## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the very extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes, following each individual volume or author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as with those possessing some authority and weight in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately clear to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the several texts of the books of Scripture. This is an exceedingly accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one weighs the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection, which is single, methodical, and chronological: six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there are gathered together for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the universal library of the clergy, or complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical science. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition sells for 1,200 French francs per thousand volumes; the Greek-Latin for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

## Volume six of the works of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux

Containing the sermons of Guerric, abbot of Igny, disciple of Saint Bernard; the letters of Guigo, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse; and also various authors who wrote about Saint Bernard’s life and deeds. Certain historical documents are added.

### [Sermons of Guerric, abbot of Igny]

[Col. 0009]

## On the blessed Guerric, abbot of Igny

**Note:** [Col. 0009] They think that he was a Belgian, specifically a canon who had been master of the school at Tournai, whom Bernard drew to himself in 1131. He became abbot of Igny, in the diocese of Reims, after Humbert, a man [Col. 0010] of outstanding piety, mentioned in the Letters and Sermons of Saint Bernard. Manrique places Guerric’s death around the year 1157. His Sermons deserve to be read with almost the same reverence as Bernard’s.

(D. Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensis*, vol. I, in the *Exordium Magnum Cisterciense*, distinction 3, chapters 7–8.)

[Col. 0009] 907–908 The venerable lord Guerric, of blessed memory, once abbot of Igny, while he was still a monk under the discipline of Saint Bernard at Clairvaux and was being nourished at the royal breasts of sacred doctrine, showed by his conduct and life that he was a worthy son of so great a Father. He had learned to climb the fortress of virtue all the higher because, in greater secrecy, by God’s great gift he gloried in the testimony of conscience concerning the title of incorruption. For, as those to whom it had been granted to know the secrets of so great a man asserted, under the guidance of grace he preserved the spotless garment of incorruption until life’s end. The Lord deigned to make clear by glorious and manifest signs how great was the purity and integrity of his life and conduct, and how pure a perfume of devotion he daily burned to God upon the altar of his heart. When, in due course, the venerable Guerric became abbot of Igny, it is beyond our small ability to say what kind of man he proved himself, or how diligently he fulfilled the office entrusted to him. In this one matter, however, he was exceedingly saddened and greatly humbled himself: because, on account of his weakness, he was compelled almost continually to leave the brothers’ community and lie in the infirmary; nor could he thus provide his brothers with an example of daily labor. Yet whatever he lacked in bodily exertion was wholly supplied by sincere piety and ardent devotion toward God. In one sermon he complains of his weakness and insufficiency, saying: “Friends have come to me from the road, but I have nothing to set before them.” How sound his sermons were in their words of doctrine is plainly shown by those brilliant, eloquent, and truly spiritual Sermons of his, which he delivered on the principal solemnities in the brothers’ community and which were taken down by the cantor of that same church.

When the faithful servant of the Lord, Guerric, having distributed his Lord’s provisions to his fellow servants with most faithful generosity, was about to pass from this world to the Father, full of days and virtues, he was struck by illness and, as the distress of that illness grew heavier, brought to his final extremity. Examining all the corners of his conscience with exceptional care, lest perhaps there should be something wrongly done and left uncorrected that might make the strict Judge offended with him and give malicious spirits an opportunity to accuse him, he remembered the little book of Sermons he had composed. At the same time he recalled that the Fathers had decreed that no one should make books without the permission of the general chapter. Groaning heavily, he summoned the brothers and said: “Behold, brothers: while I strove to watch over your progress and obey your request, I incurred the crime of disobedience, which, as Saint Samuel bears witness, is like the sin of idolatry. For I presumed, with excessive rashness and without the permission of the general chapter, to publish the little book of Sermons that I dictated at your request. Therefore bring it as quickly as possible and burn it in the fire, lest for the fault of disobedience I be handed over to the avenging flames of Gehenna to be consumed.” By God’s providence, however, it happened that the book had already been copied into other quires, God disposing something better for us also in this matter: namely, that his holy Church, and especially the Cistercian order, should not be deprived of the benefit of such learning. For, by a wonderful balance, the charm of literary knowledge swells in that volume, and the humility of Christian simplicity shines forth in it so brightly that it is not merely far from burdensome, but very pleasing to readers. Moreover, the Lord’s fiery word found in those Sermons moves, affects, and kindles the reader so powerfully that a person would have to be utterly hardened in heart not to be pricked by reading them and strive to advance toward better things.

[Col. 0011]

## Sermons throughout the year of Guerric, abbot of Igny, disciple of Saint Bernard

## On the Advent of the Lord

### 909 Sermon I. On expectation of the divine promises

[Col. 0011A]

**1.** “We await the Savior” (Titus 2:13). Truly, the expectation of the righteous is joy: they await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. “And now what is my expectation?” says the righteous man; “is it not the Lord?” (Psalm 38:8). And turning to the Lord he says: “I know that you will not put me to shame in my expectation” (Psalm 118:116), “because my substance is already with you” (Psalm 38:8): because our nature, taken from us and offered for us, has been glorified with you, giving us hope, since “all flesh shall come to you” (Psalm 64:3); and the members shall follow the head, so that the whole burnt offering may be completed. [Col. 0011B] Yet with fuller confidence, because with a safer conscience, the Lord can be awaited by the one who has been granted to say: “The substance of my little possession, O Lord, is with you,” because, whether by distributing my resources to you or by despising them for your sake, I have stored them in heaven and laid all that is mine at your feet, knowing that you are able not only to guard my deposit but also to restore it a hundredfold and add eternal life. How blessed are you, poor in spirit, because, following the counsel of the Wonderful Counselor, you have stored up treasures for yourselves in heaven, lest, if your treasures remained on earth, your hearts should likewise rot! “For where your treasure is,” he says, “there also is your heart” (Matthew 6:21). Let hearts therefore go, let them go after their treasures; let thought be fastened above and expectation suspended toward the Lord, [Col. 0011C] so that it may be yours also to say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it also we await the Savior” (Philippians 3:20). O expectation of the nations! All who await you shall not be put to shame. Our fathers awaited you; all the righteous from the beginning of the world hoped in you, and they were not put to shame (Psalm 21:5–6). Now, your mercy having been received in the midst of your temple, a choir of those rejoicing and praising sings: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9). “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined to me” (Psalm 39:2). And, recognizing the majesty of divinity in the humility of the flesh, they say: “Behold, this is our God; we awaited him, and he will save us. This is the Lord; we have waited for him;” [Col. 0012A] “we shall exult and rejoice in his salvation” (Isaiah 25:9).

**2.** As the Church in the ancient righteous awaited the first coming, so among the new it awaits again the second; as in the first it was certain of the price of redemption, so in the second of the reward of recompense. Suspended from earthly things by this hope, it longs for eternal things both happily and ardently. While others, hastening to be blessed by present things and unwilling to await the Lord’s counsel, run to plunder the booty of this world, blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord and who has not looked to vanities and false insanities (Psalm 39:5). He keeps himself from their vices as from uncleannesses, knowing that it is better to be humbled with the gentle than to divide spoils with the proud (Proverbs 16:19). Speaking with himself, he consoles himself and says: “The Lord is my portion, my soul has said; therefore I will await him. The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to await in silence the salvation of God” (Lamentations 3:24–26). “My soul has failed in your salvation, O Lord, but I have hoped beyond hope in your word” (Psalm 118:81). It is written that hope deferred afflicts the soul (Proverbs 13:12); yet, although weary from the delay of desire, it is secure because of the promise. Hoping in him alone, and hoping beyond hope, I shall add hope, just as tribulation is continually added upon tribulation and delay upon delay. For I am certain that he will appear at the end and will not deceive. **910** Therefore, even if he delays, I shall await him, because “coming, he will come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3), [Col. 0012C] beyond the appointed or opportune time. What is opportune? When the number of our brothers has been fulfilled and the time of mercy granted for repentance has been completed. Hear Isaiah, often admitted to heavenly counsels, and learn by what counsel the Lord delays judgment. “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord waits to have mercy on you; and therefore he will be exalted, sparing you, because the Lord is God of judgment. Blessed are all who await him” (Isaiah 30:18).

**3.** Therefore, if you are wise, consider how you may use the respite of this delay: if you are a sinner, for repentance, not negligence; if holy, to advance in holiness, not to fall away from faith. But if that wicked servant says in his heart, “My lord delays his coming,” and begins to strike his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with drunkards, the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know; he will cut him asunder and assign him his portion with the hypocrites: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 24:48–51). The voice of weariness and despair recorded in Isaiah seems to belong to this wicked and faithless servant: while the Lord delays, unbelievers and mockers seem to taunt his frequent messengers: “Command again, command again; wait again, wait again; a little here, a little here.” But the prophet did not conceal what punishment would follow for the wretched, when shortly afterward he added: “The word of the Lord shall be for them,” the word they mock when they say to the prophets, “Command again, command again; [Col. 0013B] wait again, wait again; a little here, a little here,” so that “they may go and fall backward, be crushed, ensnared, and captured” (Isaiah 28:13). They go backward through apostasy; they fall into crimes; they are ensnared by deadly pleasure or by some inextricable necessity of sinning, so that they neither wish nor are able to repent; they are captured by sudden death and crushed by eternal condemnation. A person does not know his end; but just as fish are caught on a hook and birds in a snare, so, says Solomon, people are caught in an evil time when it suddenly overtakes them (Ecclesiastes 9:12). Thus, lest our faith grow lukewarm because of the delay of hope, or patience grow feverish, and we begin to be among those who believe for a time but withdraw in the time of temptation (Luke 8:13), the one who gives faith, tests the faith given, and crowns the tested faith cries to us from heaven: “Whoever believes shall not hasten” (Isaiah 28:16), namely, to see what he believes. If we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience. To his bride, whom he betrothed to himself in faith, God also commands through Hosea: “You shall await me many days; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man” (Hosea 3:3). To await the Lord truly is precisely this: to keep faith with him, so that, although we lack the consolation of his presence, we do not follow an adulterer but hang in expectation of his return. Thus the Lord says in the same prophet: “My people shall hang upon my return” (Hosea 11:7). Beautifully and precisely: “shall hang,” as though between heaven and earth. Although it cannot yet grasp heavenly things, it does not wish to touch earthly things. And if it sometimes touches them, it does so only with the tips of its fingers, that is, the outermost parts of the soul, because of the necessity of our corruption, which we are compelled to serve as long as creation is unwillingly subject to vanity (Romans 8:12). It is commonly said, “He who hangs waits badly.” I say instead: “He who hangs in this way waits happily.” Therefore my soul chose hanging, and in that hanging my bones chose death, so that I might deserve to hang perseveringly on this cross until I die with it.

**911 4.** O Lord Jesus, when you were about to lay down your soul by your own power, and it was subject to your choice by what kind of death you wished to do so, your soul chose hanging, so that, lifted up from the earth, you might also draw us to yourself [Col. 0014A] and suspend us from earthly things. Nor did you allow yourself to be taken down before death, so that we too might persevere on the cross until death, and from it, as from a lofty step, ascent into heaven might be easier. Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus! We are there, there we await you—not Elijah, who may come to take us down, but Eli, that is, our Lord, who may receive us. “A little here, a little here,” if you command and command again. I did indeed believe your commands once; but help my unbelief, so that I may await and await again there, immovably, until I see what I believe. For I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. You too believe; therefore await the Lord, act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord! (Psalm 26:13–14.) Woe to those who have lost endurance and turned aside into crooked ways. What will they do when the Lord begins to look upon them? Yet although he commands that he be awaited with long-suffering, elsewhere he promises that he will come quickly: in one place forming endurance, in the other comforting the fainthearted, frightening the unprepared, and rousing the lazy. “Behold,” he says, “I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each according to his works” (Revelation 22:12); and to Jerusalem: “Your salvation will come quickly; why are you consumed with sorrow?” (Micah 4:9). Truly, the time is short, especially for each one of us, although it seems long to one burning either with labor or with love. Therefore both are necessary: that we fear the Judge who is near, and perhaps at the door for me, perhaps for you; and that, if he delays, we await him with long-suffering. Coming, that Lord will come: our fear and desire, the rest and reward of those who labor, the sweetness and embrace of those who love, the blessedness of all, our Savior Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever.

## Sermon II. How we should meet Christ when he comes

**1.** Behold, the King comes; let us go out to meet our Savior. Solomon says beautifully: “Cold water to a thirsty soul, and good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25). Good, then, is the messenger who announces the Savior’s coming, the reconciliation of the world, and the good things of the age to come. “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” (Isaiah 52:7.) [Col. 0014D] There are many, not one. Many, I say, but in one spirit, in a long succession from the beginning of the world, messengers have come to us, and the voice of all is one, their judgment at once one: “He comes; behold, he comes” (Ezekiel 39:8). “And from where,” you ask, “did these messengers come?” As it is written, “from a distant land” (Isaiah 39:3), because from the land of the living, which is separated by a great interval from this land of the dying; for a great chasm is still fixed between us and them. From there, nevertheless, prophets were sent to us, as were angels: for although they moved here in body, in spirit they were taken there when they were to be sent, so that there they might hear and see what they were to announce here. Such messengers are water of refreshment and a draught of saving wisdom for the soul thirsting for God. Whoever announces to it the Savior’s coming or his other mysteries draws and gives it water with joy from the Savior’s fountains, so that the same soul seems to answer its messenger—whether Isaiah or any of the prophets—with Elizabeth’s words, because it has drunk of the same Spirit as Elizabeth: “And how has this happened to me, that my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:34, 43.) For behold, when the voice of your announcement came to my ears, my spirit exulted with joy in my heart, eager to go out to meet God its Savior.

**2.** And truly, brothers, Christ who comes must be met with exultation of spirit. Even now, from afar, he must be greeted, or certainly greeted in return, he who sends greetings to Jacob. “I shall not be ashamed to greet a friend,” says the Wise Man (Sirach 22:31); how much more to greet him in return? O salvation of my face, and my God! How great was your condescension that you greeted servants; but how much greater that you saved them! For our salvation would not have been complete if you had sent greetings without giving salvation. You gave it—not only by later greeting with the kiss of peace, through the union of flesh, those whom you had greeted with peaceful words, but also by accomplishing salvation through the death of the cross. Let our spirit therefore rise **912** with nimble joy, run out to meet its Savior, and adore and greet him as he comes from afar, crying out to him: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 117:25–26). Hail, you who come to save us; blessed are you who come to bless us. Therefore, O Lord, grant prosperity, you who come to the human race so prosperously and savingly. Direct your way, advance prosperously [Col. 0015C] and reign. The Father, the God of our salvations, will make your path prosperous. “It shall prosper,” says the Father, “in the things for which I sent it” (Isaiah 55:11): not according to the wishes of the flesh, nor according to Peter’s will, who shrank from his suffering. “Everything that he does shall prosper” (Psalm 1:3): not according to the headlong will of human beings, but for their true salvation. Human salvation is indeed empty (Psalm 107:13), but salvation belongs to the Lord (Psalm 3:9), who worked salvation from his own blood, pouring it out as a price and offering it as drink. Come, then, O Lord, save me, and I shall be saved (Jeremiah 17:14). Come and show your face, and we shall be saved (Psalm 79:4, 8, 20). For we have awaited you: be our arm, our salvation in the time of tribulation (Isaiah 33:2). Thus the prophets and righteous, by desire and affection, went out to meet Christ who was to come long beforehand, longing, if it could be, to see with their eyes what they foresaw in spirit. Hence the Lord said to the disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke 10:23–24). Abraham our father also rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day: he saw it, though among the dead, and rejoiced. In this our sluggishness and hardness of heart are rebuked, if we do not see him with spiritual joy.

**3.** We await the anniversary of the day of Christ’s birth, which, God willing, is promised to us as soon to be seen. Scripture seems to demand that our joy be of such a kind [Col. 0016A] that our spirit, lifting itself above itself, longs in some way to meet Christ who comes; stretching forward in desire and impatient of delay, it hastens already to see what is future. I believe that the many passages of Scripture in which we are warned to meet him refer not only to the second coming but also to the first. “How so?” you ask. Because, just as we shall meet the second coming with bodily movement and exultation, so the first must be met with the affection and exultation of the heart. You know that, when we have taken up new bodies in the resurrection, according to the Apostle’s teaching, we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Even now, too, there are clouds which, if our spirits are not too sluggish or fastened to the earth, will lift them to higher things; and so we shall be with the Lord, even if only for half an hour. Your experience, unless I am mistaken, recognizes what I say: sometimes the clouds have given voice—that is, the voices of prophets or apostles have sounded in the Church—and your thoughts have been carried to such heights as though in a cloud’s vehicle; sometimes they have gone so far that they deserved, however slightly, to contemplate the glory of the Lord. Then, unless I am mistaken, you came to know the truth of that saying which the Lord rained down from the cloud that he daily sets before you as a means of ascent: “The sacrifice of praise shall honor me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49:23). Let it therefore be so: before his coming, the Lord comes to you, and before he comes to the world in general, he visits you familiarly. [Col. 0016C] “I will not leave you orphans,” he says; “I go, and I will come to you” (John 14:18). And indeed, according to each person’s merit or diligence, this coming of the Lord to each one is frequent, in this time between the first and last coming; it conforms us to the first coming and prepares us for the last. For this reason he now comes into us: lest he should have come to us in vain at the first coming, or lest at the last he should come against us in anger. By this coming he labors to reform the sense of our pride, conforming it to the sense of his humility, which he displayed when he first came; so that in turn he may reform our body of humility, conforming it to the body of his glory, which he will display when he returns. Entirely to be desired by every prayer and sought by every effort is this familiar coming, which grants us the grace of the first coming and promises the glory of the last. Because God loves mercy and truth, “the Lord will give grace and glory” (Psalm 83:12): by mercy bestowing grace in advance, by truth repaying glory.

**913 4.** Moreover, just as this spiritual coming is better than the two bodily comings in the arrangement of time, so also in the proportion of likeness it stands between them like a mediator and shares in both. The first coming is hidden and humble; the last manifest and wondrous; this one is hidden, indeed, but wondrous. I call it hidden, not because it is unknown to the one to whom it comes, but because it comes to that person secretly. Hence that glorious soul, rejoicing within itself, said [Col. 0017A]: “My secret is for myself, my secret is for myself” (Isaiah 24:16). Yet even by the one to whom it comes it cannot be seen before it is grasped, in accord with blessed Job’s confession about himself: “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; if he departs, I shall not understand” (Job 9:11). For he is neither seen while coming nor understood while departing: only while present is he the light of soul and understanding, by which the invisible is seen and the inconceivable understood. But how wondrous this coming of the Lord is, though hidden; how with sweet and happy astonishment it suspends and holds the contemplative soul in wonder at itself; how all the bones of the inner person cry out to it, “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 34:10)—those who have experienced it know. May those who have not experienced it at least earnestly desire to do so, provided that rash curiosity does not make them scrutinize the majesty and be overwhelmed by glory, but devout charity makes them sigh for the Beloved and be received by grace. For “the Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground” (Psalm 146:6); he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). Since the first coming is of grace and the last of glory, this one is of both grace and glory: in it, through consoling grace, we are granted in some measure to taste beforehand the glory that is to come. Since in the first God of majesty appeared contemptible, and in the last he will be seen as terrifying, in this middle coming he appears wondrous and lovable. Thus, because of the condescension of grace by which he makes himself lovable, he cannot be despised but is admired; and because of the magnificence of glory by which he appears wondrous, he is not a source of terror but rather of consolation. Of the first, the Seer said: “We saw him, and there was in him no appearance or beauty; therefore we did not esteem him” (Isaiah 53:2–3). Of the last even the righteous man is afraid, saying: “And who shall stand to see him?” (Malachi 3:2.) Of this one the Apostle says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18). It is utterly wondrous and lovable when God, who is love, enters the senses of the lover; when the Bridegroom embraces the bride in the unity of the Spirit and is transformed with her into the same image, through which, as through a mirror, she contemplates the Lord’s glory. How blessed are those whose ardent charity has already earned this privilege! Blessed also are those whose holy simplicity can one day hope for the same. The former already take consolation for their labor from love’s fruit; the latter, perhaps with the greater merit because meanwhile with less consolation, bear the burden of the day and the heat and await the coming of recompense. Therefore, brothers, since such sublime experience does not yet console us, let certain faith and a pure conscience console us meanwhile, so that with Paul we may say as happily as faithfully: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit for that day” (2 Timothy 1:12)—namely, for the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon III. That a person should always be ready for the coming Lord

[Col. 0018A]

# Translation — batch 001

1. Israel is ready to meet the Lord, for he is coming (Amos 4:12). And you, brothers, be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come (Luke 12:40). Nothing is more certain than that he will come, but nothing is more uncertain than when he will come. Indeed, it is so far from belonging to us to know the times or the seasons which the Father has set in his own power (Acts 1:7), that even the angels who stand before him have not been granted knowledge of that day or hour. Our own last day too is most certain to come to us; but it is most uncertain when, where, or from what quarter it will arrive—except that, as has been said before us, for old men it is at the doors, whereas for the young it lies in ambush. And would that even those kept watch over themselves who see death so ready to enter—nay, already entering. Has it not already entered in part, when it has taken possession of some parts of the body which are already wholly dead? Yet in many who are half-dead one may still see the desire of the world alive: the limbs grow cold, and avarice burns hot; life comes to its end, and ambition is prolonged. And for us also, to whom perhaps age or health seems to promise some longer span, the less death is in sight, the more, if we are wise, must it surely be suspected: lest that day, like a thief in the night, catch us unaware and unprepared. Since it is set in ambush, the less it can be seen or guarded against, the more it must be feared. There is therefore one security: never to be secure, so that fear, keeping watch over itself, may render us always ready, until security succeeds fear, not fear security. “I shall keep watch over myself,” says the wise man, “against my iniquity” (Ps. 17:24), since I cannot keep watch against my death; knowing that if the righteous man is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment (Wis. 5:7). Indeed, he triumphs in death over whom iniquity does not rule in life. How beautiful, brothers, how blessed, to triumph in death not merely securely but gloriously; by the authority of conscience, with the spirit and voice of Saint Martin, to rebuke the bloody beast if it should presume to stand before one; and gladly to open to the Judge as he comes and knocks! Then indeed you may see men like me—alas!—trembling, asking for a delay and not receiving it; wishing to buy the oil of conscience with the lamentations of repentance, yet finding that time does not suffice; wishing to turn away from those ghostly faces, yet unable; wishing to hide in the body from the face of thundering wrath, and being forced to go forth! “His spirit shall go forth, and the sinner shall return to his own earth, from which he was taken. On that day all their thoughts shall perish.” I know, of course, that it belongs to the human condition to be disturbed at the peril of departure, since even the perfect do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over; and those who are conscious of nothing against themselves, because even by this they are not justified, must necessarily fear a judgment of which they are ignorant. Yet, whether my soul has been troubled by the feeling of its condition, by lack of holiness, or by fear of judgment, the righteous man says: “You, Lord, will remember mercy, and will send forth your mercy and your truth, and will rescue my soul from among the whelps of lions” (Ps. [Col. 0019A] 56:4–5); and I, who was at first troubled, shall afterward “sleep and rest together in peace” (Ps. 4:9). God called the earth, and it heard him in trembling. For when he caused judgment to be heard from heaven, the earth trembled at the hearing alone, and, cleansed by terror, rested. Blessed are those who now so refine within themselves every dross of sin that then they need be purified by fear alone. As for me, an unprofitable and negligent servant, it goes well with me if I am saved even through fire; if, after the wood, hay, and stubble which I have piled up are burned, I escape even half-burned. And certainly, in comparison with evil, to be saved even through fire is good; but beyond doubt it is far better to be brought to completion by the cleansing of fear alone; best and most blessed of all is not to be disturbed even by fear.

2. Therefore be ready, O true Israel, to meet the Lord [Col. 0019B]: not merely so that, when he comes and knocks, you may open to him; but also so that, while he is still far away, you may run to meet him cheerfully and with rejoicing, and, as one having confidence on the day of judgment, may pray with your whole affection for his kingdom to come. If, then, you wish to be found ready at that time, “Before judgment prepare justice for yourself” (Sir. 18:19), following the counsel of Wisdom. Be ready to do every good work; be likewise ready to suffer every evil, so that your mouth may sing without reproach from the heart: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” Ready, certainly, to do worthy things with your aid; ready to suffer unworthy things. And thus ready for both, for “I will sing and make melody in my glory”: that is, I will praise and glory in each alike. And at once the righteous man rouses himself to this very end, saying: “Awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56:8–9), that is, my heart and my flesh, to rejoice in the living God: the heart, namely, on account of its particular actions; the flesh, on account of its sufferings. For the wise heart, concerned with the things above, is a psaltery sounding from above; the patient flesh, concerned with the things below, is a harp sounding from below. So too David, offering his devotion to God elsewhere, says: “I am ready to keep your commandments”; and so ready that “I was not troubled” (Ps. 118:6) when temptation rushed upon him and persecution raged. When an enemy pursued him, a servant cursed him, and a son sought his life (2 Sam. 15–18), I was nevertheless not troubled so as to fail to keep the commandments of evangelical perfection: returning good for evil to those who returned evil for good; anxious for the salvation of his persecutors, sorrowful at the death of his son; enduring reproach from a servant, but refusing to endure vengeance at the hands of a friend. Behold evangelical perfection before the Gospel: charity, patient and kind even toward the malicious whom it endures. Since, therefore, he was so ready, he surely went confidently to meet the Lord: “Without iniquity,” he says, “I ran and set straight the crooked, as far as lay in me. Rise up, then, to meet me who am coming to meet you; and since I cannot even thus reach your height unless you, stooping down, stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands: rise up to meet me” (Ps. 58:5–6), “and see whether there is a way of iniquity in me”; and if you find some way of iniquity, I know not what, remove it from me; and, having mercy on me according to your law, lead me “in the eternal way” (Ps. [Col. 0020A] 138:24), that is, in Christ, who is the way by which one goes and the eternity at which one arrives: an undefiled way, a blessed dwelling-place.


# Translation — batch 002

3. Yet I think that even before that blessed dwelling-place, if you prepare for the Lord an undefiled way, he will deign often to set his steps upon the way itself; he will enlarge your steps beneath you, so that with an enlarged heart you may run in the way of the commandments, whose beginning perhaps you complained was narrow. For Wisdom herself testifies that she walks “in the ways of justice” (Prov. 8:20); and: “He who keeps justice shall lay hold of her, and she will meet him like an honored mother. She goes about seeking those worthy of her, and on her ways she shows herself to them” (Sir. 15:1–2; Wis. 6:17). If you complain that she meets you seldom or never, see whether perhaps you have corrupted your way. For thus you have it written: “The folly of a man corrupts his way, but he will lay blame upon God in his heart.” He himself stands at the door and knocks, so that, if anyone opens to him, he may dine with him on the delights of the heavenly table. The bride speaks: “The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my bride” (Song 5:2). Open your heart to me, and I will feed it. Open your mouth to me, and I will fill it. “I opened my mouth,” says David, “and drew in the Spirit” (Ps. 118:131). For Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face, one not only to be invited but drawn into the lodging of the heart by a certain force of prayer and vehemence of fervor, as the Gospel narrative relates of the two disciples as a figure of this matter (Luke 24:28–29). And indeed for no other reason than to test the devotion of your charity, he sometimes pretends to be going farther; just as the two angels, when Lot worshipped and begged them to enter, nevertheless dissembled, saying: “No, but we will stay in the street.” But what does Scripture say? “He constrained them strongly to turn aside to him” (Gen. 19:2–3). A pious force, by which the kingdom of heaven is seized; a praiseworthy importunity, which wins Christ as a guest, or angels. But what is it, you ask, that Jesus pretends to be going farther? What, except that which Ecclesiastes confesses of himself? “I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ and wisdom herself withdrew farther from me” (Eccl. 7:24). The bride, however, explains this more clearly, expressing, indeed, our daily complaint, when she says: “I rose to open to my beloved, but he had turned away and passed on. I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me” (Song 5:5–6), just as he did not answer the Canaanite woman. You were calling upon the spirit of wisdom; you were seeking in prayer the spirit of grace. If he seems to withdraw farther from you, do not despair, but persist importunately until you receive the answer: “Great is your faith; be it done to you as you have asked” (Matt. 15:28).

4. Yet when you invite Jesus, take care not to invite the God of majesty into a foul and unworthy lodging, where a quarrelsome wife, or smoke, or dripping water would not allow even you to dwell in peace. For “his place is not made except in peace”; nor are justice and judgment anything other than the preparation of his throne. “Now,” he says, “they seek me day by day and desire to know my ways, as though they were a nation that had done justice and had not forsaken the judgment of their God” (Isa. 58:2). “Justice and judgment,” he says, “are the preparation of his throne” (Ps. 88:15). Do not make the excuse that it is costly [perhaps: presumptuous], and exceeds the resources of your poverty, to prepare a house for so magnificent and powerful a guest: you have at hand what enables you to do it. I mean what is human, because of the weakness of your flesh, or rather the narrowness of your mind. Make full confession concerning the past; have a good will for the future, for “peace [is] to men of good will” (Luke 2:14), and by this judgment and justice you have prepared a seat for the Most High. Do you wish to hear more plainly concerning confession that it must be made in preparation for the Lord’s coming? “The righteous man,” Scripture says, “is [Col. 0021B] the first accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech.” And what follows? “His friend comes” (Prov. 18:17), he who before the confession was standing at a distance as an enemy. For when he said: “I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord” (Ps. 31:5), and the Lord himself forgave it: he comes, I say, and will examine him. Indeed he will examine him, like a potent draught, searching heart and reins; reaching even to the division of soul and spirit; draining what is harmful from the marrow of the soul and the inward parts of the mind; cleansing the affections so that it may bear more fruit. Of its first fruit, confession, the Father who is the husbandman already rejoices. Yet he who after confession is sometimes present even before he is invoked, sometimes waits for you to invite him first; and, to increase your merit, often pretends to delay longer, so that by more attentive psalmody, more insistent prayer, and sweet force you may compel him to enter. Otherwise the prophet will lament that “the cities of the south are shut, with none entering” (Jer. 13:19). Therefore, when you can say: “My heart is ready, O God,” because it has been emptied of evils; “my heart is ready,” because it is full of holy desires: then diligently do what follows: “I will sing and make melody” (Ps. 66:8). And whatever the sound of the singer or psalmodist may be, let this be the intention of the mind: “Awake, my glory; rise to meet me, for, as far as I was able, I came to meet you.” O gracious Jesus, how eager and ready, how glad and festive you are in meeting such devotion! How cheerful you show yourself on these ways! “You met,” says Isaiah, “him who rejoices and does justice; on your ways they will remember you” (Isa. 64:5). For if you make melody wisely, he will come upon the undefiled way; he will come who will also illuminate your hidden things, so that you may understand the mysteries of Scripture which you do not know, and it will be yours to say: “I will sing and understand on the undefiled way, when he comes to me” (Ps. 100:1–2). Stir up, Lord, your power, that it may stir up our sloth to meet you; and come, that you may save us (Ps. 79:3), Savior of the world, who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.


# Translation — batch 003

## Sermon IV. On the solitary life and on preparing the way for the Lord

1. “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40:3). Before all else, I think, we should consider the grace of the desert, the blessedness of the wilderness, which from the beginning of grace deserved to be consecrated to the repose of the saints. The voice crying in the wilderness certainly consecrated for us the dwelling-place of the desert: John preaching and administering the baptism of repentance in the desert. Yet even before him solitude, as though an audience chamber of the Spirit, had always been dear to the holiest prophets. Far greater and more divine grace of sanctification nevertheless came to the place itself when Jesus succeeded John. Even before he began to preach to penitents, he judged that the place had to be prepared for penitents; and during the forty days he spent in the desert, as though purifying the place and dedicating a new place to a new life, he overcame the tyrant who was lurking there and all his malice and craft—not so much for himself as for those who were to be dwellers in the wilderness. If, then, you have gone far away, fleeing and remaining in solitude, remain there; there await him who will save you from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm. However great the storm of battles that breaks upon you, however great the scarcity of provisions you suffer in the desert, do not return in faintheartedness of spirit, in your mind, to Egypt. The wilderness will feed you more happily with manna, that is, with the bread of angels, than Egypt with pots of meat. Jesus himself fasted in the wilderness; but he often and miraculously fed the multitude following him in the desert. Yet more often and more wonderfully will he satisfy you, since with so much more grateful merit you have followed him in the desert with a holier purpose. For when you have thought that he has forgotten you for too long, he, not forgetful of his goodness, will console you and say to you: “I remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your espousals, when you followed me into the desert” (Jer. 2:2). Then he will indeed make your desert like the delights of paradise, and you yourself will confess that “the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” (Isa. 35:2). For just as today in many places we see even in the literal sense that prophetic saying fulfilled, “The beautiful places of the desert shall grow fat” (Ps. 64:13), and “Strangers shall eat the deserts turned into abundance” (Isa. 5:17), so every passage of Scripture which before seemed barren and dry to you will suddenly be filled with wonderful abundance and richness of spirit, by God’s blessing; so that from the fullness of your mind you may pour forth a hymn of praise, saying: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men; for he has satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things” (Ps. [Col. 0022D] 106:8–9).

2. It has surely been provided by the marvelous grace of divine dispensation that in these deserts of ours we may have the quiet of solitude and yet not lack the consolation of grace and holy fellowship. Each may sit alone and be silent because he suffers no one to interrupt him; yet there is no “woe to the one who is alone,” because he does not lack one to comfort him or, if he falls, to raise him up (Eccl. 4:10). We are in a multitude of men and yet without a crowd; we live as though in a city, yet suffer no tumult to keep us from hearing the voice crying in the wilderness—provided that we have inward silence as well as outward [Col. 0023A] silence. For, Solomon says, “The words of the wise are heard in silence more than the cry of a ruler among fools” (Eccl. 9:17). And now also, if all things within you keep the middle silence, the almighty Word will secretly flow into you from the paternal seat. Blessed therefore is he who has so gone far away in fleeing the tumult of the world, who has withdrawn so far into the secret and solitude of a quiet mind that he deserves to hear not merely the voice of the Word but the Word himself; not John but Jesus. In the meantime, however, let us hear what the voice of the Word cries to us, so that one day we may advance from the voice to the Word. “Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord; make straight his paths” (Isa. 40:3). He prepares the way who corrects his life; he makes the path straight who directs himself along the narrower way. A corrected life is plainly the straight way by which the Lord may come to us, he who in this very thing goes before us. For the steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he will so desire his way that, coming gladly upon it to the man, he may walk with him continually. Unless he who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6) goes before his own coming to us, our way cannot be corrected by the rule of truth, and therefore cannot be directed to the life of eternity. “By what means does a younger man correct his way,” except by keeping his words, except by following the footsteps of him who made himself the way by which we come to him? “O Lord, may my ways be directed to keep your ways” (Ps. 118:5), so that, because of the words of your lips, I may keep even hard ways: which, though they appear hard to the flesh because it is weak, will appear sweet and beautiful to the spirit if it is ready. “Her ways,” it says, “are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable” (Prov. 3:17). The ways of wisdom are not only peaceful but peace-making, because when a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace (Prov. 16:7). “Israel, if he had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing, and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them” (Ps. 80:14–15). Why indeed are destruction and misery in their ways, except because “they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 13:3)? Accordingly, whenever I saw a man who was restless, stubborn, quarrelsome, harassed by a most grievous temptation or scourged by tribulation, I recalled that proverb: “The wicked always seeks disputes, but a cruel angel shall be sent against him” (Prov. 17:11). Perhaps he is delivered over to the affliction of the flesh so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. Yet if at times the way of the impious prospers, “do not envy him who prospers in his way, the man who does injustices” (Ps. 36:7), because this way of theirs is a stumbling-block to them, so that they may run more freely to death the less their path is hedged in. Of these the Wise Man speaks: “The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; but at their end are hell, darkness, and punishments” (Sir. 21:11); and: “They spend their days in good things, and in a moment descend into hell” (Job 21:13). Blessed therefore are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the way of the Lord! For though they drink from the torrent on the [Col. 0024A] way, for that reason they will lift up their head; because in the end, at their dwelling-place, they will attain their head, whom they follow along the way of suffering.


# Translation — batch 004

3. Whatever therefore meets you on the way of the Lord, run with a cheerful and enlarged heart in the way of God’s commandments. For although the way seems narrow to the fainthearted, it is straight; and although it seems hard, it is undefiled. Blessed indeed are the undefiled in the way, who pass along the way of the world by so undefiled a path that they do not stain their garments; or at least, if they do stain them, they do not lose their place according to the beatitude, but wash their garments in the baptism of repentance with which John baptizes [Col. 0024B] in the wilderness, preparing the way for the Lord. Chastity is surely an undefiled way, a pleasing way by which the Lord of grace may deign to come; and the prophet sings of him: “My God, his way is undefiled.” Undefiled was the Virgin’s chastity through which he came into her womb; undefiled must also be the chastity of the person through which he comes into that person’s soul. Happy is the conscience to which that utterance applies: “God girded me with the strength of continence, and made my way undefiled” (Ps. 17:31, 33). Yet, lest you glory in chastity without the other virtues as though you had already prepared an undefiled way for the Lord, know that this way must no less also be straight and level, so that it may not be dark or slippery. For the way of the wicked is darkness and slipperiness, and the angel of the Lord pursues them (Ps. 34:6). And “the way of the wicked is dark; they do not know where they fall” (Prov. 4:19). Do we suppose, brothers, that in any of us there is still something crooked in the will, harsh in character, dark through ignorance of understanding, slippery through inconstancy of action? How then shall we fulfill the Scripture concerning the preparation of the way unless we do as it is written: “Let crooked things become straight, and rough things level ways” (Isa. 40:4; Luke 3:5)?

4. First, then, if there is in us any crooked and distorted will, it must be corrected and directed according to the rule of the divine will. Otherwise we shall seem to say, as the impious say: “The way of the Lord is not straight.” But immediately unanswerable truth refutes us, and fearful severity reproves us: “Are not my ways straight, and are not rather your ways crooked?” (Ezek. 18:29). Therefore, you who hasten to prepare the way for the Lord, first of all let your will be good, because “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4). But once in this manner you have made crooked things straight, know that rough things must no less become level ways: that is, you must level every harshness of character and lay it out into a kind of evenness of social life, lest that gentle and sweet traveler recoil, offended by the roughness of the way. Why should he not recoil, he who is meek and humble of heart and rests only upon the meek and humble, when every human feeling too shrinks from and abhors an angry and unmanageable man? But even if you have advanced so far on the way of the Lord that you have attained both a purpose of uprightness and the discipline of meekness, you have made progress indeed, but you have not attained perfection unless the word of God is “a lamp to your feet and a light to your paths.” For “in the way wherein I walked they hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141:4). And there are ways that seem straight to men, but their end leads down into the depth of hell. “The way of the wicked is dark,” as Solomon says: “they do not know where they fall” (Prov. 4:19). The Lord says this also: “He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12:35). But “the commandment is a lamp, and the law a light, and the rebuke of discipline is the way of life” (Prov. 6:23). For whoever abandons rebukes goes astray. If therefore you are wise, on a way on which you have never walked, you will not be your own teacher or guide, but will incline your ear to your masters, assent to their rebukes and counsels, and give yourself to learning and reading, lest, repenting too late, you say: “Why have I hated discipline, and why has my heart not yielded to rebukes? I did not hear the voice of those who taught me, and I did not incline my ear to my masters. I was almost in every evil, in the midst of the church and the synagogue” (Prov. 5:12–14). Hear David confess that knowledge of the law frees one from snares: “Sinners laid a snare for me, but I did not stray from your commandments.” How could you do this? “Because I acquired your testimonies as an inheritance. I rejoiced in the way of your testimonies as in all riches. Sinners waited for me to destroy me; but I escaped this because I understood your testimonies” (Ps. 118:110–11, 94–95). “The law of God,” he says, “is in the heart of the righteous, and therefore his steps shall not be overthrown” (Ps. 36:31). Hence Solomon his son also says: “The dissembler deceives his friend by his mouth, but the righteous will be delivered by knowledge” (Prov. [Col. 0025C] 11:9).

5. But would that this way by which we must receive salvation, or the Savior, were, as it is no longer dark through ignorance of the truth, also not slippery through inconstancy in action. But like Balaam, who fell while having his eyes open (Num. 22:27, 31), so we too see with open eyes through knowledge and fall through negligence. We sin willingly and knowingly, and we gladly slip; and we can blame not so much the slipperiness of the way as the purpose of the mind, that is, the foot on which we rely. For who does not walk in a slippery place while living in the world, while living in a body of clay? The fault, therefore, lies not so much in the way as in the foot, which is insufficiently firm on the way of God. But will not he who falls add that he should rise again? “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises seven times” (Prov. 24:16). For “the Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord directs the righteous” (Ps. 145:8). “For when I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, O Lord, helped me” (Ps. 93:18). Therefore, when you cannot otherwise, walk the way by falling and rising, yet always cry out to him whom you desire to follow and attain: “Perfect my steps in your paths, that my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. 16:5); and, “if there is a way of iniquity in me” (as there is, through human frailty), “lead me in the eternal way” (Ps. 138:24), so that through you, who are the way and truth, I may come to you, who are truth and eternal life: to you be glory through eternal ages. Amen.


# Translation — batch 005

## Sermon V. How one must advance in preparing the way for the Lord

[Col. 0026A]

1. “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40:3). The way of the Lord, brothers, which we are commanded to prepare, is prepared by walking, and is walked by preparing. Although you may have made much progress upon it, it always remains for you to prepare, so that from the things you have attained you may stretch and reach forward to what lies beyond; and through each advance the Lord, for whose coming the way is prepared, may meet you as though new and always greater than himself. Thus the righteous man fittingly prays: “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications, and I will seek it always” (Ps. 118:33). Thus perhaps eternal life is so called because, although providence has searched out the path of each person and appointed the limit to which that person will advance, the nature of the goodness in which you advance has no limit. Thus, when the wise and tireless traveler has been perfected, then he will begin; so forgetting what lies behind that every day he says to himself, “Now I have begun” (Ps. 76:11). He rejoices as a giant, whom nothing terrifies from running in the way of God’s commandments; and, having become Idithun, he readily leaps over the slothful who sit on the way in the force of his course. And even if he has come at the last hour of the day, “made perfect in a short time he fulfills many times,” so that he may suddenly become first from being last, and receive a crown among the first.

2. But we who speak of progress on this way—would that we had at least grasped its beginning! For in my understanding and judgment, he who has begun makes no small progress on it, provided he has truly begun and has found the way to the city of habitation. “How few,” says Truth, “are those who find it!” (Matt. 7:14). How many wander in solitude! They are all solitary, that is, all proud, who regard themselves as alone. None of them can yet say: “Now I have begun; this change is the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11). For there is no change in them, by which they cease to be what they were, because “they did not fear God” (Ps. 54:20), though “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). If it is the beginning of wisdom, it is surely also the beginning of the good way. The fear of the Lord himself immediately produces in the heart of a man that wise counsel by which he can say: “I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies” (Ps. 118:59). It persuades him to confession, which the Psalmist teaches to be the beginning of a good work: “Begin,” he says, “to the Lord in confession” (Ps. 146:7). It bends the proud man to repentance, so that he may hear the voice crying in the wilderness, commanding the way to be prepared and showing where one must begin: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3:2). The saying of Solomon agrees with this, for he instructs the untrained by a clear definition, saying: “The beginning of a good way is to do just things” (Prov. 16:5). For what is it to do just things except to do penance? Except to exact from ourselves what we owe God and to pay back what we have taken? This is the justice that walks before the Lord and prepares for him an acceptable way, as it is written: “Justice shall walk before him and shall set his steps in the way” (Ps. [Col. 0027A] 84:14). For as John precedes Jesus, so repentance precedes grace: that grace, namely, by which after satisfaction we are reconciled and received in the kiss of peace. In this way of repentance justice and peace meet one another with a welcome and joyful encounter and kiss each other: the justice of the person punishing himself, and the peace of God forgiving him. They celebrate a glad and delightful covenant of reconciliation in the holy kiss. Finally, lest this justice, by which a man makes judgment and justice concerning himself, be considered of little merit, and lest the brief prayers and vows of the lazy presume to compare themselves with the labors of penitents, let them hear what Solomon thinks of it: “The beginning of a good way is to do just things; but it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices” (Prov. 16:5). Therefore, if you see a man professed to this repentance preferring private little prayers to the regular and holy labors of which he is a debtor, press upon him this saying of the Wise Man: “The beginning of a good way is to do just things; and it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices.” Likewise, if you see a man against whom his brother has something, offering at the altar a gift either of praises or of sacraments, repeat to him the same saying: “The beginning of a good way is to do just things,” so that you may be reconciled to your brother; and it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices. This saying has also bearing upon the man who is going to give alms: first, if he has defrauded anyone, let him restore at least the principal. And you likewise should by no means believe that the voluntary offerings of your mouth are pleasing to God—the offerings, that is, which you have made to him in psalms or secret prayers—if for that reason you discharge the rule-established canon of psalms more negligently. “Have you not sinned if you offer rightly and do not divide rightly?” (Gen. 3 according to the LXX). “Make straight his paths” (Matt. 3:3; Isa. 40:3), you who prepare the way of the Lord.

3. O Lord, you have prepared paths of straightness for us, provided only that we walk rightly in them. You have set before us the law, the way of your justifications, through him, namely, whom you gave as the legislator of this holy institution, saying: “This is the way; walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. 30:21). This is indeed the way which the prophet promised: “A straight way for us, so that fools may not wander upon it” (Isa. 35:8). “I was young and now have grown old,” and, if I remember rightly, I have not seen a fool wandering from the way—although I have scarcely seen any wise man able to keep its straightness. “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent before yourselves” (Isa. 5:21)! Your wisdom leads you astray from the way of salvation and does not allow you to follow the folly of the Savior. That fool for Christ did not fail to know what evil this earthly, animal, devilish wisdom does, when he said: “If anyone seems wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may be wise before God” (1 Cor. 3:18). Desirable folly, which is accounted wisdom in the divine judgment and does not allow a man to wander from the way! This folly, unless I am mistaken, is that wisdom from above, chaste, peaceable, modest, easily persuaded, assenting to good things (Jas. 3:17). How far the man wise in his own eyes recoils from all these things, would that experience itself had never proved before our eyes! If the arrogance or stubbornness of such wise men grieves you, the peace and modesty of our fools consoles you more abundantly: the less they trust themselves, the more readily they are persuaded and assent to good things. Such fools, then, do not easily wander from the way of God, but, according to the prophet’s word, always hear the voice behind them warning: “This is the way; walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. 30:21), lest by exceeding the measure through fervor or falling short of measure through lukewarmness you abandon the prescribed law and royal way. The spirit is on the right and the flesh on the left; and these, struggling against one another, are always opposed to one another, so that we may not do whatever either this one or that one wills: lest, if we follow the impulse of the spirit beyond what is right, we turn to the right; or if we indulge the flesh beyond what is right, we stray to the left.

4. I am pleased, with your charity, to recall how greatly Isaiah extols this way of the Lord’s commandments, the way of truth which you have chosen. “And there shall be there,” he says—that is, in the former haunts of dragons, namely, in a land deserted and pathless—“a path and a way,” as may be seen today: for among wild and uncultivated people, who lived without law, there is found order of life and discipline. “And this way,” he says, “shall be called holy,” because it is indeed the sanctification of sinners and the salvation of the lost. But how greatly it excels in the power and reverence of holiness, the prophet proves from this: “The unclean shall not pass over it” (Isa. 35:8).

O Isaiah, then will those who are unclean go by another way? Rather, let all come here; let them walk by this way. For Christ especially made this way for the unclean, he who came to seek and save that which had perished on the paths of the world. What then? Shall the unclean pass along the holy way? Far from it! Let one come to it however unclean; yet he shall not pass along it unclean, because once he has passed, he will no longer be unclean. The holy way indeed admits the unclean, but immediately washes the one admitted; for it washes away every sin committed, as a true second baptism for penitents.

Here indeed—here Jesus baptizes, not John, with the baptism of repentance; here lies open the fountain of the house of David for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman. Therefore this way admits the unclean, but does not let the unclean pass through: for the way is narrow, and like that narrow opening through which a serpent, to be renewed, can come with the cast-off skin of its old age, but cannot pass through with it. Rather, new and more fittingly clothed in its nakedness, it passes through the narrow passage, stripping off all the foulness of old age which it had brought. We are rightly urged, then, to imitate the serpent’s prudence, since we cannot otherwise be renewed unless we are constrained through narrowness.

5. Indeed, Isaiah promises that we shall escape the snares of that ancient serpent if we follow, by this narrow way, the example of this new serpent. Concerning the same way he adds:

> “No lion shall be there,  
> nor shall an evil beast go up by it;  
> neither shall it be found there”  
> (Isa. 35:9).

Let us therefore be secure, provided we do not stray from the way. That lion which goes about seeking whom he may devour can set stumbling-blocks beside the road, hide snares, and terrify travellers by roaring; but he cannot harm those who persevere on the way, since the way itself is terror and punishment to him. “The way of the Lord is strength to the upright, and dread to those who do evil” (Prov. 10:29).

If, therefore, you are on the way, fear this alone: that you may not turn aside, that you may not offend the Lord who leads you by the way, so that he leaves you wandering in the way of your own heart. Apart from him, do not fear a stranger. But if you complain that the way is too narrow, look to the end to which it leads you. For if you see the end of every perfection, you will immediately say: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). If you cannot see it, believe Isaiah who sees it, who is the eye of your body. He saw it, at least in some measure, when he spoke what follows:

> “And behold, those who have been set free shall walk by this way,  
> and those redeemed by the Lord;  
> and they shall come into Zion with praise,  
> and everlasting joy upon their heads.  
> They shall obtain joy also and gladness;  
> sorrow and groaning shall flee away”  
> (Isa. 35:9–10).

Whoever thinks sufficiently upon this end, I think, not only makes the way broad for himself, but also takes wings, so that he no longer walks but flies. Therefore, brothers, always think upon the end of the rewards, and with every ability and eagerness you will run the way of the commandments. May he himself lead and bring you through it—he who is the way of those who run and the prize of those who arrive, Christ Jesus—to whom be honour and glory through all ages of ages.

## ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0029]

### SERMON I. What God as a child teaches us.

[Col. 0029B]

1. “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6): a child, ancient of days. A child in bodily form and age; ancient of days in the incomprehensible eternity of the Word. Yet even in that ancientness of his days, although he is not a child, he is nevertheless always new; indeed, he is not so much new as newness itself, abiding in himself always and renewing all things. Whatever recedes from him grows old; whatever draws near to him is renewed. Thus, in a new manner, he is new precisely in that by which he is ancient: for his eternity, without a beginning of birth and without decline into old age, is itself his ancient newness and new antiquity.

Yet the newness of this temporal birth is different: for the child was born to us, that we might be renewed; he who was born God from eternity was born for the beatification of angels. That birth was one of greater glory, but this one of more abundant mercy. This one, indeed, was for my sake, since I needed mercy, being surrounded by misery—and misery which I could not expiate.

“Show us your mercy” (Ps. 84:8), since we are not yet fit to behold your glory. Let the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appear, so that through it we may be made worthy and fit for the majesty and divinity of God our Creator to appear to us. Show us, Lord, your mercy, clothed in our misery and, by a new manner of showing mercy, working remedies from the very misery of the miserable. For this purpose the art of mercy joined the blessedness of God and the misery of man in the unity of the Mediator: so that, by the working of the sacrament of unity, through the power of the resurrection blessedness may swallow up misery, and life may devour death; and the whole human being, glorified, may pass into fellowship with the divine nature.

So completely did the divine condescension assume, without sin, all the infirmities of the flesh to which human nature is subject because of guilt, that it did not refuse even the injuries of infancy or choose beginnings other than those belonging to the common condition—except, certainly, that, born immaculate through the Holy Spirit from the immaculate woman, he cleansed the faults of our origin and consecrated for us the sacraments of a second birth.

2. Thus “a little child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6), and the God of majesty, emptying himself, conformed himself not only to the earthly body of mortals, but even to the weak and tiny age of infants. O blessed infancy, whose weakness and folly are stronger and wiser than all human beings! For the power of God and the wisdom of God work their own divine work in our human realities.

The weakness of this infant triumphs over the prince of this world, binds the strong man armed, takes the cruel tyrant captive, and releases and frees our captivity. The seemingly mute and speechless simplicity of this infant makes the tongues of infants eloquent; it causes them to speak with the tongues of human beings and angels, distributing fiery tongues. This one, seemingly ignorant, is himself the one who teaches knowledge to human being and angel alike, as truly the God of knowledges, the Wisdom of God, and the Word.

O holy and sweet infancy, which has restored true innocence to humankind, through which every age may return to blessed infancy and become conformed to you—not in littleness of limbs, but in humility of mind and godliness of conduct. Truly, you children of Adam, who are far too great in your own eyes and have grown through pride into the monstrous enormity of giants: unless you are converted and become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 18:4). “I am the door” (John 10:9) of the kingdom, says this little child: unless the height of men is bent low, the gate of humility will not admit them.

Therefore he will “strike down the heads of many upon the earth” (Ps. 109:6); and those who approach in pride, dashed back with their heads struck, will fall backward. What then? Do you still take pride, earth and ashes, after God has become humble? Are you still great in your own eyes, after God has become a little child before your eyes? He emptied himself so as almost to appear to be nothing—he without whom nothing was made—and you swell and exalt yourself without measure, imagining yourself to be something when you are truly nothing! “You deceive yourself” (Gal. 6:3), the Apostle cries to you. Even if you were something, even if you were something great, you ought all the more to humble yourself. “The greater you are,” says the Wise Man, “humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3:20), who “resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5). He himself, to become your example, though greatest of all, became the humblest and least of all.

It was not enough for him to become lower than the angels by the condition of mortal nature, unless he also became lower than human beings by the age of helpless infancy. Let the devout and humble see and rejoice; let the ungodly and proud see and be put to shame. Let them see, I say, God immense made small, and an infant to be adored: a stupendous mystery, the redemption of the devout, the glory of the humble, the judgment of the ungodly, the ruin of the proud.

O venerable and dreadful mystery! How holy and terrible is your name, O fountain of mercies and abyss of judgments! Who has drunk from this fountain and not loved? Who has contemplated this abyss and not trembled? Whoever has not loved is wicked and ungodly; just as whoever has not trembled is foolish and senseless. Yet there is no reason to fear judgment, if you do not insolently oppose mercy. For he would rather be loved than feared slavishly; and he approves more the free and voluntary affection offered by children than the forced fear extorted from slaves. Therefore, when he first manifested himself to mortals, he chose to present himself as a child and to appear lovable rather than terrible: since he came to save, not to judge, he preferred for the present that by which he might awaken love, and deferred that by which he might instil fear.

3. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his grace, when we could not even think without trembling of the throne of his glory. Here is nothing terrifying, nothing severe for you to fear, but every kind of kindness and gentleness in which to place confidence. And although power and terror are with him, for the present he entirely conceals them, until he spares the penitent and receives the confessing sinner.

Do not let it trouble you that you have sinned grievously: an injured child does not know how to be angry; or, if he is angry, he can easily be appeased. Truly, nothing is more ready to be reconciled than the mind of this child, who anticipates your peace and satisfaction for precisely this purpose, and first sends envoys of peace, so that you, though guilty, may desire reconciliation. Only desire it—desire it truly and perfectly. Not only will he grant pardon, but he will heap grace upon you; indeed, reckoning it no small gain to have recovered the lost sheep, he will hold a feast day with the angels.

It was therefore fitting for the divine gentleness that he should be at the innocent and yielding age of infancy; and he most fittingly and appropriately began the salvation of sinners at this age, so that those whom the guilt of their own conscience terrified might be consoled by the hope of a pardon not difficult to obtain.

4. O sweetest child, good Jesus, how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you and will accomplish for those who hope in you, when you have shown so much to those who do not yet know you! Truly, incomparable sweetness and ineffable loving-kindness: that I should see as a child, created for my sake, the God who created me; and that the God of majesty and glory should become not only like me in the truth of bodily nature, but should appear pitiable and, through the weakness of age, as though in need of human aid.

Truly you are the child-God, the salvation of my countenance and my God; and although you are wholly sweetness and desire, the tenderness of your limbs makes you sweeter to me. It makes you accessible to the senses and affections of little ones, who are not yet able suitably to receive you as solid food. Meanwhile it is sweet—truly sweet and savoury—to think of God as a child; indeed, it is efficacious and operative for healing and sweetening whatever bitterness of spirit, harshness of speech, or austerity of conduct there may be in us.

For I would not believe that, where the awareness and remembrance of this divine sweetness are present, there can be room for anger or sadness; rather, all indignation and bitterness with every evil shall be taken away from us. Thus, as newborn infants, we shall worthily praise the newborn infant Lord; and, in the harmony of conduct and voices, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings shall be perfected the praise of the infant and suckling Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise and jubilation through eternal ages of ages. Amen.

### SERMON II. What gift the Church received when the Synagogue rejected it.

1. “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). That he was born to us is proved from the fact that he was given to us. For he is rightly said to be born to those to whom he is seen to be given. The grace of this birth was indeed offered to all, but it was not received by all. “For faith is not everyone’s.” “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John 1:11). Moreover, he would have been born to no purpose unless he had also been given; and he would have become the Son of Man in vain if the children of men had not received him, to whom he might give power to become children of God.

Woe, therefore, to you, unbelieving, ungrateful, and impious Judaea: the kingdom of God has been taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits. Jesus was cast out of the Synagogue but received by the Church. He was cast out amidst the contradictions of the Jews and established as head of the Gentiles. Behold, a people whom he did not know served him; they obeyed at the hearing of the ear. Yet concerning you—alien children, criminal and parricidal children—there is that terrible complaint of the loving Father: “I have nourished and raised children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). But he who despises—will he not himself be despised? “Since you have rejected the word of God,” say the apostles, “and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

O blessed gentility! Behold, Jesus is brought to you. Run with hands outstretched to meet him; stretch out your hands, open wide your bosom. Let both deed and result prove your devotion. Receive in faith the Son offered to you; embrace him in affection; and let him always dwell between your breasts. And behold, I seem to hear a voice of exultation and confession from every part of the world; from the ends of the earth I hear praises, the glory of the righteous.
