There is a sound as of a multitude, as the sound of the camps of God: one voice praising and saying, “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

This, unless I am mistaken, is the Church rejoicing and praising throughout the whole world, because she embraces as born and given to herself the Son whom she sees was offered but, through the Jews’ unbelief, justly taken away from them.

> “Praise, O barren woman who did not bear;  
> sing praise and rejoice, you who did not give birth;  
> for through this Son who is given to you,  
> the children of the desolate woman shall be many more  
> than those of her who seemed to cleave to God,  
> being married to him by the bond of the law”  
> (Isa. 54:1).

“Then your heart shall marvel and be enlarged” (Isa. 60:5). Then you will say in your heart: “Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not bear, exiled and captive; and who has brought these up for me? I was abandoned and alone; where then were these?” (Isa. 49:21).

O incorrupt mother, fruitful virgin: the Son given to you gave these to you. For he is the Son of the Most High, to whom the Father adopted them, that they all might be conformed to his image and that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. “Enlarge,” he says, “the place of your tent, from east to west and from sea to sea; for you shall extend to right and left, and your seed shall inherit the nations” (Isa. 54:2–3). For this only-begotten Son of Mary is the firstborn of every creature, to whom the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8).

2. But as the barren Church, having received the Son of God, bore many children and was strengthened, so her rival the Synagogue, which had many children, was weakened when he was cast out. Therefore today the Church, rejoicing in the Son given to her, fills heaven with thanksgiving and a voice of praise; but the Synagogue sits mute in darkness—or rather wearies hell with lamentation.

Miserable and blind, why does she not perceive how plainly her God has passed over to us; how clearly, after she herself was repudiated and retained only the bill of divorce—the letter, I mean, of the law, which convicts her adulteries—the Bridegroom transferred all her dowry to his new bride? Behold, in our hands are the tablets of marriage, in the two Testaments; behold, the mysteries of anointings, the dignity of kings, the order of priests, the ministries of Levites, the worship of the temple and its vessels, the reality of sacrifices—in short, all their glory has been transferred from them and bestowed upon us, because the cause and truth of all things, the Son, has been given to us.

He has tilted the cup of the law, which is in the hand of the Mediator, from this Jew toward this Christian. And everything in it that was pure and true, he has strained out and poured over to us. The dregs alone, which have not been poured out, have remained among the Jews; they drink them: that is their portion of the cup.

3. But why do I linger over words? Can what and how great are the things given to us, when this Son is given to us, be narrated? Has not every good gift and every perfect present descended to us from him and with him alike? Has he not brought with himself to us all the riches of heaven and all the treasures of God? Though these are still hidden in him, he has nevertheless already distributed much and great bounty, as a donative to those who are to fight; yet all these are nothing compared with what he has reserved for the victors.

Who can enumerate so many gifts of charisms, so many kinds of virtues, the variety of our weapons, the helps of the sacraments, the dishes of the Scriptures, the grades and orders of ministers; in every age, sex, condition, nation, and tongue, so many trophies of martyrs, distinctions of confessors, and crowns of virgins?

“If you wonder,” says the Church, “how this multitude of riches and greatness of glory has suddenly come to poor little me, it is plainly because the Son of God has been given to us: the God of grace, the Lord of powers, and the King of glory.” Indeed, it would be more surprising if his goods did not follow their Lord, since he himself is all good things. “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33:11); how much more those who receive him? If you wonder at these things given to us through the Son, I will add—so that you may wonder more—that absolutely all things have been given to us with him. For when the Father gave us the Son, through whom and in whom all things subsist, how did he not give us all things with him? (Rom. 8:32).

“All things are ours,” says the Apostle, because the author and Lord of all is ours; so that, though we seem to have nothing, we may nevertheless be found possessing all things. You see, therefore, how great and what a gift the Son is; and how credible is what is read concerning Wisdom, which he himself is: “All good things came to me with her, and innumerable honour through her hands” (Wis. 7:11).

Why, my brothers, do I press this point so strongly? Why, except that you may learn to glory because a Son has been given to us, and reckon whatever the world can give or promise you not merely cheap and unworthy in comparison with him, but even loss for his sake? He does not give to you as the world gives. Only be grateful because he has been given to you, and labour that he may be given to you more fully and perfectly.

For he who was once given to the world in the form of flesh, and is given to believers at fixed days or hours under the species of bread, namely in the eating of his sacrament, is more often given to the devout at uncertain hours in the taste of his Spirit. The first giving is for redemption; the second, for sanctification; the third also, for consolation. The first requires right faith; the second, a pure conscience; the third, ready devotion. This raises the mind to meet grace, opens the heart to receive it, and enlarges the affection to receive as much of him as possible.

May the God of all grace, the Son who has been given to you—God blessed through the ages of ages—make not only this grace, but every grace, abound in you. Amen.

### SERMON III. On the wonderful exchange between God and humanity.

[Col. 0035A]

1. “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6): to us indeed, for he was not born for himself or for angels. He was not born for himself, that is, in order that he might begin to exist, or to exist more perfectly, through this birth; for before he was born temporally, he existed eternally, and he was perfect blessedness to himself, since perfect God was born of perfect God. Nor was he born for angels, because neither that angel who stood in the truth needed restoration, nor was the fall of the one who fell capable of restoration. Therefore “he nowhere takes hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16). He who was God born for himself became a child born for us: in a manner leaving himself and passing over angels, so that, coming all the way to us, he might become one of us; and emptying himself, he was made lower than angels, that he might become equal to us.

Therefore, he who, born eternally, was blessedness to himself and angels, born temporally became redemption to us, because he saw that we alone laboured under the ancient disadvantage of our birth. How happy, how lovable is your birth, child Jesus! It corrects everyone’s birth, restores our condition, dissolves the disadvantage, and tears up the bond of condemned nature, so that anyone distressed to have been born unto condemnation may be born again most happily. “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

We give thanks for your gratuitous and gracious birth, O God, Son of Man, through which we have access to this grace in which we stand and glory in hope of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 5:2). Truly, this is a wonderful exchange: that, taking flesh, you grant divinity! An exchange, I say, made by love, not by desire for gain; glorious indeed for your generosity, but altogether profitable for my need. Truly you are a merciful child, whom mercy alone made a child—although mercy and truth also met together in you (Ps. 84:11).

Truly, I say, you are a merciful child, born for us and not for yourself. Being born from us, you sought our gain, not your own increase; for you deigned to be born for this purpose alone, that by your abasement you might advance us and by your humiliation glorify us. You, emptied, filled us: for you poured all the fullness of your divinity into the human being. You poured it forth, but did not confuse it. Yet I would not call God poured into humanity if I heard that the Spirit had been given to this man by measure; or if anything of his whole fullness had remained with God which he had not poured out into the human being with whom he is one.

2. Rightly, therefore, is the name of the God-man “oil poured out” (Song 1:2), or rather ointment emptied out, since God was poured so utterly into humanity that the faith of the Apostle confesses that he “emptied himself” (Phil. 2:7). Yet he so emptied himself that he diminished or changed absolutely nothing in himself; nor could there be any other emptying of immutable nature than the assumption of our nature, which is “earth empty and void.”

This is truly a great emptying in the eyes of those who see it: that the brightness of glory and image of the Father’s substance should display only the form of a servant, having in that form neither appearance nor beauty. For as though it were too little for him to be emptied merely by becoming human, he also so completely stripped himself of even the glory of human flesh, made wisdom foolish, made strength weak, and diminished greatness, that both in his birth he showed himself least and in his passion the last of men; therefore they did not esteem him.

Would you see God emptied of himself? See him lying in a manger. “Behold our God” (Isa. 25:9), says Isaiah, who saw from so far away and recognized the manger of his Lord—or rather, God in the manger. “Behold,” he says, “our God.” Where, I ask? “In the manger,” he says. Yet I find an infant there. Do you call this the one who says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24), indeed whose majesty finds all the expanse of heaven narrow? I see him wrapped in swaddling clothes. Do you call this the one who has clothed himself in glory and beauty, in inaccessible light, robed in boundless light as in a garment? I hear him crying. Is this he who thunders in the heavens, under whose thundering voice angelic powers lower their wings?

“It is so,” answers another prophet on Isaiah’s behalf; “it is altogether so. This is our God, but he is emptied in order to fill you, and he chose in a manner to lack from himself in order to restore you.” The whole choir of prophets cries out with one Spirit and the same meaning, though some with differing voice: “It is so: this is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him” (Bar. 3:36), for there is none other beside him.

“But I know,” says David, “I know that the perverse and adulterous generation of the Jews will not believe this sign but will contradict it. You apostles, declare it to the succeeding generation of the Gentiles.” What shall they declare? That he whom the Jew neither notices lying in the manger nor values hanging on the cross—whom he does not see when he is wondrously born, envies when he works wonders, and mocks when he suffers dreadful things—this one, I say, this is our God for ever and ever; “he himself shall govern us for ages” (Ps. 47:15).

3. And behold, now that the apostles preach and the prophets bear witness, though the fleece has been dried, the broad threshing-floor has been drenched (Judg. 6:39–40); though the gourd has withered, Nineveh has been saved (Jonah 3–4); and the loss of the Jews has become the riches of the world and salvation for the Gentiles. All kings of the earth adore the child born to us; all nations serve him. For any who do not serve, or will not serve, are before him as though they were not (Isa. 40:17); indeed, the nation and kingdom which shall not serve him shall perish.

Yet already we see and rejoice that what the Father had promised through Isaiah has been fulfilled: “Men of lofty stature shall pass over to you; they shall be yours; they shall walk after you; they shall worship you and make supplication to you. And rightly,” he says, “because God is in you alone, and there is no God apart from you. Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Saviour” (Isa. 45:14–15).

If Jesus could ever have been said more plainly or more expressly to be God, let the Jew never believe it. Or, if he denies that these things were said of Jesus, let him show another in whom God is, and who is God, and that there is no God besides him. For he does not confess a Trinity of persons, so that he could assign a God in whom God is, in such a way that there is not another God besides him.

But, faithless one, what ought to have built you up unto godliness is a stumbling-block to you: namely, that God was hidden and a human being was set before your eyes, like mud made from spittle that might enlighten a blind man to see God. This, I say, is your scandal: that the strength of God was hidden in the weakness of flesh, and the strength of the God-man was hidden in the weakness of the cross; that his appearance was inglorious among men and his form among the children of men. Therefore you did not esteem him, but thought him “as a leper, stricken by God and humbled,” when God had placed in him the iniquities of us all (Isa. 53:4–5). He would have taken yours also, if at last you had wished to lay it down. But you, wretched one, do not lay it down; rather, you add iniquity upon iniquity: to the blood of the prophets, the blood of the Son of God and of the Apostles.

Lay upon yourself, then, since you so desire, the yoke of your iniquities, upon yourself and your children. It is more fitting for me to bear the kingdom of Christ, so that he himself may bear my iniquities. You bear the bonds of impiety and crushing bundles; let me bear the bundle of myrrh which Mary bound for me and laid, wrapped in swaddling clothes, in the manger.

4. Therefore, my brothers, you who have recognized the manger of your Lord and the Lord in the manger, whom Israel did not recognize; you, I say, for whom the Saviour was not made cheap because he chose to be merciful, but is more tender in your affection the smaller he is in appearance: sing, rejoice, and make melody: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us.” He was born of the Jews, but he was born to us, because he was taken from them and given to us.

“Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things. The Lord has made known his salvation” (Ps. 97:1–3), so fully that even the ass from among the Gentiles recognizes in the manger his Lord made hay for him, because “all flesh is hay” (Isa. 40:6). For “in the sight of the Gentiles he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97:2), which the Jew does not know, still having a veil over his face. He has the veil because he harbours jealousy; therefore he does not even see the veil, but envies that a child is born to us, a son given to us. Nor does he envy because he wishes to possess him himself, but because he desires both me and himself to perish. The jealous and wicked harlot would rather have the infant killed than given to me alive.

But the judgment of our Solomon, whose word is sharper than every two-edged sword and searches hearts and reins, did not err in finding the mother. “Give the living child,” he says, “to the Church, for she is his mother” (3 Kgs. 3:26–27). “For whoever does his will is his mother and brother and sister” (Matt. 11:50). O Lord Solomon, you call me mother; I profess myself a handmaid. “I am the handmaid of Christ: let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). Certainly I shall show myself a mother by love and solicitude as far as I can; but I shall always remember my condition.

5. O brothers, this name of mother does not belong only to prelates, although a special responsibility of maternal care and affection rests upon them. It belongs also to you, who do the will of the Lord. Indeed, you too are mothers of the child given to and in you, since you conceived from the fear of the Lord and gave birth to the spirit of salvation.

Watch therefore, holy mother; watch over the care of the newborn, until Christ, who was born to you, is formed in you. For the more tender he is, the more easily he can perish for you—though he never perishes for himself. For if the Spirit who is in you is extinguished for you, he returns to God who gave him. Watch, I say, over the care of the newborn, remembering that your rival, while sleeping, smothered the son who had been given to her. Who is she but the carnal soul, which extinguishes the Spirit through negligence and sloth?

When such people have lost the fervour of religion, they nevertheless arrogate to themselves its glory and name. From this arise the disputes of the carnal against the spiritual, even in chapters where the true Solomon presides invisibly as judge. “My son,” the carnal say, “is alive, and yours is dead. I have the Spirit of God; you do not. The love of God lives in me; in you it is dead.” They thus claim for themselves the authority of religion, whose truth the spiritual possess, in order that, after authority has been withdrawn from the latter, they may introduce customs according to the pleasure of their own judgment.

And indeed the mother wishes the living and whole infant to be given to her rival, not begrudging her the honour, provided she also possesses the virtue. But the other says: “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided” (3 Kgs. 3:26), because she wishes to keep for herself the honour of holiness and leave its labour to others. Yet the judge does not err, though he conceals his judgment for a while. Solomon’s sword finds the mother to whom he awards undivided both the affection of charity and the effect of authority, both the fervour of acting and the favour of commanding.

Therefore, brothers, you in whom faith working through love has been born of the Holy Spirit, keep it, feed it, and nourish it, as the little Jesus, until the child born to us is formed in you. By being born, living, and dying, he gave us the pattern to which we are to be conformed. Always remember that he was born only for us, chose to live only for us, and died only for us—not for himself, who had no need of this—that we might be born again through him, live according to him, and die in him, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

### SERMON IV. On the fullness of time brought by Christ.

1. “Behold, now the fullness of time has come” (Gal. 4:4). Paul understands this fullness of time either on account of the abundance of grace, or on account of the fulfillment of the preceding prophecy 928, or on account of the fuller age of mature faith. Let us consider each point. [Col. 0039A]

The Lord Christ is the fullness of every good thing; for he is full of all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God, and of all grace; indeed, in him “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). The apostles saw him “full of grace and truth,” and from his fullness all received; so much so that Paul, the last of them and as one untimely born, the chosen vessel, scattered everywhere the fullness of grace and truth which he had received from that fullness, crying out and saying: “Behold, now the fullness of time has come” (Gal. 4:4). For since the author of time was born in time, full of every good thing, why should he not have brought the fullness of time? When the heavens dropped dew from above, and the clouds rained down the Just One, when the earth brought forth the Savior, why should such abundance of heavenly blessing not have bestowed fruitfulness upon all lands? [Col. 0039B] “You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have given your goodness, and our earth has yielded its fruit” (Ps. 84:2, 13): namely, from the single grain of wheat which the Virgin’s womb brought forth, a plentiful harvest of believers springing up throughout the world.

For I do not wish you to seek this fullness of time in an abundance of temporal goods, but of eternal ones; not in the yield of fields, but of heaven. If the heavens drop dew from above and the clouds rain down the Just One; if the earth brings forth the Savior and righteousness rises at the same time; if finally in the days of the Lord there arises not only righteousness but also an abundance of peace: seek no happier times, when the kingdom of God itself is nothing other than “righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17), proceeding from these things. Indeed, the condition of our own times too is judged best and most beautiful when righteousness imposes discipline upon conduct, and abundance together with peace provides tranquility and joy of life.

Finally, “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 118:64); “the Lord has blessed the crown of the year of his goodness, and his fields are filled with abundance” (Ps. 64:12), with every spiritual grace. And who but the ungrateful would deny that this is the fullness of time? What golden age ever possessed anything comparable to this fullness of time, when the bread of angels, containing every sweetness of flavor and every delight, is set even before beasts; and not human beings alone, but beasts also, are fed with heavenly food? [Col. 0039C] “You will save men and beasts, O Lord, according to the multitude of your mercy, O God” (Ps. 35:7–8). Infinite in manifoldness is this mercy of yours, O God: you who are the bread of angels enrich and make blessed not only the tables of human beings, but, having become hay, also fill the mangers of beasts. [Col. 0039D]

You acknowledge, O merciful Wisdom, that you are debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, so that, having made both, you may provide both with necessary nourishment; and may save both men and beasts, both spiritual and animal persons, each in his own rank and order. Therefore let them “give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men” (Ps. 106:15): for he sent his Word made flesh, the medicine and food of all, so that even those incapable of the Word might nevertheless be healed and satisfied by the flesh of the Word. [Col. 0040A] Let the poor therefore eat and be filled, and confess that the blessed fullness of time has come, when they find heavenly bread prepared in their mangers without the sweat of their brow. “Will the ox then low when it stands before so full a manger?” (Job 6:5). Let it low—but from joy of spirit, in the jubilation of its heart—because it has recognized the manger of its Lord, indeed the Lord in its manger.

2. Yet I would gladly see still more plainly how great a fullness of time Christ, coming from heaven, brought with him; and at how easy and slight a price he decreed that every precious thing might be purchased. Since his days, the kingdom of heaven is bought for two small coins, or a cup of cold water, or indeed by good will alone—although even now, among so great a multitude of rich persons, it scarcely finds a buyer. [Col. 0040B]

Shame! Even we ourselves, who have already begun to buy, have already drawn up the deeds of purchase, have already received the pledge of the inheritance—even we, I say, so often withdraw from the agreement, and almost repent of having been pleased with it; we complain, we murmur, as though we had been deceived in a transaction, as though that almost-nothing which is required of us were something great. Scripture prophesied well concerning us: “‘Bad, bad,’ says every buyer; and when he has gone away, he will boast” (Prov. 20:14). And will he not rightly be able to boast who has purchased that immeasurable and eternal weight of glory 929 at the cost of this light and momentary tribulation, who has thus been saved for almost nothing?

But now one hears complaints every day on all sides and troublesome murmurings: “This is bad; that is bad; this is burdensome; that unbearable; who can endure so many and such things?” [Col. 0040C] Thus scarcely anyone, estimating the matter worthily according to its true value, says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18)—unless only at last, when it begins to be revealed. Then indeed he will boast who now disparages the purchase and groans that he is overcharged; when, that is, he has departed from the marketplace—that is, from this world, where the contract of this commerce is made—and returned to the house of his eternity, carrying with him so great a possession purchased for so little.

That man was truly according to God’s heart, a straightforward man without complaint, who was far from this craft—or rather, this sloth and unbelief—of buyers: I mean David, who said: “Because I have not known learning, O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70:15–16). [Col. 0040D] I will in no way remember my own righteousness, so as to exaggerate my labors or magnify my merits; rather, I will remember your righteousness alone, you who freely bound yourself to me as promiser. “Hear me in your truth, in your righteousness; and enter not into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142:1–2): for if I should wish to justify myself, my own mouth would condemn me. [Col. 0041A] “By this,” he says, “I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70:16): because, namely, I shall not establish my own righteousness. By this he will make me powerful, both now in battle and then in the kingdom, because I shall always confess my weaknesses. “For when I am weak, then I am powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10).

Therefore, just as he deals prudently with his cause before God who, forgetful of his own righteousness, entrusts everything to mercy, so he buys prudently who refuses to know every pretense and greed of bargaining; who, having found that precious pearl, freely and eagerly spends not only all that he has but even himself. But we, lukewarm, pretentious, ungrateful, irreligious, lovers of pleasures more than of God, can scarcely restrain ourselves from that unbelieving and utterly wicked murmur: “‘Bad, bad’” (Prov. 20:14), even after we have tasted and seen—as is written of the valiant woman—that our transaction is good.

3. A certain relentless zeal against the ingratitude and unbelief of this present age was still carrying me away; but the holy and blessed fullness of Christ’s time, of which I began to speak, calls me back, by which you are even today to be fed more fully. [Col. 0041B] Yet these two times, so different and so opposed—the time of grace and the time of malice—run together and are borne along together, although only one time is found for both.

For if now were not a time of grace, the Apostle would not say: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). And again, if now were not a time of malice, the same Apostle would not say: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16). Grace and ingratitude therefore contend within one time, as in one arena. For wisdom has long fought against malice, and for this reason has now descended into the arena of this world. It fights, I say, [Col. 0041C] unwilling to be conquered by evil, but willing to conquer evil with good.

Iniquity abounded; and though human charity had grown cold, divine charity did not grow cold. That great fire of charity was truly, as it is written, unquenchable by many waters (Song 8:7). Although the multitude of sins was already demanding the final judgment, God nevertheless sent his Son, not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Therefore, when the malice of the world, now almost completed, indicated the end of time, the coming of the Redeemer poured a new and unexpected fullness of time into human affairs. For when the world had grown old and was near destruction through the age of time, it was suddenly renewed at the coming of its Creator with the new and unexpected youthfulness of power and with a certain youthful warmth of faith. [Col. 0041D]

For faith—whose earliest period, like a kind of childhood, was among the Patriarchs, who arose at the first dawn of the Church’s birth; whose adolescence was among the Prophets—finally grew in the Apostles to the fullness of youthful strength, when it displayed to the world the heat of its power in the splendid and most courageous triumphs of innumerable martyrs. The Apostle calls this mature and full age of faith the fullness of time: when those who had been under the pedagogue 930 of the law, and differed in nothing from a slave while they were little children, now, grown up, received through the Father’s Only-begotten Son the liberty of children (Gal. 4:1–9). [Col. 0042A]

He, moreover, lest any fullness be lacking to his time, came full both of grace and truth: through grace causing the commandments of the law to be fulfilled, and through truth himself fulfilling the promises. Thus whatever had been done or said mystically throughout all previous ages was all fulfilled more truly and more fully in this fullness of time. For this very day has today presented so many mysteries and so many oracles, as though recapitulated in brief, that it may truly be said of it: “Perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many times” (Wis. 4:13).

4. Since, therefore, it is evident in so many ways that the blessed fullness of time has come, Solomon rightly checked the complaints of the foolish, saying: “Do not say: ‘What do you suppose is the reason that former times were better than the present?’ Such a question,” he says, “is foolish” (Eccl. 7:11). [Col. 0042B] For the grace of God has plainly made these times most happy for human beings; but human ingratitude has made them most wretched for itself.

O acceptable time, to which this day gave so blessed and auspicious a beginning—the day on which the eternal Creator of time was born and announced eternity to mortals! O truly day of salvation, this day on which the salvation of the world, having been born, mixed itself as a saving cup for the sick! O brothers, the Wise Man, unless I am mistaken, spoke of this day to his son: “Do not deprive yourself of a good day.” And explaining what it is not to deprive oneself, he says: “Let no portion of a good gift pass you by” (Ecclus. 14:14). He calls it a good day because today a good gift has been given—indeed, an excellent gift, a perfect gift, descending from the Father of lights; and no one knows what it is like except the one who has received it. [Col. 0042C]

But you, brothers, have received the Spirit who is from God, that you may know the things given to you by God; you who sing with the conviction of your hearts: “A Son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6). This Son is the bread of children, who today presents from himself a blessed and solemn banquet to the whole household of the Father.

5. Thanks be to you, Father of mercies, who give us today our daily bread, and have opened your hand with such generosity to fill every living creature with blessing, so that even their manger itself is found full of blessing. How wretched, brutish, and foolish—indeed, how wicked toward and envious of itself—is that creature which deprives itself of this good day, allowing a portion of the good gift to pass it by: which becomes deprived of the heavenly grace set before it, and passes a day of universal refreshment and joy in a sorrowful and fasting heart; as though the most abundant fullness of time had not yet come, and heavenly bread had not filled the mangers of the simple and humble! [Col. 0042D]

Wisdom marks such a person—wicked toward and envious of himself, ungrateful and injurious toward God—when it says: “An evil eye is set upon evil works, and it shall not be satisfied with bread; it shall be needy and sorrowful at its table.” Therefore, it says, “his soul shall not be satisfied with good things,” because his eye is upon evils, nor will his eye turn back to see good things, so as to consider with devotion and faith what has been set before him upon the great rich man’s table. “For,” it says, “the eye of the envious man is wicked, turning away his face and despising his own soul” (Ecclus. 14:10, 8). [Col. 0043A]

Without doubt, brothers, if we do not turn our face away from considering him who lies in the manger, we can be most happily fed by that very sight, and shall say: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has placed me” (Ps. 22:1–2). Then indeed we shall know that the most desired fullness of time has come, in which God sent his Son, through whom we are now filled with so great a fullness of good things. To him be blessing and thanksgiving, now and through infinite ages of ages.

## SERMON V. On the Wonderful Providence of God in Christ’s Birth

1. You have gathered, brothers, to hear the Word of God. But God has provided something better for us: that today it may be granted us not only to hear, but also to see the Word of God—if only we pass on to Bethlehem and see “this word which the Lord has made and shown to us” (Luke 2:15). [Col. 0043B]

He knew that human senses were incapable of invisible things, unteachable in heavenly things, and difficult even with respect to faith, unless the very thing concerning which faith is urged were visibly presented to their senses for conviction. For although faith comes by hearing, it comes much more readily and promptly by sight, as we learn from the example of him to whom it was said: “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:29)—that is, while you heard, you were unbelieving. Since things heard are believed more difficultly than things seen, the faith of those who have not seen is deservedly proclaimed blessed by the Lord, because they have yielded more to the authority of the word than to the experience of their own senses or reasoning.

Yet God, wishing in every way to satisfy our slowness, made his Word—which he had first made audible—even visible to us today, indeed tangible; so that certain among us could say: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and what our hands have handled concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). He was from the beginning of that eternity which has no beginning; we heard him promised from the beginning of time; we saw and touched him presented at the end of time.

Elsewhere you will find that the Word of God was made not only visible and tangible to us, but even tasteable and fragrant; for through every avenue of the senses he sought an entrance to the soul, so that, as death had entered through the senses, so life might return through those same senses. Therefore, the fact that “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14) was done for us, who are wholly flesh; so that we who formerly could only hear the Word of God may now see and taste him made flesh, and summon every sense as testimony to hearing, so that all our senses with one agreement and one voice may confess: “As we have heard, so we have seen” (Ps. 47:9). [Col. 0043C]

Yet sight was then granted incomparably more than hearing had ever been granted: for now the Word who is God is seen, whereas before it was held a great thing to hear any word from God. I have sometimes seen, brothers, a word which is from God heard with weariness; but can the Word who is God be seen except with joy? [Col. 0043D] I shall pronounce judgment first against myself: because if the Word who is God offers himself today for me to see in that which I am, and does not make me glad, I am impious; if he does not build me up, I am reprobate. [Col. 0044A]

2. Therefore if anyone among us, brothers, is found afflicted by acedia, I do not wish his ears to be wearied longer by our contemptible sermon. Let him pass on to Bethlehem, and there look upon that into which angels desire to look: namely, the Word of God which the Lord has shown us. Let him imagine in his mind what manner of thing the living and effective Word of God lies there in the manger [variant: “how it is silent there”]. If devotion only enlightens the eye of the beholder, what can be seen more delightfully or thought more beneficially? What equally builds up character, strengthens hope, and inflames charity? [Col. 0044B]

Surely this is a faithful word and worthy of all acceptance: your all-powerful Word, O Lord, who, in so profound a silence, slipped down from the royal seats of the Father into the mangers of animals (Wis. 18:15), and meanwhile speaks to us more effectively by his silence. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” what this devout and mystical silence of the eternal Word says to us. For, unless my hearing deceives me, among the things it says, it speaks peace to the people of his saints; upon them his reverence and religious example have imposed silence—and most rightly imposed it.

For what commends the discipline of silence with so great a weight and authority? What so terrifies into restraint the restless evil of tongues and the storms of words, as the Word of God silent in the midst of human beings? [Col. 0044C] “There is no speech in my tongue,” the all-powerful Word seems to confess while he is subject to his Mother; and with what madness shall we say: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11:5). Would that it were permitted me to become mute, be humbled, and keep silence even from good things, so that I might give a more attentive and diligent ear to the hidden voices and sacred meanings of this divine silence, and learn in the school of the Word under silence for as long a time as the Word himself was silent under his Mother’s discipline.

3. O brothers, if we attend devoutly and diligently to this Word which the Lord has made today and shown to us, how much and how easily might we be taught by him! For the Word has been shortened, yet in such a way that every word necessary for salvation has been completed in him, because he himself is the word completing and shortening in righteousness. And this shortened completion overflowed with righteousness (Isa. 10:23), as you remember was promised through Isaiah, because from his fullness 932 he poured righteousness over those who share in him, so that their righteousness might abound more than that of the Pharisees and Scribes; although the latter exercise themselves in so many different justifications of the law, while the former are content with the brief and simple word of faith. [Col. 0044D]

But what wonder if the Word of God shortened all his words for us, when he was willing to be shortened himself and in some sense diminished? Thus he contracted himself, as it were, from the incomprehensible immensity of his being into the narrowness of a womb; and, containing the world, allowed himself to be contained in a manger. [Col. 0045A] In heaven this Word astounds the angelic powers by his dreadful height; in the manger he feeds the simple and dull. There he is unsearchable to the most subtle intellects of angels; here he is palpable even to dull human senses.

Because God could not speak to us as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons, his Word was made flesh, so that all flesh might not only hear but also see what the mouth of the Lord had spoken. And because in its wisdom the world did not know the wisdom of God, by ineffable condescension that same Wisdom of God made itself foolishness, in order to offer itself as learnable even to the most ignorant or self-confident, and through the foolishness of preaching save those who believe. “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden your wisdom from the wise and prudent, and revealed it to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you” (Matt. 11:25–26), that a little one born for us might be given to little ones, since the height of the proud is utterly opposed to the humility of this little one, and “what is high among men is abominable before God.”

He who is truly high became little for us. This little one agrees only with little ones and rests only in the humble and quiet. Therefore, as little ones, glorying in him, sing, “A little one has been born to us” (Isa. 9:6), so he too glories in them: “Behold,” he says, “I and my children, whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. 5:18). For in order that the Father might give companions of his Son’s own age to his little Son, the glory of martyrdom began immediately, first of all, from the innocence of little children; by this the Holy Spirit signifying that the kingdom of heaven belongs only to such persons (Matt. 19:14). [Col. 0045B–C]

4. If we wish to become such, brothers, again and again let us pass on to Bethlehem, and look more attentively upon this Word made flesh by the immense God, who became little, so that in this visible and shortened Word we may learn the wisdom of God, which has become wholly humility. For all-powerful strength transferred itself for the time being wholly into this virtue. That supreme Wisdom wished meanwhile to know nothing else but this humility, of which afterward he wished to profess himself the teacher.

And this one—though I speak this, surely, for my own reproach—this one, I say, was worthily and justly made master of the humility to be taught. [Col. 0045D] Although he did not lack humility, original from his Mother and natural from his Father, nevertheless he learned it from the womb of his Mother by the things that he suffered. He was born in a travelers’ lodging, so that, taught by his example, we might confess that we are guests and pilgrims upon the earth. There also, choosing the lowest place, he was laid in a manger, so that we too might learn by deed that saying of David: “I have chosen to be lowly in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). [Col. 0046A]

He was wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that, having only what we need for covering, we might be content with these. In every way content with his Mother’s poverty and in every way subject to his Mother, he made it seem that the pattern of all religious life was already born in his birth. Blessed indeed is the simple faith of the shepherds, who, when they found the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, were not scandalized by them into unbelief, so as to think lesser things concerning him; but were rather built up unto devotion, becoming more grateful for so great a condescension. For the more deeply and utterly that Majesty showed itself humbled and emptied for their sake, the more easily and completely, if we wish to think worthily of them, did charity seize and claim all their affections for itself. [Col. 0046B]

5. Brothers, today you too will find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed in the manger of the altar; see that the lowliness of the covering does not offend or disturb the gaze of your faith, which beholds the truth of the venerable body under other forms of things. For just as Mother Mary wrapped the infant in certain wrappings of cloth, so Mother Grace covers for us the truth of that same sacred body under the ministering forms of things; and likewise Mother Wisdom covers the hidden majesty of the divine Word under enigmas and figures, so that there simplicity of faith and here the exercise of study may accumulate merit for salvation. [Col. 0046C]

For I, brothers, when I proclaim to you in my words the truth which is Christ, what else do I do but wrap Christ in rather mean cloths? Yet blessed is he to whom Christ is not less precious even in these wrappings, just as precious wares do not become cheap to a prudent person because of the old sacks in which they are clothed. It is Christ, certainly, whom I desire to deliver to you through whatever sort of words of ours, so that, according to the saying of the Apostle Peter, you may sanctify him in your hearts (1 Pet. 3:15). “Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas. 1:21). And may the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly: that is, love and remembrance of the incarnate Word, so that you may sing with as much happiness as faithfulness: [Col. 0046D] “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Therefore let us think upon Christ in the swaddling clothes with which his Mother covered him with all devotion, so that with eternal blessedness we may see the glory and beauty with which the Father clothed him—the glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father—with whom, and with the Holy Spirit, are honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0045]

## SERMON I. On Offerings to Be Brought to the Lord

[Col. 0045D]

1. “Bring to the Lord, sons of God, bring” (Ps. 28:1). It is better to bring to him than to the leech—that is, to desire—whose two daughters, pleasure and vanity, give no rest by day or by night, saying: “Bring, bring” (Prov. 30:15). [Col. 0046D] What, then, shall we bring to the Lord? Bring to the Lord the glory of gold and the honor of incense; bring to the Lord glory to his name, myrrh for his burial (Ps. 28:1–2). [Col. 0047A]

But a disciple of Christ, a son of Peter, says to me: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6), nor sacks of foreign merchandise—myrrh and incense. Will you then appear empty in the Lord’s sight and honor the cradle of the new King with no gifts? O rich poverty, O wealthy nakedness, if only it is Christian and voluntary! For what riches do you lack—not only gold, but even pure gold, gold refined by fire; not only myrrh and incense, but every kind of spice-powder? Indeed, who else can abound in riches of this kind except Christ’s poor?

“I walk,” he says, “in the ways of righteousness, that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries.” Nor does he lack the means to do so: “With me,” he says, “are riches and glory, splendid wealth, and righteousness” (Prov. 8:20–21, 18). [Col. 0047B] These are truly good possessions—the riches of salvation—in which one may take pride in such a way that righteousness is not abandoned. Brothers, this pride is the glory of those who exult in the Lord and triumph over the world because it possesses nothing so precious that it can be compared with the poverty of the saints.

O you of little spirit, why do you not take pride with me in these riches? The Master of humility does not condemn this pride but rewards it, provided that you are so great-hearted in contempt for the world that you look down upon all its glory as from a height, and count it as nothing beside the love and glory of your nakedness. You are altogether rich if you glory in poverty; and the Apostle’s congratulation will give thanks for you also: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God, because in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and holiness, so that you lack nothing in any glory” (1 Cor. 1:4–5, 7). [Col. 0047C] Very differently does the Lord address the person who applauded himself for the abundance of this world: “You say, ‘I am rich and lack nothing’; and you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked” (Rev. 3:17).

2. Certainly among riches of this kind, for which Paul congratulated the disciples, I would not doubt that gold, incense, and myrrh can be found, fit to be offered worthily and gratefully to Christ at his birth. But you say: “I am not conscious that I have received anything of the kind, nor can I find in my possession anything so precious as gold, incense, and myrrh. For, seeing my poverty, I shall scarcely beg a daily alms, maintaining a poor life.” [Col. 0047D]

Do you think, he says, that you have received nothing of the kind? Consider rather whether you have dissipated the substance received from the Father by living luxuriously. But I pass over that matter; for, as the Wise Man says, one must not reproach a person turning away from sin (Ecclus. 8:6). I would rather that you should not be reluctant to try and seek whether perhaps even the smallest part of your paternal inheritance remained with you, from which you might take a beginning for recovery. I would that you might dig within yourself; for precious treasures are accustomed to lie hidden in the depths of the earth.

That treasure was hidden in a field which compelled a man, by desire for it, to sell all that he had (Matt. 13:14). Ten Israelites said that they had treasures hidden in a field, and by this escaped the sword of the murderer (Jer. 41:8). O how many treasures of good works, how many riches of devout fruits, lie hidden in the field of the human body, and how many more in the hidden place of the heart, if only there is someone to cultivate and dig! [Col. 0048A] Nor do I mean that Platonic doctrine, that the soul learned arts before the body, and that, buried under forgetfulness and the mass of the body, they must be dug up again by learning and effort. Rather, I mean that human reason and natural capacity, with grace assisting, are the seedbed of every virtue.

Therefore, if you return to your heart and exercise your body, do not despair of finding desirable treasures; and if not gold immediately at the beginning, or incense, at least myrrh that is not useless. Do not call it useless or cheap when Christ accepts it as a gift—he who willed not only that the burial of his body should be prefigured by it when it was offered to him, but even accomplished by it when he was anointed with it. [Col. 0048B]

3. If, then, you wish to hear more plainly: myrrh in your heart is sorrow; myrrh in your body is labor, provided that either is penitential. For that both are myrrh is shown not only by the etymology of the name or the quality of its taste, but also by the medicinal efficacy of its power. Myrrh reveals the extreme bitterness of its taste even in its name; by its effect, besides its other benefits, it resists corruption. And what is more bitter in taste, or more salutary in effect, than the sorrow by which a sinner is grieved unto repentance? He recalls his years in the bitterness of his soul, saying to God: “Do not condemn me” (Job 10:2). Yet all this bitterness is nothing but myrrh, preserving him from the corruption alike of the luxuries in which he rotted and of the immortal worms which he deserved. [Col. 0048C]

And what of bodily labor? It is not so much myrrh as a bundle of myrrh, if we are willing to believe those who have recently come from the world. The rule of fasts and vigils, daily manual labor, roughness of clothing, and almost everything bitter because unfamiliar, are imposed upon them to bear as though tied together into one bundle. And indeed they would bear this bundle of myrrh most bitterly, were it not that, although they do not yet rejoice to share the sufferings of the Beloved so as to say, “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Song 1:12), nevertheless they find it exceedingly sweet to temper the bitterness of the heart by outward bitterness, as one tempers the bile of the stomach by a draught of wormwood. [Col. 0048D]

For as a stomach corrupted by immoderate use of sweet things is cleansed by a bitter drink, so those who have lived pleasantly in a conscience made bitter are never better cured than by the opposite—that is, by an austere life and practice. Especially if they are more often given to drink the myrrhed wine of the Lord’s passion: that is, if they drink the wine of compunction, which is more salutary for the sinner in proportion as it is more bitter from remembrance of sin. Therefore Jesus would not drink (Matt. 27:48), because he had committed no sin which his crucifier imputed to him: that man gave him to drink from the bitterness of an alien vine, whereas Jesus had new wine from the fruit of the true vine to drink with his friends in his Father’s kingdom.

[Col. 0049A] 4. Moreover, although bodily exercise is of little use in comparison with devotion for the perfect, such as Timothy was (1 Tim. 4:5), you yourselves, brothers, are witnesses to how useful it is for beginners and imperfect persons such as we are: how the bitterness of restraint and labor redeems our life from corruption. For you yourselves know how hearts would breed worms, how bodies would breed worms, if myrrh did not daily distill from the hands of those who labor. Is not luxury a worm? I do not know whether there is another more harmful. It enters by flattery, bites with laughter, pierces through by delight, and kills by voluntary consent.

Are not acedia and sorrow a worm? “As a moth to clothing and a worm to wood, so sorrow harms the heart of a man” (Prov. 25:20). [Col. 0049B] What of all evil desires? Are they not worms as well? “Every idle person is in desires, and desires kill the slothful person” (Prov. 21:26, 25). Blessed therefore is he whose own hands distill myrrh throughout his whole being in order to kill worms of this kind, and who has already gone beforehand to anoint his body for burial. 935 But shall I call it his own body, or Jesus’ body? Indeed, Jesus’ also. For his body is a member of Jesus. Whoever he is that has thus been anointed need not fear the worm that does not die, because the worm through which that worm dies for him is already dead to him.

5. Therefore you too have offered myrrh—and myrrh chosen and most thoroughly tested—to the Lord with the kings, being yourself a king, if meanwhile, when your hand does not suffice to offer the gold of wisdom or the incense of devotion, [Col. 0049C] you have at least consecrated to the Lord a contrite heart and an afflicted body with the bitterness of repentance. For I think—without prejudice, however, to a better interpretation—that myrrh is the first offering of beginners, then incense that of those advancing, and finally gold that of the perfect; and that therefore, when they are named together by the Evangelist, the more precious and worthy things were placed first in the order of names according to their respective merit. Elsewhere, indeed, according to the order of spiritual progress, you find myrrh set before incense, as in: “Like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense” (Song of Songs 3:6). And: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” (ibid. 4:6). For it is no small advance when one progresses from myrrh to incense: when one comes from that which serves the needs of human weakness to that which is assigned to [Col. 0049D] divine and festal sacrifices; so that one who offered the sacrifice of a crushed spirit and humbled body, not without the myrrh of bitterness, may now offer the sacrifice of praise with the incense of devotion, and, according to the Lord’s promise, such consolation may be granted to those mourning in Zion that he gives them a crown instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow (Isaiah 61:3). Then the one who mourned sings: “You have turned my lamentation into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth—my spirit of sorrow—and surrounded me with gladness,” namely with the garment of praise, “that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with grief” (Psalm 29:12–13). “For I shall rejoice with joy in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me [Col. 0050A] with the garment of salvation and wrapped me in the raiment of gladness” (Isaiah 61:10).

6. O brothers, whose garments of poverty are insufficient against this harsh winter, who say, “Who can endure before the face of this cold?” Why, I ask you, do you not put on this garment of gladness and salvation, this mantle of praise? If you praise the Lord, your soul shall be praised in the Lord; and the mantle of praise, in which he who is supremely praiseworthy is clothed, will also cover and warm you, as a hen does her chicks beneath her wings—if only you are willing. Ah, how often he has willed it, and you have not! Is this mantle too short to cover both? “You are not constrained in us,” he says, “but you are constrained in your own inward parts. Be enlarged also” (2 Corinthians 6:12–13), [Col. 0050B] and the mantle will extend itself as far as you. His hand is not shortened so that it cannot save; nor is it a great thing for him to console us, unless our perversity prevents it. O you who are cold, this mantle is warm, for it is warmth able to heat not only inwardly but outwardly. “Are not your garments warm when your land is breathed upon by the south wind?” (Job 37:17); indeed, when fire is sent into the bones and kindled fiercely (Lamentations 1:13). With this fire burn that incense; and when you have offered it with the kings, let your prayer be directed like incense before the Lord. And when, from your sacrifice, he has smelled an odor of sweetness, may he say to you: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song of Songs 4:11).

7. But now, concerning the gold of wisdom—which, as we have said [Col. 0050C], is the offering of the perfect—let the one who has attained it speak to you, since none knows it except the one who receives it. Let him, then, who has learned wisdom speak wisdom among the perfect, and from the gold he possesses fashion golden ornaments for your ears. For I do not consider that I have apprehended it; but I pursue it, if by some means I may apprehend it (Philippians 3:13, 12). Great indeed and blessed is the one who finds wisdom and abounds in prudence: wisdom in contemplation of eternal things; prudence in the administration of temporal things; or, to define the wise person more moderately, one who knows how to govern himself and another. This gold is more precious than all riches, even than incense and myrrh; and all things desired in virtues or graces cannot [Col. 0050D] be compared with it. Finally, the wise person, as a man rich in virtues and in all things, even if he is able to offer gold in sublime contemplation or prudent administration, nevertheless does not neglect to offer incense in devotion to the divine work, and myrrh in the mortification of himself. Therefore, brothers, let us offer what we have to the glory of the new King; what we lack, let us ask from him to whom we desire to offer. “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives abundantly to all” (James 1:6). “My gifts, my bestowals,” says the Father of lights, from whom is every perfect gift and every excellent bestowal. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the various ways by which God enlightens us

[Col. 0051A]

1. “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isaiah 60:1). The Light from Light has enlightened and consecrated for us this day of lights: though hidden and unknown today, it has deigned to reveal itself to the world for the illumination of all nations. For today it revealed itself to the Chaldeans by the sign of a new star, and with their firstfruits dedicated the faith of all the nations. Today it revealed itself to the Jews by the testimony not only of John, but also of the Father and the Holy Spirit, when, baptized in the Jordan, it consecrated the baptism of all. Today it manifested its glory before its disciples, when by changing water into wine it foreshadowed that ineffable mystery in which, by its word, [Col. 0051B] the substances of things are changed. Foreseeing through all these manifestations of God that the Church’s faith would be enlightened, the Spirit addresses her under the figure and name of Jerusalem: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come.” The light had indeed come; it was in the world, and the world had been made through it, yet the world did not know it. It had been born, but was not known, until this luminous day began to make it manifest. The prophet therefore says: O new Jerusalem, great city of the new King, Mount Zion, “the sides of the north” (Psalm 47:3)—that is, to be built from the two walls of circumcision and uncircumcision—arise, be enlightened, for your light has come. Arise, you who sit in darkness; attend to the light that has risen in darkness, though it is not comprehended [Col. 0051C] by darkness. “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6); and in his light you will see light, and it will be said to you: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). Attend to the eternal light that moderated itself for your sight, so that he who dwells in inaccessible light might be approached even by weak and bleary eyes. Behold the light in an earthen lamp, the sun in a cloud, God in man: in the clay vessel of our flesh, the splendor of glory and the brightness of eternal light.

2. Majesty is indeed hidden in humanity, power in humility; yet the signs of powers breaking forth do not permit doubt as to where these things come from. “The works,” he says, “which I do bear witness concerning me” (John 10: [Col. 0051D] 25). Great indeed was the testimony of John, who came to bear witness—a lamp from the light; yet much greater was that heavenly testimony which the Father and the Holy Spirit bore to the Son (Luke 3:16, 21, 22): the Father in a voice, the Spirit in a visible form, since every word stands in the mouth of two witnesses. But if even this is received too little: “The innumerable and indisputable works which I do,” he says, “bear witness concerning me” (John 10:25). Clearly the witness is incorruptible and unconquerable when an insensible creature receives a kind of perception for confession of its Creator, hears his will, and obeys his nod without hesitation. For what could be displayed to mortal senses as more divine than the sign of today’s novelty, which Jesus even sent beforehand before the beginning [Col. 0052A] of his signs? A new child cries on earth, and creates a new star in the heavens: that light may bear witness to Light, the star to the sun, and that the star may lead the kings, in the brightness of its rising, from the east to the true East—the eternally dawning splendor—that is, to the man whose name is East/Branch (*Oriens*) (Zechariah 6:12)—by a star proceeding before them not as a star, but as a rational living creature: going before on the way, stopping at the end of the way, and, as it were with a finger, pointing out the one whom they sought. But let the unbeliever object that this star was not Christ’s work, provided that he confesses it to have been the Father’s work in testimony to the Son. Yet the countless multitude and greatness of plainly divine miracles which our Jesus performed in the flesh, though not from the flesh, will overwhelm him without contradiction.

[Col. 0052B] 937

3. But let darkness cover the earth and gloom the peoples who, when light came into the world, loved darkness rather than light (John 3:19), provided that you are enlightened, Jerusalem, heavenly city, who throughout every land and people are to bear for God children of light, whom the true Light will transfer from the power of darkness into the kingdom of its brightness. Thanks be to you, Father of lights, who called us from darkness into your marvelous light (1 Peter 2:9). Thanks be to you, who said that light should shine out of darkness and shone in our hearts for the illumination of knowledge in the face of Christ Jesus (2 Corinthians 4:6). This indeed is the true light—indeed, eternal life—that we may know you, the one God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent. We know you because we know Jesus, since the Father and the Son are one (John 17:23, 11). We know, indeed, through faith, holding faith itself as a trustworthy pledge, because we shall know you by sight. Meanwhile, however, increase faith in us, leading us from faith to faith, from brightness to brightness, as by your Spirit, so that day by day we may enter more deeply into the treasures of light; that faith may become fuller, knowledge more complete, and charity more fervent and more widely diffused, until through faith we are led to the vision of your face—as by a guiding star to our Bethlehemite leader, who, coming forth from Bethlehem, rules Israel and reigns in Jerusalem: not that Jerusalem which kills the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself, but that one in which the same Lord crowns the slain, he who is the cause, power, and glory [Col. 0052D] of the martyrs.

4. With how great joy does the faith of the Magi rejoice there, seeing him reigning in that Jerusalem whom they adored crying in Bethlehem! Here he was seen in the lodging of the poor; there he is seen in the palace of angels. Here he was in infants’ swaddling cloths; there, in the splendors of the saints. Here, in his Mother’s lap; there, on his Father’s throne. Truly worthy was the faith of the blessed Magi to be rewarded with so happy a vision: though it saw in him nothing but weakness and contemptibility, it could not be scandalized so as to fail to venerate God in man and man in God. Without doubt, the star from Jacob had shone in their hearts: the morning star, the light-bearer that knows no setting, who had also kindled outwardly a star, the sign of his morning rising, [Col. 0053A] in their hearts. Of them it may altogether fittingly be understood what is written in Solomon: “The path of the righteous, like shining light, goes onward and increases unto perfect day” (Proverbs 4:18). For they first entered upon the path of righteousness at the light of the shining star; under its guidance they advanced to see the new rising of the morning light; and thus at last they came to contemplate the face of the noonday Sun, glowing on the day of his power.

5. Thus, beautifully and pointedly, in these firstfruits of the Gentiles, in these beginnings of the nascent Church, the progress of faith in each person was foreshadowed: from what it begins, how it advances, and to what at last it comes, so that the footprints of those who are fathers may easily be recognized in their [Col. 0053B] children. As they began from the sight of the star, advanced to the sight of the child, and arrived at the sight of God, so faith in us is born from the preaching of the heavenly luminaries; it is strengthened by the sight of certain images which, through a mirror and in an enigma, present God to us as if incarnate; it shall be consummated when the present, unveiled truth of realities is seen face to face by those contemplating what is now scarcely and fleetingly attained in an enigma. Then faith itself will pass into knowledge, hope into possession, and desire into enjoyment. For stars shine for us too—not one but many; except that the many are one, since their heart is one and their soul one, their faith the same, their preaching harmonious, and their life alike. If you doubt what these [Col. 0053C] stars are, ask Daniel: “Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall be as stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12:3). Paul also calls them luminaries who shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation (Philippians 2:15) and hold fast the word of life, as a brightness borrowed from eternal light, by which they are commanded to illuminate the night of this world. Therefore the Lord, source and origin of light, when he appointed the moon and stars to rule the night, said to them: “You are the light of the world”; and again: “Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:14, 16). They shine, therefore, by word; they shine by example; and by each ray of light they announce the rising of eternal [Col. 0053D] light, while by the likeness of a heavenly life they also commend the heavenly one whom they preach by voice.

[Col. 0053D]

6. Look up, brothers, to heaven; for their way of life is in heaven. Look up, and direct the eyes of your mind: if you cannot yet look upon the wheel of the sun, at least upon the gleam of the stars. Admire the splendor of the saints; imitate their faith; emulate their holiness. These stars flash like flame and point out the rising of the Light of lights. They lead to the cradle of the new King, to the chamber of the Virgin Mother—which is the inviolable mystery of faith; indeed, they will lead into the King’s temple, into the sanctuary of God the Father—which is the inconceivable reward of faith. But meanwhile, while we are not fit to search out God’s wisdom hidden in mystery [Col. 0054A] or to contemplate the majesty laid up as a reward, let us be content to admire the saints’ brightness and imitate their holiness. “My son,” he says, “have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will bestow it upon you” (Ecclesiasticus 1:33). “Do not seek what is higher than you, nor investigate what is stronger than you; but always keep what the Lord commands you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22). For the Lord’s commandment is bright, enlightening the eyes (Psalm 18:9), by which afterward you may be able to behold the very body of light itself, once you have become accustomed to move in the light of its rays—that is, in the practice of the commandments. “Light is sweet,” Solomon says, “and it is delightful to the eyes to see the sun” (Ecclesiastes 11:7). Sweet indeed and delightful, but to those for whom it is bearable. It comforts healthy eyes; it torments weak ones. And [Col. 0054B] who has sight so healthy and keen that he does not grow dim at the sight of that invisible Sun? Who is that investigator of majesty who is not overwhelmed by glory? Your brightness, O Lord, has become wondrous to me, both in itself and also because of me; for it has become too strong for me, while my vision has weakened within me, and I can no longer attain it as I could in Adam. Perhaps I can attain the brightness of the stars, though I cannot attain the Sun itself; and through that brightness I shall one day be strengthened for him.

7. Come then: arise, be enlightened, my soul, you who sat in darkness. Look upon the luminaries of heaven; lift up your eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to you, if you come to him who dwells in heaven—that is, in those mountains themselves. From the mountains, I say, help will come [Col. 0054C] to you, because the inaccessible light illuminates you wonderfully from the eternal mountains. The mountains have received light for the people, that it may descend from them to the subject valleys and plains. This, therefore, brothers, I say is the best beginning of illumination, and one suited to our weakness: that we attend to those who have been enlightened. The straightest way to find Jesus is to follow the guiding light of the fathers who went before. “The path of the righteous is straight; the straight track of the righteous is for walking” (Isaiah 26:7). Whoever follows the righteous does not walk in darkness; not only will he see, but he will possess the light of life. He will see it for the consolation of the present life; he will possess it as the inheritance of eternal life. For godliness has the promise of the life that now is [Col. 0054D] and of that which is to come. Let us train ourselves in godliness, and he who freely made himself our debtor will defraud us of neither (1 Timothy 4:8, 7, 9). Let us train ourselves in works of light; and he who hides light in his hands, declaring concerning it to his friend that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it (Job 36:32–33), will at times now show it to us as consolation for our work, and afterward give it as a reward: Jesus Christ himself, our light, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. By what stages one comes to the light of wisdom

1. “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isaiah 60:1). Blessed be the light that comes in the name of the Lord: the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us. [Col. 0055A] By its gift this day too—a day made holy by the illumination of the Church—has shone upon us. Thanks be to you, true light, who enlighten every person coming into this world, and who for this very purpose came as man into the world. Jerusalem, our mother, the mother of all who have deserved to be enlightened, has been enlightened, so that she now shines upon all who are in the world. Thanks be to you, true light, who became a lamp in order to enlighten Jerusalem, and so that the Word of God might become a lamp to my feet. Thanks, I say, to you, because Jerusalem itself, once enlightened, has become a lamp, to shine upon all who are in the house of the great householder. For it has not only been enlightened but exalted, and has been set upon that entirely golden lampstand: the city upon the mountain of mountains, once abandoned [Col. 0055B] and hated, has been made the pride of ages, so that its Gospel shines as far and wide as the empire of the world once flourished as far and wide. And if its Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who perish (2 Corinthians 4:3), in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so that the glory of Christ’s Church may not shine upon them. Yet for those upon whom it does not shine so that they may see, it shines so that they may envy; and those unwilling to be enlightened by the Church’s grace are tormented by its glory. But the Church, neither proud because of the glory in which it flourishes nor envious because of the grace in which it is powerful, implores even for those whom it endures as troublesome the light which it has received, saying: “For you enlighten my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Psalm 17:29). [Col. 0055C] They may be mine because they are predestined, but they are still darkness because they have not yet been called or justified. Call them too into your marvelous light, and they will proclaim with me your marvelous name. Although every righteous and holy person in the Church rejoices to be enlightened in such a way that he still sees and grieves that he remains dark in no small degree; and therefore, though enlightened, he must still ask to be enlightened. For the more his lamp has been enlightened, the more truly he detects his own darkness by that lamp itself. Nor should you immediately suppose this contrary to what Truth says in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matthew 6:22; Luke 11:34). It does not follow that, because [Col. 0055D] our whole work is made bright by the eye of sincere intention, all the darkness of our ignorances is immediately enlightened. For this is still the manner of our enlightenment: a person is reckoned to have progressed far into the light of truth if he can know his own deficiency and recognize what he lacks. Hence, among the wise people of this world who have discussed knowledge more soberly, the first rank of knowledge is held to be knowing that one does not know.

[Col. 0056A]

2. Brothers, you are all children of light and children of God. We are not of the night or of darkness. “For the night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12). And if we were once darkness, now we are light in the Lord (Ephesians 5:8). Yet if, because we are not darkness or children of darkness, we say that we suffer nothing from darkness, we deceive ourselves and bring upon ourselves the darkness of death, which does not deserve to be enlightened. For what does the Light of the world say, which came into the world for judgment, “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”? “Because,” he says, “you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (John 9:41). I see, however little, because you enlighten my lamp, O Lord; but because what I see is little, “my God, enlighten my darkness” (Psalm 17:29). We see much, indeed, through a mirror and in an enigma; but even that is far removed from true brightness and bright truth, which will be seen face to face. Perhaps this is why the blind man whom the Lord had begun to enlighten in Mark saw people like trees walking (Mark [Col. 0056B] 8:22–24): namely, because he saw only through a mirror and in an enigma. But when the Lord laid his hand on him a second time, he restored him so that he saw all things clearly. This will occur in us when he renews us and completes our healing by the second laying on of hands—the healing which he began by the first—restoring us in perfect brightness.

3. But to whom, when, and for how long can even this seeing through a mirror and in an enigma occur? How mercifully I would be treated, how happily enlightened I would consider myself, if I could see my sins, when daily I must mourn and say: “Evils beyond number have surrounded me, and I could not see” (Psalm 39:13). For “who understands transgressions?” (Psalm 18:13), when even a vice that deceives under the appearance of virtue kills, as though it were truly an angel of darkness transforming itself into an angel of light. Great indeed and greatly enlightened is the one who has been able and willing fully to understand transgressions; for “the deceitful person has not been able and has not been willing to understand, that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4). Of you, God, enlightener of all nations, it was sung to us: “Behold, the Lord will come and enlighten the eyes of his servants.” Behold, you have come, O my light: enlighten my eyes, lest I ever [Col. 0056C] fall asleep in death; lest sin unto death close our eyes by some pleasure and entice us to consent, or, like Ish-bosheth, finding us asleep, pierce us through (2 Kings 4:7). You have come, O light of all the faithful, and behold, today you have granted us joy in the illumination of true faith—that is, our lamp. Grant us also ever to rejoice in the Lord in the illumination of our remaining darkness. You have given the light of true faith; give also the light of true righteousness, the light of divine knowledge, and likewise the light of divine wisdom.

4. By these stages, surely, and along this path, I think you must advance, O faithful soul, so that, stripped of the darkness of this deceitful world, you may reach the homeland of eternal brightness, where your darkness shall be as bright noonday and night shall be illuminated as day. Then indeed, then “you shall see and abound, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged” (Isaiah 60:5), when the whole earth is filled with the divine majesty of unbounded light and his glory is seen in you. “House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord” (ibid. 2: [Col. 0057A] 3): that as true children of light we may walk from brightness to brightness, as the Spirit of the Lord shines before us, so that through the successive stages of virtues we may press further into the kingdom of brightness. Therefore, since we are already in the light through faith, let us advance from and through it into a greater and clearer light: first of righteousness, then of knowledge, and finally of wisdom. For what we believe by faith must then be done or merited through righteousness, afterward understood through knowledge, and finally contemplated through wisdom. First of all, the lamp of faith is kindled, by which we are to work in the night of this age. Hence it is written in praise of the valiant woman, who rose by night and, working with her hands by night and day, did not eat the bread of idleness: “Her lamp,” it says, “shall not be extinguished [Col. 0057B] in the night” (Proverbs 31:18); that is, her faith shall not fail in temptation. By this lamp works of darkness are not done; when they are done, it is extinguished. “For everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). Accordingly, such a person extinguishes the lamp of faith and puts aside the remembrance of God.
