There is no fear of God before his eyes; and, pleased by the darkness he has made for himself and by the absence of judges, he says: “Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, walls cover me, and no one looks about me. Whom do I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins.” And he does not understand that the eye of God sees all things (Ecclesiasticus 23:26–27). Good works, however, even when they are sometimes performed in secret to avoid vainglory, are nevertheless done toward the inward and eternal light—that is, under the judgment of faith and the witness of God—because they are works of light: lamps burning in the hands of those who work and await the Bridegroom’s coming. He will bring forth your righteousness like light before the sight of people and angels and will make your works shine like clear noonday, because they have been done in God, so that the judgments of all may glorify God in you and you in God.

5. How brightly righteousness shines even in the present life, and with what light it gladdens a righteous person’s conscience, the testimony of your own consciences will teach you more intimately and sweetly. Yet faith often shines and righteousness flashes, while understanding still remains dark, so that one may reverence the mystery of faith as though holding it wrapped up but not know how to unfold it; the book of Scripture may be sealed to him, as though he did not know letters; nor may he have senses trained to distinguish good from evil, truth from falsehood. Many such are in the Church: abundant in faith, rich in righteousness, almost wholly lacking in knowledge. Yet that the light of knowledge ought to be added to the light of righteousness is taught by the prophet’s saying. Having first said, “Sow for yourselves righteousness,” he added, to show what firstfruits we are meanwhile to gather from this seed: “Enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10:12). So the Apostle says: “Bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God” (Colossians 1:10). You also, David, most wise prince among the Three, sitting in your seat of wisdom: how did you understand more than the elders? “Because,” he says, “I have sought the commandments.” [Col. 0058A] Truly, I understood from the commandments, because good understanding belongs to all who practice the fear of the Lord. For the anointing that teaches concerning all things, knowing certainly in what order each thing should be learned from it, first teaches goodness and discipline, and afterward knowledge—provided that the person to be taught has first of all believed, that is, has learned the rudiments of the first principles of the teachings of righteousness. Therefore that disciple of the anointing ordered his prayer so wisely and pleaded: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments” (Psalm 118:100, 66). As though he said: I have learned the first rudiments, that is, unfeigned faith; now teach what follows: righteousness, that is, goodness and discipline, so that afterward you may advance me to the knowledge of the saints. You called me to the grace of [Col. 0058B] faith; now justify me through the goodness of love and the discipline of chaste fear, that afterward you may magnify me by the gift of spiritual knowledge. “Those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also magnified” (Romans 8:30).

6. It should certainly be known that, although this is the knowledge of the saints, not all saints are taught it, but only those in whom neither diligence lacks grace nor grace lacks diligence. Rather, both cooperate in mutual support, so that the human disciple is teachable and the Spirit is present as a diligent teacher. Since this knowledge contains various charisms, however, the governing Spirit does not readily confer them all upon one person, but distributes to each as he wills: to one, knowledge of mysteries; to another, understanding of the Scriptures; [Col. 0058C] to another, interpretation of sayings; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, that most necessary faculty resembling discernment by taste, the judgment of virtues and vices, lest vices deceive under the appearance of virtues. “They shall not harm or kill on all my holy mountain, because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord” (Isaiah 11:9).

7. But if, after and through these three—faith, righteousness, and knowledge—someone advances to wisdom, that is, to the savor and taste of eternal things, so that he can be still and see, and by seeing taste how sweet the Lord is; and so that what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered into the human heart may be revealed to him through the Spirit—such a person I would certainly call magnificently and gloriously enlightened, as one who beholds the Lord’s glory with unveiled face and over whom the glory of the Lord often rises. To such a person not a prophet, but the Spirit of the prophets, can say: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (ibid. 60:1). Brothers, not all receive this word; but let the one who can receive it receive it. The one who cannot receive it is not condemned; but the one who does not desire it is surely charged with lukewarmness. Let the one who desires it know that fervent prayer kindles this light of wisdom, just as frequent reading kindles the light of knowledge—provided that, when you read, you bring a burning lamp, that is, righteousness of works and devout experience of the senses. But you, Lord, Father of lights, who sent your only one, Light from Light, [Col. 0059A] to enlighten the darkness of mortals, grant us by the way of lights to arrive at eternal light, that we may be pleasing before you in the light of the living—you who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On our new birth and life

1. Today, brothers, a second birth is celebrated for us, which seems to have been born in due sequence from that first birth, as an effect from its cause. The birth which we have celebrated up to today is Christ’s birth; the birth which we celebrate today is ours. For in that birth Christ was born; in this one Christianity was born. Since three things make us Christians—faith, baptism, and participation in the altar—today’s day initiated faith for us, consecrated baptism, and foreshadowed the miracles of the heavenly table. It is no longer necessary to teach how the first illumination of the Gentiles initiated faith for us, how Christ’s baptism consecrated our baptism, or how that change of water into wine foreshadowed the transformation of things at the feast of the Lord’s table. But I judge it worthwhile to stir ourselves up, lest faith in us degenerate from its beginnings, lest the grace of baptism be rendered void in us, and lest participation in Christ’s cup turn to our judgment.

2. What kind of faith was handed down to us today by those Magi, its first authors, and how they indicated the greatest sacrament of faith through the mystical figures of their gifts, our fathers have discussed sufficiently and abundantly, so that no labor now remains to us in this respect except to enter into their labors. But neither the condition—indeed, the ruin—of this age particularly requires that the mystery of faith be discussed. Rather, every effort must be made that, as the Apostle says, that mystery of faith may be held in a pure conscience (1 Timothy 3:9). For behold: if today you ask about the mystery of faith, you will find nearly everyone most Christian; if you examine consciences, you will find very few truly Christian. Nearly the entire world professes in words that it knows God, but denies him in deeds (Titus 1:16); so much so that even those who seem to have an appearance of godliness are very often found almost to deny its power. [Col. 0059D] But whom do you think, my brothers, I mean to signify by this? Whom do I call persons who have the appearance of godliness but deny its power? If you understand me to mean those who walk the broad way of the world, what appearance of godliness do those display even outwardly, who are Christians only in name and take Christ’s holy name in vain, yet with full and unconstrained profession pursue what is hostile to that name? By every appearance of behavior and manner of life, they declare themselves enemies of Christ’s cross. Is this the appearance of godliness that we see in them: harlot-like dress and gait, buffoonish speech, an immodest eye, a belly worshiped as God, and every insult of life publicly and boastfully inflicted, as it were, in godliness’s face? “For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret” (Ephesians 5:12). [Col. 0060A] Let the prophet sent to them dig through their wall, that he may see yet greater abominations which they neither blush nor fear to commit before that dreadful Majesty. But what is it to me, who seem to be a monk, to judge those outside this monastery? Would that I did not have to judge even those within it. For my soul is troubled within me concerning myself, because I fear that this very appearance of godliness, which I bear with you however imperfectly, may begin to accuse me more grievously if it proves me to have denied godliness itself.

3. Indeed, brothers, I fear—whether you yourselves ought to fear it, see to it—that the saying prophesied through the Apostle concerning the last times may apply especially to us [Col. 0060B]. There, while he described the wickedness of men yet to come, such as may now plainly be read in their life and conduct, he finally concluded his long catalogue of evils thus: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). For what has the appearance of godliness as much as this which we display: the humility of tonsure and habit, moderation in food and drink, almost continuous labour, and an altogether ordered manner of life? Yet as for the very power of godliness which this outward appearance promises, I should be ashamed to confess how nearly nothing of it can be found in me and those like me, if we were not evident to everyone. For what is the power of godliness except unfeigned charity, true humility, long-suffering patience, and ready obedience [Col. 0060C]? How far you may rightly glory in these virtues and their like, brothers, I leave to your own judgment. But concerning myself I frankly confess that I know their names, but have not yet known their savour.

Accordingly, the religious habit which I wear rightly inspires me with both shame and fear, since it is supported by almost no testimony of virtue. Can I safely claim for myself the name and honour of monk when I lack its merit and power? For, as it was said before our time, “feigned holiness is doubled iniquity” (Augustine, on Psalm 63); and the wolf found beneath a sheep’s skin must be struck by a harsher sentence. Therefore you too, brothers, if you would glory safely in this appearance of godliness with which your bodies are adorned [Col. 0060D], set your hearts upon its power, so that the appearance in your bodies and the power in your hearts may show you approved both to angels and to human beings; and so that it may be as written: “All who see them shall recognize them, that these are the offspring whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61:9).

4. This, brothers, is the true godliness of Christian faith: to have the mystery of faith in a pure conscience. For in order that we might faithfully and worthily preserve unstained in a pure conscience the mystery of faith which the mystical gifts of the Magi commended to us today, Christ too was baptized today [p. 943]—not for himself but for us—and, as the Apostle says, “sprinkled our hearts clean from an evil conscience, and washed our bodies with pure water” (Heb. 10:22). How blessed, brothers, is that soul [Col. 0061A] which, thus washed unto salvation, immediately followed the Saviour, so that thereafter, cleaving to him with the Apostles, it deserved to hear that voice: “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13:10).

But “he who is baptized by one dead, and touches him again, what profit is there in his washing?” (Ecclus. 34:30). After I was washed in Baptism, I touched not one dead person, but as many dead persons as I committed works of death; and, according to the Apostle Peter, that true proverb befell me: “The dog returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in mire” (2 Pet. 2:4). What then shall I do? With what waters shall I further wash away such great defilements? I hear that, as there is one faith, so there is one Baptism; nor is there room for a second Baptism, because all of us who are baptized are baptized into the death of Christ [Col. 0061B]. As he died once, so he was baptized once, in order to prescribe for us likewise the manner and form of a single Baptism.

Perhaps I should despair of being cleansed further, had not Elisha’s trustworthy counsel, among the other consolations of Scripture, brought the despairing back to hope—even if I am wholly covered with leprosy like Naaman the Syrian and possessed by an incurable lethargy. “Go,” he says, “wash seven times in the Jordan, and you shall be clean.” If he had said, “Wash three times and you shall be clean,” I should at once have understood the threefold immersion by which the baptized are flooded, and I should have said that the whole miracle prophesied the grace of Baptism: that already then the Jordan had begun, by the power of the Lord’s Baptism, to work for the salvation of the nations. But now, when he expressly says, “Wash seven times in the Jordan,” what does this number seven mean [Col. 0061C], or what is this Jordan? Jordan, they say, is interpreted “their descent.” Whose descent? Surely that of those who are humbled unto repentance; for the more deeply they descend through the degrees of humility, the more profoundly they immerse themselves and the more fully they are washed in the spiritual channel of the Jordan.

5. “My soul is troubled within me, O God,” mindful of its sins; “therefore I shall remember thee from the land of Jordan”: that is, how in the descent of humiliation thou didst cleanse Naaman the leper. “He went down,” it says, “and washed seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and was cleansed.” Go down yourself also, O my soul, from the chariot of pride into the health-giving waters of Jordan [Col. 0061D], which now flows forth from the fountain of the house of David throughout the whole world, “for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman.” This indeed is the humility of repentance, which, flowing alike from Christ’s household and example, is now proclaimed throughout the world and cleanses the crimes of the whole world.

O you Naamans of Syria—for there is not one, but innumerable—O rich men, yet leprous; proud men, yet wretched: why do you so violently shrink from being washed in these healing waters? Why has this Jordan of ours seemed so cheap to you in comparison with the rivers of Damascus? For perhaps, when the humility and poverty of Christ are preached as things to be imitated by those seeking counsel for salvation, you say: “Are not the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel, that I should wash in them and be cleansed?” (4 Kings 5:10, 14, 12). Is it not better [Col. 0062A], and more effective for cleansing sins, to do good daily out of the abundance of the world than, by leaving everything once for all, to become poor?

But listen, Naaman. Leviathan will swallow the river of Damascus and not be astonished; but if he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth, his hope will deceive him (Job 40:18). For he does not consider it a great matter how abundantly you may overflow with any virtues apart from Christian humility. He even trusts that he can devour Christ’s poor, but the enemy accomplishes nothing in them. Damascus, according to its name, is “the city of blood,” and its waters are mixed with blood, because even the good works of carnal and worldly persons are scarcely free from any sin. And how will that which is infected with blood cleanse blood [Col. 0062B]? By what reasoning will that which is leprous cure leprosy? But our Jordan itself flows pure; and the proud will not be able to accuse you if you have been wholly immersed in it and, as it were, buried together with the humility of Christ.

6. At least listen, O Naaman, to your household: humble friends and faithful counsellors. Naaman was departing in anger from the man of God whom he had consulted; but they said, “Father, even if the prophet had told you some great thing, surely you ought to have done it.” This is indeed a faithful saying, full of reason and [p. 944] wisdom; for it is the prompting of the rational faculties of the human being, which God has kept as witnesses against the human being himself. “Father,” they say, “even if the Prophet had told you some great thing, surely you ought to have done it.” For not to believe the Prophet is an injury to God; not to try everything for one’s salvation is self-hatred and envy. What can be great in a command when salvation lies in the promise? How much less ought it to seem great or difficult to learn from Jesus, because he is meek and humble of heart, when in him are found together rest for the soul, a present remedy for spiritual leprosy [Col. 0062C], and the pledge of eternal salvation?

At last, and only with difficulty, the proud sinner is induced to go down into the Jordan and wash. Yet if he washes seven times, immersing himself wholly, more fully and more often, the effect of salvation does not delay to prove the prophetic word true. But alas, how great is the misery of our time! For not only rich lepers, but poor lepers also, are found so delicate that they scarcely permit themselves to be dipped in the healing waters as far as the ankles; or, if they have washed once, they immediately think themselves completely cleansed.

7. Elisha does not think so, but expressly says: “Wash seven times, and you shall be clean.” He knew that the humility of Christ, which we must imitate if we wish to be perfectly cleansed, has sevenfold power. The first power is that, though he was rich, he became poor. The second is that, adding extremity to poverty, he was laid in a manger. The third is that he was subject to his Mother. The fourth is that today he bowed his head beneath the hands of a servant. The fifth is that he endured a thieving disciple and betrayer. The sixth is that he was so meek before an unjust judge. The seventh is that he was so merciful an intercessor with the Father for those who crucified him [Col. 0063A].

You follow this giant’s footsteps, though from far off indeed, if you love poverty; if among the poor you choose the lowest place; if you are subject to monastic discipline; if you endure a lesser person set over you; if you patiently bear false brethren; if by meekness you prevail when you are judged; if you repay with charity those from whom you suffer unjustly. This humility truly rebaptizes without injury to the one Baptism, because it does not repeat Christ’s death but renews the mortification and burial of sins; and what was performed in that Baptism in figure is here fulfilled again in truth. This humility opens heaven and restores the Spirit of adoption: the Father recognizes the son, restored in the innocence and purity of the reborn child [Col. 0063B].

Thus Scripture rightly records of Naaman that “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child” (4 Kings 5:13, 10, 14), signifying, I think [Col. 0064A], that those who wash themselves in this way not only recover in their hearts the innocence of little children, but also claim for their bodies, in a certain sense, childlike purity through the mortification of their members. Thus it is written of one of the saints that, in the limbs of the deceased, there appeared, as it were, the grace of a seven-year-old child (said of St Martin in Sulpicius).

Behold, brothers: we who first lost the grace of Baptism amid such defilements of pleasures, behold, have found the true Jordan—the descent, that is, of the humble—where we may be rebaptized daily. This alone is required: that day by day we spare not ourselves in descending more deeply, in being more fully immersed, and in being wholly buried with Christ. Let us give thanks to him whose humility today consecrated for believers both the form of Baptism [Col. 0064B] and reserved no unlike grace for penitents. To him be glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## On the Feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Col. 0063]

### Sermon I. On the ceremony of lights customarily observed on this feast

[Col. 0063B]

1. “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 22:35). Let our loins be girded, that we may imitate Mary’s Purification; let lamps burn in our hands, that we may represent in ourselves, by a visible sign, Simeon’s joy as he bore the light in his hands. Let us, that is, be chaste in body and pure in heart, and we shall have expressed Mary’s Purification [Col. 0063C]; let us burn with devotion and shine in deed, and with Simeon we bear Christ in our hands.

Mary, however, was not so much purified as she commended to us the mystery of Purification, fulfilling the legal rite [p. 945] and signifying the spiritual reality. For what could there be in her to purify, she who conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—indeed, she who by that very conception was plainly purified, if perhaps she had previously possessed anything less of purity [variant: “had possessed”]? What, I say, had that conception to cleanse—the conception which alone can make clean one conceived from unclean seed (Job 14:4), which brought forth the fountain by which the unclean is purified, the fountain of the house of David, still open today and ceaselessly flowing “for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” [Col. 0063D] (Zech. 13:1)?

Yet the Mother of all purity accepted the outward form of legal purification in order at once to show the power of most obedient humility and to suggest the truth of evangelical purification. Where now is the person who, presuming upon holiness as deceitfully as obstinately, refuses to undergo the purgative remedies of penitents? Grant that he is holy: is he holy as the holiest of holy women, Mary, who bore the Holy of Holies? Would that, my brothers, would that we had in our sins the humility which the saints truly had in their virtues. But let us now leave this aside, so that we may continue what we have begun [Col. 0064B].

And first, we should treat of that spiritual Purification which Mary commended to us when she offered for herself and for her Son a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, were it not that our fathers, as is very well known to you, have discussed everything exhaustively. They have carefully explained how the turtledove pertains to chastity of body and the dove to simplicity of mind; nor have they omitted what is meant by the sacrifice of one turtledove or young pigeon and the whole burnt offering of the other. Yet we add this one point: the better known the mysteries are to us [Col. 0064C], the more strictly and justly their works are required of us. For “to one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4:17); and “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

2. Leaving aside, therefore, what has been sufficiently discussed, let us instead consider, if you please, what this most beautiful custom of the Church—of carrying lights today—either represents as accomplished or shows to be done. Yet I do not think this is unknown to you, even if you have never heard it explained. For who today, carrying a burning candle in his hands, does not immediately remember that old man who, receiving Jesus in his arms today, declared the Word in flesh—like light in wax—to be himself “a light for the illumination of the nations” [Col. 0064D]?

He too was surely a lamp burning and shining, bearing witness to the Light. Filled with the Spirit, he came for this very purpose into the Temple: that, receiving thy mercy, O God, in the midst of thy Temple, he might proclaim it to be mercy itself and the light of thy people. Truly, serene old man, you bore the light not only in your hands but also in your understanding. You were so illuminated that, though you saw so clearly the future illumination of the nations so long beforehand, even amid the darkness of Jewish unbelief the present brightness of our faith shone upon you [Col. 0065A].

Rejoice now, righteous elder; see now what you foresaw. The world’s darkness has been scattered; the nations walk in your light; the whole earth is full of the glory of that light which you cherished hidden in your bosom—or rather, by which you refreshed your faculties. O tinder of love: Love itself, sweet and delightful, for the reviving of the soul! Truly sweet and delightful even when you torment and afflict: a torment that delights blessedly, like a fire that refreshes healthfully.

This fire, brothers, if hidden in the bosom, does not burn garments; rather, it extinguishes that fire which, concealed in the bosom, not only scorches the garment but consumes what is clothed—that is, devours body and soul alike. “Our God,” it says, “is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24), but a fire that consumes consuming fire; for it revives the soul, caresses the mind, refreshes the spirit, and restores that which is perishing [Col. 0065B]. Simeon knew the power of this fire, he who rejoiced to carry it in his bosom and to warm his aged breast with its heat. How much more healthfully and sweetly did this fire warm our old man than Abishag the Shunammite warmed King David (3 Kings 1:17)—unless perhaps Abishag here was this same fire, namely Wisdom, by whose embrace not only are the cold warmed, but the dead also revived.

3. Therefore embrace, blessed old man, the Wisdom of God [p. 946], and let your faculties grow warm and white again as though renewed; clasp God’s mercy to your breasts, and your old age shall be in abundant mercy. “Between my breasts,” it says, “he shall abide” [Col. 0065C] (Song 1:12): even when I return him to his Mother, he will remain with me. And when he is held between his mother’s breasts, he will nevertheless abide between my breasts, and will make even my breasts drunk with abundant mercy—although not as much as his Mother’s breasts. For as she is uniquely the mother of supreme mercy, so she possesses in an outstanding way breasts of abundant mercy.

I rejoice with you and give thanks for you, full of grace, who bore the mercy whom I have received; you prepared the candle which I have accepted. You supplied the wax for the light received, O Virgin of virgins by a Virgin, when you, an incorrupt mother, clothed the incorruptible Word with incorrupt flesh. Come then, my brothers: behold, the candle burns in Simeon’s hands. Light your own candles from the borrowed light of his—that is, the lamps which the Lord commands to be in your hands [Col. 0065D] (Luke 12:35). “Come to him and be enlightened,” so that you may not so much carry lamps as be lamps yourselves, shining inwardly and outwardly, for yourselves and for your neighbours.

Let the lamp, therefore, be in the heart, in the hand, and in the mouth. Let the lamp in the heart shine for you; let the lamp in hand or mouth shine for your neighbours. The lamp in the heart is the piety of faith; the lamp in the hand is the example of deed; the lamp in the mouth is speech that edifies. Yet we must shine not only before human beings through action and speech, but also before angels through prayer, and before God through intention. Our lamp before angels is pure devotion, when we sing wisely or pray fervently in the sight of angels [Col. 0066A]; our lamp before God is a single-minded intention, that we may please him alone, whom we have chosen.

4. And lest we should seem in what we say to have followed dreams of our own imagination, let us instead prove that in all things we have adhered to the testimonies of Scripture. That faith is a lamp, Solomon testifies when he speaks of the valiant woman: “Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night” (Prov. 31:18); which we understand to mean, “Her faith shall not fail in temptation.” For of charity too, which is nothing other than faith working through love, we read in the same Solomon: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters cannot quench charity, neither can rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8:6–7).

That good work is a lamp, the Light of Truth himself indicates when he says: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” [Col. 0066B] (Luke 12:35); and, “Let your light shine before human beings, that they may see your good works” (Matt. 5:16). That edifying speech is a lamp, David says: “Thy word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105). And the Apostle Peter says of prophetic speech: “You do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19).

“The unfolding of the words of God gives light and gives understanding to little ones” (Ps. 118:130), whether Gospel words make clear the shadow of the Law, or whether the very sayings of both Gospel and Law are made clear by lucid expositions—sayings that seemed obscure to little ones who did not understand them. Thus we speak in light what was said to us in darkness [Col. 0066C]. Therefore Philip, as a figure of every ecclesiastical teacher, was called “the mouth of the lamp,” because from his mouth the Lord’s fiery utterance shone forth for the illumination of hearers.

By “word of God,” my brothers, I understand whatever his Spirit deigns to speak in you: every word, surely, that is good for the edification of faith and for the stirring up of charity. Therefore, if any one of you speaks, let him speak “as the words of God” (1 Pet. 4:11), so that even in private conversations no evil speech may proceed from your mouth, but only what serves the edification of faith, that it may give grace to the hearer; so that whoever hears may say to you in thanksgiving: “Blessed is the speech of your mouth, because thy word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105) [Col. 0066D].

That prayer too is a lamp, especially if divinely illuminated, we infer from Solomon’s saying: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a human being, searching all the inward secrets” (Prov. 20:27). For the light opened to us from above while we pray or sing psalms is the breath of life, in which we breathe sweetly. Job seems to recall this lamp when, in the sorrow of temptation, he remembers with a sigh the joy of former consolation: “Who would grant me to be as in the former months, according to the days [p. 947] when God kept me, when his lamp shone above my head, and by his light I walked in darkness?” (Job 29:2–3).

But when this lamp is said to search all the inward secrets—that is, of the mind [Col. 0067A]—we must not suppose this to be what the Lord threatens when he says that he will “search Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 1:12). This is the grace that illumines; that is the judgment that investigates. For a physician’s potion searches the inward secrets in one way, and an executioner’s sword in another. As for intention, that it too is called a lamp no one can doubt, if only he understands that Gospel saying: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22; Luke 11:34).

5. Therefore, brothers, that you may light all these lamps, come to the fountain of light and be enlightened—I mean Jesus, who shines in Simeon’s hands—that he may illuminate faith, brighten deed, furnish speech to the human being, inflame prayer, and purify intention. Thus, whether through deed, speech, or prayer [Col. 0067B], you may seek to please him in the light of the living: him who has lamps with which to search Jerusalem (Zeph. 1:12) and to examine even our light.

With all these lamps lit, O child of light, you will no longer walk in darkness; nor need you fear the sentence of the curse: “Whoever curses father or mother, his lamp shall be extinguished in darkness” (Prov. 20:20). That is, the consolation of this light will fail amid darknesses rushing in from every side: outward darkness on this side, inward darkness on that. But for you, in whom so many lamps burn within, when the lamp of this life is extinguished, the inextinguishable light of life shall rise; and at evening brightness like the noonday sun shall arise for you. When you think yourself consumed, you shall rise like the morning star, and your darkness shall be as noon (Job 11:17–18; Isa. 58:10) [Col. 0067C].

Yet you shall no longer have the sun to shine for you by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon give you light; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, because the Lamb is the lamp of the new Jerusalem—to whom be blessing and splendour for ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon II. With what affection Jesus is to be met when he comes

1. As that thanksgiving and voice of praise, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” belonged to the day of the Nativity, that is, of the Lord’s coming; and as the words that follow, “God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us,” belonged to the day of the Epiphany, that is, of our illumination; so too the subsequent words, “Appoint a solemn day in crowded assemblies [Vulgate: ‘in dense throngs’] even to the horn of the altar,” may not inappropriately, I think, be said to belong to this day, made famous to us by a solemn gathering: the day, namely, of the Lord’s Presentation, when he was solemnly presented by his Mother at the altar to the Father [Col. 0067D].

For in the words added, “Thou art my God, and I will confess thee; thou art my God, and I will exalt thee; I will confess thee, because thou hast heard me and become salvation to me” (Ps. 117:26–28), what could we understand more fittingly than the faith and confession of Simeon and Anna? She too, coming up at that very hour, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who awaited the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:38). Thus our harpist rightly urged Jerusalem to rejoice and assemble on so solemn a day: “Appoint,” he says, “a solemn day in crowded assemblies even to the horn of the altar” [Col. 0068A] (Ps. 117:27). That was no mean or lightly solemn gathering, when Jesus and Mary came from one side with the throng of parents bringing the child in order to do for him according to the custom of the Law (Luke 2:27); and Simeon and Anna came to meet them from the other with the crowd of those awaiting Israel’s consolation, to whom they bore testimony concerning him.

2. I could not believe that the prophet’s tearful complaint, “The ways of Zion mourn, because there is no one who comes to the solemn feast” (Lam. 1:4), applied to a feast having so devout and joyful a gathering—unless perhaps it accuses only a few from among the great people who were in all Judaea and Jerusalem of having come. For in comparison with so great a multitude, few came; and among those few, very few, I suppose, received him when they saw the long-awaited one present among them, as had been promised in the Father’s voice through Malachi: “Behold,” he says, “the Ruler whom you seek and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire shall come to his temple” [Col. 0068B] (Mal. 3:1).

O Jews, behold, the Ruler whom you seek is here [p. 948]: why do you not receive him when he offers himself to you? You seek and do not seek. But if you seek, seek: turn and come (Isa. 21:12). You seek one who will redeem you from the hand of human beings; you do not seek one who will redeem you from the hand of demons. You seek one who will rescue you from Roman servitude; you do not seek one who will rescue you from captivity to vices. If you truly seek a liberator, seek the liberator of your souls, who shall save his people from their sins [Col. 0068C]. If you seek one exalted, seek first one who is humble, because, as Daniel says, “God shall set the lowliest of men over every kingdom” (Dan. 4:14). If you seek a ruler of power, seek first a teacher of righteousness, because “his throne shall be established by righteousness” (Prov. 25:5), and “righteousness and judgment are the preparation of his throne” (Ps. 88:15).

Because you do not seek perfectly, therefore you do not find him even when present, as he himself foretold concerning you: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find me, because they hate me” (John 7:34–36). They will seek him absent, and will not find him even present, because they hate the light that rebukes their evil works; whereas wisdom can be sought, much less found, only through love. Simeon, indeed, because he sought with a devout and faithful desire, found what he sought; and he recognized what he found without another’s indication, that is, without human testimony [Col. 0068D]. For it is the Spirit who bears witness that Christ is truth (1 John 5:6): the power that proceeds from him, the anointing which teaches concerning all things and flows manifoldly from him—anointed in a unique manner according to his name.

3. But what, my brothers, do we think this Anointed One was like, he who anoints even those whom he does not touch? How did he anoint the bright and holy breast of our old man, when, receiving him in his arms, he clasped him to his breast and longed, if possible, to enclose him in the inmost place of his heart? What, I say, do we think that sweet and gentle one was like [Col. 0069A], as he gave himself to the most chaste bosom of the devout old man? How did he steal into his marrow—how delightful and health-giving, indeed how altogether ineffable, was the way he enfolded himself around his bones and breathed himself into his faculties?

Truly the Anointed One melted into an anointing, as though dissolved at the fire of the embracer’s love, in order that the anointing might teach what reading says but love alone learns. For how do you read? “Thy name,” it says, “is ointment poured out” [Vulgate: “poured forth”] (Song 1:2). This ointment is poured out when it is softened from a certain hardness of its own, not so that its substance flows entirely away, but so that its spices may flow forth, so that, as having nothing solid, it may be felt but not held.

Or rather, the old man’s soul melted in the embrace of this Anointed One, or ointment [Col. 0069B], so that it might say: “My soul melted when my beloved was poured into me.” Thus the infusion of the anointing is testimony to the Anointed One. It testified to the old man concerning the child, to Simeon concerning Christ, as the spirit of truth and charity: teaching by truth, anointing and enkindling by charity, and causing all the inward parts of the cold old man to become as when ointments boil.

The movement of boiling ointments is the heat of desires; their sound is the jubilation of affections saying together—if indeed they are capable of expressing anything—“Thou art my God, and I will confess thee; thou art my God, and I will exalt thee” (Isa. 25:1); proclaiming thee as “a light for the revelation of the nations and the glory of thy people Israel” (Luke 2:32). “I will confess thee,” I say, “because thou hast heard me,” daily saying with tears, “When wilt thou comfort me?” [Col. 0069C] (Ps. 118:82). Thou hast heard me, and now at last hast made me Simeon—that is, “heard”—because thou hast become salvation to me (Ps. 117:28).

Jesus, made for me from the seed of David according to the flesh, thou who according to thy divinity hast made David and all things: thou hast indeed become Saviour generally for all, but for me in particular thou hast become salvation, anointing my sickly breast and restoring its vital warmth, refreshing my soul and enlightening my eyes. For my soul had failed in longing for thy salvation, O Lord, Father of my Lord Jesus Christ; my eyes had failed in longing for thy word, saying, “When wilt thou comfort me?” (Ps. 118:82). I had become like a wineskin in frost: cold in body, dry in heart, languid in spirit, and wholly faint with desire [Col. 0069D]. But because I hoped exceedingly in the word of thy promise—that I should not see death unless I saw thy Christ—I now see what I hoped for, hold what I desired, embrace what I longed for. I see God my Saviour in my flesh, and my soul has been saved. My eyes have seen the salvation of God, and my inner [p. 949] eyes, which were languishing from want, have been enlightened.

At the touch of this child, this new human being, my youth has indeed been renewed like the eagle’s, just as I promised myself a little earlier while speaking. “I will go in to the altar of God,” where Mary offers Jesus to the Father, “to God who gladdens my old age”—or rather, who will renew my youth (Ps. 42:4).

4. Perhaps Anna’s heart also rejoiced in the Lord with no less joy [Col. 0070A]. In my judgment, she was of so much greater merit, as her purpose was loftier and her desire holier, than that Anna who was Samuel’s mother. For the latter thought of worldly things, how she might please her husband; this woman, how she might please God. The former sought offspring from her husband’s bed; this one asked for the Saviour from the Father’s bosom. Thus, by a certain foretokening of the outstanding grace that flourished in her life—and by which she deserved also to recognize and proclaim the Redeemer’s grace—she received the name Grace: an exemplar of true widowhood, a mirror of holiness, and a living image, in a body as good as dead, of every virtue.

Feeling the end of the Law and the beginning of the Gospel draw near, she had already begun to exchange Jewish rites for Christian godliness, serving rather in fastings and prayers night and day than in foods, drinks, diverse baptisms, and righteousnesses of the flesh rather than of the soul [Col. 0070B]. Therefore, scorning the blessing of children, which was highly valued in the Law, she had chosen “a better name than sons and daughters”; and for eighty-four years she had rejoiced to be a dry tree and to perch upon dry wood, like a turtledove once bereft of its mate.

5. Behold, you have a pair of turtledoves: a righteous old man and an aged widow, each chaste, each groaning with desire for the Redeemer. They undoubtedly offered themselves to the Lord and for the Lord as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God.” I call them a pair of turtledoves, certainly, not spouses but those joined together—not by the bond of marriage but by a holier mystery [Col. 0070C]: equal in faith, alike in chastity, similar in devotion, partners in the preaching of grace; both advanced in age, both perfected in holiness; who even before the Gospel dedicated in both sexes the first fruits of evangelical purity and godliness.

These two adorned your bridal chamber, O Zion, with the varied beauty of virtue, to receive Christ the King: not the walls of your Temple, but the inner sanctuary of their hearts, the secret place of their chamber, where we are commanded to worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:23), and where he is received who testifies that he does not dwell in things made by hands (Acts 7:48). In them, then, faithful Zion received Christ; in them she joyfully and gladly went out to meet her God. Elsewhere he scarcely has where to lay his head, and, according to Isaiah, “He has been perplexed, and there is no one to meet him” [Col. 0070D] (Isa. 69:16).

Yet the meeting offered by these persons is sufficient for every solemnity and joy, because a shortened consummation overflows in righteousness, and the perfected and abundant righteousness of a few easily compensates for the unbelief of many.

6. This gathering is altogether celebrated for me, this procession solemn, and festive with every joy: here come the Child and the woman who has borne a child, Jesus and Mary; there meet them the old man and the widow, Simeon and Anna; here are the Lord and the Lady, there the servant and the handmaid; here the Mediator and the Mediatrix, there their witnesses and ministers, so faithful and so devout. In this gathering mercy and truth have met one another: the mercy, namely, of redemption in Jesus, [Col. 0071A] the truth of confession in the aged pair. In this meeting righteousness and peace have kissed: while the righteousness of the devout elders and the peace of him reconciling the world have been joined together in a kiss of affection and the joy of the Spirit. Rightly, therefore, we believe that what we sang this night pertains to the gladness of this day—while preserving, of course, another and deeper meaning: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her” (Isa. 66:10). It is as though it were said: Nazareth rejoiced at the Annunciation, Bethlehem at the Nativity; you too, Jerusalem, rejoice at the Purification, because he who was conceived at Nazareth and born at Bethlehem has been received and proclaimed at Jerusalem. “Keep festival,” he says, or “assemble,” all you who love her—that is, Jerusalem: [Col. 0071B] Assemble in the Temple with festive devotion, to receive the Redeemer, all you who await the redemption of Israel.

7. But now, brothers, if your Holiness seeks, as is your custom, to be edified in a moral sense, let it consider those four illustrious persons in this procession, whose life not only illumines churches but also adorns heaven: I mean Jesus and Mary, Simeon and Anna. And, that the discourse may proceed from lower things to higher, in Anna, who served with fastings and supplications night and day, fasting and prayer are commended to us; in Simeon, who embraces Jesus with such great joy, piety and devotion; in Mary, who, although she owed nothing to the law in this matter of purification, nevertheless fulfilled the law, [Col. 0071C] humility and obedience; and in the Lord Jesus, who, “made of a woman,” was also “made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law,” charity and mercy.

For the holiness of chastity, whose praise, as I have learned, always delights your purity, shone forth in all alike, though very differently: in the elders it was the fruit of laborious continence; in the maiden, the gift of grace; in the Child, the right and property of nature—not of newly born childhood, but of inborn purity. In him is not only the origin and perfection of this virtue, but also of all virtues; from him comes the distribution of each; through him their preservation; with him their reward. Let us therefore seek from him, with the merits of the Virgin [Col. 0071D] Mary, Simeon, and Anna supporting our prayer, that he may bestow what virtue we lack and preserve what he has bestowed; so that, restoring his deposit to him intact under his own protection, we may obtain his reward—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. How Simeon Is to Be Imitated

1. An old man carried a Child: an old man full of days, a Child Ancient of Days. God had filled this old man with length of days, that he might show him his salvation in our countenance; but he was still to fill others with length of days, that he might show [Col. 0072A] them his salvation in his own countenance. Thus, full of temporal days, he carried the Ancient of ancient days, and held stored in his bosom the most sure pledge of eternal hope: that Child who would add his days to the days of the king and renew his youth like the eagle’s.

Yet, when this old man too, like Abraham, is called “full of days,” I would rather understand him as full of virtues than of years; for time has no fixed state, and, as it passes away by its own advance, it drains a person rather than fills him. Nor is it a great thing—indeed, it is rather an evil—to have lived many days if you have not grown old in virtues; since “the child a hundred years old shall die,” and “the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. 65:20). Therefore, “if a man live many years,” as Solomon says, “and rejoice in them all, he should remember the dark time and the many days which, when they come, will prove the past to have been vanity” (Eccl. 11:8).

On the contrary: “Venerable old age is not that which lasts long, nor that which is reckoned by the number of years. For the gray hairs of a person are understanding, and an unblemished life is old age” (Wis. 4:8–9). Unless Simeon had grown old in this old age, he would never have deserved to carry the crown of the aged, Christ the wisdom of God. For it is written: “Old age is a crown of dignity, found in the ways of righteousness” (Prov. 16:31). And what is that old age found in the ways of righteousness, suited as a crown for the one who finds it, except Christ, the wisdom of God? For he fittingly grants, as the reward of righteous works, the gray hairs of wise understanding, [Col. 0072C] which he will afterward fashion for the righteous into a crown of glory.

Thus holy old Simeon, that he might grow still holier in old age, found in the ways of righteousness—and truly recognized—the old age of the wise, or the wisdom of the aged made a Child, when he came into the Temple in the Spirit: for there was old age in the nursing Child, wisdom in the infant, strength in weakness, the Word in flesh. O childhood, O old age! How fittingly you are joined together in this Child’s understanding and character! Nothing is more innocent, yet nothing wiser; nothing more delightful, yet nothing more mature; nothing gentler, yet nothing more just.

2. To you, O children of men, the Word of God was already speaking by his very silence, that you might be children in malice but mature in understanding. [Col. 0072D] Some among you, like “a deceived dove without heart,” are left foolish, possessing simplicity without prudent discernment; others are wise in doing evil but do not know how to do good, and, failing to sweeten prudence with goodness, become harsh. This Child, the Ancient of Days, is a wholly fitting and pleasing tempering and seasoning for both: in childhood displaying innocence innate to himself, and from his antiquity of days bringing forth wisdom, first-born before all things.

If anyone understands himself to be imperfect in understanding or unformed in character, let him come into the Temple with Simeon and receive in his hands the Child whom Mother Mary brings—that is, let him embrace with affection the Word of God offered by Mother Church. [Col. 0073A] Stored in the bosom, he will build up the understanding, sweeten the character, and temper the whole condition of the mind and order of life with a welcome and health-giving sweetness.

Nor will Mother Church alone, in hearing, give you the Child to embrace; much more will Mother Grace give him in prayer, if only you come frequently and devoutly as a suppliant into the Temple, so that you may say daily to God: “I will worship toward your holy Temple in your fear” (Ps. 5:8). Whom the Church, preaching, offers to the ears, Grace, enlightening, brings into hearts—so much the more present and sweeter in that she entrusts naked truth to pure understanding. Mary gives Christ, who is Truth, clothed in flesh; the Church gives him clothed in speech; Grace gives him naked to be embraced through the infusion of the Spirit. Yet this itself occurs in different ways, [Col. 0073B] according to the capacity of the receiving soul or the decision of the mercy that dispenses.

For although we do not readily see the very face of supreme Truth, and he is accounted great to whom it is granted even to behold it “through a mirror, in an enigma,” still, when the Spirit enters us, we feel something of it as though naked, and our understanding is, as it were, rubbed into love of it in its nakedness. Then indeed we may rightly say and sing with joy: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your Temple” (Ps. 47:10). Blessed is the one who, that he may receive it more worthily and more frequently, prepares a fitting place for it in the innermost chambers of his heart. Blessed is that Zion which diligently and fittingly adorns its bridal chamber, that it may receive Christ the King with honor worthy of him and pleasing to him.

3. O holy Zion, soul contemplating eternal things, [Col. 0073C] consider what majesty is to be received; reflect with what care and diligence you ought to prepare a place for him. If anyone says, “And who is sufficient for these things? What adornment can be fitting for the magnificence and glory of so great a King?” David says that it is vain for anyone to plead poverty: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. 75:3); and, “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of his throne” (Ps. 88:15). Because Simeon adorned his bridal chamber with such coverings, he was therefore worthy to receive Christ with great grace.

Do you wish to see that he had found a place for the Lord in peace and had prepared a throne for him in righteousness and judgment? “There was,” it says, “a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; [Col. 0073D] and this man was righteous and God-fearing” (Luke 2:25). Simeon’s house was in peace, since he dwelt in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision and love of peace—of which Jerusalem David had heard the promise: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 124:1–2).

And, that you may know that he was a dweller in and lover of peace, and sought above all things the untroubled peace of that stable and eternal Jerusalem: when he received in his bosom Jesus, the peace of God and humankind, who came to give peace upon peace, this first utterance burst forth from the breast of the old man long meditating upon peace: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29). Since my eyes have seen your salvation—he who is our peace, making both one, not only [Col. 0074A] Jew and Gentile but also God and man, and within man spirit and flesh—this alone remains for your servant’s desires: “that in peace I may sleep and rest in one and the same” (Ps. 4:9), and that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may absorb my whole self into the harmony of that supreme and simple unity.

The peace for which I waited has come: let him who sought peace and always strove to pursue the things that belong to peace rest in peace. Thus Isaiah says: “Let peace come; let him rest in his bed, because he walked in his uprightness” (Isa. 57:2). Simeon had made his bed in peace, he who, having cast out every other care, meditated in his heart upon Jesus alone—the place where he also laid him when he had received him. He had likewise walked in his uprightness, for he was righteous and God-fearing, and awaited the consolation [Col. 0074B] of Israel, daily going out to meet with longing the one who was coming.

4. Therefore, in his being called righteous and God-fearing, understand righteousness and judgment, by which God’s throne is prepared. Righteousness is indeed shown by its own name; but judgment is rightly understood by the name of fear—or fear by the name of judgment—because fear is born not only from the consideration of future judgment, but even now produces in us a certain likeness and execution of that judgment. For though we are forbidden to judge our neighbors before the time (1 Cor. 4:5), we are commanded to judge ourselves, so that, while we judge ourselves, we may not be judged by the Lord (1 Cor. 11:31–32).

Moreover, this fear is holier when it follows righteousness than when it precedes it. When preceding, it initiates a person into righteousness; when following, it perfects and preserves that same righteousness. It does not permit one to presume upon righteousness, but makes one fear all one’s works, so that after judging oneself one may still be apprehensive of a more searching judgment, and say to oneself: “The Lord is he who judges me” (1 Cor. 4:4), who, when he receives the appointed time, will judge even acts of righteousness. Whoever is without this fear cannot be justified (Ecclus. 1:28), as Scripture testifies; because, however much he exercises himself in righteous works, others consume his strength while, wishing to establish his own righteousness, he is not subject to the righteousness of God.

5. Therefore, the Gospel, vigilantly commending the perfect righteousness of Simeon, does not say, “God-fearing and [Col. 0074D] righteous,” lest we should understand the fear which is the beginning of righteousness; rather, it says, “righteous and God-fearing,” so that from his example we may learn the fear that accompanies righteousness as its inseparable companion through every stage, advancing and protecting it. Nor do I think it without significance that it calls him not merely “fearing” (timentem), but “fear-imbued” (timoratum): the fear in question was not new, momentary, or perfunctory, but had become a settled disposition; it had deeply imbued the person’s affection, possessed his understanding, adorned his speech and countenance with modesty and gravity, moderated his actions by circumspection, and, in short, ordered the entire state of the inner and outer person.

For he who awaited the consolation of Israel did not relax his mind in empty consolations. And this too he had added to the fullness [Col. 0075A] of his righteousness: solicitous not only for his own consolation but also for that of the people, he remained suspended in long expectation.

6. Finally, that you may hear more plainly with what precious and genuine brightness of virtues that Zion—that is, Simeon—had adorned his bridal chamber, rather than with the cosmetic of colors: “The Holy Spirit,” it says, “was in him.” What could that earthly Zion compare with this adornment, amid all the manifold display and glory of its bridal chamber—that is, its Temple? If it had adorned the face of the Temple with golden crowns, what is gold but mud, even without comparison with virtue? I think that not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned as Simeon was: for Solomon lost in old age the wisdom in which he had flourished, whereas Simeon received it.

Yet your own bridal chamber reproaches you, O unbelieving Zion: although it had been sufficiently foretold to you, “Behold, the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his Temple” (Mal. 3:1), “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion; put on the garments of your glory, city of the Holy One” (Isa. 52:1), you nevertheless added absolutely nothing to the Temple’s daily service at his coming—no veils, no crowns, no additional lamps or sacrifices, no other psalms or songs. You send away without honor and without greeting him who had come to save you. Therefore this bridal chamber of yours, the house of your glory, will be left desolate to you; indeed, not one stone will be left upon another that shall not be destroyed.

But for you, Lord, faith of the nations will build a more august, spacious, and perfect Temple—the great Church from the rising of the sun to its setting; and “according to your name, O God, so also is your praise unto the ends of the earth” [Col. 0075C] (Ps. 47:11). Thus today too we heard praises: the glory of the righteous, namely the voices of those praising and saying, “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your Temple” (Ps. 47:11, 10), that is, in the communion of your holy people.

O brothers, you too have received God’s mercy—indeed, more abundantly. See that you have not received it in vain, lest by ingratitude you make grace empty. Let your devotion therefore rejoice: him whom Simeon today carried in his bosom, you glorify and carry every day in your bodies—Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Four Kinds of Our Purification

1. “When the days of Mary’s purification were fulfilled” (Luke 2:21). Scripture, recounting the mysteries of our redemption, narrates events historically accomplished for us in such a way as to signify what must morally be done by us. For when the Purification of blessed Mary is commemorated today, we are plainly reminded of our own purification. And whom would the authority of so great an example not move, when we see that she, holiest among holy women, who had nothing to be purified from, nevertheless did not refuse to fulfill the command of legal purification?

O immaculate Mother, untouched Mother, are you not conscious of your own purity—that neither conception nor childbirth violated your integrity, but consecrated it? Why, then, as though you had suffered something womanly in conceiving or giving birth, do you seek the remedies of cleansing provided for feminine weakness? “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15), so that I, chosen as Mother of supreme righteousness, may also be a mirror and model of all righteousness. I know the pride of Eve’s children, which is readier to excuse than to purge its offenses. I judge it necessary that, at the very beginning, all the examples of the new generation should counteract the vices of the old origin. The mother of transgression sinned and brazenly excused herself; let the mother of redemption not sin, but humbly make satisfaction, so that the children of men, who derive from the mother of oldness the necessity of sinning, may at least draw from the mother of newness humility in being purified.

2. O children of men, the time of purification has come, [Col. 0076B] when the Mother of supreme purity, whose purification is our feast day, both brought forth the fountain and gave us the example by which we ought to be purified. It is better, brothers, and sweeter to be cleansed by a fountain than by fire. Certainly, those who have not now been cleansed by the fountain must be cleansed by fire—if indeed they deserve to be cleansed—when the Judge himself, like a refiner’s fire, will sit refining and cleansing silver, and will purify the sons of Levi (Mal. 3:4–5). Now Christ washes with water; then fire consumes. Now the fountain is open for the washing of sinner and menstruous woman; then there is a raging flame and devouring fire, penetrating to the marrow of the soul.

For that purgatorial fire will blaze from the heat of the angry fountain before him, and will kindle round about his enemies. “Smoke,” it says, “went up in his wrath, and fire flamed forth from before his face” (Ps. 17:19). Then coals of penal purification will fall upon those who do not now apply the health-giving, desolating coals to themselves—the sort of coal, I think, which was taken from the altar and cleansed the prophet’s lips (Isa. 6:5–7). Or perhaps those coals may also be understood in this manner, of which someone is told: “Behold, coals have been given you, and you shall sit upon them; they shall be a help to you.” I leave this for you to judge.

But I assert without doubt that if the fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth (Luke 12:49) burns fiercely in us—as is the will of him who sends it—then that purgatorial fire which at judgment will purify the sons of Levi will find in us no wood, hay, [Col. 0076D] or stubble to consume. Both fires are purgatorial, but in very different ways. This one purifies by anointing; that one by burning. Here is the refreshment of dew; there, the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, by which the Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanse Jerusalem’s blood from her midst.

3. In this itself, indeed, there is much of the Lord’s mercy toward the daughters of Zion; but she whom the daughters of Zion call blessed was purified far more mercifully and gently: she to whom it was said, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” This overshadowing of heavenly power was Mary’s true purification, not that which is celebrated today only outwardly, under a certain mystical dispensation. [Col. 0077A] This certainly was the whole and true sanctification of Mother and Son, as the angel explained to her: “Therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

For mortal nature had to be purified before conceiving God, not after it had conceived him, since to conceive the Holy of Holies is supreme sanctification, and nothing can be holier than she who was made the Mother of holiness itself. Therefore, while the daughters of Zion who live more softly and dissipatedly, and perhaps experience the heat of the flesh, rightly need to be purified by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, the perpetual and singular Virgin, who alone conceived God by the overshadowing of the Spirit, was purified by the Spirit of grace alone and by the refreshment of dew.

Of all the purifications by which the mortal condition is restored, this purification of the blessed Virgin was the gentlest and happiest; for that purification of the daughters of Zion which will occur through the purgatorial fire of judgment will be, as it is the last, so also the most severe of all. Thus the one can be for us only an object of admiration, and the other only an object of dread: for we can aspire to neither the former, and, if we are wise, we always fear falling into the latter. If we are wise, we shall always cry out—more by amendment of life than by noise of words—“Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, neither chasten me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:2).

4. Therefore, between these two kinds of purification—the highest, which we do not attain, and the last, which we fear—divine mercy has necessarily and mercifully provided other kinds of purification for us, granting both time and place for repentance and many remedies for salvation. [Col. 0077C] Though these are many and varied, nearly all seem capable of being included under four kinds, lest we confuse the hearer’s memory by an unarranged multitude of matters.

These, then, I judge to be the four means by which we may fittingly and suitably be purified in these days of our purification: contrition of heart, affliction of body, works of mercy and faith, and patient endurance of tribulation. In this manner you will find four means by which Christ generally purifies the world, making purification for sins: water and blood, Spirit and fire. “This,” John says, “is he who came through water and blood. This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit [Col. 0077D] and fire” (1 John 5:6, 8).

He baptized with water and washed the disciples’ feet, consecrating also the baptism of tears that flow from contrition of heart. He shed blood, so that we too, through mortification of the body sharing in his Passion, may wash our garments in the blood of the Lamb. He gave the Spirit, so that the love of God and neighbor poured into our hearts through the Spirit may cover in us a multitude of sins. If this love is less perfect, so that it is not enough to cover sins so many and so great, that Refiner applies fire, who purifies the sons of Levi; and the fire bakes out whatever rust remains, whether by present or future tribulation, so that at last they may sing: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” [Col. 0078A] (Ps. 65:12).

Thus this world too, first baptized by the water of the Flood and afterward purified by the fire of judgment, will pass into a new state of incorruption.

5. Finally, to make some allowance for the tender and delicate: if they have no tears, recoil from hardships, and do not know how to bear tribulation, will they excuse even what Solomon commends, saying, “By mercy and faith sins are purified”? (Prov. 15:27; 16:6). What is sweeter than mercy? What more pleasant than faith? The one is oil for the limbs; the other light for the eyes. Mercy anoints the affections; faith illumines the understanding and directs the steps, so that by its light you may walk in darkness, contemplate invisible things, and meditate upon your future blessedness, already anticipated in the mind.

Sins are rightly said to be purified through mercy and faith: for mercy, bestowing from one’s own goods, redeems debts, while faith obtains forgiveness freely, even without works. Of mercy the prophet says: “Redeem your iniquities by mercies to the poor” (Dan. 4:24); and the Lord of the prophets: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Of faith the Apostle says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9); and the Lord of the Apostles: “Go; your faith has made you whole” (Mark 10:52).

Yet in this saying of Solomon, “faith” may be understood not as the faith by which we believe, but as that by which we show ourselves trustworthy, keeping faith with God and human beings. Thus what is said here, “Through mercy [Col. 0078C] and faith sins are purified” (Prov. 15:27), and a little later, “By mercy and truth iniquity is redeemed” (Prov. 16:6), may be the same thought repeated in different words. Mercy and truth—or faith—are therefore rightly joined, since unless mercy and truth meet one another in all our ways, we must fear that sins will be increased rather than purified.

For, to pass over other actions for the moment and speak of almsgiving to the poor, which the necessity of this season calls to be done more abundantly: what sin is committed even in those very acts through which sins should be purified, if mercy lacks faith or faith lacks mercy?

6. Let those therefore hear to whom stewardship has been entrusted; let those hear to whom it has not been entrusted: the former, lest they wish to be faithful in such a way as to abandon mercy; the latter, [Col. 0078D] lest they wish to be merciful in such a way as to injure faith. For some wish to be more faithful than they ought, and some wish to be more merciful than is permitted them. Those, therefore, who usurp undue mercy against faith, should hear Solomon saying: “Many people are called merciful, but who shall find a faithful man?” (Prov. 20:6). But those who, as though for the sake of faith, neglect the mercy they owe, should hear one greater than Solomon saying: “Give alms from what remains over” (Luke 11:41), so that at least your abundance may supply the need of others.

He showed great indulgence indeed to our weak and small faith in commanding not that common goods be divided equally among the brothers, but that alms be shared with them out of what remains after one’s own needs. For, without speaking of natural law, which assigns to all earth-born people in common whatever the earth, mother of all, produces: how can the use of bread administered by the heavenly Father not be common at least to those for whom the kinship of adoption is undifferentiated and the lot of inheritance common?

Grant, however, that this is the law of ordered charity: evangelical moderation has first made provision for each person’s needs. But who is there who rightly measures his own needs, who distinguishes with impartial judgment between what is necessary and what is superfluous? Let us attend to ourselves, brothers, lest we begin to be judged for the deaths of our poor brothers if we retain or spend superfluously upon ourselves that by which their life might be sustained.

And because today’s purification of the most pure and most poor Virgin has reminded us to speak of our purification, let us recognize that our purity consists above all in cutting away whatever is superfluous to us, so that, not only by the holiness of chastity but also by the simplicity of poverty, we may in some degree emulate the poor Mother of the poor Christ, whose are kingdom and dominion, now and through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V

> **[Note: Col. 0079D]** Horstius doubts whether this sermon is Guerric’s: both because it is absent from the Cologne manuscript containing his sermons, and because Guerric’s style appears more compressed and vigorous. Moreover, although it has hitherto been included among Bernard’s works, it is not worthy of so great an author.  
> **[Col. 0080D]**

### On Cleansing and Adorning the Soul for Christ

1. “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, and receive Christ the King, whom a virgin conceived, a virgin bore, and whom, after giving birth, the virgin who bore him adored.”

> **[Note: Col. 0080D]** Thus the Church sings in the Office for this day.

The Holy Spirit speaks to us, brothers—to us who are Zion, who are watchers, who lift our eyes day and night to the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us. Let us therefore adorn our bridal chamber and receive Christ the King. Behold, brothers, Christ comes into his own and is repulsed by his own; he has nowhere to lay his head. Before our doors, crying in his mother’s arms, he seeks lodging through the Holy Spirit, saying: “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion.”

Let us therefore cleanse our bridal chamber, first casting out those things which might offend Christ’s eyes as he enters; and then let us adorn it by bringing in those things in which he delights and rejoices. Perhaps one of you asks, What are the things that can offend Christ’s eyes? To him we say: Nothing so offends his eyes as pride, [Col. 0079D] which expelled the angel from heaven and the human being from paradise; which is the beginning of every sin; and which the Holy Spirit exhorts us to avoid, saying, “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9), and elsewhere, “All flesh is grass; the grass has withered and its flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:6–7; Ecclus. 14:18).

Let us see now what pride has done. It expelled the angel from heaven and the human being from paradise. Rightly does this offend Christ’s eyes, since it defiled his most beautiful work in heaven and in paradise; it made a devil of an angel and a faithless person of the newly created, righteous human being. As it is the first and greatest of sins, so it is the queen and mother of all vices.

2. We must therefore take care and diligently consider that our mind may exclude it with all its offspring, so that our bridal chamber, cleansed and adorned, may receive Christ the King who knocks outside [variant: “at the doors”]. With all its offspring, I say—the seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. These are the daughters of pride, following their mother; whatever lodging they enter, they make foul.

But what communion have we with these? What agreement has the Temple of God with idols? We have no association with them, thanks be to God: having put off the old human being with its deeds, we have put them to death with the sword of true [Col. 0080B] confession and repentance. Therefore pride, which made a devil of an archangel and an ungodly rebel against his Creator of the first human being, must have no further power in us. Let vainglory have nothing in us, since from the day of our conversion we began, with the Apostle, to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Let our glory therefore be the cross of Christ which we bear, and the testimony of a conscience cleansed through Christ’s cross, concerning which the Apostle says: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). To glory in this conscience is to give thanks to God for God’s gifts. The Apostle exhorts us to this, saying: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31; Jer. 9:24; 2 Cor. 10:17)—that is, let him glory in the Lord concerning the purity of his conscience. For “it is not he who commends himself,” and so forth.

But whoever glories in himself and pleases himself pleases a foolish person. Whoever glories in another human being, or in his heart awaits praise from another’s mouth, receives the reward of his works, anoints his own head with the oil of the sinner, and hears the prophet say to him: “Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man” (Jer. 17:6). And on the day of judgment, when they say, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” he says: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:11–12). This vainglory is a daughter of pride, and wherever it is found, it makes a person disobedient.

3. Again, after conversion, let envy have no further place in us, for through it death entered into the world. The devil envied the human being’s ascent to the place from which he had fallen; for this reason he tempted him and killed him in soul. This is that envy which always torments not great persons but little ones (Wis. 2:24–25), as holy Job says: “Envy kills the little one” (Job 5:2). For in envying another, a person shows himself inferior to the one he envies. Thus the devil envied the first human being; thus Esau envied Jacob, and Cain Abel.

Envy kills the little one, because unless he were inferior he would not grieve at another’s good. No one dies from this plague except the one who desires these earthly things, which cannot wholly come to several people. Thus, if someone desires any such thing, he envies the person who has received it altogether, or the person whose share diminishes its quantity for him. Envy kills this little person because, being unable to obtain what he envies in another, he falls into hatred, the daughter of envy.

4. Again, brothers, after our conversion let anger have no place in us, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel, it leads by stages to the pit of Gehenna: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says, ‘Raca’”—that is, utters a voice of indignation in anger—“shall be liable to the council,” where the penalty to be imposed is considered. “Whoever says, ‘Fool,’”—that is, does something either by word or blow [Col. 0081B] that causes him to be despised among the brothers—“shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22), unless he comes to his senses.

This is the anger that extinguishes the eyes of fools and sometimes disturbs the eyes of the wise, as the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). And of the anger of the fool Job says: “Anger kills the foolish man” (Job 5:2). Behold, we see two kinds of anger: one sometimes disturbs the eye; the other always extinguishes it. One comes from impatience; the other from zeal for righteousness. One comes from vice; the other from virtue.

Of the anger that comes from virtue the Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5; Eph. 4:26). As though he said: Be severe toward vice, gentle toward your brother, considering yourselves lest you too be tempted. Of the anger that comes from vice the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26); that is, let Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, not abandon your mind when it is angry, for he never dwells with anger.

We ought first to be angry, with the anger that comes from zeal for righteousness, at our own faults, and afterward at the faults of our neighbors. This anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of countenance a neighbor is corrected (Eccl. 7:4). Yet it must be subject to reason, so that it may not be excessive, but may consider the time and measure in punishing sin. This anger sometimes disturbs the wise; anger arising from vice kills fools, while it lets the tongue loose into quarrels and abuse.

5. Again, brothers, after our conversion the bridal chamber of our heart must be fortified, lest sorrow return and enter in—I mean that sorrow which works death, [Col. 0081D] which comes from the loss of temporal things. This is the sorrow that begets perverse thoughts, makes a monk murmuring, produces weariness, and compels one holding God’s plough to look back with Lot’s wife. For one cannot lose without pain what one possessed with disordered love. Let us therefore exclude this sorrow which works death, and admit that which comes from the remembrance of sins and from our pilgrimage; and let us say with the Psalmist: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!
