I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5–6). This is the sorrow that works life, of which the Apostle says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” [Col. 0082A] (2 Cor. 6:10). This is that of which the Lord says to the disciples: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). The other begets death; it begets bitterness of spirit.

6. Again, brothers, after conversion let us fortify our bridal chamber, lest avarice, which is the root of all evils, return and enter in, draw us away from the worship of the one God, and make us worshippers of idols. Of it the Apostle says among other things to his disciples: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5). See how he compares avarice to idolatry, and rightly so: for just as the idolater strives to take glory away from the one God, lest he alone possess [Col. 0082B] the name of deity, so the avaricious person stretches himself out over God’s possessions, in order to usurp alone what almighty God made for the use of many. Both are enemies of God, because each denies God what is his.

And avarice is not only love for acquiring or retaining money, but also ambition for preeminence, when one person strives to rule another. This, to speak the truth, so troubles even the poor—who once for Christ’s sake left their possessions—that contrary to right, law, and their own profession, they not only wish but even labour to rule over their brothers and fellow-servants. If their abbot or prior does not consent to their desire, they grow angry, speak against them, and call them either envious or ill-disposed toward themselves, because they do not advance them. This is the avarice which disturbs the remembrance of God’s commandments, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: [Col. 0082C] “Incline my heart unto thy testimonies, and not unto avarice” (Ps. 118:36). It is the mother of betrayal: it first led Judas, God’s disciple, to forgetfulness of God’s commandments; from forgetfulness to betrayal; and from betrayal to the noose.

7. Again, brothers, after our conversion let us fortify the bridal chamber of the heart, lest gluttony return and enter in—the vice which deprived Adam of the garment of innocence and Esau of the dignity of the firstborn. This is the pestilence which made our fathers in the desert ungrateful for God’s benefits, which compelled them to murmur against God and say: “Would that we had died in Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate garlic, onions, and melons” (Exod. 16:3; Num. 11:5–6; 14:3). This is the deadly pestilence which led them to blasphemy, [Col. 0082D] as though there were no life after this one, when they said: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (Isa. 22:13; 1 Cor. 15:32)—that is, in the life to come. They seemed to say: “We have only what we eat; after this life we hope to possess nothing in the future.”

The Apostle declares that this pestilence will perish with the human being, saying: “Food for the belly and the belly for food; but God shall destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13). This plague is threefold: it causes one to eat either before the canonical hour, or what is not permitted, or more than is necessary; and it strives to make provision for the flesh in its desires. From it arises foolish merriment, as is said of the people of Israel: “The people sat down to eat and drink, [Col. 0083A] and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6; 1 Cor. 10:7).

8. Again, brothers, after our conversion let us fortify the bridal chamber of our heart, lest luxury return and find entrance. This returning pestilence is worse than it was before. For it never returns alone; rather, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “It takes with it seven spirits more wicked than itself, and, having entered, they dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12:45). This is the pestilence which dismembers Christ’s body, which makes members of the devil out of Christ’s members. For whoever clings to some person in order to satisfy lust becomes one body with that person and becomes a member of the devil, of whom that person too is a member through the union of evil deeds.

This is the pestilence that kindles hell-fire in the human body, [Col. 0083B] so that it may be vigorous and strong for fulfilling lust; and which continually supplies fuel and strength to that inextinguishable fire, so that it may always have from its own substance the means to burn without end. Scripture gives us authority concerning these two fires, of luxury and of Gehenna. Concerning the fire of luxury it says: “All adulterers are like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. 7:4). Concerning the fire of Gehenna it says: “You shall make them like a fiery furnace in the time of your countenance”—that is, of judgment—so that they may burn inwardly, like an ignited furnace, in their conscience. “The Lord in his wrath shall trouble them” (Ps. 20:10), saying: “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27; Ps. 6:9; Matt. 7:23). And the final infernal fire will devour them, a fire which they kindled by the foul works of luxury. Let there therefore be, brothers, [Col. 0083C] the utmost care and the utmost effort among those who are in such things to escape and flee from them.

9. But we who, by God’s grace, have escaped and put off the old man, who are Zion, must make it our chief concern to fortify and adorn our bridal chamber and receive Christ the king, as the Scripture we have recited commands: “Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion.” What is it to adorn your bridal chamber? To gather virtues, by which the whole house may be adorned—its pavement and walls, as it were, with hangings and flowers.

Let the first adornment of our bridal chamber, we who are Zion, be fear, which is the beginning of wisdom—that is, the first step by which one ascends to wisdom. Of this fear Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” [Col. 0083D] (Prov. 28:14). And the Psalmist says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11), so that fear may remove harmful self-assurance and rejoicing deadly sorrow. This fear produces humility, the most precious adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber, which especially pleased Christ when he entered the virginal bridal chamber, as blessed Mary said: “For he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). This humility, I say, is the adornment of Zion—that is, of Christ’s poor—of whom he himself says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20). See how the fear of the Lord, the first step of ascent and the first adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber, produces other [Col. 0084A] adornments also: namely humility and voluntary poverty. Therefore adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, with the fear of the Lord.

10. The second adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber, and the second step toward wisdom, is godliness, of which Scripture says: “Have mercy on your own soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24); and elsewhere: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. 66:2). It has mercy on those who sin against it, bears the burdens of brethren, and chooses rather to lose any temporal goods than to contend with a brother in litigation. This godliness is certainly nothing other than worshipping God and pleasing God through God’s worship.

It produces in us gentleness, the excellent adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber, which makes us children of God, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for [Col. 0084B] they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:4; Ps. 36:11). See how godliness, the second adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber and second step of ascent, produces from itself another adornment: gentleness, which makes people children of God. Therefore adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, with godliness.

11. The third adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber, and the third step of ascent, is knowledge, which gives a person self-knowledge, so that one may think neither less nor more highly of oneself than one ought. The former—thinking too highly of oneself—makes one rush headlong into evils; the latter—not knowing oneself—makes one sluggish in every good thing. The Holy Spirit invites the Church to this knowledge in the Song of Songs: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go after the tracks of your flocks,” namely, of the heretics, “and feed your kids” (Song 1:7), that is, [Col. 0084C] carnal desires.

This knowledge gives us confidence to overcome all temptations through true faith, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:22), namely through God’s grace and free choice. We see now how knowledge, the third adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber and third step of ascent, produces in us another adornment: devout mourning, which deserves consolation from the Lord in the future. This knowledge prepares in us the sorrow and mourning of pilgrimage, so that, seeing the evils of exile which we suffer, we may mournfully desire the homeland from which we are exiled, and hear the Lord say to us: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:6; Isa. 61:2).

[Col. 0084D] 12. The fourth adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber is fortitude, fitting for those who labour to acquire true goods. This is what fortifies Zion’s bridal chamber, so that it is not lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity; it confounds the reproving and flattering tongue with these words: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119:2). This is what, becoming stronger day by day, kindles in Zion’s bridal chamber hunger and thirst for righteousness, and causes it to hear from the Lord: “Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” Therefore adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, with fortitude.

The fifth adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber is counsel, by which a person examines one’s own weaknesses, investigates one’s capacity and incapacity; and, from one’s own weakness, [Col. 0085A] considers others, spares and pities them, just as one wishes God to pity oneself; forgives others their debts, just as one wishes God to forgive oneself; and deserves to hear from the Lord: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:4, 7). Therefore adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, with counsel.

The sixth adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber is understanding. It carries the human mind above these frail things and, passing beyond all bodily substances by intellectual contemplation, is not fixed upon bodily substances; and, wishing to proceed further and draw nearer, it hears from the Lord: “Do not come near here” (Exod. 3:5); for “no man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). This understanding belongs to those whose eye has been purified by God, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5: [Col. 0085B] 8). Therefore adorn your bridal chamber, Zion, with understanding.

13. The seventh adornment of Zion’s bridal chamber is wisdom, fitting for those who contemplate eternal things with the eyes of understanding, whose citizenship is in heaven, who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. In their person the Apostle said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” As though he said: “In order that I may magnify Christ, I wish to live only for Christ; and Christ is the reward of death.” And shortly afterward: “But I am constrained by the two, having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is far better; yet to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:21, 23–24).

See what true wisdom does: it so subdues all rebellious movements of the body that one feels no further conflict in the flesh; for weak brethren’s sake, in order to announce Christ to them, it willingly endures exile; it does not heed reproaches, does not feel losses, lets go the cloak to one taking its tunic, offers the other cheek to one striking the first, and hears from the Lord: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). These are the adornments of Zion’s bridal chamber. Let us who are Zion adorn ourselves with them, and receive Christ the king, whom a Virgin conceived, a Virgin bore, and a Virgin, forty days after giving birth—that is, on this present day—presented in God’s temple.

14. For it was written in the Law that a woman who, having received seed, bore a male child should, once purified, enter the temple with her son on the fortieth day, bringing with her offerings for sin: an unblemished lamb of a year old. But if she did not have a lamb, she was to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons (Lev. 12:2, 4, 6, 8). Blessed Mary fulfilled all this, not from necessity but from humility. She abstained from entering the temple for forty days, though she did not need purification, since she conceived of the Holy Spirit without any sensual pleasure, the seal of virginity remaining intact. She offered a sacrifice, not for sin as other women did, but for humility, showing in this also that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, had not come to dissolve the Law but to fulfil it.

And behold Simeon, an aged man who had received the answer that he would not see death unless he saw the Christ of the Lord, and received him whom he awaited. He took him into his arms—that is, he embraced him between [Col. 0086A] his arms. He carries between his arms him who weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers, who fills all things and embraces all things, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace. I desire to be dissolved and to await with the patriarchs and prophets in hell his coming who will make peace between you and the human race. For my eyes have seen your salvation—your Son, whom I desired, concerning whom I received an answer from the Holy Spirit—a light for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29–30, 32). Of him Isaiah says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa. 9:2), because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

[Col. 0086B] 15. Hear, brothers, hear what Mary offers and what Simeon receives: God’s Only-Begotten, consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father, the Word in the beginning. And, that we may hear of our own benefit and consolation: the Virgin offers him whom God promised to Abraham, saying: “In your seed,” that is, in Christ, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18; 12:3; 18:18); and whom he promised to David, saying: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). This is he whom the Virgin offers: the joy of the patriarchs, the desire of the prophets, the expectation of the Gentiles, the salvation of the Jews who received him, the restoration of the fallen angels. Such is he whom the Virgin offers to God—indeed, far greater than any human or angelic tongue can express.

And though he is so great and such as he knows himself to be, it does not suffice the Virgin to offer him alone; she also offered for him the sacrifice prescribed by the Law, namely as an example of humility, to teach us how we too ought to offer him. She offered for him two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Brothers, the dove is a simple animal: it lacks gall, does not wound with its beak, nests in the clefts of rocks, feeds other birds’ young, remains beside streams so that it may flee at the sight of a hawk’s shadow, chooses better grains, gives forth a groan instead of song, flies in flocks, defends itself with its wings, and recovers its sight.

And we, brothers, when we stand before the altar to offer the Son of God to God, should offer with him and for him a pair of turtledoves: chastity of body and soul; [Col. 0086D] and two young pigeons: groaning instead of singing, with a twofold compunction—through longing for the heavenly homeland and through consideration of our misery. The dove lacks gall: let us too lack anger, which makes us sin. Let us not wound with our beak; but, when struck on one cheek, let us offer the other. Let us nest in the clefts of rocks: let us take refuge in faith in Christ’s wounds. Let us feed other birds’ young: by the word of preaching, making children of God out of the devil’s children. Let us remain beside streams: that is, as we sit beside this flow of mortality, considering the shadow of the hawk—that is, sins, which are the devil’s shadow—and the downfall of evils, let us flee its talons. Let us choose better grains: that is, better interpretations in the holy Scriptures. Let us fly in flocks: [Col. 0087A] holding a single agreement in goodness within the congregation under a shepherd. Let us defend ourselves against God’s enemies with the wings of the New and Old Testaments, or with the two commandments of love, namely love of God and of neighbour. Let us recover our sight, ever directing ourselves from the good of action toward the good of contemplation.

16. Dearest brothers, such ought we to be when we consecrate Christ’s body, when we sacrifice while consuming that which has been consecrated, when we offer you that same body for the salvation of body and soul. Such also ought you to be when you receive the sacred sacrament from our hands, knowing that whoever receives Christ’s body unworthily and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon oneself (1 Cor. 11:29).

But since one rarely finds a person who possesses all these things in oneself, let one love the person who possesses the good that one does not possess oneself, [Col. 0087B] and possess in that person what one does not see in oneself.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] It is a matter of faith that the priest alone is the proper and sufficient minister for consecrating the Eucharist, as is evident from canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea. There the Fathers, while reproving deacons because in certain places they administer the Eucharist to presbyters, and forbidding this to be done thereafter, give the following reason for their decree: “For neither rule nor custom has handed down that those who do not have the power to offer sacrifice should distribute Christ’s body to those who offer it.” The Lateran Council under Innocent III likewise decreed this, and it is reported in the chapter *Firmiter*, *Extra*, “On the Supreme Trinity.” For, after explaining the truth of the sacrament, it adds: “And certainly no one can perform this sacrament except a priest who has been duly ordained according to the keys of the Church which Jesus Christ granted to the apostles and their successors.” Isambert says nearly the same in 3, question 82, article 1. Nevertheless, it may be said that those standing by also offer and perform the sacrifice in their own way, through the priest and with the priest, who is the mediator and minister of the people. Hence the canon of the Mass formerly read: “And of all those standing around, who offer to you this sacrifice of praise”; to these words there were added: “For whom we offer it to you,” or “who offer it to you,” etc.]

For the carpenter alone does not make a house: one man brings twigs, another timber, another beams, and so forth. Those standing by ought therefore to have something of their own, as does the priest: firm faith, pure prayer, devout devotion. And it must be known that none of those standing by ought to be without firm faith. As for the other virtues mentioned above, even if all do not possess them, let them love the person who has what they do not find in themselves, and possess in that person what [Col. 0087C] they do not yet see in themselves. As Peter possesses in John the merit of virginity, so John possesses in Peter the reward of martyrdom.

17. It must also be known that we owe three things to Christ’s body, which Mary presented today in the temple and Simeon received in his arms: dignity, reverence, and fruit. Dignity: that we believe him to be the Son of God, God from God, almighty, creator of all things, judge of the living and the dead. Dignity: that we believe that immediately after we depart from the body, we shall receive from him, as from a judge, according as we have acted, whether good or evil.

For he whom Mary presented in the temple, whom Simeon received, whom we, consecrating him in our hands, lift up before [Col. 0087D] God, bless, eat, and offer to you to be eaten—he, our intimate companion, will be our judge. Let us therefore beware of being separated from him by judgment after death, when in life we are so intimate with him. Let us therefore say to him in our heart as we handle him; [Col. 0088A] let us say as we consecrate him: “Lord, after death we shall come to you; we shall stand before your tribunal to be judged. You deign to be so intimate with us in life that you are handled, consecrated, and eaten by us. Do not be a stranger to us in death, but spare us on the evil day. Let the demons who will then pursue us be confounded; destroy their strength by your power, for there is none to fight for us except you, our God and intimate companion.” This is the dignity which we owe him.

18. We also owe him reverence: namely, to examine ourselves, and, if we find our heart polluted by foul thoughts or an evil will, to keep both ourselves and others away from touching him, as from fire. For he is a consuming fire (Deut. 4:24), to whom the unworthy ought not approach, lest one be consumed inwardly and handed over to a reprobate mind. Therefore let the person polluted by nocturnal emission go outside the camp, as Moses commanded (Deut. 23:10): that is, the person who through negligence in this dark life—which wholly passes like sleep—has proceeded as far as polluted thoughts. Let such a person go outside the camp: that is, while in that condition, let one judge oneself unworthy of the fellowship of the faithful who communicate in this sacred body; let one wash one’s garments through holy confession; and after sunset—that is, once the heat and burning of temptation have died—let one return joyfully and communicate with the other faithful. This is the reverence we owe to Christ’s body, which the Virgin Mary presented in the temple on this present day, and which Simeon joyfully received in his arms.

[Col. 0088C] 19. We must also know the fruit: that is, understand what fruit we receive if we eat him worthily. Hear, brothers, not me but the Apostle saying: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion in Christ’s blood?” The cup—that is, communion in the cup—makes us have a certain communion with Christ. “And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the Lord’s body?” (1 Cor. 10:16). As if he said: The bread which we break makes us one body under Christ the head. For just as one bread is made from many grains and afterwards is converted into Christ’s body both through faith and through the holy words which Christ taught his own, so the diverse persons [Col. 0088D] who partake of this body, in the unity of faith, hope, and charity, are one body with Christ: they will come to Christ immediately after death, and reign with Christ, as with their head, without end. Him the Virgin conceived, the Virgin bore, and the Virgin presented in the temple on this present [Col. 0089A] day; he lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

962

# SERMON VI. On completing our purification, so that we may be presented to the Lord

1. “After the days of their purification were fulfilled, they took Jesus to Jerusalem.” O how happy is the person of whom it can be said: “The days of his purification were fulfilled,” so that nothing now remains for him except that they carry him into the heavenly Jerusalem and present him to the Lord (Luke 2:22). Such, surely, was that Simeon, our old man, as full of desires as he was desirable. Since, as I think, the days of his purification had long ago been fulfilled, today the days of his expectation also were fulfilled, [Col. 0089B] so that according to the Lord’s word, after he had seen the Christ of the Lord—the Christ, peace between God and humankind—nothing remained for him except to be dismissed in peace and sleep in the selfsame peace: that is, to be carried into the Jerusalem of eternal peace and presented for contemplation of the peace which surpasses all understanding.

O Simeon, man of desires, your desire has been fulfilled with good things. O blessed old man, your youth has been renewed like the eagle’s. You have now entered the heavenly, eternal, wholly golden altar of God, who makes your youth glad by the eternal vision of himself, even as he made your old age glad today by the vision of his Christ. You yourself have now been presented to the Father at that invisible altar, to whose visible altar you presented the Son today. There you embrace in an eternal and indissoluble embrace that very Son whom today you bore [Col. 0089C] in your bosom.

2. Thus the blessed old man’s desire has been fulfilled with good things: his whole expectation and desire was the Expectation of the Gentiles and their Desired One. His youth has been renewed like the eagle’s, because in a good old age the days of his purification were fulfilled. Otherwise, he could not have been capable of that newness unless during those days he had diligently purged away oldness.

Brothers, purge out the old leaven while you have time to purge it, so that, when the days of your purification have been fulfilled, you too may be found capable of that joy with which Simeon’s soul is now full. Indeed, whether we will or not, we fulfil the days given us for purification. But woe to us if the days are fulfilled and the purification is not fulfilled, so that afterwards we must be repurified by that fire than which nothing more painful, sharper, or more violent can be imagined in this life.

But who is so perfect, so holy, that when one departs hence one owes nothing to that fire? Who has burned away in oneself every dross of sin so completely that one can boast of having a chaste heart and say: “My heart is clean; I am pure from sin” (Prov. 20:9)? The elect indeed are few; but among those few, very few, I think, are so perfect that they have completed that purification of which the Wise Man says: “Cleanse yourself from negligence with the few” (Ecclus. 7:34). Certainly, if we cleansed ourselves from negligence, we would be among the few. But now, because we neglect not only the least things but even the greatest, we are far removed from the few on earth; and of us speaks he who prefers the small number of saints to the multitude of the negligent: “Among many I was” (Ps. 54:19).

3. And what today is at once so characteristic and so common among those whom the shadow of religious life shelters as negligence? To speak of myself: how often do my enemies mock my Sabbaths? How often does my soul doze through weariness, and I spend nearly the whole day in idleness, as if time could be recalled? And would that my soul so slept that, with eyes open and watchful, I miserable man did not fabricate vain and illusory dreams for myself! But now the saying has been perversely reversed: I am awake, [Col. 0090B] and my heart sleeps—indeed, with a sleep so heavy that it can scarcely ever awaken even at the thunder of that heavenly rebuke: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep; and poverty shall come upon you like a traveller, and want like an armed man” (Prov. 6:8–11; 24:33–34).

Surely the most wretched thing is that today it is judged not a loss but a gain if the days given us for purification slip away in sleep, pass and perish through negligence. A Gentile, they say, when he sat down at table and remembered that he had done nothing vigorous or memorable that day, pushed the table away with deep groaning and sorrow, crying: “O friends, I have lost a day!”

[Note: [Col. 0089] The emperor Titus, in Suetonius. Seneca complains in almost the same words, *Letters*, 1.]

Yet today we seem to say, “I have gained a day,” [Col. 0090C] if it can slip entirely away in idleness without work. Thus there is scarcely anyone who sets a value upon time, who considers privately how much one day is worth for obtaining eternity. Do you suppose there is anyone among us who demands from oneself a daily accounting of one’s days, who carefully records for oneself the losses or gains of each day, so that, if one discovers that one acted negligently today, one may punish oneself and act more cautiously thereafter? Blessed is that servant whom, when the last day comes, it finds doing so.

4. This indeed would be to cleanse oneself from negligence with the few: if the days of purification were rightly and profitably fulfilled, so that access to the holy things might at last be healthfully obtained. Otherwise, as long as anyone remains in the blood of one’s purification, eternal justice has decreed—as is written in the Law of Moses—that one should touch no holy thing and not enter the sanctuary until the days of purification are fulfilled (Lev. 12:4). Let those therefore see with what face they enter the sanctuary, with what conscience they not only touch holy things but even handle and receive the Holy of Holies, when they have not yet been freed from bloods yet undertake no effort at all toward their purification.

Do they not hear him protesting and saying: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn away my eyes; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15)? For what if I am clean from another’s blood, yet the Lord sees me trampled in my own blood [Col. 0091A] (Ezek. 16:6), as he speaks of Jerusalem through Ezekiel? What benefit, I say, is it to me if my feet are not swift to shed my neighbours’ blood, while my affections are swift to yield to flesh and blood, of which the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50)? “Cursed,” says Jeremiah, “is he who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10): that is, who spares himself the cutting off of the vices of flesh and blood. “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50:16), lest, entering the sanctuary or touching holy things while in the blood of my purification, I be found guilty of your body and blood by eating and drinking unworthily.

Yet thanks be to you, God, God of my salvation, who poured out your precious blood precisely in order to purify the uncleanness of our blood, and did not shrink from the touch of the woman with the issue of blood, who nevertheless desired healing. For you knew that no one except you, who alone are such, can make clean that which was conceived from unclean seed; and that a physician is needed not by the healthy, but by the sick—yet by those who desire to be better. Therefore, to touch the Holy of Holies is, for those who delight to remain in their own blood, a judgment of death; but for those who desire to be purified, it is a remedy of salvation, according to Simeon’s prophecy: “For this one is set for the fall and rising again of many” (Luke 2:34).

5. Brothers, you too were in blood, but you have been washed and purified. Yet, as the righteous man confesses: “Though you wash me as with snow-water, you immediately plunge me into filth” (Job 9:30–31). Not only is our condition corrupt, but our will also is weak, so that new purification is always needed for fresh filth. Yet wondrous and pitiable is this negligence of people concerning themselves: although no one may presume not to need purification, scarcely anyone fails to neglect the time granted for this, as though already most thoroughly purified.

Brothers, human days are short (ibid., 25), yet exceedingly precious; indeed, the shorter they are, the more precious, because they are days of purification, while immediately afterward will come days of recompense. Blessed are those who in these days wash their robes [Col. 0091D] and make them white in the Lamb’s blood, lest afterward their garment, if stained with blood, become fuel for burning and food for fire (Isa. 9:5). Not only fear of punishment presses us, but hope of reward also invites us to devote ourselves with every care and earnestness to purification, so that what the Son of God wished today to prefigure in himself under a certain dispensation may someday be fulfilled in us in the very reality of things.

What is that? “After,” it says, “the days of their purification were fulfilled, they took Jesus to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord” (Luke 2:23). And we too, if the times [Col. 0092A] of purification have been lawfully fulfilled by us, will be carried by the ministrations of angels into the heavenly Jerusalem, so that, standing there before God’s face, we may be his acceptable and unblemished offering. There at last we shall be wholly purified, from sin as well as from the punishment of sin. There will be the consummation—and the reward—of our purification, when the divine fire consumes us entirely as a burnt offering to the Lord.

6. Moreover, the devotion of the saints does not even now cease to emulate this same ineffable manner of most blessed purification, so far as the corruption of their bodies and the concern of earthly dwelling permit. That is: transported in mind into that Jerusalem, the true place of prayer, there in the Lord’s presence they offer, as it were, a turtledove and a dove for and from themselves; their heart and flesh exulting in the living God, because “the dove has found herself a home, and the turtledove a nest,” namely, “your altars, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. 83:4).

Yet I judge that it is no less meritorious, and perhaps more effective for purification, if we continually practise through faith that which is granted rarely, and to few, to experience “through a mirror and in an enigma”: namely, to be presented to the Lord in Jerusalem. Let us set the Lord always before our eyes, continually considering, with wakeful faith and unrelenting fear, his eyes and his judgments over us. Let this faith, brethren, be in you, and you will belong to the few; let this fear be in you, and with the few you will cleanse yourselves of negligence, for this fear readily overlooks nothing.

At last, from this beginning you will pass onward, as the Bridegroom promises the bride, “from strength to strength,” “from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18): advancing from the vision that is through faith to that which is through mirror and image; and finally, from that which is in the image of likeness to that which will be in the very truth of the face, or the face of truth. For if you steadily attend through faith to the Lord’s presence, though veiled, then one day you will also behold his glory with unveiled face, though by mirror and image. But when, the days of purification being fulfilled, that which is perfect comes, you will stand before the Lord in Jerusalem, dwelling with his countenance and beholding him without end, face to face—to whom be blessing and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## IN LENT

[Col. 0091]

## SERMON I. On tribulation and consolation

[Col. 0091D]

1. “Blessed be God, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation” [Col. 0092D] (2 Cor. 1:3–4). “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from them all the Lord will deliver them” (Ps. 33:20).

Now we suffer a twofold kind of tribulation, because we subsist not only in a twofold nature, flesh and spirit, but also live with a twofold quality: partly carnally and partly spiritually. In the world we were wholly carnal; in heaven we shall be wholly spiritual; but now we are partly carnal and partly spiritual. Insofar as we advance in the spirit, we either become more spiritual and less carnal, or remain more carnal and less spiritual. Thus a twofold tribulation now arises: for what is carnal in us is grieved by adversity, while what is spiritual is grieved by iniquity. If nothing in us were carnal, no adversity would grieve us—indeed, there would be no adversity. If nothing were spiritual, our iniquity would not grieve us but rather delight us, as it is said of some: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” [Col. 0093B] (Prov. 2:14).

Therefore our grief over adversity is carnal and according to the world; but this grief over iniquity is spiritual and according to God. The former works death if consolation is lacking; the latter works salvation if consolation is not lacking. Yet in outward adversity it matters greatly what kind of consolation the sorrowful receive, since the divine threat directs an eternal “woe” against the consolation of the rich (Luke 6:24). For often those who might have been humbled by adversity become more gravely proud through prosperity, and “their iniquity proceeds from fatness”; indeed, they boldly provoke God when he himself has given all things into their hands.

2. But when that temporal consolation abounds, we ought to be more grateful and more humble; and when it fails, more certain and more joyful concerning eternal redemption. Yet when bodily health, tranquillity of the times, or abundance of possessions is available, it must be used and administered with such moderation that it may be not an occasion for sin but an aid to virtue, and that we may make good use of good things rather than become evil through good things.

Let my soul refuse to be consoled by that consolation through which pleasure spreads itself abroad or vanity exalts itself (Heb. 12:5); and let it rather choose, with Moses and the men of Israel, to suffer affliction than to enjoy the pleasure of temporal sin. But whether we are consoled outwardly or afflicted, blessed be God, who has given inward and eternal consolation in our hearts: that is, the joy of hope, which persuades us [Col. 0093D] even to glory in our tribulations, promising that “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12).

Indeed, we bear that tribulation which we suffer inwardly from our iniquity all the more painfully because we experience it as more dangerous. For we are daily in peril of life, so that we may truthfully confess: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, because, though the dangers are grave, the remedies are easy; because, “if I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, O Lord, was helping me” (Ps. 93:17–18). And what you once portrayed bodily in Peter (Matt. 14:29–31), you daily fulfil spiritually in Peter’s children.

You commanded us to come to you upon the waters—that is, upon this great sea, broad in its expanse [Col. 0094A]. Behold, by your power we walk, but by our own weight we are burdened; and often, when the spirit of storms rushes upon us, we are driven so that we even begin to sink—that is, we are almost, at any moment, consenting to the tempter. But if we quickly confess that our foot has moved—that our mind has wavered—and faithfully call upon help, you mercifully stretch out your hand and make our step firm and straight.

3. Concerning this the righteous man sings daily: “I was driven that I might fall, but I did not fall, because the Lord upheld me” (Ps. 117:13). “But when he falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord puts his hand beneath him” (Ps. 36:24): that is, when he sins, he shall not be condemned, because he has Jesus as his advocate; for although he falls seven times a day, seven times he rises. He does not delight to lie where he falls and wallow in mud; rather, rising swiftly, he shakes himself free from the dust and washes away his filth by satisfaction.

For by this a man becomes righteous: that he is always “the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” [Col. 0094B] (Prov. 18:17), mindful of the divine counsel by which he was told: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43, according to the Septuagint). Thus it comes about that, while he judges himself and vindicates God concerning himself, he who feared God as judge has him, though guilty, as advocate. For “the Lord is righteous and loves righteous deeds” (Ps. 10:8); nor can he take up or defend unjust causes, he who, “when he has received the time,” will judge even acts of righteousness.

And yet he who threatens that he will be judge of those who proudly presume upon their righteousness promises that he will be advocate of those who humbly confess their sins. For before him, in whose sight “no human being shall be justified,” we can in no way testify more effectively to our own cause than by accusing and punishing ourselves, assigning his justice against us, and performing the part of the judge against the accused.

4. But even if in some venial matter we are deceived through ignorance or overcome through weakness, so that we cannot wholly exterminate our Jebusite, but allow him always to dwell with us in the land under our eyes, even in this our imperfection the prophetic word consoles us, speaking in our person: “We have always been in them, and we shall be saved” (Isa. 64:5). “Your merciful eyes,” says the body of Christ, “saw my imperfection, and in your book all shall be written” [Col. 0094D] (Ps. 138:16): that is, both perfect and imperfect alike shall be found written.

For the Lord promises that he will bring our imperfection to completion, speaking through the prophet Joel: “I will cleanse their blood which they did not cleanse” (Joel 3:21). Hence Isaiah, having first declared the future perfection of the heavenly Jerusalem—“Everyone left in Zion and remaining in Jerusalem shall be called holy, everyone written for life in Jerusalem”—added, to show that this holiness in the weak can be accomplished only by divine purification: “When the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and has cleansed the blood from the midst of Jerusalem.” The washing that is promised consoles me; but the manner which follows terrifies me: “By the spirit,” he says, “of judgment and the spirit [Col. 0095A] of burning” (Isa. 3:4).

“For fire will test the work of each person. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved by reason of the foundation, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:13, 15).

5. How much better it would be if we now burned with delightful love rather than then with that penal burning! How much more sweetly if we were now purified by the fire of love, so that nothing worldly might remain in us which would be found liable to the world’s conflagration; but so that, as for the three children, the furnace of Babylon might become for us a wind of dew (Dan. 3:49–50)!

Otherwise, if while living lukewarmly and negligently we heap up wood, hay, and straw for ourselves and carry hence with us so much material for fires, when we enter such a trial of purgatory, who among us will be able to dwell with devouring fire? Or who among us will dwell with everlasting burnings, when every garment too, stained with blood, “will be for burning and food for the fire”? [Col. 0095B] (Isa. 9:5).

I know indeed that, if I burned sufficiently with the fire of charity, it could also be said of me: “Her many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). But now, if I do not deserve to be purified by the fire of love, would that I might at least be purified by some fire of suffering, and that what the prophet invokes upon himself might happen to me: “Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation” (Hab. 3:16). Would that he who began might himself crush me; let him loose his hand and cut me down; and let this be my consolation, that in afflicting me with pain he does not spare me.

Nevertheless, Lord, you know the weakness of my frame. “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should be patient? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze” [Col. 0095C] (Job 6:9–12). This first I ask, Lord: “Do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger” (Ps. 6:2). But because I hear from you, “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19), and, “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5:17), correct me, Lord, in mercy and not in your fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing (Jer. 10:24), and it be said of me: “You have withdrawn him from cleansing” (Ps. 88:45).

Look upon my weakness, and temper your hand according to it, lest the violence of the blow break the heart’s endurance; but rather let tribulation produce endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope. But woe to me if I am burned daily and not cleansed, so that it may happen that it is said even of me: “It has sweated with much labour, and its rust has not gone out of it—not even through fire. Your uncleanness is abominable, because I wished to cleanse you and you were not cleansed of your filth; nor shall you be cleansed until I make my indignation rest in you” [Col. 0095D] (Ezek. 24:12–13).

6. How I fear lest this come upon us, who are daily cooked, as it were, by a purgatorial fire in the strictness of life, yet are never cleansed from our iniquity as we ought to be! And perhaps we shall not be cleansed until the Judge himself sits “as a refiner’s and cleanser’s fire,” and purifies the sons of Levi (Mal. 3:2–3).

Nevertheless, however little this fire may now accomplish, I would rather have it applied to me meanwhile than have it deferred wholly to that other fire. For if they are compared with one another, this is the medicine of one who is merciful; that is the vengeance of one who is angry. So thought he who said: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger” (Ps. 6:2).

I know indeed that even then, when my soul has been troubled, Lord, you will remember mercy in anger. I know that even amid mourning and punishments I should console myself with better hope; and to the hostile power, to which I might be delivered for a time to be corrected, I would answer in the prophet’s words: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen: I shall rise. When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. I will bear the anger of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause. He will bring me into the light; I shall see his righteousness. Then my enemy will see me and be covered with confusion” (Mic. 7:8–10). [Col. 0096B]

And on that day I shall say: “I will praise you, Lord, because you were angry with me; your fury has turned away, and you have consoled me” (Isa. 12:1). Yet why should I fear on the evil day? Why should I not rather enjoy good things on the good day and guard against the evil day? Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Why should I not now heed the counsel of the Wise Man: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly; because there is no counsel, nor reason, nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten” (Eccles. 9:10); and that of the Apostle: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:10)?

We had indeed begun with consolations, but have come to terrors, because consolation will then truly be useful when mingled with fear. Then, Lord, we shall enter into your truth (Heb. 4:3), if our heart so rejoices that it also fears your name. Otherwise, if we made you wholly secure, it would be said even of us: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the paths of your steps” [Col. 0096C] (Isa. 3:12). But we shall then truly be blessed if we rightly acknowledge our misery and grieve over it devoutly; then we shall be secure in death if we always live fearful and watchful.

## SERMON II. SATURDAY OF THE WEEK OF LENT. On the parable of the prodigal son. (Luke 15:11–32)

1. O blessed humility of penitents! O blessed hope of those who confess! How powerful you are with the Almighty; how easily you conquer the unconquerable; how swiftly you turn the fearful Judge into a most loving Father!

This prodigal son, whose wretched wandering, tearful repentance, and glorious reception we have today heard for our great edification—this prodigal, I say, though so gravely guilty, had not yet confessed, but had only resolved to confess; he had not yet made satisfaction, but had only inclined his mind toward making satisfaction. Yet from the mere purpose of conceived humility he immediately obtained pardon—the pardon sought for so long by such great prayers, implored with tears, and pursued by acts of service. Confession alone absolved the thief upon the cross; the will to confess alone absolved this man.

“I said, ‘I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5): mercy everywhere goes before. It had gone before the will to confess by inspiring it; it went before [Col. 0097A] even the spoken confession by pardoning what had to be confessed. “While he was still far away,” it says, “his father saw him and was moved with mercy; and running to him, he fell upon his neck and kissed him.” As far as these words can convey, the father seemed slower to grant pardon to his son than the son was to receive it. So eagerly did he hasten to release the guilty man from the torment of his conscience, as though the compassionate man’s pity for the wretched suffered more pain than the wretched man’s own suffering.

We do not say this in order to attribute human emotions to the unchangeable nature; rather, our own affection is sweetened toward the love of that highest goodness, while from a human likeness we learn that he loves us more than we love ourselves.

2. Observe, moreover, how, where offence abounded, grace abounded still more [Col. 0097B]. The guilty man could scarcely hope for pardon; the Judge—indeed, no longer Judge but Advocate—heaps grace upon grace. “Quickly,” he says, “bring out the first robe and clothe him; put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet; bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life.”

But to pass over all these things—the first robe, namely the sanctification of the Spirit, with which the baptized person is clothed and the penitent reclothed; the ring of faith, by which he is given a pledge; the sandals, by which he is armed to tread upon the poisons of serpents or prepared for evangelizing; the fattened calf, offered for him upon the altar; and those festal joys which, decreed for the received son, are celebrated by all heaven—to pass over, I say, all these and reserve them for treatment by the more learned: what grace and sweetness, what most happy joy, what most holy delight, is not contained in that embrace and kiss of fatherly love?

“It says, ‘He fell upon his neck and kissed him.’” When he so poured his affection upon him, what was he doing as he embraced and kissed him, except imparting himself to him—or the man to himself—and breathing himself into him, so that by cleaving to him the son might become one spirit with him, just as by cleaving to harlots he had been made one body with them? It was too little for the bowels of that highest mercy not to shut up its compassion against the wretched: it draws them into its own bowels and joins them to its own members. He could not bind us to himself more closely, nor hold us more intimately, than by incorporating us into himself and, by an ineffable power as well as charity, uniting not only the assumed body but even the spirit itself to himself [Col. 0097D].

If so great is the grace of penitents, what will be the glory of those who reign? If these are the consolations of the wretched, what will be the joys of the blessed? And he who grants this upon the way—what does he reserve in the homeland? Surely that which has not ascended into the human heart: that we may be like him and that God may be all in all.

3. But now, blessed sinner—though blessed not because you are a sinner, but because you repent of sin—what, I ask, was the feeling of your heart amid the father’s embraces and kisses, when he restored you although you had nearly despaired, when, renewing a clean heart within you, he poured back into you the joy of his salvation? And how, he says, will speech explain what the mind does not comprehend? The groanings are unutterable and the emotions inexplicable which the soul, as though pregnant with the incomprehensible, brings forth. The human heart is too narrow for them; therefore, torn open, it pours itself out, and the ardour which it conceives but cannot contain it vents and relieves as it can, in tears, groans, and sighs [Col. 0098A]. Those know these things better who have tasted them more often and more richly.

Even now, I say, when, after those embraces and kisses, you are left to consider yourself and your own condition, when you review what your case had been and how it was judged by him, and weigh there the abundance of your offence and here the superabundance of grace—what, I beseech you, does your reflection produce in you? Surely, he says, an intolerable fire burns in my meditation: on the one hand through sorrow and shame, on the other through joy and love. I would not consider myself human but stone if I were so hard-hearted that I did not grieve for or blush for myself, or so wicked and ungrateful that I were not wholly melted into joy or love for that Father.

4. Therefore guard, O blessed sinner, guard carefully and vigilantly this spirit of yours, this most fitting affection of humility and devotion, by which you may always think of yourself in humility and of the Lord in goodness. Nothing is greater among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, nothing more precious among God’s treasures, nothing holier among all charisms, nothing more salutary among all sacraments.

Guard it, I say, if you wish yourself to be guarded: the humility of that feeling and utterance by which you confess to the Father and say: “Father, I am no longer worthy [Col. 0098C] to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants.” Nothing wins the Father’s favour as does the feeling of this utterance; nor can you make yourself more worthy to be a son than by always confessing yourself unworthy. This humility not only justifies sinners, but also brings the righteous to perfection and adds righteousness to them, if indeed they confess themselves to be unprofitable servants even when they have done all that was commanded.

Let your sin always be before you, and, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, “even concerning a sin that has been forgiven, do not be without fear” (Ecclus. 5:5). God’s judgments are uncertain and hidden; one must not rashly presume concerning them, since we hold nothing about them more certainly than that “no living person shall be justified” in God’s sight, except insofar as he judges himself a sinner. Otherwise, all our righteousness is “as the cloth of a menstruous woman” [Col. 0098D] (Isa. 44:6).

Mercy received you gently and restored you mercifully; fear judgment, lest the grace given to the humble be taken away from one grown proud. You chose to be lowly in your Father’s house; you were content to become as one of the hired servants. Stand by that resolve, so that, even if you have been raised up, you may yet be advanced to greater things. Always occupy, or at least desire, the lowest place. Claim for yourself the service of a hired servant, not the freedom of a son. Worship the Father with a son’s devotion, conscious of what he has deserved from you; but be content with the humility and labour of a hired servant, conscious of what you yourself have deserved.

Never let humility displease you, the humility through which you began to please and without which you will begin to displease, however great the virtues in which you may excel and however dutifully you may seem to serve the Father. For humility is the greatest of all virtues, although it does not know itself to be a virtue. It is, as it were, the root, seedbed, tinder, incentive, sum and summit, safeguard, and discipline of all virtues. They begin from it [Col. 0100A], advance through it, are perfected in it, and are preserved through it. And while it grants to all the rest that they are virtues, if one of them is lacking or less perfect, humility itself advances through the defect of the other and makes up its loss from itself.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 0099]

## SERMON I. On abiding in wisdom

[Col. 0099A]

1. “Blessed is the man who will abide in wisdom, who will meditate on righteousness, and who will thoughtfully consider the watchfulness of God!” (Ecclus. 14:22). How aptly these words have been sung in praise of blessed Benedict, any of you whose knowledge of his life and teaching is not lacking can readily understand. How fittingly they may be applied to the instruction of our own life is shown by the very form of the words themselves: they commend, together with the reward of blessedness, the things than which nothing is more useful in life—wisdom, righteousness, and the fear of God.

“Blessed,” it says, “is the man who will abide in wisdom.” This indeed is blessedness; this is wisdom: that you abide in wisdom and hold it perseveringly. For not one who has found wisdom at once, but one who has held it, is blessed. Scripture does say: “Blessed is he who finds wisdom.” But it did not stop there; indeed it added: “and he who abounds in wisdom” [Col. 0099B] (Prov. 3:13), lest merely having found it should be thought sufficient at once for blessedness, unless, having found it, you remain with it and in it, delighting in its companionship and fellowship. Do not depart from its instruction until, by meditating on righteousness and considering God’s watchfulness, you can abound in prudence.

For Solomon also found wisdom; but, because he did not sufficiently abound in prudence or watch carefully enough over himself—since he did not cautiously guard himself against foreign women—he not only lost wisdom but fell headlong into the final folly of idolatry (3 Kings 11). Likewise the wise men of this world, who saw God’s invisible things, understood through the things made from the creation of the world, seemed to have found wisdom. But because they too did not abound in prudence and, though they knew God, did not glorify him as God, they too became foolish; and their senseless heart was darkened, even to a reprobate mind and the disgrace of shameful acts (Rom. 1:21–32).

2. Thus, as the example of these men makes plain, pride of heart drives some away from the wisdom they had found; the enticement of the flesh draws others away, as is evident in Solomon; while others, offended by some slight disturbance through levity and inconstancy of mind, abandon it: those, namely, who believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation. Why do they withdraw? Because they have no roots by which they may be held fast (Luke 8:13–14). But how will they take root unless they remain? What plant ever takes root unless it remains in the place to which it has been fixed?

So the righteous man, planted in [Col. 0100A] the house of the Lord, can neither take root nor be founded in charity except through remaining and stability of place. But if he is not rooted, he can neither flourish nor bring forth fruit that remains. And if, in some beginning of hope, he seems to flourish, it will be said of him: “Before the harvest he has wholly flowered, and unripe perfection has budded” (Isa. 18:5); and according to another prophet: “If he produces fruit, strangers will eat it” (Hos. 8:7).

Would you know how necessary stability of place is, that you may abide in wisdom and may take root and bear fruit through duration in time? Ask your father Benedict, and he will tell you that the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community are a fitting place for bearing nearly all the fruits of virtues, of which he there weaves a long catalogue (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 4). For what does he say concerning the unstable man? “Like a bird migrating from its nest, so is a man who leaves his place” (Prov. 27:8).

The turtledove had found a nest in which to place her young; she had begun to warm it and to be warmed by it; the young had advanced even to birth—and behold, she flies away and leaves the work begun unfinished. Why, from where, or where she flies, let her see for herself; or when she will compensate for the many losses she suffers meanwhile; or by what reasoning she will excuse her first pledge of faith, now made void. For I would not consider it prudent to undergo certain losses for an uncertain hope, although the progress of certain persons bids me meanwhile restrain judgment from precipitancy [Col. 0100C].

3. Certainly, the case of those who are made restless by love of wisdom is very unlike that of those of whom I had begun to speak, who recoil from wisdom when moved by a trivial and frivolous cause. For just as a person remains in the disciplines of wisdom through patience in order to learn wisdom, so those who readily lose endurance will not delay, as Scripture says, to cast it aside.

But Scripture first stated what offends them when it said: “Its testing will be in them as the strength of a stone” (Ecclus. 6:22). They stumbled at the stone of stumbling and rock of offence, whose proven power reproved and instructed the foolish and tested minds; whereas they interpreted the strength of wisdom as the hardness of a stone and complained that everything was harsh—discipline, expression, and speech. “This saying,” they say, “is harsh” [Col. 0100D] (John 6:61). Granted, the saying is harsh; but is it not true? A stone is hard; but is it not precious? Why is truth harsh to you except because of the hardness of your own heart? If your heart were softened by devotion, the solidity of truth would please you more than the emptiness of falsehood or the oil of flattery.

“This saying is harsh,” they said, because wisdom’s testing was for them as the strength of a stone; and therefore they did not remain but cast it aside and went back. They rejected the precious stone, chosen by God, for no other reason than that they judged it hard. And Christ was indeed the rock, but by power, not by hardness. He was a rock, but one that could be turned; indeed, that was turned into pools or springs of waters, where it found the hearts of the faithful soft and humble, into which it might flow.

For even those who, so quickly offended by an appearance of harshness, went back would perhaps, had they remained with the Apostles, have drunk with them from the Rock that followed them; they would have drunk rivers of living water flowing most abundantly from the rock struck upon the cross, so that even today “the people and the cattle drink”; indeed, they would also have sucked honey from the rock [Col. 0101B] and oil from the hardest stone.

4. Truly, Simon Bar-Jonah, you are blessed. The Father was already revealing to you the loving mystery hidden, as it seemed, beneath the harshness of the saying. When the Twelve were asked whether they too wished to depart, you steadfastly replied: “Lord, you have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?” (John 6:69). Clearly blessed are you, who chose to remain with wisdom and, with its household, meanwhile to be nourished at its table by the bread of the Sacrament, until, advancing from faith to understanding, you should be fed with the bread of life and understanding and given the saving water of wisdom to drink.

And blessed are you also, my brethren, who have enrolled yourselves in the discipline of wisdom and the school of Christian philosophy—provided that you remain perseveringly in wisdom. Thus, when its saying seems harsher, that is, when it commands more rigorously or rebukes more sternly, there may not be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God; rather, say steadfastly with the Apostle: “You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?”

“You fashion labour in commandment” [Col. 0101C] (Ps. 93:20), and harshness in speech; but we know that “great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30:20), which you will bring to completion for those who hope in you. But I shall always hope, even if you kill me. Indeed, then I shall hope more greatly: when you scourge, cut, burn, and kill whatever lived in me, so that not I, but Christ, may live in me. We absolutely do not depart from you, because even by killing you will give us life, and by striking you will heal us.

Truly blessed is one who abides with wisdom, enduring with constancy and faith, patiently and faithfully obedient unto death; one who does not abandon his place whenever “the spirit of one who has authority” rises against him, knowing that “the healing of discipline will make the greatest sins cease” (Eccles. 10:4).

5. Indeed, I judge that this especially belongs to the wisdom of abiding in wisdom: that restlessness or any slight annoyance should not readily shake from us any work of wisdom—for example, solemn psalmody, prayer, divine reading, the allotted daily work, or the discipline of silence. For wisdom is sung at the end: “My lips,” says the holy man, “will rejoice when I sing to you” (Ps. 70:23), while even literally “you will delight the goings forth of morning and evening” [Col. 0102A] (Ps. 64:9).

Concerning prayer too, you yourselves have the daily, sure experience of the Head that the end of prayer is better than its beginning; so that you may prove true that counsel of the Lord, so often inculcated and commended by so many examples, concerning perseverance in prayer. But if, having read, you neglect it—or cast the book from your hands before you have begun it—what fruit, do you suppose, can it produce for you? If you do not remain with Scripture until through constancy of study you become familiar with it, when, do you suppose, will it reveal itself to you? “He who has love for the word,” it says, “will be given understanding and will abound; but from him who does not have it, even what he has by nature will be taken away” [Col. 0102B] (Matt. 13:12; 25:29), because of negligence.

And concerning manual work, have you not learned sufficiently from this too that, as the denarius is given to labourers, so consolation is often reserved until the end of the work? Concerning silence, moreover, the prophetic promise is well known: “In silence and hope,” it says, “shall be your strength” (Isa. 30:15). For if you cultivate righteousness in silence and, as Jeremiah says is good, wait silently for the salvation of the Lord, amid the silence the almighty Word will secretly flow into you from the royal thrones, and the waters of Siloam, which flow silently, will water the valley of a quiet and peaceful heart with a welcome stream.

You will experience this not once but often, provided only that your silence is “the cultivation of righteousness” (Isa. 32:17): that is, provided that you meditate on righteousness, so that you persevere in the Scripture I have set before you, and thoughtfully consider the watchfulness of God.

6. Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may become manifest [Col. 0102C]. For if you meditate upon iniquity in your bed—namely, the wicked thoughts which the Evil One injects, or the fantasies which your own heart brings forth, or empty philosophies and deceptive theories, which are like the dreams of a sick man—will not your silence be a cultivation of injustice rather than of justice? If, then, you wish to dwell in wisdom, strive to meditate upon justice. “Have you desired wisdom?” it says. “Keep justice, and the Lord will provide her for you” (Sir. 1:33). But if harmful thoughts rush in, as though violently, set over yourself a manly and faithful guard, which may keep your heart with all vigilance. I mean the fear of God: it neglects nothing; it permits nothing to enter unexamined; it repeatedly questions even an angel of light: “Are you one of us, or of our adversaries?” (Josh. 5:13).

For it looks about on every side [Col. 0102D], as one ever mindful of God’s watchfulness, observing how He unceasingly beholds and judges the hearts of the children of men. It was well said: “He shall meditate with understanding” (Sir. 14:22), for he is utterly without understanding and has departed from his heart who neglects to contemplate the fear of God, who does not feel the weight of so great a majesty and judgment resting upon him. God, too, is said significantly to “look round about,” because all things, past and future alike, are present to Him: He neither looks back upon the former nor looks forward to the latter, but surveys all things alike, because simply; and that eternity is as it were a point at the midst of all temporal things, to whose unmoved simplicity the circuit and wheel of time are always equally present.

The fear of the Lord always contemplates this eternal eye, which unceasingly sees and judges all things, and makes itself anxious by this contemplation. It calls us back not only from evil deeds, but also from evil thoughts; it instructs us to meditate rather upon justice and restrains us so that we may dwell with wisdom. Thus it gradually comes about that one who is first checked by fear of judgment and punishment is afterwards nourished by love and meditation upon justice, and finally rests and delights in the companionship and embrace of wisdom. This not only casts fear outwards by pouring forth charity, but also drives weariness and languor from the soul by infusing sweetness. Thus one who had her as his companion spoke of her: “When I enter into my house, I shall rest with her; for her conversation has no bitterness, nor her company weariness, but gladness and joy” (Wis. 8:16).

May Christ Jesus, the Wisdom of God, who deigned to become a partaker of us, make us partakers of these things; He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On Trust in God

1. “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord” (Jer. 17:7). Our holy Father Benedict, blessed both by grace and by name, whose memory is in blessing, was indeed that blessed man who trusted in the Lord. For He who anticipated him with blessings of sweetness, so that he might trust in the Lord, had already [Col. 0103C] blessed him with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ, because he trusted in the Lord. Nor did the Lord give him only, in heavenly things, the blessing of all the angels, but also, in earthly things, the blessing of all nations. For among what nations is the Lord’s blessed Benedict not blessed today? Truly, “The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the just” (Prov. 10:6), him whom the grace of God has heaped full with so many blessings of heaven and earth.

Yet his blessing is not, like Esau’s, “in the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven” (Gen. 27:28), but in the richness of the Spirit and in the dew of heaven, who speaks through the prophet: “I shall be as dew” (Hos. 14:6), and to whom it is said: “Your dew is the dew of light” (Isa. 26:19). Certainly, the Father’s blessing is in Christ, to whom the Father declared: “May he who blesses you be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27:29). Therefore the man who trusts in the Lord is rightly blessed in the Lord, because he who trusts in the Lord fixes himself in Him. Where a tree fixes its root, thence it drinks the sap of life and the moisture of richness. Truly, he has sent his roots toward moisture who, to use the words of Master Benedict, has committed his hope to God, and drinks from that fountain of the supreme good the waters of life, of every blessing and grace (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 4).

2. Through this pious and faithful trust sins are forgiven; remedies for bodily healings—and still more for spiritual healings—are obtained; dangers are driven away; terrors are despised; the world is conquered [Col. 0104A]; and, finally, all things are made possible to the believer. To him who was in sins, He said: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” To those to whom healing of body or soul was granted: “According to your faith, be it done to you”; and: “Your faith has made you whole” (Matt. 9:2, 29, 22). To those frightened by the danger of shipwreck: “Have faith in God” (Mark 11:22); and: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” (Matt. 8:26). To those whom He armed against the cruelty of the world and the rage of the devil: “Take courage,” He said; “I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

And this is indeed the victory which conquers the world: our faith (1 John 5:4), provided only that it be neither lukewarm nor timid, but be trust—that is, faith unfeigned, or hope not weak. Through it not only is the world conquered, but heaven also is possessed [Col. 0104B]; man is established upon eternity, and is rooted and founded in God Himself through charity. For “those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion: he shall not be moved for ever, who is founded upon the Eternal One” (Ps. 124:1). He can no more perish than can He to whom, by cleaving, he is one spirit. “For who has hoped in the Lord and been confounded? Who has remained in His commandments and been forsaken?” (Sir. 2:11–12).

If an unbeliever says, “He was forsaken who cried on the cross: ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Matt. 27:46), I think He did not altogether forsake Him in whom He was reconciling the world to Himself. O what consolation, to be thus desolate! What love, to be thus forsaken: that you might deserve to be associated even in sufferings with the Father’s Only-Begotten, uniquely beloved Son!

3. Open, Lord, the eyes of this child—I mean one untrained and newly entered—who, when he is afflicted, thinks himself forsaken. It would be wholly new and unheard of if I saw any just man forsaken, when the Church says: “I was young, and now I have grown old; yet I have not seen the just man forsaken” (Ps. 36:25). Open, I say, O Lord, the eyes of your child, that he may see that those with us are more numerous than those with our adversaries. For the Lord of hosts is with us, and with Him is every power and the host of heaven—indeed, the favor of every creature, serving the will and judgment of its Creator. “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31). And “who is he that can harm us, if we are zealous for good?” [Col. 0104D] (1 Pet. 3:13).

That envious one may rage; but this will be to serve us. He may burn, strike, and cut to pieces; but this will be to fashion crowns. “I will love you, O Lord, my strength,” through whom every opposing power yields to me, a little worm; and the craft of the ancient dragon is mocked by your angels, sent for our service, so that, while desiring to harm, it may benefit us. I will love you, O Lord: mighty defender, prudent governor, merciful consoler, generous rewarder. Securely I cast all my care upon Him whose power cannot be overcome, whose wisdom cannot be deceived, and whose good will cannot grow weary of supplying all my need. How much better, how much safer, that He Himself should be concerned than that I should be concerned for myself! How good it is to trust [Col. 0105A] in the Lord rather than in man! And how rightly accursed is he who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord! (Jer. 17:5).

Indeed, I am needy and poor; but if the Lord is concerned for me, I am rich, I am blessed, since all things cooperate for my good. Let those, therefore, who know your name hope in you, for you do not forsake those who hope in you, O Lord (Ps. 9:11). And may your people dwell, as it is written, “in the beauty of peace, in tents of trust, in abundant rest, in everlasting security” (Isa. 32:18, 17). Truly beautiful are peace and everlasting security: to dwell in the help of the Most High, to abide in the protection of the God of heaven. Truly abundant rest is to sit at leisure beneath the true vine, the fig tree, and the olive; and, after the fullness of diverse fruits, to soothe oneself with a song of love and say: “Under his shadow, whom I desired [Vulgate: whom I had desired], I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:5). Truly sweet to the throat is that fruit, from whose taste so sweet a belch bursts forth.

4. These, then, are the tents of trust, in which true Israel dwells confidently, feeds and lies down, and has none to terrify him. And, as Wisdom promises, “He shall rest without terror, shall enjoy abundance, the fear of evils having been removed” (Prov. 1:33). It says well, “the fear of evils having been removed,” not the fear of the Lord; lest you suppose that the trust and security which we commend produce negligence, when strong trust is found only in the fear of the Lord.

For fear, while guarding against offence, preserves grace and maintains a place for trust, so long as you are not conscious that you have offended the Lord. Hence it comes that you fear Him chastely alone, and fear no stranger whatsoever besides Him. Therefore good conscience alone presumes this trust and persuades our hearts that they stand before the eternal Judge. For who can promise himself good from One whom he understands not to love him? But he who loves never distrusts, knowing that He whom hearts cannot deceive loves those who love Him, even when He rebukes and chastises. Indeed, to those instructed in wisdom of heart, the Father’s discipline does not remove but increases trust, for they know what is written: “Blessed is he who is corrected by the Lord” (Job 5:17); and: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chasten” [Col. 0105D] (Rev. 3:19; Prov. 3:12).

Therefore, when His anger has blazed up briefly, blessed are all who trust in Him (Ps. 2:13): namely, those whom consciousness of their own love consoles, because, when He is angry, He will remember mercy. And when they say, “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me,” there immediately follows: “Your fury has turned away, and you have comforted me” (Isa. 12:1), because His anger blazed only briefly, and confession of guilt so quickly appeased it.

5. Jeremiah therefore rightly compares the blessed man who trusts in the Lord to a tree transplanted beside waters. Because it sends forth the roots of its heart toward the moisture of love, it shall not fear when the heat of anger and tribulation comes. And even in a time [Col. 0106A] of drought, when heaven has been shut up for a long time and neither dew nor rain of grace descends upon it, it shall nevertheless not be anxious, as though God had cast it away (Jer. 17:7–8). For it knows itself to be planted by faith and rooted by charity beside the waters of life, which, according to Ezekiel, issue from the sanctuary, give life to all things, and have upon either bank every fruit-bearing tree whose leaf does not fall and whose fruit does not fail (Ezek. 47:3–12).

Why, then, should that blessed tree either fear the heat or be anxious about drought, when living water—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—never ceases inwardly to supply it with the life-giving sap of hope and charity? Thus its leaf is green—that is, its word is full of grace and truth—and it itself never ceases at any time to bear fruit: every work of piety [Col. 0106B]. Pleasant indeed is that springtime mildness of peace and joy, desirable that voluntary rain which God has set apart for His inheritance. But if necessity requires it, let the heat of tribulation scorch everything; let whatever Jeremiah prophesied concerning the utterances of spiritual drought come again: yet he whom trust in the Lord has rooted beside the water of refreshment (Jer. 17:6, 8), that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, shall not fear.
