Though this grace does not visibly rain down so as to flow perceptibly, it nevertheless inwardly gives life and fruitfulness in secret, as long as it preserves fidelity to its resolve, strengthens one to persevere, and supplies irreproachable speech and steadfast work.

6. Let this, brothers, be your consolation whenever other consolations, not merely carnal but even spiritual, are withdrawn from you—not through your negligence, but by divine dispensation [Col. 0106C]. Perhaps that hidden grace of the Spirit of which we have spoken is the lower watering-place, with which Achsah does not wish to be content unless the upper watering-place is added to it also (Josh. 15:19): that is, that the Spirit may be poured out from on high, the heavens may drop dew from above, and the angelic clouds may rain down the Just One—the justifying Word of God, speaking to the heart of Jerusalem.

And that watering-place is well called lower, because, flowing as it were toward the roots, it nourishes humility; while the other is upper, because, pouring itself down from above, it raises the mind in hope and exultation. Therefore, if you too, brothers, long for that upper watering-place, your desire is praiseworthy; but [Col. 0106D] if you have not yet attained it, meanwhile send your roots toward moisture: this is a wholesome remedy. He, then, who is unable to receive the joy of the contemplative life should meditate upon the justice of the active life. From this let him enrich the roots of his affections, sweeten his habits, and shape his whole condition of life, so that in him neither may the leaf wither or fall—that is, a word lightly or uselessly uttered—nor may life ever cease to bear fruit. Blessed is the tree whose leaf is for healing and whose fruit for life: that is, whose speech produces grace in its hearer and whose work produces life in its doer.

7. For this purpose, indeed, my brothers, you whom carnal generation or worldly habit had planted in a waterless land, in a land of salt marshes, have been transplanted by divine generation, or by the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, beside [Col. 0107A] the waters of refreshment: so that you for whom the axe and fire were formerly prepared because of barrenness may now, planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, flourish and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain.

Are not the Scriptures of the Holy Spirit waters of refreshment, in which we meditate day and night? Are not tears of compunction waters of refreshment, which have become our bread day and night? Are not the sacraments and aids of our salvation waters of refreshment, by which we are fed and given drink at the altar? For in all these things, as in certain streams, the fountain of wisdom that rises in the midst of paradise is led forth outside and distributes its waters in the streets. “I,” says Wisdom, “have gone forth from paradise like an aqueduct. I said: I will water the garden of my plantations; I will make the fruit of my offspring abundant with drink” (Sir. 24:41–42).

Behold: as you can gather from the mouth of Wisdom herself, who bears and plants, the garden of plantations is the assembly of children [Col. 0107B]. “Shall I, who cause others to bear, not myself bear?” says the Lord (Isa. 66:9). He bears when He implants a good will; He plants when He establishes a manner of life; He waters when He pours grace into the senses; He cultivates when He applies discipline to conduct. “Hear me, divine fruits, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water” (Sir. 39:17). Send your roots toward the moisture of life—that is, toward love of the land of the living, not of this land in which all things grow old and rot.

A tree cannot bear fruit that remains unless it fixes its root upward in heavenly things, so that it seeks and relishes the things above, not the things upon earth. What natural philosophers say—that man is an inverted tree, because the nerves of the body have their root and beginning in the crown of the head—I interpret in this sense rather: that he ought to fix the root of love and desire in heaven, in the supreme summit of all things, our head, Jesus Christ [Col. 0107C]. Whoever has sent roots thither and continually drunk from that eternal fountain the sap of life and grace shall not fear when the heat of judgment comes. But, bringing and offering the abundant fruit which he has produced, he shall receive as his reward that he may flourish for ever before the Lord, to whom belong honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On Seeking God’s Friendship Above All Things

1. “Beloved by God and by men” (Sir. 45:1). In few words he has portrayed the good and blessed man—such, assuredly, as Benedict, beloved of the Lord, is known to have been. In few words, I say, he has comprehended the sum of perfection, the fullness of grace and virtue, together with the blessedness of everlasting life and the consolation of the present life. For what can be lacking for eternal happiness to one who is loved by God? What can be lacking for present consolation to one who is loved by men?

To one who is loved by God, even if something seems to be lacking, it is lacking for no other reason than that nothing may be lacking to him, and that he may be more perfect through his seeming deficiency. For virtue is perfected in weakness. “Paul,” says the Lord, “my grace is sufficient for you” (2 Cor. 12:9). For him to whom God’s grace is sufficient, some grace may be lacking without serious loss—indeed, with no slight gain—since that very deficiency and weakness perfects virtue; and the diminution of a certain grace makes the supreme grace of God, the sum of all graces, greater and more secure in him.

Far from your servants, Lord, be whatever grace it may be that can take away or diminish your favor, by which someone becomes more glorious in his own eyes and more hateful in yours [Col. 0108A]. That is not grace but wrath, fit to be given to those with whom you are angry, those concerning whom, because of their deceits, you have set such things: casting them down while they are lifted up, and violently dashing them down while they are raised on high. Therefore, that grace alone without which no one is loved by you may remain safe in us: may your grace withdraw from us every other grace, or at least grant at the same time the grace to use it, so that, having grace by which we may serve acceptably with fear and reverence, we may, from the grace of the gift, deserve the grace of the Rewarder; and the more gracious any person is, the more pleasing may he become to you.

2. By a wonderful art, but by a still more wonderful charity, the prudent mercy and merciful prudence of God has provided for human salvation: though He loves all, He does not readily allow them to be certain or secure of His love. He hides the great abundance of His sweetness from those who fear Him for no other reason than that, while He always keeps them humble, He may always have them lovable. For there are just and wise persons, and their works are in the hand of God; yet a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future (Sir. 9:1–2).

The Ruler of all so distributes to them the grace of gifts and works that, through certain things which He grants, He gives consolation that they are worthy of love; and through certain things which He withholds, He instills suspicion and fear that they are worthy of hatred. He consoles when He visits at dawn; He terrifies when He suddenly tests. Now He kills, now gives life; now He brings down to hell, now brings back. Now He makes poor and makes rich; now He humbles and raises up (1 Sam. 2:6–7). And amid so great a variety of changes He works our salvation all the more surely as we, being more uncertain concerning it, cooperate with Him in greater fear and trembling.

Paul indeed says: “I am certain that nothing shall separate me from the charity of God” (Rom. 8:38–39). But this was truly Paul, not I or you, for whom it is expedient that all things be kept uncertain for the future. It was Paul, I say, who said this, to whom it properly belonged also to say: “I now live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20), since he had been so entirely transformed into a certain divine affection that, cleaving to the Lord, he was one spirit with Him. Yet observe this same Paul, who was at one moment so certain, at another fearful and anxious, chastising his body lest perhaps, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate (1 Cor. 9:27); observe also that he was buffeted by Satan (2 Cor. 12:7), lest perhaps he should be exalted. Thus in Paul himself you may now see how every certainty which is strengthened and confirmed for a time by the consolation of the Spirit is likewise weakened and vanishes when temptation comes.

But I, wretched and unworthy even of life itself—by what consolation, by what trust, may I presume that I am worthy of love, when all things inward and outward proclaim evident hatred against me? My life is not temptation, not warfare against sin, but willing servitude to sin. In mind and flesh alike I serve the law of sin; and I seem to have made a miserable treaty with the prudence of the flesh and the friendship of the world, both of which are hostile to God: plainly, a covenant with death and a compact with hell [Col. 0109A]. Yet I know, I know Him who said: “Your covenant with death shall be abolished, and your compact with hell shall not stand” (Isa. 28:18), because nothing can be friendly to God’s enemies, and zeal will arm, for vengeance against the enemies, not death or hell alone but every creature also.

How blessed, on that day, will be whoever is beloved by God! How praiseworthy those whose praise shall then be from God, to whom He will say in the manifest evidence of things: “You are my friends, because you have done what I commanded you!” (John 15:14). This, indeed, is the first virtue, the best gift of grace, the chief fruit of life: to deserve God’s friendship, the most certain pledge of blessedness. If He is favorable, someone may become a man’s enemy, but the enemy will accomplish nothing against him, and “the son of iniquity shall not add to harm him” (Ps. 88:23).

3. But if, after and through this highest good and cause of all good things, you also deserve that grace—that, beloved by God, you may likewise be beloved by men—what consolation is that amid the miseries of this life, what rest, what joy, what delights! Especially if you have learned not to fade away in the favor of human grace, but to burn more ardently in love for God [Col. 0109C], for whose sake you are loved by men.

Otherwise, if human favor arises from elsewhere or is referred elsewhere, what is it but a scorching wind, a corrupting or pestilential breeze, a plundering robber, a lurking murderer, a serpent in the road, a horned viper in the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider falls backward? For the vain man is raised up into pride, and by the vanity of his own mind, like a headlong horse, he is carried into ruin. Such a serpent wounds and overturns his steps, while, as if flattering his head, it causes his tender beginnings to be praised.

No differently, unless I am mistaken, does it happen to the person who, before he knows how to love, excessively desires to be loved, and who, before he has learned to be a friend even to himself, seeks to gain all men as friends. He makes riches without judgment; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and at his end he shall be a fool, when all his friends have despised him—for whose sake he himself despised God. Then the saying written will come to pass: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they have been confounded, because God has despised them” (Ps. 52:6).

4. Therefore, before all else, the love of God must be sought—that love which is both first and the end of all things—so that through it we may rightly deserve to be loved also by men, and through its pursuit may be taught how we ought to use the love of men. But when you have placed the matter in safety—namely, when the affection of your mind has been so firmly fixed that you wish to be loved only in God and for God—then I certainly desire [Col. 0110A] that the sweetness of your character, the humility of your services, and the honorableness of your pursuits should commend you to every man’s conscience; that you may spontaneously win the affection of all and be proclaimed by the testimony of all, so that religion itself, which commends you, may in just reciprocity become commendable through you.

Thus in you also, an adopted son, the prayer of the Only-Begotten will be fulfilled: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1), when, seeing the brightness of your works, men glorify your Father. We do not say this because there is any temporal sequence between the love of God and the love of neighbor, although there is an order of affection. From the beginning, both must be observed: the former must not be neglected, nor the latter disregarded, since neither God without one’s neighbor nor one’s neighbor without God can truly be loved [Col. 0110B]. Yet ordered affection cannot fail to know which of the two loves outweighs the other, which ought to prescribe form and measure to the other and set its end.

But this is what we say: it is one thing to be loved, another to endeavor to be loved. Such endeavor is dangerously undertaken by those who are ingratiating more through vanity than charity; and it is dangerously neglected by those who are austere more through pride than wisdom. For this reason they have called blessed the one who, between the two vices—vain friendliness and proud severity—has been able to hold the royal middle way of truth: that is, being full of true charity, neither pursuing this endeavor through vanity nor disdaining it through arrogance.

5. Yet such is the power and nature of true love that, even when it does not seek it, it makes itself loved in return. For truth, even without another’s support, readily commends itself to every conscience, unless the dreadful perversity of a malicious mind intervenes, ready to interpret everything malignantly. Still, some have from God a special gift for winning this holy love: the gladness of their countenance, as though anointed with oil, has poured over them a certain gracious charm and brightness, making all their deeds and words pleasing in the eyes of all, while many who perhaps love no less, indeed more, do not readily find the same grace.

But it belongs to all, “providing things good not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12:17; 2 Cor. 8:21), neither to neglect conscience through love of reputation nor reputation through confidence in conscience. For how can you flatter yourself even with respect to conscience, unless you are without complaint among the brethren—indeed, unless in all your conduct you show yourself a brother among brothers? Do you think it enough if you do not cause scandal? Rather, you cause scandal if you do not edify; if you do not, so far as your rank is concerned, glorify God everywhere by possessing good testimony within and without [Col. 0110D].

Certainly, if you are not permitted to please evil men, to whom nothing but evil is pleasing, to whom a just man is burdensome even to behold, this is not through your negligence—for you love even all enemies—but through their own wickedness, since they repay evil for good and hatred for your love. He who says, “Blessed shall you be when men hate you” comforts you (Luke 6:22), as does he who says that, if he pleased such people, he would not be Christ’s servant (Gal. 1:10).

6. But this is a wretched evil, to be lamented with every flood of tears, which not only superiors but also subjects often experience when they are zealous for their brethren with the zeal of God: namely, that even the good, though not insofar as they are good, are found to hate the good. “They hate him that rebukes in the gate” (Amos 5:10), and “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7:6), so that Paul himself groans because he has become an enemy to his children and friends by speaking truth (Gal. 4:16). Thus he too experienced what the comic poet says: “Truth breeds hatred” [Note: [Col. 0111D] Terence, *Andria* I.i.41]; indeed, he experienced also what the bride mentions: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1:5) [Col. 0111B], while I fought for their salvation.

O victorious queen, O glorious conqueror, fight: do not yield, do not withdraw, and do not grow weary. “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil by good” (Rom. 12:21). Wisdom conquers malice (Wis. 7:30); how much more weakness or imprudence? The charity of spiritual persons cannot interpret the opposition of carnal persons as malice, but rather as ignorance or the weakness by which they have been overtaken. Indeed, not even the Apostles regarded it as an insult that they were called evil by the Lord.

But why do I speak in this way, my brothers, beloved by God and by me? Is it because I suspect such an evil in any of you, against which I or my brethren must fight? Is anyone found among you, not merely rebellious, but even hard and intractable? I say these things not because this is so among you, but lest it should ever be so; lest perhaps some weakness should someday creep into someone, so that he receives no correction of charity except with charity. Thus both he who corrects and he who is corrected will be beloved by God and by men, and the memory of each will be in blessing. May He grant this through the merits of our blessed father Benedict: Jesus Christ, singularly blessed of God the Father, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On Gentleness and Faith

1. “In his faith and gentleness He made him holy” (Sir. 45:4). These words were written of Moses [Col. 0111D], but today, as I judge, they are not inappropriately applied to blessed Benedict. Since he was altogether full of the Spirit of the saints, he must much more be believed to have possessed no small portion of the spirit of Moses. For if the Lord took of the spirit of Moses and set it upon that entire assisting company of elders, who were summoned to share in the ministry (Num. 11:24–27), how much more upon this man, who fulfilled the fullness of the whole ministry all the more truly because more spiritually?

Moses was leader of those departing from Egypt; Benedict, of those renouncing the world. Moses was a lawgiver; so too was Benedict. Moses was only a minister of the letter that kills; Benedict, of the Spirit that gives life. Moses, because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, gave them ordinances that were not good, apart from a few moral precepts [Col. 0112A]; Benedict handed down only evangelical purity and a simple discipline of conduct. Moses wrote so many things difficult to understand, impossible or useless to perform; Benedict wrote a Rule of life most upright, eloquent in expression, outstanding in discernment. Finally, that leader did not bring into the promised rest the children of Israel whom he led out of Egypt; our leader, by the straight way and path of the rising sun, as standard-bearer of the army of monks, has today gone before us into the kingdom of heaven. It will therefore not be absurd to believe that he equalled the merit of the one whose ministry he is found even to have surpassed. Nor will it seem incongruous to transfer to him what is written of Moses: “In his faith and gentleness the Lord made him holy,” especially since he himself is our teacher particularly in these virtues, faith and gentleness, having lived in no other way than he taught.

2. For what was more illustrious than his faith? In boyhood, scorning the world as it smiled upon him, he trod beneath his feet the flower both of the world and of his own body as though already withered, preferring to suffer the world’s evils for God’s sake rather than prosper in it for a time. What was more like that faith of Moses which the Apostle commends when he says: “By faith Moses, when he had grown great, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time” (Heb. 11:24–25)?

And what was holier than the gentleness of our Father, whom not even the malice of false brethren plotting against his life and offering him poison instead of wine could embitter [Col. 0112C]? Scripture indeed proclaims Moses “the meekest of all men who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12:13); yet does it deny that his spirit was provoked? Does it not recall that he was angry, even very angry, against his rivals? (Num. 16:15). But I remember reading of the gentleness of our master as marvelous not only toward those who reviled him but even toward evildoers; I do not remember reading of his anger. Nevertheless, neither in him nor in Moses is the praise of holy gentleness prejudiced if a just man burns with zeal against sinners, without which gentleness is lukewarmness or cowardice. For how could that gentleness make someone holy which was condemned in Eli, who was otherwise holy? (1 Sam. 2).

“Have peace among yourselves,” commands that peaceful and gentle Master [Col. 0112D]; but first He adds, “Have salt in yourselves” (Mark 9:49), knowing, indeed, that the gentleness of peace is a nurse of vices unless the harshness of zeal has first sprinkled them with biting salt, just as mild weather causes meat to breed worms unless the heat of salt has dried it. Therefore have peace among yourselves, but peace seasoned with the salt of wisdom; pursue gentleness, but gentleness fervent with faith.

3. You too will be holy in faith and gentleness; nor will gentleness now be suspect if faith has gone before it—provided only that the faith be not feigned but true, not dead but living and life-giving. Moses’ faith was not merely living or life-giving, but steadfast and fearless, [Col. 0113A] concerning whom Paul writes: “By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s wrath.” Kings are high-spirited, but faith is more high-spirited still, since it sees their power as nothing and therefore, secure as though superior, mocks all the frenzy of persecutors; it is readier and stronger to endure than their fury is to persecute.

In that memorable faith of Moses, with which, on the occasion of today’s reading, we said that the faith of our holy father Benedict should be compared, the Apostle seems to me to commend two things: namely, that this same Moses, made an example of faith, despised this world’s prosperity and did not fear its adversities. He despised prosperity, “esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt”; he did not fear adversity, that is, “not fearing the king’s wrath.” [Col. 0113B] For each point the Apostle adds the reason why this could be so, so that we may learn whence our faith is weakened within us. “He deemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for,” he says, “he looked to the recompense.” “He did not fear the king’s wrath, for,” he says, “he endured as though seeing the Invisible One” (Heb. 11:27, 26).

Certainly, temporal things come to be counted as nothing when eternal things are kept before the eyes; human power is easily despised when divine power, as though ever impending, is feared. Faith alone accomplishes both, for its eyes are so vivid and so penetrating that it extends its lively gaze to things still to come and fixes its clear sight upon things which, though present, are nevertheless hidden. For faith, [Col. 0113C] illumined by the eternal Spirit, can be hindered neither by the delay of time nor by the burden of the body from both preceding time, by anticipating what is future, and surpassing the body, by beholding what is spiritual.

Faith has a twofold power, contemplating not things seen but things unseen; and there is likewise a twofold reason why things are unseen. Either they are unseen because they are not present, or because, although present, they are spiritual. The promised future goods are not present; God himself, who promises or threatens, is present but hidden, because he is spirit. Now faith, because it is “the substance of things hoped for,” anticipates the future goods for which it hopes as though present, and already [Col. 0113D] causes them, as it were, to subsist in the believer’s heart. Likewise, because it is “the proof of things not appearing” (ibid., v. 1), it demonstrates, establishes, and convinces itself that God, though he does not appear, is nevertheless present.

For him who said, “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. 2:6), faith was the substance of things hoped for. For him who endured “as though seeing the Invisible One” (Heb. 11:27), it was the proof of things not appearing. For when one said, “We were saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24), did he not show that what he hoped for and awaited through patience already subsisted in his heart through faith? And when one set the Lord always before his eyes, did he not hold it as certain, through faith’s proof, that he who did not appear was present? (Ps. 15:8).

[Col. 0114A] 4. What Scripture says, “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17), is altogether most fittingly applicable to this faith. For it makes a person righteous and keeps that person righteous; and, so that one may live forever, meanwhile it nourishes him with the joy of hope. What so recalls and preserves a person from sin as faith, which endures and keeps watch as though seeing the Invisible One? What so makes one rejoice in hope as faith, which always looks to the recompense?

Why, brothers, are we negligent except because we do not attend watchfully enough to the presence of our Judge? Or why are we almost swallowed up by sorrow except because we do not faithfully enough consider the promised recompense? These are indeed the two evils—negligence and sorrow—from which our unbelief grievously suffers. For [Col. 0114B] either we neglect the commandments; or, if necessity and fear restrain us from negligence, we do not work cheerfully, nor, as faith requires, are we consoled in our labor by hope of recompense. “Those who approach God,” he says, “must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. 11:6). If we do not ignore that he is, we have the safeguard of fear; if we do not ignore that he rewards those who seek him, we have the consolation of hope. Where there is the safeguard of fear, there is no place for negligence; where there is the consolation of hope, there is no place for sorrow.

Just as the fear that leads to salvation arises from faith by which God is believed to exist, so, when he is not believed to exist or is ignored, the reins are loosed for every evil. Why indeed did they become corrupt and abominable in their iniquities, except because that universal [Col. 0114C] fool said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 52:2, 1)? Or, if one is not permitted not to know God, “there is no fear of God before his eyes”; rather, “he acts deceitfully in his presence,” feigning not to know what he knows against his will, “so that his iniquity may be found unto hatred” (Ps. 35:2, 3). Most deservedly is he deceitful unto hatred who does not lack knowledge of God but has hatred of him. For how does he not hate God whose gaze he avoids, whose authority he despises, and who would wish there to be no judgment? The ignorant person will indeed be ignored; but the one who hates will also be hated. The former will be rejected by the truth of judgment; upon the latter vengeance will be taken by the severity of hatred.

5. Thus, brothers, feigned and deceitful faith, which conceals itself from itself, is more dangerous than no faith at all. [Col. 0114D] No faith says in its heart through folly, “There is no God”; feigned faith acts deceitfully in his presence through wickedness, and pretends not to know God or to be known by God, while knowingly and deliberately—indeed, foolishly and shamelessly—it sins beneath his eyes. Yet I do not know how that can be called faith which makes people feigned and deceitful rather than faithful. I know, indeed, that the earth is full of the confession of faith; yet I hear the prophet lamenting that faith has perished from the earth (Jer. 7:28). Do you suppose that, if the Son of Man came now, he would find faith upon the earth? (Luke 18:8). Would he count as faith this feigned faith of the negligent and contemptuous, by which he judges the blindness of unbelievers less severely and considers the belief of demons better? “The demons believe and tremble” (Jas. [Col. 0115A] 2:19); people believe and do not tremble. Demons revere him in whom they believe; people, while they believe in him, neither fear nor revere him, and are judged more severely for their contempt.

Therefore, brothers, let us not be deceived by the general name “faith,” as though every sort of faith were to be counted unto righteousness. Rather, let us remember how the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth defined the faith by which God is to be pleased: “Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not appearing.” This is the faith that works through love: so that hope may arise from faith at the prompting of consciousness of merits, and faith may be laid beneath as a subject and foundation upon which the eternal goods that are to be hoped for are built. “Without this faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:1, 6), and with it it is impossible to displease God. “Your eyes, O Lord, look upon faith” (Jer. 5:3), said he who stood continually before you through faith. Entirely justly and deservedly so: it is a fitting reciprocity that your eyes, O Lord, should look upon faith, because my eyes are always toward the faithful Lord.

6. But if we, brothers, are as though without faith, we put God behind our back, so that, ignoring his fear, we look instead toward vanities. [Col. 0116A] With what face, then, do we think we ought to be looked upon? Indeed, we shall be looked upon—but with what countenance? “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17). But how angry, how terrible, how unbearable that face is will at last be known when those who hate him flee from before his face. And from your face, O Lord, where will they flee except into outer darkness, into that chaos and abyss of fire and gloom? Then they will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30), judging it easier to be swallowed by the abyss of hell than to endure the face of God in anger.

But then the righteous will stand in great steadfastness. Then faith, which now stands anxiously in the Lord’s presence in order to see his will, will stand secure in order to see his glory. “Keep watch, brothers; stand firm in the faith” [Col. 0116B] (1 Cor. 16:13). The person whom faith makes watchful through fear cannot sleep through negligence; the person whom faith roots in hope cannot stagger through mistrust. “Let all that you do be done in love,” so that gentleness may be joined to faith, in order that it may be said of each of you: “In his faith and gentleness the Lord made him holy” (Ecclus. 45:4). May the Holy One of holy ones grant this, he who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0115]

### SERMON I. On the joy of this day and the praises of the Virgin Mother

[Col. 0115C]

1. Fittingly, during these days of Lenten observance, the feast of the Lord’s Annunciation occurs for us, so that those wearied by bodily affliction may be refreshed by spiritual joy, and those humbled by the grief of penitence may be consoled by the announcement of him who takes away the sins of the world. For thus you have it written: “Sorrow in a man’s heart will humble him, and he will be made joyful by a good word” (Prov. 12:25). Truly, the good word, the faithful word worthy of all acceptance, is the Gospel of our salvation, which the angel sent by God announced to Mary on this day; and day uttered unto day, the angel unto the Virgin, the joyful word concerning the Incarnation of the Word. [Col. 0115D] That word, in promising a Son to the Virgin, promises pardon to the guilty, redemption to captives, opening to those shut in, and life to those buried. In proclaiming the kingdom of the Son, that word announces also the glory of the righteous; it terrifies hell and gladdens heaven, and, just as through knowledge of the mysteries, so also through the novelty of joys, it seems to have increased the perfection of the angels.

Whom, then, would that good word not gladden in affliction? Whom would that word not console in humiliation? “Remember,” David says, “your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope; for this has consoled me in my humiliation” (Ps. 118:49–50). He had received only the word of promise; no indication of its fulfillment had yet appeared. The delay of what he desired afflicted him, but the certainty of hope arising from the faithfulness of the Promiser consoled him.

[Col. 0116C] 2. If David nourished his spirit by hope alone of this salvation which was being reserved for us, what joy, what delight ought the actual bestowal of the thing itself to have been for us? O happiness of these times! O unhappiness of these times! Are they not happy times, in which there is such fullness of grace and every good? Are they not unhappy times, in which there is such ingratitude among the redeemed? For behold, the fullness of time comes, in which God sends his Son, that he may become the Son of Man and the Savior of humankind; and behold, the enormity of the times, that sinful man should disdain his Savior. Salvation is announced to the lost, and they despise it; life is promised to the desperate, and they neglect it; God comes to human beings, and they do not rise.

A person rises who lifts himself by some devotion in order to give glory to God’s grace; a person rises who at least receives with joy the word of his own salvation. Yet I know—I know who is gladdened by that good word: surely, the one first humbled by devout sorrow in his heart: sorrow over pilgrimage and exile, sorrow over the bonds of death and the dangers of hell; one who mourns daily, lamenting that the snares of death have overtaken him and the dangers of hell have found him. [Col. 0116D] To this person, certainly, that heavenly message of today comes pleasantly; this person receives gladly the word concerning God’s Son. To this mournful and grieving person, distressed that he has been forestalled and surrounded by such great evils, the Liberator is announced not without joy—the one who will give the oil of joy instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a spirit of grief; who will indeed put an end to miseries and grant endless blessedness to the wretched. Therefore blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled; blessed are those whom devout sorrow in their heart has humbled, for they shall be gladdened by the good word.

Surely good and consoling is your word, O Lord—your almighty Word—who today came from royal seats into the Virgin’s womb, where he also established for himself a royal seat. Although he now sits there, like a king in heaven surrounded by an army of angels, he is nevertheless the comforter of those who mourn upon earth.

[Col. 0117A] 3. The Virgin was indeed chosen from a royal lineage: a noble offspring of royal stock, but a still nobler disposition of royal virtue. Thus maternal nobility might render royal honor to the eternal King, the Son of the King, and a royal throne in the virginal chamber of the Queen Mother might receive him who came from the royal throne of the Father. For in her and from her Wisdom “built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1); in her and from her he prepared a throne for himself, when in her and from her he fashioned a body for himself so perfect and fitting in every respect that it might be a house for his repose, a throne for judgment, a tabernacle for battle, and a chair for teaching.

But consider whether perhaps she is the throne of David his father (Luke 1:70) which the angel promises will be given to him—not because David sat upon her, but because she was taken and fashioned from David’s seed. And certainly, even if she is not David’s throne, yet she is “your throne, O God, for ever and ever.” Even if she is not David’s seat of rule, she is certainly a throne high and exalted above every creature. [Col. 0117B] If, moreover, anyone should interpret as the body itself that great throne which King Solomon made of ivory, the body which our Peaceful One took today from the Virgin, he will not seem far from the truth. For what follows—“and he clothed it with exceedingly yellow gold” (1 Kgs. 10:18)—is quite fitting for the same body, which the Lord has now clothed with the splendor of unbearable radiance. “He clothed it,” he says, “with yellow gold.” Certainly, if you ask the eyes of the Apostles who saw him transfigured on the mountain (Matt. 17:1–2), they will confess that the gold was exceedingly yellow—that is, that the body’s brilliance was excessive, which they could not bear—although it is customary in Scripture to use *nimis* (“exceedingly”) for *valde* (“very”). The other things which Scripture goes on to relate concerning the magnificence of that throne (1 Kgs. 10:18–20) will, I think, be more fittingly understood, if anyone wishes to expound them, of Christ’s body, which is the Church.

[Col. 0117D] 4. Yet at present I prefer to marvel at that ivory, so precious—indeed, beyond price—of virginal chastity, from which he who sits above the Cherubim chose to make himself a throne: “This is my resting-place for ever and ever; here I will sit, for I have chosen her” (Ps. 131:14). How gleaming was that ivory which pleased the eyes of so great and wealthy a King, in whose days silver was of no value! How cool, since it did not grow warm even at conception! How solid, since childbirth did not violate it! How white and ruddy at once, since the brightness of eternal light and the fire of the Holy Spirit filled it with all their fullness!

For Mary herself is whiter than snow, ruddier than ancient ivory. Chastity gave her an incomparable whiteness, and charity—or martyrdom—a glowing redness surpassing the ancient chosen ones. For a sword passed through her very soul, so that she might be mother of the supreme Virgin and Martyr, herself both virgin and martyr, white and ruddy, as her beloved is “white and ruddy” (Song 5:10). [Col. 0118A] Finally, just as Solomon, amid all his treasures and such great wealth, had nothing so precious that he judged it preferable to ivory for that work, the magnificent throne of his glory, so Mary found before God a singular grace beyond all the elect, angels and human beings alike: namely, that she should conceive and bear God’s Son, and that the power of the Most High should hew out for itself from the ivory of her body a glorious throne without hands.

That throne is indeed glorious and marvelous, concerning which Scripture testifies that “no such work was made in all the kingdoms” (1 Kgs. 10:20). This could readily be proved by the testimonies of the angels, who continually and insatiably long to gaze upon the glory and beauty of the Lord’s body. Since in all kingdoms no such work was made, let everything that has been made bend the knee to it in all the kingdoms—of heaven, earth, and hell. How blessed, therefore, is that ivory womb, from which was taken the Redeemer’s ivory flesh: the price of souls, the wonder of angels, the seat of highest majesty, the throne [Col. 0118B] of power, the food of immortal life, the medicine for sin, the restoration of health! “All who touched him were healed of their diseases” (Mark 6:56); for power went out from him and healed them all (Luke 6:19).

5. Blessed, therefore, is the womb that bore you, Lord Jesus! Blessed the chastity of the virginal womb which supplied the material for this work! Blessed indeed, my brothers, is the brightness of that ivory—that is, the whiteness of chastity. Our Solomon’s choice prefers it to neither the gold of worldly wisdom, nor the silver of eloquence, nor the jewel of any outstanding grace—provided, however, that chastity is commended by humility, since “the Lord looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48).

Accordingly Solomon, when in the song of love he proclaimed the chastity of the virgin—or bride, indeed, or bridegroom, since where their spirit is one and their flesh one, their praise too is in many respects one—wishing to teach that her chastity was adorned, and ours ought to be adorned, with other virtues, says: “Her belly is ivory, set with sapphires” (Song 5:14). [Col. 0118C] And that you may know that chastity is a receptacle of other virtues or graces, the spice-stores or perfume chambers of our Solomon are nothing but ivory houses, as David sang in that epithalamium whose title-inscription, “A song for the Beloved,” shows should be understood of Christ, Bridegroom of the Church: “Myrrh and balm and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses, from which daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Ps. 44:9–10).

The ivory bodies of the saints are houses of Christ; they are Christ’s garments; they are Christ’s members; they are temples of the Holy Spirit. From these garments of Christ, from these ivory houses, all the fragrance of virtues and gifts breathes forth to him; from them the daughters of Apostles and Prophets delight and honor the King of kings. You yourselves, my brothers, have experienced, since each of you began to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:4–5), what perfumes and fragrances have been poured in by divine generosity; how the body, once a sewer of filth, is now the venerable sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, and what was once a gulf of shameful deeds is now a kind of storehouse of graces.

[Col. 0119B] 6. “Myrrh and balm and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses.” We inhabit houses of clay; but although they are clay by the quality of their material, through the virtue of continence they become ivory. If myrrh first begins to breathe forth from them through the mortification of pleasures, other kinds of aromatic spices will follow, exhaling the manifold grace of virtues. They will breathe forth delightfully for Christ, as from his garments; they will also breathe forth widely and far to neighbors, as the good odor of Christ in every place.

As soon as Isaac perceived the fragrance of these garments of Christ, he said: “Behold, the odor of my son is like the odor of a field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). And the Bridegroom speaks to the bride, who is also his body and garment, saying: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Col. 0119C] (Song 4:11). This fragrance of incense, most pleasing to the Bridegroom, will be breathed forth by the devotion, brothers, of your hearts, if it is so fragrant and devout that your prayer may be directed like incense in the sight of the Most High and rise before him like a little column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense (ibid. 3:6).

Indeed, myrrh gives him fragrance from your bodies; it surely gives fragrance to me also. Would that incense might likewise give fragrance from your hearts, so that the Bridegroom, finding you not only chaste but also devout, may deign to visit you more frequently and say: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” (ibid. 4:6). Yet this saying seems to be a prophecy of this day, foretold long ago through Solomon and fulfilled today through Jesus. For today he came to that mountain, highest of mountains: a mountain not only of myrrh and incense but of every aromatic spice. I mean the Virgin of virgins, full of every grace, among which, I think, the myrrh of chastity and the incense of devotion especially gave fragrance to the Bridegroom. [Col. 0119D] This fragrance, my brothers, is above every aromatic spice; this fragrance draws and invites the Lord of majesty from on high, that he may bow the heavens and descend—as this day proves, when the Most High, having sent an angel from heaven, himself also descended into his Mother’s womb, while ever remaining in the bosom of the Father, with whom he lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

983 **SERMON II. On the Incarnation of the Word in Mary and in the faithful soul**

[Col. 0120A]

1. Today the Word became flesh and began to dwell among us, according to the rule of sound faith handed down to us by the definition of ecclesiastical doctrines. [Note: [Col. 0119D] That is, Gennadius.] For the Church most firmly holds, and in no way doubts, that Christ’s flesh was not conceived before it was assumed by the Word; rather, the very Word of God was conceived in assuming flesh, and the flesh was conceived in the Word’s incarnation.

Therefore, from this day the Lord of hosts is with us, the God of Jacob our protector, because today is the Lord’s assumption of us, so that glory may dwell in our land (Ps. 84:10). Truly, today you have blessed your land, O Lord—that woman blessed among women. Today you have given the gracious gift of the Holy Spirit, so that our land might yield the blessed fruit of her womb, and, with the heavens raining dew from above, the virginal womb might bring forth the Savior. The land was cursed through the deed of the transgressor; though cultivated, it produces thorns and thistles for the heirs of the curse (Gen. 3:17–18). But now the land is blessed through the work of the Redeemer: it bears remission of sins and the fruit of life for all, and undoes for Adam’s children the prejudice of the original [Col. 0120C] curse.

Truly blessed is that land which, entirely untouched—neither dug nor sown—brings forth the Savior from the dew of heaven alone and provides mortals with the bread of angels, the nourishment of eternal life. Therefore, although this land was uncultivated, it seemed a desert, but was filled with rich fruit; it seemed a wilderness of solitude, but was a paradise of blessedness. Truly it was God’s garden of delights, a wilderness whose fields brought forth a fragrant shoot; truly a well-filled desert, from which the Father sent forth the Lamb, ruler of the earth. “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, from the rock of the desert” (Isa. 16:1): that is, hew the Rock from the rock; let holy and inviolate virginity bring forth the Holy One and the Inviolate.

Indeed, in this respect Christ’s setting corresponds fittingly to his rising, and his burial to his conception: the Lamb is sent from the rock of the desert to be laid in the rock of the tomb; and he whose body was to have a tomb hewn in rock, from the beginning of his conception both hewed out a body for himself from a rock and a place in rock for that body. Thus he did not lessen the integrity of the rock when he was sent forth from it, just as he did not open the rock sealed for burial when he came forth from it.

[Col. 0120D] 2. Therefore, if “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), as the Apostle says, the Son does not fall short of his Mother, when she too is designated by the name of rock. Is she not rightly called a rock, whose purpose was firm in love of integrity, whose affection was solid, and whose very sensibility was wholly unfeeling and stony against the allurements of sin? Is not virginal integrity rightly called a rock, since by its own nature it bears nothing, and when it bears through the power of divine dew, it knows neither the opening that admits conception nor the opening that sends forth birth?

“But let the earth be opened,” says Isaiah, “let it be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). O holy Isaiah, you say, “Let it be opened”; what then is this which the Lord declares to Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened” (Ezek. 44:2)? Was only the counsel concerning the Mother’s fecundity revealed to you, while the mystery of her integrity, forever closed, remained hidden from you?

“Far from it!” he says. “No one is more conscious than I of this secret. For how could the mystery of perpetual virginity have escaped me, when so long before I prophesied: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son’” (Isa. 7:14)? You ask, then, how we can say—I, “Let it be opened”; he, “It shall not be opened.” It shall not be opened to a man; it shall be opened to the Lord, as Ezekiel himself is told there: “No man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it.” [Col. 0121B] Yet what is opened to the Lord is not the virginal integrity of the body; for, as Ezekiel added after these words, “It shall remain shut even for the prince himself” (Ezek. 44:2–3). Rather, the ear and the gate of the heart are opened, because the Word who was to be incarnate entered through the Virgin’s ear and came forth incarnate through the closed gate of the body.

For the almighty Word of God, although he assumed our weakness, diminished none of his omnipotence for himself, so that, contrary to the nature of flesh and beyond the comprehension of our understanding, he could pass his tangible body through closed and intact barriers, as he also showed to the disciples when he entered with the doors shut: what reason cannot grasp, their eyes proved.

[Col. 0121C] 3. Therefore be confident, O undefiled Virgin, O gate of the sanctuary forever shut; confidently open to the Lord God of Israel, who long ago cries to you: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved” (Song 5:2). You have no reason to fear for your integrity: God does not know how to violate what is intact, but how to restore what has been violated. If you are fitted for the Word of God, then you are not merely shut but sealed. “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (ibid. 8:6). For Jesus, impressed upon the heart and expressed in deed, is plainly an inviolable seal and defense of his bride’s chastity; and by imprinting upon her the pattern of imitation, he also imposes the safeguard of incorruption.

Therefore, O faithful Virgin, let your ear be open to hear and your mind to believe: receive through the ear the angel’s word, receive in the heart the Word of the Most High, and conceive in the body the Son of God. You also say, O blessed one, humble as you are faithful, say: “The Lord opened my ear; but I do not resist; I have not gone backward” (Isa. 50:5). “Behold the handmaid of the Lord: I stand ready for his will; indeed, I will aid it with my prayers if I can. Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). To say this, to offer such devotion, is truly to open one’s breast to the Lord; it is also to open one’s mouth and draw in the spirit. Thus indeed the earth was opened, that it might receive the dew which the heavens rained down from above and bring forth the Savior.

A noble shoot, [Col. 0122A] a righteous shoot, a fragrant shoot, the Lord’s shoot, which is now in magnificence and glory, since the same fruit of the earth is high above all things: that is, God is exalted above the heavens, and his glory above all the earth. For it makes no difference whether you call him shoot, fruit, or flower, since all these things—and indeed countless others—are the one Christ: one reality, but manifold grace, and the diverse operation of one power. Although the poverty of human understanding and speech may apply infinite names by analogy, it cannot exhaust the meaning of the reality.

He is aptly called together shoot, flower, and fruit, because from the beginning of his conception, without stages of development, he existed perfect in himself with every power and grace. In us, however, he is first a shoot, when faith breaks forth into confession or evident work; afterward a flower, when God’s sanctification blooms upon one advancing, with a certain visible beauty of virtues; and finally fruit, when blessedness satisfies the perfected person. Most beautifully and watchfully, moreover, divine providence preordained not only the mysteries but also their foreshadowings: the place where the earth brought forth the Savior, the righteous shoot, and where the flower rose from the rod and root of Jesse, was called Nazareth—that is, holiness, shoot, flower, little shrub—so that the event bore witness to the place, and the place to the event, with consonant speech; and at once the name of the place announced what was to occur, while the accomplished event indicated the reason for the name.

[Col. 0122C] 4. Forgive me, my brothers, for I who ought to have served the instruction of your conduct have perhaps lingered longer than was necessary upon admiration and praise of that ineffable mystery. What wonder if I marvel at that which astonishes the angels, if I am eager to proclaim the glory of God which the heavens declare? What wonder if I delight in what gladdens blessed spirits, justifies sinners, and glorifies the righteous?

Yet I do not know whether any formation of conduct can be more effective or sweeter than faithful and devout contemplation of this mystery, that is, of the incarnate Word. What can so stir a person to love God as God’s love for humankind, preceding humanity with such vehemence that he willed to become human for humanity’s sake? What so nourishes love of neighbor as the likeness and nature of the neighbor in God’s humanity? Nor can I think of any greater example of humility than God’s emptying of himself into the form of a servant, and a servitude greater than that of a servant. What, moreover, commends chastity equally with the fact that chastity itself brings forth the Savior? Or what more clearly shows faith’s power and merit than that the Virgin conceived God by faith and by faith merited the fulfillment of all things divinely promised to her? “Blessed,” it says, “is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (ibid., v. 45).

And so that you may know more fully that the Virgin’s conception is not only mystical but also moral: what is a sacrament for redemption is also an example for your imitation. You plainly render the grace of the sacrament void in yourself if [Col. 0123A] you do not imitate the virtue of the example. She who conceived God by faith promises the same to you, if you have faith: namely, that if you faithfully choose to receive the word from the mouth of the heavenly messenger, you too may conceive him whom the whole world cannot contain.

You may conceive him in heart, indeed even in body—not, however, by bodily act or form, but truly in your body—since the Apostle commands us to glorify and bear God in our body (1 Cor. 6:20). Therefore attend diligently to your hearing, as it is written; for “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God” (Rom. 10:17). Undoubtedly God’s angel announces this to you when a faithful preacher speaks with you concerning fear or love of God; and you must not doubt that he is called, and is, an angel of the Lord of hosts (Mal. 2:16–17).

How blessed are those who can say: “From your fear, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:17–18)! This is none other than the Spirit of the Savior, the truth of Jesus Christ. See God’s ineffable condescension, and at the same time the power of the incomprehensible mystery: he who created you is created in you; and, as though it were too little that you should have him as Father, he also wills that you should become a mother to him. “Whoever,” he says, “does the will of my Father is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50).

O faithful soul, spread wide your bosom; enlarge your affections. Do not be constricted in your inward parts: conceive him whom creation cannot contain. Open your ear to hear the Word of God: this is the way by which the spirit is conceived in the womb of the heart; by this means the bones of Christ—that is, the virtues—are joined together in the womb of one who is pregnant.

5. Thank you, Holy Spirit, who breathe where you will. By your gift I see not one but innumerable souls of the faithful pregnant with that noble seed. Guard your work, lest any one of them miscarry and cast forth the conception of the divine offspring, unformed or dead. You also, blessed mothers of so glorious a progeny, attend to yourselves until Christ be formed in you (Gal. 4:19). Take care lest some more serious outward injury harm the tender fetus, lest you introduce into the womb—that is, into the mind—anything that may extinguish the Spirit whom you have conceived. Spare, if not yourselves, at least the Son of God within you. Spare, I say, yourselves not only from evil deeds and words, but also from harmful thoughts and deadly pleasures, which indeed suffocate the seed of God. Therefore guard your hearts with every vigilance, because from them life will proceed, when the mature birth is brought forth and the life of Christ, now hidden in your hearts, is manifested in your mortal flesh. You have conceived the Spirit of salvation, but you are still in labor; you have not yet given birth. If there is travail in giving birth, there is great consolation in the hope of the birth. “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow” (John 16:21) from her labor; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish because of her joy, because Christ, the human being, will be born into the outward world of our body, which is also customarily called the lesser world. For he who is now conceived as God [Col. 0124A] in our spirits, conforming them to the spirit of his love, will then, as a human being, be born in our bodies, conforming them to the body of his glory, in which God lives and is glorified through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the signs of this mystery.

1. “Hear, house of David: behold, the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7:13–14). Today this prophecy has been fulfilled in your hearing. For today you have heard fulfilled, just as you had heard it promised, that ineffable miracle of virginal conception: today the Virgin conceived. And this sign, unheard of in earlier ages, the Lord has given in our age. As Jeremiah likewise foretold, by the same Spirit [Col. 0124B] and in the same sense: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth, because a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). For what is Jeremiah’s “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man,” except what Isaiah says: “The Lord will give a sign: a Virgin shall conceive a son” (Isa. 7:13–14)? This, surely, is what “shall encompass” means. She shall not receive from intercourse with a man, but shall conceive from herself alone, within herself, and shall clothe him in the covering of a mother’s body alone.

Otherwise, let the Jews say, if they can, what sign the Lord gave in this, if not a virgin but a young woman—as they falsely interpret it—conceived; or what new thing the Lord created if a woman encompassed a male conceived from a male. Iniquity may indeed lie to itself; but “in the abundance [Col. 0124C] of your power, O Lord, your enemies shall lie to you,” so that, while the perversity and small number of the Jews deny your power, the faith of all peoples may confess it more gloriously and abundantly. “Let the peoples confess you, O God; let all the peoples confess you, because the earth has yielded its fruit”: the Virgin has put forth Jesus (Ps. 66:6). Whether the Jews will or not, the Lord has created the newness of this miracle as a sign of their unbelief—indeed, as a sign which they contradict even today, from, I think, a persistence more hateful than their ignorance is pitiable.

2. Yet it is not foreign to the origin and habit of the viperous brood that they should contradict this sign after it has happened, since from the beginning, in their most impious father and king Ahaz, they contradicted its happening. For the Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: “Ask a sign for yourself.” “I will not ask,” he said, “and I will not test the Lord” (Isa. 7:10–12). O profane religion! O execrable piety! O deceitful humility! By not testing the Lord, as you claim, you despise the Lord. For how would you test him if you faithfully obeyed? But now how do you not grievously test him whom you provoke by open contempt?

We know indeed—we know—the deceit and envy of the Jewish root, which began even before Christ was born to envy his glory. For this Ahaz also, so far as his life and conduct allow us to understand—for he was a worshiper of idols—refused to ask for a sign when commanded for no other reason of religion or fear, except, of course, that the Lord might not be glorified. [Col. 0125A] Certainly, the Jews’ perversity is astonishing and plainly worthy of the anger of God and human beings: when they are commanded to seek signs, they refuse—not, as they pretend, lest they test God, but lest they glorify the Lord (Matt. 16:4); when they are not commanded, they test and seek them. For Jews seek signs, as it were by nature and habit; and if signs are given, they slander them and strive to deny them, thereby openly confessing that they sought while testing, not so that they might believe the one performing the miracle, but so that they might mock him if he did not perform it.

“O sinful nation, wicked seed, criminal children!” (Isa. 1:4), says Isaiah. “Is it too little for you to be troublesome to human beings—to me and to the other prophets, indeed to the whole human race—because you are troublesome also to my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign” (Isa. 7:13–14). Since you perversely walk contrary to him, he too, as Scripture says, will walk perversely toward you. You do not wish a sign to be given lest the author of the miracle be glorified; and therefore he himself will give one, so that he may be glorified and you put to shame. “Do a sign for me for good, O Lord, that those who hate me may see and be ashamed” (Ps. 85:17): thus the Son speaks to the Father concerning the Jews.

3. But I judge that the first sign which Father and Son worked, for the confusion of unbelievers and the glory of believers, as a testimony to their power and a work of our salvation, is today’s conception of the Virgin. For after the words “The Lord will give a sign” had been set forth concerning it, as though people asked what sign, the context of the Prophet added—in the Evangelist’s words—[Col. 0125C] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14; Luke 1:31). Thus either the context lacks coherence or truth, or else—what is more probable—the Jewish lie has no hiding-place.

Rightly, therefore, when “a wicked and adulterous generation” now seeks a sign, no sign is given to it except the sign of Jonah (Matt. 16:4), so that those whom the sign of power does not build up because of the perversity of their minds may be scandalized by the sign of weakness: namely, the three-day burial and death. For the word of the cross and of death is a scandal to the Jews who are perishing; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God (1 Cor. 1:18). Nor is the Son of Man less or weaker for us in the heart of the earth than in the assembly at the Father’s right hand.

The sign which they refused—whether “in the depths of hell” or “in the heights above”—we receive with full faith and devout veneration, recognizing that the Son whom [Col. 0125D] the Virgin conceives is, in the depths of hell, for us a sign of liberation and pardon; and, in the heights above, a sign and hope of exultation and glory. For he who first descended into the lower parts of the earth, in order by the blood of his covenant to draw prisoners out of the waterless pit, is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things (Eph. 4:9–10). The Lord has now raised the first sign upon the gibbet of the cross, and afterward upon the throne of his kingdom; and he has exalted the sign among the peoples of the nations, because the Jewish people contradicted him. Daily, from the four winds, he gathers the scattered members of the true Israel to this sign.

“O Root [Col. 0126A] of Jesse, who stand as a sign for the peoples, over whom kings now keep their mouths shut”: may the mouths of those speaking iniquity also be stopped—that is, of the blaspheming Jews, who still contradict the spotless sign of your conception and do not believe even the angel Gabriel when he says that no word is impossible with you (Luke 1:30–31). Blessed is she who believed, for whom this answer sufficed, and who, after asking how she would receive a Son when she knew no man, was thereafter made secure both concerning her virginity and concerning her offspring.

4. Whatever the impiety of unbelievers may chatter, for us let the Virgin conceive and bear a Son; for we have a sign for good: both Mother and Son. For us the Mother is wholly a miracle: uniquely and without example, both mother and virgin. For us the Son is wholly a miracle: uniquely, indeed incomprehensibly, both God and human. The Mother—a virgin conceiving and giving birth—is a sign to us that this one who is conceived and born is God and human; the Son, performing divine acts and suffering human things, is a sign to us that he will transform into God the human being for whom he is conceived, born, and even suffers.

Yet among all the human weaknesses and injuries which divine condescension endured for us, I consider that one of the first in time and almost the greatest in humility was this: that that unbounded majesty endured being conceived in a womb and contained there for nine months. Where else did he so empty himself? Or when did he appear so wholly to have departed [Col. 0126C] from himself? For so long that Wisdom speaks nothing; that Power works nothing openly; no visible sign reveals the majesty hidden in enclosure. He did not appear so weak on the cross, where what was his weakness immediately appeared stronger than all human beings: when, even in dying, he glorifies the thief, and in breathing out inspires the centurion; when the hour-long suffering of his passion makes not only the elements of creation suffer with him, but also subjects opposing powers to the suffering of eternal pains. But in the womb he is as though he were not; omnipotent power is inactive as though it could do nothing; and the eternal Word restrains himself in silence.

5. Yet for you, brothers, that silence [Col. 0126D] of the Word speaks; it cries out for you. It commends to you the discipline of silence. “In silence and hope shall be your strength” (Isa. 30:15), as Isaiah promises, who defined the practice of righteousness as silence (Isa. 32:17). For just as that child, conceived in the womb, advanced to the maturity of birth under deep and prolonged silence, so the discipline of silence nourishes, forms, and strengthens the human spirit; and the more secretly it does so, the more safely and healthfully it bestows growth.

The natural human being, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, does not know what the way of the spirit is or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman (Eccl. 11:5). But “my bone was not hidden from you,” says the holy man to God, “when you made me in the secret place” (Ps. 138:15) of the mind, beneath the hiddenness of silence. Nor is this mystery hidden from you, my brothers, whose experience and confession testify to me how a quiet and modest spirit is strengthened, enriched, and flourishes under silence; how, conversely, through words it is, as it were, loosened and drained by a kind of paralysis; how it grows thin, withers, and falls away dry.

Finally, if strength were not in silence, Solomon would never have said: “Like a city lying open and without the encircling of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28). But if you ask with what business the mind should be occupied in silence, we lay upon you nothing burdensome: eat your bread, as the Lord himself, conceived within, shows you by his own example. For what did the prophet say of him when speaking of the eastern gate, always [Col. 0127B] shut, in the house of the Lord, which nevertheless admitted and sent forth the God of Israel? “The prince himself,” he says, “shall sit in it, in order to eat bread before the Lord” (Ezek. 44:3).

“He shall sit in it,” he says, because he shall rest in it, of which he himself says: “This is my rest” (Ps. 31:14). He shall sit in it as upon the great throne which, as I said elsewhere, King Solomon made for himself from ivory (1 Kgs. 10:18). If you consider the narrowness of the womb, it is indeed a confined place; if the breadth of the heart, it is a great throne. Because of this breadth, even the womb became capable of such majesty. Therefore the prince sat in it and ate bread, because, he says, “If anyone opens to me, I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20).

6. This supper is not without bread, since he who dines is himself the bread of life, the bread who today descends from heaven and gives life to the world. But it is a marvelous thing if the one who dines is also that which is dined upon, and the one who eats is himself the bread which he eats. Truly it is marvelous, but true: Christ is nourished by no bread other than himself. For he is wholly bread: the Word in virtue of himself, the flesh in virtue of the Word’s union with it. Otherwise flesh profits nothing, since it is the Spirit who gives life (John 6:64); nor does a human being live by bread alone, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God (Matt. 4:4).

Every word proceeding from the mouth of God is the one and only-begotten Word of the Father, which, though simple, nevertheless contains within itself the principle and form of every divine word. Therefore [Col. 0128A] the Word feeds upon the Word; the Son lives by himself, for as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself (John 5:26). Yet by another mode, though still with ineffable blessedness, that soul was nourished by the Word, being joined to the Word himself in person; and with incomparable happiness that prince, seated in the gate of the virginal womb, ate the bread of the Word before the Lord.

You also, then, if you are wise, will perform this work in your silence: you will eat the bread of the divine Word before the Lord, preserving and pondering in your heart, like Mary, the things spoken concerning Christ. Christ will delight to eat this bread with you; and he who feeds you will himself be fed in you (Luke 22:15, 19). And that bread, the more it is eaten, will abound the more to be eaten, because grace is not diminished [Col. 0128B] by use but increased.

7. Let Jesus, conceived and carried in the womb, therefore be your example in this: just as that light and sweet burden, although it made Mary pregnant, did not weigh down her womb, so may the womb of the Church not find you burdensome or troublesome. The Church, brothers, is pregnant—not, like Mary, with Jesus alone, but, like Rebekah, with Jacob and Esau; that is, not only with the good and well-ordered, but also with the harsh and undisciplined. Yet even such persons the womb of the Church receives and embraces, for the sake of Jesus’ name, or perhaps because of some beginning of his substance in them.

But when the discordant little ones struggled with one another in Rebekah’s womb—she who had first prayed that she might conceive—her womb was afflicted by the disturbance and pain caused by the evil ones, and she almost regretted that she had conceived: “If this was to happen to me, why was it necessary to conceive?” (Gen. 25:22). If the womb of our mother should happen to complain thus of any one of us, brothers, I fear that it would have been better had that person not been conceived—except that he who raises children of Abraham even from stones does not permit us to despair even of such persons (Luke 3:8). May he soften in them, if any such persons exist, their stony heart, lest they shake their mother’s womb; may he console their mother’s womb, lest it grow weary of carrying them, whatever they may be, until Christ is formed in them—he who, perfect God and perfect human, lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## PALM SUNDAY.

[Col. 0127]

## SERMON I. How Christ became all things to the human being.

[Col. 0127D]

1. “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God” (Phil. 2:5–6), etc. Let the wicked and fugitive servant hear this—I mean the human being—who, being in the nature and condition of servitude and under the necessity of serving, yet refusing service, attempted to seize liberty and equality with his Lord for himself. Christ, when he was in the form of God, was equal not by seizure but by nature, because he was co-omnipotent, coeternal, and consubstantial. Emptying himself, he not only took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, but also fulfilled a servant’s ministry, [Col. 0128D] humbling himself and becoming obedient to the Father even unto death—indeed, death upon a cross (Phil. 2:8).

But let it seem too little to you that, though Son and coequal, he served the Father as a servant, unless he also served his own servant more than a servant serves. You were indeed made human in order to serve your Creator. And what is more just than that you should serve him by whom you were created, without whom you cannot even exist? What is more blessed or exalted than to serve him for whom service is reigning? “I will not serve,” says the human being to the Creator. “Then I will serve you,” says the Creator to the human being. “Recline; I will wait upon you; I will wash your feet. Rest; I will bear your illnesses and carry your infirmities. Use me as you please in every need of yours—not merely as your servant, but even as your beast of burden, as your possession. If you are weary or burdened, I will carry both you and your burden, so that I may be the first to fulfill my own law: ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ’” (Gal. 6:2).

“If you hunger or thirst, and perhaps have nothing better at hand, nor is another calf equally fattened ready for you, behold, I am prepared to be sacrificed, that you may eat my flesh and drink my blood. Nor need you fear that, through the death of your servant, you will suffer the loss of his service: even when eaten and drunk, I shall remain whole and living for you, and I shall serve as before. If you are led into captivity or sold, behold, sell me, and redeem yourself by my price—or redeem yourself with me myself as the price. I may seem a cheap slave; but even if I am sold away by night and secretly as stolen property, even if I am bought by the most avaricious priests of the Jews, I can at least be valued at thirty pieces of silver. With this price of mine the burial-place of strangers may be bought; by my price, life for the buried.

“If you fall ill and fear death, I will die for you, so that you may make from my blood medicines of life.”

2. Well done, good and faithful servant: you truly served; you served in all faithfulness and truth, in all patience and long-suffering. You did not serve half-heartedly, for you “rejoiced as a giant to run the way” (Ps. 23:6) of obedience; nor falsely, for after so many and such great labors you even gave your life in addition; nor with murmuring, for though innocent and beaten, you did not open your mouth. It is written, and rightly so: “The servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do worthy things shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47–48). But this servant, I ask, what unworthy thing did he do? What ought he to have done and did not do? “He did all things well,” cry those who observed his deeds, “and he made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7:37). He did everything worthily; and how did he suffer all things so unworthily?

He offered his back to the lashes; he was beaten with stripes neither few nor slight. The streams of blood flowing from so many parts [Col. 0129D] of his body are proof. He was questioned with insult and torture, as though a servant or robber subjected to interrogation in order to extort a confession of crime. O detestable pride of the human being who despises service, which could not be humbled by any other example than the servitude—and such servitude—of his Lord! And would that it might be able even thus to be humbled! Would that even now it might have and render gratitude for such humility and goodness!

But, as it seems to me, I still hear the same Lord in Isaiah lamenting the ingratitude of his wicked servant, where he says: “I did not make you serve in offering, nor did I burden you with incense. Yet you made me serve in your sins; you burdened me with your iniquities” (Isa. 43:23–24). And with what labor? Even to exhaustion, hunger, and thirst; even to sweat—sweat of blood running down to the earth (Luke 22:44); even to death, indeed death upon a cross. Not to recount everything now: struck with slaps, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, pierced with nails, perforated with a lance, given vinegar and gall to drink. “I have trodden this winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3). Therefore you who stand idle all day, attend and see whether there is any labor like my labor.

3. You surely have labored greatly, my Lord, in serving me. It would indeed be just and fair that at least henceforth you should rest, and that your servant should serve you in turn, now that his turn has come. At what great cost, my Lord, have you redeemed for yourself my useless service—you who have no need even of the ministries [Col. 0130B] of angels! By what sweet and kindly art of mercy you have recovered and subjected to yourself the rebellious servant, conquering evil with good, confounding the proud by humility, overwhelming the ungrateful with benefits! Thus indeed, thus wisdom conquers malice; thus you heaped coals of fire upon the head of the obstinate, that he might be kindled to repentance.

You have conquered, then, Lord; you have conquered the rebel. Behold, I give my hands to your chains and place my neck beneath your yoke. Only deign that I may serve you; allow that I may labor for you. Receive me as your everlasting servant, though useless, unless now too your grace be with me and labor with me, always both preceding and following. Let it precede us by first showing examples of humility and patience; let it follow us by helping us imitate what has been shown.

How happy we are, my brothers, if in this matter we hear the Apostle’s counsel: “Have this mind in yourselves which you know preceded in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 2:5). That is: let no one exalt himself above himself, but rather humble himself beneath himself; let the greater serve others; if anyone is injured, let him be first to make amends; let each obey in common even unto death. In these footsteps, brothers, we shall follow Christ in the form of God, in which he lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the knowledge and power of the cross.

1. If Paul, our teacher in faith and truth, came to us today, I think he would judge that he knew nothing among us except Jesus Christ, and him crucified [Col. 0130D] (1 Cor. 2:2). For in these days when the yearly memorial of the Lord’s passion and cross is solemnly celebrated, nothing, I think, is more fittingly preached than Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
