Indeed, on any other days, what can ever be preached more faithfully, heard more salutarily, or thought more fruitfully? What is so devout for the affections of believers, so medicinal for conduct? What so kills sins, crucifies vices, nourishes and strengthens virtues, as the remembrance of the Crucified One?

Let Paul, therefore, speak among the perfect of wisdom hidden in mystery; to me, whose imperfection even human eyes see, let him speak of Christ crucified: to those indeed who are perishing, foolishness; but to me and to those being saved, clearly the power of God and the wisdom of God—indeed, for me the loftiest and noblest philosophy, by which I mock the wisdom both of the world and of the flesh, rendered foolish. How perfect I would think myself, how advanced in wisdom, if I were found even a competent hearer of the Crucified One, who was made for us by God not only wisdom, but also righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30)! Certainly, if you are fastened to the cross with Christ, you are wise, righteous, holy, and free. Are you not wise, if, raised from the earth with Christ, you savor and seek the things above? Are you not righteous, in whom the body of sin has been destroyed so that it no longer serves sin? Are you not holy, if you have offered yourself as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God? Are you not truly free, if the Son has made you free, so that from the freedom of conscience you confidently appropriate for yourself that free utterance of the Son: “The ruler of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30)? Truly, with the Crucified One there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption; for he so redeems Israel from all its iniquities that it merits to escape free from the accusations of this ruler of the world.

2. Yet let whoever that blessed and true Israelite may be know—let him know—that this is not the merit of his own perfection but the grace of divine redemption: not because he himself has committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth, but because he whose own peculiar praise this is—namely Christ—has cleansed that person’s sins. By making purification for sins through the blood of his cross, he triumphed most fully over principalities and powers precisely where his strength was hidden. [Col. 0131C] It was hidden, but not lost, because though crucified through weakness, he lived through the power of God. It was concealed, but not inactive, because, while crucified, he crucified the old human being in all the elect. He crucified the world to Paul, and Paul to the world (Gal. 6:14). Finally, he crucified the tyrant of this world and all the ministers of his ancient tyranny. He concealed the hook beneath the bait, for beneath weakness he hid strength. And so that murderer from the beginning, thirsting for human blood, while he rushed upon weakness, fell upon power: he was bitten as he bit; he was transfixed as he assailed the Crucified One.

3. Thanks be to your cross and nails, Lord Jesus: I see the throat of that dragon pierced through, so that those who had even been swallowed up may pass through liberated. And he who was confident that the Jordan would flow into his mouth (Job 40:18) gnashes and rages because he has lost no small portion of the river that he swallowed. For from those jaws have come to us those who today sing with us the noble and magnificent triumph of the cross. They have plainly been delivered from the lion’s mouth—indeed, returned from the belly of hell. Let him, therefore, rage, gnash, and waste away whose prey has been snatched from his teeth; for Christ will rejoice that he was not crucified in vain. Let hell and death mourn: the former has been bitten, the latter killed; for heaven rejoices and the Church exults because Christ despoils hell and triumphs over death.

For in the conversion of these persons he has renewed the triumph of his passion and revived the miracles of the cross. In [Col. 0132A] them the cross has flowered again; even now the tree of life has borne this precious fruit. For how could it remain barren, when it has not merely been watered but made life-giving by the Savior’s blood? He will no longer regret that he ascended the palm tree, when he has gathered from it so great and precious a fruit. He foresaw this fruit among others when he voluntarily hastened to the cross. “I said, I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits” (Song 7:8). In few words he expressed that he suffered willingly, that through suffering he was exalted, and that he did not suffer without fruit for us. For in the statement of his purpose is shown freedom of choice; in the ascent, the loftiness of triumph; in seizing the fruits, the benefit of redemption.

You foolish Jews cried, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (2 Kgs. 2:23); but your fury could only serve his utterly free ordinance, since he had voluntarily determined to ascend. He ascended the cross by will, triumphed upon it by power, and gathered fruit from it by mercy. Thus by one act he mocked the Jew, killed the devil, and redeemed the Christian.

4. Therefore let those redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions (Ps. 106:2), say—in voice and mind—with their teacher: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14), in which the wisdom of God made foolish wicked counsel, righteousness destroyed him who had the dominion of death, and mercy set the captive free. Rightly indeed, O wise boaster, you will glory in the cross of your Lord, by whose triumph you were delivered, by whose mystery made alive, by whose example justified, and by whose sign defended.

For the logic of justice seems to demand that those who impress the sign of the cross upon their foreheads for their defense should imprint the example of the Crucified One upon their conduct for their justification, and should live by the law of him whose faith arms them. Otherwise, a soldier falsely bears the king’s mark if he does not observe his command; nor does he rightly protect himself by the sign of one whose authority he does not obey. See, moreover, how great is the perversity and abuse when enemies of Christ’s cross wish to protect themselves by the sign of Christ’s cross: secure, they indulge their passions contrary to the mercy of the cross; caught in danger, they wish to be defended by the power of the cross. Clearly they are enemies of Christ’s cross and friends of their own belly: their god is their belly, their idol is money.

Yet let whoever now deceitfully appropriates the sign of the Crucified One for himself know—let him know—that he will by no means be able to protect himself with it in that supreme necessity, when the letter *Tau* will be marked, not by human choice but by the judgment and ministry of angels, upon the foreheads of men who groan and mourn, so that those to be saved may be distinguished from the multitude of the lost (Ezek. 9:4–7).

5. Paul also, that vigorous leader of the Christian army and faithful standard-bearer, who bore in his body the marks of the Crucified One, even now in this confusion of true and false soldiers distinguished the former from the latter by a conspicuous sign, when he said: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires” [Col. 0133A] (Gal. 5:24). This is certainly a cautious and careful definition, as though reproducing the pattern stamped from the exemplar of Truth itself. What life retains as impressed, the tongue expresses more distinctly. Therefore he who had been fastened to the cross with Christ produced this pattern from the exemplar of his own conscience: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires.”

That man of great knowledge and experience knew that many either were or would be people who crucified the desires of the flesh yet allowed the vices of the heart to reign; and, conversely, many who, confident of a tranquil heart, neglected the mortification of the body. But just as divine justice sometimes chastises with the shameful afflictions of the flesh a spirit not subject to it, so, more often, the fattened body kicks back and raises new wars against a spirit now at rest. Therefore the Apostle wishes that, with both inward vices and outward desires crucified, we should cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God (2 Cor. 7:1).

For the fear of God, like nails driven in deeply, fastens us to the cross; and, as though attached to righteousness, makes us hold firm, so that we do not offer our members as weapons of iniquity but of righteousness, and so that sin, though present, may not reign in our mortal body. Certainly, that the fear of God is compared to fastening nails is David’s teaching, when he says: “Fasten my flesh, as with nails, by your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118:120). Therefore, if you do not yet prevail in extinguishing your vices, the Apostle wants you to take care at least to crucify them. He does not say, “Those who belong to Christ have extinguished vices”—a power belonging to few—but, “have crucified them,” without which there is no salvation, just as apart from Christ’s cross there is no redemption.

For this reason the Redeemer chose this manner of suffering for accomplishing and shaping our salvation: that the sacrament of redemption might become an example of justification; so that, just as he crucified the likeness of sinful flesh, condemning sin through sin, we too—indeed, much more, we—might crucify sinful flesh, crucifying sin in it even if we do not yet extinguish it.

6. Here you may recall that Moses, to appease the Lord’s wrath, crucified the leaders of the Israelites (Num. 25:4–9); Joshua—who is also Jesus—the five kings of the Amorites (Josh. 10:26). For if we wish to appease the wrath of the Lord which we have deserved, it is necessary that we crucify ourselves through continence. But our Jesus, who will lead us into the promised land, will crucify—indeed, extinguish—the vices of the five senses in us, provided, as is fitting, we hang upon the gibbets until evening. For the Savior took care to offer you in himself an example of this perseverance upon the cross, unwilling to be finished except upon the cross, or taken down from the cross before the evening both of that day and of his life.

Balaam said, “May my soul die the death of the righteous” (Num. 23:10); but you should say, “May my soul die the death of my Lord Jesus Christ, and may my last things be like his,” so that I may deserve to hang in the voluntary cross of penitence until life’s end. With what confidence, from the cross of the Son, will you commend your spirit into the Father’s hands! Indeed, with what mercy will the Father receive the one whom the Son commends!

> [Note: [Col. 0133] See similar material above, Sermon 1 on Advent, near the end; likewise in St Bernard, Easter Sermon 3, nos. 3 and 8.]

For the Son, who once undertook on the cross to plead the cause of your soul, never ceases to plead it, always interceding with the Father. Go securely; go rejoicing, where your judge is your advocate. Only let your spirit carry with it the sign of the cross—the mortification of Jesus—which you bear about in your body. May the Lord of glory, who suffered for you, brothers, and is glorified in you, deign to make you companions in his passion and glory; and, as you glory in the cross, may he glorify you in that radiance which he had with the Father before the beginning of the ages and will have through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the twofold form in which Christ is presented for contemplation.

1. The desire of our soul, “fair in beauty beyond the children of men,” is presented by this day to the children of men under now one, now another aspect: in both aspects indeed worthy to be contemplated, in both desirable and lovable, because in both the Saviour of humankind; though in the one exalted, in the other humbled; in this glorious, in that afflicted; in this venerable, in that pitiable—if indeed he may properly be called pitiable who, through the condescension of compassion, took misery upon himself, so as from his misery to bestow mercy upon the miserable; not as one who, being blessedness to himself, begged mercy from the miserable. Therefore, where he chose to appear deserving of pity, there he was also the more deserving of reverence. “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for one who would comfort me, and I found none” (Ps. 68:21). Thus he who, out of compassion for all, freely chose to become wretched, found compassion with scarcely anyone. But where, you ask, is he seen today exalted and glorious, and where humbled and afflicted? Look at the procession; hear the Passion. In these you will plainly be able to recognize what Isaiah says: “As many were astonished at him, so shall his countenance be without glory among men, and his form among the children of men” [Col. 0134C–D] (Isa. 52:14). Many were astonished at the glory, as of a triumphant victor, when he entered Jerusalem; yet shortly afterward his countenance was without glory and despised when he suffered. “When he entered Jerusalem,” says Matthew, “the whole city was moved, saying: Who is this?” (Matt. 21:10). When he suffered, shame covered his face, so that he could truly confess: “I was exalted, humbled, and confounded” (Ps. 87:16).

Certainly, when he here says that he was confounded, this must be understood in accordance with what he says elsewhere concerning the face of his body: “Shame covered my face” (Ps. 68:8), because they did not spare to spit in my face, to veil it, strike it, and mock it [Col. 0135A]. For the face of his mind, which always and immovably dwelt with the countenance of God, could neither be troubled nor confounded. “The Lord God is my helper,” he says; “therefore I am not confounded; therefore I have set my face like the hardest rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded” (Isa. 50:7). “For in thee, O Lord, have I hoped; I shall not be confounded for ever” (Ps. 30:2). “Rather let them be confounded, and not I; let them fear, and not I” (Jer. 17:18).

2. If, then, as I had begun to say, today’s procession and Passion are considered together, there Jesus is plainly seen exalted and glorious, here humbled and afflicted. In the procession he is regarded in the honour of a king; in the Passion he is seen under the punishment of a thief. There glory and honour surround him; here he has neither beauty nor comeliness [Col. 0135B]. There is the joy of men and the glory of the people; here the reproach of men and rejection by the people. There they cry to him: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes, the King of Israel” (Matt. 21:9); here they shout: “Guilty of death” (Matt. 26:66), and mock him because he made himself King of Israel. There they meet him with palm branches; here he is struck in the face with the palms of hands, and his head is struck with a reed. There he is exalted by praises; here he is filled with insults. There competing crowds spread others’ garments in his way; here he is stripped of his own. There he is received into Jerusalem as a just king and saviour; here he is condemned and cast out of Jerusalem as a criminal and deceiver. There he sits upon an ass, attended with acts of service; here he hangs upon the wood of the cross, scourged with lashes, pierced with wounds, and abandoned by his own [Col. 0135C].

Behold, here he is more than Job, whose entire condition God so suddenly and violently turned at once into its opposite. “You have heard of Job’s endurance; you have seen the end of the Lord” (Jas. 5:11), says the Apostle James. It is as if he said: Job’s endurance lasted until the restoration of his possessions; the Lord’s endurance until the end of his life. Job indeed patiently endured losses, but soon received double in his own land; Christ, filled with miseries and drenched with bitterness, departed from the world. Thus here he is more than Job: suddenly and all at once cast down, as it seemed, from the highest happiness, he met his end in an extremity of the gravest calamity. “And I have suffered these things,” he says, “without iniquity in my hand, when I had pure prayers to God” [Col. 0135D] (Job 16:18), even prayers for his crucifiers, that they might be forgiven.

3. Would not the Son therefore rightly appear, as though troubled by so great and so sudden a reversal of circumstances, to appeal to the Father in that tearful cry: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Surely thy hands made me! Thou didst lead me according to thy will, and a little before didst receive me with glory; and dost thou so suddenly cast me down? “Thou didst lift me up and dash me down,” as though setting me upon the wind and violently crushing me. “I was exalted, humbled, and confounded”; and the more confounded because then I was more highly exalted and now more deeply humbled; and as I was then raised more high, so now am I more grievously dashed down.

It is indeed just, O Father, that one who exalts himself should be humbled, and that the pride of the unworthy should be punished by a fitting abasement [Col. 0136A]; but was it likewise just that one whom thou hadst exalted should be humiliated so shamefully, and that such contempt should follow the glory which humility had earned? 994 Wast thou angry with me, Father, because for even an hour I was allowed to be honoured here? And was that very small portion which I had received of this world’s goods to be paid out before death in punishments and insults, lest afterward it could be said to me: “Son, thou hast received good things in thy life” (Luke 16:25)? Yet the honour was thine, O Father; it was the honour of the Son, because “he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.” Behold, thy enemies reproach thee, O Lord; they reproach the change wrought in thy Christ. Behold, those who shortly before were tormented by my glory and honour now exult in my disgrace and torment [Col. 0136B]. Shall I not answer my reproachers with a word, so that they may someday know by what dispensation thou hast changed thy Christ, by what counsel thou didst thus exalt him only soon to humble him, or didst humble him who was exalted?

4. Thou wilt answer, O Lord Jesus; thou wilt answer thy reproachers with a word—and a harsh word—when thou answerest them to their face with their own arrogance and convictest them of their wickedness, as they behold him whom they pierced. For when they see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty (Matt. 24:30), then they will know what they now refuse to believe: that the earlier glory of today’s procession was the mystery and figure of that later glory, just as the Passion’s disgrace was its merit and cause [Col. 0136C]. Then they will understand that Christ, now honoured and now made an object of mockery, was set as a stumbling-block and ruin for those who perish, just as he is resurrection and instruction for those who are saved; because what is the sacrament of redemption is at the same time also a lesson in edification.

For the deserts of the proud demanded that both Christ’s honour should become a scandal to their pride and his death a precipice; so that the glory of the triumphant one might rightly arouse the envy of those who perish, and the punishment of the dying one condemn them. But for those who are saved—that is, for us—it was altogether necessary that Christ, passing along the way of this world, should prepare the way for those who follow him, through prosperity as well as adversity; and that, first exalted and afterward humbled [Col. 0136D], he should hand down by his example how modesty is to be preserved in honour and patience maintained amid disgrace or pain. He could be honoured, indeed, but could not be puffed up; he chose to be despised, yet did not know how either to be cast down in faint-heartedness or to be stung by anger.

For just as on another occasion, when they wished to seize him and make him king, he withdrew and fled into solitude to pray (John 6:15), teaching by example what he also taught in word—not to desire to be lifted up on high—so now, by another dispensation, permitting himself to be honoured for a time, and nevertheless retaining in honour his customary, because ingrained, gentleness, he gave a pattern to those set in authority. Yet, so that they might learn to be gentle through humility with such discrimination that, when circumstances required it, they should rise up in zeal, the Lord immediately returned to the Temple and, having made a whip of cords, avenged the injuries done to his Father; he chose rather to provoke the priests’ fury to bring about his own death than to overlook the Temple’s profanation [Col. 0137A] (Matt. 21:12–13).

5. Therefore, brethren, that we may follow our leader with an unharmed foot through prosperity as well as adversity, let us contemplate him in the procession as placed in honour, and in the Passion as subjected to insults and pains; yet never as changed in mind amid so great a reversal of circumstances, although he “changed his countenance before Abimelech,” that is, before the kingdom [variant: king] of the Jews—a change in Christ which the blindness of the faithless reproaches. Scripture says concerning the unchangeable state of his mind: “A holy man remains in wisdom like the sun; but a fool changes like the moon” [Col. 0137B] (Ecclus. 27:12). Another Scripture says concerning the change in his face: “The wisdom of a man shines in his countenance, and the most mighty shall change his face” (Eccl. 8:1).

Truly, in thy countenance, O Lord Jesus, however changed it may appear, whether glorious or inglorious, wisdom shines; from thy countenance the brightness of eternal light radiates. Would that the light of thy countenance, O Lord, might shine upon us! Thy face, in sorrow as in joy, is restrained in itself, serene, and wholly radiant with the secret light of the heart; cheerful and pleasant to the righteous, merciful and kind to penitents. Look, brethren, upon the face of the most serene King. “In the gladness of the king’s countenance is life,” says Scripture, “and his clemency is like the latter rain” (Prov. 16:15). He looked upon the first-formed man, and at once, animated, he breathed into life [Col. 0137C] (Gen. 1:27); he looked back at Peter, and immediately Peter, pierced with compunction, breathed again toward forgiveness. For as soon as the Lord looked upon Peter, 995 Peter received from the clemency of that most loving countenance the latter rain, tears after sin (Luke 22:61–62).

“The light of thy countenance, O eternal light,” according to Job’s witness, “does not fall upon the earth” (Job 25:3). For what fellowship has light with darkness? (2 Cor. 6:14). Rather, let the souls of the faithful receive its rays: may it breathe joy into those of good conscience and healing into the wounded. Certainly the face of triumphant Jesus, as it is to be contemplated in the procession, is joy and jubilation; the face of the dying one, as it is to be contemplated in the Passion, is remedy and salvation. “Those who fear thee shall see me,” he says, “and rejoice” [Col. 0137D] (Ps. 118:74); those who grieve over themselves shall see me and be healed, like those who looked upon the serpent suspended on the wood after the serpents’ venom. Therefore may all vows bless thee, the joy and salvation of all, whether they see thee seated upon an ass or hanging upon the wood; so that, when they behold thee reigning upon the throne, they may praise for ever and ever him to whom be praise and honour through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. How Christ is to be blessed

1. “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:9). It is a voice of exultation and salvation, a voice of joy and devotion, a voice of faith and love, rejoicing at the Redeemer’s coming and declaring with prophetic joy the gladness of the redemption so long desired. “Hosanna to the Son of David,” says this household of David: salvation belongs to him who was made from David’s seed, that he might save those who are of David’s faith. “Praise the Lord, praise him, servants; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:1–2); say: “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21); blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

From the mouths of these children, O Father, thou hast perfected praise for thy Son, so that by the uncorrupted witness of simple innocence thou mightest destroy the enemy and avenger (Ps. 8:3): the Pharisee and the high priest—not avengers of the divine law, as iniquity falsely claimed for itself, but avengers of their own envy and wrath. Yet “his pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown” (Ps. 7:17). “O God, do not be silent concerning my praise,” says the Son to the Father; “for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me” [Col. 0138A] (Ps. 108:2).

The Father can deny nothing to the Son. The Father’s voice, heard repeatedly from heaven, did not keep silence concerning the Son’s praise; nor did the creatures keep silence, confessing him in so many signs and wonders to be the author of nature. Angels bore witness; demons confessed; the prophetic order sang in harmonious voices, answering one another. But this at last is perfect praise: that which is not kept silent by an age that does not know how to flatter and cannot conceal what the Spirit suggests. For what could be clearer than that children of this age neither said nor did, of themselves, things so new and so unusual? Rather, the Holy Spirit, according to his custom speaking through the mouths of the simple, bore witness to the Son [Col. 0138B].

2. Clearly the Holy Spirit, aware of Christ’s works—of what that coming of Christ would produce, and of what joy and salvation his Passion would bring forth for humankind—awakened foreknowing joys in innocent hearts, and took the service of simple faculties for himself in order to prophesy to the world the gladness of redemption. For the Spirit addressed these people, “calling those things which are not as though they were,” when through his prophet he then commanded things which today have been done by him, and which are now brought into being: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem: behold, thy king shall come to thee, just and a Saviour, himself poor and riding upon an ass” [Col. 0138C] (Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5).

“Now,” he says, “rejoice greatly, you who until now have been in sorrow; now satisfy yourself—if indeed you can be satisfied—with the ineffable joy which so satisfies desire that it makes one hunger more abundantly and more happily. Let your mouth be filled with joy and your tongue with exultation; and if neither mouth nor tongue can suffice, let jubilation overflow what affection cannot contain. ‘Shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem.’ For ‘blessed is the people that knows jubilation’” (Ps. 88:16). Blessed indeed is the people that knows and understands that today it must rejoice ineffably, when the Saviour promised and awaited from the beginning of the ages comes to it. Blessed is the people that today comes out to meet him with all the alacrity of devotion, crying aloud to him in heart and voice together: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21:9).

For in this the Son is blessed by the Father: that whoever blesses him may be filled with blessings—not one blessing, indeed, but many; since the blessing which one lends to the Lord returns upon one’s own head with multiplied interest [Col. 0139A]. “Woe to the sinful nation, wicked seed, criminal children!” To them belongs that dreadful complaint of the Lord: “I have not lent, nor has anyone lent to me; all curse me, says the Lord” (Jer. 15:10–11). This was the Jewish people, which disdained to deal with the Lord in the account of giving and receiving: unwilling to bless the Blessed One of God the Father in order to be blessed by him, it called him a Samaritan and demon-possessed, and assailed God with mad and blasphemous curses (John 8:48, 52–53). “They shall curse,” he says, “and thou shalt bless” (Ps. 108:28); for the blessing which they refused shall pass away from them to the nations. Bless our God, you nations, because he who first lent to you, going before you in blessings of sweetness, will repay those who lend to him with manifold interest in blessings of blessedness [Col. 0139B].

3. Yet I fear, my brethren, lest that complaint of the Lord should perhaps touch these times of lukewarmness and unbelief: “I have not lent, nor has anyone lent to me” (Jer. 15:10). Grace is offered but not received; a reward is promised for work, and scarcely anyone works in hope of it. The Lord lends when, distributing talents to his servants, he bestows beforehand for gain knowledge of the word or the grace of any gift. But a kindly person who has mercy and lends, lends to the Lord; as Scripture says: “He who shows mercy to his neighbour lends to the Lord” (Prov. 19:17). Indeed, whoever does anything in hope of divine recompense lends to the Lord, so that he may say: “I know whom I have believed” [Col. 0139C] (2 Tim. 1:12); I know him who said: “Whatever you spend, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35).

But we lend him either nothing, or so timidly and coldly, as if he were an untrustworthy debtor or lacked the means to repay. Great indeed was the faith of that Hebrew people: although they saw him poor, seated upon a little ass—and an ass not even his own—yet with all confidence and devotion they lent to him, spreading not only their garments on the way, but also devoting their whole selves, as far as they could, to his honour. But assuredly they understood the poor and needy one. For the prophet had given them as a sign for recognizing the Saviour the very poverty by which he was despised by the proud: “He himself is poor and rides upon an ass” (Zech. 9:9). “By this sign,” he says, “you may recognize your coming King, whose kingdom is not of this world: namely, because, to overthrow the pride reigning in the world, he will proclaim poverty or humility both in word and in example” [Col. 0139D].

4. Blessed therefore is the daughter of Zion that has learned to honour humility as heavenly armour and as a royal insignia. Wretched is her unbelieving mother, that Zion which, seeing him humble, despised him, and seeing him honoured, envied him. Blessed, I say, is the Church of the first believers, which so faithfully recognized and so gratefully received him who came in the name of the Lord. Unhappy is the synagogue of the faithless, ready to receive one who would come in his own name, but tormented by the honour of him who sought the Father’s glory. “Rebuke thy disciples,” they say, as though their simplicity could flatter, or his purity could take pleasure in empty praise. “I tell you,” he says, “that if these keep silence, the stones will cry out” [Col. 0140A] (Luke 19:39–40), because God will not keep silence concerning my praise.

Certainly it is so: if they keep silence, the stones will cry out. For at the time of the Passion these people kept silence, but the stones cried out, when, as witness to and praise of the dying one, the rocks were split and the tombs opened (Matt. 27:51–52). Certainly it is so, because now, while the synagogue is silent, in accordance with the saying, “By night I caused thy mother to be silent” (Hos. 4:5), the Church of the Gentiles cries out—living stones—yes, the stones cry out from which he who is mighty raised children for Abraham. “Praise,” says the prophet, “you inhabitants of the rock; from the tops of the mountains they shall cry out” (Isa. 42:11). Behold, today in the clefts of the rock, in the caverns of the wall, the voice of the dove resounds, crying and saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” [Col. 0140B] (Matt. 21:9).

5. Blessed is he who, so that I might nest in the clefts of the rock, endured the piercing of his hands, feet, and side, and opened himself wholly to me, so that I might enter “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle” and be sheltered “in the hidden place of his tabernacle.” The rock is indeed a fitting refuge for hedgehogs, but also a pleasant dwelling for doves: its clefts, lying open in so many wounds throughout almost his whole body, both offer pardon to the guilty and confer grace upon the righteous. Indeed, brethren, it is a safe dwelling and a tower of strength from the face of the enemy to linger, in devout and diligent meditation, upon the wounds of Christ the Lord, and by faith and love of the Crucified to shelter the soul [Col. 0140C] from the heat of the flesh, the storm of the world, and the assault of the devil.

Above all worldly glory is the protection of this tabernacle: namely, “a shade by day from the heat,” and security and concealment from storm and rain, so that by day the sun may not burn you with prosperity, nor the storm shake you in adversity. Therefore enter into the rock, O human being; hide yourself “in the pit of the earth” (Isa. 2:10); make for yourself a hiding-place in the Crucified. He is the rock; he is the earth, because he is God and man. He is the pierced rock and the excavated earth, because, he says, “they dug through my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:17). “Hide yourself in the pit of the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 2:10): that is, flee from him to him—from the judge to the redeemer, from the tribunal to the cross, from the just one to the merciful one; from him who “will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth” [Col. 0140D] to him who drenches the earth with the drops of his blood; from him who “will slay the wicked with the spirit of his lips” to him who gives life to the slain by the blood of his wounds.

Indeed, flee not merely to him but into him: enter the clefts of the rock; hide yourself in the excavated earth; conceal yourself in the very pierced hands and opened side. For what is the wound in Christ’s side but the door in the side of the Ark, for saving persons from the face of the flood? That was a figure, but this is the reality: there not only is mortal life preserved, but immortal life restored. For this reason the loving and merciful one opened his side: that the blood of the wound might give you life, the warmth of the body might revive you, and the spirit of the heart might breathe upon you as through an open and unobstructed passage. There you will hide safely until iniquity passes away [Col. 0141A]; there you will in no way grow cold, because love does not grow cold in Christ’s inward parts; there you will abound in delights and overflow with joys—ultimately when mortality has been swallowed up by the life of your head and of all the members of his body.

6. Rightly therefore does Christ’s dove, Christ’s beautiful one, for whom his wounds have prepared clefts as safe as they are pleasant for nesting, joyfully sing his praises today; and from remembrance or imitation of the Passion, from meditation upon the wounds, as from the clefts of the rock, a sweet voice resounds in the bridegroom’s ears. But upon you, my brethren, who have nested all the more inwardly in the clefts of the rock because you live more secretly in Christ and “your life is hidden with Christ in God” [Col. 0142A] (Col. 3:3), there wholly rests the duty that, as your manner of life is more quiet and more secure, so your devotion may be sweeter—especially today, when both the return of the season and the representation of the event make us, as it were, present at that solemn joy with which he was received into Jerusalem. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”: to him be blessing, kingdom, and dominion, who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

# ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0141]

## SERMON I. Jacob’s words concerning Joseph are aptly applied to Christ’s resurrection

[Col. 0141B]

1. “They reported to Jacob, saying: Joseph lives. On hearing this, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son lives. I will go and see him before I die” (Gen. 45:26, 28). Perhaps you will say to me: Very well; but what has this to do with the matter? What has Joseph to do with the joy of this day, with the glory of Christ’s resurrection? It is Easter, and you again set before us Lenten fare? Our soul hungers for the Paschal Lamb, for whom it has prepared itself by so long a course of fasting. Our heart burns within us for Jesus; we desire Jesus, yet we do not deserve to see him or hear of him. We hunger for Jesus [Col. 0141C], not Joseph; for the Saviour, not the dreamer; for the Lord of heaven, not of Egypt; not for him who fed bellies, but for him who feeds minds that hunger. At least let your discourse help us to hunger more for him whom we hunger for. For we read: “Blessed are those who hunger, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). When we hear, we hunger more. One who commends a feast also provokes appetite. If we hear of Jesus, joy and gladness will be given to our hearing, and humbled bones will rejoice. Our bones have been humbled by Lenten affliction and mourning, but still more by sorrow for his Passion; yet they shall rejoice at the news of his resurrection. Why then do you press your Joseph upon us, when, apart from Jesus, whatever you say has no savour for us—especially today, when the Paschal Lamb is eaten, when “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” [Col. 0141D]?

2. I have set before you an egg or a nut, brethren: break the shell and you will find food. Let Joseph be broken open, and Jesus will be found—the Paschal Lamb for whom you hunger; eaten all the more sweetly because he lies more deeply hidden, and sought more diligently and found with greater difficulty. You say to me: What has Joseph to do with Christ? What has the history I have set forth to do with this day? Much in every way. Recall the history, and the loving meaning of the mystery will freely disclose itself to you, provided that you have Jesus as interpreter—he who, rising even today, speaks to his disciples on the way of the killing letter, and opens the Scriptures.

For who, among all patriarchs and prophets, more plainly or more distinctly sets forth the figure of the Saviour than Joseph? To state the matter briefly, according to the saying, “Give opportunity to the wise, and wisdom shall be added to him” [Col. 0142B] (Prov. 9:9): if with faith and devotion we consider the interpretation of his name; then that he was, beyond his other brothers, “beautiful in face and handsome in appearance” (Gen. 39:6); innocent in conduct, prudent in understanding; sold by his own people and yet redeeming his own from death; first humbled even to prison and then exalted even to the throne; and finally, in reward for his work, called among the nations by a new name, “Saviour of the world” (Gen. 41:45)—if we consider all these things devoutly and faithfully, do we not immediately recognize how truly the Lord said: “In the hands of the prophets I have been made like unto [them]”? (Hos. 12:10).

[Col. 0142C] 3. But if we come now to the words which I set forth from the history, I think they will require not so much exposition as they will stir admiration and joy: namely, that Christ’s resurrection was so clearly attested by the Law and the Prophets, and that the ancient history speaks the new mysteries so aptly that, when prophecy is read, one almost seems to hear the Gospel, with only the names changed. “They reported to Jacob,” he says, “saying: Joseph lives.” What else can I understand here except: “They reported to the Apostles, saying: Jesus lives”? For by Jacob I understand nothing other than the company of the Apostles; nor, I think, without reason. Not only were they descended from Jacob; not only did they become Israel from Jacob when they passed from the struggle of the active life to the vision and rest of the contemplative; but they are also the fathers of the multitude of believers, that is, of true Israelites, just as he was the father of carnal Israelites [Col. 0142D].

Like him, they grieved inconsolably when they thought that their Joseph had perished; when they heard that he lived, they believed with difficulty and delay; when they recognized him, they rejoiced beyond utterance. “They reported to Jacob,” he says, “saying: Joseph lives.” When Jacob heard this, as though waking from a heavy sleep, he still did not believe them (Gen. 45:26). This seems to me to have been said in other words of what we read written in the Gospel: “She went”—without doubt Mary Magdalene—“and reported to those who had been with him, mourning and weeping; and they, hearing that he lived and had been seen by her, did not believe.” “After this he was shown to two on the road, and they went out and reported to the rest; neither did they believe them” [Col. 0143A] (Mark 16:10–13). Likewise in Luke: “And, returning from the tomb, they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest; and these words seemed to them like nonsense, and they did not believe them” (Luke 24:9, 11), doubtless because they were awakening from the heavy sleep of weariness and despair.

“But when Jacob,” he says, “saw all that Joseph had sent to him, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son lives. I will go and see him before I die” (Gen. 45:27–28). Thus mere words made little progress among the Apostles until they received gifts. For Jesus himself, when he showed himself present to them, persuaded them not so much by showing his body as by breathing the gift upon them.

[Col. 0143B] 4. You know that when he came to them while the doors were shut and stood in their midst, they were troubled and frightened, thinking that they saw a spirit (Luke 24:37). But when he breathed upon them, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), or when he sent that same Spirit from heaven—though another gift—these gifts were unmistakable witnesses and proofs of resurrection and life. For it is the Spirit who bears witness in the hearts of the saints and through their mouths that Christ 999 is truth, true resurrection, and life. Therefore the Apostles, who had previously doubted even after seeing the living body, after tasting the life-giving Spirit bore witness to the resurrection with great power. To conceive Jesus in the heart is so much more than to see him with the eyes or hear of him with the ears; and the Spirit’s operation upon the senses of the inner person is so much more powerful than the operation of bodily things upon the external senses.

For what room can remain for doubt where the Spirit who bears witness and the spirit to whom he bears witness are one? If the spirit is one and the perception is one, the assent too is equal. Then, therefore, as is truly said of Jacob, their spirit revived—already almost extinguished by mourning, indeed buried in despair. Then, unless I am mistaken, each of them said to himself: “It is enough for me that my Joseph lives,” because “for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” “Therefore I will go into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus appointed us, and I will see him and worship before I die, so that afterward I may never die; for everyone who sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life, so that even if he has died, he shall live” [Col. 0143C–D] (John 6:40; 11:26).

5. Now, then, my brethren, what does your heart’s joy bear witness to you concerning Christ’s love? I think—whether rightly, you must judge—that if you have ever loved Jesus, whether living, dead, or restored to life, today, when the announcements of the Resurrection ring out and resound so often in the Church, your heart glories within you and says: “They have reported to me, saying: Jesus my God lives.” On hearing this, my spirit revived: it had been sleeping from weariness, languishing from lukewarmness, or failing through excessive faint-heartedness. For the glad voice of this happy announcement raises even criminals from death. Otherwise he is surely beyond hope and should be buried in oblivion whom Jesus, returning from the underworld, left in the lowest place of hell [Col. 0144A].

You will know, indeed, that your spirit has fully revived in Christ if it says, in accordance with what follows: “It is enough for me if Jesus lives.” O faithful voice, and truly worthy of Jesus’ friends! O most chaste affection, which speaks thus: “It is enough for me if Jesus lives!” If he lives, I live, since my soul depends upon him; indeed, he himself is my life, he himself my sufficiency. What can be lacking to me if Jesus lives? Rather, let everything else be lacking: it matters nothing to me, provided Jesus lives. Indeed, let him himself be lacking to me, if it pleases him; it is enough for me provided he lives, even for himself. When Christ’s love has so absorbed a person’s entire affection that, heedless and forgetful of self, the person is conscious only of Jesus Christ and of the things that are Jesus Christ’s [Col. 0144B], then, I think, charity is at last perfect in that person.

To one thus disposed, poverty is not burdensome; such a person does not feel injuries, laughs at reproaches, despises losses, and counts death as gain. Indeed, such a person does not even think that he or she dies, knowing rather that death is a passage into life, and confidently saying: “I will go and see him before I die.”

6. Yet we, my brethren, though we are not conscious in ourselves of such purity, should nevertheless go—go to see Jesus on the mountain of heavenly Galilee, where he has appointed us. Affection will grow as we go, and at least it will be perfected when we arrive. In going, the way that was at first narrow and difficult is widened, and strength is increased for the weak. So that neither Jacob nor anyone of Jacob’s household might excuse himself from the journey, provisions and vehicles were sent, besides other gifts, to the poor old man, so that no one might plead either poverty or infirmity [Col. 0144C]. Christ’s flesh is the provision for the journey; his Spirit is the vehicle. He himself is the food; he himself is Israel’s chariot and its driver.

When you arrive, every best thing is yours—not Egypt’s goods, but heaven’s; in the best place of the kingdom your Joseph has prepared rest for you. He who first sent angels, women, and Apostles as witnesses and messengers of his resurrection now himself cries from heaven: “Behold, I whom you mourned as dead during these three days—I was indeed dead for your sake, but behold, I live, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). “Come to me, you who labour with hunger, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that I have prepared for you” [Col. 0144D] (Matt. 25:34). May he who calls you there himself bring you where, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

**1000 SERMON II. On our twofold resurrection.**
1. “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20:6). “I am,” Jesus says, “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). He himself is surely the first resurrection, and he is also the second resurrection. For Christ, rising from the dead as the first fruits of those who sleep, has by the mystery of his resurrection effected for us the first resurrection, and by the example of that same resurrection he will effect for us the second. The first [Col. 0145A] is that of souls, when he raises them with himself into newness of life; the second will be that of bodies, when he refashions the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21). Christ therefore rightly declares himself to be resurrection and life, since through him and in him we rise again, in order that we may live according to him and with him: now according to him, in holiness and righteousness; later with him, in blessedness and glory.

Moreover, just as the first resurrection of our head, the Lord Jesus Christ, is the cause and proof of the second resurrection, which will be that of his whole body, so for each of us the first resurrection of the soul, by which it returns to life from the death of sin, is the proof and cause of its own second resurrection, by which the body will be freed [Col. 0145B] not only from death’s corruption but also from every corruptibility of mortality. The Apostle plainly shows that the former is proof and cause of the latter when he says: “If the Spirit of Christ, who raised Christ from the dead, dwells in you, he will give life also to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:11).

2. Thus it is rightly said: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20:6). Holy, certainly, because of the first resurrection, which he has already attained through the renewal of the soul; blessed because of the second, which he happily awaits in the restoration of the body. Finally, the same Scripture reveals why he is blessed when it adds: “Over such as have a share in the first resurrection, the second death has no power,” [Col. 0145C] even if the first death seems for a time to have exercised dominion over them. For death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression (Rom. 5:14). But as Christ, so also the Christian rising from the dead “dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

Therefore among the blessed there, neither will the second death have power, nor will the first retain the power it held for a time. For the single death of Christ triumphed over both our deaths: freeing those already captured from the one, and those who were to be captured from the other, so that we may neither fall into that death nor remain in this one. How true, devout, and magnificent is that threat of the one dying: “I will be your death, O death” [Col. 0145D] (Hos. 13:14)! How beautifully and wonderfully he triumphed: tasting death for all, he swallowed up utterly both his own death and that of all. Truly, “death is swallowed up in victory.”

Let whoever is that blessed person, who has a share in the first resurrection, securely taunt death: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” You are conquered, you who conquered all things; and you have lost the weapons in which you trusted. For where is your sting? “The sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:55–56), which, having once pierced the root of the human race, poured the incurable poison of death through all its offspring. As the Apostle says, “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and thus it passed to all human beings” (Rom. 5:12). Thus death reigned victoriously [Col. 0146A] from the first Adam even to the second, because, just as the whole human race was bound by the law of origin in the bond of sin, so it was also bound by the debt of dying.

3. But thanks be to God, who gave us victory over both sin and death, indeed through the Lord Jesus Christ. Entirely free from sin and therefore free from the debt of death, he nevertheless voluntarily discharged that debt for us by dying, and absolved us from sin by rising again. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ died for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). In dying, he paid the penalty for our offences; in rising, he established for us the pattern and cause of perpetual justification, so that, just as Christ, rising from the dead, “dies no more; death shall [Col. 0146B] no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9), so the Christian raised together with Christ may no longer sin unto death, nor may sin any longer rule him.

This is the blessed and holy person who has a share in the first resurrection: the second death will have no power over him, while even the first death will be swallowed up in the victory of Christ’s resurrection. This is the one who has not merely recognized but also grasped the power of Christ’s resurrection and the fellowship of his passion, being conformed to his death in order to attain the resurrection from the dead. The Apostle was not mistaken when, for the sake of that gain, he counted all things formerly gain to him not only as losses but even as dung, if only he might be found in Christ, conformed both to his death and [Col. 0146C] to his resurrection (Phil. 3:7–11).

A wholly profitable exchange: to despise what diminishes and defiles you, so that you may gain Christ; indeed, if necessary, to expend not only what is yours but even yourself, so that with such great interest of immortality and glory you may deserve to receive yourself back. For who can doubt that it is a profitable transaction to sow a mortal, animal, dishonourable body so that it may rise immortal, spiritual, and glorious; to die to the world so that you may say, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21)? O lovers of gain, why do you linger over the pursuit of profit? Why do you not learn the art of gain? Why do you not despise trivial things—indeed, losses and dung—so that you may gain Christ? Why do you spend [Col. 0146D] silver “not on bread, and your labour not on what satisfies” (Isa. 55:2)? As I see it, that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world is cheaper in your eyes than your silver. Yet one cannot know how precious [variant: how great] it is who is unwilling to taste how good it is.

Would that even the miser valued himself more highly than his money, and did not expose his soul for sale out of love of it, or cast away his inmost self during his lifetime (Ecclus. 10:10). That prudent merchant and worthy evaluator of things—I mean Paul—did not make even his soul, that is, his animal and sensuous life, more precious than himself (Acts 20:24), that is, than his spirit, by which he clung in union to Christ; he was ready to lose his soul so that he might keep it unto eternal life.

[Col. 0147A]

4. Since those who possess riches enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, and those who store up silver sooner spend it on empty things than on bread—on the unleavened bread, I mean, of sincerity and truth, with which the Paschal Lamb must be eaten today—you blessed poor, children of the poor Crucified One, you, I say, who have no silver, hasten: buy and eat. Those who possess nothing buy that good far more readily and easily than those who possess much. When means are lacking, a good will is enough to purchase; and those poorer in possessions are often richer in this will. Scripture rightly invites such people: “Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isa. 55:1).

You see, happy poor person, that only a good will is required of you, [Col. 0147B] and that in it alone lies the price of so great a transaction. Do not ungratefully refuse what is offered so freely; indeed, do not lose through an ungrateful will what you have already merited through blessed poverty. Recognize how great a gain it is to have no share in the ruin of the world, so that you may have a share in Christ’s resurrection. Understand how great a happiness it is not to be intoxicated by the luxury and frenzy of the age, so that you may drink new wine with Christ in the kingdom of his Father.

The Paschal Lamb himself invites his friends to the delights of his body and blood: “Eat, friends,” he says; “drink and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5:1). This food and drink is the mystery of life, the medicine of immortality, the cause of the first resurrection, and the pledge of the second; for it is plainly the beginning in us of the divine substance. “We have become partakers of Christ,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0147C] “provided that we hold firm to the end the beginning of his substance” (Heb. 3:14).

For one who, after receiving grace, returns to his own vomit, “will vomit up the riches he has swallowed, and God will draw them out of his belly.” Or again, “his bread in his belly will be turned within him into the gall of asps.” For grace received is indeed turned into the punishment of conscience when the blood of the covenant, by which a person had been sanctified, is regarded as polluted and outrage is offered to the Spirit of grace. By this contempt and nausea the riches swallowed are vomited out, so that it may be said of such a person: “Nothing remained of his food, and therefore nothing of his goods shall endure.”

[Col. 0147D]

5. Let the one beware lest this terrible sentence perhaps strike him also: the one who, having been filled through the grace of devotion with the good things of God’s house, retains absolutely nothing of them in memory, so as to pour forth for us the remembrance of the abundance of divine sweetness—not flavour in his words, as taste in the mouth; not power in his conduct, as juice in the inward parts—but immediately vomits the whole out again in empty or buffoonish talk, thereby changing grace into wrath for himself. Truly into wrath, and terrible wrath, if what Scripture sets forth applies to him: “When he has been filled, he shall be distressed, and every pain shall rush upon him. Would that his belly might be filled, so that God may send against him the wrath of his fury and rain his warfare upon him” (Job 20:15, 21, 23).

For the Prophet rightly perceived and assented that warfare should rain down upon sinners who have not yielded the fruit of peace in response to the voluntary rain; and that fire, sulphur, and the blast of tempests should be the portion of their cup, who drank the Lord’s cup unworthily. For land that often drinks the rain falling upon it and brings forth suitable vegetation receives a blessing; but land producing thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is in burning (Heb. 6:7–8). Yet we are persuaded of better things concerning you, brothers, things nearer to salvation. Only be grateful for the grace of God; and, as you have been transferred into a new creation through the Paschal mysteries, so always walk in newness of life.

Therefore you who have become partakers of Christ through the fellowship of faith, participation in the sacrament, [Col. 0148B] and communion of the Holy Spirit, strive not merely to retain firmly to the end the beginning of his substance, but diligently to increase it. Thus, having begun through so many prerogatives of gifts to have a share in the first resurrection, sealed on the day of recognition by confidence in so great a pledge, you may claim for yourselves an everlasting right in the second resurrection; through our Lord Jesus Christ, our resurrection and life, who died for us for three days and now lives and reigns for all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the vigilance necessary for us to have a share in Christ’s resurrection

1. “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” [Col. 0148C] (Rev. 20:6). Christ, the first fruits of those who sleep, the firstborn from the dead, by his resurrection—which is first among all—consecrated for us both the first resurrection of souls and the second of bodies. In the body which he raised from the dead, he declared to souls the sacrament, and to bodies the example, of rising again.

But Christ’s single resurrection has also prepared a twofold grace of resurrection for souls themselves: they are daily restored to life from the death of sin through the working of the mystery, and especially today they rise from the sleep of sluggishness through the devotion of joy. For who is so lazy or lukewarm that, hearing today that voice full of all joy, “The Lord has risen,” he is not wholly stirred to exultation, wholly restored to life and warmed in spirit? Indeed, “my heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God,” says one [Col. 0148D] who had wholly collapsed into sorrow and despair while looking upon Jesus dead (Ps. 83:3). Jesus’ return from the tomb brings me no small profit of faith and no slight interest of joy: he is recognized as the living God, who shortly before was mourned as a dead man; and he whose death grieved my heart is now alive, and in him not only my heart but also my flesh exults, secure, through him, of its own resurrection and immortality.

O my soul, Christ says, “I lay down and slept; I awoke” (Ps. 3:6); rise also, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you (Eph. 5:14). Is not one like the dead, brothers, who still stands after the sun has risen, who is still weighed down by negligence and apathy, as though buried in the torpor of despair, when already the grace of the resurrection shines everywhere? The new Sun, rising from the underworld, strikes the eyes of those who vigilantly seek him in the morning, opening the day of eternity. This day knows no evening, because its sun shall not set again: having once set, he once rose beyond the setting-place, subjecting death to himself.

2. O brothers, “this is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:24). Let us exult in its hope, so that we may see and rejoice in its light. Abraham exulted that he might see Christ’s day; and for that reason he saw it and rejoiced [Col. 0149B] (John 8:56). For you also, if every day you keep watch at Wisdom’s doors and observe at her gates, and if you keep vigil with Mary Magdalene at the door of his tomb (Matt. 27:61), will, I think, prove with that same Mary (Luke 24:1–8) how true is what is written of Wisdom herself, who is Christ: “She is easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her. She anticipates those who desire her, in order to show herself to them first. Whoever watches early for her shall not labour, for he will find her sitting at his doors” (Wis. 6:13–15).

For he himself promised, saying: “I love those who love me, and those who watch early for me shall find me” (Prov. 8:17). Mary did indeed find bodily the Jesus for whom she kept watch, at whose [Col. 0149C] tomb she had come to watch while it was still dark. But you, who ought no longer to know Jesus according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, will be able to find him spiritually, if you seek him with a like desire, if he finds you likewise vigilant in prayer. Say therefore to the Lord Jesus, with Mary’s desire and affection: “My soul desired you in the night, and also my spirit within my inmost parts; in the morning I shall watch for you” (Isa. 26:9). Say with the voice and mind of the Psalmist: “O God, my God, from the dawning light I watch for you; my soul thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2). And see whether it will not be fitting for you to sing with them: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy, and we have exulted and delighted” (Ps. 89:14).

[Col. 0149D]

3. Therefore keep watch, brothers: intent in prayer, keep watch; watchful in your actions. Especially do so because the morning of that unending day has now dawned, since eternal light has returned to us from the underworld more serene and welcome, and the morning reception has renewed the new Sun. Truly, it is now time for us to rise from sleep, since “the night has passed and the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:11–12). Keep watch, I say, so that the morning light may arise for you—namely Christ, whose coming forth is prepared like the dawn, prepared indeed repeatedly to renew for those who watch for him the mystery of his morning resurrection.

Then you will sing in the joy of your heart: “God, the Lord, has shone upon us. This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117:27, 24), when [Col. 0150A] he permits the light which he hides in his hands to shine through to you, declaring concerning it to his friend that it is his possession and that he may ascend to it. “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? How long will you doze? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep” (Prov. 6:9–10; 24:33). And while you sleep, unaware, Christ will rise from the tomb; and when his glory passes by, you will not deserve even to see his back. Then, in late repentance, you will weep and say with the wicked: “Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us” (Wis. 5:6).

“But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 4:2); and of the one “who walks in righteousness,” “his eyes shall see the King in his beauty” [Col. 0150B] (Isa. 33:15, 17). This indeed is the blessedness of the life to come; but in a certain measure it is granted also as consolation in the present life, as Christ’s resurrection plainly proves. For over forty days Wisdom proved to us by many signs that she “goes about seeking those worthy of her; she shows herself to them cheerfully in their paths, and meets them in every prudence” (Wis. 6:17). Thus, in order that Jesus might show himself to be that Wisdom of whom these things were written, and might represent in the form of a bodily act what he does not cease to do spiritually each day—that is, cheerfully to show himself in the paths of righteousness—today he met the women returning from the tomb on the road, and on the road showed himself to the two journeying to Emmaus (Luke 24:3–4, 13–27).

[Col. 0150C]

4. Let those who walk in the paths of righteousness hear and rejoice; let them hear, I say, that Jesus deigns both to meet and reveal himself not only to those who remain devoted to contemplation, but also to those who walk justly and devoutly in the paths of action. The experience of some among you, I think, recognizes that Jesus, whom they sought as at a tomb—at the memorials of altars—and did not find, unexpectedly met them on the paths of their labours. Then they came forward and took hold of his feet: feet which sluggishness had not held back from their longing for him.

Therefore, brother, do not spare your feet too much from the paths of obedience and the journeys of works, since Jesus did not spare his own feet from the pain [Col. 0150D] of the nails even for your sake; and he is still not wearied of rewarding or relieving the labour of your feet by the embrace and kiss of those same feet. How great a consolation it will also be if he joins himself to you as your companion on the road and, through the wonderful delight of his conversation, even removes from you the sense of labour, opening your understanding so that you understand the Scriptures which, perhaps, you read while sitting at home but did not understand.

I beg you, my brothers, you to whom divine condescension has at some time granted this experience: was not your heart burning within you because of Jesus, when he spoke with you on the way and opened the Scriptures? Let those who have experienced this remember it and sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord. Let those who have not experienced it believe and strive to experience it, so that at last the ordinances [Col. 0151A] of God may become a song for them also in the place of their pilgrimage and affliction.

5. Therefore let the spirit of us all rise again and return to life, whether for wakefulness in prayer or for diligence in work, so that with a renewed and living eagerness it may prove that it has received anew a share in Christ’s resurrection. The first sign of life returning to a human being is that he is vigorous and unwearied in action; but its perfect resurrection in this still mortal body consists in opening the eyes for contemplation. Yet the understanding does not merit this before the affection has been enlarged by frequent sighs and vehement desires, so that it may be made capable of so great a majesty.

I judge that this ascending progress of resurrection, as though through certain stages, is significantly represented in the dead child whom Elisha raised. As he began to return to life, it is first said that the child’s flesh grew warm; then that he yawned seven times; and only then opened his eyes (4 Kgs. 4:34–35). The child’s flesh is the fleshy heart in one who is a little child in Christ; its first hope of life is that it may say: “My heart grew warm within me, and in my meditation a fire will blaze” (Ps. 38:4). [Col. 0152A] His garments too are warm when his land is breathed upon by the south wind—that is, by the Holy Spirit, whom the true Elisha breathes forth anew in advance.

He advances more fully and plainly toward resurrection when, through a certain desire and hunger for righteousness, he begins to yawn more frequently, in the manner of the one who said: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments” (Ps. 118:131). This yawn is the stretching of the affection, so that the spirit of life may become more capacious; and thus, after the other charisms of sevenfold grace, the Spirit of understanding and wisdom may also be infused and finally cause the eyes to open for contemplating God.

Thus the first warmth of returning life is when good action is practised; the second advance of resurrection is when affection is enlarged through prayer; perfection is when understanding is enlightened for contemplation. By these stages of virtues, by these advances in the holier life, my brothers, strive to rise ever more and more, if in some way you may attain, as the Apostle says, “the resurrection of Christ from the dead” [Col. 0152B] (Phil. 3:11), who lives and reigns for all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FOR THE ROGATION DAYS: On asking for and setting forth the bread of the word

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151B]

1. “Lend me three loaves” (Luke 11:5). Friends have come to us from the road, but I have nothing to set before them. I am not a physician, and in my house there is no [Col. 0151C] bread; therefore I said from the beginning: “Do not appoint me ruler” (Isa. 3:7). For one ought not preside who cannot be of use. But how can one be of use who is neither a physician nor has bread in his house—that is, who neither knows the art by which he may heal nor possesses the teaching sufficient to feed others?

I did say these things; but alas, you did not listen to me, for you appointed me ruler. It remained, therefore, since I could not escape the danger, that I should flee to the remedy and heed the counsel of the Wise Man: “Have they appointed you ruler? Be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclus. 32:1). But woe is me: even this has not been left to me. For as lack of skill prevents one from being over others, so weakness does not permit one to be among others; and just as I do not suffice in spirit [Col. 0151D] to minister the word, so I fail in body to provide an example.

Since, therefore, I am fit neither to preside nor to be alongside others, where can I be, unless I choose the last and safest place—namely, to be beneath all? And this indeed I can do: to think humbly—indeed, truthfully—of myself. Nothing prevents me from being subject to all in spirit; rather, truth itself strongly admonishes me to do so, even though duty compels me to preside.

2. You, Lord God, are the one who both command me to be subject and nevertheless bid me preside. From you I ask, from you I await, that you make me at once humble and useful in the ministry entrusted to me: humble, by thinking truthfully of myself; useful, by speaking rightly about you. Inspire the former in my heart; supply the latter to my mouth. Give a right and fittingly sounding word at the opening of my mouth, you who said, “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” [Col. 0152B] (Ps. 80:11), so that your whole household may be filled with blessings.

Behold, friends have come—my friends indeed, but even more yours. I have nothing to set before them unless it is lent by another. And who else is as rich or generous in lending as the Lord of all, “rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. 10:12), who opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing (Ps. 144:16), who gives generously to all and does not reproach (Jas. 1:5)—unless perhaps to the one who either asks sluggishly or ungratefully retains the grace he has received? How many hired servants in this householder’s house have bread in abundance. Because they proclaim Christ, though not sincerely, the grace of teaching is nevertheless not denied them for the sake of others. And where hired servants abound, will children be in need?

Therefore, Lord—for I fear to call you friend, but confess you as [Col. 0152D] Lord—lend me three loaves by which the friends may be refreshed, lest, if I send them away fasting, they fail on the road and I then be called to account for them, and it be said to me: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). Lend, Lord, what may advance to your profit; for when it pleases you, you will receive back what is yours with interest. Lend, I say, three loaves, if you please; or at least whatever you please, however little it may be. Even a morsel of bread will suffice for however many thousands, if only you bless it.

I know indeed that you wish us to be importunate with you: though you seem to refuse, though you excuse yourself because you have already been received into heaven and your Apostles are with you in bed, yet we should nonetheless persist in asking, seeking, and knocking. We know that teaching is not merited by innocence of life alone, through which we become friends, without the constancy of study and persistence in prayer, through which we appear importunate. Yet neither supports my plea; I set forth only the merit of those who must be fed. They deserve what I do not deserve.

3. But you, my brothers, for whose needs and on whose merits I ask these loaves, do you think that we are sufficient—either I to break them or you to eat them? I fear lest it be said to me: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search into things stronger than yourself” (Ecclus. 3:21). I fear lest it also be said to you: “You have become such as need milk, not bread” (Heb. 5:12). I know well that there are loaves with the householder which, if our infancy presumes to take them, will sooner break our teeth than fill our bellies—that is, build up our minds.

For who can comprehend, who can sufficiently explain or worthily conceive that ineffable mystery of the Trinity: how the Father is from himself, the Son from the Father, the Holy Spirit from both, and yet there are three persons in unity of substance? The foolish woman, the rash vanity of heretics, urges those with itching ears to investigate such matters, although God must be believed, not examined. “Gladly touch,” she says, “the hidden loaves.” As though you, fool, could touch what is more sublime than the angels. And why should I touch hidden loaves which I may not break or eat without danger?

It is enough for me to know that they exist, that there are three loaves. I do not mean the Trinity [Col. 0153C] of persons, but the trinity of discourses—or rather, understandings—that must be held concerning the persons: three loaves, I say, of one size and weight, one form and flavour. For whatever and however much must be thought concerning the Father must likewise be thought concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, except only that the distinction of properties makes a number of persons, just as in the Trinity, so too a number of understandings in their distinction.

4. Let us therefore leave these loaves to be broken by angelic sublimity, until, growing toward their equality, we are fit for their table. For many other trinities of loaves can be set before us from Scripture, which are more suited to our weakness. For example, so that we may not yet move far from that highest Trinity: all things are from him, through him, and in him; we have been created by the Father, redeemed through the Son, and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.

In this manner so much can be said that however hungry a friend may arrive from the road, if you set even half of it before him, he may perhaps begin to be endangered by satiety no less than formerly by hunger: abundance may overwhelm one whom scarcity had distressed. For you can set forth in threefold fashion not only him who made us, and the things made for us, but also the things written for us, so that there may be abundant refreshment in the three loaves of history, allegory, and moral instruction.

The whole content of Scripture is also divided into three parts, as though arranged into three loaves, when it treats either of natural righteousness, [Col. 0154B] literal righteousness, or spiritual righteousness; that is, before the law, under the law, and after the law, which is under grace. Nature gave right understanding; the law gave action as well; grace gave affection. The Doctor and Shepherd of the Gentiles in faith and truth also teaches that the Church should be fed by a trinity of loaves: one who builds up the Church should speak “for edification, exhortation, and consolation” (1 Cor. 14:3). For edification, that you may know what you ought to do; for exhortation, that you may will what you know; for consolation, that even amid adversities you may be able to do what you have known and willed.

Finally, not only in the subject matter of things, the senses and parts of Scriptures, and the kinds and modes of speech, but also in every end of them, you will find a certain trinity of loaves, itself quite savoury and wholesome: namely faith, hope, and love. For the whole purpose of Scriptures and sermons seems to aim at this: that we may believe, hope, and love. Indeed, love alone has been defined as the end of the commandment; and it too is in a certain manner threefold, since it must be possessed with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength.

But since a longer and varied banquet is considered a fault, we shall end the reading. It will be your task to gather the fragments that remain—that is, the subtler matters which escaped our hands. And it will be both your task and ours to sing to him who feeds us: “Blessed be God in his gifts,” who lives and reigns for all ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE DAY OF THE LORD’S ASCENSION. SERMON: On Christ’s love for us and ours for him

[Col. 0153]

[Col. 0153D]

1. “Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name” (John 17:11–12). This prayer of the Lord was made before the day of his passion. Yet it is not inappropriately suited to the day of the Ascension, when he was about to depart finally from his little children and commended them to the Father. He who created in heaven teaches and rules the multitude of angels; on earth he had gathered for himself a little flock of disciples to be instructed in the presence of his flesh, until, having attained a more mature understanding, they became fit for the discipline of the Spirit.

Thus the great one loved the little ones with great love: he had drawn them away from the love of the world, and saw them, having abandoned every hope in the age, dependent upon himself alone. Yet while he wished to associate with them bodily, he did not readily or greatly disclose this affection for them, presenting himself as more mature than tender, as befitted a teacher and father. But when the time drew near when he was to depart from them, he seemed, as it were, to be overcome by their tender affection, so that he could not conceal the great abundance of sweetness which he had hidden from them. Hence it is said that, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end” (John 13:1).

Then he poured out almost the whole force of his love upon his friends, before he himself was poured out like water for his enemies.
