Then he handed over to them the sacrament of his Body and Blood and instituted its celebration, devising—I do not know whether through a more wonderful power or love—this new manner of abiding as consolation for his departure: so that, although he departed from them in the visible form of his body, he might remain not only with them but also in them through the power of the sacrament. Then, as though entirely forgetful of his majesty, and as though doing himself an injury—except that it is the glory of love to humble itself for friends—the Lord, and such a Lord, in ineffable condescension washed the feet of his servants. By this one act [Col. 0155B] he gave them both an example of humility and a sacrament of forgiveness.

2. Finally, after the exhortation of his longer discourse, commending them to the Father, he lifted his eyes to heaven and among other things said: “Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name, and none of them perished except the son of perdition. But now I come to you: keep in your name those whom you gave me. I do not ask that you take them from the world, but that you keep them from evil”; and the rest, which this is not the time to recount, much less expound.

Yet the sum of the prayer, as the text of the reading indicates, lies in these three things, in which lies also the sum of salvation—indeed, of perfection, so that nothing can be added: namely, that they may be kept from evil, sanctified in truth, and [Col. 0155C] glorified with him. “Father,” he says, “I will that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am, that they may see my glory” (John 17:11–13, 15, 24).

O happy ones, whose advocate is the judge himself; for whom he prays who is to be adored with equal honour to the one whom he prays! The Father will not disappoint him of the desire of his lips, since with him he has one will and one power, because he is one God. Whatever Christ prays for must surely be fulfilled: his word is power and his will effect; concerning all things that are, “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9).

“I will,” he says, “that where I am, they too may be with me.” O what security for the faithful, what confidence for believers—provided only that they do not cast away the grace they have received. [Col. 0155D] For this security is not set before the Apostles alone, or their fellow disciples, but before all who will believe in the word of God through their word. “I do not pray for them only,” he says, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:24, 20).

3. But to you, brethren, it has been granted, as the Apostle says, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him (Phil. 1:29). Thus faith in Christ’s promise makes you not more negligent through security, but more fervent through eagerness; and it crowns you with a continual martyrdom in the daily conflict against vices: continual, yet easy; easy, yet sublime. It is easy where nothing beyond one’s strength is commanded; sublime where victory is won over every power of that strong armed man. Is it not easy to bear Christ’s sweet yoke? Is it not sublime to excel in his kingdom? What, I ask, is easier than to bear wings which themselves bear their bearer? What more sublime than to fly above every height of heaven, whither Christ ascended? Certainly the saints, whose youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s, shall take up wings like eagles and shall fly. Whither will they fly? “Wherever the body shall be,” he says, “there shall the eagles also be gathered” (Matt. 24:28; Luke 17:37).

4. But how, brethren, do we suppose that he will then suddenly be able to fly from earth to heaven who has not now learned, through daily exercise and practice, to flutter and fly? If you ask under what teacher or guide: did not Christ, like an eagle, today summon his young to flight when he hovered over them—that is, when he was raised up before their eyes and they long followed with their eyes as he went into heaven? He could indeed in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, have been snatched from their sight and placed wherever he wished. But certainly, like an eagle “stirring up her young to fly and hovering over them” (Deut. 32:11), he strove by love for himself to draw their hearts upward after him, and by the example of his own body promised that their bodies likewise could be lifted up. As the Apostle says, conscious of the eternal mystery, we too shall be caught up on clouds that bear us to meet Christ returning (1 Thess. 4:16). He himself ascended above the Cherubim and flew

[Col. 0156C]

upon the wings of the winds (Ps. 17:11); that is, he passed beyond the powers of the angels. Yet, stooping to your weakness, he will spread his wings, take you up, and bear you upon his shoulders—provided only that you are not a degenerate fledgling, afraid to be raised from earth and to enjoy a purer air.

5. Others fly by contemplation; you, at least, fly by love. Paul is carried beyond himself in mind and flies as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2); John, to that Word which was in the beginning. You, at least, do not drag a degenerate soul along the ground, nor allow your heart, buried by sloth in the earth, to rot away. Rather, faithfully answer the great High Priest—who today entered the Holy Places, having obtained eternal redemption, where he also stands

[Col. 0156D]

before the face of God, interceding for us—when he cries, “Lift up your hearts”: “We have them unto the Lord.” And if at any time you have sought not the things above, but the things upon earth, rebuke yourself and say to the Lord with the prophet: “What have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. 72:25). Alas, how miserably I wandered! So great was that which lay stored up for me in heaven, and which I despised; so utterly nothing was that upon earth which I so eagerly pursued! Therefore Christ, your treasure, has ascended into heaven: let your heart also be there. From there you derive your origin; there you have your Father and inheritance; from there you await the Savior. Amen.

## On the Feast of Pentecost

[Col. 0157]

### Sermon I. On God’s Love and Human Ingratitude

[Col. 0157A]

1. God is ineffable; his mercy is ineffable. As his name is, so is his work. Truly, ineffable is the loving condescension of God toward us. It was too little for the Father to give up his Son to redeem a slave, unless he also gave the Holy Spirit, through whom he might adopt the slave as a son. He gave the Son as the price of redemption; he gave the Spirit as the privilege of adoption; finally, he keeps himself entire as the inheritance of those adopted. O God—if it is permitted so to speak—lavish of himself out of desire for humankind! Is he not lavish, who expends not only what is his, but his very self, in order to recover humanity, not so much for himself as for humanity itself? Is he not lavish, who, “as he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32), likewise did not spare the Holy Spirit, so to speak, but with a new and wondrous bounty poured him out upon all flesh?

That prodigal son indeed was lavish in the outpouring of himself, who gave both his estate and himself to prostitutes; yet the father was far more lavish in recovering his lost son than the son was in ruining himself (Luke 5) — if, indeed, there ought to be any comparison of grace and money, spirit and flesh, God and human being. See with what abundance the grace of the Spirit has been poured out over the whole world: not merely to strengthen the righteous, but also to justify sinners; how, among nations everywhere, the Spirit, creating a new race of human beings, has renewed the face of the earth; indeed, what a transformation is daily wrought by the right hand of the Most High, so that suddenly the most abandoned tax collectors

[Col. 0157C]

and prostitutes may go before very many righteous persons into the kingdom of God, and the last become first. Truly, “it is not with the gift as with the offense”: for where offense abounded, grace abounded beyond measure (Rom. 5:15, 20). Grace not only forgives offenses, but also heaps up the merits of virtues; and redemption restores the fallen more exaltedly than the first creation had established them.

Certainly, in all these things, the more wonderfully God’s grace is proclaimed, the more condemnable is the hardness of humanity proved to be, if it either refuses grace when offered or does not preserve it once received. For to whom is it not offered? Upon whom does its light not shine? Who hides himself from its warmth? God has not left himself without witness in human consciences, enlightening them with the radiance of truth and warming them with the heat of goodness; since “the true light enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9), and God “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matt. 5:45).

But woe to those who rebel against the light, resist the Holy Spirit, and do not yield to the truth which they understand. Like clay hardened by the sun’s heat, they become harder through God’s goodness and benefits; they even boldly provoke him, though he has given all things into their hands!

2. But what have we to do with those who are outside? Rather, our discourse is addressed to you,

[Col. 0158A]

who have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, possessing that same Spirit as the sign of adoption and the pledge of inheritance. Like a distinctive seal, it separates vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. Yet concerning our salvation—or rather, our hope of salvation—we ought to rejoice with such modesty that we should still fear for ourselves, because of our changeableness, what we grieve over in them. For just as it is impious to despair of them, so it is rash to presume concerning ourselves. Whatever knowledge one may have of the present, there can be no foreknowledge of the future, either concerning us or concerning them. Nor is it a slight affront to the supreme power, with whom rests the decision of life and death, if one prejudges his judgments either so cruelly concerning them or so boldly concerning ourselves.

For we have been taken from their mass; and we who a little before

[Col. 0158B]

were, like them, by nature and manner of life children of wrath, have suddenly become children of grace. Let us therefore be for them an example of hope leading to repentance; and let them be for us an example of fear leading to perseverance. In us mercy displays itself, that it may be loved; in them judgment displays itself, that it may be feared. “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1): giving thanks for the one, pouring out prayers because of the other; grateful and joyful because of the one, fearful and cautious because of the other. Instructed by both, I shall rejoice before you with trembling, because I shall then walk in your truth if my heart so rejoices that it fears your name.

For this fear, made chaste by love, does not take joy away, but guards it; does not destroy it, but instructs it; does not embitter it, but seasons it. Thus it is more enduring because more modest, truer because more grave, sweeter because holier. O chaste and faithful joy! How true of you is that saying of the Wise Man: “There is no wealth above bodily health, and no delight above joy of heart” (Ecclus. 30:16). The ungodly do not rejoice with this joy; the Wise Man abominates and rebukes their foolish laughter and frivolous pleasures. “I judged laughter to be error,” he says, “and I said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” (Eccl. 2:2). “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning shall occupy the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13).

3. O good Jesus, how unlike is that joy of yours by which you meanwhile console those who renounce that false and deceitful joy! How better is your mercy than lives! How better is one day in your courts

[Col. 0158D]

than thousands! By your very poverty, how much happier do you make your poor than the world can make its own by however great an abundance—where whatever flows in flows away, and carries away with it the person who clings to it!

That poor household of Christ overflowed with other delights, when the torrent of the river that gladdens the city of God flooded it: that is, when on this day the Spirit, like a rushing stream, filled the whole house where the Apostles were sitting (Acts 2:2). For divine Truth fulfilled what it had promised through the prophet: “Behold, I will turn toward you

[Col. 0159A]

like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66:12). How much flowed into those into whom so great a stream poured! And how much flowed forth from those from whose belly flowed rivers of living water! Not only did the charity of goodwill flow from their hearts, but from their mouths also poured the force of a torrent of speech, which none of their adversaries could resist or contradict. Thus it is said of Stephen that they “could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

4. To joys of this kind, brethren, your Comforter now invites you. He desires to give the thirsty minds of those who love him drink from this torrent of his delight. “If anyone thirsts,” he says, “let him come and drink” (John 7:37). O overflowing liberality of God! O unfailing bounty of divine goodness! The Spirit, whose first-fruits he gave today to the Apostles,

[Col. 0159B]

he offers to all. He opens his treasure, the fountain of living water, both to people and to beasts, as though he too were debtor to all, wise and foolish alike. “All you who thirst,” he says, “come to the waters” (Isa. 55:1). Behold: he does not accept persons, distinguish conditions, or require merits; one need only know how to thirst and be willing to come. For grace does not admit those who are sated; but as it fills the hungry with good things, so it sends the rich away empty.

O satiety—the moth of hearts, the rust of minds, the most grievous sickness of souls—which makes one loathe God’s good word, despise the heavenly gift, and be disgusted with manna because of pots of meat! What plague is so destructive, what illness so deadly, as to make a person forgetful of salvation, laughing and wickedly secure while approaching even to the gates of death? But how, I ask, has this plague infected Christ’s sheepfolds so widely and invaded the flocks, that for very many in the Lord’s flock even their place of awe and vast solitude—the place of pasture in which they have been set—has become a place where, amid most fertile pastures and green grass, they wretchedly perish, sick with disgust?

Have they not, I ask, tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the Holy Spirit? Have they not likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come? (Heb. 6:5). For if they have not tasted God’s good word, how has their heart so often poured forth a good word, when their lips poured forth a hymn from the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness? Yet now they take part in divine praises and fall asleep; or they turn over idle and even harmful thoughts in their minds. They sit down to a book and yawn; they hear a word of exhortation and are wearied by the very hearing; they move from pasture to pasture, and are disgusted with this as with that; they are continually occupied among the dishes of life and die of hunger.

[Col. 0159D]

Whence, then, after that happy experience and sweet taste of heavenly sweetness, has this great forgetfulness and neglect of the good, this languor of mind, crept in? There remains to them only the voice of one lamenting—if indeed they are willing to lament: “I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). They were surely running well: who bewitched them to turn back? They began in the Spirit: how are they now being finished in the flesh? They feasted delightfully: how do they now perish in the ways?

[Col. 0160A]

5. Let them see, I ask, whether perhaps the enemy, who is accustomed to sow his tares over the good seed of the householder, has, after that sweet food of Christ, stained their throats with his gall, and thereby destroyed not only the desire but even the memory of the former taste. Indeed, the Apostle immediately declares to those who are such: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20–21).

Does he not seem to you not merely to drink, but to be drunk from the cup of demons, who is carried away by the frenzy of lust, anger, impatience, or similar passions? To speak of matters now more customary than criminal, I think that he too is a partaker of the table of demons—and, feeding them, is fed by them—whose mouth abounds in malice, whose tongue fashions deceits, who sits speaking against his brother and lays a stumbling-block before his mother’s son; who, even if he does not slander, willingly listens to a slanderer; who dissolves others in laughing fits by the buffoonery of foolish talk.

Let one who is such consider whether it is fitting that, after wallowing as it were in sacrificial blood and the filth of demons, he should immediately be admitted to the table of Christ and the angels. But far be it from me, my brethren, in saying this, to charge your innocence, in which I take great delight, with guilt. I say these things that you may be saved and, made more cautious by the example of others, may wash your hands in the blood of the sinner and take every care to preserve, with all vigilance, the grace of the Holy Spirit which others lose through negligence—to the praise and glory of Jesus Christ our Lord, the giver of that grace, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon II. On the Mystery of Tongues and the Gift of Tears

1. The Apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God (Acts 2:11). Surely it was from the abundance of the heart that tongues spoke within them. The exultations of God were in their throats because the love of God had been poured out in their hearts. O Lord my God, I too would surely praise you in like manner, if I were given drink in like manner. But because my soul is dry, my tongue also is sluggish. “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation” (Ps. 62:6). My lips shall pour forth a hymn—but when you have taught me

[Col. 0160D]

your ordinances: that is, when you have enabled me to taste how sweet you are, so that I may learn to love you with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength. “You are good, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances” (Ps. 118:12).

For your goodness is your anointing, by which you teach those of whom it was foretold: “They shall all be taught by God” (John 6:45). “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12). The law of the Lord, undefiled and converting souls (Ps. 18:8), is love: indeed, the fiery law which is in his right hand, which, written with the finger of God upon the breadth of the heart, makes the heart itself burn with love’s fire and causes people to glow with fiery speech. “From on high he sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” (Lam. 1:13).

O with what ease and speed, with what abundance and power, did that fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth not only instruct the ignorant but also make the impeded eloquent! Truly fiery are the tongues which that fire distributed from itself, which so kindled not only the minds but also the tongues of the Apostles that even now a devout hearer is inflamed by their words. Truly fiery was Peter’s tongue, fiery Paul’s tongue; in whose words an everlasting fire still lives, sparkling even upon our hearts, if we draw near, if we do not turn ear or mind away from their words.

2. If I had deserved to receive one of such tongues, I too would surely say: “The Lord gave me my tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise him” (Ecclus. 51:30); as it is written of them:

[Col. 0161B]

“The Apostles spoke in various tongues the mighty works of God.” I would say also: “The Lord gave me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain by a word him who has fallen” (Isa. 50:4). The Apostles and those like them, with the tongues given them, proclaim God’s mighty works, scourge tyrants, whip demons, water the earth, and open heaven; for their tongues were made keys of heaven, since tongues were sent to them from heaven itself.

But would that even a dog’s tongue were given me, by which I might first lick my own sores and then those of others, if perhaps there are any who would deem me worthy to be admitted for this very task. Blessed indeed are those whose heart love and delight in divine praise fill with joy, and whose mouth they fill with jubilation. Yet I would surely call blessed also those who lick away poison and pus from the wounds of souls, drawing it into themselves so that their own soul may be fattened with spirit and grace. For they hunger and thirst for righteousness and suffer hunger like dogs; consequently, they disdain nothing that they can take into their bodies, and they abhor no sinner whom they can convert to righteousness. “What God has cleansed, do not call unclean” (Acts 11:9) was said to the Prince of the Apostles, and in him to others. Therefore he slaughters and eats every kind of creeping thing and bird, and says: “Things which my soul formerly refused to touch are now, because of the distress of impatient longing, my food” (Job 6:7).

Indeed, it is wonderfully so: the more bitter any sinner was before conversion, the sweeter his conversion afterwards; and the more desperate, the more welcome his salvation is to us. For we marvel the more at the grace of the Savior, who, bearing the lost sheep home upon his shoulders, causes the angels to rejoice more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons (Luke 15:7).

3. Let others, then, to whom it has been granted, say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord!” (Ps. 118:103). But my soul, hungry and suffering hunger like a dog, will take even what is bitter as sweet, and what is abhorrent as desirable. Let others delight in licking the honey of the Scriptures; I, however, shall delight in licking the sores of sinners—my own, that is, and those of people like myself. The wound of sin is foul and horrible to behold; yet what savor and grace there is in licking it, no one knows or comprehends except one who hungers for the salvation of those in danger and suffers hunger like a dog. Of such it is said: “The tongue of your dogs—from the enemies” (Ps. 118:24).

But woe to the wretches who so zealously perish and so eagerly bring death upon themselves that they hide their wounds, avoid the care of dogs, and judge the roughness of the healing tongue to be the bite of deadly hatred! “They hate the one who rebukes at the gate, and they abominate one who speaks perfectly” (Amos 5:10). By “one who speaks perfectly,” I mean not so much one discoursing upon perfection as one rebuking with perfect love. Yet should I say, with perfect love or with perfect hatred? Rather, both: with perfect love and perfect hatred. For perfect hatred is nothing other than perfect love; and the perfection of both is one, which the Apostle defines when he says: “Hating evil, but cleaving to good” (Rom. 12:9).

4. But let me return to the point from which I had digressed. I desired a tongue with which I might praise God, or at least a tongue with which I might heal the sores of those confessing: in the first, seeking for myself the fruit of divine devotion; in the second, the gain of a brother’s salvation. I desired to become pleasing to you in the first and useful in the second. For from the art and office of secular poets, one of them has said:

> Poets wish either to benefit or to delight.  
> He has won every vote who has mingled the useful with the sweet.  
> —Horace, *Art of Poetry*

I desired, I say, the grace of speech by which I might serve God and you in dutiful service, so as to make some compensation

[Col. 0162C]

by word for the lesser benefit I provide by example. Yet this consolation is quite suspect to me if I say and do not do; if the supports of speech are at hand while the merits of life are lacking. Indeed, perhaps I should fear rather that God may say to me in my sin: “Why do you recount my justifications and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16).

But what shall I do? “If I speak, my pain is not stilled; and if I keep silent, it does not depart from me” (Job 16:7). Fear is troublesome on both sides, and I am constrained from two directions: my position requires speech as a duty, while my life contradicts it. But I remember the saying which I found in the Wise Man: “The soul of one who labors labors for himself, because his mouth compels him” (Prov. 16:26). Therefore I shall speak—not as my position demands, but as my understanding permits; indeed, as the Lord gives, in whose hand are both we and our words. I shall speak, I say, and bind myself with my own tongue, that at least through shame I may sometimes be compelled to labor. And if it excuses my body from the labor of hands, at least let the soul of one who labors labor for itself, so that it may say with David: “I have labored in my groaning” (Ps. 6:7). O that those unutterable groanings might be given me, by which the Spirit intercedes for the saints, so that I might labor in them! Without doubt the labor of such groanings would adequately repay me for my daily labor of the hands.

5. And you yourselves, brethren, if you have learned to desire the better gifts, ask that groanings of this sort may be poured into you by the Spirit. I do not know whether among the gifts of the Spirit there is anything more fitting or more advantageous for those encompassed by weakness and misery. I do not know whether, for the Holy Spirit who appeared in the dove,

[Col. 0163A]

any voice is more familiar or more pleasing than groaning. But this I know: in no work is such great and ready material available to us as in our groaning and lamentation—unless our pride conceals our misery from us, or our awareness is hardened by stupefaction or madness.

This is the first effect, regarding the sick whose care he undertakes, of the medicine of the Holy Spirit, who is our illumination and our salvation: namely, that the delirious person may feel and know himself, and, returning to his heart, say to the Lord with the prophet: “After you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jer. 31:19). For unless one applies knowledge, one does not apply sorrow; unless one has sorrow, one does not merit consolation. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

I think that the consolation of the Paraclete would not have found a place even in the Apostles today unless they mourned that they were left desolate. For the bridegroom’s children could not but mourn when the bridegroom had been taken away from them. Hence he said to them: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7). Unless you are left desolate by my bodily presence, the spiritual visitation will not console you. “Give strong drink,” he says, “to those who mourn, and wine to those who are of bitter spirit” (Prov. 31:6)—not, of course, to those drunk with the joy and luxury of this age. For what fellowship has righteousness with iniquity? Can they drink

[Col. 0163C]

the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons? Rather, he says, let the poor Apostles drink and forget their need (Prov. 31:6–7), so that they may say: “As needy, yet making many rich” (2 Cor. 6:10). Let those mourning the Bridegroom’s absence drink and no longer remember their sorrows, but say:

[Col. 0164A]

“Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). For if you too can say with the devout affection of the Psalmist, “I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. 68:30), the sober intoxication of this glorious cup will so enrich and gladden you that, even if you are poor, poverty will not burn your heart; and, if you grieved because you had sinned, the consciousness of sin’s guilt will no longer bite you.

6. Consider also whether the Holy Spirit himself does not come into this world for judgment, so that those who mourn may not mourn, while those who laugh may surrender themselves to eternal and inconsolable lamentation. It is therefore better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting (Ecclus. 7:3). And truly, although the wise person may at times deserve consolation so as no longer to remember sorrows—those, namely, for which he receives consolation—yet, in order to make room for new consolations, he always seeks new causes of sorrow within himself. He does not immediately flatter himself as though he were already altogether righteous; rather, the more he has begun to be enlightened, the more penetrating he becomes; the more he has begun to be justified, the more exacting he becomes as his own accuser and judge.

Therefore, I think, the Spirit the Comforter frequently comes to one who is such, because he himself has already anticipated his coming: he comes in order to grant consolation, but he anticipates it in order to teach mourning. For devout and religious mourning is found first in the Spirit’s instruction and order, and preeminent in usefulness. It is the highest wisdom of the saints, the safeguard of the righteous, the sobriety of the self-controlled, the first virtue of beginners, the spur of those advancing, the completion of the perfect, the salvation of the perishing, the harbor of those in danger; finally, it bears the promise of consolations that are present and joys that are to come. May he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages bring us to these. Amen.

## On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 0163]

### Sermon I. On the Praises of the Saint

[Col. 0163D]

1. “Ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. 1:6). Brethren, if Jeremiah—as you heard in yesterday’s reading—more bashfully than justly pleaded his youth as an excuse, so that he might not undertake the office of preaching, how much more rightly should I plead the inadequacy of my understanding? If weak age deterred one who was holy from the womb, and whom divine election manifestly sent, what face can I have for speaking, when neither my conscience supports a claim to holiness nor my learning supplies eloquence?

Was his childhood a cause of fear for him, and will my childishness not be so for me? Yet you, child and prophet of the Most High, of whom the duty of our present occasion requires us to speak today, do not permit our childishness to be accepted as an excuse, so that at least we may long, in the manner of children, somehow to stammer concerning you—

[Col. 0164C–D]

we who have not yet learned even in an easier subject to form words fully. It will be your task, O voice of the Word, voice of wisdom, to loose the bond of a tongue devoted to you; for though not yet speaking, you were able to restore the use of speech to your mute father. Nor did that interrupted faculty of speech return without great increase, since the grace of prophecy was added to it at the same time, so that each parent might rejoice that something had been granted to them from the prerogative of their son.

2. For he who was to be a prophet, and more than a prophet—indeed, who began to prophesy before he began to speak, and to perceive God before himself—also made his parents prophets. Into those who had communicated to him the substance of flesh he poured back an overflowing abundance of his Spirit and grace. Thus Elizabeth, after the child leaped for joy in her womb,

[Col. 0165A]

then herself prophesied, filled with the Holy Spirit. For her son, though not yet speaking, revealed the Lord’s hidden presence to his mother by manifest exultation. He greeted the Savior by the movement available to him, and as an eager forerunner longed to break forth to meet the Lord.

Truly incomparable is this grace; beyond estimation is the power of divine might. While Mary’s voice sounded in Elizabeth’s ears, it penetrated to John’s heart, hidden within his mother’s womb; it quickened his spirit and revived him with saving joy. To one into whom the power of nature had scarcely yet poured his whole soul, the power of Mary’s voice poured a fuller prophecy—so fully that from the son’s abundance it seems to be poured back in rich measure even into the mother.

Truly Mary was full of grace: manifestly the God of all grace was in her, from whose bounty the abundance of grace flowed so richly and magnificently—first into the Mother, from the Mother into John, and from John into his parents. From Mary’s womb indeed flowed rivers of living water, and from the midst of paradise sprang a fountain of life and grace to water the trees of paradise.

3. This noble cedar—John, I mean—stood nearest to the fountain: kinsman and friend of the Bridegroom, Forerunner, Baptist, and martyr of the Lord. Therefore, being watered more abundantly, he grew so great that among those born of women none higher could be found. He was wholly close to the Savior, approaching him more nearly than all mortals not only through the bond of blood or intimate friendship, but also through the glory of his announcement, the marvel of his birth, holiness almost from his origin, similar preaching,

[Col. 0165C]

authority to baptize, and strength in suffering. Finally, even if all else were lacking and all the heraldings of the prophets concerning him were silent, the very grace of his name alone would sufficiently and abundantly testify to the singular grace of God that would be in him.

> [Note: [Col. 0165D] For *John* is interpreted “the grace of God.”]

For it was fitting that he who was full of grace should preach the grace of God which she who was full of grace had poured forth; that one who marked out, as a kind of middle boundary, the time of grace from the time of the Law should shine forth with no ordinary grace. “For the Law and the Prophets prophesied until John” (Luke 16:16): he was the first to point out as present the one whom Law and Prophecy had promised would come.

[Col. 0165D]

4. Rightly, then, the birth of this child caused many to rejoice at that time and causes rejoicing today. Born in his parents’ old age, he was to proclaim to an aging world the grace of rebirth. Rightly does the Church solemnly venerate this birth, which grace wonderfully works and nature marvels at—especially since through it she sees faithful pledges sent beforehand of that unique birth by whose grace nature was restored. The Church proves herself neither ungrateful nor forgetful: she faithfully recognizes with what devotion and thanksgiving she ought to receive the Forerunner, through whom she recognized the Savior himself.

To me the lamp of the world is born with new joy: by his indication I recognized the true light shining in the darkness,

[Col. 0166A]

though not comprehended by the darkness. To me he is born with truly ineffable joy, with whom so many and such great blessings are born to the world. He is the first to give the Church catechetical instruction; through repentance he initiates her; through baptism he prepares her; prepared, he seals and joins her to Christ. He who trains her to live temperately also confirms her by his own death to die courageously; and in all these things he prepares a perfect people for the Lord.

5. O brethren, whose purpose—and, would that it were also your desire—is to hasten toward perfection: how quickly would one attain Christian perfection who gave this teacher a teachable mind! Even the first rudiments of his righteousness surpassed the measure of human perfection; the beginnings of his earliest age outdid the grave wisdom of old age. For one who was holy before he was born—what wonder if, in the progress of his manner of life, he was more than holy?

We may marvel at your holiness, holiest of saints; we cannot imitate it. It is wholly necessary that you, hastening to prepare a perfect people for the Lord out of tax collectors and sinners, should speak to them more humanely than you live, and should temper the standard of perfection not according to the pattern of your own life but according to the capacity of ordinary human virtue. “Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8). We, brethren, boast of speaking more perfectly than we live; but John, though living more sublimely than human beings can even understand, nevertheless speaks to them as they can hear. “Bring forth,” he says,

[Col. 0166C]

“fruits worthy of repentance.” “I speak in human terms,” he says, “because of the weakness of your flesh” (Rom. 6:19). If the fullness of every good cannot yet be in you, let there at least be true repentance for every evil. If you are not yet able to produce the fruits of perfect righteousness, let this meanwhile be your perfection: that you bring forth fruits worthy of repentance.

6. If, brethren, we wish to recall yesterday’s reading, then to the worthy fruits of repentance belongs what was said to Jeremiah—or certainly to John under the figure of Jeremiah—“that you may pluck up and pull down, destroy and scatter”; to the fruits of righteousness, “that you may build and plant” (Jer. 1:10; 18:7). Blessed is he who helps the hands of this uprooter—for he is himself God’s helper—[Col. 0166D] namely, he who, cooperating with God’s word and grace, devotes his zeal and effort to plucking up and destroying from his own affections and habits every planting which the heavenly Father has not planted; to pulling down and scattering every construction of Babylonian pride and confusion, so that thereafter he may build and plant more fittingly, and become as it is written: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones; they have cut down the sycamores, but we shall replace them with cedars” (Isa. 9:10). “Instead of the thorn-bush shall rise the fir tree, and instead of the nettle the myrtle” (ibid. 55:13): that is, every beauty and grace of virtues in place of the foulness and horror of vices.

Who, do you think, among us is so perfect as to possess even this beginning of perfection: namely, to repent so worthily and completely [Col. 0167A] that he condemns with all severity the evils he has done, utterly renouncing his former vices, so as to pluck up and destroy at the root every shoot of cursing from the field of his heart, so that from that most evil root no fruit of bitterness may ever again spring forth; and so to pull down and scatter every height exalting itself against the humility of Christ that he does not build again what he has destroyed? How happy the Church of the saints would be today; with what peace and grace the congregations of blessed poor people would flourish, if the repentance of beginners—or the righteousness of those who wish to appear perfect and holy—brought forth these fruits which it ought to bring forth!

Finally, since we possess neither the righteousness of saints nor the exact repentance of sinners, let us at least partly redeem [Col. 0167B] our lukewarmness by devout veneration of the saints, especially of blessed John, whose holiness blossomed forth so magnificently beyond the measure of others that he was believed to be the Holy of holies. Let us speak and meditate, my brethren, upon the magnificence of the glory of his holiness, so that he may make propitious to our sins him whose unique friend he deserved to be, the Son of God, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the force necessary to seize the kingdom of heaven.

1. “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Rightly, then, is his birth a joyful one for us, whose times are so fortunate that from that point the kingdom of God [Col. 0167C] has been laid open for us to seize—although righteousness was surely insufficient for us to merit it. Rightly do many rejoice at his birth, as the angel promised; under him the condition of the times was changed with such happiness that the kingdom of God, which formerly no righteousness of the innocent attained, is now invaded and possessed by the violence of penitents.

For what else should the repentance of sinners be called but violence against the kingdom of heaven? Is it not violence to seize by strength what was not granted to nature, so that those who by nature were children of wrath and Gehenna may, by the unremitting toil that conquers all things, force themselves into the inheritance of the saints and the fellowship of glory? Was not that vigorous wrestler, the patriarch Jacob, plainly violent toward God? As it is written, he was strong against God and prevailed; wrestling with him until morning, he held fast firmly and urgently when asked to release him, saying, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” I say that he wrestled with God, for God was in the angel with whom he wrestled. Otherwise the angel would not have said, “Why do you ask my name, which is wonderful?” nor would Jacob have said, “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. 32:26, 29–30); nor would the Lord have said of Jacob through the prophet Hosea, “At Bethel he spoke with us” (Hos. 12:4).

Good, therefore, was the violence which extorted a blessing; blessed the wrestling in which God yielded to a human being and, conquered, endowed the conqueror with the grace of blessing and the honor of a holier name. What then if he touched the sinew of Jacob’s thigh, and it withered, so that thereafter [Col. 0168A] he limped? It was an easy bodily loss and a consolable injury, compensated by so great a gift—especially for one who could say, “I loved wisdom above health and every beauty” (Wis. 7:10). Would that not merely the sinew of my thigh, but the strength of my whole body, might wither, provided that I might deserve even one blessing from the angel. Would that I might not only limp with Jacob, but also die with Paul, so that I might obtain by an everlasting gift the grace and name of Israel.

Jacob indeed bears a withered thigh; Paul, however, a dead body, because the Gospel brought to complete fulfillment the mortification of the members which prophetic religion had begun. Jacob limps because, thinking partly upon worldly things, he keeps one foot raised from the earth. Paul, thinking only on the things of God—whether in the body or outside the body, he does not know; God knows (2 Cor. 12:3)—yet wholly free in spirit, flies to heaven.

2. Therefore we say to you, brethren, who have undertaken to seize heaven, who have entered into contest to wrestle with the angel guarding the way of the tree of life: we say that it is altogether necessary for you to wrestle steadfastly and without remission—not, I say, merely until the enervation of the thigh, from which the generation of the flesh is propagated, but even unto the mortification of the body. Yet even this our labor cannot attain unless through the touch and favor of divine power, when it has proved your invincible constancy for itself. For thus it is written: “When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and [Col. 0168C] immediately it withered” (Gen. 32:25).

Do you not seem to be wrestling with an angel—indeed, with God himself—when he daily opposes your too-hasty desires? You wash yourself as with snow-water in order to be clean in heart and body, and he plunges you into filth. You say, “I shall become wise” (Eccl. 7:24), and he withdraws farther from you. You cry to him, and he does not hear you; you wish to approach him, and he repels you. You decide upon a matter, and it turns out contrary to you; and in nearly everything he opposes you with the hardness of his hand.

O mercy that conceals itself, which pretends to be hardness: with how great a tenderness you fight against those for whom you fight! Though you hide these things in your heart, I nevertheless know that you love those who love you, and that your sweetness is an immense multitude, which [Col. 0168D] you hide for those who fear you. Therefore do not despair; act steadfastly, blessed soul who have begun to wrestle with God. He indeed loves to suffer force from you; he desires to be overcome by you. For even when he is angry and stretches out his hand to strike, he seeks—as he himself declares—a man like Moses who will resist him; and if he does not find one, he complains and says: “There is none who rises up and holds me” (Isa. 64:7). For if his wrath were unappeasable and his sentence inflexible, Jeremiah, who had attempted resistance, would weep and say: “You were stronger, and you prevailed” (Jer. 20:7).

3. But far be it, brethren, who ask things pleasing to him—far be it that he should be strong against you, who for your sake willed to become weak even unto death! He was pierced with so many wounds and crucified over his whole body: whence, I ask, could he have strength [Col. 0169A] to resist that love which brought him, as though conquered and captured, through every kind of weakness unto death—and death upon a cross? Love is now not strong as death, but stronger than death, since the strength of God was weakened by the power of love unto death; yet his weakness was found stronger than every strong one, and his death was proved to be your death, O Death.

Therefore be armed with the power of love, whoever you are, devout invader striving to seize the kingdom of heaven; and be confident, for you will readily conquer the very King of heaven. If he seems to oppose you with any difficulty or hardness, do not lose heart, but understand with what purpose he does this: namely, that by opposition he may whet your courage, as is the nature of the high-minded and brave; that he may exercise your strength, test your constancy, multiply your victories, and increase your crowns.

4. Therefore gird yourselves, children of Israel, and be children of strength. Nothing is needed except greatness of soul and constancy, which no adversities can terrify. Let the weak say, “I am strong”; and through the joy of hope let him not know himself weak, for heaven is now, now indeed, so easily to be taken. He truly seizes heaven by violence who uses force upon his own weakness or age. Indeed, to speak more exactly, he surely uses force upon his own destruction who, when the trumpet of command sounds, does not know how to spare himself. “A man in labors,” as Scripture says, “labors for himself and does violence to his own destruction” (Prov. 16, LXX).

Gird yourselves, I say, men of valor, [Col. 0169C] and follow the leader and master of this blessed warfare: I mean John the Baptist, from whose days heaven began to be assailable. For he is the one who, like another David made captain of robbers, became leader of devout plunderers and led after himself into the kingdom of heaven that victorious army of tax collectors and sinners by this praiseworthy and religious violence. What wicked or profane person heard his trumpet, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2), and did not immediately prepare himself for battle?

Follow this leader, whose banners shine with his own blood, whose virtues and triumphs you have today celebrated with due veneration. He, unless I am mistaken, will fittingly aid those whom he has drawn after himself by example, and will commend them by his intercession, since among those born of women none is more acceptable to the supreme King, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. Again on the praises of the Saint.

1. “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). Solomon says: “Let the lips of your neighbor praise you” (Prov. 27:2). But how much more blessed and glorious it is when the lips of one’s God praise someone! For God can neither be deceived nor flatter. God does not readily praise anyone whom he sees may be puffed up by praise, or whom he foresees must be rejected in the end. A human being is rightly told not to praise a person during his life, [Col. 0170A] since he can neither know the inward things nor foresee the final ones; indeed, he must confess even concerning himself: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). For the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future (Eccl. 9:1–2).

Blessed, therefore, is he who has deserved to know by the testimony of the Judge himself that he is worthy of love—except that testimony to present righteousness does not remove, in view of human mutability, suspicion and fear concerning the future. Yet whenever God in his supporting testimony of praise deigns to render that irrefutable judgment upon a human being still subject to corruption, it is an unquestionable sign of extraordinary virtue and great perfection. It is indeed a great proclamation of righteousness when supreme Righteousness says to Noah: “I have seen you righteous before me” (Gen. 7:1). It is the mark of great merit that God testifies concerning Abraham that the promises made to him will be fulfilled on his account (Gen. 17; 22:17–18). How great, moreover, is that glory when the Lord boasts of blessed Job against the envious one: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a man simple and upright, fearing God and withdrawing from evil?” (Job 1:8). How great also was the favor when he was jealous on Moses’ behalf and confounded his detractors: “If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I shall appear to him in a vision or speak to him through a dream. But my servant Moses is not such: he is most faithful in all my house. For [Col. 0170C] I speak with him mouth to mouth, and openly; not through riddles does he see God. Why, then, were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” (Num. 12:6–8). And who in all things was like David, concerning whom the Lord rejoices because he found a man according to his own heart? (3 Kings 11:4).

2. Nevertheless, however great these men or others may have been, among neither these nor any others born of women has there arisen, according to the testimony of the One born of the Virgin, anyone greater than John the Baptist. For although star differs from star in brightness, and among the choir of holy stars that illumined the night of this age before the rising of the true Sun some shone with marvelous splendor, yet among them all none was greater or more radiant than this morning star—the burning and shining lamp [Col. 0170D] which the Father prepared for his Christ. He was the heralding star of dawn’s light, the forerunner of the Sun, announcing the approaching day to mortals asleep in darkness and the shadow of death, crying aloud: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). As though saying: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near; cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. 13:12). “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

3. We must not pass over negligently, but must consider again and again, how lofty in merit, how excellent in grace and virtue, that eye which is deceived by nothing discerned him to be—the eye which, after so many encomia of his predecessors, pronounced this judgment concerning him: that among those born of women none [Col. 0171A] greater than he had arisen; nor did it judge that anyone should be preferred to him except one from the order of angels, or one who had attained equality with angels. Nor did it touch upon his praise merely once, cursorily, or briefly; whenever an occasion for discourse arose, it delighted to linger over his praises. The Gospel history sufficiently proves this.

For this reason Mark, Luke, and John likewise dedicated the beginnings of their books to his praises: so that the authority of so great a name, placed upon the first page, might thereafter render the whole Gospel more worthy of commendation; and that the lamp, burning and shining in the very entrance and vestibule, might lead to the Light which shone in darkness but could not be comprehended by the darkness. Matthew, because the Lord’s birth had occupied him in his opening chapters, immediately after entrusting the infant to be nourished at Nazareth turned his pen to the Lord’s Forerunner and Baptist, judging that whatever he said concerning the Bridegroom would be incomplete if he kept silence concerning the Bridegroom’s inseparable friend.

This concern was no slight one not only for the Evangelists recounting these events, but also for the Prophets and Angels foretelling them: that Christ’s lamp, such a witness of the Lord, should be introduced, by whose splendor and authority enemies might easily be confounded, and from whose greatness the incomparable greatness of the Most High might be plainly shown. For when he who was greatest among those born of women testified that the One born of the Virgin so far surpassed his own greatness that he confessed himself unworthy to carry his sandals, what else was made known but that he was that great [Col. 0171C] Lord “whose greatness has no end” (Ps. 144:3), and of whom it is said: “For who in the clouds shall be compared to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88:7).

And this was assuredly John’s greatness: that he grew so great among the great because he crowned for himself his great and innumerable virtues, in which he was second to no mortal, with the greatest of all virtues, humility. When he was thought greatest of all, he voluntarily and most devoutly preferred before himself the humblest of all, and preferred him so utterly that he declared himself unworthy to unfasten his sandals (Luke 3:16).

4. Let others, then, marvel that he was foretold by the Prophets; promised by an archangel and conceived at the same time as Christ—yet Christ in the bridal chamber, John in the sanctuary; that he was born of parents so holy and noble; of elderly and barren parents, contrary to nature’s due course, by the gift of grace; holy before he was born; a prophet before he prophesied; more than a prophet, because he was an angel, carrying out an angelic office and life on earth, living in flesh beyond the flesh; and, though most innocent, nevertheless handing down a model of repentance more by example than by word; that, going before in the spirit and power of Elijah, he preceded the Redeemer’s coming and prepared his way in the wilderness; that he turned the hearts of fathers toward children and of children toward fathers; that he deserved to baptize the Son, hear the Father, and see the Holy Spirit; and finally, that he contended for truth even unto death—[Col. 0172A] so that he might precede Christ even to hell: before Christ’s Passion, he was Christ’s martyr.

Let others marvel at these things, if indeed anyone can marvel worthily. But to us, brethren, not only the wonder but the imitation of his virtue of humility is offered: he did not wish to be believed greater than he was able to be, but rather restrained, as far as he could, those who believed so, lest they err. For as the Bridegroom’s faithful friend, he was more a lover of his Lord than of himself; he wished himself to decrease so that the other might increase, and strove to increase the other’s glory through his own diminution (John 3:29–30). Before the Apostle, in deed and truth, he uttered that apostolic saying: “We do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5).

Accordingly, great is his glory in your salvation, in your Jesus, O Lord, whose righteousness and goodness it is to love those who love him and glorify those who glorify him. Great indeed is John’s glory in Jesus, great from Jesus: he glorified him both with himself through fellowship in his own glory and among human beings through the testimony of his voice. John had persuaded himself of the Wise Man’s trustworthy counsel: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord; for it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:17–18). He therefore preferred to glory soundly in the Lord rather than vainly in himself, because he preferred to be commended truthfully by the Lord rather than falsely by himself. Thus he was approved by God and human beings; his glory among human beings was truth, and with God, blessedness. Had he glorified himself, his glory would have been nothing.

5. O children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why [Col. 0172C] do you love vanity and seek falsehood? (Ps. 4:3). Why do you love vain and lying glory, and not desire the glory which is from God alone? But how do you seek it? Would that you did so by doing brave deeds, not by speaking lofty words; would that at least you spoke truths, though vainly, rather than outright lies; would that, finally, you lied only about yourselves, rather than also maligning others! This is no longer receiving or seeking glory, but rather stealing and plundering it.

For to seek glory by a way not one’s own, but contrary to one’s own—that is, by a course to which glory is not due but disgrace, not by the title of virtue but by the robbery of lying and detraction—what else is this but wickedly to seize or steal what one has shamefully coveted? Certainly, if you did not seek glory from a human being but accepted it when offered, even in this you would not walk according to truth. But what now, when you not only accept it if it is offered, but seek it when it is not offered? Finally, what when you virtually murder another with a poisonous and treacherous tongue in order to seize his glory for yourself, so that through his evil you may appear better, and through his contempt more glorious?

Let receiving or seeking glory from a human being, then, be the vanity of fools; but what is this latter conduct but the cruelty of raging persons? Let the former, to speak more mildly, be a human temptation; what is the latter but diabolical imitation? Those who belong to the devil’s party—that is, all the proud—plainly imitate the devil. For he himself is “king over all the children of pride.”

[Col. 0173A] 6. “How,” you ask, “do they imitate him?” Because the devil grew proud, he envied one better than himself, that is, God; because he envied, he spoke maliciously against him. Thus his children of pride, as soon as they are infected by his vice—that is, love of their own excellence—envy the excellence of others. Once they begin to envy, they begin, if they can, to malign, so that what they take away from others may increase for themselves.

How much more healthfully would they imitate the humility of John, who diminished himself in order to add to another; who strove to be thought less than he was thought, so that another might begin to appear what he had not been thought to be! Finally, if humility does not please on account of its own nobility and fairness, let it at least please on account of its usefulness. For there is no straighter or easier way to divine glory; nor is there any more beautiful or just way to human favor, and often none more direct: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find favor before God and men” (Ecclus. 3:20; Phil. 2:3).

This glorified blessed John before God and human beings, as does this day, which through his glorious birth brings consolation to the world, joy to heaven, and glory to God, to whom be honor and glory through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On strength and mortification.

1. Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” (Matt. 11:7). Behold that of which the bride boasts concerning the bridegroom in the Song of her love: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” (Song 2:16): John belongs to Jesus, and Jesus to John. John proclaims Jesus; Jesus commends John. Like is returned for like, and love is stirred—or rewarded—reciprocally by a requital as friendly as it is just. For Jesus says: “I love those who love me, and I will glorify those who glorify me” (Prov. 8:17). Godliness has the promise of the life which now is and which is to come; and the Lord, whom he will glorify in the future by granting a reward, begins even now to glorify by granting [variant: bestowing] praise, and exalts his witness before human beings by the special honor of his own testimony.

“What did you go out,” he says, “to see in the wilderness?” You marvel at a man dwelling in the wilderness; but through him “the beauties of the wilderness shall grow rich,” and the solitude shall blossom, when everywhere new cultivators of the desert spring up from John’s example. [Col. 0173D] Then the desert shall be like paradise’s delights, and the solitude like the garden of the Lord. Then “the glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” (Isa. 35:2). But what, I ask, did you go out into the wilderness to see? “A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11:7). Though he dwells in desert places, he is not a reed of the wilderness but a cedar of paradise, a pillar of heaven, the glory of the human race, a wonder of the world—by virtue and merit beyond the measure of human beings, by condition beneath the nature of angels.

2. He is not a reed shaken by the wind, but a palm tree stronger than every storm, which no whirlwind can shake; or rather, a cypress planted upon Mount Zion for eternity, set so high that it need not fear the violence of winds. He is not subject to the storms of this air, because he is above all the desires of the world. He has fixed his root in heaven, [Col. 0174A] where no storm-wind blows; and from there he securely scorns the threats and wars of winds and all things adverse in the world.

Let Herod be angry; let Herodias plot; let the storm boil up from within them, and let the wicked spirit of storms, which lies hidden in the abyss of their hearts, set all its powers and devices of malice in motion: nothing will terrify him, nothing move him from his judgment, from freely denouncing their incestuous marriage. For how could adversities bend one whom prosperities could not soften? At one time soft and flattering winds did indeed blow—the breezes, that is, of popular favor—yet not even they could incline him from his uprightness. “You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth.” For the Jews sent priests and Levites to ask him, “Who are you?” And he confessed and did not deny: “I am not the Christ” (John 1:19–20). Though popular favor blew upon him and common opinion flattered him—not so that he should proclaim himself Christ, but so that he need scarcely contradict those who believed it—he remained unmoved.

Again, when his disciples said to him, “Rabbi, he to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and all are going to him,” could this wind shake him or move him to grief or envy over his own abandonment and another’s multitude and glory? On the contrary, repelling and breaking the wind with unshaken constancy, he answered: “You yourselves bear me witness that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him’” (John 3:26, 28).

[Col. 0174C] 3. But what did you go out to see? “A man clothed in soft garments?” He had praised John for constancy of spirit, and now praises him for contempt of his body; finally, for the surpassing excellence of prophetic grace and the dignity of angelic office and name. By these two steps human humility strives upward toward spiritual and divine things: if it remains unmoved against the winds of rushing temptations, and afflicts the body through desire for spiritual goods. For as at the beginning the body must be disciplined, so that we may conquer temptations and sin may not reign in it, so even after temptations have been conquered we must persist in this discipline—not only from fear of falling back, but also from desire to advance. Thus, through the mortification of the flesh, the spirit becomes more vigorous; and the lighter and subtler the bond it bears, the more freely it rises toward spiritual things.

John, sanctified before he came forth from the womb, to whom it was fitting to say, “From my infancy holiness grew with me, and from my mother’s womb it came forth with me” (Job 31:18), whom no wind of temptation could shake, nevertheless neither clothed himself softly nor fed himself delicately. He knew, certainly, that a stricter discipline of life is necessary for saints to become holier just as it is necessary for sinners to become holy.

But now, thanks be to God, who has given us—if indeed he has given it—victory without struggle, pardon without repentance, righteousness without work, holiness without labor, and abundance in carnal and spiritual delights together. We are clothed, if not in purple and fine linen, at least in garments softer and warmer than purple and fine linen; we feast sumptuously every day; and nonetheless, bloated and belching after gluttony, shall we sleep with Lazarus, once poor, in Abraham’s bosom—or rather, with John in Christ’s bosom? If this is so, then our lot has plainly been better than theirs, who bought through such great labors what we delicate people possess freely. If this is so, John’s life is plainly more to be laughed at than praised, and it is more fitting to condemn than imitate the whole nation of God’s children who followed the hard and narrow way of the Father’s Only-Begotten.

4. But it seems more credible that this is not so, but rather, as Truth says, “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts [Col. 0175B] 14:21); and, as the disciple of Truth declares, “a widow living in pleasures is dead” (1 Tim. 5:5–6). Therefore, after praising his friend, most faithful in all his house, for the roughness of his clothing, the Lord says: “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8), clearly intending it to be understood that those who pursue pleasures of the flesh serve the kingdom of this world, not the kingdom of God.

Alas, what a terrible sentence I have heard from heaven against the softness of that great harlot clothed in purple: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in pleasures, give her so much torment and mourning” (Rev. 18:7). Yet would that the delicacy of luxurious people were content with these pleasures—with merely soft clothing and sumptuous food—and that the thorn-bush of pleasures did not produce in them other thorns of vices, so that all their sin might be indulgence, not debauchery. Let them see for themselves whether that innate pestilential fire has been so extinguished in them that, surrounded by so many kindlings, it cannot be rekindled—especially when winds blow from the opposite direction, that is, tempting words and wanton laughter. Yet I am accustomed to hear that it often lives even in one dying, remains vigorous in an old man, is awakened and rises even without fuel, and rages when nothing provokes it. Let them therefore see to themselves.

For I have no business judging the consciences of others, since I know that many have lived temperately and chastely amid every abundance and glory of the world; and conversely, that some have acted wickedly in rougher clothing and with more frugal food. But I also know that the king of Israel wore sackcloth next to his flesh beneath his purple robe (4 Kings 6:30), and that kings were sometimes served bread alone—whereas today a dark garment of penitents, or rather of those professing repentance, covers every kind of delicacy and softness, [Col. 0175D] and neither the riches of the world nor the arts and torments of cooks suffice for their fastidiousness.

But because in such matters each person easily finds himself a defense—one in infirmity, another in the community whose custom he follows, another in the office he holds—let them live as they wish and eat as they wish, provided only that this evil does not proceed further, namely, to that which those who wish to commit it refuse to confess because they cannot defend it. Let them not begin to be marked by the proverb concerning the wicked woman, who “eats and, wiping her mouth, says: ‘I have done no evil’” (Prov. 30:20). For concerning that great Babylon, from the midst of which these luxurious penitents seemed to have gone forth, I dare say: Let her be as purple-clad as she wishes, as luxurious as she wishes; only let her not be a harlot, nor spread her legs to every passerby.

5. Therefore, if you cannot imitate John in roughness of dress or frugality of diet, strive at least to imitate him in this: do not be a reed shaken by the wind; and, as the Wise Man says, “Do not be tossed about with every [Col. 0176B] wind, and do not go upon every path. For thus is the sinner tested by a double tongue. But be firm,” he says, “in the way of the Lord” (Ecclus. 5:11–12), lest the wind cast you away from the face of the land or place to which you have professed yourself—or from the kingdom for which you must be prepared.

A violent wind often suddenly rushes from the wilderness region and shakes the four corners of the house of Job’s children (Job 1:19), and its fall is great—if, that is, it is founded upon sand rather than rock; if it is made of reeds rather than stone. Or rather, if the person who builds and inhabits it is a reed: outwardly splendid through hypocrisy, loud through boastfulness or empty promise, inwardly empty of truth. Behemoth loves to sleep in the hiding-place of this reed, which also grows and luxuriates more frequently and more abundantly in watery places (Job 40:10, 16), where there is no lack of transitory things, but everything overflows toward extravagance (Isa. 36:7).

If anyone leans on this reed, it will pierce his hand; for if anyone summons such a person to assist in a work, or entrusts him with some duty of office, he will grievously wound through scandal the person hoping in him. Yet the Lord’s patience does not break even such a bruised reed, but bears with it so that it may be changed for the better (Isa. 24:20). At times he also rebukes the beasts of the reed-bed (Ps. 67:31), which sleep with their prince in its secret place. At times the righteous run through the reed-bed like sparks of glowing fire (Wis. 3:7); like coals of desolation they burn whatever grows there in barren wilderness, [Col. 0176D] and prepare a pure place for new fruits.

John, the voice crying in the wilderness, did this: not a reed but a spark in the reed-bed. His speech was, as it is written, “the speech of a spark to stir the sluggish and foolish heart” (Wis. 2:2), so that it might prepare the way for the Lord. May that same voice now accomplish this also in us, with the cooperation of the Word himself whose voice it was, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

[Col. 0177]

## SERMON I. On the two olive trees at the right hand of the lampstand.

[Col. 0177A]

1. “And I answered,” says Zechariah, “and said to the angel who spoke within me: What are these two olive trees at the right of the lampstand and at its left?” “These,” he says, “are the two sons of the oil of brightness, who stand before the Lord of all the earth” (Zech. 4:4, 11, 14).

The Prophet understood the lampstand which he had seen, entirely of gold, and its seven lamps upon it; nor may we now doubt, since in its light we see light. Although this light reveals other things, it does not allow itself to remain unknown, but, bearing witness of itself, says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Light according to divinity; lampstand according to humanity. And it is wholly gold, not merely gilded: because whether divinity, wisdom, or [Col. 0177B] love be signified by gold, Christ possesses all these not by participation but by substance. Though by nature we are leaden, or rather clay-like, by his grace and participation we are not gold or golden, but at most gilded. The seven lamps upon it are the seven spirits, the seven eyes of the Lord, which range through the whole earth.

Concerning these things, therefore, the Prophet was certain; concerning the two olive trees he asks what they are, and hears from the angel speaking within him: “These are the two sons of the oil of brightness, who stand before the Lord of all the earth” (Zech. 4:14). Let others interpret as they wish or can, each according to his own understanding: whether as Enoch and Elijah, who live hidden with God; or Moses and Elijah, who were seen with him on the mountain; or the two orders of preachers, namely, of the Old and New Testaments—so that those of the Old are at the left because of temporal promises, those of the New at the right because of eternal ones. Whatever does not depart from the rule of faith or disagree too greatly with the context of the reading, I accept, revere, and embrace.

2. Yet I think, without prejudice to a better interpretation, that Peter and Paul may not improperly be understood here. Indeed, it would seem absurd for anyone today to interpret it otherwise, when today the Church throughout the world sings and treats of nothing else than the praises of her Fathers and Doctors. For although it may be applied to others, I think it fits these men more especially: whether it be what the Prophet sees as two olive trees around the lampstand [Col. 0177D], or what the angel calls the two sons of the oil of brightness. Each expression explains the other—the prophetic vision by the angelic interpretation—so that they are understood to be olive trees because they are sons of the oil of brightness, and to be around the lampstand because they stand before the Lord. Since they have been reborn from the oil of the Holy Spirit, and today flourish and bear fruit like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, imparting the juice and sweetness of their richness even to the Gentile wild olive grafted into them, let the Gentile world—once barren and bitter—give them thanks. Even if it is not directly from them, it is nevertheless through them that it now abounds throughout the world in such abundant and precious fruit.

3. But you, brothers, whose substance and house are one, and likewise whose heart and soul are one: you, I say, I judge to have special cause for glorying in them, since, like shoots of olive trees, you have drawn from their root not only the sap of faith, but also a pattern of life and an example of religious order. If you are shoots of olive trees, then you are surely also sons of oil: sons of the Anointed One, who is the Christ of God. And when you approach the altar today, it will be said of you: “Your sons are like shoots of olive trees around your table” (Ps. 127:3). O shoots of noble olive trees! O well-born growth from trees so rich and fruitful! Always, I beseech you, remember [Col. 0178B] from what stock you have sprung and from what root you have grown, lest barrenness of works or bitterness of conduct convict you of degeneracy, or—God forbid—consign you as useless to the fires. Beware, I pray, of the mark of those unhappy times of which you remember the prophecy: “The work of the olive tree shall fail, and the fields shall yield no food” (Hab. 3:17). Yet I think that you must especially beware of two things: first, lest through lukewarmness you become like the olive tree “casting off its blossom,” as you read in the Prophet—so that you fail to produce the fruit which you promised in the beginnings of novice fervour; or secondly, once you have produced it, lest through pride you lose it, and Jeremiah say to you: “The Lord called your name, ‘a luxuriant olive tree, fair, fruitful, beautiful’; but alas! at the sound [Col. 0178C] of a great outcry, fire was kindled in it, and all its branches were burned” (Jer. 11:16). But, beloved, we are persuaded of better things concerning you, although we speak thus. We trust that the oil of brightness—or rather, the brightness of oil—whose sons you are, as were our fathers the Apostles, will by its anointing teach you concerning all things. It will not only wipe away sluggishness, because it is oil; it will also dispel error, because it is brightness.

4. I know that “oil of brightness” may be understood as that which proceeds from the brightness, the Son, or as that which diffuses the brightness of illumination. But I think that “oil which is brightness” may also be understood without impropriety by a shift of construction. For in its own nature the Spirit is both: spiritual anointing and invisible brightness. By its gift it works both in us [Col. 0178D]. It anoints the affections inasmuch as it is oil; it illumines the understanding inasmuch as it is brightness. Yet it is not oil from one source and brightness from another, but is itself both oil and brightness, because it is only one and the same Spirit. It anoints the affections because it is charity; it illumines the understanding because it is truth. It anoints the affections when it grants devotion; it illumines the understanding when it reveals mysteries. When it teaches goodness, so that we may be simple as doves, it anoints the affections; when it teaches knowledge [Col. 0179A], so that we may be prudent as serpents, it illumines the understanding. It illumines, so that we may have salt in ourselves; it anoints, so that we may have peace among ourselves. Therefore you will show yourself to us a son of the oil of brightness if you present yourself as gracious and anointed through good will, discerning and mature through wisdom: so that graciousness may be seasoned with truth, and charity ordered by equity.

I think that the Holy Spirit also signified this twofold power, or this effect of His gift, on account of which He chose to be called brightness, in that fire in which He, though invisible, appeared invisibly to the Apostles. For what was brightness to their eyes was, unless I am mistaken, oil to their bodily sensation: they seemed, as it were, baptized in a bath of oil when that heavenly fire was poured upon them [Col. 0179B]. Yet whatever bodily sensation that fire may have produced in them—for it matters little what was felt, but rather how it worked—I think it is both more probable and more reverent to believe that the same fire which set their hearts ablaze and enlightened them also cooled their bodies: so that their minds might burn through charity and their members grow cool through chastity. To each belonged fittingly either Jeremiah’s saying, “From on high He sent fire into my bones” (Lam. 1:13), or the Psalmist’s, “My flesh was changed because of oil” (Ps. 108:24). Unless perhaps the Spirit chose to leave something of the law of the members opposing the law of the mind, so that strength might be perfected in weakness.

5. But let us continue what we began. “These,” he says, [Col. 0179C] “are the two sons of the oil of brightness, who stand before the Ruler of the whole earth” (Zech. 4:14). Behold, you have goodness in the oil and knowledge in the brightness; receive discipline in the words, “who stand before the Ruler of the whole earth,” so that you may recognize that they were truly disciples of Him to whom we sing: “Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge” (Ps. 118:66).
