For this is the perfection of discipline, in mind as well as body: that, setting the Lord always before our eyes, we may always and everywhere stand before the eternal Majesty which looks upon us and judges us without interruption, with fear and reverence, with wakeful faith and constant devotion. “As the eyes,” he says, “of servants are upon the hands of their masters, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God” [Col. 0179D] (Ps. 122:2), observing His signals with the keenest and most unwavering attention—what He wills and what He commands—so that our devotion may obey with all speed. Thus Moses endured as seeing Him who is invisible, and could never disregard fear of the Judge who stood over him. Thus Elijah and the other Prophets said: “The Lord lives, before whose presence I stand” (4 Kings 5:16). From this, doubtless, they obtained both the grace and the name of Seers: because what they continually beheld through unfeigned faith, they deserved more frequently to behold by a created appearance. This vigilant, unfeigned, undissimulating faith is, I think, what alone—or above all—leads by a ready shortcut to perfection. It confers upon our inward and outward selves the gravity of discipline and the sobriety of modesty [Col. 0180A], and makes us continually stand, as servants disciplined in the Lord’s service. By this virtue the Apostles deserved to be called sons of the oil of brightness: as they stood before the Lord on earth by contemplating Him through faith, so now they stand before Him in heaven by contemplating Him in direct vision; and their eyes see the King in His beauty, whose fear their hearts here meditated upon. By this way, brothers, follow the Fathers of your faith and founders of your Order, so that, stirred by their examples and aided by their intercessions, you may attain where they have gone before today, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON II. How the Apostles nourish the souls of the faithful

[Col. 0180B]

1. “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Cant. 4:5–6). See to it, brothers, that you do not degenerate. To say nothing of the nobility of your father, the mother who bore you is noble, and the breasts by which you were nursed are of noble stock. Your mother is the bride to whom these words are spoken, whose breasts are praised by the voice of the Bridegroom. That these two breasts of the Church are Peter and Paul is interpreted for us not only by this day [1024], on which we drink most gladly and abundantly from the breasts of their consolation; the evident arguments of their deeds and the memorials of their teaching also prove it. By what other breasts were the children of the Church nourished, whether from the uncircumcision or from the circumcision? These, surely, I believe to be those concerning whom divine consolation once promised the little and poor Church: “Your foster-fathers shall be kings” (Isa. 49:23), and “you shall suck the breast of kings” [Col. 0180C] (Isa. 60:16). Had she not been nourished with milk so noble, she would never have grown to such a height of virtue and glory.

Peter invited little children to the breasts when he said to them: “Like newborn infants, desire milk” (1 Pet. 2:2). Paul offered breasts when he said: “I gave you milk to drink” (1 Cor. 3:2); and again: “I became among you like a nurse sitting and feeding her children” (1 Thess. 2:7). How abundantly he overflowed with spiritual milk was beautifully signified by the stream of visible milk which is said to have issued from his body in place of blood when, beheaded on this day, he gave his life for those to whom he had given [Col. 0180D] the breast. Certainly there was nothing bloody in him, but all was milky: he thought nothing carnal, nothing for himself, but only what was useful to others. Indeed, he did not so much possess breasts as was himself wholly a breast, for he so overflowed with abundant mercy that he desired not merely to draw out his whole spirit for his children, but to spend even his body.

2. Before the primitive Church of the saints on earth had received these two breasts, Peter and Paul, the Church of blessed spirits in heaven complained and said: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Cant. 8:8). For when Christ, returning to heaven, had left behind a little flock of disciples and had not yet sent His Spirit—by which the wombs were to be made fruitful and the breasts of the saints filled—the Church in heaven was, I think, concerned for the Bridegroom’s little children, whether already born or yet to be born, to whom they were to be entrusted for nourishment. For they saw that this Church was small in number, virtue, and authority, and without the breasts of teaching. The Bridegroom Himself, in the days of His flesh, had begotten some by the word of truth, and while He was with them had nursed them with breasts of edification and consolation. The Bridegroom Himself has breasts better than wine [Col. 0181A] (Cant. 1:1), that is, better than legal teaching or secular joy. The Bridegroom, I say, has breasts, lest any of the offices and names of loving care be lacking in Him: He who is Father by creation of nature, or by regeneration of grace, and also by the authority of discipline, is likewise Mother through tender affection, and Nurse through the diligence of office and care.

There were then little children whom a certain beginning of His creation nourished—but only a beginning; much care and labour still remained until they should be brought to perfection and Christ be formed in them. But when He too had left them, the heavenly spirits, though rejoicing in the return of the Only-Begotten, were nevertheless concerned for the new offspring of adoption, and seemed in their affection to complain to Him, as it were: “Who will nourish them? You nursed them, but weaned them before the time. You did not bring the young men to maturity or lead the virgins to growth: who will nourish them? Our sister is little and has no breasts. You said to Peter: ‘Feed my lambs’ [Col. 0181B] (John 21:15–16); but he himself does not yet have sufficient milk in his breasts. His compassion would quickly dry up, for he still fears more for his own skin than for the souls of the little ones. He would easily abandon the lambs in temptation, having denied under questioning the Shepherd both theirs and his own.”

But behold: when the Spirit was suddenly sent from heaven, poured out like milk from Christ’s own breasts, Peter was filled with abundant milk. Not long afterward Saul became Paul: a preacher from a persecutor, a mother from a torturer, a nurse from an executioner—so that you might clearly understand that all his blood was changed into the sweetness of milk, his cruelty into compassion.

3. With these twin breasts fastened to her breast, therefore, the Church glories not only that she is a fruitful mother, but also that she is a fortified city. “I,” she says, “am a wall, and my breasts are towers” (Cant. 8:10). A thousand shields now hang from these towers: every weapon of the mighty. The Bridegroom Himself likewise, in praise of the Bride, says in a song of love, in mystical speech, concerning these same breasts: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle” [Col. 0181D] (Cant. 4:5). In this place we understand the gazelle as the Church: keen of sight for penetrating Christ’s mysteries, agile in leaping over the thorns of this age, mighty in overcoming the venom of the ancient serpent. Her two twins, not unfittingly, I think, are understood to be these two Apostles: brothers in faith, alike in devotion, equal in merit and virtue, united in charity, joined even in their passion and death. For as they loved one another in their life, so they were not separated in death.

Now because the desires of the greatest are fed by the progress of the lesser, until, by grace breathing upon them, they raise themselves to contemplate things sublime, the following is appropriately said of these fawns: “Which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline” [Col. 0182A] (Cant. 2:16–17). When animals avoid the day’s heat, they seek the shady pastures of valleys, where the growth of lilies is usually more plentiful, until, when the gentle breeze of the cooling evening blows, they go out into the open plains or the heights of the mountains. So too our fawns, as long as the gentler breeze of the eternal day has not breathed upon them for contemplation, feed among the lilies of the valleys: that is, they delight in the virtues of the humble, or are occupied in their deeds. But when that day breathes upon their minds, they go out and leap to the richer and happier pastures of the eternal mountains. “Through me,” says the Shepherd and Door, “if anyone enters, he shall be saved; and he shall enter” the Church, “and go out”—often in contemplation, once in migration to the heavenly homeland—“and find pasture,” both here and there: here among the lilies of the field; there among the trees of paradise; here in flowers; there in fruits; here in the virtues of the saints; there in the joys of the angels.

4. Truly, there the Lord placed me in a place of pasture, when He joined me to the assembly of saints, whose belly is “like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” [Col. 0182B] (Cant. 7:2), so that it may feed at once by the taste of wheat and the sight of lilies. For what is a heap of wheat but the abundance of the divine word, gathered from every side in so many books? What are lilies but the righteous, who spring up like the lily and bloom unfadingly before the Lord? Great is their brightness in bodily holiness and purity of heart, great their fragrance in reputation, and great their medicinal power in deed and word. It is no slight food for a faithful soul to see around itself so many lilies blooming in such beauty and grace, where it may take examples of every virtue from them—though different virtues from different persons. One is more firmly grounded in humility; another more expansive in charity. One is stronger in patience; another quicker in obedience. One is more sparing through frugality; another more useful through labour. One is more devout in prayer; another more diligent in reading. One is more prudent in administration; another holier in repose. But although you admire some particular grace flowering more conspicuously in each, there are not one but many virtues in each person, like flowers in lilies. As many righteous persons as there are, so many lilies; as many virtues as they have, so many lily-flowers. Whoever therefore sees these things and rejoices in them, or even profits by them [Col. 0182D], what does he do but feed among the lilies?

5. Paul fed others; but no less he fed among those whom he fed. He fed them by his words; he was fed by their works. With his own hands he fed his own belly—indeed, another’s also (Acts 20:34; 1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:8). But he fed his mind not so much upon his own good deeds as upon those of others, since he sought not what was useful to himself but what was useful to others. “Now we live,” he says, “if you stand fast in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8). “For what is my glory, or joy, or crown? Is it not you before God?” (1 Thess. 2:19; Phil. 4:1.) Therefore the day of eternal light more often breathed upon him, and the gentler breeze of the Holy Spirit blew upon him; by its force he was caught away to inward pastures, now of paradise, now of the third heaven, “whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know,” he says; “God knows” [Col. 0183A] (2 Cor. 12:3). It was fitting that one who faithfully fed others should faithfully be fed; and that one who outwardly rejoiced in the good of the Lord’s household should be bidden to enter into his Lord’s joy and be filled with the good things of God’s house—not only this visible house, for which he laboured, but also that invisible one toward which he aspired and from which the day breathed upon him.

6. Nor, I think, should lesser things be believed of blessed Peter, since Paul’s glory is so great that he is matched with the merits of the one whom the judgment of Truth set above all others in authority and primacy. When the Father who is in heaven revealed to Peter the truth concerning the Only-Begotten (Matt. 16:2–6), what else was this than the eternal day breathing upon him, and day uttering a word to day? Whom should we believe had readier access to heaven than its very Gatekeeper [Col. 0183B], whose tongue became the key of heaven? He who had power to shut heaven against the clouds and open its gates—how should he not be believed to have entered it more frequently? Peter was once hungry [1026], and heaven was opened to him while he still stood on earth. Such an abundance of food was sent down to him that much still remained, although he slaughtered and ate very much, transforming unclean and venomous animals into holy and flourishing lilies (Acts 10:10–16). Thus he was delightfully fed among the lilies, until, when the day breathed upon him, he was gloriously fed in heaven itself.

But see: while we commend to you these two breasts of the Bride, the hour has already passed in which we wished to draw milk for you from these breasts—though on other days we can and do this same thing. For whenever we expound their words for your edification, we draw milk for you from the Apostles’ breasts [Col. 0183C]. For the present, then, let it suffice to remind you—if indeed you need reminding—that, as you love these breasts, so you should always desire their milk, that by it you may grow into salvation, until you present within yourselves the Saviour, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the words written: “Until the day breathes and the shadows decline” (Cant. 2:17)

1. Brothers, you are mistaken about me—but, I think, through love or humility rather than rashness. You suppose that I possess knowledge of the Scriptures, though I have scarcely ever touched even the first threshold of knowledge. For it displeases you, as it seems to me, that I did not pursue to the end the chapter of Scripture about which I spoke yesterday, as if I had the capacity to explain the Scriptures, or even worthily and suitably recall the explanations of others. Yet it is not my usual purpose to expound the Scripture from which I begin a sermon, but to render, from it and in accordance with it, the discourse due for its particular day.

Moreover, our master—that interpreter of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0183D] Refers to St Bernard.]—has undertaken to speak of the whole of that nuptial song and has given us hope, from what he has already published, that if he reaches the passage you ask about—“until the day breathes [Col. 0184A] and the shadows decline”—he will bring those shadows themselves into the light of understanding: what has been said or will be said in darkness, he will tell us in light. Yet you say—and rightly—that when new things come, you will cast away the old; and the cruder or more stale our old things are, the more savoury and welcome his new ones will be. For Jesus Himself keeps the good wine until the end, knowing well how our distaste should be cured.

2. Since, then, you compel me—for I see that you cannot bear delay—and the uncertain hope of the future does not satisfy present desire, I yield to you. I shall, as far as I can, restore the end of the verse of which we spoke yesterday to its beginning. For you seem to ask what it means that, when the spiritual day breathes, the shadows decline, since it would seem more logical to say that then they do not grow but diminish and fail. For if we follow the proper meaning of the word, it is for shadows to grow that they decline: such is the nature of bodily shadows, that the more they decline, the longer they lie extended; and the more they rise, the shorter they stand. Thus the poet, signifying evening, says:

> And ever longer shadows fall from the lofty mountains.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 1.)

But it must be understood that, whereas this is the property of bodily shadows, it is quite otherwise with spiritual shadows, of which we do not doubt that the Holy Spirit speaks here. For just as to decline is to grow for bodily shadows, so for spiritual shadows to decline is to be put down, diminished, or fail. Spiritual shadows are shadowy and gloomy spirits, whether demons or human beings; shadows are the darknesses of errors; shadows are the obscure significations of the ancient sacraments [Col. 0184C]. The shadows of those significations have already declined toward sunset and their end; the shadows of errors daily decline toward diminution; but the shadows of dark spirits will finally decline into hell and death. The first happened when the eternal day breathed upon us by appearing in the flesh; the second happens daily as it increasingly breathes upon us, enlightening with truth; the third will happen at the last, when it breathes upon us, radiant in majesty.

3. Yet I seem to see other shadows within us, arising in our perception, as in a kind of mirror, from other things, and either casting shadow upon us or casting shadow for us. Those which cool and darken us cast shadow upon us; those which refresh and illumine us cast shadow for us. The former are harmful and oppressive; the latter delightful and wholesome. The former arise from lower and worldly things; the latter from higher and divine things. For the human soul has been created and placed in a middle position: the world is beneath it, God above it. God is above it, from whom, to whom, and for whom it was made; that which was made for it is beneath it. For as the body exists for the soul, so its house—that is, the world—exists for the body. Therefore, when the soul bends down toward bodily or worldly things, shadows rise into it from below; when it raises itself [Col. 0185A] toward divine things, shadows from above incline over it. It forms for itself the shadow of the thing on which it thinks.

Yet concerning divine things there is a rather uncertain shadow, however much the sharpness of thought is emptied out; or rather, it is not the shadow of the thing itself, but something else stands in its place—unless that day breathes upon us. Even then, I think, nothing is seen but a shadow; though luminous and glorious, it is still a shadow, as when in the clear and shining surface of a mirror a bright image of a most brilliant thing is reflected. But to see the face of Truth Himself, or the truth of His face, is never possible for this body; neither is it possible now for this present time, nor will it ever be, until mortality dissolves the body or immortality sets it free, eternity absorbs time, and the immortal and immutable Godhead raises to Himself and establishes in Himself the spirit which is now weighed down by the body and changed by time [Col. 0185B].

4. Paul clearly distinguished the beginning of this grace from the perfection of that glory when he said: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). But even for this—that we see through a mirror and in an enigma—we need not only that the surface of our mirror be cleansed from every phantasm and shadow of bodily things, but also that He who dwells in inaccessible light may deign to incline toward us and reveal Himself, if only through the shadow of His image. However hard we strive to pass from visible things to invisible, our lowliness will grasp nothing unless that Majesty condescends [Col. 0185C]. Moses went up the mountain, and the Lord inclined the heavens and came down (Exod. 19:20). And another says: “Arise to meet me, and behold” (Ps. 58:6). Hence no shadow is seen unless it inclines; nor is it said to incline unless the day breathes: for we cannot see God even through a mirror and in an enigma unless Majesty inclines itself and the favour of grace breathes upon us.

Certainly, what is called a shadow in comparison with manifest truth is often of unspeakable glory and splendour in those whose mental mirror is transparent. Conscious of this blessed experience, Paul spoke of himself and those like him: “But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). Thus it is said in the promise: “He will fill your soul with splendours” [Col. 0185D] (Isa. 58:11). To understand that these brightnesses are shadows, hear David: “My days,” he says, “declined like a shadow.” David himself passed from brightness to brightness, as from day to day. But alas—this winter has days so brief and dark, nights so long and laborious, that the Prophet, labouring in his groaning and washing his bed with tears every night, rightly laments: “My days have declined like a shadow!” (Ps. 101:12). Truly, “one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11) of my days, because my days are like a shadow, however bright; but that one day is true and unmixed light, without shadow and therefore without evening. The continual interruption of long nights makes my days very numerous and very brief [Col. 0186A].

5. But if one asks why shadows are spoken of in the plural, when the thing of which they are shadows is one: it is because the power of the Most High now overshadows us less, now more; truth, making itself known to us, now outlines itself more obscurely, now more manifestly. And just as it does not always breathe equally, so it does not always form the same images within us. The Apostle suggests this when he confesses that he passes from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18), from a lesser glory to a greater; and the Prophet when he promises that the faithful soul shall be filled not with brightness but with brightnesses (Isa. 58:11). Thus James calls God the “Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17), although the light of which He is Father is one and unique. Yet “Father of lights” may perhaps be understood in the same way as “Father of mercies.”

6. Now, brothers, who labour under the burden and heat of the day, or, in Isaiah’s words, “in a hard spirit meditate through the day of heat” (Isa. 27:8), I would invite you to these shadows, which that serene day, breathing upon you, desires to incline as a dew of mercy upon those who are scorched. Hear the Day Himself gently inviting you to the refreshment of shadows: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). For the servant labouring under the sun, as Job says, longs for shade (Job 7:2), in which he may recover from labour for labour, perhaps for the half-hour during which silence is made in heaven. When, by the indulgence of his Prior, he has obtained it, he boasts and says: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired, I sat” [Col. 0186C]. And because in that shadow there is not merely sitting for rest, but also refreshment for satiety, he suitably adds: “And his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Cant. 2:3). Thus it was said by the Prophet: “They shall return, sitting in his shadow; they shall live by wheat and blossom like the vine” (Hos. 14:8). The servant or hired labourer whom this shadow has often refreshed will patiently await the end of his work. For you have this: “The servant longs for the shadow, and the hired labourer waits for the end of his work” (Job 7:2). In the shadow there is not the end, but a pause. The end will be the reward for the work, when all shadows have vanished and we see Him as He is—the One to whom we now say: “In your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20) [Col. 0186D]; among the angels, indeed, not in shadow but in manifest light.

7. Notice this: when those shadows from above incline over us, these shadows from below decline beneath us. For when we draw near to divine things, we overcome worldly things; and insofar as we approach even the shadow of light, we escape the shadow of death. Light and life are in heaven; death is in hell; but the shadow of death is in this earthly and dark place. Therefore, when the Spirit raises us higher between earth and heaven, we are not touched by the shadow of earthly things. And though we do not yet enjoy the full light of heaven, we are nevertheless illumined by the shadows of the eternal mountains, or certainly of that shadowy and dense mountain from which the Holy One of holy ones came.

Yet immediately, by our own weight, we are rolled back into the region of the shadow of death [Col. 0187A], where we are compelled to sit for a very long time, until we are comforted by the visitation of the Dayspring from on high. Compelled, I say—and would that we were compelled and did not take pleasure in it! Would that what we suffer arose only from necessity, not also from will or pleasure! But alas, how easily and willingly we cast ourselves down and fall asleep under the heavy shadow of the thorny and fruitless juniper tree! How negligently and securely we grow sluggish and linger amid the cares and desires of this world! Therefore Leviathan, who sleeps under a shadow, makes his bed in us—unless we take care—because he finds in our perceptions and affections the shadows of this age friendly to himself. These shadows, as Job testifies, “cover his shadow” [Col. 0188A] (Job 40:20, 17), because worldly cares and desires within us conceal from us the shadow of impending damnation, so that we do not foresee it until we stumble into it.

Breathe upon us, O Day of days; overshadow our head in the day of battle; incline over us the shadows of salvation and refreshment, and let the shadows of sluggishness and weariness—indeed, of blindness and death—decline beneath us. And though shadows from thoughts of earthly things touch us, let darknesses not cover us—that is, the denser shadows arising from love of them—but let us always breathe again into your luminous love, O Father of lights, who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

## ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0187]

## SERMON I. That Mary is mother by a twofold title, and is rightly called God’s throne

[Col. 0187B]

1. “Come, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.” [Note: [Col. 0187D] In the Office of Virgins.] “Many are called, but few are chosen.” “Blessed are those whom you have chosen, O Lord; they shall dwell in your courts” (Ps. 64:5). Indeed, you will dwell in them, so that you may reign in them and establish in them the throne of your kingdom. Most blessed of all the blessed is Mary, who from among all the elect has been singularly chosen and pre-chosen. For the Lord chose her; He chose her as a dwelling-place for Himself, saying: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, for I have chosen her” (Ps. 131:14). He dwelt in her for nine months; He dwelt with her and beneath her for many years. Dwelling in her, He filled her with the singular grace of gifts; dwelling with her, He nourished her with the incomparable sweetness [Col. 0187C] of devout conduct and the desirable wisdom of divine words.

But now, dwelling in her and with her, as He does through unending eternity, so in an incomprehensible manner, He satisfies her with the glory of beatifying visions: outwardly displaying the form of glorified flesh, inwardly impressing the form of the Word who glorifies. O Mary, says the Lord, you shall no longer be called Forsaken, nor shall your land any longer be called Desolate, as though, because you are a virgin, you were therefore barren. But you shall be called “My Will,” that is, my beloved Son in you, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you, and your land shall be inhabited. For the young man shall dwell with the virgin, and your Son shall dwell in you—or rather, if it is preferable that we not depart from the words of Scripture: “Your sons shall dwell in you” [Col. 0187D] (Isa. 62:4–5).

2. Why do you, heretic, raise your head? Why do you turn the mystery of godliness into an occasion for unbelief? She bore one indeed: he who, as he is the Father’s only-begotten in heaven, is likewise his Mother’s only-begotten on earth. For, contrary to your impious blasphemy, she did not afterward bear other children; rather, there remains inviolate—just as in the mother the seal of perpetual virginity—so in the offspring the sacrament of catholic unity. Yet this one Virgin Mother, who glories that she bore the Father’s Only-Begotten, embraces that same only son of hers in all his members; and she is not ashamed to be called the mother of all those in whom she recognizes, or knows to be in process of being formed, her Christ.

That ancient Eve was not so much a mother as a stepmother: she offered her children the prior sentence of death before the beginning of light. She was indeed called the mother of all the living; but she proved rather to be the slayer of the living, or the mother of the dying, since her begetting was nothing other than the begetting of death (Gen. III). And because she could not faithfully interpret her own name, this woman fulfilled its mystery: she too, like the Church, whose image she is, is mother of all who are reborn to life. For she is the mother of that Life by which all live; and, in bringing him forth from herself, she thereby in some manner regenerated all who were to live from her. One was being begotten, but all of us were being begotten; because, according to the principle of the seed through which regeneration occurs, we were all already then in him. For as we were in Adam from the beginning by reason of the seed of carnal generation, so we were in Christ before the beginning by reason of the seed of spiritual regeneration.

3. Furthermore, that blessed Mother of Christ, because she knows herself to be the mother of Christians by the logic of the mystery, also shows herself their mother by maternal care and loving affection. She is not hardened toward her children, as though they were not her own: her womb, once fruitful indeed, yet never exhausted, never ceases to bring forth the fruit of devotion. For the blessed fruit of your womb left you, O loving Mother, pregnant with inexhaustible loving-kindness: born from you once, yet always remaining and overflowing within you, and causing the sealed fountain of charity in the enclosed garden of chastity ever to abound. Although sealed, it nevertheless flows forth abroad, and its waters are apportioned to us in the streets. For although the fountain of charity, proper to the Church, is inaccessible to outsiders, it nevertheless delights to share its benefit even with enemies. Finally, if a servant of Christ repeatedly labors to bring forth his little children through the care and longing of charity until Christ is formed in them (Gal. IV, 19), how much more does the Mother of Christ do so? Paul indeed begot them by preaching the word of truth through which they were regenerated; Mary did so far more divinely and holily, by bringing forth the Word himself. I praise the mystery of preaching in Paul, but I marvel at and venerate still more the mystery of generation in Mary.

4. Consider, moreover, whether the children too do not seem to acknowledge their Mother, prompted, surely, by a kind of natural devotion of faith, so that at the invocation of her name they flee first, or especially, to her in every necessity and danger, like little children to their mother’s breast. Therefore I think it is not unreasonable to understand of these children what was promised to her through the prophet: “Your children shall dwell in you” (Isa. LXII, 5), provided that the sense in which this prophecy is understood principally of the Church is preserved. For even now we dwell in the help of the Mother of the Most High; we abide in her protection, as under the shadow of her wings; and hereafter, in fellowship with her glory, we shall be cherished as in her bosom. Then there shall be one voice of those rejoicing and congratulating their Mother: “The dwelling-place of all of us who rejoice is in you” (Ps. LXXXVI, 7), holy Mother of God. Do not in any way believe that dwelling in Abraham’s bosom is a greater happiness and glory than dwelling in Mary’s bosom, since the King of glory has placed his throne in her.

[Col. 0189C] 5. “Come,” he says, “my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.” Her prerogative of glory could not have been described more expressively or more elegantly than by calling her the throne of God reigning. For the divine majesty seems to grant no soul so full and intimate a participation in itself as it grants to her in whom it has specially chosen, above others, to take its seat. The Lord spoke indeed to the disciples, who, having become poor, followed the poor one: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon thrones” (Matt. XIX, 28). Elsewhere too our Champion, watching and encouraging the combatants from heaven, promises: “To him who conquers,” he says, “I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I too conquered and sat upon the throne of my Father” (Apoc. III, 21). But to his Mother, whose merit is far different, he promises a correspondingly different reward. “Come,” he says, “my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.” It is too little, he says, for you to sit beside me when I judge, unless you yourself become my seat: so that you may contain the majesty of the reigning One within you more blessedly because more intimately, and comprehend, more specially than others, the incomprehensible One. You contained the little one in your lap; you shall contain the immeasurable One in your mind. You were the lodging-place of the One journeying; you shall be the palace of the One reigning. You were the tent of the One fighting in the world; you shall be the throne of the One triumphing in heaven. You were the bridal chamber of the incarnate Bridegroom; you shall be the throne of the crowned King.

6. O Son of God, nothing displeased you in that lodging-place of yours, which your condescension so willingly revisits and so abundantly rewards. You found nothing unclean there, since there was no lust but most pure chastity; nothing ruinous, since there was no pride but humility most firmly founded; nothing dark, since unbelief had been excluded; nothing narrow, since charity had been poured abroad. The most prudent Virgin had adorned the bridal chamber, prepared to receive you, Christ the King, not merely as a guest but also to possess you as a bridegroom. She had adorned it, I say, with the manifold beauty and glory of virtues—perhaps so much more richly because it was wholly inward. He marveled at this adornment who said, “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; in golden fringes, clothed round with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 14–15); and another: “O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity!” (Wis. IV, 1). Such holiness and beauty become your house, O Lord. That beauty invited you to enter and enticed you to return. Entering, you multiplied the grace of blessing; returning, you heaped it up. When you entered, you were born as a human being in her; when you returned, you were glorified as God in her. Then you established in her a sanctuary of grace; now, a throne of glory.

7. Other thrones are indeed spoken of, and exist: namely, certain divine spirits, filled with the majesty of God presiding, placed, as we suppose, above the other subject orders. Scripture does not state what their prerogative is, though it suggests from their name that it is something. The soul of every righteous person too is called the seat of wisdom. But what is now wisdom’s seat will assuredly then be glory’s seat as well. Let that heavenly palace, then, be full of seats and thrones, and let God sit in all of them, adapting and fitting himself to each according to merits. Yet, without injury to or envy of the other seats, it is not without reason believed that there is a certain special throne of the King, high and lifted up above the glory of all—I mean Mary, exalted above the choirs of angels—so that the Mother contemplates nothing above herself except her Son alone; the Queen marvels at nothing above herself except the King alone; and our Mediatrix venerates nothing above herself except the Mediator alone. May she reconcile us, commend us, and present us by her prayers to her only Son, Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the Mutual Love of Jesus and Mary

[Col. 0190D]

1. “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love” (Song V, 8). We wish, if it please your charity, to consider how these words, sung by us tonight, may appear to pertain to the Assumption of blessed Mary. This must, it seems, be done in that manner of discourse which the authors not only of secular but also of ecclesiastical writings have sometimes employed, especially in expounding the Song from which these words are taken. For this manner of discourse, while preserving truth, employs a certain broader freedom: when a theme appropriate to the matter has been adopted, as blessed Jerome says, it speaks not so much of things really done or said as it shows the affair to have been such that the things said, even if they were not done or spoken, might nevertheless have been done or spoken, or might reasonably be believed to have been in the intention of the doer or speaker.

Mary, then, as she was about to depart in body, lay ill, as human weakness does. Now the daughters of the Jerusalem above—that is, the angelic Powers—knowing surely that the Son’s favor is to be won by service rendered to his Mother, most dutifully visited their Lady, the Mother of their Lord. And perhaps, after the courtesies of greeting, the angels first said something of this kind to her, conforming their speech to human feeling or usage just as they conformed their appearance to a human countenance:

2. “What is this, I beseech you, my Lady, that makes you seem so sick and weak? Why are you sad and listless beyond your custom? Why, since yesterday and the day before, have you not, as you were accustomed, revisited the holy places by contemplating which you nourished your love? For several days now we have not seen you either ascending the rock of Calvary, there to fill the place of the cross with tears; or worshipping at your Son’s tomb the glory of the Resurrection; or upon the Mount of Olives kissing the final footprints of him who ascended.”

For this very reason she is believed to have lived in the valley of Jehoshaphat—where her tomb too is shown, as blessed Jerome says, in a church wondrously constructed with a stone roof—so that she might not withdraw too far from the holy places, but might visit them more often; and, although she retained all things in memory, might more sweetly embrace the form of the events as though bodily imaged in the places themselves, and thus give some consolation to her love.

3. When they asked why she now abstained from these things and lay wholly confined, she said: “I languish.”

“Why do you languish? What place in your body could weakness find, when the salvation of the world dwelt in it for so long? Power went forth from the body of that Son of yours and healed all, so that even the hem of his garment healed the woman with the issue of blood (Matt. IX, 20–22; Mark V, 25–34; Luke VIII, 43–48). And could you, who held him so long in your womb, in your bosom, and in your lap, be susceptible to any weakness or sickness?”

“There is no cause,” she replied, “for your surprise, if you remember what that very body of my Son was once like. For I know how weak he was, and to how many deficiencies he was subject—willingly, indeed—I who nourished him in my womb, nursed him at my breasts, and cherished him in my bosom. I saw not only the weaknesses of infancy but also those of the succeeding ages, and served him in them as I could. Finally, not without suffering of my own, I beheld the mockery and punishments of his Passion and cross, learning in every detail how truly our Isaiah said of him: ‘Surely he bore our weaknesses and carried our pains’ (Isa. LIII, 4; Matt. VIII, 17). Why, then, should I grieve that he gave not to my body what he did not give to his own? I am not so delicate or proud that I cannot or will not suffer, however small a part of it, what he deigned to suffer. He indeed did so by a merciful will; I by natural necessity. Certainly health is one thing, holiness another. He gave holiness to my body through the sacrament of the body conceived in me; he promised that he would give health through the example of his body raised again. Finally, that you may wonder less at my weakness: I languish with love. I languish more through love’s impatience than through suffering’s pain; more wounded by charity than burdened by infirmity.”

4. “Alas!” they said, “how frequent—indeed continuous—are the causes of weakness! Good Jesus, how is it that after bearing you this Mother of yours was almost never except in weakness? At first she languished in fear, afterward in grief, and now in love. In fear, from your birth until the Passion, when she always saw your life sought by plots; in grief, throughout the time of the Passion, until she received you alive again; now she is more happily, yet more wonderfully, tormented by love and longing, because she does not hold you seated in heaven. How, good Jesus, you who enjoy the highest joy, have you become for her the cause of such a long martyrdom, that so many and such sharp swords without ceasing pass through that soul of hers, which is dearest to you! But we beseech you, Lady, what would you have us do for you? Would you at least have this Gabriel, your fellow-initiate, remain here, sit beside you, and minister to you—he who from the beginning was privy to and minister of your mystery, and deserved also to be appointed guardian of your chamber?”

The Virgin said: “There is no need. My new angel in the flesh is enough for me—I mean the disciple whom Jesus loved, whose heir to his love he left me when on the cross he entrusted him to me and me to him. Nothing is more pleasing to me than his service, because nothing is more chaste in companionship and affection, sweeter in character, more sincere in faith, or holier in speech.”

“We then,” they said, “how can we render you service?”

“Daughters of Jerusalem,” she said, “tell my beloved that I languish with love. He knows how my weakness is to be healed.”

5. “But you know,” they said, “that although he knows all things, concerning many things he asks as if ignorant. If, then, he asks what you wish applied to your wound, what shall we answer him?”

“You are companions of the Bridegroom,” she said; “this Gabriel of mine is my *paranymphus*, my bridegroom’s friend. I do not think the mystery of love should be hidden from you. I shall therefore speak—provided only that I am not judged rash, as though I sought things too great for myself. ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’ If I knew myself guilty of anything, I should be content, with Mary Magdalene, with the kiss of his feet, where forgiveness of sins is received. But since in all my life my heart has not reproached me, I do not think that I arrogantly ask for the kiss of his mouth, the grace of joys. Why, moreover, should I seem arrogant if I ask back for that mouth which he himself, both creature and Creator, fashioned for himself from me? When I held him as a little child in my arms, whenever I wished to kiss the one beautiful beyond the children of men, I was freely permitted; he never turned away his face, never rejected his mother. And if perhaps I was excessive in the impatience of longing, he nevertheless, in his own manner, complied with his mother’s wish. He delighted to fill her with the grace poured forth upon his lips, and with the sweetness with which he was wholly filled—wholly delight and desire, namely, of chaste souls. Hence, as he himself declares of himself: ‘Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst’ (Ecclus. XXIV, 29; John VI, 35). The more sweetly I tasted the grace of that mouth, the more ardently, surely, I now seek it again. He has indeed grown in glory and majesty, but he has not at all changed from that innate gentleness and goodness. That worldly maxim of pride does not apply to him: ‘Honors change manners.’ He is more exalted, but not more proud; more glorious, but not more disdainful. He will not reject the Mother whom he chose, nor by a new judgment repudiate his eternal election.”

6. “Do not fear, Mary,” Gabriel said in his customary manner: “for you have found favor with God.” Even in others who lie far beneath your footsteps, he has been accustomed to approve the boldness of this affection and prayer; for he considers nothing excessive or injurious to himself that true charity alone presumes concerning him. Then, turning to the accompanying multitude, he said: “Let us go, let us go, lest we seem to do injury to the Son himself if we delay the Mother’s glory.”

When they had returned and reported these things to their Lord, what do we suppose Jesus said except something of this kind? “I am he who commanded children to honor father and mother. I, in order to do what I taught and to become an example to others, descended to earth to honor my Father; likewise, in order to honor my Mother, I ascended again to heaven. I ascended and prepared for her a place, a throne of glory, that the crowned Queen might sit at the right hand of the King in clothing of gold, surrounded with variety. Nor do I say this because a portion of my throne is set aside for her; rather, she herself shall be my throne. ‘Come, then, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.’ In you I shall establish for myself a seat, as it were, of my kingdom; from you I shall pronounce judgments; through you I shall hear prayers. No one ministered to me more in my humility. Besides other things, you shared with me what I am as man; I shall share with you what I am as God. You asked for the kiss of my mouth—indeed, your whole self shall be kissed by my whole self. I shall not press lips to lips, but spirit to spirit, with an everlasting and indissoluble kiss; for I have desired your beauty even more ardently than you have desired mine, nor shall I seem sufficiently glorified to myself until you are glorified together with me.”

“Glory to you, Lord Jesus,” added the choir of angels. “Glory to you, Lord Jesus,” repeated the assembly of the faithful. May the glorification of your Mother redound to your glory and to our forgiveness; you who grant this, to whom belong honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On Spiritual Rest

1. “In all things I sought rest” (Ecclus. XXIV, 11). Rest is welcome to the weary. Thus this day of rest and holiday comes welcome and fittingly to you who are weary, so that, while we celebrate the rest of the holy Mother of God, not only may our bodies be refreshed by this day’s repose from the labor of harvest, but our hearts too may breathe again in the remembrance and love of that eternal rest. Yet there too, brothers, you shall reap; but you shall reap rest, you who now sow the labor of this harvest. The fruit of this labor will be that rest: rest from labor, recompense for labor, the very remembrance of which restores the strength of the faithful in their labor. It is shade for those scorched by heat, food for the hungry. Thus said she who poured forth remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song II, 5). O you who labor, you who bear the burden and heat of the day! Under the shadow of Jesus’ wings you shall find rest for your souls: “a support of strength,” as it is written, “a covering from heat, a shelter at noon” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 19), so that this confession may come from the heart as well as from the mouth: “Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Ps. CXXXIX, 8)—in the day of heat and labor, conflict and temptation. For when meditation on eternal rest casts its shade over the heads of those who labor, it not only cools them from the heat of temptations but renews their minds for labor, according to what is written of Issachar, the strong ass: “He saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear” (Gen. XLIX, 15). That is, by longing for that rest and inheritance, he willingly humbled himself for labor. Thus he too could say: “In all things I sought rest, and I shall abide in the inheritance of the Lord.”

2. Blessed is the person who seeks blessed rest in all his labors and ways: always hastening to enter, as the Apostle exhorts, into that rest (Heb. IV, 3); afflicting his body through longing for it, while already preparing and disposing his mind for that rest; living peaceably, so far as depends on him, with all people; choosing by preference Mary’s rest and leisure, while undertaking Martha’s labor and business indeed from necessity, but fulfilling it with as much peace and repose of spirit as he can, and always gathering himself back from that manifold distraction to the one thing necessary. Such a person rests even while working, just as, conversely, the wicked work even while resting. For how could those rest upon whom God sends the wheel of evils, and to whom he swore in his wrath: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. XCIV, 12)? Outside it there is only affliction and misery, and around it a mighty tempest; just as in the nature of things, whatever lies outside the simplicity and unity of a point is in motion and agitation, and any circle is driven in a more violent whirl the farther it recedes from the immobility of its principle—that is, from the middle of its center. Indeed, “the wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. XI, 9), upon whom God sends the wheel of evils; therefore they cannot enter that inward and eternal rest. Therefore destruction and misery are in their ways, because “they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. XIII, 3): because they have not sought it, so as to be able to say, “In all things I sought rest”—that is, so that in the multiplicity of their actions, by which they are troubled and trouble others, they may think upon or seek the one thing necessary. Rather, that is the voice of the righteous, who can also say: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek. Your face, Lord, I have sought; your face will I seek” (Ps. XXVI, 4, 8). They labor only from love of that rest, and altogether prefer to have rottenness enter their bones, that they may rest in the day of tribulation, rather than spend their days in good things and descend in a moment into hell.

3. Yet if anyone wishes to inquire more curiously whose voice this is most especially—“In all things I sought rest”—it is surely the voice of Wisdom, the voice of the Church, the voice of Mary, and the voice of every wise soul. Wisdom sought rest in all things, but found it in the humble alone. The Church sought rest among all the nations of the world, but found it in believers alone. Mary, like every faithful soul, sought rest in all her actions; but today at last she found it, when, after Herod’s persecution and the flight into Egypt, after so many plots and cruelties of Jewish impiety, after so many sufferings of her own arising from the Passion and death of her Son, after so many and such bitter swords had passed through her soul, it was finally granted her today to say: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. CXIV, 7). He who created me, and was created from me, rested in the tabernacle of my body; he cannot deny me the rest of his heaven. For he who freely heaps grace upon others—how shall he fail to return like for like to his Mother? Go on, Mary; go on securely in your Son’s blessings. Act confidently as queen, mother, and bride of the King. You sought rest, but what is owed you is of greater glory: kingdom and power. He whose mystery of loving-kindness and unity was indivisible with you in one flesh and one spirit desires to have his dominion undivided with you; for, with the honor of nature preserved, the Mother was joined in marriage through the twofold gift of grace. Rest, then, O blessed one, between the Bridegroom’s arms. Amid embraces and kisses he will, I think, tell you again how sweetly he rested in the tabernacle of your body, how sweet he was in the chamber of your heart. God, brothers, is not unjust so as to forget a good work: with him the memory of a kindness once received lives forever. Blessed is the one with whom God has found rest even once, in whose tabernacle he has rested even for one hour.

4. Behold, even now Wisdom cries in the streets: “In all things I sought rest.” I knocked, and no one opened; I called, and no one answered. The Son of Man, made, according to the prophet, “like a wandering man, and like a traveler turning aside to lodge” (Jer. XIV, 8–9), has nowhere to lay his head. He stands outside, his head full of dew and his locks with the drops of the night. Who among us is so humane and hospitable as to rise and open to him and bring him into his chamber, or at least show him the great prepared upper room where he may eat the new Passover with his disciples? For I tell you, brothers: unless he finds in us the rest he seeks, neither shall we find in him the rest we desire. The Lord indeed says through the prophet: “This is my rest: refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment” (Isa. XXVIII, 12). “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor; in the evil day” (Ps. XL, 2) the Lord will prepare for him, in due return, rest and refreshment. If, therefore, God reckons as done to himself the humanity shown to his members, how much more does he reckon what is done to his own Spirit, when with thanksgiving he recalls: “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matt. XXV, 35)? Shall the poverty of many saints, unable to gather wanderers or feed the hungry, be inhumane and inhospitable to the Lord, who is accustomed especially to lodge among the poor? “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, but upon the humble, quiet man who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2). O humility—narrow for yourself, broad for divinity; poor and insufficient for yourself, sufficient for him whom the world cannot contain; abundantly and delightfully refreshing him who feeds even the angels. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, except upon the humble?” “In all things I sought rest,” but I found it in a humble handmaid. None was found like her in the grace of humility; therefore in the fullness of humility the whole fullness of divinity rested even bodily. Yet it rested differently in the Son: for though the Mother was most humble, the Son was far more humble still. Therefore the sevenfold Spirit not only rested upon him, but also prepared in him diverse dwelling-places of most blessed rest for all who have learned from him to be meek and humble; indeed, he made his very self into a kind of golden couch for resting. He who deserved at supper to recline upon his breast seems to have tasted beforehand, in a certain image, the most blessed rest of this couch.

5. But let us still consider how full of reason and fittingness is the saying: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet?” For how could anything rest upon what is restless? How could an immovable column stand upon a base that shook or wavered? But who can be quiet except the humble? Who except one humble in the peace of a tranquil and restrained spirit can possess himself? “The wind drives the wicked from the face of the earth” (Ps. I, 4), and he is carried about by every wind of doctrine. “The wicked,” says the prophet, “is like a boiling sea, which cannot rest” (Isa. LVII, 20). Anger boils, greed seethes, pride swells; continual inward warfare beats a person against himself and crushes him in domestic sedition. Therefore, that the lover and giver of rest may rest in you, my brothers, take care, according to the Apostle’s counsel, to be quiet. How can this be? “I tell you,” he says, “that you should mind your own business and work with your hands” (I Thess. IV, 11). Work is a burden which, as ballast gives ships steadiness, gives rest and gravity to restless hearts and establishes and orders the condition of the outward person. As you have read, the beginning of great evils is a wandering woman, unable to endure quiet and unable to keep her feet at home; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait by the corners (Prov. VII, 10–12). Nor without reason does the Teacher of the Gentiles hold this evil of restlessness in such suspicion that he judges it must be pursued not only by rebuke but also by separation. “We beseech you, brothers,” he says, “rebuke the restless” (I Thess. V, 14). And again, in the second letter to the same Thessalonians, among other things that he thundered, as it were, from heaven against the restless: “We have heard,” he says, “that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but busying themselves with curiosities. To such persons we declare that, working in silence, they should eat their own bread. But if anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed” (II Thess. III, 11, 12, 14).

6. If anyone of this kind is found among you—which God forbid—let him be ashamed more beautifully and honorably of his own accord, before he is publicly marked so severely: namely, because he is conspicuous and is nevertheless overlooked; blameworthy and yet tolerated. But let him be ashamed in such a way that he is corrected by shame, rejoices in rebuke, and makes glad not only us but the Spirit of God, who, when he says, “In all things I sought rest,” finds it only in the quiet and bestows it only upon the quiet. Therefore through the prophet he recalls and restrains the restless: “If you return and rest, you shall be saved” (Isa. XXX, 15). Let us all, therefore, together take care to be quiet, so that in our quiet we may always be occupied in meditation upon eternal rest and be found ready for every labor through longing for it. May the blessed Mother of God, whose rest we celebrate, obtain this for us from him who rested in the tabernacle of her body and heart. He is eternal rest, Christ Jesus, to whom belong honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. That the Blessed Virgin Fulfilled the Offices of Mary and Martha

[Col. 0197C]

1. “Mary has chosen the better part” (Luke X, 42). This was written concerning Mary, Martha’s sister; but it was fulfilled more fully and more holily in Mary, the Mother of the Lord. For today the blessed Virgin Mary chose the better part—or rather, the part she had long ago chosen she today received to possess forever: namely, that she might cleave inseparably to the Lord and perpetually enjoy the Word of God. Nor is it foreign or unfitting for what was said of that Mary to be transferred to this one, since, in support of the appropriateness of the transfer, there is a likeness not only of name but also of deed. That Mary received the Lord under the hospitality of her roof; this one received him in the bridal chamber of her womb. “He who created me,” she says, “rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. XXIV, 12). That Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, heard his word (Luke X, 39); this one, diligent in caring for his humanity, “kept all the words spoken concerning him, pondering them in her heart” (Luke II, 19, 51). And when Jesus went about proclaiming the Gospel in cities and villages, Mary, his inseparable companion, clung to his footsteps and hung upon the teacher’s mouth. Thus neither the storm of persecution nor the horror of punishment could frighten her from following her Son and Master: “Mary his mother stood,” it says, “beside the cross of Jesus” (John XIX, 25). Truly she was a Mother, who did not abandon her Son even amid the terror of death. For how could she be frightened by death, whose charity was strong as death—indeed, stronger than death? Truly she stood beside the cross of Jesus: her mind was crucified together with the pain of the cross, and her own soul was pierced by as many swords as she saw wounds piercing her Son’s body. Rightly, therefore, was she acknowledged as Mother there, and her care entrusted to a suitable guardian where both the Mother’s sincere love for the Son and the Son’s true humanity toward his Mother were most fully proved.

At other times he seemed, as it were, to have disregarded his Mother: whether when, at the wedding, she requested a miracle and he said, “What is there between me and you, woman?” (John II, 4); or when, in the midst of Gospel preaching, someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand seeking you,” and he answered, “Who is my mother?” (Matt. XII, 47–48). But he needed to answer his Mother, when she sought a miracle, in such a way as to indicate that he possessed miracles from another source than his Mother; and he could not have replied better to the one interrupting the Gospel sermon by announcing his relatives, so as to show that spiritual things must be preferred to carnal ones. It was as though, in his customary manner, he said to parents seeking him while he was occupied with the business of the Gospel: “Why is it that you seek me? Do you not know that I must be occupied with the things of my Father?” (Luke II, 49).

2. Far be it that he should have despised his Mother, he who gave a law commanding that parents be honored with such care! Far be it, I say, that he should have disdained on earth the Mother whose beauty he desired from heaven! Rather, by word and example, he was ordering charity within us, teaching us to set above the carnal affections of family ties not only the love of God but also the love of those who do God’s will. For that affection is required from the hearts of us all whom the condescension of the highest Father has adopted, so that we may faithfully say with his Only-Begotten: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII, 49). This is indeed the fitting utterance of God’s children, and the Spirit himself gives no more faithful testimony to our spirit that we are children of God than when this utterance of God’s Only-Begotten resounds from our hearts. Thus Jesus proves Mary, who was his mother according to the flesh, to be his mother also on another ground: since she too did the Father’s will to such a degree that the Father foretold concerning her, “You shall be called my will in her” (Isa. LXII, 4). Therefore, where the Son seemed to have failed to recognize her, he is found to have honored her more highly: for the honor of the maternal name was doubled in her, because she bore in her mind, now inspired, that same Son whom she had borne incarnate in her womb.

3. Moreover, since Jesus had loved her, he loved her to the end, so that he not only brought his life to an end on her account, but almost brought his speaking to an end in her: for, as though among the final words of his testament, he transferred the care of his Mother—whose debtor he knew himself to be—to his dearest heir. Thus Christ divided his inheritance between Peter, who loved more, and John, who was more loved: Peter received the Church; John, Mary. This portion plainly belonged to him not only by right of kinship, but also by the privilege of love and the testimony of chastity. For it was fitting that none but a virgin should serve a virgin, so that [Col. 0199A] the blessed Virgin, languishing with divine love, might be strengthened by the flowers of chastity, and that the young man’s virginity might meanwhile receive this reward: to benefit from companionship with so great a holiness. And because he proved faithful in his service to the incorrupt Mother, he deserved also to have entrusted to him the mysteries of divinity and the secrets of the incorruptible Word.

It was fitting, I say, that no one but the beloved of the Son should attend upon the Mother of the Lord: so that the Mother, ever yearning for her Son, might breathe more sweetly in the beloved of her Son; and that the disciple, grieving that his Master had been taken from him too soon, might rejoice to have found for himself the Teacher of all truth. This was also very suitably provided, so that, when he was to write the Gospel, he might consult more intimately with her concerning each matter—she who knew all things, since from the beginning she had most carefully observed all that concerned her Son, “keeping all the words which were spoken concerning him and pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19, 51). Thus she showed herself Martha in caring for the Child’s nurture, while she is nevertheless believed to have fulfilled Mary’s part in zeal for knowing the Word.

But especially after that same Son had ascended where he had been before, the Mother, released from every temporal concern and more fully illumined by the Holy Spirit—whom, beyond those singular first-fruits received at her conception, she had received in common with the Apostles—rejoiced, surely, to be at leisure and to see that Jesus is God. This vision is indeed one of inexpressible joy and supreme delight for all who love Jesus, but above all for her who bore Jesus. For as she alone received the grace of bearing God, so she also received the prerogative of glorying [Col. 0199C] in him whom she bore. Indeed, the Virgin Mother’s glory is singular and incomparable: to see God, the King of all, in the diadem of flesh with which she crowned him; to recognize and adore God in her own body, and to see her own body glorified in God.

Meanwhile, as I think, Mary was nourished by these contemplations. She had chosen that best part, which today has not been taken away from her but perfected in her. Since she had not been negligent or slothful in Martha’s work, she was by no means left empty of Mary’s fruit. Labour belongs to action; fruit, or reward, to contemplation. “Therefore,” he says, “because his soul has laboured, he shall see and be satisfied” (Isa. 53:11).

4. We say these things to you, brethren, so that if anyone is touched by desire for that best part which is praised in Mary, he may know that it is the reward of that part which is not disapproved in Martha. It is not fitting that reward should be sought [Col. 0199D] before merit. Jacob must first be joined to Leah before he may enjoy Rachel’s embraces (Gen. 29); and he himself must first be called and be Jacob before becoming Israel.

“Have they appointed you ruler? Take care of them; and then reflect; and, when all your care has been discharged, recline, that you may rejoice because of them and receive the crown as an ornament of grace” (Ecclus. 32:1–3). For the labour of work, or the anxiety of administration, are seeds of righteousness; in return for them joys are to be reaped from the mouth of consoling mercy. Thus the prophet says: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap in the mouth of mercy” (Hos. 10:12). Yet he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessing will reap also from blessings (2 Cor. 9:6).

Certainly no one has sown with such lavish blessing as she who is blessed [Col. 0200B] among women, who poured forth from her womb the blessed seed. But shall I call him seed, or fruit? Better: both. For he who is seed to those who work righteousness will be fruit to those who reap glory: seed in the Passion, fruit in the Resurrection. Mighty upon the earth is this seed, which, falling into the earth, immediately stirred up its power in order to bring forth much fruit, and in that seed all nations were blessed. Hence it follows there: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111:2).

5. Therefore let Mary reap from her blessings; and she who sowed the blessing of all nations, let her receive in a singular manner the blessing of all nations. “All generations shall call me blessed,” she says (Luke 1:48). This is too little. All the orders of blessed spirits shall call you blessed. Today they saw the daughter of heavenly Zion ascending [Col. 0200C], “and called her blessed; and the queens praised her” (Song 6:8).

Truly Mary today reaps from her blessings, because that blessing in all its fullness, which she poured forth from herself, has been spiritually poured back into her. “Give her,” says the Holy Spirit, “of the fruit of her womb”; and let her be satisfied with him whom she bore. O Mother of mercy, satisfy yourself with the glory of your Son, and leave your remnants to your little children. You, Lady, are already at the table; we are the little dogs beneath the table. “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress,” so this hungry household awaits from you the nourishment of life. Through you we have shared the fruit of life at the table of present sacraments; through you may we share that same fruit of life at the table of everlasting joys—Jesus, the blessed [Col. 0200D] fruit of your womb—to whom be honour and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## On the Nativity of the Blessed Mary

[Col. 0199]

### Sermon I. A comparison of the Virgin’s childbirth with the vine which, though uninjured, gives forth its fragrance.

[Col. 0199D]

1. “Like a vine I have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance” (Ecclus. 24:23). We celebrate the nativity of the most blessed Virgin Mother, from whom the Life of all received birth. Today the Virgin was born, from whom the Salvation of all willed to be born, that he might grant to those born unto death the power of being reborn unto life. Today the new Mother was born, who dissolved the curse of the first mother, so that those who through the latter had been born under the sentence of eternal curse might through the former possess blessing as their inheritance [Col. 0201A].

Truly a new Mother: she brought newness to children grown old, and healed the defect both of inborn and of superadded age. Truly a new Mother, who gives birth by so new a miracle that she gives birth and remains a virgin; and gives birth to him who created all things, including his Mother herself among them. The newness of fruitful virginity is wonderful indeed, but far more wonderful is the newness of the Child brought forth. For no one who recognizes that he who was born was God will now find it incredible that the Virgin remained a virgin after giving birth. He could in no way be born to the injury of his Mother’s integrity, since he is accustomed also to restore what has been corrupted. Nor did the reality of the body he assumed detract from the Creator’s power, so as to prevent him from preserving for himself what he granted to many creatures. You will find, indeed, many creatures born without corruption of those that give them birth, and in a certain manner bearing testimony to their Creator by their own voice concerning their inviolate childbirth [Col. 0201B].

2. But let the Mother herself speak, she who knows her own mystery, and teach us both how and what she herself bore. Let her speak, however, not on the basis of a new assertion but by the ancient oracle of prophecy; for, as the Apostle Peter says, the prophetic word is a witness stronger even than miracles (2 Pet. 1:19). For what is less open to slander or admits less suspicion of falsehood than testimony divinely uttered concerning those not yet born?

Long before Mary was born, therefore, the Spirit who was to be in her assumed her voice and defended against the blasphemies of the impious both the divinity of the Son and the integrity of the Mother—his own work. Speaking in her person, if we follow the common interpretation, he said what you have now heard: “Like a vine I have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance” (Ecclus. 24:23). The context of the reading assigns these words to the person of Wisdom, that is, to the Son himself, as you know who understand the rules of Scripture; but this does not prejudice the interpretation by which they may, like many other things, be applied also to the person of the Virgin Mother. Nor are you unaware that there are more than sufficient other testimonies, serving this subject more directly and clearly. Yet your expectation ought not to be disappointed concerning what today’s reading has proposed [Col. 0201C].

3. Let Mary therefore answer the blasphemers, both for herself and for her Son; let her destroy all heresies by a single word and say: “Like a vine I have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance.” It is as though she plainly said: My childbirth indeed has no parallel among women, but it has a likeness among the natures of things. Do you ask how virginity bore the Saviour? As the flower of the vine gives forth fragrance. If you find the flower corrupted because it has given forth fragrance, then believe that modesty was violated because it brought forth the Saviour.

What objection can you raise against the aptness of the comparison? For what is virginity except the flower of an inviolate body? What is the son of virginity except sweetness of fragrance? Yet take care lest you die from the good fragrance. For to some it is a good fragrance, from life unto life—namely, to those who are saved; to others, a fragrance of death unto death—namely, to those who perish: just as the fragrance [Col. 0202A] of a flowering vineyard is so to poisonous creatures.

Certainly the spirit of the aged patriarch was refreshed by the sweetness of this fragrance when, touching his son and sensing Christ’s fragrance, he poured forth from remembrance of the abundance of that sweetness, saying: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a field full of blessing, which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). God the Father perceived the sweetness of this fragrance and, delighted by it, was reconciled to the human race when the Son offered himself as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet fragrance. We are drawn by this sweet fragrance when, through conversion, we run to him; the young women are drawn by it when, through devotion, they run after him.

Yet one is the fragrance received from the renown of preaching; another is this fragrance which is, in some manner more substantial, diffused from his garments or ointments, or perhaps from his very body. It is certainly nothing other than the power that goes forth from him, which rouses the sluggish and renews love’s fervour, making them rejoice to run in the way of the commandments [Col. 0202B].

4. Since, therefore, she brought forth so fragrant a fruit, let Mary glory and say: “Like a vine I have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance.” Aptly, “like a vine”: for her Beloved is “a cluster of Cyprus” to her (Song 1:13). From him the winepress of the Passion not only pressed out the red must of precious blood, with which the splendid cup intoxicates; holy devotion also daily presses for itself wine which gladdens the human heart and intoxicates it with the delight of joy and love.

But the taste of flavour does not intoxicate before the sweetness of fragrance draws; nor does the joy of vision gladden unless the piety of reputation first attracts. For unless we believe, we shall not understand; nor shall we taste that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 33:9). Faith is what smells; experience is what tastes and enjoys. Therefore perhaps Mary, describing her Jesus through his virtues and effects, first calls him the sweetness of fragrance; for Jesus must first subsist in us by the fragrance of his holy reputation drawing us to himself.

What is the fruit from which this fragrance proceeds, and whither it draws us, she reveals when she adds: “And my flowers are the fruit of honour and honesty” (Ecclus. 24:23). Truly this is Jesus: sweetness of fragrance inviting; honourable beauty sanctifying; honour glorifying. Sweetness of fragrance, by which we are as it were brought to the way; honourable beauty, by which we are led along it; honour, to which we are brought [Col. 0202D]. “Honourable beauty” is aptly so called, as though it were the abiding state of honour. For that honour, the state of highest dignity and glory, could not then abide in us unless the honourable beauty of life and conduct now prepared a dwelling for it. No one then will be seen, as many now are, honoured without honourable conduct, just as no one is honourable without honour.

Thus Jesus is first sweetness of fragrance for those whom he calls; then honourable beauty for those whom he justifies; finally honour for those whom he glorifies. “For those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

5. “Such, then, is my Beloved,” says Mary, “and this is my Son, O daughters of Jerusalem. This is the blessed fruit of my womb; my flowers have borne this fruit.” She does not say, “Flower,” but “flowers,” because, although the holy Virgin is one, the flower of virginity in her is manifold. Yet in Mary grace flowered in a singular and manifold way above all others: she was wholly beautiful within and without, wholly blooming with a certain flowery beauty and loveliness of modesty [Col. 0203A].

Indeed, if chastity is perfect in you also, not only will your flesh bloom anew, but a certain divine sanctification will flower over your whole self. Your gaze will not be wanton or wandering, but flower with modesty; your speech will not be lascivious or foolish, but pleasing through reserve or seasoned with wisdom. Your ears will not itch with the desire to hear novelties or obscenities, nor your palate with the desire to take sweet things. Your walk will not be disorderly, but modest; nor will your dress be—not to say prostitute-like—but not even superstitious: rather, religious. The whole bearing of your person will flower with the grace of holiness, so that when you invite the Bridegroom into your inner chamber, you may rightly say to him, “Our bed is in flower” (Song 1:15).

Indeed, you yourself will become a most beautiful flower, such as the Bride desires to support and refresh the languor of her love when she says: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5). Such a righteous person, even when his root has grown old in the earth and his trunk has died in the dust, at the scent of living water in the resurrection—that is, in the renewed flowering of the righteous—shall sprout like a lily; and shall flower eternally before the Lord: the flower from the flower, born of a virgin, the Virgin’s Son, Bridegroom and crown of virgins; the flower, I say, by whom not only the integrity of virgins but also the chastity of the continent is to be crowned. To him be glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon II. On the beauty of holy love

1. “I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope” (Ecclus. 24:24). You may remember that last year, when we spoke about the beginning of today’s reading, we assigned it, not inappropriately, I think, to the blessed Mother of God—while preserving nevertheless that interpretation according to which the whole reading properly belongs to her Son, the Wisdom of God. But far more clearly, in what we have now proposed from the same reading, the voice and person of that Virgin manifest themselves, provided that we notice how beautifully and aptly, when she says, “I am the mother of beautiful love,” and so forth, she describes her Son by these names of virtues [Col. 0203D].

The Son was known to his Mother, and surely no less than to him who said: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).
