She first knew him according to the form of flesh in which she bore him; but this is far from knowledge of that form in which the Father begot him. In the former he was at one time seen, and “there was no form or beauty in him” (Isa. 53:2); in the latter he is “the brightness of glory and the radiance of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26), with whom “there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1:17). The sight of that former form increased sin for unbelievers; the sight of this latter is reserved as a reward for the righteous.

Thus between the form of flesh and the form of the Word there is, as it were, an intermediate step from the one to the other: another form of Christ, spiritual indeed, yet one which he openly displayed in the flesh—namely, the form of the life which he lived in the body for the formation of those who were to believe. For if Christ has been formed in us according to the pattern of life and conduct displayed in him, then at last we shall be fit to behold not merely the form that was formed for our sake, but also that form which formed us [Col. 0204A].

2. In Christ there is one bodily form, another moral form, another intellectual form. In the bodily form he is our brother; in the moral form he is our teacher; in the intellectual form he is our God. He assumed the bodily form in order to fulfil the sacrament; he displayed the moral form in order to provide an example; he will reveal the intellectual, or divine, form as a reward. Yet even then to behold the bodily form, into which angels desire to look, will be no small share of glory.

Blessed, however, is the one who has now become a lover of this form which has been set forth as an example; for one who scrutinizes that form which has been laid up as a reward “shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27). He had become an admirer and lover of this form who said: “You are beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). Do you wish to know that he praised not the form of the body but of the heart, not the beauty of limbs but of character? Hear what follows: “In your splendour,” he says, “and in your beauty, set forth, advance prosperously, and reign.” Perhaps this still leaves doubt, unless he adds: “For truth,” he says, “and meekness and righteousness” (Ps. 44:5). Truly this is your splendour and beauty, by which you acquired your kingdom, most beautiful of kings: namely, truth in words, meekness in conduct, righteousness in judgments.

By this beauty you easily charmed and subjected to yourself even the hearts of enemies, being altogether desire and delight. A wondrous triumph of grace, an utterly new and most beautiful kind of victory: not to destroy an enemy unto death by strength, but to convert him to love by beauty. Behold, the whole world has gone after him, desiring the beauty of his splendour—not because it has seen his face, but because it has heard so many lovable things of his meekness, truth, and righteousness. “Out of Zion comes the beauty of his splendour,” because “from Zion the law went forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Mic. 4:2): that is, the Gospel was sent to us from there, in which a fairer face of Christ was shown—namely, the form of life and teaching which he both handed down in word and expressed in himself by example [Col. 0204D].

3. To know Christ in this form is, for the present, the piety of Christians; to know him in the form of flesh was the scandal of the Jews; to know him in the form of divinity is the blessedness and joy of angels. Therefore Paul, knowing that the flesh profits nothing apart from the Spirit who gives life, refuses now to know Christ according to the flesh (2 Cor. 5:16), so that he may devote himself wholly and more zealously to the life-giving Spirit.

Mary too seems to understand this. Desiring to commend to the affections of all the Beloved of her womb, the Beloved of her desires, she describes him not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit—as though she too said: “Though I knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now I know him so no longer.” For she too desires to form her Only-Begotten in all the children of adoption. Though they have been begotten by the word of truth, she nevertheless labours over them daily in the desire and care of piety, until they attain “to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age” of her Son, whom she conceived and bore once; indeed, as Isaiah says, “Before she travailed, she gave birth” (Isa. 66:7), because she bore without pain and knew none of the difficulty and distress of childbirth when she bore the fruit of eternal joy [Col. 0205A].

4. Commending him to us, therefore, she says: “I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope” (Ecclus. 24:24). Is this then your Son, O Virgin of virgins? Is your Beloved then such, O fairest among women? Certainly, “such is my Beloved, and he is my Son, O daughters of Jerusalem. My Beloved is beautiful love in himself; my Beloved is beautiful love, fear, hope, and knowledge in the one who is born from him.”

For he is not only the one whom we love, fear, know, and hope in; he also works all these things in us, and by these virtues, as by certain members and parts, he is perfected and formed in us. For then Christ is perfectly formed in you, according to the measure of this life; then his truth is expressed in you, if you have known and glorified the truth which he is, namely through fear and hope, and if, lest hope put you to shame, love has been poured into your heart.

If you judge it unsuitable to this interpretation that the order of these virtues or perfections differs from the order in which their names are set down—for she does not say, “I am mother of knowledge, and fear, and hope, and love,” but “I am mother of beautiful love, and fear, and knowledge, and holy hope”—perhaps something fitting and rational may be found in the very order which she gives. For just as fear is born of knowledge, and hope, joined to it, consoles fear lest it fall into despair, and love supports hope lest it be put to shame; so, in reverse order, love bears chaste fear, and fear with love illuminates knowledge, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened” (Ecclus. 2:10) [Col. 0206A]. And the more truly God is known by the illumined heart, the more confidently he is hoped in. Hence: “Let all who know your name hope in you, O Lord” (Ps. 9:11). Hope is holy, as John says when speaking of the hope of seeing God: “Everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, as he also is holy” (1 John 3:3).

5. Love is fittingly and properly called beautiful love, since charity is God and consequently supreme beauty; and this virtue is almost wholly the beauty of the Church, which her Bridegroom in the Song of Love is found so greatly and so frequently to admire and extol in her. Truly love is beautiful when it is “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.” Where the heart is pure, there is no wrinkle; where the conscience is good, there is no stain; where faith is unfeigned, there is nothing of such a kind displeasing to the Bridegroom’s eyes, to prevent him from presenting the Church to himself now as gracious and then as glorious [Col. 0206B].

By this name the love of the saints had also to be distinguished from human love: whether shameful love, which should not even be named among believers; natural love, by which parents are loved; or worldly love, by which people love one another because of the needs or desires of the world. Far away, then—far away; indeed, let love of shamefulness be nowhere at all beneath God’s eyes. Let the love of natural relationship meanwhile withdraw apart, and let the love of inward and eternal beauty alone reign, by which those who are truly beautiful love God alone, or love for God’s sake.

But you, good Jesus, beauty of the Saints, beautiful in form not only above the sons of men but even above the powers of heaven: in your splendour and beauty set forth, advance prosperously, and reign. Let your beautiful love reign so widely that it may drive shameful love from the bounds of created things and banish it; convert and draw worldly love to itself; govern and order natural love beneath itself. Thus may the world love you with that beautiful and true love by which you loved the world, O Saviour of the world, who live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## On the Solemnity of All Saints: Sermon on the Poor in Spirit

[Col. 0205]

1. “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). I recognize that well-known and noble prophecy which, as a testimony concerning himself, the Son of God uttered while not yet born in the flesh; and which, once born though not yet known, he taught to belong to himself: “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” (Isa. 61:1). Behold, the poor are evangelized; behold, the Gospel of the kingdom is announced to the poor: “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3) [Col. 0206D].

A joyful beginning of the New Testament indeed, full of new grace, inviting even the most unbelieving or sluggish not merely to hear but much more to act, when blessedness promises the miserable, exiled, and needy the kingdom of heaven. This is, I say, a welcome and auspicious beginning of the new law: at its very outset the Lawgiver gives the blessings of so many beatitudes, so that, delighted by them, people may go from virtue to virtue through these eight steps of ascent which the structure of the Gospel has set in our hearts, after the pattern and image of heavenly things shown also to Ezekiel upon the mountain of God’s visions. For this ordered eightfold sequence of virtues is clearly an ascent of hearts and an advance of merits, leading the man of evangelical perfection step by step from the lowest things to the highest, until he enters the temple in order to see the God of gods in Zion, of which the prophet says: “And its ascent was by eight steps” (Ezek. 40:37) [Col. 0207A].

2. The first virtue of beginners is renunciation of the world, by which we are made poor in spirit; the second is meekness, by which we submit and accustom ourselves to obedience; then comes mourning, by which sins are wept over or virtues are sought. There, indeed, we taste that for which we may hunger and thirst still more—righteousness, both in ourselves and in others—and we begin to be stirred by zeal against sinners. But lest excessive zeal turn into vice, mercy follows to moderate it.

When someone has learned, through these pursuits or exercises, to be righteous and merciful, he may perhaps be fit to devote himself to contemplation and to labour in cleansing the heart by which God is seen. Once trained and proved in both action and contemplation, he will then at last be worthy, bearing the name and office of a Son of God, to become a father and minister of others, and, as mediator and reconciler, to make peace between them and God; to make peace among themselves, or even with those outside, as it is written in praise of the holy fathers: “Making peace in their households” (Ecclus. 44:6) [Col. 0207C].

One who is faithful and steadfast in this office will often obtain for himself the power and merit of martyrdom, suffering persecution for righteousness’ sake—sometimes even from those for whom he fights—so that he may say: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1:5); and, “With those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. 119:7).

3. From the fact that the Lord declares even the first beginnings of those renouncing the world to be of such happiness that he says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” one may in some measure judge how great the glory and how abundant the heavenly reward are at the summit of this perfection. Blessed indeed are those who, casting aside the cheap yet heavy little burdens of this world, refuse to be rich except in the Creator of the world; who, for his sake, are as having nothing yet through him possessing all things [Col. 0207D].

Do not those possess all things who possess him who contains and orders all things, whose portion and inheritance is God? In order that nothing may be lacking to those who fear him, he dispenses all other things for their use as he knows expedient, while reserving himself for their enjoyment. When the heir of God and co-heir of Christ, grown to maturity and emancipated, is brought into full possession of the inheritance for which he waits, then he will surely have absolute right and free dominion over creatures. For now, as long as he is a child, he differs in no respect from a servant, though he is lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the Father [Col. 0208A].

Then the world will recognize its righteous and lawful heir as its lord, for whose sake it was created. It will recognize him, I say, because he is no longer conformed to it, but is transformed by the renewal of his mind into the image of God in which he was made. Yet even now “the whole world is wealth to the faithful person” (Prov. 17, according to the Septuagint).

> **Note:** [Col. 0207] This reading is familiar in Augustine, Gregory, Bernard, and other Fathers.

This is so not only because, for knowing or loving the Author of the world, he uses all worldly things as though given him for this purpose; and delights in the way of God’s testimonies—which he sees, in the created work no less than in Scripture, bearing witness to the Creator—as in all riches. It is so also because he has learned to be so content and thankful that he reckons as the riches of the whole world the almost nothing which he possesses, or even this very fact: that he possesses nothing.

Therefore Solomon rightly pronounces blessed the Church of the saints, which is poor for Christ yet so rich in Christ: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. 31:29) [Col. 0208B]. Others seize what is not their own and are always in want; the saints distribute what is their own and become richer. “For the rich have lacked and hungered, but those who seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good thing” (Ps. 33:11).

4. The more the covetous person possesses, the more he needs. Yet he possesses nothing less than that which he thinks he possesses; for he is possessed rather than possesses: a slave of money, a bondsman of avarice, a worshipper of the purse, an abominable idolater, for whom a coin is god. Beautifully, even now, divine justice takes vengeance on sinners, turning into torments the very things which they love and making their vices into punishments [Col. 0208C]. Money, when distributed or given once for all, further justifies and more truly enriches the righteous; when hoarded, it torments the miser; when squandered, it defiles the prodigal.

Truly blessed are Christ’s poor, whose faith has so outwitted the world’s wisdom that it alone has discovered the best use of riches: namely, that riches which make one poor and miserable if loved make one rich and blessed at last if they are despised for Christ’s sake. “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25), that is, to the humble; who are surely none other than the poor in spirit whose blessedness is here proclaimed.

5. Yet, though you know this, brethren, I should like to remind you that true and blessed poverty of spirit lies more in humility of heart than in narrowness of household means; it consists more in the renunciation of pride than in contempt for property. Property is sometimes usefully possessed; pride is never retained except damnably. The devil possesses nothing in the world, nor does he desire to possess anything; yet pride alone—or above all pride—condemns him.

It therefore profits little to renounce the possessions of the world unless one also renounces its ways. Indeed, it is foolish and ridiculous to strip oneself of riches while becoming entangled in the vices of the rich; to become poor in possessions without becoming rich in virtues; to leave all things yet not follow Christ, but perhaps rather assist the cause of Antichrist in Christ’s camp [Col. 0209A]. Whoever serves pride and attacks by his conduct the holy name which he professes in word or dress indeed assists Antichrist’s cause. Christ’s standard is humility; Antichrist’s is pride—or rather, that of his head, the devil, who reigns over all the children of pride and sins by pride from the beginning.

Let us therefore glory, brethren, because we are poor for Christ; but let us take care to be humble with Christ. As nothing is more detestable than a proud poor person, so nothing is more pitiable: poverty afflicts him now, and pride rejects him forever. But the humble poor person, though he is burned and purified in the furnace of poverty, rejoices in the refreshment of a rich conscience. He consoles himself by the promise of holy hope, knowing and sensing that the kingdom of God is his—a kingdom which he already bears within himself as seed or root: namely, the first-fruits of the Spirit and the pledge of eternal inheritance.

Is it not yours, brethren, that from which, as you yourselves know, you so often pluck the sweetest fruits and blessed joys, the taste of which has already made all the world’s sweetness bitter to you? For you have tasted, if I am not mistaken, and seen that your trade is good: in exchange for a thing to be freely despised and cast away, you have acquired the highest goods. Finally, “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17). If, then, we experience these things in ourselves, why should we not confidently declare that the kingdom of God is within us? And what is within us is truly ours, because it cannot be taken away against our will [Col. 0209B].

6. The Lord therefore rightly proclaims the blessedness of the poor by saying not, “the kingdom of heaven shall be theirs,” but, “the kingdom of heaven is theirs”: not only because of their most secure right, but also because of their most certain pledge and most blessed possession. It is not merely that the kingdom has been prepared for them from the origin of the world; they have already begun to be introduced into a certain possession of it. They already have heavenly treasure in earthen vessels; they already bear God in their bodies and hearts [Col. 0209C].

How blessed the nation whose Lord is its God! How near to God’s kingdom are those who already possess and bear in their hearts the King himself, whom to serve is to reign! “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is glorious to me. The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:6, 5). Let others contend over dividing this world’s inheritance; let them struggle among themselves to see which becomes more miserable. I envy them none of the things they seek; for I and my soul shall delight in the Lord.

O glorious inheritance of the poor! O blessed possession of those who have nothing! For you not only supply us with every sufficiency, but abound unto every glory and overflow unto every joy, like a measure laid up in the bosom and running over. Truly with you are riches and glory, splendid wealth and righteousness.

1044 7. Let your soul exult, O poor; let it exult, O humble, glorying in its humility. Let it look down upon all the height of this world lying far beneath its feet, and judge it unworthy of its glory to bend its majesty any further toward desire for worthless prey. What? You are now, now to be lifted into heaven, and would you at last sink into mire? Eternal things are prepared for you, and would you choose transitory things, like a dream? The court of saints awaits you, and would you prefer the company of demons? How wretched is the man who, though he was in honor, did not understand, but was compared with senseless beasts and made like them! (Ps. 48:21). Does this not plainly happen to those whom blessed poverty had made honorable in heaven, marvelous to the world, and—lest anything be omitted—even terrible to hell, but who afterward, judging poverty, humility, and sloth to be misery through blinded understanding, wished to become rich and fell into the temptations and snares of the devil; and, although lords of all things, sold themselves without price for things that are nothing? Woe to those who have lost endurance and turned aside into crooked ways! And what will they do when the Lord begins to examine them? Let them see to what they will do.

But you, to whom poverty is dear and humility of spirit welcome, immutable Truth has made secure concerning possession of the kingdom of heaven: asserting that it is yours and faithfully keeping it stored up for you—provided that you yourselves steadfastly keep to the end this hope laid up in your bosom, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON ON THE WORDS OF THE SONG OF SONGS: “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; make me hear your voice.” (Song 8:13)

[Col. 0210C]

1. In the gathering of companions and friends—that is, the Church of the saints—the Bridegroom himself, speaking to the Bride, indicates whose voice ought to be heard when he says: “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; make me hear your voice.” I am not one to whom this can seem to have been said. I am not one who dwells in gardens; rather, I seem to myself to be among those who dwell in tombs. For what are the bodies of sinners but tombs of the dead? Therefore those devoted to their bodies do not dwell in gardens but in tombs; and they provoke God until he who brings forth captives in strength cries aloud with a mighty voice, “Lazarus, come out!” and commands his disciples concerning him: “Unbind him and let him go” (John 11:43–44).

There is indeed a great difference between tombs and gardens. The former are full of every uncleanness and of dead men’s bones; the latter, of every sweetness and grace of flowers or fruits. But what if tombs are sometimes seen in gardens? For the Lord too was buried in a garden. Yet although there are tombs in gardens, are there gardens in tombs? Perhaps so—but in the tombs of the righteous. There, certainly, a most delightful beauty of gardens will spring forth, namely in that springtime of their resurrection, when their flesh blooms anew. Not only will the bones of the righteous sprout like grass, but the whole righteous person will bud like a lily and blossom forever before the Lord.

Not so the ungodly, not so those who are buried with the burial of an ass (Jer. 22:19) and, subjected to corruption without any hope of a better resurrection, find in the present a foretaste of what is to come. I had begun to say of their tombs that, as the sight of flourishing gardens recoils from their filth, so—indeed incomparably more—does the delight of spiritual joys differ from the pleasure of carnal joys.

2. You therefore, if I am not mistaken, are those who dwell in gardens: namely, you who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night. As many books as you read, so many gardens you traverse; as many sayings as you select, so many fruits you gather. Blessed are those for whom all fruits, new and old, have been stored up: that is, the utterances both of prophets and of evangelists and apostles have been laid up, so that the Bride’s words to the Bridegroom may seem spoken to each of you: “All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Song 7:13).

Search the Scriptures, then. You rightly suppose that in them you have life, since you seek in them nothing other than Christ, to whom the Scriptures bear witness. Blessed indeed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart. “Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them” (Ps. 118:2, 129). Search is necessary not only in order that mystical meanings may be brought out, but also that moral meanings may be drawn in. Therefore you who traverse the gardens of Scripture must not fly over them carelessly and idly; rather, examining each thing, like diligent bees gather honey from flowers, gather the spirit from the words. For Jesus says: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclus. 24:27). Thus, tasting what the hidden manna is like, you will utter that Davidic saying: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103).

3. From these gardens the Bridegroom, I think, leads you into other gardens, where rest is more hidden, delight more blessed, and beauty more wonderful. Absorbed in his praises amid a voice of exultation and confession, he draws you into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God: namely, the inaccessible light where he dwells, where he feeds, where he reclines at noon. For if the devotion of those who sing psalms and pray has something of that devout inquisitiveness of those asking, “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” I think they deserve to hear, “Come and see.” “They came,” it says, “and saw, and remained with him that day” (John 1:38–39).

As long as we are with the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow from alteration, we know no night; we enjoy only blessed day. When we slip away from there, we fall back into our own night. Alas for me! How quickly my days have failed; how quickly I have withered like grass! For while I was with him in the garden, I grew green and blossomed like the paradise of God. With him is a garden of delight; without him, a place of horror and vast solitude.

For I think that whoever enters his garden himself becomes a garden; his soul becomes like a watered garden, so that the Bridegroom may say in its praise: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride” (Song 4:12). Are not those a garden in whom what the Gardener himself says to the planting which his Father planted comes about? “Hear me, you divine fruits,” he says, “and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water” (Ecclus. 39:17). “Like Lebanon, have an odor of sweetness. Blossom with flowers like the lily; give forth fragrance and put forth foliage in grace.”

4. O Lord Jesus, truly a gardener, work in us what you require of us; for without you we can do nothing. You are the true Gardener: both creator and cultivator, or guardian, of your garden. By your word you plant; by your Spirit you water; by your power you give growth. Mary, you were mistaken when you supposed him to be the gardener of that poor and little garden in which he was buried. He is the gardener of the whole world; he is the gardener of heaven; he is the gardener of the Church, which here he plants and waters until, once its growth is complete, he transplants it into the land of the living, beside the courses of living waters. There it will not fear when heat comes; its leaf will be green, nor will it ever cease bearing fruit.

Blessed are those who dwell in those gardens of yours, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you. Paul dwelt in them, whose citizenship was in heaven. Often, in mind transcending himself, he traversed the paradise of blessed delight, the gardens of God’s pleasures. Passing among the roses of martyrs and lilies of virgins, he ceased even to marvel at the height of God’s cedars, and delighted rather to pluck from the fruit of the tree of life, which is in the midst of paradise: there tasting, more fully and happily, how sweet the Lord is.

Accordingly, when he returned from there, while friends listened, he poured forth more abundantly the remembrance of that sweetness; and from the abundance of his heart his mouth overflowed. For because his soul was filled as with fatness and richness, his mouth praised with lips of exultation. “The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds grace to his lips” (Prov. 16:23). Thus his heart poured forth a good word, and from a good treasure the good man brought forth good things; and he delighted the Bridegroom himself, who listened in his friends, as with a pleasing song. Truly it was a pleasing song and a sweet melody, when such a melodious instrument of the Holy Spirit, such harmony of conduct and speech, with such sweetness of love and such grace of utterance, sounded forth to Christ Jesus the jubilation of his heart.

For if a sweet tongue did not possess the force of song, it would not have been written: “Flute and psaltery make sweet melody, and above both is a sweet tongue” (Ecclus. 40:21). If the Psalmist did not know that God is delighted by such a song, he would never say: “May my speech be pleasing to him” (Ps. 103:34). Nor would the Bridegroom himself say: “Make me hear your voice; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet” (Song 8:13; 2:14), because the praises of God are in your throat—as of one dwelling in gardens, amid the delights of paradise.

Conversely: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9), who dwells in tombs. For the one whose life provokes God does not delight him by speech, but is terribly rebuked by the divine voice: “Why do you recount my righteous acts?” (Ps. 49:16). “I will not hear the songs of your lyre” (Amos 5:25).

5. But since the Scripture which I had taken up as an excuse for speaking has supplied an occasion and material for a sermon, let us, if you please, finish what we had begun from it. Therefore the words spoken by the Bridegroom, “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; make me hear your voice,” may be understood in two ways: either as inviting a devout lover to sing psalms or pray, or as stirring a holy preacher to speak. To make this more persuasive, he mentions that friends are listening: angels, in the case of one praying or singing psalms; believers, in the case of a preacher.

In the first case we see with what discipline of heart and body we ought to sing psalms or pray in the presence of angels, lest, sent away empty, they leave us empty, though they had come to carry our vows and bring back gifts; indeed, lest those who came as friends depart as enemies. Moreover, the Bridegroom himself, who stands at the door and knocks, will depart complaining if no worthy devotion from within answers and opens to him, saying: “I gave heed and listened, but no one speaks what is good. There is no one who repents of his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’ All have turned aside to their own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle” (Jer. 8:6).

But if he exhorts a preacher, he grants him confidence to speak because of the goodwill and attentiveness of his hearers: namely, because unbelievers do not contradict or dispute, rivals do not disparage or mock, and the lukewarm do not sleep or yawn; but attentive friends listen, whose love and merit may obtain word and Spirit for the evangelist. And rightly do friends listen. For this is, as it were, proper to a friend: devoutly to hear the Bridegroom’s voice. Thus John says: “The friend of the Bridegroom is he who stands”—not wandering in mind or overcome by sleep—“hears and rejoices with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29), which he recognizes even in servants.

Let us therefore prove ourselves friends in this way: whether the Bridegroom’s voice sounds through the mouth of one speaking, reading, or singing, let us stand so as to hear, that he may give joy and gladness to our hearing; and may we not only receive the word with joy, but also bear fruit in patience.

[Note.]

To these sermons of Guerric in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XIII of the Cologne edition, five others are appended, hitherto listed among Bernard’s sermons *On Various Subjects*: namely, 8, 28, 73, 76, and 79. Horstius denies that they belong to Guerric because they are lacking in the Cologne manuscript. See what has been said of these in the preface to volume three, where the sermons *On Various Subjects* were examined, and in their own proper place.

It has further seemed good to append to these sermons of Guerric the sermon of Nicholas, monk of Clairvaux, on Blessed Mary Magdalene, previously published among Bernard’s works, which we omitted through oversight in its proper place among Nicholas’s sermons in volume five. It is one of those nineteen sermons which Nicholas dedicated to Henry, Count of Champagne, and is wholly compiled from Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs.

## SERMON OF NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE

[Col. 0213]

1. Today mercy and truth have met one another, and the multitude of the Lord’s mercies has been poured upon a sinful woman. The Son of the Virgin is touched by the hands of a sinful and menstruating woman; an undisciplined woman touches God, the Son of God. Unclean, she touches the feet of him who is clean and who cleanses; a guilty woman falls at the footsteps of the Creator. The transgressor enters into the affection of the heart and returns to her heart; and the multitude of tears condemns the magnitude of her crimes. Compassion overlooks the service of the woman touching him, and that rewarding eye of majesty, in blessed condescension, does not see the urgency of her acts of devotion.

Mary kisses Christ’s feet with frequent kisses; with overflowing eyes she bathes the Redeemer’s footsteps, wipes them with her hair, anoints and moistens them with fragrant ointments. The admirer of singular distinction sees and envies; and the Pharisee’s boast reproaches them both—him for ignorance, her for presumption. But provident deliberation suspends judgment while it welcomes service, and holds back the prepared invective until Mary’s sacrifice has passed into a whole burnt offering. The angels rejoice over the sinner doing penance, and that heavenly assembly is sprinkled with the fragrance of the odor; all the sweetness of mercy encompasses [alternative: girds about] both Savior and saved. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20), and compassion outweighing the multitude of crimes shuts them out.

How great, O Lord, is the abundance of your sweetness in the sinner’s confession! How just is the rebuke of the Pharisee’s pride and misuse! The service of the obedient woman is recounted, and indirectly the wickedness of the indignant man is touched upon, the whole literal coherence of the account assailing Simon’s envy. And because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17), her many sins are forgiven because she loves much; punishment is imposed on him who neglects much. He had not been satisfied from the Bride’s breasts, nor had he put on the affection of compassion; rereading a law which knows no mercy, he knows justice.

A harsh law, proclaimed to hard and stony people, ready to strike, knowing not how to pity. A law excluding room for repentance, denying pardon, ignorant of amendment. A law that is harsh and sour wine, pressed from most bitter grapes, consecrated to fierceness, conveyed to Israel, offered to the Savior. Wine from which the teeth of those who drink are numbed: not from the fruit of that vine which the Savior drinks new in the kingdom of his Father.

2. Truly, the Bride’s breasts are better than this wine (Song 1:1). What are they? Let the apostle Paul come forward and point out to us breasts flowing with blessed milk. “Rejoice,” he says, “with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). O how brief a saying, yet how it portrays the distinctive mark of all religion! How elegantly in one clause it sets forth compassion, establishes equity, and removes envy! With these breasts Mother Church nurses those who are making progress and nourishes the perfect.

“Rejoice with those who rejoice.” Let worldly applause depart from here; let madness and worldly gladness withdraw, for “there is no rejoicing for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 48:22). Do you suppose that the mouths of those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things are filled with joy? (Prov. 2:14). Nor have those who are carried away by flattering praises known the joy of divine exultation. Will those who are clothed in purple and fine linen and feast sumptuously each day obtain joy and gladness? Far be it that material for joys should be found in the land of those living pleasantly, when the whole face of the world changes amid such great alternations, so that one who is raised up is dashed down, and one dashed down breathes again!

But there is a joy most secure in its continual delight, which the perfected mind promises itself from a secure conscience. For the mind, purely and closely cleansed from the defilement of this world, fastening the entire affection of its desire upon the keenness of divine contemplation, joyfully rejoices in the Lord and its soul exults in God its Savior. Such a soul despises threats, knows no fear, mocks false hope, and, immune from every stumbling block, rests, sleeping in peace in the selfsame good. “Great peace have those who love your law,” says the righteous man, “and there is no stumbling block for them” (Ps. 118:165). For he knew that executioners do not persecute martyrs but crown them.

The Apostle rejoices with such as these who rejoice, and, that they may rejoice more abundantly, promises with complete assurance. This joy is certain and full; and it is more certain in proportion as it is more closely impressed upon identity. This is the breast of shared rejoicing, from which the milk of exhortation is poured, by which the perfect are nourished, so that, when they have been weaned from this milk, they may feast at the entrance into the glory of God.

3. The second is “weep with those who weep.” Does the Apostle command us to weep over loss of possessions, interruption of pleasures, deaths of children, the onset of illnesses, the burden of poverty, or oppression by the powerful? Far from it! Those who weep in such ways are themselves to be wept for. Religious sorrow mourns either another’s sin or one’s own. Blessed are those whose mourning is directed toward this end, because in it they may await consoling sweetness.

O with what gentle and most sweet spirit was his spirit imbued, he who knows how to correct one who sins in a spirit of gentleness, to suspend vengeance, and through affectionate services to draw the sinner close to his heart until he is restored to life! From this breast of compassion the milk of consolation is expressed, and with this milk the Apostle feeds those unable to eat solid food. A lover of innocence, a friend of peace, compassionate toward sufferers, and rejoicing with those who rejoice, he reaches the goal of perfection when his course is completed.

These are breasts sprinkled with milky streams, better than wine, sweeter than milk, speaking mercy and breathing compassion. “Their fragrance,” it says, “is of the finest ointments” (Song 1:2). Truly worthy breasts, from which a boundless abundance of ointments is drawn off, sprinkling the city of the living God on every side with fragrant outpouring. These are the ointments which the Queen of Sheba brought to Jerusalem, of which Scripture says: “Never again were such great quantities of spices brought as those which the Queen of Sheba gave to Solomon” (3 Kgs. 10:10).

How excellently did that subtle Spirit add “finest,” who draws to himself the whole arrangement of this book! For there is a good ointment which Mary poured upon the Savior’s feet; a better one which she—if indeed the same Mary—poured upon the head of the one reclining; and a best one, which she also prepared for Christ’s whole body.

4. The first ointment is that of contrition, flowing from remembrance of sins, from a contrite and crushed spirit. With this the feet of him who walks upon the wings of the winds are anointed; here Mary worships in the place where his feet stood. They stood, I say, because she held both feet with the most powerful hand of love until she anointed both and heard forgiveness of her crimes and her dismissal in peace: “Your sins are forgiven”; and, “Go in peace” (Luke 7:47, 50).

Great mercy indeed washes away and wipes clean great misery; and it does this swiftly, since the sinner’s tears and the Savior’s pardon are joined without any interval. Her sins are forgiven and she is dismissed in peace, so that she may neither be troubled concerning the past nor insecure concerning the future. These feet are mercy and judgment. To kiss either without the other is either rash presumption or despair to be avoided.

For who, continually considering God’s mercy, does not immediately long for the repose of a more negligent life? When he reflects that the Lord of the universe took the form of a servant for servants, worked our salvation in the midst of this earth for thirty-three years, was seized, bound, pierced with a lance, crucified, and suffered all this for the children of men, he immediately flatters and deceives himself with delusive hope. He rejoices to be kept by mercy and compassions; he knows no judgment, is ignorant of justice, and thinks that what ought to be punished need not be punished.

He is mistaken who kisses the foot of mercy in such a way as not to attend to the foot of judgment; who presumes wholly upon God’s kindness, believing that this alone is sufficient for salvation: that he believes. Again, when he withdraws his mouth and touches the foot of judgment with more frequent kisses, the substance of flesh and soul is shaken, and a stronger blast strikes the state of the whole person. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God, to offend the Creator, not to know the Lord, to kick against the command of the Ruler, who has power to cast body and soul into Gehenna. Truly, as the Apostle says, there is “a certain fearful expectation of judgment” (Heb. 10:31, 27), when fire will blaze before him, the powers of heaven will be shaken, and the most powerful fire will burn up the breadth of the world while consciences tremble.

Nothing is more terrible than to see the devil’s workshop full of blood, heaped with reproaches, overflowing with torments. Who, contemplating these things for long, would not immediately tremble and be whirled into the abyss of despair? Therefore one must not linger too long upon this foot, lest the fierceness of the Judge shut out [alternative: exclude] the sight of compassion. Let the affection of the penitent soul therefore anoint both feet: now embracing mercy, now kissing judgment, offering the whole burnt offering of a contrite spirit.

See Mary steadfastly attending to the foot of judgment: although a noble and luxurious woman, she does not attend to the faces of the dinner guests, but, her body extended, rolls herself at the feet of Majesty, full of sorrow, unable to bear fear, wounded by the dart of compunction. Yet she kisses even more fervently with her lips the foot of mercy, in whose hope she clings firmly to the Redeemer’s footsteps [alternative: to those of the one reclining], until she hears: “Your sins are forgiven.”

5. Certainly precious is the ointment by which not only the earthly house but also the heavenly one is sprinkled. Yet the ingredients from which it is made are very lowly, and a great abundance of them can be found within our little gardens. Our sins, then, planted in our consciences and too numerous to count, are its ingredients. Crushed, therefore, in the mortar of repentance by the pestle of self-mortification, sprinkled with the oil of discernment, with the fire of sorrow placed beneath and cooked in the cauldron of discipline, they produce an ointment precious and acceptable to the Savior’s feet.

We have described this briefly, leaving the discerning person entirely free to apply it to circumstances. Although its material may seem more unworthy, it is nevertheless a good ointment: it fills the house, penetrates heaven, gladdens the angels, and gives back joy and gladness to the blessed city. This is the sacrifice of righteousness, because “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19).

6. The second ointment is devotion, from remembrance of God’s benefits. Truly its composition is most worthy; compared with it, the first is an insignificant sprinkling. Its ingredients are brought from the heavenly paradise and cannot be found in the land of the children of men. Virtues bestowed by God, crushed in the mortar of the breast with the pestle of most diligent meditation, drenched with the oil of exultation, with the fire of righteousness poured in and cooked in the cauldron of humility, make an ointment marvelous both in fragrance and power. It alone can be poured upon the head of the reclining Lord and offered to the reverence of Majesty.

But we gather this too briefly, reserving abundance of words for those who know how to take much from little. Nevertheless, the distinction between the two must be noted and the superiority of the second considered: for the former is “a contrite spirit, a sacrifice to God,” while the latter is “a sacrifice of praise” which honors God. We anoint the Savior’s feet, therefore, when we are pierced with compunction for sins; we anoint his head when, for bestowed virtues, we heap thanks upon the giver of virtues.

There should, however, be a long interval between the feet and the head, because it is surely a most difficult and presumptuous leap to fly from the Lord’s footsteps to his crown. For the woman who anointed the feet did not anoint the head: that prostitute is not recorded as having done either of these latter things, according to: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. 12:7). Mary therefore anointed the holy head of the Lord: already beloved, already made familiar, and long wrapped about the footsteps of that sinful woman [alternative: freed from her contagions], whom that unhappy sevenfold affliction confounded.

7. But if the two preceding ointments are of such dignity that one pleases the feet and the other the head of the Lord, where shall we find that third, which is best and surpasses all? But far be it that the Bride of Truth should disagree with Truth and boast that she has something which she cannot have! There is, then, a third ointment: that of compassion. Above all spices it is healing for every disease and danger, and it is never found ineffective against any pestilence. For of it we read: “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that they might come and anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1).

Do you see in the opening of the chapter the indication that not one or two, but scarcely three, are sufficient to buy an ointment of such composition? Do you understand that this preparation claims for itself not the feet or the head, but the whole body of the Crucified? A precious preparation indeed, sufficient for the whole body of the Creator. Observe that he received with such worthy gentleness the ointment poured upon his feet that he convicted the murmuring Pharisee by an extended parable and rebuked him with a reversed comparison (Luke 7:39–47). Likewise, when ointment was poured upon his head, he reproved the indignant disciples, declaring the woman’s work good and restraining their swollen vehemence with measured words. But this ointment, so healing and so wonderful, he did not wish expended upon his dead body; he reserved it, surely, for his living body (Matt. 26:10–13; Mark 14:6–9).

For Christ has two bodies: one which he received from the Virgin; the other, the Church, which the kindness of the Redeemer holds more dear. Indeed, he gave the former over to death and torments for the latter: delivered to the cross, joined with criminals, condemned to a most shameful death. Can we prepare such a healing preparation? All the miseries of the wretched, both of souls and bodies, viewed with the eye of compassion, are its ingredients. These, crushed in the mortar of generosity by the pestle of tenderness, softened with the oil of charity, with the fire of compassion kindled and skimmed in the cauldron of perseverance, make an ointment wondrous even to the angels.

8. There are men rich in the virtues in the house of the Lord; let us inquire whether such ointments may be found among them. Paul first comes to me, as he is accustomed to do everywhere, wholly anointed with this present ointment. “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Blessed soul, which made itself like a lost vessel, so that it might make all men’s miseries its own and bind them together in its own conscience! He had given his whole self to Christ’s whole body, becoming all things to all in order to gain all.

And that man who was simple, upright, and fearing God—see how he walked not according to man, indeed truly as a man, and, what is truer, above man. “I was an eye to the blind,” he says, “and a foot to the lame; I was father of the poor” (Job 29:15–16), and so forth. Thus this ointment had anointed him, so that he went forth more abundantly bedewed from the bridal chamber of mercy.

I recall Samuel, who not once, but throughout all the days of his life, mourned for Saul, though he knew that Saul had been removed far from the eyes of the Divinity (1 Sam. 15:35). Yet the compassion that had entered his grieving soul did not cease, pouring forth tears—unavailing indeed, yet devout. David wept for his parricidal son with continual lamentation (2 Sam. 13:37), mourning in him not the bond of flesh but the destruction of faith.

See how Joseph was wholly smeared with this honey. His brothers come, standing now not before a brother but before a lord, conscious of betrayal, guilty of murder, promoters of fratricide. Joseph sees them and, forgetting every injury, is flooded with sweetest tears; the rich fat of compassion hidden within flows outward through his eyes. Hatred flees; he knows no anger; he reserves no time for wrath; he returns good for evil, sweetness for cruelty (Gen. 45).

I had nearly forgotten Moses: he was so drenched with the dew of this sacred liquid that he is wholly flooded and flows over with it. Israel sins, and Moses strives to reconcile the sinner to the Creator; but the Lord pretends not to hear the one praying. The Creator of all promises very much to Moses, and asks Moses—whom he made—for permission to strike. “Let me be,” he says, “that my wrath may be angry against them, and I will make you into a great nation.” Moses replies: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if you do not, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:10, 31–32). Astonishing sweetness indeed! He refuses rule over another nation, and desires to be blotted out from the book of the living unless the offense of the sinners is forgiven.

9. These are the ointments of compassion and mercy, drawn off [alternative: brought forth] from the Bride’s breasts, driving away every weakness and routing passions. Blessed Mary anointed Jesus’ feet; more blessed, the same woman anointed the head of the Author; most blessed is she who prepared the dewy ointment for Christ’s whole body.

Consider with what most vehement affection of love this blessed woman loved Christ the King. “Lord,” she says, “if you have taken him away, tell me, and I will take him away” (John 20:15). Whom do you mean by “him,” Mary? Since you have made mention of no one, to whom do you refer? Do you suppose that the memory of your beloved is so present in every heart as it is in the council-chamber of your heart? “And I,” she says, “will take him away.” A marvelous thing! Will you, a most tender woman, carry and remove a fully grown man, whose body scarcely a hundred pounds of ointments could suffice for? It is ardent and impassioned speech, flowing from pure love, promising what it cannot fulfill. For nothing seems difficult to one who loves.

Who ought to despair when so great a sinner obtains not only pardon but glory? May she herself today intercede for our sins and render our Judge, her friend, favorable to us: he who is God blessed above all forever. Amen.

[Col. 0219]

## CERTAIN EPISTLES OF THE VENERABLE GUIGO THE ELDER, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE CHARTREUSE

[Col. 0219]

### ADMONITION

Horstius transferred three letters of Guigo to the Appendix because Guigo himself had a close relationship with St. Bernard, as is especially clear from Letter 11 written to him. To these three letters we add a fourth from the first volume of our *Analecta*. It was the intention to present here as well Guigo’s *Meditations*, which appear in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and the principal Statutes of the Carthusians, written by him. But the already more-than-excessive mass of other men’s works has called us back from such a plan. On Guigo, see more at Bernard’s Letter 11.

### LETTER I. TO AIMERY, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR

He warns that there are two enemies against whom one must especially fight, and that the adversaries of the Church are to be opposed not by bodily arms but by humility and penitence.

[Col. 0219D]

To Lord and friend in Christ, the most reverend AIMERY, chancellor of the Apostolic See, the brothers of the Chartreuse, his friends—if indeed this is worthy—and his own, wish that he may despise earthly things and love heavenly things.

“How welcome your presence was to us,” etc. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLIII, col. 595.

### LETTER II. TO HUGH, PRIOR OF THE HOLY KNIGHTHOOD

He teaches in what manner spiritual warfare ought to be conducted.

[Col. 0221A]

To the lords and most beloved and reverend friends in Christ, HUGH, prior of the Holy Knighthood, and all who are governed by his counsel: the servant and friends, the brothers of the Chartreuse, wish complete victory over the spiritual and bodily enemies of the Christian religion, and peace through Christ our Lord.

“Since, on returning,” etc. See the place cited above, col. 598.

### LETTER III. TO POPE INNOCENT II

He consoles the supreme pontiff amid the troubles of the schism.

To the lord and most beloved and reverend father INNOCENT, supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See: the poor brothers of the Chartreuse, his servants and sons, wish that peace which the world cannot give, and devoted service to his fatherhood, together with obedience, though it be unnecessary.

“Many prayers to the sacred ears of your apostolate,” etc. See under Innocent II, in the year 1143.

### LETTER IV. TO THE BROTHERS OF DURBON

On spurious letters attributed to Blessed Jerome.

To the beloved friends and brothers in Christ, LAZARUS, prior of Durbon, and the others serving God in the same wilderness: GUIGO, called prior of the Chartreuse, wishes eternal salvation from the Lord.

“Among other matters concerning Catholic men,” etc. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLIII, col. 593.

## [LIFE AND DEEDS OF ST. BERNARD]

[Col. 0221]

## ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING BOOKS ON THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF ST BERNARD, Concerning His Distinguished Lineage

**1057–1058**

### I.

Scarcely any saint has had so many heralds of his deeds, or writers so distinguished and of such proven reliability, as blessed Bernard. Three most eminent authors, in an unbroken narrative, have pursued his life and illustrious actions, as though by mutual agreement: namely William, formerly abbot of Saint-Theoderic near Rheims, but then a monk of Signy; Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the district of Chartres; and Geoffrey, Bernard’s own secretary—all, as it were, eyewitnesses of the events.

Others followed them: Alan, bishop of Auxerre; and, to pass over later writers, John the Hermit and many more recent authors. Among these Philotheus—a true or fictitious name—monk of Clairvaux, celebrated Bernard’s deeds in verse.

### II.

William, formerly abbot of Saint-Theoderic, but by then a monk of the monastery of Signy in the district of Regiteste in the diocese of Rheims, expressly declares in his Preface that the first book of the Life of St Bernard was written while Bernard himself was still alive, though without his knowledge. William had withdrawn there out of a desire for solitude and quiet, as Burchard, abbot of Balerne, testifies in his subscription to that first book.

The time of William’s retirement to Signy is understood from a paper book of Saint-Theoderic, in which Helinus, the abbot who succeeded him at Saint-Theoderic, is first named in 1135. The year in which William began this work is uncertain. Certainly it was after the transfer of Clairvaux monastery to a more spacious site and the construction of new buildings, as appears from sections 34 and 62; likewise after the disturbances of Church schisms had been quieted and heresies refuted, as appears from section 40; hence after 1140, and perhaps after 1145. William died before Bernard. More concerning him may be found in volume V, in the Admonition prefixed to the Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu, and in the fuller notes on Letter 85.

### III.

After Bernard’s death, Ernald, or Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, continued in a second book the Life begun by William. This was not the Bonneval in the diocese of Besançon, nor another of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Rodez, but the one in the district of Chartres belonging to the Black Monks. Bernard’s final Letter, no. 310, was addressed to this Arnold, whatever others may think to the contrary. See the fuller notes on Letter 310.

Ernald undertook this book at the request of the monks of Clairvaux, who, out of modesty, transferred this task to him, as the author himself testifies in the Preface to Book II. He died leaving the work incomplete.

### IV.

Geoffrey added three books to the preceding two. Without doubt he is Bernard’s own secretary. He must be distinguished from Geoffrey of Péronne, mentioned in Book IV, section 16; likewise from Godfrey, Bernard’s kinsman and companion in conversion, afterward prior of Clairvaux and finally bishop of Langres, who at last returned to the private life of the monks of Clairvaux and died there on 8 November 1164.

In the Preface to the following three books, Geoffrey writes in mourning that Bernard had been torn from him by a bitter death about thirteen years after Geoffrey’s own conversion. Geoffrey’s conversion must therefore be assigned to the year 1140. A native of Auxerre, he had been a disciple of Peter Abelard before his conversion, and indeed a cleric, as is clear from section 13 of the *Book of Declamations*, of which he too was the author: “Finally, we too were in the clergy.”

After his conversion he was, together with Nicholas of Clairvaux, Bernard’s secretary and companion on his journeys. After Bernard’s death he was first abbot of Igny, then, after Fastred, abbot of Clairvaux in 1162. He governed that place for about four years, according to the Chronicle of Clairvaux in Chifflet. Later, harassed by his own brethren, he resigned the abbacy in 1165 and withdrew to Fossanova in Italy. There he too was later abbot, and finally at Hautecombe, as is related more fully in the same Chronicle.

The Chronicle also enumerates some of his works: an outstanding work on the *Song of Songs*, a Life of St Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise, and several other books and sermons. Baronius preserves his letter to Henry, cardinal and bishop of Albano, vicar or legate of the lord pope, written concerning a new controversy which Geoffrey discovered upon his return to France: namely, “whether the substance of water, mixed with wine and offered in the chalice, is likewise converted with that wine into the blood of the Lord” [Col. 0223].

Also his is the treatise against the propositions of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers. We shall place this treatise, together with his other shorter works, after the books on Bernard’s Life. Finally, he also wrote against Abelard, as we shall shortly say, and composed a sermon on St Bernard, to be printed below together with his brief commentary on the Lord’s Prayer. Whether, besides the three books already mentioned, he composed the Life of Bernard whose fragments we shall print third, and the second part of the sixth book on Bernard’s miracles, must now be considered.

### V.

To the five books on Bernard’s Life just mentioned we append two books on his Miracles: one written by various authors; the other collected from the Cistercian *Great Exordium*, and from fragments of Herbert, formerly monk of Clairvaux and archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, who composed three books on the miracles of his Cistercians, published by Chifflet.

The earlier book of Miracles is divided into three parts. The first was written by Philip, monk of Clairvaux, to Samson, archbishop of Rheims; the second by other monks of Clairvaux, upon whom Philip himself imposed this task. One of them is Geoffrey, also the writer of the third part, in a letter to Herman, bishop of Constance, concerning the miracles which he had seen Bernard perform from Speyer as far as Liège.

There follows another letter by Geoffrey the monk on the same subject, addressed “to his dearest master Archenfred and to both chapters, his brothers by the same mother.” I do not doubt that this Geoffrey is the same man who wrote the latter three books of the Life. Nor do I agree with Charles de Visch, who attributes those books to Geoffrey the secretary, but that part of the book on Miracles to Geoffrey of Auxerre. That Geoffrey of Auxerre is in no way to be distinguished from Geoffrey the secretary is proved by Helinand, a monk, in these words from his Chronicle:

> “Geoffrey of Auxerre, who for a long time was secretary to St Bernard, had once been a disciple of this Peter, that is, Abelard. Among other things, he said concerning the same Peter: ‘I recall that he was once my master; he emptied the price of our redemption and in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion commended nothing other than an example of virtue and an incentive to love, etc. Blessed be God, who gave both me and you a better master’”—Bernard—“‘through whom he rebuked the ignorance and refuted the presumption of the former. According to him, Christ displayed to us three particular things in his Passion: an example of virtue, an incentive to love, and the sacrifice of redemption.’”  
> (*Among Bernard’s works, vol. II, Short Work XI, section 25.*)

“These things and many others,” adds Helinand, “the said Geoffrey wrote boldly and orthodoxly against Peter, his master.”

Nicholas of Clairvaux wrote Letter 42 to Geoffrey on behalf of the bishop of Alet. Let this suffice concerning Geoffrey and the other writers of the earlier Life and Miracles. The other writers must be discussed after the miracles themselves.

### VI.

It should not be omitted here that Pierre-François Chifflet, a learned priest of the Society of Jesus, published at Dijon in 1660 a *Dissertation on the Distinguished Lineage of St Bernard*, in order to show that the clause in the Roman Breviary stating that St Bernard was born in an honourable station falls beneath his dignity, since it is established that he was of very noble birth on both sides. He added to the dissertation an appendix containing proofs and various documents. It is useful to reduce these matters to a few points.

### VII.

Tecelinus, Bernard’s father, is described by Abbot William, chapter 1, as “a man of ancient and lawful knighthood,” that is, of proven nobility—the rank which we call equestrian. His surname was Sorus, that is, “Reddish,” from the colour of his hair, in a charter of Hugh, second duke of Burgundy, for the monastery of Saint-Marcel at Chalon. In that charter Tecelinus subscribes first, after Rainerius the duke’s seneschal, before Bernard of Montfort, Warnerius of Sombernon, and other most noble men.

“Guy of Aucy-le-Mont,” according to Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, “was on his mother’s side brother of Tesselinus Sorus of Fontaines, who was the father of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; and on another side he was brother of Ulric, under whom the abbey of Morimond was founded.” Guy’s nobility is demonstrated from his connection with Hescelina, lady of Moulins, daughter of Holdoin; and this Holdoin “had as brother Geoffrey, lord of Jona-Villa.” These matters concern the paternal line.

### VIII.

As for the maternal line, Bernard’s mother Aleth, or Alaysia—whom one author of the third Life calls Elizabeth, perhaps through a copyist’s error—was “the daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, a powerful and eminent man according to worldly rank, and deriving her origin, as many assert, from the ancient nobility of the dukes of Burgundy,” as we learn from John the Hermit, author of the fourth Life.

In the necrology of the Dijon monastery of Saint-Bénigne, where she was first buried, she is simply called a laywoman, and her memory is recorded thus: “On the Kalends of September died Alaysa, laywoman.” By this name even eminent persons are distinguished in that necrology from nuns. On this day falls the feast of St Ambrose, or Ambrosinianus, Confessor, customarily celebrated at Fontaines, according to John the Hermit. Some wrongly confuse him here with St Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Rainard, lord of Montbard, Bernard’s maternal uncle, was Alaysia’s full brother. Since Bernard’s lineage was so distinguished on both sides, it is not surprising that William, in chapter 3, calls his eldest brother Guy “a great man,” and Guy’s wife “a noble young woman”; or that his sister Humbeline is called “a noble young lady,” who proceeded “with a proud retinue and display,” in chapter 6.

These details are from Chifflet. Add that William, section 10, calls Galdric, Bernard’s uncle, “powerful in the world, renowned in the glory of secular knighthood, lord of a castle in the territory of Autun called Tuillium.” Josbert of La Ferté, situated on the Aube, was “a noble man and Bernard’s kinsman according to the flesh,” according to the same William, section 43. Finally, Rainerius the knight was brother of Godfrey, formerly prior of Clairvaux and bishop of Langres, who was related to Bernard by blood.

Chifflet further proves that the paternal line of St Bernard, known by the name of Fontaines, was propagated down to his own time through Bartholomew of Sombernon—a family into which the royal blood of the ancient dukes of Burgundy passed through marriage to an heiress daughter. We intentionally pass over the remaining things concerning Bernard’s distinguished lineage in Chifflet, whether less certain or less necessary. We add only this: the arms of Clairvaux monastery—a black shield bearing a gold or silver bend checkered by a double red line—are not derived, as some maintain, from the family arms of St Bernard, but from the family of the counts of Champagne, from whom Hugh founded Clairvaux. The six diagonal bands of gold and azure, upon a purple border, which are the emblem of the Cistercian Order, are taken from the family of the dukes of Burgundy, through whose benefits and authority the Cistercian Order was chiefly founded.

Finally, we note here that the material which you will find enclosed in brackets in what follows was added by Horstius from the Campen manuscript, or by ourselves.

# THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF ST BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, COMPRISED IN SEVEN BOOKS

[Col. 0225]

## BOOK I. BY WILLIAM, FORMERLY ABBOT OF SAINT-THEODERIC NEAR RHEIMS, THEN A MONK OF SIGNY

**1061–1062**

### PREFACE

[Col. 0225A]

As I am about to write the life of your servant for the honour of your name, O Lord God of that servant, according to what you shall grant—he through whom you willed the Church of our time to flourish anew in the ancient splendour of apostolic grace and power—I invoke as my helper that love of yours which has long been my inspirer.

For who, having even the smallest breath of life from your love, and seeing so bright and faithful a testimony of your glory and honour shine forth in a manner unfamiliar to the world, would not make whatever effort he could, lest any of yours remain unaware of the light kindled by you? Rather, so far as may be done in human writing—although you yourself do this better through the power of his works—he would have it made known and exalted, to shine before all who are in your house.

Although I had long wished [Col. 0225B] to perform some service of this kind in my turn, I have until now been prevented either by fear or by modesty. At one time I judged the dignity of the subject to be beyond me and to be reserved for worthier craftsmen; at another, I thought that after his death, when I would, as it were, survive him, this could more suitably and appropriately be done, since the man would no longer be burdened by his own praises, and the work could be carried out more safely, free from human disturbance and contradiction of tongues.

But while he remains vigorous and strong, the weaker he becomes in body, the stronger and more powerful he becomes, never ceasing to do things worthy of remembrance and always heaping great deeds upon greater. Though he himself is silent, these deeds demand a writer. Yet I am already being worn away by the pressing infirmities of this mortal body, and as all my limbs begin to show the signs [Col. 0225C] of approaching death, I feel that the time of my dissolution is at hand. I greatly fear that I may repent too late of having delayed so long what I would by every means wish to have completed before I pass away.

Moreover, the devout goodwill of certain brethren urges and encourages me strongly to this task. Since they continually attend the Man of God, they know all his affairs. They bring forward some things traced by careful inquiry, and many more at whose occurrence they themselves were present, [Col. 0226A] and saw and heard. Although they relate many splendid things which God works through his servant in their presence, their known religious character and their school of discipline free me from every suspicion of falsehood. Furthermore, they call to witness the authority of trustworthy persons—bishops, clerics, and monks—to whom no believer may refuse faith.

Indeed, I have said this needlessly, since the whole world knows these things and every Church of the saints recounts his mighty works. Therefore, seeing this marvellous material for divine praise presenting itself to all, while no one undertook it because those who could do it better and more worthily neglected it, I have undertaken to do what I can—not in the vanity of presumption, but in the confidence of love.

[Measuring [Col. 0226B] myself by myself and comparing myself with myself, I have by no means undertaken to arrange the whole life of the Man of God, but only part of it: namely, certain manifestations of Christ living and speaking in him, and certain works of his outward intercourse with people, which were seen in him by those to whom this was granted, and which we too have in part seen, heard, and handled with our hands.

For a considerable measure of that which is said of him who declares, “Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20), and elsewhere, “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3), must be understood of Bernard himself. I do not propose to narrate that invisible life of Christ living and speaking in him, but certain outward manifestations of his life, shining forth to the outward senses of humankind, through the works of the outward person, from the purity of inward holiness and the invisible conscience. These things, as all may know them, so any may in some fashion write them down.]

Especially since I have undertaken not even to arrange these matters with particular care, but at least to gather and preserve them in one place; nor are they to be published while he himself lives, just as they are not written with his knowledge. Yet I trust in the Lord that [lacuna] [Col. 0227A] will accomplish better and more worthily what we have attempted; [lacuna] will also be able to compare outward things with inward, to continue in writing his death—precious in the sight of the Lord and like his life—and to commend death through life and life through death. Let us therefore now, with the Lord’s help, undertake the work proposed.

## CHAPTER I. On the parents of blessed Bernard and their remarkable piety in educating their children; and on Bernard’s disposition and outstanding character even in childhood

### 1.

Bernard was born in the regions of Burgundy, at the town of Fontaines, his father’s native place.

> **[Note: Col. 0227D]** Appropriately, in the third Life, Tescelinus is called “lord of the lesser castle named Fontaines, which overlooks that very famous castle of Dijon and is situated on a high rock,” commonly Fontaines; there, it is believed, Bernard’s paternal house was converted into a community of Feuillant Fathers.

His parents were eminent in worldly rank, but worthier and nobler in the piety of Christian religion. His father Tecelinus [otherwise Tesselinus] was a man of ancient and lawful knighthood [Col. 0227B], a worshipper of God, steadfast in justice. For, practising the evangelical service of arms according to the precepts of the Lord’s Forerunner, he “extorted from no one, falsely accused no one, and was content with his wages” (Luke 3:14), by which he abounded for every good work. Thus he served his temporal lords with counsel and arms, **1063** while not neglecting to render to the Lord his God what he owed him.

His mother Aleth, from the castle called Montbard—

> **[Note: Col. 0227D]** Montbard.

—likewise observed the apostolic rule in her own estate. Subject to her husband, she governed her household under him in the fear of God (Eph. 5:22), devoted herself to works of mercy, and raised her children in every discipline. She bore seven children, not so much for her husband as for God: six boys and one girl. All the boys were to become monks [Col. 0227C], the girl a nun. For, as has been said, she bore children for God, not for the world; and as soon as each had been brought forth, she herself offered that child to the Lord with her own hands.

For this reason the noble woman also refused to entrust them to the breasts of strangers, as though she infused into them with their mother’s milk a certain nature of maternal goodness. When they had grown, so long as they remained under her care, she raised them more for the wilderness than for the court. She would not allow them to grow accustomed to delicate foods, but fed them coarse and ordinary fare; and thus, by God’s inspiration, prepared and trained them as though they were immediately to be sent into the wilderness.

### 2.

When she carried Bernard, the third in the order of her children, in her womb, she saw a dream foretelling [Col. 0227D] future events: namely, that she had in her womb a little dog wholly white, reddish on its back, and barking.

> **[Note: Col. 0228D]** This may be connected with Bernard’s statement in Letter 78, section 7: “When we saw evils, we barked loudly against them.” Compare Letter 230: “I point out the wolf; I stir up the dogs”; and Geoffrey’s sermon on St Bernard below, section 17.

Greatly alarmed by this, she consulted a certain religious man. At once he received the spirit of prophecy, by which David says to the Lord concerning holy preachers, “The tongue of your dogs [comes] from the enemies” (Ps. 76:24). He answered the trembling and anxious woman: “Do not be afraid; the matter is proceeding well. You shall be mother of an excellent little dog, who will be the guardian of God’s house [Col. 0228A] and will utter great barks on its behalf against the enemies of the faith. He will be an outstanding preacher, and, like a good dog, through the grace of his healing tongue will cure in many people many diseases of the soul.”

By this response, which the devout and faithful woman received as from God, she was made joyful and from that very time poured herself wholly into love for the child not yet born. She resolved to have him instructed in sacred letters, in accordance with the vision and its interpretation, by which such sublime things were promised concerning him. And so it came to pass. For as soon as she bore him in a fortunate delivery, she not only offered him to God, as she was accustomed to do with the others, but, as is read of St Anne, mother of Samuel, who dedicated in God’s tabernacle the son sought from and received from the Lord to serve there continually (1 Sam. 1), so she too offered him in [Col. 0228B] the Church of God as an acceptable gift.

### 3.

Therefore, as soon as she could, she entrusted him for instruction to the teachers of letters in the church of Châtillon—

> **[Note: Col. 0228D]** Châtillon-sur—

—which is known later to have been raised by Bernard’s own labour from secular life to the Order of Regular Canons. She did all she could that he might advance in learning.

The boy, full alike of grace and of native talent, soon fulfilled his mother’s desire in this. In literary study he advanced beyond his age and ahead of his contemporaries. Yet in worldly matters he was already, as if by nature, beginning the self-mortification of his future perfection. He was exceedingly simple in secular affairs, loved to dwell within himself, shunned public life, was remarkably contemplative, obedient and submissive to his parents, kind and agreeable to everyone, [Col. 0228C] simple and quiet at home, seldom abroad, and more modest than could be believed. He loved nowhere to speak much; he was devoted to God, in order to preserve his childhood in purity; and he was devoted also to the study of letters, through which he might learn and know God in the Scriptures. How much he advanced within a short time in this, and what discerning judgment he acquired, may be observed from what follows.

## CHAPTER II. On the integrity of Bernard as a boy, in detesting the attentions of a sorcerous woman; on the vision granted him of the newborn Saviour; and on his mother’s death

### 4.

While he was still a little boy, troubled by a severe headache, he took to his bed. A woman was brought to him, supposedly to relieve the pain by charms. [Col. 0228D] But when he, **1064**, sensed her approaching with the instruments of incantation by which she was accustomed to deceive common people, he cried out with great indignation and drove her away from himself.

Nor did divine mercy fail the good zeal of the holy boy. Immediately he felt power, and rising in the very impetus of the Spirit, he recognized that he had been freed from all pain. Because of this he made no small progress in faith, and the Lord deigned to appear to him [Col. 0229A], as once to the boy Samuel at Shiloh, and to reveal his glory to him (1 Sam. 3).

For the solemn night of the Lord’s Nativity was at hand, and all were preparing, as was customary, for the solemn vigils. When the hour for celebrating the night office was delayed a little, Bernard, sitting and waiting with the others, happened to doze briefly with his head bowed. Immediately the holy Nativity of the child Jesus appeared to the boy, revealing itself to its own child, bringing increase to his tender faith, and beginning in him the contemplation of divine mysteries.

For he appeared as though the bridegroom were again coming forth from his chamber. He appeared to Bernard as though the infant Word were again being born before his eyes from the womb of the Virgin Mother: beautiful in form beyond the children of men, drawing into himself the affections of the holy little boy, affections now by no means childish. Bernard became persuaded in his heart, and confesses it even now, that he believes this was the hour of the Lord’s Nativity.
