Those who have frequented his teaching may readily recognize how greatly the Lord blessed him in that hour, since even to this day, in matters concerning that mystery, he seems to possess a deeper understanding and richer speech. Hence later, in praise of the Mother and the Son and of his holy Nativity, he produced an outstanding little work, among the beginnings of his writings or treatises, taking its subject from the Gospel passage which reads: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee” (Luke 1:20), and the rest which follows there.

### 5.

Nor should it be left unmentioned that, even from his earliest childhood [Col. 0229C], whenever he could obtain any coins, he gave alms secretly. In this he both followed the habit of his modesty and pursued works of piety appropriate to his age—indeed, beyond his age.

After some time had passed, as the boy Bernard grew in years and in grace with God and men, passing from childhood into adolescence, his mother, having faithfully raised her children and seeing them enter upon the ways of the world, as though all that had belonged to her task had been accomplished, happily departed to the Lord.

It must certainly be noted of her that, though she had long lived honourably and justly with her husband according to the standards and honourable customs of this world, and according to the law and fidelity of marriage, for several years before her death she surpassed all others in that manner of life for which she seemed to have raised her children. So far as she could and was permitted—as a woman under her husband’s authority and without power over her own body—she herself went before them all.

For in her own household, in her married state, and in the midst of the world, she appeared for no small period to emulate an eremitical or monastic life: by sparingness in food, by plainness of dress, by renouncing worldly pleasures and display, by withdrawing as far as possible from worldly actions and concerns, and by devoting herself to fasts, vigils, and prayers. What she lacked of an assumed religious profession she redeemed by almsgiving and diverse works [Col. 0230A] of mercy. Advancing in this from day to day, she reached her end, to be perfected in the future life in that wherein she had progressed when she departed from this world.

She fell asleep while the clerics who had assembled were chanting psalms, and she herself chanted with them. Even at the end, when her voice could no longer be heard, her lips could still be seen moving and her tongue trembling in confession of the Lord. Finally, amid the prayers of the litany, when it was said, “By your passion and cross, deliver her, O Lord,” she raised her hand, signed herself, and gave up her spirit—

> **[Note: Col. 0229D]** Herbert, in Book II, chapter 23, relates that Bernard, as a novice, was accustomed to recite daily the seven penitential psalms for his mother’s soul. Having once omitted some of them, he was rebuked by Abbot Stephen [Col. 0230D]. His mother died on the Kalends of September [1 September]. Her body was buried in the church of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon and later transferred to Clairvaux.

—so that she could not lower the hand which she had raised.

**1065**

## CHAPTER III. On Bernard’s zeal in safeguarding chastity; his purpose of religious life; and the brothers and other companions whom he drew to the same resolve

[Col. 0230B]

### 6.

From this time Bernard began, according to his own custom and by his own right, to live independently. He excelled in an elegant body and pleasing appearance, was adorned with most gracious manners, endowed with a keen mind, and powerful in an attractive eloquence. He was spoken of as a youth of great promise.

As he was entering the world, many of the world’s paths began to offer themselves to him; in all of them the prosperities of this life rose up before him, and great hopes smiled on him from every side. But the unlike manners of his companions and stormy friendships besieged the kindly heart of the young man, striving to make him like themselves. Had these continued to become sweet to him, the love of chastity—the sweetest thing lodged in his heart in this life—would necessarily have become bitter to him.

The twisting serpent, especially envying this love, spread snares of temptation and by diverse encounters lay in wait for his heel. For once, when he had somewhat too curiously looked at a certain woman and kept his eyes fixed upon her for some time, he immediately came to himself. Ashamed of himself before himself, he blazed up as a most severe avenger against himself. Plunging neck-deep into a nearby pool of icy water, he remained there until he was nearly bloodless; through the power of cooperating grace he became wholly cooled even from the heat of carnal desire, putting on that disposition of chastity which he had put on who said: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, so that I should not even think upon a virgin” (Job 31:1).

### 7.

About the same time, at the prompting of the devil, a naked girl was put into the bed where he slept [Col. 0230D]. When he felt her, he quietly and silently yielded to her the part of the bed which he occupied, turned himself to the other side, and slept.

That miserable woman lay there for a while, waiting and expecting; then she touched and provoked him. At last, when he remained motionless, she, though utterly shameless, was ashamed; overcome by great horror and amazement, she rose, left him, and fled.

It also happened that Bernard was lodging with several companions at the house of a certain married woman. Seeing that the young man was handsome in appearance [Col. 0231A], she was caught in the snare of her own eyes and burned with desire for him. As he seemed the most distinguished of them all, she had a bed prepared for him apart. Rising in the night, she shamelessly approached him.

Bernard, sensing her and not lacking resourcefulness, began to cry, “Thieves! Thieves!” At the cry the woman fled; the whole household arose; a lamp was lit; the thief was sought, but could not be found. Each returned to bed; silence fell, darkness returned as before, and the others rested. But the wretched woman did not rest. She rose again and sought Bernard’s bed; but again he cried out: “Thieves! Thieves!” The thief was sought again, hid again, and was not exposed by the one person who alone knew.

Repulsed thus for a third time, the brazen woman at last ceased, overcome either by fear or by despair. When they travelled on the next day, his companions questioned Bernard, reproaching him and asking what thieves he had dreamed of so often that night. He replied: “A thief was truly there, and our hostess was trying to take from me what is more precious to me than anything in this life—namely chastity, an incomparable treasure.”

### 8.

Meanwhile Bernard reflected and considered the common saying that it is not safe to live long with a serpent, and he began to contemplate flight. He saw the world and its prince outwardly offering him many things: great enterprises and even greater hopes, but all deceptive—vanities of vanities, and all things vanity. But inwardly he continually heard Truth itself crying out and saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

Resolving to leave the world more perfectly, he began to seek and investigate where he might more surely and purely find rest for his soul under Christ’s yoke. As he sought, the new plantation of renewed monastic observance at Cîteaux presented itself: a plentiful harvest but in need of labourers, **1066**, since scarcely anyone yet turned there for the sake of conversion because of the excessive austerity of its life and poverty.

Yet these things did not frighten a mind truly seeking God. Setting aside all hesitation and fear, he directed his purpose there, judging that he could wholly hide himself there and be concealed in the secret [Col. 0231D] of God’s face from every human disturbance, and especially escape vanity—whether arising from secular noble birth, the gift of a sharper intellect, or perhaps even some reputation for holiness.

### 9.

But when his brothers and those who loved him carnally perceived that he was considering conversion, they began by every means to act so as to turn his mind toward the pursuit of learning and, by love of secular knowledge, to bind him more tightly to the world. By this suggestion, as he was accustomed to confess, his steps had almost been delayed. But the memory of his holy mother pressed insistently upon his mind, so that he often seemed to see her standing before him, complaining and reproaching him because she had not so tenderly raised him for such trifling pursuits, nor educated him in this hope.

At last, as he was once travelling to his brothers, who were with the duke of Burgundy at the siege of the castle called Grancey—

> **[Note: Col. 0231D]** Grancey.

—he began to be more deeply troubled by this thought. Finding a church midway on his journey, he turned aside. Entering it, he prayed amid a great outpouring of tears, stretching his hands toward heaven and pouring out his heart like water before the presence of the Lord his God. On that day, therefore, the purpose of his heart was made firm.

10. Nor did he receive with a deaf ear the voice that says: “Let him who hears say, Come” (Rev. 22:17). For from that hour, like a fire that burns a forest, and like a flame consuming mountains—first seizing here and there the nearer things [Col. 0232B], then advancing into more distant regions—so the fire which the Lord had sent into the heart of His servant, desiring that it should burn, first assailed his brothers, leaving only the youngest, as yet less fit for conversion, with their aged father as a consolation; then his kinsmen, companions, and friends, whomever there was hope of converting.

First of all, his maternal uncle Galdric, without delay or hesitation, as they say, went over feet-first to his nephew’s judgment and accepted conversion. He was a worthy and powerful man in the world, renowned for the glory of secular knighthood, lord of a castle in the territory of Autun called Tuillium. [Note: [Col. 0232D] Touillon.] Immediately Bartholomew also came forward—the youngest of the brothers and not yet a knight—and without difficulty, that very hour gave his assent to the saving counsels [Col. 0232C].

Andrew, though himself younger than Bernard and newly made a knight at that time, admitted his brother’s word more reluctantly, until he suddenly cried out: “I see my mother!” For she visibly appeared to him, smiling with serene countenance and rejoicing over the purpose of her sons. Accordingly, he too immediately gave his hand, and from a recruit of the world became a soldier of Christ. Nor was Andrew alone in seeing the mother of so many sons rejoicing: Bernard too confessed that he had likewise seen her.

Guy, the firstborn of the brothers, was already bound by marriage, a great man and by now more deeply rooted than the others in the world. At first he hesitated a little; but immediately reflecting and reconsidering the matter, he consented to conversion, [Col. 0232D] provided only that his wife should agree. Yet this seemed nearly impossible in the case of a noble young woman nursing little daughters. But Bernard, conceiving a more certain hope in the Lord’s mercy, unhesitatingly promised him that the woman would either consent or swiftly die.

At last, when she refused in every way, her husband, high-spirited—or rather, already anticipated by that strength of faith in which he afterward shone outstandingly—conceived, by the Lord’s inspiration, a manly resolution: he would cast aside whatever he seemed to possess in the world and undertake a rustic life, namely, laboring with his own hands in order to support himself and his wife, whom he was not permitted to leave against her will. Meanwhile [Col. 0233A] Bernard arrived, running about everywhere gathering one person after another.

Without delay, the aforesaid wife of Guy was struck by a severe illness. Recognizing that it was hard for her to kick against the goad, she summoned Bernard, begged his pardon, and was herself the first to seek consent to conversion. Finally, separated from her husband according to ecclesiastical custom, by their joint vow of chastity she entered a community of religious women, serving God devoutly there to this day. [Note: [Col. 0233D] Indeed, at Elariacum or Lariacum, commonly Lairé, by the walls of Dijon, according to the Third Life and the records of Lairé. The place is now a priory of the monastery of Saint-Bénigne, to which these religious women were then subject, just as those of Julleium were subject to Molesme. King Guntram granted the place to Saint Bénigne.]

11. Gerard, second in age after Guy, was a vigorous knight in arms, of great prudence and exceptional kindness, beloved by all. When the others, as was said, gave their consent at first hearing and on the first day, he—regarding this, in the manner of worldly wisdom, as fickleness [Col. 0233B]—with stubborn determination rejected the wholesome counsel and his brother’s exhortations.

Then Bernard, now aflame with faith and stirred to a remarkable degree by zeal for brotherly love, said: “I know, I know: affliction alone will give understanding to your hearing.” Placing his finger upon Gerard’s side, he said: “The day will come—and soon—when a lance thrust into this side will make a passage to your heart for the counsel of your salvation which you despise. You will indeed be afraid, but you will by no means die.”

So it was said, and so it happened. After only a very few days, surrounded by enemies, captured, and wounded according to his brother’s word, he was dragged away with a lance lodged in his very side, fixed in the same spot to which Bernard had applied his finger. Fearing death as though already present [Col. 0233C], he cried: “I am a monk, a Cistercian monk!” Nevertheless, he was captured and confined in custody.

Bernard was summoned by a swift messenger, but did not come. “I knew,” he said, “and foretold that it was hard for him to kick against the goad. Yet this wound is not for his death, but for life.” And so it proved. He quickly recovered from the wound beyond hope; but he did not alter the purpose or vow he had made. And although, now free from love of the world, he was still held in the bonds of enemies, and this alone delayed the fulfillment of his purpose of conversion, God’s mercy swiftly came to his aid in this also.

His brother came and labored to procure his release, but did not succeed. Since he was not even permitted to speak with him, Bernard approached the prison [Col. 0233D] and cried: “Know, Brother Gerard, that we shall soon depart and enter the monastery. Since you are not allowed to leave, become a monk here, knowing that what you wish but cannot do is reckoned as done.”

12. As Gerard grew ever more distressed, after a few days he heard in a dream a voice saying to him: “Today you will be set free.” It was the holy season of Lent. Therefore, toward the evening hour, reflecting on what he had heard, he touched his fetters, and behold: on one side the iron cracked in his hand [Col. 0234A], so that he was held less tightly and could walk somewhat. But what was he to do? The door was locked, and there was a crowd of poor people before it.

Yet he rose; and, not so much in hope of escape as from weariness of lying still, or from curiosity to make the attempt, he came to the door of the underground house in which he was bound and shut up. As soon as he touched the bolt, the entire fastening fell apart in his hands, and the door of the house opened. Going out slowly, like a man in fetters, he made his way toward the church, where the evening offices were still being celebrated.

The beggars standing before the door of the house, seeing what was happening and struck with divine terror, turned to flight without uttering a cry. When he was already nearing the church, a member of the household of his captivity came out—the brother of the man by whom he was guarded [Col. 0234B]—and, seeing Gerard hurrying to the church, said: “Gerard, you have come late.”

As Gerard was alarmed, he said: “Hurry; there is still something left for you to hear.” For Gerard’s eyes were held, and he did not at all understand what was taking place. At last, when this man had taken Gerard by the hand and helped him, still fettered, up the higher steps of the church, Gerard entered the church and then first recognized what was happening. Though the man attempted to hold him back, he could not.

In this manner Gerard, freed from the captivity of the love of this world and from the captivity of the children of this world, faithfully fulfilled the vow he had made. In this matter the Lord especially made known from what perfection of holy conduct this servant of God had received grace: in the spirit of Him “who made the things that are to come,” he was able to see what would occur as though it had already happened. For a lance was visibly present in his brother’s side when he placed his finger upon the spot of the wound soon to be inflicted, as he afterward himself confessed when questioned by those from whom he could not conceal it. [Col. 0234C]

13. But when, as we have said, the rest had been gathered with Bernard in one spirit on the first day, as they entered church in the morning that apostolic passage was being read: “God is faithful, who began a good work in you; He Himself will bring it to completion unto the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 1:6). The devout young man received it no differently than if it had sounded from heaven.

Therefore, rejoicing as the now spiritual father of his brothers regenerated in Christ, and understanding that the hand of the Lord was working with him, he began henceforth to devote himself to preaching and to gather whomever he could. He began to put on the new man; and with those with whom he had been accustomed to discuss secular learning or the world itself, he discussed serious matters and conversion. He showed that the world’s joys are fleeting, life’s miseries many, death swift, and the life after death everlasting—whether in good things or in evil.

What more need be said? All who had been foreordained to this, through God’s grace at work in them, through the word of His power, and through the prayer and persistence of His servant—at first hesitating, then pierced to the heart—one after another believed [Col. 0235A] and consented. Among them Lord Hugh of Mâcon also joined him, eminent in nobility and moral worth, and endowed with worldly lands and riches. Today, deservedly on account of his religious life and holiness, having been taken from the abbey of Pontigny, which he himself built, he presides over the Church of Auxerre with the rank and honor of bishop. [Note: [Col. 0235] Hugh III, first abbot of Pontigny, was made bishop in 1135.]

Hearing of the conversion of his dearest companion and friend, Hugh wept as for one lost, since he heard that he had died to the world. But when the two were first given an opportunity for mutual conversation, after unlike tears and groans arising from unlike sorrows, words began to be exchanged for words and realities compared with realities. As the Spirit of truth was poured into Hugh amid the words of their familiar friendship, their mutual conversation began to take on a different aspect.

Thus, having joined hands in fellowship for a new life [Col. 0235B], they became far more worthily and truly one heart and one soul in Christ than they had formerly been in the world.

14. A few days later Bernard was informed that Hugh, having been led astray by other companions, was withdrawing from his purpose. Finding an opportunity, because a great gathering of bishops was being held in those parts, Bernard hurried to recall the perishing man and to travail over him anew.

But Hugh’s aforesaid companions and corrupters, seeing Bernard, sought to retain their prey and deprived him of every opportunity to speak, blocking every avenue of approach. Yet, since he could not speak to Hugh, Bernard cried to the Lord for him. As he prayed with tears, a sudden and violent downpour of rain immediately broke out.

They had been sitting in an open field because the sky was clear [Col. 0235C] and they expected nothing of the kind. Therefore all scattered at the sudden rain and headed for the nearest village. But Bernard, holding Hugh, said: “You will endure these drops of rain with me.” When they alone remained, they were not alone: the Lord was with them, immediately restoring serenity both to the sky and to their minds. There the covenant was renewed and the purpose confirmed, which could never afterward be broken.

15. The sinner saw these things and was enraged; he gnashed his teeth and wasted away. But the righteous man, trusting in the Lord, triumphed gloriously over the world. And now, as Bernard preached publicly and privately, mothers hid their sons, wives held back their husbands, and friends turned away friends, because the Holy Spirit gave such power to his voice [Col. 0235D] that scarcely any human attachment could hold anyone back.

As the number increased of those who had agreed in this unanimity of conversion, it was as is written concerning the first children of the Church: “The multitude of them was of one heart and one soul in the Lord” (Acts 4:32); they dwelt unanimously together, “and none of the others dared to join them” (ibid. 5:12–13). At Châtillon they had a house of their own, shared by all, where they assembled, lived together, and conversed; scarcely anyone who was not of their company dared enter it.

And if anyone did enter, seeing and hearing what was done and said there, he was, as the Apostle says concerning the Christians of Corinth, in a sense convicted by all, judged by all, since all were prophesying; and, worshiping the Lord and confessing that God was truly among them (1 Cor. 14:24–25), he either attached himself to their unanimity or went away weeping for himself and calling them blessed. [Col. 0236A]

For in those times and regions it was unheard of that the conversion of a person still living in the world should be foreseen. They themselves remained in secular dress for about six months after their first resolve, in order that more might be gathered, while certain persons’ affairs were being settled in the meantime.

16. But when their number had begun to attract suspicion, lest the tempter snatch away someone from among them, God was pleased to reveal what would happen. One of them saw in a vision of the night that they all seemed to be seated in one house and, in order, each seemed to partake of a food of marvelous whiteness and flavor. While all the others received it most favorably and with great joy, he observed that two of the entire number remained without a share in that saving food.

For one of them did not take it; the other seemed indeed to take it, but, as though taking it insufficiently carefully, spilled it. Later events proved both cases true. One, before they came to the deed, turned back and returned to the world. The other began the good work with the rest but did not complete it.

I afterward saw him in the world, wandering and fleeing from the face of the Lord like Cain: so far as I could observe, a most abject man, in pitiable disgrace, yet of excessive faintheartedness. Nevertheless, in his final days, driven by bodily sickness and need, he returned to Clairvaux, when, though well-born, he was cast off by all his relatives and friends. There, renouncing property but not wholly his own will, he died—not within, as a brother and member of the household, but outside, begging mercy as a poor man and beggar. [Col. 0236B–C]

17. When the day came for paying the vow and fulfilling their desire, Bernard, father of his brothers, departed from his father’s house with his brothers, his spiritual sons, whom he had begotten to Christ through the word of life.

But Guy, the firstborn of the brothers, saw his youngest brother Nivard, a boy with other boys in the street, and said: “Come now, Brother Nivard: all the land of our inheritance looks only to you.” The boy, moved not childishly by this, replied: “So heaven is for you, and earth for me? This division has not been made fairly.” When they had spoken and departed, he remained at home with his father for the time being; but after a short interval he followed his brothers and could not be held back by either his father or relatives or friends. Their aged father and sister remained in that house consecrated to God; of them too we shall speak in their proper place. [Col. 0236D]

18. At that time the new and little Cistercian flock was living under its abbot, the venerable man Stephen. Its smallness had already begun to weigh heavily upon him, and all hope of posterity into which the inheritance of that holy poverty might be transmitted had failed: all venerated their holiness of life, but fled their austerity. Then, by this divine visitation, so joyful, unexpected, and sudden, he was gladdened that on that day he seemed to receive from the Holy Spirit this response: “Rejoice, barren woman who did not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who did not travail; for the children of the desolate are many more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1). You shall afterward see children’s children unto many generations.

[For in the preceding year, to one of those first Cistercian brothers who was already at the point of death, an innumerable multitude of people appeared near the basilica, washing their garments at a spring; and in that vision he was told that the spring was called Ennon. When he reported this to the abbot, the eminent man immediately understood the divine consolation. Then, rejoicing greatly already in the promise, and still more afterward in its fulfillment, he gave thanks to God through Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with Him and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0237D] The material enclosed in brackets has been taken from a manuscript.]] [Col. 0237A–B]

## Chapter IV. On his entry into the Order and the fervor of his novitiate; how sparing he was in food and sleep; how eager for manual labor; and on his remarkable progress in Holy Scripture

19. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1113, the fifteenth from the foundation of the house of Cîteaux [Col. 0237C], God’s servant Bernard, about twenty-three years old [variant: twenty-two], entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions and, under Abbot Stephen, submitted his neck to Christ’s sweet yoke.

From that day the Lord gave His blessing, and that vineyard of the Lord of Hosts bore its fruit, extending its branches to the sea and its shoots beyond the sea.

[Since some of his aforementioned companions had been married, and their wives too had undertaken with their husbands the same vow of sacred religious life, through Bernard’s care a monastery for religious women was built for them. It was called Julleium, [Note: [Col. 0237D] Elsewhere Juliacum, commonly Juilly. Count Milo of Bar-sur-Seine granted this place to the monastery of Molesme “that it might serve religious women under the direction of the abbot of Molesme; and four monks, appointed by the abbot of Molesme, were assigned for their governance, both of bodies and souls.” These acts took place under Abbot Guy, about the year 1115; see Bernard’s Letter 80, from a charter in Chifflet. On Julleium again below, no. 30.] in the diocese of Langres. With the Lord’s help it grew quite magnificently and remains to this day most renowned for its reputation for religious life, enlarged in persons and possessions; it has already spread to other places and has not yet ceased to yield a still more abundant fruit.] [Col. 0237D–0238D]

These, then, were the holy beginnings of the Man of God’s religious life. But the distinguishing marks of that life—how he lived an angelic life on earth—I think no one can describe who does not live by the Spirit by whom he lived. For it belongs to the Giver and recipient alone to know how greatly, from the very beginning of his conversion, the Lord anticipated him with the blessings of His sweetness [Col. 0238A]; with how great a grace of election He filled him; and how He intoxicated him from the abundance of His house.

He entered that house poor in spirit, still hidden and at that time almost nonexistent, intending there to die to human hearts and memory, hoping to remain concealed and hidden like a lost vessel. But God disposed otherwise, preparing him as a vessel of election not only to strengthen and enlarge the monastic Order, but also to bear His name before kings and nations and to the ends of the earth.

Bernard himself, however, thinking and judging nothing of this sort about himself, kept this continually in his heart and often on his lips, in order to guard his heart and preserve constancy of purpose: “Bernard, Bernard, why have you come?” And as it is written of the Lord that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), from the first day of his entrance into the novices’ cell he began to do in himself what he was to teach others. [Col. 0238B]

20. Later, when he had been appointed abbot of Clairvaux, as novices came and hastened to enter, we used to hear him preach and say: “If you hasten toward the things that are within, leave here outside the bodies which you brought from the world. Let the spirits alone enter; the flesh profits nothing.”

When the novices were alarmed at the novelty of this saying, he spared their weakness by explaining more gently that carnal desire must be left outside. But when he himself was a novice, sparing himself in nothing, he strove in every way to mortify not only the desires of the flesh, which occur through the bodily senses, but also the senses themselves through which they occur.

For when, by inward perception enlightened, he began more sweetly and more frequently to feel the sweetness of love breathing upon him from above, he feared for that inward perception from the bodily senses and allowed them scarcely more than was sufficient for companionship in outward intercourse with other people. By the persistence of continual practice this became a habit, and the habit itself was in a sense transformed into nature. Wholly absorbed in the spirit, with all his hope directed toward God, with his memory wholly occupied by spiritual intention and meditation, he saw without seeing, heard without hearing; while tasting he perceived no flavor, and scarcely felt anything through any bodily sense. [Col. 0238C–D]

He had already spent a whole year in the novices’ cell when, on leaving it, he still did not know whether the house had a vaulted ceiling—the kind we usually call a carved ceiling. For a long time he had repeatedly entered and left the church building, yet believed that at its end, where there were three windows, there was only one. His sense of curiosity being mortified, he noticed nothing of this kind; or, if he happened at times to see it, his memory, occupied elsewhere as was said, did not attend to it. For without the memory of the one perceiving, there is no perception. [Col. 0239A]

21. In him nature also did not disagree with grace, so that the words of Scripture seemed in some measure fulfilled in him: “I was an ingenious child and received a good soul; and, being rather good, I came to an undefiled body” (Wis. 8:19–20).

For the contemplation of every spiritual or divine thing, together with spiritual grace he possessed a certain natural strength of intellect. In this too he had received a good soul: a sensibility neither wantonly inquisitive nor proudly rebellious, but rejoicing in spiritual pursuits and, in matters concerning God, willingly subject and serviceable to the spirit. He had also a body never defiled by consent to any shameful act; though it was cared for less [variant: not excessively neglected] than it ought to have been [Col. 0239B], it was a most suitable instrument for serving the spirit in God’s service.

But although in him the flesh, by the gift of prevenient grace, the support of cooperating nature, and the good practice of spiritual discipline, now scarcely desired anything contrary to the spirit—that is, anything that would injure the spirit—the spirit desired against the flesh, beyond the strength and capacity of flesh and blood, so greatly that the frail creature, collapsing under the burden, has not to this day been able to rise again.

What shall I say of sleep, which ordinarily refreshes bodily labors and senses in other people, or restores the mind? From that time until today, he watches beyond human possibility. For he complains of no time more often as lost than the time in which he sleeps, considering death and sleep a sufficiently apt comparison: so that sleepers appear dead to human beings in the same way that the dead appear asleep to God.

Therefore, if he happens to hear a religious person sleeping or snoring rather loudly, or sees one lying in an unseemly position, he can scarcely bear it patiently; rather, he complains that the man is sleeping carnally or secularly. For in him scant sleep accompanies scant food. In neither does he permit his body any fullness, except that in each he considers it enough to have taken something. As regards vigils, the limit of his vigils is not to pass the whole night without sleep. [Col. 0239C]

22. Even now, his appetite is scarcely ever drawn to eating by pleasure, but by fear of weakness alone. Indeed, when about to eat, before he eats he is sated merely by the thought of food. Thus he approaches the taking of food as though approaching torture.

From the first year of his conversion, or of his leaving the novices’ cell, his constitution—always exceedingly delicate and frail—was worn down by many fasts and vigils, cold and labor, and harsh, continual exercises. His stomach having been ruined, he habitually throws up through his mouth whatever is put into it, still undigested. If any food, by natural digestion, does pass down to the lower parts, there too those parts of the body are beset by no lesser disorders of illness, and it is expelled only with severe torment.

Whatever remains is the only nourishment of his body, such as it is: not so much to sustain life as to postpone death. After eating he is always accustomed, as it were, to weigh how much he has eaten. If he ever discovers that he has exceeded his customary measure even slightly, he does not permit himself to escape unpunished. The practice of abstinence has so become natural to him that, even if he sometimes wishes to allow himself a little more than usual of any bodily refreshment, he can scarcely do so. [Col. 0239D–0240A]

Thus he was from the beginning: a novice among novices, a monk among monks, strong in spirit and weak in body. He never consented that any indulgence should be given him concerning bodily rest or refreshment, nor any exemption from common labor or work. For he regarded the others as holy and perfect, but himself as a novice and beginner, needing not the indulgences and exemptions accorded to veterans and the perfect [Col. 0240B], but rather novice fervor, the strictness of the Order, and the rigor of discipline.

23. Therefore, being a most fervent emulator of the common life and discipline, whenever the brothers performed some manual task from which he was excluded either by lack of practice or by inexperience, he made up for it by digging, cutting wood, carrying it on his own shoulders, or undertaking labors equally arduous. When strength failed, he resorted to the lowliest tasks and compensated for labor by humility.

It is remarkable that the man who had received so great a grace in contemplation of spiritual and divine realities not only allowed himself to be occupied with such things, but greatly delighted in them. Yet, with sensibility mortified as has been said—through whose curiosity or weakness, amid such bodily labors, even the minds of the most perfect must often suffer some distraction from the inward unity of the spirit, if not in intention, at least in memory and thought—he, by the privilege of greater grace, both labored outwardly in the strength of the spirit, in a sense wholly, and was wholly inwardly free for God [Col. 0240C]: in the one feeding his conscience, in the other his devotion.

Thus, during work he prayed or meditated inwardly without interrupting outward labor, and labored outwardly without loss of inward sweetness. For to this day he confesses that whatever he is able to do in the Scriptures, whatever he spiritually perceives in them, he received especially through meditation and prayer in the woods [Col. 0240D] and fields; and he often used to say among his friends, with his agreeable wit, that he never had any teachers in this matter except oaks and beeches.

24. When, at harvest time, the brothers were busily cutting grain with fervor and the joy of the Holy Spirit, he was ordered to sit and rest, being apparently incapable of and untrained in that work. Greatly saddened, he fled to prayer and begged God with many tears to grant him the grace of reaping. The simplicity of the religious man’s faith did not disappoint his desire: he immediately obtained what he had asked.

From that day he rejoiced with a certain pleasure that he was more skilled than the others in that work, and was so much more devoted to it because he remembered that he had received this capacity from God’s gift alone. When free from such labor or work, he was continually either praying, reading, or meditating.

If solitude was available for prayer, he used it; if not, wherever he was—alone or among a crowd—he made solitude of heart for himself and was alone everywhere. He read the canonical Scriptures more willingly and frequently, simply and in sequence. He said that he understood them better by no words than by their own words, and testified that whatever divine truth or power shone forth to him in them tasted more fully of its primal source than of the flowing streams of expositions.

Nevertheless, reading their holy and orthodox interpreters humbly, he did not place his own judgments on a level with theirs, but subjected them to be formed by theirs. Faithfully following in their footsteps, he often drank himself from the spring from which they had drawn. [Col. 0241A–B]

Hence, filled with the Spirit by whom all Holy Scripture is divinely inspired, he uses it to this day with such confidence and usefulness, as the Apostle says, “for teaching, for refutation, for correction” (2 Tim. 3:16). And when he preaches the word of God, whatever he brings forward from Scripture he makes so clear and pleasing, and so effective in moving his hearers concerning the matter at hand, that all who are endowed with both secular and spiritual learning marvel at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth.

## Chapter V. On the beginning of Clairvaux, the meager fare of its first monks, and its growth divinely shown

25. When it pleased Him who had separated Bernard from the world and called him, by a fuller grace to reveal His glory in him and through him to gather into one the many dispersed children of God, He put it into the heart of Abbot Stephen to send Bernard’s brothers to found the house of Clairvaux. [Note: [Col. 0241D] See the notes on Letter 31.]

As they departed, Stephen also appointed Lord Bernard as their abbot. They were indeed astonished, being mature and vigorous men both in religious life and in the world, and they feared for him on account both of his tender youthfulness, his bodily weakness, and his lesser experience of outward occupations.

Clairvaux was a place in the territory of Langres, not far from the river Alba [Note: [Col. 0241D] Commonly *l’Aube*.], an ancient den of robbers. Formerly it was called [Col. 0241D] the Valley of Wormwood, either because wormwood grew there in abundance or because of the bitter pain of those who fell into the robbers’ hands.

There, then, in a place of horror and vast solitude, those men of virtue settled, intending to make a temple of God and a house of prayer out of a den of robbers. There they served God simply for some time, in poverty of spirit, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils. They often made vegetables from beech leaves. Their bread, like that of the prophet, was made from barley, millet, and vetch. [Note: [Col. 0242D] French *vesce*, “vetch.”] Thus a certain religious man, with abundant tears, secretly carried off what had been set before him at their hospitality, as something to be shown to all almost as a miracle: that human beings—and such human beings—lived on it. [Col. 0242A]

26. But these things moved the Man of God little. His chief concern was for the salvation of many, which from the first day of his conversion until this time is known to have possessed that singularly holy breast so completely that he seemed to bear toward all souls a motherly affection.

Accordingly, a vehement conflict of holy desire and holy humility was within his heart. At one time, abasing himself, he confessed himself unworthy to be the means of any fruit; at another, forgetting himself, he burned with so ardent a longing that he seemed able to admit no consolation except from the salvation of many. Love indeed gave rise to confidence, but humility chastened that same confidence.

It happened during these events that he once rose earlier than usual for vigils. When they had been completed, and a rather long interval of the night remained before Matins, he went outside and walked around the neighboring places, praying God to accept the service of himself and his brothers. Standing thus in prayer, fixed on the desire for spiritual fruit of which we have spoken, he suddenly saw, with his eyes slightly closed, a multitude of people of every dress and condition descending from the surrounding mountains into the lower valley—so great that the valley itself could not contain them. [Col. 0242B]

What this signified is now evident to all. Greatly consoled by this vision, the Man of God also exhorted his brothers, warning them never to despair of God’s mercy.

## Chapter VI. On his great confidence in God amid difficulties; his zeal for perfection; and his sister’s conversion

27. When, before the approaching winter, his brother Gerard, the cellarer of the house, complained rather sharply to him that many things necessary for the house and brothers were lacking, that he had nothing with which to purchase them, and that under the pressure of need he could receive no consolation from words; and when no readily available property existed to be given away, the Man of God asked what would suffice for the immediate need. Gerard answered: eleven [variant: twelve] pounds.

Bernard then dismissed him and fled to prayer. A little later Gerard returned and announced that a woman from Châtillon [Col. 0242D] was outside and wished to speak to him. When Bernard went out to her, the woman fell at his feet and offered him a blessing of twelve pounds, asking the support of his prayers for her husband, who was dangerously ill.

He spoke briefly with her and sent her away, saying: “Go; you will find your husband well.” She went home and found him exactly as she had heard. The abbot consoled the faintheartedness of his cellarer and henceforth made him stronger in waiting upon the Lord.

It is certain that this did not happen to him only once, but often: whenever such need pressed, help from the Lord suddenly came to him from an unexpected source. Therefore prudent men [Col. 0243A], understanding that the hand of the Lord was with him, took care not to burden with concern for outward matters the tender mind of one newly come forth from the delights of paradise. They arranged such affairs among themselves as best they could, consulting him only concerning the inward state of their consciences and the cause of their souls.

28. Yet in this matter there almost befell them what we read once befell the children of Israel because of Moses: when, after long converse with the Lord on Mount Sinai, he came forth from the cloud’s darkness and descended to the people, his face appeared horned and terrible from his colloquy with the Lord, so that the people fled from him (Exod. 34:29–35). For when the holy man came forth from the presence of the Lord—whose enjoyment he had for some while possessed in the wilderness of Cîteaux and in the silence of a more exalted [Col. 0243B] height of contemplation—bringing among men, as though from heaven, a certain wonder of purity attained before God beyond what is human, he almost frightened away from himself all the people whom he came to govern and among whom he came to live.

For whenever he spoke to them of spiritual matters and the edification of souls, he spoke to men in the tongue of angels and was scarcely understood. Above all, in matters pertaining to human conduct, from the abundance of his heart he set before them things so lofty and demanded of them things so perfect that his saying seemed hard: so little did they grasp what was said. Again, when he heard them individually confessing to him and accusing themselves concerning the various illusions of ordinary human thoughts [Col. 0243C], which no living person in the flesh can wholly avoid, this was especially the point at which that light could have no fellowship with those darknesses: namely, that he found men whom in this respect he thought to be angels. For, tasting angelic purity in great measure, and from the consciousness of the singular grace long ago received from God, he simply prejudged the entire condition of human frailty: that no religious person could fall into temptations or defilements of such thoughts; or, if one did fall into them, he judged that person not to be truly religious.

29. But men truly religious and devoutly prudent both revered in his preaching even what they did not understand [Col. 0243D], and in their confessions, although astonished at this new hearing—because it seemed to hold out a certain seed of despair for the weak—nevertheless, according to the saying of holy Job, considered it wickedness to contradict the words of the Saint (Job 6:10). They did not excuse but accused their own weakness before the Man of God, just as no living person can be justified before God.

Thus it came about that the devout humility of the disciples became the teacher of the teacher. For when those reproved humbled themselves at the nod of him who reproved them, his zeal also began to seem suspect to the spiritual master himself as directed against humble and submissive brothers. So much so that he himself now rather accused his own ignorance [Col. 0244A], and bewailed the necessity that he was not permitted to be silent when he did not know how to speak: that, by speaking things not so much too lofty for men as unworthy of men, he wounded the consciences of his hearers; that he demanded perfection so scrupulously from simple brothers, while he had not yet found himself perfect in that respect.

For he reflected that they meditated, in his silence, things far better and nearer their salvation than they would hear from him; that they worked out their salvation more devoutly and effectively than they could learn from his example; and that through his preaching they were more likely to be scandalized than to receive anything for edification. And when he was more violently troubled and grieved on this account, and diverse thoughts rose in his heart, after many turnings of thought and torments of heart he resolved to withdraw himself from all outward things [Col. 0244B] into his inward self, and there, in the solitude of his heart and the secrecy of silence, to contain himself and await the Lord, until in whatever way His mercy might reveal to him His will concerning this matter.

Nor did the mercy of God delay its help at the fitting time. For after a few days had passed, he saw in a vision by night a boy standing beside him with a certain divine charity, and with great authority commanding him confidently to speak whatever should be suggested to him at the opening of his mouth; for it would not be he who spoke, but the Spirit who spoke in him. And from that time the Holy Spirit, speaking more manifestly in him and through him, and more abundantly supplying him at the opening of his mouth with powerful speech and understanding in the Scriptures, also added to him grace and authority with his hearers [Col. 0244C], and understanding toward the needy and poor person, the penitent sinner, and one asking forgiveness.

30. And when he had now learned somewhat how to live among men, to do and endure human things, and had begun among and with his brothers to enjoy the fruits of his conversion, his father also, who alone had remained at home, came to his sons and was added to them. After spending some time there, he died in a good old age.

> [Note: Col. 0243D] Concerning him in the Necrology of Saint Benignus: “On the third day before the Ides of April died Tecelin, monk, father of lord Bernard [Col. 0244D], Abbot of Clairvaux.”

Their sister likewise, married in the world and devoted to the world—

> [Note: Col. 0244D] Humbelina.

—while she was endangered amid the riches of the world, was at length one day inspired by God to visit her brothers. When she came as if to see her venerable brother, attended by a proud retinue and display, he [Col. 0244D], detesting and execrating her as a snare of the devil for catching souls, would by no means consent to go out and see her.

Hearing this, she was ashamed and deeply compunct; and since none of her brothers would condescend to meet her, while Andrew, her brother, whom she had found at the monastery gate, reproached her for the display of her clothing as dung wrapped about her, she dissolved wholly into tears. “Even if I am a sinner,” she said, “Christ died for such as I. Precisely because I am a sinner, I seek the counsel and conversation of good people. And if my brother despises my flesh, let the servant of God not despise my soul. Let him come and command: whatever he commands, I am ready to do.”

[Col. 0245A] Holding her therefore to this promise, her brother went out to her with his brothers. Since he could not separate her from her husband, with his first word he forbade her every worldly glory in dress and all worldly pomp and refinements; he prescribed for her the manner of life of their mother, in which she had lived for a long time with her husband, and so dismissed her.

She, most obediently complying with the command, returned home, suddenly changed according to the might of the right hand of the Most High. All marvelled that a noble, delicate young woman, by a sudden change in clothing and diet, should lead an eremitical life amid the world: persevering in vigils, fasts, and continual prayers, and making herself entirely alien to every worldly thing. For two years thereafter she lived thus with her husband—he, indeed, especially in the second year, God granting him honour, no longer presuming to violate the temple of the Holy Spirit. At last, conquered by the strength of her perseverance, he released her freely and, according to the rite of the Church, granted her leave to serve the God to whom she had proved herself devoted.

Having obtained the freedom she desired, she went to the monastery of Jully—

> [Note: Col. 0245D] In French, Juilly; see above, note 18*.

—and there, with the nuns serving God, vowed to God the remainder of her life. There the Lord bestowed on her such a grace of holiness that she was proved to be the sister of those men of God no less in spirit than in flesh.

## CHAPTER VII. On Saint Bernard’s ordination as abbot and the care of his health; likewise, on the praise of religious discipline then flourishing at Clairvaux.

[Col. 0245C]

31. When Bernard had newly been sent to Clairvaux and was to be ordained to the ministry for which he had been chosen, and the see of Langres, to which that ordination belonged, was vacant, the brothers sought where they should take him for ordination. The good reputation of the venerable bishop of Châlons, that highly esteemed master William of Champeaux, promptly presented itself from nearby, and it was decided that he should be sent there.

And so it was done. He went to Châlons, taking with him a certain Cistercian monk, Elboldo. The young man entered the house of the aforesaid bishop, his body wasted and seemingly dying, his dress likewise contemptible; behind him followed the older monk, handsome in stature and strength of body. Some laughed, others mocked, while others, interpreting the matter as it was, venerated them [Col. 0245D].

When it was asked which of the two was the abbot, the Bishop, setting his eyes upon him first, recognized the servant of God and received him as a servant of God. For in their first private conversation, as the young man’s prudence disclosed itself increasingly better than words could have done through his modesty in speaking, the wise man understood that a divine visitation had occurred in the arrival of his guest. Nor was the earnest devotion of his hospitality lacking, until, as their conversation developed into familiar confidence and freedom of speech between them, Bernard’s conscience now commended him better than his words did.

Why say more? From that day and hour they became one heart [Col. 0246A] and one soul in the Lord, so that thereafter each often had the other as guest; the Bishop’s own house became the house of Clairvaux, and not only the Bishop’s house but, through him, the entire city of Châlons became the home of the men of Clairvaux. Indeed, through him the province of Reims and all Gaul were stirred to devotion and reverence for the Man of God. For from that great bishop the others learned to receive and venerate him as an angel of God. A man of such authority seems to have foreseen in him the grace of this age, being so affectionately disposed toward an unknown monk—and a monk of such humility.

32. After a short time, however, the Abbot’s illness became so severe that nothing could be hoped for except his death, or a life more grievous than any death [Col. 0246B]. The Bishop visited him; and, seeing him, said that he had hope not merely for his life but even for his recovery, if Bernard would accept his counsel and allow some care to be bestowed upon his body in proportion to his infirmity. But since he could not easily be bent from the rigor and habitual practice of his observance, the Bishop went to the Cistercian chapter. There, before the few abbots who had assembled, with episcopal humility and priestly charity, he prostrated his whole body upon the ground and requested—and obtained—that Bernard should be entrusted to his obedience for one year only. For what could be denied to such humility in so great an authority?

Returning therefore to Clairvaux, he ordered a small house to be built for Bernard outside the cloister and boundaries of the monastery [Col. 0246C]. He ordained and commanded that no strictness of the Order be observed there regarding food, drink, or anything of the kind concerning him; that no anxiety from the whole management of the house be referred to him; but that he be left to live according to the manner he himself had prescribed [sini; alternative reading sibi, “for himself”].

33. At that same time I too began to frequent Clairvaux and Bernard himself. When I visited him there with another abbot, I found him in that little hut of his, such as is commonly made for lepers at public crossroads. I found him, by command, as has been said, of the Bishop and Abbots, released from every concern of the household, inward as well as outward, free for God and himself, and exulting as though amid the delights of paradise.

And when I entered that royal chamber [Col. 0246D], considering both dwelling and inhabitant, the house itself inspired in me, God is my witness, such reverence for itself as though I were entering the altar of God. I was so affected with delight toward that man and such a desire to dwell with him in that poverty and simplicity, that, if the choice had been given me that day, I should have desired nothing so much as always to remain there with him to serve him.

When he in turn received us joyfully, and we asked what he did and how he lived there, he smiled upon us in his noble manner and said: “Very well. I, whom rational men have hitherto obeyed, have by God’s just judgment been handed over to obey a certain irrational beast.” He meant a certain rustic and foolish man, wholly ignorant, who boasted that he would cure him of the illness from which he suffered, and to whose obedience he had been committed by the Bishop, the Abbots, and his own brothers.

While we were eating with him there, we thought that a man so ill and entrusted to such care ought to be provided for as was fitting. But, under the direction of this physician of his, we saw food offered him which a healthy person would scarcely touch except under the pressure of extreme hunger. We watched and wasted away, barely restraining ourselves by the discipline of silence from rising against that man as a kind of sacrilegious murderer in anger and insults [Col. 0247A].

But he to whom these things were done received everything without distinction and approved all alike, since, with his very sense of taste corrupted and almost dead, he could scarcely distinguish anything. For it is known that for many days he ate raw blood, offered to him by mistake in place of butter; that he drank oil as if it were water; and many such things happened to him. He said that water alone had any taste for him, because, when he drank it, it cooled his jaws and throat [Col. 0247B].

34. Thus I found him then, and thus that man of God lived in his solitude. Yet he was not alone, for God was with him, together with the guardianship and consolation of the holy angels; this was also shown by clear indications.

For one night, having poured out his soul in prayer more attentively than usual, he fell into a light sleep and heard voices as of a great multitude passing by. Awakening and hearing the same voices more clearly, he went out from the cell where he lay and followed those who were departing. Not far away was a place still thick with dense brambles and thorny undergrowth, though now far changed from what it was then. Over this place, for some time, choirs seemed to stand arranged on either side in responsive alternation, and the holy man heard and delighted in them.

Yet he did not learn the mystery of the vision until, after some years, when the monastery buildings had been transferred, he saw an oratory set up in that very place where he had heard those voices [Col. 0247C]. I, unworthy as I was, stayed with him for a few days; wherever I turned my eyes, I marvelled as though I saw new heavens and a new earth, and the ancient paths of those old Egyptian monks, our fathers, bearing upon them the fresh footprints of men of our own age.

35. At that time one could see the golden age of Clairvaux [Col. 0247D], when men of virtue, formerly rich and honoured in the world, now gloried in Christ’s poverty and planted the Church of God with their blood—in labour and hardship, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, persecutions, insults, and many distresses—preparing for Clairvaux the sufficiency and peace which it possesses today.

For they judged that they lived not so much for themselves as for Christ and for the brothers who would serve God there. They considered as nothing whatever they themselves lacked, so long as they left behind what would suffice for those brothers, both to relieve necessity and to preserve some awareness of voluntary poverty for Christ. At the very first sight, as one entered Clairvaux by descending the mountain, God was recognized in its dwellings [Col. 0248A], since the silent valley, by the simplicity and humility of its buildings, spoke of the simplicity and humility of the poor of Christ who dwelt there.

Finally, in that valley full of people, where no one was allowed to be idle, all labouring and each occupied with the task assigned, newcomers found at midday the silence of midnight, except for the sounds of work or the brothers engaged in God’s praises. Moreover, the discipline and renown of this silence inspired such reverence even in worldly people arriving there that they feared to speak—not merely evil or idle speech, but even anything irrelevant to the matter at hand.

The solitude of the place itself, hidden amid the forest’s shade and the narrow confines of the neighbouring mountains on either side, where the servants of God lay concealed, in some manner represented that cave of our father Saint Benedict in which he was once found by shepherds [Col. 0248B], so that those who imitated his life seemed also to possess something of the form of his dwelling and solitude.

For all were solitary there even in the multitude. The ordered charity of that valley, full of people, made it solitary for each person by the principle of the Order; for as one disordered person, even when alone, is a crowd to himself, so there, through unity of spirit and the regular law of silence, the Order itself guarded for each person the solitude of the heart amid an ordered multitude of people.

> [Note: Col. 0247D] See the Epistle to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu, no. 9.

36. The food was very like the simple houses and dwellings of their inhabitants. The bread seemed not so much made of bran as of earth, scarcely brought forth from the sterile soil of that wilderness by the brothers’ harsh labours [Col. 0248C]. Likewise, the other foods scarcely had any taste, except that which hunger or the love of God supplied.

But the simplicity of their novice fervour even took this away from them: reckoning as poison whatever might somehow delight the eater, they refused God’s gifts because of the pleasure which they felt in them. For when, in every kind of bodily endurance, the zeal of their spiritual Father, assisted by God’s grace, had achieved in them this result—that they now performed steadily and without murmuring, indeed even with great delight, many things that had previously seemed impossible to a person living in the flesh—the very delight gave birth in them to another murmur, all the more dangerous because they judged it more removed from the flesh and nearer to the spirit [Col. 0248D].

For, persuaded of this and as though faithfully committing it to memory under the testimony of their conscience—that every pleasure of the flesh is hostile to the soul—they thought that whatever seemed to nourish the flesh with any pleasure whatever must be avoided. They supposed, as it were, that they were being led back to their homeland by another route, when, through the sweetness of inward love, eating bitter and sweet things alike with pleasure, they considered themselves to live more delightfully in the wilderness than they had formerly lived in the world.

37. Since in this respect they somewhat suspected the daily correction of their spiritual Father—

> [Note: Col. 0249D] See Sermon 1 on the Epiphany, no. 1.

—as yielding more to their flesh than to their spirit, the matter was at one time brought before the judgment of the aforesaid Bishop of Châlons, who happened then to be present [Col. 0249A]. That man, powerful in speech, addressed them and brought his discourse to this conclusion: that every person who refuses the gifts of God because of the grace of God is an enemy of the grace of God and resists the Holy Spirit.

For he cited the history of the prophet Elisha and the sons of the prophets living with him an eremitical life in desert places: when, on one occasion, the time for refreshment had come, a certain deadly bitterness was found in the pot in which their food was being cooked; but through God’s power and the prophet’s ministry, it was sweetened by the addition of meal. “That prophetic pot,” he said, “is your pot: it has in itself nothing but bitterness [Col. 0249B]. The meal, which changes bitterness into sweetness, is God’s grace working in you. Therefore take confidently and with thanksgiving that which, though naturally less suited to human use, has by God’s grace been made suitable for your use, so that you may use and eat it. If in this you remain disobedient and unbelieving, you resist the Holy Spirit and are ungrateful for His grace.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the great severity of his life and his untiring zeal for labour amid the continual afflictions of broken health.

38. Such, then, at that time under Abbot Bernard and his instruction, was the school of spiritual pursuits in that most renowned and beloved valley [Col. 0249C]: such the fervour of regular discipline, while he did and ordered everything and built God’s tabernacle on earth according to the pattern shown him on the mountain, when he dwelt with God in the cloud in the solitude of Cîteaux.

Would that, after the first rudiments of his religious life, once he had learned somewhat and grown accustomed to be with men as a man, and to understand the needy and poor, sympathizing with human weaknesses—would that he had shown himself toward himself such as he was toward others: so kindly, so discerning, so solicitous! But immediately upon release from that bond of yearly obedience, and when he became his own master, he returned, like a drawn bow, to his former rigor, and, like a torrent held back and released [Col. 0249D], to the habit of its former course, as though exacting from himself punishment for that long rest (diutinae; alternative reading diusculae, “rather lengthy”) and for the loss of interrupted labour.

You might see a frail and sickly man trying and undertaking whatever he wished, giving little thought to what he could accomplish; solicitous for everyone, negligent of himself; most obedient to all in every other matter, but scarcely ever obedient concerning himself either to charity or to authority. For, always counting his former efforts as nothing, he devised greater things, sparing not his body, increasing his strength for spiritual pursuits, and wearing down by unceasing fasts and vigils a body already weakened by various illnesses.

[Col. 0250A] 39. He prayed standing day and night until his knees, weakened by fasting, and his feet, swollen from labour, could no longer support his body. For a long time, and while it could remain hidden, he wore a hair-shirt next to his flesh; but when he noticed that it was known, he immediately cast it aside and returned to ordinary clothing. His food with bread was milk, or water in which vegetables had been boiled, or porridge such as is commonly made for infants. His illness did not admit other foods, or he himself rejected them from a desire for frugality. If he ever used wine, it was rarely and in exceedingly small quantity, declaring that water better suited both his infirmity and his appetite.

Thus afflicted and exhausted, he scarcely ever permitted himself to be excused from the common labour of the brothers, by day or by night, or from the duties and labours of his ministry [Col. 0250B]. Physicians saw him and his manner of life and marvelled that he inflicted such violence upon nature, as if a lamb tethered to a plough were compelled to plough. When the frequent eruption through his mouth of undigested matter from a disordered stomach began to be troublesome to others, especially in the choir while they sang psalms, he nevertheless did not immediately abandon the gatherings of the brothers. Instead, having arranged and dug a receptacle in the earth near the place where he stood, he endured for some time, as best he could, that necessity of his suffering.

But when the intolerability of the condition no longer permitted even this, then at last he was forced to leave the gatherings and live apart by himself, except when he needed at times to be present at the assembly of the brothers, whether for conversation, consolation, or the requirement of cloister discipline [Col. 0250C].

49. And this was that sad necessity by which the holy brotherhood was first compelled to be able to lack the continual companionship of that holy fatherhood. In this we do indeed grieve and lament the sad result of his illness; yet we venerate the disposition of his holy longing and spiritual fervour. Nor, indeed, is the result of his illness altogether to be mourned and lamented.

For what if the wisdom of God wished rather through the weakness of that man to confound the many and great strengths of this world? And what, because of any infirmity of his, was ever left undone which ought to have been done through him according to the grace given him? In our age, what person, however robust in body and sound in health, has ever done so many things as this man has done—and does while dying and sickly—for the honour of God and the benefit of the holy Church?

How great a multitude afterward did he draw, by word and example, out of the world not merely to conversion but to perfection? How many houses, or cities of refuge, did he establish from them throughout the Christian world, so that whoever had sinned unto death and been judged guilty of eternal death might remember, turn to the Lord, flee to them, and be saved in them? What schisms of the Church did he not calm? What heresies did he not confound? What peace did he not restore among churches and peoples at variance? [Col. 0251A] These, indeed, are public matters. But as for the countless benefits he bestowed upon innumerable individuals, according to cause, person, place, and time—who could enumerate them?

41. Moreover, if an excess of holy fervour is criticized in him, this excess surely has its own reverence among devout minds; for all who are led by the Spirit of God greatly fear to reproach this excessive excess (nimium; alternative reading nimiam) in a servant of God. It also has an easy excuse among men, since scarcely anyone would dare condemn one whom God justifies by working with him and through him such numerous and exalted deeds. Blessed is he to whom alone that is reckoned as fault which others commonly presume to count as glory.

Perhaps his youth was suspect to the good young man; for blessed is the one who is always fearful. Perhaps he strove to add to that fullness of virtues which he possessed by grace some consciousness also of his own labour [Col. 0251B]. Yet his life, proposed to all for imitation, ought not to have lacked an example of frugal self-restraint. In this the servant of God, if perhaps he exceeded in excess, nevertheless left devout minds an example not of excess but of fervour.

But why do we strive to excuse him, when he himself, who fears all his works, is not ashamed even to this day to accuse himself? He charges himself with sacrilege because he withdrew his body from the service of God and the brothers, rendering it weak and almost useless through indiscriminate fervour. Yet he recovered from illness, and, weak though he was, became stronger and mighty. For the power of God, shining more brightly in his weakness, from that time until today produces in men a certain worthier reverence for him, and in reverence authority, and in authority obedience [Col. 0251C].

42. Already then he was being divinely prepared for the work of preaching, for which, as stated above—

> [Note: Col. 0251D] Chapter 1, no. 2.

—he had long before been marked out from his mother’s womb, with the testimony of divine revelation. Nor was this so at that time only, but throughout the whole period of his conversion, subjection, and prelacy: by the ordering and action of Him who ordered and acted, he was instituted for this purpose in fitting sequence. Unaware of what was being done with him, he was being prepared in this respect not only for the monastic Order but for every ecclesiastical order.

First, indeed, he devoted the first-fruits of his youth to reviving in the monastic Order the fervour of ancient religious life, applying every effort to this purpose by example and word within the community of brothers, inside the monastery enclosure [Col. 0251D]. Later, when bodily weakness compelled him to a different order of life and practice, and when, as has been said, the necessity of illness and the rule imposed by that necessity separated him more than usual from the common life of the community, this first became the occasion on which, as though exposed to people from the world—of whom a great multitude was now flocking to him—he more freely and generously made his presence available to them and preached the word of life.

And whenever obedience drew him farther from the monastery for matters common to the Church, wherever he came he could not, when about to speak, remain silent about God, nor cease to do the things of God [Col. 0252A]. Thus he became known among people in a short time, so that the Church of God, having discovered so useful a member in her body, did not neglect to employ him for whatever was needed.

And although from the first flower of his early age he had always abounded in the fruits of the Spirit, from this time there was nevertheless more abundantly added to him, as the Apostle says, “the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Cor. 12:7): namely, a more fruitful word of wisdom and knowledge together with the grace of prophecy, workings of powers, and aids of various healings. Some of these things, which I learned by trustworthy report, having been communicated to me on reliable authority by faithful men, I myself now set forth for readers.

## CHAPTER IX. On miracles performed through him and the danger of arrogance remarkably restrained in him by his relatives.

[Col. 0252B]

43. This, then, was the first sign which Christ made famous to the world through the hand of His servant. After Bernard had spent some years at Clairvaux, it happened that a nobleman and his kinsman according to the flesh, Josbert of La Ferté—

> [Note: Col. 0252D] In French, La Ferté-sur-Aube.

—a town near the monastery, fell gravely ill. Suddenly stricken, he wholly lost both understanding and speech. His son, Josbert the younger, and all his friends together were therefore all the more afflicted with grief because this distinguished and highly honoured man seemed likely to die without confession and Viaticum.

A messenger ran to the Abbot, for he was then not at the monastery. He came and found Josbert lying thus already for three days. Moved by compassion for the man, and also by his son’s tears and the lamentation of all the others, he trusted in God’s mercy and spoke boldly to them, saying: “You know that this man has in many ways burdened churches, oppressed the poor, and offended God. If you give me your word that what has been taken shall be restored to the churches, and that customary exactions, usurped to the burden of the poor, shall be relinquished, he will yet speak, make confession of his sins, and devoutly receive the divine sacraments.”

All marvelled; the son rejoiced, and the whole household exulted. Whatever the Man of God commanded was firmly promised to him and carried out. But his brother Gerard and his uncle Galdric, not a little frightened and disturbed, approached him privately regarding such a promise [Col. 0252C], rebuked him harshly, and inveighed against him more sharply. He answered them briefly and simply: “God can easily do what you find hard to believe.”

Then, after private prayer, he approached the offering of the immortal sacrifice. While he was offering it, a messenger arrived to report that the aforesaid Josbert, now speaking freely, earnestly begged the Man of God to hasten to him. Bernard came to him after offering the Sacrifice; Josbert confessed his sins with tears and groaning, received the divine Sacraments, and lived and spoke for two or three days afterward. Above all, he ordered that the measures commanded by the holy Abbot should be observed without any revocation. He also put his household in order and gave alms [Col. 0253A]; then at last, in the Christian manner and in the good hope of God’s mercy, he breathed out his soul.

44. On one occasion the holy Father was returning from the meadows when he encountered a woman carrying her little son in her arms. She had brought him to Bernard from far away; from his mother’s womb the child had had a withered hand and a twisted arm. Moved by the mother’s tears and prayers, he ordered the child to be set down. Having prayed, he immediately made the sign over the child and his arm and hand, and told the woman to call her son. She called the infant; he ran to her, embraced his mother with both arms, and from that hour was healed.

45. The brothers and spiritual sons of this blessed man marvelled at what they heard and saw concerning him [Col. 0253B]. Yet they were not, after the manner of carnal people, exalted into human glory; rather, they were apprehensive with spiritual concern on account of his youthful age and still recent religious life. In this zeal, his uncle Galdric and Guy, the eldest of the brothers, surpassed the others. They appeared to have been divinely given to him as two twin goads for his flesh, lest the greatness of his graces should exalt him.

For they did not spare him. They harassed his tender modesty with harsh words, even impugned well-done deeds, reduced all signs to nothing, and frequently afflicted this most gentle man, who made no reply, with reproaches and insults even to tears. The venerable Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres—kinsman of the holy man by blood, companion in conversion, and from that time his inseparable companion in all things—used to relate that Guy, Bernard’s aforesaid full brother, was present at the first miracle which he saw performed through Bernard’s hands.

They were passing through Château-Landon—

> [Note: Col. 0253D] French: Château-Landon.

—in the territory of Sens, and a certain young man, whose foot was affected by a fistula, begged with much supplication for the touch and blessing of the aforesaid Father. After he had been signed, he was immediately healed; and, returning through the same town a very few days later, they found him healthy and sound. Yet the often-mentioned brother of the blessed man could not be restrained even by the miracle itself from rebuking him and charging him with presumption for having consented to touch the man: so great was his loving concern for him [Col. 0253D].

## CHAPTER X. On other benefits of healing bestowed upon various persons.

46. At about the same time it happened that his uncle Galdric—who likewise, out of a zeal akin to his own, as we have said, overwhelmed his gentleness with harsh rebukes—was suffering from most severe fevers. At last, as the illness worsened and he was overcome by the very intensity of his pain, he appealed humbly to the Abbot, begging him to have pity on him and bring him the help he was accustomed to give others. But Bernard, whose spirit was sweeter than honey, first gently and briefly recalled the uncle’s frequent rebukes on such matters, and suggested to him [Col. 0254A] that perhaps he was saying this to test him. Yet when he persisted [otherwise: nevertheless], he finally laid his hand upon him and commanded the fever to depart. Without delay, at his command the fever left him, and he experienced in himself what he had criticized in others.

The same Galdric, after spending several years at Clairvaux, fervent in spirit and zealous for every good, departed this life.
