About an hour before death he was briefly disturbed, groaned terribly, and convulsed throughout his whole body; but, restored to his former serenity, he thereafter breathed his last with a most peaceful expression. The Lord, however, would not deprive the Abbot’s concerned mind of knowledge of this event. For after some days the same Galdric appeared to him in a night vision. When, in reply to Bernard’s inquiry, he reported that all was well with him and rejoiced that he was placed in great [Col. 0254B] happiness, he was finally asked what that bitter and sudden disturbance at death had meant. He said that at that hour two evil spirits had been preparing to hurl him, as it were, into a pit of dreadful depth. Terrified by this, he had trembled so violently; but when blessed Peter came to his aid, he was snatched away and thereafter suffered no harm.

47. It would take too long to recount all that divine grace had customarily revealed to him from the beginning concerning those who had departed this life, and their blessedness or even their need. Yet I shall mention one instance, which he himself sometimes recalled for the brothers’ admonition. A certain brother, of good intention but of a manner harsher toward the other brothers than it should have been, and less compassionate [Col. 0254C] than he ought to have been, died in the monastery. A few days later he appeared to the Man of God with a mournful face and a pitiable appearance, indicating that not all was going well with him as he wished. Asked what was the matter, he complained that he had been delivered over to four lizards [otherwise: torn to pieces]. At those words he was immediately driven away, as though hurled headlong, from the presence of the Man of God. Bernard groaned more heavily and cried after him: “I command you, in the name of the Lord, that you make known to me again shortly how matters stand with you.”

Then he turned to prayer for him and to the offering of the saving sacrifice. He also urged certain brothers whose holiness he knew to be greater likewise to assist the man. Nor did he cease until, a few days later, he deserved to be consoled by learning through another [Col. 0254D] revelation, as he had commanded, that the brother had been delivered.

48. [The most reverend Humbert, later founder and first father of the abbey of Igniacensis.  
[Note: [Col. 0253D] Common reading: Igny, in the diocese of Rheims, founded in 1127.]  
At Clairvaux he suffered so severely from epilepsy that, falling seven times in one day and finally becoming mentally disordered, he could scarcely be held in bed, bound by the hands of many brothers. When the venerable Abbot arrived and found the man thus afflicted—a man whom, on account of his holiness, he revered with special affection—he was filled with zeal and said: “What are we doing? Let us go and pray.” But when he entered the oratory and bent his knees, the aforementioned man fell asleep in the hands of those holding him. On the following Sunday, receiving the Sacraments from Bernard’s hand, he obtained complete recovery, so that he never afterward suffered anything of the kind.]

49. About this time famine grew severe in the kingdom of France and the neighboring regions; but the Lord’s blessing filled the granaries of His servants. Until that year, indeed, the produce of their labor had never sufficed for them. Even then, after the harvest had been gathered and every calculation carefully made, they judged that it would scarcely suffice them until Easter. When they wished to buy grain, they found no funds, since it was being sold at a price far beyond the usual one. Thus, during the very season of Lent, a very great multitude of poor people flocked to them. Faithfully distributing what they had, they themselves and the poor who came to them were cheerfully sustained, through the Lord’s blessing, from that small [Col. 0255B] store of grain until the harvest.

The adulterous wife of a poor man living not far from the monastery tormented him by sorcery. As she had threatened him in anger and fury, so by malignant incantations she brought it about that the wretched man, his flesh wasting away, could neither die nor be allowed to live. Often, indeed, he lost both the use of speech and all bodily sensation; then he returned, cruelly recalled not to life but to a more prolonged death. At last the man was brought to the Man of God, who was staying in the monastery, and the pitiful tragedy was explained to him. Greatly angered that the malice of the ancient enemy had arrogated such power to itself over a Christian man, [Col. 0255C] he summoned two brothers and ordered the man to be carried before the holy altar. There, placing a vessel containing the Eucharist upon his head, he commanded the demon, by the power of that Sacrament, to be kept from harming the Christian. It happened as he commanded; and, after such tortures, perfect faith restored the wretched man to perfect health.

## CHAPTER XI. Of the miracle of a letter written in rain yet not wetted, and of certain other marvels.

50. Brother Robert, a monk of the same holy man and his kinsman according to the flesh, had been deceived in his youth by the persuasion of certain persons and had gone to Cluny. After the venerable Father had overlooked this for some time, he resolved to summon that brother back by letter. As he dictated it, the venerable William, later the first abbot of the monastery of Rievaulx, wrote down the letter on parchment. Both were sitting together in the open air, for they had gone outside the monastery enclosure in order to dictate more privately. Suddenly an unexpected downpour broke out, and the writer—as we learned from his own account—wanted to put away the sheet. But the holy Father said to him: “It is God’s work; write, do not be afraid.” Thus he wrote the letter in the midst of rain without rain. For though it rained on every side, the power of charity protected the exposed sheet; and the grace which dictated [Col. 0256A] the letter preserved the little document as well. Because of so great a miracle, this letter has rightly been placed first by the brothers in the collection of his letters.  
[Note: [Col. 0255D] This is indeed attested by the author of the third *Life*, chapter 6 below.]

51. A principal feast was being celebrated, and a certain brother, whom Bernard had suspended from communion at the holy altar because of a secret fault, feared being noticed and could not bear the shame. With excessive presumption he approached Bernard’s hand with the others. Bernard saw him, but since the cause was hidden, he did not wish to repel the man; rather, in his inmost heart he prayed God to make some better disposition concerning so great a presumption. The man therefore received the Eucharist but could not swallow it. After striving long and hard without being able to do so, he anxiously and tremblingly kept it in his closed [Col. 0256B] mouth. When the sixth hour of prayer was completed, he drew the holy Father aside. Falling at his feet, he disclosed with many tears what he was suffering, and, opening his mouth, showed him the Eucharist itself. Bernard rebuked him, absolved him as he confessed, and thereafter he received the Lord’s Sacraments without difficulty.

52. We have also known great things to occur through him in very small matters. Once he came to Foigny, one of the first abbeys which he himself founded, situated in the territory of Laon.  
[Note: [Col. 0255D] Foigny, founded in 1121.]

As the dedication of a new oratory there was being prepared, such an incredible multitude of flies had occupied it that their incessant buzzing and movement caused intolerable annoyance to those entering. Since no remedy presented itself, the saint said: “I excommunicate them.” In the morning they found them all dead together. When they covered the entire pavement, the monks drove them out with poles and at last cleansed the church. This was so widely known and celebrated that, even among the neighboring people who had assembled in a great multitude for the dedication, the curse of the flies of Foigny became proverbial.

53. In the monastery also called Charus-Locus, that is, Charlieu, he cured a boy who was continually crying and wailing by a kiss.  
[Note: [Col. 0256D] Charlieu, in the diocese of Besançon, founded in 1131.]

The boy had wept without interruption for many days and received no consolation. He was miserably wasting away from a kind of illness not unknown to physicians. The holy Father spoke with him privately and urged him to confess his sins. Once he had confessed, his face suddenly brightened, and he asked the blessed Father to give him a kiss. Having received the kiss of peace from the Saint’s mouth, he immediately rested in complete peace; the fountain of tears dried up, and he returned joyfully and unharmed to his own home.

54. Once, when the Abbot was going out to work after the other brothers, a father offered him his lame son and begged him to deign to lay his hand upon him. The Man of God excused himself, saying that he was not of such merit that such benefits should be sought from him; restoring the power of walking to the lame belonged to apostolic, not his own, [Col. 0257A] power. Nevertheless, overcome by the father’s persistence, he made the sign over the boy and sent him away. From that hour the boy recovered, and within a few days his father brought him back, healthy and sound, with much thanksgiving, and presented him again to the Man of God.

55. Once a company of noble knights came to Clairvaux to see the place and its holy Abbot. The sacred season of Lent was near, and almost all of them were young men devoted to secular warfare. They went about looking for those detestable tournaments which are popularly called *tornetas*.  
[Note: [Col. 0257D] In French, *tournois*.]

Bernard began to ask them to refrain from arms during the few remaining days before Lent. When they stubbornly refused to heed his warning, he said: “I trust in the [Col. 0257B] Lord that He Himself will give me the truce which you have refused.” Calling a brother, he ordered beer to be served them. He blessed it and told them to drink “a draught for their souls.” They all drank, though some unwillingly because of their love for the world, fearing the effect of divine power which they afterward experienced. For once they had passed through the monastery gates, they began to kindle one another by their words, because their hearts burned within them. Therefore, God inspiring them and His word running swiftly, they returned that same hour; turning from their ways, they pledged their hands to spiritual knighthood. Some of them still serve God in that warfare; others, released from the bonds of flesh, already reign with Him.

56. What wonder, then, that mature people honor this man with devoted service, when divine power even stirs toward devotion infancy itself, still without reason and ignorant of devotion? Many know the distinguished young man Walter of Montmirail, whose uncle, Brother Walter, was among the knights mentioned above who professed the sacred warfare at Clairvaux.  
[Note: [Col. 0258D] Common reading: Montmirail.]

When this younger Walter was still an infant and had not yet completed his third month from birth, his mother offered him to the Man of God for a blessing, rejoicing and exulting that she had deserved to have so holy a man as a guest in her house. [Otherwise, uncertain and corrupt: “when he was still a yearling, able to recognize only the breast, his mother, etc.”] While the Man of God, as he always did in every place, spoke to those around him about the salvation [Col. 0257D] and edification of souls, the mother of the aforementioned infant sat beside his feet, holding him in her lap. It happened that as Bernard spoke, he at some point stretched out his hand, and the little child tried to grasp it. At length the child’s effort, repeated several times, was noticed; and, while all marvelled, he was allowed to grasp the hand he desired. Then, showing truly extraordinary reverence, he placed his other hand beneath it, held it with the first, brought it to his mouth, and kissed it. And he did this not once only, but as often as he was permitted to hold that blessed hand.

## CHAPTER XII. Of Bernard’s dispute with the devil; of the health restored to him through the blessed Virgin; and likewise of Abbot William, healed by him.

[Col. 0258A]

57. The Man of God once fell ill, and a kind of stream of phlegm flowed constantly from his mouth. His body was utterly exhausted and failing, and he came very near to the end. Therefore his sons and friends assembled as if for the funeral of so great a Father; and I myself was present among the others, for his graciousness counted me also among his friends. When he now seemed to be drawing his last breath, in an ecstasy of mind he saw himself presented before the tribunal of the Lord. Satan was also there [Col. 0258B] opposite him, assailing him with wicked accusations. When Satan had presented everything and it was time for the Man of God to speak for himself, Bernard, neither frightened nor disturbed, said:

“I confess that I am unworthy, and that I cannot obtain the kingdom of heaven by my own merits. Yet my Lord possesses it by a twofold right: namely, by inheritance from the Father and by the merit of His Passion. Content with one of these rights, He gives the other to me. Claiming it as mine by right through His gift, I am not ashamed.”

At these words the enemy was confounded, the assembly was dissolved, and the Man of God returned to himself. Since from this he expected more strongly that the dissolution of his body was near, a second and very different vision followed.

58. [Col. 0258C] He seemed to himself to be standing on a certain shore, awaiting a ship that would carry him across. When the ship reached the shore, he hurried to board it, but it moved away and struck the water. After it did this three times, the ship at last left him and went away without returning. He immediately understood that the time of his departure had not yet come. Nevertheless, his pain still increased, all the more burdensome because the hope of his impending end no longer consoled him.

As evening was already approaching, the other brothers went, according to custom, to the reading of the *Conferences*. The Abbot alone remained in the lodging where he lay, attended by two brothers. As he was suffering more violently and the pain increased beyond his strength, he called one of the two and ordered him to go quickly to pray. When the brother excused himself, saying, “I am not such a man of prayer,” Bernard compelled him by the authority of obedience. He went and prayed at the three altars in that church: the first in honor of the blessed Mother of God, and the two adjoining altars in honor of blessed Lawrence the martyr and blessed Benedict the abbot. At that same hour the aforementioned blessed Virgin appeared to the Man of God, attended by those two ministers, namely blessed Lawrence and blessed Benedict. They appeared in the serenity and sweetness fitting to them, and so visibly that from their very entrance into the cell he could distinguish each individual person. Laying their hands upon him and soothing the places of pain with most compassionate touch, [Col. 0259A] they immediately drove away all sickness. The stream of phlegm was at once dried up, and every pain departed.

59. When I myself was once sick in our house, and an illness that had extended itself far too long had exhausted and worn me down severely, he heard of it and sent me his brother Gerard, of good memory. He ordered me to come to Clairvaux, promising that there I would quickly either be healed or die. I, as though a divinely granted opportunity had been received or offered to me—either to die with him or to live with him for some time, and I do not know which I then preferred—set out at once for that place, though with immense labor and pain. There what had been promised was done for me, and, I confess, as I wished. My health was restored from a great and dangerous illness, though my bodily strength returned gradually.

Good God, what good that illness, that respite, that freedom from occupation conferred upon me! In part, what I wanted. For during that entire period of my sickness with him, his own illness, by which he too was then afflicted, assisted my need. Thus, both sick, we spent the whole day discussing the spiritual medicine of the soul: the remedies of virtues against the maladies of vices. During that time he expounded to me the *Song of Songs*, as far as my illness allowed, solely in its moral sense, setting aside the mysteries of that Scripture, because this was what I wished and had asked of him. Each day I committed to writing, as far as God granted and memory aided me, whatever I heard from him [Col. 0259C] on this subject, lest it escape me. In explaining it generously and without envy, he shared with me the judgments of his understanding and the perceptions of his experience. Though he endeavored to teach an inexperienced man many things which can be learned only by experience, and I was not yet able to understand what was set before me, he nevertheless made me understand more than usual what I lacked in order to understand them. But enough has been said of this.

60. As the Sunday called Septuagesima drew near, on the Saturday evening preceding it I had recovered enough to rise from bed by myself, and to go out and come in alone. I began to make arrangements for our return to our brothers. When Bernard heard of this, he prohibited it altogether and forbade me all hope and attempt of returning until Quinquagesima Sunday. I readily complied, since my will did not reject what was commanded and my illness seemed to require it.

When, after that Sunday of Septuagesima, I wished to abstain from meat—which, at his command and because necessity compelled it, I had eaten until that day—he prohibited this also. Because I neither heeded his warning, nor listened to his request, nor obeyed his command, on that Saturday evening we parted from one another: he silently went to Compline, and I to bed. Then the raging of my illness returned, as though recovering all its former strength. [Col. 0260A] It seized me with such violence and ferocity, and tormented me throughout that night with such destructive malignity, beyond my strength and endurance, that I despaired of life and scarcely believed I would survive until morning, merely to speak once more to the Man of God.

After I had passed the whole night in that pain, he was summoned and came early in the morning. Yet he did not bring the compassionate expression he usually wore, but rather that of one rebuking. Still, smiling, he asked: “What will you eat today?” Since, even without his speaking, I understood with complete certainty that my disobedience of the previous day was the cause of my suffering, I answered: “Whatever you command.” “Then rest,” he said; “you will not die now.” And he went away.

What more can I say? At once all pain departed, except that, worn out by that night’s suffering, I could scarcely rise from bed throughout the entire day. What pain was it, and how great? I do not recall ever having endured its like. On the following day, however, I was made well and recovered my strength. A few days later, with the blessing and gracious favor of my good host, I returned home.

## CHAPTER XIII. Of the fame of his holiness spread everywhere, the wondrous expansion of Clairvaux itself, and the spirit of prophecy granted to him.

61. While Bernard, beloved by God and men, flourished with such virtues and miracles in his valley and in the neighboring cities and regions—which the responsibilities of his household sometimes obliged him to visit—he began also to be drawn to distant lands, whether by the common needs of the Church, the charity of the brothers, or obedience to his superiors. There he restored desperate peaces between divided churches and secular rulers; with God’s aid he peacefully settled causes beyond the limits of human judgment and counsel; and, making possible many things of this sort that were impossible by the power of faith rather than by the spirit of this world—as though moving mountains—he appeared ever more marvelous and venerable in the eyes of all. Most especially, the power of preaching began to shine in him so strongly that it softened even the hard hearts of hearers to conversion, and he scarcely ever returned home empty-handed.

Later, as both his practice of speaking and his example of life advanced happily, the net of God’s word in the hand of God’s fisherman began to enclose such abundant multitudes of rational fish that the little vessel of that house seemed capable of being filled from each of his catches. Thus it came about that, in a short time, by a miracle greater than all the miracles he performed in this life, through one man weak, half-dead, and able only to speak, that valley, obscure until then, became Clairvaux in fact as well as name. A light of divine brightness, as though flowing down from a lofty summit of virtues, spread over the lowlands of the earth. From that time the mountains began to drip sweetness around the valley which had formerly been called the Valley of Wormwood and Bitterness. Once empty and barren of every good, it began to abound in spiritual [Col. 0261A] grain; and all its wildernesses grew so rich with the dew of heaven and God’s blessing, magnifying their joy by a people multiplied, that what was long ago said by the prophet to the city of Jerusalem seems fulfilled in it:

> “Still the children of your barrenness shall say in your ears, ‘The place is too narrow; make room for us to dwell.’ And you shall say in your heart, ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not bear; who then has brought these up?’”  
> (Isaiah 49:20–21)

62. Already the monastic dwelling in that narrow valley had, not without certain divine revelations, been transferred to a more level and spacious place; there it was enlarged and extended, and even now the place is too small for the multitude of inhabitants. Already the houses of that Order, daughters of that house, have filled many wildernesses on this side and beyond the Alps and the seas; and there are still people, daily arriving, for whom a place must be sought. Brothers are requested and sent out everywhere, since kings of nations and prelates of Churches, [1087] cities and regions, consider themselves blessed if they have deserved to obtain some association with that house and the discipline of the Man of God.

What am I saying? This religious way of life has advanced beyond humankind even to barbarous nations, where natural savagery has in a sense stripped off human nature itself. There, through it, beasts of the forest become human beings; having become accustomed to associate with human beings, they learn to sing a new song to the Lord. Therefore God’s fisherman, at the Lord’s command, does not cease to cast [Col. 0261C] his nets for a catch. As some depart and others succeed them in their place, the fullness of that holy congregation is never diminished. Such have been, and daily are, the marvelous catches made in Châlons, Rheims, Paris, Mainz, Liège, and several other cities; likewise in Flanders, Germany, Italy, Aquitaine, and every other region which, through whatever necessity, it once happened—or still happens to this day—that the Man of God should visit. For through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, wherever he goes, he returns full, and his fullness accompanies him everywhere.

63. Nor does he abandon those whom he sends away from himself. Wherever they are, he remains with them in constant fatherly concern; and just as rivers return to the place from which they flow, so the joyful and sorrowful affairs of his sons return daily to him. Even without any disclosure of flesh and blood, divine grace often makes known to his fatherly concern what is happening to some of them far away: what must be provided for them, what must be corrected in them, their temptations and transgressions, illnesses and deaths, and the assaults of any worldly troubles. Indeed, he often appoints prayer among the brothers around him for the particular needs of absent brothers. At times those dying in other places are also known to have come to him in a vision, seeking his blessing and permission; [Col. 0262A] undoubtedly this is brought about both by the obedience of those sent and by the charity of him who sends them.

Once I had come to him and, while speaking with him, saw and heard something which I ought not to keep silent. A monk of Foigny was present and was about to return immediately to his brethren. Having received an answer concerning the matters for which he had come, he was already leaving Bernard. But the Prophet of God recalled him in the spirit and power of Elijah, named a certain brother of that house, and, in my hearing, ordered him to correct certain hidden matters. Otherwise, he was to expect God’s judgment upon himself soon. Astonished, the monk asked who had told him this. “Whoever told me,” Bernard said, “you go and say what I tell you; lest, if you conceal it, an equal punishment for sin enfold you also.” I wondered at this; but while I wondered, in an exactly similar matter I was told far more marvelous things about him.

64. For Guy, his elder brother among his brothers, was a man whose seriousness and truthfulness all who could know him know. When we were together somewhere [otherwise: at some time] and were speaking of such things, I asked him, as friendly conversation among friends often does: “Are these tales true which one hears?” In his habitual manner and with his customary zeal he belittled his brother’s virtues, though he did not wish to trouble me. “I do not tell you,” he said, “what I do not know; but I know and have experienced one thing: many things are revealed to him in prayer.”

Then he told me how, when those hives of spiritual bees, first flowing with honey, began to produce new swarms from themselves all around and to found new houses of their Order from them, they built, at the request and urging of Lord William the bishop, the house called Troisfontaines in the diocese of Châlons.  
[Note: [Col. 0261] Troisfontaines, in the duchy of Bar, founded in 1118.]

They sent there as abbot, with monks, Lord Roger, noble according to the world but nobler in holiness, along with certain men like him. Yet the spiritual Father did not abandon the sons he had sent, but remained with them in fatherly concern and loving affection. One day the Abbot and Guy, from whose account I learned this, were alone together and speaking with one another about those brothers. Suddenly Bernard sighed deeply, his heart responding to him with something harsher than usual concerning them. “Go,” he said to his brother, “pray for them; and whatever God shows you about them, report to me.” Bernard himself was at that time confined to bed by a very grave illness.

Guy was greatly alarmed. “Far be it from me!” he said. “I am not a man who knows how to pray in that manner or deserves to obtain such a thing.” But as Bernard persisted, he went and prayed. Praying as much as he could, he poured out his soul for each one. For each of them he was filled in prayer with such sweetness of conscience, such confidence of being heard, and every grace of spiritual consolation, that his spirit rejoiced in certain faith that he had been heard in all cases except two. In those two, prayer faltered, devotion hesitated, and confidence [Col. 0263A] failed. When he reported this to the one who had sent him, Bernard at once pronounced concerning those two what the event afterward proved.

65. Abbot Roger and several of those with him were the very men whom the Man of God had once drawn from the city of Châlons, men concerning whom, or among whom, something similar had occurred even then. While he was frequently visiting Châlons at the bishop’s invitation, he once returned bringing with him a multitude of nobles and learned men, clerics and laymen. While they were still staying in the guesthouse, and he was watering the new plantings with heavenly teachings, the monk porter arrived and announced that Stephen of Vitry, their master, had come to renounce the world and dwell with them.  
[Note: [Col. 0263D] Common reading: Vitry.]

Who would not have rejoiced at the arrival of such a man, especially since the valley did not yet abound greatly in this kind of grain? Yet Bernard, as the Holy Spirit revealed to him the snares of spiritual wickedness, was silent briefly and sighed; then, with all listening, he cried out: “An evil spirit has brought him here. He came alone; alone he will return.” All were astounded, having previously been unable to contain their joy at the news of his arrival.

Nevertheless, lest he scandalize his children while they were still little, Bernard received the man and earnestly instructed him about perseverance and other pursuits of virtue. Though he knew and foresaw that the man, while promising everything, would do nothing, he admitted him into the novices’ cell to be tested alongside those who truly sought God and would persevere. None of the things he had foretold failed. Stephen himself confessed that, while he was still staying in the novices’ cell, he saw a little Moorish boy dragging him out of the oratory. Having remained there for about nine months, he finally failed; and, as had been foretold of him, just as he had come alone, so he departed alone. The enemy’s cunning was frustrated; and those for whose ruin he had prepared Stephen were instead strengthened by Stephen’s own downfall.

66. Before we leave Châlons: once, as the holy Father was returning from there, he and those with him suffered severely from cold and wind. Many who happened then to be in his company went before him and, because of the bitter cold, paid no attention to him; he followed almost alone. It happened that the horse of one of the two men with him, carelessly left free, escaped and ran out across a broad plain. They could not catch it, and the severity of the weather did not allow them to spend longer on the matter. “Let us pray,” he said. Kneeling in prayer with the brother who was with him, they had scarcely been able to finish the Lord’s Prayer when the horse, returning with complete gentleness, [Col. 0264A] stopped at his feet and was restored to its rider.

## CHAPTER XIV. Of certain other benefits divinely bestowed through him, and of his flight from honors and dignities.

67. To pass from Châlons to the city of Rheims: once, when the archbishop and people of Rheims were in disagreement, it happened that the Man of God was present to reconcile them. He was seated in the palace of that city with Joslenus, bishop of Soissons, and, with the house filled by a great multitude of clergy and people, peace was being discussed. Then before them all a wretched woman offered him her son, whom she believed to be possessed by a demon, begging for mercy. For that very day he had risen against his [Col. 0264B] mother and nearly killed her. He had become mute, blind, and deaf; with open eyes he did not see, all his senses were stunned, and he remained even without understanding.

Bernard had compassion on the miserable mother, whose perception of the boy’s suffering tortured her most intensely. He gently encouraged the wretched young man, caressing his head and face with compassionate hands, and began to speak with him, asking how he had dared to lay hands upon his mother. The youth returned to himself at once, recognized his sin, promised amendment thereafter, and was restored unharmed to his mother.

In the monastery called Alpense, among other sick people seeking his care, a woman suffering from the falling sickness came to him.  
[Note: [Col. 0263D] Incorporated into the Cistercian Order in 1136, in the diocese of Geneva.]

At that very hour, as she stood before him, she fell under a sudden attack of her illness. But the Man of the Lord took her hand and immediately raised her; nor was she healed only for that hour, but was completely cured of her illness.

68. The Duchess of Lorraine, a noblewoman but one who had not lived so nobly, once saw in a dream that man of God drawing seven horrible serpents out of her womb with his own hands. Afterwards, converted by his admonition to a religious life, she boasts to this day that she is the woman from whom he cast out seven demons.  
[Note: [Col. 0263D] Namely, in the convent of Tart, of the Cistercian Order, then near and now within Dijon, as is clear both from chapter 7 of the third *Life* and from the letters of Matthew, Duke of Lorraine, her son, for that same convent, in Chifflet. This duchess is there called Adelaide. See Letter 119.]

I knew a cleric named Nicholas, almost hopelessly given over to the world, but freed from the world through Bernard. Once he had received at Clairvaux the habit and rule of monastic life, he saw those who had fled there from the shipwreck of the world continually redeeming the losses of their shipwreck by tears. Wanting to do the same but unable because of the hardness of his heart, he begged Bernard, with great sorrow of heart, to obtain for him from God the grace of tears. Bernard prayed and obtained for him such great and unceasing contrition of heart, together with the grace of tears, that his countenance was scarcely ever found changed in any way [Col. 0265A] and his eyes scarcely ever without tears, even while eating, travelling on the road, or speaking with anyone.

69. So numerous and so great are the miracles which in this manner we have heard and seen concerning him, and the diverse forms of assistance afforded to diverse human needs, that if anyone wished to recount them all, whether orally or in writing, he might produce unbelief in the fastidious, or weariness in the unbelieving. Yet in all his works the body of his bright activity plainly declares how pure was the eye of his intention. For, by declining—not boastfully rejecting, but religiously and reasonably avoiding—the highest ecclesiastical honours and the favour of secular princes, which continually pursued him as though he were worthy of them, he clearly showed what he always sought and desired in all his activity. [At Milan and Rheims, with the clergy choosing and the people acclaiming, he was named archbishop; at Châlons and Langres, bishop; and the same would already have occurred in many other cities, had there been any hope of securing his consent.]

And although he was worthy to be compelled, by some judgment of God—and for a long time he had enjoyed among all men such singular reverence for his holiness—that he was never compelled to do anything against his will. Yet, though in this way he fled the honour of this world, he did not escape the authority belonging to every honour: worthy, in every conscience, to be feared and loved in the fear and love of God. Wherever he was present, nothing contrary to justice was dared; wherever he spoke or acted for justice, he was obeyed.

70. Supported by such authority in the Church of God, when the necessity of obedience or charity pressed upon him, he shrank from no hardship in his labour. To whose will, to whose counsel, did every height of secular as well as ecclesiastical rank submit itself so humbly? Proud kings, princes and tyrants, soldiers and plunderers, fear and revere him so greatly that one might think fulfilled in them what the Lord is read to have said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Behold,” he says, “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall hurt you” (Luke 10:19).

But among spiritual persons, and where spiritual matters are examined spiritually, his authority is far different. For as it is said through the prophet concerning the holy living creatures, that “when there came a voice from above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood still and lowered their wings” (Ezek. 1:25), so today, throughout the world, all spiritual persons, when he speaks or treats a subject, stand still, yielding to the one who goes before; and they submit their own senses and understandings to his senses and understandings. [His writings bear witness to this—those which he himself wrote, and those which others wrote down as they received them from his mouth.]

Thus the distinctions of sacred virtues commend that holy man, even to this day, before God and before men; testimonies surround him with holiness; the gifts of the Holy Spirit illumine him. And, what is greater than all these and most difficult in human affairs, all these things seem to attend him without envy. What restrains envy toward him is something greater than all envy: namely, that the wickedness of the human heart often ceases to envy a man precisely where it cannot hope to attain.

**1090**

71. Moreover, he himself either kills all envy by the example of humility, changes it for the better by the incitement of charity, or, if it is more wicked and hardened, overwhelms it by the weight of his authority. For who today is found with prudence so effective and affectionate in fostering charity where it exists and provoking it where it does not? Who is so beneficent toward all whom he can help, so well-disposed toward everyone, possessing such graciousness toward friends and patience toward enemies?—if indeed he could ever have had any enemy, since he never wished to be an enemy to anyone.

For just as friendship exists only between two persons, and can exist only between two friends, so perhaps enmity too exists only between two enemies. A person who hates, or does not love, one who loves him is not so much an enemy as unjust. But one who loves every human being and by his own virtue never has an enemy may nevertheless sometimes suffer from another’s gratuitous injustice acting as an enemy against him. Yet the charity which wholly possesses him is patient and kind: wisdom conquering malice, patience impatience, humility pride.

[Col. 0266C]

## Subscription to the Preceding Work, Added after the Author’s Death by Burchard, Abbot of Balerne

[Note: [Col. 0265D] Letter 146 is addressed to him.]

The foregoing work, written concerning the life of the most holy Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, by the venerable William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry but then already a monk of the monastery of Signy—to which he had withdrawn out of a desire for solitude and quiet—is known to have been arranged down to the time of the schism raised against Pope Innocent by Peter Leonis.

For that faithful man had a special reason for writing: the friendship and intimacy in which he had long been united with the man of God. Accordingly, he had found such favour with him that scarcely another could be found more intimate for sharing the secrets of their mutual affection and for holding conversations about spiritual mysteries. The grace of this intimacy is especially made manifest even now by the fact that the same saint wrote many letters to him, in which what he thought of him is clearly evident to those who read them. He also wrote for him the book *Apology*, and another, *On Grace and Free Choice*.

Yet William had a stronger, general reason for writing: namely, the benefit of the whole Church of God, lest, when a vessel full of desirable treasure is hidden, the treasure itself likewise be hidden. Hence one who desires it to be brought forth rightly complains, saying: “A treasure unseen, and wisdom hidden: what benefit is there in either?” (Sirach 20:32). This writer brings forth the riches of salvation, the desirable treasure, lest it should lie concealed beneath clods of earth—though it is not earth, but a most precious pearl.

Yet, contrary to his own desire, it happened to him that, as he had declared himself to fear in his preface, he was overtaken by death and did not complete what he had conceived in his mind to commit to writing. Therefore, whoever undertakes to read this work will readily understand from what perfection the pious child and religious Bernard, like another Benedict, began the first stages of his conversion. Even in his mother’s womb he appeared to have received a signification [otherwise, sanctification] from which were conceived the presages of the future holiness alike of his life and his teaching. What he also began to do when he had become a young man is narrated in the foregoing work; and thereafter he is carefully portrayed up to the man of perfection, insofar as, as has already been said, this was permitted to an excellent painter who was overtaken by death.

[Col. 0267]

# Book Two

## By Ernald [otherwise, Arnald], Abbot of Bonneval, in the Territory of Chartres

**1091**

## Preface

[Col. 0267B]

Some writers, exalting the deeds of illustrious men with praises, have celebrated them in formal language to the extent permitted by the efforts of outstanding genius and eloquent speech. When writer and work are joined in equal embrace and united in an equal bond, and talent and eloquence concur in ordering the proposed theme, the enterprise goes well: the matter, worthily and orderly arranged, reaches a calm and tranquil harbour by a direct course.

But when the sublimity of the subject, under an unskilled craftsman, is shipwrecked against rocks, and the dullness of his understanding gives way, exhausting the writer’s presumption, deliberation about correction begins too late. For what has been poured out among many cannot be recalled or corrected; and it would be more fitting for the discordance between writing and deeds to be erased than amended.

Reflecting and turning these matters over in my mind, I greatly fear that, just as I am accustomed to be indignant at the imprudence of many who, lacking knowledge and eloquence, rush into writing and, having vigorously blown their noses, draw blood, so I too, if I undertake what is above me, shall expose myself to ridicule. For who am I, that I should aspire to write the deeds of the most holy Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, who flourished in our age in singular religious devotion and learning; whose fragrance, poured out, filled the whole Church; and whose grace, through the Lord’s working, is declared by signs and miracles?

How many learned men, how many rhetoricians, how many philosophers of this world have schools sent to his monastery for the contemplative life and godly conduct? What discipline did not flourish there, where there were companies of masters and distinguished men eminent for practised understanding, who, devoted to sacred studies, teach and kindle one another by many incentives of grace? [Their unanimous community sings the Song of Ascents; and, ascending with Jacob to the summit of the ladder, sees God clearly in his splendour, radiant with a crown.]

Surely those men, lacking nothing in any grace, ought to have undertaken this labour and inscribed the memorials of the venerable Father, so that through their effort there might be a delightful page, which they might hand to their disciples to read as though it were living, and that lasting consolation might remain beside the relics of the sacred body and teaching laid there. But the humility of Clairvaux is accustomed to emulate what is lowly and to conceal what men might admire. Those noble men are ashamed to bring any tokens of themselves into public; and contempt and lowliness make them more at peace than any offer of dignity in which their profession of humility seems endangered.

For such reasons, keeping themselves within the hinges of silence, they take more delight in the sackcloth of the wilderness than in the shoe [otherwise, silk] of a palace; they now seek glory not in the pen but in the cross. Therefore, in this matter, as in other affairs of this sort, they willingly lay the burdens of their undertakings upon others. And now that the lord William of venerable memory has been taken away—he who faithfully and devoutly wrote the glorious beginnings of that holy man—the request for this work has come to my lowliness. The charity of the beloved Church has imposed it upon me: that I might cook a stew for the sons of the prophets. If through carelessness I should mix colocynths into it, Elisha, as I trust, will season it by scattering flour over it; and the affection of obedience will excuse the excesses of foolishness.

# Chapter I. On the Pontificate of Innocent II, Vigorously and Successfully Defended through the Work of Saint Bernard; Also on the Pope’s Journey into Gaul and the Check upon the Emperor

1. At that time Pope Honorius entered upon the way of all flesh (A.D. 1130). Without delay, as the cardinals disagreed in the election and the Church was divided, the greater number—sounder in judgment, men approved in life and endowed with virtues, priests, deacons, and bishops—elected Innocent, whose life, reputation, age, and learning were considered worthy of the supreme priesthood.

But the other party, supporting infamous undertakings by violence rather than reason, separately and precipitately nominated, by fraudulent contrivances, Peter Leonis—who aspired to this height—as Anacletus, and, despite the opposition of the others, ordained him. Those who belonged to the Catholic party solemnly enthroned their elected pope in the chair; they conducted him through those places where Roman pontiffs customarily hold their sittings from ancient usage; and for the time being the honour due to apostolic dignity was present.

At that time they stayed near the Lateran palace, and even their own houses no longer afforded them a safe dwelling, since Peter’s followers harassed them most fiercely. Unable to hold out there long, they found temporary shelter in the towers of certain Roman nobles allied with them. Yet loyalty did not endure even in these places. In a short time men were won over either by force, by fear of the reckless mob, or by money. For Peter had such a multitude, both through the inherent power of his lineage and through the family connections of those attached to him, that almost the whole city followed him, bound either by money or advantage.

He had indeed amassed innumerable riches, both from the exactions of the curia and from the transactions of legations, and had reserved them for the fair he anticipated. Moreover, a great accumulation of his paternal revenues, hitherto sealed up but now distributed among the people, armed for every crime a populace put up for sale. After these funds had been spent, he tore royal gifts, in the form of church ornaments, from the very altars. And when those profane Christians themselves either feared or were ashamed to break up chalices and divide golden crucifixes limb by limb, Jews, they say, were sought out to shatter boldly the sacred vessels and images dedicated to God.

Thus each man, hired for wickedness according to his degree, greater or lesser, publicly sold his assent to Peter under general oaths and stretched out hands and weapons for every kind of bloodshed; and in daily encounters they pursued with curses and swords the party which stood with Innocent.

2. The servants of God therefore took counsel; and, since they could not protect themselves by human force, chose to yield. Having secretly procured ships, they escaped down the Tiber into the Tyrrhenian Sea from the mouth of the lion and the hand of the beast. Favourable winds driving the sails, they happily reached the port of Pisa.

[When the arrival of so great men was heard and the reason why they had departed from the City was known, Pisa rejoiced that the glory of the Roman name had been transferred to her; for while Rome engraved upon itself the mark of perpetual disgrace, Pisa was preparing for itself an inscription of everlasting name and enduring fame. The dignitaries and consuls therefore came out to meet them. Falling at the feet of the lord Pope, they gave thanks that he had judged them worthy of so great an honour as to choose their city, which he deigned to illumine with his own presence.

“The city is yours,” they said, “and we are your people. We serve you at our own expense; indeed, whatever resources the republic has stored up, it shall devote to your uses. You will find no duplicity among the Pisans: they will not cling to you one moment and recoil the next; swear one moment and dissolve their oaths the next. This people does not hunger for domestic plunder and civil slaughter. Our nation is neither bold at home nor timid abroad. We are neither slaves nor masters, but fellow citizens and brothers, outdoing one another in honour, not provoking one another by seditious enterprises. At home we practise gentleness; foreigners often experience our courage. Having subdued the Carthaginians and subjected the Balearic Islands, triumphing by land and sea over pirates and criminals, we brought their captive kings in chains to Pisa. With their spoils and varied furnishings the crossroads and squares are adorned at your coming, and the rejoicing city is crowned.”

After such words, as the people came forward to meet them, the way scarcely lay open for the arrivals because of the innumerable multitude. But as they advanced slowly, the cardinals presented themselves to matrons, maidens, and little children who gazed out through the windows, longing to see them; and extending blessings on every side, the lord Pope and his company were gloriously conducted to the house of the canons of Blessed Mary and honourably received.]

3. Before leaving Rome, the lord Pope had sent envoys into Gaul to inform the Gallican Church of the course of the dissension and schism created by Peter, and to urge the bishops to arm themselves for vengeance upon this presumption and, condemning the schismatic party, to subscribe to unity. But the full nature of the affair had not yet become known to the bishops, nor had anyone ventured privately to grant his assent, until a general assembly was gathered at Étampes and they might determine jointly what they should receive and what condemn.

For France, unlike other regions prone to schisms, has never been stained by such a faction [otherwise, by accepting Guibert or Burdin]; it has not acquiesced in the errors of evil men, nor fashioned an idol in the Church and worshipped a monster in Peter’s chair. In such causes, authoritative edicts never frightened them, nor did they prefer private advantage to the common good. They did not incline to a party or defer to persons, but to causes. If necessary, they courageously resisted persecutions and did not fear losses or exile.

When the council at Étampes had been summoned, the holy abbot Bernard of Clairvaux, called in particular by the king of the Franks himself and by the principal bishops, arrived—as he later confessed—more than moderately fearful and trembling, since he did not fail to recognize the danger and weight of the affair. Yet on the journey God consoled him, showing him in a vision of the night a great Church singing harmoniously in God’s praises; from this he hoped that peace would undoubtedly result.

When they had arrived at the place, a fast was first observed and prayers poured forth to God. Then the king and bishops, with the princes, sat down to deliberate upon the matter. The counsel and judgment of all was one: that the cause of God should be entrusted to God’s servant, and that the whole matter should depend upon his mouth. Though fearful and trembling, he accepted this task at the urging of faithful men. Having carefully set forth the order of election, the merits of the electors, and the life and reputation of the first man elected, he opened his mouth and the Holy Spirit filled it. Thus, speaking as the mouth of them all, he declared that Innocent ought to be received by all as supreme pontiff. They all together acclaimed that this was ratified; after the customary praises to God had been sung, they promised obedience thereafter and all alike subscribed to Innocent’s election.

[Col. 0271A]

4. Meanwhile, the Pope himself, after settling many matters authoritatively at Pisa, in Tuscany, and in other provinces, took leave of the Pisans and gave them thanks. He was conveyed by ship to Provence, crossed Burgundy, and arrived at Orléans, where, as the bishops came to meet him, he was gladly and honourably received by Louis, the most pious king of the Franks. From there Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, a man of great virtues, conducted him to Chartres. There the glorious king Henry of the English also came to meet him with a very great retinue of bishops and nobles.

The venerable abbot, sent before him to the Pope, also brought this king to him. He had scarcely persuaded him to receive Innocent, since the bishops of England had entirely dissuaded him. For when the king resisted and refused in every way, Bernard said: “What do you fear? Do you fear that you will incur sin if you obey Innocent? Consider how you will answer God for your other sins; leave this one to me: let this sin be upon me.” Persuaded by these words, that most powerful king met the lord Pope outside his own realm, as far as Chartres. [Many things were said and done there, and many secular and ecclesiastical matters were settled.]

5. Meanwhile the lord Pope’s legates returned from Germany, bringing the assent and letters both of the bishops and of the king, as well as a public entreaty that, crossing over to them, he might grant them his longed-for presence. For they were easily persuaded to receive the one whom the others had already received. But the love and devotion of the Gallican Church detained him, and individuals and all alike sought an apostolic visitation.

Accordingly, after travelling through France, [at Rheims he summoned a council (A.D. 1131), in which, after arranging many matters for God’s honour, he crowned King Louis—while his father was alive—in place of his brother Philip. In all these affairs the lord Pope would not allow the abbot to be separated from him, but he sat with the cardinals in public business. Privately, too, all who had matters to settle consulted the man of God in secret. He in turn reported what he heard to the curia and afforded patronage to the oppressed.

When the council had been dissolved, the lord Pope went to Liège to meet the king of the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0271D] Innocent’s journey to Liège before the Council of Rheims has been shown in the Preface to volume one.] He was indeed honourably received, but that calm was quickly clouded. For the same king urgently pressed, judging the time opportune for the restoration to himself of the investitures of bishops, which the Roman Church had wrested from his predecessor, Emperor Henry, through very great labours and many dangers. At these words the Romans were terrified and grew pale, judging that they had encountered a graver peril at Liège than that which they had escaped at Rome. No counsel was available until the holy abbot placed himself as a wall before them. Courageously resisting the king, he rebuked that wicked proposal with remarkable freedom and checked it with remarkable authority.]

6. Returning from Liège, the lord Pope wished personally to visit Clairvaux. There he was received with the deepest feeling by Christ’s poor, who were not adorned with purple and fine linen, who did not come out with gilded Gospel books, but carried a rough cross in ragged companies; not with the thunder of clamorous trumpets or loud rejoicing, but with subdued chant. The bishops wept, the supreme pontiff himself wept, and all marvelled at the gravity of that community: in so solemn a joy, all eyes remained fixed upon the ground and wandered nowhere in curious observation. With eyelids closed, they themselves saw no one, yet were seen by all.

The Roman saw nothing in that church which he might desire; no furnishings stirred his gaze. In the oratory they saw nothing but bare walls. Ambition could only covet their morals, and such booty could not harm the brothers, since religious devotion could not be diminished by being carried away. All rejoiced in the Lord, and the celebration was conducted not with foods but with virtues.

There, whole-wheat bread (*panis autopyrus*) was set forth instead of fine flour; *sapa* instead of *carenum*; vegetables instead of turbot; and legumes instead of every sort of delicacy. If a fish happened to be found, it was served to the lord Pope and benefited the community by its appearance, not its consumption.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] *Panis autopyrus* is bread from which neither flour-dust nor bran has been removed, as though it retained the whole of the wheat undiminished. See Celsus, book II, chapter 17. It differs from common bread (*panis cibarius*), from which a good portion of the flour-dust has been taken and which is largely bran-like. It also differs from fine flour (*simila*), which is the pith of wheat flour—that is, the portion between the flour-dust and the second-grade flour. *Carenum*, according to Laurence of Lucca, is a kind of boiled sweet wine. But *sapa*—elsewhere denoting wine reduced by boiling to one third—is the juice of herbs; hence perhaps French *soupe*, “broth.” Here, I think, it is used for *zytum*, that is, beer, or for barley-gruel (*ptisana*). *Rhombus*, French *turbot*, is a kind of flat fish.]

7. The devil, unable to endure the glory of God’s servants, whom the presence of so distinguished a guest rendered illustrious, grew envious. While they were singing the psalms gladly and devoutly in choir, with certain cardinals also present, who delighted in hearing and seeing them, he disturbed several of the brothers with dreadful terror. One above the rest was possessed and uttered certain blasphemous words: “Say,” he cried, “I am Christ.” Several others, terrified and trembling, fled to the feet of the blessed Father.

But he turned to the others and said, “Pray.” Then, in silence, he led out those who seemed disturbed and restrained them, so that the most wicked one, who was attempting to turn an assembly of devotion into a theatre and a school of innocence into mockery, might not, as he supposed, damage the reputation of religious men, but might expose himself and find his attempts powerless. Everything was calmed with such speed that the persons standing nearby were entirely unaware of what had happened. Thus the malignant enemy, quickly rebuked, was unable not merely to cause the scandal which he was preparing for them, but even to bring the event to their knowledge.

The result was that the brothers thereafter fortified themselves with greater watchfulness; and, deservedly, Clairvaux grew thereafter in numbers and possessions, and religious life was extended through almost the whole extent of that place as its communities multiplied. From this time the holy abbot himself also shone more than usual in miracles and signs.

# Chapter II. On the Synod Held at Pisa by Innocent; Also on the Milanese, Reconciled to the Church through Bernard’s Work, and on the Possessed He Healed There

8. The lord Pope could not remain long in Gaul. Rather, as he had arranged with King Lothair, he met him at Rome and was conducted by force of arms into the Lateran palace. Many of the Roman nobles also, faithful to the Church, honourably received him. But Peter Leonis, who did not set God as his helper but was surrounded by the wickedness of his confederates, remained in towers higher and safer and mocked Lothair’s strength. Forbidding his followers public engagements, he neither exposed himself to danger for the sake of his security nor gave his enemies cause for battle; nevertheless, he impeded their free movement by engines placed above and by various obstacles.

He most obstinately avoided a meeting with the emperor. Neither threats nor blandishments moved him, and he admitted no person’s counsel concerning his position. The emperor therefore departed, leaving Innocent in Rome. But after his departure Peter made frequent raids through the City and thirsted for the slaughter of the faithful.

Innocent, understanding that his stay in Rome at that time was fruitless and unwilling that his presence should inflame the rage of that beast, returned again to Pisa. [Note: [Col. 0273D] See Letter 130.] There, after bishops from the whole West and other religious men had assembled, a synod of great splendour was celebrated (A.D. 1134). The holy abbot was present throughout, sharing in its counsels, judgments, and all its decrees. All paid him reverence, and priests kept watch before his threshold—not through any pride on his part, but because the crowd prevented ordinary access. As some went out, others entered, so that the humble man, who claimed none of these honours for himself, seemed to possess not merely a share in responsibility but the fullness of authority.

It would take too long to recount the proceedings of the council. Its principal result, however, lay in the excommunication of Peter and the irreversible deposition of his supporters; and this sentence remains in force to this day.

9. When the council was dissolved, the lord Pope sent the abbot of Clairvaux—whom the Milanese had sought with many entreaties—together with Guy of Pisa and Matthew, bishop of Albano, his legates, to reconcile the Milanese. [Note: [Col. 0274D] In the same year, 1134; see Letter 131.] They were to wash away the schism introduced in that city through Anselm and restore the straying people to the unity of the Church.

The abbot, with the aforesaid men whom he had received from the lord Pope as colleagues, added to their company and common counsel the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, whose innocence and sincerity he had tested in many matters. For it seemed good to the cardinals that an undertaking of such weight should be supported by so great a helper.

Having crossed the Apennines, they learned that the Milanese had heard that the abbot they desired was approaching their territory. Seven miles from the city all the people came out to meet him: nobles and commoners, horsemen and footmen, people of middling rank and poor alike. As though migrating from the city, they left their own homes and, in separate companies, received the man of God with incredible reverence. All alike delighted in the sight of him; those able to enjoy hearing him judged themselves fortunate. Everyone kissed his feet. Though he received this painfully, he could by no reasoning restrain them as they bowed in devotion, nor could he repel them by prohibition.

They even plucked whatever hairs they could from his garments and tore off pieces of the cloth to use as remedies for diseases, judging holy everything which he had touched and believing that they themselves were sanctified by touching or using such things. Those going before and those following applauded the abbot with joyful acclamations; after being kept for a long time amid the dense crowds, he was at last given solemn hospitality.

When the matter for which both the man of God and the cardinals had come was publicly discussed, the city, forgetting its strength and laying aside all fierceness, submitted itself so completely to the abbot that the poet’s little verse could fittingly be applied to its obedience:

> “To obey commands is for me as necessary as to will and to be able.”

10. Once all matters had been pacified, the Church reconciled, and compacts of concord established among the peoples, other affairs began to arise. As the devil raged in certain possessed bodies, the banner of Christ was raised against him; and when the man of God rebuked him, the demons, terrified and trembling before the greater power that came upon the possessed dwellings, fled away.

Behold a new embassy, carrying not a Roman decree but advancing the decree of faith according to divine laws, producing in the midst letters written with Christ’s blood and impressed with the seal of the cross—a figure which by its authority subjects and bends to itself earthly and infernal things. In our times such faith among the people, such power in one man, has not been heard of. A devout contention existed among them: the abbot attributed the glory of the signs to their faith, while they attributed it to the abbot’s holiness and believed without doubt that whatever he asked from the Lord he obtained.

Accordingly, without hesitation they brought to him a woman known to all, whom an unclean spirit had tormented for seven years. They humbly asked him to command the demon, in the Lord’s name, to flee and to restore health to the woman. The people’s faith caused the man of God no slight embarrassment. With humility as his teacher, he did not presume to attempt what was unfamiliar; yet, pressed by the people’s request, he was ashamed to resist too obstinately the charity of those who asked. It seemed to him that he would offend God and that he would appear to cloud God’s omnipotence by distrust if his own faith dissented from the people’s faith.

Thus he struggled within himself; and although he maintained that signs ought to be given not to believers but to unbelievers, he entrusted his venture to the Holy Spirit. Applying himself to prayer, and with power descending from heaven, he rebuked and drove Satan away in the spirit of strength, restoring the woman sound and calm. Those present rejoiced and, lifting their hands to the stars, gave thanks to God who had visited them from on high.

This report was heard, its fame spread abroad, and suddenly it stirred the whole city. From every direction people gathered in churches, public buildings, and crossroads; everywhere they spoke of the man of God. Publicly they said that nothing was impossible for him to obtain from the Lord; they said, believed, proclaimed, and affirmed that God’s ears stood open to his prayers. They could not in any way be satisfied with the sight or hearing of him. Some rushed into his presence; others waited at the doors until he should come out. Work in offices and crafts ceased; the whole city remained intent upon this spectacle. They came together and asked for his blessing; and each person considered it healing merely to have touched him.

11. On the third day, as the servant of God went to the church of Saint Ambrose to celebrate the divine mysteries, an innumerable crowd awaited him there. During the very solemnities of the Mass, while he sat beside the altar as the clerics sang, they brought before him a little girl whom the devil tormented with violent attack, begging him to aid the poor child and crush the demon raging in her.

Hearing the supplication of those standing by, and seeing her gnash her teeth and shriek so that she was a horror even to those who looked upon her, he felt compassion for her age and sorrow for the intensity of her distress. He took the paten of the chalice in which he was to celebrate the divine mysteries. With his fingers wetted by the liquid, praying inwardly and trusting in the Lord’s power, he applied the healing drink to the girl’s mouth and let a medicinal drop fall into her body.

Without delay, as if Satan were being burned, he could not bear the power of that infusion. Pressed inwardly by the antidote of the cross, he hastened out and burst forth trembling in a most filthy vomit. Thus, the person being cleansed and the devil put to flight and confounded, the Church sang due praises to God. After joyful acclamations, the eager people remained motionless there until the divine mysteries were completed. In full sight of all, the little girl, sound, was led home by her own people; and only with difficulty was the man of God at last released by the crowd and able to return to his lodging.

[Col. 0275D]

12. By divine judgment, at that time in Milan, according to Isaiah’s words, “the hairy ones (*pilosi*) cried one to another, and demons encountered the onocentaurs” (Isa. 34:14); and in unbridled outbreaks they afflicted many people. There was no one able to resist their insolence, since for a long time under the schism of Anselm—Peter’s supporter, who had occupied the Milanese see—mourning priests, neglected virgins, accursed consecrations, and a polluted altar had provoked God’s wrath upon the people.

But at the coming of the man of God, once Anselm’s impostures had been rejected and the Church restored under Innocent to obedience to the Apostolic See, this licence of the demons was checked. Daily the devil gave ground and fled at the prayers of the man of God; and whenever he attempted resistance, he was overcome in the very conflict and gloriously defeated.

# Chapter III. On the Expulsion of Demons from Various Possessed Persons—by the Power of the Eucharist, by Blessed Bread and Water, and by the Sign of the Cross; Also on Other Benefits of Healing
13. Among those who were afflicted was an elderly woman, a citizen of Milan and formerly an honourable matron. After the blessed Man, she was dragged by many people as far as the church of St Ambrose. For many years the devil had dwelt in her breast and had by then so suffocated her that, deprived of sight, hearing, and speech, grinding her teeth and thrusting out her tongue like an elephant’s trunk, she seemed a monster rather than a woman. Her filthy face, dreadful expression, and foul breath bore witness to the foulness of Satan, her inhabitant. When the Man of God saw her, he recognized the devil clinging to her and glued fast to her (*inviscatum*; variant: *invisceratum*, ‘embedded within’), and knew that it would not readily leave the dwelling it had possessed for so long.

Turning to the people, of whom an innumerable multitude was present, he ordered them to pray more intently; and he ordered the clergy and monks standing with him beside the altar to place and restrain the woman there. She resisted, kicking back not with natural strength but with demonic force, and, not without injuring others, struck the Abbot himself with her foot. He gently disregarded this audacity of the devil; and, seeking her deliverance, he called upon God for help, not with angry indignation but with peaceful and humble supplication, and approached the offering of the saving sacrifice. Yet as often as he signed that same sacred Host, so often, turning likewise toward the woman and making the same sign of the cross, the strong athlete assailed the wicked spirit. For whenever the sign of the cross was directed against him, that malignant one, showing that he had been struck, raged more fiercely; and, kicking against the goad, unwillingly disclosed what he was suffering.

14. When the Lord’s Prayer had been completed, the blessed man attacked the enemy more forcefully. Placing the sacred Body of the Lord upon the paten of the chalice and setting it upon the woman’s head, he spoke as follows:

> “Your Judge is present, wicked spirit; the supreme power is present. Resist now, if you can. He who was to suffer for our salvation is present: ‘Now,’ he says, ‘the ruler of this world will be cast out’ [John 12:31]. This is that Body which was taken from the body of the Virgin, which was stretched out upon the wood of the cross, which lay in the tomb, which rose from death, which ascended into heaven while the disciples looked on. Therefore, by the dreadful power of this majesty, I command you, malignant spirit, as you depart from this servant-woman of his, never again to dare touch her.”

As he unwillingly left her and could not remain longer, he afflicted her more cruelly, having great wrath because he had but a short time. The holy Father then returned to the altar, duly completed the breaking of the saving Host, and gave the minister the peace to be distributed among the people; and immediately complete peace and health were restored to the woman. Thus that wicked one, compelled not by confession but by flight, showed how great was the efficacy and power of the divine mysteries.

Once the devil had been driven out, the woman whom that pestilential executioner had for so long fried in the frying-pan of such great torments came to herself; her senses were restored with understanding, her tongue rolled back into her mouth, and she confessed God and gave thanks. Looking upon her healer, she threw herself at his feet. A mighty cry arose through the church; every age rejoiced in God; the brass instruments sounded; God was blessed by all; reverence exceeded all measure; and, if it may be said, the city in its melting charity revered the Servant of God as more than human.

15. These deeds done at Milan were heard of; throughout all Italy the reputation of the Man of God spread, and everywhere it was proclaimed that a great prophet had arisen, mighty in deed and word, who, upon invoking Christ’s name, both healed the sick and freed the possessed from demons. Great indeed was the grace granted him in curing illnesses; but his activity in expelling demons was more frequent, because a larger number of the afflicted flocked to remedies already proved, and the working of greater miracles obscured lesser effects.

Now, because of the crowds which sat at his doors from morning until evening, he could not, given his bodily weakness, endure the pressure of the populace. He therefore came to the windows of the house and showed himself to them, raising his hand and blessing them. They also brought bread and water with them; after these had been placed before him for his blessing, they carried them away as sacramental remedies. Many had gathered from neighbouring castles, villages, and towns; and at Milan the common concern alike of visitors and citizens was to follow the Saint, seek his benefit, hear his word, and see a sign. They delighted, beyond what can be believed, in his teaching and miracles.

16. There was among them a man from the outskirts, who had brought there a demoniac boy. Suddenly, before them all, at the sign of the cross which the holy Man made, the boy fell from his bearer’s arms and, dashed upon the ground, appeared motionless and as if dead, without any sensation. There was in him neither voice nor breath; only a slight warmth remained about his breast. The others therefore made way so that the bearer of the half-dead boy might proceed and be admitted to the Man of God; and the astonished multitude waited for the outcome of so pitiable a case.

The man entered to the Man of God and laid the senseless boy, unable to perceive anything, before the Abbot’s feet, saying:

> “My lord father, this boy whom I have laid before your feet has for three years now been most grievously tormented by a demon. Whenever he enters a church, is sprinkled with exorcised salt, has the sign of the cross made over him, is compelled to hear the Gospel, or is present at the divine sacraments, the devil who inhabits him is offended and is tortured more fiercely. While I was just now waiting outside the doors with the others, as you made the sign of the holy cross and stretched out your hand over the people, the demon, irritated by the power of those sacramental signs, directed itself more violently than usual to tormenting the boy; and, as you see, occupying his whole body, it has almost cut off even his vital breath.
>
> “But the boy himself, once the report had reached our home of the grace you have received from God, hoped for his own healing from the cures of others and begged me to bring him to you. I beseech you therefore, by the mercy of God, to aid with your merciful and customary compassion both my labours—for I spend burdensome and dangerous effort in guarding him—and his misery, which is as great as you yourself can see. Do not permit the demon’s rage to advance unchecked.”

He wept; and, with his face bathed in tears, he moved all those present, so that all joined together in supplication.

17. [Col. 0278B] 1099 Then the Man of God ordered them to trust in God’s mercy and gently touched the boy’s neck with the staff upon which he leaned. His brother Gerard, wishing to test the truth of what the man had said, secretly made the sign of the cross upon the boy’s back. The boy had lain for a long time stretched upon the floor before the Abbot’s feet, without movement or sensation, neither seeing nor hearing. But at the touch of the staff and the sign of the cross he growled and, disturbed, groaned.

The Abbot ordered him to be put upon his own bed. But, as though offended by an injury, he threw himself back upon the floor, ground his teeth, and bit his attendant. Seizing the hair of those present, he struggled with all the force he could to pull himself away from their hands and could scarcely be held by them.

> “Come,” said the Abbot, “bring him back to our bed.”

While the Abbot prayed and the brethren lay prostrate in prayer, the devil testified with cries to the pain of burning torment, as though he were being burned by blazing straw contained in the bed, when divine power drew near. The holy Man then ordered blessed water to be poured into the sufferer’s mouth. He would not admit it, pressing shut his lips and teeth; but at last, when a wedge had been inserted and loosened the pressure, he received it into throat and gullet, whether he wished or not.

As soon as the penetrating sanctification descended into his inner parts, the malignant force burst forth as though an antidote had been poured in; and, amid the foulest vomiting, driven out in a rushing torrent, the devil whirled forth in headlong haste with great disgrace. Suddenly he who had seemed dead lived; rising sound and unharmed from the Abbot’s bed, he embraced his patron [variant: paternal uncle] and said, “Thanks be to God, I am well.”

All gave thanks to God together, and those who had been weeping now rejoiced. The cry spread outside; the deed done within was solemnly proclaimed from the housetops; the whole city gathered for the spectacle. God was blessed, the people rejoiced, and in the Abbot, the accomplisher of so great a deed, the affection of the entire populace found rest.

18. The same Saint obtained health for many fever sufferers by laying hands upon them and giving them blessed water to drink. By touching withered hands and limbs disabled by paralysis, he restored them to soundness. Under the testimony of many, he also powerfully obtained from the Father of lights, by the making of the sign of the cross, that blind persons in that city should see.

At the same period he entered the lodging of the Bishop of Albano—Matthew, mentioned above, no. 9 [note: Col. 0279D]—whom the lord Pope had given him as a colleague in that same legation, in order to transact affairs; and they were discussing the matters entrusted to them. Suddenly a young man rushed in, whose hand was withered and twisted back against his arm. Throwing himself at Bernard’s feet, he humbly begged for healing.

Bernard, occupied with other matters, gave him a blessing and told him to go away, forbidding him, in words more severe than his custom, to trouble him further. The man was departing without having obtained what he sought when the venerable bishop ordered him to return with all speed; taking him by the hand, he handed him over to the Abbot.

> “Do not,” he said, “close the bowels of mercy against this man, who, though he obtained no benefit, obeyed you when you told him to depart. Rather, you obey; bound by the power of obedience at my command, do what he asks and grant what he seeks. Trusting in the power of him through whom he seeks healing, ask and you shall obtain, so that both we may glory in God’s gift and he in the health for which he longed.”

19. At the bishop’s command, the Abbot took the young man’s hand, invoked the Lord, and was heard.
