When he had made the sign of the cross, the sinews that had stiffened were stretched out; and the flesh which the continual [variant: adjacent] disease had frozen became mobile and flexible as its innate soundness returned. More quickly than words can tell, the limb long weakened recovered its strength.

The bishop marvelled at the effect of so sudden a power, and thereafter honoured the Man of God with still greater reverence; he himself became a witness and reporter of his miracles. He compelled him to dine there that night, obtaining his consent only with great difficulty, on the sole ground that an unbearable crowd was waiting everywhere and that departure did not seem possible without danger.

During dinner the bishop entrusted to his household servant for safekeeping the dish from which the Abbot had eaten, commanding him to set it apart and guard it with every care. A few days later the same bishop was seized by a violent burning fever. Remembering the Man of God, he ordered the servant to be summoned.

> “Bring here without delay,” he said, “the Abbot’s dish which I recently gave you to preserve.”

When the servant had brought it, he said:

> “Pour water into it, and break up small pieces of bread.”

When this had been done, trusting in the Lord and commending himself to the Abbot’s prayers, he ate and drank and recovered without any delay.

20. The number of those arriving increased, and marvellous works drew people toward him. The Man of God was granted no rest anywhere, while others procured rest for themselves from his exhaustion. Those arriving met those departing, and seekers of benefits replaced one another.

Among them a certain knight brought in his arms to the Man of God a little girl who so hated light that she always kept her eyelids shut and even held her arm before her eyes, lest any particle of light by any means reach her. At times the arms held before her were forcibly pulled away; and, when light shone upon her, she cried out and wept. Brightness was torture to her, and visible light seemed to drive spikes into her brain.

The Man of God blessed the little girl and, making the sign of the cross over her, dismissed her calmer. As she was being carried home, she opened her eyes of her own accord and herself returned on foot, without a bearer. In that same place, in the presence of many, the same Saint obtained healing from the Father of mercies for a woman afflicted by a demon.

## Chapter IV. On demoniacs healed, and on Bernard’s remarkable humility: amid so many splendid works, he always judged himself modestly.

21. He had now arrived at Pavia. The report of his miracles had preceded his arrival, and the rejoicing city welcomed a Man of such great glory with fitting joy and ceremonial. So that delay might not long suspend the people’s desire—for, having heard of the miracles done at Milan, they wished to see a sign from him—a peasant suddenly came after him, having followed him from Milan and bringing with him his demoniac wife. In a tearful voice he set forth before Bernard’s feet the inward anxieties of his wife.

Without delay, the devil spoke through the mouth of the unhappy woman in insult to the Abbot and, mocking God’s servant, said:

> “This fellow who eats leeks and devours cabbages will not drive me out of my little bitch.”

He hurled many insults of this sort against the Man of God, so that, provoked by the blasphemies, Bernard might bear the reproaches impatiently and be humiliated before the people as he heard himself assailed with unworthy words. But the Man of God understood the devil’s tricks, mocked the mocker, and, seeking no vengeance himself but leaving it to God, ordered the demoniac woman to be brought to the church of St Syrus. He wished to give the glory of her healing to the Martyr and have the firstfruits of the miracle attributed to his power.

But St Syrus sent the affair back to his guest; claiming nothing for himself in his own church, he wished the unperformed work to be brought back to the Abbot. The woman was therefore brought to the Abbot’s lodging, while the devil chattered through her mouth and said:

> “Little Syrus will not cast me out; little Bernard will not expel me.”

To this the servant of God replied:

> “Neither Syrus nor Bernard will cast you out, but the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then he turned to prayer, entreating the Lord for the woman’s health. At that the wicked spirit, as though his former insolence had changed, said:

> “How gladly I would leave this little bitch—how grievously I am troubled in her! How gladly I would leave! But I cannot.”

When asked the reason, he said:

> “Because the great Lord does not yet will it.”

The Saint asked him, “And who is the great Lord?”

He replied, “Jesus of Nazareth.”

The Man of God again asked, “How do you know Jesus, or have you ever seen him?”

> “I have seen him.”

“Where did you see him?”

> “In glory.”

“And were you in glory?”

> “I was indeed.”

“How did you leave it?”

> “With Lucifer,” he said, “many of us fell.”

All this he spoke in a mournful voice through the mouth of the old woman, in the hearing of all. The holy Abbot then replied:

> “Would you not wish to return to that glory and be restored to your former joy?”

Again changing his voice and laughing in a strange manner, he said:

> “That is delayed” [variant: “slow”].

He said nothing further. As the Man of God prayed more intently, that utterly wicked one was overcome and departed; and the woman, restored to herself, gave as much thanks as she could.

22. The man therefore returned with his wife, rejoicing throughout the journey in her recovery, and was restored to his household where his friends awaited him. All rejoiced when they heard the account of what had occurred; but suddenly joy was changed to sorrow. For when the woman touched the threshold of her own home, the devil entered her again and, more savage than usual, tore the miserable woman apart more cruelly.

What was the unhappy husband to do, or where was he to turn? To live with a demoniac seemed most burdensome; to abandon her seemed wicked. Therefore, taking the woman with him, he returned again to Pavia. When he did not find the Man of God there, he followed him as far as Cremona. He reported what had happened and tearfully begged to find grace.

The Abbot’s mercy did not fail the pious petitioner. He ordered him to enter the church of that city and wait in prayer before the bodies of the confessors until he himself came after. Mindful of his promise, at nightfall, when the others had gone to sleep, Bernard himself entered the church with only one companion. Devoting that whole night to prayer, he obtained from the Lord what he sought; and, having obtained healing for the woman, he ordered her to return safely to her own home.

But since she feared the devil’s return, as she had already experienced it, he ordered a small paper bearing the following words to be tied around her neck:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I command you, demon, never henceforth to dare touch this woman.”

The devil so feared this command that he never afterward dared approach the woman after she had returned home.

23. There was also in the same city a certain demoniac whose affliction moved many to laughter, though others of more serious disposition pitied him with the most compassionate sympathy. He barked so that, if you heard him without seeing him, you would think him a dog. When the Man of God had him brought before him and heard him barking, he groaned. He barked as dogs that have been beaten or crushed usually rage and snarl [variant: growl] at those who strike them. In the Man of God’s presence too, panting and barking, he was more violently disturbed than usual.

The devil was rebuked and cast out by Christ’s power, and Bernard ordered the man to speak. Cleansed, the man entered the church, attended the sacraments, fortified himself with the sign of the cross, heard the Gospels, confessed and prayed, and rendered and consecrated to God the other duties of a sound mind.

24. When the holy Father passed through Milan a second time in the same year, a demoniac woman was brought to him. She had been absent when the Man of God first glorified the aforementioned city with his presence. A demon possessed her which spoke now Italian, now Iberian; nor was it sufficiently clear whether it was one bilingual demon or two, each using the idiom of its own language. But it spoke now one language, now the other, so properly that you would say, “This speaker is a Ligurian; this one a Spaniard.”

She was also afflicted by weakness in her knees and trembling in her hamstrings. When she had been brought to the Man of God, with sudden spring and unexpected swiftness she leapt over the bench upon which he sat. When she was brought back and asked what was the meaning of her leap and flight, and whence so much force and swiftness had come to an old and sick woman, she replied that the devil’s presence gave her this agility: she could overtake galloping horses and leap onto their backs without any assistance.

On the following day, while she was attending in the church the divine offices that he was celebrating, she was most cruelly and for a very long time tormented before all. The Abbot pitied the woman and, having often experienced God’s mercy in such cases, commanded the devil to leave. At the command of the Servant of God, it vanished trembling. The woman recovered at once, not only from the torment but also from the contraction of her sinews.

These and many other works the Man of God performed while he was within the Alps; travelling through various places, he did good to the sick, giving sight to the blind, raising up the weak, healing those with fevers, and with especially diligent care cleansing those oppressed by the devil. The breasts which the malignant spirit had defiled he consecrated as temples acceptable to God.

25. Very many things concurred in him that were worthy of approval and praise. Some admired his teaching, others his character, others his miracles. I indeed render fitting honour to all these things; but above all, as far as I am able, I judge this higher and proclaim it more earnestly: although he was a chosen vessel and fearlessly bore Christ’s name before nations and kings; although the princes of the world obeyed him and bishops in every nation stood at his beck; although the Roman Church itself revered his counsels by a singular privilege and, as though granting him a general legation, subjected nations and kingdoms to him; although, what is judged more glorious, his deeds and words were confirmed by miracles—he never overreached himself, never walked in things too wonderful for him. Always thinking humbly of himself, he believed himself not the author but the minister of his venerable works. Though in everyone’s judgment he was supreme, in his own judgment he held himself to be least.

He ascribed to God alone whatever he did; indeed, he both perceived and declared that he could neither will nor accomplish any good except through God’s inspiration and work. Yet divine power was present in the acceptable time and day of salvation, setting apart for its Gospel the servant whose humility it had regarded and whose soul the Holy Spirit had adorned. And because no duplicity stained his sincerity, nor did any admixture of falsehood interrupt his goodness, that same Spirit remained unmoved in its place.

26. So that he might always be more resplendent and pure, he was tested daily in the furnace. Lest any rust creep upon him, he was struck, scourged, and reproved by frequent hammer-blows upon the anvil—not as punishment for guilt, but as glory for virtue. The goad of illness never failed him. Knowing that power is perfected in weakness, he experienced grace as sufficient in this respect: he saw that every movement in himself, however slightly irregular, was daily scraped away by the file of that affliction.

His flesh was weak, but his spirit willing. Since he could take less delight in the body, he took greater delight in the Lord; and no ambition of this world stirred him, for he longed only for heavenly things. How many Churches left without pastors elected him as their bishop? The Church of Langres, his own home church, elected him; Châlons elected him. Within Italy, the city of Genoa and Milan, the metropolis of the Ligurians, desired him as pastor and teacher. Rheims, the most noble city of France and capital of the province of Belgica Secunda, sought his governance. Setting all these calls aside, the offered honour did not trouble his soul, nor did his foot move to incline toward glory; the tiara and ring pleased him no more than the rake and hoe.

27. To those who asked for him, neither ever consenting nor refusing insolently or improperly, he said that he did not belong to himself but had been assigned to the service of others. When this was reported to the brethren, they replied:

> “Having sold all that we possessed, we bought the precious pearl that we had found. We cannot return to the estates we disposed of. If both the price and what was purchased should be lost to us, and we should be deprived both of our possessions and of the pearl, our expectation has been poorly provided for, if, after pouring out our oil, we must beg like foolish virgins before closed doors.”

The holy brethren had also taken counsel for themselves and were fortified by the authority of the lord Pope, so that no one could take their joy from them, turn others’ consolation into their affliction, or increase others’ abundance through their poverty. By these and other arguments the servants of God had defeated the petitioners. It was now everywhere known that God had established the Abbot in the Church as Moses had been among the Hebrew people: though Moses was not high priest, he nevertheless anointed and consecrated Aaron as high priest; and the entire Levitical succession always obeyed his ordinances.

## Chapter V. On Bernard’s return from Italy and the transfer of the monastery of Clairvaux to a more spacious site.

28. He had now crossed the Alps in the year 1135. Shepherds, herdsmen, and rustic people came down from the highest crags to meet him, shouting from afar and asking for a blessing. Returning to their sheepfolds, they crept through the mountain passes, talking with one another and rejoicing that they had seen the Saint of the Lord and received the grace of the desired blessing as his hand was stretched out over them.

At last, arriving at Chrysopolis [note: Gallic, Besançon; Col. 0283D], he was solemnly conducted as far as Langres. Near that territory the brethren of Clairvaux came to meet him; falling at his knees, they rose to kiss him. Conversing with him in turn, they joyfully led him to Clairvaux.

The brethren gathered together and received their beloved Father with wonderful devotion. Their joy was conducted without tumult and with all gravity. Their faces, indeed, could not conceal their pure delight; but their disciplined manner of action and speech did not exceed its proper limits, and their very affections restrained themselves lest they do anything in which the mark of laxness should offend the maturity of their religious observance.

During the Abbot’s long absence, the devil had been able to weave nothing at Clairvaux; nor had he meanwhile rubbed any rust upon their sincere minds. In no part was the house of God, founded upon the rock, shaken. Though absent in body, the Servant of God had so fortified and strengthened his work by the urgency of his prayers, while present in spirit, that no crack appeared likely to open in so great a structure.

No quarrels had been kept for his arrival; no hatreds, fostered in secret, burst forth in the judge’s presence. The younger brethren made no complaint against their elders concerning severity or harshness; the elders made no accusation against the younger concerning any laxness or relaxation. The condition of all was sound, their fellowship harmonious, their unity true. They were all found to be of one disposition in God’s house, in peace and holiness, climbing Jacob’s ladder and hastening toward the vision of God, whose delightful aspect shone forth above.

The Abbot, therefore, not forgetful of him who said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” [Luke 10:18], was the humbler and more subject to God because he understood that God was favourably present to his desires. He did not glory in himself because demons were subject to him; rather, he rejoiced in the Lord because he saw his brothers’ names written in heaven, their unanimity keeping them unstained from this world.

29. His venerable brethren were present in his counsels. Present was Godfrey, Prior of the same place, his kinsman in flesh and spirit, a wise and steadfast man. By his merit in religious life and prudence, he was afterward made bishop in the Church of Langres; preserving a model of holiness and not diminishing the honour of the dignity in which he stands, he perseveres to this day, praiseworthy in his comings and goings.

He, therefore, and many other prudent men concerned for the common good sometimes compelled the Man of God, whose conversation was in heaven, to descend and informed him of what the household’s need required. They represented to him that the place in which they had settled was narrow and inconvenient, not capable of containing so great a multitude; that, as the numbers arriving in companies increased daily, they could not be received within the buildings already constructed, and that even the oratory scarcely sufficed for the monks alone.

They added that they had examined a suitable level tract lower down, together with the advantage of the river that flowed below; there was there a spacious site for all the monastery’s needs—for meadows, farms, groves, and vineyards. If enclosure by woodland seemed lacking, this could readily be supplied by stone walls, since there was a vast abundance of stone there.

At first the Man of God did not agree to the plan.

> “You see,” he said, “that, with much expense and labour, the stone buildings have already been completed [note: the Corbie manuscript reads, ‘this house is prepared; the church is lofty, the stone buildings, etc.’; Col. 0285D], and aqueducts have been carried through the several workshops at the greatest cost. If we destroy all this, people of the world may think ill of us: either that we are fickle and changeable, or that excessive wealth—which we do not have—has made us mad. And since you know with complete certainty that we have no money, I tell you in the Gospel’s words that one intending to build a tower must calculate the expense of the future work; otherwise, when he has begun and failed, people will say: ‘This foolish man began to build and was not able to finish’ [Luke 14:30].”

30. To this the brethren replied:

> “If, after the completion of what belongs to the monastery, God had ceased to send inhabitants, this judgment might stand, and it would be a reasonable decision to cease from works. But now, since God daily multiplies his flock, either those whom he sends must be turned away or provision must be made for a dwelling in which they may be received. Nor is there any doubt that he who prepares inhabitants also prepares dwellings. Far be it from us, through distrust concerning expenses, to incur the risks of this disgrace!”

Hearing this, the Abbot delighted in their faith and charity and at last agreed to their counsel, though only after first pouring forth many prayers to God about the matter and receiving certain revelations beforehand. The brethren rejoiced when the word had been publicly announced.

31. The most noble prince Theobald, of holy memory, heard of this and gave much toward the expense, promising more ample aid. The bishops of the regions, distinguished men, and merchants of the land heard of it, and gladly and without compulsion freely contributed abundant assistance to God’s work. With resources abundant and workmen quickly hired, the brethren themselves devoted themselves completely to the work. Some cut timber; [others squared stones; others built walls;] others divided the river by extended channels and raised its waters to supply the mills. [The words in square brackets are taken from the Corbie manuscript; note: Col. 0286D.]

Fullers, bakers, tanners, smiths, and other craftsmen also fitted suitable machines to their own works, so that the stream, conducted through underground channels throughout the whole house, might bubble up and flow forth wherever it was useful. Finally, once appropriate services had been supplied in all the workshops, the waters that had been dispersed returned, after cleansing the house, to the main channel and restored to the river its proper volume.

The walls were completed with unexpected speed, enclosing the whole precinct of the monastery with the greatest spaciousness. The house rose up; and the newly born church, as though it had a living and movable soul, swiftly advanced and grew.

## Chapter VI. On the schism in Aquitaine, settled through Bernard’s action; and on a woman marvellously freed from an incubus demon.

32. At that time the whole Church of Bordeaux laboured under the oppression of schismatics; and in Aquitaine there was no one who could resist the prince, whose heart God had hardened. With the approval of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, who planted seeds of dissension in his heart, the prince became defender and author of the schism in the year 1135.

All who did not subscribe to the recognition of Peter Leonis were exposed to persecution: some were punished by confiscations, others by banishment, and others were driven from their own sees and compelled to live in exile. Into the ears of that Count, by repeated persuasions [variant: suggestions], hissed like the ancient serpent that crafty man who had long been papal legate in those regions. Now, cast down from so great an office, he could not endure to be bishop merely of his own single Church when he had seen himself prince and master of all Aquitaine.

He blushed to return to his original household, when the provinces of Tours, Bordeaux, and Auch had been subject to his dominion, and when all that the Ocean encompasses and bounds from the Iberian hills to the Loire had obeyed his authority. Accustomed, therefore, to plunder provinces and, under the title of justice, to make profit from cases that arose, he had amassed boundless wealth, which was to him an idol and an image of apostasy.

Seeing, then, that his authority for exactions had perished, and that the one household which had lately been thronged with many clamours now lacked revenues, this man of serpentine cunning could not bear that his hands were no longer filled with gifts. He hastened to send to Peter Leonis, asking him to grant him a legation; he himself would swear obedience and loyalty and, besides, would incline the prince of the land and all whom he could to Peter’s authority.

The man of perdition rejoiced, thinking that he had found a place in which to extend his wickedness. He quickly consented and, in order to support the error, willingly and promptly delegated to him Giles, cardinal-bishop of Tusculum, who alone among the Romans, together with Peter, bishop of Porto, had adhered to him.

33. Gerard himself, who had previously lamented that he had been mutilated, recovered his horns and thereafter began to appear more secure and more audacious. For, what he had not done before, he now went about publicly wearing the mitre, so that the very insignia of his sacred office might claim greater reverence for him among the people. He therefore assailed the Count with large sums of money, invaded his soul with poisonous arguments, and easily seduced and corrupted a man already disposed to such things. First, William, bishop of Poitiers—a worthy man, a Catholic, steadfast in the communion and defence of the universal Church—was violently expelled from the city of Poitiers, and condemned by Cardinal Gerard and his ally because he rejected Peter. There were also private reasons for which the Count had long been hostile to him; given the occasion, he most willingly pursued and disowned him.

It seemed good both to Gerard and to the Count to create without delay a bishop at Poitiers to confirm their party. They found an ambitious man, noble indeed by birth but degenerate in faith. With the assent of certain clerics, they elected him, so that they might bring his lineage into the cause with him; and, laying profane hands upon him, they did not so much anoint his execrable head as defile it. They intruded a similar monster into the Church of Limoges: a certain Ramnulf, abbot of Dorat, whom divine vengeance shortly afterward overtook. Falling backward from his horse on a level road, with one avenging stone—left there, as it were, for this purpose—driven into his head, and his brain shattered, he expired.

[Col. 0287B]

34. On hearing these and similar reports, the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, to whom Pope Innocent had entrusted the legation of Aquitaine, was deeply grieved. Setting aside other business, he determined to bring aid to the endangered Church without delay. He therefore sought out and implored the abbot of Clairvaux to help him eliminate such evils. The man of God consented, informing him that he was shortly to lead a community of monks into Brittany, to a place near Nantes which Countess Ermengard had prepared; once that house had been arranged according to its kinds and species, he promised to proceed with him into Aquitaine.

They travelled together and, to avoid many digressions, arrived together at Nantes. In that region there was a miserable woman afflicted by a wanton demon.

That lascivious demon appeared to her in the form of a knight, very handsome in appearance. By an inward and hidden suggestion, and outwardly flattering speech, he deceitfully inclined her mind toward love of himself. Having gained the woman’s consent, he spread out his arms, placed her feet upon one of his hands, covered her head with the other, and thereby endowed her with the sign of this covenant [variant: betrothed her to himself]. She had a husband, a valiant knight, wholly ignorant of this abominable intercourse. That utterly impure adulterer therefore abused her invisibly, even while her husband lay in the same bed, and tormented her with incredible lust.

35. For six years the evil remained concealed, nor did the ruined woman disclose the shame of so great a crime. But in the seventh year she was confounded within herself and terrified—both by the foulness of such continual disgrace and by fear of God, by whose judgment she feared every moment to be overtaken and condemned. She fled to priests and confessed the sin. She travelled through holy places and implored the aid of the saints; but neither confession, prayer, nor abundant almsgiving availed her. Every day, as before—and more importunately—she was harassed by the demon. At length the crime became publicly known. When it had been heard and recognized, her husband abhorred her companionship.

Meanwhile the man of God had arrived with his company at the aforesaid place. When the unhappy woman heard of his arrival, she threw herself trembling at his feet. Bathed in tears, she disclosed to him her horrible affliction and long-established deception, and said that none of the acts imposed upon her by the priests had helped her. She added that her oppressor had foretold his arrival and threateningly forbidden her to come into his presence, because it would do her no good; and that, once the Abbot had departed, he who had been her lover would become her most cruel persecutor.

Hearing this, the man of God consoled the woman with gentle words; promising help from heaven, he commanded her—for night was already approaching—to return the following day, trusting in the Lord. When she returned in the morning and reported to the man of God the blasphemies and threats which she had heard that same night from her incubus, he said: “Do not fear his threats. Take this staff of ours and place it in your bed; then let him do what he can.”

The woman did as she had been commanded. Reclining in her bed, fortified with the sign of the cross, she placed the staff beside her. He immediately appeared, but dared approach neither his customary act nor the bed itself. He nevertheless threatened most fiercely that, once the man of God departed, he himself would return to inflict punishments upon her.

Sunday was approaching, and the man of God wished the people to be summoned to church by episcopal decree. When a very great crowd had gathered there on that day, during the solemnities of the Masses, with Bishops Geoffrey of Chartres and Bricius of Nantes accompanying him, he mounted the pulpit and announced that all in the church were to hold lighted candles in their hands, for he was about to speak. He himself did so with the bishops and clerics. He then publicly exposed the unprecedented audacity of the devil and, with the assent of all the faithful present, anathematized the spirit of fornication which had burned into such horrible pollutions, even contrary to its own nature. By Christ’s authority he forbade it access both to that woman and thereafter to all women.

When those sacramental lights were extinguished, all the devil’s power was henceforth extinguished. After the woman had confessed and received communion, the enemy never again appeared to her; expelled beyond return, he fled away.

[Col. 0288C]

36. Having accomplished these things, the Abbot and the legate entered Aquitaine together. Meanwhile Gerard, with the Count’s consent, had seized the archbishopric of Bordeaux and held at the same time the churches of Bordeaux and Angoulême. But as the money which he had cast into the hands of flatterers ran out, and as the truth became more and more evident, the support of princes was now ebbing away from him, and men feared to become defenders of his treachery. He therefore stayed in places where he considered himself safer and no longer readily appeared at public assemblies.

To recapitulate briefly what occurred earlier: as soon as word first began to spread of Gerard’s schemes against the Church of God, while Pope Innocent was still staying in Gaul, our Abbot of Clairvaux and the venerable Joslenus, bishop of Soissons, were sent and came as far as Poitiers to meet both Gerard himself and the aforesaid prince. But Gerard, having already persuaded that prince, began shamelessly to hurl insults against the Catholic Church from which he was separating himself, and to withhold the obedience he had previously promised to Innocent. He called his Anacletus the worthier chosen one [variant: “more worthily chosen”], and termed all who did not obey him erring men and headless persons. Thus clerics, encouraged and armed for madness, publicly began from that day to persecute Catholics.

Yet before they had thus cut themselves off from unity [variant: before their treachery had thus been made public and hardened, he had offered, etc.], the holy Abbot had offered sacrifice to God in their church. After his departure, the dean of that church impiously—but not without punishment—destroyed the altar on which he had celebrated the divine mysteries. For shortly afterward, struck by God, as he breathed out his spirit, he saw the house in which he was dying full of demons. Crying out that a demon was cutting his throat, he asked those standing by for a knife to plunge into his own throat, so that, when the demon had been drawn out, he might live. But the devil to whom he had been given extinguished him amid these words and plunged his pestilent soul into hell.

The archpriest, too, who proclaimed the synod of Peter, invader of the Church of Poitiers, was seized by a demon before those whom he was inviting to this assembly of treachery. Divine power had also visibly inflicted vengeance upon many others who had been more ardent in that schism. Because of these and other such events, Gerard had begun to be shamed before men; and, fearing that things which could not be denied would be laid to his charge, he avoided public meetings.

[Col. 0289C]

37. Meanwhile, distinguished men who could safely dare approach the Count informed him that the Abbot of Clairvaux, the bishop of Chartres, other bishops, and religious men sought a conference with him. Their purpose, moreover, was to discuss with him peace for the Church and the removal of evil. He was persuaded not to avoid a meeting with such great men, since, after taking counsel with them, that which now seemed difficult might easily become possible, and that which appeared impossible might by an unexpected outcome be rendered possible.

Accordingly they met from either side at Parthenay. First, concerning the division of the Church and the obstinacy of the schism—which, south of the Alps, had settled only in Aquitaine like a corrupting mist—the servants of God made known to the Count in many ways and by many arguments that the Church is one, and that whatever lies outside it, like what lies outside the ark, must necessarily perish and be washed away by God’s judgment. They also cited Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive for the guilt of schism (Num. 16:31–32), showing that God’s vengeance has never at any time been absent from so great an evil.

Hearing this, the Count adopted in part a sounder counsel and replied that he could consent to obedience to Pope Innocent; but he could by no argument be induced to restore the bishops whom he had expelled from their sees, because they had offended him beyond reconciliation, and he had sworn never at any time to accept peace with them. The discussion was prolonged for a long time through intermediaries. While they occupied one another in turn with words, the man of God, taking up more effective arms, went to the holy altar to offer sacrifice and prayer. Those permitted to participate in the divine mysteries entered the church; the Count remained outside the doors.

[Col. 0290A]

38. When the consecrations had been completed and peace had been given and spread among the people, the man of God—now acting no longer as a man—placed the Lord’s body upon the paten and carried it with him. With a face of fire and flaming eyes, not pleading but threatening, he went outside and addressed the Duke in terrible words:

“We asked you, and you despised us. In another conference which we have already held with you, the gathered multitude of God’s servants pleaded with you, and you scorned them. Behold, the Son of the Virgin comes forth to you: he is the head and Lord of the Church which you persecute. Your Judge is present, at whose name every knee bends, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Your Judge is present, into whose hands that soul of yours will come. Will you despise him also? Will you likewise scorn him, as you have scorned his servants?”

All present wept and, intent upon prayer, awaited the outcome. The expectation of all hung in suspense, awaiting, I know not what divine action from heaven. Seeing the Abbot advance in vehement spirit and bear the most sacred body of the Lord in his hands, the Count was terrified and frozen. His limbs trembled and failed from fear; as though out of his mind, he fell to the ground. Raised up by his knights, he fell again upon his face. Speaking to no one and looking at no one, with saliva running down into his beard and deep groans issuing from him, he appeared epileptic.

Then the man of God approached him more closely. Striking his bent body with his foot, he ordered him to rise, stand upon his feet, and hear God’s sentence. “The bishop of Poitiers, whom you expelled from his church, is present. Go and be reconciled with him; join with him in a covenant through the holy kiss of peace; and yourself restore him to his see. Make satisfaction to God: render glory in return for insult, and throughout all your principality recall those who are divided and at variance to the unity of charity. Submit to Pope Innocent; and as the whole Church obeys him, so you too obey this pontiff, chosen by God for so great an office.”

Hearing this, the Count, overcome by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the presence of the holy Sacraments, neither dared nor was able to reply. But he immediately hastened forward, received the bishop in the kiss of peace, and with the same hand by which he had disowned him restored him to his own see, amid the rejoicing of the whole city. Thereafter the Abbot, conversing with the Count more familiarly and gently, admonished him as a father not again to rise to deeds so impious and rash, not to provoke God’s patience by such enormous crimes, and not to violate in any respect the peace that had been made.

[Col. 0290D]

39. Thus peace was restored to the whole Church of Aquitaine, while Gerard alone persisted in evil. But not long afterward, when the day of wrath came, he was miserably destroyed in his own house. Scripture says, “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16). Impenitent and dying suddenly, without confession or viaticum, he rendered up his departing spirit to him whose minister he had remained to the end.

His nephews, whom he had raised to honours in that church, found his body lifeless in his bed and monstrously swollen. It was buried in a certain basilica, but afterward Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, had it removed from there and cast elsewhere. His nephews too were later driven out of that church; his entire offspring and plantation were torn up by the root and went into exile through foreign realms, bearing complaints of so great a judgment.

When so great an evil had been buried and Gerard’s schism reduced to ashes, the man of God returned with great joy to Clairvaux. The brethren were present, gathered about his feet; they gave thanks to God, who crowns good beginnings with happier results and glorifies and exalts everywhere the humility of his servant.

[Col. 0291B]

40. Having found a period of rest, the man of God occupied himself with other pursuits. Withdrawing into a small hut woven about with ropes of rushes, he intended to devote himself alone to divine meditation. Suddenly, in that humble lodging, as though standing beside the Lord’s manger, he encountered the loving Songs and the spiritual fare of the wedding feast. He considered and marvelled that the Bridegroom, beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, upon whom even angels desire to look, had loved a dark bride, sun-darkened, and exalted her with such praise as to call her wholly beautiful and without any blemish.

He also marvelled that the bride languished with love, and carefully inquired what that charity might be whose kisses [variant: breasts] are sweeter than wine, a taste of which the soul pants to receive with such longing. Though the Bridegroom extols the bride with many praises, he nevertheless does not in all things grant her the full abundance of himself or yield himself to the bride’s desire unto the fullness of satiety. At times, when sought, he is not found; and, after long wanderings, when he is found, he is held lest he flee.

For a long time [variant: for some time] he poured out his soul in meditation upon these matters. How much he advanced, who daily feasted upon those delights, and how much he benefited us, for whom he preserved in writing the remnants of the same blessing—this is clear to those who read it.

## Chapter VII. On the cause of the schism at Rome, and the successful conduct of affairs with Roger, king of Sicily

41. Meanwhile apostolic letters summoned the man of God, and the cardinals begged him to assist the Church in its distress. His studies were interrupted, and journeys—until then continuous—were resumed at intervals. No leisure remained: the servant of God either prayed, meditated, read, or preached.

Seeing that excuses were uselessly being made [variant: put forward], [and that it was necessary to obey commands], he gathered the brethren from many regions. After sighing long and deeply, he addressed them:

“You see, brothers, amid how great tribulations the Church labours. Peter’s party, struck down by God’s action both in Italy and Aquitaine, no longer brings forth but miscarries. In these lands the defenders of schism have been scattered. At Rome a great part of the nobility follows Innocent, and many of the faithful favour him. Yet fearing the onslaught of the reckless multitude, they do not dare publicly confess the assent by which they have upheld Innocent. Peter has conspirators, ruined men whom he has corrupted with money; occupying their strongholds, he displays not the faith of Simon Peter but the tricks of Simon Magus.

“After the West has been subdued, one struggle against one people remains. While you pray and rejoice, Jericho will fall; and when, like Moses, you stretch out your hands to God, defeated Amalek will flee. Joshua fights and, that the day may be lengthened sufficiently for the completion of victory, commands rather than merely prays that the sun stand still. Faith merits both the sun’s obedience and victory over the prostrate enemy.

“Therefore, while we fight, bring us support and implore help from heaven with suppliant hearts. Do what you are doing and remain at the rank in which you stand. Although you know nothing against yourselves, do not on that account judge yourselves righteous, for God alone judges those whom he justifies, and every one, however perfect, is unaware of the searching examination of divine judgment. Do not care greatly about being judged by a human day, approving neither your own judgments nor those of others. Stand thus in the fear of God: do not, when judging anyone, ever become proud; and do not, by attending to others’ judgments, fall into trivialities. While pursuing each matter, reckon yourselves unprofitable servants. We must go where obedience calls us. We entrust and commend to God, in confidence in his mercy, the brotherhood [variant: fatherhood] of this house and your guardianship, for whose sake we undertake this labour.”

[Col. 0292C]

42. Having said this and bestowed his blessing, he departed amid the tears of all. Received everywhere with great reverence, he finally reached Rome. At his arrival both the lord Pope and the brethren rejoiced. After they had shared counsel with him, the Abbot undertook another course according to the development of events and the state of affairs. Placing no hope in chariots or horses, but accepting conversations with certain persons, he investigated what resources they possessed and what was the disposition of their supporters: whether error or malice led them to maintain and prolong so great a crime.

From private discussions he learned that the clergy who were with Peter were anxious about their situation. They knew their sin but did not dare return, lest they be marked by perpetual disgrace and held cheap among the rest. They preferred meanwhile to remain thus under a semblance of respectability rather than be expelled from their sees and exposed to public begging. Those of Peter’s own lineage replied that no one would thereafter believe them if they dismembered their family and abandoned him who was the head and lord of their kin. The rest excused treachery by their oath of loyalty; no one gave support to that party from a sound conscience.

The Abbot therefore declared to them that bonds of impiety are sacrilegious, that profane conspiracies condemned by laws and canons cannot be fortified by oaths, and that the sacraments of truth neither can nor ought to support falsehood. Those who suppose that an unlawful matter can stand under the protection of an oath, he said, are mad; for extraordinary compacts, however sanctioned under a pretext of religion, must be recalled [variant: annulled] as void and dissolved by divine authority.

When they heard these and other words of the man of God, they withdrew from Peter. As the ranks of that party were daily broken up, its bonds were shattered. Peter himself also lost heart, for he had no doubt that he was diminishing day by day and Innocent increasing. Money failed, the magnificence of the court wasted away, and the household’s services dried up. Few guests frequented his table; delicacies had been exchanged for common food; the dress of attendants was made dull by age; the mercenaries, lean and sharp-featured, were crushed by debt; and the whole pale appearance of the household indicated approaching dissolution.

[Col. 0293B]

43. Meanwhile Roger, king of Sicily, now the only prince refusing obedience to Pope Innocent, sent to him asking that he dispatch to him his chancellor Haimeric and the Abbot of Clairvaux. He likewise asked Peter Leonis to send Peter of Pisa from his side. He said that he wished to know the origin of this dissension, long since hardened; once he knew the truth, he would either correct the error or ratify the decision.

But he sent deceitfully, for he had heard that Peter of Pisa was most eloquent and second to none in knowledge of laws and canons. He thought that if Peter’s eloquence were given a hearing in public consistory, rhetorical declamations might overwhelm the Abbot’s simplicity and impose silence upon him through the force of words and weight of arguments.

To make the matter brief, both parties came to Salerno. But vengeance had already taken the field and forestalled the contrivance of so great a crime. For the king had prepared an innumerable army for war against Duke Ranulf and brought armed battle-lines into the field. Yet when he suddenly saw the Duke boldly advancing to meet him, he was terrified and fled, exposing his scattered army to plunder and slaughter. Countless soldiers were captured and killed, and he unwillingly enriched the Duke with resources and exalted his glory. All this happened to him in accordance with the man of God’s word.

For when the holy Abbot, the first of those summoned, arrived and found the King encamped, he prevented the neighbouring armies from joining battle for many days, declaring to the King: “If you enter the conflict, you will depart defeated and disgraced.” But at last, as that king’s army had grown greatly, not knowing that the outcome of war does not lie in a multitude, he scorned further to listen to the holy man seeking the things that made for peace.

[Col. 0293D]

44. The Abbot, however, powerfully exhorted Duke Ranulf and the Catholic battle-line. As he had promised the King flight, so he promised them victory and triumph. When he turned aside to a nearby village and persisted in prayer, suddenly there was heard the cry of fugitives and pursuers. Ranulf was pursuing the King’s fleeing army through that very place.

Then one of the brothers with the Abbot went out, met one of the soldiers, and asked what had happened. The soldier, being literate, replied: “I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. 36:35–36). Without delay the Duke himself followed. When he saw the monk, armed as he was, he leapt down from his horse and, falling at his feet, said: “I give thanks to God and to his faithful servant, because this victory has been granted not through our strength but through his faith.” Then he mounted his horse again and pursued the enemy.

[Col. 0294B]

45. Yet the King’s mind was not corrected by this blow inflicted upon him from heaven, nor did the storm which the exaltation of his perverse heart had heaped up subside. Rather, after those who had escaped returned from their flight, he feigned cheerfulness, raised himself up in royal adornment, and with his court surrounded by soldiers ordered both parties to be summoned. Having first instructed Peter and fired him with inducements of many promises, he ordered him to speak on the arguments for his cause.

Peter spoke first and strove to prove that his lord’s election was canonical, fortifying his words with many assertions from law and canon. But the man of God, understanding that the kingdom of God consists not in word but in power, said:

“Peter, I know that you are a wise and learned man; and I wish that sounder and more honourable affairs had occupied you. I wish that a more just and happier cause had secured you as its advocate. Then indeed no eloquence could hinder you when you argued reasonably. We are rustic men, more accustomed to mattocks than to legal advocacy [variant: declamations]; had the cause of faith not pressed us, we would have maintained our accustomed silence.

“But charity compels us now to speak, because Peter Leonis, with the Lord permitting it, tears and rends the Lord’s tunic—a tunic which, at the time of the Passion, neither pagan nor Jew presumed to tear. One is the faith, one the Lord, one baptism. We know neither two lords, nor a double faith, nor two baptisms.

“To begin with the ancient examples: there was one ark in the time of the Flood. In it eight souls escaped, while all others perished; and all who were found outside the ark perished. No one doubts that this ark prefigures the Church. A second ark has recently been built; and since there are two, one of them must be adulterous and sink into the deep. If the ark ruled by Peter is from God, the ark ruled by Innocent must be overwhelmed. Therefore the Eastern Church will perish, and the entire West will perish; France will perish, Germany will perish; Iberians, Englishmen, and barbarian kingdoms will sink into the depths of the sea. The Camaldolese [variant: Camaldulensian], Carthusian, Cluniac, Grandmontine, Cistercian, and Premonstratensian orders, together with innumerable other communities of God’s male and female servants, must collapse under one tempest into the abyss. Bishops, abbots, and the remaining princes of the Church, with millstones tied around their necks, will be received by the devouring sea.

“Has this Roger alone, among the princes of the world, entered Peter’s ark, so that, when all the rest have been drowned, he alone will be saved? Far be it that the religion of the whole world should perish while the ambition of Peter—whose manner of life has been publicly known—should gain the kingdom of heaven!”

[Col. 0295A]

46. At these words those present could no longer restrain themselves, but abhorred both the life and cause of Peter Leonis. The Abbot took Peter of Pisa by the hand, raised him up, and rose with him. “If you believe me,” he said, “we shall enter the safer ark.” Then, addressing him with saving admonitions, as he had long before conceived in his mind, he immediately persuaded him—by the cooperation of God’s grace—to return to Rome and be reconciled to Pope Innocent.

When the assembly had dissolved, the King still refused to obey. Coveting to seize St Peter’s patrimony, which is very extensive in the regions of Cassino and Benevento, he thought that by such delays he could extort from the Romans certain privileges by which that inheritance would thereafter be secured to him as his own right. Thus Herod scorned the Saviour whom he had desired when absent and scorned when present (Luke 23:8, 11). Thus almighty God gave human beings the glory which he received from the Father (John 17:22), makes those who scorn him inglorious, and raises the humbled on high.

Now concerning the cure of a certain nobleman, very well known in the city of Salerno: the physicians had failed, though their art and learning were especially strong there. As the man despaired of physicians’ help, someone appeared to him by night in a dream and told him that the holy man, effective in cures, had come to Salerno. He was ordered to seek him out and drink from the water in which he had washed his hands. He sought, found, asked for water, drank, and recovered. This report spread through the entire city and reached the ears of the King and his nobles.

Thus, with the favour of all the peoples but the King alone remaining in wickedness, the Abbot returned to Rome. He reconciled the aforesaid Peter of Pisa and certain others to the Church and united them in fellowship with Pope Innocent.

[Col. 0295D]

47. The time had come when, the iniquity of the Amorite fulfilled, the smiting angel was already brandishing his sword. Passing over the houses whose thresholds were stained with the blood of the Lamb, he came to the house of Peter Leonis and found there no saving sign. He struck the wretch, though he did not die immediately; rather, a space of three days was granted for repentance. He abused God’s patience and died despairing in his sin.

His body was borne forth in miserable pomp; his corpse was buried in concealment, and to this day that grave is unknown to Catholics. Yet his party set up another pope in his place, named Victor. They did so less from stubbornness in schism than in order that, after a convenient interval, they might more suitably be reconciled to Pope Innocent—a result which Christ promptly achieved through the hand of his servant. For that ridiculous pontiff himself, Peter Leonis’s heir, came by night to the same man of God; and he brought him, stripped of the usurped insignia, to the feet of Lord Innocent.

After this was done, the rejoicing city exulted; the Church was restored to Innocent, and the Roman people revered Innocent as shepherd and lord. The Abbot of Clairvaux was held in wonderful honour: all called him the author of peace and father of his country. Noblemen accompanied him as he proceeded, the people shouted their acclamations, matrons followed, and all eagerly rendered him service. But for how long did he endure this glory? For how long did he enjoy peace after so protracted a labour? He did not consent to receive even a day in place of a year. Once all things were settled and put in order, he could scarcely be detained five days, though he had laboured for seven years and more to repair that same breach.

As he departed, Rome accompanied him; the clergy escorted him; the people gathered; all the nobility attended him. He who was cherished by common love could not be dismissed without common sorrow. [They wept after him, asked him for his blessing, and with all devotion commended themselves to his prayers.]

[Col. 0296B]

48. Having received leave from Innocent and peace having been confirmed, the man of God returned. Bringing home great joy, he was devoutly received by the brethren with thanksgiving.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “The man of God returns home, and, displaying a double joy, is received with the rejoicing of the whole land,” etc.]

Meanwhile at Rome Innocent arranged affairs with sovereign authority, and visitors came to him from every side. Some arrived with business; others came only to rejoice with him. Processions were solemnly celebrated through the churches; laying aside their arms, the people came to hear the word of the Lord. After manifold privations, the city flourished again in abundance in a short time. Peace, once firmly established, restored and recalled what had been scattered in the time of discord. Wastes were ploughed and deserts became fertile. Each person rested beneath his own vine and fig tree; night watches fell silent, doors stood open, and every fear was excluded.

In due course Innocent restored the Church’s ruins, gathered back the exiles, restored to churches their former services, restored the depopulated settlements to those who had been expelled, and further bestowed suitable gifts. He also established at Aquae Salviae a monastery in honour of St Anastasius the martyr.

[Note: There Pope Honorius I had founded a monastic community in the year 626.]

The monastery had previously existed there, but at this time only the church remained; it lacked inhabitants. Therefore, after monastic dwellings had been built, the church restored, and houses, fields, and vineyards assigned for support, the lord Pope requested and obtained from Clairvaux an abbot and a community of brethren. Bernard was sent—

[Note: Surnamed de Paganellis.]

—formerly vice-lord of the church of Pisa, together with devout brethren, to serve the Lord in that place according to the Rule of St Benedict. That plantation swiftly prospered. Indigenous men joined it, the number of God’s servants increased, and suitable pastures soon produced abundant livestock for sustenance.

[Col. 0297A]

## Chapter VIII. On bishops of the Church produced from Clairvaux; and on the outstanding piety and severe tribulation of Count Theobald

49. The holy Abbot, returned to his studies, embraced his beloved wedding-song. From diverse regions also, as the fragrance of that religious life spread everywhere, brethren were invited to found monasteries. Once founded and established, these subjected themselves to his authority and adopted the rules of stricter discipline.

Cities of different regions also deserved bishops from this community. First, Rome was adorned with a supreme pontiff. Palestrina had Stephen, a man of complete moderation [variant: glory]; Ostia, the great man Hugh. In the Roman curia itself, Henry and another Bernard were ordained cardinals, the one priest and the other deacon. Near Rome, Nepi also flourished under Hubert. In Tuscany Baldwin, the glory of his native Pisa and a great light of the Church, shone forth. North of the Alps, Amadeus was given to Lausanne; Garinus to Sion; Godfrey to Langres; Alan to Auxerre; Bernard to Nantes; Henry to Beauvais; Giraldus to Tournai; Henry to York. In Ireland there were two bishops, Christians both in reality and in name. In the German city of Chur was Algotus, revered for wisdom, age, and grace.

These luminaries, drawn from Clairvaux, illuminated the aforesaid cities with the pure radiance of their presence. By making the glory of the pastoral office clear, they became examples to other bishops in doctrine and life, and in their high station remained always humble.

50. When Pope Innocent had died, and his successors Celestine and Lucius had also rapidly passed away, Bernard—whom we have said was formerly appointed abbot at Saint Anastasius—was made Pope of the City and was called Eugenius III. When sedition arose among the people, he shook the dust from his feet against those who quarrelled, left them, and came to France. While at Rome they were devouring and biting one another, and consuming one another, he waited peacefully until, wearied by conflicts and afflicted by losses, they longed and wished for his presence. Meanwhile, having held a council at Rheims, he humbly visited Clairvaux and displayed to the eyes of the poor the glory of the Roman pontificate. All marvelled at unshaken humility amid such exaltation, and at the strength of his holy resolve remaining firm upon so eminent a summit: so that humility joined to high office shone outwardly in his ministry, yet did not inwardly lose its strength in virtue.

A woollen tunic clung to his flesh. [Note: See the religious discipline of the supreme pontiff: he wore not a woollen under-tunic, but a tunic next to the body; nor did he add a hood even at night in bed—nor a scapular, which was not then permitted—according to Herbert, *On the Miracles of the Cistercians*, book II, chapter 35. Because of his infirmities Bernard was permitted the use of a woollen undergarment, with a similar cap: below, book III, no. 5.] Clothed in a cowl by day and night, he went thus and lay down thus. Within, he retained the habit of a monk; outwardly, in both conduct and dress, he presented himself as pontiff: undertaking a difficult task, expressing in one man the distinctive properties of different persons.

[Col. 0298A] Segmented cushions were carried about for him. His bed, covered with coverlets, was surrounded by a purple curtain; but if you turned back the coverings, you would find, beneath the woollen layers placed over them, crushed straw and heaped-up chaff. “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart”; yet he provided things good in the sight of both God and men. He addressed the brethren not without tears, mingling with his words sighs drawn from his heart; he exhorted and comforted them, and showed himself among them as a brother and companion, not as lord or master. Since the great crowd of attendants accompanying him did not permit him to remain there longer, he bade the brethren farewell, set out for Italy, and reached the City.

[Col. 0298B] 51. The holy man wrote for this pope a book of great subtlety [Note: The five books], [variant: usefulness], in which, pursuing with most penetrating inquiry both matters around him and matters beneath him, and ascending even to those above him, he discoursed so profoundly on the divine nature that he seems to have been caught up into the third heaven, to have heard certain words which it is not lawful for a man to utter, and to have seen the King in his beauty.

In those matters which are beneath a man and around him, the fellowship of morals, equality of nature, difference of offices, consideration of merits, and discernment of progress are distinguished with the utmost subtlety, and knowledge of oneself is imparted to each according to his kind. In matters above man, he contemplates heavenly things—not in the way in which angels, who always cleave to God, contemplate them, but in the way in which a man of pure heart and sincere mind can touch divine things, and in which temporal priesthood can be conformed to the heavenly hierarchy. For in the heavenly host some rule over others, and ministering spirits, at the command of higher powers, are assigned to diverse duties; some, standing nearer, receive directly from God what they are to indicate to others, whether for doing or for understanding. And since a man requires reverence to be shown to his authority, everything must be referred to the honour of the highest power; for, since man is subject to man and spirit to spirit, it is above all fitting that one be subject to God, by whose gift this pre-eminence is granted and by whose teaching it comes about that a man may attain both knowledge of himself and, through faith and hope, such approach to divine contemplation as is given and allowed to him.

[Col. 0298D] The man of God dictated, and sometimes wrote, on wax tablets, [“restoring honey, and indeed honey sweeter than before”], and did not allow what was divinely inspired in him to perish. He settled disputes of churches and troublesome appeals, which discordant clerics stirred up among themselves, calming them with a gentle breath. Sometimes, even when he rebuked more harshly, tranquillity returned; the storms subsided; and those who had come before him seditious, boiling over with bile and erupting in harangues, returned peaceful.

[Col. 0299A] 52. Above other princes Count Theobald attached himself to him. Pursuing his love in action, he devoted both himself and his possessions to the aid of Clairvaux, and placed his soul in the Abbot’s hands. Laying aside princely exaltation, he showed himself among God’s servants as a fellow-servant, not as lord, so that he might obey in all things whatever the humblest members of that house requested [variant: commanded]. He therefore bought estates, built houses, supplied resources for new abbeys; and wherever the servants of God extended their shoots, he assigned money. He did not establish a single house, as Solomon did at Jerusalem; rather, wherever persons of this form of life had settled, he took pains to provide them with necessities, as though he were preparing a dwelling of his own for Christ present on earth.

He also placed this at the disposal of the man of God: that, at his command, he would provide expenses for the work of God to any needy persons whatsoever. Seeing the prince’s ready disposition, the Abbot stirred up his compassion and especially wished him to be attentive to those who were of the household of faith. [Note: See concerning him below, book IV, chapter 3.] He advised him to found enduring temples and to arrange almsgiving with such prudence “that, continually bearing fruit through renewed and ever-reborn additions, they might continually bring forth new alms. Then he taught him in every way to have compassion on the needy, whom the goads of poverty, stinging like wasps now here, now there, drove about; he advised that clothing be given to some and food to others. He further urged him personally to visit hospitals and not to shrink from the sight [variant: at the sight] of the sick; for in this the good of mercy would be doubled, if he both saw and cared for them, if he consoled and refreshed them.

[Col. 0299C] He instructed him, as though in the elementary principles, to humble the oppressors of the poor, defend the orphan and widow, show mercy and lend, order his words in judgment, provide for the Church’s peace, and understand the function of the sword; thus making known to him the sum of princely office, and that this is required of a prince as a duty: that he should devote himself to the praise of the good and the punishment of the wicked.”

53. Receiving these and other similar wholesome counsels reverently, this reasonable man transformed the luxury of his court and the pomp of high rank into humility and honourableness. No one in his presence dared either to do or say anything unbecoming. Indeed, those who strove to please him even in this matter, whether with feigned or sincere intention, themselves often did the things in which they saw their lord take delight.

[Col. 0299D] Those who attended him more intimately therefore brought before him poor persons suffering oppression; they reported sick people lying in the streets, and any who were in bitterness and misery. He rejoiced at an opportunity for mercy offered to him, and embraced with higher favour those whom he saw to be more concerned about such matters. [Note: The words in hooks survive in the Corbie manuscript.] [And because the man of God allowed none of his own people to remain either at that court or for that cause,] he summoned two religious men of the Premonstratensian Order and placed them over his almsgiving. It was their responsibility to travel through the castles and villages in which he stayed; and he ordered that the sick and lepers residing there be abundantly fed from his own table for as long as he remained in those places.

[Col. 0300A] He further instituted that, through their ministry, other poor persons should receive generous alms appropriate to their circumstances, whether in food or clothing. He wished these men alone to have such authority in his household that they might command at their discretion the cupbearers, bakers, cooks, and other servants whatever they wished, and take whatever pleased them; nor was anyone to dare forbid anything or report it to the Count if they appeared prodigal in any respect. Yet these men feared God and desired to please both Him and the Count. They neither diminished the prince’s magnificence—he having ordered that the fullness of charity be fulfilled out of his own resources—nor wished to be found ungrateful to God by being lazy and miserly where both God’s will and the prince’s ample generosity had charged them to be ready and efficient stewards.

[Col. 0300B] Their office further included providing lodging for monks and religious men whom various business sent to the court, and supplying their necessities from the Count’s storehouse and granary. During the hard winter they also carried about, in fitted packs, clothing for the poor, skins, cloaks, and footwear—nor was grease lacking for these—which they distributed to the needy through the villages. No work of mercy was absent from that household: all shipwrecked persons had a safe refuge in that harbour.

In times of famine he did not, like Pharaoh, sell grain to the people, nor subject Egypt to himself in slavery by distributing provisions. Rather, with the holy Abbot as another Joseph and with a more divine counsellor, he freely opened his granaries to the needy. He did not drain the people of money, deceive the afflicted by trickery, or, having transferred the commonwealth to himself, heap up private treasures on earth; but, storing up treasure in heaven, an indefatigable distributor, he distributed both money and provisions with great cheerfulness.

54. A grave and dreadful temptation did not fail to assail this man who thirsted for heavenly things. Both the King and the princes attacked him; the earth was shaken and trembled; and, as if God were angry with him, plunderers and incendiaries were allowed to devastate almost everything belonging to him. The King’s army covered the face of the land, and everywhere all things were laid waste. Nor was it safe for him to resist or confront his persecutors,

[Col. 0300D] for his own people had deserted him and were openly hostile, while those who remained were set for ambushes, not for assistance. Severe straits pressed upon him on every side: he could neither protect himself at home nor make suitable provision abroad, since he did not know at all who were his own; and he utterly distrusted both the treachery of deserters and the duplicity of his adherents.

Yet amid these anxieties he turned to the Lord and sought help from heaven. Calling to him the man of God, whose counsel he chiefly employed, and not despairing of God’s mercy, he received from his answer this teaching: “that he should understand that God chastens every son whom he receives, and that corrections of this kind either cleanse or test the soul” (Prov. 3); “and that Job was more glorious when he sat on the dungheap than he would have been had he sat unharmed upon his throne with an army surrounding him” (Job 2).

[Col. 0301A] The holy man showed him that Solomon sinned in ease and, misusing the blessing of peace, slipped into vices; whereas David his father, though pursued by his son Absalom and with all Israel armed against him, remained in grace. He also explained how Satan buffeted the Apostle, who by persevering immovably in that tribulation deserved to hear that “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9–11), and that in the present life prosperity makes us more sluggish, while adversity makes us more watchful.

55. On hearing this, the venerable Count, greatly encouraged, ordered two golden vessels of immense weight and remarkable workmanship to be brought forth with all speed. In them were enclosed most precious jewels, which his uncle King Henry of England had customarily kept before himself upon the table at the ceremony of his coronation, as an exhibition of his wealth and glory. Tearing from his heart delight in such things, he ordered the jewels to be removed from their settings and the gold to be broken up, so that it might be sold and, from its price, tabernacles beloved by the Lord above gold and topaz might be founded.

[Note: Perhaps these were the jewels which Suger purchased from two abbots of the Cistercian Order: see *On His Administration*, chapter 32. The same author relates that Count Theobald gave red hyacinths for the dedication of the church of Saint Denis; in Chesne, vol. IV, p. 356.]

But Amalek did not cease from harassing Israel. Moses, however, gained victory with hands raised to heaven; and as the enemies withdrew, the holy Abbot, a concerned mediator—while the brethren cried to God and wept at home—broke into the battle-lines. In the time of wrath he became reconciliation; as divine pleadings intervened, the storms subsided, tranquillity returned between King and Prince, and the longed-for serenity of peace.

[Col. 0301]

# BOOK THREE, BY GEOFFREY, FORMERLY A MONK OF CLAIRVAUX AND NOTARY OF ST BERNARD, LATER ABBOT

1115. PREFACE

[Col. 0301B]

Eminent men have committed to writing the memory of our most illustrious father Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, for the praise of Christ and the edification of many. Having found abundant material, each according to his ability and according to the more certain knowledge of the events that came to him, they have arranged not the whole matter but certain portions of it. Yet some may think that the child of his holiness, the son of his condescension, the foster-child of his kindness, ought much less to have kept him silent [variant: ought to keep him silent]—I, whom death alone, the only thing that could do so, at last tore from his breast after about thirteen years. I ought neither remember nor utter this without sobbing.

Would that even now, holy Father, he might be pleasing to you in himself, as once he seemed, and for some time did seem, pleasing! And who else is so indebted to you, so bound to you, so wholly yours? Death, I confess, has bitten—bitten cruelly—but it has not swallowed everything alike. It has cut off, not uprooted; without mercy it has taken the portion that fell to it. It has taken sight; it has taken speech; it has also taken bodily service. Yet it has not snatched away faith in his help, still present even now; it has not swallowed hope of a future vision someday; nor, finally, has it taken away the affection of filial devotion, rooted more deeply in the memory of things past.

As I know very well, I lack both learning and eloquence, especially for a work so worthy. Yet neither the genius of Origen nor the tongue of Cicero would suffice worthily to declare your mighty works and your praises. Nevertheless, we must not despair that the prudent reader will be bound to gather the fruits of your works rather than the unworthy leaves of our words: so that, tasting the sweetness of the former more than censuring the dryness of the latter, he may not so much bite these pages maliciously as feed upon those works with delight.

[Col. 0302C] Things seen are customarily narrated more safely and more sincerely than things heard; and when poured into a third vessel they grow sour more readily. Water too is sweeter when drawn, even from a small channel, from a spring whose bubbling vein immediately replenishes it, than when taken from a stream that has already run far onward, or even from an abundant river. Therefore, leaving untouched the books of those who have written about the beginnings or the middle period of this same most blessed Father—lest I seem to build upon another’s foundation—my discourse is principally concerned with matters at nearly all of which I was present. Occasionally I also insert a few things which I learned from the most trustworthy testimony of brethren who were present.

[Col. 0302D] The reader will find this work divided into three little books. The first chiefly treats matters that seem to concern the habit, conduct, and teaching of this blessed Father. The second recounts the many miracles performed through him. The third concludes with his blessed end. This too must be noted: in narrating events, the coherence of similarity rather than of time is observed. The signs themselves and certain deeds are not written in the order in which they occurred; rather, some are inserted where they seemed to arise more suitably.

[Col. 0303A] For a discourse supported and illuminated by its own examples, like a structure upheld by suitable columns, seems more solid and is customarily received more favourably. Some matters have also been moved so as to be joined to others like them, and so that things of the same kind might adhere more fittingly to one another. This is so in the first two books; for in the third, in almost everything, the sequence of the narrative follows the order of time itself.

# CHAPTER I. A general account of the character and virtues of Saint Bernard

1. By countless signs and miracles, as the whole world has learned, God glorified his faithful servant Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, ever glorious in his saints and wondrous in his majesty. Yet, as he himself commends Saint Malachy, the first and greatest miracle that he displayed was himself.

[Col. 0303B] Serene in countenance, modest in dress, circumspect in speech, reverent in action, constant in sacred meditation, devout in prayer—and, as he himself advised others, being persuaded by frequent experience, trusting in every matter more to prayer than to his own skill or labour. [Note: See book IV of *On Consideration*, no. 12.] Great-souled in faith, patient in hope, abundant in charity, supreme [variant: profound] in humility, outstanding in compassion. Prudent in counsels, effective in affairs, yet never less idle in leisure than when he was at leisure. Cheerful in the face of reproaches, reserved in receiving services. Gentle in conduct, holy in merits, glorious in miracles; finally, abounding in wisdom, virtue, and favour before God and men.

God had made the helper of his holy soul like unto it, and had fitted his body with a special, prevenient blessing. A certain grace appeared in his flesh, yet spiritual rather than carnal. In his face shone a brightness not earthly but heavenly; in his eyes there radiated an angelic purity and dove-like simplicity. Such was the beauty of his inner man that it burst outward in certain evident signs, and, overflowing from the abundance of inward purity and plentiful grace, even the outer man appeared suffused with it. His whole body was exceedingly thin and without flesh; his very delicate skin was slightly ruddy in the cheeks.

[Col. 0303D] Assiduous meditation and the practice of compunction had drawn off whatever natural heat was in him. His hair was coloured a mixture of blond and white. His beard was reddish, sprinkled with grey toward the end of his life. His stature was of honourable medium height, though he appeared rather tall. Yet this treasure was in an earthen vessel, utterly broken and shattered on every side. His flesh suffered from many infirmities, so that in them the strength of his spirit might be perfected. Of these, the more dangerous was a constriction in the passage of his throat, which admitted nothing at all dry and scarcely anything solid; the more troublesome were weakness of the stomach and corruption of the bowels. These afflicted him continually, besides other ailments that recurred often.

[Col. 0304A] His chief endeavour was to avoid admiration and to behave as one among the rest. Yet glory pursued him as he fled, just as, conversely, it is accustomed to flee those who seek it. This proverb was often on his lips and always in his heart: “He who does what no one else does, is admired by all.” With this in view, he emulated the common life and common rule all the more, preferring in none of his actions a singular observance. For this reason, he preferred to lay aside the hair-shirt which he had secretly worn for many years rather than have it known that he wore it, declaring that he wished to be less conspicuous than one who, though of the same profession, did not follow the practices held in common with the rest.

Yet in these common observances he possessed singular purity and uncommon devotion. Neglecting nothing, he treated even the least things with diligence and attention. From his own experience he was accustomed to define a wise person as one to whom each thing has its proper savour according to what it is.

[Col. 0304B] 2. From almost his earliest years he so escaped the enticements of appetite that he largely lost even the ability to distinguish flavours. How often, deceived by the pious stratagem of those serving him, did he take one liquid for another! On one occasion, indeed, oil was offered him by mistake; he drank it and did not notice at all. This was not discovered until someone came in and marvelled at his anointed lips. His food was a morsel of bread thoroughly softened in warm water, with a few small sips.
