It was little indeed; but his stomach rejected no small portion of it undigested, lest there should be any pleasure for him in food—a food whose taking was perilous, whose retention painful, and whose rejection miserable.

[Col. 0304C] Thus, in accordance with the desire of his heart, heavenly providence had supplied this faithful servant: he did not lack the fruit of singular abstinence, yet avoided the always hateful admiration of others beneath the cover of necessity. He often told us concerning wine that, when a monk had to drink it, he ought so to taste it that the cup could not be noticed to have been emptied. Whenever he allowed wine to be set before him, he himself observed this so strictly that after not merely one drink but an entire meal, whatever its character, the little vessel from which he drank was scarcely ever seen to be less full when carried back from the table.

He could stand only with difficulty; therefore he was almost constantly seated and moved very rarely. Whenever he could withdraw from business, he was praying, reading, writing, attending to instruction and the edification of the brethren, or persisting in sacred meditation. In this spiritual pursuit he had obtained a special grace: he endured neither weariness nor difficulty, dwelling freely with himself, walking in the spaciousness of his heart, and there offering Christ—as he himself was accustomed to exhort others to do—a great upper room furnished and spread out.

[Col. 0304D] Every hour was short for his meditation and every place suitable. Yet, although thus disposed, frequently under the urging of divine fear—indeed, under the guidance of the Spirit—he set this pursuit aside for more abundant gains. He had learned to seek not what was useful to himself but what was useful to many. Otherwise, in any gathering or tumult of people, unless the matter required his attention,

[Col. 0305A] he gathered his mind with complete ease and enjoyed a certain inward solitude, which he carried everywhere with him, paying absolutely no attention to anything that sounded or appeared outwardly.

# CHAPTER II. On the visit to Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, and to the Carthusians; and on Bernard’s remarkable custody of the senses

3. After God’s servant had spent some years at Clairvaux, he conceived the desire to visit Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, and the Carthusian brethren out of devotion. The aforesaid bishop, understanding that the divine presence attended the visit of this guest, received him so gladly and reverently that he prostrated himself to the ground in reverence.

[Col. 0305B] But when the servant of Christ saw this aged bishop, renowned in reputation and distinguished in holiness, fall down before him, he was greatly alarmed; and he too fell before him. Only then, received with the kiss of peace, he complained with deep groaning that his humility had been put to shame by the veneration of so great a man. From that time he held a special place in Hugh’s heart; thereafter these two sons of splendour became one heart and one soul, and delighted in one another in Christ. For as the Queen of Sheba testifies concerning Solomon (3 Kings 10:6–7), each rejoiced that he had found in the other far more than fame had proclaimed.

4. At the Grande Chartreuse, too, the servant of Christ was received with the same affection and reverence by the most reverend Guigo, Prior, and the other brethren. They rejoiced with joy because they found him present exactly as they had previously known him by letter. Yet while they were edified in all other respects, there was one thing which somewhat troubled the aforementioned Carthusian Prior: namely, the trappings of the animal on which this venerable man rode, which were not quite plain and did not sufficiently display poverty.

[Col. 0305C] This emulous lover of virtue did not keep silent about what he had conceived in his mind. Speaking to one of the brethren, he confessed that he was somewhat disturbed and wondered about it. When that brother reported what he had heard to the holy Father, Bernard himself was no less astonished. He asked what sort of trappings they were that had thus come from Clairvaux all the way to the Chartreuse, while he had never seen or considered them and until that hour had not known at all what they were like.

[Col. 0305D] The animal was not his own; it had been lent by a Cluniac monk, his uncle, who was staying nearby, and it was equipped as that monk was accustomed to equip it for himself. When the often-mentioned Prior heard this, what he especially marvelled at was that this servant of God had so cut off his outward eyes and so occupied his inward mind that what the Prior himself had first noticed with his sight Bernard had not seen throughout so great a distance of travel.

[Col. 0306A] He also travelled for a whole day alongside Lake Lausanne without seeing it at all—or without realizing that he saw it. When his companions spoke of the lake that evening, he asked them where the lake was; and all were astonished.

5. From the beginning he had desired in every way to withdraw from business, never to go out, but to remain in the monastery. Later, considering that bodily weakness had furnished him with an appropriate opportunity, he at one time resolved upon this and observed it for some while, until the grave necessity of God’s Church, together with the command of the supreme Pontiff and of all the abbots of his Order, compelled him to go out. [Note: See letters 21 and 48, at the end.] To all these he deferred in everything as to fathers, though he was himself the father of all.

[Col. 0306B] By their command also, in his final years, besides cowl and tunic, he used a woollen cloth cut short in the manner of a cloak, and a similar cap. [Note: The wonderful strictness of the Order! A woollen under-tunic with a similar cap was granted Bernard as a relaxation, though not even Pope Eugenius used it: above, book II, no. 50. On this cap and fur caps, see below, book IV, no. 36. I interpret the woollen *pileum* as a biretta or a *calantica*.] Amid such great bodily sicknesses and labours, he never consented to use furs. In clothing, poverty always pleased him; filth never did. Such things, he said, were signs of a mind either negligent, vainly glorying within itself, or seeking petty human glory outwardly.

His gait and whole bearing were modest and disciplined: expressing humility, breathing forth devotion, displaying grace, commanding reverence, and gladdening and edifying those who saw him by sight alone. Concerning laughter, we report what we often heard from his mouth when he marvelled at the loud laughter of religious persons: “I do not remember, from the first years of my conversion, ever laughing in such a way that I had not to exert force upon myself rather to laugh than to restrain myself, and apply a spur to my laughter rather than a bridle.”

# CHAPTER III. On his rare care in speech, modesty, and grace; and on his flight from dignities

6. He who had set him apart from his mother’s womb for the work of preaching gave him a voice sufficiently strong and intelligible despite his feeble body. Whenever a suitable occasion presented itself, his speech concerning the edification of souls was appropriate to every kind of person, according to his knowledge of each person’s understanding, character, and pursuits. He spoke to rustic country people as though he had always been brought up in the countryside; he spoke to every other class of people as though he had devoted all his effort to investigating their occupations.

[Col. 0306D] Learned among the educated, simple among the simple, overflowing with instruction in perfection and wisdom among spiritual persons, he adapted himself to all, desiring to gain all for Christ. He was most carefully attentive to observe what, writing to Pope Eugenius, he uttered from the fullness of his heart: “If trivialities sometimes occur, perhaps they are to be endured, but never to be repeated. One must intervene in frivolity cautiously and wisely. One must indeed break forth into something serious which they may hear not only with profit but gladly, so that they may desist from idle things.” [Note: Book II of *On Consideration*, chapter 13.]

7. How conciliatory, persuasive, and learned a tongue God gave him, so that he knew whom and when he ought to address, to whom consolation or entreaty, exhortation or rebuke, was suited—those who have read his writings may know this somewhat, though far less fully than those who heard his words often. Grace was poured out upon his lips, and his utterance was powerfully aflame, so that even his outstanding style could not retain all that sweetness and fervour. Honey and milk were under his tongue; nevertheless, in his mouth was a fiery law, according to the saying of the Song of Songs: “Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet” (Song 4:3).

[Col. 0307B] Thus, when he spoke even to German peoples, he was heard with wonderful feeling. Although, being speakers of another language, they could not understand his discourse, their devotion seemed to be edified more from it, and to feel the power of his words more, than from an interpreter’s intelligible rendering delivered afterward, however highly skilled that interpreter might be. A sure proof of this was their beating of breasts and pouring forth of tears.

He used the Scriptures so freely and aptly that he seemed not so much to follow them as to go before them and lead them whither he wished, while following the Spirit, their author, as guide. For God had filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, in order that, as Scripture says, he might open his mouth in the midst of the Church, search even the depths of rivers, and bring hidden things to light (Job 28:11). Indeed, he once confessed that, when he was meditating or praying, all sacred Scripture had appeared to him as though laid out and expounded beneath him.

8. But who can worthily describe—or worthily marvel at—how freely he preached the Gospel? He believed that it would be an insufficient thing not to seek transient resources from his hearers unless he also repeatedly refused ecclesiastical dignities when they were offered. It was too little for him, as one engaged in warfare, to seek no pay; he would not even consent to receive insignia of office.

[Col. 0307D] Finally, like another David about to go into battle, he declared military arms too burdensome for himself (1 Kings 17:39), seeing that many, especially in his own time, were weighed down by them; and in his simplicity he triumphed more gloriously. Divine virtue had bestowed such grace upon him that, though he had chosen to be lowly in the house of God, he nevertheless bore more abundant fruit there than any who were raised on high, and illuminated the Church more brightly, as though from beneath the bushel of his humility, than others who were set upon lampstands.

Indeed, the humbler he was, the more useful he always proved to God’s people in every saving doctrine; yet he never wished to occupy the place of a teacher. Blessed indeed was he who, as Bernard himself said of one of the saints, [Note: Namely, Saint Malachy, in his Office, Antiphon 1 at Matins.] “loved the law and did not seek the chair.”

[Col. 0308A] How much more happily did he deserve to sit in the chair of virtues because he refused to preside in chairs of dignities! As righteous and strong, he laboured in evangelical preaching; as prudent and self-controlled, he always guarded himself against ecclesiastical pre-eminence. He never refused obstinately; yet, though frequently elected to the highest honours, he acted prudently—with divine grace cooperating—so that he might never be compelled to accept them. Holy Moses yielded the priesthood to his brother Aaron, but he had an impediment of speech. Our Bernard was held back from honour by humility alone, not from the work of an evangelist by any necessity.

He therefore deservedly obtained singular favour with God and men, for he offered the Gospel not only without cost in temporal resources but even without a rank of ecclesiastical dignity—though certainly not without fruit for the salvation of his brethren. He always strove to benefit God’s people and never allowed himself to preside over them.

[Col. 0308B] Yet he rarely went out to preach, except perhaps to nearby places. But whenever some necessity drew him forth, [Note: See letters 21 and 55.] he sowed beside all waters, proclaiming God’s word publicly and privately. Even this he did by command of the supreme Pontiff, and likewise at the direction of other bishops wherever one of them happened to be present. The greater he was, in humbling himself in all things, the more he deferred to priests, because he understood more fully the reverence due to the ministers of Christ.

# CHAPTER IV. On the unhappy outcome of the expedition to the East, and the murmuring against the holy man that arose from it
[Col. 0308C] 9. Nor should it be left unmentioned that, because of the preaching of the expedition to Jerusalem, the simplicity or malice of certain people took grave offence against him when its outcome proved sad. Yet we may say that this undertaking did not originate with him. For when the necessity had already stirred the minds of many, though the king of the Franks had once and again sought him for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0308D] See *On Consideration*, book II, chapter 9.], and though he had also been urged by apostolic letters, he nevertheless would not consent either to speak on the matter or to give advice, until at last he was commanded, by a general letter of the Supreme Pontiff himself, to set it forth to peoples and princes as the tongue of the Roman Church. The tenor of that letter [Note: [Col. 0308D] This letter is the first of Eugenius in volume X of the *Councils*.] was that they should undertake the journey as an act of repentance and for the remission of sins, either to free their brethren or to lay down their own lives for them.

These and similar things could truly be said concerning the matter; but what is more important should rather be said. For he manifestly preached this word, the Lord working with him and confirming the message by signs that followed. But how great and how numerous were these signs? It would be difficult even to count them, much less to narrate them. They began, indeed, to be recorded at that time; but eventually the very multitude of matters to be written, and the subject itself, overcame the writer. For sometimes in one day twenty or even more persons were healed of various ailments [Col. 0309A], and scarcely a day was free from such occurrences. In short, at that time Christ, through the touch and prayer of His servant, caused many—even those blind from their mothers’ wombs—to see, the lame to walk, the withered to recover strength, the deaf to hear, and the mute to speak: grace restoring, more wonderfully, what nature had bestowed less fully.

10. Yet by that expedition the Eastern Church did not deserve to be freed; rather, the heavenly Church deserved to be filled and to rejoice. And if it pleased God, on such an occasion, to rescue very many—not the bodies of Easterners from pagans, but the souls of Westerners from sins—who would dare say to Him, “Why have You done this?” Or what sound-minded person would not mourn more for those who returned to their former crimes, or perhaps to crimes worse than the former, than for the death of those who, in fruits of repentance, rendered to Christ souls cleansed through various tribulations? Otherwise, let the Egyptians say it, let the sons of darkness say it, who can neither see nor utter the truth: “He led them out cunningly, that He might kill them in the wilderness” (Exod. 32:12). Christ the Saviour patiently endures the reproach, which He repays with the salvation of so many souls.

The venerable Father himself recalled this saying, declaring among other things: “If one thing must result from two alternatives, I prefer that the murmur of men should be against us rather than against God. It is good for me if He deigns to use me as a shield. I gladly receive upon myself the slanderous tongues of detractors and the poisoned darts of blasphemers, so that they may not reach Him. I do not refuse to become inglorious, so that no assault may be made upon God’s glory” (chapter 1). These words he wrote in the second book of *On Consideration* [Col. 0309C].

Now when the mournful report of the dispersal of that army first resounded within Gaul, it happened that a father brought his blind son to the Servant of God to be enlightened, and overcame his excuses by many entreaties. The Saint laid his hand upon the boy and prayed to the Lord that, if the word of that preaching had gone forth from him, and if God’s Spirit had been present with him as he preached, He would deign to show it by the boy’s enlightenment. But while, after praying, he awaited the effect of his prayer, the boy said: “What am I to do? For I see.” Immediately a cry was raised by those standing by. For many were present, not only brethren but also laypeople; and when they saw the boy seeing, they were greatly comforted and gave thanks to God.

[Col. 0309D] 11. [We also believe that some have taken very pleasant notice of this: that in the very week in which his most blessed soul was released from the flesh, the Church of Jerusalem was magnificently consoled by the divine gift, as they had often known him to promise. For Ascalon was captured—that most strongly fortified city, only a few miles from the Holy City and threatening dangerously at its heel. For fifty years and more Christians had laboured against it without success; and even then it was not captured by human strength, but by divine power.

Nor is it unsuitable here to insert his own words, written in that same year to that most excellent man of the Knights of the Temple, then a minister and now also Master of the Templars, who was his maternal uncle: “Woe to our princes,” he says. “They have done no good in the Lord’s land; in their own lands, to which they quickly returned, they practise incredible wickedness, and do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph. Yet we trust that the Lord will not reject His people, nor forsake His inheritance. Rather, the right hand of the Lord will show strength, and His arm will help it, so that all may know that it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” [Note: [Col. 0309D] Letter 288.].] But enough of these matters.

## CHAPTER V. The errors of Peter Abelard and Gilbert of Poitiers, refuted through the efforts of Saint Bernard

[Col. 0310B] 12. It must also be recorded for posterity how manifoldly the teaching of the Man of God benefited the holy Church: in correcting the conduct of Catholics, restraining the frenzy of schismatics, and refuting the errors of heretics. Besides those whom he taught to live soberly, justly, and piously in this world, how many he persuaded to take a more perfect leave of the world may be seen from this: as long as he lived, he never ceased to fill the deserts of the world with those who had deserted the world. Through his ministry that prophetic saying seems to have been fulfilled even bodily: “He made the wilderness pools of water, and the waterless land springs of water. And there He placed the hungry, and they established a city for habitation. And they sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of increase. [Col. 0310C] And He blessed them, and they multiplied, and He did not diminish their cattle” (Ps. 106 [107]:35–38).

Certainly, during the days of the general schism, how faithfully the Servant of God stood in the breach before Him, to turn away His wrath; how effectively he stood, appeased it, and brought the shaking to an end; and finally, how manifestly in the time of wrath he became reconciliation—this deserves fuller treatment. For the moment, it may suffice to cite the words of Pope Innocent, writing to him on this subject:

> “With what firm and persevering constancy the fervour of your religious devotion and discernment undertook to defend the cause of blessed Peter and of your holy mother, the Roman Church, when the schism of Peter Leon was aflame; and, setting yourself as an impregnable wall before the house of God, how you laboured, through frequent arguments fortified with reason, to bring back to the unity of the Catholic Church and to the obedience of blessed Peter and of ourselves the minds of kings and princes, and of other persons both ecclesiastical and secular—the great benefit which has accrued thereby to God’s Church and to us makes plain.” [Note: [Col. 0310D] See among Innocent’s letters.]

It should also be briefly indicated how magnificently he acted, as a faithful and prudent servant, for the faith.

13. In those days there was Peter Abelard, a distinguished master and exceedingly renowned for his reputation for learning, yet treacherously teaching doctrines concerning the faith. When writings full of his most grievous blasphemies began to circulate everywhere [Col. 0311A], learned and faithful men referred these profane novelties of terms and meanings to the Man of God. Desiring, in his customary goodness and kindness, that the error be corrected rather than the man confounded, he approached him with private admonition. He dealt with him so modestly and reasonably that Abelard himself, moved to compunction, promised to correct everything at Bernard’s judgment.

But after departing from him, this same Peter, prompted by wicked counsels and unhappily trusting in his own intellectual powers and extensive practice in disputation, recoiled from the sounder purpose. He then sought out the metropolitan of Sens, because a great council was shortly to be held in that church, and accused the abbot of Clairvaux of secretly speaking against his books [Col. 0311B]. He further declared himself ready to defend his writings publicly, asking that the said abbot be summoned to the Council to state whatever he had to say. It was done as he requested.

But when summoned, the abbot utterly refused to come, declaring that this was not his affair [Note: [Col. 0311D] See Letter 187.]. Later, however, persuaded by the admonitions of great men—lest his absence should cause scandal among the people and give his adversary greater confidence—he finally consented to go. He did so sorrowfully and not without tears, as he himself testifies in his letter to Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 0311D] See Letter 190.], in which he recounts the entire affair more fully and clearly.

14. The day arrived, and a great assembly gathered in the church. There the writings of that Peter were brought forward by the Servant of God [Col. 0311C], and the propositions containing error were identified. Finally, Abelard was offered the choice either to deny that they were his, to correct the error humbly, or, if he could, to answer the arguments and the testimonies of the holy Fathers brought against him. But neither willing to repent nor able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit that spoke, he appealed to the Apostolic See in order to gain time.

Yet afterward, when that eminent advocate of the Catholic faith urged him—since he knew that nothing was to be undertaken against Abelard personally—to reply as freely as securely, since he was only to be heard and endured with all patience, not struck by any sentence, Abelard altogether refused even this. For he afterward confessed to his own people, they say, that at that hour his memory was for the most part disturbed [Col. 0311D], his reason clouded, and his inward understanding fled [Note: [Col. 0311D] See Letter 89 and the notes appended to it.]. Nevertheless, the Church that had assembled dismissed the man but punished the abomination, abstaining from condemning his person while condemning his false doctrines. For how could that Peter find refuge in Peter’s See while so far removed from Peter’s faith? Therefore the Apostolic Pontiff, involving the author himself in the same sentence as his errors [Col. 0312A], condemned the writings to fire and the writer to silence.

15. There was likewise Gilbert, surnamed of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, very deeply trained in Sacred Scripture, but one who had also searched matters too high for himself, to his own folly. For he neither thought simply nor wrote faithfully concerning the unity of the Holy Trinity and the simplicity of the Godhead. He set before his disciples hidden bread and gave them stolen water to drink; nor did he readily confess to authoritative persons what he thought—or rather, how greatly he thought foolishly. For he feared what Peter is said to have told him at Sens:

> Then your own cause is at stake when your neighbour’s wall burns.

1123 At last, however, when the scandal among the faithful over this matter was growing strong and the murmuring increasing [Col. 0312B], he was summoned before the assembly and ordered to produce the book in which he had vomited forth blasphemies—grave indeed, though enclosed in a certain wrapping of words.

Accordingly, at the Council which the venerable Pope Eugenius held in the city of Reims, Bernard, the singular champion in his time of the holy Church, confronted Gilbert closely. First he drew out all that Gilbert had sought to conceal by verbal quibbles; then, over a two-day disputation, he refuted it both by his own arguments and by the testimonies of the saints. Observing that some of those presiding had already recognized blasphemy in the doctrine but still shielded the person from accusation, he was inflamed with zeal and summoned the Gallican Church, which was his own household, separately [Col. 0312C]. Finally, by common counsel, the fathers of ten provinces and many other bishops and abbots, at the Man of God’s direction, set a new creed against the new doctrines. The names of each were also subscribed to it, so that the irreproachable faith of them all, and likewise their irreproachable zeal, might be known to the rest.

Thus at last, by apostolic judgment and the authority of the universal Church, that error was condemned. Bishop Gilbert was asked whether he consented to the same condemnation. Consenting and publicly retracting [Note: [Col. 0311D] The author of this book, Geoffrey, who himself attended the council, recounts these matters more fully in his letter to Henry, bishop of Albano. Geoffrey also published a disputation against Gilbert, which you have below [Col. 0312D].] what he had earlier written and affirmed, he himself obtained pardon, especially because from the outset he had cautiously entered upon the discussion on the condition that he promised, without any obstinacy, freely to correct his opinion according to the judgment of the holy Church [Col. 0312D].

## CHAPTER VI. The Henrician heresy suppressed in the Toulouse region, and miracles performed there

16. In the Toulouse region a certain Henry [Note: [Col. 0312D] Compare Geoffrey’s letter concerning this Henry, found after the sixth book of the *Life*, and see our Preface to volume I, article VI. For his errors, see Letter 241 and Sermon 65 on the *Song of Songs*.], formerly a monk and then a contemptible apostate, of a most depraved life and pernicious teaching, had ensnared the fickle populace of that country with persuasive words. As the Apostle foretold of certain persons, “speaking falsehood in hypocrisy” (1 Tim. 4:2), he exploited them with fabricated words. He was an open enemy of the Church, irreverently attacking both its sacraments and its ministers. And he had already advanced no little in that malignity.

For the venerable Father, writing to the prince of Toulouse, says among other things: “Churches were everywhere found without congregations, congregations without priests, priests without due reverence, and finally Christians without Christ. The way of life in Christ was barred to the children of Christians when baptismal grace was denied. Prayers and offerings for the dead, the invocation of saints, the excommunications of priests, the pilgrimages of the faithful, the building of churches [Col. 0313B], cessation from work on solemn days, the consecrations of chrism and oil—in short, every ecclesiastical institution—were mocked and despised” (*Letter* 241).

17. Under this necessity the holy man set out on the journey, having already often been asked by the Church of that region, and at last persuaded and escorted by the most reverend Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See. On arriving, he was received by the people of the land with unbelievable devotion, as though an angel had come from heaven. He could not remain long among them, because no one could restrain the crowds rushing in: so great was the multitude arriving day and night, seeking his blessing and demanding help.

Yet he preached for several days in the city of Toulouse, and [Col. 0313C] in the other places which that wretched man had frequented most and infected most grievously. He instructed the simple in faith, strengthened the wavering, recalled the erring, restored those who had been overthrown, and by his authority pressed down and crushed the subverters and obstinate, so that they did not dare, I do not say to resist, but even to stand present or appear. Moreover, though that heretic then fled and lay concealed, his paths were so obstructed and his ways so hedged in that he was scarcely safe anywhere afterward; at last he was captured, chained, and handed over to the bishop. 1124 On that journey God was glorified by very many signs in His servant, recalling some hearts from impious errors and healing other bodies from various sicknesses.

18. In the same region is a place called Sarlat [Col. 0313D]. There, after a sermon had been completed, many people offered the Servant of God loaves to bless, as was done everywhere. Raising his hand, making the sign of the Cross, and blessing them in God’s name, he said: “By this you shall know that the things commended by us are true and those commended by the heretics false: if your sick, having tasted these loaves, obtain health.”

But the venerable bishop of Chartres, that great Geoffrey—for he was present and close to the Man of God—feared this and said: “If they receive them with good faith, they will be healed.” To him the holy Father, in no way doubting the Lord’s power, replied: “That is not what I said; rather, those who taste them shall truly be healed, so that they may thereby know that we are true and truthful messengers of God.”

So great a multitude of sick people recovered upon tasting the same bread that the report was spread throughout the entire province; and when the holy man returned through neighbouring places, he avoided and feared to go there because the crowds gathering were intolerable [Col. 0314A].

19. The chief [or, first] miracle which Christ performed through His servant in the city of Toulouse was the healing of a certain paralytic cleric. At the request of the abbot and brethren, toward nightfall, the Man of God visited him in the house of the regular canons of Saint Saturninus, of whom he himself was one. He found the man dying, seemingly drawing his last breath. Having comforted the wretched man and bestowed a blessing, he departed. As he afterward confessed, the faithful servant was speaking in his heart to the Lord as confidently as faithfully: “What are You waiting for, Lord God? This generation seeks signs. Otherwise our words make too little progress among them unless You confirm them by signs that follow.”

At that very hour the paralytic leapt from his bed and ran after him; he followed and caught him, embracing his holy footprints with due devotion. One of his fellow canons, suddenly encountering him as he walked on, was terrified and cried out, for he thought him a phantom. How could he have believed that he had risen from his bed? He supposed that the soul had left the body and appeared to him in a spectral form, and he fled. But at last the truth of the matter convinced both him and the others.

Then word spread among the brethren, and they ran to the joyful spectacle; the bishop and legate himself also hurried there among the first. From there they went to the church, led by the very man who had recovered. Cries of praise to God rang out, with the healed man singing in concert; people rushed in from every side; Christ was blessed, faith triumphed, every unbeliever was put to shame, piety rejoiced, and impiety wasted away [Col. 0314C]. The Man of God then entered the cell where he was staying and ordered every entrance carefully watched and the doors barred, so that no access might be open to the crowd gathering.

[Indeed, this Bernard—for that was the name of the cleric who was healed—was not ungrateful for the bodily benefit and was more anxious for spiritual healing. He followed the Servant of Christ, professed the monastic order at Clairvaux, and received its habit. Sent again to the Toulouse region, he was made abbot there and still presides over the monastery called Vallis Aquae, “Valley of Water.”]

## CHAPTER VII. The most gracious character and outstanding virtues of the blessed man, and what he thought of his miracles

[Col. 0314D]

20. As the signs of the holy man became ever more frequent and multiplied day by day throughout his whole return journey from that province, it must not be passed over what disposition he maintained amid these events, he who had learned humility of heart and gentleness from Christ. Reflecting within himself, and at last speaking from the abundance of his heart to certain religious brethren of his household, he said: “I greatly wonder what these miracles mean, or what God has seen fit to do in performing such things through such a man. I do not think I have read anything in the sacred pages concerning this kind of signs. For signs have sometimes been performed through holy and perfect people; they have also been performed through pretenders. I am conscious in myself neither of perfection nor of pretence. I know that I lack the merits of the saints which are made illustrious by miracles; yet I trust that I do not belong to the lot of those who work many mighty deeds in the Lord’s name and are unknown by the Lord.”

He frequently and privately discussed these and similar matters with spiritual men. At last he seemed to himself to have found the appropriate conclusion: “I know,” he said, “that signs of this kind concern not the holiness of one person but the salvation of many; and that in the man through whom God performs such things, He regards not so much perfection as reputation, in order that He may commend to people in him the virtue believed to be in him. For these things are not done for the sake of those through whom they are done [Col. 0315B], but rather for the sake of those who see or hear of them. Nor does the Lord work them through such persons in order to prove them holier than others, but in order to make others more loving and zealous for holiness. Therefore these signs are nothing to me, since I know that they are granted rather to my reputation than to my life, and are done not for my commendation but rather for the admonition of others.”

Anyone who weighs this carefully will, unless I am mistaken, greatly admire this man’s disposition; and every faithful judge will consider it a greater achievement to interpret miracles so performed than to perform signs and wonders marvellously. He will likewise judge it no less useful to imitate Bernard’s affections than to marvel at his deeds, and to know the distinctions of his character rather than the signs of his works. But who is adequate for these things?

[Col. 0315C] 21. In the breast of this Man of God purity and graciousness dwelt united by an equal bond. Each was sufficiently admirable; but the union of the two was more admirable still. Hence the desires of the whole world converged so singularly upon one man: graciousness made his purity lovable, and purity made his graciousness acceptable. It was difficult to judge whether he won more favour or more reverence. For who was of conduct so strict that he did not hold the abbot of Clairvaux in the highest reverence? Who was so dissolute that he was not sweetly moved toward him?

For his breast was full of the tenderest affections; but how freely he restrained them whenever the occasion required! Most humane in affection, he was nevertheless stronger in faith. To offer a brief example, as he himself testifies in his twenty-sixth sermon on the *Song of Songs*: he celebrated the funeral rites of his own brother, Gerard—so necessary and so dearly loved a brother—with dry eyes, and with dry eyes committed his body to burial, lest affection seem to overcome faith. Yet he scarcely, or never, buried any stranger without tears. The divine hand had fashioned him to bear more abundant fruit in this way: gentleness of character softened severity, while holiness preserved authority.

For to whom could such kindness be burdensome, or such goodness fail to be honourable? We read of Solomon that all the earth desired to see his face. It is great praise; yet perhaps this man was not less great than Solomon in this respect [Col. 0316A]. Indeed, it is scarcely credible that Solomon, in all his glory, obtained a favour so universal throughout the world as this man in his humility. Rather, it would seem altogether difficult to find in any histories a single man still living among humankind who possessed, from sunrise to sunset, from north and sea, so famous and beloved a name throughout the whole earth.

22. To mention those regions from which more certain memorials are known to survive even to this day: his reputation was most celebrated both in the Eastern Church and among the westernmost Irish, in the remote borders of Spain to the south, and in the distant islands of Denmark and Sweden to the north. He received frequent letters from every quarter and answered them [Col. 0316B]. Gifts were sent to him from every quarter, and his blessing was sought from every quarter. Finally, like a most fruitful vine, he propagated his branches in every direction—except that he would not consent to send his brethren to the land of Jerusalem, although the king had prepared a place, because of pagan attacks and the unhealthiness of the climate.

Nor does that bishop appear to have claimed anything inappropriate when, after Bernard’s holy death, he consoled the brethren and praised him, among other things, because “his sound went forth into all the earth, and his words unto the ends of the world.” Yet humility of heart overcame the eminence of his name: the whole world could not exalt him as much as he alone cast himself down. All regarded him as supreme; he regarded himself as the lowest [Col. 0316C]. Everyone preferred him to themselves; he preferred himself to no one.

Indeed, as he often confessed to us, amid the highest honours and popular favour, or the favour of exalted persons, he seemed to have borrowed another man, and regarded himself as absent—as though he considered it a kind of dream. But when simpler brethren spoke with him more freely, as is customary, and friendly humility could always be enjoyed, there he rejoiced that he had found himself and returned to his own person. The modesty natural to him from childhood endured until his final day. Hence, although so great and exalted in the word of glory, he never, as we often heard him declare, spoke even in the humblest assembly without fear and reverence [Col. 0316D], wishing rather to keep silence unless urged by the promptings of his own conscience, by the fear of God, and by brotherly love.

23. We know and have proved that his patience was exercised especially by the Lord’s scourges. From the very beginning of his conversion until the day of his holy death he endured so much that his life seemed to those who knew him to be only a kind of prolonged death. Yet with regard to people too, although the occasions were rarer and perhaps offered lesser tests of patience, it should briefly be said that he did not appear lacking even in this virtue.

Since he used to say that this kind of patience was threefold—toward injuries of words, losses of possessions, and bodily assault—let us set forth at least one example of each, as they presently occur to us. The Servant of God once wrote to a bishop [Note: [Col. 0317D] Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, Letter 213.] concerning the king’s court and council, advising him to persuade the king on certain points and to counsel better measures. But the bishop, violently enraged, sent him a most bitter letter, saying in its very first salutation: “Greeting—and not the spirit of blasphemy”; as though the holy man, horrible to say, had written those things in a spirit of blasphemy.

In reply, the most gentle servant of Christ, remembering the Lord’s answer, “I do not have a demon” (John 8:49), wrote—as his extant letter still contains—“I certainly do not believe that I have a spirit of blasphemy; nor do I know that I have cursed anyone or wish to curse anyone, especially the ruler of my people.” Thereafter he regarded the same bishop as no less dear [Col. 0317B] and no less intimate; that aforesaid insult was with him as though it had never been spoken.

24. The abbot of Farfa had summoned a community of brethren from Clairvaux in order to build them a monastery; but the Roman pontiff prevented this, took them for himself, and established them elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0317D] This occurred in the time of Innocent II, who established at Rome, at Acquae Salviae, the monks requested from the abbot of Farfa. Farfa, a very illustrious monastery in the Sabine country, was then governed by Adenulf, abbot of the place from 1125 to 1144, praised in the *Chronicle of Morigny*, in volume IV of Chesne, p. 377, where he is said to have been present with Bernard in 1130 at the dedication of the church of Morigny by Innocent. Gerard, from being a monk of Farfa became a monk of Clairvaux, and is praised by Herbert in book II of *Miracles*, chapter 29.].

Deeply grieved by this, the aforesaid great man of great devotion placed under a written bond a sum collected of nearly six hundred marks of silver. Coming to the Man of God, he offered it to him, asking that, since he had not deserved to have it in his own region, a new monastery might at least be founded with it on this side of the Alps. The silver was sent for and was entirely lost. When this was reported to him, the Man of God answered nothing but: “Blessed be God, who has spared us this burden. And those who took it should be forgiven more readily,” he said. “They are Romans, after all; and the money seemed enormous, and this was a powerful temptation.”

He was also accustomed to rejoice that about ten monasteries—or sites suitable for building monasteries—had been deceitfully and violently taken from him, because he would not contend; he delighted more in being overcome than in overcoming others. 1127

25. A cleric, one of those called Regulars, once came to Clairvaux and pressed insistently to be received as a monk. The holy Father urged him to return to his own church and did not consent to receive him. The man said: “Why, then [Col. 0317D], have you commended perfection so highly in your books if you refuse to give assistance to one who desires it?” And, more violently incited by an evil spirit of anger, as afterward clearly appeared: “If I held them now,” he said, “I would tear your books to pieces.”

The Man of God replied: “I think that you have read in none of them that you cannot be perfect in your own cloister. If I remember rightly, in all my books I commended amendment of conduct, not change of place.” Then the man rushed at him like one insane [Col. 0318A] and struck him on the cheek, so heavily that redness immediately followed the blow, and swelling the redness. Those present were already falling upon the sacrilegious man; but the Servant of God forestalled them, crying out and adjuring them in Christ’s name not to touch him at all, but to lead him out carefully and take care that no one might harm him in any way. He gave this command so strictly that the wretched man, fearful and trembling, was led out and escorted away without any injury.

26. The Servant of God shone pre-eminently in the freedom of the Spirit, yet with humility and gentleness, so that he seemed in a certain manner both to fear no one and to reverence every person. He used rebukes rather rarely, proceeding instead by admonitions and entreaties. How reluctantly, and not from bitterness of heart, he spoke a bitter word was especially apparent from the fact that he very easily restrained such an impulse.

For he marvelled at the perversity of people who, when perhaps at some time upset, find it burdensome to accept any reasonable excuse or any humble satisfaction. The passion of their own agitation so delights those wretches that they hate every remedy: they stop their ears, close their eyes, put up their hands, and do everything possible to prevent an emotion once arisen from being calmed and healed [Col. 0318B]. Yet a harsh and turbulent reply sometimes restrained his rebuke no less easily than a humble and modest response; hence some said that he pursued one who yielded and yielded to one who resisted.

For he said that where modesty resounds on both sides, conversation is sweet; where it is on one side, useful; where it is on neither, harmful. For where harshness sounds from both sides, there is quarrelling, not correction; not discipline, but strife. It is therefore more fitting for a superior for the moment to overlook the matter, and, once the agitation has been healed, to correct subjects more usefully; or at least, if circumstances require it, to observe the counsel of the Wise Man, that “a fool is not corrected by words” (Prov. 18:2).

He himself speaks of rebukes received neither profitably nor patiently in his forty-second sermon on the *Song of Songs*, saying among other things:

> “Would that it were necessary to rebuke no one! That would be better. But since we all offend in many things, I am not permitted to be silent, for it lies upon me by office to rebuke sinners, and love urges me still more. But if I rebuke and do what is mine, while the rebuke sent forth does not in the least do what is its own, does not achieve that for which I sent it, but returns to me empty, like a dart striking and rebounding—what do you think, brethren, is then my state of mind? Am I not distressed? Am I not tormented? And, to appropriate for myself something of the Master’s words—since I cannot do so from wisdom—I am indeed constrained by two alternatives, and do not know what to choose (Phil. 1:23, 22): whether to be pleased with what I have said, because I have done what I ought; or to repent of my word, because I have not obtained what I wished.”

And below:

> “Perhaps you will tell me that my good returns to me, and that because I have delivered my soul, I am clean from the blood of the man to whom I announced and spoke, that he might turn from his evil way and live. But even if you add countless such things, they will by no means console me as I look upon the death of my son. As though I had sought my own deliverance by that rebuke, rather than his! What mother, even if she knows that she has bestowed all possible care and diligence upon her sick child, if at last she sees herself frustrated and all her efforts wholly ineffective, while he nevertheless dies, would on that account ever cease from weeping?”

And so much for these matters.

1128

27. Moreover, he was such a zealous lover of gentleness and peace that, if some importunate petitioner happened to extract a harsher answer from one who had refused him, he would scarcely thereafter be dismissed empty-handed with the same rebuff. For, as he confessed, he hated every scandal almost by nature; and it was exceedingly burdensome to him to bear any person’s distress—indeed, impossible not to feel it. Thus he despised no one and made light of no person’s grievance, though he set the truth and justice of God above all else. For whenever it was necessary either to rebuke the harmful actions of certain persons or to hinder their undertakings, this was done with such consideration that even those who seemed injured had ample grounds to satisfy themselves concerning him in their own thoughts. Indeed, we have seen some of these very persons—even those of whom this might least have been hoped—afterwards serve him with more devoted obedience or even cling to his footsteps.

Yet he is said to have had envious opponents, so that he might gain merit from them as well. But the glory of his name stood out so singularly that this pestilence wasted away more from despair than from envy and feared to be recognized. Indeed, it was conquered by his humility and gentleness, choked by his benefits, overwhelmed by his services. For he had certainly learned to overcome evil with good, as he says, among other things, in writing to certain brethren: “I shall cling to you, even if you do not wish it; I shall cling to you, even if I myself do not wish it. I shall do good to the unwilling, add benefits to the ungrateful, and honor even those who despise me.”  
[Note: Col. 0319D, Epistle 253, to the abbot of Prémontré, no. 10.]

[Col. 0319D]

28. Indeed, he embraced all people with such brotherly affection that, as he himself used to confess, he was more grievously wounded by the scandal of those to whom he seemed to have given no occasion for scandal. His most compassionate heart was more troubled by another’s unprovoked offence than his conscience was comforted by its own innocence. For he had less hope that what he could not see the source of could be healed; whereas he declared it a great consolation whenever he found grounds on which he could make satisfaction, either to a person on his own account or to God, troubled not without cause on account of a person.

He was deeply affected by every person’s spiritual benefit or harm; the fruit of souls and the conversion of sinners were his highest desire and highest joy. Yet he also pitied bodily necessities with most compassionate feeling. Such was his humanity that he felt compassion not only for human beings but even for irrational animals, birds and wild beasts. Nor did the effect of power fail his compassion. It happened several times that, while travelling, he miraculously delivered by the sign of the cross either a little hare fleeing from dogs and, as it seemed, about to be caught immediately, or a bird fleeing from hawks. He would tell those following him that they laboured in vain and could by no means pursue such predation in his presence.

## Chapter VIII. On the writings of Saint Bernard, and the portrait of his mind expressed in them

[Col. 0320B]

29. We have briefly outlined, according to our measure, these holy qualities of our Father. Yet he appears far more eminently in his books and is made known from his own letters, in which he seems to have expressed so fully his own image and presented a kind of mirror of himself that the Ambrosian saying may deservedly be applied to him also: “Let him sound forth his own praise, and, crowned in spirit, let him be crowned by his writings.”

If anyone wishes to know how vigilant a judge and examiner of himself he was from the beginning, let him look first at his work *On the Degrees of Humility*. If the religious devotion of a pious mind is sought, one must proceed to the homilies *In Praise of the Virgin Mother* and to the book which he published *On Loving God*. If one seeks ardent zeal against the vices of his own people or of others, let him read the work which he calls the *Apology*. If vigilant discernment tempered by that same zeal is sought, let him be heard discussing *Precept and Dispensation*. The exhortatory sermon addressed to the Knights Templar declares how faithful a commender and helper he was of every devout way of life. How far he was from being ungrateful for God’s grace is clear from what he argued, as faithfully as subtly, *On Grace and Free Will*. A diligent reader will recognize how free he was in speech, how eloquent, and how rich in knowledge alike of higher and lower things, in what he wrote to Pope Eugene *On Consideration*.

How devotedly he proclaimed another’s holiness is shown by the care with which he narrated the life of the holy bishop Malachy. In the *Sermons on the Song of Songs*, too, he is revealed both as an investigator of mysteries and as a magnificent builder of character. In the letters which he dictated to different persons on different affairs, a prudent reader will observe with what fervour of spirit he loved every form of justice and equally hated every injustice.

30. For Christ’s faithful servant sought nothing for himself; nevertheless, whatever belonged to Christ he cared for as though it were his own. What crimes did he not rebuke? What hatreds did he not extinguish? What scandals did he not restrain? What schisms did he not repair? What heresies did he not refute? What holy, honourable, chaste, lovely, reputable, virtuous, or praiseworthy discipline, arising in whatever land during his lifetime, was not strengthened by his authority, cherished by his charity, and advanced by his diligence? What thing already advanced did he not wish to spread still further? What thing perhaps fallen into ruin did he not strive with all his strength, as place and time required, to restore? Who, planning any wickedness, did not fear his zeal and authority? Who, proposing any good thing, did not, if able, consult his holiness, seek his favour, and request his help?

Who approached the sacred temple of divinity dwelling in his breast, intending faithfully to cry out over any tribulation, and laboured without effect? The sorrowful carried away consolation from him; the afflicted, help; the anxious, counsel; the sick, remedy; the poor, support. Thus he made himself the servant of all, as though born for the whole world; yet he remained free from all, attending to his conscience as though devoted solely to the care and keeping of his own heart.

31. [The Apostle indeed commends the varieties of graces (1 Cor. 12); and whoever examines carefully will find that, from the beginning, different servants of God have excelled in different gifts. We read of men magnificent in faith and distinguished by many miracles; others had a prophetic spirit and wonderfully knew future things as though present, hidden things as though laid before their eyes. The writings of the ancients likewise attest that some devoted themselves to more rigorous abstinence and cultivated frugality; that others, in their resolution of humility, despising the dignities of this age, greatly pleased the Creator of the age;  
[Note: Col. 0321D. This insertion from manuscripts varies in the edition and in certain manuscripts.]  
that others instructed very many in the doctrine of the word unto the knowledge of salvation, so that, according to the promise of Holy Scripture, they might “shine like stars unto everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3).

Others, labouring in the building of monasteries, enlarged the name of holiness; others, effectively occupied in calming the scandals and tumults of this age and advancing the affairs of God’s Church, were useful in action; others, resting spiritually in sacred meditations, were sublime in contemplation. Which of these gifts would seem lacking in our Bernard? Rather, what among them was not so outstanding in him that it alone would suffice for his praise, even if something else were absent? For although the Church of his time experienced the usefulness of his activity in very many matters, both those mentioned above and many others, the grace of contemplation nevertheless shines magnificently in him, both from visions and revelations of the Lord and from his writings, which abound in spiritual meanings.

Moreover, the fruit of the monasteries which the Lord established through him is so abundant and evident, presenting itself to human eyes, that it needs no writings to commend it. Rather, from the very multitude of these monasteries every succeeding generation will be able to receive certain proof of how many he gathered to Christ’s service, since he propagated so many everywhere. As to the rest—his humility, his refusals of dignities, and also his very scanty diet—we have treated these above. Under another heading we shall take care to record a very few instances among many concerning those things that pertain to prophecy and the manifestation of powers.]

And now, therefore, a second little book, as was stated in the preface, will relate some things concerning those matters which consist in outward signs and the manifold display of powers.

[Col. 0321]

# Book Four, by Geoffrey, Monk of Clairvaux

## Chapter I. On his return from Rome and the relics brought thence; also, on various benefits bestowed upon others through his merit, though without his knowledge

[Col. 0321D]

1. As Bernard, servant of the Lord and man of Clairvaux, rejoices and gives thanks to God in his twenty-fourth sermon on the Song of Songs, heaven’s more merciful eye looked upon his third return from Rome, and at last its more serene countenance smiled: the rage of Leo had subsided, wickedness had come to an end, and the Church had received peace. The Gallican Church received him with such rejoicing that it seemed to display no less joy at his return than it proclaimed at the restoration of peace.

He himself therefore often marvelled and complained that, when after such grievous crowds and tumults of people he judged that he must take leave of the world as though from the beginning, and as though newly undertake the purpose of sacred life, then especially he was received with fuller rejoicings and honoured with services.

On returning from Rome, the holy Father brought with him precious gifts from the bodies of the holy Apostles and martyrs, considering this no small fruit of his labour. Among these, it is worth recalling how he received a tooth of blessed Caesarius. When the martyr’s entire head was presented to him and he was invited to take from it whatever he wished, he asked for one tooth. But although the brethren who had accompanied him laboured for some time, they could not at all pull out the tooth granted to them. For two or three knives which they applied were broken, while the tooth nevertheless remained immovable. Then he said, “We must pray. For we cannot have it unless the martyr himself grants it.” After prayer had been made, he approached reverently and with incredible ease took between two fingers what previously could not be moved with iron instruments.

2. The brethren of the Temple at Jerusalem, professing a faithful knighthood, had at that time begun to possess a new house in Rome. When their aforesaid Father and special patron was returning, they kept his tunic as an exceptional blessing. In that same year a certain priest among them was desperately ill with a most severe fever. When he seemed utterly exhausted and to have reached his end, he caused himself to be carried into the oratory and the tunic of the blessed man to be placed beneath him, expecting only the outcome of death.

Suddenly caught into a kind of ecstasy of mind and as though already released from the flesh, he seemed to see his body lifeless in the very place where he lay, already surrounded by a multitude of priests holding open books and celebrating the customary solemn funeral rites. Without delay, a venerable person appeared from the altar in the face and clothing of the aforesaid holy Father. He motioned to them with his hand to be silent and at the same time forbade them by his voice to consider dead one whose life God had given to the Abbot of Clairvaux.

Immediately returning to himself, he found himself well and told the brethren what he had seen. As we have recently learned from trustworthy men, he is still alive today and lives in Aquitaine, diligently acknowledging the benefit he received by proclaiming the praise of him through whose merit he lives. If anyone is less amazed by this, let him consider that, among the innumerable miracles with which blessed Nicholas is adorned, this is commended as exceptional at the annual celebration of his feast: though far away, he diverted Emperor Constantine by a vision from the destruction of certain men.

3. Nor is what we add unlike this. Abbot Gerard of Moris—a monastery near Clairvaux—  
[Note: Col. 0323D. French *Mores*, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Langres, founded in 1153 by Samson, Archbishop of Reims.]  
testified to us that he once saw Bernard go about the choirs of brethren while they were chanting the psalms and, as he often did, rouse the sluggish, so that what remained of the vigils was sung with greater feeling and vigour. When, on the following day, he familiarly complained to him that he had visited the chanting brethren later than he ought that night, Bernard said: “During the night hours I was occupied by a bodily indisposition; but where the body could not go, the spirit came.”

Gerard was astonished to hear that he had not been bodily present, whom he himself had for so long watched with bodily sight going around both choirs, awakening the sleepers as usual, and laying his hand upon each one.

4. [While the holy Father was staying at Rome, a brother named Robert fell gravely ill at Clairvaux. A certain young man appeared to him, resembling the infirmarian brother, and commanded him to follow. He seemed to follow his guide and came to a high mountain, where he found the Lord Jesus with his angels. He heard him say to his guide, “Keep this man for me.” The Lord then put into the sick brother’s heart certain words which he sent through him to his Clairvaux.

When morning came, he whom all thought about to die immediately sat up; and, to everyone’s amazement, he had Lord Geoffrey, then prior and now bishop of Langres, summoned. In his presence he said among other things: “The Lord commands you to build spacious houses able to hold the people whom he will send to you in great number. Command the brethren of the granges to conduct themselves honourably and to offer secular people a model of good example; for woe to him through whom even one has turned back.”

About twenty days later, while he was still suffering from the same desperate illness, the admirable Father Bernard, absent in body but present in spirit, came to Clairvaux, visited the sick man, sang the morning hymns around him with a great multitude of brethren, and spent that night there beside him. When morning came, the same brother appeared well and told the brethren also how he had been delivered.]

5. We believe that the fame of the venerable William has reached many ears. Once lord of Montpellier, he now lives as a true poor man of Christ and humble monk in the monastery called Grandiselve.  
[Note: Col. 0324D. Commonly, Grandselve, in the diocese of Toulouse, founded in 1144.]  
We learned from his account what we are about to tell, as he said he had received it from the mouth of the man to whom it happened.

In the city of the Auscii, the metropolis of Gascony, a certain knight was ill. Since the raging disease had seized the lower parts of his body from the loins downward, he lay in bed for many days, with no small part of him already dead. At last, repentant and trusting in God’s mercy, he ordered himself carried, at whatever effort, to God’s servant, whose fame for powers had spread everywhere so widely. He had already travelled several days and progressed no less in faith and devotion than in the journey itself, when God, taking pity on the man, deigned wonderfully both to relieve his infirmity and spare him the exertion.

For someone met him on the road and asked who he was and where he was going. Having learned the necessity of his journey, the man said: “On behalf of that Saint I command you to return. Know that when you come home, you will be well.” God persuaded him to believe, by whose providence all these things were surely being done. He returned, and as he returned gradually received the mercy promised him, so that he did not reach home before receiving the gift of complete health.

6. [Queen Matilda of the English once displayed such devoted affection toward this servant of God that, when he came to Boulogne, she met him outside the city on foot with the people, although she herself was pregnant and already far advanced. A few days later, when the time of delivery came, she was so severely afflicted that both she and her whole household despaired utterly of her life. All her remaining property had already been assigned to the poor and to churches, and even the royal garment in which she was to be buried was being prepared, as though she were about to die at once.

Then suddenly remembering the man of God and invoking his name with full faith, in that very invocation she gave birth safely after the hopeless labour. Nor did she delay in sending a trustworthy messenger through whom she might thank her famous helper, calling the child thus born, not without reason, his child.  
[Note: Col. 0325D. See Epistle 315.]

But whenever he heard that something of this sort had occurred, he would reject it as humbly as gladly and say: “This must surely be attributed to me in the same way as to one who was entirely unaware of it.”]

[Col. 0325B]

7. In the monastery called Bellevallée,  
[Note: Col. 0325D. Of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1119.]  
near the city of Chrysopolis, a man was tormented by a demon, doing and saying marvellous things under its instigation. After the brethren had offered many prayers and that spiritual wickedness persisted shamelessly, the venerable abbot of the place, Pontius, who is still alive today, remembered that he possessed a stole which the blessed Father had once used in offering the saving sacrifice.

Without delay he took up the weapon mighty through God and confidently attacked the enemy. He had scarcely reached the threshold of the cell in which the miserable man lay when the malign spirit suddenly confessed himself conquered in dreadful cries: “Look, I am going out; I withdraw at once. I can remain no longer.” The abbot replied: “In the Lord’s name, and by the merit of the blessed man whose stole this was, I command you: depart quickly; do not delay.” At once the demon was driven from the man and the man freed from the demon.

What other person might not perhaps have rejoiced dangerously that spirits were so subject to him as to yield even to one absent? But he, when the abbot himself reported it, was unmoved and rather mocked those whom he saw stirred to great wonder over the matter. He answered with these words: “Why should not we two easily prevail over one? God could easily cast him out, especially since, as you say, I was assigned to him as companion and helper.” He often used responses of this kind on such occasions.

For as one who was truly and genuinely—not an exhibitor but an imitator—of humility, he knew that people could be dissuaded more effectively from what they marvelled at by a certain indirect and artful rejoinder than by an open denial, which, while displaying a more commendable humility, would not diminish but increase people’s estimation of him. Hence, speaking from his own experience in one place, he says: “The truly humble person wishes to be considered lowly, not to be called humble.”  
[Note: Col. 0326D. Sermon 16 on the Song of Songs.]

## Chapter II. On the spirit of prophecy and the revelation of future events in which he shone

8. This too was well known: while still living in the flesh, but appearing in spirit, he foretold to a certain brother the day of his death. A novice brother at Clairvaux, a young man of good conduct and good disposition, fell ill. The day was not far off when, after the customary year of probation, he would put on the new man—unless he first put off the man. For, perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years; his soul was pleasing to God.

On the fifth day before his last day, when a certain brother [Gerard, now abbot of the monastery of Longpont] visited him, the novice was greatly cheered. Among other words of spiritual grace he said: “Look, I shall die on the fifth day. For today our father, Lord Abbot, appeared to me with a multitude of monks and, comforting me gently, said that I would die on the fifth day.”

The report spread among the brethren, and the word was published before it was fulfilled. All awaited that day, but he himself, the blessed man, was foremost in his expectation. The fifth day was already declining toward evening, while the young man’s spirit was being raised more and more to the Lord. At last, about the eleventh hour, in the very struggle of death, with the light of his eyes wholly veiled, as is usual, attending to no one now, he was hastening toward his departure.

Meanwhile the holy Father visited him, recalled him as from deep sleep, and as though drew him back as he was departing, not allowing him to go without farewell. At his voice the young man opened his eyes; and, his face wonderfully brightened, he gazed at him for some time. We all marvelled that a mortal man—indeed, one already dying—should triumph over death so far as to rejoice with gladness at the very point of death, most beautifully displaying to us the poet’s line:

> “Begin, little child, to recognize your mother with a smile.”  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues*, 4.)

Then the holy Father consoled him and told him to fear nothing, but to hasten directly to the Lord Jesus Christ and offer him the humble greeting of his poor household. At these words, assenting as he could by an inclination of his head and a movement of his lips, he closed his eyes again and rested in peace in that same hour.

9. We have learned that many things were revealed to this servant of God through the Spirit, and that he wonderfully predicted many things without a preceding revelation. We append a few examples. Once, while the holy Father was in the city of Noyon in the house of Bishop Simon, Hervé of Beaugency was brought to him, a most charming boy of royal blood and the bishop’s nephew. On the following night Christ showed his servant what would happen after a long time: he seemed, as though during the celebration of Mass, to give an angel a kiss of peace to carry to the boy.

Certain of the revelation, Bernard declared that Hervé would renounce the world and one day become a devout servant of Christ. This promise became so famous and widespread that Hervé himself later confessed to us that, whenever the pricks of conscience accused him in his youth, it always occurred to him that it was impossible, after such a promise of the holy man, for him to die in secular dress. Nor was he disappointed in his hope. For the venerable Waleran, first abbot of the monastery of Ourscamp, made him a monk and, fulfilling an angelic office, imparted to Hervé the peace which he himself had received from the mouth of the holy Father.

Hervé’s subsequent manner of life was such that he seemed worthy of such an oracle. He succeeded the aforesaid Waleran in governing the monastery of Ourscamp;  
[Note: Col. 0327. Ourscamp, in the diocese of Noyon, founded in 1129 by Bishop Simon.]  
and finally, still healthy and sound, he knew and foretold his approaching death when Waleran himself announced it to him by revelation.

10. What we add was similar. Once the holy Father was travelling through the region of Paris. Bishop Stephen and all the others present earnestly asked him to turn aside into the city itself, but could not obtain it. Unless a grave reason compelled him, he avoided public gatherings with great zeal. Though in the evening he had arranged his route elsewhere, in the morning, as soon as he spoke with the brethren, he ordered the bishop to be told: “We shall go to Paris, as you asked.”

A very large body of clergy assembled, as they always used to request from him the word of God. Immediately three among them were pierced with compunction and converted from vain pursuits to the cultivation of true wisdom, renouncing the world and attaching themselves to God’s servant. When Bernard first saw one of them come forward suddenly during the discourse and ask for his feet, he bent down a little and spoke in the ear of a brother sitting near him: “I foresaw this man coming, just as I now see him, in a vision of the night; it was for his sake that the Lord brought us here.”

That novice afterwards lived in great purity and devotion, highly acceptable to God and people, and after some years rested at Clairvaux in a blessed end.

At another time, while the man of God was in the city of Troyes, his venerable sons Galdric and Gerard appeared to him, already released from the flesh. One had been his brother according to the flesh, the other his maternal uncle. As they passed quickly by, as though hurrying, they answered Bernard, who called them back and wished to detain them, that they had to go for Brother Geoffrey, a monk who had been their companion from their first conversion and had served God vigorously enough in building many monasteries. The holy Father at once woke the brethren and ordered haste; when he came to the monastery, he found Geoffrey that very day, as he had foretold them, already at the point of death.

11. [King Louis the Elder of France, once hostile to certain bishops of his realm, drove them from their sees and cities. This venerable man also wrote several letters, still extant today in copies, labouring for their peace. It happened that, in the presence of the holy Father, many bishops wished to bend the king’s anger. With all humility they prostrated themselves upon the ground and held his feet, yet did not thereby obtain favour.

Moved by this, the man of God, with religious resolve, reproved the king more sharply on the following day because he had despised the Lord’s priests. He also freely announced what had been revealed to him that same night: “This obstinacy,” he said, “will be punished by the death of your firstborn, King Philip. For I saw you with your younger son Louis bowing at the feet of the bishops whom you despised yesterday; and I immediately understood that, when Philip had swiftly been removed, you would ask the Church, which you now oppress, for Louis’s installation.”

Not long afterward a lamentable event fulfilled this prediction. Philip died, and his father arranged for Louis the Younger—who happily reigns today—to be anointed.]

## Chapter III. On various future events foretold by him through the prophetic spirit

[Col. 0328B]

12. The Lord delivered Count Theobald, a most faithful prince tested in great tribulation, no less marvellously than mercifully. Though exceedingly powerful in the kingdom and second only to the king, he was wholly devoted to almsgiving and intent upon works of piety. He was a most devoted lover of all God’s servants, and especially of Bernard of Clairvaux.

God allowed him to be attacked and afflicted to such an extent that, when the king and nearly all his powerful neighbours conspired against him, his escape was despaired of. Piety and religion were publicly mocked, and almsgiving disparaged. His monks and lay brothers were called his useless soldiers and crossbowmen. Such blasphemies rang out not only among outsiders, but even in his own cities and castles.

At length, when many bishops and other persons had gathered and the man of God was also present, they discussed these matters. A certain bishop, at that time extremely renowned for authority and reputation for prudence, said: “Count Theobald is in the king’s hand; there is no one who can rescue him.” Another bishop replied: “There is one who can free him.” The former, much astonished, asked who was believed able to do so. At last, hearing that God, who can do all things, could deliver him, he was not a little annoyed and said: “He can, if he appears openly, carries a club, and strikes on both sides; but so far he has not done these things.”

In this great despair, while outsiders pressed the aforesaid prince fiercely, those of his own powerful men who had deserted him nearly all attacked him more grievously. Nor did the few who seemed to remain afflict him less, since their defection from the others made them suspect as well. Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, often and familiarly consulted the man of God concerning what the Lord revealed to him in these matters. Bernard had often replied that nothing appeared to him except tribulation upon tribulation. At last, however, when asked again, he said that there would be peace in the fifth month.

And indeed peace was restored on the final day of the fifth month, Bernard himself both praying and working for it, so that there was no doubt that this most pious prince had been delivered from such severe and imminent dangers chiefly through his effort and merit.

13. [Some years later there were bitter hostilities between the same king of France and Geoffrey, count of Anjou. The cause was that the count, despite the king’s prohibition, had besieged the nobleman Gerard of Monstrelet in his very strongly fortified town, captured him with his wife, children, and relatives, and destroyed the fortification itself.

The holy man was therefore negotiating the restoration of peace, with many bishops and princes gathered for this purpose. Suddenly the count, stirred by the gall of bitterness, left everyone without greeting, mounted his horse, and departed. All were confused; the assembly was already dissolving in despair of peace; and Gerard approached the man of God asking permission to leave, as one about to return to death and imprisonment. For he had been brought to the conference under hostages.

While the man of God consoled him, Gerard wept and wailed still more grievously: “I grieve less for my own fate,” he said; “I mourn that all my people will die with me.” The blessed man, moved with compassion, said: “Do not fear. Be certain that God will help you and yours, and sooner than you can even hope.” For he recalled a vision which he had seen while coming to the conference: as though he were about to read the Gospel, he asked the holy Bishop Malachy for a blessing, and therefore he was confident that peace would undoubtedly follow.

Gerard had not yet reached the threshold of the house as he departed from Bernard when someone suddenly met him and announced that the count was returning. All marvelled to hear so swift a fulfilment of the promise. For in that same hour the count returned, and the desired peace came about.

The same count, on account of this affair, had been bound by the bonds of anathema at the command of the supreme pontiff. Yet he utterly refused to humble himself as he ought in order to be absolved or to confess his fault in the matter. Rather, as he was exceedingly high-spirited, he prayed that God might never forgive him such an offence, considering himself innocent and unjustly bound. Therefore the holy Father left him not a little saddened and said to him—for he knew the Scriptures—“With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you again” (Matt. 7:2).

That same day, when certain persons were discussing this wickedness and saying that the prince had erred grievously, God’s servant, inflamed with zeal, said: “This rashness will be punished severely enough. It is altogether impossible that, in this very year, the count himself should not either die or experience some other manifest punishment of divine indignation.” Not a few persons, both among those present and others, heard these words. They were fulfilled so swiftly that the same count died within fifteen days.]

14.
