Once Christ’s servant entered the kingdom of Germany, hastening toward the region of Mainz to restore peace between King Lothair and the nephews of his predecessor, Emperor Henry: namely Conrad, who later succeeded Lothair in the kingdom, and Frederick, father of this Frederick, who after Conrad was elected and holds the sovereignty today.

The venerable Albert, metropolitan of Mainz, sent an honourable cleric named Mascelin to meet the man of God. When Mascelin said that his master had sent him to serve Bernard, the man of God looked at him for a little while and said: “Another Lord has sent you to serve him.” The German was alarmed and wondered what he meant; he firmly maintained that his lord, the archbishop of Mainz, had sent him. Christ’s servant replied: “You are mistaken; it is a greater Lord who has sent you—Christ.”

At last understanding the direction in which the words were aimed, the man said: “Do you think that I wish to become a monk? Far be it from me; I have not thought of it, nor has it entered into my heart.” Yet though he refused, God’s servant insisted by every means that what must come to pass was not what Mascelin had planned for himself, but what God had ordained concerning him.

Accordingly, during that same journey he was converted to the Lord, bade farewell to the world, and, with many other learned and honourable persons whom Christ’s servant gathered at that time, he too followed Bernard, as had been foretold to him.

15. The Lord also changed Henry, brother of the king of the Franks, who now adorns the see of Beauvais, by a conversion not unlike this. For it happened that this same Henry came to the Man of God to speak with him about [Col. 0330C] some secular business; and, visiting the community of the brothers, he commended himself to their prayers. In the course of holy exhortation, the holy Father said to him in 1136: “I trust in the Lord that you will by no means die in the condition in which you are now placed; rather, you will swiftly prove by your own experience how much the prayer you have requested from these men will benefit you.”

This was fulfilled later that same day, not without the amazement of many; and the monastery was filled with every kind of rejoicing at the conversion of so great a young man. But while his companions mourned, and the whole household wailed as though they saw him dead, one Andrew of Paris cried out above the rest, “Henry is drunk! Henry is mad!”—sparing neither insults nor [Col. 0330D] blasphemies. Yet, on the contrary, Henry himself earnestly begged the Man of God to exert himself especially for Andrew’s conversion. The holy man said to him, in the hearing of many: “Leave the man alone. His soul is now in bitterness; do not be greatly concerned about him, for he is yours.”

And when Henry, having conceived still greater hope, persisted in asking him to speak to Andrew, the Man of God looked at him more sternly. “What is this?” he said. “Have I not already told you: He is yours?” Andrew heard these words, for he too was standing there. Being, as he generally was, wicked and strongly averse to the holy life, he turned over such thoughts within himself in silent reflection—as he admits even today: “Now I know that you are a false prophet. For I am certain that you have spoken a word, and it will not come to pass. Before the King and princes, [Col. 0331A] in every celebrated assembly, I shall not refrain from reproaching you with this, so that your falsehood may become known to all.”

But how wonderful is God in his counsels over the children of men, laughing at their vain attempts, so that his purpose may be fulfilled when and how he himself wills! For on the next day Andrew went away, calling down every evil upon the monastery where he left his master, and even wishing that the valley itself, with its inhabitants, might be utterly destroyed. Those who had heard the holy man’s prediction concerning him were deeply disturbed and astonished when they saw him depart in this manner. But God did not permit their faint-heartedness and weak faith to be tested for long. That day alone he went forward, in some measure resisting and rejecting the grace of God; but on the following night, overcome and, as it were, bound—drawn and compelled [Col. 0331B] by the Spirit of God—he could not wait for daylight. Rising before dawn and swiftly returning to the monastery, he presented to us another Saul—or rather, another Paul made out of Saul.

16. Among the others whom Christ rescued from the empty way of life of this world through the ministry of his servant, many noblemen, many wise and learned men from the regions of Flanders at one time professed holy servitude under his instruction. First among them seemed to be that Geoffrey of Péronne, who afterwards held the office of Prior at Clairvaux and died there.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] A.D. 1146; see Letter 106.]

In them that Gospel saying was quite clearly fulfilled: “Many will say to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ; behold, there’” (Matt. 24:23). For they were urged by many persuasions to choose another religious profession [Col. 0331C] and other places, until the Servant of God came upon them when they were already nearly scattered. By the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth, all their former hesitation vanished; and the will of them all alike was unshakably confirmed in his counsel.

This happened not without a sudden and wholly unexpected change of mind in some of them. For when the aforesaid Geoffrey was already following the Man of God to the monastery, he began to be assailed by a most grievous temptation. One of the brothers, looking at him, said: “What is this? Why does your face appear so altered and so heavily overshadowed by a cloud of sadness?” Geoffrey replied: “I know that I shall never again be cheerful.” When that brother, greatly troubled, reported these words to the Man of God, [Col. 0331D] he saw a holy church near the road on which they were travelling, turned aside into it, and prayed. While the others waited outside, Geoffrey, oppressed by weariness, fell asleep on a stone.

At last, when both rose together—the one from prayer, the other from sleep—Geoffrey appeared as much more joyful and cheerful than all the rest as he had formerly been sad. When the aforesaid brother gently reproached him with the gloomy saying he had uttered, he replied: “Although I then said, ‘I shall never again be cheerful,’ now I say, ‘I shall never again be sad.’”

1137. 17. This same Geoffrey, in the first period of his novitiate, was solicitous with filial affection for his father, a noble and powerful man [Col. 0332A] whom he had left in the world; and he earnestly begged the holy Father to ask the Lord for his conversion. The Man of God said to him: “Do not be afraid. With my own hands I shall bury him in this Clairvaux as a proven monk.” Both things came to pass: he became a perfect monk, and was buried at Clairvaux by the holy Father, as he had foretold.

For it was as though he could not die while the holy Father was absent. Though sick for five months and experiencing in himself the frequent—indeed continual—summons of death, he held on until the holy Father returned, so that, as he had long before promised, he might commit him to burial.

18. [The Queen of France, wife of the aforesaid Louis the Younger, had lived with him for many years and had no children. The holy man was with the King, labouring to bring about [Col. 0332B] a certain peace, while the Queen was striving in the opposite direction. When he urged her to desist from what she had undertaken and to suggest better counsel to the King, she began in the course of their conversation to lament her barrenness, humbly asking him to obtain offspring for her from God. He replied: “If you do what I advise, I too will pray to the Lord concerning the thing you ask.” She agreed, and the effect of peace was not delayed. Once peace had been restored, the aforesaid King—because the Queen had suggested the matter to him—humbly demanded from the Man of God what had been promised. This was fulfilled so swiftly that, at about the same time in the following year, the same Queen gave birth.]

19. Lord Abbot Rainard of Cîteaux, whom the holy Father, having taken him from Clairvaux, both embraced as a son and revered as a father, entered the regions of Provence to regulate certain [Col. 0332C] monasteries. While the Man of God remained at Clairvaux and was speaking with a certain brother, he was suddenly moved by inspiration and said: “The lord of Cîteaux is either dead or about to die.” The brother was greatly astonished to hear this; but he was more amazed when, a few days later, he heard the death of that abbot announced.

20. [In the same year in which the holy Father was to depart this life, three young men from the nearby town called Bar-sur-Aube entered the monastery of Clairvaux for conversion. The third of them, at the devil’s urging, returned to his vomit. The brothers were therefore more concerned for the other two, and spoke with the holy Father about this in their presence. Looking at them, he said: “This one will never suffer any temptation; the other will suffer many, but nevertheless he will prevail.” Both outcomes, as we heard them foretold, we saw fulfilled. Indeed, we often used to tell the latter, when he sometimes nearly failed in temptation and began already to depart, that it was impossible for him to be overcome whom the holy man had said would not be conquered by any temptation.]

Once the Servant of God spent the night in prayer at his monastery of Clairvaux, beseeching the Lord with his customary concentration. At that very hour, a certain poor man—truly poor in spirit—died in the guest cell. The holy Father heard his soul carried to heaven [Col. 0333A] with singing voices; and when in the morning he questioned the brothers who had been present, he discovered that the man’s death had occurred at the hour when he had heard the voices rising on high.

## CHAPTER IV. Of the miracles and various benefits bestowed by him, especially in the kingdom of France

21. When the blessed bishop Malachy, whose life full of virtues the holy man diligently wrote, rendered up his blessed soul to heaven at Clairvaux, according to his heart’s desire, the venerable Abbot, while offering the saving sacrifice for his passing, learned of his glory through the Lord’s revelation. At the same inspiration, after the sacrifice had been completed, he changed the form [Col. 0333B] of the prayer and recited the collect proper to celebrations of holy bishops rather than to commendations of the dead, saying:

“God, who hast made the blessed bishop Malachy equal to thy saints in merits, grant, we beseech thee, that we who keep the feast of his precious death may also imitate the examples of his life.”

1138. Then he approached reverently and most devoutly kissed his holy feet. Yet he would consent neither to disclose the manner and sequence of the vision to anyone nor to write it in the Life of the same bishop. When he was repeatedly asked, he gave only this answer: that it concerned his own person too closely.

[Nor is there any doubt that he concealed many similar things in the same manner—whatever things, namely, the Lord allowed him to conceal. For once at Verdun, a city of Lorraine, [Col. 0333C] when he was offering the sacrifice of praise at the tomb of the most reverend Albert, bishop of Ostia, recently deceased, for the commendation of his soul, he likewise changed the collect at its conclusion. Yet what he had seen concerning him was neither asked nor confessed, since he hardly seems to have done this without a definite revelation.]

[Note: [Col. 0333] Read “Alberic,” to whom Letter 219 is addressed and of whom mention was made above, Book III, no. 17.]

22. Concerning the grace of healings, Christ worked through this servant of his so many remarkable signs that in him too there seemed to be fulfilled what John the Evangelist testifies concerning Christ himself: “If all were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” (John 21:25). Yet let us at least set forth a few examples out of the many.

The inhabitants call a place Châteauvillain, [Col. 0333D] which, they say, is six miles from Clairvaux. There a pregnant woman had passed the entire time for giving birth; and, after several months had now elapsed without her delivering, the matter became ever more astonishing. Her labour was delayed so long that it seemed rather an illness; she was no longer believed to be pregnant but merely swollen. For who could believe that an infant could remain within its mother’s womb for a whole year? The desperate woman was therefore brought to the monastery of the Man of God in this condition.

The unfortunate woman was placed at the gate, and the cause of so great a misery was reported to the brother porter. Asked for help and moved with compassion at this unheard-of affliction, he humbly approached the holy Father, faithfully setting before him the woman’s need and faithfully carrying out the duty of his assigned message. And—marvellous operation of divine power, still more marvellous in accelerating what had been so marvellously delayed!—as though the child, long destined to be born, had waited only for this, the woman gave birth that very hour. When the brother returned to the gate, the remedy having preceded him, [Col. 0334A] he did not find the affliction which he had reported.

23. At another time, in the territory of Auxerre, near the town called Coulanges, a woman was in danger for many days because the child had come to birth but the mother had no strength to deliver. Meanwhile the Servant of Christ arrived and, in response to a request for a blessing, sent blessed water. The woman tasted it, and the child was immediately born. The venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, baptized him and gave him the name Bernard.

On the same journey and in the same territory, as a crowd of fever sufferers, as they were accustomed to do everywhere, asked the Man of God for blessed bread, a certain cleric named Girard from the castle called Clamecy—half-educated and mocking the people’s faith—blasphemed. In the very words of blasphemy he was seized by a most severe fever, and was compelled to follow the Man of God as he departed for Auxerre. Repenting before him, he obtained by many prayers the very blessing which he had disparaged. So many people who tasted such a blessing recovered their health that only the knowledge of God, by whose power these things occurred, could comprehend the number.

24. [Col. 0334C] In the territory of Meaux we saw a knight offering most devout thanks to the Man of God because, at the first taste of bread blessed by him, he had received complete recovery from a quartan fever. He had suffered so severely from it for almost eighteen months that, at the hour of its attack, he was like a madman and did not recognize even his own mother.

We also heard the venerable Gerard, bishop of Limoges, testify that a young man of his household, mortally wounded in the head, lay foaming and out of his senses. When a morsel of bread blessed by the Man of God was put into his mouth, he experienced its power so swiftly that he rose up whole that very hour.

Nor should it be passed over that this blessing preserved the very substance of the bread from every harm of corruption. [Col. 0334D] We have seen many who kept the same loaves for seven years and more, with neither colour nor flavour changed. 1139. Only a few days ago, while we were discussing these matters, the venerable abbots Girard and Henry, arriving from the regions of Sweden, testified to us that bread marked with his blessing eleven years earlier still remained with them wholly uncorrupted. We know that similar bread is preserved to this day among some of our own number, and believe that it is stored among many others as well. And now let us offer a sufficiently suitable and evident testimony to this fact.

25. The great and most honourable Eskil, archbishop of the Danes, [Col. 0335A] revered the holy Father with singular affection and honoured him with singular devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Eskil finally became a monk at Clairvaux in 1178 and died there in 1181, according to the Chronicle of Clairvaux. Letter 390 to him survives.]

He was not satisfied merely to see him in his sons, after founding a new monastery and obtaining from him the desired colony of the holy congregation. His ardent desire prevailed upon him: though a man of such authority, and uniquely powerful in those islands in both ecclesiastical and secular authority, he set aside everything and exposed even himself to many dangers and hardships. It is no great matter to speak of the expense, although we heard him himself declare that on that journey he spent more than six hundred marks of silver.

Thus he came to Clairvaux, humble though exalted: he had been drawn from the ends of the earth not by curiosity to hear wisdom, [Col. 0335B] but by zeal of faith and fullness of devotion. How much he wept there, and how he conducted himself not only toward the man whom he so singularly revered but also toward the least of the brothers, is not easy to say.

At last, as he was about to return home, he ordered, by human reasoning, that bread blessed by the Servant of God be baked again in an oven so that he might carry it back and preserve it longer, as those crossing the seas carry twice-baked bread. Hearing this, the saint would not permit so devout a man to err. Gently reproving him, he found his faith deficient in this respect: “What? Can the blessing not preserve the bread better than rebaking?” He would not agree to bless that bread, but ordered ordinary bread to be brought to him, blessed it, and said: [Col. 0335C] “Take this with you. Henceforth be in no way concerned about its decay.”

He took it; and, after returning to his own people, he boasts to this day that the defect of his faith has been refuted by the most evident reality of the matter. He did not fail to visit the holy Father’s tomb, nor is his affection for him now less than it was then; nor does he trust less in him than when he was alive, since he has no doubt whatever that he lives more truly now. He also confessed to us concerning the bread he carried back that, although the third year has now elapsed, the faith and blessing of the blessed man have kept it untouched.

26. Religious men who had come with that archbishop also told us of a miracle, worthy of remembrance, recently performed at the monastery which, as we mentioned above, he himself founded in his own land.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] He founded two monasteries of the Cistercian Order [Col. 0336D] in Denmark: one called Granadium, in the diocese of Lund; the other Esconense, in the diocese of Roskilde, which is the monastery discussed here.]

“There was,” they said, “in that same country a noble young man, related to the archbishop himself by blood, but less dear to him because of his many crimes. Stricken by a most serious illness, he scarcely obtained a visit from him, and by his hand he was brought to the monastery which he had founded. There, renouncing the world with the deepest contrition of heart, he persisted for several days in humble and most faithful confession, while suffering ever more severely from the same illness.

“At last, as it grew worse and he recognized that his end was near, [Col. 0336A] he embraced the presence of the abbot and brothers with wonderful affection. With wonderful devotion he urged them to take up spiritual arms, so that they might effectively protect the soul entrusted to them and about to depart at once, and faithfully provide it with the altogether necessary escort through the most cruel darts of the enemies that threatened it. Thus fortified by the divine Sacraments in this supplication, and in devout confidence both in the protection of these servants of God and in the Lord’s mercy, he expired, leaving all those standing round with great confidence in his salvation. The brothers then offered, as devoutly as they could, the saving sacrifice of the Lord’s body for the commendation of his soul.”

27. [Col. 0336B] Then suddenly the enemy of human salvation, apparently beyond doubt enraged by the liberation of that soul—which for many days he had believed himself to possess beyond recovery—and, by God’s permission, exercising that rage with sufficient cruelty, seized one of the brothers with a sudden frenzy. The miserable man cried out in horrible voices and could scarcely be restrained by the hands of many persons. At last he was carried away with great difficulty and bound upon a bed; he was grievously tormented, attacking with his teeth both his own limbs and those of the bystanders.

He spoke not in the language he had previously known, but in a new one which none of those present knew. Although they understood nothing of what he said, they heard him producing utterances [Col. 0336C] so fluently, smoothly, and not without coherence that they were convinced beyond doubt that he was speaking some language.

After some hours, while the brothers, deeply distressed, anxiously considered and diligently sought what they could do, one of them, conceiving a salutary counsel inspired by the Lord, advised that the holy relics deposited there by the archbishop himself in that same year—namely, some hair and beard, and one tooth of our blessed father Bernard—be brought and laid upon his breast. As soon as this was done, the wicked spirit began to cry out in horrible tones through the man’s mouth, in the German language: “Take Bernard away! Take him away! Remove him!” And it said: “Alas, Bernard, how heavy you have become! How burdensome, how unbearable you have become to me!”

As it continued for some time to cry out these and similar words, there was a brief silence. Then, suddenly cleansed by the Lord’s mercy, the same brother opened his eyes and, as if waking from a heavy sleep, marvelled greatly at the brothers standing around and at his own bonds. Rather shamefacedly, he asked what these things meant and what had happened to him. From that hour, through the holy merits of the blessed Father, he recovered his former health of mind and body, remembering absolutely nothing of what he had done or said in that most grievous state.

These things have been said by us somewhat out of order, [Col. 0337A] on the testimony of the most reverend Eskil, archbishop of the Danes, occasioned by the bread blessed by the Man of God. [Henceforth, let us continue in order with what remains.]

28. His blessing benefited not only people but also livestock and herds so frequently that on one occasion he severely rebuked the cellarer of his monastery for allowing animals to die without informing him—animals by which the poor were to be supported. Then, as was his custom, he blessed salt and ordered it to be given to the animals; immediately the disease that had arisen ceased.

We saw and learned the same thing in other monasteries: when he heard that the animals of the brothers were dying, he would sometimes come to their aid with the same remedy even without being asked, himself first reminding them of it. Gaudum is the name of a place belonging to the monks of Caziacum.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Chézy, a Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Soissons.]

When the holy man once spent the night there, he healed by prayer and blessing a lame young man who was brought before him, so that, when he returned by the same place only a few days later, the man stood before him whole and devout. In the same region, at a village called Algorrium, the people presented to him as he passed by a woman suffering from frenzy. He laid his hands on her and prayed, left her healed, and went on his way. Later we saw her in the same village meet the Man of God with thanksgiving.

29. Even in remote regions, wherever the necessity of the holy Church drew him, the power of signs followed. At Vertfeuille—for this is the name of a castle in the territory of Toulouse, where, as we recalled in the preceding [Col. 0337C] book (chapter 6), the holy Father once entered and shone with many miracles—a boy crippled and lame from his mother’s womb had recovered the use of both feet and of one hand through the memorial shrine of a certain martyr. The holy Father healed by blessing his other hand, still disabled and, as it were, divinely preserved for him, so that he too might be known to share in the saints’ power.

Cahors is a city of Aquitaine through which the Man of God passed at that time. There, besides 1141 other benefits which he bestowed on many sick persons, one of the servants of the bishop of that city, who had lost the sight of one eye through a severe wound, recovered his vision under Bernard’s hand.

Likewise, in the district of Angoulême, at a place called Castellare, after the offering of the saving sacrifice, and in the presence of the venerable bishops Lambert of Angoulême and Gerard of Limoges, they brought to the Servant of God a boy lame and crippled from his mother’s womb. His elbows and knees were joined to his navel in the form of a ball, and his feet adhered to his buttocks. After first making the sign of the cross, the Man of God touched each limb and immediately stretched and healed it with marvellous ease. Finally, taking his hand, he raised him and dismissed him walking freely. The people, at such great miracles, loudly gave praise to the Lord.

For on the following day, in the district of Limoges, in a village called Saint-Geniez—[otherwise, Saint-Germain]—many signs shone through him. Those suffering [Col. 0338A] various ailments came together from every side, and the Lord’s power was present to heal them. Among the rest, a boy of about ten years, blind from his mother’s womb, was presented to the Man of God before all the people. He spat upon his fingers, anointed the boy’s eyes, made a short prayer, and in Christ’s name opened the eyes of the man born blind.

## CHAPTER V. Of the various miracles performed by blessed Bernard in Germany—at Constance, Basel, Frankfurt, Trier, and elsewhere

30. When the blessed man once entered the kingdom of Germany, he shone so extraordinarily in the grace of healing that it can neither be expressed in words nor believed when told. Those who were present and who investigated carefully and saw with their own eyes testified that in the territory of Constance, near a village called Doniguen, eleven blind persons were given sight in a single day by his laying on of hands; ten cripples were healed, and eighteen lame persons raised up.

Yet, lest we seem impoverished amid abundance, let us commit to memory at least a few examples from the countless multitude, known to have occurred in the more renowned places. When the Man of God came to Constance and the fame of his miracles spread in every direction, the abbot of Reichenau—an ancient and noble monastery situated within Lake Constance—sent him a blind man whom he supported from his alms, and immediately received him back seeing. Heytereseim is the name of a place belonging to the diocese of that city [Col. 0338C] but very far from the city. There too, as in the other places of that province through which he passed, God was glorified by many miracles in his servant. There a man blind from birth received sight under his hand. Likewise another man, deaf and mute from birth, was given hearing and speech.

In the city of Basel, after he had, as usual, addressed the people, so that there might be fulfilled in him what is written of the holy Apostles—that “they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20)—a mute woman was brought to him and immediately spoke when he prayed; a lame man was brought and walked; a blind man was brought and saw.

31. At the city of Speyer, in the presence of Conrad, king of the Romans, who most devoutly escorted the Man of God from the church [Col. 0338D] to his lodging, they brought a lame boy and asked Bernard to deign to lay his hand upon him. Marking him with the sign of the cross and immediately raising him, he set him on his feet, and he walked freely, while all cried aloud in praise of God.

In the chapel of the bishop of that city, with the King himself watching, he restored sight to a blind woman and gave walking to a man lame from birth. Christ indeed did many other things there through his hand, but a few examples suffice. The devout King himself also presented to him with his own hands certain poor little boys, and had cause to rejoice at the healing of many.

Nor did this servant of God shine only in the aforesaid city of Speyer, but also at Frankfurt, a place in the diocese of Mainz, through innumerable miracles. For all who suffered throughout the whole region were brought to him, and so great was the crowd in 1142 that on one occasion, when the aforesaid King could not restrain the pressing throng, he removed his cloak, took the holy man in his own arms, and carried him out of the basilica.

Among the many who obtained healing there was an elderly paralytic from that neighbourhood, a well-known and honourable man. At the prayers of many of his people, and not without great effort, he was brought before the Man of God. After a very brief prayer, as was his custom, Bernard immediately raised and healed him. He appeared not only whole but strong, so that, had one seen him, one could have believed not so much that the man had been changed as that he was another person. When he began to walk vigorously, others prepared to carry off the bed on which he had been brought. But one of those standing by, Hugh, archdeacon of the Church of Toul, recalled him, mindful of that Gospel paralytic: [Col. 0339B] “Not so, not so! You shall not return empty-handed. Take up your bed and walk” (John 5:8). Placing it upon his shoulders, he sent him on his way freely, and all the people, seeing it, gave praise to God.

There too, a boy deaf and mute from his mother’s womb was lifted up by a ladder and came to the Man of God at a window. Under his hand he received both hearing and speech. A paralysed woman of the same region, rich and honourable, likewise recovered there the health she had lost long before. As she leapt up and walked, all who saw rejoiced; but above all the knights who had carried and presented her exulted. Their religious devotion seemed in fact to make them participants in his power.

At the same time, when the saint was passing near a village on the bank of the Rhine called Boppard, healing diverse infirmities throughout the province, a paralytic on a bed was brought before him. Having heard the report of his miracles, he had arranged to be carried from the aforesaid village to meet him. The Man of God laid his hand on him in the midst of the people, raised him up, and sent him back whole to his home.

32. In the same year, when the Servant of Christ entered the city of Trier, all the people, as usual, rushed out to meet him. They brought him two sisters who for four years had lost the sight of both [Col. 0339D] eyes. Making the sign of the cross over each of them, he restored the sight of light; and, seeing, they followed the Man of God with the rest.

In the basilica of the same city, after the man of apostolic grace had offered the immortal Victim at the altar of the blessed apostle Peter, a lame man was brought to him and walked; a blind man was brought and saw; a deaf woman was brought and heard. She said she had been instructed in a dream to seek the Man of God, through whose benefit she would regain her hearing.

At Koblenz, a noble stronghold of the diocese of Trier on the River Moselle, which there flows into the Rhine, the Servant of God was passing by. After he had gone a little way, he ordered a lame man who had been brought to him and signed with the cross to be set down and walk, but there was no one who obeyed. Without delay, the same lame man cried out that the contracted sinew of his thigh was loosening of itself; and, without knowing how, he felt his knee stretched, as though by another, though he had tried in every way before and had never been able to stretch it. All marvelled. What was said was tested with all speed: he was immediately set down, immediately walked, and immediately was recognized as healthy and whole.

## CHAPTER VI. Of the various and notable miracles performed at Cologne, Aachen, Liège, Cambrai, and in Spain

33. We must not pass over Cologne. It is a great city; there the Servant of God possessed great power, and the people honoured him with great devotion. In the cloister of Saint Peter, as we recently learned from trustworthy persons, there is still shown a young man once lame [Col. 0340B] but now walking freely. Presented to the Man of God, he recovered his gait through the laying on of his hand; for this reason he is publicly called his son.

Abbot Henry of Sweden, whom we mentioned above, recently told us that a noblewoman, formerly the wife of his brother, fell into frenzy from grief after her husband’s death. Remaining in that state for a long time, she was kept in bonds. Presented to the same holy Father in the aforesaid city and scarcely marked with the sign of the cross amid the clamouring crowd, she was carried back still bound, as usual; yet she had recovered her former mind and complete health.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Above, no. 24.]

In the same city, noble parents presented their deaf daughter to the holy Father. They said that she had been committed in childhood to a convent of nuns, had there entirely lost her hearing, and had spent several years in that affliction. The holy Father made the sign of the cross and touched her ears; immediately he restored both her hearing and her, now able to hear, to her parents.

Meanwhile an honourable woman, likewise a citizen of Cologne, who had lost the sight of one eye, came forward and said that she had spent much upon doctors in vain for five years. The blessed man immediately gave her sight too by the sign of the cross: freely he gave what he had freely received. In the basilica of Saint Peter, the same servant of Christ also immediately raised another matron, who had been brought in a bed, and ordered her to depart on her own feet whole. For a long time the sinews of her thighs had been so contracted that she could neither rise at all nor stand upon her feet.

[Col. 0340D] Persons who observed more carefully reported that, in the aforesaid city, during the three days he spent there, twelve lame persons were raised up, two cripples healed, five blind persons given sight, three mute persons restored to speech, and ten deaf persons to hearing, through the prayer and laying on of hands of the same holy man.

34. At Aachen, the royal seat, while the blessed man celebrated the solemnities of Mass in that chapel renowned throughout the Roman world, the King of kings and Lord of lords restored and powerfully renewed, under the hand of his servant, walking to a lame man and sight to four blind people.

At the same [Col. 0341A] time, within the territory of Liège, besides countless other events which we pass over for brevity’s sake, near the town called Fontaine, the Lord opened, at Bernard’s prayer, the eyes of a boy blind from birth. Not only were his eyes blind, but his very eyelids were shut and lifeless. Opening them with his most holy fingers, the blessed man bestowed, by God’s gift, vigour upon the eyelids and brightness upon the pupils.

Immediately the boy marvelled at the unknown light and cried out with great rejoicing: “I see the day! I see all people! I see people with hair!” Clapping his hands and dancing, he said: “God, from now on my feet will not strike against stones.”

In the city of Cambrai, while the Man of God celebrated the solemnities of Mass, a boy deaf and mute from birth was presented to him. Those who were nearest immediately set him, now hearing and speaking, upon a wooden step, so that from that higher place he might greet the people with his new speech. Nor is it surprising that the people’s wondrous devotion was immediately followed by wondrous shouting. These few examples from among many may suffice concerning what God marvellously worked in the kingdom of Germany through the hand of his servant.

35. For in Spain also, where he was not himself present, proofs of his holiness shone forth. For when the faithful and prudent servant was gathering everywhere the precious fruit of the Lord’s cross and propagating it again in every place, it happened that he sent some of his sons into Spain, desiring to bear some fruit there also, as among the other nations. Among their number was a certain Albert, a craftsman, at a place named Superadum, who, afflicted with a most grievous illness, had long lain paralysed upon his bed. Meanwhile, through his abbot, he reported his affliction to the holy Father and implored him to have pity on him. On the very day when the blessed man at Clairvaux prayed for this paralytic at the request of that abbot of his, the word of power swiftly running forth, and by the power of prayer, the man in Spain suddenly recovered, feeling as though a vessel full of water were being poured over his head. When the abbot returned and found the aforesaid brother well, he carefully asked him about the manner and time of his deliverance, and ascertained with complete certainty that, while the servant of God was praying in Gaul, the man had been cured in Spain.

36. And since we have once turned our pen toward Spain, let us also relate what happened through the man of God to the most reverend Peter, bishop of Asturias. This Peter, in the year 1144, noble by birth, a monk by profession, devoted in piety, was suffering in a certain monastery, which he himself then governed, from such severe pain in his head that he could neither observe the rule of fasting nor stand without fur caps.

> [Note: At Col. 0341D, Peter the Venerable, in his unpublished writing *On the Clothing of the Brethren*, calls them “lambskin hoods or caps.” There he prescribes that the prior of Cluny shall provide individual tunics—that is, in the common name, *frocos*—fur-lined cowls, lambskin hoods or caps, woollen garments, breeches, and *flumas*, that is, pillow-coverings. Compare the notes on Bernard’s Letters, 1.]

Hearing the widely celebrated report of the miracles accomplished through the Man of God, he sent a certain brother as envoy with his supplication and requested the aid of his intercession. The holy man sent him a woollen cap which he himself used,

> [Note: Above, Book III, no. 5.]

and promised a remedy for the sick man’s head through the power of the Lord. He received the blessing sent to him with the greatest reverence and devotion. Having confessed his sins as carefully as he could, and having clothed himself in his priestly stole, he then, as though touching Christ’s hem, took the cap of Christ’s servant and placed it upon his head. Nor was the fruit of faith and the effect of the blessing slow to follow; rather, he himself marvelled when he immediately felt a swift cure. From that time until the present day, free and sound from this infirmity, he declares to all what power he himself deserved to experience.

[Col. 0342B] Indeed, when he became bishop, he divided these gifts: he carried one half with him in his chests, most honourably, and deposited the other half in the monastery with the same veneration. He wished neither the place from which he had been called nor the see over which he had been appointed to be deprived of so great a blessing.

## CHAPTER VII. Of miracles performed by blessed Bernard in the homeland and neighbourhood of Clairvaux.

37. From this we must return also to those things which he wrought marvellously in his own region. For in this respect perhaps he seems capable of being called even more than a prophet: prophetic honour was not lacking to him, not even in his own country.

[A certain Henry, a great and powerful man in the household and family of the duke of Bavaria, had for a long time been suffering desperately from a thoroughly wretched and pitiable affliction. For he felt within his breast something as though living and moving, and was for the most part frenzied; he could neither be comforted nor be at peace, nor recognize what he feared or suffered, except that he suspected it to be a demon. Brought in this condition from Bavaria as far as Clairvaux to the Man of God, he deserved perfect restoration through his prayer. The same saint also imposed upon him a manner of life and commands to observe thereafter, and sent him home in health. For even to the present day, as we have learned by trustworthy report, he perseveres so obediently that he is not merely content with his own means, but is devoted also to works of mercy; thus the transformation of his conduct seems more marvellous than his cure.]

Musseium is said to be a village on the river Seine, a few miles distant from Clairvaux. From there they brought a man suffering from dropsy to the Man of God. Laying his hands upon him and praying, he also bound the man’s enormously swollen belly with his own belt, ordering him, once health had been restored, to bring back the belt entrusted to him. Nor was healing slow: the swelling gradually subsided. At last, about the twentieth day, he returned thin and well, bringing back both the belt and many thanks to his healer.

On another occasion, as he was leaving the monastery enclosure, they presented to him an old paralysed man from a neighbouring village called Mundivilla. Pausing briefly and praying shortly, he touched the man and ordered him to depart healed through his prayers. When he had gone away, the great crowd that had gathered to meet the Man of God praised the Lord, not without tears.

Again, as he was once returning from a journey, a deaf and mute boy was presented before the monastery gates. He spat, touched his tongue, and put his fingers into his ears. Immediately the obstructions of his ears were removed and the bond of his mouth was loosened.

38. Malenvilla is the name of a village about three miles from the monastery. Passing through it once, the blessed man touched and cured a lame girl, whom we recently learned is still alive and well. In the same period, in the year 1145, near the castle called Burdemont, two knights were discussing the powers of the blessed Father. But one, less believing, said: “If he cures this boy, from that time I shall believe more firmly.” He meant a certain deaf and mute boy brought up among them, who had never spoken or heard. A few days later, as the holy Father was passing nearby, both together took up the boy and presented him to him. He laid his hand upon the boy, signed his mouth and ears, spoke to him, and immediately dismissed him speaking and hearing.

At the town of Risnelmum, in the same region, one may still see a young man named Simon, well known enough, who was brought lame to the aforesaid servant of God and received the power of walking beneath his hand.

Barrum on the Aube is the name of a town three, as they say, leagues from the monastery of Clairvaux. There also the works of divine power often shone forth through this man of God. For, apart from those things which we took less care to investigate, because all our curiosity was overcome by the multitude of signs, Christ at various times raised four lame persons there by his prayer and laying on of hands; he gave sight to two blind persons, and hearing and speech alike to two deaf and mute persons. And near another Barrum on the Seine, a blind man was enlightened at his touch; a paralytic recovered; and a boy lame from his mother’s womb received the power of walking.

39. When our most reverend pope Eugenius III—once a monk of Clairvaux and abbot of Saint Anastasius in the city of Rome—had been raised to the apostolic see and entered Gaul, the holy man went with him; and in Bernard apostolic power was no less pre-eminent than papal dignity in Eugenius. For so great was the throng of persons suffering from various afflictions around the blessed man that, on one occasion, when the supreme pontiff devoutly entered the basilica in which he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, after the sacrifice had been completed and those seeking cure approached as usual, the pope himself was almost crushed by the crowds and could scarcely be led out by the hands of his attendants.

Of the very many things done in the company of that apostolic man, we record two which the greatness of the joy we saw does not allow us to forget. Chaleta is the name of a village lying between the castle of Provins and the river Seine. There a boy of about ten had lain paralysed since the preceding year, unable even to bend his own head unless someone else moved it. His mother and other relatives brought him on a mattress and presented him to the holy man as he passed nearby along the public road. But Bernard raised him after making the sign of the cross, set him upon his feet, and ordered him to walk. Without delay the boy leapt up and walked, glorifying God. He followed the departing saint for so long that Bernard at last ordered him, though unwilling and resisting, to return.

There, not undeservedly, great wonder and great rejoicing arose among all who saw it. But above all, his younger brother, rushing to kiss the boy as though restored from death, moved many of them even to tears. Four years later, in the same village, his mother presented this boy to the blessed man and urged him to kiss his holy feet: “This,” she said, “is he who restored you to life, and restored you to me.”

40. In the same year, 1148, when the abbots had assembled at Cîteaux according to custom, the aforesaid venerable pope was present, presiding not so much in apostolic authority as sitting among them in brotherly charity, as one of them. When the assembly had dispersed at evening, the servant of God went to the cell in which he was staying, and they presented a deaf boy to him. This boy was from the same neighbourhood and, as we learned later, while he had long been awake keeping watch over his flock, he had suddenly been struck by terror and had entirely lost his hearing. The holy Father prayed, laid his hands on the boy, and asked whether he heard. The boy cried out with wonderful devotion: “I hear, lord, I hear!” and embraced him so firmly that he could scarcely be pulled away from him. The report was heard; the boy was presented to the supreme pontiff and other persons; and this miracle became exceedingly renowned.

The holy Father had come to a monastery in the diocese of Besançon named Charus-Locus. Many abbots of his Order were with him there. A woman of that region, in the year 1146, who had been lame for a long time, was brought in a cart and presented to him. He prayed briefly, signed her in the name of the Lord, raised and cured her, so that within the same hour she returned home well.

At the same time, in the monastery of Morimond,

> [Note: Morimond, the fourth daughter-house of Cîteaux, founded in 1115 in the diocese of Langres.]

which is one of the earliest abbeys of the Cistercian Order, a monk lay so disabled by paralysis that, with almost all his limbs deprived of their proper function, he could move neither hand nor foot. The blessed man arrived, visited the paralytic, and, being asked, laid his hand upon him; immediately the sick man felt help. Yet, that the miracle might be more welcome, he recovered his limbs as if by stages: first one hand, then the other. As he was about to depart, Bernard covered the petitioner with his little cloak, and suddenly, within a short time, he obtained soundness in the rest of his body also.

In the monastery of Alba Ripa,

> [Note: Auberive, of the Cistercian Order, founded in the diocese of Langres in 1136.]

a young monk had lost the use of his voice, so that he could neither chant with the brethren nor be understood by anyone unless they stood very close to him. When the holy man visited that monastery, he blessed water mixed with wine and gave it to him to drink. Shortly afterward, a cool sweat broke forth from his breast with wonderful sweetness. Then, on that very day, freed from the same affliction, he began to chant like one of the other brethren; and this benefit remains with him to the present day.

[Many know the devout young man who was formerly a son of the Church of Lyons and is now a Cistercian monk, imitating the conduct of his holy uncle Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, whose name he also received. On hearing of this young man’s conversion, the holy man rejoiced, because he had been bound to his uncle by singular affection, and he sent him a consoling letter.

> [Note: Letter 322.]

It happened, however, that at the same time the young man was seized by fever and fell gravely ill. Receiving the letter with due reverence, he hung it about his neck in faithful devotion as a remedy for health, and to this day he rejoices that he immediately obtained complete recovery.]

41. When the holy Father once came to the monastery of Trois-Fontaines,

> [Note: Troisfontaines, of the Cistercian Order, founded in 1118 in the diocese of Châlons.]

a certain cleric of those called Regulars, an elderly and blind man, was presented to him. Bernard laid his hand upon him, made a brief prayer as was his custom, and within the same hour sent him back to his church seeing.

In the city of Troyes many miracles shone forth through this servant of God. Of these we recall two done in the presence of the bishops Geoffrey of Langres and Henry of Troyes. Relatives and acquaintances presented to him, with many prayers, a bent girl in the house of the aforementioned bishop of Troyes. So great was the crowd that, when the servant of God signed her, raised her as though wonderfully shaping soft clay in his holy hands, and ordered her to walk upright, no room could be found for her. At last they placed her upon a large table standing nearby; she walked freely upright upon it, while all magnificently praised the Lord. We have recently heard from those who know her that she too is still alive.

In the same city, a mother presented her mute daughter to the holy Father. Epilepsy had taken from her the faculty of speech. Without delay, when Christ’s servant laid his hand upon her, the bond of her mouth was loosened and she spoke correctly.

In a place of the diocese of the same city named Domnamant, after the holy man had celebrated the solemnities of Mass, a father presented his blind son to him. Bernard spat upon his fingers and anointed the boy’s eyelids; within the same hour he restored him to his father seeing. Not far from that village, at the town of Argillerias, after the celebration of Mass likewise, as he was leaving the basilica, he signed and healed a lame woman who had lived there for a long time as a beggar, filling with wonder and joy the great crowd gathered from every side.

Also, at the exit of the town called Rosnaium, they presented to the passing Man of God a paralytic man placed upon a cart, his body so wasted that he seemed to bear about only the pale image of death. When he too had been signed, he was ordered to be set down and to walk; and, healed, he followed his cart on his own feet, while all were greatly astonished and cried out in praise of God.

42. At another time, while passing through the nearby castle of Brenam, he encountered a great crowd, as an innumerable multitude always flocked to meet him everywhere and from every side. There, before the sight of all, he touched and raised a lame woman from that town. We later saw her there meeting him with the others and, beyond the others, giving thanks. In the district of Sens, at the castle called Triangulum, during the sacred solemnities of Mass, a woman whose blindness there had been known to everyone for ten years received sight under the hand of the Man of God, to the wonder of all.

At Monasteriolum also, where the Yonne and the Seine meet, while the most pious prince Count Theobald and many other powerful men stood present, they presented a paralysed woman to the Man of God as he offered the divine sacrifice. After the solemnities were completed, he touched and raised her, and in that very hour sent her home well. As she went away on her own feet, we saw in the same basilica the bed on which she had been brought lying empty.

As the same servant of Christ was passing through the castle of Joviniacum in the same diocese, they presented a blind woman to him on the public road. He stopped, prayed briefly, laid his hands upon the woman, and the Lord opened her eyes. When she was seen to see, great rejoicing followed among all present. Crying one to another, “Anna sees! Anna sees!”—for that was the woman’s name—they flocked together in greater numbers from every side.

43. Meanwhile, the holy man, hastening on, avoided the crowds and went out, when a young man, blind in one eye from his mother’s womb, followed and caught up with him. He too immediately received sight through Bernard’s blessing, and the joy of the accompanying people was doubled.

[When the blessed man once came to Auxerre, he entered the monks’ basilica to pray, where the glorious confessor of the Lord, Bishop Germanus, rests. As he came back after prayer, a lame woman, crawling on knees and hands, begged him to have mercy on her. He made the sign of the cross, took her hand, and raised her. Going out, he left her healed and sent her, walking on her own feet, to give thanks to God at the memorial of the aforesaid confessor.]

Chableia is the name of a village which has a notable basilica of blessed Martin. The estate itself belongs to the possession of the Church of Tours, where the body of that most glorious confessor lies. As the servant of God passed through this village, the people presented to him a lame young man. Immediately raised at Bernard’s prayer and walking freely, the young man was led to the aforesaid basilica of blessed Martin, while they magnificently praised the Lord, who had raised up the spirit of his Martin in Bernard.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of various signs and miracles performed indiscriminately, the outcome of which had beforehand been revealed to him in a vision.

44. Christ also more wonderfully showed beforehand in a vision some healings which he worked marvellously through the hand of his faithful servant; many he perceived in his spirit as they occurred; and to some, prompted by the Spirit, he came without being asked. From these, lest the account appear to have proceeded endlessly, we set down a few examples. We also warn, conversely, lest anyone wonder that works so great are written so briefly: for we have seen many of them done in so short a time that we could not recount them as quickly as they occurred. And though it is commonly said that nothing is easier than speech, to this servant of God, through the grace he had received, performing signs seemed easier than recounting performed signs seems to us.

As the holy Father was once leaving the monastery, a man from that region met him and presented his son for healing. For within the monastery he was less willing to lay hands upon the sick, lest, if people flocked there, the peace of the monastery should be disturbed and discipline perish. The boy was foolish and without understanding, lame, deaf, and mute. Within the same hour, by Bernard’s prayer and laying on of hands, he was freed from every affliction at once: he heard, spoke, and walked; becoming sound in mind, he entirely ceased from his former restlessness and frenzy. And when the devout father was leading his now well son to the oratory of the blessed Mother of God in thanksgiving, the brethren spoke together, reflecting on the manyfold affliction of this one boy.

45. To them the holy Father said: “It was a scourge of God and a dreadful torment by an evil spirit. For last night I saw in this very place—for it was near the river Aube, where the boy was healed—that such a boy was presented to me; when the wicked spirit departed from him, he immediately recovered complete health and the use of his limbs.” The blessed man added concerning the same vision: “When I had gone a little farther upon the same road on which we are now travelling, near the next village”—he meant the place called Longum-Campum—“a lame girl was presented to me, and the Lord restored her power of walking.”

The brethren heard and marvelled, more astonished by their expectation of the future miracle than by remembrance of the past. For what like thing had the world ever heard? They came to the place; immediately there was found a lame girl waiting for the Man of God to pass, and awaited by those travelling with him, in accordance with the word which he had spoken. Presented therefore by those who had brought her, and signed by the Man of God, she received the power of walking through God’s gift and went away giving thanks.

46. In the following year there arose a reason for the holy man to go to Langres: a most serious quarrel had arisen between the bishop and clergy of that city. On the first day he laboured without effect; when morning came and he prepared to leave, he said to the brethren: “For in a vision of the night I saw, as I entered the church, a lame woman presented to me and healed.” About an hour later, when the clergy had again assembled, peace was restored beyond all hope. With many entreaties they compelled him to enter the basilica of the martyr Saint Mamertus and, because famine had become severe, to exhort the people to almsgiving. There, while he was speaking—as he had foretold—a lame woman was presented to him and raised, to the wonder of all, but especially of those who remembered having heard beforehand what they now saw accomplished.

47. In the district of Trier there is an ancient monastery called Rutinense. Once, when the Man of God was celebrating the solemnities of Mass there, an innumerable crowd was present. Meanwhile Guntran of Sura, a town near that monastery, caused a lame woman to be brought. For a long time she had crawled upon the ground and was wholly unable to rise; grasping a little stool with her hands, she was accustomed to drag behind her her lifeless loins. But since the crowd prevented the woman from being brought to the Man of God, she suddenly recovered in the middle of the basilica; leaping up, she walked, giving thanks to God not without tears. The rejoicing people immediately carried her little stool to the altar, to present it to the Lord and to Bernard his servant.

The holy Father confessed to us concerning this cure that it had been shown to him the previous night. For he seemed to himself, in that basilica amid the surrounding people, to touch such a woman secretly and unrecognized, and to pass on; then he immediately saw her healed, rejoicing and exulting greatly within himself because he had not been recognized. On that same day heavenly light shone at Rutina in the presence of the blessed man; by its blessing two other lame women received the power of walking, and two blind women likewise received sight. Very often it happened that, while praying, the servant of God knew without doubt that divine power was present. Yet he confessed that he could express in no words the manner in which he knew this.

48. Sometimes, after he had signed certain people and passed on, he said that they had been healed; someone who returned from among those who had heard him found it to be as he had said. Once, leaving the city of Basel, he signed a deaf man and passed on. When he had gone a little way, he called Alexander of Cologne and said: “Go back and find out whether the man hears.” Alexander returned and found him hearing.

Likewise, on the same day, when he had signed another man blind in one eye and was going away, Bernard said: “God has opened his eye.” The same Alexander,

> [Note: See concerning him below, Book VI, at the end of the prologue, and Book VII, chapter 20.]

when he turned back to inquire, found this to be so. This is that Alexander who in those same days, at the holy counsels of the Man of God and the manifestation of his powers, renounced the world with nearly thirty others and followed him. A short time afterward he was made abbot of a monastery in the diocese of Toulouse called Grandis-Silva.

In the diocese of Constance, near the castle of Freiburg, Bernard laid his hand upon a blind man on the road and sent someone to see him; the man was found seeing. He did likewise to two other blind persons in the district of Cologne near the monastery called Brumvillare; when it was reported that they saw, he confessed that he too had felt the power.

49. In the territory of Sens also, in the town called after Saint Florentin, a deaf woman was presented to the Man of God. As he laid his hands upon her, he perceived by the Spirit that the power had taken effect, although she was still confused and agitated—as persons of this kind are—and cried, as she formerly had, that she heard nothing. When morning came, however, since neither she returned nor anyone else brought news about her, the saint, knowing that divine mercy had been present for her, ordered the woman to be summoned. Once found to have recovered her hearing, she came glorifying God and giving thanks to God’s servant.

The same Father was leaving the city of Metz, and, as was customary, the devout people accompanied him, together with their bishop Stephen, his brother Reynald count of Bar, and many other persons from both clerical and knightly ranks. Meanwhile, a reason arose for him to entreat the nobleman Henry of Salm concerning a matter which the bishop himself and the others assembled urged upon him: namely, that he should grant peace to the city and people of Metz, toward whom he was gravely hostile. But Henry wholly refused and swore against it, nor could any entreaties bend him.

In the midst of this, others arrived and presented a deaf man to the blessed man, begging him to deign to lay hands upon him. But Bernard, inflamed with zeal for faith—as sometimes, when necessary causes required it, a certain awe and authority shone more than humanly in his face—turned to the knight and said: “You disdain to hear us, whom this deaf man will immediately hear in your presence.” He laid his hands upon the man, signed him, and put his fingers into his ears. When the man immediately heard, Henry, frightened and trembling, fell at the feet of the Man of God, humbly making satisfaction and freely agreeing to whatever had been requested of him.

50. As Christ’s servant was once passing through the town of Brenam, he saw a blind woman begging in the street. He looked at her for a while as she asked alms from passers-by according to her custom, and said: “You seek money, and God will give you sight.” He then approached, touched her, and opened her eyes. Feeling the unexpected benefit, she marvelled no less at the greatness of mercy than at the unfamiliar light.

Among the first offshoots sent forth by this most fruitful vine, the monastery of Igniacum was happily planted and took root in the diocese of Reims. When the same saint once visited it, he was passing through a village near the river Marne called Rivolium. Samson, archbishop of Reims, a distinguished man and his most devoted admirer, accompanied him in the year 1150, escorting him with his customary reverence. An old lame man had been placed on the road to beg, and one of the brethren gave him alms. The holy abbot followed; having already passed the man, he turned back, looked at him for a while, asked those around him what he suffered from, and ordered the man brought before him. The people suspected that Bernard himself would give him something more, and said: “Lord, he is lame and cannot move; we shall carry to him whatever you wish to give.” But Bernard answered and said: “Lift him up and bring him to me.” At first they looked at one another in astonishment, not knowing what he intended to do. Then, recognizing him, they cried to one another: “It is the abbot of Clairvaux; he will immediately heal him.”

51. Certainly, whenever he could, he took care not to be recognized in villages; he forbade his companions to reveal him to any whom they met or to say anything about him. When people asked who was passing, they were to say that they were monks, or name some person travelling with them. Therefore, when the servant of God was recognized, they rushed upon him from every side, lifted the man, carried him, and presented him to Bernard. He laid both hands upon the man’s head, looked up to heaven, prayed briefly, and ordered him to be set down and to walk. The man excused himself, saying: “I cannot.” “I command you,” Bernard said, “in the name of the Lord and by his power: go, and from this hour be well.”

What more need be said? Immediately he was set down, immediately healed, immediately walked freely, filled with astonishment and ecstasy at what had happened to him. His neighbours and acquaintances likewise rejoiced together and praised the Lord, who in the abundance of his mercy exceeded both the desert and the wish of the miserable man. Thus even now the inhabitants point out the place where so manifest a sign of divine power shone forth: there the old lame man, dead in all the lower part of his body for many years, and from the loins downward entirely deprived of every function of his limbs, received health while begging for alms.

This was the holy man’s last entry into the region of Reims; for this took place one year before the holy laying-down of his body. We must now speak, though in another narrative, of that happiest consummation of his blessed acts. For anyone greatly errs who thinks that all the wondrous deeds of this most holy man can be narrated; and it is as necessary that much be passed over in silence as it is impossible to comprehend everything.

[Col. 0351]

# BOOK V, BY GEOFFREY, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX.

## CHAPTER I. Of the peace restored through blessed Bernard between the city of Metz and certain neighbouring princes, and of miracles performed on that occasion.

[Col. 0351A]

1. When, after so many and such great labours and exertions, the Lord was preparing to grant to his beloved Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the long-desired sleep of precious death and to bring his faithful servant into his rest, the spirit in him began to advance ever more readily, while his weak flesh failed. For the holy man, knowing that the prize was now near, ran more eagerly than usual; feeling the dissolution of his earthly dwelling to be imminent, he aspired with fuller desires toward the dwelling from God, the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

The flame of sacred desire, unable to contain itself within his most pure breast, burst forth in frequent tokens; his fiery speech strongly declared the intensity of his inward fervour, just as among other things the prophet describes in the holy living creatures sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze [Ezekiel 1:7]. His body lay upon a bed and was exercised by various afflictions; yet his mind, no less free and strong, performed invincibly the things that were God’s. Even amid his pains he did not cease to meditate upon or dictate some sacred matter, pray more fervently, and exhort the brethren more diligently. At the offering of the saving Sacrifice—which until his final decline he scarcely ever omitted—he sustained limbs barely joined together by the strength of his spirit, offering himself likewise as an acceptable sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness.

At that time, writing to his uncle Andrew, a Knight Templar, who was also reckoned a very great pillar of the region of Jerusalem, he says among other things: “For I am being poured out, and I do not think that I shall remain long upon the earth” [Letter 288].

2. [In those days there arose a reason why one of the brethren should be sent to distant regions of Germany on certain business. Brother Henry, a monk, was sent; six years earlier the same holy Father had brought him, together with many others, from the parts of the diocese of Constance. As he was being sent, this brother feared the dangers of so long a journey—for it was winter—but feared most of all that the holy Father might depart this life before he himself returned, and that, being absent, he might be deprived of a share in the final blessing.

But Bernard blessed him and said: “Do not fear: you will return safely, and you will find me also, as you desire.” Thus comforted, he sent him away. As the brother travelled through the territory of Strasbourg, he was crossing a river frozen hard with ice. Suddenly the ice beneath the feet of the mule on which he rode broke; he fell, and a violent current drew him beneath the ice. What could he do, submerged in the river and enclosed by ice? He remembered his Father; he remembered his promise, which could not be vain. Immediately indeed—as he still confesses today—he seemed to have the holy Father present with him. Such sweetness flooded him that he felt neither the force of the river, the discomfort of the cold, the difficulty of breathing, nor any affliction or fear.

Without delay, drawn back against the river’s current by divine power and without effort of his own, he found himself at the very opening through which he had fallen; he seized the bank, emerged unafraid, and escaped unharmed. Having completed his business, he returned safely. Finding the faithful promise fulfilled as Bernard had promised, he gave manifold thanks. Even today he remains as devoted at Bernard’s sacred tomb as he is certain that, through Bernard’s merits, he was recalled as if from a tomb—and indeed a very terrible one.

But we need not declaim on this matter. Let others compare ancient miracles and assert that he was delivered no less wonderfully than the child Placidus of blessed Benedict, and from no lesser danger. If they saw the man whom the ice-bound river restored, they might compare him with the man whom the whale vomited forth. For us, a brief and straightforward account is enough.]

3. While the holy Father was still courageously bringing the course of his life to its end in his monastery of Clairvaux, though confined to his bed, a very grave blow befell the people of Metz. Having marched out in great force [Col. 0352C] against neighboring princes—by whom that great city indignantly maintained that it had been provoked by previous affronts—many were delivered into the hands of very few. At length, hemmed in between the narrows of Frigidus Mons (“Cold Mountain,” as they call it) and the river Moselle, and charging against one another, more than two thousand, it was said, fell in a single hour: some cut down by swords, more drowned in the river.

Accordingly, seized by fierce indignation, that noble city was preparing with all its strength for revenge; while on the other side the outcome had made its opponents both stronger through abundant plunder and more daring. The certain devastation of the entire province was impending, when their venerable metropolitan, Illinus, Archbishop of Trier, grieving anxiously over what had occurred but fearing still worse things, [Col. 0352D] and bearing the fitting concern of his children, sought the one refuge amid so great a necessity, and sought out the Man of God.

Coming therefore to Clairvaux, he prostrated himself in all humility at the feet of Bernard himself and of all the brethren, begging and imploring that he would deign to oppose himself to such great evils, to which no other person [Col. 0353A] seemed able to set any limit. But the Lord, who had always directed the ways of His faithful servant and had used him as the most fitting instrument in every important cause, had somewhat relieved his bodily illness a few days before. In those days, when replying to a letter from the venerable Hugh, Bishop of Ostia, he said: “What you have heard is true. I have been ill unto death; but meanwhile, as I perceive, I have been recalled to death, and this, as I perceive, not for long” (*Letter* 307).

For he regarded mortal life as death rather than life; and thus, when he was called back from departure, he felt himself recalled not from death but to death, though he felt that it would not be delayed much longer.

4. Divine providence had often so arranged matters for him—his soul being in God’s hand [Col. 0353B] and well-pleasing to Him—that 1152 whenever some great necessity summoned him, bodily strength did not fail him, because his spirit overcame everything. Those who saw him wondered that he surpassed even strong men in endurance. For when his business was finished, as though returning to himself, he suffered from many infirmities, so that he could scarcely live when at rest, though when occupied he seemed incapable of failing.

In this final undertaking divine power was so manifestly and magnificently present with him that he seemed to draw strength from his labors. It happened that, while the parties sat on opposite banks of the aforesaid river Moselle and the faithful mediator urged what concerned peace, one party—rendered more ferocious by so great a slaughter of its enemies—stubbornly refused what was demanded. Suddenly, at last, as though driven by furies, they departed without saluting the Man of God, [Col. 0353C] leaving to everyone else only despair of peace.

Yet they did not flee out of contempt, but under the impulse of reverence for him. For they feared that he might easily bend the minds of those present, however wicked; giving too little thought to what he, through the Spirit who is nowhere absent, might accomplish even in those absent. The assembly was now breaking up in great tumult; on either side they thought only of arms and devised only malicious plans. Then the holy man, having comforted the brethren who had come with him, said: “Do not be troubled. Though peace must indeed come through many difficulties, the peace we desire will nevertheless be achieved altogether.”

He also revealed to them why he knew this, saying: “In my sleep during the night, I seemed to myself to be celebrating a solemn Mass. When, having nearly completed the first prayer, I remembered that I ought, according to custom, to have preceded it with the angelic hymn—that is, ‘Glory to God in the highest’—I blushed; and, beginning the hymn which I had forgotten and omitted, I completed it together with you to the end.” Midnight had already passed when an embassy arrived from the aforesaid princes, repentant of their conduct. The holy man turned quite joyfully to his own people and said: “Recognize the preparation for the *Gloria* promised to us for singing, and for the hymn of peace.”

Meanwhile the parties were summoned together; for several days peace was discussed, and, because of the greatest difficulties arising on both sides, hope was often abandoned. Yet all were now comforted by the holy Abbot’s very certain promise, which had become known to all, that peace would be restored. Nor was the delay itself without considerable benefit, especially to those who, afflicted with various illnesses, received bodily remedies, and also to those who were edified in faith by what they saw.

For such was the throng that, by its numbers and importunity, it almost made the work of establishing peace hopelessly difficult. At last an island in the middle of the river was selected; the leading men of both parties came there in small boats. When all had been settled according to the decision of the faithful arbiter, they gave one another their right hands and were reconciled with the kiss of peace.

5. Among all the healings which the Lord granted there through the hand of His servant, the most celebrated was the cure of a certain woman. For eight years she had suffered from a most grievous illness, her entire body being shaken by violent trembling [Col. 0354B] and severe convulsions. When, because more serious difficulties had arisen, hope of peace seemed almost to have vanished, the woman came, by the Lord’s ordering, trembling in this way—no less horrible than pitiable—and everyone assembled to see the spectacle.

When the servant of God prayed, the shaking gradually ceased before the eyes of all; and she immediately attained perfect health. This event moved even the hardest hearts to such amazement that, striking their breasts, they cried aloud with tears for nearly half an hour. Finally, such was the rush and throng of those falling down before and kissing the sacred feet of the Man of God that he was almost crushed, until the brethren lifted him up, placed him in a small boat, and pushed a little distance from the shore [Col. 0354C].

When the princes approached him and he continued, as he had begun, to plead for peace, they said with sighs: “We must gladly hear the man whom, as we ourselves see, God loves and hears; and, having heard him, do much for the sake of one for whom God does such great things before our eyes.” But he, as he was always careful suitably to decline glory of this kind, said: “He does it not for my sake, but for yours.”

6. By a similar miracle, and at a similarly timely moment, the Lord inclined the minds of the people of Metz themselves 1153 toward peace that very day. For the Saint entered the city of Metz and urgently pressed both bishop and people toward those things which concerned peace. But the wound they had received burned them bitterly: what they had planned to repay with very strong retaliation, they were compelled, contrary to their wishes, to remit [Col. 0354D].

At that very hour a paralyzed woman from the same city was brought to him. Laying hands upon her and praying, he also deigned to spread over her his own little cloak, which he himself used, and gave it to the bishop standing nearby to hold, while her weakened limbs were touched beneath that covering. When the prayer had been completed and the blessing bestowed, he raised her up. To the amazement of all, she walked sound through their midst—the woman whom they had carried in on a pallet.

Also on the river Moselle, while the blessed man was being conveyed in a little boat because of the intolerable crowd pressing about him, one of those wishing to be healed, a blind man, cried out from the bank and begged to be brought to him. As Bernard was already passing by, the man heard a fisherman traveling behind him in another boat. Immediately unfastening the cloak in which he was wrapped, he stretched it out and gave it to the fisherman, so that he might be taken into the boat [Col. 0355A]. This was done; and when he came to the Saint, in accordance with the greatness of his faith he recovered his sight with great speed beneath Bernard’s hand. In amazement he cried out that he saw hills, people, trees, and everything else.

7. A few miles from that place is a monastery called Saint-Benedict’s. There a lame boy, wholly deprived from the loins downward of every use of his limbs, used only his hands and loins in moving himself, dragging his lifeless feet behind him. His father had brought him from Burgundy and left him there four years earlier; ever since then he had been supported by the alms of the brethren.

Accordingly, as the fame of the blessed Father’s arrival and of the miracles which the Lord worked through him spread throughout the surrounding region, the brethren of the aforesaid monastery brought the same boy to him on a cart, begging that, in his customary compassion, he would aid the wretch. He consented, laid hands upon him, prayed, and in that same hour restored him to health, standing firmly and walking firmly [Col. 0355B].
