Finally, as we recently learned from the abbot of that place, the same boy continues even now in health to follow and tend the brethren’s livestock; and, if anyone wishes to know, his name is John.

Another lame man, living near the same monastery, was healed at the same time by the blessing of the aforesaid holy Father and recovered his ability to walk. Near the city of the Leuci, moreover, at a place called Gundervilla, the same man of God gave sight to a blind woman before the eyes of many people who had gathered from the whole region [Col. 0355C].

But it would be too difficult, indeed altogether impossible, to recount all the wonders of that journey. Nor is it our purpose at present to pursue signs of this kind and devote our efforts to narrating miraculous works. For here, sweetest Father, was the blessed end of your journeys, and here your final labor. In this work, no less useful than difficult, and undertaken for a peace no less desperate than necessary, the King of glory, the Lord your God, gloriously brought your labors to completion—he who has always magnificently honored you in your labors, glorifying you in His name and His name in you.

## CHAPTER II. On the most blessed, but for the brethren most sorrowful, death of the blessed man

[Col. 0355D]

8. When the reconciliation of the people of Metz had been completed and peace restored to that province, the holy Abbot returned to the monastery, already afflicted with the grave discomfort of a body on the very point of failing. Yet with such serenity of mind and sweetness of spirit he daily drew nearer to his departure, as though a sailor reaching harbor were gradually lowering his sails.

He also said plainly to the brethren: “These are the words which I spoke to you when I was ill in the past winter: that you still had nothing to fear, but that, as I believe, the dissolution of this body would threaten in the coming summer.” Yet how plainly we learned by our own experience what the holy Gospels testify concerning the Apostles: when the Lord foretold His Passion to them, the saying was hidden from them and they could not understand it 1154 [Col. 0356A]. Certainly, what the mind so vehemently dreaded was less readily persuaded to believe, especially since he himself, in compassion for his children, suppressed words of this kind.

But by his actions he was in some sense crying out: “I have completed the works which the Father gave me to do.” More and more, he laid aside activities, withdrew his affections, and, having cast ahead the ropes of holy desires with diligent intent, clung more firmly to the nearby shore and brought himself more conveniently to land. Thus, when the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of the see of Langres, consulted him concerning certain matters to be undertaken and wondered that he paid them little attention, he said: “Do not wonder; for I am no longer of this world.”

[Col. 0356B] 9. The holy Father, overflowing with the bowels of compassion and mercy, saw his beloved brethren and children miserably wasting away and withering through fear and expectation of the coming desolation and most grievous, lamentable bereavement. He refreshed them with the sweetest consolations, urging them to plant more firmly the anchor of their hope and faith, through unshakable love, in the secure bosom of divine mercy. He promised them also that he would never fail them, even after death.

With a fervor beyond the power of our speech to express, he endeavored through many tears, prayers, and entreaties to imprint upon our minds the fear of God and love of sacred purity and entire perfection. He warned and tearfully charged them that, if he had ever commended any virtue to them either by example or by word, they should emulate it, hold it firmly, and make progress in it. In different words but the same spirit, he spoke that apostolic saying: “We beseech you and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, as you have received from us how you ought to walk and to please God in all things, so walk, that you may abound more and more” (1 Thess. 4:1). Would that he persuaded as effectively as he advised affectionately.

If anyone wishes to know the extent of his illness, there survives a letter which he himself dictated to a certain friend a very few days before his holy departure from us. We have thought fit to insert it in this account, because, although even the words of others about him delight us, still more do his own words about himself delight us.

[Col. 0356D] 10. “We have received your love in love, not in pleasure. For what pleasure can there be where bitterness claims everything for itself? Except that eating nothing at all is, in some fashion, pleasant. Sleep has departed from me, lest pain should ever depart, even through the relief of numbed sensation. Almost all that I suffer is a failure of the stomach. Frequently by day and night it demands to be strengthened with a very small quantity of some sort of liquid; for it inexorably rejects every solid food. What little it deigns to admit, it takes not without severe discomfort; yet it fears a worse discomfort should it leave itself entirely empty. But if it sometimes consents to admit a little more, that is most distressing. My feet and legs are swollen, as commonly happens to those with dropsy [Col. 0357A].

“And in all these things—so that nothing may be hidden from a friend anxious about the condition of his friend—according to the inward man, as I say with less wisdom, the spirit is willing though the flesh is weak. Pray to the Savior, who does not will the death of the sinner, that He may not delay my now timely departure, but may guard it. Take care to fortify with your prayers a heel bare of merits, so that he who lies in wait may find no place to set his tooth and inflict a wound. I myself dictated these things, being in such a condition that you may recognize my affection by a familiar hand.”

[Note: [Col. 0357D] This letter is numbered 310. In certain manuscripts it bears the following title: “Letter to Arnold, Abbot of Bonneval [Col. 0358D],” who, while sending Bernard certain gifts, had anxiously inquired concerning his health.]

11. This is the text of the letter which, as we have said—and as its own words declare—the holy Father dictated when his departure was already near. From its tenor, the attentive reader may surely recognize, at least in some measure, that sacred heart: how great was the tranquility of his mind, the serenity of his soul, and the sweetness of his spirit amid the very ruin of his body; how deep the root of humility beneath the summit of confidence.

But beneath so grave a crisis, we may in some degree estimate and portray for ourselves our inconsolable grief; and, if he feels devoutly, the reader will imagine the pale bands of sons, their ravaged faces, bloodless countenances, cheeks stained with tears, and the sighs and sobs from their breasts [Col. 0357B].

[For what 1155 turmoil of thoughts there was among us, what shipwreck of souls, when a treasure so beloved was snatched from us while we were present and watching, since there was neither hope of retaining him nor any power of going with him! He was a father—but what a father, who seemed to be departing! In some sense he belonged especially to us; yet more truly he belonged to the whole world. For he was both the glory of all good persons and the terror of the malicious, so that it seemed not unfitting to sing of him: “The upright shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop its mouth” (Psalm 106:42).

While he was present, every form of holiness rejoiced; presumption was restrained; hardness was pierced with compunction. In his presence every celebrated gathering shone as though under a certain sun; in his absence it appeared dark and, in a sense, mute. How devoutly, how tenderly, each of us should cry then and even today: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” (4 Kings 2:12). You were the harbor of the storm-tossed, the shield of the oppressed; and, as blessed Job says of himself, you were an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame (Job 29:15).

You were the exemplar of perfection [Col. 0357D], the pattern of virtue, the mirror of holiness. You were the glory of Israel, the joy of Jerusalem, the delight of your age, and the unique ornament of your time: a fruitful olive, an abundant vine, a flowering palm, a spreading cedar, an exalted plane tree. A vessel of election and a vessel of honor in the house of God; a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone—solid in faith and holiness, adorned with diverse charisms as with jewels.

You were the strongest and most splendid pillar of the holy Church; the mighty trumpet of God; the sweetest instrument of the Holy Spirit, delighting the devout, awakening the idle, sustaining the weak. Your healing hand and tongue cured diseases alike: the former those of bodies [Col. 0358A], the latter those of souls. Your clothing was simple, your countenance simple, your face sweet, your appearance gracious. Your life was fruitful and your death precious, because for you also “to live was Christ, and to die gain.” If perhaps one of these was more useful to us, the other was much better for you. And what was so advantageous to you cannot fail to be joyful to us, if we have devout understanding.

Yet although it is devout to rejoice with you, good Father, who have happily entered into the joy of your Lord, it is not impious to weep for ourselves, whom, when you departed, a twofold horror more grievous than usual enclosed: life is wearisome to us and death fearful. And if it is devout to rejoice with you, who by the blessed passage of death have reached the torrent of delight for which you thirsted ardently, it is nevertheless not impious to lament our own lot [Col. 0358B], since every sweetness of living has at once been taken away from us, while the security of dying has not yet been bestowed upon us.

And if joyful congratulations are properly offered to you, blessed soul, who exult in the fullness of light, neither is lamentation over us impious, we who have been left behind: after the wondrous brightness in which we have hitherto rejoiced, we tremble all the more at the darkness entering in; after the golden age which we saw only a little while ago, we bear all the more heavily this plainly iron one which has followed. But let us turn the pen back to the order of the narrative and, with such prayers as we can, follow the passing of our patron—a passing mournful to us, but for him rather triumphant.]

12. Therefore, before this Father’s departure, the sons whom he himself had begotten through the Gospel came to him [Col. 0358C] and assailed his most loving heart with tearful entreaties, speaking these and similar words: “Do you not pity this monastery, Father? Do you not have compassion on us, whom you have nourished with maternal breasts in so great an affection of love, and warmed with paternal consolation? How can you thus abandon the labors which you labored in this place? How can you thus leave sons whom you have hitherto loved so dearly?”

Then he himself wept with those who wept; lifting his dove-like eyes to heaven and wholly receiving that apostolic spirit in his mind, he testified that he was “constrained between two” and did not know what to choose (Philippians 1:23, 22), and that he entrusted everything to the judgment of divine mercy. For paternal love urged him on one side to assent to his sons’ prayers and remain [Col. 0358D]; on the other, desire for Christ drew him to depart.

Yet humility, long ago planted and more deeply rooted in his heart, had persuaded him to say from the depths of his heart that he was an unprofitable servant and to regard himself as a barren tree, from whose life no fruit came either to himself 1156 or to anyone else. Indeed, he used to confess in familiar conversation that he could scarcely believe people when they said that they thought him as useful to them as they did. At times he also declared that he had endured no small conflict in his thoughts on this matter, since it did not seem likely either that such truthful people wished to deceive him or that such prudent people could be deceived, when he could excuse neither alternative [Col. 0359A].

He whom the whole world admired alone did not see—what was more remarkable still—the splendor of his own activity or reputation, like that ancient man, simple and upright, who declared that he had not looked upon the sun when it shone nor the moon moving in brightness (Job 31:26).

13. Finally, when the structure of his outward dwelling had now everywhere come apart and afforded the desiring soul a free departure, that great day dawned—the day which became for him an everlasting dawn. For his departure, neighboring bishops had gathered, together with a large multitude of abbots and brethren. At about the third hour of the day, the singular lamp of his generation, the holy and truly blessed Abbot Bernard, guided by Christ, happily passed from the body of death into the land of the living [Col. 0359B]. He passed from the choir of sons standing around him—who, amid heavy sobs and abundant tears, were somehow managing to sing psalms—to the rejoicing company of many whom he himself had sent on before him; to the welcoming ranks of the saints; and to the angelic hosts coming out to meet him.

Blessed was the soul which was thus lifted up by the high privileges of its merits, which the devout prayers of its lesser children thus attended, and which the sacred desires of those above thus drew onward. Blessed and truly serene was that day for him, when Christ, his full noonday, shone upon him: a day awaited throughout all the days of his life with such great longings, sought with sighs, frequented in meditations, fortified with prayers. Blessed the passage from labor to refreshment, from expectation to reward, from contest to prize, from death to life, from faith to knowledge, from pilgrimage [Col. 0359C] to homeland, from the world to the Father!

We know that much concerning this passage of his appeared to many people, and matters indeed not unworthy of narration. But it is too difficult to trace every detail and too lengthy to write them all. For even now, in many ways and by many means, his fatherly love for his children—truly living and vigorous even now, indeed more truly now—deigns through frequent revelations to console their tears and lighten their sorrow, so that as they rejoice with him more sweetly, they may grieve for themselves less anxiously. Yet if any reader, desiring a less lengthy narrative, wishes to know some of these things, we believe they should be reserved for their own and final chapter.

14. Meanwhile, as we continue the rest of the account, let us turn our minds away as forcibly as we can from that grievous groaning and roaring with which the sorrowing flock resounded when its shepherd departed [Col. 0359D]. Let us spare the page; as much as we can, let us restrain our eyes and close our eyelids against the tears with which our valley flowed at the departure of its brightness—soon to offer the whole Church the cup of its grief, though until then it had been accustomed to distill sweetness for her, pour out joys, and flow with consolations.

While the faithful minister and priest of the Most High happily enters the place of the wonderful tabernacle, to the altar of God, there to offer Him the sacred and acceptable sacrifice of his spirit, his body also, duly prepared and adorned in priestly vestments, is brought into the oratory of the blessed Mother of God [Col. 0360A]. A great grieving crowd, noble and ignoble alike, immediately assembled from all the neighboring places, and much weeping and wailing filled the whole valley.

Yet outside the monastery gates the more pitiable sex of women lamented more bitterly, because monastic discipline inexorably denied them entrance even then, while men were permitted to approach the blessed feet.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] The same discipline prevailed at Clairvaux, as at Cîteaux; it was once common among the Cistercians, except on the feast of the Dedication, when women were permitted access to the church of the Order.]

For two days the dead shepherd remained in the midst of his flock. The former grace of his most sweet countenance, not diminished but increased, fixed all eyes upon him more strongly, drew hearts to him, and buried their affections in him [Col. 0360B]. The multitude of people rushing in from every direction grew beyond measure. The press of those crowding together, holding his beloved feet, kissing his hands, and touching to him bread, belts, 1157 coins, and every other item which they wished to preserve for themselves as a blessing and use for diverse needs, was now intolerable.

Above all, people in the neighboring places, preparing for the solemn third day, awaited the time when his sacred body would be laid to rest, expecting to assemble in still greater numbers from every side. For on the second day also, around noon, so great a crowd had gathered and, filled with such zeal of devotion, had surrounded the holy body from all directions that almost no respect was shown to bishops or brethren. Therefore, fearing that something similar or perhaps worse might occur on the third day [Col. 0360C], they anticipated the hour. In the morning, having celebrated the divine Sacrifices according to custom—as they had already done for two days in the celebration of Masses and unceasing psalmody—they committed that most pure balm to its vessel, laying the precious stone in stone, the choicest pearl.

15. Thus, when he had happily completed the days of his life and fulfilled about sixty-three years, Bernard, beloved of the Lord, first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux and father of more than one hundred and sixty other monasteries, fell asleep in Christ on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], in the hands of his sons.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] That is, both directly and through the abbeys subject to Clairvaux. Bernard himself founded or adopted approximately seventy-two monasteries directly: namely, 35 in France, 11 in Spain, 6 in Belgium, 5 in England, the same number in Savoy and Ireland, 4 in Italy, 2 in Germany, likewise 2 in Sweden, and finally one each in Hungary and Denmark, according to our *Chronology*.]

He was buried on the eleventh day before the Kalends of the same month [22 August], before the holy altar of the blessed Virgin Mother [Col. 0360D], whose most devoted priest he had been. A reliquary was also placed upon his breast in the tomb, containing the relics of the blessed apostle Thaddaeus. These had been sent to him from Jerusalem in that same year, and he had ordered that they be placed upon his body, in the intention of faith and devotion that on the day of the common resurrection he might cleave to that apostle.

[Before that most sacred body was committed to the tomb, however, one of the brethren, who had suffered severely for many years from the falling sickness, came in full faith to seek help. We know him to be alive even now, and to have experienced nothing whatever of the aforesaid affliction from that hour onward [Col. 0361A].]

16. These things took place in the same year in which our blessed Pope Eugenius III, the son of that same holy Father in holy religious life, departed from this light—or rather from this darkness—to the light. His merits shine resplendently in the very city over which he presided so notably, illustrated by many miracles. Anastasius, his successor, was presiding over the Roman Church; the illustrious Frederick was reigning in the empire of the Romans; and the most devout King Louis, son of Louis, in the kingdom of the Franks. But the Son of God, Jesus Christ, held the primacy of the universal Church and the monarchy over every visible and invisible creature [Col. 0361B], in the year from His Incarnation 1153—He who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. On various revelations made after the holy Father’s death

17. As we are now to relate a few of the revelations mentioned above, let us begin with one that was foretold seven years before it occurred. There were two brethren in the monastery conversing about the holy life and blessed deeds of the holy Father. One of them, who had been brought up there from early youth, said to the other: “Do you know how many years this our most blessed Father will live?” The other replied: “I do not know” [Col. 0361C]. The first said: “I know that he will live six or seven more years in the flesh.”

How he knew this, we are now quite unable to know, because he did not reveal it even then and died before the holy Father. But the statement became known to us through the account of the other brother, who is still alive today. He was all the more astonished to have heard it then when he saw it happen just as he had heard it long before. Such a man is he that we do not doubt his testimony, nor do we think that anyone else who knows him ought to doubt it.

Nor does he testify only to this. What seems no less worthy of wonder is that, through the disclosure of the same brother, he then also learned the name and person of Bernard’s successor. For at that very time the brother plainly foretold “that Lord Robert, who today is abbot of Dunes, will be abbot of Clairvaux after this blessed Father” [Col. 0361D]. The fact that he said, alternatively, six or seven years seems to have referred to this: the end was found to be 1158 beyond the sixth year, yet within the seventh.

18. The time was now near, and the holy Father hastened toward the goal. For he was ill, as we mentioned at the beginning of this book, so gravely that his virtue seemed now to be perfected in that very illness and his departure to be near. Meanwhile the brethren persevered in prayers and entreaties to God as best they could. The Saint himself, recognizing that his desire was being delayed by their prayers, began to be somewhat better in body and assembled the brethren. He then spoke these words: “Why do you hold a wretched man? You are stronger, and you have prevailed. Spare me, I beg you, spare me; let me go” [Col. 0362A].

But first, when all the brethren, under extreme danger and fear, were humbling their souls in prayer, such a vision appeared to one of them. An innumerable multitude came out with great rejoicing to meet the Man of God beyond the monastery enclosure. In that procession, however, the brother who saw it recognized only four men going before: Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, that great lover and beloved of Bernard, whom Bernard himself mentions with praise in Book IV of *On Consideration*; Humbert, who had been the first abbot of the monastery of Igny; and Bernard’s two full brothers, Guy [Col. 0362B] and Gerard.

Thus reverently received, and having long exchanged friendly conversation after the kiss of peace, the holy and blessed Father stood with these four, while the multitude of the others waited apart. At last the aforesaid men bade him farewell and said that they must now return. He grew pale, and the sorrow spread over him revealed his inward grief. “What then?” he said. “Do you wish to depart without me?” They replied: “Your desire and ours cannot yet be fulfilled until the time of the new things comes.”

They called “the time of the new things” the time when new crops would be gathered, as the outcome plainly proved afterward, since he died in the month of August. Therefore, in the morning, the brother to whom this had been shown comforted the others, who feared the Father’s now-imminent death, and told them what he had seen and heard. Yet it was still winter [Col. 0362C].

19. At the same time another vision confirmed the former one, except that the truth fulfilled in both now proves more clearly how plainly the Lord revealed in each what was to come. For a certain brother saw, and behold, the most blessed man was preparing to ascend to Jerusalem and was already equipped for the journey. The venerable Odo, who from almost the earliest years had lived energetically and laudably in the monastery and was accustomed to discharge the duties of absent superiors, approached him reverently and said that he would go ahead.

The truth of this vision was shown as follows: that man worthy of God, Odo, successfully discharged his mission by going first to the heavenly Jerusalem—where there is truly the vision of peace—before the holy Father, who was already preparing to depart and was to follow shortly afterward [Col. 0362D].

20. Moreover, a certain abbot, living quite near him and no less devoted in affection, a few days before the most blessed departure of this Father, saw him adorned in most precious priestly vestments and suffused with surpassing glory, being conducted to the altar with immense solemnity. At his entrance the great church, resounding with loud voices, cried aloud: “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6). [Col. 0363A] For he himself was indeed a child, meek and humble of heart; and, like a little child, receiving the kingdom of God. In joy at his birth, the angelic multitude and likewise the whole Church of the Saints, while he seemed to us to be dying, rejoiced that he was being born to them; while he was coming to his end here, they rejoiced that he was beginning there—harmonizing not so much in audible voices as in equal desires. For if that whole heavenly region is moved to joy over the repentance of one sinner, what joys must it be thought to have displayed for him through whom it had received such great joy from the conversion and repentance of so many sinners? Who indeed could estimate how many people remaining in secular dress and manner of life, and how many also passing into other communities of men or women, the Lord, through the ministry of this faithful servant, granted repentance unto salvation? Or who could number those who, under his care, were brought by God’s goodness [Col. 0363B] to repentance in one hundred and sixty monasteries?

For from those alone who appeared to be his special sons—besides those who had already happily completed the course of life, and besides those who had been sent out to other places—on the day when the most blessed Father deserved to ascend from Clairvaux to the clearer mountain, he left nearly seven hundred souls dwelling there and serving the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0363] On the number of novices, see below, Book VII, chapters 12 and 29.]

What wonder, then, if he is believed to have been welcome at the court, acceptable to the King, and received with joy and exultation? For in him the grace of God was by no means empty: he labored more happily and more effectively than all men of his time and of many preceding generations; he multiplied so abundantly the talent entrusted to him and gained such great profit from the undertaking. But enough of this, lest anyone accuse us of exceeding the bounds of brevity which we promised. [Col. 0363C]

21. Indeed, in the monastery of that aforesaid abbot who had thus foreseen his birth into heaven, on the very night which the holy Father made his last before departing with us in the morning, he appeared to that abbot’s venerable prior, bade him farewell, and said: “Know that I am now departing, and shall remain here no longer.” When the prior reported this to the abbot, the abbot hastened to Clairvaux; and on that very day found, just as he had said, that the holy Abbot had already departed.

22. Brother William of Montpellier, whom we have mentioned above, had once been a distinguished man in the world, but was more distinguished in fleeing from the world. Having become a monk at the monastery of Grand-Selve, [Col. 0363D] he visited the holy Father with the greatest devotion. When he was about to return, he lamented tearfully that he would see him no more. The Man of God said to him: “Do not be afraid; without doubt you shall yet see me.”

As this most devout William awaited the fulfillment of the promise, on the very night when the blessed Father departed this life, he deserved to see him appearing to him in the monastery of Grand-Selve and saying: “Brother William.”

And he replied: “Here I am, lord.”

“Come with me,” he said.

So they went together and came to a very high mountain. The Saint asked whether he knew where they had come. He confessed that he did not know. The Saint said to him: “We have come to the foot [Col. 0364A] of Mount Lebanon. And now you will remain here, but I shall ascend the mountain.”

When asked why he wished to ascend, he said: “I wish to learn.”

William marveled and said: “What do you wish to learn, Father, whom we believe today to have no equal in knowledge?”

The Saint answered: “Here there is no knowledge, no true understanding. Above is the fullness of knowledge; above is the true knowledge of truth.”

Having spoken thus, he left him and ascended the very high mountain before his eyes. As William watched him going, he awoke, and immediately that saying which once sounded from heaven to John occurred to him: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.” Therefore, when he spoke in the morning with his abbot and brothers, he said that the holy Father had departed this life. They noted the day [Col. 0364B] and inquired more carefully; they found it to be as they had heard.

Well done, holy Father: having set the ascents in your heart in the valley of tears, you have now happily ascended from Clairvaux to Mount Lebanon—the mountain of whiteness, the fullness of light, the height of splendor. Innocent in hands and clean in heart, you have ascended the mountain of the Lord, unto the riches of salvation. You have reached the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, where you behold pure truth purely; where Christ alone is your teacher together with all the saints; where all are now taught by God. Draw us after you, we pray, and mercifully look down from the high mountain upon your Valley. Be present with those who labor; help those in peril; stretch out your hand to those who ascend. Your kindness, long experienced by us, gives us confidence—not now exhausted, but more abundantly [Col. 0364C] increased. Indeed, the vision which we append does not depart from this same confidence of ours.

23. On the night after the sacred body had been committed to burial, the holy Father plainly showed how great was still his concern for his sons, and how he loved unto the end those whom he had loved in the world. For he appeared to a certain brother in great glory, with a great radiance of clothing and countenance; and, passing swiftly by while the brother desired to hold him, said: “I have come for a certain simple brother.” The brothers heard this and marveled; but about the third hour of the day the truth of the vision was confirmed. For a brother of very commendable simplicity died; and, as is altogether credible, that happy soul was carried away with him by so great a guide, who had said that he had come for him. [Col. 0364D]

A few days later he appeared in magnificent splendor to another brother and reproved him because we had grieved over his departure. After many words of consolation, and a promise of eternal blessedness to those persevering in his obedience and teaching, he said: “Know this also, and tell the brothers: the body of a truly holy man, whose garment I too possess, is buried in the oratory.”

He meant Bishop Malachy. For he had kept for the celebration of Masses Malachy’s tunic, in which that holy man had happily fallen asleep; and when he was dying, Bernard directed that he himself should be buried in it, just as he had buried that holy man [Col. 0365A] in his own garment. Yet this saying had been wholly unknown, until this vision, both to that brother and to very many others.

Blessed bishop, whose merits the holy Father had proclaimed both living and dead. Blessed charity, which did not fail in death. Blessed fellowship, which not even that most cruel separation dissolved. For the glorious Fathers, as they loved one another in their life, so they were not separated in death.

24. About forty days later, a certain abbot from the island of Great Britain deserved happily to experience in himself the power of that sacred fellowship. At the same time as he was making, with his fellow abbots, the customary journey to Cîteaux, he had remained at Clairvaux, [Col. 0365B] desperately afflicted by two illnesses: pleurisy and a daily fever. So exhausted had he become from the prolonged affliction that the brothers, who never left him, watched only for the departure of his soul. While his mind was distressed not so much by a desire for this present life as by the desolation of his absent sons—because he would die in a foreign land—he earnestly asked to be carried to the tomb of the holy Abbot. There, having prayed with all the devotion he could muster, he intended also to visit the tomb of the blessed Bishop Malachy, located on the north side of the same oratory, and to seek help. But fearing the exertion, and being, as it were, already confident of recovery, he did not do what he had intended.

The next day he again summoned the brothers and requested their assistance in coming to the oratory. They objected, for they feared the danger. “By all means,” he said, “I must go to Saint Malachy’s tomb. For when last night I had scarcely fallen into a light sleep, I suddenly awoke and heard a voice saying to me: ‘You are now healed of one of your illnesses; if you wish to be healed of the other, seek the bishop.’” [Col. 0365C]

They did as he wished, and immediately it happened as had been told him. He was healed that same day; after very few days he set out on his journey and returned safely to his own people.

25. In this work we recognize your spirit, sweetest Father—your zeal, your concern. This is your work: that you should honor your colleague in such a way as to share with him that honor and love by which you are more truly and more happily honored in heaven. Or rather, all these things belong to your work and your gift, [Col. 0365D] O our God. For from the beginning of time you have filled the whole earth with the presence of your divinity, and one day will fill it wholly with the glory of your majesty. Yet in the meantime, visiting certain portions and places chosen beforehand by your eternal counsel in a more excellent way, you fill them with the special grace of holiness.

Grant, Lord, that the Valley may always abound in spiritual grain; you deigned to make it brighter in reality than in name by illuminating it with two stars of such outstanding brightness. Guard the house in which this twofold and most precious deposit is kept for you. Finally, let it be according to your word for us: where your treasure is, there may your heart be also (Matt. 6:21); there may grace and mercy, and the regard of continual loving-kindness, be present for all who are gathered there in your name—your name which is above every name—as you are God blessed above all things for ever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0366A]

In Vatican manuscript no. 676, this book consists of twenty-three chapters, the last of which is absent from the common editions. It reads as follows:

26. The righteous man, established by the Lord in everlasting remembrance, does not neglect the memory of his sons; after death he acts and accomplishes by miracles what, while yet alive, he foretold by his own utterances. In his works of power is seen that living and efficacious word, and the faithful testament which he made for his beloved: “I shall,” he said, “continually care for the family of Clairvaux; and, constantly nourishing my plantation with the watering of blessing, I shall show myself so present in benefits that I shall never seem to have departed from it.” [Col. 0366B]

He seeks out for us material for consolation from every quarter, so that he has recently been found, even in those lands beyond the sea, to long for our assistance. For it happened many years after the death of this saint that signs of his holiness shone forth in connection with the taking of the cross, and that he who consecrated the cross showed with what pious longing he embraced the power of the life-giving cross.

When Sarracon, commander of the Turks, had resolved to invade the city of Alexandria and the adjoining province of Egypt, and to subject them to his authority; and when Amalric, the most Christian king of Jerusalem, was requested by the Saracens of Egypt, he hastened to prepare a relief force for a sudden expedition. He feared and guarded against the future possibility that, if the Turks should come to rule in Egypt, they might [Col. 0366C] inflict greater harm on the Christians because of their proximity, while he himself would meanwhile lose the tributary revenue from Egypt. Having therefore selected soldiers and equipped an army, he hurried to meet Sarracon, going forward as far as the channel of the river Nile, which, issuing from the fountain of Paradise, waters the dry regions of Egypt.

When he came to the river, he made it passable by means of ships. Leaving for the guard of the bridge a considerable number of soldiers and footmen on either side of the river, he himself, with three hundred cavalrymen, pursued the fleeing Sarracon, following him and his great army, which was gathering fourteen thousand Turks and three thousand Arab fighting men. As they fled a day’s journey ahead of the king’s attack, messengers came and went between the two sides. Some urged the king to attack that multitude, now exhausted by hunger and fatigue and ready to be destroyed; others, on the contrary, encouraged the Turks to stand firm, asserting that the small force could very easily be surrounded by so great a multitude. [Col. 0366D]

Therefore Sarracon’s army turned about; and, awaiting the king, they formed for battle, although they had earlier been rushing headlong in flight. When night came, they encamped beside waters which separated the two armies by a fairly narrow channel. As the king slept, resting in the hollow of his shield, blessed Bernard immediately appeared to him in a dream, rebuking and reproaching him [Col. 0367A] for his sins and because he was unworthy to wear in that battle the wood of the life-giving cross, which by custom he wore hanging from his neck.

At once the king, terrified and troubled, asked forgiveness and tearfully confessed his sins to the Saint speaking with him. Then blessed Bernard, bringing his hand nearer, took the holy cross which hung from the king’s neck, and, blessing him with a threefold sign of the holy cross, comforted him, saying: “Take courage, King: in this sign you shall conquer; and in a danger of great fear, such as you have never yet experienced, you shall escape your enemies without harm.”

When he had said this, Bernard seemed about to depart, carrying away with him the cross which he had taken from the king’s neck. But the king seized him and said: “I shall not let you go unless you leave the cross with me.”

The Saint replied: “No, no, King. I have other sons who must be blessed with the sign of this cross.” [Col. 0367B]

With these words the dream departed, and the brightness of morning dawned. When daylight was granted, the two armies approached one another to engage in battle. The king’s troop attacked the abundant multitude; and he who overwhelmed in the sea the enemies of Christ’s cross cast them down beneath the banner of the cross. A thousand fell at his side, and many thousands at his right hand; Christians triumphed everywhere in Christ’s name. While they were divided among the different parts of the battle, the king himself remained alone upon a mound of heaped sand, as near to death and slaughter as he was far from all assistance from his men. [Col. 0367C]

From his elevated [Col. 0368A] position he saw Turks rushing together from every direction. He already expected his imminent destruction, except that he had some confidence in the fact that he knew he was not unknown to them. Immediately recalling the former vision and making pious vows within himself, he promised God and blessed Bernard that, if he escaped alive from the hand of his enemies, he would send to Bernard’s sons at Clairvaux the cross which the Saint had requested.

Immediately thirty of his soldiers, recognizing the king himself from a distance, challenged the Turks to fierce battle against themselves, so that, as all the force turned against them, the king might remain unknown to his enemies and safe from combat. When fifteen knights of Christ’s sacred militia saw this, they broke violently through the thickest ranks of the enemy, pursuing them, as it is written, “one pursuing a thousand, and two putting ten thousand to flight among their thousands” (Deut. 32:30). Joined to the other thirty soldiers, and having scattered and slain the enemies who met them, they reached their king with joy and victory. [Col. 0368B]

Thus it came about that the king, according to the word of our holy Father, received through the benefit of the holy cross a gift gained by the merits of that same holy Father. Moreover, this same king carefully recounted the order of the aforementioned vision in his own words to Richer, abbot of Salvation, who afterward faithfully reported it in the regions of Gaul. He was certainly a man of good testimony and honorable conduct, as far removed from suspicion of falsehood as he was free from corruptions of life. Thanks be to God. Amen. [Col. 0368C]

[BOOK SIX]

[Col. 0367]

HORSTIUS’S PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK,  
On the miracles wrought through Saint Bernard.

I. Among the saints renowned for the glory of miracles, Bernard seems to me preeminent, or to have few equals. Thus it is easy even from this to stop the mouths of those who speak wickedly and mock the miracles of later ages. For there are even now Pharaohs who harden their hearts at the sight or hearing of so many wonders, lest they be forced to acknowledge God as wonderful in his saints. There are also now deaf serpents and asps stopping their ears lest they hear the voice of the wise enchanter. Indeed, even today one may find blind and obstinate Pharisees—or worse—who dare to ascribe these things to the power of Satan.

They judge miracles superfluous after the clear light of the Gospel has been spread through the whole world; and things done later, which we have received even from men most worthy of trust, though seen and attested by the whole world, they count among fables and inventions, indeed among magical deceptions. O blind and wretched race of men, who, seeing, do not see, and hearing, do not understand! But the hand of the Lord has not been shortened, even today, so that through his faithful servants he cannot do things surpassing understanding and nature whenever this is necessary. To determine when it is necessary does not belong to us, but to him who makes all things in weight and measure, whose wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. It would be rash and impious to prescribe here laws and limits to divine power or providence.

Look only at this very life of Saint Bernard, you scourges of the saints’ glory, whose wholly exceptional holiness, apart from the fact that his writings, no less than his deeds, portray it vividly, is confirmed by so many and such testimonies of irrefragable faith that calumny itself does not dare deny it, but is compelled, even against its will and however unwillingly, to venerate him. Although miracles are not always unquestionable and infallible proofs of holiness, in Bernard sanctity of life and the grace of miracles were linked by so close a bond that anyone who dares to detract from either, or from both, in this holy man must necessarily be foolish or impious.

II. Therefore let others adorn him with one encomium or another: I gladly applaud them all, because I find no one equal to him in merits. Yet I cannot refrain from calling him, by excellence, a Wonderworker, seeing so many of his miracles and the no less wonderful testimonies of divine power operating so familiarly through him. Granted, there may be some saint who claims this title by the prescription of long usage; nevertheless, he will not begrudge Bernard admission to the fellowship of this title and honor. For holy men are not wont to rival one another in claiming praise and glory for themselves in this respect.

Bernard certainly always took pains to remove such glory from himself, knowing that all glory is owed to him who works all things in all and alone performs great wonders. Nevertheless, it is our duty to praise God in his saints, and to recall with greater diligence the miracles which holy persons have performed by divine power, to God’s glory, for the confirmation of faith and religion, or where the welfare of the Christian people required it—lest they fail of their purpose if they are neglected by us or passed over in ungrateful, or rather irreligious, silence. Their chief purpose is to maintain divine glory, reveal power, and establish especially the true doctrine of the faith, whether for refuting unbelievers or confirming believers.

To pass over now countless other things: through Bernard alone I see miracles so frequent and illustrious, published in support of arguments for the faith, that any Christian, whenever he is shaken by a temptation to unbelief, may address God in the words of Richard of Saint-Victor (On the Trinity, Book I, chapter 2): “Lord, if this is error, we have been deceived by you yourself. For these things have been confirmed among us by such great signs and wonders, and of such a kind as can be done only through yourself. Certainly they have been handed down to us by men of the highest holiness, and proved with the highest and authoritative attestation, with yourself cooperating and confirming the word by the signs that followed.”

Thus he writes. I fear that this digression has been too long; yet I cannot help recounting here words of Saint Gregory the Great (Homily 11 on Ezekiel), which are very fitting. After comparing the miracles of saints to bulwarks and their virtues to shields, by both of which Christians may even now fortify and defend themselves, he says:

> “Thus miracles testify that these holy men spoke true things about God, because they would not perform such things through him unless they spoke truly of him; and their works testify how devout, humble, and kindly they were. Therefore, if we are tempted concerning the faith which we have received from their preaching, let us behold the miracles of those who spoke, and we shall be confirmed in the faith we received from them. What, then, are their miracles but our bulwarks? For by them we can be fortified, though we do not hold these things in the power of our own choice. For we cannot perform such deeds,” etc.

I have thought it worthwhile to quote these things at somewhat greater length for the sake of those who assign little importance to miracles or put little faith in them, and who tear apart the glory of saints with calumnies rather than honoring those whom God has willed thus to honor. I hope that these matters will not be unwelcome or useless to the reader. Certainly no candid devotee of Bernard will disapprove.

III. To what Horstius has said may be added that Bernard’s miracles were so illustrious and so well known to all while he lived—indeed, even before the preaching of the cross or holy expedition, which is treated in the following book—that Berengar, the disciple and defender of Abelard, though hostile to Bernard, acknowledges them as beyond doubt in his Apology for his master. Addressing Bernard, he says:

> “Long ago winged report spread through the world the fragrance of your holiness, proclaimed your merits, and celebrated your miracles. We counted our present age blessed, adorned with the brightness of so shining a star; and we thought that the world, already owed to destruction, was sustained by your merits. We hoped that the mercy of heaven, the temperateness of the air, the fruitfulness of the earth, and the blessing of its fruits lay at the disposal of your tongue. Your head touched the clouds, and, according to the common proverb, the shade of your branches surpassed the mountains. So long did you live; so did you form the Church by chaste institutions, that we thought demons roared at your apron-strings, and we counted ourselves blessed to glory in so great a patron.”

Thus he bears witness to the truth even against his will, although in what follows he attacks Bernard for opposing Abelard.

[Col. 0369]

BOOK SIX,  
or, Miracles performed by Saint Bernard in Germany, Belgium, and Gaul in the year 1146, divided into three parts, each bearing the name of its author.

NARRATIVE OF HERBERT, [Note: [Col. 0369A] He later became archbishop of Torres in Sardinia and wrote three books on the Miracles both of Bernard and of other disciples of Bernard, concerning which see below.] ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF MORIMOND, On the book of Saint Bernard’s Miracles preserved by a remarkable miracle.

[Col. 0369A]

Recently, when the venerable Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, [Note: [Col. 0369B] He is said to have been the eighth abbot of Clairvaux and to have died in 1186; this is written in the succession of these abbots in Jungelinus, Book I, p. 25. He was also called Monoculus (“One-Eyed”); Manrique, under the year 1183, chapter 4, attaches the present miracle to him. The same Peter is reported among the omitted material in the Bollandists under 18 May.] was visiting his monasteries, [Note: [Col. 0370B] Namely, Foigny, Bonnefontaine, and Signy.] which flourish most beautifully in the province of Reims through the breath of God’s Spirit, we also traveled with him and on one day came with him to the monastery of Valroy. [Note: [Col. 0370B] La Valroy, in the diocese of Reims, a daughter-house of Igny in the line of Clairvaux, founded in 1148.] There we found an abundant multitude of Saint Bernard’s miracles, which could not be inserted into the manuscript of his Life because of the weariness it would cause readers. For if they were written out at greater length, many volumes would result.

Accordingly, since we learned that this Book of Miracles was not held at Clairvaux, we borrowed it and took it with us to have it copied. It was carried in a bag together with seven other books, both large and small volumes. When we came to the monastery of Longpont, it happened that the horse carrying these books was taken to water with the others. As it passed the ford with the reins carelessly released, it slipped into the deep part of the pond and, floundering and swimming, wandered anxiously this way and that for nearly an hour.

Those present cried out that the horse, burdened with books and clothing and with a boy riding upon it, was sinking. People rushed from every side to help. Meanwhile the animal and the boy were hidden beneath the water, except that their faces, stretched upward, appeared a little above it. A young man stripped off his clothes and pursued the endangered pair for a long time by swimming, intending to rescue them; but because the horse fled from him, he could not do so. [Col. 0371A]

At last, after a small boat had been sought and brought from a distance, the Lord had mercy and both the boy and horse were brought back and saved: not merely alive, but safe and lively. The bag containing the books, however, was found full and swollen with water like a wineskin. Because of the servants’ negligence, it remained closed for a long time. When it was eventually opened, the books, from the least to the greatest, were found so soaked and obliterated as though they had lain for a long time in the depths of the pond.

Yet this Book of Miracles alone, though it had been mixed with the other books which were waterlogged and submerged, was found uncorrupted and dry, so handsome and fresh that one would not think it had just been drawn from a fishpond, but rather taken from a bookcase. For, as may be seen to this day, not even one large or small letter in it was erased or touched by a drop of water. The other books, as has been said, appeared so blotted out by the waves and ruined like skins that they were judged thereafter unfit for any use. [Col. 0372A]

Astonished and filled with great joy, they gave manifold thanks to divine mercy, which had willed even now to glorify by such a sign the venerable merits of its beloved Bernard. We too were greatly comforted, and bore our own loss from the immersion of the books not merely lightly but most joyfully, since in their recovery—in a truly delightful catch of fish—we had drawn up from the immeasurable waters, together with the books, so great and such a miracle.

Indeed, we had a double cause for rejoicing: first, because the glory of the miracles themselves was commended, and we consider ourselves more certain of their truth through the present miracle; and second, because the boy’s life was granted, for we do not doubt that his deliverance must be attributed to the prayers and merits of this most holy confessor. [Col. 0372B]

PHILIP OF CLAIRVAUX’S PREFACE TO THE SAME BOOK,  
To Samson, [Note: [Col. 0371D] According to the Sainte-Marthe authors, he succeeded Rainald of Prades, who died in 1137, and according to Alberic’s Chronicle died in 1161; but according to his cenotaph, in 1160. Saint Bernard praises him in Letters 210 and 247.] Archbishop of Reims.

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371B]

To the dearest Father and lord SAMSON, by God’s grace Archbishop of Reims, Brother PHILIP OF CLAIRVAUX wishes progress from brightness to brightness, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

It would be great presumption, if there were not great love, for me to presume to write to Your Sublimity. For what is a servant to his lord, a disciple to his master, a monk to a bishop? There is nothing in common between me and him, since supreme dignity sets him on high and lowliness sets me below. A man buried among men ought not to be recalled to men, nor should one who has imposed silence upon his mouth be recalled to verbal ornaments and the glory of speech. You too know, lord Father, that writing ought neither to be customary for a monk, nor easy for an unlearned man, nor desirable for a penitent.

It is also hard that, while others have leisure and see that he is the Lord, I should busy myself with pen and tablets, though you know me to be broken by the martyrdom of a harsher penitence. In truth, I have learned that nothing is more effective for obtaining the riches of the Lord’s grace than to sit and be silent, and always to agree with the humble. Humility, queen of virtues, bears silence as her firstborn son; and upon it and from it depends the practice of righteousness, as the righteous one testifies when he says: “The practice of righteousness is silence” (Isa. 32:17). [Col. 0371D]

But I am advancing too far, and the course of my speech must be interrupted, because perhaps a preface is inconvenient if, by a page too long, I detain the eyes which you owe to many persons. Yet when would the littleness—or faint-heartedness—of me, your servant, have dared this, unless your humble sublimity—or rather your sublime humility—had come before or intervened, most loving Father?

You ask, therefore, that I write to you what I have learned concerning the miracles of our Father, your friend, who loves you not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. Those matters indeed needed a more diligent discussion and a more learned disputant. Yet I have not written them, but collected them; and I am certain that I heard and saw with my own eyes all of them. But those things which he performed on the outward and return journey of the conversation at Étampes, I neither saw nor heard; they were seen and heard by those who were ministers of the word, and whom I trust as I trust my own eyes.

For at that time I entered the school of Jesus and bade farewell to the world for ever and ever. We have determined to entrust both these matters and the other things faithfully recorded from the beginning of his journey to some man distinguished for eloquence and religious devotion, so that by the powerful force of words he may bring luminous deeds into the light. When you receive this letter, pray also for your Philip, who will be yours, as long as he exists, in the bowels of Jesus Christ.

PART ONE,  
By Philip, monk of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0373]

CHAPTER ONE. On Bernard’s departure toward Constance; likewise on the persons and names of those who were eyewitnesses of the miracles.

[Col. 0373A]

1. When Bernard, the true servant of the cross, was proclaiming the word of the cross in the kingdom of the Germans, it became necessary for him to speak with King Conrad concerning a matter of peace. He came to Frankfurt, a fortress situated in the territory of Mainz upon the Main, and named from the ford of the Franks. There also was present the bishop of Constance, Hermann by name, a religious man, earnestly begging Bernard to deign to travel into his region.

Many concerns opposed this request; especially the deep solicitude and heartfelt affection Bernard had for his own monks of Clairvaux, to whom he was hurrying by every means to return. For the mother could not forget the children of her womb, and he complained most grievously that he had been torn from his own heart, as it were, for almost a whole year. Yet the persistence of the lord bishop of Constance prevailed, as he pleaded at suitable and unsuitable times, now in person, now through the king and the bishops. Thus this most kindly man showed that it was intolerable to him that persons anxious for his sake should be grieved.

But the fear of the Lord prevailed still more, and his Spirit suggested that a great and open door stood before him. For this was Bernard’s purpose and practice: although his heart was full of affection, no private affection held any place with him in deliberating what was to be done; rather, the inquiry into God’s will claimed everything for itself. He therefore agreed to come with the bishop.

On the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent we entered the territory of the bishopric of Constance, and in the village named Kentingen [variant: Kentzigen, near Freiburg im Breisgau] were received with the greatest devotion of the people. From this, many miracles of divine power became manifest—miracles which, even if we were silent, the stones would cry out. Therefore we who were present considered it worthy to record them, to avoid shame and remove doubt. We have set down the names of each person; and each one testifies with certain truth to what he saw and heard.

There were with him myself; Hermann, bishop of Constance; and Eberhard [variant: Everard], his [variant: my] chaplain; two abbots, Baldwin and Frowin; [Note: [Col. 0373D] (97–98) Frowin, originally a monk of Einsiedeln, became abbot of Engelberg among the Unterwalden Swiss, and learnedly wrote several small works which we have seen in the library of Einsiedeln.] two monks also, Gerard and Geoffrey; and three clerics, Philip, archdeacon of Liège, Otto, and Franco. On the journey Alexander [Note: [Col. 0373D] See concerning him above, Book IV, no. 48, and Book I, On Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order, chapter 27; likewise below, Book VII, chapter 20. On Alexander Menol, Cistercian, 29 July.] of Cologne was added to them. He had been traveling to Rome; but seeing the works of divine power and hearing the Father’s frequent exhortation, he was pierced with compunction and converted. You will find each person’s name from the initial letters set before the accounts.

CHAPTER II. On miracles performed by blessed Bernard at Freiburg, Basel, and neighboring places.

2. HERMANN, BISHOP. The priest of the village of Herenheim, called for this very purpose, informed me that a man of his parish who had been blind for ten years was signed on the first Sunday of Advent and, when he returned home, was immediately enlightened. [Note: That Sunday in 1146, the year in which these miracles occurred, fell on the first of December, with the dominical letter F. Hence the weekdays that follow, as also the Sundays and feasts, may readily each be assigned to their respective days of the month.] I had heard this earlier from another person, and it is most certain throughout the whole region.

EBERHARD. I heard from two respectable men, one a priest and the other a monk, that two persons signed in the village of Lapenheim [otherwise Kipenheim] were similarly enlightened on that same day.

PHILIP. On Monday, while I was present, an old blind man was brought into the church; and, after the laying on of hands, as you all heard, the people cried out that he had been enlightened.

ABBOT FROWIN. I saw that man seeing, and Brother Geoffrey was with me.

FRANCO. On Tuesday at Freiburg, a mother brought a blind boy to the lodging in the morning. As she was carrying him back after the laying on of hands, the Father ordered that the boy be asked whether he could see. I myself followed, and when I questioned the boy, he replied that he saw clearly; this was also proved by many tests.

GEOFFREY. As soon as we entered the church, a lame young man received the power of walking through the sign of life.

THE BISHOP. We all saw it before the altar, while the people were crying aloud in praise of God.

EBERHARD. On that same day I saw three other lame persons raised up.

FRANCO. You all saw the blind woman who was enlightened at the entrance of the church and presented to the people.

GEOFFREY. And the girl whose withered hand was restored to health, concerning whom a chant was sung during the offerings.

GERARD. On that same day I saw a boy enlightened.

OTTO. On Wednesday, when the Father was returning to the church after the celebration of Mass, he touched the withered hands of a woman, who shortly afterwards recovered soundness. You all heard the chant; Franco and I saw the hands themselves.

GEOFFREY. Likewise, as he was leaving the village, a boy’s hand was restored before all of us. But also a lame woman, who was unable to keep up with us and whom, by the Father’s command, our Henry had gone back and carried on his horse, recovered her gait before our eyes in the very place where a girl lame from the womb had begun to walk; and the two ran together.

FRANCO. On the journey itself, a certain girl’s withered hand was restored. I handed her the Abbot’s staff, and she held it firmly.

3. THE BISHOP. Why have you omitted what he ordered on the first day at Freiburg: that prayer be made for the rich, that God might remove the veil from their hearts, because, while the poor came forward, they themselves hesitated to take up the cross? For the prayer was not ineffectual; rather, as you know, all the wealthiest men—even the most wicked—of that town were signed.

PHILIP. You also remember that old blind man who was signed on the road, and how the holy Father perceived that power had gone forth—not from himself, indeed, but from the word of power and the sign of life. For, after we had gone a little way, he sent men back to inquire whether the man could see, and he was found to be seeing.

GEOFFREY. He himself privately confessed to us that he often perceived beforehand the benefits that were to be bestowed on those whom he signed. And concerning those deaf women who, on that same day in the village of Crocingen through which we passed, recovered their hearing before our eyes at the touch of the Prior: as I heard from his own mouth, he said to God that he had not yet known any deaf person on this journey to experience a benefit; and without hesitation he touched them.

EBERHARD. Along with those two women I also saw a young man who had been enlightened at that very hour.

THE BISHOP. At Herzeretheim [otherwise Heyreresheim, as in chapter 4, no. 30], on Wednesday morning after the solemnities of Mass, I presented the girl whose hand was restored. [Note: In the Tournai notes Thursday is marked, that is, 5 December. Indeed, I strongly favour the reading “Thursday,” because those day-books are arranged according to the individual weekdays, as may be seen below. In the Mabillon and Horst editions, however, the Thursday entry is blank and Wednesday is printed twice.]

PHILIP. And I presented a boy deaf and dumb from the womb, whom you immediately heard speaking correctly and hearing clearly.

4. THE BISHOP. I myself spoke to the boy when he was signed; he immediately answered freely, and you all heard the people’s shouting.

GEOFFREY. Where did he get words he had never heard?

THE BISHOP. From Him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

GERARD. This was what the Father had said, as we talked privately on the preceding evening: that he had never yet seen in his lifetime a mute person speak. And shortly afterward: “Since,” he said, “those who are mute from birth are usually also deaf, it is very remarkable if they are ever so cured that they suddenly understand and speak a language which they had previously not known at all.”

PHILIP. We all saw the lame girl who was raised up there and recovered her gait, and the boy who was enlightened.

ABBOT FROWIN. A mother had brought a blind infant, who, once signed, had received sight; but she did not yet know this. Then I offered the boy an apple, and he stretched out his hand and seized it. Thus it was proved that he saw.

EBERHARD. When the holy man was led out of the church—or rather, carried out—I was present and saw him sign a lame man before the door. The man threw away his staff and, leaping up, walked.

PHILIP. As we were leaving, the blessed Father opened the eyes of a boy blind from birth. I saw it, as did the large crowd present and nearly all of us. Likewise, a man paralysed in the middle of his body, to whom he also gave a kiss after the sign, was immediately made whole before us; for he had previously healed his withered hand. In the village of Stieng, a woman who had been blind for four years was enlightened at a water-crossing before the people, and almost all of us saw her.

GERARD. On the same road I saw a girl whose withered hand was healed, while many watched and cried out.

5. THE BISHOP. On Friday at Basel, after he had delivered a sermon and crosses had been given, a mute woman was presented to the man of God. When he touched her tongue, the bond of her mouth was immediately loosed and she spoke correctly. I saw her and spoke with her. But which of you saw the lame man who had earlier recovered his gait, concerning whom the people so cried out?

OTTO. We all saw him.

EBERHARD. On that same day, Friday, my lord’s knights and I saw a boy whom his mother had brought blind to the holy man’s lodging and was taking away seeing.

GERARD. Very many things were done especially on that day, which we could not ascertain because of the tumult. For I heard him himself say that he had touched blind persons that day whom he believed either to have been entirely enlightened or soon to be enlightened.

THE BISHOP. On Saturday near the castle of Rinvel, a lame boy was raised up. When I heard the shouting—for I had gone ahead—I returned and found the lame boy walking amid the rejoicing crowd.

EBERHARD. At Secking, on Saturday evening, as the man of God entered the church, a boy was presented whose neck sinews were stiffened and who could not lift or turn his head. Once he was signed, he returned with the sinews loosened, lifted his head, and looked about freely. My servant, who spent the night in that lodging and saw the boy, reported this to me, together with my other companions.

6. GEOFFREY. This is the village in which, on Sunday morning, a boy’s hand was restored; another man lame from birth recovered the power of walking; and, as the village was being left, two lame persons, a man and a woman, were raised up. Having thrown away the staffs by which they supported themselves, they walked freely, glorifying the Lord. We had not gone far when, behold, a woman’s disabled hand was signed and healed. We all saw this; at each event there was a cry and great rejoicing. We also saw a man out of his mind whom the Father had signed in the same village, immediately calm, speaking sanely, and giving thanks; and we heard that he thereafter remained well. On our return, near the same village, we spoke with the priest, and he said that, among those cases of which they were certain, some had been raised up or enlightened there that very day. In the evening also, when Duke Conrad came to meet us, a lame boy recovered his gait before him and the knights, with us too as witnesses.

THE BISHOP. There too occurred something which I now pass over, but which I should like you to mention in its proper place.

EBERHARD. On that same day, at the entrance to the church at Doningen, we saw another lame man raised up and walking. On Monday morning, a man lame from the womb recovered his gait at the entrance of the same church, while I was present and saw it. A boy whom we had seen mute that morning in our lodging also spoke before us. Further, our hostess testified to us that her niece, who had been blind for forty years, from her fourth year of age, had been enlightened that very day.

GERARD. That day in the lodging I saw a blind boy enlightened.

PHILIP. And I saw a blind young woman who was enlightened near the village; many of our party and of the people also saw her.

7. GEOFFREY. We saw many things that day which we can no longer remember. Yet one comes to mind, recalled by the very greatness of the joy that I saw. I mean the woman whom we all saw raised up after having long been lame in a village through which we passed.

EBERHARD. I compared notes with my lord’s knights, and from what both they and I myself saw, we counted thirty-six miracles performed that day. Eleven blind persons were enlightened; eighteen lame persons recovered the power of walking; eleven disabled persons had their hands restored; one deaf person heard. If their total exceeds thirty-six, that is because earlier I had counted persons, but now I count signs. For many things were done for one girl: she was blind, lame in both feet, mute, and had one withered hand. We also heard the following crowd singing about many other things; but since we could not turn back, we did not see them.

8. PHILIP. On Tuesday at Schaffhausen we missed many things, because the tumult was intolerable and the Father had to refrain altogether from blessing the sick and flee, so violently did the people press one another.

EBERHARD. I myself stood before the altar urgently begging him not to lay hands upon anyone, being wholly ignorant how he could be brought out.

PHILIP. Yet at the entrance of the church a lame woman recovered her gait while I was present, and you all heard the people’s chant. We also saw another lame woman who, as we left the village, was signed on the slope above it; her sinews were immediately loosened and she walked freely.

EBERHARD. Before my eyes, in the same village, a deaf person recovered hearing, and a woman lame in both feet recovered her gait. I also heard from one of my lord’s knights, who was defending the saint of the Lord in that very crowd and was present throughout, that someone’s withered arm was healed and a lame person walked.

THE BISHOP. On Wednesday morning at the entrance of the church, while I, the people, and our brethren were present and saw it, a man lame in both feet and with one withered hand was freed from both afflictions; he walked freely and moved his hand.

PHILIP. I saw the blind boy who was enlightened there.

## Chapter III. Miracles performed by blessed Bernard at Constance and in the surrounding area

9. ABBOT BALDOWIN. After we crossed the Rhine, the chant which you heard—for you had all remained on the other side, the people having crowded onto the boats—was for the raising up of a lame boy, whom I saw.

GEOFFREY. I saw the blind old man who received sight as we passed through a village on the same journey, and a woman who had long been lame and who leapt up under the blessing hand. All who had known her before rejoiced with her; for she had arrived in a cart and returned on foot.

PHILIP. The Father signed a boy disabled in both arms. When one arm had been stretched out, one of the knights stretched out the other before all of us as he tried to offer it to him.

GEOFFREY. You all saw how the woman, astonished at unfamiliar light, rejoiced when she was enlightened beside the lake.

THE BISHOP. Our knights testify that they saw a boy paralysed in the middle of his body signed and healed. I also saw a certain knight’s son, apparently about twelve years old, whose hand was withered, as he was being brought forward. But immediately I heard people singing and asked what had happened. A knight replied that his lord’s son’s hand had been healed.

ALEXANDER. I saw this man healed.

GEOFFREY. I saw another poor young man whose withered hand was restored in a village near Constance.

10. ABBOT FROWIN. Few saw what was done at Constance because of the tumult. Yet I saw the blind man who was enlightened before the altar on Thursday. The Abbot of Reichenau had ordered that the man whom he supported as a beggar be brought forward. Also, a boy from our lodging whom I myself had caused to be brought—he was lame—was signed that day and recovered the power of walking. For three other signs, moreover, chanting was raised in the church and bells were rung, although none of us saw what was being done.

GEOFFREY. We knew none of the events so little as those done at Constance, because none of us dared mingle with the crowds; and we undertook to speak of those things which we saw. I suppose none of you saw anything done on Friday. But on Saturday morning, during the offerings, we saw a boy giving thanks to the Father with great devotion, because through his prayer he had recovered on that Friday the gait he had lost. When the holy man saw his devotion, he turned to me and said: “No one was found to return and give glory to God, except this boy.”

Earlier in that same offering, a young man deaf for twelve years, as he himself confessed, felt the benefit under the signing hand and cried out in joy and exultation that he had recovered hearing. We all saw him; some of our party also spoke with him. We likewise saw there a lame woman who recovered her gait, and a lame girl who was similarly raised up. Another girl who was deaf also recovered hearing there. These things, as you know, were done on Saturday at Constance in the bishop’s chapel.

11. PHILIP. In the bishop’s palace, as he was preparing to leave, a woman’s disabled hand was healed; I saw her.

ABBOT BALDOWIN. I spoke with that young man who had recovered hearing at the city gate, while the rejoicing people shouted.

PHILIP. On Saturday evening in the lodging at Winterthur, you saw the mute girl when her mother brought her; and you yourselves know how she later returned speaking, for, when asked many questions, she answered freely. On Sunday morning, because of the tumult, you all left the church and did not see what was happening, though you heard the cries of the shouting crowd. But I saw a boy paralysed in the middle of his body, whose arm, hand, shin, and foot—all of them disabled—divine power restored at the Father’s blessing. Two lame women also recovered the power of walking, one in one foot and the other in both; I saw these while present.

ALEXANDER. On that same day, before our eyes on the road, a lame boy recovered his gait and a deaf woman her hearing. Near Zürich [Note: Alternatively, Tigurum; the first name is attested by Bertius in his *Germania* as being in use among medieval writers.], a lame person was raised up before many who had come to meet us.

GEOFFREY. On Monday morning at Zürich, a blind woman was enlightened in the church. I saw her blind when she was brought forward; I was present when hands were laid upon her, and immediately we all saw her enlightened.

FRANCO. In the same church, a lame girl recovered the power of walking and a mute person speech, while we were present and saw it.

PHILIP. Likewise, a blind girl received sight. Many things besides were done there which none of us could see because of the tumult.

12. GERARD. After we crossed the river Lindemach [Note: Lindemagus, otherwise Limagus: the river which divides Zürich, its two banks being joined by three bridges.], on which that village lies, less than half a mile beyond it, two disabled boys recovered their hands, one mute person speech, one deaf person hearing, and a blind old man sight, before all. We saw and most certainly and carefully verified all these things, while the multitude that escorted the saint of the Lord in joy and exultation cried out at each one.

PHILIP. On that journey a lame woman, carried on shoulders, was raised up. Once the Father had signed her, he ordered that she be put down and walk. She was the woman with whom neighbouring women and all who knew her so greatly rejoiced. A deaf man likewise recovered his hearing before us that day near the hamlet through which we passed.

GERARD. On Tuesday, setting out in the morning from the village called Birbovermesdorff, before we crossed the river Rufa, we saw two lame women raised up on the road. While he was stirring them, the Father knew without any hesitation that each should be straightened. He stopped, had both put down, and they walked freely, glorifying God.

ALEXANDER. On that same day near the village, a boy with a twisted and stiff neck was healed before us and moved his head freely.

EBERHARD. You have omitted one thing which I saw, together with the great crowd of the village called Frichen, for you were all going ahead. There a cleric from the village called Seckingen urgently begged the saint of the Lord, as he entered the village, to perform some sign, because the people were exceedingly hard-hearted. And behold, they brought forward a woman who had been lame for twenty years. Once the Father had signed her, he ordered that she be put down, and she walked freely.

13. ALEXANDER. On Wednesday morning at the castle of Rinvelt, where we had spent the night, before the holy man entered the church, he healed a boy’s twisted neck in the outer courtyard and restored a girl’s disabled hand to health.

GEOFFREY. In the church, after Mass had been celebrated, we presented to him a girl who, from her mother’s womb, was blind and could scarcely see the light of the sun, nor distinguish anything else. The blessed Father anointed her eyes with spittle; she at once saw clearly and distinguished everything. There also a deaf person recovered hearing, and a blind man sight.

ALEXANDER. Another boy, whose neck sinews were hardened and drawn back so that he could not turn his head, was healed in the church at that very hour. On the road also, a contracted woman, wholly disabled, who had been carried in a winnowing-basket to meet the holy man, leapt up once she was signed, crying aloud; and there was great joy among the people. Near Basel also, a man who heard with difficulty received clear hearing.

14. On Thursday, before daylight, we set out hastily for Ronascle. On the journey itself, a deaf man recovered hearing, and a boy blind in one eye saw with both. This did not escape the Father: after he had passed them a little way, he sent men to investigate, and it was found to be so.

EBERHARD. Addressing Alexander, he said: “When he had sent you to see whether the boy had been enlightened, he turned to me, who was walking nearer, and said: ‘God has opened that boy’s eye.’”

On Friday, in the church at Ronascle, when he entered, a boy was brought who saw little with one eye and nothing with the other; he immediately saw clearly with both. We all saw him.
