Immediately another sign was also loudly proclaimed, and people said that a blind man had been enlightened; but because of the tumult we were unable to see him.

FRANCO. I saw walking among the shouting people a lame boy who, after a sermon had been delivered to the people, was raised up in that church itself and concerning whom they also cried out.

THE BISHOP. On Saturday, in the church at Berche, after the celebration of Mass, a cleric blind in one eye for five years recovered sight. I saw him giving thanks and rejoicing.

OTTO. Earlier there, a boy with a twisted neck had been healed; under the Father’s hand his sinews cracked and were relaxed, and both the boy’s father and the boy himself rejoiced beyond measure. You all heard the people singing; I saw the boy.

GERARD. We all saw a young man whose hand and entire arm were withered and who was healed there. We also saw the girl who, on the fourth Sunday of Advent, was raised up in the church at Strasbourg after the celebration of Mass; her father rejoiced so greatly and the people cried out. [Note: The Tournai notes record the following: “On the fourth Sunday of Advent, and on every weekday of that week until Saturday—that is, from 21 [read 22] December until 28 December, when the feast of the Holy Innocents is celebrated—there is nothing in the manuscript codex.” From this conclude that the miracles performed on those days have been lost, as also has the account of St Bernard’s arrival at Speyer, where he stayed in those days in order to attend the imperial diet.]

PHILIP. On that same day, before we embarked, a lame boy was raised up and walked freely before the people; those present shouted with joy, as you all heard. On Monday we travelled by boat, and those who were sick could not come near. Yet in the evening, at the lodging in Bagenbach, a lame woman recovered her gait.

GERARD. At the very hour when the woman came, we were complaining to one another that we had seen nothing that day; and she immediately began to walk without a staff, rejoicing and praising God.

## Chapter IV. Blessed Bernard comes to Speyer on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord for the assembly of the Emperor and princes, and concerning miracles performed there

15. Tuesday was the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, and we arrived at Speyer by boat. For King Conrad celebrated the feast day there; there he was crowned; there an assembly of bishops and princes was present. The holy Father came thither, desiring to restore peace among certain princes, whose hostilities kept many from the army of Christ’s cross. Yet miracles are not usually frequent in such assemblies, nor does God deign, where there is so great a throng of curious people, to reveal his glory. But the Father’s arrival was not fruitless, for there came about what, to use his own words, was “the miracle of miracles.”

For the King, contrary to the expectation of all who had assembled, was signed. The living and active word ran swiftly; there it was truly proved that the king’s heart is in God’s hand. Earlier, at Frankfurt, the blessed man had met the King privately [Note: See Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Emperor Frederick*, book II, chapter 39.], urging him to provide for his own salvation in this season of abundant mercy. When he replied that he had no intention of joining this campaign, the most gentle man was silent, saying that it did not belong to one so insignificant as himself to press the royal majesty more importunately.

Likewise at Speyer, after publicly reminding the King by name, for the second time, of the pilgrimage, as before, on the third day, when the feast of St John was being celebrated, he approached him privately with his usual gentleness. He urged him by every means to take care lest he let pass him a repentance that was easy, brief, honourable, and saving—a repentance divine mercy had devised for the salvation of sinners. At last he obtained this answer from the King: that he would deliberate with himself and consult his advisers, and give his answer on the following day.

Thereupon, during the solemnities of Mass, the blessed Father began to be prompted by the divine Spirit, contrary to custom and though no one had asked him, to say that the day ought not to pass without a sermon. In short, he spoke, and at the end of his sermon he addressed the King, not as king but as man, with complete freedom. He set before him the coming judgment: a man standing before Christ’s tribunal, with Christ commanding and saying: “O man, what ought I to have done for you that I did not do?” Then, recounting the height of royal power, riches, counsellors, courage, and bodily strength, he so moved the man by these and similar words that, in the midst of the sermon, he cried out, not without tears: “I fully acknowledge the divine gifts of grace; nor, with his help, shall I henceforth be found ungrateful. I am ready to serve him, since I am thus admonished on his part.”

He spoke, and behold, the people snatched up the word from the speaker’s mouth and cried out in praise of God; the earth resounded with their voices. The King was immediately signed and received from the altar, through the Father’s hand, the banner which he himself was to carry in his own hand in the Lord’s army. Signed with him was his nephew, the younger Duke Frederick; other princes also were signed, beyond number. On that same day, near the chapel in which the holy Father celebrated Mass, a lame boy recovered his gait while I was present. [Note: Otto of Freising, in book I, chapter 39 of the *Deeds of Frederick*, mentions this event and testifies that Bernard—whom he is otherwise by no means accustomed to favour—performed very many miracles, publicly or privately, at that time. He adds that the monk Rudolf, or Radulf, who publicly preached that the Jews ought to be killed—see Bernard, Epistle 322—was summoned by Bernard and compelled to return to his monastery, abandoning thereafter the office of preaching; the people were greatly angered and wished to stir up a riot. Finally, he adds later that Bernard’s letter, read by Conrad at the assembly at Regensburg, persuaded countless people to take the cross.]

16. EBERHARD. On Saturday morning, when the feast of the Innocents was being celebrated, I was going out of the lodging to meet the holy Father, bringing with me a knight who wished to be signed. Behold, as he looked at a blind boy amid the crowd, he said: “What does this boy want?” Since I did not fully understand his words, because he spoke in the Romance language, he said: “Bring the boy to me.” It was done as he ordered, and the boy, once signed, immediately recovered sight. I myself tested him in many ways and found that he saw clearly.

GERARD. After the celebration of Mass, the man of God was led into the chapel adjoining the canons’ dormitory. He signed a man blind in one eye, and he immediately recovered sight. Both his former blindness and his subsequent enlightenment were most carefully tested. Likewise, while returning from the church, he made a deaf person hear by impressing the sign of the cross and putting his fingers into the man’s ears. We saw and tested this.

THE BISHOP. So too the blind man whom I myself presented, who was enlightened before the altar on Sunday while the gradual was sung.

EBERHARD. I believe many things were done there which we did not see. For we often heard the people singing, and none of us could force our way in to see what was occurring. Still, I saw one deaf man who recovered hearing there, and I presented him.

## Chapter V. Other miracles performed at Speyer

17. PHILIP. On that day an assembly was held at which the Spirit was manifestly present; no one can have any doubt of this. For the King summoned all the princes and knights who had been signed. When they were all seated together, the holy Father exhorted them, not with human but with divine words. When we went out, and the King himself with the princes escorted the saint of the Lord so that the crowds might not crush him, a lame boy was presented to him before the King. He made the sign of the cross, raised the boy up, and ordered him to walk before all. Who could describe the joy and exultation with which the boy was led away?

Then the holy Father turned to the King: “This has been done for your sake, that you may know that God is truly with you, and that what you have undertaken is acceptable to him.” At that same hour, before we left the lodging, a girl was raised up and a blind woman enlightened.

EBERHARD. On Monday morning, as the holy man set out for the church, a multitude of sick people obstructed us, and we ordered them all to go on ahead. Without delay, a lame man was raised up before the altar. Whether he had been signed, I do not know. Yet I saw him walking and saw a wooden foot hanging in the church.

OTTO. In the King’s chapel, in the King’s own presence, a boy lame from the womb recovered the power of walking.

EBERHARD. That same day two others, one lame and the other bent over, were raised up and, while I was present, led to the greater church by the whole people. You all heard the shouting and the ringing bells. I had scarcely returned home when, behold, there was another cry and another ringing. I hurried to the church, and again two lame persons had been brought in, who had recovered the power of walking that very hour.

18. GERARD. In the evening, as the Father returned from the King’s court, a multitude of sick people besieged the doors of the lodging. We had them sit down in order, and he touched and healed each one. There a boy lame from the womb recovered the power of walking; another, blind in one eye, was enlightened; and a man lame for ten years was raised up. I saw these healed immediately under the blessing hand. One of our brethren testifies that he saw another deaf person recover hearing and a woman giving thanks because she had recovered from a headache.

EBERHARD. On Tuesday a blind boy was enlightened; I saw him.

PHILIP. Likewise, in the presence of the King and princes, a man recovered the sight of one eye. In the same place there occurred something at which we greatly rejoiced because a Greek duke, sent by the Emperor of Constantinople, was present. He was speaking with our Father in the King’s chapel when a blind woman was presented. Once she had been signed before him, she was immediately enlightened, and that man was deeply moved by this event. Likewise, toward evening, while the King, that duke, and many princes stood by, a lame boy was presented. The faithful man then spoke confidently, in the hearing of all: “In the name of Jesus Christ, I command you: rise and walk.” The voice of power sounded, and power followed: the boy rose and walked freely. At first his limbs or shins trembled as he walked, but little by little he grew strong before the eyes of all.

19. GERARD. Bishop Anselm of Havelberg [Note: This is Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, whose three dialogues against the Greeks were published in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*. On him see Eugenius III in Otto, book I of the *Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 61.] suffered very severely in his forehead and throat, so that he could scarcely taste anything or speak. He therefore begged the blessed man, saying: “You ought to heal me too.” Bernard pleasantly replied: “If you had the same faith as these little women have, perhaps it might benefit you.” But Anselm said: “And if I do not have faith, let your faith make me well.” At last the Father signed and touched him, and immediately all pain and swelling departed.

PHILIP. Our curiosity has been overcome, because frequent miracles shine forth every day. On the octave of the Nativity of Mary, as we were going to church, a lame boy recovered his gait in the canons’ cloister and walked rejoicing before our Father himself.

GERARD. During the solemnities of Mass, a bent boy was raised up. I saw him when his mother led him, now sound, to the altar to offer a candle for the health he had obtained.

OTTO. After the celebration of Mass, a lame woman recovered her gait; we all saw her walking.

GERARD. The King himself, the court, and the entire city of Speyer saw many benefits bestowed on the sick both that day and the following day, benefits which can never be erased from their memory. But our little sheet, on which we had noted these things, was lost through the negligence of a certain brother: may God pardon him. Yet three things come to mind, for we have no leisure to investigate the rest. On Thursday, two boys, each of whom had lost the light of one eye, were enlightened in the lodging; and a paralysed man, brought on a pallet, was healed.

PHILIP. In the King’s chapel, while the reconciliation for which the blessed Father had come expressly was being concluded, he signed a man whose head shook without interruption, and he was healed that very hour. A lame boy also was raised up there.

GERARD. In the evening, two blind persons were enlightened in the lodgings before our eyes. On Friday morning, before our eyes, a blind man recovered sight.

20. But we must go; the messenger who is to carry these things is already hurrying. Therefore we ask what the lord bishop has held in reserve.

THE BISHOP. You have done well to remind me; for, I confess, these matters had entirely slipped my memory. When Duke Conrad came to meet us, an archer in his service disparaged the word of the cross and blasphemed the saint of the Lord, saying: “He performs no more signs than I do.” When the Father stopped to lay his hand upon the sick, the man approached and saw him whom he had disparaged. Immediately he fell senseless and lay for a long time without consciousness.

ALEXANDER. I was beside him when he fell, and his horse stood motionless. But that wicked man, struck by divine power, suddenly fell backward. We were all astonished and summoned the Father. Nor did the wretch rise until the Father came down, prayed, and raised him up. Thus, having learned in himself the power which he had formerly, in unbelief, disparaged, he was signed on the following day at our Father’s command, intending to depart for the Lord’s army.

THE BISHOP. Blessed in all things is the Lord’s mercy, who has reserved for this last generation at least one of the saints of old, that, like a most burning lamp, he might consecrate this age’s darkness by his life, teaching, and miracles. Happy are you who hope beneath his wings and are satisfied from the breasts of his consolation! Happy the congregation that rejoices in so great a Father, whose glory we wretched secular men boast of possessing at least through slight acquaintance!

## Part Two. By Various Authors
## Chapter VI. Letter of the Monks of Clairvaux and Companions of Saint Bernard to the Clergy of the Church of Cologne

[Col. 0385B]

To their lords and friends, the clergy of the church of Cologne, greetings from their brothers and friends, Everard, Gerard, and Geoffrey, monks of whatever worth; Philip of Liège, Volmarus of Constance [Note: [Col. 0385D] Alternatively, Wolkemar; concerning him see below, no. 24 ff.], and the other recruits of the spiritual warfare, whom the holy man rescued from the midst of Babylon.

21. Above all, it is fitting that from the very depths of our hearts we give thanks to you, Lord our God. For you have multiplied your mercy upon us and have dealt magnificently with us, forgetful of all our iniquities, for the punishment of which [Col. 0385C] not even hell itself would suffice. And why has this happened to us—surely sinners, the worst of all—whom, by your ordering patience, the earth is compelled reluctantly to bear? Why has this happened to us, that we may breathe again under the protection of such holiness? O truly inestimable abundance of compassion! O incomprehensible abyss of divine loving-kindness! He has heaped the gifts of his grace upon the Man whom he chose, so that he might gather to him from every quarter the most desperate sinners, in whom they may more securely possess holiness laid up for them.

But you, beloved, how long will you be heavy-hearted? (Ps. 4:3.) If the mighty works done among you in these days had been done in Tyre and Sidon, would they not have repented in ashes and sackcloth? (Matt. 11:21.) We read that at a single sign three thousand people were converted from a people indeed stiff-necked, when the word of power spoken from Peter’s mouth caused a lame beggar at the gate of the Temple to walk (Acts 3–4). How many persons did the city of Cologne see raised up in a short time? Many of the people indeed were converted to that to which they were called, and most devoutly accepted the indulgence offered them by the supreme Pontiff and the penance imposed upon them.

22. But certainly, unless your righteousness exceeds that of these, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0386B] (Matt. 5:20). Laypeople belong to the world: they may lawfully think upon the things of the world. It was said to the apostles: “You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world” (John 15:19). You now occupy their places; you live upon their revenues; you hold their authority; you exercise power through their authorization; you claim for yourselves their honor. Yet—with your leave—all things are common between you and them, except conversion and manner of life, except works and will, except, finally, life itself and reputation.

If anyone sees a flock grazing upon the ground, who is surprised? But if the shepherd likewise bends downward, likewise gapes after earthly things, and seeks what is below, is that not ridiculous and a great abuse? But now, “Be ashamed, O Sidon,” says the sea (Isa. [Col. 0386C] 23:4): “Tax collectors and sinners go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31). The wound of this clergy is desperate: from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it. The Church has been enriched with earthly possessions, but stripped of virtues. For they could not dwell together long, once the King of glory, becoming poor for our sake, chose poverty so completely that he said: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Alas, alas! We see that poison has been added to the Church, as was said to Louis, whom you call “the Pious,” and who especially enriched churches. For we read in his history that he heard a voice saying to him: “You have added poison to the Church” [Note: [Col. 0386D] Others attribute this to Constantine. See Baesseus, Wednesday of the first Sunday in Lent.]. Or perhaps it seems incongruous to you to interpret [Col. 0386D] riches as poison? Christ too calls them thorns in the Gospel (Mark 4:18–19), and the Apostle defines them as the devil’s snare: “Those who wish to become rich in this world fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9). Therefore let those who wish to become poor escape, and safely sing: “The snare is broken, and we are delivered” (Ps. 124:7). Recognize the welcome voice, you who have passed through this snare: we speak of your brothers, who are still detained among you only in body.

[Col. 0387A] For the Lord’s discourse was not idle—directed, plainly, to the clergy—so that those who still persist in destruction may be the more inexcusable. Rather, may the threefold cord, which is not easily broken, draw the rest more readily, when to word and signs there is added also the example of their neighbors. As you see, abundance of material and the ardent desire by which we wish all of you to be our companions in the heart of Jesus Christ have lengthened this letter. Yet we must desist, especially because these matters were announced to you more copiously and effectively by our Father himself, with the Lord working together with him and confirming the word by accompanying signs.

Many of you have carefully read the copy of the little book which we sent to the illustrious Henry [Note: [Col. 0387D] Brother of Louis the Younger, king of the Franks.], royal more in spirit than in blood, concerning the signs which we saw from the first Sunday [Col. 0387B] of Advent until our departure from the council recently held at Speyer. Many still ask us to append an account of what occurred among you, since these things are sweeter to you because you yourselves saw them in person. A threefold consideration persuaded us to do so: first, that the new brethren, while still detained by secular affairs that must be brought to an end, may grow warm again through this reading; second, that the rest may consider what they admit when they refuse, whether enticed by pleasures or held back by faintness of heart and fear, to commit their souls to so great a Father—a man whom, certainly, once God has taken him away, many will lament tearfully because they ignored him while he called them; and third, that the noble church of Cologne may possess, as is fitting, an everlasting memorial of those events by whose presence it deserved to be exalted.

This is not because our own writing ought to be preserved, but so that those who have learning and can apply diligence may write these things more brilliantly and worthily. Nor do we doubt that far more miracles shone forth both among you and on the journey than we could then know or can now remember. But we have recorded only those most certain and thoroughly proven. We have also resolved to add those things which the power of the Almighty still works wonderfully each day through his faithful servant and devoted minister. We thought it right to preface this record with a few of the things which we saw from Speyer to Cologne, that these may be joined to the earlier narrative. Some matters too, which the venerable abbots Theodoric of Camp [Col. 0387D] and Erwin of Steinfeld [Note: [Col. 0387D] Theodoric was elected abbot of Camp in 1136. Erwin is the provost, afterwards abbot, of Steinfeld, mentioned below in no. 26; his letter to Bernard is prefixed to Sermon 65 on the Song of Songs [Col. 0388D], where he is called Everwin.] saw in person, have been recorded under their names, as we received them from them.

## 1177. Chapter VII. Miracles Performed by Blessed Bernard from Speyer as Far as Cologne

23. Since the reverend bishop of Constance is absent, let his cleric, now our brother, Wolkemar, take his place in this account and speak first himself.

**WOLKEMAR.** Would that God might command my name to be enrolled among the names of the elect! Would that, through the prayer and merits of him in whose present praise it has pleased your Holiness that this should be done first, it might be found—even last—in the book of life!

Therefore, on Friday, as the end of the previous book declares, the council of Speyer was dissolved, and we hastened to Worms. There, although he was urgently entreated, the holy Father would not remain, saying: “For I must preach the Gospel to other cities also.” For he had passed through Worms two months earlier and, after delivering a sermon, had marked an innumerable people there with the sign of Christian warfare. Yet before we departed, on Saturday, he touched the sick who had assembled. There, in my hands, two deaf persons whom I presented, while the people stood by and shouted, declared with great rejoicing that their hearing had been restored [Col. 0388B].

**PHILIP.** On the journey [Note: [Col. 0388D] Here it seems necessary to read “on Sunday,” which I find marked in the excerpts just mentioned, after Saturday, and to place it before *on the journey*, lest Sunday, which fell on 5 January, otherwise be omitted here contrary to custom.] a lame boy was raised up, as all of you truly saw.

**GEOFFREY.** On Monday, the feast day of the Epiphany, at the castle of Kreuznach, the blessed Father, returning from church, touched and raised up a boy who, as his parents and many others among the surrounding people who knew him testified, had been completely lame for six years. We ourselves immediately saw him walking as he was led to the church, while all acclaimed the praise of God.

**WOLKEMAR.** On Tuesday at Pichenbach—for thus they call the village where we spent the night—on the morning of the feast of the Manifestation, three miracles appeared which I saw with my own eyes. At the entrance of the church, a deaf man was presented; immediately the Man of God drove away his deafness with his consecrated fingers and imparted hearing. Also, at the entrance, a girl lame in one foot recovered her step. The blessed Father had not yet left the village when, behold, they offered him a paralytic on a litter. Having heard the report of his powers, this man had caused himself to be brought by wagon from a large village above the Rhine called Boppard. Him too Bernard signed, touched, and raised up, sending him home sound.

24. **GEOFFREY.** In the diocese of Trier lies a most celebrated settlement where the Rhine and Moselle meet, whence it is called Confluence, or Koblenz. Many signs were displayed there before the whole people which escaped our knowledge or memory. Yet I remember seeing a lame [Col. 0388D] boy raised up in the church of Saint Florin after the celebration of Mass. Our Frederick, who followed the Saint of God from that same village together with the excellent young man Adulf, also maintains that a blind man was enlightened there. Without the knowledge of relatives and friends, Frederick crossed the Moselle with us, clothed only in a surplice, just as he had come from the church of Saint Castor, where he was a canon. This other Joseph left his cloak with the adulteress [Col. 0389A], fled from the Egyptians, and escaped.

On the same journey, when we had gone a little way, a certain man well known in that region was brought riding on a horse. The sinew of his thigh had withered so greatly that, when his knee was bent back by the measure of a palm, that shin appeared shorter than the other. The holy man signed him and, not hesitating at all about the effect of the power, ordered him to be taken down and to walk. But there was no one to obey—perhaps because those standing by hoped too little, or understood his word too little. So the Father was silent, but the voice of power was not silent: suddenly the man cried out, feeling the sinew loosen and the knee extend as he sat upon the horse which carried him. He was immediately taken down and walked freely, magnifying God; and throughout that day he followed his healer.

Another man also, whose thigh sinew had likewise withered so that he could scarcely touch the ground with the tips of the toes of one foot, was healed on the same road, so that he freely set down his heel and walked without a staff.

**WOLKEMAR.** On Thursday, at the village of Riegemach, in the morning before we departed, a boy in my presence recovered his step, having been lame for six years, as I learned from his own parents. There too [1178] a deaf woman heard, and a blind man was enlightened. He possessed only one eye, and that too was wholly useless.

25. **GEOFFREY.** May the city of Cologne remember forever this day on which it deserved to receive the holy Man whom it had always desired. Yet because he arrived unexpectedly, the gathering of people was smaller that day. [Col. 0389C] Thus the despiser of human glory is accustomed, as far as lies within his power, always to avoid ceremonial receptions and to choose rather to enter cities secretly. Yet he can rarely do so, because a greater glory follows one who repels it.

On Friday morning, before we entered the church, a woman blind in one eye for ten years regained her sight at the touch of the blessed hand before us. She was immediately presented in the church to the clergy and lay for a long time before the altar, giving thanks to God. Meanwhile, a blind boy was also enlightened in the very lodging. The holy Father then entered the church and celebrated Mass at the altar of Blessed Mary, located in the eastern part. When he had finished, a blind girl was enlightened before all the people; and a wealthy woman, well known in the city, whose legs had been withered for three years and could not be extended at all, had her sinews loosened and immediately stood erect at the sign of life [Col. 0389D].

Likewise, when he had mounted the pulpit to address the people, an old blind man recovered his sight. Many other signs indeed occurred that day, and they often shouted aloud. But none of us was inquisitive enough to investigate them. On Saturday we also saw and learned of many things at the lodging; but because, with the arrival of the multitude of others, we neglected to write them down, they have now entirely slipped from our minds. Yet I do not think that the words which he spoke to the clergy—for that day he would not go out to the people—or how he proved by every testimony of the divine Scriptures that this form of clergy, indeed this utterly formless life, is contrary to them all, have slipped from everyone’s mind:

“You,” he said, “were marked by the prophet when he said: ‘They are not in the troubles of men, nor are they scourged with other men; therefore pride has possessed them’ [Col. 0390A] (Ps. 73:5–6). And Isaiah in the same Spirit—or rather, God through Isaiah—says: ‘Let mercy be shown to the wicked man, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has acted wickedly, and he shall not see the glory of the Lord’ (Isa. 26:10). And more expressly and by name in another prophet: ‘The princes of my people shall be cast out of the houses of their delights because of their most evil desires, and their clergy shall not profit them.’”

But of this elsewhere. Let us now return to the order of the narrative.

## Chapter VIII. Various Miracles Performed at Cologne

26. On Sunday, before Mass was celebrated, a certain blind man was enlightened by the sign of light and life [Col. 0390B] and was led to the altar. For on that day an inestimable multitude gathered for the promised sermon, such as no cleric said he had ever seen in that church. The holy Father celebrated Mass at the altar of Saint Peter, which, situated in the western part, holds the chief place in the church. There, after Mass, innumerable miracles occurred before everyone.

A distinguished woman, well known in the city, who had been blind in one eye for five years and confessed that she had spent much money uselessly on physicians, regained her sight under the signing hand. Another woman was likewise enlightened.

**ABBOT OF CAMP.** Of the many things which I saw there, only two come to mind: a deaf and mute girl, who immediately heard and spoke; and a lame young man whom divine power raised up at the prayer of its servant.

**ERWIN, ABBOT OF STEINFELD.** In the square where the blessed Man preached, because the church could not contain the people, while we stood by, a certain blind man received sight, and a crippled man received healing of his withered hand and arm.

**ABBOT OF CAMP.** When the sermon was over and we returned home, from the moment he entered the outer door until before he reached the threshold of the lodging, in my presence he raised up a hunchbacked boy; restored sanity to an insane woman; made a lame woman walk; and the blessed Father enlightened a matron blind in one eye.

**GERARD.** This was the woman concerning whom one of our brothers so marveled that a benefit could be granted so easily even to a wealthy person [Col. 0390D]; and the swiftness was indeed worthy of every admiration. For before she even appeared to have been signed, she cried out that she had been enlightened.

27. **EVERARD.** From the time we had dined, miracles never failed us that day. We know these matters with greater certainty, having examined them carefully. The holy Man stood at a window, and sick persons were offered to him by a ladder; for no one dared open the door of the house, so great was the crush and tumult. There also the daughter of a certain wealthy man, well known in the city, recovered hearing which she had utterly lost for many years. Her parents had formerly placed her in a certain convent, but the nuns sent her back because she had completely lost her hearing. She had remained thus for a long time, hearing nothing, until God opened her ears at the touch of the consecrated [Col. 0391A] hand.

A little later, a contracted woman was raised up and walked.

**GERARD.** You all saw the hunchbacked boy who was raised up that same day, and the many blind persons who were enlightened.

**WOLKEMAR.** Of those whom I saw and remember, I counted five: some blind in one eye, others in both.

**ABBOT OF CAMP.** Toward evening, a woman was enlightened who, after the laying on of hands, had remained blind for two or three hours. At last, wishing to leave and having no one to lead her, she felt her way pitifully along the wall with weeping and lamentation. We all pitied her, but immediately rejoiced with her. For she suddenly cried out that she could see; and hastening to her, we tested this by many proofs.

[Col. 0391B] 28. **GERARD.** While these things were happening inside, I stood outside and could not enter in any way. From the ninth hour until evening I remained thus with some of our brothers, unable even to approach the door or the ladder, so great was the multitude on every side. At last, when the crowds withdrew at night, I entered and immediately saw a deaf man recover hearing.

When we had supper, because a multitude of sick persons had assembled, we asked the Father to go out and sign them. Immediately, at the touch of the consecrated hand, God restored hearing and speech before us to two deaf and mute girls.

**EVERARD.** There too a certain boy and a matron of that city, both lame, were both raised up.

**PHILIP.** On Monday very early, a deaf man recovered hearing and a blind [Col. 0391C] girl sight. A little later a blind woman was enlightened; and such a tumult and rush occurred that the blessed Man could scarcely be drawn back into the lodging. I do not know whether there was a greater miracle there than that he escaped unharmed.

**GERARD.** About the third hour, a multitude of sick persons desired the Man of God to go out, pressing all the more importunately because they saw that they had little time remaining. Therefore he went out into the square and signed those seated in order. Before the eyes of all, fourteen persons were healed in that very hour: seven lame people, five deaf people, a crippled boy, and a blind woman each received the benefit they desired. At each event the people shouted, and voices thundered through the clouds in God’s praise: “Christ, uns genade. Kyrie, eleison. Die Heiligen alle helffen uns” [Col. 0391D]—“Christ, have mercy on us. Lord, have mercy. May all the saints help us” [Note: [Col. 0391D] That is: “Christ, have mercy on us. Lord, have mercy. May all the saints help us.”].

29. Moreover, the archbishop of the city was staying in that very lodging, and before him too, when the holy Father went out, he enlightened a blind boy.

**ABBOT OF CAMP.** From this point the crowd became intolerable, so that no one at all could leave or enter the house. It was therefore decided that he should be taken to the archbishop’s house, from which he could depart more freely. There a noble boy, son of the sister of the advocate of Cologne, long deaf and mute, received both hearing and speech before us all through the laying on of hands. There too a certain blind man recovered sight, and another, whose leg was withered and useless, received [Col. 0392A] healing. A girl also, whose tongue was attached to her throat and who could scarcely speak, was healed that same hour when the bond of her mouth was loosened.

We are witnesses of all these things; the city of Cologne is witness. They were not done in a corner, but publicly, that God might be glorified by all, he who is glorious in his saints. If anyone should perhaps be unbelieving or inquisitive, it would be easy to prove many of these things to him, especially those performed upon persons neither lowly nor unknown.

## 1180. Chapter IX. Miracles on the Journey from Cologne to Liège: at Jülich, Aachen, Maastricht, and Elsewhere

30. Having scarcely at last left Cologne, we came to Brauweiler, a monastery two miles distant from the city. On the road, in the presence of the people of Cologne, [Col. 0392B] who were following the Saint with due devotion, two deaf persons were presented, whose ears God opened when the blessed Father placed his fingers in them and breathed hearing into them with his consecrated mouth.

**EVERARD.** On Tuesday morning, in the church of Saint Nicholas—for the monastery of Brauweiler is dedicated in his honor, and its name is interpreted “Black Village” [Note: [Col. 0392D] Others prefer the explanation that it was named after Bruno, its first founder, as though “Bruno’s Village”.]—a blind boy was enlightened before the altar, presented by the lord abbot of Camp. The cries of the still rejoicing people had scarcely fallen silent when, behold, a deaf and mute person was granted hearing and speech.

**WOLKEMAR.** Another deaf man also received hearing while we stood by.

**ABBOT OF CAMP.** The first miracle which we saw on the road that day was the restoration of a certain man’s withered arm and hand.

**GERARD.** We saw frequent miracles on that day [Col. 0392C]; for the road was full of people, and the whole field was a city for us. The second miracle, unless I am mistaken, was a man blind in one eye, who was immediately enlightened. But in the same place something occurred at which we all marveled even more. A woman offered her now grown daughter, saying that she had been deaf and mute from the womb; and many of the bystanders who knew her testified to the same fact. She was healed that very hour by the laying on of hands, heard, and spoke freely before us.

We had not yet gone much farther when a deaf man recovered hearing.

**GEOFFREY.** Up to these miracles I was walking ahead of the crowds. But hearing such frequent songs of the people, I stopped and carefully verified what was afterwards done on the journey [Col. 0392D]. A deaf and blind woman heard and saw; three deaf persons heard; one lame woman walked; five blind people were enlightened, some in one eye and others in both. We are certain that the holy Father knew in spirit of the enlightenment of one boy who was wholly blind. For he stopped, turned toward him, and ordered inquiry whether he could see.

31. **ABBOT OF CAMP.** He had earlier done the same concerning another blind man; and after I had passed by, he sent me back to inquire. When I returned and announced that the man had been enlightened, he said: “I too had perceived it.”

In the evening we came to Jülich, a castle built by Julius Caesar, bearing distinction from his name [Col. 0393A]. Entering the church, the blessed Father saw a lame woman lying before the altar. With a new fervor of spirit, at which we all marveled, he seized her hand and raised her, with as much ease as faith. Likewise, as he entered the church courtyard, he enlightened a blind man before us and all the people.

**GERARD.** In the morning, after the celebration of Mass in the church, a blind boy received sight and a deaf man hearing. A distinguished woman, niece of the Count of Jülich, who for five years had seen nothing with one eye and so little with the other that she could scarcely keep to the road without a guide, after she was signed saw clearly with both eyes. The advocate of that castle had also lived blind for twenty years and was enlightened that same day. Many other things indeed happened, and the people often cried their customary “Christ, uns genade,” both in the castle and on the road; but a few examples out of many are enough for us.

**EVERARD.** On the road, those I remember were: a deaf boy who recovered hearing; a blind woman who recovered sight; and another lame woman who recovered her step, before us all [Col. 0393B].

Aachen is a seat, a most famous and pleasant place, more suited to bodily pleasures than to the salvation of souls; for “the prosperity of fools destroys them,” and woe to the undisciplined house. I do not say this for destruction, but would that someone might read it and correct it! Would that one of them might reflect, be converted, and live! There then, in the royal chapel at the altar of Blessed Mary, on Thursday, a blind girl recovered sight. I myself stood beside the Father, but immediately such a tumult arose that he had to withdraw.

**PHILIP.** There too an old lame man was raised up, and they immediately hung his crutches in the church itself as testimony. I myself had long kept this man back, not knowing why he wanted to approach or what he sought.

[1181] **EVERARD.** Two women, whose hands had entirely withered, were healed there in that very hour [Col. 0393C].

32. **ABBOT OF CAMP.** The holy Father extended one woman’s hand with his own; but the other was healed as if by touching the hem of his garment. For she stood behind his back and complained that she could not reach his hand. I said to her: “Put your hand upon his garment, if perhaps you can touch it.” She did as I advised; suddenly she began to grasp his cowl, and as she drew it, her fingers were extended [Col. 0393D], and she was immediately healed.

**GERARD.** Nowhere on that journey was the Father so pressed [alternatively, seized] as in that chapel, because the place was narrow and crowd drove against crowd, as one wave is accustomed to drive another headlong. For this reason we do not know many of the things that occurred. Our Gerard, then a canon of that church, who on the same day abandoned both his benefice and the world, says that five blind persons were enlightened there.

**WOLKEMAR.** Maastricht is the place [Col. 0394A] where the see of Liège was once transferred from the city of Tongeren by the most blessed confessor Servatius. There we spent the night on Wednesday in the church of Blessed Mary. On Thursday morning, after Mass, we led the Father to a raised place so that he might heal the sick without being crushed by the crowd. I was near him and knew more fully what was done, and carefully verified all matters. There five blind persons were enlightened, a deaf man heard, and a mute man spoke. Likewise another deaf man recovered hearing, and persons crippled in their hands recovered soundness.

**GERARD.** That same day in the lodging, a deaf and mute boy was presented. As the holy Father signed him, a worthy young man, Conrad, canon of Cologne, renouncing the world, gave himself into Bernard’s hands. Bernard rose to receive him, and [Col. 0394B] immediately the boy spoke and heard. The people were waiting outside; and behold, the hearing and speaking boy was restored to his parents, followed by abundant rejoicing. The boy was known in the city, and this event became most celebrated among the people. Without delay, a lame woman also recovered her step; three blind persons were enlightened; and each was led out among the people with gladness and rejoicing.

33. **PHILIP.** As the holy Man was leaving Maastricht, an occasion arose for him to turn aside to the church of Saint Servatius on account of Brother Norbert, who was a canon of that church; but Norbert immediately renounced both his benefice and the world. On that road a lame boy was raised up before us.

In the church of Saint Servatius, moreover, persons bringing a lame [Col. 0394C] man to our Father asked him to lay his hand upon him. But he said: “I do not know whether blessed Servatius will be displeased if we presume to do this in his house.” Everyone cried out and said: “Lord, he will not be displeased.” “In the name,” he said, “of our Lord Jesus Christ and of blessed Servatius, rise and stand upon your feet.” He rose without delay or hesitation, and great joy arose among the people.

These things occurred yesterday at Maastricht. Today the entire clergy had gathered at Liège—where it is exceedingly numerous—and were waiting for the Father in the bishop’s chamber so that he might address them. But behold, the Lord went before them with a word of power: a certain cleric, lame from the loins downward [Col. 0394D], so disabled that he could not stand at all upon his feet, was offered to the Man of God. Signing and touching his feeble limbs, Bernard said: “Walk in the name of Jesus Christ.” Immediately strengthened, he began to walk. And the report went out among the clergy, and they cried: “These are your works, O Christ, you who glorify your saints in this way.” To him be glory and dominion now and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] The Tournai notes state: “The manuscripts contain nothing about what he did at Liège, nor how many days he stayed there, but without any heading there follow the miracles which [Col. 0394D] he performed from Liège to Clairvaux.” Yet what was done at Liège by the holy Man will immediately be related by Geoffrey.]

## Part Three. By Geoffrey, Monk of Clairvaux

[Col. 0395]

## Chapter X. Letter of Geoffrey, Monk of Clairvaux, to Herman, Bishop of Constance

[Col. 0395A]

To his most beloved lord and most reverend Father, HERMAN, by God’s grace bishop of Constance: Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, of whatever worth, the child of his holiness, asks that in his prayers he remember his children.

1182. The miracles which we saw and learned of from Speyer as far as Liège, we described to the clergy of Cologne in the manner in which the earlier ones had been described: that, in the fashion of a conference, each of us in turn might recount the things at which we had been present. Since, therefore, a copy of that little book will not escape your attention, most blessed Father, as I trust, I have not neglected to record the remaining matters and send them to your Holiness [Col. 0395B].

It is certainly true that we were ignorant of many things even among the earlier events. No one can follow everything in passing. Yet what harmed us most, once we had left the German regions, was that your cry, “Christ, uns genade,” had ceased and there was no one to shout. For the people speaking the Romance tongue have no songs of their own, according to your custom, by which they render thanks to God for each individual miracle. Many things therefore, concealed by silence, did not reach our knowledge. Even among those things which I know with complete certainty, I have deliberately omitted quite a few, fearing perhaps that so great an abundance might produce weariness even in a very curious reader.

I say this not so much to you, whose faith I do not doubt, as to others into whose hands these pages may come: I have written nothing except what I either saw with my own eyes or learned by the most certain report of our brothers who were present [Col. 0395C].

## Chapter XI. Miracles Performed at Liège, Gembloux, Villers, Mons, Valenciennes, and Elsewhere

35. Therefore, on the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany and on Monday, we remained at Liège while our Philip concluded the secular business in which he was entangled. On Sunday, when the holy Father had celebrated the solemnities of Mass before the whole people at the altar of Blessed Mary in the greater church, a boy was presented whom they said had been lame from the womb. When Bernard signed his legs [Col. 0395D] and touched his loins, he took the boy’s hand, immediately raised him, and led him along.

The clergy immediately cried out: “We praise you, O God”; but the lowing of weeping and sobbing overcame the cry of praise. The unskilled people gave tears instead of song. There too he touched and healed two withered hands, so that they recovered both sensation and movement [Col. 0396A]. Before he had moved away from the altar, he enlightened an old blind man by the sign of the cross and made another lame man walk in the sight of the entire assembled church.

On Monday morning in the bishop’s house, after Mass, a young man blind in one eye was enlightened at the touch of the sacred hand. Under the signing hand he leapt up, crying that he had recovered sight. Without delay another man, blind in both eyes, was brought, and he too was enlightened there in that same hour. The bishop of the city was present, a careful examiner of all that Bernard did. Hearing the young man joyfully cry that he had been enlightened, the bishop asked him many questions to test whether it was true [Col. 0396B], and the man answered each without hesitation.

That day about the sixth hour the holy Father went out to sign the sick, and there a certain lame man immediately recovered his step. When they heard that he had once gone out to the sick in a more spacious house, far more people than before arrived. Therefore, after the ninth hour, he went out to them and signed those seated in order. Immediately, among those of whose cases we are certain, five blind persons were enlightened and three lame persons recovered their steps, to the fitting amazement of all. In the evening, too, in the bishop’s chapel, a deaf man recovered hearing.

On Tuesday, before we departed, three lame people were raised up in the bishop’s house itself: two women and one boy. Many other signs indeed occurred at Liège and on the journey, but a few out of many [Col. 0396C] are enough.

36. On Wednesday, setting out from the town called Huy, we hastened to the monastery called Gemblo(u)x. [Note: Perhaps Gembloux, a Benedictine monastery, in French Gembloux.] On the journey itself, an old man blind in one eye and a young man afflicted with the same disability were both restored to sight at the same time. On Thursday morning, at the aforesaid monastery of Gembloux, a lame boy was brought to the Man of God; he was immediately signed by him, regained the use of his feet, and walked before everyone. Shortly afterwards, at the entrance to the same village, another boy, crippled in both feet and hands, under the eyes of everyone regained the health of both sets of limbs. He had not gone far when, behold, a boy mute from the womb was brought to him on the road. He too was signed and healed; immediately the bond of his mouth was loosed, and he spoke correctly. On that journey two deaf persons were brought to him; and he who had made the mute speak also made the deaf hear.

In those parts a new monastery, called Villers, was being built; and a few months earlier the holy Father had sent there a community of monks. He therefore wished, even while passing through, to visit the new plantation and console his pilgrim sons. And when he began to approach the monastery, he touched, signed, and raised up a lame woman, commanding her to walk freely. In the same place he also restored the use of their feet to two lame women, and restored to a young man the sight lost in one eye, before the brethren themselves and many others who had assembled.

37. From there he hastened to the town called Fontaines, where our Philip had asked him to lodge with his relatives. On that journey a boy blind from birth was brought to him; he could not even open the eyelids of his eyes. Everyone had despaired, even those who had seen many and very great miracles. But he, without hesitation, laid his hand upon the boy and, after making a very brief prayer as was his custom, opened his eyelids with his fingers and asked whether he saw. The boy answered: “I see, lord; I see you, and I see all men with hair.” Clapping and exulting vehemently, he said: “God, God, I shall no longer strike my feet against a stone.”

On Friday, at Fontaines, before we departed, a girl’s contracted and withered hand was healed and stretched out. On the road also, near a certain village, a lame boy regained the use of his feet. From there we came to the castle called Bins, where such a multitude of people met us that the people covered the whole plain of the fields. There they brought on their shoulders a lame boy, whom the Man of God, signing him, commanded to be set down so that he might walk. The way could scarcely be cleared for his new steps: so great was the throng and so great the tumult. Yet, when set down, he began to walk in the middle of the crowd, and very many followed while leading him into the open field. His mother was present, as were his relatives and many who knew him; by their very exultation they furnished proof of the miracle.

Meanwhile, while no small portion of the people had withdrawn with the boy, the joy was doubled: another boy, likewise lame, likewise recovered the use of his feet. A third lame man was raised up on the same plain and walked before all; rejoicing, he ran and gave praise. Near the same castle one blind person was restored to sight, and two deaf persons recovered hearing at the place where he had stopped to bless and dismiss the people.

Mons is the first castle in the province of Hainaut; we spent Friday night there. On Saturday morning, before our departure, a certain old man from a neighbouring village—known to many who were present and not unknown to our Philip—recovered the light of his eyes, which he had lost many years before. A schoolboy, blind in one eye, was also restored to sight with such speed that the blessed Father had not yet withdrawn his hand before the boy cried, “I see, lord,” to the amazement of all.

38. These things were done at the lodging before the venerable Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, his clergy, and many religious men who had come from the whole province to meet the Man of God. With these same persons standing by, as he left the castle, he healed a woman’s withered hand and restored the use of his feet to a lame man. Very many miracles shone forth that day, so that many of them escaped memory. Yet these we remember with complete certainty. Two deaf women recovered hearing on the road, and a boy recovered sight in one eye. We had not gone far when, behold, in a field a woman recovered the sight in one eye which she had long lost.

On the same road there is a little chapel two miles from the aforesaid castle. There a venerable crowd had assembled to meet the Man of God, in order to see his face and receive his blessing. Nor did the Lord disappoint the devotion of his people, but showed them the desired mighty works of his power. There, before everyone, an old man who, as was said, had remained blind for twenty years was made to see; and a deaf woman heard, amid great rejoicing both of those concerned and of the people. At another place where he stopped, two boys were brought, each of whom saw with only one eye, and also a deaf woman. He did not move on until he had restored sight to the boys and hearing to the woman.

Still on that journey, near the stream Huns, before crossing it, a blind boy was restored to sight; after the crossing, two deaf women recovered hearing. We were now approaching our lodging, and behold, a lame woman recovered the use of her feet through the laying on of hands, before a large multitude of people who had come from the whole region to meet the blessed Man. Other weak and sick people also obtained their desired benefits. But it would take too long to recount every case. The town where we stayed that night is called Valenciennes, a large and populous town. There, before we entered our lodging, the holy Father, signing and raising up a lame woman well known to the people, made her walk before everyone. Setting out from there, we came to Cambrai on Sunday.

## Chapter XII. On miracles performed at Cambrai and elsewhere

39. Very many miracles occurred both in the castle itself and on the journey, but from among many we have collected a few. In the church of Saint John, after the celebration of Mass, a boy deaf and mute from his mother’s womb heard and spoke, and the crowds marvelled. He had sat mute and deaf beside me; presented before me, he heard and spoke in that very hour. The jubilation had scarcely ceased when, behold, a lame old man was raised up and walked.

There also occurred that at which, more than at the other miracles, we were astonished. A boy blind from birth, his eyes covered with a white opacity—if indeed they ought to have been called eyes, for they possessed neither colour nor function nor even the very cavities of eyes—received sight at the laying on of the blessed hand. We tested this by many signs, scarcely trusting our own eyes that sight could reside in such eyes. In the same place a woman’s withered hand also regained health. Thereupon, as the crowds pressed around the blessed Man, he was scarcely conducted into the house of the Regular Canons. There too he conferred very many benefits on the sick; but these are the cases we remember with complete certainty: two lame persons were raised up there, and a blind boy and a blind woman recovered sight.

40. On Monday, in the city of Cambrai, the holy Father celebrated the solemnities of Mass at the high altar in the church of Blessed Mary, so that, being placed in a more elevated position, he might be seen by the people and not pressed upon. As the others approached for the offering, a boy deaf and mute from his mother’s womb was brought forward. Born in a nearby village, he was known to many standing there. Those who had brought him began to entreat the Man of God to deign to lay his hand on the boy; but, fearing the press of the people, we forbade this, telling them to bring him after Mass was ended. Yet the effect of the power anticipated our expectation.

For, while making his offering, the boy kissed the sacred hand according to custom and passed on. Without delay, one of the knights of the aforesaid brother bishop came up and asked the boy, “Oz tu?”—which in Latin means, “Do you hear?” Immediately the boy too replied to him, “Oz tu?” Thus, deaf from the womb, he spoke only the words that he had heard from the mouth of the questioner. The knight therefore continued speaking to him and taught him to invoke God and name the Blessed Virgin, etc. As the boy answered each thing without hesitation, the clergy who stood nearer gathered round. Once the truth of the miracle was known, they raised their voices, magnifying and praising God who had given such power to men. The boy was lifted up and greeted the people, and the city of Cambrai exulted with joy on hearing the boy speak, who from his mother’s womb had never at any time spoken or heard.

That same day, in the bishop’s house, where he had received the holy Man with great devotion, a girl’s weak hand was healed and stretched out at his touch. In the evening a father brought his daughter, who had long been lame; she recovered the use of her feet, and he joyfully led her home. On Tuesday he healed two withered hands, and a lame woman experienced that in Bernard’s hand the grace of healings was effective. As he was leaving, he also restored sight to a blind boy at the gate; and in the field he made a deaf youth hear and a mute person speak before all the clergy and people of the city.

41. Valcellus is the name of a monastery three miles from the city itself, which this same Father of ours had formerly built by sending brethren from Clairvaux. He spent Tuesday night there, unwilling to deprive his sons of a father’s visit and consolation. In that monastery itself, on Wednesday morning before his departure, he healed by the power of his blessing a certain knight from that same region who, having been weak in feet and legs for many days, could not walk. He sent him back safe and sound to his own home, giving thanks. On the road also a deaf man recovered hearing in one ear.

In the town called Gom, near the monastery of Regular Canons called Mont-Saint-Martin, they brought a lame girl to the new Martin of our age. But he made the sign of the cross and said: “Go, in the name of Jesus Christ.” At once, when she was set down, she sprang up and walked, running and praising God.

On Thursday, at the monastery called Humblerières, a father brought to the Man of God his daughter, paralysed in one half of her body. As her sickness worsened, she had lost the use of hand, arm, lower leg, foot, and even tongue. But when the blessed Father signed her, she was healed: she spoke and walked most plainly, and moved her hands freely. That same day we came to Laon, where, on Friday in the monastery of Saint John—for he was lodging there—a deaf man recovered hearing before everyone. On Saturday also, at Reims, when the journey was already being prepared, the holy Father restored sight by the sign of the cross to a boy blind in one eye, while a multitude of clergy and citizens stood by.

## Chapter XIII. On miracles performed on the journey toward Clairvaux

42. On Sunday was the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary. Louis, king of the Franks, a most devout and most Christian prince, came to Châlons to meet the Man of God. Very many princes from both kingdoms also assembled, together with envoys of the king of the Romans and of the illustrious Duke Welf, in order that the journey to Jerusalem might be discussed by common counsel. The Man of God was so occupied by this conference for those two days that he could not go out to the people, although he was most earnestly desired. For the common good had to be preferred to private wishes.

But when he went out on Tuesday, a woman met him asking for healing of her withered hand; and according to her faith it was done for her, so that she became well in that very hour. This miracle was performed among neighbours and acquaintances, lest anyone raise the Gospel objection: “What great things we have heard were done in Capernaum, do here also in your own country” (Luke 4:23). For the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, was present: formerly a son of the blessed Man by profession, now a father by the dignity of his office. Certain princes were present also, as well as no few knights of our land.

On Wednesday, as the Desired One himself drew nearer to the desired Valley, the manifest miracles multiplied, so that, though he was proved to be more than a prophet, he did not lack prophetic honour, not even in his own country. That day, in the village of Champagne called Davamant, he celebrated the solemnities of Mass in honour of Blessed Agatha, whose feast was being observed. He had not yet withdrawn from the altar when, behold, a man brought his blind son. He anointed the boy’s eyes with spittle and touched them, and he was restored to sight that very hour.

43. In the town called Rosnay, a sick man, utterly debilitated, was carried in a cart, and nothing seemed left to him but the grave. Laying his hand upon him too, before all the people and many knights, he made him walk without delay. To the astonishment of all, the man followed the cart in health in which he had previously been carried. Likewise, upon leaving the castle, he signed a boy who for many days had been unable to walk even a single step; immediately he walked freely.

On the same road lies another castle, called by the inhabitants Brena. As the Man of God passed through it, a lame girl recovered the use of her feet through his prayer and blessing. When he had left it, a blind woman and beggar sought alms from him. Looking upon her mercifully, the Man said: “You seek silver, but God will restore your sight.” Approaching, he signed her, and before all she was restored to sight that very hour. Asked how long she had been blind, she replied that for eleven years she had seen absolutely nothing. Thus the apostolic Man, imitating the apostolic example, surpassed by a most holy generosity both the beggar’s request and her hope.

He had not gone far when, behold, a boy blind in one eye begged for a blessing and requested a touch. What could he deny one who had given to a person who did not ask? Without delay, he signed the blind eye; closing with his hand the eye by which the boy had been accustomed to see, he moved a finger before him and asked what he was doing. Certain pilgrims, hearing that the Man of God was passing by, brought their deaf companion to him with prayers. Anointing his ears with spittle and putting his fingers into them, he restored his hearing that very hour. After proceeding a little further, the man followed him, gave thanks, and received from him the sign of the cross, as he was setting out for the army of the Lord.

44. That same day we came to Bar-sur-Aube, a very famous town three miles from Clairvaux. On Thursday the holy Man celebrated the solemnities of Mass in the church of Saint Nicholas. There the people of Bar were astonished at new mighty works of divine power. [Note: For, during the offertory, four lame persons were raised up and a blind boy restored to sight before them, insofar as I infer from the variant reading noted by Henschenius, which has suffered something through a careless excision.] The Lord further magnified his servant and opened under his hand the eyes of a boy blind from birth.

In the same church after the celebration of Mass, a contracted girl, whose heels had adhered to her loins, was raised up and walked freely. Another girl, who could not stand at all, there regained health. Likewise a lame woman recovered the use of her feet; and as soon as she had been signed and felt the power, she ordered the bells rung, as they did for every miracle. In the same place two persons deaf and mute from birth received hearing and speech together: one was a boy, the other an adolescent well known in that town. One further deaf person recovered hearing, and a girl powerless in her hands from her mother’s womb was healed that very hour. As he was departing, he also restored a withered hand to health before the almshouse.

That day the good steward of the manifold grace of God was restored to Clairvaux, bearing precious sheaves, returning like the patriarch Jacob with two companies. For he brought thirty men with him, and was expecting nearly as many more to come, their vow already made and the day set. What, then, shall we say to these things? Happy indeed is he whose prayer is found so acceptable, whose touch so healing, whose speech so living and effective! Happy the soul which the Lord has filled with the oil of grace above its fellows! Happy the tongue healing the desperate wounds of so many souls! Happy the hand abounding in the grace of healings and in signs of so many powers!

## Chapter XIV. On miracles performed by Bernard at Clairvaux, Troyes, Étampes, Sens, and neighbouring places

45. The holy Father spent a few days at Clairvaux and, providing for the brethren’s rest, forbade the sick to be admitted. Yet on the very day when he was to leave, our venerable bishop brought him a young man of Langres whose one ear had been completely deaf for many years. The man immediately heard and gave thanks for the swift cure.

As the Father went out through the gate of the monastery, he found a multitude of sick persons—blind, lame, and withered—and very many amid that tumult obtained the desired healing beneath his signing hand. When he climbed the hill, he met a deaf and mute boy who had spent many days among our brethren at Fontarcia, communicating with them only by signs. Anointing the boy’s tongue with spittle and putting his fingers into his ears, he commanded him to name God. The boy began gradually to speak, but his voice still struggled in his throat. One of our brethren, noticing this, brought him again and asked that he lay his hand on his throat. Immediately he spoke freely, giving thanks to God with many tears.

For he had been deaf and mute for so long that he had entirely forgotten his own name and did not know what he was called. Barely recalling the name of the city from which he came, he said that he was a Parisian. On the same journey another deaf person heard, and two lame boys recovered the use of their feet. Near Mundivilla—for so the village is called, about two miles from the monastery—a paralysed old man was healed while we stood by and the crowds shouted loudly. The place where we spent that night is called Ville-sur-Arce.

In the morning, in the church after the celebration of Mass, an adolescent with one leg contracted was signed by the Man of God; he stretched out the sinew and walked rejoicing before all the people. Entering his lodging in the same village, and with many people rushing in, he healed by his customary blessing a boy blind in one eye and a girl mute from birth. The boy was restored to sight and the girl spoke, as all heard and marvelled. In the street also, as the people detained him while he was leaving, two maimed persons were healed. One of them also recovered the lost sight in one eye and, delivered from a double affliction, bore away double joy.

46. That same day near the castle of Bar, which the river Seine washes, before a great multitude of people assembled from the whole region, a blind boy, a blind man, a maimed girl, and a paralysed old man were healed. The old man had been brought in a cart; they said that he had been so weak for six years that he could neither sit nor turn onto his side without assistance. At the entrance of the village called Bargonium, a lame boy from his mother’s womb was raised up; at its exit, a woman recovered the use of her feet, which she had lost four years earlier.

We had not gone far when, behold, a woman blind in one eye ran after us. When she reached the Man of God, he immediately signed her; she recovered sight and returned rejoicing and praising God. At the entrance of the diocese of Troyes, in the village called Fulceria, a boy deaf and mute from birth, brought by the people, was healed of both ailments that very hour. On the road also, as we were leaving, Bernard’s blessed hand stretched out a girl’s hand, withered and contracted from birth, as though it were wax; and she was immediately healed, so that she firmly held the staff which we gave her. All marvelled—noble and powerful men of that same region who were escorting the Saint of God. Yet they marvelled still more near the village called Wanda, seeing a lame girl, mute from her mother’s womb, walk after receiving the blessing, and hearing her speak.

47. On the following day, an innumerable people assembled in the greater church of Troyes to hear the word of God from the Man of God. A dangerous and intolerable tumult of crowds pressing upon one another arose; fearing danger, the blessed Man left. When he had withdrawn to the bishop’s lodging, a multitude of sick persons followed him and waited outside the doors. A lame girl entered, and under the eyes of all, as the Man of God signed her, she regained health and walked freely. The girl was known in the city, and several of her relatives were present at that very time. Shortly afterward a boy blind in one eye was restored to sight, and two others whose hands were withered were healed, to the amazement and joy of all.

In the evening, ordering the sick waiting near the screen of the church to be placed apart, he went out to them and signed those seated in order. The venerable bishops Geoffrey of Langres, who personally saw nearly everything we write, and Henry of Troyes were present; no few clergy and laypeople from the city were present. Before them all, a lame and mute girl was brought to the Man of God. When, signed, she was led by the hand, she began to speak and said: “I cannot walk, lord, I cannot.” We were all astonished; we asked that she be signed again, and she also recovered the use of her feet.

There too, anointing a boy’s blind eye with spittle, he restored it to sight. He immediately healed, by signing and touching her, a woman lame for fifteen years, who was supported by nuns in the church of Blessed Mary, so that she could both sit—which she had previously been unable to do—and walk freely. Exulting greatly, she took the crutches which she had formerly used to hang them in the church of Saint Peter. Likewise, a young man, servant of that church, recovered there the hearing he had lost five years earlier.

The following things occurred in the same city. A certain smith, limping from a long illness so that he could not walk at all without a staff, was signed by the blessed Father and joyfully returned walking on his own feet. Then a woman brought him her epileptic daughter, to whom that illness had completely taken away the ability to speak. The blessed Man laid his hands upon her and signed her; immediately she spoke before us.

48. Leaving Troyes in the morning, as the holy Man passed through the village called Prunet, a boy was brought to him whose foot had been twisted backwards by contracted sinews, so that he could not walk at all. Those assembled shouted and raised their hands to heaven while the Man of God touched the boy. Without delay, he untwisted the signed foot with complete ease and ordered him set down. Before all he began to walk in health.

At the town which the Romance language calls Triangulum, after the celebration of Mass on Friday, a blind woman native to that castle was brought before the altar in the presence of all. When the blessed Man had laid his hand upon her, she was questioned by those standing around. “I shall soon see,” she said; and shortly thereafter: “I see clearly; I see you all. Blessed be God, who has shown me mercy.” Another woman was also restored to sight; witnesses affirmed that she had been blind for ten years. There too a lame woman recovered the use of her feet and a mute person speech, to the shouts of all, especially those of that castle, who had never before seen anything like it.

That same day, as he passed near the castle of Braium—which means “Mud”—a man met him carrying his daughter on his shoulders. She had never been able either to speak or to stand upon her feet. Immediately, under the eyes of all, she was freed from both disabilities.

49. At Montereau, where the river Yonne flows into the Seine, in the presence of Count Theobald and many other nobles and common people together, three women were healed: the first recovered hearing; the second the sight in one eye which she had lost seven years earlier; the third, who was paralysed, recovered health. She had been carried into the church on a litter; when she was signed and commanded to stand upon her feet, she stood unharmed amid the people and, leaving her litter behind, joyfully made her way home.

That same day at the town of Moret, near the lepers’ houses, they brought a boy deaf and mute from birth. His ears were immediately opened and the bond of his mouth loosed. After we had left the castle and crossed the river called Luten, an innumerable people came to meet the Man of God; there too a boy, well known to those standing around, recovered by his blessing the speech he had lost. [Note: Read *Luen*, Latin *Lupa*, commonly *Loing*, a river of the Gâtinais flowing into the Seine below Moret; see above.]

50. At Étampes, he and the others who had assembled were occupied with the business of the expedition to Jerusalem and the kingdom of France. Yet there he restored hearing to a deaf person; reason to a madman brought bound; and sight to two women, to one in a single eye and to the other in both. As he left after the council had ended, he restored sight to a blind girl by the sign of the cross.

At the village of Messa, three miles from Étampes, before all the people who had assembled, he restored hearing to two deaf persons, a man and an old woman. Passing through the town of Milly that same day, he signed and healed a sick woman so deprived of bodily strength that she could neither walk nor stand. She returned on her own feet, though she had been brought on the feet of others. There too a certain cleric recovered sight in one eye, and a lame boy his ability to walk. Likewise at Moret, a man blind in one eye, who came to meet the Man of God as he entered, was immediately restored to sight by his blessing.

At Sens, formerly the greatest city of Gaul, in the sight of the clergy assembled around him, he gave by the laying on of hands hearing to a woman deaf and blind. Apart from other things which we refrain from writing to avoid prolixity, as he entered the town called Joviniacum, a blind woman was brought to him. Her deprivation was immediately changed into its opposite: from blind she became seeing. The report spread among the people, and from every side they cried: “Anna sees!” for everyone knew her. When we departed, the people’s joy was doubled, and before all, a boy blind from birth in one eye received by the benefit of grace the gift denied by nature.

## Chapter XV. On miracles performed at Auxerre, Molesme, and elsewhere

51. Arriving at Auxerre, the most blessed Man entered the monks’ church for prayer, where that precious treasure lies, where the most holy body of glorious Germanus rests. As he came out, a lame woman met him at the gate. She could move only on her knees and hands; clinging to his footsteps, she appealed with pitiable supplication to the bowels of his mercy. The blessed Man made the sign of the cross, touched her lower back and knees, raised her in the Lord’s name, and sent her walking on her own feet to the altar of the most holy Confessor. For all the people assembled there invoked his name while the woman was being raised up. This was a miracle very well known and celebrated in that city. Everyone knew the woman, and for almost three years they had seen her carried on a litter.

The holy Man lodged in the bishop’s house. There too, before many witnesses, he freely stretched out and healed a woman’s withered hand. So also in the morning as he was departing, his blessed hand gave a similar benefit to a woman suffering from the same disability. That day, as he passed through Cableia, a lame boy was brought to him. He was immediately healed and raised up, and they led him into the church of Saint Martin. For both that church and the village itself belonged to Saint Martin, whom they marvelled to see revived in Bernard.

As the crowds still escorted him, a lame girl, whose other hand was weak, was freed from both disabilities before them. At the castle of Tonnerre, that same day, while we watched in the lodging, a woman blind in one eye was restored to sight by the sign of the cross; she went out magnifying God. Also, in the church of Saint Anianus on Wednesday, while he sat for the offering during the solemnities of Mass, they brought a blind boy. Divine power immediately opened his eyes beneath the hand of the faithful servant. Similarly, as we were leaving the castle, a blind girl before all who escorted the blessed Man recovered, at his signing, sight that she had lost many years before; and another woman blind in one eye was restored to sight near the river called Armantia.

52. That same day we came to Molesme, the monastery from which our Fathers had formerly gone forth, through whom the Cistercian church took its beginning. There is a book, the *Usages of the Cistercians*, in which the diligent reader will find this written more fully. [Note: These matters are read in the Little Exordium of Cîteaux, from which the present book of the *Usages of the Cistercians* differs; perhaps at that time it formed a single book together with the *Exordium*. Hence the antiquity of the book of the *Usages* is established—a work we think was subsequently enlarged by various additions.]

There, therefore, as stated, on Wednesday they received the Man of God with great devotion. As he sat in his lodging, a man blind in one eye entered, bent his knee, and begged for mercy. When he signed him with his sacred fingers, he touched the blind eye; immediately the man was restored to sight and gave thanks to God.

An hour later, as evening approached and the day was already declining, the blessed Man went out to sign the sick who waited outside the doors. First, a boy blind in the right eye was healed. Once signed, he shut the left eye with which he had previously been accustomed to see; discerning everything clearly, he answered at once whatever questions we put to him about objects shown.
