God granted the same benefit through the hand of his Bernard to three others suffering from the same affliction: a girl, an elderly man, and a woman; and the result in their cases likewise was carefully tested. Still in the same place, a little girl weak in her feet and lame from her mother’s womb was healed by the laying on of hands. Her mother rejoiced that she had deserved then for the first time to see her standing and walking.

53. On Thursday, as the Man of God left the monastery of Molesme, an innumerable multitude gathered from the whole region escorted him with due devotion. A lame woman who had been brought in a cart, once signed by him, was joyfully led back walking on her own feet. On the same journey, as we entered a wood, a deaf youth recovered hearing, and a woman recovered, through the laying on of the Man of God’s hands, the sight in one eye which she had lost twelve years earlier; many were present and saw it. Then two men came to meet him, and each likewise received the sight of his eye which he had lost.

We had not gone far when, behold, as crowds came running together from every direction, a lame boy whom they had brought was healed at the blessed Man’s touch and walked freely in rejoicing. Confinium is the name of a village close to our own borders, through which we passed that day. There also, before the eyes of all who had assembled, the Man of God signed and touched a blind boy and a woman lame from her mother’s womb: to the one he restored lost sight; to the other he granted a new power of walking.

Finally, as he entered Clairvaux, one of our number met him, bringing a deaf and mute boy who had for fifteen days awaited the Saint’s arrival in the monastery. The faithful boy was not disappointed in his desire. As soon as he was signed, he received hearing and speech together. At first he could scarcely name God; then, at our command, he began to invoke the name of the Blessed Virgin. At last, the bond of his mouth fully loosed, he spoke everything, pouring forth abundant tears of joy. Many brethren who had formerly known him as wholly unable either to hear or to speak also spoke into his ears and heard him form all words fully.

Asked how long he had remained mute and deaf, he replied: “It is now the third year since I became deaf and mute, and I communicated only by signs.” Saying this with tears, he blessed the Lord who had shown him mercy. We too give such thanks as we can for so great a father and patron, always glorifying and praising God, who is blessed above all things for ever.

## Chapter XVI. On certain miracles performed by Bernard at Trier, Rutila, and Frankfurt
[Col. 0407C] 54. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April, as the Man of God entered Trier, the whole populace rushed out, as was customary, to meet him. And behold, they brought to him two little girls, sisters from the same city, one five and the other four years old, suffering from the pitiable affliction of blindness. When the holy man made the sign over them, both received sight; and they were brought into the church of blessed Peter, where at that same hour he celebrated the solemnities of Mass. There clergy and people saw them; there we carefully verified the truth of the miracle. When the sacrifice had at last been completed, the Man of God sat beside the altar to lay his hands upon the sick and heal them. Immediately a lame man was brought, and he walked; a blind man was brought, and he saw; a deaf woman was brought, and [Col. 0407D] she heard. She said that she had been warned in a dream to hasten to him, by whose blessing she would receive her hearing. I do not doubt that a diligent investigator may find many other things; but I judge that these may suffice for remembrance. Yet we most certainly remember that, in the archbishop’s house, a boy blind in one eye was given sight before us.

55. Lest brevity be burdensome to you, I have added some things also from those performed at Rutila. The holy Father had seen in a dream—as he disclosed to us more privately—a lame woman seeking him in a church, although he was recognized neither by her nor by the people. He rejoiced that he was unknown, and secretly approached and made the sign over her, [Col. 0408A] then passed on; and she, suddenly amazed, rose upright. The fulfillment of this vision became manifest. For while the blessed man was celebrating the solemnities of Mass in that church, a crippled woman was brought in. For many days she had been crawling upon the ground and was utterly unable to stand upright; she moved as best she could upon her knees and with the little stools which she carried in her hands. Guntrannus of Sirco, a castle situated on the Moselle, a short distance from the aforesaid monastery, had caused that woman to be carried into the church. She had not yet come to the holy Father’s hand, when behold, his spirit secretly came to her, as he had foreseen; suddenly she sprang up from her bent posture and walked, praising and magnifying God. Seeing this, the people, who had known her formerly as lame, cried out in praise of God; [Col. 0408B] and, taking up the little stools, they immediately carried them to the altar, in order to present them to the Lord and to Bernard His servant.

There also, at his touch, a woman from the same village, lame for seven years, and a little girl crippled because the sinews of both her thighs had become stiff, so that she could neither straighten her knees nor stand erect, received the gait they had desired before all. A blind man and a blind woman were also brought to him; and, immediately making the sign of the cross, he drove darkness from each and restored light to both. But perhaps this description of ours, though too brief for the studious, may seem too long for the forgetful. Therefore, with them also in view, let us summarize what has been said, as the proverb has it. The church of Trier rang with melodious voices when, at Bernard’s touch, the lame walked, [Col. 0408C] the deaf heard, and the blind saw. The same Man of God also gave sight to two blind sisters as he entered the city, and to a boy blind in one eye in the house. At Rutila heavenly light shone in Bernard’s presence: his blessing gave walking to two lame women and sight likewise to two blind persons. In the same church, the lame woman who was carried on her knees and little stools was raised up before she reached the Man of God.

56. Once the holy Father was seated at Frankenvoert, and the sick were admitted through a window to his hand; an innumerable multitude had gathered there from every direction. And behold, among the rest there was brought a young man deaf and mute from his mother’s womb. The blessed man laid his hand upon him and immediately healed him: he heard and spoke freely. Yet he knew no language, but uttered only those words which he had heard from the mouth of someone speaking with him. This especially moved our Hugh to request that this miracle be recorded; but we had seen many similar things. On that same seat a certain wealthy and honorable matron of the same region was also brought, who had long lain paralyzed. The Man of God made the sign over her also, took her hand, and raised her, commanding her to walk freely in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the power of the Holy Spirit. He spoke, and it was done: she sprang up and walked. Then all cried aloud; but especially the knights rejoiced who had carried her on their own shoulders [Col. 0409A] and now saw her going back on her own feet. Surely their devout service seemed, in some manner, a participant in the miracle. This too prompted our friend to judge it wicked that such a miracle should be passed over in silence.

57. A third case resembles this. In a nearby village there was a man who had been paralyzed for eight years, known to everyone and deserving the compassion of all. He could not move his limbs, even if the house in which he lay had begun to burn all around him. He was carried on a mattress and laid before the blessed Father in the presence of us and many others then attending him. Touching his weak limbs after making the sign of salvation, he immediately raised him up; and he was so perfectly healed that he at once took up the sign of the cross, intending to depart for the Lord’s army—having plainly experienced its power to be so great and so swift. [Col. 0409B] When others began to carry away his bed, “Not so,” said the venerable Hugh, “rather, he himself shall carry it.” He put it upon the man’s shoulders and dismissed him; and he walked so vigorously as though he had never previously suffered any infirmity.

The fourth miracle which Hugh requested to have recorded was the restoration of a certain girl. In the evening they brought her to the lodging, carrying her on their shoulders. When the blessed man made the sign over her knees, he felt sinews contracted and hardened almost like a wooden rod. “Alas,” he said, “her sinews are wholly drawn back; she could not bend her knees, or indeed straighten them when bent, at all.” And this was certainly so: for many days she had been unable to walk on her feet, but crawled as best she could on hands and feet. Therefore, [Col. 0409C] at the Father’s blessing both sinews were immediately loosened. One of the brethren raised her up, while he held her lower legs, and they were gradually straightened. When she began to walk unharmed, we were all greatly astonished; and the Saint himself, making the sign of the cross in wonder, gave thanks to the Lord of hosts.

1192 CHAPTER XVII. On miracles wrought at Toul through blessed Bernard.

58. Let us now come to what was done at Toul. In this year the holy man entered that city four times, and never passed through it without miracles. First, on the Sunday before Pentecost, while he was celebrating Mass at the high altar in the church of blessed Stephen, a blind boy, known in that same city, was brought to him and received sight through the laying on of hands. To this day the church of Toul possesses him as a mirror of blessed Bernard’s powers and a trustworthy testimony. When he came to the city a second time, he passed through the nearby village called Calmas. Behold, a devout crowd rushed out to meet him, bringing water to be signed and blessed. By that blessing, after the manner of the Gospel miracle, it was immediately endowed with both the taste and smell of wine; and those who tasted it all bear witness. Thus even now throughout that whole region it is a most certain and celebrated miracle that at the village of Calmas water was changed into wine under Bernard’s hand. For [Col. 0410A] fresh wine was splashed upon someone’s garment, as people running together from all directions eagerly pulled at the little vessel; and for many days it retained the fragrance of most precious wine.

59. When he entered the aforesaid city of Toul for the third time, he feared the crowds; and, since a long journey still lay before him, he hastened to leave by night. Some of the people suspected this and watched for him; nor could he depart even at night without a crowd. Among them a paralyzed woman was brought upon a litter. The blessed man immediately raised her, made the sign over her in the Lord’s name, and healed her. Her cure also became known throughout the whole city; for the woman, who had long lain paralyzed there, still lives in it today unharmed. Likewise another woman, blind in one eye, [Col. 0410B] who was brought to him outside the city, received sight when he made the sign over her; this we proved most truly and certainly on this visit.

Recently, when the Man of God was received as a guest at Saint-Èvre, he adorned that monastery with many miracles: raising a lame boy, restoring hearing to a deaf young man, and granting sight to three blind persons in the name of Him who is worshipped as Three and One. I do not doubt that many miracles likewise shone forth there; but I know more certainly those done before me, and have written them with greater confidence.

EPISTLE OF GEOFFREY, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX, recounting certain miracles of Saint Bernard.

Brother Geoffrey, to his most beloved master Archenfred and to the entire [Col. 0410C] Chapter—his brothers according to the flesh: may you remember him who loves you in truth.

1. Master, I have learned by sure experience that I ought not to employ flattering words to you. For it could not escape the notice of your familiar son, whom beyond others you were accustomed to cherish more tenderly and embrace more dearly—not because you considered him worthy, but because you recognized him as unworthy—how little esteem you have for those who hunt after words. I mean, it could not escape one who clung to your side, for you plainly hold with the Apostle that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in power (1 Cor. 4:20). Why, then, multiply words? You know, lord, that I love you; you know that I need your prayers and those of your brethren; and you do not fail to know how greatly I love and how greatly I need you. Therefore I am silent about myself, knowing that I write to one who knows me.

But because I remember with what anxiety I left you and all Clairvaux together, since our lord Abbot’s intention concerning this journey seemed uncertain, I write to you, concerning whom I have greater confidence, what we saw and heard in him. Thus you may have consolation and may likewise provide it to your own. Know this, however: I write nothing except what has been established as true.

2. As we approached Poitiers, the lord Abbot began to fall ill, so that he almost began to regret not this journey but its burden. There, for our consolation and his, a voice came to him in a vision, singing: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:3). [Col. 0411A] The chant was like a versicle, and only its final cadence was lacking, in this form:

> And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

[Note: [Col. 0411] In the copy designated as taken from an old Marchiennes manuscript, a series of dots follows; hence it must be suspected that something has been omitted.]

What we should believe was signified by that omission is made clear by what follows. The next day, while he again lay down, a new song was thus put into his mouth—“The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord” (Psalm 63:11)—so that, when he awoke, he could repeatedly think of nothing else.

At Poitiers, while we were sitting at night and he was walking alone with a candle, the candle went out; and the abbot of Charroux saw him walking without light. Then, with a certain sound, as he himself confessed, the candle was rekindled, and he carried it burning back to us.

3. In the city of Bordeaux an event occurred worthy of a miracle: it converted the most obstinate minds of the clerics, so that they allowed Regular canons to be installed in the episcopal see. For seven years they had utterly disregarded excommunication over this matter: the archbishop had been in exile for five years, the church had stood vacant, its revenues had been violently plundered, and the archbishop was so hateful to all the people that, even at our arrival, they reproached all our party, saying, “These are among the archbishop’s supporters.” But the living and effective word of God changed their minds beyond the expectation of all who knew the difficulty of the affair and its exceedingly grievous entanglements.

At the castle called Bergerac, a nobleman suffering from a most severe illness was brought to him; from that hour he recovered, as we afterwards learned. [Col. 0411C] A man of that city, poor and needy, today praises the name of the Lord. His strength had been broken by a long illness, and he could neither labor nor perform any work; but, after eating blessed bread and following us for several days, he returned strong and whole. In the city of Cahors, a certain servant of the bishop, struck on the head, had lost the sight of one eye; but when Bernard made the sign over him, he received sight. There also a citizen drank water blessed by him, and it seemed to him as though a full vessel of water were poured over his head; and from that hour he recovered from a fever from which he had suffered for seven years.

4. Who could describe the devotion of the people of Périgueux? They almost suffocated him; so much so that he had to depart from them secretly. In the city of Toulouse [Col. 0411D] he was received with sufficient devotion; but within a few days they were more than sufficiently—indeed excessively—devoted. That city had a few persons favorable to the heretic, including some weavers whom they themselves call Arians. Yet those who supported that heresy were very numerous, and were the leading people of that city. Indeed, not long before our arrival, they had led astray one of the wealthier men of that city together with his wife, so that, leaving their property and little son, they withdrew to a village full of heretics and thereafter could not be brought back by any persuasion of their relatives.

Henry was summoned, and the Arians were summoned; and the people promised that no one would shelter them in future unless they came and spoke openly. It would take long to recount Henry’s flights and the hiding places of the Arians. For the Arians who were in the city fled when they heard of the signs and wonders that were being done. Their supporters renounced them, and we believe that the city has been entirely freed from every contagion of heretical perversity. Some of the knights promised henceforth to expel them and not to give them support. But if any should be greedy and choose to act otherwise, loving the gifts of heretics, a sentence was pronounced against the heretics and their supporters, and against all who had supported them: [Col. 0412B] they were to be admitted neither as witnesses nor in legal judgment; no one was to associate with them at table or in commerce. We pursued and persecuted the fleeing Henry,

[Note: [Col. 0411] Compare the preceding third book of the *Life*, chapter 6.]

but he fled all the more.

5. In the very castles which he had led astray, the lord Abbot spoke; and, while the people listened gladly, those who had been predestined to life believed. We found certain knights obstinate, though, it seems to us, not so much through error as through greed and evil will. For they hate clerics; they delight in Henry’s witticisms and in the fact that he tells them things that give them occasion and excuse for their wickedness. Nevertheless, all affirmed that henceforth they would not support him if he refused an interview with the lord Abbot. Accordingly sentence was pronounced against the heretic and his supporters, and his most wicked life was revealed to all the people: how at the Council of Pisa he had abjured all the heresies which he now preaches, and how, having submitted to the lord Abbot, he had received letters from him to become a monk at Clairvaux. We believe, with the Lord’s favor, that his malice will shortly be ended.

A land seduced by such manifold teachings of error would require lengthy preaching. But the lord Abbot seems unequal to so great a labor, and fears even more that he may be burdensome to his brethren. This, unless we are mistaken, is the meaning of the missing cadence in the chant of the versicle which he heard.

6. Having therefore received many letters from Clairvaux from various quarters, he will return with all haste; and, God willing, we believe that not long after the octave of the Assumption of blessed Mary you will see the man whom you long for, and rightly long for. Would that we knew how great and how inestimable a gift God has given us in the holy Father: a faithful advocate, a powerful protector, a good shepherd, full of grace and virtues before God and the whole world! Indeed, we learned by certain experiences that in particular places he conceals his powers through humility: when he departed, the sick were immediately healed, so that they might fare well without anyone magnifying him. Where necessity required it, however, [Col. 0413A] he preferred, as he himself confessed, to endure his own danger rather than fail to provide for their salvation.

7. In the church of Saint-Saturnin, where we were lodging, there was a Regular canon named John, highly skilled in medicine. He had lain ill for seven months, they said; from holy Easter onward he had been so weak that they expected nothing daily but his death. His lower legs had wasted away, so that they seemed no thicker than a child’s arms. In particular, the sinew of his right thigh had shriveled, so that from Easter onward he could only slightly straighten his knee. The miserable man languished half alive, daily carrying within himself the sentence of death; he was wholly unable even to rise for urination or evacuation. Because of the stench and his infirmity, he had finally been removed outside the monastery and placed in the borough, since the canons could not bear his presence.

He earnestly begged to be carried near the lord Abbot; six men carried him on a litter into a room next to our lodging. [Col. 0413B] There, visited by the lord Abbot, he confessed his sins to him and earnestly entreated him for deliverance and health. When the lord Abbot blessed him, he left the room, and we went out with him. As he walked, he was thinking and saying, like a faithful servant: “Behold, Lord, they seek signs, and otherwise we make no progress; how long will You dissemble?” Immediately the man sprang up and ran after us, so that scarcely had we entered the lodging when we saw him following us and walking—not, as he himself said, by his own strength, but by divine power. Then he went to the church, giving thanks to God; and the brethren sang with him, “We praise Thee, O God.” No one can know with what devotion he kissed the lord Abbot’s feet except one who saw it.

8. A boy of seven years, as was said, lay ill in his mother’s arms, she not knowing what his illness was. As he was returning after being blessed by the lord Abbot, he immediately vomited up a stone, which many also saw, and from that hour was well. In that same city Bernard gave sight by the sign of the cross to an elderly man who had lost the sight of one eye. He likewise gave sight to a boy blind in both eyes, and similarly to another blind person already older in age. There was [Col. 0413D] in the same city a certain woman who, feeling a sudden pain in her head, said, “I shall not eat until I come to the Man of God.” Afterwards, when her husband compelled her to eat, as soon as she tasted bread she was almost suffocated, her throat constricted, and possessed by a demon. For three days thereafter she could eat or drink nothing, until she was brought before the lord Abbot and took blessed bread and water from his hand. The lord Abbot then commanded that she spend the night near us in the chapel, wishing to come to her more privately without a crowd. During the night she began to cry out more violently, so that now the demon spoke, now the woman; and the tongue turned now to the left, [1195; Col. 0414A] now to the right, according as the speaker changed. The demon said, in the hearing of all who stood by, “I will not go out until the Abbot comes, until the little Abbot comes.” Meanwhile the lord Abbot, warned in a dream, came to her; and he left her wholly at peace, though he had found her in such torment. At daybreak he celebrated the solemnities of Mass, gave her holy Communion, and sent her home unharmed.

9. Of those whose hands were twisted to one side and fingers bent back to the other, he healed three at Toulouse and three on its borders. For while he was receiving an offering, a certain girl was brought to him; he made the sign over her hand, grasped her fingers, and opened them with complete ease. He did the same also for two others, except that, in the case of one whose hands were both contracted, he was embarrassed because bishops were present, and opened them only a little. He then entrusted her to a certain knight of the Temple who was present, that he might complete the work. He freed a fourth child from this infirmity at Dameyseria, in the sight of the lord bishop of Angoulême, who was astonished that, when Bernard made the sign over the hand and released it, it returned to a sound condition as though it were a cord, and the fingers began to open. At that same place and hour, he also made a deaf person hear and a mute person speak. He healed a fifth cripple at the castle called Green Leaf, where Satan’s seat is; and he was, unless I am mistaken, the boy of a most wicked heretic. He healed a sixth at the castle called Saint-Paul: they were among the servants of the lord legate whom a most severe fever had compelled to remain [Col. 0414C] in a foreign land, unless the heavenly medicine of blessed bread had come to their aid.

10. In the city of Albi there occurred an event which we rightly believe should be preferred to the other miracles. For the people of that city, more than all those around it, had been infected with heretical perversity, as we heard; so that, when they went out with asses and drums to meet the lord legate, who had arrived two days before us, and struck the signals to summon the people for the celebration of Mass, scarcely thirty assembled. On the third day the lord Abbot was received with great joy by the people. But he had heard such evil reports about them that he would not at all accept their devotion. On the following day, the feast of Saint Peter, so great a multitude gathered to hear the word of God that the large church could not contain them. Addressing them, the lord Abbot said: “I came to sow, but I found the field preoccupied by evil seed. Yet because the field is rational—for you are God’s husbandry—behold, I set before you both seeds, so that you may know what you ought to choose.” Beginning with the sacrament of the altar, he carefully explained point by point what the heretic preached and what the truth of faith was. Finally he asked what they chose. The whole people replied by beginning to abhor and detest heretical perversity, joyfully receiving the word of God and Catholic truth. “Repent, therefore,” he said, “all of you who have been defiled; return to the unity of the Church. And that we may know who repents and receives the word of life, raise your right hands to heaven as a sign of Catholic unity.” Thus, [Col. 0415A; 0416A] when all raised their right hands to heaven with rejoicing, he brought his address to an end. Let us also conclude the letter.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] The copy cited as note 120 adds: “At Saint-Antoine he healed a girl whose entire arm was withered.”]

Farewell.

[Col. 0415]

# BOOK SEVEN

Extracted from the book entitled *The Greater Cistercian Exordium*, distinctions 1, 2, 4, and 6.

1196 CHAPTER I. On the appearance of a deceased monk and the revelation made to Bernard concerning those of Clairvaux who would be saved.

[Col. 0415A]

1. After, by the grace liberally bestowed by God, the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth—that is, the Cistercian church—began to send forth its shoots, and after houses had already been founded at La Ferté and Pontigny, the house of Clairvaux was founded third, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115. The lord Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, of blessed memory, appointed our most blessed father Bernard its first abbot. Although the book of his *Life* treats more fully of his admirable manner of life, singular holiness, and special prerogative of signs and miracles, I nevertheless judge it fitting to record some matters omitted there, both in remembrance of so great a man and for the edification of readers, lest in this little book, fashioned concerning men of miracles, we should seem to pass over in silence that most splendid pillar [Col. 0415C] upon which the whole body of our Order rests.

2. It happened once at Clairvaux, while Mass was being celebrated in the community and the venerable Father was present, that after the Gospel had been read, water for washing the priest’s hands was lacking through negligence. While it was awaited somewhat too long, the community stood meanwhile with faces turned toward the East. As the holy Father stood in his stall between the steps of the presbytery, a monk who had died a few days before visibly appeared to him. Standing opposite him, he began to shake his head as if in rebuke. Seeing him, the servant of God recognized him and asked why he shook his head at him. The monk replied: “Oh, if you knew how many and what kind of companions you have in heaven, surely [Col. 0415D] you would guard yourselves against every negligence.” The Saint gladly heard this saying and answered: “Do you truly think that all the brethren in this monastery will be saved?” “Yes,” he said, “they will be saved. And not only they, but also all who have conducted themselves obediently and humbly in our Order will be saved.”

[Note: [Col. 0416D] Herbert attributes the same statement to Bernard in Book I, chapter 11.]

The pious Father then remembered a certain brother whom he often had to rebuke for negligence and hardness of heart and on whose account he was greatly grieved. He added, saying: [Col. 0416A] “Do you know anything certain concerning that brother’s salvation?” He answered: “The mercy of God will not fail him either.” Hearing this, the Man of God rejoiced greatly; and he observed the hard ways with his brethren all the more eagerly for the words of the Lord’s lips, the more certainly he held in his bosom the hope of eternal reward laid up for him.

## CHAPTER II. On a deceased brother delivered from the punishments of purgatory through prayers and offerings of Masses.

3. On one occasion a certain lay brother died at Clairvaux. While the brethren gathered and performed the office of commendation according to custom, an elderly monk, a man of great religious devotion, heard crowds of demons advancing in bands, crying out amid a great noisy tumult and saying: “Ah, good! Ah, now it is good! We have acquired for our allotted share one soul only from this evil valley.” When that same elder who had heard these things gave his limbs to sleep during the night’s rest, the dead brother appeared to him in a vision with a sad and mournful face, saying: “Because yesterday you heard the demons rejoicing over my punishments, come and see to what terrible torment I have been delivered by the just judgment of almighty God.” He led him to a certain pit of great breadth and dreadful depth and said: “Behold, I am frequently cast by the demons into this pit. Their cruelty is so great that, if a choice were given me, I would rather be immersed here a hundred times by human beings than once by demons.”

4. In the morning, when the aforesaid elder told the holy father Bernard what he had heard and seen—although Bernard himself had also learned these things through the Spirit—he groaned and said: “I know that, unless a grave cause existed, the demons would never have dared such presumption.” Therefore, entering the chapter of the brethren, he laid before them all the calamity of the dead brother. Then, exhorting each person’s conscience with wholesome instruction, he urged them to walk more cautiously in the way of holy religious life. He declared that the demons’ malice toward all Christians was great, but especially against those professing the monastic life. After this he earnestly urged them to aid the brother’s soul, set amid punishments, and exhorted them to appease the Lord’s anger by psalms, prayers, [Col. 0417A] and celebrations of Masses. Perhaps the merciful Father, moved by their prayers through the offering of the saving victim, might deign to defeat the tyrannical pride of the demons and deliver the brother’s soul from their wickedness.

When the brothers did this most devoutly, after a few days had passed the same deceased brother again appeared to the aforementioned elder, showing by the cheerfulness of his face that his condition had improved. When the old man asked how he was, he replied: “Thanks be to God, well.” Asked again how he had been delivered, he said: “Come and see.” Immediately he led him into the oratory of the same place, where priests stood at the individual altars, celebrating with utmost devotion the offering of the victim. “Behold,” he said, “these are the weapons of God’s grace by which I have been rescued; this is the power of God’s mercy, which remains invincible. This is that unique Victim which takes away the sins of the whole world. And truly I tell you that there is nothing able to resist these weapons of God’s grace, this power of God’s mercy, this saving Victim, except an unrepentant heart.” Upon waking, the elder rejoiced exceedingly at the deliverance of the brother’s soul. Explaining the form of this vision to the other brethren, he made them all the more devoted to the offering of the saving victim because they had deserved to experience more certainly its efficacy in the brother’s rescue.

## CHAPTER III. On a vision granted to blessed Bernard, which displayed to him the varying merits of those chanting in choir.

[Col. 0417C]

5. Once the holy Father attended the night vigils with the purity and devotion known to God alone and to himself which he habitually showed. As the slow modulation of the psalmody prolonged the vigil, the Lord opened his eyes. Looking, he saw individual angels standing beside individual monks, carefully recording on tablets, in the manner of scribes, what each monk chanted; they omitted not even the smallest syllable, however negligently uttered. But they wrote in different ways. Some wrote in gold, others in silver, some in ink, others even in water, while some wrote nothing at all. The Spirit who revealed these things also inspired his heart with an understanding of the differing modes of writing.

Those who wrote in gold signified the most ardent zeal in God’s service and an undivided attention of heart to what was being chanted. Those who wrote in silver represented a lesser ardor but nevertheless the pure devotion of the chanters. Those who wrote in ink indicated the habitual exercise of good will in psalmody of certain persons, albeit without great devotion. But those who wrote in water represented persons weighed down by drowsiness or sloth, or carried away from themselves by various thoughts: they seemed indeed to make some sound, but their hearts, drawn far away, did not agree with their voices. And—O wondrous mercy of God!—just as no evil will go unpunished, so no good, however small or however negligently performed, will go unrewarded.

But those who wrote nothing at all rebuked the lamentable hardness of heart in certain persons who, forgetful of their profession and unmindful of the fear of God, either willingly plunge themselves into deadly sleep, or else, though awake, keep their mouths closed and occupy themselves with vain and harmful thoughts, not through weakness but with deliberate intention. They do not fear to appear empty before the Lord, contrary to the command of the law. The holy Father, seeing these things and remembering the saying, “Are they not all ministering spirits sent forth to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14), rejoiced in the fervor of those making progress and, with a fatherly affection of compassion, pitied the lukewarmness of those who failed.

## CHAPTER IV. On singing divine hymns piously and devoutly, and how pleasing this is to angels.

[Col. 0418B]

6. Once solemn vigils were being celebrated, and the Man of God was present with the other brethren. While the hymn “We praise Thee, O God” was sung, he saw holy angels shining with great brightness and devout with marvelous cheerfulness of countenance. Moving through both choirs, now they stirred up one, now another; they attended the singers and stood as if rejoicing with them, striving by every means to ensure that the divine hymn should be sung with devotion. Therefore the holy man understood that this hymn was truly familiar to those angels, whom he saw taking such zealous pains that it might be sung by the brethren with fervent devotion to God’s honor. A certain spiritual brother was also granted sight, when that same hymn began, of a flame of great brilliance issuing from the mouth of the one beginning it and ascending upward.

## CHAPTER V. On the faintheartedness of brethren, raised to confidence in the divine mercy by a notable saying of blessed Bernard.

7. Once, when blessed Bernard was speaking the word of God to the brethren, he sharply reproved vices and struck terror of God’s dreadful judgment into their minds. In spirit he perceived that some who sat there were grievously troubled in their consciences and were almost falling into the abyss of despair. Then, all aflame with the spirit of brotherly love, and to the amazement of all present, he burst forth in these words: “Why are you troubled in your consciences, my brethren? Why do you regard the enormity and numberlessness of your crimes in such a manner as to forget the inexhaustible bowels of the Lord’s compassion? Truly I say to you: if Judas, that son of perdition who sold and betrayed the Lord, were sitting in this school of Christ and incorporated into this Order, he would obtain pardon through repentance.” On hearing so magnificent a word of consolation, not only those who had almost despaired because of their faintness of spirit, but all who were present, took breath again in hope of divine grace and glorified the Lord.

## CHAPTER VI. Of a certain monk who denied the reality of the sacrament of Christ’s Body and Blood, but was wonderfully brought to faith through Bernard’s care.

[Col. 0419A]

8. A certain monk of this holy Father, through the deceits of demons and the simplicity of his own understanding, had fallen into such poverty of heart that he declared that the bread and wine mixed with water set forth upon the altar could by no means be transubstantiated into the true Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore he disdained to receive the life-giving Sacraments, as though they would be of no benefit to him. At length the brethren noticed that he did not partake of the Sacraments of the altar, 1199 and he was privately summoned by his elders. Questioned, he did not deny the reason: he said that he placed no faith whatever in the Sacraments. When, despite their teaching and admonition, he would not yield or believe the testimonies of Holy Scripture brought forward, the matter was referred to the venerable Abbot. When he had been summoned and came, the holy Abbot refuted his unbelief according to the wisdom given him; but the monk replied: “By no assertions can I be induced to believe that the bread and wine set forth upon the altar are the true Body and Blood of Christ; and therefore I know that I shall descend into hell.”

> [Note: [Col. 0419D] See a not dissimilar occurrence in Herbert, book III, chapter 26.]

9. Hearing this, the Man of God, who was accustomed always to display a wonderful authority when matters were in straits, said: “What? Shall my monk descend into hell? Far be it! If you have no faith, I command you by the power of obedience: go, communicate in my faith.”

> [Note: [Col. 0419D] It was therefore an involuntary temptation; for otherwise Bernard praises the action of Malachy toward a certain [Col. 0420D] priest obstinate in a similar error, who at last, repenting of his error in his final illness, “confessed his guilt, was absolved, and asked for the Viaticum.”]

O tender Father! O truly wise physician of souls, teaching through the anointing of grace how he ought to remedy the temptations of the infirm in every case! He did not say, “Flee, heretic; go, condemned man; depart, lost one”; but confidently said, “Go, communicate in my faith,” firmly believing that his little son, whom the womb of holy desire was bringing to birth until Christ should be formed in him, would no more be estranged from the foundation of his faith than from the depths of his charity. Constrained therefore by the force of obedience, the monk approached the altar entirely without faith, as he thought; he communicated, and, immediately enlightened through the merit of the holy Father, received faith in the Sacraments. This faith he kept undefiled until the day of his death.

## CHAPTER VII. Of the crucified Christ embracing Bernard.

10. Lord Menard, abbot of Moris, a monastery neighboring Clairvaux, a religious man, related to his close companions a certain marvelous occurrence as though it concerned another, though we think it happened to himself. He spoke thus:

“A monk known to me once found the blessed Abbot Bernard alone in the church praying. As he lay prostrate before the altar, a certain cross with its Crucified One appeared to him, placed on the pavement before him; and this most blessed man was most devoutly adoring and kissing it. Then that very Majesty, separating His arms from the crossbeams, seemed to embrace and clasp to Himself that servant of God. The monk watched this for some time, transfixed in utter astonishment and, as it were, beside himself. At last, fearing that he might offend his holy Father if he saw him standing so near as an observer of his secrets, he silently withdrew, understanding and knowing, indeed, of that holy man that all his prayer and manner of life were truly beyond human measure.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Of a benefit or grace divinely obtained for an epileptic.

[Col. 0420B]

11. The holy Father once went out to visit his brethren harvesting in the field. But since he was ill and could not go on foot, he proceeded on a little ass. A certain monk who was then walking with him and driving the ass, having long suffered from the falling sickness, suddenly collapsed before him on the road and began to be grievously convulsed by that epilepsy. Seeing this, the holy man pitied him; and he prayed to the Lord for him, that this affliction might not henceforth seize him unawares.

Accordingly, from that time until the day of his death—for twenty years and more thereafter—there was granted him what he had not previously possessed, and what scarcely happens to other epileptics. Whenever he was about to fall from that illness, he sensed the attack itself for some period beforehand, 1200 so that he could suitably lie down in bed and continually avoid the injury of a sudden fall. Indeed, we believe that the holy Father, who obtained this gift for him from the Lord, could have obtained complete health for him, had he known it expedient for the salvation of his soul. But because this man was burdensome in character and exceedingly hard of heart—one to whom both the rod of correction and the staff of consolation always seemed necessary—it was mercifully granted him that, by foreknowing the danger of a sudden fall, he might continually escape it, yet not lack the goad of the health-giving illness.

## CHAPTER IX. Of a dying man who, at blessed Bernard’s command, postponed death.

12. A certain brother of Clairvaux, when he was at the point of death, was visited by blessed Bernard after Compline. Seeing that the man was near death and about to depart at any moment, he said to him: “You know, dearest brother, that our community is now weary from labor and must soon rise for Vigils. If, meanwhile, you should fall asleep and they had to interrupt their rest, they would be greatly troubled and would perform their very demanding vigil less solemnly. Therefore, that it may go well with you and that you may live eternally in the land of the living, which you are entering to possess, I command you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to wait for us until the hour of the divine office.”

The sick man replied, “Lord, I shall gladly do as you command, if only you assist my vow by your prayers.” The holy abbot then went silently to the dormitory; and he who was drawing almost his final breath did not die before the appointed time. As soon as the signal for Vigils began to be rung, the death-board too was struck, and he died. This occurred not only with this brother, but repeatedly with many others: at the nod and will of their most blessed Father their end was prolonged.

## CHAPTER X. Of a brother more concerned with material resources than brotherly charity, who died outside Clairvaux as a punishment.

13. The Man of God once heard that one of his spiritual sons, a good and religious man whom he had sent to Normandy, was suffering there from a desperate illness. He resolved to send for him and bring him back, so that this devout brother might die in his own little nest and not be deprived of the burial he desired. Yet one of his carnal brethren, named Guy, tried to oppose this plan; for, being one of Clairvaux’s stewards, he intended, I suppose, to spare expense and effort.

As he obstinately persisted in this advice, blessed Bernard said to him: “Do you care more for money or pack animals than for your brothers? Since you do not wish our brothers to rest with us in this valley, neither shall you yourself rest in it.” And so it happened. For this same Guy, though otherwise a good and religious man, was not brought to his end at Clairvaux, so that the Saint’s word might be fulfilled; rather, being overtaken by illness at Pontigny, he took to his bed there and, by God’s ordering, received there both the end of his life and the place of his burial.

## CHAPTER XI. Of Saint Bernard’s being spiritually present to his brethren at Clairvaux even while he was abroad.

[Col. 0421D]

14. When the venerable Father Bernard had spent three years in the city of Rome and in Italy, laboring to quiet the schism of Peter Leo—in which time, indeed, Christ the Lord greatly honored this His servant—he at last returned to Clairvaux. Immediately after prayer, he entered the chapter of the brethren. Since he was weary from the journey and could not speak long, he gave a brief address, but one full of consolation:

“Blessed be God, who has restored you, my most beloved brothers, to me, and restored me, whatever sort of father I may be, to you. And indeed, my little children, although during these three years I appeared to have been far removed from you, do not think that I was always absent. For know that in the meantime I returned to you three times, visiting this house and passing through its workshops; and I always departed gladdened and comforted, seeing your unanimity and your diligence in the purpose of your Order.”

15. Countless other things were said and done by this servant of God, in which it plainly appeared that he was endowed with prophetic grace: that he was often present in spirit where he seemed absent in body, and that, through the Lord’s revelation, he knew many hidden and even distant things which seemed likely to be unknown to him.

[Col. 0422B] These matters were reported to us by Lord Gerard, formerly abbot of Longpont, one of the elder monks of Clairvaux, who diligently endeavored to investigate the sayings and deeds of the holy Father. We also heard from his own account that, while this Saint of God was preaching the Word of God in a certain chapter of monks, two brethren present saw him suspended in the air above the bench on which he sat, raised about one foot from the ground.

## CHAPTER XII. Of the grace divinely granted to blessed Bernard by which, though absent, he knew his brethren’s needs.

16. This faithful and prudent steward of the Lord’s provision had at one time remained abroad longer than usual on affairs of the Church. For he was often compelled, though most unwillingly, at the command of the supreme Pontiff to go out in order to make peace, repair schism, and refute heresies. When the affairs for which he had gone out had been concluded, he returned to the monastery; and at the first opportunity he entered the novices’ cell, so that the new and tender little sons whom he nourished with milk, having been deprived for so long of the sweetness of his holy exhortation, might be refreshed all the more abundantly from the breasts of his consolation.

Wherever the holy Father went, he sowed the word of God upon all waters, and scarcely ever returned without the profit of spiritual gain. He filled the house of probation with a multitude of novices, [Col. 0422D] whose number sometimes reached one hundred, so that at the hours of the divine office, when the novices filled the choir, the monks had to stand outside, except for a few elders who supervised discipline.

> [Note: [Col. 0421] Geoffrey states above, book V, no. 20, that there were seven hundred monks at Clairvaux when Bernard died.]

17. Therefore, as we said, when he had entered the novices’ cell and by his gentle and edifying speech had made them all cheerful and more fervent in observing their holy purpose, he called one aside and said: “Dearest son, whence comes this sadness which so ruinously consumes the innermost recesses of your heart?”

The novice, hardly daring to say anything from shame, was addressed by him who knew how to show himself to all as a shepherd and not a hireling, the truly meek and humble of heart: “I know, dearest son, I know what is happening to you, and therefore I sympathize with you in a fatherly affection of compassion. During this long absence of mine, when I was compelled to lack the bodily presence of my brethren, always most dear to me, and when the Lord’s grace granted me to supply spiritually what I could not do bodily, I returned in spirit and went through each workshop, carefully examining how the brethren were faring. I also came to the novices’ cell. There, finding all rejoicing in the fear of God and girded for the labors of penitence, but seeing you alone wasting away in excessive sadness, I groaned. And when I wished by gentle encouragement to draw you to myself, you turned away from me and turned your face aside, weeping most bitterly, so that our cowl was soaked with your tears.”

Saying these things, the holy Father attacked this captive with spiritual admonitions, drove away his sorrow, and recalled him—already almost swallowed up by sadness—to the freedom of spiritual joy.

18. Truly God is wonderful in His saints; truly God is ineffable, and His works ineffable. For I do not know what I ought more to admire in this most blessed Father of ours: whether that he deserved to receive from the Lord such great and unprecedented grace, not once but repeatedly; or that, though receiving so excellent a grace, he did not keep it to himself, as his conscience bore witness, nor reveal it merely to a few intimate companions—something which itself would seem scarcely possible without danger. Rather, as we have related above, he openly declared in the public assembly, before the whole community of brethren, that this grace had been granted him; and yet his mind was so firmly established in the fear of God that he did not fear being assailed by the spirit of vanity.

It is also found in the *Gesta* of this blessed man that, while still living in the flesh, he appeared in spirit with a multitude of monks to a novice at Clairvaux who was gravely ill. He foretold that the novice would die on the fifth day; and on that fifth day, when the sun was already inclining to its setting, he visited him and commanded him to be confident and fear nothing, but to proceed straightway to the Lord Jesus Christ and offer Him the humble greeting of his family at Clairvaux. At these words the novice assented as best he could by inclining his head and moving his lips; closing his eyes, he fell asleep in the Lord that same hour.

> [Note: [Col. 0423] What these *Gesta* are has not yet been discovered by us. A similar account is related by Herbert, book II, chapter 40.]

## CHAPTER XIII. Of the calling of several Parisian clerics to the religious life.

19. On another day, when the Man of God Bernard had gone to Paris because circumstances required it [elsewhere: “was present at Paris”], he entered their schools at the request of the clerics, as was his custom. Setting before them the pattern of true philosophy, he earnestly urged them to despise the world and embrace voluntary poverty for Christ the Lord. When he had finished speaking and none of them converted, he went out sorrowful, because this had happened contrary to his hope and contrary to his usual experience. He came to the house of an archdeacon who had drawn him to his lodging, and withdrew into the oratory established there.

When he began to pray with vehement spirit, he was wholly dissolved into tears by the strongest compunction, so that the groans and sobs which he could not restrain were heard outside. Learning this, the said archdeacon began to ask Bernard’s companions the cause of so great a sorrow. One of them replied: a religious man, formerly abbot of Foigny, named Rainald, who was more privy to the secrets of the Servant of God—and from whose account we too learned these things. He said:

“This marvelous man, entirely aflame with charity and wholly absorbed in God, desires nothing else in the world except to bring the erring back to the way of truth and win their souls for Christ. Since he has now sown the word of life in the schools and has received no fruit of his word from the conduct of the clerics, he thinks God is angry with him, whose favor he has not perceived today in his preaching. Hence this storm of groaning; hence this outpouring of tears. Therefore I most confidently hope that the abundance of tomorrow’s recompense will repay today’s barrenness with great increase.”

> [Note: [Col. 0423] That sermon, *On Conversion*, addressed to clerics, is found in volume II.]

20. Therefore, when morning came, the outstanding preacher returned to the schools. At the Lord’s prompting he took the vessel of thought out into the deep and cast out the nets of Holy Scripture for a catch. When he had finished speaking, very many of those clerics gave themselves to the Lord through his hand. He did not delay to draw them, as it were, from the perils of the world and the waves of the sea, place them in hired conveyances, and bring them into the haven of salvation at Clairvaux.

At last, leaving the city with his company, he came as far as the village of Saint-Denis and spent the night there. Very early the next morning, when his brethren thought that he would set out by the direct road, 1203 he said: “We must all return to Paris, because some of ours are still there, whom we must bring away from there and join to this fold of the Lord, that there may be one flock and one Shepherd.”

As they began to enter the city, he saw three clerics coming from afar to meet him, and said to his companions: “The Lord has accomplished our errand; we shall now proceed on our way. Behold, these are the clerics for whom we came.” When they approached and learned that he was present, they rejoiced with great joy and said: “O most blessed Father, how welcome is your arrival! For we had resolved to seek you out and scarcely thought that we could catch you before you departed.” He replied: “And I knew it, beloved ones; therefore I hastened to meet you as you fled, with loaves. Let us go together, and by God’s grace I shall be the guide of your journey.”

Thus, joined to the others named above, they followed the holy man, clinging to him and serving in the spiritual warfare under the discipline of his instruction throughout all their lives.

## CHAPTER XIV. Of the wonderful gift of prophecy in Saint Bernard, and of his prophecies fulfilled.

[Col. 0425A]

21. Through the blessing of this holy father Bernard, certain of his novices put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. Speaking of them in the Spirit of God, the blessed man foretold that all of them would obtain the grace of spiritual rank and would receive the name and office of abbot. As the years followed and, at fitting times, the word of this prophecy was fulfilled in each of them, one of them, named Peter, whom the holy Abbot had sent to Sweden to the house of Nydala, lived for many years after Bernard’s death, even to old age—indeed, nearly to decrepitude—without receiving this gift of grace. For he was of a simpler nature and seemed less suited to administer so great an office. But what then? Could he, hidden at the farthest limits of the world or burdened by the infirmities of advanced age, escape the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, so that what that same Spirit had long before foretold concerning him through the mouth of His prophet Bernard should not be fulfilled?

22. Finally, after so great an interval of time, when what the holy Father had foretold concerning this man of dove-like simplicity had almost passed into oblivion, it happened that the brethren of a house of Nydala, situated on the island called Gotland, being without a shepherd, had recourse according to the general custom of the Order to their mother house, in order that through the foresight and care of the father abbot a worthy steward might be appointed for their house. And by the Lord’s will—without whose nod neither a leaf of a tree nor even a single sparrow falls to the ground—it pleased both the father abbot and the others present at the election to take the said old man into this charge. He trusted so much the more confidently in the mercy of God and the merits of his most holy Father as he humbly distrusted his own insufficiency.

When this had been done and the word formerly foretold by the Saint was recalled to memory, it was proclaimed everywhere. All who heard it marveled, saying that the promotion of so old and simple a man had been provided by divine dispensation for this great purpose: that among all the things which the Man of God had spoken by the spirit of prophecy, not even one iota or one stroke might seem to have been uttered in vain.

## CHAPTER XV. Of a thief freed from crucifixion by Saint Bernard, but thereafter religiously bound to the cross.

23. It happened once that this servant of God went to Count Theobald on certain business. 1204. As he approached the town where the Count then was, he met a large crowd of people who, by the Count’s order, were dragging a notorious and wicked thief to punishment. Seeing this, the most merciful Father took in his hand the rope by which the wretch was bound and said to his executioners: “Release this murderer to me, for I wish to hang him with my own hands.”

When the Count heard of the Man of God’s arrival, he immediately hurried out to meet him; for he had always loved and honored him with a remarkable devotion. Seeing the rope in Bernard’s hand, with which he was drawing the thief behind him, he was greatly horrified and said: “Alas, venerable Father, what did you mean to do? Why have you recalled this gallows-bird, condemned a thousand times over, from the gate of hell? Can you make him safe, when he has become wholly the devil? His correction is altogether hopeless; he will never be able to do good except by dying. Therefore, lord Father, let this man of perdition be lost, because the lives of many are endangered by his pestilent life.”

24. The holy Father replied: “I know, excellent sir, I know that this thief is most criminal and deserves the severity of every torment. Do not therefore suppose that I wish to leave such a sinner unpunished. Rather, I intend to hand him over to executioners and exact from him a fitting punishment, one which will be all the more fitting as it is longer. You had decreed that he should be finished by a short punishment and a momentary death; but I shall make him die by a prolonged torment and a death of the greatest duration. You would allow him, hung from the gallows, to remain dead on the gibbet for one or many days; I shall make him, crucified, live and hang continually in punishments for many years.”

Hearing this, the most Christian prince was silent and dared not further oppose the Saint’s words. Immediately the most kindly Father took off his own tunic and clothed his captive with it. Having cut off the hair of his head, he joined him to the Lord’s fold, making a lamb from a wolf and a convert from a thief.

> [Note: [Col. 0425D] From this Manrique reasonably infers, for the year 1146, chapter 3, that it was already customary at that time for novices to be clothed not in secular dress—as the Rule commands [Col. 0426D] and Bernard states in letter 1—but in religious garb: tunic and cowl, with tonsure added.]

Coming with Bernard to Clairvaux, he thereafter became obedient unto death, beautifully expressing in the constancy of his purpose the etymology of his name; for he was called Constantius. Thus, after surviving in the Order for thirty years, unless I am mistaken, and more, he passed to the Lord, who through the merits of our most blessed Father graciously deigned to rescue him from a double death, namely that of body and soul.

## CHAPTER XVI. With what reverence Saint Bernard was received at Milan.

25. We learned from Lord Rainald, whom we mentioned above, that when Bernard, the servant of God, once came to Milan to reconcile the schism of Peter Leo, he was received with such universal rejoicing that nearly the whole city rushed out for a league to meet him. Many indeed went out four or five miles. In short, they so delighted in him that, though they had not seen him before, as soon as he entered the city they seized him by unanimous agreement to make him archbishop rather than elected him.

When he refused, they were altogether ready to use force, had he not secretly escaped by flight. While he was seated in a very large house there, such a multitude of people surrounded him that no one could enter. Meanwhile, a citizen of that city, honorable in dress and appearance, earnestly desired by every means to approach the Man of God; finding no entrance at all, he thrust himself into the middle of the crowds, crawling on hands and feet and stepping over the shoulders of those seated, until he reached the person he desired. Seizing Bernard’s feet, he began with marvelous devotion to embrace and kiss them.

Rainald, mentioned above, who was sitting nearer, saw this and came to remove him, knowing that the holy man was greatly burdened by such 1205 veneration and service. But the man turned and said to him: “Let me be, I beg you; let me see and touch the man who is near to God and truly apostolic. For I tell you and testify in the Christian faith that I saw him among Christ’s Apostles.”

Hearing this, the monk marveled; and, wishing to know more fully, he wanted to ask him about the manner of this vision, but because of shame before those standing by he did not venture to do so. Nevertheless, he most certainly believed that the revelation had been great, because of the man’s exceedingly ardent feeling toward the Servant of God.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of the insolence of a certain heretic who insulted Bernard, wittily checked and confounded.

[Col. 0427C]

26. At one time, when the legate of the lord Pope and certain bishops had brought the holy Bernard of the Lord with them into the region of Toulouse to refute the heresy of the Manichaeans, the brethren prepared for him a mount better than usual, capable of enduring so long a journey. When he reached those regions accompanied by the bishops, a man named Henry, formerly a black monk but then a base apostate and leader of those heretics, learned of the Servant of God’s arrival. Fearing his presence, because he knew that he could not resist the wisdom and Spirit speaking in him, he hastened his flight, hid himself, and could nowhere be found at that time.

There too the Lord glorified His servant before all the people and the rulers of the land, daily performing great signs and wonders among the people through his hands. It is hard to believe how countless were the crowds that followed the apostolic man all day long, some asking instruction, others healing, and all a blessing from him.

One day, therefore, before an innumerable multitude, after he had amply warned them to preserve the Catholic faith and avoid the unclean fellowship of heretics, it happened that one of those heretics was present, apparently more powerful and more clever than the others. Seeing with bitter eye the veneration that the people gave to the Servant of God, he devised some means of obscuring the brightness of Bernard’s reputation and casting a stain upon his glory. When all that seemed necessary for the occasion had been accomplished, the Man of God had mounted his horse to depart. Then the said heretic, like a twisting serpent, came with raised head before the Man of God and cried out before everyone: “Lord Abbot, know that our master’s horse, which seems so wicked to you, is not as thick-necked and fat as this fine steed of yours.”

The meek and patient man at once answered him with tranquil face and mind: “Friend, I do not deny what you maintain. Yet you ought to know that this beast over which you insult me is a brute animal, one indeed of those which nature made bent downward and obedient to the belly. If it eats and grows fat according to its own pleasure, justice is not harmed thereby, nor is God offended; for the beast does what belongs to it. Therefore, at God’s judgment, neither I nor your master shall be charged concerning the necks of beasts; but each person shall be judged concerning his own neck. Now then, if you please, look at my neck and see whether it is thicker than your master’s neck, so that perhaps you may justly reproach me.”

Having said this, he took off his hood and, with his head uncovered down to the shoulders, showed his neck, which was long and slender. Though wasted away and thin of flesh, it was nevertheless, by heavenly gift, exceedingly beautiful and white, like the neck of a swan. All who were present, seeing it, rejoiced greatly, blessing the Lord, who had given His servant so ready and fitting an answer by which the mouth speaking iniquity was confounded and stopped.

> [Note: [Col. 0427D] To this may be referred what Otto of Freising writes concerning the cenobites of his time in book 7, chapter 35 of his *Chronicle*: “They wear next to the flesh tunics of the roughest kind, and over these other, wider garments—that is, cowls—with hoods. They differ, however, in this: some, to express contempt for the world, wear only this black garment; others, making no point of color or thickness, are accustomed to wear white, gray, or another color, provided only that it is humble and rough.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of a blind man who received sight through marvelous confidence and devotion toward the very footprints of the absent holy Father.

27. While the most reverend Father was still staying in that same region and, like one of the Apostles, was going about towns and cities, preaching the Gospel, healing every disease, and rebuking, convicting, and confuting the utterly shameful delusions of heretics, it happened that a certain blind man in that vicinity, having heard of the fame of the virtues and signs multiplied day by day through the Man of God’s hands, was encouraged by hope of recovering his health. He resolved to seek out that servant of God, in the hope that through the benefit of heavenly grace, abundantly bestowed through him upon wretched mortals, the darkness of blindness might be wiped away and sweet light restored to him also.

Hastening and anxiously asking where he might find the Saint of God, he heard that Bernard was standing amid a great multitude at a celebrated gathering, scattering the word of life. Stumbling as he went and running breathlessly, he arrived only to be struck by the sad report that the Man of God had already departed and gone elsewhere. Yet what was he to do? The desire to regain health compelled him to go farther, but the densest darkness besetting his eyes made him slow and less able to proceed. As he languished in great sadness through faintness of heart, suddenly inspired by divine grace and conceiving with his whole heart hope in the merits of the most blessed man, he said to those around him: “I beg you, by the mercy of God, lead me to the place where you know with certainty that the Man of God stood.”

When he at once obtained this through the goodwill of those present, he came to the place and prostrated his whole body upon the ground. With marvelous devotion he kissed the very dust in which the sacred footsteps of the Man of God had stood, earnestly imploring the Lord’s mercy through the merits of His servant. As he continued for some time and rubbed his eyes with that dust in full faith, suddenly, through the Lord’s mercy—who deigned even in this grace to reveal the holiness of His absent servant—he received the light of his eyes.

This event not only furnished a support to Catholics of orthodox faith, but also increased the stigma of confusion and reproach upon the vainglorious heretics. But who can adequately relate how firmly founded in humility, subdued in fear, and cautious in watchfulness this blessed man was amid every glory and honor with which he was revered by peoples, tribes, and tongues, wherever the business of the Church brought him? To say nothing of the nations of other regions illuminated by the purity of the Catholic faith, these very peoples of Gascony, whom the holy Father recalled from the jaws of profoundest heresy, as from the belly of hell, by the word of preaching and also by wondrous signs and miracles, honored him with such ardor of devotion that he sometimes yielded to their importunity and, seated in a chair, exposed himself to their wishes.

So great was the crowd of people rushing upon him to ask his blessing and kiss his sacred hands that, because his exceedingly tender and emaciated flesh could not bear the pressure and impact of so many frequent kissers, his holy hands and arms swelled like fists. From that by which others procured blessing for themselves through the power going forth from him, he himself was weakened and utterly bruised, suffering severe bodily pains. Blessed in all things be God, who in these last days deigned to raise up in the Cistercian Order a man of such perfect religious life and consummate righteousness, through whom the monastic Order might flourish anew in the ancient vigor of holy religion, and the Church of God, through the apostolic grace granted to him, might obtain very many benefits of divine mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX. Of a certain impious and blasphemous man raised from the dead by blessed Bernard.

28. At a time when the Saracens occupied the land of Jerusalem, blessed Bernard—whose soul the sword of the Christian desolation had pierced with singular bitterness—travelled everywhere, urging troops of the faithful, not only by words but also by signs and miracles, to avenge the Saviour’s wrong and to overthrow the unbelieving nation. It happened, when he came into Germany, that, leaving one day Freiburg, a notable town situated in the region of Breisgau, he was conducted, amid a great crowd going before and following, by a certain Henry, [Col. 0430B] a nobleman still young, to one of Henry’s residences, where he was to spend the night.

Now this Henry, having already received the sign of the cross, had resolved not to ride but to travel on foot until, having assembled the means for the journey, he should set out upon the proposed pilgrimage. Nevertheless, the holy Abbot ordered him to accompany him on horseback. Accordingly, mounting his horse, he immediately followed the Abbot. Seeing this, and envying it, a certain son of Belial, servant of this same Henry—a man who loved every kind of wickedness and disbelieved every good thing—began grievously to blaspheme the servant of God and to assail his master with such curses: “Go on, then, [Col. 0430C] and follow that devil; and may the devil himself seize you.”

Meanwhile two poor women came alongside, carrying between them a third woman, crippled and deprived of the use of her feet and certain other limbs. They wished to entreat the Man of God to relieve both the affliction of the sick woman and the hardship of her bearers by the remedy of the desired healing.

29. But Henry, seeing this and taking pity, said: “Lay the sick woman across the neck of my horse for me, and you hasten to the servant of the Lord and implore his help.” Yet the aforesaid servant, angered and indignant even at this charitable act of his master, reproached him still more violently, saying that he was taking the wretched woman to an enchanter, a sorcerer, and a corrupter of minds.

To him Henry said: “No; I am taking her so that, by the blessing of the Man of God, she may recover her health. And with fullest confidence in her cure I promise you that, if he does not heal her, I will give you the horse upon which I ride.” The man gladly and joyfully received these words; in complete disbelief of the miracle to be done, he both laughed and mocked—distrusting the cure no less than he rejoiced beforehand at gaining the horse.

But when the woman had been brought to the Saint of the Lord and had obtained from him the blessing she desired, she immediately rose up whole, no longer needing to be carried, as hitherto, by another’s assistance. At this sight the servant was astonished; and, driven by the onset of the evil spirit which he harboured in his breast, he hurried a little ahead, intending, when he turned to face the Man [Col. 0431A] of God, to hurl at him with all his might, in curses and insults, whatever more wicked or shameful thing Satan might inspire him to devise within. But the Lord’s vengeance immediately intervened: he fell backward upon his back, struck his neck, and expired.

Henry, suddenly struck with grief at his lamentable death, reported the mournful fall and end to the Abbot, begging him, after proceeding a little farther, to return to so sad a sight. Henry also said: “This has happened to him on your account, because he did not fear to be blasphemous and insulting toward you.” Bernard replied: “Alas! May the Lord not permit that anyone should die on my account.”

30. Returning, therefore, he applied himself to prayer, in which alone he trusted in every difficulty; and for the length of one *Our Father* he prayed silently over him. Then he immediately ordered those standing by to raise the man. When raised, since he was already dead, his head moved in a pitiable twisting motion, lacking the support of his neck. Again Bernard said: “Hold his head—hold it firmly.”

At last, approaching him and anointing and signing the injured places with his saliva, whose medicinal application he used very often, he said: “In the name of the Lord, arise.” And again: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, may God restore your spirit to you.”

The man, immediately receiving back his spirit, became a living soul—or rather, a soul restored to life—1208 while all who were present and had seen one plainly dead return to life marvelled for joy and raised voices and praises to heaven. Finally, questioned [Col. 0431C] by the same Saint of God as to how he would live and what he would do henceforth, he said: “Lord, I shall now live as you command and do whatever you prescribe, whatever you will.”

Asked by those present whether he had indeed been dead, he replied: “I was dead and had received the sentence of condemnation; and unless the holy Abbot had hurried to come, I was to be led to hell.” At the urging of some bystanders, he received the sign of the cross and set out for Jerusalem with the others. This Henry also dedicated himself to God and blessed Bernard on the same journey, and afterwards became Bernard’s monk at Clairvaux.

Since the writer had himself beheld this miracle with trustworthy eyes, and believed it to be very well known to the writers of the holy Father’s life, he grieved when he at last found that it had been passed over in silence; and, for the glory of God and of his Saint, he related it as he had witnessed it, so that every generation to come for ever and ever may hear and understand in how great glory that man ought to be held whom the Most High thus glorified.

## CHAPTER XX. On Alexander, canon and teacher of Cologne, wonderfully called to religious life through Saint Bernard

31. At Cologne Agrippina, the celebrated metropolis of Lower Germany, there was a master named Alexander, [Note: [Col. 0431] See concerning him above, book VI, chapter 1. The same account in Herbert, book II, chapter 23.] a canon and a most renowned teacher in that city. It happened that the servant of God, blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, entered Germany by command of Pope Eugenius, intending to preach the Jerusalem journey to Emperor Conrad and to the people of the land.

As he shone there with innumerable signs and miracles, the Emperor, seeing the great wonders which the Lord displayed through him, was pierced in heart and received the sign of the cross from Bernard’s hand, intending to go to Jerusalem. Nor did an innumerable multitude of people delay to do the same. Inflamed with an incredible ardour of faith, they eagerly tore away scraps and fringes from the garments of the servant of God, who was therefore frequently obliged to obtain new clothing; and whoever failed to obtain crosses made from his garments considered himself unfortunate.

Many noble and learned men also surrendered themselves to the Lord through Bernard’s hand. He led them to Clairvaux, where they became monks and thereafter brought forth great fruit for God in the Church of God. Among them was the above-mentioned nobleman Alexander. At that time he was living in the world, swollen with the pride of secular learning and adorned with the trappings of wealth and passing honour. Yet the conversion which he neither considered nor intended was accomplished in him through this wonderful ordering of God—who catches the wise in their own craftiness—as the following account will show.

32. For when the most blessed Father Bernard warned him about conversion, Alexander, puffed up with secular learning and wealth, replied that for the present he thought of and desired nothing less than taking the monastic habit. [Col. 0432C] That same night, after he had surrendered his limbs to sleep, the same man appeared to him in a vision, raising him from a bed on which he seemed to lie grievously ill and restoring him to health. Then he took the garment which he himself was wearing and clothed Alexander in it. Alexander, though he twice angrily cast the garment off his shoulders, was at length compelled on the third occasion to retain it when it was placed around his neck and fastened tightly to his body.

Then the holy Father gave him the staff he held in his hand, signifying the grace of a future office of leadership, and ordered him to depart. But when Alexander awoke, he could not yet be softened by such a revelation, but persisted in the same hardness of heart.

[Col. 0432D] 33. That same day, as the most blessed Abbot reclined at table, a fish called a perch was offered to him for refreshment. At the sight of it, the Man of God raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for a long time over the fish. Having blessed it, he sent it as an extra portion (*pitantia*) to the aforesaid Alexander. When Alexander began to taste it, at the first 1209 bite he deserved happily to experience in himself how great was the power of the servant of God’s prayer. For he was suddenly changed into another man, deeply contrite, and began to shed tears over the fish itself. He marvelled at himself, not knowing what had happened to him or why he was weeping.

At last, remembering the vision that he had seen on the preceding night, he understood that the Lord had anticipated him by His free mercy.
