Therefore, giving thanks from the depths of his heart for the heavenly calling, he immediately surrendered himself to the blessed servant of God. Bernard received him kindly; Alexander became a monk at Clairvaux and afterwards shepherd of Grand-Selve. He advanced so far in holiness of life that he later became abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux and universal Father of the whole Order.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] This is a notable passage for illustrating the dignity of the Abbot of Cîteaux. See letter 4, no. 3, and letter 5, no. 1, where he is called the “Commissioner”; compare letter 6, no. 1. The same abbot is likewise called by Herbert “universal Father of the Order,” below, no. 17.]

We have set down these things upon the faithful testimony of the same servant of God, Alexander, as we heard them from him.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the remarkable conversion of a concubinary priest, formerly a monk of Clairvaux

[Note: [Col. 0434D] Taken from the Barbellian manuscript of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Sens.]

34. A certain monk left Bernard’s monastery and discipline; casting aside his habit at the devil’s urging, he returned [Col. 0433B] to the world and undertook the charge of a parish. He was, indeed, a priest; and because sin is often punished by sin, the deserter from the Order fell into the vice of lust. He took a concubine to live with him, as is customary with many, and by her he begot children.

After many years, the Lord—who wills that none should perish—had mercy, and the holy Abbot passed through the village where this former monk lived. He turned aside to that man’s house for lodging. The former monk recognized him and received him with great reverence as though he were his own father; he ministered to him devoutly and abundantly supplied necessities both for Bernard and for his beasts of burden. Yet Bernard did not recognize him.

In the morning, when the holy Man, having said Matins, was ready to depart, he could not speak with the priest because the latter had risen for Matins and gone to church. Bernard said to the priest’s son: “Go; carry this message to your master.” The boy had been mute from birth. Obeying the command and feeling in himself the power of the one commanding, he ran to his father and expressed the holy Father’s words very clearly, saying: “The Abbot commands you this and this.”

When the father heard his son’s voice for the first time, he wept for joy and urged him to repeat the same words a second and a third time. He then asked what the Abbot had done to him. The boy replied: “He did nothing else to me; he merely said, ‘Go; tell your master these words.’”

Compunct at so manifest a miracle, the priest hastened to the holy Man and cast himself in tears at his feet. “Lord,” he said, “Father, I was your monk such and such a person; at such a time I left such-and-such a monastery. Therefore I beg your Paternity to permit me to return with you to the monastery, because God has visited my heart in your coming.”

The Saint replied: “Wait for me here, and, when I have completed my business, I shall return quickly and take you with me.” Fearing the death that he had not feared before, the man answered: “Lord, I fear that in the meantime I may die.” Bernard replied: “Know this for certain: if you die in such a state and purpose, you will be found a monk before [Col. 0434A] God.”

He departed; and, hearing that the man had recently died and been buried, he ordered the grave opened. When people asked what he meant to do, he replied: “I wish to see whether a monk or a cleric lies in the grave.” They said: “We buried him as a cleric, wearing secular clothing.” When the earth was removed, he appeared before all, not in the garment in which he had been buried, but with the tonsure and habit of a monk; and God was glorified by all.

1210 ## CHAPTER XXII. On the calling of Arnulf, a nobleman in Flanders, and the penance imposed on him by blessed Bernard

35. When the most reverend Father Bernard once entered the province of Flanders and cast God’s nets in every direction for the catching of souls, drawing many noble and learned men from the waves of the world to the shore of conversion, a distinguished man named Arnulf of Majorca, exceedingly rich and pleasure-loving, privately surrendered himself into Bernard’s hands. They jointly resolved to keep the matter secret because of certain worldly impediments, until the final day on which Arnulf would depart from his land and kindred.

For he was the head of a large household, surrounded by children and brothers and entangled in such great wealth that he could not break free without serious loss and scandal to his dependants, unless he first arranged his household wisely and cautiously. Meanwhile, while this silence was maintained and the reason for this secret undertaking was known to these two alone in the world, the word of the Lord came to a certain rustic cattle-herd while he was driving oxen to the plough, saying: “Go; tell Arnulf of Majorca that he is to take you with him to Clairvaux, where he will shortly go for conversion; and you are to be converted with him.”

The man heard the voice but saw no one. After hearing it, the poor man began to pray more attentively, that, if the message had been from the Lord, He would again disclose it to his ear. And the voice spoke to him a second time, repeating the same words. Having thus received the oracle a second time, he came to the aforesaid man and said: “My lord, I have a word for you.” When he had been led aside, he fell at Arnulf’s knees and said: “I beseech you through Christ our Lord to take me to your Clairvaux, that I may save my soul with you; and, if you wish to know, the gracious and merciful Lord has deigned, for the sake of my salvation, to reveal your secret to me.”

36. Hearing these words, the noble householder marvelled and rejoiced greatly. He accepted the man and took him with him; afterwards he had him as the inseparable companion both of his journey and his conversion; and, as we believe, he was to have him as a partner in eternal reward. When he had finished the affairs for which he had delayed, Arnulf came to Clairvaux, as lowly in humility [Col. 0435A] as he was exalted in abundance of riches. He bestowed much of his property upon that monastery and also gave gifts to several other monasteries.

Saint Bernard, greatly rejoicing in his conversion, pronounced this judgment about him before the assembly of brothers: “Christ ought to be glorified no less for the conversion of Brother Arnulf than for the raising of Lazarus, dead four days; for, buried and shut up amid such luxuries, he lay as though in a tomb and, though alive, was as one dead.”

When Arnulf confessed with groaning and many tears all the sins he had incurred in the world, blessed Bernard, observing the exceedingly bitter contrition of his heart and his ready willingness for every good work, enjoined him to say the Lord’s Prayer three [Col. 0435B] times and thereafter to persevere in his purpose until death.

[Note: [Col. 0435D] This action appears to conflict with Peter Damian’s *Opusculum* 13, where he reproves certain heads of monasteries “because, for any who come from the world, even if they have fallen grievously, they impose no penance other than that they observe the common rule of the monastery.” This may indeed be true of monasteries of more relaxed discipline, but not of stricter discipline, such as that at Clairvaux—especially where the convert’s mind is deeply affected by penitential feeling. See volume 2 of the *Analecta*, p. 346 ff.]

Hearing this, Arnulf answered sadly: “Please, most blessed Father, do not mock your servant.” Bernard said: “In what respect am I mocking you?” Arnulf replied: “Fasts of seven years, or even ten, would not suffice for me, even if I humbled myself in sackcloth and ashes; yet you command me to say the Lord’s Prayer three times and to persevere in the Order?”

The Saint answered: “Then do you know better than I what you ought to do in order to be saved? Or does it perhaps seem a small matter to you to keep the Order and persevere in it until death?” Arnulf replied: “May such wicked presumption be far from my soul. But for God’s sake I beg you: do not spare me now, so that you may spare me more fully in the 1211 future; [Col. 0435C] impose upon me now such a penance that after the death of the flesh I may reach rest without punishment.”

The blessed Father said to him: “Do as I have said, and I assure you that, once the burden of the body is laid aside, you will immediately fly to God without suffering.” Strengthened greatly by this answer, as though it had been divinely given, Arnulf thereafter could not in any degree be delayed in the course of his desire, by which he was wholly pressing on toward God, whether by any violence of temptations or by any trouble of illness.

37. He was exceedingly careful and reverent concerning the observances of the Order and the guarding of the heart; I do not recall ever having seen anyone so diligent in cleansing his own conscience. All marvelled—especially those who heard his confessions—at the daily persistence, or rather importunity, with which he did not permit them to rest, just as he himself could not rest from confessing, lamenting, and sometimes weeping over an idle word or gesture, if one ever, though rarely, slipped from him. Indeed, even over some vain and slight thought, which other people—apart from a few perfect persons—usually make light of, he judged himself with the most scrupulous severity and accused himself as though of a crime.

But because it is truly written, “Whom the Lord loves he corrects; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6), this venerable man was never without the correction of fatherly mercy, which always cut away the vices of the flesh in him and caused the virtues of the soul to spring up and bear fruit. For many years, until his death, he was scourged by serious and long-lasting ailments. He bore them all not only with patience but even gloried in them as in every kind of wealth.

It happened one time, while he was altogether crushed and weakened, that he could not stand bent over without severe pain. Yet he never omitted, for this reason, to bow deeply and devoutly in reverence to the divine Majesty at every singing of “Glory.” While the evening synaxis was celebrated in church, he stood at the back of the choir beside a monk who was likewise a most holy man. Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared there in the form of a very beautiful young monk, clothed in a cowl whiter than snow; Arnulf himself, however, did not see him.

Whenever Arnulf bowed devoutly at the “Glory” of the psalm, as was customary, the angel of the Lord stood before him and supported the supplicant’s head with his hands placed beneath it. When the aforesaid monk, standing beside Brother Arnulf, saw him and recognized from the splendour of his face and his clothing that he was an angel, he rejoiced greatly at the angelic vision. He approached to seize him and embrace him devoutly. But when he stretched out his hands to hold and clasp him, the angel suddenly vanished and withdrew [Col. 0436C] from him; then immediately appearing again, he stood in another place. Seeing him, the monk ran to him again and similarly tried to seize him. But the angel at once vanished and immediately reappeared elsewhere, so that the man’s attempt was frustrated. When this had occurred many times, the angel finally disappeared altogether; though he had offered himself to be seen, he did not at all allow himself to be held.

38. Arnulf, God’s athlete, sometimes suffered pains in his internal organs, by which he was frequently afflicted exceedingly. The illness was so severe that, as his vital breath failed, he was pressed almost to death. After lying for some time speechless and insensible, his life was despaired of, and for this reason he was anointed with the oil [Col. 0436D] of the sick. But as soon as he could breathe, he burst out in a voice of confession and praise: “All that you have said, Lord Jesus, is true.”

When he repeated this many times, those present wondered and asked how he was or why he was saying these things. He made no other response except that all that God had spoken was true. Some said that the bitterness of his pain had disordered his brain, and that he was speaking as though beside himself. To them he replied: “It is not so, brothers; but with sound head and sober mind I say that all that the Lord Jesus has spoken is true.”

They said: “We too confess that this is true; but why do you mention these things now?” He replied: “The Lord says in the Gospel that if anyone renounces the affections of parents and the riches of the world for love of Him, he shall receive a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the age to come (Matthew 19:29). I therefore experience the force of this 1212 saying in the present, and already receive my hundredfold now in this life. For the immense bitterness of this pain is so sweet to me because of the hope of divine mercy that is laid up for me in it, that I would not wish to have lacked this very pain in exchange for the world’s substance multiplied a hundredfold, which I left behind.

“If I, a sinner and unworthy man, thus confess and rejoice so greatly even in my distresses, how, we suppose, do holy and perfect men dance and exult in their consolations? For spiritual joy, which is now in hope, truly surpasses a hundred thousand times secular joy, which now exists in possession. But if anyone leaves the world and comes to conversion without deserving to receive this hundredfold, it is surely clear that he has not yet left all things perfectly, but retains with himself something from his own will, which is an evil possession.”

As he spoke thus, all marvelled that such a judgment should be uttered by a layman and an unlettered man. Yet it was plainly to be understood that the Holy Spirit, who permitted him to be grievously scourged in body, sweetly anointed him inwardly in soul; and that most holy anointing, when it touches a person, teaches concerning all things that are necessary.

This holy man, therefore, having now received double from the Lord’s hand for all his sins, was finally tested by the long martyrdom of suffering, as gold in the furnace, and fell asleep in the Lord in the most peaceful repose. We most confidently believe concerning him that, according to blessed Bernard’s judgment, as soon as he departed from the body, he came to God without punishment.

What, then, was ever lacking to this poor man of Christ on the day of his struggle? Trusting in the Lord according to the prophet, he changed the strength of the flesh into the vigour of the spirit, considering not what the flesh was able to do, but what the Order and Rule commanded. He placed as a seal upon his heart the “word fulfilled and shortened” which he had received from the holy Father: namely, that he should keep the Order in satisfaction for all his sins.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On a certain lay monk under Bernard’s discipline, who eagerly aspired to the perfection of virtues

39. “Let not the wise man,” says the Lord through the prophet, “glory in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord” (Jeremiah 9:23–24). Those who were trained under our blessed Father Bernard at Clairvaux in the disciplines of heavenly philosophy followed this pattern of divine knowledge more perfectly: not only many learned men trained in the mysteries of the sacred law, [Col. 0438A] but also very many laymen and unlettered men.

Though these did not attain the structure of human learning through which they might strive toward the summit of perfection, they nevertheless possessed illuminating grace and the life-giving Spirit, who taught them incomparably more effectively than secular knowledge concerning everything necessary. A certain lay monk of this sort, taught not by the letter but by the Spirit, was fervent in the work of God and no sluggish seeker after the better gifts. Under the teaching of the Holy Spirit he had learned not to think highly of himself, but to humble himself in all things; he carefully examined, with humility as his guide, the practices of sacred religion in the conduct of his fellow monks, holding them in great and most exalted esteem. But he entirely despised his own virtues, in which he was not moderately strong, by comparison with theirs.

Thus it came about that through the eminence of holy humility he surpassed those to whom perhaps he was not inferior in other virtues. For, what is very rare in the human race, he continually attended—not enviously, but as a devout inquirer—to what he himself lacked or to the virtues in which others flourished.

40. It happened that, while so disposed, he was one time present at the brethren’s solemn vigils. Then, having driven away deadly negligence or sleepiness, he took up the customary weapons which he knew to be most effective for defeating the enemy. He began to set his sins before himself and strictly examine his daily negligences; to accuse himself as wretched, guilty, and sinful before the eyes of the supreme Majesty; and then, as was his custom, to extol and pronounce blessed the life and conduct of his brothers.

1213 Moreover, bringing humbly into the secret chamber of his heart one brother whom he had more than once observed to surpass many others in the grace of virtues, he scrutinized with meticulous religious investigation that servant of God’s humility, charity, patience, continence, and the other gifts of spiritual grace that he found in him. In comparison with that brother he counted himself nothing but dust and ashes.

At length, unable to bear the ardour of holy humility that he had conceived in so lofty a contemplation, he could scarcely wait until early dawn, the regular time at which speaking was permitted. He summoned the most reverend Father Bernard into the parlour by a signal, asked pardon, and, enveloped in sadness, revealed the inward pain of his heart. When asked what troubled him, he said: “Woe to me, a miserable sinner, altogether empty of every good thing! This night I counted in that certain brother of ours thirty virtues, all of which he possesses, and I, a beggar, have not been able to discover in myself even the last or least of them. Therefore, lord Father, I beg you to intercede for me with the Lord, that through your holy merits and prayers I may deserve to obtain the works of virtues which, because of my sins, I have not until now been able to possess.”

[Note: [Col. 0437D] Sermon 36 on Various Subjects, no. 2.]

[Col. 0439A] 41. Hearing the disciple’s profound humility, the spiritual master—who knew his religious excellence very well, although the brother himself, distinguished by it, did not know that he possessed it because of a happy ignorance—rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. He desired and wished that all entrusted to him might always advance in virtues in such a way that, through this devout consideration of their own weakness, they might in a sense not know that they were advancing.

How greatly he regarded this praise of such humility as worthy of admiration became more evident from the fact that, in sermons delivered before the assembly of brothers, he repeatedly mentioned this same brother with fitting praise. He maintained that perhaps none of all the virtues which this true monk had enumerated in the simplicity of his heart was of such excellence as the devout humility of the observer, who neither saw nor noticed the more negligent and weaker men placed beside him, but held before his eyes with steadfast attention only those whom he knew to be distinguished in life and conduct, so that by comparison with them his own life might become vile in his own eyes.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the wonderful gift of prophetic vision, by which he knew the secrets of others, even when absent

42. The most holy feast of the Assumption, if I remember correctly, of the undefiled and immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God, was approaching; and the brethren of Clairvaux’s granges were hastening to the abbey out of reverence for so great a day. But at one of the nearer granges there was a religious lay brother who feared God. Although, because of his simplicity, he could not grasp the more perfect elements of sacred religion, he was nevertheless a man of good will and devotion, and venerated our Lady, the most gracious Mother of God, with sincere affection.

When the grange-master arranged who should go to the abbey and who should remain at home to keep watch, the care of guarding the sheep was assigned to this brother among those who were to stay behind. Though he bore this assignment most unwillingly, because he hoped and greatly desired to be present at the divine hymns and spiritual songs which he knew would be devoutly performed by that holy community in honour of the Queen of Heaven, he nevertheless dared not object and most obediently complied with the command.

Thus it came about that the holy devotion which he had conceived in mind, and which he feared to lose through the disturbance of the earthly work imposed by obedience, became more fervent: while obedience rewarded his ready will, that devotion expanded ever more within his heart like a sparkling, blazing fire.

43. Therefore, on the night of the most sacred feast, while he anxiously kept watch over his flock resting in the pasture, the sound of the Matins bell, which summoned the brothers in the monastery to offer the divine praises and which could be heard at a distance because of the silence of the night, struck his ears. Then his heart grew warm within him, 1214 and in his meditation a fire was kindled. He considered the gathering of that holy multitude, and likewise the fervour and devotion with which they would, with sincere affection, jointly render hymns of heavenly harmony to the most gracious Mother of Mercy; and how each one individually, in his own private place, would implore the protection of that blessed Virgin with prayers and sighs.

He immediately rose and, desiring according to his measure to participate in so great a devotion, stood facing the quarter of heaven in which the monastery lay, with face and mind intently directed toward it. Then, having performed as devoutly as he could the customary prayers appointed for lay brothers in place of Matins, he searched earnestly in the poor little treasury of his heart for some prayer or praise which he might offer to our Lady, the holy Theotokos, and by which he might in some manner compensate for the brethren’s prolonged and greatly extended vigils.

He found that he knew nothing besides the salutation of that gracious Lady which he had somehow learned. Taking it, therefore, as the “word fulfilled and shortened,” in which the fullness of all devotion could be found, and lifting his eyes to heaven, he added genuflections to genuflections, sighs to sighs, and salutations to salutations; and in this occupation he passed the remainder of the night and part of the dawn without weariness.

[Note: [Col. 0439D] That is, genuflections.]

For divine grace cooperated—the grace which had kindled such fervour in the heart of its poor servant. Monotony, the mother of weariness and stepmother of devotion, in a marvellous and contrary manner drove away weariness and sharpened devotion; for those most sweet words, sweeter than all honey, spoken from a simple heart and repeated ever more frequently, more swiftly obtained for the praying and sighing man the favour and grace of the universal Lady.

44. Finally, the Lord deigned to reveal by the Spirit to the most reverend Abbot Bernard that he had not laboured fruitlessly in his groaning, nor sought mercy in vain from the Mother of mercy. After the divine hymns had been completed, and the sacred mysteries in honour of the most exalted Mother of God and Virgin Mary had been most devoutly celebrated by the individual priests, he addressed the assembled brethren, in order to commend the distinction of so great a solemnity. Inflamed mightily by the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0440D], he said among other things:

> “Indeed, my most beloved brethren, it is not lawful to doubt that this night you have offered to the Lord Jesus Christ, the true King, and likewise to our special patroness, the glorious Virgin, His Mother, a holy sacrifice of devotion, pleasing and acceptable to them. Therefore you ought to hold with most certain faith that the fruit of your labour, the eternal reward, has been laid up for you with the Lord, and that that same most gracious Protectress of ours is reserved for you. Yet I wish you to know that one of the least and simplest of our lay brethren, whom obedience compelled this night to celebrate, beneath the open sky in these mountains and woods, the joys of so great a feast, has rendered to our Lady a service of Matins so joyful, so devout, so festal [Col. 0441A], that none of us, however elevated his contemplation or intense his devotion, could be preferred to his devotion—a devotion produced not by the lofty sublimity of contemplation, but by the lowliness of holy simplicity.”

When they heard this, all were amazed. The lay brethren in particular were not merely amazed but rejoiced and were greatly edified, since obedience often drew them away to various tasks on feast days as well as private days. They knew with complete certainty that, just as the enclosure of the cloister and the walls of the church do not make holy one who neglects the fear of the Lord, so the tasks which obedience imposes because of earthly necessity cannot hinder one who lifts pure hands in prayer [Col. 0441B] and desires to serve the Lord with a pure conscience.

## CHAPTER XXV. The conversion of a monk who apostasized for the third time, obtained through the admonitions and prayers of the holy Father Bernard; his fatherly chastisement; and his blessed death

45. A certain lay brother, having through his own instability left the house of Clairvaux for the third time and been received back for the third time, was at last pierced by the salutary admonitions and holy prayers of Blessed Bernard, the abbot. He began with all the inmost fibres of his heart to dread the precipice of his apostasy, in which he had already been gravely endangered three times [p. 1215]; and he earnestly sought what penance or satisfaction he might offer to the Lord for so enormous a guilt.

And, by the Lord’s inspiration, he thought and understood [Col. 0441C] that, for meriting forgiveness of sins and obtaining the grace of virtues, nothing is more effective, nothing more acceptable in the sight of the Lord, than the sacrifice of a contrite heart and a humbled spirit. This alone is able to do violence to the kingdom of heaven, and is accustomed by unutterable groanings to bend the dreadful severity of divine justice. Taking up these weapons of piety, therefore, and setting himself against himself, he first endeavoured, as far as he could, to observe all the observances of the Order without evasive negligence; moreover, he was diligent in washing away his past sins by daily prayers and lamentations. Thus he furnished a wholly salutary example, instructing those who stood, lest they fall, and those who had fallen, that they might rise.

46. But by the Lord’s ordering—He who is accustomed to apply stronger remedies to stronger sins, and who in His ineffable mercy sometimes transforms vessels of dishonour into vessels of honour and grace—decay entered the bones of the aforesaid brother. He was struck about the thighs with a most grievous ulcer, a cancerous abscess; and as the affliction increased day by day, he wasted entirely away, so that, the flesh around the ulcer being eaten away on every side, the bare bones lay exposed and the wounds swarmed with worms [Col. 0441D].

Imprisoned in his bed for many years and humbly subject to the scourges of divine correction, he endured almost as many deaths as the hours during which he lived. His suffering soul thus endured pitiable pain and anguish at the sight of his own decaying body [Col. 0442A]; and his attendants likewise suffered immense distress of heart because of the horror and stench continuously exhaled by the festering ulcer. Yet an abundant recompense before God was laid up for both parties for this labour and patience. The sick brother, meanwhile, made it his care always to give thanks for his pains and afflictions, believing in his heart and confessing with his mouth that what he received was still far less than his deserts.

47. When at last the dross of sin had been wholly smelted out in him, so that, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “when the rust is removed from silver, a most pure vessel comes forth” (Prov. 25:4), that blessed soul was finally drawn out from the furnace of purgation. Like silver tested by fire, clean and shining, it was transferred with the other vessels of mercy to the palace of the supreme King.

But before it was drawn out from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, he deserved in this life, for the consolation of all who truly repent, to taste beforehand the fruit of his labour and patience, and to sample some ineffable thing of that heavenly sweetness which he was soon to be admitted to enjoy without end. Having tasted it, as though intoxicated with heavenly new wine, he immediately burst into a jubilation of heavenly praise. With a radiant face, though unlearned and never having learned either to sing or read, he began to sing, with the sweetest melody, certain new and most delightful hymns and tunes from the songs of Zion [Col. 0442B].

48. When this sound was heard, a crowd of brethren gathered to see, with great wonder, a man oppressed by so many miseries and calamities, at the very approach of death singing and dancing triumphantly, and in some manner saying: “Where is thy victory, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:55.) “Behold, I, a great sinner and a poor little man, because I have patiently borne in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus for His name, do not fear you—shadowy phantom, mother of sorrow, destroyer of joy, and ruiner of life—but rather despise you. For I know that you have been swallowed up and utterly annihilated in the victory of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Thus our precentor, chanting melodies and in some fashion anticipating the Alleluia that is constantly sung in the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem, prophetically showed, while still placed in corruptible flesh [Col. 0442C–D], what he would do after the death of the flesh. So, rejoicing and praising, amid a voice of exultation and thanksgiving, he breathed forth that blessed soul. Blessed Bernard, gladdened by his happy end, delivered a most devout address to the brethren in chapter, commending in him the worthy fruit of repentance and setting his admirable patience before all as an example.

1216

## CHAPTER XXVI. Saint Bernard rebukes—or rather tests—the assurance or confidence of a dying man

49. A certain lay brother among the brethren of Clairvaux, innocent in life and honourable in conduct, after having been seriously ill for some time, finally came to his end. Blessed Bernard entered to visit him and, strengthening him, said:

> “Take heart, son, for you are now about to pass from death to life, from temporal labour to everlasting rest.”

But he replied with great confidence:

> “Why should I not go to my Lord and Creator? Truly I trust, and, so far as I dare presume upon the mercy of my Lord Jesus Christ, I am certain that I shall soon see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

Blessed Bernard, however, being a wise physician and watchful shepherd, feared lest in this unlearned man such confident speech proceeded more from rash presumption than from purity of conscience. He said: “Seal your heart, brother; seal your heart. What is this that you have said? How could so bold a presumption steal upon you? Why, you are that poor and wretched man who, when you possessed little or almost nothing in the world, fled to us perhaps more under the compulsion of necessity than from fear of God, at last gaining admission through many prayers. For God’s sake we received a poor man, and made you equal in food, clothing, and other comforts to the wise and noble men who are with us; and you became as one of them [Col. 0443A–B]. What then have you rendered to the Lord for all these things? And behold, it does not suffice for your ingratitude that you have freely received so many benefits from the hand of the Lord, unless you also claim His kingdom for yourself by hereditary right—a kingdom which no king or prince has ever been able to purchase, however great the masses of gold and silver at his disposal.”

50. To this he replied with a gentle expression and tranquil mind:

> “Well, dearest Father, you have indeed spoken well, and all that you have said is true. Yet, if you command it, I will speak to you, my lord and father, and briefly disclose whence such an occasion of—not presumption, but, as I hope, devotion—could arise in me, poor and wretched as I am. For if that teaching of yours is true which you have often impressed upon us—namely, that the kingdom of God is possessed neither by nobility of birth nor by earthly riches, but is acquired by the virtue of obedience alone—I have kept this single saying within myself by diligent recollection, as a word abbreviated by the Lord. I have placed it as a seal upon my heart [Col. 0443C–D], by meditating upon it continually, and upon my arm, by working diligently. Ask, if you please, all the masters and companions whom you commanded me to obey and serve, whether I was ever disobedient to any of them, or whether I ever grieved any of our brethren, by word, sign, or any other means, so far as lay in my power. If, then, I have laboured to obey all in Christ, to serve all, and through God’s grace to love all, who can prevent me from placing confidence in His mercy?”

51. When the Blessed Father received such an answer from an unlearned man, he rejoiced greatly and said:

> “Truly, dearest son, you are blessed, for flesh and blood have not revealed this wisdom to you [Col. 0444A], but the heavenly Father Himself has taught you; He Himself has set your soul toward life and led you by the straightest path to your homeland. Go, then, in confidence, for the gate of life has been opened to you.”

After the brother had died and the funeral rites had been performed, the venerable Father delivered in chapter an eloquent discourse, marked by his characteristic devotion and eloquence, upon the brother’s conduct and death. He wonderfully kindled all to love obedience by his example. For he was deeply moved by that answer, and rejoiced more for him over the virtue of obedience and the purity of his soul than if he had seen him resplendent with signs and miracles.

1217

## CHAPTER XXVII. The community of brethren sent to Sweden by Saint Bernard; how he promised one of them that he would die and be buried at Clairvaux

52. After that great eagle of great wings and many feathers—the great Father Bernard, great in merits, lofty on the wings of holy contemplation, adorned with the variety of virtues—had planted the marrow of the cedar, that is, the perfection of religion which he had received from the summit of Lebanon, that is, from the height of divine grace, in the solitude of the Valley of Wormwood, so that the same valley might through the bitterness of repentance be changed into Clairvaux, religion itself began to be transplanted over many waters: that is, to bend to the cultivation of true godliness the proud and swelling wills of various nations, like blue whirlpools of waters [Col. 0444B–C].

The same venerable Father, desiring to bear fruit among the peoples of the northern regions as among the other nations, sent a community of brethren to those parts at the request of the devout Queen of Sweden. The monks and lay brethren appointed for this purpose, to impart a pattern of religious life and discipline to rude and untamed people, were overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. With all the prayers they could make, they pleaded that they might not be sent, deprived of the presence of so great a Father, into foreign and barbarous lands. The holy abbot replied:

> “What is this, my most beloved brethren, that you are doing? Why do you afflict my soul with irrational tears and prayers? Or do I follow in this matter my own will rather than the will of God, to whom we must all obey?”

Before him lay vestments, sacred vessels, and the other implements pertaining to the ministry of divine worship, which the brethren about to be sent were to carry with them. Wishing, therefore, to assure them that this command had gone forth from the Lord, he raised a basin appointed for receiving water poured over the priest’s hands. Pressing his finger into its bottom, he said: “Behold, this shall be the sign to you that the Spirit of the Lord has sent you.”

In a wondrous manner, the hardness and inflexibility of the metal seemed to yield to the softness of his finger, so that the size of the holy joint can still plainly be discerned to this day. As much as the metal yielded inwardly, so much does it appear to project outward beyond its even surface. In testimony of so great a miracle, that same basin is preserved with the highest reverence in the sacristy of the house which the holy Father then established [Col. 0444D–0445A].

When the brethren saw that the manifest presence of divine grace was with them, they restrained the goads of devouring grief and rejoiced. Though they might go to most remote nations, hidden in the furthest region of the northern winter, not without a certain horror of spirit, they nevertheless confidently trusted that the same grace of God, through the merits and prayers of their holy Father, would accompany them.

53. Among the rest was a young man of honourable disposition and dove-like simplicity, Gerard by name, native of the province of Lower Germany, from the city of Utrecht. More impatiently grieved than the others, he said with tears to the man of God:

> “Most blessed Father, I, a wretched young man, left my father’s house and despised everything in this world that could be desirable and lovable to me. In love of religion I came to your Fatherhood, hoping to enjoy your most sweet presence, to be formed by your teaching and examples, assisted by your merits and prayers, and sheltered beneath the protection of this holy multitude from the storm of temptations and the heat of youthful desires. Above all, I desired to await my last day among the sacred bodies of our brethren resting in this cemetery. Yet behold, today you cast me from your presence; I lose fellowship with this sacred company and, in addition, shall be deprived of the burial I have desired [Col. 0445B–C]. This—yes, this—is why I grieve so deeply, for my heart is troubled within me.”

54. The blessed man, moved with compassion for the youth, sought to soothe with gentle speech the soul afflicted by grief. Foreseeing by a prophetic spirit what would happen fifty years later, he said:

> “Go, dearest son, where the Holy Spirit [p. 1218] deigns to send you, and labour in the Lord’s field as a vigorous worker. I promise you in the name of the Lord and assure you that, as you desire, you shall die at Clairvaux and await with us the glorious coming of the heavenly Bridegroom.”

Receiving this most blessed promise of his kindly Father as the earnest of his desire, the brother greatly rejoiced [Col. 0445D]. He knew certainly that the man whom manifest signs and wonders declared to be the confidant of wisdom and truth could neither be deceived nor wish to deceive.

He went forth, and in the house which he was being sent to establish with the other brethren he vigorously passed through the offices of prior and cellarer. By God’s grace he received both the title and office of abbot. Though he ascended unwillingly to this summit of dignity, preferring salvation in a humble position to danger in an exalted one, he adorned the office he received with the splendour of a most religious manner of life.

Because scarcely anyone in that land converted, owing to the scarcity of clerics, the Lord sent His faithful servant educated and discerning persons from Germany and England. Through them the discipline of monastic religion, founded in that kingdom, grew and bore fitting fruit among a people who had heard the name “monk” but had never before seen a monk [Col. 0446A].

The abbot himself entrusted all the temporal ordering of the house and every external matter to his cellarer, Abraham by name, a prudent man. He devoted himself wholly to spiritual pursuits: intent upon winning souls; watchful and diligent in God’s service; frequent in labour when otherwise free; frequent also in reading; seeking bodily support from the common resources; and endeavouring in every respect to provide his brethren with a model of devotion and religious life.

55. He also possessed such a grace of gentleness and patience that, on one occasion, when a monk whom he had corrected for an offence, prompted by an evil spirit, struck him with his fist so violently as he descended the dormitory stairs that the blow caused no slight pain, he not only did not expel the man of such perversity or subject him to a severe penalty; rather, he drew him aside and begged his pardon before him, imploring him for God’s sake to put away the resentment which he bore against him [Col. 0446B]. Whatever virtue or religious devotion he found either in himself or in his subjects, moreover, he attributed not to his own industry but to the grace of God and the merits of his most holy Father Bernard.

56. If the necessary conduct of business ever required him to leave the monastery, he showed himself to secular people so wholly and so consistently disciplined and self-controlled that both the king and the princes of that land revered and honoured him as truly a man of God; hearing him, they did many things and willingly listened to him. Even the duke of that land, a vigorous and powerful man, submitted himself in reverence to the blessed man and so humbled the height of his own princely rank before the loftiness of the saint’s holiness that he would sometimes say to his intimates:

> “Whenever I think that I am about to see Abbot Gerard, I am shaken by such fear as though every secret and hidden thing in my heart lay open to his eyes.” [Col. 0446C]

57. When he had now grown old and reached extreme old age, completing his fortieth year in office, and when his body was shaken by various infirmities, the brethren began to ask him that, just as he had lived with them for so long in common, he would also deign to receive a place of burial among them. The man of God replied:

> “Do not, I beg you, speak in this way, my children. By every means I must die at Clairvaux and, in accordance with the promise of my Father beloved by God, sleep and rest in unity with the saints who lie there in peace.”

They objected, saying: “How, Father, shall we be able to bring you back there? Besides the infirmities of advanced old age, you are shaken and weakened by so many and such severe illnesses that we think you could scarcely reach the nearest borders of the Danes while still breathing.”

He replied with great confidence:

> “The word of God, strong and mighty, living and effective [Col. 0446D–0447A], which, poured into my ears through the mouth of that most reverend man, placed in the inmost recesses of my heart the earnest of this good hope that carries me onward [p. 1219], will grant a successful outcome to this journey. Only take care to carry out what I command.”

Accordingly, he was placed in a litter set between two horses. In no small miracle, from the ends of the earth, across such distances of land and through so many perils of sea and rivers, he reached Clairvaux. There he lay for a time in the infirmary and breathed forth his spirit in a good confession. He received the burial place he desired beside the tomb of Lord Humbert, of blessed memory, who had loved him familiarly during his life. When the king of Sweden learned of his death, he declared with groaning that his kingdom and land had not been worthy for the sacred bones of so great a man to rest there [Col. 0447B].

1220

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The most blessed death of the holy Father Bernard, and the cessation of his working miracles imposed upon him by the abbot of Cîteaux

58. The venerable Father Bernard, beloved by God and men, having happily completed his days in his Clairvaux, full of days but fuller of virtues, rested in peace. Bishops, abbots, and many other religious men gathered for his death. While his funeral rites were celebrated for two days, such a multitude of people assembled that scarcely any reverence was shown either to the bishops or to the brethren. For the grace of healing which had been present while he lived never departed from him when he was dead [Col. 0447C].

For when the holy body, suitably adorned in priestly vestments, was laid out in the midst with its face uncovered and its hands likewise uncovered, a brother worn down by a long and severe illness of epilepsy approached reverently and humbly. He began with tearful prayers to implore the holy Father, as though still living, to have mercy upon him. Nor could the loving Father, still set among his children, disregard so grave a calamity of his son; but, as though saying, “Son, I sleep, but my heart is awake,” he immediately granted through God’s grace what was asked. From that hour the brother was perfectly healed and learned by blessed experience that the holy abbot lived after death.

On the day before that most precious treasure was buried [Col. 0447D], a boy came from a nearby village. Because of contracted sinews, he had a withered arm and a clenched hand. Those who were present, moved by compassion for his age and disability, encouraged him after the ninth hour of prayer to touch the sacred body, with all the greater confidence because his innocent age was less able of itself to presume upon such a thing. But when the withered arm was applied to the holy arm and the clenched hand to the blessed hand, the vigour of nature suddenly returned. The arm was healed, and the hand, freely extending and bending back its fingers before the eyes of the whole multitude surrounding the sacred corpse on every side, was restored to perfect health.

At this healing there immediately arose so great a cry from all present, shouting God’s praise [Col. 0448A], that the discipline of the brethren could scarcely restrain it. When night came, another person, weak in his whole body, was brought in; he prostrated himself before the bier and rose up healed in the presence of those chanting the psalms, then was led to the altar.

59. The lord abbot of Cîteaux, who had come with several other abbots of his Order to the funeral of the man of God, observed the great disturbance caused by the pressing crowd. Judging from the present what would follow, he began greatly to fear that, if the signs increased and so intolerable a throng of people gathered, the discipline of the Order would perish through their unruliness and the fervour of holy religion would grow cold in that place. Therefore, after deliberating on this matter, he approached reverently and, by the authority of obedience, forbade Bernard to perform signs any further.

But the Apostle says of our Lord Jesus Christ that He “became obedient unto death” to the Father (Phil. 2:8); and by His example our lawgiver, Saint Benedict, sets obedience before us in the Rule unto death (chapter 7). Thus the holy and truly humble soul of our Father was obedient even after the death of the flesh to a mortal man. For the signs which had then begun to shine forth ceased so completely that from that day onward he has never appeared to perform public miracles [Col. 0448B], although even to this day he cannot be absent to certain faithful persons—especially brethren of his Order—who cry to him amid various afflictions. It is clear that the lord abbot of Cîteaux wished only those signs not to occur which would diminish the discipline of the Order through crowds of people gathering together [Col. 0448C].

60. Several years having passed after the blessed man’s departure, there was in Italy a certain married woman whom an evil spirit, having seized her, began cruelly to torment. Her relatives and friends, greatly distressed by this pitiable misfortune, began to consider diligently whether any remedy might exist. Now there was in their neighbourhood a monastery of the Cistercian Order; and, as hope conceived from any quarter is accustomed to create confidence in minds beset by distress, they resolved by common counsel to bring the possessed woman to that house for healing. And this was done.

The unhappy woman was brought to the gate, and some of those accompanying her were sent to report so great an evil to the abbot and brethren and ask for help. The abbot took with him certain of the elders, whom he knew to be more spiritual, and went out to the sufferer with the Lord’s cross and relics of the saints. When the evil spirit did not depart after being adjured by the Lord’s cross and the holy pledges of the saints, the abbot remembered that he possessed venerable relics of Saint Bernard’s hair and beard. He had received them at Clairvaux, I think, in that same year, when travelling to the chapter meeting, as a blessing, and had continually carried them with him for protection. Saying nothing, he silently put his hand beneath his cowl, intending, after taking out those relics, to press the demon with them.

The pestilent being, perceiving this with lynx-like eyes, immediately began to grip the footstool with his feet, spit, and reveal involuntarily, by indecent movements of his whole body, what he suffered within. Then, bursting into speech, he said:

> “Come now, little abbot, what do you mean to do? What evil are you now plotting against me beneath that garment of yours? You strive in vain; you labour to no purpose. Keep your Bernard, for you will accomplish nothing.”

When the abbot said, “By the Lord’s grace and the merits of this most holy man, you shall now depart,” the spirit answered:

> “What? Have you forgotten that he is forbidden to perform signs? Knowing this, I rest secure in this dwelling of mine.”

Hearing these words, the abbot and the brethren who were with him were greatly amazed that the wicked spirit had so quickly found that prohibition to be a shield for his defence. We have briefly set down these things concerning the virtues of Blessed Bernard the abbot [Col. 0449A–B], asking the Lord’s mercy that through the merits and prayers of our most sweet Father He may guard us from every evil; and that, gathering ears of divine grace after the sacred footsteps of so great a patron, He may grant that we not be deprived of a share in eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Epilogue to the books concerning the life and deeds of the holy Father Bernard

1221

61. Lord Stephen, of blessed memory, was leader and standard-bearer among Christ’s most valiant athletes, men illustrious in the Cistercian Order. In the tenth year after the institution of the Cistercian Order he assumed the office of pastoral care in that house. Burning with desire to spread the religious life, he and his brethren suffered greatly for fourteen successive years from the weariness of their small numbers. At last, in the fifteenth year, by divine grace breathing upon them from above, he deserved to receive our most blessed apostle of the age, Bernard, together with the crowd of his brethren and companions, for probation in spiritual training. From that day onward, the Lord gave an exceedingly abundant blessing for the expansion of the Cistercian Order throughout every region of the western world [Col. 0449C].

After some years, this most reverend Father Stephen sent Blessed Bernard’s brethren to build the house of Clairvaux and appointed as their abbot the holy Bernard himself, then still a young man but surpassing many grey-haired men in maturity of wisdom and religious life, and therefore worthy of reverence. Already then, as we believe, he foresaw by revelation of the Spirit how lofty and beautiful that cedar would be in the paradise of God’s Church, and how great a multitude, gathered from different parts of the world, would be refreshed beneath the shade of its thick branches—that is, beneath the shade of Bernard’s many merits—from the heat of fleshly enticements [Col. 0449D].

62. But who could adequately estimate how great was that assembly of blessed persons, or from how many different provinces and islands it was gathered? Not to mention the inland provinces of Italy, Germany, and Gaul, even the furthest islands of Ireland, Britain, Denmark, and Sweden, which mark the end of the world, frequently sent persons to complete this assembly; and because of the holy abbot they also venerated the holy place with celebrated devotion.

Not to mention the lay brethren, whose number was far greater than that of the monks: after the blessed man’s death, eight hundred and eighty-eight profession-books were found together in one place, apart from very many others that, through negligence and the lapse of time, had disappeared and could not be found [Col. 0450A]. Whenever some from this sacred assembly, cultivated by the ploughshare of discipline and having received the seeds of virtues, had advanced so far that they might be expected to bear fruit and benefit others, they were gathered from different regions and then promptly sent out again to different regions to build monasteries. Thus, although the novices often exceeded ninety and sometimes even one hundred, that sacred community never suffered the pressures of excessive numbers.

63. Lord Henry of holy memory, first abbot of Vitae-Scholae (“School of Life”), a monastery in Denmark of the line of Clairvaux, used to relate that, while he was a novice at Clairvaux and ninety recruits were being trained in the probationary cell under Blessed Bernard’s discipline, that most merciful Father once entered to visit his sons as they reclined at table. A lay brother followed him with a basket full of cut cheese. Approaching the said Henry, who was then prior of the novices, Bernard placed with his own most sweet hand a piece of cheese before him and said this admonitory word:

> “Brother, eat, for a great journey remains for you.”

Then the faithful servant of that great Householder, who “will make His servants recline at table, and, coming forth, will serve them,” passed before all the novices, offering each an allotted portion of charity and repeating the same saying to each. In this way he delightfully refreshed their bodies and stirred their minds to concern for the narrow and difficult way which they had begun to tread [Col. 0450B–C].

Although men of virtue were frequently sent from the sacred community of Clairvaux throughout the various regions of the world to propagate the discipline of the Cistercian Order, neither Iberian heat, nor the terror of Scythian cold, nor any other harshness of climate could bend their minds from retaining with manly constancy the form of the Order which they had learned at Clairvaux, in clothing, food, and the other necessities of the body. They fittingly claimed for themselves Horace’s saying:

> “Steadfast are the minds whom no change of place alters.”

64. Not only did bishops and magnates of various provinces ask that monasteries formed by the discipline of the man of God be founded in their regions: the peoples of proud cities also chose archbishops and bishops for themselves from among his disciples. They counted themselves blessed if they could provide pastors for their souls from the fountain of so great a perfection.

Yet the most perfect founder of that most perfect community obtained this special grace before God and men: although he was most worthy to be compelled, and was on several occasions elected archbishop or bishop, he was never forcibly taken away from the poverty dear to him or compelled, against his will, to be distinguished by the summit of such dignity [Col. 0451A].

But why do we repeat these matters concerning other cities, when the very head of the world—the holy Roman Church itself, mother of all other Churches—raised from this humble fellowship, from this school of Blessed Bernard, a supreme pontiff to the fullness of power; and when the apostolic curia itself associated certain of his disciples as cardinals in its share of pastoral responsibility?

These are Your works, Lord Christ: You so glorify those who glorify You and obey Your commands that Your servants, who according to the Apostle’s command submit themselves to every human creature for Your sake (1 Pet. 2:13), are raised by You, by a judgment full of mercy, above every mortal nature [Col. 0451B].

65. Moreover, after that famous Clairvaux had sent its first and most illustrious Abbot, after thirty-one years, to the palace of the heavenly Emperor—so that he might rightly be the more powerful to help, the more nearly he beheld the face of the supreme Majesty—the vigor of holy religious life, preserved unblemished in that same glorious house through his holy successors, endured, as we were permitted, by God’s favor, to prove in the times of the venerable and God-worthy lord Peter [Note: [Col. 0451D] Afterwards the eighth abbot in order, in the year 1181] and his successor, lord Garnier, afterwards bishop of Langres. For the Lord is our witness that, when we were subject at Clairvaux to the disciplines of the cloister and the observances of the sacred Order, we saw there such religious devotion and gravity, such purity and uprightness, that we often rejoiced in the grace of God and said in our hearts that, if our most blessed lawgiver Benedict himself, whose Rule we have professed, were living in the flesh and personally governed that holy community, the institutions of the sacred Order could not have been observed more strictly in that place. For negligence, frivolity, or laxity—which is the ruin of the Order—had no place there at all; rather, a holy emulation of flourishing virtues and brotherly love was strong there. And, what is more remarkable, [Col. 0451D] the superiors still had no need to compel individuals by some harsher correction, because that holy congregation held, as though transmitted to it by hereditary succession, the practice of avoiding vices and cultivating virtues.

We also saw there elders among the disciples of blessed Bernard, venerable for the gravity of their conduct, the integrity of their religious life, prudence, and simplicity: lord Gerard, of blessed memory, the Prior; lord Geoffrey, notary of that holy man; lord Hugh of Mont-Félix, greatly beloved by him; lord Peter of Châlons; and others, both monks and lay brothers, who endured from the times of the blessed man down to our own age. Having become examples of devotion and fervor to the remaining body of that holy fraternity, [Col. 0452A] they readily showed, by their lovable manner of life, how great a fullness of perfection had shone forth at Clairvaux in its first days—since the vigorous exercise of a few elders in observing the sacred Order, and the devotion of very few, could be imitated.

66. But behold: while we speak of the purity of religious life which, not only at Clairvaux but also at Cîteaux and in the other well-ordered houses of the Cistercian Order, raised many in its early days to the summit of perfection, we recall with much fear and trembling something we once heard from the aforesaid venerable man, lord Gerard the Prior, in the chapter-house of Clairvaux. For on one occasion, as he exhorted us in sweet speech to seriousness of conduct and the keeping of discipline, [Col. 0452B] he maintained that in an earlier time the souls of deceased brethren had visibly appeared to a certain spiritual man, a monk of the same monastery, and had disclosed with pitiable lamentation that they had been assigned to places of punishment—not because they had committed some graver sin, but because they had taken less care than they ought to avoid daily negligences.

If, therefore, in those blessed times, when negligence scarcely entered through tiny cracks, the punitive correction of the strict Judge and an exceedingly painful scraping removed the rust of guilt, what are we to think of the misery of our own times, when negligence bursts in not now through tiny cracks, but through fissures—or rather through breaches—of lukewarmness? Therefore, lest after negligence and the heedlessness of sloth the death of malice and iniquity enter through our windows, [Col. 0452C] since time, which consumes all things, also weakens religious life, and since people are more inclined to pursue vices than virtues, let us cast off idleness with all our strength and strive manfully to cling to the footsteps of the fathers who went before us. Let us turn their memory over in our hearts and reread their sacred deeds frequently and gladly, so that, through the rightness of their conduct, strength for our own conduct may appear to us as from a most shining mirror. Thus, put to shame by wholesome modesty, let us learn to consider even the good deeds which we perform wholly imperfect, and always to thirst for a fuller perfection of righteousness.

But if anyone, desiring to make great progress yet unable to do so, [Col. 0452D] begins on that account, overcome by weariness, to act more slackly, let him hear what the holy father Bernard says: “I do not wish to become supreme all at once; I wish to advance little by little.” If, then, effect does not immediately follow upon the effort to advance, nevertheless everyone who wishes to advance has some degree of progress available to him, if more is not granted. Only unwillingness to advance is the occasion of every negligence and dissolution, and finally of death and damnation.

67. Therefore I beseech those who will read these things, through our Lord Jesus Christ, not to wish to read them merely out of curiosity, but to weigh carefully what in their own conduct departs from the rule of righteousness which shone conspicuously in the holy fathers; and whatever they find in themselves foreign to the path of true religion, [Col. 0453A] let them hasten to correct it wholly, in the daily conflict of vices and virtues, according to the line of truth. For just as the most foolish of all people is rightly judged to be the man who, coming upon a tree most beautiful in the greenness of its leaves and abundance of its fruit, fills his stomach with the emptiness of its leaves and remains hungry for the usefulness of its fruit, so too, by the same equity of reason, he is accounted most foolish who, rereading the most beautiful and fruitful account of the strenuous way of life of the holy fathers, runs through it like a mere chronicle or annals of kings, for the sole curious knowledge of events, and plucks nothing from what he reads to kindle in himself the fervor of compunction, to cleanse the rust of his conscience, and to balance the unevenness of his conduct [Col. 0453B] by the hand of holy devotion.

For the praiseworthy deeds of the fathers who preceded us are not described in order to serve vain and restless curiosity, but so that the unlearned may be instructed, the weak strengthened, the undisciplined may pursue seriousness, the hard-hearted may be pierced with compunction, the devout formed toward perfection, and so that through the edification and consolation of its readers the holy Church may be strengthened, and the praise of God—whose gifts are our good things—may be increased by thanksgiving.

68. Moreover, in this one respect we ask pardon of studious readers: that in certain places, retaining the sense or substance of the words that were spoken, we have taken care to clothe that same substance in a fitting form of expression. But as to the facts themselves, far be it from us—so far as lay in our power—to set down even the slightest point otherwise than the event occurred, with conscience wounded by a desire to lie. May the eternal God himself, the Son of the eternal God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who in the days of his humility, establishing the sacrament of perfect penitence and laying the foundation of true religion, said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24); and who in these last days, when the world is already growing old, faith wavers, hope totters, and charity grows cold, poured the incentive of his holy love into many hearts through the purity of the Cistercian Order, and raised up in Clairvaux the most splendid pillar of that sacred Order, namely our most reverend father [Col. 0454B] Saint Bernard—may he, I say, our Lord and God, through the merits and intercession of the holy fathers whose lives and conduct we have recorded in some measure for the edification of posterity, grant us so to cling to their footsteps, so to retain the disposition of simplicity and innocence, and so to be strengthened in true humility through continence of the flesh, that we too, by the cooperating grace of God, may one day deserve to attain that glory of eternal blessedness to which we unhesitatingly believe those same fathers have attained. Through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0453]

## FRAGMENTS FROM HERBERT’S BOOKS ON THE MIRACLES OF CISTERCIAN MONKS  
(Book I, chapters 5–7; Book II, chapters 12–14, 25)

1223

### I.—On Acardus, a monk of Clairvaux

[Col. 0453C]

1. In that same monastery there was also a religious monk named Acardus, a man noble indeed by birth, but nobler in conduct. At the command and sending of his abbot, blessed Bernard, he founded and built very many monasteries. While he was still under probation, that same most blessed father Bernard came one day, as he often did, to console the novices. When his address had ended, he drew aside the aforesaid Acardus together with two other novices and warned them in a prophetic spirit, saying:

“It will happen,” he said, “that before tomorrow this novice”—and he identified him by name—“will secretly depart. Therefore keep watch and be ready, so that you do not allow him to escape [Col. 0453D] with the plunder. And if the wretch leaves us, because he was not of us, you will nevertheless keep the spoils for us, because they are ours.”

On hearing this, they were astonished and waited silently for the outcome. Deep in the night, two of them, seeing the fugitive sleeping soundly in his bed, [Col. 0454C] began to sleep as well, for their eyes were heavy—deceived, undoubtedly, by the spirit of error. Acardus, however, because he most firmly believed that the word spoken by the holy father could not prove void, resisted with manly constancy the spirit of drowsiness, which was most troublesome to him. Now rubbing his forehead, now his temples; at one moment pulling the hairs of his beard and head, at another washing his hands and face; now rousing himself by walking from place to place, he finally overcame the deceitful sleep that oppressed him.

And when the time was near for the signal for Vigils to be sounded, behold, two Ethiopian-like giants, dressed in blackest capes, visibly entered through the door of the house. The one who went before carried a roasted hen on a spit. Moreover, on the very spit a huge serpent was impaled through head and tail, encircling that same hen on either side. With this dish he approached the novice’s place and held the steaming hen to the sleeping man’s nostrils. Immediately the novice awoke, [Col. 0455A] the demons went out and returned by the way through which they had come.

The man rose as quickly as possible and, burdened with clothing, went out after the demons. Coming to the door of the cupboard in the cloister, he tried by his devices to break open its fastening and carry away books with him. Acardus immediately roused his companions with the utmost speed and informed them of the apostate’s prophesied flight. Then together they pursued the departing man and found him shaking the bolt of the door. When he noticed that they were present, he at once sprang away; rushing in a headlong run through the gates of the orchard, he was at last stopped by the enclosure of the walls and brought back. The next day, since, unrepentant of his evils, he would not return to his senses—for he had already been given over to a reprobate mind—he was finally dismissed to go to his own place. That same day, seized by the devil, he fell into madness and did not cease raving until death.

This lord Acardus himself told us novices this account in complete good faith when he was already bent with age, since he knew everything and had seen it with his own eyes.

2. He also confessed to us that at the beginning of his conversion he endured many battles and beatings from demons and saw many of their apparitions. Often indeed, while chanting and praying in church, they lit before him many lights, like candles and lamps; these immediately vanished as an illusion at the invocation of Christ’s name. On one occasion, finally, the devil appeared to him and fought with him in a gladiatorial contest, like a wrestler in an arena. He dealt him frequent blows and wounds, and received them in return; but in the end he crushed the demon, smashed its head, and dashed out its brains. While he dragged it by the hair, he retained in his hand a portion torn from the shattered head, with flesh and bones. Immediately such an intolerable stench issued from it that it seemed nearly to exceed the limits of human endurance. When he flung it some distance from his hand, the foul monster which had appeared vanished at once; yet it left the traces of its impurity more deeply impressed. For during the course of a year such a stench continually exhaled from that hand that, from anguish of heart, he could scarcely bring it either to his mouth or to his nostrils.

This kindly man, a source of great consolation, often told us, when we were novices, many examples [Col. 0455D] by which he frequently kindled us in the love of virtues. Of these we have decided to commit at least one to writing, because we feel it cling more ardently to our affections.

### II.—On Schocelinus, hermit of the Trier district

3. “I,” he said, “when I was once staying in the bishopric of Trier in order to build the monastery called Claustrum, by the grant of heavenly grace deserved to see and know a holy man, a man truly rich and truly blessed, named Schocelinus. He was indeed the richer and the more blessed because he more truly despised and cast farther away the deceitful riches of the world, as false vanities and madnesses. For truly, the rich man is not he who has more, but he who desires less.

“This most blessed hermit abandoned the world with such fervor and loved Christ with such ardor that I think no one in our times and regions can be compared with him in contempt for visible things and mortification of the flesh. All of us can admire his life, many may even emulate it, but no one can imitate it; and therefore it must be venerated all the more. For, dying daily for Christ, he bore not one cross or death only, but countless crosses and deaths, since in all the days he lived in the wilderness he underwent, as it were, just as many martyrdoms. For what person in this mortal life, however far advanced, can live long either without human food, shelter, clothing, or all such things? Yet this manly man, a man of true virtue, transcended [Col. 0456B] human nature; deprived of all these things, he did not fail for many years, because God strengthened him.

“For fourteen years he remained a solitary wanderer, naked in all his body, roaming and hiding among mountains and forests for Christ’s love. He had the sky for his roof, air for his clothing, and the food of beasts for human food. He used wild raw herbs and their roots, and sometimes fat and acorns as great delicacies—food plainly shown to be more the fodder of brute animals than the nourishment of human beings. He preserved the rigor of this purpose with inexorable severity for a full decade.

“Afterwards, however, about four years before his death, in the heart of winter, when the most bitter season raged, the earth was buried under snow and held fast by harsher frost, so that it neither put forth herbs outdoors nor allowed roots to be dug up; then, unable to endure the pressure of hunger and that cold, like a man almost dead already, with an emaciated body clothed only in skin, he was sometimes compelled to leave the wilderness and descend, willingly or unwillingly, to nearby farms. Coming to the outlying huts of the same village, if he knew some poor person of honorable conduct lived there, he would preferably turn aside to him. Yet he refused to enter the dwelling itself; with head reclined, he rested beneath the eaves of the house, or rather in the middle of the yard. He took special care to arrive in the deep night and depart at the hour before dawn.

[Col. 0456D]

4. “The people deemed worthy to be honored by so noble a guest paid him great reverence. No inhabitant dared approach him or trouble him with conversation unless permitted or even summoned by him; for they feared, of course, lest he no longer turn aside to them if someone there importunately disturbed his rest. Sometimes they placed a little straw or an old sack for him outside the door, in case perhaps he would consent to rest upon it. They nevertheless offered him a piece of barley or bran bread, knowing well that he accepted nothing else. Of that bread he sometimes chewed a small crust, but carried the remainder with him into the wilderness as nourishment for many days.

“That exceedingly wealthy man also had tied about his loins a cheap and very short half-garment, which could barely cover only the shameful parts of his body when that unavoidable necessity compelled him to appear before people. He also possessed a very small pouch hanging from his neck or loins, in which he carried the aforesaid food. Behold the whole property of this wealthy man; behold the glorious inheritance and noble patrimony [Col. 0457A] of the servant of Christ, to whom the entire world was truly wealth. For, as one having nothing and possessing everything, he obtained all things in such nothingness. Indeed, he who enclosed the whole world in a cheap half-garment chose that half-garment alone out of, and in place of, the entire world. For what else does abundance of treasure and unlimited possession of goods give anyone, except the ability to pass and prolong this present life for a while? Yet for passing this life, a single torn strip of an old rag was enough for our poor man.

5. “When blessed Bernard heard of the virtue of his way of life, he commanded us to visit and greet the man in his name, sending him also some small gifts as a token of charity: a tunic and stockings, so that he might wear them for Bernard’s sake. We therefore set out for those regions. One day, while it was still dark, we entered the place where he was thought to be resting; and, not finding him, we asked the host where he was. The host replied: ‘This night he stayed with us in the courtyard. [Col. 0457C] When he departed and bade us farewell earlier than usual, we replied: “Why, lord father, are you leaving so early, when scarcely an hour of the middle of the night has passed?” And he said: “Some religious men are now going to come here because of me; I do not wish to be found by them at present.” He did this often also on account of others whom he likewise foretold would come to him.’

“On hearing this, we were more than sufficiently astonished that we had been detected by him so quickly in our stratagem. We had thought we had acted cleverly enough and had forestalled him unawares before he rose. In this occurrence it was plainly made known that he too was not without a prophetic spirit. Knowing, therefore, that he could not be found without his good pleasure, we arranged to send him a message through the aforesaid host, earnestly begging that, for the sake of the one who had sent us to him, he would grant us his presence.

“When at last he graciously consented, we came and saw him—not as an earthly man, but like a heavenly angel, whose whole way of life was in heaven and from heaven. Then, after we had presented the blessed bread, he humbly and reverently received the father’s greeting and put on the garments. But immediately he took them off again and said: ‘Blessed be God, who has put it into the heart of an apostolic man to deem worthy the remembrance of a sinful and miserable man. And now, for love of him, I have obediently accepted and put on the garments sent; yet I cannot wear them longer, because I have no need of them and he did not command it. But I tell you, my dearest friends, that nothing is more troublesome to me than to be compelled once again to put upon my weary and aching shoulders the hateful burden of care for the flesh, which I laid aside with such difficulty.’

[Col. 0458A]

6. “Seeing the man to be kind and approachable, and now speaking to him freely, we asked him, though with reverence, whether he still endured any trouble from the enticements of the flesh or the provocations of demons. Then he, being a cheerful man and a source of good consolation, smiled a little and began to speak thus:

“‘It has been a long time, dearest brothers, since by God’s grace I have felt myself relieved in no small degree from the passions of vices. But because the life of man upon earth is temptation, who shall boast that he has a pure heart? For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Walking amid snares and exposed on every side to hostile swords, unless we are continually fortified by the shield of divine protection, we can never guard ourselves against those who shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. Yet we trust in the Lord, because he is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able.

“‘Now I shall relate something to you by way of example, from which you may see what kinds of temptations sometimes trouble me. One day, when winter’s harshness was stiffening with a frost more intense than usual and abundant snow was falling from the clouds, I lay upon the ground, my limbs numb. Yet the almighty Creator of things, who gives snow like wool and scatters mist like ashes, had himself given me, in place of the woolen covering I lacked, a snowy covering: great and broad, and nearly a cubit thick. Spread widely all around, it covered me so that absolutely none of my body was visible. Only around my face, a stream of steaming breath coming from my mouth gradually melted the snow lying over it on every side and made a small opening.

“‘Meanwhile a little hare, fleeing the cold and snow and seeking a hiding place in which to rest, came by chance to that very opening. Drawn by the pleasant warmth, it immediately stopped and lay down there upon my head. Then the novelty of the thing made me smile, and, as frivolity stole upon me, my mind was cast down from its usual state of seriousness and slipped into the joy of vanity. Indeed, a desire came upon me to seize that little hare, as I easily could have done by reaching out my hand—not to kill or keep it, but because it is an innocent and very gentle animal, so that I might delight for a while in touching and seeing it and not fear to spend the time dedicated to penitence in that foolish pleasure.
