But, struggling for a long time against the tempter, I overcame the vain desire by God’s gift; and, keeping my body still, I let the frightened little creature rest safely until at last it departed of its own accord.

“‘Behold: this is one of the greater temptations that I remember having endured over many past days. [Col. 0459A] Although I may seem to have told it too cheerfully, perhaps in jest and to enliven you, I nevertheless blush and grieve that my thoughts are sometimes troubled by these vanities, like buzzing flies, even without consenting to indulge in vanity.’”

7. When that remarkable man had recounted these and similar things to us for our edification and consolation, he returned with the deepest humility our greeting to blessed father Bernard and most devoutly commended himself to Bernard’s prayers. Then, blessing us and bidding us farewell, like a stag released by God he ran back in free leaps to the shaded depths of the forests; and, like a bird escaped from its holder’s hand, he spread his wings into the air and flew back singing to the pathless woods.

We, seeing this, had no spirit left for further speech. In comparison with such and so great a perfection, we compared our towers to ashes and dust; and we, who had formerly thought ourselves something when we were nothing, then considered all our righteousnesses as a menstruous cloth. Thus, beating our breasts, humbled and deeply compunct, we returned to our own place.

Almost countless other great deeds are reported of that man; but because we, being far removed, have not investigated them more carefully, we leave them buried in silence, putting forward only what we received by eyewitness testimony. When this thrice-blessed man, God revealing it to him, saw that the day of his death was now imminent, he went to one of the nearer villages. There, having received the viaticum of the Lord’s sacrament, he rendered up his soul of angelic purity amid the rejoicing of angels. At his venerable funeral, religious men and innumerable crowds of people gathered in companies from every direction, buried his body honorably, and built a new church over it. Afterwards his body was transferred from there to a noble castle called Luxembourg and honorably entombed in the church of Blessed Mary. Miracles frequently occur at his tomb even to this day, and many healings and benefits are received by those who faithfully ask for them through his intercession.

Lord Acardus often related these and similar examples to us novices, strengthening the first elements of our training magnificently and raising us no little in the love of virtues. At last he too failed, passed to the Lord in a good old age, and was buried in the tomb of his brethren.

### III.—On a lay brother and convert of Clairvaux

8. There was in the same monastery a certain lay brother and convert, a religious man of supreme gentleness, who, with God as his teacher, had learned to be meek and humble in heart. Everyone bore witness concerning him that he had never been seen to become angry, nor ever, when affected by any injuries, stirred to impatience. Inspired by God, he had firmly resolved in his heart that whenever any of his brethren, justly or unjustly, made complaint against him, he would pray for them, and for each one would say at least one *Our Father* the first time. Wholesomely instructed by his example, many of the brethren of Clairvaux [Col. 0460A] keep the same custom even to this day almost as a law.

One day, while travelling alone, he had to pass through the narrow defile of a forest. There he happened upon robbers, who stripped him, took away also the horse with its packs, and left him absolutely nothing except charity. But charity was not in his wallet, nor carelessly left outside in a case; rather, it had been wisely fastened within the innermost recess of his heart by the strongest knots of patience, and therefore could not fear the violence of murderers. Since charity remained safe, the servant of God could lose nothing, because he counted as nothing whatever he lost while it remained.

After the robbers had departed and he had gone a little way, he prostrated himself in prayer, beseeching God to forgive them this wickedness. One of them, following from a distance, watched more curiously, wishing to know what he was doing. Seeing him persist for a long time in prayer, he ran swiftly back to his companions, beating his breast and saying: “Woe to us miserable and damned men! Behold, we shall all die, for we have treated so badly, to our own ruin, this most holy man and brother of so holy a monastery—for, by his own disclosure, they had learned that he was from Clairvaux. Since leaving us, he has not ceased to pray with groans and tears; and undoubtedly he even asks the Lord on behalf of his enemies.”

Hearing this, they were pierced in heart. They came and found him still intent upon prayer with knees bent. Immediately they restored everything to him, humbly begged pardon, and dismissed him in peace. Seeing this, the brother rejoiced with great joy, giving immense thanks to Christ the Savior more for the robbers’ compunction than for the recovery of his goods.

9. This good man persevered in his holy resolve until, at God’s call, he was at last gathered to his people, henceforth to receive with them the rewards of his merits. A vision concerning his glorification appeared on the very day on which he died. In a monastery far distant from Clairvaux there was a certain religious monk of great reputation, whom all sincerely loved for his holiness and all singularly honored. On the same day that the aforesaid brother died, this monk himself, dying, came to his last hour. As he seemed near death, he was taken away from human awareness, so that, deprived of every function of his limbs, he remained in ecstasy from morning until the ninth hour. At last he returned to himself, recovered strength, and only his tongue was released for speech.

Those present, astonished, urgently asked him the reason for his sudden departure and return. He answered: “Today, when I was drawn up in spirit away from the bodily senses, I suddenly found myself brought, as it were, into a paradise of delight, into a place glorious and exceedingly splendid, whose suitability, beauty, and pleasantness the narrowness of human understanding cannot measure. There was a precious abundance of vessels and ornaments; there was an infinite preparation of delights, as is customary when some most mighty king or emperor is expected. There were countless saints radiant in immense glory. Some had already arrived, while others were still coming from every region, hastening in rivalry as to a great spectacle and gathering from every side as for a solemn feast. There too the sweetness of heavenly harmony was heard, and thanksgiving and the voice of praise resounded everywhere.

“When I was greatly astonished, I asked my angelic guide about what I saw. He replied: ‘This is the new celebration of a certain new saint, today taken from the house of Clairvaux and now being solemnly introduced into these joys.’ Having said this, he ordered me to depart quickly and return to human affairs. Greatly frightened by this, I begged from the depths of my heart that I might not be sent back again from that happiness to the miseries of the body. But he replied: ‘By every means you must return to your brethren, until you announce what you have seen. When this has been done, you will immediately return and obtain a share in this eternal joy.’ For this purpose I was sent to you: to tell you what I saw, so that you too may advance in good works and persevere in goodness, knowing that reward will certainly not be lacking for your labor.”

After saying this, he bade farewell and fell asleep in the Lord. The entire community of that monastery mourned him as a man most holy and of great usefulness; all had been formed by his example and depended upon his counsel. Carefully noting the time and hour, they inquired at Clairvaux and learned that the brother mentioned above had died on the same day on which the vision had been shown. Such and so great had his manner of life proved to be that it readily gave credence to so great a miracle.

10. When certain brethren related this vision before blessed Bernard with great astonishment, he answered: “And do you, brothers, marvel at these things? I rather marvel at your unbelief and hardness of heart: you who still do not believe, or perhaps do not sufficiently heed, that voice which cries from heaven: ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth, the Spirit says, let them rest from their labors; for their works follow them’ (Rev. 14:13). To me it is clearer than light and more certain than the life I live that all who persevere obedient and humble in this purity of heart will, as soon as they have put off the flesh, immediately be stripped of every misery and clothed in the glory of immortality.”

### IV.—On Simon, abbot of Caziacum

11. The venerable man Simon, formerly abbot of Caziacum, a monastery of no small distinction among the monks of the Black Order, loved blessed Bernard with a great affection of heart, so much so that he seemed wholly dependent upon Bernard’s counsel and will. He had a great desire to abandon pastoral care and become a monk at Clairvaux. Yet blessed Bernard, knowing the man’s virtue and the grace by which he was very capable and necessary to the monastery entrusted to him, never wished, as long as he lived in the flesh, to give his consent to such a request.

One day the same abbot said to him: “Lord Father, I am now old and almost decrepit. My bodily members are failing, diseases press upon me from every side, and I feel that I am on the point of dissolution. If I should die outside Clairvaux, it will be to me an inconsolable sorrow and an irreparable loss. Therefore you must either command me to go there now, or satisfy my vows, because death hastening on permits no further delay.”

The man of God replied: “Remain in your place and do not fear. I assure you that you will die at Clairvaux.”

The man believed the holy one’s words and remained for several years more secure in his office of superiority. After the passing of the servant of God, however, unable any longer to bear the spur of his desire with no one restraining it, he relinquished his governance and went to Clairvaux. There, by God’s great gift and a great miracle, he survived seven years and, in the end, left to us all a truly remarkable example of fervor and devotion at such an age and in such infirmity.

### V.—On Gunnarius, formerly tetrarch of Sardinia and afterwards a monk at Clairvaux
12. In the same way, Gunnarius, an illustrious man, formerly a judge and tetrarchal lord of Sardinia, once came to Saint Martin of Tours for prayer. On his return journey he passed through Clairvaux, where Saint Bernard devoutly received him [Col. 0462C] and gave him abundant warning concerning the salvation of his soul. Yet Bernard could by no means convert him, although the most blessed Father, while Gunnarius was present and rejoicing greatly, restored sight to a certain blind man. When Gunnarius departed, the Saint said to him: “I have earnestly prayed to the Lord for your conversion, but for the present I have not deserved to be heard. And now I allow you to depart, because I may not detain an unwilling man. Nevertheless, know that you will return here again from Sardinia.”

The man therefore went away to his own land, carrying with him from the fiery discourse of the Man of God a spark of emulation for poverty and the religious life. Meanwhile this spark grew and burned within his breast through reflection; and afterwards, at the fitting time, it burst forth into the flame of action. When he had returned to Sardinia, those prophetic words, uttered from the holy man’s mouth and retained by him as a heavenly oracle, continually spurred his mind [Col. 0462D] and did not permit him to rest, according to Solomon’s saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly in” (Eccles. 12:11).

A short time later, when he heard of the holy man’s death, he was profoundly distressed in spirit, reproaching himself and repenting that he had not been converted by Bernard’s preaching. But what he had not done during Bernard’s life, he hastened to fulfil after his death. Accordingly, having promptly arranged everything that seemed necessary, he appointed his first-born son Baraso to rule in his kingdom, distributing his patrimony jointly among his other three children. The eldest of these, Peter by name, immediately after his father’s departure powerfully obtained the kingdom of Cagliari [Caralitanum] through marriage [Col. 0463A], and still rules it nobly today.

Gunnarius himself, while still in his forties and outstanding in bodily maturity and vigour of mind, left Sardinia and laid aside all worldly glory. Poor and humble, he entered Clairvaux. There, having now spent five times five years, he continually serves in the discipline of the Order he embraced and awaits until his change shall come. Though he left so much for Christ’s love, he considers that he has lost nothing at all; indeed, he rejoices and judges it a great gain to have cast aside earthly things for heavenly ones.

## VI.—On Saint Bernard’s return from Rome to his own community

13. The same venerable Abbot, when he had once stayed for three years in the city of Rome and in the regions of Italy in order to quell the schism of Peter Leonis [Col. 0463B]—a work in which Christ gloriously honoured that same servant of His—finally returned to Clairvaux. Immediately after prayer had been made, he entered the chapter of the brothers. Since he was weary from travel and could not speak long, he delivered to them a brief discourse, yet one full of consolation, saying: “Blessed be God, who has restored you to me, and me to you [Note: [Col. 0463D] As above, Life I, book VII, ch. 11.],” etc.

This was recorded for us by Lord Girard, formerly abbot of Longpont, one of the old elders of Clairvaux, who diligently strove to investigate Bernard’s sayings and deeds.

14. We also heard him relate that, while that Saint of God was preaching the word of the Lord in a certain chapter of monks, two of the brothers present saw him, together with the bench on which he sat, suspended in the air [Col. 0463C], raised about one foot above the ground.

Once, while this venerable Father was travelling not far from the castle of Provins, it was divinely revealed to him that one of his sons at Clairvaux had then died. He immediately descended from his vehicle and performed the office for the dead, commending the man’s soul to God. In the evening he lodged at a town called Cantamerula. The lady of that place, who had devoutly received him as a guest, presented to him her daughter, long afflicted with quartan fever, asking him to lay his hand upon her in blessing so that she might recover. He blessed and signed her, saying: “Daughter, you will suffer one further attack, and then you will be delivered.” [Col. 0463D] And so it happened to her.

On another occasion, when that most blessed man was leaving Laviniacum [perhaps Latiniacum], a noble estate situated in the diocese of Meaux, a somewhat grown girl, deaf and mute, was brought to him. They placed her upon the neck of his beast of burden. Looking up to heaven, he prayed briefly. Then he anointed her lips and little ears with his saliva, blessed her, and commanded her to call upon Saint Mary. At once the girl, who had never spoken, opened her mouth and cried out: “Saint Mary.”

A certain Roger, a religious man and monk of Clairvaux, while he was still in the world, saw this miracle performed with his own eyes [Col. 0464A]. He was deeply compuncted; and this, as he told us, was the chief reason why he gave himself to Clairvaux.

## VII.—On Fastrad, third abbot of Clairvaux

15. Fastrad, of venerable and pious memory [Note: [Col. 0463D] You have his distinguished letter among Bernard’s letters, now no. 478, where he is called Fastredus. [Col. 0464D] He succeeded Robert as abbot of Clairvaux after Bernard in 1157; he died in 1163.], formerly abbot of Cîteaux, was a man of exceptional holiness—noble indeed by birth, but nobler by the refinement of his character. Though not inadequately instructed in the liberal arts, he always devoted himself with still more ardent desire to Holy Scripture. Thus, as he advanced in wisdom and age, he kept Scripture continually before his eyes and in his hands, and would not even sit down to table without divine reading. This he did not merely at home, but also when travelling in the schools [Col. 0464B].

While he was abbot of Cambron, upon the death of Lord Robert of pious memory, who had succeeded Blessed Bernard, he was elected to govern Clairvaux. Yet he evaded coming to that election, though called by name, fearing, of course, that what he had always feared might happen to him. Nevertheless, before the delegates from Clairvaux could reach him to seek him out, rumour, flying ahead with its chatter, informed him that all had unanimously agreed upon his person. Troubled and anxious at this report, he took flight. Coming to the house of Vallis Sancti Petri, a monastery of the Carthusian Order, he hid there for several days.

While he persevered there day and night in prayer, he was caught up in ecstasy of mind; and behold, the Virgin who had borne a child, Lady of the Angels, appeared in great glory [Col. 0464C], carrying in her hands the King of Glory, her little Jesus. Seeing her, he fell at her feet and begged her to have mercy on him. The Blessed Virgin replied: “Why are you troubled, O man?” Then, placing upon his arms, as upon those of another Simeon, that noble burden which she carried, she said: “Receive my Son, and keep Him for me.” When this was done, the vision was withdrawn from his eyes. Returning to himself, he understood that the word had gone forth from the Lord, and that those committed to his care were truly sons of God and members of Christ. Forewarned by so joyful a vision, he no longer dared to resist, lest he seem to wish to oppose God’s ordinance [Col. 0464D].

16. Having undertaken the aforesaid office, how diligent, how discerning, and how exceedingly kindly a shepherd he proved himself is not for my simplicity to set forth. For as he surpassed others in the dignity of office, so also he went before them in the example and merit of religious holiness. Chaste, devout, humble, gentle, and modest beyond all whom I remember seeing in his days.

“But,” says Severus concerning Saint Martin, “there is no need to praise his frugality, since even while he was still in the world he lived so sparingly that he was thought not a student but a monk” [Col. 0465A]. For, as he himself secretly made known to certain intimate friends, two years before his conversion, although not yet fully grown in age, he devoted himself so earnestly to abstinence that he would never allow himself to be filled even with bread and water. He would never consent to take the food of flesh, even though at that time he was almost mortally ill.

After becoming a monk, I refrain from saying how soberly he lived—indeed, how rigorously he subdued his body into servitude—for, to speak the truth, he was excessively severe in this respect. I knew and observed him sufficiently in such matters, since for many years I served him at his table. For, while he pursued the vices of the flesh in himself without mercy, he seemed to show less compassion than was fitting even to the poor flesh naturally joined to him.

[Col. 0465B]

17. Moreover, how humble and restrained he was in outward dress and equipment, despite the dignity of his office, may easily be seen from this one incident. One day the monk in charge of clothing placed on his bed a cowl—or perhaps a tunic—which he wished him to wear, somewhat better than usual. The Father rebuked him, in my hearing, saying:

“What is this, my dear brother, that you desire to do? Would you separate me from communion with our brothers and set me apart by conspicuous clothing? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses. Because I am styled abbot, then, must I cease to be a monk? Was I appointed minister and servant of others [Col. 0465C] in order that I should be fattened with more sumptuous meals and adorned with more refined dress? Therefore, if you love me, if you seek my peace, if you do not disdain obedience to my commands, I beg and command you not to wish to do this again. For, since before God I am unworthy and the least of all, it is a great thing for me if I am honoured with the common food and clothing of all. From the time I was raised to the government of souls, this is the one thing I have always feared above all else, and still fear: that, through the occasion of this administration, I may abandon the poor life which I professed and lose the reward of a monk.”

Thus this man, beloved by God and human beings and pre-eminently adorned with gifts of grace, profited others not only by word and example but also moved those who looked upon him by the gracious bearing of his body and wondrous [Col. 0465D] devotion. So great was the grace of the Paraclete Spirit shining from his angelic countenance that scarcely could any believer be satisfied by the desirable sight of him—especially those who reflected on the purity of his mind and singular gentleness, which they saw, as it were, impressed by the divine hand upon the outward man as upon its own seal.

This venerable man, once he had become universal Father of the monastery of Cîteaux and of the whole Order [Note: [Col. 0465D] See above, book VII, ch. 20.], would, we believe, have borne great fruit in that office [Col. 0466A], had he not been taken away so quickly because our sins demanded it. But since we were not worthy to enjoy his most holy life longer, it was cut off like the work of a weaver while he was still setting up the warp. Yet, “having been made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many years”: for his soul was pleasing to God and worthy of the fellowship of angels.

18. Concerning his happy death, soon to come, a revelation of this kind was made to Peter of Toulouse, of blessed memory, concerning whom we have related much above. In a vision of the night he saw: behold, the Son of God coming from heaven in the clouds of heaven, accompanied by a multitude of saints, and standing in the very air. He sat upon a throne of glory, and a brightness proceeding from Him illuminated the world. At the right hand of that Majesty there appeared a most glorious tomb suspended in the air [Col. 0466B], constructed with marvellous workmanship and delighting the eyes of all who beheld it.

Before the doors of the basilica of Clairvaux stood an innumerable multitude of both sexes. With faces raised upward, they attentively watched the King of Glory, our Lord Jesus Christ, and that mausoleum itself. The aforesaid monk Peter approached the crowd and began to ask what that tomb was, which appeared before the Lord, or what it signified. Then one of them replied:

“This tomb, concerning which you inquire, belongs to a certain most holy man who is shortly to be taken from the earth. At his departure there will be great desolation far and wide in these regions. His death also shall be precious in the sight of the Lord and illustrious in the sight of human beings.”

About twenty days later, while the said holy abbot was at Paris, attending Pope Alexander concerning the affairs of the monastery and his entire Order, he was seized by illness, took to bed, and on the fifth day rested in a holy death. At last his body was brought back to Cîteaux with immense honour and buried with great devotion.

They relate that in England there was a religious man of great virtue. On the very day when Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, departed from the world, this man—being in England—saw in the spirit a certain exceedingly great angel sent down from heaven, taking up from earth an equally great soul [Col. 0466D] and leading it with immense joy to the stars. Afterwards, when Blessed Abbot Fastrad himself departed from the body, on that same day the man mentioned above saw the aforesaid angel coming to earth and lifting a soul taken from it to the heights of heaven. Though that soul appeared very great, it could not equal the greatness of the former soul.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] In all the books of Saint Bernard’s miracles there is nowhere any mention of that miraculous milk expressed by the most blessed Virgin upon Bernard. Yet we now see this miracle, before others that are far more certain, being promoted by painters and by uncritical devotees of the holy Doctor.]


# [Lives of Saint Bernard]

[Col. 0467]

# Notice concerning the remaining writers of the Life of Saint Bernard

[Col. 0467] 1233–1234. I. It seemed proper to append, by way of supplement to the preceding books, the subsequent authors who wrote of the deeds of Saint Bernard.

The first is Alanus, formerly abbot of Aripatorium, bishop of Auxerre from 1153 to 1161. In that year he retired again to Clairvaux, where he died in 1181. From the preceding five books he wove a continuous sequence of Bernard’s deeds, employing the authors’ own words and reducing them, as best he could, to chronological order.

For where Geoffrey, in book III, chapter 4, places the unhappy outcome of the Jerusalem expedition before the Synod of Sens held against Abelard, although the latter preceded it by ten years, Alanus instead places the synod before the expedition. Likewise, in book I, chapter 6 of that same work, Geoffrey relates Gilbert of Poitiers’ refutation at the Council of Reims before Bernard’s preaching against the heretic Henry; and after all these events, in book IV, chapter 1, Bernard’s return from Rome. All these matters are set out in their proper order by Alanus, who is also the first to mention the holy Doctor’s testament, omitted by the other writers.

Indeed, Geoffrey himself confesses in the preface to his third book that in his narrative he observes “the coherence arising from the similarity of deeds rather than that of time.” Moreover, Alanus permits correction of the commonly published computation of years concerning Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. For Geoffrey is said to have accompanied Bernard as a companion when Cardinal Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate, set out for the regions of Toulouse against the heretic Henry—“in the days,” says Alanus, “when Eugenius was newly risen,” and specifically in 1147. Therefore the final period of Geoffrey’s life is not to be assigned to 1138, as *Gallia Christiana* states, but postponed until after 1147, that is, to the following year. This is so both because Geoffrey exercised for fifteen years the office of legate committed to him by Pope Innocent II after 1131, according to the *Acts of the Bishops of Chartres* published in volume II of the *Analecta*; and because Goslenus, his nephew and successor in the see of Chartres, in letters granted to the monastery of Josaphat in 1151, calls that year the third of his episcopate.

What Alanus accomplished in the remainder is shown by his preface to Pontius, fifth abbot of Clairvaux. Pontius succeeded Geoffrey in 1158 and, four years later, was promoted to the see of Clermont. Therefore this writing of Alanus should be dated about 1170. For further information on him, see the notes to Letter 280.

II. The second author, who follows Alanus immediately and whom the learned Pierre-François Chifflet published at Paris in 1679 among four minor works, seems to be Geoffrey himself, the man whose latter three books on the Life of Saint Bernard, together with the second part of the *Miracles*, we printed above. This conjecture concerning the author is not slight.

For in chapter 6 he testifies that he placed first among Bernard’s collected letters the letter written to Robert because of the miracle which he had learned “from the mouth of the very man who wrote it in rain without rain.” This appears to have been the duty of a notary, an office Geoffrey held. In chapter 9 the same author adds concerning himself that his conversion took place through a sermon delivered by the holy Man in the schools at Paris. If this can be applied to Geoffrey, that sermon must be the *Sermon on Conversion to Clerics*, included among the minor works in the second volume, and it should be assigned to 1140. For Geoffrey came to conversion in that year, namely, thirteen years before Bernard’s death, as he himself testifies in the preface to the third book of Bernard’s Life.

Certainly Geoffrey speaks in much the same manner both in the preface to the third book and in the sermon on Saint Bernard when speaking of his own conversion, as does the author in chapter 6 of the following Life. Chifflet printed only certain excerpts from this author, since the remainder agreed with other authors, indeed word for word with the portion of the sixth book of the *Miracles* whose author is Geoffrey himself.

The learned man therefore judges that these were certain collections concerning Bernard’s life and deeds, prepared, as it were, as material for writing his history. Since two learned and serious men, William and Ernald, had composed the first and second books of that history, Geoffrey did not wish to obscure their pious labours with his own work. Leaving untouched the matters they had treated, he pursued the remainder of Saint Bernard’s life in three books, to be attached to the first two. These things are certainly plausible.

III. After Geoffrey’s excerpts—as we shall henceforth call him—come the two likewise incomplete books of John the Hermit on the Life of Saint Bernard. Chifflet, just mentioned, published them in the work to which he prefixed his *Disquisition on the Illustrious Lineage of Saint Bernard*.

John appears to have been called “the Hermit” from his name, not from his manner of life. Perhaps he was not even a monk, but, as he himself testifies in his second preface to Herbert, bishop of Torres in Sardinia, “formerly a regular attendant, while still a boy, among certain of [Bernard’s] disciples.” His first preface was written to Peter, bishop of Tusculum.

From this double preface the time when Peter was writing these books may be inferred. Herbert was writing in 1178; in that year Peter was made cardinal bishop of Tusculum by Alexander III. Add what John says of Abbot Robert, Bernard’s kinsman: “He lived,” he says in book I, no. 5, “for more than sixty-seven years in the monastery under the yoke of regular discipline.” John therefore wrote after 1180, since Robert did not join Bernard before 1113, having previously been offered to the monastery of Cluny.

[Col. 0469]

# The Second Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot, by Alanus, Former Bishop of Auxerre, Author or Compiler

1235. AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0469A]

To the venerable Father PONTIUS, by God’s providence abbot of Clairvaux: Brother ALANUS, humble former priest of the church of Auxerre, eternal salvation in Christ.

Many authors have undertaken to describe the life of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of blessed memory—admirable for virtues and miracles, and no less worthy of imitation—taking up a subject that offered itself in abundance to those who investigated it. We have omitted some things from this same narrative and added very few, setting it out in a shorter account; this was prompted not so much by presumption as, we believe, by reason.

First, the prolixity of writers, though their accounts be true, is commonly burdensome to readers. Secondly, Godfrey [Godefridus], the venerable bishop of the see of Langres [Col. 0469B], Bernard’s kinsman according to the flesh and his companion in conversion and fellow worker in labours according to the Spirit, pointed out certain matters in the work we have undertaken to abridge that were less consonant with truth. For having been brought up with that Saint from childhood, he had learned more accurately what he had seen than another could learn from hearsay. But death overtook that venerable priest, and he left unfinished what he had begun and desired to do.

Moreover, the series of the account itself contains repeated recapitulations of meanings, since several writers often said the same things, though sometimes in different words. And, if one looks carefully, some harsh statements are found inserted there—for example, against authoritative and exalted persons of ecclesiastical and secular power. Far be it from that Olive Tree, bearing the sweetness of its fruit in the house of the Lord, ever to render anything harsh or bitter toward anyone! His constant endeavour, while he lived in the world, was to soothe all people with the oil of his gentleness.

Certainly, the truth of our narrative possesses no uncertain assurance for us, since we have deliberately decided to omit for the sake of brevity many things which we have learned either from his own most sacred mouth or from the trustworthy report of religious persons, as well as the multitude of miracles. Therefore, if our abbreviation pleases the judgment of your purity, then, after whatever may seem fitting to your Holiness has been removed, added, or corrected, it may, with God’s good pleasure and your favour [Col. 0469D], be copied out and published without offence, if we are not mistaken. But if not, it belongs to our humility rather to conceal this little work among ourselves [Col. 0470A] than to bring it forth, lest we seem to desire to disclose what we fear will be of no benefit.

## Chapter I. On the parents, childhood, and character of Saint Bernard

1. Bernard was born in Burgundy, in the town of Fontaines, the native place of his father. His parents were distinguished in worldly rank, but more worthy and noble in the piety of Christian religion. His father, Tescelin, was a man of ancient and lawful military service, a worshipper of God and steadfast in justice. For, pursuing the evangelical military service in accordance with the precepts of the Lord’s Forerunner, he extorted from no one, falsely accused no one, and was content with his wages (Luke 3:14), by which he abounded for every good work [Col. 0470B]. Thus he served his temporal lords with counsel and arms without neglecting to render to the Lord his God what he owed Him.

His mother, Aleth [Alaidis], was from the castle called Montbard. In her own estate she too observed the apostolic rule: subject to her husband (Eph. 5:22), she governed her household under him in the fear of God, devoted herself to works of mercy, and brought up her children in all discipline. She bore seven children, not so much for her husband as for God: six males and one female; all the males were to become monks, and the female a nun. For, as has been said, she gave birth for God, not for the world; and as soon as she had brought each child forth in birth, she herself offered that child to the Lord with her own hands.

For this reason the noble woman refused to commit them to the breasts of others for nursing, as though with her mother’s milk she might in some measure instil in them the nature of maternal goodness. When they had grown for a time under her hand, she raised them more for the desert than for the court, not allowing them to become accustomed to more delicate food, but feeding them with coarser, common fare. Thus, with the Lord inspiring her, she prepared and trained them as though they were soon to be sent directly to God’s service [Col. 0470C].

2. While she had Bernard, the third in the order of her sons, in her womb, she saw a dream foretelling the future: namely, that she bore in her womb a little dog entirely white, reddish on its back, and barking. Greatly alarmed by this, she consulted a certain religious man. Immediately, receiving the spirit of prophecy, he answered the trembling and anxious woman with the words by which David says to the Lord concerning holy preachers, “The tongue of your dogs from among the enemies” (Ps. 76:24) [Col. 0470D–0471A]:

“Do not fear. You shall be the mother of an excellent little dog, who will be guardian of the house of God and will utter great barks for it against the enemies of the faith. He will be an outstanding preacher and, like a good dog, by the grace of a healing tongue will cure in many people many diseases of souls.”

The pious and faithful woman was made joyful by this answer, received as though from God, and was then wholly given over to love for the child not yet born. In keeping with the vision and its interpretation, by which such lofty things were promised concerning him, she resolved to have him instructed in Holy Scripture.

3. And this was done. As soon as she brought him forth in a happy birth, she not only offered him to God, as she customarily did with the others; but, as is read of Saint Anne, mother of Samuel, who dedicated the son she had asked for and received from the Lord to serve continually in His tabernacle (1 Sam. 1), so she too offered him in the Church of God as an acceptable gift. Therefore, as soon as she could, she entrusted him for instruction to teachers of letters in the church of Châtillon, which later, through Bernard’s own work, is known to have been raised from secular life to the Order of regular canons. She did everything in her power to ensure his progress in learning.

The boy, full of grace and strong in natural intelligence, quickly fulfilled his mother’s desire in this respect. In literary study he advanced beyond his age and ahead of his contemporaries; but in worldly matters he already, as it were naturally, began the mortification required for his future perfection. For he was most simple in worldly concerns, loved to dwell within himself, avoided public places, was remarkably reflective, obedient and subject to his parents, gracious and pleasing to all, simple and quiet at home, seldom abroad, and, beyond what could be believed, genuinely modest. He never wished to speak much anywhere; he was devoted to God, so as to preserve his youth pure for Him; and he gave himself to literary studies, through which he might learn and know God in the Scriptures [Col. 0471B–C].

## Chapter II. On his devotion, mercy, and zeal for chastity

4. While still a little boy, Bernard was troubled by a severe pain in his head and took to bed. A little woman was brought to him, supposedly to relieve the pain by charms. When he felt her approach with certain instruments of incantation, he cried out in great indignation and thrust her away from himself.

5. Once the solemn night of the Lord’s Nativity was at hand, and all, according to custom, were preparing for the solemn vigils. Since the hour for celebrating the night office was delayed for some time, Bernard happened, while seated and waiting with the others, to doze a little with bowed head. Immediately the holy Nativity of the child Jesus revealed itself to its child, imparting growth to his tender faith and beginning in him the contemplation of divine mysteries. For He appeared to him as a bridegroom coming forth anew from His chamber. He appeared as though the infant Word were again being born before his eyes from the womb of the Virgin Mother, “fairer in beauty than the children of men,” drawing into Himself the still-childish affections of the holy boy [Col. 0471D–0472A].

Bernard used to confess that he was convinced in his own mind that he had believed that hour to have been the hour of the Lord’s Nativity. Those who frequently attended his teaching could also readily observe how great a blessing the Lord had bestowed upon him in that hour, since in matters concerning this mystery he seemed to have both deeper understanding and more abundant speech. Hence afterwards, in praise of that same Mother and Son and of His holy Nativity, he produced a distinguished little work among the first of his writings or treatises. Its subject is taken from the Gospel passage: “The angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee” (Luke 1:26), and what follows there. Nor should it be passed over that, from those very years of childhood, whenever he could have any coins, he gave secret alms and pursued works of mercy suitable to his age—indeed, beyond his age [Col. 0472B].

6. After some time had passed, Bernard advanced in age and grace before God and men, and passed from childhood into adolescence. His mother, having faithfully brought up her children and seen them enter upon the ways of the world, as though all her own tasks had been completed, happily passed to the Lord. She fell asleep while the clergy who had gathered sang psalms, herself also singing. At the end, when her voice could no longer be heard, her lips were still seen to move, and her quivering tongue to confess the Lord. Finally, amid the petitions of the litany, as the words were being said, “Through Thy passion and cross deliver her, O Lord,” she raised her hand, signed herself, and gave up her spirit; so that she could not lower the hand she had raised [Col. 0472C].

Thereafter Bernard began to live according to his own custom and right. Distinguished by an elegant body and pleasing countenance, adorned with the sweetest character, endowed with keen intelligence and persuasive eloquence, he was spoken of as a youth of great promise. As he entered upon the world, many paths of the world itself began to present themselves to him; the fortunes of this life rose up for him on every side, and great hopes smiled upon him everywhere.

The unlike characters of his companions and their stormy friendships besieged the kindly mind of the young man, striving to make him like themselves. Had these continued to become sweet to him, love of chastity—the sweetest thing settled in his heart in this life—would necessarily have become bitter to him [Col. 0472D]. The twisting serpent, particularly envious of that love, scattered snares of temptations and by diverse encounters lay in wait for his heel.

7. At about this time, at the prompting of the devil, a naked girl was placed in the bed where he was sleeping. Feeling her, he calmly and silently yielded her the part of the bed which he occupied, turned himself to the other side, and slept. The wretched woman lay there for a while, waiting and expecting; then she touched and provoked him. Finally, as he remained unmoved, she—though utterly shameless—blushed, was overwhelmed with great horror and amazement, rose, left him, and fled.

It also happened that Bernard and several companions lodged with a certain married woman. The woman, observing the handsome youth, was caught in the snare of her own eyes and burned with desire for him. As he was apparently the most distinguished of them all, she had a bed prepared for him apart from the others. Rising at night, she shamelessly approached him. Bernard, perceiving her and not lacking a plan, began to cry: “Thieves! Thieves!” At this cry the woman fled, the entire household rose, a lamp was lit, and the thief was sought but not found [Col. 0473A].

They all returned to their beds; silence fell, and darkness returned as before. The others rested, but that wretched woman did not. She rose again and made for Bernard’s bed; but again he cried: “Thieves! Thieves!” The thief was sought again; again she remained hidden and was not exposed by the one man who alone knew. Repelled in this manner three times, the shameless woman at last scarcely ceased, overcome either by fear or by despair.

When they travelled on the following day, Bernard’s companions reproached him and asked what thieves he had dreamed of so often that night. He replied: “There truly was a thief present, and my hostess was trying to steal chastity from me.” [Col. 0473B]

## Chapter III. He conceives contempt and flight from the world, and persuades others thereto
8. Yet amid these things, reflecting and weighing the common saying that it is not safe to live long with a serpent, he began to contemplate flight. For he saw that the world and its prince offered him many things outwardly, promised him many things—great things, greater hopes—but all deceptive: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. But inwardly he continually heard Truth itself crying and saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29). Resolving, therefore, to leave the world more completely, he began to seek and investigate where he might more surely and purely find rest for his soul beneath Christ’s yoke.

As he searched, he encountered at Cîteaux the new planting of a renewed monastic observance: a plentiful harvest, but needing labourers, since scarcely anyone as yet turned aside there for the sake of conversion, because of the extreme austerity of its life and poverty. Yet since these things in no way frightened a mind truly seeking God, setting aside every hesitation and fear, he turned his purpose thither, judging that there he could wholly lie hidden and be concealed. But when his brothers and those who loved him carnally perceived that he was considering conversion, they began by every means to try to divert his mind toward the pursuit of letters, and to bind him more tightly to the world by love of secular learning. By that suggestion, as he himself used to confess, his steps had almost been delayed.

And when on one occasion he was going to those same brothers, who were with Duke Hugh of Burgundy at the siege of the castle called Grancey, he began to be more violently troubled by such thoughts. Finding a certain church on the way, he turned aside and, entering, prayed with a great outpouring of tears, stretching his hands toward heaven [Col. 0474A] and pouring out his heart before the face of the Lord his God. Thus on that day the resolve of his heart was confirmed.

9. Nor did he receive with a deaf ear the voice that says: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17). For from that hour, as a fire which burns a forest, and as a flame consuming mountains, first seizes on what is nearer on every side and then advances into more distant places, so the fire which the Lord had sent into the heart of his servant, willing that it should burn, first attacked his brothers—leaving only the youngest, still less fitted for conversion, with their aged father for consolation—then his kinsmen and acquaintances, companions and friends, and all persons in whom there could be hope of conversion.

The first of all was his uncle Galdric, who, without delay or hesitation, adopted his nephew’s judgment and assented to conversion. He was a worthy and powerful man in the world, renowned for the glory of secular knighthood, lord of a castle in the territory of Autun, called Tuilly. Bartholomew also, who was younger than the other brothers and not yet a knight, immediately came forward and, without difficulty, in that same hour gave assent to the saving counsels.

Andrew, however, likewise younger than Bernard and newly a knight at that time, received his brother’s word with greater difficulty, until he suddenly cried out: “I see my mother.” For she visibly appeared to him, with a serene countenance, smiling and rejoicing at the purpose of her sons. Thus he too immediately gave his hand, and from a novice of the world became [Col. 0474C] a soldier of Christ.

Guy, the firstborn of the brothers, was already bound in marriage: a great man, and already more deeply rooted than the others in the world. At first he hesitated somewhat; but immediately, considering and reconsidering the matter, he consented to conversion—provided his wife agreed. Yet in the case of a noble young woman nursing little daughters, this seemed almost impossible. But Bernard, conceiving a more certain hope in the mercy of the Lord, unhesitatingly promised him that the woman would either consent or die quickly.

At last, when she refused him in every way, her husband, nobly minded—or rather, already anticipated by that strength of faith in which he later shone conspicuously—conceived, by the Lord’s inspiration, a manly plan: casting aside whatever he seemed to possess in the world, he would undertake a rustic life [Col. 0474D], that is, work with his own hands to support himself and his wife, whom he was not permitted to leave unwillingly. Meanwhile Bernard arrived, travelling about and gathering others everywhere. Without delay, Guy’s aforesaid wife was struck by a grave illness. Recognizing that it was hard for her to kick against the goad, she sent for Bernard, begged pardon, and herself first sought assent to conversion. Finally, separated from her husband according to ecclesiastical custom, with a mutual vow of chastity intervening, she entered a community of nuns, serving God devoutly until death.

10. Girard, second in age after Guy, was a valiant knight in arms, of great prudence and exceptional kindness, beloved by all. While the rest, as has been said, yielded on first hearing and on the first day, he judged this rashness, as is the habit of worldly wisdom, and with a stubborn mind rejected the saving counsel and his brother’s exhortations.

Then Bernard, now on fire with faith and wonderfully inflamed with zeal for brotherly love, said: “I know, I know: vexation alone will give understanding to the hearing.” Placing his finger against Girard’s side, he said: “A day will come—and quickly come—when a lance thrust into this side will make an open way to your heart for the counsel of your salvation which you now despise. You will indeed be afraid, but you will by no means die.”

So it was spoken, and so it came to pass. After only a few days, surrounded by enemies, captured and wounded, he was carried away with a lance in his very side, fixed in the same place to which Bernard had applied his finger [Col. 0475B]. Fearing death as though already present, he cried, “I am a monk, a monk of Cîteaux.” Nevertheless he was captured and shut up in custody.

Bernard was summoned by a swift messenger, but did not come. “I knew,” he said, “and foretold that it would be hard for him to kick against the goad. Yet this wound is not for his death, but for life.” And so it proved. He recovered from the wound quickly, beyond expectation; but he did not alter the purpose or vow which he had made.

Though now free from love of the world, he was still held in hostile bonds; and since this alone delayed his purpose, God’s mercy quickly came to him even in this. His brother came, striving to have him released, but achieved nothing. [Col. 0475C] And because he was not even permitted to speak to him, he approached the prison and cried: “Know, brother Girard, that we shall soon depart and enter the monastery. But you, since you are not permitted to leave, be a monk here. Know that willing but being unable is reckoned as deed.”

As Girard became more and more distressed, after a few days he heard in a dream a voice saying to him, “Today you shall be set free.” It was the holy season of Lent. Therefore, about the evening hour of the day, reflecting on what he had heard, he touched his fetters; and behold, the iron snapped partly in his hand, so that he was held less tightly and could walk somewhat. But what was he to do? The door was barred, and a crowd of poor people stood before the doors.

Yet he rose, and—not so much in hope of escape as from weariness of lying there, or curiosity to make the attempt—approached the door of the underground house in which he was bound and confined. As soon as he touched the bolt, the whole fastening fell apart in his hands, and the door of the house opened. Going out slowly, like a man in fetters, he made his way toward the church, where the evening offices were still being celebrated. The beggars standing before the house door, seeing what was happening and struck with divine terror, turned to flight without crying out anything.

When he was already approaching the church, a member of the household of his captivity came out—the brother of the man by whom he was guarded—and, seeing him hastening to the church, said, “You have come late, Girard.” Girard was terrified. “Hurry,” he said; [Col. 0476A] “there is still something for you to hear.” For Girard’s eyes were held, and he did not at all understand what was being done. At length, when this man had taken Girard by the hand, though still fettered, and lifted him up to the higher steps of the church, Girard entered the church. Then, for the first time, the man understood what was happening, but could not restrain him.

In this way Girard, freed from the captivity of love for this world and from the captivity of the children of this world, faithfully fulfilled the vow he had made. In this matter the Lord especially made known from what perfection and grace of holy conduct this servant of God Bernard had begun: in the spirit of him “who makes known things to come,” he could see what was to be as though already accomplished. For when he applied his finger, the lance was visibly present to him in his brother’s side, as he afterward confessed when questioned by those from whom he could not conceal it.

11. One day Bernard entered a church with the others who had gathered with him in the same spirit. That apostolic passage was being read: “God is faithful, for he who began a good work in you will himself perfect it unto the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:6). The devout young man received this as though it had sounded from heaven. Rejoicing, therefore, as the now spiritual father of his brothers regenerated in Christ, and understanding that the hand of the Lord was working with him, he began from this point to devote himself to preaching and to gather all whom he could.

He began to put on the new man; and with those with whom he formerly used to discuss secular letters [Col. 0476C] or worldly matters, he began to speak of earnest things and conversion. He showed that the joys of the world are fleeting, the miseries of life, the swift coming of death, and that life after death will be everlasting, whether in good or in evil. In short: all who had been predestined for this, through God’s grace and the word of his power working in them, and through the prayer and persistence of his servant, first hesitated, then were pierced to the heart; one after another they believed and consented.

Among them Hugh of Mâcon joined him. Later, taken from the monastery of Pontigny—which he himself founded there as abbot—he presided over the Church of Auxerre with the deserved rank and honour of a bishop. Hearing of the conversion of Bernard, his closest companion and friend, he wept as for one lost, hearing that he had died to the world. But when at last opportunity was given them for mutual conversation, after their unlike tears and groans of unlike griefs, words began to be exchanged for words, and considerations compared with considerations. As the spirit of truth was poured into Hugh amid the words of familiar friendship, the words of their mutual conversation began to take on another aspect.

Giving right hands in fellowship of a new life, they became, far more worthily and truly, one heart and one soul in Christ than they had formerly been in the world. But after a few days Bernard was told that this same Hugh had been turned aside by others and was withdrawing from his purpose. Finding an opportunity—because a great gathering of bishops was being held in that region—he hurried to call back the man who was perishing and to travail with him again.

But the aforesaid companions and corrupters of Hugh, seeing Bernard, coveted their prey [Col. 0477A] and took from him every opportunity of speech, blocking every approach. Yet when he could not speak to Hugh, he cried to the Lord for him. While he prayed with tears, a sudden and violent downpour of rain immediately broke out. They had been sitting in the open field because the sky was clear and they expected nothing of the kind. Therefore all scattered at the sudden rain and made for the nearby village. But Bernard, holding Hugh, said, “You will endure the drops of this rain with me.” When they alone remained, the Lord immediately restored serenity both to the sky and to their minds. There the covenant was renewed and the purpose confirmed, which could not thereafter be broken.

12. The sinner saw these things and was angry; he gnawed his teeth and wasted away. But the righteous man, trusting in the Lord [Col. 0477B], triumphed gloriously over the world. As Bernard now preached publicly and privately, mothers hid their sons, wives held back their husbands, and friends turned friends away. For the Holy Spirit gave such power to his voice that scarcely any human attachment could hold anyone back.

As the number increased of those who had consented to this unanimity of conversion, it was as is written of the children of the primitive Church: “The multitude of them had one heart and one soul in the Lord” (Acts 4:32); and they “dwelt unanimously together, and none of the others dared to join themselves to them” (Acts 5:12–13). They had at Châtillon one house which was their own and common to them all, where they assembled, lived together, and conversed. Hardly anyone who was not of their company dared enter it [Col. 0477C].

Yet if anyone did enter, seeing and hearing what was done there, he was convicted by all and judged by all; and, worshipping the Lord and confessing that God was truly among them, either he joined their unanimity, or departed weeping for himself and calling them blessed. For at that time and in those regions it was unheard of that the conversion of a person still living in the world should be foreseen. But they themselves remained, as it were, for six months after their first resolve in secular dress, so that more might be gathered together while certain persons settled their affairs during that time.

13. But when the multitude was beginning to arouse suspicion, lest the one who tempts should snatch away someone from their number [Col. 0477D], it pleased God to reveal what would happen. One of them, in a vision of the night, seemed to see them all sitting together in one house and, one by one in order, as though partaking of a certain food of wondrous whiteness and flavour. While all the others received it very well and with great joy, he observed that two persons out of that whole number remained without a share in that food. One of them did not take it; the other seemed indeed to take it, but because he did so carelessly, it was scattered.

The event afterward proved both matters true. For one, before the time came for the deed, turned backward and returned to the world. The other did indeed begin the good work with the rest, but did not complete it.

## CHAPTER IV. Bernard enters Cîteaux with his companions; concerning his mortification during the time of his novitiate

[Col. 0478A]

14. When the day had now come for fulfilling the vow and accomplishing the desire, Bernard, the father of his brothers, went out from his paternal house with his brothers and with his spiritual sons, whom he had begotten for Christ by the word of life. Guy, the firstborn of his brothers, saw his youngest brother Nivard, a small boy, in the street with other boys, and said: “Come now, brother Nivard: the whole earth of our inheritance looks to you alone.” The boy, moved not childishly, replied: “So heaven is for you, and earth for me? This division has not been made fairly.”

After they had gone, he too followed his brothers a little later, and could not be held back either by his father or by kinsmen and friends. There remained of that household dedicated to God the father and the daughter, of whom we shall speak in their proper place. At that time the new and little Cistercian flock lived under Abbot Stephen. As its smallness had begun to weigh heavily upon him, and all hope of posterity into which the inheritance of that holy poverty might be transmitted had failed—since all venerated in them the holiness of their life but shrank from its austerity—he was suddenly made glad by this divine visitation, so joyful, unexpected, and sudden, that on that day the house seemed to have received this answer from the Holy Spirit: “Rejoice, barren woman who did not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who did not travail: for the children of the desolate are many more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1), [Col. 0478C] of whom afterward you shall see children’s children through many generations.

15. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1113, the fifteenth from the foundation of the house of Cîteaux, the servant of God Bernard, about twenty-two [otherwise, twenty-three] years old, entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions, and under Abbot Stephen submitted his neck to Christ’s sweet yoke. From that day the Lord gave a blessing, and that vineyard of the Lord of hosts gave its fruit, stretching its branches even to the sea and its shoots beyond the sea.

These, then, were the holy beginnings of the conversion of the man of God. But I think that no one can recount the marks of his manner of life—how, living an angelic life, he lived upon earth—unless he lives by the Spirit by whom Bernard lived. For it belongs only to the giver and the recipient to know how greatly, from the very beginning of his conversion, the Lord forestalled him with the blessings of his sweetness; with how great a grace of election he filled him; and how he made him drunk from the abundance of his house.

He entered that house poor in spirit, still hidden and at that time almost insignificant, intending there to die to human hearts and memories, and hoping to lie concealed and hidden like a lost vessel. But God disposed otherwise, preparing him for himself as a vessel of election, not merely to strengthen and enlarge the monastic Order, but to bear his name before kings and nations, and even to the ends of the earth [Col. 0479A]. Bernard himself imagined and thought nothing of the kind concerning himself. Rather, for the guarding of his heart and steadfastness in his purpose, he always had in his heart, and often on his lips, the words: “Bernard, for what have you come?”

And as it is written of the Lord that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), from the first day when he entered the cell of the novices, he began to do in himself what he was to teach others.

16. While he was a novice, sparing himself in nothing, he applied himself by every means to mortify not only the desires of the flesh, which are exercised through the body, but also the very senses through which they are exercised. For when, by the inner sense of an enlightened love, he began to experience more sweetly and more frequently the sweetness breathed into him from above, fearing for that inner sense because of the bodily senses, he allowed them scarcely so much [Col. 0479B] as was sufficient for the fellowship of outward intercourse with people.

As constant practice made this a habit, the habit itself in some manner turned into nature. Wholly absorbed in the spirit, often—with his entire intention directed to God, or his memory wholly occupied in spiritual meditation—seeing, he did not see; hearing, he did not hear; when tasting, he perceived no flavour; he scarcely felt anything through any bodily sense. He had already spent a full year in the novices’ cell when, leaving it, he still did not know whether the house had a vaulting, which we ordinarily call a ceiling. For a long time he had frequently entered and left the church building, while believing that at its east end, where there were three windows, there was only one [Col. 0479C]. Since the sense of curiosity had been mortified, he noticed nothing of this kind; or if he happened on occasion to see it, his memory, occupied elsewhere as has been said, did not attend to it. For without memory the sense of the perceiver is less effective.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Bernard’s endowments and bodily appearance

17. In him nature too did not disagree with grace, so that in him also there seemed in some manner to be fulfilled what is written: “I was a child of good natural ability and received a good soul; and, being more good, I came into an undefiled body” (Wis. 8:19–20). For in contemplating all spiritual or divine things, together with spiritual grace he possessed a certain natural power of intellect. He too received in this respect a good soul: a sensibility neither wantonly curious nor proudly rebellious, but rejoicing with spiritual goods and pursuits, and willingly subject to and serving the spirit in things relating to God. He also had a body unstained by consent to any disgraceful act, a most apt instrument for serving the spirit in God’s service.

A certain grace appeared in his flesh, but it was more spiritual than bodily. A radiance shone in his face—not earthly, certainly, but heavenly. In his eyes a kind of angelic purity and dove-like simplicity gleamed. The beauty of his inner person was so great that it broke outward in manifest signs, and the outer man also appeared suffused from the abundance [Col. 0480A] of inward purity and copious grace.

His entire body was extremely thin and without flesh. His very fine skin was moderately ruddy in the cheeks; for continual meditation and the pursuit of holy compunction had drawn to that place whatever natural warmth there was in him. His hair was coloured blond and white; his beard reddish, sprinkled with grey near the end of his life. His height was of respectable medium stature, though seeming nearer to tallness.

But although, through the gift of prevenient grace, the aid of following nature, and the good practice of spiritual discipline, the flesh in him scarcely desired anything against the spirit—that is, anything that would wound the spirit—the spirit desired against the flesh beyond the strength, beyond the power of flesh and blood, so greatly that the frail creature, falling beneath the burden, could not rise again.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the foundation of Clairvaux and Bernard’s appointment as abbot

18. When it pleased him who had separated Bernard from the world and called him to reveal his glory in him by a fuller grace, and through him to gather into one the many scattered children of God, he put it into the heart of Abbot Stephen to send Bernard and his brothers to build the house of Clairvaux. When they departed, he placed Bernard over them as abbot. They marvelled, being mature and vigorous men, and feared for him both because of the tender age of his youth, and because of bodily weakness and lesser experience in outward affairs.

Clairvaux was a place in the territory of Langres, not far from the river Aube: an ancient den of robbers, formerly called the Valley of Wormwood. There, then, in a place of terror and vast solitude, those men of strength settled, intending to make a temple of God and house of prayer from a den of robbers. There for some time they simply served God in poverty of spirit, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils. Their pottages were often made from beech leaves. Their bread was like that prophetic bread made of barley, millet, and vetches, so that a certain religious man, weeping profusely, secretly carried away what had been set before him as a guest, as though to show all men a miracle: that human beings—and such human beings—lived upon it [Col. 0480D].

But these things moved the man of God little. His chief concern was for the salvation of many—a concern known to have possessed his holy heart with such singular intensity from the first day of his conversion until the end that he seemed to bear toward all souls a mother’s affection. Thus in his heart there was a vehement conflict between holy desire and holy humility. At one time, casting himself down, he confessed himself unworthy for any fruit to come through him; at another, forgetting himself, he burned with the most ardent zeal, so that he seemed able to admit no consolation except from the salvation of many. Love indeed produced confidence, but humility chastened that same confidence.

19. It happened once, after the vigils had been completed, that he went outside and, walking about the neighbouring places, prayed to the Lord that he might accept the service of himself and his brothers. Suddenly, as he stood in prayer with his eyes slightly closed, he saw a multitude of people of various dress and condition descending from all the neighbouring hills into the lower valley—so great a multitude that the valley itself could not contain it [Col. 0481A]. What this vision portended is now manifest to all. Greatly comforted by this vision, therefore, the man of the Lord exhorted his brothers, warning them never to despair of God’s mercy.

20. One day his brother Girard, cellarer of the house, complained to him that many necessities for the brothers were lacking. The man of God asked how much would suffice for their present need. Girard answered: twelve [otherwise, eleven] pounds. Bernard then dismissed him and fled to prayer.

A little while later Girard returned and announced that a certain woman from Châtillon was outside and wished to speak with him. When Bernard went out to her, the woman fell at his feet and offered him the blessing of twelve pounds, begging the man’s prayers for her husband, who was dangerously ill. After briefly addressing her, he sent her away, saying: “Go; you will find your husband well.” Going home, she found him as she had heard.

The abbot then comforted the faint-heartedness of his cellarer and made him stronger henceforth in waiting upon the Lord. This occurred not merely once but often: whenever such need pressed, divine aid certainly came to him from an unexpected source [Col. 0481C]. Therefore prudent men, understanding that the Lord’s hand was with him, feared to trouble the tenderness of his mind—like one newly come forth from the delights of paradise—with anxiety about outward things. They dealt with such matters among themselves as best they could, consulting him only concerning spiritual and inward things.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Bernard’s preaching and the conversion of his father and sister

21. Whenever he addressed them for their edification, speaking things above human capacity to human beings, he was scarcely understood. Yet, judging it sinful, according to the judgment of holy Job, to contradict the words of the saint (Job 6:10), they did not excuse their weakness but accused it. And while those who were reproved humbled themselves at the nod of their reprover, the spiritual master himself began to suspect his zeal toward humble and submissive brothers. Thus the devout humility of the disciples became teacher to the teacher.

For he thought that in their silence they meditated matters much better and nearer to salvation than what they heard from him; and that they worked out their salvation more devoutly and effectively than they could learn from his example. He feared that they might be scandalized by his preaching rather than receive any edification from it. Troubled and saddened by this, with diverse thoughts rising in his heart, after many waves of thought and torments of heart [Col. 0482A], he determined to withdraw himself from all outward matters to inward things and to keep himself in the solitude of his heart and secrecy of silence until the Lord in his mercy should reveal to him his will concerning this matter.

But a few days later, in a vision of the night, he saw a person standing before him in brightness and commanding him with great authority to speak boldly whatever should be suggested to him in the opening of his mouth; for it would not be he who spoke, but the Spirit of God who spoke in him. From then on the Holy Spirit spoke more openly in him and through him, supplying him with a more powerful discourse and a more abundant understanding of the Scriptures, and granting him favour and authority also with his hearers. Hence he spoke both confidently and profitably for teaching, refutation, and correction; and whenever he preached the word of God, whatever he brought forward became so clear and pleasing, and so effective to move his hearers regarding the matter in question, that all marvelled at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth [Col. 0482B].

22. The aforesaid father of Bernard, who had remained at home, came to his sons and was received among them. After he had spent some time there, he died in a good old age.

Their sister too, married in the world and devoted to the world, was in danger amid its riches and delights. At length God inspired her to visit her brothers. When she came as if to see her venerable brother Bernard, attended by a proud retinue and display, he detested and abhorred her as a net of the devil for catching souls and would by no means consent to come out to see her [Col. 0482C].

Hearing this, she was deeply ashamed and pierced with remorse. Since none of her brothers would condescend to meet her, she dissolved wholly into tears and said: “Even if I am a sinner, Christ died for such persons. Because I am a sinner, I seek the conversation and counsel of the good. If my brother despises my flesh, let the servant of God not despise my soul. Let him come and command; whatever he commands, I am ready to do.”

Hearing this promise, her brother came out to her with his brothers. Since he could not separate her from her husband, at the first word he forbade all worldly display in dress and every worldly pomp; he prescribed for her the manner of life of their mother, in which she had lived for a long time with her husband; and so dismissed her. Obediently complying with the command, she returned to her home, suddenly changed by the power of the right hand of the Most High.

All marvelled that a noble and delicately reared young woman, transformed so suddenly in clothing and food, should lead an eremitical life amid the world, devote herself to fasts, vigils, and continual prayers, and make herself wholly alien to every worldly thing. She lived thus with her husband for two years. He too, overcome by the strength of her perseverance, finally released her and granted her liberty to serve the God whose servant she had proved herself to be. Having gained the freedom she desired, she went to the monastery of Jully and vowed the remainder of her life to God with the nuns serving him there [Col. 0483A]. There the Lord granted her such grace of holiness that she was shown to be no less sister to those men of God in spirit than in flesh.

## CHAPTER VIII. The abbot is consecrated by William, bishop of Châlons, who undertakes the care of his health

23. When Bernard, newly sent to Clairvaux, was to be ordained, and the see of Langres was vacant—[Note: [Col. 0483] Namely, through the absence of Joscerannus, who held the see from the year 1112 to 1125.]—to which that ordination belonged, the brothers sought where they should take him for ordination. The good reputation of the venerable bishop of Châlons, the highly renowned master William of Champeaux, presented itself; and they decided to send him there. So it was done.

He went to Châlons, taking with him a certain Cistercian monk named Elbodon. The youth entered the house of the aforesaid bishop, wasted in body and apparently dying, and contemptible also in dress, followed by the older monk, handsome in size and strength of body. Some laughed; others, interpreting the matter as it was, venerated them.

When it was asked which of the two was the abbot, the bishop, having first fixed his eyes upon him, recognized the servant of God and received him as a servant of God. For in their first private conversation, when the youth’s reserve in speaking revealed his prudence better than all eloquence could, the wise man understood that there was a divine visitation in the arrival of his guest; nor was he wanting in charitable hospitality. Taking the confidence of familiarity and freedom of speech, and holding holy conversation with him in turn, he was commended more by his conscience than by words [Col. 0483C].

From that day and hour they became one heart and one soul in the Lord, so much so that not only the bishop’s house but, through him, the whole city of Châlons became the house of the men of Clairvaux. Indeed, through him the province of Reims and all Gaul were stirred to devotion and reverence for the man of God. For from that great bishop others learned to receive and revere Bernard as an angel of God. So great an authority seemed to have foreseen in him the grace of future times, so devoted was he toward an unknown monk—and a monk of such humility.

24. A little time later, when the abbot’s illness had become so severe that nothing seemed to be hoped for except death, or a life more grievous than any death, the same bishop visited him. Seeing him, the bishop said that he had hope not only for his life but for his recovery, if Bernard would follow his counsel and allow some care to be bestowed upon his body according to the measure of his weakness. But Bernard could not easily be moved from the rigour and practice of his customary observance.

The bishop therefore went to the chapter of Cîteaux. There, before the few abbots who had assembled, he prostrated himself wholly upon the ground with episcopal humility and priestly charity, and asked and obtained that Bernard should be entrusted to his obedience for a full year. For what could be denied to such humility in one of such authority? Returning to Clairvaux, the bishop ordered a small dwelling to be built outside the enclosure and bounds of the monastery. He directed and commanded that no strictness of the Order should be imposed upon Bernard in food or drink or anything of that sort; that no concern arising from the whole administration of the house should be brought to him; but that he should live there on his own according to the regimen prescribed by the bishop.

Thus, by command of bishop and abbots, released from every concern of the house, he devoted himself to God and himself, rejoicing as though amid the delights of paradise [Col. 0484A]. That royal chamber inspired such reverence in those who saw it that they felt as though they were entering the altar of God.

A certain rustic man had been entrusted to him by the bishop to attend upon him, boasting that he would cure him. Though Bernard was so gravely ill, foods were offered to him that even a healthy person could scarcely touch except under the pressure of extreme hunger; those who saw it marvelled and wasted away. But he, to whom these things were done, received everything indifferently and approved all alike. For his sense of taste was corrupted and almost dead, and he could scarcely distinguish anything. He said that only water had taste for him, because when he drank it, it cooled his mouth and throat.

## CHAPTER IX. On the vision foretelling the removal of Clairvaux, and its wondrous discipline under Bernard

25. One night, while praying with more than usual attentiveness, he had poured out his soul over himself; and, having fallen into a light sleep, he heard voices as of a great multitude passing by. On waking, and hearing the same voices more distinctly [Col. 0484C], he left the cell in which he lay and followed those who were departing. Not far away was a place still thick with bramble and thorn-bushes, though it has now greatly changed from what it was then. Over this place choirs seemed for some time to stand, arranged on either side in alternating groups; and the holy man listened with delight. Yet he did not understand the mystery of the vision until, some years later, when the buildings of the monastery had been moved—not without divine revelations—he saw an oratory established in that very place where he had heard those voices.

26.
