At that time one might behold the golden age of Clairvaux: when men of virtue, formerly rich and honoured in the world, glorying in Christ’s poverty, planted the Church of God with their own blood, amid toil [Col. 0484D] and hardship, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many distresses; preparing for that holy valley the abundance and peace which it afterwards possessed. One might see, as it were, new heavens upon earth, and the ancient paths of the monks of old Egypt—our fathers—with fresh footprints of saints upon them.

At the very first sight, as those entering Clairvaux descended the mountain, God was known in its dwellings; for the simplicity and humility of the buildings silently spoke of the simplicity and humility of the inhabitants of the valley. In short, in that valley full of people, where no one was permitted to be idle, while all laboured and each was occupied with the task assigned to him, a visitor found at midday the silence of midnight—apart from the sounds of work, or, if the brethren were engaged in the praises of God. Moreover, the discipline and renown of that silence inspired such reverence even in secular visitors that they feared to speak there, not merely what was improper or idle, but even anything relevant to the matter at hand. The solitude of the place itself, amid the shadowy woods and the constricting mountains round about, where God’s servants lay hidden, in some manner represented that cave of the holy father Benedict in which he was once discovered by shepherds; so that those who imitated his life might seem also to possess some likeness of his dwelling and solitude.

For all there were solitary even in the multitude [Col. 0485B]. The ordered love of that valley, though full of men, made each person solitary by the rule of the Order. For just as one disordered man, even when alone, is himself a crowd to himself, so there, through unity of spirit and the rule of regular silence ordering a multitude of men, that very order safeguarded for each the solitude of his heart. Their food was very much like their simple houses and dwellings.

Such, then, in that time under Abbot Bernard and his direction, was the school of spiritual studies in that most renowned and most beloved valley; such was the fervour of regular discipline—all being done and ordered by God, who was building the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him above.

## CHAPTER X. On Bernard’s remarkable mortification in sleep, food, drink, and labour, and on his study of Holy Scripture

[Col. 0485C]

27. Would that, after the first rudiments of his religious life, he had treated himself as he treated others: with such kindness, discernment, and care. But as soon as he was freed from the bond of that year’s obedience and became his own master, he returned like a drawn bow to its former tension, and like a torrent held back and then released to the accustomed course of its earlier flow—as though exacting from himself the penalty for that brief period of repose and the loss caused by interrupted labour. One could see a frail and sickly man attempting and undertaking whatever he wished, giving too little thought to what he was able to do; anxious for everyone, negligent concerning himself; [Col. 0485D] most obedient to all others in all things, yet scarcely ever obedient, in his own case, either to charity or to authority.

For he always counted what he had previously done as nothing and planned greater things, sparing not his body and seeking to add strength to spiritual pursuits, while wearing down by unremitting fasts and vigils a body already weakened through various illnesses.

28. What shall we say of sleep, which for other people commonly refreshes their labours and senses, or restores their minds? From the beginning of his conversion he kept watch, as long as he lived, beyond human capacity; and of no time did he complain more that it was lost than the time when he slept. He regarded the comparison of death and sleep as very apt: thus sleepers appear dead to human beings, just as the dead appear to God to be asleep [Col. 0486A].

In him a scanty sleep accompanied a scanty diet. In neither did he allow his body satiety; it was enough for him in each merely to have taken something. As to vigils, the limit he set to his watchfulness was not to spend the whole night without sleep. As to food, he was scarcely ever drawn to eat by pleasure, but only by fear of exhaustion. Indeed, when about to eat, he was satisfied by the mere remembrance of food before he ate. Thus he approached taking food as though approaching torture.

His flesh was afflicted with many discomforts of sickness, so that the strength of his spirit might be made perfect in them. The more dangerous of these was in the passage of his extremely constricted throat, which admitted nothing at all dry and scarcely anything solid [Col. 0486B]; more troublesome was weakness of the stomach and corruption of the internal organs. These were continual, apart from others that occurred more often. For his constitution, always exceedingly delicate and tender, had been worn down by many fasts and vigils, cold and labour, and harsh, continual exercises; and because his stomach was impaired, he continually rejected through his mouth what he had taken in, still raw.

If something, having been digested by natural processing, passed downwards, it nevertheless emerged only with severe torment, because those lower parts of his body too were afflicted with no lesser discomforts of sickness. And if anything remained, it was whatever nourishment his body received—not so much to sustain life [Col. 0486C] as to postpone death. After eating, he would always, as it were, weigh how much he had eaten; if he found that he had exceeded his usual measure even slightly, he did not suffer for it without penalty. Indeed, the habit of frugality had so become second nature to him that, if he ever wished to allow himself somewhat more than usual of any bodily refreshment, he could scarcely do so.

29. He prayed standing by day and night, until his knees, weakened by fasting, and his feet, swollen from labour, could no longer support his body. For a long time, and as long as it could remain concealed, he wore a hair-shirt next to his flesh; but when it became known, he immediately cast it aside and adopted the common practice. For his chief concern was to avoid admiration and to conduct himself as one among the rest. Yet glory pursued him as he fled from it, just as it usually flees those who seek it.

This proverb was frequently on his lips and always in his heart: “He who does what no one else does is admired by everyone.” With this in view, he cultivated all the more the common life and rule, preferring nothing in his actions that involved singular observance [Col. 0486D]. Yet even in those common practices he possessed a singular purity and an uncommon devotion.

30. His food, with bread, was milk, or water in which vegetables had been boiled, or porridge such as is usually made for infants; sometimes it was a morsel of bread thoroughly softened in water, with a few small sips. Other things either his illness would not receive or he himself refused out of devotion to frugality. If he used wine at all, it was rarely and in very small quantity, since he declared that water suited both his illness and his appetite better.

Physicians saw him and marvelled at his way of life, and at the violence he inflicted upon his own nature—as though a lamb tied to a plough were forced to plough. For when those frequent eruptions through his mouth of undigested raw matter, caused by his impaired stomach, began to trouble others, especially in the choir during the singing of psalms, he did not immediately leave the gatherings of the brethren. Rather, beside the place where he stood, he arranged and dug a receptacle in the ground, and for some time endured that necessity of his suffering as best he could. But when the intolerability of the condition would not even permit this, he was finally compelled to leave the gatherings [Col. 0487A] and live apart by himself—except when, for consolation, for the discipline of the cloister, or for some definite necessity, he had to be present at the community of brethren.

31. Thus from the beginning he was strong in spirit and weak in body; yet he never consented that any indulgence should be shown him concerning bodily rest or refreshment, nor any relaxation from the common labour or work. For he considered the other monks holy and perfect, but himself like a novice and beginner, as needing not the indulgences and relaxations granted to veterans and the perfect, but the fervour of a novice, the strictness of the Order, and the rigour of discipline.

Therefore, as a most ardent imitator of common life and observance, when the brethren were engaged in some manual task from which either his lesser usefulness or his lack of skill excluded him, he made up for it by digging, cutting wood and carrying it on his own shoulders, or by other equally laborious work [Col. 0487C]. Where his strength failed, he had recourse to the lowliest tasks and compensated for the lack of labour by humility. It is remarkable that the man who had received such great grace in contemplation of spiritual and divine things not only endured being occupied with such matters, but took the greatest delight in them.

And, his faculty of sense having been mortified as stated above, by the privilege of greater grace he laboured in the power of the spirit both, as it were, wholly outwardly and wholly inwardly occupied with God: in the one, nourishing his conscience; in the other, his devotion.

32. During the time of labour, therefore, he prayed or meditated inwardly without interrupting his external work [Col. 0487D], and he worked outwardly without loss of inward sweetness. For whatever he understood spiritually in the Scriptures, he confessed that he had received chiefly while meditating and praying in woods and fields. Joking graciously with his friends, he would say that he had never had any teachers in this matter except oaks and beeches.

When free from labour or external work, he continually either prayed, read, or meditated. If solitude was available for prayer, he used it; if not, wherever he was—whether by himself or in a crowd—he created for himself the solitude of the heart and was alone everywhere. He read the canonical Scriptures simply and consecutively, more willingly and more frequently than anything else. He said that he understood them more by their own words than by any others [Col. 0488A], and testified that whatever divine truth or power shone out for him in them tasted better at the fountainhead of its original source than in the flowing streams of interpretations.

Yet he humbly read the holy and orthodox expositors of Scripture. He did not regard his own understanding as equal to theirs, but submitted it to be formed by them; faithfully adhering to their footsteps, he often drank himself from the fountain from which they had drawn.

## CHAPTER XI. On the miracles performed by God through him in sickness, for which he was reproved by his own brethren

33. Thus the Wisdom of God chose through the weakness of that man to confound the many and mighty strengths of this world. For what, which according to the grace given to him ought to be done through him, was ever left unfinished because of any bodily weakness? Who in our age, however robust in body and sound in health, ever accomplished as much as this dying and sickly man did, for the honour of God and the benefit of holy Church?

How many people afterwards did he draw from the world by word and example—not only to conversion, but to perfection! How many houses, like cities of refuge, did he establish from among them throughout the whole Christian world! For those who had sinned unto death and were liable to be condemned to eternal death remember, turn to the Lord, flee to these houses, and are saved in them. Who could enumerate the innumerable benefits which he bestowed individually upon countless people, according to cause, person, place, and time?

Moreover, his life, which was proposed to all for imitation, ought not to have lacked the example of frugal self-restraint [Col. 0488C]. In this the servant of God perhaps exceeded through excess; but to devout minds he left an example not of excess, but of fervour. Indeed, he was not ashamed to accuse himself for this, since he feared all his works, reproaching himself because he had withdrawn his body from the service of God and of his brethren by making it weak and almost useless through undiscerning fervour.

34. Yet though sickly, he became powerful in God’s work. For the power of God, shining more brightly in his weakness, gave him a certain worthier reverence among people; reverence gave him authority, and authority obedience. Already then he was being divinely prepared for the work of preaching, for which, as stated above, he had long before been marked out from his mother’s womb with the testimony of divine revelation (ch. 1, no. 2).

At first he devoted the first fruits of his youth to restoring in the monastic Order the fervour of ancient religious life, applying himself with every care, by example and word within the enclosure of the monastery, to the salvation of the brethren. Afterwards, when the necessity of his illness separated him from the common life of the community more than usual, this first became the occasion for him, as though exposed to people from the world—whose great multitude was now flocking to him—to make his presence more freely and generously available to them and preach the word of life.

And when obedience sometimes drew him farther from the monastery for matters concerning the common interests of the Church [Col. 0489A], wherever he came he could not be silent about God and did not cease to do what concerned God. Thus he quickly became known among people, so that the Church of God, having found so useful a member in its body, did not refrain from employing him wherever necessary. From that time there was more abundantly added to him day by day the manifestation of the Spirit that was in him for the common good: namely, a more fruitful word of wisdom and knowledge, together with the grace of prophecy, workings of miracles, and aids of various healings.

35. The brethren and spiritual sons of this blessed man marvelled at what they heard and saw of him. Yet, unlike carnal people, they were not exalted into human glory; rather, with spiritual concern they feared for his youthful age [Col. 0489B] and still recent religious life. In this zeal his uncle Galdric and Guy, the first-born of the brothers, surpassed the others, so that they seemed to have been divinely granted as two bodily goads lest the greatness of his graces should exalt him.

They did not spare harsh words, troubling his tender modesty, even maligning his good deeds, reducing all signs to nothing, and frequently afflicting this most gentle man—who offered no contradiction—with reproaches and insults even to tears. The venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, a blood-relative of the holy man, his companion in conversion, and thereafter his inseparable companion in all things, used to relate that Guy, the aforesaid brother of Bernard, was present at the first miracle which he saw performed by Bernard’s hand.

They were passing through Castrum-Nantonis, in the territory of Sens, and a young man whose foot was afflicted by a fistula earnestly begged for the touch and blessing of the aforesaid father Bernard. Having been signed, he was immediately restored to health; and when they returned through the same town a very few days later, they found him safe and well. Nevertheless, the oft-mentioned brother of the blessed man could not be restrained even by that miracle from rebuking him and accusing him of presumption because he had consented to touch the man: so greatly did he care for him in love.

36. When Bernard, the man of the Lord, had spent some time at Clairvaux [Col. 0489D], it happened that a nobleman, his kinsman according to the flesh, Josbert of La Ferté—a town near the monastery of Clairvaux—fell gravely ill. Suddenly overcome, he lost altogether both understanding and speech. His son, the younger Josbert, and all his friends were therefore all the more distressed, because that distinguished and highly honoured man was likely to die without confession and Viaticum.

A messenger ran to the abbot, for he was not then in the monastery. Bernard came and found him already lying thus for three days. Moved with compassion for the man, by the tears of his son, and likewise by the mourning of the others, and trusting in God’s mercy, he addressed them in these weighty words:

“It is known to you that this man has burdened churches in many ways, oppressed the poor, and offended God. If you will trust me, so that what has been taken may be restored to the churches and the exactions imposed to the burden of the poor may be abandoned, he shall speak again, make confession of his sins, and devoutly receive the divine sacraments.”

All marvelled; the son rejoiced; the whole household exulted. Whatever the man of God commanded was firmly promised and fulfilled. But his brother Gerard and his uncle Galdric, who were with him, were greatly frightened and disturbed; they approached him privately about such a promise, rebuked him more harshly, and attacked him more fiercely. He replied to them briefly and simply: “God can easily do what you find hard to believe.”

Accordingly, after private prayer he proceeded to offer the sacrifice of immortality. While he was offering it, a messenger arrived to report that the aforesaid Josbert, now speaking freely, was urgently begging the man of God to hasten to him [Col. 0490B]. Bernard came after offering the Sacrifice. With tears and groaning Josbert confessed his sins, received the divine sacraments, and, two or three days afterwards, while still alive and speaking, decreed that the matters especially commanded by the holy abbot should be observed without any retraction. He also set his household in order and gave alms; and thus at last, in good hope of God’s mercy, he breathed out his soul in Christian fashion. This was indeed a sign made famous in the world by Christ through the hand of his servant.

## CHAPTER XII. On the healing and death of Galdric, and the release from Purgatory of an impatient brother

[Col. 0490C]

37. At about the same time his uncle Galdric, who, from zeal of devout concern, had overwhelmed Bernard’s gentleness with harsh rebukes, as we said above, suffered from very severe fevers. At length, as the illness worsened, overcome by the very intensity of his pain, he addressed the abbot in humble entreaty, asking him to have mercy on him and bring him the help he customarily afforded others.

Bernard, whose spirit was sweeter than honey, first gently and briefly recalled Galdric’s frequent reproofs on such matters, and charged him not perhaps to be saying this to test him. Nevertheless, because Galdric persisted, he laid his hand upon him and commanded the fever to depart. Without delay, at Bernard’s command the fever left him; and Galdric experienced in himself what he had criticized in others [Col. 0490D].

The same Galdric, after spending some years in Clairvaux, fervent in spirit and an imitator of every good, departed from this life. About an hour before his death he was momentarily troubled, and, shaking terribly throughout his body, groaned. But he immediately returned to his former serenity and thereafter breathed his last with a most peaceful countenance.

The Lord did not wish the abbot’s concerned mind to be denied knowledge of this event. For a few days later the same Galdric appeared to him in a vision of the night. When, in answer to Bernard’s inquiry, he said that all was well with him and rejoiced that he had been placed in great blessedness, he was finally asked what was meant by that bitter and sudden disturbance at his death. Galdric said that at that hour two evil spirits had been preparing to cast him, as into a pit of dreadful depth [Col. 0491A], and that he had trembled thus in terror; but, when blessed Peter hastened to him, he was rescued and thereafter suffered no harm.

38. It would take too long to recount everything that divine grace had customarily revealed to Bernard from the very beginning concerning those who had departed this life, their blessedness, or even their need. Yet there was one instance that the Father himself used sometimes to recall, for the admonition of the brethren.

A certain brother, of good intention but of a harsher manner toward the other brethren and less compassionate than he ought to have been, died in the monastery. A few days later he appeared to the man of God with a mournful countenance and wretched appearance, signifying that things were not going as he wished. When Bernard asked what had happened to him, he complained that he had been handed over to four *dilaceratis* [“torn” or “rending ones”; the reading is materially uncertain].

At those words he was immediately driven away, as though hurled headlong, from the presence of the man of God [Col. 0491B]. Bernard, groaning more deeply, cried after him: “I command you in the name of the Lord to make known to me again, in the near future, how matters stand with you.” Then he turned to prayer for him and to the offering of the saving victim; he also urged some brethren, whose greater holiness he knew, to assist the same brother. Nor did he desist until, as he had commanded, he deserved to be consoled by another revelation informing him of the brother’s release.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Bernard’s illness, his rapture before the tribunal of God, and the cure of his sickness

[Col. 0491C]

39. The man of God himself once fell ill, and a kind of stream of phlegm flowed incessantly from his mouth. His body being wholly exhausted and failing, he came very near the end. His sons and friends gathered, therefore, as though for the funeral rites of so great a father. And as he seemed already to be drawing his last breath, he saw himself, in an ecstasy of mind, presented before the Lord’s tribunal. Satan too stood opposite, assailing him with wicked accusations.

When Satan had set forth everything, and it was the man of God’s turn to speak for himself, Bernard, neither frightened nor disturbed, said:

“I confess that I am not worthy, nor can I obtain the kingdom of heaven by my own merits. But my Lord possesses it by a twofold right: namely, by inheritance from the Father and by the merit of his Passion. Being content with the one, he gives the other to me; and claiming it for myself by right through his gift, I am not ashamed.”

At these words the enemy was confounded, the assembly was dissolved, and the man of God returned to himself. Since he expected from this that the dissolution of his body was now nearer, another, very different vision followed. He seemed to himself to be standing on a shore, waiting for a ship that would carry him across. When the ship reached the shore, he hastened to board it, but it drew back and struck out into the water. After doing this three times, the ship at last left him behind and went away without returning. He immediately understood that the time of his departure had not yet come.

Nevertheless, the pain still increased, made all the more grievous because the hope of imminent release no longer consoled him [Col. 0492A]. It happened, as evening was drawing on, that the other brethren went, as was customary, to the reading of the Conferences; the abbot alone remained in the lodging where he lay, with two brethren attending him. As he was more violently afflicted and the pain increased beyond his strength, he called one of the two and ordered him to go at once and pray. The brother excused himself, saying, “I am not such a man of prayer”; but Bernard compelled him by the authority of obedience.

He went and prayed at the three altars in that basilica: first, the altar in honour of the blessed Mother of God; and the two which stood beside it, in honour of blessed Lawrence the martyr and blessed Benedict the abbot. At that same hour the aforesaid blessed Virgin came to the man of God, attended by those two ministers, blessed Lawrence and blessed Benedict. They appeared with the serenity and sweetness fitting to them, and so clearly that from the very entrance of the cell he could distinguish the person of each one. Laying their hands upon him and gently touching the places of pain, they immediately drove away all sickness. For the stream of phlegm was at once dried up, and all pain departed [Col. 0492B].

## CHAPTER XIV. On his daily exercise, outstanding virtues, and manner of preaching

40. He could now stand only with difficulty, but he sat almost continually and moved very seldom. Whenever he could withdraw himself from affairs, he was either praying, reading, writing, engaged in teaching and the edification of the brethren, or persisting in sacred meditation [Col. 0492C]. In this spiritual pursuit he had obtained a singular grace: he endured neither weariness nor any difficulty, living freely with himself and walking in the spaciousness of his heart, and there preparing for Christ—as he himself used to urge others to do—a large furnished upper room.

Yet, though thus disposed, he frequently postponed this pursuit for more abundant gains, constrained by divine fear or the spirit of charity; for he had learned to seek not what was useful to himself, but what was useful to many. From the beginning he had desired by every means to withdraw from affairs and never to go out, but to remain in the monastery. Later, because of his bodily weakness, he thought he had found a fitting occasion for this, and at one time resolved upon it and maintained it for some while [Col. 0492D], until the grave necessity of the Church of God and of the supreme pontiff, together with the command of all the abbots of his Order, compelled him to go out. To all these he deferred in every respect as to fathers.

By their command also, in his last years, he used, besides his cowl and tunic, a woollen cloth cut short in the fashion of a cloak, and a similar cap. Amid so many bodily ailments and labours, he never consented to use furs.

41. Poverty in clothing always pleased him; filth never did. He said that filth was a sign of a mind either negligent, vainly self-glorifying, or seeking petty human praise. His gait and entire bearing were modest and disciplined, displaying humility, breathing piety, manifesting grace, and demanding reverence; by sight alone they gladdened and edified those who looked upon him [Col. 0493A].

People frequently heard him say, as he marvelled at the loud laughter of religious persons, that he did not remember having laughed thus at any time from the first years of his conversion onward, so that he had not needed rather to force himself to laugh than to restrain himself from it. He was carefully on guard against idle or frivolous speech, observing in practice what he had poured forth from the abundance of his heart when writing to Pope Eugenius:

“If trifles sometimes arise, perhaps they must be endured, but never repeated. One should indeed break forth into something serious, which they may hear not only profitably but willingly, and so desist from idle talk; one must intervene cautiously and prudently against frivolity.”

How earnestly he fled trifles may readily be inferred from the hatred with which he pursued detraction [Col. 0493B].

42. How unwillingly, and not from bitterness of heart, he uttered a bitter word was especially evident from how easily he restrained such an impulse. For he marvelled at the perversity and hardness of certain people, who, when perhaps troubled, find it burdensome to accept any reasonable excuse or any humble satisfaction. Their very passion of disturbance so delights them that they hate every remedy and make every effort to ensure that an agitation once begun cannot be calmed and healed.

He used rebuke more rarely, dealing rather through warnings and entreaties. Indeed, he shone outstandingly in freedom of spirit, yet together with humility and gentleness, so that in some sense he appeared both to fear no one and to revere every person. How conciliatory and persuasive, and how learned, a tongue God gave him—so that he knew whom he ought to address and when; to whom consolation or entreaty, and to whom exhortation, was fitting—may be known in some measure by those who have read his writings, though much less than by those who often heard his words.

He who had set him apart from his mother’s womb for the work of preaching gave him a voice strong enough and intelligible in a frail body [Col. 0493C]. Whenever a fitting opportunity presented itself, he spoke to every sort of person concerning the edification of souls, in a manner suited to the understanding, character, and pursuits which he knew in each, and fitting to his hearers. He spoke to rustic populations as though he had always been brought up in the countryside; to every other class of people as though he had devoted all his effort to investigating their occupations. Learned among the learned, simple among the simple, abounding in teachings of perfection and wisdom among spiritual men, he adapted himself to all, desiring to win all for Christ.

Thus it was that even when speaking to German peoples he was heard with marvellous feeling. Though, being people of another language, they could not understand his discourse, their devotion appeared more edified by his speech than by an interpreter speaking after him whose translation they fully understood, however skilled that interpreter might be; they seemed more to feel the power of Bernard’s words. The certain proof of this was their beating of breasts and shedding of tears [Col. 0494A].

For divine power had granted him such grace that, although he chose to be lowly in the house of God, he nevertheless bore more abundant fruit than many raised on high, and illuminated the Church more brightly from beneath the bushel of his humility than many placed upon a lampstand. Whenever any necessity drew him outside the monastery, he sowed upon all waters, publicly and privately proclaiming the word of God. Yet he did this itself by command of the supreme pontiff and also at the bidding of other bishops, wherever one of them happened to be present; and he showed all the more deference to priests in every matter because he had more fully understood the reverence due to Christ’s ministers.

For modesty had been innate in him from childhood and remained with him until his last day. Therefore, although he was great and exalted in the word of glory, he never, as he often testified, spoke before any assembly, however humble, without fear and reverence; he preferred to remain silent unless obedience or the urgings of his own conscience compelled him to speak in the fear of God and brotherly charity [Col. 0494B].

## CHAPTER XV. On his reputation for holiness, the growth of Clairvaux, and his care and love for his brethren

43. While Bernard, beloved by God and men, flourished with many and great virtues and miracles in his valley and in the neighbouring cities and regions, he began to appear more and more wonderful and venerable in the eyes of all. Afterwards, as he happily advanced both in the practice of holy preaching and in the example of his manner of life, the net of God’s word in the hand of God’s fisherman began to enclose such abundant multitudes of rational fish that the little boat of that house seemed capable of being filled by each of his catches.

Thus it came about that, in a short time, by a miracle greater than all the miracles he performed in this life, through one sickly man and by the cooperation of God’s grace, that valley, obscure until then, became Clairvaux both in fact and in name [Col. 0494C]. As every day a great multitude from various regions and ranks flocked there, the monastic dwelling was moved from the narrower parts of the valley—not without certain divine revelations—and afforded its inhabitants a broader and more level place.

Already the daughter-houses of that Order, and the daughters of the daughters of that house, had filled many wildernesses on both sides of the Alps and beyond the seas, as people continually flocked in and places had to be sought for them. For brethren were requested from every quarter and sent out by him; kings of nations, bishops of Churches, cities, and regions counted themselves blessed if they deserved to obtain some fellowship from that house and from the discipline of the man of God.

Indeed, through him this religious observance extended even to barbarian nations in which natural savagery had, as it were, stripped away human nature. There, through it, beasts of the forest become human beings; accustomed to live with human beings, they learn from the ends of the earth to sing a new song to the Lord. For, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, wherever he went, he returned full, and his own fullness accompanied him; while some departed and others came to take their place, the fullness of that holy congregation was never diminished in his days [Col. 0495A].

44. Yet he did not abandon those whom he sent out from himself; wherever they were, he was always with them in paternal concern. For every day, whether joyful or sad, matters concerning his sons came back to him. Often, even without any report through flesh and blood, it was divinely made known to him what was happening concerning some of them far away from him: whether anything had to be provided for them or corrected in them, as also their temptations and failings, illnesses and deaths, and the assaults of various tribulations [Col. 0495B]. Indeed, for particular necessities of absent brethren, he often appointed prayer among the brethren present around him. Sometimes also those dying in other places are known to have come to him in a vision, asking his blessing and leave—doubtless through the obedience of those sent and the charity of him who sent them.

On one occasion a monk of Foigny was present before him, about to return immediately to his own house. Having received an answer concerning the matters for which he had come, he was already departing, when the Prophet of God, recalling him in the spirit and power of Elijah, first named a certain brother of that house and, in the hearing of several persons, commanded him to correct certain hidden matters; otherwise, he should expect God’s judgment upon himself in the coming year. [Col. 0495C] Astonished, the man to whom he was speaking asked who had told him this. “Whoever it was,” he said, “who told me, go and say what I tell you; lest, if you conceal it, an equal punishment for sin engulf you also.”

Guy, brother of the man of God, the eldest among his brothers, was a man whose seriousness and truthfulness were known to all who knew him. Once, when he was speaking of religious men of this kind, although according to his habit and customary effort he played down the virtues of his brethren, he finally, unwilling to weary those among whom he was then speaking, said: “I do not tell you things that I do not know; but one thing I know and have experienced: many things are divinely revealed to him in prayer.”

## CHAPTER XVI. Of the events that occurred on his visit to Saint Hugh and the Carthusians, and of Stephen of Vitry’s feigned conversion.

[Col. 0495D]

45. When the Servant of God had now spent some years at Clairvaux, he conceived the desire to visit, out of devotion, Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the Carthusian brethren. The aforesaid holy bishop received him with such pleasure and reverence, recognizing the divine presence in the visit of this guest of his, that he prostrated himself to the ground in adoration. But when the Servant of Christ saw the bishop—advanced in age, renowned in reputation, conspicuous for holiness—falling down before him, he was profoundly alarmed. He too fell before him; and only then, received with the kiss of peace, he complained with a deep sigh that his humility had been confounded by the veneration of so great a man [Col. 0496A].

From that time he held a singular place in Hugh’s heart, so that thereafter those two sons of light became one heart and one soul, delighting in one another in Christ. At the Charterhouse also, the Servant of Christ was received with the same affection and reverence by the most reverend man Guigo, the venerable Prior, and by the other brethren. They rejoiced gladly because they found him present to be such as they had previously known him through letters.

Moreover, while they were edified by him in every other respect, one thing somewhat troubled the aforesaid Carthusian Prior: namely, the trappings of the animal on which the venerable man rode, which seemed insufficiently expressive of poverty. The lover of virtue did not suppress in silence what he had conceived in his mind; rather, speaking with one of Bernard’s brethren, he confessed that he was somewhat disturbed and surprised [Col. 0496B]. When that brother reported to the holy Father what he had heard, Bernard himself was no less astonished, asking what sort of trappings they were. For, travelling from Clairvaux as far as the Charterhouse, he had never noticed them and until that moment had not known at all what they were like. Indeed, the animal was not his own, but had been lent by a Cluniac monk, and its equipment was such as that monk was accustomed to provide for himself.

When the Prior heard this, he especially marveled that the servant of God, Bernard the abbot, had so restrained his outward eyes and occupied his inward mind that what had first offended the Prior’s sight had not been noticed by Bernard over the course of so long a journey. Likewise, travelling for an entire day beside Lake Lausanne, he paid it no attention whatever—or did not see that he saw it. For when, at evening, his companions spoke of that lake, he asked them where it was; and they were all astonished [Col. 0496C].

46. When the holy abbot frequently visited Châlons because of the aforesaid Bishop William, on one return journey he drew along with him a crowd of noble and learned clerics and laymen. While they remained in the guesthouse and he watered the new plantings with heavenly words, the porter, a monk, arrived and announced that Stephen of Vitry, their master, was present to renounce the world and remain with them. Who would not have rejoiced at the arrival of such a man? Especially since that valley did not yet abound greatly in grain of this kind.

But Bernard, while the Holy Spirit revealed to him the snares of spiritual wickedness, sighed silently for a little while, then burst into speech, to everyone’s astonishment: “A malignant spirit,” he said, “has brought him here; he came alone, and alone he will return” [Col. 0496D]. All were dumbfounded; previously, upon hearing of Stephen’s arrival, they could scarcely contain themselves for joy. Nevertheless, lest he scandalize his children, still young, he received the man and earnestly admonished him concerning perseverance and the other pursuits of virtue. Knowing and foreseeing that, though promising everything, he would accomplish nothing, he admitted him into the novices’ cell to be tested with those who would persevere.

Later Stephen himself saw, as he confessed, while he was staying in the novices’ cell, a little dark-skinned boy drawing him away from the oratory. Although he remained there for nearly nine months [Col. 0497A], he finally failed; and, as had been foretold of him, just as he had come alone, so he departed alone.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of Bernard’s remarkable authority and renown among all persons.

47. To return, then, to our account of this man of God, the abbot: so many and such great miracles were performed through him that anyone wishing to recount them all either orally or in writing might produce disbelief in unbelievers, or weariness in those prone to satiety. Yet the radiance of his works clearly showed how pure was the eye of intention in all his words and deeds. For although he always fled the honor of this world, he did not escape the authority of every honor.

For to whose will did all power—both secular and ecclesiastical dignity—ever yield so completely? To whose counsel did it humble itself so thoroughly? Proud kings, princes and tyrants, soldiers and plunderers, feared and revered him so greatly that what is written in the Gospel seems to have been fulfilled in them: “Behold,” says the Lord to his disciples, “I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19) [Col. 0497B].

Among spiritual persons, however, and wherever spiritual matters were examined spiritually, his authority was of another and far greater kind. Whenever he spoke or expounded, the others humbly submitted their own perceptions and understandings to his perceptions and understanding. In the breast of this man of God, purity and sweetness dwelt united by an equal bond: each was sufficiently marvelous, yet their union was more marvelous still. Thus sweetness made his purity lovable, and purity made his sweetness acceptable; so that it was difficult to judge whether he won more affection or more reverence [Col. 0497C].

For who, however strict his manner of life, would not revere Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux? Who, however dissolute, would not be sweetly drawn toward him? His own heart was indeed full of the sweetest affections; yet whenever necessary, he freely rebuked others in a spirit of gentleness. He was most humane in affection, but stronger still in faith. To offer a brief example: as he himself testifies, he celebrated the funeral rites of his own brother Gerard, an indispensable friend, with dry eyes, and with dry eyes committed his body to burial, lest affection seem to overcome faith [Col. 0497D].

The divine hand had formed him to bear even richer fruit, so that sweetness of character softened his austerity, while holiness preserved his authority. For to whom would such great kindness be burdensome, or such great goodness fail to be honorable?

48. It seems altogether difficult to find in any histories a single man still living among humankind who possessed throughout the whole earth a name so renowned and beloved, from the rising to the setting of the sun, from the north and the sea. To mention those provinces from which more certain records are known to survive: his reputation was most celebrated in the Eastern Church, among the westernmost Irish, in the south at the remote limits of Spain, and in the north upon the far-off islands of Denmark and Sweden. He received frequent letters from every quarter and sent replies. Gifts (*xenia*) were sent to him from every quarter; his blessing was sought from every quarter [Col. 0498A].

Therefore that bishop does not seem to have claimed anything inappropriate who, after Bernard’s holy death, while consoling the brethren, truthfully continued among other praises of him: “His sound has gone out into all the earth, and his words unto the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4).

Yet the humility of his heart surpassed the loftiness of his name. In fact, as he frequently confessed, amid the highest honors and the favor of peoples or exalted persons, he seemed to have borrowed another man for himself and considered himself absent, regarding it as a kind of dream. But when simpler brethren, as commonly happens, spoke familiarly with him and enjoyed his friendly humility, there he rejoiced that he had found himself [Col. 0498B] and had returned to his own person. And although the marks of sacred virtues commended this holy man so greatly before God and men, proofs of holiness surrounded him, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit made him illustrious, charity—which possessed him wholly—being patient and kind, overcame malice by wisdom, impatience by patience, and pride by humility.

## CHAPTER XVIII. By his authority Pope Innocent is received.

49. At that time the Roman Church was suffering under the schism of Peter Leo. Therefore, when a conference was called at Étampes in the year 1130, the holy abbot, specially summoned by the king of the Franks himself and by the leading bishops, arrived—as he later confessed—in no small fear and trembling, for he did not fail to recognize the danger and weight of the matter [Col. 0498C]. Yet on the journey God comforted him, showing him in a vision of the night the great Church singing harmoniously in praise of God; hence he hoped that peace would certainly result.

When they had come to the place, after a fast had first been observed and prayers poured out to God, the king and bishops, together with the princes, sat down to deliberate upon the matter. The counsel of all was one, their judgment one: that the cause of God should be entrusted to the Servant of God, and that the entire case should depend upon his mouth. Though afraid and trembling, he nevertheless accepted this task, complying with the admonitions of faithful men. Having carefully set forth the order of the elections, the merits of the persons elected, and the life and reputation of the candidate first elected [Col. 0498D], he opened his mouth, and the Holy Spirit filled it. Thus, speaking with the voice of all, he declared that Innocent should be received by all as supreme pontiff; and they all together acclaimed the decision as ratified. Then, after the customary praises had been sung to God, they promised obedience and all together subscribed to Innocent’s election.

50. Meanwhile the same lord Pope, having beneficially and authoritatively arranged many matters in Pisa, Tuscany, and other provinces, took leave of the Pisans and gave thanks, then sailed to Provence. Passing through Burgundy, he reached Orléans, a city of France, where he was gladly and honorably received by the most pious king of the Franks, Louis, with bishops coming out to meet him. From there he was conducted to Chartres. There the glorious King Henry of England met him, having been brought with a very great retinue of bishops and nobles by the venerable Abbot of Clairvaux; persuaded by the powerful exhortation of that same abbot, he received the Pope as his father and shepherd [Col. 0499A].

When the lord Pope’s legates had meanwhile returned from Germany carrying the assent and letters both of the bishops and of King Lothair, Bernard afterwards met that king of the Romans at Liège. In all these matters the lord Pope would not permit the holy abbot to be separated from him; everywhere Bernard performed works of mercy and offered protection to the oppressed.

Pope Innocent was thus honorably received by the king, but that serenity was swiftly clouded over. For the same king insisted importunately, considering that he had a favorable opportunity to have episcopal investitures restored to himself—investitures which the Roman Church had wrested from that king’s predecessor, Emperor Henry, through exceedingly great labors and many dangers. No counsel was forthcoming, because the Romans feared the king’s power, until the holy abbot placed himself in the way as a wall. Boldly resisting the king, he rebuked the evil utterance with remarkable freedom and restrained it with remarkable authority [Col. 0499B].

Accordingly the lord Pope returned and, without making a long stay in Gaul, later met the aforesaid king at Rome and was conducted by him into the Lateran palace. Innocent having thus been left in Rome, the emperor departed elsewhere. But Innocent, realizing that a stay in Rome at that time was unprofitable for him, returned once more to Pisa. There, after bishops from all the West and other religious men had assembled, a synod of great splendor was held. The holy abbot participated in all its counsels and decisions, and reverence was shown to him by all [Col. 0499C].

## CHAPTER XIX. Of the reconciliation of the Milanese and miracles performed by him.

51. When the council had been dissolved, the lord Pope sent the man of God, whom the Milanese had sought with many entreaties, from his side to reconcile them, in the year 1134: he was to wash away the schism caused in that city through Anselm and recall the erring to the unity of the Church. Having crossed the Apennines, when the Milanese heard that the abbot for whom they longed was approaching their territory, all the people came out to meet him seven miles from the city [Col. 0499D]: nobles and commoners, horsemen and footmen, persons of middling rank and the poor. As though they were migrating from the city, they abandoned their own homes, and in ordered companies received the man of God with incredible devotion and reverence.

All alike delighted in the sight of him, considering themselves happier than others if they could enjoy hearing him. They even kissed his feet, although he accepted this reluctantly; but by no reasoning could he restrain or by any prohibition repel persons so bowed down and devout. When the matter for which the man of God had come was discussed in public, the city forgot its strength, laid aside all fierceness, and submitted itself to the abbot’s obedience.

52. Thus, when all had been pacified, the Church reconciled, and compacts of concord confirmed among the peoples [Col. 0500A], other concerns began to arise for him. For as the devil raged and ran riot in certain possessed persons, the banner of Christ was set against him; and when the man of God rebuked him, the demons, terrified and trembling before the arrival of a higher power, fled from the bodies they possessed.

Among those afflicted was an elderly woman, a citizen of Milan and once an honored matron, who was dragged by many people after the holy man as far as the church of Saint Ambrose. The devil had dwelt in her breast for many years and had by now almost suffocated her, so that, deprived of sight, hearing, and speech, grinding her teeth and thrusting out her tongue, she appeared a monster rather than a woman. Her foul face, terrible expression, and fetid breath bore witness to the filth of Satan, her inhabitant [Col. 0500B].

When the man of God saw her, he recognized the devil clinging fast and ingrained within her, and that he would not readily leave the dwelling he had possessed for so long. Turning therefore to the people, of whom an innumerable multitude was present, he ordered them to pray more intently. He directed the clerics and monks standing nearby with him to place the woman there and hold her. But she struggled, kicking not with natural strength but with diabolical force; and, not without injuring others, she struck the abbot himself with her foot.

He gently disregarded the devil’s boldness, and invoked God’s aid for the expulsion, not in the indignation of anger but by peaceful and humble supplication. Then he proceeded to offer the saving sacrifice. Yet as often as he signed that same sacred host, he also turned toward the woman and, making the same sign of the cross, attacked the wicked spirit as a strong athlete [Col. 0500C]. For whenever the sign of the cross was directed against him, that malign being, showing himself struck, raged more fiercely; kicking against the goad, he unwillingly revealed what he suffered.

When the Lord’s Prayer had been completed, the blessed man attacked the enemy more effectively. Placing the sacred body of the Lord upon the paten of the chalice and setting it upon the woman’s head, he spoke thus:

> “Your Judge is present, wicked spirit; the supreme Power is present. Now resist, if you can. He is present who was to suffer for our salvation: ‘Now,’ he says, ‘the prince of this world shall be cast out’ [John 12:31]. This is that body which was taken from the body of the Virgin, which was stretched out on the wood of the cross, which lay in the tomb [Col. 0500D], which rose from death, which ascended into heaven before the eyes of the disciples. Therefore, by the terrible power of this Majesty, I command you, evil spirit, as you depart from this servant-woman of his, never again presume to touch her.”

As the malign spirit left her unwillingly and, unable to remain any longer, afflicted her more cruelly—having great wrath because it had but a short time—then the holy Father returned to the altar, duly completed the breaking of the saving host, and gave the minister the peace to be distributed among the people. Immediately complete peace and health were restored to the woman. When the devil had been driven out, the woman regained her right mind, her senses having been restored with reason; her tongue, rolled back within her mouth, confessed God and gave thanks. Seeing her healer, she threw herself at his feet [Col. 0501A]. A tremendous cry rose through the church, the bronze instruments sounded, God was blessed by all, reverence exceeded all measure, and the rejoicing city, melted in charity, venerated the servant of God beyond belief.

53. He had now arrived at Pavia, and the fame of his virtues had preceded his coming. The joyous city received a man of such great glory with due rejoicing and preparation. And lest delay long suspend the desire of the people, who, having heard of the miracles performed at Milan, longed to see a sign from him, a peasant suddenly came after him. He had followed Bernard from Milan, bringing with him his demon-possessed wife. He laid her before Bernard’s feet, declaring in a tearful voice his inward anguish.

Without delay the devil spoke insults against the abbot through the mouth of the miserable woman, mocking the servant of God: “This fellow eating leeks will not be able to drive me out of my little bitch” [Col. 0501B]. In this manner he hurled many insults at the man of God, seeking to provoke him by blasphemies to bear reproaches impatiently and be put to shame before the people as he heard himself assailed with unworthy words.

But the man of God understood his trick and mocked the mocker. Seeking no vengeance himself but referring the matter to God, he ordered the possessed woman to be taken to the church of Saint Syrus. For he wished the glory of the cure to be given to the saint, and the first fruits of the work to be ascribed to his power. But Saint Syrus referred the matter back to his guest: claiming nothing for himself in his own church, he wished the work, untouched, to be brought back to the abbot.

The woman was therefore brought back to the abbot’s lodging [Col. 0501C], while the devil babbled through her mouth: “Little Syrus will not cast me out; little Bernard will not expel me.” To this the servant of God replied: “Neither Syrus nor Bernard will drive you out, but the Lord Jesus Christ.” Then turning to prayer, he begged the Lord for the woman’s health.

The wicked spirit then spoke, as though his earlier insolence had changed: “How gladly,” he said, “would I leave this little bitch, being grievously tormented in her! How gladly I would leave—but I cannot.” When asked the reason, he replied: “Because the great Lord does not yet will it.” The saint said to him: “And who is the great Lord?” He answered: “Jesus of Nazareth.” The man of God asked him again: “How do you know Jesus, or have you ever seen him?” “I have seen him.” “Where did you see him?” “In glory.” “And were you in glory?” “I was indeed.” “How did you depart from there?” “With Lucifer,” he said, “many of us fell” [Col. 0501D].

He spoke all this in a mournful voice through the mouth of the old woman, in the hearing of everyone. Then the holy abbot answered: “Would you wish to return to that glory and be restored to your former rank?” Again, with a changed voice and a strange burst of laughter, he said: “That has been delayed.” And he said nothing further.

As the man of God prayed more intently, that most wicked spirit departed in defeat, and the woman, restored to herself, gave as much thanks as she could. Thus the man returned with his wife, rejoicing throughout the journey in her recovery, and was restored to his home, where his friends awaited him [Col. 0502A]. All who heard the account of what had occurred rejoiced; but suddenly their joy turned to sorrow. For as soon as the woman touched the threshold of her home, the devil entered her again, and more savage than usual cruelly tore the miserable woman apart.

The wretched husband did not know what to do or where to turn. To live with a demon was most distressing; to abandon her seemed impious. So he rose and, taking his wife with him, returned once more to Pavia. When he did not find the man of God there, he followed him onward as far as Cremona. He told what had happened and tearfully begged to find favor. The abbot’s mercy did not fail the pious petition; he commanded him to enter the church of that city and wait in prayer until he himself should follow.

Mindful of his promise, at twilight, when the others were going to sleep, he entered the church with only one companion [Col. 0502B]. Spending that whole night in prayer, he obtained from the Lord what he asked. Having secured the woman’s healing, he ordered her to return safely to her own home. But because she feared the devil’s return to her, as she had already experienced it, he ordered a little written sheet bearing these words to be tied around her neck:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I command you, demon, never again from this time forward presume to touch this woman.”

The devil was so frightened by this command that he never thereafter presumed to approach the woman after she had returned home.

## CHAPTER XX. Bernard’s avoidance of ecclesiastical dignities, and the promotion of his disciples to them.

[Col. 0502C]

54. His flesh indeed was weak, but his spirit was willing; and insofar as he could take less delight in bodily matters or in the body, he delighted the more in the Lord. No ambition of this world moved him, for he yearned only after heavenly things. How many churches deprived of pastors chose him as their bishop? His mother church of Langres chose him; Châlons chose him. Within Italy, the city of Genoa, and Milan, the metropolis of the Ligurians, desired him as shepherd and teacher. Reims, France’s most noble city and capital of the province of Belgica Secunda, sought his prelateship. But none of these calls disturbed his mind with the honor offered, nor did his foot move to incline itself toward high rank [Col. 0502D].

Yet the advancement which, so far as he could, he avoided in his own person, the Lord fulfilled in his sons, whom he had gathered from various regions and devoted to divine service. From these Rome deserved to have Eugenius as supreme pontiff; Palestrina had Stephen, a man of every distinction; Ostia, the great man Hugh. Near Rome, Nepi flourished anew under Bishop Osbert. In Tuscany, Baldwin the bishop shone forth at Pisa as a great light of the Church. On this side of the Alps, Lausanne was given Amadeus; Sion, Guarin; Langres, Geoffrey; Auxerre, Alan; Nantes, Bernard; Beauvais and likewise Reims, Henry; Tournai, Gerard; York, Henry; Arras, Andrew. In Ireland there were two bishops, Christians both in reality and in name. In Germany, at Chur, there was Algot, venerable for wisdom, age, and grace [Col. 0503A]. In the Roman curia itself Henry and Bernard were made cardinals, the one priest and the other deacon. These luminaries, drawn from Clairvaux and from the instruction of Bernard, the man of God and abbot, illuminated the aforesaid cities with the splendor of religion.

## CHAPTER XXI. Of his journey into Aquitaine and the conversion of Count William.

55. Returning from the mountainous regions, the holy Father had now crossed the Alps in the year 1135. Shepherds and rustic people came down from the highest rocks to meet him, crying out from afar and seeking his blessing. Returning joyfully to their sheepfolds, they spoke among themselves, giving thanks to God because they had seen the Saint of the Lord and received the grace of the blessing they desired [Col. 0503B]. Passing thence through Chrysopolis and being solemnly escorted as far as Langres, he finally arrived at Clairvaux. The brethren assembled together and received their beloved Father with remarkable devotion; their joy was celebrated without tumult and with every dignity.

56. At that time the whole province of Bordeaux was still suffering under the oppression of the schismatics. There was no one able to resist the prince who, with the assent of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, and as that bishop instilled the seeds of dissension into his heart, had become defender and author of the schism. For Gerard had long exercised the legation of the Apostolic See in Aquitaine; now, deposed from so great an office, he could not endure to be bishop of his own Church alone when he had seen himself prince and master of all Aquitaine [Col. 0503C].

When these two joined together in this malice, whoever would not subscribe to the reception of Peter Leo was exposed to persecution: some were punished by confiscations, others by banishment, others were driven from their own sees and compelled into exile. When the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, heard these and similar things—he to whom Pope Innocent had entrusted the legation of Aquitaine—he was deeply grieved. Setting aside other affairs, he resolved without delay that help must be brought to the Church in danger. He therefore sought out and implored the Abbot of Clairvaux to help him eliminate these great evils.

The man of God consented [Col. 0503D], informing him that he would shortly lead a community of monks into Brittany, to a place near Nantes which Countess Ermengarde had prepared; and he promised that, once that house had been established, he would set out with him for Aquitaine.

57. They went together and arrived together at Nantes. In that region there was an unfortunate woman tormented by a wanton demon. She had a husband, wholly ignorant, however, of this most abominable intercourse. That utterly impure invisible adulterer abused her even while her husband lay in the same bed, tormenting her with unbelievable lust. For six years the evil remained hidden, nor did the ruined woman disclose the disgrace of so great a crime. But in the seventh year she was ashamed within herself and became afraid because of the fear of God, whose judgment she feared might overtake and condemn her at any moment [Col. 0504A].

She fled to priests and confessed the sin. She travelled through holy places and implored the aid of the saints; but no confession, no prayer, no generous giving of alms helped her. Every day, as before and more importunately, she was harassed by the demon. Finally the crime became publicly known. When he heard and learned of it, her husband abhorred sharing a household with her.

Meanwhile the man of God had arrived with his company at the aforesaid place. When the unhappy woman heard of his arrival, she threw herself trembling at his feet. Bathed in tears, she disclosed to him the horrible suffering and the long-established mockery, and that none of the things prescribed to her by priests had helped her. She added that her oppressor had foretold Bernard’s arrival [Col. 0504B] and sternly forbidden her to come before him, because it would do her no good; and that, when the abbot had departed, he who had been her lover would become a most cruel persecutor.

Hearing this, the man of God comforted the woman with gentle words and, promising help from heaven, ordered her—for night was already approaching—to return in confidence in the Lord on the following day. When she returned in the morning and recounted to the man of God the blasphemies and threats that she had heard from her incubus during that same night, the man of God said: “Do not concern yourself with his threats; go, take this staff of ours and put it in your bed; then let him do what he can.”

The woman did as she was commanded. Lying down in her bed, fortified by the sign of the cross, she placed the staff beside herself. The demon immediately appeared; but he dared neither approach his customary work nor the bed itself [Col. 0504C]. Still, he threatened most fiercely that, once the man of God departed, he himself would return to punish her.

Sunday was at hand, and the man of God wished the people to be summoned to church by the bishop’s proclamation. When a very great multitude had assembled in the church that day, during the solemnities of Mass, with Bishop Geoffrey of Chartres and Bishop Brice of Nantes accompanying him, he ascended the ambo. Intending to speak, he ordered all in the church to hold lighted candles in their hands. This he himself did, together with the bishops and clerics. He publicly revealed the unheard-of audacity of the devil and, with the subscription of all the faithful present, anathematized the fornicating spirit—which had burned into such horrible defilements even against its own nature [Col. 0504D]—and by Christ’s authority forbade it access both to that woman and thenceforth to all women.

When those sacramental lights were extinguished, all the devil’s power was thereafter extinguished. After the woman had made confession and received communion, the enemy never again appeared to her, but, banished beyond return, fled away.

58. Meanwhile, eminent men who were familiar with the Count informed him that the Abbot of Clairvaux, the Bishop of Chartres, other bishops, and religious men wished to confer with him. Their aim was to discuss the peace of holy Church. He was persuaded not to avoid a meeting with such great persons, since, by taking counsel with them, what seemed difficult might readily become easy, and what seemed impossible might be made possible. Accordingly, they met from both sides at Partiniacum.

When they discussed the division of the Church and the obstinacy of the schism—which, south of the Alps, had settled only in Aquitaine like the corruption of a fog—the servants of God impressed upon the Count in many ways and with many arguments that the Church is one, and that whatever is outside it must, by God’s judgment, perish and be overwhelmed, as though outside the Ark. They also cited the example of Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive because of the guilt of schism (Num. 16:31–32), and showed that God’s vengeance has never at any time been absent from so great an evil.

On hearing this, the Count adopted sound counsel in part and replied that he could consent to submit to the obedience of Pope Innocent; but that he could by no means be induced to restore the bishops whom he had expelled from their sees, because they had offended him beyond reconciliation and he had sworn never at any time to accept peace with them.

The discussion was prolonged through intermediaries. While they engaged one another in alternating arguments, the Man of God, taking up more powerful weapons, approached the holy altar to offer sacrifice and pray. Those permitted to participate in the divine mysteries had entered the church; the Count remained outside the doors. When the consecrations had been completed and peace had been given and extended to the people, the Man of God, no longer acting as a mere man, placed the Lord’s body upon the paten and took it with him. With a face afire and flaming eyes, not pleading but threatening, he went outside and addressed the Duke in terrible words:

“We begged you,” he said, “and you despised us. In the other assembly of God’s servants which we have already held with you, a multitude gathered before you entreated you, and you held them in contempt. Behold: the Son of the Virgin has come forth to you—he who is head and Lord of the Church that you persecute. Your judge is present, at whose name every knee bends, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Your judge is present, into whose hands that soul of yours will come. Will you despise him too? Will you hold him in contempt as you have his servants?”

All who were present wept and, intent upon prayer, awaited the outcome. Everyone’s expectation hung in suspense, awaiting some heavenly divine act. Seeing the Abbot advancing in vehement spirit and bearing in his hands the most holy body of the Lord, the Count was terrified and stiffened. His limbs shook and failed from fear; like a man out of his mind, he threw himself upon the ground. Raised by his soldiers, he again fell upon his face, speaking to no one and looking at no one.

Then the Man of God came nearer, struck him with his foot, and ordered him to rise from his prostrate position, stand upon his feet, and hear God’s sentence.

“The Bishop of Poitiers whom you expelled from his church is here,” he said. “Go, be reconciled to him; make a covenant with him in the holy kiss of peace; and yourself restore him to his see. Make satisfaction to God: render glory in place of insult, and throughout all your dominion recall those who are divided and discordant to the unity of charity. Submit to Pope Innocent; and, as the whole Church obeys him, do not delay to obey this pontiff, so great and chosen by God.”

Hearing this, overcome by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the presence of the holy Sacraments, the Count neither dared nor could reply. At once he received the bishop in the kiss of peace and, with the very hand by which he had renounced him, restored him to his own see amid the rejoicing of the whole city.

Thereafter the Abbot spoke with the Count more familiarly and gently, warning him as a father not again to rise to such impious and reckless acts, not to provoke God’s patience by such great offenses, and not to violate in any respect the peace now made. Peace having thus been restored to the whole Aquitanian Church, Girard alone persisted in evil; but not long afterwards, when the day of wrath came, he perished miserably in his own house. Overtaken by sudden death, he gave up his spirit without confession and without viaticum. Thus, that great evil having been buried and Girard’s schism reduced to nothing, the Man of God returned with great joy to Clairvaux.

## CHAPTER XXII. On his renewed journey to Italy, the obstinacy of Roger of Sicily, and the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa

59. These things having been accomplished (in the year 1136), he had scarcely spent about one year among his brethren when apostolic letters summoned the Man of God and the cardinals begged him to come to the aid of the distressed Church. Preferring nothing to obedience, the Man of God bade farewell to his brethren and departed while all were weeping. Received everywhere with great reverence, he at last reached Rome.

At his arrival both the lord Pope and the brethren were delighted.

> [Note: [Col. 0505] That is, the cardinals. Thus Peter the Venerable, book II, letter 48, repeatedly calls Cardinal Alberic his brother and a monk.]

After sharing counsel with him, and according to the course of events and the condition of the cases, the Abbot undertook another line of action.

For Roger, King of Sicily, who alone among the princes still refused obedience to Pope Innocent, sent to him, requesting that he send him the Abbot of Clairvaux. At the same time he made the same request of Peter Leonis, that he should delegate Peter of Pisa from his side. He said that he wished to learn the origin of the dissension, which had long hardened into persistence, and, once he knew the truth, either to correct the error or to confirm the judgment. For he had heard that Peter of Pisa was exceedingly eloquent and in knowledge of laws and canons second to almost no one.

[Col. 0506D] Therefore he thought that, if Peter’s eloquence were granted a hearing in a public consistory, the Abbot’s simplicity could be overwhelmed by rhetorical declamations and silence imposed upon him by the force of words and weight of arguments. Thus both parties came to Salerno.

60. In those days King Roger had prepared an innumerable army for war against Duke Ranulf. When the holy Abbot, the first of those summoned, arrived and found the King encamped with his armed battle-lines already drawn up, he prevented them for many days from engaging, declaring to the King: “If you enter the conflict, you will depart defeated and put to shame.”

At last, when the King’s army had grown greatly and he failed to understand that the outcome of war does not depend on numbers, he refused any longer to listen to the holy man seeking the things that made for peace. But the latter powerfully encouraged Duke Ranulf and the Catholic battle-line; as he had foretold flight to the King, so he promised victory and triumph to them.

Accordingly, when he suddenly saw the Duke advancing boldly to meet him, the King fled in terror, leaving his scattered army exposed to plunder and slaughter. Countless soldiers were captured and killed, and everything happened to him according to the Man of God’s word.

For the Abbot had withdrawn to a nearby little village and was occupied in prayer when suddenly the cries of fugitives and pursuers were heard: Duke Ranulf was pursuing the fleeing royal army by that very place. One of the brothers with the Abbot went out and met a soldier, asking what had happened. The soldier, who was literate, replied:

> “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found.”  
> (Ps. 36 [37]:35–36)

Without delay the Duke himself followed. As soon as he saw the monk, although still armed, he leapt down from his horse and threw himself at his feet. “Thanks be to God,” he said, “and to his faithful servant; for this victory has been granted not by our strength but by his faith.” Then he mounted his horse again and pursued the enemy.

61. When the battle was over, the Man of God came from the little village to which he had withdrawn to Salerno; Peter of Pisa also came. The King, therefore, with his court surrounded by soldiers, ordered both parties to be summoned and to state the grounds of their case.

Peter spoke first, striving to prove that the election of his lord Peter Leonis had been canonical and laboring to fortify his speech with many citations from laws and canons. But the Man of God, understanding that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in power, said:

“Peter, I know that you are a wise and learned man. Would that sounder and more honorable business had occupied you; would that a more just cause had obtained you as its advocate. For without doubt no eloquence could hinder you while you advanced reasonable arguments. As for us, unlearned and less eloquent as we are, if the cause of faith did not press upon us, we would keep the silence we have undertaken. But now charity compels us to speak, because Peter Leonis, with this lord’s support, is tearing and rending the Lord’s tunic—a tunic which, at the time of the Passion, neither pagan nor Jew presumed to tear.

“One is the faith, one the Lord, one Baptism” (Eph. 4:5). “We know neither two lords, nor a double faith, nor two baptisms. To begin with ancient things: there was one ark in the time of the flood. In it eight souls escaped while all the rest perished; and all who were found outside the ark died. No one doubts that this ark was a figure of the Church. Another ark has lately been built; and since there are two, one of them must be adulterous and must sink into the deep.

“If the ark governed by Peter is from God, then the ark governed by Innocent must necessarily be overwhelmed. Therefore the Eastern Church will perish; the whole West will perish; France will perish; Germany, the Iberians, and the English will perish; and barbarian kingdoms will be submerged in the depths of the sea. The Camaldolese, Carthusian, Cluniac, Cistercian, and Premonstratensian orders, with countless other communities of God’s male and female servants, must all fall beneath one tempest into the abyss. The devouring sea will receive bishops, abbots, and the remaining leaders of the Church. Roger alone among the princes of the world has entered Peter’s ark; all others having been drowned, he alone will be saved! Far be it that the religion of the whole world should perish and that the ambition of Peter—whose manner of life is publicly known—should gain the kingdom of heaven.”

At these words he took Peter’s hand, raised him, and rose with him. “If you trust me,” he said, “we shall enter the safer ark.” Then, approaching him with salutary counsels, as he had long before conceived in his mind, and with God’s grace cooperating, he immediately persuaded him to return to the City and be reconciled with Pope Innocent.

The assembly having been dismissed, the venerable Abbot returned to Rome. He reconciled the aforesaid Peter of Pisa and certain others to the Church, and united them in fellowship with Pope Innocent.

## CHAPTER XXIII. After the death of Anacletus and the end of the schism, Bernard resumes his exposition of the Song of Songs and reconciles Count Theobald with the King

62. The time had come when divine mercy had determined to end the schism through the death of Peter Leonis [Col. 0508C] (in the year 1138). At that time his party set up another pope in his place, so that they might more conveniently be reconciled to Pope Innocent after a short interval. Christ accomplished this without delay through the hand of his servant the Abbot. For the substitute came by night to the same Man of God, who brought him, stripped of the insignia he had usurped, to the feet of Lord Innocent.

When this was done, the city rejoiced exultantly; the Church was restored to Innocent; the Roman people venerated Innocent as their shepherd and lord. The Abbot of Clairvaux was held in wonderful reverence, and all proclaimed him the author of peace and father of his country.

63. When all had been calmed and set in order, the man who had labored seven years and more to repair this same division could scarcely be detained even for a few days. As he departed from Rome, the clergy accompanied him, the people escorted and honored him, and the entire nobility attended him. For one honored with universal love could not be dismissed without universal sorrow.

On returning from the City, the holy Father brought with him precious gifts from the bodies of the holy Apostles and martyrs, considering this among the other fruits of his labor to be no small gain. The Gallican Church received him with such rejoicing that it seemed to display no less joy at his return than it had expressed at the news of peace restored.

Thus peace having been secured, the Man of God returned to his own community; and wherever he arrived on his journey home, he was received especially by his sons with immense rejoicing. The same Father recalled that time and work in the twenty-fourth sermon on the Song of Songs, writing:

> “At last, brothers, a more merciful eye from heaven has looked upon this, our third return from the City; and at last a more serene countenance has smiled upon us from above. Leonine fury has ceased; wickedness has reached its end; the Church has received peace; the evil one who had troubled her for nearly eight years by that dreadful schism has been reduced to nothing in his sight. I have been granted to your desires; I prepare myself for your progress. I live by your merits; I wish to live for your pursuits and salvation.”

Thus he ascribed entirely to his brethren’s merits both his life and his good deeds. Returning to holy pursuits, he resumed the epithalamium he had begun.

How effectively and manifestly the reconciliation was effected in a time of wrath is shown by Pope Innocent’s words in his letter to him:
