> “How firmly and with persevering constancy the fervor of your religious devotion and discernment undertook to defend the cause of blessed Peter and of your holy mother, the Roman Church, when Peter Leonis’s schism was inflamed; how, setting yourself as an unconquerable wall before the house of God, you labored by frequent arguments fortified with reason to lead the minds of kings, princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to the unity of the Catholic Church and to the obedience of blessed Peter and ourselves—the great benefit which has thereby come to God’s Church and to us makes clear.”  

64. After the Father’s return from the City, he had scarcely enjoyed the longed-for peace for three years when, because the kingdom of France was violently disturbed by the hostilities that arose between King Louis and Count Theobald, he was again sought out for the labor of restoring peace.

This Count, powerful in the kingdom, wholly devoted to almsgiving and earnest in the pursuit of piety, a ready lover of all God’s servants and of holy religion, adhered most devotedly to the counsels of Bernard’s holiness. When not only neighboring princes, supported by the King’s power, rose against him, but also nearly all his own followers deserted him, the Count’s escape had already turned into dispersal.

Hearing this, the holy man—who did not know how to spare himself in such matters, overflowing as he was with the bowels of compassion—resolved to oppose such great evils. At last, aided by the prayers of many religious persons, he continually cried to the Lord, and, with divine appeals intervening through him, the storms subsided. The longed-for calm of peace and tranquility returned between King and Prince.

The Man of God had conceived good hope of this peace from the beginning. As some of his brethren testified that they had heard from him, he had clearly foretold to them the swift coming of that prince’s deliverance, although it seemed almost incredible.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On his patience in illness, insults, and loss of goods

65. Amid the many fatigues of travel and labor which the holy man had undertaken for the needs of God’s Church, a daily and manifold infirmity never ceased to afflict him [Col. 0510A]. It is therefore clear that his patience was especially exercised and tested by the Lord’s scourges. From the very beginning of his conversion until the day of his holy death, he endured sufferings so great that those who knew him thought his life little more than a kind of prolonged death.

Yet, although opportunities for patience toward other people were rarer and perhaps offered slighter tests, it must briefly be said that he did not appear lacking in this virtue either. Since he used to say that this kind of patience has three divisions—injuries of words, losses of possessions, and bodily harm—let one example at least be offered for each, as they occur.

The same servant of God had once written to a bishop [Col. 0510B] concerning the King’s court and counsel, advising him in certain matters to urge and counsel the King toward better courses.

> [Note: [Col. 0509D] See Letter 224, to Joslenus.]

The bishop, deeply angered, sent him an extremely bitter letter in reply. Christ’s servant, a diligent imitator of divine kindness, answered with the utmost gentleness; nor did he afterwards hold that bishop any less dear or less familiar. The harsh reply of the prelate was, for him, as though it had never been spoken.

66. The Abbot of Farfa had called a community of brethren from Clairvaux, intending to build them a monastery; but the Roman bishop prevented him and established them elsewhere. Greatly grieved by this, the aforesaid man, eminent and of great devotion, deposited in his own country under a written bond a collected sum of nearly six hundred marks of silver. Coming to the Man of God, he offered it to him and asked him to send for the money, so that a new monastery might be founded from it on this side of the Alps, since he had not been found worthy to establish one in his own region.

A messenger was sent for the money, but, despite the venerable Abbot’s instruction, nothing was returned. When the Man of God was told of it, he gave no answer but: “Blessed be God, who has spared us this burden.” He was even accustomed to rejoice that about ten monasteries—or sites suitable for building monasteries—had been unjustly taken from him, since he did not wish to contend and took more pleasure in being defeated than in defeating others.

67. Once a cleric, dressed as a regular canon, came to Clairvaux and persistently pressed to be received as a monk. The holy Father urged him to return to his own church, but he would not consent to receive him. The man said: “Why then have you so strongly commended perfection in your books, if you refuse to give help to one who desires it?”

Then, more violently incited by a spirit of anger, as became plainly evident afterwards, he said: “If I had those books here, I would tear them to pieces.”

The Man of God replied: “I think that in none of them have you read that you cannot be perfect in your own cloister. If I remember rightly, I have commended correction of conduct, not a change of places, in all my books.”

Then the man, like one insane, rushed at him and struck his cheek so severely that redness immediately followed the blow and swelling followed the redness. Those present were already rushing upon the sacrilegious man, but the servant of the Lord stopped them, crying out and adjuring them in Christ’s name not to touch him at all, but to lead him out carefully and take care that no one should harm him in any way.

He commanded this so strictly that the man, fearful and trembling, was led out and escorted away without any injury. Truly, Bernard had learned to overcome evil with good.

Writing likewise to certain persons, he says among other things:

> [Note: [Col. 0511D] Letter 252, to the Premonstratensians.]

> “I shall remain attached to you even if you do not wish it; I shall remain attached even if I myself do not wish it. I shall render service to the unwilling, add benefits to the ungrateful, and honor even those who despise me.”

He embraced all people with such brotherly affection that, as he himself used to confess, he was more deeply burned by another person’s scandal—even when he seemed to have given no occasion for it—than by anything else.

## CHAPTER XXV. On his restrained correction, gentleness, charity, and writings

68. Moreover, he sometimes restrained his rebuke no less readily in the face of a grave and turbulent answer than of a humble and modest one. Some would therefore say of him, in like manner, that he pressed one who yielded and yielded to one who resisted.

He said that where modesty resounds on both sides, conversation is pleasant; where it is found on one side only, it is useful; where on neither side, it is harmful. For where harshness sounds from both sides, there is quarrelling, not correction; conflict, not discipline. It is therefore more fitting for a superior for the time being to overlook the matter, and, once the disturbance is healed, to correct subjects more profitably.

Speaking at times of rebukes offered less usefully or received less patiently, he maintained that rebukes ought never to be used or pressed in the evening hour, lest a disturbed brother pass a sleepless night and show himself less devout in the customary vigils.

In his forty-second sermon on the Song of Songs he says, among other things:

> “Would that it were necessary to rebuke no one! That would be better. But since we all offend in many things, I may not remain silent, since by office the duty lies upon me to reprove sinners; yet charity presses me more strongly. If I reprove and do what is mine to do, but the rebuke sent forth does not do what is its own, does not accomplish that for which I sent it, but returns to me empty, like a missile that strikes and rebounds—what state of mind do you think I then have, brothers? Am I not tormented? I am indeed constrained from two sides and do not know what to choose: whether to be pleased with what I said because I did what I ought, or to repent of my word because I did not receive what I desired.”

And below:

> “Perhaps you will tell me that my good returns to me, that I have delivered my own soul and am clean from the blood of the person to whom I announced and spoke, so that he might turn from his evil way and live. Even if you add countless things of this kind, they will not console me in the least while I behold the death of my son. As though I had sought my own deliverance by that rebuke rather than his! What mother, even if she knows that she has given all possible care and diligence to her sick son, if she finally sees herself disappointed and all her labors wholly effective, while he nevertheless dies, will ever for that reason refrain from tears?”

So much for this.

69. Furthermore, he was so great a lover of gentleness and peace that, if some wicked petitioner had wrung a harsher answer from him when he was refusing a request, that person was hardly ever afterwards sent away empty with the same refusal. For, as he confessed, he hated every scandal almost by nature; and it was exceedingly painful for him to bear the burden of any person, while it was impossible for him not to feel it.

The gratuitous scandal of another afflicted his most compassionate heart more than the innocence of his own conscience consoled it. He grieved, and scarcely hoped that something could be healed when he could not see its source. Conversely, he declared that it gave him great consolation whenever he found a means of making satisfaction—either to a person on his own account or to God on another person’s account—even if the other had been disturbed without cause.

Thus he despised no one and considered no person’s scandal insignificant. Whenever he needed either to rebuke harmful actions or to prevent someone’s attempts, he did so with such consideration that even those who appeared injured had abundant grounds to satisfy themselves about him in their own thoughts. Some of these—even persons from whom this could least have been expected—afterwards served him with greater devotion or even clung to his footsteps.

He was deeply moved by the spiritual profit or loss of every person; the fruit of souls and the conversion of sinners were his supreme desire and supreme joy. Yet he pitied bodily necessities with the tenderest compassion. He bore, in charity and with the greatest patience, not only bodily infirmities but infirmities of conduct. Indeed, he declared himself above all the abbot of those troubled in this way, not breaking the bruised reed or quenching the smoking flax.

70. Moreover, if anyone desires to know how diligently he judged and examined himself from the beginning, let him inspect Bernard’s first work, *On the Degrees of Humility*. If one seeks the religious devotion of a pious mind, one should turn to the Homilies *In Praise of the Virgin Mother* and to the book he wrote *On Loving God*. If one seeks fervent zeal against the faults of his own people or of others, let him read the work he calls the *Apology*. If one seeks vigilant zeal of heart and cautious discernment, let him hear him discussing *Precept and Dispensation*. How faithful a commender and helper of every pious form of life he was is shown by the exhortatory discourse to the Knights Templar. How far from ungrateful he was toward God’s grace is clear from the faithful and subtle manner in which he discussed *Grace and Free Will*.

How free he was in speech, how eloquent, and how rich in knowledge alike of higher and lower things, the attentive reader will recognize in what he wrote to Pope Eugenius, *On Consideration*. How devotedly he proclaimed another’s holiness is shown by the care with which he narrated the life of the holy bishop Malachy.

In the Sermons on the Song of Songs, he is revealed as both an investigator of mysteries and a magnificent builder of character. In the Letters which he dictated to diverse persons concerning diverse affairs, the prudent reader will observe with what fervor of spirit he loved all justice and equally hated all injustice.

For the faithful servant of Christ sought nothing for himself; yet he cared for whatever belonged to Christ as though it were his own. What holy, honorable, pure, lovely, reputable, virtuous, or praiseworthy discipline did his authority not strengthen from its beginnings in whatever region during his lifetime? What, once advanced, did he not desire to be further extended? What that had perhaps fallen into decay did he not endeavor with all his strength, as place and time allowed, to restore?

Who approached the sacred temple of divinity dwelling in his breast, faithfully crying out from whatever distress, and labored without effect? The sorrowful received consolation from him; the afflicted, help; the anxious, counsel; the sick, remedy; the poor, aid. He had made himself the servant of all, as though born for the whole world; yet he remained free from all, caring for his conscience as though he were devoted solely to the care and custody of his own heart.

In his presence all holiness rejoiced, and all impiety blushed, in accordance with the saying: “The upright shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop its mouth” (Ps. 106 [107]:42). In his presence every distinguished gathering shone as if under a certain sun; in his absence it appeared dark and, in a manner, mute. Finally, his healing hand and tongue cured diseases alike: the former diseases of bodies, the latter diseases of character. Let these brief remarks, though only partial, suffice for the present concerning the character of the holy Father.

## CHAPTER XXVI. He opposes Abelard and the heretic Henry

71. When he was already weighed down by many labors and was no less afflicted by daily infirmities, he desired to have rest among his brethren. But divine providence provided otherwise, so that the reward of his merits might increase: the labor of another contest was added to him.

In those days there was Peter Abelard, a famous master, renowned above all in the reputation of learning. When writings of his that were insufficiently consonant with the faith began to circulate everywhere, learned and faithful men brought certain chapters from them to the Man of God. Desiring, in his customary goodness, that the error be corrected rather than the man confounded, Bernard approached him with private admonition. He dealt with him so modestly and reasonably that Abelard himself, moved to compunction, promised to correct everything according to Bernard’s judgment.

While God’s servant remained waiting for this correction, entirely without his knowledge, a public day was appointed, through the counsel of Lord Henry, Archbishop of Sens, in the year 1140. On that day the aforesaid master and the Abbot were to meet at Sens and dispute concerning the aforementioned chapters.

It was the day on which that same bishop was to display holy relics to the King of France, the princes, and the whole people. The Abbot, though summoned, entirely refused to come, declaring that this was not his business but that of the bishops in matters of faith. Afterwards, however, bent by the counsels and drawn by the authority of great men, he finally consented to go, sad and not without tears, as he himself testifies in his letter to Pope Innocent, where he recounts the whole affair more fully and clearly.

> [Note: [Col. 0513D] Letter 189.]

The day came, and the King, the venerable Samson, Archbishop of Reims, and many bishops from both provinces assembled with a great congregation. How magnificently and profitably the faithful and prudent servant acted in that gathering, the Church assembled for this purpose plainly recognized. Pope Innocent likewise testifies more fully concerning this in a letter sent to the bishops in Gaul.

> [Note: [Col. 0514D] Letter 194 among the Bernardine letters.]

That pontiff entered the way of all flesh not long afterwards. After his death, and after the very brief pontificates of his successors Celestine and Lucius, Eugenius became Pope of the City.

72. During his pontificate, in the year 1147, a certain Henry, formerly a monk, had captured the fickle people of Toulouse by the persuasive words of his destructive teaching. As the Apostle foretold of some, “speaking lies in hypocrisy” (1 Tim. 4:2), he made merchandise of them with feigned words.

He was an open enemy of the Church, irreverently disparaging both the Church’s Sacraments and its ministers. The malignity of his perverse persuasion had prevailed so greatly that all ecclesiastical institutions were despised.

Constrained by this necessity, the holy man set out on his journey. The Church of that region had repeatedly requested him before, and now at last the most reverend Alberic, Bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, both persuaded and accompanied him.

When he arrived, the people of that land received him with unbelievable devotion, as though an angel had come from heaven. He could not remain long among them because no one could restrain the rushing crowds. Such was the multitude coming by day and night, seeking his blessing and demanding help.

Nevertheless, he preached for several days in the city of Toulouse and in the other places where that Henry had most frequented and more gravely infected. He instructed many simple persons in the faith, strengthened the wavering, recalled the erring, restored the overthrown, and by his authority pressed down and crushed subverters and the obstinate, so that they did not dare to resist him, nor even to stand near or appear.

Although that heretic then fled from Bernard’s presence and hid himself, by God’s grace his ways were so obstructed and his paths enclosed that later he was scarcely safe anywhere. At last he was captured, put in chains, and handed over to the Bishop of Toulouse.

73. During this journey God was glorified by very many signs in his servant the Abbot: recalling some hearts from impious errors and healing other bodies from diverse illnesses. In the same region is a place called Sarlat. There, after he had completed a sermon, very many people offered loaves to the Man of God for blessing, as happened everywhere. Raising his hand, making the sign of the cross, and blessing them in God’s name, he said:

“By this you shall know that what we commend to you is true and what the heretics commend is false: if your sick people, after tasting these loaves, receive health.”

But the venerable Bishop of Chartres, the great Geoffrey, was present and close to the Man of God, and was afraid. “If they receive them in good faith,” he said, “they will be healed.”

The holy Father, doubting nothing of the Lord’s power, replied: “I would not say it that way. Rather, those who taste them will truly be healed, so that they may thereby recognize us to be true and truthful messengers of God.”

So immense a multitude of sick persons recovered after tasting that bread that the report spread throughout the whole province. As the holy man returned through neighboring places, he avoided and feared going there because the crowds gathering around him were intolerable.

## CHAPTER XXVII. What Bernard thought of the wonders performed by him. On the unsuccessful outcome of the Jerusalem expedition
74. But as, throughout his return journey from that province, the signs wrought by the holy man became ever more frequent [Col. 0515C] and increased daily, we must not pass over what disposition he himself maintained amid these things—he who had learned from Christ humility of heart and gentleness. For, debating with himself in his thoughts, and speaking from the abundance of his heart, he would say to certain religious brethren of his household:

> “I greatly wonder what these miracles may mean, or why it has seemed good to God to perform such things through such a man. I do not think that I have read anything in the sacred writings about this sort of signs. For signs have sometimes been performed through holy and perfect persons; they have also been performed through pretenders. I am conscious in myself neither of perfection nor of pretense. For I know that I lack [Col. 0515D] the merits of the saints, which are made illustrious by miracles; yet I trust that I do not belong to the lot of those who work many mighty deeds in the Lord’s name and are unknown by the Lord.”

He discussed these and similar matters more frequently and more privately with spiritual men. At last he thought that he had found a fitting answer for himself:

> “I know,” he said, “that signs of this kind concern not the holiness of one person, but the salvation of many; and that God, in the man through whom he works such things, regards not so much perfection as reputation, so that through him he may commend to people the virtue believed to be in him. For these things are not done for the sake of those through whom they are done, but rather for the sake of those who see or hear of them. Nor does the Lord work these things through them in order to prove them holier than others, [Col. 0516A] but in order to make others more loving and zealous for holiness. Therefore these signs have nothing to do with me, since I know that they are displayed more for my reputation than for my life; nor are they done to commend me, but rather to admonish others.”

Surely, unless we are mistaken, anyone who weighs these words with careful reflection will admire the spirit of this man; and every faithful judge will regard it as no greater or loftier thing that signs and wonders should be marvelously worked through him than that he should interpret what had been done through him in this way. The Christian mind will also judge it no less profitable to imitate his dispositions than to admire his deeds, and to know the distinctions of his character rather than the signs of his works. Thus, through the manifold cooperation of divine grace, the teaching of the holy Man of God benefited the Church [Col. 0516B] by correcting the conduct of Catholics, restraining the fury of schismatics, and refuting the errors of heretics.

75. Before this servant of God returned from Toulouse, the reported need of the Eastern Church deeply moved the minds of many, and especially that of King Louis the Younger (A.D. 1146). Therefore the servant of Christ was requested once and again by the aforesaid king; nor did he yield to his will and request until he was at last commanded by the supreme Pontiff himself to expound the general letter to the peoples and princes. The tenor of that letter was that, for penance and the remission of sins, they should undertake the journey—either to liberate their brethren or to lay down their own lives for them.

Nor should it be left unsaid that, because of his preaching of this Jerusalem journey, some persons of limited understanding took offense against the venerable Abbot when its outcome proved sad. Yet it is certain, as we have said, that the initiative for that enterprise did not originate with him. The venerable Father himself recalls this matter in his book *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius, saying among other things:

> “As though we had acted in this undertaking with rashness. Certainly we ran in it, not as into uncertainty, but at your command—indeed, through you, by God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If one of two things must happen, I prefer the murmur of men to be directed against us rather than against God. It is good for me if he deigns to use me as a shield.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0515D] Book II, chapter 1.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Refutation of Gilbert of Poitiers, and Bernard’s Approaching Death

[Col. 0516D]

76. At that time (A.D. 1148), Master Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, was greatly practiced in the sacred Scriptures; but, searching into matters too lofty for himself, he too had written certain novelties. As scandal and murmuring among the faithful were now growing because of them, he was summoned before the Council of Reims, convened by the venerable Pope Eugenius, and commanded to produce his book. There the venerable Abbot argued against these novelties for two days, refuting them as modestly as faithfully by the testimonies of the saints. At last, by apostolic judgment and the authority of the universal [Col. 0517A] Church, the aforesaid novelties were condemned. The bishop consented to the condemnation and publicly retracted what he had written; thus, being corrected, he obtained pardon—especially because from the beginning he had promised that, without any obstinacy, he would correct his opinion according to the judgment of holy Church.

77. Thus the holy man, though already almost failing in body, was nevertheless ready and vigorous in mind. For several years he exercised in good works the zeal for God which burned within him, while his holy devotion, never failing, labored to persist in the pursuits of divine service. And when, after so many labors, the Lord was disposing to give his beloved servant the long-desired sleep of precious death and to bring his faithful servant into his rest, his spirit began to advance more and more readily toward him, while his weak flesh failed. For the holy man, recognizing that the prize was now near, ran more eagerly than usual; and, feeling the dissolution of his earthly dwelling to be at hand, he aspired with fuller desires toward the dwelling from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

The flame of sacred desire, unable to be contained in his most pure breast, broke forth in frequent indications; and his fiery speech vividly declared the intensity of his inward ardor. His body lay upon its bed, afflicted by various discomforts; yet his spirit, no less free and strong, continued unconquered in the things of God. Even amid pains, he did not cease to meditate upon something sacred, to dictate, to pray more fervently, and to exhort the brethren more earnestly. In the offering of the saving sacrifice, [Col. 0517C] which until his final decline he scarcely ever omitted, he sustained limbs scarcely holding together by the strength of his spirit, offering himself also as an acceptable sacrifice to God, a sweet-smelling savor.

At this time, writing to his uncle Andrew, a knight of the Temple, he said among other things: “For I am being poured out, and I do not think that I shall remain long upon the earth.” And while he was suffering more severely than usual, the brethren persisted in supplications and prayers to God for him. Recognizing that his desire was being delayed by their prayers, when he began to be somewhat better in body he gathered the brethren and spoke these very words:

> “Why do you keep a miserable man here? You are stronger [Col. 0517D] and have prevailed. Spare me, I beg you, spare me; let me go.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Peace of Metz Brought About Through Him

78. The holy Father was now manfully awaiting the completion of his course in his monastery of Clairvaux when a very grievous blow fell upon the people of Metz, who were severely oppressed by neighboring princes (A.D. 1153). The devastation of the entire province seemed certain and imminent. Then their venerable metropolitan, Hillinus, archbishop of Trier, anxiously grieving for the past and fearing still worse things, sought and urgently requested the one refuge in so great a necessity: the Man of God.

Coming therefore to Clairvaux, he prostrated himself in all humility at the feet of Bernard and of all the brethren [Col. 0518A] and begged and implored that he would deign to oppose himself to such great evils, which no other person appeared able to restrain. But the Lord, who had always directed the paths of his faithful servant and used him as the most fitting instrument in every important cause, had somewhat relieved his bodily illness a few days earlier. Divine providence often so arranged matters for him, for his soul’s good pleasure was in God’s hand: whenever some great necessity summoned him, the strength of his body did not fail his spirit, which conquered everything. Those who saw him marveled that he surpassed even strong men in endurance. For when affairs were sometimes completed, as though returning to himself, he suffered from many infirmities, so that he scarcely lived while at rest—he who, when occupied, did not know how to fail.

In this final undertaking, divine power and grace attended him so openly and magnificently that he seemed to gather strength from his labors.

79. It happened, while the two parties were seated on opposite banks of the River Moselle and the faithful mediator was urging what made for peace, that one party, emboldened by the slaughter of enemies whom they had recently enclosed and cut down, stubbornly refused with obstinate spirits what was demanded. At last, suddenly as if driven by furies, they departed without greeting the Man of God, leaving all the others only despair of peace. Yet they fled not from any contempt but out of fear and reverence for him. For they feared that he might easily bend even the most perverse minds of those present, failing to consider what he could accomplish through the Spirit who is nowhere absent, even in those absent from him.

The assembly was now breaking up amid great tumult; on both sides they thought only of weapons and formed only counsels of wickedness. Then the holy man, comforting the brethren who had come with him, said:

> “Do not be troubled. Although there are many difficulties, the peace we desire will nevertheless come about.”

He also disclosed how he knew this:

> “In a vision of the night I seemed to myself to be celebrating a solemn Mass. And when, after the first prayer had been almost completed, I remembered that I ought, according to custom, to have preceded it with the angelic hymn—namely, ‘Glory to God in the highest’—I was ashamed; and, beginning the hymn which I had forgotten and omitted, I completed it together with you to the end.” [Col. 0518D]

Midnight had already passed when the holy man received an embassy from the aforesaid princes announcing their repentance. Turning joyfully to his companions, he said: “Recognize the preparation for the *Gloria* promised to us to be sung, and for the hymn of peace.” The parties were therefore summoned again, and for several days peace was negotiated. Because of the great difficulties arising on both sides, they often despaired; except that all were now comforted by the holy Abbot’s certain promise, known to everyone, that peace would be restored.

80. Nor did the delay itself bring little benefit, especially to those suffering various illnesses who received remedies in their bodies, and also to those who, beholding these things, were built up in faith. For so great was the crowd that, by its numbers and importunity, it almost made the business of settling the peace hopelessly impossible. At last, an island in midstream having been selected, the leading men of each party came there in small boats.

Among all the healings which the Lord performed there through the hand of his servant, the cure of a certain woman was especially celebrated. For eight years she had suffered from a most grievous disease, with violent trembling and powerful convulsions shaking all her limbs together. When, owing to more serious difficulties that had arisen, hope of peace seemed almost to have failed, this woman came, by God’s ordering, trembling in a manner no less horrible than pitiable; and everyone gathered to see the spectacle. As the servant of God prayed in the sight of all, the shaking gradually subsided; [Col. 0519B] and the woman, feeling herself restored to perfect health, cried out: “Servant of God, I am well.”

This moved even the hardest persons to such amazement that, striking their breasts, they cried aloud with tears for nearly half an hour. Finally, so great was the rush and press of those falling down and kissing the holy footsteps of the Man of God that he was almost crushed, until the brethren lifted him up, placed him in a little boat, and pushed it a short distance from the bank. When the princes approached him and he began, as before, to urge peace, they said with sighs:

> “We ought gladly to hear the man whom, as we ourselves see, God loves and hears; and, having heard him, to do much for one for whom God does such great things before our eyes.”

But he, as always careful appropriately to avoid glory of this kind, said: “He does it not for my sake, but for yours.” There, all matters being settled according to the decision of the faithful arbiter, they gave one another their right hands and were reconciled with the kiss of peace.

It would be difficult to embrace in a complete account all the great deeds of that journey, as also the other mighty things accomplished through him by the Lord. But neither is it our purpose now to pursue signs of this kind or to devote ourselves to recounting works of power. Setting this narrative aside, therefore, we should devoutly observe that this was the blessed man’s final conclusion of his journeys and his last labor. In this work, no less useful than difficult, and concerning a peace then no less desperate than necessary, he gloriously completed his labors—he whom God had always magnificently honored in his labors.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Condition and Admonitions of the Holy Man in His Last Days, and His Precious Death

[Col. 0519D]

81. After the reconciliation of the people of Metz had been accomplished and peace restored to that province, the holy Abbot returned to the monastery, burdened by a very severe bodily illness and now close to failing. Yet, in such sweetness of mind and delight of spirit, he daily drew nearer to death as though a sailor, having reached harbor, were gradually lowering his sails. He also said plainly to the brethren:

> “These are the words which I spoke to you when I was ill last winter: that you had no further cause to fear, for the dissolution of this body would come in the approaching summer.”

But this saying was hidden from them, [Col. 0520A] and they were unable to grasp it. What the mind so intensely dreaded was not easily persuaded to believe, especially since he himself, out of compassion for his sons, suppressed such words. Yet, as though crying out by his deeds, “I have completed the works which the Father gave me to do,” he began more and more to lay aside outward activities and withdraw his affections; as though, with the cords of sacred desires diligently cast forward, he were fastening himself more firmly to the near shore and making a more convenient landing.

Finally, when the venerable bishop Geoffrey of the see of Langres consulted him about certain matters to be done and wondered that he paid them little attention, Bernard said: “Do not wonder; for I am no longer of this world.”

82. At last the holy Father, overflowing with the bowels of compassion and mercy, saw his dearest sons wasting away miserably and withering in fear and expectation of the approaching desolation of grievous and lamentable bereavement. He refreshed them with the sweetest consolations. He urged them to root the anchor of hope and faith more firmly, through unshakable charity, in the secure bosom of divine mercy; and he promised that he himself would never fail them, even after death.

More earnestly, through many tears, he begged and implored them, striving to impress upon their minds the fear of God and love of sacred purity and all perfection. He admonished them and called them to witness with tears that, if he had commended anything virtuous either by example or by word, they should imitate it, hold firmly to it, and advance in it.

Seeing the end of his days at hand, he called aside certain brethren who had long remained closely attached to him in familiar life, and addressed them thus:

> “Since I do not think that I can leave you great examples of religious life, I commend to your imitation three things which I remember that I observed, according to my ability, in the course which I ran. I trusted my own judgment less than another’s. When injured, I did not seek vengeance from the one who injured me. I wished to cause scandal to no one; and if it ever happened, I calmed it as best I could.”

See how briefly and yet how clearly [Col. 0520D] the servant of God sought in these words to implant humility, patience, and charity in the minds of his disciples, setting before them things to imitate not so much by word and tongue as by deed and truth.

83. Whoever wishes to know the nature of his illness may consult the letter written to Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, in which he says among other things:

> “Sleep has departed from me, lest pain should ever depart even through the benefit of numbed sensation. Almost all that I suffer is weakness of the stomach. It often demands strengthening by day and night with a very small quantity of some liquid; for it inexorably rejects every solid food. This little which it deigns to admit, it receives not without severe discomfort, yet it fears a worse discomfort if it leaves itself entirely empty. And if it sometimes consents to admit a little more, that proves most burdensome. My feet and legs have swollen, as usually happens to persons with dropsy. And amid all this, lest anything be hidden from a friend solicitous about the condition of his friend, according to the inward man—though I speak as a fool—the spirit is willing in weak flesh. Pray to the Savior, who does not will the death of the sinner, that he may not delay my now timely departure but preserve me. Take care to fortify by prayers the heel bare of merits, so that he who lies in wait may find no place to fix his tooth and inflict a wound. I dictated these things myself, being in this condition, so that you may recognize my feeling by a hand known to us.” (*Letter* 310)

From the tenor of this letter, therefore, the diligent reader may surely recognize, at least in some measure, that sacred heart: how great was his tranquility of mind, serenity of soul, and sweetness of spirit amid the very ruin of his body, and how deep beneath the summit of confidence was the root of humility.

[Col. 0521B]

84. Yet one may also estimate to some extent the feelings of his sons at that time: their bloodless faces, heavy sobs, frequent sighs, and anxious thoughts. For so great and beloved a treasure was still in their hands; yet they had neither hope of retaining him longer nor ability to depart with him. Still, they were in no way to mourn for him, who, happily summoned to the joy of the Lord his God, was now about to enter it; rather, they were to mourn for themselves, to whom life was then wearisome and death still dreadful.

Grievous indeed was their lot in this separation: after such wondrous light, they more greatly dreaded the darkness about to enter after his departure. Therefore, before their Father’s death, the sons whom he had begotten to Christ through the Gospel approached him and assailed his most loving heart with tearful entreaties, saying such things as these:

> “Will you not have pity on this monastery, father? Will you not have compassion upon us, whom you have nourished with the maternal breasts of such loving care and warmed with paternal consolation?”

Then he too wept with those who wept; raising his dove-like eyes to heaven, he testified that he was constrained between two things and did not know what to choose, but committed everything to the merciful judgment of God. For on the one hand paternal affection urged him to grant his sons’ prayers and remain; on the other, desire for Christ drew him to depart. Yet the humility long rooted in his breast persuaded him from the innermost affection of his heart to call himself an unprofitable servant and regard himself as a barren tree, from whose life no fruit accrued either to himself [Col. 0521D] or to anyone else.

For he was accustomed in familiar conversation to confess that he wondered and could scarcely believe people when they said that they considered him so useful to themselves. It did not seem likely either that truthful people wished to deceive or that such prudent people could be deceived, since he could not excuse one alternative or the other. The whole world admired him; he alone—what was more wonderful—did not see the splendor either of his works or of his reputation.

At last, when the structure of his outward dwelling was now loosened on every side and afforded his longing soul a free departure, after the celebration of the sacred Anointing and the reception of the most holy Body of the Lord, the great day dawned for him on which an everlasting day arose. For his departure, neighboring bishops, together with a great multitude of abbots and brethren, had assembled.

85. At nearly the third hour of the day, the holy and truly blessed Abbot Bernard, the unique lamp of his generation, happily passed under Christ’s guidance from the body of death into the land of the living (A.D. 1153), surrounded by his sons and by a choir chanting on both sides amid deep sobs and abundant tears. He passed to the joyful company of the many whom he himself had sent ahead, to the rejoicing ranks of saints, and to the welcoming hosts of angels.

Happy the soul lifted so high by the privileges of its own merits; so piously escorted by the prayers of its sons, and so drawn by the sacred desires of those above! Happy the passage from labor to refreshment, from expectation [Col. 0522B] to reward, from contest to prize, from death to life, from faith to knowledge, from pilgrimage to homeland, from the world to the Father.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Bernard’s Appearance after Death, and His Burial

86. We have heard that, concerning his passage, many things appeared to many people, and they are by no means unworthy of narration; but it is too difficult to investigate every instance, and too lengthy to write everything. We shall nevertheless set down one account, which Brother William of Montpellier—the man to whom it happened—made both true and manifest by disclosing and attesting it before his death to his spiritual father.

This man, distinguished formerly in the world but more distinguished in fleeing the world, became a monk in the monastery of Grandselve [Col. 0522C] and once visited the holy Father with great devotion. As he was about to leave, he complained tearfully that he would see him no more. The Man of God said to him: “Do not fear; without doubt you shall still see me.”

This most devout William waited for the fulfillment of the promise. On the very night when Bernard departed from this life, he deserved to see him appear at the monastery of Grandselve and say: “Brother William.” He replied: “Here I am, lord.” Bernard said: “Come with me.” When William asked where they were going, he said: “Come with me to the roots of Mount Lebanon.” When they had arrived there, Bernard said to him: “You shall remain here, but I shall ascend the mountain.”

When William asked why he wished to ascend, Bernard said: “I wish to learn.” William, astonished, replied: “What do you wish to learn, father, whom we believe today to have no equal in knowledge?” The saint answered:

> “Here there is no knowledge, no knowledge of truth; above is the fullness of knowledge, above is the true knowledge of truth.”

And with these words he left him and climbed a very high mountain before his eyes. As William watched him go, he awoke; and immediately there came to him the word which sounded from heaven to John in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). When, in the morning, he spoke with his abbot and the brethren, he declared that the holy Father had departed this life. They noted the day and inquired more carefully; they found it to be as they had heard.

87. Therefore, while the faithful minister and priest of the Most High happily entered into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, to the altar of God, there to offer the sacred and acceptable sacrifice of his spirit, his body too, duly prepared and adorned in priestly vestments, was carried into the chapel of the blessed Mother of God. A great mourning crowd of nobles and commoners immediately gathered from every surrounding place, and the whole valley was filled with weeping and loud lamentation. But the more pitiable sex of women lamented more bitterly outside the monastery gates, because, while men were allowed to approach the blessed feet, the discipline of the monastic Order inexorably denied the women entrance.

For two days the dead Shepherd remained in the midst of his flock. The former grace of his most sweet countenance was in no way diminished, but rather increased; it fixed upon itself the eyes of all, drew their hearts, and buried their affections. [Col. 0523B] The multitude of people rushing in from every side increased beyond measure. The press of those crowding together, grasping the beloved saint’s feet, kissing his hands, and placing against him loaves, belts, rings, coins, and every other sort of object to preserve for themselves as a blessing and as useful for various needs, had now become intolerable.

Above all, great numbers assembled from every side in the neighboring places, awaiting the solemn hour on the third day when his sacred body would be laid to rest. For on the second day, at about noon, so great a crowd had gathered and, packed together on every side in such zeal of devotion, had surrounded the sacred body, that they had scarcely any reverence for the bishops standing by or for the brethren. Fearing therefore that something similar, or perhaps worse, might happen on the third day, they anticipated the hour. In the morning, after they had completed the divine sacrifices according to custom—as they had already done during the two preceding days, with the celebration of Masses and unceasing psalmody—they entrusted that most pure balm to its vessel: they laid the precious stone in stone, the finest pearl in its resting place. [Col. 0524A]

88. Thus, when the days of his life had happily been completed and he had fulfilled about sixty-three years, Bernard, beloved of the Lord, first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux and father of more than one hundred and sixty other monasteries, fell asleep in the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], in the hands of his sons. He was buried on the eleventh day before the Kalends of the same month [22 August], before the holy altar of the blessed Virgin Mother, of whom he had been a most devoted servant.

Upon his breast, in the very tomb, was also placed a small reliquary containing relics of the blessed apostle Thaddaeus. Those relics, sent to him from Jerusalem in that same year, he had ordered to be laid upon his body—certainly with the intention of faith and devotion that, on the day of the common resurrection, he might rise again united with that apostle.

89. These things occurred in the same year in which the blessed Pope Eugenius III, son of the same Father in holy life, departed from this light to the Lord. His merits shine forth, made illustrious by many miracles, in the City over which he had presided with distinction; Anastasius, his successor, was governing the Roman Church. Frederick the Illustrious reigned in the empire of the Romans; in the kingdom of the Franks reigned the most devout King Louis, son of Louis; while the Son of God, Jesus Christ, held the primacy of the universal Church and the monarchy of all visible and invisible creation, in the year one thousand one hundred and fifty-three from his incarnation. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0523]

# FRAGMENTS FROM THE THIRD LIFE OF SAINT BERNARD, BY, APPARENTLY, GAUFRID, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

1275

## I. The Birth and Family of Saint Bernard

[Col. 0523D]

In the territory of the city of Langres stands a castle, once noble and very renowned, named Châtillon. It had many eminent men valiant in arms, but far more distinguished for their observance of law. Among them one Tecelin, surnamed Sorus, excelled; in the vernacular this name is customarily applied to those who are reddish-blond and nearly fair-haired. This man was noble by birth, rich in possessions, gentle in character, a great lover of the poor, a foremost cultivator of piety, and possessed of an incredible zeal for justice.

Indeed, he was accustomed to marvel that he saw justice burdensome to many to maintain; and especially—against those toward whom he was most stirred—that they should abandon God’s justice either through fear or through greed. He was a most courageous knight, but he avoided praise with no less zeal than others seem to seek it. He never used arms except in defense of his own land or with his lord, the duke of Burgundy, to whom he was especially familiar and intimate; nor was he ever with him in battle without victory coming to him.

He was a native of Châtillon, but lord of a smaller castle named Fontaines, situated on a high rock and overlooking the celebrated castle of Dijon. His wife was Elizabeth, of the finest Burgundian family, daughter of Bernard of Montbard, worthy of so great a family and so great a husband—indeed, the glory of both . . . . . Elizabeth, taught by a divine oracle, loved this son more tenderly than all the others. [Col. 0525A] Therefore she gave him his grandfather’s name, calling him Bernard.

## II. A Divine Vision Given to the Boy Bernard on the Night of the Lord’s Nativity

There was at Fontaines a church, then belonging to secular canons, but whose members lived under the strictest discipline. Bernard was educated there from childhood. On the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, while he was still a little boy sleeping in his father’s house, he seemed to see the Virgin giving birth and the Word, an infant, being born from her. Immediately the bell was rung for Vigils. His mother awoke him, carefully dressed him in canonical garments, [Note: [Col. 0525] That is, as certain devout mothers are accustomed to fit monastic garments for their little sons.] and took him with her to church, as she was accustomed to do. He himself used to say of this vision that he believed it to have been at the hour of the Lord’s birth, and that what was shown to him [Col. 0525B] had been a sign of many mysteries concerning that same Nativity which were afterward revealed to him.

## III. Concerning His Father and Brothers

Andrew said to Bernard: “See to it that none of our brothers remains in the world; otherwise divide the inheritance in the middle, since it is intolerable to be separated either from you or from them.”

What shall I say of the manly spirit of his father? Seeing six sons—and sons of such quality—depart on one day, he not only did not grieve, but rejoiced greatly; he merely admonished them to act with moderation in all things: “For I know you,” he said, “that your zeal can scarcely, if ever, be restrained.”

As the brothers were departing, only one remained, and he too was a little boy, playing in the street with other children. When his elder brother Guy saw him, he said: “Look, Nivard, you may play safely, for you will have much land.” But he replied mockingly: “May this division be under a curse, in which you have heaven and I the earth.”

The boy therefore fled daily to his brothers, wishing to become a companion in their conversion. But because he was little, they sent him back and returned him to his father. At last, unable to bear his importunity, they entrusted him to a certain priest to learn letters. When he had grown a little, he too became a novice at Cîteaux; and, after receiving the habit at the end of a year, he was returned to his brothers at Clairvaux.

## IV. The Wife of Guy, the Firstborn, Becomes Abbess of Elariac near Dijon

[Col. 0525D]

His elder brother Guy, when Bernard spoke to him about conversion, began to excuse himself on account of the bond of marriage, which he said could not lawfully be dissolved. Yet he pledged his faith and gave his right hand that he would come with his brother if he could obtain his wife’s consent. His brother immediately replied:

> “That you may be of better courage, I too pledge you in the same faith: before next Easter, either by her permission—indeed, at her own request—or certainly by her death, you shall be freed from the law of your wife.”

And he made the promise by taking his hand. Not long afterward it happened as he had foretold. The young woman, noble and beautiful, began in her chamber, with every urgency of tears, to implore her astonished husband to permit her conversion. She is the woman who even to this day perseveres at the monastery of Lairiac, situated near Dijon, a woman of virtue and mother in Christ of many virgins.

## V. He Foretells to King Louis the Elder the Death of Philip, His Firstborn Son

The complaint of the bishops against Louis the Elder, king of the Franks and father of the present Louis, is plainly explained in the letters of the blessed man directed to the Apostolic See on this very matter. One day the bishops gathered before the king, and the Abbot of Clairvaux was summoned by them. Though still young, he already seemed the chief pillar of the whole Church.

The bishops fell at the king’s feet and humbly implored him, since he had sufficiently loved and honored the Church in the past, to spare it also in this matter, lest perhaps they should be compelled to act against him more severely than they wished. But he did not sufficiently yield to their entreaties.

On the next day the venerable Abbot rebuked him more sternly, plainly threatening:

> “Because you have offended the Terrible One, him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible toward the kings of the earth, be certain that this offense will be punished by the death of your firstborn Philip. For in the preceding night I saw that you and your son Louis were falling at the feet of the bishops. I immediately understood that, when Philip died, you would beg them for what you could not accomplish except through their hands: the appointment of Louis in his place.”

Philip had already been anointed king, a young man of the greatest promise and—needless to add—exceedingly dear to his father. On hearing these words, the father’s heart was deeply moved for his son. He promised that he would make satisfaction to the bishops; but, deceived by wicked counsels, he withdrew from his promise. Not long afterward, he and all France with him mourned the most lamentable death of his son Philip.

## VI. Bernard’s Letter to His Nephew Robert, Written in Rain without Rain; Gaufrid, His Secretary, Places It First among His Letters

His nephew Robert—how he had been led astray while still a boy—is made clear by the words of the letter of which we intend to speak. Since Robert had already spent several years in another Order, Bernard wrote him a letter calling back the wandering sheep. Bernard went outside the monastery enclosure in order to dictate more privately; and William, who afterward founded Rievaulx Abbey in England, wrote down on parchment what was dictated.

Suddenly rain poured down, and the writer was afraid, for they were in the open air. The venerable Abbot said to him: “It is God’s work; do what you are doing.” A marvelous thing: their garments were wet, a long letter was being written, yet the rain did not touch the parchment at all. The letter still exists; and I myself placed it first in the collection of the *Letters*, since I had heard so great a miracle from the very mouth of the man who wrote it in rain without rain.

## VII. The Duchess of Lorraine’s twofold conversion to a better life

[Col. 0527A]

The Duchess of Lorraine—who now serves God in great humility and poverty in the monastery of nuns called Tart—was still excessively devoted to bodily pleasures when it happened that the venerable Man asked both the Duke and her concerning a certain peace settlement. As he spoke and extended his hand, it happened by chance that he touched the Duchess’s cloak. One of those standing by said with a smile: “Father, you have stretched out your hand over a religious woman.” But he replied: “Her hour has not yet come” (John 7:30).

The Duchess, hearing this—for she knew letters—was deeply pierced with compunction; and the living and effective word penetrated to the very marrow of her soul. At the same time she also saw a dream by which she was further encouraged: she perceived the Man of God drawing seven horrible serpents out of her womb with his own hand. Not long afterward, entrusting her soul to him, she renounced the world; and to this day she glories that she is the woman from whom the holy Father cast out seven demons.

## VIII. Saint Bernard promises Queen Eleanor offspring, and obtains it from God

And the principal instigator of this hostility [between King Louis the Younger and Count Theobald of Champagne] was Ralph of Péronne, Count of Vermandois, who had taken the Queen’s sister after dismissing a certain kinswoman of Count Theobald.

It happened on the feast of blessed Denis that Queen Eleanor was speaking with our Father in the church of that martyr [Col. 0527C], lamenting that the Lord had closed her womb so that she could not bear children. For she had already lived with the King nearly nine years; in the first years she had indeed conceived, but miscarried, and thereafter remained barren, now despairing of fertility. To her piteous lament the venerable Father said: “Diligently seek the things that make for peace, and I, trusting in divine mercy, promise you childbirth.”

The King himself, learning this through the Queen’s report, once reconciliation had been completed, spoke more privately with the blessed Man and demanded what he had promised the Queen, etc. That same year the Queen conceived and bore a child.

## IX. The conversion of Geoffrey himself, and of others from the Parisian schools

[Col. 0527D]

It happened on one occasion that the Man of God set out for parts of France on certain business. Both on the journey and on his return he preached, as was his custom, to the scholars of Paris about conversion. In the evening he began to be sorrowful and downcast, saying to God in his prayers: “For I greatly fear that perhaps you have forgotten me, since, contrary to custom, my journey has proved wholly fruitless: I have obtained nothing in the matters for which I came, nor has any door been opened to me among these clerics for your word.”

But at that very hour God consoled him in such a manner that he clearly knew beforehand and foretold: “I shall by no means depart from here empty.” Blessed be that day from the Lord, on which light arose for me as I sat in darkness and in the shadow of death. Blessed be the day on which the Sun of righteousness—or rather, of mercy—rising from on high visited my wretched soul; when, by one word, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, by the inestimable change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, he remade me—an exceedingly contrary and perverse man—entirely into another man, so that I might become some beginning of his creature.

[Col. 0528A]

I shall never forget this mercy, by which, so richly anticipated and so suddenly changed, I caused the minds of many to be astonished at me. Many fish were caught in that capture by the Lord’s nets, and many joined us on the journey; so that, after the year of probation had passed, twenty-one of us from this company became monks.

During that same time of our novitiate, while our Father was once absent, I began to grow physically ill and mentally distressed. I know that Satan demanded me, that he might sift me as wheat; but what was happening to me did not escape the Father. Knowing perfectly by the Spirit everything that was stirring in my heart—as I learned after his return—he prayed for me that my faith might not fail.

There, there, O Lord my God, you impressed me upon his heart more wonderfully than I was worthy of. Thanks to you, Lord; thanks to you. For how could such a place be found for such a soul in such a breast? The venerable Alberic, now abbot in the place called the Blessing of God, testifies that something similar happened to him when he was a novice.

## X. The death of Guy, Saint Bernard’s eldest brother, at Pontigny, on the feast of All Saints

[Col. 0528C]

His elder brother Guy [Note: [Col. 0527D] On him, see above, Book VII, ch. 10], while returning with him from the territory of Bourges—for he had led a new abbey there [perhaps a colony]—was seized by a severe fever. After being ill for a few days at Pontigny, on the very night on which the feast of All Saints was celebrated, he deserved to be joined to their blessed fellowship.

## XI. He brings Hugh of Vitry to monastic life

[Note: [Col. 0527D] What follows, omitted by Chifflet, is appended in Mabillon’s edition at the end of the Fourth Life [Col. 0528D]; we have placed it here as the more suitable location.]

Then he was travelling toward an appointed place, where he gathered many people from every side. One day he said to his brothers: “I have a friend at Mâcon, Hugh of Vitry [Note: [Col. 0528D] On him, see Book I of the Life, no. 13], and I must bring him also, that he too may be one of us.”

He was a noble cleric, already of mature age, abounding alike in secular and ecclesiastical resources. Those who knew him therefore began to accuse Bernard of rashness. Nevertheless, confidently and without hesitation, he hastened to him. A report had spread throughout the region that he was going to Jerusalem; for this was his pretence—that he was setting out not for the Jerusalem in which he had been, but for that in which the Lord is.

When the aforesaid Hugh saw him, he rushed into his embrace weeping and wailing; but the Man of God paid no attention at all to his tears. When Hugh had recovered himself a little, he disclosed his intention to him. And behold, grief was renewed [Col. 0529A], and the fountain of tears flowed more abundantly, so that throughout that entire day his eye did not cease.

The following night they lay together on a most narrow bed, scarcely large enough for one. Nor did Hugh then cease from tears, so that the holy Man rebuked him for not letting him sleep. But when Hugh fell asleep, it seemed to him that, after invoking the Holy Spirit according to custom, Bernard was speaking to him about conversion, and that his voice lacked no power. When morning came and Hugh again wept, Bernard, now annoyed, began to rebuke him more harshly.

But Hugh said: “Today I have not the same cause for mourning as yesterday. Yesterday I wept over you; today over myself. For I know your manner of life, and I do not fail to know that conversion is more necessary for me than for you.”

Bernard rejoiced and said to him: “Weep enough now, for these are excellent tears; do not stop.”

Afterward, when the clerics saw them walking together and rejoicing together, never separated from one another even for a moment, they tried to tear Hugh away from Bernard, fearing—or rather, now plainly recognizing—how they were moved by one spirit. They therefore held Hugh and would on no account thereafter allow the Man of God to speak with him. Bernard departed sorrowfully; but his heart nevertheless still had confidence in the Lord.

After some days, hearing of a council of bishops, he hastened there in order to see Hugh. When the clerics saw him, they looked at him with unusual hostility and surrounded Hugh on every side, lest anyone have access to him. While the bishops were seated and conferring in the field, Bernard sat among the clerics beside Hugh. He could not speak to him because of those standing by, yet he wept most copiously upon Hugh’s neck. And behold, waters flooded down and heaven gave rain, so that they scattered and ran in all haste to the nearest village.

But the Blessed Man, holding Hugh by the hand, said: “You shall stand with me in the rain.” Immediately calm weather returned, and they alone stood in the field. Hugh confessed the oath he had made: that he would by no means become a monk before a year had passed. He had done this to deceive the clerics, knowing well that the probationary period lasted a year. There, their spiritual fellowship having been wholly confirmed, they returned holding one another’s hands; and, all now despairing, no one thereafter tried to detain Hugh.

## XII. Abbot Galerannus appears to Saint Bernard

In those same years, while the Man of God remained in his Clairvaux, a religious man, Galerannus, first abbot of Ourscamp, having died at Igny, appeared to the blessed Father and received from him permission and command to enter into the rest of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0529] See Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, Book XXVII, ch. 5.]

It is quite certain that this also happened in the case of many others, so much so that, for some persons, before their death had been reported to him, he even celebrated the solemnities of Mass and offered the divine sacrifices, to the astonishment of those with him, who carefully noted the day.

## XIII. The death of Andrew, Saint Bernard’s brother

[Col. 0530A]

At the same time, while he was occupied in negotiations aimed at seeking peace, his brother Andrew ended this passing life at Clairvaux. Before the holy Father had heard anything concerning Andrew’s illness, Andrew appeared to him in a night dream together with his brother Gerard and gave him the kiss of peace. Bernard understood it to be the sign of his departure; and after a few days he heard of his death.

## XIV. On Hervé, Abbot of Ourscamp, Galerannus’s successor

But since we have mentioned the venerable Galerannus, we do not think that the things which happened concerning Hervé—his successor, no less distinguished in character and religious devotion than in birth—should be passed over in silence.

[Col. 0530B]

Hervé, a boy of royal blood, was brought up in the household of his uncle, the Bishop of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0529D] Simon]. While the holy Father was staying with that bishop, he once heard the boy singing, as the boy knew how to sing very well. Taking the song as an occasion, Bernard spoke in his customary way at length to those present about the spiritual life.

That same night, in a dream, he seemed to be celebrating the solemnities of Mass, and an angel approached and gave the boy the kiss of peace which he had received from Bernard’s mouth. Bernard thus plainly foretold that the boy would without doubt become a religious, so clearly that the boy himself did not remain unaware of the prophecy given concerning him.

Its fulfilment was awaited with certainty. Thus, many years later, when Hervé had grown up and was grievously reproached by his own conscience, he nevertheless took full comfort in the memory of that word, saying to himself, as he himself later testified to us: “You are afraid for no reason; it is impossible that you should perish. The word of the blessed Man will certainly be fulfilled in its time.”

And indeed we now see that it was so fulfilled. Moreover, that angel was Abbot Galerannus, who gave Hervé the peace received from the holy Father’s mouth. For Hervé, still a young man, fled domestic enemies and received from Galerannus the habit of religious life.

[Col. 0530C]

After succeeding him in the abbey, a man of most gentle spirit and a most fervent disciplinarian of his body, he was perfected in a short time and fulfilled many years; for his soul was pleasing to God. While still well and sound, he knew beforehand of his death, his predecessor himself revealing it to him. Without delay he began to be burdened by a severe bodily illness; and before the sixth day, resting in a blessed end, he was laid with his fathers.

## XV. Saint Bernard foreknows the conversion of others

What we have said of him—that the Saint of the Lord knew beforehand his conversion—we know also occurred in the case of very many others. Among them were Macelinus, an illustrious German youth; the venerable man Albero, who afterward became abbot in Sweden; and that great man Geoffrey of Péronne, who held and ended the office of Prior at Clairvaux.

To this Geoffrey also, while he was still in the novices’ cell and was anxious about his father, etc.

[Col. 0531]

# THE FOURTH LIFE OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT, WRITTEN IN TWO BOOKS BY JOHN THE HERMIT

1279 Here begins the letter of John the Hermit to Peter, Bishop of Tusculum, concerning the life of our blessed father Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0531A]

1. In accordance with your request and desire, most beloved Father Peter, we have judged it fitting, according to our measure, to commit to writing for your edification and that of others the life of blessed Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux, so that through his imitation and examples we may attain eternal blessedness.

Without doubt, this Saint of whom we wish to speak is worthy to be praised and venerated. For, having attained the glory of the heavenly kingdom with the saints and elect of God, he deserved to receive praise and honour in the midst of the Church. Therefore he obtained a name in holiness, and his memory lives in blessing. For it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15).

Truly this Saint is righteous, found faithful among the number of the saints, shining like fire and like a solid vessel of gold adorned with every precious stone. Therefore the Lord made him increase among his people, and multiplied his seed like the sand of the sea. His speech did not resound in human ears without effect, but by deeds and actions supplied motives for the things that ought to be done, glorious in signs and powers. Many also were found among the number of the saints whom he begot through the Gospel.

If we wished to set forth the number of miracles performed through him, the smallness of our ability would not suffice. Indeed, if we knew them all fully and could unfold them, perhaps we would not be believed. Therefore we wish at present to set forth a few, to which faith ought not be denied.

2. A certain monk, a truthful and sincere lover of the venerable Abbot, was perhaps walking with a lay brother named Humbert through a thicket adjoining Clairvaux monastery. He held in his hands a book of the Miracles of the holy Father and explained them in the idiom of the Roman language, for his own edification and that of the other.

They happened to sit down, for a brief rest, beneath a pear tree beside the road by which those labouring in the garden daily went and came. When they rose not long afterward, the aforesaid monk, through forgetfulness—as often happens—carelessly left upon the ground the book which he had held in his hand shortly before.

[Col. 0531D]

He went away and, occupied with the observances of regular discipline, eventually remembered how, where, and when he had lost it. Conceiving no hope at all of recovering it—both because he had left it near the road and because meanwhile so great a flood of rains had occurred that, even if it were found, he believed it would be good for nothing but loss—after some time he ceased seeking it, indeed seemed wholly to abandon the search; yet he was especially distressed that through his negligence he had lost the volume of the holy Man’s Miracles.

After about a month had passed in this way, he took a short walk through the garden and sat down beneath the aforesaid tree. He had neither intended to look for, nor hoped to recover, what he had lost. Yet, in a wondrous and unheard-of way, he was astonished to see the book suddenly placed before him, as though preserved by someone and newly, deliberately set beside him.

[Col. 0532A]

And, to make what occurred seem still more marvellous, both the parchment and the writing remained so sound and uncorrupted—except that the outer covering appeared sprinkled with a very few drops—as if this very book had been stored in the library with the other books.

I do not know what listeners may think of this; but for my own part, I do not hesitate to affirm that such an unusual occurrence could not have happened without a miracle. Reason persuades, and truth compels, us to ascribe it to the merits of the blessed Man.

3. In the silence of the night, after the weariness of his day’s labour, he had lain down upon his bed for a brief rest. While awake, a venerable man appeared to him, clothed in a snow-white robe, of middle height, advanced in years, white-haired, and reverend in angelic countenance.

[Col. 0532C]

He seemed to hold two books in his hands. Approaching the brother mentioned above, he handed him both and said: “Take them, look, and read.”

Struck with fear at the sudden vision, as commonly happens, but taking courage from the kindly speech, tranquil appearance, and angelic face, he replied: “Lord Father, I do not know letters. How am I, simple and unlearned, to read?”

But the other said: “Son, do not fear. Behold, the Lord is with you and will teach you; and through my intercession it will go well with you.”

Strengthened by this pious admonition, the brother took both volumes, opened them, and read, wondering and marveling within himself how this could happen. The person who stood by then departed, as though carrying one volume away with him and leaving the other with the brother; after bidding him farewell and giving him a blessing, he vanished.

What then? What we shall say is indeed wonderful to relate. For what could be more wonderful than this wonder? We all know the brother, every one of us. He was a layman only a little while before and did not even know the alphabet. Yet, God enlightening his understanding and certain brothers assisting him, he advanced in a short time so far that he knew not only how to read, but also how to sing quite competently and properly.

[Col. 0533A]

Thereafter, with practice and grace working together, he began to understand somewhat the meanings of words and gradually advanced in this sort of knowledge. He recorded the vision mentioned above in hope of divine help and of the assistance of the blessed Man, whom we believe appeared to him.

He committed to writing several of Bernard’s miracles which were either unknown to writers or had been passed over through negligence, so fittingly, so well, and so elegantly that we are repeatedly carried away in astonishment and say with the prophet David: “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes” (Psalm 117:23).

1280 Who, then, can deny that this was done miraculously? What miracle could be clearer or more manifest? First, therefore, we ascribe it to the grace of God; next, we attribute it to the merits of the Saint; finally, we assign it to the brother’s faith and obedience.

4. What more need be said? Truly this Saint is great among the number of the saints: among Angels and Archangels, among Apostles and martyrs, among confessors and virgins. For he was never defiled, but always remained a virgin and undefiled. His mind was always in God, and God was with him. Everything in him was disciplined; everything was distinguished by virtue.

[Col. 0533C]

He raised the dead, commanded demons, restored walking to the lame, speech to the mute, and health to the sick. He was humble among those near him, magnificent among the great; wondrous in writings and reputation; gentle toward the good, terrible toward the wicked; illustrious in merits, an exemplar of morals, light and mirror of Christ’s followers—especially of monks and all religious persons.

The law of God was in his heart, and his teaching shone in the Church of God like the sun in summer days. He was a staff to the lame, an eye to the blind, compassionate to the sick, generous and kind to the poor, pleasant to all, a fountain of wisdom and a pillar of justice, father of the Cistercian Order and model of virtue.

O mercy of our Creator! O kindness of Jesus Christ, who gave us such a champion! Come, dearest friends: drink and be intoxicated. For the examples of the holy Father are drink and food for the soul. With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we shall relate some of them.

I ask you, Father, to pray for me to that same Lord of ours, who is Alpha and Omega, that he may be the initiator and completer of this work.

Here begins the second letter to Herbert, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia.

You ask of me, soldier of Christ H., with the trust and charity by which you love me, that I should publish for you in writing something concerning the life or deeds of the venerable father, blessed Bernard. For when I was still a boy, I once spent much time among some of his disciples; you ask this so that your mouth may often utter the remembrance of his sweetness, and that a written account of works of such holiness may continually delight your eyes and ears.

[Col. 0534A]

Although I have seen many great things among the acts of the Man of God, things worthy of remembrance and most worthy of imitation, yet no small portion of them could be stolen away and fall from my memory, whether slipping away through the very instability of youth or failing to adhere to the tenderness of a childish mind.

Moreover, if anything has not fallen from my memory because of the wonder of the miracle or the worthiness of the deed, who am I to apply an unskilled pen to unfolding the praises of so great a Father, and to burst forth with uncircumcised lips into the praises of the Man of God? Let the deeds of saints be narrated by those whom you do not doubt have been taught by the Lord, to whom God has given a learned tongue, that they may know how to speak a word in due season.

But your friends, O God, are beyond my telling; therefore I have chosen the safer course of venerating rather than praising the holy Man, leaving wiser people to explain what he did, while I am content merely to emulate what he taught.

Yet, lest your hope—which, as I suppose, you had conceived more from affection than from my learning—be wholly disappointed, receive briefly what you already knew concerning the character of the pious Father. And while you add knowledge through the account of him, add also discipline to yourself from his deeds.

[Col. 0534B]

This man was most pure in a wondrous simplicity, so intent upon heavenly utterances that, in accordance with the Gospel faith, he despised the entire world out of love for eternal things. Retaining here nothing except a bodily dwelling-place, he lived in mind and spirit in heaven.

He was one in whose breast patience built itself a house, so that he counted it all joy whenever any adversity assailed the strength of his mind. His humility surpassed human measure, as though he had sworn to regain heaven through the perfection of that virtue through whose failure the devil fell into hell.

Throughout his life neither temperance nor fortitude deserted him: neither did prosperity dissolve him in pleasures, nor adversity break and weaken him. Chastity’s brightness clothed his body; unquenchable charity inflamed his mind, so that he was bright outwardly, burning within, and altogether desirable.

Good Jesus! How great was his diligence in obeying, moderation in commanding, gravity in exhorting, and discipline in carrying things out! He had no arrogance from authority and no haughtiness from reverence. Rather, though he surpassed all, he submitted himself to all, thereby showing himself to be the disciple of him who came not to be served but to serve.

[Col. 0534C]

He was gentle, devout, and approachable: he did not omit discipline in kindness, nor admit cruelty in severity. And what can I say of his faith and pious belief? Through it he deserved frequently to have heavenly mysteries revealed to him, while divine sacraments made themselves known to him by visible effects.
