## Here begins the prologue to the Life of Saint Bernard

Whoever, dearest brothers, wishes to write the lives of saints must first correct himself of lies and iniquities. Saints do not love lies, but condemn those who speak them. For they themselves rather affirm what is written: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

He who writes the lives of saints offends, just as he who weaves fine linen offends if his hands are stained, because their works are defiled. To weave fine linen is to write the lives of saints. To have stained hands is to be corrupted by vainglory or a wicked conscience, through which lies are fabricated. How can one who has a lie in his mind speak rightly concerning the deeds of saints?

[Col. 0535A]

I tell you, beloved ones, that this labour—namely, writing the lives of saints—weighs heavily upon me, and not without reason. For neither my own merits commend me nor learning adorns me. Yet I would rather incur the reproach of rashness than, under the cloud of disordered modesty, pass over in silence the praises of saints covered over by silence.

I call upon the Godhead, who knows all things, as witness that I intend to write nothing frivolous, nothing for the sake of human praise or gain; rather, I write what the truthful, straightforward, and holy report of elders confirms—elders whom it is as devout to believe as it is impious not to believe.

I write for servants and friends of God, whom it is most perilous to deceive, delighted alike by the holy Man’s glory and virtues. Even if I keep silent, people proclaim him, intensely marveling at the greatness of his miracles. Let no one, therefore, despise what is read. Although the greatness of what is to be told exceeds human reason and possibility, all things are possible with God, and nothing is impossible to one who believes.

[Col. 0535B]

Yet whoever doubts these things should forgive devoutly rather than accuse me of falsehood. For there is nothing in human affairs that cannot somehow be slandered or perverted through malicious interpretation. Here, however, is a matter in which human judgment can neither be deceived nor deceive. Why? Because the certainty of the matter removes doubt, and because, as Seneca says, falsehood is thin and transparent like glass (*Letters*, 79).

Again I tell you, brothers: this labour afflicts me less; but, as I hope, God’s help will make it possible for what has been begun to be completed well. Therefore I call upon you, Word through whom all things were created, that you may grant me fittingly to say true things concerning the blessed Man.

## Here begins the Life of Saint Bernard

1. The most blessed Bernard was born of worthy stock in Fontaines, his father’s town, in the district of Langres [Col. 0535D]. Noble indeed in lineage according to the flesh, he was nobler by the eminence of his mind.

His father was named Tescelin; his mother was Aalays, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, a powerful and eminent man in worldly rank, who, as many assert, traced his origin from the noble line of the ancient dukes of Burgundy. But since we have not undertaken at present to set out the history of his family, let us return to what ought rather to be said.

Bernard’s grandfather Bernard wished his daughter Aalays to be educated in letters, intending in the future to make her a nun. But God’s providence determined otherwise concerning her. When she had reached her fifteenth year, Tescelin, lord of the town of Fontaines, a man distinguished in nobility and rank and very wealthy in worldly goods, sought her in marriage. Her father, because he could not honourably refuse, granted the request.

2. After she had been joined to her husband by the law of marriage, God granted her to set the fruit of her womb upon his table, as she did.

[Col. 0536A]

For she bore six sons and one daughter, not so much for her husband as for God, as the gracious Lord deigned to show in their holy works. He enlightened their minds from his most holy Spirit. Having tasted spiritual sweetness, they renounced the devil’s service and the pomp of the world. With the effective pious exhortation of their brother Bernard—who was a burning light, though still under the bushel and not upon the lampstand—they came into the wilderness for the most strenuous life of cenobites and received the monastic habit.

Thus they all became monks and together undertook a life pleasing to God. Their daughter became a nun in the monastery of Jully. O blessed womb that bore such sons! O blessed breasts that nourished such persons! O blessed origin of this family; glorious fertility of one womb! Therefore, men worthy of God, you unanimously despised present things for heavenly glory and chose to live eternally with Christ rather than to enjoy temporary happiness by living happily for a time in this unhappy world.

But enough concerning your way of life, since the manner of history does not permit us to say more. Returning to the birth from which we began our account, we continue what we have undertaken.

3. In the order of the children, Guy was the firstborn: a disciplined man, beloved by God, wise alike in word and deed. The second was Gerard, a man of venerable life, honourable in conduct, distinguished in wisdom, prudent in counsel. The third was Bernard, light and mirror of his brothers and lofty pillar of the holy Church. The fourth was Andrew, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil. The fifth was Bartholomew, who, in the flourishing years of his earliest youth, anticipated the lives of old men and adorned an unblemished age with sincerity of mind. The sixth was Nivard, who, despising earthly inheritance, chose heavenly things before it.

[Col. 0536C]

The girl, who followed blessed Bernard in order of birth, received the name Humbeline in holy baptism. Their mother, bearing all these, as has been said, for God and not for the world, as soon as she had brought forth each child, in that very anguish and affliction of body and contrition of heart, lifted the child up from the ground with her own hands and offered it to the Lord.

O woman firm in faith and steadfast in God’s love, persevering in prayer! Blessed are you, and blessed your womb, and still more blessed the fruit of your womb. She would not permit the other women who had assembled for her childbirth, as was customary, to make the offering mentioned above. For she knew the Scriptures, especially the Davidic psalm in which is sung: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

But she offered the most blessed Bernard to the Lord not as quickly as the others, but when he was older. She did indeed offer him, and did this most devoutly; and, that he might prove more devoted toward the Lord, she entrusted him to be instructed in literary studies. With these matters thus passed over, let us turn our pen to both parents of such glorious offspring.

4. In Burgundy, as we have stated above, there was a man of praiseworthy life named Tescelin, and his wife Aalays. Both were noble according to worldly rank, but more illustrious in faith and works; and the higher they were, the humbler they were, as it is written: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Sirach 3:20).

[Col. 0537A]

It would be most difficult to recount everything concerning their faith, hope, charity, justice, and other virtues. Nevertheless, for instruction, we shall present a few things.

At one time the aforesaid man, because various disputes had arisen—as often happens among secular persons—had arranged to fight a judicial duel with an opponent who was much inferior in birth and poorer in substance. The appointed and fixed day of combat arrived, and both sides assembled.

But the venerable Tescelin, recalling the fear of God and the divine judgments in which it is said, “Judge your neighbour justly” (Leviticus 19:15), and likewise, “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16), although he was stronger and more powerful and could have overcome his enemy and won great profit from victory, nevertheless voluntarily made peace with his opponent, surrendering and abandoning without dispute whatever was under contention.

[Col. 0537B]

O great mercy, great clemency of the man! Great are the things we recount, but greater are those that follow.

5. His venerable wife Aalays likewise used, among her other notable virtues, to go about the houses, seek out the poor, sick, and needy, and distribute from her own resources whatever they required.

1283 She also took the greatest care of the lame and infirm. She used neither servants nor other attendants to perform these duties, but did it herself. She came to their dwellings and supplied each person with what was needed; in the hospices of churches she most devoutly served the sick assigned separately, scouring their pots, serving food, washing cups, and doing every other thing which servants and attendants customarily perform as servile work.

[Col. 0537C]

What more? Do we wish to relate all her virtues? Certainly not, because we would not be believed. Yet we shall set forth one especially worthy of narration: a matter full of miracle, which we ourselves heard not without wonder from a most religious abbot named Robert. He lived more than sixty-seven years in a monastery under the yoke of regular discipline. He was the nephew of that matron of whom we intend to speak, the son of her sister; and blessed Bernard addressed the first of his letters to him.

6. “The mother,” he said, “of our holy Father was exceedingly devout. Her custom was, each year on the feast of Saint Ambrose [or: Ambrosinian], to gather together all the clergy whom she could find, and on that day solemnly refresh them with food and drink in honor of God, blessed Mary, the aforesaid saint, and all the saints. Since God wished to reward her for the honor that she rendered to His saint every year, He made her aware beforehand of her death—which was to occur on the anniversary day of that same feast—on a certain day before the feast. Thus it is not incredible that she shared in the spirit of prophecy. She informed her husband, her sons, and all her household of what had been revealed to her. They all wondered; at first they did not believe that it would happen as she had foretold, but afterwards they wondered all the more.

“As the vigil of the feast approached, a fever seized her limbs. On the feast day, after the celebration of Mass, she most devoutly asked that the Body of the Lord be brought to her; and this was done. Then, strengthened by the sacrament of the most holy Anointing, after receiving the Eucharist, she had all the clergy summoned to supper according to custom. While they reclined at table, she called her first-born son Guy, directing and earnestly impressing on him that, as soon as the clergy had finished their meal, he should have them gather before her. He, most kindly obeying his kindly mother, assembled the clergy after the meal, as his mother had requested.

“The clergy were present. When they had assembled, the handmaid of Christ, rejoicing in spirit, announced that the dissolution of her body was near. They, meanwhile, earnestly prayed to the Lord for her and began the litany; and she sang psalms with them most devoutly until she breathed her last. But when the choir of singers had reached that petition in the litany, ‘By thy Passion and thy Cross, deliver her, O Lord,’ she, still unceasing in prayer, at the very point of death commended her spirit into the Lord’s hands and, raising her hand, signed herself with the sign of the holy cross; then in peace she yielded up her spirit—without doubt received by the angels and placed by God among the holy souls—awaiting with great happiness and rest the resurrection of her body on the day of the general resurrection, when Christ Jesus, our judge and advocate, shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. In this manner that holy soul departed from the temple of her holy body, and her hand, raised as it was to make the sign of the cross, remained so, before the eyes and to the amazement of all who were present.”

7. O woman inflamed with the fire of divine love, strong in faith, most patient in hope, devoted in charity! O happy and blessed woman, who attained such honor before God that you knew beforehand the day of your death, and that in your blessed passing the sign of our redemption shone so visibly over you: that sign, I mean, upon which our merciful God and Lord Jesus deigned to suffer for the salvation of the human race. Thus the departure of this blessed soul brought joy to the angels in heaven, but, conversely, grief and mourning to Christ’s poor, the widows and orphans, whose mother she had been in the world.

1284. 8. When news of her death spread everywhere, the abbot of Saint Benignus at Dijon, named Gerannus, a man of venerable life, came at once and requested the sacred body, regarding her relics as a glorious treasure. Having obtained what he requested, he and those with him—with tears flowing abundantly in an affection of piety, both through his own reverence and through the cooperative good will of her sons—bowed their shoulders and carried the holy body with them as a precious treasure. At last they came to the castle of Dijon. And behold, all the people had gone out to meet them with crosses and candles; with great joy and reverence, all accompanying the precious clay of the sacred body to the basilica of the most blessed and renowned martyr Benignus, they committed it there to burial with great reverence [Col. 0539A–B].

After this, the aforesaid abbot had six images made above her tomb, in memory of her six sons, as they are visibly shown even to the present day. Thereafter, for five years, she was accustomed to appear to her son Andrew, as the history of Lord William, the man of God, relates. And when the brothers began to discuss his conversion, she appeared to blessed Bernard, saying: “My son Bernard, do not be afraid; act manfully, and effectively complete what you have begun, for it is God’s work. For this reason posterity shall call you blessed. But I await you in the glory of God.” Having said this, she disappeared; and blessed Bernard advanced ever more in the service of God [Col. 0539B–C].

## Here begins the prologue to the second book

We desire, with pious intention, to set forth a few matters concerning the virtues of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, so that through his examples we may rejoice with those who rejoice and praise God with those who praise Him. In the first part of this little work, we recounted the beginning of his birth; here we relate some of the miracles which God deigned to perform through his hands.

But what are we to do? Can we comprehend everything? Certainly not, for we should not be believed. The children of Adam are perverse, as they have been from the beginning. But what follows from that? Must we be silent because of their unbelief? No; rather, according to our ability, we must labor in the Lord’s field. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” What we have in our heart that is worthy of utterance, insofar as it pertains to our purpose, we shall commit to writing [Col. 0539C–D].

## Here begins the second book

1. Bernard, a boy of good disposition, now having reached, as we have received from our fathers, the age of twenty-two years, sought the wilderness and, with companions given him by God, embraced the most strenuous purpose of monastic life at the place called Cîteaux. At that time there was such a scarcity of temporal goods that those assembled there could scarcely obtain clothes for proper use. Indeed, before his arrival some religious men had begun to dwell in that place, but they were very few. From that time forward our merciful Lord undoubtedly blessed them and sanctified the place itself, on account of His servant Bernard, whom He had sent to them; and He bestowed abundantly upon all dwelling there whatever was necessary [Col. 0539D–0540A].

While this most holy young man was in the novices’ cell, some of his relatives came to visit him and spoke with him. After the signal for the ninth hour, each returned home, while the most devout young man went to church for the work of God. Then, according to custom, raising his eyes to heaven and expecting to find God’s grace as before, he did not find it. He considered within himself that this had happened to him on account of some fault or sin, and found nothing except the idle talk to which he had imprudently exposed himself shortly before. Recognizing himself as guilty for this reason, he prostrated his whole body beside the altar, saying with the prophet: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury,” etc. (Psalm 6:1). After he had done this for twenty-five days, the glory of the Lord appeared to him, filled him, and gave him knowledge of the saints, so that his works might be brought to perfection in goodness.

Others also came to visit him and received permission from Abbot Stephen to speak with him. When he was led to them, he took pieces of tow and put them under his hood into his ears, so that by this device he might keep himself free from empty conversation. Thus he came to the guests, remained with them for the whole hour, and heard nothing; nor did he speak, except a few words of edification. Then, when the bell rang, he joyfully left them and came to church, his grace having thus been preserved for him by God. O man of outstanding holiness and worthy of remembrance, who, by providing for himself in this way, still edifies those who hear and shall edify them until the end—profitable not only to himself but to countless others! [Col. 0540A–C]

2. Not long afterwards, Abbot Stephen, distinguished by honorable conduct, the father of that new planting by God’s ordinance, resolved to make an offering to God from the fruit which God had given him, with manifold increase. Having sent out a community, he founded the abbey called La Ferté. Shortly thereafter he also founded two others, namely Pontigny and Val d’Absinthe, now called Clairvaux. There he appointed as abbot Bernard, a young man of holy conduct. Bernard remained there for many days with his companions, dwelling and praying in hunger, thirst, fastings, vigils, cold and nakedness, in many labors, and in various afflictions of soul and body. Yet he was unceasingly intent on meditation upon the divine utterances; day by day he vigilantly purified his faculties and freed his soul from every passion, illumining it with the light of impassibility [Col. 0540C–D].

Those first gathered there endured such want that their food was bread—not oat bread, for they would have considered such food precious—but bread roughly clumped together rather than made, from some far cheaper mixture, indeed from the very cheapest. In summer they had boiled leaves of trees for pottage; in winter, roots of herbs. O how many labors, distresses, illnesses, tribulations, anxieties, and how grievous sufferings of infirmity and need the most blessed man and the brothers sent with him endured in that place! Beech mast, other wild fruits, and certain other things which the earth commonly produces of itself were their better dishes; for they tasted neither meat nor any fat, eggs, cheese, or wine at all. Their clothing, in summer as in winter, consisted of a cowl and tunic, which were renewed very rarely. They also wore poor hose and shoes that often remained torn and unstitched for a long time before being repaired; owing to the extreme lack of leather, they bound them with cords [Col. 0540D–0541B].

O noble and great men in the world! Who brought you to these dry and dangerous places except Him who was rich in heaven and poor and humble on earth, lying in a manger—He to whom each of your blessed mothers, having brought you into the light, offered you with deepest devotion? Who then instilled in you the resolve to leave your possessions—your estates and castles, male and female servants, kinsfolk and connections, wives and children—except Him who, Creator of angels and archangels, assumed human nature for the salvation of the human race?

3. In that great want of which we have spoken, salt was lacking one day among their other necessities. The holy abbot called one of his brothers, named Guibert, and said to him: “My son Guibert, take the donkey, go to the market, and buy us salt.” But he replied, “Where is the money?” The man of God answered: “Believe me, son, I do not know a time when I possessed gold or silver. For He who has my purse and my treasures in His hands is above.” Then the brother, as though smiling, said: “If I go empty-handed, I shall return empty-handed.” The saint said to him: “Do not fear, my son, but go in confidence. For He who has our treasures, as I have already told you, will be with you on the journey and will provide everything for which I send you.”

At these words, receiving the blessing of his devout Father, he set out with the donkey for the market at the castle called Risnel, more unbelieving than he should have been. Yet the merciful and compassionate Lord did not regard his unbelief but considered the faith of His servant and gave him everything for which he had been sent. As he approached the castle and came to a certain village, he met a priest who greeted him and said: “Where are you from, brother? Where are you going?” He replied, carefully explaining the reason for his journey and the poverty of the place in which the holy Father lived with his sons. On hearing this, the priest was deeply moved; he took the brother to his house and gave him half a modius of salt and fifty solidi or more, as Guibert himself often used to relate [Col. 0541B–D].

Having received these things, he began to give boundless thanks to God and to say in his heart: “Without doubt, the word I heard from my Father is true. But in this I have sinned grievously against him: I did not believe him, but came here in unbelief.” Taking leave of the priest, he returned to the monastery. On entering, he ran to the man of God and told him all that had happened on the way. The holy Father said to him: “I tell you, son, that nothing is as necessary for every Christian as faith. Therefore have faith, and it shall be well with you all the days of your life.” From that day onward, both that brother and the others held the holy Father’s words in greater reverence.

O good Jesus, who can recount the faith possessed by this saint? I know, Lord, I know and recognize in myself that I cannot do this. Yet if anyone is eager to know more of this, let him go to the library and read the Holy Scriptures; by reading them he will be able very greatly to perceive how charitable and God-fearing this saint was, so as not to offend his Savior. For in this present history I have not undertaken to write his praises, but only to recount certain miracles or wonderful works which the Lord deigned to make manifest to the world through him [Col. 0542A–B].

4. A certain brother from the brethren of Clémentin-Pré came to visit Christ’s new planting. He was honorably received, as far as was possible, and was offered half a loaf of oat bread, which was ready at hand. Receiving it and, with great wonder at the sort of food on which they lived, taking it back to Clémentin-Pré, he reported to all dwelling there the voluntary abstinence of Christ’s servants amid the greatest poverty, their patience in abstinence, and their generous liberality in want [Col. 0542B–C].

At once the brothers of Clémentin-Pré, deeply moved and sharing their suffering, agreed jointly to assist them. Then the master of that place, a venerable man named Odo, beloved by God and men, loaded horses and donkeys and brought bread and provisions in carts. From that day to the present there has been such fellowship between Clairvaux and Clémentin-Pré that, whenever brothers of Clémentin-Pré came to Clairvaux, they were treated, in spiritual and temporal matters alike, just as one of the brethren of Clairvaux would be treated. The rites due to the dead were likewise reciprocally performed. In this way merciful Jesus provided ever more abundantly for His servants [Col. 0542C–D].

5. A woman also came bringing one hundred solidi, with which the nakedness of their feet was covered. They lacked every beast of burden except the donkey on which the abbot travelled for his visitations and by which wood was carried for necessities. Pressed by hunger, cold, and other needs, they complained to their abbot that extreme poverty compelled them to depart. On hearing this, the abbot gently and mildly consoled them, impressing on them as much as he could the fear and love of God, hope of eternal life, and divine recompense. But they, exceedingly distressed and distressed by manifold grief, would not agree at all; rather, they wished to return to Cîteaux.

When the man of God saw their despair, he finally turned to prayer. Having done so, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him before them all: “Rise, Bernard; your prayer has been heard.” When the brothers heard this, they glorified God and His holy Bernard, and said to him: “Tell us, Father, what did you ask of the Lord?” He replied: “What do you wish to know, men of little faith? Remain here, and you will know afterwards.” While they talked among themselves, giving a little time to conversation—not idle talk, but holy discourse—someone came and offered the holy Father ten pounds. Without delay, a man of Bar-sur-Aube, whose son was brought near to despair of life by an excessive illness, brought him thirteen pounds and humbly begged him to have mercy on his son. The holy abbot sent him away joyful, promising that he would find his son restored to health. On returning, the man found his son recovered, as the man of God had promised; therefore later he gave abundant thanks to God’s servant [Col. 0542D–0543B].

A short time later, God’s mercy looked abundantly and graciously upon them, so that, abounding in eternal and temporal aid, they lacked nothing in any grace, according to the saying: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God” (Psalm 34:10).

6. Twelve years later a famine arose in Burgundy so severe that people almost consumed their own limbs. Under the pressure of this same necessity, a great multitude of poor people came to the gate of Clairvaux. Because of so great a crowd, the holy abbot and his brothers took counsel and, by common decision, admitted two thousand under a token, so that alms might also be given to the others, though less. For they did not have resources by which to sustain everyone until harvest; yet the merciful Lord multiplied those resources in such a way that they sufficed for them until after the harvest, namely for a period of three months [Col. 0543B–C].

Two boys received a token, though their mother did not. Completely at a loss as to what to do, she finally conceived the plan of making, from moss, something like a child wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that by this device she might save herself from the threatening danger of famine. This she did. For some time she thus received alms, until at length the deception was discovered. When her reduced allowance did not suffice for her, she subsequently perished through the distress of famine and illness.

After her death the holy abbot, passing by, heard the boys lamenting for their mother’s death and ordered each of the passersby to ask why they were weeping. The boys explained the matter in order. Hearing this, the blessed man entered the place where the body lay and prostrated himself in prayer. While he prayed, the woman, as though waking from sleep, was restored to life before the eyes and ears of all who stood present. She gave thanks to God and to His saint, by whose merits and prayers she had returned to life; she also declared how great were the torments that she had suffered for her fault [Col. 0543C–0544A].

7. One day alms were being distributed to the poor on the side of a mountain, when rain began to fall. The saint of God happened to be there; raising his hand, he made the sign of the cross against it. This done, the rain was seen unexpectedly to divide itself to the right and left, so that not even a drop touched them.

Again, at harvest time, this miracle occurred. One night, while the blessed man slept and the monks slept all around, he heard angels in the church, with a clear and delightful voice, praising God and the blessed Virgin Mary. When he heard this, he rose secretly and walked slowly to the church, so that, standing nearby, he might more plainly see what it was. He saw the holy Mother of God between two angels; one seemed to hold in his hand a golden censer, the other incense. Led by one of them, the holy man proceeded, as it were, at the right hand of the glorious Virgin, until he came to the altar. There he heard, in an angelic voice, the antiphon *Salve Regina* sung in full to the end. He retained it in his heart and is reported subsequently to have written it down and sent it to Pope Eugenius, so that by command of apostolic authority it might be solemnly observed in churches in honor of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God. This was done, as many still testify [Col. 0544A–C].

> [Note: Alberic relates this story somewhat differently in his *Chronicle* under the year 1130. He records that Saint Bernard, having once been received as a guest at Saint Benignus in Dijon, heard before the clock, near the altar, angels sweetly singing the antiphon *Salve, Regina*. At first he believed it had been sung by the community, and said to the abbot on the following day: “You sang the Antiphon of Le Puy most excellently last night near the altar of the blessed Virgin.” The antiphon was called the Antiphon of Le Puy because Haimier, bishop of Le Puy, composed it. See note 14 on the sermon on the antiphon *Salve, Regina*, above, vol. III of the works of Saint Bernard. [Col. 0543D–0544D]]

At the dedication of the church, the man worthy of God delivered to his sons a highly persuasive sermon in the chapter house at Clairvaux. In his wonderful manner, he showed what so solemn a mystery of dedication signified in the outward appearance of consecrated things and in the acts of so devout a consecration. He also reported certain words concerning what had recently occurred in the church: “Now,” he said, “the holy angels have taken part in your celebration and have, by divine appointment, received you into the care of their guardianship.” He added words which gave it to be understood that the same place had been designated before one stone had been built upon another in its construction [Col. 0544C–D].

On another occasion, while sitting in the chapter house at Clairvaux, he spoke a wonderful and most consoling saying—indeed, a gracious saying, a word full of joy and consolation, and very necessary. Perhaps someone was there who repented and was afraid because of the remembrance of transgressions and the enormity of his sins. “Why,” he said, “do you have desolation, my brothers and sons? I tell you in Christ’s truth: if Judas, who betrayed God, were here where you are, even he would obtain mercy” [Col. 0544D–0545A].

8. He was travelling through Burgundy to reconcile the count of Forez and the count of Vienne. As he passed through a certain village, he heard from its inhabitants that two exceedingly savage beasts, commonly called *varoli*, were raging in a nearby wood. When his companions heard this, they begged him to turn back, for they preferred to make a detour of two days’ journey, or much more, rather than expose themselves dangerously to the beasts. Unwilling to agree, he replied that he would never turn aside for such a reason.

Without delay, the beasts came out into the open and confronted them with terrible gaping jaws, as though to devour them. When the brothers saw them, all immediately fled in extreme terror to the holy man, hiding about him, and cried with one voice: “Holy Father, deliver us!” He said: “Why are you afraid, men of little faith?” At this word, raising his hand, he made the sign of the cross against the beasts. Immediately they became like stones, as though they had absolutely no power to harm. Seeing this sign, all who were present rendered boundless thanks to the man of God. When the neighboring people heard of it, they greatly rejoiced, for through fear of the beasts they had not dared to go out in groups smaller than twelve [Col. 0545A–B].

Saint Bernard then proceeded to the aforesaid counts. When he sought peace from them, the count of Forez humbly agreed. But the count of Vienne wickedly opposed him, saying that he would never make peace with his adversary until he had compelled him into exile. Having gathered an army, he attacked the other’s land. Then the count of Forez, terrified with fear, begged Saint Bernard to obtain victory from almighty God. Blessed Bernard confidently promised him victory. Strengthened by this faith, he attacked his enemies, captured the count, and struck down so great a number of the enemy that scarcely anyone escaped alive. He gave thanks for this victory to Saint Bernard [Col. 0545B–C].

9. One day, while the holy man was sitting in his chapter house at Clairvaux, he delivered a great and wonderful sermon. Among other things, he said a certain word which greatly gladdened all who heard it: “Do not fear, you who keep my commands, the torments of hell; nor let the labor which you endure terrify you. For I tell you that, if you persevere to the end, on the day of the Lord’s wrath I shall give my soul for your souls.” When they heard this, the brothers gave boundless thanks to God, who had given them such a father. From that day onward, all who heard it steadfastly obeyed his commands.

And you, most beloved, who have not seen him, ought to search out his commands and diligently obey them, so that through his intercession you may reach the joys of paradise. Watch therefore and pray, lest you come into torments; for he who goes about seeking whom he may devour seeks you. He knows that through Bernard’s institutions, with God’s help, you have been delivered from his hands. For the apostle says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8) [Col. 0545C–0546A].

10. A monk named Christian planted a vineyard on the summit of a mountain near Clairvaux. The brothers of the venerable Father—namely Guy and Gerard—came and excommunicated it.

> [Note: Yet, when the removal of old Clairvaux was being discussed, the brothers informed Bernard that there was another spacious place “for vineyards,” etc., according to Ernald, book 2, no. 29, above. The same author, no. 48, relates that Innocent assigned the monastery of Saint Anastasius at Aquae Salviae to the Cistercians “with fields and vineyards.” Wine was nevertheless rarely used among the Cistercians at that time. Read Geoffrey, above, no. 2. [Col. 0545D]]

They said to him: “Brother Christian, where is your mind and where is your heart? Why did you not consider the Scripture saying that wine is not for monks?” He replied: “You are spiritual brothers and do not wish to drink wine; I am a sinner, and I wish to drink wine.” Then Gerard said: “I tell you, Brother Christian, you shall not see its fruit.”

After these words they returned to the monastery. He, however, dug and cultivated his vineyard for many years. At last he died and did not see its fruit. Much later, the keeper of the vineyard came to Saint Bernard and said: “Father, our vineyard is under anathema and cannot bear fruit.” He asked: “Why, son?” The man replied: “Your brothers excommunicated it, and since then it has borne no fruit.” He said to him: “Bring me water in a basin.” He brought it. Then the holy man made the sign of the cross and sanctified the water. “Go,” he said, “my son, and sprinkle it over the whole vineyard.” The brother departed and did as the abbot commanded; the vineyard grew and multiplied, so that those who saw it were amazed [Col. 0546A–C].

11. Once, while he was travelling by boat on the Loire, his little boat happened to strike a small bridge on which a boy was standing. The boy immediately fell into the river and was killed. His neighbors, roused by the event, ran up lamenting the dead boy. The holy man ordered that he be brought to him, and when the dead child was brought, the saint prayed. Then, before the eyes of all present, who with one voice praised God, the boy was immediately raised at the saint’s prayer.

From that day onward, loving the man of God most affectionately as a son loves a father, he later went to Clairvaux and became a lay brother there. He was called Tescelin Nascardus, because he had been taken from the water and caught like a fish [Col. 0546C–D].

12. One day, about the sixth hour, as the venerable man passed through the territory of the village called Colombey-in-the-Ditch, he found in his path a spring trampled by livestock. Stopping there, he ordered bread to be served for himself and his disciples in that same place. But because the place seemed unsuitable, they wished to go elsewhere, and said to the man of God: “Father, this is not a suitable place for eating. Let us pass on until we come to a place where we may eat more fittingly. For this place is fouled by livestock and lies beside a road constantly trodden by travellers.” But the man of the Lord would not agree to their words [Col. 0546D–0547A].

Nearby there were men of great nobility and wealth, who came from the aforesaid village to meet him, wishing to lead him to their homes. He would by no means consent to this; rather, he ordered more insistently that food be prepared for him in the aforesaid place. Then one of his disciples, named Hemeric, said to him: “What is this, Father, that you wish to do? This place stinks and is fouled by livestock, and yet you wish to eat in it.”

When the man of God heard this, he could endure no longer, but opened his mouth and began to prophesy before them all: “Hear me, brothers, and all you who are with me. I tell you in the word of truth that a time will come when many will seek this place in order to be cured in it of various illnesses. It is a holy place, as one sanctified by the Lord.” When the disciples heard this, they took bread and provisions and ate with him, as did many others; for, as we have said, more people had come to meet him. Then the man of God raised his hand, made the sign of the cross over the spring, blessed and sanctified it, and said to the servants: “Draw water and offer it to those who are eating.” The servants drew water and filled the cups; it was changed into wine. All who were present drank and gave boundless thanks to God, saying with great joy: “Truly this man is holy; truly the Holy Spirit dwells in him” [Col. 0547A–C].

13. After the meal, the blessed man called a man of the aforesaid village named John, who was very rich and prosperous. He ordered him to care for the aforesaid place, clean it of filth, and fortify it with stones, lest livestock foul it. He added: “If you refuse to carry this out, know that before your death you will suffer such poverty that at your death you will not have even a little cloth in which you may be wrapped.”

But he delayed—indeed, he refused—to carry out the blessed man’s command; and the matter happened as the saint had foretold. For at his death he could not obtain even a shroud from all his possessions, in accordance with the man of God’s word. Who could doubt that the holy man foretold these things by the spirit of prophecy? While he was still alive he prophesied many things which we saw come to pass long after his glorious death [Col. 0547C–D].

For many miracles occurred at the aforesaid spring, as he had foretold. Even now, if any member of someone’s body is burdened by any pain and is washed with water from that spring in the devotion of faith, many have known it to be restored to health. Drunk as well, its waters aid recovery from various illnesses. Indeed, if anyone suffering from the serious discomfort of fever, inspired by the confessor of Christ Bernard, has a desire to draw water and immediately drinks it, he recovers. Thus the force of fevers is extinguished, as though, upon a vast pyre, all fires were suddenly quenched by water cast upon them. When tertian and quartan fevers are burning, the pains are checked when its water is drunk [Col. 0547D–0548A].

14. There was a religious man named Odo, a part of whose body had for some time remained almost dead through the contraction of a neighboring ailment. After the blessed man’s death he went to the same spring. Having washed the diseased place with its water, he returned sound and whole. Another, tormented terribly by pain in his head and entirely deprived of sensation, was healed when bathed with water from the spring. Another had languished for seven years; when his relatives brought him to the holy spring, he was made well. Another man, named Suynus, had long suffered from a quartan fever; by drinking from the same spring he regained health [Col. 0548A–B].

A man severely burdened by illness tasted the same water; before all who saw it, a little worm like a locust came out through his mouth, and he immediately recovered. A mute man also, as those who saw it report, came to the spring and received speech. It is enough to have briefly mentioned these and many other things, seen both by us and by others—things in which unbelief would be impious—lest the length of the narrative produce weariness in its hearers.

15. Thus, at Bar-sur-Aube there were two women tormented by two demons. Their parents then brought them to the Man of God at Clairvaux, that they might be healed by him. And when they had approached the gate of Clairvaux, one of the devils said to the other devil through the woman’s mouth: “I must leave this woman.”

[Col. 0548C] “Why,” said the other demon, “must this happen?”

He said: “I cannot see Bernard or hear his voice.”

The other said to him: “For what reason?”

He replied: “When Bernard was still in the world, I wished to tempt him and take away his virginity. And as I was attempting this, he said to me, ‘Get behind me, Satan. I adjure you by Jesus not to harm me, nor ever to see me.’ Because of this adjuration, I must now depart.”

And immediately he went out of the woman, and she was healed from that hour. Those who were present praised God and said: “Truly that man is holy, and the Holy Spirit dwells in him.” While they were saying these things, the servant of God came to the gate, and they told him everything that they [Col. 0548D] had heard and seen concerning those two demons. When the Man of God heard this, he gave thanks to God and said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because you have never abandoned me. You alone are God; you alone perform great wonders. You created heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them. Hear, O Lord, my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

After this prayer, turning to the other woman, he said to the demon: “O demon, enemy of God, come out of the woman.” At this command he came out of the woman, and she was healed from that hour. Then all who were present, blessing God and offering boundless thanks to Saint Bernard, said: “There is not in this age, nor has there been since the Apostles, anyone who could do what this man does.”

[Col. 0549A]

16. One day, when blessed Bernard was in his cell with a few disciples and was oiling his sandals according to his custom, the devil appeared to him in the likeness of a black monk and said: “Abba, how are you? I have come from distant lands to see you, and I find you oiling your shoes. You ought not to do this; it should be done by your servants and attendants.”

The Man of God replied: “I have no servants, nor have I ever wished to have any. I have sons, whom I have begotten for Christ through the Gospel, and who serve me with great charity and gentleness. I truly love them and teach them the way of the kingdom of heaven, humbling myself after the example of the supreme Master, who says: ‘Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted’ [Luke 14:11]. By manifold displays of humility—indeed, by humbling himself in the highest and chiefest manner—he has left us an example, that we should follow in his footsteps.

[Col. 0549B] Therefore, in imitation of my Lord, to perform lowly and servile tasks for love of him is not merely no burden to me, but gives me the greatest delight. Go and tell your abbot to do likewise.”

The devil replied: “Give me the sandals, so that I may oil them.” Looking at him, the blessed man recognized, through revelation of the Holy Spirit, that he was the devil; and, assailing him indignantly, said: “It is not fitting that one who was created by God from the beginning in the highest blessedness and beauty should oil my footwear, when I am dust and ashes.” And he added: “Get behind me, Satan. I adjure you by Jesus Christ not to harm me or my sons in any way.”

When this was said, he immediately [Col. 0549C] transformed himself into the likeness of a tiny creature, in the sight of all who were present, and at once vanished from their eyes. Lord Abbot Gerard of Morimond, a holy man and truthful in his words, used to relate these things to us; not to give credence to his words is almost to oppose truth itself.

17. One day, when the blessed man was in the chapter-house at Clairvaux, a complaint was made concerning a monk who, when he was serving as weekly kitchen attendant, neglected to wash the bowls in the kitchen, contrary to the statutes of the Order. The holy man said to him: “My son, are you so negligent where you ought to show the greatest diligence?”

Confused by this, the monk muttered some foolish and childish excuse, saying that the kitchen duty was very mean and filthy. The blessed man replied: “My son, have you not heard what Benedict, the promulgator of our blessed rule, declares on this subject? [Col. 0550A] The Apostle likewise says that each one shall receive according to his own labor [1 Cor. 3:8].”

Then the Man of God added, prompted by holy zeal: “O most wretched pride, beginning of sin, root of all evils! How are you permitted to defile any portion whatsoever of my most holy flock? Depart, depart, with God’s help: here there is no place for you, now or ever. Flee; flee back to him who came down from heaven with you and through you.”

Having said this, he addressed the monk in this manner: “O wretched man—rather, most wretched of men, unless the Almighty has mercy on you! Where is your mind? Where is your religious profession? Take heed lest the deceiver of the human race transform himself into superstition. Whence comes such great and monstrous negligence in you? O how dangerous, how abominable is this self-exaltation! Why [Col. 0550B] do you not attend to that Gospel saying: ‘Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled; and conversely, whoever humbles himself shall be exalted’ [Luke 14:11]?

“My son, hear my discourse. I tell you in the word of truth, calling God and my conscience as witnesses, that if such humiliation proceeded from the root of true humility, you would achieve a gain more salutary and glorious for your soul by washing bowls and spoons and diligently carrying out the other tasks belonging to the kitchen office than by frequently standing at, or serving, the altar, as often happens to many.

“Work, my son, work; and in gentleness perform what has been enjoined upon you according to the statutes of the Order and the rotation of your duty. For the more lowly your labor is in the sight of the children of men, the more precious it will be in the sight of [Col. 0550C] the angels. Henceforth, in accordance with apostolic tradition, it is fitting that we labor out of necessity. For the Apostle says: ‘If anyone does not work, neither let him eat’ [2 Thess. 3:10]; and again he says of the same matter: ‘Let each one labor, working with his own hands at what is good’ [Eph. 4:28]. And what is better than serving one’s brothers in common? This indeed is what the weekly kitchen attendants do.

“Therefore, my son, be ready to wash the bowls, just as you are eager to eat what is set before you in them. Work, and thus eat more securely. For it is written: ‘You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you’ [Ps. 127:2].”

By this kind of address from the holy Father, both the monk against whom the rebuke had been made was thereafter corrected, [Col. 0550D] and the others who were present were greatly edified.

The remainder is missing.

[Col. 0551]

**PHILOTHEUS THE MONK, ENCOMIASTIC POEM ON THE LIFE AND CHARACTER OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX**

1292–1293

**PROLOGUE**

[Col. 0551A]

While I undertake to tell illustrious deeds in a feeble whisper,  
Deeds that should be set to Maeonian tones,  
What am I attempting but to call the waves back to Sicilian shores  
And confine them in little jars?

Shall I, untrained as yet to shape rough speech  
Or strike the rustic lyre,  
Sing the titles and sacred deeds of the heavenly Prince—  
He who has surpassed every measure of praise?

Who could endure that Codrus’ exile-muse should dare  
Deeds worthy of Sophoclean song?  
It would be like my trying to add light to Phoebus,  
And drawing mockery from rhinoceroses on either side.

Therefore, Bernard, it is not permitted me to utter your praises  
Or sing them upon a trembling lyre.

[Col. 0551B]

Let bright songs be rendered to you by laurel-bearing poets;  
We poor ones offer heart, mind, and prayers.

Such thoughts I had been turning over in my mind, the tablets laid aside,  
And my sins were reproaching my faint courage,  
When gentle rest stole over my wearied eyes  
And tranquil sleep possessed my exhausted breast.

Then the Goddess to whom earth, to whom all heaven renders service—  
The Virgin—seemed to pour forth these words to me:

“Fool, why do you forbid us the use of your song?  
Or deny grateful gifts to my priest?  
Begin: if you do not know it, Bernard is our glory;  
Whatever a stream possesses, it draws from our spring.

“To me that John, who was given as the guide and companion of my life,  
Was never dearer.  
He indeed remained with me through his sweet years,  
[Col. 0551C] Enjoying the sight and converse of the Virgin;  
But this man, when I already held the sceptres granted me in heaven,  
Often deserved to behold my face.

“He alone was guardian to me of my inviolate body;  
This man continually watches over the care of my name.  
But why say more? Each is joined to me by equal affection;  
Neither is less pleasing to me, nor is the other.

“Each lived an alike life free from Venus’ sin;  
One virginity belonged to their two hearts.  
For these God bestowed heavenly dwellings upon the lofty summit  
And commanded them to stand beside me.

“Come then: let him receive the honors of praise  
Which the Father granted me, and in turn give and receive them.

[Col. 0551D]

“Do you see the distinguished books he composed with excellent art,  
So that they might proclaim my name in song to the stars?  
The malignant spirit carried away those writings,  
[Col. 0552A] Which sang my praises and were destined to profit souls.

“In place of devout Jesus, it introduced the Iliad and the Greeks,  
And hid away the mystical sayings of my old man.  
While wretched men pursue empty trifles,  
These writings were found almost nowhere.

“The power of the supreme sceptre, outraged thus, did not endure  
That the faithless enemy should possess our treasures.  
For I myself admonished, by a silent breath, a certain man  
Who was bound to me by a special gift,

“That pious care might recall the scattered little books,  
The writings which taught the starry paths;  
And that, lest they be eaten away by age as the days passed,  
A printer might imprint them in small characters.

“And because the lettering had been corrupted by so long a withdrawal,  
He should first cleanse it by his own judgments.

[Col. 0552B]

“These are the things for which I urge you, easy tasks for you to undertake,  
Though they made him endure such great labors.  
But perhaps you fear that verses ploughed by a rough buskin  
May be assailed by devouring envy’s grim tooth;

“That it may reject your beginnings with haughty brow  
And contend that such things become frivolous men;  
Nor endure that a monk should call back the Aonian sisters,  
Whom he once ordered to depart with unwelcome foot.

“Excellent! Against the needless barking of these men stands  
A poet bound to me in perpetual love,  
Who lays snowy garments over rust-colored robes  
And wears the illustrious dress of Mount Carmel;

“Who celebrated my deeds in sweet-sounding song  
And the shrieking bronze wheels of cruel Costis.  
He will grant you favorable breezes and prosperous harbors;  
[Col. 0552C] With him as guide, you shall pass beyond Scylla’s hounds.

“Do you see how he refutes fools by clear reason  
And has closed their chattering mouths with an opposing hand?  
Called back from the whirlpool of the world, he applauds me  
And sings my glory in sweet utterance.

“Speak, then: what man, rich in heaps of virtues and in honor of praise,  
Was fit for me to place above my poet?  
For, if it be permitted to compare him with lofty-voiced Maro,  
Because each sings verses in an equal manner,

“Yet this man is more illustrious than that one in eternal virtues  
By as much as kindly day exceeds the night.

1295 “For what gifts could I bestow upon my client  
That would not show him to be an illustrious man?  
Do you ask how great is his power in shining eloquence?  
Such were Aristocles and the Maeonian poet.

[Col. 0552D]

“Do you ask how brightly he shines in harmless uprightness?  
Such was Elijah in the burning chariot.

[Col. 0553A]

“This man teaches how to climb virtue’s narrow summit  
And swiftly impose a limit upon vices.  
He speaks nothing but what stern Catos might praise,  
Nothing but Christ sounds from his consecrated mouth.

“While in renowned song he repeats my praises,  
He has joined a thousand men to me in eternal love.  
For so great a poem I have assigned him a heavenly dwelling  
And the highest joys of my kingdom.

“Yet envious Bavius wearies him with continual malice,  
Though his genius may match the heavenly halls.  
Could the savage murmurs of the greedy dog be lacking  
To one whom Christ adorned with no worldly distinction?

“He scorned human favor, aspiring higher,  
And longs only for the rewards of everlasting light.  
Follow his example: despise babbling trifles,  
[Col. 0553B] For virtue is accustomed to shine more brightly when oppressed.

“You will find that all men worthy of flourishing praise  
Have succumbed to the torches of envy.  
Rejoice, therefore, that we deem you worthy of such honor  
That our love may give you cause to blush.

“Begin now, led by such a stratagem, though  
The vain-speaking Apollo grants you no lyre.  
Our Cynosure shall favor your open course,  
So that the undertaking journey may be more lightly completed.

“I confess that your tongue has no eloquence, none at all;  
Yet God approves not eloquence but devout hearts.  
Cattle feed on grass, cicadas on dew,  
The tiger on the blood of four-footed beasts; God on the heart.

“Therefore, quickly launch your little boat from the shore.  
[Col. 0553C] Our breezes shall direct your course.”

She spoke, and had already glided away through the airy heavens,  
When my senses began to awaken.

I undertake a great work: grant pardon to one obeying commands;  
The Muse is forced to run with unwilling foot.  
She who once played hidden in a light epigram  
Now proceeds with Calliope’s weightier step.

Yet I shall not tell the deeds arranged in their proper order;  
I shall relate only a few marvels from a full margin.

Meanwhile, venerable Father, favor my labor;  
And be present, O Doctor of holy love.

**CHAPTER I. Saint Benedict’s supplication to God for the restoration of monastic observance, and the promise received from God.**

[Col. 0553D]

Ten centuries had sped their swift course among the stars,  
And twice as many five-year periods had run with equal pace,  
Since Christ, cutting away the contagion of the death-dealing disease,  
Had been born of the inviolate Virgin;

When every kind of good deed had fled from mortal men,  
And foul delights were the god of earthborn men.  
Everywhere were devouring envy, savagery, discord, strife,  
Pestilence, wars, famine, and fear of the enemy.

Reverence for the heavenly powers had perished in every land,  
Along with the honor and love of ancient religion.  
Indeed, your flock, holy Benedict, wandered through winding ways,  
Its reins broken and poor.

A rare and unsettled monk roamed without a fixed station  
And did not render his founder the vows due to him.

[Col. 0554A]

Then Benedict, pitying his own sheep,  
Is said to have addressed the King of heaven in these words:

“Greatest King, whom heaven, earth, and sea obey,  
Who by your will give and govern all things:  
You see how virtue has grown cold in this long age!  
You see how crime boils throughout the whole world!

“You see how all religion is tossed by adverse waves  
And falls, supported by no soldier!  
Where has gone the honor of ancient religious observance,  
Which once was well cultivated by me from tender years?

“As I died, I left my Order in so broad a dominion:  
Alas! Tell me, where now is the fervor of our Order?  
Unless you immediately look down from your lofty summit  
Upon my offspring, it is at last cast down.

[Col. 0554B]

“Rise, then, pitying the bitter lot of humankind,  
And rescue our pledges from such great evils.”

He spoke; and he who governs the entire world from on high  
Immediately received these utterances:

“Excellent leader, you who fill heaven with a varied soldiery,  
You who were lately the foremost part of our ship,  
Spare yourself, devout Benedict, this fear: through my leaders  
The walls shall be restored after your followers’ death—

“Walls shaken by so many assaults,  
Walls laid by Peter’s hand.  
Look upon the boy whom his mother offered to me  
From his tender years, and whom the land of Gaul gave as his homeland.

“The Holy Spirit, shining in his full breast,  
[Col. 0554C] Will make him equal to Moses in religious observance.  
See how, driven by the goads of my love,  
He already wears down the sacred thresholds with unceasing foot!

“See how virtue gleams beneath his lovely breast!  
Look to the work that bears witness to what is to come.  
Bands of monks, with so great a leader, will restore  
Happy times within your folds.

“After he has filled all things with angelic companies  
And ceased to order your house,  
Then Peter’s ship, long too violently tossed,  
Will rest secure under the auspices of this man.

“Thus one monk alone will guide the mighty reins  
Of the world and give laws beneath the furthest pole.  
The weapons you see rising in swollen strength  
Will become peace, reconciled by his faith.

[Col. 0554D]

“Then a golden age will arise in tranquil morals,  
And my grace toward earthly men will be greater.

“Indeed, when at the end of the age goodness shall be no more  
And faith shall have fled the whole world,  
Behold: from your branch a golden shoot shall arise,  
And nectar-like liquid shall flow from a dry mouth.

“The city of Padua shall furnish the illustrious origin of the shoot;  
From there it shall bear joyous offspring to my aid.  
It too shall produce fruit with such abundant increase  
That you will confess it had no need of your hand.

“Therefore do not be troubled by any fear lest the offspring  
Of so brilliant a stock should ever fail.”

Thus he spoke, and sent the Paraclete from the highest heaven;  
God set Bernard ablaze with his fire.

**CHAPTER II. Bernard, having brought his four brothers by birth to the same resolve, determines to enter religious life.**

[Col. 0555A]

Filled with God, he assumed a modest face and character  
And banished the evil thoughts of his mind.  
Even as a boy he enclosed divinity within his tender breast,  
And great was the beauty of his noble countenance.

Whoever looked upon him with discerning eye said:  
“This man possesses both the appearance and character of a virgin.”  
His fair face was suffused with rosy blush,  
And sweet gravity was mingled with charm.

In early youth he pondered serious matters with mature understanding,  
Though that age is wont to luxuriate in easy jesting.  
A gaze fixed on the ground, restrained smiles without a murmur—  
These were signs of modest shame.

[Col. 0555B]

His mind enjoyed a pleasing calm; and, wandering alone,  
The boy often gave such utterance to his sorrowing heart:

“Why, my mind, why, exercised in brief and wretched cares,  
Do you restlessly admit human passions?  
When will life, the burden of varied labors laid aside,  
Learn to return to its Creator?

“If I desire to behold the lofty summits of heaven,  
You press my head down by my inborn condition.  
Here my father, here my mother, here my companions, my concern,  
And every spark distracts your thoughts.

“But God himself shows me the path by which I must go  
And opens the way of sacred religious observance.  
A humble, newly built holy house lies hidden beneath a poor roof—  
Holy indeed, but not ambitious.

[Col. 0555C]

“Few fathers of Cîteaux dwell at those thresholds,  
O Benedict, who observe your rules.  
There I shall set my thresholds in the heavenly kingdom;  
This alone shall be the rest from my labor.

“Though my own fields should yield me foreign gems,  
And whatever lies open in the whole world should be mine,  
Still I should be ashamed to compare these things with eternal triumphs  
And joys that will know no final day.

“Why do I delay? Ah, madman—why squander the time given me?  
One day has added very much to my sins.”

Such words he weighed in his burning breast  
And then fixed his resolute foot in his purpose,  
When the young man, overcome by tender love for his brothers,  
[Col. 0555D] Wept and said: “This prize too must be sought.”

He spoke and summoned his brothers to the kingdom of heaven,  
Thus recalling in his mind the joys born for himself:

“Lately I wandered shipwrecked upon adverse waves;  
Now I have found the goal of the heavenly way.  
I have found the goal which unfolds the peace of the celibate life  
And the safe path of religious observance.

“Then strive with swift course to seize it with me  
And reap the gains of so great a good.  
God and heaven are the cause of our labor;  
Such rewards will make the struggle light.

“What madness it is for minds to serve fleeting riches  
When God calls them to the blessed kingdom of heaven!  
Why then, brothers, do earthly dwellings detain you?  
Free your necks from the hostile yoke.”

[Col. 0556A]

Without delay, by this most persuasive speech he compelled  
His brothers to consent and leave their ancestral homes.

Then the fire, hitherto restrained, begins to spread to neighboring persons  
And is scattered abroad with wide mouth.  
For, seeking by holy skill companions equal to himself  
And wishing to enlarge the heavenly kingdom with his flock,

The young man, conspicuous in beauty and the glory of all his own people, was not ashamed to scatter words in the midst of the public square,  
Now recalling to the people heavenly triumphs,  
Now the fearful realms of the Cerberean hound.

By his artful discourse he drew countless nations,  
Teaching that the camp of the supreme Leader alone must be followed.  
There crowds gathered in dense masses  
Wherever he turned his longed-for steps.

Then an illustrious company from a numerous host of companions  
[Col. 0556B] Clung to him, joined to him by a firm bond,  
Ready in feet and spirit to lead religious good  
In whatever direction he might wish.

One will, with equal fervor, united all the companions  
And gathered together the immense flock.  
All had one dwelling, all one food,  
And their life was full of divine fear.

And as a cold gladiator, entering upon scattered sand,  
First tests weapons fit for harmless blows,  
So these youths, wielding the weapons of monks with vigorous arms,  
Wage harsh warfare against vices.

And before putting on the sacred garments, their purple laid aside,  
They forsook their former ways.

**CHAPTER III. Bernard, with more than thirty companions, receives the habit in the monastery of Cîteaux, and there soon makes marvelous progress in holiness.**

[Col. 0556C]

Now the vowed-for day had come, on which hearts united in like resolve  
Were to be reborn in holiness,  
When the youth himself, accompanied by a renowned company of men  
And while a heavenly melody already resounded in the sky,

Was enclosed within the precincts; stripped of his former clothing,  
He now wore the garments of holy rusticity.  
A small cell received the season of his new life,  
A cell ever beloved by his judgment.

Here he learned to penetrate heaven’s highest summit.  
Here he learned whatever flows from the cultivated mouth.  
Here he learned to heal diseases with a new ointment  
And, alone, to restore dead faith to life.

Such gifts does the blessed cell, well tended through a few years,  
[Col. 0556D] Bestow upon its lover.

1298 You who tread the crossroads with eager step, tell me:  
What gains have you found in the clamorous forum?  
He did not begin to overwhelm his intellect with diverse problems  
Or entangle it in novel studies.

His first concern was to tame the raging goads of Venus  
And bring the movements of his soul into order.  
His first concern was that sins might be expiated by mournful lament,  
Before joyful hearts acquired swollen learning.

His first concern was to clothe his heart in the bright darkness of heaven  
And mortify his own senses.  
For this Christ filled his servant with such great honor  
That he often beheld the heavenly choirs.

Why recount how often the Queen of the supreme court  
[Col. 0557A] Was seen to utter nectar-sweet sounds to him?  
The Virgin often honored her servant by visiting him  
And often brought him ambrosial food.

Now hear what strength he possessed in his meditative breast;  
I myself shall relate it briefly.

Before Christ’s saving image, with bended knee,  
He offered tears, vows, and prayers;  
He looked upon the feet pierced by the cruel wound  
And the bones to be counted by their distinct marks.

Then, groaning, he poured out complaints in trembling voice,  
Words capable of moving mountain beasts:

“O glory, O balm of our suffering, Christ!  
O salvation won for me at so hard a cost!  
Blessed are you if you may turn such great punishments upon me,  
And if it is granted to me, wretched as I am, to be able to die.

[Col. 0557B]

“I would dare pluck the unripe fruits myself;  
Yet, Christ, your teeth have been stunned.  
Stars, earth, sea, pity your Lord;  
Weep for my misfortunes, stars, earth, sea.”

As he uttered these things, the image of the hanging Lord  
Loosened and moved its arms into an embrace.  
Such power reigned in the exalted prince;  
Such fervor was in his burning breast.

Thus the new soldier rejoiced in inward nectar,  
And eternal heat had seized his inmost bones,  
So that he savored nothing mortal and, ever unlearning earthly things,  
Was carried away by love of Christ.

At night he readily dissolved his eyes in tears  
And was a stern avenger of the least sin.  
He abstained from flesh and from the belly of the great fish,  
[Col. 0557C] And the simple moisture of water quenched his thirst.

By these arts he reached the citadel of highest virtues,  
Thus passing the days of his early youth in joy.

He had long lived sweet years in obscurity,  
Yet they were times full of true rest,  
When God himself, ordering all things by his devout will,  
Commanded Bernard to depart from his humble place.

A valley, bright indeed in name but brighter still in omen,  
Lay planted in a neighboring region.  
Sent there with the holy arts, the excellent Father  
Founded a cloister to be governed under his command.

The faithless man, wearied by the burden of his sins,  
Came there and, sin laid aside, was safe.  
He who formerly shone in foreign purple  
[Col. 0557D] Learned there to be clothed in humbler dress.

Nor was it shameful there to turn the fields with curved hoes  
Or draw unwilling oxen beneath bent yokes.  
There were true hope, faith, integrity, reverence, worship,  
And the beauty of ancient religious observance.

Harsh clothing, slender food, severe labors,  
And a cloister always stored with vegetables served.  
The land, so barren and poor, scarcely yielded fruit  
To the plowshare wearied by unceasing work.

Leaves that ordinarily provide beds for the poor  
Also furnished joyful fare to the monks.  
The whole community pursued fragrant virtues  
And rejoiced to submit their necks to a light yoke.

Now I shall sing the miracles which the Saint, hidden in the cloister,  
Performed and which are celebrated among the people.

[Col. 0558A]

Not far from there, fever surrounded a man with such excessive heat  
That he believed his last day had come.  
That disease could not be healed by Haemonian medicine  
Or restored to health by the physician’s hand.

They went to the revered dwelling of the exalted soldier  
And humbly begged for his merciful aid.  
He went and asked God with tears and prayers  
To grant swift help to the dying sick man.

Immediately the sick man was seen to spring up from his bed  
And walk with whatever vigorous step he pleased.  
From that time Bernard began to become known throughout the world  
And from that day grew more renowned.

Rumor flew everywhere through the neighboring cities,  
And everyone marvelled at this new work of healing.  
Germany heard and hastened with joyful course,  
[Col. 0558B] As did you who inhabit your borders, land of Baetica.

One man brought his mother, deprived of sight; another his parent;  
The wretched man ran from the furthest edge of the world.  
Each person tormented by the foul frenzy of spirits  
Went there and returned freed from the hostile enemy.

Several crippled people too were carried in litters,  
That the pious hand might renew nature’s work.  
He merely adorned their breasts with the sign of the cross;  
Thus each could enjoy the desired healing.

There was no sick person anywhere in the whole world  
Who sought the arts of Apollo and learned Machaon.  
So great was the power in the Saint’s gentle speech;  
So swift was the healing that came from his sacred mouth.

**CHAPTER IV. Bernard nobly defends Pope Innocent against the schism of Peter Leo and wondrously restores him to the Apostolic See.**

[Col. 0558C]

Meanwhile madness, sent from the Stygian stream,  
Harassed the cities of Latium with clashing swords.  
Rome, sorely afflicted by Tartarean serpents,  
Gnashes its teeth and rages in insane sedition.

The schism of Peter Leo, breaker of faith,  
Was tearing apart the temples of the all-beholding Thunderer.  
He wickedly prided himself on the titles and glory of his forebears  
And strove to attain the highest rank of pontiff.

Though another, by decree of the sacred senate of magnates,  
O Christ, ought to have held your see,  
Yet this man, overthrowing everything with cruel sword,  
Claimed every right to your temple though unworthy.

He had already driven out priests venerable for surpassing merit,  
[Col. 0558D] Himself alone powerful in the holy City.  
Those who refused to take the side of the Lion-born man—  
O crime!—fell beneath the cruel sword.

Here, amid troops raging with flashing blades,  
Christ’s body, Rome’s wealth, is plundered.  
Nor did the fury of this war confine its pest within the walls:  
Its Gorgon-like poison infected the whole world.

For the Pastor who held the lawful reins  
Entrusted many churches to men deserving of them.  
But, on the contrary, the faithless other man, violating the laws,  
Ordered churches to have priests of his own.

Therefore wars flew from this cause through Christian cities,  
While each wished to be subject to one leader or the other.  
And so the ship wandered through uncertain storms,  
[Col. 0559A] As though it were now about to perish in an uncertain sea.

The Father of true faith and teacher of the flock  
Could scarcely remain concealed in his own house.  
What should he do? If he sought harbor with a fearful oarsman,  
The helmsman struggled to sail into adverse waters.

Should Palinurus himself abandon the ship amid the waves?  
Love of holy religion forbade this.  
But at last, exhausted by the warfare of raging Leo,  
He yielded and fled, borne by the Etruscan river.

Yet as tears arose he addressed those  
Whom Christ had given to be aboard the fugitive ship:

“O companions, destined to be happy in adverse fortune,  
Provided the words of the heavenly Leader stand firm,  
Trust: aid for holy labor, unless hope has been defeated,  
Always comes from the heavenly height.

[Col. 0559B]

“That greatest Father, glory of the kingdom of the Franks,  
Whose name shines throughout the whole world—  
He indeed can bring aid to our fallen cause;  
He alone is the rest found for our long misfortunes.

“Who does not know that this man, mighty in virtue and signs,  
Can readily turn kingdoms by his hand?  
Beneath his secure star I shall station the ship;  
There it can safely lie in a tranquil shallows.”

Without delay, with its prows foaming on the Tyrrhenian sea,  
The land of Gaul received the fugitive leader.  
Thus, traversing the territory of the Franks, the supreme Shepherd  
Came through white woods to the caves.

The Fathers came out to meet the arrivals in a long procession;  
Before them went the signs of Christ-bearing crosses,  
[Col. 0559C] And they soothed the clouds with devout psalmody:  
Such was the pomp attending the humble soldier.

The Roman knight calls these men, whom he sees living  
In such great peace, blessed beyond measure.  
Now he praises the silence continually observed in the cloisters;  
Now, the riches of virgin honor.

The new arrival desired nothing there with hurried mind  
Except the brightness of surpassing love.  
Bread, apples, nuts, garden herbs, and legumes—  
These were luxuries to the men who had come.

Meanwhile the greatest Priest of Christ explained  
The reasons for his so long a journey.  
Then the Father, revering the commands of his master,  
Undertook the protection of the fugitive ship.

[Col. 0559D]

I shall not mark in wordy verse every event endured over seven years,  
Nor recount the long labors he bore  
While he desired to restore the torn faith.

I shall follow only the chief heights of the renowned deed,  
And its outcome itself shall be present in my pages.

At the summit of Rome’s dominion, Lothair held supreme power  
At the time of that great division.  
He honored the Man as a saint deservedly should be honored,  
Always rejoicing that he was at his side.

The old man approached him and asked that with strong arms  
He restore to his native land its sacred things and gods.  
He consented and, gathering a mighty force of troops,  
The king undertook the journey of holy devotion.

On one side were Father Bernard’s worthy and abundant prayers;  
[Col. 0560A] On the other, the army of the leader Lothair.  
Thus the supreme Priest advanced toward the Roman palaces,  
Protected on either side as he sat within a twofold citadel.

They had reached the most famous temples of the supreme Thunderer.  
I shall speak truth, though things difficult to believe.  
There was no need to sound trumpets, move armies, stir battles,  
Or join the hand in fiery combat.

The reverence for one monk alone, O happy man,  
Terrified bold warriors armed for savage warfare.  
But he who had been the author of so great a storm  
Heard these mournful words from a like voice:

“Peter, I was able suddenly to cut short your life  
And hurl you into the Phlegethonian lake;  
But, that you may obtain pardon through bitter groaning,  
Take three days for yourself as a great gift.”

[Col. 0560B]

The prediction was fulfilled: already the third Titan in succession  
Had shone and closed the final day.  
Immediately the sheepfolds were opened with their gates thrown wide  
And restored the scattered flocks across the broad fields.

What had been decreed by the law of raging Leo,  
The pontiff seated in the supreme City overthrew.  
Now citizens could joyfully conduct their affairs  
And the farmer at last turn the hard soil.

When all things had thus been set in order under tranquil peace,  
The Saint then went to his longed-for retreats.

**CHAPTER V. Bernard, after a happy peace had been granted to the Roman Church, returns honorably to Gaul and there renders his most holy soul to the Lord.**

Silently I pass over the miracles of the excellent Father  
[Col. 0560C] Which were performed in the course of his long journey.

For exceedingly, exceedingly happy were those  
Who received the illustrious man as a guest;  
And every people wishing to retain the sacred father  
Went out from its city to meet him upon the long roads.

1301 Each, walking in new attire, displays joy;  
Man and boy alike meet the devout old man.  
Sorrow departs; the sky resounds with joyful music,  
And the host keeps festival, ordinary tasks set aside.

Everywhere they scatter purple flowers through the crossroads,  
And incense burned on sacred altars breathes fragrance.  
Along the roads boys spread green boughs,  
And the crossroads were covered with fires laid beneath them.

So once at Jerusalem the welcoming crowd received  
The God whom a poor donkey bore as he returned.

[Col. 0560D]

But once he had at length settled on the threshold  
Of his desired lodging, the applauding crowd rushed in from every side.  
The crowd rushed in from every side, gathered in such tumult,  
That he could scarcely bring his weary foot across the threshold.

They presented so many bodies languishing with grievous disease  
To be restored by his ready hand,  
That scarcely was even a small allowance of sleep given him,  
Nor, when a meal was finished, could he take his food in haste.

Thus, after traversing the lands of the Franks, the Abbot reached  
The blessed cloister with longed-for foot.

Then you might have seen woods and the stony summits  
Of his native mountain all applauding their lord.

As a child, after a long time, is wont to seek his unseen mother  
[Col. 0561A] And joyfully bring her kisses,  
So the monks, glad at the sight of their shepherd, spring up  
And give and receive kisses on one another’s cheeks.

Then he who had lately been carried above heaven by honors,  
Whom great leaders had longed to behold,  
Behold: you might have seen the holy man, his pontiff’s rank laid aside,  
Take up hoes in his sacred hands.

And he upon whose shoulders the weary world had rested  
Is seen carrying mud in a woven basket.  
Two hundred companies applauded the heavenly King,  
Whom the good Father had drawn from every region of the world.

These things had been celebrated by peoples with such great favor,  
So did man and boy honor the holy flock,  
That the resounding whole world strove alike  
To keep the consecrated leader for itself.

[Col. 0561B]

Then the Roman churches, to be adorned with their pontiff,  
Drew Eugenius away from his humble dwelling.  
Then too innumerable cities in diverse regions  
Established for themselves from there a sacred head.

With such men at work, and no Charybdis stirring it,  
The holy ship floated over shallow waters.  
A golden age now ran its course, pride cast aside,  
And these times were darkened by no evils.
