Every crossroads resounded with divine praises;  
Now land and sea gave forth angelic melody.  
Yet far more renowned than all other valleys was this valley,  
Which was tended by the leader and father of the great flock.

Now, as the swiftly passing cycles had closed ten times six years, bowed old age had brought its final step; and his limbs, unsteady in an aging body, were broken by the burden of unceasing toil.

[Col. 0561C] Yet austere old age did not slacken the reins of his high office, nor seem able to halt his swift wheels. Rather, he pressed on more keenly than in vigorous youth, as a light horse runs toward the prizes of the palm. And as the swan, when led to the threshold of death, repeats its melodies in more musical song, so he uttered sweet strains at life’s final boundary, and the writings of the decrepit old man were wondrous.

For the Father, worn down by age, expounded eternal loves and unfolded abundant kisses in sacred modes. And, seeing the joys of heavenly life now near at hand, he laid his languishing limbs upon a humble bed. The good flock groaned and, gathered around the one lying there, spoke such words in anxious murmur:

[Col. 0561D] “Then, venerable Father, can you bear to leave your wretched children in mid-sea? What shepherd, then, will comfort the sorrowful or the sick, and spur them on with love of heaven? Father, who will protect the bewildered and helpless lambs, lest wolves tear their entrails with greedy teeth? Who will be able to unlock for the wretched the hidden knots of the Law and the mystical words of sacred utterance?

“Who then will heal our sluggish minds and cold hearts, and our wounds with a gentle hand? Ah, how hastened are the swift days of your life! Ah, how cruel are the harsh fates of your death! What good did it do us that the bearer of the keys—the Father—once took counsel for us with unwearied words,

[Col. 0562A] lest perhaps someone should stealthily take away our head from our people, our bishop, by holy cunning, if the envious Fate, having ravaged our labours too grievously, dares to take away our honoured leader? Yet you, who with an easy nod turn the stars, weave again the threads of your servant’s life which have been cut short, so that, when this house has been supported by his labour, it may more gladly see the Father it has received depart.”

The old man was moved by their words; and, raising his eyes a little, he returned this answer in a faint voice: “For me supreme rest is now at hand; glad rewards are now being prepared; at last the sweet hour of my death is here. But why do you pour out complaints in womanish speech? What good is it to hold back an old man who has not deserved this? Did I not so often tell you beforehand of my death, lest sudden grief should injure you too deeply?

[Col. 0562B] “When I have been placed in the heavenly seat, Christ will rain down greater help through our mouth. Now my understanding is surrounded by this muddy embankment and can scarcely behold its own riches. Only you, keeping the commands of your heavenly Father, go on along the path of religion which you have undertaken. Let neither flattering honour, nor wicked hardship, nor anything whatever that lies in the whole world ever call you back.

“What would it profit me if, amid trumpets and easy dances, our time had led happy days? What would past joys of pride benefit me, if I were now compelled to bear the Stygian torches? But at last Christ calls his trembling client into his kingdoms,

[Col. 0562C] and bids me go hence with swift foot. Therefore farewell, brothers, sons, and fathers; and store my words in your remembering breast.”

He had scarcely given these instructions in brief speech, soothing hearts wounded by anxious grief, when his snow-white spirit, amid the tears and groans of his own people, left the cast-off body and rose on high. The Virgin herself, radiant through the airy spaces, was seen joyfully leading the heavenly choirs; drawing the purple soul upward, she placed it on the Empyrean height and set it at her own side.

## CHAPTER VI. Saint Bernard is most rightly preferred not only to ancient heroes but also to Christian martyrs.

[Col. 0562D] Until now I had admired the arms of lofty Caesar, to whom martial Rome gave heavenly honour; Hannibal’s savage right hand, drenched in Roman blood; and the proud deeds of the renowned Macedonian leader.

I admired the Scipios, the Decii, and the stern Aemilii, raging for their country’s freedom. Nor did I less acknowledge as adorned with mighty praise the man who seared his brave hand in the swift fire; him to whom Africa gave a famous name from noble lineage, Rome being prosperous under his consulship; him who defended the piled bridge with his breast and, driven on, leapt into the rushing waters of the Tiber; and him who, lately consul at the Quirinal plough, took up arms and returned victorious from the conquered foe.

[Col. 0563A] I admired also him who, mounted on horseback and gleaming in shining armour, cast himself headlong into the cleft Forum; and him who, in the chains joined in his first warfare, dyed the Ionian waters with Tyrian blood. I thought him too borne above heaven by his titles, who held the Phrygian homes under siege; and him who, illustrious among the Trojan chiefs in proud battle, perished when drawn from the Haemonian region; and him who overcame monsters with giant strength, whence he bears the tokens of the Molorchian lion.

I had thought these men exceedingly, exceedingly blessed, because with a strong hand they had carried their name to the stars. As a simple boy I revered them with distinguished honour, when my first youth was reading light verse.

[Col. 0563B] But now, if I compare the praises of ancient fame and deeds of valour with my old Bernard, what was lately most celebrated in Thracian song now seems to me worthy of a girlish tune. Let ancient fame be silent, and the triumphs of the ancients yield to the merits that stir the Christian man. For in them there was an image of fictitious virtue; in him true virtue, *aretē* [virtue; Note: [Col. 0563D] “Virtue.”], was present in a full heart.

They offered libations to Mars and Phoebus upon cold stones; he offered a pure heart to the true God. They subdued barbarian cities by fearful wars and proud dwellings by mighty force; he subdued the fords of Tartarean Phlegethon, and all the choirs of spirits stood at the commands given them.

[Col. 0563C] They endured diverse labours in glorious warfare, deeming it beautiful to fall for their country; he endured the cold pains of continual dying, wishing to reconcile a faith torn apart. Their reward was false honour and the empty glory of renown; but for him the sole cause of labour was love of Christ.

Perhaps, after conquering regions, they gave great treasures as gifts to their country; but he, in dying, gives his wretched children gifts that will perish on no day—gifts that restored chaste morals. These are the works he wrote with sacred hand.

But why do I compare Hercules’ strength with Pygmies in song, and little streams with the Pharian sea? I shall repeat his highest praises in a changed strain,

[Col. 0563D] and, Father, sing of you by a better comparison. For why should I dare compare you with vain Romans, when you were holier than any martyr? It was indeed great to be slain by sword and flame and yet not abandon eternal faith. Greater was the task of moving amid the highest summit of affairs without allowing the mind to be weighed down by any ambition. Greater was the task of maintaining always life’s severe pinnacle and religion’s narrow path. And greater was the task of enduring with a brave heart the wars waged by the weapons of evil spirits.

Let others admire the martyr’s lightning-like racks, and the fires which Lawrence bore with eager mouth.

[Col. 0564A] Let them boast of Chrysogonus’ wounds, Paul’s chains, and Euphemia’s limbs severed by a cruel hand. Let them admire the grievous penalties borne by saints in death—battles, the cross, swords, lashes, missiles, flames. With inexhaustible heart I alone shall admire the labours which the Father bore, seized by everlasting love.

For if one gathers together the slaughter, torments, and labours of Christ’s people, and all the glory of shed blood, all will yield to the burden which that blessed man endured in wishing to sustain a house about to fall. For others felt pains in torn flesh, but he bore wounds in the midst of his heart. Therefore, by as much as the spirit is nobler than the limbs themselves, by so much was he higher than the martyrs.

## CHAPTER VII. A fine commendation of the writings, or books, of Saint Bernard.

[Col. 0564B]

After the holy Virgin and Mother had passed beyond the poles and the circles of the tenfold heaven, and beyond the nine choirs, and, mighty while her companions looked on, possesses the heavenly citadel, kingdoms never to be forsaken on any day, she has never failed human prayers or our salvation, nor seemed to despise our earthly dwellings. Rather, she has restrained the anger of the highest Prince and the arrows to be hurled against our homes. She has often seemed to bring help to wicked crime and reconcile humble defendants. She granted pardon to the wretched, and her favour rained down from her gentle mouth upon the whole world.

[Col. 0564C] She also commanded innumerable peoples, scarcely dragging their sickly bones through hunger, to have abundant feasts. And when pestilence had been cruelly cast upon Latin cities, she healed wounds sent from the Stygian depths. Our Brescia, witness of so great a benefit, has often experienced her desired favours [Note: [Col. 0564] “From this one may infer that Philotheus of Brescia was, or at least was certainly, Italian.”]:

Brescia, once torn by malignant peoples, swelled with a condition no healing hand could approach; Brescia, whose stricken head bore wounds that caused sudden death. But now, helped by Mary’s prayers, she triumphs and celebrates welcome leisure with joyful choirs. She erects beautiful churches, testifying to Mary’s special gift—works like Parian marble.

[Col. 0564D] These things and more has the most holy Mother of Christ bestowed on us, readily responding to our wretched prayers. Yet let it be permitted to my daring Muse to say this and express the feeling of my mind. Never has the gracious Virgin given the human race and our glory so great a gift as when, lately, with this welcome gift she brought forth for us these writings, fit to be read in brief notes.

She herself brought them forth; for the goddess commanded her own servant to seek the beginnings of the distinguished old man. She commanded it, and behold: writings that had been scattered throughout the world you will, by her will, read all together within one margin—writings opening heaven’s triumphant gates, writings to be received by every hand.

[Col. 0565A] For every age and sex enjoys the books bestowed, provided it speaks with a Latin tongue. Whoever you are, if you have any concern for your salvation, these will be great gifts for your soul. If you desire to contract a marriage blessed with desired offspring and submit your neck to the marital yoke, here you may pluck distinguished fruits of character, which will give your children rare names.

But if your sole concern is polished expression, here was one no less than the eminent Cicero. If, indeed, you delight in devoting yourself to pious labour and teaching untaught peoples Christ’s commands, gather here the teachings to be scattered through diverse cities: here the sought-after author will give you better things. When he wished, he soothed hearts with gentle feeling;

[Col. 0565B] when he wished, he frightened the guilty with stern speech. If you delight in serving the citizens of heaven and in lying hidden more safely in a humble hut, here is an author always to be revered by you with special honour and worthy of eternal love. Reading him again, you will joyfully walk in the highest heaven; and you will be able, sorrowful, to visit the Stygian lakes.

Before your eyes he will paint the birth of our Prince and the divine powers born in a shepherd’s house.

[Col. 0566A] Here Jesus resounds on every side in sweet melody, and the names of Mary are honoured in illustrious song. He teaches how bright trophies were set up over the Tartarean foe and how the serpent-bearing head was cut off; and by what deceits he, and by what arts the other, deceives the wretched flock feeding in holy fields.

Whoever reads cannot be satisfied; he burns as he reads and grieves when the accustomed hour of food comes. Other writings make minds swell and luxuriate excessively in scattered locks; but these establish the Paraclete in the heart of the world and kindle cold hearts with new fires. These will draw sweet tears for you from a heart of marble—the highest joys of your soul.

In short, this one book alone contains, by outstanding art, all the volumes of the new and old meaning.

[Col. 0566B] Therefore, monks, strive with all speed to seize these things and store the words in your silent breast, so that they may make you climb the starry height and hold kingdoms among heavenly choirs. You also, clients of Christ, immortal race, fix the aged champion of the Virgin deep in your heart, so that he may remove the grievous wrath of heaven and earth and open the lofty thresholds of the closed heaven.

[Col. 0565]

## NICOLAS HACQUEVILLE, MOST JUST PRESIDENT OF THE SACRED SENATE OF PARIS: ON THE PRAISES OF SAINT BERNARD AND THE SITE OF CLAIRVAUX.

[Col. 0565C] There was a hidden valley amid high mountains, then covered with dense woodland and green bramble. The ancients rightly called it Clairvaux, “Bright Valley”: they changed your name, Bitter Valley. Although shady mountains surround it on every side, none in the whole world was brighter. The water-bearing stream Alba flows through its middle; a spring gives it water as a perpetual gift.

To this place, holy Father Bernard, you were first sent to cultivate it; already at that time you were so great. You had not yet left behind difficult youthful years, yet your mind in tender flesh was old. Then this valley was planted with untended thickets; then untamed beasts lurked there. At that time it produced wild fruits;

[Col. 0565D] there was no vine-grower and no ploughman. There were no human dwellings; it was an old den of robbers. No one could travel safely in it. But after you, Bernard, sought Clairvaux and yourself established dwellings for your brothers, all things suddenly changed their former form: what had been harsh you made more fertile.

In the middle of the valley you built cells and a church consecrated to Christ, after bringing in brothers. You instructed them to lead an angelic life on earth,

[Col. 0566C] to sing divine prayers by night and day. At once an immense fame ran through the world, and Father Bernard flew upon every tongue. From every side boys, young men, and old men hastened together to bend their proud necks beneath your rule. Mothers did not restrain them, nor tender age; white-haired old age did not fear austere paths. Wealth did not delay them, nor, finally, empty nobility that comes from illustrious blood.

Henry himself, despising worldly honours—whose brother held the sceptres of France—though he was born of royal blood, nevertheless submitted himself to your authority. You ruled all kingdoms by your nod, Bernard: such honour was then accorded to virtue.

[Col. 0566D] If discord arose among great kings, everything was reconciled at your wish. Then the mad, frenzied rage of Leo was savaging the Church with ravening teeth; but your prudence broke its pestilential power and put an end to such disasters. William, reigning over the Aquitanian cities, is witness, when he, Bernard, fell at your feet.

You also scattered your brotherly ranks across the world; no land lay closed to your brothers:

[Col. 0567A] whether the land stretching toward the purple east, or that lying beneath the setting sun; whatever lands bend toward the cold Bears, or are known to lie beneath the southern pole; or the populous island that nourishes Britain’s remotest inhabitants and is broadly surrounded by Ocean’s sea. However far Europe’s borders extend, all kingdoms seek your brothers.

Our poems cannot now record everything. It is enough to have discussed these few matters out of many. This weighty subject exceeds my strength; let the man whose vein flows more sweetly sing it.

[Col. 0568A] Let this suffice for me: I have touched on these matters rapidly in song. My Muse is not equal to so great a man.

## TO THE MEN OF CLAIRVAUX.

After your Father’s precepts, while this present life still survives, press on; for it already flees with silent foot. Do not regret having despised the pleasures of a collapsing world, pleasures to be handled only for a short time. Whatever things now seem sad and bitter prepare joys after death that will not perish. After the valley’s tears, groans, and long sighs, God himself will draw you up to the high mountain.

[Col. 0567]

## ENCOMIASTIC POEM ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF BLESSED BERNARD, FIRST ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF CLAIRVAUX. BY BAPTISTA MANTUANUS. (From Book VIII of the *Fasti*.)

[Col. 0567B] Bernard’s most celebrated feast-day has come to the Belgians. He was a Belgian; he drew six brothers and one sister into Christ’s service. God inspired in all of them one work, one manner of life.

While still pregnant, his mother saw in dreams that she bore in her womb a puppy fierce in its frequent barking. Thus God showed what mouth and heart the child to be born would have against every kind of evil.

He cultivated chastity, although as a young man he suffered womanly battles: beautiful, with a rosy-white face, he tormented hearts with grievous seizures and with the fire by which Venus incestuously kindles tender marrow. When he was travelling among the Celts and pale night was already closing heaven, he entered a lodging. At night the reckless hostess, while the young man slept, wantonly clung to him and pressed side against side. He suddenly recoiled from the crime and, calling his companions with a loud cry,

[Col. 0567C] overcame the raging woman’s wickedness by the terror caused by his action. Great beauty is an evil more harmful than any herb said to grow through Thessaly’s ridges or the fields of Phasis.

He devoted his intellect to sacred teachings. Everything Christ taught, the prophets foretold, and Moses learned upon the Panchaean summit, he knew by constant meditation without any teachers; and therefore he said that he had woods as his teachers.

[Col. 0568B] He lived in poverty, but wanted clean clothing, condemning neglect and hating dirt. The concern which the crowd has for the body alone he transferred to the mind, being the keenest enemy of vices.

If nations contended or kingdoms were divided by discord, Bernard was the peacemaker. He went as envoy to cities and kings to break hatred and anger. The Germans saw him performing such an office; the Lombards once saw him, and the Aquitanians saw him. Whenever hearts wavered amid doubtful affairs, he was the interpreter who led mortal hearts from darkness to light, as a fiery lamp shining from a distant tower at night is accustomed to guide storm-tossed sailors to safe shores.

He shone with as many miracles as one may scarcely be permitted to comprehend in number: able to know people’s hidden concerns, drive away infernal spirits, and heal those laid low

[Col. 0568C] by sickness. Therefore the fame of the Man had filled the world and his name flew through foreign mouths. He is said to have founded one hundred and sixty Cistercian houses: the prudence of one man accomplished so much.

Therefore the sacred twentieth dawn of this great Father’s merits is the day on which he withdrew himself into the highest thresholds of the supreme heaven, which contains all things.

[Col. 0567]

## EPITAPH OF SAINT BERNARD, BY ADAM OF SAINT-VICTOR.

The valleys are bright; but the abbot of the bright valleys, brighter than they, gave his bright name to the world. Bright in ancestry, bright in merits, and bright in honour, he shone in eloquence, yet more in religion. Bright is his death, bright his ash, and bright his tomb; brighter still his spirit exults before God.

[Col. 0569] When the martyrdom of the Great One has been celebrated, the great martyr is gathered to him: equal to the Equal One without death.

In the manuscript codex of Anchin the poem is found with this title: “Anselm, in praise of Clairvaux, to Bernard, venerable abbot of Clairvaux,” and begins:

> “A sloping valley, which a sloping mountain overshadows.”

[Col. 0569]

## DESCRIPTION OF THE LOCATION OR SITE OF THE MONASTERY OF CLAIRVAUX.

[Col. 0569A] If you wish to know the setting of Clairvaux, let what is written here serve you as a mirror. Not far from the abbey two mountains begin. At first separated by the interval of a narrow valley, they open their jaws in a wider gap the nearer they approach the abbey. One occupies one side and half the other side of the abbey; the other occupies the whole remaining side. One is rich in vines and the other fertile in crops, furnishing a service pleasant to see and useful in practice: on the sloping sides of one grows what may be eaten, on the other what may be drunk.

On the mountain summits the monks have frequent work, pleasant indeed and more delightful than rest: gathering old brushwood and binding it into bundles for burning; uprooting scrubby thickets and making ground fit for sun and fires; clearing, pulling up, destroying, and scattering thorns and, to use Solomon’s words, “illegitimate shoots” (Wisdom 4:3), which either bind the branches of growing trees or undermine their roots, lest the stiff oak be prevented from greeting the saving stars with its lofty crown, the soft linden from spreading its arms, the cleavable and pliant ash from freely stretching upward, or the spreading beech from expanding broadly.

[Col. 0569B] Moreover, behind the abbey lies a broad plain, no small part of which is occupied by a wall enclosing the abbey with an extensive circuit. Within its bounds numerous and varied trees, fruitful in various fruits, form an orchard like a grove. Adjoining the infirmary, it relieves the brothers’ illnesses with no slight comfort: it gives those who walk a spacious promenade, and those suffering from heat a pleasant place to rest.

[Col. 0569C] The sick man sits on the green turf. When the cruelty of the dog-days, with its harsh star, scorches the earth and dries the rivers, he, beneath tree foliage, moderates the blazing stars in safety, concealment, and shade from the heat of day. For comfort in his pain, grassy fragrances delight his nostrils. The pleasant green of herbs and trees feeds his eyes, as do their immeasurable delights hanging and growing before him, so that he may rightly say: “I sat in the shadow of that tree which I had desired, and its fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs 2:3). The harmony of brightly coloured birds caresses his ears with sweet melody. For the relief of one illness, divine mercy provides many consolations, while the air smiles in bright serenity, the earth breathes fertility, and he drinks through eyes, ears, and nostrils the delights of colours, sounds, and scents.

[Col. 0570A] Where the orchard ends, a garden begins, marked out by intersecting beds—or rather divided by little streams running between them. Although the water appears to sleep, it nevertheless flows with a gentle current. Here too a beautiful sight is offered to the sick brothers, as they sit beside the green bank of the clear pool and watch little fish play beneath the glassy water and, swimming against one another, represent a martial encounter.

This water serves a double purpose: feeding fish and watering vegetables. The Alba, a river of famous name, supplies its nourishment in tireless flow. Passing through many workshops of the abbey, it leaves a blessing behind it everywhere in return for faithful service. It climbs up for this task with much labour; it does not pass through entire, yet it does not pass idly through.

[Col. 0570B] Indeed, cutting through the middle of the valley by a winding channel made not by nature but by the brothers’ industry, it sends half of itself into the abbey, as though to greet the brothers and excuse itself for not having come wholly, since it could find no channel capable of receiving all of it. If the river should perhaps rush down in flood with violent course, driven back by the barrier of a wall, it flows below where it must flow, turns back upon itself, and, flowing back, embraces itself anew.

Admitted as far as the wall, acting as porter, allows it, it first makes its rush into the mill, where it is greatly concerned and troubled about many things: both grinding grain with the mass of the millstones and separating the flour from bran with a fine sieve.

[Col. 0570C] Then, in the neighbouring building, it fills the boiler and entrusts itself to be cooked by fire, in order to prepare drink for the brothers, if a barren vintage should not respond well to the cultivator’s labour and, through lack of the grape’s blood, a substitute must be supplied from the daughter of the reed. But not even thus is it released. For the fullers, neighbours of the mill, invite it to themselves, claiming by right of reason that, as it is occupied in the mill so that the brothers may eat, so it should labour among them so that they may be clothed.

It does not object or deny anything asked of it; but, raising and lowering in turn those heavy pestles or hammers, as you may prefer to call them—or rather wooden feet, for that name seems more suitable to the leaping work of fullers—

[Col. 0571A] it completes the fullers’ work with heavy labour; and, if it is permissible to insert a joke among serious matters, it absolves the penalties of their sins. Good God, how many comforts you provide for your poor, lest they be swallowed up by excessive sorrow! How many alleviations of penalties you dispense to penitents, lest perhaps they sometimes be overwhelmed by the violence of their labour!

For how many horses’ backs would the labour break, how many people’s arms would it weary, from which that gracious stream frees us without labour, though without it neither clothing nor food could be provided for us? It shares with us, and expects no other reward for its toil under the sun than that, once it has diligently completed everything, it may be allowed to depart free. Turning so many whirling wheels in rapid revolution, it leaves so foaming that it itself seems, as it were, to have been ground and made softer.

[Col. 0571B] It is then received by the tannery, where it displays industrious diligence in preparing what is necessary for the brothers’ footwear. Next, dividing itself little by little and into many branches, it visits each workshop in its attentive course, diligently asking everywhere what work requires its service: cooking, sifting, turning, grinding, watering, washing, milling, softening—it supplies its obedience without objection.

Finally, lest anything be lacking from any of its services and lest its works be imperfect in any respect, it carries away filth and leaves everything clean behind it. Having energetically completed the work for which it came, it hastens at swift speed

[Col. 0571C] to the river, so that, acting on Clairvaux’s behalf, it may thank it for all its benefits and return a fitting greeting for its greeting. Immediately it gives back the water which it had transferred to us, and so makes one out of two that no trace of their union appears; mingling with it, it makes the river—rendered thin and slow by its departure—rush onward.

But since we have restored it to its place, let us return to the channels we left behind. Diverted from the river, they wander in passive courses through the meadows, in order to soak the earth, pour water upon it, and make it germinate, so that when the earth, pregnant in spring’s mildness, is delivered into birth, the returning grasses may not wither for lack of moisture, nor need to be watered with borrowed drops of cloud, being sufficiently nourished by the favour of their kindred river.

[Col. 0571D] These channels—or rather furrows—after completing their duty, are swallowed up by the river which had poured them forth. Alba, now gathered wholly together, hastens down the slopes in its descending course. But since we have already taken it too far and it too, according to Solomon, “returns to its place” (Ecclesiastes 1:7), let us also return whence we departed and pass over the broad expanse of the meadow in concise speech.

That place has much charm: much that relieves weary minds and loosens anxious grief; much that kindles those seeking the Lord toward devotion and reminds them of the sweetness above for which we sigh. The earth’s smiling face, diversified with colour,

[Col. 0572A] feeds the eyes with springtime painting and breathes a sweet scent to the nostrils. And when I see a flower or smell its fragrance, the meadows recall to me the stories of ancient days. When I drink in the delight of its scent, the fragrance of the garments of the patriarch Jacob comes to mind, compared to the sweet smell of a full field. When I refresh my eyes with colour, I remember that this beauty was set before Solomon’s purple: in all his glory he could not equal the beauty of the lilies of the field, though he lacked neither the art of wisdom nor the resources of power. Thus, while I enjoy an outward ministry, I am no little delighted by a hidden mystery.

Therefore this meadow is nourished by the irrigation of the river running through it and sends its roots toward its moisture; therefore it will not fear when heat comes. It stretches at such length

[Col. 0572B] that, when the sun has dried the shorn grassy fleece into hay, it is enough to tire the community for twenty days. Yet this labour is not left to monks alone. Together with the monks, an innumerable multitude of lay brothers, donors, and hired workers gathers the cut grasses and turns the mown ground with a sparse rake.

Two granges divide this meadow between them, and Alba comes as impartial arbiter and measurer to settle the dispute. Assigning each its own part by the measuring-line of distribution, it makes itself a boundary which neither dares cross in order to encroach upon the other’s portion. You would think these granges were not dwellings of lay brothers but monastic cloisters, unless teams of oxen, ploughs, and other instruments suited to rural

[Col. 0572C] labour revealed their inhabitants, and unless books were not opened in them. As regards their buildings, you would say that they suit in position, adorn in beauty, and suffice in capacity for a great community of monks.

In the part of the meadow adjoining the wall, a clear pond has been made from firm ground. Where before the sweating worker cut hay with a sharp sickle, now the water-brother sits, riding a wooden horse that moves over the slippery level of the liquid field. He has a light branch for spurs to urge his course, and for a bridle to turn it. A net is spread beneath the water to entangle the fish; bait is prepared which it gladly eats, though the hook by which the unwary creature is caught lies hidden within.

By this example we are taught to despise pleasures, because pleasure bought with pain harms;

[Col. 0572D] no one is permitted not to know that its endings are sad, except one who has either not sinned or has not properly repented of sin. May God keep far from us the delight beside whose entrance death is set, which, according to the philosopher’s description, “like a swarm of flying bees, after it has poured forth pleasant honey, flies away and, when struck, wounds hearts with an excessively clinging bite” [Note: [Col. 0571D] Boethius.].

The circumference of the lake is held by the high bank’s intertwined wicker roots, lest the crumbling ground give way to the lapping water. This lake is fed by a passing channel which, scarcely thirty-six feet away, pours into it through narrow ducts the water by which it is nourished, and returns that water through the same narrow outlet. Thus

[Col. 0573A] it remains in the same state, becoming neither larger through incoming water nor smaller through outgoing water, because it measures, receives, and rejects the same quantity.

But while I am borne with flying course over the plains, while breathless I draw my sides along the heights, or describe the purple surface of the meadow painted by Wisdom’s own hand or the mountain ridges leafy with trees, that sweetest spring, so often drunk by me and well deserving of me, yet ill repaid by me, rebukes me for ingratitude. It reproaches me that it has often served to quench my thirst; that it humbled itself not only for washing my hands but also my feet; that it rendered me many offices of humanity and kindness. It says, with deserved reproach, that I have answered a good service with bad payment; that it received the last place, almost no place at all, in the catalogue of sites, though by reason of its own dignity the first was due to it.

[Col. 0573B] And truly I cannot deny that I remembered it late, when I had remembered someone before it. Yet, silently slipping along underground courses and passages so that even a soft murmur cannot betray its transit, it covers its head everywhere and turns aside from sight, like the waters of Siloam, which flow in silence, as though afraid to appear. Why should I not think it wished to be left unmentioned, when I see that it wishes to be seen only under cover?

[Col. 0574A] This spring, then—a mark said to indicate a good spring—rises opposite the eastward sun, so that at the summer solstice it greets, face to face, the rosy countenance of the glowing dawn. It is covered and enclosed by a little, beautiful hut—or, to speak with greater reverence, a tabernacle—lest it admit dirt from any direction. Where the mountain pours it forth, the valley swallows it; and in the place where it rises it, as it were, dies—indeed, is buried. But do not expect the sign of the prophet Jonah, that it should remain hidden for three days and three nights. Immediately, a thousand paces within the monastery’s enclosure,

[Col. 0574B] as though raised from the heart of the earth, it emerges and in some fashion appears reborn, offering itself only to the brothers’ sight and use, so that henceforth its lot may be with none but the holy.

## [WORKS OF GEOFFREY OF CLAIRVAUX.]

[Col. 0573]

## SERMON IV OF GEOFFREY, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX [Note: [Col. 0573] On him see the observations on Book III of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.], ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF SAINT BERNARD’S DEATH [Note: [Col. 0573D] Delivered in the year 1163, as is inferred from §5.].

[Col. 0573C] 1. How sweet, beloved sons, should the memory of a father be today—how lovable, welcome, pleasant, celebrated! Since “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his servant,” it must by no means be neglected by mortals. The memory of so great a man must not be buried in the tomb of negligence or entombed in the sepulchre of forgetfulness. His holy name must be embraced in all things and through all things: his great works by those who hear them, his words by those who read them, and his fruit by those who consider it.

Nor is it fitting that those who knew his spiritual life should forget his bodily death: how devoted it was to God, how pure toward himself, how useful and fruitful to very many. Yet today’s memory ought to be much sweeter and far more pleasant to those who, grafted into the richness of that very good olive tree,

[Col. 0573D] are even now borne by that holy root. But it should be sweetest of all and devoted in every way for those who recall, chew over, and bring forth the memory of the abundance of sweetness which they once tasted, as they remember and tell others what they saw and heard of that man of God and what perhaps their hands touched.

Such persons speak these things among themselves, and all declare of them what a certain Wise Man said concerning blessed Elijah: “Blessed are those who saw you and remained in your friendship” (Ecclesiasticus 48:11). Moreover, in every delight drawn from the ancients, we must seek usefulness, and in all things the affection of devotion, the fruit of salvation, and the effect of edification. For our poverty needs refreshment more than delight; and, if it is not foolish, seeks food rather than luxuries.

2. And indeed, if we seek devoutly, we find both in this holy and fruitful tree. For this tree, first planted beside running waters, gave its fruit in its season. But now, as though transplanted elsewhere beside waters, it does not cease to bear fruit. The examples of his manner of life still live among us; the sayings of his mouth are still repeated; the holy aid of his prayers does not cease. We read of the children of Israel that they served the Lord all the days of Joshua and of the elders who knew all the works of the Lord which he had done in Israel (Josh. 24:31). May the generation of this blessed Father, which he himself begot visibly through the Gospel [Col. 0574D] and repeatedly brought to birth, live long! May it so follow his footsteps that—God forbid!—a succeeding generation may not have grounds for complaint against it: that, quickly turning aside from the way of life shown them, they neither entered it themselves nor afterward allowed us, their followers, to enter. For this was what he diligently urged upon you when he was about to be taken from you. And even now, unless I am mistaken—indeed, because I am not mistaken—he desires with paternal love that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “as you received from him how you ought to walk and please God in all things, so also walk, that you may abound more” (1 Thess. 4:1). No doubt he was anxious perhaps because of that dreadful saying of holy Moses which he had read, lest it might be said of some: “While I am still alive and walking among you, you have always acted rebelliously against the Lord; how much more when I am dead?” (Deut. 31:27). Nor, I fear, did the apostolic words move him any less, because he perhaps foresaw that after his departure grievous wolves would enter the sheepfolds of his disciples (Acts 20:29). Therefore may he live among us forever and never die! May he never depart, but be firmly held and never let go! May he be found to be our abbot, and you his sons; may he be your shepherd, and you the sheep of his pasture! For we, as you yourselves know, sit here today not for our own sake, but for the sake of him who loved us, provided that you have been careful above all things lest one should seem to have arisen among us “who did not know Joseph” (Exod. 1:8).

[Col. 0575B] 3. And now, dearest brothers, the things visible among us are temporal and will quickly pass away; but not so the things which we believe and also see in him. Therefore let us emulate and venerate him, though invisible, as though seeing him, observing in all things his commands, desiring also his counsels and examples, and praying as well. For the present we make use of remembrance; in a temporal observance we rejoice together; by an everlasting sight we rejoice. For is it possible that, although we are not worthy now to see him, we ourselves are likewise not seen by him? Far be it from us, brothers, far be it to entertain even the slightest suspicion of such a thing! How many things did the holy man see in the spirit even while he lived in the flesh? How much did he learn while far away? How many future things did he foresee and foretell?

I know a man whom this man of divine speech had himself caught, together with not a few others, and brought into the cell of the Novices, [Col. 0575C] where at that time many 1311 sheaves of firstfruits, according to the ordinance of the Lord’s law, were being broken and roasted. Meanwhile there arose a reason—as frequent necessity, both of his own household and of the whole Church of God, often drew him away—why the holy Father left the monastery for several days: absent only in body, not in heart or in the effective providence of his spirit, but only in the weak presence of the flesh. At length returning from his journey, he immediately visited the recruits of his Lord, whom, if I remember rightly, he was training—about eighty of them—in spiritual arms for His warfare.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] See Book V of the *Life*, no. 5.]

After greeting them and saying little, he called one of them by name and said: “Know that, after you ceased seeing me, [Col. 0575D] I saw you myself—indeed, deeply sorrowful and grievously distressed; and when, desiring peace, I gave you the kiss of peace, I myself was drenched with your tears.” Having said this, he ordered the man to come nearer; with his most merciful condescension he kissed him and consoled him magnificently. Nor is it surprising that that ray dispersed the cloud with wonderful ease and swiftness, for that vision was no longer merely a vision. For, after the departure of that blessed Father, a most severe temptation had seized the man, who had been beforehand visited by an abundant blessing of sweetness, and violent sorrow had almost overwhelmed him. But a twofold grace from holy lips—in the word of truth and in the kiss of charity—immediately drove away his sadness and restored saving joy.

[Col. 0576A] 4. And now, brothers, who will give waters of tears to our head, fountains to our eyes? Let us sigh for the light; let us sigh, dearest brothers, let us sigh to the Lord, until both streams are added to our parched land. Let our eyes pour forth rivers of waters, if perhaps they may rain upon that bosom of paternal mercy; if perhaps even now the fatherly breast may be moistened by the tears of his sons. For he whose notice did not escape the cause of a little child still crying in its infant cradle, when he was far away, and who perceived its afflicted distress, knew its sorrow, and felt its tears—what do you think? How much more certainly does he now perceive, know, and feel all that concerns us?

Or when he shall still appear to each one of us—if we behold him without any hesitation; and may our heart rejoice, and may no one take our joy from us—how, I say, will he embrace each one, address each one, and tell each one: “Because when you did not know it, I was present with you in that necessity; I heard those groans, helped those efforts, saw those tears, and received those sighs”? Yet in that expectation it is surely fitting that those whom the holy man spiritually raised while still dwelling in the flesh should meet him first, though not they alone. For Truth itself says both: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see” (Luke 10:23), and: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

5. To some also, though they did not see the holy Father in the flesh, he showed himself a gracious father in the spirit: [Col. 0576C] he brought help, took away temptation, and brought consolation. For from the washing of his sacred body, when after his passing we were rendering him the due funeral rites according to custom, certain brothers carried water to the most distant regions of the world. As we learned from their trustworthy report, now that the tenth year has passed (A.D. 1163), not only has that water remained wholly unspoiled until now, but whatever water has been poured upon it retains the same virtue. For although they have already given portions of this sacred liquid to many who sought remedies—for they affirm that it has brought help to many—yet, though the vessel has repeatedly been filled with other water, it remains to this day such as it was on the first day.

And would that in the congregation of that same blessed Father it might forever be proved true what is said to occur in the liquid: that neither its excellent colour in outward conduct, nor its taste in heavenly intention, nor its fragrance in reputation, may be changed; but that whatever you pour in may be conformed to the same grace in which the holy man stood. We have not now undertaken to narrate his virtues, but, so far as we can, to raise your minds to emulation of and reverence for him. Though you no longer see him bodily, the thoughts which the hearts of your love meditate concerning him will spiritually aid the efforts of my perception; and whatever it is difficult for my speech suitably to express, your hearts will utter to themselves in their own reflections.

Scripture says in one place 1312: “Wisdom is seen at the end” [Col. 0577A]—that is to say, the conduct of the wise is praised at the end of its completion. Hence elsewhere it says: “Do not praise a man in his lifetime”; and again: “Praise no one before death” (Ecclus. 11:30)—as though it said: Praise after death. For praise offered to one living provides an occasion for empty exultation in the person praised, and places especially upon the praiser the recognized mark of flattery.

6. For it is useful in many ways to praise one who has died. First, because, when he to whom we might give pleasure by praise is absent, all praise must necessarily be referred to God, the giver of grace. Secondly, because admiration for virtue alone remains where suspicion of flattery is removed. Thus praise of the dead, uttered in the holy congregation of believers, is wholly edifying; boasting empties merits and, in this respect, also accuses the person praised, because many profit by his praise. [Col. 0577B]

Nor do I fear that I may perhaps be thought to speak too favourably about him. Apart from the fact that nothing can be said which is not beneath his virtues, there is no one who does not count him his own, feel him to be his own, and believe him to be his own. Yet I do not set my hand to touching upon the life of so great a man through confidence in my talent or reliance on eloquence. If some master of ancient eloquence were to attempt it, he would not merely fail to adorn it by eloquence, but, conquered by the weight of his subject, would collapse beneath it. Your love urges me on; your affection gives me confidence to say something about him. His merit, as we believe, will animate this discourse, though its talent crawls; what lies low in words will be raised by deeds; and it will be seasoned by the charity poured out upon him from your hearts.

[Col. 0577C] 7. It is the customary practice of all trained in rhetoric, when they undertake to praise a person’s life, first to extol his country and origin, so that what is lacking in personal virtues may seem to have preceded in the glory of his ancestors. But in Christ we are all one, and the summit of nobility is to be counted among God’s servants. The distinction of earthly origin can add nothing to this dignity except by being despised. No one is more illustrious in heaven than one who, rejecting the lineage of his fathers, chose to be reckoned solely by Christ’s fatherhood.

I therefore pass over the already mentioned distinction of his ancestral worldly honours and the nobility of his family, which he scorned through a still greater nobility of heart. Worldly honours superfluously belonging to his relatives gave him no pleasure, for through love of truth he no longer wished them to be his own. My speech hastens rather to say how sweet his infancy was, how modest his boyhood, how grave his youth; how he surpassed every stage of life beyond what could be expected of virtue, and was always found greater, so that I think him to have been reared by a certain divine pedagogy. For grace had entered all their senses; and while Christ was taking him for Himself, the world was striving to hold him fast in every one of his own people [the reading is uncertain: *terram tamen*]. Some were bound by his sweetness; others were fastened by the attraction of companionship; others were held by admiration for the worldly virtues of the young man’s company. As many claims as his earlier grace had upon them, by so many bonds they were drawn back from his conversion. All feared to be robbed of a common ornament. And indeed, who ever received him except almost as something personally their own? What garments did he not at some time adorn? Thus they thought that a most splendid jewel and the common glory of all were being taken away from them; and they believed that all these things were not to be changed and reformed for the better, as we have seen, but were as it were dying. Nor without reason did worldly glory fear that Christ was taking him from it, for it found him the most adorned among all others and embraced him as unique.

[Col. 0578A] 8. But the young man despised what delighted the aged, exhorting himself continually in these words:

> “This life delights, but it deceives. In churches one set of precepts is recited; here another set of commands sounds in the ears. There modesty, self-restraint, and chastity are taught; here unbridled luxury is sent forth. There Christ invites to the eternal kingdom; here the devil urges toward temporal things. All that is in the world is vanity and the lust of the eyes. And the world passes away, and its lust; but he who does the will of God remains for ever” (1 John 2:16–17), as He Himself remains for ever.
>
> “Let us hasten to be torn from these snares while we are still held less tightly. Things long bound are released more slowly. It is easier to pull up tender growth than to cut down what is strong. Save your life upon the mountain, lest the evils of this way of life seize you. The poison of pleasure creeps quickly. 1313 The liberty received through Christ’s grace must be preserved for Christ. Let others admire gold and silver: metals, as I see, rule those who rule. Let others possess estates and slaves, though not without captivity of their own soul; let them rejoice in honours and prefer honour to the divine image within themselves. It is enough for me not to be a slave of vices; let salvation be my joy; let my delight and my treasure be in virtues. Sorrow will balance joys for me; and in this life too it will grant that I may be delighted and adorned by devotion to discipline, and amid these things become worthy of the heavenly kingdoms.”

Such meditation did not endure a long delay. At once, the spark nourished by such kindling broke forth into the flame of conversion. Bowing his neck to receive the yoke of the Lord’s service, he cast off the yoke of licence, understanding that the greatest kind of captivity is youthful self-indulgence. The splendour of clothing was transferred to brightness of mind; the beauty of his milk-white neck was covered with stiff cloaks; joy passed into gravity; bodily vigour was changed into vigour of soul. Strength of body migrated into strength of spirit. His handsome face grew pale through fasting, and, formerly full of healthy colour, became full of solemnity. And what more? Entirely changed from one thing into another, he appeared another man. The Lord stood by His recruit and consoled him; nor did he fail to rouse his brothers into the community, who, summoned to conversion by his example, accompanied him in virtue as they had accompanied him in fellowship.

[Col. 0578D] 9. From this point there were among them voluntary contests of purpose [alternative reading: *proposita*, “things proposed”]: whose mind was gentler toward compassion; whose food harsher; whose speech kinder; whose clothing rougher; who could speak less often and pray more frequently; whom injury moved less and mercy more; who gave more readily what he had deprived himself of; in whose mouth the world was rarer and Christ more frequent; who, amid that exaltation of virtues, seemed smaller in his own eyes; and who, as he ascended more in merit, diminished more in compunction.

What gravity was theirs then, what maturity together with it; how rare their visits from women, even relatives; and, amid so many virtues, what flight from every vanity! By the industry of these men a temple is raised for God’s elect; fitting dwellings for monks rise up, where they led on earth an angelic life: “in much patience, in watchings, in fastings, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God.” Meanwhile everyone’s love for him grew, multiplied, and spread abroad, and his fame was carried into ever more distant regions. His whole native land competed in loving service and honour toward him.

Yet he feared his own glory. Although he referred to God’s praise the honour of his good manner of life, spread far and wide, he nevertheless feared that it brought him the danger of vanity; he thought that he had received his reward in his lifetime. Every district now sent to him, in competition, those who sought God. Whoever desired Christ sought this man; plainly, whoever sought this man found Christ, for Christ flourished wholly there. He had taken possession of Bernard’s heart as of a lofty citadel and a most splendid temple. There chastity, holiness, faith, wisdom, and virtue dwelt; there justice and truth shone.

[Col. 0579B] Thus, as it were with arms poured forth and open embraces, he invited all into his embrace—that is, into the love of Christ. Everyone streamed to him from all sides in eager rivalry. For what land, what nation, still lacks its own countrymen in his monastery? What raging person did he not tame? How often did he make doves most gentle out of savage beasts? How often did he stir the bitter and sprinkle them with Christ’s sweetness; and those whose severity had been a punishment to themselves afterward became a delight to all through their grace? Finally, having tasted the sweetness of the good, they could not help hating more deeply how great were the evils they had formerly been [perhaps: “what they had formerly been”]. For, as though led into a new light, they detested the old prison of errors that had long possessed them.

10. By his prayers the diverse plague of souls was driven away. Bitterness, harshness, and rage yielded place to the liberty offered by Christ; and rest after long and grievous Pharaonic slavery was delightful. A stupendous and admirable transformation! Not by the cup of Circe, as they say, turning human beings into beasts, but by Christ’s own ministry, as by a most sweet cup, turning beasts into human beings. For what would not that persistence joined with eagerness obtain? Or what stones would not be changed into children of Abraham (Matt. 3:9), where there was such a workshop of virtues for 1314 stripping minds bare? If he did not advance a person to salvation by his exhortations, he constrained God by prayer.

For he regarded the sufferings of all as his own, wept over them as his own, and counted the progress and labours of all as his own, knowing how to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. At once he transferred both the virtues and the vices of all into the accumulation of his own merit. [Col. 0580A] For as virtue calls forth virtue, so compassion bestowed on the afflicted sanctifies. Thus he reaped in each person more than each reaped for himself. The salvation of each built up for him the fullness of glory. Energetic, prompt, and tireless, he persevered according as he discerned the character and disposition of each. He approached one privately, another publicly; one severely, another gently; and, in order to alter by correction, he often altered the very countenance of correction. Hence it was that we saw no one easily loved as much, or feared as much. For he placed these two affections in each of his own people in such a way that his love introduced fear in the beloved, and fear of discipline introduced love.

11. It is incredible how great was his concern that sorrow should afflict no one, that no solitary thought should oppress anyone; how readily he perceived what troubled each person, how he bore the minds of individuals. Moreover, with what merciful ordering did he provide that excessive labours should not burden anyone and that no one should grow dull through excessive rest. With pious affection he weighed, if one may say so, the very sleep of each brother. Constantly shaking the physically strong out of idleness, he compelled those fervent in spirit to rest. By God’s prompting, I believe, he knew the strength, the temper, and the stomach of all, truly made servant of all through Jesus Christ.

It is astonishing how one man fulfilled so many offices at once. Though especially afflicted by such varied weakness, he accompanied, though unequal in strength, under the same rule, even the strongest and those still robust from recent eating, in fasts and vigils. Visiting the sick while himself more infirm, he provided refreshment for souls and bodies alike. And lest anything should have been given too little attention, his mind always returned to such thoughts: [Col. 0580C] “This man is cold; this one is troubled in thought; that man’s work is heavy; this food does not suit this one; that man has been hurt by another. Serious is the wrong which this man inflicted; no less serious is the fact that the other felt the injury. Great diligence is needed so that offence may obtain grace: so that this man may consider the insult done to him either nonexistent or slight, while that man sighs that he has inflicted a most grievous wrong.”

This was his unceasing work and unceasing attention: to lighten Christ’s yoke for all; to turn aside whatever the devil had cast in; to dispel the cloudy darkness of sins and restore the clear skies of graces; by loving to implant love of Christ and neighbour; to renew the minds of all with joy as though they were his own heart; and to make them burn with desire for Christ as on the first day of conversion.

[Col. 0580D] 12. Hence it was that the entire community, eager for service and assembled at his name from diverse parts of the earth, differing in customs and languages, joined together in love for him. All called him lord, all father, reckoning that in him father, relatives, and all things were restored to them at once. Through his compassion for them, all had learned to bear his sufferings as their own [perhaps *computare*, “to reckon,” rather than *comportare*, “to bear”]. As the sun clothes the face of heaven according only to its own cloudiness or brightness, so that community, thirsting for heaven and devoted to heavenly pursuits, received from him clouds or serenity of mind, as it were from the sun reflected in Christ; it corresponded to him when he was in harmony with it, and disclosed itself to him when he inspired it.

Hence that grace of the Holy Spirit, spread abroad in the monastery and still enduring through his prayers, was confirmed by the example and acceptance of so great a teacher: in diverse gifts of grace, in humility, gentleness, and unfeigned charity; and in the one glory of the head amid the diversity of members. Great, amid all this, was his concern for strangers and guests. In the squalor of the wilderness he provided delights by his presence, receiving those first known to him then as though long his own, with such joy and eagerness as though he had adopted them. Almost no distress reached him which did not extend beyond him and find its limit in him.

[Col. 0581B] From every side duties of correspondence were eagerly brought to him. With what new expressions he sent answers varied for them; how weighty, how gentle, how sweet! Who did not think his house 1315 blessed, his writing-cases blessed? Speech from his mouth was so considered, his writings contained so much salvation and sweetness, that they were stored not in writing-cases or cupboards, but in an open chest. Thus very many preserve those writings in their hearts and most gladly bring them forth as a testimony of their love. Finally, who ever bound to himself such affections of friends present as the unknown persons who loved him intensely and longed for him eagerly?

13. Meanwhile, while I recall his manifold grace toward all, I pass over his infinite concern for me. Would that it had brought me no less salvation in Christ than love among you! For his charity, poured out upon all, had—if I may say so without envy—made so great an addition in me; and by his kindnesses how much lighter had he made Christ’s light yoke for me! First he fed me with milk; afterward he gave me to drink also from that overflowing stream of heavenly wisdom which was within himself. And would that the narrowness of my spirit had received as much as he strove to pour in! He would surely have prepared me for you, given you a successor worthy of your desire, and trained one fit to succeed him. But you would not readily have perceived [perhaps *sentiretis*, “you would perceive”] how great a good you had lost if your good had been restored whole to you.

May the merciful Lord, who, by stirring your minds to love my smallness, granted that I should not be absent from his tomb, grant also, through your prayers, that I may not wander far from his ways; but that, whatever I learn that he did, I may hasten to do without scrutinizing or disputing his deeds.

[Col. 0581D] 14. Meanwhile, beloved, in skimming over rather than recounting everything concerning your most diligent Father, I have repeated things known to you. For you saw, beloved, that wakefulness of care, that zeal for discipline, those tears of compassion, that constant and perpetual serenity of mind, whose evidence was his unchanging face. You saw that breadth of charity, so great in him that, if charity itself were to be portrayed, it would seem right that it should be painted pre-eminently in the likeness of this man’s face.

[Col. 0582A] Who ever thought that he had seen enough of him? To whom did he not take the place of every affection? Who administered discipline so mingled with cheerfulness? Whom did he not correct to the very pleasure of the person corrected? When did his joy ever savour of frivolity? When was his sadness not salutary? Who did not find him loftier than he had previously seen him? Always stationed on the summit of virtue, he always found room in which to grow. Moreover, under his exhortation, who in anxiety did not despise his pain? Who of savage manners did not abhor his madness? Who, being wanton, did not detest his luxury? What more need be said? “Becoming all things to all,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 9:22), he was the common remedy for all.

He had scarcely a grace which he did not possess so fully that he seemed especially to cultivate and possess it as though it were unique. Nothing readily filled him with horror, however harsh. Amid any bitter and long-endured torments, he neither improperly desired death nor feared it. For one whom it had not wearied to live amid every hardship in Christ’s service did not fear to pass into a new life through that common gate of the new life—the final necessity of humankind—which he had reflected upon beforehand.

[Col. 0582B] 15. You do not at all doubt that he now hears and sees what concerns you. Indeed, he is the one who, on the first day when he entered and vowed that most blessed covenant with the Lord, the covenant of holy life, while he had not yet laid aside secular dress, saw a lance not yet driven into his brother’s side;

[Note: [Col. 0581D] See Book I of the *Life*, chapter 3.]

and about fifteen days later pointed out with his finger the place where the wound was to be inflicted. [Col. 0582C] Now, then, released from corruptible remains, freed from bodily bonds, led out of earthly darkness, rescued from the prison of the world—is he to be thought ignorant of anything, especially of matters pertaining to the needs of his own sons? This concern is not carnal, nor should spiritual fatherhood be thought dissolved by the dissolution of flesh.

Indeed, even now he ought to hear his sons; he ought to hear from the tomb, he who was heard once while still in his mother’s womb. Thus his memory is rightly celebrated after his departure with abundant blessing, whose holiness was splendidly commended even before his birth. For just as the Lord knows those who are His, and surely knows those whom He chose from the beginning, so He also 1316 establishes for each person the times and moments [Col. 0582D] in which the mystery of His eternal love may become known either to them or concerning them. And although He has called some in childhood, some in youth, and some in old age, He has nevertheless, by a certain privilege of special grace, anticipated—indeed, as it were snatched away—in blessing a few, declaring before they were born what they would be by such signs and indications as He chose.

16. Thus He frightened this venerable mother of His chosen and especially beloved one, while she was still pregnant with her most blessed burden, by an unusual vision, but consoled her by the interpretation of that same vision. For while she was pregnant with her noble offspring, she saw a dream and related it to a certain religious solitary:

[Col. 0583A]

> “I saw and heard, as it were, a little dog wholly white in body, reddish on its back, barking in my womb; and I was frightened.”

He said to her: “Do not be afraid. You will bear a son acceptable to God, who will be an effective and eminent preacher, great and exalted in the word of glory.”

[Note: [Col. 0583D] *Ibid.*, chapter 1.]

Thus indeed our Bernard, from the time he began in whatever measure to live, began to appear wonderful. He was not yet being born, and already he was being preached—or rather, he himself was already preaching. He was not yet even nursing, yet already appeared to be praising the Lord. Nor without reason was he commended before he was born; not without reason, I say, was he magnified by a divine oracle while still a little child borne in his mother’s womb. For how truly the word of that faithful man was foretold, and how effectively fulfilled, those surely remember today who have learned more certainly in their own experience the power of his barkings and the healing grace of his tongue.

And now, Lord, whoever loves You surely loves Your dog. Would that You also may love the one whom he loved. In his speech we have plainly proved fulfilled what Scripture continues, in praise of the bride, in the Song of Songs: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet” (Song 4:3). For in few words there is evidently praise of fervour in the scarlet colour; of subtlety and breadth in the ribbon; also of restraint of the heart’s thoughts, as though the binding together of the hairs of the head; and clearly and expressly of sweetness of speech. Whose teaching, indeed, was so fervent, so subtle, so abundant, so useful, and finally so sweet and acceptable?

[Col. 0583C] 17. But why do we say that, though wholly white in body, he seemed to have a reddish back? Whiteness is chastity; whiteness is innocence of life; bodily whiteness is purity of action. But what is redness? Is it not martyrdom? If he had appeared red, would he not have been a martyr? For burdens are carried on the back, and the back is offered to blows. And though he did not fear to run [perhaps *cavere*, “take care,” for *currere*, “run”], what confessor, bearing such things, runs more in the contest than a martyr enduring the blow? Yet in human judgment, after good martyrs, glory in the world is granted to holy confessors.

But if we remember how much this servant of God bore and endured, how many and how grave things he suffered—not by the mortification of a single blow, but by long mortification of his body—we perhaps not without reason call our Bernard the equal of the martyrs, just as we call blessed Lawrence the equal of the Apostles, since we know that Bernard appeared reddish in his mother’s womb. Blessed is he who among the members of the heavenly Bridegroom was so swiftly conformed to his Head that, just as He is proclaimed “white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song 5:10), so this man in his own manner was white, and ruddy without suffering, yet reddish through patience.

[Col. 0584A] We too ought to be his imitators, as he was of Christ. For is he not an apostle, if not to others, at least to us? Are not you the signs of his apostleship before God? And not merely you few who seem even now to dwell visibly with him, but those who today live in countless places under the shadow of his name, among peoples so diverse, and often barbarous and perverse. May you not show yourselves unworthy sons of so great a Father, but white in holiness, reddish in patience, barking with zeal for the Order, with ardour for righteousness, and with the free voice of truth.

For as the surpassing whiteness of all his conduct and life joined the same Father to holy confessors and chosen virgins; as his reddish back made him equal to martyrs; and as his surpassing teaching proved him an apostolic man: so his voice in the womb will grant him both that most desirable 1317 companionship with himself and fellowship through all ages, together with blessed vision. Surely, brothers, if you agree with me in this matter, you will either wonder where to seek that same Father among those only whom we have named, or hope to find him there. As he came much desired by many into the house of the Father, he found many mansions prepared for himself. Unless perhaps we doubt that he was happily received into the prophetic company, whom in so many experiences we have often proved to possess a prophetic spirit.

Nor should it seem incredible to anyone that the holy patriarchs, as soon as that man of God entered the heavenly palace and divine temple, gladly opened to him not only their bosom but also their council-seat. For they did not judge him unworthy to be enrolled in that sacred number of their assembly, in whose seed they see, and do not begrudge seeing, so many nations blessed on every side.

[Col. 0584C] 18. You also know, beloved, that holy and supreme teachers have taught that the various classes of the elect among humankind are advanced, according to the differing quality of their merits, to the sacred orders of angels. For angels are called messengers; archangels and principalities, supreme messengers, because lesser matters are believed to be announced through the former, while certain highest and chief matters are announced through the latter. Likewise among human beings chosen by God one finds some who, though less learned and grasping small things, nevertheless faithfully announce to their neighbours what they themselves can; and others who perceive certain more exalted things and also share them without envy with all who are more perfect and more capable. The former pass hence into the angelic order; the latter receive a dwelling among the archangels.

We know that neither kind of teaching was lacking to this most blessed Father of ours. For, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, he set forth sublime matters; yet he did not refuse to condescend to the unlearned and little ones. But perhaps what appeared humbler in him was then the more wonderful and now tastes the sweeter. How often did it delight us to hear, and delight us now to remember, how this man urged rustic people and poor little women to acts of humanity suited to them! He taught them, surely, that when a neighbour lacked his usual bread, [Col. 0585A] they should cheerfully lend it to him until he could repay; that when another neighbour, perhaps occupied elsewhere, had not prepared food for himself, they should invite him in charity to share vegetables; that they should generously send him a small portion of legumes and share a meagre dish.

Likewise, he taught them to keep faith in lawful marriage and, not ungrateful for the divine benefit, not to overstep the bounds of salutary indulgence. He taught them also to render earthly dues to earthly lords and faithfully pay what is owed—whether tithes without fraud—to Him who could more justly claim even nine portions than the farmer could claim a tenth for himself. For He made the earth, gave arms, and bestowed strength on the labourer. He also hardens sown seeds with frost, waters them with rains, cherishes them with spring warmth, and ripens them beneath the summer sun. Otherwise, the man who ploughs loses his labour unless He gives the increase.

[Col. 0585B] He also earnestly warned them that fortune-tellers and their sacrilegious charms must be avoided; that they ought not, when unable to attack those who harmed them with swords, to attack them with their lips; that they ought not, by defrauding one another, pursue small gains to great ruin. Rather, they should remember Him who, though rich, became poor for our sake, and because the poor person was left to Him.

19. But if our smallness fails even in recounting small matters, when would it suffice for his greater achievements? We therefore judge it better to yield him this portion of his own praises: that his spiritual teaching—although it is clear that he wrote with a far different intention—may nevertheless become known from his own writings. For even when a lamp has been lit chiefly so that other things may be seen, it cannot itself remain hidden. Meanwhile, let it suffice for us to have recalled that he is deservedly believed to have been placed in both orders of the heavenly messengers, since in both kinds of teaching he was so faithful, so effective, so devoted.

Certainly, through those Spirits called Virtues, they say that many signs are wrought; through the Powers, demons are restrained. But if those are counted among the same orders who exercise the same works, it is surely clear that our Bernard is excluded from neither of these, since he is known to have shone so magnificently in miracles of both kinds. Between Principalities and Dominions the difference perhaps appears to be this: although both are believed to preside over the elect spirits, the Principalities, as though by office, direct what others are to do and, like vigorous commanders of the divine armies, take the lead in carrying out that work itself. The Dominions, however, in a higher rank, surpass even those obedient to them by a certain wondrous power and authority. Hence we believe that among human beings themselves those belong to the order of Principalities who preside over the other brethren in the care of administration. But those belong to the Dominions who deserve to obtain obedience itself through a special reverence for holiness. Of such persons, indeed, it is said that by the very right of purity they are called gods among human beings.

Nor is it difficult to perceive how both these things alike met in this blessed Father of ours. For he showed pastoral care for very many brethren, and obtained singular reverence and authority among almost all churches. For in whom else was such trust placed, to whom was such deference shown, whom did religious and secular persons, princes and bishops, obey so readily?

The Thrones follow, and we know that they received this name because God sits in them. And this arrangement is indeed most beautiful. For it is higher and more glorious than every dominion to be subject to the Lord. And although, after the fall of him who wished to appear like God, together with his accomplices, all the orders of angels are certainly known to be subject to their Creator by voluntary devotion, yet those in whom He is said to sit seem to possess something distinctive.

20. Above all, however, human beings must observe this: those who are more highly honored among men should be found especially subject to God. Otherwise, woe to them unless they subject all their dominion to Him, unless they set all their principality beneath the Lord of lords. Woe to those who seem to excel and preside among men unless the Lord sits and presides over them. For greater humility is necessary where there is greater authority.

The more profound and purer we have found this humility in that very Father of ours of whom we speak, the more we rejoice that his blessed soul, while still placed in the flesh, was a seat of wisdom—firm and steadfast, peaceful and humble, and therefore also so acceptable. Accordingly, we judge all the more that, now released from the flesh, it deserved to appear exalted among those heavenly seats. Where this humility has gone beforehand, knowledge does not puff up but fills—especially if the surpassing grace of charity is added. Thus the fullness of knowledge seems securely established if humility sustains it and charity cherishes it.

For this reason the eighth and ninth orders are not without cause called Cherubim and Seraphim: by these names, fullness of knowledge and ardor or burning are commended in those orders. For Cherubim, they say, signifies “fullness of knowledge,” and Seraphim “the burning ones” or “those who set aflame.” If we believe that those belong to the same order whose interpretations of names are found to agree, then we ought not to doubt, even concerning these highest and supreme orders, that our blessed Father and pastor has a place in both.

21. Certainly, those who have received from his fullness know to this day how full he was of knowledge. But how he burned with love—indeed, beyond measure—and by speaking kindled others, you especially remember, since you have often proved it by experience, so that, unless I am mistaken, you say to yourselves in silent thought: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way while he spoke to us?” (Luke 24:32). How often has someone entered this audience perhaps lukewarm and departed not moderately inflamed? His speech was intensely fiery: who would not love it? Who would not burn with love for it?

Happy, therefore, is he who thus finds rest in all things and among all; who thus follows the Lamb wherever He goes. Happy is he who thus receives the rewards of manifold merits, so that now nothing at all is lacking to him in any glory, to whom formerly nothing was lacking in any grace.

But concerning all these divisions of graces, dearest brethren, I admonish your Fraternity to glory in so great and precious a treasure in such a way, and to venerate so deeply the signs of his election, that we may zealously seek to imitate those things which are more profitable for our edification and necessary for salvation—always magnificently praising and glorifying in him the Author of that same salvation, the Giver of pardon, the Bestower of grace, the Render of glory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives as God, blessed above all things for ages. Amen.

[Col. 0587]

## Letter of the Same Geoffrey to Albinus, Cardinal and Bishop of Albano, on the Condemnation of the Errors of Gilbert of Poitiers

[Col. 0587B] To his most beloved father and lord ALBINUS, by God’s grace bishop of Albano and vicar of the lord Pope: brother GEOFFREY of Clairvaux, the least thing that he is.

1. Your Paternity had instructed our venerable brother and your special son Augustine to impose upon me, by your command, the task of making known to you carefully by letter what was discussed and what judgment was finally reached, and in what manner, at the Council of Reims which Pope Eugenius III of blessed memory held, concerning certain propositions detected and censured in the exposition of the bishop of Poitiers, Master Gilbert surnamed Porretanus.

Therefore, if I seem to obey you rather slowly, let not Your Serenity wonder: for before the vigil of the feast of All Saints I had heard no word, small or great, about this matter. On that very day, taking up pen and tablets, I began to write what I should have wished, if I could, to communicate to you more promptly.

2.
