In the same year in which the aforesaid pontiff Eugenius, seated in the chair of the Roman Church, immediately at the first report inspired no slight fear in the wicked and, conversely, confidence in all honorable persons, a great man worthy of remembrance among the good, named Arnald and surnamed “Who Does Not Laugh,” held the office of archdeacon in the church of Poitiers under the aforesaid bishop. He had not obtained it through that bishop’s favor, but had been promoted by his predecessor; for such a tree could hardly have borne fruit of this kind.

It happened that the bishop was privately admonished, as we believe, by that archdeacon, a man sufficiently faithful and eloquent, concerning certain articles of faith. Since he did not yield, he was at last publicly reproved in the church. An appeal was then made to the Roman Church, and the same question was debated before the aforementioned Pope. As he was about to go down into Gaul, he ordered both parties to appear before him in Paris at the Easter festival.

Our most blessed father Saint Bernard was present with that Pope at Paris during the same festival. Whenever any affair of Christ happened to require his presence, he immediately devoted himself to it as though it were wholly his own; no one doubted this. An inquiry was made according to the aforesaid commentary on Boethius. Asked for it, the bishop replied that he did not have it at hand. Yet a certain passage was found among the scholars, containing among other things these words:

> “If a man, to whom diverse things contribute [or: contribute] to his being, is, through the abundance of one form—for example, wisdom—called wisdom itself, according to the saying, ‘However great you are, you are nothing but wisdom’; much more is God, to whom diverse things do not contribute [or: contribute] to his being, said to be his own wisdom, his own goodness, and so forth.”

This writing was thus produced in public, and Saint Bernard disputed against the bishop, saying that it appeared a grave and monstrous assertion to say that diverse things do not contribute to God’s being, as though one thing did contribute. He also said that this comparison involving emphatic speech was far removed from God: God is not called His own wisdom as any human being may be called his wisdom, but is truly and substantially His own wisdom, His own essence, His own divinity—not as Davus was called “crime.”

The bishop denied that he had ever taught, believed, or committed to writing that divinity was not God, or that there was in God a form or essence which was not God. Going still further, he produced as witnesses his disciples: a certain noble bishop of Évreux, named Rotold, later to become archbishop of Rouen, and Master Ivo of Chartres. They testified that he had not maintained or believed that doctrine. He did so unwillingly, as we clearly observed then, but compelled by the pressure of his followers, because of the words of his booklet quoted above.

Since different persons asserted different things, the Supreme Pontiff commanded him to send that same booklet before the council which he proposed to hold that year in the city of Reims, so that it might be carefully examined, and to be ready at that council to answer more fully the charges made against him.

3. It happened that the often-mentioned Lord Eugenius gave this exposition, sent to him by the bishop, to a venerable Premonstratensian abbot, Godescalc of Mont-Saint-Éloi, who afterward became bishop of Arras, to examine. He, being an eloquent man, carefully marked the propositions and wrote on a sheet a few patristic authorities from books of holy Catholic Fathers plainly contrary to them. When he came to the council, he presented these to the lord Pope together with the booklet of the bishop of Poitiers.

In that same year the Lord removed from among us a great pillar of the Church, Lord Alberic of Ostia, worthy of all reverent remembrance. While serving as legate in Aquitaine, he had learned so much about the life and teaching of that Gilbert that the latter, conscious that he was not as he ought to be, feared the most ardent zeal of the bishop of Ostia more than that of the other cardinals of the time. Nor were there lacking persons who believed that, had that man lived, the bishop of Poitiers would never have dared, in his presence, to confess what he did confess.

The discussion came to the propositions noted by the aforesaid Abbot Godescalc. But because he himself was too inarticulate, the lord Pope gave the book, with the saints’ testimonies opposed to it, to our Father Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. Present were great men, and men by no means unlearned: Geoffrey of Oratorio, archbishop of the church of Bordeaux, of whom the bishop of Poitiers was a suffragan; Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, notable enough for religion and learning; Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, endowed with both secular and literary learning; and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, to whom King Louis of the Franks, when setting out for Jerusalem, had entrusted the administration of the whole kingdom.

These and many others, together with blessed Bernard, refuted the aforesaid propositions alike by reason and by testimonies of Holy Scripture—except that the aforesaid Geoffrey spoke less than the others, deliberately sparing the man and reserving himself for judgment, as he humbly confessed and did penance, when he heard the cardinals, whose leading members were known to have favored and indeed openly supported the defendant, promise that they would judge on the objections they had heard.

4. When we entered the consistory on the first day, the bishop of Poitiers had large volumes brought in by his clerks, while we had only a few ecclesiastical authorities on a single sheet. His supporters therefore seized the opportunity to object that we were producing abridged testimonies, whereas he offered complete codices, in which one might understand how what preceded or followed was connected to the words proposed.

Nevertheless, this proposition was produced from his codex:

> “When God is spoken of, this pertains to the substance—not to that which He is, but to that by which He is.”

While one person after another loudly accused the author and reasonably complained against him as he continued to evade the issue, Saint Bernard said to the bishop: “What need is there to dwell longer on words of this kind? The source of this scandal arises from nothing other than that many believe you yourself believe and teach that the divine essence or nature—His divinity, wisdom, goodness, greatness—is not God, but is the form by which God is. If you believe this, say so openly; or deny it.”

He dared to say: “The form of God, and the divinity by which God is, is not itself God.”

“See,” said Saint Bernard, “we have what we were seeking. Let this confession be written down.”

The Supreme Pontiff ordered it, and Lord Henry of Pisa—then subdeacon of the Roman Church, later a monk of Clairvaux, and after being abbot of Saint Anastasius, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus—at his command brought forward paper, pen, and ink. But while he was writing that confession, the bishop said to the abbot: “And you write that divinity is God.”

The other answered without agitation: “Let it be written,” he said, “with an iron stylus upon an adamantine nail, or carved upon stone, that the divine essence, form, nature, deity, goodness, wisdom, virtue, power, and greatness truly is God.”

5. The discussion then continued upon the same proposition, and it proceeded so far that the Saint said: if that form is not God, it is better than God, since God has being from it, while it neither is from Him nor has anything from Him.

I believed this especially worth recording for the following reason. When the disputation was finished, I immediately entered the library of the church of Reims, took several codices from it, and in the book of blessed Augustine *On the Trinity* found, among many other testimonies, almost the same words that Saint Bernard had raised in objection:

> “God is great only by that greatness which is what He Himself is; otherwise that greatness will be greater than God.”

Moreover, when the first proposition was being debated on the first day, I was the one who objected to the bishop, before everyone present, that the words which he was now professing he had wholly disavowed that same year at Paris before the lord Pope and the greater part of the distinguished persons present, and that he had produced witnesses that he had never believed or taught such things.

But he, very confident—and perhaps more so than he afterward wished, since he could not deny having denied them—said: “Whatever I said then, this is what I say now.”

But I, sighing deeply because I saw such great audacity being undertaken before such judges almost with impunity, said: “Then, like the king, do you have both your statement and its retraction?”

6. While the persons present were disputing over the aforesaid first proposition, the second came forward. The bishop professed that the three persons are neither one God nor one thing, although the three persons are one God—that is, by one divinity—and are one, that is, by one [thing]. This proposition was discussed at length; and at Saint Bernard’s suggestion and by the lord Pope’s command, it too was committed to writing with the first.

The authority of Athanasius was plainly set against it:

> “The hymns of the heavenly powers affirm that the Three are One and the One Three.”

On the following day we brought such large codices to the disputation that the bishop’s supporters were astonished and heard from us: “Behold, we do not have mere sheets.”

The bishop caused less intelligible words from books of blessed Hilary and from the body of canons, in certain Greek letters, to be repeatedly read—especially amid such haste and so great and such a crowd. Nor were there lacking people who spoke on his behalf, although understanding little.

That same day two propositions were added to the first two and likewise committed to writing: namely, that the same bishop truly professed that personal properties and an abundant multitude of eternal things exist without beginning, although none of them is God and none is from God.

7. The fourth proposition was that the divine nature did not assume human nature, but that the person of the Son assumed our nature—contrary to the saying of blessed Gregory:

> “Divinity came to us shod with humanity.”

And contrary to blessed Augustine in the first book *On the Trinity*:

> “Therefore, because the form of God received the form of a servant, both are God and both are man.”

Likewise, in his seventy-fifth tractate on the Gospel of John:

> “He emptied Himself, and man, etc. Who but that same Christ Jesus? But here all things are already present: the Word in the form of God, which received the form of a servant; and soul and flesh in the form of a servant, which was received by the form of God.”

And Pope Leo:

> “That nature assumed us which neither consumed its own things by ours nor ours by its own.”

After a lengthy disputation, they departed on this understanding: the lord cardinals said, “Since we have heard what has been proposed, we shall henceforth judge how these matters ought to be defined.”

This statement so stirred many hearts that, on the following day, ten archbishops, a great multitude also of bishops, abbots, and masters gathered at Saint Bernard’s. Since the cardinals seemed to have reserved judgment to themselves alone—and they knew that almost all of them favored the erring man rather than the error—it was thought necessary to send, together with the propositions of Bishop Gilbert, their own confession and symbol of faith, so that the judges might know more fully what they were judging.

They therefore wrote out an equal number of propositions as clearly as they could, setting forth in the bishop’s own words their confession, contrary to his in every respect. By the common agreement of all, and not without much deliberation, they caused it to be presented to those who were to judge. Yet they did not fear that the latter would decide anything contrary; rather, they believed that some of them were aiming to dissolve the council without any definition being made. Accordingly, beneath the document—which we are sending you last—were subscribed the names of every archbishop, bishop, abbot, and master who was present, by the consent and agreement of all.

8. Three persons were selected: the two most reverend bishops Hugh of Auxerre and Milo of Thérouanne, and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. They were to present the same document to the lord Pope and the cardinals and say:

> “Out of reverence for you, we have endured statements less worthy of acceptance, until at last we heard that you wished to judge them. Therefore we also offer you our confession, so that you may judge not one party, but both parties. You possess the written confession of that man; it is fitting that you should possess ours as well. Yet he gave you his under the condition that he was ready to correct it if anything else should seem right to you. We wholly reject such a condition and offer you ours in such a manner that you may know that this is our position, that we shall persist in it, and that we shall change absolutely nothing.”

Without delay the lord Pope replied, and ordered the message to be reported to all who had sent them: the Roman Church differed in absolutely no respect from their confession; and if any appeared to have stood for the person, they were in no way standing for the doctrine.

Consequently, in the notable palace called Thau, when the whole Church assembled and the bishop of Poitiers was questioned, he freely renounced each proposition, saying these same words: “If you believe otherwise, so do I; if you speak otherwise, so do I; if you write otherwise, so do I.”

There the lord Pope, by apostolic authority and with the assent of the whole Church that had assembled, condemned the propositions themselves, strictly commanding that no one should dare read or copy the same book, even though it had thus been condemned, unless the Roman Church had first corrected it.

When the bishop replied, “I will correct it according to your judgment,” the Pope said: “This correction will not be entrusted to you.”

9. There were other matters that the same bishop was said often to have taught his hearers in his schools, though we passed them over. Yet because of the multitude of scholars who testified that they had heard them from him many times, documents said to contain his opinions were torn and shredded before all. Indeed, when fire was requested to burn them, some said that it was enough if they were torn up. What those propositions were, I neither took care to learn then nor know even now.

As for the other propositions concerning which I received Your Dignity’s instruction, I examined carefully the book of glosses on the Psalter that the same Gilbert of Poitiers composed. On the verse, “Worship His footstool” (Psalm 98:5), I found the following written:

> “Flesh is from earth, and Christ received flesh from the flesh of Mary. This is worshiped by us without impiety, because no one spiritually eats His flesh unless he first worships.”

Thus far are Augustine’s words. Gilbert immediately added the following explanation, which is their addition:

> “I do not mean worship with that adoration which is *latria*, due to the Creator alone, but with that which is the worthier kind of *dulia*. For *dulia* is worship also offered to a creature, and it has two species: one offered indiscriminately to human beings, the other offered to the humanity of Christ alone.”

Also, in his book of glosses on Saint Paul’s Epistle, upon the passage, “Therefore God exalted Him and gave Him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9), he commented thus:

> “Some think that this name was given to the man, which can in no way be fitting. For this gift is the Son of God; this name is God, who is above every name not by mere appellation but by nature, and who received it not after His passion but rather from the Father, from whom He has all things, when He was begotten. Therefore this was not given to the man—unless perhaps someone should say that everything was given through adoption. But every knee does not bend to an adopted God, nor is he in the glory of God the Father; for this belongs to One born from God. Yet the Apostle says: ‘He gave Him the name,’ etc. I say this because the One born received it in order that by the cross it might be manifested what He received from the Father when He was begotten.”

Of these propositions, therefore, we had heard nothing, and knew absolutely nothing, at the time of that council.

10. The following passages in the writings of Pope Saint Leo appear contrary to these views; Your Discretion knows very well that their authority is confirmed by the sacred canons. For in an Easter sermon he says:

> “The creature was not assumed into partnership with its Creator in such a way that He should be the inhabitant and it the dwelling-place; but both are God by the power of the One assuming, and both man by the humility of that which was assumed. Therefore, in each nature the same is the Son of God, and nothing belongs to one nature which does not belong to both.”

Likewise:

> “In no respect dividing the visible from the invisible, the bodily from the incorporeal, let us worship in Christ the man the Word, and in the Word Christ.”

And below:

> “Faithfully believe both, faithfully worship both, and let there be no division in the unity of Word and flesh.”

The same author, in a sermon on the Nativity:

> “From the time when the Word was made flesh, it is not permitted to think of Him as God without that by which He is man, nor as man without that by which He is God; for nothing divine was lacking to that which was assumed, and nothing human to the One assuming. Human things do not prejudice divine things, nor divine things human: He who is flesh is the Word.”

The same, to Bishop Flavian:

> “The judgment of John the apostle and evangelist is: ‘Whoever divides Jesus is not from God, and this is antichrist’ [1 John 4:3]. What is it to divide Jesus, except to separate human nature from the Word?”

Augustine, in the *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* [Note: This book is not Augustine’s; it is attributed to Gennadius]:

> “He who is *homoousios* with the Father and with man is worshiped by angels and every creature, as are the Father and the Holy Spirit—not man on account of [variant: apart from] God, nor Christ together with God, but man in God and God in man.”

The same, *On the Predestination of the Saints*:

> “What did that man merit, that, assumed by the Word into unity of person, He should be the only-begotten Son of God? For in the Apostle we learn that even the Lord of glory Himself, insofar as He became man and the Son of God, was predestined. So great, so lofty, so supreme was this predestined elevation of human nature that it could have no higher point to which it might be raised.”

Jerome, in the *Breviary on the Psalms*, on “Worship His footstool”:

> “Although man was indeed assumed, and in comparison with God every creature is His footstool, yet this very footstool has been joined to God. And see what a thing I dare say about His seat: I worship the footstool just as I worship the throne. I do not understand one thing as seated and another as the footstool; rather, in Christ the whole is a throne. I do not know how it is so, yet I believe that it is. It is enough for me to know what is written and what I believe: we are called believers, not reasoners.”

11. Against the fourth proposition, as we have set it forth above, Pope Leo writes to Bishop Flavian as follows:

> “‘Have this mind in yourselves,’ says the Apostle, etc., down to ‘in the glory of the Father’ [Philippians 2:5–11]: that God exalts Him is the advancement of the assumed, not of the One assuming. Knowing that the eternal divinity of the Son received no increase from the Father, understand wisely that the same One to whom it is said, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall return’ [Genesis 3:19], is told in Christ, ‘Sit at my right hand’ [Psalm 109:1].”

The same, to the Constantinopolitans:

> “Let the adversaries of truth say when, or according to which nature, the almighty Father raised the Son above all things, or to which substance He subjected all things. For the divinity of the Word is equal to the Father in all things and consubstantial with Him; but that which grew was lesser than the One raising it. In the nature of man He received from the Father what, in the nature of divinity, He Himself also bestowed.”

Likewise, to the Emperor Leo and to the Palestinians:

> “We understand the exaltation by which God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name as belonging to that form which was to be enriched by the increase of so great a glorification.”

Likewise:

> “Whatever He received, He received in time according to man, to whom things that He did not possess are bestowed. But the form of a servant was raised into the glory of divine power; and it makes no difference from which substance Christ is named or worshiped.”

Jerome, in the *Breviary on the Epistle to the Philippians*:

> “Since the assumed man deigned to be humbled in this manner, divinity, which cannot humble itself, deservedly exalted him who had been humbled. And a name was given to him which he had not possessed before. Hence this passage must rightly be understood according to the human nature.”

The same, on “The Lord said to my Lord”:

> “The Savior explained this passage in the Gospel, saying: ‘If Christ is David’s Son, how does he in the Spirit call Him Lord?’ [Matthew 22:43]. To this Lord, then, is the command given that He should sit. For God does not sit—He sits by assumption of a body. Therefore the command to sit is given to Him who is man, who was assumed.”

Augustine, *Against Maximus*:

> “‘He gave Him the name,’ etc. He gave these things to the man, not to God. And then, the very form in which He was crucified was exalted; to Him was given the name above every name—to Christ the man, dead according to the flesh, risen, ascending. For the name above every name is given.”

12. Finally, so that this letter may now reach its conclusion: if it pleases Your Discretion to be more fully instructed concerning the preceding four propositions, a more careful disputation concerning the same is contained in the sermons of blessed Bernard on the Song of Songs.

We desire and pray that Your Paternity may always prosper well in the Lord. We commend to you our brethren of Fossanova. We should greatly wish to hear reliable news of your welfare and of the condition of Holy Church.

13. This letter had scarcely been completed by the person to whom it had been entrusted for writing when, behold, at that very hour it was the Lord’s will that what I wanted should come to hand. Before this present letter was returned to me, another document, long sought and already despaired of by me, was supplied by another brother. Nearly forty years ago I had published it on these same propositions together with the very symbol of faith which had been presented to the lord Pope and the Roman Church, on behalf of ten archbishops and almost all the bishops who were still found that day at Reims, together with the greatest and very many abbots and masters of schools, and with the names of each subscribed, through the persons mentioned above.

Therefore, rejoicing greatly, I attach that document also to this letter and send both to you, my most beloved lord, with filial devotion.

14. I have also heard that Your Diligence wishes similarly to know more fully the truth concerning the condemnation of Peter Abelard, whose books Pope Innocent II of pious memory publicly burned by fire in the city of Rome, in the church of Saint Peter, declaring him a heretic by apostolic authority. Indeed, many years earlier, a venerable cardinal and legate of the Roman Church named Cono, formerly a regular canon of the church of Saint Nicholas of Arras, had likewise burned his *Theology* while holding a council at Soissons, accusing Peter himself in his presence and condemning him, once convicted, for heretical depravity.

Therefore, if it please your desire, satisfaction will be provided through the booklet on the life of Saint Bernard and through Bernard’s letters sent to the curia. Yet I found at Clairvaux a booklet by a certain abbot of Black Monks, in which the errors of that same Peter are noted; I remember that I too saw it long ago. But, as the keepers of the books state, the first quire—carefully sought for many years—could not be found.

For this reason, it is our intention to send into France to the monastery whose abbot was the author of that book. If I can recover it, I shall have the entire codex copied and sent to you. For I believe that it should suffice for your inquiry to know what was condemned, in what manner, and why.

[Col. 0595]

## Treatise of the Same Geoffrey against the Propositions of Gilbert, Bishop of Poitiers

[Note: From a manuscript codex of Longpont.]

[Col. 0595C] 1. Reader, you will find in these sheets four propositions which were recently proclaimed and rejected in the great Church, as plainly opposed to the truth—not merely to any truth, but to that truth whose injury could not be passed over, because it especially upholds the foundation of the Catholic faith.

These are the hidden loaves which that celebrated master, Gilbert by name, Porreta by surname, had for no short time been peddling to his disciples. He had intoxicated not a few of them with stolen waters, especially youthful minds delighted by novelty: they rushed into the divine pages without the key which is Christ, and searched even the deep things of God without the Spirit, who alone knows them. Among such persons new doctrines lay concealed, but at last they came to light.

[Col. 0595D] 2. Catholic ears shuddered at the profane novelty, and zeal broke out so strongly that the aforesaid Gilbert, then already bishop of Poitiers, was arraigned concerning these matters in the presence of the Supreme Pontiff Eugenius III. He chose to deny everything, even what he had plainly been accused of confessing at Poitiers in his synod.

Yet while denying it, he employed, as was his custom, certain winding verbal quibbles, so that the apostolic man easily perceived that something of the accursed thing of Jericho was entirely hidden within him.

3. Therefore, in the same year, being about to go down into Gaul, he postponed the case; and at Paris a second examination concerning the same matter was held. Some argued for him, others for the truth of the faith, especially the most reverend Abbot of Clairvaux; but perhaps it will appear more prudent, being content with a simple account, to pass over in silence what concerns persons. There also he denied the charges and produced as his witnesses his former disciples, then fellow bishops, that he had never taught anything of the kind. Yet he had written a book upon Boethius’s treatise *On the Trinity*, with an elaborately fabricated commentary, in which he had widely disseminated the aforesaid errors—though in many places covering his serpent’s head with certain winding coils of argument. When asked for this book, he denied having it at hand; nor was it easy, especially for purposes of examination, to obtain it from his disciples. [Col. 0596D] Some excerpts, however, were produced; but he distorted even manifest propositions as far as he could, employing no slight advocacy in this matter. At last he was ordered to send the Supreme Pontiff the whole body of the book intact.

4. And a third inquiry was held in the city of Rheims, where the aforesaid pope celebrated a great council in the same year, with bishops of four kingdoms assembled—France, Germany, England, and Spain. There the possibility of dissimulation no longer remained, since he was more clearly convicted from his own writings. But he too, having prepared defenders for himself, seems to have become bolder, so that he now disdained any longer to deny what he had taught for so long a time. Thus, with shameless audacity, he professed what he had denied once and twice before so great a judge and in the presence of such witnesses; yet he cautiously added that he was ready to submit his own view to the judgment of the Church, and that he did not wish stubbornly to persist in what he had said.

5. The matter was debated for several days. There too, although very few stood for that doctrine, very many stood for the man, laboring to excuse and diminish even what they did not approve. Hence the zeal of the Church on this side of the Alps was compelled, following the sound doctrine of the aforesaid Abbot of Clairvaux, to issue a confession of its faith against these same propositions, opposing as explicitly as possible what was being said by him. At last, after all his positions had been condemned by the Supreme Pontiff, he, fearful and trembling, in a public hearing, with his own mouth renounced what he had professed; rejecting every individual point, he promised that thereafter he would neither write, say, nor even believe anything of the kind. 1326 Moreover, by apostolic authority the Supreme Pontiff forbade, under penalty of excommunication, that the volume in which manifest iniquity had been found should thereafter be read or copied—unless perhaps the Roman Church should publish it purged and corrected. We have neither heard that this was done nor hope that it ever will be done. Yet because the hearts of many scholars still seem to retain the scent with which they were once imbued, and because they have not ceased, all the more perniciously for themselves because more secretly, to read the forbidden pages, perhaps it will not be [Col. 0597C] useless, both for the correction of the present and the caution of the future, to refute likewise the propositions of the error themselves, as their author was caught setting them down in his own little book and professing them with his own mouth, and to bring forward the testimonies of the holy Fathers by which they have been, or appear capable of being, refuted.

## ON THE FIRST PROPOSITION

6. This was the beginning of the evils. A form was posited in God, by which God would be, and which would not itself be God—just as humanity is the form of a human being, not that which a human being is, but that by which he is human. This divine form or nature, which, as we have said, he denied to be God, he said was called by various names: divinity, greatness, [Col. 0597D] goodness, truth, wisdom, omnipotence. By this one form, he said, God was not only God but also great, true, good, wise, and all such things. For he contended that the Creator differs from creatures in this: creatures subsist through many forms, whereas he through one. Consequently, he dared to declare, as impiously as freely, that propositions such as “Divinity is God,” “Wisdom, truth, greatness, goodness, or omnipotence of God is God himself,” if spoken of that most simple and most excellent nature, are altogether false. But their inversions—“God is truth,” “God is wisdom,” and the rest of this kind—he held to be emphatic, as though one said of a human being: “You, utterly and entirely, are wisdom”; thereby assigning a more fitting mode of expression to God, because in a human being, who has many properties, there may be an abundance of one form, for example wisdom, whereas in God the very singularity makes such a proposition true. He held that God’s being lay in subsisting by this form; but that the form’s own being lay rather in this: that it was not this [God] by anything, but was something by this [form]—that is, God. Concerning this proposition, in his work upon Boethius’s treatise—or rather against it, for he was not expounding Boethius but opposing him—he wrote as follows:

> “Just as there is nothing by which God is except sole and simple essence, that is, *ousia* (οὐσία, ‘being/essence’); so there is nothing from which *ousia* itself is except that it is simple and that God alone is it. Hence ordinary language also has it that of God one says not only ‘God is,’ but also ‘God is essence itself.’ Quite rightly indeed. For if someone is not only wise, but also colored, great, and many things of this kind, because of an abundance of wisdom above the rest he is called, ‘You, utterly and entirely, are wisdom,’ as though nothing other than wisdom alone conferred being upon him. Much more properly is God, to whom diverse things do not confer being, called essence itself and by other names.”

The same:

> “God is his own divinity, his own wisdom.”

7.

> “Divinity is said to be in the Father, just as essence is in him who truly is.”

8.

> “Some who are childish in understanding, when they hear that God is simple, understand him and whatever is said of him under diverse names—such as God, one, eternal, person, principle, author, Father, Son, connection, and other things of the same nature and same [Col. 0598C] account—in such a way that the essence called God is also the unity by which he is one, the eternity by which he is eternal, and likewise the rest; and conversely, 1327 that the Father himself is paternity, the one is unity, the eternal is eternity, and conversely.”

9.

> “I ask whether Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated substantially of divinity—that is, of those who, because by divinity alone they are what they are, are called not only God but also divinity.”

10.

> “The Father is truth, that is, true; likewise the Son is truth, that is, true; the Holy Spirit is truth, that is, true; and taken together, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three truths but are one truth, singularly and simply—that is, one true being.”

11.

> “Whoever is a human being, such as Plato, Cicero, or Trypho; or whoever is God, such as Father, Son, or Holy Spirit: the statement that any one of the former is human and any one of the latter is God refers to the substance, not which he is, but by which he is.”

12.

> “When one says, ‘God, God, God’—the first concerning the Father, the second concerning the Son, the third concerning the Holy Spirit—there has been a numbering of those who are God, but a repetition of that by which they are God.”

13. [Now that we have heard the expositor, lest perhaps he be unfaithful, let us consult the author himself.] He does indeed call it a form, but states more plainly what he means:

> “Divine substance is form without matter, and therefore it is one; and it is that which it is, whereas other things are not that which they are. For everything has its own being from the things of which it consists, that is, from its parts; and it is this and that, that is, its parts joined together, but not this or that singly. Thus, since an earthly human being consists of soul and body, he is body and soul, not either body or soul alone. Therefore, in a part he is not that which he is. But what is not this and that, but only this, truly is that which it is; and it is most beautiful and most strong, because it relies on nothing. Accordingly, this is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing in it other than [Col. 0599B] that which it is. Nor can it become a subject. For it is form, and forms cannot be subjects. For other forms are subjects of accidents, as humanity receives accidents not because it itself does so, but because matter is subject to it. For when matter subject to humanity receives any accident, humanity itself appears to receive it. But form that is without matter cannot be a subject, nor can it truly inhere in matter.”

14.

> “Therefore this one thing, which alone is that which it is—this most beautiful and most strong thing, which relies on nothing; in which there is nothing other than that which it is; which cannot become a subject, since it is form—what sound-minded person would deny to be God? [Col. 0599C] Otherwise, if diverse things do not confer being upon God, but divinity relies on nothing, not even on one thing, let each person choose what he judges preferable.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0599D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book V, chap. 10.]

If perhaps he hesitates in judgment, let him consult Augustine. For he says:

> “God is not great by a greatness which is not what he himself is, as though God, when great, participated in it. Otherwise that greatness would be greater than God.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0599D] Boethius, *On the Trinity*, chap. 2.]

But why do we wander from the path? Let us return to Boethius:

> “But Catholics, who establish no difference, and who posit the form itself as being what it is, judging that it is nothing other than that which it itself is, rightly consider the repetition of the same thing, rather than the enumeration of different things, to occur when one says: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. Certainly you see that one is not Catholic who thinks that in God the form by which he is is one thing and that which he is another. For it has been shown above concerning form that he is form and truly one, with no plurality.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0599D] Boethius, *On the Trinity*, chap. 3.]

15.

> “I beg you, see how you may prove holy and inviolably what we have said: that the supreme God is most full of the highest good. In what way, I ask? Do not suppose that this Father of all things either received from without that highest good with which he is said to be full, or possesses it so naturally that [Col. 0600A] you imagine the substance of the God who possesses and the blessedness possessed to be different. For if you think it received from without, you may judge that which gave it to be superior to that which received it. Yet we most worthily confess him to be pre-eminent over all things. But if they are the same by nature and different only in conception, when we speak of God, the ruler of things, let whoever can imagine who joined these different things together. The highest goods cannot in any way be different from one another. Yet we have concluded that both blessedness and God are the highest good; therefore that highest blessedness must itself be the highest divinity.”

16.

> “Therefore take care henceforth to distinguish between the highest blessedness, which is the highest divinity; and, if you please, explain to us how the highest good can belong to two things, [Col. 0600B] since highest goods cannot be different from each other. For it seems harsh to assert that the highest goodness, by which all things—including God himself—are good, is something not good; but I think it must not readily be admitted either that this goodness should be counted among intermediate or lowest goods.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0600D] The same, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book III.]

But let that unique hammer of all heretics also be consulted, to see whether he appears to leave even this blasphemy untouched. At the same time observe that this is not new but, long ago worn down and debated—indeed shattered and scattered abroad—has sprouted again.

17.

> “Now hold,” he says, “with unshaken faith, that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the Trinity, and yet one God; not because there is some common, as it were fourth, divinity belonging to them, but because the ineffable and inseparable Trinity itself is so. The divinity of the Trinity, which is thought to be other than the Trinity itself, and on account of which they are said to be not three gods but one because it is one in the three, either is substance or is not substance.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0600D] Augustine, Letter 222, to Consentius.]

It is Augustine who speaks and explains your novelty to us so carefully. Answer what you think: is this divinity of yours, by whose unity alone you maintain that the three persons are called one God, substance or not? Why are you silent? He pursues both alternatives, and pursues the fugitive from either side.

18.

> “If,” he says, “it is substance, and other than the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself taken together, then without doubt it is another substance. But truth rejects and repudiates this. Likewise, if this divinity is not substance, and the Trinity is one God according to it because it is one in the three, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit ought not to have been called of one substance, but of one divinity, which is not substance. But in the Catholic faith you recognize that this is true and established: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although they are Trinity, are one God because they are inseparably of one and the same substance, or, if it is better said, essence. For some of our writers, especially the Greeks, have said that the Trinity, which is God, is one essence rather than one substance, thinking or understanding there to be some distinction between these two names; but there is no need to dispute that now. But if we call this divinity, which is judged to be other than the Trinity itself, not substance but essence, the same falsehood follows. For if it is other than the Trinity itself, there will be a second essence—which God forbid any Catholic should think. It remains, therefore, that we believe the Trinity to be of one substance, so that the essence itself is nothing other than the Trinity itself.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0601D] The same, ibid., Letter 120.]

19. What could have been said more clearly? Yet let us hear the same Augustine further:

> “Every substance which is not God is a creature; and whatever is not a creature is God. What then shall we make of that by which God is, rather than that which God is?”  
> [Note: [Col. 0601D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, chap. 6.]

The same:

> “For in the form of God, just as the Son is not one thing and his life another, but the Son himself is life; so the Son is not one thing and his teaching another, but his teaching itself is the Son. Other things called essences or substances admit accidents, through which great or however extensive a change may occur in them. But nothing better can be conceived than God; and therefore that substance or essence alone which is God is immutable, and to it, assuredly, being itself—from which the name essence is derived—belongs most fully and truly.”

These are Augustine’s words. But you, whoever you are who still hunger for the leeks and onions of Egypt, I should like you to confess which is more properly called essence: that which God is, or that by which he is God. For both are immutable; and perhaps the name “essence” belongs more fittingly to that by which whatever is, is.

20. The same Augustine:

> “The very nature or essence—or whatever other name may be used—is that which God is, whatever it may be; it cannot be seen bodily.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0601D] Ibid., book II, chaps. 2, 18.]

Likewise:

> “Just as it is absurd to say that what is white is not whiteness, so it is absurd to say that what is wise is not wisdom; and just as whiteness is called white in relation to itself, 1329 so wisdom is called wise in relation to itself. But bodily whiteness is not essence, because the body itself is essence and whiteness is its quality; hence the body is called white from it, though for the body to be is not the same thing as for it to be white. [Col. 0601D] For there form is one thing and color another, and neither exists in itself but in some mass; this mass is neither form nor color, but is formed and colored. Wisdom, however, is both wise and wise through itself.”

Likewise:

> “Mutable things are not properly called simple substances. But if God subsists, so that he can properly be called substance, something is in him as in a subject, and he is not simple—the one for whom being is the same as whatever else is said of him in relation to him, such as great, good, and whatever else is not incongruously said of God. But it is impious to say that God subsists and is subject to his goodness, and that this goodness is not his substance—or rather, essence—and that God himself is not his goodness but that goodness is in him as in a subject.”

21.

> “We say three persons of the same essence, or three persons [are] one essence; but we do not say three persons from the same essence, as though there were one thing there that is essence and another that is person.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0601D] Ibid., book VII, chaps. 1, 5, 6.]

Likewise:

> “There is, then, an unmade nature which made all great and small natures, unquestionably superior to those which it made; and thereby it is superior also to the rational and intellectual nature of which we speak, namely the human mind. But that nature superior to all other natures is God.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0601D] Ibid., book XIV, chap. 12.]

Perhaps he ought to have said, “God is by that which is superior to all other things.” Yet what great matter is it that this should be that by which God is whatever he is? Likewise:

> “Through truth, which is beheld when understood; through the highest good, from which every good comes; and through justice, by reason of which a just mind is loved even by a mind not yet just—I have urged that the incorporeal and even immutable nature, which is God, should be understood as far as possible.”

Likewise:

> “The life said to be in God is his very essence and nature. Therefore he does not live except by the life which he himself is to himself.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0602D] Ibid., book XV, chaps. 3, 5.]

What do you think? Should this man be believed—the singular teacher of the Catholic faith and conqueror of every heretical perversity—when he says, “The immutable nature, which is God, and the life which he himself is to himself”? Or rather should he be believed who says, “Not ‘that which he is,’ but ‘that by which he is’”? But again and again, let us hear what Augustine thinks.

22.

> “What happened in your heart when I said, ‘God’? A certain great and highest substance was conceived, transcending every mutable creature.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0602D] The same, Tractate 1 on the Gospel of John; Wisdom 7:22.]

Likewise:

> “We have said, as we were able, that the Son does not know temporally; that the Son’s knowledge is not one thing and the Son himself another; and that the Son’s vision is not one thing and the Son himself another; rather, the Son himself is vision, and the Son himself is the Father’s knowledge or wisdom. In God, substance by which he is is not one thing and power by which he can act another; whatever belongs to him is consubstantial with him, and whatever belongs to him is God.”

[Col. 0602D] Likewise:

> “It is indeed read, ‘And the spirit of wisdom is manifold,’ but it is also rightly called simple. It is manifold because the things it has are many; but simple because it is not other than what it has. Thus the Son is said to have life in himself (John 5:26), and that very life is himself. What else did Scripture intend to teach you except that, when you read of God and of what is in God, you should understand the nature not to be composite, but incomposite despite its composite expressions?”

Likewise:

> “Now let us come to those things which God is said to have—things which cannot fail to be possessed. For, as the Apostle says, ‘No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit who is in him’ (1 Cor. 2:11). Let us therefore ask together what things are in God. Are they not wisdom, power, light, providence, life, splendor, image, immortality, of which it is written: ‘Who alone has immortality?’ (1 Tim. 6:16). For he has all the things we have named, and all these are the Son. But that which is substantially good cannot be capable of an alien goodness, since it bestows goodness itself upon others.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0602D] Gennadius, *Definitions of a Rule*.]

Likewise:

> “The Holy Spirit, not receiving wisdom from elsewhere, is called the Spirit of wisdom. For the very thing which subsists is the Spirit of wisdom, and his nature is nothing other than the Spirit of truth. For the one truth of the one God—indeed, the one truth, one God—does not permit the service and worship of the true God to be joined with that of a creature. God alone, because he is eternal—that is, because he has no beginning—truly bears the name of essence.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0603D] Fulgentius, *To Donatus*.]

The same:

> “God has essence; he has wisdom; but what he has, that he is, and all things are one.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0603D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IV, chap. 4.]

23.

> “God is what he has. For he has eternity, and he himself is eternity. This also must be known: every substance which is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0603D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XVI.]

Likewise:

> “There wisdom is the same as essence, power the same as essence, life the same as essence; and all these are one, and one God.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0603D] Alcuin, *On the Trinity*, book II, chaps. 9 and 14.]

[Col. 0603C] 24.

> “Only a passible and created substance can suffer. Since it was called from nothing into existence by the highest essence, which is God, it stands between that from which it was made and him by whom it was made. Thus it can be affected by higher things so as to advance, just as by lower things so as to decline.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0604D] Claudianus Mamertus, *To Sidonius, On the State of the Soul*.]

25.

> “Moreover, this is a third error: when Father and Son are called of one substance, he thinks that a substance prior to them is signified, which the two equals possess between themselves, as though the expression indicated three things—one substance, and two co-heirs, as it were, of one substance.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0604D] Hilary, *On the Synods*.]

The same:

> “Through Moses, Seth is the likeness of the soul; through John, the Son is equal to the Father; and we seek some third thing, I know not what, between Father and Son, which nature does not admit.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0604D] Ibid.]

[Col. 0603D] The same:

> “God, the living power of immeasurable might, who is nowhere absent and lacking nowhere, teaches his whole self through what is his; and he signifies that what is his is nothing other than himself, so that where his things are present, he himself is understood to be present—not bodily, as though, when he is somewhere, he were thought not also to be everywhere; for through what is his he does not cease to be in all things. But what is his is nothing other than what he himself is.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0604D] Book VIII, *On the Trinity*.]

For the present, these remarks on the first proposition seem sufficient.

## ON THE SECOND PROPOSITION

[Col. 0604A]

26. The second resembles the first. Proceeding manifestly from the spring of Arius, it asserts that there is not only one substance which is God. For it teaches that two things are designated by the name “substance”: namely, *what is* and *that by which it is*—a being and essence—just as “white” and “whiteness” are sometimes said to signify a white thing and whiteness. It agrees that that by which something is is one in the Trinity: namely, that form and divine nature, the mother, so to speak, of the Trinity. But it contends that what is by this essence is not one in the Trinity, but three singular entities, three countable things with three unities: the first Father, the second Son, the third Holy Spirit. It teaches that this miracle must be believed concerning that blessed Trinity, and places the whole merit of faith in confessing that a form numerically one exists in several things. The unity of that form alone, indeed, is the reason why those whose divinity is one and common are not called several gods. Thus, if it could in any way happen that one humanity or the same whiteness—one and the same numerically—were found in three human beings, they would no longer be called three white persons or three human beings, but one. Is this the whole of that ineffable mystery, the whole account of Trinity and unity? You see the monstrous image of the Trinity painted for us; you see that what is devised is not a miracle at all but absurdity. Three branches are brought forth from one root; three bodies are attached, as it were, to one head. [Col. 0604C] “There is one essence,” he says, “but that by which they are, not that which they are.” And he who said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), ought to have said, “We are by one thing.” For there is not one thing which is both Father and Son and Holy Spirit. “Otherwise,” he says, “the Son would be Father, the Father Son, and the Spirit both of them.” Thus indeed he falls who rushes in; thus he strikes who does not see. Why should the searcher of majesty not be overwhelmed by glory? Hence came those questions, no less ridiculous than sacrilegious. For when someone made such statements as “God is Father,” “God is Son,” “God is Holy Spirit,” conceding none of them simply, he asked concerning what each was said. An exceedingly diligent investigator:

> “If you say concerning the Father, ‘God is Father,’ and this means ‘Father is Father,’ you say what is true; otherwise it cannot be true. So concerning the Son, and so concerning the Holy Spirit. For there is no thing, no substance, no one thing of which it can truly be said: ‘God is Father,’ ‘God is Son,’ ‘God is Holy Spirit.’”

Therefore he denied the combined proposition, “One God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit,” lest he should be Sabellian—or rather, lest he should cease to be Arian. He inverted propositions whenever he could, so that by reversing the words he might overturn the meaning itself:

> “Father and Son and Holy Spirit are one, or one God, or one substance. I have never denied any of these. But why? Because they are by one thing, one essence, one divinity. But if anyone pronounces it thus: ‘God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit,’ predicating the persons—this,” he says, “I plainly deny.”

27. Thus at Poitiers, in the see of the great Hilary, he who presided over the synod dogmatized when the Church was assembled. Thus in the hearing of the Roman Church and of the multitude of bishops whom apostolic authority had summoned to the council of Rheims—alas!—he did not lack supporters while making this profession among Catholics, although it was established that, when examined similarly at Viterbo and Paris, he had not answered plainly. Thus the unhappy pages from which we draw these things contain them to this day.

[Col. 0605B] 28.

> “When Sabellians hear that there are three persons of one substance, and read that analogies have been introduced in order to show the diversity arising from their properties, or their equality, cooperation, co-eternity, or procession—namely, the mind, knowledge, and love of one soul; or the memory, understanding, and will of one mind; or the brightness and warmth of one ray, and other such analogies—they suppose that, just as there is only one ray of which brightness and warmth are said, or only one mind of which memory, understanding, and will are said, so there is only one subsisting being who, while God by nature, is himself Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by personal properties. This error plainly shows them to be ignorant of the multiple use of the term ‘substance’: namely, that both what is and that by which it is are designated by this name. Lest any Sabellian, following comparisons drawn from a multivocal term—such as *ensis*, *mucro*, *gladius* (‘sword,’ ‘blade,’ ‘sword’)—or from a univocal expression—such as ‘sun, sun, sun’—in which both what is and that by which it is, that is, both the subsisting entity and subsistence, are repeated by reiterated signification, in what is predicated of the Father, Son, and their Spirit.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0605D] Gilbert’s Commentary on Boethius.]

These things have been taken from the commentary. Henceforth let Boethius himself speak, so that he may especially dissolve the fabricated devices of this impious deception.

29.

> “Relation will not make an otherness of the things of which it is spoken, but, if it may be said, of the persons.”  
> [Col. 0605D]

Blessed Augustine had taught this in almost the same words:

> “Let the Arians confess with us that in the one nature of divinity there is a plurality of persons rather than of things.”

Likewise Boethius:

> “For the Father is not the same as the Son, nor are both the same as the Holy Spirit. Yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same God: the same just, the same good, the same great, the same all things that can be predicated according to themselves. It must indeed be known that a relative predication is not always such that it is always predicated in relation to something different—as a slave is relative to a master, for they differ. For everything equal is equal to an equal; everything similar is similar to a similar; and the same is the same as what is the same. Such is the relation in the Trinity of Father to Son and of both to Holy Spirit: the relation of what is the same to what is the same. If this cannot be found in all other things, it is because an otherness akin to perishable things brings this about.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0605D] Boethius, *On the Trinity*, chaps. 5–6.]

30. The same:

> “I ask whether Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated substantially of divinity, or in some other way whatever.”

And shortly afterward:

> “From these things, therefore, we understand that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not said substantially of divinity itself, but in some other manner.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0605D] Boethius, *To John the Deacon*.]

31. Augustine:

> “We believe that the one God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0606D] Gennadius, *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.]

Perhaps the caviller is now preparing to invert the statement; but let him hear what follows:

> “The Father, because he has the Son; the Son, because he has the Father; the Holy Spirit, because he is from the Father and the Son.”

This addition, indeed, if anyone attends prudently, wholly forbids inversion and allows the statement to concern none but the one God.

32. Augustine:

> “Accordingly, it is understood that the Apostle Paul did not say only of the Father, ‘Who alone has immortality,’ but of the one and only God, which is the Trinity itself.”

Likewise:

> “The blessed and only powerful One, King of kings and Lord 1332 of lords (1 Tim. 6:15–16), who is the one, only, and true God, is the Trinity itself. Therefore God the Trinity is rightly understood to be blessed and only powerful.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0606D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, chap. 6.]

[Col. 0606C] The same:

> “For the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some way say what we cannot utter in any way, the Greeks said ‘one essence, three substances’; the Latins, however, ‘one essence’ or ‘substance, three persons,’ because in Latin essence is not usually understood otherwise than substance.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0606D] The same, book VII, chap. 4.]

The same:

> “In the seventh book, the question which had been deferred is explained: namely, that God who begot the Son is not only Father of his own power and wisdom, but is also himself power and wisdom. So too the Holy Spirit. Yet they are not at the same time three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom, just as one God and one essence. Then the question is raised how three persons are said to be one essence, or, as by certain Greeks, three substances one essence; and it is found that this is said out of linguistic necessity, so that some one name might be used in reply when it is asked what the three are whom we confess to be three—namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

33. The same:

> “Reason reaches the point that the Son is wisdom from wisdom, just as light from light, God from God; nor could we find the Spirit to be anything other than wisdom too, and all together one wisdom, just as one God and one essence. How then do we understand this Wisdom, which is God, to be Trinity? I did not say, ‘How do we believe it?’ For among believers this ought not [Col. 0607A] to be a question.”

Likewise:

> “I have already argued above in this book that the Trinity which is God must not be understood from those three things which we have shown in the trinity of our mind, as though the Father were the memory of all, the Son the understanding of all, and the Holy Spirit the charity of all three; as though the Father did not understand or love for himself, but the Son understood for him and the Holy Spirit loved for him, while he himself remembered only for himself and for them; as though the Son neither remembered nor loved for himself, but the Father remembered for him and the Holy Spirit loved for him, while he himself understood only for himself and for them; and as though the Holy Spirit neither remembered nor understood for himself, but the Father remembered for him and the Son understood for him, while he himself loved only for himself and for them. Rather, it must be understood thus: all three, collectively and individually, possess all these things each in his own nature; nor are these things distinct in them, as in us memory is one thing, understanding another, and love or charity another; but there is one thing which can do all things, namely wisdom itself. Thus it is possessed in the nature of each one, so that whoever possesses it is what he possesses, as in an immutable and simple substance.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0607D] The same, book XV, chaps. 3, 6, 7.]

34. The same:

> “The things to be enjoyed are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and the same Trinity is one supreme thing, shared by all who enjoy it—if indeed it is a thing and not the cause of all things; if indeed it is a cause. For no name suitable to such excellence can easily be found.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0607D] *On Christian Doctrine*.]

The same:

> “We have said that this one true God, who alone is naturally God, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.”

The same:

> “If the one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person, it would not be said, ‘In our image,’ but ‘In my image’; nor would he have said, ‘Let us make,’ but ‘Let me make.’ What then? We are now taught that that one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not even a single person.”

35. The same: “Because in the one true God, the Trinity, not only that He is one God, but also that He is Trinity, is naturally true: therefore the true God Himself is Trinity in persons and one in nature [Col. 0607D].” The same: “Hold principally that every nature which is not God the Trinity was created out of nothing by the Holy Trinity itself, who alone is the true and eternal God. Explain to us, if you can, what nature God the Trinity is, since the divine nature is neither God nor Trinity; or else confess that it, being not God the Trinity, was created out of nothing. For this is what the great champion of faith commends us principally to hold [Note: [Col. 0607D] *On the Rule of Faith, to Peter*].”

36. Augustine: “It is enough for a Christian to understand that the cause of created things—whether heavenly or earthly, visible or invisible [Col. 0608A]—is nothing but the goodness of the Creator, who is one and true God; and that there is no creature which is not either Himself or from Him; and that He is Trinity, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The testimonies are manifest and need no intervention by anyone [Note: [Col. 0607D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 4.].”

37. Augustine: “God is called that power ineffably great and immeasurably wise, as it is written: ‘Great is the Lord, and great is His power’ (Ps. 146:5). This power is God, and God Himself is three.” The same: “Whatever the mind knows, it loves to know. Love exists no less than between two: the lover and that which is loved. Therefore there is one love of both, and it is also a third. Yet it cannot be denied [Col. 0608B] that this whole is one soul, and that these three are one soul. For as these three are truly one soul, so this is one thing, that another, and that a third. Let this creature, then, however exalted, compare itself with its Creator, who infinitely surpasses it—except in this respect, which is far removed above it: that every goodness and every good, and all sweetness of goodness and good, belongs to the Creator from Himself [Note: [Col. 0608D] Aug., *On the Creation of Man in the Image of God*].”

38. Athanasius: “I see that I must necessarily hasten to this point: that three are one and one is three; and, if not by the reason that belongs to me as a man, at least to teach it thoroughly by authority.” The same: “The hymns of the heavenly powers show that one is three and three are one.” But our theologian here, on the contrary, shows indeed that three are one, but not that one are three [Col. 0608C], lest perhaps he follow the Sabellians. Yet let our man hear Athanasius answering his Arius: “We neither fall into Sabellius by confessing three to be one God, nor are we ensnared in the snares of your faithlessness while we frankly confess this God to be Trinity [Note: [Col. 0608D] Athanasius, *Against Arius and Sabellius*].”

39. From these statements: knowledge is God; God is Trinity. The same: “For there unity is truly Trinity, and Trinity is truly unity. Then we shall perfectly know what we now profitably believe. For we shall not deserve otherwise to perceive it unless we now confess what is true: namely, the true, coeternal, immutable Trinity, distinct in persons and inseparable, filling all things at once by its substantial power [Col. 0608D]. One simple and threefold: these three are one, and this one is three; yet not three Fathers, nor three Sons, nor three Holy Spirits. I confess three as one and one as three. These three are one God, and one God is these three.” The same: “God and Lord: true and everlasting Trinity in persons; true and everlasting unity in substance, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance. If Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, why is the Son alone said to have become incarnate? Because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another [Note: [Col. 0608D] Cassiodorus, *On the Nature of the Soul*].”

## On the Third Chapter

[Col. 0609A]

40. The third offshoot of the viperous root attributes to the three persons properties, that is, relations, which are not the persons themselves: eternal things differing numerically from one another and from the divine substance, so that there is found not a Trinity but a quaternity. For that divine substance is one thing, while each of the three properties is another thing. Indeed, it posits four eternal unities: the first belonging to that supreme nature by which God is God, and the remaining three to the three properties. Further, it says that the persons themselves are called one God by that unity, but are three by the other three unities. Here, if you attend carefully, four properties at once present themselves, since the logic of relation does not allow this inequality. For the Spirit cannot be related [Col. 0609B] to the Father and the Son without their also being related to the Spirit. Nor can they be related by the same relation as He is, lest there be one person in the Trinity without a property. As filiation differs from paternity, so production differs from procession—if one is pleased to call it by that name. Now it is necessary to assign its own unity to this also; and the number of eternal things will grow still further, if anyone carries the argument onward. For many things must necessarily spring up from this source, so that a basilisk may arise from the serpent’s root. But this controversy is above us; let it be reserved for greater minds. Perhaps, however, impiety itself may suffice for its own complete refutation, provided the reader’s diligence investigates a gloss more obscure than the text, opposed as it is to the text and laboring after convoluted veils [Col. 0609C]. If not, there is an abundance of scriptural testimonies by which every impiety, however shameless, may be overwhelmed.

41. “For the property of predication by which, of whatever one of these three is predicated, another cannot be predicated, clearly enough shows that these are different, not only from one another, but also from all those things which are commonly said of their subjects, and especially from that which is substantially predicated of one of the three under many names. This difference exists not only in number, inasmuch as this is one thing while each of those is another thing, but also in the nature of genus and in the place of definition [Note: [Col. 0609D] Gilbert’s Commentary on Boethius].”

[Col. 0609D]

42. He calls the divine substance—that, namely, not which God is, but by which He is God—one thing predicated under many names, when he says, “God is great, good, and omnipotent,” and the like. For in God wisdom, essence, truth, and omnipotence are the same; and so are whatever things we say of God in this manner. From this divine substance, therefore, he says that the personal properties—for we are certainly speaking of these—differ numerically: so that it indeed is one thing, while each of those properties is another thing. Nor does this difference suffice unless a still broader diversity of genus and definition is added. Consider, however: if here we rightly answer in Boethius’s words, since we are speaking of God, the prince of things, let whoever can imagine who joined together things so diverse. For Boethius himself plainly refutes the assertion that it belongs to the property of predication that, of whatever one of those three is predicated, another cannot be predicated. Elsewhere also he called them opposed things and denied that the one God was three persons [Col. 0610A].

43. “I ask whether Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated substantially of divinity, or in some other way.” Again: “From these things we understand that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not said substantially of divinity itself, but in some other way. For I say: if they are predicated of divinity, they are also predicated of the one, since there is only one divinity [Note: [Col. 0609D] Boethius, *To John the Deacon*].” Then the Catholic ear recoils when he says that the persons themselves are subjects of relations [Col. 0610B]. Hence Boethius himself, certainly speaking of God—for he would not so elegantly assert anything else to be preferred above all other things, as we have recalled above—says: “This is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing other in it besides that which it is. For it cannot become a subject, since it is form; and forms cannot be subjects [Note: [Col. 0610D] Id., *On the Trinity*, bk. II, ch. 2.].” Nor does Boethius differ from blessed Augustine even in this, since Augustine too teaches that in God’s substance there is not one thing that is substance and another that happens to the substance; rather, whatever can be understood in it is substance.

44. Or perhaps he may seem not to place those properties in God, but to attach them from without. For in one place he says [Col. 0610C]: “The theological persons, because, by the simplicity of that by which they are, they cannot be different from one another by an opposition of essences, are proved to be, and are, different from one another by the opposition of the aforementioned things attached from without [Note: [Col. 0610D] Gilbert, Commentary on Boethius].” Where, I ask? Outside God? Yet all things are from Him, through Him, and in Him. Finally, if anything were attached to Him from without, it would be proved to be outside truth and outside eternity. Once crucified for us, the Only-Begotten of God the Father will surely henceforth suffer nothing to be attached to Himself, to the Father, or to His own Spirit by us. Lastly, if he truly attaches those three things from without, where will be what he produced as most favorable to himself [Col. 0610D]: “In substance unity, in persons property, and in majesty equality is to be adored”? You hear, he says, “in persons, property,” and do you hesitate to believe that personal properties are eternal things which are not the persons themselves, but are in them? A moment ago they were attached from without; but Catholic faith receives neither attached nor implanted things. Surely, just as it adores property in the persons, unity in the substance, and equality in majesty, so anyone who is not foolish understands all these expressions as spoken without distinction. For there is nothing in God except what He is. Nor does that text say “properties,” though even this could indeed be understood; rather, “property in the persons,” that is, distinction. Therefore unity is adored in the substance, property in the persons, equality in majesty: that is, the substance is one, the persons distinct, the majesty equal [Col. 0611A]. Otherwise, if one delights in insisting on the words, let him adore in the persons relations—eternal things which are not God. But by us there is faithfully adored only that most simple substance and nature which is God the Trinity. Yet let us hear further how he discusses these properties.

45. “Because paternity, filiation, and connection are different, the unities also which belong to them must be different from one another; and because, although one substance may belong to another substance or to an accident, yet a substance cannot belong to an accident, the unities which belong to paternity, filiation, and connection cannot possibly be substances [Note: [Col. 0611D] Gilbert’s Commentary on Boethius].”

46. Here, if the careful reader attends, he will find no consequence in what follows: “Therefore the unities belonging to the properties cannot be substances, because a substance cannot belong to an accident.” Unless he means the properties themselves to be accidents. Otherwise, if they are not accidents, what logical force can there be in saying that, because a substance cannot belong to an accident, the things belonging to them cannot be substances? Yet not even the Master of the Properties himself wished to profess that they are accidents, setting them up as certain intermediate things between substances and accidents. Further, by what reasoning he can deny that his triad—or rather quaternity, for he discovers four, or perhaps even more, eternal unities—is a quaternity, I do not see [Col. 0611C]. It is plainly a number by which we count, a number of things different from one another. But if these things stand thus, the whole discussion of Boethius concerning numerical difference must be erased: he removes from that ineffable Trinity not only difference of number, but even the very number by which we count, wherever repetition of unities produces plurality. For, proposing a threefold difference—of genus, species, and number—he says: “Come then, let us proceed and examine each thing insofar as it can be understood and grasped.” Then, after a long discussion, he concludes:

> “Therefore in God there is no diversity, no plurality from diversity, no multitude from accidents, and consequently no number. But God differs in no respect from God, nor is He separated either by accidents or by accidental differences situated in a subject. Where there is no difference, there is absolutely no plurality; therefore neither is there number. Thus there is unity alone. For the word ‘God,’ repeated a third time when Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named, does not make three unities into a plurality of number in that which they themselves are, if we attend to things capable of being numbered and not to number itself. There the repetition of unities makes number. But in that number which consists in numberable things, repetition of unities and plurality do not make a numerical diversity of numberable things [Col. 0612A]. For number is twofold: one kind, by which we count; the other, which consists in things capable of being numbered. Thus one is the thing, unity, by which we call something one. Again, two things are in things, such as men or stones; duality is nothing but merely the duality by which two men or two stones become two; and likewise in the remaining cases. Therefore, in the number by which we count, repetition of unities produces plurality; but in the number of things, repetition of unities does not produce plurality: as if I should say of the same thing, ‘one sword, one blade, one weapon.’ For a sword may be recognized by so many terms. This repetition of unities is rather reiteration than enumeration: as if we should say, ‘weapon, blade, sword’; it is a repetition of the same thing, not a numbering of different things. Or as if I should say, ‘sun, sun, sun’: I have not made three suns, but have predicated the same thing repeatedly of one sun [Col. 0612B]. Therefore, if God is predicated of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit a third time, the threefold predication does not thereby make a number. For this threatens those, as has been said, who establish among them a distance of merits. But for Catholics, who [above, “nothing” is added] posit nothing in difference and hold that the form itself is what it is, and judge that there is nothing other than that which it itself is, it rightly appears to be a repetition concerning the same thing, rather than an enumeration of different things, when it is said: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and this Trinity one God; as weapon and blade are one sword; as sun, sun, sun are one sun [Col. 0612C].”

[Note: [Col. 0612D] Boethius, *On the Trinity*, chs. 2–3.]

47. Truly God has made foolish the wisdom of this world! For this man, so learned in letters, while reading and handling these matters, nevertheless increases numbers, multiplies unities, and divides the most simple eternity by a multiplicity of things. Finally, he establishes a Trinity in three ways: of persons, of properties, and of unities; whereas to us only a Trinity of persons is commended.

48. Augustine: “For if love is less great than wisdom, wisdom is loved less than it is. Therefore it is equal, so that wisdom is loved as greatly as it is. But Wisdom is equal to the Father, as we have said above. Therefore the Holy Spirit also is equal; and if equal, equal in all things because of the supreme simplicity which is in that substance. Therefore there are no more than three: one loving Him who is from Him, one loving Him from whom He is, and love itself. If this love is nothing, how is love itself God, if it is not?” The same: “Number, measure, and weight are God Himself. He is number without number, from whom is every number; measure without measure, from whom is every measure; weight without weight, from whom is every weight. Therefore He disposed all things in number, measure, and weight (Wisdom 11:21): as though He had said, ‘He disposed all things in Himself’” [Col. 0613A]. The same: “God is simple, immutable, and undisturbed by nature; nor is He one thing and that which He has another [Note: [Col. 0613D] *On the Trinity*, bk. VI, ch. 5.].”

49. Isidore: “God is called simple, either because what He has is not other than Himself, or because He is not one thing and that which He has another [Note: [Col. 0613D] *Etymologies*, bk. II, ch. 4.].”

50. Jerome: “God is simple and immutable by nature; nor is He one thing and that which He has another [Note: [Col. 0613D] *On the Essence of God*].” The same: “Everything which exists is either unbegotten, begotten, or made.
