But it is proper to God not to have begun.” The same: “What then do we say concerning the properties of the persons?” Let us hear him further: “For we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases*, that is, subsistences [Col. 0613B]. Thus they are one in substance, distinguished by persons and properties [Note: [Col. 0613D] *Book of Definitions, to Pope Damasus*].”

51. Gregory Nazianzen: “When I name God, be enlightened by one light and by three: by one indeed according to substance, but by three according to the properties or subsistences of each, as some think it should be said, or according to persons. For there is no difference arising from the diversity of terms when the diversity of names brings the intellect to the same meaning [Note: [Col. 0613D] *Book III on the Second Epistle to the Ephesians*].”

52. Alcuin: “Unbegotten, Begotten, and Proceeding are one nature, three properties, one God. Everything which exists either always existed and did not begin to be, or did not always exist and began to be. Therefore that which did not begin to be, but always was, is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but that which began to be is every creature [Note: [Col. 0613D] *On the Trinity*, bk. II, ch. 4.].”

53. Isidore: “It is called Trinity because a whole is made one from certain three things, as it were a ‘three-unity’; for example, memory, understanding, and will, in which the mind possesses within itself a certain image of the divine Trinity. For though they are three, they are one, because each remains in itself and all are in all. Therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are Trinity and Unity. For what is one is also three [Note: [Col. 0613D] *Etymologies*, bk. III, ch. 4.].” The final part of this testimony plainly contradicts the second chapter of this error, as the careful reader will readily observe that many of these authorities plainly oppose either two or even three chapters; but its beginning specifically opposes the third. For Gilbert expounds Trinity as three unities, writing thus: “Hence it follows that neither Trinity—that is, three unities—is predicated substantially of God.” But Isidore more faithfully interprets Trinity as the unity of three.

## On the Fourth Chapter

54. The fourth chapter remains, a poisonous offshoot indeed of the first [Col. 0614A]. Therefore there is no need to linger over it longer, since it appears to have already been refuted in its very root. For, maintaining that the divine nature is not God, he has proceeded so far, even without being asked, as to attribute the Incarnation to the person of the Son in such a way as wholly to deny it to divinity itself. He had written, concerning the same chapter in his exposition, distorting statements rightly made according to his pleasure. These are Boethius’s words: “But perhaps human nature may appear to have been converted into deity. But how could this happen, if divinity in Christ’s generation assumed both a human soul and a body?” Again: “Since in the same person divinity, which assumed, is one thing, and humanity, which was assumed, another; for it is not nature but person [Note: [Col. 0614D] Boethius, *On Person and Nature*, ch. 6.].” Why so? Do you have this from yourself, or have others taught you? I suppose it is peculiar to the expositor, with whom neither the author himself nor any of the saints seems to agree. The prophet says in the Psalm: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 94:2). Interpret it, you: “Truth,” that is, “the true one”; and let those hear whose souls are untouched by zeal for God. Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1). Interpret it: “Wisdom,” that is, “the wise one”; but not for us.

55. Augustine: “Therefore He who, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant is both God and man [Note: [Col. 0614D] *On the Trinity*, bk. III.].” The same: “For if the divine substance, far more distant and incomparably higher in its difference, could for our sake so assume human substance that one person might result, how much more credibly do other men, His holy and faithful ones, become with the man Christ one Christ [Col. 0614C; Note: [Col. 0614D] *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, bk. II, and *On the Baptism of Infants*]?” The same: “For eternal and divine nature could by no means be temporally born from human nature unless, by assuming the truth of human nature, the ineffable divinity received in itself a true temporal conception and birth.” In the same work: “The immutable truth remains such in human and divine nature that, just as His divinity, which He has immutably from the Father, is always true, so His humanity, which supreme divinity bears united to itself, is always true and immutable [Note: [Col. 0614D] *On Faith to Peter*; this book is not Augustine’s but is attributed to Fulgentius].” The same: “Although we believe one person in Christ, we nevertheless confess two substances, that is, natures: divinity and humanity, the assuming and the assumed, the creating and the created [Col. 0614D].” The same: “Divinity, coming into the Virgin’s womb, fashioned flesh for itself from her substance; assuming it for our salvation and uniting it to itself, God was born as man.”

56. Fulgentius: “This child had a true soul just as He had true flesh, so that that true divinity might assume the entire nature of man, which needed restoration, and might restore the nature it had assumed [Note: [Col. 0614D] *On the Mystery of the Mediator*].”

[Col. 0615A]

57. Gregory: “Divinity came to us shod [Note: [Col. 0615D] *Homilies*].”

58. Alcuin: “Thus Christ is full of grace and truth: just as the fullness of humanity was assumed by divinity, so in His humanity there is the fullness of divinity.” The same: “For divinity has nowhere abandoned humanity since it was assumed into the unity of His person [Note: [Col. 0615D] *On the Trinity*, bk. IV, tract 2, and bk. Cod., tract 16.].”

59. “Certainly divinity was conceived in the conception of its flesh and born in its birth; and, by participation in human feeling, it experienced the death which it had voluntarily assumed. Yet it did not lose the power of its nature, by which it gives life to all things.” The same: “The authority for all the works performed in Christ is from divinity; nevertheless it is fitting for the flesh to say, ‘I have power to lay down my life’ (John 10:18), not for divinity. For divinity did not relinquish the soul after assuming it [Note: [Col. 0615D] *To Fridegisus*].”

60. Hilary: “Nature had not failed so as to cease to be; rather, remaining within itself, the nature of God assumed for itself the humility of earthly birth [Note: [Col. 0615D] *On the Trinity*, bk. IX.].”

61. Pope Leo: “Therefore, with the property of each nature and substance preserved and converging into one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity; and, in order to discharge the debt of our nature, inviolable nature was united to passible nature [Note: [Col. 0615D] *Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord* 1.].” The same [Note: [Col. 0616D] Id., sermon 3.]: “The creature is not assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that He is the indweller and it the dwelling-place; rather, one nature is truly united with the other nature. And although that which is assumed is one thing and that which assumes another, nevertheless the diversity of both comes together in so great a unity that the one and same Son of God calls Himself less than the Father insofar as He is true man (John 14:28), and professes Himself equal to the Father insofar as He is true God (John 10:30) [Col. 0615C].” The same: “The Word became flesh by the advancement of flesh, not by any falling away of divinity; divinity so moderated its power and goodness that, by assuming what is ours, it advanced it, and by communicating what was its own, it did not lose it [Note: [Col. 0616D] *Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord* 4.].” The same: “It was necessary to establish most certainly that the Word became flesh and that the everlasting essence of the Son of God assumed the true nature of man [Note: [Col. 0616D] *Sermon on the Epiphany* 4.].” The same: “Unless the Word became flesh, and there existed so firm a unity in both natures that even the brief time of death did not separate the assumed nature from the One assuming it, mortality could never return to eternity [Col. 0615D].” The same: “That nature assumed us into its own property, by which it bent itself to whatever measures of loving-kindness it willed, yet never underwent a change into mutability. That nature assumed us, by which neither what is ours consumed what was its own, nor what was its own consumed ours. That nature assumed us, which neither severed the image of our race from the common path nor admitted the contagion of sin passing into all men [Col. 0616A; Note: [Col. 0616D] *Sermons on the Passion* 4 and 21.].” The same: “In it, though through what is ours, the Word was not changed in any part of itself either into flesh or into soul. For the simple and immutable nature of divinity is always wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase; and it so blesses the assumed nature that, glorified, it remains in the One glorifying [Note: [Col. 0616D] *To Julian, Bishop of Coos*].”

62. Finally, we briefly warn those who study knowledge more than conscience not henceforth so readily to assent to those introducing novelties in the faith. Let them be cautious not to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers, nor be carried about by every wind of doctrine. For this alone ought to have sufficed for the complete refutation of novelty—especially in matters of faith—that it is novelty. For one who sometimes twists certain carefully selected testimonies of Scripture is an author of novelty. What presumption! As though they alone had read or understood the Scriptures. Was there no Catholic before you, brother? Had our faith perished when a third Cato fell from heaven, and did your masters not know the faith? And were you yourself in error until a few years ago, before a new gospel was revealed to you while you dreamed on Parnassus? And does the universal Church still err, apart from your few disciples? As it is most shameless to say this, so it is most proud to think it and, rightly, most foolish to believe it [Col. 0616B].

63. To return to the particular chapters before us: ought those who heard doctrines so novel not to have considered how many wise and learned men the Church, sound in opinion and doctrine, had possessed not long before, who had thought and taught the evident contrary? I mean those distinguished men of Laon, Anselm and Ralph; also Master Alberic of Rheims, afterwards Archbishop of Bourges; the most faithful expositor of the divine word, Hugh of Saint-Victor; Robert Pullen likewise, chancellor of the Apostolic See; and many others besides, whose presence still endures, or whose recent memory is held in blessing. Their common judgment is extant: whatever is in God is God. Thus Master Ralph of Laon says in a certain writing: “By the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we do not understand any properties to be posited—as was said above concerning *to pyr* (‘the fire’)—which are something other than the persons themselves.” And Master Hugh: “Because in the Trinity there is One who is from none, One who is from Him, and One who is from both, the Trinity is true and unity remains perfect, because in God there can be nothing which is not God, since all that is is one.” The same: “In the nature of divinity [Col. 0617A], where there is no multiplicity or diversity, the person and that which is in the person cannot be divided [Note: [Col. 0617B] *On the Sacraments*].”

64. First chapter: That the divine essence, substance, and nature, called the divinity, goodness, wisdom, and greatness of God, and all similar things, is not God, but the form by which God is God.

65. Second chapter: That the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are neither one God, nor one substance, nor one thing.

66. Third chapter: That the three persons are three by three unities and are distinguished by three properties, which are not what the persons themselves are, but are three eternal things differing numerically, both from one another and from the divine substance.

[Col. 0617B]

67. Fourth chapter: That the divine nature was not incarnate and did not assume human nature.

Here ends the little book against the chapters of Gilbert, Bishop of Poitiers.

1339. **Confession of Faith**, issued against the same Chapters by the Fathers of ten provinces, with many bishops and abbots, under the dictation of Bernard, most reverend Abbot of Clairvaux.

I. We believe and confess that the simple nature of divinity is God; nor can it be denied in any Catholic sense that divinity is God and God is divinity. Whenever it is said that God is wise by wisdom, great by greatness, eternal by eternity, one by unity, and God by divinity, and other such expressions, we believe that He is wise only by that wisdom which is God Himself; great only by that greatness which is God Himself; eternal only by that eternity which is God Himself; one only by that unity which is God Himself; wise, great, eternal, one, and God only by that divinity which is Himself—that is, by Himself [Col. 0618A].

II. When we speak of the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—we confess that they themselves are one God and one divine substance; and conversely, when we speak of one God and one divine substance, we profess that this one God and one divine substance is three persons [Col. 0618B].

III. We believe that God alone—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is eternal, and that there are absolutely no things, whether called relations, properties, singularities, unities, or anything else of that kind, present to God from eternity which are not God.

IV. We believe that divinity itself, whether you call it divine substance or nature, was incarnate, but in the Son.

Here ends the confession.

[Col. 0617]

## Letter of the Same Geoffrey to Josbert

Containing notes on the Lord’s Prayer (Matt. 6:9–13).

[Col. 0617C]

To his beloved brother Josbert, Geoffrey: to sing and pray at once with the spirit and with the mind.

1. My brother Josbert, you asked me for an annotation on the Lord’s Prayer, arranged according to the individual clauses of that prayer in a fourfold division, so that it might cling more firmly to memory and appear neither too slight nor too diffuse. In response to your fourfold scheme, I have taken care to give you a twofold annotation in this matter, and to give it quickly, knowing that you know that he gives twice who gives promptly. Let not its perhaps somewhat obscure brevity displease you: it will aid exercise, affording an occasion for applying wisdom. “One ought always to pray and not lose heart,” says the Lord (Luke 18:1). This, which all the faithful ought to follow at the Lord’s admonition, is known to suit our profession especially [Col. 0617D]. For it is signified both by the person and by the name of Daniel, who is read in the prophet as one to be saved together with Noah and Job (Ezek. 14:14). The man of desires is also the man of prayers. He prays well always who desires well without interruption. Blessed Daniel, against whom no charge could be found except concerning the law of God. Blessed he who preferred to incur the danger of death rather than cease from prayer (Dan. 6) [Col. 0618C]. How much more fitting is it for us always to pray and not lose heart, since death threatens us if we neglect it, while life is promised to those who pray! Yet this too must nevertheless be observed: although we may perhaps sometimes pray with different words, let us always pray in such a way that no desire, no prayer, no petition of ours departs from the fountain which the most skillful Orator dictated and the singular Advocate instituted. “Thus,” He says, “you shall pray to the Father.”

2. Our Father, who art in heaven. We are taught to direct prayer to the Father, because the Son seeks his glory, and he who does whatever the Father does likewise grants whatever the Father grants. It is said in the plural, that we may always pray for one another. For as adoption is common, so too is prayer common. His prayer alone is singular whose sonship is proper to himself, according to the saying: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John 20:17), etc. “Our Father, who art in heaven.” This brief but useful and efficacious preface touches the four fibres of the heart: the affections of joy and fear, sorrow and desire. 1340 For, when we recall that we have God as Father, we rejoice in the conception of confidence; yet fear nevertheless urges us toward reverence, lest so great a Father find us unworthy, degenerate, or ungrateful. When we say, “Who art in heaven,” unless we are senseless, sorrow bites the mind because he does not yet dwell in us; and, just as heaven is exalted above earth, so we are not merely pilgrims away from the Lord, but far-away pilgrims, until we are in heaven. Yet we rightly long to become citizens of heaven and desire to be heavenly celibates, so that it may likewise be true of us: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my words,” etc., as far as “we will make” (John 14:23). It is clear that those who make [their abode] do not yet have a dwelling-place; but we rightly long and desire that they may complete [this], dwell, and remain. The Spirit remained upon Jesus; and this was the sign received by him who heard: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes” (John 1:33).

The first petition, therefore, is: “Hallowed be thy name.” The Lord’s name is indeed holy, and his holiness perpetual and perfect. But we ought to desire and pray that it may be hallowed for us, in us, by us, and from us: through knowledge and participation in his holiness; through the devout confession of heart and mouth; and through the training of neighbours in these same three things, by examples and admonitions alike. For in some sense the Lord’s holy name comes to be so for us when it is known; and, while it remains always in its own most perfect holiness, it nevertheless advances in our sanctification all the more insofar as it is more truly made known. When its invocation sanctifies us, it is hallowed in us; and its holiness increases as it is poured out and enlarged within us. It is hallowed by us when we give glory to that name. It is hallowed from us when it is not blasphemed through us. “So let your light shine before men, that the heavenly Father may be glorified by your works” (Matt. 5:16).

“Thy kingdom come.” Let it come to us, that it may be believed, hoped for, loved, and received by us; as the King says: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34). The road of the three days of God’s kingdom, both to us and to it, is our faith, hope, and charity; but it will reach the fourth dwelling when the blessed come.

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” This looks back to what preceded: “Who art in heaven”; and it must also be joined to the two prior petitions, so that the Lord’s name may be hallowed in heaven and on earth, and likewise his kingdom may come. Let thy will be done in us, that we may will nothing except after thee, for thee, according to thee, and through thee. After thee: so that, in matters in which thy will is certain, ours too may remain with firm constancy. In matters in which thine is uncertain, ours should rightly remain suspended and ready to follow wherever it sees thy will incline. Yet what the Father willed that the Son should suffer, Judas willed, and the Jews likewise willed; and yet it profited neither him nor them. Therefore, Lord, let us will for thee, so that in all things we may have thy zeal; let us will also according to thee, so that zeal may not be without knowledge, as those who persecuted thine own thought they were rendering thee service. Finally, whatever we will, let us will through thee, so that all our will may become thine: that thou mayest work in us both willing and accomplishing according to good will.

“Give us this day our daily bread”: the bread of necessity, pain, labour, life, and understanding; for the sustenance of this life, the fruit of penitence, the exercise of righteousness, and the delight of taste. Concerning this fourth bread holy Daniel said that, being in the mourning of penitence, he did not eat desirable bread (Dan. 10:3).

“And forgive us our debts,” which we incur in four ways: by failing to render to our body its due chastisement, to our heart its guardianship, to human beings humanity, and to thee glory. “As we forgive our debtors”: those who have sinned against us by causing loss, hindering progress, inflicting injury in word or deed, or bringing upon us any bodily hurt.

“And lead us not into temptation”; but may thy truth surround us as a shield, that we may not fear the terror of night, the arrow that flies, or the business that walks abroad (Ps. 90 [91]:5–6), etc. These are the faint-hearted person’s impatience in adversity and unwise insolence in prosperity; for these belong to the night. Those belong to the day: hypocrisy, unjust pretence, and unrestrained, unbridled shamelessness in public and notorious sins. The first two pertain to the double battle-line which the world puts forth; the latter to Gog and Magog, the covered and the uncovered, of which we also read in the Prophets (Ezek. 39). “But deliver us from evil”: from the bondage of sin, temporal punishment, the sentence of condemnation at judgment, and despair of remedy in hell.

[Col. 0620D] A letter of the same Geoffrey to Albinus, bishop and legate of Albano, appears in Baronius under the year 1186. It treats a question then raised in Gaul: “whether the substance of water mixed with wine in the chalice is itself likewise changed with that wine into the blood of the Lord.” Geoffrey supports the affirmative side of this controversy.

[Col. 0619]

## THE CANONIZATION OF ST BERNARD

[Col. 0619D] 1341 Among the eulogies of Bernard, this should not be assigned the lowest place: that he deserved to be the first of the Cistercian Order enrolled by solemn rite in the catalogue of saints. The exceptional holiness of the blessed man, his immense labours undertaken for the Church, and finally the heavenly attestations of remarkable miracles, to which it would have seemed sinful to subscribe only belatedly, demanded this. Scarcely ten years had passed after his holy death when the matter first began to be discussed at the Council of Tours, held in 1163, with Alexander III seated and presiding. Yet the supreme pontiff, although otherwise most willingly disposed to agree because of his reverence for Bernard, nevertheless judged that it should be deferred for a time, for the reasons he afterwards set forth in the letters of canonization:

> “For when,” he says, “we were attending with a sufficiently favourable disposition to that matter”—namely, the canonization of Bernard—“there came upon us a multitude and throng of petitioners seeking a similar thing in different provinces. Therefore, since we saw that all could not suitably be satisfied, it was determined, in order to avoid scandal, that this too should be deferred which it was necessary for the time being to deny to the rest.”

At last Alexander himself, at the request of Gerard, abbot, and the community of Clairvaux, wishing to satisfy the pious desires of his sons, decreed that Father Bernard should be enrolled among the saints. But in what year this occurred is not expressly stated in the apostolic letters, and authors differ: Horstius and Henriquez refer it to 1164, others to 1166. Yet both opinions seem contrary to the chronology, since Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, to whom Alexander’s letters are addressed, entered upon his office only in 1172. Best of all is Ciaconius, whose knowledge of Roman antiquities and papal documents gives him more secure authority: he assigns it to 1174. He is followed by the most learned Sirmond in his Notes on Peter of Celle, and by Manrique in the Annals; Alberic in his Chronicle agrees with them. There is added testimony beyond all exception from the Chronicle of Clairvaux, published by Chifflet, S.J., written by an anonymous but contemporary author:

> “In the same year,” that is, 1174, “the dedication of the church of Clairvaux, the canonization of blessed Bernard, and his elevation took place; Lord Wicard, archbishop of Lyons, formerly abbot of Pontigny, was present. And in the following year, at the General Chapter they adopted the chant for blessed Bernard and the chant of the Trinity.”

Bernard’s sacred inauguration thus fell on 18 January 1174, twenty years, four months, and twenty-nine days after his death. As for the elevation mentioned in the cited testimony, the Book of the Tombs of Clairvaux says that it was carried out some years after the canonization by Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, and Henry, abbot of Clairvaux. But the very words make sufficiently clear that this must be understood of another, more solemn translation, since they state that the aforesaid Abbot Henry, through Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, caused “the body of St Bernard to be raised and devoutly and honourably placed, as it appears today, in a marble shrine behind the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary.” Henry’s letter on this matter, though without chronological dates, will be given below. But now let us produce the letters of Pope Alexander III, by which Bernard is shown to have been enrolled among the heavenly saints by the Church.

### I. 1342 Apostolic Letter of Pope Alexander III to the Gallican Church, Concerning Blessed Bernard’s Enrollment among the Saints and the Future Solemn Celebration of His Feast in the Church

[Col. 0622A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons, abbots and other prelates of churches established in the kingdom of France: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It happened once, when we were at Paris, that certain great and venerable men mentioned the canonization of Bernard of holy memory, formerly abbot of Clairvaux. They desired it and earnestly urged us by pious prayers that, at the council soon to be celebrated at Tours, we should give speedy effect to this worthy and praiseworthy desire. And while we were attending this business with a quite favourable disposition, a multitude and throng of petitioners arrived who sought a similar thing in various provinces. Therefore, seeing that all could not suitably be satisfied, it was decided, to avoid scandal, to defer in this case also what it was necessary at that time to deny to the others.

But recently, at the insistence and through the devotion of the brothers of Clairvaux and other eminent persons, when these same prayers were renewed before us, we recalled to mind the holy and venerable life of that blessed man: how, sustained by the prerogative of singular grace, he shone not only in himself through holiness and religious life, but also radiated throughout the whole Church of God with the light of faith and teaching. Hardly any region of holy Christendom is ignorant of the fruit he produced in the house of the Lord by word and example; for he transmitted the institutions of holy religious life even to foreign and barbarian nations, extended the founding of monasteries, and recalled an innumerable multitude of sinners walking along the broad way of secular life to the straight path of spiritual life.

In particular, he sustained the most holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authorship we preside, when it was formerly labouring under the storm of severe persecution, both by the merit of his life and by the pursuit of the wisdom divinely given to him. He should therefore rightly be held in memory by us and by all the children of that Church, and revered with perpetual devotion. In the affliction of his body, moreover, he so made the world and himself crucified to each other that we trust him also to have obtained the merits of holy martyrs, since it is certain that, by the order of confession and the austerity of his life, he endured so long a martyrdom. Having weighed all this with pious consideration and laid it before the council of our brethren, trusting in the mercy of God, whom he served perseveringly and faithfully, and presuming also upon the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of this most blessed Confessor, we have commanded by authority of the Apostolic See that he be enrolled in the catalogue of saints; and we have decreed that the feast of his commemoration shall henceforth be publicly celebrated. Therefore do you, who are accustomed both to receive the institutions of that Apostolic See and to honour God more gloriously in his saints, celebrate the memory of this Saint on earth in such a way that by his prayers and merits you may receive worthy rewards in heaven.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January], in the year 1174.

### II. 1343 Apostolic Letter of the Same Pope Alexander to the King of France

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Louis, illustrious King of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The exalted majesty of your royal magnificence knows, we believe, that whatever we recognize as pleasing and acceptable to you in the honour of God, we always promote to a useful effect with great and willing spirit. We observe this especially in those works in which both the honour of God and the glory of his saints are particularly displayed; and we know that whatever is established by apostolic authority for the adornment of the Church and the honour of the heavenly King will be most welcome to you. Therefore, since Bernard of holy memory, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, was always dear to God and was pleasing and welcome both to you and to your whole kingdom, we have decreed, to the glory of God and the exaltation of the Church and of all your kingdom, that he be canonized and honoured among the most blessed Confessors by festive celebration. We do so both trusting in the mercy of God and in the merits of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and not being ignorant of Bernard’s manner of life and holiness.

We therefore exhort the royal piety of your most Christian Serenity to embrace with arms of joyful devotion this gift of heavenly grace bestowed upon your kingdom during your reign. Devoutly show him the customary piety now that he enjoys heavenly blessedness, whom you loved for his venerable holiness while he was still set in darkness. We desire that you hold the monastery of Clairvaux, which he founded and in which his venerable body also rests, commended to you in reverence for him, so that you may ever deserve to have him as your patron.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

### III. Apostolic Letter of the Same Pope Alexander to All Abbots of the Cistercian Order

[Col. 0623D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons: the abbots of Cîteaux, La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, Morimond, and all abbots of the Cistercian Order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever a fitting opportunity is offered us to respond in some measure according to your merits to the faith and devotion which you have shown toward the Church of God in our time, we willingly embrace that opportunity. Especially in matters known to breathe a distinctive virtue, we do not delay to assist your advancement. It happened in these days that the question once proposed concerning the canonization of blessed Bernard, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, which had been deferred from the celebration of the Council of Tours because of the scandal of certain others seeking similar honours, was, by God’s will, recalled to our mind; and he who works a sign of goodness with us had reserved the completion of this work of piety for our hands.

For, diligently recalling the life and holiness of this most blessed Confessor, how he was magnificent in himself in the prerogative of religious life and sanctity, and how useful and abundantly fruitful he was to the whole Church of God, but especially to your Order, by faith and teaching, we—trusting in the mercy of God and in the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and presuming upon the merits of the same holy Confessor—after taking counsel with our brethren, have judged that he should be enrolled by the authority of the Apostolic See in the catalogue of saints, and that the day of his death should be publicly celebrated in the Church. Since this so abounds to the glory and honour of the supreme Creator that it redounds also to your edification and consolation, it is especially for you to give thanks to almighty God, who has willed in these latter times to raise up in your Order a man of perfect and praiseworthy holiness. Therefore receive this gift of generosity with special devotion, and especially honour, in his celebration, God who is wonderful in the glorification of his saints.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

### IV. Apostolic Letter of the Same Pope Alexander to the Community of Clairvaux

[Col. 0624C]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gerard, abbot, and the whole community of Clairvaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As nothing remains doubtful to us concerning the religious devotion and piety which you display toward God, so the strength of devotion and faith shown by you is always manifest with certain clarity. For you could not, nor, God being the author, will you henceforth be able to appear degenerate from the grace of holiness, since you are known to be heirs of a holy Father: in whom spiritual grace abounded for merit and effective works were not lacking as an example. You know, indeed, and recall with pious veneration how Bernard of blessed memory, first abbot and principal founder of your monastery, was acceptable to God because of the excellence of his religious life and gracious to the Church of God because of the fullness of his devotion and faith. Thus you would rightly be accounted blameworthy if you were negligent in any respect either of imitating or venerating him.

It has therefore pleased us that you have exercised concern for him as for a pious Father and sought his canonization by a praiseworthy desire. We, whose heart is always disposed, beloved son Abbot, to comply with the offices of your devotion and with the religious and pious endeavours of your whole house, to yield continually to your prayers and to favour your advancement, have mercifully granted this request, that we may demonstrate toward you our grace and goodwill. Therefore, having recalled to mind the life of this most blessed Confessor—how he shone in faith, religious life, and teaching, and with what a light of conspicuous brilliance he radiated in the Church of God—we, after taking counsel with our brethren, trusting in God’s mercy and in the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and presuming upon the merits of this Saint, have judged that he should be enrolled in the catalogue of saints, and that the day of his death should henceforth be observed as a festive and solemn day. Therefore, since it is especially yours both to imitate his life and venerate his glory, strive and labour in all things to cleave to the footsteps of this holy Father and to honour the feast of his holiness, so that you who deserved to share his manner of life may be deemed worthy to share the same blessedness.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

These great memorials commending Bernard’s memory and immense merits were not sufficient unless the supreme bishop of the Church himself should also dictate, from his own lips, an Office for him. Innocent III did this at the petition of John, formerly metropolitan of Lyons and then a monk of Clairvaux, together with Rainer, monk of Heisterbach and Innocent’s confessor, in a letter given to John in 1201, as follows:

### To John, Formerly Archbishop of Lyons

We have not wished to deny what you desired to request, since from it the fruit of eternal recompense may increase both for us and for you. Requested by the brethren, you asked that, in honour of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, whom the Apostolic See had enrolled in the catalogue of saints to be venerated, we ourselves should dictate from our own lips the Collect and the other prayers, that they might be said with greater devotion, both because of the authority of the one composing them and because of the style of their composition. And behold: as far as we were able, at the urging of our beloved son Brother Rainer, we have taken care to grant your petition.

### Collect

Bring to completion in us, we beseech thee, O Lord, the pious effect of holy religious life; and may blessed Bernard, abbot and outstanding teacher, always intercede before thee for us by his merits and prayers, that we may obtain the abundance of thy grace. Through the Lord, etc.

### Secret

1345 May this offering of the Sacrament, which we offer to thy majesty in memory of the Lord’s Passion, be pleasing to thee, O God.

### Postcommunion

May the food which we have received accomplish its effect in us, almighty God, so that the food itself, consuming those who eat it, may incorporate us into itself. Who with thee, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July].

Here you see that holy Bernard was distinguished by the title of Doctor by the supreme ruler of the Church. An old Corbie manuscript containing the Saint’s life testifies that Alexander III himself had also employed it in the Mass of canonization. After the Collects, “Be present at our supplications,” etc., from the Common; the Epistle, “Thus says the Lord: I have sent you this command,” etc.; and the Gospel concerning Doctors, “You are the salt of the earth,” it adds:

> “The above-written Mass concerning St Bernard was first celebrated by Lord Pope Alexander III.”

So much concerning these matters.

### V. Letter of Tromundus, Monk of Clairvaux, to Abbot Gerard, Concerning the Canonization of St Bernard

To the reverend father and lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, Brother Tromundus, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and an increase of most ready devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0625] “Monk” should rather be read; for this Tromundus, a monk of Clairvaux, wrote several letters in the name of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux.]

The outcome of our undertaking as well as our labour shows in many ways how great your Fatherhood’s merit is before God and its favour among men. For, supported from both directions in both matters, we felt neither danger in the labour nor any obstacle in the work to be feared. Yet from the day of our departure from our own land, there was no end of fear and distress until both the concern of the business was ended and the performance of the labour completed. But blessed in all things is God, who delivered us from all things and, after the happy execution of the undertaking, restored us safely and joyfully to our own country.

And behold, our most blessed Confessor Bernard, altogether worthy of veneration, through the demands of his own merits and your praiseworthy zeal of piety, at the urgent request of the brethren whom you sent with me for this purpose, with the assistance also of your friends—among whom you abound in resources, both inward and outward, for winning the favour of the curia—has not newly been joined to the company of God’s saints, but enrolled in it. Thus, as his lot was among the saints from his mother’s womb, so he may obtain among them the title of holiness by the favour of Mother Church. Henceforth, concerning him and for his sake, we shall share a feast with the angels; we need no longer sing mournful songs for one whom we believe to resound with solemn songs in the heavenly choirs of angels.

That we omitted to undertake a similar work concerning St Malachy was done by the counsel of the chief priest, who warned us at the very beginning of our address that plurality might produce weariness and frustrate the desired effect even in the one case. It is therefore yours gratefully to embrace what has been granted in your days in the case of one, and patiently to bear what is deferred in the other; giving thanks to him who established periods and courses for the heavenly lights, so that the rising of the morning and evening star is not the same, although in both an equal glory of brightness shines forth.

The lord abbot of Casamari, by himself, his people, indeed even his resources, stood by and assisted us from beginning to end. The lord abbot of Fossanova and the bishop of Veroli, when asked, supplied aid of favour and counsel. Brother Franco, Brother Peter, and Brother Stephen supported us and the undertaking in every way. Brother Guido, through the many labours of himself and his people and through no small expenditure by a brother, enabled us to find a way through byways, because the malice of those lying in ambush more zealously than usual occupied the straight road. Brother Rocchus laboured greatly, sustaining us and the business itself by faith and prayer.

Since the tenor of your letters had warned me to serve at your expense, I moderated Roman frugality in all respects so that I did not follow Gallic extravagances. May the Lord grant us all together that the memory of this labour and undertaking may preserve for us on earth your favour and that of the brethren of Clairvaux, and may confer God’s mercy in the heights. We advise that the Mass which the lord Pope sang on the solemnity of this Saint should not be changed. We send you the same Collects.

### VI. Letter of Henry, Abbot of Clairvaux, to Stephen, King of England, Concerning the Elevation of St Bernard’s Body and the Transmission of His Finger to the King

[Col. 0627B]

A day honourable and solemn has been celebrated among us, delightful in its new festivity and festive in its abundant joy, since the revelation of the most sacred body of blessed Bernard has made it most renowned for us and flooded it with brighter light. Oh, how we wished the presence of your Majesty to take part in those joys, surely more heavenly than earthly, so that for us the splendour of so great a feast might increase from the principal glory, and for you a more abundant outpouring of richer blessing might flow from the merits of this most illustrious Confessor.

But because the great distance of a most remote land begrudged us this, we transferred our desires to a spiritual remedy and, with God’s favour, acted so that although your presence was absent there, your remembrance was not wanting. For we solemnly impressed your name, with the emblems of your piety, upon the affections of your brethren and the hearts of your sons, as was fitting; they, receiving it with abundant devotion, might in some way offer it before the gaze of the holy Father and present it in the secret chamber of the heavenly court.

Moreover, lest the occasion of bodily absence should deprive the royal treasuries of sharing in the gift discovered, we send you an honourable portion from the treasury of his relics. We deem it altogether unworthy that the piety of so great a prince should be deprived of participation in such holiness. Receive, then, a finger of that sacred hand. Because it belonged to a righteous man, it shook off every gift of earthly gain; God therefore filled it, as was fitting, with the most abundant richness of heavenly blessing. I mean that hand whose touch healed the sick, strengthened the infirm, made men steadfast, and drove demons away. It was that hand which laid the first foundation stone of our Clairvaux, for which you arrange to provide shelter.

We took care diligently to seal what is sent in a small vessel, so that either the treasure stored there might not be exposed to injury through frequent openings, or some deception of pious fraud might creep in through an impulse toward devout theft.

[Col. 0627]

## TESTIMONIES CONCERNING ST BERNARD, ABBOT

### 1. Of Supreme Pontiffs

[Col. 0627C]

Innocent II, in a letter to St Bernard:

> “The great benefit which has accrued to the Church of God and to us makes manifest with what firm and persevering constancy the zeal of your religious devotion and discernment undertook to defend the cause of blessed Peter and of your holy mother, the Roman Church, when the schism of Peter Leonis was raging; how, setting yourself as an impregnable wall for the house of God, you laboured by frequent arguments fortified by reason to bring the friends of kings and princes, and other persons both ecclesiastical and secular, into the unity of the Catholic Church and obedience to blessed Peter and to us.”

Alexander III, in the letters of canonization to the Gallican Church:

> “Blessed Bernard, sustained by the prerogative of singular grace, shone not only in himself through holiness and religious life, but also radiated throughout the whole Church of God with the light of faith and teaching. Hardly any region of holy Christendom is ignorant of the fruit he produced in the house of the Lord by word and example, since he transmitted the institutions of holy religious life even to foreign and barbarian nations.”

Pius V, in the bull *Ex innumeris*, etc., among other measures he proposes for reforming the Cistercian Order, recommends the reading of the works of St Bernard in these words:

> “Where sacred reading cannot be held according to the decree of the Council of Trent, besides those books necessary for the use of the divine office and choir, there shall at least be kept the Bible, the Catechism for parish priests recently published, likewise the works of St Bernard, and any other books that may serve the honourable occupation of monks.”

Gregory XIV devoted a full hour to meditation every morning, says Gicarella in his Life, reading the works of mellifluous Bernard; and any concepts he drew from them in his mind he carefully noted down and wrote out elegantly.

### II. Of Cardinals and Doctors of the Church

James of Vitry, bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, writes thus in chapter 14 of his *History of the West*:

> “At the beginning of their new plantation the Lord raised up for them a skilled husbandman, a prudent and holy man, whom the Lord found according to his own heart . . . namely holy Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: the most approved pearl of religious life, the lamp of the Order, and a star shining in the firmament of the Church of God. Not from man nor through man, but by God’s inspiration alone, he received a pre-eminent understanding of the holy Scriptures; and, as though he had drunk from the very fountain of the Lord’s breast, he poured forth heavenly waters into many streets. And because he was mighty in work and word, through the example of his holy and pre-eminent way of life, the teaching of heavenly preaching, and the power of miracles and marvellous works, he became for many an order leading from life to life.”

St Bonaventure, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, bishop of Albano, and member of the Order of Friars Minor, in his *Meditations on the Life of Christ*, which he everywhere adorned with Bernard’s sayings as though with jewels, speaks thus in chapter 36:

> “You have heard the most beautiful words of Bernard, who contemplates the Most High and tastes the sweetness of prayer. Ponder them, if you wish them to have savour for you. I willingly insert his words into this little work because they are not only spiritual and penetrating to the heart, but also full of beauty and stirring toward the service of God. For he was most eloquent, filled with the spirit of wisdom, and illustrious in holiness. I desire you to imitate him and to put his admonitions and words into practice; for that reason I often set him before you.”

St Thomas Aquinas, in his Sermon on St Bernard, says:

> “His mouth was therefore a precious vessel, a golden mouth, a jewelled mouth . . . With the wine of sweetness he intoxicated the whole world . . . Bernard was gold through holiness of will; a multitude of jewels through uprightness of character and a multiplicity of virtues; a precious vessel through the purity of virginity . . . There were in him nine jewels, of which Ezekiel speaks in chapter 28. These stones signify the nine orders of angels. Bernard was endowed with them because he possessed in himself the virtues and offices of all the angelic orders, as is said in the book in which his acts are written.”

Augustine Valier, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Verona, in chapter 41 of his *Ecclesiastical Rhetoric*, says:

> “There is in the books of St Bernard a certain wondrous sweetness, so that they are always read with a holy delight of soul.”

Caesar Baronius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, calls Bernard “a heavenly trumpet” in volume 12 of the *Annals*, under the year 1130, and under 1143, “another Elijah.” Under the year 1153 he writes of him:

> “Bernard, a man truly apostolic—indeed, a true Apostle sent by God—mighty in work and word, making his apostleship manifest everywhere and in all things by the accompanying signs, so that clearly he lacked nothing possessed by the great Apostles . . . He must be called at once the ornament and support of the whole Catholic Church; and especially of the Gallican Church, its highest distinction, highest glory, and highest happiness. May his most blessed memory endure continually in the holy Church, in blessing and sanctification, for the formation and discipline of morals and for the condemnation of heretics.”

Robert Bellarmine, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, says in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, was plainly an apostolic man, illustrious no less for the glory of miracles than for the splendour of wisdom.”

Likewise, in volume 2 of the *Controversies*, book 4, chapter 14:

> “The same blessed Bernard was renowned for more miracles than any saint whose written life survives.”

### III. Of Bishops
Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and later archbishop of Tours, in Letter 24 addressed to Bernard, writes: “I count it my greatest possession and prize that you have opened to me the sanctuary of your friendship. [Col. 0630B] Received into it, amid many great dangers I have experienced how powerful is the continual prayer of a righteous man.” And shortly afterward: “I therefore possess and render thanks to your religious devotion, the bosom of which I should long ago have embraced as an accused man embraces an altar, had the Pope, when consulted, permitted me to lay aside the office of bishop. While he sent me back to labour, he begrudged me glory; may the Lord not impute it to him. Meanwhile I shall hope in the shadow of your wings, until I am brought out from the pit of misery and the mire of filth.” See also his Letter 72, which is Letter 122 among Bernard’s letters.

Otto, bishop of Freising, Book I of the *Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 34, states: “At that time in Gaul there was an abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux named Bernard, venerable in life and character, conspicuous for the orderliness of his religious life, endowed with wisdom and learning, renowned for signs [Col. 0630C] and miracles.” The princes decide that he should be summoned and consulted, as though he were a divine oracle, concerning what ought to be done in this matter—namely, the overseas expedition. And below: “He was regarded among all the peoples of Gaul and Germany as a Prophet or an Apostle.”

Peter of Celle, abbot and afterward abbot of Saint-Remigius at Rheims, finally bishop of Chartres, in Book VI, final letter, writing against a certain Nicholas the Englishman—not, however, Bernard’s secretary, as has been demonstrated in connection with Letter 284—who after the holy Doctor’s death was casting a stain upon his character because he had opposed the Conception of the Blessed Virgin, thus breaks out, in 1348, into Bernard’s praise: “What holiness, what religious devotion, what prerogative of merits belongs to [Col. 0630D] this Bernard! I am nothing when it comes to recounting his holy praises. His life, his reputation, his works, writings, miracles, faith, hope, charity, chastity, abstinence, and finally the mortification in his members; his speech, countenance, bearing, and manner—all these and things like them themselves bear witness concerning him . . . . . He was the most devoted foster-son of our Lady, to whom he dedicated not merely one basilica but the basilicas of the entire Cistercian Order, and in whose praise he composed the most polished and eloquent treatises. If, then, you can touch the apple of our Lady’s eye, write against her Bernard, to whom she herself says: ‘Whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of my eye.’”

Anselm of Havelberg, in Book II of his dialogue against the Greeks: “In our times there appeared an abbot in a place called Clairvaux, named Bernard, a most devout man, distinguished by miraculous power, famed from West to East for his holiness; Pope Eugenius the Venerable, formerly a monk of his monastery, frequently honoured him with fitting reverence in councils of many bishops.” [Col. 0631A]

William, archbishop of Tyre, Book XVI of the *Sacred War*, chapter 18: “Pope Eugenius sends devout men, mighty in deed and word, to various regions of the West . . . Among them Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of immortal memory and honourable life, of pious remembrance in the Lord and in every respect worthy to be cherished, is chosen above all for carrying out this God-pleasing task. [Col. 0631B] A diligent executor of the commission laid upon him, drawing with him as fellow-ministers in the same work men beloved by God, untiring and indefatigable, though physically frail, both because of almost continual fasts and an excessively spare diet, he traverses kingdoms and journeys through regions, everywhere preaching the kingdom of God.”

William of Paris, bishop, in a sermon on Saint Bernard, extols him thus: “He lived most excellently, taught most graciously, and shone with the clearest miracles. Not human instruction but divine inspiration made him wise in what he discerned especially in the Scriptures.” And below: “As God related his mysteries to Moses, and Moses’ face shone with the brilliance of rays so that [Col. 0631C] the children of Israel could not look upon him, so he revealed many secrets to blessed Bernard, so that, illuminated with heavenly light, Bernard greatly illuminated the Church.”

Theobald, bishop—or whoever is the author of the *Life of William, Duke of Aquitaine*, chapter 2—writes: “At that time the monastery of Clairvaux was founded, and there, by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, Bernard was ordained abbot to govern it. He shone so brightly in life, virtues, and teaching that no one in the world was his equal in intellect, character, speech, style, and virtues. This is the man who in his days uprooted heresies, confounded heretics, recalled schismatics, instructed the erring, and rebuked princes.” And shortly after: “What strength in the man; what purity of soul! Seeking neither public notice nor fearing the tyrant—William—for his salvation! [Col. 0631D] How could one who fled public notice have coveted the height of a bishop’s throne? My God, how many and how great cathedral churches, deprived of their own pastors, elected him bishop! Yet mitre and ring pleased him no more than rake and hoe.”

## IV.—Kings and Great Men

Charles V, Emperor, according to Thou’s *History*, Book XXI, throughout the whole two-year period preceding his death consoled himself in the brotherhood of the Hieronymites, under the guidance of a certain Constantine, his confessor, chiefly by reading blessed Abbot Bernard.

Louis XIII, [1349] most Christian king of France and Navarre, surnamed the Just, in a diploma granted in 1618 to the Congregation of Feuillants for the establishment of the monastery of Fontaines, calls Saint Bernard “the great and most renowned Confessor, Father and Doctor of the Church, reformer of peoples, reconciler of schisms and dissensions, patriarch of religious persons, worker of wonders, and outstanding devotee of the Virgin Mother of God.” [Col. 0632A] See in Henriquez’s *Cistercian Menologium*, under 20 August, the splendid eulogies of almost all Christian kingdoms and of diverse estates, inscribed on the foundation stones of the aforesaid monastery of Fontaines in honour of the most holy Abbot Bernard; especially that of the most serene Queen Marie de’ Medici, mother of the same most Christian king, who declares in a solemn testimony that fertility had been divinely granted to her through the merits of blessed Bernard. [Col. 0632B]

Giovanni Francesco Pico, Count of Mirandola, Book II, *On the Death of Christ*, chapter 8: “But let us also hear Bernard, most devout and learned—though the populace has deprived him of this latter title, certainly through no fault or demerit of his—for by his writings, which everywhere overflow with sound and health-giving doctrine, and by his most powerful disputations against Gilbert and Peter Abelard—by means of which they returned from the crooked path of error and falsehood to the path of truth—he vindicated for himself the name of Doctor.”

## V.—Abbots and Generals

Peter Maurice, surnamed the Venerable, Letter 29, Book VI—Letter 264 among Bernard’s letters—writes: “To Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the strong and splendid pillar of the monastic Order—indeed, of the whole Church of God—Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, etc. [Col. 0632C] If it were allowed, if God’s ordinance did not stand in the way, if his life were in a man’s power, I would rather, dearest one, cling to your Blessedness in an indissoluble bond than either rule anywhere among mortals or reign. For what? Should not your welcome companionship, pleasing not only to men but to the angels themselves, be preferred by me to all earthly kingdoms? If I call you their fellow citizen, though hope has not yet passed into reality, by the grace of the merciful God I shall not be lying.”

Burchard, abbot of Balerne, in the subscription to Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, speaks of him thus: “He seems to have received sanctification in his mother’s womb, [Col. 0632D] from which were conceived the presages of his future holiness and teaching.”

Guerric, abbot of Igny and disciple of Saint Bernard, Sermon 3, on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul: “Our master Saint Bernard, that interpreter of the Holy Spirit, undertook to speak about the whole of that nuptial song—the Song of Songs—and from what he has already published gave us hope that, if he reaches the passage about which you ask, ‘Until the day breathes and the shadows incline,’ he will bring the shadows themselves into the light of understanding: what has been said or shall be said in darkness he will tell us in the light.”

Geoffrey, first Saint Bernard’s secretary, then abbot of Igny, and afterward abbot of Clairvaux, Book III of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, or the first version written by him, [Col. 0633A] chapter 7: “Moreover, he appears far more eminent in his books and makes himself known through his own writings. In them he seems to have expressed his own image and displayed, as it were, a mirror of himself, so that the Ambrosian saying too may rightly seem applicable to him: ‘Let him mark himself with praise, and, crowned with the laurel of the Spirit, be crowned by his own writings.’” See the same author’s sermon on Saint Bernard at the end of Volume VI.

Robert, abbot of Saint Michael “in Peril of the Sea,” of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the appendix to Sigebert under the year 1152: “The venerable Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, a man of admirable religious devotion and effective teaching, fulfilled the course of human life by dying on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, leaving very many evidences of his wisdom, especially in his commentaries [1350] [Col. 0633B] on the Song of Songs.”

Father Claudio Acquaviva, fifth Superior General of the Society of Jesus, according to John Bourhesius in the book entitled *The Society of Jesus Consecrated to Mary the Mother of God*, chapter 4: “He certainly honoured the Blessed Virgin and Saint Bernard with special devotion, and regarded them as helpers in every doubtful matter.”

## VI.—Doctors of Theology

Henry of Hesse, Parisian doctor and afterward Carthusian, in his treatise addressed to James, abbot of Eberbach, against the detractors of Saint Bernard, Part I, chapter 3, writes: “Where, I ask, is such a spark of devotion found, such a stream of compunction poured forth, such a goad of love applied, as in the [Col. 0633C] life and teaching of the most blessed Father Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, star of the Church, principal enlarger of the Cistercian Order, and most ardent kindler of monastic life? And what more penetrating exhorter to virtues appears, what more effective remover of vices proceeds, awakening human sluggishness to heavenly things, crushing ardour for earthly things, preventing the sleep of death, and striving, after darkness has been driven away, to make the rays of divine light shine forth? Furthermore, in his fruitful and beautiful sermons the Virgin, mother of Christ, is exalted with such glorious proclamations of praise, adorned with the most precious encomiums of purity, and proclaimed with the most perfect seals of virginity. Nor is this all: by his teachings the fabric of the universal Church glitters as though with blooming gems [Col. 0633D] and shines more gloriously through the singular elegance of his words. By the fruitful eloquence of heavenly irrigation, grace flowing in, he unlocks the riddles of Scripture, loosens knots, clarifies obscurities, and explains doubts—as does blessed Bernard, the outstanding Doctor of the Church, who, departing into the glory of his homeland, thus by the most health-giving admonitions of every holiness, by teaching, and by the examples of his life, fructified and watered the whole ecclesiastical hierarchy beneath heaven. Therefore holy Mother Church, in the fullness of her overflowing testimony—when, in his canonization, he was examined and found brighter than light in miracles, teachings, and exercises of virtues, while his heavenly life bore witness—ordained that, for his many labours, chaste conduct, and most vigorous acts, this outstanding Confessor and Doctor should be honoured with diligent studies and celebrated in resounding praises; [Col. 0634A] that he should be venerated with solemn honours and more gloriously entered in the catalogue of saints.”

Jean Gerson, doctor and chancellor of Paris, in a sermon on Saint Bernard, addresses him thus: “And you, most blessed Bernard, whom with devout faith I hold to be one of the company of those fiery spirits whom Scripture calls Seraphim, I now entreat and entreat again through your love: take the burning coal from the altar of him whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem . . . . . and, touching my lips, cleanse them,” etc. And near the end: “As I consider those things which incidentally and, as it were, externally assisted Saint Bernard in attaining the love of God, I find, among others, four: his mother’s devotion, a suitable constitution, proper upbringing, and love of solitude.” And below: “Finally, one may say that all four of these incidentally assisted Bernard in becoming a prophet and worker of miracles; among these I count as chief the things he did in converting those who fled conversion with all their might.” [Col. 0634B]

Josse Clichtove of Nieuwpoort, doctor of theology and canon of Chartres, Sermon 1 on Saint Bernard, compares him to John the Baptist: “Thirdly, our lamp Bernard was shining through the manifold composition of sacred works, which would benefit not only people of his own time but posterity for the edification of faith and morals . . . . He certainly shone upon all, not only those then present but those yet to come until the consummation of the age, through the production of many books, ever directed toward some spiritual [1351] [Col. 0634C] advancement. Their diction is so sweet that his speech flows more sweetly than honey; hence he is deservedly called the Mellifluous Doctor.” Likewise, in a preface placed before the works of Saint Bernard: “Among works laboriously produced by authors of the highest approval, the volumes of most blessed Bernard ought not to be assigned the last place. For if one wishes to consider the author, one will find him most eminent both in holiness of life and in distinguished learning. If the character and method of writing itself are examined, they will be found to proceed most sweetly, without any jarring roughness, with the greatest ease and elegance, so that speech seems to have flowed from his mouth more sweetly than honey. Finally, if the subject he treats is examined, nothing else will be found except that he brings the coverings [Col. 0634D] of Holy Scripture into the light, thunders down upon vices with the grave thunder of words, or more earnestly summons men to virtue.”

Luis of Granada, Book II, *On the Christian Religion*, chapter 27: “It would not be fitting, among so many most weighty doctors, to omit the most sweet and holy Bernard. The humbler he was and the farther removed from vain glory, the greater grace and power he obtained for performing miracles.” And chapter 11: “It is also read of Saint Bernard that, at the beginning of his glorious novitiate, he went so rapt in spirit and beside himself that he lost the use of his senses . . . . For the force of the Spirit and the taste of divine sweetness which charity brings with it had so absorbed and drawn along the powers of his soul that he had no capacity for anything except that.”

[Col. 0635A] Charles Sacci, Parisian doctor of theology, in a sermon on Saint Bernard preserved in manuscript in our monastery of Lyre, in the diocese of Évreux, recalls among other things: “He certainly extinguished, lest they spread further, the flames of the universal schism; and this through so many and such prolonged journeys and vigils that it is remarkable that a still mortal man had—indeed, had remaining—such strength for enduring affairs, travels, and night-labours. At times he watched continuously not merely through one night but through many long nights. Severe illnesses followed, which he endured not only patiently but with a cheerful spirit, and which he used to call imitators of the blessed and heavenly life. Meanwhile he neither moderated nor interrupted his study of the sacred Scriptures, which he used to say he saw set before his eyes like a certain most level plain. [Col. 0635B] He delivered innumerable sermons and wrote books with the most elegant ornament of language and the greatest speed: one book *On Contempt for the World*; one book of *Meditations*; one book *On the Passion and Resurrection of Christ*; *On Loving God*; *On the Degrees of Humility*; *On Grace and Free Will*; *On Precept and Dispensation*; *To Pope Innocent on the Heresies of Peter Abelard*; *To Pope Eugenius on Consideration*; *To the Templars, in Praise of the New Knighthood*; an *Apology to the Cluniacs*; twenty-two homilies on Psalm 90; eighty-three homilies on the Song of Songs; four homilies on the Gospel of Luke; one book on the Canticle of Mary; one book on the Life of Bishop Malachy; and indeed countless letters—though 245 of them are still in circulation,” etc. [Col. 0635C]

## VII.—Religious from Various Orders

Hugh Metellus, regular canon of the monastery of Saint-Léon near Toul, in the letter to Saint Bernard published here in Volume I, column 1780: “Your name is poured-out oil, fragrant after the manner of crushed spices. The fame of your most renowned name has passed even to the ends of the earth,” etc.

Hugh, monk of Saint-Marianus of Auxerre, in his chronicle under the year 1114: “In the same year Clairvaux was founded; its first abbot was the servant of God Bernard, a man renowned for most illustrious holiness, [Col. 0635D] through whom the Church of his time blossomed again into the ancient glory of religious life.”

1352. Andrew Silvius, a Benedictine of Marchiennes, in his *Synopsis of Frankish-Merovingian History*, writes under the year 1126: “Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, like the morning star illuminates the monastic Order and shines in holiness, teaching, and miracles in Gaul—indeed, in Germany, Italy, and England. His life is so outstanding that all that has been said or written in his praise is too little.”

Helinand, Cistercian monk of Froidmont in Gaul, Book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, chapter 8, speaks thus of Saint Bernard: “Read the most beautiful book *On Consideration*, addressed to Eugenius. From its most noble style you will be able to understand that the book’s author was wiser than Apollo, more eloquent than Demosthenes, subtler than Aristotle, more moderate than Socrates, and more discerning than Plato.” [Col. 0636A]

Caesarius, Cistercian monk of Heisterbach, Book XIV of the *Miracles*, chapter 17: “Amid that flame of dreadful schism, in which the Christian world had begun to blaze, Bernard travelled through the provinces, undid whatever ought not to have been done, and, girded with the sword of the divine word, broke the terror of arms. He was a man of such authority that, through the mouth of Bernard alone, purple-clad fathers, kings, and princes of the earth spoke as though through the common oracle of the world.”

Henry Suso of the Order of Preachers, in the *Dialogue on Eternal Wisdom*, chapter 14, addresses Saint Bernard thus: “And you too, Bernard the mellifluous, be blessed among all the Doctors of the Church; your soul was wondrously illuminated by the splendours of the eternal Word. With your honeyed eloquence, flowing from the abundance that streamed from your heart, you most sweetly set forth and exalt the Passion of Christ’s humanity, saying thus,” etc. “Rightly indeed, most holy Father Bernard, does your most sweet tongue pour forth eloquence, when the honey-flowing Passion of Christ has so sweetened your heart.” [Col. 0636B]

Denis the Carthusian, Sermon 1 on the Feast of Saint Bernard, praises him thus: “Almighty and most gracious God adorned the most blessed man, holy Father Bernard, with grace so abundant and manifold that one might truly say of him what the Saviour said of the Apostle Paul: ‘This man is a chosen vessel for me,’ etc. (Acts XI, 15); and what is read in Ecclesiasticus: [Col. 0636C] ‘No one like him has been found’ (Ecclus. XLIV, 20). For in his own time he had no equal in the world, but was truly the Apostle of his age.” And in Sermon 2: “God’s most chosen Bernard, most excellent doctor of all religious persons, light and glory of monks, exemplar and model of the devout, was anticipated by so many and such great graces from above, adorned with so many excellences, and elevated by so many privileges, that no intellects can penetrate them, nor speech or language express or adequately praise so great a man.”

Sixtus of Siena, of the Order of Preachers, *Sacred Library*, Book IV: “Bernard, pre-eminent in holiness of life and distinguished learning, imbibed the sacred Scriptures from childhood and retained them in memory throughout his life, so that whenever he attempted to write or speak, he was compelled to break forth into the words and expressions of the holy Scriptures. Hence his various writings, which may be called nothing but patchworks of the divine books, are everywhere adorned with sayings from the Old and New Testaments as though with jewelled inlays, inserted so conveniently and aptly that they seem to have been born there. His manner of teaching is almost always occupied with investigating mystical meanings and forming morals. His speech everywhere delights with sweetness and ardour and ardently kindles, so that honey and milk of words seem to flow from his most sweet tongue, and flames of burning affections to burst forth from his most ardent breast.” [Col. 0636D]

Jerome Platus of the Society of Jesus, Book III, *On the Good [Col. 0637A] State of Religious Life*, chapter 11, writes among other things: “What shall we say of Bernard? We may truly call him [1353] altogether honeyed, for, abounding in spiritual instruction, and in the best and most perfect such instruction, he has also this chief quality: he so interweaves and combines Holy Scripture into his style that he seems either himself to speak in the words of Scripture, or Scripture itself to sound through his mouth. This has, together with charm, a wonderful gravity and power.”

Peter Canisius of the same Society, *Mariale*, Book V, chapter 28: “Under Lothair II and Conrad III flourished Bernard of Clairvaux, a man most renowned in Gaul, Germany, and Italy. All deservedly admired and revered him, not only for teaching divinely inspired but also for holiness of life, often displayed in the most evident miracles. No one either wrote or lived better than he in the whole company of monks—if, that is, we accept Luther’s judgment.” [Col. 0637B]

Aloysius Gonzaga of the same Society, as is read in his *Life*, Book II, chapter 32: “He did not forgo reading Bernard, which had been so pleasant to him during life, even when near death. For in the illness that proved his last, he held Bernard so dear that he arranged for something from Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs to be read aloud to him every day.”

## VIII.—Jurists and Orators

Francis Petrarch, Book II, *On the Solitary Life*, chapter 14: “Bernard used to say that he had learned all the letters he knew—of which I do not know whether anyone in his age was richer—not from human instruction but in woods and fields, by meditation and prayer; and that he had never had any teachers except oaks and beeches.” [Col. 0637C]

Nicolas Pithou, in the letter prefixed to his treasury drawn from the works of Saint Bernard: “I have a great friendship and intimacy with Lord Charles Perrot. One day, when I had visited him as I am accustomed to do and we had conversed much, back and forth, about various matters, the first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, Saint Bernard, came up in conversation. Perrot extolled him with such high praise and held his writings in such esteem that he moved me to examine them . . . And so I found to be true what he had predicted would happen. For I derived such delight from reading Bernard that it wiped away nearly all the troubles which had so miserably tormented my mind.” The same author says below that Bernard was “a kind of pillar and support of the falling Church.” [Col. 0637D]

Justus Lipsius, royal professor and historian at Louvain, asked by Aubertus Miraeus which Fathers he judged should be read for the formation of sermons, replied in Letter 49, Century 3: “Among all the Greeks Chrysostom pleases me . . . Among the Latins Bernard captivates me and has the power to stir one up, because of his sharpness and warmth everywhere; likewise to teach and impress, because of the keen judgments that he frequently and beneficially intermingles.”

René Choppin, advocate in the supreme senate of Paris, Book II, *On Sacred Polity*: “At the same [Col. 0638A] time Saint Bernard shone forth, a monk and disciple of oaks, most learned with no teacher preceding him, who brought holiness and learning out of solitude into public renown, out of shadow into sunlight. He was as much *polygraphos*—a prolific writer—as *autodidaktos*—self-taught; something we see has happened to very few writers of this kind.”

## IX.—Illustrious Women

Saint Hildegard, abbess of Mount Saint Robert near Bingen, in a letter to Saint Bernard, describes him thus: “Two years ago I saw you in this vision, like a man looking into the sun and not afraid . . . . You are an eagle looking upon the sun,” etc.

1354. Saint Gertrude, abbess of the monastery of Helfta in the county of Mansfeld, describes the manner in which Saint Bernard appeared to her, Book VI of the *Insinuations*, chapter 51. Among other things she says: “[Col. 0638B] His most holy breast, neck, and hands seemed honourably clothed in certain golden plates interwoven with very radiant rose-coloured gems. The golden plates signified the particular elegance of his saving teaching, which he diligently pondered with a devout heart, brought forth through the service of his sacred throat by his consecrated mouth, and faithfully wrote down with holy hands for all who wished to make progress in them toward salvation. The gems, however, represented those sayings that more especially breathe forth divine love.”

Blessed Mechthild, companion of that same Blessed Gertrude in the same monastery, writes thus in the *Book of Spiritual Grace*, chapter 91: “In the midst of the Church the Lord opened the mouth of Saint Bernard, whom God had singularly anticipated with blessings of sweetness; for the Holy Spirit, flowing into him so abundantly and superabundantly, had filled him, so that, just as a wind opens a door with most rapid force, so the Holy Spirit, by its impulse, poured into him—kindled by charity—the things divinely inspired to him. He greatly illuminated the Church by his teaching; and the Lord filled him with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding. Though he poured forth much, [Col. 0638C] he retained far more in understanding, illuminated in mind beyond what can be said.”

## X.—Heterodox Writers

Martin Luther, in his *Table Talk*, chapter on the Fathers of the Church: “Bernard surpasses all Doctors of the Church; but when he disputes, he is changed into another man. There he attributes too much to free will.” [Col. 0638D]

Michael Neander writes of him thus in the preface to his *Gnomology of the Greeks*: “More of the spirit of life, teaching, and faith is found in a few pages of Lord Bernard—who did not touch philosophy, content with Scripture alone, which he had made so familiar to himself that he spoke sheer words of Scripture—than in all of Jerome, who surpassed everyone in knowledge of languages, arts, philosophy, and ancient wisdom.”

Martin Bucer, Book *On Concord*, article on Justification, calls Bernard a man of God.

John Oecolampadius, cited by Cuthbert Tunstall in Book *On the Truth of Christ’s Body in the Eucharist*: “Bernard surpassed all the men of his age in more exact judgment.”

[Col. 0639A] John Calvin, Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 11, §10, testifies: “Abbot Bernard speaks in the books *On Consideration* as though Truth itself were speaking.” Likewise, chapter 10, §17, he calls Bernard “a devout and holy writer.”

[Col. 0640A] Daniel Heinsius, Oration 3: “Who writes more sweetly than Bernard? I am accustomed to call his *Meditations* a stream of paradise, ambrosia for souls, angelic food, and the marrow of piety.”

[Col. 0639]

## Horstius’s Exhortation to Sectarians: On Reading Saint Bernard Fruitfully

### Observation

In this place Horstius reports the unfair and erroneous judgments of the Magdeburg Centuriators, extracted from their Twelfth Century, by which they impiously or unfairly carp at certain deeds and sayings of Saint Bernard under the name of superstition. The same author divided these judgments into twenty-two articles; for brevity’s sake we have reduced them to ten principal heads, lest we seem to have omitted anything.

First, then, the Magdeburg writers charge Saint Bernard with having rendered worship to the Host offered and consecrated in Mass, and with having used it to expel demons.
