Second, with having venerated relics of saints. Third, with having believed that things fortified by a sacred blessing possess a certain power. Fourth, with having defended the Roman Pontiff against his opponents and asserted for him the right of investitures against Emperor Lothair. Fifth, with having denied that salvation is to be hoped for outside the Catholic Church. 1355 Sixth, with having preached the holy expedition called the Cross. Seventh, with having sought truth from the dead and believed the sacrifice of the Mass beneficial to them. Eighth, with having performed miracles to confirm errors, as they put it. Ninth, with having propagated monastic life and led very many into it; above all, with having forbidden his own sister, though married, every display of dress, and approved her separation from her husband so that she might enter a cloister. Tenth, with Bernard himself having cast his body into an icy pool out of concern for chastity, and, in short, having treated his body with excessive harshness.

These, then, are the allegedly superstitious acts which the heretics calumniate in the holy Doctor. Horstius appended to each not so much refutations as vigorous invectives. But since they attack not so much Bernard himself as the common cause of Catholic religion, and since many writers have answered them fully and learnedly, it was not thought necessary to dwell upon them longer. [1356] Certainly, these things which the heretics accuse as superstitious may much more powerfully be turned back against them in Bernard’s defence. Since Bucer calls him a man of God and Calvin devout and holy, it is impious to suppose that he was devoted, even to death, to superstitious deeds. Accordingly, those things are by no means to be marked as superstition among Catholics which were unable to prevent Bernard from being holy and from being made illustrious by miracles from God. Moreover, if he wishes, let the reader consult the *Bernardine Confession*, drawn by Father Theodore Petre, Carthusian of Cologne, from the works of the holy Doctor; there he will find the points of Catholic doctrine arranged in definite classes.

[Col. 0639B] We have heard the various judgments of sectarians concerning Bernard. Some praise him, others blame him—unless perhaps all agree in this: that all alike condemn and reject him because he opposes their own opinions and practices. Yet the things which they disapprove as contrary to their doctrine, we Catholics consequently judge worthy of approval and embrace, because we know that Bernard and other men most holy like him taught and did such things, and thus travelled a path different from theirs. Holiness of life bears witness to doctrine; and teaching or faith cannot seem false or erroneous to us when men illustrious for such holiness have held it. Why do they wish themselves to be believed more, supported by no testimony of holiness, than most holy Bernard and the other orthodox Fathers, whose teaching and [Col. 0639C] faith are proved by so many evidences of holiness—indeed, by so many signs and miracles? Certainly a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit. For who of sound mind could persuade himself that a man teaching impious, false, absurd, and erroneous things, devoted to idolatry, superstition, and empty observances—the things which those dark critics, the Centuriators, impute to Bernard—could nevertheless grow, amid all these, in continual increases of grace before God and men and rise to such perfection [Col. 0640B] of divine love and every virtue?

Furthermore, Bernard’s writings abundantly testify what he thought concerning the principal articles of orthodox faith. But even if he had committed nothing to writing, the very course of his life would have shown sufficiently to which Church he adhered and how far he stood apart from you in doctrine and conduct. For I would now address you briefly, O sectarians, who also sometimes like to read Bernard, in the hope that perhaps you may at last be granted understanding and repentance.

For you the Mass is sheer and dreadful idolatry; yet how often did Bernard offer Mass, the true sacrifice to God? His *Life* testifies that he scarcely ever omitted it even to his last breath; and you yourselves testify to it, though not without calumny. Did he not often terrify and drive out demons by the very offering of Mass? Did he not, after offering the sacrifice, come from the altar and strike down and conquer William, Duke of Aquitaine—that obstinate supporter of schism, yielding to no threats or warnings—armed in his right hand, not with a sword, but with the sacred Host of the Lord’s Body? [Col. 0640C] Read and understand, if perhaps at last the hardness of your hearts may be conquered,” etc.

But I proceed farther than the scope of my purpose allows. I had intended only to stir you briefly, [Col. 0641A] lest you suppose yourselves wiser than Bernard. For why do you introduce a novelty condemned by the ancients, which condemns the ancients? Why do you not hold to the path by which Bernard, those holy men and confessors, and all antiquity sought heaven? If you do not believe yourselves to be in error, see by what path these men proceed; if you recognize that you are, why do you not follow guides skilled in the way? Why do you not at last return to that from which you ought never to have departed?

I indeed, to confess candidly about myself, if either from my earliest years I had been imbued with your errors, or if by whatever chance it had happened that I had turned aside from the path of truth and orthodox religion to your sects, Bernard alone would suffice to make your doctrines suspect to me—indeed, to bring one who had gone astray back onto the way of truth. For I should reason thus with myself:

[Col. 0641B] If the things which a man of such exceptional and unassailable holiness held and taught are not true, how could so great a holiness coexist with so great a falsehood? I cannot deny his holiness, which I see attested by so many most weighty men and writers beyond every objection—even by his very enemies. I also behold innumerable miracles performed in confirmation of him; to wish to deny them does not seem the part of a prudent man, while to slander them as illusions and works of Satan seems altogether [Col. 0642A] the part of a man unsound of mind, not to say malicious, since such things could have been done only by divine power. But to believe that deeds of this kind were performed in confirmation of errors would truly be the part of a wholly impious man, blasphemous against God and injurious to his saints. Here I may rightly employ that notable saying of a certain holy Doctor: “Lord, if this is error, we have been deceived by you. For these things have been confirmed among us by such great signs and wonders—such as can be done only through you yourself; they have certainly been handed down to us by men of the highest holiness and proved with the fullest and authoritative testimony, while you yourself cooperate and confirm the word by the signs that follow.” [Note: [Col. 0641B] Richard of St Victor, *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 2.]

I say this for your benefit, O sectarians, because I acknowledge myself a debtor both to wise and foolish; although [Col. 0642B] you seem, over and above those who teach you, to understand and be wise yourselves. Yet I wonder what is in your minds when you read Bernard, who differs from you by the whole heaven, while conscience doubtless protests against your preconceived opinions. Read henceforth: this alone I pray and urge—read, I say, and, if you have any concern for salvation, understand. Behold: I set before you Bernard, the light of holiness and guide of truth; or, if you prefer, I commend to you him who is the true light—indeed, the way, the truth, and the life.

# Bollandist Acts

[Col. 0643]

## COMMENTARY ON SAINT BERNARD, CONFESSOR, FIRST ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, FATHER AND DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH, IN THE TERRITORY OF LANGRES IN GAUL

By John Pinius, priest and theologian of the Society of Jesus. (*Acta Sanctorum Bollandiana*, August, vol. IV, 20 August, p. 101.)

### § I. Year and place of birth; illustrious lineage

[Col. 0643A]

1. Among the great men who, like the most brilliant stars of God’s Church, have illumined the world by doctrine, virtues, and miracles, Saint Bernard plainly deserves and occupies an altogether singular place. His name has been spread and celebrated everywhere to such a degree that scarcely any saint seems to have found so many heralds of his deeds—writers so excellent, of such tested fidelity and acknowledged authority. This will become clear both from the three especially distinguished biographers, who transmitted his most outstanding acts to posterity in continuous narrative, as though by common agreement, and whom we shall cite below; and from the documents of others, of which we shall speak later. Whatever, in the course of this commentary, [Col. 0643B] we shall say beyond what others have previously said will serve either to confirm, elucidate, or amplify the Life and miracles of the honey-flowing Doctor, beginning with his birth, concerning which various matters call for consideration.

2. First, concerning the year of his birth, the authors agree so completely that it lies beyond all controversy. For the most illustrious Angelus Manrique, Bishop of Badajoz, in volume I of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year of Christ 1105, the eighth of Cîteaux, chapter 1, no. 3, says:

> “Concerning the time, it is altogether certain that he was born in the year 1091, namely in that year in which Blessed Peter of Cava, formerly a monk of the Cluniac monastery, reverently indeed, but magnificently, declined the use of the mitre offered him by Urban II at the Council of Benevento. You may see this written in the acts of his Life (in Baronius under this year). Thus there were shown in Bernard, even then, presages that he would offer and despise such things. You will readily prove that he was born in this year if from 1113, when he entered Cîteaux, you subtract the twenty-two years that he then had—[Col. 0644A] a point on which all historians agree.”

Add the more recent writers, who assign the Saint’s birth to the already mentioned year 1091. So much for the time. Of the place in which our Saint began life, the aforementioned author of the *Annals*, Manrique, writes as follows in no. 2:

3. “All who write his Life testify that Bernard was born at Fontaines (elsewhere this place is called Fontes; in common usage, Fontaines), a town so called from its springs, the residence and lordship of his father. It lies about half a league from Dijon, the noble and renowned court of the Dukes of Burgundy, between the strongly fortified castle of Talant (commonly Talen) and the castle of Fontaines.”

Manrique there describes this from Guillaume Paradin, *On the Ancient State of Burgundy*, folio 140 in his edition. In our Basel edition, p. 165 and following, the following is read:

> “There is a most delightful plain, its walls washed on either side by the two rivers Suzon and Ouche … Talant rises above the city, a castle fortified both by the nature of its site and by art … Opposite it lies a castle named from its springs, which Bernard, most holy abbot, made illustrious by his most famous beginnings; formerly the house [printed: *dominis*, ‘lords’] of the lords of Châtillon, today a sacred dwelling for Christ.”

Mabillon, editor of the works of Saint Bernard, appended to the end of the second volume various Lives of the same Saint, beginning at column 1601, and afterwards added other documents concerning him. After quoting in a note at the said column, from the third Life, that Tescelin, the Saint’s father, is there called “lord of the lesser castle named Fontaines,” etc., he observes in the same place that Bernard’s paternal house, as is believed, “was converted into a convent of the Fathers of the Feuillants.”

The Reverend Father Chrysostom Henriquez, in his Cistercian martyrology for this day, states the matter more expressly than he proves it, writing thus of the Saint:

> “He happily came forth into the light at Fontaines in his paternal house, which, out of reverence for so great a man—since in it he had the first beginnings [Col. 0645A] of his life and holiness—was converted into a monastery for the reformed Cistercians of the Feuillant congregation. On the foundation stones of that sacred building, praises of the most holy Father Bernard and splendid encomia were inscribed in fine letters; lest these remain hidden beneath the ground, I judged that they ought to be copied here.”

But we refrain from transcribing them here, since they may be read there. The undertaking is connected with the year 1619, in which, as the same inscription indicates, the first stone was laid on 6 January “by command and in the name of Louis XIII, Most Christian King of France and Navarre, and of his most serene consort Anne of Austria.”

4. But with respect again to Fontaines, the castle or town of Saint Bernard’s birth, Manrique warns in the cited no. 2 that it must not be ennobled beyond its merits or enriched with other places attached to it.

> “Modern writers,” he says, “when they read that it was the town of his father, invent a county and attach to it several other villages, over which Tescelin, from Fontaines, supposedly exercised rights.”

He cites Brito, who published a Cistercian chronicle in Portuguese, book I, chapter 14:

> “But he produces no testimony whatsoever; indeed, antiquity itself protests, for in book I, chapter 1, of the Life of Saint Bernard, I read rather that he was a knight content with his military pay, though thereby he had abundance for every good work. Nor would that author have detracted from Tescelin, Bernard’s father, if he had possessed more extensive titles; for a little further below he enumerated even lesser titles in full concerning the uncle Galdric: ‘A holy man and powerful in the world, renowned for the glory of secular knighthood, lord of a castle in the territory of Autun called Ticilium [elsewhere Tuillium; commonly Tovillon].’ Therefore, he did not possess the rich revenues of a county or another dominion, when his chief revenues, if not his only ones, are described as military pay. It is quite enough if he possessed a suburban estate belonging to a jurisdiction other than that of the duke himself.”

Thus Manrique reasons, and, in my judgment, rightly.

5. Yet the *Fragments* in Mabillon, column 1275, from the third Life of Saint Bernard, apparently by Geoffrey, monk [Col. 0645D] of Clairvaux (we shall henceforth call these the *Fragments of Geoffrey*), do not entirely agree with the words he added: “whose chief revenues, if not his only ones, are described as military pay.” There it is said:

> “This man was noble by birth and rich in possessions.”

From what has been said, the Life of Saint Bernard contained in our manuscript marked P. Ms. 13 is convicted of error when it writes: “Bernard … was a native of the town of Châtillon in Burgundy.”

Although it is so certain that our Saint sprang from noble stock that no prudent person can raise any controversy against it, we shall nevertheless not act without purpose if we confirm and illustrate this point.

6. “His parents,” writes Manrique, no. 4, “were the aforesaid Tescelin and Alaide. Our countrymen report that he was related by blood to the Dukes of Burgundy and consequently descended from the kings of France; that she was from the family of the Counts of Cornelien, of high descent from the kings of Portugal, and related in the third degree of consanguinity to Henry of Portugal, the first Count and father of King Alfonso—thus binding all Christian princes to Bernard by a close bond of blood. I find only this in William of Saint-Thierry, book I, chapter 1, and Alan of Auxerre—one formerly an abbot, the other a bishop, and both contemporaries of Bernard:

> ‘His parents were distinguished according to worldly rank; and Tescelin served his temporal lords so faithfully by counsel and arms that he did not neglect to render to the Lord his God what he owed.’

To these may be added the following from the fourth Life, written by John the Hermit, in Mabillon, col. 1281:

> “Most blessed Bernard … [Col. 0646B] sprang from a worthy stock: noble indeed in the lineage of the flesh, but nobler in the loftiness of his mind. His father was named Tescelin; his mother, Aalays, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, a powerful and great man according to worldly rank, and descended from the nobility of the ancient Dukes of Burgundy, as many assert.”

But let us return to Manrique.

7. “Yet,” he says, “in Guillaume Paradin, a Burgundian author who treats of the Dukes of Burgundy, I find the families of Châtillon and of Saffres, to which each parent belonged, counted among the illustrious houses of that former kingdom—for those who afterwards became dukes had formerly been kings; but I do not read of royal descent or origin. I should like to transcribe his words from folio 93:

> ‘There are also many other illustrious families, such as that of the Cornejors, from which came Godfrey, standard-bearer of the little banner.’

And, after listing quite a number of others, he says of the two families of the holy Doctor:

> ‘Then come the Châtillons, from whom came that holy Bernard, most holy Abbot of Clairvaux and no less distinguished by the monuments of his genius. You Châtillons and Saffres therefore have reason to boast, since you have given from your own body so radiant a sun of religion to the Christian commonwealth—a man of whom it is commonly said what Homer once sang of Nestor: that speech sweeter than honey flowed from his mouth.’”

So far Paradin, who, I think, declares Bernard’s mother Alaide to have sprung from the Saffres, and Tescelin from the Châtillons: families certainly illustrious among the Burgundians, but not equal to royal splendour. I do not deny that the Counts of Châtillon, from whose family Tescelin came, may perhaps have been related by blood to the Dukes of Burgundy, and Bernard through them, though remotely. The honour of a king loves judgment; the honour of saints requires certain truth. Nor is the nobility of Bernard’s father one that needs the recommendation of borrowed adornment. We write these matters as certain on the authority of a trustworthy author from that province, whose account agrees with ancient statements; we shall write greater things if they are supported by witnesses worthy of belief.”

These are the candid and sincere words of the most illustrious Manrique.

8. Hence it follows that the Roman Breviary could have said more—indeed, I might say ought to have said more—about Saint Bernard’s birth than merely τὸ (‘the’), *honesto loco natus* (‘born of honourable rank’). In 1660 our Father Peter Francis Chifflet published at Dijon a *Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux*, to which he appended proofs and various documents. In the preface to that dissertation he rightly complains of the Breviary’s aforesaid wording, which is certainly far too modest and beneath the Saint’s dignity.

> “For,” he says, “anyone reading this who knows nothing else of Bernard’s birth would easily suppose him born of common parents, such as peasants or artisans, or others of the same sort; whereas it is certain that he was exceedingly noble on both his father’s and mother’s side … Add also,” besides other observations he makes there, “that this lowering of Bernard’s birth does some injury to the most holy man, who deserved so well of the Church, since it deprives his virtue of a certain splendour and, as it were, its own foundation—if every prudent person truly judges that virtue placed and implanted in nobility rises higher and shines more brilliantly.”

He divides the plan of his work as follows:

> “First he undertakes to demonstrate that Bernard was noble; next, that he belonged to the equestrian order, which in those times was commonly called *Militia* [knighthood]; further, that his origin in that rank was ancient; and finally that, through his mother Aalyd—who was daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard—he was descended from the ancient Dukes of Burgundy.”

9. Mabillon summarized the matter briefly before the first Life of Saint Bernard, written by Abbot William and edited by himself from col. 1061. Speaking thus of the paternal line on p. 1059:

> “Tescelin, Bernard’s [Col. 0647C] father, is said by Abbot William, chapter 1, to have been a man of ancient and lawful *militia*—that is, of proven nobility, which we call equestrian. He had the byname Sorus, that is, reddish-haired, evidently from the colour of his hair, in the charter of Hugh II, Duke of Burgundy, for the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Chalon. In that charter Tescelin subscribes first, after Raimerius, the duke’s steward, and before Bernard of Montfort, Warnerius of Sombernon, and other most noble men. (See Chifflet, proofs appended to the mentioned dissertation, p. 426.) According to Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, Guy of Aucromont was, on his mother’s side, brother of Thescelin Sorus of Fontaines, father of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux; and on another side he was brother of Ulric, under whom the Abbey of Morimond was founded. (See Chifflet, dissertation, section 7, pp. 416–417.) Guy’s nobility is proved from his marriage connection with Hescilina, lady of Moulley, daughter of Holdoin; and Holdoin had as his brother Geoffrey, lord of Joinville. So much for the paternal line.”

10. “As for the maternal line,” he says, “Bernard’s mother Aleth, or Alaysia—whom one writer of the third Life calls Elizabeth, perhaps through a copyist’s error—was the daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard,” etc., which we have already quoted above, “as we learn from John the Hermit, writer of the fourth Life. In the necrology of the Dijon monastery of Saint Benignus, where she was first buried, she is simply called a laywoman, and her memorial is entered thus:

> “On the Kalends of September [1 September] died Alaysa, laywoman.”

By this name even distinguished persons are customarily distinguished in that necrology from nuns. On this day falls the feast of Saint Ambrose, or Ambrosinian, Confessor, which, according to John the Hermit, was customarily celebrated at Fontaines. Some wrongly confuse him here with Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan. (Chifflet discusses this more fully in section 6.) Rainard, lord of Montbard, Bernard’s uncle and Alaysia’s full brother, was such a man. Since Bernard’s lineage was so illustrious on both sides, it is not surprising that his eldest brother Guy is called “a great man” by William in chapter 3; that Guy’s wife is called a noble young woman; and that his sister Humbelina is called a noble young woman, who went about with proud retinue and display, in chapter 6. These things are from Chifflet. Add to them that Galdric, Bernard’s uncle, is called by William, no. 10, “powerful in the world,” etc. (as we have said above); and that Josbert of La Ferté, which lies upon the Aube, was a noble man and Bernard’s kinsman according to the flesh, according to the same William, no. 43. Finally, the knight Rainerius was the brother of Godfrey, former Prior of Clairvaux and Bishop of Langres, who was related to Bernard by blood.

11. “Moreover Chifflet proves that Saint Bernard’s paternal family, which bears its designation from Fontaines, continued down to our own times through Bartholomew of Sombernon—a family into which the royal blood of the ancient Dukes of Burgundy passed through affinity with an heiress daughter in marriage. (See Chifflet, [Col. 0648C] section 7, p. 418.) We deliberately omit the remaining matters which, in the same Chifflet, seem either less certain or less necessary concerning Bernard’s illustrious lineage. We add only this: the arms of the monastery of Clairvaux—a gold or silver bend, chequered with a double red line, upon a black shield—do not derive, as some wish, from Saint Bernard’s family arms, but from the family of the Dukes of Champagne, from whom Hugh, founder of Clairvaux, came. The six bands of gold and azure slanting diagonally downward on a purple border, which is the emblem of the Cistercian Order, were taken from the family of the Dukes of Burgundy, by whose benefits and authority the Cistercian Order was chiefly founded.” On this matter see Chifflet, section 1.

12. Therefore one should not listen to the writers whom Chifflet there enumerates: “Barnabas de Montalvo, Mariana, book X of the *History of Spain*, chapter 12, Boniface Simonetta, book I of his *History*, and several other recent writers,” who maintain that the Saint sprang from the family of the Dukes of Burgundy whose head was Robert, King of the Franks. They accordingly proclaim him related by blood not only to the kings of France but also to those of Spain and Portugal, “thus binding all Christian princes to Bernard by a close bond of blood,” as Chifflet adds from Manrique, whom we too cited above. “They think they prove this from the ancient arms of the Cistercian Order,” but wrongly, as has just been indicated.

Hence Tamayo, so often corrected in our work, deserves correction here again when, in his Spanish Martyrology for 20 August, in the notes, he assigns as the first cause of “Saint Bernard’s cult in Spain that he was most closely connected by blood with Alfonso, surnamed the Emperor, King of Castile,” citing Alfonso Sánchez. But enough and more than enough has been said concerning the most illustrious lineage from which Saint Bernard sprang. It was not only the splendour of his father’s and mother’s families, but also their great integrity of life and true piety toward God—qualities shining forth in both parents of the Saint—that secured for him no slight ornaments of praise, as we shall now see.

### § II. Parents, brothers, sister, prophecy, upbringing, studies

13. Manrique reports the following relevant matter under the aforesaid [Col. 0649B] year 1105, no. 5:

> “His parents, distinguished according to worldly rank, were rendered more distinguished by virtue and piety—whether because these are rarer in the noble and therefore more precious when found, or because abstinence from superfluities together with abundance of useful things made them sufficient not only for themselves but for others, and munificence won them distinction. The mother especially, beneficent toward the poor and continually devoted to works of mercy, was not merely distinguished but dear to everyone. Their marriage was increased by seven children, born more for the Cistercian family than for their own: Guy, Gerard, Bernard—for he was third in birth order—Andrew, Bartholomew, Nivard, and Humbelina: six males, all destined to become monks, and one female, who became a nun.”

See our notes on them at chapter 2 of book I of the Life of Saint Bernard. It pleases us here to add, for parents blessed with offspring so numerous and so devout, the eulogies by which they are celebrated in the writers of the Life of the honey-flowing Doctor. Of Tescelin, Bernard’s father, the second Life, whose author or compiler is Alan, chapter 1, in Mabillon, col. 1235, says that he was “a man of ancient and lawful knighthood … a worshipper of God and steadfast in justice.” In the *Fragments of Geoffrey*, col. 1275, mentioned above, he is praised because he was:

> “Gentle in manners, a great lover of the poor, an eminent cultivator of piety, and possessed of an incredible zeal for justice … Furthermore, he never used arms except either in defense of his own land or with his lord, the Duke of Burgundy, to whom he was exceedingly familiar and intimate; nor was he ever with him in battle without victory attending him.”

14. This same man joined singular gentleness to the supreme zeal for justice that burned in him, according to John the Hermit in the same Mabillon, col. 1282. For:

> “When at one time the aforementioned man … had agreed to fight in single combat with an adversary much inferior to him in rank and of lesser means, the appointed and fixed day for the contest arrived. Both sides assembled. But the venerable Tescelin, mindful of the fear of God and the divine judgments … although he was stronger and more powerful and could overcome his enemy and gain the greatest profit from victory, voluntarily made peace with his adversary, surrendering and relinquishing without dispute whatever was at issue. [Col. 0650A] O great piety, great clemency of the man!”

That he was conspicuous for many duties of Christian justice may be inferred from the brief but forceful praise which I quoted above before no. 4: “He had abundance in his resources for every good work.” What followed? At Saint Bernard’s admonitions he renounced the world and died with the odour of sanctity.

15. William, in book I, chapter 1, no. 1, of the Life of our Saint, records the following concerning his mother:

> “Aleth, the mother, was from the castle named Montbard. Keeping the Apostolic rule in her own order, subject to her husband, she governed her household under him in the fear of God, devoting herself to works of mercy and rearing her children in every discipline … When they had grown up, as long as they remained under her hand, she brought them up more as in a desert than at court, not allowing them to become accustomed to more delicate foods, but feeding them on coarser and ordinary fare.”

Among Geoffrey’s *Fragments*, col. 1375, this distinguished woman is called “worthy of such lineage and such a husband—indeed, the glory of both … Instructed by a divine oracle, Elizabeth loved this son more tenderly than all the others, and therefore gave him his grandfather’s name, calling him Bernard.”

John the Hermit, from col. 1282, says:

> “The venerable Alays … amid her other notable virtues, was accustomed to go about the houses, seek out poor, sick, and needy persons, and give them from her own resources what was necessary. She had the greatest care also for the lame and disabled. She used neither servants nor other attendants in carrying out these offices, but did it herself: she came to their dwellings [Col. 0650C] and supplied each with what was needed. In the hospices of the churches she most devoutly ministered to the sick, according to their several needs: she cleaned their pots, offered food, washed their cups, and did all the other things which servants and attendants customarily perform as servile work. Why say more? Shall we recount all her virtues? Certainly not, for we should not be believed. Yet we shall bring forward one thing most worthy of narration, a matter full of miracle and not heard by us without wonder, reported by a most religious abbot named Robert, who lived for more than sixty-seven years in a monastery under the yoke of regular discipline. He was the nephew of the matron of whom we wish to speak, being the son of her sister; and it was to him also [Col. 0650D] that Blessed Bernard addressed the first of his letters.”

16. The substance of the matter related more fully in the aforesaid Life is that this most upright woman foretold her own death and, having most devoutly prepared herself for it with the Church’s final aids:

> “Commending her spirit into the hands of the Lord, she raised her hand, signed herself with the sign of the holy cross, and surrendered her spirit in peace … When that holy soul had thus departed from the temple of her holy body, her hand, raised as it was to make the sign of the cross, remained so, while all who were present looked on in wonder. O woman inflamed with the fire of divine love, strong in faith, most patient in hope, devoted in charity!”

But now let us draw in our sails. The most illustrious Manrique treats, under the year 1105, no. 8 and following, of the immense gathering at her blessed death; of her body’s being requested from and granted by the monks of Saint Benignus, and honourably buried there; likewise of her appearance to her children, her translation to Clairvaux, and the year of her death. Documents concerning her life and death, together with her epitaph, are included among the proofs of Chifflet’s dissertation from p. 431. We have already indicated, in the omitted notices for 4 April, vol. I of that month, p. 320, that she is commemorated with the title Blessed in the menologies of Chrysostom Henriquez, Bucellin, and Chalemot. We also said that the following was read concerning her in the book of burials of Clairvaux:

> “Likewise there lies there the noble lady Aleydis, of pious memory and most devoted to God, mother of the excellent Doctor and our Father, Blessed Bernard, first [Col. 0651B] Abbot of Clairvaux.”

From Manrique we assigned her death to the year 1105, as may be seen in our annotations on chapter 1 of the Life of Saint Bernard. Meanwhile, we do not venture to grant the title Blessed to that most pious woman until certain documents from another source establish that she received public and lawful cult. Reader, you have what we judged should be mentioned here concerning the Saint’s parents.

17. From this most fortunate root of marriage there sprang those seven most beautiful flowers of whom we spoke a little earlier. We now wish to proceed to Saint Bernard’s birth, upbringing, and the rare gifts both of divine charisms and of character and intellect which shone forth in him from earliest age, so that they seemed clearly to foreshadow the greater deeds he would later perform.

First, that great man shared with other great men the feature that signs preceded his birth. For while his mother was pregnant, she saw in a dream a beautiful white puppy, reddish on its back, which did not cease barking even within the womb. She brought the matter to a certain religious man.

> “Immediately, inspired with a spirit of prophecy, he replied to the trembling and anxious woman with what David says to the Lord concerning holy preachers, ‘The tongue of your dogs from your enemies’: ‘Do not fear; all is well. You will be mother of an excellent puppy, who will be guardian of God’s house and utter great barks for it against the enemies of the faith. For he will be an outstanding preacher and, like a good dog, by the grace of his healing tongue will cure in many persons [Col. 0651D] many diseases of the soul.’”

This is according to William in the *Life*, chapter 1.

18. Let us also hear Geoffrey, fourth Abbot of Clairvaux, in his sermon on the anniversary of Saint Bernard’s death, in Mabillon, col. 1309 and following. The sermon was delivered in 1163, as may be inferred from no. 5 itself. In that sermon, no. 15, he says this concerning the same Saint:

> “Though he called some in childhood, others in youth, and others in old age, yet he anticipated—indeed, as it were, snatched away—certain persons, few though they were, by a kind of privilege of special grace in blessing; and while they were not yet born, he declared by such signs and indications as he willed what they would be. Thus he startled this venerable mother of his chosen and beloved one, while she was still pregnant with her most blessed burden, by an unusual vision; but by the interpretation [Col. 0652A] of that same vision he consoled her … Thus indeed our Bernard, from the moment he began in any manner to live, began to appear wonderful. He had not yet been born, and already he was being proclaimed—or rather, he himself was already preaching. He was not yet even at the breast, and yet he already appeared to be praising the Lord. Nor without reason is he thus commended before he is born; not without reason, I say, was he magnified by a divine oracle while still a little child borne in his mother’s womb.”

19. Hence Burchard, Abbot of Balerne, in the subscription which he appended to book I of the Life after William, its author, had died, says:

> “He who, even in his mother’s womb, seemed to have received a signification [variant: sanctification], from which were conceived presages of the future holiness alike of his life and teaching.”

But his mother, rejoicing at such a presage and already then anticipating the joys to come to her from such a son, “was wholly transformed into love for him not yet born,” as William says in chapter 1, “thinking to give him for instruction in sacred letters”—although, as may be supposed, others were intended for knighthood according to their country’s custom—and striving earnestly to do whatever could contribute to this end, “in accordance with the character of the vision and interpretation by which such sublime things were promised to her concerning him,” as the same author adds. And so it was done.

20. Meanwhile, “after Aleth had given birth,” as the most illustrious Manrique recounts in no. 7, “she had always followed the custom of offering her newborn infants to God, then taking them back after the offering to nourish them with her own milk—either because a mother who remained whole, for women who do not nurse seem to halve the duties of mothers, claimed greater right over those offered and thus offered more of them to God; or because the offering itself, enclosed within both those maternal offices, might be innate rather than extraneous in every respect.” William (whom henceforth, when citing passages from Manrique, we shall call *Guillermus*) and Alan explain the reason a little differently, writing in book I, chapter 1:

> “As though with her mother’s milk she infused into them, in some manner, her own goodness of character.”

In Bernard I read something special. First, as to the offering: as soon as she had brought him forth in a happy birth, she not only offered [him] to God, as she was accustomed to do with the others, but, as we read of Saint Anne, Samuel’s mother, who dedicated [variant: destined] to perpetual service in God’s tabernacle the son she had asked and received from the Lord, so she too offered [him] in God’s Church as an acceptable gift.”

This is from the two biographers just cited.

> “Bernard was presented in the temple so that, even thus from the beginning of his life, he might begin to appear a son of the Virgin Mother. Next, as to milk, Burchard adds that he never wished to suck any other. For, as they report of him, he never suckled at a nurse’s breast except that of his own mother. Thus, already then a partner in her vows before he was conscious of them, and though not yet commanded, he obeyed in all things, a fellow-worker in the maternal piety and offering once conceived by her—himself not only the victim, but also fellow-priest.”

Thus Manrique, who rather rhetorically amplifies Burchard’s words, “For, as they report [Col. 0653A] of him, he never suckled,” etc. (see Surius on this 20th day of August after book I of the *Life*; for I read nothing concerning this matter in Burchard’s subscription which we are to publish). The same Burchard continues concerning Bernard’s infancy, in these words:

> “From his mother’s womb there came forth with him signs of goodness: a comely face, a pleasing countenance, dove-like eyes. Whatever served in him as a sign of goodness by nature’s gift passed, through grace’s gift, into virtue. An infant, not yet speaking with the tongue, he seemed already to speak through grace received.”

21. But to these remarks concerning the exceptional prerogatives of nature and grace, several particulars must be added from William and Alan, chapter 1. Concerning his pursuit of letters and the excellence of his intellect, they relate:

> “As soon as she could,” Bernard’s mother “placed the boy in the church of Châtillon—known later to have been raised through Bernard’s own efforts from secular life to an order of Regular Canons—in the care of masters to be educated in letters, and did all she could to ensure that he should advance in them. The boy, full both of grace and natural talent, quickly fulfilled his mother’s desire in this. For in the study of letters he advanced beyond his age and ahead of his contemporaries.”

Nor is this surprising, since, besides the strength of intellect with which he was endowed, he diligently avoided the other diversions of early life which draw the mind far elsewhere.

> “For in worldly matters he was most simple, loving to dwell with himself, avoiding public life, wonderfully thoughtful … seldom abroad.”

Add to these our copy from the Aurea Vallis manuscript, sent by the Reverend Father Alexander Wiltheim, rector of the Jesuit college at Luxembourg, where the copy reads:

> “In matters pertaining to letters the boy possessed a most penetrating intellect, learning more easily than all his contemporaries whatever was taught by his masters.”

22. Burchard’s wording in Surius is as follows: “Weaned from the breast and now passing into boyhood, he already showed a certain maturity, surpassing the claims of childhood.” Nor did he cultivate himself only by those studies through which childhood is ordinarily formed toward humane learning; “but he was also devoted to the study of letters, through which he might learn and know God in the Scriptures,” according to William and Alan, ch. 1. Hence [Col. 0653D] one may see, says Manrique under the year of Christ 1105, ch. 2, nos. 6–7, “that what is commonly said of him—that he received theology infused by God, and that he himself used to say that he had learned amid beeches and oaks—must be referred rather to his advances than to his beginnings, and to a higher and more certain contemplation of things than could be obtained in the schools. Otherwise, he was imbued with the rudiments of theology—rudimentary indeed, given the character of that age—yet nonetheless imbued with them, and not moderately conversant with Holy Scripture.”

23. Manrique also holds that he applied himself to poetry, reporting in the same place, nos. 7–8:

> “I am not unaware that it was once written of him that, from almost the first rudiments of his youth, he practised poetry, [Col. 0654A] publishing verses in the vernacular tongue which were spread far and wide throughout all France and had not become obsolete even after many years; and that he also not only challenged but surpassed brothers otherwise most dear to him, not to mention his fellow-soldiers in study, in contests of rhythm and displays of keen invention. Yet these assertions—being unworthy of any credit, since they were cast as an insult by a condemned author, Berengar, disciple of Abelard, in the *Apology against Blessed Bernard*, printed at Paris in 1616, which nevertheless in this year 1632 the sacred tribunal of the Inquisition in Spain judged should be entirely suppressed,” as Manrique himself notes in the margin—“might perhaps be true nevertheless, though then hurled forth in rage. Certainly Bernard’s rhythmic prayers addressed to the individual members of the suffering Saviour, [Col. 0654B] to Christ the Lord and to his Virgin Mother, and others of that kind, reveal the brilliance of his genius. Even today one reads his little book called *Floretus*, composed in heroic, and not inelegant, verse, in which he treats clearly and exactly of vices and virtues, the sacraments, and all the mysteries of our faith.

24. “Nor is it, as appears, a spurious production; for John Gerson, an ancient and weighty theologian, received and published it not only as Bernard’s work, but illustrated it with a fairly extensive commentary, which the reader will find printed in folio at Lyons by John Marion in 1720, and elsewhere as well. Bernard therefore cultivated poetry considerably, and exercised it upon more sacred subjects. Nor would it be strange if, having once changed his subject matter and yielding to place, time, and age, he displayed some form [Col. 0654C] of it.”

Thus Manrique judges. But I do not set myself up as arbiter in this matter, both because I read nothing about it in the earliest biographers, and because, whether it is so or otherwise, it contributes little to the praise of the holy doctor. By so many other labours he attained that glory that it need not at all be sought from poetic trifles of this kind. Moreover, Mabillon’s *Admonition concerning verses and rhythms ascribed to St Bernard*, found in volume II, col. 891, may be consulted. There he reports that he does not think the verses and rhythms which he appends should be attributed to Bernard. But we shall speak below also of the holy man’s writings, insofar as is sufficient for our purpose.

## § III. Heavenly favours bestowed upon the saint; his purpose of adopting the monastic life; obstacles overcome against it; companions gathered to the same purpose; his wondrous mastery over human hearts; life before his entrance among the Cistercians.

[Col. 0654D]

25. Besides the adornments of intellect and learning through which the Saint shone beyond what childhood permits, we must deservedly recognize in him outstanding morals and special favours of divine grace. Let William be heard in ch. 1, no. 5 of his *Life* as printed by us:

> “Already amid worldly matters he was, as though naturally, beginning the mortification of his future perfection. He was obedient and subject to his parents; kind and agreeable to all … and, beyond what could be believed, modest; nowhere loving to speak much; devoted to God, that he might preserve his childhood in purity.”

Divine mercy anticipated this innocent [Col. 0655A] manner of life with blessings. For, as William relates in ch. 1, no. 6:

> “While still a little boy he was afflicted with a severe headache and took to his bed. A little woman was brought to him, as though she would ease the pain by charms, ‘or magical tricks.’ When he perceived her approaching with the charm-working instruments by which she habitually deceived common people, he indignantly cried out, drove her away from him, and cast her off. Nor did divine mercy fail the good zeal of the holy boy; immediately he felt power, and, rising in that very impulse of the spirit, knew himself freed from all pain.”

26. What of the fact that, besides this bodily health, an altogether singular grace of soul was granted him by the Lord, [Col. 0655B] when, while still a boy, the boy Jesus appeared to him … like a bridegroom going forth anew from his chamber? The infant Word appeared to him, as though once more being born before his eyes from the womb of the Virgin Mother, as is written in the same place. With what streams of divine grace and what honey of anointing the future mellifluous doctor was sprinkled through that appearance may readily be understood both from the nature of the event itself and from the fruit that later followed from it. For the same biographer immediately says:

> “Those who have frequented his teaching may easily observe in what blessing the Lord anticipated him at that hour: for even to this day, in matters belonging to that mystery, he seems to have at hand both a deeper understanding and a fuller discourse. Hence later, in praise of the mother and the child [Col. 0655C] and of his holy Nativity, he produced a distinguished little work,”

which is discussed in the same place.

From these facts, then, it follows that in Bernard heavenly favours corresponded to merits, and merits to favours, from his very childhood; and, as I said above from Burchard, “whatever he possessed as an indication of goodness by nature’s gift passed, through the gift of grace, into virtue.” Not a little also contributed to this the wonderful mercy toward the poor which was in some way innate in him even then. William says in the same place, no. 7:

> “Nor should this be passed over: from his very childhood, whenever he could have any coins, he gave alms secretly, thereby both accommodating himself to his own modesty and pursuing works of piety appropriate to his age—indeed, beyond his age.” [Col. 0655D]

But since these matters already reported may be called either the beginnings or the preludes of far greater things to be related concerning the saint, we must now see how excellently, as his age gradually increased, the adornments of virtues and heavenly graces increased with it.

27. “But when,” as William has it in the place cited, “some time had passed, and the boy Bernard, increasing in age and grace before God and men, passed from childhood into youth, his mother … happily departed to the Lord.” After his mother’s death Bernard, left in the world, aroused great expectations concerning himself because of the singular graces with which he was endowed. Great hopes smiled upon him; [Col. 0656A] friendships besieged him; terrible snares were laid against his chastity. Yet at so slippery an age he triumphed most uncorrupted through a perilous conflict and stood unharmed amid those fires. But since William treats these matters vividly in ch. 1, it is enough to have indicated them briefly here.

“Yet these victories,” as the most illustrious Manrique testifies under the year 1110, ch. 2, no. 6, “were not without a reward, which he received even in this life. The anonymous Frenchman, book VII, ch. 9, in his *Acts*—which, as he says, he received from John the Hermit, Bernard’s contemporary, and therefore claims a more assured authority—relates that, many years later, when the holy man governed Clairvaux, certain women possessed by demons were brought to him to be freed by him. Before the saint arrived, the demon driven from [Col. 0656B] one woman—or rather departing of his own accord—cried out that he could not resist Bernard, since he had been handed over to obey him in all things: Bernard, while still living in the world, had been violently tempted by that demon in works against chastity, yet had remained wholly unconquered. Recounting these and similar trophies over the common enemy, the holy man gloriously triumphed through God’s grace.”

We have just seen Bernard living in the world; now let us follow him, in Manrique’s words under the year just mentioned, no. 7, as he turns from the world to a more perfect life.

28. “Then indeed,” he says, “in the very flower of youth, in the twentieth year of his age—when others are commonly delayed the more because the heat of desire rises more violently and overwhelms the fervour of the spirit—he, on the contrary, through the prevalence [Col. 0656C] of that same grace restraining every rebellious movement, began to feel the first calls of the wilderness; he began then to meditate on flight from the world and on Cîteaux, deeply fixed in his heart: a saving refuge for one in peril, a remedy for one infirm, a preventive medicine for one strong. The rays, like those of the sun, of that heavenly sphere then shining upon earth—already illumined by moon and stars, that is, by Stephen and his companions—were awaiting him, though he least expected it.”

Whoever wishes to read in the biographers the description of this first conversion may consult William, ch. 2. There he will also find the efforts of Bernard’s brothers and friends, who did everything possible “to divert his mind toward literary study and, by love of secular knowledge, bind him more closely to the world.”

[Col. 0656D] 29. This is stated there very briefly. But the most illustrious Manrique, under the year 1111, in the sole chapter, no. 4, enlarging upon it, relates that his brothers added:

> “Men are not born for themselves alone, but to benefit the commonwealth—indeed, the world. Monks hiding in the wilderness and fleeing the world help no one either by learning or by example. Rather, under the respectable name of contemplation, they disguise idleness and devote themselves to sloth and inactivity; sustained by others’ alms, they are, as the Emperor Tiberius once said of others, idle for themselves and burdensome to others. Let them then shake off idleness by working and seeking their food from their own sweat; let them relieve the burden of others as well. Such was the report concerning that new kind of monks recently established on the estate of Balne. [Col. 0657A] Yet a young man of such great promise, outstanding in natural gifts, character, and intellect, and granted to the world for the glory of his own family, as they believed—or rather for common service—ought not to be enslaved to the country and the plough. There are many left for tilling fields to whom no other duties can be assigned. He himself owes service to public affairs, lest, if he hides in a deserted and trackless land the talent entrusted to him by God, he incur condemnation,” etc.

30. Although the schemes of his brothers and friends did not alter the pious young man, steadfast in his purpose, they nevertheless caused him some delay. For, as William reports, ch. 2, no. 11, “by this very suggestion, as he used to confess, his steps had been almost delayed.” The manuscript of Aulne says more:

> “They urged him toward literary studies, by which path they hoped they could most easily keep him back. Their argument pleased him, and a day was fixed on which his brothers would provide the necessities for his journey, and he would thus set out for Germany.” [Col. 0657B]

But there is no counsel against the Lord. Bernard overcame every obstacle through the working of the Holy Spirit, which recalled to his mind the memory of his most pious mother, and the hope and expectation of a better and higher destiny that she had conceived—and already tasted—in regard to her most beloved son. Let us hear William on this matter in the cited place:

> “The memory of his holy mother importunately pressed upon his mind, so that he seemed often to see her appearing before him, following him and reproaching him because she had not brought him up so tenderly for this sort of foolishness, nor educated him in this hope.” [Col. 0657C]

31. The manuscript of Aulne agrees with William:

> “Hastening toward the appointed day and place, he suddenly began to turn over in his mind the image of his mother and was confounded that he was disappointing the hope she had conceived concerning him and doing nothing for her who had brought him up so tenderly.”

Thus Bernard was restored to the former course of his heavenly calling; and at last he was conquered—or rather, he emerged crowned as victor over himself and his brothers. Obeying divine and maternal admonitions, he devoted himself wholly to God’s service, in which to serve is to reign. Indeed, he brought over to his own [Col. 0657D] conviction and happily joined to the fellowship of the same monastic institute those very brothers who had earlier been his principal opponents in his most pious resolution to embrace a better life. He begot them in Christ Jesus and, from being their brother by blood, became their father in the spirit.

Let us continue with William:

> “First of all, his uncle Galdric, without delay or hesitation, went over, as they say, feet first to his nephew’s opinion and to consent to conversion.”

The brothers followed afterward. In what order and manner these things happened, with what ardent Holy Spirit, and with what remarkable prophecy on some occasions, the same biographer William relates individually and movingly. Manrique connects these events with the year of Christ 1112, the fifteenth of Cîteaux, where he also gives a fairly extensive narrative of what took place.

32. But a wondrous and altogether heavenly power moved Bernard [Col. 0658A] when, thundering forth the word of God, he strove to enlarge the little flock of the Lord which he had gathered, by new additions. For, according to William, “as he preached publicly and privately, mothers hid their sons, wives held back their husbands, friends turned friends away; because the Holy Spirit gave his voice such power that scarcely could any affection hold anyone back.” This new and youthful preacher had received from the Spirit working within him such powerful mastery over human hearts.

Among the many remarkable conversions, however, one deserves no low place: that which occurred in Hugh of Mâcon, whom William praises in no. 15 as “distinguished by nobility and excellence of character, possessions and worldly riches; who today, on account of the merit of his religious life and holiness, having been taken from the monastery of Pontigny which he himself built, rightly and honourably presides over the church of Auxerre as bishop.” The biographer then recounts his calling to a more perfect life. Since the account of this event extant in William differs from that found in our copy from the manuscript of Aulne, we did not think the reader should be deprived of the latter. Here, then, is its text.

33. One day he said to his brothers: “I have a friend at Mâcon, Hugh of Vitry, and he too must be brought in, so that he may be one of us.” He was a noble cleric, already of rather mature age, abounding in both secular and ecclesiastical possessions. Those who knew him began therefore to accuse Bernard of rashness. Nevertheless, confident and without anyone’s hesitation, he hastened [Col. 0658C] to Hugh.

There was a report in the region that he was about to go to Jerusalem. Thus he himself gave out, intending to go not to the Jerusalem in which he had been, but to that Jerusalem in which God is. When the said Hugh saw him, weeping and wailing, he threw himself into Bernard’s embrace. But the man of God paid no attention whatsoever to his tears. When Hugh had recovered himself a little, Bernard disclosed his purpose to him; and behold, the grief was renewed and a more abundant fountain of tears flowed, so that his eye did not rest throughout that whole day.

The following night they lay together upon an exceedingly narrow bed, scarcely large enough for one of them. Hugh still did not cease from tears, so that the holy man reproved him for not allowing him to sleep. But when he had fallen asleep, he seemed to himself, having as usual invoked the Holy Spirit, to be speaking with Hugh about conversion [Col. 0658D]; and power was not lacking to his voice.

34. When morning came, Hugh again wept. Bernard, now taking it ill, began to rebuke him more severely. But Hugh said: “Today I have not the same cause for mourning that I had yesterday. Yesterday I wept over you; today I weep over myself. For I know your manner of life, and I do not fail to know that conversion is more necessary for me than for you.”

Bernard rejoiced and said to him: “Weep enough now, for these tears are excellent; do not cease.”

Thereafter, when the clerics saw them walking together and rejoicing together, never separated from one another even for a moment, they tried to tear Hugh away from Bernard, fearing—or rather now openly recognizing—that they were moved by one spirit. Holding Hugh, therefore, they would by no means allow [Col. 0659A] the man of God to speak with him further. Bernard departed sorrowful, yet his heart still had confidence in the Lord.

After some days, hearing that a gathering of bishops was being held, he hurried there in order to see Hugh. When the clerics saw him, they looked upon him with grim eyes, contrary to custom, and surrounded Hugh on every side so that no approach might be open. While the bishops were seated in a field and conversing among the clerics, Bernard sat beside Hugh. He could not speak with him because of those standing by, but he wept copiously upon Hugh’s neck. And behold, the waters poured down and heaven gave rain, so that they scattered and hurried to the nearest village; but the blessed man, holding Hugh’s hand, said: “You shall stand with me in the rain.” Immediately fair weather returned, and they alone stood in the field.

[Col. 0659B] 35. Hugh confessed the oath he had made: that he would by no means become a monk until a year had passed. He had made this oath to deceive the clerics, for he knew well that there was an annual probation. There, with their spiritual fellowship wholly reaffirmed, they returned holding each other’s hand. All now despaired, and thereafter no one attempted to detain Hugh.

From this new victory of Bernard grew a new triumph in his praise, altogether singular because of so great a man whom he added to the monastic institute. It is pleasing to append Manrique’s conclusion, which, concerning Hugh’s conversion under the year of Christ 1112, ch. 2, from no. 3 onward, he adds in this manner:

> “From these things you may see Bernard’s almost immeasurable power even at the very beginning of his conversion: namely, his closing heaven with clouds and again [Col. 0659C] opening its gates according to his will, the Lord obedient even before a word was uttered to the thought of a man; so that Bernard’s tongue, and even then his heart, might be proved to be keys of heaven. You may further see the happy times of the primitive Church renewed, and those first callings of Christ, preferring neither relatives nor strangers; miracles and wonders renewed, by which men were drawn to the Gospel.”

36. What that holy flock did in the meantime, before entering the monastery of Cîteaux, may be read in William. From him I select these words from no. 17:

> “As the number increased of those who had agreed upon this unanimity of conversion, as we read of the first children of the Church: ‘The multitude of them [Col. 0659D] had one heart and one soul in the Lord’; they dwelt together in unanimity, and no one else dared join himself to them. For at Châtillon they had one house of their own, common to all, where they assembled, lived together, and conversed; scarcely anyone who was not of their company dared enter it … They themselves remained for about six months after their first resolve in secular dress, so that more might be gathered together while, in the meantime, the affairs of certain persons were being settled.”

These, indeed, were the beginnings of those great things which St Bernard afterward accomplished excellently and successfully, through himself and others, for the glory of God, the good of the Catholic Church, and the spread of the monastic institute. Let us now accompany him and his fellowship as they enter [Col. 0660A] beneath the roof of the monastery of Cîteaux.

## § IV. Novitiate; virtues practised within it; reception of the habit; religious profession; exercises of soul and body.

37. “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, the fifteenth from the foundation of the house of Cîteaux, Bernard, servant of God, about thirty-three [elsewhere, twenty-two] years old, entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions, and under Abbot Stephen submitted his neck to Christ’s sweet yoke.” Thus William, ch. 3 of the *Life*.

Under this year, ch. 2, no. 1, Manrique makes several observations about the number of companions:

> “Nor,” he says, “were all admitted without selection. Robert, a young man, was rejected because he was too tender in age; if he returned more mature, he was to be received. Meanwhile I note that perhaps this is why some report that only thirty men came, while others say that Bernard came with thirty: namely, because Robert was counted among them, though the postponement—not removal—of his probation left him, as it were, in doubt for either account.” [Col. 0660B]

Nor does the little book entitled *The Beginning of the Monastery of Cîteaux*—which we call the *Lesser Beginning of Cîteaux* to distinguish it from the *Great Beginning of Cîteaux*—raise the number of companions above thirty. This is evident from the words of ch. 17 of the same *Lesser Beginning*, cited in Bertrand Tissier, to be mentioned more fully later, and written by St Stephen:

> “Therefore in those times the Lord visited that place. For by God’s grace he sent at one time to that church so many learned clerics, noble laymen, and persons powerful and equally noble in the world, that thirty entered the novices’ cell together with joy, [Col. 0660C] and, contending well and bravely against their own vices and against the incitements of evil spirits, completed their course.”

38. And immediately, Manrique says in no. 2, “The same event, but beginning somewhat further back, is set forth in an ancient poem which is said to remain even today at Cîteaux, inscribed upon a tablet hanging on the columns of its church.” He recites the poem there as follows:

> In the year one thousand and ninety-one together,  
> Fontaines gave Bernard his birth.  
> Then, only seven years having elapsed,  
> The Cistercian order began in this monastery.  
> When it had at last grown to fifteen years,  
> The holy man received the religious habit within it  
> Under Stephen, bringing thirty companions.

[Col. 0660D] What is said there about the religious habit is corrected shortly afterward, as needing correction “by a sponge,” by the aforementioned author of the *Cistercian Annals*, as we shall presently see. In the same place, nos. 3–4, he continues:

39. “But Stephen, forewarned by God through the oracles already reported above, and from the coming of these men conceiving a firmer hope of things to come, rejected only Robert because he was a boy—though he was to be admitted if he persevered, as we shall note. All the rest he gladly admitted, not indeed to receive the religious habit immediately, since in those days this was not customary before the year of probation was completed, but to be tested in secular dress, which after a completed year was at last to be laid aside.

“I infer both points from Bernard’s letter to this same Robert, the first among all the saint’s letters, if not in time, then in the dignity of the miracle performed while it was being written—a miracle to be related by us in the year in which it occurred. First, from these words:

> ‘You came from the world to Cîteaux, Robert, as you yourself bear witness. You asked, you sought, you knocked; but because of your still tender age, though against your will, you were deferred for two years.’

“Second, from the words added a little below:

> ‘After this, tested for a year according to the Rule in all patience, continuing steadfastly and without complaint, after the year you freely made profession; then, for the first time, having laid aside secular dress, you received the religious habit.’” [Col. 0661A]

40. How abundantly the Lord enriched the coming of these new ascetics, and especially of Bernard, with heavenly gifts and with the expansion of the Order, we learn from William at the beginning of ch. 3:

> “From that day the Lord gave blessing, and that vineyard of the Lord of Hosts yielded its fruit, stretching forth its branches unto the sea and its shoots beyond the sea.”

Add to this what he had just said at the end of ch. 2. Indeed, the *Lesser Beginning of Cîteaux*, in the passage cited above, testifies that through the example of St Bernard and his other companions, very many people, weary of human affairs, had already come to Cîteaux:

> “Encouraged by their example, old men and young men, and persons of different ages in different parts of the world, seeing that in these men what they had formerly feared impossible—the observance of the Rule—was possible, began to flock there, submit proud necks to Christ’s sweet yoke, ardently [Col. 0661C] love the hard and harsh commands of the Rule, and wonderfully gladden and strengthen that church.”

41. Bernard earnestly endeavoured to preserve the fervent spirit which he had brought with him from the world into the monastic novitiate, to kindle it ever more and more with fresh fuel of heavenly flames, and to adorn it with the ornaments of solid virtues. In speaking of his novitiate, William in ch. 3 opens a broad field for describing his way of life and due praises, as may be seen there more fully. Yet, kind reader, here are a few specimens selected from the many things said there:

> “How he lived an angelic life on earth, I think no one can recount who does not live by the spirit by which he lived.”

And immediately:

> “He entered that house … [Col. 0661D] intending there to die to the hearts and memories of men, and hoping to hide and lie concealed like a lost vessel. But God disposed otherwise, preparing him as a vessel of election not only to strengthen and enlarge the monastic order, but also to bear his name before kings and nations and unto the end of the earth.”

Yet the holy novice was utterly little in his own eyes, “thinking or judging nothing of the sort concerning himself; rather, for the guarding of his heart and steadfastness in purpose, he always had in his heart, and often also on his lips: ‘Bernard, Bernard, for what have you come?’”

42. Finally, there follow in the same place, no. 23:

> “While he was a novice, sparing himself in nothing, he strove by every means to mortify not only the desires of the flesh, which are effected through the bodily senses, but even the senses themselves through which they are effected … He scarcely allowed them as much as sufficed for the fellowship of outward intercourse with men. Since the force of continual practice had brought this into habit, the habit itself became in some manner nature to him. Wholly absorbed in the spirit, with every hope directed toward God by intention, and all memory occupied by spiritual meditation, seeing he did not see, hearing he did not hear; nothing tasted pleasant to one eating; he scarcely felt anything through any bodily sense. He had already spent a whole year in the novices’ cell when, on leaving it, he still did not know whether the house itself had a vault, which we customarily call a ceiling.” [Col. 0662A]

William there recounts more, with high praise of the novitiate undergone by our saint and of the most splendid virtues with which he was adorned.

43. The fourth *Life*, published by Mabillon and written by John the Hermit, book II, from col. 1284, recounts an example which makes clear how severely the holy novice punished even the slightest faults:

> “Therefore, while the most holy young man was in the novices’ cell, some of his relatives came to visit him and spoke with him. But after the signal for the ninth hour, each returned to his own place, and the most devout young man went to church for the work of God. Then, according to custom, raising his eyes to heaven, he thought to find the grace of God as before, but did not find it. He considered within himself that this had happened to him for some fault or sin; and he found nothing except the idle talk to which, shortly before, through imprudence, he had exposed himself. [Col. 0662C] When he understood himself to be guilty for this reason, he prostrated his whole body beside the altar, saying with the Prophet: ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath,’ etc. Having done this for twenty-five days, the glory of the Lord appeared to him, filled him, and gave him knowledge of the saints, so that his works might be completed unto good.”

44. “Others also came to visit him and obtained permission from Abbot Stephen to speak with him. As he was being led to them, he took pieces of tow and put them under his hood, in his ears, so that by this contrivance he might keep himself free [Col. 0662D] from idle conversation. Thus he came to the guests and remained with them for the whole hour, hearing nothing. He spoke only a few words of edification. Then, when the bell rang, he rejoiced, left them, and came to church, his grace being thus preserved for him by God. O man of outstanding holiness and worthy of remembrance! By providing for himself in this way, he edifies those who hear even now, and will edify them to the end, being beneficial not to himself alone but to countless persons.”

If that biographer means, in the second example, that Bernard was wearing a hood while still a novice—and therefore, according to what will shortly be said, not yet clothed in the monastic habit—it does not seem sufficiently consistent with another account which I shall immediately present. Meanwhile, one may infer from this how zealously the most devout young man strove after solid perfection, since he disciplined in himself with such exactness even the slightest blemishes which seemed capable of hindering him ever so little. Manrique makes some observations concerning Bernard’s solemn profession and that of his companions under the year of Christ 1114, ch. 1, no. 1 and following, writing thus:

45. “The following year, namely the year of Christ 1114, the seventeenth of Cîteaux, was favourable to the solemn vows [Col. 0663A] of Bernard and his companions … The authors suggest rather than affirm that Bernard and his companions professed the Rule after a year. I do not think this occurred without a mystery. For it is not the habit that makes the monk, but profession; indeed, since they did not even wear a novice’s habit then, as we showed in the preceding year, it appears quite remarkable that their entry is described by everyone but their profession related by no one. Perhaps this was left to the constancy of men of God, who, once they had put their hand to the plough, would undoubtedly complete what they had begun.

“Nevertheless they professed the Rule of the blessed Father Benedict according to the rigour of the congregation of Cîteaux, and then for the first time were clothed in the monastic habit and tonsured. It has pleased me to note this final point as well. For, just as probation was customarily exacted without the habit, so also without tonsure in those times. I have as witness Caesarius of Heisterbach, writing a hundred years later about a novice then his contemporary, book IV of the *Dialogues*, ch. 51:

[Col. 0663C] 46. “‘A certain novice, having spent the year of probation quite peaceably at Himmerod’—a Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Trier—‘and having expressed his will for stability in the Chapter, was to be shaved into a monk. The one who was to shave him was sharpening the razor—that is, the shaving blade—upon a strap, and at that very hour so grieved him,’ etc.

“From this you may see that no one was customarily shaved before expressing the will for stability. This is more remarkable in Caesarius’s time, when novices already wore the cowl and hood, the badge of religion—perhaps so that they might not be held by that mark if they wished to depart halfway through their year of probation. Therefore, in the earliest times of the Order, candidates were tested in secular habit and tonsure. Later, though tonsure was postponed, a habit was permitted, however very unlike the monastic one; this, as we see, still remains today. Finally, in the course of time it came about that they received habit and tonsure together, perhaps a practice first introduced by the newly arisen mendicant orders and gradually extended also to our own.” [Col. 0663D]

47. But, leaving this brief digression, let us return with Manrique to the solemn profession. In no. 4 he notes the following concerning its order:

> “There are those who affirm that Bernard was the first to pronounce the vows; this, he says, is doubtful to me. His tenderer age and deeper humility prevented the master of all from being preferred to the others. Otherwise Hugh would not have been sent first to found Pontigny in Champagne; nor, when Bernard had been appointed abbot of Clairvaux, would all [Col. 0664A] have been seized by the astonishment described by Abbot William in book I, ch. 3 of his *Life*: ‘They marvelled indeed, as men mature both in religion and in the world, and feared for him both on account of the tender age of his youth and on account of bodily weakness and lesser experience of outward affairs.’

> “I should think that they were admitted before that year and then professed in the order of their ages, with either nothing or little changed; except perhaps that clerics preceded married men, and married men the unmarried. Let this brief preliminary survey suffice concerning the profession omitted by the ancient writers.”

48. To this belongs also the saint’s unremitting fervour and the art of reaping divinely infused into him. On these matters Manrique, in the passage cited, from no. 8 records the following:

> “Meanwhile Father Bernard and his companions, fervent in spirit [Col. 0664B] as they were in their new state, persevered in prayers, wore down their bodies with vigils and fasts, devoutly sang the divine praises in choir, and nevertheless worked with their hands, kept silence, applied themselves to reading, and without interruption practised the remaining observances of the religious life—without complaint—while Stephen, formerly their instructor, now marvelled at them and truly experienced the vigorous leaders whom shortly before he had called novices. Indeed, William says much of Bernard’s virtues, as do all who wrote the Life of the blessed man—matters which it would be too lengthy to transcribe here. But what they relate about his skill in reaping, miraculously bestowed upon the servant of God, since it contains a particular lesson perhaps less approved of, or at least less practised, in our times, we do not think should be passed over in silence.”

This is especially so because it makes manifest [Col. 0664C] the remarkable manner in which divine providence dealt with our saint: when it pleased to have a man so great, born to accomplish undertakings of the highest importance, begin his ascent to such great and numerous deeds from the lowly and modest labour of reaping, as we shall now see.

## § V. The art of reaping divinely granted to the saint; departure from Cîteaux for the monastery of Clairvaux; various notices concerning it; the year in which it was founded

49. The holy man had made up for his ignorance of reaping, as Manrique relates in no. 9, “in the following year, other tasks having been assigned in place of the harvest-work. Although those tasks involved no less labour, their practice was easier, and they suited limbs readier for daily work than reaping, which returns only after a year. [Col. 0664D] Yet to be separated alone from the rest, and not to reap with the reaping brethren, distressed his soul, ardent for the common life. Nor was there always something else to do; nor, if there were, was it permitted to him, since his strength had failed through bodily weakness and excessive abstinence and vigils.

“Let those hear this who think such external works to be of little value before God. Let those hear it who assign the entire business to the mind, holding the body so exempt from labours that they judge it less fitted for contemplation if it is wearied. Bernard—the future illustrious doctor of the Church, indeed its oracle and pillar of faith; under whose leadership and command the necks of schismatics were to be subdued and heretics trodden down; Bernard, granted to the world to strengthen all Catholics and establish the very throne of the Roman pontiff [Col. 0665A]; Father Bernard, who was to move kings and kingdoms, and at last the whole Christian world, at his command; whose words councils adopted while he was still living, and to whom even sacred Scripture was to be submitted, as though to the key-bearer of heavenly mysteries (this must be understood suitably, lest Manrique say too much)—Bernard, I say, as he took the first step toward all these things, began with skill in reaping. This skill, obtained from God through tears and granted not without a miracle, commends both tears and miracles as useful even for attaining the summit of a doctor’s office in the Church.”

50. William narrates the event, chapter 3, no. 27:

> “At harvest time, while the brethren were busily engaged in cutting grain with fervour and the joy of the Holy Spirit, he himself, [Col. 0665B] being as it were incapable of and unskilled in that work, was told to sit and rest. Greatly saddened, he had recourse to prayer, asking God with many tears to grant him the grace of reaping. Nor did the simplicity of faith disappoint the desire of this religious man. For immediately he obtained what he asked.
