From that day he rejoiced, with a certain delight, that in this labour he was more skilled than the others; and he was so much the more devoted in this work because he remembered that he had received the ability for it from God’s gift alone.”

Manrique judges that this grace given to Bernard belongs to the year of Christ 1114, “because,” he says, “after making his profession, the man of God was present at Cîteaux only for gathering this one harvest; for in June of the following year he was to be transferred, as we shall say, to Clairvaux.”

It remains for us now to consider [Col. 0665C] how, having been transferred there, or having gone from Cîteaux thither with the others, he began his administration of the abbey of Clairvaux, of which he was the first abbot. The year in which he was raised to the abbatial dignity is confirmed by ancient verses which, as Manrique observes under the year 1115, chapter 1, no. 6, many manuscripts append to Bernard’s works, and which he there gives:

> The thousandth year is counted with three fives,  
> And likewise the hundredth, when the holy man is made  
> Abbot, and follows the decrees of the earlier Fathers;  
> He becomes teacher of the brethren, light of the faith, rule of morals.

51. Bernard’s brethren were sent with him to found the monastery of Clairvaux, as William his biographer testifies, book I, chapter 3, no. 28:

> “When it pleased Him who had separated him from the world and called him, that He might reveal His glory in him with fuller grace . . . He put it into the heart of Abbot Stephen to send his brethren to build the house of Clairvaux. As they departed, he also appointed Lord Bernard himself as their abbot.” [Col. 0665D]

Manrique further mentions, in no. 5, others joined to him, and then in no. 6 says:

> “That Stephen should place Bernard over such great men—young in age, having scarcely passed his twenty-fourth year, weak in body, entangled or hampered by shyness, and lacking every kind of experience—appeared marvellous in everyone’s eyes, and perhaps for that reason was declared later. Certainly William seems to imply that he was by no means named before the departure,”

from the words I have just quoted from him, [Col. 0666A] “As they departed, he also appointed Lord Bernard himself as their abbot,” and from the words immediately added by the same biographer:

> “They marvelled indeed, as men mature and vigorous both in religion and in the world, and feared for him both because of the tender age of his youth, his bodily weakness, and his limited experience of outward affairs.”

But it is nothing new for divine providence to use weak instruments to accomplish the greatest things, as the many and great outcomes in Bernard proved. Concerning his departure from the monastery of Cîteaux, it seems fitting here to make some observations with Manrique.

52. “Moreover,” he says under the year just cited, no. 7, “I shall not hesitate to transcribe word for word the departure of a new community, as it was customarily made in the Order and as described by Caesarius of Heisterbach, because it displays solemnity combined with devotion.” He cites in the margin Caesarius’s homily for the third Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany, in these words:

> “Twelve monks, in the place of the twelve Apostles, are sent out with a thirteenth, the abbot, who is set over them in Christ’s place, to found a new abbey. A cross bearing the image of the Lord is given into the hands of him who is leaving the oratory with that cross; the twelve appointed for this follow him, as the Apostles followed Christ.” [Col. 0666B]

Thus he, from Caesarius; and there you see the number assigned to this new colony. “Therefore,” as the same Manrique adds, “after the cross had been placed in Bernard’s hands by Father Stephen, he went first, like father and leader of all; immediately his brethren and sons departed [Col. 0666C] to seek a site among the people of Langres. As they were about to leave, you might have seen tears falling in profound silence, while only the voices of all the monks chanting sounded amid sobs. For the restraint externally governing their limbs scarcely prevailed over their inward emotions; nor could one distinguish those who were to remain from those departing, until, at the gate of the house, the very hesitation of those standing separated them from those going forward. Such was the devout indeed, but sorrowful, aspect of Cîteaux when Bernard and his companions departed.”

53. Before we leave the Cistercians at Cîteaux with our holy abbot for Clairvaux, since the holy man there laid the first foundations of a more perfect life, and afterwards illustriously adorned and extended that community both by himself and through others whom he joined to those ascetics; since we have already so often mentioned the Cistercians, and shall do so again, we think it not irrelevant to add here certain notices concerning this most pious and celebrated school of ascetic life. We shall point out more information in authors who have written about it than we shall gather here at length and in detail, lest the discourse range too far.

Its founder was St Robert, first abbot of Molesme, whose acts were long ago illustrated by us in volume III for April, on the twenty-ninth day of that month, from page 662. There, moreover, § 2 of the Preliminary Commentary on his Life, page 664 and following, treats of the beginnings of the monastery and Order of Cîteaux, and of St Robert’s transfer to it, which occurred in the year of Christ [Col. 0667A] 1098. He was likewise the first abbot of Cîteaux; but not long afterward, having resigned his office among the Cistercians, he returned to the monks of Molesme, who pressed for his return before the supreme pontiff Urban II. This may be seen at greater length in the said Commentary, § 3, together with other matters pertaining to this praiseworthy holy founder.

54. Gaspar Jongelinus describes the site in his *Notice of the Abbeys of the Cistercian Order*, page 6:

> “Cistertium (Cîteaux), the chief monastery and head of the Order, under the Rule of St Benedict, is situated in the diocese of Chalon-sur-Saône, about five leagues distant from the city of Dijon . . . in the duchy of Burgundy.”

Now, after Cîteaux’s first daughter, the monastery called La Ferté, in the diocese of Chalon-sur-Saône on the river [Col. 0667B] Cron, and after its second daughter, called Pontigny, situated in the territory of Auxerre—as may be seen in Jongelinus from page 16—there followed Cîteaux’s third daughter, Clairvaux. There we again meet our most holy abbot, whom we have for a while left at Cîteaux as he set out thither. That place too, rendered famous far and wide by the saint’s rule, virtues, and miracles, deserves that we set forth the following documents on its site, foundation, and praises before proceeding further.

55. William the biographer, chapter 3, no. 28:

> “Clairvaux was a place in the territory of Langres, not far from the river Aube, an ancient den of robbers, which in antiquity was called the Valley [Col. 0667C] of Wormwood, either because of the abundance of wormwood growing there or because of the bitter suffering of those who fell into the hands of robbers there.”

And in chapter 4, no. 40, the same author says of the same place:

> “The solitude of the place itself, amid the shadowy woods and narrow passes of the surrounding mountains, in which the servants of God lay hidden, in some fashion represented that cave of our father St Benedict in which he was once discovered by shepherds; so that, as they imitated his life, they might seem also to possess some likeness of his dwelling and solitude.”

Nicolaus Hacqueville, president of the Parliament of Paris, records in a poem [Col. 0667D] on the praises of St Bernard and the site of Clairvaux that the valley was surrounded not only by mountains but also abounded in a perennial spring, besides the waters of the Aube flowing through it. The poem was reprinted by Mabillon, editor of the works of the same Father, in volume II, col. 1305:

> A hidden valley lay amid the mountains, then covered  
> With lofty forest and green bramble . . .  
> The water-bearing stream of the Aube flows through its midst;  
> A spring gives you water in its perpetual bounty.

56. In the edition of the works of St Bernard just mentioned, from col. 1306, there is a description of the position or situation of the monastery of Clairvaux. Besides much else that may be read in the same description—which circulates among Bernard’s works under an uncertain author, though apparently a monk of Clairvaux, according to Manrique under the year 1115, chapter 2, no. 1, and is not without wit—the following is noted in Mabillon’s edition, col. 1309:

> “This spring [Col. 0668A] . . . rises opposite the east, so that at the summer solstice it greets face to face the rosy countenance of the glowing dawn . . . Where the mountain ejects it, the valley swallows it; and where it rises, there in a sense it also dies—indeed is buried. But do not expect the sign of the prophet Jonah, that it should remain hidden for three days and three nights. At once, a thousand paces within the monastery enclosure, as if raised from the heart of the earth, it flows forth and appears in a fashion restored to life, offering itself only to the sight and use of the brethren, so that henceforth its lot may be with the holy, and not with others.”

Thus he alludes to the said spring. Manrique, already cited, explains the etymology of the house thus in no. 5: “The monastery received the name Clairvaux, a bright valley, because of the character of its occupation and discipline, its former bitterness having been changed.” Hence the verse:

> Into a bright valley he transformed the bitter valley.

William, chapter 3, no. 28, reports of the holy abbot and his companions, the first inhabitants of the place:

> “There, therefore, in a place of horror and vast solitude, those men of virtue settled, intending to make from a robbers’ den a temple of God and a house of prayer.” [Col. 0668B]

57. Manrique, under the aforesaid year 1115, chapter 2, no. 1, does not seem to have regarded the foundation of this often-mentioned place as sufficiently certain, when he states concerning the first arrivals there:

> “Whether they found it by chance or sought it after being directed is uncertain. It is certain that they reached a rather dreadful place, said to have been a robbers’ refuge . . . I should suppose that, lacking every resource, they chose this place, useful to none of the inhabitants; indeed harmful, and therefore much more easily obtained.” [Col. 0668C]

We too must therefore speak of the first donation or foundation of the place. In volume I of Mabillon’s edition, containing the genuine works of the holy Father, col. 45, there is Letter 31, written by Bernard himself to Hugh, Count of Champagne, in which he says:

> “Can we forget the old affection and the benefits which you have so generously bestowed upon our house?”

By these words the holy Father professes grateful remembrance toward Hugh, the first founder of his monastery of Clairvaux, as is established from an instrument first published by Pierre-François Chifflet among the proofs of his *Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard*, page 513, taken from the Clairvaux autograph. (It appears above in the notes to St Bernard’s Letter 31, *Works*, vol. I.) [Col. 0668D]

58–59. In Mabillon’s note on the above-mentioned letter of St Bernard—one of the notes to volume I of that holy Father, placed at the end of volume I already mentioned—the following observations relevant to our subject are made after the foundation charters just given from Chifflet, col. 19:

> “As regards the year of the foundation, which is not stated in these charters: the same author, namely Chifflet—consult him in the Appendix to the *Dissertation*, chapter 20—following the *Chronographer* of St Marianus of Auxerre, assigns it to June of the year of Christ 1114. All agree concerning the month; but as to the year, since both external and domestic documents seem to oppose this date—among them the *Exordium Cisterciense*, distinction 2, chapter 1, and the tablet attached to the tomb of St Bernard, which expressly state the year 1115—it seems preferable to adhere to the opinion long received. Otherwise Bernard would scarcely have made his profession in June 1114, while Hugh himself, who granted the site, was still in the East. Clairvaux, therefore, was first founded by Hugh, Duke of Champagne; later, in 1135, it was transferred to a more spacious site and endowed with a new building through the assistance of Theobald, Hugh’s successor. Thus Theobald acquired among some the name of first founder, those persons confusing the relocation with the foundation, as Manrique rightly observes in his *Annals* under the year 1115, chapter 1.” [Col. 0669A]

This opinion, which pleases me more than Chifflet’s, I explain and confirm as follows.

60. Chifflet’s other argument, which he places first for the year 1114, rests on this ground: “Morimond, the younger daughter, namely the fourth in number among the daughters of Cîteaux, began in July of that same year, on the eleventh day of the month; while Clairvaux is considered the third in order of birth.” But Jongelinus places the foundation of Morimond in 1115; Manrique does the same under that year, chapter 1; likewise the Sammarthani in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, page 673.

The documents of Clairvaux which Chifflet adduces against the year 1114 for the foundation of Clairvaux in the specified Appendix are: first, the ancient verses:

> The thousandth year is counted with three fives,  
> And likewise the hundredth, when the holy man is made  
> [Col. 0669C] Abbot . . . [lacuna]

“Next, the tablet attached to the tomb of St Bernard, which reads: ‘In the year of the Lord 1115, in the month of June, [St Bernard] was sent with his blood-brothers and his community to this place, now called Clairvaux, but formerly called the Valley of Wormwood.’”

Chifflet replies to the verses:

> “Unless my conjecture deceives me, those verses indicate Bernard’s consecration as abbot . . . This could scarcely have occurred before the year of Christ 1115 . . . Therefore the chroniclers of Morimond and Auxerre recorded the foundation of the monastery from their first arrival at Clairvaux, which fell in June 1114; but the monks of Clairvaux reckoned it from the inauguration of the abbot.” [Col. 0669D]

But against this is the fact that the phrase *creatur*, “is made,” in the said verses seems better referred to Bernard’s appointment over the monastery of Clairvaux, entrusted by St Stephen to Bernard when he departed with his companions from the monastery of Cîteaux—as was discussed above—in conformity with the words of the tablet. To these words I find no answer there in Chifflet, though they state clearly and distinctly: “In the year of the Lord 1115, in the month of June,” our saint was sent, certainly with the authority of an abbot, having then been appointed or made such by his superior, though not yet consecrated by a bishop in that month. More will be said of this consecration in the following section.

## § VI. He is consecrated abbot of Clairvaux; the monastery’s privations relieved by miracles; spiritual food offered to the monks of Clairvaux by the saint, warned through an apparition

[Col. 0670A]

61. William, book I, chapter 4, has handed down the following concerning the saint’s consecration:

> “When Bernard, newly sent to Clairvaux, was to be ordained to the ministry to which he had been called, and the see of Langres, to which that ordination belonged, was vacant, the brethren, wondering where they should take him for ordination, soon learned of the good reputation nearby of the venerable bishop of Châlons, the highly esteemed master of William of Champeaux; and it was decided that he should be sent there. And so it was done.”

Chifflet, in chapter 20 of the Appendix to the *Dissertation* cited above, from page 676, raises and resolves on the basis of William’s text just quoted the following difficulty:

> “How,” he asks, [Col. 0670B] “was the see of Langres vacant in 1115, when it is established that Jocerannus was bishop of Langres from 1112 to 1125, as we reported from the Chronicle of St Bénigne, page 505? But the answer is ready: the see of Langres was then vacant in an improper sense—not because there was no bishop of Langres at that time, but because in that year 1115 he was absent from his bishopric, perhaps on a journey to the thresholds of the Apostles, or to certain synods frequently held in those very times by Guy of Vienne, apostolic legate throughout Gaul.”

Thus Chifflet. How our saint, “having taken with him Elboldo [variant: Elbodo], a certain monk of Cîteaux,” as the said William narrates in the same place, [Col. 0670C] went to Châlons and entered “the house of the aforesaid bishop”; how some despised him, even to mockery, because of his outward bodily appearance, while the bishop held him in the highest reverence; and how great a friendship sprang up between them from their first meeting, not without the broad diffusion of Bernard’s name throughout all Gaul—you will find in the same William.

62. I shall not add the other matters which this biographer had previously related concerning the privations of the monastery of Clairvaux in its first days and their various reliefs; likewise concerning its immense growth, shown in a vision to the holy abbot and afterward proved true by the event; and finally concerning his zeal for perfection and his sister’s conversion. The same writer of the *Life* may be consulted on these matters, chapters 3 [Col. 0670D] and 4.

Yet John the Hermit relates differently the exceedingly severe poverty by which divine providence saw fit to exercise and test the holy abbot and his subjects; and by various examples, exceedingly illustrative of the same saint’s glory, he proves that divine provision was made for those great temporal necessities at Clairvaux. I therefore judge that Abbot William should be supplemented from the said John, who, in book II, col. 1285, no. 2, after speaking of scarcity of food, adds the following concerning clothing:

> “Their clothing, both in summer and winter, consisted of a cowl and tunic, which were renewed very seldom. They also used cheap leggings and shoes that often remained torn and split for a long time before being mended; because leather was so excessively scarce, they tied them with cords. O noble men, great in the world! Who brought you into these dry and perilous places, if not He who was rich in heaven and poor and humble on earth, who lay in a manger?”

Behold now the abbot’s uplifted spirit and his complete confidence in God’s timely aid amid so many miseries.

63. The same writer of the *Life*, from col. 1285, no. 3, continues:

> “In that great poverty of which we have spoken above, salt failed them one day among their other needs. The holy abbot called one of his brethren, named Guibert, and said to him: ‘My son Guibert, take the ass, go to the market, and buy us salt.’ But he replied: ‘Where is the money?’ To him the man of God said: ‘Believe me, son, I do not know the time when I possessed gold or silver. But He who holds my purse and my treasures in His hands is above.’ [Col. 0671B]
>
> “Then the brother, almost smiling, said: ‘If I go empty, I shall return empty.’ The saint said to him: ‘Do not fear, my son, but go confidently. For He who holds our treasures, as I have just told you, will be with you on the road and will supply everything for which I send you.’
>
> “At these words, having received the blessing of his pious father, he went with the ass to the market at the castle called Risnel, more unbelieving than was proper. But the pious and merciful Lord did not regard his unbelief; rather, He considered the faith of His servant and gave him all that he had been sent to obtain. Thus, as he approached the castle and came to a certain village, he met a priest, who greeted him, saying: ‘Where are you from, brother, [Col. 0671C] or where are you going?’ He replied and carefully explained the purpose of his journey and the poverty of the place in which the holy Father lived with his sons.”

64. “When the priest heard this, he was deeply moved, took the brother into his house, and gave him half a measure of salt and fifty shillings or more, as Guibert himself often used to recount. Having received these things, he began to give immense thanks to God and to say within himself: ‘Without doubt the word I heard from my father is true. But in this I have sinned grievously against him: I did not believe him, but came here unbelieving.’ Taking leave of the priest, he returned to the monastery. When he entered it, he ran to the man of God and reported everything that had happened to him on the way. [Col. 0671D] The holy Father said to him: ‘I tell you, my son, that nothing is so necessary for every Christian as faith. Therefore have faith, and it will go well with you all the days of your life.’ From that day onward, both that brother and the others held the words of the holy Father in greater reverence. O good Jesus, who can recount the faith possessed by this saint?”

John the biographer then presents another example, no. 4:

65. “A certain brother of Clementiniprati, arriving to visit Christ’s new planting, was honourably received as far as possible. He was offered the half of an oat-bread which was at hand. Having received it and, with great astonishment at their way of life, brought it back to Clementiniprati, [Col. 0672A] he announced to all living there the voluntary abstinence of Christ’s servants amid the utmost poverty; their patience in abstinence; and their lavish generosity in need.

“Immediately the brethren of Clementiniprati, deeply moved and sympathetic, unanimously agreed to assist them. Then the superior of that place, named Odo, a venerable man beloved by God and men, loaded horses and asses and conveyed loaves and provisions in carts. From that day until the present there was such a fellowship of brotherhood between Clairvaux and Clementiniprati that, whenever brethren of Clementiniprati came to Clairvaux, they were treated in spiritual and temporal matters just as one of the monks of Clairvaux would be. The offices for the dead were likewise reciprocally rendered. [Col. 0672B] In this manner pious Jesus provided more and more for His servants.”

The following is added in no. 5: “A certain woman also arrived bringing one hundred shillings, with which the nakedness of their feet was covered.”

Two further occurrences follow, which Manrique assigns to the immediately following year, 1116. Yet, continuing the sequence of John the biographer’s narrative, we append both here from him, beginning with the following:

66. “They lacked all animals except one ass, by which the abbot was carried on his visitations and wood was brought for necessities. Compelled by hunger, cold, and other privations, they complained to their abbot that extreme poverty forced them to depart. Hearing this, the abbot consoled them gently and mildly, urging upon them as far as he could the fear and love of God, together with the hope of eternal life and divine recompense. But they, most sorely pressed and distressed by manifold affliction, absolutely refused to agree and preferred to return to Cîteaux. When the man of God saw their despair, he finally turned to prayer. [Col. 0672C] When he had done so, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him in the presence of all: ‘Rise, Bernard; your prayer has been heard.’

“When the brethren heard this, they glorified God and their holy Bernard and said to him: ‘Tell us, Father, what did you ask of the Lord?’ He replied: ‘What do you wish to know, you of little faith? Remain here, and you will know afterward.’ As they spoke among themselves, spending a little time in conversation—not idle talk, but holy discourse—someone came and offered the holy Father ten pounds.” [Col. 0672D]

67. The aforesaid writer of the *Life* records the other occurrence thus, from col. 1286:

> “Without delay, a man of Bar-sur-Aube, whose son was afflicted by such severe illness that his life was despaired of, brought him thirteen pounds, humbly begging him to take pity on his son. The holy abbot dismissed him cheerfully, promising that he would find his son well. On returning, the man found his son restored to health, as the man of God had promised. For this reason he afterward gave abundant thanks to the servant of God. A short time later the mercy of God looked upon them richly and kindly, so that, abounding in eternal and temporal help, [Col. 0673A] they lacked no grace, in accordance with the saying: ‘Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.’”

To these remarkable and serious events let us add a spurious and apocryphal miracle from Manrique under the year 1116, chapter 1, no. 5, where he sets it forth and rejects it in these words:

68. “A tradition accepted among the inhabitants relates that horses, accustomed to wander without a driver and to range among the neighbouring peoples in collecting the alms of the faithful, which they immediately brought back to the monastery, were robbed by the townspeople of a nearby village, either in mockery or plunder; and, instead of bread, were loaded with stones of enormous weight. When Father Bernard learned of the outrage—for the horses groaned under the weight and so revealed the affair all the more quickly—and cursed the perpetrators’ impiety, they hold as certain that the earth suddenly split in two and swallowed up the place together with its inhabitants, while the church alone remained unmoved. There are those who believe that, in memory of so great a miracle, the church too is gradually swallowed up, namely by the thickness of one silver gros each year; and they point out the church, the site, and the stones, by which greater credence is built up for the tale. [Col. 0673B] Thus there is no land whatsoever that does not suffer from the fables of its inhabitants, from which not even holy men are altogether immune. Whether another somewhat similar curse, by which the same saint is said to have struck Verfeil, a sizeable place in Aquitaine, while preaching in that province, is of the same kind, we shall consider in its proper time. For now it is enough to have intermingled this with serious matters, as it were in passing.”

Manrique might usefully have added that it is highly beneficial to overturn traditions of this merely popular kind and distinguish false miracles from true ones. This applies especially in the case of St Bernard, who is so richly endowed with almost countless true miracles that they neither ought nor can be covered over with false ones, lest these detract in any degree from the credibility of the former. [Col. 0673C]

69. “There remained a second and greater hunger: that of spiritual food, namely the word of God. Father Bernard either preached too timidly or kept altogether silent, lest through excessive zeal and inexperience of affairs he should, as he thought, wound the consciences of the brethren; or, to use Abbot William’s words, lest they should be scandalized by his preaching rather than receive any edification from it. But He who had checked the first hunger by a miracle did not permit the second to grow, since it had to be restrained for the greater good of the Church. [Col. 0673D] For Bernard had been assumed by God Himself into the ministry of the word, charged with the office of preaching, and fitted by divine power for so great a work,” as Manrique says under the year 1116, chapter 1, no. 6.

This matter is treated more fully by William in book I, chapter 4, of the saint’s *Life*, from which I select the following:

> “Nor did the mercy of God delay its help until the opportune time. For after only a few days had passed, he saw in a vision of the night a boy standing by him with a certain divine charity [variant: brightness], and authoritatively commanding him to speak confidently whatever should be suggested to him in the opening of his mouth, because it would not be he who spoke, but the Spirit speaking in him. From that time the Holy Spirit, speaking more manifestly in him and through him . . . gave him, among his hearers also, grace, [Col. 0674A] authority, and understanding concerning the needy and poor man, the penitent sinner, and one asking forgiveness.”

Manrique, just cited, further adds in no. 7, from Caesarius on the Octave of the Nativity of the Lord:

> “When on one occasion he was dictating something, and had at hand a testimony suitable to the present place, he wished to reserve it until the end, fearing a failure there; but he heard a voice from heaven saying: ‘If you reserve this, another will not be given to you.’ Thus the saint himself, though speaking, no longer spoke, but the Holy Spirit who was in him.”

Since therefore the temporal and spiritual affairs of the new community of Clairvaux had been so prosperously and happily ordered through divine favour, let us turn to another matter most suitable for the praise of that monastery and indeed of its first abbot himself. [Col. 0674B]

## § VII. The growth of the monastery of Clairvaux foreseen by its holy abbot; difficulties concerning Canons of St Victor admitted there; the date of the event; the saint’s remarkable patience, while ill, with an unskilled physician; his father’s conversion

70. Hear how the foreknowledge of our abbot concerning the vast influx of secular persons and religious men to the monks of Clairvaux—for, as William relates in chapter 3, no. 29, he saw a multitude of men of diverse dress and condition descending from every side into the lower valley, so great that the valley itself could not contain them—was fulfilled at this time.

“For,” says Manrique under the year 1116, chapter 2, no. 1, “as the fame of that house became celebrated [Col. 0674C] throughout all Gaul, many religious men, abandoning their own residences, sought Bernard’s guidance at Clairvaux, desiring, though veteran leaders—indeed veterans discharged after approved service—to become novices there.”

Immediately afterward, the aforesaid author of the *Annals* proves this by the authority of the *Great Exordium*, book I, chapter 4. But because I do not find the passage there in Tissier’s edition, I transcribe it here on the credit of Manrique who reports it:

> “After the house of Clairvaux was founded through the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that its most fragrant reputation for sacred religion might become to many an aroma of life unto life, among the rest whom the hidden counsel of divine goodness summoned from different parts of the world, many religious [Col. 0674D] men who seemed perfect in the observance of religion in their own places heard that the Lord had so especially and excellently magnified His mercy toward that house and its most holy abbot. Therefore, coming as new recruits from the labours of a hermit’s warfare (*eremitae*; perhaps *eremiticae*, “eremitical”), they most fervently desired, in devotion of spirit, to be joined to a fellowship of such great holiness.”

71. “Among these, the first, or among the foremost, to stand out were Humbert, afterwards the first abbot of the monastery of Igny; Raynald; Peter surnamed of Toulouse; William; and Gerard of Farfa. Though they lived not in one place but in different provinces, widely distant from one another, from the very rudiments of childhood [Col. 0675A] they so devoted themselves to divine service that, flourishing in every grace of virtue, they might have seemed to have little need of formation through the examples of others as though more perfect.”

As to the chronology, Manrique observes: “Moreover, among those listed there, although perhaps not all—for that is wholly uncertain—some nevertheless must be assigned to this year, especially Humbert, a man of immense holiness, of whom we shall say more below. For Bernard himself, the Father, testifies in a special sermon on Humbert’s death that he came to Clairvaux at its very beginning.” This sermon is printed in Mabillon’s edition of the works of St Bernard from col. 1066 onward; in it the same holy Father says: “He lived with us for thirty years, from almost the very beginning [Col. 0675B] of this monastery.” Mabillon observes in his notes appended to this sermon that this most worthy man had lived as a monk for twenty years from early youth in the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu, under the Rule of St Benedict, before withdrawing to Clairvaux. This occurred about the year 1118. The sermon itself is placed by Mabillon under the year 1148.

72. What kind of a man Humbert was, how great, and how worthy a son of Father Bernard, is most plainly evident, first, from that elegant and moving sermon which I mentioned, a discourse suffused alike with the highest praise of him and with the tenderest emotions of love toward him on the part of that same saint. Secondly, as Manrique reports, no. 3, [Col. 0675C] from the author of the *Exordium Cisterciense*, St Bernard himself “set before himself God’s servant Humbert as an example of perfection to imitate, striving to admire his virtues and to judge his merits great and exalted; he regarded him as a model of holiness, a pattern of religious life, and a mirror of monastic purity,” etc. Manrique treats of his death in volume II, under the year of Christ 1145, chapter 8; and of Igny (Igny-en-Tardenois), in the diocese of Rheims, where we have said that he was abbot, see the previously cited Jongelinus, p. 41.

73. “In this same year, certainly not long afterward, I judge that there were added,” says Manrique, no. 6, “in order that the vision of the holy Father might be more fully accomplished, certain regular canons of St Victor in Paris—the house [Col. 0675D] founded by William of Champeaux before he became bishop of Châlons—who were more than others aware of Bernard’s holiness and revered him although they had not yet seen him. They … through frequent letters of their founder … visited Clairvaux and, falling at Bernard’s knees, earnestly begged to be received for probation, intending, if approved, to remain permanently. He, being prudent in affairs and most scrupulous in respecting another’s right, neither wholly admitting nor rejecting them, decided that William himself should be consulted: as the founder of that congregation, as a man equally holy and learned, and, what gave access and confidence, as one dear to himself. The devout bishop had sent the men to Clairvaux [Col. 0676A] and had prompted them to change their manner of life. Therefore, when Bernard consulted him, he gave, it is said, an answer consistent with himself: that the canons ought to be received, for reasons which may be read in Manrique. Yet he added that, as a suppliant, he begged his friend to intercede and, as bishop, so far as he could, enjoined it—not for strangers but for sons. The holy bishop acted thus without jealousy; not because zeal for his own foundation, indeed for his order, was lacking—for he himself, having resigned the archdeaconry, had put on the habit of a regular canon—but because zeal for God prevailed in the holy man. Father Bernard, relying on such counsel, or rather constrained by such authority—and he had consulted certain others about the same matter—admitted the canons to probation.

[Col. 0676B] 74. “But Gelduin, abbot of St Victor … bitterly distressed at finding himself deprived of his sons, without even knowing it … summoned his canons and resolved to write to Bernard a letter which was indeed humble and full of reverence for the man of God and the entire convent of Clairvaux, yet threatening nevertheless, brandishing, or preparing to brandish if they did not withdraw, the sword of excommunication against the novices. Upon receiving this, Father Bernard—whose mind was always equally steady in the face of insults and praise, and firmly directed to the good—is known to have sent the following answer.” Anyone wishing to see it entire will find it as the third among Bernard’s letters, in Mabillon, vol. I, cols. 13–14, where it is likewise assigned to the year 1120, of which I shall speak shortly. Meanwhile, what the holy man did in this [Col. 0676C] affair is sufficiently plainly indicated by the conclusion of the letter:

> “Since they have been received in such a manner and on such terms, far be it from us to think that your integrity has been injured in receiving them, or ought to be injured in retaining them—provided, however, that if during the year of probation … they should happen to abandon what they have begun and wish to return to you, we do not keep them against their will. Otherwise, most holy brethren, it is not your concern vainly to attempt, by an unconsidered anathema, to impede the spirit of liberty which is in them—unless perhaps, which God forbid, you make it your business to seek what is yours rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ.”

75. If you ask what was afterward done concerning them, Manrique, no. 10, says that he does not doubt that they were retained, “though no further record of them survives, whether this resulted from the authority of William, of Father Bernard, or of both.” Nor was this first dispute in this matter the last. “For this first controversy,” Manrique testifies, “conducted over persons, was followed by many others, most of them serious; and more were impending, had not Bernard, both retaining his own right and refusing to invade another’s, met them—repelling many, postponing few, but firmly retaining those once admitted, as the sequence of the history itself will show.” These matters concern the first little flowers planted in the most delightful garden of Clairvaux under Father Bernard and cultivated by his care. As Manrique adds, no. 11, he gave those entering the monastery this warning: [Col. 0677A] “If you hasten toward the things that are within, leave here outside the bodies which you have brought from the world. Let spirits alone enter: the flesh profits nothing.” Explaining these words, the author says that “this saying would have deterred many, had Bernard not, sparing the weak, explained it as referring to carnal desire and affections, which they were to leave outside and never again take up.”

76. I shall now fulfil what I recently promised concerning the year of St Bernard’s third letter, especially because its date is characteristic for fixing the time of the controversy just discussed between the men of Clairvaux and the Victorines of Paris. Manrique, no. 10, under the previously cited year 1116, says that the deeds of William himself—whose exhortation and counsel Bernard employed—show plainly that these events must be assigned to that year, or at least must not be deferred for [Col. 0677B] long: “For he died in January of the year 1119; as John Picard, whom Manrique had shortly before cited in notes on St Bernard’s letter, observed from the necrology of St Aulph of Corbeil. Therefore, though the letter was written after this year, 1116, as the affair progressed, yet the affair itself, or at latest the following year, having begun with the admission of the men, can scarcely be called into doubt.”

77. But Manrique does not appear to have established a sufficiently firm footing here. William of Champeaux, also surnamed “the Venerable,” is praised by the authors of the *Gallia Christiana* among the bishops of Châlons, [Col. 0677C] and it is asserted there that “he departed this life in 1121, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, as the tables of St Stephen and Alberic teach.” The same year is given by Mabillon in his notes on Bernard’s third letter. Indeed, that this bishop did not die in 1119, as Manrique wished, is argued in these terms in the notes there: “Cardinal Conon, legate, came in 1120 to the monastery of Morigny near Étampes, bringing with him as a great helper William, bishop of Châlons, who had directed the higher schools, that is, theological schools; and at that time, possessing zeal for God, he shone above all the bishops of all Gaul in knowledge of the divine Scriptures. This is from the Chronicle of Morigny. Hence you may refute those who place his death [Col. 0677D] in 1119.” Consequently, according to what has been stated, the regular canons’ arrival at Clairvaux need not necessarily have occurred in 1116, or in the immediately following year; nor need Bernard’s letter have been composed before 1120. Let us therefore say that we see no difficulty in placing both events in 1119 or 1120.

78. Under the said year 1116, chapter 3, Manrique presents the holy Father suffering from a serious illness caused by excessive austerity of life; William of Champeaux wonderfully concerned to restore his health; and a little hut prepared for this purpose. Then under the year 1117, chapter 1, no. 4, he recounts how the man’s health was entrusted to a wholly unskilled peasant, [Col. 0678A] and the very serious hardships which he endured. We do not copy those events here, but refer the reader to the biographer William, chapter 4, where he recounts what he saw. There also you will find the saint refreshed by an angelic vision; and in chapter 5, the former, very severe rigor of life resumed by the holy man. What the same author of the *Life* had previously stated in chapter 4, no. 34, concerning the saint’s father’s conversion to the monastic life, Manrique connects with the aforesaid year 1117; see chapter 3, no. 8. The cited William touches very briefly upon this conversion; elsewhere, however, the account is longer, clothed with various accompanying details and with actions attributed to Bernard in the matter, though these require some examination.

[Col. 0678B] 79. In no. 9 of the chapter just noted, Manrique quotes from Vincent of Beauvais, *Mirror of Morals*, book III, part 3, distinction 22, at the end:

> “When blessed Bernard had converted all his household and they had followed him, his father remained disobedient to him, persevering in his hardness. Once, when Bernard was preaching in his father’s village and his father would not obey him, he ordered fire to be brought. This having been done, he applied it to an old trunk standing before the church door. As he endeavoured to light it, it could not be kindled but smoked. Then he directed everyone to gather there after their meal for a sermon, and that each should bring with him a small bundle of vine-shoot twigs and throw it [Col. 0678C] upon the trunk. When this was done, he ordered fire to be applied; and when the bundles had caught fire, the trunk too was kindled, sending forth a very great blazing fire. Then blessed Bernard began a sermon on the torments and fire of hell, and on how the disobedient, with bundles of their sins cast upon them, would be tormented in hell. He preached so excellently on this that his own father, hard and disobedient, followed him into cloistered obedience.”

The author of the *Cistercian Annals* draws this from Vincent; but since Vincent does not agree with himself elsewhere, I fear that he does not agree with the truth.

80. Manrique expresses the point thus: “Since, in the same moral work, he testifies that the same event happened in different ways, he seems, by contradicting himself, to deprive his own statements of credibility. Certainly, he agrees in both accounts that wood was applied to the trunk and set alight; but in book II, part 3, distinction 4, he had narrated the rest very differently:

> “When this was done, the dry wood quickly caught fire; but the trunk, slowly, around its middle, emitting from its extremities foul moisture and most dreadful smoke, maintained the fire for a long time. Then the saint began to speak about the punishments of hell and told his father that he was like that trunk: here he could not be kindled by the divine fire; but in hell, unless he did penance, he would burn forever and emit foul smoke. Pierced by these words, the father followed him and became a monk.”

Thus Vincent disagrees with himself … and does not agree with the biographer William, who is above every exception. William says simply of him in chapter 4, no. 34, without mentioning the place of conversion, the person through whom [Col. 0679A] it occurred, or the manner in which it happened: “His father also, who alone had remained at home, came to his sons and was received among them.” He seems, however, to have spent only a short time as a monk; for, as William immediately adds, after living there for some time, he died in a good old age. Chrysostom Henriquez entered him in his Cistercian Menology on 23 May. Mabillon, in a note to the first book of William’s *Life*, makes the following brief observation from the necrology of St Benignus, III, concerning his death and monastic profession: “On the Ides of April died Tescelin, monk, father of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.”

## VIII. The monastery of Trois-Fontaines distinguished by the holy man’s prophecy and miracle; whether in 1119 he sent his own men into Portugal; he is prepared by withdrawal from affairs to carry out great undertakings.

[Col. 0679B]

81. Under the year 1118, chapter 3, no. 1, Manrique relates that another monastery was built in his diocese of Châlons by William of Champeaux, of whom we have spoken; wishing to bind himself more closely to Bernard, he requested that a colony be sent there from Clairvaux, chosen by the holy abbot. The place was named Trois-Fontaines, perhaps from the springs flowing there, and it was the first-born daughter of Father Bernard. Jongelinus discusses this monastery on p. 38. We mention it here because the holy man distinguished it by a notable prophecy and afterward also by a splendid miracle. The prophecy is found in William the biographer, chapter 7. Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, gives this brief account of the miracle in book IV of the *Life*, chapter 7 of Mabillon’s edition, no. 41:

> “When the holy Father once came to the monastery of Trois-Fontaines, a certain cleric, one of those called regulars, an aged and blind man, was presented to him. Bernard laid his hand upon him and made a brief prayer according to his custom; and in that same hour he sent him back to his church able to see.”

82. The immediately following year, 1119, contains, in chapter 3 of the repeatedly cited annalist, an account of the historical controversy whether St Bernard at that time sent ascetics selected by himself into Portugal to propagate there the monastic way of life. [Col. 0679D] Brito affirms it in book I, chapter 2; but Manrique raises several arguments against him. Manrique sets out the alleged event as follows in chapter 3, no. 1:

> “Bernard Brito constantly asserts, book I, chapter 2, that after Matins on the feast of the sacred Forerunner in this year, the same Forerunner appeared to Father Bernard and ordered him to send monks to the furthest shores of Spain facing the west, to establish [OCR: *erigendo*, ‘establishing,’ rather than *exigendo*] a monastery and dedicate it under his name; and that this was not to be anywhere whatever, but in a place first designated from heaven, where miracles succeeding miracles would increase hope by the earlier wonders, and the later would confirm faith in the former. He further said that those to be sent would find in those regions a hermit, by whose counsel and help they would successfully complete the undertaking. Bernard then [Col. 0680A] selected eight monks: Bohemond and Aldebert, the former to be abbot and the latter prior; John, Bernard, Sisinand, Roland, and Alan—the eighth he left unnamed—and sent all of them to Portugal shortly afterward, adding a letter written to the hermit John Zirita by name, for he had revealed even the Baptist’s name, briefly setting forth the affair.”

Manrique recites the words of this letter from Brito and then adds the following, no. 3 and subsequent sections.

83. “At the time when the glorious Forerunner of Christ had appeared to Bernard at Clairvaux, the same author affirms that he appeared in Portugal to John Zirita, who was living the eremitical life beside the River Baroso; and that he told him of the arrival of the monks and of the monastery to be built by them, so that they might not seek out one unaware or ask one unwilling, but find one awaiting them. Brito treats these matters more fully as belonging to the present year; the rest occurred at the beginning of the following year. But, lest we distract the reader, we shall set them down here in consecutive order. Therefore the monks sent by Father Bernard, having crossed the Pyrenees in midwinter and traversed nearly all Spain, came to the borders of Lamaca—now called Lamego. There John Zirita met them, and by this very fulfilment of the prophecy strengthened their wavering hearts; already weary of the long journey, they saw its reward surpass their toil. Afonso I, son of Count Henry, ruled Portugal; he was then himself a count, later to be distinguished by the royal title. Descended from the dukes of Burgundy, and consequently joined to Bernard the Burgundian—already celebrated in fame—both by blood and spirit, he could readily be persuaded by John to grant the sons of Bernard whatever land they might choose. He confirmed the donation by a privilege, issued by this same king at Araduca, commonly Guimarães, not many days after the men’s arrival, in the following words,” which Manrique quotes there from Brito. It is dated: “The charter was made … on the Kalends of March, in the era 1158,” corresponding to the year 1120 of the common era. “That they crossed the Pyrenees,” Manrique adds, “in the very winter is shown by the date: the first of March—or, more correctly, the first day after the winter season—so that we must either admit that they spent the entire three months idle if they had arrived before them and done nothing, or that during those very months they crossed the Pyrenees, frozen stiff with wintry snow and cold.”

84. Further, what Manrique then recounts from Brito in nos. 6 and 7—namely “that Bohemond built small cells for himself and his companions …; that a place marked by a light shining at midnight … gave a happy omen for building the monastery; that letters of Bohemond to John” and of John to Bohemond, copies of which are produced there, bore witness to these things; “that an illustrious Portuguese prince … and all the nobles, among them the archbishop of Braga, aware of the miracles, provided aid for the work of construction and for the celebration of divine worship; one gave seventy marks of silver, from which crosses and other vessels might be made, another sacred vestments which he used in celebrating the solemnities of Mass”—all this, I say, it is enough here to have compressed from the fuller account given there. Having set this out, it is worth hearing the arguments by which Manrique, modestly indeed but aptly, calls the foregoing story into question. These, then, he advances against it.

85. “First,” he says, no. 8, “and this is the chief point of all, Father Bernard presents a difficulty. A little after this year—though in fact after it, as I shall shortly show—he dissuades Artand [variants: Artald, Artaud], abbot of Preuilly, his contemporary and fellow abbot, from foundations in Spain, because they are situated far away, a place to which it is not expedient to exile one’s sons. You have the saint’s quite explicit letter, Epistle 75, written to him in these words:

> “I have heard … concerning you that you wish to build an abbey in Spain from your holy convent. This has naturally caused me great astonishment: what reason, what counsel, or what advantage can there be in your wishing your sons to be exiled to a place so distant, to be sought out, moreover, and built at such expense and labour?”

Thus the holy Father. Had he already sent sons to Spain, he would never have condemned another for sending them there. Would he have dissuaded someone from doing what he himself had done? Moreover, that the letter was written after this year is evident even from the fact that Preuilly, whose abbot Artand was, had been founded in the preceding year, 1118, and could not have contemplated producing an offspring when it had scarcely professed sons whom it had received and whom it was to send out [printed: *transmissum*; apparently for *transmissurum*]. Certainly neither Clairvaux, although most fruitful, bore offspring before three years had passed, nor Bonneval before four, nor the other houses before more years had elapsed.

86. “The letter, then, was written after this year, but before 1122, when the Order, expanded through Germany without any danger, was less exposed to fears of this kind. Hence it is no wonder that in the following years, namely in 1130, the same saint, having changed his policy to suit the circumstances of the time and the experience of events, should have ennobled Spain with his monks—first by Moreruela, in the diocese of Zamora, of which more will be said below, and then by several other monasteries to be founded or reformed, as the sequence of the history itself will show.”

The Portuguese history agrees with these arguments of Manrique, drawn from St Bernard’s letter and from chronology. But as to the date of the letter, Mabillon’s edition of the works of St Bernard, col. 76, differs greatly from Manrique, assigning it to the year 1127. The further this chronological reckoning removes the letter from the time to which Brito attaches that remarkable Cistercian colony in Portugal, the more clearly it shows—even apart from the other arguments—that the story does not stand securely.

Besides the argument which Manrique drew from the said letter, he advances another from the very history of the alleged event, speaking thus in no. 9: “The story itself is suspicious in its own right; it contains several matters, not a few, which [Col. 0682A] have little flavour of the antiquity of that period: that Afonso ruled Portugal in that year, though Brandão, royal writer and profoundly skilled in Portuguese antiquities, proves at length in part III of the *Monarchia Lusitana*, book VIII, chapter 26—producing Afonso’s own testimony—that he was then either too young, being only ten years old, or, because his mother retained her dower lands and therefore the principality of Portugal, was not raised to the throne before his twenty-eighth year; that the prince gave seventy or more marks of silver for making crosses from them; that the archbishop of Braga gave the monks sacred vestments which he himself used, though it is certain that at that period they could use neither those silver crosses nor silk vestments such as befitted a great prelate of the Church, according to their own institutions; that Bernard, most loving of his sons, exposed them, shivering and almost naked in the middle of winter—clothed, as it was said, only in two loose garments—to the snow of the Pyrenees, without providing for them, and neither anticipated nor waited, when he could have done so, for a more suitable season.” So Manrique. Add that Afonso’s blood relationship with Bernard is sought too remotely, and thus is not sufficiently aptly sewn into the present story, as appears from the materials cited above, § I, no. 12.

87. A second argument against Brito’s colony is supplied to Manrique, no. 10, by “the monastery of Moreruela, once pre-eminent through the most holy Froilan and Atilan, the one as abbot and the other as prior, which, as even the history from which Brito drew admits—and Brito himself does not dare deny—first received the Cistercian observance in Spain. Yet it is certain that it had not received it ten years later. Certainly, even if Cîteaux had been its model, it waited five years, as we shall see in its place; and another five-year period must be added to this, as even the authors of Moreruela do not deny. They are content with that antiquity which rests on certain trust in ancient documents, especially the concordant records of Clairvaux and Cîteaux, while no document or author that I have seen says otherwise.”

88. Finally, Manrique’s last argument against the often-mentioned migration to Portugal is drawn from a combined mass of various considerations. Here it is in his own words, no. 11: “What of the fact that the letter produced as Bernard’s savours too little of Father Bernard? What of the fact that it reports a revelation such as we nowhere else see him make? What of the fact that other authors are silent about it, and that those who narrate the smallest things are found to have kept silent about a whole apparent accumulation of manifestations and miracles? What of the fact that every ancient memorial of the Order affirms that the monastery of St John of Tarouca in Portugal was constructed many years later, namely in 1131? What of the fact that monasteries became numerous and productive through frequent foundations only from that year onward, while for a long time before it they were either wholly unheard of or, if one existed, remained barren? For what Brito adds concerning St Christopher, commonly called de la Foens, suffers precisely the same difficulty, as we shall see in its place.”

At last Manrique concludes the present controversy: “I have set forth these points with the aim of raising doubt rather than deciding, and leave them to the reader’s consideration, myself uncertain in judgment and neither affirming altogether nor wholly denying.” Such was his modest conclusion. We, however, to whom it matters nothing whether the Cistercian—or rather Clairvaux—vine extended its branches to the sea sooner or later, that is, to Portugal, assign far greater weight to Manrique. He seems to us to have established the case of the present controversy so fully and clearly that Brito’s history, which he here refutes, ought to be regarded as highly suspect. It follows also that the two letters concerning Bernard’s dispatch of Clairvaux monks into Portugal—one addressed to King Afonso of Portugal, the other to John Cirita, both formerly published under Bernard’s name—were not without reason relegated to the Appendix of that holy Father’s letters in Mabillon’s edition, cols. 371–372, after his genuine letters. But enough and more than enough of these matters. Let us return to France and to the deeds of our holy abbot at Clairvaux, concerning which Manrique supplies various information under the next year, 1120.

89. After that author, in chapter 3, no. 1, had treated of distinguished men in the world who embraced the companionship at Clairvaux, some drawn by the holy abbot’s teaching and others stirred by his unceasing preaching, and of the assistance necessary to promote it, he adds that sorrows succeeded the joys of the same household. For, says the same annalist, no. 2, [Col. 0683C] “amid its prosperity, lest they should trust themselves too much, they endured other, harsh and adverse things: Father Bernard was separated from his sons, to the greater grief, it is uncertain whether his own or theirs. The cause lay in himself. For, while he succumbed in body before spirit to the excessive rigor of which we have spoken, he repented—earnestly indeed, but too late—of the penance carried beyond his strength. He was compelled at last to leave the community of brethren, which he had retained for too long, and to live separately. God, as appeared, so disposed this, that, freed from those common duties, from then on he might live not for himself or his own alone, but for others—indeed for the whole Church, to the great benefit of the entire Christian world, which was to employ his work in all things.” William narrates the event in the *Life*, book I, chapter 5. The holy Father himself blamed himself for that excessive austerity, as may be seen there.

90. “But,” as Manrique rightly observes, no. 4, “He who from the beginning of the rising Church has been accustomed to choose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong, prepared through Bernard’s very incapacity a most abundant fruit. For, released from the convent as we said, his illness gave him time for business through leisure; gravity of countenance through pallor; weight to his words through weakness; and through physical decline, as though death were imminent, it won everyone’s esteem. It was as though his fleeting life gained a greater return: fear, as is usual, urged desire, and dread of loss commended its worth.” Consult the end of the chapter of the *Life* just cited. Thus this period of leisure splendidly prepared the holy man for the affairs of the highest importance that followed.

## IX. Whether the place of Prémontré was given by St Bernard to the Premonstratensians; his affection toward them and toward St Norbert; the mutual services and praises of the Cistercian and Premonstratensian Orders.

Following Manrique’s example, I intend here to present the noble pair of friends, Saints Bernard and Norbert. Although he treats of them before Bernard’s separation from his own monks, of which we have just spoken, he nevertheless inserts the present topic under the same year 1120, in which we are now engaged with him. Under that year, then, chapter 2, no. 1, the praised compiler of the *Cistercian Annals* gathers the following material for our purpose:

> “At about the same time the great light of the Church, Norbert … founded, to the great good of the whole Church, the illustrious Order of Regular Canons called Premonstratensian from its first place … Of all places, Norbert preferred this one, obtained through the generosity of the most blessed Father Bernard, to whom it had first been given; fitting in itself and recommended by its donor for laying the foundations of his household. Since the matter concerns an illustrious order, not only contemporary with the Cistercian Order but also close to it, I shall explain it by beginning somewhat further back.”

Manrique continues the narrative of this event in nos. 2 and 3, where it may be read. It suffices for our purpose that the place of Prémontré belonged to the Cistercians before it passed to the Premonstratensians, by Bernard’s gift. The holy doctor himself expressly affirms this in the letter written after St Norbert’s death to the abbot of Prémontré, letter 253 in Mabillon, col. 250, where, among other benefits conferred by him upon the Premonstratensians, he says:

> “First, the very place of Prémontré in which you dwell was ours, and you received it by our gift. For Brother Wido—the name of the first inhabitant of the place—had previously given it to us through the hand of the bishop.”

92. This passage in the letter is not without difficulty. Mabillon’s notes address it thus: “Some hesitate here in explaining Bernard, because it is certain that the first church at Prémontré, dedicated to St John the Baptist, was granted by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, to Norbert through an exchange made with the monks of St Vincent of Laon—commonly St Vincent de Laon—to whom it belonged, as Hermann, monk of Laon, soon to be cited, testifies in book III, chapter 4. Yet in chapter 10 the same author, an eyewitness, relates that ‘a larger church on the other side of the hill’ was later built by Abbot Hugh, with an imposing monastery attached. Its site, or at least a portion of it, undoubtedly came to the Premonstratensians from Bernard or the Cistercians, who had received it from Wido the hermit. What Bartholomew himself contributed is taught by his letter in the Appendix to this volume, col. 385. See Mabillon’s fuller notes on the aforesaid letter 253, col. 74, where Hermann the monk is cited, book III of *The Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon*, chapter 4, saying:

> ‘Coming therefore to the aforesaid place of Prémontré, they entered, in order to pray, a certain church built there in honour of St John the Baptist. This belonged by right to the monastery of St Vincent of Laon,’ etc.

From these facts, a recent writer in notes on the *Life of St Norbert*, chapter 19—see what I shall say shortly—declares himself at a loss in explaining Bernard’s grant, which he understands to have been made by the Vincentian monks through the hand of Bishop Bartholomew.

93. “But even though six hundred arguments of this kind stood against it, Bernard’s word must possess irresistible authority; and if you consider the matter a little more carefully, you will easily reconcile the apparent contradictions. For it is certain that the monastery of Prémontré, in its first establishment, was not situated on the site where it was first founded by St Norbert, but on the other side of the hill, to which Hugh, Norbert’s successor and the recipient of this letter, had transferred it. The same Hermann mentions this both in the cited place, where he relates St Norbert’s foreknowledge of the monastery’s transfer, and in chapter 10, where he describes the change at Prémontré as follows:

> ‘But when Hugh saw that that little church’—namely, that of St John the Baptist, which the Vincentian monks had granted, as he had stated in chapter 4—‘could no longer suffice for the great multitude which had assembled and was daily increasing by God’s grace; and when he knew too that Lord Norbert, as was said above, had foreseen in spirit that a larger church would be built on the other side of the hill, he took counsel with his brethren and asked Lord Bishop Bartholomew, as founder and father of the place, to come and, when all the workshops had been arranged, lay the first stone in the church’s foundation.’

Thus the first dwelling or church may have been granted by our Vincentian monks—that is, Benedictine monks—but what prevents this second one from having been granted to the Premonstratensians by St Bernard, who had previously received it from Wido the hermit? Let the two letters of Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, which seem to answer these points, be read.

94. Therefore, the place granted to the Premonstratensians by St Bernard, and explained in this way, in no respect conflicts with the foundation charters of Prémontré, which were drawn up in the name of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, and in which that place is said to have belonged to the monks of St Vincent; likewise, St Norbert is said to have received it from Bartholomew himself, to whom it had first been granted by Adalbero, abbot of St Vincent, Seifrid, his successor, later confirming the transaction—as may be seen in the fuller notes already cited, where the aforementioned charters are quoted. Consult our volume I for June, under the sixth day of that month, pp. 862 and following, where, among the *Norbertine Analecta*, chapter 2 presents three diplomas of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, and examines the difficulty proposed and resolved above. Yet the method given there by us on p. 864 for disentangling it does not please me as much as that which I set forth a little earlier from the notes cited.

Whatever little arguments you may advance against this disputed donation, Bernard’s word, as was rightly said above, must carry irresistible authority. For he could and ought to have known perfectly well, and retained in the most recent memory, what he had given and to whom; likewise, from whom, at what time, and in what manner he had previously received what he later gave. Nor do I see how this can be denied unless one brands that most holy man with the stain alike of imprudence and impudence, and even of open falsehood—not to say lying. Far be that! I therefore wonder that the truth of this donation was not sufficiently known, and consequently not sufficiently securely approved, by a certain Premonstratensian author; while another, a Cistercian, undertook to defend it with labour that seems to me altogether unnecessary, indeed superfluous. For Bernard’s word ought to stand—if the Premonstratensian had not scattered this question abroad in public. Understand the matter from what follows.

95. Among the materials concerning St Bernard which I have at hand is a manuscript little dissertation, briefly demonstrating how the holy Father Bernard could truly say in his Letter 252 [otherwise 253] that the Premonstratensian Fathers possessed the very place of Prémontré through his gift. Receive the opening of the dissertation:

> “The Reverend Dom Polycarp de Hertoghe, a religious of St Michael’s at Antwerp, of the Premonstratensian Order, wrote in his annotations on the Life of St Norbert (this Life appeared with the annotations in 1656, printed by Plantin at Antwerp), on chapter 19, folios 346 and 348, that he could not see how St Bernard, in Letter 252, says that the Premonstratensians possess the very place of Prémontré through his gift; since the diplomas of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon (parts of which he produces), clearly show that the said place, formerly belonging to the monks of St Vincent at Laon, was given by that bishop himself to St Norbert and his brethren, by an exchange more advantageous to those monks. Unless perhaps St Bernard counts himself among the Benedictine monks of St Vincent by reason of their common Rule; or unless, when it is said that the monks of St Vincent had formerly inhabited that place for a long time, the words ‘for a long time’ must be extended to a much earlier period, when that place had belonged to them. These arguments are excessively frivolous—so much so that I have thought it worthwhile briefly to refute them here and to bring forward other, sounder reasons.”

[Col. 0686D] I refrain from transcribing those reasons here. What has already been said is sufficient. After the end of the little dissertation its author, Carolus de Visch, a religious of Dunes, says: “I was composing this in June 1663.” Leaving behind these frivolous subtleties, let us return to the earlier path and establish the holy Doctor’s veneration, and thus his love, for St Norbert.

96. In Letter 8 to Bruno, bishop-elect of Cologne, after St Bernard had been consulted by him about accepting the episcopate of Cologne, Bernard writes among other things at the end:

> “You have Lord Norbert, whom, being present, you can better question in person about such matters. For that man is so much the readier for us in unfolding divine mysteries, as he is known to be the nearer to God.”

This letter is dated by Mabillon to the year 1131, but in our volume I for June, which I cited a little earlier, p. 815, it is assigned to 1132, the third-last year of St Norbert’s life. Very brief indeed, yet nevertheless illustrious, is the praise inserted in Letter 56, addressed to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres:

> “What you ask of me concerning Lord Norbert—namely, whether he is going to Jerusalem—I do not know. For a few days ago I had the privilege of seeing his face and of drawing many things from the heavenly pipe—that is, his own mouth,”

etc. This is altogether an honourable expression from the Saint’s pen, since in Sermon 22, *On Various Subjects*, in Mabillon, col. 1129, the same Doctor calls Ambrose a “heavenly pipe.” Letter 56 is assigned by Mabillon to about 1128.

The following fragment may be added from Letter 253, mentioned above, where the holy Doctor, writing in 1150 to the Premonstratensian abbot—St Norbert having long since died, and this being the date assigned to the letter in Mabillon’s edition—says: “I have always fostered and advanced your Order as far as lay in my power.” He then proves this by striking arguments; finally, after excusing all that had given occasion for complaints—and who does not know that complaints not infrequently arise even between the best of friends?—he declares that a close bond of friendship both exists, has existed, and will exist between himself and them, saying thus, col. 253:

> “I shall cling to you, even if you do not wish it; I shall cling to you, even if I myself do not wish it. Long ago I bound myself by a strong bond, by that unfeigned charity which never fails. With those who are troubled I shall be peaceable; to those who trouble me I shall also yield place to wrath, lest I give place to the devil. I shall be overcome by quarrels; I shall overcome by acts of service. I shall render aid to the unwilling, add benefits to the ungrateful, and honour even those who despise me. And now my soul is sorrowful because I have offended you on whatever occasion; and it will remain sorrowful until it is relieved by your forgiveness. If you delay, I shall go and keep watch at your doors; I shall persist in knocking, I shall press on in season and out of season, until I either merit or extort a blessing.”

So deeply had the friendship long ago contracted with St Norbert taken root in the innermost breast of our Saint, that afterward he persevered with such affection toward Norbert’s Order.

97. Hence it should not be surprising—indeed, who would not think it very reasonably?—that St Norbert returned mutual tokens of esteem and goodwill to our Saint, who was so intimately disposed toward him; that the two often maintained friendly intercourse; and that the bond of attachment between them was strengthened especially from the time when, joining the weapons of their sacred preaching, they attacked the errors of Peter Abelard. For I judge that the following statement, made by Abelard himself in the first letter written in his and Heloise’s name, chapter 12, must be understood of both champions of truth:

> “They stirred up against me certain new apostles, in whom the world placed great trust; one of whom boasted that he had restored the life of regular canons, the other that of monks. These men, by preaching, etc.”

Thus he, shamelessly casting upon their true praises the false stain of empty glory.

But I do not have at hand particular documents by which I might show the ways in which the founder of the regular canons returned equal marks of favour to St Bernard, except those alleged by Manriquez from no. 6 onward:

> “That Father Norbert, not alone toward Bernard alone, but that all his sons cherished the Cistercian family and its monks with no less reverence, is persuaded to me by two arguments, each effective: one on Norbert’s behalf, the other on behalf of his followers.”

98. “Certainly, in Norbert it is quite remarkable that, after receiving the place of Prémontré and the heavenly oracle concerning that place; after gathering many disciples through whom the vision had already in part been fulfilled, and was shown to be still to be fulfilled in its remaining particulars, he nevertheless sought counsel about adopting the Cistercian institute, and about establishing no other. This the Acts of his life sufficiently indicate when they report that many religious persons, bishops as well as prelates—doubtless consulted by the man of God—gave diverse answers.” From the Life in Surius, 6 June, chapter 22, where this occurs:

> “When many religious persons, bishops as well as abbots, offered various counsels, one recommending the eremitic life, another the anchoritic life, another the Cistercian Order to be adopted.”

Thus, when St Norbert was considering the foundation of an order, the Cistercian Order came under deliberation—whether this consideration arose from St Bernard, its wonderful propagator, or from the expansion of the flourishing Cistercian family, or from both together.

99. [Col. 0688C] “But, as Manriquez rightly adds in no. 7, He who through the holy man was preparing a new adornment for His Church, to be encircled in the same golden garment by a variety of religious orders, lest Cîteaux, deprived of Norbert, should have no share in his family, repaired, in imitation of Cîteaux, the imminent ruin of the newly risen sun. For when Norbert was promoted to the archbishopric, destruction threatened the abandoned flock, and all conceived this one hope of salvation: that they should imitate the statutes of the Cistercian Order, its annual Chapters, and its contempt and rejection of every superfluity.”

Consult the Life of St Norbert in Surius, chapter 46, from which I extract this:

> “That father whom Norbert had appointed his successor was installed and consecrated in the church of Prémontré; and the other two—whom, as had been said a little earlier, the man of God had directed to appoint one as father in the church at Antwerp and the other in that at Floreffe—were installed in the two other places mentioned above. Two others had already been consecrated in two further churches, St Martin’s at Laon and Viviers. These five, together with a sixth, whom the abbot of Prémontré had sent immediately after his accession to the place called Bonne-Espérance, seeing the impending dissolution of the Order in many places and fearing a greater one to come, assembled on the appointed day in the determined place. Cutting away whatever at that time seemed superfluous in their houses, they resolved thereafter, following the example of the Cistercian Order, to return together every year to correct the defects of their Order. When this had been published in other places, they were six in the first year, nine in the second, twelve in the third, and eighteen in the fourth; and thereafter they multiplied throughout all the world, as their words, deeds, and works bear witness down to the present day.”

The foregoing is confirmed by the Life of St Norbert in our cited volume, chapter 16, p. 852. In the notes on that chapter it is indicated that Norbert was succeeded by Hugh, his first companion, of whom discussion had occurred above on chapter 5; that Waltmann was assigned to Antwerp and Richard to Floreffe; and so forth. Likewise Walter and Henry were consecrated in the churches of Laon and Viviers, men of whom, as also of their monasteries, mention had been made in chapter 13. The unnamed sixth man above is Odo, first superior of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance in Hainaut, near the town of Binche, as may be seen in the notes shortly to be cited.

Finally, observe in passing the following concerning the time of the Chapter just mentioned:

> “The holy man ordained and commanded that from all the churches which, either in his lifetime or after his death, should follow the pattern of his institute and rule, all abbots and provosts should every year, on the feast of St Dionysius, assemble at the church of Prémontré … and, gathered together, should celebrate a general Chapter in that same place.”

So testifies Jean le Paige in the *Bibliotheca of the Premonstratensian Order*, part 1, book II, chapter 34, from which I have taken these words.

100. “Furthermore, these and similar ties of likeness and likewise of mutual love,” Manriquez concludes in no. 8, “bound the two families so closely that ancient writers hardly speak of one without speaking of the other as well. Hear Robert, continuator of Sigebert:

> ‘In these times the canonical Order of Prémontré and the monastic Order of Cîteaux, like two olive trees before the Lord, supplied the world with the light of piety and the richness of devotion; and, like fruitful vines, spread the branches of religious life everywhere,’”

etc.

Let Laurence of Liège also be heard, in the *History of the Bishops of Verdun*, which in the earlier edition of Acheri’s *Spicilegium* is in vol. XII, p. 325, and in the later edition in vol. II, p. 255. Joining the two Orders in charity, merits, and praise, he says:

> “Then followed those two cherubim spreading their wings in the midst of the Church and looking mutually upon the mercy-seat with faces turned toward it: that is, two most illustrious Orders, protecting the Church by their devotion and emulating one another in mutual charity with hearts turned toward God. One, the Cistercian, under Bernard, abbot of most holy name, restored the monastic order, now almost fallen, to the first norm of apostolic life.
