The other, rightly and by name Fore-shown by God [*Praemonstratus*], begun under Norbert, archbishop of Parthenope, shook the ecclesiastical order free from the mud of worldly vanity. You might believe these two Orders to be the two prophets in the Book of the Apocalypse, sent by God near the end of the world and clothed in the sackcloth of penitence; the two olive trees of heavenly mercy and the two lampstands of divine grace. Thus in every way they mortify themselves; thus they water the world with the word of faith; thus they enlighten it with the radiance of merits,”

etc.

Having dealt with this noble and holy pair of friends and with the most illustrious character of both families, we are called back to pursue further Bernard’s affairs, as the purpose of our undertaking requires.

## § X. Freedom from business compensated by holy leisure; flies killed miraculously; the extraordinary force of preaching in converting others; an apparition concerning the salvation of those who duly persevere in the Cistercian Order; sinners brought to amendment by miracles through the holy Father

Manriquez begins the immediately following year, 1121, with St Bernard. Separated from his sons, the more free he was for the business of others, the more he was enlightened by God, both through wisdom infused from heaven and through miracles. For both gifts of divine bounty toward the man, consult William, *Life*, book I, chapter 5.

And indeed he compensated the time free from business with holy leisure. For, according to Alan, chapter 10, no. 32, col. 1248 in Mabillon, when free from external labour or work, he continually either prayed, read, or meditated. What he wrote in these times is related by Manriquez in nos. 6 and 7.

As for what the compiler of the *Cistercian Annals*, chapters 3 and 4, relates concerning dissensions resulting from the frequent transfer of monks from the black habit to the white, and the letters written by St Bernard on that occasion, I do not see that these concern us enough to be transcribed here at greater length; nor does the famous prodigy of flies killed by the Saint’s word, since William explains it in book I of the *Life*, chapter 6, no. 58. But what of the holy abbot’s preaching?

102. “The zeal of Father Bernard,” to use Manriquez’s words for the year 1122, chapter 6, “was vigorous and drew from the world many learned men, many nobles, many powerful persons. Indeed, he scarcely ever left Clairvaux [read *egrediebatur*, ‘went out’] without bringing back with him a troop of novices, filling that heavenly hive from which new swarms came forth daily. William and Alan add to his Châlons catch—for so they call it, borrowing the name from fishing—a Parisian one, which I therefore suspect occurred about this year. (William treats of the fruitfulness of his preaching in the *Life*, book I, chapter 7, and Alan in chapter 15.) But what the Parisian catch was like, and how the first attempt was unsuccessful, then fruitful, and finally, with an added accession, overflowing—filling Clairvaux with novices, the angels with joy, and all France with wonder—the author of the *Great Exordium* recorded for posterity. He learned its truth from Rainald, then Bernard’s companion and later abbot of Foigny … who was present.”

The *Great Exordium*, published by Tissier, distinction 2, chapter 13, tells the event:

> “Moreover, on one occasion, when Bernard, the man of God, had gone to Paris on necessary business, he entered, at the request of the clerics, their schools as was his custom. Showing them the pattern of true philosophy, he earnestly exhorted them to contempt for the world and to undertake voluntary poverty for Christ the Lord. But when he had finished speaking and none of them had been converted, he departed sadly, because, contrary to his desire and contrary to his usual experience, this had happened to him.”

103. He then came to the house of a certain archdeacon who had brought him to his lodging, and withdrew to an oratory established there. When he began to pray with vehement spirit, he was wholly dissolved into tears by the most powerful compunction, so that the groans and sobs which he could not restrain could be heard outside. Learning of this, the aforesaid archdeacon began to ask his companions what was the cause of such great sorrow. One of them answered—a religious man, formerly abbot of Foigny, named Renald, who was more privy to the secrets of the Servant of God, and from whose account we have also learned these things:

> “This wonderful man, wholly inflamed with the fire of charity and wholly absorbed in God, desires nothing else in the world but to be able to lead the erring back to the way of truth and to win their souls for Christ. And because he has just sown the word of life in the schools and has received no fruit of his word in the conversion of the clerics, he thinks that God is angry with him, since today he has not felt God’s favour in his preaching. Hence this storm of groans; hence this outpouring of tears. Therefore I most certainly hope that the abundance of tomorrow’s satisfaction will repay today’s barrenness with great interest.”

104. “Accordingly, when morning came and the eminent preacher returned to the schools, at the Lord’s bidding he put out the ship of his thought into the deep and cast the nets of sacred teaching for a catch. When the sermon was ended, very many of those same clerics gave themselves to the Lord through his hand. Bernard at once did not delay to draw them, rescued from the peril of the world as from ocean waves, into the harbour of Clairvaux, placing them in hired vehicles. At last he departed from the city with his company, came as far as the village of Saint-Denis, and spent the night there. In the early morning, when his brethren supposed that he would set out by the direct road, he said: ‘We must return to Paris by all means, because some of ours are still there, whom we must also bring from there and join to this fold of the Lord, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.’

105. “As they began to enter the city, he saw three clerics coming from afar to meet him, and said to his companions: ‘The Lord has sped us on our way, and now we shall continue our journey. See: these are the clerics for whom we came.’ When they approached and learned that he was there, they rejoiced with great joy and said: ‘How welcome is your arrival, most blessed Father, for we had intended to come to you; we scarcely thought that we could overtake you as you departed.’ He answered them: ‘And I knew it, beloved; therefore I hastened to meet you in your flight with loaves. Let us go together, and by God’s grace I shall be the guide of your journey.’ Joining the others mentioned above, they followed the holy man, clinging to him and exercising spiritual warfare under the discipline of his instruction all the days of their lives.”

This account is somewhat long, indeed, but faithfully narrated. From it shines forth the wonderful power of speech in the holy Father, by which, like a sacred magnet, he drew the hearts of young men strongly and sweetly, so that they might bear the Lord’s yoke from their youth.

Moreover, it also happened that “the Saint in these actions,” as Manriquez continues in no. 6, “preached Christian philosophy not with a premeditated discourse, but with an impromptu one—certainly inspired by God—and taking occasion from the very subject-matters of the schools, however slight.” This is from Vincent of Beauvais, whom he cites in the *Speculum Morale*, book II, part 2, distinction 6. The text which Vincent there produces may be seen at its source, since the preceding extracts are sufficiently long, and a very long road remains to us in illustrating the affairs of the holy Doctor.

106. Thus with Manriquez we proceed to the year of Christ 1123, which provides us with many remarkable matters concerning the holy man that must be related. There, chapter 2, no. 1, he recounts this example from Caesarius, Homily 8 after Epiphany:

> “At one time, when St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, still a young man, was standing at Mass, and a certain negligence occurred there in the ministry of the altar, a venerable person appeared to him with a sad expression and said: ‘If monks knew how greatly they grieve the holy angels present here when they are lukewarm and negligent in this sacred ministry, and how greatly they gladden them when they see them devout and fervent, they would become more careful.’ When the blessed man asked him concerning the state of the monks, he replied: ‘All who persevere in the Cistercian Order shall be saved.’”

These words are cited from Caesarius there under that year, no. 1, whether they should be assigned to that same year or to earlier years, since the Saint is called an abbot still young. What precisely was this negligence, what person appeared visibly to the holy Father, and in what more extensive terms that prophecy was explained, Manriquez adds in no. 2 from the *Cistercian Exordium*, book II, chapter 1, whose authority confirms what was said above. I give the text from Tissier’s edition, distinction 2, chapter 1 of the *Great Exordium*:

107. It happened once at Clairvaux, while Mass was being celebrated in the convent in the presence of the same venerable Father, that after the Gospel had been read, water for washing the priest’s hands was lacking through negligence. While it was awaited somewhat longer, the convent meanwhile stood facing east. Then the holy Father, standing in his stall—that is, a seat in the choir of the church—before the step of the sanctuary, saw visibly a monk who had died a few days before. Standing opposite him, the monk began to shake his head as though rebuking him. The Servant of God, seeing him, recognized him and asked why he shook his head at him. He replied:

> “Oh, if you knew how many and what companions you have in heaven, surely you would guard yourselves against every negligence.”

The Saint, gladly hearing this word, answered:

> “Do you truly think that all the brethren who are in this monastery will be saved?”

“Yes,” he said, “they will be saved; and not only they, but all who have lived obediently and humbly in our Order will be saved.”

The pious Father, remembering a certain brother whom he had often had to correct for negligence and hardness of heart, and over whom he therefore grieved greatly, added:

> “Do you know anything certain concerning that brother’s salvation?”

He replied:

> “God’s mercy will not fail even him.”

On hearing this, the holy man rejoiced exceedingly; and, holding more confidently within his breast the hope of eternal reward, he guarded the hard ways with his brethren all the more eagerly because of the words from the Lord’s lips. This is the account there.

108. Manriquez adds some other matters; but before we recount them, it is worthwhile here to consider what he says in no. 5 and following concerning the prophecy of eternal blessedness for all who persevere in the Order:

> “But as regards the promise of salvation for all who remain in the Order, let the reader accept another very similar one, made from heaven to a most holy monk, named Gerard—whether of Clairvaux is uncertain—while he was at the point of death, Bernard the Father being alive and testifying to it; provided that the little book circulated among Bernard’s works under the title *Teaching of Blessed Bernard* is truly his.”

Manriquez cites the following from it:

> “Moreover, be prepared to obey with a cheerful mind and countenance. Think of that monk named Gerard, who, despairing beyond measure of God’s mercy, fell mortally ill and lay for three days with his eyes closed, in an ecstasy of mind. When the abbot visited him, he opened his eyes and said: ‘Obedience is good. I have been before Christ’s tribunal; I saw the souls of the saints and Christ himself face to face, saying to me: “Behold, your place is among your brethren. No one of your Order shall perish, if he loves the Order; either he shall be purified in death or shortly after death. Those who are saved from your Order shall receive a lot in the order of the apostles, or of the martyrs, or of the confessors.”’ And saying this, after receiving communion, he departed.”

After citing these words, Manriquez says: “Thus far Bernard, or whoever may be the author of that little book, evidently ancient and of such a character as to have deserved to be regarded as Father Bernard.” That work, whose author Manriquez doubts, is found in Mabillon’s edition of the works of St Bernard, volume II, tome V, among doubtful works wrongly attributed to Bernard, col. 800 and following.

109. But concerning that prophecy, the cited annalist confirms the matter thus in no. 6:

> “We read that something similar occurred at Clairvaux under Abbot Pons, and we shall relate it below in its place, so that the word might stand not only in the mouth of two but of three witnesses and be impressed more deeply on the minds of all. Similar, I say, I believe, but not identical. For Bernard, who died before Pons’s administration, would not have related an event under Pons; and suppose the work not Bernard’s but that of another, younger man from Clairvaux. Yet the distinction of names also seems to indicate a difference in the persons concerned: one, as we have just seen, was called Gerard; the other, as we shall also see below from the *Great Exordium*, Bernard.”

Consult volume II of the *Cistercian Annals*, at the year 1167, chapter 6, no. 2 and following, where this occurrence is narrated; also Bertrand Tissier, *Library of the Cistercian Fathers*, vol. I, distinction 2 of the *Great Exordium*, chapter 26.

110. Finally, the same author of the *Annals* explains this point in chapter 2, no. 7, under the said year 1123:

> “Meanwhile I note that these promises, and any similar ones, ought so to raise our spirits to hope that they can bring them absolutely nothing of presumption or false security: they are for those who keep the observance, who will receive the same promises from the stronger word of the Gospel; while transgressors have already placed themselves outside the Order and therefore outside hope of the promised reward. Hear Caesarius speak thus in Homily 8 after Epiphany: ‘Let not these words deceive us, brethren. If there were among us—God forbid!—thieves, possessors of private property, conspirators, and persons like them, such persons are not of the Order, because the Order excommunicates such people. But he who does not share communion is an outsider.’”

Thus Caesarius. The *Exordium* states this more clearly, or at least more readily, when it promises the reward of future glory not to everyone remaining in the Order, but to those who live humbly and obediently. The promise, then, is made to those who observe the holy Rule and therefore the Gospel; it is in no way favourable to transgressors. So far the source.

Before I proceed elsewhere, I may usefully warn my reader in passing that the predictions reported concerning those dying in the Society of Jesus are altogether remarkable, as may be seen in the *Posthumous Glory of St Ignatius*, its founder, volume VII for July, on the thirty-first day of that month, pp. 851–852.

111. Here now, reader, are the matters which Manriquez had prefaced in nos. 3 and 4 concerning sinners brought to repentance by miracles through the holy Father. William, *Life*, book I, chapter 6, no. 57, tells the example of a brother whom Bernard had suspended from receiving the sacred communion; the man, overcome by human respect, received the Eucharist with the others but could not swallow the sacred host until the holy Father absolved him when he repented.

What need is there for me to mention the other example, equally remarkable and difficult for Manriquez to understand? In the already cited no. 4 he calls it “the work not of virtue but of a gift and of a most special inward movement; something rather to be admired than imitated.” I narrate the deed on the authority of the Cistercian *Great Exordium*, where it is found in these words:

> “A certain monk of this holy Father, through the deceits of demons and the simplicity of his own understanding, had fallen into such poverty of heart that he said that the bread and wine mixed with water which are offered on the altar could in no way be transubstantiated into the true body and blood of Christ. Therefore he scorned to receive these life-giving sacraments as though they would avail him nothing. At length his brethren noticed that he did not participate in the sacraments of the altar, and his elders privately confronted him.”

112. “Asked the reason, he did not deny it: he said that he placed no faith whatsoever in the sacraments. Since he would not yield to their teaching and admonitions, nor believe the testimonies of Holy Scripture adduced, the matter was brought to the venerable abbot. When summoned, he came; and when the holy abbot, according to the wisdom given him, addressed his unbelief, he answered:

> ‘No assertions will ever induce me to believe that the bread and wine offered on the altar are the true body and blood of Christ; and therefore I know that I shall descend into hell.’

When the man of God heard this, as he was accustomed to show a remarkable authority in circumstances of difficulty, he said:

> ‘What? Shall my monk descend into hell? Far be it! If you have no faith, by the power of obedience I command you: go, receive communion with my faith.’

O loving Father! O truly wise physician, who by the anointing of grace taught himself concerning all things how he ought to remedy the temptations of the infirm! He did not say: ‘Flee, heretic; go, condemned man; depart, lost one.’ Rather, he said with confidence: ‘Go, receive communion with my faith,’ firmly believing that his little child, whom the womb of sacred longing was bringing forth until Christ should be formed in him, would be alien neither from the bowels of his charity nor from the foundation of his faith.

Compelled, therefore, by the power of obedience, the monk—wholly without faith, as it seemed to him—approached the altar and received communion; and immediately, through the power of obedience and the merits of the holy Father, he was enlightened and received faith in the sacraments. He preserved that faith undefiled to the day of his death.”

This is found in Tissier, *Great Exordium*, distinction 2, chapter 6. But Tissier, explaining in notes at the end of volume I of the *Library of the Cistercian Fathers* what may initially appear difficult to understand here, says: “The monk of whom this account speaks was troubled by scruple and involuntary uncertainty; otherwise the Saint would not have commanded him to communicate, nor would the monk have said that he knew he would descend into hell because he did not believe.” We are mistaken if the reader, having maturely weighed the whole matter with its circumstances, will not rest content with this explanation.

## § XI. Sudden conversion of certain knights; a barren vineyard made fruitful; other reports concerning this vineyard; mutual ties between the monks of Clairvaux and the Carthusians; the Saint’s beneficence toward the Premonstratensians

“At the same period—for the year is still uncertain, and some place it far too late, though without justification—not a few noble magnates of France, while seeking military glory throughout the world, making dangers and enemies for themselves, and seeking not revenge but an affront, increased the number of brethren at Clairvaux by embracing the manner of life they had formerly dreaded.” Thus Manriquez writes under the said year 1125, chapter 3, no. 1, from William; see below, *Life*, book I, chapter 6, no. 61, where that noble cohort of knights, as William calls it, is suddenly converted by a wonderful transformation.

But remarkable are the things which the cited Manriquez records under the same year, chapter 4, nos. 1, 2, and 3, concerning the vineyard at Clairvaux:

> “We conjecture from the sequence of its history that it was planted about this time. At first barren, then fruitful, then both at once, it was always a portent of obedience. A certain brother named Christopher, appointed by the holy Father over external affairs, planted it in such spare hours as he had, without Bernard’s knowledge; for, as we have said, many matters were not referred to Bernard, lest his mind descend from divine to earthly concerns with lesser profit. But Gerard and Guy, Bernard’s brothers, regarding wine as an excessive luxury and therefore unbecoming to the austere life of monks, opposed the undertaking, rejected the labour, and persistently tried by every means to dissuade Christopher from what he had begun. He, on the contrary, insisted that brethren labouring in the field could scarcely be sustained without wine; that there were many sick and weak persons who needed to take it even as medicine; and that, if it were necessary for no use at all, it could easily be sold and many other things bought with its price, things of which the house undoubtedly stood in need … And these reasons seemed sufficient to Guy not to condemn the undertaking altogether.

[Col. 0696B] 114. “But Gerard, fervent as he was in zeal, … turned to him (that is, the planter of the same vineyard) and burst out with these words: ‘Brother, plant and cultivate the vineyard; yet you shall never taste of it, for you will always find it unfruitful.’ A remarkable event, worthy to be on everyone’s lips. Though planted and cultivated by industrious labor, in fertile soil and under favorable sun and air, the vineyard nevertheless remained barren for many years; nor did the earth produce fruit from it before it received the planter and held within itself his dead body … But let us relate two other wonders that followed in the same vineyard. After the planter’s death, when it still bore no fruit, the monks approached Father Bernard. It is uncertain whether Gerard too had then died. They humbly and faithfully reported that the vineyard would remain forever in that barren state through the curse of that most holy man, unless it were blessed by Bernard himself. Then the holy Father ordered water in a basin to be brought to him and, once blessed, sprinkled over the vineyard. When the water had been sprinkled, as though it were dew sent from heaven, the planting sprouted; and, as it had once been barren in obedience to Brother Gerard, so thereafter it obeyed Bernard by becoming fruitful, and compensated for its delay by abundance—so that the first miracle might appear not to have done harm, and the second more glorious. These things are from the anonymous Frenchman, book VII, chapter 7, translated by Silva; an author both ancient and equally worthy of credit.”

115. That event is described with less embellishment and greater simplicity by John the Hermit in the Life of St Bernard, in Mabillon, cols. 1288 and following, no. 10. From him, as from the genuine source, I transcribe it here:

“A monk named Christian planted a vineyard on the summit of the mountain nearest Clairvaux. And the brothers of the venerable Father came, namely Guy and Gerard, and excommunicated it, saying to him: ‘Brother Christian, where is your mind, and where your heart? Why did you not consider the Scripture saying: “Wine is not for monks”?’ But he replied: ‘You, brothers, are spiritual and do not wish to drink wine; I am a sinner and wish to drink wine.’ Then Gerard said: ‘I tell you, Brother Christian, you shall not see its fruit.’ After these words they returned to the monastery. But he dug and cultivated his vineyard for a long time. At last he died, and did not see [Col. 0697A] its fruit. Yet after a long time the keeper of the vineyard came to St Bernard and said: ‘Father, our vineyard is under an anathema and cannot bear fruit.’ He said to him: ‘Why, son?’ He replied: ‘Your brothers excommunicated it, and from then on it has borne no fruit.’ He said to him: ‘Bring me water in a basin.’ And he offered it to him. Then the holy man made the sign of the cross and blessed the water. ‘Go,’ he said, ‘son, and sprinkle it over the whole vineyard.’ The brother departed and did as the abbot commanded; and the vineyard grew and multiplied, so that those who saw it marvelled.”

You see here a mode of narration differing from the foregoing, yet in both cases the substance of the event is the same.

116. Concerning the words in the latter narrative, “And the brothers of the venerable Father came, namely Guy and Gerard, [Col. 0697B] and excommunicated it,” a difficulty may be raised; and indeed it is raised in Mabillon’s notes here against that excommunication, from col. 1287, where we read:

“And yet, when the removal of old Clairvaux was under discussion, the brothers informed Bernard that another site was spacious enough for vineyards, etc., as Arnold testifies in book II, no. 29. The same author likewise states at no. 48 that the monastery of St Anastasius at Aquae Salviae was assigned by Innocent to the Cistercians with its fields and vineyards. Although at that time the use of wine among the Cistercians was rare. Read Geoffrey above, col. 1117, no. 2.”

But we shall attempt to remove this difficulty for the reader.

117. We reply, then, to Arnold’s passage first by distinguishing the persons. For, since the names of the brothers are not there stated, why must Guy and Gerard necessarily be understood there? Why could not two other brothers of St Bernard be meant, namely Andrew and Nivard, who were still alive at that time? For Manrique, at the year 1141, chapter 4, no. 2, relates that they were present with the holy Father at the deathbed of their sister Humbeline, while Guy and Gerard had already died.

Second, we reply by distinguishing the times. Suppose that both of these were then present and mentioned vineyards when the removal of old Clairvaux was being discussed, concerning which see Manrique at the year 1135, chapter 3. If you go back from there to about the year 1123, to which the above excommunication of the vineyard was assigned, you count about twelve years lying between that incident and the removal. Thus, in the meantime, through a change of circumstances, they could very easily have changed their former will—by the persuasion, agreement, or command of the saint himself—so that the Cistercian or Clairvaux community, which was growing remarkably, might be supported from the annual produce of vineyards.

“For wherever the holy Father went, he sowed the seed of God’s word upon all waters, and scarcely ever [read: ever] returned without the interest of spiritual gain, filling the house of probation with a multitude of novices, whose number at times extended to one hundred; so that, when the novices filled the choir at the hours of the divine office, except for a few elders who attended to discipline, the monks were compelled to stand outside.” On this matter see the same annalist at the year 1135, chapter 3, no. 2, citing the author of the Great Exordium; I have just reproduced that text from Tissier’s edition, distinction 2, chapter 12. From what has been said, the answer is also clear to the objection drawn from the monastery of St Anastasius, on which see Manrique at the year 1140, chapter 8.

118. But, to return from this digression to that wondrous vineyard, there remain several further things reported about it. Manrique testifies to them at the year 1123, chapter 4, no. 4, where he says:

“The elders of Clairvaux further add, from a tradition received from their fathers, that after some years of fertility, when its grapes were already swollen and nearly ripe, the same vineyard was struck and so battered by hail from heaven that it scarcely retained two clusters which could be saved for the vintage. One of these was given to a pregnant woman who craved it—or asked for it as though she craved it. But from the other, pressed by Bernard’s hands into a huge wooden vessel which still survives today, the must increased within a short time to such an extent that it overflowed and ran from the vessel. Thus Villalpando, in his Itinerary, testifies that in the year of Christ 1599 he saw there a wine-vessel of unusual size, and consulted old men who confirmed the tradition, he having been sent there by the most reverend Abbot of Fitero to inspect the antiquities of that house. Thus that vineyard—never without wonder, never without obedience, and always illustrious no less through barrenness than through fruitfulness—continues even to this day, after more than five hundred years, and is called the Great Vineyard, whether from the extent of the place [Col. 0698C] or from its events. These matters have been stated partly by anticipation, because we judge that this is the more expedient course in these minor matters.”

But let the credit of this exceedingly wondrous narrative rest with its authors.

119. At this point it is also pleasing not to overlook the singular bond of love by which St Bernard and his community were bound to the Carthusian ascetics through a mutual tie of friendship. I find some matters on this subject connected with the year 1123 now under discussion, and some deferred to the following year. Let us state the former here. Accordingly, in the same place, nos. 4 and following, the author cited writes thus on this matter:

“He bound to himself the Carthusian monks, who had arisen in the world not long before Cîteaux—a great luminary of the Church—so completely that the Charterhouse was no less his than Clairvaux. A Carthusian received as his guest, and drinking in with his own eyes what he had earlier learned by report, returned to his own people and stirred their minds; already inclined and loving, he made them break forth also into outward expressions. Therefore Guigo, prior of the Great Charterhouse, and his brothers, having learned of the holiness of the Father and his sons, and of the multitude flocking to Clairvaux, began to venerate those men … and, as the flames of love burst forth, to call forth men who were silent, to rejoice in their blessings, and of their own accord to write and send letters in which they greeted Bernard—though still unknown to them—with the most ardent affection.”

120. There survives the holy man’s reply to them, a most eloquent witness to their mutual love, sprinkled throughout with marks of his tenderest affection and highest reverence toward them. It is the eleventh among his letters; but because it is long and may be read there, we do not transcribe it here. In Mabillon’s edition it is assigned to about the year 1125. There also survives the twelfth letter, addressed to them and shorter than the former, in which he excuses himself for having gone into those parts on very pressing business and not seeing them. In that edition it is printed without a date; but Manrique assigns it to the year 1127 and reproduces it there, chapter 2, no. 6. Concerning another journey which the holy Father made to the Charterhouse, Geoffrey may be consulted, book III of the Life, chapter 1, no. 155 of our edition. Concerning the man’s affection for other houses and ascetics of the same order, and also toward St Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, see the Cistercian annalist at the year 1123, chapter 3, nos. 8 and 9.

121. How greatly the same most blessed Father esteemed the Premonstratensians, and how he promoted the spread of their order, is shown by the same writer from the benefits and services bestowed by Bernard upon it, which he assembles under the year 1124, no. 7. Add to these a certain place in the forest [that is, wood] called Orta, granted by Louis the Younger through the intervention of Lord Bernard of blessed memory, abbot of Clairvaux, as the abbot of St Marianus of Auxerre acknowledges in letter 282 in Chesne, included among the Writers of the History of France, vol. IV, p. 666. St Marianus of Auxerre is mentioned in the synopsis of churches or monasteries of the Premonstratensian order in Paigi, Bibliotheca of the same order, part 1, book II, p. 326. Although the favors by which the holy Father supported the Premonstratensian order were discussed above, § 9, the chronological arrangement to which the aforesaid Manrique attaches this subject has led me briefly to recall it here.

## § XII. Apparitions of the dead; assistance rendered to them; a prophecy concerning a novice who would leave secretly; the archbishop and people of Reims reconciled; evil customs reformed in the Gallican Church.

The Cistercian annals again portray St Bernard as illustrious through many marvellous favors of heaven, at the aforesaid year 1124, in their customary manner and in a manner worthy of the merits of that most blessed Father, whose whole course of life was almost an uninterrupted collection of miracles. There, chapter 2, nos. 1 and 2, occurs the precious death at Clairvaux of Galdric, Bernard’s uncle according to the flesh, but his son and disciple in the spirit. When the enemy of the human race attempted to disturb his blessed passage from this mortal life to immortality, the Prince of the Apostles stood beside the dying man, drove away the evil demon, and rescued Galdric’s soul from danger. After his death Galdric appeared to Bernard in glory and revealed the event to him, as William, familiar with them both, testifies in his faithful narration in book I of the Life, chapter 5, no. 52.

“But,” Manrique continues there, [Col. 0700A] no. 3, “as regards the anticipatory or subsequent apparitions of sons who were dying, absent, or present, the same author, William, records them as so frequent that they can scarcely be committed to writing. Let him be heard at the place cited, no. 53: ‘It would be a long task to relate all that divine grace was accustomed from the very beginning to reveal to him concerning those who had departed this life, their blessedness, or even their need.’”

What is more, this remarkable man, passing, so to speak, through the threshold of both worlds—present and absent, the present age and the age to come—through the inspiration of the divine Spirit knew them with equal ease and without any distinction, and provided for his sons with a father’s care both in life and in death. Consult William, book I of the Life, chapter 7, from no. 69 onward, and chapter 5, no. 53.

123. That he rescued them from expiatory flames, if perhaps they had carried over from this life into the next some trace of human dust, by which even the minds of saints are defiled, is shown by an event that may be read in William, book I of the Life, chapter 5, no. 53. But that this entirely singular grace descended from the holy Father to his sons—who, enlightened by such visions, were aware of the punishments and thus labored diligently to appease divine justice, receiving both the fulfillment of their prayers and a share in the liberation of the souls whose purification they had procured—we infer, I say, that this grace descended from the Father to his sons from the writer of the Great Exordium, distinction 2, chapter 2.

[Col. 0700C] On one occasion a certain lay brother died at Clairvaux. While the brothers gathered together and the office of commendation was being performed according to custom, a certain elderly monk, a man of great religious devotion, heard troops of demons proceeding in their companies and crying out with loud clamour: “Ah, how good it is now! Ah, how good it is now! From this evil valley alone we have gained one soul for our allotted share.” When the same elder had surrendered his limbs to sleep in the quiet of night, the deceased brother appeared to him in a vision, with a sad and mournful expression, saying: “Because yesterday you heard the demons rejoicing at my sufferings, come and see to what terrible torment I have been consigned by the just judgment of almighty God.” And he led him to a certain well of vast width and dreadful depth, and said: “Behold, I am often thrown into this well by demons, whose cruelty is so great that, if a choice were offered me, I would rather be plunged here a hundred times by human beings than once by demons.”

124. “But when morning came, and the aforesaid elder reported to blessed Father Bernard what he had heard and seen—though Bernard himself had also learned it through the Spirit—he groaned and said: ‘I know that, unless there were a grave cause, the demons would never have dared attempt such a thing.’ He therefore entered the chapter of the brothers and laid before all of them the misery of the deceased brother. Then, with salutary exhortation appealing to each person’s conscience, he warned them to walk more cautiously in the way of holy religion, affirming that the malice of demons against all Christians is great, but especially against those who profess the monastic life. After this, earnestly urging them to aid the soul of the brother placed in torments, he exhorted them to appease the Lord’s wrath by psalms and prayers, and also by celebrations of Mass: perhaps the merciful Father, moved by their prayers, might through the offering of the unique sacrifice overthrow the tyrannical pride of the demons and deign to free the brother’s soul from their wickedness.

125. “When the brothers did this with the utmost devotion, after a few days had passed the same deceased brother appeared again to the aforesaid elder, indicating by the cheerfulness of his face that his condition had improved. When the old man asked how he was, he answered: ‘Thanks be to God, well.’ Asked again how he had been delivered, he said: ‘Come and see.’ And immediately he brought him into the oratory of that place, where priests with their ministers stood at each altar, celebrating with the greatest devotion the offering of the saving sacrifice. ‘Behold,’ he said, ‘these are the weapons of God’s grace by which I have been rescued; this is the power of God’s mercy, which remains invincible; this is that unique sacrifice which takes away the sins of the whole world. And I tell you truly that nothing can resist these weapons of God’s grace, this power of God’s mercy, this saving sacrifice, except an unrepentant heart.’ When the elder awoke, he rejoiced exceedingly at the liberation of his brother’s soul. By explaining the manner of this vision to the other brothers, he rendered them all the more devoted to the offering of the saving sacrifice, because he had deserved to experience more certainly its efficacy in the brother’s rescue.”

The author of the Cistercian annals assigns this history to the year of Christ 1124, on the occasion of the aforementioned apparition of Galdric, which, he says, “may deter sinners from vices and console penitents, for whom God has provided such remedies. Therefore, because these things are useful, plainly singular, and concern the same subject of apparitions, though the year is still unknown, let the reader take them kindly,” as he advises there, chapter 2, at the end.

126. Returning thence to the year 1124, the same writer, chapter 3, nos. 7 and 8, records the holy Father’s prophecy concerning a novice who would leave secretly. He relates it in a manner both dreadful and marvellous from the Great Exordium, so often cited already. This tragic story is narrated in Tissier, distinction 3, chapter 20:

“A certain old man named Achard, noble by birth but nobler in the dignity of his conduct, was in charge of the novices at Clairvaux. He was powerful in the word of edification and consolation; and in the vigor of his youth, by the command and mission of his abbot, blessed Bernard, he had devoutly founded and built very many monasteries. Now a veteran and an old man of completed military service, appointed to train recruits, he diligently fulfilled his office. From what he had learned through long experience, he daily formed their still-untrained minds through exhortations against the threefold cord of flesh, world, and devil, which is difficult to break. He also made them more cautious against vices by examples, both ancient and recent; and from his own mouth we have heard some of these, which we shall touch upon.

“When Achard himself was still a novice, the venerable Abbot Bernard one day entered to console his novices, as he often used to do. When his discourse had ended, he drew aside the said Achard with two other novices and warned them beforehand, speaking thus in a prophetic spirit: ‘It shall happen,’ he said, ‘that that novice’—and he identified one by name—‘will secretly depart before tomorrow. Therefore watch and be ready, and do not allow the fugitive to escape with plunder. And if the wretch departs from us because he was not of us, nevertheless retain for yourselves the spoils, because they are ours.’ When they heard this, they marvelled and silently awaited the outcome. But deep in the night, although two of them saw the fugitive fast asleep in his bed, they too began to sleep; for their eyes were heavy, the spirit of error undoubtedly deceiving them. Achard, however, because he most certainly believed that the word spoken by the holy Father could not prove void, resisted with manly constancy the spirit of drowsiness that grievously troubled him. Now rubbing his forehead, now his temples; at one moment plucking the hairs of his head and beard, at another washing his hands and face; now walking from place to place to rouse himself, he finally overcame the deceptive sleep that oppressed him.

127. “And when the signal for Vigils was near to being rung, behold, two Ethiopians of almost gigantic size, clothed in blackest capes, visibly entered through the door of the house. The one who went before carried a roasted hen [Col. 0702C] on a spit [that is, a roasting-spit]. Moreover, a huge serpent was fastened through head and tail upon the very spit, encircling the same hen on either side. With this dish, then, they approached the bed of the false novice and applied the smoking hen to the sleeper’s nostrils and hands. Immediately upon his awakening, the demons departed, and by this dreadful visible sign they showed what they had invisibly been doing within his heart.

“When that wretch had awakened, not as Jacob from the sleep of contemplation, but as a contemptible apostate from the sleep of deception, he immediately rose and, laden with clothing, went out after the demons. Coming to the door of the cupboard in the cloister, he attempted by his devices to break its fastening and carry off books with him. But the said Achard very quickly awakened his companions and indicated by signs and gestures the prophesied flight of the apostate. They pursued him together as he withdrew and found him shaking the door-bolt. When he perceived them, that evil man immediately sprang away, rushed headlong through the gates of the orchard, and was finally caught within the enclosure of the walls and brought back. When day came, since he remained unrepentant and refused to come to his senses, because he had already been given over to a reprobate mind, he was finally allowed to go away to his own place. That same day, seized by the devil, he fell into madness and did not cease raging until his death.

128. To this terrible example of a false novice most miserably punished, we add a happier event, altogether remarkable for the saint’s glory, which Manrique, writer of the Cistercian Annals, presents thus at the same year 1124, chapter 4, no. 1:

“At about the same time, when the archbishop of Reims was at variance with the people and neither side was willing to yield to the other, though many others had sought to make peace, Bernard alone in Gaul seemed able to accomplish so great a work. For he was powerful alike in word and deed; while he confirmed by signs what he said, men were ashamed not to obey one whom even irrational creatures, indeed demons themselves, obeyed. A blind, deaf, and mute man, restored in his senses and at the same time freed from a demon, presented the palm of obedience to both parties.”

This notable miracle is found in William, book I of the Life, chapter 7, no. 73. There I read indeed that it happened at the time when it occurred … that the man of God was present to reconcile them—that is, the archbishop and people of Reims—and likewise that peace was being discussed in the palace of the same city. Yet in that chapter I do not read that peace followed at that time from Bernard’s miracle, which is there reported as having happened before all, in a house filled with a great multitude of clergy and people. Still, it seems that this may not imprudently be supposed or believed: the praised biographer left it implicitly to be understood when he had stated that the man of God was present to reconcile them. For what else does it mean that the man of God, endowed with such great gifts of grace and nature, with supreme authority among men and a wonderful power of bending their minds, was present to establish concord, than that it was truly established by him at that time—especially since the miracle of which I spoke was then performed? It is also credible that many others had sought that peace, but without result, as Manrique relates; William, however, does not say this in the place cited.

129. The same Cistercian historian also assigns to the year mentioned the labors and fruit of St Bernard and other Cistercians in reforming the Gallican Church. “When ecclesiastical prelates,” he says at no. 3, “throughout Gaul somewhat loosened the reins of moderation and by a secular and slightly profane manner of life represented the apostolic life less faithfully, Stephen and Hugh, Bernard and John, with the other chosen Fathers of Cîteaux, began to labor by word and example that they might be brought back … to a more fruitful rule of life … Moreover, the bishops of the metropolitan see of Sens, the metropolitan of Sens himself, Suger abbot of St Denis, and his entire convent are witnesses to how much they achieved by their labor.”

The most eminent Baronius speaks thus of this matter at the year of Christ 1127, no. 13, in the edition of 1629:

“For the bishops of the province of Sens had made progress through the example of the Cistercian monks and through the words and letters of St Bernard, especially the bishop of Paris whom we have mentioned, and Suger, abbot of St Denis at Paris, who had tightly bound that monastery, wholly released from monastic discipline, with the clasp of regular observance. On that account St Bernard rejoiced with him and sent him a congratulatory letter,” namely letter 78, reprinted in Mabillon, col. 77 and following, where it is likewise assigned to the year of Christ 1127.

Thus this chronological assignment does not agree with Manrique’s. At the beginning of the cited letter, “A report has gone forth,” those matters are noted—namely, those concerning his, that is Suger's, conversion, no doubt brought about through Bernard’s admonitions about the year 1127—although the reformation of the monastery of St Denis by Suger is placed, perhaps prematurely, in the Chronicle of Nangis under the year 1123.

130. Concerning the metropolitan of Sens, Baronius adds at the year designated shortly before:

“Moreover, that Henry, the archbishop and metropolitan of Sens himself, likewise admonished by the letters of St Bernard—and indeed by more lengthy letters—was converted to a better disposition and diligently fulfilled the duties of an excellent shepherd, incurred for the same reason the indignation of the prince himself, that is, Louis king of the French; and not merely a moderate indignation, but precisely such that St Bernard, together with the other abbots, had again to write to Pope Honorius and to the cardinal chancellor, even crying out that bishops suffered persecution because of their most well-ordered life,” etc.

What that reformation was, so displeasing to the Most Christian King, may be seen in the same place. Concerning the bishop of Paris mentioned above, we shall speak with the Cistercian historian at the year of Christ 1127; meanwhile we shall continue with him to the year of Christ 1125 and the year immediately following.

## § XIII. Grain multiplied; a demon driven out; a woman restored to life; rain turned aside; the Saint’s former health restored, through the patronage of the Mother of God; refutation of the error concerning Antichrist’s imminent coming; exchange of letters with the Roman court.

The year of Christ 1125 opens, in the Cistercian historian, chapter 3, no. 1, a public stage for a conspicuous miracle of the first rank.

“Famine,” he says, “was becoming severe throughout all Gaul and both Burgundies; nor was the grain brought there from Flanders, however great its quantity, sufficient to feed the peoples. When human resources failed, the charity of Bernard and divine power multiplied the granaries of Clairvaux, otherwise meagre.”

Since that wonder is described by William, book I of the Life, chapter 5, near the end, it is superfluous to recount it here. Nor could the Saint’s fatherly mercy towards the needy be confined within the domestic walls of Clairvaux monastery; it also spread further abroad, as appears from his letter to the duchess of Burgundy, letter 121, in Mabillon’s edition, col. 127. There the merciful Father of the poor concludes: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Distribute your grain to Christ’s poor, that you may receive it again eternally with increase.” Manrique assigns this letter, printed there without a year, to the aforesaid year 1125.

132. In the same place, no. 3, he adds another miracle and gives the reason why he records it under that year. Since it may be read in William, just cited, it is enough here to give Manrique’s summary. It reads:

“A wife’s treachery attacked the man by sorceries … and she whose adultery had defiled his marriage-bed pursued with implacable hatred him whom she had once injured. A demon tortured the man relentlessly. But the man of God, by prayers, extinguished the spells and drove out the demon more swiftly than one can speak, through the presence of Christ’s body. Because William relates that this happened in the time of famine, and thus in this year,” the same Cistercian historian indicates that he will then recite it from William.

But he defers to the following year, 1126, two wonders performed by the holy man on the occasion of the famine. We shall attach them here to the events just narrated, from John the Hermit in Mabillon, col. 1287, no. 6:

“A famine arose in the regions of Burgundy so severe that people almost consumed their own limbs. Under the pressure of the same need, a great multitude of poor people came to the gate of Clairvaux. Therefore, because of so great a multitude, the holy abbot and his brothers took counsel; and by deliberate decision they admitted two thousand under the token, so that alms might also be given to others, though in a smaller amount. For they had no resources from which all could be maintained until harvest; yet the merciful Lord multiplied those resources so that they sufficed them until after the harvest, that is, for the period of three months.”

133. “Accordingly, two boys received a token, while their mother did not. Being utterly at a loss about what to do, she eventually conceived the idea of making, from moss, something like a child wrapped in swaddling-clothes, in order by this device to rescue herself from the danger of the approaching famine. She did so, and for some time received alms in this way, until at last the fraud was discovered. When her allowance was reduced and what she received was insufficient for her, she subsequently perished under the distress both of famine and illness. After her death, the holy abbot, passing by, heard the boys wailing for their mother’s death and ordered each of the passers-by to inquire into the cause of their grief. The boys explained the course of events. On hearing this, the blessed man entered the place where the body lay and prostrated himself in prayer. [Col. 0705D] While he prayed, the woman, as though awakened from sleep, was restored to life before the eyes and ears of all who stood present, giving thanks to God and to His Saint, through whose merits and prayers she had returned to life. She also declared how great torments she had suffered for her fault.”

Here is another miracle, performed on behalf of and for the sake of the poor, which follows there at no. 7:

“One day alms were being distributed to the poor on the side of the mountain when rain threatened. By chance the saint of God was standing there, and, raising his hand, he set the sign of the cross against it. When this was done, the rain was seen unexpectedly to divide itself to right and left, so that not even a drop touched them.”

134. Let us return with Manrique to the year of Christ 1125, temporarily set aside by us. There, chapter 3, nos. 4 and 5, he speaks of the Saint’s failing health, visions, and the recovery of his former health through the visitation and most gracious touch of the Virgin Mother of God and Saints Lawrence and Benedict. William the abbot reports the event, book I, chapter 6, no. 63, a witness beyond every exception. The holy Doctor mentions the aforesaid illness in letter 37 to Theobald, count of Champagne—on which matter see Mabillon’s notes to that letter—when he writes to him in these words: “That I heard you were concerned about our illness, I regard as by no means a small kindness. For in this I recognize your gracious regard toward me,” etc. That letter is assigned by Mabillon to the year of Christ 1128; hence, if that dating stands, it seems to follow that the adverse health of the blessed man of which I spoke should be placed somewhat later, about the year 1127. Yet consult Manrique’s conjectures concerning the date of this illness in the cited passage, no. 8.

135. Proceeding to the year 1126, the same author writes, chapter 3, no. 1, about the error by which it was then believed that Antichrist’s coming was not far off, an error opposed by the holy abbot.

“Meanwhile a rumor spread among the faithful occupied the minds of the credulous populace: Antichrist’s coming was already imminent. And, wonderfully enough, its authorities were neither doubtful nor ordinary, but most weighty and holy men, among them Norbert, who affirmed the matter as though he had received it from heaven. But after consulting Father Bernard about the oracle and examining it, he moderated his judgment. Thus the rumor was dispersed through Bernard’s efforts.”

Relevant here are the things reported in letter 56 of the same holy Father to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres:

“But when I asked Norbert what he thought about Antichrist, he solemnly declared that he knew most certainly that Antichrist would be revealed while the present generation still endured. But when he wished to explain to me, as I asked, the basis of that certainty, I did not think that, after hearing his answer, I ought to believe it as certain. In short, however, he maintained this: that he would not see death unless he first saw a general persecution in the Church.”

Concerning the rumor then spread about the said coming of Antichrist, Baronius, at the year 1106, no. 27, in the edition of 1629, relates:

“As regards Antichrist, there was indeed an opinion among men of no ordinary standing that Antichrist would be revealed in this century; among them was Norbert, a man most renowned in the reputation of this age. Concerning him St Bernard wrote the following to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres,”

from which we have just given the matters relevant here. And the cited Baronius adds there: “These are St Bernard’s words concerning the oracle. It is customary to relapse into this belief: when holy men had often foreseen that great persecutions of the Church would come, they thought that, because of the very magnitude of these events, the times of Antichrist were at hand.”

[Col. 0707A] 136. The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, no. 2, decides as follows concerning St Norbert’s oracle, uttered about that persecution: “Although Baronius did not state expressly what great persecution of the Church was made known to St Norbert by revelation, it is easy to conjecture that it was the one which the Church suffered under Innocent II at the hands of Peter Leo [indeed, Leo], the most obstinate antipope. It began about the year of salvation 1130, thus four years before St Norbert’s death, and continued for almost a decade. Thus both the sound teaching of Father Bernard and Norbert’s unfailing prophecy—and the divine instruction of each—were confirmed by the events themselves.” Nor were there lacking those who, taking occasion from this rumor, aspired to the name of Christ—or rather, of Antichrist; proof is furnished by those matters [Col. 0707B] produced by the same author of the *Cistercian Annals*, no. 3, where he also observes that undoubtedly more would have sprung up had Bernard not more firmly opposed the rumor which had gained prevalence.

But since we have touched upon that widely circulated and, at the time, extremely harmful talk concerning Antichrist’s imminent coming, it will not seem irrelevant, for the benefit of the learned and inquisitive reader, to set down here the following observations, since they are very well suited to the present subject, though they were published long ago.

137. In the edition of the works of St Bernard made public under Mabillon’s care, volume I, col. 13 and following, there are extensive notes on the said works, both by the most learned [Col. 0707C] Mabillon himself and by Horstius, celebrated for bringing the Saint’s works to light. At column 23, Mabillon, already cited, takes occasion from the fifty-sixth letter of the holy Doctor, addressed to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, to make various observations at length, though learnedly, drawn from the aforesaid Horstius:

“Not only Norbert, but many of the ancient Fathers as well—to say nothing of more recent men—were at times persuaded that Antichrist and the last day of the world stood at the doors, as may be seen in Jerome, Pope Leo, Gregory the Great, and St Augustine himself. For, from the wickedness of the times and from the signs foretold by Christ as preceding the world’s end, many of which were already then [Col. 0707D] appearing, they did not seem to themselves to draw this conclusion without reason. And, to trace the matter a little more deeply, from the very times of the Apostles there have always been various judgments, conjectures, opinions, and prophecies of many persons concerning Antichrist and the end of the world. Most philosophers and astronomers, many impostors as well, jesters and peddlers of trifles, and likewise certain fanatical heretics, wished to appear as prophets here and wiser than other mortals. But events have already mocked most of their prophecies and convicted those prophets of vanity and falsehood. The following age will likewise mock the remaining predictions, which still look to the future, so that it may be clear how truly it was said: ‘It is not for you to know times or seasons’; likewise: ‘But of that day no one knows.’ It will not displease the reader if [Col. 0708A] we give a few examples from among very many.”

But lest their account draw us farther than is fitting from our present purpose, we refer the reader there.

138. “These matters,” Horstius continues at col. 24, “seemed worth recalling on the occasion of the aforementioned prophecy about Antichrist—not, however, in disparagement of Norbert, a most holy man, whom Bernard elsewhere calls a heavenly pipe. For he was not alone: several holy Fathers also thought or foretold that the end of the world was not far off in their own time; and a catalogue of them is drawn up in the same place. But observe that holy men spoke of the world’s end for a very different reason from those whom we mentioned above, the astronomers. The latter spread such inventions either from observation of the stars and planets [Col. 0708B]—which is excessively deceptive in predictions generally, but especially in this one—or from certain sayings of Scripture twisted into a false meaning, or from a mere desire to lie and deceive, or from pursuit of popular applause and reverence. Holy men, however, because of the horror of crimes and evils flooding everywhere throughout the whole world, thought that the world could scarcely stand any longer and that nothing remained except that it should soon collapse under the weight of sins and iniquities, God’s wrath, of course, forestalling the limit appointed for the world.”

This is enough gleaned from Horstius concerning Antichrist’s coming. Whoever wishes for more on the subject should consult him. We therefore leave this digression and proceed, with the Cistercian historian, to continue the thread of St Bernard’s affairs which we interrupted for a while.

139. “The fame of the holy man,” he says in no. 4, “growing daily more illustrious, and the favor shown him by princes both within and without, everywhere gave peoples hope that through him they would obtain whatever they desired. And he who had hitherto been known only to the French, now becoming known to the Roman curia as well, was taken up as a suitable mediator before the pope and the cardinals, to intercede for churches and individuals. The matter is proved by the Saint’s various letters, so many witnesses to his great authority among the highest men. There survives his Letter 13 to Pope Honorius, by which he asks that Alberic’s election to the bishopric of Châlons be ratified. Concerning this Alberic one may consult [Col. 0708D] Mabillon’s notes in volume I, col. 33, where the said letter is assigned to the year of Christ in which we ourselves are now engaged, 1126, contrary to Baronius’s view. Manricus writes of this as follows in no. 6:

“Cardinal Baronius assigns Bernard’s letter mentioned above to the year 1129, as also other letters which we shall immediately produce; but undeservedly. For this letter is proved to be Bernard’s first to Honorius, both because Bernard’s name is suppressed and from the context itself. At that time he either considered himself unknown to Honorius, or at least did not regard himself as known well enough to presume. Yet letters from him to the same pope, written before that year, survive; Baronius himself had transcribed them earlier, and we shall set them out more fully in their proper places.”

Whether the holy man obtained his wish for Alberic, as expressed in this letter, see the same Manricus, no. 5. In no. 7 he deals with another letter to the praised Honorius, the fourteenth, introducing his copy with these words:

140. “Not long afterward, the church of St Benignus at Dijon, renowned above all for antiquity and religious observance, but still more renowned and dear to Bernard because it was entrusted with the remains of his mother Alcidis—add also of his father, according to Mabillon’s note on this letter—appealed to his favor while a dispute with the monks of Lisieux was pending. This was his second letter to Honorius, written with a pen still timid and not yet running freely, though now expressing its author’s name, as to one known.”

Moreover, the esteem in which the holy abbot was held [Col. 0709B] among the cardinals of the Roman curia is established by the letters he wrote to them: namely, Letter 15 to Haimeric, chancellor of the Apostolic See; and Letter 16 to his dearest lord Peter, cardinal priest. To these may be added Letter 17 and those following. What more need be said? Let these things suffice as examples, since both the man’s letters and other evidence abundantly establish that he was held in the highest esteem by great and humble alike. How strong and fearless he showed himself against the powerful men of that age, when justice required it, is indicated by what we are now to relate.

## § XIV. Actions on behalf of Stephen, bishop of Paris, against Louis the Fat; the fulfilled prophecy of his son’s death; the holy abbot’s labors refreshed by heavenly consolations; whether St Felix of Valois was brought to him or educated under him

[Col. 0709C]

The Cistercian chronicler, under the year of Christ 1127, which we now enter with him, chapter 1, recounts the lineage, power, and character of Stephen, bishop of Paris; Bernard’s letters to him and their result; likewise the violent assault made upon the same Stephen by Louis, king of the French; furthermore, the appeal for the favor of the Cistercian Chapter, and the envoys sent by Stephen together with letters intended to restrain the king’s raging anger. Then, in chapter 2, the praised chronicler, continuing the same subject, treats of the anger of the same King Louis, restrained by Cistercian envoys and by fear of the interdict to which he was bound; but after the interdict was lifted by Pope Honorius, [Col. 0709D] that anger at once flared up again when the reins were loosened. I have thought it sufficient to indicate these matters in passing, because they prepare the way for what we shall relate concerning the Saint’s threats and prophecy against the king. That concise summary which we have given may be compared with the fuller treatment in the said chronicler, whose account is here followed, and with Mabillon’s observations in the extended notes to the letter addressed to King Louis—understand, Louis the Fat—which stands as Bernard’s forty-fifth letter. One may also consult what Pagius has in his *Historical-Chronological Critique* for the year of Christ 1127, nos. 13 and 14.

142. Meanwhile, what did Bernard, that high-minded and fearless champion of justice, do? The holy man omitted absolutely nothing, as the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 2, no. 3, relate, which he did not attempt. . . . “Indeed, Paul Aemilius, in his account of Louis, and others have reported that Bernard added severe threats and declared that heavenly vengeance would shortly come unless he repented. ‘The bishops who begged him,’ he says—that is, Louis—‘he drove away from his knees; and Bernard the abbot is said to have announced to him, in his impenitence, that the avenging wrath of heaven was at hand.’ Gaguin, an authority of no slight credibility, adds that the same Saint specified the kind of punishment and aptly foretold to the furious father the untimely death of his firstborn: ‘This obstinacy of yours, O king,’ he says in Book VI of the *History of France*, ‘shall be punished by the death of your son.’”

Furthermore, the truth of this prediction is established by passages inserted from elsewhere into the text of the biographer Geoffrey, Book IV of the *Life*, in our chapter 1, at the end, where the following is found. On account of this matter—that is, King Louis’s obstinate refusal—“the man of God, moved by religious zeal, rebuked the king more harshly the next day because he had despised the Lord’s priests, and freely announced what had been revealed to him that very night: ‘This obstinacy shall be punished by the death of your firstborn, King Philip. For I saw you, with your younger son Louis, bowing at the feet of the bishops whom you despised yesterday; and I immediately understood that, when Philip had quickly been removed, you would ask the Church which you now oppress for the substitution of Louis.’” This indeed was fulfilled not long afterward, namely in the year of Christ 1131, by a pitiable accident. For, as Pagius reports under the year just mentioned, no. 12, from Orderic and pseudo-Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel: “Philip, a boy recently anointed king, while riding a horse in the city of Paris, was thrown headlong when a pig happened to run beneath the horse’s feet, and his sudden and miserable death brought mourning upon the French on the third day before the Ides of October [13 October].”

143. But was King Louis moved to genuine repentance by Bernard’s so grave and sorrowful pronouncement? Not at all—perhaps because he did not think that God would avenge a crime which the supreme pontiff had left unpunished. Mabillon briefly explains the event in the notes cited shortly before, col. 21, while speaking of the Saint’s prophecy and its fulfillment:

“The prince, somewhat turned from his purpose by such freedom of speech, revived his courage at Pope Honorius’s letters dissolving the interdict [Col. 0710D] and pursued his wicked undertaking more ardently. Bernard, bearing this impatiently, sent letters full of just complaint to Honorius, both in his own name and in that of Geoffrey of Chartres. See Bernard’s Letters 46 and 47.”

Finally, as Mabillon continues at col. 22, that stubborn and inflamed dispute seems to have ended at the Council of Troyes in 1128, or at least not long afterward, by Honorius’s own authority. Bernard gave thanks for this, writing to him again in Letter 49: “For thereby the constancy of the bishop of Paris was assailed by grievous insults and injuries, but not shaken, because the Lord put forth His hand when You put forth Yours.”

As for that Stephen, Mabillon adds the following: “Moreover, Chesnius proves expressly in his notes to Abelard that this Stephen of Paris, formerly chancellor, is distinct from Stephen de Garlande, the seneschal, mentioned in the *Annals of Teulfi*; and this is also made sufficiently clear by a letter of Geoffrey of Chartres in volume III of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, p. 160, in which he writes that St Bernard was chosen to make peace between Stephen of Paris and Stephen de Garlande.” With respect to Louis further, whom St Bernard, writing to Honorius in Letter 49, calls another Herod—the phrase is softened by Mabillon in a shorter note to that letter, col. 57—it is certainly worth remembering with what religious devotion and penitence he ended his life in 1137, as may be seen more fully in the observations [Col. 0711B] on Letter 45, among the extended notes already cited, col. 22.

144. But how can I adequately recount the heavenly consolation that received Bernard after the great troubles which he had borne with a thoroughly manly and unconquered spirit? Let the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 3, no. 1, be heard:

“Bernard, then, restored to Clairvaux and to his sons, enjoyed the desired quiet all the more affectionately because it came more slowly and seldom, and was not thereafter, if possible, to be abandoned. Among many other fruits, he experienced two fruits of it, strengthened by two visions from God, both angelic and both remarkably commending the monastic order, choir, and chant. In one vision heavenly spirits were writing down the prayers of those chanting in choir, doubtless to be presented to the divine majesty; in the other, they were rousing and laboring to promote the devotion of the chanters. Both visions were for the glory and consolation of all monks, indeed of all churchmen.”

Hear the events from the author of the *Great Exordium of Cîteaux*, in Tissier, distinction 2, chapter 3:

“On one occasion the holy Father attended the night vigils with the purity and devotion known to God alone and to himself, with which he was accustomed to attend them. And while the slow modulation of psalmody prolonged the vigils, the Lord opened his eyes—that is, the holy Father’s—and behold, looking about, he saw angels standing beside individual monks; and they were carefully taking down on little tablets, in the manner of notaries, what each monk was chanting, so diligently that they omitted not even the smallest syllable, however negligently uttered.

145. “They wrote, however, in different ways. Some wrote in gold, others in silver; some in ink, others even in water; while some wrote absolutely nothing. The Spirit who revealed these things also inspired his heart with an understanding of the different kinds of writing. Those who wrote in gold signified the most ardent zeal in the Lord’s service and complete attention of heart to what was being chanted. Those who wrote in silver declared a lesser fervor but nevertheless a pure devotion in the chanters. Those who wrote in ink marked the habitual good will of certain persons in psalmody, though not with great devotion. But those who wrote in water represented those who, oppressed by drowsiness or laziness, or carried away by vain thoughts, seem indeed to make some sound, but whose heart, drawn far away, does not at all accord with their voice. And, O wonderful mercy of God! For as no evil shall go unpunished, so no good, however small and however negligently done, shall go unrewarded.

146. “Moreover, those who wrote nothing rebuked the lamentable hardness of heart of certain persons who, forgetting their profession and unmindful of the fear of God, either immerse themselves deliberately in deadly sleep, or else, while awake and with mouths shut, occupy themselves with vain and harmful thoughts—not from weakness, but by deliberate intention—and do not fear to appear empty before the Lord, contrary to the precept of the law. The holy Father [Col. 0712B] who saw these things, remembering that saying, ‘Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?,’ rejoiced at the fervor of those making progress, but also, with a father’s compassionate affection, pitied the lukewarmness of those falling short.”

In the same work, chapter 4, another blessed vision is recorded in these words:

“On one occasion solemn vigils were being celebrated, and the man of God was present with the other brothers. While the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—‘We praise thee, O God’—was sung, he saw holy angels shining with great brilliance and devout with a marvelous cheerfulness of countenance. Running through both choirs, they now roused this man and now that; they attended the singers, stood by as though rejoicing with them, and strove by every means to ensure that the divine hymn should be sung with devotion. [Col. 0712C] Thus the holy man understood that the hymn was truly divine and familiar to the holy angels, whom he saw devoting such earnest labor so that the brothers might sing it to God’s honor with fervent devotion.”

Then, on the occasion of this hymn, the following is added:

147. “A certain spiritual brother was also granted a vision when the same hymn was begun: from the mouth of the one beginning it burst forth a flame of great splendor and rose upward.”

Manricus, chapter 3, no. 4, says concerning this subject: “I find two observations recorded by the Fiterian which the reader may readily accept. First, the angels’ rousing is not to be understood materially, as waking from sleep, but spiritually, as stirring the mind to devotion: so that those who were lukewarm might become fervent, and the fervent might be made more fervent. Second, the person beginning the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, from whose mouth the fiery flame was said to burst and fly upward, as seen by that devout brother, was none other than Father Bernard, upon whom, by the office entrusted to him as abbot, lay the duty of beginning the hymn. This practice, received from the beginning at Cîteaux, we see observed even today.”

The same historian, no. 10, relates a particular event concerning St Bernard which, as he recites it from another author, I likewise transcribe here:

148. “In the recently published history of Segovia,” he says, “concerning the beginning and progress of the most holy family which God established under the invocation of the Holy Trinity for the redemption of captive faithful people, I find it recorded that one of its first founders was Hugh of Valois, nephew through the sister of Count Theobald, who was afterward called Felix of Valois. Together with Blessed John, called of Matha, he laid the happy foundations of that distinguished work. I find, I say, that this saint was born in this year and, after baptism, was brought by his mother to Clairvaux, to be offered there to almighty God through Bernard and to receive the holy Father’s blessing. I have not wished to omit what is related by the author of that history, Book I, chapter 5, although I do not yet know whence he drew it, nor am I unaware that in other matters he mixes in, he departs somewhat from the truth. Certainly there is no chronological inconsistency; and if Hugh, or Felix, was truly Theobald’s nephew, he had no other relation nearer than Bernard from whom to seek, before God, an intercessor from his very cradle. And it is no slight glory for Bernard to have had so great a fosterling or client, one who would illuminate the world and that age by miracles and merits, and fill subsequent ages with glorious offspring.”

149. As you see, Manricus reports rather hesitantly, and not without reason, this matter concerning the offering of this saint to God at Clairvaux by our Saint. For what follows? The origin and education of St Felix of Valois do not yet appear to have been established with sufficient solidity. The writer of the account we have reported is far too recent and of authority insufficiently tested to command belief on his own; Manricus does not even state his name, nor does he produce ancient documents to confirm the present event. We may therefore desire proof of better standing before assenting to it. Yet lest we decide anything too hastily in a matter not yet sufficiently ripe, we defer it until 20 November, when St Felix of Valois must be considered, and perhaps more light will then arise for our successors to disprove or confirm the present account.

The same must be said of what is found in the *Life* of the same saint by the Reverend Father Master Brother Francisco de St Augustine Macedo, a Portuguese Minorite, published in Latin at Rome in 1660. In chapter 2, in florid language indeed, but without citing any author, he describes the present subject in these words:

“Eleanor gave milk to Felix when he was born, but sought to season it with honey. Therefore she went to Clairvaux and sought Bernard, whom she knew to be a heavenly honeycomb. He instilled honey into the infant with his words and did not withhold an embrace, because Bernard believed that he had come among lilies and roses. Before the altar he offered the blooming pledge to God like a little bundle. The one who saw him carrying the boy in his arms believed Bernard to be a bee.”

150. There are some who say more, as I understand from a modern author who published the lives of the saints in French in three volumes. For, under 20 November, in the *Life of St Felix of Valois*, he affirms that certain persons maintain that Felix went to Clairvaux for sacred instruction under the discipline of St Bernard. Yet just as the preceding story of St Felix, whom his mother allegedly brought as an infant to Bernard and whom he offered to God, has thus far seemed to me scarcely credible, so much less credible does the claim appear that the same St Felix was trained in the practices of religious life under our Abbot’s discipline, so long as I do not see it supported by suitable testimonies.

## § XV. The treatise on grace and free will; attendance and authority at the Synod of Troyes; whether the Rule of the Knights of the Temple was composed by the Saint

151. The composition of this treatise, by which the holy Doctor earned an immortal title of merit before the whole Catholic Church, is assigned to the aforesaid year of Christ 1127 by the author of the *Cistercian Annals*, who makes several observations concerning it in chapter 4 of that year. It is found in Mabillon, volume I, col. 603 and following, and is there elucidated by this preliminary notice at p. 601:

“Bernard composed this treatise before 1128, that is, before the thirty-eighth year of his life. It treats of grace and free will, on the occasion of a discussion with a certain man, whose name I do not know, to whom the holy Doctor seemed to attribute too much to grace, as though he left free will nothing to do in human actions.
