The principal aim of the book, therefore, is to establish what parts grace and free will respectively have in the work of salvation. It teaches much concerning the free will of God, angel, and human being—unfallen, fallen, and blessed—and likewise concerning the grace of the first human being before and after the fall. It is a small book, yet one containing more richness and solid teaching than great volumes of books [Col. 0714C] treating this theological question. Its style is vigorous, full of lively genius and light; its words are fitting and suited to its subject; its expression is easy, not artificially sought but seemingly natural; neither bloated nor thin, but rich and sinewy; elegant, well-proportioned, and pleasing; not languishing in the commonplace vocabulary of the schools, nor barbarous or uncultivated. It is not so compressed as to flow sparingly and drop by drop, yet not so copious as to burst forth like a torrent after a dam has broken and its channel run dry. Rather, it flows evenly with a steady course and grave majesty, indicating an unfailing spring, filled not from another source but from its own—or rather, from God’s gift and continual meditation upon Scripture, especially the Apostle [Paul].” No. 48.

[Col. 0714D] 152. “Geoffrey, in Book III, chapter 8, of the *Life of Bernard*, says of this treatise: ‘How grateful he was to God’s grace is clear from the faithful and subtle manner in which he argued concerning grace and free will.’ Nor should the words of Letter 52 to Cardinal Haimeric, written in 1128, be passed over: ‘The aforesaid bishop, Geoffrey of Chartres, asked me for some of my little works to send to you; but there was nothing at hand which I deemed worthy of your study. Yet I have recently published a little book on grace and free will; I shall gladly send it to you when I learn that you wish it.’ The book was addressed to William, abbot of St Thierry, Bernard’s particular friend, to whom were also addressed the *Apology* published above, col. 525 and following, and several letters.”

Thus the most learned Mabillon introduces the reader to this highly praised little work of the holy Doctor, which he also explained with notes. Let us now move with the Cistercian historian to the year of Christ 1128, very honorable to the holy Father, as will become clear from what is to be said on the occasion of the Council of Troyes, which he adorned with his presence, even against his will.

153. Baronius places it in the year of Christ 1127, but Pagius corrects him in the *Critique* under that year, no. 11, in these words:

“The Council of Troyes, attended by Matthew, cardinal bishop of Albano and apostolic legate, the archbishops of Reims and Sens, and various bishops, was celebrated only in the following year. For John of Michaëls, clerk of the council, says in its preface that it was held ‘on the feast of St Hilary’—namely 13 January—‘in the year 1128 from the incarnation of the Son of God, and in the ninth year from the beginning of the aforesaid knighthood,’ namely that of the Templars. This year of the Incarnation is also found noted in a manuscript codex of the Victorine library at Paris and in James of Vitry’s *History of Jerusalem*. Tyre indeed says that this council confirmed the Order of the Templars, founded already nine years before; but since he begins the year of the Incarnation there either on 25 March or at Easter, and since it is certain that the council assembled in January, Tyre can only be understood to mean January of the following Christian year. Some learned men, failing to attend to his method of reckoning the years of the Incarnation, have either alleged that the numbers in Tyre were copied incorrectly or resorted to futile interpretations. Therefore the year 1128 of the Dionysian era was still, in January, the year 1127 for Tyre, and the ninth year ending from the foundation of the Templar Order.”

These remarks concern the year of the council; its acts are treated from William of Tyre, Book XII, chapter 7, in Labbe, volume XX of the *Councils*, col. 922.

154. Therefore Matthew, legate of the Apostolic See and president of the council, wishing to add still greater weight of authority to the matters being transacted there, desired that, besides the archbishops of Reims and Sens, their suffragans, and abbots, the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, as William of Tyre, whom I have just cited, records—adding also the abbot of Pontigny with many others—should attend the same council.

“But Bernard,” Manricus says under this year, chapter 1, no. 3, “who had once resolved not to leave his monastery, as he had written to Peter Leo, likewise a cardinal legate, two years earlier, was dragged away only with difficulty and great reluctance, giving every reason and every excuse, and sparing neither the poor health which detained him nor his own insufficiency.”

There survives St Bernard’s Letter 21 to Legate Matthew, in which he excuses himself for not coming when summoned to deliberate on affairs. Mabillon dates it, col. 38, toward the end of 1127. As to who this Matthew was, of whom we have spoken above, Mabillon observes in the same place:

“Matthew, formerly a canon of Reims, then a Cluniac monk at St Martin-des-Champs, afterward cardinal and bishop of Albano, a man of remarkable holiness according to Peter the Venerable, is the person to whom this letter was written, as the Council of Troyes of 1128 was impending; see the fuller notes, col. 16.”

Moreover, the features of this letter are such as to impress the reader with the Saint’s wonderful humility and to give the clearest testimony that a man so great in the eyes of others was truly small in his own. He also ends it with this clause of submissive obedience: “Yet may you know—you, Father, I say—that I am ready and have not been troubled, to keep your commands. It will belong to your indulgence to spare me where you decide that I should be spared.”

[Col. 0716B] 155. Why mention his letter to Theobald, count of Champagne? It may be read in Mabillon, col. 51; it is Letter 39, assigned there to the year of Christ 1127. In it Bernard exhorts him to conduct himself honorably and reverently toward the bishops assembled in his city of Troyes for the council. After reciting an excerpt of it, the Cistercian annalist says in no. 5: “Thus far the holy Father to Theobald, seeking obscurity for himself but honor for the Church, and the reverence to be shown to prelates, whose fellowship he did not judge himself worthy to share.”

Concerning the letters written by the Saint to Peter Leo, which Manricus mentioned shortly before, note a few things in passing, so to speak. Mabillon, in notes to Letter 17, col. 35—addressed to Peter, cardinal deacon and legate—observes: “This Peter is undoubtedly different from Peter, also a legate, but a cardinal priest, as we have proved in the preface to this volume.” He then adds whom this Peter seems to have been.

Pagius, in his critique of Baronius under the year of Christ 1125, discussing Cardinal Legate Peter, whom Pope Honorius II sent against Pons, former abbot of Cluny and usurper of their monastery, no. 3, judges him to be “different from Peter Leo, because Peter Leo had already been a cardinal priest from 1120, according to Onuphrius, and certainly in 1121, as we saw under that year. Furthermore, this Peter, to whom the case of Pons was entrusted by Honorius II, can be none other than Peter, cardinal deacon and legate, to whom St Bernard wrote Letter 17 in the usual ordering. His legation could have been carried out in no other year during this period than the current one. From this he concludes that St Bernard’s letter, which Mabillon dates about 1127, belongs entirely to this year,” as do two others, namely Letters 18 and 19, sent by Bernard to the same Cardinal and Legate Peter, “because in the following year, as he adds, Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, and Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, exercised the legation in Gaul. Mabillon, in § 4, no. 39, of his preface to the edition of the works of Abbot St Bernard, had already suspected that Peter, cardinal deacon and legate, to whom the aforesaid letters of Bernard are addressed, was the man who came into Gaul by Pope Honorius’s command against Pons, abbot of Cluny; but for me this is certain and beyond doubt.”

Thus far Pagius, who also observes under the year of Christ 1127, no. 12, that Baronius wrongly refers St Bernard’s seventeenth letter to the Council of Troyes. For while the holy abbot excuses himself in it because, though summoned, he had not come, . . . there he says that he speaks of another journey unknown to us.

156. But as regards the Council of Troyes, at which, as we said, the holy Doctor attended together with several others, how can I describe the man’s authority, by which, like the sun among the stars, he shone among the other Fathers of that synod? For in Miraeus, in the *Cistercian Chronicle* under 1128, after listing their names, these words are found: “The aforesaid Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux was not absent; the Fathers mentioned above praised his opinion with free voice.” The same words appear in Labbe, volume X of the *Councils*, col. 924.

In the prologue to the Rule of the Templars, given to them at the said Council of Troyes, in the same work, col. 923, and in Miraeus just cited, the clerk of the frequently mentioned council testifies that the task was entrusted to the holy abbot: “I, John of Michaëls, by God’s grace have merited to be the humble scribe of this present document, by command of the council and of the venerable abbot of Clairvaux, Bernard, to whom this task was entrusted and due.”

Here, however, one may ask whether the Saint composed the Rule prescribed for the Templars. Manricus and Miraeus affirm it; Mabillon denies it in volume I, in the notice to the Saint’s sixth work in volume II, *In Praise of the New Knighthood*, addressed to the Knights of the Temple. To that work, which appears at col. 543 and following, the editor prefixes the following remarks relevant to the present question:

157. “Miraeus published the Rule of the Templars from the Victorine manuscript, and inserted it in his Cistercian Chronicle, ‘as having been,’ he says, ‘dictated by St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux (as is clear from the Prologue).’ This Rule consists of as many chapters as the Rule of St Benedict, from which it is for the most part taken word for word—namely, seventy-two chapters. Before the prologue it is entitled as follows: ‘Rule of the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon.’ Manrique, under the year 1128, chapter 2, agrees with Miraeus in assigning this Rule to Bernard as its author, and adduces two passages from the prologue to prove it. The first passage reads thus: ‘Although indeed the very great number of religious Fathers who assembled in that council by divine prompting lends authority to our composition, we must not pass over in silence those in whose presence, and while they delivered their true opinions, I, John of Michael, [of] the present document, etc.’—words which we have already given a little above. But these words do not signify that Bernard composed any Rule for the Templars; rather, that he entrusted to John of Michael the office of scribe laid upon himself. Nor is anything further proved by the following words [Col. 0718A], which are reported after the enumeration of the Fathers of the Council of Troyes in this manner.

158. “The master of the knighthood himself, Hugh by name, was indeed present, and brought with him certain of his brethren—for example, Brother Godfrey, Brother Roval, Brother Geoffrey Bisol, Brother Pagan of Montdidier, and Archambaud of Saint-Aignan. This Master Hugh, with these disciples, made known to the above-named Fathers, according to what his memory supplied, the manner and observance of the modest beginning of his military Order, which took its origin from Him who says, ‘I am the Beginning, who also speak unto you.’ It therefore pleased the Council that this counsel, there carefully examined by the file and consideration of the divine Scriptures, should nevertheless, under the direction of the Pope of Rome and [Col. 0718B] the Patriarch of Jerusalem, and also with the assent of the Chapter of the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of the Temple which is in Jerusalem, be committed to writing and inviolably observed.” From these words we understand only that the Fathers decreed that a Rule should be prescribed for the knights by their agreement, after consultation with the Roman Pontiff and the Patriarch of Jerusalem; Bernard, however, is by no means asserted to have been its author. Indeed, Alberic of the Cistercian Order writes that the Rule of St Augustine was imposed upon those same knights. Hence in the English Monasticon they are assigned to the Order of St Augustine. It would be very surprising if Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, a Cistercian monk not far from Clairvaux, had been unaware of this Rule of Bernard and had attributed another in its place to the knights [Col. 0718C] who still existed in his time.”

For these reasons the most learned Mabillon denies that St Bernard composed the said Rule; and, not being satisfied with these arguments, he adds the following others:

159. “William, Archbishop of Tyre, in chapter 7 of book XII of the work already mentioned, relates that to those same knights, who before the Council of Troyes ‘numbered only nine, a Rule was instituted by the command of Pope Honorius and of Stephen, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and a white habit was assigned,’ whereas before they had used ordinary dress. ‘Afterwards, however, in the time of Pope Eugenius, as it is said, they began to sew crosses of red cloth upon their mantles,’ both the knights ‘and [Col. 0718D] those brethren of theirs called sergeants.’ Their estate increased so enormously that, ‘at the present day,’ says William, they have about three hundred knights in their community, ‘clothed in white cloaks, apart from the brethren.’ From these last words we infer that the Rule attributed to Bernard as author was written only after William of Tyre; for in chapter 21 certain ‘false brethren from regions beyond the mountains, falsely claiming to belong to the Temple, and certain things that had grown up among the knights themselves without discretion or the counsel of the common chapter and must be entirely cut off,’ are noted and censured—namely, because ‘formerly servants and squires had white garments, whence intolerable harms arose.’

160. “There was no general chapter of the Templars before the Council of Troyes; before it there was no distinctive habit for the knights, but only ordinary dress. White was granted them by the Fathers of the Council, sergeants excepted. Clearly, even from these words alone, it may be understood that this chapter at least was added long after the time of the Council. Chapter 7 not only does not commend hearing the divine office while standing, but even censures it, and ordains that it be heard while sitting. Such an ordinance would certainly never have entered Bernard’s mind. Chapter 61 decrees that sisters are henceforth not to be kept. This indicates that the Order was not newly established. Whether John of Michael was the author of this Rule, I leave for others to judge.” Yet that the most holy Father, though not in this matter, was nevertheless elsewhere a benefactor of the Templars, is related by Manrique, chapter 3, [Col. 0719B] nos. 5 and 6.

## § XVI. The complaints of the Roman Curia refuted by the holy Doctor; the notorious schism of the pseudo-pope Anacletus suppressed by him; the year of the murder of the venerable Thomas, Prior of Saint-Victor

161. Affairs of the common good, to which Bernard was not infrequently summoned even unwillingly, stirred up great complaints against him, not to say hatreds. There is no need to transcribe here the substance of this matter, recounted at length by the Cistercian historian under the year of Christ 1129, since it may sufficiently be understood from the saint’s Letter 48, addressed to Haimeric, Chancellor of the Roman See, in which he refutes the unjust accusations made against him with a vigorous and intrepid pen. Here, then, reader, is an excerpted fragment from that letter. Observe, however, that the writing was directed not to Cardinal Haimeric alone, but also to other cardinals, whom he calls brethren; on this see Mabillon’s notes to the letter. It follows that the Roman Curia resounded with calumnies against him, as is plainly inferred from the holy man’s reply, from which I extract the following:

“Does truth then bring hatred even upon one poor and needy? Can not even misery escape envy? Shall I complain, or shall I glory, that I too have become an enemy by speaking the truth? By speaking the truth, or by doing what is right? . . . What in me, good sirs, has displeased your brotherhood? Was it because at Châlons a man utterly notorious was removed from the stewardship entrusted to him, because in the Church of Verdun, over which he presided, he had squandered his lord’s goods? Or because in the city of Cambrai Fulbert, the manifest destroyer of his monastery, was compelled to yield to Parvin, whom all testify to be a faithful and prudent servant? Or because at Laon God’s sanctuary was restored from a brothel of Venus? Is it for these things that I am—not, I say, stoned, but torn to pieces, so that I may receive something less from my Lord? And I should answer this deservedly and with all glory, if I recognized anything of my own in these matters.

162. “But now, why am I judged for deeds of others? Or, if they are mine, why as though they were evil? Since no imprudence can doubt, no impudence deny, that all these things were done justly and nobly . . . [Col. 0720A] A new kind of detraction, and truly bearing some resemblance to the work of Balaam, who, brought and hired to curse the people, instead heaped blessings upon them . . . But . . . it matters nothing to me concerning things of which I was not the author. Let them praise them if they wish, or blame them if they dare: in the first case, the Lord of Albano; in the second, the Lord of Reims; and in the third, the same man, Archbishop and Bishop of Laon at once, together with the king and many other reverend persons, who certainly do not deny that they were the authors and leaders in these matters. If they acted well, what is that to me? If otherwise, what is that to me any more? Is all the blame mine alone, solely because I was present—a man fit only for hiding-places? . . . I was present . . . I cannot deny it; but summoned, but dragged there. Would that I had not gone [Col. 0720B] to those affairs! Would that I did not go to similar ones! Would that I had not recently gone where I saw tyranny, armed by apostolic authority—alas!—violently directed against the Church, as though it had not raged sufficiently of itself. Then at last I felt, according to the prophet, my tongue cleaving to my palate,” etc.

163. “For such reasons, even if there were no other, it grieves me to take part in causes in which I especially know that I have no part. It grieves me, but I am drawn in. Yet from this necessity, through whom might I better hope to be withdrawn than through you, excellent sir? . . . Let it be decreed, if you please, that the noisy and importunate frogs are not to come forth from their caverns, but are to be content with their marshes. Let them not be heard in councils; let them not be found in palaces. No necessity, [Col. 0720C] no authority, should be able to drag them to lawsuits or business . . . Yet even if I remain hidden and silent, I do not think that the murmuring of the churches will cease, unless the Roman Curia ceases, at the will of those attending it, to do injury to one who is absent. Farewell.”

Thus the great man vigorously refuted the unjust complaints against him, replying to the accusations so freely because, conscious of no fault and surrounded by the mighty company of his virtues, his conscience stood secure against slanders. Some matters occurring in the quoted fragment are explained by Mabillon, both in his shorter notes on the said letter and in his fuller notes, column 22. Manrique, under the year of Christ 1129—which, as I previously indicated from him—chapter 7, no. 8, reports a prophecy of St Bernard; but of this below.

[Col. 0720D] 164. What the holy Doctor had written in the letter to Haimeric cited a little earlier—that it was his counsel and purpose “never, unless the cause of our Order alone should require it, to leave the monastery, except at the summons either of a legate of the Apostolic See or certainly of my own bishop when the see is vacant; whom, as you well know, it is altogether unlawful for our humility to resist, save under a privilege of some superior authority”—what, I say, the holy Doctor then wrote, in restricting his departures from the monastery and his beloved solitude for the public good by these most equitable conditions, found application in the year of Christ 1130, on the occasion of the notorious schism which the ill-occupied and turbulent pseudo-pope Peter Leonis, adopting the name Anacletus, stirred up in the Church of God against Pope Innocent II.

Because this subject is one of the chief ornaments through which St Bernard earned among posterity an immortal name and glory never to be effaced by oblivion, we should not wonder that the most learned Mabillon returned to it in a revised treatment, and illustrated it from the evidence of various ancient monuments in that excellent General Preface which he prefixed, § 4, to his re-edition of Bernard’s Works. Therefore it has seemed fitting here to reprint the labor of the praised Mabillon, who has so excellently deserved of the republic of letters through this and so many other monuments which he brought to light—not indeed all of it, but so much as is sufficient for our purpose. Those remarks which the author himself inserted in the words of others I shall enclose in parentheses.

165. “Although Baronius and other ecclesiastical writers,” he says, “have written much concerning the schism that arose between Innocent and Anacletus after the death of Honorius II in the year 1130, some points nevertheless require fuller explanation; these we shall endeavor to supply from a reading of ancient monuments.” Then, after a few intervening words, the aforementioned Mabillon develops and illustrates the present subject as follows:

“Peter Leonis, a Roman of the Leonine family, was first made, if we believe Onuphrius, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian by Paschal II; then cardinal priest of Santa Maria in Trastevere, of the title of Callixtus, by Callixtus II in the year 1120. [Col. 0721C] ‘This Peter,’ as we learn from the Chronicle of Morigny, ‘was the son of Peter, son of Leo. Leo, however, passed from Judaism to Christ at Easter—that is, at the Passage—and deserved to be baptized by Leo and distinguished with his name’—understand Leo IX. ‘This man,’ namely Leo, a convert from the Jews, ‘being very learned, became eminent in the Roman Curia and begot a son named Peter, who was thereafter to be of great fame and great power.’

166. “At that time there arose that most turbulent conflict concerning investitures between the King of the Germans, who by succession from Charlemagne was Patrician of the Romans, and the Roman Church. In it this man proved so vigorous in arms, prudent in counsel, and faithful to the Roman Church that the Pope entrusted to him, together with the other fortifications in Rome, that tower also which seems to hold the likeness of that city—the Tower of Crescentius, situated on the Gallic side at the bridge over the Tiber—and held him more intimate than the rest. Growing wonderfully through this opportunity, he improved daily in his position and increased in wealth, possessions, and honors.”

These matters had to be set forth beforehand, because the understanding of the event depends on Peter’s lineage, Judaism, power, and the Tower of Crescentius—which they call the Castle of Sant’Angelo, and in which Anacletus defended himself. The Chronicler of Morigny continues:

“Among his other offspring—of which, according to some, Antichrist boasted a very great multitude of both sexes—he begot this Peter, of whom the present discourse now speaks; having been educated in letters, he was called by some the forerunner of Antichrist.” (I consider that reproach to have been bestowed on him from what followed, or from the event.) “For the sake of study he went to Gaul and Paris; and, as he was returning to his native country, he assumed the monastic habit at Cluny, a most wealthy and holy monastery. After being there for some time instructed in regular observances, he was recalled to the Curia by Pope Paschal II at his father’s urging, and was made a cardinal in the time of Pope Callixtus. Along with that Gregory who later became Innocent II, he was sent to Gaul, where he held councils at Chartres and Beauvais.”

There is no mention here of the title of cardinal deacon, which Onuphrius says was granted to Peter Leonis by Paschal. In this matter the authority of the Chronicler of Morigny, a contemporary, is stronger.

167. “Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Angelo, is said to have been created by Urban II, and later sent as legate to Gaul by Callixtus II with Peter Leonis in the year 1124. With him he visited Sées, a city of Neustria, as Orderic testifies in book XII, p. 877. Vincent, in chapter 49 of book II of the Life of Stephen of Grandmont, writes of this legation as follows: ‘The most eminent cardinals Gregory and Peter Leonis—between whom there was later a schism concerning the papacy—when sent to Gaul and performing their legation in the regions of Limoges, came together to this man of God, Stephen.’ Both in fact subscribed as legates to the charter of Abbot Suger in the year 1125, in Chesne, vol. IV, p. 547: [Col. 0722C] ‘I, Peter, cardinal priest and legate of the Apostolic See, praise and confirm. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo and legate of the Apostolic See,’ etc.

“At the same time Bernard wrote certain letters to Peter, cardinal deacon and legate—namely Letters 17 and following—and I once thought with Manrique that he was Peter Leonis himself. But since it is certain that the Peter to whom Bernard writes was a cardinal deacon, not cardinal priest, those letters cannot apply to Peter Leonis.

168. “Meanwhile Pope Honorius died in the middle of February in the year 1130. The Chronicler of Morigny assigns the preceding year, following the French custom by which the beginning of the new year was reckoned from Easter. Then ‘the cardinals,’ says the same chronicler, ‘who were present there with the chancellor, Haimeric, and sat beside the ailing Honorius, set over themselves a certain Gregory’—that is, the man just mentioned—‘distinguished for learning and religion; and, as some say, they clothed him too hastily with the pontifical insignia. They say this was done by way of dispensation, in order to frustrate the hopes of a certain Peter, who seemed to aspire to the papacy in a worldly manner. This Peter was the son of Peter, son of Leo,’” and so forth—the things that we reported above concerning him.

Suger expresses the event more clearly in his Life of Louis the Fat, among Chesne’s Writers of French History, vol. IV, p. 317. He says: “The greater and wiser members of the Roman Church, after Honorius had died, had agreed, in order to avert turmoil in the Church, that the election should take place at Saint Mark’s and nowhere else, and should be celebrated publicly in the Roman manner by all together. [But] those who, through assiduity and familiarity, had been closer to the Apostolic Lord, not daring to assemble there through fear of the tumultuous Romans, before the death of the Lord Pope had been publicly announced, chose as supreme pontiff the venerable Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. But those who favored the party of Peter Leonis, having invited others to Saint Mark’s according to agreement, when they learned of the Lord Pope’s death, elected that same Peter Leonis, cardinal priest, by the desired consent of many bishops, cardinals, clergy, and Romans”; and thus the destructive schism was produced.

[Col. 0723B] 169. “Innocent’s election, therefore, was the earlier, but hasty and not made by the whole body of electors. ‘But since the party of Peter Leonis prevailed,’ Suger adds, ‘both by the support of his kinsmen and by the protection of the Roman nobility,’ Innocent left the City and sailed toward the regions of Gaul. Having sent messengers to King Louis, he sought his aid. For this reason Louis convened at Étampes a council of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men, and, by their counsel, made inquiry more into the person than into the election. He acknowledged Innocent, on Bernard’s authority; and the votes of the whole council concurred in Bernard’s judgment, as Ernald testifies in book II, chapter 1 of his Life.

Thereupon, as Suger himself relates, he was sent by the king to meet Innocent as far as Cluny, whose Abbot Peter the Venerable and monks had preferred Innocent to Anacletus, their former monk, as we shall note later on Letter 126. The king himself met the pope as far as the monastery of St Benedict at Fleury, together with his queen and sons; and, bending “his royal head as before the tomb of Peter, he prostrated himself at his feet.” Following his example, Henry, King of England, likewise met Innocent [Col. 0723C] at Chartres, fell most devoutly at his feet, and promised him obedience, his own and that of his people.

“Innocent then, visiting the Gallican Church, made his way into the regions of Lorraine. When Emperor Lothair met him most splendidly in the city of Liège, with a great assembly of archbishops, bishops, and nobles of the German kingdom, he humbly offered himself as the pope’s groom in the square before the episcopal church. He hastened on foot through the midst of the holy procession toward him, holding in one hand a staff for defence and in the other the bridle of the white horse, and conducted him as his lord. When the whole procession had dismounted, he bore him along, supporting him, and made the eminence of his fatherhood renowned among known and unknown alike.”

These things occurred in the year 1130. Here Suger says nothing of Bernard, though from Ernald we learn that Bernard was Innocent’s constant companion in his journey through Gaul.

170. Mabillon then observes what was done at Liège at this time, citing the manuscript Magdeburg or Saxon Annals under the year 1131: “On the Sunday before Mid-Lent, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, a most celebrated assembly of thirty-six bishops and princes was held at Liège, in the presence of the Lord Apostolic Innocent, King Lothair, and the queen.” This council had been preceded by the Synod of Würzburg, as the same Annals, written by a contemporary author, state: namely, “a council of sixteen bishops convened by the king in October, at which the Archbishop of Ravenna, legate of the Apostolic See, was present; there Gregory, who is Innocent, [was] elected and confirmed by King Lothair and all assembled there.”

After the assembly at Liège Innocent, Suger testifies, returned to France, spent Easter at Saint-Denis, and “after three days had passed after Easter, came to Paris. Thereafter, visiting the churches of Gaul . . . after travelling for some while by land, he chose to remain at Compiègne.” Soon afterwards, after holding a council at Reims, as Suger relates—and indeed “on 14 November,” according to Dodechin—Louis the Younger there received the royal insignia from Innocent on the eighth day before those Kalends, as Robert, continuator of Sigebert, recorded.

“The manuscript Saxon Annals, under the year 1131: Pope Innocent, again gathering ecclesiastical men”—that is, after the Synod of Liège—“and crowds of the faithful, presided for several days over a great synod at the city of Reims on the feast of Saint Luke.” Suger adds that the pope, “after the council was dissolved,” remained for a time at Auxerre and finally returned to Italy with Lothair. The Chronicler of Morigny likewise places the stay at Auxerre after the Council of Reims.

171. “Ernald, in book II, chapter 1 of the Life of Bernard, places the Council of Reims before that at Liège, and writes that Innocent went from Liège to Clairvaux and then, [Col. 0724C] after a brief stay in Gaul, made for Rome with Lothair. But it is certain that the Synod of Reims was later than that of Liège, both from Suger’s narrative and from the Saxon Annals, but above all from the Chronicle of Morigny, in which Innocent’s journey is carefully described. Mabillon soon supplies its text, as well as other matters which may be seen there, lest we stray too far from our subject.

“Meanwhile Peter, or Anacletus, left nothing undone in order to attach all the more eminent men possible to his side. Among the bishops Gerard of Angoulême adhered to him; he had held the office of legate under the immediately preceding popes and hoped to obtain the same office from Anacletus. The same Gerard drew William, Count of Poitou, over to Anacletus’s side. Moreover, to secure the counsel of Roger, Duke of Apulia, Anacletus gave him his sister in marriage and crowned him King of Sicily, as Orderic testifies in book XII . . . All these many and great disturbances, which I have perhaps described more fully than the place permitted, caused Bernard much trouble. He wrote various letters in every direction to reconcile the schismatics to Innocent and to keep the faithful in their duty; he also undertook various journeys for the same cause, as may be understood from the following letters and from book II, chapters 6 and 7, of the Life.

172. “It remains here to discuss Gerard, Bishop of Angoulême, whose character was admirably described by Arnulf, first Archdeacon of Sées and then Bishop of Lisieux, in a treatise against him [Col. 0725A] which our Acherius published in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*. Mabillon then portrays his most shameful crimes more fully from that same author.

“Through those grievous and long-lasting times of schism, how great were Bernard’s labors and how many his journeys may be understood, as we have said, from his Life and letters. For this cause he went to Italy three times; and at last, through his work, the schism was suppressed after Anacletus died in 1138. The schismatics then substituted Victor as antipope, ‘not so much from obstinacy in schism as in order that, after some delay, they might be more conveniently reconciled to Pope Innocent. And indeed Victor himself went by night to the holy man’—that is, Bernard—‘and he, stripping him indeed of his usurped insignia, brought him to the feet of the Lord [Col. 0725B] Innocent,’ as Ernald testifies in the Life, book V, chapter 2, no. 137, in our edition.”

And this was the end of that most grievous and long-lasting schism, which was most happily and honorably suppressed by the tireless cares and labors of our holy hero Bernard. Ernald, just mentioned, recounts at greater length from no. 129 the deeds Bernard performed in this cause; and the matters which I have already set forth from Mabillon’s Preface will throw light upon his narrative. Yet I judge it suitable to our present purpose to add some points individually.

173. First, this was alike memorable and exceedingly glorious for the Saint: he “opened his mouth and the Holy Spirit filled it,” as Ernald testifies in chapter 1, no. 85. Chosen, surely, by that same Spirit, Bernard alone was the mouth and tongue of all the Fathers assembled in the Council of Étampes in this most weighty affair. “For, speaking alone with the voice of all,” says the same biographer, “he declared that Innocent should be received as supreme pontiff by all; and all together acclaimed the decision as ratified. Having sung praises to God according to custom, they then promised obedience, and all subscribed together to Innocent’s election.”

Other actions undertaken by the holy man in this cause are known from his letters. In Letter 124 he exhorts Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, to acknowledge Innocent as the lawful pontiff, and among several other things sets out these prerogatives of Innocent’s right: “A threefold cord is not easily broken. The election of the better men, the approval of the greater number, and—what is more effective than these—the testimony of character, commend Innocent to all and confirm him as supreme pontiff.”

In Letter 125, to Geoffrey of Loroux—on whom see Mabillon’s note—he seeks Geoffrey’s help in establishing Innocent’s pontificate, whom, he says, “the Church rightly receives, since both his standing has been found clearer and his election sounder, clearly prevailing both in number and in worth of those electing.” Finally, in Letter 127 to the bishops of Aquitaine, he nobly defends the same cause against Gerard of Angoulême, who acted as a partisan of the schismatic; he depicts Gerard’s character and exposes his evasions.

174. Moreover, regarding William, Count of the same Aquitaine, who was wickedly drawn over to Anacletus’s party by Gerard, Bishop of Angoulême, Manrique indeed relates the matter under the year 1130, chapter 4; but we defer it, together with other matters, to another time, when we shall treat of his conversion through St Bernard to a better life. The same author, in chapter 5, reports what the holy man did in the case of the venerable Thomas, Prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, who was sacrilegiously murdered. But Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year of Christ 1135, no. 5, proves against several writers whom he there cites that Thomas’s murder belongs to the year 1133; this chronology had already been shown by Mabillon in his fuller notes on Letter 158 of St Bernard.

The cited author of the Cistercian Annals, chapter 6, no. 8, writes that St Bernard was asked by the Genoese to become their bishop [Col. 0726B] (see Ernald, *Life*, book II, chapter 3), but in vain. He observes that there befell him the saying of William in book I of the *Life*, chapter 14: “Although he was worthy to be compelled, by some judgment of God and by the singular reverence for his sanctity which long since prevailed among all, he never at any time was compelled to do anything against his will.”

## § XVII. The journey of Pope Innocent II to Liège with St Bernard, who defended the Church’s right against King Lothair; his alleged journey into Artois; the conversion of Guerric and many others; Pope Innocent’s visit to Clairvaux; St Bernard’s authority at the Council of Reims; his refusal of the mitre of Châlons

175. Having related, under the year of Christ 1131, chapter 1, the journey of Pope Innocent II with St Bernard [Col. 0726C] to the people of Liège, and the honorable reception given them on their arrival by King Lothair, who showed the Vicar of Christ most submissive reverence, as we have already said above in § 16, the Cistercian chronicler goes on, from no. 3, to explain an event which makes it clear that the praised pontiff very fittingly and opportunely joined our holy man to himself as companion on this journey.

For Lothair, in that humble abasement of himself in favor of Innocent, sought, as Manrique puts it, “to turn everything to his own advantage, and to attempt gain from piety and power from religion. Lest he should serve Innocent gratuitously, he dared to demand among his services the investitures of bishops, formerly usurped from the Church but, as we saw above, firmly recovered by Callixtus II. He thought that the pontiff, still an exile from Rome—indeed a fugitive—and therefore in need of his assistance against his rival, would deny nothing to one who asked; and that Anacletus would have to grant him everything even had he merely remained silent and accepted events.”

This was Innocent’s greater conflict: if he conceded, he would almost betray the Church, buying the tiara at the cost of Peter’s rights—indeed, of Christ’s true patrimony—and would thereby be unworthy of the pontificate; but if he refused, he was liable to be deserted by Lothair, and through the very abandonment by that king to divide yet more, and more hostilely, the Church which had long been divided and shaken. Then for the first time Innocent realized that Bernard had by no accident or human design come thither, nor had been brought merely to enjoy settled peace, but to calm disturbances which were already emerging and, unless checked, would rage more violently.

176. “But how all this was done, and how the firmness of Father Bernard checked the threatening storm, will be best told in the words of the other Bernard, Abbot of Bonneval, whom with Mabillon we more correctly call Ernald, so that our statements may carry greater credibility and weight.” In book II, chapter 1, no. 87 of the *Life*, he says:

“After the Council of Reims was dissolved, the Lord Pope met the King of the Romans at Liège.” (But it has been demonstrated from Mabillon’s Preface, presented by us in the immediately preceding section, that Innocent’s journey to Liège occurred before the Council of Reims.) “He was honorably received indeed, but that serenity was quickly clouded over. For the same king pressed importunately, judging the time opportune for the investitures of bishops to be restored to him, which the Roman Church had recovered from his predecessor, Emperor Henry, through very great labors and many dangers. At this word the Romans were terrified and grew pale, judging that at Liège they had encountered a danger graver than that which they had escaped at Rome. Nor was any counsel at hand, until the holy abbot set himself up as a wall. For boldly resisting the king, he rebuked the wicked utterance with remarkable freedom and restrained it with remarkable authority.”

So speaks that entirely trustworthy biographer. The holy Father himself also alludes to this in Letter 150, directed to Pope Innocent. There, while praising him for various good deeds and stirring up his zeal against the ambition of Philip, who sought by unlawful means to seize the See of Tours, Bernard recalls this to him: “Nor did the barbarous sword threatening your neck at Liège compel you to yield to the importunate and wicked demands of an angry and raging king.”

177. From this we infer, first, that the action of King Lothair on that occasion is not narrated sufficiently truthfully or graphically by Otto, Bishop of Freising, in his *Chronicle*, printed at Frankfurt in the year of Christ 1585, book VII, chapter 18, p. 149, where the following is written concerning it: “Without delay, yet first modestly setting forth how greatly the kingdom had been weakened by love for the churches, and at what loss to himself he had surrendered their investiture, he promised aid to the Roman Church.”

Secondly, we infer how utterly the most lying Peter the Cassinese deacon departed from the truth—and is to be refuted, as Baronius says under the year of Christ 1131—when, in favor of that same Lothair, to whom, as we shall say in the appropriate place, he later attached himself, he asserted against the plainest truth concerning investitures that they had been granted to Lothair by Pope Innocent at that assembly at Liège. Thus he says in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, chapter 99: “Innocent, therefore, entering Germany, was received near Liège by King Lothair, confirming to him the staff and ring according to the ancient custom.”

The *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, published some years ago at Milan among the *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. IV, was reprinted and annotated. In the notes on chapter 97 of book IV, p. 555, the writer of those notes attempts to soften the term “lie,” used by Baronius; but Peter’s manifest falsehood cannot be cleared by this. Moreover, “investiture” is the handing over or placing in possession, from *vestire*, “to put in possession,” as Du Cange says in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin Writers*, vol. III, col. 1520 of the latest edition. The learned author there adds much concerning the various modes, forms, or symbols by which such transfers were made, and confirms them by examples which may be read in his work.

Among the events then performed in the city of Liège must also be counted the coronation of King Lothair, carried out there by Pope Innocent in Bernard’s presence, as the Cistercian Annals under the year 1131, chapter 1, no. 5, recount at length; and they continue thus in no. 6:

178. “While Innocent was staying at Liège, Father Bernard went to Arras, a city of the Gallo-Belgian province in Artois, to visit the miraculous wax candle recently sent down from heaven and brought by the Mother of God. This is reported there on the authority of Ferréol Locrius, who, in his *Belgian Chronicle* under the year 1130, describes that journey in these words:

> St Bernard came to Arras in order to see and venerate, among other things, the sacred wax candle recently brought from heaven by the Virgin Mother of God. When he had seen it and celebrated it with his praises, the honey-tongued doctor was filled with such spiritual sweetness that, for perpetual remembrance, he caused a cross to be erected in the old cemetery of the Abbey of St Vaast, in the district called the Count’s Court [Col. 0728C]. For that was indeed the fitting place, where Bernard, standing, attained the fulfilment of his vows: nearby, namely, the sacred pledge of his hidden treasure was then kept, in the street named after the Magpies. This monument—by which I mean the cross—endured until the year 1647. At that time, because it was falling into ruin, the ascetics of St Vaast decided to restore it and to endow it with a more august form; and so today we see another [cross].

Thus Locrius, from the records of Dom Pronier, the senior prior of St Vaast. I should certainly like to see the accounts of our holy abbot’s journey to that prodigious candle confirmed by other documents.

179. Locrius had prefaced the history of this candle under the year 1105, writing as follows concerning it:

> At Arras, in the cathedral church, that wax candle—most celebrated throughout the Belgian world—was brought down from heaven by the Mother of God herself to two actors or minstrels (*histriones seu citharoedi*; Iperius calls them *joculatores*), Iterius of Paulinat and a Brabanter named Norman. It was a prompt and singular remedy for extinguishing the burning fire—concerning which we have spoken under the year 1092 and elsewhere. From this candle, although nothing whatever has hitherto been diminished from it [Locrius flourished at the beginning of the seventeenth century and died on 22 August 1614, according to Valerius Andreas’s *Bibliotheca Belgica*], indeed although it often burns and is miraculously increased, many other candles have been made: those of Bruges, Valkenburg, Boulogne, Noyelles, Ardres, Blandecques, and so forth. The following write concerning the aforementioned candle: Molanus, in the *Natales Sanctorum Belgii* under 6 February; Meyer, in Book IV of the *Annals [Col. 0729A] of Flemish Affairs* under 1095; and Malbrancq, *On the Morini*, Book IX, chapter 15. [Col. 0728D]

“Moreover,” Locrius adds, “this candle of Arras, enclosed in a most noble pyramid occupying the middle of the lesser marketplace—the pyramid was erected in 1215—is carried annually with a very solemn procession to the cathedral church; and, after vows have there been paid and two candles each weighing forty pounds have been offered, it is brought back to the town, to its own chapel, on the Sunday within the octave of the feast of Corpus Christi.” But let us now return from this digression to our path.

180. “I should think,” says Manriquez under the year 1131, chapter 1, no. 8, “that it was in this same year that Guerric—destined to be a great increase to the whole Order—followed Bernard, leaving all things behind, in order to be trained by him at Clairvaux. Previously, from being master of the school of Tournai, he had been promoted, by the fragrance of his sanctity and learning, to be a canon of the principal church of that place [Col. 0729B]. Moreover, the remarkable conversion of as many as thirty educated, wealthy, and noble young men, among whom were Geoffrey of Péronne and Robert of Bruges, both eminent men—the conversion which writers call the ‘capture of Liège’—cannot at all be deferred beyond this year. For Robert of Bruges, one of their number, is recorded not long afterward as having been placed over the monastery of Dunes; and, so far as I know, no other journey of Bernard to Liège intervened.

“Because this conversion was both more numerous in its number and more distinguished in its quality, I shall first set it forth in the words of Geoffrey of Clairvaux, who attached himself to Father [Col. 0729C] Bernard not long afterward and learned everything from his mouth and from that of the converts themselves.” In the *Life*, Book IV, chapter 2, no. 204, he says:

> Among others whom Christ rescued from the vain manner of life of this world through the ministry of His servant, many noblemen and many wise and learned men from the regions of Flanders at one time professed the sacred service under his teaching. The foremost among them seemed to be that Geoffrey of Péronne, who afterward fulfilled the office of prior at Clairvaux and died there in that office.

He died about A.D. 1146, according to Manriquez under that year, chapter 11, no. 9. The same author, under the year in question, 1131, chapter 2, resumes and separately treats the history of these men’s conversion as a singular event attended by various circumstances [Col. 0729D]. But since so vast a field remains to us in recounting Bernard’s so many and so great deeds in every quarter, let the reader consult the Manriquez just cited, Bernard’s Letter 109, addressed to Geoffrey and his companions, and the biographer Geoffrey, Book IV of the *Life of our Saint*, chapter 2.

181. In the same place, no. 5, Manriquez attempts to establish the chronology by connecting their conversion with the year 1131. But Mabillon, in his brief notes on that letter, says:

> Hermann, monk of Tournai, is to be understood as speaking of these men in Volume XII of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 479, where, concerning St Bernard, he says: “Many famous clerics, both from the Church of St Mary at Tournai and from the diocese itself, followed Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, for the sake of conversion.” [Col. 0730A]

Hermann relates this event on p. 476 after the twenty-fourth year of the pontificate of Simon of Noyon, who began to hold office in 1122. Therefore this letter—as Manriquez judges—cannot be assigned to 1131, nor consequently can the conversion of Geoffrey and his companions. “Further,” Bernard says in this letter, “I set my shoulders beneath this burden, though they are already weary.” From this Mabillon concludes “that Bernard was then already near old age.”

182. But Manriquez, under 1131, chapter 2, no. 5, answering those who object that, because of Bernard’s old age, “Geoffrey’s conversion occurred fifteen years or more later, when the Saint was preaching the Cross at Liège [Col. 0730B] under Conrad and Eugenius—the latter pope, the former emperor,” replies:

> This seems probable to me, were it not opposed by the recorded conversion, simultaneous with Geoffrey’s, of Robert of Brussels—or rather, Bruges. It is established that this could not have occurred in that year. For Robert was placed over the monastery of Dunes eight years before, namely in 1138—on which all agree—and was sent there by the holy Father. Therefore he could not previously have failed to be a novice, to have made profession, and to have lived as a monk for some considerable time.

The objection from the weary shoulders, intended to prove that the Saint was then old, is not compelling, especially in a man rendered almost unfit by the frailty of a failing constitution and the severity of illnesses, and of whom physicians had long before judged that he could scarcely be preserved without a miracle [Col. 0730C]. Thus, according to Manriquez, he could speak in this fashion even though not yet old.

As for Manriquez’s assertion that Robert of Bruges was converted together with Geoffrey of Péronne, he had proved it in chapter 2, no. 3, from the tombs at Clairvaux, in which, he says, we read: “Together with the illustrious Geoffrey of Péronne, treasurer of the Church of St Quentin, he received the habit in this Clairvaux.” I do not see that this chronological knot can easily be untied if the conversion mentioned above by Manriquez and Mabillon concerns the same persons and the same time; it is otherwise if there were two conversions, differing in time and persons [Col. 0730D]. Certainly, in the text cited by Mabillon, the name of no convert is given; but there is more than enough of these perplexities.

183. The Cistercian historian, under 1131, chapter 3, treats of Pope Innocent, who, on returning from Liège, first visited Cluny and then Clairvaux; of the hospitality there extended to the pope—Ernaldus describes this in Book II, chapter 1, of the *Life of St Bernard*—and of the monks there troubled by a demon but calmed by Bernard, according to Ernaldus; likewise of the Council of Reims and its chronology. (See what we have set out above, §16.)

That the holy man attended that council is related by Manriquez, chapter 4. “Meanwhile,” he says there at no. 3, “Innocent, travelling through France, awaited the day appointed for the synod. Whether Bernard accompanied him or not is less explicitly stated. Certainly, while the council was in session, the weight of all affairs rested with Bernard.” This is attested by Ernaldus, Book II, chapter 1, no. 87, who committed the following account of Innocent to memory:

> Having thus travelled through France, he summoned a council at Reims. There, after arranging many matters to the honour of God, he crowned King Louis—his father Louis the Fat still being alive—as king in place of his brother Philip. In all these affairs the lord pope would not allow the abbot to be separated from him, but kept him at his side with the cardinals in public business. Moreover, all who had private concerns consulted the man of God more secretly. He in turn reported what he had heard to the court and provided protection to the oppressed. [Col. 0731A]

Thus the holy doctor not only attended the Council of Reims, but also shone among the Fathers assembled there with splendid authority. But did he deliver two sermons there?

184. Both [Col. 0731B] are found in Mabillon among the spurious works of St Bernard, Volume II, col. 735 and following. On the first, entitled “To the clergy assembled at the Council of Reims,” the following judgment is inscribed:

> It is not Bernard’s. He would have regarded it as proud and improper to call all bishops and prelates “brothers,” much less “devils,” as is done here at no. 3. Whoever the author may be, the whole is compiled from patchwork extracts of Bernard; it was delivered before the pope and by his command, as appears from no. 1.

Before the second, “To the pastors assembled in synod,” these words are prefixed: “Whoever the author may be, it is neither inelegant nor unworthy of reading.” Manriquez, chapter 4, no. 7, judges them thus:

> I should think that Bernard’s addresses at that council, together with some of his other minor works, have been lost, and that these which circulate under his name were composed by an author of inferior eloquence and delivered in a less important council. [Col. 0731C]

185. To the distinction conferred upon our most highly esteemed abbot in this year may be added, first, his election to preside as bishop over the see of Châlons, according to the chronicle of Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, published by Leibniz in Volume II of the *Accessiones historicae*. There, on p. 269, this event is reported under 1131:

> When blessed Bernard had been elected bishop of Châlons, he refused; and through him Geoffrey, abbot of St Medard at Soissons, became bishop of Châlons. [Col. 0731D]

Second may be added two miracles: by one he raised up and healed a woman who had long been lame; by the other he restored to health a boy who was crying without ceasing. The first is attested by Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, in the *Life*, Book IV, chapter 4, no. 232; the second by Abbot William, in the *Life*, Book I, chapter 6, no. 59. Both occurred at the monastery of Charlieu, in the diocese of Besançon, founded in 1131, which Manriquez mentions among Bernard’s daughter houses in chapter 8 and refers to there also. The Sainte-Marthe brothers likewise discuss it in Volume IV of the *Gallia Christiana*, p. 225. St Bernard names it in Letter 197, to Peter, dean of Besançon [Col. 0732A], and in Letter 198, to Pope Innocent.

## § XVIII. Very many converted by the holy Father; the Genoese reconciled; a letter subsequently written to them; their grateful disposition toward the Saint; the year in which he came to Rome; acts concerning monastic affairs, empire, and priesthood.

186. Under the year 1132, the Cistercian *Annals*, chapter 1, no. 7, report a notable prophecy of the holy Father in these words:

> The holy Father … strengthened by words and examples alike the novices whom he had brought from Belgium and the many who flocked to him from the whole world—for ancient records report that he trained as many as one hundred novices, and that not once only. When Geoffrey of Péronne, in the first period of his novitiate, anxiously and with filial devotion prayed the holy Father more earnestly to implore the Lord for the conversion of his father, a noble and powerful man whom he had left in the world, the man of God said to him: “Do not fear. With my own hands I shall bury him in this Clairvaux as a tested monk.” Both things came to pass. [Col. 0732B]

This is narrated by Geoffrey in Book IV, chapter 2, of the *Life*, whose words I have quoted, and where he also relates the fulfilment of the matter.

How vigorously and successfully the great man laboured to defend the pontificate of Innocent II in France and Italy is clear from what has preceded in §16. But here let us speak more particularly of certain splendid actions accomplished by him in Italy, as we are about to accompany him there with the aforementioned Innocent.

187. Ernaldus, in Book II, chapter 2, of the *Life*, writes thus concerning Innocent’s departure from France:

> The lord pope could not remain long in France; but, as he had arranged with King Lothair, he went to meet him at Rome. [Col. 0732C]

That journey to Italy occurred in the same year, 1132. It is described at greater length by Pagi in his critical examination of Baronius under that year, no. 1 and following; there you will also find that they conferred with one another in Lombardy before reaching Rome.

Manriquez, chapter 1, no. 8, under the same year, says: “After greeting Lothair following their conferences, Innocent sends Bernard to Genoa, while he himself proceeds to Pisa, intending, if possible, to restore peace between the two cities. That peace had long been disturbed and, besides continual slaughter and devastation, was doing no small harm to the pope’s cause.” [Col. 0732D]

The undertaking, of the greatest importance, succeeded to the satisfaction of both parties. The same annalist, chapter 6, no. 1, commemorates its outcome thus:

> Long dissensions disturbed the two peoples, namely the Genoese and Pisans; and while each side sought revenge for even slight injuries, greater troubles arose, passing first into complaints and quarrels, then into hatreds, and finally into public wars. … The Genoese were then more prosperous and more powerful and were therefore thought slower to hope for peace. But behold: Bernard, sent by Innocent, checked their fierce spirits in a moment and calmed them instantly, so that they were ready promptly to carry out whatever he commanded. There was no hesitation, no delay. He came, he saw, he conquered; by his mere appearance he subdued whatever he wished. This was reported to Pope Innocent, and it was agreed that the Pisans should intervene. The sole obstacle to peace being confirmed there—although the Genoese obeyed Bernard and submitted themselves to his arbitration—was the absence of the other party. Thus he who had come as legate to negotiate peace scarcely had to discuss it, since it was almost obtained before it was proposed. But the short time he remained there he gave rather to preaching the word, proclaiming salvation to souls with greater fervour because all heard him more eagerly and more fruitfully. [Col. 0733A]

188. “Now, the reverence with which he was received, and the honour in which he was held, displaying outwardly the worship rendered to him even while alive, can most fittingly be learned from the same Saint’s congratulatory letter written to them a year later [Col. 0733B]. It confirms them in their undertaking, but is also historical.” It is Letter 129 among Bernard’s letters. I extract from it the following, which confirms both what has just been said and what is to be said below:

> That our visit to you last year was not idle, the Church shortly afterward proved in her need—the Church from which we had been sent. You both received us honourably and entertained us during the short time we were among you. … Certainly, as we are not forgetful, neither are we ungrateful. May He who can, and who was the cause of it, repay you—God. For how can we recompense that homage of reverence, that service, that affection full of love and grace? It is not that we delight in favour shown to ourselves, but that we rejoice with your devotion. O those festive days, though few! I shall never forget you, devoted people, honourable nation, illustrious city. Evening, morning, and noon, according to the Prophet’s custom, I recounted and proclaimed; and the eagerness to hear was as great as the charity of the hearers. We bore the word of peace; and, when we found children of peace, our peace rested upon them. … Wonderful swiftness, because great was the need. I endured neither delay nor difficulty: in almost one day I sowed and reaped and carried home with rejoicing sheaves of peace. For this was the harvest which I reaped: to exiles, captives, fettered persons, and prisoners we brought joyful hope of escape and return home; to enemies, fear; to schismatics, confusion; to the Church, glory; to the world, joy; and so forth. [Col. 0733C–D]

189. Mabillon’s brief notes, col. 139, state that the Genoese truly experienced the words “I shall never forget you” in 1625, when Bernard was invoked for aid in the war against Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy. Manriquez explains the event more fully in the chapter 6 cited above, no. 6:

> The Genoese have been accustomed to rely so firmly upon the holy Father’s words, “I shall never forget you, faithful people,” and indeed they experienced their truth, that almost five hundred years later—in the year of Christ 1625, scarcely seven years before the time at which we write—when they saw the most excellent prince Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy, ravaging the towns of their territory and threatening them at scarcely five miles from the city [Col. 0734A], despairing of all human assistance, they appealed to the faithfulness of the most holy Father. After other provisions, they made the following vow:
>
> Henceforth we promise and vow to enroll and number among the guardian saints of our republic Saint Bernard, who, while living among men, pledged in his letters that he would never forget us. We shall celebrate his feast day and ensure that it is celebrated by our people and clergy, with the consent of the most illustrious archbishop and the most reverend bishops. In this principal church, or in another at our discretion, we shall build a chapel dedicated to him. On the same day of St Bernard, every year in perpetuity, we shall cause a solemn procession to be held and a solemn Mass to be celebrated at his altar, we ourselves devoutly attending. Finally, during the solemnities of the said Mass, by the duke’s own hand, we shall pay in perpetuity each year dowries to twelve girls, as they are called—namely, one hundred pounds to each of them—for this present year and thereafter. In testimony of this matter, we command that this document, publicly read by our undersigned secretary, be received and subscribed, and authenticated by our seal. Given in the cathedral church, Sunday, 25 April 1625. [Col. 0734B]

190. Thus spoke the Genoese as the ruin of their republic pressed upon them. How favourably that vow succeeded according to their desire was shown by events not long afterward. For the holy Father, delaying his aid only until it might be proved to be his, graciously appeared on the very eve of his feast with a Spanish fleet sent in aid, [Col. 0734C] soon to put the hostile forces to flight. There was no one in that populous city who did not recognize Bernard’s protection: the Saint was present, and the benefit received had to be repaid.

These matters have been mentioned incidentally on the occasion of the letter and should be recounted more fully in their proper chronological place. I may add that the memory of this benefit remains fresh and is still celebrated with festivity and devotion not only at Genoa, but among Genoese throughout the world. Certainly, in Spain, where they frequently attend the court of the Catholic king on business, they jointly celebrate the Saint’s annual feast devoutly, and year after year are generous in their own monastery church. We ourselves witnessed this when, in the preceding year, we acted as envoy of the venerable University of Salamanca to the most powerful king of Spain [Col. 0734D]. But enough on these things.

191. Let us return from this brief digression with Manriquez to the chronological life and deeds of St Bernard. The same historian, under 1132, chapter 7, no. 10, treats of Bruno, designated for the see of Cologne, who consulted the holy Father as to whether he should accept its governance; he adds Bernard’s reply, Letter 8 in the collection. In chapter 8, no. 8, he gives the Saint’s Letter 96, addressed to Richard, abbot of Fountains—of the diocese of York, commonly York in England—and his companions, who had passed from another order into the Cistercian order; Bernard praises them for renewing religious discipline. In the cited chapter, no. 9, follows Letter 95 to Thurstan, archbishop of York, praising his charity and generosity toward religious persons. In chapter 9, no. 3, occurs the Saint’s reply, Letter 94, to the abbot of a certain monastery in the diocese of York, from which a prior had departed with several brothers. Finally, in no. 4 of the same chapter, follows his letter to Henry, king of the English, seeking the king’s favour for monks whom he had sent to found a monastery [Col. 0735A].

Mabillon’s edition gives the letters the titles just stated. The purpose which the holy man set before himself in them—although occupied with so many affairs, yet, as we have seen above, tireless for the good of the Church and, as we have just said, a patron of the expansion of his religious family—will be understood from Mabillon’s brief notes on Letter 94. On the occasion of the address to the abbot of a certain monastery in the diocese of York, mentioned shortly before, he names that abbot, the monastery, and other particulars:

> Namely, Geoffrey, abbot of the monastery of St Mary in the diocese of York, of the Order of St Benedict. From that place twelve monks departed with their prior; because they were not permitted to flee to the Cistercians, they took refuge with Thurstan, archbishop of York. Bernard praises him in the following letter for the protection he gave them. Compare the fuller notes and Letter 313 to the same Geoffrey. [Col. 0735B]

And on Letter 95 he observes:

> What Thurstan did in defence of the aforesaid monks, who had taken refuge with him out of a desire for greater perfection, is shown by his own letter, to be printed after Bernard’s letters from the *Monasticon Anglicanum*. [Col. 0735C]

192. The year of Christ 1133, in which Pope Innocent II and King Lothair came to the city of Rome, is most worthy to be marked with a white stone because of the various deeds which our holy abbot performed in its course and left to be recorded for posterity. Accordingly Manriquez, under this year, chapter 1, no. 2, relates:

> When all stood before the entrance into the City, and Innocent lacked the resources by which the undertaking of entering it could be managed, Bernard alone provided aid in every way amid every danger and necessity. From the very entrance into the City, he wrote to Henry, king of England, whom he himself had drawn to Innocent’s side, a letter brief indeed, but vigorous and sharp, and all the more effective for being shorter. [Col. 0735D]

This is Letter 138 among the Saint’s other letters, in which he asks the said king for aid for Pope Innocent. It reads:

> To wish to instruct you, especially on matters concerning honour, is either foolish or shows complete ignorance of you. Therefore it is enough simply to state the matter, and to do so briefly. … We are at the entrance of the City; salvation is at the gates; justice is with us. But this food does not please the Roman soldiers. Therefore with justice we appease God; with soldiery we terrify our enemies. We lack the necessities necessary even for the barest needs. You yourselves know better what must be done in order that your work may be completed—the great and honourable reception which you gave Lord Pope Innocent. [Col. 0736A]

That is, in recognizing Innocent at the Council of Chartres, according to the fuller notes on this letter and Book II, chapter 1, of the *Life*.

193. Cardinal Baronius, as Manriquez observes, no. 4, appears to suppose under the following year that Father Bernard did not go to Rome with Innocent in this year, indeed that he did not even cross into Italy. He recognizes only three of Bernard’s arrivals there: two in 1134, and a third two years later. His words under 1134, no. 14, are these:

> Moreover, it happened three times that the same St Bernard came to Italy to Pope Innocent. The first was in this year, when he came to Pisa for the council; the second, shortly afterward in the same year, as the author of his *Life* attests in these words: “When the holy Father passed through Milan for the second time in the same year,” etc. The third arrival was when Emperor Lothair went to Italy with an army, and the schism was ended by the death of Peter Leo. [Col. 0736B]

The words of the author of the *Life* which Baronius indicates occur in our text, Book II, chapter 3, no. 188. But the most eminent author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* is refuted by Manriquez, no. 5:

> Whatever may be said of those arrivals, which we shall treat in their proper times, the letter just cited is an abundant witness that Bernard also came with Innocent in this very year: “We are,” he says, “at the entrance of the City.” Moreover, his mission to the Genoese, mentioned above, proves the same thing, as does another mission to Conrad, Duke of Swabia, which I shall shortly cite. [Col. 0736C]

Add that it is known from the Cistercian *Exordium* that the Saint was exiled from his own sons for three years while he remained in Italy to quiet the schism; and these three years can scarcely, if indeed at all, be identified unless counted from 1132 to 1135.

194. For from 1135, when it is certain that he remained in Gaul, to 1137, when he is again recorded as having returned from the Roman curia, we can identify not three but only two years. Let the reader consider the words of the *Great Exordium*, which Tissier prints in Distinction II, chapter 11:

> The venerable Father Bernard, having at one time remained for three years in the city of Rome and in the regions of Italy in order to quiet the schism of Peter Leo, etc. [Col. 0736D]

Manriquez adds: “This was the sole reason why he left his sons for so long. Therefore Bernard, assisting Innocent in this very year—as cannot be called into doubt—must be believed to have been sent with St Norbert, the archbishop, to Anacletus, in order, if possible, to restore him to the Church.”

Pagi also discusses the distinction of St Bernard’s three journeys to Italy in his *Critica Baroniana* under 1134, no. 10. He praises Manriquez for having correctly distinguished the three Italian journeys and answers this objection:

> It does not matter that Bernard’s name is not mentioned in Emperor Lothair’s letter, quoted by us under the preceding year, although some bishops and abbots are named in it. For not all bishops and abbots present at the courts of emperors and kings subscribed the diplomas; consequently, not all were named in them. [Col. 0737A]

195. What Manriquez had just conjectured concerning the Saint’s being sent to Anacletus together with St Norbert produced no result from the journey undertaken for that purpose by the holy men, if both were sent. For, he says at no. 6, they found Anacletus inflexible before the words of the saints, not to be softened by any concessions or reasons, according to Ernaldus, Book II, chapter 2, of the *Life of St Bernard*:

> He also most obstinately avoided a meeting with the emperor; he was moved neither by threats nor by blandishments, nor did he accept counsel concerning his position from any person whatsoever. [Col. 0737B]

Let Lothair’s entry into the City and his imperial coronation there be regarded as inserted here. On these matters I nevertheless quote the *Chronicle* of Otto of Freising, Book VII, chapter 18:

> The king, trusting more in courage than in soldiers, advanced as far as the City. There, having energetically accomplished what he could with a few men, he was crowned by the supreme pontiff Innocent in the church of the Holy Saviour, called the Constantinian church, and received the title of emperor and augustus. Peter [Leo], at that time, held the church of blessed Peter, where it was customary for emperors to be crowned.

But Peter, having little confidence in advancing his cause by success and hoping rather to secure it by delay—though inferior in strength, he was safer in his positions—“did not set God as his helper, but, surrounded by the wickedness of his allies and remaining in higher and safer towers, mocked Lothair’s power. He forbade his own men to meet in open battle, neither exposing himself to danger nor giving his enemies cause for conflict; nevertheless, from superior engines and by various obstacles he impeded their free movement,” according to Ernaldus cited above [Col. 0737C].

196. But after Lothair left Rome, Peter raised his head; and Innocent too considered that it would better serve his interests to return again to Pisa. Hear Ernaldus speaking thus in the same place:

> Leaving Innocent in Rome, the emperor departed elsewhere. But after his departure Peter made frequent sorties through the City, intent upon the slaughter of the faithful. Therefore Innocent, understanding that remaining in Rome at that time was fruitless for him, lest his presence should inflame the rage of that beast, returned once more to Pisa. There, gathering bishops from the whole West and other religious men, he celebrated a synod of great splendour. [Col. 0737D]

We shall speak of this synod under 1134, when it was held. Meanwhile, certain further matters are to be added; the Cistercian *Annals* treat them in chapter 2.

197. “Innocent,” they say, “while staying at Pisa, sends Father Bernard as legate to Germany, to reconcile Conrad, duke [of Swabia], after the long schism mentioned above—for it had lasted eight years—with the new emperor, on equitable terms agreed by both sides, such as Lothair’s childlessness made possible. Meanwhile Roger, formerly duke of Sicily, but then pseudo-king created by Anacletus, having learned of the holy Father’s departure and thinking he had thereby found an opportunity to weaken the constancy of the Pisans, approaches them with envoys and letters. He promised them much if they abandoned Innocent and joined Anacletus; he threatened them with still more if they remained faithful—both with sharpness and intensity, as is the manner of princes. The Pisans yielded to neither entreaties nor terrors, having learned perseverance from the holy Father and adhering wholeheartedly to Innocent. When this was reported to Bernard on his journey, he judged them worthy of eternal praise and composed the following letter to them [Col. 0738A].”

The letter may be read as Letter 130 among Bernard’s letters. Baronius, under 1133, no. 10, calls it worthy of perpetual remembrance. Let us now briefly pursue, as is our practice, the actions reported to have been performed by Bernard on the same journey, from contemporary writers, because they concern this year.

198. First, that he converted many men who would serve under his leadership at Clairvaux and fill the vacant places of the founders is attested by the abbot of St Thierry. Among the “captures”—as he himself calls them—made by the blessed man, he records the famous capture at Mainz, Book I, chapter 13, of the *Life*; in our division, Book I, chapter 7, no. 68. But in this capture of men at Mainz, the conversion of Mascelin was made particularly famous, as Manriquez continues at no. 4, by his resistance and Bernard’s prophecy: Bernard told the unwilling man that he would be converted, and finally drew the resistant man to God [Col. 0738C]. Consult Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, Book IV, chapter 2, no. 201, of the *Life*, where the event is related more fully.

“I should think,” says Manriquez, no. 5, “that on this journey also the Duchess of Lorraine was converted by him, a distinguished woman, no less exceptional in the condition of sin than as a penitent.” You have the event in William the biographer, Book I, chapter 7. Moreover, as Manriquez adds at no. 8, with respect to the Duchess of Lorraine, chronology establishes that she was Alcide [rather, Atheleid or Adelaide], sister of Emperor Lothair and wife of Simon, to whom she bore Matthew, who would succeed him in the duchy of Lorraine [Col. 0738D].

How that duchess, persevering in holiness and righteousness, was held in special affection by the man of God; how she deserved to see him freed from the prison of the body and ascending to heaven; and how she was thereby more strongly confirmed in goodness—a daughter following her father and a disciple her teacher through labours to glory—Manriquez recounts among the deeds of our Saint on the said journey, no. 9, in the following words:

199. “When the same saint, as we said, had again met Father Norbert at Rome and had been joined to him by new bonds of charity, he added further new tokens of affection. Hence it came about that, on this same journey, when he had turned aside for a little while to Cambrai in order to visit the newly born community of Vaucelles, he took care to obtain from Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, the most noble and wealthy abbey of Tongerlo [Col. 0739A], to be handed over freely to the Premonstratensians. A reliable witness—the deed of donation—confirms that this was done chiefly at his instance; Aubertus Miraeus publishes it.”

That instrument is found in the same author’s *Cistercian Chronicle*, published at Cologne in 1614, pp. 90 ff. The following fragment, transcribed from it, will suffice for our purpose:

> “I therefore, Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, judged that the petition of the religious men—namely Waltmann, abbot of the men of Antwerp, and Bernard of Clairvaux—ought to be approved.
