They begged that I should grant liberty to the church of Tongerlo, so that in it brethren of the Premonstratensian Order, living under [Col. 0739B] the Rule of blessed Augustine, might be able freely and peacefully to serve God. Judging this petition good, and therefore graciously granting it, I make the aforesaid church of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary free from every exaction and from the customary provisions due for the support of the canons serving God and his holy Mother there. Then … I willingly establish that, in appointing an abbot, the sounder part of the convent shall have free authority; but the person elected is to be presented to the bishop of Cambrai,” etc.

Among the several persons subscribing their seals appears “S.,” that is, the seal of “Bernard of Clairvaux.” “These things were done at Cambrai in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the reign of Conrad, ever Augustus.” Yet Burchard is said to have died in 1131 in the new edition of the *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 27 [Col. 0739C].

200. Concerning the benefit which the holy abbot, by his embassy just discussed, brought to the common good of the Church and of secular rulers, Manricus speaks thus, no. 10: “Now, as regards the fruit of the embassy: it is established that Bernard obtained peace and, after reconciling Lothair and Conrad, secured peace for the Empire for a long time.”

On these matters the Polish history, from the collection of Johann Pistorius of Nidda, printed at Basel in 1582, says the following under the year 1126, vol. II, book V, p. 485:

> “In Germany and Italy, Conrad the Swabian, together with his brother Frederick, had taken up arms against Emperor Lothair, until, defeated by him, they were reconciled through the efforts of Bernard [Col. 0739D], abbot of Clairvaux, renowned for his learning, piety, and holiness of life.”

Thus it came about, as Manricus adds, that in a plainly similar cause the realm owed no less to Father Bernard than the priesthood owed to him; and that he who had secured the Church’s pontiff also secured for the world no less its emperor.

Yet I cannot fully reconcile what the above-mentioned Cistercian historian asserted—namely, that Bernard “secured peace for the Empire for a long time”—with what Pagi says in his *Baronian Criticism* under the year 1135, no. 12. There, discussing the princes of the Empire swearing peace with Emperor Lothair, he transcribes, among other things drawn from the Hildesheim Chronicler for that year, the following:

> “On the feast of Saint [Col. 0740A] Michael, at the place called Mühlhausen, Conrad, brother of Duke Frederick, was reconciled to the emperor.”

He then observes: “Already in 1133 Conrad had returned to favor with him—Trithemius dates it 1134 in the *Hirsau Chronicle*—but some disagreement must afterwards have arisen between them. Unless perhaps these statements are to be understood of a less solemn act of concord previously entered into by them; whereas what is said to have happened at Mühlhausen concerns a reconciliation publicly confirmed by oath in an assembly of princes, after the first agreement—perhaps itself sworn, but performed with a less solemn rite.”

## § XIX.—Proceedings at the Council of Pisa and at Milan

201. The year of Christ 1134, which we now approach with the Cistercian historian, was made especially illustrious by the renown of the great Father Bernard, attended by the highest commendation of his venerable name: both through deeds and miracles performed among the Milanese and elsewhere in Italy, and through the Council of Pisa, held there in this year. All these things provide us with a noble subject for the praises of this most holy man.

“Innocent,” says Manricus, chapter 1, no. 1, “had appointed a council to be held at Pisa in this year of Christ 1134; he himself was to attend, as was a great part of the Church, and Father Bernard, by command of the same pontiff. But behold: as he was hastening thither, envoys from Milan intercepted him, intending, if possible, to take the saint back with them, so that through him they might be reconciled to the pontiff and through him to Lothair.” The latter had succeeded by election to the place of the deceased Emperor Henry. It has nevertheless been said above that Conrad [Col. 0740C], duke of Swabia and nephew of the same Henry through Henry’s sister, claimed the kingdom by right of blood. See the year 1125, chapter 1, no. 6. We have likewise reported, on the authority of Conrad’s own brother Otto of Freising, that he was received by the Milanese, anointed by Archbishop Anselm at Modicia, or Modoetia—the seat of the kingdom of Italy, where emperors customarily received the Iron Crown, as Baudrand notes—and acclaimed king of the Romans; this may be seen in the place shortly to be cited.

Therefore, remaining firm—or obstinate—in this allegiance, while adhering to Conrad they rejected Lothair; and because of Conrad they also opposed Innocent. For Innocent, bound first by the protection inherited from Honorius and then by many, and not trifling, obligations [Col. 0740D], had promoted Lothair’s party and cause.

202. “But now that Lothair had been crowned, and Conrad had been reconciled with him through Bernard, since they were bound by no oath of pledged loyalty and otherwise wished to be reunited to the Church, having abjured Anacletus they sought [perhaps, ‘pursued’] the favor of pope and emperor through the same Bernard. This was the public occasion of the embassy. But besides this there was another, particular reason concerning many persons who, struck by the reputation for sanctity of Bernard and his disciples, converted, and already despising the pleasures of the world, either had anticipated the arrival of the holy Father or at least, having been anticipated by God, awaited it, intending to entrust themselves to his instruction. From these, I think, the envoys were chosen, as though they might more effectively persuade the holy Father by their very purpose of conversion [Col. 0741A].

“And the most gracious Father would at once have turned aside to them, had not the time of the Pisan Council been pressing, from which, without violating obedience to the pontiff, he could by no means be absent. He replied, however, requesting a short delay, that he would present himself after the council. And since that city was being recalled to the unity of the Church, its first error having been wiped away, chiefly through the efforts of the Milanese clergy, he first wrote this letter to the clergy.”

These are taken from Manricus. But whether this letter was composed first or not, it nevertheless stands first, before two others, in their collection.

203. In that letter, which stands as no. 132 in the said collection, the holy Father congratulates the clergy of Milan on the success just mentioned and postpones his coming to them. He begins it thus:

> “Blessed are you by the Lord, through whose zeal and industry your city has been delivered from error and, abandoning schism, has returned to Catholic unity … And I too, brethren, desiring to become a participant and companion in your joy, was coming to you with our beloved brethren, your messengers, as you requested, intending to give fuller satisfaction, according to reason and the good pleasure of God, concerning the matters about which you wrote to me. But because the time is short in which we must hasten to the Council of Pisa, do not be troubled to wait until our return.”

This is addressed to the clergy. In Letter 133, addressed to the citizens of Milan, by whom he had been invited to make peace, he writes that he rejoices that his assistance has been sought for this undertaking and bids them hope for his return after the Council of Pisa [Col. 0741C].

In Letter 137, written after the same council to the Empress of the Romans—Richera, as Mabillon adds in the margin—concerning Milanese affairs, the holy man indicates that the Milanese were not received into favor by the pontiff until they themselves had received Emperor Lothair. Hence he commends them to the empress’s clemency. But I shall speak of that letter below also.

The holy Father himself gives the names of the envoys mentioned shortly before, in Letter 134:

> “I, brethren, stirred by such great joy, but also summoned by you through our most beloved brethren Otto and Ambrose, whom you sent for this very purpose, had resolved [Col. 0741D] to come to you with them,” etc.

The letter is entitled, “To the converts newly made at Milan.” He congratulates them on their conversion and promises that, when the council is concluded, he will see them.

204. The title or heading of this letter seems more probably to have led Baronius into error under the year 1134. For when he writes, no. 8, “By this time the Cistercian religious order had been planted at Milan and had propagated itself with fruitful offspring,” Manricus, chapter 1, no. 7, notes against Baronius that this is wrongly said.

But let us hear Mabillon in his shorter note on the same letter:

> “From this title Baronius infers that, before Bernard’s arrival at Milan—that is, before 1134—a Cistercian community had been sent there and some monastery founded to which these novices had devoted themselves. But Ughelli, in vol. IV of the *Italia Sacra*, col. 197, judges that the first Cistercian monastery in that city was Chiaravalle, which he proves was founded not before 1135, two miles from the city. Therefore, by the name ‘novices’ in this letter, we must understand those who, newly converted through Bernard’s activity as he made for the Council of Pisa, had already wholeheartedly devoted themselves to his instruction. Ughelli’s date for the foundation of the monastery is established from an ancient inscription and from the earliest documents of the place, in which it is consistently called Caravallis, not Claravallis. See Letter 281.”

So Mabillon. The letter to which he refers is headed, “To Abbot Bruno of Caravalle.” On it he observes:

> “Earlier editions read *Claravalle*; but manuscripts of better authority prefer *Caravalle*, and the local documents of Caraevallis support them. Caravallis is a notable Cistercian abbey near Milan” [Col. 0742B].

Now let us return to Bernard. You have heard, kind reader, what the holy abbot did before reaching the Council of Pisa. We now set forth with what veneration he was admitted to it, with what authority he took part in its proceedings, and with what benefit he served it.

205. Ernaldus, book II of the *Life*, chapter 2, left the following remarks relevant to our subject:

> “Innocent … again returns to Pisa, and there, with bishops gathered from the whole West and other religious men, a synod of great renown is celebrated. The holy abbot was present throughout in the deliberations, judgments, and all determinations. Reverence was shown him by all, and priests kept watch before his threshold—not because of any arrogance, but because the crowd prevented common access. As some went out, others went in, so that the humble man, claiming none of these honors for himself, seemed to be not in a share of responsibility, but in the fullness of authority” [Col. 0742C].

Thus Ernaldus, a most faithful writer of the *Life* and a witness beyond all exception. This, then, was now the third council—as Manricus observes on this passage, chapter 2, no. 1, “I do not include that of Troyes”—“in which Bernard was deferred to in all things: one for declaring Innocent supreme pontiff, two held under him.”

The praised biographer then proceeds to the acts of the council, which he briefly summarizes as follows:

> “It would take long to relate the proceedings of the council. Its substance, however, consisted in the excommunication of Peter [Leonis] and the irreversible deposition of his supporters; and this sentence endures to this day.”

Pagi has more on this council in his *Baronian Criticism* under the year 1134, where he also discusses its date.

206. It is suitable to extract from him, for our purpose, what he reports there, no. 3, concerning King Louis of France when he considered obstructing that synod. Some disagreement existed between Innocent II and Louis VI, king of the Franks; therefore St Bernard sent Letter 255 to King Louis and warned him not to hinder a council so necessary at that time to the Church [Col. 0743A] and kingdom and destined to redound to the king’s own honor.

> “‘But the heat is excessive,’ they say. ‘As though we had bodies of ice,’ Bernard says … Yet if anything has proceeded from the rigor of apostolic authority, on account of which the serenity of your highness judges herself rightly disturbed, your faithful servants who will be present will strive with all their power that it may be recalled or moderated as is fitting for your honor. Among them, we too, if we can do anything.”

On the saint’s mention of the heat, Mabillon observes in his notes on that council: “The king forbade the French bishops to attend, on the pretext of excessive heat.”

The council’s business having been completed, the holy Father fulfilled the promise previously given to the Milanese, to come to them. It is my intention to divide this expedition, so illustrious for so great a man, into several parts.

207. Let us first consider for what ends he was sent there by the supreme pontiff. Pagi, mentioned shortly before, sets them out thus, no. 6:

> “Landulf the Younger, chapter 41, in Puricellus’s *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 360, mentions the reconciliation of the Milanese with Innocent II and says: ‘Pope Innocent held a synod at Pisa, at which, with Bishop Robaldo [of Alba] representing them, Thealdus de Landriano, archpriest of the church of Milan’”—he seems to have been successor of Stephen of Guandeca, who in the preceding year had greatly harassed Anselm, archbishop of Milan, as we said there—“‘Amizo de la Sala, archdeacon [Col. 0743C], Anselm of Rho, deacon [elsewhere, “ordinary” is added], and many other ordinary clergy of the same church, together with the primicerius, a priest of the decumani, swore fidelity to Pope Innocent, contrary to the customary dignity of Milan and of its church.’”

For the Milanese, who had hitherto retained their ancient liberty, persuaded themselves that the oath of fidelity decreed by Gregory VII, now required of bishops, was contrary to the dignity of their church.

208. “But the Cremonese did not on account of this oath of fidelity release the Milanese knights whom they held captive. Pope Innocent, however, confirmed the deposition and expulsion of the oft-mentioned Anselm de Pusterla from the Milanese bishopric. Yet the aforesaid men who had sworn fidelity, fearing these dangers to the city and church of Milan, delayed returning to Milan unless they had a protector who would confirm before the Milanese people Anselm’s expulsion, reduce Conrad’s coronation—performed in 1128—to nothing, summon the people of so great a city, and establish them in love for Emperor Lothair and in unity with Innocent himself. To accomplish these things the pope had, from God [Puricellus and others: ‘indeed’], a fitting angel, such as Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, was” [Col. 0743D].

Thus far Landulf, cited from Puricellus; Pagi inserts some words of his own among Landulf’s, as is clear from the parentheses. Moreover, the *Milanese History* of Landulf the Younger, or Landulf of Saint Paul, was republished not long ago among the writers of Italian affairs issued at Milan, vol. V of that collection, and was furnished with notes. I compared the text above quoted from Puricellus’s edition with the most recent edition, as you may see from the variant readings I added from it in the margin. In that new edition one may also consult the notes on chapter 41 of Landulf, contained in the said volume from p. 513 [Col. 0744A].

209. Let us secondly consider who were sent with Bernard from the Apostolic See to Milan to accomplish a task of such great weight. Ernaldus the biographer, book II, chapter 2, no. 91, after what he had stated about the Council of Pisa, commemorates the companions of this distinguished embassy as follows:

> “When the council had been dissolved, the lord pope sent the abbot of Clairvaux—whom they had sought with many entreaties—to reconcile the Milanese; and he sent with him Guido of Pisa and Matthew, bishop of Albano, from his own side, that they might wash away the schism caused in that city through Anselm and recall those who had strayed to the unity of the Church. The abbot, therefore, together with the aforesaid men whom he had received from the lord pope as colleagues, added to their company and common counsel the venerable man Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, whose sincerity and innocence he had proved in many matters. And it seemed good to the cardinals that a business of such weight should be supported by so great a helper” [Col. 0744B].

We add the following information. That Geoffrey, called de Lèves, governed the church of Chartres most worthily from 1116 to 1138, according to the Sammarthani in vol. II of the *Gallia Christiana*, where he is praised at length. Guido of Pisa is discussed by Ciaconius in the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals*, vol. I, col. 987; likewise, Matthew of Albano is treated at col. 960 ff., where he is honored with the most splendid praises.

Landulf the Younger, chapter 42, speaking of Bernard’s entry among the Milanese, assigns him only these companions:

> “The aforesaid abbot, without delay, entered Milan with the bishop of Chartres and Robaldo of Alba.”

The notes identify the latter as “the man whom the Milanese, after Anselm’s deposition, had chosen as archiepiscopal vicar to perform the offices.” But Ernaldus is of too much value to us for us here to depart from him by even the breadth of a fingernail [Col. 0744C].

210. Let us thirdly consider the wonderful entry of the holy man among the Milanese, like a miracle; and, if one gathers all its attendant circumstances together, a most exceptional reception, perhaps without any comparable example in the reception of saints. Hear Ernaldus, *Life*, book II, chapter 2, no. 91, already cited:

> “Having crossed the Apennines, when the Milanese heard that the abbot they desired was approaching their territory, the entire people went out to meet him seven miles from the city: nobles and commoners, cavalry and infantry, persons of middling rank and poor alike. As though they were migrating from the city, they left their own homes; and, divided into separate companies, with unbelievable reverence they received the man of God. All alike delighted in the sight of him; those who could enjoy hearing him judged themselves blessed. All kissed his feet; and although he took this with distress, no argument could restrain them in their prostrate devotion, no prohibition repel them [Col. 0745A]. They even plucked whatever hairs they could from his clothing and tore off pieces of the cloth as remedies for diseases, judging holy all things that he had touched and believing themselves sanctified by touching or using them. Those going before and those following applauded the abbot with joyful acclamations; and, after he had long been held within the dense throng of companies, they at last brought him to a solemn lodging.”

This was at the church of Saint Lawrence, according to what will be said below at the beginning of §20. What could have been done more illustrious for the saint’s praise, or more suited to the Milanese people’s most ardent affection for him, than such lavish public expressions of veneration, joy, and acclamation?

211. And what of the fact that, because of the multitude surrounding him, there was no way of approaching him? The author of the *Great Cistercian Exordium*, distinction II, chapter 16, says:

> “When, therefore, he was sitting there—that is, at Milan—in a certain very large house, such was the multitude of people around him that no one could enter.”

Indeed, there he was thought of as an angel fallen from heaven and as a man close to God. For, as the same author immediately adds:

> “Meanwhile, a certain citizen of that city, honorable in dress and appearance, desiring by every means to approach the man of God but finding no entrance anywhere, forced himself into the midst of the crowd, crawling on hands and feet and stepping over the shoulders of those sitting down, until he reached the one whom he desired. When he had seized his feet, he began with wondrous devotion to embrace and kiss them. Seeing this, the aforesaid Renaldus [Col. 0745C], who stood nearer, came up to remove him, knowing that the holy man was greatly burdened by veneration and services of this sort. But the man turned and said to him: ‘Let me be, I beg you; let me see and touch a man close to God, a truly apostolic man. For I tell you, and testify in the Christian faith, that I saw him among Christ’s apostles.’ Hearing this, the monk was astonished and, desiring to know more fully, wished to ask him about the manner of this vision; but from embarrassment before those present he did not presume to do so. Nevertheless, he most certainly believed that this was a great revelation, on account of which that man was so vehemently moved toward the servant of God.”

I shall speak below, no. 215, of Renaldus, the witness to this matter.

212. Let us fourthly consider how vigorously he handled the cause of his embassy, and how gently he accomplished the business committed to him, without resistance from the nobles or discord among the common people. For, according to Ernaldus just cited:

> “When the matter for which both the man of God and the cardinals had come had been publicly discussed, the city, forgetful of its strength and laying aside all fierceness, submitted itself to the abbot in such a manner that the little verse of the poet could not inappropriately be applied to its obedience:
>
> *To obey commands: for me, to will it is as necessary as to be able.*”

But what this praised biographer states in general terms, the saint himself expresses more specifically in his letter to the Empress of the Romans, Lothair’s wife, mentioned above in this paragraph, no. 203. Let us give the saint’s own words:

> “Certainly the Milanese were not received into the favor of the lord pope and the unity of the Church until, openly rejecting and renouncing Conrad, they received our lord Lothair as their king and lord, and confessed him as Augustus, emperor of the Romans, together with the whole world. And, concerning the injury done, they promised, upon the holy Gospel having been touched, that they would make fitting satisfaction to you according to the counsel and command of the lord pope” [Col. 0746A].

Pagi places this letter, written by him in 1134 when he returned to Milan for the second time, under the same year, no. 9.

213. Let us fifthly consider how the most holy man transformed the morals of the Milanese into a better pattern, with a success not to be regretted. Landulf, chapter 42, testifies to this in the following words:

> “Meanwhile Prince Conrad, having adopted a higher counsel—namely, after he had abdicated the kingdom and returned to favor with Lothair—became standard-bearer of Emperor Lothair, and this aforesaid abbot”—he had just spoken of St Bernard—“entered Milan, a city which he indeed shaped as he wished. At this abbot’s command all ecclesiastical ornaments seen in the city’s church—of gold, silver, and rich cloth—were put away in chests as though despised by the abbot himself. Not only men but women also were tonsured; clothed in hair-shirts and the cheapest woolens, they were converted to every kind of religious life [Col. 0746C]. Water was changed into wine,” etc.

But the miracles wrought there by the holy man will be treated later. Besides these honors with which our abbot was adorned while performing the office of envoy among the Milanese, others are at hand, which we shall give in the next paragraph.

## § XX.—He refuses the governance of the see of Milan; chronological observation; the Cistercian Order propagated there; his distinguished service to the Humiliati; benefits bestowed on the Milanese

214. We have just spoken so fully of the deeds most splendidly performed by the saint at Milan that not a few things remain to be said. Let us sixthly consider that our apostolic envoy was held in such veneration and affection by the Milanese people that, with the most ardent wishes of all, they demanded him as their bishop. Landulf the Younger, chapter 42, relates this as follows:

> “At last, in order that they might have that abbot as archbishop, the same people ran with hymns, praises, and their customary *Kir.*—on which see the notes to this chapter—to the church of Saint Lawrence, where he was lodged. But that abbot would not endure it; instead he said: ‘Tomorrow I shall mount my palfrey—that is, my pacing horse—and if it carries me beyond you, I shall not be to you what you ask.’ And so he departed from Milan” [Col. 0746D].

Puricellus, explaining Bernard’s answer in the *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 368, says:

> “By this answer the holy abbot, then wishing to proceed to Pavia and Ticinum, seems to us not obscurely to have alluded to what happened to St Ambrose, when, refusing the government of the Milanese Church offered to him, he at last fled even from the city itself. Leaving the city at midnight, as Paulinus narrates in his *Life*, and thinking he was going to Ticinum, he was found in the morning at the gate of the city of Milan called the Roman Gate” [Col. 0747A].

But Puricellus’s conjecture concerning this allusion of St Bernard is wholly uncertain. Thus the modesty of this divine man refused the most honorable dignity offered him, according to his usual practice on other occasions of this kind. The fact is confirmed by Ernaldus the biographer, *Life*, book II, chapter 3, from which I briefly extract, no. 110, the following relevant words:

> “Within Italy, the city of Genoa and Milan, the metropolis of Liguria, desired him as pastor and teacher.”

Thus there, among other mitres refused by this most modest man, it is asserted that this occurred among the Milanese.

215. Why should I pass over in silence the testimony of the author of the *Great Cistercian Exordium*, who in distinction II, chapter 16, transmitted the following to posterity?

> “We learned from the report of Lord Renaldus, whom we have mentioned above, that God’s servant Bernard, when he once came to Milan to reconcile the schism of Peter Leonis, was received with such rejoicing by all,” etc. “In short, they were so delighted with him that, although they had not seen him before, as soon as he entered the city they unanimously seized upon him for archbishop rather than elected him [Col. 0747C]. When he refused, they were fully prepared to use force unless he secretly escaped by flight.”

Who, then, was this Renaldus or Rainaldus? He is the same man “to whom three letters of Bernard survive, overflowing with milk and honey beyond the ordinary manner,” as Manricus writes under the year 1121, chapter 5, no. 9. These are nos. 72, 73, and 74 among the other letters. He was likewise abbot of Foigny, commonly called Fusniac, in the diocese of Laon, and indeed the first, as Mabillon affirms in his note on Letter 72; but Manricus, just cited, denies this. He was also the faithful companion of St Bernard at Paris who, as was reported above, §10, no. 103, from the author of the *Great Cistercian Exordium, “was more privy to the secrets of the servant of God.” Thus credibility is given to the narrative previously reported from this man.

216. From what has just been set forth concerning the holy Father’s arrival in the city of Milan after the Council of Pisa, it is abundantly clear that the mitre of that see was offered him there in the year of Christ 1134. It is therefore astonishing that Sigonius should have erred so grossly in his chronological calculation of this event by placing it in 1123. For in vol. II of his works, most recently edited at Milan, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book X, col. 650, I read the following under that year:

> “When Honoricus, bishop of Milan, died on the third day before the Kalends of June, that dignity was offered, because of the remarkable reputation for his holiness, to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. But he refused it,” etc.

I say nothing here about Honoricus; the notes on that year may be consulted concerning him. In Panvinius’s *Ecclesiastical Chronicle* I find the same chronological error under the often-mentioned year [Col. 0748A]. Puricellus refutes, in the *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, no. 331, others who wrongly date the arrival of St Bernard, abbot, in the city of Milan to the year of Christ 1119. Since they have erred so miserably that they do not deserve refutation here, the same author may be consulted regarding them.

Thus, in 1134, the Milanese, disappointed in their most ardent desire—to promote the holy man to the archiepiscopal chair and so retain him among them—yet wishing to possess the Father in his sons and the sons in their Father, requested ascetics of the Cistercian Order.

217. Let us seventhly consider how greatly St Bernard benefited the Milanese and the Cistercian Order when he propagated the latter among them. “There was at hand,” as Manricus narrates in the year indicated above, chapter 2, no. 9, “a plentiful harvest: persons had already been converted before the saint’s arrival, but many more were called by him and responded without any hesitation. There survives a rescript of the same holy Father to Peter, then bishop of Pavia, in which he shows that the glory of the many conversions experienced at this time, though attributed to himself, should be referred to God alone,” according to what he says in that Letter 135:

> “If good seed, cast into good soil, seems to have borne fruit, the glory belongs to him who gave seed to the sower, fertility to the soil, and increase to the seed. What share do we have in these things? I certainly shall not give Christ’s glory to another; yet I shall claim it for myself with much greater scruple. Assuredly, it is the law of the Lord that converts souls, not I. The testimony of the Lord is faithful and makes the little ones wise, not I. It is the hand, not the pen, that is praised for the fine formation of letters. I confess, if I am to attribute much to myself, my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” [Col. 0748C].

From this, then, the immense multitude of people converted to a more perfect life may plainly be understood. “Therefore,” Manricus continues, no. 10, “to satisfy the devotion of both groups and return sons of peace for what he had received, he—being otherwise disposed to extend his community—assented to their pious and devout request. A place not far from the city was designated, watered by natural springs and pleasant; and he agreed that a building should be erected there [Col. 0748D] for monks to be brought from Clairvaux. Carlo Sigonius relates that Guido, captain of the Eastern Gate, contributed not a little to this building.” The reader may consult him, book XI of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, col. 671, in the latest Milanese edition. Let us continue with Manricus.

218. “I found in a manuscript of Robert Rusca, recently sent to me from Rome,” he says, “through the kindness of the most reverend Father Lord Hilarion René, abbot of Holy Cross in Jerusalem—whom our college at Salamanca formerly had as a pupil, and we had as a hearer and friend—that the same designated place was marked out by heavenly light, illuminating the boundaries of the house amid the darkness of night. The monastery was given the name Chiaravalle in memory of the other Clairvaux, whose very name comforted the Milanese so long as they were not granted the enjoyment of the holy abbot” [Col. 0749A].

But, from what was said above in §19, no. 204, on the occasion of Letter 134, Manricus appears more probably to be mistaken in this derivation and allusion of the name *Clara Vallis*.

219. Let us eighthly consider what the holy Father did in favor of the order of brethren called the Humiliati while he was staying at Milan. Pagi, under the year 1134, no. 14, collected the following on this subject:

> “While Bernard was staying at Milan, he gave a rule to the Third Order of the Humiliati. Indeed, according to Tristan Chalco, they had originated this Order as early as 1119; but before Saint Bernard they were not religious persons. Puricellus, cited above, no. 375, asserts that they were called the Brethren of the Convent [*Fratres de Convenio*], which Chalco too committed to writing; and Puricellus adds: ‘An order of Brethren of the Convent is called by that name even to this day, and in its own emblem bears this holy abbot as its patron.’ Puricellus further states that a manuscript codex containing the privileges of the Humiliati is preserved in the library of the Milanese basilica. At its beginning is found:
>
> ‘Saint Bernard came to Milan and there became renowned for many miracles and built a monastery’—namely Chiaravalle … ‘Through him certain magnates and noble citizens of Milan, made drunk with the divine Spirit, adopted for themselves and their households a manner of life in religious dress, living together’—this was then their institution. ‘Thus Saint Bernard was the first founder of this Order. Hence brethren of this Third Order are still in some places called brethren of Saint Bernard. These brethren of this Order remained separately in religious dress for fifty-four years before a rule was granted them by the Roman Church. But in the year 1199, on the penultimate day of May, a rule was granted them by Pope Innocent III. Therefore it should be known that the brethren of this Third Order were the founders of the first and second Orders of the Humiliati’” [Col. 0749B–C].

220. Galvaneus Flamma, chapter 255 of his *Greater Chronicle*, cited by the aforementioned Puricellus, no. 375, writes: “The nobleman Guido, captain of the eastern gate, was a particular helper of blessed Bernard in founding the monastery of Chiaravalle near Milan, from his wealth, in the year of the Lord 1135 . . .; and this Guido established the third [Col. 0749D] order of the brethren de Convenio (“of the assembly/convent”) of Saint Bernard at the eastern gate, on the feast of Saint Vincent; Innocent III confirmed it, and it was called by Innocent III the Third Order. These brethren de Convenio founded the order of the Humiliati brethren, and visited them.” The same Galvaneus, who lived in the fourteenth century, confirms this in the book entitled *Manipulus florum*, chapter 171, in Puricellus at the same place; but in the latest Milanese edition of that *Manipulus*, chapter 169. “Although Saint Bernard and Guido were founders of the Humiliati, who before either of them had neither a rule nor a religious habit, this association had nevertheless already begun earlier, as Puricellus proves by the testimony of Saint Antoninus, part II of the *Chronicles*, title 15, chapter 23; Raphael of Volterra, book XXI; [Col. 0750A] Tristanus Chalcus; and others. Sigonius is therefore mistaken in connecting the beginning of this Order with the year 1046, as may be seen in his *History of the Kingdom of Italy* under that year.”

From these matters we understand that a definite rule of life was prescribed at Milan by Saint Bernard for the said brethren. Although this is sufficient for our purpose, we shall briefly append the following observations to this fact.

221. Galvaneus Flamma, in the cited chapter 169 of the *Manipulus florum*, writes that this happened in 1135, a year with which he connects the Saint’s return to the city of Milan. For, writing under the year 1134, he immediately adds: “In the following year Blessed Bernard returned to Milan . . . He organized the Order of Saint Bernard, whose members are now called brethren of the Assembly,” etc. But Puricellus, cited above, [Col. 0750B] p. 63, likewise affirms that this was done at the return of which I spoke; he differs, however, as to the year, maintaining that the event occurred “about the time when Saint Bernard was again in Milan during this year”—but in the chronological index prefixed to his cited work he marks the year as 1134. We shall deal later with that return.

Moreover, the same author, p. 632, does not admit that this Order was called the Third from the name of Innocent III; for, he says, others think differently, and better. Hippolyte Hélyot, vol. VI of the *History of the Monastic Orders*, etc., chapter 19, treats at length of the religious of the Order of Humiliati and of their suppression. There one may see the various opinions of writers concerning its origin; the alleged derivation of its name; [Col. 0750C] and the three distinct states of the Order. Having discussed the first of these, the cited writer affirms that the second began in 1134, adopting, on Saint Bernard’s advice, a manner of life different from the former, etc. He then adds the Third Order, under the Rule of Saint Benedict, etc., and says that it continued until the Humiliati were extinguished. Why, how, and by whom this was done may be read there. It now pleases us to recount other benefits bestowed by Saint Bernard upon the Milanese, which the Saint himself records.

222. In letter 131, which Mabillon assigns to the year of Christ 1135, and prefixes with this summary: “Since the Milanese, though reconciled to Innocent, appeared nevertheless to waver in duty and obedience, he urges them to preserve steadfastness, recalling the recent benefits of the [Col. 0750D] Roman Church toward them”—and should we not add, also, his own? Benefits obtained in part or entirely through the Saint’s interposition of his own authority, as it is fair to believe. In that letter, I say, he thus recalls them:

“God deals well with you; the Roman Church deals well with you. He acts as a father; she acts as a mother. And truly, what ought she to have done for you and has not done? If you asked that honorable persons be sent to you from the curia for the honor of God and yourselves, it was done. If you asked that what your unanimity had established concerning the election of your venerable father be confirmed, it was done. If you wished to be permitted what the sacred canons judge unlawful except in a case of great necessity—namely, the translation of a bishopric into [Col. 0751A] an archbishopric—it was granted. If you asked that your fellow citizens be freed from the chains of the Piacenzans—which indeed I neither wish nor am able to pass over—this too was done. In this last matter, what reasonable petition of a daughter has suffered, I do not say refusal, but even delay from her loving mother? Behold, to complete all: the pallium, the fullness of honor, is at hand.”

223. So that the matters which the Milanese had requested and obtained, as Saint Bernard reported above, may be better understood, Mabillon observes in his notes on the aforementioned letter, concerning the honorable persons sent to them: “There were sent with Bernard Guido of Pisa, Matthew of Albano, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres,” according to the biographer Ernald, chapter 2, no. 91, in our edition, “namely, to reconcile to the Roman Church the [Col. 0751B] Milanese, who had produced a schism because Anselm, the archbishop elected by them, had been deposed. On the phrase τὸ, ‘your venerable Father,’ he notes: Ribald, namely, who was elected by them in place of the rejected Anselm. By ‘the translation of a bishopric into an archbishopric,’ as the holy Father put it, understand,” he says, “the restoration of archiepiscopal dignity, which had been withdrawn from that church by the pope because of the schism. See the other notes.”

He explains what the holy man wrote concerning the chains of the Piacenzans as follows: “For when both sides were contending against each other in war, many Milanese had been carried away captive by the Piacenzans.” On Ribald or Robald and Anselm, Pagi may also be consulted under the year 1134, nos. 11 and 12. It remains for us to discuss the wonders then performed at Milan, as well as elsewhere in Italy, by our great Wonder-worker.

## § XXI. He shines forth through miracles at Milan; goes to Pavia and Cremona; absent in body from his sons, present in spirit; his letters to them and to Emperor Lothair; his return to his own; events and date.

224. The miracles by which God—wonderful in His saints—made illustrious among the Milanese this His servant, in whose most upright life, merits, and apostolic labors He was well pleased, are described by Ernald, book II of the *Life*, chapter 2. From that author they were inserted into the *Cistercian Annals* under the year of Christ 1134, chapter 1. But since those wonders are related more fully in the said *Life*, it will suffice [Col. 0751D] here to present them in summary, in order to continue the sequence of the acts of Saint Bernard which we are elucidating.

Here, therefore, are the words of the cited biographer: “So great a faith among the people, so great a power in a man, has not been heard of in our times. There was among them a devout rivalry: the abbot attributed the glory of the signs to their faith, while they attributed it to the holiness of the abbot. They were so wholly convinced about him that they believed he obtained whatever he asked from the Lord.”

Nor did their judgment deceive them. For, as the same biographer immediately adds: “Without any hesitation they bring to him a woman known to everyone, whom an unclean spirit had tormented for seven years; and they humbly beg him to command the demon, in the name of the Lord, to depart, and to restore the woman to health. . . . He gives himself to prayer; then, by power sent down from heaven, he rebukes Satan in the spirit of might and puts him to flight, restoring the woman sound and tranquil. . . . This report was heard, and the fame spread far and wide. . . . From every side people assemble through the churches, the public halls, and all the crossroads. . . . They publicly say that nothing is impossible for him which he asks from the Lord. . . . Some rush into his presence; others wait outside the doors until he comes out. Work and crafts are abandoned. . . . They run together and ask to be blessed; and each considers it salutary to have touched him.”

225. “On the third day,” the author continues, “the servant of God went to the church of Saint Ambrose to celebrate the divine mysteries. There, while an innumerable multitude of people waited, during the very solemnities of Mass, as he sat beside the altar while the clerics sang, they brought to him a little girl violently tormented by the devil, and begged him to help the poor child. . . . Hearing the supplication of those present, and seeing the person gnashing her teeth, . . . he pitied her age. . . . Therefore he took the paten of the chalice in which he was about to celebrate the divine mysteries, and, after pouring liquid over his fingers, . . . applied the healing drink to the girl’s mouth and infused a medicinal drop into her body. Without delay, as though Satan were being burned, . . . he hurriedly came out . . . and burst forth.”

The same writer of the *Life*, having spoken of the demons’ liberty being checked through the holy man, then treats of demons being expelled from various possessed persons. But because to recount these individually, while preserving the force and style of the author—who describes them at length and with feeling—would lead us into too lengthy a discourse, let the reader go to the source itself. There he will also find other miraculous cures wrought by our Wonder-worker.

Let us therefore leave Milan for a little, since it has long detained us while we recount the most illustrious deeds there performed by the Saint; and let us proceed elsewhere with him as he departs thence—to Pavia, namely, and Cremona.

226. Sigonius, in the latest Milanese edition, vol. II, book II, col. 671, under the said year 1134, has the following: “Thence—that is, from Milan—by Innocent’s command, he set out to pacify the cities of Lombardy among themselves, and went to Pavia and Cremona. But since he achieved nothing among the Cremonese, he reported their obstinacy to Innocent in these words: [Col. 0752D] ‘The Cremonese have become hardened, and their prosperity destroys them; they despise the Milanese, and their confidence deceives them. Placing their hope in chariots and horses, they have frustrated me and made my labor vain.’”

Sigonius takes these words from the opening of our apostolic man’s letter to Innocent, numbered 314 in Mabillon’s edition, formerly 318, and assigned to 1134. Louis Cavitelli, in his *Annals of Cremona* under the same year, records: “Saint Bernard obtained absolution and pardon for the Milanese when sacred rites had been forbidden them by the supreme pontiff because they had adhered to Conrad the Swabian, and when shortly afterwards, having abandoned Conrad, they adhered to Lothair. He then went to Cremona and [Col. 0753A] Pavia in order to reconcile the inhabitants there and their confederates with the Milanese; but, having accomplished nothing, he returned from Cremona to Milan.”

The year of this return will be discussed a little below. After returning there, Bernard freed a woman in a moment from the miserable torment of a demon and from the contraction of her sinews, as Ernald relates at length in book II of the *Life*, chapter 3. Nor, when he went to the Pavians and Cremonese, of whom I have just spoken, did Bernard refrain from restraining demons, as the same cited biographer testifies; there are further details in that place. He concludes these matters thus: “These,” he says in chapter 3, no. 108, “and many other things the man of God did while dwelling within the Alps; travelling through different places, he did good to the sick, giving sight to the blind, raising up the weak, curing those afflicted by fever, cleansing especially those oppressed by [Col. 0753B] the devil . . . and consecrating as temples acceptable to God the hearts which the malicious spirit had defiled.”

227. Immediately afterward the biographer turns aside to praise the man: “Above all,” he says in no. 109, “I judge this more sublime . . .: that, although he was a chosen vessel and fearlessly bore the name of Christ before nations and kings; although the princes of the world obeyed him, and bishops in every nation stood at his nod; although the Roman Church itself revered his counsels by a singular privilege and, as though granting him a general legation, subjected nations and kingdoms to him; although even . . . his deeds and words were confirmed by miracles . . .—he always thought humbly of himself. . . . Though in the judgment of all he was supreme, in his own judgment he regarded himself as the lowest. He ascribed to God alone whatever he did,” etc.

Add the weaknesses and diseases by which he was tested like gold in a furnace, as well as his contempt for dignities, inasmuch as he never smiled upon any of the many mitres offered to him. Consult, please, the cited writer of his *Life*, who recounts more fully the matters I have just drawn from him.

228. Nor, while he was obliged to live outside Clairvaux, which he loved so dearly, was he so occupied with the most serious affairs of the Church that he forgot the sons left there, or failed to know what was being done there while he was far away. Rather, absent in body but present in mind and spirit, he came among them, visited them, and inspected them.

The fact is proved from the saint’s own words, [Col. 0753D] which, after returning from Italy, he soon spoke among the Clairvaux brethren in chapter, as the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 2, chapter 11, teaches in the following account: “The venerable Father Bernard, having once spent three years in the city of Rome and in the regions of Italy in order to quiet the schism of Peter Leo . . ., at last returned to Clairvaux. Immediately after prayer had been made, he entered the chapter of the brethren. Since he was weary from his journey and could not speak long, he delivered a brief discourse, yet one full of consolation, saying:

‘Blessed be God, who has restored you, my most beloved brethren, to me, and me—such as I am—as your father, to you. And I indeed, little children, although during these three years I may have seemed far removed [Col. 0754A] from you, do not think that I was always absent. For know that during that time I returned to you three times, visiting this house and walking through the workshops; and I always departed gladdened, always consoled, seeing your unanimity and your earnestness in the resolve of our Order.’”

229. “Innumerable were the things which this servant of God said and did, in which it clearly appeared that he was endowed with prophetic grace: that he was many times present in spirit where he seemed absent in body; and that, by the Lord’s revelation, he knew many things hidden and even far removed, which people thought were unknown to him. These matters were reported to us by Lord Gerard, formerly abbot of Longpont, one of the ancient elders of Clairvaux, who diligently strove to investigate the words and deeds of the holy [Col. 0754B] Father.”

Thus it is written there. From the same source we may be permitted to add this also, although it belongs to another subject, which follows there: “We also heard him report that this holy man of God, while preaching the word of God in a certain chapter of monks, was seen by two of the brethren present suspended in the air above the bench on which he sat, raised from the ground by about the measure of one foot.”

But the narrative of the Saint’s return to his own, which we have just mentioned, including his unknown and wondrous visitation of them, seemed, as it were, insufficient for his paternal heart; he further wished to console them by letters. “Two letters of his to them survive: one, when he was being sent into Apulia, which will be considered below; the other written, as I believe,” says Manrique under this year [Col. 0754C] of Christ 1134, chapter 4, no. 7, “during this three-year period,” and he gives it in that place. It is letter 143, and Mabillon assigns it to about 1135, with a prefatory title from which you may learn the occasion for its composition. In it the holy man excuses his prolonged absence as being no less burdensome—indeed more burdensome—to himself than to his own brethren. Meanwhile he briefly reminds them of their duty.

Moreover, under the same year, the cited Cistercian historian devotes all of chapter 7 to William, formerly abbot of Saint-Theodoric near Rheims and later a monk of Signy, who committed the first book of Saint Bernard’s *Life* to writing and has repeatedly been cited by us above. But we shall consider him below, when treating the writers of Bernard’s *Life*. In the meantime, [Col. 0754D] let us examine the deeds of the most holy abbot which are assigned to the following year of Christ, 1135.

230. There, then, the historian just mentioned, chapter 1, no. 1, preparing the way for the letter sent by Saint Bernard to Emperor Lothair, which we shall discuss immediately, says several things beforehand about Roger, duke of Sicily, who was ravaging Italy, etc.; then he adds:

“Therefore Innocent, providing both for himself and for all, sends envoys in this year 1135 to Emperor Lothair: let him come, defend Church and kingdom, protect Italy by arms . . . and recover what the invader has wrongly seized. This was nearly the first important embassy in Church affairs under Innocent which was not entrusted to Father Bernard—whether because he recoiled from stirring up war against Christians, however rebellious; or because, seized with longing for his own brethren and now absent for three years, he was hastening his return to Clairvaux; or, finally, because he was being reserved by God for Aquitaine and for William’s conversion, a task to which he was more useful. Yet he wrote to the emperor, almost sounding the trumpet for battle, certainly inviting him to defend Church and Empire. Indeed, when the emperor had been deceived by a false report and was consequently delaying Innocent from defending a certain church which was suffering unjustly, Bernard, in the freedom of spirit with which he was endowed, boldly rebuked him and advised him to desist from his undertaking.”

I do not transcribe the letter itself; it is found among Bernard’s other letters as no. 139, and the aforementioned editor assigns it to about the year of Christ 1135.

231. Having thus far set forth the apostolic labors and miracles of the holy Abbot while he was in Italy, it remains that we follow him as he returns thence to his own in the year just mentioned, with Ernald, book II of the *Life*, chapter 3, no. 112: “He had now crossed the Alps, and shepherds, herdsmen, and rustic folk came down to meet him from the highest crags. They shouted from afar, asking for a blessing; and, returning to their folds, they crept through the mountain passes, speaking among themselves and rejoicing that they had seen the Saint of the Lord,” etc.

How he was received by his most beloved brethren of Clairvaux the cited biographer adds immediately afterward. Since the Saint had thus been restored to his own, we must see what was done among them. The *Cistercian Annals* under the year 1135, chapter 2, no. 1, say: “First, upon entering his Clairvaux and, according to custom, pouring out prayers in the oratory, he is said to have gone into chapter.” Immediately afterward they attribute to him the address to his brethren taken from the author of the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, which I gave above in no. 228.

The same *Annals*, no. 2, then write of the flourishing observance of religious discipline and the remarkable harmony of the brethren. Consult Ernald, whom I have just cited. They add, no. 3, that monks were chosen by the holy Father to plant his offspring among the Milanese; no. 4, his letter to Emperor Lothair on behalf of the Pisans, which is letter 140 among his other letters; likewise, no. 7, his letter to Pope Innocent, letter 178, on behalf of Albero, [Col. 0755D] archbishop of Trier. Mabillon, however, assigns this last to 1139, following Brover; in chapter 3, they discuss the transfer of Clairvaux; and finally, the law of Muhammad translated from Arabic and dedicated to the Saint.

232. Lest this last matter seem surprising to anyone, I offer the text of Manrique in the said *Annals*, chapter 3, no. 11: “At the same time, as John Picard noted in his notes on letter 227, Peter Mauricius sent Bernard a very lengthy letter, containing among other things a brief narrative of Muhammad’s life, which Peter, although he admits it to be most fabulous, took care to have translated into our language.”

Moreover, that this treatise or translation was not only sent to Bernard but also dedicated to him is proved by the letter prefixed to the same work, with which it is circulated in publication. “Since this letter is otherwise important and worthy of these *Annals*, and because it is by no means included among Peter of Cluny’s other letters, I judged that it should not without reason be transcribed here.” But it may be read there, no. 12. That Peter was abbot of Cluny is stated there in the same letter. Such, then, was the state of affairs after Saint Bernard had returned to his beloved sons at Clairvaux.

As a concluding addition, I append some remarks on the year in which this return occurred, since it has been mentioned more than once above and writers do not seem to agree in determining its date.

233. In the Bernardine Chronology, published together with the Saint’s works by Mabillon at the end of the first volume, col. VI, under 1135, [Col. 0756B] there is discussion of Bernard returning from Italy through the city of Milan, etc. Galvaneus Flamma, indicated by us in § XX, connects his return to the Milanese with the same year; but Puricellus, whom I cited there, assigns it to 1134.

From the text of Ernald, book II of the *Life*, chapter 3, I infer that he himself connects that return of the Saint with the things he did at Pavia and Cremona. For, having spoken of these, he adds: “When the holy Father passed through Milan for the second time in the same year,” etc. Manrique, under the year 1135, chapter 1, no. 4, says: “That is, ‘within the year’; for thus I understand it.” Manrique understands it in a manner consistent with what he had said concerning the deeds of the same holy Father after his return to the Milanese, assigning these to the said year 1135; and likewise consistently enough with the deeds he narrates of Saint Bernard among the Pavians and Cremonese, which he assigns to 1134, as may be seen in his discussion of that year, chapter 4. Events occurring within an undetermined year, or over a period of twelve months, may fall within two specified years, so that they happened partly in one and partly in the other.

But I should rather incline to the opinion which places the events among the Pavians and Cremonese, as well as the return to the Milanese, not merely within one year but within the same year, so that there is no need, with Manrique, to force Ernald’s phrase “in the same year” into the sense “within the year.” Indeed, Bernard’s journey to the Milanese and return, his embassy to the Pavians and Cremonese, and his departure across the Alps are all connected with the same year, 1134, to use Sigonius’s wording, by the said Sigonius in *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book XI; see col. 669 and following of the latest Milanese edition, and Pagi’s *Critica* under the same year.

## § XXII. William, Duke of Aquitaine, converted from schism to the unity of the Church by Saint Bernard; a possessed woman freed by him at Nantes; various observations concerning Duke William.

234. The utterly deplorable state of Aquitaine, with Duke William hostile to Catholics and raging against bishops, and with Gerard of Angoulême, the pseudo-legate, introducing schismatics who rendered obedience to the antipope Anacletus, is more than sufficiently shown both by Saint Bernard himself and by his biographer Ernald.

For in letter 126, addressed to the bishops of Aquitaine against the same Gerard of Angoulême, in which he nobly defends the cause of Innocent as legitimate Pope, the holy abbot says among other things of this bishop, col. 134: “He dares—what I say with tears—to drive out by his own feet the saints who refuse to worship the beast which opened its mouth for blasphemies, to blaspheme the name of God and His tabernacle. He attempts to set altar against altar; he is not ashamed to confound right and wrong. He strives to intrude abbots over abbots and bishops over bishops; to remove Catholics and promote schismatics. Wretched and pitiable are those who consent to be so promoted, and by such a man. For he traverses sea and dry land to make one bishop; and when he has made him, he makes him twice as much a son of Gehenna as himself.”

Mabillon assigns this letter to about 1132. The biographer named shortly before, depicting the tragic scene in Aquitaine, says with feeling in book II of the *Life*, chapter 4: “At that time the whole Church of Bordeaux labored under the oppression of schismatics; nor was there anyone in Aquitaine who could resist the prince, whose heart God had hardened. With the consent of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, who instilled into his heart the seeds of dissension, he became the defender and author of schism.”

235. “Whoever did not subscribe to the reception of Peter Leo was exposed to persecution: some were punished by losses, some by banishment, and others were driven from their own sees and compelled to live in exile. [Col. 0757C] In that count’s ears the crafty man—like the ancient serpent—kept hissing repeated persuasions. He had long been legate of the Apostolic See in those regions, but, having now been cast down from so great an office, he could not bear to be bishop of his church alone.”

The aforesaid author of the *Life* skillfully depicts there the other crimes of this evil-doer, given over to wickedness. Let the reader consult the same *Life*, to be reprinted after this Commentary, and he will become more fully informed of the mournful scene of the present tragedy, Gerard on one side and Duke William on the other mutually lending one another their assistance.

Nor did Saint Bernard permit his own help to be wanting for the good of the Church. Consult his letter 125, assigned to 1131. And does not letter 127—dated about 1132, written in the person of Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, and addressed to William himself, count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine, against Anacletus and for Innocent—show the holy abbot’s concern for Aquitanian affairs?

236. Yet you might call these lesser aids bestowed by the Saint’s labors for the benefit of this province, if you compare them with what follows. Ernald, cited above, after describing the evils troubling Aquitaine, continues in no. 119:

“Hearing these and similar things, the venerable man Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, to whom Pope Innocent had entrusted the legation of Aquitaine, was deeply grieved. Setting aside other business, he resolved without any delay that aid must be given to the Church in peril. [Col. 0758A] Therefore he sought out the abbot of Clairvaux and begged him to help in eliminating such great evils. The man of God agreed . . . and promised . . . to go with him into Aquitaine. Thus they went together . . . and . . . together came to Nantes.”

There the holy Father freed a woman who for fully six years had had a very shameful intercourse with a most impure spirit. After other remedies had first been tried in vain, he freed her by his staff, pronounced an anathema upon the demon, and expelled it. Ernald describes the event at greater length in no. 119 and the following sections.

In this journey one might say that divine providence wished to display that miracle in Bernard as a kind of forerunner and omen of Duke William’s great conversion, which later followed through God’s favorable aid and the Saint’s tireless efforts; and likewise of the destruction of the devilish deceit which troubled Aquitaine.

237. After these deeds against the malignant spirit had been performed by the holy man at Nantes, the abbot and legate entered Aquitaine together, according to the cited writer of the *Life*, no. 122. He immediately continues to relate why Gerard of Angoulême was remaining . . . in those places where he considered himself safer, and no longer readily appeared at public assemblies.

Thus, because of the withdrawal of this instrument of the devil, Bernard had easier access to Duke William and a more favorable opportunity of speaking with him. For because of the matters which Ernald had there set forth, and others of the same sort, Gerard began to be confounded before men; fearing that things which could not be denied might be brought against him, he avoided public meetings, as the same author immediately adds. The way toward a successful outcome was therefore made somewhat smoother than before.

“It was reported,” says Ernald, no. 124, “to the count through distinguished men who dared more safely to approach him, that the abbot of Clairvaux, the bishop of Chartres, other bishops, and religious men sought an interview with him. . . . He was persuaded not to avoid a meeting with such great men. Accordingly, they came together from both sides at Partiniacum”—commonly Partenay, a city or town of France in the province of Poitou.

What took place in this meeting may be read in the said *Life*, where it is likewise described in what wondrous manner Saint Bernard brought about Duke William’s conversion. Two aspects of it should rightly draw the reader into astonishment: first, the force of the Holy Spirit and a kind of heavenly inspiration by which the great man was moved; second, the immense change in so proud and obstinate a prince which followed in so short a time. The same biographer sets both vividly before our eyes.

238. Our Father Godfrey Henschen, in the preliminary Commentary on the *Life of Saint William the Great*, hermit at Stabulum Rodis in Etruria, vol. XI for February, 10 February, from p. 433 onward, endeavored—by labor no less painstaking than worthwhile—to examine and disentangle the deeds of this Saint, which had been entangled in many fables and errors, according to the balance of truth. I shall briefly transfer here what bears upon our subject.

Care must be taken not to confuse this William with the former one. The same Commentary, § 4, warns that this man must be distinguished from the other. Moreover, the same place supplies other points which illuminate the foregoing account of William of Aquitaine and his conversion.

In 1130 he acknowledged Pope Innocent II, but, misled by others, adhered in 1131 to the antipope Anacletus. Saint Bernard and Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, admonished him in vain in the same year 1131, contrary to Manrique under 1130; the cited Henschen thinks that these events occurred in the following year, when news first began to be heard of what Gerard was plotting against the Church of God. This is drawn from book II, chapter 6 of Saint Bernard’s *Life*—chapter 4, no. 122, in our division.

He records that this Saint then wrote his notable letter concerning that schism to the bishops of Aquitaine, letter 126 among the others; and afterward sent one to William, duke of Aquitaine, written in the person of Hugh, duke of Burgundy. We have spoken recently of both letters. In the one addressed to Duke William appears this clause: “Through the most Christian Lothair, the false accusers have lately been caught in their own lie.” Hence he concludes that the letter was written after Lothair, having brought Innocent back with him into the City in 1133, was crowned Roman emperor by Innocent.

239. He next adds the Council of Pisa, at which Saint Bernard was present in 1134, and the Milanese whom he reconciled with Innocent. We have dealt with these matters above. He adds to them the meeting of the same Saint with Duke William in 1135, and the Duke’s restoration by Bernard to obedience to the Apostolic See.

The aforementioned commentator then cites a fragment from letter 128 of the holy Doctor, addressed to the same Duke, from which we give the following:

“I remember, most excellent Prince, that I departed from you some time ago with this disposition and intention: that with all my affections I desired good for you and yours, and with all my efforts, wherever I could, I desired to assist your salvation and honor. For I did not return deprived of the fruit of my visit to you; rather, beyond the expectation of many, I joyfully carried back with me the peace of the Church, amid the rejoicing of the whole land. But I wonder by what means, or by whose counsel, that wondrous change wrought by the right hand of the Most High was so suddenly changed for the worse, that you again expelled from the city the clerics of Saint Hilary to the injury of the Church, and stirred up God’s anger against yourself more heavily than before. Who has bewitched you to depart so quickly from the way of truth and salvation?”

From this we have a new instance of Bernard’s care and a new merit in Aquitanian affairs and in the Church of God. Since it is most plainly clear from the words of the letter just cited that it was not written before William’s conversion, nor long afterward, I do not sufficiently understand how it can be assigned by Mabillon to the year of Christ 1132.

240. Nor would it be superfluous to read in the said Commentary that, in 1136, the Duke ravaged Normandy in war with the count of Anjou; that many were punished by diarrhoea; and that in 1137 he undertook a pilgrimage to Saint James and died there on 9 April. This is from Orderic Vitalis, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, which he completed in the fourth year after William’s death, in the Christian era 1141, when he had lived for fifty-six years among the Normans in the monastery of Saint-Evroul, having become a monk in 1085—that is, fourteen years before Duke William was born, as may be seen there.

That he died at Compostela is proved there from these words of Orderic: “In the year 1137, in the third week of March, King Stephen came into Normandy. . . . At the same time William, duke of the Poitevins, mindful of the evils which he had recently wrought in Normandy, was moved by repentance and set out as a pilgrim to Saint James. Then, on Friday of the Preparation, 9 April, he was fortified by Holy Communion and died reverently before the altar of the blessed Apostle.”

Moreover, in the often-cited Commentary, § 5, historians of the twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth centuries are adduced who agree concerning the death of Duke William at Compostela; § 6 treats of the *Life* embellished by Theobald, which, as you will find in § 7, remained unknown until nearly the sixteenth century, and there its various errors are also noted; § 8 rejects the fiction of Buchet and others concerning Duke William’s feigned death, as well as forged diplomas and the fabricated testament of Duke William.

241. These points, then, have thus far been extracted in summary from Henschenius’s Commentary [Col. 0760C]; together with many others, which he has laboriously arranged in the same work, they are of great service in avoiding confusion of events, times, and persons, and in attaining fuller knowledge of William, Duke of Aquitaine, whom St. Bernard brought back to better fruit, with most abundant benefit to the Catholic Church and an immortal memory of his name among posterity. But before I withdraw my hand from this tableau, I should like the designated Commentary to be compared with, and the following matters weighed: what Manrique writes under the year of Christ 1136, chapter 1; and what he relates in chapter 2, together with Henschenius’s historical Commentary, which appears after the Life of St. William the Hermit. It remains, after these matters—which we have narrated in one unbroken course of discourse [Col. 0760D] concerning the repeatedly mentioned conversion, so that, being interrupted from elsewhere as little as possible, it may be all the clearer and more intelligible—to meet St. Bernard as he returns to his brethren at Clairvaux from the holy Aquitanian expedition.

## § XXIII. The Song of Songs expounded by the holy Doctor; various circumstances and adjuncts of that work noted; its praises.

242. Ernald, in Book II of the *Life*, chapter 4, toward the end, says: “When, therefore, the great evil raging in Aquitaine had been overwhelmed, and Gerard’s schism reduced to ashes, the man of God returned to Clairvaux with great joy. . . . Having found . . . some time of quiet, he occupied himself with other pursuits; and withdrawing into a small cell woven about with twisted *pisatii* cords [material uncertain], he resolved to devote himself alone to divine meditations [Col. 0761A]. And suddenly there came to him, in a humble lodging, as though standing by the Lord’s manger, songs of love and the spiritual fare of a wedding-feast.”

The praised biographer pursues this point there at greater length and with pious feeling. This recollection alone of Bernard’s work supplies us ample material for a more extended discussion. Therefore, in order that its dignity may shine out more brightly, we divide the subject into several parts. First, let us speak of the time when that most holy Doctor applied his mind to this illustrious work—that is, to writing the Sermons on the Song of Songs. Secondly, at whose urging he wrote them. Thirdly, why they remained unfinished. Fourthly, how often, in what manner, in what place, and at what time they were delivered. Fifthly, in what year and why they were interrupted. Sixthly [Col. 0761B], concerning their manuscript copies. Seventhly, concerning their continuator. Eighthly, concerning the dignity and praises of this work.

The most learned Mabillon, in his new edition of the works of St. Bernard, vol. I, p. 1263, has a Preface to the fourth volume of that holy Father, containing his Sermons on the Song of Songs. From it I extract the following. On the time—which I proposed to address first—he says:

“Bernard undertook this remarkable work in 1135, after his return from Aquitaine, as is clear from Book II, chapter 6, of his Life. That the work was begun about the season of Advent in that year, 1135, we understand from the opening of the second Sermon: ‘For behold how many will rejoice at this Nativity of his which is shortly to be celebrated,’” etc.

243. By whose counsel or prompting he undertook that work is indicated in the praised Preface in these words:

“That Bernard of Portes, a Carthusian, was, if not the author of this undertaking, at least its instigator, is evident from Bernard’s Letter 153 to him. In it the holy man, when his exposition of the Song of Songs, or some spiritual work, was urgently requested, pleaded his own insufficiency; but at length yielded to the petitioner’s insistence—whether this is to be understood of taking up the work, or of publishing and sending the work already begun. The second interpretation is preferable, particularly because Geoffrey, in the passages just cited”—namely, Book II, chapter 6, and Book III, chapter 8 (but Ernald is the author of Book II of the *Life*, Geoffrey of Book III)—“does not say that Bernard of Portes intervened with authority to induce him to undertake this work [Col. 0761D]; indeed, he sufficiently suggests that the holy man of his own accord applied his mind to this meditation. The words of Letter 153 favor this view: ‘I yield to your importunity, so that the performance may remove suspicion. This is a matter between friends. I no longer spare my modesty. Truly, provided what you wish is done, I shall not remember my folly. Behold, I am having a few sermons on the beginning of Solomon’s Song of Songs, recently delivered, copied out; and, though I have not yet published them, I shall send them to you as soon as possible. When I receive time, Christ commanding my occupations, I shall attempt to proceed in this work.’

244. “From these words one can infer only that Bernard of Portes asked our Bernard for some spiritual work, and that the first Sermons on the Song of Songs were sent to him. I do not know whether the passage in Sermon 1, no. 2, should be explained of this Bernard: ‘But I think that he who came to us from the road, our friend, will now have nothing with which to murmur against us, since he has also consumed this third loaf.’ I leave that for others to judge. Finally, the earlier sermons were sent to Bernard of Portes with Letter 154, in which we read: ‘I send you the sermons on the opening of the Song of Songs which you requested and I had promised; after reading them, I ask that, as soon as you conveniently can, you advise me by your reply whether I should proceed or desist.’ This too may likewise be understood of the copying and sending of the work itself [Col. 0762A].”

245. Mabillon, their editor, gives the following reasons why these Sermons were not completed by their author:

“Although Bernard delivered these Sermons to his brethren at Clairvaux almost daily, he could not, in the eighteen years that he lived afterward, complete the work he had begun, being continually interrupted by various affairs of Church and kingdom, and even by the troublesome frequency of visitors, of which he complains more than once. Thus at the end of Sermon 3: ‘But behold, the evil of the day calls us away. For those whom they now announce as having arrived compel me rather to break off than to finish a pleasing discourse. I shall go out to the guests, lest anything be lacking in the offices of that charity of which we are speaking.’ And in Sermon 52, no. 7: ‘All too seldom is an hour of leisure granted me, free from arriving visitors.’ Yet it is remarkable that the holy Father, distracted by the care of a great household and by pressing business, was equal to meditating upon discourses of such lofty wisdom [Col. 0762C] and delivering them day by day.” Thus he.

246. Now, concerning the fourth point which I previously set down—namely, the various circumstances of these Sermons: how often, in what way, where, and at what time the holy man delivered them—form your judgment from what follows. For, as Mabillon just indicated, he delivered them daily.

“This,” he says, “the author himself also testifies in Sermon 22, no. 2: ‘It is certainly no small fatigue and labor, namely, to go forth every day and to draw even from the manifest streams of Scripture,’ etc. He delivered these Sermons on feast days, and indeed almost continuously, as is evident from Sermon 83, where he says that he had already devoted three successive days to explaining one passage. Moreover, he delivered these Sermons orally [Col. 0762D]. Hence at the end of Sermon 42 he says: ‘My infirmity, which you know, does not allow me to proceed further.’ And at the end of Sermon 44: ‘And enough of this. For my infirmity bids me rest, as it often does.’

247. “The holy man did indeed use meditation and prayer in arranging the matter of his Sermons; but sometimes, from the abundance and fullness of his mind, he produced them without having written them beforehand, as several places prove. For many things in these Sermons are said extemporaneously. Such is the passage in Sermon 36, where he rebukes the sleepy and says: ‘I thought I would fulfill in one sermon what I promised concerning the twofold ignorance; and I would have done so, had it not seemed too long to the fastidious. For I observe some yawning and others even sleeping. Nor is it surprising: the vigils of the preceding night—for they were exceedingly long—excuse them.’ But nothing proves those extemporaneous remarks so clearly as the passage from Sermon 9, no. 6: ‘Another meaning occurs to me, which I had not proposed, but which I shall by no means pass over.’

“The holy man further implies that the Sermons, once delivered, were afterward copied down by the disciples in these words: ‘They were written as they were spoken,’ he says in Sermon 54, no. 1, ‘and taken down with the pen, as were the other Sermons, so that what may perhaps have escaped can readily be recovered.’ Relevant also is what is read in Sermon 77, no. 2: ‘But if these things which we say are perhaps committed to writing, they will disdain to read them’ [Col. 0763A].

248. “Bernard delivered these Sermons repeatedly in the assembly of the brethren, with novices present, as appears from Sermon 63, no. 6, but not with the lay brothers present, since they did not attend gatherings of this kind. Hence he often indicates that his hearers were skilled in Holy Scripture; he testifies that they outstrip him in native ability in Sermons 15, no. 2; 16, no. 1; and 39, no. 2.

249. “Moreover, the hour at which these Sermons were delivered was sometimes morning, before Mass—as has been said concerning other Sermons in the Preface to the preceding volume—and sometimes evening. Understand two passages as referring to the morning time, in which he dismisses the address because of manual labor and the divine office. Thus at the end of Sermon 1 he says: ‘But the hour passes which urges us to go out to the work of our hands, both poverty and the Rule’s institution.’ But a passage more explicit for this purpose occurs in Sermon 47, which he interrupted because the hour of the divine office was imminent.
