For the evening time there is clear testimony in Sermon 71, no. 15: ‘For while I have been speaking at greater length, the day has declined.’ But enough of such small details, which nevertheless suit this place not ill [Col. 0763C].”

250. For the fifth point I mentioned above—namely, in what year and why those Sermons were interrupted—receive the answer from their editor:

“Bernard had completed altogether twenty-four Sermons in 1137, the year in which he departed for Italy to settle the schism. On returning the following year, he returned to the work he had interrupted, repeating Sermon 24 with a different beginning and a different ending; from these arose the diversity of readings which we shall discuss in its place. The holy man composed the sixty-fifth Sermon and the following one, which begin from the exposition of the verse, ‘Catch for us the little foxes,’ against the Cologne heretics, on the occasion of a letter written to him by Everwin, provost of Steinfeld; and for that reason it seemed proper to prefix that letter to those two Sermons. Finally, Sermon 80 was delivered after the Council of Reims, celebrated in 1148 in the presence of Eugenius, at which the error of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, was condemned, as Bernard himself recalls in that Sermon [Col. 0763D].”

251. With respect to the sixth point, concerning manuscript copies of the aforesaid work, and the seventh, concerning its continuator, Mabillon may be consulted in the cited place. There he treats of the number of Sermons, and on that occasion notes that in Vatican codex no. 665 [Col. 0764A] there is a preface found neither in printed editions nor in any manuscripts. He gives its opening, but it may be read there. Nothing in that Preface accords with Bernard’s style or genius. The Preface is followed by only eighty-three Sermons, under this title: “Here begins the exposition of the blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, on the Song of Songs.” He observes that this title is differently recorded in other codices.

Then he says: “This exposition ends in the third chapter of the Song, at the verse, ‘On my bed I sought him through the nights’; from there Gilbert of Hoyland, likewise an Irish Cistercian, continued it as far as this verse in the fifth chapter: ‘My beloved is white and ruddy,’ publishing forty-eight Sermons. He was indeed a man not much inferior to Bernard in gravity and piety of speech. But while endeavoring to proceed further with the exposition, death removed him from human affairs, as though indignant with him—if we believe Sixtus of Siena—for daring to continue anew Bernard’s interrupted labor and wishing to carry it to completion. Sixtus is mistaken in saying that Bernard’s work was begun in the last year of his life. We shall include Gilbert’s Sermons in the following volume.” Thus he.

“Besides this,” he continues, “Bernard dictated another, shorter exposition to William, Abbot of St. Thierry, as William himself testifies in Book I, chapter 12, of his *Life*. But a more fitting occasion to speak of it will occur in the fifth volume, where we shall report Bernard’s concise commentary on the first two chapters of the Song [Col. 0764B].”

252. There remains the eighth point of this subject, which I promised above to discuss: the dignity and praises of this most highly celebrated work [Col. 0764C]. In the often-mentioned Preface its editor extols it in these terms:

“Although all the works of St. Bernard are filled with the rich substance of solid piety and learning, two especially ought to be esteemed by all: the books *On Consideration* and the Sermons on the Song of Songs. For in those books is contained, in elegant compendium, whatever is holier in the sacred writings and in councils, whatever is more salutary in the writings of the ancient Fathers and in papal decrees prescribed for the governance of the Church. But in these Sermons, whatever is scattered through the other works of the holy Doctor for the formation of morals and the kindling of piety; whatever concerns vices and virtues [Col. 0764D], and the whole spiritual life—all this, I say, is treated in these Sermons more solidly and more sublimely. From the coverings and figures of mystical allegories, the mysteries of all perfection are drawn forth in a manner no less delightful and useful than elevated; so that these Sermons should be regarded as a kind of chaste delight for devout persons.

253. “We call this manner of writing delightful and useful. For this is, in Bernard’s own testimony, the utterly wondrous and pitiable condition of human souls: although they perceive so many things outwardly by the liveliness of their intelligence, they nevertheless altogether need certain figures and riddles of bodily likenesses, in order that from visible and external things they may be able, at least in some measure, to infer invisible and internal things. This is most excellently accomplished in these Sermons [Col. 0765A].”

Afterward Mabillon, setting a conclusion upon his Preface to the Song of Songs, says: “What Guerric, Abbot of Igny, himself a most devout disciple of the holy Doctor, thought of these Sermons, he reveals in Sermon 3 on Saints Peter and Paul, which appears with others in vol. VI: ‘Our master, that interpreter of the Holy Spirit, undertook to speak of the whole of that nuptial song, and gave us hope, from what he has already published, that, if he came to the place concerning which you ask, “until the day breathes and the shadows incline,” he would bring the very shadows into the light of understanding; what has been said, or will be, in darkness, he would tell us in the light.’ Such are Guerric’s words.”

Nor should I pass over what Manrique writes under the year of Christ 1135, chapter 6, no. 10:

“This is that work of Father Bernard which, because he was hindered by other business—though none of it was foreign to him if it concerned charity—and was at last forestalled by death, he did not complete; nor would that great sun of the whole Church, an angel alike in doctrine and purity of life, the angelic Doctor St. Thomas, undertake to complete it, as though distrusting his own ability to equal the Saint’s sweetness. Hence, when asked by the brethren of Fossanova, where he also rendered his final breath to God, he is said to have replied: ‘Give me Bernard’s spirit, and I will complete Bernard’s works’ [Col. 0765B].”

## § XXIV. A new Order established in England by Bernard’s counsels; prophecies; a miracle; journey to Rome against the schismatics; happy success of the undertaking.

254. The author of the *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, under the year of Christ 1135, chapter 8, no. 8, writes as follows, mentioning a new Order established in England by St. Bernard’s counsels:

“At the same time, by the counsels of Father Bernard, whom its founder himself consulted, the Order of Sempringham was founded in England by Gilbert of Sempringham, a most holy man; and his own achievement proved that he had received a heavenly spirit especially for the instruction of virgins.”

To this might be added what is brought forward there, in no. 9 and following, for fuller knowledge of the matter; but, lest we be too lengthy, we refer the reader there. From this point we pass with Manrique to the year of Christ 1136, where, chapter 3, no. 1, he relates a notable prophecy of the holy Abbot in this manner:

“This same year was both sad and joyful for the brethren of Clairvaux and Pontigny because of the death of Bernard’s elder brother. It was joyful for the latter because they were enriched with the relics of a holy body; sad for the former because they were bereft, since he was forestalled by illness at Pontigny and thus did not have burial at Clairvaux. In accordance with Father Bernard’s prophecy, he showed himself obedient even in death. But the occasion of that prophecy, sorrowful yet only too true, the author of the *Great Exordium* has left in writing in connection with the death of that glorious man himself.”

I quote the text as follows from Tissier’s edition, distinction 2, chapter 10:

“When once the man of God—namely, our holy Abbot—heard that one of his spiritual sons, a good and religious man whom he had sent to Normandy, was suffering there from an illness judged desperate, he resolved to send for him and bring him back to himself, so that the devout brother might die in his own little nest and not be deprived of the burial he desired. Nevertheless, one of his brothers according to the flesh, named Wido, strove to oppose this plan, because, being one of the stewards of Clairvaux, he wished, I suppose, to spare expense and labor [Col. 0766A].

255. “When he stubbornly persisted in this advice, Blessed Bernard said to him: ‘Is your concern for money or beasts of burden greater than for your brethren? Therefore, because you do not wish our brethren to rest with us in this valley, you too shall not rest in it.’ And so it came to pass. For this same Wido, although otherwise a good and religious man, was not brought to his end at Clairvaux, but, forestalled by illness at Pontigny, lay sick in bed there and, by God’s ordering, received there both the end of his life and the place of his burial [Col. 0766B].”

The holy man did not merely foretell the fate of brother Wido, or Guido, who was to die outside Clairvaux; he also announced his death, if what Manrique recounts from Brito in no. 3 is true:

“Arnold, a witness cited by Brito, states that Bernard was informed by revelation of the impending departure of the absent brother. . . . He then enjoined prayer upon all the brethren, that they might accompany the departing soul. But he immediately ordered them to cease from it and not to pray for Guido, but rather that Guido would intercede with God for them. ‘Brethren,’ he said, ‘ask Guido to pray for us; he has received the time and place so that he may do so.’ . . . Arnold recounts these deeds at Clairvaux, while at Pontigny Guido, casting off the bonds of flesh, exchanged mortal life for a better one through life-giving death [Col. 0766C].”

These are Manrique’s words from Brito. Reader, if you wish, you may consult him in Book IV, chapter 7. We should indeed have preferred that this event were attested by Ernald, the biographer so often cited, so that we might be more certain concerning it. Under the aforesaid year, chapter 7, Manrique treats of the beginnings, founder, and location of the monastery of Alba Ripa, commonly Auberive; and on that occasion he passes to the account of a miracle performed there by the holy Father, which may be seen in Geoffrey’s *Life* of him.

256. The holy Abbot came to the aid of the Church’s lamentable condition in Italy, and by his customary skill and authority calmed the storm raging there against Christ’s vicar. Manrique gives a synopsis of his actions under the year 1137, chapter 1, no. 1:

“Father Bernard was peacefully meditating the sweetest nuptial song of the Bridegroom, and had now nearly completed, in twenty-three Sermons, the first four verses of the first chapter, when, behold, at the beginning of the present year, namely 1137, he again crossed the Alps into Italy, intending at last to put an end to the long war. Campania and Apulia were suffering under Anacletus, with Roger of Sicily not merely favoring him but, under the specious title of piety—as is the way of men—sacrilegiously occupying the Church’s lands. Indeed, that great and illustrious head of Western monasticism, Monte Cassino, a no insignificant part of the Roman Church, from which so many true Popes had proceeded, had then defected from the true Pope—whether from fear or affection for Roger, who can decide?—and had insolently inclined to Anacletus. Its Abbot Seniorectus having been removed, it had set over itself Rainald, ordained by Anacletus himself and destined to promote his party. Finally, Anacletus possessed Rome. Although its leading men now stood for Innocent, the obstinate populace—either conscious of former crimes, or, amid troubled circumstances, hoping for better fortune, which commonly awaits the most abandoned persons—was found to remain more stubborn than faithful, and, if not for him, nevertheless to stand against Innocent [Col. 0767A].”

Such is Manrique’s account of the state of affairs.

257. He proves the chronology as follows in no. 2:

“Thus, when affairs were distressed, Bernard was called in the name of all as their sole comfort; and this was done immediately at the beginning of the incoming year, certainly before Pisa had been abandoned by Innocent, who, as Falco of Benevento records in his Chronicle, departed from there in March: ‘In the year 1137, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent, in the month of March, in the fifteenth indiction, the aforesaid apostolic lord Innocent, who was then staying at Pisa, having taken counsel, came from the city of Pisa to the city of Viterbo, in order to confer with the aforesaid Emperor.’ Thus Falco concerning Innocent’s departure from Pisa. But that Bernard was summoned by him before he had resolved to go to Viterbo is demonstrated by the fact that Innocent was sought at Pisa but was no longer found there, as we shall shortly see.”

That the holy man was summoned by apostolic authority to assist the Church in such disastrous circumstances, Ernald testifies at the beginning of Book II, chapter 5, of his *Life*:

“Meanwhile apostolic letters summon the man of God, and the cardinals entreat him to come to the aid of the distressed Church. His studies are interrupted, and those which had lately been continuous are resumed amid intervening journeys. No leisure remains: the servant of God either prays, meditates, reads, or preaches [Col. 0767C].

258. “Seeing, therefore, that excuses were vainly spent [variant: offered]—and that he had to obey the commands—he summoned brethren from many regions, and, after long and deep sighing, addressed them” in a fatherly speech, commending the happy success of the journey he was undertaking to their prayers, etc., as may be seen in the cited place. “Having said this and given them his blessing, he departed while all wept; received everywhere with great reverence, he finally reached Rome.”

As you see, the praised biographer recounts the Saint’s journey very briefly, mentioning nothing of his companion on the way and nothing of a stay at Viterbo. Both points will be supplied from elsewhere, after I first report certain matters from the *Cistercian Annals*, under the said chapter 1, no. 4. Their author says:

“Meanwhile I note that it is better established by tradition and frequent paintings than by ancient testimonies that, when the holy Father, about to cross the Alps, mounted a carriage, the devil, envious of the Church’s peace hoped for from his arrival, broke a wheel—whether to delay the journey begun as much as he could, or, if he could, to throw down the holy man. But Bernard himself, filled with the spirit of prophecy and no less with prudence and courage, powerfully commanded the demon who had broken it to put himself in the wheel, to turn with it, and to carry the carriage. Thus, it is said, he who had delayed the journey advanced it, and he who had hindered its voluntary traveler was compelled to carry him, becoming at once an object of ridicule and an example. There are ancient and modern pictures printed at Rome, from which the modern writers Perales, Book II, chapter 16, Montalvo, and others drew [Col. 0768A].”

Let this story stand for what it is worth. The same Annalist adds the following concerning the journey:

259. “The most beloved Father, torn away from his sons, first made for Pisa, from which he had been summoned, thinking that he would find the Supreme Pontiff there. But when he learned that he had departed, he followed him as he went as far as Viterbo, where he was received with the highest honor by him and all the cardinals. Then, when the Pope and Emperor had agreed to prosecute the whole matter by arms, dividing their forces so as to conquer Campania from one side and the March from the other, that they might more easily gain possession of the City at last,” the holy Abbot thought the affair should be undertaken at Rome by another method, as Ernald reports—not at Viterbo, as Manrique does.

For after the cited writer of the *Life*, no. 131, had said that the Saint reached Rome, he immediately adds:

“At his arrival both the Lord Pope and the brethren rejoiced; and, after they had shared counsels with him according to the course of events and the state of affairs, the Abbot undertook the matter by another way. Placing hope neither in chariots nor in horses, but holding discussions with certain persons, he inquired [Col. 0768C] what resources they had, what were the intentions of their supporters, and whether error or malice had led them to persist and continue in so great a crime,” etc.

These matters may be read more fully in Ernald, in the same chapter. Manrique, having cited a portion of them, says: “It pleased them to send the holy Doctor to Rome, to bring back to Innocent as many as he could.” Thus, according to Manrique, the foregoing occurred at Viterbo; according to Ernald, at Rome. But the latter’s view does not seem to me as probable as the former’s, both because of what has already been set forth from Falco’s Chronicle concerning Pope Innocent’s journey from Pisa to Viterbo, and because of the testimony of St. Bernard himself. Mourning the death of his brother Gerard, Bernard says in Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs, vol. I of Mabillon’s edition of his works, col. 1359:

260. “I remember, Lord, my covenant and your mercy, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. When last year we were at Viterbo for the cause of the Church, he fell ill; and when his illness worsened and his summons seemed near, I took it most grievously that I should leave my companion in pilgrimage, that companion, in a foreign land, and not restore him to those who had entrusted him to me, since he was loved by all, as he was most lovable. Turning to prayer with weeping and groaning, I said: ‘Wait, Lord, until our return. Restore him to his friends; then take him, if you will, and I shall not complain.’ You heard me, O God: he recovered; we completed the work which you had enjoined; we returned rejoicing, carrying sheaves of peace [Col. 0769A].”

It follows, first, that the holy Father was at Viterbo and remained there for some time; and not merely once, but twice—first in 1133, as Letter 151 testifies, and again in 1137, of which this passage speaks, as is observed in the notes to the said Sermon. That Sermon, in col. 1353, is marked as delivered in 1138; whereas Letter 151, addressed to Philip, intruder [variant: elected bishop] of the Church of Tours, is assigned to the year of Christ 1133, col. 154. Secondly, it follows that in his later Italian journey the holy man took with him his brother Gerard, who was most dear to him.

261. Manrique did not distinguish this journey from the earlier one in no. 6. Hence it happened that he fused into one and the same time events of different dates, as is clear from his words there:

“While Bernard was staying at Viterbo, it happened that Philip, the pseudo-elect of the Church of Tours—for Heribert had died in the preceding year, and Philip, his predecessor’s nephew, had violently intruded himself and, though still a young man, occupied that see—it happened, I say, that Philip sought Rome to be ordained a pseudo-bishop by the pseudo-Pope. Thus cut off from the Catholic Church, he was a young man otherwise familiar to Bernard and distinguished by many gifts of mind. When Bernard learned that he was in Rome, he wrote him a brief but sharp letter, no less sweet and full of affectionate love.” A copy of it is immediately quoted there and appears in Mabillon, cited col. 154.

But that the letter addressed to Philip belongs not to 1137 but must be referred back to 1132 is established from Mabillon’s note on Letter 150, addressed to Pope Innocent, in which the holy Doctor says: “The spirit of Gislebert, they say, has revived in Philip, plainly his nephew in the flesh and heir of his ambition.” Let Mabillon now be heard:

“Gislebert, or Gilbert, was the predecessor of Hildebert, who was transferred in 1125 from the see of Le Mans to that of Tours and held it for six years and as many months, as we noted on Letter 122. On his death Philip, Gislebert’s nephew, invading the see by evil practices with Anacletus’s support, gave occasion for this Letter and for the following Letter, which was written earlier.

262. “Philip having been compelled to yield, Hugh was canonically appointed in his place. Read the *Analecta*,” published by Mabillon himself, “vol. III, p. 338.”

In the notes to Letter 122, written by the said Hildebert to Bernard but placed in this order among Bernard’s letters, the following is observed:

“Hildebert, the author of this letter, governed the Church of Le Mans from 1108 to 1125, when, after the death of Gislebert, he was appointed to the metropolitan see of Tours. This is established both from Orderic Vitalis in Book X under the year 1098 and from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, printed in vol. III of the *Analecta*, where Guy, his successor in the see of Le Mans, is recorded as consecrated in 1126 after long disputes. He governed Tours for only six years and as many months. Thus the aforesaid *Acts* state, with which the Chesne copy agrees, as does John Maan in his *Metropolis of Tours*, and indeed also Orderic under the year 1125, p. 882, where he assigns Hildebert nearly seven years as archbishop. Therefore Hildebert did not survive to 1136, as is read in *Gallia Christiana*, but died in 1132, the year in which John Maan likewise places his death [Col. 0770A].”

Three conclusions therefore follow from what has been said: first, that the holy man stayed at Viterbo twice and in different years; second, that Manrique confused the two stays; and third, that the letter which the same Saint wrote to Philip must be restored to the year of Christ 1133, as Mabillon showed. But let us return to the Saint as he leaves Viterbo.

263. “Meanwhile,” as Manrique relates in no. 7, “when Gerard had recovered, Father Bernard immediately left Viterbo; ascending to Rome, he met men individually, assembled them collectively, pressed upon all that Peter, the abominable author of the schism, must be detested, and Innocent followed, and the Church’s unity preached; he rebuked those who divided it and completely closed off the evasions of excuses,” etc.

But what pretexts the rebels advanced, and what arguments the Saint brought against them to uncover and overcome their faithlessness, Bernard—or rather Ernald, Abbot of Bonneval—relates in these words, which may be seen in our chapter 5. But how great was the power of the speaker’s eloquence; how great the movements of mind in the rebels caused by his powerful discourse; and how great the fruit for God’s Church of the mission undertaken by the holy man among the Romans, is clear from the praised biographer, who recalls the outcome of the matter in no. 132 as follows:

“Having heard these and other discourses of the man of God, they fell away from Peter; and daily, as the ranks of that party broke apart, its bonds were shattered. Peter’s own spirit also wasted away, because he did not doubt that he himself was daily diminished, while Innocent increased,” etc. [Col. 0770C]

## § XXV. Events said to have occurred among the men of Monte Cassino in St. Bernard’s presence are partly false and partly plausible; his bodily infirmity and his desire to return to his brethren.

265. The most eminent Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 1137, after setting forth the state of the schismatics in the city of Rome, asserts in no. 5 that our Saint “prolonged his stay there for a long time, with great benefit to Catholics.” But if what is found in Peter the Deacon, a writer of that period, in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, is true, he must have been in Campania in July and discharged the office of legate at Monte Cassino.

The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year just mentioned, chapter 2, nos. 1 and 2, reports that Lothair was summoned by the men of Monte Cassino, previously attached to Anacletus and Roger, so that through him they might be reconciled to the Church. He adds what occurred here at Monte Cassino, omitted by Falco—whose Beneventan Chronicle he had cited—and preserved only by Peter, or circulated under Peter’s name. Manrique indeed admits that these matters are true, or at least plausible; they may be read in the aforesaid Peter’s *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 107 and following, from p. 563 [Col. 0771A] of the latest edition, printed among the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. IV, at Milan, together with notes elucidating that Chronicle.

“But what is said to have occurred in the presence of Lothair,” Manrique continues there, “seems to deviate too far from the truth; and therefore, lest any part of it be imputed to us, it is fitting to write it in Peter’s own words. Except that I first observe that, whoever may have been the author of that history, beyond other errors of which I shall speak below, he also selected a year that is not merely uncertain but contradictory: namely, the following year, 1138, in which Innocent had already returned to Rome and Lothair had even departed from Rome.”

265. He then quotes the author’s words from Book IV, chapter 110 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, which in the specified Milanese edition are numbered Book IV, chapter 109. [Col. 0771B] We here abridge them from Manrique’s text, selecting from the same material as much as suffices for our purpose:

> “In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the year of His Incarnation 1138, in the first indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the seventh year of the reign of Emperor Lothair [Milan edition: sixth], while the same most invincible prince was residing at Acquae Pensiles, and Peregrinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, was likewise sitting in council with very many archbishops, bishops, and abbots, Girard, Cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross, was sent as advocate for the Roman Church, and Guido Cardinal, both of whom afterwards became Roman pontiffs.”

[Col. 0771C] Among the others named there occurs “Robert [Milan edition: Norbert], Abbot of Clairvaux. . . . On behalf of the Church of Monte Cassino, the hearers were Henry the duke, son-in-law of the emperor, Conrad the duke,” and many others whose names are set down there. “When silence had therefore been made, the emperor said: ‘In this assembly there shall be a discussion not only of present and temporal matters, but also of future and eternal things. We likewise, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, have thought it fitting to attend this council and to weigh the importance of what shall be said.’” These are the words from the said *Chronicle* as quoted by Manrique. I do not give the variant readings found in the Milanese edition, apart from two.

266. Manrique, in nos. 4 and 5, censures the proceedings of this session as spurious [Col. 0771D]:

> “From these,” he says, “you may plainly see a controversy between the Roman Church, head of all others, and a particular member utterly unworthy of her; an unworthy tribunal for those contending, secular for ecclesiastical persons and churches. Finally, it was an act unworthy of Pope Innocent, who would have appointed cardinals and Bernard as delegates for this affair—so that, even from these points, whoever wrote it may be convicted of falsehood. And Robert (or Norbert, as the Milanese edition has it), Abbot of Clairvaux, no less exposes the fiction as a fabrication.”

He immediately adds the account of a disputation said to have continued at length for five days between Cardinal Girard and Peter himself: the latter acting as defender of the Church of Monte Cassino, the former of the Roman Church. The principal point of the dispute was whether the Cassinese monks, after renouncing Anacletus, were to bind themselves to Innocent by an oath. A further question was added concerning the election of an abbot and what right the Vicar of Christ possessed in it. “Peter then adds,” as Manrique continues in no. 6, “a second disputation, continued for three days, with a Cistercian monk”—so he calls him—“in which he was easily able to gain his object against an adversary apparently invented for himself.”

Manrique inserts this second disputation into his *Annals*, in the same no. 6 and the following sections; but we give neither disputation here. Baronius sharply criticizes both under the year of Christ 1138, no. 14. Let us set forth his words.

267. “The proceedings concerning the disputation of the cardinals with Peter himself before Emperor Lothair, fabricated by someone at will, since they are proved false in many ways [Col. 0772B], we consider unworthy to be interwoven in the *Annals*. Thus God resists a liar: although the one who spins the web of falsehood be crafty and cunning, He darkens his understanding as though by an enchantment, so that he cannot see what is clear to others and may thus be convicted of falsehood from it.”

And shortly afterwards, having quoted the beginning of those proceedings, Baronius continues in no. 15:

> “This place called by the author Acquae Pensiles—where was it? The same author asserts above, Book IV, chapter 109 (but in the latest Milanese edition, chapter 108), that it was near Melfi. For he says: ‘The monks, striving to hasten their flight, came first to Melfi, then from there to Lake Pensile’—in the said edition, p. 565, it is commonly called *Lago Pesole* in the notes—‘where the whole army of the emperor had encamped with Pope Innocent.’ But it happened that the emperor was there not in this year but in the preceding year, when he descended with his army into Apulia, as has been shown above in its place from the authority of writers of that same period. How then does Peter assign the present year and the indiction of the present year, and record a definite day in July of that year, when neither emperor nor pope was at Acquae Pensiles? Innocent was living at Rome at that time, and Emperor Lothair had already withdrawn from the City toward Cisalpine Gaul.”

268. “Moreover, who is said to have been present there at the public disputation with the cardinals as Robert, Abbot of Clairvaux, when none other than Saint Bernard was at that time Abbot of Clairvaux? Further, how could Innocent have tolerated Emperor Lothair presiding as judge between the cardinals and the monks of Monte Cassino, when, as we have seen, he took it with the greatest indignation that Lothair had heard the case of monks disputing among themselves? These things, and others, prove that the appended proceedings are wholly fabricated; as is also the great disgrace of those schismatic monks, who are represented as arguing with such audacity against the Roman Church. Thus those proceedings should not have been dated in the thirty-eighth year after eleven hundred, but in the thirty-seventh; not in the first indiction but in the fifteenth; not in the seventh year of Emperor Lothair, but in the fifth; and should be corrected in other respects as well [Col. 0773A], as we have said.”

So far Baronius. To this criticism, among other things, the above-mentioned Cistercian historian adds in no. 9:

> “One might add: who was that Cistercian, then held in such esteem by all, to whom the defense of a public cause would be entrusted, yet so insignificant that he should remain anonymous, unknown even to the man whom he was attacking? Was it Bernard, whom the writer preferred to omit rather than name falsely again? But Bernard would not have stood at a distance: pope and emperor revered him, and the world saw him seated among the cardinals. Nor would he have been summoned to the contest if the contest had not been entrusted to him,” etc.

269. Such, then, are the charges by which both these writers denounce the proceedings at Monte Cassino as spurious and fabricated [Col. 0773B]. Yet the author of the historical-juridical *Excursus* interwoven into the Milanese edition of Peter the Deacon’s *Chronicle*, pp. 566 ff., endeavors at length and laboriously to defend Peter’s narrative against the accusations of Baronius and Laureti. How he answers them may be seen there. But the argument I shall add here—one which I do not find touched on either by Baronius, Manrique, or the author of the said *Excursus*—namely, the time when Emperor Lothair died, appears to carry great weight against the disputed proceedings at Monte Cassino.

This argument, developed by Pagi in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year of Christ 1138, I apply to the present issue [Col. 0773C]. Thus in no. 6 he observes against Baronius:

> “At no. 12 and following, Baronius postpones the death of Emperor Lothair until December of the current year. But that Lothair died in the preceding year . . . ought to be beyond all controversy. Robert of Monte, Abbot Dodechin, the continuator of Lambert of Schafnaburg, the Hildesheim chronicler, and others everywhere report that Lothair died in the preceding year and that Conrad succeeded him in the current year; his charters demonstrate this conclusively. We shall overthrow Baronius’s foundation under the following year.”

Those charters are also mentioned in no. 3. Pagi continues in the said no. 6:

270. “Falco says in his *Chronicle* under the year 1137 [Col. 0773D]: ‘In this year the aforesaid emperor . . . died in the regions of Tuscany.’”

What Pagi adds concerning another place of death has no bearing on our present controversy, any more than does the question of where Lothair’s body was conveyed, which he discusses there. Concerning the day of Emperor Lothair’s death, he writes from the authorities he cites in no. 7: “In the middle of the night between the third and second Nones of December he ceased to live.” Since he was crowned emperor in June 1133—see Baronius and his critic—it follows that he died in the fifth year of his reign.

Now the argument which has seemed proper to employ against the Cassinese session rests upon chronology. Baronius indeed applies other chronological marks to the events said to have occurred there [Col. 0774A], as we have just related; but he could not invalidate them from the emperor’s death, because he places it in 1138. Nor could Manrique, who assigns that year to Lothair’s death in chapter 7 under the year 1139.

But let us see what the author of the historical-juridical *Excursus*, p. 567, replies to Baronius’s argument drawn from chronology:

> “First,” he says, “he charges an error in the year, and consequently in the indiction. But historical credibility would fare badly if such slight errors darkened and destroyed the truth of the remaining particulars. Further: our handwritten manuscript, from which this material was taken, does not read ‘in the seventh year of Lothair’s reign,’ as the Venetian edition, which misled Baronius, wrongly has it; but ‘in the sixth year,’ which denotes the thirty-eighth year of Christ.”

[Col. 0774B]

271. But critics of more discerning judgment may reply, first, that chronological errors in historical documents darken and render suspect the truth of their remaining contents when other difficulties of the same tendency occur in them. Secondly, that the chronological correction adopted in the cited *Excursus* is worthless, as is clear from the year of Emperor Lothair’s death, for Conrad succeeded him in 1138. Thirdly, that they cannot understand how Peter the Deacon could have brought Lothair onto that contentious stage as its presiding officer on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the seventh year of his reign—or, if you prefer, in the sixth—when he never lived to see the sixth year of his reign, much less that day, having died a year and a half, and more, before it. This is said of Peter the Deacon, not merely spectator and witness of the event, but, as they maintain, its principal actor and advocate [Col. 0774C]. Fourthly, if this controversy was truly written by Peter and not attributed to him by another—see the *Excursus*, p. 570—how can it be conceived that he wrote it in such a manner as to stumble so grossly in chronology? And how likewise did he substitute another name for Bernard’s?

Yet I do not set myself up as arbiter between the accusations stated above and their defense in the *Excursus*, by comparing all the objections and replies together, lest I stray too far afield. This I say: it does not seem to me certainly established that Peter the Deacon was the genuine author of the frequently mentioned Cassinese disputation, that it truly took place in the manner reported, and consequently that Saint Bernard attended it [Col. 0774D]—the investigation of which has so long diverted us from our purpose. But whether he was staying there or elsewhere at that time, he did not live in idleness, but was engaged in advancing the affairs of the Catholic Church, being consumed by that fire of the Holy Spirit which could not rest. Whatever may be thought of the said controversy, it is recorded that the holy abbot was at Monte Cassino on another occasion and at another time.

272. “It is established,” says Manrique under the year 1137, chapter 3, no. 1, “that the Cassinese . . . received Innocent after renouncing Anacletus, their obedience being confirmed by an oath, which, in the presence of the leading men of both courts, the abbot was the first of all to swear.” He reports this from Peter the Deacon, whom he cites, Book IV, chapter 116. In the latest edition the event is narrated in Book IV, chapter 115; the monks then followed, as you will find there [Col. 0775A], and in chapter 118.

Manrique adds in no. 4:

> “As for the election of Abbot Rainald, lest even that should be dealt with without the sons of Benedict, it was entrusted to Bernard for examination, with two cardinals added, Haimeric and Girard, who were to decide whether it should be confirmed or invalidated, whether the election once decreed should be overturned or preserved. The matter was debated at length on both sides. But when they finally recognized it to be void, so that they might carry out the affair with more mature and more agreeable judgment, and not without a full hearing of the party,”

the same annalist says, reporting from Peter the Deacon what was done in this case. The Milanese edition, Book IV, chapter 119, p. 583, reads:

> “At the breaking of day, Aymericus, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Roman Church, Gerard, Cardinal of the Holy Cross, and the Abbot of Clairvaux were sent by the same pope, in order that they might examine the aforesaid Rainald and, in accordance with the sanction of the canons, remove him from the government of the abbey.”

And after other acts in this affair, subsequently narrated, chapter 122, p. 595, contains these words:

> “On the following day they again went up to the monastery and sat in the chapter-house, where, after the Abbot of Clairvaux had delivered his discourse, the cardinals, by apostolic authority, prohibited the same Rainald from holding the abbey of Monte Cassino,” etc.

Thus Saint Bernard took part in these proceedings with no small authority in speaking, if what is read in Peter the Deacon is altogether genuine and authentic.

273. “When affairs at Monte Cassino had thus been arranged,” as Manrique narrates in no. 5 [Col. 0775C], “and the towns throughout Campania which Roger had violently subjected to himself and Anacletus had been subdued, while Innocent was preparing to travel toward Rome, Bernard’s health, already weak, failed beyond its usual degree of exhaustion. Worn out by labors, his body was sustained by spirit alone. There survives a letter written by him this year to the abbots assembled at Cîteaux, which portrays a dying man.”

Understand the subject of the letter from the title prefixed to it: “He desires these”—namely, the abbots—“to be aware of his labors and sufferings, perhaps thus excusing his absence. He certainly wishes to die not abroad, but among his own.” It is the one hundred and forty-fifth among Bernard’s other letters, and is printed in Mabillon’s edition from col. 150, where it is marked as written about the year now under consideration, 1137.

## § XXVI. Saint Bernard sent by Pope Innocent to restrain Roger; Roger’s defeat foretold and obtained from heaven by the holy man; the softening of Roger’s disposition; proceedings in the case of the schism and their circumstances

[Col. 0775D]

274. The holy Father’s bodily health was indeed extremely bad, or rather almost nonexistent; but nevertheless, as Manrique reports under the year 1137, chapter 3, no. 6, “there was no cessation from labor, nor was a truce granted to his failing strength. Innocent and Lothair, proceeding to Rome, took the holy doctor with them, since both believed that without him nothing happy, nothing prosperous could occur. Nor did hope deceive men otherwise prudent.”

At Rome he advanced the affairs of the Church so effectively that shortly afterwards he did not hesitate to write the following to his brethren at Clairvaux [Col. 0776A], in Letter 144:

> “Even on this occasion I would tell you, for your consolation, how necessary the presence of our littleness is, or has been, to the Church of God, if it did not smell of glory. But now it is better that you should learn this from others.”

From this it may be understood that the holy man managed the common cause at Rome in such a way as to leave little or nothing there still requiring action. Manrique continues:

> “But while matters were proceeding more favorably at Rome, everything in Campania was again thrown into disorder; the cities recovered for the Church were again lost, conquered, devastated, surrendered, and returned to the party of Anacletus. The emperor’s departure brought Roger the duke, and Roger brought every evil with him—evils to be driven away by the merits of Bernard alone, so that victory might be ascribed to God alone. But what evils followed the emperor’s departure we can draw from no source better than the letter written by Guibald, the new Abbot of Monte Cassino, to the emperor.”

Manrique excerpts it from Book IV, chapter 127 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*; in the new edition the letter stands in Book IV, chapter 126. There, in tragic and impassioned narration, is set forth the barbarous scene of events and the lamentable calamity of a rage more than bestial, which filled up every measure of cruelty in a frightful manner, as may be read there in detail. What was done meanwhile amid circumstances so desperate?

275. “But the pious prince,” as the Cistercian *Annals* continue in no. 8, “broken by old age and illness and near death [Col. 0776C], could not assist the abandoned cause; and victory was reserved for Father Bernard, so that it could not be taken from him by another. The holy doctor had accomplished much in peace, and with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, had quenched the fiery darts of the most wicked adversary. But, not being opposed to an armed soldier, he had not wielded a material sword against the Church’s enemies; he had not driven the rebels into slaughter or flight, having rendered them obedient before battle by his words, or dismissed them to obey in time. Therefore, lest he should be deprived even of this kind of victory, divine providence brought it about that he alone—humble, poor, and dying—should be set against a victorious army, in order that he might restrain Roger by words if possible [Manrique: ‘being about to restrain’]; if not, by arms, and by arms against which those who had been defeated and routed would then have no power whatever to dare anything [Col. 0776D] against the victors. Baronius mentions the counsel of Innocent alone. But in Bernard—I shall shortly quote the letter—I also read the emperor’s consent.”

276. Here, reader, is Baronius’s text under the year 1137, no. 28:

> “What did Pope Innocent do on hearing this? Having learned in reality how vain is human aid, hoping against hope amid such desperate circumstances, he set against the raging assaults of the Sicilian tyrant, against the fierceness of the avenging and victorious army, one humble man, yet powerful by God’s strength, to turn the victorious enemies of the holy Roman Church to flight. He knew this to be the kind of work of God: namely, that He chooses the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong. Thus, sheathing at Christ’s command the drawn sword raised in defense of the Church, he turned to spiritual weapons powerful through God, taking the shield of faith and, securely receiving upon it all the darts of the wicked one, hastened unharmed to wound his adversary. How was this done? Listen to Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, whom he had left at Rome to bring back to the Church those led astray by schism—as, above, we heard it related—whom he sends as an envoy of peace to the tyrant Roger, breathing threats and slaughter against all who were in communion with Pope Innocent,” etc.

277. But Bernard himself seems to indicate in Letter 144 that this was done not merely at Pope Innocent’s command but also at the most earnest request of Emperor Lothair and the Roman Curia. Addressing his brethren of Clairvaux, he says:

> “Yielding to the most urgent request of the emperor, to the apostolic command, and also to the prayers of the Church and of the princes, grieving and unwilling, weak and infirm, and—to confess the truth—bearing about the pale image of a fearful death, we are drawn into Apulia.”

Let us now relate what was accomplished in this embassy of the great man to Roger. “First of all,” says the recently cited Baronius, “we think it necessary to warn that the author who wrote the acts of Saint Bernard confuses two embassies, when he affirms that Cardinal Aimeric the chancellor was sent with Saint Bernard, and likewise Cardinal Peter of Pisa on Anacletus’s side. For those matters concerning cardinals sent by either side occurred later, as is quite clearly evident from Falco of Benevento, who was present and committed them to writing. Saint Bernard was therefore sent first; afterwards, at Roger’s request, the cardinals were sent, when, humbled by God, he began willingly to listen to the words of peace which he had despised.”

Having noted this point, which he will later develop, let us narrate the history of the event.

278. “There remained,” say the Cistercian *Annals*, chapter 4, no. 1, “on Lothair’s side Duke Rainulf, faithful both to the Church and to the Empire, but far inferior to Roger in forces, as in fortune. For he led few men, and men defeated and therefore timid, who did not despise flight, by which they might escape extreme dangers. Roger’s spoil and numbers supplied strength and spirit to his resources and power [Col. 0777D], now made confident by victory. Therefore Father Bernard was sent to Roger, and first of all he sought to dissuade him from war, prevent battle, instill concord, and ratify treaties of peace.”

But let us hear Abbot Ernald of Bonneval, Book II of the *Life*, chapter 5, no. 132:

> “Meanwhile Roger, king of Sicily, who alone now among the princes refused obedience to Pope Innocent, sent to him, asking that he send to him his chancellor Aimeric and the Abbot of Clairvaux. He made the same request of Peter Leonis, that he should delegate to him Peter of Pisa from his side. . . . Yet he sent deceitfully, because he had heard that Peter of Pisa was most eloquent and second to none in knowledge of laws and canons. He thought that, if a hearing were granted to that man’s eloquence in a public assembly, the abbot’s simplicity could be overwhelmed by rhetorical declamations. . . . In short, each side came to Salerno. But vengeance had taken the field and had forestalled the scheme of so great a crime. For, when the same king had prepared an innumerable army for war against Duke Rainulf, . . . he was suddenly terrified at the sight of the duke boldly advancing to meet him, fled, and exposed his scattered army to plunder and slaughter. With countless soldiers captured and killed, he unwillingly enriched the duke with resources and raised him high in glory. All this indeed happened to him according to the word of the man of God,”

as we shall relate shortly, after restoring to a better chronological order what the biographer here recounts by anticipation, using the praised Falco, vol. V, p. 124 of the Milanese edition.

279. “Meanwhile,” he says, “the Abbot of Clairvaux, a very admirable and discerning man, who had come to that king to calm the disturbance of so great a dissension, tried to bind treaties of peace between the king and the duke. But because of the many and diverse matters in dispute between them, concord had not yet pleased the power of God the Savior to be bound. Why say more? The king himself divided his army and steadfastly prepared it for battle; likewise the duke wisely arrayed all his own men. . . . At once the king’s battle-line was overthrown. And the king . . . when God’s judgment came upon him, struck with fear, was the first himself to turn his back and flee.” The same writer then discusses his defeat and the spoils carried off by the victorious Duke Rainulf, adding, “on the second . . . day remaining”—that is, the thirtieth day, according to what will be said in the section immediately following—“of October this battle was fought.”

Thus, at about the same time occurred Saint Bernard’s prophecy, by which he foretold defeat to Roger and victory to Duke Rainulf. See Ernald in the indicated chapter, where he writes in no. 133:

> “For when the holy abbot, the first of those who had been summoned—or, more probably, summoned only later—arrived and found the king encamped in the field, he prevented the neighboring battle-lines from engaging for many days, declaring to the king: ‘If you enter battle, you will depart defeated and confounded.’ . . . But he encouraged Duke Rainulf and the battle-line of the Catholics with powerful words, and as he promised flight to the king, so he promised victory and triumph to them.”

Indeed, that heavenly warrior obtained this remarkable victory by his prayers. For “when, as Ernald testifies, he had turned aside to a nearby little village and was intent on prayer, suddenly the cry of those fleeing and those pursuing was heard. For Rainulf was pursuing the fleeing royal army through that very place. One of the brothers who were with the abbot went out and met one of the soldiers, asking what had happened. But he said: ‘I saw the wicked man exalted . . . and I passed by, and behold, he was not.’ Without delay the duke himself followed; and when he saw the monk, armed as he was, he leapt from his horse and, falling at his feet, said: ‘I give thanks to God and to His faithful servant, because this victory has been granted not by our strength, but by his faith’ [Col. 0779A]; and mounting his horse again, he pursued the enemy.”

That illustrious triumph, therefore, with the Judge granting victory, was prayed for, obtained, and granted by the holy man from God, the Lord of hosts; it was secured by heavenly rather than military arms.

280. Roger meanwhile, stubbornly driven into flight with a great defeat, since he could not resort to arms, turned his mind to stratagems. The historian of Clairvaux explains the matter thus in no. 4 [Col. 0779B]:

> “Roger, having received an unexpected blow, became more fearful and did not dare advance further until he should recover his forces and power. Awaiting—or rather creating—a favorable time for this, so that he might not meanwhile be troubled by Rainulf, he devised a crafty expedient suited to the moment: namely, to cast Bernard into hope of his conversion and, with arms removed from both sides, to commit the affair to disputations.”

We shall relate the event from the *Chronicle* of Falco of Benevento, noting also its chronological setting:

> “On the second day remaining in October, as we have said, this battle of which we spoke above was fought. Then the aforementioned king,” Falco continues, “fleeing in such a manner with his followers by night, reached the castle of Paludi on the following day and then hastened to Salerno. Not many days later, Rossemannus, the Beneventan prelate [Col. 0779C], having taken counsel with the judges of the city and certain wise men, hastened to comfort the king and offer him the city’s services. He further requested that the king grant the people of Benevento the liberty of their possessions which the aforesaid emperor had conceded.”

The king consented, as is evident from the charter of privilege which Falco produces, dated in the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, November, first indiction.

281. Having narrated the acts performed by Duke Rainulf after his victory, “Near the castle of Paludi,” says the same chronicler, p. 125, “surrounded by the valor of his men, he encamped on the day before the Kalends of December.”

Now what Abbot Ernald of Bonneval had related above, whether by anticipation or confusedly, first concerning the arbitrators requested by King Roger and sent to Salerno to establish peace, and then concerning Rainulf’s victory [Col. 0779D], we arrange from the foregoing and the following facts in such a way that the proceedings in that assembly of envoys from Innocent’s side and Anacletus’s side seem to belong here, and therefore not to Bernard’s first meeting with Roger. At that first meeting, the holy Father more probably urged, but did not persuade, Roger to agree to this conference. They belong rather to another meeting, after the defeat inflicted upon him.

For Falco adds these words to those last cited by us, from which I infer that what he first asserts applies either to the holy man’s first conference with the king before the battle, or else was confirmed at the second conference after the battle:

> “While the aforesaid Abbot of Clairvaux, a very admirable and discerning man, was conversing with the said king about a treaty of peace and the unity of the Church [Col. 0780A], the king repeatedly agreed with that abbot that three cardinals from Pope Innocent’s side, who had been present at his election, should come to the king, together with three from Anacletus’s side, and explain to the king the procedure of each election. The king would then, having heard the procedure, choose the holier and more just election of the two sides.”

Note *agreed*, that is, he then ratified the arrangement about which Bernard had previously dealt with him, but fruitlessly, as I interpret it. Thus the summons which Roger had formerly rejected was now put into execution. For “immediately,” Falco continues, “a delegation was sent to Pope Innocent and Anacletus, and the king’s command was dispatched with swift speed.” Ernald himself also signifies this quite clearly. For, after describing Roger’s defeat, he writes in no. 134:

> “Yet the king’s mind was not corrected by this blow inflicted upon him from heaven, nor did the storm subside which the pride of his perverse mind had gathered. But when those who had escaped returned after the flight, feigning cheerfulness, he raised himself in royal array; and, with his court crowded with soldiers, he ordered both sides to be summoned. Having first instructed Peter and inflamed him with the incentive of many promises, he ordered him to speak concerning the grounds of his cause. Peter therefore first endeavored to prove the election of his lord canonical,” etc.

282. But since the praised author of the *Life* proceeds to treat the proceedings of this case and their circumstances neither sufficiently distinctly nor fully [Col. 0780C], we shall supplement him from Falco. First, therefore, let us consider the persons who took part in these proceedings. Although we have seen above from Ernald who were called to it, nevertheless nothing prevents us from recalling the matter here also from Falco and confirming it:

> “It therefore pleased them,” he says, “and their counsel having been confirmed, Aimeric the chancellor and Girard the most venerable cardinal arrived at Salerno from Innocent’s side, together with the aforesaid Abbot of Clairvaux, to debate this election. From Anacletus’s side Matthew the chancellor, Cardinal Peter of Pisa, and another cardinal named Gregory likewise hastened there.”

Why Peter of Pisa had been summoned by Roger, we set forth above from the said biographer.

[Col. 0780D]

283. Secondly, let us consider the proceedings of this case. Ernald, chapter 5, no. 134, mentions the holy Father’s contest with Peter of Pisa. How fittingly and powerfully the holy man argued in it is made clear from his words, produced by the same biographer, and from the approval of his hearers. For “at these words,” he says in no. 136, “those who were present could no longer restrain themselves, but abhorred both the life of Peter Leonis and his cause.” Moreover, his adversary was so overthrown in the first encounter that he could not resist or contradict the arguments advanced by his holy antagonist, as the same biographer testifies when he immediately adds:

> “But the abbot, taking the hand of Peter of Pisa, raised him up and himself rose with him: ‘If you trust me,’ he said, ‘we shall enter the ark more safely.’ And, approaching him with saving admonitions, as he had long before conceived in his mind, by the cooperating grace of God he immediately persuaded him, upon returning to Rome, to be reconciled with Pope Innocent. When the assembly was dissolved, the king was still unwilling to obey.”

You see that this author confines the proceedings of the present case to one meeting, whereas Falco extends them much further when he records them in these words:

> “When all those whom we named a little earlier had thus assembled, the king, being a man of shrewd mind and provident counsel, first examined Innocent’s side, remarkably and beyond belief, for four days until evening; then he investigated Anacletus’s side likewise for four days.”

[Col. 0781B]

284. “Having therefore carefully and diligently heard the parties of each election, the king ordered all the clergy and people of the city of Salerno to assemble, as well as the bishops and abbots of monasteries who had gathered. Before them he began in this manner:

> ‘Lords and brothers, we believe that your prudence is not unaware of the reason for which I have caused these cardinals . . . to be summoned. . . . But since our mind is hindered by many questions and various answers, I cannot by myself bring an end to this great affair. Therefore, if it pleases these lord cardinals, let them write down the procedure of each election, and let one cardinal from each side go down with me into Sicily, where, God favoring us, we are to celebrate the feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ our Savior [Col. 0781C]. There we shall find wise archbishops, bishops, and other men of prudent mind, by whose counsel I have until now followed Anacletus’s side. . . .’

> To this Cardinal Girard replied: ‘We shall indeed send Cardinal Guido of Castello . . . to come with you into Sicily, as you request. . . .’”

When these things had been done, each returned home. On the following day the aforesaid Cardinal Girard returned with his companions; but the said Cardinal Guido alone remained behind, intending to depart with the king as had been arranged. From Anacletus’s side likewise another cardinal was sent. These matters having been completed and a ship prepared, the king crossed over into Sicily.

285. Before proceeding further, let the reader observe that Ciaconius, in *Lives of Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals*, vol. I, col. 968, states that this Guido governed the city of Benevento for a time as its prefect, when Innocent II left it on his way toward Rome—see Pagi’s *Critique* under the year 1137. Therefore nothing prevents his having been present at Salerno with the other cardinals, although he was not named among them above [Col. 0781D].

A second point I would note is that Falco’s silence about Saint Bernard’s address to Peter of Pisa and Peter’s consequent conversion to obedience to the legitimate pontiff ought in no way to prejudice the authority of the biographer Ernald. Although Falco is silent, Ernald explicitly affirms these things; and Ernald’s principal aim was to collect Bernard’s deeds and transmit them to posterity, whereas Falco’s was not. Moreover, not all authors who treat the same subject write down everything [Col. 0782A]. How often is it necessary to supplement one author from another? Make the same judgment about other acts of our saint which Falco left unmentioned but Ernald records. Ernald could easily have learned them either from “a certain brother among those who were with the abbot,” or elsewhere, since they happened not secretly but openly.

286. Let us consider, thirdly, the place where these proceedings occurred: namely Salerno, where the cardinals met with St. Bernard—the scene of the laureled victory which he won over Peter of Pisa—although another place in Sicily was requested from King Roger, and obtained, for the further discussion of the case. Yet I do not remember reading that Bernard also went there; indeed, he does not seem to have proceeded thither, as is indicated by what I shall relate from Ernaldus concerning his return to Rome [Col. 0782B]; nor do I know whether anything was transacted there, or what it was. That Roger had not yet submitted himself to Innocent is apparent from what will be said below. Moreover, the city of Salerno was honoured not only by the saint’s presence, but also by a distinguished miracle wrought through him. Ernaldus writes of it, book II, chapter 5, no. 136, and adds that it “was spread abroad throughout the whole city and reached the ears of the king and his nobles.”

Let us consider, fourthly, the time of this affair. It was conducted at Salerno in the year of Christ 1137, toward its end, apparently in December. For Roger had said above: “Let one cardinal from each side come down with me into Sicily, where … we shall celebrate the feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ the Saviour.” Here ends the embassy of the most blessed abbot [Col. 0782C]; and we now begin to speak of his return to the City, relating what he himself did in the following year.

## § XXVII. The Saint Returns to Rome; Peter of Pisa Is Reconciled to the Church, as Is Victor, Anacletus’s Successor; Roger Likewise Abandons the Schism; a Sacred Pledge Given to Bernard as He Leaves Rome; He Leaves His Tunic There; Various Chronological Points

287. The Cistercian historian thus opens the year of Christ 1138: “Let Bernard’s return to Rome inaugurate the beginning of the year for us: Peter of Pisa having been reconciled to the Church; Anacletus failing, scarcely deserted by his followers before he had deserted himself—for once accustomed to pontifical trappings, he preferred to lose his soul rather than the title [Col. 0782D] of pseudo-pontiff. Let us sketch in the manner of the ancients how each event took place, and some of them even by months and days. The author of his Life has briefly recorded both the saint’s return [the edition incorrectly reads *reversum*] to the City at this time and likewise the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa. ‘Therefore, with the favour of all the peoples, the king alone—that is, Roger—remaining in malice, the abbot returns to Rome; he also reconciles the aforesaid Peter of Pisa and certain others to the Church, and binds them in alliance with Pope Innocent.’”

Manrique continues: “But that Peter of Pisa’s reconciliation occurred on the fourth day of January is shown by the fact that Anacletus, surviving three days, is recorded to have died on the seventh of the same month. Antoninus testifies that he was reconciled three days before Anacletus’s death … Part II, title 17, chapter [Col. 0783A] 1, §4: ‘Abbot St. Bernard reconciled Peter of Pisa himself to Pope Innocent. After three days Peter Leonis died unrepentant.’ Falco of Benevento, cited by Baronius under the year 1134—or rather 1138—expressly records that he died on the seventh of January.” Thus, under the year 1137, p. 125, Falco says: “In this year Anacletus, who lived under the name of pontiff, died on the seventh day of the current month of January. He had sat for seven years, eleven months, and twenty-two days.”

288. But Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius* for the year of Christ 1138, no. 1, observes that Baronius and others wrongly assign Anacletus’s day of death, and postpones it on the following grounds:

“Falco, who begins the year from the Kalends of March, says under the year [Col. 0783B] 1137: ‘In this year Anacletus,’ etc. Baronius, no. 1; Mabillon, in the fuller notes on St. Bernard’s letter 126; Papebroch, in his *Chronological-Historical Essay*; and learned men elsewhere generally interpret the day mentioned by Falco as the seventh day of January. But Peregrini, in his notes on Falco, rightly explains Falco’s manner of speaking as referring to January at its end, and shows that a ‘standing,’ ‘approaching,’ or ‘present’ month is a month coming to its close. Du Cange subsequently demonstrated this with various examples in the *Glossary of Medieval and Later Latin*, under the entry *mensis stans* … Therefore Anacletus died on the twenty-fifth day of January, which is the seventh day counted from the last day of the same [Col. 0783C] month. From that last day Falco, and those who employed this mode of expression, reckon the first day of a given standing month. Ordericus, book XIII, p. 915, confirms Peregrini’s explanation, saying: ‘Peter Anacletus, who had usurped the apostolic see for nearly seven years, died suddenly while sitting in the chair on VIII Kalends of February’—that is, 25 January … Falco had defined the duration of his usurpation, which Ordericus gives in a round number and says was about seven years; but copyists corrupted the numbers,” etc.

From these chronological arguments of Pagi it follows that the death of Anacletus, the pseudo-pontiff, must be moved from 7 January, as others maintain, to 25 January. Accordingly, Peter of Pisa’s reconciliation with Innocent [Col. 0783D] II falls on the twenty-second day of that month, according to the statement drawn from St. Antoninus. One may also consult the note on another passage of Falco in the Milan edition mentioned above, p. 129.

289. Ernaldus narrates Anacletus’s disastrous death in book II of the *Life*, chapter 5, no. 137. St. Bernard likewise writes of it to Peter of Cluny in letter 147. But when the head of this schismatic faction had been cut off, another sprang up. Falco recounts the event on pp. 125–26, from which I select the following:

“When the aforesaid Anacletus had died, his cardinals … sent to King Roger, announcing Anacletus’s death and asking whether, if it pleased him, they should appoint a pope. The king therefore, in order to obstruct the cause of Pope Innocent, [Col. 0784A] assented to their will … Having returned to Rome and gathered their supporters, in the middle of March they established Cardinal Gregory as their pope and invader, and called him Victor. But with God’s mercy helping, that heresy and usurpation prevailed only a short time. For, after not many days had passed, the aforesaid brethren of Anacletus, recognizing so great a disturbance, came to themselves and, by the Lord’s favour, made a firm peace with the aforesaid Lord Pope Innocent. Both they and all his adversaries turned to his allegiance; and that wicked man who had appeared under the name of Victor laid aside his vestment and mitre and submitted himself to the will of Pope Innocent. Thus the whole Roman city rejoiced with great joy and exultant glory, [Col. 0784B] and Pope Innocent himself is brought into the unity of the Church …”—that is, he alone is recognized as pontiff of the Church.

So far Falco, who records the outcome of this most desired event, but not its cause, which must be ascribed to St. Bernard.

290. Ernaldus, no. 137, explains it as follows: “His party—that is, Anacletus’s—appointed another pope for themselves in his place, not so much out of persistence in schism as in order that, by a delay of some time, they might more conveniently be reconciled to Pope Innocent. Christ accomplished this without delay through the hand of His servant. For that ridiculous pontiff himself, Peter Leonis’s heir, came by night to that man of God; and he brought him, stripped of the insignia he had usurped, to the feet of Lord Innocent. When this was done, the city rejoices in gladness [Col. 0784C] … The abbot of Clairvaux is held in wonderful reverence; by all he is proclaimed the author of peace and father of his country,” etc.

A eulogy of St. Bernard’s merits, pronounced by Christ’s vicar on earth, who spoke from experience and expressly testified what that great man had contributed to the Church, to Peter’s see, and to his own pontificate, is found in the *Life of the Holy Father*, book III, chapter 2, no. 163.

291. What should I omit concerning the time and manner in which these things happened, and concerning the day on which the holy abbot left Rome? All these particulars are found in letter 317 of Mabillon’s edition, otherwise 320, sent by the Saint to his prior Geoffrey:

“On the Octave of Pentecost, on that very day, God fulfilled our desire by giving unity to the Church and peace to the City. For on that day all the sons of Peter Leonis together humbled themselves at the feet of the lord pope; and, becoming his liege men, they swore him liege fidelity. The clerics likewise who had been in schism together with the idol which they had set up—that is, Victor the antipope—humbled themselves at the feet of the lord pope, promised him obedience according to custom, and there was great rejoicing among the people. Had we not awaited this peace with a certain assurance, though it had long been concealed from us, we should have come long ago. Henceforth there is nothing to keep us here … Behold … I come quickly, and my reward is with me: Christ’s victory and the Church’s peace. On the Friday after that day one of our number left the city. Therefore we shall come, we shall come with exultation, [Col. 0785A] bearing sheaves of peace.”

Thus far the holy man. When, with his customary modesty of spirit, he says that “we awaited this peace with a certain assurance,” would I attribute too much to him if I said that he had known it beforehand, God revealing the matter to him? So that the word *ligius* may not delay anyone, Mabillon explains it in his notes on this letter, col. 296: “A *ligius* is one who, by reason of fief or subjection, is bound to render his lord complete fidelity against every person whatsoever.” Du Cange sets forth several writers’ opinions concerning the origin and etymology of *ligius* in the *Glossary of Medieval and Later Latin*.

292. Moreover, the cited letter of St. Bernard supplies material for two observations. The first concerns the month and day on which he left Rome; the other, whether Roger was among the “sheaves of peace” of which the holy Father wrote above. Roger was first duke of Sicily, then crowned king by the legate of the antipope Anacletus, and finally declared king by Innocent II.

Baronius, under the year 1138, no. 12, denies that Roger should be counted among these sheaves, saying: “Moreover, even after Anacletus’s extinction and Victor’s removal, Roger still refused to recognize Innocent as supreme pontiff.” Falco, p. 126, affirms the contrary; after relating the submission of the pseudo-pontiff Victor and his followers to Christ’s vicar Innocent II, he adds:

“After not many days had passed, the aforesaid Apostolic Lord, having taken counsel, came to Albano, intending, after gathering an army, to go [Col. 0785C] to Duke Rainulf; but, struck by illness, he could not go. Meanwhile King Roger, having gathered an army, came into the borders of Apulia, intending to subject to his authority the cities which the emperor had taken from him. Duke Rainulf, perceiving that king’s arrival, stirred up all the regions of Apulia so that they might stand unanimously against his fury. Without delay they hastened at full speed to the duke mentioned, and thus resisted the king’s ferocity for nearly two months. Meanwhile, as has been reported to us, the aforesaid king accepted Lord Pope Innocent as father and lord, and commanded the city of Benevento and all parts of his kingdom that he had accepted him as father and lord. [Col. 0785D] Having received his letters, we too called that man lord and father.”

Thus, according to the cited Falco, Roger is said at last to have been led from the obstinate error of schism into the right way. Whether this occurred through Bernard’s prayers, his words, or the example of the others just discussed who submitted themselves to the lawful pontiff, we willingly allow ourselves to be persuaded that this change belongs among the sheaves of peace so happily gathered by him in Italy. This is the first observation.

293. I had also proposed to speak of the second observation: namely, when our Saint left Rome. On the Octave of Pentecost itself, as we learn from the holy Doctor’s letter, the schismatics embraced the Church’s unity [Col. 0786A]. The octave day of Pentecost in 1138 fell on 29 May. The Friday after that day is assigned for his departure from the City, and that was 3 June. On that day, then, if no intervening impediment delayed the holy Father, he set out for his Clairvaux brethren.

At last that famous schism came to an end. It had been checked in its beginning by that great man, opposed during its course, and finally conquered; now, through his agency, it was uprooted completely. Yet, “having at last attained the Church’s desired peace,” to use Manrique’s words, no. 10, “after enduring the storm for seven years, he scarcely enjoyed five tranquil days. For he was born not for himself but for the common good: so that he might himself reap no fruit in life, he always produced fruit for another, being readier to sow than to gather, and reserving the whole harvest for others.”

Ernaldus, abbot of Bonneval, chapter 5, no. 138, expresses the matter thus: “The abbot of Clairvaux is held in wonderful reverence and is proclaimed by all the author of peace and father of his country … But how long did he endure glory? How long did he enjoy peace after so prolonged a labour? He did not consent to receive a day in exchange for a year. When all things had been calmed and settled, he could scarcely be kept for five days, though he had laboured for seven years and more to repair that very schism [Col. 0786B].”

294. But before we accompany the holy Father on his return to his own, certain matters remain to be mentioned which the author of the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 2, observes to have occurred at Rome before his departure.

First, he writes of Bernard’s fatherly concern for his Alpine sons when Garinus, abbot of the Alps, was promoted to the see of Sion and a new ruler of the monastery had to be chosen there. See St. Bernard’s letter 143, addressed to these same Alpine monks, with the following summary: “He commends the Alpine monks, who had associated themselves with the men of Clairvaux under the Cistercian Order, and consoles them for the absence of their Father, who had been raised to a higher rank. He then counsels them concerning the election of a new abbot.” In this monastery, as may be read in book I of the *Life of our Saint*, chapter 7, no. 73, a woman suffering from epilepsy was restored to health by him.

Next, the same annalist, no. 3, treats of Humbert, abbot of Igny [Col. 0786D], to whom there survives a letter from the holy man, numbered 141, in which “he sharply rebukes him for rashly and without consultation abandoning the office of prelate.”

Third, the same Manrique, no. 4, mentions the constrained election to the see of Langres and the complaints of those who elected. But what they did at Rome, what St. Bernard did, and what Pope Innocent did in this matter may be learned from Bernard’s letter to Innocent, numbered 164.

Fourth, the author mentioned adds at no. 6 that the holy man settled the dispute between the monks of Saint-Bertin and those of Cluny.

Fifth and finally, at no. 8, he describes Peter of Cluny’s exceptional reverence for St. Bernard. This brief account will suffice.

295. Furthermore, “as Father Bernard was about to leave the City,” as the aforesaid *Annals*, chapter 3, no. 1, relate, “Innocent honoured him with gifts suitable alike to the giver and recipient: not perishable gold or silver, nor things purchased with gold and silver, but the precious treasure of sacred bones, themselves attested even by a miracle and approving Innocent’s gift. Certainly, in the tooth of St. Caesarius the martyr, there occurred a remarkable thing which Geoffrey of Clairvaux narrates in the *Acts of Bernard* … book IV, chapter 1.”

For that tooth, which no force had previously been able to pull from the martyr’s head, was afterward removed by the holy abbot with incredible ease, after he had first offered prayer; or, so to speak, it obeyed the fingers of him who took it away. The cited biographer narrates this event more fully, and there likewise records that, through the tunic of this same St. Bernard, which remained with the Templars at Rome before his departure from the City, a certain priest among them, suffering from a most severe fever even to the point of despairing of life, was restored to his former health [Col. 0787B].

296. How great a longing for himself the holy man left behind at Rome when he departed may clearly be gathered by anyone from these words of Ernaldus the biographer, book II, chapter 5, no. 138:

“As he departed, Rome accompanied him; the clergy escorted him; the people came out to meet him; the entire nobility attended him. He could not be dismissed without common sorrow, for he was cherished with common love. They weep after him, ask him to bless them, and with every devotion commend themselves to his prayers [Col. 0787C].”

Then, “having received leave from Innocent, peace having been confirmed, the man of God returns; carrying home the greatest joy, he is devoutly received by the brethren with thanksgiving.”

But we shall meet the holy Father returning to his Clairvaux brethren with Ernaldus once we have first supplied his silence concerning several events which occurred on the journey undertaken to reach them, gathering them from other sources.

## § XXVIII. Affairs Conducted for the Church of Langres; Care for the Novices of Clairvaux; Continuation of the Sermons on the Song of Songs; Death of Blessed Gerard, His Full Brother; Geoffrey Advanced to the See of Langres; St. Hugh Helped in Spirit and Body; Journey to Dunes; Death of St. Malachy

[Col. 0787D] 297. Miracles were accustomed to accompany the holy man when he undertook journeys for the common good of the Church. Did he then perform none on his Italian journey when he was returning to Clairvaux? The Cistercian historian, under the year 1138, chapter 3, no. 3, identifies none with certainty; nevertheless, he believes Bernard made that journey not without miracles:

“The remainder of the journey, at least through Italy, has been omitted by the ancients. Nor should it be believed that it was completed without miracles, which, however, because they had become common and no longer astonishing, were almost reckoned among ordinary occurrences, lest they lose their value through frequency.”
