Let us therefore enter Gaul. When St. Bernard reached it, he found an opportunity to render the Church of Langres a service both fruitful and wholly necessary. For, after crossing the Alps, as the cited historian reports [Col. 0788A], no. 4, when he was already almost at Clairvaux’s gates, he was compelled to turn aside to Lyons in order to prevent the consecration of the bishop-elect of Langres.

For the people of Langres had named as their bishop—contrary to divine and human law, contrary to promises, and contrary to the command of Pope Innocent, despite the intervention of the son of the duke of Burgundy—a man who was a monk merely by profession, but degenerate in life and morals, and so infamous in reputation as to be disgraceful. The saint therefore first shuddered when this betrayal by such important persons reached his ears, especially by the metropolitan of Lyons; and he grieved for the fate of the Church dear to him, should what was reported prove true. Lest he allow her to be exposed to a wolf, he left his sons and addressed the fathers … But what was then done at Lyons, let us relate from the same letter which he wrote to Innocent and which we cited above.” It is letter 164, to which we refer the reader.

298. These matters having thus been arranged among the people of Lyons, the holy Father revisited his most beloved sons at Clairvaux. Carrying home the greatest joy, as we reported shortly before from Ernaldus, he was devoutly received by the brethren with thanksgiving; and words are unnecessary to express the affection with which this occurred.

The first concern occupying that fatherly heart was wholly directed toward the novices of his monastery at Clairvaux. For, immediately upon entering, he went without delay to their cell, according to the Cistercian historian, chapter 4, who commends the holy Father’s outstanding love for his sons from the following passage of the *Great Exordium*, found in Tissier, distinction 2, chapter 12:

“Therefore, when the entanglements of the causes for which he had gone out had been resolved, he returned to the monastery as soon as opportunity allowed. He entered the novices’ cell, so that the new and tender little sons whom he fed with milk might, the longer they had lacked the sweetness of his holy exhortation, be refreshed all the more abundantly from the breasts of his consolation … When, therefore, as we said above, he had entered the novices’ cell and, in his gracious and edifying speech, had made them all cheerful and more fervent in observing their holy purpose, he called one of them aside and said to him: ‘Dearest son, whence comes this sadness, which so ruinously consumes the inmost recesses of your heart?’

[Col. 0788D] 299. “The novice, however, scarcely daring through shame to say anything, was addressed by him who was truly meek and humble in heart, and who knew how to show himself to his sheep as a shepherd rather than a hireling: ‘I know, most beloved son, I know what is happening to you, and therefore I sympathize with you in a fatherly affection of compassion. During this long absence of mine, when I had been compelled to lack the bodily presence of my brethren, ever so dearly desired by me, the Lord’s grace granted me to make good spiritually what I could not do bodily. Returning in spirit, I went through each workshop, carefully examining how the brethren were faring; I also came to the novices’ cell. There I found all rejoicing in the fear of God and girded for the labours of repentance, but I saw you alone wasting away in excessive sadness, and I groaned. When I wished to bind you to myself by soothing words, you shrank from me; turning your face away from me, you wept most bitterly, so that our cowl was soaked with your tears.’

“Having said this, the holy Father addressed the captive with salutary admonitions, drove away his sorrow, and recalled one almost swallowed up by sadness to the freedom of spiritual joy.”

So it is related there. Yet from the preceding words—that “this faithful and prudent steward of the Lord’s provisions had at one time remained abroad longer than usual because of the Church’s affairs; for he was frequently compelled, though most unwillingly, to leave at the command of the supreme pontiff, in order to make peace, repair schism, and refute heresies” [Col. 0789B]—it is not sufficiently clear whether the event I have narrated, which Manrique connects with this stated return of St. Bernard to Clairvaux, really occurred then, or on another of several occasions. But whatever its date, the cited Manrique, no. 2, confirms the matter as follows:

“Geoffrey, the earlier author of the *Exordium*, who was Bernard’s confidential attendant during his lifetime and, after his death, also his successor in the abbacy, though not immediately so, left in writing in a sermon which he delivered about Bernard to the brethren in chapter that this consolation of the desolate novice was accomplished not only in words but also with a kiss.”

He then confirms the occurrence in these words: “‘Having said this,’ he says—that is, the holy Father—‘and bidding him come nearer, he kissed him with that most compassionate dignity of his.’” And shortly afterward, as he adds, “a twofold grace of holy lips—in the word of truth and in the kiss of charity—at once drove away the sadness [Col. 0789C].”

300. But to what sacred meditations did he devote himself, now returned to his own and again at home? After narrating his return, Ernaldus the abbot says in chapter 5; and the same biographer says in chapter 6: “The holy abbot, having returned to his studies, embraces his beloved bridal song.” The compiler of the *Cistercian Annals*, no. 3, affirms this too and explains it more distinctly:

“Then, resuming at the brethren’s request his interrupted work on the Song of Songs, he added the twenty-fourth sermon to the twenty-three he had already delivered, beginning from the point of interruption.”

Let the holy Father himself be heard in Sermon 24 on the Song of Songs, which he begins thus:

“This is now the third time, brethren, that our return from the City has been regarded by a more merciful eye from heaven and, at last, a calmer countenance from on high has smiled upon us. The Leonine rage has been stilled; malice has come to its end; the Church has received peace. The wicked man who had troubled her with a dreadful schism for almost eight years has been reduced to nothing in His sight. Have I then been restored to you freely after such great dangers? I have been granted to your desires and devote myself to your advancement. By your merits I live; I wish to live for your pursuits and your salvation. And since you desire me to continue what I long ago began on the Song of Songs, I gladly accept it and judge it fitting rather to repair the interrupted [Col. 0790A] discourse than to begin something new,” etc.

301. Two observations will serve to elucidate the beginning of this sermon. The first is drawn from Mabillon’s notes upon it. At col. 1346 he observes that there is a marked variation in the introductions from the opening of the sermon to the place he identifies there, and adds:

“From this variation arose great confusion in most printed editions, in which both introductions are given, but incorrectly. For the variation arose because Bernard delivered this same sermon twice: first, with the shorter introduction, in 1137, before departing for Rome for the third time; then, when he returned from there in 1138, he repeated it with the other introduction in order to resume the interrupted work with this final sermon. One royal manuscript, no. 4511, accordingly repeats the same sermon with a double introduction; likewise one manuscript formerly belonging to Thou and Colbert gives it once here with one introduction, and again after Sermon 60 with the other [Col. 0790B].”

302. The second observation is from the *Cistercian Annals*, no. 4: namely, that the holy Father indicates at the beginning of the same sermon that he had “now returned from the City for the third time.” The compiler of those *Annals* warns that this should be understood rather of the Curia than of Rome: “He had returned once from a place this side of the Alps and twice from beyond them; otherwise the sequence of the history itself has taught us that he had crossed the Alps only twice thus far. But we have more than once seen that the Curia, wherever it was located, was called Rome and the City. Thus when Bernard visited Innocent at Viterbo in the preceding year, he is nevertheless said to have been received by him at Rome.”

For further proof, Ernaldus is cited: “Saying this and blessing them all as they wept, he departed; received everywhere with great reverence, he finally arrived at Rome, at whose coming both the lord pope and the brethren rejoiced.”

Manrique proves his assertion by a similar example: “So too the venerable John and Ilbod are said to have gone to Rome and returned from there when Paschal II was at Troyes, and to have brought back a privilege from there; for the Curia was called Rome by reason of the See, even if it happened to be established elsewhere.” See the Cistercian *Little Exordium* in Tissier, chapter 10, and the *Cistercian Annals* under the year of Christ 1100, chapter 3 [Col. 0790D].

303. Under the often-mentioned year 1138, chapters 5 and 6, the writer of the same *Annals* gathers many varied matters concerning the precious death, in the sight of the Lord, of Blessed Gerard, St. Bernard’s full brother, and the events occasioned by it. Truly moving are the things which the holy man thought, said, and did at the death of his most beloved brother. One should certainly read the words which the mellifluous Doctor uttered in Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs, where, in a most sweet alternation and blending of sorrow, love, tears, and mourning, he continually interweaves these feelings and exalts Gerard with the fullest praises, invoking his aid as one already admitted to the fellowship of the heavenly beings [Col. 0791A]. We have treated of him under 13 June, in volume II for that month, p. 699.

The cited Manrique then continues in chapters 7 and 8 the cause of the Church of Langres which he had interrupted, and the renewed efforts of those who had broken faith. For what has already been set before us concerning it, read above; the cited author recounts the difficulties that subsequently occurred in the same controversy. But we shall offer from him a synopsis of the matters there related individually.

304. The bishop-elect of Langres therefore again endeavours to secure his consecration, while his patrons among the people of Langres employ fresh schemes for this purpose. On the side of that elected man, who was a monk of Cluny, stood the venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, like a father defending his son and setting his own authority against that of St. Bernard. He accuses Bernard of excessive credulity, while excusing the other from blame.

Why say more? He appeals to Louis, king of France; Bernard, meanwhile, appeals to Pope Innocent. Various measures are pursued on either side by the litigants in this matter, as may be seen in letter 164 sent by the Saint to the same pontiff. St. Bernard, however, pursued his cause with such steadfast and unconquered spirit, and pressed so vigorously against that bishop-elect and man unworthy of the mitre—or rather against the abuses connected with him—that no entreaties could move him from his purpose.

Peter of Cluny also addressed letters to Innocent, which Manrique gives in chapter 7, no. 7, and likewise to St. Bernard, which may be read there at no. 8 and following. After this, in chapter 8, the same historian proceeds to discuss the attempted consecration of the bishop-elect of Langres. He says that its execution could not be prevented by Bernard’s one letter to the supreme pontiff, numbered 167, nor by the other addressed to the cardinals, numbered 168, which he quotes. Yet the holy man, always most tenacious of a purpose once conceived for justice and the common good, left nothing untried to secure a happy outcome to this controversy.

305. In letter 165 he praises and encourages the supporters and defenders of the good cause; in letter 166 he again appeals to Pope Innocent. After so many labours he obtains the result that the acts done in favour of the man wholly unworthy of the see of Langres are annulled and abolished [Col. 0791D]. For the consecrated man is removed from the episcopal throne; a new election is instituted; and a new bishop is appointed.

First, as Manrique writes near the end of chapter 8, “Father Bernard was chosen, whom even the defeated party most ardently desired. But when he absolutely refused the burden, although several other suitable persons were proposed, beyond expectation and every intention, one Geoffrey, prior of Clairvaux, appeared before all: truly a great man, whom all wished for, whom all requested, and from whom none at all dissented.”

So he says in chapter 9, adding the king’s hostility toward the new election, Bernard’s letter to him, numbered 170, and Peter of Cluny’s steadfast love for the holy Father. Peter, says the aforesaid annalist, no. 6, “having found the king compliant in all things, at last sorrowfully tore Geoffrey away from himself,” and immediately praises Geoffrey [Col. 0792A].

This controversy of Langres is also discussed in volume IV of the latest edition of *Gallia Christiana*, beginning at col. 575. A collection of Geoffrey’s acts is given there beginning at col. 577, where it is said that “his election obtained its full effect only in the year 1139.” William, book I of the *Life of St. Bernard*, chapter 6, no. 51, calls him “the holy man’s kinsman by blood, his companion in conversion, and from that time his inseparable companion in all things.” Ernaldus, in the same *Life*, book II, chapter 3, no. 114, says: “Geoffrey the prior was present … his kinsman in flesh and spirit, a wise and steadfast man … preserving the form of holiness,” etc.

Such was the end of the very serious difficulties and disputes in the affair of Langres. The holy man, accustomed elsewhere to conquer by the highest steadfastness and unwearied labour, won a distinguished palm for justice by placing upon them a triumphant conclusion beneficial to the Church of Langres. But now let us continue to gather other deeds of the most holy abbot.

306. Among the matters related by the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 10, concerning Hugh, who had embraced the monastic way of life of the Cistercian Order, belongs the holy Father’s letter to him, formerly numbered 351 and now 322 in Mabillon, in which he “praises his resolve to lead a religious life, fortifies him against temptations, and urges him to constancy and perseverance.” We treated St. Hugh long ago under 1 April, beginning at p. 46, as also of his life and public cult [Col. 0792C]. Chalemot likewise announces and praises him in his list of saints, etc., of the Cistercian Order under 16 March.

Nor shall I depart from my purpose if, together with Manrique, no. 7 of the chapter just cited, I relate “how he was healed by Father Bernard through medicine and skill combined with miracle, although it is clear that this does not concern the present year, since no other certain year is specified,” etc. Vincent of Beauvais relates the event in book XXIX of the *Historical Mirror*, chapter 33:

“After this he began to afflict himself by excessive fasts, so that he seemed almost to be losing his senses and memory. Meanwhile St. Bernard, who was then living, came to him by God’s providence and ordered him to be sent to the infirmary, and that vigils should be sung for him each night before they were sung for the other sick, so that afterward he might have general permission to speak wherever he wished. And thus, through God’s mercy, he recovered in a short time [Col. 0792D].”

307. The Cistercian historian, chapter 13, no. 8, investigates whether St Bernard visited the Dunes. First he cites Aegidius de Roca—rather, de Roya—who, in the Belgian Annals under the year 1138, affirms it in these words: “Blessed Bernard came into Flanders, established Robert as abbot at Dunes, and obtained from Count Theodoric privileges for the monks of Dunes, namely, as much land as they could cultivate with their own ploughs,” etc. To this author the same historian adds Meyer, who, in Book V of the Annals of Flanders, under the year [Col. 0793A] 1138, left the following note:

> “In the same year Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, came into Flanders to preach, where by holy sermons and salutary examples he led very many to a devout and blessed life. Among them was one Arnulph, surnamed of Majorca, who guarded Bernard’s teaching with such earnestness, and endured long and severe illnesses before his death with such patience, that Bernard often gave thanks to God for his conversion and steadfastness, saying that he had been tested like gold in the furnace. At Furnes, moreover, while he was preaching the word of God, he gave the monks of Dunes the Cistercian observance, and made there his own monk Robert—whose letters still survive, a native of Bruges by country and birth—abbot; and Robert flourished in such renowned holiness that, when Bernard himself was already near death, he was chosen abbot of Clairvaux.”

308. Yet Manrique does not accept that coming of the holy Father. In the passage just cited he writes:

> “As I regard his arrival in this year as doubtful, so I ought not—indeed could not—pass over what weighty authorities have recorded. But I judge it more likely that he remained at Clairvaux, weary of his long exile, and that he entrusted nothing, however difficult, to anyone other than Robert.”

But these two arguments do not seem very weighty. Not the first, which is drawn from weariness: for that strong man was not deterred by so many other hardships, undertaken with tireless labour for the common good; why, then, by this one? Nor the second: for although he placed great confidence in Robert’s merits, what prevented him from manfully swallowing the inconveniences of this journey, so as to establish the beginnings of that new foundation with greater solemnity and security? Although we do not know whether he had particular reasons that summoned him there, and therefore cannot affirm it with certainty, neither can we certainly deny that he had them—especially since, besides the authors cited, others have committed his arrival in Flanders to memory, and more distinctly than the two previous writers whose words we have given.

For our Malbrancq, volume III of *De Morinis*, Book X, chapter 3, p. 188, speaks thus:

> “Moreover, Lord Bernard came into Flanders and cultivated the district of Iseræ, or the territory of Furnes, by his salutary sermons; and in cultivating it he turned aside to Fulco’s company, and filled it so with the fragrance of his spikenard that Fulco and all his disciples did not hesitate to subject themselves and all that they possessed to Bernard’s rule—even those who lived by the castle and wood of Ruholt. The same disposition likewise possessed Count Theodoric and Countess Sibylla, who had as yet settled nothing, whether concerning revenues or a permanent structure . . . Therefore Bernard did indeed approve the gift offered . . . . . but he considered that the men of Clairvaux must take the lead, and that the matter should there be dealt with more maturely.”

So Malbrancq, assigning Bernard’s arrival among the Morini, in the chronological index prefixed to that volume, to the year of Christ 1137—an opinion we reject. Indeed, he seems there to speak inconsistently, because he says that this arrival occurred after the schism had been overcome; but the famous schism which Bernard extinguished ended in the year of Christ 1138.

309. Anthony Sander, in *Flanders Illustrated*, Book IV, *The Affairs of Bruges*, chapter 1, p. 248, writes the following concerning the aforesaid Robert, relevant to our purpose; we transcribe it here on his authority:

> “In his time Blessed Bernard came into Flanders, and at Furnes delivered a honeyed sermon to the Canons of St Walburga on the Nones of April [5 April], in the year 1138. Near the monastery of Dunes there was then a chapel sacred to St Lawrence, in which he himself offered the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass. On that account it was held in the highest veneration almost down to our own times; but it has been utterly destroyed by the fury of the recent war.”

The Reverend Lord Charles de Visch, prior of the monastery of Blessed Mary at Dunes, in his *Library of Writers of the Sacred Cistercian Order*, under the name Robert of Bruges, affirms that Robert was “stirred up by the preaching and holy conduct of the divine Bernard when he visited Flanders,” etc. Let the reader compare these many testimonies already produced with Manrique’s small doubt, and see whether, in this controversy, it is more probable to stand by that doubt alone or by those testimonies. For matters concerning the abbey of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Dunes, formerly in the district of Furnes but later transferred to the city of Bruges, the above-mentioned Sander may be consulted from p. 246 onward. Thus far concerning the saint’s deeds in 1138.

[Col. 0794C] 310. In the following year, 1139, Manrique inserts much concerning St Malachy, archbishop in Ireland, a most celebrated and apostolic man there, who also embraced the observance of Clairvaux and whose Life St Bernard wrote. The Roman Martyrology records his annual commemoration on 3 November. Meanwhile, let us undertake the narration of other deeds of St Bernard, for whose accomplishment divine providence chose him in a singular manner and distinguished him with the highest splendour while he performed them most honourably.

## § XXIX. Peter Abelard: his talent and character; his errors rightly attacked by St Bernard; Bernard’s remarkable encounter with him; Arnold of Brescia, Abelard’s disciple

[Col. 0794D] 311. The year of Christ 1140, memorable for errors attacked and overcome by St Bernard, supplied great praise for the victor, notable benefit for the Church, and abundant material for writers. Let Peter Abelard, or Abailard, first enter the scene: that notorious wanderer from the right path, brought back to better ways by the work and skill of the same saint. The collection I propose concerning this affair will contribute to a fuller explanation of the Life of our holy doctor, continued by Geoffrey, Book III, chapter 2, no. 164, where he speaks as follows:

> “There was in those days Peter Abelard, an eminent master and most famous for his reputation for learning, but teaching perfidious doctrine concerning the faith. When writings of his, full of most grievous blasphemies, began to fly about everywhere, learned and faithful men reported to the man of God these profane novelties of words and meanings.”

Let us first consider Peter himself, presenting an image of his studies, intellect, and character. Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius*, under the year of Christ 1113, no. 13, says:

> “At this time there flourished in France Peter Abelard of Nantes, who composed the history of his misfortunes in his first letter written to a friend. Born for literary study, as he himself asserts, he learned it easily, especially dialectic; eager to learn this, he travelled through various provinces disputing. He came to Paris to William of Champeaux, then pre-eminent in this teaching both in fact and reputation. William at first received him favourably, but afterward found him most troublesome, because he refuted some of his opinions; and, while still a youth, presuming excessively upon his own ability, he opened schools at Melun, a few leagues from Paris, and at Champeaux, the village where William was born.”

But let us hear Abelard himself, in Letter 1, chapter 2:

> “From this beginning of our schools, my name began so to spread in the art of dialectic that not only the reputation of my fellow students, but even that of the master himself, gradually waned and was extinguished.”

312. “From this it came about that, having a higher opinion of myself, I transferred our schools as soon as possible to the castle of Corbeil, which is nearer to the city of Paris, so that our importunity [variant: ‘opportunity’] might from there give more frequent assaults in disputation.”” Thus he. Let us continue with Pagi:

> “Meanwhile William of Champeaux, in the current year, as Alberic teaches in his *Chronicle*, was made bishop of Châlons; yet he did not abandon his customary pursuit of teaching philosophy. Abelard came from Corbeil to Paris to his school. But since he again proved most troublesome to his master, he himself devoted himself to teaching dialectic, and after some time returned to Melun and reopened his school there. At last he lectured on Holy Scripture at Paris; and Peter Lombard, afterward bishop of Paris, used his theology in composing the *Sentences*, as John of Cornwall, Lombard’s own pupil, relates in his *Eulogy* to Pope Alexander III.”

Here, reader, you have something concerning Abelard’s talent and studies. Now learn concerning his character—or rather his love-affairs—from Pagi, who continues thus in no. 14.

313. “Fulbert, a canon of the cathedral church of Paris, asked him to instruct in spare hours his niece Héloïse, a noble maiden, outstanding in beauty and still more outstanding in learning; later famous throughout all France for her education, exceptional gifts of mind, and mastery of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages. He was to teach her not only languages but also philosophy and the other liberal arts. But Abelard, ensnared by love for her, ensnared her too by his own love; and she conceived by him a son named Astrolabe. He wished to mitigate that crime by an honourable marriage, with Fulbert’s consent. Meanwhile, while he attended to his schools, he placed Héloïse in seclusion among the nuns of Argenteuil, warning her nevertheless not to take the veil. But Fulbert and Héloïse’s relatives, believing that he had deceived them, cruelly mutilated him in the part in which he had sinned and made him a eunuch. Thereupon, overwhelmed with shame, he took the monastic habit in the monastery of St Denis near Paris. She, however, received the veil from the bishop in the monastery of Argenteuil near Paris, where she later became prioress and abbess.”

314. Then, in no. 15, after inserting some remarks concerning the fame of Abelard’s school—since Adam, abbot of St Denis, permitted him to teach at the request of others—and also concerning the filthiness then prevailing among the ascetics of that abbey, as reported by Abelard himself, whom he says that “I frequently and vehemently rebuked, sometimes privately and sometimes publicly, and thus made myself excessively burdensome and hateful to them all. Delighted especially by the daily insistence of our pupils, they found an opportunity to remove me from among them”—after these insertions, I say, Pagi adds:

> “But while the hatred of great and small alike burns against him, he indulges his own intellect too much and despises others; and as his hand is against all, so the hands of all are armed against him. He is charged with various errors, as we shall see when speaking of the Council of Soissons in 1121 and that of Sens in 1140. We had to treat these matters somewhat more fully because his Works were not brought out of obscurity and illustrated with notes by André Duchesne until after Baronius’s death, in the year 1616. See what we shall say under the year 1166 concerning Goswin, abbot of Anchin.”

Thus far Pagi. We have both transcribed the foregoing and will add more below, in order to supplement and elucidate the brevity of Geoffrey the biographer. From his words concerning Abelard’s errors—or, to use Geoffrey’s term, blasphemies—it seemed proper to gather what follows. Yet, to avoid quibbling, I do not dispute concerning the intention of Abelard’s mind, but concerning the meaning which the writer’s words themselves present.

315. Let us therefore consider secondly in what respects Abelard taught perfidiously concerning the faith, as Geoffrey said. The works of this author were published by Francis Ambrose in Paris in 1616, together with an apologetic Preface for the writer. In it he adduces seventeen chapters which “the great Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, is said to have sent to Pope Innocent II, found, if one may believe it, partly in the book of *Theology*, partly in the book of *Sentences*, partly in the book entitled *Know Yourself*; the last two books Abelard denied were written by him. Of these detestable errors anyone may say: ‘Alas, can so great a crime fall upon anyone?’” After this preface he gives those chapters, which were afterwards transcribed by Manrique under the year 1140, chapter 4. Then the author of the apology sounds the trumpet against St Bernard and others in this controversy, on Abelard’s behalf. But this is not the place to examine or refute that apology at length. Below I shall speak for St Bernard and likewise against Abelard, as much as our purpose requires.

316. As to Abelard’s errors, there survives the saint’s celebrated 190th letter, entitled: “To Pope Innocent concerning certain errors of Peter Abelard.” Yet in Mabillon’s edition it is placed among the holy doctor’s Treatises, Treatise 11, from col. 643, with Mabillon’s prefatory Admonition from p. 635. At the end of that Admonition he says:

> “After I had written this, our Jean Durand, who was then at Rome, sent me from a faulty Vatican manuscript, no. 663, the *Articles of the Heresies of Peter Abelard*, prefixed to the following letter—undoubtedly the very articles which Bernard says at the end of this letter that he had collected and sent to the pope. Therefore it seemed fitting to place them here before the letter, for the elucidation of the letter itself.”

Mabillon gives this warning; but we refer the reader both to those articles and to the letter itself. Meanwhile, in defence of the justice of St Bernard’s cause, some further observations should be made concerning Peter Abelard’s errors from the material Mabillon has learnedly gathered on this subject.

317. In his general Preface to the new edition of the Works of St Bernard, no. 53, Mabillon observes:

> “First, it may be noted that, long before Abelard had any dealings with Bernard, he was summoned by Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, to the Council of Soissons held in 1121. There his book *On Theology*, containing erroneous propositions, was given to the flames, and its author was confined in the monastery of St Medard. After leaving it, he continued, in various wanderings here and there, to disseminate his earlier doctrines. Hence he was called a heretic by many. Bearing this name with indignation, he dragged Bernard—whom he believed to be the author of this reproach—unwilling and reluctant, to the Council of Sens in 1140. There Abelard was again heard before bishops and other distinguished men of the second rank, and refuted by Bernard; his doctrine was examined and again condemned, while he himself remained untouched, appealing to the Apostolic See. But when he learned that the sentence of the synod had been approved by Innocent II, he abandoned the appeal. At the urging of Peter the Venerable he withdrew to the monastery of Cluny, and finally rested in a praiseworthy end at the monastery of St Marcellus near Chalon.”

These facts, traced somewhat further back, sufficiently show the erroneous character of his doctrines concerning the faith. Moreover, while writing abusively against Bernard and raising his horns, he brings his perverse doctrine into clear light, as can be seen in Mabillon’s prefatory Admonition just mentioned. “We mention this,” he says in col. 637, “so that all may at last understand how impiously Abelard, if not in thought, at least in writing, treated both the Incarnation and the grace of Christ; and how justly Bernard said in Letter 192: ‘When he speaks of the Trinity, he savours of Arius; when of grace, he savours of Pelagius; when of Christ’s person, he savours of Nestorius.’”

318. A little below, Mabillon rightly repeats:

> “We mention these things, I say, so that those who detest these errors may be ashamed to take up Abelard’s cause against Bernard, whom they do not hesitate further to accuse of rash judgment against Abelard and excessive heat. In almost the same fashion William of Conches explains the mystery of the Trinity; his errors likewise are refuted by William, abbot of St Thierry, in a letter to Bernard. Nothing can be more disastrous for religion than when philosophers attempt to explain the mysteries of our faith by reason alone.”

Soon afterward the same author treats the whole Abelard affair from a letter of Geoffrey, notary of St Bernard, to Henry, cardinal and bishop of Albano. The words of that letter may be read both there and in Duchesne’s notes on Abelard cited in the same place. I omit what is narrated in volume XII of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 478 and following, concerning a vision of Henry, canon of Tournai, reported to the Fathers of the Synod of Sens and to Bernard.

319. To make still clearer the justice of the cause and the prudence of our most wise doctor in pursuing Abelard’s errors with such ardent zeal—although what we have already set forth would be more than enough—we add a few points concerning his defenders. “First,” says Mabillon in his general Preface, no. 55, “Abelard himself is brought forward. In his *Apology* he complains that certain things had maliciously been imputed to him, above all that ‘the Father is full power, the Son some power, and the Holy Spirit no power’—words which he says are not so much heretical as devilish in their abhorrence, and which he affirms cannot be found in his writings. But concerning this and the other propositions, see the observations on Bernard’s Treatise 11. Meanwhile, in the same *Apology*, Abelard admits that through error he wrote some things which he ought not to have written, but adds that he did nothing through malice or pride; and he declares that, if he has exceeded through excessive speech, he is always prepared to make satisfaction by correcting or deleting his own ill-considered words, and finally that, as a son of the Church, he receives all that the Church receives and rejects what it rejects. Good. We do not wish Abelard to be a heretic. It is enough for Bernard’s cause that he erred in certain matters, which Abelard himself does not deny.”

320. “What then does Otto of Freising, Book I, chapter 47, bring against the holy doctor, or in support of Abelard? He says, no doubt, that Bernard was zealous from the fervour of Christian religion and credulous from habitual gentleness, so that he abhorred masters who clung too confidently and excessively to human arguments and secular wisdom, and readily listened whenever anything discordant with Christian faith was said to him about such men. Yet these very things redound to the holy doctor’s glory. For nothing belongs more to a Catholic doctor than to check at once such persons, who attribute more than is right to philosophical subtleties—especially when they coin new terms capable of leading the unwary into error. Moreover, to speak with William in Book I of the *Life*, no. 41: ‘If an excess of holy fervour is reproved in him, that excess surely has its own reverence among devout minds . . . Happy he whose only fault is judged to be what others commonly presume upon as glory.’ Yet Otto himself, however favourably disposed to Abelard, admits that Abelard excessively diminished the three persons of the most holy Trinity, used unsuitable illustrations, and on that account was JUDGED A SABELLIAN HERETIC at Soissons in a provincial synod. What wonder, then, if, when he again repeated the same doctrines, he was ill-spoken-of among lovers of sound faith?”

[Col. 0799B] 321. “As for Berengar of Poitiers, who wrote an *Apology* for Abelard, his teacher, against the Synod of Sens and Bernard, we need not concern ourselves greatly with him: both because he was a man of no account and of no authority, and because, having returned to a sounder mind, he no longer wished to be the defender of the propositions charged against Abelard. For although they might have had a sound meaning, they did not sound sound. He would have suppressed his book if he could, as he himself testifies in a letter to the bishop of Mende. Furthermore, although we no longer possess all Abelard’s works in which he scattered his errors, nevertheless among those that remain there are many THORNY PASSAGES, as the Parisian theologians noted, who placed A PROTECTIVE CHARM AGAINST EACH OF THE MORE DANGEROUS SAYINGS at the beginning of his works. Among these one could indeed wish that the apologetic Preface were erased.”

Thus Mabillon speaks forcefully for St Bernard, but modestly and learnedly, as was his custom, against Abelard and his defenders.

322. Moreover, he defends the holy doctor’s cause splendidly in his notes to Bernard’s Letter 187. After an outline of Abelard’s life and a letter of Pope Innocent against Abelard and Arnold of Brescia, whom he commands, as “fabricators of perverse doctrine and assailants of the Catholic faith,” to be separately confined “in religious places,” and their books of error “burned by fire,” he answers the objections made against Bernard and for Peter Abelard. Here is a synopsis of the matter. First he answers the objection against the holy doctor drawn from Otto of Freising; then the testimony of Peter the Venerable for Abelard; then the devices intended to undermine the authority of the Synod of Sens; and finally the arguments advanced against the Roman pontiff in Abelard’s case. These matters are there developed more fully. The affair of St Bernard against Abelard, discussed here so far, is likewise woven into the *Cistercian Annals* under the year of Christ 1140, chapter 2 and following. These are the points which seemed worth adducing concerning the present controversy. From them it follows that Peter Abelard, transformed from a keen dialectician into an ill-employed theologian, wrote erroneous doctrines in matters of orthodox faith and was convicted of them; consequently, his supporters and defenders are patrons of a bad and hopeless case. Bernard’s authority, on the other hand, remains intact: he deserved exceedingly well of the common good and triumphed over the errors of that scribbler, who even today smells so foul among thoroughly Catholic men that Abailard is listed among the authors proscribed in the first class in the *Index of Books Prohibited by the Holy See*, p. 390 of the Roman edition of 1711. After the two preceding points—one concerning Abelard’s character and life, the other concerning his doctrinal errors—both expanded in aid of Geoffrey the biographer, whose account we are illustrating, let us add another.

323. Let us therefore consider thirdly a circumstance which occurred in the saint’s encounter with Peter before the Fathers of the Synod of Sens. For the event itself, the same biographer may be consulted. He reports this circumstance concerning Abelard in Book III, chapter 2, no. 165:

> “For afterward he confessed to his own people, as they say, that at that hour his memory had for the most part been disturbed, his reasoning darkened, and his inward understanding had fled.”

Who can deny that this altogether remarkable event, both in regard to Abelard and in regard to Bernard, occurred by God’s singular providence—God deposing from the throne of reason one who was mighty in his own eyes through talent and eloquence, and exalting the humble Bernard? The annalist of Clairvaux explains the matter under the year of Christ 1140, chapter 3, nos. 1 and 2:

> “The holy Father declined the battle and altogether refused the contest, not claiming equality in a duel with the master: a rustic before the philosopher, reared among beeches and oaks before the most practised professor of the schools. What had he to do with scholastic questions? What with subtle disputations? What with ingenious arguments? How, in such matters, could a poor monk have achieved anything, when the cause of faith and the Church was entrusted to him? There were masters of distinguished name in the Church itself; there were also Hugh and Richard, the Victorines, in the Parisian academy, to whom the task could more safely be committed. He would advance the Catholic cause as much as he could by prayers, since prayer is more familiar to a monk than disputation. By these and similar words—more humble because wiser—he did not refuse himself to the Church, but refused glory to himself. Yet when the wishes of all had turned toward him and all demanded Bernard alone for the battle, lest not so much his own presumption as the defence of Christ’s cause should seem wanting, he at last consented, to receive from God himself what he should render to Him.”

Thus Manrique. Relevant here is Bernard’s Letter 187, addressed “to the bishops to be summoned at Sens against Peter Abelard.”

324. In this, moreover, was the marvel: “that at that same hour,” as Manrique adds in nos. 5 and 6, “a man of many words and of the easiest and readiest flow lost both talent and memory to such a degree, and lost words to such a degree, that he remembered absolutely nothing ever said or written by himself—neither the subject matter nor the terms of things. . . . Thus divine providence brought it about that he who had arrived trusting in his own strength and glorying in the multitude of his subtleties departed confused, carrying away shame and disgrace instead of the victory which he had long before foretold.”

325. Abelard’s disciple, follower, and advocate was Arnald—or Arnold, or Arnolph—of Brescia, of whom we have spoken briefly above and shall speak more fully later. In Letters 195 and 196 the holy doctor vividly depicts the perverse doctrines and destructive effects of this deceitful flatterer and heretic. Relevant here are Bernard’s words about him, inserted in the same Letter 195:

> “You will see a man openly rising against the clergy, relying on military tyranny, rising against the bishops themselves and raging indiscriminately against every ecclesiastical order.”

Baronius, under the year 1140, no. 3, says: “This occurred when, after Innocent’s death, he made his way to Rome under Pope Eugenius”; and thus he judges these words, among others, to have been written prophetically by the saint. Below, when we discuss this pope’s elevation to the See of Peter, we shall present a vivid picture of this most impious profaner of ecclesiastical hierarchy, so that the reader may know how exactly St Bernard’s prophecy was later fulfilled, and how wisely he had beforehand exposed and disclosed this heretic’s pestilential poison for the common good.

## § XXX. The saint wins a cleric by dice; gives another man money with which to gamble for himself; rescues a criminal from death and makes him a monk; he patiently bears an injury; the death of his sister Humbelina; he defends the oppressed; his acts in the conflict of priesthood and kingship

326. The year of Christ 1141 follows. We shall find the holy abbot transferred from external affairs to domestic ones, and contemplate him intent upon the concerns of Clairvaux. “The community being depleted,” as the *Cistercian Annals* state under the same year, chapter 3, no. 1, “Bernard year after year supplied more and more men for new monastic foundations: some converted by preaching; others, who resisted through their own vices, were drawn by miracles.” An example is the famous gambling—or deceiving—cleric, who, while he takes a horse, is himself caught by the saint in an agreeable and wonderful manner. The story is there described from Caesarius of Heisterbach, cited in Homily 5 for the Third Sunday after Pentecost, in these words:

> “When the holy Father was one day riding along the road, wandering clerics, whom they call *everandini*, met him. He urged them to conversion. One said to him: ‘I will play dice with you. If fortune favours me, give me your horse; if it favours you, I shall follow you into the monastery.’ The saint replied, ‘Let the will of the Lord be done.’ Immediately the man drew out loaded dice and threw eighteen points. The monks were troubled and did not understand God’s design. But the blessed man, placing hope in Christ, picked up the dice for the man’s salvation and cast them. And behold: twelve pips appeared on two dice, while the third, divided into two halves, showed six pips on one side and five on the other. Terrified at the sight, the cleric followed the man of God to Clairvaux and became a proven monk. This event remains very famous to this day in the schools of the Parisian masters.”

This is from Caesarius, who flourished in the thirteenth century.

327. In a similar manner, so to speak, divine providence played through St Bernard when he brought back to his former manner of life, by means of gambling, another man who was weary of the religious order and ready to renounce it. Manrique, no. 2, reports the fact from Vincent of Beauvais, whom he cites as recording the following in Part IV, Distinction 13, of the *Mirror of Morals*:

> “We read in the Life of St Bernard that he had received as a monk a certain man who had been a gambler. When the man wished altogether to leave the order, the saint asked what he knew how to do by which he might gain his living. He replied that he knew how to do nothing except gamble with such-and-such a game. St Bernard said to him: ‘If I entrust you with capital, I want you to come every year to render an account to me and divide the profit.’ ‘So be it,’ he said; and, receiving thirty shillings, went away gladly. After a short time he lost it and returned in shame to the gate. When blessed Bernard heard this, he went there gladly and spread out his lap so that they might divide the profit together. But the man said: ‘I have gained nothing, but have lost your shillings. Yet if you are willing to receive me, you may have me as your capital.’ The saint said to him: ‘It is better that I receive you than lose everything at once.’ And he received him, rejoicing at his recovery.”

328. Furthermore, learn from the following story how the holy man delivered a wicked man, condemned to death, from both evils and brought him to the finest fruit. It occurs in the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, in Tissier, Distinction 2, chapter 15; Manrique indicates in no. 3 that it happened about this same time. Hear the event:

> “It happened once that the same servant of God went to Count Theobald on certain business. As he approached the town where the count then was, he encountered a large crowd of people who, by the count’s command, were dragging a notorious and criminal robber to execution. Seeing this, the most merciful Father seized in his own hand the rope by which the wretch was bound and said to his executioners: ‘Give this murderer to me; for I wish to hang him with my own hands.’ When the count heard of the man of God’s arrival, he immediately hurried out to meet him. For he always loved and honoured him with a wonderful devotion. When he saw the rope in Bernard’s hand, by which he was drawing the robber behind him, he was greatly horrified and said: ‘Alas, venerable Father, what is this that you have wished to do? Why have you recalled this gallows-bird, condemned a thousand times over, from the gate of hell? Can you save him, since he has already become wholly a devil [variant: wholly the devil’s]? His correction [variant: amendment] is altogether hopeless; nor can he ever do good except by dying. Therefore, lord Father, let this lost man of perdition go to destruction, for through his pestilential life the lives of many are endangered.’”

329. “The holy Father answered: ‘I know, most excellent man, I know that he is a most wicked robber and deserving of the most severe bitterness of every torment. Do not therefore suppose that I wish to leave such a sinner unpunished. Rather, I intend to hand him over to executioners and take worthy vengeance upon him; and it will certainly be the worthier in proportion as it is longer-lasting. You had decreed that he should be brought to an end by a brief punishment and momentary death; but I shall make him die by prolonged torment and a most lingering death. You would permit the thief, once hanged, to remain dead on the gibbet for one day or several; I shall make him, nailed to the cross, live and hang continually in punishment for many years.’ On hearing this, the most Christian prince was silent and did not dare further to contradict the saint’s words. Immediately, therefore, the most kindly Father stripped off his own tunic and clothed his captive in it; having cut off the hair of his head, he joined him to the Lord’s flock, making a lamb from a wolf and a convert from a robber. Coming with him to Clairvaux, he thereafter became obedient until death, beautifully expressing in the constancy of his resolve the etymology of his name: for he was called Constantius. Having thus survived in the Order for thirty years, if I am not mistaken, or more, he departed to the Lord, who through the merits of our most blessed Father deigned mercifully to rescue him from a double death, namely that of body and soul.’”

Thus the author of the *Exordium*. Concerning the aforementioned Theobald, count of Champagne, the *Cistercian Annals* treat in various places; their index may be consulted, as may Ernald, the biographer, Book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 6, and Geoffrey, Book IV, chapter 2.

[Col. 0803C] 330. The compiler of the same *Annals*, after these three deeds which we have just related, adds under no. 6 one of another kind: namely, “the execrable crime of a certain regular cleric, who struck the holy abbot a blow; and, in retaliation for the rebuff, proved the judgment of him who repelled him and exalted his patience—a patience which princes and kings revered, though his face had been dishonoured by a sacrilegious hand and smitten not merely with redness and pain, but with swelling.” See Geoffrey, book III, chapter 3, where this matter is narrated more fully. The aforesaid Manrique observes at the end of chapter 3 that, since no certain year was attached to each of the matters he had related, he had gathered them together into one place; and, following his example, we judged that we ought to do the same.

The same author writes in chapter 4 of the most pious death of Humbelina, the blood sister of St Bernard, who both there and elsewhere is called by the title of saint; but for our part she seems hitherto to be ranked only among the venerable, until her public cult is established. Manrique accordingly records that the holy Father was present with her during her illness until her death; he then recounts their mutual conversations and Bernard’s recall—he had left her for a while—through the agency of an angel striking the board. But, he says, no. 8, this body “is reported to have been committed to holy burial, Bernard celebrating the funeral office and amid these things rejoicing and weeping; yet joy prevailed, especially when she appeared to him in glory, congratulating him on the reward which she had merited at his exhortation.” Thus he.

331. But we have something bearing against the chronology to which the same historian assigns the death of the venerable Humbelina, who elsewhere is called Humberga. In our volume IV for June, on the 23rd day, beginning at page 608, there was published the *Life of St Peter the Monk*, prior of Jully near Molesme in Champagne, Gaul. In chapter 3 of Peter’s Life it is said that an angel informed him that Humberga would shortly die. Our Peter Francis Chifflet had previously brought this Life out of obscurity and published it in print in his treatise *On the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux*, beginning at page 134. In the observation which he gives concerning the year and day of the death of the aforesaid prior of Jully, pages 155 and following, he determines that he departed this life in the year of Christ 1136.

“Whence it is evident,” as he says from page 156, “that Angelus Manrique went far astray in the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year of Christ [Col. 0804B] 1141, chapter 4, no. 1, where he says that Humbelina, St Bernard’s sister, was still alive in 1140 and not long after piously fell asleep in the Lord in 1141. For if Prior Peter, who was present at her death, died in June of 1136, how was she still among the living in the fifth year thereafter?” It is enough here briefly to indicate this from him; it is developed there at greater length. Chifflet’s observation also tells against Baillet, who, under 21 August in the Life of Humbelina which he published, places her death in the year 4141 [clearly an OCR error, probably 1141]; and likewise against another Frenchman in the *Life of St Bernard* published at Paris in 1704, book IV, page 350.

332. The Cistercian historian committed some other matters concerning St Bernard to writing under the said year 1141, chapter 5. “At the same time,” he says in no. 1, “the venerable Guido, abbot of Charolles in the diocese of Besançon, being oppressed by every sort of injustice by the pseudo-provost of a neighbouring convent—a man otherwise ruined and profligate—appeals to the supreme head of the Church, intending to proceed to Rome for a hearing before him. There survives Bernard’s earnest letter to Innocent on his behalf, sharp against the offender, which so commends the cause of the one that it describes the character of both.”

Then the letter is recited there, which is number 198 in the collection and may be read in the source itself. He again urgently commends the same affair to the same vicar of Christ, as is clear from the immediately following letter addressed to him under this title: “He asks that the sentence pronounced on behalf of religious persons unjustly oppressed be confirmed, and that ears be given no further to calumnies.” Manrique writes in the same place, no. 4, concerning the judges who pronounced sentence for Charolles and how its execution was delayed; and in no. 6 he observes that “in Bernard ... it ought not to be thought remarkable if he would not permit the children whom he pursued with such close care to be harassed by the more powerful. For so great was the protection of the poor implanted in him by nature but perfected through grace, that he would not suffer even brute animals to be oppressed in his presence; and he said that others attempted this in vain, since he himself would prevent it as long as he could.” Geoffrey’s *Life*, book III, chapter 4, may be consulted.

333. But another and more perilous storm exercised the labour and skill of the holy man. Hear the account from the cited *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 6:

“In this same year Louis the Younger, undisciplined in conduct because of his age, fierce through power, loosening the reins of disobedience against the Church and rebelling against Innocent, attacked even Theobald—toward a man, however holy, whom he had long hated—with an old enmity. Was it because he found him favourable to the Church and to Innocent, and therefore opposed to himself? This was Bernard’s cause, and that of the whole of Cîteaux, under a double title: first, because it was the Church’s cause; then, because it was Theobald’s, managed through Bernard and our brethren. ... Scarcely any affair was more grave, difficult, or laborious, given the ever-slippery will of kings—and more slippery whenever they are carried headlong by anger or vengeance. Bernard was, after a long time indeed, equally an iris [a rainbow, i.e. a reconciler] toward the king and on the king’s behalf.

“The first occasion of the quarrels was Peter, given by the pope as shepherd to the church of Bourges, long widowed since the death of Alberic. The king judged it unseemly that he had been consecrated without his consent, and injurious if he should be admitted. Nor were courtly counsels lacking, according to the custom of the court: not to guide him, but often, while urging obedience itself, to drive him headlong. Theobald alone, count, proved more steadfast than the rest when he contradicted him, and more faithful; but the more faithful he was, the more he became hated and provoked the king’s vengeance against himself.”

On these matters Robert—or rather pseudo-Robert, as will be said in §32—and Sigebert’s continuator write under this year. Their text is immediately added in the cited *Annals*:

“In this same year, namely 1141, a dissension arose between the Roman pope and Louis, king of the Franks, whence the Gallican Church was troubled. For, Alberic archbishop of Bourges having died, Peter was sent by Pope Innocent and consecrated shepherd of the same church; but, rejected by King Louis because he had been consecrated without his consent, he was by no means received into the city. Since Count Theobald was believed to support his party out of reverence or affection for the pope, the enmity which had seemed to be lulled began to revive between the king and him.”

After Manrique has recited these words, the following is added in his *Annals*: “In the precipitancy of his anger Louis added an oath: that while he lived, no one consecrated without consulting him should ascend to the episcopal see. And among the French there was such superstition that they counted it shameful not to fulfil whatever they had confirmed by oath.”

334. “Moved and troubled by these things, Bernard, guarding against still greater evils, devoted an entire year, first with fruitless effort and then successfully, to restoring peace between priesthood and kingdom. The holy man himself speaks confidently of this in the following year, writing to Louis in Letter 221: ‘You know with how great labour, with how great [Mabillon: and how great] concern, throughout the whole preceding year, I devoted myself [ibid.: applied myself] to seeking your peace.’

“Therefore he first approached the king, that he might come to his senses; then Innocent, that he might spare him. But when the former would not withdraw from disobedience, alleging the sacred obligation of his oath, and the latter, grieving that the keys of the Church had been despised, threatened the king with anathema, Bernard did what remained: he wrote to the four cardinal bishops of the curia—among whom was Stephen, his beloved son—asking them to take counsel for the Christian commonwealth and, if possible, soften Innocent. Let the Father pardon the son; the old man the young; the ecclesiastic the secular ruler; finally, the priest the king, who would indeed wish to yield but did not sufficiently dare, for shame at incurring the reproach of a violated oath. And behold a copy of the holy Father’s letter, which will also incidentally confirm what has been said.”

The letter which Manrique immediately recites is number 219 in the collection, and in Mabillon’s edition bears this heading: “To the three bishops of the curia, Alberic of Ostia, Stephen of Palestrina, Igmar of Tusculum, and Gerard the chancellor.” The notes observe among other things: “In some copies, ‘four.’ But the common reading is better. For Gerard the chancellor, named here in fourth place and afterward made pope under the name Lucius II, was not a bishop.” This is further confirmed by the fact that the same letter is assigned to the year of Christ 1143 in that edition. And indeed, at that time the affair for which the holy man laboured had a good outcome; but discord had scarcely been lulled before fresh disputes disturbed the peace, as Manrique records from no. 6 onward, and as will presently be said from him more fully.

## § XXXI. That dispute, scarcely lulled, breaks out again in fresh dissensions; Bernard’s new labours to settle it

335. What we said at the end of the immediately preceding paragraph that Bernard had undertaken, he obtained, as Manrique reports in the place indicated: “It was established that no anathema was then pronounced against the king. Indeed, convinced by the holy man’s admonitions, he agreed with the pope that Peter should be installed in the see of Bourges. The king’s favour toward Theobald also was secured by definite agreements, for which two men were chosen on the king’s side—namely Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris, whom the holy doctor had long before converted to better ways, as we noted in the proper place. On Theobald’s side there were likewise two others, both a bishop and an abbot of Cîteaux: namely Hugh of Auxerre and Bernard, to determine conditions and effect a settlement for both sides.

“But among the other provisions, this in particular was established—the provision which, after peace had later been disturbed, the holy Father recalled to both royal advocates in Letter 222: that if any controversy or dissension arose concerning those agreements, they should neither do nor seek any harm against one another until the matter had been aired and examined before us three together and the lord of Auxerre, who were then mediators and ought, should any controversy arise, to be reconcilers.” But it is worth recounting what difficulties again intruded upon this scarcely established peace.

336. It was the year 1142, as the *Cistercian Annals* relate under that year, “when the dissensions between the pope, Theobald, and King Louis, scarcely yet lulled, flared up afresh in new quarrels. And perhaps the anger which could not break out against Innocent rushed with greater violence upon Theobald. Ralph, count of Vermandois, furnished the occasion: having repudiated his wife, he took Petronilla, daughter of Duke William and sister of the queen, in addition. Consanguinity was sought as a pretext for the divorce; nor were witnesses lacking for the royal desire, and three bishops were found among the chief men to pronounce sentence for Ralph—yet secretly and, as it were, through darkness, as though their own conscience protested and could not bear the sight of the sun amid notorious crimes.

“Then Theobald, zealous for his sister and for marriage, approached Bernard to seek both counsel and aid. But the holy Father, having learned the truth and grieving first over the violation of the sacrament, then over the injury done to a prince whom he dearly loved, appealed to Innocent as avenger of both and sent him the following letter on behalf of Count Theobald.” This letter is recited there; it is number 216 among Bernard’s letters. The cited *Annals* continue in no. 3 to relate what followed.

337. “Upon receiving these letters, Innocent sent Ivo, cardinal priest, into Gaul with full authority, so that through him the cause of the divorce might be decided. Having investigated and discovered the truth, he compelled Count Ralph, under anathema, to dismiss his new bride; he declared him, since he was disobedient, excluded from the communion of the faithful; he placed his land under interdict; and he suspended from sacred orders and entrance into church the three bishops by whose authority the whole matter had been done—all in justice and according to the mind of the sacred canons.”

On these matters Robert, Sigebert’s continuator, writes under this year; Manrique quotes his words as follows: “Ralph, count of Vermandois, dismisses his wife and marries Petronilla, the queen’s sister. At the insistence of Count Theobald, Ivo, legate of the Roman See, is sent, who excommunicated Count Ralph and suspended Bartholomew bishop of Laon, Simon bishop of Noyon, and Peter bishop of Senlis, who had effected that divorce.”

The *Annals* continue: “In the meantime the legate entered upon the way of all flesh and, by his own death, confirmed the sentence. For after he had been removed from the midst, when perhaps the heated zeal might have been softened, the Roman pontiff alone remained to be approached, and he could not easily be persuaded.” Thus Manrique. See Achéry’s *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 480.

But Louis, as the said *Annals* add in no. 4, “when he saw himself frustrated and saw that the disgrace which he had brought upon the count by rejection of his sister had fallen upon the queen’s sister, ... had recourse to arms ... and, contrary to right, justice, and the agreements, without awaiting or consulting the arbiters, attacked Count Theobald as an enemy, ravaging all his dominion with sword and fire. The cruelty went so far that the pious count, to avoid the slaughter of the faithful, plunder, rape, and the other evils of war which alike envelop victors and vanquished, was compelled to swear that he would obtain absolution from the pope—either preferring his own disgrace to the safety of his citizens, or buying time by the promise of an absolution which Innocent might either deny or, if granted, revoke.” Bernard reveals the affair in Letter 217 to Innocent.

338. “Then the supreme pontiff,” Manrique continues in no. 6, “yielding to Theobald in view of his merits ... lifted the anathema, intending immediately to renew it unless the adulterers repented and separated.” Power perceived that it had once again been deceived and that the vengeance by which it had thought itself newly entangled had again vanished. Attributing all this to Bernard—for who else could have prevailed with the pope?—Louis sent him a letter of excessive complaint, to which Bernard replied freely according to his custom, yet reverently.” He stood steadfastly for justice, rejecting the king’s unjust demand in Ralph’s case and warning the same king not to oppress the innocent or provoke against himself the supreme King. This letter survives as no. 220 among the others.

Afterward, indeed, the effort and care of the most holy Father in settling this public affair of such great enterprise and consequence were without the desired result; yet they were not brought to the point of ceasing to exert further labour upon it. Letter 221 may be consulted.

339. But what meanwhile did King Louis do? Let the aforesaid *Annals*, chapter 2, no. 1, be heard: “Louis, however, was not exasperated—which is rather remarkable and shows a better disposition in a young man—nor did he disdain a reply from the man of God. Rather, he sent him a long letter, weaving excuses and complaints by which he attacked Theobald on many counts, and Bernard too on certain points: that he had evaded the oath through deceit, while the land nevertheless remained under interdict; that he was binding to himself by marriages the count of Flanders and the count of Soissons, with whose aid he rebelled against the king; that Ralph had been solicited by him, with Bernard’s knowledge and complicity, since Bernard promised him forgiveness of sins if he wished to adhere to Theobald.

“After the king had written these and similar things in reply, Bernard appealed to his two counsellors and arbiters of the agreements, Joscelin and Suger, through whom—as men acquainted with the whole truth—he might be brought back far more effectively, and more easily as friends.” This letter is number 222 among Bernard’s letters.

Let us proceed to Manrique, no. 7: “But when the holy doctor sent the letter either accidentally opened—whence an occasion was taken, as though he had acted disrespectfully—or when Joscelin, from a guilty conscience, judged it rather biting, he returned an exceedingly biting answer, and the more blameworthy he was, the more impatient. So far did he go that he was not ashamed to say that the Saint had spoken in a spirit of blasphemy, as Geoffrey affirms in his *Life* and as the holy man’s own reply testifies.” See this in Letter 223; consult the latter in book III, chapter 3, no. 175. We observe in passing, however, that Mabillon’s edition does not assign that letter to the year 1142, in which we now stand with the *Cistercian Annals*, but to 1143. From these things it is meanwhile sufficiently understood that St Bernard attempted everything to bring a remedy to this most lamentable controversy between the two contending princes; yet his effort had so far been fruitless, as will be plain from the events which afterward followed.

## § XXXII. Bernard’s further attempts to relieve the tragic dissensions of Gaul; he undeservedly loses the favour of Pope Innocent

[Col. 0809A]

340. As we pass from this point to the year of Christ 1143, there presents itself to us a most disastrous scene in the affairs of Gaul. To change it into a happier one, how many and how great labours did not the holy man undertake—labours certainly all the harder because they were denied the desired fruit.

“The affairs of Gaul,” says Manrique under this year, chapter 1, no. 1, “were rushing toward a worse state, and Louis, having broken the bonds of piety, raged every day more irreligiously and more fiercely against Theobald. This happened in the year 1143 ... in which Bernard, grieving and sorrowing, wrote this letter to the cardinals of the curia, especially to Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, his beloved son, containing the miserable condition of Gaul.” This letter is number 224 in Mabillon’s edition. I extract the following:

“You ... know how I too stood for the king in the presence of my lord, absent in body indeed but present in spirit, that I might speak good concerning him. For he promised good things. But now, as he repays good with evil, I am compelled to write the contrary. ... Holy things are trampled underfoot among us; the Church is shamefully enslaved. For episcopal elections are prevented from taking place; and wherever the clergy have dared to undertake one, the elected man is not allowed to exercise the episcopal office. Finally, the Church of Paris sits in grief, deprived of her own pastor, and no one dares breathe a word concerning the appointment of another. It is not enough that episcopal households are stripped of their present goods: a sacrilegious hand also rages everywhere against lands and persons, claiming for itself from them the revenues of an entire year.

341. “The king entrusted to his brother Robert the functions of bishop, and Robert, exercising arbitrary power over all the lands and goods of the Church, ... daily offers to heaven sacrifices far from peaceable: the cries of the poor, tears of widows, lamentations of orphans, groans of prisoners in chains, blood of those slain. ... Moreover, the king, after no little effort on our part, had made peace with Count Theobald ... and behold, he seeks opportunities to withdraw from his friend. The great charge brought against the count is this: that he contracts marriages between his children and the barons of the king. The enlargement of affection is suspect to him, and he does not think himself king if the princes love one another. ...

“Therefore he openly transgresses the conventions and settlements of peace and does not keep the agreements which his lips have set forth. Finally, he has recalled to his house and counsel an adulterous and excommunicated man whom he had, by formal agreement, expelled; and, to practise greater wickedness, the king and advocate of the Church again joins himself with many other wicked men—equally excommunicated, perjured, incendiaries, murderers—against a lover and defender of the Church, as cannot be doubted. ... In addition, according to his custom, he compels bishops to curse those who ought to be blessed and again to bless those who ought to be cursed. ... With what face, I ask, does a man who persists with his own cousin in almost the third degree of consanguinity—as is plainly known—labour so earnestly to prescribe rules of consanguinity to others?

342. “And indeed, whether there is consanguinity between the son of Count Theobald and the daughter of the count of Flanders, and likewise between the count of Soissons and the daughter of Count Theobald, I do not know—for I have never knowingly commended, nor do I commend, unlawful marriages—but you should know, and my lord should know, that these marriages are forbidden.”

These are among many other things by which Bernard presses Stephen. And, as Manrique reports in no. 6, he wrote matters not unlike these “to the other bishops whom he knew adhered to the pope, so that they might oppose such great evils as far as they could. Why he did not then write to Innocent himself we shall explain below under this same year.” On the said King Louis, Horst’s notes in Mabillon on Letter 224, column LXX, may be consulted. There also the almost third degree of consanguinity mentioned above is explained, as likewise in the shorter notes, column 209. Pagi writes under the year of Christ 1142 concerning Count Ralph of Vermandois repudiating his wife and taking another. Thus we see St Bernard straining every nerve to relieve the utterly ruined affairs of Gaul. Having briefly noted these points on the preceding letter, let us continue the present discussion with the cited *Cistercian Annals*, where nos. 7 and 8 say the following.

343. “Meanwhile the Saint himself and Hugh, who had been arbiters of the agreements for Theobald and were appointed by Innocent to seek peace for the Gallican Church—as Bernard makes no slight suggestion in his letter to Innocent—left nothing whatever untried: they met the king, brought the nobles into the matter, invoked divine and human law, set forth the losses of war, and declared that whichever side conquered, the kingdom would perish, without which the king himself could not stand. For whose was that land which was being laid waste? Whose were the people against whom he raged? Would not compensation have to be made from his own treasury? ... These things they urged concerning temporal losses; but they spoke of still greater matters concerning reputation and honour, and greatest of all concerning salvation,” as is explained there at greater length.

“By these and similar means, now through letters, now in person, they persevered in approaching the king, respectfully and firmly rebuking, entreating, and reproving him in all patience and teaching. And already a meeting appointed at Corbeil promised better things, had not the king, scarcely hearing the counsels of the holy men and insisting, according to the manner of princes, that nothing be granted to him unless everything was granted, withdrawn in anger and fury, impatient of equity—not merely disobedient, but unwilling even to listen. Then the holy men, confounded by this shameful rejection but nevertheless steadfast for the peace of the realm, wrote him the following letter through Brother Andrew, one of their dearest friends and, as appears, familiar to the king.” It survives in Mabillon as Letter 226.

Moreover, “this Andrew, of Baugé, as is added in the text of the letter, was celebrated and employed in various affairs. He subscribes the principal documents of the abbey of Caricamp in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, page 329, and is found with Bernard as a witness to the agreement made between Louis the Younger and Algrimus, archdeacon of Orléans, in volume IV of Duchesne, page 764.” Mabillon gives this and more in his shorter notes on the same letter. So much in passing.

344. Also relevant here, as we continue to recount other things done by the holy and common Father for establishing peace, is Bernard’s letter to Joscelin, bishop of Soissons. Bernard wrote it alone, forgetting the injury received—or rather, loving him the more because he remembered it ...—as Manrique says in no. 10. It is number 225 in Mabillon. But what was the result of efforts so pious and strenuous alike? The aforesaid compiler of the *Annals* says in no. 11:

“Nothing was obtained from the king by letters. ... Therefore in this year, by an outstanding act of impiety, the king at Vitry—others call it Vitriacum, a town within Theobald’s dominion—first destroyed the walls, then by fire the church itself, into which almost all the townspeople had fled. He burned sacred and profane things, men and women, adults and children. One thousand three hundred souls perished—others give a greater number—who, as though protected by the holiness of the place, had awaited safety from religion. The king is then said at last to have been struck by a tardy repentance and to have wept, yet not to have been ready to amend his sin.”

On these events Robert, Sigebert’s continuator, writes under this year: “King Louis captured Vitry, the castle of Count Theobald. When fire was applied, the church was burned, and in it thirteen hundred souls of both sexes and all ages were consumed by fire. King Louis is said to have wept, moved by pity; and for this reason some think that he undertook the pilgrimage to Jerusalem.”

345. “From the occasion of these words, I believe,” says Manrique in no. 12, “Paul Aemilius confuses the times and relates that Father Bernard was summoned by the king to implore God’s mercy through him, as though he were already repenting.” He gives the following words of Paul Aemilius in his account of Louis the Younger:

“When he had been admitted and received most graciously by the king, and saw his weeping and learned the cause of his sorrow, he said: ‘Unless these tears quickly dry up, they can extinguish the memory of the fire of Vitry. Only add steadfastness and strength to them; and lest they be like a woman’s lamentation, show a manly and truly royal spirit. Before the anger of the offended deity arms itself against you, turn against the enemies of temples and against barbarous religion the fires which you brought upon temple and altars.’”

Manrique does not transcribe the rest of what Aemilius pursues at greater length, but indicates that he treats the affair “as though Bernard had in this very year and on this occasion urged Louis toward the Jerusalem expedition. Yet these events, separated by at least three full years, are far apart; one occurred under Innocent and the other under Eugenius, with two other popes, though of short reigns, intervening. They are confused in history without cause. The memory of the earlier crime could have impelled the king; Bernard too could have recalled it, even though it had been committed two years previously. And Louis was still at odds with Theobald and could not be reconciled with him until after a year, as we shall mention in the proper place.” Thus far the Cistercian annalist. While correcting Paul Aemilius’s chronology, he gives us occasion to note something regarding the year 1143, to which he assigns the atrocity perpetrated at Vitry by King Louis the Younger.

346. In his *Critique of Baronius*, under 1141, no. 3, writing of the dispute between Innocent II and Louis VII, king of the Franks, Pagi relates in no. 4 the following from William of Nangis’s *Chronicle* under 1142: “The king stirred up almost all his nobles to make war with him against Count Theobald. Then in 1143 the king captured Vitry, a town of Count Theobald, where, when fire was applied, the church was burned and 1,300 people of both sexes and all ages perished in it.”

But Pagi immediately observes that the Chronicles of Gembloux and Châlons nevertheless say that Vitry was burned in 1142. He accepts their dating under 1143, no. 1, where, after recounting the miserable condition of the Gallican Church, he says: “The basilica of the castle of Vitry, however, was not burned in this year, as Baronius reports in no. 6 from pseudo-Robert of Mont, but in 1142, as we showed under 1141.” Manrique above used this same pseudo-Robert; and though Nangis supports him concerning the year 1143 which he assigns, the other two chronicles cited stand against him.
