347. But the other Robert of Mont, whose genuine *Additions* and *Appendix* to Sigebert were published by Achéry after the works of Guibert, abbot of Nogent, printed at Paris in 1651, relates the following under the year 1141, page 762:

“Louis, king of the Franks, afflicted Count Theobald and devastated his land, especially in Champagne, where he burned a very fine castle, namely Vitry; there a very great multitude of persons of both sexes and all ages were burned.”

Thus the other Robert, who apparently appended the burning of the castle of Vitry by prolepsis to the harassments stirred up by Louis against Theobald in 1141—the year in which, as we said in §30 from the *Cistercian Annals*, Theobald was attacked by him—unless one prefers, with another manuscript indicated in Achéry’s marginal note on pages 760 and following, to read 1142 instead of 1141. This other Robert of Mont, I say again, is the genuine one; see the observation on him in Achéry, page 715.

Oudin, in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume II, from column 1625, has collected various particulars about this author. Among them is this point relevant to our subject: “He carried his Chronicle from 1112, where Sigebert had ended, to 1182. But the Appendix to Sigebert, published among the distinguished writers of Germany, is for the most part by another author, namely from 1110 to 1155. The genuine appendix to Sigebert’s Chronicle, written by Robert of Torigni—as he is also called—from the autograph manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael of the Mount, together with his additions to Sigebert, was published by the most learned Lucas d’Achéry,” mentioned above by us. But lest chronological discussions of this kind divert us from our historical thread, we say below, under the year 1144, that the discordant princes King Louis and Count Theobald were reconciled through the efforts of St Bernard. For the present, let us proceed with Manrique, who continues his subject in chapter 2 of the aforesaid year 1143.

348. “The holy Father mourned these public evils when he suddenly experienced private ones also, from a quarter he least feared; sorrow upon sorrow and grief upon grief was added. Without his knowing it, he had lost Innocent’s favour, which he had earned by so many labours and services. The goods of Cardinal Ivo, the legate, had been distributed to the poor although they ought to have been reserved for the pope. The distribution was charged against Bernard on two grounds: because he had been designated as distributor in the will, and because he had put himself forward, voluntarily, as promoter of the poor’s cause.

“Two abbots had been present while Ivo was at the point of death, so that the property bequeathed might pass, through them together with Bernard, into the possession of the poor. Both went to Clairvaux to seek Bernard, as was fitting; but since the Saint, occupied in matters concerning peace, was not found, they carried out alone what Ivo had ordered, lest the will be delayed longer. It seemed difficult to Innocent that anything should have been done without Bernard being consulted; and in that cause the Saint was suspect, because it was his own—the cause of the poor—and one to be preferred to private interests.

“Now once favour has somehow been lost, such being commonly the human condition, what had pleased before began to become offensive. Almost nothing, it was said, was done in the Church without Bernard; and scarcely a single pope sufficed for his frequent letters and intercessions, though the pope had been given to the whole Church and could not comply with one man’s wishes. Let the abbot confine himself within his monastery, or at least within Gaul; let there be something not carried out according to his judgment. ... Thus he who had once used Bernard in every region of the world to secure his tiara, after securing it condemned what he had chosen; and he who urged Bernard to plead for him would not permit him to plead with him for others.”

349. “When Bernard learned of the Pope’s indignation against him, he wrote him an apologetic letter, as Baronius says under 1143, defending his cause and powerfully excusing himself, showing that he had committed no fault to merit such indignation.” This is the last letter which the holy Father wrote to Pope Innocent, number 218. Although it may be read elsewhere in print, it deserves to be reprinted and read here also, with some passages omitted for brevity:

“I had thought,” says the holy man, “that I was at some time something, even if only a little; but now, as I perceive, I have been reduced utterly to nothing, without knowing it. For I would not say that I was altogether nothing then, when the eyes of my lord were upon his servant and his ears open to my prayers. ... But now I say deservedly that I am not merely something small but nothing, because since yesterday and the day before yesterday he has turned his face away from me. Why is this? What sin have I committed? I confess it was a great one if the money of Cardinal Ivo of good memory was distributed at my discretion and not at his own command. I am not so dull as not to know that whatever he did not give away from his possessions belongs to the Church.

350. “But now hear the truth plainly. ... When the man put off the mortal man [i.e. died], I was absent—indeed, very far away. Yet I heard from those who were present that he made his will; and what he did, he did and wrote. He himself distributed his goods as he wished, to whom he wished. What remained, he entrusted for distribution to the two abbots then attending him, and likewise to me, though I was absent, because the poorer houses of the saints were known to us. When those abbots came home and did not find me—for at that time I was detained by your command in affairs of seeking peace—they nevertheless divided the money as seemed good to them, not merely without my connivance but without my knowledge of what they did. Let indignation now, if it please you, yield to manifest truth. ...”

351. “For I have also learned that you were displeased with me over my many letters; I need no longer fear this, for I shall readily amend. I know, I know: I presumed more than was fitting, paying too little heed to who I was that I presumed to write so frequently to whom I did. . . . Henceforth I shall, if I can, add discretion—knowledge—to my zeal, and put my finger upon my mouth. For it is more tolerable that I should offend some friends than that I should weary the Anointed of the Lord with many petitions. And even now I have not dared to write to you concerning the dangers threatening the Church, [Col. 0814C] the grave schism which we fear, and the very many hardships which we endure. But I have written to the holy bishops attached to your side: from them you may hear, if you wish to know, what I have written.”

It is pleasing to append, by way of conclusion, Baronius’s words for the year 1143, no. 5, which he adds to the foregoing letter quoted by him: “It happened exactly as the Wise Man says (Eccles. 7): ‘Slander unsettles the wise man’; so that St Bernard was diminished in Pope Innocent’s esteem because of his detractors, to such an extent that, although this same saint had rendered such numerous and great services and benefits, these were consigned to oblivion; no account was now taken of them, and he himself fell from Innocent’s favour. Whether, after receiving these letters from him, Innocent [Col. 0814D] had a more equitable disposition towards him is not known to us. But if Bernard’s crops withered in this land under the scorching wind, surely elsewhere he gathered unto eternal life the seeds which he had sown in the land of the living—not by human, but by divine vision. Thus let men learn not to put their hope in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.”

These are Baronius’s words, as true as they are weighty, occasioned by this letter, which, as I indicated above, was the last which the holy Doctor wrote to Pope Innocent II—now defending himself in a cause so just and so directly his own, whereas previously he had so often defended others’ causes. That pontiff died in the same year, 1143, on 24 September; Celestine II of that name succeeded him on the following day. The latter’s reign was brief; for the cause of the former’s death, see Baronius and Manrique.

## § XXXIII. The Cistercian Order propagated in Sweden by the holy abbot; a miracle and a prophecy; disputes in France settled by him; he is honoured by the Patriarch of Jerusalem

352. The Cistercian chronicler, at the year previously mentioned, chapter 7, while treating of the spread of monasteries, records three remarkable things about the holy Father in connection with the foundation of Nydala in the kingdom of Sweden and in the diocese of Linköping. One was a miracle confirming the brethren sent there; another, a prophecy by which he foretold to a certain brother the place of his death; and the third lay in the manner in which that prophecy was fulfilled. Here is the first, from the author of the *Great Exordium*, in Tissier, distinction 4, chapter 28:

“The same venerable Father, desiring to bear some fruit among the peoples of the northern regions as among other nations, sent a community of brethren to those parts at the request of the pious woman, the queen of Sweden. When the monks and lay brothers who had been selected for this purpose—that they might impart the form of religious life and discipline to uncultivated and untamed men—were overcome with excessive grief and, with all the prayers they could offer, begged not to be sent to foreign and barbarous regions, where they would be deprived of the presence of so great a Father, the holy abbot replied: ‘Why do you afflict my soul with irrational tears and prayers? Or do I follow my own will in this matter, rather than the will of God, whom we all ought to obey?’ [Col. 0815C]

353. “Now garments, sacred vessels, and the other implements belonging to the ministry of the divine office, which the brethren who were to be sent had to take with them, had been placed before him. Therefore, wishing to assure them that this word had proceeded from the Lord, he lifted a basin intended to receive the water poured over the priest’s hands, pressed his finger into its bottom, and said: ‘Behold, this shall be your sign that the Spirit of the Lord has sent you.’ In a marvellous manner the hardness and inflexibility of the metal appeared to yield to the softness of his finger, so that the exact size of the holy joint may still today be clearly discerned. As far as it appears to have sunk inward, so far does it seem to have projected beyond the outer level. In testimony to so great a miracle, that same basin is preserved with the greatest reverence in the sacristy of the house which the holy Father then established.

“But when the aforesaid brethren saw the manifest presence of divine grace, they checked the goads of their devouring sorrow and rejoiced. Although they might approach, not without a certain horror of spirit, nations most remote and hidden in the furthest region of the northern winter, they nevertheless confidently trusted that the same grace of God, through the merits and prayers of our holy Father, would accompany them.”

So much there concerning the miracle. The same author immediately adds the following concerning St Bernard’s notable prophecy:

354. “Among the others there was a young man [Col. 0816A] of honourable character and dove-like simplicity, named Gerard, born in the city of Maastricht, in Lower Germany. More impatiently distressed than the others, he said with tears to the man of God: ‘Most blessed Father, I, a wretched young man, have left my father’s house and despised everything that could be desirable and lovable to me in this world. Drawn by love of the religious life, I came to your fatherhood, hoping to enjoy your most sweet presence, to be formed by your teachings and examples, helped by your merits and prayers, and sheltered beneath the protection of this holy community from the storm of temptations and the heat of youthful desires. And what I desire above all else is to await my final day among the sacred bodies of our brethren resting in this cemetery. [Col. 0816B] Yet behold: today you drive me from your presence. I lose fellowship in this holy company and, moreover, shall be deprived of the burial I have desired. This, indeed, this is why I grieve so deeply: for my heart is troubled within me.’

355. “The blessed man took compassion on the youth and endeavoured with gentle speech to soothe his soul afflicted by sorrow. Foreseeing and foretelling in a prophetic spirit what would happen fifty years later, he said to him: ‘Go, dearest son, wherever the Holy Spirit deigns to send you, and labour as a vigorous worker in the Lord’s field. In the name of the Lord I promise you and make you secure that, as you desire, you shall die at Clairvaux and together with us await the glorious coming of the heavenly Bridegroom.’ [Col. 0816C]

“Receiving this joyful promise of the devout Father as the earnest of his desire, that brother rejoiced exceedingly, knowing certainly that the man whom clear signs and miracles declared to be a follower of wisdom and truth could neither be deceived nor wish to deceive. He therefore went forth and, in the house to establish which he was sent with the other brethren, vigorously discharged the duties of prior and cellarer. By divine grace he obtained alike the name and office of abbot. Although he ascended unwillingly to that summit of rank—preferring salvation in a lowly place to peril in a high one—he nevertheless adorned the office he had accepted with the splendour of a most religious way of life.”

Thus far the praised author of the *Great Exordium* concerning the prophecy which the holy Father had made to Gerard. Having related Gerard’s virtues—see also the *Cistercian Annals*, vol. II, at the year 1150, chapter 10—he proceeds to recount how the prophecy was later fulfilled. Thus he continues concerning Abbot Gerard:

356. “When he had now grown old, reached decrepit age, completed his fortieth year in prelation, and his body was shaken by various infirmities, the brethren began to beg him that, just as he had lived with them for so long in common, so he might also deign to receive a place of burial among them. The man of God replied: ‘Do not, I pray you, speak thus, my sons. In every way it is necessary that I die at Clairvaux and, according to the promise of my Father beloved by God, sleep and rest in peace together with the saints who lie there.’

“When they objected and said: ‘How, Father, shall we be able to bring you there, when, in addition to the infirmities of advanced old age, you are so afflicted and debilitated by so many and such great ailments that we think you can scarcely arrive breathing at the nearest borders of the Danes?’ he replied with great confidence: ‘The word of God, mighty and strong, living and effective, which was poured into my ears through the mouth of that most reverend man and planted in the inner chambers of my heart the earnest of this good hope which bears me onward, shall grant a successful outcome to this journey. You, only take care to fulfil promptly what I command.’ [Col. 0817A]

357. “Accordingly, a litter having been arranged between two horses, he was placed in it; and, not without a great miracle, he arrived at Clairvaux from the ends of the earth, across so great expanses of land and through so many perils of sea and rivers. There, lying for some time in the infirmary, he breathed out his spirit in a good confession. He received the place of burial he had desired beside the little tomb of Lord Benedict the Dwarf, of blessed memory, who had loved him familiarly during his life. When the king of Sweden learned of his death, he declared with groaning that his kingdom and land had not been worthy for the sacred bones of so great a man to rest in it.” [Col. 0817B]

Manrique assigns Gerard’s death to the year 1190, as may be seen in volume III of the *Cistercian Annals*, at that year, chapter 4. Jongelinus, writing on the abbeys of the Cistercian Order in the kingdom of Sweden in his *Notitia abbatiarum ordinis Cisterciensis*, book VIII, p. 36, cites several details that may shed some light on what has already been recounted. For, concerning the foundation of Nydala—which he also assigns to the year 1143, as Manrique does—he says that its first abbot, Lord Gerard, was born at Maastricht on the Meuse in Belgium. Thus is removed the ambiguity in the author of the *Great Exordium*, who, in saying that Gerard was “born in the city of Maastricht, in Lower Germany,” leaves it uncertain whether he means Maastricht on the Rhine or Maastricht on the Meuse.

Furthermore, from what the praised Jongelinus had previously stated in the cited place about Alvastra or Alvastrum—founded in the same year, 1143, and in the same diocese of Linköping, and owing its beginnings, he affirms, to Sverker, the illustrious king of Sweden—and from his remarks concerning the kings of Sweden buried in that abbey, light is thrown upon the unnamed king of Sweden mentioned in the *Great Exordium*. For, according to Jongelinus: “Besides others, Sverker, king of Sweden, who died in 1150, chose burial here . . . Likewise his son Charles, king of Sweden, slain by Canute the Dane, was buried in this monastery in 1168 beside his father . . . King Sverker, slain in the Danish war, died in 1208, or alternatively 1210,” etc. [Col. 0817C–D] Therefore the statement concerning Gerard—“When the king of Sweden learned of his death,” etc.—appears to refer to this king, according to the sequence set out above in Jongelinus. Our Riccioli, moreover, gives the succession of Swedish kings in volume III of his *Reformed Chronology*, catalogue 41, where Sverker II, son of Charles VII, is marked at 1192.

[Col. 0818A]

358. Having thus brought our collection of St Bernard’s deeds down to the year of Christ 1143, the immediately following year, 1144, opens for us a serene calm after the most severe storm of dissensions between King Louis and Count Theobald, which the work of the holy man had stilled and which we had temporarily interrupted. Lucius II of that name then occupied Peter’s chair. Manrique, for this year, chapter 1, recounts under this pontiff, from pseudo-Robert of Mont in the Appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, an event accomplished in that year: “Through the mediation of the abbot of Clairvaux, the hostility which had flared up between King Louis and Count Theobald was appeased.” To this most fortunate outcome very aptly belongs the exclamation which Manrique adds: “A peace worthy of Bernard as mediator, and one which all good men had most earnestly desired.” [Col. 0818B]

Two writers of St Bernard’s Life have preserved the manner in which these things occurred. First, it is most worthy of narration how the man of God instructed Theobald, by devout and holy counsels, to bear a steadfast and exalted spirit amid so many and such harsh adversities of fortune. Ernaldus describes these matters at length and movingly in book II, chapter 6; lest the discussion run too long, we refer the reader there.

359. From this it is understood that this tragic and bloody dispute between the two princes was indeed happily settled by our holy peacemaker. Yet it must further be added that it was settled in such a way that Bernard, raised up in hope against all hope and moved by a prophetic spirit, foretold the successful outcome of an event most earnestly desired but scarcely expected. Read Geoffrey, book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 2, no. 198. Although he does not add on what terms and with what result that peace was concluded, a most abundant benefit followed from it, as the writer of the *Cistercian Annals*, no. 7, reports:

“The ancient authors are silent concerning the terms agreed upon, content to relate the peace that was made. Yet it is certain that it remained so firm and unshaken that Louis, after divorcing Eleanor, daughter of William, duke of Aquitaine, because she was bound to him by a tie of consanguinity for which no dispensation had been granted, and after Constance, daughter of Alfonso VIII, king of Castile, had died in childbirth before even a full year of marriage had elapsed, married Adela, daughter of Theobald. By her Philip, surnamed Augustus, was born, who succeeded to the kingdom and was to bind grandfather and father more closely together.” [Col. 0818C–D]

Such, then, was the outcome of this most serious dissension: useful and honourable to Theobald, glorious to Bernard.

360. The holy Father was also held in veneration by the Patriarch of Jerusalem, as is indicated by a fragment of the Lord’s Cross which the latter sent to him from Jerusalem. The aforesaid annalist discusses it at the year 1144, chapter 4, and, on that occasion, says that “in this very year salvation was obtained once and again through the intervention of the same saving wood, making believers more devout.” See Baronius at the same year, 1144. There survives Bernard’s letter no. 175, in which, having been anticipated by this Patriarch’s letter and given that sacred pledge, he shows himself mindful and grateful for both honours. But that letter differs greatly from the year 1144; in Mabillon’s edition it is dated about 1135. The Patriarch was William, a Gallo-Belgian, as is stated there in the notes: formerly a hermit of Tours, Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1130 to 1145. Further information concerning that Patriarch follows in the same notes. [Col. 0819A]

## § XXXIV. Arnold of Brescia, a heretic; the fulfilment of St Bernard’s prophecy, especially under Pope Eugenius III; his election and commendations; Bernard’s letters to him

361. Above, at the end of paragraph 29, several things were briefly set forth concerning this mad impostor. St Bernard had foretold his unrestrained fury against every order of the Church everywhere, as was there observed in connection with Peter Abelard. This was indeed shown most clearly to have been fulfilled under the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III, who was raised from the Cistercian Order to Peter’s chair in the year 1145. Let us therefore portray in living colours the promised and here transferred likeness of Arnold of Brescia, from Otto of Freising, book II of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, chapter 21, col. 719 of the latest Milanese edition, volume VI among the writers of Italian affairs:

“Arnold, a man of Brescia, of whom mention has been made above, entered the City under the guise of religion and, to use the Gospel’s words, wearing a wolf beneath a sheep’s skin. He stirred the hearts of the untutored populace—that is, the Roman people who stood with the senate against the pope—into that faction, inflaming them to audacity by his alluring doctrine; and he drew, indeed led astray, an innumerable multitude after himself. This Arnold, an Italian by birth from the city of Brescia, a cleric of that church and ordained only as a reader, had formerly had Peter Abelard as his teacher. He was a man not dull by nature, but more copious in a flood of words than in weight of thought; a lover of singularity and eager for novelty—the sort of mind inclined to devise heresies and foment the disturbances of schisms. [Col. 0819B–C]

“Returning from study in France to Italy, he assumed a religious habit in order to deceive more effectively. He attacked everything, gnawed at everything, spared no one: a detractor of clerics and bishops, a persecutor of monks, flattering laymen alone. For he said that neither clerics possessing property, nor bishops possessing regalian rights, nor monks possessing estates could be saved on any grounds. All such things, he said, belonged to the prince and ought, through his beneficence, to pass only to the use of laymen. Besides this, he is reported not to have held sound views concerning the sacrament of the altar and the baptism of infants. By these and other means, too lengthy to enumerate, while he disturbed the Church of Brescia and maliciously expounded the pages [variant: *personas*, ‘persons’] of Scripture to the laypeople of that land, whose ears itched against the clergy, he was accused by the bishop of that city and religious men in the great council held at Rome under Innocent in 1139. The Roman pontiff therefore decreed that silence should be imposed upon the man, lest his pernicious teaching spread further; and this was done. Thus he fled Italy and made his way beyond the Alps. There, in the German town of Zurich, taking up the office of teacher, he sowed his pernicious doctrine for some days. [Col. 0819D–0820A]

362. “But when he learned of Innocent’s death, he entered the City near the beginning of Eugenius’s pontificate. Finding it roused in sedition against its pontiff [lacuna], he stirred it up still further, putting before it the examples of the ancient Romans, who, by the mature counsel of the senate and the courage, discipline, and integrity of their young men, had made the whole world their own. He taught that the Capitol should be rebuilt, senatorial dignity renewed, and the equestrian order reformed. Nothing in the administration of the City, he said, belonged to the Roman pontiff; ecclesiastical jurisdiction ought to suffice him.

“The evil of this poisonous doctrine indeed began to prevail to such an extent that not only were the houses of Roman nobles and cardinals, and their splendid palaces, torn down, but even reverend persons among the cardinals were shamefully dragged about by the frenzied mob, some having first been wounded. While these and like acts were done by him constantly and irreverently over many days—that is, from the death of Celestine down to these times—and while the sentence justly and canonically pronounced against him by the shepherds was scorned in his judgment as entirely devoid of authority, he at last fell into certain persons’ hands. Captured in the borders of Tuscany, he was reserved for the prince’s judgment; finally he was hanged by the prefect of the City, and, his body reduced to ashes on a pyre, his ashes were scattered in the Tiber, lest his body be held in veneration by the foolish populace.” [Col. 0820B–C]

Reader, here you have Arnold of Brescia’s portrait painted in its native colours. Bernard therefore truly and aptly foretold his most wicked and seditious schemes, as though seeing them beforehand from a watchtower and comprehending much in few words, when in letter no. 195 he applied to him the following words: “You will see a man openly rising against the clergy, relying on military tyranny, rising against the bishops themselves, [Col. 0820D] and raging savagely against every ecclesiastical order everywhere.”

363. It was on account of that turbulent Arnoldist faction that Pope Lucius II, who had immediately succeeded Celestine II, died; Baronius explains the affair at greater length at the beginning of the year 1145. The same cause which removed Lucius also promptly raised a new successor in the dead man’s place. “The see did not stand vacant,” Baronius continues there, “but suddenly—as St Bernard says in letter 237 of Mabillon’s edition—a successor was elected because of the imminent danger. For after Lucius’s death, fearing the tumultuous Roman Arnoldists, the cardinals assembled unanimously in the church of the monastery of St Caesarius. There, by God’s prompting, they judged that a Roman pontiff should not, as customary, be chosen from the body of the cardinals; instead they turned their eyes upon Bernard, abbot of the monastery of St Anastasius at Tre Fontane, of the Cistercian Order. Not long before, under Pope Innocent II, he had been appointed to that house by St Bernard. A native of Pisa, distinguished in uprightness and richly endowed with prudence for conducting affairs, he seemed most suitable for that most disastrous time, in which the City burned with civil war of this sort. Since they had found him most sagacious, they elected him by equal consent and in complete unanimity.” [Col. 0821A]

The writer of the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 1, no. 4, says: “Whether it was owing to the man’s practical ability or to his holiness that this office was conferred is uncertain. Baronius, though he rarely follows uncertain authorities, unquestionably reports that both were considered; the others mention only the holiness of a man otherwise simple and less fitted to transact affairs, unless instructed by unction as his teacher.” Thus he speaks. We have just given Baronius’s words.

364. “But others,” says the same Manrique, no. 5, “weaken the claim of the man’s practical ability and ascribe everything to holiness alone.” Among others cited there, St Antoninus speaks of him thus, part II, title 17, chapter 1, §7: “Although he had previously been simple, God endowed him with marvellous grace and eloquence.” But Manrique, assigning him both prerogatives, of nature and grace, says in the same no. 5: “I should think that the dove-like purity of a man otherwise industrious and prudent was pre-eminent, and that he had not wished to extend himself beyond the monk while he remained within the limits of his profession. But as pontiff he loosed the reins of his own practical ability, which, nonetheless inspired by God, flew even beyond mortal capacity; many of his deeds testify to this.” Baronius, cited above, writes of the consecration of the praised pontiff.

Moreover, Manrique, no. 7, judges worthy of notice something Baronius omitted and the author of the *Belgian Chronicle*, whose passage and words he supplies, recorded: “When some cardinals, perhaps because they found the elected man more resolute than they had wished, sought to invalidate his election, the holy man neither lost courage nor readily yielded to them. Rather, having pronounced an anathema against the innovators, he stood firm manfully and rendered their attempts ineffectual. Thus, though he had previously scarcely consented to those who elected him, he resisted those who opposed him; and as he had not in any way sought election, so he did not allow himself, once elected, to be deposed—humble no less than steadfast, declining from faint-heartedness no less than from pride.” [Col. 0821B–D]

I have chosen to say rather more concerning this most worthy vicar of Christ because he was Bernard’s disciple, friend, and son, and therefore also the glory of the most holy Father, who dedicated to him the books *On Consideration*. You have a letter of Eugenius, then abbot, to Bernard in Mabillon, no. 344; likewise another by him when already pope, prefixed to Bernard’s letter no. 273.

365. But what shall I say of Bernard’s letters to him, which Baronius calls wholly golden at the year 1145, no. 4, and which he inserts in full in his *Annals* there, no. 5 and following? I shall employ some passages from them, after first giving the following account of them from the Cistercian historian, chapter 2.

The daily increasing fury of the Arnoldists and the pressing affairs of the City and the world prevented the pontiff from reporting by letter to Bernard—formerly his Father, but by then his son, and always most beloved—the change that had come over and concerning him, so that Bernard might either grieve with him or give thanks. But the holy Father, who had long known by public report of his son’s elevation, but did not yet know of the rebellion against him, waited for the desired messenger or letter by which he might gladly read that Bernard had been changed into Eugenius [lacuna] and that he himself was called son. Meanwhile he was also pressed by the requests of the Archbishop of Canterbury, engaged in litigation against the Archbishop of York—against whom Bernard was still acting on behalf of his disciple Henry Murdac. At last Bernard himself broke silence first, addressing the new Pontiff in the letter praised above, which is Mabillon’s no. 238. Here are some excerpts from it. [Col. 0822A–B]

366. He therefore congratulates himself upon having so great a son, indeed now a father, and expects every blessing from his government: “Since I have once begun, I shall speak to my lord. For I no longer dare call you son, because the son has become father and the father has become son. He who came after me has been made before me; but I do not envy it, because I trust that I possess in him what was lacking to me—him who came not only after me, but also through me. For, if you deign, in a certain sense I begot you through the Gospel. What then is our hope, our joy, and crown of glory? Is it not you before God? In short, a wise son is the glory of his father.

“Yet henceforth you shall not be called son; rather, a new name shall be called upon you, which the mouth of the Lord has named. This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, and many will rejoice in this change. For just as of old Abram became Abraham and Jacob Israel; and, to put before you examples drawn more particularly from your predecessors, Simon became Cephas and Saul Paul: so my son Bernard has been promoted into my father Eugenius—a change altogether joyful and beneficial, as we hope. This is the finger of God, raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit among princes and hold the throne of glory.” [Col. 0822C–D]

367. St Bernard had not, however, so completely laid aside all the authority he had once possessed over his son that, in sending him this letter, he failed freely and fatherly to add some notable counsels to his congratulations. He immediately continues:

“It remains that, now that this change has taken place in you, the Bride of your Lord also, committed to you, may be changed for the better, and henceforth be called no longer Sarai but Sarah. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding. If you are the Bridegroom’s friend, do not call his beloved ‘my princess,’ but ‘the princess,’ claiming nothing in her as yours except that for her, should it be necessary, you ought even to lay down your life. If Christ sent you, you will consider that you came not to be served but to serve; and to serve not merely with your possessions, but with your very life, as I have said.” [Col. 0823A]

Then, after some intervening remarks, this most holy man assumes various feelings—joy, fear, and dread. “Therefore,” he says, “since she has such confidence in you as she has not appeared to have had in any of your predecessors for many generations past, the whole Church of the saints everywhere rightly rejoices and glories in the Lord; but especially that Church whose womb bore you and whose breasts you sucked. What then? May I not rejoice with those who rejoice? Shall I not be one of the number of those rejoicing? I rejoiced, I confess, but with trembling. I rejoiced, but at the very point of my rejoicing fear and trembling came upon me. For although I have laid aside the name of father, I have not laid aside fear, anxiety, or, finally, a father’s affection and inward feeling. I consider the rank, and fear the fall; I consider the pinnacle of dignity and behold the face of the abyss lying below. . . .” [Col. 0823B]

368. “Indeed, you had chosen to be lowly in the house of your God and to recline in the last place at his banquet; but it pleased him who invited you to say: ‘Friend, come up higher.’ Thus you have ascended on high. Do not be high-minded, but fear lest perhaps one day you utter that miserable cry: ‘At the presence of your wrath and indignation, you lifted me up and dashed me down.’ You have received a higher place, indeed, but not a safer one; a more exalted place, but not a more secure one. This place is terrible—truly terrible. The place, I say, in which you stand is holy ground: it is Peter’s place, the place of the prince of the apostles, where his feet stood. It is the place of him whom the Lord appointed lord over his household and ruler over all his possession. If perchance you depart from the Lord’s way, he was buried in that very place, that he may stand as a witness against you. . . . Thus far.

“But the reason why I have written to you before the proper time is this.” We have already prefaced this letter with Manrique’s summary of that reason. [Col. 0823C]

369. Having stated the reason, St Bernard signifies what he desires for the Church and its new pontiff; finally, he exhorts him to strong and great-hearted resolve and to continual remembrance of death, concluding his letter in these words:

“Be strengthened, therefore, and be resolute; let your hand be upon the necks of your enemies. Claim for yourself by steadfastness of mind and vigour of spirit the portion which the almighty Father gave you beyond your brethren, and which he took from the hand of the Amorite with his sword and bow. Yet in all your works remember that you are a man, and let the fear of him who takes away the spirit of princes be always before your eyes. How many deaths of Roman pontiffs have you seen with your own eyes in a short time! Let your predecessors themselves remind you of your own most certain and most swift departure; and let the brief duration of their rule tell you of the fewness of your days. Therefore, amid the allurements of this passing glory, continually meditate upon your last things; for those whom you have succeeded in the see, you shall without doubt follow to death.” [Col. 0823D–0824A]

These, then, are the passages which I judged should be transcribed here from that distinguished letter of Bernard to Eugenius, full of fatherly feeling.

370. The phrase, “How many deaths of Roman pontiffs have you seen with your own eyes in a short time!” gave Horstius occasion to ask why the lives of Roman pontiffs are so short. His note on this letter, found in Mabillon’s longer notes on the letters of St Bernard, col. LXXII, deserves to be heard:

“It may reasonably seem remarkable why Roman pontiffs are so short-lived that Peter alone is thought to have reached his twenty-fifth year, while premature death has carried off very many after only a few years, or a few months, indeed not many days, though we see that very many emperors and kings have lived much longer lives. The matter is wholly worthy of investigation. But who knows the mind of the Lord? Yet I see that the same question was put to Blessed Peter Damian by Pope Alexander, which he carefully treats and explains; what he writes is altogether worth reading. See among the letters, book I, letter 17, otherwise *Opuscule* 23.

“‘You once earnestly asked me what cause seems to me to explain why the bishop of the Apostolic See never lives long, but ends his final day within a short period of time; so that after the holy Apostle Peter, who presided for about twenty-five years, no Roman pontiff afterward equalled that duration of episcopal rule. Indeed, in modern times scarcely anyone is raised to the summit of that see who passes the limit of four, or at most five, years. As we consider this, a prodigious astonishment, so to speak, arises, because this necessity of a short life is found in no other Church in the whole world. But insofar as the mystery of the divine dispensation is revealed to mortals, it seems to us that this order of heavenly judgment is arranged for this reason: to instil fear of death into the human race, and to show clearly, in the very primacy of glory, how contemptible the glory of temporal life is.’” Etc. [Col. 0824B–C]

Damian, I admit, confined the lives of the pontiffs within excessively narrow bounds when he did not extend them beyond four or five years. Yet they seem to me to have been compressed into briefer limits still, if one consults the history of the pontiffs. St Bernard therefore rightly exhorts Eugenius in this letter to learn, from the exceedingly brief reigns of his predecessors, to regard his own as uncertain. Thus far Horstius.

Bernard’s letter to the cardinal fathers who elected Eugenius, also elegant and marked by various expressions of feeling, may be read in the source itself.

## § XXXV. Pope Eugenius withdraws to Viterbo; while celebrating sacred rites there before Armenians, he performs a miracle; St Bernard’s writings against the intruded Archbishop of York; certain domestic affairs; the ambition of the notorious Nicholas of Arremar; etc.

[Col. 0825A]

371. The compiler of the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 3, treats of the entry of Arnold of Brescia into the City and of the populace there stirred up by him. We have already said enough above concerning the outrages of this turbulent man. “But Eugenius,” the same author continues (§3), “avoiding the fury of the frenzied Roman citizens, withdrew to Viterbo; where, remaining until the end of the year, he seemed not so much to yield as to give place to anger, which, once it had boiled over [perhaps: *deferbuerit*, ‘cooled down’], could more easily be restrained. Yet first he struck Jordan and his associates with an anathema; and he enlisted the Tiburtines, the ancient enemies of the Romans, as auxiliaries, so that, harassed by them, they might more readily come to their senses.” [Col. 0825B] See Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 31. “But,” says Manrique, “we shall speak of these matters in their proper time.”

Meanwhile, so that happier matters might be mingled with sad ones and each might temper the other, the scene changes; and he adduces that passage from Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals* for this year, §27: “There occurred what the divine oracle, uttered by the mouth of Truth, had declared concerning the predestination of the saints: ‘They shall come from East and West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while the children of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness’; so that, while the Romans fall away, peoples hasten from afar; while those who are near deny, those who are far off profess, that thus at least all who hate Zion may be put to shame.”

The same father of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, in treating this year, and Manrique likewise in the cited chapter 3, record several embassies of foreign peoples to the Apostolic See. Among the events said to have occurred, however, the following remarkable miracle, reported by Baronius from Otto of Freising, seems not to be passed over; though, to avoid excessive length, we shall compress it.

372. “At that time also,” says Baronius, §29, “while Eugenius was staying at Viterbo, he received embassies from the East, from Armenia and Syria, as is reported by Otto, who was present and faithfully wrote even what he saw.” From Otto’s own book VII, chapter 32, we therefore extract the following:

“At that time envoys of the Armenian bishops and of their metropolitan—envoys from almost the furthest East—approached [Col. 0825D] the Supreme Pontiff at Viterbo, and, offering him on behalf of that church complete submission, explained to us, in the presence of many others, at the old palace, the reasons for their journey. … Between them and the Greeks there is agreement in certain matters concerning the rite of sacrifice, but in others disagreement. For they use leavened bread (a point refuted by Pagi under the year of Christ 1145, §8), as the Greeks do; but they do not add water to the wine, as we and the Greeks do. … Since they differed among themselves concerning these and other matters, they chose the Roman Church as judge, came to seek counsel, and asked that the form of sacrifice according to her custom be imparted to them. The Roman pontiff received them graciously, admitted them to the solemnities of Mass and to the secret prayers of the sacrifice, [Col. 0826A] and carefully directed them to observe what was done there.

373. “While they were doing so, … one of them, invested with episcopal rank, as he afterwards related in full court, on the octave of Saint Martin, when the dedication of the church of Saint Peter is customarily celebrated, saw, while the Supreme Pontiff was performing the divine mysteries, a ray of sunlight gleaming in splendid brilliance above his head, and two doves ascending and descending within it. As he looked more carefully this way and that and found no opening through which that light could have been admitted, he recognized it as divine and, further inflamed toward obedience to the Roman See, disclosed to all what he had seen. But the venerable Father, attributing this not to his own merits, maintained rather that it had been shown him from heaven because of that man’s faith: namely, that the church from which he had been sent might recognize the power of the Sacraments flooded with the light of truth, and thereafter learn with what reverence and in what form it ought to handle them.”

Thus far Otto of Freising. We have all the more willingly interwoven into this Commentary the things he records, because the outstanding marvel which occurred while Pope Eugenius was conducting the sacred rites strongly commends reverence for that pope, and therefore also reflects upon Bernard himself and upon his sacred Clairvaux community.

374. The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 4 for the present year, §1, displays Pope Eugenius’s concern for the faithful in the East and proceeds to recount what was then done by the pontiff, by Christian princes, and especially by Bernard himself for the expedition of the holy war and the defence of the Holy Land. But because he pursues the same theme through several succeeding years, interweaving with it other matters unrelated to the subject, we believe that the understanding of events so memorable, their chronological order, and the manner of the narrative will be better served if we join together in one continuous account what he separated for chronological reasons and interrupted with other histories, presenting under one view the deeds of several years, from the year of Christ 1146 onward. We refer the reader there.

For the peace concluded by Pope Eugenius with the Romans, its conditions, and the common joy with which the same pontiff was received at Rome, Manrique may be consulted in the cited chapter 4, §§10–11. Meanwhile let us proceed to chapter 5 of the year 1145 in the aforementioned *Annals*, which Manrique opens as follows.

375. “Meanwhile Bernard, prompted alike by his affection for his own people and by his zeal for the public good, was urged by Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, and by the leading men of the English Church, to act against William, the intruder at York, on behalf of Henry, his [spiritual] son.” He considered that the cause, long begun and debated, had still not been settled through the deaths of three popes, and remained pending, not without grave injury to justice and to the Church itself. He therefore wrote a second letter to Pope Eugenius, forceful and vigorous, openly [Col. 0827A] declaring what the first had more covertly suggested: that useless branches must be cut off and fruitless trees uprooted.”

Immediately thereafter, §2, the letter is quoted. It is no. 239 in Mabillon’s ordering. “Pope Eugenius, however,” Manrique says in §4, “when he had learned the state of the cause, preserved unchanged since Innocent’s death, and deferring to his predecessor’s judgment, confirmed by his letters that reliance was to be placed on the oath of the dean of York, which William had most insistently demanded: unless the dean should remove by oath the charge of intrusion, among others brought against William, the election was to be declared invalid and null. The dean at first withdrew himself from judgment, feigned ignorance, and avoided conferences. At last, when compelled by censures, though he wholeheartedly favoured William, he nevertheless gave more weight to truth and religion than to friendship; finally he again pronounced the man an intruder, said so again, and declared the election void and invalid, with Henry’s election to be held thereafter.”

376. “Then William, struck by his own sword and seeing his own weapons turned against him, judged that he must take refuge in the later letters of Innocent, genuine or forged; and, by a new device, he gave Eugenius the matter to deal with, so that he should henceforth write to Father Bernard that he was zealous for the church of York and wished to remove that idol from its midst, but that he still hesitated over the more suitable means of deposing him. Then the holy Father, steadfast for truth and for his son, yet also zealous for Innocent, who was being accused of duplicity in his [Col. 0827C] letters, again brandished his pen against William. Strengthening the pope, and drawing even from the good acts which he had heard Eugenius had performed, he wrote him such a letter.”

It is found in the edition just cited as no. 240, though there assigned to the year of Christ 1146. Events fulfilled Bernard’s wishes. For Eugenius, “overcome by the merits of the case and Bernard’s urgency, at last adjudged that William should be deprived and Henry appointed in his place. Indeed, after summoning and consecrating him, he soon honoured him, as custom required, with the pallium; and thus honoured, sent him back to York,” says Manrique, §7. He then also reports the sacrilegious acts committed by supporters of the deposed man. On this subject there is a letter of Saint Bernard [Col. 0827D] in Mabillon’s edition, no. 252; the reader may consult the note to it, where it is dated to the year of Christ 1147.

377. In chapter 6 the Cistercian historian, taking up his pen to write of certain private and domestic concerns of his order, speaks of the successor in the headship of Saints Vincent and Anastasius at Rome of Peter Bernard, who had been raised to the chair of Peter. This was Rualenus. Bernard, as is narrated there in §§2–3, reluctantly endured the removal from himself of “the dear son whom he loved more tenderly than the others …, although he strongly resisted and prayed that he might be allowed to rest in his father’s bosom. But obedience to the Supreme Pontiff finally prevailed. … Yet when Rualenus remained in Rome, sluggish or humble, [Col. 0828A] neither changing his spirit with his place nor permitting himself to be moved by the allurements either outwardly of the court … or inwardly of his office as superior; rather, persistently requesting Father Bernard by letters and messengers to secure permission for his return, the holy Father, compassionating him with his customary paternal affection but nevertheless deferring to Pope Eugenius, by whose election he had chiefly come there, wrote him such a letter,” no. 258, asking that he be sent back.

But it happened that Eugenius “not only did not grant the request, but wrote more severely to Bernard, as though Bernard were unwilling to please him. Then the holy abbot imposed silence on Rualenus and on himself in this matter, and wrote again both to Rualenus and to Eugenius: to the latter, to show that the obedience had been voluntary; to the former, that he should obey,” as [Col. 0828B] Manrique says, §5. These are letters 259 and 260.

378. The historian just mentioned, chapter 8, writes of the blessed death of the venerable Humbert, a monk of Clairvaux, who died in Saint Bernard’s hands, and concerning whom the holy man addressed a sermon to the brethren, extolling his virtues with deserved praises. It is found among Bernard’s other sermons in Mabillon’s edition, col. 1066 and following, but is assigned to the year of Christ 1148. See the notes there.

The same author, in chapter 8, §10, says: “In this very year, so far as may be gathered from the sequence of the writings and from Bernard’s life itself, Father Bernard, interrupting his sermons on the *Song of Songs*, undertook, for the benefit of the monks during Lent, to explain the psalm *Qui habitat* [‘He who dwells’]; he completed it in seventeen sermons.” These are interwoven among the saint’s other sermons in the cited Mabillon edition, col. 827 and following; but they are dated to about the year 1140, as may be seen in the note to the sixth sermon.

379. The ninth chapter of the *Cistercian Annals* consists of a rather long narrative presenting to the reader the crafty devices of a certain hypocritical man, by which he insinuated himself intimately into Saint Bernard’s friendship and familiarity, intending by this means to acquire great renown, for which he was exceedingly greedy. Although it matters little to our purpose if this story is omitted, yet, because it has a natural connection with the deeds of the holy abbot, we shall compress part of it from Manrique. “Nicholas of Arremar, a young man, handsome in appearance, with manners either cultivated or feigned, but with talent and eloquence almost miraculous—so that Peter the Venerable of Cluny cherished him and others held him in admiration—when he saw Eugenius occupying the highest seat of the Church and Father Bernard [Col. 0828D] held in the highest estimation, resolved to go to Clairvaux. … He considered that Father Bernard, now burdened with old age and illnesses and entangled in affairs beyond his strength, needed a secretary who could imitate his weighty phraseology, his inverted scriptural passages, and his sweet style; and that he, if anyone, was suited to this office. … Once admitted to this service, through daily use he would become more capable; through greater familiarity, more useful and almost indispensable; and would soon attain what he desired: to become known to the world through the holy Father. … This was Nicholas’s sole motive for feigning conversion and his aim in simulating a more perfect zeal for religious life. But his feigned devotion feared Bernard as a detector, and he thought he could conceal himself better if he were first commended to Bernard’s sons, as simpler men, and then through them to the saint.

380. “Accordingly, under the pretext of seeing companions … or visiting that holy house, … he arrived there while Bernard was absent. … There, as though suddenly warmed with zeal and drawn by the holy way of life of God’s servants, he marvelled at their life, praised the men, … and called himself unhappy because he lacked so great a good. If he were admitted to the company of the saints, he declared that he would be blessed even in this life. If only he dared to hope—if only he dared to ask! … These and similar remarks, first spread through the community and then addressed to the prior and elders, were so gladly received by all that Bernard’s absence alone prevented them from assenting to the petitioner’s wishes. … Finally all agreed that Arremar should meanwhile return and persevere in his original vocation until the Clairvaux monks could make it known to Bernard upon his return, and Bernard in turn could present and commend the vocation to Peter the Venerable, so that the necessary approvals might be secured.” … Thus he departed from Clairvaux not without tears—whether genuine or feigned, who would dare judge? But because Bernard’s affairs detained him longer than usual, the man, unable to endure delay, crafty and shrewd, concealing vices under a show of religion, first persuaded the venerable Theobald, prior of Arremar, to make the same request. Then, having him both as partner in his plan and helper in his prayers, he wrote this letter to the elders of Clairvaux, calculated to win them by its style, whether because it was effective and forceful with them or because it might lighten the burden of their father.”

A copy of this letter follows there. After it has been quoted and several other matters narrated, which may be read in that place, the author recounts what Nicholas did once his desire had been granted and he was in the monastery of Clairvaux, in order to attain his predetermined goal of acquiring a great name.

381. “The outwardly upright and modest manners of the crafty young man on entering Clairvaux, his keen and lively intelligence, his sweet and easily adaptable style, and then his constant service [Col. 0829D] won him favour with the holy abbot. All these things, approved and praised by others—especially by Peter, abbot of Cluny, whose judgment Bernard greatly respected—strongly recommended Nicholas to Bernard. And perhaps amid these very things a spark of self-love lay hidden, since a man desirous of rest and solitude found in him someone to whom he could entrust even difficult affairs. Thus the way was opened for Nicholas’s desire, as the holy Father used his pen in many matters, and others followed Bernard’s example. Through these writings Nicholas soon became known throughout the whole world. … Thus Nicholas quickly acquired the celebrated name for which he had so ardently longed.”

Manrique gathered these and many other matters concerning this hypocrite under the present year 1145, chapter 9. There, §13—and Pagi, after him, in the *Critica* under the year 1146, §13—he maintains that Nicholas’s fraudulent conversion must be placed in 1145, correcting Baronius, “who supposes that Nicholas was discovered in the following year and denounced to Pope Eugenius; whereas he revealed himself much later, as the whole course of the history will plainly show,” says the same Cistercian historian. “Nor is it credible,” as Pagi rightly writes, “that Nicholas should have been discovered so quickly by Saint Bernard as a forger and yet not immediately dismissed from his service.”

So much, then, for that impostor at present. It will later be useful to remember these matters, along with others that I append here for a fuller knowledge of Bernard’s history, in which Nicholas afterwards played his part wickedly and fraudulently, when we return elsewhere to the same subject.

382. I follow the most learned Mabillon, [Col. 0830B] who in the second part of his preface to volume III of Saint Bernard’s works carefully notes various matters concerning this notorious Nicholas from p. 712 onward. Mabillon reports as follows what I was saying from Manrique concerning his character and natural gifts:

“Nicholas was French by nation; from early youth a monk in the monastery of Arremar [commonly Montier-Ramey], in the diocese of Troyes, four leagues from that city. He was a man of facile and versatile talent, readily entering into the affections of others, very highly cultivated in letters for his time, and placed in charge of instructing others among his Arremar brethren. He was dear to the leading men of that age: Atto, bishop of Troyes; Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny; Peter of Celle; Henry, brother of Louis the Younger; and others.”

Mabillon immediately treats of Nicholas’s admission to Clairvaux; but enough has already been said above on that matter. Regarding “the office of secretary entrusted to him,” Mabillon says: “Bernard had several secretaries because of the various matters continually referred to him. The chief was Geoffrey, and Nicholas was joined to him.” The things in which Nicholas himself there describes his *museum*—his study or writing establishment—are evidence to the author of the said preface that “Nicholas himself also had secretaries under him.”

I do not transcribe the matters related in the same preface concerning the exchange of books; the tunic sent to him by a friend and returned by him as insufficiently suited to his order; or, finally, the letters by which he kept up intercourse with friends. The reader may readily consult Mabillon’s cited preface concerning these. Yet I shall extract some matters from it [Col. 0830D] that bear more closely upon our purpose and therefore upon Bernard’s history. They occur at col. 715 and following.

383. “Nicholas was a friend, even a cherished favourite, of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny. Bernard repeatedly sent him to Peter, so that the secret matters of their hearts and their reciprocal affection might be entrusted to this intermediary. On this subject read Peter’s letter, no. 264 among Bernard’s letters. But at last—O unhappy condition of mortals!—Nicholas abused Bernard’s indulgence and trustfulness, forged his seal for evil purposes, and finally fell into a dreadful apostasy, which it is doubtful whether he ever seriously corrected.

“Bernard informed Eugenius of the corrupted seal in letter 284, without naming Nicholas, such being the holy man’s charity: ‘We have been endangered by false brethren, and many letters forged under our falsified seal have fallen into the hands of many; and—what I fear more—it is said that the falsehood has even reached you.’ In letter 298, to the same Eugenius, he laments Nicholas’s disastrous fall, now no longer concealing the author because the crime was public: ‘That Nicholas went out from us because he was not of us; and he went out leaving foul traces behind him. I had known the man long before, but waited either for God to convert him or for him, like Judas, to betray himself. … And this has happened. Besides books, money, and much gold, three seals were found upon him as he was leaving: one his own, another the prior’s, and the third ours. … As for his shameful acts, by which the land is defiled and which have made him a byword to all, I refrain from polluting my lips and your ears.’”

Bernard adds that, should Nicholas dare to go to Eugenius’s court, as he had boasted that he would, he deserved, as much as anyone, perpetual confinement. This fall occurred in 1151, as is clear from Bernard’s mentioned letter 298 to Eugenius, written that year, and from letter 388 of Peter the Venerable, concerning the election at Grenoble made in the same year. In that letter Nicholas is praised as still dear to Bernard and Peter and as the faithful messenger between them both.

384. It is further observed in the frequently mentioned preface that this Nicholas must be distinguished from another Englishman of the same name. Its words are these: “All suppose that he fled to England and took refuge in the monastery of Saint Albans, and that he is the Nicholas who, after Bernard’s death, disparaged and attacked Bernard’s opinion concerning the conception of the Mother of God, and had Peter of Celle as his opponent. This man too was called Nicholas; but that he was English is clear from two letters of Peter addressed to him, book VI, letter 23, and book IX, letter 10,” whose words are there quoted. “But from what has been said it is clear that Nicholas of Clairvaux was, before his flight, very well known and intimate with Peter; that he was not English but Gallic or French; and therefore that he must be distinguished from that Englishman.”

385. [Col. 0831D] “But where then, you ask, did the French Nicholas take refuge? After wandering about in various directions, he finally settled in his monastery at Arremar, where, once Bernard had been taken from the living, he could live safely and without fear.” The proofs may be seen in the same preface, which also states, from Nicholas’s own words, what position or status he held in the monastery of Arremar.

“Thus Nicholas lived among the Arremar brethren,” says Mabillon, “as his own master. Truly a miserable condition for a man who had been Bernard’s disciple and secretary! But who should wonder, when angels themselves fell from heaven? In this especially he displays his vanity: he boasts of the multitude of his friends, as he was accustomed to do on other occasions.” The letter adduced there as proof also indicates “that Nicholas was born in Champagne; but that the cause of his fall must be sought nowhere but in vain glory and pride, which drive most men mad. … From all this it appears what Nicholas’s character was: vain, inconstant, restless—one of those from whom scarcely anything good may ever be hoped. But what his end was, we do not know.”

But now it is time, after this digression, to return to our subject.

§ XXXVI. Services rendered to the public good of the Church and to the Apostolic See; a synopsis of what the man of God did and suffered for the holy war.

386. The *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 1 under the year of Christ 1146, record that the venerable Peter Mauricius, abbot of Cluny, went to Rome to Pope Eugenius. Saint Bernard’s letter 277 to the same Vicar of Christ survives, warmly commending him. “The venerable abbot at length arrived at Rome,” as Manrique writes there in §6, “where he was received by Eugenius not merely kindly but reverently, as one whom, even had Bernard said nothing, Eugenius knew to have deserved well of the whole Church and, from its beginning, especially well of Cîteaux.” More concerning Peter appears there.

The same *Annals*, chapter 3, §1, report Pope Eugenius’s second flight from the city of Rome and its circumstances: “While the pontiff governed the world from the City, providing for all now personally and now through vigorous legates, he experienced the city’s rebellion again and again withdrew. He who had recently been received with branches and hymns was, scarcely three months later, attacked with stones and blasphemies and driven into flight.” Then §3 states:

“When this second sedition of the Roman city had reached Bernard’s ears at Clairvaux through public report and letters from friends—though Baronius refers it to the earlier revolt—he was inflamed, as usual, with zeal for justice, brandished his pen as a sword, and first wrote to the Romans, reproving, entreating, and rebuking them; but soon also wrote to Emperor Conrad, so that, if the obstinate persisted, they might nevertheless be restrained by arms through him.”

The letter sent to the Romans is printed among Bernard’s letters republished by Mabillon as no. 243; another, addressed to Conrad, immediately follows it. Both are there assigned to the year 1146; both give clear proof of the ardent zeal with which the holy man burned for the public good of the Church and the See of Peter, as will be evident to anyone who reads them. Pagi also observes under the present year 1146, §1, that both letters belong to that year, against Baronius, who quotes them under the preceding year.

387. In the immediately preceding paragraph we promised to treat, in this year and those following, of the holy expedition of Christian princes against the unbelievers in the East, in a single continuous narrative so that the matter might stand out more clearly. We now fulfil that promise, first setting out what Mabillon briefly writes in §7 of his General Preface. It may serve [Col. 0833A] as a synopsis for understanding in outline the longer narrative of this history which we shall begin in the following section.

“Among Bernard’s final labours,” he says, “must be counted his preaching of the holy expedition to the Holy Land. How much labour and trouble this undertaking brought him may readily be understood from his *Life* and writings. The occasion of this expedition, as we learn from Otto of Freising, arose through Louis the Younger, king of the Franks. Pressed by a desire to go to the holy places—because his brother Philip, bound by the same vow, had been prevented by death from fulfilling it—he disclosed his plan to the princes of the realm. They decided that Bernard should be consulted. When the holy abbot was summoned, he judged that a matter of such importance should be referred to the examination of the Roman pontiff. Eugenius highly commended and approved this judgment, granting authority to preach and move all minds to this end to the aforesaid abbot, who was regarded by all the peoples of Gaul and Germany as a prophet or apostle. Armed at last with apostolic letters and having stirred many minds to the overseas expedition, Bernard marked King Louis with the cross at Vézelay, together with Thierry of Flanders, Count Henry, son of Theobald of Blois, other counts, barons, and nobles.

388. “Meanwhile, a certain monk Radulf, likewise preaching the cross in Germany, incited Christians to kill Jews. Bernard restrained the man by letters and himself undertook the preaching of the holy expedition in the eastern realm of the Franks—that is, in the part of Germany situated upon the Rhine. Conrad the emperor accordingly convoked a general assembly at Speyer. Bernard went there and persuaded Emperor Conrad, together with Frederick, the son of Conrad’s brother, and other princes and distinguished men to take the cross, performing numerous miracles publicly and privately. Bernard softened Duke Frederick of Swabia, who was deeply troubled that his son had taken the cross; ordered the monk Radulf to be shut up again in his cloister; and, in his own place, gave Abbot Adam of Ebrach as a companion to Conrad, who was setting out for Bavaria, to press forward the business of the journey.

“There survives Bernard’s letter on this matter to the eastern Franks, now no. 363; it is immediately followed by another to Henry, archbishop of Mainz, for the restraint of Radulf. ‘Thus,’ Otto says, ‘not only from the Roman Empire but also from the neighbouring realms—namely western Francia, England, and Pannonia—countless peoples and nations were stirred by the report of this expedition to take the cross; and suddenly nearly the entire West became so quiet that it was held unlawful not merely to start wars, but even for anyone to carry weapons in public.’

389. “This great movement throughout the West was attributed to Bernard’s preaching. But because the expedition did not succeed according to hopes, all the odium of its unhappy outcome was likewise cast upon him, according to the common habit of mortals, who judge matters by their outcomes. There was scarcely any other thing that afflicted Bernard’s mind with greater sorrow, and that not so much for his own sake as for God’s. Hence, at the beginning of book II of *On Consideration*: ‘If one of two things must happen, I prefer that men should murmur against us rather than against God. It is good for me if he deigns to use me as a shield. I willingly receive upon myself the slanderous tongues of detractors,’ etc.

“Almost everyone’s mind was so disturbed by this result that the holy doctor calls blessed the man who was not scandalized by it. Finally, how great Bernard’s sorrow over this was is clear both from letter 288, which he wrote on this subject while lying in bed, perhaps from grief of mind, and from letter 386 among Bernard’s letters, written to Bernard himself by John, abbot of La Case-Dieu, who consoles the holy man because he had heard that he was distressed by the expedition’s adverse result.

390. “Yet there were those who undertook to defend Bernard’s case. Among them, not least in rank, must be counted Otto, bishop of Freising, who was not generally very favourable to Bernard. In book I of *The Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 60, Otto makes a digression to excuse the outcome of that expedition, in which he himself took part. At the end of this digression, philosophical rather than historical, he concludes in Bernard’s favour:

‘If we say that that holy abbot was inspired by the Spirit of God to stir us up, but that we, through our pride and self-indulgence, failed to observe the salutary commands and therefore deservedly suffered losses of things and persons, this is not inconsistent with ancient arguments or examples.’

He adds only one qualification: that the spirits of prophets are not always subject to prophets; by this he seems to indicate that it is uncertain whether Bernard formed his judgment concerning this expedition and its outcome through the divine Spirit.

391. “Nevertheless Bernard himself, at the beginning of book II of *On Consideration* addressed to Eugenius, where he defends his action against slander, does not deny that he was divinely impelled to it. ‘We proclaimed peace,’ he says, ‘and there is no peace; we promised good things, and behold turmoil.’ Then he adds in his own defence: ‘As though we had acted in this undertaking from rashness or frivolity. Certainly we ran in it, not as into uncertainty, but at your command—indeed, through you, at God’s command.’ And later, after setting out the reproaches levelled against him by men—‘How do we know that the word came forth from the Lord? What signs do you perform that we may believe you?’—he replies, addressing Eugenius: ‘There is no need for me myself to answer these things: my modesty must be spared. Answer for me, and for yourself, according to what you have heard and seen.’ By these words he doubtless modestly indicates the miracles performed by him in confirmation of his preaching.

392. “But Geoffrey most excellently vindicates his holy Father from slander in book III, chapter 4, of Bernard’s *Life*: first, because the original proposal for that expedition did not proceed from him. For, though the need had already moved many minds, and though the king of the Franks had once and again sought him out for this purpose, and even though apostolic letters had urged him, Bernard did not consent even to speak or give advice on the subject until at last the pope himself, by a general letter, commanded him to address peoples and princes as the voice of the Roman Church. Secondly, because the office of preaching, which he had undertaken through obedience, was divinely confirmed by so many and such great miracles and signs that it would be difficult even to count them, much less narrate them. Finally, if by that expedition the Eastern Church did not deserve to be delivered, the heavenly Church surely deserved to be filled and made joyful: namely, through the death of those who, in fruits of repentance and purified through various tribulations, rendered their souls to Christ. Indeed, this is precisely what John, the holy abbot of La Case-Dieu, informed Bernard that he had learned by revelation.

“But why delay in defending Bernard? His authority is so great that long ago his life, outstanding holiness, and teaching were approved in the common judgment and estimation of all, even of the heterodox.”

§ XXXVII. The actions of Pope Eugenius, King Louis, and Saint Bernard for the holy war; the preaching and miracles of the man of God; the supreme command of the military enterprise entrusted to him alone but declined by him; the people of Langres reconciled; his authority interposed in other disputes.

393. Geoffrey, formerly a monk of Clairvaux, Saint Bernard’s secretary and afterwards abbot there, writes in book II of his *Life* concerning the unhappy outcome of the holy war carried by Christians into the East, while Bernard’s preaching sounded its summons far and wide, and concerning the murmuring against the holy man which then arose. He has left us ample scope for further discussion, so that we may illustrate in fuller detail this subject, which Mabillon shortly before presented generally in synopsis.

The Cistercian historian relates in chapter 4 that certain foundations of this holy expedition were laid in the year of Christ 1145: “Meanwhile Eugenius, considering in his heart and pondering deeply what he had heard concerning the injuries inflicted in the East upon the Christian people by the unbelievers—Edessa having been captured, Antioch thereby endangered, and Jerusalem itself brought into peril—[lacuna] thought that common arms ought to be taken up against the Saracens. Whether Louis anticipated him or was anticipated by him is uncertain. It is certain that both agreed on this: one would proclaim the expedition and the other undertake it; neither would do anything without Bernard. But let us hear Otto, an author of the same age and present at almost all these events, relate these very matters with the authority he possessed among all.”

In book I of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, chapter 34, Otto records the following, taken from the latest Milanese edition, volume VI, col. 668: “Louis, having secretly cherished the desire to go to Jerusalem, because his brother Philip, bound by the same vow, had been forestalled by death, and unwilling longer to delay his purpose, summoned certain of his princes and disclosed to them what he was turning over in his mind.

394. “At that time there was in Gaul a certain abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, called Bernard [Col. 0836A], venerable in life and character, distinguished in the observance of religion, endowed with wisdom and learning, renowned for signs and miracles. The prince decided that he should be summoned, and that he should be consulted, as though an oracle from God, concerning what ought to be done in this matter. The aforesaid abbot was summoned, and his counsel was requested concerning the will of the prince just mentioned. He, judging it rash to give an answer concerning so great an undertaking on the basis of his own authority, replied that the best course was to refer the matter to the hearing and judgment of the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, an embassy having been sent to Eugenius, the whole business was laid before him. Recalling the examples of his predecessors—namely, that Urban, on a similar occasion, had restored to the unity of peace the Church overseas and the two patriarchal sees [Col. 0836B], Antioch and Jerusalem, which had been severed from obedience to the Roman See—he assented to the wishes of the aforesaid king for the enlargement of the Christian religion, granting to the above-named abbot, who was regarded among all the peoples of Gaul and Germany as a prophet or apostle, authority to preach and to move the minds of all toward this purpose. Hence a letter of his, directed to the king and his princes, is found in the following form.”

Immediately the same author adds that letter in chapter 35; but because it is rather long, and was printed by Baronius and Manrique under the year of Christ 1145, we do not transcribe it again here.

395. Moreover, writers cited by Pagi under the year of Christ 1145, no. 13, report that Louis VII, king of the Franks, undertook his eastern expedition by vow because he was remorseful [Col. 0836C] over the burning of the basilica of Vitry, together with the thirteen hundred persons who had fled into it (see what was said above, §32). It would be lengthy to recount individually the preparations made in Gaul before that expedition under the said king: such were the assemblies at Bourges, concerning which Pagi writes under the year just cited, no. 12; and likewise at Vézelay, under 1146, no. 3.

Concerning the former, he says: “Odo of Deuil, a monk of Saint-Denis and successor of Suger in the abbacy of that monastery, composed seven little books on the expedition of Louis VII, king of the Franks, to the East [Col. 0836D]. These were brought out of obscurity by Pierre-François Chifflet in his *Assertion of the Illustrious Lineage of Saint Bernard*, and may enrich ecclesiastical history.”

He then quotes from the first book of that Odo several matters concerning both those assemblies. But the praised Odo writes various things in the same first book about the assembly at Vézelay which concern Saint Bernard. Besides other matters that may be read in Chifflet, I select the following words of Odo, from page 11:

“In the year of the incarnate Word 1146, the glorious king of the Franks … that he might be worthy of Christ, began at Vézelay, at Easter, to follow Him by carrying his cross … The abbot also [of Clairvaux], fortified by apostolic authority and by his own holiness, and a very great multitude of those assembled, were likewise present … [Col. 0837A] And because there was no place in the castle that could contain so great a crowd, a wooden platform was erected for the abbot outside in the field, so that he might speak to those standing around from on high. He ascended it with the king, adorned with the cross.”

396. “And when the heavenly instrument, according to its custom, had poured forth the dew of the divine word, they began from every side to cry out, demanding crosses, crosses. And when he had scattered rather than given out the bundle of crosses prepared beforehand, he was compelled to tear his own garments into crosses and scatter them. He labored at this as long as he remained in the town.
