I refrain from writing of the miracles that occurred there at that time, by which it appeared that this undertaking pleased the Lord: lest, if I write a few, people should fail to believe that more occurred; or, if many, I should seem to have omitted the subject. At length [Col. 0837B], when it had been decreed that they should set out after a year, all returned joyfully to their homes. But the abbot, beneath a frail and almost lifeless body concealing a vigorous spirit, flew about wherever he went preaching, and in a short time those carrying the cross multiplied beyond number.”

For the assembly at Vézelay, Otto of Freising, just cited, chapter 36, may also be consulted; for those at Laon and Chartres, Pagi under the year 1146, no. 6. Under no. 5 he names the more notable persons marked with the cross. Pope Eugenius did not personally preside over the conference at Vézelay; for, according to Odo, page 12: “He himself indeed desired to lay the first hand, in person, to so holy a work; but, impeded by the tyranny of the Romans, he could not. He delegated this charge to the holy abbot Bernard of Clairvaux.” Indeed, Pagi shows that Eugenius came to Gaul only in 1147, there, no. 5, against others whom he cites under 1146 and corrects to this year, no. 2. Manrique, under 1145, chapter 4, no. 9, may likewise be consulted on this matter.

397. We have quite recently mentioned the assembly at Chartres, so far as was sufficient for our present purpose; yet the remarkable office entrusted to the holy abbot in the council assembled there for the expedition of the sacred soldiery properly calls for fresh mention here. Baronius, under the year of Christ 1146, writes of the summoning and celebration of that council and of the distinguished persons assembled in it. Then he asks, no. 3: “What was done there?” And he replies:

“Above all, this is plainly astonishing [Col. 0837D], and will amaze all who hear it: namely, that there the holy Bernard himself was chosen by the unanimous consent of all as commander of the entire war, to act as chief of the army, to whom all the soldiers and even the princes themselves should be subject. This was decreed in the council by universal consent. Lest you think this a fable, the letters of Saint Bernard to Pope Eugenius, treating of these matters, must be set down here: first, commending Eugenius’s zeal from the letters written by him, encouraging him toward further action, and finally recounting what was done in the Council of Chartres.”

398. I transcribe what follows from Letter 256 of the saint in due order, where the preceding matters may also be read:

“Further,” he says, “concerning that report which, unless I am mistaken, you have already heard—how at the assembly of Chartres (by what judgment I greatly wonder) they chose me, as it were, leader and prince of the army—let it be certain to you that this neither has been nor is a matter of my counsel or my will; nor does it lie within my power, so far as I measure my own strength, to attain to such a position. Who am I, to draw up battle-lines of camps, to go forth before the faces of armed men? And what could be more remote from my profession, even if strength were available, even if skill were not lacking? Yet it is not for me to instruct your wisdom. You know all these things. I ask only, by that love through which you are especially indebted to me, that you do not expose me to human wishes; but that, since it especially rests upon you, you seek the divine counsel and endeavor that, as [Col. 0838B] the will is in heaven, so it may be done.”

Mabillon, in his note upon this letter, advises readers to consult the letters of Peter the Venerable and of Suger concerning this assembly.

399. When “Eugenius first received Bernard’s letters,” according to the Cistercian historian under the year 1146, chapter 5, “and learned of the military preparations that had begun in Gaul and, if they were advanced, might easily be expected to extend far into other provinces, he judged that the sails should be spread to favorable winds. Thinking that no other sailor should be employed than the very man who had begun the voyage so successfully, he writes back eagerly to Bernard himself: not that he needs his material sword or military command—though the princes of Gaul also ask for this—but only his spiritual sword, that is, the sword of the Spirit, which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, is the word of God. Let him summon war with the priestly trumpet; let him preach, rebuke, reproach the Christians: the places of our salvation are in straits; our brethren are endangered and miserably destined for slaughter; those places are to be profaned sacrilegiously and impiously, while Christians themselves remain idle and luxuriate in leisure, unless they come to their aid. Let him instill rage—or, more truly, zeal—against the unbelievers into the faithful peoples, and stir the whole Christian world against the despisers of the cross. This embassy of Eugenius—once his son, now his friend, now his father, and indeed acting in the name of the whole Church—was to be undertaken eagerly by the man of God, who had never spared himself any labors or dangers for that cause.” Manrique says that Geoffrey recounts these and similar commands sent once and again by Eugenius to Bernard. Let the reader consult Geoffrey the biographer, Book III, chapter 2.

400. “When the court was dissolved, and the king,” continues the same annalist, no. 3, “and the pontiffs had returned to their own places to prepare what was necessary for the journey, Father Bernard traveled through the neighboring places and cities, preaching throughout the provinces, with no unequal success. Frequent miracles added the voice of power to his voice, and by these the faithful were so aroused that all but deserted the cities and left the towns empty, following the saint in order to serve Christ beneath the sign of the cross.”

Besides Odo, who spoke a little earlier of miracles, we have an unanswerable witness in Geoffrey at the place just indicated. Speaking of the signs by which the Lord confirmed the holy man’s preaching, he says: “But how many and how manifold were they? How great a number, difficult even to count, still less to recount! For they had begun to be recorded at that very time; but the sheer multitude of what had to be written finally overcame the writer himself and his subject. On one day, indeed, twenty or even more were sometimes healed of various infirmities, and scarcely was any day free from such events. In short, at that time Christ caused more people, through the touch and prayer of His servant—even those blind from their mothers’ wombs—to see, the lame to walk, the withered to recover strength, the deaf to hear, and the mute to speak.”

It is pleasing to hear the saint himself concerning the immense multitude of those signed with the cross. Writing to Eugenius about it in Letter 247, in Mabillon, he says: “You commanded, and I obeyed; and the authority of the one commanding made obedience fruitful. For I proclaimed and spoke, and they multiplied beyond number. Cities and castles are emptied; and now seven women can scarcely find one man to take hold of: so everywhere widows are left behind while their husbands yet live.”

401. Bernard accomplished these things by his living voice in places where he was present. But what need is there to say how much he achieved, by fiery letters suited to kindle the hearts of the faithful, in places from which he was absent because he could not go there, or could not go there so quickly? Consult the Cistercian historian, chapter 5 cited above, no. 8. “Moreover,” he says, “amid the preparations for war, in that same year he reconciled to peace the bishop and clergy of Langres, who were in conflict with one another. A foreseen miracle intervened, and peace was prophesied in the miracle, at a time when it was thought less likely to be achieved.” The matter is related by Geoffrey, Book IV of the *Life*, chapter 5, no. 239.

Chapter 6 of the Cistercian annals contains the acts of Pope Eugenius against the unbelievers and Bernard’s letter to him on behalf of Samson, archbishop of Reims. That letter, among Bernard’s letters published by Mabillon, is numbered 247. From the editor’s note on it:

“It was formerly customary for kings to receive the crown in a ceremonial rite on principal feasts, as occurred here at Bourges before the Jerusalem expedition. The archbishop of Bourges claimed that this was due to him in his own church. Therefore, when Samson performed it at Bourges, despite the protest of Archbishop Peter, Eugenius forbade Samson the use of the pallium [Col. 0839D]. You have papal letters on this matter in the *Patriarchate of Bourges*, from other notes.”

From these matters, I say, it is clear, first, that this sentence, in which the cause of King Louis the Younger was involved, was delivered not without danger that zeal for the said expedition might either grow cold altogether or be wholly extinguished. Second, it is clear that the holy man properly intervened with his authority to settle this controversy, especially if one considers its circumstances.

402. Let us hear Manrique, chapter 6, no. 7: “Samson … was a prelate of unblemished reputation … always numbered among Louis’s dear friends, and then still dearer after he had bestowed the crown … The promulgated sentence disturbed the king, princes, and people; although just, although proceeding from zeal for God, it nearly tore the whole overseas expedition, for which all were so ardent, from the hearts of the faithful by angering the king. But Bernard … whether from affection for Samson, whom he loved deeply; or reverence for his outstanding religious devotion, by which he excelled among the other prelates of Gaul; or finally through deference to, or fear concerning, the king—deference, I say, for his holy zeal, through which, at such expense, through such personal labors, and through so many dangers by land and sea, he was preparing the eastern expedition; but also fear lest, if he should perhaps be angered by contempt from the pontiff, he might be recalled from his purpose—wrote this letter to Eugenius, full not merely of zeal but of prudence, with the paternal authority he possessed and the freedom he always used in the causes of Christ.”

## § XXXVIII. A wicked preacher against the Jews repressed and brought to better conduct by the holy Doctor; a warning against forgers of his letters

[Col. 0840B]

403. The author of the Cistercian Annals, chapter 7, records a most savage persecution of Jews stirred up among Christians in Gaul and Germany. The occasion was a barbarous deed attributed to that faithless sect: at Norwich in England, it was said that they had crucified a boy named William. He had long before been treated as a martyr in the Bollandists, 25 March, vol. III for that month, p. 588 and following, in connection with the year of Christ 1144. The trumpet of persecution was a hermit named Radulph, who incited Christians against them by his preaching. The eastern expedition against the Saracens [Col. 0840C], which Saint Bernard was promoting so vigorously, provided an additional opportunity. Since this matter bears a certain relation to the history of the holy war now under discussion, we shall relate it briefly from the praised compiler of the Annals.

The savage slaughter of the innocent boy particularly harmed the Jews, already everywhere hated by the Christian people. “Hence,” he says, “Christian hatred against them increased; and, as zeal passed into vengeance, the cruel greed for the wealth in which they abounded led many to conspire for their destruction. Once wrath had been inflamed against the Saracens as enemies of Christ, the transition to the Jews was easier. There survives a letter of Peter the Venerable to the king of Gaul, severe against that people, worse and more pernicious than the people of the Saracens, and urging that, if they were not to be assigned to the final punishment, they should at least be deprived of the goods which they had extorted from Christians through crimes” (a fragment of the said letter is quoted in the same Annals). Thus Peter, who was the more moderate, urged the confiscation of all their goods; others cried that they should be put to death.

404. “But among the rest, a certain hermit named Radulph, whether from excessive zeal or eagerness to win popular favor, usurped the office of preaching as though sent by Bernard; and he preached the cross against the eastern Saracens, but extermination and death against the Jews at home.”

Let us hear Otto of Freising speak of him, Book I, *Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, chapter 37:

“Meanwhile, the monk Rudolph, a man indeed wearing the habit of religion and diligently imitating the strictness of religious life, but only moderately furnished with literary knowledge, entered those regions of Gaul which border upon the Rhine. He stirred up many thousands of people from Cologne, Mainz, Worms, Speyer, Strasbourg, and other neighboring cities, towns, and villages to receive the cross. Yet he heedlessly inserted this point into his teaching: that Jews dwelling everywhere in cities and towns should be slaughtered as enemies of the Christian religion. This seed of teaching took root and grew so firmly in many cities and towns of Gaul and Germany that, when very many Jews had been killed in this turbulent uprising, many fled for protection beneath the wings of the Roman prince. Thus it happened that not a few of them, fleeing such savagery, took refuge to preserve their lives in the prince’s town called Noricum or Nuremberg [Col. 0841B], and in his other fortified places.”

So far Otto on that false apostle.

405. “The bishops grieved,” Manrique adds, no. 4, “at the shedding of blood, the violation of the law of nations, the deserted cities, and the fact that they were being treated with contempt by a single monk. Under the pretext of preaching the cross on Bernard’s commission, without merely failing to consult them but against their resistance, he was throwing nearly all Germany into disorder. Henry, archbishop of Mainz, therefore sent complaining letters to the holy Doctor, because he had supposedly appointed such a man in his place—for this was believed—through whom matters so grievous and scandalous were preached under the appearance of zeal and justice. Then the holy Father, both to clear himself of this calumny and to repress the spreading evil, first wrote to the same archbishop of Mainz, and then to all the bishops of Germany.”

The text of the letter to Henry, archbishop of Mainz—number 365, formerly 323, in Mabillon’s edition—contains, among other things:

“The man discussed in your letter has come neither sent by man nor through man, nor indeed by God. If he boasts that he is a monk or hermit, and from this assumes for himself liberty or the office of preaching, he may know, and ought to know, that a monk has not the office of teaching but of mourning; for a town ought to be a prison to him, and solitude a paradise. Yet this man holds the opposite: solitude as a prison, and a town [Col. 0841D] as a paradise. O man without sense, O shameless man! His folly has been set upon a lampstand, that it may appear to all who are in the house. There are certainly three things in him most worthy of rebuke: usurpation of preaching, contempt for bishops, and license for approved homicide.”

The further remarks which he adds, accusing this false teacher and defending the proposition that a Jew’s life must not be taken, may be found in the said letter.

406. Also worthy of reading there is Letter 363, formerly 322, in which the holy man—as its title states—exhorts men to take up arms against the unbelievers for the defense of the Eastern Church. Further, he teaches that Jews must not be persecuted, much less killed, by a certain turbulent preacher. It is addressed to the archbishops, bishops, and all the clergy and people of eastern France and Bavaria.

Moreover, this letter is like a trumpet-call to the sacred expedition, of which William of Tyre speaks as follows in Book XVI, chapter 18, of his *History of the Holy War*, praising Saint Bernard in terms consistent with other commendations of that holy herald of sacred warfare given above in our present subject:

“A man of immortal memory and a mirror of honorable conduct, Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of devout and in every respect most worthy remembrance in the Lord, was chosen above all others for carrying out the aforesaid God-pleasing task. A diligent executor of the charge entrusted to him, drawing along with himself beloved fellow-workers of God in the same undertaking, active and tireless though weak in body because of nearly continual fasts [Col. 0842B] and an excessively spare diet, he traveled through kingdoms and went about the regions, everywhere proclaiming the kingdom of God,” etc.

407. But to return to the matter of the Jews, it will not be irrelevant to hear the Otto of Freising cited above:

“The aforesaid abbot of Clairvaux, teaching that such doctrine must be guarded against, sent messengers or letters to the peoples of Gaul and Germany. In them he demonstrated clearly from the authority of Holy Scripture that Jews, because of the excess of their sins, were not to be killed but scattered. He also cited the testimony of the Psalmist in Psalm 57 [rather, 58]: ‘God will show me over my enemies: do not kill them.’ And likewise: ‘Scatter them in your strength.’”

So far that historian, chapter 38. I shall conclude the account of the false and deceiving teacher Radulph by setting forth two points to observe. The first is that Radulph’s rashness was not only restrained by the holy man, but that he himself was brought by him to better conduct. Otto of Freising attests this in Book I cited above, chapter 39, where he writes concerning our abbot:

“Coming also to Mainz, he found Rudolf remaining in the highest favor with the people. Having summoned and admonished him not to assume, contrary to the rule of monks, the word of preaching on his own authority by wandering through the world, he finally induced him to return to his own monastery, after promising obedience to Bernard.”

Although this was done when Saint Bernard had gone to Germany to proclaim there the eastern military service of the cross, we join it here to the preceding history of Radulph, adding besides Manrique’s exclamation in chapter 8:

“Thus Bernard restrained by persuasion the man whom neither the prelates of the Church nor princes had restrained by the force of their power; and more swiftly than one can say it, he came, saw, conquered—removing the sin while preserving the sinner.”

It is true, however, that the people of Mainz, who had adhered to Radulph, bore his departure impatiently; for I read in Otto, chapter 39 cited above, that this occurred “while the people were greatly indignant and, unless recalled by consideration for his holiness, even wished to raise a rebellion.” So great an authority had this false apostle acquired among the deceived people. “But,” as Manrique adds concerning the holy Father, “reverence for him restrained them all; and, since they did not dare approve what Bernard had once condemned, his simple word was law to them.” This is the first point which I wished to note; I now add the second.

408. In Letter 363, which I cited, the holy Father writes:

“It is also necessary, dearest brethren, that you be warned of this: if anyone, desiring to hold primacy among you, should wish by his own expedition to precede the army of the kingdom, let him by no means dare to do so. And if he pretends that he has been sent by us, it is not true; or if he displays letters as though given by us, declare them wholly false—indeed, I will not say stolen,” etc.

The compiler of the Cistercian Annals comments upon this passage of the letter in chapter 7, no. 9:

“While Cardinal Baronius relates these matters, he is of the opinion that, when the saint calls upon all to refuse letters said to have been sent by him, knowing them to be false, he was warning them against Nicholas: the very man whom, in the preceding year, he had received as a monk at Clairvaux. Above we saw him writing in the name of Father Bernard to the count and nobles of Brittany; later we shall say that he was accustomed to counterfeit Bernard’s seal and style, to the grave harm both of Bernard and of others. But, as Manrique rightly observes, I should not believe that the holy Father discovered him so quickly, especially since he was to remain in Bernard’s service for several years. Nor is there any reason to resort to uncertainties when we possess what is certain. Since Radulph preached under Bernard’s name, which was the source of Henry of Mainz’s complaint, Bernard guarded against a similar fraud.”

Recall what I earlier set forth concerning Nicholas of Arras. Of Radulph I have just said some things by anticipation; others I shall say shortly, when the occasion is offered by the German journey undertaken by Saint Bernard, partly to restrain him and partly to arouse the princes of that region for the holy war.

## § XXXIX. He travels through Germany for the sacred military expedition; gift of tongues; force and fruit of his preaching; miracles; conference with Saint Hildegard; conversion of Alexander of Cologne

409. A twofold cause summoned the holy man into Germany. Otto of Freising, just cited, Book I, chapter 39, expresses both in these words:

“Having therefore aroused innumerable people in western Gaul to the overseas expedition, Bernard resolved, under the name of preaching, to set the eastern kingdom of the Franks in motion: both that he might soften the mind of the Roman prince by the word of holy exhortation to receive the cross, and that he might impose silence on Rudolph, who, on the occasion of the Jews, was repeatedly stirring up the people in the cities to seditions against their lords.”

These, then, were the two motives that moved the holy man to go to Germany. The twofold result he sought corresponded to them, besides other results not so much sought by the holy Father himself as freely offered to him. But account must also be taken of the time when he went there.

410. Baronius, under the year of Christ 1146, no. 25, says: “As the present year was drawing toward its end, he went to Germany.” But Manrique, under the same year, chapter 8, no. 2, judges it far more probable that this journey occurred earlier. Let us weigh his reasons:

“Cardinal Baronius thinks that he departed near the end of this year, moved, I suppose, by the prologue to the history of his miracles, which begins with the first Sunday of Advent. But since it is written in the same history, chapter 15, that on this occasion the holy Father was absent from his sons for almost a year, and elsewhere that he returned to Clairvaux not long after the feast of the Purification in the following year, we are compelled, against Baronius, either to say that he visited Toulouse against Henry before going to Germany, or that he entered Germany before the end of the year. The miracles, however, began to be written down not from his first entry but from his arrival at Constance. In any event, I judge this far more probable and also more consonant with the narrative itself. However that may be, when the saint entered Germany he kept both ends attentively in view: to summon Christians against the Saracens and to draw them back from attacks upon the Jews.”

We have already discussed these matters, including, by anticipation, the conversion of Radulph, which properly belonged in this place. It remains now to treat the former matters individually.

411. “It is established first,” Manrique asserts, chapter 8, no. 4, “that at the end of October he stayed in the city of Worms and marked many with the cross for the holy war. For when, at the beginning of January in the following year, he again visited the same city, Philip [Note: [Col. 0843] Rather, Volkmār, cleric of Constance, later a monk.], then an archdeacon and later a monk, who was present, writes as follows”—words found below in Book VI of the *Life*, part II:

“He had passed … through Worms two months before, and, after delivering a sermon, had marked there an innumerable multitude with the sign of Christian military service.”

What followed? “At Frankfurt,” as the same annalist continues, chapter 8, no. 4, “he met the emperor to transact certain business with him and, as it were incidentally, to suggest the holy war and sow seeds that would later bear fruit at Speyer. Yet he did not find the man—though most reverent and obedient toward Bernard—readily disposed in this matter. That he shrank from the overseas journey and could not be persuaded to undertake it is clearly attested by the author Philip, a brief but eyewitness narrator of all that occurred, when he describes the events at Speyer in Book VI of the *Life*, part I, chapter 2:

‘For the blessed man had previously met the king privately at Frankfurt, warning him that he ought in the season of abundant mercy to provide for his own salvation. When the king replied that he had no intention of undertaking this military service, the most gentle man fell silent, saying that it was not for his own lowliness to press the royal majesty too insistently.’”

Hence it is clear that the holy Father needed great power in speaking and persuading in order to bend Conrad, then so disposed in mind, later at Speyer in the direction he desired.

412. But we cannot leave Saint Bernard at Frankfurt for other places in Germany without relating what he accomplished there. Helmold the priest, in his *Chronicle of the Slavs*, published at Frankfurt in 1556, chapter 60, p. 128 and following, records the matter as follows:

“About those days events arose that were new and astonishing to the whole world. For while the most holy Pope Eugenius presided and Conrad III guided the helm of the kingdom, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, flourished. His renown for signs was celebrated with so great a reputation that crowds of people flowed to him from all the world, desiring to see the wonders worked through him. Having gone forth into the German land, he came to the famous court at Frankfurt, where King Conrad had then by chance assembled in festal state with a great gathering of princes. While the holy man devoted himself especially in the churches to healing the sick in the name of the Lord, with the king and highest powers standing by, it was uncertain amid so many crowds what each person suffered from or whom he might perhaps help. Our count Adolph was there, desiring to know more certainly from a divine operation the power of the man.

413. “Meanwhile a blind and lame boy was brought to him, and there could be no doubt of his disability. The most discerning man began carefully to try whether he might perhaps, in this boy, obtain proof of the saint’s holiness. The man of God, as though divinely instructed, provided a remedy for his unbelief: contrary to his customary practice, he ordered the boy to be brought to him. For he merely signed the others with words; but this boy, brought before him, he received in his hands and restored his sight by prolonged handling of his eyes. Then, taking hold of his contracted knees, he ordered him to run to the steps, giving manifest evidence that both sight and walking had been restored.”

Helmold relates these acts of Bernard at Frankfurt.

414. From there, as the *Chronicle of Hirsau* of Trithemius says—reprinted in 1690 at the press of the monastery of Saint Gall, under the year 1147, p. 415—“descending by boat, he came to Bingen, where Hildegard, a nun and most devout virgin of Christ, had built a monastery on the hill of Saint Rupert. With her he is said to have exchanged sweet conversations concerning future blessedness. For the holy servant of Christ was known to the divine Bernard both through her writings and through the reports of many, and had been approved in the Lord. When he arrived, after the customary prayers and courtesies of greeting, he ordered the volumes to be presented which she had written under divine inspiration. Having carefully examined part of them, and marveling beyond what can be expressed, he is said to have told his companions: ‘These writings have not been devised by human means, and the merely natural person cannot grasp them unless, through love, he has been inwardly and in his soul re-formed into the likeness of God.’”

More of what the saint is said to have spoken at that time may be read there. This benefit seems not to have been sought by him when he was traveling toward Germany, but to have been freely offered after he was already there: namely, that he might strengthen Hildegard against human reproaches, if this conversation with her is historically sound. I add this qualification because some things tell against it.

415. For Manrique, having related this conversation from Trithemius in chapter 8, nos. 6 and 7, quotes Trithemius’s conclusion in no. 7:

“But the holy servant of the Lord, Bernard, taking leave of the virgin of Christ Hildegard, continued his intended journey down the Rhine. At Boppard he healed a paralytic in the midst of the people by laying his hand upon him. Then he ascended Trier through the channel of the Moselle, and in that city, before all the people looking on, healed three blind men, one lame man, and a deaf woman.”

But the aforementioned Cistercian historian adds: “This is from Trithemius; as to its date, it is of doubtful credibility. For it is omitted by Philip, who, from the conference of Conrad and Bernard at Frankfurt, describes the acts of the saint day by day. Nor had the holy woman herself, as Trithemius says in the *Chronicle of Sponheim*, occupied the territory of Bingen with her convent before the year 1148.” This saint is treated by the Bollandists and the Roman Martyrology on 17 September; she will also be mentioned again below.

Here we do not add the two letters which Manrique, nos. 8 and 9, recounts: one sent by her to the holy Father, the other by him to her. For a greater and far more illustrious abundance of material presents itself to us in the holy man’s travels through Germany, proclamation of sacred arms, and most frequent manifestations of miracles there. Let us therefore accompany him in that journey; yet we shall not give here those matters concerning the places of his German journey, his companions, and the very frequent, well-attested miracles of every kind performed by our great wonder-worker, both there and upon his return to his people at Clairvaux, while the Lord confirmed his preaching with so many and such great accompanying signs. Rather, we refer the reader to the book of these miracles, which we shall reproduce below and endeavor to elucidate with notes.

416. “It must nevertheless be counted a miracle that, although the holy man preached in his native tongue—namely French, of which the Germans were wholly ignorant—he nevertheless moved the people who heard but did not understand him to compunction even unto tears,” as Manricus observes, chapter 9, no. 5. He confirms the matter from Homily 16, *On the Infancy of Christ*, by Caesarius, a contemporary author, from which he cites these words: “In the time of Emperor Conrad, when St Bernard was preaching in Germany in the French language, he so kindled the people that they wept most abundantly; and although at that time they did not understand his words, afterwards, when a most skilled interpreter explained the saint’s sermon, the people were not moved.” Such, plainly, was the power of that most potent preacher when present, speaking, and aflame. These facts are confirmed still more strongly by Geoffrey, *Life*, book III, chapter 1, no. 158, who, writing of the wondrous grace of his speech, says to our purpose:

“Thus it was that, even when he addressed German peoples, he was heard with remarkable feeling; and their devotion seemed to be edified more by his discourse—which, being men of another language, they could not understand—than by the intelligible speech of any most accomplished interpreter speaking after him. They seemed, moreover, to feel more strongly the power of his words. A sure proof of this was the beating of their breasts and the shedding of tears.”

It is therefore not surprising that the way to this holy preacher was eagerly sought by hearers in the most frequent and densely packed throngs. On this matter see, among the miracles, chapter 1, in connection with the miracles performed at Constance, some of which Trithemius likewise records in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1147.

417. The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, in the same chapter 9, nos. 11 and 12, thus recounts the remarkable and distinguished conversion at Basel, obtained from the holy man, of Alexander of Cologne; nor shall we permit it to be omitted here. “We have seen above,” he says, “that this man, when setting out for Rome, encountered Bernard; indeed, having seen—or rather experienced in himself—the works of divine power, of which I shall speak presently, he at last yielded to the holy man’s counsels and joined himself to him as a companion on the journey, intending to become a monk at Clairvaux. But from another source we must learn where and in what order these things happened.

“We have the place from Godfrey, notary of the holy Father, who relates that the man was converted at Basel. For, when the saint was leaving the aforesaid city, he mentions Alexander and immediately adds: ‘This is Alexander who, in those same days, following the sacred counsels of the man of God and the manifestation of his powers . . . followed him.’” This is from book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 6, no. 241; see also book VI of the *Life*, or *Miracles*, part I, chapter 1, no. 283. But what manner of man he was, and in what way and order he was converted, is taught by the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, in Tissier, distinction 1, chapter 25:

“Near Cologne Agrippina, the distinguished metropolis of Germany, there was a certain master named Alexander, a canon—of St Mary ad Gradus, as the marginal note states—and a most famous teacher in that city.

418. “It happened that the blessed servant of God, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, entered Germany at the command of the holy Pope Eugenius, in order to preach the journey to Jerusalem to Emperor Conrad and to the people of the land. While he there shone forth through countless signs and miracles, the emperor, seeing the great wonders which the Lord displayed through him, was pierced in heart and received from his hand the sign of the cross, intending to depart for Jerusalem. Nor did an innumerable multitude of people delay to do likewise. So inflamed were they with an incredible ardour of faith that, competing with one another from every side, they tore away strips and fringes from the garments of the servant of God—who was therefore often compelled to procure new clothing—and counted themselves unfortunate if they did not merit to possess crosses made from his clothing. Many noble and learned men also committed themselves to the Lord through his hand; Bernard led them to Clairvaux, where they became monks and thereafter bore the greatest fruit in the Church of God.

419. “Among these was the aforementioned nobleman Alexander. At that time he was a young man, puffed up with the pride of secular learning, adorned also with the insignia of wealth and transient honour, and thinking of nothing less than conversion. But God, who catches the wise in their own craftiness, brought this about by a wonderful sequence of events, as what follows will show. When the most blessed Father Bernard urged him to convert, he, swollen with secular knowledge and wealth, replied that for the present he was thinking of and desiring nothing less than to assume the monastic habit.

“That same night, after he had given his limbs to sleep, the same man of God appeared to him in a vision. He raised him from the bed upon which he seemed to be gravely ill, restoring him to health. Then he took the habit in which he himself was clothed and clothed Alexander with it. Alexander once and then a second time angrily cast off from his shoulders and rejected the same habit; but at the third time it was thrown around his neck, tightly fastened to his body, and he was compelled to keep it. Then the holy Father placed in his hand the staff which he held, signifying the grace of his future prelacy, and commanded him to depart.

420. “On awakening, however, Alexander was as yet unable to soften in response to such a revelation, but persisted in the same hardness of heart. That same day, when the most blessed abbot reclined at table, a fish called a perch was served to him for refreshment. At the sight of it, the man of God raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for a long time over the fish; then, blessing it, he sent it to the aforementioned Alexander as his portion. As Alexander began to taste it, at the very first bite he was granted happily to experience in himself the power of the prayer of the servant of God. For he was suddenly changed into another man, deeply compunct, and began to shed abundant tears over the fish itself. He marvelled at himself, not knowing what had come over him or why he was weeping. At last, recalling the vision he had seen the night before, he understood that by the Lord’s gratuitous mercy he had been forestalled. Therefore, giving thanks from the depths of his heart for the heavenly calling, he immediately committed himself to the blessed servant of God.

“Bernard received him kindly; he became a monk at Clairvaux and afterwards pastor of Grandselve. He advanced so greatly in holiness of life that he later became abbot of the Cistercian monastery—the ninth, as the marginal note has it—and universal father of the whole Order. We have drawn these facts from the trustworthy report of Alexander himself, that servant of God.”

Mabillon, in book VII of the *Life of St Bernard*, excerpted from the *Great Cistercian Exordium*, observes at the phrase “universal father of the whole Order,” col. 1209: “This is a notable passage for illustrating the dignity of the abbot of Cîteaux. See Epistle 4, no. 3, and Epistle 5, no. 1. . . Herbert likewise calls the same abbot ‘universal Father of the Order’ below, no. 17.” Moreover, that wondrous conversion of Alexander was once again among the fruits which Bernard, before his German journey, did not seek but which were freely offered to him during it. Let us now say how powerfully the holy man acted in persuading Conrad to undertake the holy war.

## § XL. Emperor Conrad Enrolled in the Sacred Warfare; St Bernard’s Journeys through Germany; His Return to France; Miracles; the Assembly at Étampes; the Unhappy Outcome of the Eastern Expedition Wrongly Imputed to the Saint

421. Conrad, as the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 10, relate, was thinking of nothing less than taking the cross and, abandoning the western Empire, directing arms toward the remote regions of the East. This was especially so because Germany was aflame with civil wars, some princes being divided among themselves and perhaps ready to divide themselves from the Empire unless restrained by his presence. Yet he had appointed a general assembly at Speyer, at which Bernard was to be present, to convene on Christmas Day.

See book VI of the *Life*, which concerns the miracles, part I, chapter 2. There you will also find the saintly preacher’s happy success in attaining his intended end: Conrad and his younger nephew Frederick, together with innumerable princes, were signed with the cross. Add also the miracles related there. Nor was Bernard’s labour fruitless when he restored the quarrelling German princes to concord, as Otto of Freising testifies in book I of *The Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 42. His words seem clearly to imply this:

“Thus, when countless peoples and nations, not only from the Roman Empire but also from neighbouring kingdoms—namely western France, England, and Pannonia—had been stirred by the report of this expedition to take the cross, suddenly almost the entire West became so peaceful that it was considered unlawful not only to wage war but even for anyone to carry arms in public.”

422. What is reported among the miracles performed at Speyer, part I, chapter 2, no. 302—“When . . . we went out, the king himself with the princes escorted the saint of the Lord, lest the crowds crush him,” etc.—is expressed more clearly and movingly by St Antoninus, part II of the *Histories*, title 17, chapter I, § 6. Speaking thus of Bernard: “At the city of Speyer such was the concourse that King, or Emperor, Conrad, lest the people crush him, laid aside his cloak, took him in his own arms, and carried him out of the basilica.”

The *Cistercian Annals*, cited a little above, record at no. 6 that at Speyer the saintly Father saluted an image of the Virgin Mary three times, and that it once returned his greeting, all hearing. Then, at no. 8, there is discussion of the milk of that same Virgin with which he was sprinkled, and also of the greeting addressed to him by the most blessed Mother of God in the famous monastery of Afflighem; that event is assigned to the following year. But we shall examine these matters below. Other things now call us: the deeds accomplished by the holy man as he left Speyer and travelled through other places in Germany.

423. The compiler of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1147, chapter 2, nos. 1 and 2, says: “The assembly having been dissolved, and after bidding farewell to Emperor Conrad and to the bishop of Constance, whom he had hitherto had as companion on the road, or rather as his guide, the holy Father, about to leave Speyer, took with him the abbot of Kamp of his Order and, swiftly travelling through the remaining cities of all Germany”—“which must be understood suitably”—“and making them illustrious by miracles, preached the word of the cross against the enemies of the cross. . . . But let the reader learn from his travelling companions, whom he brought with him and who were present at everything, what cities he visited and at what times.”

We direct the reader to book VI of the *Life*, or *Miracles*, part II, chapter 3, where there is an account of the assembly at Speyer being dissolved, the saint’s passage through the city of Worms, and the miracles. From there the holy traveller went to Coblenz and Cologne, with signs accompanying him as usual, as may be seen in the chapter just cited. Why should I recount the other deeds he performed after leaving Cologne: at Aachen, Maastricht on the Meuse, Liège, Gembloux, Villers, Cambrai, and elsewhere? Spain itself was not excluded, although he was not there—indeed, he was never there—as will later be proved more fully. Concerning the saint’s innumerable miracles, the most splendid testimonies of writers survive, and there will be occasion below to discuss them. One might say that God, supremely good and great, “who alone performs great wonders,” shared with His incomparable wonder-worker such riches of miracles from the infinite treasury of His omnipotence that He seems not to have wished them bounded by number, place, time, or persons—especially when this great man was summoning the peoples of the West to holy war.

424. “While these things were being done through the holy Father,” says Manricus, chapter 4, “Conrad, who had previously received from his hand at Speyer the banner of the holy war, summoned a general assembly in Bavaria, to be held at the beginning of February, in order to arrange all necessary matters for the expedition. Since Bernard could not attend, he appointed in his place the venerable Adam, abbot of Ebrach, whom we have mentioned above, and wished him to be furnished with both apostolic and his own letters, by which they might discharge the office of subdelegates—for this too had been granted. . . .”

Otto of Freising, who was present, describes what was done there in book I of *The Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 40, connecting the event with February. Among other matters he says: “At that same time three bishops received the cross: Henry of Regensburg, Otto of Freising, and Reginbert of Passau,” together with other distinguished men mentioned there. What, meanwhile, was St Bernard doing? Let us hear Geoffrey, book VI of the *Life*, or part III of the *Miracles*, chapter 6.

425. “It was Sunday, the feast of the Purification of blessed Mary; and Louis, king of the Franks, . . . met the man of God at Châlons. Very many princes of both kingdoms also assembled . . . so that the journey to Jerusalem might be discussed by common counsel.” The same author subsequently recounts many miracles performed by Bernard on his journey toward Clairvaux, which will be given by us elsewhere.

The history of the holy war, however, requires that we not pass over in silence the acts of the assembly at Étampes, where the final decisions concerning the departure for Jerusalem were taken on Septuagesima Sunday in the year under discussion, 1147. Accordingly, Odo of Deuil, cited above, writes from p. 13 concerning this assembly or conference:

“Louis the king therefore summoned all to Étampes on *Circumdederunt me*, that they might jointly choose what they would jointly endure. As they were eager in coming, so, would that they had been prudent in choosing! For when, at the appointed place and time, a multitude of bishops and nobles, glorious as well as great, had assembled, the aforesaid abbot, Bernard—worthy indeed to be proclaimed—also appeared in person. He brought news, and by both his presence and his report made the assembly joyful. For he had come from Germany, where he had joined the king and the magnates of the realm to the soldiery of Christ’s cross. Then letters from diverse nations were read, envoys heard, and these proceedings continued until evening. Thus they passed a joyful day, and postponed what remained until the morrow.

426. “The next day came, more joyful than fortunate. Among those present were persons who, from reading and experience, declared the Greeks treacherous. But the king and his men, who rightly feared the strength of no nation, would that they had feared treachery! Yet, since there is no counsel or prudence against God, they chose the route through Greece, there to die. Thus the second day ended, but not prosperously.

“Then the noble envoys of King Roger departed in confusion, their demeanour plainly showing their lord’s sorrowful feeling. They warned us of Greek deceit, which we afterwards experienced. Nor is it surprising if powerful and wise King Roger desired the king’s welfare, provided he loved the Franks, being himself descended from our regions. Finally, by the grace of the Trinity, the third day dawned. The assembled persons first invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit—would that they had invoked it in like manner the day before!—then, after a spiritual discourse by the holy abbot, they proceeded to discuss the protection of the kingdom. Meanwhile, a day at Pentecost was appointed for those departing.” More is found there.

427. Nor did the holy Father leave Étampes devoid of miracles. Departing thence likewise, he made his journey back to Clairvaux illustrious through the brilliance and multitude of his wonders; as he entered it, he healed a deaf and mute boy. These things are accurately related in book VI of the *Life*, or part III of the *Miracles*, from which we too shall later offer them to the reader for reading. We give the same notice concerning many other things which happened at Trier, Metz, Toul, and Rutila, and which will be treated below.

Meanwhile, there may be added these matters noted by Arnoldus Raissius in the supplement to John Molanus’s *Natales Sanctorum Belgii*, under 20 August: “In the duchy of Luxembourg he also once visited the monastery of Clairefontaine, which to this day is inhabited by nuns of the Order of St Bernard himself. There is seen there a spring which even today, because St Bernard blessed it, retains the name Fountain of St Bernard; drunk with faith and devotion, it is believed to afford relief against illnesses. He passed through a village situated on the borders of the same duchy, called Rutila, where descendants preserve the tradition of the fathers that at that time St Bernard, as though exulting, broke out into these prophetic words: ‘O Rutila, Rutila, you will one day shine red [*rutilabis*].’ No one will deny that the man of God thereby foretold the introduction into that place, almost three hundred years later, of Carthusians, who still dwell there, if he considers Bernard’s most ardent affection for the Carthusians.”

So writes Raissius. I should prefer evidence from earlier writers. To these may be added the prophecy concerning the monastery of Beaupré, related by the cited Raissius. Manricus treats the reform of the monastery of Aulne under the year 1147, chapter 3, at the end. I shall speak of the monasteries of Gembloux and Villers in § 47. On Villers Abbey see p. 343; on Gembloux, pp. 342, 344, and 393.

428. But before we proceed with the remaining matters concerning the Eastern expedition, let us add to the almost infinite miracles by which our incomparable wonder-worker made illustrious the apostolic labours of his German journey one miracle of the first rank. Chifflet published, in *St Bernard’s Illustrious Lineage Vindicated*, pp. 81 ff., the *Chronicle of Clairvaux*, extending from A.D. 1147 to 1199, by an anonymous monk of Clairvaux, from an old manuscript of that monastery. The chronicle begins thus: “In the year of the Lord 1147, blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, preached the cross in Germany; he performed many great miracles, among which he also raised from the dead the man concerning whom there is an account in the book of the Miracles of Lord Herbert.”

Now, lest we spend more time than is enough gathering events of the holy war which lie outside Bernard’s own history, Otto of Freising, so often cited above, writes of the departure of Conrad and Louis for the East in book I, chapter 44; of their arrival in chapter 58; of Conrad’s return in chapter 59; and of the unhappy outcome of the holy expedition in chapter 60. Why mention Odo of Deuil, Baronius, Pagi, and others?

429. Concerning this lamentable tragedy—which we must wonder at and revere in submissive silence, but cannot investigate, much less comprehend—let us repeat the Apostle’s saying in Romans, chapter 11: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” Add the saying of the royal prophet: “Your judgments are a great deep”; and likewise: “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is upright.”

What, after these things, was St Bernard—who had earned imperishable merit in that holy expedition through so many and such great cares, journeys, labours, and miracles—to do? What was his temper and feeling amid the reproaches by which that most upright man was attacked, as though he himself had been responsible for that most calamitous and lamentable catastrophe? Shall we seem to anyone to depart from the truth if we say that Bernard, great as he was in his entirety, needed all of himself to digest so bitter a morsel?

Yet, ever the greatest of men, sustaining himself by his own virtue in adversity no less than prosperity, he possessed his soul in patience. After that disaster, bitter in every respect—whether one considers the welfare of the Christian world, the salvation of so many souls, the enlargement of the divine glory, had the Lord willed otherwise, the calumnies levelled against the holy Father, or, finally, all that lay outside himself—he nonetheless remained inwardly upright upon the lofty summit of a heroic mind. As was his custom, he allowed his service to be lacking nowhere when he saw that it might be useful in public affairs.

Indeed, under this very year 1149, when Louis VII, king of the Franks, and Emperor Conrad returned from the unhappy Jerusalem expedition, Manricus presents St Bernard as occupied with good works, as may be read there. See what we shall later say near the end of § 48; likewise §§ 49 and 50. Under the year 1150, chapter 1, Manricus offers Bernard’s most just defence from book II of *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius. Recall what we set forth above in § 36, where Bishop Otto of Freising himself—though not otherwise much disposed to favour Bernard—defends the man of God and lays blame upon the sins of Christians.

For further confirmation, these words may be added from the *Chronicle* of Geoffrey, monk of the monastery of St Martial at Limoges and subsequently prior of the monastery of Vigeois in the same diocese, who flourished in the same century. In Labbe, vol. II of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, the cited chronicler writes in chapter 52 concerning the Christian army: “That army made no progress at all because they behaved without discipline. Therefore many fell away and countless numbers perished because of their iniquity. Before the journey they carried off the treasures of churches by pledging false securities; they afflicted the lowest populace with cruel exactions; in pomp and pride they followed the humble Christ, and in vain they strayed from the most just and most humble one.” Thus he writes.

## § XLI. The Holy Doctor’s Conflict with Gilbert of Poitiers

430. Just as the perverse doctrines of Abelard were suppressed by St Bernard, so the errors of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, were defeated by the same holy man and earned him great hostility. The events of this most serious affair, in which the holy doctor conducted himself with such great praise, are related by Manricus under the years of Christ 1146, 1147, and 1148. Let us therefore return to these and explain the passage which Geoffrey left noted on this matter in book III of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 2, no. 166:

“There was Gilbert, surnamed of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, greatly practised in sacred letters, but also searching into matters too high for himself, to his own folly.”

He was a native of the same city, as Otto of Freising affirms in his *Frederick*, book I, chapter 46 of the edition cited above. From pupil he became master, and from master eventually bishop in the same place. “From youth he had subjected himself to the discipline of great men, trusting more in their weight than in his own talent. Such first was Hilary of Poitiers; afterwards Bernard of Chartres; lastly Anselm and Ralph of Laon, brothers. From them he had drawn not slight but weighty learning. His hand was not quickly withdrawn from the rod; his learning did not diverge from moral discipline and gravity of life. He had applied his mind not to jokes and entertainments, but to serious matters. Hence it was that, preserving gravity both in gesture and voice, he showed himself difficult in speech as in action, so that what he said could never be grasped by childish minds, and scarcely even by minds trained and practised in learning,” according to the testimony of the same Otto, chapter 50.

431. Mabillon, in the general preface to his new edition of the *Works of St Bernard*, § 5, no. 58, says: “I think that this Hilary is none other than the great Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, whose authority Gilbert abused, according to Geoffrey’s testimony. Bernard of Chartres is known to me from no source other than Otto’s testimony. Ralph of Laon is very well known from Guibert, Herman, monk of Laon, and Geoffrey, notary of St Bernard—see here vol. VI, col. 1338, that is, at the end of Geoffrey’s tract against Gilbert of Poitiers—as is also Anselm, his brother, dean of the Church of Laon. While composing commentaries on the Psalms, Paul’s epistles, and Boethius, Gilbert philosophizes in certain matters concerning the Godhead and other articles of religion otherwise than was permissible.”

Otto, in the same chapter 50, thus recalls Gilbert’s errors: “Among other matters charged against him concerning the divine majesty were four articles: namely, that he asserted that the divine essence is not God; that the properties of the persons are not the persons themselves; that the theological persons are not predicated in any proposition; and that the divine nature was not incarnate. Besides these, he put forth other lesser articles: namely, that, by diminishing human merit, he said that no one except Christ merited; that, by invalidating the sacraments of the Church, he said that no one is baptized unless he is to be saved; and other things of that sort.” Consult Geoffrey’s tract.

432. He also disseminated his errors, offering others poison infected with blasphemies. For, as Geoffrey relates in book III of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 2, no. 166, “he set before his disciples hidden breads and gave them stolen waters to drink; nor did he readily confess to authoritative persons what he savoured—or rather how greatly he raved.” But the orthodox took it to heart to set an antidote against his poison.

Mabillon describes the events from no. 59 in these words: “When the bishop had delivered a discourse in a numerous gathering of his clergy and disseminated the same errors, two of his archdeacons, Arnald and Calo, brought the matter before Eugenius III, then coming to France, at Siena in Tuscany. The pontiff referred examination of the case to France. Meanwhile, the archdeacons drew Bernard to their side. An examination was held at Auxerre and Paris, and judgment delivered at the Council of Reims in 1148. Otto briefly records what was done at each meeting; Geoffrey, Bernard’s notary, does so more fully. He wrote both a treatise on the events concerning this matter at the Council of Reims and, forty years later, a letter to Henry, cardinal bishop of Albano. Both writings are printed here at the end of vol. VI.”

433. “Of the meeting at Auxerre, which Otto alone mentions, we have discovered nothing distinctive; but there is considerable material concerning the Paris meeting. Geoffrey reports that it was held at the Easter solemnity, and therefore in 1147, since, according to Otto, the Council of Reims was celebrated in mid-Lent of the following year—indeed, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, according to the Appendix to Sigebert. Therefore Gilbert appeared at Paris before the pontiff, cardinals, bishops, and other venerable and learned men, to answer concerning these articles. The proceedings continued for several days.

“Two masters were produced against him: Adam of the Petit-Pont, a subtle man and recently made canon of the Church of Paris; and Hugh of Champfleury, the king’s chancellor. They solemnly affirmed that they had heard certain of the propositions from Gilbert’s own mouth. Meanwhile, while many objections were made from both sides, he is reported, among other things, to have said: ‘I confess that the Father is one thing as Father and another as God; yet he is not this thing and this thing.’ Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, took the statement with indignation. These things occurred on the first day.

“On another day, when he was accused of having called the three persons ‘three singulars’ in a prose text on the Trinity, the archbishop of Rouen—Hugh III—aggravated the charge, saying that God ought rather to be called one singular. This is approximately Otto, bishop of Freising’s account of the Paris meeting.

434. “Geoffrey treats it somewhat differently, prefacing it with a synod held at Viterbo concerning the same case. He mentions one accuser of Gilbert before the pontiff, Archdeacon Arnald, to whom he gives the surname ‘Who Does Not Laugh’ [*Qui non ridet*]. At the Paris meeting, however, he sets Bernard alone against Gilbert, upon whom, wherever the concern of Christ touched him, the whole affair immediately devolved as though it were entirely his own.

“When the bishop was asked to produce his own commentary on Boethius, containing the suspect articles, he answered that he did not have it at hand. The bishop denied that he had ever taught, believed, or committed to writing that the divinity was not God, etc. He produced as witnesses principally two of his disciples: namely Rotrou, bishop of Évreux and later archbishop of Rouen, and Master Ivo of Chartres—undoubtedly another man than the celebrated Ivo, bishop of Chartres. I think this was Master Ivo, a regular canon of the abbey of St Victor near Paris, afterwards created cardinal by Innocent II, to whom Bernard’s Epistle 193 is addressed.

“In these disputes the pontiff ordered the aforementioned book to be brought to the future council which he intended to celebrate that same year in the city of Reims. It was, however, deferred to mid-Lent of the following year, though still within one year of the Paris meeting, which, as we have said, was held at the preceding Easter feast.

435. “Meanwhile, at Eugenius’s command, Godescalc, then abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi near Arras and afterwards bishop of that city, examined the author’s commentary on Boethius which had been sent to him. From it he extracted the suspect articles and noted from the books of the holy Fathers authorities contrary to them. Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate in Aquitaine, would have contributed more concerning Gilbert’s life and doctrine, had premature death not removed him shortly before.

“Finally, at the Council of Reims, they came to the examination of the articles noted by the aforementioned Abbot Godescalc. But because he was too inarticulate, the pope handed the book, with the testimonies of the saints contrary to it, to St Bernard. The council consisted of bishops from four kingdoms: France, Germany, England, and Spain. Among them were great men, not moderately learned: Geoffrey of Le Dorat, archbishop of Bordeaux, of whom Gilbert was a suffragan; Milo, bishop of Thérouanne; Joscelin of Soissons; and Suger, abbot of St-Denis. Louis, king of the Franks, setting out for Jerusalem, had committed the administration of the whole kingdom to Suger; Otto adds that this was according to the prerogative of that monastery. Geoffrey of Le Dorat, although he did not approve Gilbert’s doctrine, favoured the man.

436. “On the first day, when they entered the consistory, Gilbert arranged for great volumes to be brought in by his clerks, alleging that his adversaries adduced only truncated testimonies. Bernard said, ‘What need is there to linger longer over such words? The origin of this scandal comes from nothing else than that many people believe that you believe and teach that the divine essence or nature—his divinity, wisdom, goodness, and greatness—is not God, but a form by which God is God. If you believe this, say so openly or deny it.’

“He dared to say that this form was not God. Then Bernard said, ‘Behold, we have what we sought. Let this confession be written down.’ The supreme pontiff gave this command; and Lord Henry of Pisa, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, later a monk of Clairvaux and, after being abbot of St Anastasius, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, went at his command and brought a sheet, pen, and ink [*incaustum*, that is, writing ink].

“As he wrote this confession, Gilbert said to Bernard: ‘And you write that divinity is God.’ Bernard replied: ‘Let it be written with an iron stylus and an adamantine point.’ After much disputation back and forth, the cardinals said that they would thereafter decide the matter. The bishops, disturbed that the cardinals reserved the decision of the case to themselves alone, appealed to Bernard to compose propositions contrary to Gilbert’s articles together with a creed of faith, lest the council be dissolved without action—as very many of the cardinals who favoured Gilbert wished.

437. “Accordingly Bernard did so. The bishops then presented to the pontiff for confirmation the confession subscribed by them, through Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, and Abbot Suger. They easily obtained this. Finally Gilbert was summoned into the assembly in the notable palace called Tau—the residence of the archbishop of Reims was so called because of the shape of the Greek letter *tau*—and freely renounced each of the articles he had advanced. The pontiff condemned these articles together with the author’s book, strictly commanding that no one dare read or copy the same book until the Roman Church had first corrected it. When Gilbert said that he would correct it at the pope’s direction, the pope refused. These details are gathered from Geoffrey.

438. “Otto has certain particulars in chapter 56, and likewise some points at variance with Geoffrey. First, he relates that Gilbert’s examination began after the synod had ended and its decrees had been promulgated; then, when the middle week of Lent had passed [Col. 0857B] and the sacred season of Passion Sunday was beginning, Gilbert was summoned before the assembly for judgment. Next, after he had read books of the orthodox Fathers in his own defence, Eugene, weary of the matter, raised the question which Geoffrey attributes to Bernard: would Gilbert simply say whether he believed that the supreme essence was God? Exhausted by the prolonged debate, he answered thoughtlessly, ‘No.’ A notary immediately took down the saying as it fell from his lips. When the assembly was dismissed, Gilbert spent all that remained of that day, together with the following night, soliciting his cardinal friends, of whom he had not a few. On the following day his written statement was read aloud and the bishop was required to give its rationale. He then explained his opinion [Col. 0857C] thus: if the name God be understood of nature itself, he granted that it was God; but not if it were understood of person, lest, if he made that profession without qualification, he should be led to assert equally of the essence whatever is said of any person; and thus be compelled to confess that, just as the person of the Son, so the divine essence without qualification, had been incarnate and had suffered.

439. “He further supported this distinction by testimonies from the Fathers, Theodoret and Hilary, and by the authority of the Council of Toledo. When the Abbot of Clairvaux wished to define that authority and had put forward certain words displeasing to the cardinals, Gilbert asked that this be written down; but Bernard, [Col. 0857D] as Geoffrey records, replied: ‘Let it be written with an iron stylus and an adamantine nail.’ At last the holy abbot met with the bishops and, together with them, set forth his faith against Gilbert’s propositions. The sacred senate of cardinals took this act of the Gallican Church so seriously that they complained of it to the pope—both against the bishops and against Bernard himself—because, as though putting the final hand to a judgment about to be rendered, they had dared, without consulting them, to put their faith in writing; whereas the matter belonged to the Roman See. Finally Bernard, summoned by the pope’s order to appease the cardinals, humbly and respectfully replied that neither he nor the lord bishops had defined anything concerning the aforesaid propositions; but because he had heard from that same bishop of Poitiers that [Col. 0858A] his faith should be written down, he had therefore, unwilling to do so alone, simply set forth what he thought under their authority and testimony.

440. “When this humble and moderate answer had been received, the aforesaid indignation of the cardinals subsided, yet on the condition that the said document, having been issued without consultation of the curia and thus lacking the weight of authority, should not be held in the Church as a creed. And so nothing could be decided concerning the three propositions because of the foregoing disturbance. Otto says this is not surprising; and he adds that Gilbert differed from the other bishops insofar as they professed nature incarnate, but in the Son, whereas Gilbert professed the person of the Son incarnate, not without his nature. On the first point only the Roman pontiff decided: no line of reasoning in theology was to divide nature from person; nor was God to be called ‘by the divine essence’ merely in the ablative sense, but also in the nominative. Gilbert reverently accepted the judgment of the supreme pontiff and, having received his archdeacons again into favour, returned to his own diocese with unimpaired rank and full honour.

441. “In all this Otto plainly appears to have been very favourable to Gilbert; hence it is not surprising that in what follows he doubts whether the aforesaid Abbot of Clairvaux, in this affair, was deceived as a man by the frailty of human weakness, or whether the bishop, as a most learned man, escaped the Church’s judgment by shrewdly concealing his intention. Yet when Otto was near death, as Radevicus testifies, book II, chapter 11, [Col. 0858C] he ordered his book, in which he had written these things, brought to him and entrusted it to religious men, that, if he seemed to have said anything in favour of Master Gilbert’s opinion which could offend anyone, it might be corrected at their discretion. On this entire controversy Geoffrey rightly refers readers to Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs, namely Sermon 80, in which the holy man does not hesitate to declare heretics those who continued to defend Gilbert’s opinion, although he spares the author’s name because of his repentance. These, then, are the matters which Mabillon learnedly collected concerning the case of Gilbert of Poitiers, against whom the holy doctor was chosen as antagonist. He has treated it sufficiently in its historical relation to our subject, so that we do not seem to need to have recourse [Col. 0858D] to Baronius and Manrique. Yet to what has been said may be added the account of Geoffrey the biographer, book III of the Life of our saint, chapter 2, for the sake of which passage the foregoing has been transcribed here. Finally, concerning the matters repeatedly cited above by Mabillon from Otto, Otto himself may be consulted in *Frederick*, book I, chapters 46, 47, 50, 51, 52, 55 and following.

## § XLII. Henrician heretics restrained by Father Bernard; miracles performed by him among the people of Toulouse for the destruction of their errors

442. As I proceed through chapter 2 of the recently cited Geoffrey, another passage presents itself for elucidation—no. 168 and following in our edition—concerning the Henrician heresy suppressed in the region of Toulouse and the miracles there performed in confirmation of the orthodox faith, which [Col. 0859A] Bernard, the great athlete of the Church, defended splendidly and successfully against that most pernicious sect both by word and by writing. With respect to chronology, the events in this affair are assigned to the year of Christ 1147 by Baronius, Manrique, and Pagi. This Henry had formerly been a monk, but was then, as Geoffrey says, a contemptible apostate, of most wicked life and pernicious doctrine. The same biographer immediately enumerates that teaching in the saint’s own words, quoting a fragment of Letter 241 to the prince of Toulouse, about which we shall shortly say more. Baronius also lists the errors of this utterly impious man from Peter of Cluny; and Manrique, drawing on him, marks them under the same year, chapter 12, in these words: “That baptism must [Col. 0859B] be denied to infants; that churches and ecclesiastical buildings are constructed superfluously; that the Lord’s cross ought not to be honoured or worshipped; that the body of the Lord is not present in the sacrament of the altar; that it is vain to pray for the dead; that God is mocked by ecclesiastical chants and hymns.” Thus he speaks of Henry’s blasphemous doctrines.

443. The same Cistercian historian immediately continues: “Inflamed against these errors, Pope Eugenius decreed a legation and appointed as legate Alberic, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, than whom he knew no more outstanding man in the sacred college, to oppose the serpent-like evil effectively. Alberic urgently requests Bernard as his companion; without him nothing great could be done throughout the world; through him all things would be successfully accomplished. Though the man was worn out and broken by so many journeys, he was still necessary: one who would not refuse himself to a Church in need. His health, however beneficial, must be risked, and his very life also, lest, if the people of Toulouse perished, the plague should spread to neighbouring provinces. Bernard was therefore assigned as companion to the man, torn away from his sons for the third time that year, though already after a long journey. Under this necessity,” says Geoffrey, “he set out, having often before been asked by the church of that region, Toulouse, and at last persuaded and brought back by the most reverend Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See. But first he called Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, [Col. 0859D] to share his burden of care, a man great indeed in reputation and no less powerful in wisdom than in holiness. Then he sent to Alfonso, count of Saint-Gilles, this letter announcing his arrival,” which Manrique inserts in his history. Apart from the fragment of it which I have just indicated as extant in Geoffrey, I have thought it unnecessary to excerpt other portions of that letter, since they are readily available to readers.

444. Yet I shall not omit to give its encomium, which Baronius composed under the year of Christ 1147, no. 20, before weaving it into his *Annals*: “By God’s favour this letter still survives, like the sword preserved in the sanctuary with which Goliath’s head was cut off; and it is also powerful for smiting the remaining enemies of God.” After reproducing it, the celebrated author of the *Annals* thought the following worthy of being appended, no. 23: “You have heard, reader, whence this pseudo-apostle came and for what purpose: namely, an apostate from religious life, so that, after casting off every bond by which he had been restrained from dissolving into works of the flesh, and being free to accomplish every evil he wished, he taught the children of men this liberty of the flesh. But when Saint Bernard describes Henry, he seems plainly to paint in the same colours the unhappy heresiarchs of our own time, likewise issuing from apostasy and hurling themselves headlong into the gulf of lust, like swine into the mire.” Thus far Baronius—and wisely.

445. Geoffrey, cited above, records the holy man’s arrival in the city of Toulouse, [Col. 0860B] the crowds that rushed upon him in their most ardent devotion, and the great fruit produced. He then appends the miracles by which God was pleased to confirm the preaching of the herald of orthodox faith and conqueror of the errors opposed to it. But I shall discuss prodigies in the following section, after first adding to the matters already related certain particular notices that illuminate the Henrician poison and the holy Father’s labours against it. Mabillon long ago applied himself diligently and learnedly to this subject in §6 of his General Preface to the Works of Saint Bernard; and it is pleasing to transfer the following here:

446. “The Henrician heresy especially exercised Bernard’s zeal for the Christian cause; he vigorously assailed it in deeds and writings. . . . Henry, whom the holy man calls an apostate monk and Geoffrey after him, is called a pseudo-hermit in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, in the third volume of the *Analecta* published by the aforesaid Mabillon. There his character and perverse actions are accurately described. From what place he originated is not sufficiently indicated by these words: ‘At about the same time, namely under Bishop Hildebert, in the districts of the neighbouring regions there arose a certain hypocrite, whom his own conduct, depraved morals, and detestable doctrine proclaim worthy of punishments fitting for scorpions and parricides. Under a feigned name of holiness and learning, while practising shameful crimes, he boasted that from mere sight he could know the hidden transgressions of every mortal. Two of his disciples, sent to Le Mans, reached the suburbs of the city on Ash Wednesday. [Col. 0860D] In accordance with their master’s custom, they carried staffs and a banner of the cross, displaying by colour and outward conduct the appearance of penitents. Deceived by this appearance, the people of Le Mans received them as angels. Bishop Hildebert also received them kindly; when about to undertake a journey to Rome, he charged his archdeacons, among other things, to allow that pseudo-hermit Henry a peaceful entry and permission to address the people.’” He later had ample cause to regret this.

447. “From this, perhaps, someone may infer that Henry came from the region near Le Mans, to which he first administered the poison of his perverse doctrine. For if he had already been known from elsewhere, the learned and discerning bishop Hildebert would not have admitted him so readily into his city. Yet he could have come there from a distant region, perhaps even from Italy, as we shall say later. When Henry entered the city, the common people, as usual, applauded the novelty. Indeed, many of the clergy provided him with food and prepared a platform from which that preacher might address the crowds; he was extraordinarily eloquent. When they had heard him, the people turned in fury against the clergy, treating them as pagans and tax collectors, so that they threatened their servants with tortures and would neither sell anything to them nor buy anything from them. Indeed, they had resolved not only to destroy their houses and scatter their goods, but also to stone them or hang them from the gallows, had not the prince and leading men resisted their wicked attempts.

448. “Although it learned this late, the clergy of Le Mans forbade Henry and his companions to preach, publishing an edict. Therefore Henry, having learned of Hildebert’s return, withdrew to the castle of Saint-Calais, by no means abandoning his undertakings but daily breaking out into worse deeds. Meanwhile, when Hildebert had returned from his journey to Rome and wished to impart his blessing to the people, he was treated with indignity by a populace corrupted by the heretic’s speeches. He then approached the seducer and asked what office of order he held. Henry replied that he was a deacon; being ordered to leave that province, he secretly fled, intending similarly to disturb and infect with his viperous breath the other regions, unless rumour outstripped him.” Thus far from Hildebert’s acts.

449. “Meanwhile two disciples of Henry, Cyprian and Peter, recovered from his deceptions, as is attested by Hildebert’s circular Letter 78, in which their master is described thus: ‘This Henry was a great snare of the devil and a renowned armour-bearer of Antichrist. The aforesaid brethren adhered for so long to him, who feigned religious devotion by his appearance and learning by his words, until both the filthiness of his life and the error of his doctrine became known to them. But when they discovered that his ways were not right, they first returned to themselves, and then came over to us. He had infected our diocese to such a degree that the clergy resisting him could scarcely preserve their liberty within the walls of the church.’” Thus Hildebert learned too late how much danger threatens from the incautious approval of new teachers who corrupt the minds of their hearers [Col. 0861D] under an appearance of piety.
