450. “From this it is clear that Henry infected Le Mans long before he entered the region of Toulouse, whence Bernard expelled him. For the journey to Rome undertaken by Hildebert while still bishop of Le Mans, at the time when that infamous impostor sowed his tares at Le Mans, occurred before 1125, the year in which Hildebert moved to the metropolitan see of Tours. Bernard, however, did not travel to the region of Toulouse until 1147. Certainly in Letter 241, which the holy man wrote to Count Alfonso while stationed in the Toulouse region, he sufficiently implies this in the following words: ‘Inquire, if you please, how he left the city of Lausanne, how Le Mans, how Poitiers, how Bordeaux.’” This, indeed, seems to be the sequence of that apostate’s journey, who began his preaching from Lausanne and then from Le Mans.

451. “And perhaps he had come to Lausanne from Italy, whence refuse of this kind migrated into the regions of Gaul: remnants of the Manichaeans, as also those heretics of Cambrai brought from Italy, who were condemned in the Synod of Arras in 1125; at that same time similar plagues perished by fire at Orléans. Indeed, the *Cistercian Exordium*, book VII, chapter 17, calls the Henricians Manichaeans, recounting that the papal legate and other bishops came with the holy man to the Toulouse region to refute the Manichaean heresy. [Col. 0862B] Now how the name and errors of Manichaeans may be attributed to heretics of this sort and to their followers is clearly shown by the most illustrious bishop of Meaux in his excellent work on the variations of heretics, book XI.

452. “The same Henrician heretics spread among the people of Périgueux, under Pontius as their leader and standard-bearer, as is taught by Herbert’s letter in the third volume of our *Analecta*, where the peculiar fictions of those Pontians are reported. Hence Bernard went to the peoples of Périgueux, or Périgord, as appears from the third part of book VI, which concerns his miracles, no. 4; there it is recorded that he found many Arians among the people of Toulouse and put them, as well as the heretic Henry, to flight. Henry himself, moreover, is said first to have been condemned at the Council of Pisa and entrusted to Bernard in order that he might become a monk at Clairvaux. But, after receiving letters from Bernard to the monks of Clairvaux, he preferred obstinately to persist in the error he had once embraced rather than return by this short path to the way of salvation.

453. “Bernard portrays Henry in vivid colours in the aforesaid Letter 241, writing that he was learned and bore an appearance of piety, but was addicted to gambling and prostitutes. He mentions approximately the following impious doctrines of his: no regard was due to priests and clerics; the sacraments and feasts were to be abolished; baptism was to be denied to infants. Of a different class was the heretic mentioned by Hildebert in Letter 51, who rejected the intercessions of the saints and wrongly attempted to draw Hildebert himself into support of his sect.”

## § XLIII. Other heretics opposed by the Saint

454. The cited Mabillon asks, “Whether those heretics whom Bernard attacks in Sermons 65 and 66 on the Song of Songs were the same as the Henricians. I was once persuaded that they were no others; but after the discovery of the letter of Everwin, abbot of Steinfeld, which gave occasion to those sermons, the opinion must be changed. For these were heretics of Cologne: agreeing with the Henricians in some points, but differing from them in many. Everwin distinguishes the Cologne heretics into two classes. One group said that the Church existed only among themselves, as though they alone followed Christ’s footsteps. In food they forbade the use of milk [Col. 0863A] and everything made from it. In their sacraments they covered themselves with a veil and claimed that daily they consecrated their own food and drink into Christ’s body and blood; all others, they said, were far from the truth in their sacraments. Besides baptism in water, they admitted another baptism in fire and spirit, by the laying on of hands alone. They rejected our baptism along with marriage. Finally, they said that each of their elect, or baptized members, had the power to baptize others who were worthy, and at his own table to make Christ’s body and blood.

455. “The others denied to the Church’s priests, because they lived in a secular manner, the power of consecrating and administering the other sacraments, except baptism, which they bestowed only on adults, not infants. They considered every marriage fornication, except that contracted between a male virgin and a female virgin. Finally, they rejected the suffrages of the saints, fasts, and other mortifications of the body, as also purgatory and suffrages for the dead. Thus the Henrician and Cologne heretics shared one disposition: hatred of the Church’s ministers, sacraments, infant baptism, and marriage. Their few peculiar points indicate not a distinct type of sect, but only a certain diversity among its branches. In a word, they were different branches springing from the same root. Nor do I doubt that those Cologne heretics emerged from Tanchelm’s workshop.”

456. Distinct from the foregoing mass of heretics, at least in name, were those who called themselves Apostolics. Concerning them, the Cistercian historian writes under the year 1147, chapter 14: “The Henrician heretics having been suppressed and for the most part reconciled to the Church, the holy Father was now returning to his own people. Behold, he encountered another sect of men who wished to call themselves Apostolics. They were a rustic and country breed, without a teacher or leader to follow, but for that very reason more difficult to dissuade: each had to be approached separately, and with them neither Scripture nor reason could be used. When the saint had returned to his sons, after so often resuming the Song interrupted for the Church—that is, for the Bride—he said in Sermon 66: ‘They are rustic men, unlearned, and altogether contemptible. But, I tell you, they must not be dealt with carelessly. [Col. 0863D] For they make great progress toward impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer.’ And after a few intervening words, the holy doctor says: ‘Ask them for the author of their sect: they will name no one. What heresy has not had its own heresiarch from among men? The Manichaeans had Mani as their leader and teacher; the Sabellians, Sabellius; the Arians, Arius; the Eunomians, Eunomius; the Nestorians, Nestorius. Thus all the other plagues of this kind are known individually to have had individual human teachers, from whom they derived at once their origin and their name. By what name or title will you classify these people? By none. For their heresy is not from man, nor did they receive it through man,’” etc.

457. Since they had neither an author nor a name, the saint testifies in the same epistle that they wished to call themselves Apostles, in these words: “I am not unaware that they boast that they alone are Christ’s body. But let those persuade themselves of this who also hold themselves persuaded that they have power daily at their own table to consecrate Christ’s body and blood, so that they may nourish themselves into Christ’s body and members! Certainly they vaunt themselves to be successors of the apostles and call themselves Apostolics, yet cannot show any sign of their apostolate.” You have Saint Bernard’s words about these heretics. If you consider his phrase, “By what name or title will you classify these people? By none,” it is more probable that they differed from the Henricians both in name and in founder. Nevertheless Mabillon counts them among the Cologne heretics in his note on the passage just quoted, observing: [Col. 0864B] “I do not know whether Bernard would have said this if those Cologne people had had Henry, from whom the Henrician heretics took their name, as their founder. Yet the doctrines of both were similar, as is evident to one comparing Letter 240. Everwin notes two classes among the people of Cologne, whom Bernard distinguishes only obscurely at the end of Sermon 65.”

458. Against such utterly impure and perverse doctrines of the sectarians, therefore, the holy doctor drew his pen. See his already cited Sermons 65 and 66, and also the most eminent Baronius under the year of Christ 1147, who concludes the matter with this encomium of the holy man: “Since I know with certainty that he was divinely enlightened in knowledge, sent and proved by God through the power of many miracles, endowed with outstanding holiness of life, and a friend of God, I am confident, clinging most closely to him who clung to God; and I lament in Christian charity those utterly ruined innovators who, struck by precisely the same boundless blindness, pay more deference to the brutal heretics who follow these most wicked men than to Bernard. Thus one may rightly cry out with Jeremiah: ‘Be appalled, O heavens, at this.’”

459. What the aforesaid Geoffrey reports concerning the miracles performed by the holy doctor among the people of Toulouse in confirmation of orthodox faith against the Henrician mass is so scanty that it deserves supplementation from other documents. Let that which is read in the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, in Tissier, distinction 2, [Col. 0864D] chapter 18, come first. “While the most reverend Father was still staying in the same region, Toulouse, travelling about towns and cities as one of the apostles, preaching, healing every infirmity, and rebuking, convicting, and refuting also the most shameful ravings of the heretics, it happened that a certain blind man in that neighbourhood, having heard the report of the virtues and signs multiplied day by day through the hands of the man of God, was encouraged by hope of recovering health. He resolved [perhaps ‘had resolved’] to seek out that servant of God, in the hope that by the benefit of heavenly grace, which was abundantly bestowed through him upon miserable mortals, the darkness of blindness might be wiped away and sweet light restored to himself also. Hastening, therefore, and anxiously inquiring where he might find the saint [Col. 0865A] of God, he heard that he was standing amid a great multitude at a certain celebrated gathering and scattering abroad the word of life.

460. “When he arrived there, stumbling with his feet and running breathlessly, he was struck by the sad report that the man of God had already departed and gone elsewhere. Yet what was he to do? The desire to regain his health compelled him to pursue him farther, but the thickest darkness that enveloped his eyes made him slow and less able to move. As he languished in great sorrow, his courage failing, he was suddenly inspired by divine grace and conceived with all his heart hope in the merits of the most blessed man. He said to those standing by: ‘I beg you, by [Col. 0865B] God’s mercy, lead me to that place where you most certainly know that the man of God stood or sat.’ This he immediately obtained through the goodwill of those present. Coming to the spot, he prostrated himself on the ground with his whole body and, with wondrous devotion, kissed the very dust upon which the holy footprints of the man of God had rested. He earnestly implored the Lord’s mercy through the merits of his servant. While doing this, and rubbing his eyes with that very dust in full faith, he suddenly received the light of his eyes, through the mercy of the Lord, who deigned even by this grace to manifest the holiness of his servant though absent. This deed brought not only support to Catholics in their orthodox faith, but also increased the mark of confusion and disgrace upon the boastful heretics.” Thus far the *Exordium*.

## § XLIV. Hardened heretics punished by God; Bernard’s holiness and miracles held in highest veneration at Toulouse; he did not go thence into Spain

461. Yet our holy wonder-worker advanced God’s cause and the true faith among the people of Toulouse not only by divine favours, but also chastised with punishments those who, hearing the Lord’s voice through Bernard, hardened their hearts. The following is from the chronicle to be cited shortly: “The blessed religious man Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, distinguished in life and learning and inflamed with zeal for the faith, at one time visited the land sick from the misfortune [*disgratia*, i.e. calamity] of such great unbelief. He hastened to approach the castle of Verfeuil, which at that time flourished with a military [Col. 0865D] and popular multitude, intending that, if he could extinguish there the heretical depravity which had greatly infected the place, he might more easily prevail against it elsewhere. When he began in the church to address those who were the chief persons there, they left the church, and the people followed them. The blessed man followed them and began to proclaim God’s word in the square. But they hid themselves in houses on every side. He nevertheless continued preaching to the little crowd around him; but they made a din and beat upon the doors, so that the people could not hear his voice or the word of God. Shaking the dust from his feet as a testimony against them, to declare that they were dust and would return to dust, he departed from them; looking back upon the castle itself, he cursed it, saying: ‘Verfeuil, may God dry you up.’

462. “This curse continues with evident signs. For at that time, as ancient tradition relates, there were in that castle a hundred households of knights, possessing horses with their trappings and arms, who did not return to another’s oats but to their own. From that time true poverty, like an armed man, began frequently to assail them; frequent hail, sterility, sedition, and even war allowed them little rest. Indeed, when I myself was a child, I saw the noble Lord Isarn Nebulatus, formerly the chief lord of Verfeuil, who was said with good reason to be a hundred years old, living in utmost poverty at Toulouse and content with one nag [*roncinus*]. But the fact itself plainly shows how and how severely, by God’s judgment, punishment fell upon many lords of that castle who were ruined. For what the holy man had cursed could not be restored until the count of Montfort gave the castle to the venerable Father Lord Fulk, bishop of Toulouse; from then it gradually began to be reformed after the lords had been expelled, as the following account will show in its proper place.” These matters are narrated in the chronicle of Master William of Puylaurens, published by Catel at the end of his *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, chapter 1. I explain two terms occurring in the text. *Viridefolium*, in the vernacular Verfeuil, is a castle in the diocese of Toulouse, near which Saint Dominic later debated with the Albigensian heretics. Here *roncinus* means a smaller, ordinary horse: French *roncin*, *roucin*, or *rossin*. Consult Du Cange’s *Glossary*. These details supplement what Geoffrey recalls concerning Saint Bernard’s miracles among the people of Toulouse.

463. His miracles and preaching, as well as the fame of his exceptional holiness, aroused there a wonderful veneration for him. This is clear from the fact that, even upon his arrival at Toulouse, and indeed perhaps before he had wrought any sign among them, he was already held there in the highest affection. Let Geoffrey, book III, chapter 2, be heard: “When he came, he was received by the people of the land with incredible devotion, as though an angel had come from heaven. He could not stay among them, because no one was able to restrain the crowds rushing upon him,” etc. What of this? “The multitude of people who pressed forward to request a blessing and kiss his holy hands was so great that his most tender and wholly wasted flesh could not bear the repeated pressing and assault of those kissing him; his holy hands and arms swelled like fists. From that by which others sought blessing for themselves through the power that went forth from him, he himself was weakened, utterly bruised, and endured severe bodily suffering.” This is from the *Great Exordium*, distinction 2, chapter 18, after the signs of the holy man performed in the region of Toulouse have been related.

464. The distinguished veneration conceived for him there, deeply implanted in people’s minds [Col. 0867A] and publicly renowned, could not be uprooted or even obscured by a malicious, heretical slanderer; indeed, it shone still more brightly when the fellow’s chatter in attacking the man of God was blunted by his prudent answer. The *Great Exordium*, distinction 2, chapter 17, tells the incident: “At a certain time, when the lord pope’s legate and other bishops brought with them the holy Bernard of the Lord into the region of Toulouse to refute the Manichaean heresy, the brethren prepared for him a better mount than usual, one which could suffice for so long a journey. When he had arrived in those regions accompanied by the bishops, a certain Henry, a black [Benedictine] monk but then a contemptible apostate and leader of those heretics, learned of the coming of God’s servant. Fearing his presence, because he knew that he could not resist the wisdom and spirit speaking in him, Henry hurriedly fled into hiding and could nowhere at that time be found.

465. “There also the Lord glorified his servant before all the people and the princes of the land, daily performing through his hands great signs and wonders among the people. It is not easy to believe how innumerable were the crowds that followed the apostolic man all day long: some sought instruction, others healing, and all a blessing from him. On one day, then, in the presence of an innumerable multitude, after he had spoken to them at length of preserving the Catholic faith and avoiding the unclean fellowship of heretics, [Col. 0867C] there happened to be present one of those heretics who seemed more powerful and more astute than the rest. Seeing with a bitter eye the veneration paid by the people to God’s servant, he sought to do something by which he might somewhat cloud the brightness of Bernard’s reputation and stain his glory. Now when all that seemed necessary for the occasion had been completed, the man of God had mounted his horse to depart. Behold, the aforesaid heretic came before the man of God with head raised, like a twisting serpent, and cried out before everyone: ‘Lord Abbot, know that our master’s horse, which appears so bad to you, is not as thick-necked and fat as this steed of yours.’

466. “Hearing this, the meek and patient man immediately answered him with tranquil face and mind: ‘Friend, I do not deny what you assert. Yet you ought to know that this beast of burden, about which you taunt me, is a brute animal—one, certainly, of those which nature has made prone and obedient to the belly. If it eats as it pleases and grows fat, justice suffers no injury from that, because a beast does what belongs to it. Therefore your master and I shall not be called to account at God’s judgment for the necks of our beasts, but each person shall be judged concerning his own neck. Now then, if you please, look at my neck and see it; and if it is thicker than your master’s neck, perhaps you may justly rebuke me for it.’ Having said this, he removed his hood and, his head being uncovered down to the shoulders, [Col. 0868A] his neck was seen to be long and slender. Although it was worn away and thin in the flesh, it was nevertheless, by a heavenly gift, exceedingly beautiful and white, like a swan’s neck. When all those present saw this, they rejoiced with great joy, blessing the Lord, who had given his servant so ready and fitting an answer, by which the man might be confounded and the mouth of those speaking iniquity stopped.”

467. When the Cistercian annalist, under the year 1147, chapter 13, had explained how excellently St Bernard had conducted himself in preaching at Toulouse, he reports and refutes the opinion of those who maintain that the man of God travelled to Spain. If this opinion were true, he observes, that journey would have to be connected with this year for two reasons: “first, because in it the monastery of La Espina was founded, as we shall say in its proper place; secondly, because the passage from Toulouse is easier, since that province borders upon Spain.” So he writes, adding arguments against this ill-founded opinion; but we shall draw ours from elsewhere.

While we were at Madrid in the year of Christ 1721, the most reverend and distinguished Lord Adrian de Coninck, a blood relative of the praised author, very kindly shared with us the posthumous manuscripts of the eminent Nicholas Antonio, well known to the republic of letters through the *Bibliotheca Hispana* which he had published.

In these manuscripts this most distinguished Spanish writer is wholly engaged in attacking and demolishing the fabulous inventions and apocryphal fabrications of the notorious—or rather, to speak frankly, infamous—pseudo-chronographers. Let us therefore set out here what we have extracted from his manuscripts for our present purpose. He refutes a passage of the disguised Julian Peter, archpriest of St Justa, printed in that author’s *Adversaria*, p. 96, no. 418.

468. “It is likewise new and hitherto unheard of—indeed, utterly false—that St Bernard, the most holy abbot of Clairvaux, was in Spain, along with all the falsehoods and absurdities contained in the passage just cited.” Thus I read there in the *Adversaria*:

“After Emperor Alfonso took the city of Toledo and restored it to the Christians, he ordered that it should be called the imperial city, the capital of the empire of Toledo and of Spain; and, as has been said, he was crowned emperor by the authority of Pope Anastasius IV. Therefore Bernard of Clairvaux calls him so. This holy man came into Spain with his brother Bernard, and visited the monasteries at Toledo of St Clement and St Dominic of Silos; and afterwards he wrote to the nuns of St Clement. He founded in Spain the monastery called La Espina.”

The praised Nicholas Antonio rebukes this fabulist as follows:

“First of all, he childishly confuses the two Alfonsos VI and VII. For the sixth captured Toledo from the Moors; the seventh, nephew of the former through his daughter Urraca, was the one whom he had already taught us in the *Chronicle* to have been crowned emperor by the authority of Pope Anastasius . . . although each of them is called emperor by him, because they were in fact so styled.

469. “Next, the assertion that St Bernard wrote to this Alfonso VII, assigning him the title of emperor, is equally false; or at any rate, nowhere among the letters of the holy abbot will you find evidence of the fact. Two published letters are addressed to Alfonso, but to Alfonso I, king of Portugal: namely, 308 and 367; they have nothing to do with Julian.

“Moreover, that Bernard came into Spain is expressly denied by Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, spiritual child of the holy Father, who declares that he was present at all the events which he narrates. He is the author of the second book—otherwise called the third, fourth, and fifth—of the *Life of St Bernard*, as is clear from the preface to this part in editions arranged through the efforts of the most distinguished Jacques Merlon Horstius (we possess the Paris edition of 1658). Most explicitly, after entitling chapter 6 of book IV concerning various illustrious miracles performed at Cologne, Aachen, Liège, Cambrai, and Spain, he prefaces his account of the Spanish miracles thus: ‘For in Spain also, where he himself was not present, signs of his holiness shone forth.’

“This testimony of Geoffrey is used by the most learned Benedictine writer Fr Antonio Yepes, vol. VII, century 7, year 1146, fol. 370, col. 4, to refute someone’s error. Our own Juan de Mariana committed this error in his *History of the Affairs of Spain*, book X, chapter 12, under the year 1123: deceived by the not obscure words of the holy abbot addressed to Peter the Venerable upon his return from Spain, Letter 227—which is 228 in Mabillon’s edition—he believed Bernard to be speaking of himself. Nor do we find any corroboration whatsoever of the alleged letter directed to the holy women of St Clement in the city of Toledo, which professes to commend in some fashion a faith that is in ruins.

470. “The procession of falsehoods is closed by the attribution to that same most holy man of the foundation among us of the monastery of La Espina, situated in [a pleasant place] between the two kingdoms of Castile and León, six leagues from Valladolid and five from the city of Toro. It takes this name from a thorn of the Lord’s crown preserved there, which it boasts was given, as Louis the Younger, king of France, passed through Paris, to the founding lady of the house, the infanta Sancha, sister of Emperor Alfonso VII.

“The same Yepes relates the matter in the same vol. VII, under the year 1143, chapter 1, fol. 328. He adduces and explains documents which might in some sense signify that the monastery, suitably endowed, was offered and handed over to Bernard in person: namely, the charter of endowment itself, in which the devout princess says that she gives as a gift to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the inheritance of St Peter of La Espina; and likewise a certain privilege of King Alfonso, Sancha’s brother, drawn up for the enlargement of the same house. Yet such documents are customarily said equally of persons absent as of persons present, when gifts and offerings are made for their benefit.

471. “Indeed, the constant tradition of that house is that St Bernard, having sent his brother Nivard into Spain—Julian reads ‘Bernard’—and having mentioned in a letter addressed to Sancha that Nivard had returned to him from there and from her, employed Nivard’s hand and industry as the recipient of the pious donation and in the work of building. This tradition is confirmed by these rough but ancient verses, which the members of the house report as being inscribed in various places upon its old walls and woven into its hangings:

*PETIT AEDIFICAT DITAT SANCIA / BERNARDUS PER NIVARDUM / ALFONSVS PROTEGIT / APERIT SPINEA CORONA PETRVS.*

“Sancha petitions; Bernard builds through Nivard; Alfonso endows; Peter protects; the thorny crown opens.”

For that religious house was first dedicated to Peter, prince of the apostles, and its church was afterwards called that of St Mary.

“Julian falsely said that Bernard visited the monasteries of the nuns of St Clement at Toledo and of the men of St Dominic of Silos, thus inventing the arrival among us of the most distinguished abbot.”

472. Moreover, Manrique treats of the foundation of St Peter of La Espina under the year 1147, chapter 18. From St Bernard’s Letter 301, cited above, he admits that Nivard’s arrival in Spain is more certain than the outcome of his mission—whether Nivard was the youngest by birth among the saintly doctor’s brothers according to the flesh, or another person.

If anyone desires to know more concerning the pseudo-Julian Peter, archpriest—as he styles himself—of St Justa at Toledo, let him consult the praised Nicholas Antonio, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, chapter 8. There that learned author examines his works, reproves them as false and fabricated, and strips the mask from their disguised inventor. In chapter 9 he produces eighteen passages from which anyone may see clearly that Julian’s *Chronicle* and *Adversaria* are refuted.

473. Indeed, Tamayo himself—otherwise so credulous, and so miserably naïve and excessive an admirer of pseudo-chronicles of this sort—was compelled to declare in his *Spanish Martyrology*, vol. II, for 3 April, p. 469:

> “Throughout these *Adversaria* of Julian we see such absurdities of glossing that we should be compelled to swallow iron rather than them.”

But let these observations concerning the fabricated Spanish journey of St Bernard be introduced, so to speak, incidentally. His true achievements are certainly so numerous in extinguishing schisms and uprooting heresies that there is no necessity whatever to attach a false one to him. It now seems fitting to add to the deeds which we have previously recounted as performed by him in this sphere, in removing evils from the Church of God, his countless beneficial accomplishments, or his success in reforming the morals of the Christian commonwealth.

## § XLV. The holy Father fruitfully devoted to reforming the morals of clergy, monks, and laypeople

474. We owe the matter and structure of this subject, and acknowledge the debt, to the most learned Mabillon, who says as follows in § 3 of his general preface to his new edition of the works of St Bernard:

> “The holy man everywhere laments and deplores the corrupt morals of his age, especially among the ministers of the Church. He brought most of them to better conduct, so that the entire condition of the Church and clergy—above all, the Gallican clergy—was thoroughly transformed by his counsels and sermons and restored to its ancient dignity. Indeed, he supplied the Roman See with Eugenius, a most holy man; and in him he instructed and stirred up all Roman pontiffs to the proper and lawful exercise of their dignity, by the truly divine books which he published *On Consideration*. Among bishops, he recalled Henry of Sens, Stephen of Paris, and very many others from a courtly manner of life to morals worthy of the episcopal rank; and he produced many of his own men as bishops for the example of others. He gave salutary counsels to all clerics in his sermon *On Conversion, to Clerics*.

> “Whoever wishes to see all these matters carefully should read book VI of the French *Life of St Bernard*, the latter three books of which are woven, with great devotion and notable selection, from Bernard’s writings. Concerning the morals and office of bishops, one should read especially Letter 42, to Henry of Sens, now placed among the treatises in vol. II. Therefore it is deservedly said in the book *On the Bishops of Verdun* that Bernard is the man ‘upon whose counsels kingdoms and the churches of Gaul now rest,’ as the author says in d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 311.

475. “He possessed a wonderful grace in speaking, such that not even his own style, though outstanding, could retain all that sweetness and all that ardour. Indeed, God had given him a conciliatory, persuasive, and learned tongue, so that he knew whom and when he ought to address: to whom consolation or entreaty, to whom exhortation or rebuke, was fitting. Those who have read his writings may know this to some extent, though far less than those who often heard his words. If we are thus inflamed by reading his writings, how much more those who heard him speaking! It is therefore not surprising that through him God accomplished so many and such great things for the salvation of the people of his time.

476. “Who could explain what, and how great, were the things which he achieved in rekindling the original fervour of the monastic institution? His outstanding letters and writings on this subject, the book *On Precept and Dispensation*, the *Apology to Abbot William*, and various sermons testify to it. In them he urged monks to retain and restore the chief rule of the ancient Fathers: namely, the labours and austerities of penance, moderation and humility, poverty, contempt for the world, love of solitude and silence, and continual progress. He understood that the hinge of the whole monastic way of life turns upon these things.

> “Thus Peter the Venerable, in Letter 228 among Bernard’s letters, no. 30, not undeservedly calls him ‘the milky and mighty pillar on which the structure of the monastic order rests,’ and ‘a shining star’ which in his time gave remarkable light, by his example and word, not only to monks but also to the whole Latin Church.

477. “In his book *On the Bishops of Verdun*, Lawrence of Liège compares the Cistercian and Premonstratensian orders to the two cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat. One of these, the Cistercian, under Bernard, abbot of most holy name, restored the monastic order, now almost fallen, to the first norm of apostolic life. ‘And in the space of this three-year period,’ he says, ‘the Cistercian order increased to about two hundred abbeys, great in name, merit, and number; and it had already begun to spread even among the barbarous Sarmatians and the remotest Scythians.’ Such was the power of Bernard’s fame and reputation for holiness, and that of his disciples.

“Consequently Bernard himself, though merely a son of the Cistercian order, was regarded almost as its founder; and from his monastery of Clairvaux the order was in his time called the Order of Clairvaux, indeed afterwards even the Order of St Bernard. Innocent VIII nevertheless prohibited this in the letters uniting the monastery of Clairvaux with the Cistercian order.

478. “Thus in the letters of Albero, bishop of Verdun, quoted by the recently praised Lawrence, the abbots of Trois-Fontaines and La Chalade are called members of the Order of Clairvaux. Peter of Celle likewise calls it the Cistercian, or Clairvaux, order in book I, letter 24. Thus in the letter of Samson, bishop of Reims, which is numbered 435 among Bernard’s letters, the Order of Clairvaux is mentioned more than once. It may, however, be said that the name ‘Order of Clairvaux’ often denotes only the Clairvaux line, not the entire order.

479. “What and how great was the strictness and severity of either the Cistercians or the men of Clairvaux under Bernard need not be set out here, since it is more than sufficiently evident both from Bernard’s letters and writings and from his *Life*, especially book I, chapter 5. There the first inhabitants of Clairvaux are said to have served God in poverty of spirit, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils. They often made their dishes from beech leaves. Their bread was of barley, vetch, and millet.

“William, an eyewitness, writes thus; and Bernard, in Letter 1 to Robert, says that vegetables, beans, porridge, and coarse bread with water were the Cistercians’ delicacies. Fastred likewise gives no other fare in his letter among Bernard’s correspondence. ‘Their economy in food is so great,’ says Stephen of Tournai in Letter 72, ‘that they use only two dishes, which the field provides from legumes or the garden from vegetables. They use fish so much more rarely as it is more commonly heard of than seen among them.’ You may find more in the same author and in Peter of Celle.

480. “This vigour [perhaps ‘severity’] of the order continued not only to the end of the twelfth century, as appears from Peter of Blois, Letter 82, but also beyond the middle of the thirteenth century, as James of Vitry testifies in chapter 13 of his *Western History*. ‘They do not eat meat,’ he says, ‘except in serious illness. They do not ordinarily consume fish, eggs, milk, or cheese,’ etc. We Frenchmen even now see the same severity of life flourishing again among the most devout monks of Blessed Mary of La Trappe and some other imitators of theirs. By their purity of life, austerity, love of solitude, silence, labour, and other religious virtues, they establish as possible in practice what we read, and scarcely believed, of Bernard and his disciples.

481. “James of Vitry adds in the following chapter that the weaker sex of women did not venture, from the beginning of the order, to aspire to the severity of so strict an observance; but that this later became customary. Nevertheless, during Bernard’s lifetime women were not wholly without participation in this institution. This is proved by Herman, monk of Laon, in book III of *The Miracles of Holy Mary*, chapter 17, where he treats of a small monastery of Cistercian virgins at the Laon Parthenon, built by Bishop Bartholomew. There the nuns, under Abbess Guiburge, laid aside all linen and fur garments and wore only woollen tunics. They sought their livelihood in silence by working continually with their own hands, not only spinning and weaving, but also digging in the fields, clearing felled woodland with axe and hoe, and pulling up thorns and brambles. In every respect they imitated the life of the monks of Clairvaux.

482. “The discussion would proceed too far if we were to bring forward all the distinguished men and women, known to us, whom Bernard drew to monastic life: such as Henry, son of Louis VI, king of the French; Ermengard, duchess of Brittany; Adelaide of Lorraine; and countless others of both sexes. Yet it is a scarcely less praiseworthy and admirable achievement that he persuaded those remaining in the world to adopt a most devout and upright way of life.

“Above all princes Count Theobald attached himself to Bernard, placing both himself and his possessions at Clairvaux’s disposal and putting his soul into the abbot’s hands. Laying aside the height of princely station, he showed himself among the servants of God as a fellow servant, not a lord, ready to obey in everything that even the least member of that house might require. Ernald the abbot, from whom we have reported the foregoing, testifies what this great prince accomplished at Bernard’s urging and exhortation, both in building, endowing, and assisting monasteries, in relieving the poor, and finally in discharging the office of an excellent ruler. Bernard’s letters concerning him also testify to it. The noble and illustrious lady Beatrice emulated Theobald’s devout zeal, as we learn from Letter 118.

[Col. 0873D] 483. “Finally, the conversion of Duke William of Aquitaine shows how greatly Bernard’s authority availed in reforming human morals: from a most obstinate schismatic he made him an exceptionally obedient and devout prince. To conclude briefly with Geoffrey: ‘What crimes did he not rebuke? What hatreds did he not extinguish? What scandals did he not restrain? What schisms did he not repair [Mabillon: “restrain”]? What heresies did he not refute?’”

These are the matters Mabillon collected concerning the moral improvement, spread everywhere by the great Bernard throughout every class of people in the Church of God. What concerns heresies and schisms, overcome by the man’s skill and labour, has been treated by us elsewhere at considerable length.

## § XLVI. Whether St Bernard was greeted by an image of the Mother of God at Speyer; whether he was sprinkled with her virginal milk

484. Above, in § 40 of our preliminary Commentary, we reserved for this place three notable occurrences attributed to the most holy Father. The first concerned an image of the Virgin Mother of God, which, after being greeted three times at Speyer by the holy man, is said to have returned his greeting once, “with all hearing,” according to Manrique under the year 1146, chapter 10, no. 6. The second concerned the virginal milk of that same Mother of God, with which St Bernard is reported to have been sprinkled, according to the same author, ibid., no. 8. The third was that he was greeted by the voice of the most blessed Virgin Mary among the monks of Afflighem. Let us speak of each.

The Cistercian historian just cited relates the first from Johannes Nauclerus, who, speaking of the matter, says:

> “They agree on this: Bernard came to Speyer, where there was then such a great throng of people to venerate him that the emperor deigned to carry him away in his own hands, lest the crowd trample him. Three circles remain in the pavement of the principal church where, prostrate upon the ground, the man of God is said to have greeted the Virgin Mary three times. To him the Virgin Mary said, ‘Hail, Bernard!’”

Johannes Nauclerus writes this in Generation 39 among other things which he records under the year of Christ 1142. Manrique attempts to confirm this miraculous greeting of the Mother of God by proceeding as follows:

> “The words are engraved in the circles which the faithful are accustomed to sing at the end of the antiphon which from its beginning we call *Salve Regina*. Father Bernard is confidently reported to have recited it as ending in the words, ‘and after this our exile show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus’; and, more confidently, to have added to the recitation that threefold invocation. Moved by this, and accepting the homage, the image of the Virgin was heard to return the saint’s greeting in like manner: ‘Hail, Bernard!’”

So he writes. Upon this I offer certain observations to the reader who is free from party spirit and loves truth.

485. First, Johannes Nauclerus is sufficiently well known. I read that he was German by nationality, Swabian by birthplace, and provost of Tübingen by rank. He published a universal chronicle, briefly comprising memorable events of all ages and nations from the creation of the world down to the year 1500. He flourished, however, at the end of the sixteenth century, and therefore about four centuries after the saint’s death. Nor does the *τό* (*to*, ‘the word’) *fertur* (‘it is said’), which Nauclerus uses, fail considerably to weaken the credibility of the event.

Testimony of better quality therefore seems necessary if the aforesaid greeting of Bernard by the Mother of God is to be accepted as historically true. This is especially so because, in book VI of the *Life of St Bernard*, or part I of the miracles, chapter 2, where eyewitnesses report with the highest fidelity and accuracy so many and such great marvels concerning the man of God that occurred at Speyer, they say not a word about this greeting. Yet it would have contributed so much to the saint’s glory that they should not have passed it over in silence. Nor can I conceive how they could have been ignorant of the event, since, as Manrique cited above says, it happened “with all hearing it.”

486. Although we do not wish, from the silence of the ancient writers on this matter, to decide with certainty that this greeting is false, yet before we admit it as true we earnestly ask all those particularly learned and devoted in Bernardine matters to furnish the republic of letters with suitable documents by which this occurrence—which seems to us less than probable—may become truly and historically credible.

Nor does the Reverend Father Augustine Sartorius, a Cistercian ascetic, establish the matter when, in his *Cistercium bis tertium*, printed at Old Prague in 1700, title 4, *On St Bernard as Propagator of the Cistercians*, p. 91, he writes thus of the statue which greeted the saint:

> “This very statue of the Virgin, down to our own age, preserves enduringly, by the outstanding devotion of the faithful, the memory of the Mother of God and her Mellifluous client.”

For this memory or tradition, whatever its worth—would that it were not merely popular!—does not seem at all to weaken the arguments proposed above. Hear now the absurd folly with which William Eysengrein, whom we shall cite shortly, disfigures this story under the year of Christ 1147:

> “When Bernard had uttered these words, a voice breaking forth from the image declared, in the hearing of all present, that Bernard had come in a manner pleasing to God and all people. Struck by this voice, Bernard, in amazement, forbade the image, saying that women ought to keep silence in church.”

This is mere trifling in a matter so serious. Our Papebroch, in his manuscript *Roman Journey*, undertaken in 1660, p. 39, writes among other things concerning the statue at Speyer which is said to have bidden St Bernard “hail”:

> “All our students gather before it every day before five o’clock and sing the *Salve* with litanies.”

So he writes. Their devout faith and religious affection toward the Virgin Mother deserve praise. But what shall we say concerning the milk of the Mother of God with which they maintain that the holy Father was sprinkled, if they judge that it must be understood in a physical or real sense, rather than a mystical one?

487. That occurrence, which I mentioned second above, must now be examined somewhat more fully. Manrique narrates it in these words, no. 8:

> “There are not lacking authors, and grave ones, who think that that virginal favour, never sufficiently praised by anyone though always praised by all—Bernard’s sprinkling with Mary’s milk—should perhaps be referred to this same time. It was first related by William Eysengrein in his *Speyer Chronicle*—would that Manrique had identified the year!—approved by Canisius and Coster—he does not say where—and confirmed by our Bivarius, book II of *Bernard Vindicated*, § 10, and others, namely Henriquez in his *Menology*, 13 May.
>
> “For us, although the favour itself is certain—yet some have not failed to deny it, as Johannes Bertelius is noted in the margin, Dialogue 8—the place and time still remain doubtful, on however slight and crude a foundation. Of the time scarcely anything can be written. As for the place, if anything certain can be known, I judge that it should be referred to Châtillon. But these and other similar matters must be discussed more fully under the death of the man of God, to which place we deliberately reserve them.”

But, considering the order and clarity of this question, we shall pursue in continuous discourse the matter which we have now begun to discuss, bringing back from the year 1153, chapter 12, to which Manrique transferred it, his fuller narrative.

488. “The notable favours shown to Father Bernard by Christ and the Virgin, under which he is commonly depicted—now sprinkled with the milk of the Virgin Mary, now embraced by the arms of the crucified Redeemer—and another favour, though less common yet no less certain, in which the Mother offered the Son to that same saint: since I have found no fixed time connected with them, I have deliberately reserved them for this place.

> “And indeed, it is established that they are received rather by tradition than by writing: by that constant tradition handed down, as it were, from fathers to sons, the credit of which is sometimes no less, but rather more unshaken. I admit that in ancient matters it is rarer, and is expressed more by paintings than letters, but is not therefore to be valued less,” etc.

Thus the Cistercian historian prefaces his account, and immediately begins with Christ, of whom we shall speak below. Then, in no. 6, he proceeds concerning our subject:

> “As regards the milk of the Blessed Virgin, it is even more commonly received and widespread in sacred images. Authors differ more about the time and place than about the favour itself; that it was granted to Bernard, no one doubts. The only person I have seen who calls it into question is Johannes Bertelius, in Dialogue 8 on the Rule of St Benedict; but on so coarse and grossly foolish a basis that he does not deserve refutation by us. ‘No one doubts,’ he says, ‘that Mary preceded Bernard by many centuries.’ As though anyone had ever imagined that the sacred Virgin, mortal and capable of suffering, offered Bernard her breast to suck, or as though, after her glorious departure, she did not remain eternally enduring, glorious then in heaven and in her images on earth.
>
> “But passing over these things because they are trivial, I see no one else who has doubted.”

489. “It is true, however,” he says, “that authors differ concerning the place. Some refer it to Speyer, when Father Bernard had devoutly greeted the Virgin Mother as merciful, loving, and sweet. But it is perhaps more probable that it happened not at Speyer, but at Châtillon, a town of the Lingones, and not amid so great a crowd: when the holy Father, humbly setting out for one of those legations to which he was accustomed to be sent, implored the help of the Virgin Mother. At that time the Son is believed to have been offered by the Mother for Bernard to receive, so that in carrying him, whether outwardly in his hands or inwardly in his heart, he might give himself wholly to him, and, under his protection, fear nothing.”

Thus far the Cistercian historian. Since, as we have seen above, he candidly admits that this remarkable favour of the virginal milk was first related by William Eysengrein in the *Speyer Chronicle*, and since no more ancient monuments are assigned from which that chronicler might have received this tradition, who can fault us if we say that the tradition of this favour granted to Bernard is recent? Bernard died in the year of Christ 1153, whereas Eysengrein wrote in the sixteenth century, having carried his *Chronicle* down to the year 1561. Can the confirmers or approvers named by Manrique—later than, or contemporaries of, Eysengrein—truly add any historical weight to Eysengrein’s first transmission of the tradition? Add that this chronicler gains little authority for himself when he either first produced, or adopted from another, that absurdity which we censured above in no. 486.

490. But let us not conceal the other materials which Manrique gathers from no. 7 onward:

> “There exists an authenticated document of the Reverend Lord Edmund of the Cross, then abbot of Cîteaux, sent in 1599 to Ignatius Firmin of Fitero—this document itself I have among his other papers—speaking of this favour in the following terms: ‘In the church of St Berolus in the castle of Châtillon-sur-Seine, in the diocese of Langres, there was formerly constructed an image, held in veneration and honour, of Blessed Virgin Mary. While St Bernard was praying, this image miraculously offered him her Son in the church, saying: “Bernard, receive my child, the Redeemer of the whole world.” Then, beyond all the power of human nature, as though he were Christ’s natural brother, when the breast of the said image was received in his hand, it immediately and miraculously distilled upon the blessed Bernard, her devoted servant, three drops of milk flowing from the breast of that same image.’”

Thus far the testimony of the venerable abbot, which Antonius Hiepius, under this year, chapter 5, Francis Bivarius, book I of *Bernard Vindicated*, and others mention. Henriquez too, in his *Menology*, for 13 May, mentions an icon—I suppose the same one—and a French inscription which, translated into Latin, attests the earlier part of the favour. It reads:

> Bernard, my greatly beloved chaplain,  
> Take, receive from my hand  
> Sweet Jesus, Saviour of the world.

This seems to state that she offered the Child Jesus to Bernard while he was still living and praying.

491. “The same Chrysostom Henriquez mentioned above,” Manrique adds in no. 8, “introduces another, still more recent, testimony, transmitted, as he says, from Châtillon of the Lingones itself to the reverend abbot of Châtillon in Verdun, from whom he testifies that he received it. In it, beyond the tradition of the event, the same reporter testifies, with witnesses produced, that the sacred image still remains today and—wonderful to relate—still preserves, or rather repeats, the memory of the event:

> ‘At Châtillon there is an image of the Blessed Virgin which is said to have sprinkled holy Bernard with a certain milk. Since he burned with singular love for the Blessed Virgin, she showed herself to be a mother also to him, as he prayed tirelessly before the aforesaid image. In the said castle there was a chapel, in the left part of which stood the image of the Blessed Virgin. There a certain soldier named Picant lived; while carrying out his duty by making his rounds of the castle during civil wars, he testifies that more than fifty times he heard voices singing “Hail, Star of the Sea” in the said chapel.
>
> “‘For the said miracle is remembered to have occurred when St Bernard uttered, “Show thyself to be a Mother.” When the wars had ceased and the castle was destroyed, the image was carried away for safer preservation into a church. There it is kept in a conspicuous and elevated place with great veneration and a concourse of people, especially when the need of the time requires it. Thence it is taken by three priests prepared by a three-day fast and is borne with greatest devotion in solemn procession, together with the relics of St Verolus, by a great number of virgins who have likewise first observed a three-day fast. There are people at Châtillon who say that this same image, when it is moved, distils drops of milk.
>
> “‘Two priests of proven life still live there: one is called Edmund; the other Clement, formerly tutor to the lord lieutenant Gaillard. They clearly and publicly affirm that such an abundance of milk flowed into the hands of a third priest, now dead, named James Viandot, that he had to go to the sacristy and wash his hands there.’”

Thus far the account. If these things are certain, they confer great authority upon the event, indeed authority almost beyond human belief.

492. “Philotheus,” Manrique continues in no. 9, “relates the favour of the milk more tersely and concisely, but says that it was granted to Bernard more than once:

> Why tell how often the Queen of the highest theatre  
> Was seen to utter nectar-sweet sounds to him?  
> Often the Virgin was accustomed to honour her servant  
> By visiting him, and often bringing ambrosial fare.

“In Hiepius I read also a tradition that Christ appeared to Bernard together with his Mother, and that they offered the saint, standing between them, blood and milk respectively, as though competing with one another: the former remaining from Christ’s wound, the latter from the Virgin’s breast; both heavenly, both illuminating and fertilising Bernard’s lips. Then the saint, having venerated both and bearing equally unwillingly to be deprived of either, finally burst forth into words commonly attributed to Augustine:

> Here I am fed from the wound; here I am suckled at the breast.  
> Set between them, I do not know to which I should turn.

“But I believe that it was the devotion of pious minds, rather than the truth of the event or a simultaneous occurrence, which joined these things together more closely. I do not see knowledge of this tradition in any other approved author; nor do I think such things easily to be believed, much less asserted. There are also among the works of Nicholas Salicetus certain other things attributed to Father Bernard, too unworthy of confidence to deserve a place in these *Annals*.”

So he writes. I shall make some observations on Philotheus and Salicetus at the end of the following paragraph. “Ignatius Firmin de Ibero, monk of Nucales in Spain . . . and afterwards appointed abbot of the very celebrated monastery of Fitero in the kingdom of Navarre,” is praised in the *Cistercian Library*, p. 167.

493. Sartorius, cited above, also contends that this favor of the Virgin’s milk, discussed earlier, must be understood in a physical and real sense, not merely a mystical one [Col. 0879A]: “If some assert,” he says on p. 91 and the following page, “that Bernard was indeed suckled by the Virgin, but not in the flesh, or with bodily lips, nor by real and physical milk, but only in spirit and through some mystical influence, this is plainly to cast suspicion upon the ancient truth, which has been established by so many pens and so many brushes for five or more centuries—as though those ancient writers had not known, as well as we do, how to distinguish between that mystical influence and a physical and real one. Both kinds of suckling must be granted to Bernard: that in the spirit and this in the flesh. The latter must not be denied, since this is precisely what the ancient and trustworthy historians chiefly intended.”

So far Sartorius speaks generously enough. Yet would that he had at least brought forward some single suitable document in support of that “ancient truth, established,” as he wishes it, “for five and more centuries,” and had removed the suspicion which he says is cast upon the event. Who, pray, are “those ancient writers”? Who are the “ancient and trustworthy historians” whom he mentions but does not name? For the reply may indeed be made to him in the words of Mabillon—a man most deeply versed in matters concerning St Bernard, himself trustworthy, and highly deserving for his work on Bernard’s writings, virtues, and miracles—which he notes at the end of the Fragments from Herbert’s books on the miracles of Cistercian monks, in his often-cited edition, cols. 1231–1232:

> “In all the books of St Bernard’s miracles there is nowhere any mention of that miraculous milk expressed by the most blessed Virgin upon Bernard [Col. 0879C]; and yet we now see this miracle, above others most certain, being peddled by painters and by uncritical devotees of the holy Doctor.”

494. The Venerable Guibert, abbot of St Mary of Nogent, whose third book *On the Pledges of the Saints*, ch. 3, §4, p. 355, was published at Paris in 1651 and annotated by Acherius, rejects the milk of the Virgin Mother which, he says, “is said to be kept to this day at Laon … in a crystal dove.” On this passage the editor of Guibert makes various remarks in his notes and observations, pp. 575 ff.; but I extract one only, and the one most relevant here:

> “Some writers report that the same Queen of Heaven poured milk also into blessed Bernard of Clairvaux [Col. 0879D]; but let those who have examined the deeds of that man, written by three contemporaneous authors with whom Bernard was on most intimate terms, judge on what truth they are supported. For how can it be that, after recounting more than a hundred miracles, they consigned this most remarkable one to oblivion? Thus John Bertelius, book VIII, on the Rule of St Benedict; whom Chrysostom Henriquez refutes in the Cistercian Menologium for 13 May, and Angelus Manrique in the *Cistercian Annals*, vol. II, year 1153, ch. 12.”

We have just recently said who answers Bertelius here; and we have also indicated above what Chrysostom Henriquez’s arguments are which Manrique brings forward in defense of the truth of the present occurrence. Indeed, if anyone weighs carefully and without party spirit the arguments of these two Cistercian writers [Col. 0880A], and compares them with the argument of Bertelius and Mabillon—though it is, as they call it, a negative one—I shall be much mistaken if he does not award the palm to the latter rather than the former. Arguments of this sort, though merely negative, are not infrequently of greater force, considering the circumstances of events and writers, than affirmative arguments. Finally, the reasons drawn above from paintings and popular devotion do not deserve a more laborious refutation. From what has thus far been argued on either side in this controversy, we conclude that the opinion seems nearer the truth which does not admit that St Bernard was physically or really sprinkled with the milk of the Mother of God.

## §XLVII. The salutation of an image of the Mother of God at the monastery of Afflighem; Jesus fixed to the cross, releasing his arms from it and embracing Bernard.

[Col. 0880B]

495. There is a tradition that the holy man, while at the Benedictine monastery of Afflighem, situated in Belgium between Brussels and Aalst, was greeted by an image of the Mother of God. Concerning that other and altogether singular favor of the Virgin Mother of God toward St Bernard, which I had undertaken above to discuss, the following is handed down. “The famous monastery of Afflighem,” as Manrique writes under the year 1147, ch. 3, while treating of places in Belgium visited by the man of God, “was visited by the holy Father in passing. It is the constant tradition of that church that he strove, by repeated prayer [Col. 0880C], though unsuccessfully, to have the monks reformed according to the Cistercian rule; but that nevertheless he left behind his staff, with which he was accustomed to support his feeble limbs, as a pledge of friendly affection. They preserve and venerate it even today. Moreover, the men of Afflighem affirm, producing ancient records, that something greater happened there; and because it was published by Arnaldus [Raissius] a few years ago and bears many marks of truth, I have thought it pleasing to add it in his own words.”

Accordingly, the aforesaid Arnold Raissius, in the Supplement to John Molanus’s *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, under 20 August, left these remarks for posterity:

> “In the same monastery there was once to be seen a sacred statue of the Blessed Virgin which addressed blessed Bernard under Abbot Godescalcus. The following verses, extracted from the annals of the said monastery, attest the fact:
>
> Bernard says to Mary: ‘Hail to thee, blessed Virgin, mine!’  
> And I, the image, willingly return to thee: ‘Hail, Bernard!’”

496. “The Chronicle of Gembloux supports this, saying as follows: Before the devastation of Belgium and the undermining of the Catholic faith within Belgium itself, there was at the monastery of Afflighem an image of the Mother of God. As Bernard took leave of it, he said, ‘Farewell, gracious Mary.’ But holy Mary replied, ‘Farewell, Bernard.’ This image of blessed Mary bore Christ in her arms. It was carved from white and rather soft stone, sprinkled somewhat with black sand—called by the people of Brabant *labender-steen*—five feet or more in height, and altogether ancient in workmanship and appearance, with a veil hanging from the head upon the shoulders. [Col. 0881A] In this latest period the image was thrown from its base and broken by a certain insolent scoundrel, who thought it wooden and intended to make a fire from it. Two other sculptures were made from its fragments: one is preserved at Afflighem; the other was given by the prior to the Jesuit Fathers at Brussels.”

Having recounted from Raissius these things concerning the celebrated salutation of the Mother of God, let us hear what Manrique adds in no. 9: “Thus Afflighem and Speyer contend over the image of the Mother of God which returned Bernard the Father’s greeting, and each puts forward a tradition resting upon and established by ancient monuments, against which hardly anyone will dare to proceed. Let neither be defeated, but let both prevail; and let pious credulity persuade itself that the favor was repeated, which alone remains to be done.” But while Manrique speaks thus, he clings to the surface and does not penetrate to the heart of the matter.

497. For the question here is not one of “pious credulity.” Who would deny that the tradition of Afflighem—and, if one wishes, also that of Speyer, discussed above—may be piously believed? But it is another matter to prove its truth from contemporary witnesses or writers of the event, or from historically certain documents. Let us therefore briefly examine the testimonies cited from Raissius.

Antonius Sanderus, in the *History of the Affairs of Afflighem*, included in his published *Brabant*, relates similar matters to those just reported, p. 8; so too does the Continuation of the Chronicle of Afflighem, published from various records of that abbey in Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, vol. X [Col. 0881C], pp. 610 ff. In the History in question, p. 613, it is further stated that this image of the Mother of God was held in the highest veneration among the said monks: for “the custom had prevailed” among them “that in the morning they never went from the dormitory into the church without greeting this image through the Angelic Salutation.”

This continuation is preceded in the same volume of the *Spicilegium* by a history of the said monastery. Its editor writes to the reader on p. 23: “We have added a continuation or epitome of that history, composed from ancient and authentic records by Dom Odo Cambier, likewise of Afflighem, while he was alive and especially well versed in antiquarian matters.” The date of this writer or compiler is shown by the words with which he ends his little work: “Most recently, in our own times, Benedict Haeftenus has adorned the most holy and illustrious Father Benedict with the greatest splendors.” For in 1644, while provost there, he published the twelve books of *Monastic Investigations*, dedicating them to the most illustrious Lord Jacob Boonen, Archbishop of Mechelen and prelate of the abbey of Afflighem.

498. We have another Chronicle of Afflighem, marked MS N. 5, upon which our own Herbert Rosweyde wrote in his own hand that it had been excerpted “from a very recent Afflighem manuscript.” This indicates that the Chronicle was either collected from elsewhere by a very recent writer of that time [Col. 0882A], or copied by him from another compiler. At its end I find the year 1514 distinctly recorded; for although other matter concerning the monastery of Afflighem follows, namely a fifth book divided into three parts, it does not contain chronology but matter altogether different.

The following is read in the said Chronicle: “In the year 1148—Sanderus, p. 10, writes 1146—Lord Peter voluntarily laid down the burden of the abbacy; in his place Lord Godscalcus was appointed, a young man of good promise, because he sprang from a noble and holy family.” Later it says: “In the year of the Lord 1164, Lord Godscalcus laid down the burden of pastoral care,” etc. During this time of Godscalcus’s government, mention is indeed made of “St Bernard”; but I find there nothing concerning the salutation bestowed upon the holy man by the statue of the Mother of God, although Raissius above affirmed that it happened “under Abbot Godscalcus,” while the Continuation of the Chronicle of Afflighem in Acherius states that it occurred “at the beginning of this prelacy.” Since the event ought to have been very famous among the monks of Afflighem and highly honorable to their monastery, it seems surprising that the aforesaid compiler or copyist supplies nothing about it. From the Chronicle of Gembloux, cited above, however, it follows that this miraculous image of the Mother of God was known at the monastery of Afflighem before the dreadful tragedies in Belgium stirred up by heretics in the sixteenth century, and was accordingly honored as such.

499. More ancient records of this tradition [Col. 0882C] are not readily available to us. In Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux and companion of the holy man on his Belgian journey, who gives a detailed and accurate itinerary of that journey in part III of the miracles, or book VI of the *Life*, ch. 5—an itinerary which may be inspected at the place cited, rather than being repeated here to the reader’s weariness—it will suffice to note the names of the places at which the holy man stopped. Thus, after preaching in Germany for the Holy War, he went from Liège to the town of Huy, or Huum, in the diocese of Liège; from Huy to Gembloux; then he sought Villers, or the monastery of Villers; thence the town of Fontaine; from Fontaine he moved to the castle of Bins, that is, Binche, a Belgian town in the county of Hainaut; at Binche he was received at the castle of Mons, now Mons in Hainaut [Col. 0882D]; afterward at Valenciennes, a city of the diocese of Cambrai; at the monastery of Humblieres; at Laon and Reims; and finally he returned to his own monastery of Clairvaux.

From this you see that the holy man returned by the Franco-Belgian region, not by the Flemish-Belgian region in which the monastery of Afflighem is situated. This journey which we have described concerns the time at which the oft-mentioned prodigious event is said to have occurred at Afflighem. But we cannot establish from the foregoing itinerary that our saint stopped there at that time, nor do we remember reading it in another early biographer. Yet Sanderus, among the praises of the monastery of Afflighem, p. 7, reports that St Bernard thus commended it:

> “Around the year 1147, when he had observed with his own eyes the holy life of the men of Afflighem, he is said to have declared: ‘Everywhere I found human beings; here, however, angels. Truly Afflighem: where the spirit is afflicted.’ Thus the records of that place have it.”

500. Although Geoffrey says nothing of St Bernard’s arrival among the monks of Afflighem, it does not follow that he did not visit them. For the contrary is found in our manuscript Chronicle of the Abbots of Villers, marked MS 9, A, and noted as transcribed from a Rubeaevallis manuscript, parchment folio, from the first part of the *Novale Sanctorum*. The final year I find there distinctly recorded is 1333. After the prologue, the said chronicle begins thus:

> “When St Bernard had once entered Brabant for the sake of preaching, in order to gain some fruit there as in other nations, he visited the monastery of Afflighem and delivered two sermons there. In memory of this, the men of Afflighem are said to preserve the staff upon which he was accustomed to support his weak limbs. But when he had wished to unite them to the Cistercian Order and they had not wished it, he entered the monastery of Gembloux; and, being received there kindly, he left in it his chasuble, which is still there.”

The same things are recorded in the printed Chronicle or History of Villers in Martène’s *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. III, from col. 1269. Raissius, the same writer cited above, describes as follows the memorial left by the holy Father to the monks of Gembloux: “He gave them his chasuble, hanging down everywhere in the ancient fashion, and a stole with a maniple, [Col. 0883C] upon which are images beautifully embroidered in gold thread, as I myself once had occasion to see.”

From what is subsequently noted in the cited chronicle—“When Lord Gyroldus had resigned, Lord Fastradus became the third abbot of Villers, and these two observed the Sabbath for nearly five years. But when, in the year of the Lord 1151, St Bernard visited this place and celebrated the divine offices in the oratory, he called together many abbots at Reims and there settled a controversy which had arisen between us and the church of St Foillan the martyr”—from these words, I say, it follows that St Bernard visited his sons at Villers more than once.

Raissius maintains that the holy Father “by prophetic spirit … affirmed [Col. 0883D] that more monks would pass to heaven from that place than from any other monastery of the same Order; as, in subsequent times, happened, or may most plainly be gathered,” he says, “from this Supplement of mine, in which we have described no fewer than thirty religious from that monastery, all renowned for holiness of life.” So Raissius. But let us return to our subject, from which we have briefly digressed.

From what we have so far set forth concerning the celebrated tradition of Afflighem, we draw three corollaries. First, we by no means wish to represent it as false or apocryphal. Second, we regret that we cannot, as we would wish, demonstrate it more strongly as historically certain. Third, we shall not stand in the way of the most devout ascetics of Afflighem continuing to remain in possession of their tradition [Col. 0884A].

501. Since we are here wholly occupied in collecting the heavenly favors reported to have been granted to the most holy Father, we shall proceed in the same manner as above and recount other charisms of this kind. The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1153, ch. 12, no. 2 and following, writing of the singular prerogative with which Christ the Lord honored his most beloved servant, says:

> “The author of the *Great Exordium*, of surpassing authority, records that, when Bernard tenderly greeted his image hanging upon the cross itself, it loosened its arms and rushed into the greeting man’s embrace.”

The event is described in Tissier, distinction 2 of that work, ch. VII [Col. 0884B], in these words:

> “Dom Menardus [variants: Medardus and Gerardus], formerly abbot of Moris, a monastery neighboring Clairvaux, a religious man, related to his intimates, as though about another person, a certain wonderful event which we nevertheless think happened to himself. He said: ‘I know a certain monk who once found the blessed Abbot Bernard alone in church at prayer. While he was prostrate before the altar, there appeared to him a cross with its Crucified One lying upon the pavement before him. This most blessed man was devoutly adoring and kissing it. Then that Majesty itself, having separated its arms from the ends of the cross, seemed to embrace that servant of God and clasp him tightly to itself. As that monk beheld this for some time, he stood stupefied in excessive amazement and was, as it were, beside himself. At last, fearing that he might offend the holy Father if Bernard should see him standing so near, like an observer of his secrets, he silently departed, understanding and knowing, surely, of that holy man that his entire prayer and manner of life were truly above human measure.’”

We venerate this most devout story with great admiration, supported as it is by the testimony of the often-mentioned *Great Exordium*, a testimony certainly worthy of belief. It is also found in book II, ch. 19, of Herbert, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, in Chiffletius cited above, p. 283. In Tissier’s notes on both Cistercian *Exordia*, found after p. 262 [Col. 0884D], the following is observed: “What is said about Christ being seen to embrace St Bernard did not happen at Moris, as is commonly believed, since that monastery was founded at the time of the holy Father’s death.”

502. It is useful here to add from Manrique who this Menardus or Medardus was, who testifies to these sacred delights of Bernard. Under the aforesaid year, ch. 17, taking occasion to discuss the foundation of the monastery of Moris, he says: “Having received the site, Bernard sent a convent and placed over it as abbot Blessed Medardus—namely the man to whom we said that the sacred image of Christ embracing Bernard appeared, whether in a vision or in reality. This man of God, intimate with the saint and himself a saint, deserved to see many other visions, especially concerning the father whom he loved; from these we shall transcribe one … written by Geoffrey.” But, reader, see this event in book IV, ch. 1, of the *Life of St Bernard*. Manrique gathers much further material concerning the aforementioned favor of the Crucified One in ch. 12, which must also be taken into account here.

503. He continues thus:

> “An old panel in the cloister refectory of the monastery of Clairvaux agrees with this, depicting the favor and bearing an inscription. It affirms the former point—that the event happened not once but several times—and probably supposes the latter: that it occurred in reality, not merely in vision. Elsewhere, it says, it is related that, when Blessed Bernard had composed a most devout prayer beginning:
>
> [Col. 0885B]  
> Hail, salvation of the world,  
> Hail, hail, dear Jesus:  
> To join myself to your cross  
> I would truly desire; you know why.
>
> Grant me possession of yourself;
>
> and recited [variant: delivered] it before an image of the Crucified One, then the image of the Crucified One, freeing its arms from the cross, embraced [variant added: and kissed] him. It is piously to be believed that this happened to him several times. Bernard Villalpando transcribed this inscription from the panel itself in 1199, when he had been sent there by the abbot of Fitero to examine this and other matters. Antonius Hiepius also mentions it, in the same words, in the seventh century under this year, 1153, ch. 5,” [Col. 0885C] where the variant readings just noted occur.

504. “Nicolaus Salicetus and Philotheus, about two hundred years ago more or less, likewise support this: one writing in prose, the other in verse. Salicetus does so with such assurance that he produces an ancient prayer addressed to Bernard the Father, in which the same embrace of Christ is mentioned. First, in his *Antidotary of the Soul*, he transcribes Bernard’s words to Christ under this title: ‘Most devout prayer of Blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, which, when he once spoke it before an image of the Crucified One, the image itself bent down from the cross and embraced him.’ He then adds a prayer to Bernard, in which Bernard, as though adjured by this sweetest embrace, is asked to intercede for others with him [Col. 0885D] from whom he deserved so great a favor.

“Indeed Henriquez, in his *Menologium*, for 23 March, positively asserts that an embrace was recorded in a certain book of the Cistercian monastery, with the very day on which it occurred specified—namely, the twenty-third day of March: ‘The image of Christ hanging on the cross embraces Bernard on the twenty-third day of March.’ And in the annotations: ‘As it is recorded in the Martyrology of Cîteaux.’ If this is so, it adds no slight weight to all the rest.”

505. “But Philotheus, an author of the same period—for he wrote when Bernard’s works had recently been printed, which the very ancient copies still surviving today show to have seen the light with the birth of typography in Europe—Philotheus, I say, an author of the same century, reports this same embrace of Christ no less clearly after depicting the holy Father praying before Christ’s image in these very verses:

> O Christ, glory and alleviation of our sorrow!  
> O salvation won for me by such harsh toil!  
> Blessed, if you turn such sufferings upon me,  
> And if it be granted me, wretched as I am, thus to die.  
> I would dare to pluck fruits before their time;  
> Yet, O Christ, your teeth were astonished.  
> Stars, earth, and sea, have pity on your Lord;  
> Weep for my misfortunes, stars, earth, and sea.  
> As he uttered these things, the image of Christ hanging there  
> Loosed its fastened arms into an embrace.

“So far Philotheus; and what we shall report below will show that this favor of Christ the Lord did not stop with Bernard [Col. 0886B], but passed on to his sons.” Thus the Cistercian annalist.

506. To the matters just related I add fuller information concerning the three writers named by him: Philotheus, Villalpando, and Salicetus. The Reverend Dom Charles de Visch, in the *Library of Writers of the Sacred Cistercian Order*, p. 281, does not seem to have had a sufficiently clear understanding of Philotheus’s date. He says that Philotheus was “a monk of the Cistercian Order and wrote, in learned and flowing verse, a notable treatise *On the Life and Character of St Bernard*, printed at the end of the works of that same holy Father”; but he says nothing about the author’s time. This may nevertheless be inferred from Philotheus’s prologue, in which the Blessed Virgin is introduced encouraging him to write by the example of Baptista Mantuanus, whom I find to have died in 1516. Philotheus therefore wrote after him.

In the same *Cistercian Library*, p. 53, Villalpando is praised, and his works are there listed. “He was still alive in 1626,” as is there stated. Salicetus “flourished in 1480 and thereafter,” according to the cited bibliographer, p. 251, where he also treats of his books.

It remains only, before we proceed to elucidate the final years of the life of the holy Father Bernard, to preface some matters pertaining to earlier years.

## §XLVIII. The conversion of Arnulf; heavenly glory promised to him; victory, as reported, granted to the king of Portugal; a journey with Pope Eugenius; services rendered to St Malachy, whom Bernard knew to be in heaven; concern for the king of France; his brother, a Cistercian ascetic, and another likewise.

[Col. 0886D]

507. Not the least part of St Bernard’s glory was the conversion of the illustrious Arnulf of Majorica, both because it was itself wonderful and because the manner in which the holy man brought it about was wonderful. Manrique includes it under the year of Christ 1147, and in the same place, ch. 6, reports from the author of the *Great Exordium*, who describes Arnulf’s splendor and the order and manner of his conversion.
