The passage is found in Tissier, distinction 3, ch. 17. Here are the words:

> “When the most reverend Father Bernard had once entered the province of Flanders, cast out the nets of the word of God for the catching of souls, and drawn many nobles and learned men from the waves of the world to the shore of conversion, among the rest the illustrious Arnulf [Col. 0887A] of Majorica, rich and luxurious, secretly gave himself into his hands. Their mutual counsel was to keep the matter silent, because of certain worldly impediments, until the last day on which he was to leave his land and kindred. For he was a great householder, adorned with sons and brothers and entangled in such great wealth that he could not withdraw himself without loss and grave scandal to his own people, unless he first arranged his household wisely and cautiously.”

After the writer of the *Exordium* has set forth Arnulf’s splendor and the manner in which he wholly entrusted himself to the holy Father, he proceeds to explain how wonderfully divine mercy dealt with him, that he might attain the intended end of his vocation.

508. “Meanwhile, while they kept this whole matter silent and these two alone in the world knew the cause of this secret business, the word of the Lord came to a rustic cattle-herd while he was driving oxen to the plow, saying: ‘Go, tell Arnulf of Majorica to take you with him to Clairvaux, whither he will soon go for conversion; and be converted with him.’ He heard the voice but saw no one. When the voice had spoken, the poor man began to pray more attentively that, if the speech had gone forth from the Lord, he might reveal it again to his ear. And he spoke to him a second time, repeating the same words. Having thus received the oracle for the second time, he came to the aforesaid man and said: ‘My lord, I have a word for you.’ When Arnulf had led him aside, he fell at his knees, saying: ‘I beseech you through Christ our Lord [Col. 0887C], take me to your Clairvaux and save my soul with your own. And if you desire to know it, the Lord, gracious and merciful, has deigned, for the sake of my salvation, to reveal your secret to me.’ On hearing these words, that noble householder was greatly astonished and delighted. He received the man and took him home with him; and afterward he had him as an inseparable companion both on the journey and in conversion, destined, we believe, to be a companion in eternal recompense as well.”

Thus divine providence saw fit to strengthen and advance Arnulf’s vocation by issuing a heavenly oracle for this very purpose. Nor did he, upon hearing the Lord’s voice, harden his heart.

509. For, as the author of the *Great Exordium* continues, “When [lacuna] the affairs [Col. 0887D] for which he had delayed had been completed, he came to Clairvaux, as lowly in humility as he was exalted in abundance of riches. He bestowed much from his property upon that monastery, and also lavishly gave gifts to several other monasteries. Blessed Bernard, greatly rejoicing in his conversion, pronounced this judgment concerning him in the assembly of the brethren: ‘Christ is no less to be wondered at and glorified for the conversion of Brother Arnulf than for the resurrection of Lazarus, dead four days; for, shut up and buried amid such luxuries, he lay as though in a tomb and was, as it were, living while dead.’”

But it is worth hearing from the cited author how gently and fatherly the holy man treated Arnulf, as he washed away in the sacrament of penance the filth of sins contracted in secular life:

> “When he confessed to him with groaning and many tears all the sins he had committed in the world, Blessed Bernard, seeing the most bitter contrition of his heart and his willing disposition toward every good work, imposed upon him the saying of the *Our Father* three times and perseverance in his resolution thereafter until death.”

510. “Hearing this, Arnulf answered sorrowfully: ‘I pray you, most blessed Father, do not mock your servant.’—‘In what,’ Bernard said, ‘do I mock you?’—Arnulf replied: ‘Fasts for seven or ten years would not suffice for me, even were I humbled in sackcloth and ashes; and you command me, Father, to say the *Our Father* three times and persevere in the Order?’—And the saint said to him: ‘Do you then know better than I what you must do in order to be saved? Or do you perhaps think it a small matter to keep the Order and persevere in it until death?’—But Arnulf answered: ‘Far be such wicked presumption from my soul! But for God’s sake I beseech you, do not spare me now, so that you may spare me better in the future; and impose such a penance now that, after the death of my flesh, I may come to rest without punishment.’—To him the blessed Father said: ‘Do as I have said; and I assure you that, once the burden of the body has been laid aside, you will immediately fly to God without suffering.’”

Strengthened beyond measure by this answer, received as though divinely given, he thereafter could not be delayed in any degree from the course of desire by which he wholly hastened toward God—not by any violence of temptations, nor by any distress of illness. He was exceedingly careful and fearful concerning observance of the Order [Col. 0888C] and custody of the heart, so that “I remember seeing no one so zealous in cleansing his own conscience.” From these final words it follows that the narrator was not merely Arnulf’s contemporary but knew him very well. The remaining details, by which the praise of this most devout ascetic is subsequently developed, may be seen in the same author. It was altogether fitting not to pass over this remarkable conversion, whose glory is notably conveyed to St Bernard from Arnulf as from a son to a father.

511. The Cistercian historian, under the year 1147, ch. 9, gives an account of Alfonso I, king of Portugal, who, intending to capture Scalabis—commonly Santarém—made a vow to Christ on behalf of the Cistercians. He adds that the holy man promised him victory, obtained by Bernard’s prayer and seen and announced at Clairvaux. The chronology also contributes an argument, though Manrique admits there is a difficulty about it. There is likewise a letter of the king to Bernard, and another from Bernard to the king. Yet we should more confidently support this reported event if Manrique had produced writers of sounder and more ancient authority than Brito and Brandão. Among the matters which Manrique recounts about this affair, some occur that do not entirely favor the establishment of its truth. For, after reporting certain things from a “recent inscription,” as he admits, he observes that “there are more matters there, but they anticipate the date.” Then, after laying out the event, he adds [Col. 0889A]: “These things Brito takes from ancient copies; but since they introduce Gerard, Bernard’s brother, as speaking—though he is certainly known to have died seven years before—they appear not merely suspect, but corrupt and spoiled by certain additions.”

512. We briefly indicate what is more fully reported in the *Cistercian History* under the year 1148, ch. 5: namely, that Pope Eugenius, setting out for Trier and taking Bernard with him, held a council concerning the revelations and writings of St Hildegard the virgin; that he sent the bishop of Verdun to her; that he approved her writings and revelations; and so forth. But these matters may be read there. See also what we have previously stated concerning this virgin in §39.

The same *Cistercian History*, under the year just mentioned, ch. 6, continues thus:

> “Pope Eugenius spent three months at Trier. After these, returning to France, he visited Clairvaux—the cradle of his religious life—then Cluny, and finally Cîteaux; he presented himself to both families and fostered them both. Bernard was his constant companion on the journey, and did not even then desist from continuous miracles. He nearly brought his most loving son and father—indeed, the father of the whole Church—to the point of peril to life. Such a crowd of people followed the saint wherever he went that even the pontiff, unable to escape the crush, was overwhelmed by the multitude and with difficulty was at last rescued from danger.”

Geoffrey describes the event in book IV, ch. 5, of the *Life*, where he also recounts the miracles. Manrique, ch. 9, writing of St Malachy, collects various matters from the life of that most worthy bishop, solemnly and movingly transmitted to posterity by St Bernard, including the things performed by him during the last time of his earthly life. In ch. 10 he writes of the illness of that same most holy pontiff after his reception by the men of Clairvaux, of his foreknowledge of death, of his most devout preparation to meet it, and of his most sweet falling asleep in the Lord, also graced by a miracle. But these and other matters, expressed by Bernard’s honeyed pen, may be seen in that splendid *Life of Malachy* which I mentioned; from it most clearly appears how highly our saint esteemed that saint, and with how tender an affection he embraced him.

513. What he relates in the preface to that same Life, addressed to Abbot Congan, deserves notice in the very words of the holy Father: namely, that Malachy, as he was now breathing his last, bestowed this upon him. He tells it thus: “I hastened there, that the blessing of the dying man might come upon me. And he, though he could no longer move his other limbs, was strong enough to give the blessing: lifting his holy hands above my head, he blessed me, and I possess that blessing as an inheritance.” Yet the greatness of his affection and esteem went still further. For, as Manrique relates in chapter 11, “when the body was being prepared for burial, while it was being stripped of its clothes to be washed and clothed again after the washing, the devout abbot—as we noted above—by a pious and friendly, indeed faithful, theft secretly took away the tunic in which the saint had fallen asleep, having exchanged it for one of his own. [Col. 0890A] He used it on more solemn feast days when offering the sacrifice of the Mass; and finally, when he died, he was buried in it. Geoffrey, who wrote Bernard’s Life, relates the matter, concealed from all during Bernard’s lifetime but revealed and disclosed by him after his death. . . .”

Moreover, in the funeral Office of St. Malachy, “when the venerable abbot, offering the saving Victim for his passing, came to know his glory through the Lord’s revelation, and, inspired by Him, had now completed the sacrifice, he changed the form of the prayer and introduced the collect which belongs to celebrations of holy bishops, not to the commendation of the departed, saying: ‘O God, who hast made the blessed bishop Malachy equal in merits to thy saints,’” etc. See Geoffrey, book IV, chapter 3, from whom I have extracted these things.

[Col. 0890B] 514. The *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 11 cited above, no. 3, reports that the holy man did something similar on another occasion. I transcribe the following:

“Antonius Demochares, in the preceding century, published from the book of *Antiquities* by Master Richard of Wassebourg, archdeacon of Verdun—and in our own century both he, in his catalogue of the bishops of Verdun, and John Chenu published it in the same words—that the same saint, less than sixteen years earlier, while celebrating for Albero, bishop of Verdun, did this very thing: ‘Albero of Chiny dies in the year 1131’ [supply: ‘dies’]. But the Sammarthani, to be cited presently, write that he was then promoted to episcopal rank. It is reported that Blessed Bernard, while singing Mass for him, changed the collect for the dead into the collect for confessors.”

So they say. [Col. 0890C] We dare neither deny nor affirm it; certainly actions of this kind, once performed to manifest glory, lose much of their force if they are repeated. What then? John Pistorius also notes that precisely the same thing was done a third time for Alberic, cardinal bishop of Ostia, whom we said had died in the preceding year, in his *Belgian Chronicle* under 1138:

“In the fourteenth year of Conrad,” he says, “the lord Alberic, cardinal bishop of Ostia, dies at Verdun. At his tomb Blessed Bernard, celebrating Mass for him, when he came to the collect after the sermon [perhaps: after Communion] for the dead, omitted it and said the collect for a confessor.”

515. “Yet it is possible that these two are the same person, owing to the identity of place—namely Verdun—and the small difference between the names Alberic and Albero; an error may have slipped in which cannot easily afterward be distinguished. What is certain we note in its proper places; for doubtful matters, it is enough to have touched on them in passing.” Thus far the author of the *Cistercian Annals*.

Among the Sammarthani, in *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Verdun, p. 1167, I likewise read concerning Albero of Chiny: “For him, while celebrating Mass, Blessed Bernard is said to have changed the collect for the dead into the collect for confessors, when that Albero, namely, fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1158.” Is that really so, when St. Bernard himself had already fallen asleep in the Lord in 1153? It follows, therefore, that either the event is apocryphal or the year is wrong.

Manrique above wrote that Alberic had “died in the preceding year,” that is, in 1147; [Col. 0891A] but “the fourteenth year of Conrad” falls in the years of Christ 1151 and 1152. Accordingly, the alteration of the collect related above ought, according to Manrique, to have occurred about five years after Alberic’s death. This by no means agrees with Pistorius, whom he cites; and hence the event might appear apocryphal, were there not other considerations making it more likely to be true. These are:

1. The matter occurs in Geoffrey, book IV of the *Life of St. Bernard*, chapter 3, even though it was not written by Geoffrey himself but inserted into Geoffrey from a manuscript in Horst’s edition, and also distinguished from Geoffrey’s text by brackets [ ] in Mabillon’s edition. In that Mabillon edition, the margin of the passage notes that, instead of “Albert,” as the text has it, [Col. 0891B] the name “Alberic” should be read.

2. It is there said that the event occurred at the tomb “of one who had died . . . recently before,” namely Alberic.

3. In the chronicle of Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Châlons, published by Leibniz in volume II of the *Historical Accessions*, and whose author flourished in the thirteenth century, the said alteration is explicitly narrated on p. 320 in these words: “In the year 1151 . . . the lord Alberic, cardinal bishop and legate of Ostia, dies at Verdun. At his tomb Blessed Bernard, celebrating Mass, when he came to the post-Communion, omitted the collect for the dead and said the collect for one holy confessor.”

From this, the deed of St. Bernard seems sufficiently confirmed, and the year 1147 assigned by Manrique to the death of Cardinal Alberic refuted—as also in Ciaconius, *Lives of Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals*, vol. I, col. 993, where this same alteration of the collect also appears.

Let these remarks have been made on the occasion of St. Malachy. Manrique, chapter 11 cited above, no. 4, may also be consulted concerning him. There he gives the epitaph inscribed on St. Malachy’s tomb, which, as it is said there, was “composed by Father Bernard and continues even today under his name.” Other matters which Bernard committed to writing in prose concerning this holy bishop are listed in the course of the same chapter. Manrique concludes it as follows:

“Furthermore, with regard to Malachy’s coming to Clairvaux . . . lest, even after his death, he should be disappointed in his desired hopes, we shall relate under the year 1153, when it is known to have occurred, not only the pallia granted to Ireland by Eugenius, but also the enlargement of its archiepiscopal sees, promoted by Bernard and established as four in number according to the provinces of that island.”

But now other matters call us, which Manrique relates under the year 1149.

516. In chapter 1, no. 5, the holy man again appears intent upon the public good. By letters sent to Suger, abbot of St. Denis and, during the absence of King Louis the Younger, governor of the French monarchy, he earnestly endeavoured to prevent the detestable single combat between Robert, the king’s brother, and Henry, son of Count Theobald, which had then been appointed by both sides for a fixed time. Consult letter 376 among Bernard’s letters in Mabillon’s edition.

Letter 377, written to the same man, [Col. 0892A] breathes the holy Father’s singular concern for the welfare of the kingdom of France and its king, who had not yet returned to his own people after the unhappy outcome of the holy war. And does not the letter written in Bernard’s name by Nicholas to Emperor Manuel of Constantinople, commending to him the Christian army during that overseas campaign, show that the holy man kept excellent watch over the common good of the Christian commonwealth? That letter is printed in the cited *Cistercian Annals*, no. 9.

517. No less illustrious for the holy Father was the conversion to the observance of Clairvaux of Henry, brother of King Louis—venerable to the world, and, in view of the circumstances, remarkable. Let us hear Manrique, chapter 3, no. 7:

“He came to Bernard at Clairvaux to discuss certain affairs of the realm; but Bernard exchanged the matters which he himself had brought concerning an earthly kingdom for a heavenly one, calling the man and drawing him by the power of word or prayer.”

Robert of Torigni, circulated under that name, connects the event with the year of Christ 1149: “Henry,” he says, “brother of Louis, king of the Franks, despising the garb of the world, put on the monastic garb for Christ at Clairvaux.”

But in what way this conversion occurred is told by Geoffrey in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Life of St. Bernard*. The same biographer seems clearly enough to indicate that the saint knew of the event before it happened, when he testifies that the holy man foretold these things to Henry: [Col. 0892C] “I trust in the Lord that you shall by no means die in the state in which you now are; rather, you shall swiftly prove by your own experience how much the prayer of these brothers of Clairvaux, which you have sought, will benefit you.” This was fulfilled later that very day, not without the amazement of many.

518. But the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High through Bernard was especially marvellous, and foretold by him beyond all expectation, in Andrew, who had accompanied the aforesaid Henry, his lord, to Clairvaux. He railed against Henry as a drunkard and madman, spewing out insults and blasphemies, inwardly accusing the holy Father of being a false prophet, and on the next day cursing his monastery with dreadful imprecations. His lord’s conversion was the cause. Yet, overcome by a powerful impulse of the Holy Spirit during the following night, he rose before daybreak, returned to the monastery, and displayed himself as though changed from another Saul into another Paul. The biographer just cited testifies to this and describes the wonderful transformation at greater length.

## §XLIX. He commands wild beasts; reconciles those at variance; restores a dead person to life; aids the bishop of Orléans; answers the abbot of Prémontré; illness, religious profession, and episcopate of Henry, brother of the king of France; prophecies of the saint; water changed into wine; death of Count Theobald.

519. “In this same year, namely 1149,” so far as may be inferred [Col. 0893A] from the sequence of the history, when the counts of Vienne and Forez [perhaps *Forestae*; below, “count of Forez”] were attacking one another, “Father Bernard was called to settle the affair and calm their passions. . . . The author of the discord opposed the counsels of peace, and two wolves encountered on the road, raging with a madness surpassing their natural savagery, . . . terrified those who were coming and almost turned all of them back from their undertaking. His travelling companions considered retreating, lest they expose the saint to danger, to the detriment of the Christian commonwealth. But the blessed abbot, aflame with charity and fervent in faith, not to be moved from the work of peace, the angel of peace, did not so much despise the danger as remove it.”

These are from the Cistercian historian under the year just indicated, chapter 5, no. 1. But receive, reader, the sequence of the event from John the Hermit, *Life of St. Bernard*, book II, no. 8, col. 1288 of Mabillon’s edition:

“He was going into Burgundy, intending to reconcile the count of Forez and the count of Vienne. As he passed through a certain village, he heard from its inhabitants that two most savage beasts, commonly called *varoli* [Note: [Col. 0893D] I read the word as so called on account of their variegated colours.], were raging in the nearby wood. When his companions heard this, they begged him to turn back, because they preferred to make a detour of two days’ journey, or much more, than to expose themselves to the beasts’ danger. Unwilling to consent, he replied that he would never turn aside for such a reason.

“Without delay, behold: the beasts came out into the open and met them with terrible open jaws, as if to devour them. When the brothers saw them, all immediately fled in extreme terror to the holy man, [Col. 0893C] hiding around him, and cried out with one voice: ‘Holy Father, deliver us!’ But he said: ‘Why are you fearful, you of little faith?’ At these words, raising his hand, he made the sign of the cross against the beasts. They at once became as stones, as though wholly deprived of any power to harm. Seeing this sign, all who were present gave the man of God boundless thanks. When the neighbouring people heard of it, they rejoiced greatly; for, from fear of the beasts, they had not dared to go out in groups of fewer than twelve.”

520. “Departing from there, St. Bernard came to the said counts. When he sought peace from them, the count of Forez humbly consented. But the count of Vienne wickedly resisted, saying that he would never make peace with his adversary until he had compelled him to go into exile. Having assembled an army, he invaded the other’s land. Then the count of Forez, terrified by fear, begged St. Bernard to obtain victory for him from almighty God. Blessed Bernard confidently promised him victory. Strengthened by this faith, he attacked his enemies, captured the count, and struck down so great a number of the enemy that scarcely anyone escaped alive. He gave thanks to St. Bernard for this victory.”

Thus far John the Hermit, the biographer. A little later, at no. 11, col. 1289, he committed another illustrious miracle to writing in these terms:

521. “While he was once sailing on the Loire, his small boat happened to strike a little bridge, over which a boy was standing. The boy immediately fell into the river and was killed. The neighbours, roused by the commotion, came running and mourned the dead boy. The holy man ordered him to be brought to him; and when the dead boy had been presented, the saint prayed. Then, before the eyes of all present, who with one voice praised God, the boy was immediately raised to life at the saint’s prayer.

“From that day onward, loving the man of God most affectionately as a son loves a father, he afterwards went to Clairvaux and there was converted. He was called Tescelin Nascardus, because he had been taken from the water and caught like a fish.”

Manrique, just cited, no. 3, also treats of this miracle, but doubts whether it occurred “on this journey or another”; nevertheless he judges that it was certainly performed “about this time.” He adds the following exclamation: “Thus Bernard, compared with Martin—as we have seen above in many other respects—is also found like him in this: a glorious raiser of three dead persons: a blasphemous man whom God had punished with death; a woman who died at Clairvaux; and this youth drowned in the river, whom he delivered from the jaws of death.”

But the same annalist shows that he had not sufficiently ascertained here the name of the author from whom these matters were drawn. For after narrating the affair of the two counts which we gave above, he cites “an ancient author whom Sylva translated.” But after the miracle of the man drowned in the waters and restored to life by the holy man, he adds: [Col. 0894C] “These are from the same Gallic author from whom Sylva drew; and we have thus far followed him. Many consider him John the Hermit; others think him another person, but a contemporary and of unimpaired trustworthiness, whose statements it is not permissible to doubt.”

522. But the curious reader will ask whence comes this etymological allusion: “called Tescelin Nascardus, because he had been taken from the water and fished like a fish.” I reply: I think Tescelin was his own name before the drowning and was not changed afterward. This is confirmed by the fact that St. Bernard’s father bore the same name. Hence it may be inferred that Tescelin was a personal name, and one at least sometimes given to people; so that the question seems to concern the surname Nascardus alone. Receive concerning it the following highly probable conjecture.

Ménage, in his *Etymological Dictionary, or Origins of the French Language*, under the word *nasse*, collects the following: “*Nasse*, a fisherman’s instrument, from the Latin *nassa*. Festus: ‘A *nassa* is a kind of fisher’s vessel from which, once the fish has entered, it cannot get out.’ Isidore, book IX, chapter 5: ‘A *nassa* is woven of twigs like a net for catching fish.’ Plautus: ‘By Hercules, today I shall never seek bait from that fish-trap.’ Silius Italicus:

> No otherwise does the skilful fisherman, beside the glassy waters,  
> weave from osier, with wide-open mouth, a light fish-trap.

These seem exceedingly apt for resolving the question proposed: as though you were to say that he was called Nascardus because, through Bernard’s power, he was drawn from the water as fish are commonly drawn from a *nassa*, a fish-trap. It remains that we should not omit a few other matters concerning Bernard which the author of the *Cistercian Annals* has under the year already mentioned.

523. In chapter 7, he relates that the bishop of Orléans, on Bernard’s advice, embraced the observance of the Cistercian Order. We shall trace the circumstances of this matter, which had been drawn out for a considerable time, somewhat further back, as Manrique wishes. Thus the same historian, under the year of Christ 1146, chapter 2, no. 8, says:

“At about the same time—as is plainly evident from the sequence and connection of Bernard’s letters—the steadfast zeal of Eugenius [the pope] for truth either drove, induced, or drew the bishop of Orléans (the tables seem to indicate Manasses) to Clairvaux, after he had laid aside or cast off his mitre. Noble by birth . . . but worldly in conduct . . . he dishonoured, by the frivolity of his manners and pernicious examples, the gravity of the French Church and the insignia of pontifical dignity. . . . Accused before Eugenius . . . he resolved at least through intercessors to mitigate and obtain pardon for what he could not defend through witnesses, and he stirred almost all France to move Eugenius or reconcile him. . . . King Louis wrote for him, and the nobles wrote; the venerable Peter Maurice also wrote. Bernard alone, in all France, could never be induced to write. Indeed, when Eugenius, unmoved by the prayers, ordered the man to appear for judgment . . . Bernard confirmed his resolve by a letter then at last sent in the following tenor.”

A fragment of this letter relevant here follows; it may be read in Mabillon at the beginning of letter 245. “Strengthened by these letters,” the Cistercian historian continues in no. 9, “the pope appointed a formal day for the accusers, which he likewise made known to the accused. . . . But what was done with him and in him, and how . . . while the suit was still pending and not yet hopeless, when he was to make his purgation before the bishops, he nevertheless voluntarily divested himself of the episcopate, chose as his master the one man whom he had found not favourable to him, Bernard, and became his humble monk and son at Clairvaux in the year 1149, when this is known to have occurred [perhaps: ‘happened’], after the litigation had been prolonged so far . . .—we shall relate more conveniently in our usual manner.”

524. He describes this event at length under the year 1149, chapter 7, just cited, [Col. 0895D] where it is shown that the bishop of Orléans was indeed summoned to make purgation; but after mature deliberation with St. Bernard as to whether it was wiser to renounce the mitre or contest the matter, he laid aside the episcopate on the holy man’s counsel and put on the habit of a Cistercian monk.

What the holy Father afterward did in the bishop’s favour before Pope Eugenius is evident from Bernard’s letter 246, addressed to him, which Mabillon assigns to the year of Christ 1146 and which begins: “It is time that I too should write, no longer for a bishop, but for a poor and humble monk,” etc.

In his shorter notes on letter 245, Mabillon observes two points that do not agree with the account just quoted from the annalist of the Cistercian Order. He differs from him both in naming the bishop of Orléans [Col. 0896A] and in fixing the time of his resignation from the episcopate. Briefly commenting on the words of the letter, “For the bishop of Orléans,” he says: “That is, Elias, who, accused of grave crimes, when he could not bend Eugenius either personally or through the king or his friends, voluntarily resigned the episcopate in 1146, as appears from other notes and the following letter.” For from the year in which that letter is marked as written, and from the words I cited from it a little above, that prelate was then no longer a prelate but a monk. In the more extensive notes to the same letter, his accusation is placed in the year 1144; other matters may be seen there.

525. The Cistercian historian, under the year of Christ 1150, chapter 3, mentions difficulties which arose between the two most distinguished orders, namely Prémontré and Cîteaux. A letter written by the abbot of Prémontré gave St. Bernard occasion to reply to that abbot in a letter which, among Bernard’s letters in Mabillon, is number 253. In it he considers the complaints raised by the Premonstratensians and, answering each of their points, composes a free and vigorous defence of himself and his own. He concludes it in terms excellently expressing the great goodwill he bore toward the Premonstratensian community and his desire to secure peace with it.

526. The historian just mentioned writes the following in chapter 6:

“Meanwhile Henry, Louis’s brother, whom in the preceding year we mentioned as converted and awaiting, as he himself said, the solemn day of his betrothal [whether before or after profession is not sufficiently clear], fell into a severe and rather dangerous fever through the great change in his life and diet. Bernard the Father felt no small grief, for he venerated in one of royal blood his noble contempt for glory. . . . It seemed by no means advisable to Bernard and the brothers to bring physicians and medically prepared remedies into the community; but not to help the sick Henry seemed almost inhuman. Therefore he was taken to Paris for treatment. . . . Though ill, the royal youth departed neither in a carriage nor in a litter, nor riding a horse adorned with more fitting trappings. He rode with rustic trappings, such as befitted a monk who counted his being both son and brother of kings far less highly than his monastic profession.”

A letter of Nicholas, whose words are quoted there, may be read concerning his departure and his travelling companions. Then, in chapter 7, the same Henry, after he had made solemn vows to God and had been restored to his former health and to his Clairvaux, was promoted to the episcopal see of Beauvais. How Bernard acted in this matter, how Henry acted, and what means were used to secure the consent of both, may there be read more fully. We have here combined material from the two cited chapters.

For the death at Clairvaux of Geoffrey of Amay, as the holy Father had foretold, see Manrique, chapter 6. In chapter 8 he treats of that notorious and infamous Nicholas; but we have already gathered the history of that sycophant above by anticipation of time.

527. The year of Christ 1151 follows. In chapter 1, Manrique, among other things, treats of the death, foretold by St. Bernard, of Raynald or Rainard, a great man in the Cistercian Order and abbot of the same monastery. On this matter consult Geoffrey the biographer, book IV, chapter 3, no. 19, of the *Life of the Holy Father*. Then, in the Cistercian history, no. 8, follows the death of Suger, abbot of St. Denis, whom we have praised above. Bernard’s letter 266 survives, written to him as death was now threatening, in which he exhorts him to meet it without fear.

Letter 270, to Pope Eugenius, concerning a Carthusian prior against certain transgressors after disputes had arisen among them, is also connected with the present year 1151. See Manrique here, chapter 2, and Mabillon’s notes on that letter.

“In this same year,” as the Cistercian historian holds in the same chapter, no. 9, “Bernard, discharging his task and writing his customary book *On Consideration* to Pope Eugenius, laments many things in the Roman curia which ought to be corrected by him; but especially the frequent missions to Spain, profitable indeed to the envoys, but not merely useless to the Church—harmful.” He then quotes a passage from book III of the same work. But the historian would more correctly have deferred this to the year 1152, for reasons to be assigned by us in the paragraph immediately following.

From these things it follows that even in the final years of his life the holy man, as he had done earlier, was never without attention to opportunities—whether deliberately sought or spontaneously offered—to contribute his efforts to the public benefit of the Church or to the particular good of some community or person. Add to this what Manrique observes under 1151, chapter 6:

“In this same year Baronius notes, from a manuscript of the Vatican Library, that the *Decretum* was compiled by Gratian, a Benedictine monk: ‘The *Decretum* of Gratian, monk of St. Felix at Bologna, of the Order of St. Benedict, was compiled in that monastery in the year of the Lord 1151, in the time of Pope Eugenius III.’ Yet I read that this too was not done without Bernard in the notes to the *History* of John Dubravius, book IX, letter G: ‘At the exhortation of St. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux,’ they say, ‘Gratian compiled the decrees of the popes.’”

So Manrique observes.

528. And immediately afterward, no. 7: “Let a rather remarkable miracle of Bernard, performed about this time but continuing for many years afterward, close the chapter: a fountain of fetid water changed into a fountain of wine. . . . Since I have not been able to obtain John the Hermit, who transmitted this to memory, let the reader receive it from Sylva, who copied him.”

But since the account is readily available in the *Life* composed by this John and published by Mabillon after our Chifflet, and is there narrated differently, we give the event from Mabillon’s edition, cols. 1289–1290:

“One day, about the sixth hour, as the venerable man was passing through the boundary [*finagium*, that is, the border] of the village called Colombey-in-the-Ditch, [Col. 0898A] he found in his path a spring trampled by cattle. As he stopped there, he ordered bread to be served to himself and his disciples in that place. But because the place seemed unseemly, they wished rather to move elsewhere, and said to the man of God: ‘Father, this is not a suitable place for eating. Let us go on until we come to a place where we may eat more decently. For this place is defiled by cattle and lies beside a road daily trodden by travellers.’

“But the man of God would not yield to their words. Some men nearby, eminent in rank and wealth, came from the aforesaid village to meet him and wished to bring him into their houses.

[Col. 0898B] 529. “He would by no means assent to them, but ordered food to be prepared for him more and more insistently in the aforesaid place. Then one of his disciples, named Hemeric, said to him: ‘Father, what is this that you wish to do? This place stinks and is defiled by cattle; and do you wish to eat in it?’ When the man of God heard these words, he could bear it no longer. He opened his mouth and began to prophesy before all, saying: ‘Hear me, brothers, and all you who are with me. I tell you in the word of truth that a time will come when many will seek this place in order to be cured there of various ailments. The place is holy, since it has been sanctified by the Lord.’

“When the disciples heard this, they took bread and provisions and ate with him, together with many others; for, as we said above, many had come to meet him. Then the man of God, raising his hand, made the sign of the cross over the spring, blessed and sanctified it, and said to the servants: ‘Draw water; give it to those who are eating.’ The servants drew water and filled the cups, and it was changed into wine. All who were present drank and gave boundless thanks to God, saying with great joy: ‘Truly this man is holy; truly the Holy Spirit dwells in him.’”

530. “After the meal, the blessed man called a certain man from the aforesaid village, named John, who was very rich and prosperous, and commanded him to care for the aforesaid place, cleanse it of filth, and fortify it with stones, lest cattle defile it. He added: ‘If you are unwilling to fulfil this, know that before your death you will suffer such want that, when dying, you will not have even a rag in which you may be rolled.’

“But since he delayed—indeed, refused—to carry out the blessed man’s commands, the outcome followed as the saint had predicted. At his death, out of all his possessions, he could not obtain even a winding-cloth, according to the word of the man of God. Who could doubt that the holy man foretold these things by the spirit of prophecy? While still alive, he also foretold many things which we have seen come to pass long after his glorious departure.

“For, as he predicted, many miracles occurred at the aforesaid spring. Even now, if a limb of anyone’s body, burdened by whatever pain, is washed with the water of that spring in the devotion of faith, many know that it is restored to health. Taken as a drink, the water also benefits persons suffering from various ailments. If anyone is troubled by the distress of a severe fever and, through the inspiration of Bernard, Christ’s confessor, desires to draw it, as soon as he has drunk it he recovers. Thus the force of fevers is extinguished, as though you saw every flame in an immense pyre suddenly quenched when water was thrown upon it. When the fires of tertian and quartan fevers are kindled, once the water has been drunk, it restrains their pains.”

531. You will find in Manrique, chapter 6, that the death of Theobald, count of Champagne—often mentioned above—fell in this year 1151. There also are many other matters: the integrity of his life, drawn from various writers there named; his burial place; the illustrious honour paid to his family by royal marriages; Bernard’s letter 271, a witness to his sincere friendship toward him; and finally Theobald’s alleged monastic profession, rejected as apocryphal.

## §L. The pilgrimage of the archbishop of Lund to St. Bernard; Bernard attends his departure with a miracle; the chronological setting of the books *On Consideration*; various prophecies; disturbances in Lorraine settled; the sons’ grief in the Father’s final illness; his care for them.

532. We have reached the year of Christ 1152, the next-to-last of the great Father’s life. Under that year, chapter 3, the Cistercian annalist speaks thus:

“Meanwhile the venerable Eskyllus [otherwise Eskilus, Eschilus], archbishop of Lund, [Col. 0899C] primate of the Danes and legate of the Apostolic See throughout Denmark . . . resolved to visit Clairvaux, intending to visit the holy Father through so many dangers by land and sea, through expense and the hardships of travel. Concerning that pilgrimage Saxo Grammaticus, p. 310, toward the middle, says: ‘At the same time Eskyllus, exhausted by domestic affairs beyond his strength, while seeking more earnestly to provide for rest, obtained from the king with difficulty permission to depart. He made for the noble monastery of France called Clairvaux, and there exchanged the harsh manner of life of his native country for the gentleness of voluntary pilgrimage, finding among foreigners a more pleasant way of life than he would have had among his fellow citizens.’”

But what this author relates here is set forth more fully in Geoffrey, book IV of the *Life of St. Bernard*, and in the *Great Exordium*, distinction 3, chapter 25.

533. The same Manrique adds that this venerable prelate desired to lead a private life at Clairvaux, leaving aside his mitre; but the holy Father at that time dissuaded him from this because he was a man highly useful—indeed necessary—to many. The cited annalist also recounts remarkable things, highly honourable to St. Bernard, concerning bread preserved from corruption for a long time by his blessing alone, and concerning a tooth and hairs of the holy man which Eskyllus carried away with him when he departed Clairvaux. Since these are to be presented later from the same Geoffrey whom I have just indicated, let the reader consult him.

The aforesaid Eskyllus, after laying aside the mitre, joined the monks of Clairvaux [Col. 0900A] after the holy Father’s death; and the annals of the Order make frequent and honourable mention of him. Henriquez announces and praises this man in his Cistercian *Menology* under 10 April.

534. This year also belongs to the completion placed by St. Bernard upon his golden work *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius. Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius* under the year of Christ 1152, no. 2, discusses its chronology and composition as follows:

“Baronius speaks under this year of the five books *On Consideration*, elaborated by St. Bernard for Pope Eugenius and outstanding among his works. But the holy doctor did not complete them in one continuous course, as Baronius thought; rather, he sent them to Eugenius at different intervals, as Mabillon observes in the preface to volume II of the *Works of St. Bernard*.

“He first published one book in 1149, when Nicholas, monk of Clairvaux and secretary to St. Bernard, before his departure wrote to Peter the Venerable: ‘I send you the book of the lord abbot of Clairvaux to the lord pope.’ This is letter 7 of book VI. Nicholas left the holy doctor soon afterward, as we have said in its place.

“Furthermore, Bernard sent the second book to Eugenius in 1150, after the unhappy outcome of the Jerusalem expedition; at the beginning of that book he offers an apology for it. He wrote the third in this year, after the death of Hugh of Auxerre; for in chapter 2, no. 11, speaking of him, he says, ‘the holy bishop having died.’ In no. 20 of that book, he declares that it was published by him in the fourth year after the Council of Reims. Baronius cites his words. Finally, he completed the fourth and fifth books shortly afterward, if not together with the third.”

535. At last our historical collection concerning the affairs of St Bernard has been brought down to the year of Christ 1153. This was for the man of God the end of this mortal life and the beginning of blessed immortality. The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, under this year, ch. 1, no. 2, observes from Bernard’s own letter: “At the beginning of the year, that is, in midwinter, Bernard fell ill unto death.” This is no. 307 among the letters of Bernard published by Mabillon, written to the Lord of Ostia and there dated to the year of Christ 1153. The holy Father writes to him concerning our subject as follows:

> “Further, I have learned that you are concerned about the condition of [Col. 0900D] my body. What you have heard is true: I have been ill unto death; but meanwhile I have been recalled from death, and this, as I feel, will not be for long; for I am far weaker than can be believed. Yet I say this without prejudice to divine Providence, which can also raise the dead.”

From this it is clear that the saint was then afflicted with a most desperate illness. But Geoffrey, in Book V, ch. 2, of the *Life*, testifies when the worsening sickness at last brought him to his end. There he describes the man’s most blessed death, though most grievous to the brethren, and recalls him addressing them thus:

> “These are the words which I spoke to you when I was ill last winter: that you had nothing yet [Col. 0901A] to fear; that in the coming summer, as I believe, the dissolution of this body was impending.”

Moreover, the same biographer had already related, in Book V, ch. 1, how the saint conducted himself in his grave illness, exercising an unconquered and heroic spirit in burning zeal and pious occupations.

536. “Meanwhile the brethren,” as the same writer of the *Life* relates in ch. 3, “persisted in their prayers and entreaties, so far as they could before God. Hence the saint himself, recognizing that through their prayers his desire was being delayed, when he had begun to recover somewhat in body, gathered the brethren together and spoke these same words: ‘Why do you hold back a wretched man? You are stronger, and you have prevailed. Spare me, I beseech you, spare me; let me depart.’”

Manrique adds the following, [Col. 0901B] no. 4:

> “Nevertheless, full of the spirit of prophecy and no less meanwhile burning with fatherly love, he consoled the mourners, promised delay, instilled confidence, raised all to hope, and promised that he himself would be deferred until summer, granting a truce to grief: ‘These are the words which I spoke to you when I was ill last winter,’ etc.”

Therefore, as Manrique continues in no. 5, “while they wavered in uncertainty between hope and fear, and scarcely—or rather, not even scarcely—hoped that the long-imminent sentence of death could be deferred, a vision confirmed those perhaps less trusting in Bernard’s words.” This is explained by Geoffrey in the already indicated ch. 3. “This,” as the Cistercian historiographer observes, “was the third vision concerning Bernard’s death; yet it was followed by a fourth, which confirmed that it was to be deferred, if less clearly, still not too obscurely.” It foretold that Odo, one of the elders of Clairvaux, would die before the holy Father. Read it in the biographer so often named; add the author of the *Great Exordium*, distinction 3, ch. 6. Since there follows the holy Father’s assurance or prediction concerning the heavenly glory that would befall Odo immediately after death, I also transcribe the following from that *Exordium*:

537. “For after the aforesaid vision, Odo, that servant of God, worn down by bodily sickness, came to his end. When blessed Bernard entered to visit him, he saw him trembling and anxious, as though he had lived less than perfectly and therefore still awaited in uncertainty the Judge’s sentence. He addressed [Col. 0901D] him thus: ‘Why do you tremble, why are you troubled, O blessed soul? From the days of your youth you have rendered devoted service to Christ through many and great labours, and do you fear to depart? Go on, go on in security. I tell you in truth that you will reach your Creator by a straight course and appear holy before him.’

“Strengthened by this consolation from his beloved Father, humble Odo . . . truly laid hold upon life. But in order that the holy Father might prove true, by the obedience of pious humility, the judgment which he had pronounced concerning him, while the holy body still lay on the ground, before it was carried away for washing, he approached reverently and devoutly kissed the sacred feet of the God-worthy dead . . . The remains of his blessed body were laid, out of reverence for his holiness, in the tomb in which, as I have said, Humbert of pious memory had been placed.” [Col. 0902A]

538. But another prophecy of the holy man is altogether remarkable. Manrique, ch. 2, believes it belongs to the first months of this year, 1153, and brings it forward from the writer of the *Great Exordium*. It is related thus in Tissier’s edition, distinction 3, ch. 27:

> “The most noble prince Gunnar, formerly judge and lord of Sardinia, *detrachalis* [perhaps *tetrarchalis*, ‘tetrarchal’], having at one time sought, for the sake of prayer, St Martin of Tours, was on his return journey passing through Clairvaux. Received devoutly by blessed Bernard and abundantly admonished also concerning the salvation of his soul, he did not at all consent to conversion, although the holy Father, in his presence and while he was talking at great length, had given sight to a certain blind man. To him as he departed, the man of God spoke thus: ‘I indeed have earnestly asked the Lord for your conversion, but for the present I have not deserved to be heard. And now I permit you to depart, because I may not hold you against your will; nevertheless, know that you will return here from Sardinia.’
>
> “He therefore went away to his own country; but the words which he had heard from the mouth of the man of God incessantly pricked his mind, while the Spirit suggested inwardly that a prophecy which so great a prophet had uttered about him could not be wholly brought to nothing. A short time later, when it was announced to him that the blessed man had passed from this world to the Father, he was violently shaken in mind, reproaching himself and deeply repenting that he had not been converted by that man’s preaching. Immediately, then, he was wholly inflamed by that fire which the Lord sends into the hearts of his elect [Col. 0902C] and wills to be vehemently kindled. Unable to endure any delay whatever, he established his first-born son to rule in his stead in his kingdom. He himself, still only forty years old, in the prime of bodily age and vigour of mind, abandoned Sardinia and despised all worldly glory; poor and humble, he entered Clairvaux. There, under the discipline of the Order which he had embraced, perseveringly serving until decrepit old age—indeed, until death—he boasted that he had exchanged an earthly kingdom for a heavenly one.”

539. “Various disturbances in Lorraine,” as the *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, ch. 4, report, “among the people of Metz awaited Bernard as an angel of peace, perhaps reserved for this very purpose. Indeed Illinus [elsewhere Hilinus], metropolitan of Trier, under whom the see of Metz lay, came to [Col. 0902D] Clairvaux and humbly and suppliantly urged the same saint to bring aid to such great evils.”

Geoffrey relates the matter in Book V, ch. 1, of the *Life*, adding that in this case, as had occurred on other past occasions, the man of God was divinely restored in strength sufficient for the success of so great a task. “The Lord,” he says, “who had always directed the paths of his faithful servant and employed him as the most fitting instrument in every principal cause, had somewhat relieved his bodily sickness a few days beforehand.” And shortly afterward:

> “This divine Providence had indeed often ordained with respect to him . . . that, whenever some great necessity summoned him, though his spirit conquered all things, his bodily strength should not fail . . . In his final work divine power was so manifestly present that he seemed to draw strength from his labours.” [Col. 0903A]

Meanwhile, the cited *Annals*, no. 4, say: “Already arms and cries were heard on either side; each side raged, one from the heat of vengeance, the other from the exaltation of recent victory. When the holy Father, warned by a vision to yield to no refusal, was at last to obtain whatever he wished, he followed the bishop of Trier and reached the camps which stretched far along the banks of the Moselle and were on the very point of rushing upon each other.”

540. How many and how great were the marvels which divine Providence here, as it were in a throng, heaped upon the holy man! Marvellous was his journey to those regions, he being scarcely a single moment removed from the journey to eternity; marvellous, in a matter of peace so utterly desperate, was the certain and confident prediction of its favourable result; and marvellous, finally, was the settlement of those most dreadful discords. For “the leading men of both parties . . . after all matters had been settled according to the decision of the faithful arbiter, Bernard, gave one another their right hands and were reconciled with the kiss of peace,” as Geoffrey testifies. He will instruct the reader more fully by describing the whole course of the affair.

“For men,” as Manrique rightly observes, no. 6, “were overawed by the weight of Bernard’s authority; they were overawed by miracles, since both sides deemed it wicked not to listen to one whom God heard and whom nature herself obeyed. Besides others, two blind men who received sight at the touch of the man of God, and likewise two lame persons granted free movement, showed that God was present in Bernard.” Then he reports from the same [Col. 0903C] Geoffrey the famous cure of a woman shaken for eight years by violent trembling and powerful convulsions of her limbs, as also the healing of another woman afflicted with paralysis. Consult Geoffrey himself at the place cited above. After recounting what occurred on this final and altogether memorable journey of the most holy abbot, he addresses him thus in conclusion of the aforesaid first chapter:

541. “Moreover, it would be exceedingly difficult, or altogether impossible, to embrace all the mighty works of that journey. Nor is it our purpose at present to pursue such signs or devote our labour to recounting works of power. For here, sweetest Father, was the blessed end of your journeys, and here your final labour. In this work, no less useful than difficult, and undertaken for a peace no less desperate than necessary, he gloriously completed your labours: he who had always magnificently honoured you in your labours—the King of glory, the Lord your God—glorifying you in his name and his name in you.” [Col. 0903D]

So Geoffrey. In ch. 2 he treats of the saint’s return to the monastery of Clairvaux and of the joy of spirit with which he was filled. Here are a few of the many things he writes:

> “When reconciliation had been achieved for the people of Metz and peace restored to that province, the holy abbot returned to the monastery, already burdened by the severe discomfort of a body on the point of failing. Yet in such sweetness of soul and delight of spirit he daily drew nearer to his departure as though a sailor in harbour were gradually lowering his sails. He also said plainly to the brethren: ‘These are the words which I spoke to you when I was ill last winter,’ etc.” [Col. 0904A]

These words have been quoted above.

542. Manrique, ch. 7, commemorates the grief of Clairvaux’s sons over the desperate condition of their most loving Father, in these words:

> “Now the holy Father drew near to death; now death to victory; now victory to triumph. Now the blessed angels, now the heavenly spirits, awaited a new citizen with joy; indeed, the demons themselves awaited Bernard’s departure with such rejoicing as they could, since through him they had lost so many thousands of souls. Only the brethren and sons, about to be deprived of the consolation of so great a Father and the guidance of so great a master, mourned in sorrow, ready to redeem his life even with their own. For they counted departure under him as happiness, and life without him [Col. 0904B] as misery. You might have seen men almost beside themselves, nearer, it seemed, to death than he whose loss they deplored.”

Let one of them, Geoffrey, be heard, Book V, ch. 2, of the *Life*:

> “Under so grievous a crisis, he may in some measure estimate our inconsolable grief and picture to himself, if he feels compassionately, the pale companies of his children, wasted faces, bloodless countenances, cheeks stained with tears, and also the sighs and sobs of their breasts.”

543. Then the same biographer directs to his holy Father an apostrophe full of expressions of the tenderest affection, deepest reverence, and most abundant praise; but, lest I repeat work already done, I do not transcribe it here. I likewise omit other things which [Col. 0904C] he adds concerning the sons’ approach to their Father, their words and his, and their weeping. The Father also consoled his dearly beloved offspring. In addition, the sweet and concerned Father instructed them by counsels toward religious perfection—see Geoffrey at the place cited—with tears mingled, through emotion, in truly fatherly speech, exhorting the pledges most dear to him.

Nor shall I pass over those three counsels by which, in place of a testament or final will, the most gracious Father is said by Alan, in Mabillon, vol. II, cols. 1271 and 1272, to have addressed his beloved sons:

> “Therefore, seeing that the end of his days was at hand, he called aside certain brethren who had long been united to him in familiar companionship and addressed them as follows: ‘Since I do not think that I can leave you great examples of religious life, I commend to your imitation three things which, in the course in which I ran, I remember observing according to my ability: I trusted my own judgment less than that of another; when injured, I did not seek revenge upon the one who injured me. I wished to give offence to no one; and whenever it arose, I quieted it as best I could.’” [Col. 0904D]

To these deserve to be joined what Manrique states that he read in additions to the *Great Exordium*, Book VII, ch. 10, expressed in these words:

> “As the sweetest swan, which, led to the threshold of death, is accustomed to sing with melodious and sweet modulation, so also Blessed Father Bernard, now at the end of this present and perishing life, uttered words far sweeter and more honeyed; so that, because of joy mingled with sorrow, all who were present dissolved into tears amid immense grief and unutterable groans.” [Col. 0905A]

## § LI. Illness; death revealed; the alleged letter of the Duchess of Lorraine; visits of distinguished persons; death; body; miracles ended through obedience

544. “If anyone wishes to know the nature of his illness, there exists a letter which he himself dictated to a certain friend a very few days before his holy departure from us,” according to Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 2, of the *Life*, who also recites it there. Here is the following fragment from it:

> “Sleep has departed from me, so that pain may never depart, even through the benefit of stupefied sensation. Failure of the stomach is almost all that I suffer . . . My feet and legs are swollen, as [Col. 0905B] ordinarily happens with dropsical persons. And in all this, lest anything be hidden from a friend concerned about the condition of his friend, according to the inward man—though I speak as a fool—the spirit is willing though the flesh is weak.”

This letter is numbered 310 and entitled *To Arnold, Abbot of Bonneval near Chartres*. Mabillon notes that in ancient documents he is commonly called Ernald, as in vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 390, and in Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who praises his letters. We deeply regret that all of them have perished. The fuller notes teach that the second book on the *Life of Bernard* ought to be attributed to Ernald.

545. Manrique, ch. 7, nos. 7 and 8, writes concerning two other revelations, in addition to those already mentioned, by which the saint’s death was foretold. Let us set forth his words:

> “At this very time, in an abbey near Clairvaux—though it is not yet sufficiently certain which it was—a fourth revelation of the saint’s death both informed and invited the abbot to be present, if he wished, at the death of the saint, at which the whole heavenly court would be present to assist.”

The event is related and confirmed by Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 3. But whether that abbot thought the event not so near at hand, or did not place full faith in this revelation, or was occupied by other pressing business, this heavenly warning was followed by another. Manrique, at the cited no. 8, says that this was made by St Bernard himself to the provost of the aforesaid monastery. Since the biographer just praised relates it briefly, I transfer it here from him:

> “In the monastery [Col. 0905D] of that aforesaid abbot, who had thus foreseen his death, on the night which the holy Father, about to depart from us in the morning, made his last, he appeared to the venerable provost, bade him farewell, and said: ‘Know that I am now departing and shall remain here no longer.’ When the latter informed the abbot, the abbot hurried and came to Clairvaux, and on that very day found that the holy abbot had already departed, as he had said.”

This, as Manrique observes, no. 8, was the fifth revelation of the most holy Father’s death, and, so far as we know, also the last. It certainly occurred on the final night, after which at the following dawn he was to depart to the Lord.

546. As the time of death approached, a messenger is said to have come to him from Lorraine and to have brought him letters from the Duchess, formerly converted by the holy man. What she wrote in them, and what answer the saint gave, may be read in the Cistercian historian, ch. 7, no. 9. After narrating the matter, he adds: “These things are from an old anonymous manuscript, as he calls it, from which Brito testifies that he drew them.” Brito may be consulted, Book III, ch. 28, where a manuscript codex, fol. 64, is indeed cited and other authors named. But let the credibility of the event rest with those who assert it, since Geoffrey, so diligent and accurate a writer of the events occurring toward the end of St Bernard’s life, mentions none of them.

William treats of the remarkable conversion of this Duchess Adelaide in Book I, ch. 7, of the *Life*, and Geoffrey’s *Fragments*, col. 1277. See what I said above, § 18, no. 198. Finally, Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 2, of the *Life*, bears witness that the holy man, now near death, was honoured by the company of distinguished [Col. 0906B] persons:

> “At last, when the fabric of his outward dwelling was already everywhere dissolved . . . that great day dawned on which the day of his perpetual rising arose; and for his departure the neighbouring bishops had assembled, together with a large multitude of abbots and brethren.”

Then, giving the time of death, he says: “At almost the third hour of the day . . .”—Manrique, ch. 7, no. 11, says about three hours before noon—“he departed from the body of death.” He then gives other chronological indications: “Having completed about sixty-three years . . . on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, he fell asleep in Christ in the hands of his sons,” namely in the year of restored salvation 1153. The said biographer, after inserting several matters to be treated immediately, also notes this year, saying: “These things happened in the same year in which our blessed Pope Eugenius III . . . departed [Col. 0906C] from this light.”

547. At the very moment when the most blessed Father rendered his most pure soul to his Creator, a truly extraordinary vision honoured his most blessed passage from this life. Manrique, no. 13, relates it thus from additions to the *Great Exordium*, Book VII, ch. 10:

> “At the very moment in which he breathed his last, the most compassionate Mother of God, the special patroness of Blessed Bernard and most generous rewarder of her own, was seen in the room in which the holy man lay, having with her in attendance an innumerable multitude of angels and heavenly spirits, as befitted the Queen of Heaven and Lady of Angels. Before the sight of all who had come to the funeral, she snatched, as it were, the most holy soul of the man of God from his mouth and led it, with the same company, even to the inner courts of heaven, while the angels rejoiced and sang heavenly hymns through the air, so that she might in no wise prove forgetful of those who remembered her devoutly. Likewise, the same Queen of Heaven was seen to place the soul of our Blessed Father Bernard at her side in heavenly blessedness.” [Col. 0906D]

Philotheus cast this account of the apparition into verse in his encomiastic poem on the life and character of St Bernard:

> When, amid the tears and groans of his own,  
> the snowy spirit, casting off the body, departs on high,  
> the most radiant Virgin herself was seen, joyful,  
> leading the heavenly choirs through the airy paths.  
>
> And drawing up the purple soul, she set it upon  
> the empyrean height and placed it at her own side. [Col. 0907A]

Thus far concerning this apparition. But Geoffrey has left nothing written about it, which surprises me. What is to be said about the holy body laid out, the crowd of people, and the burial?

548. The body of the deceased abbot, duly prepared and clothed in priestly vestments, was carried into the oratory of the blessed Mother of God, according to Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 2. A very great multitude of people gathered around it and filled the whole valley with weeping and lamentation, as follows in the same passage:

> “For two days the dead shepherd remained amid his flock, while that former grace of his most sweet countenance, not diminished but increased, fixed all eyes more firmly upon itself, drew their souls, and buried their affections. What more? The multitude of people rushing in from every side increased beyond measure; the crush of those gathering became intolerable—seizing his beloved feet, kissing his hands, applying loaves, belts, coins, and every other object which they wished to preserve for themselves as a blessing.” [Col. 0907B]

Indeed, on the second day the crowd surrounding the venerable body and awaiting the burial of that most sacred pledge, intended for the third day, was so importunate that the hour of burial was moved forward, to avoid the inconveniences feared. Consult the biographer just mentioned, who relates these matters more fully. Moreover, one of the brethren, suffering severely and for a long time from epilepsy, approached the body in full faith and asked its aid before it was committed to the tomb; he recovered perfect health, as may be seen in the same writer, although this healing has been inserted into his text from another source. Consult also the *Great Exordium*, distinction 2, ch. 20.

549. Nor was the holy Father kind only to his son and member of his household; he also showed himself merciful to outsiders. Let the *Great Exordium* be heard in the place just indicated:

> “On the day before that most precious treasure was laid away, a boy arrived from a nearby village, with an arm shrivelled through dryness of the sinews and a contracted hand. Those present, moved with compassion for his age and infirmity, invited him with all the greater confidence to touch the sacred body after the ninth hour of prayer, because his innocent age had less boldness to presume this for itself. But when the withered arm was applied to the holy arm and the contracted hand to the blessed hand, immediately, as natural strength returned, the arm grew sound; and the hand, freely extending and bending its fingers, was restored to perfect health before the eyes of the whole multitude which surrounded the sacred funeral from every side. At his cure so great a cry of all present immediately arose, shouting in praise of God, that the discipline of the brethren could scarcely restrain it. When night came, another person, weak in his whole body, was brought; he fell down before the bier and, while psalms were being sung, rose up and was led to the altar.” [Col. 0908A]

So the *Great Exordium* of the Cistercian Order.

550. But great power of miracles must have gone forth from the body of our abbot after his death, since he is said to have been commanded not to continue them any longer, Goswin, abbot of Cîteaux, forbidding it. Hear the event from the author of the *Great Exordium*, distinction 2, ch. 20:

> “Indeed Lord [variant adds: Goswin], the Cistercian [variant adds: abbot], who had come with many other abbots of his Order to the obsequies of the man of God, considered the great importunity of the tumultuous people and inferred future events from the present. He began to fear greatly that, if the signs multiplied and so intolerable a throng of people flocked there, the discipline of the Order would perish through their disorder [Col. 0908B] and the fervour of holy religious life would grow cold in that place. Therefore, after deliberation on the matter, he approached reverently and, by the power of obedience, forbade him to perform signs any further.
>
> “But since the Apostle says concerning our Lord Jesus Christ that he became obedient to the Father unto death, and our lawgiver St Benedict, following his example, sets before us obedience unto death in the Rule, the holy and truly humble soul of our Father was obedient to a mortal man even after the death of the flesh. For the signs which had then begun to shine forth ceased so completely that, from that day forward, he was never seen to perform public miracles. Yet he cannot fail, even today, those faithful persons—especially brethren of his own Order—who cry out to him in their various afflictions. For it is clear that the lord of Cîteaux wished only that those signs should not occur which would diminish the discipline of the Order through throngs of people gathering.” [Col. 0908C]

551. Moreover, it will not be out of place here to recount from the *Great Cistercian Exordium*, just mentioned, what occurred on account of this commandment to an infernal spirit possessing a woman. Being ordered by the merits of St Bernard to leave, it boasted of Bernard’s obedience, so that it might not be compelled to abandon the dwelling it occupied. Understand the event from that work:

> “Several years having then passed after the blessed man’s departure, there was in a region of Italy a certain married woman whom an evil spirit, having seized her, began to torment cruelly. Her relatives and friends, deeply distressed by so lamentable a calamity, began carefully to consider whether any remedy might exist. Now there was in the neighbourhood a certain monastery of the Cistercian Order; and, as a hope conceived from any source usually gives confidence to minds in distress, they resolved by common counsel to bring that possessed woman to the same house for healing. And this was done. The wretched woman was brought to the gate, and some of those accompanying her were sent to announce so great an evil to the abbot and brethren and to seek aid. The abbot took with him certain elders whom he knew to be more spiritual, and went out to the sufferer with the Lord’s cross and relics of the saints. When that evil spirit did not move at all after being adjured by the Lord’s cross and the sacred pledges of the saints, the abbot recalled that he possessed venerable relics from the hair and beard of St Bernard. He had received them, I believe, in that same year, when going to the chapter at Clairvaux, as a blessing; he always carried them with him for his protection. Without saying anything, he silently put his hand beneath his cowl, intending, after drawing out these relics, to press the demon with them.” [Col. 0909A]

552. “When that pestilent being perceived this with lynx-like eyes, it immediately began to scrape the footstool with its feet and spit; by the unseemly movement of the whole body it unwillingly betrayed what it suffered within. Breaking into speech, it said: ‘Come now, little abbot, what do you intend to do? What evil are you now contriving against me under that garment of yours? You strive in vain, you labour to no purpose. Keep your Bernard, for you will accomplish nothing.’ When the abbot said, ‘By the Lord’s grace and the merits of this most holy man, you will now come out,’ it replied: ‘What? Have you forgotten that he was forbidden to perform signs? Knowing this, therefore, I rest secure in this dwelling of mine.’

“When the abbot and the brethren with him heard these words, they marvelled greatly that the wicked spirit had so quickly found that prohibition as a shield for its defence.” [Col. 0909B]

## § LII. Various apparitions after the blessed Father’s death; tomb; epitaphs; eulogies; miraculous water in which his holy body had been washed; anniversary sermon; description of body and character

[Col. 0909C]

553. “Most holy men in various parts of the world beheld his blessed soul ascending to heaven; but two in particular are commemorated, one in England and the other in Gascony. The latter was Count William of Montpellier, whom we have already mentioned as converted long before at Grandselve, then sent thence into Spain, but perhaps now returned; the former was anonymous, but of great holiness and not unused to similar revelations. Both saw this on the very day of his death, but one speaking, the other only seeing.”

Concerning the Englishman, the author of the *Great Exordium*, Book I, ch. 38, says:

> “They report that in the region of England there was a certain religious man of great virtue who, on the very day on which Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, departed from the world, while he was in England, saw in the spirit a certain very great angel sent from heaven, taking up from the earth an equally great soul and carrying it with him in immense joy to the stars.” [Col. 0909D]

With these words the Cistercian annalist begins his eighth chapter. The same historiographer then adds, from Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 3, another apparition which befell the aforesaid William on the very night on which the holy abbot departed from this life; the reader will find it there described more fully.

554. Manrique adds a third to these two: “an apparition,” he says, “made to a regular canon four from Clairvaux, who afterward assumed the monastic habit at Clairvaux.” He says that he records the event from an anonymous French writer translated by de la Silva. It runs as follows:

> “On the same day on which the saint died, indeed at the very same hour, he seemed in sleep to see many monks radiant in white cowls, proceeding slowly two by two and carrying the body of the blessed man from his cell to the church where his funeral rites were being celebrated. Awakening, troubled by the death and vision, he was torn by doubt whether the holy doctor had already departed from the world, and whether prayer ought to be offered for him, or rather to him, as one who might intercede for others. Suddenly, transported outside himself, he saw a star of immense brightness and beauty; and by a voice falling clearly from heaven he learned that it was the soul of his friend and Father, which would shine eternally before the throne of God.” [Col. 0910A]

After setting forth this vision, he says: “There you also have another similar one, which occurred in Italy.” Thus far the compiler of the *Cistercian Annals*.

555. Receive another account, found in the same historian, no. 5, from additions which he cites to the *Great Exordium*, Book VII, ch. 10:

> “Doctor James of Paradise, who belonged to the Carthusian Order, reports that in the hour in which Blessed Bernard happily departed from this world, thirty thousand persons died. Among them was also a certain dean of the church of Lincoln, who, while he lived, was a man of praiseworthy life. Fleeing worldly honours, he chose a solitary life in a certain wilderness, in which he lived most holily for twenty-five [Col. 0910C] years. This dean also died, therefore, on the same day as our most blessed Father Bernard. After death he appeared in great glory to the bishop of Lincoln, for the admonition of that bishop and of all hearers, saying to him: ‘Do penance, amend your life, correct your conscience, abandon pride together with avarice; otherwise you will never possess heavenly glory. For the salvation of a human being is not so easy as many believe. For when I was presented before God’s fearful judgment, thirty thousand souls were present, among whose number Blessed Bernard and I were saved; three descended into purgatory; all the rest fell [Col. 0910D] into hell.’ Having said this, the dean disappeared. But blessed be God in his saints and holy in all his works, who deigned thus to glorify our holy Father Bernard in every people and nation.”

In the *Carthusian Library*, by Fr Theodoricus Petreius, it is noted: “James of Clusa, otherwise of Paradise—although some consider them to have been distinct persons—before entering the Order was doctor of sacred theology and public professor; afterward a member of the Carthusian house at Erfurt. He wrote a treatise *On the Apparitions of Souls after Their Departure from Bodies* . . . and died in the year . . . 1465, or thereabouts.”

556. There are many other visions by which the Lord God manifested the glory of his most faithful servant after his death. Let Geoffrey, Book V, ch. 3, of the *Life* be read; from it I condense the following:

> “On the following night, after the holy body had been committed to burial, the holy Father clearly showed how great a concern he still bore for his sons . . . Appearing to a certain brother in great glory . . . and swiftly passing by while that brother wished to hold him, he said that he had come for a certain simple brother . . . About the third hour of the day the vision was proved true. For a certain brother died . . . and, as is altogether credible, he carried his soul away with him. A few days later he appeared very magnificently to another brother [Col. 0911A] . . . ‘Know this also,’ he said, ‘and tell the brethren: the body of a truly holy man, whose garment I too possess, is buried in the oratory.’ He meant Bishop Malachy. For Bernard had kept for the celebration of his Masses the tunic in which that saint had happily fallen asleep, and, when dying, had ordered himself to be buried in it, just as he had buried that holy man in his own garment. Yet this fact had been altogether unknown, both to the brother himself and to very many others, until this vision.” [Col. 0911B]

Many other apparitions of St Bernard, remarkable in their kind, will be given by us later in the account of the man’s posthumous glory. Meanwhile, let us proceed to other matters.

557. Therefore, on the third day after his death, his body was buried. Geoffrey, Book V, chapter 2, reports that, as the blessed abbot had directed, relics of the blessed apostle Thaddaeus, sent to him from Jerusalem in that same year, had been laid upon his most sacred breast. [Col. 0911C] On the occasion of the burial, a few points should also be noted concerning the epitaphs. Manrique, chapter 9, gives the following judgment of them:

> “The praises or epitaphs with which they adorned Bernard’s tomb when the saint himself had been buried, and which circulate together with his Works, are inferior in quality to their number.
