They are feeble for the grandeur of their subject—now harsh, now cold, or, if they occasionally grow warm, uneven; certainly they seem numerous because none is adequate. Yet I would not believe this happened without a divine disposition: that minds otherwise of the highest excellence should, as it were, be blinded in Bernard’s light, and that gifts which would have remained for praising [Col. 0911D] others should fail in his case, as though he alone were sufficient to himself; and, crowned with the laurel of the spirit of wisdom, he had come to be crowned not by others, but by his own writings.”

Baronius appears to have assented to this conjecture under this year and to have approved it by his own judgment. Having begun, but scarcely sampled, the praises of the Saint, he hastens on to Adam of Saint-Victor, one of Bernard’s chief panegyrists, and finally concludes: “Let these things redound to the praise of the praiser of St Bernard . . .”

558. “Since the epitaph by Adam of Saint-Victor genuinely sounds sweeter than the others, I have thought it proper to transcribe it here, omitting the rest; for it is said to be found among the epitaphs of Lord Bernard. It is worded thus:

> Bright are the valleys; yet, among the bright valleys, the abbot  
> [Col. 0912A] Brighter than they gave a bright name to the world.  
> Bright in ancestry, bright in merits, and bright in honour;  
> Bright also in eloquence, but more so in religion.  
> Bright is his death, bright his ashes, and bright his tomb;  
> Brighter does his spirit rejoice before God.

Thus Adam of Saint-Victor played upon and alluded to the brightness of the holy abbot and of the place. The rest are languid, and were worthy neither of Bernard’s works nor of these Annals.”

There is therefore no need to resort to such panegyrics. A little below we shall produce other testimonies concerning the Saint from men of the greatest weight, of every rank and condition; not excluding even heterodox writers from the company of those who praised him, for they too contributed their share to Bernard’s renown. Indeed, if it is permitted to add our own judgment of the holy Father to the encomia of most wise men, it follows most plainly, both from what has been said in the course of this commentary, and from what will be said below in his Life and thereafter in the posthumous Glory prepared by us in his honour, that the following titles belong to him—not as shadows, but as true and genuine designations. He was therefore a most holy man and should most deservedly be called the light and pillar of the Catholic Church; the support of the Apostolic See; hammer of heretics; apostle; prophet; wonder-worker; angel of peace; instrument of almighty God; model of religious perfection; propagator and glory of the Cistercian Order; and, finally, a chosen vessel for undertaking great deeds and bringing them to a happy conclusion in times not merely most difficult but even most desperate. [Col. 0912B–C]

559. “On the anniversary solemnity of his sacred death, Geoffrey, his secretary, who later became abbot of Clairvaux, delivered a most elegant sermon. Although it is full of many errors in the later editions which circulate, it was published together with the Saint’s works under this opening: ‘How sweet today, beloved sons, ought the memory of a father to be’; as Manrique observes, chapter 9, no. 5. We have mentioned this sermon several times in §1 of this Commentary, no. 18, where the year in which it was delivered is also indicated. Concerning its author, let the reader consult the observations in §63.

“Remarkable, however, is what is reported in the said no. 5 concerning the water with which the body of the Saint, after he had died, had been washed: even many years later it was health-giving and miraculous. Let us hear the sermon’s words:

> ‘To some also the holy Father, who had not seen him in the flesh, showed himself a kindly father in the spirit: he brought help, removed temptation, and brought consolation. For some brethren carried to the most remote regions of the world water from the washing of his sacred body, when, according to custom, we rendered him after his passing the obsequies due to him. And, as we learned from their reliable report, although ten years have now passed, not only does that water remain to this day wholly unspoiled, but it retains the same grace, whatever has been poured upon it. For although they have given some of that sacred liquid to many persons seeking remedies—for they affirm that it has brought help to many—yet, after the vessel has repeatedly been filled with other water, it remains to this day as it was on the first day.’” [Col. 0912C–0913A]

560. Concerning the exceptional gifts of grace with which the holy man was endowed, Geoffrey, the writer of the Life, states the following in Book III, chapter 1:

> “He was serene in countenance, modest in bearing, circumspect in speech, restrained in action, assiduous in holy meditation, devout in prayer, and . . . in every matter he trusted prayer more than his own industry or labour; great-souled in faith, long-suffering in hope, lavish in charity, etc. A certain grace appeared in his flesh, yet more spiritual than bodily. A brightness shone in his face—not earthly, assuredly, but heavenly. In his eyes there radiated a certain angelic purity and a dove-like simplicity. So great was the beauty of his inner person that it burst outward in certain clear signs, and, abundantly suffused from the fullness of inward purity and grace, the outer man also appeared so.”

The same biographer, in the cited place, continues to describe his physical appearance:

> “His entire body was exceedingly thin and without flesh; even his very delicate skin was moderately red in the cheeks . . . His hair was coloured blond and white. His beard was reddish, sprinkled with grey near the end of his life. His stature was of honourable medium height, though he appeared rather tall.” [Col. 0913A–B]

561. The holy man’s body, however, was weak and subject to very many ailments. Let us again hear the cited Geoffrey:

> “Moreover, this treasure was in an earthen vessel utterly shattered and broken on every side. For his flesh suffered under the many burdens of infirmities, so that in them the strength of his spirit might be perfected. The more dangerous of these lay in the passage of his very narrow throat, which admitted nothing at all dry and scarcely anything solid; more troublesome were the weakness of his stomach and the corruption of his internal organs. These were continual with him, besides others which frequently occurred.”

I shall not recount the virtues of the man and his manner of life which the praised biographer describes there; rather, I direct them to be read in the source itself, lest I become unduly lengthy by describing individually everything written there. Meanwhile, I wish that the same author had represented what his facial formation was like—what the features of his forehead, mouth, and eyes were. But since neither he did this, nor do I know it to have been done by any other ancient biographer, I shall attempt below, insofar as I can, to supply this deficiency from elsewhere. [Col. 0913C–D]

## § LIII. Portraits; cell; chalice; pilgrimages to the Saint’s body

562. I possess three impressions representing the likeness of St Bernard. One bears the following inscription: “True likeness of St Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, enlarger of the sacred Cistercian Order.” Yet the truth of that likeness—that is, the perfect correspondence of this impression with its prototype—is asserted there but not proved.

Another image, wholly unlike the first, is prefixed to the French Life of St Bernard printed at Paris in 1704. Its inscription declares this to be the true likeness of the holy man, namely, engraved in copper from a painting sent from Rome and taken from his own face in 1152, when he was sixty-two years of age. That image represents a countenance at once graceful and venerable, joined with paternal gentleness; but I fear that it is affected. For the holy Father’s body was so emaciated that the skin scarcely covered the bones, while the bones themselves scarcely held together with the remaining structure of his extremely weak body—already, so to speak, morally dead before natural death. Consult what I have just set forth from Geoffrey near the end of §52. Brief also is the passage in Bernard’s Letter 144: “Bearing about the pale image of fearful death,” etc. [Col. 0914A–B]

563. Entirely different from the aforesaid images is the likeness of the holy man found in Puricelli, among the monuments of the Ambrosian basilica at Milan and of the monastery now Cistercian—such is the title of the learned author’s work—volume I, p. 623. This one pleases me more than the two preceding images because it possesses greater authority in our estimation than they do. Puricelli writes of it, p. 622, no. 370:

> “This has been engraved in copper quite faithfully from another of equal size, which the Father General sent from France in recent years to his monks in this Ambrosian monastery, now Cistercians, commending it with this encomium: that among all likenesses hitherto engraved in copper, none had ever corresponded more closely to the true and natural likeness of the holy abbot.” [Col. 0914B–C]

564. Nor should I pass over in silence here some matters which Manrique writes at the end of chapter 9 under the year 1153 concerning St Bernard’s chamber and certain other things:

> “Meanwhile I note that the blessed chamber still exists today, about forty feet long and twenty-six broad, with a square stone in one part of the floor upon which the Saint’s straw bed was placed. In the middle of the stone a hollow is visible, the purpose of which is uncertain; and there are those who say it was excavated for placing a fire there, so that his lack of natural heat—for this was especially the Saint’s ailment—might be remedied. In the same chamber may also be seen the wooden bed upon which he lay when he gave up his spirit, preserved whole and uninjured through the years out of reverence for the Saint. Finally, among the relics of Clairvaux, of which we may perhaps have something to say later, the cited Inventory of Clairvaux displays: ‘A small wooden casket silver-plated, whose lock is of silver, full of relics, namely, of the priestly vestments of St Bernard our Father Abbot.’ For this is the heading prefixed in the Inventory. Likewise, a beautiful but small chalice, with its foot and round knop wholly well gilded, both inside and outside, together with its paten and spoon, also gilded, weighing one mark and five ounces; and, because of reverence for St Bernard, who was accustomed to use it in the sacrifice, it occupies the first place in the Inventory.”

But perhaps we shall set forth more concerning the Saint’s relics in his posthumous Glory, if fuller information about them reaches us. [Col. 0914C–0915A]

565. Besides the matters concerning the burial of the most blessed Father, which we have related a little above, we now proceed to speak of pilgrimages piously and devoutly undertaken by various persons in the first period after his death to his venerable tomb. The Cistercian historian, under the year 1154, chapter 1, no. 1, says:

> “When Father Bernard had been translated to the heavens, vows were made at his tomb, as at other holy places, by crowds from almost the whole world. The first, or among the first, was Eskil, the illustrious primate of Denmark, mentioned above, who in this year 1154—the fifty-seventh of Cîteaux—came from the farthest ends of the earth to Clairvaux.”

And shortly afterward, giving the reason why he assigns Eskil’s arrival to this year, as also that of the Sardinian ruler mentioned immediately below, he continues:

> “Therefore . . . at the beginning of spring, he who two years earlier had visited Bernard, having learned from Geoffrey’s writing of the glorious passing of the man, arrived to venerate his tomb.” [Col. 0915A–B]

566. That arrival is also narrated and confirmed by the words of the *Great Exordium*, distinction 3, chapter 25, where the following is read:

> “Not long after this—that is, after he had returned from the monastery of Clairvaux—a most sorrowful report struck his ears concerning the death of the blessed man, his special friend. Lord Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, who had been secretary to that most holy abbot for no small time, wrote him a little book concerning his death. Then his heart grew warm within him, and in his meditation a fire was kindled. He regarded as vain, transitory, and perishable all things that may hinder a man’s purpose from the straight course by which one tends toward the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Therefore, commending to God and the princes of the earth the church over which he had laudably presided, leaving parents and kinsmen, acquaintances and friends, and bidding farewell to the very soil of his native land, he came as a distinguished exile to Clairvaux. He visited the tomb of the blessed man, his once intimate friend, and chose to live and die at his most sacred grave; there too, by God’s gift, he afterward received the habit of holy religion.”

So it is written there. But recall what we set forth in §50, no. 532, concerning the monastic profession at Clairvaux which he desired while St Bernard was still alive. Add what the aforementioned Manrique observes shortly afterward, no. 4. [Col. 0915B–D]

567. “In the same year and at the same time,” Manrique continues, no. 5, “so far as one may conjecture, the ruler of Sardinia, whom we mentioned above, having placed his firstborn upon the throne, abandoned the kingdom; and he who hitherto had refused to adhere to Bernard while he lived adhered to his ashes, becoming a humble monk at Clairvaux.”

We infer from the same *Great Exordium* that he was drawn to the Saint and enrolled in the rule of Clairvaux. I explained the matter in §50, no. 537, when another opportunity arose there to discuss his journey to Clairvaux. I count it among the pilgrimages to the holy man’s tomb, as also the one narrated in the praised *Exordium*, distinction 3, chapter 28:

> “The venerable man Simon, formerly abbot of Chézy, a monastery of no little distinction among the monks of the Black Order, loved blessed Bernard with great affection of heart, so that he seemed wholly dependent upon his counsel and will. He had a great desire to abandon pastoral care and become a monk at Clairvaux. Yet holy Father Bernard, knowing the man’s virtue and the grace by which he was very capable and greatly needed for the monastery entrusted to him, never, so long as he lived in the flesh, wished to grant him consent concerning such a request.” [Col. 0916A–B]

568. “One day, therefore, the same abbot said to him: ‘Lord Father, I am old and almost decrepit; my bodily limbs are failing, illnesses press upon me besides, and I feel myself already beginning to dissolve. If I should die outside Clairvaux, it will be an inconsolable grief and irreparable loss to me. Therefore, you must either now order me to leave and permit me to fulfill my vows, because hastening death no longer allows me to delay.’

“To him the man of God replied: ‘Remain in your place, and do not fear. I assure you that you will die at Clairvaux.’

“The man believed the Saint’s words and for several years remained more secure in his office of prelate. But after the passing of the blessed man, when no one restrained him and he could no longer endure the impulses of his desire, he relinquished his government and went to Clairvaux. There, by a great gift of God and a great miracle, surviving seven years—something wholly remarkable at such an age and in such infirmity—he left to us all at the end a wonderful example of fervour and devotion.” So it is written there. [Col. 0916B–C]

569. Although those two pilgrimages are not clearly and distinctly said by the author who mentions them to have been undertaken for the purpose of seeing and honouring the precious deposit of the sacred body laid at Clairvaux, yet since it seems probable that this cause also, either as primary or at least as secondary, to speak with the philosophers, influenced the journey of those who went to that monastery, we thought it not far from the truth—following Manrique’s example—to say that these two journeys were undertaken by them in honour of that venerable pledge possessed by the monks of Clairvaux, whose daily consolation they would enjoy for as long as they lived, having been enrolled in their order.

“For thus,” says Manrique, no. 6, “all venerated Bernard’s ashes: religious men in Simon of Chézy; princes in Gumarus, or Gunnar; bishops in Eskil—not by undertaking a pilgrimage alone, but by establishing their dwelling among them and living according to the rule of the same Saint, which was judged more excellent and, in his absence, more arduous.”

Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of St Benedict*, volume III, under the year 854, no. 80, supplies this information: “The abbey of St Peter at Chézy, which lies on the river Marne below Château-Thierry in the diocese of Soissons, etc.” I have wished to note this because mention occurred above of the superior of that abbey. [Col. 0916C–0917A]

## § LIV. The holiness, learning, and authority of St Bernard in the Church

570. Mabillon illustrates the headings here prefixed in §2 of his General Preface. See volume I of the works of St Bernard, cols. 25–26, in our edition.

## § LV. Various testimonies in praise of St Bernard collected together

571. It is fitting to confirm by many and varied testimonies concerning this same holy man the immortal praises of our most holy abbot, illustrated by the most learned Mabillon and transcribed by us from him in the paragraph just cited. They are indeed found in the introduction to the works of St Bernard published at Cologne by Merlo Horst; but because the praised Mabillon published them in a better order, it seemed proper for us to conform to him. Accordingly, at the end of the second volume, he divides the present subject among various ranks of persons. [Col. 0917A–B]

To what the Mabillon edition relates concerning St Pius V, however, the Bollandist editor adds another passage from the Life of that praised pontiff by Giovanni Antonio Gabuzio. There, Book IV, chapter 13, the following is reported of him:

> “While he was at table, he wished both great cleanliness in all things and, above all, continual sacred reading to be observed; and he especially arranged for St Bernard’s books *On Consideration*, addressed to Eugenius, to be frequently read aloud—books which clearly teach what must be considered for the honour of God, the good of the whole Church, and the salvation of souls. Carefully weighing the seriousness of their teachings, he diligently reflected within himself upon what he should carry out in his own time and place.” [Col. 0917B–C]

## § LVI–LVII. Whether St Bernard’s Works were collected by the command of the Mother of God; Mabillon’s edition; the holy doctor’s traits as a writer

572–616. I had prepared for the press what the illustrious Manrique collected under the year of Christ 1153, chapter 10, concerning the genuine, doubtful, and spurious writings of the holy doctor, employing the work both of other authors and especially of Cardinal Bellarmine in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. But, having reconsidered the matter, I changed my plan. Lest I should, as the saying goes, put my sickle into another’s harvest by laboriously treating a subject which properly belongs to bibliographers rather than hagiographers, I resolved to forgo this labour and refer readers on this question to Mabillon’s edition, for reasons to be assigned immediately.

It is nevertheless useful to recall that certain works of St Bernard have been cited in this Commentary: namely, in §§15 and 54, *On Grace and Free Will*; in §§23 and 28, the *Sermons on the Song of Songs*; and in §50, the book *On Consideration*. Add that Geoffrey the biographer enumerates certain genuine works of the holy Father in Book III, chapter 5 of his Life as given by us. But, on the occasion of the present subject, a certain matter discussed by the above-cited Manrique must briefly be examined. I set out the matter. [Col. 0917C–0918A]

617. That historian, then, maintains that St Bernard’s Works were collected by command of the Mother of God. To establish this, he brings forward Philotheus’s testimony:

> “In order follow the books which the holy doctor left: a vast volume of works, but far surpassing in weight what it does in bulk; all gems, or rather gold. Concerning these, among Bernard’s praises, Philotheus . . . when they had recently been collected and published, declared confidently, with a certain pious but poetic licence, that the human race had received no greater gift of this kind from the Virgin than the enjoyment of Bernard’s writings.”

These words are found in the Mabillon edition, volume II, chapter 7, col. 1304:

> Yet let this bold Muse have spoken,  
> And have expressed the feelings of my heart:  
> Never has the kindly Virgin, *Parthenice*, given  
> So great a gift to the human race and our honour  
> As, together with her own welcome gift, she lately brought forth for us  
> These writings to be read in brief pages.

618. After quoting these verses of Philotheus, Manrique adds the following:

> “He attributes this gift to the Virgin because, by her command, the Saint’s little works were collected and gathered into one volume for public use, and saw the light.”

Thus he writes. He soon quotes the following couplet from the same poet, confirming the matter:

> She herself indeed brought them forth, for the goddess commanded  
> Her own client to seek out the writings of the excellent old man.

This would be a fact worthy of remembrance if its truth were sufficiently established. But several considerations militate against it. First, the reported command is very confused. For I ask: who was this particular client? In what place, in what manner, and at what time did this occur? By what documents is it confirmed? Second, painters and poets make frequent and characteristic use of episodes. It follows that this commanded collection of the works must be established by testimony of better authority before we give it our assent. Since we have just referred the reader to Mabillon’s edition of St Bernard’s works, it will not be irrelevant to give a brief account of it. [Col. 0918B–C]

619. This most distinguished editor published all St Bernard’s works—genuine, spurious, and doubtful—in six tomes bound in two volumes. The first volume contains the first four tomes, that is, all the Saint’s genuine works; the second, containing the last two tomes, namely the fifth and sixth, presents the remainder. He put both volumes, revised in a second edition, to press at Paris in 1690, after the first edition had appeared there in 1667. Mabillon names at the end of the General Preface the collaborators who worked diligently on the edition of 1690. Yet we always cite him, not them, as the principal author.

Above, I said that Mabillon published all the holy doctor’s works, even though certain letters written to him had not reached his hand. “Certainly,” he says in §1 of the General Preface, “I judge that no unpublished writings of Bernard survive, at least none of any importance, except certain letters which are still sought,” and he identifies them there. What was added in the edition of 1719 may be learned from the General Preface at its end. In the notices prefixed to the smaller works which the learned editor relegated to the second volume, he separates spurious, doubtful, or uncertain works from genuine ones, with such success that he won the palm from all who had preceded him in this field of learning, according to the heterodox Cave, who is therefore in no way open to suspicion here of flattery or false praise. Cave gives him this encomium: “He distinguished the supposititious works from the genuine ones most excellently; no one ever made the distinction more certainly or judged of them more learnedly.” These are Cave’s words in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*. [Col. 0918D–0919B]

620. Moreover, the exceptional and not easily imitated qualities of the Mellifluous Doctor’s writing—imbued, of course, with the special anointing of the Holy Spirit who spoke through him—are expressed by Mabillon in his General Preface prefixed to the first volume, §1, no. 3, in the following language, at once clear and weighty:

> “For in his writings shines an intellect naturally noble, generous, and elevated, yet humane, civilized, and honourable; an eloquence as though inborn, without artifice, not without ornament, but with native ornament; a compact style, vivid discourse, fitting expression, lofty thoughts, devout affections, spontaneously arising charms, speech throughout breathing one God and heavenly things. He burns—not scorching, but enkindling. He pricks and stimulates—not to irritate, but to move. He reproves and rebukes—not to disparage, but to draw. He argues, threatens, terrifies, but by loving rather than by indignation. He caresses, but does not flatter; praises, but does not exalt. He presses gently and touches sharply without causing hurt; he delights, refreshes, and pleases.

> “For, as Sixtus of Siena says, his speech is everywhere sweet and ardent; it so delights and ardently inflames that honey and milk of words seem to flow from his most sweet tongue, and flames of burning affections to burst forth from his most ardent breast.” [Col. 0919B–C]

621. “Moreover, his learning is by no means ordinary, full of the words and substance of Holy Scripture, and so adhering to the judgments of the Fathers that it is nevertheless felt to be his own. Thus he writes concerning divine matters, grace and free will, morals and the duty of popes, clerics, monks, and laypeople, in such a way as to show a fountain, not a stream or channel. Shall we then wonder that so great a man is loved? That his writings are acquired, read, and worn out by everyone? That editions of them are produced without number? That learned and scholarly men devote their labour to enlarging, elucidating, and restoring them to their original integrity? That Rome herself, mistress and teacher of the world, which once reverenced Bernard as teacher—indeed, even as reprover—permitted the books *On Consideration*, first offered to Eugenius III, then most elegantly copied by order of Nicholas V, and finally published from pontifical presses under Clement VIII, while she was about to publish the whole of Bernard, if Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, had likewise devoted his labour to the whole Bernard? It is therefore less surprising that in the capital of the Gauls so great a light of Gaul deserved to be honoured by royal printing.” Thus far Mabillon. [Col. 0919C–0920A]

## § LVIII. Various editions of the holy doctor’s Works; an opinion falsely attributed to him; why and what Bernardine chronology is given here

622. “Among the foremost indications of Bernard’s merit and worth is nothing more striking than the very frequent and repeatedly renewed editions of his works, whether before or after the invention of printing. For their numerous editions demonstrate how widely Bernard is acquired, how eagerly he is read, and finally how universally he is loved.” These are Mabillon’s words in §1 of the General Preface, where he immediately appends a long and careful discussion of so many and diverse editions of the same Works, beginning with the Mainz edition made by Peter Schöffer in 1475, which he judges to have been the first.

How much diligence, accuracy, and labour that Benedictine editor expended in order that his edition might appear as correctly as possible becomes entirely clear to anyone who reads what he adds on this subject in the cited Preface. In the Preface reproduced in the edition of the Works of 1719, I find the following added concerning him: “Throughout his life, though occupied with other studies, and those most weighty, he devoted every care and all diligence to discovering and polishing Bernard’s Works.” [Col. 0920A–C]

623. To the various printings of which I spoke may incidentally be added that the Reverend Father Lord Godfrey Bouvart, of the Cistercian Order, an ascetic at the celebrated and flourishing monastery of St Bernard in the territory of Antwerp on the Scheldt, took no little care to examine and note a great many diverse copies of the printed works of the same Saint. Among other things written here by him concerning the same Saint on 15 March 1737, he says: “I add here a series of editions of the same Saint’s works which I have been able to find in catalogues of libraries, auctions, and booksellers, in prefaces to the Works, and elsewhere.” The catalogue which he appends begins with the Mainz edition of 1475 and ends with Mabillon’s edition, reprinted at Paris in 1719, so that it identifies forty different editions in all. [Col. 0920C–D]

624. But before leaving this subject for others, I must take issue with a certain Catholic writer who attributed to our holy doctor an opinion alien to sound doctrine. We have already dealt in §54, no. 574, with heterodox persons who concoct poison from Bernard’s honeyed substance. Whether Catholic authors may also be found who either understand certain matters in his works less correctly or criticize them wrongly, I am not ready to say, and I forgo an elaborate inquiry, since this matter properly belongs not to our tribunal but to theologians, whose responsibility it is to explain the holy Father rightly understood, as they do the other doctors of the Catholic Church. My concern here, therefore, is with a certain Catholic author who believed he had found something in Bernard which is not in Bernard. Understand the matter.

625. Lucas Castellinus, in his treatise *On the Certainty of the Glory of Canonized Saints*, chapter 1, point 23, §3, takes issue with those who assert “that St Bernard followed the error of those who denied that the souls of the righteous enjoy eternal glory before the day of the Last Judgment, as Alphonsus de Castro writes of him in Book III of *Against Heresies*, under the heading ‘Beatitude,’ after the sixth heresy, § ‘Blessed Bernard.’” What Castellinus subsequently adduces in defence of the holy doctor may be read in the place just cited.

Mabillon, however, treats the subject more fully in volume I, p. 709, where he examines St Bernard’s teaching concerning the intermediate state of souls. Natalis Alexander also defends the holy doctor in volume VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, published at Paris in 1714, discussing this matter on pp. 527–528. If anyone desires further information concerning Alfonso de Castro, a Spaniard by nationality and a Franciscan by profession, let him consult Wadding’s *Writers of the Order of Friars Minor* and Nicolás Antonio’s *Spanish Library*. [Col. 0920D–0921B]

626. Although I am not unaware that the introduction to the works of St Bernard, published at Cologne by the eminent Jacques Merlo Horst, contains a chronology of the life and writings of the same holy Father, with a preface to the reader, I nevertheless thought that Bernardine chronology should also be considered here. The purpose is that the deeds performed by this great doctor and assigned in this preliminary Commentary of mine to fixed computations of years from the author of the Cistercian Annals may receive new—or even better—light if they are displayed here, as it were, in a single view. Thus they may deservedly be compared with Manrique’s chronological system, which I have followed in the said Commentary, and this system may be confirmed or corrected from that one wherever it perhaps goes astray. Indeed, who will deny that chronology is history’s bright torch?

I therefore present the chronology published by Mabillon at the end of his first volume, not Horst’s chronology. For since the former was arranged and published after the latter, we should not be surprised that the later one is of better quality, being arranged by a man who, after Horst and the other editors of St Bernard’s works and writings, applied himself earnestly and wisely to re-editing and elucidating them. See the beginning of volume I of our edition. [Col. 0921B–D]

## § LIX–LX. St Bernard solemnly enrolled in the canon of saints

627–661. Just as the honour of the great Father’s admission to the number of the Saints was distinguished both for the man himself and for the whole sacred Cistercian Order by the manner and circumstances in which that sacred and solemn act was performed, so scholars disagree concerning the year in which it occurred. Mabillon says in volume II, col. 1341, among Bernard’s encomia:

> “Not to be placed last is the fact that he deserved to be the first of the Cistercian Order to be solemnly entered in the roll of Saints. The extraordinary holiness of the blessed man, his immense labours undertaken for the Church, and finally the heavenly attestations of remarkable miracles demanded this; it would have seemed wrong to delay assent to them. Scarcely ten years had passed from his sacred death when the matter first began to be discussed at the Council of Tours, held in 1163, at which Alexander III sat and presided. Yet the supreme pontiff, although otherwise most willingly disposed to agree, because of his veneration for Bernard, nevertheless judged that it should be postponed for a time, for the reasons which he afterward set out in the letter of canonization.” [Col. 0921D–0922A]

662. “For,” he says, “while we were devoting a sufficiently favourable disposition to the same business—namely, Bernard’s canonization—there came upon us a multitude and crowd of petitioners who sought a similar thing in various provinces. Since we saw that we could not suitably satisfy everyone, it was decided that, in order to avoid scandal, this matter too should be deferred, because what had to be refused to others for the time being ought also to be postponed in this case. Finally, at the request of Abbot Gerard and the community of Clairvaux, Alexander himself, desiring to satisfy the devout wishes of his sons, willed that Father Bernard be enrolled among the saints.” Thus Mabillon.

As I indicated above, that matter was highly honourable to our holy abbot, to the entire sacred Cistercian Order, and especially to the ascetics of Clairvaux; this will become evident from the apostolic letters which we shall shortly reproduce. [Col. 0922B]

[Col. 0922C] **663.** Meanwhile, it must also be determined to what year that canonization ought to be assigned. The same editor of Bernard’s works mentioned above discusses the matter as follows in the cited column 1341:

> “But since the year in which this occurred is not expressly stated in the apostolic letters, authors are not of one opinion: some, such as Horst and Henriquez, refer it to the year 1154; others to 1166. Yet both views seem contrary to the chronology, since Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, to whom Alexander’s letters are addressed, entered upon his office only in 1172. Better than all of them is Ciaconius in his account of Alexander III, whose knowledge of Roman antiquities and pontifical documents makes him a safer authority: he places it in 1174; and he is followed by the most learned Sirmond, in his Notes on Peter of Celle, book IX, letter 9, and by Manrique in the *Annals*. Alberic in his *Chronicle* agrees with them. There is added testimony beyond all objection from the *Chronicle of Clairvaux*, published by the Jesuit Chifflet, written by an anonymous but contemporary author.”

**664.** Accordingly, in that *Chronicle*, published by Chifflet in his book composed to establish the noble lineage of St Bernard of Clairvaux, p. 84, the following is recorded under the year of the Lord 1174:

> “In the same year occurred the dedication of the church of Clairvaux, the canonization of blessed Bernard, and his elevation. Lord Wichard, archbishop of Lyons, formerly abbot of Pontigny, was present. And in the following year, in the general chapter, they adopted the chant for Blessed Bernard and the chant of the Trinity.”

From this it follows that this sacred act, by which Bernard was enrolled by solemn rite among the company of the blessed, must be restored to the year 1174 and fell on 18 January, distinctly specified in the apostolic letters. Thus, as Mabillon calculates, it occurred twenty years, four months, and twenty-nine days after his death—plainly so if one counts backward from the stated year and day of the month to 20 August, in the year of Christ 1153, the day and year of the saint’s death.

Concerning his elevation, mentioned in the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* just cited from Chifflet, discussion will return below, after we have produced the ancient documents—though they have elsewhere been published together with the works of St Bernard—which illustrate the sacred inauguration of the man enrolled among the saints.

In the edition published in 1719, the apostolic letters are preceded by an epistle from Traimund, or Tromund, monk of Clairvaux, to Abbot Gerard, by whom he had been sent to Rome to press for the canonization of the blessed doctor. But since the reader gains no great advantage from reading what is mentioned in that letter, I do not judge it should be transcribed here. There follow the letters of Alexander III concerning the canonization of St Bernard, already published above; see col. 2595.

**665–672.** From all these testimonies and proofs of the highest veneration for the blessed man while living, manifested by the Apostolic See in decreeing for him public honours among the blessed, we must conclude that scarcely any canonization in the Church of God up to that time was celebrated with greater solemnity than that of St Bernard. Accordingly, it was most honourable both to the man himself, to the entire Cistercian Order, and especially to the ascetics of Clairvaux.

## § LXI. Prayers for the Mass composed by Pope Innocent III himself; elevations of the body; altars; relics transmitted to various parts of Europe

**673.** Besides the other, altogether singular honours of which we have just spoken, commended in writings by Christ’s vicar Alexander III when he admitted St Bernard into the assembly of the blessed, another exceptional event occurred: afterward another supreme pontiff not only prescribed that Bernard’s office should be recited at the sacrifice of the Mass, but even composed it with his own lips.

Hear the account from Mabillon, mentioned above, who relates it thus from column 1344:

> “Such monuments of praise were insufficient for Bernard’s memory and immense merits, unless the supreme head of the Church should also compose his office with his own lips. This Innocent III did at the request of John, formerly metropolitan of Lyons and then a monk of Clairvaux, and also of Rainer, monk of Heisterbach and Innocent’s confessor, in a letter given to John in the year 1201.”

The said author immediately reproduces the letter there in these words:

**674.**

> “To John, formerly archbishop of Lyons. We have not been unwilling to grant what you desired to request, since from it there will accrue both to us and to you the fruit of eternal recompense. For, at the brothers’ request, you asked that, in honour of Blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, whom the Apostolic See had enrolled in the venerable catalogue of saints, we ourselves should compose, with our own lips, the collect and the other prayers—both because of the authority of the composer and because of the style of the composition, so that they might be said with greater devotion. And behold: as far as we were able, at the urging of our beloved son Brother Rainer, we have seen to it that your petition was heard.
>
> “Collect: ‘Bring to fulfilment in us, we beseech thee, O Lord, the devout effect of holy religion; and, in order that we may obtain the abundance of thy grace, may Blessed Bernard, abbot and outstanding doctor, always intercede with thee for us by his merits and prayers. Through the Lord,’ etc.
>
> “Secret: ‘May this offering of the sacrament, which we offer to thy majesty in memory of the Lord’s Passion, be pleasing to thee, O God.’
>
> “Post-Communion: ‘May the food which we have received produce its effect in us, almighty God, so that, eating it, we may be incorporated into it. Who with thee,’ etc.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, 10 July.”

**675.** Having produced these passages, Mabillon adds:

> “Here you see St Bernard distinguished by the title of doctor by the supreme ruler of the Church. A very old Corbie manuscript containing the saint’s life testifies that this title had also been used by Alexander III himself in the Mass of canonization. After the preliminary prayers from the common, ‘Attend to our supplications,’ etc.; the Epistle, ‘Thus says the Lord: I sent to you this commandment,’ etc.; and also the Gospel concerning doctors, ‘You are the salt of the earth,’ the following is added: ‘The above-written Mass of St Bernard was first celebrated by Lord Pope Alexander III.’”

**676.** Let us now return to the elevation of the holy doctor, which we briefly indicated in the preceding paragraph from the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* in Chifflet. There we saw that the dedication of the church of Clairvaux, the canonization of St Bernard, and his elevation were connected with the year 1174. Manrique, under that year, chapter 2, no. 2, postpones the elevation, saying:

> “The great Belgian Chronicle mentions, under this same year, the dedication of the church of Clairvaux and the canonization of St Bernard, though it confuses them with the elevation of the saint’s body, which is nevertheless known to have occurred four years later.”

But since the author of the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* is contemporary and beyond all objection, whatever may be the case with the *Great Belgian Chronicle*, he does not seem to us chargeable with error in assigning that elevation to 1174, if he can be explained in another way. And surely he can, if, following Mabillon, we admit that two elevations occurred at different times. For Mabillon observes in column 1341:

**677.**

> “As regards the elevation mentioned in the cited authority—that is, the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* in Chifflet—the book of the tombs of Clairvaux says that it was performed by Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, and by Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, some years after the canonization. But the words themselves sufficiently show that this must be understood of another, more solemn translation, since they indicate that the aforesaid Abbot Henry arranged this elevation through G., archbishop of Lyons.”

The words of the book of the tombs of Clairvaux are reported by Manrique, whom Mabillon cites under the year 1178, chapter 3, no. 1, on the occasion of Godfrey of Sorit, who was among those present:

> “When Godfrey heard of the canonization of Blessed Bernard by Pope Alexander III of happy memory, and of the intended translation of the body of the same Blessed Bernard under Lord Henry, the seventh abbot of Clairvaux, he came to the general chapter and hastened thence to Clairvaux. There he most diligently took part in the ceremony with the archbishop of Lyons and the co-bishops.”

**678.** Then, from the same book, in Henry’s epitaph, Manrique says, no. 2:

> “At Clairvaux he gloriously completed two good and magnificent works, apart from innumerable other good deeds. For Blessed Bernard, whom Lord Pope Alexander III had already canonized and whose day of deposition he had commanded the universal Church to celebrate joyfully, he caused—after venerable bishops and other reverend persons had assembled from various places—the venerable father, our Lord Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, formerly abbot of Pontigny, to elevate and re-elevate him with great joy and the exultation of the whole Gallican Church, and to place him reverently and honourably in a marble shrine behind the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, as may still be seen today.”

Do not these testimonies make it altogether likely and consonant with truth that two elevations of St Bernard’s body occurred: one in 1174, less solemn; the other in 1178, more solemn?

**679.** Moreover, a letter of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, concerning this latter elevation—though it bears no chronological date—survives in Mabillon, cols. 1345 and 1346, addressed to Stephen, king of England. It contains the following:

> “A day honourable and solemn was celebrated among us, joyous with a new festival and festive with abundant rejoicing; for the uncovering of the most sacred body of Blessed Bernard made it most celebrated for us and suffused it with a brighter light. How we wished that the presence of your majesty might share in those joys, heavenly rather than earthly! Thus the splendour of so great a feast would increase for us through the honour of such a principal glory, and for you a richer abundance of blessing would flow, by some marvellous channel, from the merits of that most illustrious confessor.
>
> “But because the great distance of a most remote region denied us this, we transferred our wishes to spiritual aid and, God being favourable, did what we could: though your presence was absent, your remembrance was not lacking there. For we solemnly impressed your name, with the emblems of your piety, upon the affections of the brothers and the hearts of your sons, so that, received with great devotion, they might in some manner offer it to the gaze of the holy Father and present it in the secret chamber of the heavenly court.”

**680.**

> “Furthermore, lest the occasion of bodily absence should deprive the royal treasuries of a share in the discovered gift, we send you an honourable portion from the treasury of his relics. We consider it wholly unworthy that the piety of so great a prince should be deprived of a share in so great holiness.
>
> “Receive, therefore, a finger of that sacred hand. Since the righteous man had shaken from it every gift of earthly gain, God filled it, as was fitting, with the most abundant fullness of heavenly blessing. I mean that hand whose touch healed the sick, strengthened the infirm, confirmed men, and put demons to flight; that hand which laid the first foundation-stone of our Clairvaux, for which you are planning to provide buildings.
>
> “We have taken care to seal carefully in a little vessel what is sent, lest either the treasure deposited there be exposed to injury through frequent opening, or some deceit of pious fraud creep in through an impulse of devout theft.”

**681.** What, then, shall we say of the other notable honours honourably bestowed upon the man enrolled in the canon of saints? The author of the *Cistercian Annals*, writing under the year 1174, chapter 2, no. 2, concerning that solemnity, says: “I should suppose that on the same feast an altar was also consecrated to the saint; very many such altars were being erected in his honour in other churches as well.”

In the same place, no. 3, the Cistercian historian adds:

> “Certainly in this year the bishop of Tarentaise, now weakened by age but ready and inclined toward every good work, at the request of the same bishop of Langres—Walter was in question—and of the brothers of Longvadum, came to Longvadum and consecrated a new altar and cemetery in honour of the holy Father. The people assembled and competed among themselves as to who could more fittingly honour the new sacred rites.”

[Note: [Col. 0925] Longum-Vadum: Longvadum, a Cistercian house in the diocese of Langres, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, founded in 1149.]

**682.** Sacred pledges which travelled into various regions of Europe considerably increased the honour of our saint. I shall set down here those which have come to my knowledge, though I am fully persuaded that many others are preserved either among Cistercians or elsewhere.

In the Cistercian Calendar printed at Dijon in 1617, under 17 May is marked: “Translation of our holy father Bernard to Avignon.” This may perhaps be understood of some portion of his sacred relics. We have just spoken of the most precious pledge, namely the finger of St Bernard which Abbot Henry sent to Stephen, king of England.

In the history of the royal abbey of the Virgin Mother of God at Soissons, printed at Paris in 1675, book IV, chapter 2, p. 398, it is related that around the year 1400 Lord d’Honcourt gave his daughter Agnes a silver reliquary containing relics of St Bernard, St William, and twenty others. But in the catalogue of relics, p. 403, I find mention of St Bernard’s garments, not of any part of his body.

Mabillon, vol. I, col. 362, in the notes to letter 410—formerly 366—of the holy Father, on the occasion of the abbey of St Victor outside the walls of Paris, of the Regular Canons of the Order of St Augustine, reports that the saint’s cowl is preserved in that abbey’s treasury, a perpetual memorial of his love for it, together with the charter from which St Bernard’s seal hangs; “concerning which,” he says, “see above at letter 284.”

**683.** Spain possesses a portion of a rib five fingers long and five other smaller relics, as noted in our manuscript, which was drawn from the inventory of relics, or *lipsanologium*, as it is elsewhere called among us, of the royal monastery of St Lawrence at the Escorial.

What of Italy? In volume IV of Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*, among the material concerning the bishops of Genoa, under Otto, col. 850 of the latest Venetian edition, there is discussion of the love and veneration shown by St Bernard, while alive, toward the Genoese, and also of their recourse to the saint after his death when war broke out in Italy in 1625 (see our Commentary, § XXIII). They feared for their liberty. Indeed, the Genoese not only chose him as their patron and protector, but also sent Augustine Centurione as ambassador to Gaul, that he might adorn our abbot’s tomb with the public honour of a continuously burning silver lamp, as you will find there in Ughelli.

The following words, at col. 851, are relevant:

> “Abbot Claudius Argenterius of Clairvaux received Centurione with the monks so honourably that, with the consent of the same monks, he judged that, once St Bernard’s tomb had been opened, the envoy should be presented, on behalf of the people of Genoa, with a rib taken from the saint’s body. The gift would be all the more welcome to the Genoese because it was known that until then no one had obtained either, after the stone had been lifted from Bernard’s tomb, sight of the body with his own eyes, or relics separated from the other limbs to carry away.”

**684.**

> “Moreover, so great a concourse of people received the rib from the saint’s body when it was brought to Genoa that nothing more magnificent could have been done in those processions. Enclosed in a silver vessel, it was brought into the metropolitan church to secure the saint’s perpetual protection.”

From this, reader, infer that the two arms of St Bernard, one of which the Cassinese monks of St Catherine at Genoa and the other the Friars Preachers at Santa Maria Novella in Florence boast of possessing, must have belonged to some other St Bernard. For it is certain that, in the presence of Centurione the envoy, Abbot Claudius, and a large multitude of Clairvaux monks, St Bernard’s body was found so whole and uninjured that not even the smallest part appeared to have been detached from the rest of the body.

Yet at least the finger was then absent from the remaining body, according to what was said shortly above. Ughelli, in the cited vol. IX, in presenting the metropolitan church of Cosenza, col. 185, lists among the sacred relics preserved in its metropolitan basilica “the arm of Bernard the abbot”—certainly not Bernard of Clairvaux, as follows from what we have just cited from the same author, unless it was sent there after 1625, which would need proof. From this infer what should be said of the arm of St Bernard which Masini, in his *Survey of Bologna*, claims on 20 August to be held by the nuns of St Leonard.

**685.** Raissius, in the supplement to John Molanus’s *Natales sanctorum Belgii*, records the following relics of St Bernard in Belgium, fol. 170v:

> “At Cambron I once saw … one chasuble of this honey-tongued doctor. The ascetics of St Bernard in Brabant, on the River Scheldt, at the second milestone from Antwerp, likewise rejoice that they possess one chasuble of their father and patron, together with one complete joint of his sacred hand.”

But on 14 February of the year in which I write, 1737, when I was in the lodging, or “refuge,” as they call it, which those ascetics possess in this city of Antwerp, I was told that the joint had been stolen.

In the same place, fol. 170, there is mention of St Bernard’s spring in the monastery of Clairefontaine in the duchy of Luxembourg. When drunk with faith and devotion, it is believed to bring aid against illnesses. Other sacred relics remain to be indicated in the following paragraph.

## § LXII. Other sacred relics among the Belgians; his Office; proper lessons; whether the Saint, as these say, was the author of the antiphon *Salve Regina*; public honour rendered to him in Paris, Liège, and Rome

**686.** In his *Hierogazophylacium Belgicum*, Raissius mentions many other relics of St Bernard, namely: p. 314, two notable bones in the cathedral church of St Mary at Tournai; p. 82, Bernard’s name in the list “On the bones of saints” at the abbey of St Aubert, Regular Canons of St Augustine, at Cambrai; p. 218, a bone at the Premonstratensian abbey of Floreffe in the territory of Namur; p. 227, a chasuble with stole and maniple at the Benedictine abbey of Gembloux, situated between Brussels and Namur in Gallic Belgium.

Raissius himself says:

> “That very chasuble, which I have seen more than once—and in which I, though unworthy, have more than once offered the sacrifice of Mass to God the Father—marvellously breathes antiquity. For it is not, like our present chasubles, open at the sides and divided in two, but closed all round in a circle, descending to the middle of the shin. Hence, while celebrating, the priest supports both its lower side-edges, gathered up over his arms; for it has neither sleeves nor openings through which the priest’s arms may be put out.”

**687.** To these are added other remains recorded in the same *Hierogazophylacium*: p. 298, a hair-shirt and cloth of St Bernard the abbot at the Benedictine abbey of Mariacolum in the territory of Landrecies in Hainaut; p. 459, bones and the cowl of Bernard, prelate of Clairvaux, at the Cistercian nunnery of Salzinnes near Namur; p. 80, among the relics of the Cistercian abbey of Orval in the duchy of Luxembourg:

> “There, moreover, we saw the gilded chalice of Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux, which he used in the sacrifice of the Mass and which he left there in the time of Constantine, first abbot of Orval.”

P. 515, speaking of Les Vaucelles, or Vallis-Cella, a Cistercian abbey in the district of Cambrai, the same collector of relics says:

> “There we saw St Bernard’s undershirt, a singular remedy for pregnant women against the perils of childbirth.”

On p. 3 he records “the staff … with which he used to support his feeble limbs, and which he left to the monks of this place”—that is, the Benedictines of Affligem in the territory of Aalst—“as a memorial.”

**688.** Nor would it be foreign to our purpose to make some observations concerning the cult with which the saint was honoured in the Church after he had been enrolled among the saints. Baillet, at the end of the *Life of St Bernard*, drawing on Gavanti, notes that his Office was subsequently established by the Pope with a semidouble rite; but that St Pius V raised it to a double rite, while changing its prayer and ordering the homily still read today to be inserted. On this point see Gavanti, *Thesaurus sacrorum rituum*, vol. II, p. 160.

We possess a copy of proper lessons marked with this title:

> “These nine lessons, customarily read at Matins on the feast of St Bernard, have been taken from the breviary of the church of Fontaines parish; they contain certain matters omitted in his Life.”

Above this title is written: “A gift of the Most Reverend Father General of the Feuillants”—that is, of the Fulians—and the name John Bona is appended. His merits are sufficiently known, and he is praised by Ciaconius among the *Lives of Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals*, vol. IV, col. 793. Hippolyte Hélyot treats, in his *History of Monastic Orders*, etc., vol. V, part IV, chapter 38, from p. 401, of the reformed religious of the Cistercian Order, who are called Feuillants in France and Reformers of St Bernard in Italy. These points having been noted, reader, here are the aforesaid lessons.

**689. Lesson I.** The most blessed Bernard was born at Fontaines, a town in the district of Langres, as the worthy offspring of his father. Noble indeed in lineage of flesh, but nobler in loftiness of mind. His father was named Tescelin, and his mother Aleth, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, a powerful man descended from the noble stock of the ancient dukes of Burgundy. By God’s providence they had six sons and one daughter. But since we have not undertaken here to expound the history of his family, let us at least relate a few miracles from his life, as the Lord grants.

**Lesson II.** One night, then, Blessed Bernard was awake while the monks all around were sleeping. He heard angels in the church clearly and sweetly praising God and the Blessed Virgin. Hearing them, he rose secretly and immediately went to the church, so that, standing near, he might see more clearly what this was.

**Lesson III.** He saw the holy Mother of God in the midst of the angels. One of them held in his hand a golden censer; another held incense. Led by one of these, the holy man proceeded, as though at the right hand of the glorious Virgin, as far as the altar. There he heard, in an angelic voice, this antiphon sung, *Salve Regina*, entire from beginning to end. Having retained it by heart, he is said afterward to have written it down and sent it to Pope Eugenius, so that by command of apostolic authority it might be solemnly observed in the churches in honour of the Virgin Mother of God. This was done, as many still testify.

**690. Lesson IV.** Once, when the blessed man was sailing on the Loire, his boat happened to strike a small bridge, upon which a boy was standing. The boy immediately fell into the river and drowned. At the news, neighbours ran together, lamenting the dead child. Bernard ordered him brought to him; when the dead child had been brought, the saint prayed, and the boy, in the sight of all, was raised to life by the saint’s prayer.

**Lesson V.** There was a religious man named Odo, one part of whose body remained for some time almost dead, lying immobile because of paralysis. After the death of the blessed man, he arrived there. Having washed the afflicted part with water sanctified by the blessed man, he returned sound and unharmed.

**Lesson VI.** Another, cruelly tormented by a headache and entirely deprived of his senses, was healed when sprinkled with water from a spring sanctified by St Bernard. Another had languished for seven years; brought by his parents to the sacred spring, he was made well. Another had suffered from quartan fever for a long time; by drinking from the same spring, he recovered health.

**691. Lesson VII.** At Barru [perhaps *Barrum*] on the Aube there were two women tormented by demons. Their parents then brought them to the man of God to be cured by him. When they had approached the gates of Clairvaux, one of the devils said through the woman’s mouth to the other: “We must leave this woman.” “Why,” said the demon, “must this happen?” He replied: “I cannot see Bernard or hear his voice.” And immediately he left the woman, and she was healed from that hour.

**Lesson VIII.** Those present at this miracle praised God, saying: “Truly that man is holy, and the Holy Spirit dwells in him.” As they said this, the servant of God came and, giving thanks, prayed.

**Lesson IX.** After praying, he turned to the other woman and said: “O most wicked demon, enemy of God, come out of this woman.” At that voice the demon left the woman, and she was healed from that hour.

**692.** I explain certain words occurring above. *Negatus* means “drowned” or “suffocated in the waters.” See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, vol. IV, col. 1165 of the latest edition. *Incommota contractionis*—in our manuscript written either wrongly or in a form now not sufficiently intelligible as *in commota*—I explain from the sense as meaning “without movement because of paralysis.”

Whether St Bernard composed the antiphon *Salve Regina*, as was indicated above in Lesson III, will be examined immediately. If in the seventh lesson *Barrum super Albam*, or *Barri*, with “town” understood, should be read, it is in the French province of Champagne.

These many and varied signs of public veneration toward the holy doctor, which it seemed appropriate to gather in this paragraph and the immediately preceding one, prove that he both deserved and obtained an estimation common to all, equal to his public and private endowments. Add that the Faculty of Theology at Paris, as a token of grateful memory for the benefits rendered by our saint to that body against Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, and certain other diseased members, goes each year on 20 August to the Bernardines in order to celebrate solemnly a Mass accompanied by a sermon, as Baillet testifies at the end of the *Life of the Most Holy Doctor*.

The Roman people, in memory of benefits received from the holy man when Rome was in very great distress, offer him a chalice with four tapers, according to Piazza in the *Hemerologium Sacrum* for 20 August.

**693.** In Edmond Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, vol. VIII, from col. 1486, among the statutes of the church of Liège made in the years of the Lord 1336 and 1337, the following is recorded:

> “Moreover, moved by pious reflection and a reasonable obligation, we enact and ordain that special devotion, and some recompense for such great gifts, be rendered every year on his feast to the good confessor and outstanding doctor, Blessed Bernard the abbot. For by his presence while alive, in solemn Masses and frequent preaching, and by divine and wonderful signs and miracles, he illuminated the holy church, city, and country of Liège, as we find recorded in our histories. Namely, his feast is to be celebrated in this church with three lessons from his proper legend and a special collect, with the *Te Deum*, and with the Hours and Mass from the Common of one Confessor not a Bishop.”

**694.** A question previously deferred to this point—whether St Bernard composed the antiphon *Salve, Regina*—will now be examined. First, it does not seem certainly established that the holy man was the first author of that antiphon. Secondly, if another was its author, it is not sufficiently clear who that person was. Both points will appear from the arguments in which different writers designate different authors of the same antiphon.

Among Bernard’s spurious and non-genuine works, which Mabillon gathered into his second volume, are four sermons on that antiphon. He explains there, at col. 721 before the first sermon, why he denies them to this saint. The author of that work, saying in the cited place, “This song … composed by saints,” obscures rather than resolves the matter, since he names none of them and seems to indicate more than one.

Indeed, that passage gave Mabillon, in the notes at the end of vol. I, cols. 117 and 118, occasion to discuss the present question and to put forward and examine various views. Yet he reaches a doubtful and uncertain conclusion, as is clear from the following words, which we reproduce.

**695.**

> “Wion proves at length, in *Lignum Vitae*, book V, chapter 105, that the author of this antiphon was Herman the Cripple, a Benedictine monk, adducing various testimonies of later writers; but this text seems somewhat opposed to that opinion. For I nowhere read that Herman was distinguished by the title of saint. Moreover, John the Hermit, book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 7, relates that St Bernard heard the antiphon *SALVE REGINA* sung by an angelic voice, entire from beginning to end; and that, having retained it by heart, he is said afterward to have written it down and sent it to Lord Pope Eugenius, so that by command of apostolic authority it might be solemnly observed in the churches … ‘And this was done,’ etc. From this passage the angels would have to be called the authors of this prayer. Other words from the same sermon, close to those cited above, seem to allude to this: ‘This song came forth poured from the highest lips.’
>
> “Alberic relates this story somewhat differently in his *Chronicle* under the year 1130. He records that St Bernard was once received as a guest at Dijon, at St Benignus, an abbey which, he says, Bernard always loved because his mother was buried there. Before the hour of the office, Bernard heard angels around the altar sweetly singing the antiphon *SALVE REGINA*. At first he believed it was the community, and on the following day said to the abbot: ‘YOU SANG THE ANTIPHON OF LE PUY EXCELLENTLY LAST NIGHT AROUND THE ALTAR OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN.’”

**696.** It was called the “Antiphon of Le Puy” because Haimar, bishop of Le Puy, composed it … Hence, at a certain Cistercian general chapter, he obtained permission for this antiphon to be received by the whole Order; and this was done. Haimar, or Aimar, or Adhemar, was bishop of Le Puy and an especially devoted worshipper of the Blessed Virgin in the time of Pope Urban II.

But William Durand, in book IV, chapter 22 of the *Rationale*, reports that Peter, bishop of Compostela, composed this antiphon; Claudius a Rota asserts the same in his notes on Pseudo-Liutprand. To what I have thus far reproduced from Mabillon, I have no additional material to add which would make the original author of the famous antiphon clear from uncertain and unknown.

## § LXIII. The first three writers on the Saint’s deeds

**697.** Above we spoke of things Bernard wrote for others or to others. We shall now treat of Bernard himself as described by others, that is, of the historians of his life. Mabillon praises them especially well in his notice prefixed to the books on the Life and Deeds of the holy Father, found in vol. II, p. 1057, using these words:

> “Scarcely any saint has had so many heralds of his deeds, so outstanding and trustworthy writers, as Blessed Bernard. His life and illustrious acts were pursued in continuous narration, as if by agreement, by three most distinguished authors: namely William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims, but then a monk of the monastery of Signy; Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the district of Chartres; and Geoffrey, Bernard’s own secretary—all, as it were, eyewitnesses of the events. Others followed them: Alan, bishop of Auxerre; and, to pass over other later writers, John the Hermit and many more recent authors. Among these Philotheus—whether a real or fictitious name—a monk of Clairvaux, sang Bernard’s deeds in verse.”

698. After these prefatory remarks on the biographers, Mabillon illustrates the first three—and the principal—writers on the deeds of the holy Doctor with the following observations:

> “That the first book of the *Life of St Bernard* was written during Bernard’s lifetime, though without his knowledge, is expressly asserted in its preface by its author William, formerly abbot of Saint-Theoderic, but then already a monk of the monastery of Signy, in the district of Regitesten [uncertain reading], in the diocese of Rheims, whither he had withdrawn from a desire for solitude and quiet, as Burchard, abbot of Balerne, testifies in the subscription to that same first book.”

The date at which William embraced a more retired life is more certainly known than that at which he began his book on the *Life of St Bernard*. Concerning both points Mabillon, cited above, writes:

> “The date of William’s withdrawal to Signy is understood from the parchment book of Saint-Theoderic, in which Helinus, his successor at Saint-Theoderic, is first named in 1135. In what year William began this book is not known. Certainly it was after the transfer of the monastery of Clairvaux to a more spacious site and the construction of new buildings, from nos. 34 and 62; likewise after the schisms in the Church had been settled and the heresies refuted, from no. 40; and thus after the year 1140, perhaps after 1145. Moreover, William died before Bernard. More concerning him may be found in volume V, in the prefatory notice to the letter *To the Brethren of the Mount of God*, and in the fuller notes on Letter 85.”

699. Mabillon judged these points concerning the biographer who composed the first book on the deeds of St Bernard worthy of notice. How far he carried the *Life*, and what matters he treated in it, may be learned from Manrique under the year of Christ 1153, chapter 11, no. 1:

> “He wrote of Bernard’s beginnings, lineage, native country, parents, youth, conversion, monastic life, and his government of the then newly founded monastery of Clairvaux, together with the remaining matters, down to the schism of Peter Leo.”

But when this golden author was torn away by death from continuing his work, another golden author was not lacking to carry it forward. It is worth hearing Mabillon, identified above, on him:

700. “The *Life* begun by William,” he says, “was continued, after Bernard’s death, in a second book by Ernald, or Arnald, abbot of Bonneval—not the Bonneval in the diocese of Besançon, nor the other Cistercian house in the diocese of Rodez, but that of the Black Monks in the district of Chartres. To this Arnold was written Bernard’s last letter, Letter 310, whatever others may think to the contrary. See the fuller notes on Letter 310. Ernald undertook this book at the request of the monks of Clairvaux, who, out of modesty, transferred this task to him, as the author testifies in the preface to the second book. He left the work unfinished when he died.”

At approximately what date he was engaged in writing the *Life of St Bernard* may be learned from the notes on Book II, chapter 3, of that same *Life*.

> [Note: [Col. 0933] From these notes it is inferred that Ernald wrote this neither before 1139 nor after about 1169. EDITOR.]

These two writers of the *Acts of St Bernard* were succeeded by a third. The matters that the reader should know about him are supplied by Mabillon, the same authority cited above. Let his words be given:

701. “Geoffrey added three books to the preceding two: doubtless none other than Bernard’s own secretary. He must certainly be distinguished from Geoffrey of Petrona, mentioned in Book IV, no. 16; and likewise from Godfrey, Bernard’s kinsman and companion in conversion, later prior of Clairvaux and finally bishop of Langres, who eventually withdrew to the private life of the monks of Clairvaux and died there on 8 November 1164. Geoffrey, however, writes mournfully in the preface to the three following books that Bernard had been torn from him by a bitter death about thirteen years after Geoffrey’s own conversion. Hence Geoffrey’s conversion must be dated to the year 1140.

702. “A native of Auxerre, before his conversion he was a disciple of Peter Abelard and was indeed a cleric, as is clear from the *Book of Declamations*, of which he too was the author, no. 13: ‘Finally, we too were among the clergy.’ After Bernard’s conversion, he was, together with Nicholas, secretary of Clairvaux, Bernard’s companion in his journeys. Then, after Bernard’s death, he was first abbot of Igny, and afterwards abbot of Clairvaux after Fastred in 1162. He governed there for approximately four years, according to the Chronicle of Clairvaux in Chifflet; but subsequently, harassed by his own monks, he resigned the abbacy in 1165 and withdrew to Fossanova in Italy. There he too was afterwards abbot, and finally at Hautecombe, as is related more fully in the same Chronicle. Some of his works are listed there: namely, an important work on the *Song of Songs*, a *Life of St Peter, Archbishop of Tarentaise*, and several other books and sermons.

703. “Baronius has his letter to Henry, cardinal and bishop of Albano, and vicar or legate of the Lord Pope, written about a certain new controversy which Geoffrey discovered upon returning to France: namely, whether the substance of the water mixed with the wine and offered in the chalice is likewise, together with that wine, converted into the blood of the Lord. Also his is the booklet against the propositions of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers; after the books on Bernard’s *Life*, we shall include this booklet with his other shorter works. Finally, as we shall shortly say, he also wrote against Abelard, and published a sermon on St Bernard, to be printed below with a short commentary on the Lord’s Prayer. Whether he composed, in addition to the three books just mentioned, the *Life of Bernard* whose fragments we shall give in third place, and the second part of the sixth book on Bernard’s miracles, must now be considered.

704. “To the five books on Bernard’s *Life* we append two books on his miracles: one written by various authors; the other collected from the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order* and from fragments of Herbert, formerly a monk of Clairvaux and archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, who composed three books on the miracles of his Cistercian monks, published by Chifflet. The first book of miracles is divided into three parts. The first was written by Philip, monk of Clairvaux, to Samson, archbishop of Rheims; the second by other monks of Clairvaux, upon whom Philip himself imposed this task. Among them is Geoffrey, author also of the third part, in a letter to Herman, bishop of Constance, concerning the miracles which he had seen Bernard perform from Speyer to Liège. This is followed by another letter by Geoffrey, on the same subject, to his most dear master Archenfred and to both Chapters, his brothers of the same mother. I do not doubt that this Geoffrey is the same man who wrote the latter three books of the *Life*.

705. “For I do not agree with Charles de Visch, who assigns these books to Geoffrey the secretary, but that part of the book *On Miracles* to Geoffrey of Auxerre. That Geoffrey of Auxerre is by no means to be distinguished from Geoffrey the secretary is proved by the monk Helinand in his *Chronicle*, in these words:

> ‘Geoffrey of Auxerre, who for a long time had been secretary to St Bernard, had at one time been a disciple of this Peter [that is, Abelard]. Among other things he said of that same Peter: “I recall that he was once my master, who, by rendering void the price of our redemption, commended nothing else in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion than an example of virtue and an incentive to love, etc. Blessed be God, who gave both me and you a better master”—Bernard—“through whom he reproved the ignorance and confuted the arrogance of the former. According to him, Christ displayed for us three special things in his Passion: an example of virtue, an incentive to love, and the sacrifice of redemption.”’

This appears in Bernard, volume II, Short Work XI, no. 25. “This same Geoffrey,” Helinand adds, “wrote strongly and in a Catholic manner these and many other things against Peter, his master.” Nicholas of Clairvaux wrote Letter 42 to Geoffrey on behalf of the bishop of Alet.”

These remarks on Geoffrey and the other writers of the earlier *Life* and of the miracles may suffice. The other writers must be discussed after the miracles themselves; but shortly we shall weave them into this our preliminary Commentary.

706. The Cistercian historian may also be consulted concerning the three biographers just praised, under the year of Christ 1153, chapter 11, no. 4. Among other things which he records concerning them, he commends their reliability and fixes the date of their writing as follows:

> “Bernard, therefore, had these three writers of his works, men distinguished for religious devotion and learning; all were no less eyewitnesses, so that they could neither have been mistaken nor be believed to have wished to deceive. William, as I have said, wrote while the saint was alive; Abbot Arnold immediately after his death; Godfrey two years later. For when speaking of the blessed bread carried by Eskil to Denmark, he says that it was then in its third year and was nevertheless preserved uncorrupted: the third year, I say, from Eskil’s arrival at Clairvaux during the saint’s lifetime. We have recorded, on the authority of the *Great Exordium*, that this occurred in the year of Christ 1152, at least one year before the death of Father Bernard.”

707. “Accordingly Trithemius requires incidental correction in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he not only makes Arnold a Cistercian—thus, as though by entering one of our men among his own, he compensated for the countless writers whom he takes away—but also states that he flourished about 1160. He is no less wrong in this than in the other point. For Godfrey by no means undertook the work while Arnold was alive, who without doubt would have completed the subject in a manner worthy of it. Therefore, since Godfrey undertook it, as is plainly evident, about the year of the Lord 1155, this clearly proves that Arnold had died earlier; and consequently that Godfrey continued what Arnold, who had begun it, was utterly unable to complete.”

## § LXIV. Other biographers after the first three; later writers; the Lives in Surius, Horst, and Mabillon; why Mabillon’s text is preferred by us for printing over the others

708. A little earlier I deferred to this place the remaining writers of Bernard’s *Life*, who after those listed in §63 transmitted to posterity the deeds and miracles of the holy Doctor. Mabillon did not omit the labour of recording various matters helpful for understanding this subject. Here, reader, is what I read in him, volume II, p. 1233: “The first,” he says, “is Alanus” . . . See the remainder above. These are the observations made by Mabillon, mentioned above, about these biographers published by him.

709–713. Moreover, I am persuaded that the reader will not dislike further information about later biographers. Their catalogue was compiled and sent here by the Reverend Lord Godfrey Bouvart, whom I praised above in §58, no. 623. He there mentions Philotheus, Gilbert of Hoyland, Caesar Baronius, Laurentius Surius, and Zacharias Lippeolus; but it will suffice to transcribe here the following from the same catalogue. They are as follows and are listed in this order:

Francis Caesar, monk of Dunes, 1483. Bernard de Rosergio, archbishop of Toulouse, 1474. William Flameng, canon of Langres, 1528. The Congregation of Regular Observance at Rome, 1587. John Alvarez of Aragon, 1595, in Spanish. Christopher Gonzales, 1601, in Spanish and Latin. Chichere Bailly of Cîteaux, 1601, in French. Philip Malabayla, 1634, in Italian. Anthony Le Maître, under the name Lamy, in French, 1644, 1655, 1663, 1674, 1684, etc. Theophilus Raynaud, S.J., 1657, 1665. Anonymous, in French, Dijon, 1653. Nicholas Hacqueville, Paris, 1667. 714. Lucas Bartolottus, abbot, in verse, 1682. Joseph Almonazid, in Spanish, 1682. Francis Giry, in French. Peter Ribadeneira, in Spanish. Father Viel, in French, 1603. Peter Lenain, in French, 1697.
