Francis Joseph Bourgoin, in French, 1704. Gaspar Verstockz, in Flemish, 1650. The religious of Baudeloo, in Latin and Flemish, 1613.

Indeed, a *Life of St Bernard* was even written in Chinese, possessed by the lord abbot of Sambernardin on the Scheldt, as the praised Bouvart adds to the preceding catalogue. To the biographers already named may be added two other modern French writers: Adrian Baillet, in the *Lives of the Saints*, printed at Paris in 1704; and Villefore, who published the saint’s *Life* there in the same year.

715. But since the *Life* in Surius, mentioned above, is everywhere in common use, I judge it important for the reader not to be ignorant of Horst’s remarks on that *Life* in the address to the reader prefixed to the *Lives* which he published. There he observes:

> “Having compared this *Life* with that which until now has customarily been published together with the works of St Bernard, I found it to differ considerably in wording and in substance. At first I wondered—since I had not yet obtained a manuscript of the *Life*—why or how this had happened. I suspected whether perhaps Surius had here also employed something of that customary and familiar freedom which he had used in most other Lives of the Saints. But the style of these authors, which requires no polishing, scarcely admitted the suspicion: it is in itself, and in accordance with its purpose, sufficiently polished and elegant. I say nothing of the fact that the style familiar to those saintly and learned men, especially in that age, possesses something distinctive and moving, and a certain hidden energy for stirring the reader’s affections, which our writers do not attain so readily.

716. “Let others, therefore, mark out Surius’s diligence as ill-timed; I believed him here to be free from fault. For I observed differences not only of words, though less frequently, but also of substance between the two editions—and of such a kind as easily to free Surius’s edition from the charge of some recent alteration, since it was fuller and richer than the published text and undoubtedly seemed to rest upon the authority of some manuscript exemplar. Yet while I wavered in this uncertainty, there was at last offered to me what I had anxiously sought: an ancient manuscript copy of the *Life of the Holy Father*, from the library of the famous Cistercian monastery of Kamp. Upon examining it, I immediately absolved Surius of every suspicion, for it corresponded to the Surian edition, though in many respects it was far more correct and fuller; indeed, it also had a book of miracles attached. From this, therefore, kind reader, we present to you the *Life of St Bernard*. What you see enclosed in these marks, ( ), you should understand to be lacking in the editions hitherto published and now newly inserted from the manuscript.”

Such are, among other things, the remarks which Horst makes to the reader about his edition. Although this learned and diligent man devoted to perfecting it a labour altogether exceptional and useful, we nevertheless judged that Mabillon’s edition rather than his should be reprinted by us.

717. First, Mabillon’s edition moved us because he gave Horst’s work further attention, having that editor before his eyes. Secondly, because he enlarged it, as will become clear in the course of the *Life* which he published and as he himself indicates in the notice before its first book, saying: “At the end we note that those things which you find enclosed in brackets in what follows were added either by Horst from the Kamp manuscript or by us.” Thirdly, because Mabillon’s exemplar, which we shall print, is more corrected than Horst’s, as we were able to perceive when we compared the latter with the former. Fourthly, because it is illustrated with new and learned notes, to say nothing of its various readings. We use the edition in our possession, which was published at Paris in 1690. The reader should meanwhile know that not all the *Lives* found in the said editor will be committed to print by us, for reasons shortly to be given.

718. We shall also make a new division of the chapters, and the chapters themselves will be divided into new numbered sections. Yet we shall give the old division of the five books after the preface to the first book; it will thereafter also be marked in the margin of our edition. Likewise the titles of the miracles, or sixth book of the *Life*, will be given after its preface. Besides the notes by which we shall endeavour to elucidate this book, account will also be taken of the observations sent here from Tournai in September 1672 by the Reverend Father Joseph Ignatius of St Anthony, a Discalced Carmelite. We shall also present a synopsis of the miracles in the *Posthumous Glory of St Bernard*, providing for the convenience of those who either lack leisure to read the longer and numerous accounts of those miracles, or prefer certain selected narratives suited to a sermon, which they may appropriately offer to their hearers according to the subject of their discourse and thus have more readily at hand.

## § LXV. The equipment and fidelity with which the most illustrious Manrique wrote his *Annals*, and consequently the deeds of St Bernard woven into them; concerning the author of the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*

719. In the *Library of Writers of the Sacred Cistercian Order*, the Reverend Lord Charles de Visch praises Angelus Manrique as born of a most noble family, possessing a keen, ready, and universally capable intellect, and as having advanced so remarkably in philosophical and theological studies that he was an object of admiration to his professors. The same bibliographer adds that Manrique was endowed with great abundance and elegance of speech for preaching and for inclining his hearers to whatever emotion he wished, and that he exercised this office amid the greatest crowds and applause, being invited to it from every quarter. He was also a man of the highest counsel in the gravest affairs; and, appointed to the chair of theology in the University of Salamanca, he adorned this office magnificently for many years, with the highest renown of his name. The cited bibliographer likewise lists his various works. He was advanced to the episcopal see of Pax Julia or Augusta—commonly Badajoz—by Philip IV, king of Spain, in the year of Christ 1644, though Nicholas Antonius, to be cited shortly, gives the immediately following year; see the work there mentioned. Eminent encomia with which other learned men honoured Manrique are found before the first volume of the *Annals of the Cistercian Order*. Nicholas also discusses the praised author in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, where he writes that Manrique died in the city of Badajoz in 1649. Such was the man whom the *Annals of the Cistercian Order* obtained as their author.

720. Moreover, that Manrique was equipped with an excellent store of documents before composing the same *Annals* is abundantly clear from the preface to volume I of that work, where he says in no. 4:

> “Four libraries were available to us, with which Salamanca is richly furnished: the domestic library of the Cistercian college, inferior to none; that of Luis Bernardo de Quiros, formerly chief professor of Holy Scripture, collected through his industry. No less accessible to us through the kindness of their owners were three external libraries: one from the royal college of the Society of Jesus; two from those commonly called the Major Colleges, namely Saint Bartholomew’s and Oviedo’s. This last—once the glorious care of that great man Diego Covarrubias—was almost more used than all the rest. The remainder was supplied by manuscripts sought everywhere from France, Italy, the Low Countries, and Germany; by the very autographs left by Ignatius Firminus, a Spaniard and abbot of Fitero; and by the Vatican, which for three years stood open to Leander Vadillo, a man of distinguished learning, sent to Rome for this purpose as soon as we began to contemplate these *Annals*.”

721. Since truth is the first essential quality of a genuine historian, Manrique left testimony in the same cited place, no. 8, in most serious words—and indeed confirmed it by an oath—that he had kept this alone before his eyes:

> “We do not doubt that we have omitted much: who could gather everything? Much has been narrated otherwise than it occurred: who, amid such a varied multitude of events, does not sometimes see dimly or fall asleep? This we affirm upon oath: nothing has knowingly been altered by us; nothing intentionally added or removed which we thought relevant to history. Nor have we attributed anything to our own Order which we consider another’s, being more desirous of true glory than false. We are not those who seek praise at another’s loss: Cîteaux has no need of stolen goods.”

Thus the most illustrious Manrique frankly professed that, if he did not always and everywhere attain the truth, he nevertheless always and everywhere followed it in his work. This is why we have mentioned these matters.

722. And indeed, as he testifies that he was most tenacious of truth, so he writes no less plainly that he was most desirous of correction wherever he had departed from it. He concludes his preface in the place just cited with these words:

> “Would that there were those who corrected, who deleted! Would that there were also those who added and showed how little we have done, by bringing to light more of what we have not done. Father Bernard sent a book together with a knife to Cardinal Matthew, the legate, so that he might cut away, with the author’s own blade, whatever imposture he judged worthy of excision. We should wish to send our *Annals* to all learned persons with knife and pen: with the knife, to cut away what has entered through error; and with the pen, no less, to add what is missing through ignorance. May God, I wish, inspire many to do this!”

723. Now, since we have very frequently used above the book entitled the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, which, divided into distinctions and chapters, is found in F. Bertrand Tissier, doctor of theology and prior of Bonfont in Therasia of the same Order, in the *Library of Cistercian Fathers*, p. 13 and following, the nature of our undertaking seems to require that we acquaint the reader with this work, using the matters which Tissier prefixed to it. Regarding the title, he gives this warning:

> “In the manuscript codex of the monastery of Foigny which I use, this title is found: ‘Here begins the narrative of the beginning of the Cistercian Order: how our Fathers, leaving the monastery of Molesme in order to recover the purity of the Order according to the rule of Saint Benedict, founded the fruitful church of Cîteaux, which is the mother of us all; since from it, as from a most pure spring, the streams of all the churches of our Order have flowed forth; and concerning certain venerable persons, conspicuous in every form of religious life, who flourished at Cîteaux and Clairvaux.’ But since this book is commonly called the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, just as the preceding work—there, from p. 1—is called, by contrast, the *Little Exordium*, I have preferred the aforesaid title.”

724. Concerning the author he continues:

> “Angelus Manrique says in the *Annals* that the author of this *Great Exordium* is unknown. But the Foigny codex has these words: ‘This book was composed by a certain abbot named Conrad, of the monastery of Eberbach, who had been a monk of Clairvaux.’ He plainly indicates at the end of this work that he professed the monastic life at Clairvaux, where he asserts that, in the time of Blessed Peter and Lord Garnier, afterwards bishop of Langres—the former the eighth and the latter the ninth abbot of Clairvaux—he was educated in the cloister’s discipline at Clairvaux, namely about the year 1180. Eberbach, over which this Conrad is said to have presided, is a monastery in the line of Clairvaux in the diocese of Mainz. The author himself mentions it with the highest praise in distinction 5, chapter 17, and elsewhere, though there he does not state that he is abbot of that house. But whoever the author of the book may be, I judged it most worthy of reading and very useful, and thus deserving of a place at the head of the *Library of Our Fathers*.”

725. Horst also praises this work in his *Introduction to the Works of St Bernard*, p. 70, prefacing the seventh book of the *Life of St Bernard*, which he printed from the praised *Exordium*, with the following words:

> “We have excerpted this book word for word from the book *On Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order*, which we received in manuscript at Koblenz from the college of the Society of Jesus. The Carthusian Fathers of Cologne procured for us another copy of the same work from the Charterhouse at Wesel. A third was supplied by Father N. of the Society of Jesus, copied in his own hand at Emmerich; he had also added notes of variant readings, and his diligence was of great assistance to us. The reader should be warned concerning that book, lest he be misled when he finds here and there these titles: *Exordium of the Cistercian Order*; *Book on Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order*; likewise *Book on the Beginning of the Cistercian Order*. Henriquez frequently cites them as though they were different books, whereas they are one and the same—although perhaps elsewhere it bore a different title. This one may readily discover, when one finds in the single book *On Illustrious Cistercian Men*—for this title alone appears in the three manuscripts I saw—what Henriquez brings forward as though from different books. I wished to warn you of this in order to avoid the confusion occasioned by the said author, all the more because he divides the *Exordium* into books but the work *On Illustrious Men* into distinctions. Nevertheless, let us hear that same writer’s judgment about this book.

726. “‘That book which we call the *Exordium of the Cistercian Order* is, as it were, the foundation stone of all the histories of our Order and a writing of the highest authority.’ And a little later: ‘For my part, whenever I turn over this book, I cannot sufficiently admire its piety, the gravity of its style, the weight of its judgments, and the remarkable events related there. I dare say that in its kind it is among the greater and more precious treasures enjoyed by the Church, and ought to be regarded as such by the faithful.’ Thus Henriquez, *Apparatus to the Cistercian Menologium*, chapter 4. I willingly agree with him: it is, indeed, a book worthy to be published entire.

727. “I see that Aubertus Miraeus, who has deserved well of monastic history, wished this as well. I wonder that no one from the Cistercian family has undertaken the task. I myself would put my hand to it, if I did not fear putting my sickle into another’s harvest. Moreover, the author of this book was close to the times of St Bernard, for he associated familiarly with men who had lived together with Bernard, and relates here almost from their mouths what is narrated. Thus you may see upon what faith and authority these accounts rest.”

So he writes. The wish of these learned men was fulfilled when Tissier published the work. Examples demonstrating its merit are supplied by our preliminary Commentary. Mabillon too, after Horst, published the seventh book of the *Life of St Bernard*, excerpted from the same *Exordium*, in volume II, cols. 1195 and following; this indicates that he too held that work in high esteem. That it was enlarged by additions is clear from Manrique, who cites them, as may be seen in our preliminary Commentary, §50 at the end; §51, no. 547; and §52, no. 555. Finally, whether the author of the *Exordium* himself collected or wrote the events which occurred during his lifetime, or whether other matter was later added, we have repeatedly cited both the *Exordium* itself and its author in the preliminary Commentary.

## § LXVI. Which Lives are not reprinted by us, and why; certain other works passed over

728. We shall reprint and annotate the six books on the *Life and Deeds of St Bernard* which have long been printed by Horst and Mabillon, as indicated above. To these *Lives* we shall add, with Mabillon, the *Fragments* from Herbert’s books on the miracles of Cistercian monks, though not all of them. We shall not, however, add the seventh book on the *Life* of the same saint, which is excerpted from the book entitled the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, second distinction, as is indicated in Mabillon’s edition; for Horst’s edition, consult what I have stated above, §65, no. 725. The reason for excluding these books from our edition is that we have drawn from them and woven into this Commentary various deeds of the holy Father related there. If any notable matters remain, account may also be taken of them in the *Posthumous Glory*.

Nor shall the *Life* composed by Alanus, formerly bishop of Auxerre, which is found in Mabillon, be published anew.

729. For that biographer “wove together from the five preceding books a continuous series of Bernard’s deeds, using the authors’ own words and arranging them, as best he could, in chronological order,” as Mabillon observed in §64, cited by me. Moreover, he was the first to mention the holy Doctor’s testament, omitted by other writers, as was there stated. But since, following Manrique, we have provided for chronological order in our preliminary Commentary and have given there a Bernardine chronology; and since we shall publish the earlier biographers from whom Alanus compiled and abridged his *Life*, what need is there to commit it to print again and unnecessarily increase the already vast bulk of material concerning St Bernard?

730. But let Alanus himself be heard in the prologue to the same *Life*:

> “We, omitting some things and adding very few, give in a briefer account material from the narratives of several authors who had already written the Acts and miracles of the holy man.”

What Mabillon just said about the testament, which . . . he was the first to mention, seems to concern the three counsels which the holy Father left to his sons for imitation when he was near death; Alanus treats these in chapter 30, and we gave them above from him in §50. After this *Life*, Mabillon appends *Fragments from the Third Life of St Bernard*, apparently by Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, in eight chapters. Consult §64. These fragments have more than once been useful to us in the preliminary Commentary and perhaps will be useful later, if anything remains worthy of notice. Next there is given the Fourth *Life*, written in two books by John the Hermit. Matters concerning this biographer are found in the section just indicated, §64. Since his *Life* has already been reprinted twice, we have judged that we should refrain from reprinting it, being persuaded that the original biographers will sufficiently serve the readers’ benefit, the saint’s glory, and finally our own purpose. If, however, it contains some distinctive matters which it is important for the reader to know, account may also be taken of them.

731. The editor of the *Lives of St Bernard* whom I have just named, at col. 1292, presents material omitted by Chifflet from Geoffrey, “above,” he says, “at col. 1278, after article 10,” and later discovered. This is followed by the panegyric poem of the monk Philotheus on the *Life and Morals* of the same saint; Charles de Visch places him among the writers of the Cistercian Order in his *Library*. The poem also appears in Horst’s edition. Add two others in praise of the holy Father: one whose author is named as Nicholas Hacqueville, most upright president of the Paris Parlement; the other by Baptista Mantuanus, from Book VIII of the *Fasti*. Yet we readily allow these poetic rivulets to be absent from our edition, where we abound in the genuine springs of the most ancient biographers.

At this point it is not unwelcome to recall what is found in Mabillon, col. 1306:

> “In the manuscript codex of Anchin is read a poem bearing this title: ‘Anselm to Bernard, venerable abbot of Clairvaux, in praise of Clairvaux,’ beginning as follows:
>
> ‘A sloping valley, which a sloping mountain shades.’”

After this brief observation, a description is there given of the position or site of the monastery of Clairvaux. It also appears in Horst and was cited by me above, §5, no. 56.

732. These are the matters concerning which I wished to forewarn my reader. If, however, in the *Lives* excluded from this edition, beyond those materials already inserted in advance from them into this preliminary Commentary, there should appear other documents which I find very conducive either to the saint’s glory or to the reader’s instruction, I shall give them a place after the *Lives*, in the *Posthumous Glory of St Bernard*. In that work will be collected many and notable things concerning the man, which it has seemed fitting to defer until then. At length, therefore, having measured, so to speak, a long voyage across the sea, I furl my sails and introduce the *Acts*. I have already informed the reader above, at the end of §64, what principles have been observed by us in printing them.

*(There follow various studies concerning the Life of St Bernard, which appear above.)*

[Col. 0943]

# POSTHUMOUS GLORY AND SUPPLEMENT TO THE LIFE AND MIRACLES OF ST BERNARD, AND ALSO TO OUR PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

## CHAPTER ONE. Public veneration; the spread of monasteries; most recent information concerning the saint’s tomb and relics. His shadow, and other sacred relics.

[Col. 0943C] 1. What was said in the Preliminary Commentary, § 62, concerning the Office of St Bernard and the public veneration paid to him may be supplemented by the following. Among the selected statutes of the general chapters of the Cistercian Order, preserved from various manuscript codices by Martène in volume IV of the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, I read the following under the year 1321, col. 1506, no. 3:

> Likewise, since by the obligation of monastic profession we are bound to reciprocal gratitude in charity, the general chapter has beneficially decreed in the following manner, etc., that a service be held for St Hugh, the first abbot of Cluny, because in the said house and throughout his whole order a solemn service is celebrated for our father St Bernard.

From this it is clear that the Office of St Bernard was then celebrated with a solemn rite among all Cluniacs. Public veneration is also indicated by the fact that the holy man’s patronage was invoked against contagious disease. For, after the Life and Miracles of St Adrian, a special patron against pestilential infection—published in French at Luxembourg in 1636 by Fr William Hardigny of the Society of Jesus, together with several other short treatises—St Bernard is numbered, on p. 260, among the other saints favourable against this disease. The author adds that in 1625 the saint’s aid against it was invoked at Lier, near Antwerp, in his chapel. Perhaps, indeed, this was in the sacred building of the Cistercian nuns of Blessed Mary of Nazareth outside the walls of Lier, where, as I hear, there is every year a large and beneficial concourse to the saint on 30 August and throughout the octave.

2. Above, in the third part of the Miracles, chapter 7, no. 343, are related the deeds performed at Ruitz. The place is commended by the grateful remembrance of the people of Ruitz, who have honoured their great Deliverer with a distinctive cult. Raissius testifies to this in the supplement to Jean Molanus’s *Natalia Sanctorum Belgii*, for 20 August, fol. 170, where he writes:

> He also made this place illustrious—the village of Ruitz, namely—by miracles, when he restored three lame women and two blind persons to health. In perpetual memory of this event, an image was erected to St Bernard in the church itself; I have seen it. Annual processions are made to it on the Friday after Pentecost, when, according to ancient tradition, the devout people believe that these miracles occurred there. Peter Haymam, prior of the said monastery, communicated these matters to me while I was there.

3. John Cognatus, commonly called Cousin, in book III, chapter 50 of his *History of Tournai*, affirms that the people of Tournai are greatly indebted to St Bernard and may rightly regard him as patron and protector of the bishopric of Tournai. By his intervention and influence with Pope Eugene, they obtained a bishop of their own, whereas previously they had been subject to the bishop of Noyon. For this reason, he says, the man’s likeness was painted in a glass window on the north side, around the choir of the cathedral church, above a painted representation of the restoration of the bishopric. This favour—the granting to the people of Tournai of a new and proper bishop, through Bernard’s support—occurred, as Alberic testifies in his Chronicle under the year 1148:

> At the city of Tournai, which for nearly four hundred years had been under the bishops of Noyon, at last, through the intervention of St Bernard, Pope Eugene installed a new bishop, and the church recovered its ancient privilege. The first bishop was called Anselm, the second Gerard, the third Walter.

Yet the favour which Alberic, cited above, relates under the year 1148 occurred in 1146, as is evident from the bull itself of Pope Eugene III. It is printed in volume II of the new edition of Miraeus’s *Diplomata*, p. 1167. The lord of Castillon, in his *Sacred Chronology of Belgium*, p. 405, declares that he possesses an authentic copy of this bull, dated 1146 according to the reckoning of the most distinguished and learned censor of this volume.

Nor shall I leave unmentioned the religious cult of St Bernard instituted among the monks of Anchin, in French Belgium near Douai, when his relics were brought there by the abbot of that monastery. Ferreolus Locrius, in his *Belgian Chronicle* under the year 1179, recounts the following from the Chronicle of Anchin:

> In 1179 Simon, ninth superior of the monastery of Anchin, while returning from the Roman council, turned aside to Clairvaux and obtained, by entreaty, relics of Blessed Bernard from the abbot of that monastery. Having brought them to Anchin, he honoured them with great solemnity.

The matter is likewise related in *Gallia Christiana*, volume III of the latest edition, col. 412, under Simon I, the ninth abbot of Anchin. Add, from Manriquez, that Paul, abbot of Palaciola in Old Castile in Spain, devised a special observance in honour of the saint when he prescribed that, in the confession customarily said at the beginning of Mass, St Bernard the Father should be invoked immediately after the Blessed Virgin: “I confess to God, to Blessed Mary, and to Blessed Bernard.” We have drawn this from the appendix to volume IV of the *Cistercian Annals*, p. 629, by the said Cistercian historian, among other matters inserted under the year 1550.

[Col. 0946B] 4. The glory of our saint especially shone among posterity through the remarkable expansion of his offspring of Clairvaux. William writes on this subject in book I of the Life, chapter 7, above. Although I had resolved not to treat this topic separately in my notes on that passage, it seemed appropriate here to add what follows in order to illustrate the biographer’s statement.

In Geoffrey, book V of the Life, chapter 2, no. 262, the first abbot of Clairvaux is called the father also of more than one hundred and sixty other monasteries. This must be understood to mean that the holy Father raised up a large part of so many founded monasteries not immediately in person, but through his offspring. Yet what his sons did themselves may deservedly be said to have been done by Father Bernard in his sons; and thus that happy and fruitful expansion pertains to the saint’s posthumous glory. Mabillon observes at the passage of Geoffrey just cited that the holy abbot founded these monasteries both in person and through abbeys subject to Clairvaux. For Bernard himself, he says, established or adopted about seventy-two monasteries: thirty-five in France, eleven in Spain, six in Belgium, five in England, and as many in Savoy and Ireland; four in Italy, two in Germany, likewise two in Sweden, and finally one each in Hungary and Denmark, according to our Chronology. The reader will also find that Chronology in § 59 of our Preliminary Commentary.

Therefore Pope Innocent III, in the apostolic letter to the Gallican Church inserted in § 60 of our Preliminary Commentary, deservedly admires this singular distinction among the holy man’s other qualities, praising him because he transmitted the institutions of holy religion even to foreign and barbarian peoples and extended the foundation of monasteries.

5. Another vicar of Christ on earth, Gregory IX, added a notable honour to the perpetual memory of the holy man in the same connection. In the bull by which he enrolled St Dominic, founder of the Order of Friars Preachers, among the saints, he says this of St Bernard:

> After these—that is, the first preachers of the New Law and the sons of St Benedict, of whom he had spoken—the Lord Christ, as though renewing a weary army and restoring rejoicing after lamentation, yoked white horses to the third chariot: the brethren of the Cistercian and Florensian Orders. Like flocks that have been shorn, abundant in the offspring of twofold charity, he made them rise from the washing of repentance, with St Bernard, the ram of the sheep, going before in the strength of the Spirit with which he was clothed from on high, and in the abundance of grain in the valleys; so that, liberated through him, those who pass onward may cry to the Lord in strength, sing a hymn, and set the camp of God’s armies above the sea.

There remain some matters to be noted concerning the present state of St Bernard’s body and tomb.

6. On this subject I add the following, along with some other matters pertaining nearly to the same theme. All these will supplement what was said in § 50 of our Preliminary Commentary concerning the saint’s body and his testament or last will; in § 51 concerning the tomb; and in § 53 concerning the cell, and so forth. After those matters had there been set forth, new information was subsequently sent to us. We owe its grateful record to the Reverend and Most Distinguished Dom Candidus Briger, Cistercian, most worthy prior and doctor of sacred theology at the Valley of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Field of Lilies, commonly Lilienfeld, in Lower Austria and the diocese of Passau.

When I had explained to this man, as he was departing for the general chapter that opened at Cîteaux in early May of this year 1738 and honoured our museum by his presence while passing through, my desire to learn more about the present state of St Bernard’s body, he undertook to make it his concern. Nor did he do less than he had promised, as appears from his most courteous letter sent here from Cîteaux in Burgundy, on 8 May 1738, while the general chapter was actually in session. From it I extract the following information which Briger was able to discover for our purpose at the monastery of Clairvaux.

7. “The body … rests buried beneath the ground. The head, stripped of skin and flesh—what we commonly call the skull—is enclosed in a silver shrine and kept in the place where the church treasury is stored. There too stands a silver tomb, but it contains absolutely nothing except the holy man’s cowl. His tomb, behind the high altar in the church of Clairvaux, rises about eight feet above the ground and is faced with small marble columns; a statue of the holy man stands upon it. At the foot of the tomb an altar is erected, upon which the sacrifices of Mass are offered to God. The front and sides of the sepulchre have the form shown by the enclosed slip of paper, though roughly drawn with a brush. Nevertheless, the lord abbot of Clairvaux, whom I met here today concerning this matter, promised that he would send a more accurate one.”

The outcome fulfilled the promise. For, in the name of his Most Reverend Lord, the abbot of Clairvaux, the Reverend Dom John Anthony Macuson, apostolic protonotary and master of novices of the same abbey, sent here from Clairvaux on 29 July 1738 a better drawing of St Bernard’s mausoleum. The drawing which I received has been reduced here by our engraver from a larger format to a smaller; he has endeavoured accurately to reproduce the face of the tomb according to the model placed before him, as you see in this impression.

[Col. 0948A]

[Col. 0948B] The reader will learn what the sides of the mausoleum are from the second diagram. Above both, as it was sent here, rises the saint; but a handwritten note states that in the first, not in the second, his true clothing is represented. Here it is:

[Col. 0948D]

[Col. 0949A] 8. The praised Briger continues to describe the remaining relevant matters in these words:

> On the front of the tomb are seen two tablets fastened with iron chains. The first has this inscription:
>
> HERE RESTS SAINT BERNARD, FIRST ABBOT OF THE SACRED MONASTERY OF CLAIRVAUX.
>
> On the other tablet are read the following words:
>
> TESTAMENT OF THE MOST BLESSED BERNARD, ABBOT: I LEAVE YOU THREE THINGS TO OBSERVE, etc.

See our Preliminary Commentary, § 50, no. 543, where these words are not added: “Behold, I leave you charity, humility, and patience.” After this, Briger’s aforementioned letter gives the testament of the holy Father in metrical form; and, having spoken of these tablets, he adds: “Moreover, the house—or rather cell—almost entirely wooden, and the bed on which he yielded up his spirit, still survive at Clairvaux today.”

9. If anyone desires more information concerning the monastery of Clairvaux itself, let him consult the French *Hodoeporicon*, or Literary Itinerary, of two religious of the Order of St Benedict from the Congregation of St Maur, written by Edmund Martène, part I. There, at p. 99, he will read that in the cemetery discussed there may be seen the graves of St Bernard’s brethren, as well as the saint’s cell, which William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, ordered built for him to afford comfort while he suffered bodily infirmities. See our Preliminary Commentary, § 7, no. 78, and book I of the Life, chapter 4, no. 37.

The said *Itinerary*, p. 100, further relates that there was no fireplace in this cell, for St Bernard was so mortified that he would not permit a fire to be made for himself. Yet beneath the holy man’s bed was a large stone, pierced in several places, under which a small fire was kindled to warm the room without his noticing it. Moreover, nothing could appear plainer than this room and St Bernard’s bed, which is still preserved there today. A small chapel adjoins this cell; it was probably built so that he might celebrate at an altar. It is affirmed that he died there, and an inscription may be read there which states this quite clearly. The matters I have drawn from this *Itinerary* shed somewhat more light on what was set forth shortly above and in § 53, no. 564, of the Preliminary Commentary.

[Col. 0949D] 10. Besides the matters already mentioned from Martène, he also makes mention of St Bernard’s chalice, p. 99, and of his chasuble, p. 104. There he also treats of a large silver chest which some bishop of Saintes caused to be made for the placing within it of St Bernard’s relics. But he adds that the religious, fearing that, if his bones were removed from the tomb, very many princes—who could scarcely be refused—would ask for some of them, preferred that they should remain there.

It is also said that at Clairvaux the saint’s shadow may be seen upon the stone on which his body was washed after death. Martène declares, however, that he does not know whether the matter is as miraculous as it is believed to be. For, he says, the shadow cannot be seen from every direction; one must stand in a particular position to perceive it. He judges that this could occur naturally through the reflection of light. Such is his account. Whatever the case, this reflection of light is certainly remarkable; but whether it occurs through a miracle in the strict sense, I leave undecided.

Meanwhile, let us hear Chrysostom Henriquez on this subject in book I, distinction 4, chapter 51 of his *Fascicle of the Cistercian Order*:

> In the sacred monastery of Clairvaux there exists a wondrous and continuous miracle, which has greatly commended the virtue of the holy abbot. On the stone where his body was washed according to the custom of the Order, the shadow of that body remains to this present day and is clearly and visibly seen by everyone. When heretics attempted to erase the memory of so great a miracle and hollowed out the stone itself with various instruments, the shadow descended and could in no way be erased, as I learned from the Reverend Dom Adrian Cancellier, abbot of Dunes.

11. In another *Itinerary*, published at Paris in 1724, the aforementioned Martène writes of the celebrated Cistercian abbey of Cambron in the territory of Mons in Hainaut, p. 198, that the chasuble of St Bernard shown there inspires devotion. It is not of cloth of gold, silver cloth, or silk, but woven from plain cotton. It is used on the saint’s feast day and at the first Masses of religious.

The same author, p. 40, among other matters which he reports concerning Valleclara—listed above in our Bernardine Chronology, part I, under the year 1134—mentions St Bernard’s mantle, which in French he calls *la coule*, and says that it is preserved there. It is worth observing here that among Bernardines there are two kinds of mantle: one white, a very ample garment which Bernardine ascetics use in ceremonies and when attending the Office; the other black, likewise a very ample garment, used by Bernardines only in towns and when walking through streets. This is from the French-Latin Dictionary published at Trévoux in 1704, under the word *coule*.

12. In the same Martène’s very extensive *Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, etc., volume VI, there is produced the foundation charter of the Cistercian monastery of Blessed Mary of Altaripa, daughter of Charilocus in the line of Clairvaux. At col. 317, among the chief sacred relics of that monastery, is listed:

> The stole of our most holy Father Bernard, made from a coarser cloth of dark grey colour, with which this holy Father adorned our sacristy when, travelling to and returning from Germany, he passed through this monastery.

In a booklet concerning the relics kept at Aachen, printed there in 1734, among the ornaments of the church of the Virgin Mother, p. 46, is listed a chasuble made in the Greek manner, woven of smooth, dense blue silk, with a cross embroidered on it in pearls. The same booklet states that the mellifluous doctor Bernard used this chasuble in that church for the sacrifice of the Mass in 1146, and that afterward he restored sight to four blind persons and the power of walking to one paralytic.

## CHAPTER II. Various appearances and predictions of St Bernard

[Col. 0951]

### § I. He appears to a Cistercian monk and to a lay brother; having comforted the latter, he foretells him a successful outcome in his affairs.

[Col. 0951A]

13. In § 52 of the Preliminary Commentary, I related various appearances after the holy man’s death, and said that I would deal with others in his posthumous glory. Let first place here, therefore, be given to the one found in Tissier’s *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 3, chapter 14:

> It happened one day, when Prime was being sung in choir and he—that is, William, whom I shall shortly describe more fully—was standing in his place among those chanting the psalms, rendering to the Lord the calves of his lips with a voice of exultation. And behold, St Malachy appeared to him while he was awake and singing psalms, Malachy formerly bishop of Ireland, who lies honourably buried in the same church. He sat in a chair beside the altar, wonderfully adorned with ring, staff, mitre, and the other pontifical ornaments, as though he were about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass after the end of that Hour. It was then the anniversary day of the death of that most blessed bishop, which is also the solemn commemoration of all the faithful departed. Blessed Bernard also appeared with him, the most happy shepherd and patron of the same church. He too shone in precious white garments and wore a mitre, but not an infula. [Note: Are *mitratus* (“mitred”) and *infulatus* (“wearing an infula”) not commonly synonymous? How then are they distinguished here? I suspect the writer intended to indicate that St Malachy appeared wearing a mitre from which ribbons hung down on either side, whereas Bernard wore a mitre without these ribbons. For some have thought that the word *infulae* derives from *inferus* or *infra*, “below,” because of the ribbons which hang down from it below, as is indicated in Vossius’s *Etymological Dictionary of the Latin Language*.] And rightly so.

14. For Bernard was the master of the household in his own home, honouring and rejoicing over his venerable and special guest. Out of fitting honour for his most beloved guest, he most willingly yielded to him the solemnities of Mass, especially on that day when the holy bishop had entered the heavenly court and had first been honoured with heavenly hymns. Thus the blessed Father himself showed himself dutiful and assiduous toward the same holy bishop and in the service of his altar.

The blessed prelate, leaning upon his pastoral staff, kept his eyes steadily fixed upon the choir. St Bernard, however, looked now at the bishop, now at the community, now at the altar itself, as one solicitous for them all. This vision appeared visibly, plainly, to that servant of God while he was awake and looking with his bodily eyes, for as long as one psalm was sung by the community during that Hour. When the psalm ended, the vision ended; but thereafter the devout impression of that vision could not end in the beholder’s heart.

Thus far the *Great Exordium* on one appearance of the holy Father. Another follows there immediately; it is written in the following words and was shown to the same William.

15. On another day the same Blessed Bernard likewise appeared to him, glorious in face and bearing. When he saw him, William fell at his feet, praying and asking something of him. The saint said to him: “What do you wish me to do for you?” And he replied: “My lord and father, if I have found favour in your eyes, tell me whether I am to be saved.” The saint said to him:

> Is this a small matter that you ask? Today, as I departed from paradise, how many thousands of people I left outside the gate, who are tormented by just such fear, not knowing whether they are held worthy of love or of hatred.

Having said this, he gave him an answer concerning the matter for which he had asked. But what definite answer he gave is unknown to us, because the man, avoiding the plague of vain glory, refused to disclose it. For he was a prudent man, restrained in speech, and very careful not to say anything that might savour of his own glory. Yet the confidence of his speech and the cheerfulness of his face gave sufficient indication that he had received from the holy Father a pleasing answer concerning such a matter.

16. This is the William whom we mentioned above, in distinction 2, chapter 22: he saw the spirit of fornication, in the form of a phantom prostitute, wandering inquisitively through the infirmary, and from what he heard and saw from her predicted to Dom Robert, abbot of Clairvaux, the apostasy of two young men. Their shameful flight, following immediately, proved this prediction true. Before joining the Cistercian Order, this William lived for a long time in the monastery of St Albinus at Angers, as is stated at the beginning of the cited chapter 14, where many other things concerning him may be read. In Manriquez’s Cistercian Menology he is listed with the title “Blessed” on 19 November and is called a disciple of St Bernard. On the two appearances just given, Herbert, book I of *Miracles*, chapter 4, may also be consulted.

17. The praised *Exordium*, distinction 4, chapter 33, records another appearance:

> There was at Clairvaux a certain religious lay brother, named Lawrence … a spiritual and devout man in all his manner of life, who persevered unceasingly with remarkable constancy in prayer and compunction. Thus, for many years, while he guarded day and night in the sacristy the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, he could scarcely ever be found there otherwise than continually engaged in prayer and watering the pavement with prolonged tears. … After the passing of Blessed Bernard, it happened that the same brother was sent by Dom Philip, venerable prior of Clairvaux, to Roger, king of Sicily, on business of the same church. When he had entered Rome and learned that this king had very recently died, he was dismayed in spirit and had absolutely no idea what he ought to do at such a juncture. Remembering his holy father Bernard, under whom he had often been sent on various business and had gone and returned successfully, he turned with many groans and tears to prayer and invoked the same saint of God, saying: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer, why have you forsaken us? Alas, holy Father, what shall I say, or what shall I do, poor and wretched man that I am, deprived of every counsel and help?”

18. “While you lived and at your command, I went securely to diverse lands and nations; everywhere I was received for your favour, carrying, as I did, your greetings and letters, which kings and bishops, together with all others, received as a blessing sent from heaven. The noblest rejoiced to be ennobled by your gifts of blessing. But now that you have died, my favour has died with you as well; there will be no one now to extend a helping hand to a stranger and needy man. And behold: the king who loved you with sincere affection is dead, and his son has risen in his place, a boy who perhaps does not know you. If I should wish to approach him while he is still so far away and should happen to be rebuffed, it would be an inconsolable grief to me, after the weariness of such labour and such a long journey, to return with the matter unfinished—I who, while you lived, used to return to your Clairvaux laden with every good thing.”

19. “But if I return at once and leave the business unattempted, I fear to be accused of sluggishness and folly. I beg you, extend help and give counsel to one in need; do not despise the groaning of your pitiable servant.”

That same night this most blessed Father appeared to him and magnificently comforted him, saying:

> Brother, why did you think fit to distrust so greatly God’s mercy and my intervention? When or where have you experienced the failure of my help in your necessities? Or do you perhaps now consider me less powerful, since I have been admitted into the powers of the Lord, than I was formerly when I lived in the flesh? Go, therefore, in confidence, for all things will turn out favourably; and in this very matter you will know that I sent you.

While the saint spoke these words and many others, the brother wholly melted in spirit through the excessive ardour of devotion; and as his heart gave birth to immense joy, tears of devotion also burst forth outwardly.

[Col. 0953D] 20. When he awoke, his eyes and cheeks were wet; he found even the pillow upon which he had laid his head soaked on every side by the same flood of tears. Accordingly, at first light he set out. When he had left the city, he came upon a band of merchants travelling to Sicily for trade. When they learned that he was from Clairvaux, they immediately welcomed him gladly into their company and at their table, supplying him freely each day with everything necessary. At last, when he entered the presence of the king of Sicily, he found great favour in his eyes. Not only did he obtain a successful issue in the business for which he had been sent to the king’s father; the king also opened his treasures and, for the soul of that same father, sent through the brother a substantial sum of gold with great devotion for the building of the new church of Clairvaux.

21. When the aforesaid brother returned to Rome, he found such favour there also that he received an abundant blessing from the gifts of cardinals and other Romans. Through their generosity, he led ten buffaloes out of the City. To the immense astonishment of all, protected by God and aided by the merits of his holy Father, he brought them safely as far as Clairvaux. …

It happened that he had to pass through a certain town ruled by leaders of brigands; no one could escape their hands unscathed unless perhaps he prevailed by force. Now, when dawn was already reddening and he was leaving a meadow where he had spent the night with the animals, he earnestly begged the Lord and St Bernard to rescue him from the imminent danger. And behold, at a distance he saw what seemed to be two men coming to meet him, each holding a lighted candle in his hands. As they gradually drew nearer and were already almost upon him, they suddenly vanished from his sight, giving the servant of God great confidence that he would escape.

He then entered that nest of the devil; immediately he was stopped, and men rushed in from all sides to seize their spoil. But by God’s will, certain honourable men arrived at that very hour. Recognizing that he was from Clairvaux, they delivered him from the hands of his attackers and allowed him to depart with all his possessions, etc.

22. Our Preliminary Commentary, § 27, narrates what took place between Bernard and the Roger mentioned above. Yet what has just been related concerning the journey undertaken by Lawrence to deal with that Roger does not accord with chronology. According to Baronius, who assigns Roger’s death to the year of Christ 1152, how could St Bernard have appeared to this religious brother as one deceased, when Bernard died only in the following year? Likewise, how could that lay brother have guarded day and night for many years in the sacristy the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, etc.?

If, however, with Pagi, you defer Roger’s death to 1154—where, in no. 4, he treats the matter expressly—the first difficulty is indeed removed, but the second remains. Nevertheless, it does not follow that the history of the foregoing appearance is false. A remedy is supplied if the phrase “for many years” is deleted; this circumstance could easily have been inserted here by some careless or unskilled copyist or interpolator. As for the construction of the new church of Clairvaux mentioned above, *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV, col. 129, states under Guichard, archbishop of Lyons:

> He was present at the dedication of the church of Clairvaux in 1174.

But concerning the year of that dedication, see also our Preliminary Commentary, § 61, no. 676.

### § II. He appears to two monks of Clairvaux and prevents their apostasy; confirms a young man in his monastic resolve; restrains a fire; shows himself to one near death; and to another sick man.

23. Herbert, book I, chapter 28, recounts that a monk of Clairvaux who was thinking of abandoning his resolution came to his senses after seeing St Malachy and St Bernard in a dream, the latter beating him with his staff. Let us give Herbert’s words:

> One of the brethren of Clairvaux, corrupted in mind by the devil’s prompting so that he was already preparing to apostatize to the world, saw in a vision of the night Blessed Bernard and St Malachy walking through the dormitory, visiting and blessing those resting there. When, in the course of their visitation, they came to his little bed, St Malachy said: “This perverse man turns over nothing good at all in his heart, but has already consented to the devil’s persuasion and is on the point of returning to the vomit of the world.” On hearing this, Blessed Bernard said to him: “So you seek to flee? And where, wretch, will you flee from the face of the Lord? Believe me: you have conceived such thoughts to your own harm. For flight will no longer please you once you have escaped from my hand.”

24. Having said this, he began to strike him repeatedly with the staff he held, saying: “Behold the wages you deserve. Rise now, and flee, if you can.” When the brother awoke, he found himself so sore and bruised by those blows that he had to be taken to the infirmary and confined to bed. Calling for the prior, he confessed the evil he had intended and the punishment he had suffered for it. Having received penance, he came fully to his senses, and thereafter the desire to flee no longer seized him.

In the same work, chapter 31, an appearance of a similar nature is related in these words:

[Col. 0955C] 25. Another brother of the same monastery, an honourable and religious man, told me about himself—though with embarrassment—that in the beginning of his conversion, when he was severely troubled by the spirit of fornication, he resolved in his heart to yield to the tempter and, casting off the habit of religion, return to the world. While he was anxiously seeking an opportunity to depart, Blessed Bernard, who had died shortly before, stood beside him in a vision, rebuking his sluggishness and reproving the wickedness which he had conceived in his mind and was striving to carry out in deed. When the brother answered that he had struggled for a long time [indeed, that he was struggling] and could no longer bear the violence of the temptation, the saint said to him:

> Know beforehand that many struggles still await you. But act manfully and do not fail, for the Lord will be with you as a helper in due time, to deliver you.

26. “Therefore I promise you that, if you persevere in the Order until the end, you will be saved. But if perhaps anyone attempts to harm you, on the last day I shall answer for you and lay down my soul for your soul.”

Strengthened by this promise, the brother could thereafter not be moved from his stability. Even now, having completed five times five years in the Order, he fights manfully to this day and, after so many victories, awaits with greater certainty the salvation promised him.

27. The same author, Book II, chapter 9, dealing with a certain young German who was wonderfully converted at Clairvaux to the monastic life and became distinguished by outstanding holiness and divine manifestations, relates an event relevant to our subject [Col. 0956A], which occurred during the holy Father’s lifetime. I excerpt what follows:

A certain excellent young man, native to the regions of Germany, was travelling to Paris for the sake of study, accompanied by his teacher. As he passed through the house of Clairvaux, that master, seeing the community and discipline of the place, was, by some judgment of God, pierced with compunction for the moment; he asked and obtained permission to be received for conversion. When he asked the young man to remain with him, however, the latter wholly refused. For he greatly recoiled from the company, even from conversation, of Cistercian monks; and he had often asked the Lord that he might never be granted conversion to that order. Accordingly, while his master begged him and the brothers of the monastery exhorted him, he resisted stiff-neckedly and could not be overcome by any engines of preaching [Col. 0956B].

That same night, as he pondered their admonitions in his mind, a voice came to him from God, saying: “If you depart from here and arrive in Paris, you will die before Pentecost; and without doubt you will die.” At this voice the young man was greatly astonished; yet the hardness of his heart could not then be softened.

28. On the following night, when he had yielded his limbs to sleep, he seemed to himself to have sunk into the mud of a deep well. As he lay there in despair, blessed John the Evangelist suddenly appeared above, at the edge [perhaps *l. oram*, “at the rim”] of the well, in the face and dress of blessed Bernard, together with another saint whose name has escaped me. This latter was likewise very similar to a most religious man named Gerard, porter of Clairvaux [Col. 0956C]. Seeing them, he earnestly begged them to have pity on him.

Blessed John answered him: “Do you, who despised to assent to sound counsel, now ask help from us?” When he promised to do whatever pleased him, John said: “Will you then become a monk in the monastery of Clairvaux?”

“Yes, my lord,” he replied; “most willingly I will.”

When he had firmly promised to fulfil this without delay, they immediately drew him out of the depths and allowed him to go free.

29. Therefore, when morning came, he asked to be brought as quickly as possible before blessed Bernard. Though he had not previously seen him, he at once recognized him by his face and clothing, knowing certainly that this was the very man whom, on the preceding night, he had deserved to have as his deliverer on condition of conversion [Col. 0956D]. Greatly amazed and compunct, he immediately surrendered himself to that holy man. Kindly received by him, while still of tender age he at once put on, to the wonder of all, the grey hairs of gravity and wisdom.

The other charismatic manifestations recorded there concerning him do not belong to the present subject. Yet the conclusion of the chapter cited contributes to the greater credibility of the history which we have just related, where Herbert confirms the matter:

“All these things which I have related above, and many more besides—which, though I consider them great, I have nevertheless passed over out of love of brevity—I learned by the secret account of that same servant of God, on the condition, namely, that they should remain secret with me until his death. But because, now called by the Lord, after completing twenty-six years in the Order, he died as happily as he had lived sincerely, I, released from the bond of this promise [Col. 0957A], have included in the present page the aforesaid revelations—in which I remember that I myself was no little consoled—for the consolation of others also.”

30. In Manrique, volume IV of the *Cistercian Annals*, in the Appendix, among the materials found on p. 659, no. 13, under the year 1592, appears the following apparition:

“In August, on the day of Father Bernard, the newly planted woodland was miserably consumed by fire, while the abbot and the greater part of the Benedictine community of Saint Peter of Eslonza were present. They had come with our monks to celebrate the solemnity of the holy Father. Rumour spread that both Fathers, namely Benedict and Bernard, had appeared to one of them and checked the advancing flames so that they should proceed no farther; for, as the wind drove them in the opposite direction, there was reason to fear that they would consume everything” [Col. 0957B].

Note that the *saltus novalis* (“newly planted woodland”) is identified in this Appendix, p. 602, no. 18, as situated in the kingdom and diocese of León.

31. Herbert, Book II, chapter 29, recounts certain wonderful things concerning Gerard of Farfa, an old man of admirable piety and eminent sanctity. He adds the following:

“To this man, now at the point of death, blessed Bernard appeared, adorned with an angelic face and white clothing, yet in the same bodily bearing and appearance which he had before his death. As Gerard watched him enter, supporting his aged and venerable limbs with a staff, he signalled by hand and voice, as best he could, to his attendants that they should rise for the approaching Saint and quickly prepare a seat. They marvelled and asked of what saint he spoke, but, oppressed by illness, he could not answer [Col. 0957C]. Afterwards, when his power of speech returned and they asked the same question again, he confessed that he had seen blessed Bernard comforting him with gentle words. After blessing him, Bernard also blessed the whole house, adding these very words: ‘This is my house, which I have built. May the Lord guard it for ever and ever, unto ages of ages.’”

Herbert, Book III, chapter 10, may be read concerning Geoffrey, bishop of Sorrento, who, while suffering from a severe throat ailment that physicians had almost despaired of curing, was healed by the holy man appearing to him.

## § III. He manifests himself three times to a certain brother; likewise appears to Blessed Mary of Oignies; foretells heavenly glory to another and death to Ascelina; marvellous discovery of a book of miracles, and a monk’s literacy.

[Col. 0957D]

32. To the apparitions mentioned above may be added three others, narrated in the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 4, chapter 7, in these words:

“A certain brother of the Order of Regular Canons, being eager for spiritual progress and a zealous seeker of the better charisms, greatly desired to submit himself to the instruction of blessed Bernard and to join the community of Clairvaux. Yet he could by no means attain this while the holy Father himself was living. When Bernard died, and the report of his precious death reached him, he was deeply distressed in spirit, crying out that he was miserable and unworthy because he had not deserved to gain his desire.

“But after a few days that venerable Father appeared to him in a vision [Col. 0958A], like a vigorous labourer girded for work in a very broad field. In it were visible countless sheaves of a wheat harvest, from which he had gathered a great multitude into one large stack; and he persistently continued to carry together and heap up those that remained, which were also far more numerous. Seeing this, the brother immediately understood that the heap of sheaves represented the multitude of brothers whom that outstanding preacher, while he lived in the flesh, had gathered to Christ the Lord; and that countless others remained, who through his merits and example were to be brought to the grace of salvation. He therefore rejoiced greatly; and, not despairing that he himself would be one of them, he went as quickly as possible to Clairvaux, asking and obtaining admission to probation.”

[Col. 0958B]

33. By this apparition of the holy man, then, the brother was called to the novitiate at Clairvaux. A second apparition made to him discloses what favour he received there from that same saint:

“While he was a novice there, and was turning in his mind almost unceasingly and insatiably the memory of the blessed man, one Sunday, near the end of the night offices, sleep began to steal over him, exhausted and afflicted in many ways. And behold, the most reverend Father, whose love burned within him, appeared and graciously addressed him, admonishing him continually to direct his intention toward God, with daily shedding of tears. If he did so, he might confidently expect divine mercy and that Father’s own visitation. Having said this, he withdrew into his tomb [Col. 0958C], which stood there before the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mother. This withdrawal was so visibly perceived that the brother did not know whether he had seen it asleep or awake.

34. “When he opened his eyes and reflected on the most loving Father’s admonition in sweet remembrance, the Father suddenly appeared to him again while he was fully awake and offered himself to be seen by bodily eyes. He stood close before him, so that he might easily have been touched by hand, looking intently at him and, as it were, testing whether he slept or woke, after the manner of those who awaken sleepers for the night offices. As the novice gazed at him, stunned and amazed, he who appeared immediately vanished. And, wonderful to relate, it seemed to the novice that he had entered, almost tangibly, into his inmost heart [Col. 0958D].

“Thus greatly inflamed in love for God and for that most blessed man, he was trained day by day to embrace the new life with spiritual joy and exultation. Finally, on the following night, while likewise attending the brothers’ vigils, he experienced there such and so great a grace of divine visitation as he had never before felt in all his life. He rejoiced that he had obtained it all through the merits of him whom he loved. And as for many days he repeatedly poured forth the memory of the abundance of this sweetness, he shed abundant sweet and devout tears, with which he could not be sated day or night.”

Thus far the *Great Cistercian Exordium*, which also treats of the life and death of the praised brother, who continually followed in the footsteps of Saint Bernard.

[Col. 0959A]

35. James of Vitry, author of the Life of Blessed Mary of Oignies, recounts an apparition of Saint Bernard which befell her in these words:

“Blessed Bernard, father and light of the Cistercian Order, once appeared to her as though winged, and spread his wings around her. After he had sat with her for a long time at the chancel-screen [read *cancello*, not *cantello*] of the church, and she asked what kind of wings these were, he answered that, like an eagle in lofty flight, he had reached the lofty and subtle matters of divine Scripture, and that the Lord had revealed to him many things concerning heavenly mysteries.”

36. Herbert, in the books *On Miracles*, Book II, chapter 28, relates the following apparition of the holy man:

“A monk died there”—the Abbey of Domus Dei, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, had previously been under discussion—“young indeed in years but advanced in the maturity of religious life. They also affirm of him that, by the Lord’s gift, he preserved the flower of virginity until death. Strengthened by a marvellous hope, he so longed to be dissolved and to be with Christ that he seemed to fear nothing except being delayed from death and remaining in the body; and he would have grieved deeply if anyone had either promised or wished him a reprieve.

“On the very day of his departure blessed Bernard appeared to him with the aforesaid Brother F. [that is, Franco], who said to him: ‘Brother Bernard’—for this was the young man’s name—‘behold, I bring you our holy Father Bernard, so that I may place you in his hands.’ The blessed Father received him with his merciful right hand and said: ‘Today you shall be with me in paradise.’ Having said this, they vanished” [Col. 0959B–C].

Then the monk told the brothers what he had seen and heard, adding: “If I live until tomorrow, I have not spoken truth; but if I depart today, let that departure itself confirm my words.” The brother accordingly died that same day, so that all which the holy Father had said to him might be fulfilled.

The Cistercian historian, under the year 1195, chapter 3, no. 7, records that the holy man appeared to Ascelina on the night of his death and announced her death to her. Ascelina was a virgin in France, Saint Father Bernard’s niece according to the flesh and disciple according to the spirit. We mentioned her under the title “Blessed,” following Henriquez in the Appendix to the *Cistercian Menology*, among the omissions for 18 May; her cult may be examined on the 23rd day of this month of August [Col. 0959D].

37. John the Hermit, who wrote the Life of Saint Bernard, in the letter prefixed first to that Life and reprinted by Mabillon in volume II, relates this wonderful apparition at col. 1279:

“A certain monk, a true and sincere lover of the venerable abbot, was walking by chance with a lay brother named Humbert through brushwood adjoining the monastery of Clairvaux. He held in his hands a book of the holy Father’s miracles and expounded its contents in the vernacular Romance language, for the edification both of himself and of the other. It happened that they sat down for a brief rest beneath a pear-tree by the road along which those working in the garden went and came daily. When they rose again not long afterwards, the aforesaid monk, forgetfulness stealing upon him—as happens very often—carelessly left on the ground the book which he had held in his hand shortly before [Col. 0960A].

38. “He went away and, occupied with the pursuits of regular discipline, eventually recalled how, where, and when he had lost it. But, conceiving no hope whatever of recovering it—both because he had left it close to the road and because meanwhile there had been so great a flood of rain that, even if it were found, he believed it could be of no more value than if lost—after some time he ceased looking for it; indeed, he seemed to give up altogether, though deeply distressed that through his own negligence he had lost the volume of the holy man’s miracles.

[Col. 0960B]

39. “About a month passed in this way. After a short walk through the garden, he sat down again beneath the aforementioned tree, with no intention of searching and no hope of recovering what he had lost. Then, in a marvellous and unheard-of manner, he was amazed to see the book suddenly set before him, as though preserved by someone and only then freshly and deliberately placed beside him. And, so that what happened may be believed still more wonderful, both the parchment and the writing had remained so sound and uncorrupted—except that the outer covering seemed to have been sprinkled with a few drops—as if that same book had been stored in the library with the other books.

“I do not know what those hearing this may think; but for my own part I do not hesitate to affirm that so extraordinary and unusual an event could by no means have occurred without a miracle. Reason persuades, and truth compels, us to ascribe it to the merits of the blessed man” [Col. 0960C].

40. “In the silence of the night, after the fatigue of the day’s work, he had lain down on his little bed for a short rest. While awake, a venerable man appeared to him, clothed in a snow-white robe, of middle height, very aged, white-haired, and august with an angelic face. He seemed to hold two books in his hands. Approaching the brother mentioned above, he handed him both of them, saying: ‘Take them, look, and read.’

“Startled—as commonly happens—by the terror of the sudden vision, but taking confidence from the gracious speech, tranquil appearance, and angelic face, the brother replied: ‘Lord Father, I do not know letters. How can I read, being simple and unlearned?’ [Col. 0960D]

“And he said: ‘Son, do not be afraid. Behold, the Lord is with you and will teach you; and, through my intercession, all shall be well with you.’

“Strengthened by this devout exhortation, the brother took both volumes, opened and read them, marvelling and wondering inwardly how it could be so. The person standing by then, as though carrying one book away with him and leaving the other with the brother, gave him farewell and disappeared after bestowing a blessing.

41. “What then? What we are about to say is indeed marvellous. What could be more marvellous than this marvel? We all know the brother: until shortly before, he was a layman and did not even know the alphabet. Yet, God enlightening his understanding and certain brothers assisting him, he quickly advanced so far that he knew not only how to read, but also how to sing quite properly and suitably [Col. 0961A]. Thereafter, with practice and grace working together, he began somewhat to understand the meanings of words and gradually to advance in such knowledge.

“He wrote down the aforesaid vision in hope of divine help and of the aid of the blessed man whom we believe appeared to him. Some of that saint’s miracles, either unknown to writers or omitted through negligence, he committed to writing so fittingly, so well, and so elegantly that we are repeatedly carried away in admiration and say with the prophet David: ‘This was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes.’ Who, then, can deny that this happened miraculously? What miracle is more open, what more evident? Therefore we ascribe it first to the grace of God; next, we attribute it to the merits of the saint; finally, we assign it to the brother’s faith and obedience” [Col. 0961B].

## § IV. Certain prophecies of the holy man.

42. Although our preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Bernard, and the Life itself, contain so many and such great prophecies as prove with the utmost clarity that the holy man deserves the highest renown in this kind of gift, besides his other outstanding prerogatives, the subject has not been exhausted there to such an extent that no examples remain whose knowledge I would wish to withhold from my reader.

In the *Literary Journey*, discussed above in chapter 1, no. 9, part 2, p. 201, is narrated a prophecy of our holy abbot. When he came to Villers to found a monastery there, and was on the mountain—for the monastery lies between two mountains [Col. 0961C]—he is said to have planted his staff in the ground and foretold: “In this place the souls of many shall be saved.” That staff, having taken root, grew into a tree which survived until the year 1697, and died at the same time as Abbot Thomas. This gave occasion for the composition of these four verses:

> A phoenix once hidden in Villers’ soil,  
> I die likewise as Thomas dies.  
> I have lived through five and a half centuries and a year,  
> Since Bernard’s sacred right hand planted [perhaps *serit*, “planted”] me.

43. The holy man is reported to have foretold to a novice the day of his death in the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 2, chapter 12:

“It is also found in the acts of this blessed man that, while still living in the flesh, he appeared in spirit at Clairvaux with a multitude of monks to a certain novice who was seriously ill. He foretold that the latter would die on the fifth day; and that, on that fifth day, when the sun was already declining to its setting, he visited him and commanded him to sit up and fear nothing, but to hasten directly on his straight course to the Lord Jesus Christ and offer him the humble greeting of his family of Clairvaux. At these words the novice, assenting as best he could by an inclination of the head and movement of the lips, closed his eyes and fell asleep in the Lord at that same hour” [Col. 0961D–0962A].

The matters recorded there in the same *Exordium*, chapter 14, concerning certain novices raised to abbatial rank are certainly also worthy of notice: exactly as the holy Father had foretold, not one of them was excepted. Hear the event.

44. “At the blessing of this holy Father, some of his novices, putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. Concerning them the blessed man, speaking in the Spirit of God, foretold that all would attain the grace of spiritual dignity and receive both the name and office of abbot. As years passed and suitable times came, the word of this prophecy was fulfilled in each of them [Col. 0962B].

“One of them, named Peter, had been sent by the holy abbot to Sweden, to the house of Nydala. After the latter’s death, Peter lived for many years, into old age and indeed almost into decrepitude, without receiving this gracious office, because he was thought of simpler character and less fit to administer so great an office. But what then? Could he, hidden even in the ends of the world, or bearing the infirmities of advanced age, escape the omnipotence of the Holy Spirit, so that what that same Spirit had foretold of him so long before through Bernard, his prophet, should not be fulfilled?

45. “Finally, after so long an interval, when what the most reverend Father had foretold concerning this man of dove-like simplicity had almost passed into oblivion [Col. 0962C], it happened that the brothers of a certain house of Nydala, situated on the island called Godandia [Gotland], being left without a shepherd, had recourse, according to the general custom of the Order, to their mother-house, that through the provision and care of the father abbot a worthy steward might be appointed for their house. By the Lord’s will—without whose nod neither a leaf of a tree nor a single sparrow falls to the ground—it pleased both the father abbot and the others present at the election to take the aforesaid old man into this burden of care. Thus he might trust all the more confidently in the mercy of God and in the merits of his most holy Father, in proportion as he more humbly distrusted his own insufficiency.

“When this was done, and the word once foretold by the saint was recalled and published everywhere, all who heard it marvelled and said that the promotion of so old and simple a man had been provided by divine dispensation for this sole purpose: that, of all that the man of God had spoken through the spirit of prophecy, not even one iota or one stroke should be seen to have been uttered in vain” [Col. 0962D].

We discuss the praised Peter among the omissions for 10 June. Gotland, moreover, is a sufficiently well-known island in the Baltic Sea and needs no further explanation.

# CHAPTER III. Supplement to the miracles.

[Col. 0963]

## § I. Various bodily infirmities healed; a dying man’s time of death fixed; a miracle wrongly attributed to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; why an epileptic was not wholly cured; a dead man restored to life.

[Col. 0963A]

46. Chrysostom Henriquez, in the *Fascicle of Saints of the Cistercian Order*, Book I, distinction 4, chapter 51, says:

“Not many years after the death of the devout Father, Gundisalvus, abbot of Moreruela, a Cistercian monastery in the kingdom of León, was afflicted by gout and could scarcely endure the severity of the pain. Nevertheless, with the utmost reverence and devotion he applied to his ailing limbs a portion of Saint Bernard’s habit, preserved in that monastery among its other relics; immediately all pain departed, and he obtained complete health.

“Suerus, abbot of Nucales in Spain, had carelessly swallowed a fishbone and was nearly choked. At last, as the illness worsened, he lay in bed at the point of death, abandoned by the physicians [Col. 0963B]. Then the prior of Moreruela touched the swollen throat of the sick abbot with the girdle which he wore and which, from devotion, he had laid upon the tomb of the holy Abbot Bernard when he visited Clairvaux. At once the bone went down; he was wholly freed from every discomfort of illness and consequently from danger of death.”

Bernardus Britto relates these two miracles, Book III, chapter 29.

47. The things related in our preliminary commentary, § 49, concerning the prodigious spring are wholly marvellous. Add to what we there prefaced for reading about it the following from John the Hermit in Mabillon, col. 1290:

“There was a religious man named Odo, a part of whose body had remained almost dead for some time, contracted through a neighbouring affliction. After the blessed man’s death, he went to that same spring. Having washed the diseased part with it, he returned sound and unharmed. Another, violently afflicted by headache and wholly deprived of sensation, was healed when sprinkled with the spring. Another had languished for seven years; brought by his parents to the holy spring, he was restored to health. Another man named Suynus had long suffered from quartan fever; by drinking from that spring he received health. Another, afflicted with a very serious illness, tasted the same water; a little worm resembling a locust came out through his mouth in the sight of all [Col. 0963C–D], and he immediately recovered. A mute man also, as those who saw it report, came to the spring and recovered speech.
