It suffices to touch briefly on these and many other things, seen both by us and by others, to disbelieve which would be impious, lest the length of the narrative cause disgust to hearers.”

48. Among the holy man’s miracles may also be counted his singular command by which the death of a monk of Clairvaux was deferred. The event is found in Mabillon among the excerpts from the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, col. 1200, and in Herbert, Book I *On Miracles*, chapter 13, from whom I transcribe it:

“One of the brothers of that place, namely the monastery of Clairvaux, lay at the point of death. After Compline blessed Bernard entered to visit him; and, seeing the man near death and on the very point of departing, said: ‘You know, dearest brother, that our community is now fatigued by labour and must soon rise for vigils. If, while you are meanwhile [perhaps *l. interim*, rather than *iterum*] asleep, it must interrupt its sleep again, it will be greatly troubled and will perform the very long vigils with less solemnity. Therefore, that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land which you are about to enter and possess, in Christ’s name I command you to wait for us until the hour of the divine office.’

“The brother replied: ‘Lord, I shall do as you command, provided that you support my wish by your prayers’” [Col. 0964A–B].

49. What need of more words? The Father went to the dormitory, and the brother did not die before the appointed time. As soon as the signal for vigils began to be rung, the board was struck and he died. This happened not only to that brother, but repeatedly to several others also: their end was deferred for one or more days at the command and request of the Father.

So that the reader may know what is meant by “the board was struck,” Manrique, under the year of Christ 1141, chapter 4, no. 6, says that it was once customary throughout the Church, and remains so in the Cistercian Church even today, to signify the death of persons by repeated and harsh blows on a board. He then adds other matters. But let us continue with the remaining wonders of our great miracle-worker [Col. 0964C].

50. Among these, Mabillon incorrectly includes, at col. 1109, the remarkable conversion of a concubinary priest and former monk of Clairvaux, given from the Barbellian codex of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Sens. For our Saint Bernard played no part in this conversion. Nevertheless, I find that same remarkable conversion attributed to the holy abbot of Clairvaux in Horstius, Book VII of the *Life*, p. 77, from the Paris edition which he cites.

51. Herbert, Book II, chapter 20, has preserved the memorable story of a monk who suffered from epilepsy and, through the merits of Saint Bernard, received the ability to foresee the onset of the illness, lie down in bed, and avoid injury from a sudden fall. I quote Herbert’s text:

“The holy Father once went out to visit his brothers harvesting in the field. Because he was infirm and could not walk on foot, he rode on a little ass. A monk walking with him then, and driving the ass, had long suffered from the falling sickness. Suddenly, before him on the road itself, he fell and began to be grievously convulsed by that epilepsy. Seeing this, the holy man pitied him and prayed to the Lord for him, that the affliction should no longer seize him unawares. From that time until the day of his death—during the twenty years and more that he lived thereafter [Col. 0964D–0965A]—he was given what he had not previously possessed, and what scarcely ever happens to other epileptics: whenever he was about to fall from the same illness, he perceived it some time beforehand, so that he could suitably lie down in bed and continually guard against injury from the sudden fall.”

52. We believe, indeed, that the holy man obtained no more for him from the Lord because he could have secured complete health for him had he known it to be expedient for the salvation of his soul. But because that man was hard to bear in his conduct and exceedingly hard of heart, and seemed always to need both the rod of correction and the staff of consolation in order to be saved, it was mercifully granted him to avoid continually, by foreknowledge, the danger of a sudden fall, while not being deprived of the stimulus of a health-giving disease.

## § II. A dead man restored to life.

[Col. 0965B]

Tissier, in the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 2, chapter 19, tells a miracle which deservedly ought to be reckoned among the foremost. Hear the event, described there in these words:

“At a time when the Saracens occupied the land of Jerusalem, blessed Bernard—whose soul the sword of Christian desolation had pierced with singular bitterness—travelled about everywhere, exhorting crowds of the faithful, not only by words but by signs and miracles, to avenge the injury done to the Saviour and to overthrow the unbelieving nation. It happened that he came into Germany. One day, leaving Freiburg, a notable town situated in the region of Breisgau [Col. 0965C], he was conducted by a nobleman named Henry, still a young man, to one of Henry’s residences, where he was to lodge overnight, with a large crowd following him.

53. “Henry himself, having now received the sign of the cross, had resolved to travel on foot until he had gathered the equipment and expenses for the proposed pilgrimage and set out upon its journey.

> [Note: In Tissier’s marginal note [Col. 0965D], the sense at this point is said to be incomplete. Perhaps the words immediately following in our copy [Col. 0966D] from the manuscript of Saint Matthias are missing: ‘Nevertheless the holy abbot ordered him to accompany him on horseback.’]

“Having therefore mounted his horse, he immediately followed Bernard as he departed. Seeing this with envy, a certain man of Belial, Henry’s servant, a man who loved every kind of wickedness and disbelieved every good thing, said to the servant of God: ‘Go on, follow that devil; and may that devil himself seize you!’

“Meanwhile two little women approached, carrying between them a third woman who was deprived of the use of her feet and certain other limbs, and was contracted. They wished to entreat the man of God to relieve the misery of the sick woman and the burden of those carrying her by the remedy of the desired cure [Col. 0965D]. Henry, seeing her and taking pity, said: ‘Place the sick woman for me across my horse’s neck, and hasten to the servant of the Lord to ask aid.’

54. “The aforesaid servant was everywhere indignant and impatient at this act of his lord’s compassion. He fiercely reproached Henry, as if he were carrying the wretched woman to an enchanter, sorcerer, and corrupter of minds [Col. 0966A]. Henry replied: ‘No: I am carrying her so that she may recover health through the blessing of the man of God. In the most certain confidence of her recovery I promise you that, if he does not cure her, I shall give you the horse I am riding.’

“The servant received these words gladly and gratefully. In his complete disbelief that a miracle would be performed, he both laughed and scoffed: he disbelieved equally in the cure and rejoiced beforehand at obtaining the horse. But when the woman was brought to the Saint of the Lord and obtained the blessing she desired, she immediately rose whole, no longer requiring, as hitherto, the assistance of others to carry her.

55. “When the servant so often mentioned saw this, driven by the rush of the evil spirit he bore in his breast, he hurried up, turned toward the face of the man of God, and hurled at him with all his force every wicked or disgraceful thing which, Satan inspiring him, he had conceived inwardly—cursing and reviling him [Col. 0966B]. But the Lord’s vengeance immediately came upon him: he fell backwards, supine, struck his neck, and breathed out his spirit.

“Henry, at once struck by grief at this lamentable death, reported the mournful fall and death to the abbot. When he had gone a little farther, Henry begged him to return to so sad a sight. Henry also said: ‘This happened to him because of you, because he did not fear to be blasphemous and insulting toward you.’ ‘Alas!’ said the Lord, ‘that anyone should die because of me.’

56. “Bernard therefore returned and devoted himself to prayer, in which alone he trusted in every difficulty. He prayed silently over him for the length of one *Our Father* [Col. 0966C], and immediately commanded those standing by to raise him. When raised, since he was already dead, his head, lacking the support of the neck, rolled about in every direction with pitiable motion. Again Bernard said: ‘Hold his head, hold it firmly.’

“At last he approached and, anointing and signing the places of injury with his saliva—whose medicinal application he very frequently used—said: ‘In the name of the Lord, arise.’ And again: ‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, may God restore your spirit to you.’”

57. But he, immediately having received back his spirit, became a living soul—or rather, one restored to life. All who were present and had seen a dead man so visibly and miraculously revived marvelled for joy and raised their voices and praises to heaven. At last, when questioned by the same holy man of God how he would live and what he would do henceforth, he said: “Lord, I shall now live as you command, and do whatever you prescribe, whatever you wish.” Asked also by the bystanders whether he had already been dead, he answered: “I was dead, and had received the sentence of condemnation; and unless the holy abbot had hastened to come, I was irrevocably to be led down to hell.” At the exhortation of certain bystanders, he also received the sign of the cross and departed with the others for Jerusalem. This Henry devoted himself to God and blessed Bernard on that same journey, and afterwards became Bernard’s monk at Clairvaux. Since the writer himself had beheld this miracle with trustworthy eyes and believed it to be well known to the writers of the Life of the holy Father, he grieved when he discovered that it had at last been silently omitted; and, for the glory of God and of His saint, he recounted it just as he had witnessed it, so that every generation to come for ever and ever might hear and understand in how great glory he ought to be held whom the Most High thus glorified. So far that account. This story is also found in Horstius and Mabillon, *Life*, Book VII, chapter 19.

58. We have a copy noted as taken from the monastery of St. Matthias near Trier, after the books on the Life of St. Bernard, and it bears the following title:

> A glorious miracle, written down by a certain monk of Clairvaux together with what follows: how St. Bernard raised a dead man, matters omitted from the Life.

We pass over what follows this miracle in this copy; but note that the foregoing story is recorded there as well. Meanwhile, we are surprised that so illustrious a miracle, of the first rank, is not found among the countless others which writers beyond every exception, with the greatest faithfulness and diligence, recorded—as we saw above—when they accompanied the holy wonder-worker as he summoned the peoples of Germany by the sacred trumpet to the eastern expedition, and most carefully observed the miracles he performed. One may meanwhile consult what appears in the Preliminary Commentary, §40, no. 428, concerning a dead man restored to life by the saint while preaching in Germany, from the *Book of Miracles* of Lord Herbert. Yet I do not find this miracle in Chifflet’s edition of that author; and consequently it is not established for me whether it is identical with the preceding one or another miracle.

## § III. The remarkable manner in which the father of St. Bernard is said to have been converted, considered more carefully; a cart, though its axle was broken, carried farther on; Humbert’s falling sickness cured; another aided in spirit and body; etc.

59. In the Preliminary Commentary, §8, we reported that St. Bernard’s father entered the monastic life, forsaking the world. The remarkable manner in which this happened was there related from Vincent of Beauvais, and it was observed that one passage did not agree with another. That remarkable manner, I say, contained something which displeased Manrique and myself. I also noted that the biographer William had left nothing written about it. Yet the following, read in Fr. Jacob Eckard’s *Writers of the Order of Preachers*, vol. I, pp. 188–189, among the writings of Fr. Stephen of Bourbon, or of Bellavilla, who flourished in the thirteenth century, the century immediately after Bernard, makes this account more probable. Although the said Commentary quoted two passages of the same Vincent concerning this conversion, both nearly similar to that which the aforementioned Stephen relates, I have nevertheless judged that Stephen’s narrative should also be transcribed here, so that it may be compared with Vincent’s, because it is brief. Stephen accordingly records the event and its circumstances as follows:

60. “I heard,” he says, “that when Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux had converted all his brothers and made them monks, while his father alone remained in the world, more hardened, Bernard came to his village. Preaching there beside a most ancient tree-trunk in his father’s presence, and seeing his hardness, he ordered the men who had brought dry wood around the trunk, as he himself had commanded, to kindle a fire. When this was done, the dry wood quickly caught fire; but the trunk slowly, around its middle, gave off foul moisture and most hideous smoke from its extremities, and preserved the fire for a long time. Then the saint began to speak about the punishments of hell. He told his father that he was like that trunk, which could not be kindled by the divine fire, could neither weep for its sins nor sigh toward God; but that he himself, unless he did penance, would burn, weep, and emit stinking smoke in hell for ever. At these words the said father was pierced with compunction, followed him, and became a monk.”

And Stephen adds, in further confirmation of the event: “I heard these things in the very place where the sermon was delivered, from Lord Calo, lord of Fontaines, great-grandson of Blessed Bernard, at the place of Bernard’s birth, called Fontaines.”

61. In our copy from the manuscript of Aulne Abbey, mentioned in the Preliminary Commentary, §2, no. 21—and whose exemplar, as I gather from its beginning and course, is that same one, or similar to that from which the extracts surviving under Geoffrey’s name in Mabillon were taken—the following remarkable event is related. The author is described in its heading as a disciple converted by St. Bernard to the Order at Paris:

> It happened in the early years, at harvest-time, that the venerable Bernard, speaking with a certain brother, sat on the slope of the wood which, from the lofty hill, overlooks that present establishment—the context having just concerned Clairvaux. And behold, before him a cart was broken which lay brothers, with oxen drawing it, were bringing down loaded with sheaves. The axle was broken, so that it held together by scarcely the breadth of a finger. The brothers, distressed, complained to the abbot about their serious loss, since they did not know how they could bring the sheaves, which were on the point of falling, into the grange. But he made the sign of the cross from a distance and said: “In the Lord’s name, go on as far as the threshing-floor.” The grange was situated so far from that place that a shouting voice could scarcely be heard from there. When the cart reached the threshing-floor, as though it had now completed the service of obedience, its axle—which until then had been prevented from falling apart—broke, and the cart fell at that very hour. At this the brothers were greatly comforted.

62. The following is related in the manuscript just praised:

> Nor shall I pass over what happened to the most reverend man Humbert, afterwards abbot of Igniacum [perhaps Igniac or Igniacensis]. When he came to Clairvaux, he was already rather advanced in age and accustomed to suffer from falling sickness. Seized, therefore, by his customary illness, but much more violently than usual, he fell seven times in one day, so that, driven into frenzy, he tried to bite with his teeth those holding him in bed. When the man of God saw this, inflamed with zeal for faith, he said: “What are we doing? Let us go to prayer.” Entering the oratory and bowing himself, the prayer of the righteous man immediately penetrated heaven and obtained the desired result. For Humbert at once fell asleep in the brothers’ hands; and on the next day, receiving the divine sacraments from the hand of the holy and blessed man, he was made well. Living many years thereafter, he never again suffered from an illness of this kind.

This event is related above among us in Book I of the *Life*. Yet since it is not in William’s actual text but was inserted into it from another source, the truth of the event is confirmed by the cited copy of the highest authority.

63. Let the reader forgive me if I add here, from the same manuscript of Aulne Abbey, the healing of the soul which the author candidly and gratefully acknowledges that he himself received from St. Bernard among the miracles he relates: when the holy man enlightened his eyes as he sat in the darkness of this world and, as it were, in the shadow of death, and directed his feet into the way of peace.

> “I ought not,” he says, “while speaking of others, to forget myself, lest perhaps I be found ungrateful.”

Then, after setting forth the notable fruit which the saint won among the scholars of Paris, the same author speaks of himself thus:

> “Blessed be by the Lord that day on which light arose for me as I sat in darkness and in the shadow of death! Blessed be the day on which the sun of righteousness—or rather, the Dayspring of mercy—visited my wretched soul from on high! I was a man excessively hostile and perverse; yet in a single word, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, by the inestimable change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, He recreated me wholly into another man, so that I might be some beginning of His creation. Never shall I forget this mercy, by which, being so abundantly anticipated and so suddenly changed, I caused the minds of many to be astonished at me. Truly many fish were caught in that haul by the Lord’s nets, and many joined us on the road, so that, after the year of probation had passed, twenty-one of this company became monks.”

From these words what was stated in the Preliminary Commentary, §10, about the catch at Paris is supplemented and confirmed. The antiquity and authority of this writer, from whom both this material and the preceding passages recently quoted from him were extracted, are also commended.

64. Immediately afterward, the same writer relates that he was cured by the same holy man when his body was sick and his mind afflicted:

> “Indeed, at the same time of our novitiate, when our Father was once absent, I began to be sick in body and afflicted in mind—I know that Satan had demanded me, to sift me like wheat. But what was happening to me did not escape the Father; and, as I discovered after his return, knowing perfectly by the Spirit all that was taking place in my heart, he prayed for me that my faith might not fail. There—there, O Lord my God—you wondrously impressed me upon his heart beyond what I was! Thanks to you, thanks to you! For how could such a soul have such a place in such a breast?”

The venerable Alberic, now abbot in the place called God’s Blessing, testifies that something similar happened to himself when he was a novice. For, driven by a sudden and most vehement temptation, he nearly yielded; but venerable Bernard, who was a day’s journey away, learned this through the Lord’s revelation and, rising in the night at that same hour, hurried to comfort him.

65. I reduce to a summary several other things which I read in the writer just cited. In a village near Châtillon, a man had suffered a flow of blood for many days. As the saint happened to pass that way, he signed him with the cross and stopped the bleeding, before the eyes and to the astonishment of all. But on the following night the affliction returned. The holy man ordered his book to be sent to the man and laid upon his head; and he recovered. An adulterous woman had so afflicted a poor man from Champagne—having, as was said, threatened to attack him by sorcery—that the wretched man, his flesh consumed, could neither die nor be allowed to live [lacuna]. When he had been brought to the man of God [lacuna], he ordered the sick man to be carried by two brothers before the altar; and, when a vessel containing the Body of Christ had been placed beneath his head [lacuna], the man shortly recovered.

The conversion of the monk who had for the third time fallen away from the Order, obtained by the admonitions and prayers of St. Father Bernard, might have been woven into this paragraph, as also his penance and his patience under God’s fatherly chastisement. At the happy completion of this, as is related in the passages immediately to be cited, blessed Bernard [Tissier adds: “greatly”] rejoiced and delivered a most devout address to the brothers in chapter. In it he commended the worthy fruit of the man’s penance and his admirable patience, proposing him to all as an example. But since the narrative of the event is rather long, it may be read in Horstius and Mabillon, *Life of St. Bernard*, Book VII, chapter 25; and in Tissier, *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 4, chapter 16.

## § IV. Synopsis of the innumerable miracles of St. Bernard

> **Note.** The synopsis of miracles which I promised in the Preliminary Commentary, §64, no. 718, I have deferred to this place. There I explained the reasons that moved me to provide it. The manuscript copy was most kindly shared with me by the most reverend and distinguished Lord Alexander Adriaenssens, most worthy abbot of the celebrated monastery of St. Bernard in the territory of Antwerp, on the Scheldt. This synopsis was compiled by the Reverend Lord Bernard Timmermans, pastor of the chapel of St. James, formerly superior and master of novices in that abbey. Its citations follow the order of the earlier edition, which comprises the five books of the *Life* and the sixth book, concerning miracles, as is also done in our edition; except that in this edition a new division of chapters and numbers has been made. For passages which occur from Book VII, let the reader consult our Commentary prefixed to the books of the *Life*, §66, and the discussion after Book VI, from p. 351, concerning the Fragments from Herbert published by Mabillon. Add also what has been related above in the *Posthumous Glory*. Moreover, we divide this synopsis into two sections, adding to each numbers and notes in the margin. These are the points on which I had to warn my reader; nothing now remains except to produce the synopsis itself, transcribed here in the words of the distinguished compiler.

[Col. 0970D]

## SECTION I. Sick persons, blind, deaf, mute, lame, crippled, deformed, foolish, frenzied, and others restored to health by St. Bernard

66, 67. William, Book I, chapter 9, no. 43, relates the first miracle performed by St. Bernard: namely, that he made Josbert, lying at the point of death and unconscious, speak freely. The man confessed his sins, arranged his other affairs well according to the holy Father’s counsel, and died two or three days later.

While absent, Bernard healed a man dangerously ill, saying to the man’s wife: “Go; you will find your husband well.” And so she found him. Chapter 6, no. 27.

He suddenly healed his uncle Galdric of a fever. Chapter 10, no. 46.

He suddenly healed William himself, the author of the book, who had relapsed and was afflicted even to death because he would not obey the holy Father concerning the eating of meat, when he had now consented to eat. Chapter 12, no. 60.

He healed a woman of falling sickness. Chapter 14, no. 67.

The bishop of Milan ordered the dish from which the holy Father had eaten to be brought; he ordered water to be poured into it and small pieces of bread placed in it. He ate and drank, and without delay recovered from the violent heat of fever. Book II, chapter 3, no. 19.

A nobleman despairing of medical help drank water from Bernard’s hand-washing and recovered. Chapter 7, no. 46.

A priest desperately ill and apparently at the point of death was suddenly healed by the tunic of St. Bernard. Book IV, chapter 1, no. 2.

He restored Brother Robert of Clairvaux, who was at the point of death, to his senses. No. 4.

He healed also a knight on the road, so that he could in some fashion be brought to the holy man. No. 5.

68. At the first taste of bread blessed by Bernard, a knight received complete recovery from quartan fever, from which he had suffered severely for almost eighteen months, even to the point of delirium. Chapter 4, no. 24.

In the same place, no. 23, the author indicates a multitude of fever patients cured, including a certain cleric seized by a most severe fever as punishment because, mocking, he had blasphemed the people’s faith. But, when he was contrite, St. Bernard healed him.

A young man seized by fever, on hanging around his neck a letter received from the holy Father, was immediately healed. Chapter 7, no. 40.

He healed a woman who for eight years had suffered a terrible illness, which violently shook all her limbs at once with severe trembling and powerful convulsions. Book V, chapter 1, no. 5.

By laying on of hands he made one near death suddenly walk. Book VI, chapter 13, no. 44.

Likewise, he healed there a boy who for many days had not been able to walk even a single step.

Likewise, a woman so deprived of bodily strength that she could neither walk nor stand. Chapter 14, no. 50.

In the same Book VI, another person healed of fever is related in no. 3 of Geoffrey’s letter after Book VI.

There also he heals a nobleman suffering from a most severe illness.

Likewise there, a poor man whose strength had been broken by a long illness.

Likewise there, he heals a regular canon half-dead, no. 7.

Likewise there, a boy suffering from an unknown illness who vomited up a stone after the blessing.

He healed his own brother Gerard of illness, Gerard himself testifying to this. Sermon 26, final number, on the *Song of Songs*.

69. It is evident from Book II, chapter 3, no. 15, that he healed many others of various diseases besides the twenty-three just mentioned, where it is said that “he had the greatest grace in cures of illnesses.” “Laying hands upon many fever patients,” says the same author, no. 18, “and giving them blessed water to drink, he obtained health.” And, travelling through various places, “he did good to those who were sick … healing fever patients.” Book III, chapter 6, no. 18, relates that an immense multitude of sick persons recovered after tasting bread blessed by him: all who tasted it, according to the promise made by the holy Father. It is therefore evident that the authors recorded only a few individually in comparison with those whom he healed of diverse illnesses; this will also be confirmed by the following third article.

70. At Clairvaux he healed the most reverend Humbert—afterwards founder and first Father of the monastery of Igniacum—of a severe illness of epilepsy. Book I, chapter 10, no. 48.

Likewise, by laying on of hands, he healed a woman made unable to speak by this illness. Book VI, chapter 14, no. 47.

Likewise, a certain monk, though only in part: so that he might foresee an attack in order to guard against injury, because Bernard knew that this was more expedient for the monk’s soul. Book VII, chapter 8.

While absent, he healed a paralytic named Albert in Spain. Book IV, chapter 6, no. 35.

Likewise, touching her beneath his cloak, he healed a paralytic woman. Book V, no. 6.

Book VI records twelve others healed of paralysis, ten of whom, unless I am mistaken, are those mentioned in Book IV, chapters 5 and 7.

71. He healed a dropsical man by girding him with his belt. Book IV, chapter 7, no. 37.

He healed Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, who suffered most grievously in his forehead and throat, so that he could scarcely taste anything or speak. Book V, chapter 5, no. 19.

He healed a man who lay unconscious and without sensation for a long time because he had disparaged the holy Father’s miracles. There, no. 20.

He healed an incessantly crying boy by a kiss. Book I, chapter 11, no. 23.

He healed Peter, bishop of Astorga in Spain, of a headache by sending him his cap, which was placed upon him. Book IV, chapter 6, no. 36.

Book VI mentions another healed of headache.

He cured a swelling of the head. Book IV, chapter 4, no. 24.

Book VI mentions one healed of trembling of the head.

72. Let us come to the blind, deaf, lame, maimed, and so forth. I pass over the manner of healing unless some remarkable circumstance occurs. I am content merely to cite Book VI without chapter and number, because I neglected to note them, judging it unnecessary.

He healed a girl unable to bear light. Book II, chapter 3, final number.

He gave sight to a blind boy as testimony that he had preached the eastern expedition by divine inspiration. Book III, chapter 4, no. 29.

He healed a boy blind in one eye. Book IV, chapter 1, no. 6.

In the same place, another deprived of both eyes from his mother’s womb. No. 7.

I omit many others whom the same Book IV records as given sight, since Book VI appears to mention the same people.

Book V records a blind man and a blind woman given sight.

Book VI records 184 persons given sight, for the most part blind in both eyes, some in one eye, and many blind from their mother’s womb.

Book VII, chapter 18, mentions one person given sight by kissing the ground and rubbing his eyes with it, having heard that the holy Father had touched it in passing. Thus you have 191 blind persons individually recorded as given sight.

73. Book VI records eighty-six deaf persons who received hearing.

The same Book VI records thirty-one mute persons who received speech.

Book VII, chapter 21, mentions one such case.

Book I, chapter 9, no. 44, records the healing of a boy who from his mother’s womb had a withered hand and a twisted arm.

Book II, chapter 3, no. 18, records withered hands and limbs disabled by paralysis restored to health, including the withered hand of a young man twisted back to his arm.

Book IV, chapter 4, no. 29, records two maimed boys healed. Those healed of maimed limbs whom it records later are also mentioned in Book VI, which here records fifty-seven healed persons with maimed limbs and withered hands. Chapter 9, no. 32, indicates many others healed of a similar infirmity. Book VI records three persons healed whose arms were withered or unable to move.

74. He healed a young man of a fistula in the foot. Book I, chapter 9, final number. To this category belong the lame who received the power of walking through the holy man.

Book I, chapter 2, no. 54, mentions one.

Book IV, chapter 4, nos. 28 and 29, mentions two whom it records subsequently and whom Book VI also cites.

Book V, no. 7, likewise mentions two.

Book VI records 157 lame persons set upright, of whom a few were bent.

There, chapter 15, no. 51, a person crawling on knees and hands is healed.

Book VI records eleven contracted and wholly incapacitated persons healed; Book VII, chapter 19, one.

Book VI records five healed who could not raise their heads.

75. He healed a foolish and mentally deficient boy, who was also lame, deaf, and mute. Book IV, chapter 8, no. 44.

Book VI records two foolish persons restored to sound mind.

He healed Henry, a great and powerful man in the household and service of the duke of Bavaria, who was in large measure delirious and suffered desperately from other afflictions. Book IV, chapter 7, no. 37.

The same Book IV, chapter 4, commemorates a frenzied woman healed.

Likewise another, chapter 6.

Book VI likewise records a frenzied man healed.

Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, he saves a man about to drown.

## SECTION II. Dead persons restored to life; death deferred; offspring obtained; women in childbirth aided; authority over demons, beasts, and elements; other stupendous miracles; conversions; punishments inflicted on the obstinate; reconciliations; innumerable prodigies of the holy wonder-worker

76. He raised three dead persons. Book VII, chapter 19, mentions one, suddenly dead as punishment for blasphemy against the holy Father. Another raised from the dead is mentioned in Book II of his *Life*, published by John the Hermit. A third—a woman, namely, raised from the dead—is mentioned by Barnabas of Montalbo, *Cistercian History*, Book III, chapter 63. See chapter 30 of the *Medulla of the Life of St. Bernard*.

He calls back one at the point of death and, as it were, draws back one departing, not permitting him to go without a farewell. Book IV, chapter 2, no. 8.

At the holy Father’s command, a dying man postpones death to a more suitable time. Book VII, chapter 9.

He foretells and obtains a child for the barren queen of France. Book IV, chapter 3, no. 18.

Matilda, queen of the English, invokes him while absent and gives birth, though she and the birth were despaired of. Book IV, chapter 1, no. 6.

He marvellously causes a woman pregnant for a whole year to give birth. Chapter 4, no. 22.

There likewise, he delivers another woman in peril during childbirth by blessed water which she drinks.

77. We must now speak of the miraculous power he had over demons. Book II, chapter 3.

“In casting out demons,” says Arnald, Book II, chapter 3, no. 15, “his activity was more frequent.” Likewise: “Those most severely oppressed by the devil he purified with more careful effort.” Chapter 4, no. 24.

Among others individually mentioned, Book I records a demoniac, deaf, blind, and mute man healed, chapter 14, no. 67.

Book II, chapter 2, no. 10, mentions a woman; no. 11, a girl; chapter 3, no. 13, a woman; no. 17, a boy and a woman; at the end of no. 20, a woman; chapter 4, again a woman, namely nos. 21 and 22; no. 23, a man; and no. 24, a woman and several demoniacs delivered.

Book IV, chapter 1, no. 7, records a demoniac healed through the stole used by the holy Father in Mass. Book VI records another.

He freed a monk agitated by the devil in the manner of a demoniac. Book II, no. 7.

Book II, chapter 6, nos. 34 and 35, records a woman marvellously delivered from an incubus demon.

He frees a man from sorceries. Book I, chapter 10, at the end.

Add to these what is narrated in Book II of the *Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, chapter 7, likewise on tradition. When the holy Father was summoned to Rome by Innocent II, at the end of the schism, he miraculously repaired the breakage of a wheel of the cart in which he rode, broken through the wiles of a demon.

78. There follow several miracles unrelated to the grace of healing, from which it will be clear that Bernard miraculously commanded the elements and beasts, and so forth.

While not yet a religious, he miraculously obtained rain. Book I, chapter 3, no. 14.

He miraculously obtains strength for work. Chapter 4, no. 14.

By a miracle he helps his own in their scarcity. Chapter 6, no. 27.

He multiplies provisions. Chapter 10, no. 49.

He writes a letter in rain without being rained upon. Chapter 11, no. 50.

A man unworthy to receive the Eucharist cannot swallow it when the holy Father, who knew him to be unworthy, prays; but after confessing to Bernard, he swallows it without difficulty. No. 51.

He clears an oratory of a multitude of flies by excommunicating them—improperly speaking, of course, as stated elsewhere. No. 52.

He makes an unbroken horse stand still at his feet. Chapter 13, at the end.

He suddenly obtains for a certain Nicholas the gift of tears. Chapter 14, no. 68.

He obtains sudden spiritual consolations for Geoffrey of Péronne, afflicted with excessive sadness. Book IV, chapter 3, no. 16.

He obtains victory for Duke Ranulf. Book II, chapter 7, no. 44.

Likewise for Duke Theobald, at the end of Book II.

Likewise for the Portuguese against the Saracens. Thus the *Medulla of his Life* states.

He miraculously extracts a tooth from the head of Blessed Caesarius. Book IV, chapter 1, no. 1.

79. When a plague was spreading among livestock, he blessed salt and ordered it to be given to them, and the plague immediately ceased. “We have seen and learned,” he says, “that this also occurred in other monasteries,” etc. Chapter 4, no. 28.

Several times, by making the sign of the cross, he marvellously saved either a little hare fleeing and seemingly about to be immediately caught by dogs, or a little bird by hawks. He told those pursuing them that they were trying in vain and could by no means practice such predation while he was present; for the gentle man abhorred it. Book III, chapter 7, no. 27.

He changes water into wine. Book VI, chapter 17.

He miraculously lights a candle without fire. No. 2 of the letter at the end of Book VI.

The cold rigidity of air yields to the softness of his finger. Book VII, chapter 27.

His blessing preserves bread from all corruption for many years; and he promises this to Eskil, archbishop of the Danes, when the latter is insufficiently confident. Book IV, chapter 4, nos. 24 and 25.

80. There follow several conversions accomplished not without miracle. The rest, as Alexander III also testifies in the bull of canonization of the holy Father, are innumerable.

I do not doubt that the conversion of the more than thirty companions with whom he entered Cîteaux was miraculous—at least in some cases. Book I, chapter 3.

Add the conversion of his sister, chapter 6, no. 30.

He converts a company of noble knights through blessed drink and makes them all monks. Chapter 11, no. 55.

He converts the duchess of Lorraine. She had seen Bernard in a dream drawing seven horrible serpents from her womb with his own hands, etc. Chapter 14, no. 68.

He converts Duke William of Aquitaine in a remarkable manner; William afterward died a holy death. Book II, chapter 6, no. 38. Likewise Peter of Pisa, chapter 7, nos. 45 and 46; and Victor the antipope, no. 47.

Likewise, a certain venerable cleric, Mascelin. Book IV, chapter 3, no. 14.

Likewise Henry the German, king of France. Book IV, chapter 3, no. 15.

81. Likewise a certain Andrew, who resisted more strikingly than the others just mentioned. There.

Likewise Geoffrey of Péronne, with several others, no. 16; likewise his father, a noble and powerful man, no. 17.

Likewise the nobleman Henry of Salins. Chapter 8, no. 49.

He converts most obstinate clerics. No. 3 of the letter after Book VI.

Likewise, the people of Albi, most obstinate in the Henrician heresy. There, no. 10.

He orders a monk doubtful about the truth of the Eucharist to communicate in his faith, and converts him. Book VII, chapter 6.

> **Note.** See Preliminary Commentary, no. 111.

He converts various Parisian clerics to religious life. Chapter 13.

He frees a robber from crucifixion and makes him holy. Chapter 15.

He converts his blasphemer, raised from death. Chapter 19.

82. By means of a fish offered to him and first blessed, he makes Alexander, canon and teacher of Cologne, a religious. Chapter 20.

He converts a concubinary priest and an apostate monk. Chapter 21.

> **Note.** See above, no. 50.

Likewise, a monk apostatizing for the third time. Chapter 25.

These are brief remarks concerning those converted by the holy Father, whose conversion should be regarded not so much as an example as as a miracle, as may be seen in the relevant passages. Hence Gerson, doctor and chancellor of Paris, rightly says: “Among miracles, in my judgment, the chief are those which he performed in converting persons who fled with all their might from being converted.” But such persons had for the most part already been listed.

83. It is also established that several who obstinately resisted the holy man were punished by God. Among them: a certain Ramnulf, abbot of Dorat, Book II, chapter 6, no. 33;

Several persons possessed by a demon, no. 36;

Peter of Leon, antipope, chapter 7, no. 47;

His supporter Gerard of Angoulême, chapter 6, no. 39;

Geoffrey, count of Anjou, Book IV, chapter 3, no. 13;

A certain cleric Gerard, Book IV, chapter 4, no. 23;

Likewise Thomas of Beverley, whom the holy Father himself testifies was snatched away by a sudden and dreadful death, Letter 108, no. 3.

I pass over the various reconciliations which he brought about, not without miracle, between private persons and public bodies; between kings and princes; between cities and cities; between these and the Church; between bishops and clergy. Thus he deservedly is called an angel of peace.

84. Count now the miracles individually enumerated, and you will find 676. But that these are few in comparison with those not individually enumerated is now evident from what has been said, and will be confirmed in the following article, in which the Reverend Pastor previously praised shows that St. Bernard’s miracles are innumerable. Manrique, however, writing under the year of Christ 1183, chapter 4, says the following relevant to our subject. An opportunity had been offered him to discuss the *Book of Miracles* discovered by Peter the One-Eyed, abbot; Herbert’s narrative of this matter appears above at the beginning of Book VI, and the cited Manrique also quotes it from the same author:

85. “I find,” he says, “in no. 5 something noteworthy concerning this book, which Ignatius Firminus of Fitero left recorded after comparing it with five others, and with John the Hermit, and likewise with the *Exordium* and Caesarius, whose subject is in part not dissimilar. Beyond the works performed, as it were, in a mass and indiscriminately—just as, when all were to taste bread which Bernard had blessed, and there was a great multitude of loaves, he promised healing—more than 1,170 miracles which the Saint performed are reported among the individual and more special miracles.”

His words, as found in Manrique, run as follows:

> “For I found 221 persons blind from birth given sight; 180 mute persons speaking and deaf persons restored to hearing; 126 lame persons granted the power of walking; 184 maimed persons and persons weak in strength and hands; 125 contracted persons restored to the free use of their limbs; 11 insane persons; finally, three dead persons restored to light and life, and sixty healed of other illnesses.”

[Col. 0977]

## PIOUS DONATIONS MADE TO THE MEN OF CLAIRVAUX IN THE TIME OF ST. BERNARD

Those marked with the numerical references 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10, and 11 are now published for the first time. They were most kindly shared with us by M. RIBIÈRE DE JUBENVILLE, alumnus of the School of Charters.

### I. JOCERANNUS: IMMUNITY FROM TITHES  
(*Cartulary of Clairvaux, Grange-Abbey, IVa.—Year 1121.*)

In the name of the highest and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Jocerannus, by God’s will bishop of the church of Langres, while in the bosom of the mother church’s basilica, together with our archdeacons and many other religious persons, and in the presence also of our lord and father Humbald, primate of Lyons, with his most reverent retinue, we were unanimously deliberating concerning the condition and governance of that same church, the lord Bernard, the devout abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux—which God had revealed in our times—appeared before our gaze, asking and most humbly requesting that we make a privilege, fortified by the protection of our authority, concerning the estate of that place, its immunities, and certain other necessary matters, and solemnly confirm it by the decree of this present charter. Since we resolved gladly to comply with his just and reasonable petition, we took care, by the judgment of so many men, duly to bring into effect whatever he seemed to request as worthy of justice and propriety.

First, therefore, we decree, command, and confirm for that place and for the brothers now present and those who shall succeed them hereafter firm immunity and perpetual liberty in Christ, saving the canonical obedience and subjection due to the bishop of Langres. Concerning their possessions and labours, we command that, wherever in our whole bishopric they and their household may carry on work of stock-raising or agriculture, they shall have their tithes; and that they shall possess those tithes, from the hand of the bishop of Langres, to whom the distribution of tithes properly belongs, for the support and reception of their poor.

If, however, any priest who today possesses those tithes by an earlier grant should refuse to concede this most lawful gift of our dispensation and persist in such hardness of heart, we nevertheless forbid those who succeed him to suppose that those tithes can be given to them by anyone contrary to our authority, or to presume henceforth to receive them. But if it should happen, as God may direct, that the aforesaid brothers work on any lands or places previously granted by the bishop to another church, monastery, abbey, or hospice, let them seek them in brotherly love; and, if they can obtain them, let them have them. If anyone should presume, by rash audacity, to act against the charter of this our ordinance, let him incur the wrath of God and the sentence of condemnation; and unless he quickly comes to repentance, let him endure the infernal punishments with the miserable rich man.

I, Humbald, of the church of Lyons. Sign of Guilencus, dean. Sign of Ayrard, archdeacon. Sign of Guarnerius, archdeacon. Sign: I, Jocerannus, bishop of Langres. Sign: I, Gocelinus, archdeacon of the church of Langres. These things were enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, indiction 5, the third year of Pope Calixtus II, while Louis was king of the Franks and Jocerannus bishop of the church of Langres. I, Durandus, notary of the church of Langres, acting in the place of Fulk the chancellor, wrote, dictated, and read this aloud.

## II. GIFT OF GUIDO, ABBOT OF MOLÈSME

*(Cartulary of Clairvaux, Bellus-Mons, III.—Year 1131.—In the margin: “Guido, abbot of Molèsme, gave everything he possessed in the place called Heis.”)*

It is time, according to the Apostle, to do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith. Accordingly I, Guido, by God’s forbearance abbot of the monastery of Molèsme, with the praise and consent of our chapter, most devoutly approve and grant to the church of Clairvaux and its brothers, to possess forever, absolutely everything that we have hitherto possessed and that belonged to our right in the place called Heis, provided, however, that an annual rent of twelve pence be established, which that church shall take care to pay ours each year about the feast of Saint Remigius.

In order that this gift of our devotion may remain permanently unshaken for the aforesaid brothers and may be an example of charity to all others, I commit it to writing and secure it with our seal. Sign of David, prior; sign of Aymon, subprior; sign of Martin, third prior; sign of Raingerius, chamberlain; sign of Robert, sub-chamberlain; sign of Gualterius, cellarer; sign of Robert, sub-cellarer; sign of Peter of Raveriis; sign of Enjorrannus, chaplain.

This was enacted at Molèsme in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, while King Louis reigned, Wilencus was bishop of Langres, Hugh was duke of Burgundy, and Theobald was count.

## III. REGULAR CANONS REPLACE SECULAR CLERGY AT THE CHURCH OF ST. LUPUS

*(CAMUSAT, Promptuarium sacrarum antiquitatum Tricassinae dioecesis, fol. 297.—Year 1135.—Compared with the original.)*

[lacuna] It happened that Count Theobald, of blessed memory, after consulting religious men—Hugh, bishop of Auxerre; Hatto, bishop of Troyes; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of good memory; and William, abbot of the aforesaid Saint-Martin—carefully considered how he might restore to religious observance the church of the aforesaid St. Lupus, which through the negligence of certain persons seemed and was said to have grown slack in divine worship. It pleased the aforesaid prince and religious men, with the consent of all the canons of St. Lupus, that, upon the departure of the secular brethren then presiding over the church, regular canons should be put in their place, so that what the former performed less honourably, the latter might serve the Lord more solemnly and with greater devotion.

Therefore, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1135, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November], the aforesaid religious men selected certain brothers from the church of St. Martin and transferred them to the church of Blessed Lupus, to serve the Lord there as had been arranged. They remained there without an abbot of their own for one year, six months, and twelve days, subject to the governance and oversight of William, abbot of St. Martin. In 1137, on the second Ides of June [12 June], Gerard, prior of St. Martin, was appointed and set over the aforesaid brothers as abbot, a man of remarkable simplicity and ignorant of secular affairs.

## IV. IMMUNITY FROM TITHES

*(Cartulary of Clairvaux, Campigny, XXXIV.—Year 1136.)*

Let it be known to those present and future that Lord Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, sought and obtained from Ebrard, abbot of Molèsme, and his chapter, the tithe on the labours of the brothers of Clairvaux from whatever they cultivated within the bounds of the parish of Champigniac, which was said in ancient times to have belonged by right to the church of Molèsme. It was therefore granted and confirmed by these letters that neither the monks of Molèsme nor anyone acting for them should ever receive tithes from the brothers’ labour or livestock, however these might be produced for the use of the church of Clairvaux, whether by monks, lay brothers, or hired workers; rather, the men of Clairvaux should hold them forever, without objection or lawsuit.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, in the common chapter of Molèsme, in the presence of both aforesaid abbots. Present among the persons of the church were Atho, prior; Peter and Fredericus, subpriors; and the whole convent.

## V. CHARTER OF KING ALFONSO

*(Journal de Trévoux, August 1739, p. 1875.—Year 1142.)*

In the name of God.

Since it is fitting that every faithful person make God’s ministers participants in the goods bestowed upon him by the supreme Giver, so that through them we may be made participants in heavenly goods, therefore I, Aldephonsus, by divine mercy king of the Portuguese, newly made king with God’s help, because I recognize myself as more indebted than all others, desire to offer myself and all that is mine to the Most High, so that both I and my successors, who are to reign forever, may acknowledge that they hold the kingdom from the hand of the Lord, who has now delivered it to me, in order that with steadfast heart and perfect charity I might defend the Christian faith against the wrongs of unbelievers and enrich the holy Church from the revenues of the kingdom, so that the kingdom may thus be holy, dear to God, and established forever.

And because I have already made myself and all that is mine tributary to Blessed Peter and his successors, now desiring also to have the Blessed Mother of God as my advocate before God, with the consent of my vassals, who established me upon the royal throne without foreign assistance, I place and decree as placed under the protection, defence, and patronage of Blessed Mary of Clairvaux myself, my kingdom, my people, and my successors. I ordain and command all and each of my successors who lawfully enter upon the inheritance of this kingdom to grant each year to the same church of Holy Mary of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order, situated in the kingdom of France in the diocese of Langres, fifty maravedís of tested, good, acceptable gold, in the manner of a fief and vassalage.

If anyone of the aforesaid order should enter our dominion, or should build a monastery there, the persons and possessions of such a monastery shall be under the king’s protection and patronage, so that no one may molest, trouble, disturb, or despoil them of their goods. If this should occur, they shall be restored to their former liberty at whatever hour, time, or moment this can be done with greater advantage. Therefore the goods of such monasteries and persons shall be as royal goods, and the king shall have the same care for them that he ought to have for his own.

But if any king or tyrant—whom we do not believe will be born from our loins—should harass the aforesaid persons or take away their goods, let him understand that he is usurping not my inheritance or theirs, but that of the Virgin; and, as faithless to his lord, under whose protection we commit our kingdom, let him be deprived of that same kingdom, and let his seed not flourish upon the earth. Let the brothers in the said monastery of Clairvaux and others of their order devoutly commend the condition of our kingdom to God, assist my soul and those of my parents by masses and vigils, and restore the altar of Blessed Mary from the fief or vassalage. Lord Abbot Bernard and his successors in perpetuity shall possess this fief forever on the day of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

And therefore, Virgin Mother of my Lord Jesus Christ, in whose praise this order shines forth as established, I, your humble servant Aldephonsus, king of the Portuguese, ask that you defend my kingdom from the Moors, enemies of the cross of your Son; preserve this crown free from every external dominion; and strengthen upon the royal throne descendants of mine who will be faithful servants and providers of the fief.

If anyone should attempt anything against this testimony of vassalage and fief, if he is a vassal, let him be expelled from our kingdom; but if—may the Lord not permit it—he is a king, let him be accursed by us, not counted among our stock, stripped of every dignity by the Lord God who gave us the kingdom, conquered by his enemies, and buried in hell with Judas the traitor.

The charter was made in the church of Lamego, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April], in the year 1142. I, King Aldephonsus. Egas, president of the court, confirms. Peter Pelaides, standard-bearer of the court, confirms. Evas Ropinias, prefect of Colom., confirms. Pelagius de Saura confirms. Gondisalvus de Saura attests. Rosendus Alvar attests. Alphonsus Egea attests.

## VI. CHARTER OF QUEEN SANCIA

*(MANRIQUE, Annals of the Cistercian Order, II, p. 87.)*

In the name of the Holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good”; and it is not enough to refrain from evil unless what is good is done. Likewise: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”; “he who fears God will do good”; and “it shall go well in the end for one who does good.” Therefore I, Sancia, sister of Alfonso, emperor of the Spains, instructed and admonished by these and other examples, of my own free will and under no compulsion, for the redemption of my soul and of those of my parents, give to you, Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the estate of Saint Peter of Spina and the estate of Saint Mary of Aborridos: namely, lands, vineyards, meadows, springs, cultivated and uncultivated mountains, with entrances and exits on both sides, that is, with all the boundaries belonging to them, in order that there, with my aid, you may build a monastery in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ and his Mother, in which your monks and members of your order, continually attending, may beseech God for their sins, mine, those of my parents, and those of all the faithful, both living and dead.

But if anyone, whether from among my own people or outsiders, impelled by wicked greed, should wish to invalidate this gift of mine, he shall by no means be able to bring this about; but if it should happen—may it not!—let him first restore all the aforesaid things twofold, and then pay to the king, or to whomever you shall entrust with the assertion of your right, a fine of one thousand pounds of the purest gold; and moreover let him be accursed, and, like Dathan and Abiram, let the earth swallow him, and let him suffer the pains of hell with Judas the traitor. Amen.

This charter of gift was made on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January], in the era 1134, while Emperor Alfonso, with Empress Berengaria, ruled in León, Toledo, Zaragoza, Córdoba, and all Spain.

I, the aforesaid Queen Sancia, who ordered this charter to be written, confirmed it before these witnesses:

Lord Peter, bishop of Segovia, confirms. Lord Loysius, bishop of León, confirms. Lord Peter, bishop of the see of Palencia, confirms. Gutter Fernandes confirms. Martinus Moniez confirms. Nicolaus Pelagii confirms. Count Pontius of Cabrera confirms. Count Manric confirms. Count Amergot confirms. Cid, witness, confirms. Belid, witness, confirms. Duaya, witness, confirms. All the witnesses of my court, beholders and hearers of this grant.

## VII. CHARTER OF THEODERIC, COUNT OF FLANDERS

*(Cartulary of Clairvaux, Counts of Flanders, I.—Year 1142.)*

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Theoderic, by God’s grace count of the Flemings, considering in good will the welfare and peace of churches, have judged it fitting that I should agree with the wishes of religious persons and grant assent to their just petitions; and I have resolved to bring this into public effect, considering it not merely honourable but fruitful for my soul in God.

Accordingly, responding devoutly and favourably to the pious requests of the venerable and holy-minded Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, deservedly to be commended through the ages in his own right, I have wished and granted in perpetuity that throughout the whole land and at all crossings under my lordship, county, or power, the abbey of Clairvaux and all abbeys descended from Clairvaux, or yet to descend from it, and also those proceeding from the abbeys which themselves proceeded from the monastery of Clairvaux, shall be wholly free, in going and returning, from toll and passage-dues. In order that this may remain valid, stable, and undisturbed, I have ordered it confirmed by the impression of my seal, by my authority, and by the subscriptions of my barons.

Witnesses of this grant: Roger, provost of Bruges; William, castellan of Saint-Omer; Rodulf, castellan of Bruges; Gislebert, castellan of Bergues; Baldwin of Bailleul; Anselm of Bailleul; Theoderic, chamberlain; Walter Gonela; Hugh of Fareseles; Robert, abbot of the Dunes; Brother Osto and Brother Robert, Knights Templar.

Enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, indiction 5, concurrent 3, epact 22.

*(Original on parchment, preserved in the archives of Aube. The seal is missing; it hung by silk cords.—On the back one reads in twelfth-century writing:)*

> “Of Theoderic, count of Flanders, concerning the liberty of the abbeys of Clairvaux.”
>
> “Charter of Theoderic, count of Flanders, concerning immunity from customary dues throughout his whole dominion.”

*[Col. 0984B] And in fifteenth-century writing:*

> “Counts of Flanders, first.”

## VIII. MIROSLAW, ONE OF THE MAGNATES OF BOHEMIA, AT THE URGING OF HENRY, BISHOP OF MORAVIA, FOUNDS AND ENDOWS THE CISTERCIAN MONASTERY OF SEDLEC

*(BOCZEK, Diplomatic Codex of Moravia, I, 221.—Year 1143.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, future as well as present, that while the most serene Lord Vladislaus, duke of the Bohemians, was reigning with his most noble wife Lady Gertrude, a certain magnate of Bohemia named Miroslaus, divinely prompted partly by fear and partly by love, wishing to provide for his salvation, and having often heard from men wiser and more advanced in years that neither the unity of charity can subsist without the worship of true religion nor service pleasing to God be offered, resolved to love religious persons and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace.

Having therefore considered the varied ways of life of holy men according to their different professions, yet all tending toward the dwelling-places of the one heavenly Father’s house, he chose certain brothers of the Cistercian Order to procure for him mediators with Christ. As this pious and holy intention grew warmer day by day through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he obtained for himself a community of brothers to be committed from the cloister of Waldsassen. The venerable Abbot Gerlacus, inclined by this request toward holy observance, sent a community of brothers into Bohemia. Having received them with holy desire, the aforesaid Lord Miroslaus, with the consent and attestation of the aforesaid venerable duke of Bohemia Vladislaus, with Otto, bishop of Prague, confirming by canonical authority, and with the urging and attestation of the venerable Lord Henry, bishop of the Moravians, freely gave in perpetuity to God and to Saint Mary, Mother of God, for the use of the aforesaid brothers, the place called Sedlec with all its appurtenances.

First he established that monastic order should be observed there inviolate in perpetuity according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian fathers. Then, when the suitable time came and divine grace assisted, a church fit for divine service and appropriate to that order was founded at Sedlec. From the beginning of its foundation, the following possessions, whose names are recorded below, were freely conferred upon it for the use of the church itself and the brothers serving God there, without anyone’s objection: Solnic, Hothonici, Podollani, with all their appurtenances; Gradische with water, meadows, and woodland; Sdebudici; at Pobor, a manor with land; Odolen and the land of Donatus; Bilani, Maleionici, Lubenici, Glusow, and Cacin, with all their appurtenances as far as the stream flowing around the forest of Porra.

Moreover, in order that a better end might follow this good beginning, the aforesaid Miroslaus, earnestly intent on providing thereafter also for the aforesaid church, having only one son, ordained that if this son should die without a male heir, or if thereafter the line of sons should fail in an heir, then, without objection from kinsmen or blood-relatives, his whole inheritance should revert to the use of the church at Sedlec. Dersislaus also, son of Miroslaus’s sister, having no son, so disposed of his inheritance.

Inflamed by divine love, therefore, both the venerable duke and the reverend fathers, Lord Otto, bishop of Prague, and the venerable Henry, bishop of the Moravians—by whose prudent counsel Bohemia was governed and adorned—decreed that no person whatsoever might rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away, diminish, or in any manner invade its possessions, or harass them with vexations; but that both the place itself and its possessions, and everything whatsoever that the church of that place possessed from the beginning, or might in the future acquire, by the grant of bishops, the bounty of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, should be preserved whole and remain inviolate.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person should hereafter attempt to disturb the aforesaid church or its possessions, let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the wrongdoing committed. But upon all who protect the often-mentioned church or its possessions may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal blessedness. In order that this charter of ordinance and privilege may remain valid and free of every ambiguity, the often-mentioned faithful servants of Christ—the duke, namely, and the venerable father bishops—confirmed it with the marks of their seals.

## IX. GIFT OF HATTO, BISHOP OF TROYES

*(Montieramey.—Years 1122–45.)*

I, Hato, by God’s grace bishop of the church of Troyes, to the beloved sons Guido, abbot, and the monks of Montieramey, in perpetuity. The authority of our office exhorts us to cherish religious places and to sustain from the goods of the Church the brothers dedicated there to divine service. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your prayers out of pious regard, we have given to you and your monastery, with the approval of Manasses of Villemaur, our archdeacon, the old cemetery of Clareio and the chapel which is in that cemetery, at the request of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of good memory.

This is granted, however, on the condition and understanding that the priest of Clareio shall never receive anything there; rather, what those living there offer, or what those dying there leave, shall belong exclusively to the monks. Present at this gift were reputable persons: the aforesaid Manasses of Villemaur, archdeacon; Manasses, archdeacon of Rumilly; Odo, archdeacon; Falco, archdeacon; Gibuinus, cantor and archdeacon; and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, at whose request all these things were done and granted.

*(Original on parchment, without date; written on the back: “Concerning the old cemetery of Clareio given to us.”)*

*(The seal is missing; it hung by a double parchment tag. Preserved in the archives of Aube, Montieramey collection.)*

## X. CONFIRMATION BY THEOBALD, COUNT OF BLOIS, OF THE GIFTS OF JOBERT OF LA FERTÉ

*(Cartulary of Clairvaux, Counts of Champagne, V.a.—Year 1145.)*

I, Theobald, count of Blois, wish it to be known to all persons, present and future, that Jobert of La Ferté, being about to depart for Jerusalem, granted to God and to Saint Mary of Clairvaux everything that he possessed in the village of Petrecini, retaining absolutely nothing either for himself or for his heir, except that, if he should return from Jerusalem, he shall receive into his hand, if he wishes, and hold during his life, as long as he wishes, that share of the common property which he divided with three other lords of the same village—namely lordship over the people and jurisdiction. After his death, however, this same share shall return into the hand and possession of the aforesaid church.

But all the remainder—that is, whatever he held as his own property either in the village or its district and did not hold in common with the other three—whether he lived or died, he gave to that same church to possess forever, without any revocation. At La Ferté he invested Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, with this gift, with the approval of Gertrude, his wife, in the presence of Lord Godfrey, bishop of Langres, and ourselves. I, moreover, from whose fief it was held, approved the same gift with Henry, my son, and therefore ordered this charter to be drawn up.

Witnesses of this gift are Hilduinus of Vendœuvre, Walter of Bernon, Peter Bursaldus, knights of the count; also Hugh, lord of Beaumont, his brother-in-law; Roger of Orgiis; Wiard of Villa; and John, mayor of the same village.

This was done at La Ferté in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1145, while Louis, son of Louis, was reigning as king of the Franks.

*(Original on parchment, preserved in the archives of Aube. The seal is missing. It hung by a double tag.—On the back one reads: “Charter concerning the gifts of Josbert of La Ferté; seal of Count Theobald. Counts of Champagne: fifth.”)*

## XI. GIFT OF FREDERIC, SURNAMED “THE SAVIOUR”

*(Cartulary of Clairvaux, originals. Common charters, II.—Year 1147.)*

Let it be made known to our posterity that Fredericus, surnamed Salvator, with the approval of his wife Hersende, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything he possessed in the district of Gundree Hispaniae, retaining nothing. Moreover, both in other places and in that same district, he granted to the brothers of that place everything which they could either already have acquired, or might hereafter acquire, from those who held of him, from his fief. Witnesses are Hugh of Bugeio; Pontius of Saint-Lupus; Hugh, servant; Odo, his son. Leiardis, the daughter, and her husband Frederius, approved this same gift; witnesses being Jheremia, brother of Frederius; Frederius, their nephew; Letardus; and Guido, chaplain.

Likewise, in the same district, Drogo Crassus, with the approval of his present wife and his sons Wicardus, Milo, Guido, and Agno, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything he possessed or was held from him.

Hugh of Villa, with the approval of his wife Heldiard and his sons Guido, Everard, and Bencelin, and his daughters Gertrude, Altrude, and Emmelina, with Agno, Lambert, and Fulco as witnesses; and Rainald, son of Everard, son of Aalerm, with the approval of his mother Lezvid and daughters Lescelina, Emmelina, and Gertrude, granted to the same monastery everything they possessed in the same district; witnesses again Agno, Lambert, and Fulco. Guido of Wangionis-rivulet, from whose fief that possession descended, approved this gift. Likewise, he granted whatever the brothers might acquire from his fief in other places; his wife Aalaydis likewise approved this. Witnesses are Guido, prior of Saint Stephen; Odo of Clement Meadow; Martin of the House of God; Everard, son of Garengerius; Lebaudus, king.

Likewise, in the district of the village, Guiardus of Juvencourt, with the consent of his brothers Philip and Arlebald, freely gave the monastery of Clairvaux the share of allod that he possessed, and divested himself of the common property he held in the village and in the inheritance of Juvencourt. Witnesses are Milo Mahart, Haimo Viveus, and Agno Viridis.

Richard and Paganus, brothers of Villa, gave to God and Saint Mary of Clairvaux everything they possessed from Airablo as far as the Aube, and thence towards Clairvaux from the wood as far as the Aube, together with everything that we possessed either from their heirs or from their men. Their mother Beatrix approved this gift, as did their sisters Luca and Belosa, Rainerius, son of Luca, Adelina, Richard’s wife, Rainaldus, his son, and Beatrix, his daughter, surnamed Sylvestris. Witnesses are Rainerius of La Ferté, Guido son of Odelinus, and Durandus the Miller. Egidius, son of Rainaldus, made a similar gift from his share, and offered it by placing one book upon the altar. Witnesses are Rainerius of La Ferté; Guido, son of Odelinus; Rainaldus of Petrecini; and his son Guido.

Maria, daughter of Humbert of Molenvilla, approved the gift which her father had made to the monastery of Clairvaux in the pastures of Villa. Witnesses are Ricoldus, Aimo, and Bernerius of Molenvilla.

Let it also be made known to our posterity that Josbertus of La Ferté, son of Isobertus Rufus, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux, with the approval of his wife Gertrude, everything he possessed at Petrecini and everything he possessed in the district of Petrecini. Witnesses are Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to whom and into whose hand this gift was made; Everard of Brecons; Aimo Bocardus; Paganus of Villa; and Gaufridus Felenia. The same Isobertus also granted to the aforesaid monastery all the gifts which his father had given, and whatever the brothers of that place could acquire or had acquired from him or his heirs, from his land and his fief, together with all assents throughout his whole land, with the approval of the aforesaid [wife; name omitted in the source]. Witnesses are Hugh of Beaumont, brother of the aforesaid Gertrude; Hilduinus of Vendœuvre; and Count Theobald, who approved this, since it derived from his fief.

Clarembaudus of Capis, with the approval of his wife Aaliz, gave the monastery of Clairvaux whatever the brothers of that place might acquire from his fief. Witnesses are Anculfus of Capis and Gauterius of Supraponte. After Clarembaudus’s death, his sons Clarembaudus and Hugh Rapina granted the same; witnesses Hilduinus of Vendœuvre and Gaufridus Furnerius.

Walterius, son of Walterius Pinetus, and Henry, his brother, son of Freerius, with the approval of the same Freerius, Henry’s father, and of Vilricus [wife or associate of Walterius; reading uncertain], gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything they possessed at Petrecini and in its district, retaining nothing; and they granted that they would not take throughout the whole land of Clairvaux the toll which they took at Petrecini. Hugh, son of Freerius of Brion, made a similar gift from his own share; witnesses Rainaldus of Petrecini, Guiardus son of Odelinus, and Rainaldus Chardon of La Ferté. Hugh, viscount of La Ferté, from whose fief this was held, approved these gifts, with the approval of his wife Ildeberga and both their sons Erebaud, Roric, and John, and their daughters Lancenna and Isabel. The same Hugh also granted that, if any legal challenge arose concerning these gifts, he would settle it peacefully.

Witnesses to the aforesaid gifts of Walterius and Henry, to Freerius’s approval, and to the approval of Hugh the viscount, are Bartholomeus Coquilla, Gonterius of Buxeriis, Rainerius of La Ferté, and Guiardus of Capis. Witnesses to the approval of the viscount’s wife and of his sons and daughters are Rainerius of La Ferté, Guiardus of Capis, Everard of Brecons, Garinus, and Aimo Viridis. Count Theobald and his son Henry, from whom the aforesaid viscount held, also approved this. And in order that it might stand more firmly, at the request of Hugh the viscount, Count Theobald undertook that, if at any time a legal challenge should arise from these gifts and the viscount could not suppress it, Count Theobald would hold in his own hands all the remaining fief which the viscount held from him until he had completely settled it.

Adelina, wife of Bartholomeus Coquilla, with the approval of her son Guicardus, her daughter Gertrude, her husband Bartholomeus himself, her father Hugh of Ostrecort, and his son Auno, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything she possessed at Petrecini and throughout all its boundaries, into the hand of Godfrey, bishop of Langres. Witnesses are Hugh, dean of Belona; Everard, priest; Rainerius of Rocha; and Hugh Chavaucheia. Matoldis, Adelina’s mother, and Hugh, Adelina’s son, approved this. Witnesses are Hugh, dean; Everard, priest; Morellus, knight of Clermont; and Rollanus of Petrecini.

Guilelmus Guarescous of Covlenz, with the approval of his wife Isabel, from whose inheritance this came, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything he possessed in the district of Petrecini, retaining nothing; his son Rainaldus approved it. Witnesses are Hugh, his squire; Radulfus of Covlenz; and Radulfus, his son, canon of Langres. Emmelina, Isabel’s mother, and Ilbertus, son of the same Emmelina, approved this gift. Witnesses are Rainerius, Emmelina’s brother, and many others who were there. Thomas, Isabel’s brother, likewise approved it in the presence of Godefidus [sic], bishop of Langres, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; witnesses Ebrard of La Ferté, his son Guido, and Giremus of Britinniacum.

Erbertus of Bar-sur-Seine gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything he possessed in the village of Petrecini or in the district of that village, retaining nothing, together with everything there held from him. His brother Thomas, Thomas’s wife Ildiardis, and Thomas, his son, approved this. His other brothers, Humbertus and Hagano, and his nephew Guiardus also approved it. Witnesses are Guido, count of Bar-sur-Seine; his son Milo; Milo of Valvurio; and Richard of Cacenniacum. Rocelinus of Vendœuvre, his son Gaufridus, and Hulduinus, brother of Roscelinus, from whom he held, approved it. Witnesses to this approval are Radulfus, chaplain of the count; Martin, prior of Radulf’s castle; Odo of Mont-Omer; Josceranus Rigandus of Pringerium. Afterwards Richard, son of Thomas, approved this gift; witnesses Guiardus, son of Everard of Vacua Silva; Deodardus; and Seguino.

Stephanus Raerius, with the approval of his wife Lucia, from whose inheritance this came, and with the approval of his sons and daughters Hugh, Guido, Henry, Gertrude, and Floretia, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything he possessed in the district of Petrecini, retaining nothing. Witnesses are Simon, son of Isobertus; Gontard of La Ferté; Roger, Stephen’s brother; Stephen, chaplain; and Olbertus, chaplain of Blois.

Aimo Bocardus gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever he possessed at Petrecinum, in the territory of Petrecinum, without any reservation. Rainerius of Gronai made a like gift from his share in the same village and territory, with the assent of his wife Ascelina, their son Lambert, and their daughters Ildiardis and Ermengard. Witnesses: Milo Crassus and Scotus Venator. All this was granted by Goriardus, his brother, [Col. 0990B] and Bruna, wife of Aimo himself. Likewise Bencelina gave to the same monastery whatever she possessed there, on the same terms, with the assent of her son Simon and his wife Galiena. Guiardus of Capis made the same gift from his share. Witnesses to all these acts: Agno Viridis, Bartholomeus Coquilla, Milo Crassus, Everardus of the Vill, and Landricus. Drogo made the same gift from his share; witnesses: Guiardus of Capis and Seguinus of Vacua Silva. Peter of Aissi likewise made the same gift from his share, with the assent of his wife Abelina; witnesses: Erbertus, priest, and Guiardus of the Vill.

Marco of Vegniac gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever he possessed at Petrecinum, without any reservation, with the assent of his wife [Col. 0990C] Emmelina and his son Henry; witnesses: Hugh of Veniac, Garnerius, and Sirebellus of Bar-sur-Seine. The gift made by Marcus was also made, from his own share, by Milo Crassus of Firmitas, Marcus’s son-in-law, with the assent of Milo’s wife Supplicia and his son Marcus. Ermengardis, Supplicia’s sister, consented to the gift of Marcus and Milo. Witnesses: Rainerius of Firmitas, Hugh of Confinio, and Guiardus, son of Odelinus of Firmitas. Milo’s other children, Henry and Sera, also consented to his gift; witnesses: Hugh of Veniac, Garnerius, and Sirebellus of Bar-sur-Seine.

Rolannus of Petrecinum gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever he possessed in the same village and its bounds, without reservation, with the assent of his wife [Col. 0990D] Richildis; his sons Clement and Bernard and another Bernard; his brother Paganus; and Anscherius, the latter’s nephew. Witness: Silvester, together with the two above-mentioned men, Paganus and Anscherius.

Richardus and Paganus gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever they possessed from Petrecinum as far as Ermeniorii, which lies beside Gaudricus’s hill, as divided by the Roman road; that is, whatever they possessed in the land of Jurvilla and Warencemont. Their mother Beatrix approved this gift, as did their sisters Luca and Belosa; Rainerius, Luca’s son; Adelina, Richardus’s wife; Rainaldus, his son; and Beatrix, his daughter, surnamed Silvestra. Witnesses: Rainerius of Firmitas, Guido son of Odelinus, and Durannus the Miller. Egidius, [Col. 0991A] son of Rainaldus, made a like gift from his own share and offered it by placing one book upon the altar. Witnesses: Rainerius of Firmitas; Guido son of Odelinus; Rainaldus of Petrecinum; and his son Guido.
