Hugh Bouez of Jovencort gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever he possessed in the territory of Juvilla and Warencemont, without any reservation, with the assent of his wife Bertha, surnamed Poma, their sons Odo and Hugh, and their daughter Goncelina; witnesses: Stephen, priest, and Guido son of Odelinus.

Odo and Peter, sons of Milo Debois, with the assent of their mother Dameron and their sister Agnes, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever they possessed in the land of Jurvilla and Warencemont, without any reservation. Raherius approved this gift, as did his wife Bona Amica, their sons Guido and Milo, and their daughter Magaleh. Witnesses: Theobald, nephew of the priest; [Col. 0991B] Walterius; Iterius of Beloun; Hugh; and Peter.

Simon of Chameon gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever he possessed in the valley of the Dead Spring as far as Emmauricus’s spring, and whatever he possessed on the hill called Middle Hill, with the assent of Hilbertus of Bar, from whose fief he held it. Witnesses: Isobertus Rufus and Rainerius of Pulleries. At another time Odo, Simon’s brother, granted the share which he possessed in Middle Hill. Witnesses: Henry of Aconvilla; Gibertus the Carpenter; and Peter, son of Henry.

Roger of Esclantia, with the assent of his sons Hildierius and Hugh, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever the monks had cleared in the wood and [Col. 0991C] at Acunvilla. He also granted a certain portion of woodland beside the Dead Spring which had not yet been cleared, and granted that we might have all our woodland rights (*assantiae*) everywhere in the remaining wood, except cultivation of the land. The countess made a like gift from her own share, with the assent of her husband Odo. For these gifts, however, an annual rent of twelve denarii of Troyes currency shall be paid to them; this rent must be paid to their steward at Acunvilla between the Kalends of October and the Kalends of November. The above-mentioned Roger, from whom she held it, and Roger’s sons Hildierius and [Col. 0992A] Hugh, approved the countess’s gift. Stephen of Grangia, from whom Roger held it, also approved the gift of each of them. Hilbertus of Bar, from whom the said Stephen held it, gave his approval. Roger and his sons, Stephen of Grangia, and Hilbertus of Bar also agreed that, should any claim arise concerning these gifts, they themselves would entirely extinguish it. These gifts were made into the hand of Guido the monk, in the presence of Dominicus, provost of Bar. Witnesses: Radulfus, dean of Bar; Hildierius, master of the House of God; Falco, Herbertus’s son-in-law; and Galterius Scotus. Gaufridus, son of Herbertus, also approved all these acts. Witnesses: Radulfus, dean of Bar; Hildierius, master of the House of God; Odo Rufus; Lambertus; and Girardus of Langres.

Gilo, son of Rainaldus of the Vill, gave us a meadow beside the bank of the Aube called Croipratum, and approved everything which his father had given us in the territory of [Col. 0992B] Gondea Hispania: namely, Girard’s meadow, Hugh’s meadow, Garinus’s meadow, and all other things which we hold from his father. Witnesses: Remigius, chaplain of the Vill; Guiardus, son of Odelinus; and Engelrannus the smith.

Gaufridus Felenia gave Berold’s meadow, in the territory of the Vill, to the monastery of Clairvaux, with the assent of his brother-in-law Airardus; witnesses: Peter Ventarius, Arbertus, and Bernard. Lancenna, wife of Airaudus, granted this gift, with the assent of their children Girardus, Rainerius, Guiardus, and their daughter Galia; witnesses: Bernard, mayor; Guiardus, priest; and Theodericus.

I, Godefridus, by the grace of God bishop of Langres, approve the entire charter on this page, strengthen it with my own seal, and confirm it in perpetuity to the monastery of Clairvaux. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1147, in the reign of Louis, son of Louis, king of the Franks. The sign of Jocelin, archdeacon. The sign of Pontius, archdeacon. The sign of Warnerius, archdeacon. The sign of Guiardus, archdeacon. The sign of Fulco, archdeacon. The sign of Humbertus, dean.

(Original on parchment.—Red wax seal suspended by a double tag.—Archives of Aube.)

# Various Additions to the Books on the Life and Deeds of St Bernard, Illustrating the Beginnings, Origin, and Posthumous Glory of Saint Bernard, and the Clairvaux and Cistercian Antiquities of the Sacred Cistercian Order

# The Greater Exordium of the Cistercian Order

[Col. 0993]

On the antiquity and very great authority of this book, Fr Chrysostom Henriquez writes as follows in the *Menologium of the Cistercian Order*, Apparatus, chapter IV:

> The foundation stone, as it were, of all the histories of our Order, and a work of the highest authenticity, is that book which we call the *Exordium of the Cistercian Order*. For its venerable antiquity is admired not only by us, members of the Cistercian family, but all standard authors hold it in high esteem. For experts in ecclesiastical antiquities everywhere find in it distinguished testimonies by which to establish and confirm their opinions and histories. For my own part, whenever I turn over this book, I cannot sufficiently admire its piety, the dignity of its style, the weight of its thoughts, and the wonderful events related there. And I would venture to say that, in its kind, it is among the greater and more precious treasures enjoyed by the Church, and ought to be esteemed as such by the faithful.

The author—or rather compiler—of this book, following the example and modesty of the ancient Fathers, suppresses his own name and attributes everything that he writes to the diligence and useful labour of others, as he expressly acknowledges in Book I, chapter 2:

> I think it worthwhile to set down for future generations how the Cistercian Order took its beginning, and with what abundant blessing of God’s grace it was endowed from its very outset; as holy men, who were founders of this sacred religious life from its beginning, have partly handed it down to us in written records, and as we have partly learned it through the reports of our elders. Thus those whom divine grace may deem worthy to call to our Order in ages to come, if they judge it worthy to read this page of our littleness, which we have laboured over for their consolation, may consider from what noble royal breast they were nourished, and blush to be found degenerate sons, etc.

It is consequently evident that the author of the said book is not expressly identified for us. Yet it is certain that, whoever he was, he was aided by the writings of Archbishop Herbert, Prior John, and the monk Goswin, although he does not name them, but speaks generally; as he says in Book VI, chapter 10:

> What we have received as having been written here and there by diligent men, we have brought together into one whole, for a clearer knowledge of events and a greater benefit to readers.

Although his name is entirely unknown to us, at least this is clear: he was a monk of Clairvaux, as he himself testifies in these words, Book I, chapter 2:

> If anyone is troubled that we have mentioned only the elders of Clairvaux and not also those of Cîteaux, let him know that we, as members of the Church of Clairvaux, have been able to investigate more intimately and effectively the sacred endeavours of our own elders. Nor do the things which we have written concerning the sincere manner of life or blessed end of a few men, in fulfilment of our promise, prejudice the holiness of the innumerable servants of God who, both at Cîteaux and throughout the whole Order, have valiantly endured their spiritual contests.

Although he was not a disciple of the holy Father Bernard, it is nevertheless certain that he knew some of Bernard’s spiritual sons and was intimately associated with them, relying upon their accounts for what he writes about the deeds and lives of the saints. For, speaking of blessed Raynald in Book II, chapter 13, he says:

> One of them replied, a religious man, formerly abbot of Foigny, who was more deeply acquainted with the secrets of the servant of God—that is, Bernard—and from whom we also learned these things that have been related.

He was also intimately associated with the blessed Gerard, abbot of Longpont, a disciple of the same Bernard, as is read in Book II, chapter 10:

> These things were communicated to us by Lord Gerard, abbot of Longpont, who, being one of the elders of Clairvaux, was eager carefully to investigate the words and deeds of the holy Father.

Near the end of Book VI, chapter 10, he adds:

> There also we saw elders among the disciples of Saint Bernard, venerable for the gravity of their morals, the integrity of their religious life, prudence, and simplicity.

He saw the golden age in which such perfection flourished in the Order, and he was able to enjoy—and did enjoy—the familiarity and presence of so many holy Fathers, who strictly observed that original vigour and rigour of our Order in which it had been established by its first founders. The same author testifies to this in the final book of his work, saying:

> Moreover, after that illustrious Valley [Clairvaux] had sent its first and most illustrious abbot, after one [read: eight—most aptly corrected by Master Dom Ignatius de Ybero, perpetual abbot of Fitero, in the first edition of the *Greater Exordium*: Pamplona, 1631, folio; editorial note] and thirty years, to the palace of the heavenly Emperor, so that he might now be the more powerful in helping because he beholds more closely the face of the supreme Majesty, the vigour of holy religious life continued unimpaired in that House through his holy successors, concerning whose virtues we have understood something from above; as, in the times of the venerable and God-worthy Lord Peter and his successor Lord Warnerius, later bishop of Langres, divine favour granted us to establish.

From this it is apparent at what time he lived at Clairvaux. Finally, I say that this book had not several compilers but one, and that the same man began and completed this work, as he himself clearly states. For after saying in Book I, chapter 2, “I think it worthwhile to describe more carefully for future generations,” etc., he adds in the final chapter of the whole work, “As we declared in the beginning of this volume,” etc. Thus he refers to what he had promised to write at the beginning of the work, and to the order which he had proposed to observe.

[Col. 0995]

# The Greater Exordium of the Cistercian Order

(*Library of the Cistercian Fathers*, Fr Bertrand Tissier, Bonfontaine, 1660, folio, vol. I, p. 13.)

[Note.]

In the manuscript codex of the abbey of Foigny which I use, this title or inscription of the following work appears:

> Here begins the account of the beginning of the Cistercian Order: how our Fathers, having departed from the monastery of Molesme in order to recover the purity of the Order according to the tenor of the Rule of Saint Benedict, founded the fruitful Church of Cîteaux, which is the mother of us all; for from it, as from a most pure spring, the streams of all the churches of our Order have flowed forth; and concerning certain venerable persons, conspicuous in every form of religious life, who flourished at Cîteaux and Clairvaux.

But because this book is customarily called the *Greater Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, just as the preceding work is called, by contrast, the *Lesser Exordium*, I have preferred the title stated above.

Angelus Manrique says in the *Annals* that the author of this *Greater Exordium* is unknown. Yet the Foigny codex contains these words: “This book was composed by a certain abbot named Conrad, of the monastery of Eberbach, who was a monk of Clairvaux.” That he professed the monastic life at Clairvaux is indicated plainly enough at the end of this work, where he states that he was trained in the cloistral disciplines at Clairvaux in the days of Blessed Peter and Lord Garnerius, later bishop of Langres—of whom the former was the eighth and the latter the ninth abbot of Clairvaux—namely about the year 1180.

Eberbach, over which this Conrad is said to have presided, is a monastery of the line of Clairvaux in the diocese of Mainz. The author himself mentions it with high praise in Distinction V, chapter 17, and elsewhere, although he does not there state that he was abbot of that place. But whoever may have been the author of the book, I judged it most worthy and useful to read, and deserving of a place at the head of the Library of our Fathers.

It remains to note that one or even more gatherings of this book, before chapter 15, which dealt with Blessed Alberic, have perished, so that absolutely nothing is now said about him. Since chapter 37 states that the body of St Stephen was buried beside the tomb of his predecessor, namely Alberic, it is clear that the place of Alberic’s burial was formerly explained in this book; otherwise an unknown thing would be explained by an unknown thing. See Manrique, vol. I, *Annals*, year 1106.

# First Distinction

[Col. 0995]

## Chapter I. That the Lord Jesus, in his teaching, handed down the pattern of perfect repentance

The eternal God, Son of the eternal God, our Lord [Col. 0996] Jesus Christ, Creator of all things and Redeemer of all the faithful, while in the days of his humility he was working salvation in the midst of the earth, preached to the world the saving way of perfect repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” [Col. 0997A] (Matt. IV).

Thanks be to the inestimable mercy of God, who at last, looking with a more serene eye upon the wretched race of Adam’s children, tempered through the incarnate sweetness of his Word the severity of the Law, which mercilessly exacted eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and every kind of retaliation for every offence, saying: “Repent.” And lest weak human beings should be terrified by the word “repent,” that is, “undergo punishment,” he immediately took care to sweeten the severity of the foregoing pronouncement with a consoling word, a word worthy of all acceptance, adding: “For the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.”

For what person of sound judgment, though weak, though delicate, would not patiently—indeed gratefully—bear the momentary burden of present punishment, not only in order to escape the eternity of future punishment, but also to become a participant in the heavenly kingdom which never ends? Yet since blessed John the Baptist and forerunner of the Lord, preaching repentance in the course of his forerunning ministry, judged that fruits worthy of that repentance ought to be produced (Matt. III), we must earnestly inquire what is the pattern of perfect repentance that seems sufficient for obtaining worthy fruits.

But where should we seek this pattern more fittingly than in the words and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the master of masters? When a certain man who possessed many goods asked the Lord what he should do to obtain eternal life, and the Lord set before him the commandments of the Law, and he said that he had kept all of them from his youth, the Lord added: “One thing still lacks to you. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me; and you will have treasures in heaven” (Matt. XIX).

But he, who was accustomed to offer not himself but his possessions, and not all of them but only a part, and indeed a very small part—namely tithes, first-fruits, and other legal offerings—and who thought this a great thing, heard the word of consummate righteousness and recoiled. Drawing [Col. 0997C] his heart down to earth, he went away sad; for, as Truth itself testifies, those who affectionately love the riches they possess are saved only with difficulty (ibid.).

How differently blessed Peter was disposed! How abundantly drenched with the dew of heavenly grace was he cooled from the heat of worldly desire, when he said to the Lord, with humility no less than confidence, concerning himself and his fellow disciples: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee” (ibid.). Here indeed we find the pattern of perfect repentance, which the Saviour advised to the man seeking counsel for salvation and handed down also to his disciples who followed him, although we read that some lived chastely and humbly amid riches and all the glory of the world.

But since the privileges of a few do not make a common law, those who strive after the height of perfection much more safely obey the voice of the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke IV).

## Chapter II. That the practice of common life began with the primitive Church, and that from this the institution of monastic religious life took its beginning

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus, traces the origin of monastic life to Elijah, Elisha, and the sons of the prophets. From Philo it is evident that this manner of life flourished throughout Egypt, and especially around Alexandria. [Col. 0998D]]

[Col. 0997D]

Indeed, it was fitting that the Wisdom of the supreme Father, who had come to hand down the norm of perfect righteousness, should immediately stamp this norm distinctly upon the little flock of the Church in its very birth; so that all who, stirred by their example, proposed to walk the arduous and narrow way, formed by the teaching of so great a Majesty and strengthened also by the example of such great Fathers, might run the way of the Lord with enlarged hearts, saying to the Lord with the Psalmist: “Because of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. XVI), knowing that thou wilt render the hundredfold which thou hast promised and add eternal life besides.

After the Lord had suffered in the flesh, risen from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sent to his disciples the Holy Spirit whom he had promised, the crowds of believers having now multiplied, the brightness of that same spiritual life which we call perfect repentance began to shine forth more clearly. For, as Luke testifies, “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, and none of them said that anything which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. Those who possessed fields and houses also sold what they possessed, laying the prices at the apostles’ feet” (Acts IV).

The same blessed Luke testifies how great a reverence that exalted manner of life produced in the hearts of unbelievers, when he says that “none of the rest dared join themselves to them, but the people magnified them” (Acts V). Nor was this school of the primitive Church trained in heavenly disciplines at Jerusalem only: at Antioch also, under the masters Paul and Barnabas, it flourished most gloriously; and there the disciples were first called Christians.

Philo too, the most eloquent of the Jews, wrote much concerning their most fervent zeal in the Lord, in the book which he entitled *The Contemplative Life*. It is likewise clear that the name, life, and institution of monks and cenobites took their beginning from them.

But when the word of God had been spread throughout every region, and the sound of the apostles’ preaching had now gone forth into all the earth, it was necessary that the ark of holy Church—which in its upper parts, as an image of this most perfect religious life, was confined to the cubit of unity, but in its lower parts enlarged the bosom of charity—should receive the faint-hearted and those less fit for the height of perfection, so that the mercy of almighty God might most graciously save not human beings alone, but even the beasts themselves; that is, those who through weakness defile themselves with the dust of earthly possessions.

From this point that noble commonwealth which the Lord Jesus Christ had founded and the Holy Spirit strengthened—in which, though none possessed anything, yet no one [Col. 0998C] among them was needy—began to be divided into private property. Christians began to use possessions freely, but in such a way that they did not place earthly things before heavenly things and, by administering temporal things well, might more easily attain heavenly things.

## Chapter III. That the monastic order, strengthened through blessed Antony and the other holy Fathers, shone forth excellently

Although mother Church, accommodating herself to the multitude of the imperfect, loosened the reins of a more relaxed way of life, nevertheless from the very beginning of the Church’s birth down to our own times there have never been lacking men of virtue. Burning with the most fervent fire of divine love, rejecting also the enticements of a more relaxed life, they have held with tireless zeal of devotion to the uprightness of the common life, which alone is the stable foundation of perfect repentance preached by the Lord Jesus; and they handed it down to their successors to be maintained through many rules and examples of holy conduct.

Among these the first, or chief, were Antony, Pachomius, and Basil. Antony, the first of these, displaying in his heart the law of charity, written not in ink or letters but by the Spirit of the living God, left disciples most perfect in their own most perfect manner of life. Such were Macarius, Paphnutius, Pambo, Isidore, and many others, who became Fathers of monasteries throughout Egypt and the Thebaid. Leading countless companies of monks along the path of perfect repentance, they triumphed most gloriously over the world, its prince the devil, and all his host.

Pachomius, distinguished by apostolic grace, wrote Rules for monks which he had learned at an angel’s [Col. 0999A] dictation. In conformity with these he polished an infinite multitude of living stones and brought them together for rebuilding the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Blessed Basil also, bishop of Caesarea and eminent doctor of the Church, wrote a Rule for monks; and this Rule, as our blessed Father Benedict testifies, [Note: [Col. 0999D] Benedict, final chapter of the Rule.] is a most upright norm of human life, by which one may attain the heavenly homeland without stumbling.

Thus the whole Church of the East flourished conspicuously for a long time through adherents of monastic religious life, following the teaching and examples of virtue of these most venerable Fathers. This was also attested, shortly before our own time, by Anselm of blessed memory—first bishop of Havelberg, later archbishop of Ravenna—in the disputation which he held with the Greeks concerning the obstinacy of their schism and set down in an elegant style.

When he had been sent as ambassador by Lothair, the most Christian emperor of the Romans, to the emperor of Constantinople, and carefully examined the observances of different religious bodies, he saw in the monastery called Pantocrator—that is, “of the Almighty”—nearly seven hundred monks serving the Lord under the Rule of blessed Antony. In the monastery called Philanthropos—that is, “lover of humankind”—he saw about five hundred monks serving the Lord under the Rule of Saint Pachomius. He also saw very many monasteries bearing the sweet yoke of the Lord under the Rule of blessed Basil.

## Chapter IV. On the institution and authority of the Rule of the holy Father Benedict: how by the grace of God it flourished and flourishes to this day

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who illumined the East by the presence of his most sacred humanity, sent in his stead to the West those whom he found worthier and more exalted in his Church, namely the most blessed chief apostles [Col. 0999C] Peter and Paul. Thus the peoples of the West, taught by the instruction of the Holy Spirit, might come together with the peoples of the East into the same fullness of faith: into the precious mystery of faith which Peter received not through flesh and blood but through the inspiration of the supreme Father; and likewise into the Gospel which Paul learned not from a human being nor through a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. So from all peoples one bride of Christ the Lord might be formed, without spot or wrinkle.

The same grace which bestowed upon the East the aforesaid holy Fathers to establish and strengthen the discipline of the monastic order, in the graciousness of its mercy also endowed the West with a man of no lesser merit: namely our most holy Father Benedict. He possessed not only the spirit of Antony and Basil but, as blessed Pope Gregory testifies, was filled with the spirit of all the righteous. Like a most pure and brilliant star, by his singular prerogative of holiness, his surpassing purity of life, and finally the inestimable glory of signs and miracles, he shone most brightly from the West to the East. Thus, whatever divided gifts the East rejoices to possess in diverse Fathers, the West may rightly glory that it possesses all of this in its one most holy Father Benedict, filled with the spirit of all the righteous.

This most reverend Father of ours wrote a Rule for monks which he learned through long exercise in the virtues, not from a human being but through the anointing of him who teaches humanity knowledge. In it the Holy Spirit, the wondrous craftsman, joined the fullness of perfection with most moderate discretion in so subtle a union that, however religious a person may be, he finds in it means for further progress; and however faint-hearted or infirm he may be, he finds remedies for his infirmity equally in it.

For who, for example, will be so strict an adherent of righteousness, so fervent a zealot for holy religious life, that, if grace leading him has enabled him to ascend the twelve degrees of humility described in the Rule, and if, as his merits increase, he has advanced so far as to reach the sixth and seventh—namely, the last degree of the first set of six and the first of the second set of six—which number signifies perfection, and which, doubled in these degrees of humility, demonstrates through the Rule of the teacher the love of God and neighbour that is the sum of perfection: who, if he examines himself without pretence and carefully searches all the corners of his accusing conscience, will not, I say, measuring his strength and sensing his deficiency, immediately cry out in tears with the Apostle that “he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. VI)?

Again, who will be so delicate and infirm that he cannot find remedies suited to his weakness in the observances of the Rule, in the most moderate discretion with which its fasts, vigils, labours, and other institutions are arranged?

Therefore, when the same legislator says in the final chapter of that Rule that not every observance of righteousness has been described in it, calls it the least Rule for beginners, and sends those who desire to press on to the summit of perfection to the teachings and rules of the ancient Fathers, he does so, as blessed Bernard testifies, from humility. He did not wish to appear arrogantly to make himself equal to the ancient Fathers in writing his Rule, and in this also took care to provide for the humbling of his own conscience.

Blessed Gregory too, an apostolic man, [Note: [Col. 1000D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, II, chapter 36.] commends it, no less by merit than by office, as distinguished in language and pre-eminent in discretion. By his authority he tacitly urges monks, abandoning the practices of other institutions perhaps less judicious, to receive with devoted hearts the Rule of God’s beloved Father Benedict, pre-eminent in discretion, and to form the whole order of their lives according to its norm.

In a council subsequently held in Gaul, it was decreed by common resolution that monks dwelling throughout the provinces of Gaul and Germany should abandon the institutions of other Rules, receive in all their monasteries the Rule of the aforesaid Father, and observe in all their conduct the form prescribed by him.

According to the model of this holy Rule, many monasteries throughout Italy were reformed, and many were newly built by the venerable Father. In them multitudes of monks, serving the Lord in the spirit of humility, produced fruits worthy of repentance like true Israelites.

## Chapter V. That blessed Benedict, at the request of the bishop of Le Mans, sent his holy disciple Maurus into Gaul to found monasteries

Not only Italy, but also the threefold division of Gaul, [Col. 1000D] sprinkled with the sweet fragrance of this holy religious life, eagerly desired with praiseworthy longing to accept the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden—that is, the observances of the holy Rule.

It therefore happened that the distinguished bishop of the city of Le Mans sent his envoys to the venerable Father Benedict: his archdeacon Flodegarius and his steward Harderadus. With most devout earnestness he asked that Benedict would deem it fitting to send him some brothers from his monastery, to build for him in the regions of Gaul a monastery according to the observances of the Rule of the holy Father.

Blessed Benedict accordingly summoned his disciple Maurus, whom he had reared from childhood in the fear of God, and sent him with other religious brothers into Gaul. There Maurus built a monastery illustrious alike for its religious life and wealth; he became father of a great multitude of monks and, adorned with signs and virtues, rested in peace.

It is reported that in that same monastery a pound of bread and a *hemina* of wine, which Saint Benedict sent there, are preserved to this day in memory of antiquity and out of reverence for so great a Father. From that time monastic religious life grew and multiplied throughout all the provinces of Gaul under the Rule of Father Benedict, the monks serving Christ the Lord, the true King. Many, inspired by divine grace, flocked to it; trained in the duties of holy discipline, they bore in patience the fruit of good work from the soil of their hearts.

But in the time that followed, when barbarians burst into Gaul and the Lord resolved to chastise the sins of his people through repeated pagan invasions, many monasteries of the saints were either burned by fire or destroyed to their foundations. Those which remained fell into such negligence that scarcely a trace of the ancient religious life could be found in any monasteries.

Yet the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ permits his Church, when charity has grown cold [Col. 1001B] and iniquity abounds, to be scourged by diverse tribulations; but he never closes to her the depths of his mercy. So too, without doubt, he does not cease at opportune times to restore through men of virtue the monastic order, which continually falls into ruin through the corruption of human weakness.

## Chapter VI. That blessed Odo, abbot of Cluny, vigorously restored through the grace of God the fallen monastic order
Source/review notes: One proposed column-reference insertion at Col. 1006B necessarily requires correcting the surrounding sentence rather than duplicating it; the supplied draft otherwise translates the source substantively.

Hence it was that blessed Odo, the outstanding ruler of that most noble monastery of Cluny, rose to so lofty a summit of holiness that, according to the grace bestowed upon him by the Lord, he restored in every respect to the ancient vigor of sacred religious life the monastic Order, which in his time was altogether plunging headlong to ruin. For, to speak briefly of the moral collapse of that age: when this venerable Father Odo began, as was fitting, strictly to maintain in his monasteries the rigor of regular discipline, certain other monks [Col. 1001C], seeing some of his brethren washing or anointing their undergarments, or performing any other lowly tasks, and also carefully keeping silence—using signs instead of words when necessary—were moved by an excessive bitterness of anger. “O wretches,” they said, “what are you doing? What law, or what Order, commands you to devote yourselves to such base and servile tasks? Where, I ask, does Scripture command this, that you should use your hands in place of your tongue? Are you not plainly convicted of insulting the Creator himself, when, abandoning the natural use of the tongue and the instrument of speech, you irrationally make a commotion with your hands?”

But the blessed man, thinking little of the chatter of disputatious persons and false monks, admonished his brethren by word and example to advance toward better things. Whenever he was invited by religious men, he went readily, restoring monasteries that had fallen into disorder to the rigor of the Order, or founding new ones. How strictly the monks under his discipline observed its rule may be known from this single proof of their virtue [Col. 1001D], which we wish to relate in order to show their steadfastness of spirit. Once, as some of them were travelling, they were surrounded by robbers amid the darkness of midnight. They were captured with all their belongings, dragged away, stripped, and subjected to insults; finally they were thrown into chains. The robbers were both astonished and angered that, amid such evils as they themselves inflicted, they could not force even a single word from them. Like mute and tongueless men, as though they did not feel loss or abuse, they persisted in silence until, after the solemn office of the night and morning praise had been completed and dawn was shooting forth its rays, they loosed their tongues to speak with praiseworthy discretion—the tongues which they had previously restrained under an even more praiseworthy rule, out of the fear of God and the discipline of the Order.

Nor did he restore the condition of the sacred Order in Gaul alone, but in Italy as well. He also went to the special monastery of Saint Benedict in France [Col. 1002A], where, as is said, that most holy body rests, invited by the most blessed Father Benedict himself, as is recorded in the deeds of Saint Odo. For one day, while the monks of that place sat in the cloister and were not ashamed to occupy themselves with quarrels and buffoonery, holy Father Benedict visibly appeared to a monk before the gate of the monastery and said to him: “Go and tell these brethren that they greatly distress me by their perverse conduct. Therefore I shall now go and bring from Aquitaine a man according to my heart, so that he may rebuke these perverse men and restore the discipline of the Order in this monastery of mine.”

The monk was astonished; hastening to the brethren, he reported, in the hearing of all, what their spiritual father had commanded, and left them all dismayed and stunned. Yet with great amazement they asked one another who this person might be of whom the holy Father had spoken; trembling, they suspected that it would be blessed Odo himself [Col. 1002B], as the subsequent outcome proved. Thus Odo, the most devoted follower of Father Benedict, came to the aforesaid place. Although he suffered many tribulations and insults from those who loved ruinous liberty more than the rigor of regular life, nevertheless, by the grace of God and the help of holy Father Benedict, he very commendably reformed the discipline of the Order in that monastery.

Moreover, the particular monastery of this God-beloved Father Odo, called Cluny, which shines even to this day as most great and noble—great in the multitude of its brethren, noble in its possessions, riches, and glory—and also the monastery from which Father Odo withdrew with his brethren to Cluny, are known from written records to have produced men of such consummate perfection, such excellence, and such worthiness before God. Therefore we are pleased to insert into this small work two exceedingly delightful miracles selected from among them, so that the prudent reader [Col. 1002C] may judge the rest from these two.

## CHAPTER VII. Of the brother in whose hand crumbs of bread were changed into most precious pearls.

It was an ordinance of the monastery that, after the brethren seated at table had finished their meal, they should carefully gather up and consume the crumbs that fell from the fragments of bread, lest they be found negligent before God even in this matter. It happened one day that one of the brethren, a watchman not careless of his conscience, sat at table with the others. When the meal was over, he gathered the crumbs according to custom into the palm of his hand, kept his fingers closed around them, and attended to the reading with great sweetness of heart. But before he had consumed them, the reader suddenly ended the reading at the prior’s signal.

What was he to do? He was permitted neither to throw them away nor now to eat them, since on either side he faced the danger of transgression. Therefore he kept them enclosed in his hand [Col. 1002D], thinking that this fault of negligence could be removed only by the remedy of confession and penance. After grace had been said, he made the sign for confession, drew the prior aside, fell upon his face, and asked pardon, revealing his negligence with great simplicity of heart. The prior rebuked his fault, as was fitting, and asked what he had done with the crumbs. “Here, lord,” he said, “they are in my hand.” When the prior commanded him to show them, he stretched out his arm and opened his hand; and behold, in his palm there were found most precious pearls instead of crumbs.

Would that certain negligent brethren might deign to consider this brother’s praiseworthy fervor—those who, when the reading has ended, if they happen to have a morsel in their hand which they wish to eat, or if something remains in the cup which they desire to drink, do not hesitate to do so without regard for the fear of God. Yet the custom of the sacred Order teaches that from the moment the reader begins to say, “But thou, O Lord,” [Col. 1003A] no one ought to take any food or drink whatsoever. But why, we may ask, did almighty God wish to perform so glorious a miracle, apparently so unnecessary, even in matters so small? Certainly, so that it might become plainly known to all how greatly he delights in brethren who are fervent in spirit within the community, who observe with care, because of fear of him, not only the greater but even the smallest commands.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of a dying brother who saw a multitude of white-clad persons coming to him.

A certain brother at Cluny, having guarded his life commendably in every fervor and devotion of sacred religious life, was struck by a fatal illness and brought to his last hour. As he struggled in his final agony, now close to death, he opened his eyes and saw a great multitude of monks entering to him. They were all clothed in white garments, of that kind of vestment [Col. 1003B] which in ecclesiastical usage is called an *alba* [white robe], as the communities of that Order customarily clothe themselves on principal solemnities.

Seeing them, and thinking that they were the community of brethren, he began greatly to wonder why they were entering to him clothed in white. With something like indignation he said to the infirmarian attending him: “What is this, dearest brother, that I see? When was our community accustomed to come to a dying brother clothed in white?” The infirmarian replied that the community of brethren had not yet come. “What are you saying?” he answered. “Do you not see the great crowd of brethren around me, all clothed in most radiant white *albs*, and outdoing one another in coming to celebrate my funeral rites?”

When the infirmarian heard this, although he himself saw nothing of the kind, he understood that the religious brother was seeing a vision of blessed spirits. Shortly afterward that holy soul was released from the flesh and, as we believe, happily passed from the valley of weeping, from the tents of Kedar—that is, from the blackness of sin—to the white-clad citizens [Col. 1003C] of the heavenly Jerusalem, whom while still living in the flesh he had deserved to see.

After the most reverend Father Odo, the aforesaid monastery of Cluny was governed by abbots conspicuous for religion. The foremost were the holy and God-worthy Majolus and Odilo, and, in more recent times, blessed Hugh. Spreading the Cluniac Order far and wide throughout all the lands and islands of Europe, they handed down to their subjects the undefiled path of monastic Order. In that great and religious house too, among the other exercises of spiritual life, there grew up a most salutary custom, full of every piety: that, for the liberation of the souls of departed believers, that holy multitude of brethren should diligently devote itself to devout prayers and the celebration of Masses, and should obtain either that the punishments assigned to them be mitigated, or that, released from every punishment, they be transferred into rest.

Moreover, besides the daily persistence in prayers and psalms, the pious diligence of the Fathers decreed in that house that solemn offices [Col. 1003D] for the departed faithful should be held at stated times during the year. Thus the solemn day of the faithful departed, which the holy and universal Church customarily celebrates with a solemn office after the feast of All Saints, is said to have taken its beginning from the Church of Cluny.

## CHAPTER IX. How blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, healed a paralytic.  
*[In this chapter too the author laments the monks’ negligence and the decline of the Cluniac Order.]*

But since we have mentioned blessed Hugh, who laudably governed the monastery of Cluny in recent times, we shall recall one of his miracles for the benefit of readers. It will be all the more pleasing because it is known to have occurred in a more recent age, and because we learned of it through the reliable account of the venerable William, formerly superior of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, [Col. 1004A] and afterward abbot of the Paraclete, which belongs to the Order of the house of Saint Victor.

Near the city of Paris there stands a monastery of regular canons. In it, one of the brethren of that community lay so disabled by paralysis that he could not rise from his bed without another’s assistance. By chance the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, came there. The brethren, greatly rejoicing at his arrival, conceived no slight hope of restored health for their sick brother. They approached the man of God and humbly asked him to obtain by his prayers from almighty God health for the brother who had long suffered from illness.

It is said that this monastery possesses half of the chasuble of blessed Peter the Apostle, which, as is fitting, is held by the brethren in great veneration. Therefore the holy man of the Lord could not refuse what fraternal charity requested; rather, with the inmost affection of piety he implored the Lord’s mercy for the health of the sick brother. Finally, after the most sacred mysteries had been celebrated [Col. 1004B], he approached the altar and reverently took from it the aforesaid portion of blessed Peter’s chasuble. Coming to the sick man, he covered him with the sacred garment; holding his hand, he began to sing in a measured voice that antiphon, “Peter the Apostle said to the paralytic,” changing two words in it: namely, *dicit* [says] for *dixit* [said], and “Robert” for “Aeneas,” because the sick man was called Robert.

As he held the man’s hand and sang, “Peter the Apostle says to the paralytic: Robert, arise and make your bed” (Acts 9), he immediately rose, every weakness of his limbs utterly banished. All who were present glorified God, who had deigned to manifest the power of his blessed Apostle Peter through the merits of venerable Hugh. For the holy abbot could all the more readily obtain so glorious a miracle from divine generosity because he attributed it not to his own merits but to the power of his special patron, blessed Peter the Apostle. The noble Church of Cluny [Col. 1004C] glories that it is named in honor of that apostle’s revered name, and the whole community of brethren most devoutly attends to his sacred veneration.

Under Fathers so holy and so distinguished in every form of religious life, the Cluniac Order shone most brilliantly and became for many “the savor of life unto life.” So much was this so that blessed Henry, Augustus, emperor of the Romans, the second of that name—whose memory is blessed before God and humankind—hearing the report of that religious life, visited Cluny and, offering gifts and revenues as imperial magnificence required, most devoutly commended himself to the prayers of the brethren.

If the choice were now given us, we might delight to cry out with blessed Peter the Apostle and say to the Lord: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17). It would indeed be good for all who attain the summit of monastic religion if the discipline of the Order, corrected and renewed to the line of truth by the holy Fathers, might endure unshaken; if deadly negligence were driven away; and if the fervor of sacred religious life might flourish everywhere [Col. 1004D] in every respect. But what are we doing, when the Wise Man laments that nothing beneath the sun can remain in the same state? What are we doing, when negligence—which, alas, is found even in the manner of life of religious persons—is so prone to vices?

Woe once, and woe a second time, and a third time also! Woe to you, negligence: mother of disorder, rust of minds, moth of hearts, corruption of morals, flight from discipline, overthrow of religious life, weakening of virtues, evil beast, most crafty little fox! With such deceitfulness do you efface your tracks that, when you bite, you are not felt; when you demolish, you are not seen; and you are discovered only after the gravest injury has been done. How many evils you have wrought! How many you do work! How many evils—may God avert it!—you are, not without reason, feared to be about to work! O detestable negligence, how slight, how insignificant, how wholly without importance you appear in human eyes, so that you are judged scarcely worthy even of rebuke! Yet whoever despises you as so small gradually falls.

Who [Col. 1005A] would believe, unless experience made it credible, that a tiny drop, when it first begins to fall in a gentle trickle, could penetrate the hardness of a stone? Or who, seeing a new and rigid ring placed upon a finger, would suppose it could be worn away by use? Yet true is the saying:

> The drop hollows out the stone; the ring is worn away by use.  
> *(Ovid, *Epistulae ex Ponto*, IV, Elegy 10.)*

So too—and we cannot say it without great sorrow of heart—negligence, creeping in little by little, destroys religious life. “The leech has two daughters,” says the Wise Man, “crying, ‘Bring, bring’” (Prov. 30). O how many there are who seem to have abandoned the broad ways of this world that lead to death and to have taken hold of the narrow and constricted way that leads to life; yet, because they do not at all avoid the embrace of this most wicked leech, this detestable harlot—that is, negligence—they produce from that viperous seed two daughters, worse than their mother: namely pleasure and vanity. Without cessation, without any interruption whatsoever [Col. 1005B], they cry to their wretched mother, saying, “Bring, bring.”

These are those who separate themselves, sensual persons, not having the Spirit; those who, wearing the habit of religious life, are known by their tonsure to lie to God; those who, shut up not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own, regard the pleasure of their desires as law; those who, though they ought to be nourished in scarlet, embrace dung; those who, placed in a place of pasture, daily move from pasture to pasture and yet die of hunger; whose food is the root of junipers and the husks of swine; whose wine is dragons’ gall, from the most bitter cluster of transgression; those who, while professing bodily chastity and holiness of spirit, nevertheless do not fear to imitate the example of a wicked and shameless woman, who eats in secret and, wiping her mouth, says, “I have done no evil” (ibid.); those who rejoice in such things and count it delight to live under the thorns of disorder.

And what will these wretches do when God begins to look upon them? Certainly, we learn by the facts themselves [Col. 1005C] how rightly the prophet lamented that “the gold has grown dim, the finest color has changed, the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4). Yet it is not for us to bite too sharply at the faults of others, lest perhaps it be said also of us that, while we are dim-sighted regarding our own affairs, we see keenly in the faults of others.

Let whoever wishes read the *Apology* of blessed Bernard, abbot, which he wrote to the venerable William, abbot of Saint-Thierry. There he will find how the gold has grown dim and the finest color changed. There, I say, he will find how that noble religious life of the Cluniac Order, of which we have already said much, darkened and clouded by foreign and adulterous customs—indeed, by desolations—has degenerated from the former integrity of its purity and holiness.

But to what end are these things? What is our purpose in recounting and emphasizing the formerly most perfect religious life, and afterward the most miserable dissolution, of another Order—a dissolution which today we see with our own eyes [Col. 1005D]? Surely our intention is this: that we who, through the grace of God, serve the Lord in the monastic Order renewed and corrected to the path of truth by the Cistercian Fathers, may become more cautious through the fall of others, may “wash our hands in the blood of sinners,” and may always remember that our blessed Father Benedict commands in the Rule that negligence and forgetfulness be wholly avoided. Let us also continually recall that apostolic saying: “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). For we know most certainly that our own affair is at stake when the neighboring wall is on fire.  
*(Horace, *Epistles*, I.18.)*

## CHAPTER X. How the brethren who founded the Cistercian Order, while they were still living at Molesme, were enlightened by divine grace.

Now I think it worthwhile to describe more carefully for future generations [Col. 1006A] how the Cistercian Order took its beginning, and with how abundant a blessing of God’s grace it was flooded from its outset. This we have learned partly from written memorials handed down to us by holy men who were founders from the beginning of this sacred religious life, and partly from the testimony of elders. Thus those whom divine grace may deign to call to our Order in ages to come, should they deem it worthy to read this little page of our insignificance, which we have composed for their consolation, may consider from what noble royal breast they have been nourished, and blush to be found degenerate children.

Moreover, not devotion and the usefulness of the matter alone invite us to this work; a certain necessity also compels us. For monks of the Black Order, especially those living in the provinces of Germany, do not cease, wherever and before whomever they can, to disparage our sacred Order. They assert that our holy Fathers departed from the monastery of Molesme in scandal and disobedience, against the will of their abbot. How shameless a lie this is, the course of the following narrative, setting forth the event more fully, will plainly show.

For monks of the Black Order assert that our holy Fathers departed from the monastery of [Col. 1006B] Molesme in scandal and disobedience, against the will of their abbot. How shameless a lie this is, the course of the following narrative, setting forth the event more fully, will plainly show.

For our purpose is, with God’s favor, not merely by the fullest reasoning but also by the weight of the most authoritative testimony, to stop the mouths of those who speak iniquity; and to furnish our brethren, who perhaps hitherto have not known these things so clearly, with instruments for refuting the falsehood of malicious detraction, supported by the testimony of sincere truth. O always blind impiety of foolish rivalry! Although it sees with its eyes and recognizes by reason, by divine and human judgment alike, that the Cistercian Order has been exalted upon the candlestick of virtue and honor in order that it may shine upon all who are in the house of God, nevertheless by stealthy whisperings it strives to turn away from its love and veneration all whom it can—as though its own honor increased by just so much as it could detract from the reputation of its neighbors.

But since, according to the Apostle’s judgment [Col. 1006C], “not he who commends himself is approved, but he whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10), after we have shown from the letters of the supreme pontiff, and likewise of the cardinals and bishops who dealt with this matter of such great piety, how reasonably and how authoritatively the Cistercian Order was judged and approved by human judgment at its beginning, we shall then take care to show how it was approved by divine judgment as well.

For it is clear to all sound-minded persons that almighty God approves that religious life which he has deigned from its beginning to pour over with such blessings of gifts, and within which he has raised up so many Nazarites of such perfection and holiness. But who could adequately estimate, much less recount, how gloriously the vigor of sacred religious life has shone forth in different parts of the world, not only in the greater but also in the least houses of the Cistercian Order? How exalted in virtues [Col. 1006D], how grave and humble in conduct have its prelates been; how devout, how most patient in bearing voluntary poverty for Christ, and how ready for every good work its subjects; how frequently persons of the Order’s religious life have been glorified by revelations and heavenly visitations; and how many, refined by the straits of voluntary tribulation, have passed by a happy death, without the fire of purgatory—which is exceedingly rare among another class of people—to the land of the living, to see the God of gods in Zion.

Yet lest the abundance of illustrious persons should seem to have made us poor in speech, after we have described more carefully the beginning of the sacred Order in order to cheer the devout and restrain lying detractors, we shall also briefly touch upon some of the virtuous pursuits of certain most reverend Fathers, namely the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux; and upon the memory of those elders who, having become imitators of the most pure religious life at Clairvaux, left their memory [Col. 1007A] blessed to posterity. Through these accounts every faithful and devout person may advance, strengthened in faith; while the faithless detractor, cleansing the jaundiced eye of his heart, may learn not to disparage the religious Order but rather to imitate the devotion of religious persons. Or else, struck by the rays of truth made manifest, he may witheringly groan that the material for malicious disparagement has been taken away from him.

If anyone is troubled that we have mentioned only the elders of Clairvaux and not those of Cîteaux also, let him know that, as members of the Church of Clairvaux, we have been able to investigate the holy pursuits of our own elders more intimately and effectively. Nor do the things we have described concerning the sincere manner of life or blessed consummation of a few persons prejudice the holiness of countless servants of God who have manfully labored in spiritual contests both at Cîteaux and throughout the whole sacred Order.

Therefore, when, as we have said above, the monastic Order had fallen into such a torpor of negligence [Col. 1007B] that, for persons coming to conversion, not so much progress as danger seemed to threaten in many places, and no hope of restoration smiled anywhere, almighty God—who calls and justifies in time those servants whom he has foreknown from eternity, that he may one day glorify them eternally—while all things held the middle of silence, sent his Holy Spirit from the heavenly secrets, from the royal thrones, into the hearts of certain brethren (Wisdom 18). They lived in a monastery situated in the region of Burgundy, called Molesme.

These servants of God were few in number, but strongly inflamed by that fire which the Lord Jesus casts upon the earth and wills to be vehemently kindled. As they heard the daily readings of the Rule in chapter, and observed that the Rule [Col. 1007C] commanded one thing while the customs of the Order maintained another, they were deeply grieved. They saw that they and the other monks had promised by solemn profession that they would observe the Rule of blessed Father Benedict, but were by no means living according to its ordinances.

At first they frequently conversed privately among themselves, lamenting their transgression and carefully considering how they might find a remedy for so great an evil. But afterward, when the matter had been brought out into public, the others, being carnal and unable to say with the prophet, “From on high he sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” (Lam. 1), began to ridicule the servants of God and to harass them in every way they could, so that they might desist from so holy a purpose.

But those who were led by the Spirit of God, and were therefore free, paid no heed to their malevolent attacks. Turning with all the effort of their minds toward God, they begged in most urgent prayers that the Lord’s mercy might deign to direct them to such a place as would allow them to fulfill the vows of their lips, which they had confirmed according to the Rule but had not observed. Then, considering that the Apostle warns that not every spirit [Col. 1007D] is to be believed (1 John 4), and that the Rule which they desired in every way to observe perfectly commands that one who has presumed to do anything without the abbot’s permission be rebuked, they humbly approached their abbot. They set forth their complaint concerning the transgression of the Rule, disclosed the most fervent desire of their vow, and humbly prayed that, by his counsel and assistance, they might accomplish what, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they had conceived in their minds.

By God’s prompting, the abbot was for the moment moved to compunction. He praised the purpose of God’s servants and most firmly promised not only that he would offer them counsel and help, but that he himself would be their inseparable companion in so holy a purpose. Hearing this, those brethren humble in spirit were greatly strengthened. Then for the first time they understood that the word had truly gone forth from the Lord and that in this desire they were not following dreams of their own hearts, but the right hand of the living God working powerfully within them.

## CHAPTER XI. That Lord Robert, the abbot, and the brethren with him, desiring to renew monastic religious life, approached the legate of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1008A]

Thus those high-spirited men, destined to become commanders and standard-bearers of innumerable soldiers of Christ, eager not so much for novel as for great undertakings beneficial to the whole world, continually considered among themselves how they might suitably bring what they piously desired into effect. By prudent judgment of reason they wisely recognized that they ought by no means to presume to change their place or Order without the consent of the Apostolic See.

At that time the legate of the Apostolic See in the regions of Gaul was the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, a man to be revered for religious devotion, prudence, and authority. The aforesaid abbot and the brethren, who burned with desire to renew monastic religious life, approached him. They humbly disclosed the fervor and desires of their hearts [Col. 1008B], complained that the customs of their Order differed excessively from the Rule which they had professed, and sorrowfully confessed that they had thereby knowingly incurred the crime of perjury. They added that they wished to order their lives anew according to the ordinances of the Rule of their holy Father Benedict, and steadfastly demanded that, in order that they might more freely carry this out, the same legate should extend to them the support of his aid through apostolic authority.

The lord legate, being prudent and discerning, carefully considered their arguments and declared that they were commendably moved. Favoring their spiritual vows with joyful auspices, he exhorted them by the following letter to accomplish with complete freedom what they had conceived in a pious mind.

## CHAPTER XII. Letter of Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See, by which the beginning of the Cistercian Order was founded upon his authority.

[Col. 1008C]

“HUGH, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See, to ROBERT, abbot of Molesme, and to the brethren with him who desire to serve God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

“Let it be known to all who rejoice in the advancement of holy mother Church that you and certain brethren, your sons, of the monastery of Molesme, stood before us at Lyon and professed that you wished henceforth to adhere more strictly and perfectly to the Rule of most blessed Benedict, which until now you had observed tepidly and negligently in that monastery. Since it is clear that this cannot be accomplished in the aforesaid place because of several hindering causes, we, providing for the salvation of both parties—namely, those departing from there and those remaining there—have judged it beneficial that you should withdraw to another place which divine generosity may designate for you, and there serve the Lord more beneficially and [Col. 1008D] peacefully.

“Therefore, when you were present before us—namely Robert, abbot, and the brethren Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Letald, and Peter—we advised you then to observe this holy purpose, together with all whom you shall decide regularly and by common counsel to associate with yourselves; and we command that you persevere in it, confirming it forever by apostolic authority through the impression of our seal.”

After this, the aforesaid abbot and his companions, relying upon such great and such authoritative support, returned to Molesme. From that community of brethren they selected companions who rejected the seductive allurements of a more relaxed life and burned with ready mind to observe purely and simply the purity and simplicity of the sacred Rule. Thus, between those who had stood before the legate at Lyon and those summoned from the monastery, there were twenty-one monks who entered upon the narrow and constricted way out of desire for a more perfect life and for observing the Rule of Saint Father Benedict according to the letter.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, and in what year of the Lord’s Incarnation, the holy Fathers of the Cistercian Order departed from Molesme and went to the wilderness of Cîteaux.

[Col. 1009A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, Lord Robert, abbot of the monastery of Molesme, founded in the diocese of Langres, and with him the brethren whose hearts God had touched—preferring to be wearied in labours for God together with their beloved Father Benedict rather than be dissolved in the comforts of this life—departed from Molesme. They eagerly made for the place which, through the Lord’s grace, they had previously foreseen as suitable to their purpose: namely, the wilderness called Cîteaux. This place lay in the diocese of Chalon and, because of the density of its woodland and thorns, was then inaccessible to people and inhabited only by wild beasts. Therefore, when the men of God came to this place of terror and vast solitude, [Col. 1009B] and perceived it to be the more suitable for the religious life which they had long conceived in their minds and for which they had come there, precisely insofar as it was more contemptible and inaccessible to secular people, they cut away and cleared the dense woodland and thorns. With the will of the bishop of Chalon and the consent of the person to whom the place belonged, they began to build a monastery there.

Accordingly, in the same year mentioned above, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March], the solemn feast-day of the most holy Benedict—which a twofold joy then made especially celebrated because Palm Sunday fell upon it—while angels rejoiced and demons wasted away, the community of Cîteaux, and thereby the religious order of Cîteaux as a whole, took its beginning through men wholly prepared for the Christian philosophy. This was a prudent design: those who had resolved to arrange the rule of divine service and the whole order of their life according to the pattern laid down in the Rule should happily begin it especially on the birthday of him who, through the life-giving Spirit, had given that law for the salvation of many. [Col. 1009C]

Behold the supreme and eternal Shepherd. Leaving the blessed sheep on the heavenly mountains, in pastures of everlasting greenness, he descended by the condescension of his grace to seek one sheep wandering in this valley of tears. Establishing the folds of mercy by a new ordering of his compassion, he raised over them the sign of salvation, so that his dying and sickly little sheep—entangled in the thorns of desires and carnal pleasures and wandering through forests of vices—might hear the voice of the dove inviting them to the folds of mercy; might enter the inn of the true Samaritan, there to be healed with the wine of repentance and the oil of forgiveness of sins; and might finally lay hold truly upon the sign of salvation.

For just as, at the beginning of grace, when Christ the Lord our Saviour was born, the world, though unaware of it, received the pledge of a new redemption, an ancient restoration, and eternal blessedness; so, in these latter days, when charity had already grown cold and iniquity was everywhere abundant, almighty and merciful God planted the seed-plot of that same grace in the wilderness of Cîteaux. [Col. 1009D] Watered by the rain of the Holy Spirit, it received a most abundant growth of spiritual richness, growing and advancing into a great tree, exceedingly beautiful and fruitful, so that peoples, tribes, and tongues of diverse nations rejoice to rest beneath its shade and satisfy themselves from its fruit.

Moreover, the lord archbishop, legate of the Apostolic See, by whose blessing, command, and authority so great a good had received a firm foundation, considered the poverty of God’s servants. Since in the barren place they had occupied they could neither survive nor erect buildings at all unless they were supported by the aid of some powerful person, he wrote to the illustrious prince Odo, then duke of Burgundy. He requested and urged him to foster and support Christ’s poor, who possessed zeal for the glory [Col. 1010A] of God and for the monastic Order, and to assist their needs in a manner worthy of the magnificence of his principality. Duke Odo of Burgundy assented to this request and counsel; delighted also by the fervour of those brethren, he completed entirely at his own expense the wooden monastery which they had begun in their poverty. For a long time he supplied them there with everything necessary and also abundantly relieved them with lands and livestock.

## CHAPTER XIV. How that place, with the consent of the bishop of Chalon, to whose diocese it belonged, was canonically raised into an abbey; and concerning the departure of the abbot who had come there.

At the same time, the abbot who had come there received from the bishop of Chalon, to whose diocese that place belonged, the pastoral staff and the care of souls, by command of the aforesaid legate. He canonically caused the monks who had come with him to make their stability firm in that place. Thus that church, protected alike by divine and human favour and fortified also by apostolic authority, was raised into an abbey to be ordered according to the Rule of Saint Benedict the Father. [Col. 1010B]

Not long afterwards, however, the monks of Molesme, acting by the will of their lord Abbot Geoffrey, who had succeeded Robert, sent messengers to the Roman curia. They importunately requested Pope Urban that the aforesaid Abbot Robert be restored to his former place, that is, to the church of Molesme. Moved by their importunity, the lord pope directed his legate, namely the venerable Hugh, that, if possible, the same abbot should return and that the monks who loved the wilderness should remain in peace.

## CHAPTER XV. On the advancement of blessed Stephen, the second abbot of Cîteaux; what institutions he added to the still new Order; how the Order increased under him; and by what virtues he shone.

[Col. 1010C] After the death of its shepherd, the church of Cîteaux, still poor and small, assembled to deliberate concerning the election of an abbot without respect of persons.

> [Note: [Col. 1009D] This concerns the death of Alberic, for Stephen succeeded him. What had been written concerning Alberic himself [Col. 1010D] has fallen out, as I noted after Manrique in the preface.]

Through the intervening grace of the Holy Spirit they elected a good man, Stephen by name, English by nation, who had departed from Molesme with them: a man of conspicuous holiness, adorned with the grace of every virtue, a lover of the wilderness and a most ardent emulous follower of holy poverty.

In his youth this blessed man left his land and kindred and, as a pilgrim, visited the thresholds of the holy apostles. On that journey he did not occupy himself with idle tales, as commonly happens; rather, devoting himself with his companion to divine praises, he sang the entire Psalter every day. When he had fulfilled his pilgrimage vow and, returning from the city, had entered Gaul, he came to the above-mentioned monastery of Molesme and received there the holy habit of the monastic Order. Later, when the proposal of renewing religious life had arisen in that house, he was foremost among the foremost [Col. 1010D] in labouring with most fervent zeal. By every means he strove that the place and Order of Cîteaux should be established—an Order of which he himself was afterwards, by God’s ordering, to be made an outstanding shepherd and teacher.

When this had been accomplished through the Lord’s gift, as we have said, he immediately began, like a faithful and prudent steward, to consider with the most devoted purpose of mind how he might advance and elevate his newly founded Order, still wavering in many respects because it had not yet been cultivated by fully developed institutions and still bore the mere scent of poverty. He sought to strengthen it by such governance that it might bear abundant fruit for the Lord Jesus.

Therefore, after summoning his brethren and taking counsel with them, both he and his brethren forbade any duke of that land or any other prince ever to hold his court [Col. 1011A] in that church, as they had been accustomed to do on feast-days. Then, lest anything should remain in the house of God—where they desired to serve God devoutly day and night—which savoured of pride or superfluity, or might at some time corrupt the poverty that guards virtues and which they had freely chosen for God’s sake, they decreed that they should retain no crosses of gold or silver, but only wooden ones painted in colours; no candlesticks except one of iron; no censers except those of copper or iron; no chasubles except of fustian or linen, without gold or silver cloth; and no albs or amices except of linen, likewise without gold or silver cloth. They entirely gave up all rich cloths, copes, dalmatics, and tunics. They nevertheless retained chalices not of gold but of silver, and, if possible, gilded; a silver reed [fistula], and, if possible, gilded; and stoles and maniples of cloth only, without gold or silver. They decreed that altar coverings should be made of linen, plain [Col. 1011B] and without imagery, and that cruets for the service of the altar should be without gold and silver.

By these and similar holy and God-pleasing institutions, God’s servants strengthened their new Order. Of those things which they had formerly used, they completely cut away some as contrary to true humility, while exchanging others for better customs that more strongly expressed holy poverty. They made the crooked ways of pleasures straight into continence, and the rough ways of vanity and pride into the level paths of righteousness, so that, according to the prophet, even fools cannot go astray on this way (Isa. 35).

How many, cultivated in the Cistercian Order by the hoe of discipline, yield fruits of continence, who, had they been placed elsewhere where the rigour of discipline did not flourish at all, would easily have been cast down through the monstrous prodigies of pleasures and carnal desires. Therefore our holy Order must by no means be regarded as an invention of human beings, but as truly handed down by the teaching of the Holy Spirit. At fitting times he does not cease, through his humble servants, to restore the brightness of holy religion, which the negligence of the human heart—inclined toward evil from youth—never ceases to darken, so that no flesh may glory before the Lord (1 Cor. 1). Far from all religious persons be that blasphemous utterance of those who trust in their own prudence and industry and say: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things” (Deut. 32). [Col. 1011C]

Thus, while the venerable Abbot Stephen and his brethren advanced daily to greater virtue, and proved by happy experience that their trade was good—namely, to give earthly, temporal, and perishable things and receive heavenly, eternal, divine things—one matter interrupted their spiritual rejoicing and subjected them to no small sadness: few in those days came to them for conversion. The holy men longed to entrust to their successors, for the salvation of many, the heaven-sent treasure of virtues. But nearly everyone who saw or heard of the unfamiliar and almost unheard-of severity of their life hastened to withdraw from them in heart and body rather than to approach them, and despaired altogether of their perseverance.

But the mercy of almighty God, who had deigned to inspire this spiritual warfare in his servants, decreed magnificently to enlarge and perfect it for the profit of many, as what follows will show. For when they were almost approaching the door of despair, they cried out to the Lord in most devout prayers because they were nearly without successors. They begged that the Lord might deign to pour out upon them the bowels of his mercy. The Lord heard their prayers through the merits and prayers, as we believe, of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, to whose holy name our Order is especially dedicated, and also of our most holy Father Benedict, whose Rule the aforesaid brethren had promised to observe in its entirety. And the Lord stirred up [Col. 1012A] the spirit of a young man named Bernard.

Although he was a youth, noble, refined, and learned, he was so inflamed by the mighty fire of divine love that, abandoning every pleasure and wealth of the world, and ecclesiastical dignities also, he devoutly resolved, as the first-fruits of the Lord’s harvest, to imitate the most austere manner of life of the Cistercians. O how wonderful is God in his works! How swiftly his word runs! How easy he shows those things to be for himself, when he wills them, which are impossible among human beings! For although not only nobles and rich people, but even those of middling station and the poor themselves, seeing the Order’s severity, refused to come to them, this youth, so tender and refined, as though he had emerged from the wine-cellar of God’s prevenient grace and were intoxicated with the wine that gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103), fervently and eagerly travelled about preaching the word of vocation which he had heard in the whisper of his heart’s secret ear. He wished to offer it to others also, [Col. 1012B] as it is written: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22).

Thus it happened that, accompanied by his brothers, relatives, and friends, and by other noble, learned, and powerful men in the world, thirty persons together eagerly entered the novices’ cell in the church of Cîteaux. Beginning in the spirit of fortitude to contend against the vices of the flesh and the incitements of evil spirits, they persuaded other people, not by words but by deeds, that all that severity of the Order which they had shunned was nothing other than the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden. Provoked by their example, an innumerable multitude of people of different ages and conditions—nobles, persons of middling rank, and poor persons—so filled that inn of Christ wrapped in the swaddling-clothes of his innocence that they wonderfully gladdened the brethren who had been afflicted by weariness and despair over future generations. From the pool of rational fish, with the little wings of pious intention and the scales of holy action declaring their purity, overflowing streams of many [Col. 1012C] monasteries came forth and occupied every part of the western world.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Abbot Stephen learned of the expansion of his Order through the Lord’s revelation and the appearance of a deceased brother to him while he was awake.

The Lord deigned mercifully to show beforehand by revelation to his humble servant, Lord Abbot Stephen, this grace inspired by divine visitation shortly before it came to pass. For, as related above, they were oppressed by heavy grief because they were nearly without successors. It happened that one of them, having completed the course of his present life and approaching death, was about to be brought into the joy of his Lord as a servant of a warfare whose service had been completed, and to receive the prize of his labour.

When he was already at the point of death, the venerable abbot, deeply afflicted by weariness arising from his despair of future successors, dared to presume something—something which might have been ascribed to rashness had not the piety of his purpose excused one who presumed. For since it is clear that intention judges all human actions, we believe that, before the eyes of the Lord, the piety of his intention and the severe pressure of necessity removed the blemish of presumption. Therefore, while that brother, as already stated, lay at the point of death awaiting the end of his life, the holy abbot came to him and spoke as follows:

“You see, dearest one, in what weariness and dejection of spirit we are placed. We have in some fashion entered the narrow and constricted way which our most blessed Father Benedict set before us in the Rule; but whether this way of life of ours pleases God or not is not sufficiently clear to us, especially since all the neighbouring monks judge us to be inventors of novelties and instigators of scandal and schism. Above all, my heart is pierced by the sharpest dart of sorrow at our small number. One by one, each day, we are removed from the midst by death; and, as I greatly fear, this religious life newly begun will come to an end together with us, [Col. 1013A] since until now the Lord has not deigned to associate with us capable persons suited to the humility of holy poverty, through whom we may hand down to posterity the pattern of this institution of ours.
