Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love we have entered the narrow and constricted way which he himself sets before his followers in the Gospel, and by the power of obedience, I command you: after your death, return to us at such time and in such manner as the grace of that same Lord shall decree, and make us certain of our condition, as far as his mercy wills.”

The sick man replied: “Father and lord, I will gladly do what you command, if, helped by your prayers, I am able to bring your command to fulfilment.” He spoke, and shortly afterwards happily ascended from the vale of weeping to the mountain of joy, the mountain of eternal blessedness.

A few days afterwards had passed. The venerable abbot, while engaged with the community of brethren in labour, gave the signal for rest, as was customary. He too withdrew a little from the others and, intent upon meditation, sat with his head covered by his hood. And behold: that deceased brother, flooded with the glory of great brightness, suddenly stood before him, yet seeming rather to be borne in the air than to stand on the ground. Asked how he fared and what his condition was, he replied:

“Father, I fare well—exceedingly well. May it be well with you also, for through your teaching and care I have merited a share in that endless joy, that incomprehensible peace of God which surpasses all understanding. In order to gain it, I patiently and humbly endured the hard labours of our new Order. Now, in accordance with your command, I have returned, announcing to you, Father, and to your brethren the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since you commanded that I should make you certain about your condition, know and hold firmly, with [Col. 1013C] every scruple of doubt excluded, that your life and way of life are holy and pleasing to God. Drive away from yourself as quickly as possible the sorrow which so greatly consumes your heart because you are leaving no successors; turn instead to spiritual jubilation and rejoicing, for the children of barrenness will yet say in your ears: ‘The place is too narrow for us. Make room, that we may dwell’ (Isa. 49). For behold, from this very time the Lord will begin to do great things with us, sending us many persons. Among them will be very many noble and learned men, who will fill this house so that, flying forth from here like swarming and overflowing colonies of bees, they will penetrate many parts of the world; and from the blessed seed of the Lord, which by his grace has taken root in this place, they will bring into the heavenly granaries manifold sheaves of holy souls gathered from every part of the world.”

On hearing this, the holy abbot, filled with joy and exultation, gave thanks to divine mercy from the inmost marrow of his heart. By this happy experience he proved how truthfully Scripture testifies that the Lord does not forsake those who hope in him (Pss. 9 and 16). [Col. 1013D] The heavenly messenger was preparing to depart, but—wonderful to relate—he did not presume to do so without the blessing of his spiritual father. He said therefore to the abbot: “It is time, Father and lord, that I return to him who sent me; and so I ask you to dismiss me strengthened by your blessing.”

In astonishment and fear the abbot replied: “What is this, I ask, that you are saying? You have passed from corruption to incorruption, from vanity to truth, from darkness to light, from death to life; and do you ask a blessing from me, who still groan miserably beneath all these things? This seems contrary to every principle of law and reason. Rather, I ought to be blessed by you; and I beg you therefore to bless me.”

But he replied: “It is not fitting thus, Father. The power of blessing has been conferred on you by the Lord, since you are established in the height of dignity and spiritual teaching. But for me, your disciple, who through your saving instruction escaped the defilements of this world, it is desirable to receive your blessing. Nor indeed shall I depart from here until I have received your blessing.”

The abbot, filled with amazement and wonder and not daring to resist further with obstinacy, raised his hand and blessed him. Thus that holy soul vanished, restoring to invisible mysteries the visible appearance it had assumed. [Col. 1014A]

On another occasion, one of the same brethren, about to enter upon the way of all flesh, saw in a vision an innumerable multitude of people near the oratory of that church, washing their garments in a certain most brilliant fountain. In that vision he was told that the fountain was called the Fountain of Ennon.

> [Note: [Col. 1013D] *Ennon* is a Hebrew word.]

When he reported this to the abbot, the eminent man understood that divine consolation was signified by it. Greatly rejoicing then in the promise, and afterwards still more in its fulfilment, he gave thanks to God. For after the Lord had tested the patience and faith of his servants through various tribulations and much poverty for fourteen continuous years, and had found them faithful, in the fifteenth year after the foundation of the house of Cîteaux the Dayspring from on high visited them by sending the persons mentioned above. In those same days the church increased in meadows, vineyards, fields, and estates, yet did not diminish in religious devotion. [Col. 1014B]

## CHAPTER XVII. How blessed Abbot Stephen, through the spirit of prophecy, discovered certain secrets of his novice.

The servant of God Bernard, who was afterwards to become the first abbot of the church of Clairvaux, while still a novice at Cîteaux, was accustomed every day to say silently the seven penitential psalms for the soul of his mother. But one day, when [Col. 1014C] after Compline he had begun those psalms, he omitted them before completing them—whether through forgetfulness, I do not know, or through sleepiness. Coming to his bed, he refreshed his limbs in sleep-giving rest and did not render the customary refreshment to his parent.

But the abbot, knowing the negligence through the Spirit, met him the following day and said: “Brother Bernard, where, I ask, did you leave those psalms of yours yesterday, or to whom did you entrust them?” Hearing this, the youth, being modest and God-fearing, blushed and began to wonder inwardly, saying: “Lord God, how has this matter become known openly, when I alone was conscious of it?” Understanding that he had been detected by a spiritual man, he fell at the abbot’s feet, confessed his negligence, and asked forgiveness. Having easily obtained it, he took care thereafter to be found more attentive in observances both private and public, and not readily to transgress what he had resolved upon mature deliberation to observe.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning a fish brought down from heaven to Saint Stephen, and food granted by God.

[Col. 1014D]

On one occasion Stephen, the poor abbot for Christ’s sake, had been bled. Because of the poverty of the house, the cellarer—upon whom, by the Rule’s command, rested the care of the poor and sick—had nothing at hand from which he could prepare even a somewhat better meal for his poor and sick abbot. Loving his abbot with sincere charity, he ran about to see whether he might find something somewhere by which he could show outwardly the charity burning within. And behold, a large bird flew up, carrying in its claws a fish of no small size. Immediately, before the eyes of the astonished brethren, it dropped the fish and departed, leaving the cellarer abundant prey from which he could sufficiently provide for his abbot’s bleeding.

At another time the most holy feast of Pentecost was near, and on that most sacred day scarcely enough bread could be found in the house to suffice for the brethren. Then the brethren, greatly rejoicing as though they were being fed upon that very poverty which they endured for God’s sake, began to sing the Mass of that great solemnity with utmost devotion and jubilation of heart. Behold, before Mass was finished, they received with much thanksgiving a generous blessing suddenly sent to them, from a source they had not expected, out of the storehouses of God’s grace. [Col. 1015A]

In these and similar matters, the man of God perceived how truly Scripture says that nothing is lacking to those who fear God (Ps. 33). Greatly wondering at the abundance of the Lord’s mercies upon himself and his brethren, he advanced more and more in holy religion and gloried in the straits of blessed poverty as though in every kind of wealth.

## CHAPTER XIX. On this saint’s devotion and humility.

[Col. 1015B]

Moreover, how attentive a hearer he was of the holy Rule—

> [Note: [Col. 1015D] Saint Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 19.]

—which commands us to stand in singing psalms so that our mind accords with our voice, will be evident from the following account. It was his custom, after the collation had been read, when entering the church, to hold the church door with his hand and press it firmly with his fingers as though making a sign. People commonly make a mark or knot in this way in order, when reminded by it, to impress more firmly upon memory what they do not wish to forget. When he did this frequently, one day a brother whose familiarity gave him boldness asked why he did it. The holy father replied: “I tell all the thoughts which I am compelled to admit during the day, because of the duty laid upon me of ordering the house, to remain outside and by no means presume to enter with me. They are to wait until I find them here after Prime has been said.”

On hearing this, [Col. 1015C] that brother was greatly edified, understanding clearly that the holy father’s manner of life surpassed the ordinary negligence of others. How great was the humility of this true shepherd, not a hireling; and how much he hated every display of pride, is sufficiently shown by his pastoral staff, with which he used to walk in festal processions. Preserved to this day in the treasury at Cîteaux out of reverence for so great a father and held in great veneration, it appears not to differ greatly from the common walking-sticks upon which old and weak persons are generally accustomed to lean.

This is the father of our most blessed Father Bernard in holy religion. This teacher, so perfect, merited to have so perfect a disciple. By their teaching and examples, even to this day innumerable vessels of captivity are taken away from the king of pride—that is, the devil—and incorporated into Christ the Lord, the true king of humility.

## CHAPTER XX. How Saint Stephen sent a brother to a market without money to buy necessities, foretelling that everything would turn out well for him.

[Col. 1015D]

At a certain time, when the house of Cîteaux was severely pressed by poverty, the venerable Abbot Stephen called one of his brethren. Speaking to him in the Spirit of God, he said: “You see, dearest brother, that we are greatly constrained by want; and our brethren are near to being endangered by hunger, cold, and other hardships unless help is quickly given them. Go therefore to the approaching market at Vézelay, and buy there three wagons, with three strong draft-horses for each of them, which we need most urgently to carry our loads. When you have loaded those wagons with cloth, provisions, and other necessary things, bring them with you; you shall return to us with joy and prosperity.”

The brother replied: “Father and lord, I am ready to obey your commands, if you give me money to buy those supplies.” The venerable abbot answered, magnificently trusting in God’s mercy amid his poverty: “Brother, know truly that when I anxiously and carefully sought the means by which to relieve our brethren’s needs, only three denarii could be found in this whole house. Take them, if you wish; and whatever else is lacking, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ will provide for you. Go then in confidence, for the Lord will send his angel with you and make your journey prosperous.” [Col. 1016A]

The brother set out and, when he arrived at Vézelay, was received as a guest by a certain faithful and God-fearing man. When this man learned the reason for his journey and the brethren’s need, he immediately went to a very wealthy neighbour of his, who was hopelessly ill and nearly dying, distributing his possessions among the poor. After he had told this sick man of the want of the Cistercian monks, whose holiness was already renowned in those regions, the aforesaid brother was summoned to his house. From the dying man he received so large a sum of money as alms that he could buy sufficiently with it everything which the abbot had directed. [Col. 1016B]

Having obtained three carts with nine draft-horses, he loaded and equipped them with everything he knew to be useful for the brethren’s needs. Thus, having arrived empty-handed, he returned full and rejoicing to his brethren in accordance with the abbot’s prophecy. As he neared Cîteaux, he sent a messenger to inform the abbot both of his arrival and of the result. Hearing this, the venerable father rejoiced exceedingly in the Lord. Summoning all the brethren together, he said: “The God of mercies, the Lord, the God of mercies, has acted freely and generously. Truly, Lord, our provider and shepherd, you have dealt nobly—truly, beautifully—with us, opening your hand and filling our want with your blessing.”

Then, after arranging a procession, they went out to meet the approaching brother as far as the gate. The abbot himself proceeded clothed in sacred vestments and carrying the pastoral staff, while ministers went before him with the cross and holy water. They solemnly received, therefore, with much thanksgiving, that alms—not as something granted by a human being, but as a blessing sent from heaven by the Lord and mercy from God their Saviour. [Col. 1016C]

Now this prudent and spiritual man, as may be understood, intended by this celebrated reception of the gift to admonish his children, both those then present and their successors, to retain the grace of this miracle in continual meditation and to learn from it, in all their needs, confidently to trust in God’s mercy. For he never abandons those who hope in him, but is always the most merciful comforter of his poor and a helper in times of need, in tribulation. From that day onwards, therefore, as spiritual goods always abound in that house through the Lord’s generosity, temporal goods also did not fail, although economy in all things is observed according to the institutions of the Order. [Col. 1016D]

## CHAPTER XXI. How the church of Cîteaux founded monasteries in different dioceses; and concerning the institution of the general chapter and the privilege obtained by Lord Abbot Stephen and his fellow abbots from the Apostolic See.

After, through the generosity of divine grace, the number of persons in the church of Cîteaux had increased, the mother of many children began now to rejoice, though she had formerly grieved for a long time in mourning over her barrenness. That vineyard of the Lord of Hosts also began to send out its shoots far and wide and establish cities of refuge in diverse places [Col. 1017A] and regions, so that those who had shed the blood of souls, fleeing to them (Deut. 19; Josh. 20), might, through the death of the supreme High Priest—who once entered the holy places through his own blood—be counted worthy to find eternal redemption (Heb. 9) and everlasting release from their exile.

Indeed, the abbeys which that same church established in various dioceses grew daily with such abundant and powerful blessing from the Lord that, from the time when Firmness was founded—the first-born daughter of the house of Cîteaux, and one which already beautifully prefigured by the meaning of its name the firmness and stability of the Order—within eight years twelve monasteries were found to have been built, counting both those specially sent out from Cîteaux and those which sprang from them. It was indeed a most pleasing spectacle, and in this they also proved themselves imitators of the most blessed Father Benedict, whose life and institutions they desired with their whole effort of mind [Col. 1017B] to emulate: just as he established twelve monasteries under appointed fathers and handed down to them the precepts of his Rule to be observed, so these men, in the renewal of the Order according to the same Rule, established twelve monasteries. In likeness of Christ’s twelve apostles, made drunk by the grace of the Holy Spirit, these might offer the cup of salvation to the whole world.

But before the Cistercian abbeys began to flourish, the most reverend Father Stephen, inspired by the Holy Spirit and with the counsel of his brethren, composed the decree called the Charter of Charity. In it we are taught how the monasteries of our Order, spread through diverse regions of the world and different in their diverse languages, may be joined together through a marvellous bond of charity and mutual rendering of honour, and become one Church, one Order, and finally one body in Christ. He judged that this decree should be called the Charter of Charity because its ordinance, rejecting every burden of exaction, [Col. 1017C] seeks only charity and the salvation of souls in matters divine and human.

Among the other provisions which, for the preservation of peace and charity and for maintaining the discipline and governance of the holy Order, were arranged with remarkable foresight by the blessed man and his brethren in the Charter of Charity, this is found especially eminent and worthy of every acceptance: that all the abbots of the Cistercian Order should assemble once each year at Cîteaux, celebrate a general chapter, and deliberate most diligently concerning the ordering of their whole life and the preservation among themselves of an unbroken peace; so that their manner of life, frequently rehearsed and strengthened by the authority of the divine Scriptures, might not readily grow lukewarm but might flourish through the long course of many years. For this reason, from that time until the present, the reverend Fathers of the Cistercian Order visit their mother once every year and celebrate a general chapter; and, instructed by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, they decree that the chapters more fully set forth in the book of Definitions—like antidotes compounded from diverse ingredients and wholly necessary for the salvation of souls—be observed throughout the brotherhood of our congregations.

But the devout Father Stephen, considering that such matters ought by no means prudently to be undertaken without the authority of the Apostolic See, and following the religious example of his predecessor, sent to Rome, with the approval of his fellow abbots and brethren, humbly petitioning Lord Pope Calixtus, then pontiff of the Apostolic See, to decree that what he himself, together with his fellow abbots and brethren, should establish for strengthening the discipline of the monastic Order might by apostolic authority remain forever valid and inviolable. The supreme pontiff graciously assented to his petition and issued the following decree in confirmation of the Order.

## CHAPTER XXII. Decree of Pope Calixtus Confirming the Cistercian Order

[Col. 1018A]

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Calixtus II, elected in the year 1119.]

“CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons in Christ, STEPHEN, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“By the Lord’s ordering, we are seen to have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See, so that, through his aid, we ought to promote religion and confirm by the authority of our office those things which have rightly been established for the salvation of souls. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, we grant your petition the assent due to charity; and, rejoicing with paternal affection in your religious life, we set the hand of our confirmation to the work of God which you have begun.

“Indeed, by the consent and common deliberation of the abbots and brethren of your monasteries, and of the bishops in whose dioceses those monasteries are situated, you have established certain chapters concerning the observance of the Rule of blessed Benedict and certain other matters which seemed necessary to your Order and place. You seek that these, for the greater peace of the monastery and observance of religious life, be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See. Therefore, rejoicing in your advancement in the Lord, we confirm those chapters and that constitution by apostolic authority, and decree that all shall remain valid forever. We expressly prohibit in every way any abbot from receiving your monks without a regular letter of commendation. We also forbid anyone to presume to receive your lay brothers or professed members for residence [perhaps: “for the habit”].

“If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person should presumptuously undertake in any way to oppose this our confirmation and your constitution, let that person, as a disturber of monastic religion and peace, be struck with the sword of excommunication by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and by our own authority, until satisfaction has been made. But whoever proves its guardian shall receive the blessing of almighty God and of his holy apostles. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the Blessed Father Stephen Recognized through the Spirit the Unworthiness of His Successor, and of His Precious Death

When the blessed Father Stephen had vigorously administered the office entrusted to him according to the true Rule of humility of our Lord Jesus Christ, worn out by great age so that his eyes were dim and he could not see, he laid aside pastoral care, desiring to devote himself to God alone and to himself through the savor of holy contemplation. A certain man, unworthy of the honor, named Guy, succeeded him. Though richly endowed with outward gifts, like a whitewashed tomb, inwardly he was filthy with the corruption of vices.

At the very beginning of his elevation, as he was receiving the professions of the brethren according to custom, Stephen, the servant of God, saw in the spirit an unclean spirit coming to Guy and entering his mouth. Scarcely one month had passed when, by the Lord’s revelation, his impurity was uncovered; and the spurious planting which the heavenly Father had not planted was immediately uprooted from the paradise of God.

When the time was at hand for the old man, who had earned rest by his labors, to be brought into the joy of his Lord and, from the lowest place of poverty which, in accordance with the Savior’s counsel, he had chosen in this world, to rise to the banquet of the supreme householder, the brethren assembled. Some abbots of his Order also came—whose number, it is said, had by that time grown to twenty—to attend with most devout services and prayers their faithful friend and most humble Father as he returned to his homeland.

As he lay in his death-agony and drew near to death, the brethren began to praise among themselves a man of such great merit, saying that he could go securely to God, having produced so great fruit in the Church of God during his lifetime. Hearing this, he gathered what strength he could and said to them in a voice as though reproving them:

“Be silent, brethren, be silent. What are you saying? Truly I tell you that I go to God trembling and anxious, as though I had never done anything good. For even if there was any good in me, or if through my littleness any fruit could arise through the cooperating grace of God, I greatly fear and tremble lest perhaps I have retained that same grace within me less worthily or less humbly than I should.”

Thus armed with the shield of perfect humility, which sounded from his mouth and flourished in his heart, he put off the human person; and, powerfully repelling all the darts of the most wicked adversary, whether fiery or sulphurous, he passed safely through the aerial powers [Col. 1019B] and ascended to the gates of paradise to receive his crown. The remains of his sacred body were reverently buried beside the relics of his predecessor, so that those who had been one spirit and one faith in this life might also possess an equal glory in eternal blessedness. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Life and Excellent Character of the Most Reverend Fastrad, Abbot of Cîteaux

We have inserted into this work matters full of edification concerning the holy life of the holy and God-beloved Fastrad, abbot of Cîteaux, which a certain religious monk of Clairvaux, a witness of truth who was also privileged to enjoy the friendship of so great a man, wrote down. We have also inserted certain admirable matters concerning the elders of Clairvaux, as we find them arranged in his little book, so that what he placed here and there, mingled with other narratives, may here, reduced to order and joined to similar material, shine forth more clearly [Col. 1019C] and serve more profitably for the reader’s benefit.

Thus he writes:

Fastrad, of venerable and devout memory, formerly abbot of Cîteaux, a man of outstanding holiness, was noble indeed by birth, but nobler still through the excellence of his character. Though by no means slightly initiated into liberal studies, he nevertheless always devoted himself with more ardent desire to sacred letters; so that, as he later advanced in wisdom and age, he kept them continually before his eyes and in his hands, and would not even recline at table without divine reading. He did this not only in his own house but also while travelling in schools.

While he was abbot of Cambron, when Lord Robert of devout memory, the elected successor of blessed Bernard, died, Fastrad was elected to govern Clairvaux. Yet he pretended not to come to that election, even though he was called by name, fearing lest what he had always feared might happen to him. Nevertheless, before the delegates from Clairvaux could reach him to seek him out [Col. 1019D], rumour, flying ahead with its chatter, informed him that all had unanimously agreed upon his person.

Troubled and anxious at this report, he fled and came to the house of the Valley of Saint Peter, a monastery of the Carthusian Order, where he hid for several days. As he persisted there day and night in prayer, he entered into ecstasy of mind. And behold, there appeared to him in great glory the Virgin who had borne a child, Lady of the Angels, carrying in her hands the King of Glory, her little Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] The Blessed Virgin appeared to him. This story may still be seen painted in glass in the church of the Valley of Saint Peter.]

When he saw her, he fell at her feet, begging her to have mercy upon him. The blessed Virgin answered him: “Why are you troubled, O man?” Then, placing in his arms, as in those of another Simeon, the noble burden which she carried, she said: “Receive my Son, and keep him.”

[Note: [Col. 1019D] These are not the words of the author of this book, but of an earlier author [Col. 1020D], whom he introduces as speaking in this and other chapters.]

[Col. 1020A] When this was done, the vision was taken from his eyes; and, returning to himself, he understood that the word had gone forth from the Lord, and that those entrusted to his care were truly sons of God and members of Christ.

Forewarned, then, by this joyful vision, he no longer dared to resist, lest he appear to wish to oppose God’s ordinance. Having accepted the government of so distinguished a monastery, it is not for our simplicity to set forth what a discerning, watchful, and most kindly shepherd he showed himself. For as he surpassed others in the office of dignity, so he also went before them by the example and merit of religious holiness. He was chaste, devout, humble, gentle, and modest beyond all those whom I remember seeing in his lifetime.

There is no need, as that Severus says of blessed Martin, to praise his frugality; for even while still in the world he lived so sparingly that he was thought to be not a scholar but a monk. As he himself privately disclosed to some close associates [Col. 1020B], two years before his conversion, though not yet mature in age, he devoted himself to abstinence in such a way that he never wished to be satisfied even with bread and water. And although at that very time he had been ill almost to the point of death, he never consented to eat meat.

Once he had become a monk, I forbear to say how soberly he lived—or rather, how strictly he abstained—and reduced his body to servitude, since, to confess the truth, he was excessive in this regard. I observed enough of him in such matters, for I served him at his table for many years. Since he relentlessly persecuted the vices of the flesh in himself, he seemed also to have too little compassion, as was fitting, even for the wretched flesh itself, in which they naturally reside.

But how humble and temperate he was in outward dress and equipment, considering the dignity of his office, may easily be seen from this one thing which I shall relate. One day, when the monk in charge of clothing had placed upon his bed a cowl—or perhaps a tunic—with which he wished him to be clothed, somewhat better than usual, the Father rebuked him in my hearing and said:

“What is this, my dear brother, that you wish to do—separate me from the fellowship of our brethren and make me conspicuous by distinctive clothing? Because I bear the title of abbot, must I therefore cease to be a monk? Was I appointed minister and servant of others so that I ought to be fattened with more sumptuous fare and adorned with finer clothes? Therefore, if you love me, seek my peace, and do not disdain to obey my commands, I beg and command you not to wish to do this again. For since I am the least of all and unworthy before God, it is a great thing for me if I am honoured with the common food and clothing of all. Since I was raised to the governance of souls, this is the one thing I have always feared and still fear above all others: lest, through occasion of this administration, I abandon the poor life which I professed and lose the reward of a monk.”

This man, beloved by God and by human beings and splendidly adorned with the gifts of charisms [Col. 1020D], instructed those subject to him not only by word and example, but also moved those who looked upon him with wondrous devotion by the most gracious bearing of his body. So great was the grace of the Paraclete Spirit shining in his angelic face that scarcely could any one of the faithful be satisfied with the sight of him, so delightful to behold—especially those who considered the purity of his mind and his singular gentleness, which they saw as though divinely impressed upon the outward man, like a seal proper to him.

Adorned with these ornaments of virtue, this venerable man was, when the Church of Cîteaux—the mother of us all—lacked a shepherd, chosen by equal vote and common counsel as universal Father of the monastery of Cîteaux and of the whole Order [Col. 1021A], the abbots and monks attending the election having been attracted by his sweet fragrance. Having accepted this office, he would, we believe, have produced great fruit in it, had he not been taken away so quickly because our sins demanded it. But because we were not worthy to enjoy his most holy life longer, it was cut off like a thread from the weaver while still being woven. Yet he, perfected in a short time, fulfilled many years; for his soul was pleasing to God and worthy of the fellowship of angels.

Concerning his happy departure, soon to occur, the following revelation was made to one of the elders of Clairvaux, Peter of Toulouse, of blessed memory, concerning whom we shall say something later. In a vision of the night he saw: behold, in the clouds of heaven, the Son of God came down from heaven, attended by a multitude of saints; he stood in the air itself, seated on the throne of glory, and a radiance proceeding from him illuminated the world. At the right hand of his majesty there appeared a most glorious monument suspended in the air, wrought with marvellous workmanship and greatly delighting the eyes of those who gazed upon it [Col. 1021B].

Before the doors of the basilica of Clairvaux stood an innumerable crowd of both sexes, their faces raised upward as they intently watched the King of Glory, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the mausoleum itself. The aforementioned monk Peter approached that company and began to ask what the tomb was which appeared before the Lord, and what it signified. One of them replied:

“Know that this tomb of which you inquire belongs to a holy man who will shortly be taken from the earth. His departure will bring great desolation throughout these regions far and wide; yet his death will be precious in the sight of the Lord and illustrious in the sight of human beings.”

After the vision had passed, the elder who had seen it began to be troubled and sorrowful as he thought upon it. On the following day, when I saw his face clouded and displaying signs of inward grief, I asked him the cause of his sadness. At length, when much entreated, he explained to me in order the vision he had seen [Col. 1021C]. Knowing him to be endowed with much grace and frequently honoured by the Lord with great consolations, I thought and believed that the word seen by so holy and perfect a man could not fail altogether to be fulfilled.

About twenty days later, suddenly and unexpectedly, the most sorrowful report of that same most holy abbot’s death struck our ears—a report more grievous than any, we believe, which had occurred in that time for many days past, either in these regions or in the entire Cistercian Order. Nevertheless, in accordance with the manner of the foregoing revelation, his death was, as we truly trust, precious in the sight of the Lord and renowned and illustrious in the sight of human beings.

For while he was in Paris attending Lord Pope Alexander concerning the affairs of his monastery and of his whole Order, he was seized by illness and took to his bed; within five days he rested in a holy end. [Col. 1021D] At his death, the entire dignity of the Roman Curia stood by him, so that Lord Pope himself, anointing him with his own hands and strengthening him with the apostolic blessing, compassionately shared the suffering of the dying man with deep affection and rejoiced over him when dead. Not only the Pope, but also the most devout king of the Franks, Louis, who was likewise present with his court, mourned the most holy man with great lamentation as a most beloved father and shed many tears over him. At last his sacred body was brought back to Cîteaux and buried with great devotion.

It is therefore clear that the blessed Father’s happy consummation and the splendour of his most celebrated funeral were plainly signified by the radiance of that most precious monument set before God. I shall also briefly relate another vision concerning this most devout Father. Although I do not know who saw it [Col. 1022A], I know certainly that I have heard it often and from many persons.

They say that in England there was a religious man of great virtue who, on the very day when blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, departed from the world, although he himself was in England, saw in the spirit a great angel sent from heaven, taking up from the earth an exceedingly great soul and bearing it with immense joy to the stars. Later, when the blessed abbot Fastrad, of whom we speak, departed from the body, that same man saw, on that very day, the same angel descending to earth and lifting up a soul taken from it to the heights of heaven. Though it appeared great and illustrious, it was in no way comparable in greatness to the former.

I have related these things concerning the life of the most blessed Father and his precious death in a brief account, not intending to encompass in writing all his life and works—which are surely great and altogether beyond my littleness—but only so that those matters known, as I understood, either to myself alone or to a few persons with me might not perish after being committed to a written memorial.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Wonderful Conversion of Lord Alexander, Abbot of Cîteaux

(See above, *First Life of St Bernard*, book VII, in this volume, col. 431.)

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Revelation Which the Blessed Monk Christian Was Worthy to See Concerning Lord Abbot Rainard and the Community of Cîteaux

Rainard, a venerable man and formerly abbot of Cîteaux, having heard the reputation of the blessed monk Christian, desired to speak with so holy a man. He therefore wrote to the lord abbot of La Charité, under whose care Lord Christian was, requesting that he send Christian to him with [Col. 1022C] due reverence. The abbot summoned one of the brethren, whom he knew suitable for this task, and entrusted that servant of God to him, so that he might be conducted, as ordered, to the house of Cîteaux.

One day, as they journeyed and had said together the regular sixth hour according to the time of day, the monk travelling with the man of God withdrew apart so that each might privately chant the Hour of Our Lady by himself; for permission had not yet been granted for the Hours of the Blessed Virgin to be sung publicly.

[Note: [Col. 1021] Note the custom of reciting the Hours of the Blessed Virgin: first privately, afterward in choir and publicly.]

As the man of God went on alone, he was suddenly caught up in ecstasy of mind. With tears streaming from his eyes and his face raised to heaven, he swayed in different directions so that he could scarcely remain on the horse which he rode. The other monk, seeing this, greatly feared lest perhaps he should fall from the horse; nevertheless, giving honour to God, he did not presume to approach more closely, but patiently waited to see what outcome the matter would have.

A little later the elder returned to himself. His travelling companion [Col. 1022D] reverently approached and humbly began to ask him, if he had seen anything relating to God’s honour and the edification of one’s neighbour, to deign to reveal it to him. The servant of the Lord answered with cheerful countenance:

“My dear brother, I pray you, in what direction is the house of Cîteaux situated?”

Although he had never seen Cîteaux or ever travelled the road that led there, he stretched out his hand straight toward that region of the sky where the monastery lay and said: “Is it not in this direction?”

The monk, marveling, replied: “Yes, holy Father.”

Then he burst forth in exultation, in heart and voice: “O blessed brethren who dwell at Cîteaux! O how blessed and holy is that community, which strives to serve the Lord so sincerely and devoutly day and night!” Then, turning to the monk, he said: “Just now, as you saw, when I entered [Col. 1023A] into ecstasy of mind, I was caught up in the spirit to Cîteaux. I saw the community of monks standing in its order in the choir, suffused with great brightness and most devoutly rendering praise to God. Above that community I saw another community of holy angels standing in the same order; they too shone with the brightness of a far greater light and seemed to rejoice at the brethren’s devotion. In that upper choir I saw the lord abbot, as though standing in his stall; he too, surrounded by fitting glory, sent forth rays of great light.”

When the brother asked whether he had seen the lord abbot shining with a brightness equal to that of the angels, the elder replied: “You should know that, in this mortal and corruptible life, however much one advances, one cannot be clothed with a glory of brightness equal to that of the holy angels.” Hearing this, the brother was greatly edified and knew without doubt that the lord abbot of Cîteaux was of great merit before God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Vision through Which Lord John, Formerly a Monk of Cîteaux and Afterwards Bishop of the Church of Valence, Was Converted

[Col. 1023B]

John, a bishop venerable for his life, who had been taken from the Cistercian Order and governed the Church of Valence vigorously enough, had, while still living in the world, resolved in his heart to cast away the vanity of the world and, having received the religious habit, to serve the Lord in the Order and house of Cîteaux. But as he delayed through negligence what he had profitably resolved, that fervour of good intention gradually began to grow cold in his mind.

Meanwhile, he travelled to Saint James for prayer. When he had returned home from that pilgrimage, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision that same night, together with his blessed apostles Peter and James. Blessed James had a certain most beautiful book [Col. 1023C], which he held open before the Lord, and in it was written the name of that cleric. The Lord said to Saint Peter: “Erase his name from my book, for he has drawn back from his purpose.”

Blessed James approached the Lord and said: “I beg you, Lord, spare him, for he is my pilgrim, and he will now hasten to correct himself.” As the aforesaid cleric, frightened and trembling, confirmed this and promised it, the Lord said: “And who will make me secure of this?” Blessed James replied: “Lord, I am his surety.”

The cleric awoke; and while he marvelled within himself at these things, he fell asleep again and saw the same vision. Blessed Peter held the aforementioned book open before the Lord, and in the place where the cleric’s name had been written there appeared this inscription: “We will make for you little chains of gold, inlaid with silver” (*Song of Songs* 1).

When the vision had passed, he awoke and followed with his whole soul the grace of God calling him. Leaving behind all the world’s vanities, he hastened to the house of Cîteaux; there, once tested and found faithful, he received the monastic habit. Advancing in religious life and wisdom in that same house, he later became abbot of Bonneval. From there he was also raised to the bishopric of the city of Valence. Governing it vigorously for many years, he endured many adversities there in defence of justice.

Let those, I pray, attend to this who resolve to do something good and neglect to bring it into effect; who think themselves bound by no guilt if they fail to perform the good which they have resolved to do, provided they have not vowed it. For blessed Gregory plainly teaches:

[Note: [Col. 1023] Gregory, *Homily 3 on Ezekiel*, at the end; also cited in 17, question 1, chapter “Qui bona.”]

If anyone, established in a lesser good, resolves to do some greater good, that person has already made the lesser good unlawful for himself; and if he does not perform what he has resolved, then, though in human eyes he may appear to remain in the lesser good, in the eyes of God, who sees all things, he has nevertheless fallen from the greater good. For God will come as judge not only of deeds but also of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

Certainly, the servant of whom we speak is known to have made no vow, but only to have delayed through negligence what he had simply resolved. Yet that most subtle searcher of hearts judged the matter so seriously that he ordered him to be erased from the book of life, unless he made haste to bring into effect the good he had conceived in his mind [Col. 1024C].

These few matters concerning the virtues of the most reverend Fathers of the monastery of Cîteaux, which could come to our knowledge, we have set down in a faithful account. We know most certainly that that most holy house was illustrious for men perfect and consummate in every form of religious life; and we confess that our littleness was less fitted to investigate their virtues.

## CHAPTER XXI. Lord Robert, Second Abbot of Clairvaux

Lord Robert, abbot of Dunes, succeeded the most blessed Father Bernard in the government of the monastery of Clairvaux. The Lord deigned to reveal his appointment six or seven years before the elevation itself occurred. For, so long before that time, two brethren of Clairvaux were speaking of the blessed accomplishments of their beloved abbot Bernard.

“Do you know,” one said to the other, “how long our Father will yet live?”

When the other replied that he did not know, the first said: “I know that he will live six or seven years, and that Lord Robert, now abbot of Dunes, must succeed to the government of this monastery.”

When this came to pass by God’s gift, that religious abbot exercised pastoral care all the more humbly because he judged himself inferior in merits to his predecessor. The more outstanding he considered the virtues of the one who had gone before, the more he despised in himself whatever good he could do. Thus it came about that, while he offered the appearance of great religious devotion, his own life nevertheless seemed base to him in comparison with one better.

In the time of this venerable abbot there was at Clairvaux a certain religious monk who saw a glorious vision, which the Lord deigned to show for the consolation of his humble family at Clairvaux. But the brother who was worthy to see that vision was uncertain whether he saw it sleeping or fully awake; yet he believed rather that he saw it awake and caught up in ecstasy [Col. 1026C].

On the Monday of Easter, while he was at Vigils in the choir of Clairvaux, the hand of the Lord came upon him there. And behold, above in the air, opposite the middle of the choir, there appeared to him a shining and glorious right hand. It blessed the community present, confessing his holy name in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and impressed upon it, once and then a second time in a long sweep, the sign of the life-giving Cross. The Spirit revealing mysteries spoke in the heart of the beholder and said: “This is the arm of the Ruler; this is the right hand of the Almighty.”

On that same day, the most noble man Andrew, archdeacon of Verdun, was converted there. He had come for prayer, yet at that time had no intention of conversion. But when he entered the chapter of the brethren to seek the support of their prayers, he saw the order of that holy multitude and their life like that of angels [Col. 1026D]. He was deeply pierced with compunction, and when the Spirit of the Lord rushed into him, he was changed into another man.

He abandoned the world with such fervour that he did not return to his own people even for an hour—not even to greet friends or arrange his household and affairs. Rather, he immediately left all things behind, breaking rather than settling his ties, that he might cleave more swiftly to Christ. And so that the double impression of the Cross might appear more plainly, another cleric, named Geoffrey, entered with him: lower indeed in birth, but perhaps not inferior in uprightness of character and noble conversion.

Both men, therefore, having entered together and persevered together in the Order, fought the good fight; and now, their contest completed, they share in the eternal blessing. The aforesaid Andrew, however, endured many trials in the newness of his conversion; but the heavenly right hand which had bestowed the blessing kept him unharmed through them all. For he was like a very tender worm in wood, exceedingly soft and delicate, so that the right hand of the Lord might triumph in him all the more gloriously in proportion as the vessel in which it worked its power was weaker. Since he could scarcely unlearn the softness of his former manner of life and regarded the labor of his newly begun undertaking as altogether too arduous, he thought, like Lot, that, having left Sodom, he could not save his life on the mountain. He therefore resolved to turn aside to some Order of more relaxed observance. Although he had already often revealed this to his spiritual father, the venerable Robert, and had for some time restrained himself from this purpose by means of Robert’s saving admonitions, at last one day, overcome by faintheartedness of spirit and by the storm, he declared that he could endure no longer. [Col. 1027B]

Then the abbot, by many entreaties and gentle persuasions, obtained from him the promise to do violence to himself and hold out patiently until the third day. Having at last scarcely gained this concession, he entered the chapter of the brothers and appointed that the community should pray to God for him. The compassionate father himself also turned to the Lord with the full effort of his mind and prayed most devoutly that the Lord in His mercy might deign to preserve the little sheep which the devil was attempting to snatch away.

That same day, when this novice came to table, he found a dish of peas set before him. This sort of pulse he was accustomed to loathe above all others, so much that it sometimes even made him nauseated. Looking upon the stew which he so greatly abhorred, he was troubled, and, though hunger compelled him to take something, he could scarcely persuade his reluctant stomach to accept it. And, O good God, how rich Thou art in mercy, accommodating Thyself to the tender and delicate, so that in all things the purpose of Thy will may be fulfilled and Thy holy name glorified! When the aforesaid novice had barely begun to taste the food he hated, he felt a certain wondrous sweetness, so that its excellence of flavor surpassed meat or fish. On discovering this, he immediately seized a spoon, drew the bowl nearer, and, forgetful of moderation, devoured the cooked legumes to the bottom. While eating, he frequently put his finger into his mouth, thinking that he might discover bits of bacon-fat, in which he supposed those legumes had been fried. When the meal was finished, he hastened to the abbot and anxiously asked whether he had ordered that stew to be enriched with fat, or deliberately seasoned with any other grease for his sake. The abbot denied it; the cooks were then questioned about the dish as well. They too declared truthfully that they had added nothing except salt and water. Hearing this, the neophyte joyfully recognized the miracle of God’s visitation toward him; and, giving thanks to God, he could thereafter not be moved from his chosen Order. [Col. 1027D] Since, by God’s great gift, on the second and third days and for a long time afterward he continued to perceive the aforesaid sweetness in foods of this kind, experience, his teacher, finally taught him that the Lord is able, when He wills, to bestow upon legumes and vegetables, for the consolation of His servants, the same delight of taste that He has given to meats and fishes. Hence he often said that he now took greater pleasure in eating peas and vegetables than formerly in eating fattened poultry and game.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Concerning the elder who foresaw in the spirit the apostasy of a certain monk and foretold it to Lord Abbot Robert

But since we have related a sufficiently pleasant example concerning these two athletes of Christ, to encourage the tender and delicate not to shrink from conversion—for the hand of the Lord is not powerless to sustain, strengthen, and confirm in the sacred Order even those however luxurious in upbringing—we now set forth a very sad example concerning two others. Having assumed the habit of religion, they turned back after Satan, lest anyone incorporated into the holy Order should immediately promise himself security, when he ought then first to set his hand to mighty deeds and, unless he strives lawfully, shall by no means attain the crown set before him.

One of the elders of Clairvaux, named William, advanced alike in religious life and age, whom Lord Abbot Robert himself greatly venerated for his holiness, once lay ill in the infirmary under the pressure of bodily sickness. One night after Matins, while the other sick men were resting, he, being most fervent, kept watch and prayed in bed as was his custom. And behold, a demon entered through the door of the infirmary and appeared manifestly to his eyes in the dress and countenance of a harlot. Passing before him, she wandered about as though seeking someone. In the middle of the room a lamp was burning; shining brightly, it made the wanton movements and lascivious gestures of that monstrous creature plainly visible. Thus the phantom prostitute went about, surveying all things with roving gaze and examining almost every bed, carefully investigating who slept and who kept watch, in case perhaps she might recognize one of her own there; whether anyone might meet her consenting to her flattery and seduction. She passed quickly by one, gazed more lingeringly upon another, visited this one from afar, drew nearer to that one; sometimes she even gently laid her hands upon the mouths of those at rest. She wished to leave nothing untouched, nothing unexamined; and what she continually works inwardly through suggestion, she visibly performed—by the Lord’s permission, for our warning—before the eyes of that spiritual man. [Col. 1028C]

At length, finding the one whom she sought, she stopped before his bed. He was a young monk, newly made a monk. Then, thrusting out her shameless hand, she moved back the covering a little at the side of his head and, gently touching and rousing the sleeper, said aloud:

> “O senseless man, what are you doing here? Rise quickly and follow me; and tell your companion also to come out after you. I shall wait for you outside at the door.”

Having said this, the obstinate beast hurried away and went out through the door by which she had entered. The young man awoke, sat up in bed, rubbed his forehead with his hands, and looked this way and that, wishing to know who had awakened him. Seeing no one, he laid his head down again and fell asleep—but not in the Lord.

When morning came, the man of God who had seen these things informed his abbot, Lord Robert of pious memory, of the course of events. The latter, like a good shepherd anxious not to lose any sheep entrusted to him, privately questioned the young man about his thoughts, admonished him more carefully, and instructed him more cautiously. The answer he received was that the young man was troubled by no shameful thought whatsoever, but was drawn by a most steadfast will toward perseverance in his purpose. Yet iniquity lied to itself (Psalm 26 [Vulgate]). For the way of confession was blocked in his heart under the devil’s presidency, so that he might not enter through the gate of penance into saving pardon.

When the abbot reported the young man’s answer to the aforesaid man of God, he replied: “Wait a little, and from the outcome of the deed you will prove that what I said is true.” Why say more? Not many days passed, and behold, that young man, driven by the furies of lust, forgetful of God’s dreadful judgment, broke the bond of his profession and, returning to the vomit of the world, became a vile apostate. Thus at last he was caught by the seduction of that phantom harlot.

The companion whom he had been ordered to lead forth with him had himself been a novice with him and had received the sacred habit with him, though in vain. Having been sent to another house, when he heard that his companion had cast off the yoke of the Order, he too, breaking the bond of his profession, did not delay to apostatize with him. It therefore became plainly known that that spirit of fornication, which according to the prophet “blows coals in the furnace” (Isaiah 54), had kindled in their hearts the poisonous delights of carnal pleasure and thereby deceived them both. May the almighty and merciful Lord keep the inextricable bonds of this wickedness far from His weak little servants; for, according to blessed Job’s saying, “the sinews of his testicles are intertwined” (Job 40).

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Concerning the joyful vision which Lord Abbot Robert saw at the death of a certain spiritual man

One of the spiritual sons of the most reverend Father Robert had run with unbending zeal along the narrow and arduous way which leads to life. At last it pleased the Lord to put an end to his labors, that, falling asleep in peace in unity, he might rest. When the hour was already at hand in which he was to be summoned from the course of this world and invited to the heavenly prize, the lord abbot had lain down in his bed with the other brothers in order to rest. And behold, the sleep of the Lord fell upon him, and in a dream he saw two most beautiful youths, strikingly radiant in countenance and dress. They scattered throughout the choir of Clairvaux lilies, roses, violets, and flowers of diverse kinds in abundance, so that the entire pavement seemed painted and made beautiful with various colors.

At this sight he marveled greatly and, as though jealous for the simplicity of the Order, said to them: “What has seemed good to you, good youths, that you should, contrary to our custom, strew this pavement with flowers and introduce such novelty into our monastery?” They replied: “Do not marvel at these things, nor hinder us in carrying out our office; for a new feast of a certain new saint will now be celebrated in this choir, at whose solemnity the angels shall rejoice and a hymn shall be sung to the Lord in Sion.”

They were still speaking, and were carrying the mind of the seer and hearer of these things away in wonder, when suddenly the hurried clatter of the board awakened the sleeper. By the customary signal he was summoned, so that he might carry out outwardly, in accordance with the dignity of his office, the celebration which he had learned inwardly in the spirit was to be observed. He ran quickly with the other brothers to the man and, with great devotion, commended his soul, believing and confidently trusting that this was that new saint concerning whom the holy angels would immediately celebrate a new feast and new joy when he was received into rest. [Col. 1029C]

O blessed—and truly blessed—are those whom Thou hast chosen and taken up, Lord, who now in this life so purge out from themselves every dross of sin through the ardor of penance that, in that life to which one passes through the death of this present life, where the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Sion by the dreadful spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning (Isaiah 4), they require no purification, but immediately attain the rest of blessedness without any hindrance of sin.

Lord Robert of blessed memory, the second abbot of Clairvaux, having faithfully, wisely, and humbly employed for the profit of souls the talent entrusted to him, was brought into the joy of his Lord. Though not equal in merits to his most holy predecessor, he was nevertheless joined to him in blessedness, that he might rejoice with him in heaven whose worthy successor he had deserved to be on earth in so religious a community. His bodily remains were laid in a tomb constructed in the wall of the cloister of Clairvaux, near the church door, where other perfect monks, truly worthy of God, likewise rest; concerning whom we shall say something in what follows.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Concerning Lord Pontius, fifth abbot of Clairvaux and afterward bishop of Clermont; and concerning certain holy monks, his brothers and sons

In the third place, the blessed Fastradus, to be named with all reverence, of whom we have spoken above, presided over the monastery of Clairvaux. When, as the preceding matters show, he was taken up to govern the Church of Cîteaux, Lord Geoffrey—formerly notary of our holy Father Bernard, greatly beloved by him, and the author in honeyed speech of the final three books of Bernard’s Life—was appointed as the fourth pastor and abbot of Clairvaux. After he had resigned some years later, the venerable Pontius, abbot of Grandselve, was raised to the dignity of this office by the common election of the abbots and brothers of Clairvaux, because of the merit of his religious life and prudence.

While still a monk in the house of Grandselve, one of the daughters of Clairvaux in the region of Toulouse—a house in which, it is established, many men of distinguished and great merit had existed from the beginning—this servant of God strove by every means to crucify the world to himself and himself to the world; to cut away the vices of flesh and heart; to pant after the heavenly fatherland with vows and sighs of sacred desire; and eagerly to seek the friendship and familiarity of elders whom he knew to be eminent in spiritual life and religion, so that by their examples and exhortations he might be renewed day by day in the spirit of his mind and, advancing through daily increases, rise above the knowledge of adverse philosophy. [Col. 1030B]

Among the others, he attached himself especially to one who was master of the novices in that house, a man of exceptional virtue and grounded in every purity of the virtues. This man, therefore, like an elder worn out by his labors, began to think upon the rest of eternal happiness, to despise everything belonging to the world and the flesh, and to long with all the marrow of his heart for the most blessed presence of Christ our Lord. He had a most ardent desire “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1), “for this is by far the better.” As he stood in this contest of spiritual desire and daily said in his prayers, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41 [Vulgate]), the most sacred day of the Lord’s Supper came upon him, on which, as is customary, the community was solemnly to approach the Lord’s table and partake of the life-giving sacraments.

When the hour of the divine sacrifice was at hand and the brothers in their order approached the altar to receive holy communion, he too came among the others, eager to partake of the divine gift. Having received holy communion, while he still held that saving Eucharist in his mouth, his soul melted within him because of the inexpressible sweetness of divine love. Through impatience of sacred desire, he put his finger to his throat and asked his soul that he might die, pouring out the following prayer to the Lord:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, Savior of humankind, who didst deign, for us sinners, to take from the womb of the immaculate and undefiled Virgin Mary this most pure and innocent flesh, which I, unworthy as I am, have presumed to receive: if this petition of Thy servant, such as it is, does not displease Thee, I pray and beseech the mercy of Thy compassion that through this passage of my throat, through which I must now send down the heavenly food, the bread of eternal life, Thou wilt henceforth permit no earthly bread, nor any other earthly substance whatsoever, to pass in any manner.”

Saying this, he sent down the Host of salvation which he held in his mouth with the utmost joy and devotion, into the interior rather of his soul than of his body. Immediately, therefore, as though the Lord had answered him, “Be it done to thee as thou hast asked,” at that same hour and in that same place his bodily strength suddenly began to fail, and on the third day—that is, on Holy Saturday of Easter—he fell asleep in the Lord, to be eternally satisfied by the vision for which he had sought with such sighs and prayers, into which angels desire to look (1 Peter 1). Blessed is the man who thus fulfilled his desire! Happy the prayer which deserved so swift an effect of its petition!

The aforesaid Lord Pontius, then a monk of that same monastery, who loved him singularly and devotedly rendered assiduous service to him in sickness and death, asked whether he was severely oppressed by bodily pain. He replied that he was peaceful and tranquil and felt no discomfort, except only in his throat, where he had placed his finger; there, he said, he felt some pain. [Col. 1031A]

As Lord Pontius was moved with wondrous devotion toward one dying so happily, he approached him and, with great contrition of heart, earnestly begged him that, if it could come about by divine permission, he would return to him after death and inform him of what had happened to him. The man assented. A few days after his death, he returned to the aforesaid brother, shining with great brightness and transparent throughout his body like crystal or the purest glass. He said to him:

> “I make known to you, dearest friend, that through the Lord’s mercy I have been received into great blessedness. This body, in which you see me, has been granted to me until the day of the general resurrection, when I shall recover my own body, which now swarms with worms and is reduced to dust, incomparably more excellent and glorious than this one. Meanwhile I rest most sweetly in this body, which is altogether suited to me and so transparent that I see most clearly from each of its limbs and all its parts as though from eyes; and my whole body is everywhere to me as if it were one single eye.”

> [Note: It is scarcely probable that the appearing monk is reported to have said that the body in which he appeared was given to him as a gift until the day of resurrection: [Col. 1032D] for what use would such a body be to him rather than to others—or indeed, what use would it be to them?]

In one foot of that same most pure and transparent body, however, there appeared the darkness of a certain spot. With a somewhat sorrowful expression he spoke of it thus: “This spot which you see was contracted by my negligence: namely, because I used sometimes to go sluggishly to the daily labor, and did not follow with the zeal I ought the community of brothers going out to manual work.” That holy soul made known these and many other most wonderful things to the aforesaid monk, and at length, departing from him, left him greatly edified and consoled.

Let those pay attention, I beg, who are accustomed not only to go sluggishly to labor but even to stay away from common labor for any trifling reason, since it is certain that every institution of the Order is holy and pleasing to God and cannot be neglected without grave danger to souls. [Col. 1031C]

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Concerning a dying brother who disclosed to Lord Pontius the glory shown beforehand to him

The servant of God Pontius had deserved to see the aforesaid vision for our consolation, we who bear the burden of the day and heat in the Cistercian Order. In the time that followed, when his merits had increased, he was appointed to govern that same Church. He adorned his place of dignity with fitting conduct, exercising pastoral care with due authority while not losing the gentleness and innocence of a sheep.

It happened in the days of his prelacy that the Lord, by a hidden dispensation of His dreadful judgments, sent into that house a violent plague, so that within two months about forty-five brothers were taken away. Almost all of them accepted death with so great a desire of piety that they seemed already to have foreseen from heaven that, after the miseries of this life, they would immediately become partakers of the life of eternal blessedness. Many of them indeed foresaw the heavenly grace to be bestowed upon them and deserved to receive what they had foreseen. To give credibility to our words, we shall relate, by way of example, a few instances out of many.

There was there a monk of most approved conduct who died in the aforesaid epidemic. When he had reached his final hour, the board was struck after Compline, and the brothers assembled to strengthen him for his departure. While the monks sang litanies and psalms around him, he too, strengthened by the Lord, chanted with the others in such voice as he could. When the psalmody was completed, Lord Abbot Pontius gave the signal and ordered the community to depart, because he saw the sick man chanting and thought that he would still draw breath for some time. [Col. 1032A]

When the brother saw this, he stretched out his hand to indicate to the abbot that he should make them remain a little longer, because he knew that he would depart almost immediately. Seeing that the most fervent man, because of the strictness of regular discipline, did not wish to break silence after Compline even at the point of death, the abbot could not restrain himself for joy. Breaking silence himself, and first saying, “Bless,” he said: “I beseech you, most beloved brother, since I see that the Lord is with you, tell us, if anything has been revealed to you concerning that blessed hope which you await, so that we too may take breath in the Lord and rejoice with you.”

Then the sick man replied: “To answer briefly what you ask, father, know that I have seen things which it is not permitted to speak. Yet I can say this one thing: if I alone surpassed the merits of all human beings, I should still certainly not be worthy to obtain the glory of eternal blessedness which has been prepared and shown beforehand to me, and which I am now about to possess.” Having said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Concerning a fainthearted brother whom Lord Abbot Pontius magnificently encouraged to penance

A brother of great religious devotion, named Bernard, lived at that time in the same monastery. At the beginning of his conversion, as he considered more attentively the enormity of his sins and the justice of the strict Judge, he was so moved by fear that he nearly fell into despair. When the venerable abbot Pontius learned this, he tried by many examples and admonitions to persuade him that anyone who confesses and repents, however guilty, is never deprived of pardon. When he still could not satisfy him in this way, he added: “I make myself surety for your salvation, and let my soul be demanded in place of yours, provided that you obediently persevere in this Order.”

Strengthened greatly by this promise, the brother completely conquered the spirit of distrust by which he was assaulted and, rejoicing in the Lord with trembling, thereafter accustomed himself to sing of mercy and judgment. Though noble by birth, he considered no nobility of value except becoming poor for Christ and serving the poor. He had been appointed infirmarian for the poor in the guesthouse. Attending to them with the utmost care, he did not serve them as strangers and beggars, but as his own lords and as members of the Son of God. If he saw among them anyone sick, ulcerated, or swarming with worms, he devoted every work of compassion to that person—washing, wiping, and refreshing him—and attended him continually like a mother beside her sick child. [Col. 1032D]

While the servant of God did not cease to do these and similar things, it happened that in the aforesaid epidemic he departed to the Lord. Seeing his companions taken away daily, he too greatly desired “to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” The merciful Lord, who is always near to servants whose hearts are contrite and spirits afflicted, decreed to fulfill his desire. A slight fever arose, and when he began to be mildly ill, he lay down in bed. When the lord abbot came in to visit him, he wondered that a man of such fervor should be confined to bed for so slight a cause. Smiling, he said: “Do not fear, my brother Bernard, for you will not now die, but will yet eat with us of our beans and vegetables.” But he replied: “I do not fear, father, I do not fear; rather, I trust in the Lord that I shall no longer be disappointed of my desire.”

Why say more? After four or five days, the small spark grew into a great fire; and the fever which had been considered a one-day fever became fatal. Then the abbot reproved his own judgment and recognized that the brother’s prediction concerning himself had prevailed.

As the hour of his departure drew near, the brother was anointed with sacramental oil. Once the anointing was completed, he was immediately in the spirit; caught up in contemplation, he lay for a long time without sense or movement, so that he seemed almost dead. Meanwhile the heavens were opened to him, and with unveiled face he deserved to behold the glory of God, so that he could say: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32). As he lay for a long while as though lifeless, searching out the secrets of heaven not through presumption but with grace as guide, at length he returned to himself; the very joyfulness of his expression sufficiently showed where he had been. [Col. 1033B]

The compassionate father approached and asked how he was. He answered: “It is well with me, lord father, by God’s pardon. And now, dearest father, I release you from the debt of your pledge, giving many thanks for your care toward me, a sinner. For a promisor is rightly released when the fulfillment of his promise has already been secured.” The abbot, having forgotten that former obligation by which he had made himself answerable for the soul of this brother, wondered what he meant. The brother then reminded him more plainly:

> “Have you then forgotten how formerly you made yourself responsible for my salvation? I therefore make you free from that surety, because I am now secure of my salvation through the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then the abbot began anxiously to inquire how he could have known this. When the brother refused by every means to tell him, the abbot, seeing that his prayers accomplished nothing, commanded him in the Lord’s name, by the power of obedience, to reveal for the edification and consolation of many what he had seen. Hearing this, the sick brother spoke thus:

> “Since the power of obedience forbids me to keep silence concerning the truth, I shall tell you a matter to which perhaps you will give doubtful credence. But, that I may make this testimony credible, know that with the end of my speech I shall also receive the end of my life. Let your charity know, then, that I—although wretched and unworthy—have been presented to our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and have seen Him face to face; not, however, in His divinity, but only in that most blessed form of humility which He deigned to assume for us. By His most gracious mercy I have received remission of sins, and I have through His grace the hope of eternal happiness laid up in my bosom. From His own most holy mouth I have also heard that all who persevere obediently in this Order until death will receive eternal salvation from Him. I have seen our brothers who have departed from the world resting in great blessedness, and I have foreseen my own place, which, through the Lord’s mercy, I am now to receive among them.”

Having said these things, he fell silent and immediately rendered up his blessed soul.

Let us gird ourselves for penance, brothers, and with this penitent man let us go beforehand to meet God’s face in confession and contrition of heart, so that afterward we may deserve with him to see God’s face in joy of heart and exultation of spirit. Truly, according to God’s testimony, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11). Behold this great sinner: at the beginning of his conversion, considering strictly, as he ought, the number and enormity of his crimes, he had nearly fallen into despair. Enlightened by divine grace, he raised himself up against himself, striving amid tears and the mourning of repentance, and in the assiduous service of the sick, daily to offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart and humbled spirit. Therefore, while still placed in this frail body of mortality, he deserved, for the consolation of all truly penitent persons, not merely to see appeased the face which he exceedingly feared as angry and sought in every way to propitiate, but also to contemplate it forgiving his sins with most gracious gentleness and inviting him to the glory of eternal blessedness. [Col. 1034A]

For the kingdom of heaven does not come to those who sleep and are negligent, who conceal their sins, or who presume upon the number of years which they have spent in holy conduct; rather, it comes to those who keep watch and labor day and night in the voluntary exercise of observing God’s commandments.

Thus Lord Pontius of holy memory, abbot of Grandselve—whose holiness and religious devotion may be estimated from such perfect and devout disciples as those of whom we have spoken—was, both by divine and human election, appointed father and shepherd of the Church of Clairvaux and of the whole generation of Clairvaux, so that, as it is written, “let the holy person still be sanctified” (Revelation 22), and that he who was found faithful in little might be set over many good things of his Lord (Luke 19). While he watched with vigilant care over the Lord’s flock and sought in his prelacy not his own profit but the Lord’s, the lamp kindled by the kindness of the Holy Spirit was not to remain hidden under a bushel. At the Lord’s call, and through the united endeavor of clergy and people in election, he was raised to be bishop of Clermont. Exalted to the honor of the episcopate, he did not abandon monastic humility. He showed these two graces wonderfully joined in himself: the dignity of the high priesthood made the purity of monastic humility more commendable, while, in turn, the vigor of religious life gave authority to the bishop. Thus, feeding and instructing by word and example the people over whom he had been appointed bishop, he appeared distinguished among the bishops of his time. At last, having honorably completed the course of his life, he rested in peace, about to receive from the Lord the reward of his labor. [Col. 1034C]

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning blessed Gerard, sixth abbot of Clairvaux

After Lord Pontius, who had been the fifth abbot of Clairvaux from Saint Bernard, was raised to the summit of the episcopate, blessed Gerard, abbot of Fossanova—a man praiseworthy in every respect for purity of conduct and integrity of character—was appointed sixth abbot of that same Church. He was to fulfill the perfection of the number six both in his life and in his death.

This venerable father, acceptable to God and dear to humankind, was adorned with such grace that the whole body of brothers, beholding him as the most flourishing flower of paradise, venerated him with wondrous affection. For one whom God had sprinkled with grace necessarily had to be loved by all. Christ, indeed, the author and giver of every virtue, in whom are hidden all the treasures not only of wisdom and knowledge but also of compassion and grace, so filled this servant of His with the nectar of spiritual gifts that he did not fear not only to believe in Him and serve Him happily, but even to suffer a hard and dreadful death for Him.

For if tribulation proves the quality of one’s faith, and if it is established that the one who perseveres therein possesses perfect charity, it is clear that this blessed man was perfect in both. Like a good and faithful servant, in tribulation he took care to preserve an unfeigned faith and to bring forth charity from a pure heart and good conscience. He even loved the enemy cruelly thirsting for his blood, valuing the life of the soul more highly than that of the body, shrinking less from death of the flesh than from injury to faith, and preferring to struggle for righteousness rather than, through fearful silence, to conceal the dishonor of the Order and danger to souls. Let us therefore set forth, as briefly as we can, how, after a praiseworthy life conspicuous in every form of religious devotion, he came to the palm of martyrdom. [Col. 1035A]

A certain monk, noble indeed by birth but base in conduct, wandered everywhere contrary to the form and propriety of the Order, frequenting the courts of princes and shamelessly involving himself in secular affairs. In his whole manner of life he showed himself more a wandering monk (*gyrovagus*) than a cloistered monk.
