Lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, inflamed with zeal for justice and devotion to the Order, ordered him to be apprehended. Taking away both his horses and all his possessions, he entrusted him to the venerable Lord Peter, abbot of Igny, so that, restrained in Peter’s house by regular discipline and deprived of every license for wandering, he might do penance, even unwillingly.

Although the good shepherd had acted with the praiseworthy intention of correcting his brother’s error, that malicious man, forestalled by sinister suspicion, murmured that this had been done from an unsound intention. Accordingly, where he ought to have improved, he became worse. Conceiving the devilish spirit with his whole mind, he breathed a dreadful poison of savagery and cruelty and, like a most cruel beast, thirsted for the blood of the compassionate father.

Meanwhile it happened that Lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, entered the regions of Germany, in order to visit the monasteries which Clairvaux possessed in those parts. On the journey he came to Trier, the metropolis of Belgica Prima. Once called most noble and a second Rome, it now shows by the desolation of its ruins what it once had been. In the suburb of this city stands the renowned monastery called by the name of St. Matthias, because the entire body of that most holy apostle rests there, having been brought from Judaea and honorably deposited there by the Empress Helena, mother of Constantine the Great. The authority of the place is further enhanced because the bodies of the disciples of the blessed apostle Peter—namely Eucharius, [Col. 1035C] Valerius, and Maternus—are suitably placed in the crypt of that same church and are venerated with great devotion by the faithful. Sent forth by the aforesaid apostle, these blessed men were the first to preach the word of salvation and the trophy of the Cross to the peoples of Germany; and in their own days they conspicuously adorned three most distinguished German cities—Trier, Tongeren, and Cologne—with the honor of episcopal office.

Coming therefore to the aforesaid city of Trier, Lord Abbot Gerard sought lodging at the monastery of St. Matthias, and was received with every kindness by the abbot and brothers of that place. But he, who had turned aside there not so much for bodily convenience as for spiritual profit, rose in the silence of the untimely night, went to the oratory, entered the crypt, and prostrated himself before the tombs of the aforesaid confessors of Christ, both in body and in mind, intending to seek, by their intercession, divine help for himself and his own through earnest prayers. And when prolonged prayer had obtained the grace of devotion, the infused devotion enlarged his mind; and his enlarged mind [Col. 1035D] became capable of heavenly secrets. Suddenly he saw the same confessors of the Lord standing near him, radiant with heavenly grace. One of them, Eucharius, addressed him in these words:

“Brother, do not be afraid, nor let your heart be alarmed at the sight of us. For we are those who, sent forth by the apostle Peter, first preached Christ in these regions: I, Eucharius, and these likewise, my brothers Maternus and Valerius, whose aid you have sought by visiting our tombs. Therefore, rejoicing also in your faith and devotion, we have come to you by God’s will, to give you counsel concerning the matters which occupy your heart. Your will and the purpose of your heart are that, released from the office of prelation and relieved of the biting tumults of business, you may begin to devote yourself to God alone and to yourself. But you must know that this wish of yours is not according to God’s will. Therefore I advise and admonish you not rashly to abandon the rank of honor which you have attained through the grace divinely bestowed; rather, be steadfast and act courageously, for the time is near when you shall be visited by the Lord, and for your labors you shall receive the unfading crown of glorious victory.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1035D] St. Maternus and the others are falsely said here to have been sent by St. Peter into Germany. For Maternus himself is recorded as having been chosen by Constantine as judge against the Donatists, about three hundred years after the time of St. Peter, as Optatus writes at the end of Book I. Likewise curious, useless, and unworthy of the blessed Gerard, soon to be a martyr, is the prayer in which he sought to have revealed to him what Maternus had done and where his soul had been during the forty days [Col. 1036D] in which he is said to have been dead before being raised by St. Peter. Add that Caesarius and this author do not agree concerning the answer. It is therefore easy to judge that this account was fabricated by Germans, in order to carry the origin of their Church back to the apostolic age—something others have elsewhere attempted contrary to the truth of history.

Having spoken thus, they vanished, leaving the abbot who had heard and seen these things strengthened alike by astonishment and wonder. Meanwhile he hastened on his journey, visited the houses for which he had entered those regions, and by his welcome presence and teaching made the brothers more fervent in the praises of God and in observance of the holy Order. He repeatedly recalled in his mind the sweetness of the aforesaid [Col. 1036B] vision, and diligently pondered the force of the words he had heard: namely, that he would soon be visited by the Lord.

Moreover, beginning to think more earnestly about the same saints who had appeared to him, he wondered greatly where the soul of blessed Maternus had been, or in what kind of life it had lived, during those forty days in which his body lay in the tomb before he was restored to life by the apostle’s staff. And, as if moved to repentance, he groaned because, although in the aforesaid vision he had had a sufficiently fitting opportunity to ask, he had not asked this at all.

When the business for which he had gone had been completed, he returned to Trier, but did not lodge at St. Matthias. For a powerful and wealthy man of that city had earnestly obtained from him, when he had been there previously, a promise that on his return he would deign to bless his house. Received as a guest in that house, before [Col. 1036C] going to bed he spoke privately with his lay brother, commanding him to saddle two horses before dawn and to go alone with him to St. Matthias. The man obeyed; and, when Matins had been said at the proper time, the abbot devoutly visited the bodies of the saints for prayer. While he persisted more intently in tearful prayers, by God’s great gift he merited to see the same saints in the same form as before.

Then St. Eucharius looked at the abbot, stretched out his hand toward St. Maternus, and said: “Behold, this is my brother Maternus. Ask him what you wish.”

When Gerard hesitated and, through reverence and the glory of their countenances, did not dare to reply, blessed Maternus addressed him thus:

“Rightly, dearest brother, you hesitate to ask boldly what you desire to know, because to wish to search out so deep an abyss of God’s judgments, wholly inaccessible to human senses, appears presumptuous.

> **Note:** [Col. 1036D] On this vision and the preceding one, see the note above.

“Yet because you are a pious rather than a curious inquirer, I shall disclose to you, insofar as you can receive it, the mystery of this secret. You think upon and turn over with diligent attention of mind where my soul was, or in what kind of life it lived, during those forty days in which my body lay in the tomb; and with ardent pious longing you desire to know this. Know, then, that just as an infant enclosed within the womb lives, yet does not perceive, so I lay in the bowels of the earth, sleeping in my body the sleep of death, yet living in my soul to God, in whose almighty presence I was even then what I was afterward to be, when restored to life, in the eyes of men.” [Col. 1037A]

Strengthened therefore by this double vision and address, Lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, strove, advancing day by day, to offer Christ diligent service; he was so much the more certain of his approaching end of life because he knew that the heavenly messenger who had foretold it could neither be deceived nor wish to deceive.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Lord Gerard is cruelly murdered while visiting the monastery of Igny.

Accordingly, in the same year in which he had seen this blessed vision, as the time approached when the holy abbot should become an offering to Christ and, as a follower of the spotless Lamb, shed his blood for justice as He had done for the universal Church, he resolved to visit his houses according to the institutions of the Order, and among the others decided also to go to Igny. But the brothers, because they suspected the bestial rage of that false monk—whom, as related above, the lord abbot had rebuked and [Col. 1037B] bound under penance in that same house—warned the lord abbot to take greater care, lest perhaps, as they greatly dreaded, the lamp in Israel should be extinguished.

Yet he, fearless of death and wholly committing himself to the divine will, said that he could not omit the duties belonging to his office merely because death might be imminent. And when he was ready for the journey and already preparing to leave, a spiritual brother came to him and asked to be permitted to speak with him privately. Having obtained this, he began with tearful sighs to beg him not to undertake the journey he had planned, saying that it had been shown to him in a revelation that, if he then came to Igny, he would be killed by a cruel death.

The man of God answered him: “Dear brother, I thank you for your concern for me; but I want you to know that I do not make my soul—that is, this temporal life—more precious than myself, nor is it at all fitting that, frightened by an anxious imagining of death, I should neglect what I am bound to do by the duty of the office which I unworthily discharge. For who knows whether my Lord is testing me? And who, likewise, does not know that God is almighty, and that, if He wills, He can most easily avert the death which you say is imminent, and which I trust, with a secure conscience, that I have not deserved? But if He does not will it, we, as His unprofitable servants, must in every respect obey His will. Therefore let His will be done concerning us and you.”

So he spoke; and, commending all the brothers to divine grace, he set out in a spirit of fortitude upon the journey he had planned and arrived at Igny. There he was received with much reverence, as was fitting, by the abbot of that place, Lord Peter of blessed memory, and by all the brothers; and he showed himself pleasant and gracious to everyone. As he spoke publicly and privately to each one concerning the salvation of souls and observance of the Order, he ordered that even that man of whom we have spoken above—not a monk but soon to become a detestable parricide—be summoned to him. [Col. 1037D]

When he had come, the holy Father, soon to be an offering to Christ, began in the gentlest words to admonish him to bear patiently what had been done for the salvation of his soul. He said that he bore him no resentment whatever, but was indeed ready to embrace him as his dearest son if he could perceive his amendment in signs of holy humility and patience. But that man, who had become one spirit with the devil, a murderer from the beginning, lest the crime of horrible parricide which he had long conceived in his mind should in any way be disclosed and he thus be deprived of the accomplishment of his malice, pretended, with lowered head like a most cunning serpent, humbly to hear what was said. He even uttered with his mouth words of gentleness and peace which he did not have in his heart.

The brothers rejoiced; and, deceived by the garb of false humility with which that pestilent man had clothed himself lest he be discovered, they hoped for fruits worthy of repentance. They thought nothing less possible [Col. 1038A] than that in so short a time, by committing so horrible a deed, he would entangle himself in the snare of eternal death and damnation.

The next day, when the brothers had gathered to perform the office of the nocturnal synaxis, and, according to custom, the lord abbot had been offered leave on account of his travel to depart after Matins and relieve through night rest the fatigue incurred on the journey, he remained, being fervent in spirit. Attentive and wakeful through the whole period of the vigils to the divine praises, as though by a foreknowing spirit he already perceived what was to come upon him, he prepared himself for the approaching contest.

Why say more? When Lauds had ended and, according to the custom of the Order, Prime was immediately joined to them, the lord abbot left the choir and went up to the dormitory; thence he was about to descend to wash his hands, so that, when the Hour had ended, he might come more ready to celebrate the sacred mysteries. That execrable man—not a monk but a parricide—wickedly observed this and more wickedly followed him. In the dormitory, at the place which he had judged suitable [Col. 1038B] for committing so great a crime, he concealed himself in ambush like a lion ready for prey.

The man of God then returned and, walking through the dormitory toward the stairs by which one descends into the cloister, reached the place of ambush. And behold, that son of perdition suddenly sprang forth, attacked him, and plunged a sharp knife, long and broad, into his entrails; cruelly tearing, cutting, and stabbing, he reached as far as the spine of his back. But just as the true Lamb of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was silent—not indeed before His shearer, but before those who pierced His sacred hands and feet—and did not open His mouth, so too this true imitator and offering of Christ, before the terrible tearer and piercer of his entrails, uttered not merely no cry but scarcely any sound of pain.

Then that murderer, hateful to God and abhorred by men, feeling the cage of ribs resisting him so that he could not pierce the sacred body as he wished, added still worse torments to grievous torments. Turning and turning back the detestable dagger within the entrails, he strove by every means to ensure that the holy Father should not escape his hands alive. But the gentle shepherd, shuddering at his execrable persistence, said to him in a mild voice: “I beg you, brother, spare me. Let your hand now cease, for in no way can I live any longer.”

At this voice the wicked man fled in swift flight, and, having become the prey of demons, bore with him the avenging consciousness of so great a crime. The venerable abbot, however, gathering his strength, descended, pierced with so horrible a wound, by the stairs leading to the church. But when he reached the lowest steps, feeling himself fail because of the excessive loss of blood, he fell and lay as though lifeless. By God’s prompting the sacristan, walking through the church, came upon him lying there; but in the darkness he could not discern who he was or why he lay there. Greatly terrified, he quickly lit a candle; and when the light was brought near, he recognized the holy Father. [Col. 1038D] At once he cried out lamentably and repeatedly cried, “Alas, alas!” causing all the brothers to gather at so wretched a sight. Lord Abbot Peter himself was also present, and, seeing the martyr of Christ rolling in his blood, revealed the inward pain of his heart through tearful sighs.

Accordingly, he was carried in the hands of the mourning brothers to the infirmary. When he had rested a little and recovered his spirit, he began to give immense thanks to almighty God for allowing him to be punished in the present life by so harsh a death, lest after death he should pay heavier penalties for his sins and negligences in the places of purgation. He survived for three days, if I remember correctly. During that time, fortified by the sacraments of the Church, he sighed for the blessedness of the future life with devout prayers and pious vows of holy desire. He forgave his murderer from his heart and earnestly begged all who were present that, if the man should perhaps be caught, [Col. 1039A] he might suffer no harm from anyone. He commended his special sons at Clairvaux to divine grace with the inmost affection of his heart. Thus that holy soul, released from the flesh, penetrated, as we believe, the ethereal heaven all the more freely because it had deserved to be purified here more severely in the furnace of tribulation and in the dreadful extremity of death.

His sacred body, placed upon a bier, was honorably carried to Clairvaux, divine psalms and hymns resounding all along the way, and Lord Abbot Peter himself accompanying the funeral with great reverence. There, I think it not inappropriate to relate, for the commendation to posterity of the memory of so great a martyr, by what sublime and manifest revelation the same abbot merited to be assured of the glory of his martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How Lord Abbot Peter was assured by revelation of the glorification of Gerard, Christ’s martyr.

When the Mass for the commendation of the [Col. 1039B] blessed soul was being solemnly celebrated by the community of Clairvaux, as is customary, the aforesaid Lord Abbot Peter stood at the sacred altar, intending in his customary devotion to offer the saving sacrifice. Although he presented a cheerful countenance to those looking at him, he was nonetheless very sad and grieving over the so undeserved death of the pious Father, especially because the Lord had allowed so monstrous a crime to be committed in his own house, namely Igny. As he was agitated by various thoughts and considered whether this perhaps had happened because of his own sins, he suddenly saw in visible form most blessed Bernard standing at the right side of the altar, and Lord Gerard, whose death he mourned, at the left. Both shone with the glory of inestimable brightness.

As he stood astonished and bewildered at this sight, blessed Bernard said to him: “Why, I ask, do you mourn as dead one whose passing death, changed into the eternity of blessed life, is precious in the sight of the Lord?” Then, stretching out his hand toward Gerard, the martyr [Col. 1039C] of Christ, who stood at the left side of the altar, he said: “Behold, this is my brother, for whose funeral you are performing the due rites. The more cruel and undeserved was the death which he seemed to have endured in the eyes of men, the more greatly has he been exalted by the Lord, and has merited to receive the portion of his calling among the conquering, purple-clad companies of martyrs.”

After these words, that joyful vision was withdrawn from the eyes of the beholder. But such joy and certainty regarding the glorification of his beloved friend succeeded in the heart of him who had merited to see and hear these things that he no longer thought Gerard to be mourned as dead. Rather, every cloud of sorrow and doubt being driven away, he judged that he should be regarded as a most faithful intercessor before the mercy of almighty God.

We heard this revelation from Lord Gerard of pious memory, formerly prior of Clairvaux and afterward abbot of Eberbach. Those who had lived with him know what a man he was in truthfulness, purity, and innocence. We also heard the elders of Clairvaux relate concerning him that, when he came before the hands of most blessed Bernard in order to commit himself through him to the Order and to the house of Clairvaux, that venerable Father, speaking in the Spirit of God and in the hearing of those present, bore witness to his innocence, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile” (John 1). [Col. 1039D]

When the solemn funeral rites had therefore been completed, grief mingled with joy, and when his spiritual sons rejoiced over so great a Father—not so much mourning his temporal death as rejoicing in his glorious victory, by which, dying bravely for justice, he triumphed over the enemy—his holy body was reverently laid before the doors of the oratory of Clairvaux, in the cell which had formerly been constructed to receive the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, in a sarcophagus raised above the pavement.

Then, as the report of his precious death spread everywhere—how he, innocent, had been punished by a cruel death for justice and zeal for the Order—it reached the ears of the supreme pontiff, Alexander of blessed memory. Since he had loved Gerard with special affection because of reverence for his holiness, he was deeply grieved at his so undeserved death and judged that the perpetrator of so great a crime should be excommunicated and excluded from the fellowship of all the faithful.

After some years had passed, that cruel executioner who had committed so great a crime, moved by repentance, went to the supreme pontiff and fell at his feet to seek mercy. When the apostolic lord asked who he was and what evil he had committed, the man said: “I am he who killed Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux.” When the lord pope heard the name of the abbot once dear to him and saw before him the author of his death, he shuddered all over and, violently disturbed, as it is said, pushed him away with his foot rather indiscreetly, saying: “Go, son of perdition.”

Hearing this, the wretched man rose quickly and departed. The cardinals [Col. 1040B] present reverently approached and suggested to the lord pope that, although the man was most wicked, he ought not to be dismissed without mercy: the Lord Jesus had prayed on the cross for His crucifiers, and it was not fitting for his apostolic office to leave posterity so harsh an example of despair. Alarmed by their words, the pope ordered that parricide to be summoned at once. For he had not rejected him for that moment in order that he should be deemed beyond hope, but so that the horror and enormity of such a monstrous crime might be more deeply impressed upon his heart, and that by this he might be moved to endure every severity for his crime.

But how terrible is God in His counsels concerning the children of men, since no one can correct the person whom He has neglected. For when, at the pontiff’s command, the servants searched everywhere for that miserable sinner, he could not be found in the consistory, the palace, or even throughout the entire city. Where he went, or by what end he perished, remains unknown to this day. [Col. 1040C]

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning Lord Henry of pious memory, seventh abbot of Clairvaux, afterward cardinal bishop of Albano.

When blessed Gerard, the sixth abbot of Clairvaux, had been glorified by the palm of martyrdom, Lord Henry, abbot of Hautecombe, longing in desire, life, and character for the sabbath-rest of the people of God now resting in the seventh age—to whom the Spirit says, “that he may rest from his labors” (Rev. 14)—was elected spiritual Father, in the seventh appointment, of that noble community of Clairvaux, sincere in religion.

This venerable Father, noble indeed by birth but far nobler through the nobility of his virtues, had from the first years of his youth been placed in the sanctuary of the Lord. He set his hand to mighty deeds, choosing rather to bear the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden (Matt. 11) than to be called and to be a son of Belial—that is, “without yoke.” He desired more to be humbled with the meek for Christ the Lord than to divide spoils with the proud, and thereby to fall into the portion of him who is king over all the children of pride (Job 41). [Col. 1040D]

He passed the days of his youth in such purity and innocence, and had so put on the gray hairs of wisdom in his tender years, that, while he had scarcely yet reached the threshold of manhood, he deserved, by the merit of religion and prudence rather than age, to be set as mediator between God and human beings; and, made the vicar of the Son of God, to receive alike the name and office of father and shepherd. Yet he administered this prerogative of honor—or rather this burden of care—once undertaken, with such readiness of faith and devotion that the inward Judge, the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, who sets a seal upon the hand of every person so that each may know his own works, finding him faithful in a lesser stewardship, resolved to raise him by a greater grace of gifts.

Indeed, now of more mature age and with virtues become habitual, [Col. 1041A] when he had become abbot of Clairvaux, he by no means neglected in himself the rigor of discipline by which he compelled others toward the path of justice. Rather, insofar as the dignity of his office allowed, he bound himself to the fellowship of the common life and at times, when occasion allowed, sweated at manual labor with the other brothers. Moreover, the sound counsel which the Wise Man gave to all those in high station—“The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3)—and how acceptable it is to God when a prelate, for fear of Him, does not disdain to mortify his flesh even through hard and lowly work, the merciful Lord deigned to show to this servant of His. For He wished wonderfully and mercifully to correct him for a certain negligence which he had incurred while applying himself too ardently to manual labor, and which he did not think so serious.

> **Note:** [Col. 1041D] Henry’s fault was only venial: he did not leave off manual labor and arranged for another to administer the anointing which he ought to have administered personally—perhaps thereby causing scandal among his own people. [Col. 1042D]

For it happened once that the same venerable abbot, during the mowing season, was busy gathering hay in the meadows of the grange situated beyond the river Aube, near the monastery of Clairvaux. [Col. 1041B] There he was working vigorously with his brothers. And behold, while he was applying himself more ardently to the work, a brother arrived in haste, reporting that one of the sick lay brothers, his illness worsening, was near death and therefore desired the grace of anointing. But the abbot, knowing that the others were strengthened by his presence and stirred to work more zealously, was deeply reluctant to be torn away from the work. Therefore he sent one of the elders as his deputy, to administer to the sick man the customary rite of anointing. When this had been done, the brother, properly fortified by the Church’s sacraments against the powers of the air, ended his life in peace.

Afterward, one day, when Compline had been said and the brothers, while it was still broad daylight, had placed themselves in their beds, the lord abbot too lay awake in his bed. As he lay there, a monk who had shortly before died—the aforesaid brother—appeared visibly to him and said:

“Know, [Col. 1041C] lord Father, that the brother who recently died, as soon as he laid aside the clothing of the flesh, was presented by holy angels before the throne of glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. There, when his life was examined with the most exact scrutiny, the investigation finally proceeded to an examination of what had been done concerning him as he lay at the point of death. And when the kindly Judge asked whether all things customarily done for dying brothers had been duly performed for him, the answer was that they had been duly performed, except only that the abbot, while he persisted more ardently in manual labor, had neglected to anoint him in person and had sent a deputy in his place. Therefore the Lord, calling me, as I stood with the others before His dreadful majesty, said to me: ‘Go, and on My behalf tell the abbot that for this negligence he is to recite the seven penitential psalms every day for the whole time of his life.’”

Having said this, the heavenly messenger, after reporting outwardly what he had heard within, returned to the Lord who had sent him, from whom, although appearing outwardly, he had never departed inwardly. The abbot, however, with much trembling and astonishment pondering in his mind what he had heard, gave thanks from the depths of his heart to the divine mercy. By his own experience he proved that the Apostle’s statement concerning the Lord rests upon irrefragable truth: “He cares for us” (1 Pet. 5). [Col. 1041D]

Accepting with most humble obedience the penance imposed upon him by the Abbot of all abbots, he took such care to observe it that, even after becoming cardinal bishop of Albano, he was accustomed to tell his familiar associates that, if he were pressed by such a necessity that one of two things must absolutely be done—namely, on the holy day of Easter or of the Nativity of the Lord, either omit Mass or omit those psalms—he would rather omit Mass. [Col. 1042A]

Blessed, therefore, is God in His gifts and holy in all His mercies. In these last days He consoles His humble servants by revelations so clear and evident, so that, being thereby drawn away from visible things, we may set the foot of faith more firmly upon things invisible, knowing with complete certainty that He alone is the one and only Lord of visible and invisible things, who by His incomprehensible majesty makes the homeland of earth and the homeland of heaven one commonwealth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the lay brother who, through God’s grace and the prayer of the venerable Abbot Henry, escaped the sentence of damnation.

A certain lay brother had indeed lived for some time at Clairvaux, but had not been formed under the most chaste discipline of the Clairvaux brethren; rather, he had been transferred there from another house. Until the very point of death, with dreadful hardness of heart, [Col. 1042B] he hid in the abyss of a most evil conscience, without confession or repentance, the exceedingly grave crimes he had committed in his former house. Almighty God, in whose dominion and will all things are placed, deigned both generously and mercifully to rescue him from the gulf of eternal damnation, already looming directly over his head.

For, oppressed by a most severe illness and sensing that death was near, he was enlightened by divine grace, which sometimes has mercy upon wretched and unworthy sinners, and wished, when a confessor had been called, to confess his sins. But the grim host of malignant spirits, which insofar as it can always opposes the grace of God, feared that through the saving antidote of confession it would lose a sinner whom it presumed it could soon seize, long ensnared in its nets. It rushed upon him with such force of malice that, his power of speech being lost and remaining so for a considerable time, he seemed already mute and to be drawing his final breath.

But the merciful Lord, who knows both how to spare those who entreat Him and [Col. 1042C] how to overthrow the proud—as once, in the silence of midnight, looking upon that typological army of Pharaoh through the pillar of fire and cloud, He crushed it—so now, in the silence of midnight, rebuking and putting to flight, as we believe, through the intercession of blessed Bernard and of the saints who rest at Clairvaux, the tyrannical pride of the demons, He freed His accused servant and, restoring the use of his tongue, encouraged him to receive the sacrament of confession.

At last, while the brothers of the infirmary watched anxiously over him and no one now expected anything but his death, behold, as midnight approached, he suddenly opened his eyes and, speaking clearly, informed the brothers that he wished to confess. Then the venerable Lord Abbot Henry was summoned quickly. The man confessed to him, speaking in the bitterness of his soul and saying:

“I, an unclean sinner, I the most shameful of all offenders, confess to God and to you, Father, that when I was formerly in my monastery, named Esrom, situated in [Col. 1042D] Dacia, I fathered a son by a certain prostitute; and to this day I have made neither confession nor penance for such a crime. Accordingly, when I became speechless, malignant spirits seized my most wretched soul and carried it to the infernal places. There I saw the punishments to which, once I have shortly been stripped of the body, I shall be consigned for punishment. There also, to increase my damnation, I found my son, long since dead, reproaching and condemning my iniquities in words such as these: ‘Alas, detestable sinner! Alas, accursed betrayer of chastity and religious life! Would that you had never been born, would that you had never reached adulthood; would that, as though you had never existed, you had been carried from the womb to the tomb! For, at the prompting of your malice, I have deserved to be brought into these miseries!’”

Troubled and distressed beyond measure by what I had heard and seen—both because of the punishment laid to the charge of this my son and because of my own condemnation, now immediately impending—[Col. 1043A] I was thus afflicted. When the discerning and prudent Father, Lord Abbot Henry, had heard this, his heart was profoundly moved at so great a tribulation of a sinner endangered in his final struggle. Addressing the man with saving words, he began, with every earnestness of reasoned compassion, to encourage him to hope for pardon. By effective admonitions he counselled and urged him never in any way to despair of the ineffable mercy of the most powerful Redeemer, but with the full devotion of faith to cry out and say to him: “I believe, Lord, that even if I should be plunged into the depths of hell, your mercy has power to deliver me from there” (Job 30).

At last, after penance had been imposed and absolution granted, the abbot left the sick man and returned to the dormitory. Scarcely an hour had passed when, at the sick man’s request, the abbot was summoned back again; and he returned without delay. The sick man said to him:

“I beg you, lord Father, have mercy on me and pray for me, a wretched sinner. For now, after I spoke with you, I was brought back to the places of punishment. There it was also made known to me that, because of the confession which I made through God’s mercy, and because of the penance which I received, through God’s grace I shall be delivered from the abyss of eternal condemnation; yet in the punishments of purgatory I must pay for the crimes I have committed and all my sins, down to the last farthing. But because I confessed less than purely, and cannot be saved without a pure confession, behold, by God’s great gift I have been permitted to return a second time, so that I may hasten to vomit forth, through the saving draught of confession, the poison which still gnaws at my conscience. I therefore confess to God and to you, Father, that I presumed to take one tunic from a certain brother without permission, and that until now I have lived without confession or penance for this sin of private ownership and disobedience.”

Thus the devout and pious Father Henry, [Col. 1043C] greatly marvelling at so abundant a manifestation of divine goodness toward so great a sinner, and rejoicing like a good shepherd over a sheep that had indeed been lost but was now found, again granted absolution, imposed penance, and with the tenderest affection of compassion commended the sick and penitent man to God’s grace. The sick man too, while the abbot prayed, became more tranquil; and, by the very serenity of his face, indicated that his state had improved. He again fell silent and, after a short interval, rested in peace.

Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? If God justifies, who is there that condemns? (Rom. 8.) To his omnipotence alone it is both lawful and possible, out of the same mass of the human race, to make one vessel for dishonour and another for honour; nor can anyone say to him, “Why have you made it thus?” His judgments are true and justified in themselves; and his mercy, from everlasting and unto everlasting, is upon those who fear him. Just as none among all the children of men, so neither can any among all the powers [Col. 1043D] of the angels comprehend it. For Augustine, that knower of heavenly mysteries, says concerning the saying which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6): “Whom the almighty Father draws, or whom he does not draw; why he draws that person or does not draw him—do not seek to investigate or judge this, if you do not wish to err.”

Moreover, just as those are exceedingly blessed who deserve to be saved by so special a privilege of grace, such as the man of whom we have spoken, so, conversely, those are exceedingly wretched and unhappy who, following such examples, put off confessing their sins until the point of death, rashly and most impudently presuming that they too will obtain that same grace in their last moments. For the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I will not gather their assemblies with blood” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate]); because few who persist in the blood of sins obtain this grace. Nor do the privileges of a few [Col. 1044A] make a general law. Therefore, when those who so arrogantly presume upon God’s mercy, and through their own negligence lose the time of grace presently at hand, have passed beyond the time of grace, and the horror and darkness of everlasting death have darkened the light of this life, then, as fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so wretches shall be taken in an evil time. Then they shall experience, in most just and severe judgment, the tremendous majesty of almighty God—which now, because he most benignly overlooks human sins on account of repentance, they despise—punishing sins with punishments that shall never end.

Accordingly, the most reverend Father Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, while advancing daily to better things through increasing virtues and while the renown of his holiness spread brightly everywhere, was raised, by the will and election of the supreme pontiff, with the approving counsel of the brother-cardinals, to be cardinal bishop of Albano. Having attained that dignity, he so fulfilled those duties which belonged to a pontiff [Col. 1044B] that he was by no means forgetful of his former profession and humility. Outwardly he displayed an authority worthy of the priesthood; inwardly, however, offering the mourning of a monk in a contrite spirit and humble heart, he hastened to please the gaze of the inward Examiner.

Having become bishop, he did not consign his Clairvaux to oblivion, but always loved it with sincere affection, devoting himself with most faithful zeal to its honour and advantage, both in the Roman curia and elsewhere, wherever he was able. When he had happily completed the days of his life, he was buried at Clairvaux, in the place which he had chosen for himself and ardently preferred. This place lies between the memorials of the holy confessors of Christ, Bernard and Malachy; and he selected it beforehand as his burial-place with the intention that, adhering to those saints on the day of the general resurrection, he might obtain through the merits of his most holy companions whatever merit he himself lacked.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the venerable man Lord Peter, the eighth abbot of Clairvaux

[Col. 1044C]

After the universal mother, namely the holy Roman Church, which possesses the fullness of power, had associated Lord Henry, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, in her share of pastoral care, the abbots and brothers of Clairvaux earnestly sought whom they should appoint in his place. At once, from close at hand, the most fragrant sweetness of virtues in Lord Peter, abbot of Igny, of whom we have spoken above, presented itself. He had obtained this special favour from the people of his time: that he should be acclaimed as holy and good, chosen from among thousands.

They therefore unanimously elected him—the worthy successor of worthy men—as the eighth abbot of Clairvaux: worthy, I say, that, ascending to a higher place because of the reverence due to his humility, he should be appointed minister of the Lord’s temple, which is built of living stones, concerning which Ezekiel says that “its ascent was by eight steps” (Ezek. 34 [as cited]). By this the Holy Spirit signifies that through the eight steps of the principal virtues one ascends to the eighth degree, that of eternal blessedness.

Although, before undertaking the government of the Church of Clairvaux, this servant of God had been regarded by all as perfect and holy, he nevertheless began to stretch himself toward a new contest, as though his former manner of life had counted for nothing. By every means he strove to give his voice “a voice of power”: that is, not to destroy by his deeds what he taught with his mouth, but to show all that was just and holy more by deeds than words. He kept constantly before his eyes the footsteps of the fathers who had preceded him, especially those of our most holy Father Bernard, whose unworthy vicar he judged himself to be.

Although he flourished in other virtues, he was so adorned by the grace of gentleness that in his bearing, his walk, his face, and his speech nothing appeared except the effects of holy humility, which had taken deepest root in his heart. [Col. 1045A] Finally, having entrusted nearly the entire temporal administration of the house to its cellarers and stewards, he resolved to devote himself to God alone and to attend to the salvation of souls. Whenever he could be free, he sat alone in silence in the chapter room, his face lowered to the ground, so that any of the younger or weaker brothers, struck by a multitude of temptations or burdened by any distress, might have free access to him. According to the grace given him, he immediately strengthened such a brother to endure the struggle undertaken for Christ, by salutary counsels and most sweet words of edification.

Moreover, how rigorous a chastiser of his own body he was sufficiently appears from this: he never wore two tunics and two cowls together, but either one cowl and two tunics, or one tunic and two cowls, even in the harshest cold; and he used boots very rarely. He devoted himself so earnestly to frugality [Col. 1045B] and economy that, using even the common foods most sparingly, he showed that he sought rather whatever support might sustain the frail body than indulgence in the provocations of gluttony.

He always held in his heart, and often upon his lips, that he was unworthy and insufficient to govern so great a house; that he was less fit and less discerning than was required of one to whom so great a multitude of abbots and brothers from every part of the world ought to look. Thus he is said on one occasion to have spoken to the king of the Franks, who was a kinsman of his:

“See, my lord king, that I, such a little man, of no standing whatever, lacking even judgment and reason, have undertaken to govern so exalted a house; and I greatly fear that through my imprudence and insufficiency the condition of Clairvaux, which has hitherto remained unimpaired, may be shaken.”

Delighted by his humility, the king answered:

“Why, lord Father, do you cast yourself down into such faint-heartedness that you wish to abandon the care of the souls which, with God as author, you have undertaken to govern? I beg you, do not do this. Rather, according to the grace bestowed on you by the Lord, do not neglect diligently to exercise care over the Lord’s flock. Only be abbot within, in those matters which concern God’s honour and the salvation of souls; I shall be abbot without, in all matters which concern the benefit of your house—protecting your possessions, rendering them free from every levy, and striking with the vengeance of royal punishment anyone who, with malicious intent, presumes in any manner to trouble you.”

The glorious revelation which we have set out above, through which he was judged worthy to see and hear, not only with spiritual but also with bodily eyes and ears, the glorification of Christ’s martyr Gerard, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, more clearly demonstrates this blessed man’s most pure and God-pleasing way of life in holy religion. How richly he was filled with the sweetness of heavenly grace, and how effective an intercessor he was for criminals and sinners, is plainly declared by that remarkable and truly memorable conversion, at the end of his life, of Baldwin, a knight and most wicked sinner. We shall recount how this occurred, not to promise impunity to the guilty, but for God’s honour and the consolation of penitents. The same most reverend abbot, earnestly entreated by a certain brother, explained it to him in order; and not to place faith in that abbot’s words would be to disparage all religion. The brother committed to writing what he had heard; and we have therefore expressed in his own words what we are about to relate.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How almighty God, through the merits and prayers of the venerable Abbot Peter, granted the fruit of repentance to a most wicked sinner

There was a knight named Baldwin, lord of a castle situated in the territory of Rheims and called Guise. A warlike man and vigorous in arms, he daily committed many evils, having cast aside the fear of God. He was frequently engaged in robbery, arson, slaughter, and other similar works of the devil. Yet this one good quality seemed to be present in him: he sincerely loved and magnificently honoured the most holy man Peter—then abbot of Igny and afterwards of Clairvaux—together with the whole house of Igny, and placed great confidence in his merits. Nor was this in vain, as the event showed, so that the saying might be fulfilled which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matt. 10).

While Baldwin was still in the vigour of manhood, it happened that, oppressed by a deadly sickness, he was brought to the point of death. He therefore sent a messenger in all haste, asking and beseeching the aforesaid abbot to deign to come to him. Arriving quickly, the abbot found the man already almost consumed and utterly deprived of the use of speech. But, as the holy abbot prayed, our Lord Christ in his abundant kindness immediately granted the sick man the ability to speak [Col. 1046B] and the will to confess.

After making his confession with great contrition of heart, he wished at once to leave the world and take on the habit of holy religion. His wife, however, who loved her husband’s body more than his soul, very obstinately prevented this. The vow was therefore delayed for the moment, until she had utterly despaired of his recovery and at last gave her consent. Rejoicing greatly that permission for his conversion had been obtained, he immediately had himself carried to the aforesaid house at Igny, intending to become a monk there if he lived. But as death hastened, his soul was immediately released from his body, groaning in most bitter contrition and repenting intensely that he had spent the time of repentance without repentance.

After his death many revelations concerning him were made to the aforesaid abbot and to the other elders of the place. Since it would take too long to recount them all, we have taken care to record a few out of the many. Thus, on the very night on which he died, he appeared in a vision to a religious man, as though rising from the bed in which he seemed to lie oppressed by grave illness. When the man attempted to lend him assistance, Baldwin said:

“Brother, there is no need for you to weary yourself. For holy Benedict, beneath whose wings I have fled, though unworthy, is my strongest helper; and he sends me to your lord Abbot Peter, that I may become a monk through him.”

On that same night, while the venerable abbot was very anxious and concerned for the soul of the sinner, now penitent, he began to consider in his mind how he might aid a dead man weighed down by so vast a burden of sins. While he was thinking this, suddenly someone stood before him whose face he did not recognize, though he believed him to have been an angel of the Lord. Answering his thoughts, he said: “He needs great help.” There was no doubt that he meant the dead man. Having said this, he immediately vanished from his sight.

Accordingly, the holy abbot, having received such an answer from God, [Col. 1046D] was wholly melted by the balm of compassion and brotherly mercy. At once he turned to prayer, went about the altars of the saints, and from the depths of his heart implored their aid for the salvation of the dead man. As he continued this for a long time with ardent affection of compassion, sleep began to steal over him, as over one sorrowful and weary through the weakness of human frailty. When his eyelids were lightly closed, and he seemed neither fully awake nor fully asleep, Satan suddenly appeared to him. With a terrifying face, fiercely raging in threat against him, he said: “What? Will you take Baldwin away from me?” Having said this, he leapt upon him in a furious assault, constricting and crushing him violently.

Awakening immediately, the abbot found himself so bound in all his limbs that he could not move them; but the word of God was not bound. He therefore said to that insatiable murderer:

“I adjure you, unclean spirit, by the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, which he deigned to shed on the cross for us wretched sinners, and by his glorious Mother and Virgin Mary: do not presume to harm this soul, which has confessed and repented.”

Having said this, the devil, compelled by divine power, left him and fled. Understanding from his release that the dead man had been delivered, he resumed his perseverance in prayer and continued to pray more and more earnestly. For at that hour he was filled with so great a grace of devotion and conceived in his mind such confidence in God’s mercy as he had never experienced in all his life. He therefore believed without hesitation that the supplications of himself and his brethren on behalf of the dead man had been heard by God.

When morning came and he was presiding over the chapter of the brethren, he earnestly asked and carefully exhorted them all together to pour out devout prayers for the soul of the sinner who had fled to them in his last extremity of need. Appointing many lengthy prayers, he himself took care, for almost thirty days, to offer nearly every day the sacrifice of our redemption for Baldwin’s soul. Throughout that entire thirty-day period scarcely a day passed on which the said abbot did not see the dead man, Baldwin, appear to him—at times while asleep, and at times, more wonderfully still, while awake. Sometimes Baldwin was seen standing before him with bent knees and joined hands, begging him not to cease praying for him.

It happened at that time that a certain abbot of monks of the Black Order, whom the knight had once gravely injured while still alive in the flesh, came to the same house at Igny as a guest. The most reverend Abbot Peter rejoiced that the Lord had provided him with this further occasion to help a sinful soul. He led the aforesaid abbot to the dead man’s tomb and begged him, for Christ’s love, to absolve Baldwin of the injury which, at the devil’s prompting, he had committed against him. The other immediately granted what was asked, without delay, both for the honour of God [Col. 1047C] and from the compassion of brotherly mercy.

Then, behold: on that very night the dead man appeared joyfully to Lord Abbot Peter, showing him his body cleansed of the leprosy with which he indicated that he had long been defiled. Moreover, there appeared upon his face the completely closed scar of an immense wound; its recent healing showed that the guilt of the offense committed against the abbot had been erased.

After this, when the Lord wished to show that the prayers of the holy abbot and his brethren for that penitent’s soul had been heard in his sight, on the holy day of Preparation, when the divine office had begun at about the ninth hour—at that very hour, I say, at which the Lord Jesus Christ deigned to undergo the punishment of the cross and taste death for sinners—the venerable abbot, vested in priestly garments and presiding beside the altar, saw two young men appear, radiant in face and in shining silk garments. Walking at Baldwin’s right and left, they led the dead man to the altar. As they passed before the abbot, they turned toward him and said: “Behold Lord Baldwin.”

The dead man himself was clothed in black garments, yet they were fine and handsome garments, seemingly made of a fabric called *isembrun* [material uncertain]. Seeing this, the holy abbot rejoiced greatly, understanding, without doubt, in the black garments the sign of repentance and in Baldwin’s presentation at the altar a sure indication of reconciliation. To remove from the heart of God’s servant every scruple concerning this reconciliation, Baldwin, who had formerly often appeared to demand the help of intercession, thereafter appeared neither to the abbot himself nor to anyone else. By this too he made clear that, through God’s great mercy, he had been received among the penitents and into the places of purgation, where souls are to be refashioned into God’s likeness.

Who, I ask, can sufficiently estimate the depths of divine goodness and mercy toward us wretched sinners? But just as the Catholic mother Church most certainly believes that the Lord Jesus shed his most innocent blood in his Passion and death for sinners and ungodly persons, so it is altogether uncertain who belongs to the sacrament of this redemption and who does not. We are therefore rightly forbidden to judge or to pronounce a hasty sentence concerning even the most wicked sinner. For although we may in some fashion estimate what a person is today, we can by no means know what he will be tomorrow. Not only do some, by God’s grace, pass from sins and vices to the remedies of repentance; but also—something to be mourned with every fountain of tears—some at last fall away, by God’s terribly severe judgment, from virtues and holy works into vices.

Therefore let him who stands take heed, in fear and trembling, lest he fall; but let him who has fallen be anxious by every means to rise again. For wherever the tree of human nature falls in the death of the flesh, whether to the south or to the north, there it shall remain (Eccl. 11): that is, either with Christ, who is true life, in eternal blessedness, or with the devil, who is true death, in the perpetual misery of condemnation.

Consider therefore, reader, how dear and acceptable to God was this blessed Abbot Peter, through whose merits and prayers he granted this grace to a sinful man who, because of the multitude and enormity of his crimes, had scarcely seemed ever able to breathe again from the abyss of profound death. If he is known to have been so perfect before undertaking the governance of Clairvaux, shall we think that no merits accrued to him after he deserved to become pastor and ruler of this religious house? Of this house, as blessed Bernard testifies in one of his sermons, God gathers each year the finest and most precious revenues of souls.

Indeed, merits accrued to him. By later holiness he multiplied his earlier religious life with many increases of virtue. He so chastened in himself Martha’s restless occupations [Col. 1048C] that with all the affection of his mind he embraced Mary’s repose through the pursuit of sacred contemplation. He so taught his subjects to walk the narrow and constricted way that he demonstrated in his own holy conduct that the law which he imposed on others must first be observed by himself.

Having therefore praiseworthily completed the days of his life, he paid the debt owed to all humanity. Having sown for a time in tears, he closed his eyes in the death of the flesh and eternally reaps, in the joy of immortal life, the sweetest sheaves of his labours. His venerable body was honourably laid in a sarcophagus raised above the pavement, in the cell where, as we said above, Christ’s martyr Gerard had been placed. There, sleeping and resting in peace together with his blessed companion, he happily awaits the day of the general resurrection and the glory then to be rendered to the saints.

## Recapitulation of the matters set forth above

From the spacious and flowering field of the virtues and the praiseworthy life of the most reverend Fathers—the blessed Alberic, first abbot, and blessed Stephen, second abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux; likewise the most holy Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux; and their successors—we have, I think, not uselessly plucked these things and set them before our brethren devoted to reading, and desirous also of profiting by reading, like flowers in their freshest bloom. We pray for the mercy of almighty God, that he may deign to raise up, not only at Cîteaux and Clairvaux but throughout our whole Order, fathers who emulate such religious devotion and perfection. Thus may all of us who have resolved to bear in the Cistercian Order the burden and heat of the day, which our founders bore with tireless zeal and handed down for us to bear, not merely learn from sacred reading the examples of the preceding Fathers, but also, enlightened and strengthened by the teaching of the Fathers of the present time, deserve to be received within the folds of the Lord’s sheepfold, where, entering and going forth, [Col. 1049A] we may find the pastures of life.

Let no one suppose that we have written these things concerning the holy manner of life of the Cistercian and Clairvaux abbots as though fathers distinguished in life and religious devotion had not also flourished in other houses of our Order—especially in those which, together with Cîteaux and Clairvaux, are recognized as heads of the Order: namely La Ferté, Pontigny, and Morimond. For we know most certainly that in various monasteries of our Order there have been fathers flourishing through the grace of diverse virtues, through whose merits and prayers the vigour of discipline and the fervour of holy religion are preserved, with the Lord’s help, throughout our congregation to this day. Yet we believe that the matters we have learned about the fathers of the principal houses of the Order suffice as examples. Their holiness is believed to be more eminent, without prejudice to the others; and their authority may be expected more readily to kindle the reader’s mind to reverence and love for holy religion.

# THIRD DISTINCTION. Concerning certain brothers and disciples of St Bernard, and other religious of Clairvaux

[Col. 1049]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Lord Gerard, brother of St Bernard and cellarer of Clairvaux

[Col. 1049B]

Let us now turn our pen to the elders who flourished under our most blessed Father Bernard and afterwards at Clairvaux: men truly religious, exalted through contempt of the world, fervent in zeal for the Order, shining like the stars of heaven through the grace of diverse charisms, tirelessly watchful in mind through the pursuit of holy contemplation. They adorned the name and habit of monk with holy morals and an excellent manner of life; and, in order truly to be what they were called, they laboured with remarkable constancy of devotion.

First among them, as the firstborn whom the Law commands to be offered to the Lord, we shall not unreasonably place Lord Gerard, formerly cellarer of Clairvaux, the full brother of our holy Father Bernard and greatly beloved by him. The more difficult he seemed to have found it at the beginning to consent to conversion, the more steadfastly and sincerely did he afterwards cling throughout his whole life to the practices of that same conversion.

For when God’s servant Bernard, in his youth, delicate as a most tender little worm in wood, had been forestalled by the Holy Spirit and resolved to set his hand to mighty things, and had vowed to the Lord the grace of conversion conceived in his mind, he was also, inflamed by that same Spirit, gathering companions for conversion from every side. His other brothers had already yielded assent to his saving counsels; but Gerard accepted that beneficial advice more reluctantly. For he was a knight vigorous in arms, strong in the vigour of youth, possessed of great prudence and exceptional kindness, and loved by all; he had driven the root of his heart more deeply into the pomps and vanities of this world.

When, with an obstinate mind, he rejected his brother’s counsels, Bernard, now afire with faith and extraordinarily stirred by zeal for brotherly charity, said: “I know, I know: affliction alone will give understanding to the hearing.” And behold, a spear fixed in the side of that same brother appeared to him as a present foretoken of things to come. Then, placing his finger upon the spot in Gerard’s side where he alone saw the spear, he said: “The day will come—indeed, it will come quickly—when a spear fixed in this side will make a passage through to your heart for the counsel of salvation which you despise. You will indeed be afraid, but you shall not die.”

So it was spoken, and so it was done. For after very few days had intervened, Gerard was surrounded by enemies, captured, and wounded according to his brother’s word. Receiving a spear in that very side, in the very place predicted, and terrified as though death were already present, he cried out: “I am a monk! I am a monk of Cîteaux!” Nevertheless, he was captured and confined in custody. He soon recovered from his wound beyond hope, [Col. 1050B] but he did not alter the purpose or vow which he had made.

When his brother laboured to procure his release but achieved nothing, Gerard began to grieve and worry more and more because he was prevented from fulfilling the vow he had made to the Lord, whereas, when freedom had been his, intoxicated by love of the world, he had scorned both to make and to fulfill such a vow. Since Bernard was not even permitted to speak with him, he came to the prison and cried out: “Know, brother Gerard, that we shall shortly depart and enter the monastery. Since you are not allowed to go out, be a monk here, knowing that what you will but cannot do is counted as done.”

Thus, while at one time shut in prison and bound in fetters, he learned that it was hard for him to kick against the goad of God’s grace. He learned, I say, with what calamities and bitterness the galling sweetness of love for this world is filled. Finally, after he had been sufficiently and beneficially chastised by the Lord for his obstinacy, one night he heard in sleep a voice saying to him: “Today you shall be set free.”

That same day, toward evening, his fetters were broken by divine power and the bars of the prison opened of their own accord. Gerard went out and walked freely through the midst of those who had captured and imprisoned him. Thus, delivered by God’s great mercy from a double captivity—that of body and that of soul—he could rightly say: “Your rod and your staff, Lord, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22 [Vulgate]). He came to Cîteaux with his brothers and the others who had sworn the same vows of spiritual warfare, to fulfill the vow he had made to the Lord with all the greater humility and devotion because he knew, taught by so manifest a miracle, that the power both to make the vow and to fulfill it existed in him solely through divine grace.

Later, when the most reverend Father Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, had sent blessed Bernard and his brothers, with other religious men, to establish the house of Clairvaux, and had appointed the venerable Bernard abbot over the others, Lord Gerard was made cellarer in that same house. How vigorously, prudently, and humbly he administered the office entrusted to him we shall explain better in the words of blessed Bernard himself than in ours. For, when after Gerard’s death the venerable abbot delivered, in the assembly of the brethren, an address filled with most loving grief in his noble eloquence, he said among other things:

> [Note: [Col. 1049] Funeral oration on the death of Gerard, Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs:]

“Do you know, my sons, how just is my grief? How grievous is my wound? You see, indeed, how faithful a companion has left me on this path which I was walking: how watchful in care, how untiring under burdens, how gracious in manner! Who was so necessary to me? To whom was I equally dear? He was a brother by birth, but a still truer brother by religion. I beg you, who know these things, grieve for my loss. I was weak in body, and he carried [Col. 1051A] me; faint of heart, and he strengthened me. I was sluggish and negligent, and he roused me; unforesighted and forgetful, and he reminded me. Why have you been torn away from me? Why snatched from my hands, man of one mind with me, man after my own heart? We loved one another in life: how are we separated in death? A most bitter separation—one which nothing but death could have effected. For while living, when would you have left me alive? It is wholly death’s work: a dreadful divorce. For who would not have spared so sweet a bond of love between us, save death, the enemy of all sweetness? In every new matter that arises, I look for Gerard, as I used to do, and he is not there. Alas! Then I groan in misery, like a man without help. Whom shall I consult amid uncertainties? To whom shall I entrust myself in adversities? Who will bear the burdens? Who will ward off dangers? Did not Gerard’s eyes everywhere go before my steps? Did not your breast, Gerard, know my cares better than my own did, encounter them more intimately, press them more urgently? [Col. 1051B] Did you not, with that persuasive and powerful tongue of yours, most often rescue me from worldly conversations and restore me to the silence of a friend?

“The Lord had given him a learned tongue, that he might know when he ought to speak. Thus, by the prudence of his answers and by the grace bestowed on him from above, he satisfied both those within and those without; so that almost no one asked for me if Gerard had happened first to meet him. He met those who came, placing himself in their way lest they disturb my leisure. If there were people whom he could not himself satisfy, he brought them to me; the rest he sent away. O industrious man! O faithful friend! He showed love to his friend and did not fail in the offices of charity. Who departed from him empty-handed? If rich, he carried away counsel; if poor, assistance. He did not seek what was his own, he who thrust himself into the midst of cares so that I might have leisure. For, being most humble, he hoped for greater fruit from my repose than if he himself were at leisure. Yet at times he asked to be released and to yield to another, as though someone might [Col. 1051C] provide better. But where could such a man be found? He was not held to his office by any self-willed attachment to it, as often happens, but solely by regard for charity. Indeed, he laboured more than all and received less than all, so that, while he often supplied others with necessities, he himself lacked many things—for example, food or clothing.

“Thanks be to you, brother, for every fruit of my labours, if there is any in the Lord. To you I owe it if I have made progress, if I have been of use. You became entangled, and through your service I sat at leisure, or rather was more holily occupied in divine service, or more usefully applied myself to the instruction of my sons. For why should I not have been secure within, knowing that you were at work without—you, my right hand, the light of my eyes, my breast and my tongue? But why did I say that he worked without, as though Gerard knew nothing of inward things and had no share in spiritual gifts? Those spiritual persons who knew him know how his words breathed the Spirit. His companions know how his character and pursuits did not savour of the flesh, [Col. 1051D] but burned with the Spirit. Who was more strict than he in keeping discipline? Who more severe in chastising his body? Who more absorbed in contemplation, more subtle in argument? How often, while discussing matters with him, did I learn things I did not know; and I who had come to teach departed more taught.

“Nor is this surprising in my case, since great and wise men likewise testify that this happened to them with him. He did not know letters, but he possessed the understanding of their inventor, and he possessed also the enlightening Spirit. He was greatest not only in great matters, but also in small. For example, in buildings, fields, gardens, waters—in short, in every craft and work of country people—what, I ask, in this whole sphere escaped Gerard’s skill? He was readily master to masons, smiths, farmers, gardeners, shoemakers, and weavers. And though by the judgment of all he was wiser than all, he alone was not wise in his own eyes. Would that the curse, ‘Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes’ (Isa. V), touched many others, even if less [Col. 1052A] wise, no more than it touched him. I speak to those who know these things, and who have experienced and ascertained still more concerning him. Yet I refrain, because he is my flesh and my brother. This, however, I add without hesitation: he was useful to me in all things and before all others—useful in small and great matters, private and public, outside and within. Rightly I depended wholly on him, because he was everything to me. He had left to me almost only the honour and name of steward; he himself did the work. I was called abbot, but he presided in solicitude. Rightly my spirit rested in him, through whom I was free to delight in the Lord, to preach more freely, and to pray more securely. Through you, my brother, my mind was sober, my rest pleasing, my speech more effective, my prayer more abundant, my reading more frequent, and my affection more fervent.

“Alas, you have been taken away, and with you all these things at once. Together with you have gone all my delights and joys. Now cares rush upon me; now troubles assail me from every side; and distresses find me alone from all quarters. They alone have remained to me now that you are gone; alone I groan beneath the burden. I must either lay it down or be crushed by it, because you have withdrawn your shoulders. Who will grant that I may die soon after you? For I would not die for your sake, nor deprive you of your glory. But to survive you is labour and pain. Come forth, come forth, tears, which have long desired to come forth. Come forth, because he who had blocked your passage has passed away. I confess that I am not insensible to sufferings; I dread the death of myself and of my own. Gerard was mine—utterly mine. Was he not mine, who was a brother by blood, a son by profession, a father by solicitude, a partner in spirit, closest in affection? He has departed from me; I feel it, I am wounded, and grievously. Forgive me, sons—or rather, if you are sons, make allowance for a father’s lot. I grieve for you, dearest Gerard: not because you are to be lamented, but because you have been taken away. And perhaps I ought rather to lament over myself, because I drink the cup of bitterness. ‘Where is thy victory, O death? Where is thy sting, O death?’ (I Cor. XV). Gerard does not fear you, phantom image! Gerard passes through the midst of your jaws to his homeland, [Col. 1052C] not merely secure, but rejoicing and giving praise.

“Therefore I weep first over my own wound and this house’s loss. Next I weep over the needs of the poor, whose father Gerard was. Certainly I weep also over the state of our whole Order and our profession, which drew no slight strength from your zeal, counsel, and example, Gerard. Finally, though not over you, yet because of you I weep. In this I am wholly and grievously afflicted, because I love deeply.”

## CHAPTER II. On the praiseworthy abstinence of Lord Gerard, cellarer

This is the testimony which the most reverend Father Bernard bore concerning the life and conduct of his beloved brother Gerard. We have extracted it from his long discourse in various places and set it down continuously in order to show the virtues of so great a man. We know that the darkness of flattery was wholly far removed from the words and thoughts of so great [Col. 1052D] a Father of ours; nor was he drawn by affection of blood to praise Gerard by even one word beyond what unalloyed truth judged him worthy to receive. Therefore, if his testimony is true—indeed, because it is true—it is plainly evident that Gerard, servant of God, was perfect in virtues. The administration of external affairs, which so often turns many aside from the path of cloistered discipline and plunges them into the abyss of worldly conduct, did him no harm in his great observance of true religion.

Who can worthily marvel at this proclamation of such great praise: that, labouring more than all, he received less than all; that he was not held in his office by any desire of self-assertion—something extremely rare in our own times—but solely by regard for charity; that, while supplying necessities to others, he himself lacked many things? To demonstrate how strict he was in observing discipline and how severe in chastising his body, we shall offer one of his praiseworthy deeds as an example [Col. 1053A], so that those who strive to investigate the virtues of the saints for their own advancement, if they are fervent in religion, may have something to imitate; while, if they are lax or weak, they may have reason to grieve for themselves.

Gerard, servant of God, used to make the rounds of the granges in accordance with the duty of his office, content with the brothers’ common table and fare, drinking water with them himself; nor did he readily permit anything other than the common dishes to be set before him. It happened once that he fell ill when he was about to go to a grange. A lay brother who was to travel with him, knowing this, went to the prior and reported that the cellarer was ill. He said that he feared Gerard’s weakness would become worse if he drank water at the grange as was his custom. By the prior’s command, then, he took along a small vessel full of wine, Gerard being wholly unaware of this. At table he offered it to him as he sat with the brothers, making the customary sign on the prior’s behalf that, because of his illness, he alone should use that small quantity of wine.

But how could that most fervent champion of poverty and common life consent to this—that while all the others drank water, he alone should enjoy a cup of wine? A vessel full of water had been placed in the middle, from which the brothers were to drink. After deliberating briefly within himself what he ought to do, he at once rose and, taking the little vessel of wine, poured its contents, in the sight of all, into the jug containing water, making a sign that all should drink in common. He preferred to put his body at risk through illness rather than, even in such a slight relaxation of abstinence, bring a stain upon his conscience. The brothers, at once delighted and edified by this religious act, drank that water with greater pleasure than if he had served them the most precious wine. [Col. 1053B] For they read in the life and conduct of their excellent cellarer how contemptible the enticement of the flesh is: he would not agree to take a cup even to preserve or recover his bodily health if thereby he might seem to give the weak an occasion for scandal.

## CHAPTER III. On the precious death of the venerable man Gerard

[Col. 1053C]

When the holy Father Bernard had entered Italy for the third time, summoned by Pope Innocent, to put an end to the schism of Peter Leo, and was everywhere renowned for great signs and miracles, he kept his cellarer, Lord Gerard, continually with him as a most faithful helper and prudent adviser. It happened, however, when they were at Viterbo, that Lord Gerard was seized with a very severe illness and lay confined to bed, causing the venerable abbot intense distress and dismay. As manifest signs of death announced that the end was near, Bernard, servant of God, suffered most painfully at the thought of leaving the companion of his pilgrimage—and such a companion—in a foreign land, and of not restoring him to those who had entrusted him to Bernard, since Gerard was loved by all, as he was indeed most lovable. With weeping and groaning [Col. 1053D] he turned to the Lord:

“Wait, Lord,” he said, “wait until our return. Restore him to his friends; then take him, if you wish, and I shall not complain.”

But how could the pious and merciful Lord disregard His most humble servant, asking in his own cause with such contrition of heart, when He continually accustomed Himself to hear him so readily and so graciously in the causes of others? Contrary to everyone’s expectation, Gerard was recalled as though from the gates of death to life and quickly recovered. Their business having been completed, peace restored to the holy Roman Church, and the Leonine fury wholly extinguished, they returned to their homeland, bearing sheaves of peace amid the rejoicing of the whole land.

Not long afterwards, as though the Lord had now satisfied the prayers and desires of His faithful servant Bernard, Gerard again suddenly began to lose his bodily strength and gradually drew near to his end. He had patiently borne Martha’s occupation because of the office imposed upon him, but had embraced Mary’s leisure with all the effort of his mind. [Col. 1054A] Feeling, therefore, that he would certainly depart and pass from the laborious cares of this world to the repose of eternal blessedness—where, beginning to be at leisure, he would taste and see that the Lord is sweet, and demonstrate that no carnal or worldly desire had held him in his office—he raised his eyes to heaven and said:

“God, you know that, so far as it depended on me, I always desired to devote myself to quiet and to be at leisure for you. But your love held me bound, as did the will of the brothers and zeal for obedience; above all, the fraternal love of my abbot and brother.”

About midnight, the last night which he spent with wretched mortals, his face wonderfully brightened, and he suddenly burst forth in a voice of exultation into David’s words, to the amazement of those present: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights” (Ps. XLVIII). For to this blessed man day was already dawning though it was still midnight, [Col. 1054B] and his final night was illuminated as day; indeed, that night was his illumination amid the delights of the eternal light, which is Christ the Lord. For how are darknesses not changed into light where a man dies singing and sings in dying? You, O hostile death, are employed for joy though you are the mother of sorrow; employed for glory though you are glory’s adversary; employed as an entrance into the kingdom though you are the gate of hell; as the pit of destruction, for the finding of salvation.

The brothers present, astonished at the novelty of so great a marvel, hurried quickly to report to his beloved brother, Saint Bernard, that the man exulted and triumphed over death. Though weak and ill, Bernard hastened there and, while Gerard listened, completed in a clear voice the final words of the psalm which Gerard had been singing. Raising his eyes to heaven, Gerard said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). Repeating the same saying and frequently doubling the words, “Father, Father,” he turned to the holy abbot and his brother, his face radiant, and said:

“How great is God’s condescension in being the Father of men; [Col. 1054C] how great is the glory of men in being God’s children and God’s heirs. For if children, then heirs.”
