Thus that holy soul, released from the flesh in joy and exultation of spiritual gladness and joined to the hymn-singing choirs of angels, sought the starry dwellings in freer flight, because the hostile host of evil spirits could find nothing of its own in her. His holy abbot and brother devotedly rendered to his funeral the due office of commendation and burial, with the sweetest affection of heart. Yet although others wept, he did not weep; rather, with great constancy of faith he restrained the tears that were ready to burst forth, lest he seem to mourn and weep as dead one whom he did not doubt had been born, through his death, into eternal life and everlasting glory.

## CHAPTER IV. On the most reverend Father Humbert, formerly prior of Clairvaux

[Col. 1054D] After the house of Clairvaux had been founded by the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, and its most fragrant reputation for holy religion had become to many an odour of life unto life, the hidden counsel of divine goodness summoned from diverse parts of the world, among others, many religious men who seemed perfect in the observance of religion in their own places. Hearing that the Lord had so especially and excellently magnified His mercy toward that house and its most holy abbot, they came, like new recruits from the labours of a completed military service, and with most fervent devotion of spirit desired to join the fellowship of such holiness.

Among the first or foremost of these were Humbert, first abbot of the monastery of Igny; Renald; Peter surnamed the Toulousain; William; and Gerard of Fars. Although they lived not in one place but in separate and distant provinces, from the earliest elements of childhood they had devoted themselves to divine service [Col. 1055A] so completely that, flourishing in every grace of virtue, they seemed scarcely to need instruction from the examples of others as though those others were more perfect. Yet, through frequent and trustworthy report, they learned of the honey-sweet delight of holiness by which our holy and blessed Father Bernard surpassed all others of his time, like a cedar exalted on Mount Zion. Therefore, as men truly meek and humble of heart, and not passing with deaf ear over the saying of the Apocalypse, “Let him who is holy be sanctified still” (Apoc. XXII), they counted their former attainments as nothing and stretched forward to the things ahead. They submitted themselves with willing and most humble purpose to the instruction of so great and spiritual a Father. In return, the blessed Bernard always embraced them with one singular affection of charity, in reverence for their holiness.

We shall now briefly recall the most pure and truly monastic conduct of the most reverend Father Humbert. Concerning the others we shall say, in their proper place, what the Lord grants. Humbert, servant of God, having been placed in the sanctuary of the Lord from childhood, had already served the Lord vigorously in religion for twenty years [Col. 1055B] when, desiring a more perfect and holy life, he came to Clairvaux, almost at the very beginning of that house. There he shone with such gifts of virtues and was adorned with such a grace of gentleness and charity that, like one of the heavenly seraphim, he kindled the whole congregation mightily toward the love of God by the intense fervour of his conduct.

Blessed Bernard himself, standing at the summit of virtues by the special prerogative of this holy congregation blessed by God, and having no need to beg from another person the increase of religious life, nevertheless had learned by the anointing of the Holy Spirit to seek lower things rather than higher. He had set before himself God’s servant Humbert as an example of perfection to imitate. He strove to admire Humbert’s virtues, considered his merits great and exalted, and regarded him as the pattern of holiness, the model of religion, [Col. 1055C] the mirror of monastic purity. Compared with Humbert, Bernard considered his own conduct of no account; in view of Humbert’s holy fervour, he chastened his own—even most fervent—endeavours day and night as though deficient. For he knew that every person falls short when compared with the weak, whereas through contemplating the perfect, even one accomplished in virtues finds further increases of virtue, because of that praiseworthy earnestness of holy humility. Hence Blessed Bernard himself says in one of his sermons:

“Would that we sinners had, in our sins, that humility which holy men have had in their virtues!”

Accordingly, the venerable Humbert was later sent to build the monastery of Igny and was appointed its first abbot by Blessed Bernard. He bore with the greatest impatience the removal from him of poverty, humility, and subjection—things dear to him. [Col. 1055D] Finally, unable to endure that bleary-eyed Leah, that is, the restless tumult of worldly affairs, should be imposed upon him in place of the beautiful Rachel of holy quiet and contemplation, he laid down the burden of pastoral care, although Saint Bernard was unwilling and resistant. Returning to Clairvaux, he placed upon his noble neck the yoke of subjection and obedience, because no neck is noble unless it is flexible. He bore this yoke tirelessly to the end of his life, as though it were the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden.

When he had grown old, and the vigour of his body failed with his limbs decaying, and he was further troubled by various afflictions of ill health, his spirit nevertheless remained vigorous and fervent in God’s work. Thus, though the strenuous labours of the Order could scarcely be endured by the strong age of young men, he, old and almost decrepit, underwent them patiently—indeed, cheerfully. The relaxations and merciful allowances granted to the aged out of compassion [Col. 1056A] he not only did not seek, but would not accept when others wished to grant them. After spending about thirty years at Clairvaux, he completed his blessed contest and joyfully underwent death—not to be consumed by it, but, through it, to triumph most gloriously in the assumption of new life, then in soul and afterwards in body. Deeply troubled by his passing, Blessed Bernard declared in a discourse before the assembly of brothers what he thought of Humbert’s most excellent conduct. [Note: [Col. 1055D] Sermon on the death of Humbert.]

## CHAPTER V. From that sermon it is inferred that the holy old man Humbert was perfected in virtues

Consider, reader, as though in a small picture, a man of perfect virtue elegantly portrayed before your eyes. You may rightly say that this blessed man, having become a monk, “kept watch over the acts of a monk”: by most diligent effort he laboured to be in truth what he was by habit and name, judging it utterly unworthy to glory in the empty name of monk without the work of virtue. He knew that virtue is a step to glory, and that grace is altogether vain and beauty deceitful when virtue does not bring them forth. Therefore, most blessed Father Humbert, that ironic epitaph will be far from you—the one by which a certain man is reported to have been mocked after death, because in life he had gloried in the empty name of monk without the work of virtue:

> If a black garment, a shaven head, and a broad cowl make anyone righteous, this man was righteous.

O how far light is from darkness! How great a gulf is fixed between the children of wrath and the children of grace! How different a judgment receives, as they depart hence, the falsely religious and the truly religious! Humbert was not among the foolish virgins who, having taken their lamps, forgot through detestable negligence to take oil with them. He was among the prudent. Of him—not a painted flatterer, but his true eulogist—says that he was more composed than all [Col. 1056C] men whom he had seen in his days, one and the same man, constant at every time and every hour. In fine terms, though in other words, this presents the definition by which the poet defines a wise man:

> Constant to himself, wholly smooth and round.  
> (Horace, *Satires*, II.85.)

That is, to remain one and the same at every time and every hour.

It should further be known that this blessed man fulfilled the office of prior under Saint Bernard at Clairvaux. By their teaching and examples of virtue, the whole of Clairvaux was watered like a garden of delights and a paradise of the Lord; and in each individual and in all together the fountain of righteousness sprang up unto the gaining of eternal life. Since his memory shall be in blessing for every generation of brothers who are to serve the Lord at Clairvaux, the venerable body of the most reverend Father Humbert was also laid in the monument in which, as stated above, Lord Robert, the second abbot of Clairvaux, was buried. It stands under an arch in the cloister wall near the chapter house. [Col. 1056D] There, too, the coffin holding his sacred bones bears the inscription of his name, so that the brothers seated in the cloister, learning from reading of his most fervent efforts in holy religion—which were so great and magnificent that the most blessed Father Bernard did not hesitate to commit them to written memorials—and having at once before their eyes the tomb of his sacred ashes, may grow warm in spirit, flee forgetfulness, drive far from themselves torpor and negligence, and never suppose that they will attain the crown set before monks except through the arduous labours of cloistered discipline.

## CHAPTER VI. On Lord Odo, formerly subprior at Clairvaux

There was among the elders of Clairvaux a man named Odo [Col. 1057A], who for many years vigorously discharged the office of subprior in that house. He was truly poor in spirit and humble in heart. From almost the first years of that house, he underwent eagerly its severe labours—not only those of voluntary poverty, but those also of harsh necessity, by which in its early state the house was frequently constrained through scarcity of resources. Thus he was observed to be more fervent in the praises of God when he seemed in some degree deprived of bodily means of support.

His disposition possessed such sweetness, and he led the brothers’ assembly with such gentleness, when the prior was otherwise occupied, as he constantly guided and brought them back while they went to and returned from work, that even today that holy congregation recounts the memory of the abundance of his sweetness with joy. When the faithful shepherd, Saint Bernard, as the ruin of his sacred body grew more frequent, approached ever more closely the laying aside of corruptible life and entrance into blessed incorruptibility, almighty [Col. 1057B] God—who never despises the desires of the humble—granted this blessed Odo, according to his heart’s desire, that he should die before the holy Father, lest, after the golden ages that had flourished most delightfully under so great a Father, he should be compelled to see with mourning eyes the iron age soon to follow.

The Lord also deigned to reveal beforehand to one of the brothers in a clear vision that this would happen. For a certain brother saw in a vision of the night that the most blessed man Bernard was preparing to go up to Jerusalem and was already at the point of setting out. The venerable Odo reverently approached him and said that he himself would go ahead. The truth shown by this vision was fulfilled thus: the man worthy of God, about to set out for the heavenly Jerusalem—where is the true vision of peace—and to be followed shortly afterward by the holy Father, went before on his blessed embassy.

After this vision, God’s servant Odo, afflicted by bodily sickness, came to his end. [Col. 1057C] When Blessed Bernard entered to visit him, he saw that Odo was afraid and anxious, as though he had lived less than perfectly and therefore still awaited the uncertain judgment of the Judge. Bernard addressed him thus:

“Why do you tremble? Why are you troubled, blessed soul? From the days of your youth you have rendered devoted service to Christ amid many and great labours—and do you fear to depart? Go on, go on in security. I tell you truly that you will arrive by a straight course at your Creator and will appear holy before him.”

Strengthened by this consolation from his beloved Father, humble Odo set out with a more peaceful countenance toward his departure. Soon, putting off the human being, he lost death and truly laid hold of life. To demonstrate through an act of pious humility that the judgment he had pronounced about Odo was true, the holy Father approached reverently while Odo’s holy body was still lying on the bier, before it was taken for washing. He devoutly kissed the sacred footprints of one worthy of God, openly showing all how great an honour is due to those who are exercised without pretence in the practices [Col. 1057D] of the rule they have professed and delight in the way of God’s commandments as in all riches.

The remains of his blessed body were laid, out of reverence for his holiness, in the monument in which we said that Humbert of pious memory was placed. There he rests in blessed repose, awaiting the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who “will transform the body of his lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III). The Psalmist says in speaking to the Lord: “Can the seat of iniquity cleave to you, which devises toil in a command?” (Ps. XCIII). For, if one may say it, what are all the affliction, pain, and distress of the present time for God’s elect but a certain contrivance of toil? For their present tribulation, momentary and light, works in them an immeasurable weight of glory in the height of eternal life (II Cor. IV). The venerable Odo is most certainly hoped already to have reached this in soul [Col. 1058A], and afterwards to be about to attain it in body.

## CHAPTER VII. On Lord Guerric, formerly monk of Clairvaux and later abbot of Igny

Lord Guerric, abbot of Igny, of holy memory, while still a monk at Clairvaux under the discipline of Blessed Bernard and nourished at the royal breasts of sacred doctrine, proved by his character and life that he was no unworthy son of so great a father. For he had learned to ascend the citadel of virtues all the more exaltedly because, by God’s great gift, he more secretly rejoiced in the title of incorruption, through the testimony of conscience. As those to whom it had been granted to know the secrets of so great a man maintained, guided by grace he preserved the spotless garment of incorruption to the end of his life.

Moreover, the Lord deigned to declare by glorious and manifest signs how pure and upright were his life and conduct, and what an exceedingly [Col. 1058B] pure incense of holy devotion he daily kindled for God upon the altar of his heart. It happened once that he was appointed to read the lesson at Vigils. As he moved from his stall and came to the step of the presbytery, in order to bow as was customary, a certain other spiritual monk, who was accustomed to investigate with diligent interest his holy pursuits in the Lord—not wasting away through pestilent jealousy or envy, but wishing to be stirred by Guerric’s examples to better things—watched him go. As he bowed devoutly before the step of the presbytery, behold, an angel of the Lord came from heaven, seen by the aforesaid spiritual brother, and clothed him in a most white and splendid garment. Leading him reverently through the middle of the choir, the angel ascended with him to the lectern; and, standing beside him until he had read the entire lesson, performed the office of attendant with great reverence.

When the reading was finished, the angel again led him through the middle of the choir [Col. 1058C] and accompanied him as far as the step of the presbytery. As Guerric made the customary act of satisfaction before that step after the readings, the angel of the Lord took back the heavenly garment and vanished from the sight of the one who saw these things. The brother to whom, by so great a condescension of divine grace, it had been granted to know this hidden gift of divine goodness was greatly edified by the glorious vision. He learned that the man concerning whom he had deserved to see such things was truly a servant of God, approaching angelic purity and, like Benjamin most beloved of the Lord, dwelling with Him all day in the chamber of holy contemplation.

In due course the venerable Guerric was made abbot of Igny. What manner of man he showed himself to be, and how vigorously he fulfilled the office entrusted to him, is not for our littleness to declare. Yet his most lucid, discerning, and truly spiritual sermons, which he delivered to the communities of brothers on the chief feasts and which were taken down by the cantor of that church, clearly show how sound and rich was his teaching. [Col. 1058D] But that heavenly craftsman, who customarily polishes vessels of mercy through various pressures and blows so that they may be distinguished from vessels of wrath, allowed this servant of His to suffer continuous and serious illnesses. He endured these afflictions most patiently, knowing that he would receive from the hands of the supreme King a crown in the future proportionately more glorious the more cheerfully he had laboured in the present contest.

Yet he was excessively grieved and greatly humbled himself because, through bodily weakness, he was almost continually compelled to leave the assembly of brothers and lie in the infirmary, and could not give his brothers the daily example of labour as he could offer them the word of holy preaching. But whatever he lacked in bodily exercise was wholly supplied by the affection of sincere devotion and his burning devotion to God. In one of his sermons [Col. 1059A] he laments his weakness and insufficiency as follows. [Note: [Col. 1059D] Sermon on Rogation Days.]

> “Friends have come to me from the road, but I have nothing to set before them. I am not a physician, and there is no bread in my house. Therefore I said from the beginning: ‘Do not appoint me ruler.’ For one who cannot be of benefit ought not to preside. But how can one be of benefit who is neither a physician nor has bread in his house—that is, who knows neither the art by which to heal nor the teaching by which to feed? This indeed I said, but alas, you did not hear me, for you appointed me ruler. It remained, therefore, since I could not escape the danger, that I should flee to the remedy and hear concerning this the counsel of the Wise Man: ‘Have they made you ruler? Be among them as one of them’ (Ecclus. XXXII).
>
> “But woe is me: not even this has been left to me. For just as lack of skill prevents one from being over others, so weakness does not permit one to be among others; and just as in spirit I am not sufficient to minister the word, so in body I fail to provide an example. Since, therefore, I am fit neither to preside nor to be with others, where can I be [Col. 1059B] unless I choose the lowest and safest place: namely, to be subject to all? This indeed I can do: by holding humble—indeed, true—opinions of myself. Nothing prevents me; rather, truth itself strongly counsels me to be subject to all in spirit, although I am compelled to preside in office. You, Lord God, are He who commands me to be subject, and nevertheless commands me to preside. From you I ask that you make me at once humble and useful in the ministry entrusted to me: humble, by thinking truly of myself; useful, by speaking rightly of you. Inspire the former in my heart; supply the latter to my mouth. Grant a right and well-sounding word at the opening of my mouth—you who said, ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it’ (Ps. LXXX)—that all your household may be filled with blessings.”

## Chapter VIII. With what strictness Lord Abbot Guerric examined his conscience at his death.

Consider, reader, the purity of conscience of this holy man [Col. 1059C], who so confidently declares it easy for himself to do what divine kindness grants only to very few and most perfect persons: namely, to be subject to all in spirit, although compelled by office to preside over them. When the faithful servant of the Lord, Guerric, having with most faithful distribution apportioned his lord’s provisions among his fellow servants, was full of days and virtues and about to pass from this world to the Father, he was seized by illness. As its discomfort increased, he was brought to his last extremity.

As he examined more carefully every corner of his conscience, lest anything perhaps done wrongly and left uncorrected should make the strict Judge angry with him and give malignant spirits an opportunity for accusation, he remembered the little book of Sermons which he had composed. At the same time he recalled that the Fathers had decreed that no one ought to make books without permission of the General Chapter. Groaning heavily, he summoned the brethren and said:

> “Behold, brethren: while I strove to watch over your advancement and comply with your request, I have incurred the crime of disobedience, [Col. 1059D] which, as holy Samuel testifies (1 Kings 15), is like the sin of idolatry. For I rashly presumed to publish, without the permission of the General Chapter, the little book of Sermons which I dictated at your request. Therefore bring it here at once and burn it in the fire, lest for the fault of disobedience I be handed over to the avenging flames of hell to be consumed.”

But by God’s providence it happened that the book had already been copied into other quires; God thus disposing something better for us in this matter, so that holy Church—and especially the Cistercian Order—should not be deprived of the benefit of so great a learning. For with wonderful balance the charm of literary learning abounds in that volume, while the humility of Christian simplicity shines so brightly in it that it is not merely not burdensome, but exceedingly pleasing to its readers. Moreover, the Lord’s fiery utterance, found so powerfully in those sermons [Col. 1060A], moves, touches, and kindles the reader in such a way that anyone is hard of heart who is not pierced by their reading and stirred to strive for better things.

Thus this just and God-fearing servant of God, having corrected by severe examination the fault that troubled his conscience, now sighed more gladly and eagerly for heavenly things. By the vows and desires of holy devotion he sought the most delightful and blessed presence of Christ the Lord; and shortly afterward, leaving the wretched society of mortals, he deserved, as we piously believe, to be satisfied with that presence.

## Chapter IX. Concerning Lord Robert, monk of Clairvaux and afterward abbot.

Lord Robert, once abbot of Notre-Dame, and kinsman of St Bernard according to the flesh, had assumed in his youth the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden at Cîteaux. Later, when the most reverend man of God Bernard had been established as the first abbot of Clairvaux, Robert was trained under him in heavenly discipline in that same monastery. While he was taught by the pious Father to repel the impulses of the flesh by holy prayers, and to tame the unruly and restless movements of youth by manual labor, vigils, and fasts, the delicate young man, overcome by faint-heartedness and wearied by the constant sacred exercises, heard with too little patience the admonishing word behind him.

Meanwhile, when the Cluniac brethren heard that this young man had committed himself to the Cistercian Order, they were greatly angered, maintaining that he could by no legal right have done this, since his parents had promised him as a boy to their monastery in accordance with the Rule of St Benedict. In support of this assertion, they pointed to land which, they said, his parents had granted to the Cluniac monastery along with him. Since the authority of Blessed Bernard prevented them from daring to reclaim him openly, they turned to craftier arguments [Col. 1060C].

A certain prior was sent by the chief prior himself of that great house, to entrap the young man, if possible, with flattery and persuasion, so that, renouncing the Cistercian Order and leaving Clairvaux, he might of his own accord transfer himself to Cluny. When the aforementioned prior came to Clairvaux, people believed that he possessed inwardly the appearance of piety which he displayed outwardly in face and dress. But alas, faith is safe nowhere, and therefore we are all deceived. Alas for that woe threatened against the sinner who enters the land by two paths (Ecclesiasticus 3): his divided heart rends the conscience, and even in religious life—something which we cannot say without groaning—the thorns of duplicity and curse are sometimes discovered to sprout.

This prior of whom we speak approached the masters of the brethren and asked permission to speak with Brother Robert, declaring that he had come to visit and console him. But who would have refused this to such a man? Who would not have believed that Christ’s new recruit would receive an increase of virtue from the edifying words of so great an elder, and thus become stronger in repelling vices? But alas: beneath the lamb’s skin a wolfish mind was found; and he who was believed to urge virtue persuaded the still inexperienced soldier to abandon his post and throw down his arms, voluntarily delivering himself—not so much by free as by miserable choice—to a cruel enemy [Col. 1060D].

Why say more? He urged and persuaded the delicate young man to flee the hard labors of the Clairvaux monks and embrace the soft observances of the Cluniacs, which breathe more of flesh than of spirit. So the little sheep followed the wolf, not knowing that he was rushing into the dreadful abyss of apostasy. The venerable Father Bernard, though he took this deed very grievously, nevertheless concealed his feelings, lest he seem to have inflicted retaliation in any respect upon those who had injured him.

After he had for some time kept silence, however, he resolved to recall the same brother by letter. As he dictated it, Lord William of Rievaulx, afterward the first abbot of that monastery, wrote it down on parchment. Both were sitting outdoors together, for they had gone beyond the monastery enclosure in order to dictate more privately. Suddenly an unexpected shower broke out, and the writer, as we learned from his own account, wished to put away the sheet. The holy Father said to him: “It is God’s work; do not fear to write.” He therefore wrote the letter in the midst of rain, without rain. Although it rained on every side, the power of charity covered the exposed sheet; and the charity that dictated the letter also preserved the page. Because of so great a miracle, this letter was deservedly placed first by the brethren in the collection of Bernard’s letters. Its text began: “Long enough, and more than long enough, have I endured, beloved son Robert,” etc.

## Chapter X. How dangerous it is for one professed in the Cistercian Order to turn aside to another Order.

[Col. 1061B]

When he received and read this letter, that brother, as soon as he recognized the handwriting of his loving abbot and kinsman, perceived with how deep a love he had dipped his pen. At the same time, considering how differently life was conducted in the place where he then remained and in the place which he had rashly left, he was compuncted and came to his senses. Though late, he groaned that he had erred—or rather, that others had led him into error. Conceiving with his whole mind the spirit of liberty, he duly abandoned the place to which he had gone unlawfully; and, returning to Clairvaux, he advanced so far under the discipline of Blessed Father Bernard that, as his virtues increased, he was afterward appointed abbot of Notre-Dame.

By this example we are plainly taught that no one who has professed the Cistercian Order can turn aside to adherents of another religious community or Order without grave peril to his soul. Indeed, to confess the truth candidly, he loses the greater good which he weakly abandons, and cannot attain the lesser good which, by choosing the greater, he has made unlawful for himself. Furthermore, unless he repents, he will not escape the mark of perpetual shame branded upon him by the most foul cautery of apostasy [Col. 1061C].

That our assertion may be believed without the scruple of doubt—for every word stands by the mouth of two witnesses—we add another example in confirmation of the truth. A certain abbot, one of the sons of Clairvaux and ruling an abbey in Italy, though otherwise religious, was deposed from the office of prelacy for a certain fault of his. Bearing this deposition less patiently than he ought, and driven by indiscreet sorrow, he abandoned the Cistercian Order and went over to Cluny. There, while for some time he served the Lord in simplicity of heart according to the institutions of that Order, God, who alone looks upon simplicity of heart, remembered his former labors in the Cistercian Order. By a revelation He deigned to show him that he could not save his soul in that Order: for although in men’s eyes he seemed to remain in a lesser good, before God’s sight he had fallen from a greater good, and therefore had rendered the lesser good altogether unfruitful for himself [Col. 1061D].

Wholesomely warned by this revelation, the old man was not ungrateful for God’s grace so mercifully recalling him from his error. Immediately withdrawing his foot from the precipice of transgression, he returned as quickly as possible to Clairvaux. There he did penance for his past error; afterward he completed his life in holy conduct and rested in a blessed end.

## Chapter XI. Concerning the monk Rainald, who saw Blessed Mary visiting the brethren at harvest.

> [Note: In relating this visitation, Caesarius names St Anne instead of St Elizabeth [Col. 1061D]. But since he praises the book of Clairvaux [Col. 1062D] as known to this author, Caesarius himself is thought to be mistaken.]

[Col. 1062A]

There was at Clairvaux a certain religious monk, worthy of good remembrance, named Rainald: a man of good simplicity, fearing God and retaining his innocence from childhood to old age. Of him that elder, whom we mentioned above as having committed to written record many things concerning the religious persons of our Order, especially the senior monks and lay brothers of his Clairvaux—and whose writings we have incorporated with the same fidelity with which he expressed them—writes as follows:

> “The man of God Rainald, although before his conversion he spent thirty years in secular dress, nevertheless did not live in a secular manner. Applying himself to works of piety, he was careful to glorify and bear God in his body. Among the other good works which he did with an undivided heart, he also dedicated bodily integrity to the Lord [Col. 1062B]. Assisted by God’s grace, he passed from his mother’s womb to the day of his death along an undefiled path, overcoming the incitements of lust and the impurities of the flesh.
>
> “After receiving the monastic habit in the monastery of St Amand, he spent twenty years and more there in holy conduct, giving all men no small proof of his holiness. Then, burning with a greater ardor for virtue, he came to the house of God at Clairvaux, driven by divine zeal, though first forewarned by God through many revelations. I refrain from saying how many labors and troubles this blessed man endured from the brethren of that Order, who envied his happy deeds and wished to turn him aside from such a purpose, since I wish to spare my readers weariness.
>
> “When he was received at Clairvaux, he immediately girded himself manfully for a new warfare, and, though an old soldier, showed himself among us a most valiant recruit: all day mortifying himself in labor, vigils, fasts, and the other observances of holy discipline. He possessed an unceasing zeal for prayer and a wonderful abundance of tears in prayer [Col. 1062C].
>
> “One day, having gone out with the others to labor at the wheat harvest, he withdrew a little from the community and began with great delight of mind to watch the reapers. He reflected and marvelled that so many wise, noble, and delicately reared men should expose themselves to labor and hardship for Christ’s love, receiving the blazing heat of the sun with such joy as though they were plucking the most sweetly fragrant fruits in a garden of delights, or feasting most luxuriously at a table full of rich dishes. Then, lifting his eyes and hands to heaven, he gave thanks to the Lord for having joined him, though unworthy and sinful, to so great a multitude.
>
> “While he turned these and like thoughts over in his mind and could scarcely contain himself for the immensity of his joy, suddenly there appeared to him what seemed to be three venerable ladies, with rosy faces and shining white garments. One of them, who went before the others, appeared more radiant in clothing, more beautiful in form, and taller in stature [Col. 1062D]. They descended from a nearby hill and approached the community of brethren harvesting grain on that hillside. When he saw them, disturbed and astonished by excessive wonder, he cried out:
>
> “‘Lord God, who are these women, so beautiful and venerable, who, unlike other women, are approaching our community?’
>
> “As he spoke thus, a man of venerable white hair, clothed in a white robe, stood beside him and said: ‘The greater one, who goes before the others, is Mary herself, the virgin mother of Jesus Christ; those who follow are St Elizabeth and St Mary Magdalene.’
>
> “When he heard the Mother of the Lord named, all his inward parts were moved by tenderness at that name, for he loved her intensely. Again he asked: ‘And where is she going, my lord? Where is our Lady going?’ He replied: ‘She comes to visit her reapers’ [Col. 1063A].
>
> “When these words had been spoken, the person who was speaking suddenly disappeared. At this sight the man of God wondered still more within himself. Turning his eyes back to the holy Mother of God and her companions, he gazed upon them with astonished sight. Walking with measured steps, they came one after another to the community. Once they entered it, they began to walk separately among the monks and lay brothers, here and there, as though bestowing the grace of visitation. At last they vanished from the watcher’s eyes and returned to heaven, from which they had come. The man of God remained fixed in place and could not move until the miracle was over.
>
> “How much he advanced because of such a visitation, and how much he increased in love for God and for His most blessed Mother, his exemplary conduct and daily growth in virtue showed [Col. 1063B]. He often received many other revelations from God, but chose rather to conceal them than to speak of them, in order to avoid the vice of vainglory. Indeed, he had kept this very vision silent for almost eight years; only a short time—forty days, if I remember correctly—before his death did he disclose it to me, though unwillingly and in a sense compelled, on the following occasion.
>
> “One day, as we were conversing familiarly about the salvation of souls, I knew him to be a just and holy man, often visited by the Lord. Trusting in the love which I bore him and which I perceived him to bear me, I dared to ask and request something from him. For Christ’s love and His mercies, I began to entreat him from the depths of my heart and to press him earnestly to reveal to me, for God’s honor, one of his consolations—namely, the one by which he judged I might be most edified. Compelled by such entreaty, he narrated to me the vision mentioned above [Col. 1063C].
>
> “But with what emotion did he tell it! God Himself is witness with what fear and trembling, with what a flood of tears, with what groans and sighs he uttered it. Groans and sobs breaking from the depths of his heart often interrupted his speaking voice, as if he were at that very hour beholding the vision itself.
>
> “After fourteen days had passed, the Lady of the Angels appeared to him in a vision, cutting and preparing white and precious garments with which he was soon to be clothed. When she had prepared them, she bound them together and, departing, took them with her. Seeing this, he followed her and cried after her: ‘Ah, my most dearly desired Lady, when shall I have these garments which you have deigned to prepare for me?’ The most holy Mother of God said to him: ‘When you come to me, then you shall receive them.’
>
> “O joyful vision! O certain promise—indeed, made all the more certain by its swift fulfillment [Col. 1063D]. When morning came, this servant of God entered to visit me as one who was ill. At that time I was sick almost unto death; the illness was exceedingly severe, so that even the physicians despaired of my recovery. For this reason I had been anointed with the oil of the sick the preceding day, because they believed I would die quickly.
>
> “When he came to me, he felt deep compassion for me. To console me somewhat, he told me the vision he had seen that same night, declaring and maintaining that it had been shown to him not for his own sake, but for mine. For he was most humble in heart and presumed nothing of this kind about his own holiness. I immediately answered him:
>
> “‘Do not, I beg you, most loving father, do not alienate your blessing from yourself by an unfavorable interpretation. The garments prepared for you from heaven will never belong to another; rather, through God’s mercy they will remain safe and intact for you. But urgently beseech that most merciful visitor of yours that, in the good pleasure of her mercy, she may deign to prepare for me whatever other garments she wishes [Col. 1064A]. For she is powerful and gracious, rich toward all who invoke her.’
>
> “Why say more? I, who was considered near death, whether I wished or not, was recalled to endure the hardships of this life. But he, who appeared sound and well, survived no more than twenty-five days afterward. At last, when he had happily completed the course of his life, he laid aside the garments of corruptible flesh and undoubtedly received the robe of immortality, through the most blessed Mother of God whom he had devoutly served, in accordance with the faith of that promise.
>
> “Nor should it be passed over in silence that, six days before his falling asleep, while he was alone in church after Compline and intent upon prayer, the death-board sounded suddenly in his ears, but only with two strokes. When he heard it, he immediately sprang up and sought the infirmary, thinking that one of the sick brethren there was about to die. But when he had learned with certainty that no one there was then at the point of death, it occurred to him that he himself was the person for whom this sign had been made, and that the sound of the board signified his own departure [Col. 1064B].
>
> “At this remembrance of death he was suddenly seized with dread; trembling and shuddering of the flesh came upon him, and he immediately began to suffer from fever. As the illness worsened, he finally came to his last end. While he lay in bed, he turned over almost without ceasing in heart and speech the salutation of the blessed Virgin Mother, which he had always been accustomed to repeat; and with the words of that most sweet oracle he breathed out his blessed soul.
>
> “It happened that a lay brother, a man of religious conduct and good repute, departed to the Lord on that same day. Thus the funerals of both were celebrated together, and both were buried in the same tomb. While this was taking place, a spiritual man was shown in a vision that two most beautiful temples were being built at Clairvaux: one in the monks’ infirmary, the other in the lay brothers’ infirmary [Col. 1064C]. But the first was much nobler and more honorable—or more beautiful—than the other.
>
> “It is therefore clear that in the twofold building of temples and in the twofold stroke of the death-board, the death of both men—precious in the Lord’s sight—was plainly signified. The difference between the temples indicates the difference in their merits: although we believe that both were holy, one was holier than the other before God. Yet each received from the treasures of God’s mercy as much as the Mother of grace deigned to bestow.”

## Chapter XII. Concerning the monk who heard the board as a sign of his death.

In the same month in which the aforementioned servant of God departed to the Lord, a similar event occurred there. In the same monastery there was a sacristan named Gerard, a man eminent in good morals and truly religious [Col. 1064D]. In accordance with the prophet’s counsel (Lamentations 3), he bore the Lord’s yoke from youth and “lifted himself above himself,” because, while still tender and weak, he set his hand to difficult things. Nourished at the breasts of kings and happily trained in chaste discipline, he continually grew and advanced toward what was better; and, by God’s great gift, he never experienced the corruption of the flesh, as those intimate with him testify.

When the hour approached at which he was to pass from the world to God, one day, after Compline, he remained in the church as usual. Suddenly a sound came into his ears, as though the board for the dying were being struck repeatedly. On hearing it, he thought that one of the brethren in the infirmary was then dying. A little later, when he learned with complete certainty that no human being had made that sound, he recalled the prophetic board which the man of God Rainald had heard as a sign of his death. For this account had already spread among the brethren and had made them all astonished and amazed [Col. 1065A]. As he considered these things, it entered his heart that through that sign he himself would pay the debt of death.

At the remembrance of death the hairs of his flesh suddenly stood up, and fear and trembling came upon him. A fatal fever immediately seized him, and within ten days he was consumed and happily departed. We cannot pass over in silence this feature of his devout piety, for we saw and rejoiced in what seemed a miracle wrought by God through him—or rather, in him. As he drew his last breath and no longer had the strength to speak, for nearly three or four hours he held his hands joined and stretched out motionless toward the cross, as though bound together by some cord. Though the other members of his body were repeatedly tossed this way and that under the pressure of pain, his hands, which, as we have said, he extended toward the cross, were never separated from each other and never drawn back to himself; thus, even in death, he showed what he had often done in life.

## Chapter XIII. Concerning the servant of God Peter, who was accustomed to see the Lord Jesus on the altar at the time of sacrifice.

[Col. 1065B]

Among the others in that blessed house of Clairvaux who, by the examples, exhortations, and prayers of our most holy Father Bernard, had grown strong in the spirit and learned to climb the height of virtue, there was an old man named Peter, surnamed the Toulousain, a man of great purity and devotion. From childhood he had one constant zeal and desire: to crucify himself to the world and the world to himself. In youth, before he submitted himself to the Cistercian Order, he lived in solitude, mortifying the old man within himself by many fasts and labors, and daily offering to the Lord upon the altar of his heart the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.

Constantly eating wild herbs and bread made with lye, he served Christ there for a long time, and, God protecting him [Col. 1065C], bravely overcame countless wars of temptation from malignant spirits. Later, having learned through widespread report of the holiness of Blessed Bernard, abbot, and of the monastery of Clairvaux itself, he went to that place with great fervor of spiritual longing. There, amid so great a congregation of righteous persons, like one in the Lord’s tabernacle, he hoped to live more safely in security and shelter from storm and rain, and under the discipline of the aforesaid Father to attain what perfection he lacked. There he served Christ the Lord happily for many years and persevered until the end of his life.

While he was still alive, the Lord deigned to appear to him in a vision, seated upon a lofty throne with thousands of saints around Him. Peter seemed to be led before the Lord for judgment. When he had been presented before the fearful Majesty, frightened and trembling, he fell at the feet of Him who sat upon the throne, begging Him to have mercy upon him. The Lord said to him: “What do you wish Me to do for you?” He answered: “Lord, that I may be saved.” And the Lord said to him: “Go; turn quickly to My service, and persevere continually in it, and the salvation which you ask shall not fail you” [Col. 1065D].

Holding this promise as the surest pledge of eternal salvation, the servant of God Peter completely forsook the world and devoted his whole self to divine service.

He therefore girded his loins with strength and strengthened his arm to overcome the spiritual wickednesses that afterward assailed him fiercely for many days and years. Above all, he endured the assaults of the spirit of fornication, which continually pricked him, asleep and awake alike, with great stings of temptation. For this reason, profoundly angry with himself, he afflicted his body incredibly by labor and hardship, many vigils and fasts, and other torments of penance. His mind was so disturbed that he often resolved to cut off his genitals [Col. 1066A], since he could find no other remedy for the temptation.

Nor should it be silent that the ancient enemy was often seen by him in various forms. On one occasion he appeared in human shape in the choir at Clairvaux, with burning eyes and a terrible countenance. He was huge in stature and very deformed. He wore an utterly black cowl whose sleeves were shortened and barely reached to the elbows, while the rest of his arms was uncovered. This malignant apostate came and stood before the man of God, looking at him with proud eye and apparently angered that he so stubbornly resisted his suggestions. The man of God was stupefied in mind and held as though bound, unable to move. At last, when God visited him, he fortified himself with the sign of the Lord’s cross. By its power the destructive apparition vanished and did him no harm, except that it increased the burning of temptation.

A few days later it appeared to him again in the same place, taking the form of a monstrous beast [Col. 1066B], partly resembling a savage lion and partly a rapacious eagle. The obstinate monster stood against the most valiant athlete, threatening him fiercely and gaping at him with mad jaws, as though it were about to devour him alive. Yet it was restrained by divine power and could not touch him. At last, when Christ’s name was invoked, the phantom beast suddenly disappeared. Once it had gone, the man of God immediately endured such a blaze of the passion mentioned above that he clearly recognized that there had been present the smith of Isaiah, “who blows coals in the fire” (Isaiah 54).

Seeing that the violence of the temptation exceeded the measure of his endurance, he formed a settled resolve to cut himself off, preferring to risk himself before God in this respect rather than fall into the abyss of lust. He awaited nothing but an opportunity to find a razor or some other instrument suitable for this purpose. But the merciful and compassionate Lord, the helper in due season, in tribulation (Psalm 9), He who alone considers labor and sorrow, did not wish to desert His servant in so great a struggle. Instead, He “made with the temptation a way of escape, that he might be able to bear it” (1 Corinthians 10) [Col. 1066C].

Accordingly, while he slept, an angel of the Lord appeared in the form of a young man, saying that he was an expert physician and had come for that purpose: to cut him and cure him of that passion. Peter gladly accepted this and at once placed himself at the angel’s disposal. While he was being cut, he endured with complete patience both the hand of the cutter and the severity of the pain. When he awoke, he thought that the amputation had truly and physically been performed upon him. But when he discovered that the members of his body remained intact while the temptation had been cut out at the root, so that afterward he felt no distress from it whatsoever, he gave thanks to divine grace as was fitting. He took care to run all the more eagerly in the way of God’s commandments, since he had deserved to experience more abundantly God’s goodness in his temptations [Col. 1066D].

> [Note: Caesarius also relates this eunuchization, but errs in the circumstances, as may be seen in his *Distinctio* 4, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* [Col. 1065].]

From that time onward, once the incentives of carnal passions had been extinguished within him, the Lord began to visit him “with the blessings of His sweetness” and fill his soul with splendors (Isaiah 58), so that he could rightly say: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Thy consolations have made my soul glad” (Psalm 93). From then on, as the Lord rebuked “the beasts of the reeds” (Psalm 67), the stings of the flesh ceased from him completely, and the Spirit of all consolation rested upon him.

For the Lord magnified His mercy in dealing with him (Psalm 125), storing up upon him gladness and exultation and satisfying his desire with every good thing. Having long made him drink the wine of health-giving bitterness, He afterward deigned to intoxicate him with the nectar of sweetest contemplation. Among God’s other gifts [Col. 1067A], he had received a special grace of devotion in prayer, especially in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. Thus the brethren who assisted him at Mass marvelled beyond measure at the abundance of tears that he was accustomed to shed there.

The Lord revealed to him many great heavenly secrets and visited him very frequently with innumerable consolations, whether asleep, awake, or carried beyond himself in mind. If all these were committed to writing, they would fill a great volume. Yet, because it would be long and burdensome for me to set down in writing everything known to me concerning this blessed man, I shall relate particularly at least one event, which conscience urges me not to keep wholly silent, as I heard it from his own mouth. It is of such a kind and greatness that faithful hearers may easily believe or judge the rest from this one thing. I fear—indeed, I greatly fear—to offend my God if, through my silence, I allow a glorious and marvellous matter to perish, a matter entrusted to me alone or perhaps to only a very few by this servant of God [Col. 1067B], none of whom, I think, survives today. In it, we trust, God may be glorified and the faith and devotion of many strengthened.

Therefore, while this blessed man stood at the sacred altars offering the life-giving sacraments, at the very moment of receiving, as he held the most holy body of the Lord over the chalice in his hands, there appeared in the form of a beautiful child that child “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”: our Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man. He is meek and humble of heart, accustomed to hide Himself from the wise and exalted and to reveal Himself to little ones.

When Peter saw this, trembling before the splendor and awe of that Majesty, he closed his eyes, for he did not dare look upon the Lord. Yet even with closed eyes he saw Him as he did with open ones. When he turned his face to the other side and remained for some time with shut eyelids and his face thus turned away [Col. 1067C], he nevertheless saw Him as though set before him: sometimes upon his hand, sometimes upon his arm. In a wondrous and ineffable manner, it was as if he had other eyes fixed in the back of his head or in his temples, through which he beheld Him.

God gladdened that man with this revelation, so sweet and marvelous, not once or twice but frequently: for almost every day during four or five months Christ appeared to him. If the appearance sometimes seemed delayed for a little longer, he had such familiarity with God and such confidence in His mercy that he prolonged the completion of the sacrifice and was unwilling readily to conclude it until, with the joy of God’s salvation restored to him, he deserved to receive the customary blessing.

As has already been said, I have taken care to tell this faithfully and simply, as I learned it from the report of the man upon whom so great a grace was bestowed. For, as I sought to attach myself to him with affectionate devotion because of his holiness, and depended greatly upon his comfort and conversation, I drew this vision from him, as I did many others, by earnest prayers and a certain force of charity [Col. 1067D]. But this was on condition that I would not presume to reveal it to anyone before his death—a condition which I was readily able to observe. For he survived only a short time thereafter; at last, having happily completed his struggle, he was gathered to his fathers. With God’s favor he now rests at Clairvaux, where he had lived religiously and had always desired, with ardent devotion, to close his final day.

## Chapter XIV. Concerning the venerable monk William, whom an angel of the Lord rebuked for his fault and enjoined penance upon him.

There was at that time at Clairvaux a venerable monk named William, advanced alike in years and in religious life. For nearly fifty years, [Col. 1068A] serving the Lord in the monastic habit, he continually crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, and prolonged a martyrdom of long and unceasing suffering. Before he had joined the Cistercian Order, he had lived for a long time in the monastery of Saint Albinus at Angers, where, living religiously, he presented himself as a pattern of good works and gave the brethren of that place hope of great holiness. Accordingly, he was held in great reverence both by the abbot and by the whole community, and was loved by all.

There was on the monastery’s estate a certain place which seemed more secluded and better suited to the quiet of religious life. With the abbot’s consent, therefore, he went there with a few brethren. There, shut up in a narrow cell, he lived for many years, both to afflict himself by stricter abstinence and not to burden weaker brethren by his more austere manner of life. Thus, redoubling fasts and prayers by day and night, he not only utterly refused meat and the richer [Col. 1068B] dishes which those brethren sometimes used according to the monastery’s former custom, but also frequently abstained from Lenten food and even from the drinking of water, sustaining his frail body on the scantiest fare.

He did not, however, attain this virtue of abstinence without great difficulty. Rather, after long torments of hunger, after unutterable groans and sobs, God’s grace cooperating, he at length drove from their proper seats the native enticements of belly and throat, together with his other vices. One day, therefore, when one of the monastery’s elders came to visit him, he ordered a meal of meat to be set before him, because he seemed weak and exhausted by a long journey. But the old man replied that he would by no means taste meat unless the brother who had ordered it served would, for charity’s sake, share the meal with him. Compelled in some measure by his familiar affection and persuasion, and, as he later confessed, tempted by however slight a desire for that dish, he consented [Col. 1068C] to eat. When the meal was finished, the elder bade farewell to his friend and host and returned to the monastery. Immediately after his departure, the brother came to himself and began to draw deep sighs from the bottom of his heart and to groan heavily because he had broken the resolve of so long a time for so trifling an occasion.

He had scarcely begun to think such things when, suddenly, someone knocked at the window of his cell. When he opened it, he was terrified and stood astonished at the sight of the visitor. The figure had a most reverend countenance and bearing, wondrous beyond the measure of human beings; William had seen none like him in all beauty. His garments were white and precious; the hair of his head was like white wool and like snow. His face, shining with singular beauty, showed him to be rather an angel than a man. The words of his mouth were full of sweetness and grace and wonderfully breathed forth heavenly wisdom. In short, whatever appeared in him seemed beyond human nature. Yet he went barefoot and said [Col. 1068D] that he was a pilgrim, come from distant regions to visit him.

After a gentle greeting, he began, as though he knew and examined the brother’s thoughts, to address him in friendly and affectionate reproof concerning the matters which he was turning over in his mind:

“You rightly groan; you rightly mourn over your transgression, by which you have now broken the long-standing resolve of praiseworthy frugality for the sake of pleasurable charity. Charity is not good when it destroys charity. That kindness is blameworthy which harms souls in order to indulge bodies. Now hear the example I set before you.

“In the regions of Spain there was a consecrated woman living as a recluse. Feeding on bread and water, or sometimes half-raw vegetables, she courageously subdued the unruliness of the flesh through sober and chaste conduct. Once, at the devil’s prompting, this evil desire came upon her: she wished to eat meat. For a long time she resisted the temptation vigorously; but when she could no longer bear the enemy’s most violent suggestions, she gave her hands over to unlawful desire and was drawn into consent. [Col. 1069A] She therefore ordered a dish of meat to be prepared for her. When it had been placed upon the table, before presuming to taste it, she prostrated herself in prayer and, with a tearful voice, begged the Lord not to permit her to touch the food prepared, if He knew that it would be dangerous to her soul’s salvation.

“Rising from prayer, she went to the table and, after giving the blessing, removed the cover under which the meat dish was concealed. And behold: instead of the meat which had been served, three young ravens, squawking and featherless, appeared on the platter. At the sight, the consecrated woman was greatly terrified. Calling the sister who served her, she inquired into the truth of the matter. But the latter, under the adjuration of God’s dreadful judgment, replied that she had placed not unfledged little birds but three pieces of cooked meat on that very table. The woman’s cell stood on the bank of a certain violent and great river, which burst forth from rocky mountains [Col. 1069B] and, rushing along a rugged course, descended in a precipitous current to the lowlands.

“Therefore the handmaid of God rejoiced and gave thanks that her prayer had been heard; now she abhorred the eating of meat much more violently than she had formerly desired it. She ordered the chicks of blackness and evil suggestion, together with the dish which held them, to be thrown into the aforesaid river. Cast into the stream, they could in no way be separated from one another; but, as the vessel floated on the waves, they were at last carried into a certain pool near that same cell, where a hollow in a huge rock holds a plentiful gathering of waters. There they have now been continually whirled about through many courses of time; and even to this day, as testimony to this miracle, they are seen floating upon the waters in the same vessel.”

> [Note: [Col. 1069D] This reported continuous circling of the raven chicks is doubtful, since it is mentioned by no one else.]

As the man spoke these things and similar matters, the brother was deeply compuncted by the delightful character of his discourse. Falling on his face and shedding tears, he sought pardon for his guilt. Having accepted penance, he deserved to receive from him not merely absolution of sins but also abundant consolation [Col. 1069C]. And when he was now speaking with him confidently, he began to ask who he was. The visitor answered him: “It is not yours at present to know who I am, nor to learn whence I come or where I go.”

Then the brother said: “I beg you, my lord, at least enter among us today, and let us minister to you.”

The other replied: “I need neither your bread, nor your clothing, nor your dwelling; rather, I abound in every good thing, and I have food to eat which you do not know of [John 4]. I am concerned only for your salvation; and you likewise should be concerned for it.”

With these words he departed in haste, and was so suddenly withdrawn from the beholder’s eyes that he seemed rather to have vanished than to have gone away. The brother immediately summoned the brethren who served him and ordered them urgently to pursue the departing man and, with many entreaties, compel him to accept lodging. They went out very swiftly; but though they ran here and there, they could find no trace of him whatsoever. Therefore the man of God most certainly believed [Col. 1069D] that an angel of the Lord had been present—one able to know the secrets of his heart and to refresh him, grieving for his transgression, with so sweet a consolation. From that blessed presence he conceived such devotion and grace in his soul that, nearly twenty years later, when he told me these things, he still could not refrain from tears because of excessive tender feeling.

In the course of time, when the celebrated name of Blessed Bernard the abbot, the fame of his virtues, and the most illustrious religious life of his monastery had everywhere become known to the aforesaid man, his spirit could not rest until he submitted himself to Bernard’s most blessed guidance, so that he might become most fervent from fervent, and most holy from holy [Col. 1070A]. Received by Blessed Bernard the abbot and joined to the desired community of Clairvaux, he shone with such grace of virtues that he appeared wondrous in every holiness, even to the most perfect.

To him the merciful Father sent many great consolations through His Spirit and revealed many things to him from the secrets of heaven, as we have learned with certainty. Yet, because he feared falling into the plague of vainglory, he told very little of the many things revealed to him, and told even that to very few people. It happened one day, while Prime was being sung in choir and he stood in his place among those chanting the psalms, offering to the Lord the calves of his lips in a voice of exultation, that Saint Malachy, formerly bishop of Ireland, appeared to him while he was awake and chanting. Malachy lies honorably buried in that same church. He sat in a chair beside the altar, wonderfully adorned with ring, staff, mitre, and the other ornaments of a bishop, as though he were about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass after the end of that Hour. [Col. 1070B]

It was then the anniversary of the death of that most blessed bishop, which is also the solemn commemoration of all the faithful departed. Blessed Bernard also appeared with him, the most blessed pastor and patron of that same church. He too shone in white and precious garments and wore a mitre, though not the episcopal band. And rightly so. For he was master of the household in his own house: showing deference to and rejoicing with his venerable and special guest, and anticipating his beloved guest with fitting honor, he most willingly yielded to him the solemnities of Mass, especially on the day on which that holy bishop had entered the heavenly court and had first been honored with heavenly hymns. Accordingly, the blessed father showed himself attentive and diligent toward that holy bishop and toward the service of his altar.

The blessed bishop, leaning upon his pastoral staff, kept his eyes fixed continually toward the choir. Saint Bernard, however, looked now at the bishop, now at the community, now at the altar itself, as one solicitous [Col. 1070C] for all. This vision appeared visibly, manifestly, to that servant of God as he remained awake and looked with bodily eyes, for as long as one psalm was sung by the community during that Hour.

When the psalm ended, the vision ended; yet the devout emotion inspired by that vision could not thereafter end in the heart of its beholder. On the following day, Blessed Bernard himself appeared to him again, glorious in face and bearing. When the brother saw him, he fell at his feet, praying and asking something of him. The saint said: “What do you want me to do for you?”

He replied: “My lord and father, if I have found favor in your eyes, tell me whether I am to be saved.”

The saint answered: “Is this a small matter that you ask? Today, when I was leaving paradise, how many thousands of people I left outside the gate—people who are indeed tormented by such fear, not knowing whether they are counted worthy of love or of hatred.”

> [Note: [Col. 1069D] Saint Bernard does not appear to be speaking of the dead, as though their fate were uncertain, but of the living, who are said to have approached heaven’s gate through good works, yet remain uncertain of their salvation.]

Having said this, he gave him an answer concerning [Col. 1070D] the matter for which he had entreated him. But what definite answer he gave is unknown to us, because, avoiding the plague of vainglory, William would not tell us. He was a prudent man, grave in speech, and took great care not to say anything that might savor of his own glory. Nevertheless, from the confidence of his speech and the cheerfulness of his face, it was sufficiently understood that he had received from the holy Father a joyful answer concerning this matter.

This is the William mentioned above,

> [Note: [Col. 1070D] Above, Distinction 2, chapter 22.]

who saw the spirit of fornication, in the form of a phantom prostitute, curiously roaming about the infirmary; and from what he heard and saw from her, foretold to Lord Robert, abbot of Clairvaux, the apostasy of two young men. Their shameful flight immediately afterwards proved this prediction [Col. 1071A] true. There are also many other things known to us concerning this man of God which could stir the devotion of readers, but we keep them silent, both in consideration for fastidious readers and because we hasten to relate other matters. Thus this blessed and holy man, as he lived faithfully, so also died happily; full of days and virtues, he passed to the Lord and, by the Lord’s gift, obtained the burial in the most holy community of Clairvaux which he had desired and sought with all his prayers.

## Chapter XV. Concerning Lord Gerard of Farfa, a monk of great holiness

Gerard of Farfa, beloved by God and by human beings, whose memory is in blessing, and whom Blessed Bernard honored above others with a singular favor because of his singular purity and holiness, showed himself wondrous and exceedingly lovable to the whole community [Col. 1071B] in every form of religious observance. While he was still a monk at Farfa, a famous abbey of Tuscany, the Lord revealed to him in spirit that he had been transported to Clairvaux and was performing an office there: going around the various workshops with two basins, he poured water over the brethren’s hands for washing.

The outcome showed what this signified: he was to be one who would wash away the failings of the brethren of Clairvaux by a daily—indeed, almost continual—flood of tears from his eyes, as though with two ewers. When, therefore, by this sweet revelation he had received a foreknowledge of future things, a vehement fire of holy desire immediately blazed within him. His spirit could not rest at all until he was joined to the company of Christ’s poor, to whose service he recognized that he had been divinely assigned.

Though he flourished in other virtues, the grace of holy compunction had filled his breast with a special prerogative, so that the dove-like pupils of his eyes [Col. 1071C] rarely rested. Rather, like twin springs, they soaked his face nearly everywhere—especially at the celebration of the divine mystery—with a great rain of tears. He possessed a singular grace with God and with human beings, which all admired; they looked upon his face as the face of an angel standing among them and said: “This is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and for all our community” [2 Maccabees 15].

The Lord undoubtedly gave him many consolations in secret. Yet, being modest and humble, he preferred that his virtues remain hidden; and, because of reverence for his holiness, no one dared trouble him with questioning about such things. A certain novice named Julian, a priest of honorable life who had come to Clairvaux from the order of regular clerics, once saw an unclean spirit wandering wantonly about the choir in the likeness of a goat. When [Col. 1071D] it came before him, it stood for a while and began to mock him with open mouth, shaking its obscene head toward him and chattering its teeth together with the finest rapidity. When it left him, it came and stood before Gerard, the man of God, and likewise began, with shameless gestures, to ridicule him as a frolicsome animal.

More mocked and blown upon by Gerard, it immediately vanished like smoke, and the novice saw it no more. Having soon received permission to speak with Gerard, he asked whether he had seen anything in choir during that Hour. The elder, perceiving that Julian knew the secret, confessed that he had seen a phantom goat which had mocked both himself and Julian with its slippery motions. When the novice heard this, he was greatly amazed; and thereby he understood that Gerard saw many things of this sort, although, as his conscience bore witness, he kept his secret hidden between God and himself.

Although this man of God was exceedingly weak in body, being almost ninety years old, [Col. 1072A] neither old age nor weakness could hinder his customary good practices. Instead, through the tireless fervor of his spirit, he seemed daily to grow young; scarcely could he be kept in the infirmary even when grave illness compelled it, and scarcely could he be kept back even from the labor of harvest. Once, while oppressed by a very serious illness, he lay in bed in a more secluded little room. One night the lamp burning there went out. Seeing this, a brother then serving him rose and went to relight it. But finding all the workrooms locked on every side, he returned sadly without fire; having secured the door of the cell, he lay down again and fell asleep.

In the depth of night, when the holy man wished to rise for his necessities, the brother rose too, grieved that there was no light for him. Looking at the nearby fireplace, in which there had been no fire for eight days, he saw there a considerable heap of burning coals. Lighting the lamp from them, [Col. 1072B] he immediately looked back again at the same fireplace, but found not only no coals there, but could not detect even the slightest trace of warmth in it.

When Gerard lay in the final sickness of which he died, and was already at the point of death, Blessed Bernard appeared to him, adorned with an angelic countenance and white garments, yet in the bodily stature and appearance which he had had before his death. When Gerard saw him coming in toward him and supporting his aged and venerable limbs with a staff, he indicated by hand and voice, as best he could, that the others should rise at the saint’s arrival and quickly prepare a place for him to sit. They wondered and asked of what saint the old man spoke, but the pressure of illness prevented him from answering. Afterwards, when he regained the strength to speak, they asked again; he confessed that he had seen Saint Bernard consoling him with gentle speech. Bernard blessed him and, making the sign of the cross, [Col. 1072C] blessed the whole house as well, adding these very words:

“This is my house, which I built. May the Lord preserve it for ever and ever.”

Strengthened by the blessing of his most holy father, Gerard, the man of God, joyfully paid the debt of death, to be satisfied from the fountain of eternal life for which he had thirsted with such longing. Some time later he appeared in a vision to a religious lay brother named Lawrence, joyful and resplendent, fittingly adorned with precious garments, and told him that by God’s grace he possessed everlasting joy and glory. When the brother earnestly begged to receive his blessing and intercessions, Gerard blessed him and replied:

“I do not cease to pray, not only for you, but also for the whole body of the Church itself. Yet I make this small complaint: the infirmary brethren, in excessive haste, prepared me for burial while I was still alive and breathing, and carried me away from the place of those at the point of death as though I were entirely lifeless.”

[Col. 1072D] After several years had passed following his death, when the new cloister and new church—begun by the permission and blessing of Blessed Bernard—had been completed, his sacred bones were removed from the place where they had first been buried. They were placed with due honor, in reverence for his holiness, in the shrine in which, as stated above, the venerable Fathers Robert the abbot, Humbert the prior, and Odo the subprior had been laid.

## Chapter XVI. Concerning the wondrous grace specially bestowed by God on a monk of perfect religious life

A distinguished young man, native to the regions of Germany, went to Paris for study in the company of his master. As he passed through the house of Clairvaux, his master, seeing the community and discipline of the place, was moved by some judgment of God and asked—and obtained permission—to be received [Col. 1073A] at once for conversion. When he asked the youth to remain with him, the latter would not consent at all. He strongly recoiled from both the company and conversation of Cistercian monks and often prayed God never to give him the will to come to that Order for conversion.

Accordingly, stubbornly resisting his master’s request and the exhortations of the monastery’s brethren, he could be overcome by no engines of preaching. But who can adequately marvel at how wonderful God is in His counsels concerning the children of men, and at how inviolably the secret of His eternal predestination stands: how, that is, He mercifully changes the minds of His elect, laughs at their vain efforts, and further directs wills opposed to Himself toward the path of piety, so that in them and through them, in the place, manner, and time which He decreed from eternity, the purpose of His will may be fulfilled?

That same night, while the aforementioned youth turned the brothers’ [Col. 1073B] admonitions over in his mind, a voice came to him from God, saying: “If you depart from here and arrive in Paris, you will die before Pentecost, and without doubt you will die.” At this voice the young man was greatly astonished; nevertheless, the hardness of his heart could not yet be softened. On the next night, when he had given his limbs to sleep, he seemed to himself to be sunk in the mud of a deep well. As he lay there in despair, Blessed John the Evangelist suddenly appeared above him at the well’s mouth, in the face and bearing of Saint Bernard, who was then still alive in the body, together with another saint who likewise seemed very like a religious monk named Gerard, porter of Clairvaux. When the youth saw them, trembling and anxious, he earnestly begged them to have mercy on him.

Blessed John replied: “You disdain to follow sound counsel, and yet you ask help from us?”

When he promised that he would do whatever pleased them, if only he might deserve to escape the imminent danger, John said: “Then do you wish to become a monk in the monastery [Col. 1073C] of Clairvaux?”

He replied: “Yes, my lord; most willingly I do.”

When he had firmly promised this, they immediately drew him out from the depths of the pool and allowed him to go free.

Therefore, when morning came, he asked to be brought as quickly as possible to Blessed Bernard. Though he had never seen Bernard before, he immediately recognized by his face and bearing that this was certainly the one whom, on the preceding night, he had deserved to have as his deliverer on the condition of his conversion. Greatly astonished and compuncted, he at once gave himself to the holy man. Bernard received him kindly; and while still young, the youth immediately put on, to everyone’s amazement, the gray hairs of seriousness and wisdom. His aforesaid master, however, quickly fell away from his good purpose and tried to overthrow him too; but he could not move the novice, who was established in Christ’s love.

Thus this delicate and very tender youth, being fourteen years old, set his hand to mighty things. To the rejoicing of angels and human beings, he undertook to bear [Col. 1073D] Christ’s sweet yoke and, like a lamb, was harnessed to the plough of the Order he had embraced. Through the Lord’s mercy, from the first beginnings of his conversion he put on the strength of a young bull, yet retained the gentleness of a lamb. From his earliest years he shone with such preeminence of graces that his companions rejoiced with deep affection at the beauty and fragrance of his conversion, and eagerly strove to be shaped by the examples of holy devotion and humility which shone in him.

A religious and spiritual brother of that same monastery testified to me that he had once seen the following vision. He watched that youth singing the Invitatory before the altar. The image of the cross above the altar, as if delighted by his melody, came down from the cross and approached him. Spreading its arms, it graciously embraced him, held him closely to itself, and kissed him. When that brother saw this, he recognized that the youth’s soul was holy [Col. 1074A] and pleasing to God, and that he had been granted a special access of great familiarity with God’s mercy.

This most beloved servant of the Lord remained all day with Him as though in a bridal chamber and enjoyed most sweetly His blessed presence through the sweetness of contemplation. By the aforesaid vision, indeed, the Lord deigned to make known how fully He had filled His servant with love and grace. Since he was devout and fervent in all the exercises of the holy Order and continually sought the Lord’s mercy through the practice of holy compunction, an angel of the Lord once appeared to him in a dream and brought him into a glorious chamber. There he seemed to see the Lord Jesus Christ hanging on the cross, while His blessed mother, the Virgin Mary, stood beside His cross with Blessed John the Evangelist.

Upon entering, he sensed such a fragrance of sweetness as though he had entered a chamber of spices sprinkled with every aromatic powder. Seeing [Col. 1074B] the Lord of majesty, in most compassionate condescension, set before him the marks of His Passion and cross, he fell with his face to the ground in adoration and began with all his heart’s inmost strength to beg for His blessing. He received it through the Lord’s gracious generosity and immediately awoke. That vision was shown by evident signs not to have been vain or deceptive: the fragrance of heavenly nectar which he had inhaled in sleep left his whole inner person, when awakened, suffused with an anointing of wondrous sweetness. For three continuous days thereafter he rejoiced to be renewed and illumined by the same blessing.
