On another night, while intent upon prayer, he deserved to hear with bodily ears angelic voices resounding in the air with sweet and splendid harmony. The height of those voices was so great that no possible effort of human voices could rise to it. After he had delighted in them for some time, the pleasantness of the heavenly melody was at last taken from his ears; but there remained in his heart an immeasurable joy of devotion conceived from it [Col. 1074C], so that, often pouring forth the memory of that abundance of sweetness, he was moved by wondrous devotion and wholly transformed into joy.

Now made conscious of heavenly secrets, he went on increasing and growing, like Father Abraham, until he became very great [Genesis 26]. Yet, what surpasses every kind of greatness: the more richly he was endowed with the higher gifts of heavenly grace, the more carefully he showed himself humble, not only before God but also before his brethren. He presumed nothing unusual and nothing singular in his manner of life, though within that common life he was singular in the devotion of his singular purity.

But because grace is always increased in the humble, the Lord further deigned to make His servant manifest [perhaps: glorify], so that he might deserve to see with bodily eyes, in the most blessed form of His humanity, our Lord Jesus Christ—Him whom the heaven of heavens and their hosts, whom cherubim and seraphim praise together in heavenly harmony, and upon whom angels desire to look [1 Peter 1]. [Col. 1074D]

It happened once, when this blessed man of whom we speak had shared in the fasting and prayer of the sacred days of Lent, and, with Ruth the Moabite, had dipped the morsel of pious action in the vinegar of salutary compunction [Ruth 2], that the most sacred day of the Lord’s Resurrection dawned. As the brethren celebrated the solemn vigils with the utmost devotion, as the greatness of such a day required, he opened the bosom of his inward meditation and began to consider more closely the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection. Burning with a feeling of compassion, he was wholly dissolved in tears.

And behold: after the second lesson had been read, as the community sang the responsory *Angelus Domini* (“The Angel of the Lord”), the Lord Jesus Christ, who had kindled the fire of devotion in his heart, suddenly appeared before the brother as he watched and wept. He stood before him in the middle of the choir, stretching out His hands as if showing them to him. In His most blessed palms the places of the nails appeared most clearly [Col. 1075A], so that blood seemed to flow from the fresh wounds themselves.

At the sight of the Lord, the brother rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; but, astonished and as though beside himself, he did not know what he ought to do in the short time available. He wished to spring into the middle of the choir and grasp the Savior’s feet, but embarrassment and reverence for the community held him back, lest he be thought mad. For he did not know whether the appearing Lord was seen by himself alone or equally by the others. He wept copiously; his heart melted within him through tender feeling because of the immeasurable sweetness of the love of Him whom he beheld.

This appearance of the Lord lasted until, in the responsory then being sung, the words *iam surrexit, venite et videte*—“He has now risen; come and see”—had been fully sung with the same deliberateness with which that holy community customarily sang them. Who can fittingly explain how much he profited from that vision, and how, when every movement and every affection of his soul had been refreshed and renewed, he wholly blazed with love for Him whom he had seen? Only the giver and recipient know how joyful were the days he thereafter spent with his Beloved, crying out with the Bride not so much in spoken words as in the affections of his heart: “I have found Him whom my soul loves; I have held Him and will not let Him go” [Song of Songs 3]; and with the Patriarch Jacob: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” [Genesis 32].

Since, in keeping humility, he sought to extend further the foot of confidence, so that, according to the divine promise, every place on which his foot trod might become his, he deserved to be enriched with grace of still more excellent gifts. For he who, as has been said, had beheld with blessed eyes the most sweet humanity of Christ our Lord was also admitted, by the wondrous condescension of God’s grace, to contemplate the eternal mystery of the indivisible Trinity, insofar as this was possible for a human being still enclosed in mortal flesh. [Col. 1075C]

For it happened on the holy day of Pentecost, while the brethren were zealously celebrating the sacred vigil and were already singing the divine hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise You, O God”—in which the praise foreshadowing evangelical grace is figured. The entire community sang, bowing down in honor of the Holy Trinity as was customary, the mystical words by which one God is proclaimed and adored under the distinction of three persons: *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth*—“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Hosts.”

During that very bowing, the aforesaid servant of God began—not investigating, nor striving to break into the secret entrusted to faith, but in reverent fear, trembling, and wonder—to meditate in the simplicity of his heart on how lofty and incomprehensible was the mystery of so great a majesty: a mystery to know which is life, and eternal life; according to which to be wise is wisdom without error; in which to delight is pleasure without comparison; to which to be conformed is to recover the likeness of God that we lost in Adam; to serve which is to reign; without whose grace all nations are as though they were not, so are they before it; and which in the life to come will be for all the saints peace surpassing all understanding and joy without interruption or passage of time. [Col. 1075D]

When that act of bowing in divine reverence had been made and the brother rose again, the intellectual eyes of his mind were suddenly opened. As though entirely carried outside himself, he saw a vision of the Trinity, which is God, glorious and wondrous; and he understood it to be more marvelous, worthy, and excellent than all the visitations by which he had ever deserved to be visited by the Lord.

O happy soul, in which the fire of divine love had so burned away the dross of sin and rust of negligence that it deserved, in this corruptible life, in some measure to taste beforehand and foretaste that sweetness, that blessedness, which the Lord reserves as a reward for His elect. Blessed likewise was that most blessed Father Bernard, under whose discipline disciples of such perfection are known to have flourished at Clairvaux.

[Col. 1076A] Thus gladdened and strengthened by such visitations and consolations from the Lord, that true monk devoted himself to daily lamentations, sighing and longing to lay down the burden of corruptible life, so that, contemplating in its own purity the face of the Lord which he had beheld through a mirror and in an enigma, he might become one spirit with Him. When asked, for God’s honor and the edification of his neighbor, to disclose some of the matters in which he had been visited by the Lord, he did not readily consent, fearing indeed that this might perhaps displease the Lord. Yet, constrained by many entreaties, he revealed with trembling and profound humility the things we have mentioned and certain others. Although we know these to be great, because our purpose hastens on to other matters, we have omitted them for the sake of brevity.

Yet he would by no means consent to explain the manner of the visitation in which he had deserved to see the blessed Trinity, who is God, asserting that he would never presume to reveal it to anyone, unless perhaps it were granted him to know the divine will on the matter. What he did wish to disclose, he made known on the condition that it should be kept in silence until his death; and this was carefully observed. Having completed twenty-six years in the Cistercian Order—which in his youth he had so greatly abhorred—he died at the age of forty. As he had lived in sincere devotion, so, too, when released from the flesh, he died a happy death; and, “made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many years, for his soul was pleasing to God” (Wisdom 4).

Now it delights us, in fear and exultation alike, to cry out with the Psalmist and say to the Lord: “I will sing to thee, O Lord, of mercy and judgment”; for “neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains; for God is judge: he humbleth this man and exalteth that man” (Psalms 100 and 74). For behold, that master of whom we spoke above, who undertook the work of piety not under the guidance of grace but of presumption, and had tried to set his hand to mighty things, like seed sown upon [Col. 1076B] rock believed for a time, but in the time of temptation quickly withered away. But this man, whose faith and holiness we have described, though in some measure resisting and reluctant, was taken up by mother Grace. Not content merely to admit him into the common company of God’s servants, she also deigned, after cleansing him from negligence, to raise him with a few others to the summit of perfection and divine contemplation. Therefore, just as “blessed is he whom thou hast chosen and received, O Lord: he shall dwell in thy courts” (Psalm 64), so surely all who forsake thee “shall be put to shame; those who depart from thee shall be written in the earth” (Jeremiah 17).

## Chapter XVII. How the eminent man Arnulph was converted through St Bernard

(See above, *The First Life of St Bernard*, book VII, col. 434, down to the words: “that is, that he might observe the Order in satisfaction for all his sins?” Here receive what Mabillon did not give in his extracts.) His earnestness in penance surely reproves our lukewarmness and negligence. We too have undertaken this same Order as penance for our sins, and yet not only live lukewarmly and negligently, but even blush not, on account of some trivial indisposition, to abandon the brothers’ vigils or to enter the infirmary. Yet this servant of God would not consent to enter the infirmary unless his sickness bore the sentence of death; moreover, though at times suffering severe weakness, he devoutly remained at the vigils of God’s service.

Irrevocable time flies—nothing is more precious, yet nothing is held more cheaply by us. While we avoid the punishment undertaken in this present life for the Lord’s sake, we incur it a hundredfold in the life to come. But if anyone pleads the weakness of his flesh, let him know that it is written that those who fear God lack nothing, and that the Prophet was young and grew old, yet did not see the righteous forsaken (Psalms 33 and 36). For who has hoped in the Lord and been confounded? Who has remained in [Col. 1077A] his commandments and been forsaken? That this may be made clearer not only by the testimonies of Scripture but also by the examples of the Fathers who preceded us, we append two miracles of God’s grace, so that through them both our lukewarmness may be convicted and our weakness strengthened for the struggle of the contest.

## Chapter XVIII. Of the monk who was freed from severe headache by the power of Christ’s sacraments

A brother named Peter, later to become abbot of Clairvaux, while in his youth striving in the observance of the holy Order to offer himself daily as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, began to suffer a most grievous pain in his head. For all who desire to live piously in Christ endure the persecutions of the enemy; and God, who works all things for the salvation of the elect, permitted this. This strong soldier of Christ bore the suffering patiently, always striving to give thanks amid pain and to restrain from murmuring the viper of self-will.

Although he desired with the prophet that “rottenness might enter into his bones,” so that he might deserve to rest in the day of tribulation (Habakkuk 3), he was nevertheless more troubled in mind because his spirit, most ready for every arduous exercise of virtue, was unable, owing to the weakness of the flesh, to follow his desire. One Sunday night, while attending the sacred vigils and feeling himself more sharply afflicted than usual by the said ailment, he thought of leaving the choir and going to rest. But immediately, by God’s inspiration, he reconsidered and resolved to endure for the Lord’s sake until the first hour of daylight, since on that day he was to partake of the undefiled mysteries of the precious Body and Blood of Christ.

When the first hour had passed, although the intensity of the pain had not ceased, he nevertheless resolved to bear it and not leave the community until after the principal Mass, so that he might receive holy Communion. And when, now about to communicate, he approached the altar step and, bending his knees, sought there with most devout humility the customary pardon, behold: suddenly something like a huge mass of lead fell from the crown of his head. Passing down through the middle of his forehead and striking the pavement, it made no small crash. He plainly felt the shock and fall of that mass, though he saw nothing; astonished at so strange an event, he was greatly amazed.

O wonderful mercy of our Redeemer! Because this brother felt most grievous pains and yet, out of reverence for Christ’s sacraments, was as though he did not feel them, as soon as he received those sacraments in faithful devotion, he recovered from all his former sickness at that very hour. He was so completely healed that he suffered no further discomfort from it thereafter. Nor was he ungrateful for God’s grace: he advanced so greatly in holy religious life that, having first received the office of pastoral care at Igny and later at Clairvaux, he adorned the title of abbot by his life and conduct. Leading his subjects by the way of true humility, he was the good fragrance of Christ in every place. [Col. 1077B]

## Chapter XIX. Of the brother to whom the Blessed Virgin Mary gave a heavenly ration in a vision

There was likewise at Clairvaux a monk who, though a man of good will, was physically delicate and infirm, and therefore excessively curious and superstitious in regulating his food and obtaining remedies. But the merciful Lord, who is accustomed compassionately to correct those who err, wished to bring him back to the way of truth. In order that he might know and understand how salutarily Scripture urges us to cast all our care upon Him, because He cares for us (1 Peter 5), He deigned to grant this simply erring man a visitation in the following manner.

The brother saw in a vision of the night that the whole body of brothers was hastening to church, as though to celebrate the Lauds of divine service. At the door of the church stood she who is at once so humble and so exalted: Mary, the gracious Virgin, Mother of Mercy. Carrying what seemed to be a little box of precious electuary, she graciously gave, with her own hand, a spoonful from it to each brother entering the oratory; and with wondrous sweetness she refreshed those who tasted it.

At this sight the brother rejoiced greatly, thinking to himself that he too ought to become a participant, without hindrance, in that heavenly nourishment. But when he came to the hand of that most merciful provider, the most kindly dissembling and truly gentle Virgin repelled him, saying: “Do you need our medicine? Are you not a wise physician, and do you not yourself carefully attend to your own care? Go then, go, and use your medicines as you please, for I care for those who cast their care upon the Lord and upon my Son.”

When he heard this, he blushed; and, asking forgiveness, he promised her that he would no longer concern himself with himself, but would commit the whole care of his life to God and to her. At this promise, the general refuge of all Christians—but the particular protector of her special servants, the Cistercian brothers—most graciously granted pardon, accepting his satisfaction, and bestowed upon him the nourishment of the healing ration. Having tasted the blessing of the heavenly antidote, the brother immediately recovered from his delicacy and infirmity. Renouncing all medicines and more refined foods, he adopted the common fare. Thus, with God’s grace cooperating, he soon put on beauty and strength together with health of both body and soul. [Col. 1077C]

Where now are those brothers who seem to follow the schools of Hippocrates more than the school of Christ? Excessively attached to the health of their mortal flesh, they employ the whole summer, with all their attention, in seeking or gathering every sort of cheap wild herb or root. Yet in winter they are no less busy drying, crushing, grinding, and combining these things; and, though they will not obtain the effect of medicine, they hurl themselves into the guilt of self-will alone—a self-ownership found to be more dangerous. Let them learn, I pray, let them learn from the examples above to trust more in the Lord than in Galen, to hope more in the Queen of Heaven than in the herbs of the earth. Let them know with complete certainty that, at the dreadful judgment of the just Judge, God, they will be judged not concerning bodily constitution but concerning their profession; there, too-late repentance will make them wish that they had cared more for their souls rather than spent their whole lives uselessly occupied in seeking the health of their flesh.

## Chapter XX. Of the venerable old man Achard, formerly master of novices at Clairvaux

An old man named Achard, noble by birth but nobler in the dignity of his way of life, had charge of the novices at Clairvaux. He was powerful in the word of edification and consolation. Even in the vigor of his youth, under the command and mission of his abbot, blessed Bernard, he had been a devout founder and builder of many monasteries.

Now a veteran and an old soldier discharged from service, appointed to train recruits, he vigorously fulfilled his office. From what long experience had taught him, he formed still-untrained minds by daily exhortations against the threefold cord—flesh, world, and devil—which is not easily broken. By examples both ancient and recent he also made them more watchful against vices. We shall accordingly relate some matters, as we heard them from his own mouth.

When Achard himself was still a novice, the venerable Abbot Bernard came one day to console his novices, as he often did. When he had finished speaking, he drew the said Achard aside with two other novices and warned them in a prophetic spirit, saying: “It will happen that this novice”—and he designated one by name—“will secretly depart before tomorrow. Therefore watch and be ready, and do not allow him to escape in flight with the plunder. And if the wretch goes out from us, because he was not of us, nevertheless keep the spoils for yourselves, since they are ours.”

On hearing this, they were astonished and silently awaited the outcome. In the deep of night, two of them saw the fugitive soundly asleep in bed and then themselves began to sleep also. Their eyes were heavy, for the spirit of error was deceiving them. But Achard, because he most certainly believed that a word uttered by the holy Father could not prove void, manfully resisted the spirit of drowsiness that sorely troubled him. Now rubbing his forehead, now his temples; now pulling at the hair of his head and beard; now rubbing his hands and face; now rousing himself by walking from place to place, he finally overcame the deceptive sleep that oppressed him.

As the time approached for the signal to be rung for vigils, behold, two Ethiopians, gigantic in appearance and clothed in blackest cowls, visibly entered through the door of the house. The one who went first carried a roasted hen on a spit. A huge serpent was fixed by head and tail upon the very spit and encircled the hen on either side. Bearing this dish, they approached the bed of the false novice and held the steaming hen to the sleeper’s nostrils. He immediately awoke; and the demons departed, having displayed by this terrible visible sign what they had been invisibly doing in his heart.

When the wretch awoke, he did not awaken like Jacob from the sleep of contemplation, but like a base apostate from the sleep of deception. He immediately rose, burdened himself with clothing, and went out after the demons. Coming to the door of the cupboard in the cloister, he tried by his contrivances to break the fastening and take books away with him. But Achard swiftly awakened his companions and indicated by signs and gestures the apostate’s prophesied flight. [Col. 1077D]

[Col. 1079C] Thus all together they pursued the departing man and found him shaking the bolt of the door. When that wicked man perceived them, he immediately leapt away. Rushing at a headlong run through the gates of the orchard, he was at last stopped by the enclosure of the walls and brought back. When day came, since he was unrepentant in evil and would not return to his senses—for he had already been given over to a reprobate mind—he was finally dismissed to go to his own place. That same day he was seized by the devil, fell into madness, and did not cease raging until his death.

The venerable old man Achard also confessed to us that, at the beginning of his conversion, he endured many battles and scourges from demons and saw many of their apparitions. For often, while he was chanting and praying in church, they lit before him an abundance of lights, as if candles and lamps, which immediately disappeared as emptiness at the invocation of Christ’s name. On one occasion the devil appeared to him and fought with him in a gladiatorial contest, as in a wrestling-school. He inflicted repeated blows and wounds upon the devil and received them in turn. At last he subdued the demon, smashed his head, and dashed out his brains. As he dragged him by the hair, he held in his hand a portion of the shattered head, torn away with flesh and bones. Immediately such an intolerable stench issued from it that it seemed to surpass the measure of human endurance. When, in horror and loathing, he shook it from his hand to a distance, the foul monster that had appeared immediately vanished, though it left the traces of its uncleanness deeply impressed. For throughout the space of a year such a stench continually issued from that same hand that, in anguish of heart, he could scarcely bring it to his mouth or near his nostrils.

While this servant of God was at one time staying in the regions of Germany to establish a monastery situated in the territory of Trier and called Claustrum, it was divinely granted to him to see and speak with a holy man—a man truly rich, a great solitary. For a long time this man had wandered naked through mountains and forests in those parts, without roof or clothing, for Christ’s name, sustaining the life of his mortal body upon wild herbs and their roots. He bore with unbelievable patience the heat of summer and the most severe cold of winter. Thus once, when the winter frost grew more intense than usual and much snow fell from the clouds, he had nowhere to flee from the snow and cold. Lying naked upon the ground, he was wholly covered by a considerable thickness of snow, and no sign of his body appeared there except a small wand-like stream of steaming breath issuing from his mouth, which slightly melted the snow lying upon it. Lord Achard used to recount to his novices the admirable virtues and patience surpassing the measure of human frailty of this blessed man; in this way he greatly strengthened them in the rudiments of their training and powerfully kindled in them the love of virtue.

## Chapter XXI. Of Lord Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, later bishop of Sorres

[Col. 1080B]

Lord Geoffrey, of holy memory, once a monk of Clairvaux and later bishop of the Church of Sorres in Sardinia, before being promoted to the episcopate, was once in the choir at Clairvaux, earnestly fulfilling to the Lord the vows of his lips with the other brothers. He deserved to behold with blessed eyes the following vision, as we received the account from him.

He saw a glorious and splendid procession coming from the northern side of the oratory, as though from the cemetery. Passing before the sanctuary, it proceeded by a straight path toward the infirmary. In this procession appeared acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests. Arranged in their several orders, seven by seven, they went in fitting order, some before others. The acolytes wore white stoles and carried individual candles in their hands, though these seemed more like fire than wax candles. Precious tunics adorned the subdeacons, shining dalmatics the deacons, and splendid garments of pure silk the priests themselves. Each bore in his hands the fitting vessels of his ministry.

After them came a great company of white-clad persons, likewise arranged and proceeding reverently. Last of all followed the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, accompanied on right and left by the blessed apostles Peter and John. This most merciful *Theotokos* shone with such beauty and brightness of face and attire that the whole basilica gleamed from the radiance issuing from her. Meanwhile the form that revealed these things spoke in the heart of the beholder and said: “This is the Queen of Heaven; this is the Lady of Angels.” Passing thus solemnly, as we have said, before the step of the sanctuary, they finally went out of the oratory through the door that leads toward the infirmary, and so vanished from the beholder’s sight.

But in that infirmary an old man, venerable and a priest of holy conduct, named Tescelin, had long lain ill. Like an obedient son he had most patiently borne the scourges of the loving Father. At that time, placed in his final extremity, he was struggling in death; shortly afterward he exchanged the bitterness of temporal life for the sweetness of everlasting life. Therefore Geoffrey, the man of God who had seen these things, firmly believed that such a procession had appeared as a sign of that man’s passing and blessedness.

O how sublime are the good things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him! (1 Corinthians 2). For if the soul that fears God, departing from the body, is met with such splendid spiritual pomp, with what rejoicing, we think, and with what joy will it exult in possession of the heavenly homeland, where it shall be filled with the sweetest vision of its Creator! [Col. 1080C]

## Chapter XXII. Further visions of the same servant of God, Geoffrey

[Col. 1081A]

On another occasion, while the same servant of God was standing in church with the other brothers to chant, he plainly saw an unclean spirit, in the likeness of an ape, passing through the middle of the choir. When the ridiculous beast came and stood before him, it looked at him with a scornful and contemptuous eye and mocked him for some time with its nostrils spread wide. After it had passed him and finally gone out of the choir, it appeared no more.

At one time this blessed man was ill and suffered grievous discomfort in the region of his throat. The illness grew day by day, eventually becoming chronic and nearly despaired of by physicians. He was especially distressed in spirit because the arteries having been constricted by the disease, he had lost the strength to chant and sing in church. Therefore, turning to blessed Bernard, he prayed day and night with many tears that he might deserve to recover the gift of singing. The compassionate father, moved by his prayers and tears, appeared to him in a vision. Touching and blessing the painful place with his hand, he made the sign of the cross upon it. When the man of God awoke, he found himself healed, wonderfully recovered his ability to sing, and thereafter suffered no impediment from that illness.

At another time it happened that a spiritual brother, whom he loved especially in Christ, fell gravely ill. The illness was extremely severe, so that he was thought to be dying. The said man, wasting away with excessive grief, began, to prove himself a true friend, to persist earnestly in tearful prayers. For the recovery of his beloved he stood “in the breach” before the Lord. But while he was continually laboring in his groaning, someone stood beside him in a vision and said: “Behold, the brother for whom you are so afflicted will be restored to health; yet another whom you love with equal spiritual love is about to depart in his place.” And so it occurred. For the one who had seemed near death recovered, while at that same time there died a certain venerable and holy old man called Renald of Cluny, whom Geoffrey likewise loved in Christ with wonderful affection. [Col. 1081B]

Furthermore, being excessively concerned for his deceased mother, and since his eyes shed long streams of tears for her—he had indeed been given much grace of tears—he urgently begged the Lord to deign to reveal to him whether she was still undergoing punishments or had already received the rest of pardon. After he had long wearied himself in this supplication, a voice at last came to him divinely, saying: “Why do you seek to extort by importunate prayers what is not due to your knowledge? Only pray for your own, and they shall be saved.”

## Chapter XXIII. How it was shown to him by revelation that he would become a bishop; and of his precious death at Clairvaux

[Col. 1081D] The man of God, Geoffrey, was once at prayer when, behold, a certain venerable figure appeared to him in a vision and placed a gold ring on his finger, a presage, that is, of the pontifical dignity soon to come. For in that same year, as he himself informed us, he was appointed to the episcopate of the Church of Sorres. He governed it vigorously through seven years and, preserving his own life in all purity, nobly honored his ministry and left posterity a worthy example of holiness.

When the end of his calling drew near—known to God alone—he left Sardinia and came to visit Clairvaux, whose son he was and in which he had most earnestly wished to be buried. Seeing it from afar, he raised his eyes and sighed toward heaven, praying the Lord with all his heart that, if he were to die within three years—for he had resolved always to visit the same house at least once within such a span—the Lord would never again permit him to be separated from it, lest perhaps he might die elsewhere and be deprived of the burial he desired.

He entered the monastery dear to him and remained there in health for some time, while all the brothers rejoiced at the presence of so great a guest. At last, however, he was seized by an acute illness, was sick for several days, and, as the disease worsened, came to his end. After he had been anointed with holy oil and fortified with the viaticum of Christ’s sacraments, at that same hour—indeed, almost at that same moment—to the wonder of all, he fell asleep in the Lord. He passed away about midnight on the feast of the Dedication of the church of Clairvaux.

The venerable abbot of that monastery, who knew very well the purity of his conscience, was closing the eyes of the now lifeless body. With great devoutness of faith he cried out: “O sweet and venerable Father, may almighty God grant that I may come as soon as possible into your company.” While rendering the office of commendation for his sacred funeral, he was moved by such tender feeling that he could not restrain the tears that burst forth, and moved even hard-hearted persons to weeping.

When this holy priest first began to fall ill, it was revealed concerning him to one of the brothers of that monastery that he was soon to depart. Then, a few days later, while that brother was attending the vigils of divine service, he saw in the spirit a bed carefully prepared with soft cushions and suitably adorned with snow-white coverings. It was reserved for that bishop, evidently signifying the repose of eternal happiness to which he would shortly be taken.

On the same night in which he died, after his body had been placed in the church, when the signal was rung for the solemn vigils of the Dedication, the said brother awoke and immediately began to think of the deceased bishop. At once a voice sounded in his ears, speaking of the dead servant of God and saying: “Behold, now, from the beginning of this signal, all the saints of God receive him into their fellowship.” Hearing this voice, the brother rejoiced greatly. He rose, came into the choir, and stood chanting with the others, continually turning over in his mind the glorification of the blessed man. [Col. 1082B]

As the morning Lauds were celebrated, he looked and saw, behold, an abundance of lights divinely kindled upon the walls of the church around the deceased bishop for about the space of one hour, so numerous that they could not be counted.

Thus, beholding with bodily eyes the light of spiritual brightness, he was deeply moved. Giving thanks to God for all that he had seen and heard, he said inwardly in the joy of his heart: “O Lord God of hosts, blessed are all who hope in thee” (Psalm 83). Truly blessed is this holy man whom thou hast chosen, O Lord, and received: “he shall dwell in thy courts” (Psalm 64). For I believe and trust that he is now worthy to be counted among thy saints and elect, since, walking by the way of humility in this present age, he strove faithfully to obey thy commandments.

When two months had elapsed after the burial of the blessed man, the same brother was in the choir, keeping vigil and chanting at vigils, when suddenly he entered into ecstasy of mind. Behold, the blessed bishop appeared to him, putting on priestly vestments and, as it were, preparing to celebrate Mass, while the brother assisted him by folding back the chasuble over his arms. At that very hour this verse was being sung in church: “And I shall go in unto the altar of God, unto God who giveth joy to my youth” (Psalm 42).

Having thus briefly recorded the life and death of this holy man, it is fitting here to add a miracle worthy of narration, which the same servant of God joyfully affirmed that he had seen. The bishop had resolved that a certain old and ruined basilica of his should be pulled down and restored to a better condition. When he ordered the altar itself to be demolished in his presence, a rough and ancient little chest was discovered in it, containing relics of saints. Among those relics the Body of the Lord had been placed. It was found so sound and whole, so clean and white, and utterly free from all corruption, as though it had only just been deposited there. Certainly no one was found in that land who remembered having seen either the construction or the consecration of that church or altar. [Col. 1083A]

At the sight of so great a miracle, all who were present rejoiced greatly; strengthened in faith, they glorified God, recognizing that it was indeed the most sacred Body of the Lord, of which it is truly written: “Thou wilt not give thy holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15).

The same blessed bishop departed from this world in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1178, on the third Ides of November [11 November], and was buried with fitting honor beside the venerable Godfrey, formerly bishop of Langres. Under blessed Bernard, Godfrey had fulfilled the office of prior at Clairvaux; then, raised thence to the height of episcopal dignity, he honored the ministry entrusted to him in many ways by living holily and religiously. [Col. 1083B]

## Chapter XXIV. Of Lord Baldwin, monk of Clairvaux, later bishop of Pisa

Among the shoots flourishing in the richness of heavenly grace which the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts—that is, the Church of Clairvaux—sent forth to be transplanted beside many waters, that is, to be raised in pontifical honor over the peoples of diverse regions, Baldwin shone forth wondrously as a special glory of his native soil. Following the teaching of the most reverend Father Bernard, he despised all the pomp and pleasures of the world. Dying to the world itself, he began to live at Clairvaux, and rejoiced that he had preferred the true riches of voluntary poverty to the enticements of deceptive riches.

For, learning from the Apostle to become foolish so that he might become wise (1 Corinthians 3), he rejected riches which exhaust rather than fill a person, and embraced with the whole desire of his mind those riches which work in him an immeasurable weight of glory in eternal blessedness. Having become an imitator of the most perfect monks, he learned to ascend from the lower spring, in which sins are bewailed, to the upper spring, in which one sighs with unutterable groanings for the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Already worthy to live not for himself alone but also to benefit many others unto salvation by word and example, he was called by God to receive the archbishopric of the Church of Pisa, the metropolitan see of Tuscany.

Having attained the eminence of this great dignity, he shone with so great a light of spiritual wisdom and exercised his office with such authority and freedom of spirit, while showing such gentleness and humility that he proved himself a true monk at the summit of the episcopate. Not only the Cistercian Order, but all the faithful throughout Italy rejoiced exceedingly and gave thanks to God, who had granted in their time this most splendid pillar and immovable support to His holy Church. [Col. 1083C]

But since we lament that in human affairs nothing can be blessed in every respect, it happened, at the devil’s instigation, that on his account a grave and dangerous war arose between the peoples of Pisa and Lucca. Even after his death, inflamed by factional strife, it continued for several years and could scarcely at last be restored to the bond of peace and concord. What occasioned this conflict is of no concern here. This alone we say: as divine revelation disclosed, that war was harmful and penal to the soul of so great a bishop.

Some time after this blessed prelate’s falling asleep, there was in the island of Sardinia a priest of honorable life, who presided there over a parish church. That church stood outside the town and at a distance from every human habitation. [Col. 1083D]

One day, therefore, while he was celebrating Mass, at the time of communion [Col. 1084A] he found the sacred Host upon the corporal broken and divided of itself into two parts, though he had previously consecrated it whole and uninjured. When he saw this, troubled and anxious with fear and amazement, he completed the sacrifice. When the service was ended and the others had been dismissed, he remained there alone. Grieved by the sign which had occurred, he went outside and stood on the eastern side of the same church, with his back against the wall of the building and his face turned eastward.

As he stood thus for some time, thinking fearfully and anxiously about what had happened to him, his spirit groaned within him, and suddenly the hairs of his flesh stood on end. Then, as some external power, I know not what, rushed upon him, he began to be held fast and constrained so that he could by no means move from that spot. And behold, with open eyes he saw innumerable crowds, mounted and on foot, passing before him at a rapid pace. Among them were persons of both sexes, of different ages and [Col. 1084B] conditions; and among them he recognized many whom he had formerly known alive in the flesh.

One of them, formerly known and dear to the priest, approached him and, halting, began to speak familiarly with him. When the priest asked what that infinite multitude of crowds was, and what it was doing, the other replied: “They are the souls of people released from the flesh. All, according to the diversity of their faults, are subjected to various punishments, and thus continually wander far and wide through the world in their recurring course. Some of them are to be delivered more quickly, some more slowly; but the punishments of some remain incapable of release.”

While he was saying this, the priest looked and saw the aforesaid bishop passing before him with downcast face, as though patiently bearing the sentence of the strict Judge, and saying to the hostile power which for a time insulted him, with the prophet: “Rejoice not over me, my enemy, because I have fallen: I shall arise. When I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be my light” (Micah 7).

When he saw him, the priest was struck with profound amazement and cried out in the terror of great [Col. 1084C] astonishment: “Woe is me, a wretched sinner! What is this that I see? Is this our lord Baldwin, formerly Archbishop of Pisa, who was taken from the monastery of Clairvaux?”

The one speaking to him answered: “It is indeed he.”

And the priest said: “Then has a monk of such profession and a bishop of such perfection been assigned to punishments—he whom we hoped was already rejoicing in heaven with the angels?”

The other replied: “Know certainly, and do not doubt at all, that he is truly holy, a pontiff of exalted merit, and that great shall be his glory before God. But because war has now long been waged on his account between the peoples of Pisa and Lucca, his rest is deferred until the discord between them is brought back to peace.”

After this there appeared to the same priest a column of immense radiance, whose brightness seemed to shine beyond the ordinary power of the sun, extending from heaven down to earth [Col. 1084D]; and through it a soul, led by an angel, was hastening to the stars. When the priest asked what this was, the other answered: “This is the soul of Constantine, formerly judge and lord of Torres. For nine years she has stood, from the day of his death until now, beneath the eaves of his house, continually exposed to winds, rain, and cold, and there has paid the penalties for his transgressions. But because he was merciful and generous toward the poor, rendered judgment for those who suffered injury, and moreover left the body having confessed and repented of the evils which he had committed, he has obtained mercy from God. Therefore on this day he deserves to be freed from all evils and, filled with every good, to be admitted into eternal blessedness.”

That priest saw and heard these things, and many others, concerning the secrets of the other life. Among them it was also said that he himself would die in that same year; and his death, which followed, proved this true. Thus almighty [Col. 1085A] God wished it to be known that the soul of His beloved pontiff, though righteous and holy, yet darkened by however slight a rust of sin, could not enter the kingdom of purity or behold the splendor of the noonday light in which the heavenly Bridegroom rests, until his guilt had been expiated and peace restored among the disputants, he might deserve to hear from that same Bridegroom: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved; you are altogether beautiful, and there is no stain in you. Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (Song of Songs 4).

What, then, are we to suppose was signified to us by the division of the sacred Host, except that such revelations take place for the warning and correction of mortals only by the nod and will of our Redeemer—especially when something of this kind happens to be seen by religious persons?

## Chapter XXV. Concerning Lord Eskil, formerly Archbishop of the Danes, afterwards a monk of Clairvaux

The illustrious man Eskil, to be named with every reverence [Col. 1085B], formerly Archbishop of the Danes and legate of the Apostolic See in the northern islands, but afterwards a humble monk of the Cistercian Order and professed member of the monastery of Clairvaux, when still an adolescent of about twelve years, was sent by his parents into Saxony for the sake of study. There, in Saxony, that celebrated Church of Hildesheim was then flourishing and was frequented by a renowned concourse of clerics from diverse regions.

After staying there for some time, he fell into a most serious illness. Wasting away under a long infirmity, he was at last despaired of by the physicians, and arrangements were accordingly made for him to be anointed with the holy oil. While priests and other faithful persons stood around his bed for this purpose, he suddenly fell into agony and was deprived of every function of limb and sense, so that he was considered nearly dead.

Released from the senses of the flesh, he was led in spirit to a certain dwelling, wholly inwardly like a burning furnace. As [Col. 1085C] he drew nearer and wished to examine it more closely, a burst of fiery vapor caught the unwary youth and immediately dragged him unwilling into that flame-belching furnace. When he at once began to burn, and thought that nothing but eternal fire remained for him, behold, by God’s mercy there appeared to him on one side of the lodging an opening, like a narrow passage, leading from doorway to doorway, which also seemed free from flames. Seeing it and encouraged by hope of escape, he crawled with all the effort he could to that place of coolness. Making his way through it toward the door, he quickly went out and fled, panting and trembling before the devouring fire.

Soon he found a royal and spacious palace; entering it, he saw there the Queen of Heaven, Lady of the Angels, shining with wondrous countenance and raiment and seated upon a throne of glory. Trembling and breathless, he approached her and urgently begged her to have mercy upon him. She immediately looked upon him disdainfully [Col. 1085D] and addressed him threateningly, asking how he had dared to appear in her presence; she commanded him to depart as quickly as possible and return to be tormented in the fire.

Among those standing by the Mother of Mercy appeared three venerable men: one was the bishop of that city, another the dean, and the third likewise some person holding an office in the same church.

When the aforesaid youth saw and recognized these men, he tearfully begged them to deign to intercede for him with that most gracious Lady. As they did so most devoutly, that most merciful dissimulator replied to them: “What is this, that you presume to ask on behalf of this most worthless young man, who is unworthy of my regard? For this perverse and fickle boy has never once offered me my salutation.”

When they begged that, in her accustomed mercy, she would forgive the sins and ignorances of his youth if he promised to amend himself henceforth, [Col. 1086A] the trembling youth approached her again, beseeching her and saying: “Have mercy on me, most gracious Lady; have mercy on me, restorer of the human race. Do not close against me, wretched as I am, the inexhaustible bowels of your mercy; for from now on and forever I am ready to serve you and to venerate you above all things after God. If my father knew of this calamity of mine, he would gladly spend the greatest weights of gold for my deliverance.”

As he uttered such words in a mournful voice, the most blessed Virgin, true Mother of Mercy, looked upon him with serene countenance and said: “What then? Do you think that you can redeem yourself before me for an adequate price? You might perhaps appease me in this way, if you paid me a fitting price for your redemption.”

Then, greatly cheered by these words, he approached more confidently and said: “Yes indeed, most merciful Lady, I shall redeem myself most fully; and whatever your graciousness commands me, I shall do most willingly. Only be favorable to me, and do not send me any longer [Col. 1086B] to be tormented in that fire.”

The Queen of Virgins answered him: “I therefore wish you not to neglect to render to me five modii, one from each of the five kinds of grain.”

On hearing this, he gladly accepted and eagerly answered: “What you impose is dear and most pleasing to me, O dearest Lady; and I shall give into your granary a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.”

When he had firmly promised this upon his faith, and had given the aforesaid intercessors as sureties, he was dismissed to return to the world of human beings. Restored to himself, he immediately opened his eyes and, having recovered the use of speech, rose and sat up in his bed. At once he burst into rejoicing and began to cry aloud in great joy: “Blessed be God! I have been delivered, and I shall burn no more.”

All who were present, seeing that youth recalled from the gate of death crying out thus and exulting for joy, were greatly amazed [Col. 1086C] and asked him the reason for such happiness. For a long time he could say nothing else but: “Thanks be to God. I shall not burn; I shall not burn.” After repeating this often, he finally turned to them and related in order what had happened to him and what he had seen.

One of them, a good and learned man, took care to speak privately with and instruct the youth, who was uncertain about the vision. He said: “Know beforehand that you will become a man of great name and will attain a rank of highest dignity in the Church. When, by God’s favor, you have obtained it, you must, in honor of God and of the holy Virgin Mother, build five monasteries of different Orders from your own resources, in which, according to the meaning of the measure set before you, there shall be at least twelve persons continually serving in divine worship.”

On hearing this, he was silent for the moment; but he remained continually concerned as to what outcome the matter would have. Moreover, [Col. 1086D] in the vision it was made known to him that the three venerable men who had interceded for him, while they still lived in the flesh, would depart from the world in that same year. Their death, which followed shortly thereafter, likewise proved this true.

In the course of time, as the aforesaid youth increased alike in age and wisdom and had become an excellent man, he was appointed by the Lord to govern the Church of Lund, which is regarded as the metropolitan see of Denmark. Having at length ascended the summit of the dignity prophesied to him, he immediately knew that the time had come to fulfill his vow. Under the figure of the five kinds of grain, according to his interpretation of the vow, he had vowed to the Queen of Heaven that he would found five monasteries of different Orders.

Finding the opportunity, he took care to summon from the remote regions of Gaul, where he had learned the fountainhead of religious life lay, not merely five but still more communities of spiritual profession [Col. 1087A]. Among them he secured two communities of the Cistercian Order: one from the very house of Cîteaux and another from Clairvaux. He planted them in the best places of his land like fruitful vines bringing forth the wine of righteousness.

For, in order perfectly to redeem himself and to render, as he had promised, a good and overflowing measure to his most gracious deliverer, he was unwilling to be satisfied with the foundation of five monasteries; but he strove to build others and still others, from gifts both his own and those of other faithful people. He also labored to root out entirely the rites of paganism, with which that land was still in great part imbued, to shape all people beneficially by the practices of Christian discipline, and to strike down the proud and contemptuous with the sword of vengeance.

Thus, armed with zeal for justice, he strove to eliminate every harmful and superstitious thing and to provide for his people whatever would benefit the salvation of their souls. Thus we may think that, in all the times before him, no bishop had sat in that metropolitan see [Col. 1087B] who had borne so much fruit in the Church of God as he did.

And the Lord, for whose honor and love he did all these things, took care to give to his voice the voice of power; those whom he bound in the bonds of anathema, God Himself punished by dreadful death. Thus a certain rich and powerful adulterer, whom the venerable priest had publicly excommunicated at the Lord’s Supper, was cruelly suffocated by an evil spirit on the most holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, together with the adulteress and two sons born of the adultery, and was dragged down to hell for eternal punishment.

He venerated Saint Bernard, the most reverend abbot of Clairvaux, with a singular affection and worshipped him with a single-minded devotion, although Bernard was far distant from him. Nor was he content merely to see him in his sons when he had built a new monastery and obtained from him, as we said above, the desired swarm of the sacred congregation. A vehement desire prevailed upon him that a man so uniquely powerful in authority should, setting aside [Col. 1087C] all that was his, also entrust himself to many dangers and labors.

He therefore came to Clairvaux, humble and exalted in person; he had been drawn from the ends of the earth not by curiosity to hear wisdom, but by zeal of faith and fullness of devotion. How greatly he wept there, and what manner of conduct he displayed not only toward the man whom he so uniquely revered, but also toward the least of the brethren, is not easy to say.

Finally, when he was about to return home, he ordered, by ordinary human reasoning, that bread blessed by the servant of God should be baked again in an oven, so that he might carry it back and preserve it longer, just as those who cross seas customarily carry twice-baked bread. But the holy abbot rebuked him kindly, finding his faith deficient in this matter: “What then?” he said. “Will the blessing not be able to preserve that bread more effectively than rebaking it?”

He would not consent to bless it; instead, he ordered ordinary bread to be given to him [Col. 1087D], blessed it, and said: “Take this with you. Henceforth have no concern about its spoiling.” He took it, returned safely to his own people across many expanses of land and sea, and rejoiced that the defect of his faith had been refuted by the most evident reality of the event.

Not long afterward, the saddest report struck his ears: his special friend, the blessed man, had fallen asleep in death. The news was sent to him in a little book on Bernard’s passing by Lord Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, who had for no short time been secretary to that most holy abbot.

Then his heart grew hot within him, and in his meditation a fire was kindled. He reckoned as vain, transitory, and perishable everything that can impede a person’s purpose from the straight course by which one tends toward the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Therefore, commending to God and to the rulers of the land the Church which he had laudably governed, taking leave of parents and kinsfolk, acquaintances and friends, and of the very soil of his native land, this distinguished exile came to Clairvaux. He visited the tomb of the blessed man who had formerly been his intimate friend [Col. 1088A], and chose to live and die at that most sacred tomb. There also, by God’s gift, he later received the habit of the holy religious life.

For he trusted no less in Bernard dead than formerly in Bernard living, since he did not at all doubt that he lived more truly after death of the flesh. The more withdrawn he was from ecclesiastical and secular business, the more earnestly he strove to devote himself to divine service, to watch diligently every day—indeed almost continuously—in devotion to sacred prayer, to offer God for his past sins the myrrh of a contrite heart and humbled spirit, and more earnestly to entreat the grace of heavenly blessing with the incense of pious compunction.

On one occasion, while he stood alone in his oratory, awake and praying, there appeared to him a brother of the same mother, who had died long before. He had fallen slain by an enemy sword and, overtaken by death, had not received the viaticum. While alive, this brother had on one occasion wronged the same archbishop [Col. 1088B] unjustly and had not, before death, been reconciled to him by satisfaction.

When he came before him, he bowed his head humbly and pleadingly, as though asking pardon for the offense or begging the aid of prayers. He stood for some time before him, saying absolutely nothing, but indicating by his bowed head his own calamity and need. The archbishop likewise said nothing to him, since he was so disturbed in mind by excessive fear and amazement that he was scarcely master of himself.

Yet of that dead man he could discern only the head, neck, and uppermost part of the shoulders. For the remaining part of the body seemed to be burning so fiercely that he could distinguish no bodily features at all, nor see anything except the flame which occupied him entirely. After appearing thus pitiably for some time, he was at last taken from his sight; but he left his brother’s soul [Col. 1088C] crushed with great sorrow over its distress. On the following day, coming into the chapter of monks, the archbishop obtained many offerings of Masses and prayers for that dead man.

## Chapter XXVI. Concerning the blessed end of two pilgrims to the Lord’s Sepulchre, uncles of Lord Eskil

But since we have mentioned the brother of so great a pontiff, I think it by no means inappropriate also to recount the death, precious in the sight of the Lord, of his two uncles—a death which they deserved through the marvelous grace of God. For we hope that devout minds will be kindled in the love of Christ if the wondrous and truly joyful mercy of this same our Redeemer toward a most wicked sinner is set forth in the hearts of readers.

These two brothers, born of the most illustrious blood of the Danes, seemed to rank highest among the nobles of that land after the king [Col. 1088D]. One of them, named Eskil, was a warlike man, swollen with worldly power; fierce and terrible in spirit, he shed much blood and committed innumerable evils daily. The other, named Svend, was conspicuous for a holy life and was bishop of Viborg. He far surpassed the nobility of his most exalted lineage by the excellence of his manners and the prerogative of his virtues.

Loving his brother’s soul sincerely in Christ but strongly abhorring his tyrannical life, he regularly endeavored to rebuke him privately and urge him to repent of his wickedness. But since he made little progress in this pious intention, one day, while they were speaking together, the venerable bishop urged him to take the sign of the Lord’s Cross and set out for Jerusalem.

The other answered that he could by no means do this unless the one giving the counsel went with him. On hearing this, the faithful and true friend gladly accepted and immediately promised [Col. 1089A] that he would do what was asked, preferring to expose himself to such dangers and labors rather than fail to rescue his brother’s soul from the lion’s mouth.

Having arrived there safely, they adored with great devotion the glorious Sepulchre of the Lord and the life-giving wood of the holy Cross upon which the salvation of the world hung. Then, as they traveled through the other holy places, visiting, venerating, and adoring them most devoutly, they came to a certain place not far from Jerusalem, called by the inhabitants “Our Father,” because the Lord Jesus Christ is said to have given His disciples the form of prayer in that place and to have composed that prayer there. There was there a small church, built in a plain and humble manner.

When these pilgrims learned that this was the place from which the fountain of prayer, springing into eternal life, had first burst forth from the mouth of the Son of God and had been conveyed through all parts of the world with such abundance of blessing to instruct the hearts of believers, they entered the oratory [Col. 1089B]. Drawing from the fountain of the Savior a spirit of piety and confidence, they poured out to the Lord a prayer from a pure heart, beseeching that their sins might be forgiven and that they might be delivered from every evil.

Nor was the regard of heavenly mercy lacking to their prayers, as the event showed. For when they immediately came to the River Jordan and had drunk of and been sprinkled with that sacred water, one of them—namely, the great sinner Eskil—placing magnificent confidence in God’s mercy and pouring out his soul in prayer, cried to the Lord and said:

“Almighty and merciful God, be gracious, I beseech You, to me a sinner; do not despise the soul of Your servant, unworthy though he is—a soul which You have drawn out from the depth of evils and, after so many shipwrecks of my crimes, mercifully brought to the harbor of repentance. And now, Lord God, my frailty is greatly suspect to me, as is the long-established habit of sinning; I greatly fear myself, lest perhaps, when I have returned to my homeland, the flattering lure of prosperity and the enticing occasion of sin compel me to fall back into my former wickedness [Col. 1089C].

“Therefore, most merciful Father, rich in mercy toward all who call upon You, if it seems good in Your eyes and if You know it to be expedient for the salvation of my soul, I beg Your most indulgent goodness, now that the vow of this pilgrimage has been fulfilled, to deign to release me from the bond of this body and, released also from the chains of sins, command me to be led into a place of refreshment.”

When his prayer was completed, he immediately knew that the end of his life was at hand and that Christ would shortly fulfill his desire. Having received the sacraments, he took leave that same hour of his brother and the others present with him; and at once, in holy confession, he rendered up his soul.

O incomprehensible mercy of our Savior God! Does it not seem to you that in this sinner the person of that prodigal son is truly presented—the son who squandered his substance with the harlots of vanities and pleasures [Col. 1089D]? While he was still far off, the Father of mercies saw him; moved with mercy, He commanded that he be quickly clothed in the first robe of innocence. Thus He hastened to release the miserable man from the guilt of his conscience, so that the father’s mercy was almost slower in granting pardon to the guilty man than the unhappy man himself was in receiving pardon.

For what else was it that this most wicked sinner prayed thus on the very threshold of repentance and obtained so swift an effect of his petition, except that, as the bowels of divine mercy were poured out upon him, he was stripped of the misery of corruptibility, clothed in the robe of blessed immortality, marked with the ring of divine love, his feet of affections shod with the sandals of eternal purity, and festive banquets proclaimed throughout heaven for the reception of the lost son?

When the venerable bishop saw that his brother’s soul, for whose salvation he had been so concerned, had been received so swiftly and so blessedly, he too was vehemently moved by the desire to depart. He prayed that his own soul might die and said [Col. 1090A]:

“I give You thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because You have heard my prayer; You have seen my tear, with which I so often begged You to receive my brother’s repentance. Therefore I beseech You, most merciful Son of God, do not allow me to be separated from him any longer, but command that I too be received now with him in Your peace, so that we may depart together and, by Your gift, together attain Your mercy. O mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, truly to be embraced and loved!”

He had scarcely finished the prayer which he had poured forth with most ardent devotion of faith when, behold, the Lord called him. He suddenly began to lose bodily strength and knew that the end of his passing life was near. Having promptly arranged what seemed necessary in view of the briefness of time, he ordered those standing by to carry his body, together with his brother’s body, to the aforementioned church called “Our Father.” They had longed for it with a sincere affection of piety inspired by the Lord, and he commanded that, without delay [Col. 1090B], they should have them buried there.

Thus, entrusting the people committed to him anew to divine providence, praying eternal goods for them all, taking leave of and blessing those present, he happily fell asleep in the Lord.

And the Lord performed a great miracle: having obtained the fulfillment of their desire, the pilgrims, once the vow of pilgrimage had been completed, also ended the pilgrimage of their present exile. Both departed from the world together, in one place and on one day; both were carried together to the place they had determined upon and received burial there.

The aforesaid little church, which had previously been small and ruinous, was razed to the ground and rebuilt in a larger and more beautiful form from their alms, which they had liberally assigned there for this very purpose. Their bodies now rest there, honorably entombed.

The kinsman of these most blessed pilgrims was Eskil of blessed memory, formerly Archbishop of the Danes. Drawing from them not only the sap of blood relationship but also of faith and devotion, and encouraged by the example of his own family, he resolved to live as a pilgrim and die as a pilgrim for Christ the Lord. Therefore, leaving the most exalted dignity in which he held a singular preeminence in his own land, he received the habit of the Cistercian Order at Clairvaux and most generously supplied the poverty of Christ’s poor out of the abundance of his riches. Thus he himself became poor and was joined to the number of those poor; having ended his life in the best manner of conduct, he was buried in the presbytery of that place before the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mother. Henceforth his memory shall be in blessing among the monks of Clairvaux from generation to generation [Col. 1090C].

Such persons, so exalted in honors and reverend in dignities, drawn by the fragrance of the virtues of our most blessed Father Bernard and by the purity of the sacred Cistercian Order, preferring the reproach of Christ to all the splendors of Egypt, chose rather to be temporarily chastened under the discipline of the Order than to be eternally tormented amid the costly favors and false honors granted them.

## Chapter XXVII. Concerning the noble prince Gunnar, afterwards a monk of Clairvaux

[Col. 1090D]

For the most noble prince Gunnar also, formerly judge and lord of the *detrachalis* [uncertain title] of Sardinia, once went to Saint Martin of Tours for the sake of prayer. On his return he passed through Clairvaux and was devoutly received by Blessed Bernard. Although the holy Father admonished him at length concerning the salvation of his soul, he did not consent to conversion, even though, while Gunnar was present and talking much, the holy Father gave sight to a certain blind man.

As he was departing, the man of God spoke to him thus: “I have indeed earnestly asked the Lord for your conversion, but for the present I have not deserved to be heard. And now I permit you to go, because it is not lawful to keep one who is unwilling. Yet know that you shall return here again from Sardinia.”

[Col. 1091A] He therefore went back to his own country, but the words he had heard from the mouth of the man of God continually stung his mind. The Spirit suggested inwardly that the prophecy which so great a prophet had foretold about him could not entirely fail.

A short time later, when he was told that the blessed man had passed from this world to the Father, he was greatly shaken in mind. He reproached himself and deeply repented that he had not been converted at Bernard’s preaching. Immediately he was wholly kindled with that fire which the Lord sends into the hearts of His elect and wishes to be fiercely inflamed. Unable to bear any delay, he appointed his firstborn son to rule in his stead in his kingdom. He himself, still only forty years old and outstanding in bodily maturity and strength of mind, left Sardinia and, despising all worldly glory, entered Clairvaux poor and humble. There, serving perseveringly under the discipline of the Order which he had embraced until decrepit old age—indeed, until death—he rejoiced that he had exchanged an earthly kingdom for a heavenly one [Col. 1091B].

## Chapter XXVIII. How the venerable abbot Simon, leaving his abbacy, made profession at Clairvaux

The venerable Simon, formerly abbot of Caziac [Caziacum], a monastery of no small distinction of monks of the black Order, loved Blessed Bernard with great affection of heart, so that he seemed wholly dependent upon Bernard’s counsel and will. He had a great desire to abandon pastoral responsibility and become a monk at Clairvaux.

Nevertheless, the holy Father Bernard knew the man’s virtue and the grace through which he was very fit and indeed greatly needed for the monastery entrusted to him. Therefore, as long as Bernard lived in the flesh, he was never willing to grant consent to this request.

One day the same abbot said to him: “Lord Father, I am old and nearly decrepit. My bodily limbs are failing, illnesses press upon me besides, and I feel myself already dissolving. If I should fail outside Clairvaux, it will be inconsolable grief and irreparable loss to me. Therefore you must either order me now to depart and fulfill my desires, since death is hastening and permits me no further delay.”

The man of God answered him: “Remain in your place and do not fear. I make you secure: you shall die at Clairvaux.”

The man believed the words of the saint and remained for several years, more at ease, in his office. But after the blessed man’s passing, since he could no longer endure the goads of his desire without anyone restraining them, he resigned his government and went to Clairvaux. There, by God’s great gift and a great miracle, he survived for seven years and at the end left all of us a truly remarkable example of fervor and devotion in such age and infirmity [Col. 1091C].

## Chapter XXIX. Concerning the elder who saw Blessed Mary presiding over the chapter of monks

A certain elder of Clairvaux, a religious and devout man, once saw in a vision—as we heard from his own mouth—the most blessed Virgin Mother presiding over the chapter of monks, radiant in countenance and apparel. In that chapter she seemed to occupy the abbot’s place and to discharge his office [Col. 1091D].

She held in her lap the blessed fruit of her womb, the little child who was born to us; and the whole convent of monks sat about her in its proper order. The elder who saw these things marveled and greatly rejoiced in the presence of the glorious little child, beautiful beyond the children of men, and of that sacred mother who had borne him. But as his eyes were dazzled by the brightness of the light, he could not sufficiently fix his gaze upon their faces.

When the chapter had been completed and the assembly was about to be dismissed, the commanding Virgin turned to that elder who sat at her right hand [Col. 1092A], graciously impressed upon his mouth the kiss of peace, and moreover offered him the blessed fruit of her womb to behold and embrace. Having done this, she turned to the other elder who sat on her left, kissed him likewise, and similarly presented to him the joy of her heart to behold.

Then all the monks present, receiving heavenly peace on both sides from those elders, rejoiced in jubilation and gladness of heart at the presence of so great a Queen, cherishing in her lap the salvation of God. When that assembly was thus dissolved, the vision was taken from the eyes of its beholder.

The elder conceived such devotion from the sweetness of this vision that he understood the chapter house to be nothing other than God’s inner sanctuary and the gate of heaven. Therefore, as often as he had to pass before that house, he would almost always bow toward the place in which he had seen the Mother of Mercy seated with her adorable Son.

## Chapter XXX. Concerning a certain brother to whom the Lord Jesus Christ appeared with Saint John the Evangelist

[Col. 1092B]

A certain brother, devout and God-fearing, burned with the desire to make progress and devoted himself day and night to holy meditations. He loved the most blessed John the Evangelist with a special affection; he was nourished with wonderful devotion by John’s writing and memory, striving to pluck from his sayings thoughts like pomegranates, with which, having strewn the bed of his conscience, he might refresh it with the fragrance of virtues against the stench of vices.

It happened once, on the vigil of All Saints, while Mass was being celebrated in the community, that he stood in his place in choir, crushing in the little mortar of his heart, with the pestle of watchful concern, the incense of sacred devotion in preparation for receiving so great a feast. And while, as customary, that Epistle from the Apocalypse was being read, he delighted in those very words with wondrous sweetness. At last, at the final verse [Col. 1092C], where it is said, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity,” and the rest which follows (Rev. 5), his whole soul melted within him in the fire of divine love, and he was flooded with such an abundance of joy that, through the immensity of his gladness, he could scarcely contain himself. Thus, wholly carried away into jubilation, he was wholly beside himself, beholding Christ alone as though present with the eyes of his heart and embracing him with the arms of burning faith and devotion.

While he still stood there in this state, and that heavenly banquet abundantly refreshed his mind, before Mass had yet ended the sleep of the Lord fell upon him—slight indeed, but sweet through divine grace. Immediately, he who had poured the aforesaid joy into him while awake graciously manifested his presence to him while asleep: the Lord Jesus Christ, together with his beloved apostle John. Addressing that apostle while the brother listened, he said:

> “Long ago I showed you this revelation, not for your sake alone—for you already possessed certain knowledge and certain confidence concerning my power and love [Col. 1092D]—but especially for the sake of the rest, who likewise love me, so that they too, recognizing my glory, may have confidence in me.”

Awakening at these words, the brother was filled with great joy: first, because of the grace granted him in the Lord’s visitation and consolation; and second, because of the Lord’s own testimony to the truth of the Apocalypse—especially since he had heard with sorrow that certain heretics disparaged this holy book, asserting that it had not been written by the blessed apostle John.

About fifteen days later, when the aforesaid brother, greatly troubled by his sins, took care to anticipate the face of the Lord through confession and daily contrition of heart, the Lord Jesus Christ stood before him in a vision with the same apostle John. The apostle spoke first, with the brother listening:

> “If anyone wishes to obtain perfect pardon from the Lord, he must punish his sins by persistent weeping and repentance.”

The Lord replied [Col. 1093A]:

> “Whoever wishes to come to me must ardently desire this very thing.”

Later, on the feast day of that same Saint John, he saw in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ with his glorious mother entering a great palace, in which paradise was said to be. When they had entered, the gate remained open. Wondering and considering within himself why that gate was not shut, he was told:

> “This is the gate of life. Once the Lord has entered through it with his mother, it will not be shut, but shall stand open to all the faithful until the Day of Judgment.”

Hearing this, he rejoiced and exulted, saying within himself: “Then the entrance to paradise is open also to me. Therefore I shall enter the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.” When he began to enter, an ineffable joy and sweetness immediately received him; penetrating and filling all his senses, it allowed him to desire nothing else and think of nothing else [Col. 1093B] except to remember the mercy and justice of God alone.

Awakening amid this wonderful sweetness, he still thought that he was in the delights of God’s paradise. But immediately, feeling himself surrounded by the motions and senses of this corruptible life, he understood that such happiness had not yet been granted to him for enjoyment, but had been bestowed upon his taste in a slight foretaste in order to awaken in him heavenly desire. Shaken by these and similar revelations from the bed of sloth, torpor, and negligence, and vehemently inflamed with the ardor of divine love, that brother, like Issachar, “a strong ass,” put his shoulder beneath the burden of penance to bear it without turning aside, so that he might deserve to attain the rest which he had seen.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Of the brother who saw the Lord Jesus Christ descend from heaven at the death of a certain brother

[Col. 1093C]

The Lord permitted a certain monk of the community of Clairvaux, a spiritual man endowed with good character, to suffer on one occasion from a very severe illness, in order—as he says in the Apocalypse, “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3)—to refine within him the dross of sin. But before he reached the critical day, by divine direction he was caught up into an ecstasy of mind and remained almost half the night as though outside himself, seeing and hearing many things which it is not our purpose now to recount.

That same night a certain devout young man died there, a monk of remarkable gentleness and patience, who, tortured by a most severe sickness for very many years, had endured a harsh and prolonged martyrdom. As he died, drawing out his final breath for a long time, he uttered frequent groans of lamentation because of the bitterness of his pain. When the aforesaid sick man heard him lamenting, he said within himself: “This lament will soon be turned into song, and eternal joy will now take possession of the end of this suffering.”

As he thought these and similar things, behold, a certain invisible presence stood before his bed and, for a long time, admonished him; at almost every groan uttered by the dying man, it richly sweetened his nostrils and throat with a marvelous and unfamiliar fragrance and sweetness [Col. 1093D]. Then he felt, sensibly and plainly, as though a heavenly power were entering into him and most sweetly anointing the innermost chambers of his heart.

When he had been refreshed by this wonderful anointing and in a sense wholly renewed, suddenly there appeared to him a certain opening in heaven, through which he seemed to direct his gaze as far as the third heaven. And a voice from on high sounded in his ears, crying:

> “Let all the earth be silent; let all wickedness depart: Christ is coming.”

At that very hour it seemed to him that the Lord Jesus Christ, the consoler of the poor and humble, descended from heaven and filled the whole house with his blessing. The brother to whom it was granted to see these things was filled with such cheerfulness [Col. 1094A] and grace that he thought himself to be in God’s paradise, and, exulting in the jubilation of his heart, said:

> “Lord my God, behold, this is the eternal life which you promised us. And now, if with opened eyes I were permitted to see and always possess this good which I feel and hold, my joy would already be full and perfect.”
