Soon afterward, when the hour of that young monk’s departure was at hand, the board was struck; and when the brethren had assembled to commend his soul to the Lord, it was immediately freed from the body of this death, and, as eternal gladness entered, pain and groaning fled from it. For we believe and devoutly trust that he did not disdain to lead that soul into his rest—he, Jesus Christ our Lord, who for its sake deigned to descend to earth.

While the body was being committed to burial, another brother of good conduct, by the Lord’s revelation and with open eyes—as he himself testified to us—saw what seemed like a bier come forth from the tomb and rise upward into the air. The aforesaid sick man, by the Lord’s mercy, recovered from his illness. Greatly consoled by what he had seen, heard, and also been permitted to experience at the brother’s death, he gave thanks to God.

Moreover, for many years afterward he received, not continuously but frequently and abundantly, the sweetness of that blessing which he had experienced like hidden manna, in an extraordinary fragrance or most excellent taste, insofar as that gracious and sweet Spirit, who breathes where, when, and as much as he wills, deigned mercifully to pour it into his poor servant. Nor did he experience this grace of sweetness only in sleep or ecstasy, when the bodily senses were asleep or stunned, as perhaps happened in that agony; rather, while his body was awake and his senses alert, whether praying, chanting psalms, reading, or doing something else, he felt that same grace divinely bestowed.

How rich and generous you are in your mercy, O Lord, toward all who call upon you, toward all who seek your name [Col. 1094C], toward the small and great alike: hiding the taste of inward sweetness and delight from those who are wise and great in their own eyes, and revealing it to your little ones, who reckon all things of this world as dung so that they may gain you in your sweetness!

## CHAPTER XXXII. Of the man of God Boson, who heard the singing of angels at the death of a certain brother

We do not think that the venerable man Boson, distinguished by birth and character, should be passed over in silence. He was one of the firstborn sons whom the most blessed Father Bernard begot in Christ through the Gospel. In his noble manner of life he showed well enough from what royal breast he had been nourished, and with what rudiments of chaste discipline he had been imbued from the beginning.

This patient man and son of peace appeared so kindly and so gentle to everyone that none of us [Col. 1094D] ever saw him angry or disturbed. Rather, standing immovable in faith amid adversity and prosperity, he always remained tranquil in mind. When he had reached extreme old age and was so deprived of strength that he could scarcely walk even supported by a staff, he nevertheless never consented to indulge in idleness or to give his body rest. Instead, through various exercises of labor, he compelled it to serve the spirit.

Once, while we were speaking together more privately and mutually nourishing one another through discussion of the devout and desirable deaths of certain brothers which we had often happened to see, this venerable man testified to us that at the death of a certain devout brother he had heard the choirs of blessed spirits singing sweet melodies in the air and joyfully carrying the deceased man’s soul to the rest of eternal blessedness. The higher they ascended, the more their voices became faint below, until, once received into heaven, they could no longer be heard [Col. 1095A].

When that blessed old man himself, called by God in peace, gave up his spirit as though falling asleep, such serenity and grace suddenly shone upon him, and his face appeared glorified by so marvelous a transformation, that—with the devotion of all bearing witness—we could in no way doubt that the presence of the blessed spirits and the most serene regard of our God were there [Col. 1096A]. For never had we seen in anyone dying or dead such brightness in a transformed countenance. Therefore, all giving thanks to God, we performed the rites and office of commendation all the more cheerfully because through so marvelous a sign we had been made more certain of his glorification.

## FOURTH DISTINCTION. Of other monks, as well as lay brothers and novices, of Clairvaux

## CHAPTER I. Of the monk Alquirinus, whom the Lord Jesus visited as he was dying

[Col. 1095B]

There was at the monastery of Clairvaux a monk named Alquirinus, whose integrity of character accorded with his profession: a religious and spiritual man, temperate in food, humble in dress, and exceedingly harsh in the mortification of his body. He was so restrained and moderate in matters apparently pertaining to bodily use that, having driven away every pleasure and vanity, he used even necessities most sparingly, although occasions to exceed the proper limit frequently presented themselves.

He was skilled in the art of medicine, and although the great and noble of the land continually sought his services and dragged him, unwilling and reluctant, through various places, he nevertheless showed greater concern for the needy and poor, devoting every care to their treatment. Nor did he merely heal their illnesses and sores; he also handled with his own hands, so graciously and carefully, the rotting flesh and limbs running with pus of the sick, that he might have seemed to be tending Christ’s wounds [Col. 1095C]. And indeed this was so. For he did everything for Christ, and Christ counted everything as done to himself—he who will say at the end to those who pursue works of mercy: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25).

Accordingly, the Lord often visited his servant with secret consolations and wonderfully encouraged him in this work of ministry. On one occasion, therefore, he saw the following vision at Clairvaux. First he heard what seemed like a heavenly forerunner crying with a herald’s voice:

> “Behold, Christ is coming. Rise and go out to meet the Savior.”

As all hurried eagerly to see the Lord, he too ran and stood at the door of the cloister through which Christ was expected to come. When the Lord entered, he approached and worshiped him, begging to receive blessing and mercy “from God his Savior” [Col. 1095D] (Ps. 23). Having received these, he began to gaze upon him more attentively and to suffer with him in a wondrous affection of compassion. For he appeared to him as one suffering and weak, pierced with nails and wounded by a lance, as though he had been taken down from the cross that very hour, so that blood flowed abundantly from his fresh wounds.

The Lord himself held clean linens, like corporal cloths, pressing them upon those wounds and, after wiping away the blood, throwing them down to the ground. Gathering them up with the greatest reverence, kissing them with much devotion, and preserving them laid up in his bosom as though they were the redemption of his soul, the brother kept them.

Frequently refreshed by these and similar revelations from the Lord, he did not cease until the end to do good to everyone, but especially to pilgrims and poor people who were sick. How severe he was in preserving penance and how strict in chastising his body is sufficiently apparent from this [Col. 1096B]: while he devoted the service of healing to all the needy with the fervor of charity, he exempted himself alone from such care. Although he was sickly and weak in body, he never consented to administer bodily medicine to himself, but committed himself wholly to God, because “he has care for us” (1 Pet. 5).

For he knew that the powers of the soul are perfected in bodily weakness (2 Cor. 12), and that a monk concerned to retain the little consolations of his flesh cannot receive spiritual consolations from the Lord, while neglecting to taste and see that the Lord is sweet. Having therefore honorably completed the course of his life, when the time was near for him to receive eternal reward for his labors and works of holy mercy, he was seized by illness and came to the end.

When the venerable Abbot Pontius, whom we mentioned above, came to visit him, he asked what he was doing and how he was faring. He replied:

> “Well, dearest Father; all is altogether well with me, because I go—indeed, I go—to my Lord.”

“But,” said the abbot, “do you not endure bodily suffering with difficulty, and do you not fear the straits of death?”

“I,” he said, “regard all things as tranquil and all things as joyful, because I have already been anticipated by the Lord with blessings of sweetness. These have taken all sorrow from my heart and nearly all pain from my body” [Col. 1096C].

The abbot replied:

> “I beg you, my beloved brother, for God’s sake tell us, for our edification, whether anything has been divinely revealed to you.”

Then he said:

> “Just now, before you entered here, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to me, though I am wretched and unworthy. Gazing upon me with a favorable and serene countenance, and showing the most blessed marks of his Passion, he said: ‘Behold, your sins have been wiped away from before my face. Come therefore in safety; come and see and kiss my wounds, which you so greatly loved and so often tended.’ Strengthened by such a promise, I no longer fear death, because this hope of mine is laid up in my bosom” (Job 19). “And know that on the next night”—it was the vigil of Saint Martin—“I shall depart while the Work of God is being celebrated in church, at such an hour.”

He died, therefore, that same night and at the very time he had foretold. Now, as we truly trust, he rests from his labors (Rev. 14), and, like a dove made white upon snow, nests in the clefts of the rock (Song 2): that is, he embraces and worships the most sacred wounds of Christ the Lord, who is God above all, blessed forever. Amen.

## CHAPTER II. Of the brother who possessed a wonderful grace of compunction, whom the Lord greatly consoled

A certain brother of the same monastery, fearful and anxious because of the sins by which he had grievously offended God, spent an entire day walking in sorrow and refused to put an end to tears and lamentations. He knew that verbal confession without contrition of heart [Col. 1097A] is judged insufficient before God for obtaining pardon. And when the scroll of the fear of God, in which “lamentations and woe” are written (Ezek. 2), had for some time embittered the belly of his conscience with salutary bitterness (Rev. 10), at last, by the breathing of divine grace, the parchment of God’s love, on which a song is written, became in the devotion of his heart “sweet as honey” (Ezek. 3).

He began to taste beforehand certain first fruits of his labors and to learn by experience that God does not despise the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled spirit (Ps. 50). For while he continued in the great bitterness described above, one night he saw in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ, clothed as though in priestly vestments and celebrating Mass. Whenever, according to the rite of sacrifice, he turned toward the people, he lifted in his hands the chalice from the altar and offered it for all present to see. Yet in that chalice there was nothing except the tears with which blessed Mary Magdalene, weeping and repenting, had watered his feet in Simon’s house [Col. 1097B].

When the aforesaid brother, lying at the Lord’s feet, saw this, he asked him:

> “I beg you, Lord, why do you show us this chalice with the tears that are in it?”

He replied:

> “So that all may see and know how much contrition of heart and penitential grief please me. For, as an example of repentance, I have preserved so long at my feet the tears of this sinful woman as she wept and repented.”

The more he learned how acceptable tears of repentance are to the divine majesty, the more his spirit was stirred and inflamed within him, so that in reading, chanting psalms, and meditation he sought nothing else and pursued nothing else except to form his mind for lamentation and awaken in himself the grace of compunction. He knew that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence and that the violent seize it with such weapons (Matt. 11).

The Lord further consoled his servant, who was continuously being afflicted in the frying-pan of discipline through sorrow over his evils [Col. 1097C]. In a vision of the night, he saw himself struggling and in peril, as though in a very deep lake. When all hope of escape was gone, behold, the Lord Jesus Christ, a helper in due season, suddenly came to him, walking barefoot on the waters. When he came to him, he graciously lifted the miserable man out of the waters into his bosom and placed him in a meadow delightful with most pleasant greenness.

Considering the grace of so great a condescension, the brother fell at the feet of the Lord Jesus; rejoicing in spirit through the immensity of his joy, he began, with an insatiable desire of devotion, to clasp and kiss the Savior’s gracious footprints. Upon waking, he carefully examined the vision and interpreted the lake in which he had been submerged as the depth of vices; the bosom of grace into which he had graciously been lifted, as forgiveness through pardon; and the flowery meadow into which he had been transferred, as the verdure of eternal rest.

Therefore, turning to the Lord with his whole mind [Col. 1097D], as though his previous labors had been slight, he began to stretch himself toward what lay ahead. By fasts, vigils, and continual prayers, with tears and unutterable groanings, he asked the Lord that, under grace’s guidance, he might be worthy to experience in reality the abundance of pardon prefigured for him in the image of the vision, and that divine mercy might deign to show him this by some signs.

The Lord, dispenser and governor of all virtues, determined to console him as he continually labored in his groaning and regularly ate the bread of sorrow. One night, strongly moved by the desire of which we have spoken above, he attended the brothers’ vigils. And behold, as he chanted psalms and prayed, he suddenly entered into an ecstasy of mind. He saw a certain figure lightly and gently drawing a sharp razor, as though insensibly, over his head; in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, it seemed to shave his beard, neck, and crown, declaring by this sign the goodness of divine pardon to the weeping and sighing man [Col. 1098A]. Yet it left a few hairs here and there, signifying, I think, the blemish of daily negligences, without which this life is not lived.

Frequently raised up by these and similar consolations, the brother, through the Lord’s inspiration, learned to breathe in hope of pardon; giving thanks for benefits received, he yearned for greater things.

O happy humility of penitents! O blessed hope of those who perfectly bewail their sins—how powerful you are with the Almighty! How, as servants, you conquer the unconquerable! How quickly you turn the dreadful Judge into a most merciful Father! You will receive the highest joy of eternal purity all the more sweetly to the degree that you now consent to be cleansed from the leprosy of vices more deeply in the descent into the Jordan.

## CHAPTER III. Of the monk to whom the Eucharist bestowed the grace of a marvelous taste

A certain brother, fervent [Col. 1098B] and diligent in the observance of holy religion, once partook, on the Lord’s Day and according to the custom of the Order, of the body and blood of Christ. It then seemed to him, throughout that whole day thereafter, that he held the sweetest honeycomb in his mouth. On the following Sunday, after similarly receiving the Eucharist, he experienced the same grace for three uninterrupted days. On the third Sunday, after again receiving the divine nourishment, he was granted the same sweetness for a whole week.

From that time onward, he experienced in many ways and for a long time the sweetness of this bread of life—sometimes less often, sometimes more often—as the Holy Spirit, giver of grace, deigned to grant it to his poor servant. It happened, however, that on one occasion, while rebuking one of his friends for a fault, he exceeded the proper measure of just reproof. Yet before receiving from the altar the gift of the divine sacraments, he did not take care through satisfaction to soothe the conscience of the brother whom he had exasperated [Col. 1098C].

Therefore, presuming to receive the peace-offering while his brother had not yet been reconciled, instead of the honeyed sweetness of spiritual delight by which he had formerly been accustomed to be refreshed and restored, he trembled in horror as a most bitter bitterness, more bitter than gall and wormwood, infected his throat. Accordingly, recalling his guilt as swiftly as possible and doing penance through the humblest satisfaction for the fault of his insufficiently discerning rebuke, he took care henceforth to observe more diligently that apostolic saying:

> “You who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6).

Let all who are emulators of the Order, all who burn in spirit with zeal for justice, attend, I beg, to this example. Let them attend, I say, and observe more cautiously, lest perhaps they turn the measure of just correction into weapons of rage, and through indiscretion draw the cup of amendment which they attempt to offer to their brothers into destruction for both themselves and others: while they tear themselves apart through anger and, by exasperating what they ought to amend, make it fester, compelling others to break out into excuses excusing sins [Col. 1098D].

## CHAPTER IV. Of the monk who endured many conflicts with demons and was granted to see the Lord Jesus Christ

To rebuke our sluggishness and awaken our devotion, we shall bring forward one of the combatants: a man who, in the monastery of Clairvaux, labored beneath the yoke of monastic discipline from youth to extreme old age and endured such numerous and bitter conflicts with demons that, unless the Spirit had helped his weakness, flesh and blood could by no means have borne such malice from spectral shadows.

Serving the Lord in all holiness and righteousness, he had preserved bodily integrity from his mother’s womb through God’s great gift. In testimony to his twofold purity, the Lord deigned to reveal to him many things from the secrets of heaven [Col. 1099A]. Once, while he prayed alone in a certain lodging after prolonged vigils, the hairs of his flesh suddenly stood on end, and he began, more than usual, to be troubled by the terror of the night.

And behold, a crowd of demons burst in through the door in a mass, as though pressing one another because of the multitude entering, and filled the whole house. They made a noise on every side and turned the man himself, though praying, now here, now there. When he perceived this, immediately armed with the sign of the cross, he began to seek frequent pardons and drove them away with salutations to the Blessed Virgin.

On the following night, when he returned to the same place in order to pray, behold, again the hostile powers, rushing on in the force of fury, struck the stone wall of the dwelling with such tremendous violence—as a battering ram strikes a wall—that they shook the entire house. When the man of God raised his eyes toward a large window opened in that wall, he saw standing in it a winged demon [Col. 1099B], in the likeness of a griffin or ostrich. It menaced him, as though it were about to rush upon and devour him.

Seeing this, he recognized the demon’s devices. Calling upon the Savior’s name, he opposed the sign of the cross to the savage apparition and drove it away. Having suffered many mockeries and conflicts of this kind for a long time, this excellent wrestler never ceased to strike and strike back, waging without truce, by unceasing attention, battle against spiritual wickedness.

He received from the Lord a spiritual grace attained by very few people. Whenever he wished, he was accustomed, directing his eyes into the air, to see in daylight with bodily eyes crowds of demons wandering everywhere in dense troops; their number was so infinite that it could not be estimated because of its immensity. Although they usually appear in many forms, there was one form—or rather deformity—in which he most often saw them.

In bodily outline, they seemed monstrous human beings: giants in stature, Ethiopians in color, serpents in swiftness, lions in ferocity; with large and swollen heads, protruding bellies, short and hunchbacked bodies, long necks, slender arms, and likewise exceedingly long legs [Col. 1099C]. When they stood anywhere in the air, their bodies could be distinguished limb by limb. But when they wandered to and fro in roving motion, nothing was perceived of them except spectral shadows and dark masses. On clear days, when the sun shone in its strength, he was accustomed to see such visions more frequently and distinguish them more clearly.

At one time blessed Augustine, the outstanding doctor of the Church, appeared to this venerable man in a vision and led him through innumerable places of punishment as far as the very entrance of the Gehenna pit. Looking down from above into it, with trembling limbs and a soul throbbing from unbearable fear, he saw that gulf of the Tartarean abyss full of dreadful cries and accursed howlings of wretches ever living in devouring fire. For them death is most bitter—the worst of all deaths: namely, to be unable to die.

Then, retracing his steps, Augustine led him from that place of horror and darkness into the region of blessed joys. He showed him the light-filled seats and dwelling places of most blessed souls, where, stripped of their bodies, they lived an incorruptible life and rested in greatest happiness in the peace of Christ, which surpasses understanding, awaiting the regeneration of their bodies. Then Saint Augustine said to him:

> “Behold, you have seen the ultimate ends of good and evil. Choose what is good in your eyes. If you resolve to keep the way of righteousness, which is abundantly set forth in my books, you shall receive a portion in the land of the living with all these. But if you wish to follow your desires, you shall be numbered for the sword with those whom you saw, cast, by the dreadful indeed but just judgment of God, into the accursedness of oblivion.”

When the vision ended and the man had returned to himself [Col. 1100A], he was wholly shaken and greatly terrified, gripped by a twofold fear: lest he lose the glory of the blessed and also lest he incur the punishment of the reprobate. From that time onward, he began to love the most blessed doctor Augustine more sweetly and to meditate more savoringly upon his writings.

It happened at one time that he fell ill at the House of God, the Abbey of the Cistercian Order, situated in the district of Bourges. At that place, moreover, a brother of honorable conduct fell mortally ill. When he had already been laid upon straw, it happened by chance that he breathed his last while the infirmarians were absent.

The aforesaid brother, lying there in his bed and languishing under grievous bodily illness, saw plainly with bodily eyes, by the Lord’s revelation, that soul emerge from the body in a long stream, like the smoke of incense proceeding from a censer. When it had entirely emerged, it gathered itself into one ball and stood suspended in the air above the body, at a height of four or five cubits [Col. 1100B]. Its appearance was like a dense yet translucent little cloud, spread out as if to the measure of one modius. It remained there motionless until, attended by the prayers of the brethren and strengthened by priestly commendation, it might deserve to receive guidance for the dangerous and unknown journey.

When the brother saw this, he called the infirmarians with whatever sound and voice he could manage. They hurried at once, struck the board for the dead, and the brethren ran together for the funeral rites. When the community was present with cross and holy water, and priestly commendation had begun, that soul departed as though secure, and the cloud which had been seen vanished.

At another time, it happened that the aforesaid man of God attended the divine offices on the Lord’s Day in a certain parish church. When the offertory had been said, and the ministration of bread and wine mixed with water had been placed upon the sacred table, the Lord Jesus immediately appeared to him, standing above that altar in the form of a child, beautiful beyond the children of men. He appeared so plainly and for so long [Col. 1100C] that the vision almost continued until the sacrifice was completed.

Yet the priest of that place who celebrated Mass was a man of dishonorable and criminal life. Therefore, whenever that priest had his back turned to the altar—whether receiving the offerings of the faithful, delivering an address to the people as is customary on a feast day, or doing something else—that holy child stood before the chalice. But whenever the priest faced the sacrament, that holy little child, as though recoiling from the priest’s unclean breath, stood far away behind the chalice.

When the brother saw this, he was deeply moved and dissolved wholly into tears, so that the flood of tears sometimes hindered the sight of his eyes from beholding the most sweet Redeemer. When the revelation was complete, he glorified God, who had deigned to show him such things. And he truly understood that difference in merits makes no difference in sacrifices, because the effect of the sacrament in no respect depends upon the priest’s power or merit, but upon the Savior’s institution and grace [Col. 1100D].

## CHAPTER V. Of the old man to whom the Lord Jesus appeared while he kept vigil on the day of Parasceve

By *Parasceve* is meant here the day on which the memory of Christ’s Passion is celebrated in the Church. Among the Jews every Friday was called *Parasceve*, that is, “Preparation,” because on that day food and other necessities were prepared for the following Sabbath day, on which it was not permitted either to cook food or to do anything of that kind. Therefore, because Christ was crucified on the Parasceve of Passover, the day of his Passion is called Parasceve. Ecclesiastical writers do not call days by the names of idols, as secular people do, who, like pagans, speak of the day of Mars, Jupiter, Venus, and so forth.

A monk of the aforesaid monastery, advanced alike in religion and in years [Col. 1101A], was once sitting in the cloister on the holy day of Preparation, with a book before him, when the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, His hands and feet stretched out upon the cross, as though He had been crucified at that very hour. This most blessed vision, though brief and almost momentary, was nevertheless so manifest and effective that the devout remembrance of it could never afterwards be erased from the seer’s heart. For as one who pours oil upon a burning furnace makes the whole blaze up, so the grace of this revelation more abundantly and perfectly illumined with the flame of holy desire the inward heart of that old man, already kindled by the long practice of holy conduct. Thus, setting ascents within his heart and advancing from strength to strength, he completed, if I am not mistaken, his fortieth year in the Order; and at last, laying aside the burden of corruptible flesh, he deserved to behold in Zion the God of gods—not in the image of weakness, as before, but in the glory of majesty.

## CHAPTER VI. How mercifully the Lord admonished a certain cleric to convert.

[Col. 1101B]

God is ineffable, and His works are ineffable. For who can worthily express how wonderful He is in His saints; by what wondrous and manifold ways, in time, He calls those whom He foreknew from eternity and predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son; so that, even from among those who seemed through their crimes to be wholly swallowed up in the mass of perdition, He rescues some by mighty power and transfers them into the kingdom of brightness of that same beloved Son? Among these was a certain young cleric, rich, noble, and devoted to the world in the inclination of his purpose. By fatherly chastisement God mercifully rescued him from the abyss of pleasures, teaching him not to hope in the uncertainty of riches, nor to follow the wantonness of slippery youth, but through the hard labours of repentance to attain the true riches of eternal life.

This pampered young man, unwilling to observe that holidays had been instituted for clerics by the holy Fathers [Col. 1101C] so that they might “be still and know that the Lord Himself is God,” not so that they might devote themselves to chess or dice or any devilish trifles, often used to waste the day with his contemporaries and companions in spectacles and various games. Once, therefore, when many people gathered at a certain house for amusement, to spend the day as usual in theatrical applause and frivolities, this young man also came there, that he too might feed his young goats upon the spectacle of vanity. Some gamblers were there playing dice; and, in order to look down upon them better from above, he lay leaning forward upon a table placed there.

And behold, suddenly something like a human hand came upon him, striking him for a long time with an invisible scourge. It battered his head, shoulders, and whole back with repeated blows, as though a lash were striking from above. He lay motionless, not knowing what to do or where to turn. Through the extremity of his pain he wished to break out into cries and lamentation [Col. 1101D], but through shame, because of the crowd making a noise around him, he did not dare, lest he be thought mad; and he bore the torment of the blows with great difficulty. Returning, however, into himself and seeing death as though already imminent before his eyes, he reproached himself in the sight of the Lord, groaning in the bitterness of his soul and saying:

> “Alas for me, O Lord my God! Now my sins have found me; and behold, I am already dying and descending with sorrow into hell, lacking the fruit of repentance. O Father of mercies, Lord my God, if You look upon the affliction of a sinner set in distress, and mercifully rescue me, though unworthy, from this present danger, I promise, vow, and pledge that I shall not be ungrateful for Your benefits; but, despising at once all things that belong to the world, I shall give myself over to You as Your servant for ever.”

While he spoke these and similar things in his heart before the Lord, a voice came to him, saying: “If you are willing to go to Clairvaux for the sake of conversion, you shall be safe both in soul [Col. 1102A] and in body.” At this voice, taking breath and understanding that he had been visited by the Lord, he immediately answered: “Behold, I give myself as servant to God and to the house of Clairvaux.” He was still turning these words over in his heart when, as the scourge at once departed, all pain also vanished.

Feeling the mercy shown to him, he did not immediately yield to flesh and blood. Had a horse been available, he would not have endured even the delay of one hour before fulfilling at once the vow he had made. Nor did he admit that carnal thought of returning home, consulting parents and friends, putting his house and household in order, letting out his revenues, lands, and rents. Rather, breaking with all these things instead of settling them, and reckoning them all as dung for Christ’s sake, he obtained a horse that same day and at dawn on the following morning set out on his journey, fleeing from the face of the world as from the face of a lion, that he might dwell in solitude.

Coming, then, to Clairvaux with most fervent desire to fulfil his vow [Col. 1102B]—Clairvaux, which had formerly been called the valley of wormwood—and explaining to the brothers the manner and sequence of his conversion, he was received with affection all the more joyful because, through these judgments, the brothers humbly presumed that his life and manner of conduct pleased the Lord. Having been received and tested, and found faithful through the Lord’s gift, he put off the old man with his deeds; and, putting on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. IV), he embraced with such earnestness the arduous labours of the Cistercian Order until the end of his life that all who beheld his most holy manner of life plainly saw that the first summons of his conversion had truly come from Him who rebukes and chastens those whom He loves, and with fatherly compassion scourges every son whom He receives (Apoc. III; Heb. XII).

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning a novice whom blessed Bernard frequently visited in a vision.

[Col. 1102C]

A brother of the Order of Regular Canons, eager to advance and desirous of the better charisms, longed greatly to submit himself to the instruction of blessed Bernard and to join the community of Clairvaux, although he had not been able to attain this while the holy Father himself was alive. When Bernard died, the brother was deeply overwhelmed on hearing of his precious death, calling himself wretched and unworthy because he had not deserved to obtain the object of his vow.

A few days later the venerable Father appeared to him in a vision, girded like a vigorous labourer to work in a very broad field. In it there appeared innumerable sheaves of the wheat harvest. From these he had gathered a great multitude into a large heap, while he persisted in carrying together and piling up the remainder, which were still left and were far more numerous. On seeing this, the brother immediately understood that the heap of sheaves represented the multitude of brothers whom that distinguished preacher had gathered to Christ the Lord while he lived in the flesh; and that countless others remained who were to be brought, through Bernard’s merits and examples, to the grace of salvation. Therefore, rejoicing greatly and not despairing that he himself would be among them, he went to Clairvaux as quickly as possible, requesting and obtaining admission to probation.

While he was still a novice there, turning over in his mind almost constantly and insatiably the memory of the blessed man, one Sunday near the end of the night-office sleep began to steal upon him, weary and afflicted as he was in many ways. And behold, the most reverend Father, whose love inflamed him, appeared, graciously addressing him and admonishing him to direct his intention continually toward God, with a daily outpouring of tears. If he did this, he might confidently expect divine mercy and Bernard’s own visitation. Having said these things, he withdrew into his tomb, which stood there before the altar of the blessed Virgin Mother [Col. 1103A]. This withdrawal was so evident that the brother did not know whether he had seen it sleeping or awake.

When he opened his eyes and reflected with sweet recollection upon the admonition of that most compassionate Father, Bernard suddenly appeared to him again, now fully awake, and offered himself to be seen with bodily eyes. He stood close before him, so that he could easily have been touched by hand, looking attentively at him and, as it were, examining whether he slept or woke, after the manner of those who rouse sleepers for the night-office. As the novice stared, stunned and astonished, he who appeared immediately vanished; and—marvellous to relate—it seemed to him as though Bernard had sensibly entered into his inmost heart. Thus, greatly kindled in love for God and for that most blessed man, he was trained day by day to receive the new life in spiritual joy and exultation.

Finally, on the following night, while similarly attending the brothers’ vigils, he experienced there such great grace of divine visitation as he had never before felt in his life [Col. 1103B]. He rejoiced that he had obtained all this through the merits of him whom he loved. As for many days he frequently poured forth the remembrance of the abundance of this sweetness, he shed copiously sweet and pious tears, with which he could not be satisfied day or night. When his year of probation had passed, he received the holy habit with great devotion, striving by continual meditation and perpetual diligence to preserve undefiled the garment of innocence with which he was clothed not so much outwardly as inwardly. Thus, following with unwearied effort, according to his measure, in the footsteps of the venerable Father whom he uniquely loved, and ending his life in good perseverance, he was, as we trust, joined with him in heaven, whose companionship he had ardently desired and diligently sought while still on earth.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning a monk to whom the Lord Jesus Christ appeared once and then a second time.

[Col. 1103C]

Another novice brother in the same monastery, having resolved to seek the Lord with his whole heart, was accustomed frequently to pray with hands joined or outstretched, whenever he could suitably do so. One night, therefore, at the beginning of the vigils, while he was in choir, with closed eyes and hands stretched out toward God, the Lord Jesus Christ suddenly came there, speaking to him and saying: “Stretch out your hands to Me.”

At this voice the brother opened his eyes and was greatly astonished; but he could not easily determine whether he had heard this asleep or awake. Yet from this voice he conceived much fervour and devotion in his mind, and thereafter took care to preserve the same form of prayer. Some time later, when he had become a monk and was standing more privately in a corner of the same church, praying, as he was accustomed, with attentive mind and joined hands, he was suddenly in the spirit. And behold [Col. 1103D], the Lord Jesus Christ stood before him, receiving the brother’s hands within His own hands placed beneath and outstretched, and as though admitting him to profession. When the man returned to himself after this, he rejoiced exceedingly; and, taught now by happy experience, he most certainly believed that the divine presence is everywhere, but especially—as our lawgiver St. Benedict testifies [Note: [Col. 1103D] St. Benedict, Rule, chapter 19.]—when we apply ourselves to the work of God, whether in prayer or psalmody.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Brother Ansulph, who saw the Lord Jesus hanging upon the cross.

A man of great devotion and endowed with great grace, named Ansulph, while still a novice at Clairvaux, saw in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ appearing to him as though hanging upon the cross. As it seemed to him, two other novices who were with him in probation were also there [Col. 1104A]. When he had humbly worshipped the Lord and begged in most lowly prayer that He would have mercy upon himself and his companions, the merciful Lord looked upon him and blessed him, and also one of the two novices mentioned above.

But when the novice who saw these things perceived that the third had not been strengthened by the Lord’s blessing, moved by brotherly compassion, he began to entreat the Lord more earnestly not to exclude him from the bounty of His blessing. The Lord answered that this man was by no means to be blessed, but rather belonged to the mass of the accursed. Awakening at these words, the novice rejoiced greatly in the blessing by which he and his companion had deserved to be blessed by the Lord; but he waited in uncertainty to see what would become of the one concerning whom he had heard such a sad sentence.

On the third day, therefore, that third neophyte broke the bond of the Trinity, as though to express the sad etymology of his own name. For his name was Malgerus [“ill-fated spear”]; abandoning the Order, he returned to the vomit of secular life and became a contemptible apostate [Col. 1104B]. But the other two, strengthened by the blessing of the Lord, through His mercy possessed the blessing as an inheritance; and by persevering justly and piously in their resolution until the end of life, they showed that they belonged to the lot of those blessed by the Lord.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the brother who in a vision kissed the right hand of the Lord as it blessed him.

A brother of the same monastery, having turned himself with great desire to seek the Lord, and continually ruminating in sweet meditation upon the remembrance of our gracious Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, once saw Him appearing to him in a vision. Concerned for his salvation, he earnestly begged for His saving blessing, saying: “I beseech You, Lord [Col. 1104C], bless me, that I may be saved.”

But the gracious Lord, who had deigned to appear to His poor servant for this purpose, that He might mercifully grant him some drop of His sweetness, raised His holy right hand and blessed him. Immediately, in that same vision, the brother seemed filled with inexpressible joy; and, grasping in devout confidence the most blessed right hand by which he had deserved to be blessed, he kissed it with great devotion and said: “I give You thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because You have blessed me; and I shall be saved.”

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the brother who saw blessed Mary Magdalene in a vision.

To another religious and devout brother it was granted in the spirit to see blessed Mary Magdalene standing before the altar with a most radiant face and habit. At this sight the brother was filled with great joy. While he reflected in his mind, wishing and praying, and sighing with the great ardour of holy desire, that the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God—to whom he served most devoutly night and day—might likewise be shown to him, a voice spoke to him in the vision itself, saying: “You must know that you are not yet fit to behold the most sublime brightness of the immaculate Mother of God and Virgin. Therefore strive, grow, and advance as much as you can, that you may someday deserve to see her” [Col. 1104D].

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the great progress of a certain lay monk.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Bernard commends, in the sermon *On the Height and Lowliness of the Heart*, the humility of a convert who, while reckoning the virtues of another, judged himself to lack them [Col. 1104D].]

(See above, *First Life*, book VII, col. 437.)

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning a convert whose devotion St. Bernard knew through the Spirit.

(See ibid., col. 439.)

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the vision seen by a brother at the death of another brother.

[Col. 1105A]

A brother of holy conduct, worthy that the Lord should deign to reveal His secrets to him, once saw in a vision that he was, as it were, placed in the infirmary at Clairvaux. And behold, certain precious garments of mantles and silks were being cut and prepared in that house by venerable persons. Greatly astonished at the novelty of this, he was told: “These ornaments, at which you marvel so much, are prepared for one of the daughters of the abbot of Clairvaux, who is now about to go forth to her wedding. And because she has less beauty in herself than befits her lineage, she must at least possess the fragrance and adornment of precious garments, by which she may please the eternal Bridegroom. Into His most pure bridal chamber there can in no way enter not merely a stain of sin, but not even a wrinkle [Col. 1105B] of negligence which the indulgence of His most kindly love has not covered.”

At that same hour the death-board was sounded, and a brother died there. It was found concerning him that, although he had led an innocent and gentle life, he had nevertheless been somewhat negligent and lax in his work. Therefore, since his own merits did not furnish him with the grace of complete adornment, it was necessary for the brothers to provide him more abundantly with adornment from their prayers.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the lay monk who learned the Mass in a dream.

The Holy Spirit, distributor of heavenly gifts, who dispenses to individual believers, as He wills, every good gift and every perfect gift descending from the Father of lights, deigned to grant a certain unlearned lay monk a special and marvellous gift of His grace. This blessed man, named Walter, not inferior in faith and devotion to learned and literate men, held the office of keeper of the vestments at Clairvaux for a long time. He provided clothing for the brothers with much sweetness of charity, not according to respect of persons but according to the needs of those in want. He was also dear and acceptable both to God and to men through the purity of his innocent life.

Once, as he rested in his bed, a venerable person appeared to him in sleep and commanded him to enter the oratory as quickly as possible and devoutly sing Mass to the divine Majesty. Greatly astonished at the novelty of this command, and at the same time considering the lowliness of his own person [Col. 1105C], he hesitated through modesty; but, constrained by the authority of the one commanding and not daring to resist, he swiftly obeyed. Undertaking the unfamiliar task and clothed in priestly vestments, he celebrated in his dream a Mass of the Holy Spirit with great devotion.

When he awoke, he knew by heart that same Mass which he had previously wholly unknown, being unable to read [Col. 1105D]. He retained it in memory for many years thereafter, and endeavoured to ruminate upon it more sweetly in his meditations and prayers because he delightedly remembered that he had learned it not from human teaching but by divine inspiration.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the great patience of a certain convert in his sickness.

(See above, *First Life of St. Bernard*, book VII, col. 441.)

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the convert to whom knowledge of the divine Scriptures was granted.

The infirmarians of Clairvaux used to recount with great joy and wonder [Col. 1106A] concerning a convert of religious life a certain marvellous and memorable grace which the Lord deigned to grant him before his death. For when the mother of grace had resolved to reward the merits of his good life, and he had lain ill for some time, the illness at last grew severe, and the clearer signs of death foretold the imminent dissolution of his little body.

And behold, as the Holy Spirit breathes where He wills and when He wills, the man’s understanding was illumined by a new and truly astounding miracle, and his tongue was opened. This rustic man, who had never learned letters, began to use Latin speech fluently, expounding certain remarkable sayings from the sacred Scriptures, though uttering nothing except what accorded with sound doctrine. The lay brothers, who did not know letters, wondered at this novelty; and having summoned the monks as quickly as possible, the sick man continued in their hearing to unfold the mysteries of the Scriptures in eloquent speech [Col. 1106B]. Moreover, he sang certain sweet melodies concerning the mysteries of the holy Church in modulated tones, melodies never customarily heard anywhere, so that he astonished his hearers by the novelty of the miracle and soothed them by the sweetness of the song.

But what did almighty and merciful God intend to make known to mortals by granting such an unusual grace to a simple and rustic man, except this: that in the eternal blessedness of His kingdom, according to the Apostle’s saying, “there shall be neither Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, learned nor unlearned” (Col. III); but, according to the Prophet, all shall be taught by God (Isa. LIV; John VI), and: “All, from the greatest of them to the least, shall know me, says the Lord” (Jer. XXXI)?

Would that restless men, who go round sea and land to be filled with the chaff of letters and puffed up with the vanity of knowledge, that men may call them rabbis and masters, that they may boast of being jurists and decretists, dialecticians and sophists—so that in the business [Col. 1106C] of piety they may serve greed and ambition—would attend to this example! Would that, I say, they would receive and understand with the ear of the heart that, just as the loftiness of divine knowledge was granted at his death to this rustic and unlearned man, who endeavoured simply to walk in the fear of God, and knowledge of heavenly mysteries was opened to him, so conversely they themselves will remain foolish and senseless at their death, when they vomit forth the riches of knowledge which they swallowed without the fear of God, and God draws them out from their belly. [Note: [Col. 1105D] An allusion to Job XX.]

We say this not in order generally to condemn seekers after knowledge, but in order to teach every person first to lay the foundation of the fear of God in the trench of humility; for the fear of God, according to the true definition, is the beginning of wisdom. Then let him build upon it as much knowledge as he will; for knowledge never puffs up where divine and brotherly charity alike build up.

Thus this new theologian of whom we have spoken, who began with the fear of God and deserved to attain the summit of perfect wisdom at the end [Col. 1106D] of this present life, after for some time delighting his hearers like a most sweet cup with a variety of sayings and the modulated sweetness of songs, at last passed from this world to the Father in a good confession, to be happily absorbed into the abyss of eternal light. As I think, he had received its firstfruits in this life only in order to make us run the more eagerly in the fragrance of the ointments with which he was anointed (Song I), since we should recognize that the fountain of true wisdom lies open only to the meek and humble.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the convert oxherd who saw in a vision the Lord Jesus driving oxen with him.

A convert in one of the granges of Clairvaux held the office of oxherd, a man pure and of great simplicity [Col. 1107A]. He promptly and devoutly performed all that his superiors enjoined upon him, and most patiently endured his daily labours for the sake of divine reward. Once he saw in a dream the Lord Jesus Christ beside him, a most delightful sight, holding the goad in that most sweet hand of His and, on the other side of the pole, driving the oxen with him.

When he awoke and reflected upon the gentleness, kindness, and sweetness of his most compassionate fellow-worker, the fire of vehement desire suddenly blazed in his heart. He sighed for Him and desired to see face to face Him whom he had deserved to have as a fellow-worker in a blessed vision. Since he greatly desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I), the gracious Lord, who walks with the meek and whose converse is with the simple, did not wish to delay the desire of His poor servant. The same brother was soon seized by illness and lay in bed; and on the seventh day [Col. 1107B] he ended labour and pain with death, and happily attained everlasting life with eternal rest, which is Christ the Lord.

At his final hour, his most reverend abbot, blessed Bernard, came to him in visitation, to take leave of his returning son, whose conscience he knew to be pure and simple, and to fortify with his blessing one preparing to depart against the robbers of spiritual wickedness. When Bernard learned from the sick man’s own account of the vision just described, he greatly rejoiced. After he had died, Bernard confidently declared of him that he had walked with God and that God had truly worked with him; and therefore the Lord had taken him away. For the compassionate Almighty could not abandon His servant in the supreme struggle when He had deigned to be his companion and fellow-worker in labour.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the great humility of a certain convert.

[Col. 1107C]

(See above, *First Life of St. Bernard*, book VII, col. 442.)

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the convert after whose death the Lord deigned by a glorious revelation to show how great his perfection had been in life, and how great the blessedness he attained in death.

In the aforesaid monastery there was another convert, a religious man of great gentleness, who through the teaching of divine grace had learned to be meek and humble of heart. The other brothers testified of him that he had never been seen to become angry, nor ever, when provoked by any injuries, to break out into impatience. By God’s inspiration he had firmly resolved in his mind that whenever he was complained against by any brothers, justly or unjustly, he would pray for them and say at least one *Our Father* for each of them. Instructed by his example [Col. 1107D], many brothers of Clairvaux retain the same custom to this day almost as a law.

Yet, if the devotion and humility of this blessed man were acceptable to God and pleasing to men, let those who act in the contrary way consider what answer they will make to God on the day of His dreadful judgment. If they happen to be complained against by anyone, they become exasperated and break out into impatient words; they cannot conceal the resentment they conceive against those who complain of them, or even seek an opportunity, impelled not by the spirit of charity but by that of resentment, to complain in return against those who accused them, with all the exaggeration they can command.

Once the aforesaid man of God, travelling upon business of his church, had to pass alone through the narrow defile of a certain wood. There he happened to fall into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, seized also the beast he rode with its small baggage, and left him absolutely nothing except charity alone [Col. 1108A]. But charity had not been carelessly left outside in a little chest; it had been wisely bound within the deepest recess of his heart by the firmest knots of patience, and therefore it could not fear the violence of assassins. Charity being safe, the servant of God could lose nothing, since whatever he lost while it remained was as nothing.

When the robbers had gone and had proceeded a little distance, he threw himself down in prayer, beseeching the Lord to forgive them this impiety. One of them, however, returned by God’s prompting and followed the brother from afar, watching inquisitively to discover what he was doing. When he saw him persist long in prayer, he ran swiftly back to his companions, striking his breast and saying: “Woe to us, wretched and condemned men! Behold, we shall all die because in our wickedness we have treated so badly a man so holy, a brother of so holy a monastery.” For, he himself having revealed it, they had learned that he was from Clairvaux. “For,” he said, “since leaving us [Col. 1108B], he has not ceased to pray with groaning and tears; and undoubtedly he is even begging the Lord for his enemies.”

Hearing this, those robbers were pierced in heart. Swiftly returning, they found him still intent upon prayer with bended knees. They immediately restored everything they had violently taken from him, humbly asked forgiveness, and let him go in peace. Seeing this, the brother gave boundless thanks to Christ the Saviour and rejoiced exceedingly more over the compunction of the robbers than over recovering his property.

This good man, having persevered commendably in his holy resolution until the end of his life, was at last called by the Lord and gathered to his fathers, to behold the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, from that time and for ever. On the very day of his death, the following vision appeared concerning his glorification.

In a monastery far distant from Clairvaux there was a monk of religious life and great reputation [Col. 1108C]. For his holiness all the brothers of that monastery sincerely loved him and each particularly honoured him. On the same day on which the aforesaid brother died at Clairvaux, this monk also came to his final hour in death. When he seemed already near death, he was snatched away from human awareness, so that, deprived of all use of his limbs, he lay motionless from morning until the ninth hour. Only a little breath remained in his breast, distinguishing him from a dead man.

Thus, from morning, as has been said, until the ninth hour, he remained in ecstasy. At last he returned to himself, recovered strength, and his tongue was again loosened for speech. Those present, astonished, asked him the cause of his sudden departure and return. He answered:

> “Today, when I was drawn away from bodily senses and lifted up in spirit, I suddenly found myself brought, as it were, into a paradise of delight, a place most glorious and exceedingly splendid, whose fitness, beauty, and loveliness the narrowness of human understanding is insufficient to estimate. There appeared there great glory and much variety of precious vessels and other ornaments, and an infinite preparation of delights, as customarily occurs at the coming of some most mighty king or emperor. There were also innumerable saints there, shining with immense brightness. Some had already arrived; others were still coming from every quarter, hastening as though in rivalry toward a great spectacle and gathering from all directions as for a solemn feast. Moreover, the sweetness of heavenly harmony was heard there, and thanksgiving and the voice of praise resounded everywhere.
>
> “As I was greatly astonished at what I saw and heard, I asked my guiding angel what was the cause of so great a solemnity and joy.” He answered: “This is the new celebration of a certain new saint, taken today from the house of Clairvaux and now solemnly introduced into these joys.” Having said this, he ordered me to depart quickly and return to human affairs [Col. 1109A]. As I greatly detested this prospect, I begged from my inmost heart that I might not be sent back any further from that happiness to the miseries of the body. But he replied: “You must by every means return to your brothers, until you announce what you have seen. When this is done, you shall immediately return and obtain a share in this eternal joy. For this purpose I have been sent to you, to declare to you the things I have seen, so that you also, doing good, may advance and persevere in goodness, knowing indeed that the reward shall not fail for your work.””

Having said these things, he immediately took leave of them and fell asleep in the Lord. The entire community of the monastery mourned him with great lamentation, since he was a most holy man and of great usefulness; all had been instructed by his example, and all depended upon his counsel. Carefully noting the time and hour, they made inquiry at Clairvaux and learned that the brother mentioned above had died on the same day on which this vision had been shown. His manner of life was found to have been so great and such that it readily gave credence to so great and such a miracle [Col. 1109B].

When one of the brothers told blessed Bernard of this vision with great wonder, Bernard answered thus:

> “And do you, brothers, marvel at these things? I marvel rather at your unbelief and hardness of heart, because you still do not believe, or perhaps pay too little heed to that truthful voice crying from heaven: ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. Henceforth, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours’ (Apoc. XIV). To me it is clearer than daylight and more certain than the life I live that all who persevere obedient and humble in the purity of this Order will, as soon as they have put off the flesh, immediately be stripped of every misery and clothed in the glory of immortality.”

Hearing from the mouth of so great a Father this testimony concerning the purity of the Order, the brothers were greatly strengthened. Praising the Lord’s mercy for the glorification of the brother who had pursued the purity of the Order with all his strength, they too strove not to shrink from the ways of a stricter life [Col. 1109C], that they might deserve to become partakers in the glorification promised to those who walk for Christ’s sake in the narrow and strait way.

Would that we also, who hear or read these things in these last times, in which, as charity has grown cold, lukewarmness and negligence have begun to enter everywhere, might grow warm again to imitate the vigour of the fervour and devotion of the holy Fathers. Otherwise, though we have beginnings of conversion like theirs, we may become degenerate through reprobate conduct; and, since we neglect the purity of the sacred Order, be estranged from the holy purity of that highest blessedness and assigned to that place “where no order is, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job X).

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the brother whom St. Bernard warned in a vision not to yield to temptation.

After the passing of the most reverend Father Bernard, there was at Clairvaux a brother who, at the beginning of his conversion, [Col. 1109D] like a new soldier, endured frequent assaults of the enemies and bravely received the repeated darts of temptations upon the shield of patience. Above all, he felt the spirit of fornication so grievously hostile that he could scarcely drive away, by the hand of holy contrition and prayer, the fantasies of miserable flesh which that malignant one continually strove to inject into his heart; crushed in this frying-pan, he went about sorrowful all day long. The affliction of this most troublesome conflict increased daily, and the inexperienced recruit did not possess such patience as to think that he could endure the violence of the harsh passion any longer. He therefore resolved to yield in spirit to the tempter, cast off the religious habit, and return to the world.

And when he was already anxiously watching for an opportunity to depart, the blessed Bernard, who had died shortly before, appeared to him in a vision, rebuking his sluggishness and reproving the wickedness which he had conceived in his mind and was striving to accomplish in act. When the brother replied that he had resisted for a long time, but could no longer [Col. 1110A] bear the force of temptation, the saint said to him:

> “Know beforehand that many conflicts still await you. But act manfully and do not fail, for the Lord will be with you as a helper in times of need, to deliver you. Therefore I promise you that, if you persevere in the Order to the end, you shall be saved. But if perhaps anyone tries to harm you on the last day, I will answer for you, and I will lay down my soul for your soul.”

O truly faithful friend, loving father, mighty helper! After the death of his flesh, proving himself still more faithful in the blessed life, he so graciously visited this wavering little sheep, already on the point of falling into the abyss of apostasy; he cherished him with gentle consolations, strengthened him with exhortations, and by God’s grace led him back from the precipice of death to the paths of life. Encouraged by so great a father’s promise, the aforesaid brother wholly expelled from his heart the spirit of faint-heartedness and distrust. Incredibly strengthened for the contest of struggle, [Col. 1110B] he could thereafter be moved from his steadfastness by no devices of the evil spirit or violence of temptations. Rather, as had been foretold him, sweating through the contests of many struggles, he deserved, through God’s grace, to carry off the triumph of victory over them all; persevering in the holy Order until the end of his life in the best manner of life, he happily attained eternal salvation, according to the pledge of his father beloved of God.

## CHAPTER XXII. Of the brother to whom St Malachy and Blessed Bernard appeared and who was chastised for his fault

Another brother of the same monastery, so corrupted in mind by diabolical prompting that he was now planning to apostatize from God and make a pact with hell—that is, to return to the world—saw in a vision of the night blessed Bernard and holy Malachy, the most reverend patrons of that place, walking through the dormitory and visiting the brothers resting in their beds one by one, [Col. 1110C] blessing them.

When, in the course of their visitation, they came to the bed of the man who saw this, they neither looked upon him so kindly nor strengthened him with the blessing by which they had fortified the others; rather, they stood before him as if angry. Then blessed Malachy said to Saint Bernard:

> “This wicked and restless man, harboring no good whatever in his heart, does not fear to devise iniquity in the chamber of his heart. Already, with an inclining will, he has assented to the devil’s persuasion, so that he may return as soon as possible to the vomit of the world.”

Hearing this, blessed Bernard said to him:

> “Do you seek to flee from my monastery? And where, wretch, will you flee from the face of the Lord? Believe me: you have conceived these things to your ruin. I know, I know: ‘affliction alone will give understanding to what is heard.’ Since you neglected to correct yourself through the fear of God, chastised by deserved blows, you will not attempt to flee any further.”

Having said this, he began to strike him repeatedly with the staff which he held, saying:

> “Behold the wages you deserve. [Col. 1110D] Rise now and flee, if you can.”

When the brother awoke, he found himself wholly battered and bruised by those beatings, so that he was taken to the infirmary and confined to bed. Trembling and afraid, he begged the brothers attending him to bring the prior to him as soon as possible. When the prior had been summoned, he confessed with great contrition of heart the wickedness which he had conceived in mind and intended to carry out in deed, and also the punishment which he had suffered for it. The prior rebuked his sloth and sluggishness as he deserved, and imposed penance for the guilt of instability. The brother then truly came to his senses, and the desire to flee never again seized him. For, having profitably learned how hard it was for him to kick against the goad of grace that spurred him, he thereafter strove, with fear and trembling, to cooperate with that same grace, which was mercifully working his salvation within him.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Of the lay brother who deserved to see holy angels at his death

[Col. 1111A]

A certain lay brother of the brethren of the aforesaid monastery once fell ill. He was a religious man of praiseworthy conduct, who, in the simplicity of his heart, had run with an unoffending foot along the narrow and confined way by which one goes to God, as became clear at his death. For when he had completed his good course and had now come to his last moments, he saw, with open eyes, holy angels standing present by his bed. When he saw them, wonderfully rejoiced, as though already triumphing over death, he said to the brothers standing around:

> “Do you not see the angels of God who have now arrived? Ring the board at once, therefore, for they are awaiting my departure.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, released into precious death, he immediately rendered up his blessed soul. Nor is there any doubt that the spirits of the blessed ones whom he had deserved to see beforehand received it [Col. 1111B] and led it with them to the joys of everlasting blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How a lay brother who washed his stockings without permission was divinely punished

Since we have already said much, for the edification of those making progress, concerning the eminent morals, religious manner of life, and precious death of the holy Fathers, I now wish, as a warning to the negligent, to insert the negligence of a certain brother and the punishment which he divinely endured for that negligence. Thus, just as those who desire to advance are stirred by examples of virtue toward better things, so every negligent person, terrified by the vengeance of divine correction, may fear to transgress not only the greater but even the lesser institutions of the sacred Order.

A certain lay brother in one of Clairvaux’s granges presumed to wash his stockings without his master’s permission. He had gone out [Col. 1111C] alone and stood on the bank of a stream flowing near the grange, engaged in the work he had begun. Alas, wretch! He did not consider that those who presume to violate the purity of the sacred Order even in the smallest matters grievously offend. While, therefore, as we have said, he persisted in this rash undertaking, to which he had not his master’s conscience as witness, he heard a voice crying out, as though one person were speaking to another:

> “Strike him, strike him.”

Without delay the same lay brother felt himself struck by two most severe blows, one on the head and the other on the feet. Trembling and pale, he hurried back to the grange and, with trembling lips, told the brothers what he had done, what he had heard, and what he was suffering. They immediately sent him to the abbey, where he confessed, with all the humility he could muster, both his sin and the penalty of his sin. He said that the same blows which he had received invisibly were gradually creeping inward, one from the side of his head and the other from the side of his feet; [Col. 1111D] and that he would certainly meet the end of his life when the blows joined one another in his heart.

The outcome proved this true: after a few intervening days, that brother ended his life in a good confession, going to God, we believe, all the purer because he had deserved to be punished for his fault by a more terrible death. But what do we suppose is the reason why that righteous Judge, the Lord of Hosts, who judges the whole world in equity, so often seems to pass unequal sentence for a similar fault? It is certain that the wisdom of God, which disposes all things not only sweetly but wisely, neither wishes to deceive nor can be deceived.

How many there are today who are covered by the religious habit and called by the name of monks, who, although according to their Rule and Order they have renounced private ownership, nevertheless, after the example of Ananias and Sapphira, do not hesitate with rash presumption to possess property! The power which went forth from the mouth of the apostle Peter punished those persons with terrible death (Acts 5), while no stroke touches these; on the contrary, they seem to spend their days in prosperity—would that they were not about to descend in an instant into hell! Yet even in the Cistercian Order itself, which, by God’s grace, is pure and untouched by so monstrous a vice as private ownership, there have been, or are, since the time when that brother received the sentence of such harsh death for a fault that seemed slight, persons who, lightly committing lesser offences without regard for the sacred Order, are accustomed to imply or say, “What is it? How much does it matter?” They do not heed what is written: “He who despises small things shall fall little by little” (Ecclus. 19). [Col. 1112A]

Yet almighty God does not punish them immediately—not because it is now less grievous a sin than it was then to wash something without permission or to do another thing without the superior’s command, at the time when God chose sternly to strike such acts as an example for posterity, but because he is gracious and merciful and deigns, by his most kindly patience itself, to call us to the remedies of confession and penance. But if there are any—may God avert it!—who think that they can do these supposedly slight things without grave danger to their souls, and who neglect to wash away such transgressions by the fitting fruits of confession and penance, then, as the bilge-water of negligence gradually swells while they care less and less, the ship of their conscience will undoubtedly sink into the depths unless God comes to its aid.

Therefore let all of us, who are bound by the title of profession to the most illustrious Cistercian Order, strive with every diligence to keep not only its greater but also its lesser institutions, lest—God forbid!—the fervor of the Order grow lukewarm and perish in our time, and we, if found guilty of such great sacrilege before the righteous Judge, be swept away with the wicked by his stern sentence, so that we may not see the glory of God. [Col. 1112C]

## CHAPTER XXV. Of the monk who presumed to sleep without stockings, and was therefore forbidden by a divine revelation to become abbot

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Caesarius says that this incident of a monk sleeping without stockings occurred in Gaul; but neither he nor this author adduces a suitable place or witness. And if there was any fault, it was slight and was erased by penance. But I make no judgment concerning this.]

Since, as the foregoing shows, we have learned with what severity an offence was punished which was indeed committed deliberately, but, in my opinion, was by no means incurred through contempt, I wish to recount another somewhat similar occurrence—though it happened not at Clairvaux but in another house of the Cistercian Order. By this we may prove that even the transgression of the least commands is not of slight weight before God, and that the sloth of our minds may be roused by this double example, as by a hand of vigilance, to awaken to its own safeguard.

A certain Cistercian monastery was vacant of an abbot. Father Abbot was summoned so that, in his presence and with his advice, the brethren of that house might, according to the institutions of the Order, choose a suitable person as father and shepherd of souls. When the time of election approached, and Father Abbot had learned each man’s vote and wishes both from private and public conversations, he found that the sounder party, unanimously and in agreement, had settled upon a certain person who happened then to be absent but was expected to arrive immediately. That person was the chief cellarer of the house.

On the night before the day of election, Father Abbot heard, by divine revelation, a voice saying to him:

> “See that you do not appoint as abbot that monk who presumed to sleep without stockings.”

At this voice the venerable abbot was greatly alarmed, and pondered with much astonishment and uncertain thought what the Lord might deign to indicate to him by it. The person mentioned above, who was thought fit for the dignity of so great an office, had arrived late on the day before the election. Very early the next morning, making the sign customary for confession, he drew Father Abbot into the chapter-house and humbly confessed that once, while travelling and overcome by excessive heat, he had presumed to remove his stockings and sleep without them.

Then the elders and those of more mature counsel met with Father Abbot to deliberate about the election. They all began, with one vote and one judgment, to seek the very man whom the secret of the divine revelation had judged should be deprived of such honor. Father Abbot therefore informed them more privately what had been divinely commanded to him, and advised them to elect another person, saying that it was impossible for him, against his conscience, to be disobedient to the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Of the remarkable fervor of John, formerly prior of Clairvaux, of sweet memory

[Col. 1113B]

I think it will be fitting, for the edification of posterity, to recall by the service of the pen a man of virtue, John, formerly prior of Clairvaux, of sweet memory, whom earthly condition has carried away. Taking fire from the warmth of the house of Rechab—whose name is interpreted “ascending,” that is, from the fervor of the heavenly discipline handed down by holy Father Bernard—he set ascents in his heart. With such unwavering constancy he observed the boundary of paternal tradition that, regarding the wine of carnal pleasure or worldly pomp as a pestilential poison, he would in no way consent to drink it at all.

The manifestly miserable poverty of our own time requires us to do this, for lukewarmness and negligence have become so strong that today each person thinks himself very fervent if he is not found altogether [Col. 1113C] lukewarm and lax. This vigorous man, then, exercising the office of prior at Clairvaux for many years, administered this share of responsibility with such cheerfulness of spirit and endurance of bodily labor that he seemed to have set as a seal upon his heart the saying which blessed Father Benedict proposes to the provost, or prior, of a monastery:

> “The more he is set over the rest, the more diligently he must keep the precepts of the Rule.”

[Note: [Col. 1113D] St Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 65.]

He was therefore exceedingly prompt and eager in performing divine things, resting neither by night nor by day. Above all, he devoted all his mental care to the sweetness of psalmody, which in that sacred community was rendered with much deliberation and intensity of voice; so that it might indeed be a cause of astonishment and admiration to all, though an example for imitation to few. The Lord had given him an instrument quite suitable for the work of devotion: namely, a deep and powerful voice. He took care to spend it happily in the service of the Giver, knowing, to be sure, that streams of graces should without loss be restored to their own spring, that they might flow forth again more abundantly.

He stood in the midst of the young women with timbrels, as superior to the others by the dignity of his office, so also surpassing all in the fervor of holy devotion and the raising of his voice; chanting and striving to go before the princes, that is, the angelic spirits joined with those who chant, ready to offer the devotion of the chanters in the sight of the divine Majesty as the fragrance of sweetest incense. Nor did he consider it a slight loss to his conscience if, owing to hoarseness or some bodily infirmity, he happened to render the solemn synaxis of psalmody with less than his usual eagerness. Yet this happened very rarely, because along with his other gifts he had received from grace a sound body of sufficient strength, ready, at the will of the spirit governing it, for every good work. [Col. 1113D]

[Col. 1114A]

But who could worthily admire or suitably express the unbending vigilance of his mind in God’s service? During the very long, daily span of the sacred vigils, he encouraged himself to endure that arduous labor, manfully drove away acedia, sloth, and drowsiness; and, if through the frailty of human nature he ever found himself even rarely dozing, with what stern rebuke did he reprove his own negligence! To preserve the uninterrupted course of the vigils unbroken, as though warned by a reminder, he had ingeniously fitted a piece of wood to the upper part of the stall where he stood. If, wearied by the length of the vigils, he began to doze, the inclination of his nodding head would meet the wooden mallet, which struck it and by its sudden blow made him more alert for watching.

Moreover, whenever he happened to be free at other times for manual work, he frequently showed himself far from idle in that exercise as well, exhorting the faint-hearted to endure labor not so much by voice as by example. Especially at the time of cutting and harvesting, when those blessed martyrs of Clairvaux are, as it were, fried in a frying-pan all day long, he clung to work so persistently that he thought himself daily washing away by sweat, on those laborious days, all the negligences of other times.

To remember that he was a stranger and sojourner upon earth, possessing here no abiding city but seeking the future one, he took as little as possible from the substance of the world. By the beauty of sobriety and frugality he chastened his body, because the strength of the soul is perfected in the mortification of the flesh.
