He kept the same moderation and humility in clothing, always choosing and embracing coarse, old, patched garments, but fleeing costly, soft, and fine ones as a kind of plague. To say nothing of other things, he would not allow even the pillow of his bed, upon which he was accustomed to rest his weary head after nocturnal vigils and daily labors, [Col. 1114C] to contain feathers of any kind; he stuffed it with hay and straw and lay down thus, not a deaf hearer of the maxim read in the *Lives of the Fathers* but avoided by many as too harsh: “Every bodily rest is abominable.”

O blessed—and rather desirable—lowliness and self-abasement in true humility of this holy man, contrasted with the arrogance, in most wicked presumption, of that abbot of whom we have learned by reliable report that, while governing a certain Cistercian monastery in the regions of Saxony, he did not deign to use cloth made from the wool of that country, but each year had costly Flemish cloths purchased for himself, so that by such adornments he might satisfy his pleasure and vanity!

After that man died, when the monks were dividing his garments among themselves, the prior of the house kept one of his tunics. When, on a certain solemn night, he put it on as though out of reverence for a feast day, he cried out terribly, as if he were being burned by glowing sheets of fiery bronze, and flung the detestable garment far away from him. Once thrown down, it appeared to emit sparks from itself like glowing iron. Astonished at the miracle, the others who had taken something from that accursed property brought their individual portions into the middle with all speed and placed them together in one place, while very frequent sparks flashed from every side as though from a blazing furnace. Nor did the deadly prodigy cease until neighboring abbots had been called in as witnesses of so fearful a judgment of God.

Not so humble John, not so! He considered the reproach of Christ’s humility more precious than all the pomps of Egypt (Heb. 11). He did not seek costly clothing, but longed with prayers and desires for the glorious garment of the angels.

## CHAPTER XXVII. With what constancy of mind the venerable prior John trampled the pleasures of the flesh

[Col. 1115A]

Yet in these and similar exercises of holy religion and devout labor, he possessed such constancy of mind and long-suffering patience that, although he sweated in daily struggle, he did not readily allow himself to steal any refreshment of temporal consolation. Except when extreme necessity pressed, he would never consent to leave the brothers’ vigils or enter the infirmary.

It happened once, while he was attending the sacred vigils, that he was afflicted by bodily illness and could not perform the songs of psalmody with his customary vigor. As he felt the sickness becoming increasingly severe within him and creeping diffusely through his vital parts, although his thoughts strongly urged him to leave the choir, he nevertheless remained—sad indeed, and considering [Col. 1115B] lest, oppressed by the severity of this illness, he might be compelled to enter the infirmary, which as far as he could he had always tried to avoid.

When the solemnities of the vigils had ended, he went to a more private place, and there, with no witnesses present, he spoke to himself all the more safely because more secretly:

> “What now, miserable John? What will become of you now? Are you ill? Overcome by such a little discomfort, will you enter the infirmary, which is accustomed either mercifully to restore bodies laboring under the scourges of God or terribly to expose the consciences of those pretending to be scourged? Very well indeed: you will go up to a bed spread and adorned with softer mattresses; and the softer things in the cellar and the more delicate things in the store-rooms will be prepared more carefully for your flesh, subject to death and decay, in deference to the office which you hold unworthily. And so, by your example, more negligent brothers will be encouraged to pursue comforts for their own flesh. Must you then interrupt the course of your penance because of this luxurious illness? Why do you not rather presume upon the mercy of God, who is able to moderate your sickness, so that he may exercise your body and you may not be compelled to diminish anything of the labor of penance, which is the seedbed of eternal blessedness?”

By God’s direction, a monk was nearby in the place where the man of God was speaking thus to himself. Separated from him only by the partition of a wall, he clearly heard the whisper of that devout murmur. He immediately hurried to the most reverend Abbot Gerald, whom we mentioned above, and informed him what he had heard from the prior. Summoned by the abbot, John was compelled, scarcely yielding even to obedience, to enter the infirmary, although the growing severity of his illness itself seemed to require it.

But it is not for our littleness to expound how vigorously, judiciously, and wisely he administered the office entrusted to him; how kindly, devoutly, and charitably he showed himself to his brothers; or how firm and authoritative he proved when the discipline of justice demanded it. [Col. 1115D] He accommodated the delicate and weak, yet he never allowed novel customs—usurped contrary to the form of the Order and smelling more of flesh than spirit—to steal into Clairvaux during his time as prior. He knew that, through the negligence of superiors, such customs readily sprout up to overthrow religion and destroy souls.

He knew, certainly, that just as superiors are blessed who keep the traditions of the Fathers uninjured through the strength of discipline, so those are most miserable who, through their own negligence and carelessness, allow religion to grow lukewarm and the Order to perish. For once religion has been ruined, it cannot be reformed without the gravest scandal and disturbance to both superiors and subjects. He kept watch most carefully not only in greater matters but also in smaller occasions, wherever they might arise. Thus, on one occasion, he could by no means patiently endure that one of the elders, altogether decrepit and nearly toothless, should, by the indulgence of the venerable Abbot Gerard, eat the infirmary’s bread in the gathering of the brothers. [Col. 1116A]

This impatience did not arise from the wasting pest of envy, but from the fervor of religion and zeal for the Order. He said:

> “Were there not old and weak men before us in this holy house, from whom yet nothing such as we now presume was ever appropriated? Did they not receive bodily relaxations and indulgences more at the discretion of the one commanding than at the demand of their own will, and in such a way that mercy bestowed upon them did not at all conflict with the customs of the Order? We know, indeed, that some of them had flown so far above the cares of the flesh through the loftiness of their spiritual life that even in extreme old age they considered themselves miserable if they were found inferior to others in vigils or fasts; nor would they consent in any way to receive bodily comforts offered to them by their superiors.

> “We must fear, and fear greatly, lest, while our holy predecessors began powerfully in the Spirit and completed still more powerfully in the Spirit, we, beginning in the Spirit, be completed in the flesh—God forbid! (Gal. 3). Therefore, if there is among us an old man worn out by meritorious labors who cannot stand in the ranks of the community because his limbs are failing, it is better that he receive leave and spend his time of need in the infirmary than that, while remaining in the community among those who abstain and somehow sustain nature with coarser food, he seek the comforts of the infirmary. For I am certain that each shall receive his own reward according to his labor (1 Cor. 3), that he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly (2 Cor. 9), and that the Judge who threatens terribly and says that he will search Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph. 1) will, by the most searching examination, inquire on what pretext and under what necessity each person has avoided the burden of the day and heat which we have undertaken to bear in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts.”

Thus, in this zeal of holy fervor and splendor of religious life, John, foster-child of God’s grace, having praiseworthily completed his life and being about to receive from the supreme householder the daily denarius, and besides it a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing—which he had gained for himself through many labors, vigils beyond measure, and vigorous performance of God’s service—was seized by illness and lay down in bed.

When the venerable men Eskil, formerly archbishop of the Danes, and Alan, formerly bishop of Auxerre, came to visit him, they saw that this most fervent man did not yield even in this very grave illness so far from his accustomed rigor as to refresh himself at least with garments suited to his sickness and weakness. Moved by compassionate zeal, they ordered somewhat more manageable clothing to be brought, which they knew fitting for so great a person and such an illness, asking him to deign to wear them for relief. Then the strong athlete of the Lord, looking rather severely at the garments laid before him, said:

> “Will a soft and delicate garment make me more blessed than a coarse and rustic one? Or what profit will there be in losing, at the approach of death, the humility which from the first years of my religious life I have taken such care to preserve? Believe my lowliness: so long as breath remains in my body, I shall not depart from the lowliness through which I chose to be despised in the house of my God (Ps. 83), nor shall I give my enemies occasion to put me to shame when I speak with them in the gate (Ps. 126). But when, at the Lord’s call, I put off these dying limbs, now on the point of death, dress and adorn this rotten sack of flesh as much as you please; for I trust that it makes no difference to me what is done with the living mass once it is devoid of spirit.”

Fortified by such constancy of faith and virtue, the man of God John put off the substance of corruptible flesh and deserved to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. His body rests in peace, buried with fitting honor beside the sacred bones of the brothers of the old abbey, whose patience and [Col. 1117A] humility he had by no means sluggishly imitated.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Of the venerable Lord Gerard, monk of Clairvaux and later abbot

See above, *The First Life of St Bernard*, book VII, col. 444.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Of the vision by which a certain novice of Clairvaux was freed from his temptation
A certain cleric of the Order of Regular Canons came to Clairvaux, desiring a stricter and more secluded manner of life. He was devoutly received, and he too was careful to adorn the beginnings of his novitiate with the flowers of a sweet-smelling way of life. But because he found it very difficult to unlearn the sweetness of his former life, and the severity of the new one he had undertaken tasted less pleasantly to the palate of his heart, [Col. 1117B] storms of diverse temptations began to boil up from within him. Such, indeed, men coming from another Order into the Cistercian Order must experience much more than secular persons coming in from the world.

Before the eyes of his heart there appeared images of the practices to which he had long been accustomed; and the crafty enemy persuaded him that these had been reasonable and honorable. But his mind, still unformed, fled from and recoiled from the Cistercian observances which he was then obliged to learn, as though they were rustic and less agreeable. Yet divine mercy deigned to draw back from error and confirm in good purpose this wavering, tossing little sheep, already looking back toward the shameful backward step of apostasy.

In a vision by night he beheld—and behold, in the clouds of heaven came the Lord of majesty, Jesus Christ the Son of God, King of kings and Lord of lords, as though now about to judge the world in righteousness and render to each according to his works. Then, while the whole human race hung in great fear [Col. 1117C] and trembling before this examination, all the several Orders which are in God’s Church assembled separately and apart, exceedingly anxious about the observances and ceremonies of their Rule and Order, lest the most severe Judge, in that most subtle scrutiny of his, discover that they had done anything improperly.

Would that those men took heed of this who profess the Rule of blessed Augustine and daily read each of its sentences in their chapters, yet do not fear to live secularly, to be called secular, and to be so; indeed, they even glory in it. Or those who, although they profess the Rule of Saint Benedict by their habit and outward appearance of religion, by an entirely secular way of life keep faith with the world, and are known through their tonsure to lie to God.

Meanwhile the aforesaid novice saw a certain illustrious Order, of a great multitude, standing apart from the others. In its midst stood a most splendid young man, adorned with heavenly glory, who appeared to be the leader and protector of that divine [Col. 1117D] host. When that sacred assembly moved from its station in order to appear before the Lord, the aforesaid young man went before them with great joy, giving the entire company of followers no small confidence of obtaining mercy. The other Orders, moreover, yielding with utmost reverence as they came and bowing as they passed by, seemed in some fashion to congratulate them upon the prerogative of their blessedness.

Even the Lord Jesus himself, the splendor of the Father’s glory—though he is omnipotence of fearful and ineffable majesty—nevertheless, in the sweetness of tenderness, pity, and compassion, like the gentlest little worm of the wood, received the young man in the kiss of peace and illumined him and all his fellowship with the glory of his divine brightness.

The novice who saw this began, in immense wonder, to ask what was that congregation of the righteous which had merited to be honored by the Lord with so special a prerogative above the other Orders. He was told that [Col. 1118A] it was the Cistercian Order; and that the splendid young man was the most holy Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux.

As soon as he heard this, he returned to himself as though from an ecstasy and said inwardly: “Was I not a novice in the Cistercian Order, in that great house of Clairvaux? Why then, wretch that I am, do I lie sluggish in idleness and not hasten to join this most illustrious company, so that I may become a partaker with them of eternal blessedness?” Saying this, he began with all his strength to make swift strides, but, hindered by some obstacle, he could not advance. For something like a twisted and knotted branch of a tree, with tangled curves, gripped his feet and shins so tightly that, although he strove with all his might to break the impediment, he labored in vain.

Therefore, greatly angered with himself because so trivial an occasion deprived him of so great a good, while he was wholly occupied in freeing himself, he awoke. Prudently considering his vision, he turned, awake and sober, against the snares of the temptation in which he had been entangled, the indignation which [Col. 1118B] he had conceived while sleeping. With such severity did he banish from his heart the images of his former customs—images which he had once delighted to receive and with which he was wont to commit fornication—that he no longer allowed them to rule him. But he embraced with the whole desire of his mind the sacred institutions of the Cistercians, which, though they are a mirror of righteousness, had been made contemptible in his estimation through the working of malignant spirits. In them, by the hard and narrow way, not running as one uncertain, he attained the crown of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXX. How demons wished to harm a certain lay brother, but could not.

A certain lay brother, one of the shepherds of Clairvaux, being a good and religious man, performed the duty entrusted to him with every care and with the gentleness [Col. 1118C] of the fear of God. But the envious enemy of every good, exceedingly provoked by the devotion and simplicity of his way of life, attempted to contrive some wickedness against him. With God’s help, however, the devices of his deceit dashed back upon himself and were reduced to nothing.

Once, when this brother was at the sheepfolds, keeping watch and holding the night watches over his flock, behold, there suddenly arose in the air a great commotion of whirlwinds and a violent storm of winds fighting among themselves. Frequent thunder also roared, crashing terribly on every side; and most frequent lightning, bursting from heaven, struck immense fear and horror into human minds.

The aforesaid brother therefore rose, repeatedly fortifying himself with the sign of the cross; trembling and anxious, he invoked the name of the Lord and humbly implored the aid of all the saints. As he stood in prayer, he began to hear the noise and shouting of what seemed [Col. 1118D] a vast army rapidly approaching those parts. The nearer they came, the more clearly their voices sounded. Among them were heard not only human cries and the blasts of trumpets, but also the roars of beasts and monsters of diverse kinds, and terrible voices.

When they came with immense noise as far as the sheepfolds, as though they would tear the sheep themselves to the bone, they were driven back by divine power while the brother prayed more intently. They could by no means enter; but, dividing into companies and swiftly passing to either side, they did them no harm whatever. Nevertheless, two of them, enormous in stature and blacker than soot, turned aside toward the praying brother. After standing a little while before him, one said to the other: “Truly the devil leads us, and he has now made us come here. Did I not tell you sufficiently that we are not permitted to pass through good?”

Having spoken thus, they departed swiftly, as if in winged flight; and when they had gone a little way, [Col. 1119A] all the dwellers in darkness vanished with them. The brother himself who saw this vision made it known to us under the attestation of truth. Indeed, his manner of life was such that we thought it sinful not to place faith in his words. It is therefore clear that the opposing powers are forbidden to pass through the goods of the righteous, unless perhaps, for some compelling reason, they are divinely permitted to do so.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the brother to whom the Lord Jesus appeared with his glorious mother.

In the house of Fontis-Mauriniacum there lived a certain lay brother named Robert. Sent there from Clairvaux, he was by no means forgetful of the religious life and discipline which he had learned at Clairvaux, but in his entire conduct gave the brothers of that place examples of virtue and devotion.

Among the other works of piety which he diligently [Col. 1119B] offered to the Lord, this was preeminent: he devotedly persevered in the service of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, and frequently and sweetly pondered the memory of his special patron, Bernard. Having happily completed the course of this present life, he deserved to foresee, in a prophetic vision, the certainty of his salvation and also the day of his death.

Five days before his falling asleep, he saw in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ and the most blessed Mother of God, with Saint Bernard the abbot, standing in a garden of delights whose charm and glory were so immeasurable that human speech could not explain them. The brother who saw these things stood apart and humbly entreated the regard of divine mercy.

Then the most merciful Mother said to her Son: “Lord Son, what will you do with this poor man of yours?”

And the Lord said to her: “Whatever pleases you, Mother.”

She, the protector of the poor and [Col. 1119C] comforter of the humble, answered: “I wish, then, that you send him into your rest.”

He said to her: “Let it be done for him as you wish.”

The most blessed Virgin replied: “And when shall this be?”

The Lord said: “Let him come on the fifth day, and be saved.”

When the vision had passed, that brother reported to the others what he had seen and heard, leaving them astonished and awaiting the appointed day. To prove the certainty of the revelation, as the illness which oppressed him grew worse, on the fifth day, according to the Lord’s word, he departed from the body and was taken into that rest and peace which surpasses all understanding. The most blessed Virgin, Mother of God, deigned to obtain this for him through her most merciful prayers.

Blessed, therefore, are all who trust in her and diligently persevere in her service with watchful devotion, because as a most generous rewarder she will return into their bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6). The brothers of that same monastery, greatly edified by so happy an assumption [Col. 1119D] of the man of God, also became emulators of the discipline of Clairvaux which they had seen in him. They applied themselves all the more eagerly to veneration of our Lady, the holy Theotokos, because they knew that nothing they could devote to her service could perish.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the monk to whom it was said: “Your sins are forgiven you.”

Among Christ’s athletes who exercised in the spiritual wrestling-school within the arena of Clairvaux was a vigorous director of the contest, named Enarrandus. Formerly a noble knight in the world, he abandoned worldly pomp and exchanged vain soldiery for fruitful warfare. Having joined the soldiers of the Temple of the Lord and proved faithful among them, he was also made master [Col. 1120A] of the soldiers of the Temple. In that office he learned to direct the energy of his soul and the strength of body which he had received from the Lord, not against citizens but against enemies; and prudently hoped from his valor not for earthly applause but for the reward of heaven.

But because that warfare, knowing nothing of Mary’s repose, was wholly occupied with Martha’s laborious concerns—which can scarcely, or never, be carried out without the dust of faults—in order that he might take the vows of an even holier warfare, he betook himself to Clairvaux. As before the second warfare had ennobled the first, so now the third surpassed the second.

He began not to exercise bodily strength but to break it with fasts, vigils, and many labors; and he applied himself to mortifying his own will, proving himself a lover of voluntary poverty, which alone is the true warfare of Christian religion. He was diligent in contrition and prayer, earnestly imploring, with daily tears, the mercy of Christ the Lord for his former offenses.

After practicing such things for a long time, he became, [Col. 1120B] according to the prophet, “a man seeing his affliction under the rod of the Lord’s indignation” (Lamentations 3). The merciful Lord now wished to add unleavened bread—that is, the grace of consolation—to his wild lettuce—that is, to the bitterness of his repentance—without which the Lamb of eternal life cannot be eaten. Thus the Lord deigned to bestow upon him, mourning and afflicting himself, the abundance of his forgiveness.

Once, while engaged in prayer, coming before the Lord’s presence with confession and supplication for his sins, he was suddenly caught up in an ecstasy of mind. He saw the Lord Jesus Christ saying to him in a most gentle voice: “Your sins are forgiven you.” Immediately released from the ecstasy and returned to himself, he was greatly comforted. Giving thanks to God, he learned thereafter to “serve the Lord with fear and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2). Growing old in an excellent manner of life, full of days he was gathered to his fathers, to receive from [Col. 1120C] the Lord the reward of his labor: eternal life.

This venerable man also related to us a memorable miracle of God which had recently occurred. He had heard it from certain most honorable brothers and his fellow soldiers, and it had happened in their presence, as they had more certainly ascertained the matter.

In the regions of Germany there was a knight, valiant and noble by birth, who, when the time of his present life was completed, gave up his spirit. After he had lain dead for a long time and the time for burial was already at hand, his soul suddenly returned and the man appeared alive again. Throwing back the covering, he opened his eyes and sat up on the funeral bier.

[Note: [Col. 1119] If the knight rose again, as is said here, though otherwise destined for damnation, it must altogether be supposed, although it is not stated, that he then made sacramental Confession.]

All who were present were astonished; the weeping and lamentation of the mourners immediately ceased, and they asked the man raised from the dead the cause of so great a marvel. In the presence of his wife and his brother, who was to succeed him in his inheritance, he began to speak thus:

“When,” he said, “I closed my eyes in death, I was immediately led to the tribunal of the Judge for examination. [Col. 1120D] There, weighed in the balance of justice, I was found to have less than was necessary for salvation. And when the sentence of damnation was rightly about to be pronounced, through the intercession of the saints who were present there I was permitted to return to you and seek from your mercy a remedy for the two matters which principally harm me: namely, the very great burden of debts, and the unlawful bond of marriage.”

Then, turning to the woman, he said: “You know, my beloved wife, that, being related by a line of affinity, we contracted an unlawful marriage, for which we are both held guilty of eternal death. Recognize that one remedy alone remains: if, abandoning worldly pomp, you join yourself to Christ’s marriage through monastic profession, you will obtain pardon for me and glory for yourself.”

She gladly accepted this and promised that she would do it at once. Then, summoning each of [Col. 1121A] his creditors, he ordered his brother to satisfy each one according to his demand. Among the rest, however, a certain Jew came forward demanding three hundred solidi owed to him. Fixing upon him a stern face and flashing eyes, to the amazement of all present, he said: “You have no right in heaven, nor on earth, nor in any creature of God. Yet, lest we seem to judge you before the time…”

Then he ordered that payment in full be made to him, just as to the others. Having said these and many similar things, he again laid back his head and gave up his spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning a religious lay brother of Clairvaux named Lawrence.

There was at Clairvaux a religious lay brother named Lawrence, whom we also mentioned above—

[Note: [Col. 1121D] Distinction III, chapter 15.]

—when, writing some matters concerning the venerable lord Gerard of Farfa, we made mention of him. This man, then, [Col. 1121B] was spiritual and devout in all his conduct, continually persevering with remarkable constancy in prayer and contrition. For many years, while he guarded day and night in the treasury the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, he could scarcely ever be found there at any hour otherwise than intent upon prayer, watering the pavement with prolonged weeping.

He had acquired, through God’s grace and not without great labor, this height of purity and devotion. For at the beginning of his conversion he was harassed by many temptations and exercised in prolonged battle against the poisonous suggestions of malignant spirits. One night, after Matins had ended, while he was alone in a certain dwelling, behold, an unclean spirit, bellowing and wailing, wheeled about him in wandering circuits. The brother made the sign of the cross upon his forehead and asked who it was.

The shape-shifting deceiver, in order to strike greater fear into a mind still untrained and tender, replied: “I am he who tempted and scourged [Col. 1121C] Job.”

Hearing this, since he was still new to the holy way of life, the brother was greatly afraid and fled from the face of the malignant spirit; and he did not see it again.

After the passing of blessed Bernard, it happened that the same brother was sent by the venerable lord Philip, prior of Clairvaux, to Roger, king of Sicily, on business of that church. When he had entered Rome and learned that the same king had died very recently, he was deeply troubled in spirit and did not know at all what he ought to do in such a crisis.

Remembering his holy father Bernard, under whom he had often been sent on various business and had prosperously gone and returned, he turned to prayer with many groans and tears, invoking the same saint of God and saying: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horseman” (4 Kings 13), “why have you forsaken us? Alas, holy father, what shall I say, or what shall I do, poor and wretched little man that I am, deprived of every counsel and help? While you lived and at your command, I went confidently [Col. 1121D] to diverse lands and nations. Everywhere I was received because of your favor, bearing, of course, your greetings and letters. Kings and bishops, with all others, received them as a blessing sent from heaven; and all the nobler persons rejoiced to be ennobled by your gifts of blessing.

“But now that you have died, my favor too has died with you; there will no longer be anyone to extend a helping hand to a stranger and needy man. And behold, the king who loved you with sincere affection has died, and his son has risen in his place—a boy who perhaps does not know you. If I choose to seek him, so far away as he still is, and happen to suffer rejection from him, it will be an inconsolable grief to me, after the fatigue of so much labor and such a long journey, to return with the business unaccomplished—whereas while you lived I was accustomed to return to your Clairvaux laden with every good thing. But if I return at once and leave the undertaking unattempted, [Col. 1122A] I fear being charged with sluggishness and folly. Stretch forth help, I pray; provide counsel for one in need; and do not despise the groaning of your pitiable servant.”

That same night, therefore, the same most blessed Father appeared to him and greatly comforted him, saying: “What has come over you, brother, that you should so distrust God’s mercy and my intercession? When or where have you found my aid lacking in your necessities? Or do you perhaps think me weaker now, when I have been admitted into the powers of the Lord, than I was formerly while I lived in the flesh? Go, therefore, in confidence, for all things will turn out favorably; and in this very matter you shall know that I have sent you.”

While the saint said these and very many other things, the brother entirely melted in soul through the excessive ardor of devotion; and while his heart gave birth to immeasurable joy, tears of devotion also burst forth outwardly. When he awoke, he found his eyes and cheeks wet, and perceived that even the pillow upon which he had rested his head [Col. 1122B] was soaked on every side by the same flood of tears.

Setting out early in the morning, after he had left the city, he found a band of merchants traveling to Sicily for trade. Recognizing that he was from Clairvaux, they immediately received him gladly into their escort and table-fellowship, and daily supplied him freely with every necessity. At last, entering the presence of the king of Sicily, he found great favor in his eyes. He not only obtained a successful outcome in the business for which he had been sent to the Father, but the king also opened his treasuries and, with great devotion, sent through the same brother no small sum of gold for the building of the new basilica of Clairvaux, for the soul of that Father.

When the aforesaid brother returned to Rome, he nevertheless found such favor there that from the gifts of cardinals and other Romans he received a very abundant blessing. Their generosity enabled him to lead from the city as many as ten buffaloes; and, with the immense astonishment [Col. 1122C] of all, God protecting him and the merits of his holy Father assisting him, he brought them as far as Clairvaux.

For who can sufficiently marvel that a weak and elderly man, with only two little boys, could drive such animals of enormous size and ferocity—animals which surpass even oxen in bulk and strength—safe and unharmed through so many perils of places, through so many schemes of robbers and brigands, on so long a journey? This is especially remarkable since, as they assert, that kind of animal had until then never been seen anywhere in the whole West on this side of the Alps. He could scarcely avoid for even one day the attacks and violence of evil men; yet, with God guarding his faithful servant through the prayers of Saint Bernard, he passed through all these things unhurt.

It happened that he was obliged to pass through a certain town controlled by leaders of robbers, from whose hands no one could escape uninjured unless he prevailed by force. Now, as the dawn already [Col. 1122D] shone red in the morning, when he was leaving a meadow in which he had spent the night with the animals, he earnestly begged the Lord and Saint Bernard to rescue him from the imminent danger. And behold, he saw at a distance what seemed two men coming toward him, each carrying a lighted candle in his hands. As they gradually approached and had almost reached him, they suddenly vanished from his sight, and gave the servant of God great confidence of escape.

Entering that nest of the devil, he was immediately stopped, and men ran in from every side to seize the plunder. But at that very hour certain honorable men arrived by God’s will. Recognizing that he was a man of Clairvaux, they delivered him from the hands of his assailants and let him depart with all that he had. At last he reached Clairvaux, bringing in, to the wonder of everyone, beasts of a new kind. Their offspring multiplied, and from that place they now spread daily through many provinces.

The brother himself returned to spiritual pursuits and with all eagerness submitted his aged shoulders to the sacred discipline which Saint Bernard had handed down. In pious confidence he trusted that through Bernard’s merits and prayers he would be delivered from eternal evils and enjoy everlasting goods—Bernard who had mercifully freed him from the manifold dangers of his present journey and deigned to bring him safely to his Clairvaux.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Account of a certain spiritual monk of Clairvaux.

A certain religious and spiritual monk of the community of Clairvaux lived for a long time in one of the houses of Clairvaux in the regions of Dacia. Returning to Clairvaux on one occasion, he recounted to his brothers, for their edification, a joyful miracle worthy of all acceptance, which, he affirmed, had recently occurred on the border of [Col. 1123B] Saxony.

In those same regions there was a monastery of the Cistercian Order, in which a monk of great religious devotion and marvelous humility served the Lord devoutly in simplicity of heart. He was fervent and devout in every observance of the sacred Order, despising and humbling himself in all things. Above all, however, he devoted himself to silence and quiet, continually giving himself to prayer, contrition, and reading. Wherever he could, he was always drawn to prayer or reading with wonderful delight. Yet in reading he sought the fruit of devotion more than learning, and delighted in it as in all riches.

When the hour of his departure from this world drew near, as he was gravely ill and had already been anointed with the oil of the sick, he requested that his body be washed at once and clothed in the garments in which he was to be buried. The brothers objected to this novelty and delayed [Col. 1123C] doing it; but as he persisted in his request, they granted what he wished out of reverence for his holiness.

When this had been done, he said to those standing by: “Let each of you return to his duties, for I am not going to die now. Rather, on the following day, after the servants’ meal, the Lord will call me.” All the brothers were thus held in expectation by this prophecy of the man of God. The next day dawned, and at the very hour he had foretold, the sound of the board summoned everyone swiftly to perform the office of commendation for the departing man.

They did this all the more devoutly because they more surely hoped that the dying man would soon be glorified in eternal life. The brother, now drawing his last breath, was suddenly illumined by divine grace; and with a joyful face he said to those around him: “Behold, now there enters to us that beloved of the Lord, blessed John the Evangelist.”

After he had been silent a little while, he said again: “Behold, now comes the blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary.”

After a short interval, suddenly illuminated by greater grace, he added in a clear voice: [Col. 1124A] “Come, brothers: behold, now comes the Lord Jesus Christ, and with him a multitude of holy angels and other saints.”

Having said this, he was immediately caught up in the jubilation and exultation of his heart, because of the sweetness of him whom he beheld. He began to sing and to intone that antiphon:

> Come to his aid, saints of God; hasten to meet him, angels of the Lord.

And thus, singing, he gave up his soul. Seeing the man exulting in death and dying in song, the brothers quickly took up the same antiphon as though from his own mouth, and sang it through in a loud voice with deep affection of devotion.

The aforesaid elder faithfully made these things known to the brothers of Clairvaux and vehemently kindled their hearts to contempt of the world, self-abasement, and love of God. May all who read or hear these things become imitators of them, knowing with complete certainty that the more despised a person has been in this world, and the more desirous of silence, quiet, and humility, the more glorious and exalted [Col. 1124B] he will appear before God in the world to come.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the bright lights of Clairvaux.

Let it be enough, then, that we have spoken thus far concerning the bright lights of Clairvaux, and also concerning that most brilliant sun which, rising from that conspicuous valley, illumined all parts of the world with the rays of its brightness. Yet we have gathered only a very few flowers from the spacious and most flourishing meadow of that blooming blessed valley, in order to kindle within ourselves the fervor of sacred devotion. Drawn by the loveliness of their radiant beauty and refreshed by their sweet fragrance, may we learn, with all vigilance of mind, to despise the world with all its vanity and pleasure and to long for the homeland of eternal brightness—in the book of true theology, in which are written lamentations, song, and woe.

But who is so fit for these things? Therefore, what else remains to us except [Col. 1124C] to eat the bread of sorrow in the bitterness of contrition, so that our tears may be our bread day and night; that with all the marrow of our hearts we may sigh for those of whom we have spoken? Perhaps the heavenly guests, moved by mercy, may cast down at the mouths of barking puppies beneath the table even some small fragments of those sublime delights, by which we may be sustained, lest we fail on the way of repentance.

Moreover, just as in the Fathers mentioned above we have learned how generous God’s mercy is toward his saints, and how merciful his regard toward his elect who keep the commandments of life without pretense, so in the examples that follow we shall show with what kindness he sometimes forgives sinners, and with what severity he sometimes strikes offenders. Thus may we embrace mercy, prepared for every good work; yet, if we should find ourselves rather negligent in the way of God’s commandments, may we always ponder with fearful mind the curse pronounced against those who perform God’s work negligently.

## DISTINCTION FIVE. Containing salutary admonitions, demonstrated by examples, concerning the danger and punishment of certain vices.

[Col. 1123]

## CHAPTER ONE. Admonition of Lord Gerard, Abbot of Clairvaux, concerning not swearing and the danger of those who swear.

[Col. 1123C]

Of blessed memory Lord Gerard, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, whose precious death in the sight of the Lord we described above [Note: [Col. 1123D] Distinction II, ch. 27], was accustomed on occasion to restrain his brethren from the habit of swearing. To do so more effectively, he took care, by way of example, to relate a terrible occurrence which had recently befallen a certain swearer. He said that the venerable bishop of Cahors had made the matter known to him; the bishop’s chaplain also, a very worthy man, affirmed that he had been present.

There was, then, in those parts a certain carnal man who, while once playing at *alces* [a game, perhaps dice] and losing through dice that fell badly for him, swore in a furious voice whatever mad thing came into his mouth. When he had almost lost everything, another accursed gambler approached; pushing him aside in swelling indignation, he said: “Give way, fool, give way. I will play for you, since you know neither how to play nor how to swear.”

And when he too, being a son of perdition, was likewise losing, inflamed with devilish rage he began to swear by every member, inward as well as outward, of our Lord Jesus Christ, as though in order, wishing to leave nothing at all unsworn. Thus he uttered certain horrible and unheard-of oaths—or rather blasphemies—such as the devil, the instructor, indeed the true destroyer, of his heart and mouth, devised. But when with furious and blasphemous mouth he had exhausted every member of our Lord, God and man, he added to the sum of his condemnation by swearing also by the most holy members of His undefiled mother. With dreadfully rash presumption he strove to tear them all apart, one by one and in succession, with his poisoned tooth, so that all present who were of sound mind stopped their ears at the face of the blasphemer and reviler and beat their breasts.

The sacrilegious swearer had not yet completed all his oaths when, behold, divine and fitting vengeance suddenly struck and pierced the criminal with an invisible blow, as though of lightning, giving a dreadful manifestation of offended Majesty. Struck down, the blasphemer fell; thinking that someone had pierced him with a material sword, he cried out with a horrible groan: “Alas, alas, wretch that I am! Who are you that have killed me?”

After writhing on the ground for a long time and emitting deadly groans, at length, under the compulsion of the evil one to whom he had been delivered, he expelled his abominable soul, to be burned in Tartarean fires. When his body was stripped for washing, a fresh wound was found in his back, gaping with a terrible opening, as if some exceedingly large axe had been plunged there, so that the innermost parts of his heart, liver, and lungs were entirely visible. At this sight the swearers were terrified, seeing that the zeal of the Lord of hosts had punished the impious and blaspheming swearer with so grave a judgment.

As the swiftly spreading report drew trembling neighbours from every side to see the thing, one of his close associates hurried mournfully toward him. As this man travelled, a dead man appeared to him, whom he had known while alive, and said: “Do you recognize me? I am that deceased man, formerly not unknown to you. I know where you are going, but you weary yourself in vain. For he whom you think to find alive has already been swallowed by death. Yet there is one thing that I do not wish to conceal from you: the Lord Jesus Christ suffers many insults and injuries from those who revile Him, patiently awaiting, like a patient requiter. Nevertheless, He does not easily endure injuries and insults against His immaculate mother; rather, He either punishes them sooner with present punishment, or, if perhaps He reserves them for the future, strikes them more bitterly than other evils.”

When he had thus finished speaking, that dead man who was speaking vanished. [Note: [Col. 1125D] Caesarius relates the same thing concerning that blaspheming gambler as is related here. The statement that God avenges injuries to His Mother sooner than injuries to Himself is made lest she be thought despised and held of little account by God [Col. 1126D]; but the majesty of God, even when He does not punish, cannot fail to be held in reverence.]

The man then reached the place and found his friend already dead, as the dead man had foretold; and by reporting what he had heard, he added terror to terror and miracle to miracle.

The aforesaid venerable Abbot Gerard also affirmed that another impudent and execrable swearer had lived near the borders of the aforementioned city of Cahors. When he presumed with most filthy mouth to swear by the sacred and hidden members of the blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, he was immediately delivered to an unclean spirit and for a long time was tormented and distorted by the most severe suffering. His eyes were turned, his whole face swelled monstrously, and he stretched his burning tongue, thrust far out from his mouth. After being tortured by this long and horrible torment, he finally yielded his miserable soul to demonic spirits; nor did he draw back in death the unbridled tongue which he had thrust out.

By these and similar examples Lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, deterred his brethren from becoming accustomed to oaths. For although the habit of swearing is dangerous to every person, it is most certain that monks and all religious persons cannot employ even the smallest oaths without grave danger.

## CHAPTER II. On the Danger of Possessiveness

Lord Abraham, formerly abbot of La Prée, one of the daughters of Clairvaux, and of most devout memory, preserved, through Christ’s grace, the flower of virginity together with the fruits of good works—without which chastity is not of great account before God—until the completion of an unstained life. This most holy man, endowed with a singular grace of gentleness, bore the Lord’s yoke with unwearied zeal from his youth through all the days of his life.

While he was still young both in age and in religious life, he hid without permission a small strip of new cloth in his bed, intending to mend a garment. But when shortly afterwards he looked for it and, after turning over the bedding everywhere, did not find it, he went away astonished. His conscience reproaching him, he took care to erase as quickly as possible, by private confession, the petty theft he had furtively committed.

O great power of confession! Great likewise is the mercy of the Redeemer, who has in a manner placed the whole hope of human salvation in the sacrament of Confession. For just as no multitude or enormity of crimes and wicked deeds can prevent grace from raising one who confesses purely and humbly from the depths of the abyss and placing him on the height of heaven, so surely even the smallest sins cast one who neglects to confess them down from the height of perfection into the depths of miserable ruin.

Thus the aforesaid young man, who prudently saw that his slight sin could not be removed without the remedy of confession, was after a short interval washing dishes alone in the kitchen when, behold, that little piece of cloth fell through the air and was placed in his hands as though someone carried it there, so that he might wipe material dirt with the very thing on account of which Satan had tried to defile his soul with the stain of private possession. Recognizing it with complete certainty, and looking all about without seeing anyone in that house, neither above nor below, he clearly discovered that it had been stealthily taken by an unclean spirit, but that after his confession it had not been able to retain it.

Therefore, giving thanks to God in fear and also in joyful exultation of heart, he understood how carefully and fearfully those who have professed a life of pure and perfect poverty must guard against possessions of this kind, however small. For even a certain nun, as is read, endured the devil’s accusation at death because of a small thread of silk which she had placed in her bed without permission.

Another monk of the Cistercian Order, when stricken with illness and come to his last hour, had already lost the power of speech. He saw an unclean spirit, in the likeness of an ape, sitting on a rod placed beside the wall, where his scapular hung. In that old and torn scapular the brother had recently sewn, without permission, a small strip of cloth. The impure spirit gently handled it, repeatedly kissed it, licked it with his tongue, and stroked it with his hand.

Seeing this, the monk groaned; and because he could no longer speak, he pointed with his outstretched forefinger and stammered in half-formed, broken words as best he could, indicating that they should drive away that most wicked mocker. The brethren standing round him wondered and long questioned what he meant or wished to say. At last, through divine mercy, he recovered the use of his tongue and said: “Do you not see that obscene being sitting on my scapular and licking with his most filthy mouth that patch which I recently presumed to sew upon it without permission? Drive out the criminal at once, therefore, and remove the patch from the garment, lest this slanderous and impious mocker insult me at the end.”

Although all looked intently, they could not see the evil spirit whom he saw. They removed the scapular from its place, and the most wicked reviler immediately departed. The sick brother, having received penance for his fault, again became speechless; and shortly afterward died in a good confession.

We all, therefore, who profess the pure and undefiled religious life of the sacred Cistercian Order, renouncing the world and everything that belongs to the world, and indeed even ourselves, must take the greatest care not to give a stain to our consciences, or matter for accusation to our most cruel enemies, by giving, receiving, or possessing even the least and meanest things without permission. At the departure of Israel from Egypt—that is, of the soul from the body—they will press upon us from behind with more cruel reproach, more wicked insult, and more severe vengeance, punishing such transgressions by God’s just judgment, in proportion as we could now more easily avoid them if we kept the fear of God continually before our eyes, as the Rule commands us.

## CHAPTER III. How Great Is the Danger of a Monk Dying Without His Habit, That Is, His Cowl

[Note: [Col. 1127D] Caesarius also relates the story of the monk who died with his cowl removed. But in the present time the sick are treated far more humanely; and, as in the use of meat, so also in clothing, dispensations are customarily granted to the sick.]

[Col. 1127C]

The distinguished Lord Jordan of Fossanova, a Roman by birth and a monk of honourable conduct, from Fossanova, one of the houses of Clairvaux, told us of a great miracle which the Lord permitted to occur in a Cistercian monastery in Italy for our admonition and correction.

A monk there, having run devoutly and humbly along the path of regular discipline as far as the goal appointed for him by the Lord, fell mortally ill. As his departure approached, he burned with the great heat of fevers. Attendants insufficiently discerning, and insufficiently attentive to the sacramental significance of the monastic habit, removed his cowl to relieve the heat and clothed him in a scapular; and while thus remaining through their negligence, he gave up his spirit.

But before his body was committed to the earth, the man who had died suddenly appeared alive again. To the astonishment of all, he began to speak as follows: “When, in the death of the flesh, I closed my bodily eyes and, removed from the senses of the flesh, opened spiritual eyes in the life of the soul, I was immediately received kindly by holy angels and brought to the gates of paradise in the habit in which I had put off the covering of the flesh—that is, without a cowl.

“When my guides attempted to bring me in and place me in the dwelling of eternal blessedness, the angelic spirits who appeared to hold the office of gatekeepers there looked at me closely. Discovering that a monk was without monastic clothing, they immediately shut the gates and excluded me, saying: ‘Is this man to be received into the order or rest of monks without a cowl?’

“Thus repulsed, I remained outside, fearful and trembling, fearing indeed to undergo the sorrowful sentence of damnation. But my guides interceded for me, saying that, apart from this matter, I had been a worthy man and sufficiently devoted in the observance of the monastic Order. Yet the immediate answer was that it had been established by an eternal law that a monk could in no way enter those gates without the monk’s habit, that is, the cowl.

“As I became more and more distressed, and greatly feared lest I be wholly excluded from the gates of eternal blessedness, I suddenly heard from those same holy gatekeepers that the merciful Judge, the Lord Jesus Christ, had passed sentence that I should return to human life, so that, having received penance for my negligence and been clothed again in my cowl, I might thereafter enter the gates of paradise without obstacle.”

On hearing this, the brethren gave thanks to God with much joy and amazement, to Him who alone does wonders. But the brother who had returned to life immediately received penance, put on his cowl in confirmation of his words, and departed in peace.

It is therefore clear that the monastic habit, in which the form of the cross is also expressed, possesses great mystery if the life of the monk is maintained. Thus we read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that it was shown to a certain holy man: he saw the same grace of the Holy Spirit which he had seen come upon the sacrament of baptism later descend also upon the monk’s habit when it was blessed.

## CHAPTER IV. On a Lay Brother from Whose Memory a Grave Sin Had Slipped Away

After a great mortality had once occurred in the house of Grand-Selve under the venerable Father Pons, afterwards abbot of Clairvaux, a devout lay brother there, named Stephen, fell ill. Touched by a desire to die, he scarcely consented to take any food, but with continual prayers and sighs begged that he might deserve to be led out from this vale of weeping, from this prison of the most severe exile of the sons of Adam.

Thus the Lord granted him his heart’s desire. When the infirmarian who had diligently ministered to him saw him dying with such devotion and tranquillity of heart, he too was vehemently kindled with a desire for death and said to him: “I beseech you, dearest brother: since I see that you are soon to be delivered from the miseries of this age and happily introduced into the joy of your Lord, when you come to our Lord Jesus Christ, may you obtain for me also from His goodness a swift passage.”

He replied that his aid would not fail him, if it were permitted. A few days after his death had passed, he appeared in a vision to this infirmarian and said: “Behold, received in peace, I see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, which incomparably surpass every delight of flesh and blood. And now, in fulfilment of my promise, I return to you to bring you help—not, however, the help which you rashly asked for, but that which I have known to be more expedient for you.

“Remember that, while you were still in the world, you committed such-and-such a grave offense, from which you have not yet deserved to be absolved by contrition of heart and confession of mouth. Confess it, therefore, and quickly do penance; for if it is not erased by confession before death, it will remain irredeemable after death.”

Upon waking, the brother recalled that grave sin which he had committed twelve years earlier, but which had been wholly erased from his memory by fatal forgetfulness. He therefore hastened to be freed by confession and satisfaction. Giving thanks to God, he clearly learned that the intercessions of the saints are not sought in vain, and that the sacrament of confession must not be held cheap, without which even sins unknown in this manner are thus imputed.

## CHAPTER V. On the Danger to Those Ashamed to Confess Their Sins

[Col. 1129A]

Since the Lord mercifully dispelled the ignorance and forgetfulness of the aforesaid brother and drew him to the saving remedy of confession, it now seems fitting to show how liable to condemnation are those who, forgetful of God’s dreadful judgment, either conceal or are ashamed to confess grave sins they have committed, blinded by vain and useless shame—of which Scripture says, “There is a shame that brings sin” (Sirach 4). Trusting in works of virtue which perhaps they have acquired in the course of time, they deceive themselves, though it is written: “He who sins in one thing”—that is, in confession—“will lose many good things” (Ecclesiastes 9); and: “He has become guilty of all” (James 2).

Lord Arnold, abbot of Belle-Loc, a faithful and religious man, told us of a glorious miracle. He said it had been related to him by a holy man, a prior of the monastery of Châlauc, in whose presence the event itself occurred.

There was in the Limousin a matron of most devout conduct. Though bound by marriage, she applied herself to fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and other religious practices, and appeared to live a regular life in secular dress. But in her youth she had committed a grave sin. Greatly ashamed of it, she never wished, because of excessive shame, to confess it to anyone.

Nevertheless, whenever she confessed to her priest, she made a veiled mention of this crime and ended her confession thus: “Of all my sins which I have now uttered and which I have not uttered, I confess myself guilty before God and before you.” Whenever she pronounced this conclusion and, as it were, seal upon her confession, she drew long sighs from the depths of her heart and at once dissolved wholly into tears.

After she had done this frequently and consistently for many years, her priest, being prudent and diligent, noticed that something deadly lay hidden in her heart. He tried by many means to draw it from her through confession. But as he made no progress by this concern, he advised her to visit the above-mentioned prior of nearby Châlauc and disclose her whole conscience to him as to a most holy man. The priest had privately taken care to forewarn the prior about this matter.

When the woman came to him and confessed, he could draw nothing from her beyond what the priest was accustomed to hear. It then happened that she fell ill and died without having confessed it. Since she lay dead for a long time, her burial was delayed while her daughter, who had been summoned from another more distant village to the funeral rites for her mother’s body, was late. When at last the daughter arrived in haste, uttering loud cries and moving everyone present to lamentation, the dead woman suddenly came to life through the most merciful power of almighty God; and as the soul returned to its own body, after the sad divorce there occurred a sweet reunion of spirit and flesh.

Then, as though awakened from a heavy sleep, she spoke thus to her weeping and lamenting daughter: “Do not be afraid, daughter. Let your eyes cease from weeping, for by God’s mercy I have now returned to life. Untie the hindering bonds of the wrappings in which I am confined, that I may rise.”

The bindings were removed with all speed, and the woman, raising her head, sat up. At her command the priest was quickly summoned. Everyone else withdrew, and the deadly infection was at once discharged and washed away through confession.

Afterwards, when people flocked together to see the miracle, the woman herself, now witness and herald of the inestimable grace of God wrought in her, explained the whole course of events to all. She described how she had been delivered through the intervention of the most merciful Mother of God and Virgin Mary:

“I, a miserable sinner, while I lived in this life among men, seemed to stand upright in human eyes because of the good works I performed and the religious life that I displayed; but before the eyes of almighty God I lay in the ruin of death. With impious rashness I did not fear to become a transgressor of His command. For the Lord established in His holy Church that no one can be saved without confession.

“Although I frequently made a pure confession of my other sins, I never dared confess to any human being a certain grave sin which I committed in my youth, because of excessive shame. For that reason I rendered all the good works I did fruitless and useless to myself. Yet I used almost every day to confess this fall of mine to the most blessed Mother of God, Mary, before her altar or image, or wherever I could, with repentance, mourning, and tears; and with pitiable complaint I implored her mercy, that she would not allow me to undergo the sentence of eternal condemnation for this sin of mine.

“But after I paid the debt of death, I was immediately surrounded on every side by malignant spirits. They cruelly seized me, drove me, examined me, and drew me toward the torments of hell to be damned, with the bitterest reproach for my sin. Meanwhile I recalled the alms I had given, my fasts, vigils, prayers, and other good works in which I had laboured for a long time. I wondered that, as though guilty of every crime, I was assigned to the torments of Gehenna without any mercy.

“I sought the light of my works; but immediately the pestilential corruption of my unconfessed sin rose terribly from the depths of my conscience, so clouding and darkening my eyes that I could in no way behold the rays of the true and eternal light which is acquired through almsgiving and good works.

“Alas! Then, though far too late, I understood that these were the wages of my obstinate and darkened heart. Then I was compelled not merely to know but to experience how ruinous it is for wretched mortals not to obey the commands of their Lord and Creator.

“Thus, deprived of every counsel and help, I remembered that I had often confessed with tears and lamentation to the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin the very sin for which I was receiving a just sentence of condemnation. Immediately conceiving some little hope, I prayed—not so much in words as in vows and sighs—to her, the true Mother of Mercy and sole hope of the wretched, that she would not abandon poor me, placed at the extremity of necessity.

“Without delay, that same comforter and protector of all who flee to her came like the morning star and the brightness of noon. She terrified and rebuked the demons who were mocking me because they had presumed to attack her little servant. She ordered them at once to put down their prey and leave her there until a judgment should issue from the Lord concerning what He commanded should be done.

“When the wicked spirits obeyed more swiftly than speech, that Mother of Mercy approached the blessed fruit of her womb, our Lord Jesus Christ, adored Him, and said: ‘I beseech Your mercy, Lord Son, do not hand over to the beasts that soul which has so often bewailed her transgression before my image.’

“The Lord answered her: ‘You know, beloved Mother, that she cannot be saved without confession.’

“But she said: ‘Lord, all things are possible to You. I beseech You, do not put to shame the face of this poor woman, who placed her trust in me and sought by many good and righteous works, though not according to knowledge, to appease Your countenance.’

“The Lord said: ‘Since it is not right that you should suffer refusal from Me in any petition, and since outside the flesh there is no place for confession and penance, it pleases Me that this soul, restored to its own body—which sinned grievously and retained it still more grievously within itself—should humbly confess in repentance; and then, being immediately brought back, it may at last receive mercy in due order.’

“Therefore, at the Lord’s command and through the diligent care of our most merciful Lady, a good angel was sent to me. Rescuing me from all the expectation of the malignant spirits, he restored me to my own body, as you see. Now that confession has been made, it is time for me to depart, never to return, but to sing eternally the mercies of the Lord, who, though I was unworthy, has so worthily withdrawn me from His dreadful judgment, mercy itself going before and following after.”

When she had said these things, she rested her head upon the bier; fortifying herself with the sign of the holy cross, she gave up her spirit.

Would that whoever, pierced by the dart of eternal death through some criminal sin, reads or hears this example might be moved to the saving remedy of confession and penance, knowing without doubt that no one will obtain pardon from the Lord who has scorned to humble himself before His vicar—that is, his prelate or priest.

But if anyone should try, without the foundation of confession, to build works of virtue upon the emptiness of presumption; or should presume upon a confession made at the last because of his own good works; or in still greater madness dream for himself something like what we have now related, let him know that the higher he has flown without the wings of confession, the more grievous will be his fall. Confession at the last is granted all the more difficultly in proportion as it is presumed upon more proudly. Singular privileges bestowed through divine grace upon very few persons utterly exclude general application.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] This story, though almost incredible, nevertheless appears certain. Our author says that he received it from Arnold, abbot of Belle-Loc; and Arnold asserted that he had heard it from the prior of Châlauc [Col. 1132D], who was an eyewitness. No one, however, should presume upon it or fail to provide for his own salvation.]

From these things it follows that it is much better, while opportunity remains and we are still in this body, to anticipate the face of the Lord in pure confession than, persisting in our obstinacy, to bear on the day of the general resurrection the never-ending mark of eternal shame and reproach before angels and human beings; and moreover to be struck by the dart of dreadful malediction, when it is said to the wicked and unconfessed: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

## CHAPTER VI. With What Mercy the Lord Corrected the Sleepiness of a Devout Monk; with What Severity He Rebuked the Sloth of Another, Lukewarm and Negligent Monk

[Col. 1131C]

In the aforementioned monastery of Grand-Selve there was a spiritual monk, endowed with great grace. Although he continually struggled with the fault of drowsiness and strove to render to the Lord, as was fitting, the pure service of devotion in psalmody, he could not overcome the frailty of nature in this respect.

Once, therefore, while standing in his place in choir and seeming to chant sluggishly and sleepily, a venerable person whose face he did not recognize stood beside him. Rousing the sleeping man, this person took hold of him by the garment over his breast and seemed to try to pull him out of the choir. As he was being drawn away, he opened his eyes, saw him, and said: “Who are you, lord, and why do you drag me so?”

He replied: “And you—why do you sleep so?”

It was as though he said: “Did you rise from your bed and enter the choir in order to make yourself a laughingstock to your enemies by sleeping and nodding your head, rather than in order to sing eagerly to the Lord your Creator in the presence of His holy angels?” Having said this, he released him and immediately vanished.

The brother who had deserved to be so mercifully corrected by the Lord for his sleepiness, shaking off in the fear of God the sleep of torpor and negligence, thereafter took care to be found more watchful in keeping vigil and chanting psalms.

There was another monk in the same monastery, named Bernard. Although he appeared strong in a youthful and vigorous body, he conducted himself more slackly than the others, showing himself lazy at manual work and sleepy at vigils. He was therefore no small burden to his companions and was noted everywhere for idleness, especially in church, where he was found particularly negligent.

One night, when the precentor of the monastery, weary of finding him asleep at vigils, awakened his excessive laziness more sternly than usual, Bernard rose in anger and went to the dormitory. As he approached the necessary house, behold, a crowd of demons stood at the door, shouting against him with tremendous noise and terror, repeatedly crying: “Seize him! Seize him!”

At hearing this he was suddenly filled with horror; hastily taking flight, he ran swiftly back into the church. When he reached his stall, trembling and gasping, he immediately suffered a failure of heart, fell to the ground, and lay for a long time without movement or sensation, as if lifeless [lacuna]. Carried thence in the hands of the brethren and brought to the infirmary, after he had somewhat recovered from that terror and returned to himself, he was questioned by the brethren about what had happened. Relating the event in order, he testified that he had paid the penalty for his obstinacy and sleepiness. A novice who was in the oratory at that very hour also testified that he had heard the same tumult and clamour of demons.

Thus that lazy and negligent brother, beneficially chastened by the goad of divine correction, learned that sloth, sleepiness, and idleness, and other plagues of this sort, truly are dung which oxen—that is, those strong in the fear of God—cast away, that is, abhor and detest. With this very dung unclean demons never cease to stone every lazy and useless person, to their great shame (Sirach 22).

See, then, how great is the difference between negligence contracted through infirmity, where amid daily struggle the vigour of the mind washes itself, as it were, in snow-water and strives to render pure service to the Lord—yet, lest it grow proud and arrogant, is stained with the filth of sleepiness—and miserable idleness, which throws away spiritual weapons, voluntarily surrenders itself to enemies, and is not merely drowsing but sleeping and snoring, at times more deeply in choir than in bed, without any alertness of mind resisting the malignant spirits who mock and say: “Bow down, that we may pass over” (Isaiah 51).

This difference is finely expressed by the twofold example we have related. The athlete of Christ mentioned above, fighting indeed through grace but yielding through weakness, was made more vigilant for his own protection by the gentle address of a good angel. But the other, whose sloth and folly we have exposed, was pursued by a troop of malignant spirits with terrifying and shameful cries, and was made distraught and nearly beside himself.

Let us take examples from the good, choosing rather to contend manfully with men of virtue in the spiritual contest. Yet let us so sympathize from the heart with the lukewarmness of the lazy and useless that we nevertheless strive by every means to flee their negligence, whether for hope of divine recompense or for fear of the fire of Gehenna.

For the elders of Clairvaux used to relate of our most blessed father Bernard that, when on one occasion he was present at the night watches, he saw an angel of the Lord, bearing a censer filled with heavenly incense, passing through both choirs. Those whom he found awake, chanting psalms, and praying, he refreshed in heart with the sweetest nectar of spiritual spices, removing weariness and sharpening their devotion. But those whom he saw sleepy, slothful, and useless, he passed by with a kind of indignation, judging them in no way worthy of the heavenly ration.

The venerable father Lord Richard, formerly abbot of Savigny, also made known to us a certain wonderful grace, experienced, I think, by very few, concerning a devout and holy [Col. 1133A] abbot who was abbot in one of the houses of Savigny. Divine generosity had deigned to bestow it upon him because of the merit of his devotion. For, when he had utterly banished from his heart not only carnal desires but even carnal thoughts, and kept vigil, chanted psalms, and prayed in purity and devotion of mind, with grace breathing down from above, he was accustomed to perceive through his nostrils the influx of a certain unfamiliar fragrance: a nectareous sweetness of cinnamon, frankincense, and balm, incomparably surpassing the fragrance of every perfume. He also felt poured into his throat a sweetness as of heavenly manna, containing within itself every flavor and every delight of sweetness. Like a living fountain springing up in his mouth and flowing thence into the inward parts of body and soul, it suffused and affected his whole man with marvellous sweetness, so that he could aptly say [Col. 1133B]: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118 [119]). Happy the soul which deserved already to taste and see, not only in itself but even in its body, though still corruptible, “that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33 [34]). For there can be no doubt that such an excellent gift, granted to anyone, powerfully extinguishes carnal desires in him, vehemently kindles spiritual ones, and melts the entire soul in the fire of divine love.

Moreover, it suggests the flight of evil spirits, indicates the presence of holy angels, and proclaims, by an experience both happy and true, the longed-for regard of divine mercy. Thus, yes thus, the Lord knows how to console those humble persons who are vigorous and devoted in his service. He also knows how to terrify the idle and inert, who pursue the comforts of their flesh beyond due measure, thereby declaring in a sense by present judgment what the prophet announces will be disclosed at the future examination (Mal. 3): namely, what difference there is [Col. 1133C] between one who serves the Lord and one who does not serve him; between one who vows to the Lord and fulfils the vow, and one who vows but does not fulfil it. Of the latter, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture (Eccl. 5), it would have been better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to render what was promised.

Therefore, what the Lord chose to do visibly and bodily in the persons mentioned above, with different recompenses according to the quality of their merits, we must know with complete certainty to be carried on spiritually and invisibly in all who profess the service of God. For just as the merciful condescension of God secretly visits, relieves, cherishes, and consoles those mindful of their profession, who, weary under no pressure of labor or vigils, readily and eagerly perform each day the course of psalmody and hymns with devotion, so indeed a horrible swarm of demons does not cease to foul those forgetful of their profession, unwilling, as the saying goes, to touch with the tips of their fingers the arduous labors of vigils and God’s service, with various fantasies of deceptions and passions; and it endeavors to make them, day by day, more inclined [Col. 1133D] toward the most perilous abyss of lukewarmness and negligence.

## CHAPTER VII. How great is the danger of seeking holy orders ambitiously

[Note: [Col. 1133D] The story concerning the ambitious seeker of orders is uncertain.]

Let the ambitious hear; let those impatiently panting after holy orders or ecclesiastical benefices listen to this example of an ambitious man. Let them hear, I say, and tremble; and, considering in lesser matters what they have to fear in the greatest, let them at last fear rashly to thrust themselves into the patrimony of the crucified Lord. For an inheritance hastily acquired at the beginning will lack blessing at the end, when the same Lord of majesty—who was crucified through weakness—is angry (Prov. 20).

A monk of the Cistercian Order, who had brought his life to its close in a very devout manner of living, was removed from the temptations and miseries of this changeable life when death [Col. 1134A] intervened. After his death, the sacristan of that house was sitting awake one night in his bed, as the time for the vigils was approaching, awaiting the clock’s signal. Suddenly the spirit of that same brother stood before him, clothed as though with a solid and tangible body, and addressed him in a sorrowful voice:

“Lord sacristan, I am that brother who has lately died; but I beg you to consider compassionately why I have now come to you. While I was still living in the body, although by God’s grace I zealously exercised myself in the observances of the Order, I nevertheless sinned grievously in one matter: I carnally desired the sacred order of the diaconate, and I was greatly agitated, without regard for the fear of God, to ascend to this rank of honor. And, what is still more serious, I left the body without worthy repentance for this sin, because I did not think it to be of so great a weight as I found it to be after death. But the merciful Lord has for this purpose [Col. 1134B] now permitted me to appear to you: that I, who can now merit nothing by myself, may be aided by the prayers of our brothers, who can still obtain God’s mercy both for themselves and for others. Therefore, I beseech you by the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: disclose my calamity to the prior, and ask him to absolve me in chapter and to deign to enjoin upon the brothers a general prayer for my deliverance. And, that you may know that what you see and hear is by no means a phantasmal illusion, you will find, as proof of the truth, the psalter which the porter sought in chapter some days ago and has not yet found, laid away in such a place.”

But although the sacristan had heard and seen these things and greatly wondered at so unusual an occurrence, he was a man of mature judgment. Thus, on that day, he said nothing to anyone about the matter, thinking that perhaps he would be mocked as a dreamer or as one deceived by demons.

The following night, while [Col. 1134C] he was again awake and sitting on his bed, thinking more attentively about what had happened the preceding night, the same dead man again appeared to him, awake and astonished as before, and said:

“You do not act rightly, Lord sacristan; you do not act rightly toward me, who bear the wrath of the Lord because I sinned against him—into whose hands, how dreadful it is to fall, may you never experience! Oh, if you knew how grievous even the least punishment now is for a soul released from the flesh, surely you would not act so negligently, but would strive with all your strength to come to my aid. Therefore I call upon you again and again by God: do not delay any longer, but hasten to carry out my request, for I hope that through the prayers of our brothers I shall obtain mercy from God, the most merciful Judge.
