And that every scruple of doubt may be removed from your heart, and that you may not doubt that I am indeed the man whom you knew well a little while ago when I was living in the flesh, behold: take from my hands the psalter which the porter sought in chapter and has not yet [Col. 1134D] found.”

The sacristan therefore took the psalter from his hands, profoundly amazed at such unheard-of wonders of God, since he truly is the one “who alone does great wonders.” The sacristan further wished to know whether the body which he saw was solid and tangible, and whether it was subject to touch as well as sight. Having a rod near him, he took it and, as though to satisfy himself by experimental touch, lightly swung it; but immediately, meeting no resistance whatever, it passed through the appearing body as through empty air.

When morning came, he made known to the prior and the brothers what he had seen and heard. He also produced the psalter he had received as a pledge of truth. Thus, through the common prayers of the brothers and the celebration of Masses, the soul of that brother was, as we believe, released from its punishments and, through God’s mercy, attained fellowship in eternal blessedness.

But why does almighty God, in these last times [Col. 1135A] of the present age, cause so much concerning the state of souls to become clear which had formerly lain hidden, so that by open revelations and manifestations the life of souls after death, and the disclosure of the age to come, seem in some measure to press upon us and to be on the very point of opening itself? Is it not what blessed Pope Gregory says: “The nearer the present age comes to its end, the more the age to come is already, as it were, touched by that very nearness and disclosed by clearer signs”?

Woe, then, to those who, while such great and manifest signs of God’s dreadful and eternal judgment break forth, still, according to the Apostle, pursue shameful gain and think godliness a means of profit; who do not fear by right or wrong to force themselves into sacred orders and ecclesiastical honors. And whereas the Apostle also says that no one ought to assume honor for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was (Heb. 5), these men, on the contrary [Col. 1135B], are not ashamed with proud eye and insatiable mind to beg for every kind of ecclesiastical dignity by entreaty, payment, and service—not in order, intent upon vigils, fasts, and prayers, to labor watchfully for the gaining of souls, but to satisfy gluttony and the belly, vanity, pleasure, and pride of life. Unless they come to their senses and repent, their condemnation will be harsher and more unbearable than that of all other people, in proportion as they have not feared unworthily to seize divine sacraments and carnally to arrogate to themselves the sacred orders of Christ’s vicars.

But what are we doing—or rather, with what rain of tears shall we be able to lament that the whole race of Adam’s children is so generally infected by this plague of ambition that the more religious, holy, and perfect a man strives to be, the more ashamed he is to admit that he is assailed by this subtle vice of a weak mind? For, as blessed Bernard testifies in one of his sermons, we are a noble creature, since we were created in God’s image. We all aspire upward, all strive toward heights, and all pursue lofty things. Nor would desire for elevation be a vice at all, if none of those eager to ascend were to transgress the law [Col. 1135C] set beforehand by the Most High. But because sin has intervened, making our intention crooked, our reason blind, and our will weak, it is necessary for us, because of our imperfection, to be pierced in our hearts, torn apart in confession, humbled by the labors of repentance, and wholly vigilant lest we ever give our members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. That is, we must never allow ourselves to be detected by neighbors or superiors as suffering from the disease of ambition through empty flatteries, pretended services, or any enticements resembling agreeable manners.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the danger of disobedience

[Note: [Col. 1135D] This author ought to have rendered credible, by giving proper names, what he relates concerning the punishment of the disobedient brother, as he did in the following [Col. 1136D] chapter in making credible the account of the devout but disobedient pastor.]

Since the Apostle says concerning our Lord and Savior that he became obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2), and since our most blessed lawgiver Benedict extends obedience even to impossibilities [Note: [Col. 1136D] St Benedict, Rule, ch. 68], [Col. 1135D] while the Lord himself declares concerning the prelates of his Church, “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10), it is greatly to be lamented that those who profess the sacred religious life, and vow obedience above all things and before all things, sometimes break forth into such a swelling of pride and disobedience that they can be moved neither by prayers nor terrified by threats into being willing to abate the heat of their madness.

Therefore I think it necessary to bring forward an example of disobedience, so that those who, with the gall of anger stirred and the ulcer of pride inflamed, neither fear God nor respect people, may, when they hear how dreadful is the judgment by which God resists the proud, learn rather to humble themselves and obey with the meek than to divide the spoils of obstinacy and arrogance [Col. 1136A] with the proud.

A lay brother of the Cistercian Order became disobedient to his prior. He contemptuously refused in his proud mind to do what he had been commanded, and neither fear of God nor the brothers’ gentle admonitions could induce him to obey the one commanding him. Indeed, with swollen and undisciplined answers, he babbled that he would never do it.

Meanwhile the sun declined toward its setting and the day closed. Full of the gall of rancor and bitterness, and not afraid to persist in his contumacy, he placed himself upon his bed as though to rest, heedless of the apostolic injunction: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4). But behold: at the first nocturnal signal, before he had fallen asleep, while he was still satisfying the vice of dreadful pride by devising evil in his heart, two wicked spirits, blacker than soot and more cruel than dragons, appeared standing before his bed. One of them said to the other, as though asking, “Who is this lying here?” [Col. 1136B] The other replied, “A lay brother.” Then the first speaker said again, as though indignantly: “Not at all; he is a disobedient man.” Immediately the other added: “Then, if he is disobedient, let us drag him to the gate.”

No sooner said than done. Laying hands upon the wretch, shaking him harshly from his little bed, and stopping his mouth so that he could not cry out, they cruelly dragged this disobedient and obstinate man from the dormitory and the company of obedient brothers. Then, carrying him through the air, when they had come outside the monastery enclosure, they began—horrible to say—to mock him, tossing him from one to the other as people at play throw and catch a ball. After tormenting him for a long while, they left him, withdrawing from him for a time. But, O cruel and insatiable wickedness of the devil! Shortly afterward they returned; and when they had begun again, as before, to mock him, behold, the signal for the service of almighty God suddenly sounded. At its ringing [Col. 1136C], terrified as though thunder from heaven had crashed down upon them with a roar, they fled. But they threw the wretched lay brother—now no longer proud and obstinate, but fearful and trembling like a little deer—into a marsh that was there.

Pulling himself out of it as best he could, he sat beneath a tree, wholly blackened and fouled by the marsh’s mire. While he sat there overwhelmed by grief and distress, fearing that the ghostly shapes of the demons would immediately return, a certain venerable figure suddenly stood before him and said:

“Take courage and do not be afraid, for those evil ministers of darkness, avengers of pride and obstinacy, will not presume to harm you any further. But these things befell you by the just judgment of God because you did not fear to be so proudly disobedient and rebellious toward your elder.”

When morning came, because that lay brother did not appear among the other brothers and could not be found despite a thorough search through the workshops [Col. 1136D], they all suspected that he had secretly departed and returned to the vomit of the world. The site was so situated that those responsible for the kitchen had to draw clean water outside the gate for use in the kitchen. Therefore, the brothers then serving in the kitchen office went out very early in the morning to draw water and saw that lay brother sitting beneath a tree like a madman. They hurried back and informed the prior and brothers what they had seen.

The prior therefore took several brothers with him and went outside to him. Seeing him in such a miserable state, he asked why he sat there and what harm had happened to him. But the man, threatening to bite with dog-like jaws at the brothers who wished to approach him, and staring fiercely at each one [Col. 1137A], said: “You all saw me made sport of by evil spirits throughout this night, and none of you cared to bring me help.”

The brothers immediately understood that he had paid certain penalties for the sin of his own disobedience and contumacy. At the prior’s command he was taken to the infirmary, and there, lying for a long time and suffering from the same madness, he learned from the things he endured not to be obstinate and rebellious; and, as it is written, “Vexation alone gives understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28). Therefore, as pride and rebellion are incomparable evils, so the proud, arrogant, and rebellious will be punished, condemned, and tortured beyond example. May their sentence be far from all of us who have resolved to love God with sincere and humble charity and, for his sake, to submit and obey his vicars, our prelates, in every care.

## CHAPTER IX. Again, on the danger of disobedience

[Col. 1137B] There are, however, some who, although they avoid with all due care this gross and, as it were, openly ruinous disobedience, nevertheless, being less cautious in lesser commands imposed through obedience, easily overstep the boundary of obedience. Even if afterward they try to wash away the guilt of disobedience by confession and penance, they are found to do so more perfunctorily than with true contrition of heart. I shall therefore not hesitate to set before these also an example of disobedience, so that those for whom the bread of falsehood—that is, the appetite of their own will—has proved sweet against their prelate’s command may, frightened by this example, come to their senses. Otherwise perhaps the stolen bread may turn in the stomach of conscience into the gall of an asp; and so they may vomit up the riches of disobedience which they had greedily swallowed, and God may draw them out of their belly.

In the province called Germany beyond the Rhine, also called by the general name Saxony [Col. 1137C], in the territory of the city of Paderborn, founded by Emperor Charlemagne, there stands a monastery of nuns called Aroldisseium [Aroldessen]. Dedicated to the holy name of the most holy apostles, the sons of Zebedee, it is known to have been of great religious rigor and the strictest discipline from ancient times. A venerable man named Peter, chosen from the Order of Regular Canons, was at one time over this monastery, since the institution of that monastery itself was ordered according to the Rule of blessed Augustine.

This man was a diligent investigator of God’s commandments and a devoted performer of them: radiant in charity, humble in disposition, exceptional in chastity. Like a faithful friend of the bridegroom and attendant of the bridegroom, he zealously guarded with watchful devotion the chastity of the brides of his Lord entrusted to him, and manfully repelled every robber who would corrupt their integrity, lest they violate the bridal chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom. Though rich in good qualities, he considered this one practice the chief jewel, like a precious pearl, in his way of life: to persist with sincere affection of heart in holy veneration of the Mother of God; frequently, with great devotion, to offer in her honor the saving victim and singular sacrifice by which the sins of the world are taken away; to choose her as his advocate in all his needs; and to implore her aid with tearful and continual prayers.

Moreover, he had made this praiseworthy practice his custom: whenever he heard the honey-sweet name of that blessed Virgin and Mother pronounced, if there was no opportunity to ask pardon, he would reverently bow his head and bend his knees slightly, offering as devoutly as he could the angelic salutation to that Mother of Mercy.

At last, after happily completing the contest of the excellent struggle, the time came in which he would experience that true saying of the heavenly oracle: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). For, seized by illness, he began to burn with fever; and the more the signs of death as they broke forth announced that death was near, the more earnestly he began to implore the aid of his special patroness, our Lady: that she might deign [Col. 1138A] to come to the departure of her little servant and protect him from the utterly wicked cruelty of evil spirits.

A few days before his death, he called to himself the prioress of that place, a very prudent and devout virgin named Gisela, along with certain of the senior sisters, and said:

“Behold, I am entering upon the way of all flesh; and although, according to my measure, I have striven to render pure service to the Lord, nevertheless, because no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, I fear the uncertain sentence of the strict Judge. But I make known to you that tomorrow, about the sixth hour, the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, Queen of Heaven, Lady of the World, will deign to visit me, however poor a servant I may be; and, as I hope, believe, and trust [Col. 1138B], to rescue me from this world’s exile and take me with her to the bright dwellings of the heavenly homeland. What I do not presume to be able to attain by my own merits, I confidently claim for myself through her most holy merits.

“Therefore have the entire house cleaned as quickly as possible; arrange and adorn the seats; and, about the hour which I have named, command all the sisters to be present with incense and candles. And when I begin the verse from the sequence for the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, ‘You, Queen of Heaven,’ let all the sisters together joyfully chant the sequence from that verse to the end with eager devotion.”

The prioress and the other sisters present immediately believed his words, since they knew his holiness and innocence. But a lay brother named Theoderic, standing at the head of the bed where the man of God lay, disbelieved what was being said and spoke thus in his heart: “O truly fickle and weak [Col. 1138C] female sex, believing every word! Behold, this man, standing at death’s door and losing his senses, speaks nonsense; and these sisters think that his words, as though proceeding from reason or founded upon truth, must immediately be carried out.”

As he thought these things, the holy priest raised his head with such strength as he could and directed his eyes toward the place where the lay brother stood. “Are you there, Brother Theoderic?” he said. When Theoderic answered, “I am, lord,” the priest said, “Come here to me.” He immediately approached. “Give me your hand,” he said.

The lay brother was astonished, and still regarded him as somewhat not in possession of himself; yet he did not dare to oppose the holy man’s words and gave him his hand. The man of God seized it and tightly clasped Theoderic’s fingers with his own: “As it is true,” he said, “that I hold your hand in my hand and clasp your fingers with my fingers, so it is true that I have spoken through the power of God’s grace. And know that what you say in the secret [Col. 1138D] of your heart is false: namely, that I am delirious and, with mind disturbed, do not know what I am saying.”

Thus, by this prophetic and truly divine rebuke of a single unbeliever, the cloud of all doubt was wiped away from the hearts of the rest, and all rejoiced together that so great a grace had been bestowed from heaven upon their spiritual father.

The next day dawned, and the hour predicted by the man of God drew near, as the sun hastened toward the middle of the sky. The whole community of sisters, assembled with the lay brothers, awaited the coming of the most devout Queen of Heaven all the more confidently because he who had foretold it had demonstrated it by a more manifest miracle. So great a reverence was poured into the minds of all present at the stated hour that none standing there could lawfully doubt that some divine power had arrived.

The blessed priest himself, his face wonderfully serene, his eyes raised to heaven and his hands extended upward, began the verse he had foretold, singing: “You, Queen of Heaven, this little people celebrates with devout hearts.” [Col. 1139A] But who could fittingly describe with what devotion and compunction, and with what affection of piety, that same sequence was chanted by the sisters? Meanwhile the servant of God lay in agony and, caught up in ecstasy, learned by revelation many things concerning heavenly secrets and the state of that monastery, which he afterward disclosed to the prioress and senior sisters.

But while every eye was fixed upon him, his face suddenly grew clouded, and his furrowed brow gave signs of sorrow and great anguish. Breaking into speech, he uttered these words in wretched lamentation:

“Why, most loving Lady, do you leave your poor little servant in this dregs of mortality, though you deigned to console one unworthy by so gracious a visitation? You have graciously granted to one now at the point of death your sweetest presence, so long desired by such great longings and sought by prayers and tears; and now, returning to the homeland of life and the joys of paradise, do you deny fellowship in your company to a wretch?”

As he repeatedly cried [Col. 1139B], “Most loving Lady, most merciful Lady, do not abandon me. With you I wish, with you I wish,” turning all to weeping and lamentation, he suddenly returned to himself. After resting a little because of the excessive exhaustion of his frail body, he dismissed the others, retained the prioress with a few senior sisters, and spoke as follows:

“Command that a little liquid be brought for refreshment, so that, once the dryness of my tongue has been relieved and the rheum in my throat cleared, I may more readily utter what I must say.”

The prioress quickly brought a little wine in a small vessel with her own hands. But as soon as she reached the threshold of the house where the man of God lay, he—though unable to perceive by sight or any bodily sense what she carried—cried out: “No, Lady Prioress; do not bring us wine, for ‘wine lays bare secrets’ (Ecclus. 27), and ‘wine causes the wise to fall away’ (Ecclus. 19).”

Hearing that she had been detected by so evident a spirit of prophecy, she trembled so greatly that she could scarcely turn back her step. [Col. 1139C] Then, refreshed with a little water, he began thus:

“Would that I, wretch that I am, had understood more carefully, before experiencing the punishment, how great is the guilt of disobedience! Would that I could imprint this upon your minds as necessity requires! For behold: because of the guilt of disobedience, my most gracious Lady has now left me in this valley of tears and has not judged me worthy, passing under her protection through the powers of the air, to penetrate the secrets of heaven.

“But hear what my disobedience was. It happened on one occasion that very many priests of this diocese, deceived by an imprudent calculation, observed the September Ember fast at an unlawful time; and I too fell into this error, paying insufficient attention to the rulings of the canons. At the next synod, when those who had observed the fast at an unlawful time accused themselves of this transgression, it was commanded by virtue of obedience that whoever knew himself guilty of this offence should ask pardon and acknowledge himself culpable [Col. 1139D]. While the others whose conscience accused them, preferring to endanger their reputation rather than their conscience, humbly did what was commanded, I, wretch that I am, giving more regard to my Order and reputation than to truth—because I was one of the Church’s prelates and was thought to possess some religious standing—alas, unable to bear the disgrace of shame, was ashamed to ask pardon publicly. This is my sin; this is the offence of disobedience for which today I am deprived of so great a good: repelled from following the universal Lady, the Mother of Mercy, I have been called back from entry into eternal life and everlasting glory to the miseries of this mortality.”

The prioress then asked whether he had not washed away the stain of that sin in the bath of confession and penance. When he asserted that he had confessed it not once but many times, she added in astonished amazement: “Woe to me [Col. 1140A], a sinner, Lord Father! What, then, shall we say of the sacrament of confession? If forgiveness has been denied to you who confessed not once but many times, who else can now hope for pardon through confession of sins?”

He answered with a saying worthy of remembrance: “You must know that, according to the intention or contrition of the person confessing or doing penance, the purpose of judgment—or the remission of pardon—is shaped. Because I, wretch that I am, neglected to weigh my sin according to its true seriousness and did not confess it with the contrition and compunction of heart that were required, I have not yet deserved to obtain forgiveness.”

After he had spoken these things sadly and mournfully, the hearts of the sisters who were present were shaken with great terror and were kindled no little toward pursuing purity of obedience. He survived for three days afterward, if I remember correctly, mourning his sin all the more bitterly because he had more clearly experienced the strictness of divine judgment. [Col. 1140B] As he died, he foretold that a great mortality would occur in that house; and this followed immediately after his death. Thus he ended his days in peace and, full of good works, was gathered to his fathers.

Yet he lost through the sin of disobedience that festal and utterly glorious assumption, by which, had guilt not intervened, he would deservedly have been taken up with the blessed Mother of God Mary and the multitude of holy angels. May all of us who have professed obedience be frightened by his example, so that we may never rush into the vice of disobedience; or, if through the corruption of human weakness we should fall, may we hasten to wash it away with worthy laments of repentance.

## CHAPTER X. On the danger of conspiracy

In the province called First Germany, whose metropolis is Mainz, in the territory of the city of the Wangiones, that is, Worms, there stands a monastery [Col. 1140C] of the Cistercian Order, of the line of Clairvaux, which in the German language is called Schönau, meaning “beautiful island.” In this monastery, during the time of the abbot Lord Godfrey of good memory, the evil one once stirred up an occasion of the gravest scandal, as follows.

In earlier times, through negligence—or rather, the indiscreet indulgence—of its prelates, a practice contrary to the form of the Order had presumptuously grown up in that house: lay brothers, like monks, were given new boots every year. When the aforesaid vigorous man had been brought from another house and had obtained the highest rank of honor in that church by divine and human calling, not through the prerogative of money or flesh and blood but by merit of life and distinction of prudence, he found that the lay brothers delighted in this rash extravagance. Inflamed with praiseworthy zeal, he judged that this most pernicious presumption ought to be corrected.

Accordingly, in private deliberations and publicly in the chapters of the brothers, he began [Col. 1140D] openly to state the case against this unauthorized innovation; to warn, entreat, and at last command that, if possible, the crookedness of a perverse custom inconsistent with the Order’s uprightness should be cut away without the scandal of dissension. But because the poison of dreadful presumption adhered to the minds of the carnal brothers with the most tenacious glue of miserable obstinacy, so that it could not possibly be torn away without scandal, the prudent man preferred, according to blessed Gregory’s teaching, that scandal should arise rather than truth be abandoned.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Gregory, Homilies on Ezekiel, Homily 7.]

The lay brothers therefore began first to mutter in corners and whisper; then, as their conspiracy gradually strengthened, they meditated open sedition in unrestrained madness. The instigator of the whole evil and author of the conspiracy was a certain lay brother entrusted with the care of the brothers’ dormitory and the keeping of their boots. Filled with a diabolical spirit and [Col. 1141A], according to the prophet, “casting silence down in every place” (Amos 8), he approached now individuals, now several together, persuading and urging them never, on any pretext of entreaties or threats, to allow their custom—fuel for insolence and an incentive to pride—to be taken from them.

And O how marvellously—indeed, how lamentably—the spirit of pride ensnares those whom it has once deceived, so that, puffed up with the swelling of contumacy and arrogance, they do not fear to undertake as light and easy the arduous and harshest labors which, if compelled to endure them for God, they would judge intolerable! When the lord abbot first discovered their whispering, he commanded by virtue of obedience that whoever broke silence should fast on bread and water that same day if he did so before the meal, or the next day if afterward. The man of whom we have spoken—not a convert, but a pervert—took care to observe this sentence, not from love of virtue, but in order to stir up hatred against his abbot [Col. 1141B]. For since he broke silence almost daily in fomenting the conspiracy, he fasted almost every day on bread and water, intending thereby to inflame the brothers’ minds against the abbot who had promulgated so harsh and inhuman a sentence.

Meanwhile the most sacred celebration of the Lord’s Advent approached; and the storm of conspiracy, increased and strengthened by secret whisperings, thundered on every side, now threatening a public scandal of the gravest kind. For the aforesaid false convert had given a most wicked counsel, which he pressed with most criminal urgency: namely, that on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, when the lay brothers from the granges had assembled, they should, with one consent, go up to the monks’ dormitory during work-time and, taking the boots from each man’s bed, cut them bit by bit with iron and tear them apart with their hands. Yet although this monstrous and infamous wickedness of theirs did not escape the awareness of the venerable [Col. 1141C] abbot, he nevertheless dissembled, as it is written: “The prudent man shall keep silence in an evil time” (Prov. XI). But the farther, amid such straits, human counsel and help alike stood away, the more earnestly he resolved to call upon the merciful heart of divine compassion. Proclaiming a general prayer to the monks, he urged that each should implore the Lord’s mercy according to his ability, that in His mercy He might deign to devise some better remedy for so great an insolence of the carnal brethren.

The principal and festive solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity was now at hand; and a few days before that solemnity, while the lord abbot was presiding over the chapter of lay brothers, the aforesaid standard-bearer of dissension and minister of Satan was denounced by certain of his accomplices for excessive abstinence and for having completely shaved his beard with a razor—something the wretched man had indeed done with the intention of provoking a scandal. They denounced him not from zeal for the Order nor from regard for brotherly charity, but from a desire to exercise malice. When the lord abbot [Col. 1141D] gently asked him why he had done this, and understood from his swollen and disorderly answers that his wickedness was fully developed, he was kindled with a praiseworthy zeal for justice and spoke prophetically to him before all:

“Brother, I ought indeed to have approached your obstinate mind with salutary admonitions, if perhaps you might return to your senses from the snares of the devil, by whom you are held captive to do his will. But since the beam of pride has so darkened the eye of your heart that I do not presume to be able to cast it out through my humility; and since I see you so alienated in mind that you mock our admonitions rather than receive them, therefore before all who sit here I confidently pronounce concerning you that, unless you speedily and without delay return to your senses and come in a humbled spirit to make satisfaction, you will shortly feel the terrible judgment of almighty God; and, as it is written, [Col. 1142A] ‘In the time of vengeance the Lord shall destroy thee’ (Ecclus. V). Behold, again and a third time I say to all here who possess sound understanding: just as the gracious and merciful Lord gives grace to the humble, so the terrible God, by the unbending line of His righteousness, resists the proud (I Pet. V). Therefore you, who are a public enemy of the peace and observance established by the holy Fathers, shall, if you persevere in wickedness, bear a most severe judgment within a few days. For I trust in the Lord Jesus and in His glorious Virgin Mother, whose useless servants we are, that they will not suffer this house—distinguished from its very foundation by the bond of brotherly charity and by the discipline of praiseworthy manners—to be corrupted by your excessively wicked obstinacy.”

The prayers of the brethren groaning beneath the infection of inward discord had now risen to the ears of the Lord of Hosts; and the angel of the Lord, having received judgment from Him, passed through those whose foreheads he found marked with the sign of Tau [Note: [Col. 1141D] An allusion to Ezekiel IX.], [Col. 1142B] that is, with the banner of Christ’s humility. But he struck and immediately destroyed the wretched author of the conspiracy, upon whose forehead he saw impressed the character of the beast and of the dragon, who is king over all the children of pride (Job XLI); and with him he scattered the whole whirlwind of scandal and cloud of presumption.

For on the evening of the day preceding the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, after he had descended from the dormitory following Compline, the infirmarian of the lay brothers met him. This infirmarian seemed to be, as it were, the second leader of the same conspiracy, and he often discussed with him the poisonous counsels of dissension. Suddenly the man began to utter cries of pain with loud groaning; his face grew pale, his nostrils contracted, and his eyes rolled from their proper position: grim signs plainly showed that death was immediately at hand. The other, disturbed, saw him already staggering and, lest he be dashed to the ground by a sudden fall, clasped him around the middle. But the death was so sudden that [Col. 1142C] before he could reach the ground, he breathed out his wretched soul in the hands of the ill-fated companion who held him.

Then the leaders of the conspiracy were thrown into confusion; trembling seized those who had been stout in their obstinacy; all the instigators of dissension and schism grew numb. How good Thou art, Lord Jesus, to those who hope in Thee! How sweet is Thy mercy in the time of tribulation, like the morning dew and like timely rain in days of drought! For Thou art King of kings and Lord of lords, who sittest upon the throne of judgment, scattering every evil by Thy glance (Prov. XX); Thou who, by the terrible death of one sinner, restrained many sinners, and mercifully freed that house—because works pleasing to Thee had been found in it—from the whirlwind of a scandal long premeditated and stirred up.

The lay brothers ran from every side to their standard-bearer. Him whom on the following day they had resolved to follow as their leader in carrying out an unheard-of crime, they now carried—O good Jesus—his dead body amid a pitiable tumult to the infirmary; and, overwhelmed with fear and trembling, they laid him in the place where the brethren [Col. 1142D] customarily pass from this life. For Thou didst not permit Thy most sacred solemnity, on which peace was first announced to the earth through the ministry of angels, to be defiled by the disturbance of discord and schism.

When the board for the dead gave its signal and struck the ears of all—especially because they knew no one there to be so near death—the lord Theobald, then sub-cellarer, later abbot of the same place, and afterward chosen as prelate of the mother church, namely Eberbach, one of the foremost daughters of Clairvaux, through whose revelation we have learned these things, at that very moment was devoutly performing, as best he could, the prayer which the lord abbot had prescribed against the obstinacy of the conspiracy, though it had until then been forgotten. Hearing the sound of the board, he hurried to the infirmary [Col. 1143A]; and when he learned who had died, he marveled greatly at God’s judgment and swiftly summoned the lord abbot, who had perhaps then descended from the dormitory, to perform the office of commendation for the dead man.

The abbot too came quickly. When the covering which shrouded the body had been removed from the head and he saw the face of the man lying there, he clapped his hands and, drawing sighs from the depths of his heart, said: “Alas, most wretched man! Behold how you lie destroyed by divine judgment, without repentance for your wickedness.” Repeating this again a second and third time, he said: “Would that you had not despised my admonitions with an obstinate mind! Would that you had not eternally shut God’s mercy away from yourself!”

After considering for some time what he ought to do, he at length judged it more prudent to perform the customary office of commendation, bring the body into the church, and summon all the brethren, monks and lay brothers alike, on the following day, so that they might determine together [Col. 1143B] what ought to be done in such a case. When the assembly had gathered, the lord abbot spoke thus in the hearing of all:

“You know, dearest brethren, in what perverse purpose of a depraved heart and malicious will this man was caught. Unless the strict sentence of God’s judgment had quickly taken him from our midst, he would not have feared, together with his accomplices—whom he had enticed to this by whisperings and wicked persuasions—to brand this house, which has hitherto endured in the best peace and concord, with the searing iron of a most grievous scandal. Therefore, since we all know his perversity but do not know his confession or repentance, I judge that his body ought by no means to be placed among the bodies of our brethren; and I trust that I determine this not from any rashness, but by the balance of just judgment.”

On hearing this, the lay brothers were terrified and grew pale; and they humbly begged to be allowed to speak apart with the senior monks. Having obtained this by the lord abbot’s indulgence [Col. 1143C], they withdrew to deliberate. Soon they returned, and both monks and lay brothers prostrated themselves before him, pleading with many urgent prayers that mercy not be denied to the dead man. The lay brothers pledged and solemnly affirmed, under attestation of the divine Name, that if the lord abbot tempered the strictness of his judgment and did not deny common burial to the deceased, though less worthy, they would abandon every intention of their conceived malice and would in no way raise the matter of new boots again.

Moreover, some of the elders said that, apart from this affair, the man had otherwise been quite respectable; and that men ought not to pronounce judgment without mercy against one whom perhaps divine mercy had punished temporally for this very reason: lest he should be able to bring his conceived malice to effect, for which he would have deserved eternal damnation.

The lord abbot therefore considered that this was expedient for the occasion [Col. 1143D], and feared lest the latter error become worse than the former if the lay brothers, who might easily be calmed on this occasion, should break out into some greater scandal. At the same time, he feared for himself if he pronounced a harsher judgment more hastily than was proper, since the sentence concerning conspirators had not yet been promulgated by the general chapter. He therefore assented to their petition; and, after the customary solemnities of Masses and funeral rites had been celebrated, the dead brother was committed to the earth among the bodies of the brethren.

Blessed in all things be God, who mercifully and compassionately delivered that house, hanging from the lofty cliff of malicious conspiracy and already on the point of being hurled into the deepest abyss of grave scandal. Thus it seemed, when the brother had been buried, that the dregs of all discord had in some manner been buried with him. And the entire holy congregation boasts to this day that no foul traces of those most ardent little foxes were found afterward in that house.

But the lord Theobald, whom we mentioned above [Col. 1144A], had long been united to the deceased brother by the friendship of close familiarity. They had mutually bound themselves, both in life and in death, that when either died, the other would assist him with the suffrages of prayer. Since that same lay brother, before the storm of conspiracy, had been a man of no negligible religious devotion, Theobald knew that a friend is proved in the extremity of need. Greatly grieving for the danger to the soul of one whom he had loved familiarly while alive, he resolved to offer prayer for him yearly. For he firmly believed that, even if the offerings of prayer brought no benefit to the dead man because of his merits, the fruit of his own good will could not be lost to himself.

After he had poured out humble prayers to the Lord for him throughout that entire year, when the year’s cycle had turned, the deceased appeared to him in a vision, showing by his mournful face that he had undergone a sad judgment. Asked how he fared, he answered that from the hour of his death until that time [Col. 1144B] he had paid the penalties of most grievous torments in punishment for his obstinacy and rebellion, though he did not altogether despair of God’s mercy.

Indeed, whether this was a simple dream or the mystery of some revelation, it is as rash to define as it is pious to restrain a hasty judgment upon the soul of a deceased brother. Perhaps the dreadful destruction of temporal death was an aid to everlasting mercy, because mercy shines more clearly when mercy and judgment look upon one another from opposite sides. Certainly, how serenely the Lord regarded this house is proved by the church of Eberbach. For when, much later, the question of new boots was stirred up by the most malicious prompting of demons, thorns of so many scandals and calamities sprang forth that one would rather weep for them than attempt to explain them in words.

Let this, therefore, be set before us as an example and memorial of humility and caution: if ever that ancient serpent, the inveterate enemy, [Col. 1144C] should attempt in the places where we live to sow the tares of discord and conspiracy because of the customs of the Order, let us not be slow, in the fear of God, to flee the violators of peace and concord as asps and basilisks. Let us instead rise up courageously with the children of peace, who endeavor from zeal for God to uproot and destroy evil customs presumptuously adopted contrary to the form of the Order; and let us set ourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord (Ezek. XIII). For this must often be said and remembered without forgetting: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV; I Pet. V).

## Chapter XI. On the danger of excommunication

Although the minds of all who are called by the Christian name are, through the faith in which they have been instructed, persuaded almost by nature that the sentence of excommunication is nothing other than separation from God and estrangement from eternal life, nevertheless, because hearts [Col. 1144D] benumbed through negligence are sometimes moved more by examples than by words, I have judged it necessary to show how greatly this final sentence is to be feared by a rational creature. It sometimes subjects even an irrational creature either to death or to the gravest calamity, so that wretched man, against whom the dart of anathema is especially aimed because of the merit of pride, may reflect what he ought to fear for himself when beings incapable of experiencing reason are struck by the sword of anathema through the power of the divine Name.

Louis the Pious, Emperor Augustus, son of Charlemagne, who first magnificently endowed the churches of Christ throughout Gaul and Germany from the vast revenues of the imperial treasury—and thereby deserved to be surnamed “the Pious”—and who, as is reported, heard a voice saying to him, “Louis, you have added poison to the churches,” founded in Saxony, on the bank of the great river Werre, a monastery of monks. In accordance with imperial magnificence he exalted it most nobly with riches and honor, and decreed that, to distinguish it from Old Corbie in Gaul, it should be called New Corbie. In this monastery, in the time of the emperor Frederick [Col. 1145A] of blessed memory, there was an abbot named Conrad. In keeping with the pompous custom of imperial abbots, amid the other enticements of secular glory, he wore gold rings. His disposition, I think, was far different from that of the first abbot of Clairvaux, truly poor and humble in spirit, of whom it is written that he delighted more in a rake and hoe than in a tiara and ring.

It happened on one occasion that he had a gold ring which was precious to him. One day, while sitting at table, he took it off in accordance with courtly custom in order to wash his hands. Through some interruption of trifles—I do not know whether serious matters or not—it was left rather negligently upon the table. Meanwhile a domestic bird, a raven, which the abbot’s household retained as a pet, flew in. With no one at all noticing, [Col. 1145B] it seized the ring in its beak and, unaware that it was guilty of theft, carried it by swift flight to its little nest. But after hunger had been satisfied by the meal and all rose when the tables had been removed, the abbot discovered his loss. Blaming his servants’ negligence, he ordered the ring immediately sought everywhere; but because the true culprit’s guilty awareness deceived everyone, it could not be found.

The abbot therefore suspected both guests and servants. Deeply angered, he commanded the parish priests of the town—an extremely large and wealthy town situated not far from the monastery walls and subject to the abbot’s jurisdiction—to pronounce publicly the most severe sentence of excommunication against whoever had not feared to stain himself with this crime. When this was done, just as the testimony of conscience made innocence an ornament in all rational beings in this matter, so irrational nature itself could not escape paying the temporal penalties of the anathema—penalties which the weakness of its transitory condition prevented it from paying eternally. [Col. 1145C] The wicked thief, though unaware of his fault, began gradually to weaken, to loathe food, to make more sluggishly the playful croakings and the other foolish actions of an irrational creature by which it had been accustomed to entertain the minds of foolish people who neglected the fear of God. Then it even began to shed its feathers; and finally, as its flesh wasted away and even the plumage fled the corruption, it appeared pitiable and marvelous to all who saw it.

One day, while the abbot himself was present, his household discussed among themselves this extraordinary transformation of the bird, affirming that so unusual a thing could not happen without cause. One of them said to the abbot, as if joking: “My lord, you should consider whether perhaps this is the thief you seek, and whether this dreadful affliction which you see indicates the bond of anathema in which it is entangled.” All were astonished at the remark. The abbot ordered one of the servants [Col. 1145D] to climb quickly into the tree in which the bird had its nest and carefully turn over the bed made from straw and a tangled mass of twigs. As soon as he climbed up, the servant recovered the ring, rescuing it from filthy defilement, and, not without the amazement of all present, returned it to the abbot’s hands.

Thus the wretched thief, who was paying the most severe penalties for theft yet did not know itself guilty of theft, was revealed, as we believe, by divine direction. On the counsel of prudent men, the lord abbot ordered those who had pronounced the sentence of excommunication to lift quickly the anathema they had directed against the offender, since the loss had been restored. Once this [Col. 1146A] was done, just as the bird had earlier seemed gradually to fail and to languish day by day from its pestilential wasting, so afterward it began by degrees somehow to revive and grow vigorous again, until it was fully restored to its former appearance and lost health—not without a great miracle of God.

It is also found in the deeds of our most blessed father Bernard that, when he had been invited to the dedication of the new church of the monastery of Foigny, so countless a multitude of flies had gathered in the newly plastered church because of the smell of fresh lime, and caused such disturbance to those entering that the brethren greatly feared lest the solemnity of dedication, to be celebrated the next day, might be hindered by their nuisance. When this was reported to the holy Father, employing his customary confidence in God, he said: “I excommunicate them.” In the morning all those flies, struck by the dart of anathema [Col. 1146B] and dead, covered the whole pavement so completely that they had to be gathered into a heap with poles and carried away by porters.

We have also heard of a certain knight who deserved to be publicly excommunicated because of his wickedness. As he sat at table and threw bread to dogs, the dogs, terrified by the smell alone of the polluted bread, drew back and would by no means consent to touch it. How fearful and watchful, then, ought a person to be who, led by reason and grace, can avoid evil and do good, lest he fall under so terrible a sentence of destruction and separation, when an irrational creature that cannot sin and is therefore not liable to pay penalties for sin is sometimes seen to be punished through the severity of anathema.

## Chapter XII. On the danger of indiscreet confessors, and praise of discreet ones

[Note: [Col. 1145D] Many considerations make that narrative about discreet and indiscreet confessors suspect. 1. The first confessor does not seem to have been so indiscreet, and many would follow him in a similar case. 2. What sort of knight was he, who could kill a confessor as though he were a chicken with impunity, while everyone [Col. 1146D] muttered? 3. That nocturnal vigil appears fabulous, especially since the place, time, and persons of so celebrated an event are not specified. Certain other matters, especially chapters 20 and 21, are uncertain.]

How beautifully Holy Scripture calls discretion [Col. 1146C] the mother of virtues! Like a sacred boundary placed midway between virtues and vices, it separates them from one another by discerning foresight; it blows away vices veiled in the appearance of virtues; it enriches and orders the virtues themselves through devotion; it does not cast aside one weak in faith, but receives him with maternal compassion. It does not wound the sinful consciences laid bare before it through the shame of confession by the harshness of rebuke, but soothes and raises them by kindly consolation. And if the penitent’s faint-heartedness is so great that even the gravest crimes—which one could scarcely hope might be removed by the sacrifice of a humbled spirit and contrite heart even with the mourning of many years—may readily be forgiven, it persuades him of this through sweet exhortation.

Not so many shepherds in the Church of God: by their indiscreet and impetuous spirit they scatter the Lord’s flock. Ignorant of the virtue of discretion and lacking the precious *lingua eucharin* (‘gracious tongue’; reading uncertain)—with which the festering wounds of the sinful soul are licked in order to bring them to health, [Col. 1146D] they wound more deeply those whom they should heal. Empty of compassion, by exaggerating a harsh and prolonged penance they introduce into the weak a kind of seedbed of contempt and despair.

We do not say this as if those who impose a fitting penance on sinners according to the quality or quantity of their crimes do wrong. Rather, where a discreet confessor sees the penitent so faint-hearted that, not only from shame at the crime committed but also under the burden of the penance to follow, he is pale, trembling, and failing in spirit, [Col. 1147A] he must for the present conceal the matter altogether. He must sustain the soul wearied by fear with the milk of sweet consolation and the gentleness of pious exhortation, until strengthened by his kindness it becomes able to receive the more solid food of fruitful penance.

But how dangerous it is to be ignorant of the force of discretion, not to know, in accordance with the Apostle, how to become weak with the weak (II Cor. XI), and not to weigh the condition of the penitent; and likewise, with what praise the discreet confessor ought to be exalted, who through the anointing of grace teaching him concerning all things knows how to conform himself to the condition and ability of each penitent—I shall endeavor to impress these points on the reader’s mind by a most beautiful and very pleasing example. Thus, whoever is holy and discreet may advance still further in discretion; whereas whoever is harsh and indiscreet, struck as it were by the hand of this admonition, may hasten to wipe away the stains of indiscretion. Nor should he consider it burdensome to learn, through attentive reflection, with what zeal of compassion he ought to bring forth the little ones of God’s Church until Christ be formed in them [Col. 1147B].

A certain knight, adorned with the titles of nobility, wealth, youth, and great strength, and thereby puffed up in the mind of his flesh, despised divine and human laws alike and confounded civil law with natural law. Filling everything with arson, robbery, seditions, and murders, he made light of right and wrong alike. In short, to sum up all his evils: he neither feared God nor reverenced men.

He had, however, a faithful wife, devoted to every piety of the Christian religion insofar as this was possible under so cruel a husband. Loving her husband with sincere charity, she mourned his perversity with unceasing tears and, moved by an affection of spiritual rather than carnal love, poured out continual prayers to the Lord for his amendment. Moreover, whenever she saw that his swollen mind had cooled from anger and that his more cheerful face showed some happiness, she approached him with salutary admonitions. With many exhortations and tears she begged him at last to cease from such great evils and, through the humility of confession and penance, to appease the face of the Lord [Col. 1147C].

But he sometimes repelled his excellent wife, who was zealous for his salvation, by dangerous evasion, and at other times by stormy indignation. He told her that this will was not yet in him; that he ought rather to devote himself to warfare and military affairs; and that he could not endure the reproaches of relatives and friends, who would taunt him if, idling and languishing in sloth, he did not repay his enemies, when they inflicted wrongs upon him, with a vengeance double or even triple.

Though she was often thus rebuffed, the excellent woman was in no way broken by despair, she who bore her husband in the womb of holy desire. She did not cease to press chaste counsels upon him, whether welcome or unwelcome, until at last, wearied by the persistence of her goodwill and softened also by marital affection, he spoke to her thus: “Behold, at your counsel I am willing to confess; but where shall I find such a confessor as I may safely entrust with my conscience, and who will show himself kind and humane to me?”

Immediately she, thirsting for her husband’s salvation with the most ardent affection of compassion, gladly seized this saying from his mouth as an auspicious omen: “My lord,” she said, “I shall procure for you a trustworthy and humane confessor. Only do not depart from this good and holy purpose.”

Accordingly, while she sought a spiritual physician suitable for healing the long-standing and manifold wounds of a sinful soul, she found a priest of religious life indeed, but—alas!—ignorant of the grace of discretion: skilled in spiritual treatment, but unable to distinguish the conditions and temperaments of the sick. This venerable matron, therefore, in feminine simplicity judging every religious man also to be discreet, brought her wretched husband to him [Col. 1148A]. She advised and begged him not to hesitate to make a pure confession, yielding in no way to shame and embarrassment, not as to a man but as to Christ the Lord.

When he had done this as best he could, the priest was astonished to hear crimes so numerous and so enormous. The man whom he ought to have drawn from the deepest pit of perdition by the healing balm of compassionate consolation, he miserably hurled into the abyss of renewed—indeed doubled—despair by the blade of indiscreet severity. For he said to him:

“Certainly, good man, if your transgressions were confined within any bounds of moderation, and if so great an enormity of crimes and wicked deeds did not envelop you, I would willingly offer you the counsel available to me. But since it is clear that you have committed deeds of such a kind and magnitude as the sacred authority of the canons has decreed must be reserved for the examination, not of any priest, but of the supreme pontiff alone, I advise and urge you to seek the thresholds of the Apostles as quickly as you can, humbly lay open your conscience to the pontiff of the holy Apostolic See, and not shrink from undertaking the labor of penance according to his direction.”

At these words that fierce mind, which had seemed somewhat softened and humbled, roared as though it had been struck in the forehead by the strongest blow of a stone. Cruelty returned, and the wretched man, wholly turned to madness, said: “Then am I to expect nothing else from you, to whom I humbled myself so as to disclose my conscience?” The priest simply replied that for the present he had no better or sounder counsel. At once that son of Belial, to whose eyes blood was as nothing, drew his sword and cut off his head. Then, returning to his wife, he disclosed the sad outcome and the blood of the defiled confession.

She was terrified and grew pale; almost lifeless from the excessive sorrow of her heart, she answered the detestable news of parricide not with words but with mourning and tears. Yet when did charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith [Col. 1148C]—charity which had taken deeper root in the breast of this excellent wife—ever yield to difficulties, be driven back by the barrier of perversity, or be crushed by the hammer of malice, which the Wise Man declares strong as death and hard as hell (Cant. VIII)? Indeed, the more harshly it was repelled, the more vigorously it persisted. Nor did it cease until the judgment of compassion was brought to victory and, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, the unbelieving husband was saved through the believing wife (I Cor. VII).

This second Theodora burned with a most fervent desire to save this second Sisinnius; and she was truly another Natalia, striving, if possible, to make of her husband another Adrian. Her eye did not sleep: now setting before her husband the terrible judgment of God, now impressing upon him the brevity and instability of this present life, until, through the cooperation of God’s grace, she again drew from him a willingness to confess.

Then, like a most discerning bee, she began with pious carefulness to seek whether she could find not merely a confessor but a discreet confessor [Col. 1148D], one who knew how to instruct in a spirit of gentleness a man overwhelmed by many sins; one who knew that the bruised reed must not be broken altogether, lest the last state of her wretched husband become worse than the first. And, by the will of the Lord—whose judgments are an exceedingly great abyss, who according to the depth of His good pleasure sometimes calls even the most wicked to life, but leaves those who presume upon their innocence in the hand of their own counsel—she found a bishop distinguished for religious devotion, eminent for discretion, fit for winning souls, and most suited to the undertaking pursued by this strong woman.

To him, therefore, this second Naaman the Syrian—stricken by the contagion of spiritual leprosy from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head—was brought for washing in the descent of the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1147D] An allusion to IV Kings V.], that is, in the humility of pure confession, through the power of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1149A], so that henceforth he might indeed be dead to sin but live to God.

When the confession had been made and the stomach of his conscience had been emptied of the poisonous humors of gall, the prudent and compassionate physician entirely concealed the knife of cutting and the fire of cauterization, and approached the half-dead man with the ointment of sweetest consolation, saying:

“Your sins, my friend, by which you have offended God and wounded your soul, are indeed grave. But whatever their kind or number, what are they beside the incomprehensible abyss of divine compassion? No more than a drop from a bucket beside the expanse of the sea. Therefore I urge you to take courage. And since by God’s grace you have received the antidote of confession, do not shrink from taking the draught of penance also, though it is somewhat bitter; for divine authority has decreed that confession can benefit no one without it. It will be my task to temper this healing draught of penance for you in such a way that through it you may escape the danger of eternal death [Col. 1149B] and not be deprived of a share in everlasting life.”

When he hesitated and, on merely hearing the word “penance,” gave no answer, the bishop said: “What do you think, dearest brother? Will you be able to offer some small sacrifice of penance for such great sins of yours?” He replied: “A severe and prolonged penance I can neither undertake nor desire; but if, in accordance with your promise and with due regard for moderation, you impose upon me something which does not exceed the measure of my abilities, I shall try to undertake what you urge.” And the bishop said: “Consider, then, with me now, and let us measure your strength, so that we may enjoin upon you only what you think you can accomplish.—What then?—Are at least some easy fasts possible for you? Or might generous almsgiving prove burdensome to you?” But he said: “I can do none of these things. For I am unable even to fast until the third hour; and a daily, unconsidered outpouring of my property would very quickly bring my household [Col. 1149C] to utter poverty.” The bishop said: “If you think you can do none of these things, at least agree with us in this: either visit the Lord’s sepulchre as a pilgrim for your sins, or go to the thresholds of the apostles at Rome, or to the body of Saint James in Galicia, so that through their intercession you may deserve to receive forgiveness of your sins.”

Immediately that knight, strong indeed in body but exceedingly small and weak in heart, unable to restrain his rising indignation, answered resentfully: “Why do you speak such useless words without cause? If I depart from my land for the journey of a single day, all that is mine will at once be exposed to robbery, arson, plundering, and destruction; and when I return and find nothing, I shall be the reproach of my kindred and friends, the mockery and derision of my enemies. Far be it from me that I should incur so grave a loss both of my honor and of my estate!”

What could even the most skilled physician do [Col. 1149D] when the sick man was wretchedly wasting away and failing in his hands, while utterly rejecting every remedy? What, I ask, could he do for one who shrank back, not merely from cutting and cauterizing, but even from fomenting and anointing? Here compassionate discernment and holy fellow-feeling had necessarily to perform their office, lest that dying, languishing little sheep, for whom Christ died, should be devoured by that ancient dragon, who “swallows a river and does not marvel,” but is confident “that even Jordan shall flow into his mouth” (Job 40)—the Jordan, that is, of penitents.

Therefore, while the bishop weighed in the uncertain balance of his mind what he ought to do or say in such a crisis, he was suddenly enlightened by divine grace and said to him with a cheerful face: “Come then, most valiant knight! Can you at least keep silence for one night for your sins?” Though he was inclined to despair and was by no means willing, as Scripture says, to labor and use force against his own destruction, yet on hearing this [Col. 1150A] word, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, he said: “If all my sins are forgiven me for the silence of a single night, I will do as you advise.” But the bishop, conceiving in full faith a confidence in the Lord’s mercy, and fearing that if the man suffered a relapse he might again entangle himself in every crime, answered: “Do only what I judge; and under whatever form of penance or obedience, humble yourself before God and His vicar, holding firmly the resolve not henceforth to commit sin grievously; and I will answer for your soul on the day of the fearful judgment of God the just Judge.”

Thus an agreement truly wonderful was made; a compact almost without precedent was established; an exchange of commerce unheard of through the ages was entered into: that, for the silence of one night, crimes and most grievous and countless enormities of many years might be remitted. Yet such is the power of obedience, and such the loftiness of charity, that what the pious mind of the brother desiring to save a soul [Col. 1150B] presumed upon from the abundant goodness of his God could by no means be rendered void.

Meanwhile the star of day was declining toward the west and the darkness of night was drawing on. The true shepherd, truly worthy of the name and honor of bishop, led his penitent to the church. Before the doors of the church, this new recruit of Christ, lately a veteran soldier of the devil, was carefully instructed concerning faith, patience, perseverance, and the manifold cunning of demons; and, because “unless a man contend lawfully, he shall not be crowned” (1 Tim. 2), he was above all admonished, and the bishop repeatedly impressed upon and commanded him, that whatever he heard, whatever he saw, whatever terrors or shudders he felt, he should utter no word at all until morning came and the bishop himself should arrive with the cross of the Lord and by his blessing restore to him the use of speech.

Then, sufficiently instructed by his inexperienced trainer in how he ought to exercise himself in the spiritual arena, he was led into the church, while angels rejoiced and demons raged. [Col. 1150C] After prayer had been made, he was stationed before the altar and again admonished by the bishop to remain steadfast. Then everyone withdrew; the bolts of the doors were firmly secured; and he was left in the hand of God.

Surrounded by the fear and horror of night, he learned at last to become gentle, to lay aside the arrogance of pride, to change the beastly rage of cruelty into meekness, to invoke with trembling lips the mercy of God which he had formerly despised in his swelling pride, and to pray humbly that divine mercy would not abandon him in this struggle of perilous combat. The sinner, who sins from the beginning, saw these things; he became angry, gnashed his teeth, and wasted away. He grieved bitterly that by this new device of mercy he was being driven from his ancient possession, and summoned the whole troop of malignant spirits to spread snares of cunning and deceit.

Accordingly, in the first part of the night, while the penitent, fearing all dangers in his frightened heart, strained his ear for a sound, he suddenly heard what seemed like [Col. 1150D] the church doors being opened. He saw phantom merchants—or rather demons in the guise of certain traders—entering, ostensibly to purchase precious garments belonging to his household. Each of them, as though carrying cloths of varied color, great fineness, and high value, laid them down before him. Then, pretending sympathy, they addressed him:

“Why, lord, do you follow that hypocrite who is trying to deceive you, who has even brought you to such folly that amid the darkness and horror of night, among the tombs of the dead, you sit like a madman bereft of sense? Or will you not be able, at a later age and in a more fitting manner, to do penance for your sins—provided only that you do not now become the reproach and mockery of your enemies? For all your relatives and friends, hearing that you have suddenly become insane, lament and mourn; but your enemies dance for great joy and hasten with most greedy desire to seize your possessions. Therefore, hearing of your calamity, we have come to you and shall wait, for whatever period you please to extend, for the payment for the cloths we have brought, should you wish to purchase them; and perhaps, at our exhortation, you may deign to recover from madness and regain your former honor.”

When those most heated and malicious spirits saw that he was in no way moved by their words and that they could extract no answer from him, they departed in confusion, intending shortly to devise the appearances of another temptation.

But about midnight, while the aforesaid knight was considering more attentively the things he had seen, he heard in the distance what seemed to be the clatter of horsemen hurrying tumultuously and hastening toward the church where he sat. When they had approached the doors of the church, they leapt swiftly from their horses and began to cry out in mournful voices: “Is our most beloved companion and kinsman [Col. 1151B] here?” They were demons in the likeness of certain relatives whom he had loved with special intimacy and whom he had very often had as companions in enormities and crimes.

Then, as it seemed to him, they broke down rather than opened the doors and entered to him. Now using grieving, now indignant voices, they called him by his own name and said: “Alas, alas! Sweetest of friends and kinsmen, what necessity has brought you to this lamentable madness? And who could have persuaded you to this voluntary and insane calamity? Who would believe that a prudent and capable man, vigorous in affairs, skilled in military discipline, and most experienced in martial conflicts, could suddenly fall into such madness as to forget his kinsmen and friends, neglect even his own honor, not hesitate to subject himself to the extremity of unhappiness and misery, and expose all his goods to robbery and arson?

“You must know that all your enemies, whose pride and audacity you used to check with manly constancy by the strength [Col. 1151C] of your courage, rejoice and exult on hearing that adverse fortune has cast you down and humbled you. Like victors rejoicing over captured spoil, they are arranging their bands and intend in tyrannical cruelty to seize everything that belongs to you and subject it to their dominion. Moved by this malice of theirs, therefore, we have come to urge you, dearest friend, that, casting away the madness in which you are entangled and summoning your companions and fellow-soldiers as quickly as possible, you may meet your enemies with a strong hand. Otherwise, if—God forbid!—you disregard friends who are zealous for your honor and delay in leaving, then after your fertile fields and all that belongs to you have been consumed by robbery and fire, you will begin too late to be ashamed of and disgusted by this folly.

“For what greater madness could there be than to believe that your sins will be forgiven for the silence of a single night—a thing that that pseudo-bishop invented out of his own heart, not for any benefit to you, but so that, by somehow gratifying your martial spirit, he might seem to speak things pleasing to you!”

Amid all these intricate contrivances of most subtle deception, the penitent, enlightened by divine grace, persevered unmoved. He gave no answer at all to their chatter, but allowed them to depart empty-handed and without result from their malice, tearing themselves apart with anger and fury. Therefore, when the ministers of impiety, the fabricators of falsehood, saw themselves frustrated in every device of their cunning, and saw the greatest sinner—over whose apparently certain destruction they had congratulated themselves—through the power of obedience restored to life, as it were in a moment of time, they were exceedingly inflamed with envious rage. They decided now to proceed by cruelty and torments, so that, if possible, one who had not yielded to flattery might at least, compelled by terrors and sufferings, utter some little word of whatever sort. Thus the precious ointment of salvation, being crushed in the mortar of obedience by the pestle of patience, might be spilled through the vice of impatience.

[Col. 1152A] Thus, when a great part of the night had already passed and the time of cockcrow was near, behold: the malignant spirits appeared to the penitent, no longer in an alien guise as before, but in their own form—deformed and foul in body, savage in face, threatening in eye, and breathing out in their fury the dreadful poison of malice. Surrounding him on every side, they rebuked him in terrible voices:

“O condemned knight, dregs of crimes, cesspool of wickedness, Charybdis of enormities, what is this vain hope by which you are deceived? Can you henceforth be anything other than one of us, you who have surpassed even demons in dreadful crimes and wicked deeds? O how foolish, vain, and senseless is this thought of yours: that for the silence of one night you can escape our fellowship and throw from your neck the yoke of our master, by whose mark you are already branded for service in the kingdom of death! Therefore, lest you pay fitting penalties for despising us and experience the anger of those whom you may have appeased, if you wish, depart quickly from here. By our favor, rejoice in every pleasure of the sweet world during the vigor of your flourishing youth; and, after your enemies have been conquered and covered with shame through our aid, bear home a most glorious triumph.”

So they spoke to him. But the strong athlete of God, who shortly before had been so faint-hearted in patience, now established by the merit of faith and obedience upon the most firm rock, that is, Christ, despised alike their deceitful flatteries and their terrifying rebukes. Manfully maintaining his proposed silence, he provoked the demons to such madness that, turned to fury, they rushed irreverently upon him and tore him with most savage blows. Though wounded by the bruising of the blows, he was left glorying in the testimony of an uninjured conscience.

Having therefore overcome the nocturnal terror of the first temptation, and, for his second victory, having been protected by the shield of divine grace from “the arrow that flies by day,” he was nevertheless, for a third time, fortified by the breastplate of patience against “the pestilence that walks in darkness,” namely the devil’s cruelty. [Col. 1152C] What remained for him but the “noonday demon,” which rises so much the more fiercely amid the splendor of good works as it presumes more easily, through the exaltation of the heart and boasting in virtues, to overthrow him?

The dawn was already scattering its ruddy rays; and the sinful man, yet now penitent, glorious in the grace of God through these three triumphs over subdued diabolical wickedness, and wholly changed into another man, eagerly awaited the arrival of the bishop, who had promised to come at daybreak in order to receive his lawful penance. Truly this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76); truly, “Blessed is the man whom Thou instructest, O Lord, and teachest out of Thy law, that Thou mayest give him rest from evil days, until a pit be dug for the sinner” (Ps. 93)—the pit of eternal perdition and the abyss of never-ending confusion. “Who shall bring an accusation against Thy elect, O Lord?” (Rom. 8). When Thou openest, O Lord, who is there that can shut? When Thou, O Lord, callest forth by the power of Thy voice Lazarus, dead four days, [Col. 1152D] mortally stinking with the horror of vices and moreover pressed down by the stone of evil and inveterate habit (John 11), who dares say: “Why dost Thou do thus?” To Thee, O Lord, for the justification of sinners, who have rotted like beasts in their own dung, be praise, honor, power, and dominion for ever and ever!

But the most envious eye of Leviathan, the ancient serpent—who fell from the height through the sin of pride, yet sees everything lofty through his desire for glory (Job 41), and therefore envies everyone who ascends to the height which he himself lost—seeing that penitent rejoicing in the grace of God over his victory, the insatiable murderer undertook to tempt him by a very different and much more dangerous path than before. For, knowing that the bishop would soon arrive, he summoned his Tartarean ministers and devised a most deceitful spectacle. The ravening wolf himself put on the garb of the pastor in a presumptuous counterfeit deserving punishment; the most cruel [Col. 1153A] tyrant assumed, by an ill-omened prodigy, the person of a bishop; and he furnished the ministers of darkness, bathed in false light, as though they were ministers of righteousness.

Suddenly the ridiculous apparition came forward. The false bishop, intending to deceive, advanced adorned in a most splendid robe, cheerful in face, apparently reverend in dress and bearing, so that he might be thought anything rather than a devil. Attendants of falsehood followed, themselves deceitfully decked in white garments, as though priests, Levites, and clerics of the lower orders. Each carried what looked like a vessel belonging to the Church: some sacred vessels of the altar, others vestments for the holy sacrifice, and others, as though bearing books for the divine office, carried them in impure hands.

Thus the changeable and winding dragon, transformed into an angel of light, approached with a retinue of impiety pretending to piety; and to the sinful man, now strengthened by God’s grace for penance, he vomited forth with a serene expression the deadly poison of deception:

“O servant of God, great is your patience; unconquered is your faith, [Col. 1153B] since you have kept the obedience prescribed to you uninjured and reduced the seducing spirits to nothing in all their malice and deceit. For you must know that their most wicked plots have by no means escaped us: throughout this whole night, by manifold fraud they tried to break your patience, nullify your faith, and utterly ruin your obedience. Yet, with the Lord protecting you, they have been deprived of the result of their malice.”

The other wicked spirits, standing there in the guise of priests, deacons, and other clerics, joined this pestilential flatterer. They extolled his victory with extraordinary praises. Some praised him because he had not deigned even to look upon, much less touch, the appearance offered to him; others because he had put relatives and friends, possessions, and everything worldly beneath the fear of God. But all together proclaimed that he had most patiently endured the cruelest beatings and asserted that he would be a companion of the martyrs.

Then that chief—no bishop, but an artificer [Col. 1153C] of deceit—said: “Come, brother: you have fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept obedience like a good athlete. Now it remains, since dawn has shone, that you receive permission to speak and set forth to us in order how you triumphed over those wandering spirits, for we desire to hear this from you.”

Meanwhile the foster-child of God’s grace, whose eyes and ears Satan was mocking with such apparitions, was greatly troubled in his thoughts. For the same deceitful spirits who mocked him outwardly in visible form inwardly, invisibly, enticed him by their viperous suggestions to believe their lies. But how could the most malicious plotters harm one whom the most merciful pity of God had decreed to save? For the ancient enemy does not cease in a thousand ways to tempt wretched mortals, because he learns who is elect only by his own defeat and confusion.

Thus, as we have said, while he turned over anxiously and uncertainly in his mind whether he ought to speak or not, suddenly, by the inspiration of God’s most secret grace, he remembered that the bishop had said he would come with the cross of the Lord. Carefully surveying with his eyes all the things which those most unworthy bearers carried in wicked hands as though they were sacred insignia, he shrewdly perceived that the saving sign was not among them. For though Satan can counterfeit and lie about all other things, he cannot at all reproduce the wondrous sign by which he was conquered and reduced to nothing. Greatly terrified, and now restraining the voice about to break forth from his throat, he understood that all that white-clad multitude were ministers of darkness and had fabricated the display of that false religion in order to deceive him.

But when he who had once been Lucifer, and was now Night-bearer, together with the other apostate spirits, saw that all the devices of their deception were being nullified and that by a sinful but penitent man they were, in every subtlety of theirs, despised and cast away like a menstruous cloth, [Col. 1154A] they were struck with terror as if by the presence of the very highest divinity working its power in a fragile vessel.
