Like smoke they vanished, and no longer dared to harass with their most wicked deceits the man whom they saw protected beneath the shadow of the wings of God’s grace and incapable of being caught in the snares of their plots.

Therefore, after the enemies of all good, together with their prince, had been defeated and confounded, the bishop arrived according to his promise with the cross of the Lord, surrounded by a great company of the sacred clergy, marked not by a feigned but by a true and genuine religion. When, after prayer, he greeted his recluse and commanded him to speak in the Lord’s name, the man, still fearing the perils of the night, could scarcely be persuaded to loosen his tongue into words. For, having experienced the manifold snares of demons, he thought, like the Academics, that everything must be doubted and distrusted his ability to distinguish truth from falsehood. At last, when he saw the sign of the holy cross—which alone, he knew, demons tremble at and flee—he reverently bowed his head and adored it. Asked by the bishop whether he had kept the brief but salutary penance enjoined upon him, and whether he could add anything further in satisfaction, he answered:

“I, Father, in order to preserve obedience, have struggled through immense contests and most perilous combats within this brief span of time. Therefore I give thanks to our Savior God, who has deigned to show me this night, wretched and unworthy though I am, how obstinately I have hitherto been an enemy of my own salvation, and how madly I enslaved myself to the ruinous service of a cruel tyrant.”

At these words all who were present were astonished and wished to know what had happened. At the bishop’s command that he declare without delay what he had seen or heard, he recounted, to the wonder of all, the tragedy of diabolical cunning, and moreover displayed the wounds that testified to tyrannical cruelty, by whose bruising his back and other limbs had become swollen. [Col. 1154C] While they all together gave thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ for the unutterable gift of His mercy, the bishop smiled with grateful joy and said to him:

“What then, brother, do you think? Do you wish to be satisfied with this penance alone, or do you still consent to undertake a lawful penance according to the ordinances of the Church?”

But he, wholly forgetful of his former weakness and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit to endure whatever most grievous labors might be required, replied: “Lord Father, whatever your fatherhood commands, I will perform willingly and devoutly, provided only that I may escape the fellowship of malignant spirits. How detestable and bitter their society is—terrible as it is to experience it—would that wretched mortals might likewise be able to know and avoid beforehand! Therefore I am ready to undertake solemn Lents, prolonged fasts, vowed pilgrimages, and whatever else accords with lawful penance; for through the grace of God I have become certain that sinners cannot return to life without the bitterness of penance.”

But who could worthily express how greatly the bishop rejoiced, or how much all who were present, and all his kinsfolk and friends who were of sound mind, gave thanks to God when such holy, humble, and devout words resounded from the mouth of a sinner who, only the space of one night before, had been most proud and obstinate and had utterly rejected every penance? Above all, his admirable wife, worthy of honorable remembrance, rejoicing with special exultation, blessed the Lord because through the constancy of holy prayer and pious exhortation, through her labor and diligence, she had drawn her husband—joined to her in carnal union—to the spiritual and most chaste nuptials of the immaculate Lamb.

Behold what sweet, pleasant, and salutary fruits the power of holy discernment produced; and conversely, what bitter, pernicious, and deadly fruits the vice of miserable indiscretion brought forth. For the priest mentioned above, who had undertaken to heal the sick man, ignorant of the discernment of virtues and failing to understand how kindly and compassionately he ought to have treated a weak conscience, brought temporal death upon himself, while doubling for the man whom he ought to have restored to life the burden of eternal death. [Col. 1155A] But this blessed bishop, because he excelled magnificently in the virtue of discernment, when every resource of compassion seemed to have failed him, found through the shrewdness of pious discernment a means by which to cast down the proud man for his health and raise the humbled man to life.

## CHAPTER XIII. How dangerous it is to delay one who wishes to confess, at whatever hour.

The Apostle James testifies that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1), thereby rebuking the foolish philosophy of those who attribute the light of good works and the quickening of understanding to free will, seek to establish their own righteousness, and therefore are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10). For who can adequately weigh the many hazards and calamities to which the weakness not only of human flesh but even of the human mind is exposed if it is abandoned by grace even for a moment, since we do not know what we ought to pray for unless the Spirit helps our weakness (Rom. 8)?

Therefore, reader, I ask that you bear patiently if I briefly add another example, as I think very necessary, concerning the sacrament of confession. In it there will appear with the utmost clarity both how liable to lamentable ruin is the blindness of the human mind corrupted through free will, and again how powerful and effective is grace for saving that which had perished. Grace, indeed, could have preserved it from that very fall, had not Adam’s sin—according to the notable saying [Col. 1155C] of Ambrose—been necessary, a sin erased by Christ’s death; so that noble nature, created in the image of God, might recognize what it is by itself and what by grace, and might not forget the mercies of the Lord for ever.

In one of the monasteries of the Premonstratensian Order, a certain brother was at one time assigned the office of infirmarian. By outward appearances he seemed to possess suitable religious seriousness and honorable conduct. But alas! He was discovered to be weighing “weight and weight,” both of which are abominable before God (Prov. 20), on a deceitful balance. Outwardly he pretended through hypocrisy to be sober and a lover of frugality; inwardly, however, secretly giving free rein to gluttony and voracity, he most wickedly consumed, without fear of God’s judgment, the more lavish food which he might have prepared for the sick, and the more delicate foods entrusted to his fidelity on account of the sick persons’ need.

It happened that after he had for some time subjected himself with culpable recklessness to this most wicked vice, he was, by some judgment unknown to me, touched with compunction for an hour and resolved to confess. Therefore, on the holy Vigil of Pentecost, about the ninth hour, when the abbot of that place was about to put on sacred vestments to celebrate the office of that day, he approached him and made the sign of confession, as is the custom for those wishing to confess. But the abbot, thinking that he wished to mention some everyday negligences, refused, indicating that he should seek a more suitable time for confession, since he himself was about to proceed immediately to celebrate the most sacred mysteries.

Rejected, the brother went away sorrowful because he had not been allowed to obtain the effect of confession for the crime, full of every shame and disgrace, which he was about to confess. He feared lest the little spark of fear of God then kindled in him should grow cold through this delay, and lest shortly afterward he should not find himself able to endure the shame that brings glory, [Col. 1156A] but should instead fall into the shame that produces sin (Ecclus. 4).

Seeing this brother afflicted by such grief and inclined toward despair, the malignant spirits, enemies of the human race, rushed upon him like robbers upon an orphan. They gave the wretched soul—who had defiled itself, contrary to reason, order, and every beauty of law and decency, through the unseemly pleasure of its flesh—to drink the gall of hardening and the wormwood of despair. Moreover, by most violent persuasion they impelled the man, now deranged in mind, against his own throat.

Finally, from the hour when he was rejected until evening, tossed by the machinations of demons amid various ruinous thoughts, he became foolish and was removed from the wisdom of God, which says: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present among learned thoughts” (Prov. 8). In most unhappy madness he resolved to imitate Judas the betrayer, hated by heaven and earth, who perished between the two. The evening assembly for that most holy feast was already being conducted by the brethren. He, as though detained in attending to the comfort of the sick, abandoned his station and withdrew himself from the assembly of the brothers. Wretched man, he did not understand that he could be deceived all the more readily by the snares of malignant spirits the more he presumed to separate himself from the congregation of the righteous praising God.

Why say more? At last overcome by weariness and despair and falling into hatred even of his own life, the fool entered into a pact with death and struck a covenant with hell. On that very holy night of Pentecost, plunging a knife into the throat whose pleasure he had satisfied by disgraceful enticement, he made the same being the instigator of his most wicked self-killing whose prompting he had not feared to follow in pursuing Cyclopean voracity. Then the apostate spirits rejoiced with most wicked delight, with the special and unrestrained exultation they are wont to show whenever they can overthrow someone from the number of the religious. Ignorant that their presumption would soon be checked by divine judgment, [Col. 1156C] and acting as though they had already obtained a complete victory, they formed a plan to remove and carry away the half-dead man, lest, before he wholly expired, he might be found by the brethren and by some means of mercy be recalled to the aid of confession and penance, and thus the princes of Tartarus might lose their wicked prey.

But when that brother appeared neither at Vespers nor at the sacred Vigils in his place in choir, the abbot remembered the sign of confession he had made and the rejection he had suffered. He trembled all over and, as though his spirit already forewarned him lest what he did not know had happened might indeed have happened, began to fear with grievous contrition of heart. Quickly, fearful and anxious, he summoned certain brothers and sent them to seek the man, believing that whatever misfortune had befallen him would be imputed to himself by God the just Judge, because he had presumed, although under evident necessity, yet with insufficient discernment, to reject one who wished to confess.

The brother was sought in the infirmary and in the other places where he was hoped to be found, but nowhere discovered. At last, however, those who had been sent searched even every hidden corner more carefully. In the sick persons’ privy they found the knife, the instrument of a dreadful crime, stained with blood, and the pavement likewise reddened with much blood; these gave certain evidence of the sad event of a murder recently committed. [Col. 1156D]

At the sight, the brothers sent to search were horrified and turned pale, and they lamented that the cruel malice of him who was a murderer from the beginning had prevailed against their faint-hearted brother. But when, searching more diligently through every hidden and dark place, they tried to discover what had become of the body which they supposed to be dead, and could find no trace at all of either living or dead man, they were struck with even greater amazement. They hastened back and reported to the abbot and brothers the mournful occurrence of their brother’s death.

Immediately grief and mourning arose among all: with one voice they lamented their brother’s fall in pious compassion. But he mourned more impatiently than the rest who, holding the name and office of shepherd, was marked as having provided an occasion for the loss of the wretched little sheep. Meanwhile the day of Pentecost, to be observed with festive devotion, dawned. The brethren, celebrating the solemnities of the Masses with utmost devotion out of reverence for so great a day, humbly begged the clemency of almighty God to deign, in His customary mercy, to reveal to them what had happened to that brother.

But the goodness of divine clemency, which incomparably exceeds both the merits and the prayers of suppliants, was not content merely to grant what was requested. By a more abundant gift of grace, it wished to show how graciously it had placed the hand of its mercy beneath that sinner’s fall, lest one who deserved punishment for his fault should be crushed by the presumption of diabolical malice. For the unanswerable judgment of the merciful justice of God did not allow him to receive judgment without mercy, since, fearing judgment, he had desired to flee beneath the wings of mercy through the assistance of confession and penance, though through the negligence of his superior he had been unable to obtain it. Nor did God permit that the most sacred day on which the Holy Spirit abundantly illuminated the hearts of His primitive Church so as to enlighten all nations should be defiled by the deadly victory of the adverse party.

For behold, while the sacred mysteries were being celebrated, one of the brothers, standing apart beneath the tower which supported the bells, happened to look upward. He saw that man, truly wretched through his own misery yet plainly blessed by the magnificent grace of God, lying headlong upon a steep wall, hanging from the wall from the loins downward and seemingly about to fall at once. Astonished, the man who had seen him called the others. Looking more closely, they discovered him to be the very man whom they had supposed had perished in body and soul, ensnared by the frauds of the enemy. But, expecting to find merely a lifeless corpse, [Col. 1157C] they brought ladders and climbed up; and, through the mercy of Him who permits none of His predestined ones to perish, they found the man still breathing.

When those who had climbed up made this known to the others with cries mingled with joy, all exulted—especially the abbot, who, weeping and lamenting, kept declaring himself guilty of that man’s death. From all sides the cry was repeated: “Glory to you, Christ God; glory to you, Holy Spirit God!” Then, by the abbot’s order, he was lowered with the utmost caution and care and carried to the infirmary. All beheld and marvelled at the gaping, dreadful wound in his throat, wondering joyfully how one so mutilated could live in such wholeness of health; he was laid upon a bed. After he had rested a little, the brothers came near and compressed with their hands the opening of his horribly gaping throat, so that the breath of life might not escape by the wrong passage, testing whether he might somehow be able, even thus, to utter words. [Col. 1157D]

But merciful God, who had powerfully rescued him from the tyrannical malice of the ancient enemy, also deigned, contrary to the force of failing nature, to grant to this man the faculty of speech for the praise of His glory—the grace of confession. When the devout curiosity of the investigating brothers perceived this—that, against every law of mortal nature, this brother too had been restored to health—the abbot at once dismissed everyone else and finally received, by a truly great gift of God and a stupendous miracle, the confession that had been imprudently delayed; and he enjoined suitable penance upon the man confessing. So that the gift which the Holy Spirit, who is called the compassion of God, had deigned to grant on the most exalted day of His feast might be full and complete, the man thereafter strove all the more eagerly and devoutly for purity of holy conduct, because he had learned in his own person with greater certainty that those who, though distinguished by the outward garb of religion, do not fear to defile their consciences with hidden crimes lie exposed to the venomous bites of Leviathan, the ancient serpent. [Col. 1158A]

Therefore, just as the Apostle testifies, “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15); so without doubt whatever mighty works of God have been performed in His holy Church were performed for our instruction. Accordingly, all who have received by God’s grace the care of souls should beware lest, for any reason or necessity whatsoever, they presume to defer without the grave weight of discernment one committed to them who wishes to confess; lest they oppose the Apostle’s saying, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5); and lest perhaps one who could now be recalled to life, going through that very rebuff into an alienation of heart, should soon afterward disdain to return to life.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the danger of discord

Since the Lord says in the Gospel, “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5), and likewise the Apostle gives the salutary warning, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4), it is deeply lamentable that some even among the religious relax the reins of anger too carelessly and sometimes break forth into the dregs of strife and discord. While they desire to remain unconquered outwardly, they are grievously wounded within; and while outwardly defending small and worthless matters, inwardly they lose great and precious things. For, loving to retain a temporal possession, they grow more angry than is fitting if it is taken away, and thereby lose the incomparable treasure of true love.

Therefore, so that anyone pursuing the religious life may remember himself to be a temple of God and dread to offend by the passion of anger or discord the Lord of majesty dwelling within him, I shall not shrink from recording, as a warning for the sluggish, how a certain religious priest, because he did not fear to violate in his neighbour the peace which the citizens of heaven announced to earth-dwellers when the King of heaven was born on earth (Luke 2), lost a remarkable grace specially bestowed upon him by the Lord. [Col. 1158B]

This priest, commendable in life, did not languish in idle sloth, but earnestly laboured to ensure that the quality of his conduct did not fall short of the excellence of his rank. Above all, in the offering of the saving victim—wherein the Son is offered to the Father to take away the sins of the world—he took care to sacrifice himself in the presence of the supreme Godhead through the sacrifice of a contrite heart and a humbled spirit.

He had a parishioner who, although occupied with the affairs of secular life, perhaps was not inferior to his pastor in soundness of faith and sincerity of devotion. Instructed religiously by the priest’s teaching and example, this man continually wore down the thresholds of the church; he attended the celebration of Mass as a diligent observer and, knocking at heaven by the persistence of his holy prayers, spoke with the Lord in the simplicity of his heart during the time of the divine sacrifice. [Col. 1158C]

The Lord, wishing to make known the merit of both men to the praise and glory of His name, opened the eyes of this layman, both spiritual and bodily. During the celebration of the sacred mystery he began to see our Lord Jesus Christ with blessed eyes, standing upon the altar beside the holy chalice, mercifully anointing the consciences of both men with the wondrous sweetness of His presence.

When the consecration of the divine sacraments had been duly completed and the kiss of peace was to be conveyed to the people, the priest, following the custom of some, first kissed the sacred host. At that very moment the gracious Lord came near and most graciously offered the kiss of peace to His minister. O how great is the kindness of our Redeemer! How much the devout and pious simplicity of some persons obtains from their God: that they seem, in some measure during this mortal life, to taste beforehand that ineffable sweetness of the eternal vision of God which is generally reserved for all the elect at the end!

The man admitted to so reverent a mystery of divine contemplation kept his secret to himself, according to the prophet. Although he frequently saw Him who is “fairer in form than the children of men,” he would reveal nothing to the priest, lest either he himself be charged with vanity for lightly disclosing so great a mystery of God without grave cause, or the priest, to whom such grace had been granted by the Lord, should deprive himself of that grace through the vice of pride. [Col. 1159A]

Meanwhile, a little pig belonging to a poor man had become accustomed to enter, by stealthy incursions, the garden of the aforesaid priest—a garden green with various herbs and vegetables and, as it were, smiling upon its gardener through the vitality of its growth. Since the animal could find nothing in its master’s house, owing to the scarcity of food, with which to fill its belly, it was forced to beg this elsewhere. The priest, then, being greatly distressed that his garden was being ravaged, repeatedly warned the poor man to keep his pig at home. He repeatedly drove the pig, as it rooted up the tender vegetable plants, beyond the garden enclosure with the violence of blows; but when this achieved nothing, he was at last provoked by grief to kill the pig. [Col. 1159B]

The poor man, learning of his animal’s death, groaned that he had lost a great part of the support of his meagre means. Wishing to take legal action against the priest so that he might restore the loss inflicted upon him according to the laws, he was scorned and dismissed to the detriment of his case, the priest countering with an exaggerated account of the damage to his garden, because “a poor man lies everywhere.”

Thus the priest, remaining unreconciled to his poor brother, rashly approached to offer the victim of true reconciliation. But the Lord Jesus, who was made for us by God the Father “righteousness, redemption, and reconciliation” (1 Cor. 1), did not deign to manifest His presence to one stained by the plague of discord.

Behold, the man of God mentioned above, standing and praying most devoutly during the action of the sacred canon, expected to see, as usual, Him “upon whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1); but, disappointed of his hope, he was greatly troubled. He saw the priest utterly stripped of the grace bestowed upon him and overshadowed, as it were, by a cloud of divine displeasure. [Col. 1159C]

What he had kept hidden for some time in modest humility, with conscience alone as witness, he did not, necessity requiring, choose to suppress in silence. Taking the priest aside, he privately told him what kind and how great a grace he had lost, warning and beseeching him that, if he had fallen into some sin, he should hasten as quickly as possible to cleanse it by the remedy of confession and penance, if perhaps he might deserve to receive again, through the abundant kindness of our Redeemer, the grace he had lost.

The priest, dismayed in spirit, replied that he knew himself guilty of no criminal offence, nor did his conscience reproach him more than usual even concerning the faults that can arise in daily life—except only that, unwilling to tolerate the destruction of his garden, he had killed that poor man’s pig and had not yet been reconciled to him through the humility of satisfaction.

Both men therefore understood that the Lord, protector of the poor, had avenged the injury done to His poor man with a punishment all the more severe because it was hidden. The priest hastened to make satisfaction to the Lord’s little one through adequate recompense for the damage inflicted. [Col. 1159D]

Whether he recovered that exalted grace which he had lost, however, is unknown to us. For the servant of God, who shared that grace with him—or perhaps possessed it before him—disciplined himself with censorious silence, lest he presume to reveal God’s mysteries indiscriminately without some definite necessity.

Moreover, because the hardness of the human heart is stirred only with difficulty to guard itself, we shall further prove, even by the testimony of the enemy himself, how dangerous the vice of discord is. Though unwilling and compelled, he betrays the truth; yet he sometimes seems to utter such words as are known to be warnings for the faithful.

In a certain monastery of nuns, the provost of the place was at one time discussing with the sisters the sale of a possession belonging to the monastery. As commonly happens when parties defend their own view as supported by sounder judgment, a serious discord arose between him and the sisters. The provost said that administration had been entrusted to him and forced the entire affair, by the authority of his office, according to the decision of his own will. The sisters, who maintained the opposite position, withdrew deeply scandalized. [Col. 1160A]

There was in the same monastery a laywoman afflicted by an unclean spirit. For her deliverance the sisters laboured together daily in persistent prayer; and, that they might press the destructive spirit more strongly, they had her partake more frequently of the Lord’s sacraments.

On the following day the provost, making light of the sisters’ scandal, approached the altar of God—troubled himself, together with those same sisters, who were even more grievously troubled—to offer the peaceful victim. When the consecration of the divine gifts had been performed according to custom, he had the afflicted woman brought before him also, so that she might receive the Eucharist. [Col. 1160B]

Then the evil spirit, resisting in a wondrous manner, began to utter savage and terrifying cries. Rebuking the provost with most bitter invective, it said:

> “O most wretched and unfortunate of men, what are you doing? You breathe from your whole breast the deadly poison of rancour and discord; moreover, you stand guilty before the eyes of supreme Majesty of gravely scandalizing the Lord’s little ones. Yet you rush, at once imprudently and irreverently, to consecrate, handle, and eat the flesh of the Most High? Know certainly that you would have acted more wisely had you not entered the house of God today than by scorching your conscience with the branding iron of such presumption.”

Though it was compelled by many exorcisms and prayers to yield reverence to the divine sacraments until the woman whom it tormented had communicated, it could scarcely, and only with great difficulty, be compelled to permit her to receive the grace of the Eucharist from the hands of one defiled by the vice of dissension and strife. [Col. 1160C]

From this we gather that through our negligence our enemies gain strength against us, and that the more prone a person is to sin, the more difficult it is for him to escape the most dreadful yoke of the prince of darkness. How diligently the vice of discord must be avoided, and how swiftly one must return to the bond of peace and concord, is sufficiently shown also by that great John called “the Almsgiver,” who, because of his incomparable generosity and compassion toward the needy, was called in Greek *Eleēmōn*, that is, “Merciful.”

This blessed bishop, while patriarch of Alexandria, the great city, opposed Nicetas, a patrician of the same city, who wished to post in the marketplace certain adulterated laws concerning merchandise—laws that smacked more of exaction and avarice than of the restraints of just laws. The generous patriarch foresaw that this would burden the poor, who are the pasture of the rich, and resisted magnanimously. Thus, disturbed by a most serious dispute, they departed from one another in discord. [Col. 1160D]

But the gentle shepherd, who had learned from the supreme Shepherd, the Lord Jesus Christ, to be meek and humble of heart, could have defended his conscience by the testimony of the stronger case and disregarded the offence of the man who, inflamed by the heats of avarice, was irrationally agitated. Yet, because of the fear of God, as the sun was hastening to set, he sent the patrician through religious clerics a memorable saying: “My lord Patrician, the sun is at its setting.”

Struck to the heart by these words, the Patrician rose quickly and ran to clasp the feet of the venerable patriarch. Thus the true imitator of Christ’s meekness, striving to bend himself to the height of humility, extinguished in his neighbour’s heart the tinder of proud discord.

## CHAPTER XV. In praise of patience

[Col. 1161A]

But, O how fitting a place is this for remembering the admirable patience of a certain brother, who, striving to be peaceable with one who hated peace and, according to the Lord’s command, to pray even for his enemy, through the Lord’s compassion tore from his brother’s heart the poisonous roots of long-standing malice. He merited to receive as a most devoted and obedient follower the man whom he had long endured as a most violent persecutor.

Accordingly, in a monastery of the Cistercian Order there once sprang up, from some cause of hostility, seeds of dissension and hatred between two brothers. One of them persisted in the malice of discord; the other, swiftly recovering his senses through God’s grace, hastened to uproot with the rake of compunction what he recognized to be growing evilly within himself. [Col. 1161B]

The more that malicious man attempted, by secret or open attacks, mockery, or slanders, to bring his brother’s spirit to bitterness, the more this other man, humbling himself in the humility of the fear of God, vigilantly blunted by confession, tears, and prayer the spurs of envy and impatience which the adversary tried to sharpen in his heart.

But what do you not compel in mortal breasts, execrable corruption of malice and envy? For all that this patient and humble brother did for his conscience—giving place to wrath and, in accordance with the Gospel command, offering the other cheek to one striking him—the perverse and swollen man twisted into evidence of pride and contempt for himself. The more the former tried by his patience to soften that savage mind, the more the latter, driven by the frenzies of his malice, was inflamed by wretched envy ever more and more to persecute the innocent man. [Col. 1161C]

Thus it came about that, changed into the bitterness of an alien vine, he did not fear to profane what was holy, proscribe justice, and confuse right and wrong, provided only that he could disturb the tranquillity, cloud the grace, and blacken the reputation of the man whom he persecuted with most wicked hatred.

For, seeing that the unconquered strength of his opponent’s mind triumphantly rose above every contrivance of his wickedness and, with the foot of steadfast patience, trod on the neck of his malice, this most savage wolf came to his abbot, pretending to be a sheep, raging with sharper envy. He most wickedly accused his brother of a detestable crime which he had wickedly fabricated, seeking, if possible, to humble by the leaven of a most evil lie and a corrupted reputation the man whom the honour of innocence rendered glorious.

When the falsely accused brother was summoned to answer the charge, knowing it is written that “he is cruel who disregards his reputation,” he candidly declared that he was not conscious of this crime and voluntarily offered to undergo whatever test might be chosen to prove his innocence. Yet, since he knew the human heart to be prone from youth not only to do evil but also to suspect evil in another, he grieved deeply that a word once spoken had given occasion for scandal concerning him to the weak. Though he could safely say with the Apostle, “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1), he could not patiently endure being harassed by the malice of the day through groundless suspicions. [Col. 1161D]

Nevertheless, heedful to follow the counsel of the Apostle, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12), and also fearing lest continual grief, nourished by the stings of impatience, might turn into hatred of his adversary, he turned the whole force of the grief raging within him toward a work of devotion. With continual prayers and tears, both for himself and for his rival, he implored the mercy of the Lord and the compassion of the most blessed Mother of God: that divine grace might strengthen him in charity, restrain in his rival the magnitude of malice, and, by the binding power of its sweetness, pierce him with compunction so as to remove the tinder of scandal.

Nor did he labour vainly in his groaning, nor did the pupils of his eyes flow with the waters of an idle devotion. But the Lord, who consoles the humble and receives the afflicted, heard his voice; and in him was fulfilled what the most wise Solomon says: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, He will turn even his enemies to peace” (Prov. 16). [Col. 1162A]

For some time he had offered to the Lord, in the simplicity of his devotion, the sacrifice of a contrite heart and a humble spirit. Yet the grief that consumed his heart did not cease: grief both at the stigma of dishonour which he had incurred though innocent, and at the destruction of his brother, who, infected by the poison of lying and hatred, was perishing. It happened that one night, in this state, he stood in his appointed place in choir for the solemnity of Vigils.

And behold: at the remembrance both of his own calamity and of his brother’s peril, a fountain of tears began to bubble up from the deepest marrow of his heart. It truly drew the sources of its streams from the fountain of the house of David, opened “for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13). As it sprang forth, tears flowed from his eyes—not against the man who caused them, so that he might be confounded and perish, he who had prepared the pit of confusion and destruction for the one shedding them—but so that he might recover his senses from the snares of the devil, by whom he was held captive at his will, and regain the blessedness and glory of eternal life. [Col. 1162B]

Intoxicated, therefore, by the most pure wine of charity which gladdens the heart of man—and whose more worthy portion and higher praise consists in loving enemies and praying for persecutors and slanderers—he could not remain among the brothers. Quickly seeking solitude, he prostrated himself in prayer before one of the altars, that the bubbling fragrances of his most ardent compunction might have freer opportunity to evaporate and, like a rod of smoke, to penetrate the heavens.

There, remembering in his mind all the Lord’s mercies from the beginning, and likewise the inexhaustible bowels of compassion of the most blessed Mother of God, he humbly begged that Mother of Mercy, known as the hope of the wretched, to deign to take up both his own cause and that of his adversary. For in pious confidence he presumed that a matter, however entangled, for which the Mother of supreme compassion would not refuse to perform the office of advocate before her most merciful Judge and Son, could be settled only in the order of mercy. [Col. 1162C]

Nor did the magnificent effect of compassion that immediately followed disappoint the simplicity of his faith. For behold, while in great contrition of heart he repeatedly said: “Merciful Lord, have mercy; merciful Lady, Mother of God, Virgin Mary, aid a wretch utterly deprived of all counsel and help,” and was still turning the words of this devout murmur in heart and mouth, there appeared that spiritual protectress of the poor and special refuge of the wretched—the Virgin Mother of God, our Lady. She brought the desolate man no ordinary or moderate consolation, but precisely such great and fitting consolation as it became the Queen of Heaven, Lady of the world, Mother of Mercy, and hope of the wretched to grant to one whom she had deigned to visit.

The brothers were already singing the final verse of the psalm which the choir was then chanting to the praise of God, when the brother looked up, his eyes shedding tears. He saw that exalted Lady of angels, the hope of the wretched, coming toward him as if from the right side of the altar, with a countenance, bearing, and manner befitting the Mother of Mercy, venerable and radiant with the brilliance of immense light. [Col. 1162D]

A most splendid young man followed her, himself notably adorned with heavenly glory. Meanwhile, when the psalm had ended, the brothers said the glory to the Holy Trinity and, as is customary, all bowed together in reverence for supreme Majesty. The blessed Virgin stopped and reverently bowed her most exalted head—the head to which no creature is equal, except only that One who, in her sacred and virginal womb, was assumed by the Word of God into unity of person, from the sacred and of the sacred womb; that head, I say, both so humble and so high. She remained bowed as a truly humble handmaid of the Lord until the brothers had finished, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 1163A]

After this, raising herself and turning her face toward the brother in distress, she comforted him with honey-sweet words:

> “Man of God, let the tears now cease from your eyes, and let the bitterness of grief that sorely afflicts your heart depart from you. For there is a reward for your work: according to your measure, you have become an imitator of the Lord and my Son’s highest innocence and loftiest charity. You have not only endured your adversary’s violence with equanimity, but, bearing devout concern for his salvation, you have not hesitated to humble yourself for him before the Lord in mourning and tears. Therefore know that, because of the sincere devotion of your faith, I have obtained from the Lord glory for you and pardon for your rival.”

The brother, admitted to so great a height of heavenly mysteries that he saw with bodily eyes the venerable Mother of the Lord, revered by all the orders of angels, was not at all afraid. Indeed, he could not be disturbed, since he saw the Mother of sweetness and security. He said to her confidently:

> “I beseech you, Lady, who are you, who speak so graciously to the heart of your little servant? And who is this young man who is with you?”

> “I am Mary, Mother of God,” she said, “and this young man is John the Evangelist, to whose chaste care my most gracious Son, hanging upon the cross for our salvation, committed me.”

The brother said:

> “If you then are she through whom salvation came to the human race, whom the whole creation reveres and praises, why, I ask, do you too bow your honourable head, as though you were one of the rest, even before the angelic powers?”

The most merciful Lady replied:

> “You should know that whenever glory is rendered upon earth to the Holy Trinity with fear and reverence, all the powers of heaven are moved and stirred to praise their Creator.” [Col. 1163B]

When these words had been spoken, the blessed vision was withdrawn from the sight of the beholder. Yet at the same hour as the appearance of the blessed Virgin, so wondrous a sweetness of nectarean fragrance refreshed with gracious inspiration not only the inner heart of that brother, who was wasting away in sorrow and anxiety, but also the hearts of all who were then devoutly chanting in choir. It could readily be understood that this was not the fragrance of material spices but wholly of divine power: “Who shall speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord, or make heard all the praises of His mercies?” (Ps. 105).

Truly His ways are unsearchable, and the works of His compassion incomprehensible. For that envious slanderer and accuser of his innocent brother, who, so far as lay in him, had extinguished alike his neighbour’s life and honour with the sword of a cruel lie, deserved indeed to be struck by that terrible sentence in which the Lord says to the children of Israel: “If you walk contrary to me, I too will proceed against you and chastise you with seven plagues for your crimes” (Lev. 26); and by that saying from the Psalm: “You have loved evil more than goodness; therefore God will destroy you utterly” (Ps. 51). [Col. 1163C–D]

Although he deserved, I say, to hear this, he did not hear it. Rather, through the patience of the innocent man and the most humble intercession of fraternal charity grieving devoutly for him, he deserved to hear that evangelical householder displaying the bowels of compassion to the prodigal son and saying:

> “Quickly bring the first robe of compunction and put it on him, lest he walk naked and they see his shame; and give a golden ring of confession upon his hand, so that, washed in the waters of confusion which bring glory unto salvation—for in confession all things are washed—he may receive the seal of innocence; and give sandals of fruitful penance upon his feet” (Luke 15),

so that, walking in the paths of righteousness, he might thereafter not dash the feet of his affections against the stones of malice.

Indeed, when the fragrance of that most sweet odour which issued from the virginal body of the undefiled Mother of God reached, among the others deemed worthy of this grace, even the foul cavern of his breast, polluted by envy and hatred, he was immediately pierced with compunction and beneficially inflamed by that fire which the Lord Jesus sends upon the earth. He began to weigh his crime in the balance of truth, to judge himself guilty, wretched, and deserving of every torment, and correspondingly to pronounce blessed the innocence of the brother whom he had slandered with a false charge. [Col. 1164A]

At last, unable to bear the goads of his accusing conscience, he resolved in his mind to cease every form of persecution of his brother. Once the fabricated story of his crime had been disclosed by confession, he would make satisfaction to him, according to his abbot’s judgment, with all the humility he could.

When morning came, the brothers, not without great amazement, asked one another what the sweetness of the great fragrance which they had sensed while chanting during the night might signify. The man conscious of this great mystery went privately to the abbot, simply revealing what he had seen and heard and affirming that the very hour of the blessed Mother of God’s appearance was the hour in which the fragrance of heavenly sweetness had been poured into the nostrils of those chanting. [Col. 1164B]

The abbot marvelled and found it difficult to credit his words, since the greatness of so glorious a miracle exceeded what one might expect from the man’s person. But behold: to confirm the truth, that malicious defamer of his innocent brother arrived, pale and trembling. Weeping and lamenting, he confessed that the drama of that detestable crime had been fabricated by himself under the compulsion of envious malice, rather than grounded in truth. He mourned in great contrition of heart that he had burned with persecution of his brother in many ways and for a long time.

Asked whence such sudden compunction and recognition of his sin had come to him, he replied that he too, though unworthy, had been suffused with the same grace of the most sweet fragrance that had touched the others; and that as soon as the anointing of the heavenly gift penetrated the depths of his heart, he had wonderfully revived into hatred of malice and love of innocence. The abbot reported what he had heard to certain spiritual elders, and together they gave thanks to the Lord for the grace of divine compassion amid such great marvels. [Col. 1164C]

But the brother who by his patience had converted his human enemy to peace and had crushed the devilish enemy beneath his feet eagerly revisited the place where he had learned these heavenly mysteries. As he worshipped most devoutly there, where he remembered that the sacred feet of the Queen of Heaven had stood, he joyfully found, in confirmation of the vision’s truth, that the stone bore the blessed footprints and breathed forth in its fragrance the honey-sweet odour he had perceived in that very vision.

When the abbot learned this from the brother’s swift report, he took with him certain religious brothers and approached the indicated place with fear and reverence. Proving by facts what he had heard in words, he inhaled the sweetness of the wondrous fragrance. Having shared counsel with his brothers, he ordered the same stones to be dug out and placed in a fitting location in the sacristy as a memorial of so great a miracle. [Col. 1164D]

Behold: we can prove literally and, as it were, by touch that “the peacemakers are blessed, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5). Conversely, as the foregoing portions of this chapter show, even those who seemed through their religious life to be counted among the children of God are deprived of fellowship in that exalted name if they neglect to preserve the bond of peace and concord in the unity of fraternal charity, unless they hasten to return to the tranquillity of peace, without which no one shall see God (Heb. 12).

Therefore let us pray, brothers, that through the sweetness of His Holy Spirit the Lord may extinguish in us the bitterness of discord and remove from our hearts the plagues of rancour and ill will, through which religious persons living a common life are known sometimes to be placed in grave danger. Thus, all being of one mind and feeling the same toward one another, as children of God—for we are children of peace—may we dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the danger of those who recite the psalms negligently

[Col. 1165A]

The Psalmist exhorts us to render the daily due of divine service to the supreme Majesty with fear and reverence, saying: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. 2). But since the weakness of the human heart, prone to negligence from youth, easily grows lukewarm in spiritual exercises—especially where repetition breeds weariness, as in the course of continual psalmody—we have judged it fitting, for the correction of the negligent, to disclose how our Lord Jesus Christ deigned personally to rebuke the blasphemous negligence of a certain cleric. Thus the minds of the negligent may awaken all the more readily to their amendment, as they weigh with fearful heart the majesty of Him who rebukes them more attentively.

Blessed Anno, Archbishop of Cologne and founder of the monastery of Siegburg—where likewise the ashes of his sacred body await the glory of the future resurrection—was of such holiness and [Col. 1165B] authority in the Church of God as is clear to all who read the history of his life. Whenever this venerable priest could withdraw from external business and from company, he devoted himself with particular attention to psalmody with one of his clerics, whom he had foreseen to be suitable for so religious an occupation. Yet this man, whom devotion did not make willing, but whom necessity, I suppose, compelled to render such continual hymns, became thoroughly wearied by the repetition of this pious work. At times he began to omit half the words, and sometimes even whole words, so that at every recitation of the *Gloria* he mentioned only the first and third Persons and entirely passed over the middle one.

As day succeeded day, this most wicked negligence went unnoticed and uncorrected, because the holy bishop fixed the attention of his heart upon those verses assigned to him by the alternating lot. One evening, when the bishop had laid himself upon his bed to rest, before falling asleep he [Col. 1165C] heard what seemed the voice of a man hurriedly and negligently saying: “Glory to the Father, and to the Holy Spirit,” and repeating the same thing a second and third time. Having heard this, and being wholly unable to discern what the voice signified for him, he fell asleep. Then the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him—He who is “fairer in form than the sons of men.” Stretching out his hand, with two fingers—the thumb and little finger—folded into the palm, He held the three middle fingers upright. Then, touching the index finger of the other hand with the index finger of His right, He said: “Behold, the Father.” Immediately, touching the middle finger in like manner: “Behold, the Son.” Finally, touching the ring finger: “Behold,” He said, “the Holy Spirit.” Then He added:

“When these three Persons, who are one God, are worshipped with equal honour by the whole Church, why do you not rebuke the blasphemies of your cleric, who, at every singing of the *Gloria*, withholds the honour of praise from me, who am the middle Person in the Trinity?”

Awakening after this delightful [Col. 1165D] vision, the priest of God rejoiced greatly at a visitation from such Majesty. Hurrying to test with the bodily ear what he had heard in the spirit, he summoned the cleric after rest and began the customary psalmody. Listening more carefully to what discipline he maintained in singing, he learned with certainty that, at the conclusion of each psalm, through culpable negligence the cleric reduced the Trinity to a duality, passing over the Person of the Son. He therefore chastised him at once with a severe rebuke, as was fitting, and under grave threat commanded him thereafter to sing more distinctly and devoutly.

This same blessed bishop, by the power of Him who reveals mysteries, was once caught up in spirit and learned all the tribulations and calamities destined to oppress the Church of God until the end of the world. Returning to himself, he languished for some time not only in mind but also in body from horror at the vision he had seen. When devout men urgently begged him to disclose, for the edification of the faithful, the [Col. 1166A] mysteries he had seen, he answered their inquiries only with these words:

“Woe, woe, woe to all the corners of the earth, because of those who are called bishops and rulers of souls, by whose teaching and example the people of God ought to have been formed so as to render pure service to the Lord!”

Moreover, how greatly this dangerous negligence must be shunned and guarded against—whereby the course of psalms or any prayers whatsoever is run through without attention, without devotion, hurriedly, and by skipping over at times half or even whole words—is clearly demonstrated also by the book entitled *On the Miracles of the Most Blessed Mary, Mother of God*. There it is found that a certain religious virgin, according to the number of the psalms, daily offered the Queen of Heaven, Mother of Mercy, one hundred and fifty angelic salutations together with an equal number of genuflections. But because, on account of their multitude, she performed them with less worthy devotion than she ought, she was admonished by that same Lady of ours to cut away two parts and to render to her daily fifty salutations [Col. 1166B] together with fitting genuflections, attentively and unhurriedly. Thus she plainly indicated that a little service offered with devotion is more acceptable to God and to herself than much rendered negligently and without devotion.

What answer can those give who trust in a multiplication of prayers or psalms uttered anyhow—who boast that they can run through fifty, or even a whole psalter, in the briefest space of time? Let them learn, I pray, from these examples that God does not weigh how much is offered in His sacrifice, but with what affection of piety it is offered; nor can that be called a holocaust which has not been wholly set ablaze by the flame of devotion. But if anyone has grown, through God’s grace, to so great a height of perfection that he is able to render both much and devoutly, for such a person, according to Scripture, “the law is not laid down” (1 Tim. 1). As in this life, surpassing the vows and merits of the imperfect, he sows good seed without weariness of mind or body, so in the life to come he shall inherit an [Col. 1166C] immeasurable weight of eternal glory, like a star brighter than many constellations.

## CHAPTER XVII. How great a good it is to render God’s service diligently in the daily vigils.

David, outstanding among prophets and most illustrious among patriarchs and kings—the holy man whom the Lord did not so much find as choose according to His heart—was the first of mortals to establish choirs of psalm-singers to confess to the Lord that He is good, that His mercy endures for ever (Pss. 105, 106, etc.). Handing down to Solomon his son the ordering of the house of God, together with the ranks and turns of the singers, he said: “All these things came to me written by the hand of the Lord.” He thus plainly showed that whatever grace, beauty, and virtue the Jerusalem that wanders on earth possesses, groaning under the burden of sinful flesh, all this descends from the fullness of the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 1166D] above, which is therefore free, whose fellowship is wholly united, and in whose streets the sweetest *Alleluia* is sung without interruption.

After the pattern of that city, those who dwell on earth and the children of humankind, adorned with the holiness of charity, chastity, and innocence, strive with diligent devotion to render the proclamations of praise to the Lord their Creator. Although all the faithful in the Church of God pursue this performance of divine praise according to their capacity, yet by true judgment the arduous labour of the Cistercian Order is preferred in this aspect of devotion to the regular obligation of the other Orders. Its professed members, rising for vigils shortly after midnight—and sometimes around midnight—despise the sweetness of early-morning sleep and persevere in labour and hardship until sunrise. In many vigils they strive to anticipate the face of the Lord with confession, prayer, and praise, saying with the Psalmist: “For thy sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. 43); and: “Because of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16).

But how great a merit [Col. 1167A] it is before almighty God to keep watch diligently in His holy and daily service, and likewise how great a danger it is to abandon the vigil-station without urgent necessity, we shall show by a twofold example. Thus those who, kindled by the fervour of the Holy Spirit and finding savour in the song of sacred psalmody, do not recoil from burdensome length but strive to praise God and purify their hearts by liveliness of voice and spirit, may hear the testimony to their work with joyful ears and take comfort in God’s grace. But those oppressed by the vice of sloth and drowsiness, who neither fear God nor are ashamed before men, easily abandoning the joyful fellowship of God’s service and hurrying to the repose of bed, should not neglect to consider to what cruel tyrant’s dominion they subject themselves. Warned by a terrible example, they should take care to cast away the torpor of idleness, lest after this life they be tormented with atrocious punishments for their very sluggishness.

When the holy Father Bernard, [Col. 1167B] first abbot of Clairvaux and worthy of mention with every sweetness of spiritual love, was communicating to peoples, tribes, and tongues of diverse nations the perfection of monastic religion—which he had learned more fully and purely than all the people of his time from the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift—and was building monasteries of the Cistercian Order throughout the world by sending out brethren, from the offerings of the faithful, he founded the monastery of Eberbach. It lay two leagues from the walls of Mainz, the first metropolis of Germany, at the request of the venerable elder Aubert, Archbishop of that city, not far from the bank of the Rhine, the great river and chief among all rivers.

This house, therefore, receiving very great growth through the blessing of so great a father and reproducing its mother-house admirably, rivals to this day the eminence of its revered mother in religious observance, wealth, celebrated reputation, the integrity of its members, the authority of its superiors, and the great number of its community. Thus, throughout all [Col. 1167C] the provinces of Germany, the Church of Eberbach shines as a special mirror of religion and honourableness.

Indeed, faithful neighbours and also certain more distant people, drawn by the good fragrance of the virtues of that holy congregation, customarily sought from its fullness the gravity of its counsel, the aid of its prayers, and protection in dangers; they also generously relieved from its abundance the need of Christ’s poor. Some, prompted by devotion, were accustomed to celebrate the principal feasts there. Among these was a certain knight, valiant in arms, distinguished by birth, and not insignificant in devotion, named Conrad. He customarily celebrated there the solemn day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin and Mother, and attended devoutly from beginning to end the sacred vigils, which were greatly prolonged out of reverence for so great a day. Thus, aided by the prayers of that holy multitude, refreshed by the exhortation of the solemn sermon, and fortified by the divine sacraments of the Masses, he might return more joyfully to his own home and bring blessing to his [Col. 1167D] household.

For though entangled in the chances of secular life and concerned with worldly matters, he humbly recognized that he was not a fruitful vine. Nevertheless, like a most ready elm, he strove by temporal gifts to sustain the spiritual vine together with its fruits. It happened, however, that on one occasion he was hindered by more pressing household affairs and arrived too late for the said feast. Going to bed when the night was already deep, and laying his limbs, wearied by the fatigue of travel, upon the bed, he was overcome by deep sleep and did not hear the signal for vigils, by which the brethren were roused to render divine praise.

Awakening an hour later, when the melody of the chant resounded in his ears, he sprang quickly from bed. Coming into the church, he sat down sorrowfully before one of the altars in the south part of the church, where guests customarily attended the divine offices. Wishing, as he sat, to compensate for his negligence, he strove somehow to share in the holy devotion which throughout the whole church was fervently expressed in rivalry both in singing [Col. 1168A] and in prayer. But, oppressed by the deceit of drowsiness, he grieved that he was insufficiently alert for keeping watch and praying. Angry with himself, as the vigils dragged on he now stood, now sat, and sometimes rubbed his forehead and temples with his hand, attempting by this sort of art to overcome the violence of sleep.

Meanwhile, considering with what eagerness of voices and minds the brethren attended to divine praise, and at the same time recoiling from the weakness of his own flesh, he spoke to the Lord as if offering an excuse, with the astonishment of great admiration:

“Lord God, what is this endurance, extended beyond the capacity of human frailty, by which these brethren seem to have passed beyond the limits of corruptible nature, being put to death for thee all day and night? For behold, though they exercise themselves in daily vigils and fasts, and though on this night they have scarcely taken any sleep, nevertheless [Col. 1168B] they are shown to offer with entire eagerness of spirit vows of praise to thee, their Lord and Creator. But I, a miserable sinner, am unable to endure, for thy name, even the somewhat prolonged vigils of a single night—vigils which these men boast of enduring continually for the reward of eternal life—so that they yield to no hardships whatsoever, but grow still more ardent to undertake those same struggles again.”

Amid these meditations of pious complaint, his eyelids closed briefly and he slipped into a light but blessed sleep. He saw two figures, conspicuous for the beauty of heavenly loveliness and venerable in monastic dress, coming out from the choir of singers toward him. One of them, as though answering his thoughts and commending the excellence of the labour and vigils expended in God’s service, spoke to the knight—who knew no letters—not in his native language, German, but in an elegantly composed Latin verse:

[Col. 1168C]

> Such sufferings only the blessed have deserved to endure.

Having heard this, he immediately shook off sleep, opened his eyes, and, retaining by God’s great miracle the words he had heard, gave thanks to God. Though he could by no sharpness of understanding discern the force of the saying, he nevertheless surely hoped that it signified something good for him. He therefore spent the rest of the night, having bravely driven away drowsiness, in watching and praying with as much devotion as he could. He burned with great desire and wished for daybreak, so that he might disclose to some learned person the divine oracle graciously revealed to him through God’s abundant kindness before it slipped from his memory, and might by that person’s aid attain also an understanding of the words.

When morning came, he waited for a suitable opportunity to speak and privately approached the prior of that place, a very devout man. He simply disclosed what he had seen and heard. Asked to repeat the angelic verse, this unlearned and illiterate man [Col. 1168D] uttered the Latin words without difficulty and repeated them until they were so firmly impressed on the prior’s heart that they could not be erased by the fleeting frailty of failing memory.

Wonders more wonderful than before followed. Since he had learned this mystery not merely for his own sake, but much more so that he might become a joyful herald of the blessedness of those whose endurance he had admired in pious simplicity, the Lord deigned to make the matter still more manifest. For as soon as he communicated to a discerning mind the words he had heard but not understood, and through the prior’s interpretation grasped their meaning, he went back to the repository of memory and found it entirely empty. Nor could he ever afterward utter even the least syllable of the verse which he had learned for an hour.

Greatly edified and strengthened in God’s grace, he truly believed the Lord to be the guardian of that place. He then pledged an annual payment in that church, which he faithfully took care to pay every year for as long as he lived. Therefore, whoever [Col. 1169A] casting away fear arising from bodily frailty and dispelling faintheartedness, strives to show himself vigorous and devout in God’s service, should await with all the greater confidence the blessedness and rest of the heavenly homeland, since by this recent miracle the Lord deigned to grant His faithful an earnest of good hope.

The aforesaid prior was named Meffrid. Toward God he was a man of outstanding religious devotion, while in worldly matters he possessed exceptional authority. Amid the dreadful storms of the schism which, in the days of Pope Alexander, by the faction of Emperor Frederick tortured the Church of God with prolonged dismemberment, he preserved his house by the foresight of marvellous diligence, lest it be utterly destroyed.

To this servant of God, among the other gifts of grace in which he happily abounded, the secrets of revelations were also sometimes divinely disclosed. As he was sometimes consoled by the visitation of blessed spirits, so he was also terrified by the apparitional shadows of malignant spirits, [Col. 1169B], that he might be rendered purer.

There was in the same house a young man named Henry, of Strasbourg origin, robust and vigorous in body, but ugly with spiritual leanness and weak in heart—such men, alas, as in our times we see and lament in great numbers, fearing more to be physically mortified for a time than to be consigned to the punishments of Gehenna. Though this young man was marked out from the other brethren for sluggishness and idleness in all the observances of the Order, he sinned more gravely in the performance of divine service, which he neglected in every way. He could certainly have performed it more vigorously than many others, had he not hidden the hand of his natural strength beneath the armpit of excessive sloth. Furthermore, he often used to leave the collect of the sacred vigils, as though because of illness, and was not ashamed to go to bed to rest his miserable flesh.

The venerable prior desired to heal this detestable negligence with fatherly concern, now publicly and now privately, by warning, beseeching, [Col. 1169C] and rebuking him—but in vain. The young man valued bodily comfort more highly than the rest of the soul; and therefore, as a foolish estimator of things, he “fed the barren woman who does not bear, and did no good to the widow” (Job 24).

Meanwhile it happened that this undisciplined brother, fleeing labour and discipline, left his place at the vigils as he was accustomed to do and departed from the choir, so that, after saying the morning office for the sick as briefly as possible, he might satisfy the pleasure of his flesh by returning to bed. But the Lord, wishing to show the watchful prior how justly he was moved with zeal and how great was the ruinous danger of that brother’s negligence—or rather, contempt and pride—opened his eyes. He saw the brother leave his stall, bow slightly before the altar step, and hurry toward the choir door. A most hideous demon leapt upon his neck and rode him, gesticulating in marvellous ways and cackling, all the way to the entrance of the infirmary—to speak in the usual expression, fitting for such idleness.

Soon afterward, when he came out [Col. 1169D] of the infirmary, the savage driver again leapt upon his shoulders, and drove him, like a truly irrational beast drawn by the halter of sluggishness, with the whip of most shameful softness, to the side of the bed in which he eagerly desired, to his harm, to rest.

How much happier and wiser it would have been for this foolish beast to follow the holy devotion of that pious beast, which in the simplicity of its heart said to God: “I became as a beast before thee, and I am always with thee” (Ps. 72). He would then have deserved to have as rider the One “who rides upon the setting,” to destroy sin and establish righteousness, rather than him who entangles wretches in the bonds of everlasting calamity for the delight of temporal pleasure.

In the end, no one can correct a person who has neglected the fear of God. That wretched man despised the admonitions of the excellent prior, who told him what he had seen concerning him. He did not take care to retain the vigour of cloistered discipline even on the surface; rather, following the deadly counsels [Col. 1170A] of his ungrateful rider, he abandoned the Order and became a contemptible apostate, so as to spend his days amid the false goods—or rather corruptions—of this world and to descend in an instant into hell.

Therefore, as we hope the foregoing example will be an incentive to devotion for those who do not shrink from the labours and vigils of divine service, so surely this latter example must indicate grief and sorrow of heart to the tender, the delicate, and those incapable of arduous labours. But those who possess strength and health of body and voice, yet through most shameful idleness disdain to be wearied with labours for God, should greatly fear that their end may resemble that of this man whose miserable life, but still more miserable apostasy, we have related.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How dangerous it is to perform the vigils of God’s service lukewarmly.

[Col. 1170B] Moreover, concerning idleness, negligence, and sleepiness in God’s service, and also concerning the phantasms and illusions which those who are more lukewarm, even while sleeping in choir, suffer unwillingly through the assaults of demons, there is a more subtle and detailed account in the revelations of a certain servant of God. He lived in Britain, in a certain Cistercian house called Strata Florida; and the Lord deigned to fill him with a spirit of foreknowledge for the correction of His servants.

This servant of the Lord had from his youth striven to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones, and to observe more exactly the holiness of the sacred Order. On a feast of Pentecost, when he rose at the sound of the clock and began to sing the morning office of Our Lady, he suddenly felt a new devotion, never before experienced, enter into his heart. Growing more and more throughout the prolonged span of the vigils, it [Col. 1170C] refreshed his inner and outer person alike with marvellous eagerness.

When the brethren began the hymn, “O all ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord” (Ps. 102 [Vulgate]), in which every creature is invited to bless and praise, he saw with his bodily eyes an angel of the Lord descend through the window opposite him into the middle of the choir in a splendour of great brightness, carrying in his hand a thurible filled with heavenly incense. Proceeding toward the altar, the angel censed it, as is customarily done at Mass on solemn feasts; then he moved toward both choirs and passed through them, offering the life-giving fragrance of spiritual spices to the monks who were awake and singing psalms.

When the singing choirs came to the verse, “Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit,” the angel of the Lord was making the circuit of them all in order and had reached the brother to whom it had been granted to see these things. Then this brother, inflamed with wondrous devotion of piety, as though saying with the Prophet, “I opened my mouth [Col. 1170D] and drew in breath, because I desired thy commandments” (Ps. 118), stretched out his whole body to draw in the breath, so that, bending low, he might sing praise more fervently to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But the angel of the Lord took from the thurible with two fingers a coal burning most fiercely and brightly, and cast it into the mouth of the man drawing breath. Passing through his whole body, it set all his inward parts aflame with the sweetest fire, so that he could truly say with the prophet: “From on high the Lord sent fire into my bones” (Lam. 1).

Unable to bear the burning of that desolating coal, which beneficially consumed vices within him, he fell to the ground pale and bloodless. He was carried thence to the infirmary and remained there three days without voice or movement, as though dead. But after three days, at the same hour at which he had been caught up, he returned to himself. By the fire in which he had happily burned, he was so cleansed from every fleshly corruption that weighs down the soul that he could see absent things as though present [Col. 1171A] with spiritual eyes. He also described the temptations of the monks of his house, by which they were troubled whether awake or asleep, and explained their manner and causes. Thus many of the brethren, stirred by his exhortations, strove after the holiness of a purer life.

He further said that every night, and especially on Sundays and feast days, an immense multitude of demons assembled in the choir of psalm-singing brethren. Their execrable office was nothing other than to mock the brethren in many and diverse ways, turn their minds away from attention to God’s service, and insult the lazy and sleeping with most malicious applause and laughter, moving with wandering swiftness from one sleeping man to another and back again.

They wore on their heads certain hoods of old rags, most filthy and exceedingly foul-smelling, soaked within and without as though with the pus of scabby sores. Beneath them they hid their ghostly faces [Col. 1171B], as though afraid of being recognized. Approaching each monk, they watched with most cunning scrutiny whether he was awake or asleep. If they found him asleep, they immediately shook all the stench and corruption of their rotten hood into his face. Then, as if at a signal, very many gathered before him and did not leave as long as he slept, sending him phantasms and shameful dreams.

But from those whom they observed awake and singing psalms they fled as from fire, so that they could not endure at all the breath proceeding from the mouths of those singing and praising God. Therefore, since our consummate blessedness and happiness in eternal life will be continually to praise the Lord and our Creator not only without labour but also with the highest delight, before our eyes are closed in death and the tongue created to praise God is bound to the dust, let us sow, though with labour, the good seed of God’s service. In its [Col. 1171C] season we shall reap, exulting with unspeakable joy. Conversely, those who now do not fear to sow thorns and thistles of lukewarmness and negligence in the soil of their flesh will reap fire and punishment as vengeance upon their transgressing conscience, when those same malignant spirits—who now never cease enticing the slothful, feebly overcome by the pleasure of their flesh, to rest—will cruelly heap torments upon those to be punished.

Moreover, the authority of the book called *The Lives of the Fathers* is not without reason adduced as support and confirmation of truth for these, as it were, more recent and therefore apparently less authoritative revelations. For there it is written that, when a malignant spirit told one of the holy Fathers that he and his companions often attended the brethren’s vigils, the Father prayed to the Lord that He might reveal to him the truth of the matter. Coming to the brethren’s collect, [Col. 1171D] he saw demons like Ethiopians running throughout the church and, by phantasms, representing before his own eyes everything which the praying and psalm-singing brethren were turning over in their hearts. As afterward became clear from each person’s confession, he recognized that the vain and perverse thoughts and deadly pleasures which brethren suffer during the hour of divine service arise from the suggestions of demons.

Therefore we must cry out with contrite spirit and humble heart together with the Psalmist: “Do not deliver, O Lord, the souls confessing thee to the beasts; and do not forget for ever the souls of thy poor” (Ps. 73).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the danger of religious persons living softly in this life.

How fearful and dreadful is the trial of purgatorial fire, in which the Lord, according to the Prophet, [Col. 1172A] “washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanses the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4), as the Lord Himself also testifies through another prophet, saying: “And I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed” (Joel 3); and as the prophet likewise says of the Lord, that He “will be like a refining fire and like fuller’s soap; and He will sit refining and cleansing silver, purifying the sons of Levi” (Mal. 3)—would that those who do not fear to waste their days in frivolities, negligences, and sleepiness would attend to this.

Concerning this fearful trial, I remember reading in a certain collection that a monk at the point of death, before he departed, was caught up in spirit and led to infernal places. He saw—something we cannot recount without horror—many souls transfixed on spits and pointed poles at an enormous fire, roasted and grilled like geese. Their most cruel torturers, with bellows and other instruments of fire, [Col. 1172B], strained with all their might to intensify the torments of the wretched.

Others placed burning pans and frying-pans beneath them, carefully collected the fat flowing from the blazing limbs of those lying there, and then poured it back, bubbling and exceedingly hot, upon those from whom it had flowed. He observed that this punishment was more intolerable to them than the other tortures.

After this he was taken to a certain place of refreshment, where he found a multitude of souls resting as if after some heavy labour. Asked by his angelic guide whether he knew who they were, he replied that he did not. But the holy angel said to him:

“Those whom you saw roasting at that enormous fire are men of your Order. Although they have not defiled themselves with mortal sins, nevertheless they have not taken care, as Scripture commands, to serve the Lord in fear and trembling. They have not sought to keep the strictness of discipline or patiently endure quiet and silence. In short, they have not zealously pursued, as they ought, the solemn devotion of vigils and prayers, nor the [Col. 1172C] laborious performance of psalmody; but, being inquisitive, jesting, restless, superfluous, slothful, lazy, sleepy, and given to gestures, jokes, and frivolities, they have not feared to violate the purity of their monastic profession.

“After they have been purified by the utterly just sentence of God the righteous Judge in the punishments seen above—some for a shorter, others for a longer time, according to the duration or quality of their transgressions—they are brought by the mediation of God’s grace to this place of refreshment. Here, resting after those dreadful punishments, they await with patience the perfection of their blessedness.”

It is therefore clearer than light that revelations of this sort, by the dispensation of divine mercy, become more frequent as the end of the world draws nearer. Since charity grows cold in many because iniquity and negligence abound, God’s elect, having through this incentive a spur to charity, may grow warm in spirit all the more, as He is thought to be near at hand whose face is preceded by the want of every good thing.

[Col. 1172D] What, then, is indicated to us by the fact that the aforesaid brother saw the infernal stokers carefully collect the fat and pour it back upon those from whom it dripped, increasing their punishment? Surely this: the more anyone in this life spared himself against his profession, satisfying the pleasure of his flesh with the fatness of disordered repose, the more, when assigned to purgatorial places in the other life, he will be compelled to pay in punishments. Thus the Lord says through the Prophet of that scarlet harlot who intoxicates the whole earth with the cup of fleshly pleasures and the wine of worldly pomp: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. 18).

Therefore, brothers, let us awaken at the sound of this thunder, and with attentive minds hear what our Father, Blessed Bernard—most perfect even among monks and most venerable among the Fathers—thought concerning these daily and very harmful negligences of ours [Col. 1173A]. In a sermon [Note: [Col. 1173D] It appears after the sermons on St. Andrew.] which he delivered on the life and character of Humbert of blessed memory, formerly prior of Clairvaux, when he was exhorting the brothers to emulate the purity of that man’s manner of life, he says among other things:

> “For the rest, brothers, I tell you that if you followed in his footsteps, you would not so easily lapse into vain thoughts and idle speech, jokes and buffoonery; for in these you waste much, both of your life and of your time. Time flies irretrievably; and while you think you are avoiding this very slight punishment, you incur a greater one.
