For know this: after this life, in the places of purgation, what has here been neglected shall be repaid a hundredfold, down to the last farthing. I know that it is hard for a undisciplined person to take up discipline, for a talkative person to endure silence, for one accustomed to wandering about to remain steadfast; but it will be harder, and much harder, to endure those future afflictions.”

Moreover, how reverent, eager, and careful we ought to be in carrying out the divine praises [Col. 1173B], not only that we may obtain the grace of our Lord and Creator, but also that we may be able to escape the inextricable deceits of evil spirits, the same venerable Father teaches in the forty-eighth sermon on the Song of Songs, saying:

> “For in our Rule it is permitted to place nothing before the work of God. By this name Father Benedict wished the solemn offices of praise [Note: [Col. 1173D] This passage is now found in Sermon 47 on the Song of Songs.], which are daily rendered to God in the oratory, to be called, so that from this it might appear more plainly how intent he wished us to be upon that work. Therefore I admonish you, dearest ones, always to take part in the divine praises purely and vigorously. Vigorously, indeed, so that, as you stand before the Lord reverently, you may also do so eagerly: not sluggish, not yawning, not sparing your voices, not cutting words in half, not skipping entire words, not mumbling through the nose in broken and weakened voices with something womanish; but bringing forth the words of the Holy Spirit with a manly sound and affection, as is fitting. Purely, however, [Col. 1173C] so that while you chant, you think of nothing other than what you chant. Nor do I say that vain and idle thoughts alone must be avoided: even those thoughts must be avoided, at least in that hour and in that place, which the officials among the brethren are compelled, as if by necessity, to entertain for the common need. Indeed, I would not advise receiving even those things then which perhaps a little earlier, while sitting in the cloister, you had read in books—things which you are now carrying away fresh from this audience of the Holy Spirit as I expound them orally. They are wholesome things; yet you do not profitably turn them over in your minds while chanting. For at that hour the Holy Spirit does not accept with pleasure whatever else you may offer, if you neglect what you ought to offer.”

Such are the words of Blessed Bernard. What, I ask, are we to think of ourselves when in that hour and in that place we entertain perverse and harmful thoughts, if the holy Father judged that not only vain and useless thoughts, but even necessary ones, ought to be avoided during psalmody? Here indeed, here the instability of our hearts, when detected, is put to shame, according to the Prophet: as a thief is ashamed when he is caught; so that even the more perfect among us must needs say to God with mourning and groaning of heart: “Enter not into judgment with thy servants, O Lord, for in thy sight no living person shall be justified” (Psalm 142). Yet it is one thing for the mind sometimes to fly away from attention to the psalmody through the weakness of mortal nature, and quite another through slothful inertia to make no resistance, with any vigour of mind, to perverse and harmful thoughts. And therefore, as the cause is different for those who sin pardonably and for those who sin gravely, so too will the judgment be different which they receive as deserved by their merits.

## CHAPTER XX. On the danger of those who presume to sing in the service of God wantonly or for applause

[Col. 1174A]

Now, as I consider how this prophetic man rebukes the most wretched and excessively superstitious parsimony of certain persons, saying, “Not sparing their voices, not mumbling through the nose in weakened voices with something womanish” [Note: [Col. 1174D] St Bernard, Sermon 47 on the Song of Songs.], I recall a terrible occurrence which, on the report of the venerable abbot of Morimond, we learned had befallen one such man.

For there are some to whom, although the Lord has most generously lent the instruments of His praise, they nevertheless lend them to the Lord most sparingly. They are readier to seek through those same instruments the glory of men than the glory of God; and though, by sparing their voices, they entirely neglect the daily course of psalms and hymns, lest the sharpness of their voices perhaps be blunted, whenever an occasion and opportunity to glory in themselves and in their voices [Col. 1174B] smiles upon them, they immediately show themselves strong, skilled, and ready to sing and to raise their voices on high.

The aforesaid abbot therefore said that there was a monk in one of the monasteries of the Cistercian Order who, delighting in the gift of a most noble voice, disdained to expend its strength in the common labour of God’s service. Rather, pursuing his own glory, he joyfully—but without fear—cheerfully—but with no devotion—sang in festive celebration those responsories assigned to him as the special privilege of his voice.

It happened, however, on a feast of the Lord, that while in all the chants which the community of brothers sang together to the praise of God he stood as if mute and tongueless, he sang his own responsory verse in his customary wanton manner—not plainly in low notes, but shaking his voice in high, or rather the very highest, notes, and fashioning ringing melodies by the flexibility of his voice. When he had finished, so that he might understand from whom a reward for his ridiculous singing was to be expected, [Col. 1174C] a little demon appeared, in the form of a foul and dark Ethiopian boy, before himself and the others around him, who both saw and heard. Clapping with unclean hands and laughing in a strange fashion, it cried out:

> “Oh! Oh! He sang well—very well; it was sung excellently!”

Let everyone, therefore, who has received from God the grace of a pleasing voice know that it is a dreadful evil thereby to feed the malice of demons by singing wantonly and for applause, from that by which he ought to have honoured God, rejoicing devoutly and humbly. Therefore we must strive with all our strength that, according to the moderation prescribed for us by our holy Order, and likewise according to the authority by which the Rule we have professed instructs us, each individually and all together may chant psalms and sing to our God with gravity, fear and trembling, and humility.

Certainly the irony of diabolical malice might, above all things—or even by itself—have been able to bring a blush and a suffusion of shame to our faces and arouse us to guard ourselves. But because hard human hearts reverence the testimony of the spirit of truth more than the mockery of the lying spirit, we shall not pass over in silence what, even in our own times, a certain holy virgin of outstanding religion and special abstinence disclosed concerning this wantonness of singing, having been instructed by divine revelation.

For when the lord abbot of Cîteaux, father and patriarch of our entire holy Order, had once come to visit her, amid their sweet conversations about eternal life the abbot began earnestly to ask that this handmaid of God seek from God a revelation for him concerning what had, through negligence, most contrary to the purity of true religion crept into the Cistercian Order. After obtaining a delay and pouring out prayers to the Lord, she replied:

> “Know, lord Father, that there are three things in your Order which especially offend the eyes of the supreme Majesty [Col. 1175A]: namely, the multiplication of estates, the excess of buildings, and wantonness of voices.”

Accordingly, all who have been admitted to the sacred clerical Order and assigned by the judgment of holy Church to the office of psalmody and singing, if they exceed the bounds of moderation, gravity, and humility, should know that they make an offering rightly indeed, but by no means distribute it rightly. And they must fear the Lord’s threat spoken through the prophet: “My soul has hated your solemnities” (Isaiah 1). For when enemies mock your Sabbaths, almighty God by no means deigns to accept what the enemy derides.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the danger of prelates who love their relatives according to the flesh

The Apostle, speaking of those who exercise on earth the role of the supreme householder, and who have been appointed in the Church as stewards of the mysteries of God, says: “Here moreover [Col. 1175B] it is required among stewards that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4). Some, alas, fearing this examination and scrutiny too little, if by divine grace they are called to a share in pastoral care, immediately glory as though they had been raised to the fullness of honour. In their prelacy they seek with every care not only what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ, but also what belongs to their own kinsfolk. For their relatives’ advancement they do not fear to squander and dissipate the patrimony of the crucified Lord—that is, the goods of the Church—which, upon their promotion, they vowed by a pledged sacrament to preserve intact.

What is still worse: if they have advanced any of their nephews by educating and training them so that they appear capable of being distinguished by the exercise of some office, drawn more by affection for flesh and blood than by concern for their neighbours’ good, they appoint them as their successors, not remembering the judgment of the all-seeing God even in that terrible hour of their departure. Therefore we shall relate how almighty God, who glorifies those who glorify Him and makes contemptible those who despise Him, chose to reveal, for the correction of the living, the intolerable torments to which one such man was assigned after the death of the flesh. Perhaps those who provoke the Lord, hearing this, may fear to suffer such things and, with the severity of vengeance before their eyes, desist from their disordered love for relatives.

An abbot of a certain monastery had raised from childhood a monk who was his nephew, and had brought him to a commendable way of life. It happened that the same abbot, with the moment of his final lot imminent, was about to enter upon the way of all flesh. While the brothers whom he had governed mourned his impending loss—for he had been a prudent and provident man—and deliberated concerning the appointment of another, with different men holding different views, it was decreed by common consent, lest the matter through party interests fall into contention, that they should entrust their wishes and counsels to him as to a spiritual father [Col. 1175D], since he knew more fully the consciences and merits of each. And whomsoever he should name orally as his successor, that man they would unanimously elect abbot without opposition.

But alas, how tenderly bound are those to the ties of their relatives whom the ardour of charity has not yet perfectly separated from the love of the world. For when the aforesaid abbot, in that fearful hour of his departure, ought to have remembered the justice of God alone and to have provided, according to God alone, for those who rendered him pure obedience, he was wrongly enticed by affection for flesh and blood. He designated to those brothers his aforementioned nephew, saying that he was devout in religious life and prudent and thoughtful in external affairs. Though this was true in part, nevertheless he had given such counsel by no means with a sincere intention, namely, out of concern for the brothers’ welfare. Rather, as may be inferred from the punishment that followed, his purpose was to make his own kindred more illustrious through his nephew’s advancement [Col. 1176A]. The Lord deigned to show to that successor, who had acquired his dignity less than canonically, how severe was the sentence to which the dying abbot had been condemned for this offence.

There was in that monastery a pleasant place, suited for refreshment, and in that place a spring bubbled forth with clear streams and a gentle murmur. Pleasant with luxuriant grasses along the edge of its channel, it soothed the souls and eyes of those who approached it, both by its liveliness and by the lovely green of the grass. While he still breathed the breath of life, the dead abbot was accustomed often to visit this place for refreshment; there, relaxing his mind exhausted by the heat of gnawing cares, he allowed it to pour itself out the more freely because the place was more secluded.

His successor decided to maintain the same custom of relaxation, and he too frequented the place—more inclined, I think, to pursue the comforts of the flesh which he had seen in his predecessor than to draw from that predecessor’s way of life an example of any virtue [Col. 1176B]. One day, as he approached the aforementioned place in his accustomed manner, he heard from what seemed to be the bottom of the spring a voice weeping piteously and repeating, “Alas! Alas! Woe is me!” Greatly terrified and dismayed, when he came nearer and listened more carefully, he recognized it as the voice of his deceased predecessor, the abbot, from the quality of that voice, long familiar to him.

Then, with lips trembling from astonishment, he asked who it was that wept there so. The same voice replied as though from beneath the water:

> “I am that kinsman of yours, once abbot, but now a wretched spirit, whom you succeeded in governing this monastery, to my great shame and misery.”

Asked why he wept so, he replied, “Because I burn.”

Asked again why he burned, when the religious life he had led in the body seemed to deserve rest rather than torments, he said: “You are the cause of my burning.”

And the abbot said [Col. 1176C]: “Why or how am I?”

“Because,” he said, “when the brothers over whom I was unworthy to preside sought a person beneficial to the salvation of their souls and, after God, entrusted to me their wishes and counsels, alas, blinded by the allurement of the kinship by which you were joined to me, I gave counsel not according to the fear of God but according to the folly of my own will, that they should raise you to the summit of this dignity. Therefore, by the just judgment of God, condemned to torments in this element of water, I burn, melt away, and fail; and, when I have been reduced almost to nothing, I am restored in order to endure the same torments again. But if you wish to prove more certainly that what you hear is not idle fancy, have a bronze lampstand brought and slowly lowered into the water.”

At once, at the abbot’s command, a bronze lampstand was brought and gently placed into the water. By a wondrous miracle it was melted by the surface of that water—which appeared cold—as wax flows before fire, or as mist is driven away before the sun. With what severity, then, will the judgment of God’s just tribunal condemn those who make their relatives rich and eminent from the money or possessions of the churches entrusted to them, if he deserved to be punished in this manner who presumed to advance, to the eminence of a spiritual office, a person perhaps sufficiently suitable, with regard more to blood than to charity [Col. 1176D]?

We have now, then, treated for some time, on the occasion of the account concerning Lord Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, of blessed memory—who endeavoured to warn his brothers against the danger of habitual swearing—and have taken care to set forth briefly the dangers of various vices and negligences for the exhortation of readers. For we know that examples move the minds of simple brothers more than words. A devout mind, which seeks from reading the fervour of spiritual compunction rather than the instruction of puffing-up knowledge, when it repeatedly turns over the memory of an event and, as it were, feels it by the hand of thought, is kindled more strongly by it toward the love of virtues and horror of vices [Col. 1177A] than if it ran through ten thousand maxims written on little sheets.

Having discharged this, as it were, large debt, let us return to our Clairvaux, from which we had gone out with Isaac to meditate in the field upon the various mighty works of Christ our Lord. Thus at last let the course of our narrative, woven for the edification of many concerning the religious manner of life of the venerable Fathers and their death precious in the sight of the Lord [Col. 1178A], be brought to its fitting conclusion. For even a little stream flowing beside meadows, drawn off through the fixed courses of its channels, enriches every dry place, causes withering grasses to grow green again, and, when all have been sufficiently watered, gathers itself back into itself; restored to its own bed, it flows on with the vitality of its proper course.

## SIXTH DISTINCTION. Containing various matters concerning the sacrament of the altar and confession, the souls of the dead, and certain other subjects

[Col. 1177]

## CHAPTER I. On the incautious contemplation of a monk of Clairvaux, and on the danger facing contemplatives

[Col. 1177B]

The Lord, speaking to blessed Job concerning the manifold cunning of the ancient enemy under the figure of Leviathan, says: “The sinews of his testicles are entwined” (Job 40): plainly instructing every person that no one can escape the inextricable knots of Satan’s most subtle deceits without the aid of divine grace.

But if all who bear the Christian profession and strive, under the guidance of humility, to ascend to the heavenly glory from which proud Satan fell with his angels, must earnestly consider the Apostle’s words, “See that you walk carefully, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5), and again, “Lest we be outwitted by Satan; for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 2), with how great a vigilance, we may suppose, must those watch who have undertaken to serve the Lord in monasteries out of a desire for a more sacred life [Col. 1177C], and to fight spiritual wickedness with spiritual weapons?

Those are indeed deceived and carried away by a most foolish error who suppose that only the tumultuous business of the worldly mill, and not also the quiet silences of the monastic bedchamber, lie open to the enemy’s snares. For the crafty enemy is accustomed to set so much subtler traps the higher anyone climbs the ladder of virtues and the more confidently he believes himself to have escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world.

Therefore we shall set forth, as a warning to contemplatives, the most grievous temptation of a certain spiritual man, which he incurred by contemplating indiscreetly in the leisure of his silence. Thus may those who, applying themselves with more fervent zeal to reading, commit diverse sayings to memory and from them first sharpen the eye of meditation, then also that of contemplation, always remember the saying, “He who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Proverbs 25), and profitably humble themselves in the fear of holy humility, rather than childishly presume to fly in the dangerous light of contemplation [Col. 1177D].

There was at Clairvaux a certain elder of most pure religious observance, which, under our venerable Father Blessed Bernard, bestowed in that same holy house the grace of perfection even upon many rather simple men; he had become a zealous imitator, devoted to the daily exercise of virtues. Because of the gravity of his wisdom, the maturity of his counsel, and the holiness of his outstanding manner of life, he was judged able to benefit not himself alone but others also. He was therefore appointed abbot of the Church of Foigny, one of the more distinguished daughters of Clairvaux and one more conspicuous for religious observance.

Set, therefore, in honour, and continually weighing the burden of that honour lest, according to the Prophet, he should fail to understand the danger of honour (Psalm 48), he administered the dignity of the pastoral office with the humility fitting a spiritual man. At length, withdrawing his aged shoulders from the care of his laborious prelacy, he preferred the companionship of Rachel—more barren indeed, but more delightful—to the embraces of Leah, fruitful though they were, yet very dangerous [Col. 1178B].

He therefore returned to his Clairvaux; and, like a chick not degenerate, restored to its own little nest, he was moved to examine his daily conduct and gathered back to himself the motions and affections of his heart which had long been scattered in every direction through the occasion of prelacy. Following the example of his most holy Father Benedict, he dwelt with himself. Intent upon spiritual studies and wholly removed from the noise of talkative occupation, he devoted himself to prayer, reading, compunction, and sacred meditation, knowing that against the poisonous suggestions of worldly display and fleshly allurements there is no more effective antidote.

Drawn on by the persistence of continual meditation and enticed by its sweetness, he now began, with the subtlety of holy contemplation, to examine all the divine mysteries; he took delight in examining them, exulted in the joy of his heart, and said with the Psalmist to the Lord: “Wonderful are thy testimonies, O Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out” (Psalm 118). Since he diligently offered, with the fruit of good works, the saving victim through whom we have been redeemed and reconciled to God the Father, he meditated more sweetly upon the height of this unsearchable mystery the more frequently he repeated it, representing the most profound humility of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 1178C].

But would that he had taken care to be as cautious and fearful a contemplative as he was devout—especially amid so wonderful a depth of such great mysteries, where every argument of human reason fails and only the oracle of sacred faith is to be consulted. For while he pondered in wonder, and wondered as he pondered, how the bread and wine set forth upon the altar were, through the power of God, transubstantiated into the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ our Lord and Redeemer, he searched more than he ought and relied too presumptuously upon the eye of reason. He attempted rashly to investigate by the audacity of reason the sacred mystery entrusted to the hiddenness of faith.

Yet, as Blessed Bernard testifies, if reason attempts to break into what belongs to faith, it is judged a burglar [Note: [Col. 1177D] Bernard, Letter 190, and elsewhere.]; and Blessed Gregory says that faith has no merit when human reason supplies experimental proof [Note: [Col. 1178D] Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels.]. Indeed, the aforesaid elder paid too little heed to the counsel of the Wise Man, who advises one who finds honey to eat sparingly, lest perhaps, being satiated, he vomit it up (Proverbs 25); and to the Apostle’s warning, “Do not be wise beyond what is fitting, but be wise unto sobriety” (Romans 12). While he investigated too greedily the sweetness of the sacred mystery, unsearchable, as I think, even to angelic spirits, he did not show the reverence owed to supreme Majesty. He struck against the stone of stumbling, and the Lord turned away in anger from His servant.

But when the good Spirit—or rather, the Spirit who is goodness—withdraws the rays of His light, the malignant spirit immediately brings in the darkness of its malice [Col. 1179A], harassing the soul, now wavering, with diverse thoughts and shaking reason, now tossed about, with the worst spirit of doubt. For while, concealing from himself the darkness of his mortality, he presumed as though with unveiled face to behold that which faith most certainly establishes, by the just judgment of almighty God he fell from the certainty of faith into the uncertainty of opinion. Blinded by presumption, he judged impossible what he could not comprehend by reason.

For faith, as the Apostle most elegantly defines it, is “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11). “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” (Romans 8). But if we are commanded patiently to await what we cannot see in this valley of mortality, in this body of sin and death, until it may be fulfilled in us in the homeland of eternal brightness, where God will be all in all, let us restrain the eyes of the heart from the vice of restless curiosity. For, as the Wise Man testifies: “An inheritance to which one hastens too early in the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Proverbs 20) [Col. 1179B].

As soon as that incautious contemplative perceived this evil of doubt secretly creeping into the dispositions of his soul, he trembled utterly. He strove with the vigour of his mind to disperse the darkness of diabolical cunning, but he could not. For just as a restless will is free, by voluntary decision, to cast itself headlong into a pit, so it is not likewise free by its own power or effort to climb out of the pit.

Therefore, when the rudder of faith had been violently torn away by the stormy spirit of presumption, the ship of this wretched man’s conscience was battered by the strongest waves of destructive thoughts. All the malicious spirits, with every deceit of their wickedness, strove toward this end: that the man whom they had violently disturbed from certainty of faith should now be hurled from the cloud of doubt into the densest darkness of blasphemous assertion; namely, that, following the example of Berengar, who was the first inventor and defender of this impious heresy [Col. 1179C], he might think and say that the bread and wine set forth on the altar are by no means, after consecration, the true body and true blood of Christ.

But almighty and merciful God, who had delivered His servant to the angel of Satan to be buffeted, so that this presumptuous man might learn not to be presumptuous, and who had allowed him, while he too arrogantly searched into the highest degree of knowledge—reserved for blessed life alone—in this miserable life and in this flesh of sin, even to fall away from the stability of faith, nevertheless did not permit him, while he hung upon the dangerous cliff of doubt, to be cast headlong into the abyss of heretical depravity.

Thus he went about miserably withering and wasting away within himself from anguish of spirit and the violence of temptation. He dared not approach the sacred mysteries which he had formerly celebrated with the greatest devotion, and groaned that by the merit of his presumption he had been consigned to this dreadful suffering. In a wonderful manner, he recognized and grieved over his error, but nevertheless he could not disperse the cloud of that error. And, as holy Pope Gregory says of Blessed Mary Magdalene: “She loved and doubted; and the more she remembered the sincerity of her former devotion, the more, weeping, she detested the blindness of her perverse opinion” [Note: [Col. 1179D] Gregory, Homily 25 on the Gospels.].

The affliction of this destructive temptation increased day by day, and seized not merely his inner person but even his outer person as well. Thus, as strength of mind and bodily vigour failed together, he was compelled frequently to rest in the infirmary and endure his condition as best he could. When his former spiritual sons, the brothers of Foigny, heard that their once most beloved Father was oppressed by such grief and affliction, they came to him and, by gentle entreaties, respectfully persuaded him to return with them to Foigny [Col. 1180A], hoping that, refreshed by their dutiful charity, he might receive some alleviation of his distress and breathe again from the anguish of the temptation that pressed him so heavily.

But because, as the poet elegantly sings,

> “He who runs across the sea changes his sky, not his mind”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.11.27),

and because, as the Wise Man declares, “No one can set right whom God has cast aside” (Ecclesiastes 7), neither change of place nor the encouraging exhortation of those brothers could pluck the sting of temptation from the old man’s heart. The time for mercy upon him had not yet come; a harsher punishment still pressed upon his rash presumption.

Thus, almost to the final end of his life, he was worn away in this frying-pan of blasphemous doubt and, like gold tested and purified in the furnace of tribulation. At last, through the Lord’s mercy, he received the light of faith in its fullness. Thereafter he retained the stability of belief with so much greater humility, and withdrew the eye of contemplation from the unrest of unlawful inquiry, in proportion as, through the experience of his own calamity, he had learned that God resists the proud and restrains the presumptuous [Note: [Col. 1179D] Reginald is not to be charged with the sin of unbelief, but only with an involuntary movement against [Col. 1180D] faith; because he could not overcome it, he was distressed in mind, judging himself with excessive scruple guilty of sin.].

Whoever, therefore, subject to cloister discipline, has by the Lord’s gift obtained Mary’s leisure, and finds it sweet, through keenness of intellect, to search the divine page, must always remember that he is a disciple, not a master. Otherwise, stirred by the subtlety of his intellect, he may attempt, to his own harm, to break into things sealed by the seal of faith; or rashly presume to investigate anything which the most watchful ingenuity of the holy Fathers has passed over without investigation because of reverence for, and the depth of, the mysteries of God.

## CHAPTER II. On the excellence of faith in the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood, and on the discernment of contemplations
[Col. 1180C] Certainly, the difference between the inquiry born of curiosity and the reflection produced by piety; between contemplation which humble devotion brings forth in simplicity of faith and purity of conscience, and meditations which descend from the arrogance of presumption, we shall now make still clearer, so that, as we have frightened the presumptuous in their own spirit, we may likewise soothe the humble and devout in the Spirit of God. Surely that foremost and greatest contemplative, from whom, in the “Most Bright Valley” (Claravalle), the whole religious life of devotion and contemplation took its beginning—I mean blessed Bernard—who writes copiously concerning how the rashness of presumptuous contemplation must be avoided and with what reverence the weakness of human reason must submit to the sacred mystery of faith, makes this sufficiently clear in one place, saying:

> [Note: Col. 1180D. Book II, chapter 3.] “I speak confidently: I believe in the Holy Trinity, which I do not understand. What is sounder for faith than this brief saying, simpler for merit, or more faithful for devotion?”

Moreover, he magnificently demonstrated—not in words only, but also through the performance of miraculous deeds—that he held just as firmly the same simplicity of faith concerning the sacrament of the altar which he here [Col. 1180D] briefly expresses concerning the Holy Trinity. When he had once entered Italy, and the fame of his miracles shone everywhere because of the very effective grace which he possessed for driving out unclean spirits, he ordered a woman possessed for a long time by a most savage demon, who had been brought to him, to be led into the church, knowing, no doubt, that she could not be healed as easily as the others. He himself approached the altar and celebrated the sacred solemnities of Mass. When the consecration of the sacred gifts had been completed according to custom, he placed the Lord’s body upon the paten and held it over the head of the woman, foul and horrible with the filth of the evil spirit, saying: “Here is your judge, wicked one,” [Col. 1181A] and the rest of what is contained in the book of his life. Thus, by faith and by the power of the divine sacraments, he forcefully expelled that hellish Cerberus, whom he had been unable to drive away by the customary efficacy of prayers.

On another occasion, when he was unable by any warnings or exhortations to bring back to the summit of humility and to the unity of the Catholic Church the Count of Poitou, who was stubbornly supporting the schism of Peter Leo and refusing submission to Pope Innocent, he entrusted to divine power a matter which seemed impossible to human effort. He entered the church to offer the saving sacrifice through which life, salvation, peace, and unity are granted to wretched mortals. The prince, together with the others whom a sentence of excommunication had excluded from entrance into God’s house, waited before the doors of the church. Once the sacred mysteries of the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood had been duly celebrated, the man of God—now acting no longer according to man—before [Col. 1181B] peace was distributed among the people, reverently placed upon the paten the heavenly manna, the utterly pure fruit of the Virgin’s womb, while all who were present marvelled. As they waited in great astonishment for the outcome, he took the paten itself, containing the precious deposit, the pledge of eternal salvation, and went out. With a fiery countenance, and in a voice not pleading but threatening, he addressed the prince in words full of authority, beginning thus:

> “We entreated you, and you scorned to hear us. Behold, the Son of the Virgin, the Son of the most high Father, has come out to you: that Son, I say, who redeemed the holy Church at the price of his most innocent blood, which you, so far as lies in you, do not fear to rend and throw into confusion. The Judge of the universe is here, into whose hands that soul of yours will come; before the fearful throne of whose judgment you must render an account of the deeds of your whole life. Resist him, if you can.”

When the count saw the venerable abbot holding in holy hands the heavenly sacraments, dreadful to all the orders of angels [Col. 1181C], and with burning speech piercing the secrets of his guilty conscience, he could not bear the presence of supreme majesty. His blood grew cold throughout his limbs, and he fell to the ground as though lifeless. As he lay there, foam issued horribly from his darkening lips; as though about to breathe his last, he shook his vital parts with repeated sobs. After he had lain thus miserably for some time, while those present wept and beat their breasts, the prophetic man approached, struck him with his foot, and, by the power of him whom he bore while being himself borne, commanded in an authoritative voice that he rise, be reconciled with the bishops whom he had driven from their sees—some of whom were present—and show himself henceforth to be more a son of the Catholic Church than a supporter of schismatics. By God’s cooperating grace this was immediately done, as the book of his deeds more fully relates, quite beyond the expectation of all who were present and knew how exceedingly obstinate [Col. 1181D] that prince’s mind had been in the schism. Thus both clergy and people of the land, freed from the madness of Peter Leo by the power of the undefiled sacrifice and the faith of the man of God, and restored to the unity of holy mother Church, praised the Lord’s mercy.

O how great is the piety of faith, of which the Apostle declares excellently that it has “promises of the life that now is, and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). O truly wondrous craftsman, the Holy Spirit, who joins highest things to lowest by so wonderful a glue of charity: so that the most splendid, most pure, and most sweet bread of angels, containing every delight—the Word of God—may, through the most blessed humanity of that same Word, be granted to worms of the earth to eat; and that a small portion of earthly substance, which could be despised merely by looking at it and considering it, when consecrated according to the rule of ecclesiastical tradition, may be transubstantiated into the true body and true blood of Christ our Lord, becoming the sweetest nourishment. Thus the pious rational but wretched beast, deliciously refreshed, may become a sharer in the glory of blessedness with rational [Col. 1182A] yet blessed nature! Yet these most exalted works of God, which in the ineffable condescension of his grace he bestows upon wretched mortals, are manifest indeed to faith but blind to reason. Therefore to believe them belongs to piety; to investigate them, to rashness; to know them is life, and eternal life.

Does not this saint seem to you, together with holy old Simeon, not only to acknowledge in the depth of the mystery the loftiness of majesty, but also openly to show it to others: beneath the accidents presented to bodily senses and eyes—that is, visible appearance, weight, and taste—he does not investigate Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, by the rashness of reason, but believes, reveres, and worships him in the simplicity of faith, and in the same constancy of faith presents him fearfully to the proud?

Let, then, the rashness of human reason now cease from wishing to investigate what has been sealed with the seal of faith and denied to mortal nature to know. Though it limp with the foot [Col. 1182B] of knowledge, like the patriarch Jacob, who was content with his simplicity, let it nevertheless plant the foot of faith more firmly with the apostle Peter, who by the power of faith detected and destroyed the duplicity of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), so that through the devotion of faith it may someday deserve to attain the fullness of knowledge. For what does it matter to you, in your curiosity, to know by what order you receive the life-giving benefit of the heavenly Giver, provided you possess it in its efficacy, prove it in its usefulness, and further experience, so far as is lawful, with glad manifestation the manifold glory of signs and wonders which God has never ceased to work in the sacrament of the altar from the beginning of faith until now?

But, passing over greater matters, let me, a small man, speak of the lesser miracles of God. Although he is exceedingly great and praiseworthy in great things, he nevertheless works wonders more gloriously in the smallest things. With what kindness he deigned to relieve the alarm of that abbot who, finding a spider in the holy chalice at the hour of the divine sacrifice, full of faith drank it together with the sacrament, wisely observing that death could not prevail over life [Col. 1182C]. On that same day, while being bled, he was astonished and frightened to see the very spider emerge intact with the blood from the little wound. With what sweetness, too, did the merciful Lord teach another priest that one thing is seen at the altar and another must be believed. This priest, encountering a similar case and armed with no lesser faith, did not hesitate to take death together with life; but when evening had already come, feeling an itch in his foot, he scratched it and pulled out the spider which he had swallowed, with no part of its little body crushed or mutilated.

But how astonishing and worthy of wonder must this be judged: that the same venomous little creature, which, even when received into the vital organs, could in no way harm those who displayed sincere faith and due reverence toward the Lord’s sacraments, is reported, though remaining at a distance, to have terribly killed certain persons who approached those same fearful sacraments with shameless irreverence. For it is read in the acts of Emperor Charlemagne that, when [Col. 1182D] the same religious Augustus was hearing Mass with his customary devotion on a certain solemn day, the deacon appointed to read the Gospel at that Mass had not feared, on the preceding night, to defile himself with the unchaste embraces of a little woman for whose love he pined. Although his conscience was branded by this most grave sin, and though he did not fear the judgments of God, terrible in his counsels over the children of men, he presumed to read the holy Gospel. Afterwards he would also, with the same impudence, have performed his ministry in the sacred mysteries with unclean hands, according to the dignity of his office, had not divine vengeance swiftly removed the rash man by severe punishment. For behold: while he uttered sacred words with polluted lips, the aforesaid little creature let itself down from above, from the ceiling of the oratory, by its thread over the head of the defiled reader once, twice, and three times. On the third occasion, while the emperor watched, it stung the foul head and immediately killed the wretch.

If, then, O curious man, you cannot by any sharpness of human reason determine [Col. 1183A] by what route or channel that little creature crept through the hidden intricacies of the veins, or how, escaping from the stomach the natural downward course of the intestines, it reached the lowest parts of the body by crawling unharmed between flesh and skin, how will you be able to know in what order or manner the bread and wine placed upon the altar become the true body and true blood of Christ? For if, according to the prophet, “you have grown weary running with footmen” (Jer. 12), how will you contend with horses? That is, if you find yourself wrapped in the densest darkness of mortality in these smallest matters, with what face or rashness do you presume restlessly to investigate the most exalted works of God? Concerning the sacrament of the altar, therefore, let us say as someone said concerning martyrdom: “Let us give all to God, and nothing to ourselves.”

Accordingly, one who wishes to advance in holy religion must devote himself in every way to correction of morals and purification of heart, but must attend more chastely to the mysteries of Holy Scripture through contemplation [Col. 1183B], since the field of exercise and labor belongs to the untrained and imperfect, while the bed of contemplation belongs to the humble and devout. But what sort of humble persons, or what sort of devout persons, do you suppose? Certainly not just any such persons, but those who have long been dead to the vices of curiosity, vanity, and pleasure, and have ascended the citadel of holy humility and perfection; those who can say to the Lord with the Psalmist: “In the way of thy testimonies, O Lord, I have delighted, as in all riches” (Ps. 118).

But whoever has not yet been established by God in this brightness of virtues, so as to walk in their light all day long, but still has his understanding surrounded by the darkness of vices, ought to know, though he may flourish in subtle intelligence and possess keenness of reason, that it is more expedient for him to pray and to meditate repeatedly upon the psalms, to read more sparingly, and in reading itself to seek not knowledge that puffs up but the Spirit that gives life; not to become eloquent, but sober-minded, as the Apostle warns: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 12). He should not boast that he knows what he does not know, but should keep his knowledge before God and himself, as befits a monk, in humility of conscience. Otherwise the satirist—rather, the unclean spirit—may mock him because his knowing is so insignificant that it amounts to nothing unless another knows that he knows it.

Hence, since Augustine, the most learned of teachers, says: “To pray and to read are both good, if one is permitted; if one is not permitted, it is better to pray than to read,” we greatly wonder at certain persons who almost wholly, or wholly, neglect the utterly necessary benefit of prayer and devotion, yet devote themselves to reading and meditation throughout days and nights—as though he were not painting upon emptiness or carrying dust in the wind who multiplies knowledge in a conscience not yet cleansed of vices. And the more the subtlety of contemplation flies upward without the fullness of perfection, the more, as we have found in many cases, it lies exposed to perilous downfall [Col. 1183D].

Therefore, since such persons must greatly fear lest, displaying only the brightness of lamps while neglecting the richness of oil—that is, glorying solely in the clarity of knowledge without the gentleness of devotion and humility—they be rejected with the foolish virgins by God the just Judge, who expelled the first-created humans from Paradise because of their disordered appetite for knowledge, let us all take care, each of us take care, diligently to offer to the Lord our God, upon the altar of devotion, the sacrifice of a contrite heart and humble spirit: for forgiveness of sins, for acquisition of virtues, and also for avoiding the misery of eternal death and gaining the glory of everlasting blessedness.

But if anyone, with grace as guide, can advance [Col. 1184A] so far in the constancy of sacred devotion as to establish the goodness of religious life and the discipline of unfeigned humility upon the foundation of a steadfast conscience, then he may safely ask with the Psalmist to be taught knowledge (Ps. 118). Yet he must not presume that he will gain the efficacy of saving knowledge merely by diligent reading and meditation, but much more by the anointing of him “who teaches man knowledge” (Ps. 126). For, as the Psalmist testifies, it is vain for every person to rise before the dawn of perfect humility in eager pursuit of knowledge; and therefore it is altogether necessary first, sitting in penitence, to eat the bread of sorrow (ibid.), that is, of compunction, and only then to rise to the light of knowledge or contemplation. For arrogant vanity will find no place for pride in knowledge where maturity of goodness and discipline has filled every corner of the conscience.

## CHAPTER III. On the happy end of a monk who desired to die at Clairvaux

John the apostle and evangelist, who by sacred inspiration revealed the secrets of the Word of God [Col. 1184B], so far as mortals sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death may lawfully know them, was exiled to the island of Patmos for the testimony of that same Word of God. Among the many mysteries of heavenly revelation, for the consolation of all who labor in the way of God and groan beneath the weight of temptations, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). Giving the reason for this same blessedness, he adds: “From henceforth, the Spirit says, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow them” (ibid.).

Meditating diligently upon the joyful remembrance of this blessed death, through which one passes from labor to rest, from corruption to incorruption, from death to life, from misery to happiness, and from faith to knowledge, they too sighed for it with continual prayers and desires, saying: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41). They also bestowed upon others who were dying a pious affection of congratulation and compassion. Thus it is read of blessed Abbot Bernard that he scarcely ever [Col. 1184C] buried a dead person without tears of compassion; and the most reverend John, Patriarch of Alexandria, forgetting the authority of his exalted rank, personally approached any faithful persons who were dying. Sitting before them, he watched their final struggle with much pious feeling; with his own hands he closed the eyes of the dying, and most devoutly commended to divine grace the souls departing from their bodies.

Blessed Malachy, bishop of Ireland, likewise remembered his last things in all his works, so that he might deserve to receive a blessing on the day of his death. Once he came to Clairvaux, and because of reverence for his holiness gained the friendship and familiar companionship of our holy father Bernard. His soul clung to the soul of the man of God with such ardor of holy charity, and he was so inflamed with desire to die at Clairvaux, that upon returning to his homeland, throughout the remainder of his life he devoutly offered to the Lord this chief petition: that he might die both at Clairvaux [Col. 1184D] and on the day of commemoration of the souls of all the faithful departed, and that, reduced himself to ashes beside the ashes of his beloved abbot, he might through divine generosity deserve to await the glory of the blessed resurrection. Nor was he disappointed in his hope, since the Lord granted him his soul’s desire. He received the place as glory, the day as merit, and the triumph of companionable rest as the prerogative of his merits.

A certain brother followed the faith and devotion of this glorious bishop, Balsam by natural name no less than by the fragrance of his holy conduct. He was a monk of St Anastasius, a Cistercian monastery situated by the walls of the city of Rome. Once, when business entrusted to him brought him to blessed Bernard at Clairvaux, he saw the discipline of that holy and numerous community and its mature observance of the sacred Order. His heart grew warm within him, and in meditation [Col. 1185A] fire blazed forth, so that, unless charity—which does not seek its own—had commanded otherwise, he would have preferred to live and die at Clairvaux to all the riches and delights of the world.

Yet, lest he leave empty-handed and such a religious desire be deprived of its due reward, he asked the holy abbot with most humble prayers, and because of the fervor of his devotion obtained, that at his death the whole service might be performed for him by the community of Clairvaux. Having gained this, he now considered Clairvaux his own and himself a monk of Clairvaux, and rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Returning home, from that time onward he always performed special offices for each brother of Clairvaux whose death he learned of, and, in addition, each year said twelve Masses for all the rest whose end he did not know.

This most devout man, although obedience compelled him to be continually occupied with the concerns of the monastery, in which he was very useful and necessary, nevertheless strove to redeem for himself this portion of time [Col. 1185B]: amid these occupations, besides the common observances of the Order and other good works which he did with God alone as witness, for eight years he said the Psalter every day and received discipline at least daily. How pleasing to God his holy life was is clearly shown by the one miracle which we now add. Once, sent on business of his monastery to Lord Pope Alexander, who was then staying in France, he happened to fall into the hands of certain schismatics supporting the party of the antipope Octavian. Immediately they insultingly took him down from the mule on which he rode and ordered him confined in custody. One of these robbers mounted the mule of the man of God and wished to lead it away; but the animal, resisting with marvellous movements and leaps and, as though fighting for its master, wholly refused to go. Though they beat the innocent beast from every side with spurs and whips, they could not overcome it. Instead, it moved backward and always struggled toward the forbidden direction, defeating all their efforts [Col. 1185C].

Seeing that a miracle was divinely being worked against them, the schismatics, at last overcome both by weariness and by the miracle, released the holy man and ordered him to mount the same mule before them and depart. When the servant of God was received again, the animal at once, in complete gentleness and to the wonder of all, went forward without delay or compulsion, walking eagerly and carrying the master whom it gladly recognized.

That desire to die at Clairvaux, which he had long conceived in fruitful devotion, continually increased by daily encouragement and always lived in his heart. But as the day of his calling approached—a day known to God alone, who is accustomed to hear the desire of the poor—the Lord himself, who works all things for the salvation of his elect, arranged that he should come, on another pretext, even to the house of Clairvaux, which he had always desired to be the place of his death and burial. For it happened that the aforesaid house of St Anastasius, which was [Col. 1185D] a daughter-house of Clairvaux and of which he was a most devoted monk, lacked a spiritual pastor. Therefore, sent by the supreme pontiff himself and by his brothers, he came to the house of Clairvaux to choose from there a new abbot at the discretion of the father of that house. Yet he came more truly sent by the Lord, so that, departing from the sea of this world, he might now at last reach the harbor of his desire.

While he remained there for several days, edified, moved to compunction, and stirred to devotion by everything he saw and heard in that holy community, it happened that one of the brothers reached the end of his present life. At the sound of the death-board he saw the very devout gathering and procession of that great body—monks and lay brothers alike—the solemn performance of the commendation, the pious chanting at the lifting of the funeral, and the long, ordered procession of the great multitude. He also saw the sacred service of priests and ministers offering the saving sacrifice for the soul of the deceased brother [Col. 1186A], and likewise the religious vigils of psalmody around the dead man’s body. Entirely dissolved in pious feeling, and desiring with a burning heart to deserve a share in this benefit for which he had always longed, he asked his soul with a loud groan that it might die, crying from the inmost marrow of his heart to the Lord and saying: “Let my soul, Lord, die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like theirs” (Num. 23).

When the funeral solemnities had been duly celebrated and the body borne to the tomb, and when, according to custom, the community had gone in a wide circuit like a crown around the graves both of the newly buried man and of the other brothers resting there, the psalms belonging to the burial having now ended, the antiphon *Most Merciful Lord* was being sweetly sung by the whole body of brothers. Meanwhile the aforesaid servant of God, casting his eyes about [Col. 1186B]—not as instruments of curiosity but of piety—joyfully beheld that holy multitude like an angelic choir. Melted within himself by every feeling of sweetness and devotion, since obedience prevented him from becoming one of them in life, he longed and prayed in the heat of fervent desire that at least by dying he might deserve to become one of them.

When the antiphon had been sung through, at its conclusion, where it says, “Lord, have mercy upon the sinner,” all asked forgiveness according to custom and made humble prayer for the soul of the deceased brother. The servant of God too asked that same forgiveness with the others and prayed the same words in an ardent spirit of piety. The fountains of his eyes burst open, and, watering his face with a most abundant shower of tears, he asked not only rest for the dead man but also for himself a swift end of life in that same house. Immediately, therefore, as divine mercy willed to bring the desire of its little servant into effect, a fatal fever seized him in that very place. Afflicting him with diverse illnesses until his death, and cleansing the rust of creeping sins—without which this present life is not lived—it made him gain his wish as happily as swiftly [Col. 1186C].

On the following night, when he had given his limbs to sleep, heaven was opened to him. There he saw our Lord Jesus Christ, his most blessed mother our Lady, St Bernard, and a great multitude of other saints in great glory. He rejoiced so much in their most blessed vision that he already counted himself almost one of them. As his illness increased, he gave thanks to God in great patience; by confession of the mouth, contrition of heart, and devotion in holy prayer, he begged that a portion might be given him in the land of the living. Thus, reaching his final hour, he rested in a holy end before the tenth day: “Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord” (Ps. 127). Such a man venerates and loves the good things that he sees in others; and although he himself watches over the pursuit of virtues according to his ability, he nevertheless trusts that, through the intervening merits of his brethren, he may obtain the prize of his own labor more fully and perfectly [Col. 1186D], if he can attain the fellowship, in life or death, of those whom he judges better than himself.

Behold this servant of God, whose truly happy end we have described. Taught by God not to think highly of his own virtues but always to fear because of his imperfection, he longed with burning desires for the blessed companionship of the most holy community. What the virtue of obedience denied him while he lived, the most merciful rewarder of that same obedience kindly restored him in death; and he associated him in heaven with the ineffable glory due only to perfect monks—those whose sacred ashes he had preferred, with humble sighs of desire, to join even in burial on earth.

## CHAPTER IV. Likewise, concerning a lay brother who asked the Lord to let him die at Clairvaux

We know that the grace of dying at Clairvaux was [Col. 1187A] granted by divine generosity not to this man alone but also at times to certain others. In our own times, likewise, we have seen and rejoiced in the fulfillment of the joy of a servant of God who burned intensely with such a desire; and from it we took no small encouragement to bear the burden and heat of the day under the discipline of Clairvaux.

The time of the general chapter was approaching, and abbots of the Cistercian Order were hastening to Cîteaux from all parts of the world. Among them, a certain abbot, governing one of the daughter-houses of Clairvaux in the regions of Spain, was making the long and laborious journey to the mother of his community, that is, Clairvaux. In his company he had a certain lay brother, upright in conduct and remarkable in devotion. Having often heard in his homeland the nectar-like report of the religious life and holiness of the house of Clairvaux, this man was stirred in spirit and desired to see Clairvaux, to which its most illustrious abbot had given a renowned name throughout the world by the radiance of his holiness.

Having set out on the journey to the chapter [Col. 1187B], the nearer he came to his desired Clairvaux, the more he wished, if it might be, not only to see it but also to draw there the thread of his final lot. When he came so near that he could see from afar the pinnacle of the sacred church, the ointments of devotion bubbling up at the sight of that revered place with the fire of charity, he was wholly melted into piety. Raising his hands and eyes to heaven, he poured out to the Lord a short prayer, yet one most sincere in the fullness of faith, crying out in a manner and saying:

> “O Lord, if the petition of a poor and sinful man does not displease thy majesty, let this holy place, which keeps the pledges of so many holy souls now reigning with thee, be my rest for ever and ever. Here, Lord, if thou deignest, let me rest, because I have chosen it.”

Entering, therefore, the place of the wonderful tabernacle which God, not man, established (Heb. 8), he simply venerated the tombs of the special patron and protector of that place, St Bernard, and of his distinguished companion, blessed Malachy [Col. 1187C]. He devoutly prayed that he might deserve swiftly to receive the effect of his desire. Nor was the effect of his pious petition delayed: he suddenly began to fail in bodily strength, was taken to a sickbed, and hastened joyfully and eagerly toward death’s struggle as though invited to a feast.

After he himself disclosed it and his abbot bore witness, monks and lay brothers alike learned that he had obtained from the Lord this swift death because of his desire to die at Clairvaux. That holy community greatly rejoiced and, piously rejoicing with him as he happily died, joined him as he departed to its most holy fellowship with prayers and desires of good will. Anointed with sacramental oil and strengthened by the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, he breathed out his spirit, protected by the prayers of the brethren, within a few days, in the midst of so great and holy a multitude—abbots, monks, and lay brothers—as he had desired. The abbots who had assembled at Clairvaux on the Nativity of St Mary before the Cistercian chapter were still remaining there, unless I am mistaken [Col. 1187D]. The great and venerable assembly celebrated his funeral with solemn and devout offices, and, adding earth to earth, together glorified the wonderful God in his saints, who had deigned to show in this poor man how much sincere petitions of suppliants avail before him.

Moreover, who could doubt that, through the abundance of divine goodness, certain people are sometimes granted that which is lacking to them in their own merits, to be supplied by the merits of others? For where any weak and imperfect person is perfectly incorporated into the Church in religious life, the merits of the perfect cover the deformity of the imperfect, provided that these imperfect persons [Col. 1188A], with pure intention, become imitators according to their measure of perfection and sacred religion and are snatched away from this world. As the Psalmist sings: “With the holy thou wilt be holy, and with the innocent man thou wilt be innocent” (Ps. 17).

Nor should any religious church be believed merely to support, protect, and fortify at death its weak members, still vigorously fighting in the flesh of sin, by the merits and prayers of its members. Rather, and much more, it ought to be hoped that it does this in its members who, after the labors of their sacred warfare accomplished, are glorious in the rest and blessedness of veterans. Thus a certain elder of perfect religious life among the brothers of Clairvaux, who had received from the Lord the grace at times to see invisible things, testified that the souls of brothers already released from the flesh meet a soul about to be released from the flesh with no less—indeed, with greater—number and devotion than brothers still animating their bodies; and that they labor with most dutiful charity so that it may escape the malicious accusations of evil spirits who meet it from the opposite side with great savagery, and may obtain a share in true light and eternal blessedness [Col. 1188B].

Therefore, just as we rightly pronounce happy those who, after the exercise of hard and laborious penitence, deserve to be supported in death by the suffrages of brothers both living and dead, so we surely lament as wretched—and, so to speak, more unhappy than all people—those who do not consider why they took on the religious habit, but corrupt their lives by depravity of conduct. Although they may be borne to the tomb with honorable offices from the living, they obtain nothing from the aid either of the living or of the dead; but those who have sown the thorns of dissolution will receive eternal fire as the wages of their malice.

## CHAPTER V

> [Note: Col. 1187D. The histories in chapters 5 and 6 are pious—would that they were certain.]

Concerning a religious man whose funeral the souls of the departed were seen to celebrate.

Indeed, if perhaps anyone is troubled by the scruple that the aforesaid elder said that the souls released from the flesh come to meet brothers departing this life at the moment of death [Col. 1188C], let him not, I pray, take offense either at the holy man for saying these things or at us for writing them down as though they were false. Rather, let him bear with us patiently; and true testimony will prove that we affirm that such things have not only been known in a special manner by holy men, but have also at times, by the will of the almighty Creator, been seen with bodily eyes and heard with bodily ears. Thus mortal man may doubt the less concerning the wretched or blessed condition of the soul after death according to the quality of its merits, the more clearly he perceives that the subtle and invisible substance of that same soul can, at the Creator’s command—to whom all things are possible—be joined and, so to speak, mingled with those living in the flesh. Despising utterly this present life, which he knows to be frail and passing, let him prepare himself with every care, watching over good works, for that life toward which he runs at every moment.

In the regions of Lesser Brittany [Col. 1188D] there once lived a layman who, although devoted to secular business and occupied with the management of his household, was nevertheless faithful and God-fearing, and, according to his measure, devout in keeping God’s commandments. Among the other good works which he did, publicly or privately, with God alone as witness, he had made it his custom, whenever going to or returning from church, or whenever passing through a cemetery on any other occasion, to offer the Lord a devout prayer for the souls of the faithful resting there.

It happened that, when the term of his life was fulfilled and he was about to depart from this wicked world, he lay sick in bed. Feeling himself now near death, in the darkness of midnight he sent for his priest, asking him to deign to come and visit him with the sacrament of the Lord. But the priest, overcome by sloth and—alas!—loving the comfort of his own flesh more than the salvation of the soul [Col. 1189A] of his parishioner, refused to go. He nevertheless sent in his place his deacon, named Daniel, a man of good conduct. Gladly obeying and promptly fulfilling his orders, Daniel administered viaticum to the dying man and did not delay in returning home.

As soon, therefore, as that poor man—poor in worldly goods but rich in merits—received for his defense Christ the Lord, the giver of everlasting health and imperishable riches, he joyfully put off the human being, and, as we believe, entered the gates of paradise with Him who deigned to become the receiver of the poor, and obtained the bright dwellings of the blessed spirits.

As the deacon returned and approached the church door, he found it open, although he had left it shut and most securely barred. Greatly astonished and turning uncertain thoughts over in his mind, he was immediately fixed by divine power in that spot, so that he could not move away from it. And behold, suddenly in that cemetery [Col. 1189B] a voice was heard crying and saying:

> “Arise, all you faithful; arise at once, and come out from your tombs, all of you who rest in this cemetery, so that, gathering in the church, we may commend the soul of this our most beloved departed brother, and repay him for his kindness. For as often as he used to pass through this cemetery, so often he customarily offered a special prayer for us.”

At this voice the dead began swiftly to arise, and there was a great crash and commotion as they came forth from their tombs. In the church, moreover, many candles appeared, fixed here and there to the walls, illuminating the same basilica with abundant light. When those dead persons had entered it, they began there to praise the Lord together in sweet melody and solemnly to chant the Office of Commendation, so that, while one said the collects and prayers, the others added “Amen” and the remaining responses, as is customary in a choir of chanters.

When the commendation [Col. 1189C] was completed, a cry was again raised that each should return to his own place. When they had gone out of the oratory, there was again a sound and collision of tombs as they replaced themselves in them. Then those lights visible in the church began gradually to fail, until they were wholly extinguished.

When this had been done, that cleric was released from the place where he had stood fast; entering the oratory, he put away there the sacramental vessels which he had brought with him. When he returned to the priest’s dwelling, the latter, measuring others by the scale of his own idleness and supposing that no one could easily stay awake in the depth of night, seemed to pity the man for his exertion and urged him quickly to return to bed and sleep. The deacon replied:

> “This is no time for me to rest; rather, it is time for you to rise and work. For the sick man, for whose funeral we must proceed, has now died.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, a messenger came, announcing the death of the aforesaid man and demanding the priest’s presence. Therefore, though unwilling, the priest rose [Col. 1189D], went without delay with the deacon, and rendered the service due to the pious funeral.

That deacon, however, was by no means ungrateful for the favor of God’s grace, which had so graciously visited him. Deeply moved and compuncted by the vision he had seen, he left everything that he had or could hope to have; departing from his land and kindred, he received the religious habit at Tours in the monastery of St. Martin. There, living a religious life and keeping the memory of the faithful departed, he advanced in merit and was later made prior of that same church. He disclosed the aforesaid revelation privately to certain close acquaintances. Yet, because of the wondrous novelty of the event, it could not be concealed in silence, but quickly came to the knowledge of the abbot of that place. Wishing either to be reliably informed of so incredible a matter or to have it wholly suppressed, the abbot assembled the community of brothers [Col. 1190A] in chapter and questioned the same prior before them all concerning this report, strictly commanding and adjuring him by virtue of obedience not to conceal the truth from them.

Constrained at last by this adjuration, the prior, though he would have wished to spare his own embarrassment and prevent this from occurring in public, nevertheless, for the honor of God and the edification of his neighbor, shamefacedly and fearfully explained what had happened to him. When the truth was known, the aforesaid abbot, being a good and religious man, gave thanks to God for such unheard-of wonders—this prophetic revelation in some manner prefiguring the sacred mystery of the future resurrection. Establishing a general rule in his monastery, he commanded that whenever any of the brothers happened to enter the cemetery, they should not be reluctant to say at least once the Lord’s Prayer for the faithful resting there.

Therefore let no one think it frivolous or absurd that we have said that the souls of departed brothers sometimes attend the departure of dying [Col. 1190B] brothers and strive more earnestly to rescue them from the dangers then pressing upon them. For by this present example we are manifestly taught that they devote themselves to helping all the more fervently and devoutly as a person in this life has been more diligent to keep their memory and offer the aid of his prayers to mitigate the sentence of the strict Judge.

For what else is suggested to us by what is recorded above in this volume concerning Lord Geoffrey of Sées, bishop of blessed memory [Note: Above, Distinction III, chapter 21; Col. 1189D]? While he was still a monk at Clairvaux, one night during the sacred vigils, as he was cheerfully chanting psalms and praying, he plainly saw coming from the northern side of the church—that is, from the court in which the bodies of the departed brethren rest—a great multitude clad in white. Passing before the step of the presbytery, it went out through the door leading to the infirmary. At that same moment, in the infirmary, a certain old man of good conduct [Col. 1190C] was struggling in his last agony. Does this not mean that the blessed souls of the departed brethren came to receive into their fellowship their brother as he put off the garments of corruptible life, and to drive back the phalanxes of malignant spirits seeking to accuse him?

So far as we understand, however, these things are to be thought only of those souls which have been freed from every fault together with every punishment and have already attained the happiness of eternal blessedness; likewise, they are to be thought of those dying persons who have merited by the religious conduct of their past life to be supported in the danger of death by the protection of blessed souls.

## CHAPTER VI. On the knight delivered from the danger of death by the souls of the faithful

Since, however, by relating this memorable miracle we have shown how the souls of the faithful repaid at his death the kindness of one who devoutly prayed for them, it is now pleasing to relate how certain persons who diligently [Col. 1190D] prayed for the faithful departed, or gave alms on their behalf, were delivered by the aid of those same souls from the dangers of this present life and from the swords of enemies hanging over their necks. Thus every religious person may be assured that he will not be deprived of the reward of his labor if he extends compassionate affection and active assistance to souls suffering punishment according to the sentence of God, the just Judge. For he may learn that even certain laymen, who were more fervent in this form of devotion, escaped the perils of utter calamity because of this work of mercy.

For nothing is more acceptable to God than compassionate affection, since the merciful love of supreme compassion caused the supreme blessedness of the Godhead to descend from heaven to earth to help the wretched. And because the souls of the departed, now unable to merit anything by themselves, receive more gratefully [Col. 1191A] the benefit of intercession bestowed upon them by the living, inasmuch as by it they feel their punishments either mitigated or more quickly ended—punishments which, because their sins required it, they know must have been harsh or long-lasting.

Accordingly, a certain knight, secular in activity and habit, endeavored to restrain his secular mind by zeal for good works. Frequently reflecting that he was mortal and would die in his own time, he often commemorated the dead before God with such prayer and devotion as he could. He had resolved that no necessity or haste should ever prevent him, when passing through a churchyard, from stopping, turning his face eastward, attentively saying the Lord’s Prayer for the souls of the faithful, and humbly begging the Lord to have mercy on the departed.

It happened that on one occasion he was so suddenly surrounded by enemies lying in wait for him that he had to face the danger of death immediately or secure his life by flight. Therefore, fleeing with utmost speed [Col. 1191B], he happened in his running to reach the enclosure surrounding a cemetery. Since he found no shorter route by which to escape those whom he fled, he leapt quickly over the entrance of the enclosure and pressed on, breathless, through the middle of the cemetery.

But while running, he remembered his custom, which he had preserved unbroken for a long time. He was troubled at heart and anxiously weighed in his mind what he ought to do in so critical a situation. Either he must pay the spiritual debt owed to the souls of the faithful at the risk of his life, or his conscience held him guilty before God, the just Judge—as a violator of his duty, although God can preserve those who trust in Him in however narrow an extremity of necessity. But since in such pressure of time and danger he had no leisure for lengthy deliberation, the piety of faith quickly overcame the fear of bodily frailty. Scorning death, he resolved not to withhold from the faithful departed their accustomed aid of prayer; rather, if it pleased the Most High, to die pierced by the swords of his enemies above the tombs [Col. 1191C] of those for whom he prayed.

Thus he stopped running and stood still. Calming his troubled mind, he turned his face eastward as was his custom and began to say the Lord’s Prayer with all the more sincere devotion because he thought that he was offering this his final prayer to God and, as it were, his last farewell to the faithful departed.

Meanwhile his enemies, driven by the most cruel rancor of deadly hatred, rushed upon him with rapid steps. Seeing the man whom they thirsted to kill standing reverently, they supposed that fear of death had made him stand rigid. As though they were now to achieve their cruel desire by immediately committing the crime they hoped for, they rejoiced wickedly, though not with impunity. For as, in mad headlong fury, they hastened to break into the cemetery enclosure, violate the sanctuary of God’s church, and sacrifice, after the example of the first fratricide, the victim standing with bowed neck and lowered head [Col. 1191D], behold, they suddenly saw a great multitude of armed men filling the whole cemetery. We may reasonably believe that these were the souls of the departed for whom he prayed. Surrounding their intercessor with a close-formed crown, they watched with holy concern so that he might complete without impediment the prayer he had begun for them; but against his adversaries they terribly brandished swords and spears.

Those men, hateful to God and murderers in the mere wicked desire of their hearts, saw this sudden change and the armed crowd threatening them. Stupefied and mentally overwhelmed, they swiftly took flight. Having come to destroy another’s life by cruel slaughter, they now considered it the greatest gain if they could preserve their own by escape.

The devout man at prayer saw and felt none of this. When he had completed his prayer, he resumed the course which, constrained by piety in such an emergency, he had interrupted. With swift speed he made his escape, as though fleeing the hands of enemies who pursued him; and he was astonished and afraid that he had been able to escape the swords of furious enemies so near at hand [Col. 1192A].

After some time, however, the cloud of enmity was dispersed by the ardor of charity, and the beauty of peace was firmly restored between the parties. In friendly conversation, the enemies asked him what reason there had been for his standing motionless and not moving from the place when death threatened him; while he asked why they had spared his life when they had had the opportunity to destroy him. When each learned the truth of the mystery from the other, they magnificently praised the Lord, who alone does great wonders. Both they and many others who could learn of so great a miracle were powerfully stirred to pray for the faithful departed. May we too, and all who happen to read or hear these things, not be reluctant to imitate this in religious devotion!

How astounding, and how worthy of a proclamation of admiration, will be judged the event divinely wrought concerning Eusebius, duke of Sicily, which has now been spread by writing through many regions of the world [Col. 1192B]. He had as his adversary a certain prince who, raised high by great wealth and the glory of earthly eminence, placed his hope in the strength and multitude of his army. Eusebius, committing his confidence to God, did many good works for the deliverance of the souls of the faithful. By a great miracle of God, through an army of souls sent to him from heaven, splendidly equipped with snow-white horses and arms, he received into surrender both his rival and his entire army. Encouraged by the admonition of those same souls, who gave him thanks for benefits bestowed upon them and exhorted him to aid the departed, he resolved to perform many more good works than before for the deliverance of the souls of the faithful, throughout the cities and churches subject to his authority.

O how certain of victory may he be who fights with mercy and prayers! O by what irrefutable witness of truth is supported the saying: “He who prays for another labors for himself”!
