This was granted to the religious prince of whom we speak in the highest crisis of his honor, and likewise to the devout knight whom we mentioned above in the extreme danger of his life, to experience most happily and excellently. For if it is believed to be a work of mercy to pray for faithful brethren and neighbors who still can perform works of righteousness and merit the rewards of righteousness, how much more should it be judged a work of mercy worthy of every approval to intercede for the souls of the faithful, who can now neither perform works of righteousness, by which good merits are gained, nor any longer have recourse to remedies of penance, but are compelled only to pay the penalties of their sins and negligences under the just judgment of the Divinity [Col. 1192C]?

## CHAPTER VII. On the priest who, saying, “May they rest in peace,” heard many voices answering, “Amen”

[Col. 1192D]

Yet although they can no longer act by themselves, they are sometimes found, by the wondrous and joyful gift of almighty God, to cooperate and in some way rejoice together with those who labor for them. We heard by the most certain report of elders that this happened many years ago to a monk of religious life, and we know that it was also set down in writing for the memory of posterity.

In the province called Germany beyond the Rhine, commonly called Saxony, there was in former times, while the Cluniac Order still flourished in its proper condition, a monk in the monastery built within the walls of the city of Paderborn, of the Cluniac Order, and dedicated to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul. In accordance with his name, he loved Christ; for his personal name was Amo. Since he was endowed with priestly rank, he sought to adorn his holy office with holy conduct [Col. 1193A], and celebrated the divine mysteries with the devotion fitting for a spiritual minister.

So that he might offer the undefiled sacrifice more devoutly because more secretly, in the ark of a contrite heart, he customarily frequented a certain chapel consecrated in honor of St. Alexius. It was separated from the church of that place only by the intervening cemetery, and he went there to say Mass. Thus he necessarily crossed the cemetery continually in going and returning. Going to the sacred building or returning from it, he extended the hand of devout prayer, without wearying of the repetition, to the faithful departed. Reflecting that after his own days were finished he too would be reduced to ashes, he devoutly considered the expiations of those reduced to ashes and humbly prayed that their punishments might be mitigated.

One day, after celebrating the sacred mysteries, as he returned and diligently paid, as he was accustomed, the pledge of holy prayer to those to whom mercy had made him indebted, he completed his prayer and added at its conclusion [Col. 1193B], “May they rest in peace.” He clearly heard a great multitude answer him, saying, “Amen, amen.” Hearing this, he trembled all over. Thinking that these were the voices of the souls for whom he prayed, he marveled and was afraid that they were invisibly so close to him. Thereafter he pursued the practice of his good custom, which he had hitherto devoutly maintained, with all the more eager watchfulness, because he joyfully recognized through the novelty of so unusual a miracle that the service of his devotion was acceptable to God and grateful and fruitful to the souls of the faithful.

Holy and salutary, therefore, is the thought of praying for the dead, that they may be released from sins (2 Maccabees 12).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the boy who confessed his sins after death

[Note: This history is certain. It is discussed more fully in the notes to volume III of the *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, on Distinction III, chapter 25. Here it need only be noted that it is not correct to say that the soul was withdrawn by the suffrages of the living from eternal punishments [Col. 1194D], since no mortal sin is remitted except in this life; once it has been remitted, the soul is not assigned to infernal punishments and therefore does not need to be liberated from them.]

O eternal Wisdom of God, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High [Col. 1193C], reaching mightily from end to end while disposing all things sweetly (Wisdom 8)! You say through the prophet: “My mercy shall not fail, and I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (Exodus 33). What more, what more excellent, what sweeter thing could human nature, subject to sins and vices, have expected from your most merciful goodness than this: that you so mercifully pity your poor, namely, that through a communication passing between the dead and the living—a communication exceedingly wonderful and possible only to your omnipotence—the former disclose to the living the faults and negligences which, while the flesh still lived, they had insufficiently corrected, and seek more earnestly the aid of holy prayer; while the latter presume, by the authority of power granted to them, to absolve souls now placed before your dreadful judgment, and by the devout offering of the unique sacrifice together with persevering holy prayer, are able to raise them to the joys of paradise?

But behold, O most kind and merciful Son of the living God, and Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Lord Jesus Christ, something still more sublime and sweet has flowed to us from the honey-bearing rock of your sweetness [Col. 1193D]. You are shown to have granted, to one of your least ones, all the more mercifully because undeservedly, the sacrament of confession, the profound and unutterable groans of a contrite heart, and also the baptism of most bitter tears of penance. Human weakness would not dare to presume that this could occur; yet, when it has occurred by the immense gift of your mercy, one rightly marvels and reckons it among the greatest proclamations of your praise.

I ask those who will read these things not to disparage them as falsely written, for the event occurred within our own memory, as even today certain trustworthy persons of the Cistercian Order testify.

It is known to all who could know so great a man, or learn the report of his virtues, how richly Lord Hugh, abbot of Bonneval, of blessed memory, was adorned with the grace of spiritual gifts [Col. 1194A]. He had in his service a boy who ran errands, exceedingly useful for the needs of travel through the liveliness and quickness of his service. Therefore he was dear and welcome both to the abbot himself and to the others who managed external affairs.

It happened, however, that in the middle of the days of his youth he was compelled to undergo the dreadful separation of spirit and flesh and pay the cruel tribute of harsh death, which spares neither age nor rank. For suddenly seized by grave bodily illness, he mourned as the vigor of his flourishing youth withered through daily decline, and learned by experience how truly the Wise Man says that youth and pleasure are vanity (Ecclesiastes 11). At last, despairing of the present life, he began, insofar as the weight of illness allowed—or rather, as the merciful Lord deigned to inspire him—to think fearfully of the state of the life to come [Col. 1194B]. Tearfully grieving that, through the impulse of his slippery age, he had committed many offenses against God and his Creator, he sought the remedy of confession as the single plank for those shipwrecked upon the great and broad sea of this world.

But whether, overtaken by death, he did not obtain what he devoutly desired, or whether, after confessing, he was not canonically absolved because of the simplicity or negligence of his confessor, we do not know. Yet the miraculous event of a confession made after the death of the flesh proves that assistance was provided less adequately than was fitting for such a youth, one indeed of the Lord’s little ones, by those by whom he ought to have been helped both in dying and after death.

One night, as the aforesaid venerable Abbot Hugh rested in his bed, the same youth, now dead, appeared to him in a vision, showing the countenance and bearing of one grieving and in distress. Then [Col. 1194C], approaching with great reverence, he properly placed his knees upon the knees of the holy abbot, stretched his supplicating hands toward his breast, and prostrated himself over the venerable limbs of the reclining man, as if in prayer. With tearful entreaty he asked that the abbot would deign to receive his confession.

Thereupon he made his confession, weeping and lamenting, setting out with complete distinction the particulars of the circumstances and events in which he said that he had sinned. Among these, he confessed that he had fallen even into certain criminal sins, with such sighs and such an abundant outpouring of tears that scarcely could the bitterness of so great a contrition and compunction be found in any living person. When his confession had been made, uttering yet deeper groans and adding more copious tears to his tears, he prayed with the greatest contrition of heart that the abbot would have mercy on him and deign by his holy prayers to make favorable to him the heavenly Judge—just toward the righteous, terrible toward sinners, yet promising pardon to the penitent [Col. 1194D].

Meanwhile the religious abbot melted wholly within himself through compassionate pity at the tears and sighs of so great a compunction. As he tried, from the expansiveness of mercy, to answer the distress of the wretched youth, he awoke. Reflecting on what he had seen and heard, and feeling himself urged by certain inner promptings to pity the dead man, he understood that the vision was not vain.

But so that every scruple of doubt might be removed from his heart—wondrous to say!—the marvelous mercy of almighty God permitted him to prove by a material experience, confirming the vision’s truth, what the spiritual substance had seemed to do spiritually. For when he felt with his hand the place in which the penitent soul had lain prostrate, pouring out tears of repentance [Col. 1195A], he found the covering with which he was covered so wet that it was as if the spirit which had seemed to shed those tears spiritually had possessed in itself the moisture of a liquid element.

But in these and similar wonders of divine power, if the judgment of reason alone is consulted, what is reported begins to appear unbelievable; but if divine power is acknowledged, it ceases to appear wonderful. Therefore the reverend abbot, no longer doubting, absolved in the chapter of brethren the soul which the mercy of Christ the Lord had entrusted to him for assistance. Offering satisfaction to God for its sins by his own prayers, those of his brethren, and devout celebrations of Masses, he withdrew the wretched soul, guilty of eternal death, from its punishments and made it, as we devoutly believe, a participant in immortal blessedness through the grace of God. Thus he showed that what was impossible with men is possible with God through the force of holy charity, to which even impossibilities yield.

## CHAPTER IX. On a prioress admonished by revelation to make confession

[Col. 1195B]

The Apostle, speaking in his manner of the depth of God’s mysteries, says: “That through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3). And the Lord, recounting to blessed Job the works of His omnipotence, says: “Who shall make the harmony of heaven sleep?” (Job 38).

For mortal nature cannot know with what sweetness, and with what deeply inward delight, that harmony delights and refreshes those lofty powers of blessed spirits through the works of grace—the manifold wisdom of God—by which He joins His holy Church, rescued from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, that is, the defilement of sin, to their sacred fellowship, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

For, on the testimony of Wisdom and Truth Himself [Col. 1195C], we have learned that it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota or one stroke of the law of His grace to perish (Matthew 5); that is, that even the smallest occasions through which even the least among the people of God receive the remedies of salvation should be so delayed that they fail to be brought into effect.

Accordingly, we shall note by way of example the subtle occasion by which that same gracious Wisdom—whose watchful care is for the salvation of human beings and before whose eyes all things are naked and open—deigned to admonish one of His handmaids concerning the condition of her conscience. Thus every person of sound understanding may burn with a stronger love for that Wisdom, the more sweetly he hears Her proclaim, through an instrument of wisdom familiar to him, that Her delights are with the children of men (Proverbs 8).

A certain prioress of a monastery was a virgin greatly devoted to God. With prudent care she held both herself and the sisters subject to her to the strictness of regular discipline. Although her holy way of life was pleasing to God [Col. 1195D], there was one thing which stained her purity, though she herself did not at all perceive it in her conscience. In her childhood she had committed a certain sin which, neglected through childish dullness and then swallowed up in oblivion by the length of time, had so disappeared that she did not remember having done anything of the kind.

But the merciful Lord did not wish His devoted handmaid to be put to shame by her enemies in the gate because of a sin concealed not by embarrassment but by forgetfulness. Therefore, in the following manner He deigned to reveal to her both what and when she had done wrong. One night, as the venerable prioress slept, a certain woman appeared to her in a vision—the woman who had once nursed her as a little child and, so far as tender age could receive it, had instructed her in the first rudiments of discipline [Col. 1196A]. Addressing her by her own name, as she had formerly addressed her when she was a child, she said:

> “Gilla, my daughter, what are you doing? How long will you remain numb through negligent disregard and not wash away, by the remedies of confession and penance, that sin which you committed in your childhood while you were entrusted to my care?”

When she had also informed her of the nature of the sin, the prioress, as though overcome with shame and recalling what she had done so long ago, replied:

> “Can the sin committed by a weak and foolish age, whose reason had not yet fully unfolded through the exercise and growth of life, be judged so serious that I must make so full a confession of it and do penance for it?”

But the woman said:

> “Do you then think that any sin whatsoever is of slight weight if it has not been wiped away by the shame of confession and the labor of penance? Listen carefully, then, to what I say. Know for certain, and do not doubt in the least, that just as images are seen painted on curtains or walls, represented by definite outlines and the expressed features of limbs, so in the soul of every [Col. 1196B] person who has in any manner been able in life to possess discernment of good and evil, even the least sins which he has committed are marked by a foul impression—except only those which, through God’s grace, have been forgiven by the offices of confession and penance.”

At these words the prioress shook off sleep. Astonished by what she had heard, she thought and reconsidered it more carefully and found that the vision was not vain. She truly remembered that she had done such a thing in childhood as she had heard in the vision. Yet, from the time when she reached the years of discretion and assumed the religious habit, it had never struck the attention of her conscience, because it had wholly fallen from her memory.

Therefore, giving thanks to God, she confessed and did penance all the more sincerely and humbly because she rejoiced that she had obtained this through the generosity of God’s goodness alone. Thereafter she was all the more watchful concerning both her past and impending sins because, through this divine revelation, she had learned more certainly that those deceive themselves who, flattering themselves on account of ignorance [Col. 1196C] or forgetfulness, rashly promise impunity to their consciences.

[Note: Above, Distinction V, chapter 4; Col. 1195D.]

Above, too, in this volume there is contained an account of a certain deceased convert who appeared in a vision to another convert still living, and recalled to him a sin which he had committed twelve years earlier while still a layman, but which had slipped from his memory through deadly forgetfulness; and he advised him to confess and repent of it as soon as possible, uttering a warning that must be heard with fear and trembling: namely, that a sin not at all absolved before death remains incapable of absolution after death. What then shall become of sins which shame at confession, weariness at harsh penance, or—what is more dangerous than these—confidence arising from a religious life long continued urge one to conceal, if that handmaid of God needed to be admonished even by revelation to confess and repent of a sin committed in her childhood, and if this brother heard that pardon would be denied after death for a grave sin which forgetfulness concealed, unless it had been duly absolved before death? Truly it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10); for God is terrible in his counsels toward the children of men. It is therefore beneficial for every person, and especially for one professed in religion, diligently to reconsider the past years of his life in bitterness of soul and, without dissembling, to judge himself by confession of the mouth, contrition of the heart, and the performance of good works, if he does not wish to be condemned with this world. For the narrow way that leads to life scarcely receives those who are unburdened and unencumbered, because the righteous person is scarcely saved; but it wholly rejects those weighed down and spread out by the cares and pleasures of this age. Nor is it a hindrance to one wishing to enter the gate of life, however much he humbles himself; but it is a dreadful evil if he allows himself to rise even a finger’s breadth, however obliquely, above the threshold: for he will immediately strike against it and, his head shattered, fall down.

Yet we trust in the Lord Jesus that, if anyone in his youth has followed the paths of a more lax life and entangled himself in crimes and wickedness; if, awakened by him who says, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11), he rouses himself amid the snares of death clattering around him; and if, endeavoring to return to the paths of a stricter life, he examines his conscience with anxious and careful scrutiny not once but often—indeed, throughout the whole course of his life—and purely confesses whatever he finds in it; and if furthermore, confessing to God in prayer with the grief and tears of repentance both the sins he remembers and those which perhaps he does not remember, he continually humbles himself for them, he will not lack the fruit of repentance. But, as the Apostle says, “he who does not know shall not be known” (1 Cor. 14); so certainly, if anyone refuses to seek, in proportion to the multitude of his iniquities, the multitude of the Lord’s mercies, mercy will, as we deservedly fear, forget him; and he, whoever he may be, will bear a most severe judgment both for those sins he remembers and for those which perhaps he does not remember.

> [Note: Col. 1195D. That error of childhood, if it was to keep the woman liable, must have been committed with some awareness or scruple of the grave crime [Col. 1196D], and must have presented itself to her adult mind; otherwise she would have obtained pardon for it through general contrition.]

## Final Recapitulation of What Is Contained in This Volume

Having completed what we considered necessary to write concerning the beginning of the Cistercian Order, and likewise concerning the venerable men conspicuous in every form of religious life who flourished at Cîteaux and Clairvaux, together also with examples which, because of the similarity of the subject, we have inserted, as I think not inappropriately, in suitable places near the end, we request this return of favor from our reader: that, if he finds anything in this little work by which he feels himself kindled to love of virtues, hatred of vices, and fervor of holy devotion, he may give thanks to God, without whom nothing good is done, and to the Fathers through whose industry these things have come to our knowledge [Col. 1197C]; and that he may deign to grant us, by whose no small labor they were compiled and formed into one body, the assistance of pious prayer.

For we have not written these things as authors of some new work; rather, as we stated in the preface to this volume [Col. 1198A], we have gathered into one, for a clearer knowledge of events and greater benefit to readers, what we found scattered in writings by diligent Fathers. We have nevertheless taken care to weave into the continuation a few chapters which we learned by reliable report from devout and trustworthy persons—thus preparing food for the sons of the prophets by cutting up and boiling herbs gathered in the field of the ancient Fathers, while judging it a crime to cut false colocynths, like deadly hellebore, into the vegetables.

Consideration of a twofold purpose moved us to undertake this labor. First, we wished to give our brothers, who profess our sacred Order in more remote parts of the world and embrace the holy house of Cîteaux as the head and mother of us all, and likewise the holy house of Clairvaux more dearly because of blessed Bernard, certain knowledge of the beginning of our Order; and to reveal for their edification how lofty and how most worthy of imitation was the life led by the first Fathers of each house [Col. 1198B]. Secondly, we wished to remove an occasion for calumny from the monks of the Black Order, who disparage our Order before laypeople and those ignorant of the facts, saying that it began in presumption and that our Fathers who first departed from Molesme went forth without their abbot’s permission. How false this is, the opening portions of this volume testify most fully.

Far be it that presumption—the mother of ruin and stepmother of stability—had any part in the religious purpose of these holy men! Far be it that the voluntary sacrifice of God’s servants should not have been full of reason and divine authority, by which, sweating under many labors and hardships, they did not hesitate to offer themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, upon the altar of the daily cross, so that, with God’s aid, they might restore the purity of the monastic Order, rescued from the filth of laxity and the abyss of transgression, by their own labor and industry, for the salvation of many, to the ancient state of sacred religion [Col. 1198C]! The leader and standard-bearer of these most valiant athletes of Christ was the lord Stephen of blessed memory, whom we have mentioned above, etc. For the remainder, see above in the First Life of St Bernard, book VII, col. 449.

## The Noble Lineage of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, Vindicated

Also included are minor works by Odo of Deuil, John the Hermit, Herbert, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, and several other writers concerning the history of the twelfth century after Christ, edited and prepared by Pierre-François Chifflet, priest of the Society of Jesus.  
(Dijon: presses of Philibert Chavance, 1660, quarto.)

[Col. 1199]

## To the Most Reverend Father and Lord, Dom Peter Henry, Most Worthy Abbot of Clairvaux

There are many things, most reverend sir, which claim this little work for you alone above all others. First, there is that almost proverbial law of the Wise Man: “To the place whence the rivers flow, thither they return, that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1:7). From the rich storehouse of the library of Clairvaux I formerly received from your predecessor of blessed memory, Claude l’Argentier, Odo of Deuil, Herbert, Archbishop of Torres, John the Hermit, and indeed all the best things in this volume. These same things ought now to be restored by me to you with better right: for he brought it about that they should come to me, while you have also brought it about that they should be made public through me.

Further, the works contained here not only came forth from your Clairvaux, but especially illustrate it, and teach how many “mountains this splendid valley,” to allude to Sidonius, “has sent into heaven.”

> [Note: Col. 1199. In *Eucharisticus*, addressed to Faustus.]

Which of your ascetics would not be set aflame by these examples, when he reads here of the holiness of life of his ancient Fathers, their familiar intercourse with God and the heavenly powers, the confidence of the dying, their exultation and triumphs as they fly in a straight course from their beds to the eternal dwelling-places of the blessed? Those who owe you this favor will be those who see these histories, worthy of cedarwood and everlasting memorials, emerge from the dust and darkness of moths into open light.

Why say more? This book contains in particular marvelous things concerning St Bernard. To whom then should it be dedicated, if not to you, who not only bear the title of abbot of Clairvaux but also fully “fill the measure of so great a name—which is the chief point”? I speak historically: there is no trope here, no exaggeration. From your first novitiate, tested through all the ranks of regular offices, you so discharged the duties of these positions and so shone before your brethren that they especially desired you as their common Father: one in whose bosom they might rest, by whose counsels they might be governed, and by whose way and moderation of life they might be stirred to better things. Permit me to say to you what is prompted not by a desire to flatter, but by love of what is fair, good, and true.

Two qualities above all may be admired in the great Bernard, whose seat you occupy. On the one hand, his fatherly affection toward his own, and that *philanthrōpia* [love of humankind], as it is called, and graciousness in conversation; on the other, zeal and vigor of spirit in rebuking vices, and especially in assailing rebels against the Church. Those who know you well love these same qualities in you. Your own boast that they are so loved and cherished by you, as sons by the best of parents. You are always such in the conduct of affairs that the courtesy in you, seasoned with gravity, strikes every eye. Nor would I say that, when the matter demands it, you lack the sting of severity.

I shall relate what happened at Clairvaux nearly two years ago, and what I myself learned from eyewitnesses. Several important men reclined at your table, and the company of guests was, as it were, a group of twelve. One guest among them, a young man of distinguished family, was provoked by the conversation to reveal the venom of his mind. He was, they say, of the condemned Jansenist party, and among them more than ordinarily unrestrained. Thus, in blind fury, he uttered certain impious things against the relics of the saints and certain irreverent things against our most holy lord Pope Alexander VII. You did not tolerate the insolence of this presumptuous man. Rising to your feet, you commanded him to be silent, sharply rebuked his rash audacity, and threatened that, unless he stopped, he would immediately be expelled by you from the dining room and house in disgrace. Your reproof benefited the young man. As though struck from heaven, he suddenly fell silent. You then declared in a serious address your own convictions concerning the sacred things and mysteries of our religion, and your profound reverence for the Roman pontiffs; and you impressed those same convictions upon your guests and, through them, upon very many others [Col. 1201].

Proceed in these pursuits, most reverend abbot. Thus you will continue to represent Bernard, whom you represent in office, also in conduct. Thus, after this life well and happily spent—which I pray may be long—you will be added as a new star to him and to your other predecessors already received into heaven. This I desire; this I vow.

Dijon, 2 February, in the year of the Christian era 1660.

Rev. Fr. T.

Your most devoted servant, Pierre-François Chifflet, priest of the Society of Jesus.

[Col. 1201]

## Preface to the Seven Books of Odo of Deuil on the Departure of Louis VII, King of the Franks, Surnamed the Younger, for the East

1. Deuil—commonly called Devil—is a village in the district of Paris, made famous by the martyrdom of St Eugenius, first bishop of Toledo. From it this Odo, a monk of Saint-Denis, both derived his origin and took his name. He writes concerning the king’s journey to his abbot Suger, left as administrator of the Frankish kingdom. Odo himself was the king’s travelling companion, his chaplain and confidant, almost continually attached to the king’s side, acquainted not only with his deeds but also a participant in his counsels.

That pilgrimage occupied two full years. Odo explained the course and varied fortunes of the first year more accurately than any other writer. He writes, moreover, from the same place from which the king himself wrote to Suger on the same subject: namely, Antioch in Syria, which they reached after suffering many hardships, on 19 March 1148, a Friday within the third week of Lent. We have therefore appended the king’s letter to this narrative, so that each may shed light upon the other. What the king conveys to Suger in scarcely a whole page, Odo expounds to him in seven books; and these books, long desired and eagerly sought, we now at last publish from a Clairvaux manuscript.

He begins with the assembly of bishops and magnates at Bourges on Christmas Day, which was the beginning of the Dionysian year 1146. There Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, after speaking at length on the devastation of Rohes or Edessa and the intolerable oppression of Christians by the Turks, moved the minds of all to bring assistance. Further, we read in a Cistercian manuscript chronicle, in Robert of Torigni, and in several others, that King Louis undertook this pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulchre in fulfillment of a vow, remorseful because he had burned the church of the castle of Vitry with the 1,300 persons of the mixed multitude who had taken refuge in it enclosed within. An ancient chronicle of St Peter of Châlons assigns this crime of the king to the year 1142.

Whatever the case, for that expedition the coming Easter—31 March—was appointed for taking up the cross according to custom; and the place was the castle of Vézelay, famed for the former relics of Blessed Mary Magdalene and for the benefactions of Count Gerard and his wife Bertha. There, an immense people, fired by the king’s example and the preaching of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, vowed themselves for the pilgrimage in the following year. This plan was highly approved by Pope Eugenius III. Meanwhile, an assembly was appointed at Étampes for *Circumdederunt me*, that is, Septuagesima Sunday, which in that year 1147 fell on 16 February. There the vows of the holy military service were confirmed, and the inspection of the whole army was ordered for Metz on the Wednesday after Pentecost. The Rhine was crossed at Worms, the Danube at Regensburg; thence the route ran through Bavaria, Hungary, and Bulgaria into the dominions of Manuel Comnenus, emperor of the Greeks.

Forgetting the faith pledged to the Latin Christians, Manuel secretly made an alliance with the Turks against them. Under the pretext of friendship he gave guides who led not only the flourishing French army but also that of Emperor Conrad of Germany through trackless forests and craggy mountains; they were then exposed to Turkish ambushes and stripped of provisions, baggage, horses, arms, and men, almost reduced to nothing. Odo himself, an eyewitness, sets this tragedy before his Suger almost as though before his eyes. The world was astonished that the great preparations and endeavors of the two most powerful kings should have come to nothing within a few months. Nor were there lacking those who then devised a serious calumny against Bernard, the instigator of this war, because—such is the folly of the crowd—they judged counsels by their outcomes. But the evident holiness of the man sufficiently cleared him, and divine power itself supported his apostolic zeal by many signs and miracles.

Odo wrote to Suger with the intention that Suger, just as he had written the life and deeds of Louis the Elder, surnamed the Fat, might likewise commend to posterity the history of his son Louis the Younger. But Suger’s death intervened before it could appear complete: he died on 13 January 1152, in the Dionysian era. Odo of Deuil, elected as his successor, governed the monastery of Saint-Denis as abbot for eighteen years. From the published preface to the *Deeds of Louis VII*, which end with the divorce of that king and his wife Eleanor, I think I perceive that these were Suger’s work, or at least begun by him, and subsequently continued and at times interpolated either by Odo or by some other, later writer.

[Col. 1203]

## The Topical and Chronological Particulars of This Itinerary

1. At Christmas, and thus on the very first day of the Dionysian year 1146, at Bourges, in an assembly of bishops and magnates, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, delivered an address on the devastation of Rohes, or Edessa, and the oppression of Eastern Christians by the Turks. An assembly concerning this affair was appointed at Vézelay for the following Easter.

2. On Easter Day, 31 March of that same year 1146, at the preaching of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, an expedition to the Holy Land was resolved upon at Vézelay. Crosses were first taken up by King Louis the Younger and his wife Queen Eleanor, then by countless others following their example. A full year was granted for military preparations.

3. In 1147, at the king’s command, bishops and leading men of the kingdom were summoned to Étampes for *Circumdederunt me*, that is, Septuagesima Sunday, which was 16 February. The route through Constantinople was chosen. Those who would administer the kingdom while the king was abroad were appointed: Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, together with Count William of Nevers. But not long afterward, William withdrew to the Charterhouse, where he took the monastic habit in fulfillment of a vow. A gathering of the forces and an inspection of the army were ordered at Metz for the approaching Pentecost.

4. Shortly afterward, Pope Eugenius III arrived from Rome and celebrated Easter, 20 April, at Saint-Denis. There the king received from his hand the royal banner, along with the wallet and blessing. Departure was appointed for the Wednesday after Pentecost. Samson, archbishop of Rheims, and Count Ralph of Vermandois were substituted for Count William of Nevers as governors of the kingdom.

5. The king came by Verdun to Metz for Pentecost. A few days later the whole army assembled there; it was led onward and reached Worms on the feast day of the apostles Peter and Paul, 29 June.

6. After crossing the Rhine at Worms, they made for Würzburg, or Herbipolis, by a journey of three days, and thence, at the same distance, to Regensburg, where the army was carried across the Danube.

7. From Regensburg, by following the Danube, they came in three days likewise to Passau. From there they reached the New City, or Neuburg, in approximately five days. From Neuburg to the gates of Hungary was a journey of no more than one day.

8. They crossed Hungary in fifteen days. Then, at the entrance to Bogaria, or Bulgaria, was Bogarian Belgrade, as it is customarily called in order to distinguish it from the Hungarian city of the same name.

9. Brundusium, a poor little city, is only one day’s journey from Belgrade. From Brundusium they reached, on the fifth day, a Greek city named Niš.

10. From Niš it was four days to Hesternit, and four more thence to Philippopolis. Already at Philippopolis, Alvisus, bishop of Arras, had died on 6 September, having been sent ahead by King Louis as ambassador to the emperor of the Greeks at Constantinople.

11. From Philippopolis to Adrianople was four days’ journey; from Adrianople to Constantinople, five.

12. At Constantinople King Louis celebrated the feast of St Denis with the Greeks.

13. When the king had left Constantinople for Romania, following his army, the sun was darkened in the middle of its disk on Sunday, 26 October. This eclipse was made notable by the consecration of the basilica of St Stephen at Châlons, together with its high altar, by Pope Eugenius III and bishops and cardinals then present, in solemn rite on that very day and hour. We learned this from the ancient records of that church, a copy of which we provide for the reader at the end of this little work.

14. Meanwhile, the German army, which had taken the shortest but most dangerous road from Constantinople toward Antioch by Iconium, was almost destroyed by Greek treachery and Turkish arms. Their emperor Conrad, having lost thirty thousand of his soldiers, came to King Louis seeking help and consolation, and held a conference with him near the beginning of November at Lake Nicaea, beside the castle of Lupadion.

15. After the feast of St Martin, the king came to the castle of Esseron, thence to Demetrias, and finally to Ephesus, leaving Smyrna and Pergamum to his left. In the Ephesian valley, also called Decervion, he celebrated Christmas and several following feast days.

16. From there they proceeded toward Laodicea through the fords of the Maeander River. At these fords the Franks inflicted a great slaughter upon the Turks, though not without loss to themselves; for there, among others, Milo of Nogent drowned in the waters.

17. On the third following day they reached Laodicea. From there the French army was led into the mountains, hemmed in by the ambushes alike of Turks and Greeks, and in January 1148 a great part of it perished. The remnants of the forces celebrated the Purification of Blessed Mary at Sattalia, a city remembered by the ancients as Attalia (Acts 14:24).

18. Then, having decided to seek Antioch by sea, they waited five weeks for favorable winds; the voyage then took three weeks, and they reached Antioch on Friday after mid-Lent, 19 March. From there both King Louis and Odo of Deuil sent letters to Abbot Suger.

[Col. 1203]

## Letter of Louis VII, King of the Franks, Surnamed the Younger, to Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis and Administrator of the Kingdom

Written at Antioch in Syria, when the king had reached it by ship, in 1148, on Friday after mid-Lent, 19 March.

(It is number 39 among the published letters of Suger.—See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, col. 1365, under Suger.)

[Col. 1205]

## The Work of Odo of Deuil, Who Was Present, on the Departure of Louis VII, King of the Franks, Surnamed the Younger, for the East, Divided into Seven Books

### Letter of Odo to His Venerable Abbot Suger

[Col. 1205A] To Suger, venerable abbot of the Church of Blessed Denis, Odo of Deuil, least of his monks: greetings.

The desire lies within me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish it: namely, to set down for you some suitable account of the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, which you may commit with your pen to everlasting remembrance. For I am still held in the contest of the journey, hindered both by inexperience and by labor. Yet we must sometimes attempt even what we cannot do, so that by our effort we may encourage valiant men to undertake what we desire but cannot accomplish.

For I, having abundantly experienced the kindnesses of the glorious King Louis on the journey to the Holy Sepulchre and having adhered more closely to his familiarity, possess indeed the desire to return thanks, but lack the strength to bring it to effect. Let this be credited to Blessed Denis [Col. 1205B], for whose love the king did this, and to you, because he received your monk in your stead. You, however, owe him much on your own account: for he especially loved you in his kingdom and, led by zeal for the propagation of the faith, entrusted the kingdom to you when he left it for a time. Even there, however, he watched over his own affairs, trusting them to your tested fidelity and singular wisdom.

You wrote the deeds of his father; but it would be a fault to defraud posterity of knowledge of the son, whose every age is a model of virtue [Col. 1206A]. For when he began to reign, almost a boy, the glory of the world was not for him a source of pleasure, but gave growth and splendor to his virtues. Therefore, if someone begins to describe his deeds only from the Jerusalem journey, he will cut away from future kings a very great part of the example set before them by God. For we admire more in the boy Nicholas his Wednesdays and Fridays without nursing and his other early indications than the wonderful holiness of his episcopate.

Therefore you, to whom reverence is rightly due for writing of the son, since you first brought the father to light by your pen, and who rightly owe this service, having enjoyed the more abundant favor of both, begin from childhood, where virtue began to arise. You know this better, because, like a foster-father, you learned it more intimately. But I, though hampered in expression and not in knowledge of the events accomplished on the journey to the Holy Sepulchre—for, like his chaplain, I was often present when he rose and when he lay down—will, as though stammering, offer you a summary of the truth, to be embellished by literary eloquence [Col. 1206B].

Nor should you be reluctant to perform what you owe because you hear that several people claim this task. Rather, take pleasure in it if one who has deserved the praise of all receives the praises of many.

## First Book

[Col. 1205C] In the year 1146 of the Incarnate Word, the glorious Louis, king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, son of King Louis, being twenty-five years old, undertook at Vézelay, at Easter, to follow Christ by bearing his cross, so that he might be worthy of Christ [Col. 1206C]. On the preceding Christmas, when that same devout king held court at Bourges, having deliberately summoned bishops and magnates of the kingdom to his court more generally than usual [Col. 1207A], he first disclosed to them the secret of his heart.

Then the religious bishop of Langres spoke in a manner worthy of a bishop concerning the devastation of Rohes, called by its ancient name Edessa, the oppression of Christians, and the insolence of the pagans; and from this mournful subject he stirred up much weeping, urging all to serve with their king in bringing aid to the Christians on behalf of the King of all. There burned and shone in the king zeal for the faith, contempt for pleasure and temporal glory—an example surpassing every speech. Yet what the bishop sowed in words and the king by example, they did not reap immediately. Another day was therefore appointed at Vézelay, at Easter, when all might assemble unanimously in the Passion of the Lord and, at the Resurrection, those whom heaven inspired might exalt the glory of the cross [Col. 1207B].

Meanwhile, ever watchful in his undertaking, the king sent envoys to Rome to Pope Eugenius concerning this matter. They were gladly received and gladly sent back, carrying letters sweeter than all honey. These imposed obedience upon the king, moderation in arms and clothing upon those taking up Christ’s sweet yoke, promised remission of all sins and protection for their children and wives, and contained certain other matters which seemed useful to the holy care and prudent judgment of the supreme pontiff. Eugenius himself desired to be personally the first to set his hand to so holy a work, but was prevented by the tyranny of the Romans. He therefore entrusted this responsibility to Bernard, holy abbot of Clairvaux.

At last the day desired by the king arrived [Col. 1207C]. The abbot, fortified by apostolic authority and his own sanctity, was present, as were the immense multitude of those summoned, at the same place and time. The king therefore received the emblem of the cross sent to him by the supreme pontiff, and many nobles with him. Since there was no place in the castle able to contain so great a crowd, a wooden platform was erected for the abbot outside in the field, so that he might speak from on high to those standing around. He mounted it with the king adorned with the cross. And when the heavenly instrument had, in its accustomed manner, poured forth the dew of the divine word, people everywhere began crying out, “Crosses! Crosses!” and demanding crosses. When he had scattered rather than distributed the bundle prepared for them, he was compelled to tear his own garments into crosses and scatter them. He labored at this for as long as he remained in the town [Col. 1207D].

I refrain from writing of the miracles which then occurred there and by which it seemed that this undertaking pleased the Lord, lest, if I write a few, people should not believe that more occurred; or, if I write many, I might seem to have omitted material. At last, after an edict that they should set out a year later, all returned joyfully to their homes.

The abbot, concealing beneath a slight and almost lifeless body a vigorous spirit, flies everywhere preaching, and in a short time those bearing the cross were multiplied beyond number. The king, as though now having found his joy in the propagation of the faith and in the hope of an abundant future army, sent envoys to King Roger in Apulia. He wrote back favorably on every point. Moreover, he sent back noble men who promised that his kingdom would supply provisions, ships, and every necessity, and that either he himself or his son would accompany the expedition [Col. 1208A].

The king also sent others to the emperor of Constantinople, whose name I do not know, because it is not written in the book of life. This man drew up a long scroll of extravagant flattery and, calling our king holy, friend, and brother, promised many things which he did not fulfill in deed. But of this elsewhere. The king also sought assurances from the kings of Germany and Hungary concerning markets and passage; and received their envoys and letters according to his wish. Many dukes and counts of those regions, stirred by his example, likewise wrote that they would join him on the expedition. Thus everything proceeded at his command.

Meanwhile rumor flies, crosses the sea to England, and penetrates the recesses of other islands. Seafarers prepare ships, intending to go with the king by sea. But while the king, reviewing all matters, arranged the condition of the realm and secured peace for his subjects in time to come, envoys from every quarter assembled at Paris [Col. 1208B]. When he returned, they all appeared together; they presented the solemn charters of emperors and dukes and promised in word and writing whatever he had asked. The king could choose whom to trust and in whom to place his confidence. But it was his custom that those who shared his counsels should also share his labor. He therefore summoned them all to Étampes at *Circumdederunt me*, that they might jointly choose what they would jointly endure.

As they were eager in devising, so would that they had been prudent in choosing! For when an assembly, as glorious as it was great, of bishops and nobles had gathered at the appointed place and time, the aforesaid abbot—worthy both of being mentioned and praised—also appeared, bringing news [Col. 1208C] which made the assembly rejoice on both accounts. For he came from Germany, and had added that king and the magnates of his kingdom to the warfare of Christ’s cross. Then letters from various regions were read, envoys heard, and these proceedings extended until evening. They spent the day in joy and postponed what remained until the next day.

The next day was happier than it was fortunate. Those present at the assembly stated, as they knew from reading and experience, that the Greeks were deceitful. Yet the king and his men, who rightly feared the strength of no peoples, would that they had feared their treachery! But because there is no counsel or prudence against God, they chose the route through Greece in order to die. Thus the second day ended—not auspiciously.

[Col. 1208D] Then the noble envoys of King Roger departed in confusion, sufficiently making known by their sorrowful bearing their lord’s feelings, and warning us of Greek treachery, which we afterward experienced. Nor is it strange that King Roger, powerful and wise, desired the king’s company if he loved the Franks, being himself descended from our regions. At last, by the grace of the Trinity, the third day came round; and the assembly, having first invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit—would that they had likewise invoked it on the preceding day!—and then heard a spiritual discourse from the holy abbot, proceeded to discuss the guardianship of the kingdom.

The king, according to his custom, restraining his power under the fear of God, gave the prelates of the Church and the magnates of the kingdom freedom to choose [Col. 1209A]. They went to deliberate, and after a short while, having chosen what was best, the holy abbot went before them as they returned and said: “Behold, here are two swords. It is enough.” He meant you, Father Suger, and the count of Nevers. This greatly pleased everyone—if only it had pleased the count himself as well. But he had dedicated himself to the Charterhouse, a resolution which he soon put into effect, and neither the prolonged prayers of the king nor of all others could recall him. Thus the burden of both offices was finally placed upon you alone; you bore it with unshaken peace and, through its lightness, perceived it to be Christ’s burden.

Meanwhile, a day was appointed at Pentecost for those who were to depart, and at Metz for the forces to gather there from every quarter for the glorious and humble prince they longed for. After this, lest anything of blessing or grace be lacking, Eugenius, Roman pontiff, came and celebrated the Lord’s Easter in the church of Blessed Denis with fitting honor. Many from many regions flocked to see both marvels: the king and the apostolic pope as pilgrims [Col. 1209B]. The pope confirmed what had been well arranged, set many disorders in order, and awaited the king’s departure. That year the appointed departure fell on the Wednesday after Pentecost. Thus all conspicuous things befell the king favorably.

When he sought from Blessed Denis the banner and permission to depart—such had always been the custom of victorious kings—the sight of him stirred all to very great weeping, and he received the blessing born from the deepest affection of all. As he went onward, he performed an act praiseworthy, though imitable by few and perhaps by none of his rank. For after first visiting every religious community in Paris, he finally went outside the city to the establishments of the lepers. There I certainly saw him attend with only two witnesses and exclude the whole remaining multitude of his attendants for a long time [Col. 1210A].

Meanwhile his mother, his wife, and countless others hastened ahead to Saint-Denis. When he afterward arrived, he found the pope, the abbot, and the monks of the church assembled. Then, prostrate most humbly upon the ground, he venerated his patron. The pope and the abbot opened the little golden door and drew out somewhat the silver shrine, so that, having kissed and seen him whom his soul loved, the king might become more eager. Then, receiving from the altar the banner, the wallet, and the blessing from the supreme pontiff, he withdrew into the monks’ dormitory away from the crowd. For the press of people, and his mother and wife, who amid tears and emotion were almost breathing their last, did not permit delay [Col. 1210B]. But to wish to describe the grief and lamentation there would be as foolish as it would be impossible.

That day, retaining only a few of his own men, he ate with the brothers in the refectory; afterward, having kissed them all, he departed, accompanied by the prayers and tears of everyone.

## Second Book

[Col. 1209C] Lengthy discourse is always wearisome to one occupied with many matters. Therefore I fear that my account has run on too diffusely without pause. But grant me, I beg you, Father, this fault. I was present at joyful events; writing down the names of my homeland and recalling its affairs, I lingered without weariness over what I had joyfully seen. Pleasant things do not soon bring fatigue. But now, girding myself for hardships under a new beginning, I am about to enter foreign regions—in speech as we did in deed—and I shall henceforth bring the laborious matters to an end more quickly.

After the glorious king had departed from the church of Saint-Denis, nothing memorable was done in his kingdom—unless perhaps you wish it recorded that, in the care of the realm, he gave you the archbishop of Rheims as a colleague. Yet I do not know whether Count Ralph, since he was then excommunicated, ought to be excluded from the fellowship of our narrative [Col. 1209D]: lest the secular sword be lacking to you two, he was added as a third, so that a threefold cord might not easily be broken (Eccl. 4).

Let us therefore turn our pen to Metz, since it was there that we assembled. There the king, although by right of lordship he found nothing his own, nevertheless found everyone subject to him by favour, as he had already done at Verdun, almost as though they were servants. Having pitched his tents outside the city, he awaited the incoming army for a few days and established measures necessary for peace and other public benefits. The princes confirmed these by oaths and pledges; but because they themselves did not keep them well, neither have I retained them.

[Col. 1210C] From there he sent ahead to Worms prudent and religious men: Alwis, bishop of Arras, and Leo, abbot of Saint-Bertin, to prepare on the Rhine, which flows past that place, shipping for the army that followed. They accomplished this excellently, gathering so great a multitude of vessels from every direction that no bridge was needed. The clergy and people of that city received the king very solemnly on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. Here we first experienced the foolish arrogance of our people.

For the soldiers crossed over and, having found a sufficiently broad expanse of meadowland, the lord king chose to wait for the venerable Arnulf, bishop of Luxeuil, with his Normans and Englishmen. Provisions flowed to us by river from the city, and there was continual traffic of our own people and the inhabitants. [Col. 1210D] At last a quarrel arose. The pilgrims threw boatmen into the river. Seeing this, the citizens ran to arms and, after some had been wounded, immediately killed one man. The pilgrims were disturbed by this crime; the poor cried out “Fire!”—a calamity for the citizens, but also for certain of our own people, namely wealthy merchants and money-changers. Yet, by God’s will, the wiser men of both parties restrained the foolish men of both parties. The citizens nevertheless remained afraid; withdrawing the vessels from both banks, they removed the supplies. But the religious bishop of Abbeville, having with difficulty secured a vessel, [Col. 1211A] crossed with certain barons, calmed the crowd, and promised the citizens security. Afterwards the ships were brought back; traffic resumed as usual, and necessities were supplied to us.

Here was first proved the evil omen that had been feared concerning the people. Thereafter many of the multitude separated themselves from us through the Alps, because everything was bought at a higher price because of the crowd. The king also moved camp, having sent ahead to Regensburg the venerable bishop of Arras, together with the chancellor and the abbot of Saint-Bertin, on account of envoys from the emperor of Constantinople, who had been awaiting the king there for many days.

At that city all crossed the Danube by an excellent bridge and found an abundant multitude of ships, which carried our baggage and a great many people [Col. 1211B] as far as Bulgaria. Some even loaded two-horse and four-horse wagons onto ships, to compensate for the former loss in the wildernesses of Bulgaria. But they proved more useful in hope than in fact, both before and afterwards. We say these things for the caution of posterity. For when there was a very great multitude of four-horse wagons, if one was obstructed, the delay was equal for all; but if they found several roads, all sometimes blocked them at once, and pack animals, avoiding their obstruction, very often encountered a more serious one. From this came frequent deaths of horses and many complaints about short daily marches.

The clergy and people of this city received the king very royally. But since this cannot be repeated as often as they freely demonstrated the devotion of their hearts, it must be said once for all that every town, castle, and city as far as Constantinople rendered him royal honour—more or less, but all according to their means. Their will was equal, but I say “more or less” because their ability was not equal. Therefore, after the tents had been pitched and the king lodged, the emperor’s envoys, summoned, came. Having greeted him and performed their ceremonial reverences, they stood awaiting an answer; for they would not sit unless commanded. After the command, placing the small seats they had brought with them, they sat down.

[Col. 1211D] There we observed what we later learned to be a Greek custom: when their lords are seated, all their retainers alike stand. You might see young men standing motionless, heads bowed, their eyes raised toward their own lords, ready in silence to obey them by a mere nod. They do not wear cloaks, but rich men are dressed in silk garments, short and closed all round; with tight sleeves, unencumbered, they always walk like fighters. The poor dress themselves in the same fashion, apart from the cost. I ought not, and partly cannot, fully translate their documents. Their first and largest portion sought favour with such absurd humility that its excessively affected words—because they did not arise from genuine feeling—would, I should say, disgrace not only an emperor but even an actor. It is therefore shameful [20] to be detained by such things when proceeding to others. For although the French may be flatterers, even if they wished, they cannot equal the Greeks.

The king, though with embarrassment, first tolerated the whole being explained, but did not know from what source it proceeded. [Col. 1212A] At last, when envoys in Greece came to him frequently and always began with such a preamble, he could scarcely endure it. The religious and high-spirited Godfrey, bishop of Langres, once sympathizing with the king and unable to bear the delay of narrator and interpreter, said: “Brothers, do not repeat so frequently his glory, majesty, wisdom, and religion. He knows himself, and we know him well; but state more swiftly and freely what you want.”

Yet even among certain laymen this proverb was always known:

> “I fear the Danaans, even when they bring gifts.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.49

The final portion of the documents, which concerned the matter at hand, contained two demands: namely, that the king should offer the emperor no city or castle from his own realm; indeed, that he should restore to him anything belonging by right to the emperor if he expelled the Turks from it; and that this should be confirmed by oaths of the nobles. The first seemed sufficiently reasonable to our wise men; but concerning the second the legal question was long debated. Some said: “He may claim from the Turks, by price, legal title, or force, what may belong to him by right. But why ought he not to claim it from us if he sees that we possess it on some occasion?” Others said that the territory in question ought to be named, lest disputes might later arise from an indefinite proposal.

[Col. 1212C] Meanwhile several days passed, and the Greeks alleged delays, fearing, as they said, that the emperor, taking precautions for himself, would burn the fodder and destroy the fortifications. “For,” they said, “he has declared that he will do this if we delay—as though he knew from this that you do not come peacefully. And if he does so, afterwards you will not find necessities in full on the route, even if he wishes it.”

At last certain men on the king’s side swore concerning the security of his realm; and the Greeks, on behalf of their emperor, confirmed by a similar oath that they would provide a suitable market, fair exchange, and other things judged useful for our people. What could not be settled between them they reserved for the personal meeting of the kings. After this, one of them, named Demetrius, departed in haste; another, called Maurus, remained with us. Then Alwis of Arras, Chancellor Bartholomew, Archembald of Bourbon, and certain others were chosen to be sent ahead with Maurus to Constantinople—for among other things the letters required this. They therefore proceeded more quickly, having undertaken the embassy; the king followed more slowly, as the crowded host allowed.

In what we write, descriptions of notable deeds serve as examples; names of cities serve for guidance on the route; and the character of regions serves for travellers’ caution. For travellers to the Holy Sepulchre will never be lacking, and, if it please God, they will be more cautious because of our experiences.

Thus Metz, Worms, Würzburg, Regensburg, and Passau are very wealthy cities, each three days’ march from the next. From the last named there are five days’ march to Neustadt; from there, one to the gates of Hungary. The intervening country is wooded, and unless provisions are brought from the cities it cannot supply an army [Col. 1213A] with food; nevertheless, it abounds in streams, springs, and meadows. When I crossed this region, it seemed rough to me because of its mountains; now, by comparison with Romania, I judge it flat.

On this side Hungary is bounded by muddy water; on the other it is separated from Bulgaria by a clear river. In its midst it has the river Drava, which, like a roof, has one bank sloping and the other steep; hence even slight rain makes it overflow, and, aided by neighbouring marshes, it submerges places at some distance as well. We heard that it had suddenly flooded many Germans who had preceded us; but where their camp had been, we could scarcely ford it. There we had small and few boats; consequently the horses had to swim. Though they found an easy entrance and a difficult exit, they crossed with labour, [Col. 1213B] but, by God’s will, without loss.

All the other water of this land consists of lakes, marshes, and springs—if indeed they are springs—which travellers make by digging the earth a little, even in summer; except for the Danube, which flows fairly straight through it and carries by ship the riches of many lands to the noble city of Esztergom.

This land is so rich in pasture that Julius Caesar’s pastures are said to have been there. There, as we desired, we had both market and exchange. It extends for fifteen days’ march. Then, at the entrance to Bulgaria, rises a fortress called Belgrade of Bulgaria, in comparison with a city of the same name in Hungary. From there, one day’s march away, with a certain river intervening, is the rather poor city of Brundusium. [Col. 1213C] What remains to be said of it is, so to speak, wooded meadowland, or a pasture-bearing wood. It abounds in things that grow spontaneously and is suitable for other produce if it had cultivators. It lies neither flat nor harsh with mountains, but among hills suitable for vines and grain, watered by very clear streams and springs. It lacks rivers, yet from there to Constantinople we needed ships.

At the fifth day’s march stands Niš, the first but small city on this side of Greece. Niš, Hesternit, Philippopolis, and Adrianople are cities four days’ march apart, and from the last to Constantinople there are five days. The intervening land is flat and abounds in villages, castles, and every good thing. Mountains stand right and left, near enough to be visible and far enough away to enclose a broad, rich, and pleasant plain. So much for this.

But we must move forward and backward. Many things offer themselves to be written, but the narrative must not be confused by a multiplicity of events. Causes proceed side by side, but sequence must be preserved in the account. For king and emperor alike have come to my mind at Regensburg. But since the king is my principal subject, I am nevertheless compelled to insert a few shared actions concerning the emperor.

The German preceded our king in place and time. Our king set out at Pentecost; the other at Easter. Our king moved his foot from Saint-Denis; the other from Regensburg. Yet the latter’s earlier passage benefited ours: because there are many rivers in his territory, our king found new bridges over them without his own labour or expense. To tell the truth, he set out very imperially, with a naval equipment and a land army. And rightly, for the Hungarians were then his enemies.

[Col. 1214A] Thus the high-spirited emperor entered Hungary with naval and infantry forces, having an abundant body of soldiers with him in ships, and horses and people beside him on land—as befitted and became a prince. There was a certain man named Boris, who claimed a hereditary right in that kingdom. Concerning this, Stampas had sent letters to our king [24], fully setting forth the complaint and humbly requesting justice. When this Boris came to meet our king, following up his letters, he showed in whom he could place confidence: the emperor. He set out his case to him, promised much—or rather, as we heard, gave much—and received from him hope of obtaining his right.

But the Hungarian king, knowing that he could be conquered more easily with gold than with iron, scattered much money among the Germans and escaped their attack. Boris, disappointed in his empty hope, concealed himself as best he could, waited for the king’s passage, and, for some purpose unknown to me, secretly mixed himself among the French. It is said, however, that the two princes knew this, and that Boris, through the favour of the emperor of Constantinople, whose niece he had as his wife, attached himself to them quite favourably.

[Col. 1214C] Covered and protected by such a veil, he proceeded with the army through Hungary. Meanwhile the Hungarian king, fearing and honouring ours, sought his favour through envoys and gifts, but avoided a meeting by the intervening Danube. He desired an interview with one whom report had commended to him and events had revealed; but, fearing to sail to our bank, he humbly begged the king to deign to come to his own bank.

The king, easily overcome by affection and humility—as was his custom—took certain bishops and dukes with him and complied with his wish. Then, after kisses and embraces, they established peace, confirmed friendship, and arranged that henceforth our pilgrims should pass safely through Hungary. This done, our king dismissed the Hungarian joyfully. Royal gifts followed him: horses, vessels, and clothing. The Hungarian king was still preparing to honour our king and his nobles as far as he could, [Col. 1214D] when he learned that Boris was among the French.

He therefore sent men to present to the king their new covenant of affection and peace, and humbly request that his enemy, who was hiding in the army, be handed over to him. All this happened at night. The king, unaware of the whole deception, did not believe it at all. But at last, as they persistently affirmed and requested it, he consented. They therefore advanced joyfully, more boldly than prudently, for Boris, aroused naked from bed by the uproar of his pursuers, escaped. They returned in confusion.

The fugitive, however, not being foolish, when he had left the tents while making for the river, encountered a groom on an excellent horse. He fought courageously with him for the horse. The groom shouted and resisted, prevailing more by his cry than by strength. Men came together [Col. 1215A] from every direction; they seized Boris as a thief and brought him to the king, beaten, filthy with mud, naked except for his breeches. All took him for a thief. But prostrate before the king, although he did not know our language and the king then had no interpreter, he nevertheless revealed who he was by inserting certain familiar words among barbarous sounds and repeatedly naming himself.

He was immediately clothed honourably and held until the next day. The Hungarian king, who had pitched his tents near us and, having already experienced Boris, feared him, immediately learned what had happened, both because he was nearby and because fear made him watchful. He therefore demanded Boris from the king as from a friend and, as though it were owed by the covenant of friendship, promising in addition much—indeed, things scarcely credible—for this purpose. In like manner he solicited the leading men [Col. 1216A] by entreaties and payment. But he could not extort anything from the king by the persistence of requests or gifts except what the common judgment of wise men had first decided [26].

The king acknowledged him as his friend, but said that he ought not, for that man’s sake, to do anything unbecoming toward a pilgrim. At last the bishops and other nobles were assembled; after the matter had been considered, they judged that a king should keep peace with a king, and preserve the life of a nobleman, though captured: for both would be crimes—to sell a man to death, and without reason to break the compacts of a friend. Therefore the Hungarian king, not trusting our people, withdrew sadly and sought safer and more remote parts of his realm. Our king, treating Boris quite honourably, led him out of Hungary with him.

## Third Book

[Col. 1215]

[Col. 1215B] Up to this point we had been at play, because we had suffered neither losses from human malice nor feared dangers from the cunning of treacherous men. But once we entered Bulgaria, the land of the Greeks, courage endured hardship and judgment found exercise.

As we were about to enter the wilderness, at the poor city of Brundusium we loaded ourselves with provisions, supplied especially by Hungary through the Danube. There was such a multitude of ships there, brought by the Germans, that they would have sufficed the citizens for a long time in building houses and for firewood. Our men took the smaller of these and, crossing the river, brought over necessities from a certain fortress of Hungary not far away.

Here we first encountered copper currency and *stammas*; sorrowfully we gave—or rather lost—five denarii for one of the latter, and a mark for twelve solidi. [Col. 1215C] Behold: at the entry into their land, the Greeks are stained by perjury. For you must now remember what has already been said: namely, that they had sworn on behalf of their emperor to provide our people with a suitable market and exchange.

Thereafter we crossed the wilderness and entered a most beautiful and wealthy country extending without interruption as far as Constantinople. Here wrongs first began to be committed and encountered. For the other regions, which sold us necessary things adequately, found us entirely peaceful. But the Greeks guarded their cities and castles, lowering merchandise down by ropes over the walls; yet food supplied with such delay did not suffice for our multitude. Therefore the pilgrims, unable to endure scarcity amid abundance, obtained necessities for themselves by plunder and robbery.

[Col. 1215D] Some nevertheless considered this to have been the fault of the Germans who preceded us. Since they plundered everything, we found that they had also burned certain suburbs. For Philippopolis, grievous though it is to relate, had outside its walls a noble Latin borough, which supplied necessities abundantly for payment to those arriving. While the Germans were sitting in its taverns, a juggler appeared under an evil omen. Although he did not know their language, he sat down, contributed his share, drank, and after a long bout of gluttony drew out a snake which he had, as if charmed, in his bosom. He placed it upon an earthenware cup set on the ground and, among men whose customs and language he did not know, exhausted himself in other juggler’s tricks.

The Germans, as if they had seen a prodigy, immediately rose in fury, seized the performer, and tore him to pieces. They imputed the crime of one man to all, saying that the Greeks wished to kill them with poison. The city was thrown into commotion by the disturbance in the suburb, and the duke, with a crowd of his men, went out unarmed but hastily to calm the crowd. But the Germans’ eyes, troubled by wine and rage, saw not weapons but movement. Therefore, in anger, they met those running toward them for peace [Col. 1216C], thinking that vengeance for a killing was being demanded of them. The others fled and were received into the city.

Then, taking their bows—for these are their weapons—they went out again, put to flight those who had put them to flight, killed and wounded men, and, having driven all from the suburb, ceased. Many Germans were killed there, especially in their lodgings, and were thrown into pits for their money. Recovering courage and arms, in order to avenge their disgrace and the deaths of others, they returned and burned almost everything outside the walls.

The Germans were also unbearable to our people. For on one occasion some men of our royal host, avoiding the pressure of the multitude and therefore travelling ahead, lodged beside them. Both parties went to market; but the Germans would not allow the French to buy anything until they themselves had first taken enough from it. A quarrel arose—indeed, a squawking; for where one attacks another with loud voice without understanding him, it is squawking. The French, striking and being struck, returned from the market with provisions. But the Germans, because they were numerous and despised the pride of the few Frenchmen, [Col. 1217A] took arms against them and attacked furiously; the French likewise armed themselves and resisted bravely. But God ended that wickedness through the swift arrival of night.

That night their fire could neither be extinguished nor soothed, for at dawn they rose again more fiercely in frenzy. But their wise men, throwing themselves at the knees of the foolish, calmed their madness by humility and reason. Thus the Germans, going ahead, threw everything into disorder, and therefore the Greeks fled our following peaceful host. Nevertheless, gatherings of churches and all the clergy came out from the cities with their icons and other Greek ceremonial display, always receiving the king with fear and due honour.

The duke of Hesternit, the emperor’s kinsman, also remained constantly with the king along the road and caused peace to be kept for the inhabitants and, in part, a market to be supplied for the pilgrims. [Col. 1217B] He served the king very honourably with provisions, retaining little or nothing of them for himself: now he distributed everything among the rich, now among the poor. Accordingly peace was more strictly observed where he was, because there was less need and greater fear.

Many detachments preceded and followed the king, obtaining abundance for themselves either from the market, if they could, or from plunder, because they could do that. At last they came to Philippopolis, where the venerable Alwis, bishop of Arras, while carrying out an embassy to Constantinople, had died in holy confession on the eighth day before the Ides of September [6 September].

Here, after a long illness had become more severe between the feast of Saint-Bertin, whose monk he had been, and the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, tears arose—tears for which he had always had the gift. Calling together his monks and clerics, he said: “Dearest ones, celebrate the feast of Saint-Bertin with due honour; but because I shall not be with you for the solemnity of the Blessed Mary, grant me what favour you can: anticipate that feast, take the books, and solemnly chant the entire service for me.”

[Col. 1217C] They obeyed sorrowfully and chanted the whole service of day and night at greater length. Whenever he heard that distinctive “Ave” or the name of the Virgin, he rose, at the very point of death, with a feeble but devout effort. Afterwards he surrendered his soul to the Virgin, whose memory he then held so devoutly. His body received honourable burial outside the city in the church of Saint George, before the altar [Col. 1217D; 30].

When the king afterwards came to his tomb, he grieved that he had died and, with his bishops and abbots, repeated mournful funeral rites for him. It should also be known that we ourselves certainly saw fever sufferers first sleep beneath the bier and then upon the tomb, and afterwards give thanks to God and to the deceased bishop for their recovery.

Having briefly interrupted these matters, I should like to lead the Germans to Constantinople—indeed, convey them across the strait as well—for the matter must be related in the order in which it happened. They advanced boldly enough but not wisely enough. For, finding wealth everywhere in that land and having no self-restraint in it, their infantrymen who fell behind were killed while drunk, and their unburied corpses defiled everything. Hence, to the French who followed, dead Germans did more harm than armed Greeks.

[Col. 1218A] When they reached Adrianople, they found people preventing their passage to Constantinople, partly by resistance and partly by counsel, asserting that the sea was narrower and the land more fertile at Saint George of Sestos [perhaps Xystos]. But their emperor held in equal contempt those who resisted and those who counselled. Continuing therefore in the direction he had begun, he found about midway a meadow watered by a small river or torrent and bounded by the neighbouring sea. While he spent the night there with tents pitched, rain broke over them—moderate, as we heard, upon them, but in the mountains so overflowing that it carried them away rather than sprinkled them.

For the swollen, swift torrent engulfed and swept away the tents in its path and all that they contained, hurled them into the nearby sea, and drowned many thousands of the Germans. [Col. 1218B] The emperor and the surviving multitude, bearing so great a disaster not without grief but nevertheless as though without loss [31], rose and came to Constantinople, seemingly made bolder by the event.

Before the city lay a spacious and beautiful circuit of walls, enclosing varied game, watercourses, and ponds. There were also certain trenches and hollows, which afforded animals hiding places in place of woods. In that pleasant place certain palaces shone with excessive magnificence; the emperors had built them for their pleasure in the spring season. Into this place of delights, to speak the truth, the German emperor burst, [Col. 1218C] destroying almost everything on every side and taking the Greeks’ pleasures for his own uses before their very eyes.
