The imperial palace, singular in that it rises above the city walls, overlooks this place and delights the gaze of those dwelling in it. Yet if such a spectacle brought astonishment or suppressed pain in the Greek emperor, he requested a meeting with the German through his men. But one feared or refused to enter the city, the other to leave it; and neither moderated his customs or his habitual arrogance for the other.

Meanwhile the king of the French, whose custom it was always to temper royal majesty with humility, earnestly sent word to the German emperor that he should await him on this side of the strait, so that men whose shared purpose had undertaken the same labour might enjoy the same counsel. But the German, hastening on with the ardour with which he had begun, accepted from the Greek emperor a guide for the road—or rather for error and death—and crossed over.

Although I have already written, and it is true, that innumerable men of his army had already died, we nevertheless heard from Greeks who counted the crossing force that he crossed the strait with nine hundred thousand and five hundred and sixty-six [perhaps ninety] men. [Col. 1218D; 32] He then came to Nicomedia, where his followers, after a quarrel arose, created a schism. The emperor made for Iconium; his brother Otto, bishop of Freising, and many nobles with him held to the coast. We shall recount their mournful and swift reverses in their proper place and time; but let us return for the moment to our own people.

The venerable bishop of Metz, his brother Renald, count of Monçon, and the bishop of Toul, unable to endure the Germans, were awaiting the arrival of the peaceful prince with a considerable army. But the Greeks forced them to cross the strait by whatever injuries they could inflict, especially by withholding the market, saying that they had confirmed an agreement with their emperor that they would allow none of the Germans to remain there.

[Col. 1219A] The royal envoys who were still staying in the city, hearing this and believing it true, ended the dispute by this agreement: that the Germans should cross and, awaiting the others, should have a suitable market on the far side. This having been done, a few Frenchmen who had arrived later remained behind. When they urged and tried to compel the others to follow, but could not obtain it, the Greeks sent against them an immense multitude of Pechenegs and Cumans. These had also killed many of our people by ambushes in the wildernesses of Bulgaria.

The French climbed a certain mound of earth and fenced themselves in with two-horse and four-horse wagons; they resisted manfully. There our people first suffered want, because they had no market and their attackers did not cease. In the city, although the royal envoys learned this only late, they approached the emperor in great agitation. Having learned of the treacherous crime, they complained about those who had crossed on the previous day, and especially about those Christians who were being attacked by unbelievers in the city.

Then the emperor, as if he could not otherwise restrain the Pechenegs [33], ordered our people to come closer and lodge below him, at the foot of the palace, and ordered a market to be provided.

[Col. 1219C] On hearing the message, they left their makeshift enclosure and proceeded, as though fearing nothing, to the place they had been ordered to go. But behold: some Pechenegs pursued them, while others tried to occupy their position. Swiftly and bravely returning, they stoutly resisted both the pursuers and those occupying their position. There many infantrymen, throwing away some of their possessions so that they might flee more easily, lost them.

Then certain envoys, more fiercely inflamed—namely Everard of Breteuil, Manasses of Buges, Ansel, seneschal of Flanders, and certain others—judging it better honourably to suffer death themselves than disgracefully to watch their own men suffer it, armed themselves, left the city, joined their companions, and shared their danger.

But the master of the Temple, Lord Everard of Barres, Chancellor Bartholomew, Archembald of Bourbon, and certain others confronted the emperor and overcame by argument the man whom they could not then overcome by force. He swore that he had not known of this, asked pardon for his people, caused ours to lodge beside the palace, and, all disturbance having been driven away, ordered a market to be provided.

[Col. 1219D] The envoys would have been satisfied, had they not proved one crime by another. For they learned that he was at peace with the Turks. The man who had written to the king that he would go with him to wage war against the unbelieving peoples, and that he had won a new and glorious victory over them, was certainly known to have confirmed a twelve-year truce with those same peoples.

His treachery was further increased and made plain by this: through his kingdom only the German multitude travelled safely. For the bishop of Langres, the count of Warenne, [Col. 1220A] and certain others who had sent a small advance party to Constantinople to prepare arms and provisions for the journey, had suffered great losses of property and grieved over the wounds and deaths of their men. Nor did this happen only once. From the time we entered his land, we suffered the robberies of his people, because we were inferior in strength.

Perhaps this might have been tolerable; it might have been said that the evils we suffered were deserved by the evils we had done, had blasphemy not been added. For if our priests celebrated Masses upon their altars, they afterwards purged them as though profaned, by sprinkling and washing them. All the wealthy have private chapels, adorned with paintings, marble, and lamps, so that each of them could deservedly say: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house” (Psalm 25 [26]), if the lamp of orthodox faith shone in them. But—alas, wickedness!—we heard that their crime is punishable by death: whenever they contract marriages with our people, before the spouses come together they rebaptize the one baptized according to the Roman rite.

Other heresies of theirs are known to us, concerning the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the Holy Spirit. But none of these would stain our page unless it suited our subject.

For these reasons they had incurred the hatred of our men; indeed, their error had spread even among the laity. On this account they were judged not to be Christians, their slaughter was counted as nothing, and our men could with greater difficulty be recalled from plunder and robbery. But let us return to the king, who, although he received new messengers from the emperor almost every day, nevertheless complained of delays among his own people, [Col. 1220C] because he did not know what was happening to them. They always brought good news, never showed the contrary, and were believed the less because all invariably began with the same preface of flattery. He accepted their *polychronia*—for so are called the expressions of reverence which they offer not only to kings but also to any of their superiors, bowing head and body most submissively, whether with knees fixed upon the ground or even with their whole bodies prostrate—but despised it. Sometimes the empress wrote to the queen, and then the Greeks wholly became women, casting off every masculine strength both in speech and in spirit. They lightly swore whatever they thought we wished, yet kept neither faith with us nor shame before themselves. For it is their general [Col. 1220D] opinion that perjury committed for the sacred empire is not reckoned as perjury. Nor should anyone suppose that I am pursuing a hateful race of men and inventing out of hatred things I have not seen; for anyone acquainted with Greeks, if asked, will confess that when they are afraid, they abase themselves excessively and make themselves contemptible, while when they prevail, they grow proud through the harsh oppression of their subjects.

Moreover, they laboured with great effort in counsel to make the king turn aside from Adrianople to Saint George of Sisto, and cross there more swiftly and conveniently. But the king was unwilling to begin what he had heard the Franks had never done. Therefore, following the Germans who had gone before by the same tracks, though not under the same auspices, he continued on. When he had come within one day’s journey of Constantinople, his own messengers met him, bringing reports about [Col. 1221A] the emperor which we have already related in part. Then there were those who advised the king to turn back, seize the exceedingly rich land with its castles and cities, and meanwhile write to King Roger, who was then attacking the emperor most vigorously, and, with his naval aid, assault Constantinople itself. But woe to us—indeed, to all subjects of the apostle Peter—that their voices did not prevail! We proceeded; and as we approached the city, behold, all its nobles and wealthy men, both clergy and laity, came forth in companies to meet the king and received him with due honour, humbly begging him to enter to the emperor and fulfil the latter’s desire to see and speak with him. The king, pitying the emperor’s fear and complying with the request, entered with a few of his own men, and found him waiting in the portico of the palace with sufficient imperial magnificence. They were nearly of the same age and equal in stature, differing only in manners and dress. At length, after mutual embraces and kisses, they went within, where, two seats having been set down, they sat together. Surrounded by the circle of their men, they spoke through an interpreter. The emperor inquired after the king’s condition and wishes, wishing him what belonged to God and promising him what belonged to himself—would that he had been as truthful as he was courteous! If bodily gesture, cheerfulness of countenance, and words revealed the heart’s inner feelings, those standing around would have proved that he loved the king with excessive affection; but such evidence is plausible, not conclusive. After this they parted from one another as brothers, and the nobles of the empire conducted the king outside to the palace where he was lodged.

## Fourth Book

[Col. 1221]

[Col. 1221B] Constantinople, the glory of the Greeks, rich in fame and richer in possessions, is shaped into a triangle like a ship’s sail. At the inner angle it has Saint Sophia and Constantine’s palace, within which is a chapel honoured by most sacred relics; on its two sides it is enclosed by the sea. As we approached the city, we had the Arm of Saint George on our right and, on our left, a certain channel issuing from it and extending for nearly four miles. There stands the palace called Blachernae. Though founded on low ground, it rises in fitting loftiness through expense and art, and, offering a threefold delight to its inhabitants through its threefold boundary, looks out in alternating views upon sea, plains, and city. Its exterior beauty is almost incomparable; [Col. 1221C] its interior surpasses whatever I could say of the exterior. It is painted everywhere in gold and varied colours; the floor is paved with marble in painstaking workmanship; and I do not know whether subtle art or precious material contributes more to its value or beauty.

The third side of the city’s triangle faces the plains, but is fortified with a double wall and towers, stretching nearly two miles from the sea to the palace. It is neither strong in construction nor are its towers raised very high; but, as I think, the city trusts in its own multitude and its long-established peace. Below the walls lies open land which admits ploughs and hoes, containing gardens that supply the citizens with vegetables of every kind. From outside, underground conduits flow in and abundantly furnish the city with fresh water. The city itself is filthy and foul-smelling, and in many places [Col. 1221D] condemned to perpetual night. For the wealthy cover the streets with their buildings, leaving filth and darkness for the poor and for strangers. There murders, robberies, and other crimes that love darkness are committed. Since life in this city is lived without law—having, as it does, almost as many masters as rich men, and nearly as many thieves as poor men—every criminal there has neither fear [Col. 1222B] nor shame, where crime is neither punished by law nor brought openly to light. In everything it exceeds measure; for as it surpasses other cities in wealth, so too in vices.

It also has many churches, unequal to Saint Sophia in size but not in beauty; as they are admirable in loveliness, so they are to be venerated for their numerous pledges of saints, that is, holy relics. Those who could entered them: some through curiosity to see, others through faithful devotion. The king too, with the emperor as guide, visited the holy places; and upon returning, overcome by urgent entreaties, he ate with him. That banquet, as it had illustrious guests, so it satisfied ears, mouth, and eyes alike by the splendid display, the delicacies of the dishes, and the pleasing applause of entertainments. Many of his own men [Col. 1222C] feared for the king there; but he, having entrusted his own care to God, feared absolutely nothing in faith and courage. For one who has no intention of doing harm does not readily believe that harm will be done to him, although the Greeks displayed no sign of treachery; for I believe they would not have rendered such diligent service had they harboured good intentions. They concealed the wrongs they had suffered, intending to demand payment after the crossing of the Arm. Nor was it counted against them if they closed the city gates against the multitude, because many of their houses and olive groves had been burned—whether from scarcity of firewood or from the insolence and drunkenness of fools. The king repeatedly had their ears, hands, and feet cut off, yet could not even so restrain their madness. Indeed, one of two things was necessary: either to kill many thousands at once or to endure very many of their evils.

The market, [Col. 1222D] therefore, supplied us quite abundantly by ship; and before the palace, or even in the tents, we had a suitable exchange rate, while it lasted: one *stamma* for less than two denarii, and thirty-three solidi for a mark.

But after we had crossed the city in three days’ marches, we were losing one *stamma* for five or six denarii, and one mark for twelve solidi. [Col. 1223A] Moreover, while the king was awaiting those coming through Apulia and crossing between Brindisi and Dyrrachium, the feast of blessed Dionysius occurred, which he celebrated with the veneration due to it. The emperor learned of this—for the Greeks observe this feast—and sent to the king a chosen multitude of his clergy, each supplied with a large candle painted in varied colours and gold, thereby enhancing the splendour of the solemnity. They differed from our clergy in their form of words and chant, but were pleasing in sweet modulation. For blended voices—the stronger with the slender, that is, eunuch voices with male voices, for many of them were eunuchs—softened the hearts of the Franks. By the graceful and restrained movements of their bodies, the clapping of hands, and the bending of their limbs, they also offered pleasure [Col. 1223B] to the eyes.

We recount the emperor’s services so that his deceit may be clear: he displayed the affection which we are accustomed to show our dearest friends, yet harboured a disposition which could not be appeased except by our deaths. Certainly no one could know the Greeks save by experience or a spirit of prophecy. But the bishop of Langres, rejecting their faith, despising their services, and predicting the evils which we later experienced, urged that the city be taken. He demonstrated that its weak walls—of which a great part collapsed before our men—could, without delay or labour, be overcome by cutting the conduits and withdrawing its fresh water; likewise, that its populace was inert. That prudent man, holy in spirit and religion, said that, once that city had been taken, it would not be necessary to conquer others, [Col. 1223C] because they would freely offer obedience to whoever possessed their head. He added that it possessed not the reality of Christianity but merely the name; and that, though it ought itself to bring aid to Christians rather than hinder them, a few years before the emperor had attacked the prince of Antioch in order to conquer him. He first took Tarsus and Mamistra, many castles, and a very extensive territory; after expelling the Catholic bishops of the cities and installing heretics in their place, he besieged Antioch. Although he ought, having gathered Christian forces, to drive back the neighbouring pagans, he relied on their assistance to exterminate Christians. But God, knower, judge, and avenger of these deeds, willed that he should strike himself with a poisoned arrow and end his unworthy life by a slight wound. This man who now reigns, [Col. 1223D] heir to his father’s gains and crimes, retains for himself the rights of churches and the other things which his father wickedly acquired, and likewise covets those things which he himself desires. He has already extorted homage from princes; and, setting altar against altar, he established his own patriarch in the city, in contempt of Peter’s patriarch. It is for your judgment whether you ought to spare one under whose rule neither Christ’s cross nor sepulchre is secure, and whose destruction would bring nothing contrary to your purpose.

When the bishop had finished his speech, some approved what he said. But the greater number, who disapproved, replied in this fashion and similarly: “We cannot judge concerning these men’s faith, being ignorant of their law. That he attacked Antioch was evil; nevertheless, he may have had grounds of justice unknown to us. [Col. 1224A] It is certain that the king recently spoke with the pope and received neither his command nor counsel about this matter. We and he have come to visit the Lord’s sepulchre and, by command of the supreme pontiff, to blot out our sins through pagan blood or conversion. Now we can assault a most wealthy city of Christians and become rich, but we must kill and be killed. Therefore, if the slaughter of Christians washes away sins, let us fight. Likewise, if ambition does no harm to our dead, if dying on the road to acquire money is worth as much as devoting ourselves to obedience to the supreme pontiff and to our vow, because riches please us, let us enter upon dangers without fear of death.”

Such was their dispute; and advocates of either opinion invoked justice on their own side. [Col. 1224B] Yet I believe that the bishop would have prevailed, had not the Greeks been stronger in stratagems than in force. Suspecting our delay, they dared not urge us to cross, yet, by partly withholding the market and stirring our men with reports about the Germans, they drove them toward the crossing. First they reported that the Turks had gathered a numerous army, and that the Germans had killed fourteen thousand of them without loss to their own men. The following day, with a more favourable outcome, they pressed still more strongly for the ill-fated crossing. For they said that the Germans had reached Iconium and that, before their arrival, the frightened population of that city had fled. Since they themselves were hastening onward, one emperor wrote to the other [Col. 1224C] that he should come and, by defending it, possess what had been conquered without his own labour. By these spurs the army was stirred, and it murmured against the king’s delay, some envying their profits, others their fame. Thus the king, overcome both by Greek counsels and by the complaints of his own men, crossed before those whom he had been awaiting arrived. And the emperor, just as he eagerly wished this, so swiftly prepared an abundance of ships.

But when the king had [lacuna: “crossed,” or something similar] the Arm [Note: [Col. 1223D] Here “crossed,” or something similar, is lacking.], he spent fifteen days awaiting a part of his army, and a further fifteen likewise enduring Greek trickery. They had obtained the opportunity which they had awaited and dared reveal what they had conceived. Yet the madness of our men gave them coverings for their wickedness. Hence many said that what they did to us was not malice but [Col. 1224D] vengeance. He judges partially who knows a matter only in part; nor can he make a right judgment who does not know the cause in its entirety. They could indeed have been offended, but not appeased.

Behold, we crossed, and ships bearing provisions and money-changers followed us. They spread out their wares on the shore; tables gleamed with gold and were adorned with silver vessels which they had purchased from our men. Men came from the army to exchange necessities; those who coveted what was not theirs joined them. Thus, one day, a certain Fleming, worthy of whips and flame, seeing immense wealth and blinded by unrestrained greed, cried, “Haro! Haro!” and seized what he desired; by his audacity and by the value of the plunder he encouraged men like himself [Col. 1225A] to crime. And because fools go everywhere—for in the exchange-market, as many as were killed, so many were fools—those who had their money ready fell everywhere. The uproar and fury grew; booths collapsed; gold was trampled and carried off. The money-changers fled, despoiled, through fear of death. Their ships received the fugitives and, hauled away from the shore, carried back to the city very many of our men who had been buying food. These men were beaten and stripped; the city too stripped its guests as though they were enemies.

These events were reported to the king. Inflamed with anger, he sought the criminal; when the count of Flanders handed him over, he was at once hanged in sight of the city. Then the king hastened to seek out the lost goods, granting pardon to those who restored them and threatening like punishment to those who concealed them. And lest they fear or be ashamed before his presence, [Col. 1225B] he ordered them to restore everything to the bishop of Langres. On the next day those who had fled on the preceding day were recalled, and whatever they could swear they had lost was fully restored to them. Very many claimed more than was due to them, but the king preferred to make good from his own resources what was lacking rather than let the peace of his army be violated.

After this he chose men to demand from the emperor what his people had lost and to restore a market to the army: Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, distinguished in eloquence and piety, and Bartholomew the chancellor. Since the king, ever swift to correct wrongs, pressed them, they crossed early enough and, through the good offices of the custodian, entered the palace; but they could not speak with the idol. That day they were each other’s consolation: paintings served as food, [Col. 1225C] and, with night coming on, a marble floor served as mattress or bed. On the following day, when that profane man had risen about the third hour, they were summoned before him, sober and sleepless, and discharged their embassy concerning satisfaction for his men and the complaint of ours. The bishop’s prudent and gentle eloquence would have made him sufficiently tractable, if that serpent could have been charmed by anyone; but, deaf after the manner of an asp and swollen with venom, he became other than the man they had previously seen—or rather, he was revealed as the man whom they had not previously recognized beneath a covering of deceit. Yet the bishop persisted and prevailed in part: the army obtained a market, and an exit was opened to his pilgrims whose goods had been lost. The emperor said that he would still speak with the king and soon send messengers ahead. [Col. 1225D] A private necessity pressed the bishop to return, lest he observe a three-day fast with him. The emperor still pretended goodwill in order to do greater harm, providing a market, but sparingly; intending to speak with the king, but slowly. Thus, while he sent messengers and sent them back, several days passed, and the Franks consumed what they had prepared for the journey.

He wanted the king to return to his palace; the king wanted the conference to take place on his own bank, or from horseback in the sea. At last, through messengers, he disclosed what he had craftily delayed: he demanded as wife for a certain nephew of his the king’s kinswoman whom the queen had with her, and demanded the homage of the barons for himself. For this he promised guides for the journey, and everywhere a suitable market and exchange; wherever these were lacking, they might take plunder; if a castle or city refused such provision, [Col. 1226A] it might be taken, provided that, after the spoils were removed, it was left empty for him. He further offered the king gifts worthy of a king, and each baron gifts suitable to his rank.

When this was heard, delay was again necessary: both because the count of Maurienne, the marquis of Montferrat—uncles of the king—the count of Auvergne, and many others whom we awaited had pitched their tents beyond the city in our sight; and because the barons disagreed over the emperor’s demand. The Greeks, however, who had been accustomed to urge the crossing, delayed it by forbidding it. Therefore the distinguished knights, scattered through the mountains and making provision for delay and journey alike, filled the army with plunder, purchasing passage for their own men at the Greeks’ expense. Thus the Greeks offered what they had forbidden; and, once transported across, our men received those whom they had awaited.

Meanwhile, while what the emperor demanded remained uncertain, Count Robert of Perche, the king’s brother, secretly removed his own kinswoman from the queen, withdrawing both himself and certain barons from homage to him, and his kinswoman from marriage to the emperor’s nephew. Thus he went ahead to Nicomedia; and the king, with bishops and other barons, considered the emperor’s case. Some, especially the bishop of Langres, said: [Col. 1226B] “Behold, the impious man reveals what he previously concealed: he demands your homage, though he might have been your servant, promising shamefully what victory ought to have won. But we, dearest friends, should prefer honour to advantage and obtain by force what he offers as if to men greedy and afraid. For it is shameful, while we have so glorious a lord present, to render homage to an unbeliever.”

Others, however, [Col. 1226C] whose number and reasoning prevailed, answered in this manner: “By custom we may have several lords after the king, whose fiefs we possess, while we preserve our principal allegiance to him. If we judge this shameful, let us abolish the custom. But now the emperor, fearing for himself, demands our homage. Therefore, if it is shameful that he fears us, if it is dishonourable to do to the emperor what we ourselves do to lesser men, let us decline. But if the emperor’s fear, or the practice of our custom, neither injures the king nor brings shame upon us, let us yield to our custom; let us spare his fear for our own benefit, and, providing for the necessities of the journey, let us desire the advantages. None of us knows [Col. 1226D] this land; therefore we need a guide. We are hurrying against pagans: let us make use of the peace of Christians.”

While these things were happening, almost all whom the king had awaited crossed over. I am grieved to recount their names, because I witnessed their untimely deaths; and perhaps it would weary a reader who seeks an example of usefulness or virtue. Since the emperor alone was now the cause of further delay, the king ordered the camp moved. Hearing this, the emperor hastened after him with messengers sent in advance, appointing a certain castle for their conference, where he secured himself by assembling ships from the nearby sea. The king, emulous of the Germans—whose good fame he had gladly heard and sought to match swiftly—was unwilling either to delay or to refuse the conference. Therefore, while the army went ahead, he turned back, [Col. 1227A] taking with him the glory of the barons and a ready multitude of knights. Yet he took it ill that the emperor demanded the homage of his men, but considered useful for God’s service what the emperor promised. If he were a Christian, he ought to provide it without any demand; but he said that, having already experienced our people, he feared for his kingdom. Unless they gave him such satisfaction, whatever might be useful to them in his territory would have to be avoided. The king, fired by haste against the pagans, preferred to bend the sternness of his spirit to the emperor’s will rather than delay God’s service for any reason.

When they met, they first set forth the terms: namely, that the king would take from him neither castle nor city belonging to his jurisdiction. This was a sufficiently reasonable and moderate demand, followed by an equally generous but deceptive promise. In order that imperial favour might answer royal peace, [Col. 1227B] he added that two or three of his leading men would proceed with the king, conduct him by the direct route, and provide a suitable market everywhere. Where this failed, he would endure without complaint the plundering of castles and the seizure of cities, provided that, after the spoils had been taken, the land remained empty for him.

At that time King Roger of Apulia was pressing him fiercely and successfully, conquering many places. Had he been able to join our king to himself against Roger, he would have poured out upon him every abundance of treasures. But when he could not bend him to this, whether by continual entreaty or incredible promises, [Col. 1228A] they mutually bound themselves to one another by treaty concerning the matters stated above. Then, after receiving the homage of the barons and honouring the king with gifts sufficiently imperial, the king hastened after the army; that sacrilegious man, stained with new perjury, remained behind freed from fear, providing for only a few days the market needed for a long time, and never supplying the promised guides for the road.

On that day the sun saw a crime which it could not bear; but, lest it seem to equal it with the Lord’s betrayal, it served the world only half its course and hid itself by half. Therefore, while the army proceeded after leaving the king and saw the sun in the shape of half a loaf for a great part of the day, it feared that he who shone above others in the light of faith, burned in love, and was sustained by heavenly hope might, through Greek betrayal, be deprived of some portion of his light. But another, equally lamentable event occurred. For the emperor of the Germans, betrayed by his guide and secretly abandoned in the hollows of the mountains, with many thousands of his men pierced by Turkish arrows, was compelled to retreat, as we shall later relate. Once we learned this, we interpreted the heavenly prodigy more correctly, saying that our king and the German emperor were one sun, because they shone with the light of one faith; and that this sun shone half-bright and concealed the rays of half its circle when, while the king continued his course with his usual ardour, the Germans were retreating.

## Fifth Book

[Col. 1227]

[Col. 1227C] Constantinople, proud in wealth, deceitful in manners, corrupt in faith: just as all fear it because of its wealth, so it is to be feared by all for its trickery and faithlessness. Yet if it lacked these vices, it could be preferred above all places for its temperate air, the health-giving fertility of its soil, and easy passage for spreading the faith. For it has the Arm of Saint George, which is a sea in the abundance and saltiness of its fish, but a river in its breadth, and may be crossed to and fro seven or eight times in a day without danger. Beyond lies Romania, a very extensive land and extremely rugged with rocky mountains, extending in its southern part as far as Antioch and having Turkey on its eastern side. Although all of it had belonged to the Greeks by right, the Turks possess a great part of it; having expelled the Greeks, they destroyed one part of the country; [Col. 1227D] where the Greeks still hold fortifications, they share the revenues.

By such service they retain what the valour of the Franks who conquered Jerusalem had liberated. That inactive people would have lost everything; but, purchasing gold with gold, they defend themselves with hired soldiers of diverse nations. Yet they continually lose ground, and, though possessing much, cannot hold all at once; for foreign strength does not suffice one deprived of his own. Nicomedia first showed us this: overgrown with brambles [Col. 1228C] and thickets, its lofty ruins reveal its former glory and the inertia of its present masters. A certain sea-channel, rising from the Arm and ending there after a third day’s journey, helped it in vain.

From here three routes lead to Antioch, unequal in length and unlike in character. The route which turns to the left is shorter, if it had no obstacles, and could be completed in three weeks; but after twelve days it presents Iconium, the seat of the Sultan, a most noble city, and after another five days, once the Turks have been passed, the land of the Franks. A strong army, fortified by faith and numbers, would despise these things, but would be deterred by the snows of the mountains in winter. The route which keeps to the right [Col. 1228D] is more peaceful and more plentiful, but through coastal windings it causes travellers a delay three times as great, having rivers and torrents to fear in winter in place of snow and Turks. The middle route is tempered by the advantages and disadvantages of either side: longer than the shorter route but safer; shorter and safer than the longer route, but poorer. Therefore the Germans, who had preceded us, having made a division, mostly set out with the emperor to the left, under an ill omen, through Iconium. The remainder, however, turned right with his brother, following [Col. 1229A] everything leftward. But the middle lot fell to us, moderated by the misfortune of either side.

Thus, when, leaving Nicaea on our left, we were encamped above its lake, stirred by Greek reports both to hurry after the Germans and to be hurried along, noble men sent by their emperor after the king arrived. They sorrowfully reported to us, contrary to our wish and expectation, that the Germans had fled back to Nicaea. Hearing this, our men grieved in astonishment and were astonished in grief that so strong an army had failed so suddenly and that the enemies both of God and of ourselves had so easily triumphed over our companions. They were asked for the order, manner, or cause of so great a disaster; but perhaps all these terms are improper, since confusion has no order, excess no measure, and that for which no reason precedes has no cause. Yet it had both a bad beginning and a bad end, as those who were able to escape that calamity taught us.

At first they were sufficiently just accusers of themselves: they had trusted excessively in their own strength, while offending God more frequently and beyond their usual manner. Then they cursed the idol of Constantinople, who, when he had given them a guide and betrayer of the road, [Col. 1229B] had, so far as lay in him, cast down Christian faith, established paganism, encouraged the cowardly hearts of the Turks, and chilled the ardour of our men. Led by their guide to Nicaea, they were ordered to load themselves with provisions for eight days, intending with such supplies to reach Iconium.

But when both the days and the food were spent, they thought the road would likewise be finished; yet, hemmed in by mountains and engulfed among their crags, they could have inferred its boundlessness. Nevertheless, deceived by their guide—or rather, their harsh deceiver—they endured postponement from one tomorrow to the next, and then to a third, and were driven farther into trackless mountains. At last, believing the army still alive to be already buried, that traitor fled by night along shortcuts known to himself and summoned a very great Turkish multitude to the prey. At dawn on the following day, when the standard-bearers, as usual going ahead and now angry with him, sought their guide but could not find him, they suddenly saw that the Turks had occupied the mountain crags; they grieved especially that the man for whom they searched had escaped without the fitting payment for his crime. These events were made known to the emperor both by the report [Col. 1229C] of his men and by the sun. In that crisis he consulted his wise men, but too late, because they were not choosing good out of evil, but the lesser of evils. They had to go forward or withdraw; but hunger, the enemy, and the unknown labyrinth of the mountains prevented advance; hunger likewise, and fear of disgrace, prevented retreat. In retreat there was at least some hope of escape, though with dishonour; in advance, certain death without truth or praise. What, then, was hungry courage to do? Would it flee in God’s service, when it was not accustomed to flee in its own? Or would it press on vainly, immediately to die, though, if preserved, it might still serve God? Certainly it would prefer a glorious death to a shameful life; but if shame stains either alternative, it is better to be preserved shamefully through valiant actions than to perish shamefully without redress.

With this reasoning [Col. 1230A] the yielding Germans did what they were not accustomed to do: condemning retreat in their judgment, they conceded it for the time, with the hope of correction; they did what they could and wished what they ought. Therefore all armed themselves to endure hunger. They had for food exhausted and dying horses, and for warfare against the pursuing enemy only a certain distinguished count, Bernard by name, with his own men. As they returned thus in formation, they lengthened their marches seeking food, while labour and hunger diminished their strength. The Turks, meanwhile, tested them little by little and, once their weakness was known, attacked them more fiercely from day to day.

At length that illustrious count, worthy of praise and lamentation, while waiting for the weary and supporting the weak, remained behind beyond a certain mountain after the army had crossed it and night had come on. The Turks [Col. 1230B] encircled him from afar and shot at him, killing him and his men more easily than they had hoped, without loss to themselves. For that man lacked bows and crossbows, while hunger and labour had taken away the swift horses of the armed men. The Turks did not wish to fight hand to hand; nor did he possess weapons with which he might defend himself at a distance; nor could the hungry horses carry armed men against the enemy. Greatly to be mourned is that agile youth which, often drawing the sword and having sheep-skins for shields, runs swiftly and boldly against the enemy only to encounter flying death midway.

When the holy pope forbade hawks and dogs and imposed restraint upon the arms and dress of knights, he acted wisely and beneficially; whoever did not consent to his command acted foolishly and to no benefit. Yet I wish he had likewise equipped the foot-soldiers: retaining the weak, he should have given every strong man a sword instead of a wallet [Col. 1230C] and a bow instead of a staff, because the weak and unarmed are always a burden to their own side and prey to the enemy. On the following day the count was sought, he who had habitually offered himself willingly for the defence of his men; it was learned that he had not come late to the army, but had perished on the road with his men beneath Turkish arrows. All mourned his death, relying greatly as they had upon his strength and counsel, and because a like death threatened them all.

All who could do so therefore armed themselves; and, as famine and the enemy raged more fiercely than usual, they hastened on. For the Turks now feared nothing from afar once they recognized that there were no bows and no swift horses. Thus they pressed not only the rear, but shot arrows also at the foremost and the middle ranks. [Col. 1230D] I cannot describe the losses of that march, in which the emperor himself was wounded by two arrows: while some hurried onward, the weak were left behind, and amid the central mass a rain of arrows slew the unarmed. Thus at last they came dying to Nicaea. There the starving rushed to food, which the Greeks, as far as they could in such necessity, sold at an excessive price, demanding swords and coats of mail rather than gold, so that they might strip the army completely bare. The greater part of it, its strength exhausted and possessions lost, wishing to return home, went to Constantinople; but before they could obtain either a market or passage, more than thirty thousand of them, as we heard, were killed by hunger.

But the emperor, deprived of human comfort and trusting in divine aid, steadfastly made his way after the king, seeking his company for God’s service. Messengers sent ahead by him found the king above the Lake of Nicaea, as has been said, and reported what we have described, begging him to come to meet the emperor who followed, bringing help and counsel to one in need. The king grieved for his companion’s loss as for his own; and with a great company of barons he willingly and swiftly went to meet him in person, in answer to his request. They embraced one another and exchanged kisses bedewed with tears of compassion. At last they determined that the king should await the emperor at the castle called Lupar, while the latter, having taken provisions at Nicaea, should hasten after him.

Thereafter the Greeks began to withhold a market from our men; but the latter could not look upon abundance and yet starve. Thus many, scattered about, seized what they would more gladly have bought; while others bought plunder from them, considering themselves more just if in any manner they lived from their own resources. So they came to Lupar, where by agreement they awaited the Germans, whom thereafter the Greeks daily despoiled of goods and life, as the locust devours what the palmer-worm has left (Joel 1). At last the emperor and his knights, wearied out, since they could not escape—even though the enemy were few—by resisting manfully with arms, dismounted and went miserably forward on foot, enduring more bravely. But the poor, unencumbered by baggage in their flight, hastened after the king, not fearing the greedy because of their poverty. The emperor also entreated the king through messengers to hurry to meet them with an armed force, either to bury their bodies or to preserve some remnant of life for those half alive.

Accordingly the constable Ivo of Niella, count of Soissons, hastened at the king’s urging; and, as the Greeks fled, he freed the exhausted Germans without difficulty. Indeed, as they themselves later reported, if the constable had not come so swiftly, all would at once and in one place have met their death. Alas, what a pitiable fate: that fierce Saxons and Batavians, and other Germans—whom we read in ancient histories once made Roman courage afraid—should now have perished so miserably through the deceit of the feeble Greeks! In its own time the slaughter of the Franks too shall be related, and there shall be an unbearable double grief. Both peoples will have cause for perpetual mourning, unless sons avenge the deaths of their fathers. Yet divine justice gives us, who have endured Greek crimes, hope of vengeance; and our peoples are not accustomed to bear shameful injuries for long.

Meanwhile we console our sorrowing hearts with these thoughts; and, so that posterity may know the deceitful deeds of the Greeks, we shall continue the account of our misfortunes. When the emperor had been brought to the king’s tents and lodged on the other side of a certain river, the king crossed over to him in boats and came on foot, courageous and compassionate, manly and weeping, to console him. The emperor, like a shipwrecked man reaching harbor, received his words with the greatest gratitude; and very humbly asked him for what he needed. Then, beginning thus, he set forth his circumstances with sufficient firmness:

> “Lord King, whom nature has made my neighbor and kinsman, and whom God has preserved in my need as my protector, I need not recount my misfortunes to you, for it is superfluous to show someone what he already sees. They are indeed grievous; yet know that I am angry because of them not with God, but with myself. God is just; but I and my people are foolish. When I led forth from my kingdom a numerous and wealthy army, if I had rendered fitting thanks to the Giver of good things, perhaps he who gave it would have preserved it. When I was about to enter barbarian lands, if I had amended my life in the present and mourned for the past in devout satisfaction, God would not have punished faults that had been corrected. When I expected victories over the Turks, if I had not swelled with pride in my own numbers but had humbly placed my hope in the God of hosts, God would not have subdued uncorrected obstinacy. Yet by his grace I am still safe, I still possess wealth, and I persevere in the purpose of his service. For I believe that I would not have emerged wealthy and unharmed from so many dangers, nor would I have found you, at the point of death, ready to aid me, [Col. 1232C] unless God had provided that I might still be of some use in his service. Therefore I do not wish henceforth to be separated from your company, nor to be stationed either in the foremost or the rearmost position, because I could neither drive back enemies who met us nor endure those who followed without loss to those in the middle. Apart from this, let my tents be placed wherever you wish. But I ask that my number be increased from among your companions.”

When he had concluded this speech, anxious in his fresh grief and speaking through the interpretation of the bishop of Metz, he moved the hearts of all to tears. Then, on the counsel of bishops and barons, the king assigned to him his uncles, the count of Maurienne and the marquis of Montferrat; his kinsmen, the bishop of Metz and his brother Count Renald; and certain others. He judged that they should lodge together, so that he might be able to take counsel from him at close hand.

## Book Six

[Col. 1231]

[Col. 1231D] The king therefore, loving the emperor for his person, almost preferring him to himself because of his age, and reverencing him because of his fortunes, broke camp and, after the feast of Saint Martin, came to the castle called Esseron. Meanwhile, while the grief was fresh and while he still remembered royal service, I approached the king, set before him the injuries which he was inflicting on Saint Dionysius concerning the castle of Estufin and Hescelingis, and reminded him of the excommunication which he had heard the pope pronounce over this matter at Easter. Rejoicing that he had an opportunity to serve his patron, he did not delay, but immediately ordered the possessors of these places to be shown to him.

I replied that the emperor himself held one tower in the castle, and Duke Frederick, who was present, another; and that the duke solely possessed the remainder. On hearing this, he sought out each of them, personally and through his agents: first privately, then publicly. He begged on his own behalf; he exhorted them for the appeasement of God and for the glorious martyr; he pressed the emperor’s household over this matter and renewed his importuning. But the emperor at first gave evasive answers, hoping that the king, wearied by delay, would abandon what he had begun. The king, however, did not desist from his honorable and religious petition until the emperor revealed how immovable he was in his error and how ungrateful for benefits:

> “Although this is not our present subject, Father Suger, it is nevertheless fitting that you should know it, so that you may pray more devotedly for him who honors you when present and loves you when absent. The king, moreover, intended to hasten to Philadelphia; the road thither was fully eight days’ journey, but he had not a full supply of provisions. When the emperor learned this, while the king and the barons were present, he spoke about it, and perhaps unknowingly offered us, in full cups, a lesson drawn from his own misfortune. ‘As it is the part of courage,’ he said, ‘to imitate brave deeds, so it is the part of prudence to be made cautious by another’s misfortune. When I recently had an army which no unbelieving people could have withstood, it yielded through hunger to those whom it could have subdued if it had possessed provisions. In this matter the condition of us two is equal: just as you fear no people’s power, so you have no weapons against hunger. Behold, two roads are set before you: one shorter but destitute; the other longer and well supplied. Yet it is certainly better to live honorably for a long time in abundance than to perish quickly and disgracefully in want. A delay which preserves a strong army in plenty is better than one which restores it exhausted or starving. Therefore I advise you to keep to the coast, and preserve the strength of your soldiery for God’s service, though it arrives more slowly.’”

The king accordingly assented to a speech more plausible than truthful, and was soon to suffer losses and dangers. He turned aside toward the coastal city of Demetrias: a place which the part of the army taking the direct route reached in half a day, but which he himself would scarcely reach on the third day. For he had strayed into certain hollows; and, striking against the crags of mountains, while he skirted or climbed them he did not approach his intended destination, but by turns drew near to hell and to the stars. On the third morning we saw a small village inhabited by peasants, companions of beasts. When the others fled, we captured one of them; by his assistance we were led out that same day before Demetrias, to our companions, who had been greatly afraid for us.

Our first and greatest loss was made in those mountains. When our pack animals died, we greatly enriched the wild Greeks with gold and silver, arms and clothing; yet because we escaped, we bore this loss with equanimity. There was there a winding and extremely swift torrent which had to be forded eight or nine times in a single day. Had it swelled only a little more with rain, no one could either go on or return; each would necessarily have waited in his own place, mourning his sins, for the end of life.

After this we returned to the coastal windings, finding almost every day rocky and steep mountains, and deeply cut riverbeds which it was laborious to cross even when empty. If these had been swollen by snow or rain, their rushing waters could not possibly have been swum by horseman or footman. There we found many ruined cities, and others which the Greeks had contracted from their ancient extent above the sea, fortifying them with walls and towers. From them we obtained food with difficulty because of the burden imposed by our multitude, and at an excessive price because of their greed. Someone who was not there may perhaps say that these places ought to have been taken, and that what could not be had at a fair price ought to have been seized for nothing. But they had towers and double walls for defense, and ships at sea for escape. What advantage would there have been if our men had captured one of them with delay, danger, and effort, only for its citizens to escape after taking the city’s spoils?

The villagers also hid their animals in the mountains; thus, after emptying their houses, they sold from ships food at whatever exorbitant price they pleased, and stripped the poor during so long a march of gold and silver, arms and clothing. Whenever they could find ships, some entered them, setting aside the danger of shipwreck, in order to be carried wherever Greek treachery or winter storms chose. Others, whom their condition had condemned to servitude, considered it easier to remain in Greek service.

Nor should it pass unmentioned that, to the astonishment of the inhabitants, we easily forded three rivers on this route, contrary to custom; and each immediately flooded with rain after our crossing. Hence it was regarded as a miracle that, contrary to what was usual, rain and winter spared us. Thus, passing Smyrna and Pergamum, we came to Ephesus, which amid the ruins of its ancient glory retains venerable remains of its former condition: the tomb of Saint John, on a mound of earth, enclosed by a wall against the pagans. There the king received messengers of the emperor with letters. They said that Turks beyond number had gathered against him and advised him to take refuge in the emperor’s castles. But when the king held both fear of the Turks and the emperor’s favor in equal contempt, they offered other proposals equally worthy of scorn, setting forth the injuries which the king had done them and declaring that they could no longer restrain their men from vengeance. [Col. 1234D] Rejecting these without reply, he proceeded, intending to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord in the valley of Decervion; and the German, regretting that he had not seen the emperor of Constantinople, returned to winter with him.

Accordingly, on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord, after the tents had been pitched in a very rich valley, the Turks, guided by Greeks, laid their first ambush while our horses were grazing. Our distinguished knights resisted courageously and cautiously; they joyfully took first-fruits from the heads of the enemy, and by that terror secured peace during the festival days. While we devoted ourselves there to divine praises and rest, the sky grew darker—as though divine providence meant to be dried up before our eyes—and sent rains, by which the streams of the valleys overflowed and the mountains became white with snow. (Yet thereafter, by God’s will, until Satellia the air was neither horrible with cold nor clouded with rain.) Finally, after the fourth day, when the swollen waters had run off and the sky had cleared as the rains were driven away, the king, fearing that he might be cut off by the torrents if the snows melted or heavy rains descended, left the Ephesian valley and, taking provisions, hurried toward Laodicea.

On this route, amid steep mountains, was the Maeander River, deep and broad from its own waters, but then more swollen by waters from elsewhere. With its channel it divided the middle of a broad valley, and immediately made its bank passable for a vast multitude. There the Turks divided themselves, thinking that some would harass the advancing army with arrows, others would prevent the river’s timid fordings, and both groups, when they yielded before our men, would be safe in the refuge of the mountains. When we came there, we found bands of Turks occupying the crags of the mountains; others had exposed themselves upon the plain to test the army; and the rest had massed beyond the river to prevent the crossing.

But the king, gathering his baggage and the weak in the middle, protected the front, rear, and flanks with armed men. Thus he advanced safely, though making little progress over two days’ marches. For the enemy on either side delayed him by cunning rather than strength, being trained and swift in flight and bold in pursuit. Since, therefore, he could have neither peace nor battle with those who attacked boldly and retreated skilfully and swiftly, he wished to cross; but he did not know the river’s ford, and, with the Turks preventing him, it could not be tested without danger.

About noon on the second day, one part of the Turks assembled behind the army, as they had agreed, and another above the river, where the entry was easy for our men and the exit difficult toward the Turks. Then they sent three of their number across to shoot arrows at our men; as they shot, both sides thundered with a united cry, and the Turks fled by whatever way they could. But the distinguished counts Henry, son of Count Theobald; Thierry of Flanders; and William of Mâcon rushed after them like a whirlwind, and more swiftly than words can tell penetrated the steep bank, the rain of arrows, and the Turkish multitude. The king likewise, encountering those who were shooting from behind with loosened reins, put them to flight, cut them down, and drove those whom the speed of their horses aided back into the hollow mountains. Thus each assault of our men quickly and easily strewn the fields, as far as the mountain refuges, with the bodies of both groups.

There a certain Amiradus was captured, brought before the king, examined, and killed. A small city of the emperor was nearby, bearing the diminutive name Antiochia; it lay open as a refuge for the fleeing pagans, and here the emperor passed from being a deceitful traitor to being an open enemy. The king would have stormed it to seize the fugitives who had shut themselves in, but provisions were nearly lacking, and no spoils could be taken in a poor village. Certainly there were those who said that they had seen, before our men at the river crossing, a certain white knight whom they had seen neither before nor afterward, and who had struck the first blows in the battle. [Col. 1236A] In this matter I wish neither to deceive nor to be deceived. Yet I know that in such straits so easy and celebrated a victory could only have come through divine power; nor could the iron rain of the opposing multitude have fallen without death or wounding, God granting us victory without loss, had not Milo of Nogent drowned in the river. On our route the Turks and Greeks had adjoining territories, and we knew them both to be unanimous enemies against us.

They therefore mourned their dead and summoned others from nearby for vengeance, intending to return on the seventh day in greater numbers and more boldly. We, with foolish confidence, came to Laodicea on the third day. Here I recall that Count Bernard, who, returning from Iconium with the emperor, laid down his life for his brothers; for here, with the bishop of Freising, the emperor’s brother, another count of the same name and fortune perished through a similar betrayal. The duke of this city, though he ought to have led them out of the mountains, instead led them through impassable places into Turkish ambushes. There, after the count and many others had been killed, those who could escape fled by hiding; while the duke and the Greeks whom he had led divided the spoils with the Turks.

The same man, either fearing the king for his crime or wishing to harm him by another means, emptied the city of every useful thing. Avoiding the now-recognized treachery, he devised another equally harmful. The impious man knew that as far as Satellia—a distance which afterward took us more than fifteen days’ march—provisions could nowhere be found, and that all must necessarily die of hunger if food could not be obtained from the emptied city either by purchase or by force. The king therefore consulted the bishops and other leading men. Although no one doubted the king’s prudence except himself, he nevertheless always managed public affairs by the counsel of many. This was indeed prudent humility: he preferred many men to himself alone, elders to himself as a young man, and the tested experience of others to his own judgment. What he could do as lord, what he knew as a wise man, he generously deferred to his subjects.

Those who were accustomed to debate other matters and sometimes to disagree with needless subtlety over conjectures drawn from diverse considerations were now astonished, unable to find a suitable course in this crisis, and grieved because they could see no escape from the common danger. They sought food in a city intentionally emptied—having strength to take it and wealth to buy it—but because what was sought was not there, both powers were useless for this purpose. Nevertheless, it was decided to seek out the fugitive citizens along the mountain paths and, after securing peace with the sellers, to bring them back.

When this had been partly done—for they were found but not brought back—we proceeded and lost one day in this way, with Turks and Greeks before and behind us on our route. There were mountains still wet with German blood, and the same enemies who had killed them stood ready. The king, wiser too late, seeing the troops of these enemies and the corpses of the others, drew up his ranks. In this matter Geoffrey of Rancon earned everlasting resentment. The king had sent him forward with his uncle, the count of Maurienne. About noon on the second day there was an accursed mountain with an easier passage. The king had intended to cross it during the entire day and had ordered that tents should not be pitched there. Those who arrived first came fairly quickly, since no one impeded them; forgetting the king, who was then protecting the rear, they climbed the mountain and, when others followed, pitched their tents on the far side about the ninth hour.

The mountain was steep and rocky. We had to climb its slope; its summit seemed to us to touch heaven, while a torrent in the hollow valley descended into hell. The advancing multitude increased, pressed each other, became packed together, halted, could not look ahead for the horse, and clung in place rather than advancing. Pack animals slipped from sheer rocks, overthrowing all whom they met down into the depth of the abyss. Stones too, dislodged from their places, wrought their own destruction. Thus, while people spread out far and wide seeking paths, all feared either their own fall or the thunderous descent of others. Meanwhile the Turks and Greeks, preventing with arrows those who had fallen from rising, gathered on the far side and rejoiced at such a spectacle in hope of evening advantage. The day declined, and the heap of our equipment continually grew in the gorge.

But this was not enough for the enemy: they dared more and crossed to our side, because they no longer feared the first ranks and did not yet see the last. They struck down men, and the unarmed crowd fell or fled like cattle. A cry arose which pierced heaven and reached the king’s ears. The king did what he could; but no help then came from heaven except night, and when night came the disaster ceased. Meanwhile I, who as a monk could do only this—to call upon the Lord or urge others to battle—was sent to the camp and reported the matter. In alarm they ran to arms; they hastened to return, but could scarcely go because the roughness of the ground and the oncoming crowd impeded them.

The king, left in danger with some nobles, had with him neither ordinary knights nor servants with bows; for he had not prepared himself for the peril which, by common agreement, was to have been crossed the next day. Disregarding his own life in order to free the dying crowd, he forced his way into the rear and bravely met those slaughtering the ranks just ahead of him. He presumptuously attacked an unbelieving people a hundred times more numerous, and one greatly aided by the terrain. There a horse could not merely fail to run, but could scarcely stand; and the slower attack weakened the blow of a wound. Our men hurled their lances on slippery ground by their own strength, not that of their horses; while the enemy shot safely, bracing themselves against crags, trees, or stones. The released crowd fled, carrying their baggage or leading those who carried it, exposing in their place the king and counts to death. That lords should die so that servants might live would be a mournful exchange, unless the Lord of all had given such an example.

The flowers of France withered before they bore fruit in Damascus. At the account of this I am bathed in tears and groan from my inmost heart. Yet a sober mind may find consolation in this remedy: their valor will live on forever in the world; and, with their errors corrected, their fervent faith earned them at the end the crown of martyrdom. They fought, and each man made a heap of bodies around himself, lest he die unavenged; but the number of attackers, replenished from the multitude, did not diminish. Their horses were killed—horses which, though unable to run, could still bear the weight of arms—and mailed foot-soldiers were submerged amid the dense enemy as in a sea. As they spilled the entrails of the unarmored, they were divided one from another.

In this the king lost a small but glorious company; yet retaining a royal spirit, nimble and manly, he climbed by the roots of a certain tree—which God had provided for his safety—onto a crag. The enemy crowd climbed after him to capture him, while a more distant throng shot at him where he stood. But by God’s will his coat of mail protected him from the arrows; and with his bloodied sword, lest he be captured, he defended the crag, cutting off many hands and heads. Not recognizing him, finding him difficult to capture, and fearing an attack upon them, they returned before nightfall to gather plunder.

## Book Seven

[Col. 1237]

[Col. 1237D] The baggage-carrying crowd was still passing nearby, since the more densely it was packed, the more slowly it fled through the precipices. Coming to it, the king became a horseman from a foot-soldier and went with them as evening was already darkening. Then panting companies of knights came out from the tents to meet him. Seeing him alone, bloodied, and exhausted, they knew without asking, and groaned over what had happened; and they mourned, without consolation, nearly forty absent royal counts: namely, the count of Warenne and his brother, Evrard of Breteuil, Manasses of Bulles, Guacher of Montgaie, and others. But I do not name them all, lest the account be judged needlessly long.

They burned with spirit and were strong in numbers, but it was night, and the enemy occupied the opposite side of the deep abyss. Therefore they had neither place nor time to pursue further. They came with the king to the tents very late. Those who had been afraid there were now grieving in certain sorrow, but, with the Lord preserving them, were partly consoled. That night was sleepless, while each man either awaited one of his own who would never come, or joyfully received one arriving naked, his loss set aside. Meanwhile all the people judged Geoffrey worthy of hanging, because he had not obeyed the royal order concerning the day’s march. Perhaps he had his uncle, who shared his guilt, also as a protector against punishment; for since both were guilty, and the king’s uncle had to be spared, one ought not to be condemned without the other.

The following day dawned without dispelling the darkness of grief. The enemy army appeared, joyfully covering the mountains with its rich multitude. Our men, impoverished since yesterday, mourning both their men and possessions, cautiously and slowly advanced in formation to preserve what remained, all security having been driven away. But the king could not bear the poverty of the nobles and compassionately accommodated himself to those of lesser rank; he banished the want of both so generously that he seemed to have forgotten that he had lost anything with them.

Hunger was now afflicting the horses, which for many days had eaten little grass and no grain. Food was now failing the men, who still had twelve days’ journey ahead; and, having learned this, the enemy harassed us more confidently and, like a beast made fiercer by tasting blood, more greedily after profit. Against them the master of the Temple, Lord Evrard of Barres—venerable for religion and a model of virtue in warfare—vigilantly and prudently preserved his own resources and, as far as he could, bravely protected those of others. The king likewise loved and willingly imitated their example, and wished to bring the army into the same order, knowing that, if powerful hunger weakened its strength, unity of spirit would strengthen the weak.

Therefore it was decreed by common counsel that all should establish mutual fellowship and brotherhood with one another in this danger, rich and poor pledging their word that they would not flee from the field and that they would obey in all things the masters appointed over them. They appointed a master named Gislibert, with associates to each of whom he assigned fifty knights. They were commanded to endure those who harassed them until the command was given, because the enemy quickly fled; and, when ordered to resist, they were warned to return immediately when recalled. Once the rule was known, they were taught also to keep their positions, so that no one in the first rank should go to the last, and the guards of the flanks should not become confused.

Those whom nature or fortune had made foot-soldiers—for many nobles, their possessions lost or spent, went in the crowd in an unfamiliar manner—were stationed at the very rear, so that, having bows, they might withstand the enemy arrows. The king also, lord of the rules, wished to be subject to the rules of obedience. Yet no one dared to impose any command upon him, except that he should have a strong battle-line and, as lord and guardian of all, should reinforce the weak by sending them companions from it.

The march proceeded according to the command. We rejoiced as we descended from the mountains onto the plain and, protected by our guards, endured the enemy’s bold assaults with almost no loss. On the road were two streams a mile apart, whose muddy depths made crossing difficult. We crossed the first, waited on the far side for the rear ranks, and raised with our hands the weak pack animals from the mud. The rearward knights and foot-soldiers, almost mingled with the enemy, likewise crossed unharmed, defended by mutual courage.

[Col. 1240A] We were making for the second stream, intending to pass between two crags from whose summits the marching crowd could be shot with arrows. The Turks hurried to them from both sides, but our knights occupied one of them first. The Turks climbed the other and threw their hair down from their heads to their feet; we were told that this sign foretold that no fear would move them from such a place. But that sign then proved false, or signified nothing, because the mass of our foot-soldiers immediately drove them off. Yet while they contended from the mountaintop, the knights considered that their flight might be cut off between the two streams. Therefore, with permission from the master, all attacked them unanimously; and, avenging the deaths of their own men and their personal losses, killed those whom they could catch. Many of these, coming to the mud, found in a fitting place both death and burial.

While the fury of anger slew the fugitives and their flight grew longer, hunger was lighter for everyone and the day more joyful. But the Turks and Greeks devised many means for our destruction; for, though formerly enemies, they had entered into a pact for this purpose. Gathering flocks and herds from every side, they let them graze over and foul before us whatever fire could not burn. Consequently exhausted or dead horses were left upon the road, with their loads, tents, clothing, arms, and many other things, which our men burned lest they remain for the enemy—except those things which the poor carried away.

The army therefore ate horseflesh—and had it in abundance; animals unfit for carrying burdens provided a remedy against hunger. [Col. 1240C] Even the rich were content with such fare when they had a cake baked under the ashes from flour. By such provision hunger was moderated; and, with fraternity as our rule, we put the enemy to flight four times and always conquered them, protecting ourselves by prudent exertion as far as Sattalia without any loss of strength—except on that day when we made Geoffrey of Rancon the precursor of death and disaster.

In this city the emperor’s envoy Landulf, who, as he himself admitted, had come there partly with the Turks, was eagerly awaiting our destruction; or, should we arrive and inquire about the emperor, he was preparing an evasive reply. But because no one came to litigation, the complaints ceased: the hungry needed provisions, the weary rest. Thus he, conscious of guilt, compelled the nobles, on the pretext of legal proceedings, to renew peace with the emperor. Then the exceedingly heavy rains which had spared us on the road came upon us; soaked from above and below, in small tents—for the larger ones had been left behind—we celebrated the Purification of Blessed Mary. Certainly, throughout the whole journey, the king did not omit Mass or the Hours on a single day, neither because of flooding rains nor because of the pressure of enemies.

We had an abundance of food, though at a higher price than usual; but for the horses that remained we could find no fodder at any price, since the Greeks were deceitfully arranging matters thus, as many of our people said. They, however, pointed to the harshness of the country and said that they had none. Outside the city, as far as a certain river, lay a stony plain; beyond were enemies, preventing merchandise from coming in from outside and preventing fodder. [Col. 1241A] Thus the horses did not even have grass, unless armed soldiers led them out and brought them back.

The king, therefore, seeing that the few horses left were not recovering in rest but dying from hunger, and that none were offered for sale in the city, summoned the barons and spoke about proceeding onward. Where horses were dying of hunger, he said, soldiers had no place of rest. Moreover, it was the part of one who repented of his vow to delay it for the sake of rest; it was the part of the devout to hurry the weary and sick toward the goal of their undertaking, so that those whose souls God took from such labour might be crowned as martyrs.

But they, maintaining obedience to their lord and offering their vow such perseverance as was possible, said:

> “As it is the king’s part to command brave deeds, so it is the prudent soldier’s part to dare what is possible. All the ordinary soldiers of your army have, during these days, cast aside their arms and become foot-soldiers; [Col. 1241B] and many of the nobler men are among them. One cannot buy horses because he has lost or spent all that he possessed; another, though something remains to him, finds none for sale. They have learned from these citizens that by sea Antioch is three short, rich, and safe days’ journeys away, from harbour to harbour; whereas by land it is forty days, impassable because of torrents, occupied by enemies, and continuously afflicted by want. For this reason they do not wish to entrust themselves to the sea; and with them goes a multitude of foot-soldiers, whose strength for labour and means for sustenance now fail. The Greeks promise abundant shipping from all the neighbouring villages and islands. But we wish to die and live with you, and we shall gladly follow whatever course pleases you.”

The king answered them in royal fashion and in his own words:

> “While I am rich, no proven man shall lack; nor shall he be deemed proven who does not patiently endure poverty with me in necessity. Let us therefore select these persons, replenish them from our own resources, and commit to shipping the unarmed crowd [71] which has always burdened us, for whose sake provisions have been dearer and our march slower. Let us ourselves tread the road of our fathers, to whom incomparable valour gave worldly renown and heavenly glory.”

To this they replied:

> “We do not wish, nor are we able, to diminish the praise of your fathers; but they were treated more gently up to this point than we have been. For when they had crossed Constantinople and the strait, having attained the object of their vow, they immediately encountered the Turks and their lands; vigorous in military action, they enriched themselves by capturing cities [Col. 1241D] and castles. But we found deceitful Greeks in their place, whom, to our harm, we spared as Christians. Enervated by idleness, worn down by tedium and hardships, we have spent almost all that we had. Some, through foolish confidence or harsh poverty, have even sold their arms, or abandoned them when their horses died. What you command is indeed honourable, but for the reasons stated it is not safe. Still, putting labour and fear aside, we shall do it if we can find horses with which to restore the soldiers.”

When those sought were too few to suffice and, through weakness, of no use, they forced the king, willing or unwilling, to try the perils of the sea, so that God might permit his patience to be tested “in perils at sea, in perils in the wilderness, in perils from the nations, in perils from false brethren,” as with Paul (2 Corinthians 11).

Finally, the governor of the city and the emperor’s envoy were consulted on this affair. They gave an answer suited to their own pleasure and promised that ships would soon arrive for the entire army. Meanwhile winter inflicted what it had delayed: rain, snow, thunder, and lightning came; and the wind we had soon hoped for from the Lord was delayed for five weeks, as were, even more, the ships [72] which we expected on the Greeks’ promise. Knowing that they had only a short time, the Greeks practised every evil they could: they stripped us through the goods in the market and, so far as their counsels could achieve it, deprived us of life. Both healthy and sick found whatever their condition required, [Col. 1242B] but the amount of the price oppressed them. A hen cost ten solidi; a single egg, six or five denarii; one onion or head of garlic, seven or eight, the price varying with its size. We had two walnuts for one denarius. Those whose horse or mule remained exchanged it for bread, or sold it in the market like an ox. Such was our arrangement with the Greeks: to sell without payment and to buy dearly without measure.

The Turks learned from the Greeks that the soldiers lacked horses, and, taking advantage of that security, unanimously prepared to attack the army. When this became known to the king, he concealed near himself the wealthier men, who had still preserved their warhorses, though starving, and the brothers of the Temple. [Col. 1242C] When the Turks appeared and came on, he suddenly forced them, by killing them, to cross the river back again without a bridge, and thereafter to believe that excellent horses were plentiful in the army.

Meanwhile the Greeks made ready ships, as they did everything else, at an unheard-of price. One man paid four marks to Antioch, where, as they themselves had predicted, we were to arrive on the third day. A few small vessels were presented to the king as though a free gift from the governor and the emperor’s envoy; he distributed them among bishops and barons. He wished to take them, but bore the price with difficulty and, concealing useless complaints in silence, sought ships for the rest of the army as had been promised. Yet while the rich waited for the poor, they delayed this long, and by such robbery stripped both groups of their possessions. [Col. 1242D]

I believe we purchased the repose of this city more dearly than all the hardships of the entire journey. Those ignorant of these matters will say that the city ought to have been taken and vengeance exacted for the citizens’ treachery.
