Let them reflect that, hemmed in on right and left by domestic and foreign enemies, without provisions, we were besieged; that lofty towers cannot be thrown down without engines, nor double walls quickly undermined. The governor and the emperor’s envoy could indeed have been seized when they came to the king; but the citizens would not have surrendered the city for their hanging. It was abhorrent to the king, contrary to his custom, to take it by this treachery and to attempt the common danger without capturing it.

May God spare the German emperor, whose fate we were seeking to avoid and whose ignorant counsel we followed when we fell into these evils. But how shall God, the just judge, or man spare the Greek, who by deceitful cruelty killed so many Christians from both armies? [Col. 1243A]

Thus the mass of newly impoverished people, wearied, robbed of silver, corrupted by disease, and aware of the Greeks’ lie about the ships, came to the king and set before him their wish and poverty in words such as these:

> “Lord King, we rightly stand ashamed in the presence of your majesty; nevertheless, trusting in your goodness, we dare to ask this. When, trusting the Greeks, we refused to go with you by land, we were idle in one respect and deceived in another. Now, driven by poverty, we wish to do what we then refused, even without a leader. We are going to our death; but, God willing, we may be able to escape the present danger. Perhaps the sword of the Turks [Col. 1243B] will be more tolerable than the treachery of these citizens after your departure.”

The king pitied them with his customary compassion [74] and supplied their want with such lavish generosity that one would have thought he had previously spent nothing, or had thereafter neglected all concern for his own household. Then, wishing them to be safe on the road, he made an agreement with the emperor’s envoy and the governor: they were to receive five hundred marks from him; the Greeks were to escort them with a strong force beyond the two nearby rivers; afterwards they were to provide a suitable escort able to lead them safely to Tarsus. In the city the weak and infirm were to be received until, having recovered and found shipping, they could follow the others.

Greedy for silver and fearful of the Turks, the Greeks first spoke with the Turks and, as we then thought, [Col. 1243C] divided the payment with them. Returning with the wealthier citizens, they jointly swore the agreement as stated above. The silver was paid; they ordered the weak to enter the city and the others to prepare for departure on the following day. The king still provided for his people, gathering whatever horses he could find and giving them to proven soldiers. Fearing treachery where he had most often found it, he sent the Count of Flanders and Archambault of Bourbon as far as the departure of those people; he himself embarked with the blessing of those who remained.

On the following day the army on foot awaited its guides. And behold: the Turkish host, having learned through the Greeks that the king had departed, came against them as against certain prey. Against them the Count of Flanders and Archambault of Bourbon drew up their battle-lines—spirited, but slow, because they had few and weak horses. They met the enemy, fought, and put to flight those who had come for plunder. But since there was no one able to pursue them swiftly, few of them were killed.

After this they demanded from the governor, the emperor’s envoy, [Col. 1243D] and the citizens the fulfilment of the agreement they had sworn to the king. For the first time, pointing to the impossibility caused by the Turks and winter, they excused themselves. In this they lost several days and many words, and they could not overcome the Greeks by law, reason, or honour. At last, abandoning their complaint concerning the escort, they scarcely obtained permission for our people to lodge within the wall of a fortified work, and for a market to be supplied there until shipping arrived. Once this was done, the king’s men went to the ships, grieving that they could not avenge their wrongs. [Col. 1244A]

Then the Turks approached the city, entered and departed freely, and openly conferred with the Greeks. Our people saw themselves tightly enclosed between two kinds of enemies and walls, like sheep in a fold; those who dared neither go out nor enter could there be shot. The wall was low and curved, and so great a crowd could not cling to it; therefore those farther away lay exposed to wounds. From suitable positions the Turks discharged arrows and wounded or killed some.

Then courageous young men began to leap down from the wall, taking up bows, in order to defend their own lives and those of their companions, or to sell their deaths dearly. Seeking peace through force, they compelled the enemy to retreat farther away. They would have had peace, but the Greeks were killing them without inflicting wounds: the Greeks had shut up the healthy with the sick in a cramped and filthy place. [Col. 1244B] While hunger killed some as their money failed, and pestilence consumed others beside the corpses, many fell—not because the Greeks inflicted death, but because they waited for it.

For this reason two companies of three and four thousand brave men died lest they die, judging it the same thing to die outside and to live within. Taking up arms, they went out to cross two neighbouring but unequal rivers. They crossed the first easily, but at the second were stopped by a double obstacle. [76] The stream could be crossed only by swimming, and the enemy gathered there could be passed only by fighting; yet both could not be done at once. Therefore, turning back, they were routed, captured, or killed. The thirst of the Turks was quenched with their blood, and the Greeks’ deceit turned to violence.

The Turks returned to see those who remained [Col. 1244C] and thereafter bestowed generous alms upon the sick and poor. But the Greeks compelled the stronger persons into their service and beat them instead of paying wages. Some Turks bought our coins from their companions and distributed them with full hands among the poor; the Greeks, on the other hand, took away whatever remained from those who possessed anything.

Thus, fleeing cruel partners in the faith, they went safely to unbelievers who had compassion on them; and, as we heard, more than three thousand young men joined the departing Turks. O pity more cruel than any treachery! By giving bread, they took away faith, although it is certain that, content with service, they compelled no one to deny it. But God, execrating the city, struck its citizens so severely with sudden death [Col. 1244D] that many houses were left empty, and the survivors, stunned and afraid, considered abandoning it altogether. The emperor likewise, contrary to God in his judgment, because the city had provided the king with a market and shipping, stripped it completely of gold and silver. Thus God and the emperor held opposite views, yet each punished the city.

When the king had completed five weeks in that place, some of his ships were broken or damaged, yet, by God’s will, not sunk; he spent three more weeks being shipwrecked on the way to Antioch. The losses and perils he endured were severe, Father Suger; but you should be consoled that he survived. His labour will also benefit him, since he is known, safe amid perils and joyful after losses, to have borne all things steadfastly and wisely. [77] His one grievous adversity was that of his subjects, for whom he always provided according to his ability, judging that a king is born not for himself but for the benefit of others; and that, as it belongs to a king to have compassion, so it belongs to him never to fear poverty.

He subordinated royal caution and the protection of the first or last guard to valour; taking turns at night watch, he endured the cold of nights and the heat of days under his mail-shirt. In so many labours he was preserved whole and without medicine, through the practice of holiness. [Col. 1246A] For he always met the enemy’s power after receiving the divine sacraments, and, returning from the enemy, sought Vespers and Compline, always making God the alpha and omega of his actions. Liberal as a king, courageous as a prince, fierce as a soldier, lively as a young man, mature as an elder, he adapted himself to each place, time, and virtue; through valour he sought human favour, through religion divine grace.

[Col. 1245]

**78. The date of the solar eclipse mentioned by Odo at the end of Book IV above, col. 1228.**

(From an old parchment of the cathedral church of St Stephen at Châlons, a copy of which, received from the hand of the reverend Lord Cuissote, dean of that church, was sent to us by the Reverend Father Henri Bacio, rector of the college of Châlons.)

[Col. 1245B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Lest, through disuse, the darkness of forgetfulness be brought upon human minds concerning the person through whose agency our church was consecrated, we commit this to written record, so that future posterity may have something it can clearly recognize in times to come.

For this purpose, at the request of our venerable bishop Bartholomew, Pope Eugenius III came to this city and was honourably received. He was accompanied by the cardinal bishops: Alberic, cardinal bishop of Ostia; Imar, cardinal bishop of Tusculum; Jordan, cardinal priest of St Susanna; Julius, cardinal priest of St Marcellus; Hugh, cardinal priest of St Lawrence; Guy, chancellor and cardinal deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian; Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angelo; Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin; Humbald, cardinal of SS. John and Paul; Sigibert, cardinal of St Mark; Octavian, cardinal deacon [Col. 1245C] of St Nicholas in Carcere; Odo, cardinal deacon of St George; Guy, cardinal priest of St Lawrence in Damaso; Guy, cardinal deacon [79] of St Mary in Portico; John, cardinal deacon of St Mary the New; Guy, cardinal deacon of St Potentiana; Haribert, cardinal deacon of St Anastasia; John, cardinal of St Adrian Martyr; our bishop Bartholomew; Theobald, bishop of Paris; Bernard, bishop of Auxerre; and Hugh, bishop of Nevers.

The aforesaid bishops consecrated the church by walking around it inside and outside and sprinkling it with holy water. The pope consecrated the high altar in honour of the Holy Trinity, St Mary, St Stephen the protomartyr, St John the Baptist, St Valerius and St Vincent, martyrs, and SS. Chrysanthus and Daria. At the request of our venerable bishop Bartholomew, he deposited in the altar, together with another reliquary, relics of the virgin Nympha, which he carried with him. When these things had been done, he solemnly celebrated Mass. Our bishop and Hugh, bishop of Nevers, served as the cantors at the Mass. As soon as the Mass had begun, an eclipse of the sun visibly appeared. After the celebration of Mass, the Apostolic Lord went with the bishops and cardinals into the bishop’s garden, where he delivered a sermon to the people on the feast of that day.

[Col. 1246C]

Done publicly at Châlons, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November [26 October], in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1147, while the most glorious King Louis, son of King Louis, was reigning in Gaul. In that same year, inspired by God’s mercy, he had set out abroad with his wife, the venerable queen Eleanor, and a very great army, for the liberation of the Church of Jerusalem.

> **[Note: [Col. 1245C] Robert of Torigni, in the Appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1147:** “There was a solar eclipse on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], on Sunday, from the second hour until the fifth hour.” Read “the seventh day before the Kalends,” which the letter E assigned to that year also shows to have been Sunday. In Claude Robert, *Gallia Christiana*, under Bartholomew, the fifty-fifth bishop of Châlons: “In his presence Eugenius III dedicated the greater basilica in 1147, on the seventh day before the Ides of November [7 November].” Read: “the seventh day before the Kalends.” The Sammarthani, in the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, give the year as 1148, from, as they say, the records of Châlons. [Col. 1245D] But in these records the year is noted as 1147.
>
> Concerning the hour and magnitude of this eclipse at new moon, which we read was observed both at Châlons and Constantinople, the Reverend Father Peter Courcier of our Society, theologian and distinguished astronomer, when asked by me, answered thus in a letter dated Pont-à-Mousson, 11 June 1658: “The middle of the eclipse ought to have occurred at Châlons at 9:20 in the morning; its magnitude there was more than ten and a half digits. At Constantinople its middle and greatest obscuration ought to have occurred at 1:12 in the afternoon; its magnitude there was almost six digits.” All this accords well with the testimony of writers of that age who saw it. Robert of Torigni extends the duration of the eclipse from the second to the fifth hour; namely, using the ancient unequal hours, counted from sunrise, as in the Gospel. Thus the third and a half hour was the middle of the eclipse, while the second was its beginning, at which Pope Eugenius III happened to begin the solemn Mass at Châlons [Col. 1246D] at the principal altar of St Stephen. It was then about the eighth hour after midnight. Moreover, when Odo reports that at Constantinople the sun was seen in the shape of half a loaf, that one half shone, and that it hid the rays of a semicircle, he could not have expressed more distinctly an eclipse of six digits.]**

[Col. 1247]

# CHRONICLE OF CLAIRVAUX

Continued from the year of Christ 1147 to the year 1192. By an anonymous monk of Clairvaux. (From an old manuscript of the same monastery.)

[Col. 1247A]

**81. In the year of the Lord 1147**, Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, preached the cross in Germany and performed many great miracles, including raising the dead man mentioned in the book of the *Miracles* of Lord Herbert.

**In the year of the Lord 1148**, Blessed Malachy died at Clairvaux.

**In the year of the Lord 1153**, Blessed Bernard died; Abbot Robert presided for three and a half years.

**In the year of the Lord 1154**, Roger, king of Sicily, died; and Gunnarius, judge of Sardinia, surrendered himself to Clairvaux.

**In the year of the Lord 1155**, St Milo of Thérouanne flourished, of whom the *Life of Lord Norbert* says:

> “In Norbert faith, in Bernard charity, [Col. 1247B] in Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, humility shone forth.”

**In the year of the Lord 1157**, after Abbot Robert died at Clairvaux, Fastred of Cambron was elected abbot. His miraculous life and promotion are recorded in the book of the *Miracles* of Lord Herbert. In his first year died at Clairvaux Abbot Berlo, formerly of Savigny, who came to the Order with thirty abbeys and submitted himself to Blessed Bernard. This is he who rests near Abbot Robert with other persons.

**In the year of the Lord 1159**, the general schism began between Pope Alexander and Octavian, and lasted nearly nineteen years.

[Col. 1247C]

**In the year of the Lord 1161**, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres and formerly prior of Clairvaux, resigned his bishopric and returned to Clairvaux, to the embraces of his Rachel.

**In the year of the Lord 1162**, Henry, bishop of Beauvais, brother of the king and a monk of Clairvaux, became archbishop of Reims; and Lord Fastred, abbot of Clairvaux, was promoted to be abbot of Cîteaux. Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Igny, was then promoted to be abbot of Clairvaux and presided for about four years. Being excellently trained in letters, he produced a notable work on the *Song of Songs* and wrote several other books and sermons.

**In the year of the Lord 1163.** On the three kings: how, under Emperor Frederick, they came from Milan to Cologne through Archbishop [Col. 1247D] Rainald. To the same year we assign the matters related in the book of the *Miracles* of Lord Herbert concerning the mortality that occurred at Grand Selve Abbey under Abbot Pons.

[Col. 1248A]

**In the year of the Lord 1164**, the holy Abbot Fastred of Cîteaux died at Paris in the pope’s presence. In the same year, on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November], Geoffrey, formerly bishop of Langres, died at Clairvaux.

**In the year of the Lord 1165**, Alan, bishop of Auxerre, resigned his bishopric and returned to Reigny; he often stayed at Clairvaux, where he afterwards died. In the same year, Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Clairvaux, seeing hostility stirred up against him by certain persons, whether justly or unjustly, resigned the abbacy. Pons of Auvergne, a noble and religious man, who had been abbot at Grand Selve, became abbot of Clairvaux. He presided for five years.

[Col. 1248B]

**In the year of the Lord 1166**, the storm of schism raged between the false pope, whom the emperor supported, and Pope Alexander, whom our Order favoured. It therefore happened that monks of our Order were expelled from the Empire, especially from Burgundy, and that the abbeys of France were divided up.

**At the end of the year of the Lord 1170**, Pons, abbot of Clairvaux, became bishop of Clermont in Auvergne. Lord Gerald, abbot of Fossanova, was chosen abbot of Clairvaux. He was a native of Auvergne. He presided for five years. We possess his *Life*.

**At the beginning of the year of the Lord 1171**, Blessed Thomas of Canterbury was martyred; and in the same year [Col. 1248C] St Gundric the hermit died in England; we possess his *Life*.

**84. In the year of the Lord 1172**, Gilbert, formerly abbot of Hoiland in England, who composed sermons on the *Song of Songs* in the manner of Blessed Bernard, died at Reigny.

**In the year of the Lord 1173**, St Aymon, monk of Savigny, died; his *Life* is held at Clairvaux.

**In the year of the Lord 1174**, St Peter of Tarentaise, archbishop, died in the twenty-third year of his pontificate. His *Life* was written by Lord Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Clairvaux. In the same year the church of Clairvaux was dedicated, Blessed Bernard was canonized, and his body was elevated; Lord [Col. 1248D] Guichard, archbishop of Lyons and formerly abbot of Pontigny, was present. In the following year, at the general chapter, they adopted the Office of Blessed Bernard and the Office of the Trinity.

**In the year of the Lord 1175**, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends [Col. 1249A] of November [16 October], Gerald, abbot of Clairvaux, was martyred at Igny.

**In the year of the Lord 1176**, Lord Henry, abbot of Hautecombe, was promoted to be abbot of Clairvaux and presided for about four years. As soon as his son, Lord Gerald of Fossanova, had become abbot of Clairvaux before him, he put Lord Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Clairvaux and then devoted to contemplation, in charge of Fossanova. Likewise, when he himself was transferred from Hautecombe to Clairvaux, he arranged for the same Abbot Geoffrey to be promoted to Hautecombe in his place.

**In the year of the Lord 1178**, the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Sorra in Sardinia, died at Clairvaux during the dedication of Clairvaux and was buried beside [Col. 1249B] Bishop Geoffrey. Shortly afterwards the bishop of Auxerre was placed with them. In this year Lord Herbert, monk of Clairvaux, who had been abbot of Mores, composed at Clairvaux the book of *Miracles*. Therefore, whenever the same book says, “this or that happened three, four, or seven years ago,” we should begin with this year and calculate backwards. This is the testimony of Lord Goswin, formerly monk of Clairvaux, who lived for a long time at Chéminon and died at Boulancourt.

Goswin wrote a certain book of *Miracles* for Gerald, abbot of Eberbach, and says in its prologue:

> “John, prior of Clairvaux, caused a fine volume to be compiled, in which miracles and visions of different persons were written down for the edification of readers. Moreover, Lord Herbert, who had once been chaplain to Lord Henry the abbot, published a very large volume of diverse visions and miracles. By God’s providence, he afterwards became archbishop of Sardinia.”

These are Goswin’s words. A monk of Clairvaux named Ancher accompanied this Herbert; he became bishop of Sorra and, after Herbert, archbishop of Torres. At this time the virgin of Christ Emelina was buried at Boulancourt; Lord Goswin mentioned above related certain marvels about her.

**In the year of the Lord 1179**, reconciliation took place [Col. 1249D] between Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick; and the same pope held a great council in Rome, in the Lateran palace. [86] At that council Lord Henry, abbot of Clairvaux, was made cardinal bishop of Albano. In the same year King Philip was crowned at Reims and reigned for about forty-four years. Peter of Igny, one-eyed, was elected abbot of Clairvaux; we possess his *Life*. He is found to have presided for seven years.

**In the year of the Lord 1180**, at Trois-Fontaines, during a visitation conducted by Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, at the beginning of March, it happened that the venerable Abbot Alard was killed by a hypocritical monk.

**In the year of the Lord 1181**, the venerable Eskil, archbishop of the Danes, died [Col. 1250A] at Clairvaux after taking the habit of the Order. He had long remained at Clairvaux and had appointed in his place an archbishop in Denmark named Absalon. Henry, bishop of Albano, sent as legate into Burgundy, deposed two archbishops, of Lyons and Narbonne; by a miracle he captured the castle of heretics called Val; he presided at the general chapter at Cîteaux; and in the following year, in the time of Pope Lucius, returned to the curia.

**In the year of the Lord 1182**, a community was sent from Clairvaux to found the abbey of Boccan in Hungary.

**In the year of the Lord 1183.** Up to this time St Hugh, abbot of Bonnevaux, lived. He is the one who first freed [Col. 1250B] a woman encased in iron from iron needles; afterwards St Peter of Tarentaise perfectly healed her from stakes—that is, wooden pins—protruding from her arm. Another miracle is ascribed to this St Hugh and is contained in the book of Lord Herbert: the miracle of Cursor, who after death confessed his sins to him in tears. The rest concerning the life of this saint, Lady Prioress, if you should wish to have it, you will, God willing, have a conversation with us.

**In the year of the Lord 1184.** In the house of nuns situated near Boulancourt, under the care of that house, there flourished at this time, in the highest repute, a certain virgin of Christ, Ascelina, prioress of that place. Concerning her most excellent life, a few matters occurring here ought briefly to be inserted from the fairly lengthy narrative of Lord Goswin.

The mother of this Ascelina was a blood relative of Blessed Bernard and Bishop Geoffrey, born in a village near La Ferté-sur-Aube. When she was about thirty years old and subject to a husband’s authority, she prayed the Lord to deign to take from her whatever appeared to obstruct her salvation. When her husband had died, she left the world with her five-year-old daughter, submitting herself to Blessed Bernard’s counsel. This concerns the mother.

Ascelina herself, still a girl of five, in a more secluded place stretched out her hands to heaven, raised her eyes, and prayed the Lord to deign henceforth to preserve the virginity entrusted to her. This was then a cause of great astonishment. Likewise, [Col. 1250D] while her mother was pregnant, she heard from a man seen in white clothing that she carried a daughter who would be of great merit before God. And St Glodesind of Metz appeared to the mother and said: “Your daughter, without doubt compared with me, will be equal to me in merits,” etc.

Boulancourt Abbey adopted the Cistercian Order, and mother and daughter, with Blessed Bernard’s permission, transferred to the abbey of nuns at Poligny. There Ascelina illuminated all the sisters by her example. The abbess of the place was the daughter of Blessed Bernard’s brother, etc.

**In the year of the Lord 1186**, the most reverend Peter, the one-eyed abbot, died at Clairvaux. Lady Prioress, I believe you possess his *Life*, and therefore I pass over him briefly. Then Garnier, abbot of Alba Ripa, [Col. 1251A] was promoted to be abbot of Clairvaux and is known to have presided for six years.

**In the year of the Lord 1187**, the land of Jerusalem was lost.

**In the year of the Lord 1187**, Lord Henry, bishop of Albano, appointed legate by Pope Gregory VIII, carried out the office entrusted to him with every diligence. First, in accordance with his instructions, he ordained that from the present year for five years the faithful people should eat Lenten food every Friday, and that on Wednesday and Saturday all in health should abstain from meat. The lord pope also forbade himself, his brother cardinals, and servants the use of meat even on Monday throughout the same years.

The said legate came from there to Mainz, after the meeting of king and emperor at Yvois. There the emperor was signed with the cross along with sixty-eight great princes. From there he came to Liège, where he signed Bishop Ralph with the cross; and, by his own arrangement, transferred sixty-six clerics, who had surrendered their benefices into his hand, from one church to another so that they might both avoid simony and not lose their benefices. In this year are assigned the matters contained in the short history of Wales concerning Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 1251B] who belonged to the Cistercian Order, and concerning his legation.

Meanwhile and amid these affairs, Henry, cardinal bishop of Albano, issued a certain treatise to his brethren at Clairvaux. He laboured for peace between the king of France and the king of England, and between Count Philip of Flanders and the Church of Arras. This lamp of such quality was extinguished at Arras on the Kalends of January [1 January]. His body was brought back to Clairvaux with honour and buried in the middle of the two saints, behind the high altar: that is, between St Malachy and St Bernard. [Col. 1252A]

**In the year of the Lord 1190**, a notable miracle occurred concerning an image of the glorious Virgin Mary and an image of her infant Son. You will find it at the end of the book of Clairvaux’s *Miracles*, under “The Cupboard of Psalters.”

**In the year of the Lord 1191**, in the lands overseas, the city of Acre was recovered by the Christians. Among the other princes who died before Acre, the noble Count Philip of Flanders also died. [Col. 1252B] His bones were brought to Clairvaux and honourably placed in a stone sarcophagus in his own chapel.

**In the year of the Lord 1192**, Blessed Malachy was canonized. Manasses, bishop of Langres, returned from overseas with the king of France, died in the same year, and was buried at Clairvaux. Garnier, abbot of Clairvaux, was elected bishop of Langres. At Cologne at this time died the reverend and most religious priest Everard. Lord Goswin, who saw these things in the spirit, related much concerning his life and death and concerning the places through which his soul passed after death.

[Col. 1251]

## Epitaphs of Certain Illustrious Men  
*(From a manuscript codex of the monastery of La Charité, diocese of Besançon, Cistercian Order.)*

**90. Epitaph of Louis, king of the Franks, composed by Master Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris.**

[Col. 1251C]

*(This epitaph of Louis, said to be Louis VII, or “the Younger,” is reported by Duchesne, *Rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 444, but without the author’s name.)*

That pious Louis the elder passes on to his heir—  
in name, throne, faith, and no less in piety.

The Church, a handmaid, sorrowful and poor under some king,  
flourished beneath this king: free, glad, and strong.

[Col. 1252C] A humble king, a peaceful king, he set before himself  
David and Solomon as examples, ruling himself and his own.

Chaste as far as the bond of marriage permitted;  
gentle as far as the rule of justice allowed.

Fasting, watching, praying, he was devoted to every manner  
of divine worship and service.

His tongue poured out living prayers, his devout eyelids tears,  
his diligent hand coins for the poor.

By these merits the holy man seized heaven by force;  
taken to heaven, the earth gives you back to yourself.

[Col. 1251]

**91. Verses of Master Simon, surnamed “Golden Goat,” canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, a most eminent and rapid composer of verse, which he wrote at the request of Count Henry.**

### I. Epitaph of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux

[Col. 1251C]

*(This epitaph was published with the works of Saint Bernard, without naming its author.)*

Behold, hidden at Clairvaux is its most illustrious abbot,

[Col. 1252C] greatest among the great, yet small in his own eyes.

The summit of religious life, light of the world, glory of monks,  
voice of the Word, sanction of peace, lover of justice.

Accomplished, swift; exalted, poor, rich  
in arts, intellect, lineage, clothing, and goods.

[Col. 1253A] He needs a title of praise whose praise is not addressed to all,  
whose honor and fame can still increase.

Yet if I would praise him whom the world still mourns and proclaims,  
my praise lacks praise.

Hard things he endured, evil things he loathed, and all things he built up;  
vain things he despised; God and rest he loved, and now possesses.

### II. Likewise, verses by the same author on Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, formerly abbot of Pontigny

**EPITAPH**

The bishop of Auxerre, renowned throughout the world,  
ascending heaven in mind, left his limbs upon the earth.

Outstanding in understanding, birth, and goodness; illustrious and honorable—  
Hugh, brief in name, abundant in speech and hand.

**92.** Both wealthy and poor: poor for himself, rich toward the needy.

[Col. 1253B] Unequal to none, and none was his equal.

Service, terror, favor, gifts, and prayers  
could not recall him from the norm of justice.

In him alone the virtue of mercy triumphed,  
when after justice he was bound to be merciful.

As October closed its twice-five days,  
he closed the end of his days, now possessing a day without end.

### III. Likewise, verses by the same author on Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis

There has fallen the Church’s flower, jewel, crown, pillar,  
banner, shield, helmet, light, and summit:

Abbot Suger, exemplar of virtue and equity,  
grave in compassion, compassionate in gravity.

Great-souled, wise, eloquent, generous, honorable,

[Col. 1253C] present in judgments in body, self-possessed in mind.

Through him the king prudently governed the affairs of the realm:  
he governing the king, the king was as though king by his kingship.

While the king remained overseas for many years,  
this man presided over the kingdom, performing the king’s office.

[Col. 1254A] What scarcely any other could join in himself, he joined:  
a worthy man among men and a good man before God.

He adorned the noble Church’s see with praise, repelled its losses with strength, and enlarged its choir with men.

The seventh light of the Theophany took away his light;  
the true Theophany gave true light to the man.

### IV. **93.** Likewise, verses by the same author on Count Theobald

That Count Theobald has passed away, renowned everywhere—  
more truly father than son of Mother Church.

Great in honor, mighty in arms, distinguished in birth,  
keen in mind, clear in speech, noble in bearing.

Humble toward the lowly, terrible to the timid, harsh to the unjust,  
simple toward the simple: he was all things to all.

For the joyful, the poor, monks, and the sick he provided

[Col. 1254B] without ceasing help, gifts, churches, and houses.

His work was to preserve the good and punish the guilty;  
his work was to live justly and speak what was just.

You could see every virtue shining in him;  
and they contended together to make the man admirable.

Our France mourns, bereft of so great a protector:  
as she stood while he stood, so she lies now that he lies.

Thus the tenth day of January was his last,  
for whom one day with God is better than thousands.

### V. Epitaph of Eugene, Roman Pope

The honor of City and world, but now the grief of City and world:  
a ruler mighty in the world lies as dust in the City.

Into this sacred vessel, by the gracious favor of the full fountain,  
God freely poured gifts pleasing to heaven.

[Col. 1254C] Great God, mighty to give great gifts, through you he possessed  
a tongue skilled to teach the faith and a hand trained to give material aid.

Angelic manners, devotion, and an honorable end  
give him to you as your servant; grant rest to your servant.

# On the Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, Written by John the Hermit

[Col. 1253]

## Preface

**94.** John was called “the Hermit,” I think not by condition but by surname—for we have learned that several families bearing this name still survive in Gaul. He wrote two books *On the Life of Saint Bernard*, at the urging of Peter, cardinal-bishop of Tusculum, and Herbert, archbishop of Torres in Sardinia. Both were his closest friends; hence he calls Peter his “most beloved Father,” and Herbert a “Soldier of Christ,” indicating that Herbert was most closely bound to him by confidence and affection.

He appears to have followed the example of the Evangelist of the same name. For as that John wrote his Gospel last, as Jerome says in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, namely in order to gather what his predecessors had omitted, so this John likewise committed to a commentary those things concerning Saint Bernard which no one else had yet recorded.

The time of this writing may be inferred from Peter. It is certain that Pope Alexander III created him cardinal-bishop of Tusculum in December 1178. He seems first to have become known to John the Hermit when, not long afterward, he came into Gaul as legate of the Apostolic See and, among other acts, removed certain abuses from the convent of nuns of Saint-Cyr, as Stephen of Tournai teaches us in Letter 88 to G., archbishop of Sens. He was certainly absent from Rome in 1179, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April], the date on which we have seen a bull given at the Lateran by Alexander III to the nuns of Ulmet, Peter being absent and other cardinals subscribing. But Peter had returned to the City by the election of Pope Lucius III in August 1181, and was soon made vicar of the City by that pope; thereafter he remained constantly at Rome for many years.

**95.** Yet John the Hermit himself clearly reveals the year in which he was writing, about the middle of Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*. He says that he received what he was then writing from Abbot Robert, Saint Bernard’s nephew, who had lived in the monastery under the yoke of regular discipline for more than sixty-seven years. For if Robert entered Cîteaux with Saint Bernard in 1113, as is probable, the sixty-seventh year of his monastic life was 1180.

Therefore anyone is mistaken who supposes this man to be the John the Hermit mentioned by Angelus Manrique in the *Cistercian Annals* under the year 1115: the one who promoted the foundation of Morimond and inhabited a cell in a marshy and nearly inaccessible place not far from the town of Aigremont, on the borders of Champagne and Lorraine. For this John belonged to a much later age. He says that he had not even seen Saint Bernard; yet he relates that he was asked to write something concerning him because, as he himself says in his letter to Herbert, “while still a boy, I had formerly been constant among some of Bernard’s disciples.”

But, unless my conjecture deceives me, this John was prior of Clairvaux: the very same person of whom Goswin, once a monk of Clairvaux, writes in the prologue of the book of *Miracles* addressed to Gerard, abbot of Eberbach: “John, prior of Clairvaux,” he says, “caused to be compiled a fine volume in which miracles and visions of various persons were recorded for the edification of readers.”

And I am mistaken if I have not handled with these hands the very volume of Prior John mentioned by Goswin, which the most reverend Lord Claude L’Argentier, of pious memory, abbot of Clairvaux, most graciously showed me. In it, together with the *Life of Saint Bernard* by John the Hermit and the *Life of Blessed Peter, Prior of Jully*, are found Herbert’s three books *On Miracles*, other visions, and very many anonymous miracles.

Thus, in maintaining that Prior John was the compiler of this codex, Goswin did not deny that he was an author. Since the work is composed from various little writings, some written by John the Hermit and some by others, I do not hesitate to affirm that this John the Hermit was himself prior of Clairvaux—perhaps the same man whose commemoration the Cistercian Menology records on 21 May.

Finally, reader, you should be advised that the Clairvaux codex, **96** compiled through the care and command of Prior John, was called by some the book of Herbert *On Miracles*, because Herbert’s work on this subject, divided into three books, occupied by far the largest part of that volume. Accordingly, in certain editions of Saint Bernard’s works, the remarkable account is cited “from the book of Abbot Herbert” concerning a volume containing certain miracles of Saint Bernard which was found undamaged after having been left outdoors through carelessness and lying exposed for about a month to heavy and continual rains.

But it should have been cited from John the Hermit’s letter to Peter, bishop of Tusculum, which introduces the *Life of Saint Bernard* written by him. It is found in the same Clairvaux codex as Herbert’s book *On Miracles*, but written in another hand and a different style. Herbert himself says not a word about this matter.

[Col. 1255]

# Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, by John the Hermit

See above, the fourth Life of Saint Bernard, col. 531.

# On the Life of Blessed Peter, Prior of the Nuns’ Monastery of Jully and Monk of Molesme

[Col. 1255]

## Preface

**97–132.** We formerly copied this Life from a codex of the monastery of La Charité, diocese of Besançon, Cistercian Order, and afterward compared it with the Clairvaux codex, in which, however, the preface was lacking. The hands of these codices seemed to reveal to us that the author was a contemporary of the Blessed Peter about whom he writes.

Now, since it is highly probable that this Peter, companion of Stephen his countryman—the third abbot of the Cistercians—was one of the twenty-one monks of Molesme who founded the Cistercian community, and likewise one of those who returned to Molesme with Abbot Robert after two years, so that Peter belongs to both the Benedictine and Cistercian Orders, it may seem surprising that the day dedicated to his annual commemoration is found inscribed in no Martyrology or Menology of either Order.

For he lacks none of the ornaments of complete sanctity, unless perhaps he has not been vindicated by apostolic authority—which is uncertain. Certainly, he seems to deserve a pre-eminent place among the illustrious men not formally recognized, with whom the annals of the Benedictines and Cistercians are strewn.

But the reason for this silence is readily available: the plundering of the archives of Molesme and the ancient destruction of the nuns’ house at Jully—of which today nothing remains beyond the ground itself and a small chapel bearing the title of a male priory. Through these calamities both Peter’s sacred remains perished and whatever had been recorded concerning him in calendars or necrologies. Thus, apart from this Life, as though recovered from shipwreck, **133** nothing concerning him appears to survive.

Indeed, this Life is all the more precious because it is so rare. It was not even known to Angelus Manrique, author of the *Cistercian Annals*. The things which he reported concerning the blessed passage to heaven of Humberga, or Humbelina, sister of Saint Bernard—certainly derived from these Acts of Blessed Peter—he received from the French writer William the Fleming, who had used this very Life of Blessed Peter. You, reader, will drink more purely from the fountain itself.

But observe, in chapter 11, the erroneous reading of the Clairvaux codex, where King Philip is said to have married a daughter of Theobald, Count of Champagne, in accordance with Blessed Peter’s prophecy. This is certainly false. For Aalis, daughter of Theobald, was the third wife of King Louis VII, surnamed the Younger, and mother of Philip Augustus. Therefore we have retained the name Louis in the text from the Charité codex.

[Col. 1257]

# Life of Saint Peter, Prior of the Nuns’ Monastery of Jully and Monk of Molesme

## Prologue

[Col. 1257A] **134.** Whenever we celebrate the festivals of the saints in their annual recurrence, we ought, in praise of Christ, to recount some of their deeds suitable for the profit of Christian faith. For whatever is praiseworthy in his saints is truly Christ’s gift.

Indeed, by praising his saints we cease to be children of wrath and become accustomed to be children of mercy. And though we cannot be made equal to those same saints by the merit of our deeds, yet through the merit of our praise and veneration of them, and through their intercession, we shall somehow be able to become like them.

By the favor of divine mercy, we believe that we shall share in the recompense of those whose holy memory we strive to celebrate in worship; namely, because in our veneration of his righteous ones we revere the presence of the same Lord who is their head, who [Col. 1257B] says: “Whoever receives one whom I send receives him who sent him” (John 13). Likewise, we do not doubt that in praising the righteous we praise the same Lord, as the Prophet indicates in saying: “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Psalm 150).

Therefore we ought [Col. 1258A] to praise glorious men in their generations, men great in virtue and endowed with wisdom. Though their bodies may have met whatever death, they nevertheless rest in peace, and their names live through generations of generations. We ought both to declare their wisdom to the peoples and solemnly proclaim their praise in the churches.

From their company let us exalt Blessed Peter, prior of Jully, with more illustrious praises. Many volumes might have been written concerning his deeds and virtues, had sloth—the companion of negligence—not besieged his fellow monks. Entangled in worldly concerns, they suppressed in ruinous silence a work most worthy of reverence.

But his devoted daughters, over whom, by God’s gift, he presided and among whom he died and was buried, gathered for themselves the few surviving fragments concerning his Life. By divine grace assisting us, we have reduced these to a little book lest they perish: so that through sweet remembrance he may live on earth in human mouths, he whom it is evident reigns in heaven with the Lord of spirits.

Here ends the prologue.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 1257]

### I

Saint Peter, then, was a native of England, born to parents noble according to worldly rank. When the years of childhood had passed, he began with a receptive mind to labor in the study of the liberal arts. He pursued this throughout childhood and youth, fixing his mind upon it with fuller attention until manhood.

[Col. 1257C] **136.** By such exercise in learning he drank in the food of divine wisdom, so that the more he was filled, the more he hungered, as God’s Wisdom itself says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24).

He also frequently attended church assemblies, and whatever was there recited from the divine Scriptures he stored in the treasury of his heart. When he had departed, he pondered with most intent meditation what he had learned. Thus, while still of tender age, he began to store grains of divine seed in the granary of his heart, so that when older he might have something with which to refresh his hungry spirit, or from which to dispense to his fellow servants in due season their measure of spiritual wheat.

Although as a boy he attended school with boys, he avoided their frivolity. Seeking no idleness, but attending to his own profit, he presented himself in a sense as more cloistered than scholastic. He most willingly [Col. 1257D] read those things which formed character, nourished devotion, produced contempt for the world, and impressed upon his heart the discipline of holiness.

He had assumed a disciplined manner and a worthy bearing of his whole body. Thus the outward signs of virtues visible in him made him beloved by all [Col. 1258B] and venerable: a less elaborate care of body and clothing, rarer speech, a more cheerful expression, a more modest gaze, a more measured walk, and the beauty of self-restraint.

Finally, giving himself to the teaching of the Gospel and not being a deaf hearer, he began in childhood to place the building of good works firmly upon the rock, which he happily completed in old age.

### II

**137.** Saint Peter, then, setting his heart upon the law of life and discipline, began with utmost earnestness to turn from evil and do good. And rightly so, for on these two duties the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

Hearing the Lord in the Gospel show the paths of life and say, “Whoever does not leave father and mother, brothers and sisters, and all that he has, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), he determined, like another Abraham, to depart as a pilgrim from his land, kindred, and father’s house. After both parents had died, he bade farewell to his brothers and only sister and, leaving everything he possessed, followed Christ calling him.

In his heart he sang and said: “Direct my way before you, O Lord” (Psalm 5); “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior; I have waited for you all the day” (Psalm 24); and: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth. Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Psalm 85).

Leaving his native soil and crossing the English sea under God’s guidance, while his mind dwelt in heaven, Blessed Peter came as a pilgrim and stranger into Gaul. There he remained for a time, visiting the shrines of saints and frequenting the company of religious people. Neither by day nor night did he cease from divine discourse and prayer.

At last, while entering the regions of Burgundy as a devout explorer of holy places, he found a young man of most continent life, English by nation and named Stephen. Led by the same desire as Peter, Stephen had made his way into that region. Peter saw and approved his life and character and joined himself to him as friend and companion.

Thus, having entered into a covenant of holy fellowship, they lived together, **138** striving to outdo one another in showing honor, restraining every impulse toward wrongdoing and fleshly impurity, putting to death their own desires, and sacrificing unlawful cravings. They guarded their hearts with all diligence, knowing that life proceeds from them.

They devoted themselves so earnestly to prayer that every day they sang the entire Psalter in alternating verses. At length, divinely inspired, they set out for Rome for the sake of prayer. Entering the shrines of the apostles Peter and Paul, they offered before the sight of the divine majesty the calves of their lips and a sacrifice of the heart fattened with the oil of inward devotion.

They also visited the churches of other saints, everywhere knocking upon divine ears with most earnest prayer and everywhere offering a rich whole burnt offering for the remission of their own sins and those of their companions, and for gaining the gifts of the heavenly promise. When they had satisfied their personal devotion, they left the City and returned to Burgundy, whence they had come. By the Lord’s providence they arrived at Molesme. There they cut off the hair of their heads, exchanged secular clothing for the religious habit, and wholly dedicated themselves to divine service.

### III

Blessed Peter, then, having entered the monastery, shone out in all his conduct like the morning star among the stars, like a great lamp. He emulated the perfect in goodness, set before himself the virtues of saints as examples, and strove to present himself as a sanctified vessel so that he might receive God as a dwelling guest within the lodging of his mind.

He did not sow evils in the furrows of injustice, nor reap the fruits of scandals. He was swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. There was in him no root of avarice, no swelling of pride or arrogance. He restrained the enclosure of his mouth from idle and vain speech [Col. 1260A] and permanently abstained from detraction by silence.

At appointed times he applied himself to reading and at appointed times to prayer. Since the monastic custom did not permit him to recite the Psalter with his companion Stephen as they had been accustomed to do in the world, they imposed this rule upon themselves: each day one would chant half the Psalter, and the other would complete the remaining half. Blessed Peter retained this practice nearly to the end of his life.

At one time, while Blessed Peter was staying, at the abbot’s command, in one of the cells belonging to the abbey, it happened that the new Cistercian planting—which, fleeing the tumult of peoples and the whirlpool of the world, strove in solitude to devote itself to God alone—was deprived at once of father and shepherd. Seeking the compassionate assistance of its mother, it, by the counsel of God-fearing men, canonically appointed the aforesaid Stephen as its abbot.

[Col. 1260B] Peter prayed most devoutly and continually before the Lord for Stephen’s prosperity and welfare. Reflecting that his friend was burdened by various cares and could not complete the half of the Psalter assigned to him, this excellent man of prayer undertook to complete the whole on behalf of both himself and his companion. O man supported by love! O true disciple of Christ and imitator of the Apostle, who says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

### IV

It once happened that the man of God, hindered by the affairs of certain laypersons, delayed longer than usual in rendering his daily Psalter. Then, after [Col. 1260C] the sixth hour, mindful of his vowed obligation, he withdrew to an unoccupied and secluded place; asking pardon for his negligence, he began to sing the customary Psalter.

When he had completed the greater part of it and pronounced the verse, “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm 103), he saw at his left the one who transforms himself into an angel of light. Approaching Peter, he took the codex which Peter held in his hand as though to read it. Running here and there and muttering certain things with foul mouth, he distracted God’s servant from prayer.

As Peter continued to pay attention to him, behold, the angel of the Lord stood at his right. At his appearance that malign being fled, throwing down the Psalter which he had unworthily held.

Then Blessed Peter, strengthened by the angel of light, began to weep intensely: both because the Lord had deigned to visit him and because he had delivered him from the evil spirit. From that time he possessed discernment of spirits and began to be distinguished by divine revelations. From that time also he applied himself more attentively to prayer, reading, and contemplation.

At one time the man of God was anxious about a sister whom he had left in the world with his brothers, and he prayed God to grant her the Spirit of counsel. One night, therefore, he saw in a vision that an angel led him into his native land. Leading him into a cemetery, the angel showed him a recent grave and said: “Here is buried the body of your sister [Col. 1261A]; but her soul stands before the Lord of spirits. Henceforth do not be anxious about her.”

### V

While Blessed Peter, still a novice, was staying in Germany at a cell of the monastery of Molesme called Ysodenges, and was loved and venerated by all on account of the merit of his holiness, it happened that a most wicked official died suddenly. His wife greatly loved the man of God; running to him, she earnestly begged him to pray to the Lord for her husband.

Moved with compassion for her sorrow, Blessed Peter bent his knees in prayer and prayed most devoutly. When the woman returned home, she found alive the husband whom she had left dead. He urgently desired the man of God to come to him.

When Blessed Peter came, the man confessed among other things that he had been suspicious of his wife. The saint of God imposed penance upon him and gave him the viaticum. Having arranged his household, he departed to the Lord on the third day.

At another time, while the same blessed man was staying at La Ferté-Gaucher, and on the night of Pope Mark was chanting Matins with an open book and lighted candle, reciting the psalm “O God of praise” (Psalm 108), the ancient enemy stood beside him, chanting with him.

When the saint was angry with him because he disturbed him, the evil one said: “Look, Peter, at the monk stealing the brethren’s clothes in the dormitory.” The saint of God looked and, although walls intervened, beheld with spiritual eyes the thief carrying away all that he could steal [Col. 1261C], leaving the monastery with the things taken, and hiding in a secure place.

As Blessed Peter watched this, it happened through diabolical deceit that the candle which he held in his hand fell upon the book and burned a leaf. It is displayed to this day as proof of the miracle.

After Matins had been sung, the brothers returned to their beds and, not finding the garments which they had left there, were distressed. They ran to the man of God **142** and complained that their possessions had been taken by theft. He directed them to remain silent until morning. When day came, he told them what he had seen at night and indicated where the thief lay hidden with the things he had taken. Going there, they found everything as the man of God had foretold.

### VI

[Col. 1261D] In the same cell, a certain cleric to whom the prior owed money stole the monastery’s chalices and censers and hid them in a nearby place. When the monks learned of this, they searched long and diligently but could not find them. Distressed, they came to the man of God and sought an answer from him as from a prophet.

He said to them: “I shall tell you where he is, if you give him back to me unharmed.” When they had promised this, he showed them where the thief was hidden. They went and found what they had lost, and brought the thief unharmed to the man of God, as they had promised. Peter reproved him like a father, refreshed him in charity, and dismissed him in peace.

On one occasion peas were being boiled for the brothers’ meal. One of the monks called Peter [Col. 1262A] and commanded him quickly to prepare the peas. Peter, accustomed to offer obedience eagerly to both superiors and inferiors, did not hesitate. With bare hands he took the boiling pot and poured out the water, feeling no heat; obedience protected him, and both hands appeared uninjured.

The monk who had commanded this, seeing that Peter had not felt the burning, repented that he had acted wrongly. Falling at Peter’s feet, he asked forgiveness. O how rightly did material fire not harm one whose mind had been fortified by the grace of the Holy Spirit against every fleshly desire.

**143.** A certain boy, familiar to him, was suddenly struck by illness and swelled throughout his body. Coming to Peter, he asked for assistance. Moved with compassion for his pain, the man [Col. 1262B] of God prayed and mixed certain names of Christ into a drink for him. When he drank it, he immediately became well.

### VII

It is certain that he was so distinguished by divine revelations that he frequently and readily foretold what was occurring in distant regions. When the lord of La Ferté-Gaucher, named Elias, had gone to Jerusalem, his mother continued in prayers and almsgiving for him with pious affection. One day, sadder than usual, she came to the man of God to ask how matters stood with her son. For she knew the spiritual man possessed true knowledge of those who were absent.

But she found him at prayer and caught up in ecstasy. When she called to him a third time and could not draw him from the sweetness [Col. 1262C] of contemplation, she hastened to return home. The prior of the house met her; hearing from her the reason for her grief and wishing to console her, he compelled her to return with him.

Finding the man of God still occupied in prayer, the prior said: “Brother Peter, I command you in the name of obedience to tell this lady what the Lord has revealed to you concerning her son.”

As though awakening from sleep, Peter replied: “If you had not called me back so quickly from the vision, I should have known completely all that is happening to him. Yet know that he lies at sea with an acute fever”—and he immediately added—“and a hen is being sought for him to eat, which is sold to them for one gold piece. Recovering from his illness, he will soon come and bring you an ivory comb, but to me an excellent cup.”

[Col. 1262D] **144.** The lady departed after hearing the man of God’s answer and was not disappointed in her desire. For after a short time had passed, she received her son safe and sound, just as she had heard.

### VII

At one time, after the Office of Terce had been celebrated, the same saint remained in the oratory in order to pray. A monk passing before him saw him laughing in prayer. When the prayer was completed, the monk privately asked why he had laughed while praying. Peter, wishing to keep his secret concealed, told him: “One year from today I shall tell you.”

When the year had passed, the monk came back and said: “Father, I beg you, fulfill what you promised. The year has now passed; come then, tell me why you laughed in prayer.”

He replied: “After the hour of Terce had ended, two brothers remained in their seats [Col. 1263A] and engaged in vain and idle words. I saw a demon sitting behind the altar beside the wall, writing down their buffooneries and idle words. When they considered getting up to sing the canonical Hours—for this was the third time they had done so—the devil, bewildered, did not know what to do or write.

“At last, rising and devoting themselves to prayer, they repented before God because they had acted wrongly. When the devil saw that so many negligences had been erased by so small a satisfaction, he became indignant and full of rage. Tearing with hands and teeth the paper on which he had written, he pulled so violently that he struck the back of his neck against the wall and dashed it hard. That,” he said, “is why you saw me laugh.”

At another time a brother passed before him [Col. 1263B] and saw him drive away certain invisible spirits, breaking straws in contempt of them; then he saw him call others to himself, rise, and rejoice with them. When the prayer was complete, the brother asked why he had done this.

The saint replied: “Those spirits whom I was driving away were demons seeking to hinder my prayer; and those whom I welcomed were holy angels, who consoled me.”

One night, while he was devoting himself to prayer after Matins, the soul of the abbot of Nizelle appeared to him, asking his blessing and the aid of his prayers; for at that very hour the abbot had departed from the body. Peter most devoutly commended the soul to God, to whom all things live.

When morning came, he told the prior and brothers that the abbot of Nizelle had departed from the world. They sent to the aforesaid [Col. 1263C] monastery and discovered that the abbot had died at the very hour when his soul had appeared to the holy man.

By these and many other virtues Blessed Peter was held in highest renown far and wide.

### IX.

In the territory of Langres there stands a most famous monastery of women, called Jully, from Julius Caesar. Its most holy community, deprived of a spiritual father, earnestly begged the abbot of Molesme, to whom that place belonged, that blessed Peter might be given them as pastor, desiring to be holy with a holy man and to live innocently with an innocent man.

But Abbot Guy, who then governed the Church of Molesme, would not assent to this request [Col. 1263D], wishing to appoint another over that house. At length, overcome by the entreaties of the illustrious Count Theobald and Andrew, lord of Baudemont, he consented and ordered Peter to come to him without delay. Peter promptly set out in obedience and hastened toward Molesme.

When the day was already declining, he came to the ford of Ricey, a place two miles from Molesme, and wished to cross. He entered a whirlpool said to have no bottom; and as soon as his boy set foot in it, he was swallowed by the water and vanished from sight. When the man of God saw this, he raised his holy hand and made the sign of the cross. Immediately the servant emerged and crossed cheerfully with him to the bank.

Then Robert, a knight and lord of that place, met him. Delighted by the presence of the man of God [Col. 1264A], he took him into his house and entertained him splendidly. Seeing Peter’s servant soaked with water, he asked by what route he had crossed the ford. The man of God told how he had escaped the danger. The astonished knight gave thanks to God, who had delivered His saint, declaring that no one had ever crossed by that place.

On the following day Peter came to Molesme, and the abbot entrusted to him the care and governance of the Church of Jully. On arriving there, he was received with joy and devotion, as though an angel of the Lord sent from heaven. Thus our Jacob entered the tent of his Rachel; he entered the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of his God. Thus, indeed, the violet of humility was joined with the roses of penitence and martyrdom, and with the lilies [Col. 1264B] of chastity and virginity, which the right hand of the heavenly gardener had planted in the garden of Jully. For the flowers of Jully lack neither roses nor lilies.

Thus the Lord remembered His mercy and His truth, and, as He had promised through the prophet, gave in the wilderness the thorn and the cedar, the myrtle and the olive tree (Isa. 41). Blessed Peter showed himself a thorn by rebuking sinners; a cedar by contemplating heavenly things; a myrtle by compassionating the sick; and an olive tree by showing mercy to the wretched.

Thus blessed Peter, entering the place predestined for him by God, advanced from strength to strength, rising from the strength of action to the strength of contemplation. Indeed, the Lord had bestowed such grace upon His servant that he often, like [Col. 1264C] a true prophet, announced without hesitation things yet to come. If anyone wished to confess sins to him and had perhaps forgotten some sin, Peter, foreknowing it by the Holy Spirit, immediately disclosed it.

### X.

A certain nun in the aforesaid monastery once fell ill, and her illness was mortal. Having confessed her sins to the man of God, she had through negligence forgotten to confess one offence. Not long afterward this was revealed to blessed Peter while he was praying for her soul.

One night the aforesaid nun appeared to him, confessing her sin with such loud cries that the man of God thought she had been heard by all who were present. [Col. 1264D] The saint imposed a penance upon her as though she were still alive—namely, the seven penitential psalms—which he himself recited before God for her soul with such compunction of heart that a stream of his tears showed everyone where he had prostrated himself in prayer.

He therefore made himself an oratory beside the church, in the cemetery, where he devoted himself day and night to prayer and contemplation, vigils and fasts. The souls of penitents often came to him there, begging the aid of his prayers. There also he enjoyed visions and converse with holy angels, who very often instructed him concerning heavenly things and foretold the future.

When holy Humberga, sister of blessed Bernard [Col. 1265A], the first abbot of Clairvaux, worn out by a long illness, awaited the end of her life, her brothers and many other religious men came to her, wishing to be present at her most holy passing. Among them was blessed Peter. On the third day, after Compline, he visited her; and, seeing that she had not yet departed, he blessed and signed her with the cross, and was returning to bed with his chaplain Vincent.

Then an angel of the Lord met him in the cloister’s parlour and said: “Return quickly, for that holy soul is now about to depart from the body.”

The saint replied: “What am I to do? Religious men are outside, having come for this purpose, to witness her end, and they are already asleep.”

The angel said to him: “Then I will go and awaken them; you return quickly.”

The angel of the Lord accordingly went back [Col. 1265B] and struck the board so forcefully that those who were asleep awoke and rose trembling. They therefore hurried together, with great devotion, to behold the departure of that holy soul.

### XI.

The fame of the blessed man thus grew throughout all Burgundy, so that many noble men and women came to him for his blessing. Among them came a noble matron to confess her sins. A black dog followed her, which no one saw except the holy Father alone. As she confessed her sins, the holy man of God struck her with a rod and imposed a penance; and so the demon, which had appeared in the likeness of a dog, disappeared.

[Col. 1265C] But the great and venerable Theobald, Count of Champagne, came to him with a great retinue, praying and requesting his blessing. After departing from him joyfully, he sent his pregnant wife to Peter again. When the saint looked upon her, he declared that she would bear a daughter who would become lady of France. This later came to pass: for the glorious King Louis [Note: [Col. 1265] In Clairvaux: Philip. See the Preface.] married her, and, in accordance with the word of the man of God, obtained dominion over the kingdom.

Nor should this be passed over: while standing at the holy altars, he was often seen by some to be raised about a cubit from the ground into the air, undoubtedly supported by the hands of angels, whose manner of life he imitated while still on earth.

[Col. 1265D] A certain lay brother, named Gerald, fell from a height and was so shattered throughout his body that he lay lifeless. They placed his body in a sack and brought it to blessed Peter. Peter poured out tears and prayers over him and obtained for him life and health.

On one feast-day of holy Parasceve, after the solemn rites had been completed, his chaplain Vincent said to him: “Today, servant of God, while you celebrated the holy mysteries, I saw a splendid light shining around you, and the candles glowing with a flame brighter than usual.”

The saint replied: “I command you, in the name of obedience, not to tell anyone of this as long as I live.” For he avoided the glory of men [Col. 1266A], wishing his virtues to lie hidden just as though they were vices.

### XII.

When blessed Peter had shone forth by very many virtues and miracles, God, who was disposing something better concerning him, caused him to fall into the illness from which he died. He then often summoned the virgins over whom he presided, consoling them and instructing them concerning the kingdom of God. When many religious men heard that he was ill, they came to him; among them was Hatto, prior of Molesme, who remained with him as long as he survived.

One day, as this Hatto entered Peter’s room, he saw the entire chamber in which he lay shining with an extraordinary brightness. As soon as Hatto set foot inside, it disappeared. When he asked [Col. 1266B] Peter the cause of the brightness, Peter answered: “I give thanks to my God, who has granted me testimony to my vision. For an angel of the Lord stood beside me, commanding me to tell Count Theobald not to cross the sea and go to England to take the kingdom for himself, because it has not been predestined for him by God.”

When Count Theobald heard that the man of God was ill, he sent his chaplain to visit him. Through that chaplain the man of God sent him many secret messages, foretelling that after a few years he would wage war with the king of the Franks, and that he would be victorious in it if he protected churches and their possessions from invasion.

Again, on a certain day when the aforesaid Hatto entered to him, the man of God rebuked him and said: [Col. 1266C] “Why did you come in so quickly? Three virgins, lately deceased in this house, were standing before me upon the monastery’s bedspread, holding branches and sweet-smelling flowers in their hands. They were speaking with me of heavenly secrets and of the glory of eternal life.”

After this he was caught up in ecstasy and said that he had seen two angels holding the banner of the cross in their hands and singing: “My people” (*Popule meus*; Micah 6). He then added that he had seen demons hurling fiery arrows against him, while, on the other side, holy angels sent forth arrows of light and extinguished the devil’s arrows.

### XIII.

When he perceived that his last day was near, he summoned the daughters whom he had begotten in Christ [Col. 1266D] and urged them to perseverance and endurance of temptations, saying that through many tribulations one enters the heavenly kingdom.

As his spiritual daughters wept before him and begged him to obtain from the Lord for himself life until some later time, he sweetly consoled them and answered: “My dearest daughters, do not hinder my desire. For if I do not depart now, you will not have me present at the feast of Saint John; but if I depart while among you, know that I shall be an intercessor before God on your behalf. And I promise this also, trusting in God’s mercy: none of those upon whom I have bestowed the veil shall lose the heavenly kingdom.”

After this [Col. 1267A] the aforesaid Hatto advised him, according to the custom of religious persons, to surrender the keys of his priory before dying. He replied: “Not at all. Rather, I shall bear my priory before God, and I shall be an intercessor for those whom the Lord committed to my care; and I shall protect this place and its inhabitants. And because the time of my departure is at hand, hasten to anoint me with holy oil according to custom.”

Thus, anointed with holy oil and strengthened by receiving the Lord’s Body, blessed Peter bade his household a final farewell and blessed them. Full of holiness and renowned for miracles, he happily passed to Christ from exile to the kingdom, from earth to heaven, and from the body.

The monks of Molesme intended to remove his body for burial at Molesme [Col. 1267B], until, by divine disposition, it was secretly restored through the hand of Henry the secretary to the grieving community of nuns. They received it like manna from heaven and rushed upon it, striving to water it with tears. They lamented that they had lost their most loving shepherd, who healed them by his touch, reconciled them to God by his prayers, comforted them by his conversation, and protected them by his merits.

After the customary vigils had been celebrated around the body and the solemnities of the Masses completed, he was buried with the greatest honour by religious men beside the altar of the holy Mother of God, Mary ever Virgin. There his prayers and benefits flourish, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

### XIV.

[Col. 1267C] After the passing of blessed Peter, prior of Jully, many persons of both sexes began to flock to his tomb, desiring through his merits to obtain pardon for their sins and healing from diverse infirmities.

A boy assigned to the monastery’s services lost his senses through the devil’s prompting. Brought with great difficulty to Saint Peter’s tomb, he recovered his senses as soon as he rested there, and returned home joyful and glad.

A woman from the neighbourhood, likewise deprived of her senses, was brought to the tomb of the holy Father and was healed as soon as she touched it.

A nun of Jully named Prisca, while eating an apple, had a piece of it stick in her throat, so that it could move neither upward [Col. 1267D] nor downward. As she was in danger, she was brought to the blessed man’s tomb; immediately she spat out that piece of apple and was delivered.

Peter the elder of Châtillon, afflicted by violent fevers, came to Jully. After sleeping beneath the saint’s tomb, he was restored to health.

Henry, chaplain of Fontaines, exhausted by extremely severe fevers and hoping to end his life there, had himself carried to Jully. When he came to the saint’s tomb and rested there, he was restored to health; on the next day, after celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he cheerfully returned home.

A certain man from the neighbourhood of Jully, possessed by a demon, [Col. 1268A] howled like a wolf, roared like a lion, bellowed like an ox, and imitated the voices of every kind of beast. Bound with difficulty by many men, he was brought to the memorial shrine of the holy man. There he barked like a dog for a long time, tore himself, and spoke nonsense. At length, through the merits of God’s servant, after a few days he was freed from the demon, received the gift of health, glorified the Lord, and returned home.

### XV.

Archembaud of Raveries had a swelling caused by illness in his throat, so that he could swallow no liquid. Worn down by prolonged fasting and fearing the danger of death, he devoutly visited the tomb of the man of God, seeking his help. When he had rested there in a short sleep, he awoke, spat out the affliction together with blood, and returned home in health [Col. 1268B].

Raynald, priest of Sanivey, mad and filled with a demon, shouting, howling, and uttering blasphemies, was brought to the blessed man’s tomb. After remaining there a few days, he was restored to health through blessed Peter’s prayers.

A boy from Molesme, caught in theft, was put in fetters to be hanged the following day. All night long he invoked the aid of blessed Peter; in the morning he was set free and glorified God.

Lady Cacelina of Bar-sur-Aube came to Jully with offerings. Going to the saint’s tomb, she prayed for the recovery of one of her nieces, who was unable to walk. When she returned home, she found her niece walking [Col. 1268C]. On asking, she learned that the girl had recovered on the very day and hour when, while at Jully, she had commended her to the blessed man.

On the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, a boy from the granges of Jully, rising in the morning, encountered the ancient enemy. The latter gradually appeared to grow, stretching his head up to the clouds; seizing the boy, he strove to draw him toward himself. Terrified and deprived of his senses, the boy pulled his hand back toward himself; it became fixed behind his back, so that he could move neither hand nor arm. Brought to the memorial shrine of blessed Peter, he recovered the use of his hand and arm as soon as he slept there.

A certain matron used every year to feed the community of Jully on the anniversary of the blessed man. [Col. 1268D] One year, when that day was approaching, she ordered her servant to see whether the chest contained enough grain to suffice for the nuns’ meal. He returned and reported that the chest held no more than one cartallum (a measure) of grain. Hearing this, she became very sad. By chance, on the following day she went to the chest and found it full of grain. Greatly rejoiced, she celebrated blessed Peter’s anniversary with deep devotion, since through his merits she had found abundance of grain in her chest.

A certain woman living not far from the monastery had a small son. Angry with him, she said: “I commend you to the devil, most wretched of boys.” [Col. 1269A] At the mother’s words, the ancient enemy seized the boy’s hand and began to draw him toward himself. Feeling this, the boy in terror pulled his hand back toward himself; it adhered so firmly to his breast that by no means [Col. 1270A] could it be pulled away. Seeing this, his mother, weeping and wailing, brought him to the burial-place of the blessed man. As soon as he slept there, he recovered the health of his injured hand.

[Col. 1269]

### Observation concerning the year and day of the death of blessed Peter, prior of Jully

[Col. 1269A] We would once have had the anniversary day of the birth into heaven of blessed Peter of Jully recorded in the Martyrology or Necrology of Jully, had the wars, by which the monastery of Jully itself was utterly destroyed, left anything remaining. Only a conjecture survives from chapter 13 of his *Life*, where, near death, he is reported to have addressed his spiritual daughters standing by him, by whose prayers he was held back in his sick body, in these words: “My dearest daughters, do not hinder my desire; for if I do not die now [Col. 1269B], you will not have me present at the feast of Saint John.” Therefore, it appears that he departed to the heavenly realms on the eve of that feast, that is, on 23 June.

We learn the year of his death from chapter 12 of his *Life*, where, lying ill in his final sickness, he addresses Hatto, prior of Molesme, thus: “An angel of the Lord stood by me, commanding me to tell Count Theobald not to cross the sea, going to England to take the kingdom for himself, because it is not predestined for him by God.”

King Henry I of England died without legitimate male issue on 1 December in the year of Christ 1135; that day then fell on a Sunday, as Orderic Vitalis notes in Book XIII of his *History*. Adela, the king’s sister, had borne to Stephen, Count of Blois, Theobald and Stephen. The younger of these, Stephen, had seized his uncle’s vacant kingdom; and, with the great consent of every estate, had been accepted and crowned king in London by William, Archbishop of Canterbury, on 15 December [Col. 1269C].

This change of affairs naturally stung Theobald the elder, surnamed the Great, highly skilled in political and military affairs alike. With his uncle Henry, king of the English, he had more than once invaded the French kingdom with united forces against Louis the Fat, as Suger relates in his *Life of Louis the Fat*. Therefore, while Theobald was considering a crossing into England with an army, behold, he was warned in the name of blessed Peter of Jully that it was fixed and pleasing to God that he should abandon his plan of expedition.

Orderic appears to refer to this when he says in that same Book XIII: “The Normans, meeting his brother Theobald—namely, Stephen, already king at that time—at Neubourg, wished to set him over themselves. But in the meeting itself they heard from a certain monk, who was Stephen’s envoy, that all the English had received Stephen and wished to obey him and appoint him their king. Immediately, with Theobald’s assent, all resolved to serve one lord, on account of the honours which the barons possessed in both regions. Theobald therefore, though he was the elder, angered that he had not received the kingdom, hastened to the great [Col. 1270A] affairs pressing upon him in Gaul.”

From this we conclude that blessed Peter died in the year of Christ 1136, and indeed on 23 June.
