It is thus clear how far Angelus Manrique erred in the *Cistercian Annals*, under the year of Christ 1141, chapter 4, no. 1, where he says that Humbelina, Saint Bernard’s sister, was still alive in 1140 and died piously in the Lord not far from 1141. For if Peter the prior, who was present at her death, died in June 1136, how could she still have been alive [Col. 1270B] in the fifth year thereafter?

I know that it may be objected, from Orderic Vitalis, Book XIII, that the kingdom of England together with the duchy of Normandy was offered to Count Theobald in 1141, while his brother Stephen, king of the English, was held captive. If he refused to seek that kingdom at blessed Peter’s warning, there will be no ground upon which the *Cistercian Annals* may be reproved for assigning Humbelina’s passing to about that year, nor will blessed Peter’s death have to be fixed in 1136.

Certainly King Stephen fought and was captured at the Purification [Hypapante], on 2 February, which in 1141, as Orderic observed, fell on Sexagesima Sunday. But see what that author adds: “In mid-Lent the leading men of the regions of Mortain assembled and held a conference on public affairs. There Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, and the Normans approached Count Theobald and offered him the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy. But he, prudent and religious as he was, refused to be burdened by the weight of such great [Col. 1270C] cares; rather, subject to certain conditions, he granted the royal right to Geoffrey, son-in-law of King Henry: namely, that Geoffrey should relinquish to him the city of Tours, which was held of his fief; should free his brother King Stephen from chains; and should restore in full to Stephen and Stephen’s heir the former honour which he had possessed during the lifetime of his uncle.”

From this it may be understood that blessed Peter’s death did not belong to the year 1141. For Count Theobald was warned by Peter, while Peter was grievously ill, in the month of June; whereas in mid-Lent, about the Ides of March, Theobald transferred to Geoffrey of Anjou, the former son-in-law of Henry, sometime king of the English, the kingdom which had been offered to him.

Add to this that, when near death, blessed Peter foretold to Count Theobald that after a few years he would be attacked in war by the king of the Franks. This war, according to Robert of Torigni, began in 1140 and lasted three years; it fits exactly with the oracle delivered a few years earlier, namely in 1136, when, according to our calculations, blessed Peter flew from the prison-house of the body to the citizens of heaven.

## Three Books on Miracles by Herbert, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia

[Col. 1271]

### Preface

It appears that Herbert was Spanish by nation and from León by birthplace, from Book II of his *Miracles*, chapter 1. There he reports that he often saw and knew intimately a certain Dominic, a solitary monk from the monastery of Carrezeda, in the region of Iberia, not far from the city of León.

The house of Carrezeda or Carraceta did not receive the white habit together with the Cistercian Rule until the year 1203, as the *Cistercian Annals* inform me, under the year of Christ 1127, chapter 6, no. 8. Thus that remarkable old man Dominic was one of the black Benedictines. When Herbert often met him and observed the holy man’s groans and abundant tears, he too dissolved with him wholly into lamentation and weeping.

These, unless I am mistaken, were the seeds of a more perfect life in Herbert. Later, having assumed the monastic habit at Clairvaux and been trained among Saint Bernard’s disciples, he drew in the original spirit of the sacred Cistercian Order from fellowship with them and with other religious men, whose company he especially sought.

At that time, for several years, as he himself says in Book II, chapter 25, he served at the table of Abbot Fastrad, a man of every virtue. From 1157, after Robert, Saint Bernard’s immediate successor, Fastrad presided over Clairvaux for five years; then, in 1162, he was made Abbot of Cîteaux, and two years later, in 1164, departed this life, famous for holiness.

When Herbert was already mature in age and experience, the government of the abbey of Moris was entrusted to him. Later he returned to Clairvaux, and, while chaplain to Henry, Abbot of Clairvaux—who shortly afterward was appointed cardinal-bishop of Albano—he wrote the three books *On Miracles* in the year of Christ 1178, twenty-five years after Saint Bernard’s death, as may be gathered from Book I, chapter 31, and Book II, chapter 13.

Therefore, as the author of the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* observes, all other dates must be investigated from this one year whenever Herbert says that this or that event happened three years, seven years, or more previously.

Not long afterward he was promoted to the archbishopric of Torres in Sardinia. Soon John the Hermit presented him with certain accounts concerning the life and deeds of Saint Bernard which earlier writers had omitted, and which John, having received them from the mouths of some of Bernard’s disciples, had published at Herbert’s encouragement.

In Chrysostom Henriquez’s *Menologium* and *Fasciculus of the Saints of Cîteaux*, and likewise in Angelus Manrique’s *Cistercian Annals*, very many passages occur cited from the book *On the Beginning of the Cistercian Order* and its Appendix, or from the book *On the Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order*, or from John the Hermit’s *Life of Saint Bernard*, which were copied from these books of Herbert.

This explains why, in the *Life of Saint Bernard* by John the Hermit, one finds far more chapters cited by these authors than we have here produced from an old autograph manuscript. Herbert’s untitled work (*ἀνεπίγραφον*) stood immediately after John the Hermit’s composition and was carelessly attributed to John himself, being regarded as a kind of continuation of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

We provide the very source, and the reader will wonder that it lay hidden for so long in the manuscripts of Clairvaux, considering both the author’s credibility and the gravity and usefulness of his narratives. In the manuscript code, the chapters of the three books were distinguished only by numerical signs and not by titles; we have prefixed to all of them titles of our own, drawn from the subjects of the individual chapters themselves.

Perhaps Sardinia, notorious for the unhealthiness of its climate, will one day instruct us concerning Herbert’s death and his episcopal acts. Of it the poet said: “When death comes, Sardinia is in the midst of Tibur.” Yet I dare say that when Herbert arrived at that island—such was the pleasantness of his virtues—Sardinia became Tibur in the midst of it.

The book of Life will give his full history, in which, as Augustine says, “the blessed read without the syllables of time, and their book shall never be closed.”

[Col. 1273]

## Three Books on Miracles by Herbert, Archbishop of Torres in Sardinia

### Book I

### Chapter I. Concerning Rainald, first a monk of Saint-Amand and afterward of Clairvaux, a man of great religious devotion, to whom the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, appeared with Saints Elizabeth and Mary Magdalene, visiting the brethren who were reaping; and who, some days before his death, afterward showed him the white and precious garments she had prepared, in which he would be clothed when he came to her.

[Col. 1273A]

There was in the monastery of Clairvaux a monk named Rainald, a man of good simplicity, fearing God and preserving his innocence from infancy to old age. Although before his conversion he had lived for thirty years in secular dress, he did not live a secular life. Rather, always devoted to works of piety, he was careful to glorify and bear God in his body [Col. 1273B].

For, among the other things which he did with an undivided heart, he also dedicated the integrity of his body to the Lord. With God’s aid, from his mother’s womb to the day of his death, he passed untouched through the incitements of lust and the impurities of the flesh.

Having received the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint-Amand, he spent twenty years and more there in holy conduct, giving everyone no small proof of his holiness. Then, burning with a greater ardour for virtues, he transferred himself to the house of Clairvaux through zeal for God, though previously forewarned by God through many revelations.

I forbear to relate how great were the labours and troubles that this blessed man endured from brethren of that Order who envied his successful deeds and desired to overthrow this purpose [Col. 1273C], lest I weary readers.

When received at Clairvaux, he immediately girded himself manfully for a new warfare, and, though an old soldier, again showed himself among us a most valiant recruit—mortifying himself all day long in labours, vigils, fasts, and the other observances of holy discipline. He had an unceasing devotion to prayer and, in prayer, a marvellous abundance of tears.

One day, therefore, when he had gone out with the others to labour in the wheat harvest, he withdrew a little from the community and began with great delight of spirit to observe [Col. 1274A] the reapers. At once pondering and marvelling within himself that so many wise men, so many noble and delicately reared men, for Christ’s love exposed themselves to toil and hardship and accepted the blazing heat of that sun with such cheerfulness, as though they were gathering sweetly fragrant fruits in a garden of delights or feasting most delectably at a table full of the most lavish dishes.

Then, raising eyes and hands to heaven, he gave thanks to the Lord that He had joined him, unworthy and sinful though he was, to so holy a multitude. While he turned these and similar thoughts in his mind, and could scarcely contain himself for the immensity of his joy, behold: three venerable women suddenly appeared to him, their faces rosy and their white garments shining. One of them, who went before the others, was [Col. 1274B] more resplendent in dress, more beautiful in form, and taller in stature.

They were descending from a nearby hill and approaching the community of brethren who were reaping crops on that hill’s slope. Seeing them, he was troubled and astonished by the greatness of his wonder, and exclaimed:

“Lord God, who are these beautiful and most venerable women, who, contrary to the custom of other women, are approaching our community?”

As he spoke thus, a man of venerable white hair, clothed in a white robe, stood beside him and said: “The greater one, who goes before the others, is Mary, Virgin Mother of Jesus Christ. The others who follow are Saint Elizabeth and Saint Mary Magdalene.”

When he heard the Mother of the Lord named, all his inmost being was moved by devotion to that name which he loved so deeply. Again he asked: “And where is she going, my lord? Where is my Lady going, I beseech you?”

The other replied: “She comes to visit her reapers.”

When these words had been spoken, the person who was speaking suddenly disappeared. At this sight the man of God marvelled still more within himself, and, turning his eyes again toward the holy Mother of God and her companions, he gazed fixedly at them in astonishment [Col. 1274C].

Walking with measured steps, they came one after another as far as the community. Having entered it, they began to walk separately here and there among the monks and lay brothers, as though for the grace of visitation. At last they vanished from the observer’s sight and returned to the heavens from which they had come [Col. 1275A].

The man of God remained rooted to the spot and was unable to move from it until the miracle had ended. How greatly he advanced through such a visitation, and how much he grew in love of God and of His most blessed Mother, was shown by his life, worthy of imitation, and by his daily increase in virtues.

Many other revelations too he received from God, but in order to avoid the mire of vainglory he preferred to keep them silent rather than speak of them. For even this vision mentioned above, which he had kept concealed for nearly eight years, he disclosed to me—though I was unworthy—only a short time, namely forty days, before [Col. 1275B] his death, unwillingly and, as it were, under compulsion, on the following occasion. One day, as the two of us were speaking familiarly about the salvation of our souls, I knew that he was a just and holy man, frequently visited by the Lord. Trusting in the love with which I loved him and felt myself loved by him, I dared to ask and request something of him. Thus, for Christ’s love and for the sake of His mercies, I began earnestly to entreat him and strongly to press him to reveal to me, for God’s honour, one of the consolations he had received—specifically, the one by which he judged that I would be most edified. Compelled by this entreaty, therefore, he told me the aforesaid vision. But with what emotion did he do so? God Himself is witness with how much fear [Col. 1275C] and trembling, with what a flood of tears, he related it; so that groans and sobs rising from the depths of his heart repeatedly interrupted his voice, as though at that very hour he were seeing the vision itself.

Fourteen days having then passed, that same Queen of Heaven, Lady of the Angels, appeared to him in a vision, cutting out and preparing for him white and precious ornaments with which he was shortly to be clothed. When she had prepared them, she bound them together into one bundle and, departing, carried them away with her. When he saw this, he followed her and cried after her, saying: “Alas, my most longed-for Lady, when shall I have these ornaments which you have deigned to prepare for me?” [Col. 1275D] The most holy Mother of God replied: “When you come to me, you shall receive them.”

O joyful vision! O certain promise! And indeed it proved all the more certain and all the more joyful because it was fulfilled so quickly. When morning came, that servant of God entered to visit me, as though I were sick. At that time I was ill almost to death, and my weakness was so severe that even the physicians despaired of my recovery. For that reason, on the preceding day I had been anointed with the oil of the sick, since they believed that I would die very soon. When he came to me, he compassionately shared my suffering with great tenderness; and, in order to console me somewhat, he related the vision which he had seen that same night. He judged and declared that it had been shown to him not for his own sake but for mine [Col. 1276A]; for he was most humble of heart and presumed nothing of that kind concerning his own holiness.

I immediately replied: “Do not, I beseech you, most loving Father, do not alienate your blessing from yourself by a sinister interpretation. The ornaments prepared for you from heaven will never belong to another; by God’s mercy, they will remain safely and wholly yours. But earnestly implore your most gracious visitor that, according to the good pleasure of her mercy, she may prepare for me whatever other garments she wishes. For she is powerful and kind, rich toward all who call upon her.”

Why say more? I, who was believed to be near death, whether I wished it or not, was called back to endure the miseries of this life; while he, who appeared healthy and sound, survived no more than [Col. 1276B] twenty-five further days. At last, having happily completed the course of his life, he laid aside the garments of corruptible flesh and, through the most blessed Mother of God, whom he had devoutly served, received without doubt the robe of immortality, according to the faithfulness of her promise.

Nor must it be passed over in silence that, six days before this man of God’s death, while he was praying alone in church after Compline, the board for the dead was suddenly struck in his hearing, but only twice. On hearing it he immediately sprang up and sought the infirmary, thinking that someone had died there. But when he learned for certain that no one there had then died, it occurred to him that he himself would soon die and that, in the sound of the board, the passing of his own death was being signified to him. At this remembrance [Col. 1276C] of death he was suddenly shaken throughout; fear came upon him and his flesh shuddered. He immediately began to suffer from fever, and as the illness grew worse he finally came to his end.

While he lay sick, he almost continually recited, in heart and action, the greeting to blessed Mary which he had formerly been accustomed to repeat. With the words of that same oracle he breathed forth his blessed soul. It happened that, on that very day, a certain lay brother—a man of religious life and good repute—also passed to the Lord. Thus their funerals were celebrated together, and both were buried together in the same [167] tomb. While these things were taking place, a spiritual man was shown in a vision that two most beautiful churches were being built at Clairvaux: one in the monks’ infirmary, the other [Col. 1276D] in the infirmary of the lay brothers. But the first was far nobler and more beautiful than the other. It is evident, therefore, that in the double construction of the churches and in the double stroke of the board for the dead, the death of both men—precious in the sight of the Lord—was clearly indicated. The difference between the churches signifies a difference in merits: for although we believe both to be holy, yet we believe that one was holier than the other before God.

## CHAPTER II. On Gerard, sacristan of Clairvaux, whom the board for the dying, struck by an invisible hand, warned of his approaching death.

In the same month in which the aforesaid servant of God [Col. 1277A] passed to the Lord, a similar event occurred there. In that same monastery there was a sacristan named Gerard, a man distinguished by good character and truly religious. Following the Prophet’s counsel, he bore the Lord’s yoke from his youth and “lifted himself above himself” (Lam. 3); for while still tender and frail in age, he set his hand to mighty things. Nourished at the breasts of kings and happily brought up under chaste discipline, he continually grew and advanced toward better things; and, by God’s great gift, he was, as they say, never acquainted with the corruption of the flesh.

But as the hour drew near when he was to pass from the world to God, one day, while he remained in church after Compline as usual, there suddenly came a sound to his ears, as though the board for the dying were being struck with repeated [Col. 1277B] blows. Hearing this, he thought that one of the brethren was then dying in the infirmary. A little later, when he had learned with complete certainty that no human being had made that sound, that prophetic board came into his mind which the man of God Rainald had heard as a sign of his own death; for this report had already spread among the brethren and was being widely circulated. As he reflected on these things, it came into his heart that he himself was on the very point of departing from the world.

Then suddenly the hairs of his flesh stood on end; fear and trembling came upon him. At once a fatal fever seized him, and before the tenth day, consumed by death, he happily departed. We cannot pass over in silence this detail of his devout piety: we saw and rejoiced at what seemed a miracle wrought by God through him, or rather in him [Col. 1277C]. For when he was drawing his last breath and no longer had strength to speak, for nearly three or four hours he held his joined and outstretched hands motionless toward the cross, as if they had been bound by some cord. Though, under the pressure of pain, he repeatedly tossed the other members of his body here and there, he never separated the hands which, as we have said, he stretched toward the cross, nor ever drew them back to himself. What he had often done while living, he showed even when dead.

## CHAPTER III. On Peter of Toulouse, monk of Clairvaux, wonderfully delivered from the most importunate temptations of the flesh; who afterwards was accustomed to see the child Jesus in the consecrated Host.

[Col. 1277D]

There was another elder in the same monastery, named Peter, surnamed of Toulouse, a man of great purity and deep devotion. From childhood he had always had one purpose and desire: to crucify himself to the world and the world to himself. In his youth, before submitting himself to the Cistercian Order, he lived in solitude, mortifying the old man within himself through many fasts and labours, and daily offering God the sacrifice of a contrite spirit. At length, continually living on wild herbs and bread made with lye, he served Christ there for a long time and, God protecting him, courageously endured innumerable wars of temptation from evil spirits.

Later, having learned through widespread report of the holiness [Col. 1278A] of Saint Bernard and of the monastery of Clairvaux itself, where, amid so great a congregation of the righteous, as in God’s tabernacle, he might live more securely, hidden from the storm and sheltered from the rain, he came with great fervour of heart to that place, placing himself under the discipline of the aforesaid Father. There he persevered for many years, until the end of his life.

While he was still young, God deigned to appear to him in a vision, seated upon a lofty throne, with thousands of saints about Him. Peter seemed to be led before God for judgment. When he arrived, fearful and trembling, he fell at His feet [170] and begged Him to have mercy on him. God said to him: “What do you wish Me to do for you?” He replied: “Lord, that I may be saved.” [Col. 1278B] God said to him: “Go, quickly turn to My service, and persevere continually in it; for eternal salvation will not fail you.”

Strengthened by this most happy promise, he utterly forsook the world and devoted himself wholly to divine service. He therefore girded his loins with strength and strengthened his arm for the overthrow of spiritual wickednesses, which afterwards fiercely assailed him for many days and years. Above all he endured a most troublesome spirit of fornication, which continually pricked him with great stings of temptation both asleep and awake. Therefore, violently indignant with himself, he afflicted his flesh beyond belief through labour and hardship, vigils, fasts, and other torments of penance. His mind became so troubled and distressed that he often resolved to cut off his genitals, when he could find no other remedy for the temptation.

Nor should this be left unsaid: that ancient enemy appeared to him many times and in many forms. On one occasion he appeared in human shape in the choir of Clairvaux, with burning eyes and a terrible face. His stature was huge and exceedingly misshapen. He wore a rough, blackest cowl, the sleeves of which were cut short and scarcely reached to the elbows, while the rest of his arms was bare. This evil apostate came and stood before the man of God, looking down upon him with a proud eye and seeming indignant that he withheld his assent from the enemy’s counsels [Col. 1278D]. The man of God was stupefied in mind and held as if bound, so that he could not move. At last, when God visited him, the destructive monster vanished at the sign of the Lord’s cross; it did him no harm except to increase the fire of that temptation.

A few days later it appeared in the same place in the form of a monstrous beast, partly like a savage lion and partly like a rapacious eagle. Threatening him fiercely, it raged against him with a furious open mouth, as though about to devour him alive. But it was restrained by divine power, so that it could not touch him. Then, at the remembrance of Christ’s name, the phantom beast suddenly disappeared. Upon its departure, the man of God immediately suffered such a blaze of the aforesaid passion that he plainly recognized the presence there [Col. 1279A] of that infernal smith of Isaiah, “who blows the coals in the fire” (Isa. 54).

Accordingly, seeing that the violence of the temptation exceeded the measure of his endurance, he formed a fixed resolution to cut himself off, preferring to risk himself before God in this respect rather than fall into the abyss of lust. He waited only to find a razor or some other tool suitable for this purpose. But the merciful and compassionate God—the helper in times of need, in tribulation; He who alone is holy and alone is Lord—would not abandon His servant in such a struggle, but “with the temptation made a way out, that he might be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10).

Thus, while he slept, an angel of the Lord appeared in the form of a young man, saying that he was a skilled physician and had come for that purpose: to cut him and heal him of that passion. Peter gladly accepted this and immediately yielded himself to the angel’s will. As he was cut, he endured with every patience the hand of the one cutting him and the sharpness of the pain. When he awoke, he thought the amputation had truly and physically been performed upon him. Yet he eventually learned that the members of his body [172] remained intact, while the temptation had been so utterly cut out by the roots that afterwards he felt no distress whatever from it.

From that time, when the incentives of carnal passions had been extinguished in him, God began to visit him more abundantly in the blessings of His sweetness and to fill his soul with splendours, so that he could say with the Psalmist: “According to the multitude of my sorrows [Col. 1279C] in my heart, Thy consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93 [94]). Thereafter and henceforward, God having rebuked “the beasts of the reed,” the stings of the flesh wholly ceased from him, and the spirit of immeasurable consolation rested upon him. For God magnified His mercy in dealing with him, storing up joy and exultation upon him and satisfying his desire with every good thing. Him whom He had long given to drink from the wine of health-giving bitterness, He afterwards more abundantly made drunk with the nectar of sweetest contemplation.

Among God’s other gifts, he had received the grace of spiritual devotion in prayer, especially in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. [Col. 1279D] Hence the brethren who assisted him at Masses marvelled exceedingly at the overflowing abundance of tears with which he was accustomed to be wholly flooded there. God revealed to him many great things from the secrets of heaven, and very frequently visited him with innumerable consolations, whether sleeping, waking, or carried beyond himself in ecstasy. If all these things were committed to writing, they would fill many volumes.

Since it would be lengthy and burdensome for me to set down in writing everything that has come to my knowledge concerning that blessed man, I will simply recount at least one thing, which conscience pressing me I do not dare wholly to suppress, just as I heard it from his own mouth. It is so remarkable and so great that, from this one instance, faithful hearers may readily believe or judge [Col. 1280A] the rest. For I fear—indeed, greatly fear—to offend our God if by my silence I allow to perish a glorious and wonderful matter entrusted to me by that man of God, perhaps to me alone or perhaps to very few people, none of whom, I think, survives today; a matter in which God may be glorified and the faith and devotion of many may increase.

Accordingly, while that blessed man stood at the holy altar offering the sacraments, at the very moment of communion, as he held the most holy body of God above the chalice in his hands, there appeared in the likeness of a beautiful little child that little one, beautiful above the sons of men: true God and true man, God Jesus Christ, He who is meek and humble of heart, accustomed to hide Himself from the wise and proud and to reveal Himself to little ones. When [Col. 1280B] he saw this, trembling and astonished, he first closed his eyes because of the splendour and reverence of that majesty; for he did not dare look upon God. Yet even with his eyes closed he saw Him just as when they were open. When he turned his face to the other side and kept his eyelids shut for some time, he nevertheless saw Him, with his face thus turned away, as though He stood before him—now upon his hand, now upon his arm—in a wonderful and ineffable manner, as though he had other eyes fixed in the back of his head or at his temples, with which he gazed upon Him.

This most sweet and wonderful revelation made that man of God glad, not once or twice but often and innumerable times, so that frequently for four or [Col. 1280C] five months He appeared to him almost every day. If at times He seemed to delay longer than usual, Peter’s familiarity with God and confidence in His mercy were so great that he would prolong the completion of the sacrifice and would not readily wish to finish it until, when joy had been restored to him, he deserved to receive the customary blessing of God the Saviour.

As has already been said, I have faithfully related these things in plain truth, as I learned them from his own account. For as I endeavoured to attach myself to him with affectionate familiarity because of his holiness, and depended greatly upon his comfort and conversation, I extracted this vision from him, as well as many other things, by earnest prayers and a certain violence of charity—yet on condition [Col. 1280D] that I should presume to disclose it to no one before his death. This condition I was easily able to observe, for he survived only a short time thereafter. At length, his blessed struggle completed, he was gathered to his fathers, with whom he now rests at Clairvaux, God being gracious; there, living religiously, he had always ardently desired to close his final day as well.

## CHAPTER IV. On William, first a monk of Saint-Albin at Angers and afterwards of Clairvaux, to whom many things were divinely shown and revealed.

At the same time and place there was another venerable man, named William, advanced both in years and in religious life. Having served God in the monastic habit for nearly fifty years, he continually crucified his flesh [Col. 1281A] with its vices and desires, and endured a prolonged daily martyrdom. Before entering the Cistercian Order, he had lived for a long time in the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers. There, by his religious life, he presented himself as a pattern of good works and gave his followers an example of great holiness. Thus his fellow monks, and likewise the abbot himself, held him in great reverence and loved him with a remarkable affection of charity.

There was on monastic property a place which seemed more solitary and more suited to the peace of religious life. With the abbot’s consent, he withdrew to it with a few brothers. There, shut up in a narrow cell, he dwelt for many years, both in order to afflict himself by stricter [Col. 1281B] self-denial and not to burden weaker brethren by his more austere manner of life. So, multiplying fasts and prayers by day and night, he not only altogether rejected flesh-meat and the richer dishes which the brethren sometimes ate under the monastery’s former custom; he frequently also abstained from Lenten food and even from drinking water, sustaining his weak body on the scantiest fare.

He did not attain this virtue of abstinence without great difficulty. But after long torments of hunger, after unutterable groans and sobs, God’s grace cooperating, he finally drove out from their natural seats the inherent enticements of belly and palate, together with his other vices.

One day, when one of the monastery’s elders came to greet him, he ordered a meal of meat to be set before William, because he seemed weak and exhausted from a long journey. William replied that he would in no way eat meat unless the man who had ordered it served would share it with him. The elder, compelled by friendly affection and persuasion [Col. 1281C] and, as he later confessed, by some small appetite for the dish itself, agreed to eat. When the meal was over, the guest said farewell and departed.

After he had gone, the brother immediately returned to himself and began to draw deep sighs from the bottom of his heart and to groan intensely because he had broken the resolve of so long a time on so trifling an occasion. He had scarcely begun to entertain these thoughts when suddenly someone knocked at the window of his cell. When he opened it, he was startled and struck dumb by the sight of him. The visitor was a person of most reverend face and bearing, marvellous beyond human measure; William had seen no one like him in all beauty. His garments were white and precious, the hair of his head like white wool, and his face shone with singular beauty like snow. He seemed to indicate an angel rather than a human being. The words of his mouth were full of sweetness and grace and wonderfully breathed heavenly wisdom. Indeed, whatever appeared in that man seemed to be above human nature.

Yet he walked barefoot and said he was a pilgrim who had come from distant regions to visit William. After a gentle greeting, he began to rebuke him with familiar and friendly correction concerning the matters William had been turning over in his mind, as though he knew and saw [Col. 1282A] his thoughts. He said:

“You rightly groan; you rightly grieve over the fault by which you have now broken a long-standing purpose of praiseworthy abstinence for the sake of a pleasing kindness. Charity is not good when it destroys charity. That compassion is not to be approved which injures souls in order to foster bodies.

“Now hear an example which I shall set before you. In Spain there was a holy woman living as a recluse. Subsisting on bread and water, or sometimes half-cooked vegetables, she courageously subdued the wantonness of the flesh by sober and chaste conduct. At one time, by the devil’s prompting, she was struck with a desire to eat meat. Although she resisted the temptation long and hard, when she could no longer endure it she yielded, as it were placing her hands in the enemy’s hands, to consent. She therefore ordered a meat dish to be prepared for her.

“When it had been placed upon the table, before she dared taste it she prostrated herself in prayer, beseeching God with a tearful voice not to allow her to touch the prepared food if He knew it harmful to her soul. Rising from prayer, she went to the table and, having made the blessing, removed the cover that concealed the dish of meat. And behold: in place of the meat which had been set out, there appeared on the platter three young ravens, crying out and without feathers. At this sight the holy woman was terrified; and, summoning the sister who attended her, she inquired into the truth of the matter. Under oath before the dreadful judgment, the attendant answered that she had set on that same table not featherless little birds but three [Col. 1282C] pieces of cooked meat.

“The cell stood on the bank of a great and violent river, which burst from rocky mountains and, rushing through a rugged course, fell in swift descent toward the lower country. Therefore the handmaid of God, rejoicing and giving thanks that her prayer had been heard, ordered that the young birds be thrown there together with the very dish in which they were contained. Cast into the stream, they could in no way be separated from one another; rather, as the vessel floated upon the waves, they were at length carried down into a nearby bend of the same dwelling-place, where a hollow in a huge rock holds back a great mass of water. There they have constantly revolved through the passage of many ages, and to this day [178], as testimony to this miracle, they are seen floating upon the waters in that very vessel.”

As the man finished speaking these and similar things, the brother was touched by his most pleasing discourse. Falling upon his face and shedding tears, he asked forgiveness. Having received penance, he deserved to receive from him not only absolution for his offences but also abundant consolation. Then, as he began confidently to speak with him, he asked who he was and whence he came. The noble visitor answered: “It is not yours to know now who I am, nor to learn whence I come or where I am going.”

Then William said: “I beseech you, my lord, at least enter with us today, that we may minister to you.” He replied: “I need neither your bread, nor clothing, [Col. 1283A] nor lodging; rather, I abound in every good thing and have food to eat which you do not know. Only I am concerned for your salvation; be yourselves likewise concerned for it.”

Having said farewell, he departed hastily and was so suddenly withdrawn from the observer’s sight that he seemed rather to have vanished than gone away. William immediately summoned the brethren who attended him and ordered them urgently to pursue the departing visitor and, with many entreaties, compel him to accept lodging. They hurried away and ran here and there, but found not even a trace of him. Hence the man of God most certainly believed that an angel of God—or rather, the King of Angels and Lord Jesus Himself—had been present, since He could speak such things and discern the secrets of his heart. From that blessed presence his mind conceived and brought forth such devotion and grace that nearly twenty years later, when he told me these things, he still could not restrain his tears because of overwhelming loving emotion [Col. 1283B].

As time went on, the renowned name of blessed Bernard and the greatness of his virtues came to William’s attention through the fame that proclaimed them everywhere. His spirit could not rest until he gave himself to be governed by Bernard’s most blessed instruction, so that the most fervent might make him more fervent and the holiest make him holier. Bernard received him kindly and admitted him to the desired community of Clairvaux. Such grace of virtues shone in William that he appeared marvellous in every holiness, even to those who were themselves perfect [Col. 1283C].

The merciful God sent him many great consolations through His Spirit and revealed to him many matters from heavenly secrets, as we know for certain. Yet because William feared falling into the plague of vainglory, he related very few of these many things, and those only to very few people.

One day, while Prime was being sung in choir and William stood in his place with those chanting the psalms, Saint Malachy appeared to him as he kept vigil and sang. Malachy lies honourably buried in that same church. He sat in a chair beside the altar, splendidly adorned with ring, staff, mitre, and other episcopal insignia, as though he were about to celebrate the solemnities of Mass after the conclusion [Col. 1283D] of that hour. It was the anniversary of that saint’s death, the solemn day of All the Faithful Departed. Blessed Bernard also appeared with him, the most blessed pastor and patron of that church. Bernard likewise shone in precious white garments and was mitred, though not wearing the infula. And rightly so: he was the master of the household, who in his own house yielded and paid honour to his venerable and spiritual guest, joyfully conceding to him the solemnities of the Mass, especially on that day on which the holy bishop had entered the heavenly court and first been honoured with heavenly hymns.

Therefore the blessed Father himself showed diligent and devoted service [Col. 1284A] toward the same holy bishop and in the ministry of his altar. The blessed prelate, his eyes fixed, leaning upon his pastoral staff, continually faced the choir. Saint Bernard, on the other hand, looked now at the bishop, now at the community, now at the altar itself, as one concerned for all. This vision, so manifest and subjected to bodily eyes, appeared to that servant of God for as long as a single psalm lasted during that hour of Prime. When the psalm ended, the vision ended; but the devout feeling inspired by that vision could not thereafter end in the heart of the one who had seen it.

On another day the same blessed Bernard likewise appeared to him, glorious in face and bearing. When William saw him, he fell at his feet, praying and asking something of him. The saint said: “What do you wish me to do for you?” William said: “Lord Father, if I have found favour in your eyes, tell me, I beseech you, whether I am to be saved.” The saint replied: “Is this a small thing that you ask? Today, when I departed from paradise, how many thousands of people I left outside the gate who are still tormented by such fear, not knowing whether they are deemed worthy of love or of hatred.” Having said this, he gave William an answer concerning the matter for which he had pleaded. But what definite answer he gave him is unknown to us. For William was circumspect and reserved in speech, and took great care not to say anything that might savour of his own glory. Nevertheless, the confidence of his speech and the cheerfulness of his face [Col. 1284C] made it sufficiently clear that he had received from the saint a joyful answer concerning the matter.

At another time, while this servant of God was in the infirmary, suffering from bodily illness, on a night after Matins, when the others were resting, he—as was his fervent custom—kept watch and prayed in bed. Behold, a demon entered through the door of the house and visibly appeared to him in the dress and appearance of a beautiful woman. Passing before him, she wandered about in circles as though seeking someone. In the middle of the room there was a lamp burning brightly, whose abundant light made the wanton movements and lascivious gestures of that shameless monster plainly visible.

The phantom harlot went about, searching everywhere with roving gaze and examining almost every man’s bed: who slept and who woke; whether perhaps she disturbed one of her own there; whether anyone might respond by consenting to her flattering and seductive invitation. She passed one quickly, looked longer at another, visited one from a distance, approached another more closely, and sometimes gently brought her hands as far as the faces of the sleeping. She wished to leave nothing untouched, nothing unexamined; and what she always works inwardly by suggestion, she then outwardly represented through shameless signs. At last, finding the one she sought, she stopped before his bed. He was a young monk, recently made a monk. Then, stretching out her impudent hand, she slightly removed the cover from the side of his head and, lightly touching the sleeper, said in a clear voice: [Col. 1285A] “O senseless man, what are you doing here? Rise quickly and follow me; and tell your companion also to come out after you. I shall wait for you outside at the door.”

Having said this, the obstinate beast hurried away and left through the door by which she had entered. The youth, awakened, sat up in bed and, rubbing his forehead with his hands, looked here and there, wishing to know who had awakened him. Seeing no one, he laid his head down again and fell asleep—but not in God.

When morning came, the man of God who had seen these things informed Abbot Robert of the sequence of events. Robert privately questioned the youth concerning his thoughts and received from him the answer that he was not troubled in any degree by an impure thought, but was being drawn with the firmest will toward perseverance in his resolution. For the devil, now ruling his heart, had blocked the way of confession, lest saving pardon might enter through the gate of penance. When the abbot reported the youth’s answer to the aforesaid man, he replied: “Wait a little, and from the outcome of the deed you will prove that what I said is true.”

Why say more? Not many days passed, and behold, that youth, driven by the furies of lust, broke the bond of his profession and, returning to the vomit of the world, became a contemptible apostate. The companion whom he had been told to bring out with him had entered the novitiate with him and had been made a monk with him. Transferred to another abbey, when he heard that his companion had cast off the yoke of the Order, he too broke the bond of his profession and did not delay in becoming an apostate with him [Col. 1285C]. Thus it became plainly known that the spirit of fornication, in accordance with the aforementioned vision, had led both men away. This holy man, full of days and virtues, passed to the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. On Achard, monk of Clairvaux, founder of many monasteries, who, when Herbert was still a novice, related to him many things that he had seen.

(See above, *First Life of Saint Bernard*, book VII, col. 453.)

## CHAPTER VI. [184–86] On Schocelinus, hermit of the region of Trier: a man of great holiness and remarkable contempt for human affairs, whom Saint Bernard also visited through his envoys and honoured with gifts; whose body, translated to the church of Blessed Mary in the castle of Luxembourg, was celebrated by miracles.

[Col. 1285D]

(See the same work, col. 455.)

## CHAPTER VII. [187–93] On a lay brother and convert of Clairvaux, accustomed to pray for his enemies, whose precious death was attested by a divine vision. Which of Saint Bernard’s followers enter heaven by the straight way.

(See the same work, col. 459.)

## CHAPTER VIII. [194–97] Two angels strew the choir with flowers for Robert, abbot of Clairvaux, signifying the merit of a monk then dying.

Robert, the venerable Father, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, a religious man and praiseworthy in every respect, [Col. 1286A] once, while resting in his bed, saw in a dream what seemed to be two youthful young men, strikingly radiant in face and dress. They were scattering in abundance, throughout the choir of Clairvaux, lilies, roses, violets, and flowers of various kinds. Amazed at the sight, he said to them: “What has seemed good to you, good young men, that you should, contrary to our custom, strew this pavement with flowers and introduce such a novelty into our monastery?” They replied: “Do not wonder at this or take it ill, for at this very moment a new feast-day of a certain new saint is to be celebrated in this choir.”

At that same hour a religious brother of good reputation died in the infirmary. When the death-board was sounded for him, the same venerable [Col. 1286B] Father awoke from sleep and hastened to him with the other 198 brothers. With great devotion he commended the man’s soul, most firmly believing and trusting that this was the new saint of whom the holy angels, upon his reception into rest, were immediately to celebrate a new feast and a new joy.

## CHAPTER IX. A vision shown at Clairvaux upon the death of a brother of good will indeed, but somewhat negligent.

Another brother saw in a vision certain precious garments of cloths and silks being cut and prepared in the infirmary at Clairvaux. Greatly astonished by the novelty of this, he was told: “These ornaments at which you wonder have been prepared [Col. 1286C] for one of the daughters of the abbot of Clairvaux, who is now proceeding to her wedding. Because she has less beauty in herself than befits her rank, she must at least possess the fragrance and adornment of costly clothing, so as to please her husband.”

At the same hour the board was sounded, and a certain brother died. It was found concerning him that, although he had possessed a good will, he had nevertheless been somewhat negligent and slack in practice. Therefore it was necessary that the brothers should bestow from their prayers a more abundant adornment upon him to whom his own merits had not granted the grace of perfect beauty.

## 199 CHAPTER X. The brothers of Igny are represented in an angelic vision by the emblem of lilies.

[Col. 1286D]

Likewise at Igny—which is no undistinguished monastery among the daughters of Clairvaux—a revelation of this kind was shown to a man of approved manner of life. In a vision of the night he beheld two angels coming from heaven. Of the many lilies visible in the cemetery of that monastery, they cut four and carried them with them to the stars. When he saw this, he said to them: “Why, I beg you, do you cut down our lilies?” One replied: “Do not wonder at it, brother, for the lilies are ours. We shall now carry these four away with us; the rest, moreover, we shall gather little by little hereafter when the time is fitting. Not even one will be able to remain, until we have transferred them all.”

Immediately, therefore, four good and religious brothers died in the same monastery; and it is certain that they were signified by the four lilies cut from the cemetery. Yet in the statement that none there would be left behind until all had been transferred into heaven, no small consolation was left to us little and weak ones, who groan among the feeble members of Christ, grieve over our imperfection, and in grieving cry out into the ears of the Father of mercies: “For he knows our frame” (Ps. 102); and: “If thou, O Lord, shouldst mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall endure? For with thee there is propitiation” (Ps. 129). Likewise: “Thine eyes saw my imperfection, and none among them”—that is to be understood, “shall perish,” as blessed Bernard explains—(Ps. 138).

## 200 CHAPTER XI. Arnulf of Majorca, a man exceedingly powerful in the world, becomes a monk at Clairvaux; Saint Bernard assigns him only three Lord’s Prayers in penance for the sins of his whole life; he declares that he has received the hundredfold from the Lord in this life; he dies holily.

[Col. 1287B]

Arnulf of Majorca, a very rich and luxurious man, a Fleming by nation, secretly committed himself to blessed Bernard. They both agreed to conceal the matter because of certain worldly impediments, until the last day on which he would leave his land and his kindred. For he was the head of a large household, surrounded by sons and brothers and entangled in such great wealth that he could not break away without grave harm and scandal to his people, unless he had first arranged his household wisely and cautiously.

Meanwhile, while they kept everything in silence and those two alone in the world knew the reason for this hidden undertaking, the word of the Lord came to a certain rustic cattle-herd as he was driving oxen to the plough, saying: “Go, tell Arnulf of Majorca to take you with him to Clairvaux, whither he will shortly go for conversion; and be converted with him.” He heard the voice but saw no one. After this had happened, he began to pray more intently that, if the speech had come forth from God, He would again disclose it to his ear and speak to him once more, repeating the same words. Having therefore received the oracle a second time, he came to the aforesaid man and said: [Col. 1287D] “A word has come to me for you, my lord.”

When he had been led aside by Arnulf, he fell at his knees and said: “I beseech you through Christ: take me with you to your Clairvaux, and save my soul with your own. And, if you wish to know, this and this was announced to me.” On hearing the revelation, Arnulf was greatly amazed and delighted. He took the man in and brought him home with him; he had him as an inseparable companion on the journey and in conversion, and, as we believe, was also to have him as a companion in eternal recompense.

When this venerable man came to the aforesaid monastery, he bestowed much of his wealth both upon it and upon many others. Blessed Bernard also publicly pronounced this judgment concerning him: “Christ,” he said, “is no less to be wondered at and no less glorified for the conversion [Col. 1288A] of Brother Arnulf than for the raising of Lazarus, dead four days; for Arnulf lay enclosed and buried amid such luxuries as though in a tomb, living as one dead.”

When Arnulf confessed with many groans and tears all the sins that he had contracted in the world, blessed Bernard, seeing the most bitter contrition of his heart and his willing disposition toward every good work, imposed upon him the penance of saying the *Our Father* three times and thereafter persevering in his resolution until death. On hearing this, he spoke almost resentfully: “Please, most blessed Father, do not mock your servant.”

“In what,” Bernard asked, “do I mock you?”

He replied: “Fasts of seven or ten years would not suffice for me, even if I were humbled in sackcloth and ashes; yet you command me to say the *Our Father* three times and persevere in the Order!”

The saint said to him: “Then do you know better than I what you ought to do and how you may be saved?”

He answered: “Far be such wicked presumption from [Col. 1288B] my soul. But for God’s sake I beg you: do not spare me now, so that you may spare me more fully hereafter. Impose upon me now such a penalty of penance that, after the death of the flesh, I may attain rest without punishment.”

The blessed Father told him: “Do as I have said, and I assure you that, once you have laid aside the burden of the body, you will immediately fly to God without distress.”

Strengthened as though by a divinely given answer, he was thereafter so firm that no violence of temptations and no affliction of bodily illness could in any degree retard the course of his desire, by which he was wholly advancing toward God. He was most careful and fearful in guarding his heart; indeed, I remember seeing no one so diligent in cleansing his own conscience. All—especially those who heard his confessions—marveled at his daily insistence, or rather importunity. He would not permit them to rest, just as he himself could not rest, while confessing, mourning, and weeping—not only over an idle word or gesture, should one ever, though rarely, escape him, but even over some vain and trivial thought. Others, apart from a very few, would have regarded such matters as of little or no account; but he judged himself in them most scrupulously and accused himself as though of a crime. [Col. 1288D]

One day, while Vespers were being sung in the church, he was standing in the rear choir beside a monk who was likewise a most holy man. Behold, an angel of God appeared there in the form of a most beautiful young monk, clothed in a cowl whiter than snow, though Arnulf himself neither saw nor knew it. As Arnulf bent, according to custom, at the *Glory* of the psalm, the angel stood before him and supported the worshipper’s head with hands placed beneath it.

When the aforementioned monk saw him and perceived from the radiance of his face and clothing that he was an angel, he rejoiced greatly at the angelic sight. He approached, wishing to seize and devoutly embrace him. [Col. 1289A] But as he stretched out his hands to hold and clasp him, the angel suddenly vanished and withdrew; then immediately appearing again, he stood elsewhere. Seeing this, the monk again ran to him and tried in the same way to take hold of him. But the angel at once vanished and immediately reappeared in another place, and the man was frustrated in his attempt. After this had happened several times, the angel finally disappeared altogether; though he had offered himself to be seen, he did not allow himself to be held.

Since it is truly written that “God loves correction, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12), the correction of fatherly mercy never failed this venerable man. It always cut away in him the vices of the flesh and everywhere increased the virtues of the soul. For many years until his death, he was scourged by grave and prolonged afflictions. He not only endured them with equanimity, but even gloried in them as in every kind of wealth.

Once, when he was more harshly afflicted than usual by intestinal pains from which he suffered severely, he was distressed almost to death. For some time he remained speechless and unconscious, so that he was despaired of and was therefore anointed with the oil of the sick. But as soon as he could first draw breath, he suddenly burst into rejoicing and said: “All that you have said is true, Lord Jesus.” He repeated this again and again. Those present were astonished and asked how he was and why [Col. 1289C] he said these things. He answered nothing but that all that God had spoken was true.

Some said that the bitterness of the pain had disturbed his brain and that he was speaking as one out of his mind. He replied: “It is not so, brothers. With sound head and sober mind I say that all God has spoken is true.”

They answered: “We too know that. But why do you say it?”

He replied: “The Lord says in the Gospel that whoever leaves this and that for love of him will receive a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the age to come (Matt. 19). I therefore experience the force of this saying now, in the present, and already receive my hundredfold in this life. For the immense force of this pain is so sweet to me, so pleasing to me, because of the hope of divine mercy laid up in it, that I would not wish to have lacked this very pain in exchange for the world’s wealth, multiplied a hundredfold, which I left behind. And if I, a sinner and unworthy, am so strengthened and made glad by God even in my afflictions, how, do we suppose, do holy and perfect men dance and exult in their consolations? Truly, spiritual joy, which now exists in hope, surpasses by a hundred thousand times secular joy, which now exists in possession. Whoever has not yet deserved to receive this hundredfold plainly has not yet left all things perfectly behind, but retains something from his own will, which is evil property.”

As he said this, all marveled that such a judgment had been uttered by an unlettered layman. It was plainly given to be understood that the Holy Spirit, who allowed him to be severely scourged in body, was gently anointing him inwardly in soul. Whoever that most sacred [Col. 1290A] anointing touches, it teaches concerning all the things that it works.

Thus this holy man, having now received double from the hand of the Lord for all his sins, tormented at last by a long martyrdom and tested like gold in a furnace, fell asleep in the Lord in most peaceful rest. We most confidently believe of him that, in accordance with blessed Bernard’s judgment, as soon as he left the body he came to God without punishment.

## CHAPTER XII. A man is compelled to conversion at Clairvaux by blows inflicted by an invisible hand.

[Col. 1290B]

There is in the same monastery a venerable religious man whose name, while he still lives, we do not wish to disclose. While he was a cleric and a pampered youth, he sometimes occupied himself with games together with companions of his own age. Once, when many gathered at a certain house for amusement, intending to spend the day in the customary way with theatrical applause and trifles, this young man also went there to feast his eyes upon the spectacle of vanity.

Some gamblers were there playing with dice. To see them better from above, he lay leaning forward over a table placed there. Suddenly there came upon him what seemed to be a human hand, beating him continuously with an invisible scourge. It struck his head and entire back with frequent blows, as though beating down upon him with a club. [Col. 1290C] He lay motionless, not knowing what to do or where to turn. In the extreme anguish of pain he wanted to break out in cries and lamentation, but shame before the people around him prevented him; he bore the torment of the blows with difficulty.

Reproaching himself, he spoke in the bitterness of his soul, saying: “Alas for me, Lord God! Now my sins have found me; behold, I am already dying and descending to hell in pain, lacking the fruit of repentance. Oh, if you would grant me time to amend, how great is my willingness to obey you in all things!”

While he spoke these and similar words in his heart before God, a voice came to him, saying: “If you are willing to go to Clairvaux for conversion, you shall be saved in soul and body.”

He replied: “Behold, I give myself as a servant to God and to the house of Clairvaux.”

But once he had resolved this in his heart with firm will, the scourge immediately withdrew and all pain vanished. Seeing this, he immediately refused to yield to flesh and blood, nor did he endure the delay of even a single hour, except that a mount was not immediately available. On that same day it was obtained, and at first light the next morning he set out. Reckoning house, household, fields, revenues, rents, and everything he possessed as dung for Christ’s sake, he left them behind. He came to Clairvaux and has remained there [Col. 1291A] until this day, sufficiently demonstrating by his manner of life that that first call to his conversion truly came from him who reproves and chastises those whom he loves, and in fatherly mercy scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12).

## 207 CHAPTER XIII. By Saint Bernard’s command, the death of a monk of Clairvaux is delayed.

When one of the brothers of that place was at the point of death, blessed Bernard entered after Compline to visit him. Seeing that the man was near death and on the very point of departure, he said: “You know, dearest brother, that our community is now wearied from its labor and must shortly rise for Vigils. If, while you sleep again, it must interrupt its sleep, it will be greatly troubled and will celebrate the lengthy Vigils less fittingly. Therefore, that it may go well with you and that you may live long upon the land into which you are entering to possess it, I command you in Christ’s name to wait for us until the hour of the divine office.”

He replied: “Lord, I shall do as you have commanded, provided that you assist my vow with your prayers.”

Why say more? The Father went to the dormitory, and the brother did not die before the appointed time. As soon as the signal for Vigils began to sound, the death-board was sounded, and he died. This happened repeatedly not only with that brother but with several others also: their end was extended by one or more days at the Father’s command and wish. [Col. 1291C]

## 208 CHAPTER XIV. Holy angels stand around the bed of a dying monk at Clairvaux.

A lay brother (*conversus*) of the aforementioned monastery, a religious man of good works, came to the end of his life. With open eyes he saw holy angels standing present by his bed. Immediately he said to the brothers around him: “Do you not see the angels of God who have just arrived? Sound the board as quickly as possible, for they await my departure itself.” When he had said this, his soul immediately departed. There is no doubt that the holy angels, whom he had deserved to see beforehand, received it.

## CHAPTER XV. Christ the Lord appears in sleep to a cattle-herding brother of Clairvaux, goading oxen with him, pressing the plough-handle, and cutting the ground with the plough.

[Col. 1291D]

Another brother held the office of oxherd in the same monastery, a pure man of good simplicity. Once he saw in a dream the Lord Jesus Christ beside him, a most delightful sight: with his own most sweet hand Christ held the ox-goad and, from the other side of the yoke-pole, drove the oxen with him. On seeing this, the brother immediately fell ill and took to his bed; after six days, he ended his labor and pain with death.

Blessed Bernard, who knew the man’s conscience to be pure and simple, thought on this vision as the brother himself recounted it and greatly rejoiced. When the brother died, Bernard confidently declared that he had walked with God; indeed, he had truly labored with him, and therefore God had taken him away. The almighty Merciful One could not abandon his servant in the final struggle, for he had deigned to be his companion and fellow worker in labor. [Col. 1292A]

## CHAPTER XVI. An unlearned lay brother of Clairvaux, near death, speaks much in Latin concerning the Holy Scriptures.

The infirmary brothers of Clairvaux often recount with joy and wonder the case of a lay brother of honorable life. When he came to death, he began to speak Latin. Though he had never learned Latin letters, he discussed certain marvelous matters from the sacred Scriptures in eloquent speech, uttering absolutely nothing except what accorded with sound doctrine. Moreover, he produced in modulated tones certain sweet songs that were nowhere customarily heard, so that those who saw were astonished by the novelty of the miracle and soothed by the sweetness of the singing. After doing this for some time, he finally rendered up his soul in a good confession, and the final joy of that light took possession of him. [Col. 1292B]

## 210 CHAPTER XVII. A lay brother of Clairvaux leaves three times and is received three times; at last, truly and long repentant, he tastes eternal blessedness shortly before death.

Moreover, another lay brother, having in his fickleness left the same [Col. 1292C] house three times and been received back three times, finally groaned deeply. Adding the pains of remedies to the pains of his wounds, he strove to erase former evils by present lamentations, as though driving out a nail with a nail. At the same time, by different considerations, he instructed those still standing not to fall and those who had fallen to rise, through his salutary example.

And lest anything perhaps be lacking to him for the complete recovery of eternal salvation, God so ordained that decay entered his bones. Struck about the thighs by a cancerous ulcer, he wasted away, so that, with his flesh eaten away on every side, his bare bones lay exposed and his wounds swarmed with worms. The distress of his illness increased day by day. Imprisoned for many years upon his pallet, he was subjected almost to as many deaths as hours that he lived.

Thus there were pitiful pain and anguish for his suffering soul, and for his attendants immense stench and horror from the sight of the wasting ulcer. Yet an abundant recompense for this labor and endurance was laid up with God for both. The sick man constantly strove to give thanks in these afflictions, believing and confessing that what he received still fell far short of his deserts.

And because it is truly written, “Take away the dross from silver, and a most pure vessel will come forth” (Prov. 25:6), when the dross of sin had at last been purified away, that soul was finally brought out from the furnace of purification. Like silver tested by fire, clean and shining, it was transferred with the other vessels of mercy to the palace of the highest King. [Col. 1293A] Before it came out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, God granted it to foresee his glory and to taste beforehand something ineffable of that heavenly sweetness in whose endless enjoyment it was soon to be admitted.

On receiving this, he immediately burst forth in a jubilant proclamation of heaven. With brightened face he began to sing, in a most sweet melody, certain new and exceedingly delightful hymns and tunes from the songs of Zion. When this sound was made, a multitude of brothers gathered to see, with great wonder, a man placed amid pain and ordinary death, yet forgetful of death and unaware of pain—indeed, one who, mocking death in death, seemed already to say: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is thy victory, O death? Where is thy sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:54).

Thus, singing and glorifying God, in that very hour of sorrow he saw all things prosperous and joyful; and as though he already played upon his harp with the other saints, so, joyful and praising God in a voice of exultation and thanksgiving, he sent forth his soul to God. Blessed Bernard was greatly gladdened by his happy end. Accordingly, in a most devout address in chapter, Bernard praised in him the fruit of repentance and set his remarkable patience before all as an example. [Col. 1293B]

## 212 CHAPTER XVIII. Christ the Lord appears, shortly before his death, with the twelve apostles to Gerard, lay brother of Moris, a most gentle and religious man.

A lay brother named Gerard was a very religious man in the house called Moris, a God-fearing man and an exceedingly severe disciplinarian of his body. He struggled against vices with such fervor of spirit that, when troubled by unlawful impulses, he would roll upon nettles on the ground and rub his body and limbs against them. By doing this very often, he forcefully repressed the goads of wanton flesh and beneficially extinguished the incentives of lust by a penal fire.

He was a most gentle man, and took great pains to live among the brothers without complaint. While suffering his final illness, he called one of his attendants to him and said: “Dearest brother, I recall that the day before yesterday I offended that particular man”—he identified him by name—“through a fault which, I fear, was mine. I immediately cast myself down and asked and obtained pardon from him; but whether he forgave me from his heart is uncertain to me. Go, I beg you, to him and again, in my stead, plead with him for God’s sake to pardon a suppliant fully and from his heart.” [Col. 1293D]

When this had been obtained, he blessed God and said: “Now I shall die gladly, because, as I believe, all matters have been set at peace. I believe that I have a good peace and love with all, and that I desire for all precisely what I desire for myself.”

Then, as the moment of his departure drew near, joyful in face and spirit, he said to those around him: “Come, my brothers: rejoice in the Lord and rejoice with me, for the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God the Father, has now come to me with his twelve apostles. And behold, he now remains in our church, [Col. 1294A] awaiting my departure; nor will he leave it until I depart with him.”

When he had finished this speech, he immediately ended also in death. There is no doubt that he was received in peace by him who had awaited him with ineffable condescension. A brother named Josbert, a man of advanced age and proven holiness, told me this under divine attestation, just as he heard it from Gerard himself, whom he attended in death.

## CHAPTER XIX. A monk of Clairvaux repeatedly sees evil demons in dreadful forms; he sees Saint Augustine, who leads him both to places of punishment and to the abodes of the blessed; he sees a monk’s soul depart from its body and hover in the air until it is fortified by priestly commendation; finally, during Mass, he sees the infant Jesus recoil from a wicked priest.

[Col. 1294B]

We know another of the sons of Clairvaux, a man likewise most holy, whose name we do not wish to disclose because he remains subject to present vanity. Renouncing the world in youth, he has now passed, I believe, his fortieth year in the monastery. There, serving God in all holiness and righteousness, he has also, by God’s great gift, preserved bodily integrity from his mother’s womb.

The Lord Jesus supports him with many consolations as a testimony to his innate purity and reveals to him many matters from the heavenly mysteries. He has also received from the Lord a spiritual grace attained by very few people. For almost whenever he wishes to look upward intently into the air with fixed eyes, he is accustomed to see by daylight, with bodily eyes, globes of demons wandering everywhere in crowded bands. Their number is so great that it cannot be estimated for immensity. Though they commonly appear in many forms, there is one form—or rather deformity—in which he sees them more frequently.

According to the outlines of bodies, they appear to be monstrous men: giants in stature, Ethiopians in color, serpents in agility, lions in ferocity. They have large heads and protruding swollen bellies; their bodies are short and hunchbacked. They have long, thin necks and equally very long arms and legs. When they stand somewhere in the air, he can readily distinguish their bodies limb by limb. But when they roam hither and thither in restless movement, he perceives nothing of them except ghostly shadows and whirling coils. On clear days, when the sun shines in its strength, he is accustomed to see such visions more often and distinguish them better. [Col. 1294D]

Once, while he prayed alone in a certain lodging after a prolonged vigil, the hairs of his flesh suddenly stood on end and, before the terror of the night, he began to be disturbed beyond his usual manner. Behold, a crowd of demons rushed through the door in a mass and, as though pressed together by the multitude entering, filled the whole house. They made noise everywhere and shook the praying man himself from side to side.

When he perceived this, armed at once with the sign of the cross, he began repeatedly to ask pardon and, frequently repeating the salutation of blessed Mary, swiftly drove the whirling phantoms from his oratory. On the following night, when he returned to the same place to pray, behold, the hostile powers again hurried on in a fury and struck the stone wall of that dwelling with a violent blow, like a battering ram applied to a wall, so that the entire building shook.

When the man of God lifted his eyes toward a large window opened in that wall, he saw standing in it a domestic demon, in the likeness of a griffin or ostrich, threatening him as though it were about to rush upon and devour him. On seeing this, he recognized the devil’s devices; invoking the Savior’s name, he set the sign of the cross against the savage apparition and put it to flight. Having suffered many such mockeries and combats, this outstanding combatant does not cease even to this day to be struck and to strike back. [Col. 1295B]

One night, while he was outside the house and stood in the courtyard in prayer, he saw before him a bright lamp suspended in the air. Whenever he approached it, it was carried upward so that it could not be grasped; and whenever he moved back a little, the lamp descended again and remained in the same place. After this happened many times, what he saw finally vanished, and the meaning of the apparition did not become sufficiently clear.

Nor do I think this should be passed over: at one time blessed Augustine appeared to him in a vision, leading him through innumerable places of punishment and as far as the entrance to the very pit of hell. Looking down from above into it, with trembling limbs and a soul throbbing from unbearable terror, he saw that Tartarean gulf of the burning abyss, full of dreadful cries and howls of wretches, living an accursed life forever in devouring fire. For them the bitterest death, the worst death of all deaths, is inability to die.

Turning back from there, Augustine led him out of the place of horror and darkness and brought him into the regions of happy joys. He showed him the light-filled seats and most blessed dwelling places of souls, where, stripped of their bodies, they lived and rested most happily in the peace of Christ that surpasses all understanding. Then Saint Augustine said to him: “Behold, you have seen the ultimate ends of good and evil. Choose what is good in your own eyes. If you resolve to keep the way of righteousness, which has been abundantly set forth in my books, you will have a portion in the land of the living, in glory with all these. But if you wish to follow your own desire, you are to be numbered with those who are under the anathema of oblivion.” [Col. 1295D]

When the vision ended and he had returned to himself, the man trembled all over and was filled with violent horror, constrained by a double fear: lest he lose the glory of the good, and lest he incur the punishment of the reprobate. From then on, he began to love the most blessed doctor Augustine more sweetly and to ponder his sayings more delightfully.

It happened once that he fell ill in a house of God, an abbey of the Cistercian Order. Another brother of honorable life was then also mortally ill there. When that brother had already been laid upon the floor, it happened by chance, in the absence of the infirmary attendants, that he breathed his last. The aforementioned brother, lying there in his bed and languishing under severe bodily affliction, saw plainly with bodily eyes, the Lord revealing it to him, that soul emerging from the body in a long stream, like the smoke of incense coming forth from a censer.

When it had wholly emerged, it gathered itself into a single sphere and stood suspended in the air above the body, at a height of four or five cubits. His spirit was like a dense yet translucent little cloud, spread out to approximately the measure of one *modius* [a Roman dry measure]. It remained there motionless until, attended by the brothers’ prayers and fortified by priestly commendation, it deserved to receive guidance for the perilous and unknown journey. [Col. 1296B]

When that brother saw this, he summoned the infirmary attendants by whatever sound and voice he could make. They immediately hurried over, sounded the death-board, and brothers came running from every side for the funeral rites. When the community was present with the cross and holy water and the sacramental commendation had begun, the soul then proceeded as though now secure, and the smoky mist that had been visible disappeared.

At another time, it happened that the aforementioned brother attended the divine offices on a Sunday in a parish church. When the Offertory had been spoken and the ministry of bread and chalice had already been placed upon the holy table, the Lord Jesus immediately appeared to him standing upon the same altar in the form of a very beautiful little child. He appeared so plainly and for so long that the vision persisted almost until the sacrifice was completed.

Yet the priest of that place who celebrated Mass was a man of disgraceful and wicked life. Whenever that priest had his back to the altar—whether receiving the offerings of the faithful, addressing the people as is customary on a feast-day, or doing anything else—the holy child stood before the chalice. But whenever the priest faced the sacrament, the sacred little child, recoiling as though from the breath of the unclean priest, stood far away from him behind the chalice.

When the brother saw this, he was deeply compuncted, so that a flood of tears sometimes hindered his sight of the vision. [Col. 1296D] When the revelation was complete, he glorified God, who had deigned to show him such things. He truly understood that difference in personal merits does not produce a difference in sacrifices, since the efficacy of the sacrament in no way depends upon the priest’s virtue and merit, but upon the institution and grace of the Redeemer.

## CHAPTER XX. Robert, priest of Amiens, lover and preacher of chastity. There also, a certain chaste woman, accustomed to see the infant Jesus at the time of sacrifice: he voluntarily comes to the upright, but recoils from the wicked.

In the city of Amiens there is known to dwell a priest named Robert, a man of upright life, an outstanding lover and preacher of chastity, who, because of his exceptional holiness and wisdom, is loved and honoured by all the people. This venerable man is shown to possess great care and effectiveness in persuading his faithful subjects, by word and example, to love celibacy, so that very many of them abstain—not only from unlawful intercourse, but even from the marriage bed—some frequently and others continually. There was also there a devout woman who, burning with desire for chastity, had left her marriage bed although her husband resisted. He approached the aforementioned priest and began to complain against his wife. When the woman was summoned and rebuked by him, and would not consent to his admonitions, she heard:
