“You must choose one of two things: either obey the laws of marriage, or obtain from the Lord, through earnest prayers, your husband's consent.”

[Col. 1297B] She replied: “The first of these is altogether intolerable to me; the second exceedingly desirable.”

Accordingly, having received from the priest a respite of eight days, she applied herself fervently to fasting and tearful prayer. The Lord had mercy on his handmaid and, hearing her petition, within the course of a week so inflamed her husband's mind with love of continence that thereafter he was unable to be drawn into female embraces, even had his wife consented.

There is another holy and modest woman in the same city who, with her husband’s approval, has persevered for many years in this same resolution of chastity. To her the Lord deigns to reveal concerning the sacrament of the altar mighty things which very few people deserve to see. For when the most holy mysteries were being celebrated in church, she was accustomed very often to see the Lord Jesus Christ standing in the air above the holy chalice, in the form of a little child gleaming more brilliantly than a sunbeam, so that her eyes were dazzled by the radiance of the light. At the time of reception, that sacred little child enters the priest’s mouth together with the communion itself; and nevertheless, coming also to that same blessed woman, he visibly and tangibly enters her mouth, so that her throat and inward parts are filled with ineffable sweetness and joy. Yet she sees this grace descend upon only three priests in the same city.

Once, however, when a priest of dishonourable life was celebrating, [Col. 1297D] the woman saw the same child appear dark and as though sprinkled with blood over his whole body. He also disdained to approach the priest or enter his mouth. Seeing this, she began to weep most abundantly, understanding, surely, and grieving that the man was inwardly pierced by a deadly wound, for which so terrible a sign appeared outwardly.

## CHAPTER XXI. A Norman church-servant sees, during the divine sacrifice, a priest deprived of the kiss of the child Jesus because of the hatred by which he was stirred against his godfather-in-law. He also sees, during Rogationtide, a woman’s frivolous songs scorned by angels and received with laughter by demons.

I learned what I relate from the account of the holy and venerable Richard, formerly abbot of Savigny. In Normandy there was an honourable priest who had a parishioner, a man equally upright and God-fearing, whom he had made matricularius—church-servant—of his church. In great simplicity of heart this man sought the Lord; and therefore he obtained what he desired. Whenever the said priest celebrated the divine mysteries, the church-servant almost daily saw a glorious little child appearing above the altar. When the priest, about to give the peace to the people, kissed the sacred Host according to the custom of some, the sacred child approached the priest and graciously offered him the kiss of peace with his mouth.

It happened that the sow of a poor man, who was both the priest’s spiritual kinsman and his fellow villager, frequently entered the priest’s bean-field. Since the man neglected to restrain it, the sow was at last attacked and killed by the priest’s dogs and retainers. Thus the two men entered into a quarrel and parted in anger; and, anger giving birth to hatred, a number of days passed without reconciliation. Then grace was withdrawn from the priest, and the church-servant no longer saw the customary blessing descend upon him. Privately addressing him, he challenged the man concerning the injury to his conscience, asking what evil he had committed and also telling him what divine gift he had lost. Greatly terrified, the priest confessed that the injury done to his spiritual kinsman was the cause of this loss. Hastening to be reconciled with him, he at last scarcely deserved to receive again the grace he had lost.

[Col. 1298C] During the Rogation Days, when clergy and people extended their procession by walking a considerable distance, it was customary that, whenever the clerics paused, the women should in turn take up singing. The aforementioned guardian of the church, through the Lord’s revelation, saw in the air two separate companies of good and evil spirits, each accompanying the procession continually at its side. Therefore, when the clerics repeated psalms and hymnody, the apostate angels fled, the good spirits drew near, and with great rejoicing applauded the divine melodies. But when the women in turn sang frivolous little songs, the kindly spirits flew higher away, while the malign spirits came closer and, with foolish songs, clapping, and extraordinary bursts of laughter, mocked them. [Col. 1298D]

## CHAPTER XXII. A brother of Clairvaux, accustomed after receiving the Eucharist to taste honeyed sweetness in his mouth, once communicated after rebuking a friend too severely and felt a most bitter taste, like wormwood.

A brother of Clairvaux, when on one Sunday he received holy communion in the customary manner, thought at that time and throughout the following day that he held a most sweet honeycomb in his mouth. On the following Sunday, when he similarly received the Eucharist, he experienced like graces for three continuous days. On the third Sunday too, when he again received the divine food, he deserved to feel for a whole week the sweetness previously granted only once. Thereafter, this blessing of sweetness was multiplied for him, and he felt it for a long time, now less often and now more frequently, as pleased the Giver of grace.

It happened once that, reproving one of his friends for a fault, he exceeded all measure in the vehemence of his justified rebuke. Since he received the sacrifice of peace before being reconciled with his brother, he thought that he had put into his mouth the most bitter food of wormwood. He to whom this happened disclosed it privately to us. We do not doubt that it was true, since we know that a like grace has happened often to many persons and continues to happen today.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Another brother of Clairvaux, on the holy day of Preparation, saw the Lord Christ as though crucified at that very hour.

[Col. 1299B]

There is also another monk among the sons of that same monastery, a man advanced in years and religious observance, who has spent, if I am not mistaken, more than forty years in the Cistercian Order. Once, as he sat in the cloister on the holy day of Preparation, with a book before him, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him with hands and feet stretched out upon the cross, as though he had been crucified at that very hour. This most blessed vision, although brief and almost momentary, was nevertheless so clear and effective that the devout remembrance of it can no longer be erased from the seer’s heart. I could name this man, [Col. 1299C] had I not been forbidden by him; and I know him to be of such purity that he would not be ashamed, even for his soul’s sake, to speak the truth.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Christ, appearing in ecstasy to an elder monk of Clairvaux, says: “Your sins are forgiven you.”

Another elder of the same place, a religious man most worthy of every honour, was once engaged in prayer and was carried beyond himself in mind. Behold, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him and said: “Your sins are forgiven you.” When the vision ended and he had returned to himself, he gave thanks to God and was greatly consoled; for at that time he had been anxious and sorrowful [Col. 1299D] because of these same offences.

## CHAPTER XXV. A young monk, wrongly interpreting the devout tears of his abbot while he adored the cross on Good Friday, is immediately grievously tempted by a demon to cast off the monastic habit.

There is a venerable abbot among the sons of Savigny, a holy and very spiritual man, whose name and monastery we do not presently wish to state, lest he perhaps be burdened thereby. The Lord frequently visits him as a faithful and well-working servant, and reveals to him many things from his secrets.

Once, while he was devoutly adoring the Lord’s cross on Good Friday, he could not restrain from public view the tears of his devotion. Seeing this, a young man with a carnal mind began to interpret those tears, judging them hypocritical and wholly lacking in purity. Immediately, at the devil’s prompting, a vehement desire came upon him to cast off the monastic habit, resume secular life, sew a cross onto himself, and undertake the journey to Jerusalem.

While he was thinking these things, it was divinely revealed to the abbot what evil that ancient sower of tares had cast into the heart of the novice brother. For he saw the invisible adversary himself standing before him in the likeness of a Jerusalem pilgrim, marked by palm branch, wallet, and staff and covered with a pilgrim’s cloak. The demon was disputing with the young man and, pressing him hard, thrust a finger even into his mouth.

When the divine office had ended, the abbot was careful to meet the brother privately. By the authority of obedience, he commanded him to say what he had resolved in his bewitched heart at that most holy hour before the Lord’s cross. Recognizing that the spiritual man had detected him, the brother shamefacedly confessed everything and humbly promised henceforth to amend himself. Then the abbot likewise did not delay to disclose to the brother what he had seen, and thereafter made him cautious and fearful concerning his thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The same abbot saw a demon in choir offering every monk red wine in a cup; one of them tasted it and was assailed by a spirit of fornication.

On another occasion the same venerable man again saw clearly a demon moving about in choir, [Col. 1300C] offering, one by one, to the monks in a glass cup what appeared to be red wine. While each rejected it, only one received and drank it; and immediately the phantasmal deceiver vanished.

The abbot summoned that brother and compelled him by the authority of obedience to state what shameful thing he had been entertaining in his mind at that time. He confessed and did not deny that he had then been fiercely tempted by a spirit of fornication, so that he was on the very point of apostatizing and satisfying his own pleasure. When the abbot disclosed what had been revealed to him, the brother, pierced with compunction, strongly recoiled from the evil he had intended. Having accepted penance, he firmly resolved in his heart no longer to yield to the tempter. [Col. 1300D]

## CHAPTER XXVII. A demon seen in the form of the monk Simon leads the lay brother Christian out of the monastery.

Albert the smith, a brother of Burlandicourt, a good and highly credible man, told me that, while he was once standing at Vigils in a corner of his monastery, he saw an evil spirit emerge from the monks’ choir in the form of a monk named Simon. When it came to that corner, it seized by the cloak a lay brother named Christian, who stood beside Albert, and drew him out of the church.

Brother Albert therefore thought that the monk had led Christian out because of some urgent need. But after a long interval had passed and neither returned, he observed the said Simon singing in choir and was greatly astonished. Coming with a light to the lay brother’s bed, he found that Christian had fled with a large bundle of clothing. On the following day, when he asked Simon whether he had taken that lay brother out after Matins, Simon truthfully declared that he had done no such thing.

Later, after he had consumed all that he had carried off, that infamous deserter returned to the gate and obtained mercy to be received back. When Brother Albert asked him whether he had seen the one who drew him out of the oratory, he answered:

“I myself saw no one. Yet I know that, though I struggled for a long time, I was finally drawn away and enticed by my own desire, and yielded to the devil. But because my conscience continually reproached me, I did not depart without great fear.”

The wretch was received back and promised henceforth to be steadfast; yet in that very same week he again did not fear to depart, dragging himself backward after Satan. But he was soon recalled by the never-ceasing mercy of Christ through a serious illness. He returned sick and wretched; received again, he confessed and repented, and died within the third day. [Col. 1301B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. A monk of Clairvaux, contemplating abandonment of his resolve, sees Saint Malachy in a dream and is struck with Saint Bernard’s staff, whereupon he returns to a sound mind.

[Col. 1301C] One of the brethren of Clairvaux, his mind corrupted by diabolical prompting so that he intended to apostatize and return to the world, saw in a night vision blessed Bernard and Saint Malachy walking through the dormitory and blessing those who rested there as they visited them. When, in the order of their visitation, they came to his bed, Saint Malachy said:

“This perverse man turns over absolutely no good thing in his heart, but has already consented to the devil’s persuasion that he will soon return to the vomit of the world.”

On hearing this, Blessed Bernard said to him:

“So you seek to flee? And where, wretch, will you flee from the face of the Lord? Believe me: you have conceived such things to your own hurt. For flight will no longer please you once you have escaped from my hand.”

Having said this, he began to beat him repeatedly with the staff he held, saying: “Behold the wages you deserve. Rise now, and flee, if you can.”

When the brother awoke, he found himself so sore and battered from those blows that he was taken to the infirmary and confined to bed. Summoning the prior, he confessed the wickedness he had intended and the punishment he had suffered for it. Accepting penance, he came wholly to his senses, and the desire to flee never again seized him. [Col. 1301D]

## CHAPTER XXIX. A lay brother of Clairvaux, trusting in his obedience, dies happily.

A lay brother among the brethren of Clairvaux had fallen seriously ill and at last reached his final hour. [Col. 1302A] Blessed Bernard entered to visit him, and, strengthening him, said:

“Take heart, son, for you are now about to pass from labour to everlasting rest, from death to life.”

With great confidence he replied:

“Why should I not go to my Lord? I truly believe and trust that I shall soon see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

But the blessed Father, being a wise physician and watchful shepherd, feared, of course, that in this rustic man such a confident answer might arise more from reckless presumption than purity of conscience. He said:

“Sign your heart, brother, sign your heart. What is this that you have said? Whence could the boldness of such presumption have crept upon you? Indeed, are you not that poor, wretched man? Formerly, perhaps, you used to walk without hose and shoes, or even half-naked; and when you were perhaps afflicted by hunger and cold, you fled to us and at last obtained entrance by many prayers. For God’s sake we received you in your need and made you equal in food, clothing, and all other communal provisions to the wise and great men who are with us; and you became like one of them. What, then, have you rendered to God for all these things? And behold: it is not enough for your ingratitude to have received so many benefits freely from the hand of God, unless you also claim his kingdom for yourself by hereditary right—a kingdom which no king or prince could ever acquire by however great weights of gold and silver.”

To this the man replied with a calm countenance and tranquil mind:

“Good, dearest Father—you have indeed spoken well, and everything you said is true. Yet, if you command it, I shall speak to you, my lord and father, and briefly explain whence so great an occasion for presumption—or rather devotion—could arise in one so poor and lowly as I. For if that preaching is true which you so frequently impress upon us, the kingdom of God is not possessed through nobility of flesh or earthly riches, but is acquired by the virtue of obedience alone.

“This one lesson, as a word abbreviated by the Lord, I have retained through diligent remembrance, placing it as a seal upon my heart through continual meditation and upon my arm through careful action. Ask, if you please, all the masters or companions whom you commanded me to obey and serve, whether I have ever been disobedient to any of them, whether I have grieved any of my brothers by word, sign, or any other means within my power. If, by God’s grace, I have made it my business to obey everyone in Christ, to serve everyone, and to love everyone, who can prevent me from trusting in his mercy?”

When the blessed Father received such an answer from this rustic man, he rejoiced with great joy and said:

“Truly, dearest son, you are blessed, because flesh and blood have not revealed this wisdom to you, but the heavenly Father himself has taught you. He has set your soul unto life and led you by a most straight path to your homeland. Enter now in security, for the gate of life has been opened to you.”

After the brother died and his funeral rites had been celebrated, the venerable Father delivered in chapter an eloquent discourse, with his characteristic devotion and eloquence, on the brother’s manner of life; and by his example he wonderfully stirred everyone to love obedience. For he was deeply moved by the brother’s answer, and rejoiced more for the virtue of his obedience and the purity of his heart than if he had seen him shining with signs and wonders.

## CHAPTER XXX. At the death of a certain religious brother, harmonious musical strains of angels were heard. Boso, one of Saint Bernard’s firstborn sons, shone marvellously over his whole face after death.

We do not think that the venerable Boso, eminent by birth and character, ought to be passed over in silence. [Col. 1303B] He was one of the firstborn sons whom our most blessed Father Bernard begot in Christ through the Gospel. In his noble manner of life he showed sufficiently how he had been nourished at a royal breast and how he had been imbued from the beginning with the rudiments of angelic discipline.

A patient man and son of peace, he appeared so kind and gentle to everyone that none of us ever saw him angry or disturbed; amid adversity and prosperity alike, he remained always of tranquil mind. When he was old and so broken in strength that he could scarcely walk with the support of a staff, he nevertheless never consented to indulge in idleness or grant repose to his body. Rather, always working at something in the garden, in the house, or wherever he might be, he did not know how to eat bread in idleness.

When the Lord called him and he gave up his spirit in perfect peace, as though falling asleep, he suddenly shone with such serenity and grace, and his face appeared glorified by so marvellous a transformation, that, as the devotion of all bore witness, we could in no way doubt that the presence of blessed angels and the most serene regard of our God were there. For we had never seen in any dying or dead person such brightness in a transformed countenance.

This venerable man, as we were once privately conversing and mutually nourishing one another by recounting the desirable and holy deaths of certain brethren which he had often happened to see, declared to us that at the death of a certain religious brother they heard choirs of blessed spirits singing sweet melody in the air and joyfully carrying the dead man’s soul to joys. The higher they ascended, the fainter their voices became below, until at last the great distance of the airs shut all sound out from hearing. [Col. 1303D]

## CHAPTER XXXI. Shortly after Saint Bernard’s death, a man who had contemplated departure because of the force of fleshly temptations is strengthened in his resolve by Bernard’s appearance.

Another brother of the same monastery, an honourable and religious man, told me of himself, though with shame, that at the beginning of his conversion, when he was grievously goaded by the spirit of fornication, he resolved in his mind to yield to the tempter and, casting off the religious habit, return to the world. While he was carefully seeking an opportunity to leave, blessed Bernard, recently dead, stood beside him in a vision. He rebuked his sloth and reproved the wickedness which he had conceived in his mind and was striving to carry out in deed.

When the brother replied that he had struggled for a long time and could no longer bear the violence of the temptation, the saint said:

“Know beforehand that many struggles still await you. But act manfully and do not fail, for the Lord will be with you as a helper in due time, to deliver you. Therefore I promise you that, if you persevere in the Order to the end, you shall be saved. And if anyone should perhaps attempt to harm you, on the last day I shall answer for you and lay down my soul for your soul.”

Strengthened by this promise, the brother thereafter could not be moved from his stability. Even now, having completed his twenty-fifth year in the Order, he fights manfully to this day and, having already gained many victories, awaits with greater certainty the salvation promised him. [Col. 1304B]

## CHAPTER XXXII. A lay brother named Walter is commanded in a dream by a venerable maiden to celebrate a Mass, which he subsequently retained in memory.

Walter, the vestiarian of Clairvaux, who died a few years ago, was an honourable and religious man, though a layman and illiterate. While he was once resting in bed, a venerable maiden appeared to him as he slept, led him into the oratory, and commanded him to sing Mass. Clothed therefore in priestly vestments, he celebrated in a dream, with great devotion, the Mass of the Holy Spirit. When he awoke, he knew by heart the same Mass which previously, since he did not know letters, he had wholly not known; and he retained it in memory for many years thereafter. [Col. 1304C]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. To a certain abbot at prayer, and to several others, fragrances of marvellous sweetness are breathed into the nostrils and tastes into the palate.

A certain venerable and religious abbot is known to preside over one of the Savigniac monasteries in England. We know with complete certainty that he is endowed with a special prerogative of holiness and grace. Although he had lived carnally in the world, he later turned to the Lord with his whole heart and, continually longing for him with all desire, deserved happily to experience in himself the saying of the blessed Apostle: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5).

For while he persists in prayer, through the inspiration of grace from above he is accustomed to feel flowing into his nostrils the nectar-like sweetness of some extraordinary fragrance, surpassing by far the scent of cinnamon, incense, balsam, and every perfume. Nor only this: he also feels poured into his throat a sweetness like heavenly manna, containing within itself every taste and every delight of sweetness. Like a living fountain springing up in his mouth and flowing thence into the inward parts of body and soul, it fills and affects both his outer and inner person with marvellous sweetness, so that he can say with the Psalmist: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118 [119]).

To this soul, received by God into such grace, may fittingly be applied that sweet bridal-song from the Song of Songs: “Your lips, bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your prayers is above all spices” (Cant. 4). This gift, once granted, is very often poured out anew not only while he prays, but also while he chants psalms, reads, meditates, and works.

Thus, forestalled by God with this twofold blessing of sweetness, now experiencing one, now the other, and now both together, that soul is wholly carried away into jubilation. Rejoicing inwardly in marvellous delight and sweetness, it is known already to taste beforehand, even in a corruptible body, as it were some firstfruits of paradise’s delights.

What we report about the aforesaid man we learned by revelation from the venerable and holy Father Richard, formerly abbot of Savigny, who testified that he had heard this very thing from the man himself.

If anyone perhaps judges it unbelievable, let him know that we too have heard similar things concerning many persons. Yet among this great number there is one very well known to us, of whom we know without doubt that he frequently receives from God the same grace, wholly not unlike this one, as we learned from his own report. We believe his assertion no less completely than our own eyes. For we trust that his purity is such that he would sooner allow himself to be run through with a sword than presume to lie in matters of this kind.

Since, then, we believe that many, indeed innumerable, saints formerly received such grace from God, it is very surprising that we find either little or no mention of it in the writings of those who described their lives. We suppose this occurred for one of two reasons: either those saints themselves, according to the prophet, kept their secret with God and did not disclose it to others; or perhaps the narrators of their deeds thought little of the grace mentioned and judged it altogether unworthy of memorable report.

Yet, as far as my own understanding goes, it is plain that this gift is by no means to be reckoned among lesser gifts. Wherever and to whomever it comes, it powerfully extinguishes carnal desires, vehemently kindles spiritual ones, and makes the whole soul melt in the fire of divine love. Moreover, it signals the flight of evil spirits, indicates the presence of holy angels, and announces, by an experience at once blessed and true, the much-desired regard of divine mercy.

Who, then, should now judge incredible what we have heard of Saint Bernard: namely, that he saw an angel moving about in choir with a censer, censing those who prayed and sang psalms, but passing by the negligent and sleepy? For we see the same thing now occurring in such a soul, not merely spiritually but perceptibly. Just as though some visible maiden were frequently standing by that soul as it prayed and thirsted for God, as if with a heavenly censer, and burning before its face incense of many spices, so that soul is indeed refreshed at the time of visitation by extraordinary fragrances. Wherever it turns, it finds even the air itself sprinkled with such scents.

Happy the soul which has deserved already to taste and see, not only in itself but even in its body, though still corruptible, that the Lord is sweet. Happy the one to whom it is given to say truly: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30 [31]). I would call truly blessed the soul—sinful indeed, but confessing and truly penitent—which you, most merciful Jesus, not only cleanse from sins but also, in your ineffable condescension, so often visit, console, and refresh with that hidden manna which no one knows except the one who receives it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The most blessed Virgin Mother of God appears to a certain brother and, once and again, gives him assurance of his salvation.

We know another brother in the same monastery, a most religious and devout man, who has sincerely loved Christ from childhood. He possesses exceptional purity of body and soul and makes himself lovable to all by a special kindness of character. While still a novice, as he prayed more earnestly to the Lord and his saints for the salvation of his soul, he was once carried beyond himself in mind. Behold, the blessed Apostle Paul appeared to him, clothed in priestly vestments, and said:

“Do not fear, for you shall obtain more fully the salvation you desire.”

This man always embraces the remembrance of the most blessed Mother of God with singular devotion, and receives many consolations from this same Lady, our Lady. On one occasion the most blessed Virgin herself appeared to him. Taking his hand with great condescension, she led him along a royal road. When they came to a certain imperial and light-filled dwelling, the blessed Mother went inside and commanded him to wait outside the doors, saying:

“For the present you must remain here outside, since you are not yet fit to be admitted within.”

On another occasion the same Mother of Mercy likewise appeared to him, magnificently consoling him and saying:

“Act manfully, and do not fear, for where I am, there you also shall be with me.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. From Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx: an account of certain nuns accustomed to be carried beyond themselves in contemplation.

I am pleased to insert here the account of the venerable abbot of Rievaulx, which he himself gives in his published Commentary on the Burdens of Isaiah, speaking as follows:

> [Note: Aelred, Sermon 2 on Isaiah, chapter 13; Col. 1305D.]

[Col. 1307A] I know that in monasteries of virgins which, under the venerable and most reverently named holy Father Gilbert, daily send abundant fruits of chastity to heaven, there was—or perhaps still remains—a holy virgin. Having excluded from her breast every love of the world, every carnal affection, every care for the body, and all anxiety about outward matters, she began, in a certain fervour of mind, both to loathe earthly things and to desire heavenly ones.

It happened one day that, as was her custom, she gave herself to prayer. A certain marvellous sweetness came upon her and extinguished every movement of her soul, every wandering of thought, and even the spiritual affections which she had for her friends. Immediately her soul, as though bidding farewell to all that is in the world, was carried above itself; and, received by an ineffable and incomprehensible light, she saw nothing except that which is, and which is the being of all things.

For that light was not bodily, nor was it any bodily likeness; it was not spread out or diffused so as to be seen everywhere. Rather, it itself was not contained, yet contained all things, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, just as being contains whatever is, and truth whatever is true. Filled with this light, she began no longer to know according to the flesh Christ himself whom she had formerly known [Col. 1307B] according to the flesh, because Christ Jesus, the Spirit before her face, had led her into truth itself.

As she remained in this ecstasy for no small length of time, when the sisters knocked, she could scarcely return to the bodily senses which she had left behind.

[Col. 1307C] Since this happened to her frequently, and after much entreaty she at last explained to the others the manner of her ecstasy, a great many began to emulate the excellence of this vision. Accordingly, withdrawing themselves from every worldly care and anxiety and devoting themselves to continual tears and prayers, many received the same grace—so that even amid the gatherings of the sisters they were often, against their will, flooded with light.

There was there a certain virgin, a woman of great discernment, who, knowing that not every spirit is to be believed, attributed all this either to illness or to phantasmal illusions; and, so far as she could, discouraged the sisters from such frequent visions. When she asked the woman who was regarded as superior among them why nothing of the kind had happened to her, the latter replied: “Because you do not put faith in us, nor do you love in others a virtue which you do not yourself possess. Ask God,” she said, “that, if this comes from him, the same thing may happen to me.”

When they had prayed for some days and had achieved nothing, she again asked the woman mentioned above why this was so. She replied: “You must renounce every attachment to this world and to all mortals, and occupy yourself with the remembrance of God alone.” “What?” she said. “Am I not to pray for my friends and benefactors?” The other answered: “At the time when you wish to ascend to higher things by the contemplation of the mind, it is necessary that you commend and entrust to God all whom you love and, as though about to depart from the world, bidding farewell altogether to every creature, sigh for the sight of him whom you love.”

Still unconvinced, she asked that by the other’s prayers she might obtain the fulfilment of her desire, if these things were from God. “Yet,” she said, “I do not wish my soul to be so raised up and snatched away from the body that the memory of all things, especially of my friends, should be erased from my mind. It is enough for me to know whether these things are from God.”

Thus, on Good Friday, while she was tossed by anxious thoughts, the woman of whom we spoke, flooded with light, suddenly began in an ineffable manner to be drawn upward into her and lifted to higher things. But she, unable with her weaker eye to bear that inaccessible light shining into her, requested, as best she could, to be recalled to contemplation of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, after seeing, as if in a swift rapture, that which is, she was brought down from higher things to lower and transferred into another spiritual vision. In spirit she saw the Lord Jesus hanging on the cross, fastened with nails, pierced by a spear, blood flowing from five openings, and looking upon her with a most gentle eye. Then she dissolved into tears; and, at last returning to herself, she gave credence to the sisters and judged herself less fit for this light.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1307]

### 241 CHAPTER I. On the remarkable austerity of life of Dominic, a solitary near the city of León; and on the evil and good spirits appearing to him almost without ceasing.

[Col. 1307D]

In the region of Iberia, not far from the city of León, there is known to be a certain solitary, a man of most outstanding holiness: a man truly Dominic not less in deed than in name. He did not emerge recently from worldly life, with the first fervour of a novice, to enter the eremitical combat; but from the house of Carrezeda, a celebrated monastery of great religious observance in that region, where from boyhood he had lived a most holy religious life, he set out—already advanced in years and perfected in virtue, with his superior’s consent—as a valiant soldier for a singular contest. Thus, having overthrown Goliath, he might at last bring back two hundred from the hands of the Philistines in return for the hundred foreskins he had promised.

This upright and temperate man reduces the sustenance of his body to such spareness that, fasting every day except Sunday at all seasons, he takes refreshment at evening with bread and water. Since through old age nearly all his teeth have fallen out or become loose, so that he cannot chew anything solid, he uses warm water in which to soak dry bread. Yet occasionally—though this happens rarely—there is set before him, as a great delicacy, the juice of half-cooked vegetables or legumes seasoned only with salt, in which he softens the hardness of his bread so that he may swallow it. Apart from this, he forbids to his body, with such persistence, flesh, fish, cheese, eggs, oil, wine, and every nourishment of that sort, that this weak and aged man seems to exceed the measure of discretion in the matter. Because of the rigour of this endurance, very many judge him not a man of flesh, but as it were of stone or wood. He also increases the bodily penance by the roughness of haircloth, lest the flesh, growing wanton through any pleasantness of food or clothing, become insolent.

[Col. 1309B]

Moreover, out of zeal for contemplation he seeks and loves the repose of solitude to such a degree that he greatly avoids the company and conversation of almost all people, especially secular persons. At times, for an entire month, or for as much longer as he can, he refrains from speech with mortals for the sake of converse with God. If pressing necessity at last compels him to speak, he is always carefully on guard against idle and unnecessary matters, strives to be brief in speech, and more often endeavours to cut off discourse once begun than to spin it out.

Then, when the little door of the cave in which he has buried himself alive is opened, he nevertheless closes his eyes to the world, and at once falls asleep and rests in that same reality. For, as I heard from his own mouth, he enjoys an extraordinary and indescribable delight in that silence; and his mind always delights in God, always in heaven, contemplating with angels and saints, and is, as it were, intoxicated from the abundance of God’s house and from the torrent of delight by a certain first-fruits sweetness of everlasting goods—a sweetness which very few believe in, and far fewer in the present age experience.

[Col. 1309C]

Who could adequately recount the hundreds and thousands of prostrations by which he daily afflicts himself in supplicating and praying to God? Moreover, the uninterrupted diligence of watching, praying, and chanting psalms, by which he daily martyrizes himself and offers himself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, can neither easily be described nor easily believed. For besides the daily portion of the divine office, which day and night at the regular hours he renders threefold or fourfold, from the moment he rises for vigils he is accustomed, before daybreak, with incredible devotion to sing—or rather lament—the entire Psalter.

For what else can I say, when his whole prayer, singing, and even conversation, with the fire of charity always burning on the altar of his heart, can scarcely occur without tears and sighs? By God’s gift I have known many men of virtue; but, to confess the truth, I remember seeing in no mortal such and so great a grace of compunction as in this man of God.

Very often it happens that, while praying or chanting psalms, feeling the word of God burn with great force, he suddenly becomes entirely inflamed. Drawing most ardent sighs from the depths of his heart, he is compelled by the force of compunction that hinders him to interrupt what he was saying and give himself over to inexpressible groans, in which he seethes violently with panting spirit.

[Col. 1310A]

Then, as the fire of divine love increases in the furnace of his breast, desires for the holy virtues likewise glow there with utter fervour, and tears, pouring forth as if from a boiling cauldron, burst out more abundantly. For as an affectionate mother is wont with unrestrained mourning and wailing to grieve for her only child, whom she loved with the greatest tenderness, when that child has been slain, so this perfect man laments and bewails with miserable weeping and roaring the defect and barrenness which he attributes to his own soul; the prolongation of his present exile, which he endures with utmost distress; and his long separation from Christ, whom he loves most ardently and bears it grievously to be apart from.

[Col. 1310B]

Once this storm of great emotion—outwardly disclosed by the groans and sobs, as it were, of inward tumult amid a flood of many waters—has arisen, it can scarcely be calmed for a long span of time. What is more remarkable, this happens not once or twice but many times by day and night, whether he is praying, reading, conversing, or doing anything else.

When I often saw this—for it was granted me by God to see this man Dominic frequently and to know him intimately—when, I say, I beheld such things, whether I wished it or not, I myself dissolved with him entirely into mourning and tears. I was indeed astonished and marvelling beyond measure how his aged, broken little body, exhausted by so many and such great fasts, vigils, and other labours, could suffice for such contrition of heart and such shedding of tears, especially since, from the beginning of his conversion, he is said almost always to have done what scarcely anyone is believed able to do even for a short time.

[Col. 1310C]

But it is clearer than daylight that the God of all virtues, who bestowed so wonderful a grace of compunction upon the devout soul, himself also granted, by no smaller miracle, strength sufficient for the worn and enfeebled body to sustain the same gift. When the hour of contrition and anxious lamentation has passed, serenity of heart returns. Then, caught in an ecstasy of mind, he most sweetly enjoys God’s delightful presence through contemplation. Thus the servant of Christ, now considering his own misery, now contemplating divine goodness, always walks most safely upon the royal road: neither cast down by the troubles of temptations nor lifted up by successes in virtue.

Having briefly set forth these things about the holy man’s manner of life, we must consider by what adversaries he is continually attacked and by what helpers he is wonderfully strengthened. For just as tribulations never fail one who lives piously in Christ, so through Christ consolations always abound in him.

One night, while he was still living in the monastery, he rose for the brothers’ vigils and came, as usual, into the choir. There he found an unclean spirit in his stall, resembling the brother who stood next to him in choir. Thinking it was that brother, he signalled to him to give him space and move himself to another stall.

[Col. 1311A]

When he continued doing this for some time and the other did not move, he eventually grew impatient with annoyance, stretched out his hand, and touched him, intending to turn him toward himself as though he had not seen him and make him depart to his own place. Seizing him by the garment and drawing him a little toward himself for inspection, he found that the evil one immediately vanished and returned to the nothingness from which it had previously come.

At another time, while he was travelling, three wicked spirits met him, like bandits girded with swords, carrying bows and arrows in their hands, apparently ready to strike and rob. They wished, I think, to terrify the man of God and drive him away in fear. Seeing them and taking them for assassins, he was somewhat afraid, yet he neither turned aside from his route nor stopped. When he approached more closely, the phantasmal robbers immediately vanished from his sight.

[Col. 1311B]

Innumerable are such mockeries and assaults by which deceitful and wandering spirits daily harassed him. Often, when he was in his cave, they appeared in masked forms, or assaulted him about his person even invisibly: now inducing terrors, now inflicting blows. Often in the night hours, a troop of demons, like a band of robbers, would suddenly rush in; as though doors had been broken open, they would enter tumultuously and rage against him with great fury and noise. But he, armed with the sign of the cross, was not permitted to be harmed.

[Col. 1311C]

It happened once, as he sat in his lodging, that he lifted his gaze to heaven and fixedly contemplated the brightness of the sun itself against its ray. And behold, that twisting Leviathan appeared in the form of a fiery dragon. Descending along the same ray of the sun, it rushed in sudden flight upon his face, as though to devour him alive. Seeing this, terrified at the sight of the pallid serpent, he shuddered all over and, nearly lifeless, cried out the name of Christ in gasping cries and opposed the standard of the Lord’s cross to the deadly beast.

Repelled by heavenly power, since it could not harm him, the beast nevertheless flew importunately about his face and menaced him fiercely from every side as he moved away. Since the holy man could not evade the demon’s insolence, he closed his eyes and covered his face with his clothing, yet this did him no good. Remarkable as it is to tell, he saw that masked appearance with his eyelids shut just as he did with them open; nor could that subtle and penetrating nature be barred by any obstacle of garments.

[Col. 1311D]

When he saw that he could not escape the sight of the terrible beast, he at last opened his eyes and freely allowed himself to see what in some manner he could not avoid seeing. Then more and more demons appeared, resembling serpents and diverse animals, in crowds; immediately they filled the entire dwelling from top to bottom. Their inequality in number, diversity in kind, and deformity in shape were so great that they could not possibly be described. Many of them appeared fiery in colour.

Then, rushing upon the man of God, they surrounded him like bees and blazed like fire among thorns, attacking in angry motions and striking him with many blows. Although they seemed fiery, however, he felt no power of burning from them. For, circling about him in whirling motion and darting most swiftly through the air, they often mocked his head and body and frequently dashed against his very face. They afflicted God’s servant in many ways, but, as has been said, did not torment him with any burning.

[Col. 1312A]

Afterward, when the holy man went out as far as the door in order to take a little breath from their assault, he nevertheless saw innumerable multitudes of demons roaming through the air in massed whirlwinds, filling everything in every direction from earth to heaven. These too were so unlike one another in their inequality, so terrible in their monstrousness, and so misshapen in their deformity, that human sense could in no way endure so many kinds of monsters and phantasms of furies unless heavenly power defended it.

The aforementioned man said—and this must not be omitted—that the unclean spirits did not lay aside, at the sign of the cross, those spiritual forms in which he always saw them in the air; but at the sign of life they immediately put off the forms into which they had phantasmatically transformed themselves.

[Col. 1312C]

From that day to the present, this servant of God has not ceased to see a vision of this kind daily—or rather, throughout the whole day while awake—by day and night, in darkness and in light, with eyes shut and with eyes open. Yet the terrors and afflictions which he endured from them with difficulty at the beginning he has now completely escaped through God’s grace. Although the wicked still always walk around him and, like shameless officers, do not cease visibly and impudently to thrust themselves upon him, he now despises their obstinate persistence so completely that he fears flying fleas and flies far more than them.

For, because it is truly written, “The angel of the Lord will encamp round about those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Ps. 33), that Angel of great counsel, that Lord of the heavenly powers, after permitting his devoted soldier to be tested for some time amid so great an encounter with evil beings, at last, moved by mercy, appointed strong helpers from the army of heaven.

[Col. 1312D]

Strengthened by their blessed presence, he might henceforth safely persist in fighting in the battle line. Thus his eyes were opened, and he saw beside him an innumerable multitude of angels and saints, gleaming with immense light. When he beheld them, he exulted in great joy and, giving thanks to God, said within himself: “Truly, these are the camps of God” (Gen. 32). “And now by experience I have learned that the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior” (Jer. 20). “Though the camp of the devil stand against me, my heart shall not fear” (Ps. 26). “For the Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies” (Ps. 117).

[Col. 1313A]

From that time, these same light-bearing spirits have not ceased most graciously to visit this servant of God and to refresh him ineffably with great consolations. Yet he never wished to explain clearly to me, even when I earnestly asked him, the manner of this appearance: that is, in what bodies or forms he was granted to see them. He always regarded the fault of boastfulness with great suspicion; accordingly, he spoke even of these things in fear and trembling and with many tears, lest some vanity steal in, offend God, and cause him to suffer even a small diminution of that grace.

Still, he openly said that he received their joyful visitation and presence frequently and almost continuously in the brilliance of a great light. Therefore he was accustomed to pray more often in a darker place, since there he was flooded more abundantly with this light—which, as it were indiscriminately, he saw with eyes shut or open.

[Col. 1313B]

The holy man also made known to me that he had never openly revealed this wonderful gift of almighty God, which he had possessed already for many years, to anyone before. Here too his great humility is evident: in order to restrain the sickness of vainglory, he held silent for so long concerning a gift of such high eminence.

What, then, shall we say, brothers? What dignity and grace do we suppose belong to a man still clothed in corruptible flesh, who always has before his sight the presence of good and evil spirits: the latter on the left, lest perhaps he be exalted; the former on the right, lest he be shaken? On the left is the rod of correction, by which he may be instructed; on the right the staff of support, by which he may be strengthened. In evil beings he recognizes what must be reproved and avoided; in good beings he understands what must be loved and sought.

[Col. 1313C]

It should be known that this man, as we learned partly from him and partly knew by experience, has from God this spiritual grace: by the prophetic spirit he foresees many things, and scarcely anything important occurs around him which is not beforehand divinely revealed to him. His conscience has now been so calmed through the Holy Spirit, and the nature of his body so purified, that even when asleep he experiences little or no phantasmal disturbance or illusion; and he scarcely ever dreams anything that does not signify something to him.

Moreover, I do not think I should pass over the fact that this same servant of God, like the one who says, “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isa. 24), set before my eagerness a certain hidden word, as if for smelling, but would not explain it for tasting. For he made known to me that he knew a man who for a full three years had daily received from heaven an account.

[Col. 1313D]

When, after much entreaty, he at last admitted that he himself was that man, I proceeded to ask what sort of account it was that was sent to him from heaven. He answered that this saying was deep and sealed, and must not at present be opened by him to anyone without God’s approval. Yet he declared this to be the first and greatest among the spiritual gifts bestowed upon him, and the one for which he judged himself most indebted to God.

[Col. 1314A]

We have briefly outlined in a simple narrative these remarkable features of the holy man’s life, insofar as we deserved either to see them in him or to hear them from himself. Without doubt there are many other, perhaps much more wonderful, marks of his mighty deeds, most worthy of memorable report, if they could in any way have become known. For who can sufficiently estimate by how many daily advances in virtue he is raised up, with what splendours in his soul he is filled, or what new and wondrous things he perceives day by day through sight and hearing? He has almost laid aside the attachment and use of the present age and has now, in a certain manner, become capable and an inhabitant of the invisible world and the age to come. Conversing with incorporeal natures as though bodily, he grasps by sighted faith the certainty of invisible things and experiences it through bodily sense.

[Col. 1314B]

Truly blessed are all who fear God. Truly happy are those who trust in him. And now in this man Dominic we plainly recognize that God’s grace and mercy are upon his saints, and his regard upon his chosen ones.

### 252 CHAPTER II. Christ the Lord appears to a novice of Clairvaux, blesses him and one of his companions, but passes over a third, Malignus in both name and fact, who abandoned the Order three days later.

A certain religious brother named Anfulsus, endowed with great grace, while still a novice at Clairvaux, saw in a vision our Lord Jesus Christ appearing to him on the cross. As it seemed to him, two other novices were there, who were still undergoing probation with him. After he had worshipped humbly, the Lord, moved by mercy, looked upon him and blessed him, and likewise blessed the other of the two novices mentioned above. Seeing this, he began to ask him to bless the third in the same way. But the Lord replied that this man was not to be blessed, but rather belonged to the mass of the accursed.

[Col. 1314D]

On the third day afterward, that third novice, in wicked conduct fulfilling the sad etymology of his name—for he was called *Malignus*, “Evil”—abandoned the Order and returned to the vomit of secular life, becoming a contemptible apostate. But the other two, who deserved to be blessed by the Lord, will, through his mercy, possess the blessing as an inheritance. The aforementioned Anfulsus has already rested in a holy end; the other shows, by persevering justly and devoutly in his purpose, that he belongs to the lot of the blessed. The man who saw it himself made known to me this vision which I have recounted.

### 253 CHAPTER III. On the day after Easter, a monk of Clairvaux, while in choir, saw on high a shining right hand emerging from the midst, which once and again blessed the chanters by tracing in the air the saving sign of the cross.

We know another brother in the same monastery who saw such a vision, though he does not know whether he saw it sleeping or awake. Yet he believes he saw it while awake and in ecstasy. Thus, on Easter Monday, while he was at vigils in the choir at Clairvaux, the hand of the Lord came upon him. And behold, high in the air opposite the middle of the choir, there appeared to him a resplendent and glorious right hand. It blessed the present household as they confessed his holy name and impressed upon it once and twice the seal of the blessed cross. The Spirit revealing mysteries spoke in the heart of the seer and said: “This is the arm of the Ruler; this is the right hand of almighty God.”

### CHAPTER IV. Andrew, formerly archdeacon of Verdun, a most noble and refined man, is converted at Clairvaux with Geoffrey; when he despaired of persevering, peas of exquisite flavour appeared to him, though seasoned only with water and salt.

[Col. 1315B]

On that same day there was converted there a most noble man, Andrew by name, archdeacon of Verdun. He had come there to pay a visit, but for the present had no intention of conversion. Yet, having entered the chapter-house to request the help of their prayers, he saw the order of that holy multitude and, as it were, their angelic way of life. He was deeply moved, and when the Spirit of the Lord suddenly rushed upon him, he was immediately changed into another man. He abandoned the world with such fervour that he would not return to his own people even for an hour, whether to bid farewell to friends or to arrange his household and possessions.

[Col. 1315C]

Instead, he immediately left everything, breaking rather than untying his ties, that he might cleave more swiftly to Christ. To make the twofold impression of the cross more evident, another cleric, named Geoffrey, gave himself with him. He was indeed of humbler birth, but perhaps not inferior in probity of character and nobility of conduct. Thus both entered; both persevered in the Order, fought the good fight, and, their contest completed, became partakers of eternal blessing.

It should be known, however, that this Andrew endured many temptations during his probation. He was like a most tender woodworm, exceedingly soft and delicate, having from his mother’s womb been brought up amid many wrappings and attentions. Since he found it difficult to unlearn the softness of his former mode of life and judged the labour of his newly begun life excessively arduous, he thought, like Lot after leaving Sodom, that he could not save his life on the mountain. He therefore proposed to transfer to some Order of less strict observance.

[Col. 1315D]

Having already often told the abbot of the place, Lord Robert, of this intention, one day, overcome by faintheartedness of spirit and temptation, he declared that he could no longer endure in any way. Then the abbot, by many entreaties and gentle persuasions, obtained from him a promise to force himself to endure for only three more days. When this was at last secured with difficulty, he arranged for prayer to be made to God for him in the community.

That same day, when the novice came to table, he found peas set before him. This was a kind of legume that he habitually detested above all others, so much that it sometimes even made him nauseated. But when he began to taste them, he discovered in them a remarkable sweetness, such that the excellence of their flavour surpassed the eating of meat.

[Col. 1316A]

As soon as he perceived this, he immediately seized a spoon and drew the bowl nearer; then, forgetting moderation, he devoured the cooked legumes to the bottom. While eating, he repeatedly put a finger into his mouth, thinking that he might detect pieces of bacon fat, in which he supposed the legumes had been fried. When the meal was over, he hastened to ask the abbot carefully whether he had ordered that dish to be seasoned especially for his sake with fat or any other grease. The abbot denied it, and the cooks were questioned about the dish as well. They too solemnly declared that they had put nothing in it except salt and water.

[Col. 1316B]

On hearing this, the novice joyfully perceived the miracle of divine visitation bestowed upon him. Giving thanks to God, he could afterward no longer be moved from his intended Order. When on the second and third days, and long afterward, he continued to experience the aforementioned sweetness in food of this kind, he eventually learned through experience, his teacher, that the Lord is able, whenever he wills to console his servants, to grant legumes and vegetables the same grace of flavour which he has given to flesh and fish. Therefore he often said that he now took more pleasure in eating peas and vegetables than formerly in feasting on fattened fowl and game.

### 256 CHAPTER V. A monk of Clairvaux is blessed by Christ the Lord appearing to him.

A brother of the same monastery, when he had turned with great desire to seek the Lord, once saw him appearing to him in a vision. Concerned about his salvation, he earnestly begged for his saving blessing, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, bless me, that I may be saved.” And he blessed him there in that place. Seeing this, the brother rejoiced with great joy. Embracing the most blessed hand by which he had deserved to be blessed, he kissed it with immense devotion and said: “Lord Jesus Christ, I give you thanks because you have blessed me, and I shall be saved.”

### CHAPTER VI. A wonderful fragrance and taste, bestowed on a certain brother of Clairvaux together with a heavenly vision.

In the aforementioned monastery we know there to have been a monk who was once grievously ill with an acute sickness. Before he reached the critical day, he entered into an agony and for nearly half the night was, as it were, outside himself, seeing and hearing many things which it would now take too long to recount.

[Col. 1317A]

That same night a certain young religious man died there: a monk of remarkable gentleness and patience, who, tormented by a very severe illness, had undergone a harsh and prolonged martyrdom for very many years. As he was dying, drawing out his final breath for a long time, he uttered frequent groans of lamentation because of the bitterness of his pain. The aforementioned sick man, hearing him lament, said within himself: “That lament will soon be turned into song, and everlasting joy will very shortly overtake the end of this pain.”

While he was thinking these and similar thoughts, behold: a certain invisible presence stood before his little bed and remained for a very long time. At almost every cry which the dying man uttered, it abundantly filled his nostrils and throat with a wonderful, unfamiliar fragrance and sweetness. Then he felt, as it were, a certain heavenly power sensibly and manifestly entering into him and most sweetly anointing the inner chambers of his heart.

[Col. 1317B]

While this continued for a long time, suddenly there appeared to him a certain opening in heaven, through which he seemed to see as far as the third heaven. A voice was heard in his ears, crying and saying from on high: “Let all the earth be silent; let all malice depart; Christ is coming.” Then it seemed to him that the Lord Jesus Christ descended there and filled that whole house with his blessing. He himself was flooded with such sweetness and grace that he thought himself in paradise and said: “Lord our God, behold this eternal life which you promised us. This is that happiness, that sweetness, which you have prepared in your goodness. And now, if with eyes unveiled I were permitted to see and always to possess this good which I feel and hold, my joy would already be full and perfect.”

[Col. 1317C]

Soon, when the hour of departure was at hand, the board was struck; and when all had assembled to fortify the brother at his death, that soul was taken up. Freed from the body of this death, and eternal joy entering in, pain and groaning fled from it. I believe, and truly trust, that he did not disdain to introduce it into his rest who deigned to come to earth for its sake: Jesus Christ our Lord.

While the body itself was being committed to burial, another religious and devout brother, with God revealing it to his open eyes—as he himself testified to us—saw what seemed to be a bier proceeding from the tomb and ascending toward the heavens.

[Col. 1317D]

The aforementioned sick man recovered from his illness by God’s will and, greatly consoled by what had happened, gave thanks. In order that he might become more certain of the revelation received at the brother’s departure, in the course of time it was granted him from heaven to deserve afterward, after many days and years, to feel—not continuously indeed, but often and abundantly—the very sweetness of blessing which he had then experienced in a most excellent smell or taste, according as that gracious and sweet Spirit, who breathes where, when, and in what measure he wills, deigned mercifully to pour it into his poor servant.

And he felt this same grace of sweetness divinely bestowed not only in dreams or ecstasy, with the bodily senses asleep or stupefied, as perhaps happened in that agony, but while his body was awake and his senses alert: while praying, chanting psalms, reading, or doing something else.

### 259 CHAPTER VII. A novice at Clairvaux sees blessed Mary Magdalene standing before the altar, but is for the present denied a vision of the most blessed Mother of God.

A religious and devout brother, while still a novice in the same monastery, was granted to see in spirit blessed Mary Magdalene standing before the altar in shining face and attire. At the sight, he was filled with great joy. As he thought in his heart, desiring and beseeching that the most blessed Mother of God might visibly be shown to him, a voice came to him in the vision itself, saying: “You must know that you are not yet fit to behold her. Strive therefore and accomplish as much as you can, that you may at some time deserve to see her.”

### CHAPTER VIII. Prayer with hands joined or outstretched confirmed by several appearances of Christ.

Another novice brother in that place, having resolved to seek the Lord with his whole heart, used, whenever opportunity permitted, frequently to pray with hands either joined or outstretched. One night, therefore, at the beginning of vigils, while he was in choir with closed eyes and hands stretched out, intent upon God, the Lord Jesus Christ suddenly came there and spoke to him, saying: “Stretch out your hands to me.”

[Col. 1318C]

At this voice the brother opened his eyes and was greatly astonished. He could not easily discern whether he had heard it asleep or awake. But from this voice he conceived great devotion and fervour in his mind, and afterward carefully retained that manner of prayer. Some time later, now a monk, while he stood and prayed in a corner of the same church, his mind intent and his hands joined, he was suddenly in the Spirit. And behold, the Lord Jesus Christ came to him, receiving his hands held beneath and outstretched, and, as it were, admitting him to profession.

When the man returned to himself after this, he rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. Taught now by this happy experience, he most certainly believed that the divine presence is everywhere, but especially where, as Saint Bernard says, we stand either praying or chanting psalms.

### CHAPTER IX. On a certain young German who was marvellously converted at Clairvaux to monastic life and was distinguished by outstanding holiness and divine manifestations.

An eminent young man, native to the regions of Germany, was going to Paris for the sake of study, accompanied by his teacher. As they passed through the house of Clairvaux, the teacher, seeing the community and discipline of the place, was, by some judgment of God, touched with compunction for a time; he asked and obtained admission for conversion of life. When he asked the young man to remain with him, however, he absolutely refused. For he strongly shrank from the society and even the conversation of Cistercian monks; [Col. 1319A] indeed, he had often asked the Lord never to allow him to be converted to that Order. Therefore, though his teacher urged him and the brethren of the monastery exhorted him, he stiff-neckedly resisted and could not be conquered by any engines of preaching.

That same night, as he pondered their admonitions in his mind, a voice came to him from God, saying: “If you leave here and arrive at Paris, you will die before Pentecost—without doubt, you will die.” At this voice the young man was greatly astonished, yet the hardness of his heart could not then be softened.

The following night, when he had given his limbs to sleep, he seemed to himself to be sunk in the mud of a deep well. As he lay there in despair, blessed John [Col. 1319B] the Evangelist suddenly appeared above at the rim of the well, in the countenance and dress of blessed Bernard, together with another saint whose name has escaped me; he too was exceedingly like a most religious man named Gerard, porter of Clairvaux. When the young man saw them, he urgently begged them to have mercy on him. Blessed John answered him: “You despise yielding to sound counsel, yet you ask help from us?” When he promised that he would do whatever pleased them, John said: “Do you then wish to become a monk in the monastery of Clairvaux?” “Yes, my lord, most willingly I do.”

When he had firmly promised to fulfill this without delay, they immediately drew him out of the deep place and allowed him to go free. At dawn he asked to be brought as quickly as possible before blessed Bernard. Although he had never seen him before, he immediately [Col. 1319C] recognized him by his countenance and dress, knowing with certainty that this was the very man whom, on the preceding night, he had deserved to have as his deliverer on condition of conversion. Greatly amazed and compunct, he at once gave himself to that holy man. Received kindly by him, he soon, though still young, put on the gray hairs of gravity and wisdom, to the wonder of all. His aforesaid teacher, however, quickly fell away from his good purpose and tried to overthrow him with himself, but could not move the young man who was founded in Christ’s love.

This refined and very tender youth, then, being fourteen years old, set his hand to mighty things, to the rejoicing of angels and men; he undertook to bear Christ’s yoke and was set, like a lamb, to the plough of the Order he had embraced. But soon, through God’s mercy, he put on the strength of a young ox while retaining the gentleness of a lamb. From his earliest years he shone with such excellence of graces that his companions, deeply moved by the beauty and fragrance of his manner of life, rejoiced and gazed upon him in wonder as upon the most blooming flower of paradise. A religious and spiritual brother of the same monastery testified to me that he once saw the following vision. He watched this young man singing the invitatory before the altar. The image of the crucifix that stood upon the altar, as though delighted by his melody, came down from the cross; coming with arms outstretched, it graciously embraced [Col. 1320A] him, clasping him tenderly to itself and kissing him. When that brother saw this, he understood that the soul was holy and pleasing to God, and had spiritually obtained ready access to great familiarity with His mercy. Thus this most devoted lover of the Lord remained with Him throughout the day as though in a bridal chamber, most sweetly enjoying His blessed presence in contemplation.

One night, therefore, an angel of God appeared to him in a dream and led him into a glorious chamber. There the Lord Jesus Christ seemed to be hanging upon the cross, while His blessed mother Mary stood beside His cross with John the Evangelist. When he entered, he sensed such a fragrance of sweetness as if he had entered a perfumed cell sprinkled [Col. 1320B] with every aromatic powder. Falling upon his face, he worshipped the Lord and deserved to receive His blessing. When he awoke from sleep, he continued, while awake, to perceive for three successive days the sweet fragrance which he had sensed in sleep.

On another night, while intent upon prayer, he deserved to hear with bodily ears angelic voices resounding in the air with sweet and splendid harmony. The pitch of those voices was so high that no human exertion, however great, could rise to it. After he had delighted in them for some time, the sweetness of the heavenly hymnody was at last taken from his ears; but the immense joy of the devotion conceived in his heart remained for a very long time, [Col. 1320C] so that, often pouring forth the recollection of the abundance of that sweetness, he was stirred with wondrous devotion and wholly transformed into joy.

Moreover, on one occasion, when he was at vigils in the church of Clairvaux on Easter Day, he began to reflect more intently upon the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection. Burning with an affection of piety, he dissolved wholly into tears. And behold, suddenly the Lord Jesus Christ, who had kindled the fire in his heart, appeared before him, who was [*jugulanti*, sic; reading uncertain] and weeping, and stood in the middle of the choir with His hands spread out, as though showing them to him. In His most blessed palms the places of the nails appeared most clearly, so that blood seemed to flow from the wounds themselves as though fresh. Seeing the Lord, the brother rejoiced with very great [Col. 1320D] joy; but, astonished and as if beside himself, he did not know what he ought to do in the brief moment available. He wished to rush into the middle of the choir and seize the Savior’s feet, but shame and reverence for the community restrained him, lest he be thought mad. For he did not know whether the appearing Lord was seen by himself alone or likewise by the others. He wept most abundantly, and his heart melted within him in piety because of the immeasurable sweetness of the love of Him whom he beheld.

At that hour, however, the responsory *The Angel of the Lord* was being sung in church. The apparition continued until the choir had finished singing these words: “Now He has risen; come and see.”

On the Day of Pentecost, while at vigils [Col. 1321A] the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* was being sung, at the aforesaid verse, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” after the bow customarily made then, this brother, rising upright, deserved openly to behold a glorious and marvelous vision concerning the Trinity, which is God. He believed it more excellent than all the other visions he had ever deserved to see. Yet he explained to me absolutely nothing about the manner of that vision—what it was or of what sort it was—asserting that he would never dare disclose it to anyone unless he should first be granted to know God’s will concerning this. Whether he later revealed it to anyone is unknown to me. Indeed, concerning the other visions mentioned above, he said that he greatly regretted having told them [Col. 1321B] to anyone, fearing that this itself might displease the Lord; and he had resolved to bury in perpetual silence the many other things he had seen, and whatever he might thereafter happen to see.

I learned all these things which I have related above, and very many others—which, though I consider them great, I have omitted for love of brevity—from the secret account of that servant of God, on the condition that I should keep them secret until his death. But now that the Lord has called him, and after completing twenty-six years in the Order he died as happily as he had lived sincerely, I am released from the bond of that promise. Therefore I have set down on this page, for the consolation of others as well, the aforesaid revelations, in which I remember having found no small consolation.

## CHAPTER X. A monk of Clairvaux, most devoted to the veneration of St. John the Evangelist, learns many things concerning divine matters through him.

[Col. 1321C]

We know also that in the same place there was a monk who feared God. While living in that monastery, one day, on the vigil of All Saints, he stood in choir with the others. He loved blessed John the Evangelist with special affection and took much delight in his writings and remembrance. As was customary, the epistle from the Apocalypse was read at Mass, and he enjoyed a marvelous sweetness in the very words. At last, at the final verse, where it is said, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity” (Rev. 5), [Col. 1321D] and the rest that follows, his entire soul melted within him in the fire of divine love. He was flooded with such an abundance of joy that, because of the immensity of his delight, he could scarcely contain himself. Thus wholly carried away in jubilation and wholly beside himself, he beheld Christ alone as though present with the eyes of his heart and embraced Him with the arms of his inner being.

While he stood there and his mind was richly refreshed by that heavenly repast, before Mass was even finished, the sleep of the Lord fell upon him—slight indeed, but delightful and sweet. For immediately the Lord Jesus Christ, who had poured the aforesaid joy into him while awake, graciously manifested His presence to him as he slept, together with His apostle. The brother heard Him address the apostle and say: “I showed you this revelation long ago, not [Col. 1322A] only for your sake—for you already had sure knowledge and sure confidence in my power and love—but especially for the sake of the others who love me in the same way, so that they too, knowing my glory, may likewise put their trust in me.”

When the brother heard this, he immediately opened his eyes and was filled with great joy, both because of the granted grace of the Lord’s visitation and consolation and because of God’s own testimony to the truth of the Apocalypse. This especially consoled him because he had heard with grief that certain heretics had once dared to disparage that holy book, blaspheming and asserting that it had not been written by St. John the Apostle.

About fifteen days later, when the aforesaid brother was greatly anxious and compunct because of his sins, the Lord [Col. 1322B] Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision with that same apostle. Then that blessed apostle spoke first, saying: “Whoever wishes to obtain perfect forgiveness from the Lord must earnestly punish his sins by weeping and repenting.” The Lord answered: “If anyone wishes to come to me, he must ardently desire that very thing.” Instructed by these and similar words, the brother learned, together with Ruth the Moabitess, always to dip his morsel in vinegar; and, eating unleavened bread with wild lettuces, to rejoice in the Lord with trembling.

Later, on the feast day of St. John himself, while attending vigils, he again saw [Col. 1322C] in an ecstasy of mind that same apostle before his own altar, clothed in priestly vestments, as though about to celebrate Mass. After a short interval, a light sleep overcame him; and suddenly the Lord Jesus Christ passed before him with His glorious Mother. As soon as they entered a certain palace said to be paradise, its gate remained open. As he wondered why that gate did not close at all, it was said to him: “This is the gate of life. Once the Lord has entered through it with His Mother, it remains open to all the faithful until the Day of Judgment.”

When he understood this, he said within himself: “Then the entrance of paradise is open to me also. I shall therefore enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even unto the house of God.” As he began to enter, [Col. 1322D] an ineffable joy and sweetness received him. When he had shaken off sleep and had been awake for some time, he thought that he was still in paradise, since that joy continued in him for so long and sufficiently showed that the Author of joy had been present there.

## CHAPTER XI. St. Bernard declares, by God’s revelation, that the souls of many penetrate heaven immediately upon leaving the body, by a free and unimpeded passage. Likewise, that all who persevere in the Cistercian Order while its discipline flourishes will be saved. He foretells to his brother Guy that, because he took excessive concern for the affairs of the community of Clairvaux, he would die outside Clairvaux.

Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, once entered, as was his custom, to console the novice brethren [Col. 1323A] who were then under probation, numbering more than one hundred. After he had powerfully inflamed them, by much exhortation and consolation in his ardent eloquence, with love for heavenly things, he finally added:

“Brothers, you will be blessed if you are willing to persevere in the discipline of the Order which you hold; for this is indeed the royal way, the holy way, the secure way, which leads by a straight path to everlasting joys. For I tell you truthfully that I have often seen—not merely in dreams, as commonly happens, nor by a vision, but in prayer and wakefulness, through a manifest revelation—the souls of monks, lay brothers, and novices ascend from this valley of tears, immediately after leaving their bodies, by a free and unimpeded passage to the heights, and penetrate without hindrance the open ways of heaven.

“If these things make you glad, listen gladly: I shall add matters still more joyful. It happened once in this monastery, while I was hearing Mass with the others in the community, that, through the negligence of the ministers, water was lacking for washing the priest’s hands. While it was being sought and brought, the action of completing the sacrifice was thereby delayed longer than it ought to have been. Immediately afterward, there appeared to me in the choir one of our monks, a venerable and religious man who had died not long before. Standing and looking at me, he began to shake his head as though stirred by some indignation against me. When I recognized him, I at once asked what he meant by appearing so suddenly and unexpectedly and shaking [Col. 1323C] his head at me. He answered:
