“‘If your brethren knew how many and how great companions and friends they have in heaven, they would certainly take great care to avoid every negligence, lest they offend them—especially because all of them belong to their fellowship.’

“When I heard this gladly, a certain slothful brother, who seemed more negligent than the others, immediately came into my mind by God’s inspiration. I asked concerning him: ‘What then? Do you think that this brother’—and I designated him by name—‘can in any way be saved?’ He answered: ‘This man too will be saved, and all the rest likewise will without doubt be saved.’ Having said these things, he vanished from my sight and returned to the heaven from which he had come, filling me with inexpressible joy because of so great a consolation.

“But you, little children, must not think that this promise of the heavenly oracle belongs exclusively to those brethren who were dwelling within this place at that time. Rather, believe firmly and hope that you yourselves, together with all others who serve God in this house or in this Order until the end, will all, through God’s mercy, be saved and have been jointly designated by that heavenly messenger.”

Very many of those who heard this account of blessed Bernard still survive and remember it with joy, especially John, a religious man and capable steward of the same monastery. He attended that sermon gladly and most steadfastly asserts that it was the chief support of his own [Col. 1324A] perseverance in the Order. Many likewise affirm that this servant of God, when on one occasion he spoke in chapter, recounted for their consolation those same words concerning the visions of souls which we have reported above, addressing those present themselves.

When this servant of God heard on one occasion that a good and religious man among his spiritual sons, whom he had sent to Normandy, was suffering there from a desperate illness, he determined to send for him and bring him back to himself, so that the devout brother might die in his own little nest and not be deprived of the burial he desired. Yet one of his brothers according to the flesh, named Guy, tried to oppose this decision. Being one of the stewards [Col. 1324B] of Clairvaux, he intended, I believe, to spare expense and labor. As he persisted stubbornly in such opposition, blessed Bernard said to him: “Is your concern for money or pack animals greater than your concern for your brothers? Since you do not wish our brothers to rest with us in this valley, you yourself will not rest in it either.”

And so it came to pass. For this Guy, although otherwise a good and religious man, was not brought to his end at Clairvaux, in fulfillment of the saint’s word. Instead, overtaken by illness at Pontigny, he took to his bed and there, by God’s ordering, received both the end of his life and his place of burial.

## CHAPTER XII. St. Bernard refuses Simon, abbot of Cîteaux, of the black Benedictine Order, transfer to Clairvaux while Bernard lived; yet he foretells that Simon would die at Clairvaux, as later occurred.

[Col. 1324C]

(See above, *The First Life of St. Bernard*, Book VII, col. 461.)

## CHAPTER XIII. Gunnarius, tetrarch of Sardinia, in fulfillment of St. Bernard’s prediction, becomes a monk at Clairvaux after Bernard’s death.

(See the same work, col. 462.)

## CHAPTER XIV. St. Bernard, while living at Rome for three years, repeatedly visits his own brethren at Clairvaux. Other marvels concerning him.

(See the same work, col. 463.)

## CHAPTER XV. St. Bernard rescues Constantius, condemned to hanging and being led to the gallows, from the executioner; with Count Theobald’s consent he tonsures him at Clairvaux and clothes him in the monastic habit.

[Col. 1324D]

It happened once that this servant of God went to Count Theobald on certain business. As he approached the town where the count then was, he met a large crowd of people who, by the count’s command, were leading a notorious and criminal robber to execution. At the sight, the most merciful Father took in his hand the rope by which the wretch was bound and said to his executioners: “Release this murderer to me; for I wish to hang him with my own hands.”

When the count heard of the man of God’s arrival, he hurried at once to meet [Col. 1325A] him, for he had always loved and honored him with a remarkable devotion. Seeing in Bernard’s hand the rope by which he drew the robber behind him, he was greatly horrified and said: “Alas, venerable Father! What is this that you have intended to do? Why have you recalled this gallows-bird, condemned a thousand times over, from the gate of hell? Can you save a man who has now wholly become a devil? His reformation is altogether hopeless; he can never do good except by dying. Therefore let this man of perdition perish, for the lives of many are endangered by his pestilential life.”

The venerable Father replied: “Excellent sir, I know—indeed I know—that this man is a most wicked robber and worthy of every severity of torment. Do not think, then, [Col. 1325B] that I wish to leave such a sinner unpunished. Rather, I intend to hand him over to executioners and exact from him a fitting vengeance—one which will be all the more fitting inasmuch as it is longer lasting. You had decreed to finish him by a brief punishment and momentary death; but I shall make him die by prolonged suffering and a death of the greatest length. You would have allowed him, hung upon the gallows, to remain dead upon the scaffold for one or several days; I shall make him, fastened to the cross, live and hang continuously in punishment for many years.”

When he heard this, the most Christian prince was silent and did not dare further to contradict the saint’s words. The most kindly Father immediately took off his own tunic and clothed the prisoner with it. Having cut the hair [Col. 1325C] of his head, he joined him to the Lord’s fold, making a lamb from a wolf, a convert from a robber. He came with Bernard to Clairvaux and thereafter remained obedient to him until death, surviving in the Order for thirty years, I believe, and more. His name was Constantius; we ourselves also saw and knew him.

## CHAPTER XVI. St. Bernard refutes a heretic who speaks against him by a prudent answer.

At another time, when the legate of the lord pope and other bishops were taking that man of God with them into the region of Toulouse in order to refute the heresy of the Manichaeans, the brethren prepared for him a better riding horse than usual, capable of enduring so long a journey. When he had come into that land accompanied by bishops, a certain Henry—formerly a black monk, then a vile apostate and leader of those same heretics—having learned of the servant of God’s arrival, feared his presence, knowing that he could not withstand the wisdom and Spirit speaking in him. Therefore he hastened his flight, went into hiding, and could nowhere then be found. There also God glorified His servant before all the people and princes of the land, daily working great signs and wonders among the people by his hands. It is not easy to believe how countless a multitude followed the apostolic man all day, while some sought instruction, others healing, and all sought his blessing.

[Col. 1326A]

One day, therefore, in the presence of an innumerable crowd, after he had extensively admonished them to preserve the Catholic faith and beware the filthy heresy, it happened that one of those heretics was present, a man who seemed more powerful and prudent than the rest. Seeing with an evil eye the veneration which the people offered to God’s servant, he sought some means to obscure somewhat the brightness of Bernard’s reputation and cast a stain upon his glory.

When all that seemed necessary for the occasion had been completed, the man of God mounted his horse to depart. Then the aforesaid heretic came before him, like a serpent raising its head, and cried out before everyone: “Lord Abbot, know that the horse of our master, which seems so poor to you, is not so thick-necked and fat as this fine steed of yours.” Hearing this, the gentle and patient man immediately answered him with tranquil countenance and mind: “Friend, I do not deny what you assert. Yet you ought to know that this beast of burden concerning which you mock me is a brute animal, one indeed of those which nature made prone and obedient to the belly. If it eats and grows fat according to its inclination, justice is not thereby injured and God is not offended, because the beast does what belongs to it. Therefore your master and I shall not be arraigned at God’s judgment over the necks of our animals; but each person will be judged over his own neck. Now, if you please, look at my neck and see: if it is thicker than your master’s neck, then perhaps you may rebuke me for that.”

Having said this, he removed his hood and, bareheaded down to the shoulders, showed his own neck: it was long and slender. Although it was wasted and thin in flesh, it was nevertheless, by heaven’s gift, exceedingly beautiful and white, like a swan’s neck. When all present saw it, they rejoiced greatly, blessing God, who had given His servant an answer so ready and so fitting, by which the mouth speaking wicked things was put to shame and stopped.

## CHAPTER XVII. At Paris, he leads some clerics, converted partly by words and partly by tears and groans to a holier manner of life, with him to Clairvaux.

[Col. 1326D]

On another occasion, when this man of the Lord had gone to Paris because necessity required it, he entered their schools, as usual, at the clerics’ request. Setting before them the pattern of true philosophy, he earnestly exhorted them to despise the world and embrace poverty for Christ the Lord. When his address was finished and none of them was converted, he departed sorrowful, because, contrary to his hope and contrary to what usually occurred, this had happened to him. Coming to the house of a certain archdeacon who had drawn him to his lodging, he withdrew into an oratory situated there. When he began to pray in a vehement spirit, he was so compunct in mind that groans and sobs which he could not restrain were heard outside.

When the aforesaid [Col. 1327A] archdeacon learned this, he began to ask Bernard’s companions what could be the cause of such great sorrow in him. One of them replied: he was a religious man, formerly abbot of Foigny, named Renald, who was more aware of the servant of God’s secrets and from whose report we have learned these things. He said to the archdeacon:

“This remarkable man, wholly inflamed with the fire of charity and wholly absorbed in God, desires nothing else in the world except to bring those who wander back to the way of truth and win their souls for Christ. Since he has just sown the word of life in the schools and has not received immediate fruit from the conversion of the clerics, he thinks that God is angry with him, whose favor he has not today perceived in his preaching. Hence this tempest of groans; hence this outpouring of tears. Therefore I now most certainly hope that the abundance of tomorrow’s sowing will compensate today’s barrenness with great increase.”

At dawn, when he returned to the schools, this eminent preacher, at the Lord’s prompting, put out into the deep with the vessel of thought and let down the nets of words for a catch. When his address was ended, very many of those clerics gave themselves to the Lord through his hand. He immediately drew them from the danger of the world as from waves of the sea, put them into hired vehicles, and did not delay to bring them into the harbor of Clairvaux.

At length, leaving the city, he came with his company as far as the village of Saint-Denis and spent the night there. Early the next morning, when his brethren supposed that he would set out by the direct road, he said: “We must certainly return to Paris, [Col. 1327C] because some of our people are still there. We must also bring them away from there and join them to this fold of the Lord, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.”

As he began to enter the city, he saw three clerics coming toward him from afar, and said to his companions: “The Lord has discharged us; now we shall proceed on our way. Behold, these are the clerics for whom we came.” When they approached and learned that he was present, they rejoiced greatly and said: “O most blessed Father, how welcome is your arrival! For we had resolved to go to you, and scarcely thought we could catch you as you were leaving.” He answered: “And I knew it, beloved ones. For that reason I hastened to meet you as you fled, with loaves. Let us therefore walk together, and through God’s grace I shall be the guide of your journey.”

Joined, therefore, to the others mentioned above, they followed the holy man, clinging to him and obeying him until their deaths.

## CHAPTER XVIII. At Milan, a certain man affirmed that he had seen St. Bernard among the apostles.

Renald likewise informed us that when this servant of God came once to Milan to reconcile the schism of Peter Leo, he was received there with such universal rejoicing that nearly the entire city rushed out to meet him for a league. Many of them proceeded four or five miles. Indeed, they were so pleased with him that although they had not seen him before, as soon as he entered the city they seized him by unanimous consent and made him archbishop rather than elected him. When he refused, they were wholly ready to use force even to the death, had he not secretly escaped by flight.

As he sat there in a very large house, such a multitude of people surrounded him that no one could enter. Meanwhile, one of those citizens, honorable in dress and appearance, earnestly desired by every means to approach the man of God but could find no entrance. He climbed into the crowd, crawling on hands and feet and stepping over the necks of those sitting there until he reached him. Seizing Bernard’s feet, he began to embrace and kiss them with remarkable devotion. Renald, mentioned above, who stood [Col. 1328B] closer, saw this and went to remove him, knowing that the holy man was exceedingly burdened by such reverence and attentions. But the man turned and said to him: “Let me be, I beg you; let me see and touch a man close to God and truly apostolic. For I tell you, and testify upon the Christian faith, that I have seen him among the apostles.”

When the monk heard this, he was astonished. Wanting fuller knowledge, he wished to ask him the manner of this vision; but, because of the bystanders, he did not dare for shame. Nevertheless, he most certainly believed that it had been a great revelation, since the man was so deeply affected toward the servant of God.

## CHAPTER XIX. Christ crucified appears to St. Bernard at prayer and, releasing His arms from the cross, embraces him.

[Col. 1328C]

Lord Menard, formerly abbot of Moris, a religious man of pious memory, related to us as though concerning another person a certain marvelous vision which we nevertheless think happened to himself. He said:

“I know a monk who once found blessed Bernard the abbot in church praying alone. While Bernard lay prostrate before the altar, there appeared a cross with its crucified figure, placed on the pavement before him. This most blessed man worshipped and kissed it with the greatest devotion. Then that Majesty, separating His arms from the ends of the cross, seemed to embrace the servant of God and clasp him to Himself. As the monk watched this for some time, he remained dumbfounded by excessive amazement and was as though beside himself. At last, fearing that he might offend the Father if Bernard saw him hovering so near as an observer of his secrets, he withdrew silently, understanding and knowing that the prayer and whole manner of life of that holy man were truly beyond human measure.”

## CHAPTER XX. St. Bernard obtains for an epileptic monk that he may foresee his illness, lie down, and avoid injury from a sudden fall.

The holy Father once went out to visit his brethren harvesting in the field. Because he was infirm and unable to travel on foot, [Col. 1329A] he went on a little ass. A certain monk was then walking with him and driving the ass. Since this monk had long suffered from the falling sickness, he suddenly collapsed before Bernard on the road itself and began to be grievously convulsed by the epilepsy. Seeing this, the holy man took pity on him and prayed to the Lord for him, that this affliction might no longer take him unawares.

From that time until the day of his death—for twenty years and more afterward—it was granted to the sick man what he had not previously possessed, and what scarcely ever happens to other epileptics: whenever he was about to fall from the same illness, he foreknew it for some time beforehand, so that he could lie down upon a bed in time and continually avoid the injury of a sudden fall. The holy man who obtained this lesser gift from the Lord for him, we believe, could have obtained complete health for him if he had known it beneficial to the man’s soul. But since the man was difficult in disposition and exceedingly hard of heart, so that both the rod of correction and the staff of consolation always seemed necessary for his salvation, it was mercifully granted him to escape continually the danger of a sudden attack through foreknowledge, while not being deprived of the spur of a health-giving illness.

## CHAPTER XXI. St. Bernard appeared repeatedly, not long after his death, to a man who was first a regular canon and later a monk of Clairvaux.

[Col. 1329C] A certain brother of the Order of Regular Clerics, being eager to make progress and a zealous seeker of the better gifts, greatly desired to submit himself to the instruction of blessed Bernard and to be joined to the community of Clairvaux. This man, being four days’ journey from Clairvaux, on the very day and at the very hour when the aforesaid servant of God departed from the world, being overcome by drowsiness contrary to his custom, fell asleep upon a bench. It was about the second hour of the day. And behold, there appeared to him in a vision a great and splendid procession of monks of the white Order, such as he had never before seen. They were honourably carrying the holy body, as though from the place where the aforesaid Father had died, into the church, and were performing the due rites of burial.

But on the fifth day afterwards, [Col. 1329D] when the grievous report of the death of that most holy man reached his ears, he immediately perceived that Bernard had departed from the world at the hour in which he had seen the aforesaid vision. And indeed it was so. Then, struck by the newness of the dreadful wound, he was violently cast down in spirit, calling himself wretched and unworthy because he had not deserved to obtain the fulfilment of his desire. Therefore, giving free rein to tears, he gave himself wholly to lamentation. When evening came, before sleep received eyes wearied by weeping, he began to consider more attentively concerning that holy man whether, received in peace by the Lord, he enjoyed heavenly blessedness and was now to be invoked together with all the saints; or whether perhaps, drawing with him something from the dust of the world, he still needed the aid of prayers.

While [Col. 1330A] he turned this over in his mind and earnestly desired to know the matter, he was suddenly caught out of himself and saw in the spirit a shining star rising from the earth and, in a most direct course, piercing the heights of heaven. At once it was made known to him that this was the soul of blessed Bernard, which, like a distinguished star, pure and bright, had taken its place upon the pinnacles of heaven.

A very few days having passed, while he was before the altar intent upon prayer and devoutly performing the office for the dead for the soul of that same holy man, he came into an ecstasy of mind. And behold, that same servant of God again appeared to him, notably adorned with pontifical mitres, and likewise rising from the earth and being borne by a direct path into heaven. Forewarned by these and similar revelations, from that time [Col. 1330B] the brother was accustomed to keep a special commemoration of that most blessed man and to honour him spiritually, reckoning him among the greatest friends of God, without any doubt concerning his glorification.

In those same days that same servant of God again appeared to him in a vision, like a vigorous labourer, girded for work in a very broad field, in which there were innumerable sheaves of wheat harvest. Of these he had already gathered a copious multitude into one great heap. Yet he still perseveringly laboured to carry together and heap up the remaining sheaves, which were far more numerous. When he had seen this, he immediately understood that the heap of sheaves represented the multitude of brethren whom that outstanding preacher, [Col. 1330C] while he lived in the flesh, had gathered to Christ God, and that there still remained innumerable persons who were to be brought by his merits and examples to the grace of salvation. Therefore, greatly rejoicing and not despairing that he himself would be one of them, he went to Clairvaux as quickly as he could, requesting and obtaining admission.

While he was still there as a novice, and turned over in his mind the memory of the blessed man almost unceasingly and insatiably, one Sunday near the end of the night offices sleep began to steal over him, weary and afflicted as he was in many ways. And behold, the same servant of God appeared to him in a vision, graciously addressing and warning him to direct his intention continually toward God, with a daily outpouring of tears; if he did so, he might confidently await both divine mercy and Bernard’s own visitation. Having said this, he withdrew into his tomb, which was situated there. This withdrawal was so evident that the brother did not know whether he had seen it asleep or awake. When he opened his eyes and pondered the most merciful Father’s admonition in sweet recollection, Bernard suddenly appeared to him again while he was fully awake and offered himself to be seen with bodily eyes.

He stood close before him, so that he could easily have been touched by hand, attentively observing him and as though examining whether he slept or woke, as those do who rouse sleepers for the vigils. He was clothed in the monastic habit and almost resembled a monk standing beside that novice in choir. Thinking that he was this very monk, the novice wondered greatly why he was staring at him [Col. 1331A] with such fixed eyes. But when he turned his gaze and saw the same monk still beside him, the figure which had appeared immediately vanished. Then, through the Spirit’s revelation, the brother knew that it had been that same servant of God, who had deigned to show his desired presence to one poor and desolate.

For after he vanished from him, it seemed to the brother that Bernard had entered, as it were tangibly, into his inmost heart. Hence, set fiercely ablaze in the love of God and of the most blessed man, he was immediately caught wholly into jubilation and was, as it were, beside himself. Finally, on the following night, while similarly present at the brethren’s vigils, he experienced there such great grace of divine visitation as he had never before felt in all his life. He did not doubt that he had obtained it all by the merits of that same saint. And for many days, as he repeatedly poured forth the recollection of the abundance of this sweetness, he shed abundant sweet and devout tears, with which he could not be satisfied by day or night.

## CHAPTER XXII. The remarkable conversion to monastic life, through the help of St Bernard, of Alexander: first a canon and teacher at Cologne, afterwards abbot of Grand Selva, and finally of Cîteaux.

It happened on one occasion that the same servant of God, at the command of blessed Pope Eugenius, entered Germany to preach the journey to Jerusalem to Emperor Conrad and to the people of that land. While there he shone forth in innumerable signs and miracles. Seeing the great wonders which the Lord displayed through him, the emperor [Col. 1331C] received the sign of the cross from his hand, intending to set out for Jerusalem. Nor did an innumerable multitude of people delay to do the same. Inflamed with an incredible ardour of faith, they eagerly tore from every side strips and fringes from the garments of the servant of God—who was often compelled to obtain new clothing for this very reason—and anyone who did not deserve to possess crosses made from his clothing judged himself unfortunate.

Many noble and learned men among them likewise gave themselves to God through his hand. Led by him to Clairvaux and made monks by him, they thereafter produced the greatest fruit in the Church of God. One of these was Alexander, a venerable man, then a canon and celebrated teacher in the city of [Col. 1331D] Cologne. When the most blessed Father urged him to convert himself to the Order, he, swollen with secular learning and wealth, replied that at present he desired and considered nothing less than assuming the monastic habit.

That same night, when he had surrendered his limbs to sleep, the same venerable man appeared to him in a vision, raising him from the couch on which he seemed to lie grievously ill and restoring him to health. Then he took the habit which he himself wore and clothed Alexander with it. Alexander, having angrily thrust the habit from his shoulders once and a second time, was at length compelled on the third occasion to retain it when it was placed about his neck and firmly bound to his body. Then the blessed Father also placed in his hand the staff which he held, signifying the grace of a future prelacy, and commanded him thus to depart.

When Alexander awoke, however, he was not yet able to be softened by such a revelation, but persisted in the same hardness of heart. That same day, when the most blessed abbot reclined at table, a fish called *perca* was brought before him to refresh him. Seeing it, the man of God raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for a long time over the fish. Then, blessing it, he sent it as an extra portion to the aforesaid Alexander. When Alexander began to taste it, at the very first bite he was granted to experience happily in himself the power of the servant of God’s prayer. For he was suddenly changed into another man, deeply contrite, and began to shed abundant tears over that food. He wondered at himself, not knowing what had come over him or why he wept. At last, remembering the vision he had seen on the preceding night, [Col. 1332B] he understood that by the Lord’s free mercy he had been anticipated. Therefore, giving thanks for the heavenly calling, he immediately gave himself to the blessed servant of God. Bernard made him a monk at Clairvaux; afterwards he became shepherd of Grand Selva, and advanced so greatly in holiness of life that he was later made father and patriarchal abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux.

We have set these matters down on the faithful report of Alexander himself, that servant of God.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, learns by God’s revelation that the seven penitential psalms which St Bernard, while still a novice, customarily recited daily in silence for the soul of his mother had one day been omitted by him.

[Col. 1332C]

While blessed Bernard was still a novice, he used daily to say in silence the seven penitential psalms for the soul of his mother. But one day, after beginning the said psalms after Compline, he omitted them before completing them—whether through carelessness, I know not, or forgetfulness—and came to his bed and fell asleep. Abbot Stephen, learning of the negligence through the Spirit, met him on the following day and said: “Brother Bernard, where, I ask you, did you leave those psalms of yours yesterday after Compline? Or to whom did you entrust them?” Hearing this, the young man, being modest and God-fearing, blushed and fell at Stephen’s feet.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, to whom God wonderfully supplied three wagons with nine horses; and who, having laid aside his governance, saw an unclean spirit enter the mouth of Guy, appointed in his place.

Accordingly, the venerable Stephen one day called one of his brethren and, speaking to him in the Spirit of God, said: “You see, beloved, that we are pressed by great want. Unless help is quickly brought them, our brethren are near to perishing through hunger, cold, and other hardships. Go, therefore, to the market at Vézelay, which is soon to be held, and buy there three wagons and, for each of them, three strong draught horses, which we especially need [Col. 1333A] for carrying our burdens. When you have loaded these wagons with cloth, food, and other necessary things, bring them back with you in prosperity and joy.”

The brother replied: “I am ready, lord Father, to obey your commands, if you give me money with which to buy these supplies.”

The abbot replied: “Here are three denarii, the only ones found in this house. Take them, if you wish; for whatever else is lacking, the mercy of our God will provide for you. Go, then, in confidence, for the Lord will send his angel with you and will make your journey prosperous.”

The brother set out, and when he arrived at Vézelay he was received as a guest by a certain faithful and God-fearing man. When this man learned the purpose of his journey [Col. 1333B] and the brethren’s need, he immediately went to a very wealthy neighbour of his, who was desperately ill and nearly dying, and was distributing his possessions to the poor. When he had told the sick man of the need of the Cistercian monks, whose holiness was already celebrated in those regions, the aforesaid brother was summoned to the man’s house. From the dying man he received, as alms, such a sum of money that he could sufficiently purchase everything the abbot had ordered.

Having obtained the three carriages with nine draught horses, he loaded and equipped them with everything he knew necessary for the brethren’s use. Thus he who had arrived empty-handed returned to his own people full-handed. Approaching Cîteaux, [Col. 1333C] he sent a messenger to inform the abbot alike of his arrival and of his success. Hearing it, the venerable Father greatly rejoiced in the Lord. Summoning the brethren together, he said: “God, the Lord of mercies, the God of compassion, has acted freely and generously. Truly, nobly and graciously hast thou dealt with us, O Lord, our provider and shepherd, opening thy hand and filling our want with blessing.”

Then, arranging a procession, they went out to meet the arriving brother as far as the gate. The abbot himself went forth in sacred vestments, carrying the pastoral staff, while ministers similarly vested preceded him with the cross and holy water. Thus they solemnly received, with much thanksgiving, that alms—not as a gift bestowed by a man, but as a blessing sent from heaven by the Lord and mercy from God their Saviour.

It is also read in the *Deeds of the English* concerning this blessed man [Col. 1333D] that, while he was still a young man in the world, he once went to Rome with a certain companion [Note: [Col. 1333D] Peter, afterwards prior of Jully.] for prayer. Throughout that journey, they customarily sang the entire Psalter every day without interruption. At length, after entering the monastery of Molesme, the same venerable Stephen laboured with most fervent zeal and strove by every means to establish the place and Order of Cîteaux, of which he himself was afterwards, by the Lord’s ordinance, to be made an outstanding shepherd and teacher.

Accordingly, when worn out by great old age, and when his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see, he laid aside pastoral care in order to devote himself now to himself and to the Lord alone. A certain man unworthy of such honour succeeded him, named Guy. Though he possessed outward gifts to no small degree, like a whitewashed tomb, inwardly he was foul with the rottenness of vices. At the very beginning of his promotion, while he was receiving the professions of the brethren according to custom, that same servant of God Stephen saw an unclean spirit come to him and enter into his mouth. Hardly a month passed, and behold, by the Lord’s revelation his impurity was exposed, and that spurious plant, which the heavenly Father had not planted, was at once uprooted from the paradise of God. [Col. 1334B]

## CHAPTER XXV. Fastrad, formerly abbot of Cambron, then of Clairvaux and afterwards of Cîteaux: a man of venerable speech and great virtues, divinely commended even in death.

(See above, *First Life of St Bernard*, book VII, col. 464.)

## CHAPTER XXVI. A certain abbot is warned from heaven not to strive further to lay aside the burden of his office. The same man had formerly been freed from extremely severe and frequent headaches by the miraculous descent, as it were, of a mass of lead into the middle of his forehead.

A certain holy abbot, one of the sons of Clairvaux, while he burned wholly with Christ’s love, strove by every means to lay down the burden of pastoral office, so that he might more freely give himself to the repose of contemplation. On one occasion, therefore, having left his monastery as though never to return, he withdrew for a few days to another abbey, eagerly seeking and expecting release from the aforesaid governance. One night, while he was attending the vigils, awake and chanting with the others, he saw in an ecstasy of mind blessed Bernard appearing to him. Greatly cheered by the vision, he began earnestly to entreat Bernard to deign to lead him to the Lord Jesus Christ, whose most blessed presence he desired with excessive ardour.

The most blessed Father immediately took him with himself and, bringing him where he wished, presented him to the Lord the Saviour. When he had been introduced, he fell at Christ’s feet, worshipping and begging him to have mercy on him. The Lord replied: “If you wish me to be merciful to you, then make profession to me.” Hearing this, he most willingly assented and, joining his hands in Christ’s hands, gave himself to him, professing and promising obedience to him until death.

When the profession had been made and [Col. 1335A] the revelation ended, he returned to himself troubled and wavering in mind. He did not certainly know what was signified to him by that vision or promise. Yet he suspected that he had been thwarted in his desire and bound by the bond of that profession so that he no longer dared, without divine command, to lay aside the burden of pastoral office which he bore with difficulty. On the next day, while standing at the altar and holding the most holy Body in his hands, he began to pray from the depths of his heart that the Lord would deign clearly to show him his will in this matter. And behold, at the very moment of receiving communion, a voice came to him from God, saying: “As long as you live, you cannot have a successor.” Made certain by this answer, he stayed his foot from flight and strove to submit his own will to the divine judgment.

At the beginning of his conversion and youth, this venerable Father was frequently afflicted by severe headache. Yet he was more troubled in spirit because his weak flesh could not, as he wished, follow his spirit, which was most ready for every difficult work of virtue. One Sunday, therefore, while attending the solemn vigils, feeling himself pricked by the said ailment more than usual, he considered leaving the choir to go out and rest. But, inspired by God, he immediately resolved to force himself and endure until Prime. When Prime had passed, although the immense pain did not cease, he again determined to endure until Mass, however severe the pain, so that he might receive holy communion.

As he was about to communicate and approached the step of the altar, seeking there in the accustomed manner forgiveness on bended knees, behold, a mass as though of lead suddenly fell from the crown of his head. It came down through the middle of his forehead [Col. 1335C] and fell upon the pavement with no slight impact. He clearly felt the jolt and fall of that mass, yet saw nothing. Astonished at so strange an occurrence, he was greatly dumbfounded. But as soon as he had received holy communion, he recovered from that infirmity in that very hour, and was so perfectly cured that thereafter he felt no trouble from it.

We learned all that we have related concerning this man from his own more private account to us.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Baldwin, knight and lord of Guise, a man of evil deeds, dies at Igny in the monastic habit; afterwards he repeatedly appears to Peter, abbot of Igny, and is at last, after long purification through the prayers of the abbot and monks, received into heaven.

[Col. 1335D]

A certain knight named Baldwin, lord of the castle called Guise in the territory of Rheims, was a warlike man and valiant in arms. Setting aside the fear of God, he daily committed many evil deeds, frequently engaging in robbery, arson, slaughter, and the like. This alone seemed good in him: he sincerely loved the most holy man Peter, abbot of Igny, together with all his household; he honoured him magnificently and put great confidence in his merits. Nor was this without result, as the outcome showed.

For while he was still in the vigour of life, it happened that, oppressed by mortal sickness, [Col. 1336A] he was brought to the point of death. He therefore sent for and summoned the aforesaid abbot. Coming quickly, the abbot found him already almost spent and deprived of the use of his tongue. But at the holy abbot’s prayer, the sick man was immediately granted, by the great gift of God, both the power of speech and the grace to make confession. When this had been done, he immediately wished to forsake the world and assume the religious habit. But his wife, who loved his body more than his soul, opposed him; and so his vow was delayed until she had altogether despaired of his recovery and finally gave consent.

He was then brought to the aforesaid house at Igny, to become a monk there if he lived. But as death hastened, his soul was immediately released, groaning and deeply repentant because he had spent the time of repentance without repentance. When he had died, many revelations concerning him were made to the aforesaid abbot and to the other elders of the place. Since it would take too long to recount them all, we have taken care to record a few out of many.

That same night on which he died, he appeared in a vision to a certain religious man, as though raising himself from his bed. When the man sought to assist him, Baldwin said: “Brother, you need not weary yourself. For Saint Benedict is my most powerful helper; and he himself sends me to your lord Peter, the abbot, that I may be made a monk by him.”

That same night, while the venerable abbot himself was deeply anxious and concerned for him, he began to consider how he might assist a dead man burdened by so great a weight of sins. While he thought upon this, suddenly someone whose face he did not recognize stood before him—whom he nevertheless believed to have been an angel of the Lord—answering his thoughts and saying: “He needs great help.” There can be no doubt that he spoke of the dead man. [Col. 1336C] Having said this, he immediately vanished.

Having received this answer from God, the abbot immediately devoted himself wholly to prayer, going round the altars of the saints and earnestly imploring their intercession for the dead man’s salvation. Meanwhile sleep began to creep over him, as though he were sorrowful and weary. His eyelids closed, and he seemed neither wholly awake nor wholly asleep. Suddenly Satan appeared to him, roaring threateningly against him and saying: “What? Will you take Baldwin from me?” Having said this, he sprang upon him, constricting and crushing him violently.

The abbot immediately awoke and found himself so bound in all his limbs that he could not move them. But the word of God was not bound. Therefore the man of God said to Satan: “I adjure you, unclean spirit, by the blood of Jesus Christ, which he shed for us wretched sinners, and by his glorious Mother and Virgin Mary, that you do not dare to harm this soul, confessed and repentant.” When he had said this, the devil left him and fled.

In his release, understanding that the dead man had been freed, he resumed his steadfastness in prayer and pressed his petitions again with ever greater urgency. In that hour he was flooded with such grace of devotion and conceived in his mind such confidence in God’s mercy as he had never experienced in his life. Hence he did not doubt that the petitions of himself and his brethren for that dead man had been heard by God.

Then, prescribing many and prolonged prayers for the brethren in common, he himself also took care to offer the sacrifice of our redemption for the soul of the dead man almost daily for thirty days. Throughout the whole thirty-day period, scarcely a day passed on which that dead man did not appear to the aforesaid abbot, whether asleep [Col. 1337A] or awake, sometimes even kneeling with hands joined and beseeching him not to cease praying for him.

It happened during this time that an abbot of the monks of the black Order, whom that knight had once grievously injured, came to the house of Igny for lodging. Seeing this, the aforesaid abbot of that place led him to the dead man’s tomb, begging him, for Christ’s love, to absolve Baldwin from the injury which, at the devil’s prompting, he had committed against him. When this was done, behold, that very night the dead man appeared joyfully to the aforesaid abbot of Igny. He showed him his body cleansed and free from the leprosy by which he had shown himself formerly to be defiled. Moreover, upon his face appeared a scar, wholly formed over an immense wound; its fresh healing showed that the sin which he had committed against the abbot had been erased.

After this, on the holy day of Parasceve, that is, Good Friday, when the divine office had begun at about the ninth hour, the venerable abbot of Igny, vested as a priest, was sitting beside the altar. Two young men appeared to him, with radiant faces and shining in silken garments. Walking on the right and left of that knight, they led him as far as the altar. Passing before the abbot, they said: “Behold Lord Baldwin.” The dead man himself was clothed in black garments, but good and handsome ones, which appeared to be of *ysembrunus* [material uncertain]. Seeing this, the venerable abbot rejoiced greatly, understanding without doubt in the black garments the sign of repentance, and in Baldwin’s presentation at the altar a sure token of reconciliation. Since thereafter the dead man no longer appeared, [Col. 1337D] the abbot was made even more certain of his absolution.

We drew out this account in sequence from that same servant of God, after first urging him with many entreaties. To disbelieve his assertion is to detract from all religious devotion.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the plague which devastated the monastery of Domus Dei; and the happy passage to the heavenly realm of Abbot Franco and the monk Bernard.

At the abbey of Domus Dei, one of the daughters of Clairvaux, there occurred in this year a great mortality, so that within thirty-five days no small number of brethren were taken away, and sometimes four or five were buried in one day. Yet they hastened toward death—or rather toward death’s harbour and life’s gate—with such eagerness and desire that those dying pitied the living and the living envied the dying.

Among them was taken away the venerable Franco, abbot of that place, of holy memory, who rendered his blessed soul to Christ the Lord on the holy day of Parasceve. Already crowds of people from neighbouring regions stream in from every direction to his tomb because of the many healings and benefits which they feel that they receive there from the Lord.

Four days later, that is, on Monday in Easter week, there died there a monk young in age but advanced in the maturity of religious life. It is also affirmed concerning him that, by the Lord’s grant, he preserved the flower of virginity until death. Strengthened by a marvellous hope, he desired so greatly to be dissolved and to be with Christ that he seemed to fear nothing except being delayed longer from death and remaining in the body. He was greatly grieved if anyone either promised or wished him a reprieve.

On the day of his departure itself, blessed Bernard appeared to him with the aforesaid Abbot F[ranco], who said to him: “Brother Bernard”—for that was the young man’s name—“behold, I bring you our holy Father Bernard, that I may deliver you into his hands.” The blessed Father, receiving him with his gracious right hand, said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise.” Having said this, they vanished.

Then the monk told the brethren what he had seen and heard, adding: “If I live until tomorrow, I have not spoken the truth. But if I depart today, let that very departure confirm my words.” Thus the brother died on that same day, so that all that the holy Father had said to him was fulfilled in him.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Certain wonders concerning Gerard of Farfa, a man of admirable devotion and outstanding holiness, to whom St Bernard appeared when he was near death; and who also complained after death that he had been buried prematurely while still living and breathing.

[Col. 1338C]

Gerard of Farfa, beloved by God and men, whose memory is in blessing, was honoured by blessed Bernard above others with special favour because of his singular purity and holiness. He appeared to all marvellous and exceedingly lovable. While he was still a monk at Farfa, a famous abbey of Tuscany, he saw by the Lord’s revelation in the spirit that he had been transferred to Clairvaux. He was there performing the office of going around the individual workshops with two basins and pouring water over the brethren’s hands for washing.

[Col. 1338D] The outcome taught what was undoubtedly signified by this: he was to be the man who, by a daily—indeed, almost continual—flood of tears, as though from two ewers, washed away the brethren’s failings. So fully had the devotion of compassion, in longing for Christ, filled his breast that his pupils, like two fountains unable to be silent, nearly everywhere, but especially during the celebration of the divine mystery, drenched his face with a great flow of tears.

He possessed a singular grace both with God and with men, which all marvelled at. They looked upon his countenance as the face of an angel standing among them and said: “This is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city” (2 Maccabees 15:14).

[Col. 1339A] God gave this man many consolations in secret. But he, being modest and humble, preferred that his virtues remain hidden; and no one dared trouble him with inquiry concerning such matters, out of reverence for his holiness. Although he was extremely frail in body, being already nearly ninety years old, he nevertheless seemed daily to grow young again through the untiring fervour of his spirit. He could scarcely be kept in the infirmary even when sickness compelled him, and could scarcely be restrained even from the labour of harvest.

Once, while oppressed by a most severe illness and lying in bed in a rather secluded little room, it happened one night that the lamp burning there went out. Seeing this, a brother who was then attending him rose and went to relight it. Finding all the workshops shut and no fire anywhere, he returned sadly; after securing the door of the cell, he lay down again and fell asleep.

Deep in the night, when that holy man wished to rise for necessities, the brother rose too, grieved that he lacked a light. Looking, however, at the little furnace nearby—in which there had been no fire for the preceding eight days—he saw there a considerable heap of burning coals. He lit the lamp from them; but when he immediately turned his eyes again to that furnace, he found not only no coals, but could not detect in it even the slightest trace of warmth.

A certain novice named Julian, a priest of honourable life and religious devotion, who had come to Clairvaux from the Order of Regular Clerics, [Col. 1339C] once saw an unclean spirit wandering about the choir in the form of a kid-goat. When it came before him, it stood there for a while and began to mock him with open jaws, shaking its obscene head toward him and grinding its teeth together very finely. When it withdrew from him, it came and stood before Gerard, the man of God, and began similarly to ridicule him with lewd gestures, like an insolent animal. But Gerard mocked and blew it away even more; immediately it vanished like smoke, and that novice saw it no more.

Having promptly obtained leave to speak with Gerard, the novice asked him whether he had seen anything in choir at that particular hour. The old man confessed that he had seen a phantom kid-goat which, with playful movements, was mocking both him and Julian alike. Hearing this, the novice marvelled greatly, and thereby understood that Gerard saw many things of this kind, though he reported few of them.

When this man was now at the point of death, blessed Bernard appeared to him with an angelic countenance and adorned in white clothing, but in the bodily bearing and condition which he had before death. As Gerard watched him approach, supporting his aged and venerable limbs with a staff, he signalled by hand and voice, as best he could, to those attending him that they should rise for the approaching saint and quickly prepare a place for him to sit. They were astonished and asked of what saint he spoke; but, pressed by illness, he could not answer.

Later, after recovering the power of speech, when they asked again, [Col. 1340A] he confessed that he had seen blessed Bernard consoling him in gentle speech. After blessing him, Bernard also blessed the entire house, adding these words: “This is my house, which I built. May the Lord guard it for ever and ever.”

When that holy man had rested in the Lord, some time later he appeared in a vision to a religious lay brother named Laurence, joyful and radiant and fittingly adorned in precious garments, indicating that through God’s grace he possessed everlasting joy and glory. When the brother, prostrate upon the ground, begged that he might obtain Gerard’s blessing and intercession, Gerard blessed him and replied: “I do not cease praying not only for you, but also for the whole body of the Church itself. Yet I complain somewhat of this: because of excessive haste, the brethren buried me while I was still alive and breathing.” [Col. 1340B]

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning Laurence, lay brother of Clairvaux, who, rescued from many dangers by the help of St Bernard, brought ten buffaloes from Italy to Clairvaux.

Accordingly, since mention has arisen of the aforesaid Brother Lawrence, I think I should relate something that I learned about him. This man, then—as we all knew—was a spiritual man, always devoted with remarkable persistence to prayer and compunction; so much so that for many years, while he kept the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy in the sacristy day and night, he could scarcely ever be found there at any hour otherwise than intent upon prayer and sprinkling the pavement with prolonged tears. Now, at the beginning of his conversion, while he was troubled by many temptations, one night after Matins had ended he was alone in a certain dwelling. And behold, an unclean spirit, bellowing and lamenting, circled about him in restless wandering. But he, having made the sign of the holy cross upon his forehead, asked who it was. The demon replied: “I am he who tempted and scourged Job.” Hearing this, the brother, still a novice, was afraid at the demon’s appearance, fled, and heard him no more.

After the passing of blessed Bernard, it happened that this same brother was sent by the venerable Philip, prior of Clairvaux, to Roger, king of Sicily, [Col. 1340D] on business of that Church. When he had entered Rome, he learned that the same king had very recently died. He was dismayed in spirit and wholly uncertain what he ought to do. Therefore, turning to prayer, he invoked blessed Bernard with groaning and tears, saying:

“My father, chariot of Israel and its driver, why have you forsaken us? Alas for me! Holy father, what shall I say, or what shall I do, poor and wretched as I am, deprived of every comfort? While you lived, and at your command, I often went safely far away among foreign peoples; and everywhere, for love of you, I was received with great favor. I bore your greetings and letters, which kings and bishops, together with all others, received as a blessing sent from heaven; and all the nobler men rejoiced to be ennobled by your blessings. [Col. 1341A] But now that you have died, my favor too has died with you; nor will there now be anyone to extend a helping hand to a stranger and needy man. And behold, the king who sincerely loved you is dead, and in his place his boy-son has arisen, who perhaps does not know you. If I should wish to approach him, still so far away, and should happen to suffer rejection from him, both labor and expense will be lost. But if I return at once and leave the business unattempted, I fear to be accused of sluggishness and folly. Stretch out help, I pray; offer counsel to one in need; and do not despise the groaning of your pitiable servant.”

That same night this most blessed Father appeared to him and splendidly comforted him, saying: [Col. 1341B] “What has made you, brother, distrust so greatly the mercy of God and my own intercession? When or where have you found my help lacking to you in your necessities? Or do you perhaps judge me now less powerful than I was formerly in the world, now that I have been admitted into the powers of the Lord? Go, then, in confidence: all things will turn out favorably, and by this very matter you will know that I myself have sent you.”

While the saint spoke these and many other things, the brother himself, through the overwhelming ardor of devotion, melted wholly within his soul; and, as his heart gave birth to immense joy, tears of devotion burst forth outwardly as well. When he awoke with eyes and cheeks wet, he found that even the pillow on which he had rested his head had been soaked all around by the same flood of tears.

Therefore, setting out early in the morning, after leaving the city he found a company of merchants travelling to Sicily for trade. Recognizing him to be from Clairvaux, they immediately received him gladly into their escort and fellowship, and daily supplied all necessities without charge. At last, when he came before the king of Sicily, he found great favor in his eyes; and he obtained not only a successful outcome in the matter for which he had been sent to the Father, but the king, opening his treasures for the soul of his own father, devoutly sent through this brother no small sum of gold for the construction of the new basilica at Clairvaux.

When the aforesaid brother returned to Rome, he nevertheless found such favor there that, by gifts from cardinals and other Romans—contrary to the usual practice—he received a very abundant blessing; indeed, through their generosity he led as many as ten buffaloes out of that city and brought them all the way to the house of Clairvaux, to the great astonishment of everyone. [Col. 1341D] For who could sufficiently marvel that a weak and elderly man, with only two little boys, could drive animals of such enormous size and ferocity—which surpass oxen two- or threefold in bulk and strength—through so many hazardous regions and amid so many schemes of robbers and bandits, from Rome to Clairvaux? This is especially remarkable since, as they say, that species of animal had hitherto been seen nowhere in all the West on this side of the Alps. [Col. 1342A] He could scarcely avoid for even one day the assaults and violence of evil men; yet he passed through all of them unharmed, God and the holy Father Bernard everywhere protecting their faithful servant.

It happened, however, that he was obliged to pass through a certain town whose rule was held by chieftains of robbers, from whose jaws no one could escape unharmed unless perhaps he prevailed by force. As dawn was already reddening the sky, when he was leaving a meadow where he had spent the night with the animals, he earnestly implored God and Saint Bernard to rescue him from the impending danger. And behold, from afar there appeared to him what seemed to be two men coming toward him, each carrying a lighted candle in his hand. As they gradually approached and had almost reached him, they suddenly vanished from his sight, giving God’s servant great confidence that he would escape.

Thus entering that nest of the devil, he was immediately stopped, and men ran from all sides to seize the prey. But at that very hour certain venerable men arrived; recognizing him as a man of Clairvaux, they delivered him from the hands of his assailants and allowed him to depart with all that was his. At last he reached Clairvaux and, to everyone’s amazement, brought in beasts of a new kind, which, multiplying by their offspring, are propagated daily and from that place are now spread through many provinces.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A monk who died at Burlancourt is revealed to a holy man to be equal in merits to the holy martyrs John and Paul.

[Col. 1342C]

A religious brother from Burlancourt, named Gerard, contracted elephantiasis; and though he lived apart from the others for a long time, he bore the Father’s scourge with such equanimity and persevered so constantly in thanksgiving that the others, marvellously delighted and edified by his praiseworthy patience, glorified God and regarded him as a martyr. At last, having completed his blessed struggle, he escaped alike pain and death and deserved to be received with blessed Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom.

That same night, while the corpse was being watched in the church and the brothers were chanting psalms around it according to custom, such a revelation was made to one of them, a most holy man who had long exercised the office of abbot. In an ecstasy of mind he saw, and behold, three venerable persons appeared in great glory around the dead man’s body. One of them struck the body with a rod, and a dove came forth from it, flew away, and sought the heights. Then one of these persons said: “Like a dove it seeks the springs above.” The second added: “Without hindrance it penetrates the heavens.” The third likewise said: “It is made equal to the merits of the holy John and Paul.” Having said this, they immediately vanished from the spectator’s eyes. The holy man therefore understood that that soul was of great merit, since in merits it had been joined with such martyrs.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A certain devout man who died in the territory of Meaux was found standing upon his knees and the joints of his left hand on the bare ground, while holding his right hand to his breast as though striking it.

[Col. 1343A]

In the territory of Meaux, in a village called Béthune-Basoches, nearly seven years ago there died a certain servant of Christ, poor indeed in temporal possessions but rich in virtues. Though clothed in secular dress, he followed the monastic life in practice. While still younger, urged by friends, he allowed himself to be bound by the chain of marriage. But when his wife was soon taken away, he utterly refused to enter a second marriage; instead, he devoted his members thereafter to the virtue of continence, until old age and decrepitude.

He served the Lord day and night in fasting and prayer and constantly attended to other divine services. For almost ten years before his death, he had been accustomed to communicate every Sunday. Although the church was far from his own dwelling, he never ceased to go there frequently, spending much time and effort upon this task; for he was old and infirm and had to walk upon three feet. One Sunday, having arrived at church with great difficulty and received the most holy mysteries as usual, he suddenly began to lose his bodily strength, so that he could not return to his hut. Therefore he turned aside to the dwelling of a man living nearby. Lying in bed throughout that day, [Col. 1343C] he became gravely ill; and on the following night, called by the Lord, he rested in peace.

When morning came and people entered to visit him, they found him placed in prayer and dead in this manner. Having risen from his bed and being without a covering except only drawers, he stood upon his knees and the joints of his left hand on the bare ground; his right hand he held raised and applied to his breast as though striking it. His little body stood upright and motionless, while, with his head thrown back, his face looked toward heaven. Thus the lifeless corpse, upheld by divine power and resembling a living rather than a dead man, showed plainly after death what he had been accustomed to do before he died.

People hurried from every side to see so devout and heavenly a miracle—a thing surely no more wonderful in the dead body than in the man himself while living, or rather dying. For which is more wondrous: that a mortal man should meet approaching death while praying and standing, and in dying should not collapse from his posture; or that an inanimate body should not fall after death? Both indeed are wondrous; both belong to divine power and grace. For who besides you, Lord, could bring it about that your servant, strengthened by an unconquered constancy in prayer, should rise from his bed even at the very point of death; and, against the assault of death, as against the blow of a torrent or a thunderbolt, should stand with knees bent and body erect, and standing and praying should yield up his soul—and further, that the clod of an inanimate corpse, so called from falling, should not fall to the ground? Truly these are your works, these are your miracles, Lord Jesus, who love the poor and show favor to no person; but [Col. 1344A] “in every nation, whoever fears you and works righteousness is acceptable to you” (Acts 10). All who saw these things, having previously known his most honorable manner of life, gave immense thanks to the Lord; and, recognizing that he was truly a servant of God, they honorably buried his most holy body with great devotion and reverence.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. A Cistercian monk, habitually especially devoted to prayer and reading, sees first Saint John the Evangelist, then the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and finally Christ the Lord himself coming to meet him as he yields up his soul.

[Col. 1344B]

In a certain monastery of the Cistercian Order there lived a monk of honorable conduct. As he was fervent and devout in every observance of his religious life, he was especially intent upon prayer and reading; wherever possible, he was drawn to reading with wonderful sweetness. Seeking the fruit of devotion rather than devotion itself, he delighted in it as in every sort of riches.

When the hour of his calling approached, he was seriously ill and had already been anointed with the oil of the sick. He asked that his body should immediately be washed and dressed in the garments in which he was to be buried. The brothers, objecting that this was unusual, delayed doing it; but as he persisted in his request, he at last obtained what he wanted. When this had been done, he said to those standing around: “Let each of you return to his duties, for I shall not die now, but tomorrow, after the servants’ meal.”

On the next day, at the hour he had predicted, when he was drawing his last breath, brothers came together from all directions to strengthen him at his departure. Then he, illuminated by the divine Spirit, said with a joyful face: “Behold, blessed John the Evangelist is now entering.” After being silent a little while, he said again: “Behold, now the holy Mother of God, Mary, is coming.” And after a short interval he said once more: “Come, brothers: behold, now the Lord Jesus Christ is coming.” Having said this, he at once began to sing and intoned the antiphon, saying, *Subvenite* (“Come to his aid”). And thus, singing, he gave up his spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. A brother struggling with death sees a demon in the form of a monkey, mocking him and continually licking a piece of cloth which he had sewn onto his worn scapular without his superior’s permission.

Another monk, when he had reached his last hour and had already lost the power of speech, saw an unclean spirit in the likeness of a monkey sitting on a pole set beside the wall, where his scapular was hanging. On that old and torn scapular the brother had recently sewn, without permission, a small torn piece of cloth. The unclean spirit fondled it with pleasure, repeatedly kissed it, licked it with his tongue, and stroked it with his hand.

When the monk saw this, he groaned. Since he had already lost speech, he indicated by extending his forefinger and, stammering half-formed and broken words, signified as best he could that they should remove that most evil mocker. They marvelled and for a long time asked what he was saying or meaning. At last, through divine mercy, he recovered the use of his tongue and said: “Do you not see that foul demon sitting upon our scapular and licking with his filthy mouth that little patch which I recently presumed to sew onto it without permission? Drive out the villain, then, [Col. 1345B] and remove the patch from the garment, lest that slanderous and impious mocker insult me to the end.”

Although all looked intently, they could not see the wicked spirit visible to him. They removed the scapular from its place, and the malignant reproacher immediately departed. The brother then received penance, became speechless again, and shortly afterward died in a good confession.

## CHAPTER XXXV. A monk, having removed his cowl because of the heat of fever, put on a scapular; dying in this dress, the gate of Paradise was shut against his soul until he returned to his body, asked for the cowl, and received the penance imposed for having put it aside.

[Col. 1345C]

A certain brother was mortally ill. Burning with the great heat of fevers, he removed his cowl to relieve the heat, put on a scapular, and in that state breathed out his spirit. After death, when he was brought to the entrance of Paradise, the gatekeepers shut the gate and excluded him, saying: “Is this man to be received among the order or rest of monks without a cowl?” Thus repulsed, he remained outside, fearful and trembling, afraid of hearing and undergoing the sentence of damnation.

When his guides interceded for him, saying that, apart from this matter, he had proved a worthy man and had lived among the others without reproach, he was commanded to return to human life and, having received pardon, to come back at once wearing a cowl. Returning to his body, [Col. 1345D] he told all that he had seen; he put on the cowl and received penance, then departed in peace. It is clear, therefore, that the monastic habit—in which the form of the cross is also expressed—contains a great mystery, if the monk’s life is maintained.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Abbot Abraham of La Prée in Berry: while still young he was taught to appropriate nothing whatsoever, not even the least thing, without permission; he distinguished Jews by their stench; and, because of angelic purity of mind and body, he was honored by the Virgin Mary, Mother of God herself, with astonishing tokens of favor.

Abraham of most devout memory, once abbot of La Prée, was, as they say, a most holy man endowed with singular gentleness. By Christ’s gift, he preserved the flower of virginity until death and bore the Lord’s yoke from youth until the end of his life. While still young both in age and in religious life, he secretly put away in his bed a small scrap of new cloth, intended to mend a garment, without permission. But when shortly afterward he looked for it and, though he turned the bedding over everywhere, could not find it, he departed in wonder; and, rebuked by conscience, he hastened to erase this furtive little act of theft by private confession.

A little later, while he was alone washing bowls in the kitchen, behold, that scrap of cloth suddenly descended through the air and was cast into his hands as though someone had carried it. Recognizing it with certainty, and looking all about him, he saw no one either above or below. He clearly learned that it had been stolen by an unclean spirit but could not be retained after confession. Indeed, he also perceived how carefully and fearfully those who have professed a pure and perfect life of poverty must guard against such possessions, however small. For even a certain nun, as is read, suffered the devil’s accusation at death because of a slender thread of silk which she had placed on her bed without permission. [Col. 1346B]

This good and devout man, because of his exceptional purity of body and soul, was accustomed to receive many consolations from the Lord and his saints, especially from the most blessed Mother of God. At times the same most holy Queen appeared to him in a vision and foretold certain things that would happen to him; and after the sweetest words of that most devout visitation, she impressively deigned to place upon his chaste lips a chaste kiss from her own most pure mouth.

One night he seemed to himself to be contending in debate with faithless Jews concerning the Christian religion. When the dispute had continued for a long time, such a great stench, exhaled from these reprobate people, infected his nostrils that he awoke because of the sharpness of the most foul odor. After shaking off sleep, he continued for many days thereafter, while awake, to smell the same foul uncleanness which he had first smelled while asleep. Nor was this all: whenever he had occasion to speak with Jews or see them close at hand, to enter their houses or pass before them, [Col. 1346D] he was accustomed to smell the same most dreadful exhalation. We learned these things which we have related of the aforementioned man because he himself disclosed them to us privately.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. A monk of Fontenay sees certain wondrous things in his final illness, foretells his death, and is illuminated by a divine radiance.

At Fontenay, a noble monastery of the Cistercian Order, a monk of outstanding conduct was struggling in his final moments. One feast day, when all the sick who were able to rise had gone to the morning Mass, a person appeared to him suddenly, venerable in shining face and dress. Approaching the bed of another sick man, this person urged him with many words to follow, so that he might be led by him into a most serene place, full of every delight and joy. But the sick man’s face clouded over, and he made a slow and lukewarm reply. The holy visitor rejected him and passed on.

Coming to the monk mentioned above, [Col. 1347A] he made the same proposal. The monk rose gladly and, giving thanks from his whole heart, wished to follow him immediately. But the heavenly messenger instructed him to remain for the present and also told him the time and hour when he would shortly return for him. When the holy visitor disappeared, the sick man took care to make known to the brothers all that he had seen.

As evening approached, he called his attendants and said: “Prepare what is necessary for my burial, for I shall depart this night. Yet do not keep watch around me or be anxious, for I shall call you at the proper time when the hour comes.” In the deep night, while everyone was resting, he began to cry out: “Rise, and strike the board at once, for my time is now fulfilled.” At that hour all the lamps in the infirmary happened to have gone out. When the brothers rose, they suddenly saw around the dying man, though the moon did not shine, a brightness of such great light that it illuminated the whole house and they could even read a book by it. This light lasted until lamps had been lit, after considerable delay; thus many of the community who arrived first still found it present. [Col. 1347C] Seeing and hearing all that had happened, the brothers were greatly gladdened and comforted, gave thanks to the Lord, and celebrated the holy man’s funeral rites with immense devotion.

But the other sick man, who had not willingly agreed to the invitation of the heavenly messenger, remained for a long time afterward in that same illness and, until death, did not rise from the bed into which he had descended.

I have briefly recorded this consummation of the aforesaid brother from the trustworthy account of the venerable Hugh of Flavigny, formerly prior of the same Fontenay. Since mention has arisen of that same man, I have thought it good to insert here something [Col. 1347D] which the venerable William of Spiriac, nephew of Saint Bernard and monk of the aforesaid monastery, told us concerning him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Hugh, prior of Fontenay, a man of great religious devotion and learning, dies holy on the feast day of Saint Augustine itself, as he had desired; and his blessed soul, met by Saint Augustine together with other heavenly beings, is led into heaven.

This aforementioned Hugh was a wise and well-conducted man, fervent in religion, strong in the grace of virtues, and eminent in literary learning. He was an assiduous investigator of all divine writings, but especially a most ardent lover of the books of Saint Augustine. He honored that saint with extraordinary affection and, because of the special devotion he bore him, often confessed that he desired to die on Augustine’s feast day.

But divine mercy, which in compassion forestalls holy desires by inspiring them and follows them by assisting, made this servant attain his desire: on the very feast of blessed Augustine, just as he had wished, he departed from the world as happily as faithfully. That night a revelation of this kind was made to a religious monk of the monastery. He saw a procession of white-clad persons coming down from heaven, entering the church, and standing around the body that was being watched there according to custom. One of them, tall of stature, glorious and radiant in face and clothing, approached that monk and began to speak with him. [Col. 1348B] The monk asked who they were and for what purpose they had come. The saint replied:

“Those whom you see are angels of God and other saints. I myself am Augustine, bishop of Hippo. The reason for our coming is that we may lead the soul of this brother with us to the stars.”

When the revelation was completed, the beholder rejoiced and glorified God and that blessed bishop. He understood and knew that Augustine truly appears honorable and glorious in God’s sight: that great priest, illustrious teacher of the Church’s teachers, exalted in the word of glory, who, as he had not ceased in life to cherish his devoted servant, so in death did not delay to aid him and lead him with himself into glory.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The blessed death of a devout priest, a novice at the monastery of L’Aumône, is commended by several heavenly pronouncements.

A certain venerable priest, distinguished for the uprightness of his life, was chaste, sober, God-fearing, and always intent upon works of mercy. Yet, in order to attain greater purity, he presented himself to the house of L’Aumône and greatly desired, after receiving the habit, to be joined to the fellowship of the brothers. But the abbot of that monastery, knowing him to be a just and perfect man, delayed receiving him. The priest was very necessary to a nearby monastery of religious women, for whom he faithfully ministered and celebrated the divine mysteries. The abbot therefore kept him in that office through many entreaties, though unwilling.

When on one occasion he found himself burdened by bodily illness, he hurried to the aforesaid monastery of L’Aumône. Received for probation, within a few days he departed at the Lord’s call. As he labored at the end, the same revelation was shown that night to two religious brothers of that house, neither of whom knew anything at all of the other’s experience.

They saw a company of blessed spirits flashing with immense radiance and sweetly singing in melodious harmony descend from heaven and enter through the larger window in the front of the church. Coming into the monks’ choir, [Col. 1349A] they commended to the Lord in solemn office the soul of the dead man whose body seemed to lie there, and lifted the praises of divine glory to heaven with tuneful voices.

While the aforesaid monks were seeing this vision, the board was struck for the dying novice, now about to breathe his last. The brothers rose to strengthen the brother’s departure with their prayers. After the commendation had been made and the body laid in the church, one of the two who had received the aforesaid revelation, moved by great devotion, remained for the vigil with certain others appointed for it. The other returned to the dormitory, lay down again, and fell asleep.

And behold, a most venerable person appeared to him, sternly reproving the sleeper and saying: “How long will you sleep, sluggard? Behold, holy angels coming from heaven are keeping watch around the dead brother; and your companion, together with others, is attending the funeral, keeping vigil and chanting psalms. Yet you, wretch, snore in your bed and are weighed down by idle sleep.” Then he, terrified by the voice that reproached and rebuked him, awoke; springing from bed, he came quickly to the oratory and promptly joined those chanting psalms around the dead man.

The next day, when he reported both visions to the abbot, they both wondered who that companion could be, who had been said to be keeping watch with the others. Shortly afterward, when the other brother disclosed the vision he had seen, they learned that it was he who had been designated by the name of companion: because he had been admitted with the other to behold the glorification of that brother, so that the matter might stand by the mouth of two witnesses and such a report be made credible.

## CHAPTER XL. At the monastery of Fontmorigny, in the diocese of Bourges, the monk Robert is divinely forewarned of the blessed death he would undergo five days later.

At the house of Fontmorigny there lived a brother named Robert, who had been sent there from Clairvaux. He saw in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ, his most blessed Mother, and the blessed Abbot Bernard standing in a garden of delights, whose loveliness and glory were so immense that they could not be expressed in speech. He himself stood at a distance and pleaded from the depths of his heart for a look of divine mercy.

Then the most devout Mother said to her Son: “Lord Son, what will you do with this poor man of yours?” And the Lord said to her: “Whatever pleases you, Mother.” She replied: “Then I desire you to send him into your rest.” The Lord said to her: “Let it be done to him as you wish.” The most blessed Virgin answered: “And when shall this happen?” The Lord said to her: “Let him come on the fifth day and be saved.”

When the vision had passed, the brother told the others what he had seen and heard. As the illness he had previously endured grew worse, [Col. 1350A] on the fifth day, according to the Lord’s word, he departed from the body and entered the rest for which he had hoped.
