The brothers testified of him that he was a religious man and a son of peace, worthy, as they thought, to be brought into the joy of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XLI. Margaret of Saint-Omer, a girl of exceptional beauty, to avoid marriage, in an astonishing but not imitable act cut off the tip of her nose together with her upper lip.

A certain venerable girl named Margaret, very prudent and beautiful, born at Saint-Omer in Flanders, was being forced by her parents into marriage. With resolute spirit she refused, declaring that she could never marry anyone except Christ. But they, on the contrary, pressed in every way and, because she would not accept their prayers and persuasions, prepared to use force.

The day of betrothal had now arrived. With the suitors present, including the young man who wished to take upon himself the yoke of marriage with her, the girl was asked for her consent. As she wholly refused, her parents directed threats and harsh words at her. Meanwhile, while they were disturbed over this answer and occupied with futile counsels among themselves, the virgin, with zealous concern for her chastity and regarding her own beauty as an enemy of modesty, withdrew into a chamber. Taking up a polished and sharpened piece of steel which she had prepared, she forcibly cut away the tip of her nose together with her upper lip, cutting them off at the root.

When her parents entered, she offered them the lip and nose with which she had mutilated herself and seemed to address them in these words: “Behold my blooming beauty; behold that which pleased most in me. Take it now, if you wish, and carry it to my new husband.” When they saw this, they immediately cried out; filling everything with wild lamentation, they were pierced by overwhelming grief and nearly fainted. The supposed bridegroom and those who had come with him returned sadly and ashamed to their homes.

The father and mother, judging it a great disgrace to endure the sight and company of their disfigured daughter, removed her from their household and ordered her to live separately in another dwelling which they had dedicated as a hospital for the poor. But the girl, rejoicing in her self-contempt, longing for Christ’s sufferings and reproaches, not only bore living with beggars patiently, but eagerly offered herself as a humble attendant and servant to the sick and infirm. She was always diligent in attending the dying, preparing food, making beds, tending injuries and wounds, wiping ulcers, washing filth, and omitting no work of mercy.

After she had done these things for nearly three years, lest anything should be lacking to her in all patience and fullness of merits, the Lord’s providence struck her, according to her desire, with the sore of leprosy. When many noticed it but no one told her, fearing to distress her, [Col. 1351A] her mother drew her aside and disclosed the appearance of the pale corruption. Hearing this, she was immediately seized with such exultation that she nearly suffered a failure of heart. As though she had suddenly seen the heavenly gate opened to her, she burst into a cry of joy and exclaimed with tears: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because you remember me. And now, Lord, you have given me a sign for good, in which I receive the surest proof of your mercy.”

She then withdrew from the common society of people and entered the community of lepers. There she humbled herself before all so greatly that she alone seemed to be a leper; she served everyone so thoroughly that she alone seemed sound. All marvelled at her singular humility and patience; all venerated in her most exalted holiness and greatly rejoiced in her company, for they did not doubt that Christ dwelt in her.

After the completion, therefore, of the year of her separation, it pleased the Most High to associate His devoted handmaid with the heavenly company; and He also deigned, through the Holy Spirit, to signify to her the time of her release. One day, when her mother came to visit her, and she herself accompanied her as she was returning some distance from her dwelling, she finally bade her farewell and said: “Go in peace, mother, and pray for me, for you will no longer see my face alive in the flesh.” Yet when her mother heard this, she did not wholly believe it, because she saw her more cheerful than usual and displaying no sign of approaching death. But shortly afterwards, when a sudden illness brought her near to death, she received the viaticum of the Lord’s sacrament and yielded up her spirit in holy confession. As she herself had foretold, her mother, although living not far away, was unable to arrive at the hour of her death. In relating these matters, we do not so approve the indiscreet vehemence of the girl, by which she laid hands upon herself, as to set it before others for imitation; rather, we greatly admire and venerate the most ardent affection of divine love and the zeal for preserving chastity in a young virgin.

## Chapter XLII. On the nun who dug out her own eyes, radiantly beautiful in a wondrous manner, in order to safeguard her modesty. The wickedness and unhappy end of William, king of the English.

[Col. 1351D]

A certain king of the English, named William, a carnal and very lustful man, grievously oppressed the churches in the land subject to his rule. A revelation of this kind was made to a certain monk, a man of outstanding holiness. He saw the Lord Jesus Christ sitting upon a throne, and a multitude of saints complaining about the king because he was giving their churches over to destruction. The Lord answered: “He shall be granted a period of thirty days to amend his ways; and if he does not correct himself meanwhile, then at last let him undergo the penalties of due vengeance.” When the revelation had ended, that holy man hastened to report these things to the king. The king despised hearing them, and did not cease to add bloodshed to bloodshed.

[Col. 1352A] A few days later the same king entered a monastery of virgins, in which, as report proclaimed, there was a most beautiful girl. Though she possessed the blooming loveliness of her whole body, the grace of even greater beauty appeared in her eyes, which shone in her face like two carbuncles. When the girl was seen, the tyrant was captivated by her eyes; and, indulging in sacrilegious desire, he ordered the abbess to have her brought to his bed at night. Otherwise, he threatened that he would take her by force and likewise devastate the whole monastery. On hearing this, the spiritual mother groaned, and her heart was greatly troubled, seeing a most grave danger impending on either side: either she must incur the savage fury of the raging tyrant, to the ruin of her house, or—an abominable thing—prostitute the bride of the Lord to a seducing adulterer.

[Col. 1352B] When, pale and trembling, she disclosed to the aforesaid virgin the cause of her distress, the latter, inflamed by the divine Spirit, answered: “Be of good courage, lady mother, and do not be troubled; but confidently entrust this whole matter to God and to me. Only take care to inform the prince that I am prepared to come to his bed at the approach of evening.” Why say more? The noble virgin was brought into the decorated bedchamber and awaited the king’s arrival there alone. Then, strengthened by wondrous courage, she seized a digging-tool which she had already prepared, tore out her own eyes with it, and placed them upon a dish. She presented this new and unexpected dish to the arriving king and said: “Come now, my lord king: behold [Col. 1352C] the glittering jewels which, to the injury of Christ, you so passionately desired in His handmaid. Look carefully, and see whether you will ever be able to sate yourself upon so great a beauty.” Seeing the holy girl thus disfigured and bloodied by her gouged-out eye-sockets, the king recoiled in extreme horror; and at once sprang back from her and withdrew in great confusion.

It is read in the *Deeds of the English* concerning that profane king that, a short time before his death, many adversities occurred in his kingdom, and many things concerning his end were seen and foretold. Most terrible of all was this: the devil visibly appeared to people in remote woodland places and spoke to passers-by. Moreover, in the district of Bervescira, in the village of Hansteda, [Col. 1352D] for fifteen uninterrupted days a spring flowed so abundantly with blood that it stained the neighboring ford. He heard these things and made light talk of them, caring neither for his own dreams about himself nor for the visions of others. Edinerus, a distinguished historian, says that Saint Anselm, whom this same king had exiled, came to Marcigny in order to lay the grievances of his troubles before the conscience of blessed Hugh of Cluny. While there the conversation turned to King William, the aforesaid abbot said that, on the preceding night, that king had been led before God and judged; after judgment had been weighed, he had received the sad sentence of condemnation. How he knew this, he did not then explain, nor did any of those listening inquire.

## Chapter XLIII. At Fontaines, a monastery of the Order of Fontevraud, a nun appeared after death to her companion, testifying that she possessed great repose, but that she did not yet enjoy the sight of God until, on the definite day she named, that companion should be joined to her, so that both might together be received into glory.

[Col. 1353A]

In the monastery of holy virgins of the Order of Fontevraud, called Fontaines, two holy virgins, placed there almost from the cradle, were nurtured for Christ. When one of them departed from the body, she appeared a few days later to the survivor and said: “I make known to you, my beloved sister, that I now possess great repose; but I cannot be admitted to behold the face of the Lord without you. Prepare yourself, therefore, and come as swiftly as possible, so that we may be presented together to the Lord.” She also foretold to her [Col. 1353B] the time of her death, at which she herself finally ended her life.

## Chapter XLIV. On Mary, a girl of the monastery of Carmus, who was first most diligent in giving every kind of help to the sick, then became paralyzed, and was distinguished, both in illness and at death, by the light of prophecy and by other eminent gifts and privileges of holy souls.

In the district of Soissons there is known to be a convent called Carmus, of the aforesaid Order of Fontevraud, full of holy virgins. There was there a most holy girl named Mary, who entered the monastery at the age of nine and departed to the Lord at nineteen. For many years she was assigned to the care of the sick, and served them all with such devotion and diligence that every one marvelled at her constant attention and fervor. At last, by the Lord’s ordering, lest anything should be lacking to her merit, she was struck with paralysis and languished for a very long time. Bereft of every use of her limbs, she was unable not only to rise from her bed but even to lift foot or hand, or to move her throat in order to eat. Accordingly, prepared draughts of flour and clarified broths from certain cooked foods were made for her, more for swallowing than for eating.

[Col. 1353C] Yet, in proportion to the multitude of pains which she suffered in her body, she received many consolations in her heart, and much was divinely revealed to her. On one occasion she called her infirmarian and said: “Go, I beseech you, and tell that beloved sister of ours to pray more earnestly for her mother, because she has just died [Col. 1354A] and needs her intercessions.” When the sister learned this from the infirmarian’s report, her heart was moved at her mother’s death. Turning to prayer, she invited the other sisters also to intercede with her for the mother; and, after a messenger had been swiftly sent, she finally learned that her mother had departed from the world on the day and at the hour foretold.

It happened once, when all were resting in the depth of night, that one of the sisters heard a commotion of people conversing with one another in the room where the sick woman lay. Wondering, she rose and came to discover what it was. As she approached quietly, she saw that place gleaming with immense light; and, drawing aside a little the curtain that hung there, she beheld the sick woman sitting [Col. 1354B] in a chair, which she had never been accustomed to do. Her bed, moreover, had been newly remade with every care. Immediately terrified by what she had discovered, the sister returned and summoned the infirmarians to see what she had seen. When they arrived together, they found the sick woman laid back in bed and very carefully covered. The following day, when she had been strongly pressed by many entreaties and commands, she finally confessed that two sisters of the monastery who had died earlier—whose names she gave—had been sent from heaven to visit her; they had remade her entire bed by turning it over, and had relieved the afflicted woman with consoling words.

Thus, when the handmaid of Christ had been exhausted by so prolonged an illness, she was at length overcome by death and gathered to her people. On the very day when she departed from the world, a revelation of this kind was made to a spiritual and holy sister among them. She saw the most blessed Mother of God descend into that same house, and two nuns of that monastery, long since dead, arrive with her. Recognizing them, she asked who that most venerable Lady was and for what purpose she had come. They answered: “She is our Lady, the Queen of Heaven, who has now deigned to come to the great feast which is to be celebrated here today within the house—a feast greater than any that has occurred in this church for many days and years past.”

# Book Three

[Col. 1353]

## Chapter I. A monk of Grand-Selve, a man of great perfection, appearing after his death to the monk Pontius—who afterwards became both abbot and bishop—reveals to him several remarkable things concerning his state.

[Col. 1353D]

At the house of Grand-Selve, one of the daughters of Clairvaux, in the region of Toulouse, there are known from the beginning to have been many spiritual men of great merit. Among their number stands the venerable and holy Father Pontius, who was first abbot of that place and afterwards of Clairvaux, and is now bishop of Clermont. From his own report we learned almost everything that follows concerning that house.

There was there a monk, master of the novices, a man of exceptional holiness, who had a great desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. On Maundy Thursday, after receiving Holy Communion, [Col. 1355A] while he still held that Eucharist in his mouth, a great exultation of God arose in his throat; and, pressed by an overwhelming desire, he asked that his soul might die. Placing his finger against his throat, he poured out this prayer to the Lord: “Christ, almighty Savior, if this petition of mine does not displease You, I pray and beseech You that from this time forward no earthly food may pass through the passage of this throat.” When he had made this prayer, he suddenly began to lose his bodily strength, and on the third day, Holy Saturday, fell asleep in the Lord.

The aforesaid bishop, then a monk of the same monastery, who loved him dearly and devotedly rendered him attentive service in illness and death, asked him whether he was grievously oppressed by bodily pain. He replied that he was calm and tranquil and felt nothing distressing, except only in his throat where he had placed his finger; there, he said, he felt pain for a while. Then Pontius earnestly begged him to return to him after death, if permitted, and make him certain of what happened to him. A few days later, the dead man returned to the aforesaid monk, resplendent in great brightness and transparent throughout his body as though crystal or the purest glass. He said to him: “I make known to you, dearest friend, that through the Lord’s mercy I have been received into great blessedness. This body, in which you see me, has been granted to me until the day of regeneration, [Col. 1355B] when I shall recover my own body, far surpassing this one in incomparable glory and splendor. Meanwhile I rest most sweetly in this one, for it is wholly suited to me and so transparent that, from every limb and every part of it, as from eyes, I see most clearly; my entire body is in every direction to me as though it were one single eye.”

A dark spot appeared on this dead man’s foot, concerning which he said: “This stain which you see was incurred by me through my negligence—namely, because I was sometimes accustomed to go sluggishly to the daily labor.” The blessed man made known these and many other very wonderful things to the aforesaid bishop; then, leaving him at last, he left him greatly edified and comforted.

## Chapter II. A man restored from the dead said, among other things, that the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, visits the monastery of Grand-Selve three times daily.

[Col. 1355D]

Humbert of Poitiers, monk of Grand-Selve, a man of venerable humility and holiness, used to relate that, while he was in a place subject to the same monastery, a certain layman of honorable conduct, having fallen ill unto death, had himself carried to that place out of devotion to the faith. As his illness worsened, he died; and, restored to life not long afterward, he recounted many things that he had seen. This one thing, however, he said as chief among the rest: namely, that the blessed Mother of God visited the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1356A] three times a day—at the time of the vigils, of the Masses, and of Compline.

## Chapter III. A monk of Grand-Selve, falling asleep at vigils, is drawn out of the choir.

There was in the same convent a spiritual man, endowed with great grace, who, while once standing with the others in choir to sing the psalms, was overcome by heavy drowsiness. A venerable person whose face he did not recognize stood beside him; waking the sleeper, he seized him by the garment over the chest and drew him out of the choir. As he was being dragged, he opened his eyes, saw him, and said: “Who are you, lord, and why do you drag me so?” The other replied: “And why do you sleep so? Did you rise for vigils in order to sleep, or to keep watch?” Having said this, he released him and immediately vanished. Thereupon, in the fear of the Lord, the monk shook off from himself the sleep of torpor and negligence, and thereafter took care to be more watchful and ready for keeping vigil.

## Chapter IV. A lazy monk, drowsy at vigils, is terrified by demons.

There was also in that monastery another monk, named B., who, though robust in his youthful and vigorous body, conducted himself more slackly than the rest, showing himself lazy at manual work and sleepy at vigils. He was therefore burdensome to his fellow residents and everywhere marked for idleness, [Col. 1356C] especially in church, where he was found most negligent. One night, when the monastery’s precentor had awakened him, sleeping at vigils, with more than usual severity, he rose in irritation and went to the dormitory. As he approached the necessarium, behold: at its door was a throng of demons shouting against him with immense uproar and terror, repeatedly crying, “Seize him! Seize him!” On hearing this, he was utterly horrified. Hastily taking flight, he ran swiftly back to the church. When he reached his stall, trembling and breathless, he immediately fainted and fell to the ground; without movement or sensation, he lay for a long time as if dead. Carried to the infirmary, after he had recovered somewhat from that terror, he told the brothers, who questioned him, what had happened to him.

[Col. 1356D] Thus beneficially awakened by this goad of divine chastisement, the brother thereafter took care to be found more vigilant and ready in guarding himself. Moreover, a novice who was then in the oratory testified that he too had heard the same commotion and cries of demons. Roger, a venerable and religious man, superior of that monastery, who had been present and remained beside that brother in choir, related this to us.

## Chapter V. At Grand-Selve, many monks, carried off in a short time by a deadly disease, show that an excellent grace is stored up for them in heaven.

A great mortality once occurred in that monastery [Col. 1357A], so that within two months about forty-five brothers were taken away. Nearly all of them received death with such a longing for piety as though they had already foreseen from heaven that an excellent grace was stored up for them. Many of them indeed foresaw it and deserved to receive what they had foreseen. To establish trust in these words, we shall relate, by way of example, a few cases out of many.

## Chapter VI. A dying monk at Grand-Selve tastes beforehand the glory prepared for him, surpassing the merits of all humankind.

There was at that time a monk there of most approved conduct, who died in that epidemic. When he had reached his last hour, the board was struck after Compline, and the brothers assembled to fortify him at his departure. While the monks sang the Litany and psalms around him, he, strengthened by the Lord, sang the psalms with the others in such voice as he could. When the psalmody had ended, the aforesaid abbot Pontius ordered the community to depart, because he saw the sick man singing and thought that he would still draw breath for some time. When the brother saw this, he stretched out his hand and signaled to the abbot to make them remain there a little longer, because he knew that he was about to depart at once in a short while.

[Col. 1357C] Seeing this most fervent man, and seeing that, because of the rigor of regular discipline, he did not wish to break silence after Compline even at the point of death, the abbot could not contain himself for joy. Breaking silence himself and first saying “Bless,” he said: “I beseech you, sweetest brother, since I see that the Lord is with you, tell us, if anything has been revealed to you concerning that blessed hope which you await, so that we too may take heart in the Lord and rejoice together with you.” Then the sick man said: “To answer briefly what you ask, know that I have seen things which it is not permitted to speak. Yet I can say this one thing: even if I alone surpassed the merits of all human beings, I should nevertheless not yet be worthy of the future glory which has been prepared and shown to me, now that I am on the very point of departing.” Having said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.

## Chapter VII. The appearance of two dead men at Grand-Selve, for the salvation of the living.

[Col. 1357D]

At the same time another lay brother there was ill. Drawn by a desire to die, he had already remained three days without food. A certain monk there, venerable and of honorable conduct, was likewise struggling in his final extremity; he was, if I am not mistaken, cellarer of the same monastery. When he had already yielded up his spirit, the aforesaid Stephen said to his infirmarian: “Prepare food for me, my beloved brother, for I must eat. Our cellarer has just come here, rebuked me for excessive fasting, and ordered me to eat.” The infirmarian replied: “Brother, what are you saying? The cellarer has just died [Col. 1358A], and you say that he came to you and commanded you to eat.” The sick man replied: “Believe me, brother, he came to me; and he is no longer dead, but has escaped death and lives more happily. For just as he was leaving me, I saw him entering into the brightness of a great light, whose flashing rays I was unable to gaze upon with my eyes reflecting them.”

Food having been prepared, the brother ate; and, after a short time, he breathed out his spirit in holy confession. As he was dying, the aforesaid infirmarian begged him, once received into glory, to pray for him and obtain from the Lord a swift passage for him. He answered that his help would not fail him, provided this were permitted. A few days passed, and he appeared in a vision to the same infirmarian and said: “Behold, received in peace by the Lord, I now return to you to bring aid in accordance with my promise; yet not the aid which you rashly asked for, but that which I knew was rather expedient for you. Remember that, while you were still in the world, you committed a certain grave sin, for which you have not yet deserved absolution through confession. Confess it, therefore, and quickly do penance; for if it is not erased by confession before death, it will remain incapable of being remitted after death.”

[Col. 1358B] When the brother awoke, he recalled that grave offense which he had committed twelve years before but which had been wholly effaced from his memory by deadly forgetfulness. He therefore hastened to gain release through confession and satisfaction; and, giving thanks to God, he plainly recognized that the intercessions of saints are not sought in vain, and that the sacrament of confession must not be held in slight esteem, without which even sins of ignorance are imputed in this manner.

## Chapter VIII. B., infirmarian of the poor, a most devout man, sees Christ the Lord Himself shortly before death, and the place prepared for him in heaven.

There lived at that time in the same convent a most devout brother named B. At the beginning of his conversion, when he considered attentively the magnitude of his sins and the justice of the strict Judge, he was so moved by fear that he nearly fell into despair. When the aforesaid abbot learned this, he tried by many examples and counsels to persuade him that anyone who confessed and repented, however guilty, was never deprived of forgiveness. Since he could not yet satisfy him in this way, he added: “I make myself guarantor for your salvation, and let my soul be required in place of yours, provided that you remain obedient in this order.”

[Col. 1358D] Greatly strengthened by this promise, the brother utterly overcame the spirit of distrust by which he was assailed; and, rejoicing in the Lord with trembling, he thereafter became accustomed to sing of mercy and judgment. Though noble by birth, he considered no nobility except becoming poor for Christ and serving the poor. He was appointed infirmarian of the poor in the hospice. Attending to them most diligently, he served them not as strangers and beggars, but as his own lords and as members of the Son of God. If he saw anyone among them sick, ulcerated, or swarming with worms, he devoted every work of mercy to that person—washing, wiping, and refreshing him—and attended continuously, like a mother to her sick child.

[Col. 1359A] While God’s servant did not cease to do these and similar things, it happened that he departed to the Lord in the aforesaid epidemic. Seeing his companions taken away daily, he too greatly desired to be dissolved and likewise to be with Christ. When a slight fever arose and he began to be mildly ill, he lay down in bed. The aforesaid abbot entered to visit him and wondered that a man so fervent should be confined to bed for so slight a cause. Smiling, he said: “Do not be afraid, Brother B.; you will not die now, but will still eat with us of our beans and vegetables.” But he replied: “I am not afraid, Father, I am not afraid; rather, I trust in the Lord that I shall no longer be disappointed of my desire.”

Why say more? As the fever increased, he was anointed with holy oil. Immediately after the anointing he was in the spirit, and lay rapt in contemplation for a long period without sensation or movement, so that he seemed almost dead. Meanwhile the heavens were opened to him, and with unveiled face he deserved to see the glory of God, so that he could say: “I have seen [Col. 1359B] the Lord face to face.” When he had returned to himself, the abbot asked how he was. “I am well,” he replied; “may it be well with you too. And now, dearest Father, I release you from the obligation of your pledge.” The abbot, having forgotten that former obligation, did not know what he meant. Then the brother reminded him more explicitly: “Have you forgotten how you once made yourself responsible for my salvation? I therefore make you free from that surety, because I am secure of my salvation through Christ’s mercy.”

The abbot then began anxiously to investigate how he could have learned this. Though he refused by every means to tell it, he was finally constrained by many commands and entreaties, and at last said: “Because the virtue of obedience prevents me from concealing the truth, I shall tell you a matter to which perhaps you will give doubtful belief. But, that I may make this testimony credible, know that with the end of my speech I shall also receive the end of my life. Let your love know, therefore, that I, though wretched and unworthy, was presented to our Lord and Savior and saw Him face to face—not, however, in His divinity, but only in that most blessed form of humility which He deigned to assume for us.

[Col. 1359D] “From His most holy mouth I also heard that all who persevere in obedience in this order until death shall obtain eternal salvation from Him. I likewise saw our brothers who have departed from this life resting in great blessedness; and, through the Lord’s mercy, I foresaw my own place, which I am to receive with them.” When he had said these things, he fell silent and immediately rendered up his blessed soul.

## Chapter IX. Geoffrey, bishop of Sorres, when still a monk at Clairvaux, saw a solemn procession of the heavenly orders proceeding toward the infirmary; they are believed to have guarded the departure of the soul of the venerable old priest Tecelinus.

The venerable Geoffrey, of holy memory, formerly bishop of the Church of Sorres in Sardinia and a monk of Clairvaux before he was raised to the episcopate, once, while in the choir of that convent, deserved to see with blessed eyes the following vision, as we secretly received it from him. There was a splendid and glorious procession of saints, coming from the north side of the basilica as though from the cemetery; it passed before the sanctuary and proceeded directly to the infirmary.

[Col. 1360B] In that procession appeared acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests, arranged seven by seven in their respective orders, each group proceeding before the next in fitting sequence. The acolytes were clothed in white stoles and carried individual candles in their hands, though these seemed more like fire than wax candles. The subdeacons were adorned in precious tunics, the deacons in shining dalmatics, and the priests themselves in distinguished silk chasubles; each also carried in his hands the vessels appropriate to his ministry. Behind them came a great company of white-clad persons, likewise arranged in order and with reverence.

[Col. 1360C] Last of all followed the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, accompanied at her right and left by the blessed Apostles Peter and John. She herself shone and flashed with such beauty of countenance and attire that the whole basilica gleamed from her brightness. Meanwhile the spirit revealing these things spoke in the heart of the beholder and said: “This is the Queen of Heaven; this is the Lady of the angels.” Passing before the altar with such solemnity, as I have said, they at last went out of the oratory through the door leading toward the infirmary and vanished from the observer’s eyes.

Now, in that same infirmary there had long lain ill a venerable old man and priest of honorable life, named Tecelinus. At that time he had been brought to his last extremity and died shortly afterwards. Therefore the man of God who had seen these things firmly believed that such a procession had appeared as a sign of Tecelinus’s passage and blessedness.

## Chapter X. Several remarkable things divinely seen by, or concerning, Geoffrey, bishop of Sorres. The Body of the Lord found by him incorrupt.

On another occasion, while the same servant of God stood in church with others to sing the psalms, he clearly saw a demon in the likeness of a monkey passing through the middle of the choir. When the ridiculous beast came up to him, it looked at him with an angry eye and contemptuously mocked the man for some time with wide-open nostrils. After it had passed him, it went out of the choir and appeared no more.

[Col. 1361A] It happened once that the same servant of God suffered severely in the region of the throat. The illness had become chronic and was almost despaired of by physicians. He was greatly distressed in spirit, chiefly because, his windpipe having been constricted by illness, he had lost the strength to sing psalms in church. Therefore he turned to blessed Bernard and day and night, with many tears, prayed that through Bernard’s intervention he might deserve to regain the gift of singing. On one occasion blessed Bernard appeared to him in a vision and, touching and blessing the painful spot with his hand, impressed upon it the sign of the holy cross. When the man of God awoke, he found himself healed, recovered wonderfully his strength for singing, and thereafter suffered no hindrance from that illness.

[Col. 1361B] At another time, one of his close companions fell gravely ill and was thought to be dying. Greatly distressed, the aforesaid man earnestly besought the Lord in tearful prayers for the recovery of his beloved friend. Someone appeared to him in a vision and said: “Behold, the brother for whom you are so afflicted will be restored to health; but another, whom you love equally in spiritual affection, will depart in his place.” The first man recovered; but at that same time there died a venerable and holy old man called Renald of Cluny, whom Geoffrey also loved with wonderful affection in Christ.

Moreover, when he was excessively anxious concerning his dead mother and his eyes poured forth streams of tears for her over a long time—for much grace of tears had indeed been bestowed on him—he urgently begged the Lord to reveal to him whether she was placed in punishments or in rest. A voice then came to him from God: “Why do you seek by importunate prayers to wrest [Col. 1361C] from Me what is by no means due to your knowledge? Only pray for your own, and they shall be saved.”

Once while he was at prayer, a venerable man appeared to him in a vision and placed a gold ring on his finger, clearly a presage of the dignity that was soon to come. For in that same year, as he himself informed us, he was raised to the episcopate of the Church of Sorres. Governing it vigorously for the course of seven years and preserving his own life in all purity, he left to posterity a worthy example of holiness.

As the end of his calling approached, known to God alone, he left Sardinia and came to visit Clairvaux, whose son he was and in which he greatly desired to be buried. When he saw it from a distance, he raised his eyes and sighed toward heaven, praying with all his heart that, if he were to die within the span of time during which he had always visited that same house at least once, he might never again be permitted to be separated from it, lest perhaps he should die elsewhere and be deprived of the burial he desired.

[Col. 1362A] Having entered the aforesaid monastery and remained there well for some time, he was eventually seized by an acute illness. He was ill for several days and, as the sickness worsened, came to his last extremity. After he had been anointed with holy oil and fortified with the heavenly viaticum, at that very hour—indeed, almost at that very moment—to the amazement of all, he fell asleep in the Lord. He died around midnight, on the feast of the dedication of the church of Clairvaux.

When the venerable abbot of that monastery, who knew very well the purity of Geoffrey’s conscience, was closing the eyes of the now lifeless body, he exclaimed with great devoutness of faith: “O sweet and venerable Father, may almighty God grant that I come into your company.” As he performed the office of commendation for the funeral, he was moved by such an affection of piety that he could not restrain his flowing tears, so that he moved even the hard-hearted to weeping. This most devout Father died in the year of grace 1178 and was buried in the church of Clairvaux beside the venerable Godfrey, formerly bishop of Langres.

When this man began to fall ill, it was revealed concerning him to one of the brethren of that monastery that he would shortly depart. Then, a few days later, when that same brother was attending the brethren’s nocturnal vigils, he saw in an ecstasy of mind a bed carefully prepared with soft supports and fittingly adorned with snow-white coverings, which was being kept for that bishop—plainly signifying the rest of eternal blessedness to which he was soon to be received.

On the very night on which he died, when his body had been laid in the church and the signal for vigils was sounded, [Col. 1362C] the aforesaid brother awoke and immediately began to call the said bishop to mind. At once a voice came into his ears, speaking to him of the dead man of God and saying: “Behold, now, from the beginning of this bell-signal, all the saints of God receive him into their fellowship.” He therefore rose, came into the choir, and stood with the others to chant the psalms. When Matins Lauds were being celebrated, he looked and saw, on the walls of the church around the dead man’s body, abundant lights kindled by God for about the space of an hour, so numerous that they could not be counted. When that brother beheld this, he was deeply moved to compunction; and, giving thanks to God for all that he had seen and heard, [Col. 1362D] he said within himself: “Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who trusts in you. Truly blessed is this saint whom you have chosen and received. He shall dwell in your courts. For I believe and trust that, through your grace, he is now worthy to attain among your saints and elect the blessedness of rest and the brightness of light.”

After two months had elapsed, while the same brother was in choir, awake and chanting at vigils, he again suddenly entered into an ecstasy of mind. And behold, the aforementioned bishop appeared to him, putting on priestly vestments and as though preparing to celebrate Mass; and that brother, assisting him, turned the chasuble back over his arms. At that hour this verse was being sung in church: “And I shall go in unto the altar of God, to God who makes my youth glad” (Ps. 42 [Vulgate]).

[Col. 1363A] That same holy man related that, when he had ordered a certain old and ruinous church to be repaired and an altar was demolished in his presence, he found within it an old, rough little casket containing relics of saints. Among those relics the body of the Lord had been deposited. It was found so sound and whole, so clean and white, and entirely untouched by any corruption, as though it had been placed there only very recently. Indeed, in that region nobody could be found who remembered having seen the construction or consecration of that church or altar. At the sight of so great a miracle, all who were present glorified God, recognizing it to be the most sacred body of the Lord, concerning which it is truly written: “You will not permit your Holy One to see [Col. 1363B] corruption” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate]).

355  
## CHAPTER XI. How Hungerus, his father, and his brother Rodulph were wonderfully converted to the Premonstratensian Order.

In the territory of Meaux, in a village called Acejum, there lived a cleric named Hungerus. While he was still a little child, his mother was nursing him in her lap. Seeing the infant clean and bright, flourishing with a blooming face, she joyfully said to her husband: “Look, my lord, what a beautiful child God has graciously bestowed upon us.”

But he, being a faithful man devoted to God, replied: “The child is indeed beautiful, and he will be a fine cleric, if it please God Jesus Christ.”

Hearing this, she raged against such words and spoke like one [Col. 1363C] of the foolish women, saying: “Alas! What have you said, madman? Will you take my only son from me and make him a cleric? Far, far be it that the staff of our old age, the hope of our posterity, should be destined for the office of a cleric!”

She had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, the child was suddenly struck by epilepsy, falling and foaming in his mother’s arms; he was twisted by such a violent seizure that his mouth was almost drawn round to his ear. At this sight the woman, shaken by overwhelming terror, turned pale and cried out with groaning: “Alas, alas, Lord God, how wickedly I have spoken and how perversely I have acted! I, I am that sorrowful and wretched woman who has deserved your indignation; for what sin has this innocent little child committed? [Col. 1363D] Turn, I beg you, your hand upon the head of his ungrateful and faithless parent, provided only that my son may live and may safely be bound forever to your service.”

She immediately set out, carrying the half-dead child to the monastery of nuns called Fontanis, two leagues away. Having placed the still-breathing infant upon the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, she prayed with loud cries and tears, saying: “Most merciful Mother of God, I entrust to you and restore to you my only son, that he may live for you and serve you as long as he lives in clerical ministry.” When the prayer was ended, the child was healed through the intercession of the most blessed Virgin and recovered perfectly from that epilepsy, which, just as he had not suffered from it before, he never suffered from afterward.

In the course of time, [Col. 1364A] when he had been educated in letters and admitted to holy orders, he gave himself, by God’s gift, to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Vallis Severa, not far from the city of Soissons, in the Premonstratensian Order. There he lived most devoutly for many years and persevered until his death. His father, who had begun through a pious vow, followed his son to the same place; there he too lived obediently and piously, and at last departed to the Lord in a good confession.

Moreover, a brother of this same cleric, named Radulph, once fell ill almost to the point of death. In the agony of illness, he saw himself descending with great terror through a certain dark and deep valley, as though entering the lower parts of the earth. Meanwhile, [Col. 1364B] he encountered the community of the aforesaid monastery together with his brother. Other brethren said to him: “Brother of Hungerus, why do you not rescue your brother? Do you not see how he is perishing, descending 357 into hell?”

Afterward, when the man had returned to himself, he was greatly stricken by these words. Though he had previously given no thought at all to conversion, he immediately summoned his brother and, through his hand, gave himself to the aforesaid monastery. There he is still alive, leading a most devout and honorable religious life.

## CHAPTER XII. A child drowned in water is placed upon the altar of the blessed apostle Peter and returns to life; afterward he becomes a cleric and finally a Cistercian monk.

At the same time and in the same village, another cleric, [Col. 1364C] likewise related by blood to the man just mentioned, was, while still a little child, wandering alone through his guardians’ neglect. By chance he slipped a short distance from a bridge into a stream. The brook was narrow and muddy. As the current carried the child farther away, his head was submerged in mud at the bottom of the water, while his feet floated above the surface as though swimming. He thus remained hidden in the water for a long time before he could be found, enough time in the meantime for one to travel half a league.

His mother, meanwhile, was indoors occupied with some work; as though her mind already foreknew the impending grief, she began to feel distressed and sorrowful within herself. Recalling her child, she immediately left the room. When she did not find him [Col. 1364D] in the house, she cried out: “God and holy Mary, where is my son?” Hurrying to the bridge where the child had fallen, she looked around everywhere but could not see him. Then, going farther on, she began to run through lanes and streets, seeking and asking about her son.

At last she returned to the bridge and, walking along the bank of the little stream, saw the soles of the infant’s feet floating above the water, while his head was stuck fast in the mud. When she perceived this, she immediately leapt into the stream at a run, drew out the lifeless little child, swollen and distended like a wineskin. Raising his feet and pressing his head downward, she caused the great quantity of water that had entered his belly to flow back out in a copious [Col. 1365A] discharge.

When a crowd gathered, many people took the child from the mother’s hands. They wished to bring him into the house and bury him; but she utterly resisted, saying: “My son shall not be taken into the house until he has been presented to the Lord in the church. For I trust in his ineffable mercy that today I shall receive my son alive and well.”

They went on; but after proceeding a little way, they began to turn back, saying: “Why are we exhausting ourselves in vain when we see that the child is dead? Is he to be recalled from the dead?” Nevertheless, the mother persisted, insisting by every means that he be carried to the Lord’s church. When she had compelled them, as they turned back, no fewer than four times, they finally reached the church and [Col. 1365B] placed the infant upon the altar of the most blessed apostle Peter. After he had lain there for some time and prayer had been made to the Lord for him, he suddenly yawned and, opening his eyes, called for his mother. Immediately taken down from the altar, he suckled the breast offered to him; then, walking here and there through that same basilica, he appeared to all, alive again and well, while they marvelled.

359  
At the sight of such a miracle all rejoiced, glorifying God and his blessed apostle Peter, through whose intervention they believed that the dead child had returned to life. Therefore, lest they remain ungrateful for so great a grace, his parents offered the boy to the Lord and designated him for clerical office. Moreover, the father himself undertook a journey to Rome with great devotion and took care to give thanks before [Col. 1365C] the body of the blessed Prince of the Apostles.

In the course of time, the child was educated in letters and admitted to holy orders. Later he voluntarily received the religious habit; adding vow to vow, he lives to this day, serving the Lord with fear in the Cistercian Order.

## CHAPTER XIII. A deserter and apostate cleric, brought near death by a fatal sickness, could not be shorn by any means when he begged to have his clerical tonsure restored.

In Great Britain, in the diocese of Lincoln, not far from the monastery called Park, there was a cleric who, though already a deacon, cast aside his holy orders and also abandoned his tonsure. Later, when he had been brought to the point of death by a mortal illness, he finally confessed that he had been a cleric and had exercised the office of deacon. Moved by repentance, he asked that the mark of the crown be restored to him.

Accordingly, when razors, scissors, and other instruments of that sort had been brought to shave him, no skill and no force [Col. 1365D] could cut his hair or restore the circle of his tonsure. Thus the transgressing cleric died without the clerical sign, becoming a dreadful sign and example to clerical deserters and apostates.

## CHAPTER XIV. A sick monk of Clairvaux, superstitious about dietary observances and the provision of medicines, both recovers his strength and lays aside excessive self-concern through the marvelous providence of the most merciful Mother of God.

[Col. 1366A]

They relate that recently there was at the monastery of Clairvaux a monk who, though a man of good will, was physically delicate and ill, and was excessively solicitous and superstitious in observing dietary restrictions and obtaining medicines. The blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary appeared to him in a vision, standing at the door of the oratory. Carrying a box of precious electuary, she gave each brother entering the church a spoonful from it and refreshed those who tasted it with marvelous sweetness.

When the aforementioned brother approached, so that he too might receive a portion of heavenly nourishment from the hand of that most merciful provider, [Col. 1366B] she repelled him, saying: “You are a wise physician and diligently care for yourself; you have no need of our medicine. Go then, go, and treat yourself as you wish, for those who cast their care upon the Lord are our concern.”

When he heard this, he was ashamed. Asking forgiveness, he promised that he would no longer meddle with concern for himself, but would entrust the whole care of his life to God and to her. Then she mercifully assented, granted pardon to the penitent man, and bestowed upon the one she was healing the food of a health-giving portion. Having tasted that blessed sweetness, the brother immediately recovered from his delicacy and infirmity; thereafter content with the community’s ordinary food and assistance, he put on beauty and strength together with bodily health [Col. 1366C].

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Alquerius, monk of Clairvaux: though one who despised himself, he was most diligent, out of love for Christ, in caring for the sick, especially the poor; and he deserved to receive blessing and healing from Christ’s wounds.

In the same church there was a venerable monk named Alquerius, a religious and spiritual man: moderate in food, humble in clothing, and a very severe disciplinarian of his own body. He was so restrained and temperate in matters which seemed to concern bodily use that, having banished every pleasure and vanity, he used even necessities most sparingly [Col. 1366D].

Skilled in medicine through strong experience, he devoted the service of his art, insofar as he could, to all who needed it; only himself did he exclude from such care. Though sickly and weak in body, he never consented to apply bodily medicine to himself. Although great men and even leaders among the nobility continually sought his services and frequently pulled him unwillingly this way and that, he nevertheless gave the fullest care to the service of the needy and poor, being more attentive to them. He treated not only their illnesses and sores, but also, insofar as he was able, most diligently supplied their needs in clothing and food.

Moreover, he handled with his own hands the rotting flesh and pus-dripping [Col. 1367A] limbs of the sick so worthily and so carefully that he seemed to be tending Christ’s wounds. And indeed it was so: he did everything for Christ, and Christ counted it all as done to himself, who said: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25). Hence Christ himself often visited his servant with secret consolations and wonderfully encouraged him in this work of ministry.

On one occasion he saw the following vision at Clairvaux. First he heard, as it were, a heavenly messenger crying out in a herald’s voice: “Behold, Christ is coming; rise and meet the Savior.” While everyone hastened eagerly to see him, he too ran and stood at the cloister doorway by which he knew Christ would come. When [Col. 1367B] the Lord entered, he approached and worshipped him, beseeching him to receive blessing and mercy from God his Savior.

Having received this, he began to gaze more attentively upon him and, with a wondrous affection of compassion, suffered with him. For Christ appeared to him as grieving and infirm, nailed fast with nails and pierced by a lance, as if he had been taken down from the cross that very hour, so that blood flowed abundantly from his wounds. The Lord himself held clean cloths, like corporals, and pressed them to those wounds; after wiping away the blood, he cast them onto the ground. The brother gathered them with the greatest reverence and kissed them with excessive devotion, preserving them folded in his bosom as though they were the redemption of his soul.

Frequently refreshed by the Lord through these and similar revelations, [Col. 1367C] he did not cease until the end to do good to all, but especially to pilgrims and poor sick people.

At last, when he had completed the course of life, he came to his final day. When the venerable Abbot Pontius came to visit him, he asked how he was and what condition he was in. He replied: “Well, dearest Father; all is entirely well with me, because I go—I go to my Lord.”

“And what then?” asked the abbot. “Do you not endure bodily suffering with distress, and do you not fear the straits of death?”

“I,” he replied, “regard all things as peaceful, all things as joyful, because the Lord has anticipated me with the blessing of sweetness, which has taken every sorrow from my heart and almost every pain from my body [Col. 1367D].”

The abbot answered him: “Come then, my beloved brother: I beg you, for God’s sake, tell me whether anything has been divinely revealed to you.”

He then said: “Just before you entered here, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to me, wretched and unworthy though I am. Showing a gracious and serene countenance and the marks of his most blessed Passion, he said: ‘Behold, your sins have been wiped away from before my face. Come therefore in safety; come, see, and kiss my wounds, which you loved so greatly and tended so often.’ Strengthened by such a promise, I now do not fear death, because this hope of mine has been laid up in my bosom. And know that on the coming night—I mean the vigil of blessed Martin—I shall depart, while the day office is celebrated in church, and at such an hour.”

He died [Col. 1368A] that same night, at the time he had foretold; and now, as we truly trust, he rests from all his labors, having found the Lord whom he had sought with his own hands.

## CHAPTER XVI. Christ shows a certain brother, troubled and contrite over his sins, how highly he esteems the tears and mourning of penitents.

A brother of the monastery of Clairvaux, groaning and anxiously afflicting himself without cease because of the sins by which he had grievously offended God, went about the whole day sad and sorrowful, setting no end to his lamentation and weeping. After he had remained for some time in such bitterness of heart, he saw one night in a vision the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1368B] clothed in priestly vestments and celebrating Mass. Whenever, according to the rite of sacrifice, he turned toward the people, he lifted in his hands the chalice from the altar and offered it to the sight of all present.

There was nothing in that chalice except the tears with which blessed Magdalene had bathed his feet in Simon’s house. As the aforementioned brother, stationed beside the Lord’s feet, recognized these things, he asked him: “I beg you, Lord, why do you show us this chalice with the tears in it?”

“So that all may see,” he replied, “and know how pleasing to me are contrition of heart and the mourning of repentance; for, as an example to penitents, I have kept so long the tears of this sinful woman [Col. 1368C] weeping and repenting at my feet.”

## CHAPTER XVII. By another marvelous vision, Christ the Lord instilled in the same brother hope of pardon and his mercy.

At the same time, while that brother still daily tormented himself with sorrow for his evils, he saw in a dream of the night that he was struggling and in peril in a most deep lake. When all hope of escape was already gone, suddenly the Savior came, walking barefoot upon the waters. Having reached him, he lifted the wretched man in his arm and, with mercy and dignity, held him in his bosom; then, drawing him out of the waters, he placed him in a green and pleasant meadow. When the brother saw this, he immediately fell at Christ’s feet and, in the immensity [Col. 1368D] of his joy, began to exult in spirit, clinging to and kissing the Savior’s holy footprints with insatiable desire.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A vision on the same subject, shown to the same brother.

One day, burning with desire to know whether he might deserve to obtain pardon from the Lord, he began urgently to persist, beseeching the divine mercy with unutterable groans and sighs and longing for this to be intimated to him in some manner. The following night, while he was in this disposition and attending the brethren’s vigils, he suddenly entered an ecstasy of mind. And behold, someone—he knew not who—stood 366 before him, gently and pleasantly passing a sharp razor, as though without sensation, over his head. In a moment, [Col. 1369A] in the twinkling of an eye, he seemed to shave his beard, neck, and tonsure.

Yet, by leaving a few hairs at one point, he perhaps indicated the fault of drowsiness by which that brother, although unwillingly, was still heavily burdened. Raised up by these and similar consolations, that brother, through the Lord’s inspiration, learned to breathe again in the hope of pardon.

## CHAPTER XIX. At Domno-Martino, a village in the territory of Toul, the Eucharist, together with its sacred pyx and corporal, escaped the flames when everything around it was consumed by fire.

In the territory of Toul, in the village called Domno-Martino, on a certain vigil of Easter, because oil happened to be lacking in the church for preparing the lamps, they placed [Col. 1369B] a lighted candle before the altar, to burn there throughout the night. It had been set somewhat carelessly upon the floor over a certain apse; by chance it fell thence and rolled as far as the step of the altar. The flame, licking around it, immediately seized the hanging cloth and burned it; as the fire raged, all the altar coverings with which it had then been richly and solemnly adorned were likewise consumed.

In the morning the priest and ministers entered the church and saw what the fire had done around the altar: everything had been reduced entirely to ashes and cinders. Yet the body of the Lord, together with the wooden pyx in which it had been placed upon the altar and upon the very linens, was wholly untouched by the fire raging on every side, so that even the silk cloth covering the little vessel appeared [Col. 1369C] completely unharmed.

When the priest used a broom to gather the ashes from the altar for depositing in a clean place, he found among them—wonderful to tell—the most sacred corporal. Since it had been laid and wrapped among the altar linens, he had thought it altogether consumed with them. But when he immediately unfolded it, it appeared entirely sound and white, as though it had been carefully laid in a chest. At this sight all the people rejoiced greatly, marvelling at and magnifying the omnipotence of the Redeemer.

A certain devout monk of Clairvaux related this to us. While still in the world, he had himself lit that candle before the altar and, as the nephew of that priest, saw all that occurred [Col. 1369D].

## CHAPTER XX. The sacrament of the Eucharist, stored in a chest, is changed into flesh and disclosed by a sign of divine light.

We learned from Louis, the most Christian king of the Franks, that two years ago such a miracle concerning the body of the Lord occurred in the district of Arras. On holy Easter Day a certain woman instructed her son, who was going to church, that after he had received communion he should endeavor to bring home with him the body of the Lord for her two little children remaining there. Wishing to carry out his mother’s orders, the boy took two sacred offerings from the sacristy without the priest’s knowledge and brought them to her.

Receiving them, she distributed one to the children to receive communion; the other, carefully tied up in her gown, [Col. 1370A] she stored in a chest. A few days later one of her little boys saw immense lights, divinely kindled around that chest, illuminating the entire house with great brightness. Seeing this, the child hastily summoned his mother, pointing out in word and gesture the abundant lights shining before his eyes. When the mother looked intently but was wholly unable to see anything, she tried to unlock the chest with its key, but no force or art whatever could accomplish it.

Greatly amazed and astounded, she hurried to bring the priest himself to behold the miracle. When he quickly arrived and could not see the brightness which the child saw, he immediately took the key from the woman’s hand and, without any difficulty, rapidly opened the chest. Opening it, he found the gown in which the Eucharist had been tied stained with blood, and the same most holy host changed into the appearance of flesh, while the outward form of bread remained. At this sight the priest and those with him marvelled greatly; worshipping the divine body, they bore it to the church with honor and reverence and worthily placed it in the sanctuary [Col. 1370B].

369  
## CHAPTER XXI. In the district of Chartres, the greater part of a most sacred host is changed into flesh.

From the same source mentioned above, we learned that this year such a sign [Col. 1370C] concerning the same sacrament occurred in the district of Chartres. A certain priest, while offering the sacrament, found before the fraction that the body of the Lord had been changed for the greater part into the appearance of pure and most beautiful flesh; yet the circular form and letters of the same host still plainly appeared upon it. The part of the host, however, which the priest had held between his fingers retained only the appearance of bread.

When the priest and all the people present saw this most marvelous thing, they were astonished; rejoicing in the Lord with trembling, they placed the Eucharist in the sacristy, where it is still honorably kept in a crystal vessel. Recently, when certain chaplains and clerics of the aforesaid king of the Franks—faithful and honorable men—affirmed to us the truth of this matter as certain, one among them was present who, before God as witness, declared that he had seen with his own eyes the Eucharist itself changed in the manner we have described [Col. 1370D].

## CHAPTER XXII. On a Friday, while a priest was offering sacrifice, the Eucharistic host was changed into flesh and the chalice into blood.

We also heard of a similar miracle concerning the same sacrament, though we do not know when or where it occurred. A priest of honorable conduct, while offering sacrifice on a certain Friday, found before receiving communion that the consecrated host had been changed into the likeness of flesh, and that the sacrament in the chalice had been changed into the appearance of blood [Col. 1371A]. Seeing this, he was not in the least dismayed, but received all of it with faithful mouth.

When Mass had been completed, he disclosed to his bishop what had happened. The bishop rebuked him for not reserving such a great gift of God for him to see. On the following Friday, when the priest again celebrated Mass, the same miracle happened to him, and he reserved it for the bishop’s inspection. When the bishop saw it and displayed it for all to see, he gave immense thanks to almighty God and commanded that the sacrament be kept in the church with fitting veneration, as an incomparable treasure.

## CHAPTER XXIII. While a sacrilegious priest was celebrating Mass, after the consecration and shortly before he wished to receive communion, the sacred bread vanished from the paten and the blood from the chalice in an instant.

[Col. 1371B]

Peter, abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims, an honorable and most devout man, related in the chapter-house at Clairvaux a matter known with absolute certainty, which, he affirmed, had happened in that same year. Yet he did not wish to name the person to whom it had happened, because he did not wish to defame him. He said:

“A certain secular priest was summoned before the lord pope and accused in his presence of a criminal offense. When questioned by him—even under threat of anathema—he chose rather to be excommunicated than to confess the truth about the crime he had committed. Since he could not be convicted by lawful testimony, he was finally dismissed as an accused man apparently innocent, reserved for the judgment of him [Col. 1371C] who is not deceived.

“After returning home, though his conscience bitterly reproached him, he laid aside his secular habit, but not his secular disposition; entering a monastery of clerics, he professed a regular life there. After he had spent much time in it, he would not in any way confess the just sentence of excommunication by which he had been bound by the supreme pontiff; yet, with punishable presumption, he continually dared to exercise the office of priest.

“One day, while he was offering sacrifice and the *Agnus Dei* had already been said, he placed the body of the Lord upon the paten, according to the custom of that order. Having bowed his head slightly before it, he at once raised himself to receive communion in the usual manner. But—wonderful to tell—at that very hour, by angelic ministry, as we may rightly believe, the heavenly bread was invisibly taken from the paten, and the blood from the chalice [Col. 1371D]. When that priest saw this, he was immediately troubled, contrite, and astounded, clearly understanding and knowing by what just and terrible judgment of God it had happened. He quickly went to his spiritual father and, finally contrite and repentant, confessed his wickedness—which, while he still kept silent, heaven itself had already revealed.”

372  
## CHAPTER XXIV. At Belesmo, a village in the territory of Châlons, the Eucharist secretly sent to a dying woman is made public by an evil spirit.

In the territory of Châlons, in the village called [Col. 1372A] Belesmo, there was seven years ago a priest named William, a dissolute and very immoral man. A layman once came to him and begged him, on behalf of a poor woman of his parish who lived in the nearby countryside, to visit her promptly and administer the viaticum to her as she was dying.

But he, being lazy and negligent, refused to go. Entrusting the body of the Lord to that layman, he said: “Go and tell that cleric who lives in the same village that he is to visit the dying woman and give her this Eucharist.” It was night. As the man went away with the Lord’s sacrament, he found in the road an unclean spirit lying there, like a dead person covered with a white shroud. Seeing it at first, he was frightened; but immediately, armed with the sign of the cross and trusting in the power of the sacred body, he moved a little aside and passed on.

Then the one who had seemed dead suddenly rose and cried out to him: “Unless he whom you carry were now your protection, you would surely have come here to your harm.” Having spoken thus, the deceitful ambusher vanished. Thus, harmfully innocent and uselessly useful, he not only could not accomplish the evil he wished, but even, compelled by the Lord, confessed a truth he did not wish to tell [Col. 1372B].

## CHAPTER XXV. When the Eucharist was brought to a wicked man near death, before he received it he was lifted into the air by demons and dashed to the ground.

[Col. 1372C]

In the province of Flanders, we learned that a terrible occurrence took place not long ago. A certain carnal and perverse man, when he was approaching death, was brought the Lord’s sacrament in order to receive communion. On seeing it, the light of his eyes immediately failed; as though struck by a great bolt of lightning, he roared terribly. His body convulsed, he sprang from his bed, was seized by demons and lifted on his back upward into the air; then at once, falling outside the bed, he burst apart in the middle and vomited forth his unhappy soul.

The body of the Lord was shaken from the priest’s hand and, falling upon that same bed, came down upon a linen cloth. The priest himself, struck by overwhelming terror, lost his reason. Though he remained alive for a long time afterward, [Col. 1372D] he never recovered his senses; instead, having become like a beast, he received his daily maintenance from the household of the count of Flanders.

374  
## CHAPTER XXVI. A lay brother of Le Bec, near death, is freed from the assaults of demons through the prayers of the entire community; fortified with the sacraments, he departs this life in a good confession.

A lay brother among the brethren of Le Bec, a monastery of the Cistercian Order in Normandy, being near death, was urged by the brethren to confess and receive holy communion; but he vehemently recoiled from this and refused with a stubborn mind. The brethren labored throughout one day [Col. 1373A] to persuade him; but, finding that their own efforts could accomplish nothing in this matter, they resolved by common counsel to offer special prayer for him in the community.

All the brethren therefore assembled in the church and, multiplying litanies and psalms amid weeping and lamentation, implored the Lord to rescue that soul, so endangered, from the depth of evils and not permit it in any way to die in such damnation. When the prayer was finished, the sick man began to cry and say: “Come, brethren, help quickly and bring the Lord’s sacrament, lest the opposing party come again and find me unprepared. For just now an immense troop of demons was present. Pressed on every side by them, I was so constrained that I could give no answer to your promptings concerning my salvation.

“And behold, our brethren again—monks and lay brothers alike—formed into one battle-line and rushed upon the demons with great force. Each attacked one opponent; with mighty hand and uplifted arm they drove them all completely away and, through God’s mercy, delivered me.”

Hearing this, the brethren rejoiced with great joy. They immediately went and offered him the most holy body of the Lord. Contrite and repentant, he received communion with immense reverence and devotion, and at once yielded up his spirit in a good confession [Col. 1373B].

## CHAPTER XXVII. A lay brother of Longpont who kept one denarius and one young cow without permission, on receiving the Eucharist at Easter, thought that a burning coal had been cast into his breast.

[Col. 1373C]

In the monastery of Longpont, a certain lay brother had from the beginning kept for himself, without special permission, one denarius and one heifer. Therefore, on the day of Easter, when he had received the sacred offering, it seemed to him that someone had thrust a burning coal into his breast. He immediately left the oratory and went to his lodging; driven by nausea, he at once vomited what he had received into the ashes, before he could seize any vessel to catch it. Then, having summoned the abbot of the place, he confessed the offense he had committed and the imminent danger he had thereby incurred. On the following day the abbot related in chapter, for the brethren to hear, all that had happened [Col. 1373D]; and because of the negligence shown toward holy communion, he imposed upon us who were present a common penance. Moreover, as his illness worsened, this same lay brother took to his bed; and after languishing for a very long time, whether he afterward recovered is uncertain to us.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Eucharist, hidden at the threshold of a stable for the health of swine, is revealed by God and found to have been transformed in large part into flesh.

We knew a certain nun who, abounding in great virtues, was also shown to possess the gift of prophecy. Recently the Lord appeared to her and deigned to reveal the following, saying: “My faithful people treat me more disgracefully [Col. 1374A] than Jews or pagans. For they have just made me a swineherd, keeping my body secretly and most vilely deposited in a pigsty in the neighboring village, lest the pigs perish through plague or mortality.”

When the handmaid of God made this saying public, they immediately began a diligent investigation, even under threat of anathema, to discover who had perpetrated so great a sacrilege. The guilty man, seeing that he could no longer remain concealed, at last confessed the evil he had done, showing also a hidden hole in the threshold of the doorway in which the Lord’s body had been concealed. When the entrance was opened, they found the most holy host already transformed in large part into the likeness of flesh. Seeing, indeed, that the holy thing had been given to dogs and the pearl set before swine [Col. 1374B] (Matthew 7), the faithful groaned deeply; and, taking the sacred object from the unholy place, they carried it back to the church with great fear and reverence, and fittingly placed it in the sacristy, as was fitting.

## CHAPTER XXIX. A poor peasant, having received the Eucharist on Easter Day and retained it in his mouth, sewed it into his garment in hope of relieving his poverty; afterward, when he was endangered by illness and disclosed it, it was found wholly flesh.

Likewise, we have learned that such a thing happened in the diocese of Chartres some twenty-four years ago. A certain peasant, a very poor man, had heard from some malign impostor or other that, if he continually carried the Lord’s Body about with him, he would soon abound in riches. Therefore, having received the most holy Body of the Lord on Easter Day [Col. 1374C], he kept it whole in his mouth. He immediately sewed it into the hem of his cloak and carried it about with him for a long time; yet poverty and misery never at any time failed him.

This man, then, struck by a fatal illness, came to the point of death. Seeing himself near death, the wretch at last came to his senses and learned by pitiable experience the truth of the Apostle’s saying: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 6). Grieving and repentant, he confessed the theft he had committed with sacrilegious mouth, and disclosed also the unworthy wrapping in which the most worthy Body had been placed. The priest therefore took the garment and, unsewing it before the people standing by, found the sacred host [Col. 1374D], retaining indeed its former shape but wholly transformed in nature and appearance into flesh.

When this was reported to the bishop of Chartres, he immediately took care to come to that place with a great company. Taking up that incomparable treasure and bringing it with the highest honor to the city itself, with an innumerable clergy and people coming out to meet him, he solemnly brought it into the church of the Blessed Virgin Mother; there he placed it fittingly and exaltedly, to be preserved with the utmost reverence.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Eucharist thrown into a hive of bees is found, after three years, whole and unharmed on the uppermost comb.

Another peasant, having wickedly lent a credulous ear to the poisonous whispers of a certain sorcerer, [Col. 1375A] was persuaded that, if he blew the Lord’s Body into his hives while retaining it in his mouth, the bees would prosper greatly from this, send out more frequent swarms, and make more abundant honey. Having therefore received the Eucharist and retained it in his mouth, he came to the apiary. As he went about blowing into each hive, it happened that the sacred host slipped from his blowing mouth and entered one of the hives through an opening. Immediately, by divine action, it flew upward and was suitably placed upon the upper comb, where it remained concealed for three years.

When that expert whisperer looked more curiously inside and failed to find it, he treated the matter with contempt and went away; nevertheless, he carefully marked that particular hive so that it would not be moved. After three years, seized by a grave illness, he knew death to be at the door. Summoning a priest [Col. 1375B], ashamed and repentant, he acknowledged the bold act deserving punishment which he had proudly presumed to do, and the intolerable loss which he had afterward carelessly incurred. When the priest asked whether he recognized the hive into which the host had fallen, he replied that he knew it very well and did not delay in showing it at once.

Then, when the basket had been broken open, the priest and the many persons present found the Lord’s Body carefully and honorably stored in the upper place, altogether as whole and beautiful as though it had been placed there that very day.

## CHAPTER XXXI. In Sardinia, many things concerning the punishments of the next life are revealed by God to a certain priest.

There was on the island of Sardinia a priest of honorable conduct [Col. 1375C], who was also in charge there of a parish church. That church stood outside the village and was remote from every human habitation. Once, while he was celebrating Mass there, at the time of communion he found the host upon the corporal broken and divided of itself into two parts, though he had consecrated it before whole and sound. When he saw this, troubled and anxious, he completed the sacrifice with fear and amazement. When the service was finished and the others had departed, he remained there alone.

Going outside, he came and stood at the end of the same church, with his back against the wall and his face turned [Col. 1375D] toward the east. While he stood there for some time in this position, thinking fearfully and anxiously about what had happened, he groaned in spirit, and the hairs of his flesh suddenly stood on end. Then some external power, he knew not what, rushed upon him, and he began to be held fixed and constrained so that he could in no way move from that spot.

And behold, with his eyes open he saw crowds of an innumerable multitude, mounted and on foot, passing before him at rapid pace. Among them were persons of both sexes, of different ages and conditions; and he recognized many whom he had formerly known alive in the flesh. One of them, formerly known and dear to him, approached and, halting his step, began to speak familiarly with him. When the priest asked what that infinite multitude of crowds was, and what it did, he replied that they were souls released from the flesh [Col. 1376A], all assigned to various punishments according to the diversity of their offenses, and thus always wandering far and wide through the world in a recurring course. Some among them were to be released more quickly, others more slowly; yet the punishments of many remained incapable of release.

While he was speaking, the priest, looking closely, saw one of them passing before him, at whom he was greatly terrified. He said: “Woe is me, a miserable sinner! Is that our lord Baldwin, formerly archbishop of Pisa, taken from the monastery of Clairvaux?” The dead man replied: “It is he indeed.” And the priest said to him: “Then has this monk of so great a profession, and bishop of such great perfection, been assigned to punishments—he whom we thought already rejoicing in heaven with the angels?” He replied: “Know certainly that he is holy, a man of lofty merit, and his glory before God is great. [Col. 1376B] But because a long war is now being waged on his account between the peoples of Pisa and Lucca, his rest is deferred until their discord is brought back to peace.”

While these things were being said, behold, another man came: formerly a rich and very powerful knight, carrying in his lap great weights of silver, under whose burden he walked exceedingly weighed down and afflicted. When the priest recognized him, he asked why he too was subjected to such punishment.
