The dead man replied: “This perverse and impious man lived far too carnally and tyrannically, and therefore has been assigned to everlasting punishments. Once, when setting out for Jerusalem, he took this money with him in order to distribute it, redeem his sins, and make friends for himself from the mammon of unrighteousness. But, at the devil’s prompting, he defrauded his soul of works of mercy and, returning home, brought back with him the provisions of the poor. As he had gathered them from evil, so too, to heap evil upon evil, he did not hesitate to spend them wickedly.” [Col. 1376C]

While he said this, behold, there appeared a column of immense radiance, shining beyond ordinary power, stretched from heaven to earth; through it a certain soul, led by an angel, was hastening toward the stars. When that priest saw it, he again asked his interlocutor what it was. He answered: “This is the soul of Constantine, formerly judge and lord of Torres. For nine years, from the day of his death until now, it has stood in the dripping water from his own house, always exposed to winds, rains, and cold, and there paid the penalties for its offenses. But because he was merciful and generous toward the poor, rendered judgment to those suffering injustice, and moreover departed confessed and repentant of the evils he had committed, he has obtained mercy from the Lord; and on this day he deserves to be freed from every evil and brought, to be filled with every good, into eternal blessedness.” [Col. 1376D]

The aforesaid priest saw these things and many similar matters that would take too long to recount; and his interlocutor instructed him about everything he asked. Finally [Col. 1377A], he also asked concerning himself. The other replied: “To answer briefly what you ask, know without doubt that you will die this year and receive according to what you have done.” Having said this, he at once bade the priest farewell and passed on; then the whole apparition disappeared with him.

The priest, restored to himself and deeply affected by what he had seen, made remarkable progress in the fear of God. Although he had previously lived honorably, thereafter he lived much more strictly. He made known the vision he had seen to certain religious and wise persons; and in that same year, as he had heard, he departed from the body and died in good confession.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A Saracen girl, most eager for the Christian religion, is slain by a Christian but depraved knight for defending her chastity, and is numbered among the martyrs by Pope Alexander III.

[Col. 1377B]

The matter I relate has become very well known and spread throughout Spain. Recently, in that region, there was the daughter of a wealthy Saracen, who, faithfully believing in Christ, strove to attain Christianity. She spoke to a certain Christian knight, saying: “Let your love know that I sincerely believe in your God and ardently desire the grace of baptism. Therefore, if you will take me to your land and make me a Christian, I shall give you the great treasure that I have stored away, and I shall also give myself to you in marriage. But if perhaps you do not wish to have me [Col. 1377C] as your wife, I shall give you half of that money and reserve the rest for my own support.”

The knight agreed, and they gave one another their right hands in pledge of fidelity. They secretly left pagan territory, accompanied by a certain little boy who was in their service. Coming to a certain castle of the Knights Templar, they could not enter, since it was customary at that time for the gates of that stronghold not to be opened because of nocturnal ambushes. They turned aside into a nearby thicket, where, having kindled a large fire, they ate and drank of the provisions they had brought with them.

When the meal was finished, the knight, driven by the frenzy of lust, wished to lie with his companion. She recoiled from this with all her strength and resisted him in every way, saying: “Listen, good Christian: what is this that you are attempting, by which you will destroy both yourself and me? You have been reborn in Christ; I am a pagan. We may not yet join ourselves to one another. Or do you seek to use me as a prostitute? Did I therefore despise the temporal honor and glory of my parents, to make myself a harlot in a foreign land? Is this, then, the Christian purity which, under your instruction, I delighted to seek? Remember, I beg you, [Col. 1377D] your Lord God, and remember that in his faith and truth you undertook to treat me honorably. Show reverence, therefore, for your Christ, and do not wish to dishonor his captive by so great an outrage. If you wish to have me as your marriage-partner, wait a little while, until the reproach of my paganism is washed away in the font of baptism, and then we shall be joined by a lawful bond. But if, as I said, you perhaps reject marriage with me, take the portion of my property that belongs to you and allow me to devote myself to Christ.”

As she said these things, he was moved to no pity, but, growing ever more mad with lust, threatened quickly to kill her unless she at once submitted to his command. But she, steadfast in Christian fashion, declared freely that for the protection of her chastity she would rather choose a glorious death than buy an ignominious life at the cost of prostituted chastity. Then the frenzied and deadly knight drew his sword, cut off her head, and burned much of her cast-off body in the fire.

[Col. 1378B] But heavenly justice, looking down from heaven, did not allow an impiety of such magnitude to remain unavenged for long. Immediately, prepared at the Lord’s command, a terrible dragon came forth from a nearby cave. Hastening to the same place and opening its dreadful mouth, it attacked the son of perdition. When the wretch saw that monstrous beast suddenly threatening him, he at once shuddered all over and, having no confidence of resistance, began to flee. The beast swiftly pursued and overtook him, seized him from behind with its deadly teeth, dragged him at once into its cave, and, in vengeance for such cruelty, devoured him with a most bitter bite.

The aforementioned little boy, seeing these things, fled, shaken with excessive terror. At dawn he came to the castle and recounted in order all that had happened. The Templars therefore went out and found the spoils of the dead and the half-burned body of the most blessed martyr, together with her head. They carried it away and buried it with devotion and reverence. Subsequently, an embassy was sent even to Pope Alexander; he directed that she be buried with honor in the church and regarded as a martyr among martyrs, since she had died for the love of chastity and, baptized in her own blood, had merited, through the Lord’s gift, the crown of martyrdom. [Col. 1378C]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The monks of Burlencourt are deterred by a fiery apparition from digging up the treasure of which a certain man had dreamed.

[Col. 1378D] A man from the village called Lousa, in the diocese of Châlons, had often dreamed that a certain statue, hidden in the ground in a nearby grove from ancient times, was to be found by the monks of Burlencourt. He took care to tell the brethren of this vision. Repeating this frequently, he eventually persuaded them to search. Sixteen brethren went to the place, with the dreamer leading the way, and began to dig into the earth, more in hope of fortune than from a desire to find the statue.

The spot lay at the entrance to the wood, and outside it there stretched a very broad level plain. When they had dug a little, a small fire appeared to them on the plain [Col. 1379A], a mile away, seeming like a burning torch. As they watched it closely, they saw it coming directly toward them. The nearer it came, the larger it appeared. The little fire moved onward, growing into a pyre; before long it became in their eyes a huge furnace or some burning house. Seeing it rush terribly onward and now threaten them at close quarters, they were greatly disturbed and terrified, wholly ignorant what to do or where to flee from the devouring fire.

In so great a crisis there was but one remedy: to implore the divine mercy, which alone could help. Turning therefore to prayer, in great tribulation and distress they begged the Lord to deliver them from immediate death. Then that fiery globe, at the Lord’s command, was checked and stopped in the middle of the field, separated from them by about the distance of one acre. It was suspended in the air, some four or five cubits above the ground. After remaining motionless in this way for a time, it finally returned whence it had come, through the Lord’s mercy; as it withdrew it began to grow thinner, and thus gradually failing, it vanished completely.

The brethren departed, leaving the diabolical statue with its treasure to the prince of darkness. Wholesomely chastened, yet not killed, they learned to hope in the Lord rather than in the uncertainty of riches, knowing surely that it is incomparably better to support oneself by vigorous labor of one’s hands than, living idly [Col. 1379C], to seek wealth from unrighteous mammon or from the accursed thing of Jericho.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Margaret, a devout woman in the diocese of Roskilde, long tormented by her barbarous husband and finally cruelly killed, is divinely distinguished by the incorruptibility of her sacred body and by other miracles.

In the diocese of Roskilde there was a woman named Margaret, meek and humble of heart, endowed with great simplicity and innocence. She devoted herself continually to good works and bore with equanimity the injuries often inflicted on her. But she had an impious and cruel husband, who presented himself to her not as a husband and equal, but like a most dreadful tyrant and persecutor [Col. 1379D]. He hated her for her innocence and simplicity, regarding her as foolish and senseless. He was continually hostile toward her, assailing her all day with abuse, crushing her with blows, and inflicting many evils upon her.

But she, as though she did not feel it and as though she had no rebukes in her mouth, strove to overcome evil with good, and was peaceable with those who hated peace. Moreover, a certain wicked woman—the sister, if I am not mistaken, of that same peasant—wasted away with great envy against her, continually inflaming her brother to hatred and persecution of her.

Once, then, when that malicious husband, with his sister present and urging him on, had beaten the innocent woman nearly to death and could not yet satisfy his inexorable cruelty with her sufferings [Col. 1380A], he added murder to complete his condemnation. They laid her on her back between two supports, pressed heavily down upon her from above, and thus suffocated her by a violent death. When she was utterly dead, they put a noose around her neck and hung her from a beam in the corner of the house.

Having perpetrated so great a crime, the impious murderer began to feign grief and lamentation, inviting all the neighbors to mourn with funeral wailing. Clapping his hands together, howling and crying aloud, he said: “Alas, alas! Come, all friends and neighbors, and grieve with me. Come, I say, and see how my unhappy and foolish wife, in my absence and without my knowledge, destroyed herself—how, assaulted by the devil, she strangled herself with a noose.” When this wicked deceiver, by such lamentations, had persuaded the people to believe him, they cast out the corpse with great disgrace and dragged it far away like a dead dog to the shore of the sea. There, covering it lightly with beach sand, they laid it with two robbers who had recently been hanged and buried there. [Col. 1380B]

The waves of the sea frequently struck that place, gradually washing away the sand heaped over the dead and throwing it into the neighboring marsh, so that the bodies appeared partly exposed. After two years had passed, a certain blind man was walking near the aforesaid place and turned aside to that marsh to wash his hands and face. As soon as he began to bathe his eyes in that water [Col. 1380C], through the Lord’s mercy he was healed and received his sight.

When he realized this, immediately stunned with amazement, he cried out: “Christ, Son of God, what has happened to me? Behold, I see the sea, the dry land, and all things around me. Am I seeing this in a dream, or is this truly happening to me? Whence comes this light to a blind man? Whence joy to a wretch? Whence health to one without hope?” When, as his sight continued, he truly knew that he was healed, he at once began joyfully to run ahead of his guide, praising God. Coming to the nearest village, he told everyone what had happened to him.

All then ran to that place [Col. 1380D], and every afflicted person who entered the same water was immediately healed of whatever sickness held them. Desiring to learn the source of that blessed power of healing, they began to dig up the graves of the condemned. When they came upon the corpses of the robbers, such corruption and putrefaction appeared in them, and such an intolerable stench tainted the air itself, that nearly everyone fled with nostrils stopped. They immediately heaped the removed sand back in a mound over the unclean bodies and hastened to look upon the body of blessed Margaret.

When they uncovered it, it appeared so incorrupt and beautiful from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head that it seemed like a living rather than a dead body. Moreover, such a sweet fragrance breathed forth from it [Col. 1381A] that they thought it sprinkled with every kind of perfumed powder. Having found the precious pearl, they gave thanks and rendered great praises to the giver of so great a gift; drawing her out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, they carried her to their church with due reverence.

Then her murderer was seized and examined with threats and tortures. Since he could no longer conceal the matter, he confessed the whole truth in the hearing of all. When these things were reported to the bishop and the leading men of the city, an innumerable clergy and people came at once, carried the venerable relic with due honor to the episcopal see, and solemnly placed it in the principal church with devotion and joy. There, at her tomb, great crowds of people flow together from all directions, both neighboring and distant [Col. 1381B]; and so many miracles occur there that they cannot be comprehended because of their excessive multitude.

## CHAPTER XXXV. An evil demon attempts to avenge the injury done to its image when it was broken and burned.

A certain honorable brother of the monastery of Fontenay, before his conversion, once went to pagan lands for the sake of trade. He had with him as a companion another young Christian. While they stayed there, it happened that they wandered alone into a grove for recreation. Coming to the pleasant seclusion of a certain place [Col. 1381C], they found there an enormous idol, wooden within and coated with pitch without, standing upright like a log against the trunk of a tree. Those from the neighboring village who showed themselves especially devoted—or rather especially deranged—in the service of that abominable deity came there secretly to worship or sacrifice.

Inflamed with zeal for the faith, the Christian youths smashed the execrable statue to pieces, then immediately set fire beneath it and reduced it to ashes and cinders. When this was done, they took flight quickly, lest they be discovered by its fanatical worshipers and suffer a like punishment. For they did not yet have such courage as to dare do this openly.

On the following night, when the future lay brother of Fontenay had given his limbs to sleep [Col. 1381D], that nocturnal spirit appeared to him, pitch-black and dark in the likeness of the burned idol. Throwing hot ashes, which it held in its hands, into his eyes, it said: “Behold, yesterday you burned me, and today I shall burn you.” The youth awoke and felt great pain and torment in his eyes, which persisted for a long time thereafter and grievously afflicted him.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. When the Christian faith is introduced into Slavonia, demons flee from it with a dreadful noise, like an army defeated, routed, and put to flight in battle.

In the region of Slavonia, which has recently been converted in large part to the Christian faith, many monasteries of the Cistercian Order are now known to have been founded. The monks serving the Lord there have received from the supreme pontiff authority to baptize, because of the daily conversion of pagans. It happened that some of these brothers, invited by certain faithful people, were to come on an appointed day to one of the nearby villages, in order to baptize the multitude of pagans there who, having recently received the faith, were seeking the grace of regeneration.

On the preceding night, before they arrived, a great sound and roaring was heard there [Col. 1382A], like that of a large army making noise through the streets and squares of the village throughout the whole night. It seemed as though this army, fiercely attacked by another army and at last overcome, was turning its back and departing in great turmoil. The people of the place all heard the noise and flight of those withdrawing, but saw no person; they were astonished and afraid, not knowing what this new occurrence was or what good or evil it portended.

On the next day the monks came to the same village and baptized a great crowd of both sexes. Then it became plainly known to all the faithful that the tumult of the night had been nothing other than legions of demons fleeing, at the Lord’s rebuke, from the people they had possessed; they could not endure the presence of the blessed angels and the coming of the Holy Spirit. All were greatly consoled in the Lord by this event, especially those neophytes who had been delivered from unclean condemnation. [Col. 1382B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. A pagan woman, tormented by the sprinkling of holy water, converts to the faith of Christ.

[Col. 1382C]

A certain pagan woman, mingled among a gathering of believers, was by chance sprinkled with holy water. Feeling it and recoiling greatly, she immediately suffered intolerable pain and burning, as though she had been immersed up to the neck in a cauldron of boiling water. Although she was tormented for a very long time and invoked the gods of idols for help, not only was the burning of her body not diminished [Col. 1382D], but it was increased. At last her affliction gave understanding to her hearing, and she knew truly that there was no salvation for her in those gods. Therefore, invoking the name of the Savior and receiving the saving washing, she immediately received health of body and soul; thus made a believer, she was joined to the companies of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. King Olav, afterward a martyr, was reproved and grieved when, through inadvertence, he shaved a stick with a knife on the Lord’s Day; having gathered the shavings and burned them upon his hand as a punishment, he remained unharmed by the flame.

On a certain Sunday, the glorious King and martyr Olav found where he was sitting a little stick and shaved it with the knife he held in his hand, forgetting that it was Sunday. For in Norway feast days are observed with great diligence, and people do not presume voluntarily to do anything, great or small, on them. One of those attending the king saw that he was shaving the stick on Sunday but did not dare to say openly that it was Sunday. Instead, he reminded him with these words: “My lord king, tomorrow will be Monday.” [Col. 1383A]

At this reminder the king came to himself. Greatly grieved because he had shaved the stick on Sunday, he gathered the shavings, laid them upon his hand, and burned them by applying fire. When they were burned, his hand appeared unharmed. The miracle once celebrated in Babylon in the case of the three children was renewed: the fire retained its natural power to consume the pieces of the stick, but was altogether unable to harm the hand of the innocent king.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. A bishop accustomed to uttering ridiculous remarks appears after death with ulcerated and swollen lips; he is released through the silence for several days of seven brothers.

[Col. 1383B]

Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, frequently admonished a certain bishop by rebuking him, urging him to abandon the ridiculous words he had wickedly made a habit of uttering. [Col. 1384A] He added that unless the bishop corrected his life in the present, after death he would appear deformed, with swollen lips and foaming mouth. The bishop did not reform. He died. He appeared to a certain priest and, as the saint had foretold, showed a mouth with ulcerated, swollen lips. He tearfully sought the Father’s help, though he had refused to heed his merciful correction.

The priest reported to the Father what he had seen. The abbot took pity and hastened to heal the bishop’s transgression by the silence of seven brothers. He chose seven brothers and commanded them to keep silence for seven days on the bishop’s behalf. The seventh transgressed and broke silence. The bishop returned to the priest, accused the broken silence, complained of the transgression, and ascribed the delay in the healing of his mouth to the disobedience of the seventh man. Hearing this, the abbot found the transgressor and restored the seven-day observance by another silence. When this was completed, the bishop appeared for the third time, thanking the abbot, clothed in a bishop’s mantle and showing his healed mouth. [Col. 1384B]

# DISQUISITION ON THE ILLUSTRIOUS LINEAGE OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1383]

[DISQUISITION.]

## 395 PREFACE

[Col. 1383C]

I would readily concede the point to those who think that the Sacred Congregation of Rites ought to be approached regarding that clause of the Roman Breviary in which Saint Bernard is said to have been born “of honorable station.” For anyone reading this who knew nothing else of Bernard’s birth could easily suppose that he sprang from common parents—farmers, perhaps, craftsmen, or others of the same rank—whereas it is established that he was extremely noble on both his father’s and mother’s side.

Certainly truth ought to shine forth in all history, and especially in those accounts which Catholic churches throughout the world proclaim in the divine offices; otherwise, if truth should seem neglected anywhere in them, an opportunity would be provided for enemies of the faith to calumniate, and likewise to call into doubt other portions of the sacred readings that declare mysteries and matters necessary for salvation. Add that this disparagement of Bernard’s birth does some injury to a most holy man who deserved exceedingly well of the Church [Col. 1383D], since it takes away from his virtue a certain splendor and, as it were, its foundation—if every prudent person rightly judges that virtue placed upon, and implanted in, nobility rises higher and shines more illustriously.

Yet I do not wish the noble lineage of the holy man to be established by trivial arguments or testimonies of obscure authority. Let us examine the whole matter more carefully. In order to advance something certain and solid, we must first demonstrate that Bernard was noble; next, that he belonged to the equestrian order, commonly called in those times the *Militia*; further, that his origin within that rank was ancient; and finally, that through his mother Aalydis, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbar, he was descended from the ancient dukes of Burgundy [Col. 1384C].

## SECTION ONE. The coat of arms of the Cistercian Order was not derived from Saint Bernard’s family arms.

Bernard Barnabas de Montalvo, Mariana in Book X, chapter 12 of his *History of Spain*, Boniface Simonetta in Book II of his *History*, and several other recent writers maintain, descended from that house of the dukes of Burgundy whose head was Robert, king of the Franks. Accordingly, they proclaim him a kinsman not only of the kings of France, but also of Spain and Portugal—so that, as Angelus Manrique says in the *Cistercian Annals*, [Col. 1384D] year of Christ 1105, chapter 1, no. 4, they bind all Christian princes to Bernard by a close bond of blood.

They believe that they prove this from the ancient arms of the Cistercian Order. Since these, they say, are identical with those known to have been used by those ancient dukes of Burgundy—namely, three golden bands on an azure shield; or, in present terminology, six bands of gold and azure slanting downward to the right within a purple border—they suppose that this custom was derived from Bernard, who was descended from the family of those dukes. Thus, they hold, the ancient Cistercian Fathers, who acknowledged Bernard not indeed as the first founder of their Order, but as its propagator and special [Col. 1385A] patron, adopted his family arms as their own.

Philip of Saint John the Baptist, recounting this in his Italian *Life of St Bernard*, Book III, chapter 29, rightly denies that the Cistercians had Bernard, their own foster-son, in view when selecting their arms. Rather, they looked to that family of the dukes of Burgundy by whose benefits and authority their Order was chiefly founded and grew into a great people. As for his further assertion that these were the hereditary arms of Tecelinus, St Bernard’s father—the arms depicted beside St Bernard’s likeness nearly two hundred years ago by Hermann Schedel in the *Chronicle of Chronicles*, namely, on a black shield a bend chequered in double rows of gold and red—many suppose these to be the very ancient arms either of St Bernard himself or of Clairvaux Abbey. We shall examine this separately and more carefully below. [Col. 1385B]

398

## SECTION TWO. The nobility of St Bernard is shown by the nobility of his sister Humbelina, and likewise of his sister-in-law, the wife of his brother Guy.

Bernard had five brothers and one sister, all born of the same father and mother, in this order. Guy was the firstborn; Gerard the second; Bernard the third; Humberga, named after her maternal grandmother, or Humbelina, the fourth (for this was her order of birth, according to John the Hermit in the *Life of St Bernard*); Andrew the fifth; Bartholomew the sixth; and Nivard the seventh and last. Their birth and condition [Col. 1385C] were common to them all. The brother of a noble full sister could not fail to be noble.

Concerning Humberga, or Humbelina, Bernard’s sister, William the Abbot, Book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 6—a witness beyond every major objection—writes:

> Their sister too, married in the world and devoted to the world, while she was in danger amid worldly riches, was at last moved by God to visit her brothers.

He then relates how she came to Clairvaux with a splendid retinue and display; how the brothers rebuked her; and how they earnestly admonished her to shape her life after the example of their common mother Alys. Having shed many tears, she departed; and he then adds:

> All were astonished that a noble and delicately reared young woman, by a sudden change in dress and food, should lead an eremitic life in the midst of the world.

I wish that we had an earlier writer than Brito who stated with him that Humbelina’s husband was the brother of the duchess of Lorraine. I think it wrong to indulge in conjecture. Let us turn to Guy’s wife.

399

If, as was customary in marriages, equality of rank was observed between spouses, Guy is found to have been noble from his noble wife. William the Abbot, Book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 3, says:

> Guy, the firstborn of the brothers, was already bound by marriage, a great man and, more than the others, firmly rooted in the world. At first he hesitated somewhat; but immediately weighing and reconsidering the matter, he consented to conversion, provided that his wife also agreed. Yet this seemed almost impossible in the case of a noble young woman who was nursing little daughters.

And shortly afterward:

> Finally, in accordance with ecclesiastical custom, she was separated from her husband by a mutual vow of chastity, and entered the community of holy women, where she has until this day served God devoutly. [Col. 1386A]

Bernard Brito, in his *Cistercian Chronicles or Annals*, says that Guy’s wife was the daughter of the Count of Floresta—perhaps he meant Forestes, or Forez. If this is correct, she was of the highest nobility, since in those times the families of counts were almost equal to those who are now princes, and most of them were connected with kings themselves either by blood or at least by marriage. Yet one would wish Brito to support his assertion with some testimony from antiquity. For my purpose, it is enough that she was noble, even on the testimony of William the Abbot.

After she was separated from her husband, who had entered the Cistercian Order, I suppose she became a nun at Jully, or Julleium, [Col. 1386B] which William the Abbot, Book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 4, in Surius under 20 August, states was the first monastery constructed to receive noble women who renounced the world following the example of Bernard and his companions. We are surprised that these very words are omitted in certain editions of the same work. Yet Jacobus Merlonus reports them from manuscript 400 in his Paris edition of St Bernard’s works of 1645. There is no doubt that their author is William the Abbot, though he seems to have added them later to the *Life of St Bernard* already published by him, as often happens; hence they are not found in many copies:

> Since some of Bernard’s aforesaid companions had been married, and their wives too had entered with their husbands into the same vow [Col. 1386C] of holy life, a convent of holy women was built for them through his care. It is called Julleium, in the diocese of Langres. With the Lord’s help it grew very greatly and is, to this day, most renowned for its religious life, enlarged in persons and possessions, and already propagated into other places, nor does it yet cease to yield still more abundant fruit.

Therefore, when that former wife of Guy withdrew to Jully about the year of Christ 1113 or 1114 and gave that new monastery its beginning, she appears, after some years, to have led a colony from it to Pratum Longum, commonly Pralon, only about four leagues’ journey from the city of Dijon toward Sombernon, and to have laid the foundations of that convent about the year of Christ 1140, with the assistance of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and Godfrey, bishop of Langres. I am led to this opinion by an old local tradition, also affirmed in certain ancient documents: namely, that there was at Pratum Longum an abbess, a sister of St Bernard, in whose favour the lords of Fontaines and Sombernon bestowed many goods upon that house. Ancient charters, which we carefully examined in their original form, attest these benefactions. From one of them it appears that the house was founded and built in the presence and through the care, among others, of Bernard, [Col. 1386D] abbot of Clairvaux, and Godfrey, bishop of Langres.

Now only two women are said to have been Bernard’s sisters in the world: Humbelina, his one full sister; and another by affinity, namely the wife of his brother Guy, who was commonly called his sister as well. William the Abbot, Book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 6, affirms that Humbelina became a nun at Jully; and the author of the *Life of Blessed Peter*, then prior of Jully, testifies that she died there, commending her devout soul to God, among others, in the presence of her own brother St Bernard. It follows that Guy’s wife must be understood as Bernard’s sister who spent her life in the monastery of Pratum Longum.

Moreover, we heard from the mouth of an aged abbess of Pralon that, some years ago, when the ground of the oratory, being too low and therefore too damp, was being raised by several feet with brought-in material—so that many graves had necessarily to be disturbed—a lead coffin was found in the chapel of Blessed Mary, in which, according to report, the bones of a sister of St Bernard were enclosed. The nuns of Pratum Longum also possess in their sacristy several relics of Blessed Bernard, among them the alb and chasuble in which he performed the sacred rites; and a gilded silver chalice, broad and rather shallow like a paten, very similar to another which the monks of Clairvaux still devoutly preserve as St Bernard’s own chalice. [Col. 1387B]

## SECTION THREE. Neither St Bernard’s full sister nor his sister-in-law were nuns of the Cistercian Order, but Black Benedictines.

I digress for a while in order to restore to their own Order those women whom I have asserted to be both noble and nuns. The resolution of this question depends upon the character [Col. 1387C] of the Rule of the houses in which they lived.

I have said that Humbelina both made profession and died at Jully. Guy’s wife, however, was veiled at Jully, then transferred to Pratum Longum, and ended her life there. The monastery of Pratum Longum still exists today, and from its origin it belonged to the Order of Black Benedictine nuns. Hence, several centuries ago, in a petition to the king to recover the then alienated village of Changeio, the nuns of that place declared themselves to be of the Order of St Benignus of Dijon—that is, of the Order of Benedict—which the monks of St Benignus then followed and still follow.

Nor is this less certain of Jully. It was founded by Milo, Count of Bar-sur-Seine, assigned to Guy, abbot of Molesme, and administered by Benedictine monks of Molesme down to the present day. Blessed Peter, prior of Jully, who was present when Humbelina died there, was himself a monk of Molesme, and had accompanied St Robert when he was ordered to return from Cîteaux to Molesme. After the convent of nuns at Jully was destroyed, the chapel alone remains, bearing the title of a priory and holding revenues attached to it; even now it belongs to Molesme Abbey. [Col. 1387D]

This makes it surprising that scarcely any writer on Cistercian matters fails to assert that Humbelina was, if not the first foundress of Cistercian women, at least a nun of the Cistercian Order. Did Humbelina alone live as a Cistercian among Benedictine women? Or, if all the nuns at Jully were Cistercians, could they have been governed by Benedictine monks of Molesme—white by black—as though Jully were a member under an alien head?

The women of the Cistercian Order would certainly act wisely and devoutly if they adopted St Bernard’s sister, illustrious for sanctity of life, as their patroness, provided that they acknowledge her to have been not a Cistercian but a Benedictine. If they wish to know something certain concerning their own beginnings, they should understand that in the district of Tart, only one hour’s journey from Cîteaux, the first ascetic house for girls following the Cistercian observance began to be founded under Goceranus, bishop of Langres, around the year of Christ 1125, and was completed in 1132 under his successor Guilencus; Elizabeth as abbess and Mary as prioress being set over the new congregation. [Col. 1388B]

I do not deny that this monastery was derived from the Benedictine house at Jully, just as Cîteaux had previously been derived from Molesme. Thus William the Abbot could truly say, in the passage cited above, that Julleium or Jully had already been propagated into other places when he was writing. And Tart Abbey seems to have been, as it was first in origin, so also the head of all the other houses of the same sex and Order.

Accordingly, in a bull of Pope Innocent III issued in the year of Christ 1200, eighteen abbeys subject to Tart are enumerated. Their abbesses were accustomed each year, on the feast of St Michael, to assemble at Tart Abbey for a general chapter, over which presided the abbot of Cîteaux himself or someone acting in his place. This is testified by Guy, abbot of Cîteaux, who calls Tart Abbey a proper daughter of the house of Cîteaux, and makes it highly probable that through Tart and its eighteen offshoots all, or most, convents of Cistercian nuns were derived.

The house of Tart indeed numbered among its distinguished nuns Adelaide, sister of Emperor Lothair, widow of Simon I, duke of Lorraine, mother of Matthew, duke of Lorraine, his brother Baldwin, and their sister Agatha, countess of Burgundy. This Adelaide, as Matthew the duke, her son, testifies under the year 1142, “poor in possessions and spirit through the change of the right hand of the Most High,” had assumed the purpose and habit of holy life in the church and community of Tart. [Col. 1388D] This monastery of Tart, once renowned for wealth and religious life, is now deserted by nuns, who were transferred to Dijon in the year of Christ 1623. Thus Jully and Tart, those two most celebrated houses of nuns which the first ardour of the discipline of Molesme and Cîteaux had produced, now retain nothing of their ancient religious life except the devout ashes of so many holy virgins, whom the last day of the world will raise to the embrace of the eternal Bridegroom.

## SECTION FOUR. St Bernard was, through his father, of the equestrian order, then called the *militia*, and in that rank of ancient and unblemished descent.

In former times the *militia* was almost twofold: one form concerned office or service; the other, rank and honour. The *militia* of service [Col. 1389A] was either armed or urban—that is, civil. The armed kind was again subdivided into the field service sent against an enemy, and garrison service, to which was entrusted the care of towns and fortresses. Civil service was threefold: palatine service, in the household of a prince; robed or forensic service, in the courts; and literary service, concerned with public rescripts. On these matters Charles Loyseau writes learnedly in Book I, chapter 1 of *On the Rights of Offices*, correctly observing that palatine service too was girded with arms, but almost for display rather than, like what is properly called armed service, for the conduct of operations.

The *militia* of rank or honour was scarcely distinct among the Romans from the higher grades or prefectures of the service which we have called official: for example, the offices of tribunes, primicerii, senators, ducenarii, biarchs, patrol-leaders, and others, concerning which Jerome writes against Jovinian and likewise others who treat military affairs. But among the peoples who occupied the Roman Empire throughout Europe, there existed another honorary *militia*, commonly called by the French *chevalerie*. This held a grade of nobility above the common level, exactly like our barons—or rather, like the knights of the collar, called *chevaliers de l’Ordre*, so named from the collar, an insignia either of the *militia* or of the equestrian order. [Col. 1389B]

The Middle Ages called this *militia* in the eminent sense, κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “pre-eminently,” and called those advanced to it *milites*, “knights.” Hence, in ancient charters, epitaphs, and necrologies, one constantly sees the most noble men who were neither counts, dukes, nor princes called *milites*; indeed, those called *milites* in Latin writings are called *chevaliers* in French. Even today, in the Parliament of Paris, where all senators’ names are annually recited in Latin according to ancestral custom, the First President is honoured with the title *miles*, while in the other parlements of the kingdom he is called in French *chevalier*.

The rites for conferring this knighthood varied among different nations, as did its insignia, which it is not my task here to pursue. There were two paths to it: birth and deeds. For in every well-ordered commonwealth the passage from the temple of Virtue to the temple of Honour has always been open. This may be understood even from an imperial rescript of Frederick II, in Peter of Vinea, Book VI of the *Letters*, chapter 17, by which the emperor creates a knight who had deserved well of his majesty, although his father had not been a knight. “Although,” he says, “our constitutions provide that those not born of the race of knights cannot become knights.” [Col. 1389D] Understand: unless by their own virtue and outstanding deeds they earn that favour for themselves from the prince.

Certainly, just as it is said of the consulship in Novel 46 of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, *On Persons Honoured and Who Is to Be Preferred in Rank*, that even emperors were adorned by it, so it is certain that the sons of counts and dukes, indeed even of kings themselves, were customarily decorated with this knighthood. Thus, under 26 January, the Necrology of St Benignus records the death of “Henry, knight, our friend.” This was certainly no other than the son of Duke Robert, grandson of King Robert, father of Hugh and Odo, dukes of Burgundy, and likewise forefather of the kings of Portugal. His son Duke Odo I established his anniversary to be celebrated the next day, that is, 27 January, at the monastery of St Seine, assigning certain annual revenues for this observance.

Why, then, was Henry at his death honoured only with the designation “knight”? The reason was that he died before his father Duke Robert; otherwise he should both have been regarded and called duke, unless, at his death before his father, he had left the duchy to pass from his grandfather to his grandsons. Hundreds of similar examples occur of illustrious, indeed royal, young men who were created and called knights when their age and state of life so allowed. For the children of knights were all noble, and belonged to the military—or, as we now say, equestrian—Order; yet they were not knights [Col. 1390B] until, through the belt and sword or some other ceremony, they were made knights by the prince.

Tecelinus himself, a knight who became a monk after begetting sons, bore at death no title but that of monk. The necrology of St Benignus: “On 11 April died Tecelinus, monk, father of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.” Likewise Bernard himself is nowhere called a knight, since from boyhood he had been destined for the clerical life; nevertheless, he was the son of a knight, and thus stood at least one degree above other nobles.

Yet among these knights there were various, as it were, grades, if one considers lineage or nobility derived from knighthood. Some were new men—that is, the first of their line to be awarded knighthood for some outstanding deed and service rendered to their country or prince. Others descended from a long succession of knightly ancestors. If the latter could show that four or more lines of ancestors, both on the paternal and maternal side, had stood in the rank of knighthood, they were certainly accounted nobler than new knights or sons of new knights. This was precisely the lineage of St Bernard, whose father Tecelinus is described by William, Book I, chapter 1 of the *Life*, as “a man of ancient and lawful knighthood.” [Col. 1390C]

The French translator did not understand the force of this expression when he wrote of Tecelinus: *qu’il passa beaucoup de temps dans les charges de la guerre qu’il exerça dignement*—“that he spent much time in the offices of war, which he discharged worthily.” Whatever may be said of armed or palatine service, in which we neither affirm nor deny that Tecelinus was enrolled, we interpret those words according to the usage of that age to mean that Tecelinus was not a newly made knight, nor the first in his family to hold that rank, but sprang from a long and uninterrupted succession of ancestors in the knightly estate. In French we would say: *de l’ancienne chevalerie, sans tache ou mésalliance en son extraction de plusieurs lignes, ou de temps immémorial*—“of ancient knighthood, without stain or unequal marriage in his descent through many lines, or from time immemorial.”

This would be considerably confirmed if it were certain that Tecelinus descended from the most noble knightly lords of Châtillon-sur-Seine, as William Paradin maintained in *On the Ancient State of Burgundy*, pp. 93 and 140, and in Book II of the *Annals of Burgundy*, p. 189. Perhaps he drew this from a genealogy of St Bernard said to have been copied at Fontenay Abbey near Montbard. There Tecelinus is made the son of Werric, count of Châtillon, brother of Godfrey, bishop of Langres, [Col. 1391A] and of Andrew, a knight of the Temple; and certain other particulars are inserted in St Bernard’s paternal and maternal pedigree which would require stronger proof to establish their credibility.

Paradin may also have consulted Robert of Mont in the appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle*. Under the year 1115, he represents St Bernard as both illustrious by birth and native of the castle of Châtillon in Burgundy. This was also the assertion of Vincent of Burgundy, commonly called Vincent of Beauvais, in the *Historical Mirror*, vol. IV, Book XXVII, chapter 22; of Baptista Platina in the *Lives of the Popes*, under Paschal II; of Hartmann Schedel in the *Chronicle of Chronicles*, published at Nuremberg in 1493, folio 198; of Jacobus Philippus of Bergamo, Book XII of the *Supplement to the Chronicles*; and of Paulus Aemilius, Book V of *The Deeds of the Franks*, under Louis the Fat and Louis the Younger. The assertion of them all is doubtful.

For although Bernard, still a boy, spent several years at Châtillon-sur-Seine under teachers of letters, it is established from William the Abbot and John the Hermit in their *Lives* that he was born at Fontaines. This nevertheless seems to have furnished Paradin an occasion for saying that Fontaines lay within the jurisdiction and lordship of the ancient lords of Châtillon, so that, when we read that St Bernard was Fontainois by birth and home, we might not doubt that he also belonged to the Châtillon family. But below we shall discuss St Bernard’s Fontaines genealogy more carefully. For the present, William the Abbot is sufficient for us, on whose authority it is certain that Tecelinus was a man of ancient and lawful knighthood.

[Col. 1391C] A fact of no slight importance also contributes to his distinction: in the charter of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy, concerning the cell of Floriacum on the Ouche, granted to the monastery of St Marcellus of Chalon in the year of Christ 1104, among the duke’s familiar nobles, Tescelinus, also surnamed Sorus, is listed in the first place after Rainerius, the duke’s seneschal, before Bernard of Montfort, Warnerius of Sombernon, and other most noble men. We shall provide the charter itself among the documentary proofs.

## SECTION FIVE. Through his mother Alys of Montbard, St Bernard derived his origin from the counts of Tonnerre, and indeed from the ancient dukes of Burgundy.

[Col. 1391D] The recent writers praised by us in the first section, if they wished to establish St Bernard’s descent, ought to have produced some testimony from earlier authorities. By God’s favour, we have discovered this in the *Chronicle of St Peter the Living at Sens* and in John the Hermit’s *Life of St Bernard*, which he intended as a kind of appendix and supplement to that common and earlier *Life* which consists of five books.

I begin with John the Hermit, who says this concerning Bernard’s family:

> Therefore the most blessed Bernard was born at Fontaines, a town of his father in the district of Langres, as a worthy offshoot. His lineage according to the flesh was noble, but nobler still in the exaltation of his mind. His father was named Tescelinus; his mother Aelaiz, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, a powerful man and great according to worldly rank, deriving his origin, as many assert, from the ancient nobility of the dukes of Burgundy. [Col. 1392A]

John, apparently prior of Clairvaux and called “the Hermit” from his family rather than from a solitary manner of life, wrote to Peter, bishop of Tusculum, and to Herbert, formerly a monk of Clairvaux and archbishop of Torres in Sardinia, about thirty years after St Bernard’s death. If already at that time many asserted that Bernard’s maternal line was descended from the ancient dukes of Burgundy, who would now prudently deny it?

We do not, however, think that it follows from this that Bernard was a kinsman of those dukes of Burgundy descended from King Robert, or of those who are now kings of Spain, France, or Portugal. For the words “as many assert” sufficiently show that this descent from the dukes was traced farther back than Duke Robert, son of King Robert, who had preceded John the Hermit by not a full hundred years. It remains uncertain whether this descent was from the stock of Hugh the Great, Richard, Manasses, or even from those earlier dukes for whom the ducal office, by royal grant and decision, was personal and for a fixed period, not perpetual and still less hereditary. [Col. 1392B]

I now demonstrate St Bernard’s descent from the counts of Tonnerre. The *Chronicle of St Peter the Living at Sens*, under the years of Christ 715, 1065, 1113, and 1114, reports that St Ebbo, formerly count of Tonnerre, became a monk of St Peter the Living, then its abbot, and finally archbishop of Sens. He had sisters, Ingoara and Leoteria, who gave to the monastery of St Peter the Living from their inheritance, among other things, the villages of Rictiacum and Pauliacum. In these villages Bernard the Knight, lord of Montbard, and his wife Humberga received a fourth part from Gerbert, abbot of St Peter, in the year 1065.

Their sons Milo and Rainard thereafter held these tributary villages from the hand of the abbots of St Peter the Living, after their forebears: Milo held Pauliacum, which he sold to the abbot of Molesme in the year 1113 for 150 pounds of denarii, soon becoming a monk in that same year; while Rainard held Rictiacum. [Col. 1392D]

From this chronicle of Sens we learn:

1. First, that Milo, because he is stated to have become a monk in 1113, received the monastic habit not at Clairvaux, as some have thought, but at Cîteaux with St Bernard, whose maternal uncle he was; thence he passed first to Clairvaux and then to Fontenay Abbey.

2. That the name Humberga, from which Humbelina is formed by diminution, was transmitted from the maternal grandmother to St Bernard’s sister. Thus the author of the *Life of Blessed Peter*, prior of Jully, at whose hands she gave up her blessed spirit, calls her.

3. That Humberga was St Bernard’s maternal grandmother; or at least that Bernard, her husband, was descended from the counts of Tonnerre, since they possessed at least some part of those villages, Pauliacum and Rictiacum, in the allod of the counts of Tonnerre. Otherwise their sons Milo and Rainard could have held the whole villages under a rent from the benefaction of the abbots of St Peter the Living, even if they were not related to the counts of Tonnerre. [Col. 1393A]

4. That Peter Roverius, in *Reomaus*, under Bernard II, forty-first abbot of Reomaus, p. 183, incorrectly reports from the *Chronicle of St Peter the Living* that Milo of Montbard was the son of Rainard. The chronicle nowhere says this. Original Fontenay charters establish that Milo was Rainard’s brother, and that both had a sister Aleyde, by whom St Bernard was born. From John the Hermit’s *Life of St Bernard* in part, and in part from the *Chronicle of St Peter the Living* under the year 1065, it is gathered that all these were children of Bernard and Humberga, lord and lady of Montbard.

5. The *Chronicle of St Peter the Living*, in the passages cited, teaches that Montembarrum and Montembardum are used interchangeably. It also indicates that this lordship bore the title of county, at least for a time, when it mentions a lawsuit between the count of Montbard and Clarembaud of Cappy. It is therefore unsurprising that the families of Montbard and Tonnerre were then joined by marriage, since each possessed the same comital honour and rank. This lends support to John the Hermit—or rather to Abbot Robert, St Bernard’s nephew—when they assert that Aleyde of Montbard, Bernard’s mother, derived her origin, in the judgement of many, from the ancient nobility of the dukes of Burgundy. [Col. 1393C]

This also opens room for the conjecture that this lineage was connected by marriage even with kings themselves. In that ancient age, when royal daughters and younger brothers of kings married out, royal bloodlines spread into the families of dukes and counts; so that, although their rank was unequal, their blood was the same. This may be seen among the dukes and counts of Burgundy, Provence, Aquitaine, Champagne, and other French dominions, who, as genealogists know, nearly all boasted royal kinships.

## SECTION SIX. On the nobility of Alys, St Bernard’s mother: the difficulty is resolved from the day of her death, entered in the Necrologies of St Benignus under 1 September, in which she is called merely a laywoman, without any title of illustrious birth.

[Col. 1393D]

Henriquez, in the *Cistercian Menology*, assigned the date of death of Alys or Aleyde, St Bernard’s mother, to 4 April. His argument was that he had read that she died on the very feast day of St Ambrose. Now although the Roman Church chiefly celebrates Ambrose of Milan on 7 December, the day of his ordination, it is nevertheless established from Paulinus in his *Life* and from others that Ambrose died under the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, in the year of Christ 397 according to the common era, on Holy Saturday, which then fell on 4 April. Many other churches celebrate that date as Ambrose’s feast.

John the Hermit, on the report of Abbot Robert, who was St Bernard’s cousin, says that Aleyde died on the feast day of St Ambrose, to whose cult she was intensely devoted. William the Fleming, formerly a canon of Langres, in his *Life of St Bernard* composed by himself in seven books in French, takes Ambrose here to mean the Doctor, and therefore the bishop of Milan. Gundisalvus de Silva translated the Fleming into Portuguese. Hence the widely circulated opinion that Alys died on the feast day of St Ambrose, bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church.

But John the Hermit nowhere calls this St Ambrose either “Doctor” or “Milanese.” There was another Ambrose, more frequently called Ambrosinianus, patron of the village and castle of Fontaines. It is far more probable that this saint was yearly honoured with solemn offices by the lady of the place. [Col. 1394B] The feast of this Ambrosinianus is still celebrated, and has been celebrated from time immemorial, in the parish of Fontaines on the Kalends of September, 1 September. This is proved by the records of St Stephen’s at Dijon, drawn up more than five hundred years ago.

Now consider what the old necrologies of St Benignus contain, among whom the body of this most holy matron was committed to burial:

> On the Kalends of September died Alasya, a laywoman.

In another copy one reads *Alaysa*. And lest you doubt that St Bernard’s own mother is designated by these words, know that many nuns are entered in the same books of obits; that among the laywomen is Cunigunde the Empress, on 3 March; and that several queens, duchesses, countesses, and other women, however illustrious by birth or wives of men of the military or equestrian Order, are called simply “laywomen,” and nothing more. This was the modesty and most accepted custom of that ancient age. Thus there is nothing surprising in the attribution to St Bernard’s most noble mother and wife of the knight Tecelinus of this single designation, “laywoman”; nor should you now doubt that 1 September was the final day of Aleyde, or Alys. [Col. 1394C]

This is especially confirmed by the fact that, since so distinguished a matron buried at St Benignus could not have been omitted in the necrology of St Benignus, no woman of this name is found entered in the two necrologies of that monastery either on 4 April, 7 December, or on any other day, unless distinguished from St Bernard’s mother by the title of duchess or nun, or by some other identifying mark.

Who that saint Ambrosinianus was, or where in the world he lived, I would not dare affirm. For I regard as suspect his *Life*, contained in a Fontaines manuscript written scarcely eighty years ago. In it he is said to have been born in the Sarmatian city of Asian Iberia, to have become bishop of Sarlat after Nicephorus, and finally a martyr distinguished by many palms. I read that the bishopric of Sarlat in the province of Bordeaux was established by Pope John XXII in the year of Christ 1317. I find no other episcopal see called Sarlat in the Christian world, just as I find no city named Sarmatica.

I observe only, as I have already noted, that St Ambrosinianus is honoured at Fontaines on 1 September as the proper patron of the place, although the parish of Fontaines is entered in the catalogues of the churches of the diocese of Langres under the name of St Martin, its older patron. This is evidently because of the chapel dedicated to St Martin, which still survives beneath the hill of Fontaines and is said formerly to have been the mother church of the whole castle or village. Moreover, certain relics of St Ambrosinianus were enclosed in the altar consecrated in the crypt of St Stephen’s at Dijon on 13 September in the year of the Incarnation of Christ 1171 by Guichard, archbishop of Lyons. [Col. 1395A]

416

## SECTION SEVEN. The illustrious lineage of St Bernard is confirmed from the various marital connections of his family.

The ancient lords of Joinville were a family so illustrious that it is better known than needs proof. [Col. 1395B] Let John of Joinville stand in place of all witnesses: in the Life of St Louis, King of France, he calls the Count of Burgundy his maternal uncle. This was John, Count of Burgundy from the house of the Counts of Chalon, and lord of Salins, son of Stephen, Count of Burgundy, and brother of Beatrice, Joinville’s mother. Moreover, Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, tracing the kinships of the Lords of Joinville with the Counts of Joigny, the lords of Vangion-river, Apremont, Grandpré, and others, states that Hescelina—wife of Guy of Aucromont, uterine brother of Thescelin, lord of Fontaine—belonged to that family. Thus he writes under the year of Christ 1109:

> The aforesaid Geoffrey, lord of Joinville, had a brother named Holdoin, who died in youth and left three little children, [Col. 1395C] namely Walter and Wither, who died without children, and Hescelina, lady of Muilly. A certain nobleman of Aucromont, named Guy, son of Fulk of Sarcelles, married her, and begot Werric, father of Walter of Muilly. This Guy of Aucromont was, on his mother’s side, brother of Thescelin Sorus of Fontaine, father of Blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux. They had other brothers: Holdoin, grandfather of Alberic of Esmancés, and Hainon of Colombey, father of Abelin. Moreover, Guy was, on another side, brother of Ulric, under whom the Abbey of Morimond was founded.

Thescelin could not have been connected, whether by consanguinity or marriage, with so many very noble families, unless he too were highly noble. The Sorus mentioned here by Alberic [Col. 1395D] is the same as Thescelin Saurus in a charter of Hugh II, Duke of Burgundy, dated 1106. Julius Caesar Scaliger writes concerning *halec* [herring], in Exercise 126, §2: “Salted and cured by smoke, it is called *Soret* in France from its colour, by a Gothic word; the term has also remained among Italians for the colour of a horse’s coat: for they call reddish-brown *sorus*.” Thus Thescelin was called Sorus or Saurus—that is, reddish-brown—apparently because his hair and beard gleamed with a golden fiery hue. For Geoffrey likewise says of St Bernard, Thescelin’s son, in his Life, book III, chapter 1: “His hair had a blond and fair colouring; his beard was reddish-brown, sprinkled with grey toward the end of his life.” See Jean Nicot’s *Treasury of the French Language*, under *Saure* and *Saurir*, and Ménage’s *Origins*, under *Soret*. Germans call reddish-brown [Col. 1396A] *Surich*; hence I conjecture that this word derives from one of the three ancient languages of the Gauls—the same language which, in another work, we have proved to be identical with German. Let us now proceed to his descendants.

We read of the marriage of Humbelina, Thescelin’s daughter and Bernard’s sister, but know of no offspring. She certainly should not be passed over in historical silence, since there is discussion of this woman’s worldly softness, almost transformed into an anchoritic severity after her brothers’ rebuke at Clairvaux, and of her monastic profession at Jully, undertaken with her husband’s consent. But Guy, Thescelin’s eldest son, had daughters still of tender age, as we have reported from Abbot William, when he withdrew to Cîteaux; indeed, they are said to have numbered no more than two. To at least [Col. 1396B] one of them her father’s and grandfather’s estate must have descended; perhaps the other followed her mother into a monastery.

From the Chronicle of Clairvaux published here by us, under the year 1183, we learn that one of these daughters of Guy was abbess of the Benedictine nuns of Polengy, in the diocese of Langres. When the Abbey of Bourlencourt, formerly Benedictine, adopted the Cistercian Order, the most holy virgin Ascelina migrated from Bourlencourt to Polengy by St Bernard’s permission, accompanied by her mother. This mother was a kinswoman of Blessed Bernard and of Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres, and was born in a village near La Ferté-sur-Aube; she may have been the daughter of Holdoin or Hainon, uterine brothers of Thescelin Sorus. We believe that another [Col. 1396C] daughter of Guy, heiress of the lordship of Fontaine, married Bartholomew of Sombernon, who is known also to have been lord of Fontaine—namely, through his wife’s dowry. Thus St Bernard’s paternal line has been propagated into various families down to the present day. For the descendants described in the Fontaine table as deriving, through Andrew, Thescelin’s brother, into the families of the Counts of Tonnerre and the Dukes of Burgundy, are found not to accord sufficiently with certain historical records.

Bartholomew of Sombernon, I say, was the husband not of Guy, Bernard’s father, already then a monk, but of Thescelin’s daughter, heiress in her own right, and consequently lady of Fontaine. Through her dowry he became lord of [Col. 1396D] Fontaine. Records of him at this time survive in the charters of Tart, Prâlonge, and St Stephen of Dijon. The Sombernon family was extremely illustrious, since by inheritance it entered the family of the Dukes of Burgundy, related to it by marriage. This did not occur through William of Montagu, great-grandson of Hugh III, Duke of Burgundy, as André Duchesne thought in volume II of his *Burgundy*, but through Alexander, William’s son and Hugh’s great-great-grandson, the first lord of Sombernon of ducal royal blood.

William, Alexander’s father, had married Jacquette, daughter of Hervey, lord of Sombernon, with the dowry of the fief of Malain. Hervey of Sombernon, son of Walter, grandson of Guy, great-grandson of Carnerius, had as wife Maingardis, also called Blanche; by her he had, besides Jacquette, a son John. When Hervey died in 1239, Jacquette had already been given in marriage to William of Montagu with the dowry of the lordship of Malain; he left his son John heir to the lordship of Sombernon under the care and guardianship of his mother Blanche. But when John died some years later, although the entire inheritance belonged to Jacquette, the title of Lady of Sombernon, along with complete administration, remained with the widow Blanche for the whole of her life. Meanwhile Jacquette died in October 1259, styled in the Necrology of Buxières by no title other than Lady of Malain; and not long after her, William her husband died. Their son and heir Alexander of Montagu bore only the title [Col. 1397B] Lord of Malain, even in 1265; indeed, until the death of his maternal grandmother Maingardis, or Blanche. When she finally died in 1272, he first began both to be called and to be lord of Sombernon, as the nearer heir of the said Maingardis in intestacy, in his own words. These facts are established especially by the records of Buxières and of the Priory of Bonvaux, nearly four miles from Dijon, commonly designated there as the Church of Blessed Mary of the Valley of Scholars, near Talant. From them it appears that neither William of Montagu nor his wife Jacquette ever possessed Sombernon, but only their son Alexander, after the loss of both parents, ultimately acquired that inheritance through the death of his maternal grandmother [Col. 1397C] Maingardis, or Blanche, not before 1272. So much concerning the principal line of the Lords of Sombernon.

Another branch, however, diverged from the Sombernon family: [Col. 1398A] the lords of Fontaine. Bartholomew, who established it through the daughter of Guy, lord of Fontaine, had two sons, Calo and Thescelin, the latter named after his maternal great-grandfather. The Necrology of St Benignus says of Calo: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September died Calo, lord of Fontaine, our friend, who gave us his share of Magnomont.” I think that Garnerius, lord of Fontaine, was Calo’s son or grandson. Many of his benefactions to churches survive, as late as 1230, a date which he does not seem to have survived by much; for in certain charters of Prâlonge, under 1234, one reads: “The lord Garnerius of Fontaine, knight, of good memory.” And by 1232 he seems already to have been succeeded by the knight Calo, son of Lord William of Saulx, of Sauz. The latter’s epitaph survives in the aforesaid Priory of Bonvaux, where he is called “Lord Calo of Sauz, [Col. 1398B] knight, lord of Fontaine,” and is recorded as having died on the day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord 1272. Calo of Sauz seems to have succeeded his childless maternal uncle, Garnerius, lord of Fontaine, being himself the son of Garnerius’s sister, who had married William of Sauz. The descendants of Calo of Sauz passed into the families of the lords of Saffres, Saigney, and Cléron. Moreover, the families of Noiron, Grancey, Charney, and others most renowned in Burgundy, distinguished by titles of baronies, counties, or marquisates, are mentioned as either kinsfolk or at least relatives by marriage of Blessed Bernard. It is not my purpose to trace their exact genealogies. Let this suffice to show that [Col. 1398C] Bernard, who is said to have been born merely in an honourable station, may most truly be affirmed to have been born not only of a noble but also of an illustrious family.

[Col. 1397]

## Proofs and elucidations of matters asserted or proposed in the *Disquisition on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux*

### I. 422  
*(From the Chronicle of St Peter-le-Vif at Sens, under the year 715.)*

[Col. 1397D]

King Dagobert the Younger died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February; he reigned in Francia for five years, etc. In the time of this Dagobert, St Ebbo, Archbishop of Sens, shone forth by miracles and was renowned for nobility. He was born at the castle of Tonnerre, and was count and lord of that district; yet, by the merciful providence of God, he was handed over by his parents for instruction in letters. By God’s gift, he surpassed all his fellow students and excelled them in both wisdom and eloquence. When he lost his parents, and was acclaimed to the rule of the castle and district which belonged to him by hereditary right, he secretly fled and served God in the monastery of St Peter-le-Vif under the authority of its abbot. In the course of time, after the death of the abbot of that place, [Col. 1398C] he became abbot. Afterwards, upon the death of Archbishop Gericus, 423 his uncle, [Col. 1398D] he was placed, by the acclamation of all clergy and people and with the king’s consent, in the episcopal see of Holy Mary and St Stephen the Protomartyr, and became illustrious for signs and miracles.

In the same place, a few verses later:

> In those days Lady Ingoara, consecrated to God and sister of St Ebbo, made over to Blessed Peter by testament her inheritance, which lies in the district of Tonnerre, when Chrodolin was abbot. After Chrodolin’s death, Viraibodus succeeded him. In his time, another sister of Blessed Ebbo, Leoteria, and Mummia, likewise consecrated to God, gave all their inheritance to Blessed Peter, while their brother Blessed Ebbo was still alive and confirmed the gift. These two sisters lie in the monastery of Blessed Peter, in the oratory of St Mary, where St Ebbo himself was also [Col. 1399A] buried; after his death he became illustrious by innumerable miracles.

Under the year 1065:

> In the year 1065 Bernard, knight and lord of the castle of Barremont, and his wife Humberga, negotiated with and received from Abbot Gerbert and the monks of that place the fourth part of the village called Richey, and of the church of that village, and likewise of the village called Poiseul.

Under the year 1074:

> In the year 1074 the monastery of Molesme was founded.

Under the year 1113:

> In the year 1113 the Abbot of Molesme bought from Milo, son of Bernard of Montbard, for one hundred and fifty pounds of deniers, the village [Col. 1399B] called Poiseul. This village, with its appurtenances, belongs to the gifts which Ingoara and Leotheria gave to the Abbey of St Peter-le-Vif at Sens, as did Richey; both were sisters of St Ebbo. They also gave, in the district of Tonnerre, the village called Fontaine, with all its appurtenances and adjoining lands; and in the district of Lassois, Bagneux and the aforesaid Poiseul, in whose parish Molesme Abbey is situated. Hearing of this purchase of the village of Poiseul, which was an allod of St Peter-le-Vif, Arnald, Abbot of St Peter-le-Vif, went to the aforesaid abbot with two of his monks—namely, Helduin the prior and Gerard the cellarer—and [Col. 1399C] lodged a complaint. The aforesaid abbot replied that he would speak with Milo, the seller, now a monk, who in this same year, 1113, had entered Cîteaux among St Bernard’s companions, and with others whose advice he needed; he would answer by the Rogation Days, which were to come first. This was done at the end of the year in question, namely on the seventh day before the Ides of March.

(It continues, under the year 1114, by relating that the monks of Molesme did not appear on the appointed day; that Arnald the abbot complained, when Bishop Joscerannus of Langres happened to come to Sens, both of the Abbot of Molesme and of Rainard of Montbard, who had withheld for more than eight years the rent from Richey and Poiseul, concerning which the dispute arose. But as the suit was drawn out at greater length by the various evasions of the Molesme monks, at last, in 1116, Bishop Joscerannus, after hearing the cause in his autumn synod, adjudged those villages away from both the Abbey of Molesme and Rainard, lord of Montbard, and awarded them to Bernard, Abbot of St John of Prâ, that is, of Réome. Rainard of Montbard then protested and exclaimed that he and his predecessors had held the Church of Richey as rent-paying from the hands of the abbots of St Peter-le-Vif for more than a hundred years; it had been wrested from him by episcopal force, and the Abbot of St John’s monastery had occupied it, without the knowledge of Abbot Arnald of St Peter-le-Vif. Arnald the abbot subsequently describes his appeals: first, before the Bishop of Langres, the Duke of Burgundy, and other magnates assembled at Châtillon, on behalf of the Count of Montbard and Clarembaud of Châpays; then at Sens before Conon, Bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See; and finally before Pope Calixtus II, down to 1120. He indicates that no other judgment in the case was made [Col. 1400A] because Abbot Arnald failed in both age and strength, and finally resigned his abbacy in 1124.)

### II. Thescelin Sorus; Warnerius of Sombernon, 1104  
*(Formerly copied by Pierre Naturel from the records of St Marcellus of Chalon.)*

Let all, present and future, know that Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, son of Odo, laid claim to servile rights over certain people in the dependency of St Marcellus called Fleurieux. The prior of St Marcellus repeatedly complained of this to the duke himself and to his prudent men, until, in the succession of time, they came to Lord Hugh, venerable Archbishop of Lyons, likewise nephew of Hugh by name. This prior of the aforesaid place also complained to him repeatedly of the same claim. After many complaints, it happened that the same prior, Hugh namely, came to the aforesaid village to plead a case with a certain knight, and that lodging was supplied to the duke in that village through which his route passed. There, through prudent men—namely Joscerannus, cantor of the Church of Chalon, [Col. 1400B] Rainerius, the duke’s seneschal, Thescelin surnamed Sorus, Bernard of Montfort, Warnerius of Sombernon, Milo of Frolles, Achard of Châtillon, and the duke’s other household men—the prior approached the duke, asking him to relinquish the aforesaid claim, so that his father and he himself might deserve to receive from God forgiveness for their sins.

Persuaded by the counsel of his aforesaid household men and struck with divine fear, the duke, acknowledging both his father’s sin and his own, said that he would do what the prior requested, but on the condition that he should receive some temporal gift in this world, while in the world to come his father and he might gain eternal reward. The prior therefore gave him one palfrey and two hundred sous in Dijon coinage. In addition—and this was what the duke greatly desired, and the principal reason why he made this agreement—an anniversary was established to be celebrated henceforth and forever in the church of St Marcellus by the prior and the brethren dwelling there, for his father; and one poor person was to be fed in perpetuity in the aforesaid dependency, Fleurieux, for both father and son. Once this agreement had been granted and confirmed on both sides, the duke went to the church of Fleurieux, in the time of Pope Paschal, on the Wednesday of Easter week. Before the altar, in the sight and with the approval of the men named above and many others, he released, relinquished, and gave up whatever right he justly had in the said claim; nor would he seek anything more from those men and women then living—whose names were Odilo, Warembert, his brother Stephen, Gausbert, and the others named there—with their wives and sisters and all their descendants already born or thereafter to be born. In [Col. 1401A] the same agreement, the duke also ordered his provost, then and forever, that neither the current provost nor any successor should hold a court at Fleurieux. If anyone subject to the authority of Fleurieux should injure one of the duke’s men, the duke’s provost was first to come before the prior, so that the injury might be remedied there if possible. Otherwise, before any retaliatory harm was done, the case was to be heard before the duke or before one to whom the duke entrusted it. If the person appointed by the duke did not decide the matter, the action was again to return before the duke.

He also commanded and forbade that none of his hunters, none of his *Bernarii* [a term uncertain in function], nor any of his servants should exact payment or commit violence at Fleurieux; nor should the prior of that place allow them to do so, nor any peasant give them anything. So that this agreement might always remain certain and ratified, bearing witness before God and the saints at whose altar he stood, and in sight of all present, he knelt until the completion of *Miserere mei, Deus* [“Have mercy upon me, O God”], and placed the book he had received upon the altar for the remission of his own sins and those of his father, with the kiss of peace and truth.

Hugh himself, Duke of Burgundy, confirmed this charter, his brother Henry approving it likewise. In the chamber of the Abbot of Dijon, named Jarento, he placed it in the hand of the venerable Archbishop of Lyons named above, with the praise and consent of Hugh the duke’s seneschal, Guy and Rainald of Grancey, Walter the constable, [Col. 1401C] and many others; in the presence of the reverend bishops Robert of Langres and Berard of Mâcon, and Hugh, Abbot of Auxerre; and in the presence of Hugh, Count of Troyes, and many canons of Lyons. Done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1104, indiction 12, concurrent with leap year, epact 22.

### III. Thescelin Saurus, 1106  
*(From the autograph of St Benignus of Dijon.)*

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in which year and on which day the venerable Lord Pope Paschal consecrated the church of Dijon, with Richard, Bishop of Albano, Aldo of Piacenza, Leodegarius of Viviers, Lord Robert of Langres, and Norgaud of Autun adhering to and attending him, after the placement of the holy relics in the altar, I, Duke Hugh, admonished by the Lord Pope, promised into his consecrated hand that I would leave the Church of Dijon in the same peace and liberty in which my uncle of good memory, Duke Hugh and monk, had left it. I also remitted and ended certain exactions and injustices committed by my officials, granting that henceforward all the houses of the monks of Dijon should be free from every molestation and jurisdiction of mine and of my men. In the borough also called the cloister, I granted that, if [Col. 1402A] a theft had been committed and the outcry came to the monks and their officers, they should administer full justice—by which we understand a fine of sixty sous.

I also approved and confirmed the toll of the gate of Dijon, which my father had granted from the monks of Dijon’s own wine, wherever they might be situated; and I added thereto the toll of the castle of Beaune from my own revenue. What I had done at Plombières for my father’s sake, I confirmed for them, and did the same at Villers, retaining this provision: that twice yearly I should have lodging at Villers. I placed this gift, made with the approval of my magnates, in the hand of the Lord Pope, and my brother Henry approved it. Witnesses: Savaric of Vergy; Valo, abbot of Lantonne; Rainerius, seneschal; Josbert, viscount; Hugh of Grancey; [Col. 1402B] Hugh of Poiseul; Thescelin Saurus; Hainon of La Roche; Walter of Tilley; Widric; his brother Hugh; Aymo of Châtillon; William of Til-Châtel; Benzo; Milo of Frolles.

### IV. Anniversary of Henry, son of Robert, Duke of Burgundy: seventh day before the Kalends of February  
*(From the records of Odo I, Duke of Burgundy, by which he gives four mills to Abbot Gregory and the monastery of St-Seine, for celebrating the anniversaries of his grandfather Robert, his father Henry, and his brother Hugh; third day before the Ides of April, 1093, indiction 1, concurrent 5, epact 20.)*

I grant all this so that the anniversary of Duke [Col. 1402C] Robert, celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; of my father Henry, celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of February; and of my brother Hugh, whose death occurred on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, may be observed.

### V. 430 Monument at Clairvaux of St Bernard’s mother  
*(From Chrysostom Henriquez, *Fasciculus Sanctorum Ordinis Cisterciensis*, book II, distinction 41, chapter 4.)*
