Likewise, there also lies a noble Lady of pious memory and most devoted to God, Aleydis, mother of the outstanding doctor and our Father Blessed Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux. She was first buried [Col. 1402D] at Dijon, in the monastery of Blessed Benignus; afterward, as the Lord willed and dealt mercifully with us, she was translated to Clairvaux, to awaken humility in us and enlarge our devotion, and was placed before the altar of the Holy Saviour, in the year of the Lord 1250, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### VI.  
*(From Chrysostom Henriquez’s Cistercian Menology, the day before the Nones of April.)*

In Gaul, Blessed Aleydis, mother of our most holy Father Bernard: though living in the world, she did not live worldly, but most lovingly instructed the sons whom she had borne to Christ. Glorious in many virtues and holy works, [Col. 1403A] on the day and at the hour she herself had foretold, she happily rested in the Lord amid the chanting of psalms.

### VII. 431 Chapter IV of the first book of the Life of St Bernard, composed in seven books by Guillaume Flameng, resident at Clairvaux and formerly a canon of Langres. Printed at Troyes by Jehan Lecoq for Mace Panthoul, bookseller. Undated. On the holy life and death of St Bernard’s mother.

After a certain time, as St Bernard grew in age and in grace before God and all people, and passed from childhood into adolescence—that is, about the age of twelve or fourteen—his mother, Aalet of the Castle of Montbard, having reared her children well and holily, [Col. 1403B] who were already entering the world, left this world, as though she had fully accomplished everything which was her duty to do, and went into the company of our Lord.

It should not be passed over in silence concerning her that, after she had long lived with her husband justly and honourably according to the faith and law of marriage, for many years before she died, so far as was possible and lawful for a married woman under her husband’s power and authority, who did not possess power over her own body, she wished to lead and follow the life which she had taught her children, and in fact did so. For although she remained in her house according to the order and profession of marriage, among worldly people, she led a hermit’s and religious life: eating little and no delicate foods; in lowliness and humility of dress and clothing; fleeing the pleasures, pomps, and vanities of the world; withdrawing and distancing herself, as far as she could, from the affairs, works, [Col. 1403C] and cares of the world; persevering in fasts, vigils, and prayers. What she lacked through not having made profession, she redeemed and compensated, to the utmost of her power, by almsgiving and other works of mercy. Thus she led this holy life, advancing day by day until the day of her death.

Among her other noble and excellent virtues, the devout lady was accustomed to go about [Col. 1403D] the houses, diligently seeking out the poor and sick, and giving them from her own goods what they needed. She also felt the greatest concern and compassion for poor, weak, and helpless people. She would have no help from manservant or maidservant in doing these things; rather, she wished to do them herself and alone. She herself went to their houses and poor dwellings, giving each person what he or she needed. She also visited the hospitals of the churches very devoutly and served the sick charitably: scouring their pots, cleaning their bowls, washing their cups and glasses, serving them food, and doing most humbly all [Col. 1404A] other menial tasks which male and female servants are accustomed to perform while serving their masters or mistresses.

She had also this praiseworthy and memorable custom: every year, on the feast of St Ambrose, she gathered to herself at Fontaine all the clerics she could find. On that day, in honour of God, of the glorious Virgin Mary, of the holy Doctor, and of all the Saints, she solemnly gave them a meal of wine and food. Finally, our Lord, wishing to reward the honour that, as has been said, she paid each year to the glorious holy Doctor, revealed to her some time before the Saint’s feast [Col. 1404B] that she would die on that very approaching feast-day. In this it is evident that she shared in the spirit of prophecy.

Thus the good lady, certain of her death, told and declared to her husband, children, and whole household what had been revealed to her. They were all greatly astonished. At first they would not believe that what she said could happen; but they were still more astonished when it was fulfilled as she had told them. For soon came the vigil of the feast, on which the lady was seized with a fever. On the feast-day itself, after Mass had been celebrated, she most devoutly requested that the body of our Lord be brought to her; [Col. 1404C] and this was done. Afterwards, when she had received the sacrament of holy unction and then the precious body of our Lord, she had all the clerics summoned and called to take their customary meal.

When they were seated at table, she called Guy, her eldest son, and expressly commanded him, as soon as the meal was over, without fail to bring all the clerics before her. Guy, most kindly obeying his kind and gentle mother, immediately after the said meal summoned all the clerics together and did as his mother had commanded. When the clerics had all come into her presence, the most devout servant of God, rejoicing [Col. 1404D] in spirit, told them that the hour of her death was near and humbly commended herself to their prayers. Then all together began devoutly to pray to God for her, saying psalms and prayers. She likewise said them with them and prayed most devoutly to God as long as speech remained to her. When she could no longer speak, so that her voice could no longer be heard, 434 she still moved her lips and tongue without ceasing until her final breath, praising and praying to our Lord and commending her soul to him.

Finally, as the clerics were saying the litany, when she heard: “By thy Passion and Cross, deliver her, O Lord,” she raised her [Col. 1405A] right hand, making upon herself the sign of the Cross. In doing so she yielded up her spirit to God, so that she could not lower the hand she had raised, but it remained uplifted as it was. All those present marvelled greatly at this. The holy lady was deeply mourned, especially by the poor, widows, and orphans, to all of whom she was a mother and singular nurse.

Her death was immediately known and announced throughout the surrounding region. Without delay the venerable abbot of St Benignus of Dijon, named Gerannus, came to Fontaine. He earnestly asked and begged to have the holy body, deeming it a glorious treasure. When this good abbot, both through reverence for and honour of her person, and through the intervention and goodwill of the good lady’s children, had obtained what he asked, he and those he had brought with him, weeping with compassion, received the holy body as a precious treasure and reverently bore it upon their shoulders to Dijon. Then the whole people of Dijon, who had set out to meet them with crosses and candles, came forward in great joy and veneration. Thus the body was honourably led and accompanied by all the people to the Church of St Benignus, in which the noble and holy lady was buried with great reverence.

Afterwards the venerable [Col. 1405C] abbot caused six beautiful images to be made above the lady’s tomb, in memory of her six sons. They remained there for a long time, and, as is to be believed, remained until the translation of the holy body, when it was later brought to Clairvaux. For in the year 1250, about ninety-seven years after St Bernard’s death, by God’s will, to ennoble and magnify Clairvaux forever and to stir its inhabitants to greater devotion, the holy lady’s body was transferred from St Benignus to Clairvaux. There, in the church, in the Chapel of the Holy Saviour, which stands in the middle of the ambulatory, directly opposite and near the tomb of St Bernard, it was [Col. 1405D] honourably placed and deposited on the nineteenth day of March, where it still rests today in that chapel called *Salvatoris*.

### VIII. Epitaph of Lady Aelis or Aelet, mother of St Bernard, composed by the same Guillaume Flameng

At Clairvaux in this sepulchre  
Lies Lady Aeleth, humble among the high-born,  
Born at Montbard, where she received her upbringing;  
Then she married the lord of Fontaine.

There she lived through years and weeks  
Under Thescelin, her splendid husband;  
[Col. 1406A] Yet in performing her human duties  
Her heart was devout and virtuous.

The noble lady had seven children,  
Six sons and one wise daughter,  
All victorious and triumphant  
Over sin and vain custom.

436 By her holy speech the mother  
Gave them admonition,  
As though for life in a hermitage  
Or entry into religion.

She humbly offered them to the Creator,  
One after another, as they were born.  
She gave them nourishment from her breast,  
And they were never fed on other milk.

[Col. 1406B] In this way they received nature  
And the good manners of their notable mother;  
Wherefore they eventually became virtuous,  
For a good tree bears profitable fruit.

Thus the lady governed herself  
After the manner of a religious woman;  
Serving God in body and soul,  
She was merciful.

Her devout household she maintained  
Under the fear of God,  
With food not delicately prepared,  
But contented it with coarse fare.

Of her children St Bernard was the third;  
[Col. 1406C] She dreamed of him while she carried him,  
And nonetheless willingly heard  
The interpreter who told her the truth.

For assuredly her dream signified  
That he would be a holy preacher,  
To correct the world, which was  
Full of sins and transgression.

From that time she bestowed special care  
On Bernard, the precious child.  
437 First she offered and presented him  
To Jesus Christ, the glorious King.

And, to make him rich  
In letters and wisdom,  
At spacious Châtillon  
[Col. 1406D] She placed him to learn learning.

When her children were grown and mature,  
She applied herself to ordering her household,  
Continuing almsgiving and good works,  
Watching at night in fasting and prayer.

Living thus as in religion,  
It pleased God to provide for her death,  
To grant her recompense  
With the Saints at the heavenly banquet.

Then an illness seized her,  
By which she departed this world;  
And without difficulty she rendered to God  
Her soul, pure and clean:

For, like one who is founded
[Col. 1407A] In complete devotion,

by profound contemplation

she received her last anointing.

The people of the Church, together with other household members—

clerics, priests, and laypeople—were present at her end,

chanting the litany,

as befits the worthy sacrament.

Then, answering with a devout heart

and showing that she was a holy lady,

at a certain point she humbly signed herself;

and, doing this, rendered her soul to God.

438 But before rendering her soul to God,

she made the sign of the Cross;

and she could not restore to its place

[Col. 1407B] her noble and distinguished right hand.

Thus passed away that most worthy woman,

accustomed to virtuous conduct,

who in the church of Saint Benignus

was reverently buried.

Thereafter Saint Bernard did not cease night and day

to urge his brothers and friends

that they ought to go and take up their abode

in a devout place, abandoning worldly goods.

But Andrew, who at that time was a good knight,

was negligent and slack in this matter.

At last, when he had pressed the point greatly,

he saw his mother, who was admonishing them.

[Col. 1407C] Saint Bernard and Andrew his brother,

speaking of religious life

after their mother’s death,

had a clear vision of her.

She smiled before their eyes

at their good intention,

and showed them an exhortation

to proceed from good to better.

In the year called twelve hundred and fifty,

the holy lady, exalted with God,

was carried from Dijon to Clairvaux,

to inspire pleasant devotion in us.

After the place had been prepared

in that fair site named Saint-Sauveur,

[Col. 1407D] 439 by worthy persons she was placed and laid there

near her son, Saint Bernard the Doctor.

Let us pray God devoutly

that He may preserve us from rashness;

and that, through the intercession

both of the son and of the mother,

He may make this monastery flourish

in every venerable virtue.

Then, after this austere life,

may they grant us His everlasting glory.

AMEN.

## IX. A certain sister of St Bernard, abbess of Pralon  
(Extract from the archive of the abbey of Pralon.)

[Col. 1408A]

A petition of the abbess and convent of Pralon, undated and addressed to an unnamed king, testifies that these ladies requested from His Majesty the restoration of their grange of Changé, then alienated. It had been given to them by the lords of Fontaines, their founders, in consideration of and as an endowment for the natural sister of Saint Bernard, then abbess of that abbey of Pralon.

## X. 440. Charter of the foundation of the convent of nuns at Jully

[Col. 1408B]

I, Milo, count of Bar, forewarned by divine admonitions, wish by these present letters of mine to make known to all Christians girded with the breastplate of faith and marked by that name the gift which I made of Jully as the proper possession of the Church of Molesme. Thus, if at any time some faithless man, ignorant of all goodness, should through crafty evasion rise up against my grant after me among my descendants, when this present writing is produced, let him know that, confounded by his own importunity, he must yield to truth.

Consider, I pray, the mercy of God in His ineffable judgment: the former inhabitants of the aforesaid castle of Jully, because they chose to dedicate it to demons rather than to God, are shown to have been subjected to desolation; and now, after a very long abandonment, the Lord through me assigns it, so to speak, to the possession of the faithful.

[Col. 1408C] Therefore, providing for the salvation both of myself and of my living and dead parents, I grant the castle of Jully, which belonged to my predecessor, namely Count Milo, to God and to His holy Mother Mary of Molesme, with all its appurtenances, as the parish of Saint Andrew—formerly established below it—contains them, with the approval of my wife and my sons.

And not only what remained under my own lordship there, but also whatever those holding from me have given or shall give from it to the Church of Molesme, I approve and confirm, on this condition and in this devotion: that the same place may serve religious women wholly, and that everything given to them by me or made over by others, as stated above,

[Col. 1408D] may remain assigned to their benefit and sustenance; and that these women may be able peacefully to serve God under the direction of the abbot of Molesme. At my request, Lord Guy, abbot of Molesme, and his convent established their manner of sustenance and life thus: from their own provisions and labor, from the cultivation by their oxen, and from the alms of the faithful, they shall receive their common food and clothing. They shall have no male or female slaves, churches, tithes, or villages; but, if such things are given to them by any man or woman, they shall remain to the church of Molesme. The women of Jully may retain other movable property.

Land also, if granted to them beyond what they cannot cultivate with their own ploughs, is conceded to the monastery of Molesme. For their governance in body and soul, four monks shall be assigned by the abbot of Molesme, to guard them in the Lord from every fault of private possession and wandering.

[Col. 1409A] If any one of them dies, the prayer and benefaction owed to the brethren of the church of Molesme shall also be rendered for her. Moreover, fur garments, apart from coverlets, are forbidden them in perpetuity.

> [Note: Col. 1409A] Pope Eugenius III, in a bull of the year 1145, says that this foundation of the convent of Jully was confirmed by Joscerand, bishop of Langres. Joscerand entered office in the year of Christ 1112, according to the Chronicle of Saint Benignus under the Paschal cycles; he resigned in 1125, on the feast-day of Saint Mammes. This foundation seems, however, to have been made in the very year 1113, in which Saint Bernard entered Cîteaux with his companions, or not much later. This is indicated by Abbot William, *Life of St Bernard*, book I, chapter 4, in Surius, p. 443, after the words: “And his branches beyond the sea.” There he reports that, since some of Saint Bernard’s companions were married and their wives along with their husbands had undertaken the same vow of holy life, through Bernard’s care a convent of holy women was built for them, called Jully, in the diocese of Langres. I know that Anna is mentioned as abbess of Molesme in the Chronicle of Sens under the year 1113. But Guy could have succeeded her in that same year, or in one of those immediately following, under whose rule the castle of Jully was assigned to devout women renouncing the vanity of the world.]

## XI. Warnerius of Subernum, his brother Bartholomew, and his sons Hervey and Guy, founders of the abbey of Pralon in the time of Saint Bernard  
(From the autograph of Pralon.)

I, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, make known to present and future generations that Warnerius of

[Col. 1409B] Subernum, with the approval of his sons Hervey and Guy, gave to the house of Pralon as alms, through the hand of the venerable Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and through ours, when the same house was built, the use-right of all his land: in its woods, for making timber, for pannage, for fuel, and for all the needs of the house; also fishing in his waters and pasture throughout all his land.

Bartholomew, brother of the same Warnerius, likewise made this gift from his own share and approved his brother’s gift. Warnerius of Age and Guy Garellus also made a similar donation to the aforesaid house from their lands. And all this was, after a long time, acknowledged at

[Col. 1409C] the aforesaid house in our presence.

The witnesses of this matter are the venerable abbots … [lacuna] of Saint Benignus, Albert of Saint Stephen of Dijon, Lambert, canon and sacristan of the church of Langres, Robert, dean of Subernum, and Wiard of Saint-Bury.

## XII. Foundation of the monastery of nuns at Tart, in the diocese of Langres, transferred within the walls of the city of Dijon in the year of Christ 1623  
(From the autograph in the archive of Tart.)

In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The gracious and almighty God, head and ruler of the holy Church, mercifully supplies the poverty of the poor from the abundance of certain of His faithful, so that in eternal recompense the abundance of the poor may repay the want of the rich with reward.

But modern gifts are usefully recorded in written memorials, to efface death’s counterfeit oblivion, so that mercy and truth may seem in this respect also to meet one another beneficially. Therefore we make known to present and future generations that, in the time of Guilenc, bishop of Langres,

[Col. 1410A] while Hugh governed the duchy of Burgundy, religious women were gathered in the place called Tart. By the concession and confirmation of the chapter of Langres, an abbess named Elizabeth was set over them, under whom a certain Mary held precedence over the others.

At the request, and also by the purchase, of the duke himself and his wife Matilda, a certain knight, Arnulf Cornutus, with his wife Emilina—who was afterwards buried there—gave that place to the religious women through the hand of Lord Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, in accordance with the determination previously made by Lord Christopher, or Lord Goceran, formerly bishop of Langres, together with woods and waters, pools, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

The witnesses to this matter are Simon of Vergy; Hugh, the duke’s son; Humbert

[Col. 1410B] of Favernay and his son Stephen; Aymo Caynus and his son William; Humbert of Fouché; Scotus; Milo of Pluvault; Guy of Vernot; Hugh of La Roche and his son Guy; and Aymo Rufus of Dijon.

These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, the eleventh indiction, concurrent V, epact I.

Those who held the place itself from Arnulf in fief made and conceded this gift: Lecelin of Longchamp, Aldo of Pruney, and his brothers Pons and Hugh, as well as Peter of Pluvault and his wife Mabilia, and all their children. Pagan of Pluvault also approved and conceded the same; and after his death, his wife Droa and their son Odo did likewise.

The ministerials of the same place also approved it: Hugh, Lambert, Aymbert, and Dominic, the deans, with their brothers, sisters, and children; likewise Durannus the mayor and his brother Unaldus, with their wives and children; Raynald the mayor, with his wife and children; Letald and his brother; Brutinus and his brother; Guy Pervers; Arnulf Gorgia; and other retainers.

[Col. 1410C] Finally, Arnulf, to increase the alms, at the request of his wife Emilina, from whose estate it came, gave to the religious women the tithes of Robore, the fishermen of Genle, and the fishery in the water. This gift was made into the hands of Elizabeth the abbess and Mary the prioress, before Bishop Goceran, Duke Hugh and his son Odo, Robert of Cristol, Maurice of Genle, and his son Hugh, and Simon of Vergy.

[Col. 1410D] Let all also know that Walter, priest of the village of Tart, gave the tithes of that place to the aforesaid church and religious women, with the approval and command of Bishop Guilenc, and of Arnald, dean of Dijon, so that perpetual remembrance might there be made for him.

The witnesses to this gift are Duke Hugh and Matilda, Odo and Hugh,

[Col. 1411A] and their sons Henry and Raymond, Aymo Rufus, William of Marigny, and Hugh Candart, his paternal uncle.

I, Hugh, duke of Burgundy, make known and confirm by this letter the gift which I made to God and holy Mary and her religious women of Tart, so that they may continually remember me. I therefore gave them, with the approval of my wife and my sons Odo, Hugh, and Raymond, the estate called Marmot, with its appurtenances, for cultivation and for whatever may be necessary to them.

The witnesses to this matter are Gosbert the viscount, Bartholomew of Fontaines, Gosbert of Grancey, Aymo Rufus, William of Marigny, William of Orguil, Odo Caynus, and Peter Gaberous.

> [Note: Col. 1411D] Since, according to the Chronicle under the Paschal cycles, Joscerand resigned the bishopric of Langres in the year 1125 on the feast of Saint Mammes, and Guilenc succeeded him on 27 September, it is evident from this charter that the monastery of Tart began at least in that year 1125, while Joscerand was still bishop; but that it was completed with buildings and enriched with sufficient goods in the year 1132.

## XIII. 446. Matthew, duke of Lorraine, in consideration of his mother Athelais having become a nun at Tart, assigns to the monastery of Tart a fixed annual measure of salt at Vic; with the approval of his wife Bertha, his brother Baldwin, and his sister Agatha. Year of Christ 1142  
(From the autograph of Tart.)

[Col. 1411B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Spiritual and carnal law requires us to do honorable things for friends, especially for those whom, after God, we are commanded and bound to love more closely by the tie of blood and the bond of charity. This is the saying of the Apostle: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

I therefore,

[Col. 1411C] Matthew, by the gift of divine permission duke and margrave of the Lorrainers, make known to all, future as well as present, that, inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, I conceived a heartfelt affection of deepest love in the service of my venerable mother, Duchess Athelais. By a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, poor in possessions and spirit, she had undertaken the purpose and habit of holy life in the church and community of Tart.

Therefore, invited by grace and by compassionate love for my most gracious and sweetest mother, for the remedy of my soul and the salvation of my predecessors and successors, with the approval and concession of my wife Bertha, and also with the consent—indeed, at the request—of my brother Baldwin and my sister Agatha, I granted by a most free gift, through the hand of the venerable Stephen, bishop of Metz,

[Col. 1411D] five *sesses* of salt at Vic to Abbess Elizabeth and the sisters of the church of Tart, to be advanced perpetually in the regular life. They shall possess them for ever freely and absolutely, without any reservation; and for this alms they shall more devoutly intercede with the mercy of God both for me and for the souls of my father and my kindred.

Finally, as a sign and safeguard of a perpetual record, we decreed that this donation should be strengthened canonically and lawfully by episcopal instrument, seal, and anathema,

[Col. 1412A] so that no violence or claim of our successors may hereafter alter it.

We have also employed suitable witnesses of both estate and rank, clerical as well as lay, appointed under our seal, most ready defenders for establishing the truth in time of need.

The witnesses of this matter are Walter, master and archdeacon; Embert, priest of Vic; Gislebert of Épinal; Jordan the physician; Albert of Romont; Walter of Gislebertviller; his brother Raimbaud; Odowin of Maillane; Welf of Mélisey; Rainer of Nancy; Arnulf of Gislencourt; Ulric of Arches; and Drogo of Nancy.

Of the household of Saint Stephen: Gerard of Jussey; his brother Guidric; Richard of Rinporth;

[Col. 1412B] Albert of Ventosa; Albert of Siey; Walter of beyond the Moselle; Theobald the butler; Bertran of Chastel; Haiméric of Vigneulles; Nicholas of Port-sur-Seille; and John Botes of Vic.

Of the duke’s household: Simon of Parroy; Gerard, advocate of Bruyères; his brother Warner; William of Arches; Folmar of Mucuns; Peter of Aleia; Bertald of Bithis; and Walter, provost of Nancy.

In the happy reign of King Conrad, in the pontificate of Innocent, indiction V, epact XXII.

## XIV. 448. Frederick, count of Toul, and his wife Hawidis confirm in the year of Christ 1142 the gift of salt receivable at Vic, which Matthew, duke of Lorraine, had shortly before granted to the monastery of Tart  
(From the autograph of Tart.)

[Col. 1412C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Frederick, unworthy count of Toul by the favor of God’s mercy, and my wife Hawidis, providing for the salvation of our souls and expecting recompense from God, have by free transfer given to the church of Holy Mary of Tart, to the venerable Abbess Elizabeth, and to the sisters serving God there, five *sesses* at Vic, through the hand of R., count of Bar, and Odo of Molesme. These had previously been given to them by Duke Matthew and his brother Baldwin, with the consent of their sister Agatha.

But because transfers of worldly possessions are often altered by the claims of successors,

[Col. 1412D] we considered it useful, in order to prevent this, to commit the matter firmly to the knowledge of posterity. Therefore, because we received the aforesaid gift as part of our inheritance, we freely gave what we had received and confirmed it with our seal, appointing suitable witnesses, by whose authority the matter may remain established and secure for ever.

Their names are these: Stephen, dean and archdeacon of the greater church; Hugh of Gondrecourt, archdeacon; Albero; Bovo; Renaud, count of Bar; Henry, brother of Count Frederick;

[Col. 1413A] Odo of Molesme; Falco of Mandales; Humphrey; and Ulric of Dommartin. Of the city: Henry the advocate, Henry of Cazenval, and Fulco of Saint-Vaast. Of the count’s household: Walo of Fontenoy and his brother Wiard.

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1142, indiction V, epact XXII.

## XV. From the acts of the general chapter held at Tart in the year 1268, on the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel

First, whereas it was formerly prudently ordained and decreed by the venerable father Lord Boniface, former abbot of Cîteaux, that abbesses who, detained by any reasonable circumstance, could not come in the year in which they were bound to come to the general chapter of Tart, should excuse themselves through prioresses or other respectable nuns of their houses, with letters: it is decreed that the abbess of Mostellot, who did not excuse herself either by a suitable messenger or by letters, but—what is worse—has remained absent from the aforesaid chapter for three continuous years as disobedient and rebellious,

[Col. 1413B] shall not enter the abbesses’ stall until she has personally presented herself to the house of Tart. Nevertheless, every Friday in the meantime she shall be on bread and water; and at the following general chapter, unless she can lawfully excuse herself to the person presiding over the aforesaid chapter, she shall be deposed from the government of the abbey as rebellious and disobedient.

Likewise it is decreed that all abbesses and nuns coming every year to the said chapter, so long as they are in the convent, shall not omit to attend personally, with the others, all the hours and vigils in church.

## XVI. 450. The abbey of Tart, of nuns of the Cistercian Order, head of many others  
(From the autograph of Tart.)

I, Guy, called abbot of Cîteaux,

> [Note: Col. 1413D] This appears to have been Guy II of that name, the sixteenth abbot of Cîteaux, from the year 1190 to 1202; afterwards cardinal-bishop of Palestrina and archbishop of Reims. The Cistercian necrology says of him: “On the third day before the Kalends of August died Lord Guy, archbishop of Reims, formerly abbot of Cîteaux.” The abbeys here enumerated as subject to the abbey of Tart are listed in this order in the bull of Pope Innocent III, dated to the year of Christ 1200: “Moreover, the abbey of Beaumont, the abbey of Étain, the abbey of Oulnies, the abbey of Poulangy, the abbey of Benfaes, the abbey of Colonges, the abbey of Mustraloz, the abbey of Chambenoit, the abbey of Droitval, the abbey of Lude, the abbey of Moleise, the abbey of La Selle, the abbey of Monastier, the abbey of Boiserotes, the abbey of Renoth, and the abbey of Saint Mary of Bourgueil.”

make known to present and future generations that Arnulf Cornutus and his wife Amelina, with the consent and by the purchase of Duke Hugh of Burgundy and his wife Matilda,

[Col. 1413D] through the hand of Lord Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, gave to certain nuns who had committed themselves to the house of Cîteaux the place called Tart, in order that an abbey might be built there.

In that place Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, founded an abbey of nuns living according to the institutions of the Cistercian

[Col. 1414A] Order, and there appointed an abbess in accordance with the form of the Cistercian Order.

Let all therefore know that the aforesaid abbey of Tart is a proper daughter of the house of Cîteaux, so that the abbot of Cîteaux has full power to correct and order whatever he finds there requiring correction and ordering, both in head and members, and to elect and remove its abbess according to the form of the Order.

Moreover, all the abbeys belonging to it—namely Beaumont, Étain, Poulangy, Beaufaes, Colonges, Valbaions, Corcelles, Mosterlet, Chambenoit, Droitval, Moleise, Lesclèche, Monastier, Boiserotes, Renoth; also the abbey of Lumine Dei, of Lude, and of Oulnies; and any others which may belong to it hereafter—belong by perpetual right

[Col. 1414B] to the care and direction of the house of Cîteaux.

451 Furthermore, it should be known that the abbesses of the aforesaid abbeys are bound to assemble every year at the aforesaid abbey of Tart, on the feast of Saint Michael, for the general chapter, which the abbot of Cîteaux holds either personally or through someone to whom he has entrusted his authority—except for those who remain absent by indulgence of the abbot of Cîteaux himself.

At this general chapter of abbesses, complaints must be made according to the form of the Order before the abbot of Cîteaux or his representative; and whatever requires correction and ordering must, without any contradiction, be corrected and ordered at his judgment and disposition.

## XVII. 452. Life of Saint Ambrosinianus, bishop and martyr  
(From a manuscript of the parish of Fontaines near Dijon, whose patron is Saint Ambrosinianus and where he is honored on the Kalends of September.)

[Col. 1414C]

### I.

There was a certain man, born of noble stock, named Agarus, in the Sarmatian city situated in the regions of Iberia, a country of Asia. He had a wife, likewise of most noble birth, named Sanna. Both were righteous, both feared God and observed His commandments, and they scarcely associated with others, lest perhaps they should offend God in word or deed.

At that time a tyrant king who worshipped idols ordered everyone to be compelled to sacrifice, and those refusing to be punished with diverse torments and various tortures. Agarus and Sanna, therefore, seeing the king’s ferocity,

[Col. 1414D] resolved to depart from there as soon as possible and journey to another city, mindful of the Savior’s saying: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10).

Having sold everything, they finally withdrew to Artemita, situated on the borders of Armenia in the same region of Asia. There,

[Col. 1415A] first resorting to the shrine of most blessed Giles, they gave thanks to God; then, buying a small house, they determined to settle and remain there.

### II.

Both being childless, after living righteously and modestly for ten years, they finally received offspring by divine intervention, and not without a miracle. For the woman serving as midwife, who had lost the sight of one eye, recovered her sight immediately while receiving the child.

When this was spread abroad and established as true among the city’s inhabitants, they began, even contrary to the custom concerning newborns, to celebrate his day with festal rejoicing, praising and blessing God, “who alone does great wonders.” Meanwhile, when the matrons asked the parents by what name they wished him to be called, they experienced another miracle.

[Col. 1415B] For, while the child hung at his mother’s breast, the first word he uttered was: “Ambrosinianus.” All were astonished, and seeing the name as if brought from heaven, said: “Let him be Ambrosinianus.” Thus, brought to the sacred waters, he was called Ambrosinianus.

### III.

When he had spent his childhood years simply at home, like the patriarch Jacob, and was in his seventh year, he was entrusted to the liberal arts. In diligence he surpassed his superiors, and in humility his inferiors. And lest abundance of possessions, as often happens, or youthful frivolity should make him in any degree proud, he devoted himself with all zeal to abstinence.

For he yielded nothing to bodily pleasure; he was frequent in vigils, constant

[Col. 1415C] in prayers, and outstanding in fasts. You would scarcely have found him in church unless praying, or outside it unless reading, unless the necessity of an imposed useful task hindered him. This brought no small admiration to not only his fellow pupils but also his teachers.

### IV.

Thus Ambrosinianus, excelling in learning and virtues, when he had reached twenty years of age, returned to his father’s house. Having remained there a few days, he resolved to renounce everything and leave the world, realizing that it was not safe to dwell with the serpent.

Bidding farewell to his parents, after long stages of travel he finally came to Sarlat. There he was kindly received by Nicephorus, bishop of that city, greatly loved, and finally ordained. He attained such virtue

[Col. 1415D] and excellence that he surpassed all others in the diligent performance of his office. Moreover, through a bond of devotion he was so attached to the bishop that he was not permitted to leave him by even one step.

One night, while both were keeping vigil in prayer and constant reading, it happened that the bishop, now worn out by old age, extinguished the light. At once he clearly saw an angel of God give Ambrosinianus a light. Astonished, he said: “Ambrosinianus, what does this mean?” He replied: “My father, the grace of God.”

### V.

At daybreak the bishop called together the leading men of that city. When he had explained the miracle to them, he declared Ambrosinianus most worthy of the episcopate. All, astonished at so new a matter, freely consented, except

[Col. 1416A] one of them, whose son sought the episcopal office upon the bishop’s death. But while dissenting, by God’s will he immediately expired before them all.

At so unprecedented a sight there was a great gathering of people. Ambrosinianus urged all to pour out humble prayers before God. He prayed too, and lay prostrate in prayer until the dead man rose from death. All marveled and rejoiced with the greatest exultation, praising and glorifying God, who had given such power to men. Thus at last the holy Ambrosinianus, though unwilling, was made bishop of Sarlat.

### VI.

Ambrosinianus, raised to the highest rank of the episcopate, attained such holiness, compassion, and justice that at that time he had no equal.

[Col. 1416B] For he restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute; moreover, he restrained many afflicted by demons. Thus the fame of his holiness spread through all the provinces of the world, so that people from every direction, eagerly desiring to see him, flocked thither and came to him because of his frequent miracles, for which they were held and moved by the strongest longing.

His parents too came running, blessing God who had given them such offspring. But the pious father, seeing himself entering upon such great honors, prudently wishing to counter the danger of ambition threatening him, and having learned from his parents who he was and why they had been exiles and fugitives from their native land, resolved to return there. At last he departed from Sarlat,

[Col. 1416C] all grieving, after having made most holy provision for his bishopric.

### VII.

Having entered Sarmatia, Ambrosinianus publicly undertook evangelical disputation. Immediately shrines were destroyed, idols abandoned, and everywhere the trophies of the Cross were displayed and raised up.

Meanwhile it was learned and reported to the king that a certain follower of the Cross had arrived in Sarmatia, who said that the gods were paying in hell the penalties for their crimes, and that Christ, the true Son of God, ought to be worshipped by all. He was ordered to be sought out; when found, he was bound, beaten, spat upon, and thus brought before the king’s gaze.

The king said to him: “Are you the man whom report has proclaimed as daring, with most criminal boldness, to profane the most sacred worship of the gods and publicly preach that some God, I know not whom,

[Col. 1416D] crucified by the Jews, ought to be worshipped?”

He answered: “Hear, most sacred king: do not think them gods, but rather demons. For God is one, by whose power I proclaim words of salvation, and I desire to gain all for Him; would that you too were not ashamed to know Him.”

“If,” said the king, “you do not cease from such folly, I shall have you killed by various punishments.”

To this he answered nothing.

### VIII.

The athlete of God left the king’s presence, and on the following day boldly entered a shrine full of idols. He ordered them all broken up and ground into powder. Then, drawing the sword of evangelical preaching there, he established more than three thousand persons in the faith and baptized them.

Again he was seized, beaten, and by the king’s command cast into prison, so that there he might perish from hunger.

[Col. 1417A] But God, caring for His servant, sent an angel from heaven, who not only healed his wounds but also supplied him with food. When many days had passed, the impious king, seeing the saint of God unharmed, said angrily: “Does it seem no small matter to you that you have despised our laws and, moreover, broken our gods? Choose one of two things: either sacrifice or die shamefully. For if you sacrifice, I shall set you over much.”

But the strong athlete was neither frightened by threats nor seduced by flattering words.

### IX.

The tyrant therefore, seeing the constancy of his spirit, ordered him suspended on the rack by torturers and his sacred sides pierced with iron combs. He also ordered salt scattered into the wounds of his blows. But amid these things the man of God stood unmoved, saying that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

At last the impious king ordered him beaten and crushed with hammers and iron clubs until he breathed out his soul.

[Col. 1417B] When this was done, his soul, whiter than snow among the angelic choirs, was seen by the worshippers of Christ. The king, unwilling to spare even his remains, exposed his body for dogs to devour. Frustrated in this desire, he ordered several others, almost killed by hunger, to be brought forward.

But meanwhile, when one of them smelled the bloodless body, he was immediately driven mad; rushing with swift step to the king, he bit him, so that the king too was turned to madness.

Those who had been instructed by blessed Ambrosinianus, seeing this,

[Col. 1417C] praised God, honorably buried his body, and founded a great basilica in his honor. Peoples flock there from every direction to his tomb in order to recover health, and they are not disappointed, this being granted to the honor of His servant by Jesus Christ our Lord.

## XVIII. Feast-day of Saint Ambrosinianus on the Kalends of September. Bartholomew, lord of Fontaines  
(From Part II, chapter 44, of the cartulary of Saint Stephen of Dijon.)

Since, as charity grows cold, iniquity abounds and truth gradually diminishes among the children of men, lest falsehood should ever prevail against truth, we commit to the written knowledge of present and future generations that Bartholomew, lord of Fontaines, once came to the chapter of Blessed Stephen of Dijon, and, while Lord Herbert the abbot, Warnerius the provost, and the other canons resident there were present, requested that a certain *journel* of uncultivated land lying before the gate of his castle should be granted to him and to his heirs who after him should be lords of that castle, at an annual rent.

[Col. 1417D] The lord abbot, with the approval and consent of the whole chapter, granted it to him on this condition: that if he or his successors did not render the rent due at the appointed time, they should be excommunicated

[Col. 1418A] until they paid it.

Therefore, on the Kalends of September, the feast-day of Saint Ambrosinianus, who is honored there, they fixed an annual rent of six coins to be paid.

On Bartholomew’s side the witnesses are: Guy of Mont-Roy; Guy of Hauteville; Pagan of Chaze; Guy of Échannay, knights; Robert, his mayor; his brother Vaslius; Ulric; and Warnerius. On the canons’ side: Engalrannus, their servant; Lambert the baker; Girbert the shoemaker; and, of Aqueductu, Ansius, Amicus, and his brother John, and many others.

## XIX. Relics of Saint Ambrosinianus  
(From the same cartulary.)

[Col. 1418B] In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1171,

> [Note: Col. 1417D] This year 1171 is reckoned from Easter, or from 25 March, and precedes by nearly nine months the Dionysian era begun from Christ’s Nativity. For in the Dionysian year 1170 the epact was I and the solar cycle III.

with epact I and solar cycle III, an altar was consecrated in the crypts of Saint Stephen by Lord Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, in honor of God and His holy Mother Mary, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Blaise, Saint Giles, and all the saints.

There were placed there relics of the wood of the Lord, of the Lord’s sepulchre, of the sepulchre of blessed Mary and of Saint Peter the apostle, of the garment of Saint John the Baptist, of the bone of Saint Lawrence, Saint Leodegar, Saint Medard, Saint Ambrosinianus, and Saint Honoratus.

On the same day, that is, on the Ides of September, the cemetery before the church of Saint Stephen was consecrated by that archbishop.

## XX. 459. Rainerius, knight, brother of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres. 1141  
(From the autograph charters of Saint Eugendus of the Jura.)

[Col. 1418C]

In the name of the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. GEOFFREY, bishop of the holy church of Langres, to ADON, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Eugendus, and to his successors in perpetuity.

Whenever the settlements of ecclesiastical disputes and the securities of peace between Churches are desired to be faithfully preserved for the future, it is worthwhile that the truth of the matter be recorded most firmly in written characters. Therefore I, Geoffrey, bishop of the holy Church of Langres [Col. 1418D], have wished it to be made known to the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, how, by God’s assent, the claim of the monks of Melun against the monks of the monastery of Saint Eugendus in the Jura, concerning the upper and lower churches of Barren, has been settled.

For letters having been delegated to us and to our venerable brother Hugh, by the grace of God bishop of Auxerre, by Innocent, supreme pontiff of the holy and universal Church, we, by his decree and after consultation with both parties, appointed a day for the administration of justice. When both parties—the monks of the Jura [Col. 1419A], namely, and those of Melun—had assembled with their abbots on that day and had most carefully set forth their allegations, the men of the Jura defending their right by apostolic privileges, episcopal grants, and determinations, while the men of Melun failed in their proofs, we resolved, in order to decide so great a controversy, to seek with both parties the presence of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

Having therefore taken the counsel of so great a man and of the other religious men who were with him, we—who, by the office entrusted to us, ought to secure fraternal peace, preserve to each Church its own right, and cut away reckless claims with the sickle of justice—considering the strength of the Jura monks’ case and the weakness of that of the Melun monks [Col. 1419B], have suppressed that long-debated claim. We have granted in perpetuity to the Church of the Jura, to possess without any opposition, those churches with their appurtenances concerning which the dispute was conducted, with the approval of Alard, abbot of the Melun monks, in his chapter, where were Raymond the prior, Jordan the subprior, Garin the cellarer, Arembert the sacristan, Anscher the cantor, Walter the physician, and many other monks of Melun.

Lest these things should be erased through forgetfulness in succeeding times, we have ordered them committed to writing and marked them with the impression of our seal. Whoever, therefore, attempts to act against the text of this present decree shall incur the wrath of God [Col. 1419C] and be subject to the bond of our anathema, until he has made worthy satisfaction for his presumption. And since witnesses must be admitted in every determination of a case, the witnesses to this matter are Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, by whose prudent direction these things were done; Guy his brother; Master Anselm; Walter of Troyes; Gerard of Montsaugeon; Hugh of Rivière, canons of Langres; William of Marzy and John, canons of Lyons; Ralph, dean of Bar; John, chaplain of Saint-Macou; Peter, chaplain of Barville; Peter, clerk, son of Guy Gontier; Robert, son of Odo Rufus; Rainer, knight, brother of the bishop of Langres; Renaud, nephew of Hugh the viscount; and Leobaud of the bridge of Arienne.

[Col. 1419D] These acts were done in the year 1141 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

## XXI. Guy of Sombernon, his wife Emengardis, and his nephew Odo of Mirabel. 1149.  
*(From the original charter of Prâlon.)*

In the name of the Lord. I, ODO, duke of Burgundy, wish it to be known to those future and present that Guy of Sombernon solemnly enfeoffed the church of the nuns of Saint Mary, established on the estate of Moloy, with all the territory in Moloy that was under his right, through my hand, as far as the boundary of the territory of Savigny, as far as the boundary of the territory of Baume, and the boundary of the land of [Col. 1420A] Meuilley; and toward Chaux as far as the path which, beyond the wood of Agey, leads those coming to Meuilley; and toward Mâlain as far as the hollow of the hill which lies behind, alongside Sarratte. This was done with the approval of Emengardis his wife and of Odo of Mirabel his nephew.

He also promised on faith given into my hand that, by the coming Rogation Days, he would peacefully relocate elsewhere in his land all inhabitants of that territory, and that, after notice of the appointed term, he would deliver the land vacant and entirely free to the Church, free of claims by them and by all others, whether monks or laymen, who had hitherto inhabited it. As for the vineyards which peasants possess there, the nuns were either to purchase them or receive a suitable rent in compensation. Likewise, concerning the share in the mill which [Col. 1420B] Huguerus held there, the nuns were either to purchase it or receive from the man a suitable rent from it.

Moreover, he granted as a pledge the mill at Chaux which Guy himself claimed, together with the other mills. When he has redeemed this and the other mills, he has agreed that one of those mills shall be given to the aforesaid Church for perpetual possession. If anyone, therefore, should defraud or diminish these gifts, he asked that I should be the Church’s protector against the claimant; and, so that all the foregoing may remain ratified and unshaken, he earnestly urged that the present charter be secured with my seal.

The witnesses are I myself, Odo, duke of Burgundy; Guy Garrels; Herluin of Tercenay; Garnerius of Agey; Peter, steward of Châtillon; Morel of Clermont; and Warnerius, son of the mayor of Fleurey.

These acts were done in the year 1149 from the Incarnation, in the twelfth indiction, the ninth epact, the fifth concurrent, while King Louis reigned and Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, was living.

## XXII. Bartholomew of Sombernon, called of Fontaines; his sons Chalo and Theselin. 1154. Saint Antellus is Saint Antidius, bishop and martyr of Besançon.  
*(From the original.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Autun, since [Col. 1420D] what we speak passes away whereas what we write remains, judge it useful to record in enduring writing what ought to be commended to the memory of posterity.

Let it therefore be known to those present and to posterity that Bartholomew of Fontaines, and his sons Chalo and Theselin, Guy Garrel and his son Odo, Lady Abba and her son Bartholomew, on the day when Theobald Garrel was buried in the cemetery of Moloy, granted to God and the church of Blessed Mary of Moloy, for the remedy of their souls, the land-rent of Curcelles, to be possessed freely in perpetuity. This condition was, however, imposed: that the aforesaid Church should pay them each year three sextaries, one sextary to each of the three persons aforesaid, half in wheat and the other half in *tremois*.

[Col. 1421A] It should be known that the sons-in-law of the said Theobald, who had married his daughters, both they and the daughters themselves, wished and approved that this gift be made. One of them, namely Buirus of Vitel, retained for himself the site of a mill at Curcelles, on this condition: that in building the mill Buirus should bear half the expense and receive half the profits and milling dues; while the church should pay the rest of the cost and receive half the profit.

The aforesaid land lies where the path divides, leading from Saint Antidius toward Unce. Moreover, the aforesaid men who made the said gift graciously granted to that church a certain portion of land adjoining the district of Saint Antidius. We do not wish it to be concealed [Col. 1421B] that the land-rent and tithes of the aforesaid territory are brought into the Church’s own right.

The witnesses of this gift and agreement were Robert, dean of Sombernon; Nicholas, priest of Moloy; Arnulf, knight of Échannay; Guy of La Cour; Lethold of Vergy; Peter of Saint Antidius; and Alemannus of Sombernon. We further wish it to be known that Robert Safredus and his brother Abba, with the consent of their children Stephen, John, and Galter “without land,” confirmed by oath that they would uphold the aforesaid gift.

The witnesses of this grant and oath were Peter the priest, William the physician, Bartholomew of Sombernon, and his sons Chalo and Theselin; Guy Garrel and his son Odo; Humbert [Col. 1421C] Garrel; William of Hartheu; Odo Berard; Morand Thuri; Renaud Guy of Sombernon; Barnuinus of Drea; Morel of Clermont; and Albert of Chace. In order that this gift may remain forever unimpaired, we have ordered that the present charter be drawn up, authenticated with the character of our own seal, and strengthened by the names of the witnesses.

Done in the year 1154 of the Incarnate Word, in the second indiction, the fourth epact, and the fourth concurrent.

## XXIII. Walter, lord of Sombernon; his brother Garnerius. 1188.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part I, charter 6.)*

[Col. 1421D]

I, WALTER, lord of Sombernon, make known to all that Haimo, son of Humbert of Moloy, in my presence gave in alms to the brothers of Bussières, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his parents, six rent-pennies which he claimed in respect of the territory of Trois-Vallées. Concerning this, he promised to provide warranty against all persons bringing a claim. For this he received twenty-two sous of good Dijon currency from the benefice of the church of Bussières.

If, however, Haimo should in any way fail in furnishing that warranty, I and my brother Garnerius are answerable, because he shall restore to the aforesaid brothers, out of the money which he received, twenty sous, and he shall demand no more from them until he has wholly extinguished [Col. 1422A] every claim. Haimo’s mother Hodierna, his brother Guy, and his sister Petronilla approved this at Sombernon, in my hall before the chamber.

The witnesses are Martin the cellarer, Guy, and Gerard, monks of Bussières; Garnerius, lord of Montillot; Lord Variminus and his son John of Dree; Humbert of Échannay; Marischotus, provost of Sombernon; and many others. And, that this may remain ratified, at the request of both parties we have secured it with the impression of our seal.

This was done in the year 1188 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Anseric held the abbacy of Bussières and Hugh governed the duchy of Burgundy.

## XXIV. Gerard li Broz, lord of Asnières, son of Lord Bartholomew of Fontaines. 1206.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XII, charter 1.)*

[Col. 1422B]

I, ODO, duke of Burgundy, make known to all present and future that Gerard li Broz, lord of Asnières, acknowledged in my presence that Lord Bartholomew of Fontaines, his father, had given and granted to the church and brothers of Bussières, in perpetual alms, rights of pasture throughout the whole district of La Chalor, and of the old mill, and of the *genili*, etc.; he himself and Margaret his wife, lady of Asnières, etc. Since he had wrongfully withheld this alms of his father, he sought and received absolution [Col. 1422C] from the aforesaid brothers.

The witnesses of this acknowledgment and approval are Bernard, abbot of Fontenay; Hugh the cellarer; John of Montbard, monks of Fontenay; Bernard, lord of Spissa; Acuns, knight; and Tecelinus of Nogent. That all this may be ratified, I have ordered it strengthened by the protection of my seal, in the year 1206 of the Incarnate Word.

## XXV. Walter, lord of Sombernon; his wife Jacoba; their sons Hervé and Walter; his father Guy; his maternal uncle Hervé; and his grandfather Garnerius. 1208.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XII, charter 2.)*

I, WALTER, lord of Sombernon, make known [Col. 1422D] to present and future that I have given to the brothers of Bussières, in alms, half the meadow of La Chalor, with the approval of my wife Jacoba and my sons Hervé and Walter, for as long as I hold the pledge-right of Lord Guy of Venarey. I have likewise approved and confirmed for them everything which they now possess through the bounty of the alms of Lord Hervé, my maternal uncle, Lord Guy, my father, and all my predecessors, or which they acquired by alms or purchase from their holdings or mine.

In order that this may remain ratified, I have secured the present charter with the impression of my seal.

This was done in the year 1298 of the Incarnate Word.

## XXVI. Garnerius of Fontaines, nephew of Gerard, knight of Asnières. 1210.  
*(From the original charter of Prâlon.)*

[Col. 1423A]

I, ODO, duke of Burgundy, make known to present and future that Gerard, knight of Asnières, surnamed li Broz, with the approval and consent of his wife Margaret, gave to the church and nuns of Prâlon, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his predecessors, in perpetual alms, everything which he possessed at Échannay, whatever he possessed in the two mills of the old mill, and whatever they might acquire from what belonged to his holding.

This alms was approved [Col. 1423B] by the nephews of Gerard himself, Guy of Venarey, Garnerius of Fontaines, and many others. The witnesses present were William, abbot of Fontenay; Robert the prior; and Odo, monk of Fontenay. That this may be ratified, I have strengthened the present document by the authority of my seal.

This was done in the year 1210 from the Incarnation.

## XXVII. Walter, lord of Sombernon; his wife Jacqua; his brothers Garnerius and Guy; his sons Hervé and Walter. 1210.  
*(Extract from the original held at the Temple of Beaune.)*

[Col. 1423C]

I, WALTER, lord of Sombernon, make known to all that, with the consent and will of my wife Jacqua, I have given and freely granted in perpetuity to God and the brothers of the Hospital of Jerusalem the Maison-Dieu of Sombernon, with all its appurtenances which I then possessed. I have freely granted to the men of the said house the entire right of use in my lands, pastures, waters, and woods, just as to my own men; and I have granted the right of use in my woods for the needs of the house of the Hospital at Dijon.

Moreover, I have granted to the house and brothers whatever they may be able to acquire in my land and from my fief by purchase or alms, excepting the town and the castle, on this condition: namely, that the duke of Burgundy shall be unable to acquire any lordship in the aforesaid house which I have given, through the Hospitallers. [Col. 1423D] My wife Jacqua, my brothers Lord Garnerius of Montillot and Guy, lord of Torcy, and my sons Hervé and Walter approved this gift. That it may remain more firmly ratified, I have strengthened these letters with the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1210.

## XXVIII. Hervé and Walter of Sombernon, sons of Walter and Jacoba. 1217.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 1.)*

We, WILLIAM, by the grace of God bishop of Langres, wish it to be known to all who read or hear this charter that Hervé, son of Lord [Col. 1424A] Walter of Sombernon, with the approval and grant of his brother Walter and of Lady Jacoba, his mother, on the very day on which his father was buried in the cemetery of Bussières, gave to God, the house of Bussières, and the brothers there serving God, for the soul of his father and of all his predecessors, in pure and perpetual alms, whatever he possessed, without any reservation, in the whole tithe of Mâlain.

In order that this alms may remain ratified forever, at the request of the said Hervé we approve it and confirm it by the protection of our seal.

This was done in the year 1217 of the Incarnate Word.

## XXIX. Hervé, lord of Sombernon; his paternal uncle Garnerius; Garnerius’s wife Aaliz; their daughter Agnes, a nun; their sons Garnerius, John, and Walter; Elizabeth, wife of the younger Garnerius. 1220.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part X, charter 12.)*

[Col. 1424B]

I, HERVÉ, lord of Sombernon, make known to all who inspect the present charter that Lord Garnerius of Sombernon, my paternal uncle, in the illness from which he died, while I heard and approved it, gave to God and the church of Saint Mary of Bussières, for his soul, in pure and perpetual alms, whatever he possessed in the tithe of Cormarrin, in all its revenues and without any reservation, except for two sextaries of wheat which he had earlier given to his daughter Agnes, a nun of Prâlon.

This was approved by his wife Lady Aaliz, his sons Garnerius, [Col. 1424C] John, and Walter, and Elizabeth, wife of Garnerius. In order that this may be held ratified forever, I have secured the present charter with the impression of my seal.

This was done in the year 1220 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

## XXX. Hervé, lord of Sombernon. 1225.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 6.)*

I, HERVÉ, lord of Sombernon, make known to all who inspect the present charter that, for my soul and the soul of my father and of all my predecessors, I have given to God and the brothers of Bussières, in pure and perpetual alms, [Col. 1424D] two *muid* of pure wine, for use at Masses, to be taken annually from my vineyards of Mâlain, which lie in the territory called Rooles, and to be rendered every year at vintage-time.

In order that this may be ratified, I have caused the present charter to be strengthened by the protection of my seal.

This was done in the year 1225 of the Incarnate Word.

## XXXI. Garnerius of Fontaines. 1230.  
*(From the original charter of Prâlon.)*

I, GARNERIUS OF FONTAINES, part-lord of Blaisy, make known to all by inspection of the present document that, for the remedy of my soul and those of my predecessors, I have given and granted, in pure and perpetual [Col. 1425A] alms, to God, Blessed Mary of Prâlon, and the nuns there serving God, for peaceful possession, the land on which stand the chapel, the press, and its grange at Changey. I have also given the same nuns a vineyard lying beside the said grange and a field adjoining that vineyard.

For the aforesaid vineyard, however, two sous of annual rent are due; and similarly, for the field, two deniers are to be paid in March. Moreover, through my land I have granted the said nuns full common use for grazing the flocks and herds of the house of Changey. Should they cause anyone damage, the damage alone shall be restored, without a penalty.

Further, in the thirds of Blaisy, namely at the castle, I have given the said nuns one sextary [Col. 1425B] of grain by the measure of Sombernon, half wheat and half oats, forever to maintain the lamp of the dormitory of the aforesaid nuns. In order that this may be ratified and firm, I have caused the seal of Hugh, dean of Saint-Seine, to be affixed to the present document. The said grain is to be paid annually at harvest-time.

This was done in the year of Grace 1230.

## XXXII. Garnerius of Fontaines. 1230. Otho and Kalo of Sauz, sons of William of Sauz. September 1231. Elizabeth of Fontaines. Emeniardis, abbess of Prâlon.  
*(From the cartulary of Clairvaux.)*

[Col. 1425C] In February 1230, GARNERIUS, knight of Fontaines, having a third share in the lordship and jurisdiction of the village and districts of Fontaines, grants the men of Clairvaux perpetual common use for every kind of livestock in the pastures of his village and district of Fontaines. Likewise, he grants a third share of Changey and its districts, with the approval of Gertrude, Garnerius’s wife, and of his nephews Garnerius of Blaisy and his brother Pons.

In September 1231, OTHO and KALO, brothers, young noblemen of Sauz, sons of Lord William [of Sauz], confirm to the men of Clairvaux the aforesaid gifts made to them by Lord Garnerius of Fontaines.

In December 1223, ELIZABETH of [Col. 1425D] Fontaines, with the consent of her children Guiard and Adelina, gives the brothers of Clairvaux a vineyard in the valley of Corrant.

In July 1235, EMENIARDIS, abbess, and the whole convent of Prâlon, by common consent and for the need and benefit of their house, sell to the brothers of Clairvaux, for forty livres of Dijon currency, their vineyard situated below Fontaines, toward the castle of Talant.

## XXXIII. Kalo and Otheninus, sons of William of Sauz. 1232.  
*(From the original charter of Prâlon.)*

We, Master ROBERT, chaplain of the duke, and O., deans of Christendom at Dijon, make known [Col. 1426A] to all who inspect the present letters that Lord Kalo, knight, and Otheninus his brother, sons of Lord William of Sauz, appearing in our presence, have forever quitclaimed to the abbess and nuns of the church of Blessed Mary of Prâlon whatever the said nuns had and held at Changey in rights of pasture and all other things. They have likewise forever quitclaimed to the same nuns whatever they themselves could in any manner claim at the said place of Changey.

In testimony of this matter, at the request of the said brothers Kalo and Otheninus, we have affixed our seals to the present letters.

Done in the year of the Lord 1232, in November.

## XXXIV. Garnerius of Fontaines, of blessed memory. 1234.  
*(From the records of Prâlon.)*

[Col. 1426B]

We, Brother DROGO, called abbot, and the convent of Clairvaux, make known to all who inspect the present letters that, whereas Lord Garnerius of Fontaines, knight, of blessed memory, had given us in perpetual alms a third share of the lands, trees, buildings, jurisdiction, and everything held at the place called Changey, we have leased that same alms in perpetuity to the abbess and convent of Prâlon for one *muid* of good and lawful oats. This is to be paid to us by the said nuns, or to our messenger, by the Dijon measure, annually [Col. 1426C] at Changey, on the day after the Nativity of Saint Mary, Mother of God.

If it should happen that the said nuns do not pay the said *muid* of oats at the aforesaid place and time, they have willed and granted that, whenever this happens, we may seize and retain in our possession both what we have leased to them and what they hold, or shall hereafter hold, otherwise at Changey and at Fontaines, in lands, vineyards, buildings, movable and immovable property, until the aforesaid *muid* of oats has been fully paid to us, together with all charges and damages which we have incurred through delay in its payment. The nuns shall be bound, concerning those damages and charges, to accept upon the simple word of the master of our house at Dijon, whoever he may be at the time.

[Col. 1426D] It should further be known that they may not alienate or put beyond their control anything which they hold at Changey and Fontaines, either from us or otherwise, except into our hands, provided that we are willing to give them, for what they wish to alienate in those places, as much as any other person or Church would give.

That these things may always remain ratified and firm, we have caused the present letters to be strengthened with the protection of our seal.

Done in the year of Grace 1234, in August.

## XXXV. Hervé, lord of Sombernon; his wife Blanche; their son John. 1239.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 2.)*

[Col. 1427A]

I, HUGH, duke of Burgundy, make known to all who inspect the present charter that Hervé, lord of Sombernon, of blessed memory, who was buried in the cemetery of Bussières, gave to God, Blessed Mary, and the brothers of Bussières, for the remedy of his soul and the souls of his predecessors, in pure and perpetual alms, with the approval, will, and consent of Lady Blanche his wife, five households of persons at Mâlain, with all their goods, reserving nothing in any respect for himself or his heirs.

Thereafter [Col. 1427B] the said Lady Blanche, widow of the said Hervé, exchanged those five households with the abbot and convent of Bussières for half a *muid* of grain, half wheat and half oats, by the measure of Sombernon, to be received every year in perpetuity at the grange of the lord of Sombernon at Mâlain, without opposition by any person. She thereby delivered possession and lordship to the brothers of Bussières, in such a manner that they may have, hold, and possess the said half-*muid*, and may freely, peacefully, and lawfully dispose of it forever by right of ownership, without a claim by the heirs of the said Hervé, the aforesaid Blanche, or any other persons.

Thus whoever for the time being holds the said grange or agricultural estate of the lord [Col. 1427C] of Sombernon at Mâlain shall pay the said half-*muid* of wine to the brothers of Bussières, without awaiting any further order from the lord of Sombernon. Lady Blanche, lord of Sombernon, swore into the hand of the abbot of Bussières to observe all these things fully, never act against them, and defend them against all persons. The aforesaid Blanche also promised and undertook that, when her son John, whom she had by the aforesaid Hervé, should reach a suitable age, she would cause him to grant, approve, and confirm the aforesaid alms.

That this alms may remain ratified and firm, I, Hugh, duke of Burgundy, have strengthened the present charter with the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1239, in May.

## XXXVI. Blanche, lady of Sombernon. 1242.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 3.)*

[Col. 1427D]

I, BLANCHE, lady of Sombernon, make known to all who inspect the present letters that Lord William Fromunt and Peter his brother, appearing in my presence, acknowledged that they had given and granted to God, the church of Blessed Mary of Bussières, and the brothers there serving God, in pure and perpetual alms, for the remedy of their souls, half of a certain meadow of theirs situated in the territory of Varoilles, and the whole tithe which they had and ought to have in the territory of Poiseul, etc.

In memory and testimony of this matter, [Col. 1428A] at the request of both parties, I have caused the present letters to be strengthened with the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1242, in May.

## XXXVII. William of Montagu, lord of Mâlain, and his wife Jacqueta. 1255.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 4.)*

We, WILLIAM OF MONTAGU, lord of Mâlain, and JACQUETA, wife of the said William, make known to all who inspect the present charter that, whereas the religious men, the abbot and convent of Bussières, had and ought annually to receive six sextaries of grain, by the measure of Sombernon, at our grange of Mâlain, from the alms of Hervé, late lord of Sombernon, of blessed memory [Col. 1428B], we, seeing that the aforesaid abbot and convent, and their agent, underwent no slight trouble on account of the said six sextaries, and wishing no longer to burden them or make them toil improperly concerning the aforesaid alms, have given, granted, and quitclaimed to them, in exchange and substitution for that grain, in pure and perpetual alms, our oven at Savranges, with all rights and appurtenances of that oven, etc.

Further, we have given and granted to the aforesaid brothers of Bussières, in pure and perpetual alms, whatever right we have or shall hereafter have in all the tithes and thirds of all the territories and districts of the village of Savranges, etc. [Col. 1428C] We further confirm and approve for the brothers of Bussières all the alms and liberties which the lords of Sombernon have granted to those brothers, in lands, woods, meadows, waters, grazing lands, and pastures, from the foundation of the said house of Bussières to the present day.

Since we have no seal, we have caused the seals of the venerable men Hugh, abbot of Saint-Seine, and Peter, archpriest of Flavigny, to be affixed to the present letters.

Done in the year of the Lord 1255, in August.

## XXXVIII. William of Montagu, his wife Jacqueta, and their son Alexander. 1259.  
*(From the cartulary of Bussières, part XIII, charter 5.)*

[Col. 1428D]

We, Brother HUGH, by divine permission humble abbot of Saint-Seine, and John of Sauz, dean of the same place in the diocese of Langres, make known to all who inspect the present letters that William of Montagu, lord of Mâlain, a young nobleman, and Alexander his son, having appeared especially and personally in our presence for this purpose, with prudent deliberation and desiring with all their heart to provide for the repose and salvation of the soul of Jacqueta, formerly lady of Mâlain, widow of the said William and mother of the aforesaid [Col. 1429A] Alexander, gave and granted, for the remedy and salvation of her aforesaid soul and of the souls of Jacqueta’s predecessors and their own predecessors, in pure and perpetual alms, to God, the church of Blessed Mary of Bussières of the Cistercian Order, and the religious men, abbot and convent serving God there—in whose church the said woman was committed to perpetual burial—half a *muid* of grain, divided equally between wheat and oats, by the measure of Sombernon, as an annual and perpetual rent.

The aforesaid William and Alexander assigned this half-*muid* of grain to the said abbot and convent, or to their agent, to be paid and delivered every year in perpetuity henceforth, before the feast of All Saints, from their two mills situated on the pond of Mâlain and from the rents and proceeds of those mills. One is called the mill of La Rochette and the other the mill du Mileu. On this account, the said abbot [Col. 1429B] and convent are bound henceforth, each year in perpetuity, to celebrate in their church the anniversary of the said Jacqueta on the Tuesday immediately following the feast of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, etc.

For the strength and testimony of all these things, at the request of the said William and Alexander, we have affixed our seals to the present letters.

Done in the year 1259, in October.

## XXXIX.  
*(From the necrology of Bussières.)*

On the Tuesday after the feast of the apostle Bartholomew: the anniversary of Jacqueta, lady of Mâlain, who gave us half a *muid*, equally of wheat and oats. We are to have a double and general *pittance*, as her charter provides. [Col. 1429C]

## XL. Alexander of Montagu, lord of Mâlain. 1265.  
*(French original.)*

I, ALEXANDER OF MONTAGU, lord of Mâlain, make known to all those who shall see and hear these present letters that, for the remedy of my soul and of my ancestors, I have given, quitclaimed, and granted to God, to Our Lady, and to the abbot and convent of La Boissière, whatever right I have, or may hereafter have, by reason of fief or for any other reason whatsoever—saving the jurisdiction, lordship, and guardianship, as we had them—which I retain in the land that Sir Aubert of Savigny, knight, gave to God, to Our Lady Saint Mary, and to the abbot and convent of La Boissière, for the remedy of his soul, in perpetual alms. That is to say, two pieces of land containing about five *journaux* of land, etc.

Because I have no seal, at my request there have been placed upon these present letters, so that they may have force and validity, the seal of the honourable baron Sir John of Sauz, dean of Saint-Seine, and the seal of the religious woman Aaliz, abbess of Prâlon. This was done in the year of Our Lord 1265, in the month of October. [Col. 1429D]

## XLI. Calo of Sauz, lord of Fontaines; his wife Dannez; and their sons John and William. 1267.  
*(From the original charter of Blessed Mary of Bonvaux, near Talant.)*

[Col. 1430A]

In the name of the Lord, Amen. In the year of His Incarnation 1267, in the month of August, I, CALO DE SAUZ, lord of Fontanis, knight, being of sound mind, make known to all who shall inspect these present letters that, considering and reflecting that nothing is more certain than death, and nothing more uncertain than the hour of death, I therefore, wishing to anticipate the day of my final harvest by works of mercy and to provide for my soul and for the soul of Lady Dannez, my wife, for the remedy of my soul and that of my aforesaid wife, and of our ancestors, and also for my anniversary and that of my said wife, to be celebrated perpetually every year in the church of the Valley of Blessed Mary near Talant, have given, granted, and offered, as alms and perpetual inheritance, by a donation made among the living, to God, to the aforesaid church of the Valley of Blessed Mary, and to the prior and brothers of the Order of the Valley of Scholars there serving God, whatever I have, may have, or ought to have in the villages, territories, and appurtenances of Dez and Altavilla: in lands, clearings, holdings, rents, thirds, and all other high rights whatsoever.

And with respect to all and each of these things, I have wholly divested myself and, through the hand of Brother Girard, then prior of the Valley of Blessed Mary, have by corporal delivery invested the said … prior and brothers and put them into true lordship and true and perpetual corporal possession. I acquired all and each of the aforesaid things from Lord Hugh of Patoes, knight, and Renerius, his brother, as a free allod, by lawful title of purchase. I promise in good faith that henceforth I shall not, either myself or through another, oppose the aforesaid donation and grant, tacitly or expressly; and I specially bind my present and future heirs to hold and observe all these provisions perpetually.

All and each of the aforesaid things, I, DANNEZ, wife of the said Lord Calo, and we, JOHN and WILLIAM, sons of the same Lord Calo and Lady Dannez, approve, will, and grant; and we promise in good faith to hold and observe them perpetually, each of us severally promising that henceforth neither we nor others acting for us shall oppose any of the foregoing, nor cause, consent to, or permit another to oppose them, by reason of dower, marriage settlement, avowry, acquisition, ownership, succession, or in any other manner whatever.

In testimony and security of all these matters, we, the aforesaid Calo, Dannez, John, and William, requested and caused the seals of the venerable men Lord Peter, dean of the duke’s chapel, and Master Alberic, dean of Christianity of Dijon, to be affixed to these present letters.

Done in the aforesaid year and month.

XLII. At the priory of Bonvau, of the Order of the Valley of Scholars, five quarter-leagues from Dijon, beyond Plombières and after the mountain of Talant: in the right wing of the church there is a tomb raised upon four pillars, about three feet above the pavement, bearing this epitaph around all its edges.

[Col. 1431A]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1270, ON THE SECOND DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER [31 October], DIED LORD BALO DE SAVZ, KNIGHT, LORD OF FONTANIS. PRAY FOR HIM, THAT CHRIST MAY GIVE HIM THE CONSOLATION OF LIFE. AMEN.

His shield bears a fess across the middle and three birds in chief.

XLIII. Alexander of Montagu, Lord of Sombernon. 1272. (From the original document of Blessed Mary of Bonvau, near Talant.)

[Col. 1431B]
