I, ALEXANDER OF MONTAGU, Lord of Sombernon, make known to all who shall see and hear these present letters that Amiars, called Blanche, formerly Lady of Sombernon, now deceased, in her last will, being long ago in a sound state of mind, for the benefit of her soul and for the celebration every year of her anniversary in the Church of the Valley of Our Lady near Talant, of the Order of the Valley of Scholars, gave and granted to God, to the said church, and to the prior and brothers of the said Valley of Our Lady, in pure and perpetual alms for ever, as one able to do so, her whole share of the tithes of Vilebarni, issuing from her own head, with all revenues whatsoever.

On the condition that, if that share were not worth one hundred Viennois sols each year, she wished and granted that the deficiency should be supplied from the thirds of the said place, which were and issued from her own head, as I affirm. And I, heir of the aforesaid Amiart, called Blanche, considering and desiring the repose of the soul of the said Blanche, for the celebration of the said anniversary, and in return for fifteen Viennois pounds, which the said prior and brothers have given and paid me in ready money, and of which I acknowledge myself paid, approve, will, grant, and confirm the said alms.

[Col. 1431D] And I promise, upon my bodily oath given upon the Holy Gospels, to maintain, keep, defend, and warrant it against all persons for ever, to the full extent of right; and that neither I nor another on my behalf shall oppose it, tacitly or expressly. To maintain and keep this, I bind my heirs, the said tithes, and the thirds; and I will that, to maintain and keep it, I and my heirs may be compelled for ever, as in the case of a matter adjudged or acknowledged in judgment and hearing before the court of my lord the Duke of Burgundy.

In testimony whereof I have petitioned and requested that the seal of the court of my said lord the Duke be affixed to these letters, together with the seal of the honourable man my lord Anxeri, archdeacon of Dijon in the Church of Langres.

This was done in the year of grace 1272, in the month of March.

XLIV. Alexander of Montagu, closest heir ab intestato of Maingerdis, Lady of Sombernon. 1293. (From the original document of the priory of Bonvau, near Talant.)

In the name of the Lord, Amen. In the year of His Incarnation 1293, in the month of June, I, Alexander of Montagu, Lord of Sombernon, knight, make known to all who shall inspect and hear these present letters that Maingerdis, called Blanche, formerly Lady of Sombernon, of good memory, in her last will and while in sound condition, gave and bequeathed in pure and perpetual alms to God, to the church and brothers of the Valley of Blessed Mary near Talant, of the Order of the Valley of Scholars, for the remedy of her soul and for her anniversary to be observed yearly in the said church, her share of the tithes of Vilebarni, which issued from the head of Maingerdis herself, namely in all revenues and proceeds whatsoever.

[Col. 1432B] On the condition, however, that if that share of the said tithes were not worth one hundred Viennois sols of annual and perpetual revenue, Maingerdis herself wished and granted to the said brothers that the deficiency should be made good to them from the thirds of the said place, which likewise belonged to and issued from the head of the said Maingerdis. All and each of the foregoing, the said Maingerdis was able to do both in law and in fact, as I firmly acknowledge that all and each of the foregoing are true.

And for the love of God and out of pious regard, and also for fifteen Viennois pounds, which the said brothers gave and paid me in ready money, I approved and confirmed all these aforesaid matters, as the closest heir of the said Maingerdis ab intestato; and I also promised to warrant the said donation to the said brothers and their successors against all persons.

And since, out of my necessity, I have sold and quitclaimed in perpetuity, for myself and my heirs, to Morel called le Borne of Flavigny all the aforesaid things contained in the donation, or those upon which the said one hundred sols had been assessed and assigned, the said Morel, for himself and his heirs, by reason of the things sold to him by me, is bound to render and pay every year and in perpetuity to the said brothers and their successors three setiers of grain by the measure of Flavigny, in compensation for all the foregoing things donated to the same brothers and their church by the said Maingerdis. I also give the said brothers seven quartels of oats as an annual rent, to be received and collected yearly and in perpetuity, before the feast of Saint Martin in winter, from those receiving and collecting my thirds of Sombernon.

Done in the presence of Hugh of Chalon, notary of Dijon; Lord John of Chaigniac; and Lord Walter of Comerrien, knights, witnesses summoned for this purpose, in the aforesaid year and month.

XLV. Arverius, Lord of Sombernon; Herverius, Lord of Saffres. 1233. (From the original.)

I, Arverius, Lord of Sombernon, make known to all who shall inspect these present letters that, after I gave to my dear and faithful Herverius, Lord of Saffres, the fief of Socé, he redeemed from me the pledge which I held in that fief, for one hundred Dijon pounds; and I am bound in good faith to warrant this pledge to the said Herverius and his heirs. And so that this may be ratified and firm, I have affixed my seal to these present letters in testimony of the matter.

Done in the year of the Lord 1233, in the month of March.

XLVI. Gilla, widow of Herveus, Lord of Saffres; Guido, their son. 1249. (From the royal archive at Paris.)

To her most reverend lord TH., King of Navarre, Count Palatine of Champagne and Brie, GILLA, Lady of Saffres, greeting and reverence with honour.

We make known to you that Lord Herveus, Lord of Saffres, our husband, died in his return from overseas parts. We therefore beseech your reverence, humbly requesting that you receive Lord Guido, knight, our son, Lord of Saffres, into homage for that fief for which our aforesaid husband was bound to you in homage. We, moreover, have fully released our right to the said Lord Guido, our son, Lord of Saffres, etc.

Given on the Saturday after the Epiphany of the Lord, in the year of the Lord 1249.

XLVII. Evilo, Count of Saulx; his wife Regina; his sons Guido and Girard; and his brother William. (From the pancarte of Albaeripa, drawn up in 1135, in the time of Wilencus, Bishop of Langres.)

Evilo, Count of Saulx, with the approval of his wife Regina, his sons Guido and Girard, and his brother William, likewise gave whatever he had in the above-mentioned districts, or whatever anyone held from him there; and, beyond these, all the aforesaid easements throughout all his lands.

XLVIII. Wido, Lord of Saulx; his wife Elizabeth; and his children Bartholomew and Beatrice. 1203. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

I, Wido, Lord of Saulx, make known to those present and future that I have approved for the brothers of Albaeripa, with the consent of my wife Elizabeth and of my children Bartholomew and Beatrice, whatever right I had in that part of the *vauria* of Archotoros which lies between Praalais and the water that descends from Vivex into the Alba. They were invested therein in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1203, on the second day of April. Simon, knight of Aspre, had challenged their right to it on account of a certain agreement between them: namely, that if the aforesaid brothers should acquire anything in the already-mentioned part of the *vauria*, one half should belong to Simon, provided, however, that he first repaid them half the price for which they had bought it.

XLIX. Evilo, Count of Saulx; his brother Villermus; and his son Guido. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

Let all present and future know that Rainaldus of Grancé, with the approval of his wife Agnes, and Evilo, Count of Saulx, with the approval of his brother Villermus and his son Guido, gave to God, to Saint Mary of the Valley of the Saviour, and to the brothers living religiously there, throughout the district of Corilimont all easements, both in lands and woods: for pasturing animals, building houses, cultivating land, and other customary uses, free of every rent and customary due.

This was done through the hand of Bishop Wilencus. Witnesses: Jocerannus, former bishop; Godfrey, prior of Clairvaux; Guido, monk of Clairvaux; David, canon of Saints Gemini; etc. Rainaldus, son of Rainaldus of Grancé, approved this gift, etc.

L. The brothers of the Valley of the Saviour give themselves to Albaeripa. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

I, Godfrey, by God’s grace called Bishop of the Church of Langres, wish it to be made known to future as well as present persons that the brothers of the Valley of the Saviour gave themselves and their small holding to God and Saint Mary of Albaeripa, into the hand of Lord Raimbald, first abbot of that place.

That place, namely the Valley of the Saviour, had been given by Robert, Bishop of Langres of pious memory, to a certain cleric named William, a Norman by nation, for the performance there of God’s service and for building. He and the brothers who were with him, under him and after him, from that time onward, during the times of my predecessors Jocerannus and Wilencus, bishops of Langres—some brethren dying and others succeeding—possessed it peaceably until our time, no challenge troubling them.

I therefore, yielding not unjustly to their rightful petitions, have kindly granted and by the authority of our seal confirmed this aforesaid place, given by the aforementioned brothers to the house of God at Albaeripa and to the brothers serving God there. Whoever shall presume to oppose the gracious donation of our above-named predecessor Bishop Robert and our own, let him be anathema until he makes fitting satisfaction for it.

LI. Evilo, Count of Saulx; his wife Regina; his sons Guido and Girard; and his brother Willermus. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

For the preservation of the memory of transactions, I, GODFREY, by God’s grace Bishop of Langres, wish by the attestation of these present letters to make known that, etc. Willermus of Saulx challenged the easements and rights of use claimed by the house of Albaeripa and the Valley of the Saviour in the district of Corilimont, and the pastures in the district of Columbe, asserting that the brothers of Albaeripa or of the Valley of the Saviour, or their animals, ought to have no rights of use whatsoever in the aforesaid districts.

Accordingly, when a day for determining the right between the parties had been appointed before us at Buxerolles, Abbot Rainerius of Albaeripa produced two valid charters, sealed with the seal of our predecessor Wilencus, Bishop of Langres, and strengthened by the record of witnesses. One of them contained a writing that Evilo, Count of Saulx, with the approval of his wife Regina, his sons Guido and Girard, and his brother Willermus, had given to the House of God at Albaeripa all easements throughout all his lands.

These easements are, namely, in waters for fishing; in woods for fuel, building, and the pasture of swine and other animals; free of rent and customary due. Both sides having therefore been heard and their causes carefully examined, it was adjudged by just judgment that all these things should belong to the House of God at Albaeripa, every challenge removed, as those valid charters testified.

Witnesses to these matters are Pontius, archdeacon; Alnaldus, then dean; Brother Morelli; Lord Odo of Grancé; and Lord Rainerius of Maresc.

LII. Guido of Saulx, formerly Count of Langres. (From the cartulary of the Church of Langres.)

[Col. 1435C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Amen. Let all present and future persons know that I, HUGH, Duke of Burgundy, have given and granted in perpetuity, as alms, to the bishop of the Church of Langres—namely, to my paternal uncle Walter and to his successors in the bishopric—the county of Langres, which I received from Guido of Saulx by exchange. I surrendered it into the hand of the same Walter, with the approval of my sons Odo and Alexander; also of Henry, Count of Bar, my kinsman, who had received the aforesaid county from me as a fief; and with the confirmation and approval of this donation by his brothers Theobald, Rainald, and Hugh. If they had any right in that county from their predecessors, they granted it as alms to the aforesaid church and renounced every claim arising from it. The same donation was further approved by Guido of Saulx, his sons Otho and Henry, and the children of that same Otho.

[Note: [Col. 1435D] Bishop Walter died on the seventh day before the Ides of January [7 January] in the full year 1178, as his epitaph in the Charterhouse of Lugny, which he founded, states; that is, in the completed year 1178 and thus in the beginning of 1179. Reckoning its beginning from Christ’s Nativity, it places the foregoing documents, dated a little before his death, at [Col. 1436D]. The necrology of Lugny, under 7 January: “The Reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Lord WALTER, Bishop of Langres, our founder and brother, died; he was buried at the side of the high altar in our church.”]

Witnesses are the clerics Manasserus, dean of Langres; Peter, dean of Bar; Ebrardus, provost of Saints Gemini; the knights Gerard of Reon, Viardus of Moriers and his brother Simon; Peter of Bar, servant of Henry, Count of Troyes; Bonius, provost of Châtillon; and Peter, mayor of Châtillon.

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1179.

LIII. Henry, son of Guido, Count of Saulx, son of Evilo. 1179. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

I, WALTER, by God’s grace Bishop of Langres, wish it to be made known to present and future persons that Henry, son of Guido, Count of Saulx, through our hand surrendered and approved to the House of God at Albaeripa, to possess by perpetual right, whatever his aforesaid father Guido had given or approved for the same house.

Witnesses: Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, my nephew; Peter, dean of Bar; Hunaldus, our chaplain; Rainaldus, cellarer of Clairvaux; the above-mentioned Count Guido, father of Henry; and Milo Delfosse.

Done at Châtillon in the year of the Lord 1179.

LIV. (From the same cartulary.)

I, WALTER, by God’s grace Bishop of Langres, wish it to be made known to present and future persons that Guido, Count of Saulx, surrendered to the House of God at Albaeripa whatever he challenged or claimed to possess in the district of Arcfrait, which long before his father, namely Count Evilo, had given as alms to the same house and which Guido himself had approved. The aforesaid Count Guido also approved for the said house the pledge of the meadows of Perregné, which belonged to his holding.

Witnesses to this are Hugh, then abbot of Fontenay; Rainaldus, cellarer of Clairvaux; and Milo Delfosse, knight. Otto, son of the count, approved all these things.

LV. (From the same cartulary.)

I, WALTER, by God’s grace Bishop of Langres, wish it to be made known to present and future persons that Henry, son of Wido, Count of Saulx, through our hand approved for the House of God at Albaeripa what he claimed in Arcfrait, which Eubolus, Count, grandfather of Henry himself, had long before given as alms to the aforesaid house, with the approval of his son, the aforesaid Wido.

Witnesses for Henry are Lucas, abbot of Charliou; Peter, abbot of Accinct; Wido, Count, Henry’s father; and Milo, canon and brother of the count. In the year 1170.

LVI. Foundation of the collegiate church of Saulx by Guido, Lord of Saulx, 1197, with the approval of his wife Elizabeth and his son Bartholomew. (From the original document of the church of Saulx.)

[Col. 1437A]

I, GUIDO, Lord of Saulx, make known to all present and future persons that, for the salvation of my soul, and of my father and mother, all my predecessors, ELIZABETH my wife, and my children, I have established canons in the church of Blessed Mary of Saulx, and have freely given them seven holdings in the castle of Saulx, suitable for building houses, to possess in perpetuity.

I will that these houses be so free that, if anyone flees to them before hands are laid upon him, or puts his goods in them, he shall be safe, with his goods, under their protection, unless he has been convicted of an offence subject to high justice. I have also given them lands for their own use, to be cultivated for crops or for the planting of vines.

Moreover, I have granted that, if any canon receives someone under his safe-conduct, that safe-conduct shall not be violated either by me, by my men, or by anyone over whom I have authority. I have also made available to them all my waters for fishing.

I have likewise granted that, if any canon has offered his wine for sale and meanwhile I prohibit, by edict, the offering of wine for sale—so that no one except myself may sell wine—that canon may nevertheless sell the wine already set out for sale. I have also given them four pounds in rents in the village of the castle and in my other land; all tithes of my grain and livestock; and a fourth part of the tithes of Saulx.

Further, I have granted the aforesaid canons that they may have at Saulx free holdings for freely retaining persons who choose to remain under their authority, so that, together with my men, they may enjoy full and unrestricted use of the woods and other things belonging to the castle of Saulx, free from every exaction of myself and my men.

Moreover, if any of my men gives them as alms a meadow or land from which I receive no rent, or if any knight holding a fief from me gives it as alms, sells it, or pledges it, I willingly grant this. My wife Elizabeth and my son Bartholomew approved all these things.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1197.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] Garnerius, Bishop of Langres, confirmed this foundation in the same year, 1197; soon afterwards Rainaudus, Archbishop of Lyons, confirmed it without date; and finally Pope Celestine III confirmed it at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November [22 October], in the seventh year of his pontificate.]

LVII. Wido, Lord of Saulx; his wife Elizabeth; and his children Bartholomew and Beatrice. (From the cartulary of Albaeripa.)

I, WIDO, Lord of Saulx, make known to present and future persons that I have approved for the brothers of Albaeripa, with the consent of my wife Elizabeth and my children Bartholomew and Beatrice, whatever right I had in that part of the *vauria* of Archotoros, etc., in which they had been invested in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1203, on the second day of April.

LVIII. (From the cartulary of the church of Saulx.)

I, Guido, Lord of Saulx, make known to present and future persons that I have granted my canons of Saulx the right to acquire for their church, whether by pledge or purchase, one half of the tithes of Saulx: namely, the share of G. de Blaisé and the share of R. de Corporey. No one except themselves may acquire those tithes, not even my heirs, unless it be for the benefit of their church of Saulx. My wife Elizabeth and my son Bartholomew approved and granted this.

[Col. 1438B] Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1209.

LIX. (From the cartulary of the church of Saulx.)

GUIDO, Lord of Saulx, at the request and prayers of Lady Elizabeth, his wife, suffering her last illness, gives to the church and canons of Saulx, for the remedy of her soul, one hundred Stéphanais sols, to be paid yearly on the feast of the Circumcision of the Lord. “My son Lord Bartholomew,” he says, “has approved and granted this alms to the aforesaid canons.”

Done in the year of grace 1222.

LX. (From the cartulary of the church of Saulx.)

GUIDO, Lord of Saulx, for the anniversary of his brother Lord Hugh, canon of Langres, gives to the church and canons of Saulx two setiers of grain, to be paid yearly, with the approval of his son Bartholomew. 1222.

LXI. (From the cartulary of the church of Saulx.)

GUIDO, Lord of Saulx, for the salvation of his soul and that of Elizabeth his wife, gives four setiers of grain to the chapter and church of Saulx. 1231.

LXII. James, Lord of Saulx; his wife Mary of Mont-Saint-Jean. (From the records of the church of Saulx.)

James, Lord of Saulx, with Mary his wife, founds the chapel of St James at Saulx, with a revenue sufficient for the food and clothing of one priest who is to serve in the said chapel. On Wednesday after the feast of St Michael on Mount Gargano. 1248.

On the same day and in the same year, he gives the canons of Blessed Mary of Saulx one fourth part of the tithe of Saulx, receiving from them sixty Viennois pounds.

LXIII.

I, JAMES, Lord of Saulx, knight, make known to all who shall inspect these present letters that, by divine favour, wishing to fulfil the vow of the cross in overseas parts, I freely, generously, and graciously give, cede, and quitclaim to the canons of Saulx in perpetuity two houses with their carts, etc., for them to hold and possess perpetually as freely as my grandfather, that is, the father of my father, granted them to the canons, etc., with the approval of Mary, wife of James, in the year of the Lord 1248, in the month of July.

In the same year and month, he placed one fourth of the tithe of Saulx, both great and small, into the hands of the canons of Saulx, for seventy pounds of good and lawful Stéphanais money, which he received from them.

LXIV.

In the year of the Lord 1249, in the month of March, Mary of Mont-Saint-Jean, Lady of Salion, formerly wife of Lord James, Lord of Salion, who died overseas, by his command gives to the church of Blessed Mary of Saulx twelve mines of grain—one half rye and one half mixed grain—by the measure of Saulx, to be received yearly from the thirds of Saulx, on the condition that the canons are bound to celebrate, in the said church at the altar established in honour of St James, one Mass every day, either personally or through another, for the said deceased James and his ancestors, except on Sundays, feast days and their octaves, and the octaves of feasts of nine lessons.

John of Passavant, Lord of Saulx, who then had as his wife Mary of Mont-Saint-Jean, widow of James, Lord of Saulx, confirmed this donation or foundation in the year of the Lord 1250, in April.

LXV. William, Lord of Saulx; his mother Mary; and his wife Margaret. (From the records of the church of Saulx.)

[Col. 1439C]

William, Lord of Salion, *domicellus* [young nobleman], October 1284.

William, lord of Saulx, young nobleman, with the consent of Margaret his wife, gives to the Canons of Our Lady of Saulx seven quartels of *conseel* [apparently a grain measure], to be paid every year on the feast of All Saints, for the remedy of the soul of the late Lady Mary, his wife, formerly Lady of Saulx, in the year of grace 1285, in the month of August.

William, Lord of Salion, young nobleman, and Margaret his wife, give to the canons of the church of Blessed Mary of Salion five mines of grain, for the yearly observance of their anniversary. February 1286. The seal is, it seems, a lion rampant.

In the same month and year, the same William, young nobleman and Lord of Salion, makes his testament. Among its executors he names first Pontius, knight, his maternal uncle, Lord of Ventoux. Among other seals, he orders the affixing of the seal of the venerable man, his dearest maternal uncle, Lord Stephen, Lord of Mont-Saint-Jean.

LXVI. Philip, Duke and Count of Burgundy, Lord of Saulx. (From the records of the church of Saulx.)

On 8 March 1442, Philip, Duke and Count of Burgundy, ratifies the goods, rights, and privileges of the Canons of Saulx as lord proprietor of the castle and town of Saulx; because of this transfer of domain, it was called—and is still called today—Saulx-le-Duc.

LXVII. Extracts from original documents in the Dole archive of the royal chamber of accounts.

Concerning Joan of Chalon, wife of Robert, son of Robert II, Duke of Burgundy, and Agnes, daughter of King St Louis.

In January 1292, William of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Saint-Aignan in Berry, assigns a dower estate to his wife Eleanor, daughter of Amadeus, Count of Savoy.

[Col. 1440B] In the same year and month, the county of Tonnerre was conveyed to William by his aunt Margaret, Queen of Jerusalem and Sicily. In the following year, 1293, she founded the hospital at Tonnerre, where, until her death, in a rare example, she rendered herself the servant of the sick and poor. From the records of Tonnerre.

In the year 1296, on the Friday before Saint Catherine’s day, William, Count of Auxerre and Tonnerre and Lord of Saint-Aignan in Berry, appoints and establishes as his attorney his father John of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, to receive four thousand *petits tournois* pounds, which the noble baron Amadeus, Count of Savoy, his honoured and beloved lord, owed him on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on account of the marriage of Lady Eleanor his wife, daughter of the said Amadeus, Count of Savoy.

In February 1299, William of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Tonnerre, makes a certain agreement with his beloved uncle Robert, Duke of Burgundy.

In the year 1308, Eleanor of Savoy, widow of William of Chalon, Count of Auxerre, and afterwards wife of Dreux of Merlot, Lord of Sainte-Hermine, claims her dower rights from John of Chalon, her father-in-law, father of the deceased Count William and guardian of William’s children, his grandchildren.

In the same year 1308, on 27 June, Philip, King of the French, consents that Dreux of Merlot, Lord of Sainte-Hermine, and his wife, widow of the late William, Count of Auxerre, transfer the right of wardship and custody of the children whom she had borne to William to their grandfather, namely John of Chalon, William’s father, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort.

On 10 November 1309, Margaret of Beaujeu, widow of John of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, is present at the homage performed to John, her grandson, and Joan, her granddaughter, children of the aforesaid William.

A title dated May 1311 declares that Hugh, Archbishop of Besançon, was administrator and general governor of John and Joan of Chalon, children of William of Chalon, formerly Count of Auxerre and Tonnerre. William was the nephew of the said Archbishop Hugh, and the son of John of Chalon, formerly Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, who was brother of that same archbishop. Hugh of Neblans, Lord of Courtenay, was guardian of the said children.

At Chalon, on the Tuesday after Trinity in the year 1321, Agnes, daughter of Monsieur Saint Louis, duchess, and her son Odo, Duke of Burgundy, on one side; and Amadeus, Count of Savoy, and John, Count of Auxerre, on the other, negotiate the marriage of Robert of Burgundy, son of the said duchess and brother of the said duke, with Joan, sister of the said John and daughter of the daughter of the said Count of Savoy. Present were Edward of Savoy; Amadeus, his brother; Guichard, Lord of Beaujeu; and Louis of Savoy, Lord of Vaud. One article of this treaty was that Joan would bring to her husband as dowry, among other things, the County of Tonnerre.

In September 1321, Joan of Chalon, wife of Robert, son of the Duke of Burgundy, renounces all her claims against her brother John of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, in consideration of his having granted her the County of Tonnerre as her portion.

On the Sunday before the Nativity of Our Lady in 1325, Robert of Burgundy, son of Robert, formerly Duke of Burgundy, together with his wife Joan of Chalon, formerly Countess of Auxerre and Tonnerre and Lady of Saint-Aignan in Berry, concludes a treaty with John of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, brother of the said Joan.

On 28 August 1344, Philip of Vienne renders an arbitral judgment in the dispute between John of Chalon, Lord of Arlay, and Margaret of Merlot, his wife, on one side; and John of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Lord of Rochefort, on the other; concerning the dowry of Eleanor of Savoy, mother of the said Margaret, for which the said Count of Auxerre, together with his sister Joan, Countess of Tonnerre, was surety.

LXVIII. Documents of 1126, issued by Guilencus, Bishop of Langres, concerning the foundation of the abbey of Morimond, previously made in 1114 by Ulric, or Odolric, Lord of Acrimont. (From the cartulary of Morimond.)

[Col. 1441D]

Guilencus, by the mercy of God bishop of Langres, faithful steward and kindly administrator of the benefices and alms which I have learned were liberally bestowed upon the church of Morimond, come forward as witness and authenticate [this record] by the impression of my own seal. First, a certain layman named John, religious both in habit and in spirit, sought and received the site of Morimond from Lord Odolric of Aigremont and his most noble wife Adelina. Immediately this same John approached Robert, then bishop of Langres, and, through my intervention, having received blessing and permission, faithfully built up the site granted to him, according to his strength and ability. After the death of that bishop, the said John, enjoying the favour of Jocerannus, who had succeeded Robert in the bishopric, and moreover having the counsel of Lord Odolric, offered and granted the site he had received to the abbot and chapter of the New Monastery [Note: [Col. 1441D] This means Cîteaux.] for the amendment of his life toward a better one. And when Stephen, abbot of the New Monastery, came, he received the site from Odolric and his wife, and from the bishop and chapter of Langres; and the cemetery of Morimond was marked out and blessed by the bishop.

Afterward Odolric, relying on the liberality of his own spirit and acting with his wife’s counsel, enlarged the site and granted a certain tract of land commonly called Gualdinvillare [Col. 1442B]. He himself, with his wife, many nobles, and the inhabitants of Frasnet, walked its bounds, defining his gifts by fixed boundaries. Moreover, with his wife he granted from all his fiefs and freeholds, near and distant, fishing rights in the waters, wood for fire and for various crafts, pasture through the lands, and rights of use in the woods for the animals’ needs. Fulco, Rainerius, and Gerard, sons of Odolric, granted all these gifts. Witnesses with me to all this, who saw and heard it in person, are Hugh the knight called Lupa, Odolric of Provenchères, Girard of Dommartin, Hugh of Mosa, Arlebaud of Varennes, Rocelin of Bourbon, etc.

And because Odolric held these lands—namely Morimond and Galdinvillare [Col. 1442C]—from the count of Clermont in fief, the aforesaid abbot swiftly obtained confirmation from that count in full court, etc. Then the aforesaid abbot of the New Monastery established as abbot in that place a man wholly venerable, named Arnald, directing the monks faithfully to observe the Rule of blessed Benedict which they had learned. Thereafter, when I, at that time dean and archdeacon, succeeded by God’s appointment to the bishopric, Odolric with his wife and the above-named sons consecrated by perpetual legal gift to the brethren of Morimond all the land of Frasnet and Galdinvillare, as far as the boundaries of Romans and Damblin, as the stream flowing from Old Morimond runs past.

I confirm and strengthen all these gifts under anathema [Col. 1442D], and entrust them to my archdeacons for confirmation.

Sign of Lambert, treasurer.  
Sign of Jocelin, archdeacon.  
Sign of Airard, archdeacon.  
Sign of Guy, archdeacon.  
Sign of Fulco, archdeacon.  
Sign of Garnerius, archdeacon.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1126, in the pontificate of Pope Honorius, in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and in the episcopate of Guilencus of Langres.

I, Durannus, notary of Langres, acting in place of Fulco the chancellor, dictated and read aloud [this document]. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1441D] From the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne under the Paschal Cycles: Robert, who had succeeded Rainard in the bishopric of Langres in 1077, died in 1110. Jocerannus succeeded him two years later [Col. 1442D], but finally resigned in 1125 and left Guilencus as his successor in the bishopric from 27 September. From this it is understood that John had already been a hermit at Morimond at least by 1110, and before the death of Bishop Robert [Col. 1443D]. But an old inscription in the cartulary of Morimond fixes the day and year when Morimond Abbey was founded under the Cistercian rule [Col. 1444D], and lists its first twenty-four daughter houses in the following order.]

Morimond Abbey was founded on 11 July, in the year [Col. 1443A] 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord. The number and order of abbeys established by monks of Morimond are as follows: first Bellevaux; second La Crête; third Le Champ; fourth Eberbach; fifth Theuley; sixth Clairefontaine; seventh Berges; eighth Bethany; ninth Belleprairie; tenth Holy Cross; eleventh Villers; twelfth La Couronne; thirteenth Scala Dei; fourteenth Belledon; fifteenth Bonnefont; sixteenth Aiguebelle; seventeenth Mont-Saint-Georges; eighteenth Francavalle; nineteenth Valdora; twentieth Silvacane; twenty-first Brisenrz [uncertain reading]; twenty-second Mont-Dieu; twenty-third Charrubium; twenty-fourth Eisaie.

From some of these, many others have, by God’s working, been spread through various lands.

506. LXIX. Rainerius, lord of Aigremont, confirms to the monks of Morimond the gifts of his father Ulric, or Odolric. 1148. (From the cartulary of Morimond.)

[Col. 1443B]

I, Humbert, by the grace of God dean of the Church of Langres, make known to all the faithful the gifts which Lord Rainerius of Aigremont made and acknowledged before us to the Church of Morimond, in the presence of Lords Rainard and Rainerius, his nephews, and Pontius and Jocelin, archdeacons of our church, at the time when Pope Eugenius entered Langres. These gifts are those which his father Ulric had bestowed upon the Church of Morimond from its foundation: namely, rights of use in the waters throughout all his land, and woodland for fires and for timber-work, etc. Witnesses [Col. 1443C]: Gerard, brother of that Rainerius; Gerard of Beaumont; etc. His wife also granted the same, etc.

Therefore, that this gift may remain firm and secure, we protect and confirm it by our authority and by the seal of the chapter of Langres. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1148; concurrent 4, indiction 11, epact 28.

LXX. Gerard Sineterra, brother of Rainerius, lord of Aigremont. (From the same cartulary.)

Let all know that Lord Rainerius of Aigremont gave in perpetuity to Blessed Mary of Morimond Abbey and to the brethren serving God there a small piece of land above the abbey, on this condition: that they should plant a garden there. Present at this gift and witnesses are Gerard Sineterra, brother of the said Rainerius; Hugh, steward of Frasnet; and his son Gerard. [Col. 1443D]

LXXI. Ulric the canon and Gerard Sineterra, brothers of Rainerius, lord of Aigremont. (From the same cartulary.)

I, Godefridus, by the grace of God bishop of Langres, make known to all faithful persons present and future, and confirm by the seal of our authority, that Rainerius, lord of Aigremont, with the consent and approval [Col. 1444A] of his brothers Ulric the canon and Gerard Sineterra, granted and conveyed in perpetual right to the brethren of Morimond a certain tract of land: everything enclosed within the boundary running and dividing in a straight line from the corner of Brother Stephen’s orchard to the beginning of the new pond, where there had been a bridge whose road led to Blanchart, toward Morimond. Witnesses to all this are Lambert, abbot of Belleprairie; Roland the knight; and Gerard and Ulric, brothers of Rainerius himself. His daughter Agnes also granted and approved all this.

LXXII. Enlargement of Molême Monastery. (From the charters of Molême.)

[Col. 1444B] I, Hugh, count of Champagne, son of Count Theobald, desire it to be known to all faithful members of holy Church, present and future, that, guided by a higher counsel, I have resolved to enlarge the church of Molême from my own revenues, knowing most certainly that I shall have a greater share in heavenly things in proportion as I have more richly honoured that church. Therefore I give and grant to that church, for perpetual possession, from property under my jurisdiction, the village called Rumilly, together with authority and jurisdiction over that village after my death, in woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, male and female serfs, and in every customary use—excepting the wife of Leobaud of Troyes and their children—and, for the present, half the revenues as investiture [Col. 1444C].

I also give the said church revenues from the sale of salt, namely the saltworks of Bar-sur-Aube, and jurisdiction over the saltworks if anyone commits an offence concerning them. Likewise, in the estate at Isles, I give what my father had given: namely the village of Saint-Theobald of Volva, two mills situated upon the bank of the Seine, my entire cultivated estate commonly called Cumina, other portions of fields belonging to my jurisdiction, and the meadow adjoining the wall of Troyes, which my brother Count Odo gave to the church of Saint-Quentin of Troyes; I give and grant these for perpetual possession. At Isles I also give and grant the manorial oven. Likewise, I give the mill of Largicourte as I hold it, a certain cultivated estate by the bank of Vallis Coloris, and a third share in the mill [Col. 1444D] and a third share in the oven.

To this gift I added, in the territory of Reims, the village of Saint Walburga, otherwise called Dyona, with its appurtenances and jurisdiction. My wife Constance, daughter of the king of the Franks, and Countess Adela, wife of my brother Stephen, together with her sons, my nephews, approved all these things. Manasses, archbishop of Reims, with his clergy, gave his assent to this gift concerning matters which belonged to him.

These things were enacted at Troyes, on 2 April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1104, indiction 12; [Col. 1445A] epact 22, concurrent 5, while Paschal presided as Roman pontiff, Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, was dealing with ecclesiastical business at Troyes in a general council, and Philip reigned as king of the Franks.

This gift of the aforesaid possessions, solemnly made by me to the church of Molême and read aloud in the church of Troyes before the whole synod, was approved by the said cardinal and generally commended by the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and clerics sitting with him. To strengthen it, I caused these suitable and sufficient witnesses to be entered in this charter. They are Daymbert, archbishop of Sens, and Radulf, archbishop of Tours; the bishops Ivo of Chartres, Humbald of Auxerre, Herveus of Nevers, Marbod [Col. 1445B] of Rennes, Robert of Langres, Norgaud of Autun, Hugh of Châlons, and Philip of Troyes; Regnaud the provost; and Girard, Jocelin, and Droco, archdeacons. Also the abbots Ilgond of Marmoutier, Lambert of Pultariensis, Radulf of La Celle, and Otho of Arremar. Lay witnesses were Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine; Milo, lord of Chacennaic; Wido, lord of Vangionis Rivus; Gaufred, son of Ottrannus; and Renerius of Châtillon.

After these matters had thus been performed in the council of Troyes and solemnly authenticated by a sentence of excommunication, so that they could not thereafter be infringed, I myself came to Molême to transact my own affairs and theirs, accompanied by noble men: Hugh Borel, duke of Burgundy; William, count of Nevers; the said count of Bar; Airard, count of Brienne; Hugh [Col. 1445C], count of Risnel; Jofred, lord of Calvimont; Roger, lord of Joigny; and Pontius, lord of Traînel. Robert, the first abbot of that place, honourably received me and them with his monks. After prayer, I approached the high altar. In the presence of the said duke and the four counts and aforesaid barons, I surrendered to the same church for perpetual possession the half of Rumilly which I had retained during my lifetime before coming to Molême and had planned to give there after my death—for the church already possessed the other half in full. Drawing a ring from my own finger and laying upon the altar the gift of full authority over Rumilly, I conveyed the said authority [Col. 1445D] to the church, adding that if anyone of my household should wish to give anything to that church, he should be permitted to do so. I grant that this shall remain ratified and firm forever.

The said counts of Nevers, Bar, Brienne, and Risnel, and the said barons standing with me, saw that I had so granted to that church what belonged to my household. Moved by my example and induced by my prayers, each of them, together with the said duke, granted to the same church for perpetual possession whatever the monks of that church might in any manner acquire in the future from their respective households. Witnesses with me are Walter, viscount of Clamecy; Hugh of Tilly; Andrew, count of Ramerupt, giver and grantor to the church of what belonged to his household; Hugh [Col. 1446A], surnamed the Breton, his son; Gaufred, son of Ottrannus; Leobaud and Grimaud of Troyes; and the boy Theobald, son of Count Stephen, my brother.

The said count of Bar added to his grant by giving that church fishing rights in his waters near his village of Vertoil. I also, when later setting out for Jerusalem, went to Molême for prayer, and there added to the preceding gift all the men with their wives and children who lived at Troyes under the authority of Rumilly. I granted security to them all, whose heads belong to the said church under the authority of Rumilly; and I further granted that the church should possess those who remained at Troyes or at Isles under that same authority, so that nothing [Col. 1446B] should be diminished or detached from it, except the wife of Leobaud and her children.

Although these gifts of mine and of the said princes, including the said duke, were conferred upon the church of Molême at different times, I nevertheless wished them all to be gathered together in this document and, that they might henceforth remain inviolate, fully confirmed by the impression of my seal together with the witnesses written above. If anything from the gifts of my father, my brothers, or myself is written here less fully than justice requires, I do not on that account remove from this confirmation those things which could not be set down in writing for remembrance, but which had nevertheless long ago been given to the church by myself and by them. Rather, I decree that, just like the written instruments recorded here which that church has hitherto held, they shall remain wholly fixed.

[Col. 1446C] This was done and confirmed at Châtillon-sur-Seine in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1108, in the presence of these witnesses: William, count of Nevers; Airard, count of Brienne; Milo of Bar; Hugh, count of Risnel; Wido of Wannelruc; and many others. Moreover I, Count Theobald, devoutly following in the footsteps of the said Hugh, my uncle, when he was setting out in devotion for Jerusalem, at his request confirmed by my seal that the church of Molême should possess forever whatever he himself had confirmed to it. Further, I willingly granted and ratified to them whatever that church might in any way acquire from my household, witnesses being Milo, count of Bar; Wido, lord of Vangionis Rivus; and many others.

LXXIII. Letter XXXI of Saint Bernard to Hugh, count of Champagne, who had become a Knight Templar.

[Col. 1446D]

If you have become, for God’s cause, a knight from a count and poor from rich, then indeed we rejoice for you, as is right, and glorify God in you, knowing that this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Yet the fact that your welcome presence has been withdrawn from us, by some judgment of God I do not know, so that we cannot even sometimes see you—though, if it were possible, we should never wish to be without you—we confess we do not bear with equanimity. For what? Can we forget our old love and the benefits which you so generously bestowed upon our house? May God himself, for whose love you did this, never forget you eternally! For our part, as far as lies within us, we are by no means ungrateful: we retain in mind the memory of the abundance of your kindness, and, if permitted, we would show it in deed. Oh, how gladly we would have cared for both your body and your soul, had it been granted that we might be together! Since that cannot be, it remains for us always to pray for him whom we cannot have present, as one absent.

LXXIV. 513. The first foundation of Clairvaux Abbey by Hugh, count of Troyes, hitherto commonly unknown. (From the Clairvaux original.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Here begins the charter of Count Hugh:

Let all present and future persons know that [Col. 1447B] I, Hugh, count of Troyes, give to God, blessed Mary, and the brethren of Clairvaux the place itself called Clairvaux, with its appurtenances, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, and waters, retaining absolutely nothing for myself or my heirs. Witnesses: Acard of Reims, and Peter and Robert of Orléans, my knights. And it should be known that Geoffrey Felonia gives his pastures in the territory of Juvencourt, in wood and plain alike, at all times. If the animals of the said brethren cause any damage, only the principal loss shall be restored, without a fine. I gave all this in the presence of the above-named witnesses.

It should also be known that Lord Josbert of La Ferté, surnamed Rufus, and Lord Rainaud of Perceris gave the same brethren pasture and rights of use throughout [Col. 1447C] all their land, especially in waters, woods, and meadows, in the territory of Perrecin.

Witnesses to this are Acard of Reims and Robert, my knights. Likewise it should be known that I, Hugh, count of Troyes, approve and grant to the same brethren free and undisturbed possession of the land and wood of Aretela.

We, Joscerannus, bishop of Langres, and Hugh, count of Troyes, confirm these gifts by the seal and my ring.

(In the former seal Jocerannus is depicted seated in a bishop’s chair; in the other, Count Hugh.)

LXXV. Hugh, count of Troyes; his father Theobald; his mother Adelaidis; his brother Odo; and his wife Constance. 1097. (From the charters of Molême.)

[Col. 1447D]

We resolve to transmit to the knowledge of the faithful, both present and future, that the meadow situated beside the wall of the city of Troyes, not far from the church of Saint-Quentin, which Count Odo, son of Count Theobald, had in his lifetime given to the church of Molême, was most willingly granted by his brother, who had succeeded him in his honour, namely Count Hugh. At an Easter festival, while holding his court at Molême in the year 1097 of the Lord’s Incarnation, at the request of Robert, abbot of that place, he granted not only that meadow but all gifts whatsoever which his father Count Theobald, his mother Countess Adelaidis, and his brother Count Odo had bestowed upon the church of Molême [Col. 1448A].

The count himself also gave a certain gardener—the keeper of the meadow—with his wife and children, and all revenues and judicial rights which he possessed therein by right. Witnesses to all these aforementioned matters are Wido of Vangionis Rivus, Dudo, vidame of the city of Châlons, and many others. Constance, wife of the said Count Hugh and daughter of Philip, king of the Franks, granted all the aforementioned matters in the chamber of Walter of Beauvais, in the presence of these witnesses: Gaufred, son of Ottrannus; Odo the priest; and many others. To make all this more ratified and authentic, in the presence of Lord Gaufred of Ottrannus, the countess sent a certain coin through Lord Nivelon onto the altar [Col. 1448B] of Saint-Quentin.

LXXVI. Hugh, count of Troyes, son of Theobald and husband of Constance. 1100. (From the charters of Arremar.)

Hugh, count of Troyes, son of the most noble Count Theobald, and his wife Constance, daughter of Philip, king of the Franks, being certain of their shared mortal lot and solicitous for eternal life, etc.

For they approach the church consecrated in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul, commonly called the monastery of Arremar, but anciently named Mansus Corbonis. For the salvation of their souls, they gave it by hereditary right to possess whatever any knight or servant who held something from their benefice has given, or may wish to give, to it; and they consent to this throughout all the land subject to their authority. Moreover, they gave that church whatever they possessed at Haute-Rive, etc. [Col. 1448C]

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, indiction 8, 21 October.

Witnesses to this gift are Milo, count of Bar; Rainard, count of Juvignac; Andrew, lord of Ramerupt; Guy of Vangionis Rivus; Ingelmer, provost of the Greeks; etc.

LXXVII. Hugh, count of Troyes, about to depart for the Lord’s Sepulchre. 1113. (From the charters of Arremar.)

[Col. 1448D]

Let all faithful people of Christ, present and future, know that the memorable Hugh, count of Troyes, about to depart in pious devotion for the Lord’s Sepulchre, added to the many great benefactions he had bestowed upon the church of Arremar a thing long and earnestly sought: namely, the jurisdiction which he held around Desda, outside Quarantania, specifically at Mont-Herbert, Pruciac, Ruliac, Novavilla, and all other places belonging to Desda, etc. Among the witnesses: Milo, count of Bar; and Airard, his brother, count of Brienne.

Done publicly at Troyes, in court, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1113.

LXXVIII. Arveius of Saffra, son of Arveius and the countess; his brother Galterus; and his wife Gila. (From the original in the archive of the nuns of Pralon.)

[Col. 1449A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be made known to all the faithful who inspect this charter that Lord Arveius of Saffra granted to the abbess and nuns of Pralon free and undisturbed possession, in perpetuity, of a third part of the grain tithes of Saffra, which the same nuns hold as alms from the gift of his father Arveius, for the soul of the lady countess, mother of the said Arveius. They may collect the said share of tithes wherever and through whomever they wish.

He also gave the said nuns [Col. 1449B] a place suitable and appropriate for building one house in the same village, subject to the approval of John, chaplain of the same village, and William Frosmunt of Maalein. But if the nuns and brethren of the same abbey should wish to pledge, sell, or otherwise alienate this alms from their house, they may not do so except into the hand of Lord Arveius, or of one of his men who is neither a knight nor of noble birth, or into the hand of the House of God of Saffra, or of the said John the chaplain. Galterus, his brother, and his wife Gila approved all this; for that agreement she received ten sheep from the house of Pralon, and Arveius himself received one hundred sols in Dijon currency.

That it might be held ratified forever, the said Arveius affixed his own seal to this writing and, at his request, caused the seals of Hay, archdeacon of Flavigny, and H., archpriest of Vitteaux, to be affixed.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1204, with these witnesses: Ebrard of Flavigny; I. of Saffra; Hay of Ys; Reygmund of Grossobosco, priests; Guy of Bassy and William Frosmunt of Maalein, knights; and Humbert of Coium. [Col. 1449C]

It should further be known that the said house of Pralon may not take a tithe in the canal.

518. The seal of Herveus, lord of Saffra, hanging by a parchment strip between the seals of Hay, archdeacon of Flavigny, and H., archpriest of Vitteaux.

[Col. 1449D]

LXXIX. Warnerius of Sombernon; his wife Istiburgis; their daughters Anna and Addila; Gozelinus of Sombernon. In the year of Christ 1020, the twenty-fifth of King Robert, indiction 3. (From the original of Saint-Bénigne.)

[Col. 1450A]

In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It belongs to servants of God to enrich, enlarge, and exalt Christ’s Church with their own resources. For unless it were enriched, there would be no means by which Christ’s poor might be sustained. “Make friends for yourselves,” Christ says, “from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Therefore, contemplating the joys of this dwelling, I, Count Walo by name, my brother Walter, Warnerius of Sombernon, and Humbert the advocate, together with his brother Girard [Col. 1450B]—and also what Christ himself says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11)—have given to the church of Holy Mary and Saint Benignus, martyr of Christ, a part of our inheritance situated before the gates of the castle of Sarmasia.

This land is bounded before the doors of that monastery: by twelve field-perches in width on the northern side; by thirty-four perches in length on the eastern side; by fourteen and a half perches in width on the southern side; and by thirty-four and a half perches in length. If we ourselves, or any of our relatives, incited by the goad of greed, should attempt to act against this donation, he shall not be able to recover what he claims; rather, having been convicted, he shall pay one hundred pounds of gold to the place against which he attempted to bring a claim [Col. 1450C]. If he should persist in his wickedness, let him know that he is to be condemned under anathema with Judas the betrayer. And that this donation may remain firm and stable, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and asked our faithful men likewise to confirm it.

Sign of Walo, formerly count, and of his wife Judith, and of his sons Aymon and Hugh. Sign of Walter, his brother. Sign of Warnerius and of his wife Istiburgis, and of their daughters Anna and Addila. Sign of Humbert the advocate, his wife Ermentrude, and his son Hilerannus. Sign of Girard, his brother. Sign of Bertrada, his sister. Sign of Theobald, his nephew. Sign of Gothefrid. Sign of Gislerius. Sign of Arlebaud; likewise, sign of Arlebaud the cleric. Sign of Tezelin Rastelli. Sign of [Col. 1450D] Hugh. Sign of Aldo. Sign of Gozelin of Sombernon. Sign of Girard. Sign of Girbert. Sign of Algerius.

These things were publicly enacted at the castle of Sarmasia in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1020, in the twenty-fifth year of Robert’s reign as king of the Franks, indiction 2.

I, Girbert, unworthy deacon, asked to act in place of Lord Beraldus the chancellor, wrote and subscribed [this document].

XXX. (From the Necrology of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon.)

On 11 April died Tecelinus, monk, father of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

On 19 August died Calo, lord of Fontaines, our friend, who gave us his share of Magnomont.

[Col. 1451A] On 31 August died Wido, knight of Sombernon.

On 1 September died Alasya, a laywoman. This is Saint Bernard’s mother, formerly buried at Saint-Bénigne; in the more recent necrology she is written “Alaysa.”

On 11 October died Ebalus, count of Saulx.

On 22 October died Itisburgis, our friend, mother of our abbot. This is the wife of Warnerius of Sombernon.

LXXXI. The church of Saint Martin of the Meadow at Fontaines in Champagne, with the chapel in the upper village of Fontaines. 1120. (From the original of Saint Stephen of Dijon.)

In the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity, Father, [Col. 1451B] Son, and Holy Spirit. Whenever the offices of ecclesiastical administration are renewed by synodal decrees, and the praises and good deeds of worthy predecessors are recounted to posterity, we have judged it fitting, through the example of charity and imitation of justice, faithfully to investigate according to the custom of the ancients, and to deal by more authoritative instruments with the disposal of those things especially which in our time are kindly bestowed upon religious persons and members of the household of faith.

Therefore I, Jocerannus, by divine appointment bishop of the Church of Langres, while together with the most reverend assembly of the whole clergy we were discussing in a plenary synod the condition and advancement of this mother church, the regular canons of the church of Saint Stephen of Dijon came [Col. 1451C] before us: Lord Gualo the prior and other religious men. They asked and entreated that, as belonged to our episcopal jurisdiction, we should prepare letters of our authority, authenticated by the impression of our own seal, concerning the church of Blessed Martin in Champagne, which they had long asserted had formerly belonged to their church by right, and concerning other properties which they had acquired within our bishopric through the administration of ourselves and our faithful men.

Freely assenting to their just petition, upon the counsel of our archdeacons and of that sacred assembly, we restore and grant to them, saving the rights of the Church of Langres, that church of Blessed Martin of the Meadow, called in Champagne, with its chapel in the upper village of Fontaines [Col. 1451D]. We also give and confirm to them in perpetual right, without prejudice to the customs of the Church of Langres, the church of Gemelles with its chapel in the village of Picamgis; and the church of Ormantiac, located within the bounds of the city of Langres itself, with its two chapels, one known to be at Roseries and the other in the episcopal village of Mardoo. By this instrument of the present charter we entrust these grants to our archdeacons for confirmation.

Sign of Guilencus, archdeacon.  
Sign of Guarnerius, archdeacon.  
Sign of Ayrard, archdeacon.  
Sign of Gocelmus, archdeacon.  
Sign of Guy, archdeacon.

These things were enacted in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1120, in the pontificate of Pope Calixtus, [Col. 1452A] in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and in the episcopate of Jocerannus of the Church of Langres.

I, Durannus, notary of the Church of Langres, acting in place of Fulco, chief of the chancery and archchancellor of that church, wrote, dictated, and read aloud [this document].

LXXXII. The castle of Saulx passes from private lords into royal hands; hence, after being assigned to the dukes of Burgundy, it began commonly to be called Saulx-le-Duc. (From Claude Robert’s *Gallia Christiana*, at Dijon, under Robert de Salione, twenty-second among the deans of the duke’s chapel.)

It appears from charters subscribed at Paris in March 1302 that Philip the Fair, king of France, gave this castle of Saulx to his eldest son Louis—later king, surnamed Hutin—on the condition that if Louis became king or died without children, it should pass to the duke of Burgundy [Col. 1452B]. Then, from other letters written at Longchamp in May 1303, it is clear that the same King Philip gave the same castle, subject to feudal allegiance, to Robert, duke of Burgundy and chamberlain of France. Finally, a diploma of John of Chalon, seventy-third bishop of Langres, issued at Châtillon-sur-Seine in 1331, contains a settlement between that bishop and Odo, duke of Burgundy, by which the duke rendered homage to the bishop for this castle, in the same manner as James, or Jaquin, former lord of the said castle, had rendered it to earlier bishops.

LXXXIII. Relics of Saint Ambrosinianus. 1203. (From the charters of the Carthusian house of Lugny.)

[Col. 1452C]

In 1203, the church of the lower house was dedicated and its altar consecrated by Lord Heldum, bishop of Langres, on 6 October. Among the relics enclosed in that church are numbered relics of the blood of Saint Benignus, and relics of the blessed Medardus and Ambrosinianus.

LXXXIV. John, Cecilia, and Guillermeta, children of Humbert of Fontaines and of his widow Bona. William of Fontaines, knight. 1282.

(From an original of the family of Saffra.)

In the name of the Lord. Amen. In the year of his Incarnation [Col. 1452D] 1282, in April, we, John, Cecilia, and Guillermeta, children of the late Humbert of Fontaines, make known to all who inspect these present letters that for our advantage and necessity we sell, grant, and quitclaim in perpetuity to Lord William of Fontaines, knight, a garden situated at Fontaines, between the garden of Belin of Tyois and the garden of John Major of Fontaines, for the price of fifty Viennese sols. From the said William we have received and had full payment in coined money. Therefore, wholly divesting ourselves of the said garden, we have corporally invested the said William and his heirs in it.

I, Bona, mother of the said sellers, approve and grant this sale [Col. 1453A]. Furthermore, we Bona and the aforesaid sellers promise and are bound, each for the whole, under pledge of all our property and by our oath bodily sworn upon the holy Gospels of God, to warrant the said garden completely free in perpetuity to the said William and his heirs against all persons in every court, at our own expense; to do and provide all that ought to be done and provided in a suit for eviction; and henceforth not to oppose this in any respect, either silently or expressly, whether by ourselves or others. We consent that we be compelled to observe the foregoing, as by a judgment rendered, through the court of the lord duke of Burgundy, to whose jurisdiction, for this purpose, we submit ourselves and our heirs. In testimony whereof, we petitioned for and obtained the affixing to these letters of the seal [Col. 1453B] of the said court.

Done in the presence of Hugonin of Chalon, notary of Dijon; Humbelet called Chartreir; and Martin son of Brecon, witnesses called for this purpose, in the aforesaid year and month.

Seal of the court of Dijon.

LXXXV. John of Fontaines, esquire. 1276. (From an original of the family of Saffra.)

525. In the name of the Lord. Amen. In the year of his Incarnation 1276, in December, I, Hugonin of Fluray, esquire, son of the late Guy of Fluray, make known to all who inspect these present letters that for my advantage and necessity [Col. 1453C] I sell, grant, and quitclaim in perpetual inheritance to John of Fontaines, esquire, for himself and his heirs, three sestiers of grain, by the measure of Sombernon. The said John owed these to me as an annual rent upon his thirds at Aubigny, and I held them from him in fief, for the price of sixteen Viennese pounds, from which said John I have received and had full payment in coined money, etc.

LXXXVI. Herveus, lord of Saffra. January 1232. (From the original of Saffra.)

I, HUGH, Duke of Burgundy, make known to all who inspect these present letters [Col. 1453D] that I have seen the letters of my most dear father Odo, Duke of Burgundy, who gave and granted in perpetuity to Hervey, lord of Saffres, and to his heirs who shall be lords of Saffres, that he could not retain under himself his men who should remain under him, except at Beaune and at Dijon. And I, who greatly desire to uphold my father’s gift and grant, have confirmed, 526 approved, and promised to the said Hervey and his heirs who shall be lords of Saffres that I cannot retain under myself his men who shall remain under me, except at Beaune and at Dijon. And that this may remain ratified, firm, and stable, I have delivered to the aforesaid Hervey these present letters strengthened by the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1232, in the month of January.

LXXXVII. Beatrice, widow of William de Sauz, knight; John and William, their sons. 1265. (From the original in the chamber of royal accounts at Dijon.)

[Col. 1454A]

We, GUY, by the grace of God bishop of Chalon, make known to all who inspect these present letters that Lady Beatrice, widow of the lord William de Sauz, knight, now deceased, personally appearing before us for this purpose, acknowledged before us that she held and had received, with the approval and consent of her children John and William, from the illustrious man Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, and his heirs, everything which she possesses in the parish of Saint-Romain d’Andenay and at Saprade, both in her own right and in the right [Col. 1454B] of the said William, her husband now deceased—namely, lands, meadows, men, waters, pastures, tithes, customary dues, censuses, lordships, jurisdictions, and all other things whatsoever—for twenty Viennese pounds. The said Lady B. acknowledged before us that she had received and held herself fully and entirely paid in coined money for these, as she confessed before us. The said lady also promised before us, by her oath personally sworn upon the holy Gospels of God, 527 to hold firmly and observe in perpetuity all the things named above. In memory and testimony of this matter, at the request of the said lady and of John and William, her children, we have delivered to the said duke these present letters, strengthened by the protection of our seal.

Given in the year of the Lord 1265, in the month of May.

LXXXVIII. Bernard de Marey, Squire, Lord in part of Fontaines-lès-Dijon; Marie de Fontaines, his mother. 1462. (Drawn from the treasury of the Abbey of Cîteaux.)

[Col. 1454C]

In the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1462, on the twentieth day of February, I, BERNARD de Mairey, Esquire, Lord in part of Fontaines-lès-Dijon, make known to all present and future that, for a very long time, I have had, and still have at present, great devotion to God my Creator, to the glorious Virgin Mary his mother, and also to my lord Saint Bernard, because he was born at the castle of the said Fontaines and departed from the lordship of that place; and because I am sprung and descended from that lordship and line. Considering also [Col. 1454D] that in his youth he was received as a novice, and made profession in the church and monastery of Our Lady of Cîteaux; toward which church and monastery I have likewise long had, and still have, very great devotion, etc.

Thereupon he gives to Abbot Humbert and the convent of Cîteaux the fourth part of the castle, fortress, and fortified house of the said Fontaines, in which he had his dwelling; which had fallen to him from antiquity, by reason, he says, and through the 528 death and passing of the late Lady Marie de Fontaines, formerly my mother, whose soul may God have, and also through a partition made with the other co-lords of the said Fontaines. Likewise, about twenty-five men or dependants whom he had in that place. Likewise, the fourth part of the mayoralty and of the [Col. 1455A] middle and low jurisdiction which he held in the place, bounds, and territory of Fontaines. Likewise, a banal oven, and several parcels of vineyards and arable lands which he held in the same territory. All this upon condition that the said abbot and convent of Cîteaux should be bound to construct at their own expense, in the said castle of Fontaines, a chapel in honour of God and Saint Bernard; and there to say, or cause to be said and celebrated, one Mass every Friday of the year in perpetuity, for his intention; and to celebrate his anniversary in the church of Fontaines during his life, and after his death in that of Cîteaux, on the third day after the feast of Saint Bernard.

It appears that this Bernard de Mairey, lord in part of Fontaines, did not survive this [Col. 1455B] gift for long, since his brother Alexander, claiming to be his heir, ceded the right which he might have in this succession to Jean de Poictiers, knight, lord of Vadans, etc., on the twenty-ninth day of April after Easter, as we shall say immediately below.

In the obituary book of Cîteaux are read the following words: “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September died Lord Bernard de Fontaines, who gave to the church his share which he had in the lordship of the castle of Fontaines; we sold it and received four hundred Tours pounds for it.”

This accords with what the abbot and religious of Cîteaux stated in the petition which they presented to the court on the last day of April 1614 against [Col. 1455C] the Feuillants, who, from the year 1613, had acquired by purchase the castle of Fontaines in order to convert it into a church and monastery of their reform. They said that the Duke of Burgundy had not been willing to consent to the mortmain settlement of the aforesaid properties given to the abbey 529 of Cîteaux by Bernard de Mairey; this obliged the said abbot and religious of Cîteaux to dispose of them for the sum specified in their obituary book.

Bernard de Mairey did not survive for long the gift which he made on 20 February 1462, the year then being reckoned from Easter; for on 29 April after Easter 1463 his brother Alexander, then castellan of Vadans, made an inter vivos gift of the entire succession [Col. 1455D] of his brother Bernard, recently deceased, to his good master and lord Jehan de Poictiers, knight, lord of Arcis, Vadans, and Souvans, maintaining the nullity of the gift made to the abbot and religious of Cîteaux by his brother Bernard, since he claimed to be his heir. Now, if Bernard de Mairey died between the following 20 February and 29 April, he did not therefore die on 18 August, the day on which his obit is recorded. That day was instead the anniversary founded by him and attached to 23 August; hence one must believe that the gentlemen of Cîteaux, for some reasons and for the convenience of their church, judged it appropriate to anticipate it by five days.

LXXXIX. Milo de Fontaines, burgess of Dijon; John de Fontaines, his son; Nazaria, John’s wife; Haymo, a clerk, and John, their sons. 1237. (From the original of the Dominican friars of Dijon.)

[Col. 1456A]

I, HAYMO DE ASIREY, then mayor, and we, the aldermen of the commune of Dijon, make known to all who inspect these presents that Lord Milo de Fontaines, burgess of Dijon, and John de Fontaines, his son, with the approval and consent of Nazaria, the wife of the said John, and of Haymo, a clerk, and John, their 530 sons, sold, transferred, and granted to the venerable Lady Alais, Duchess of Burgundy, the house and holding which they possessed [Col. 1456B] at Dijon above the bank of the Suzon, between the holding formerly belonging to the brothers Valet and Renaud de Mailley and the house of Lambert de Besua. Before us the said Milo and his son John divested themselves of that house and holding and personally invested the aforesaid duchess with it. The said Milo and John promised and are bound lawfully to warrant this sale in perpetuity to the said duchess and her successors against all claimants. They acknowledged before us that they had been wholly and fully paid, in coined money, the price of this sale, namely fifty Dijon pounds. It should be known that the said duchess bought the aforesaid house and holding in order there to construct a house and building [Col. 1456C] for the use of the brethren of the Order of Preachers. In testimony of this matter, at the request of the said duchess and at the prayer of the said Milo, John, Nazaria, Haymo the clerk, and John, we caused the seal of the said commune to be affixed to these present letters.

Done in the year of the Lord 1237, in the month of June.

XC. Odo of Champagne, nephew of Counts Raynald and William of Burgundy. (From the original of the metropolitan church of Besançon.)

HUMBERT, by the grace of God Archbishop of Besançon, to present and future persons: the truth of the transaction in perpetuity.

The concern entrusted to our office urges us with a pressing spur to watch more diligently over the peace and tranquillity of churches. Therefore, by the attestation of our seal, we transmit to the knowledge of posterity what has been done. Accordingly, a long-standing dispute between the mother church of Besançon and Odo, nephew of Count William, concerning the rent-paying dependants whom he claimed by right of the lordship of Quingey, was brought to this conclusion of perpetual peace. The venerable Odo remitted to the aforesaid church, for the soul of his uncle Count Raynald, all that claim concerning the cottars, whether just or unjust, in the presence and with the approval of Robert, provost of Quingey. The same Odo also gave and granted to the same church all those rent-paying dependants, if any had passed from the lordship of Quingey to the land of the canons, [Col. 1457A] and those who reside and dwell on their land; likewise those who, leaving their lordships, dwell at Besançon and are more properly their men than another lord’s. The aforesaid Odo strengthened this settlement by his seal. Likewise Count William approved it and sealed it with his seal. Therefore, if anyone should henceforth trouble the church of Besançon concerning this claim, let him be subject to excommunication and become alienated from the body and blood of Christ.

Given at Besançon in the year 1155, indiction II.

XCI. Odo, nephew of William, Count of Mâcon. (From the original of the metropolitan church of Besançon.)

Because, hindered by earthly cares, we consign many things to oblivion, we have resolved to transmit to the memory of posterity, as worthy of remembrance, [Col. 1457B] 532 that Count G. of Mâcon and his sons Stephen and Gerard—as Hugh, the precentor, more aptly and reasonably divided in the porch of the rock, and as Landric, the dean, and the other canons of the Church understood to their advantage—approved, indeed granted to the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Besançon, the gift which his nephew Odo had made.

Witnesses: Senoric, chaplain, who wrote this; Abbot Guy; Stephen and William, brothers of Chayx; John the physician; Richard, knight of Arbois; Remigius de Montebarry; Herbert and Henry, citizens of Besançon; and Pontius the goldsmith.

XCII. Odo of Champagne, kinsman of Empress Beatrice. 1166. (From the original in the Dole archive of the Counts of Burgundy.)

[Col. 1457C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. FREDERICK, by the favour of divine clemency Augustus, Emperor of the Romans.

If imperial clemency has judged that those whom sincerity of faith, uprightness of conduct, and the ardour of unwavering devotion render commendable ought especially to be considered worthy of honours and enriched with great benefactions, Odo of Champagne has deservedly merited honour. Illustrious by birth, a kinsman of Beatrice, our most noble consort, conspicuous for integrity and every excellence of conduct, he has hitherto served us with such ardour of pure loyalty and devotion that no stain of wickedness clouds the integrity of his reputation, nor does any blemish of dishonour darken the brilliant countenance of his virtues. Therefore, 533 let the diligence of all our faithful men in Burgundy, present as well as future, know that we, together with our most beloved consort Beatrice, permit our most faithful Odo of Champagne to possess throughout his lifetime Quingey, L’Isle, Lobium, and all these places with their appurtenances, as Count Raynald was accustomed to possess them during his life. This permission is such that neither he during his life, nor after his death his wife, nor his legitimate sons or daughters, may claim anything in all these things by right of fief or inheritance; rather, they shall freely revert to the emperor, empress, and their children. [Col. 1458A] The aforesaid Odo gave to us, the empress, and our children his allodial estate in the village near Dole called Champ-Pagan, and whatever allodial estates he may acquire during his life within the Empire; and he received them back from us as a fief, so that he may hold and possess them during his life by benefice-right, just as he holds Port and Scanlint from us as a benefice. After his death, his legitimate sons and daughters shall hold and possess, as a fief from us, the empress, and our children, both the allodial estates and the fiefs—specifically and by name, Port and Scanlint. But if it should happen that the aforesaid Odo dies leaving no legitimate son or daughter surviving, all the allodial estates which he now possesses or shall henceforth acquire in our Empire, and all the fiefs which he shall hold from the county—especially and by name Port and Scanlint—shall freely revert, without any right of reclamation, into the hands of us, the empress, our sons, and our daughters, to be held and possessed; so that we may do and ordain concerning them, without contradiction from anyone, [Col. 1458B] whatever we wish. That this may be more truly believed and inviolably observed in the course of time, we have ordered this present charter to be written and distinguished by the impression of our seal, suitable witnesses being present, in whose presence these things were done: Herbert, bishop-elect of the church of Besançon; Arducius, Bishop of Geneva; Peter, Bishop of Toul; Hugh, Abbot of Cluny; Everard, treasurer of Besançon; Almo, chaplain; Matthew, Duke of Lorraine; Ulrich, Duke of Bohemia; Louis, [Col. 1458C] Count of Ferrette; Ulrich of Hurningen; Albert, Count of Dillingen; Henry, Count of Nassau; Count Stephen and his brother Count Gerard; Gaucher of Salins; Guy, abbot; Gerard of Fonvens; Peter of Ceys; Amadeus, Count of Montbéliard; Giselbert, Viscount of Vesoul; Richard, provost; Richard and William of Scavys; Gerard Strabun; Gaymar of Cicun and Odolo; Amalric of the Jura; Henry of Saint-Quentin; and many others.

The sign of Lord Frederick, most invincible Emperor of the Romans.

I, Henry, protonotary, acting in place of William, Archbishop of Vienne and Archchancellor of all Burgundy, have authenticated this.

These acts were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1166, indiction XIV, in the fourteenth year of the reign of the most glorious Lord Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, and the twelfth of his empire.

Given at Dole upon the river Doubs, the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July].

XCIII. Odo Champenois of Champlitte. 1200. (From the original of Balerne Abbey.)

535 Let present and future persons know that I, MARGARET, Countess of Burgundy, with the counsel of Count William and of the noble men Hugh de Chayx, Humbert de Mutnet, and many others, have given to God, to Blessed Mary of Balerne, and to the brethren serving there, for the celebration of the anniversary of my lord Otto, Count of Burgundy, and of his predecessors, and for my soul, one burgess at Arbois, named Gerard de Montaney, with his children, all his successors, and his goods and possessions, in perpetual right, free without any reservation, customary service, or exaction.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1200, in the village of Sentens.

Witnesses: Odo Champenois of Champlitte; Fromund de Tramelay, brother of the archbishop; Odo d’Aspremont; and Peter de Mouprey.

Given by the hand of Master Alexander, notary, into the hand of Abbot Guy.

XCIV. Odo of Champagne, brother of Louis, about to visit the land of Jerusalem. 1202. (From the original of the church of Saint Stephen at Besançon.)

[Col. 1459B]

Let all, future as well as present, know that ODO of Champagne, about to visit the land of Jerusalem, for the salvation of his soul, and of 536 his brother Louis and his predecessors, freely and in perpetuity granted to the church of Saint Stephen at Besançon the holding of Aymon Grucel, with its tenement and his heirs, at Paygné.

Witnesses of this matter are Richard de Chawis, Pontius de Frites, Pontius de Mimirey, Tibert de Montfaucon, Humbert, Odo, and Senoric [Col. 1459C] de Quingey.

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1202, epact 25, concurrent 1.
