XCV. Hugh, Count of Troyes; Odo, his disinherited son. (From Pierre Pithou, *On the Counts of Champagne*.)

EON, or EUDES, according to the genealogy of Saint Arnoul of Metz, which alone I have followed here, having found no mention of this man elsewhere—unless he is the person to whom King Louis gave the castle of Vitry after taking it from Count Theobald, and who is called in one chronicle the nephew of that Eudes; whereas, conversely, the Abbot of Saint-Michel calls him Theobald’s nephew.

HUGH, or HUES, Count of Troyes, who in the charter of Sarmoise, mentioning his mother Alix and his brother Philip, is styled Count of Champagne. He married Constance, daughter of King Philip, from whom he was separated on grounds of consanguinity. He had another wife as well, whom certain records seem to call Lombard; and he had a son named Hugh, or Eudes, whom he disinherited and sold his county to his nephew Theobald. It is read that, when going overseas—where he died on 14 June—he left this second 537 wife pregnant. This Eudes is more likely to be the man who, out of resentment for this, assisted King Louis against Theobald; the king gave him the castle of Vitry, which he had taken in 1143. For at that time the son of the elder brother called the children of younger brothers his nephews.

XCVI. Hugh, Count of Troyes and Bar-sur-Aube; Constance, his wife; Countess Adela and her son Simon, Count of Bar-sur-Aube. 1101. (From the records of Saint-Oyend in the Jura.)

[Col. 1460A]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. As it is right to refuse an unsuitable request to one who asks wrongly and improperly, so it is right to grant what is asked to one who petitions worthily. Therefore I, HUGH, Count of Troyes and Bar-sur-Aube, acceding to your petitions, venerable Abbot Hubert, approve and grant to the church of Saint-Oyend in the Jura and to the monks dwelling on Mount Bar that they shall possess in perpetuity the alms and gifts which Countess Adela and Count Simon, of blessed memory, made there: namely, the mountain itself [Col. 1460B] with the little settlement built there; Arces; Corcelle; the land of Colombe; the land of Rufy; half the tithe of the dependent village; the land of Saint-Libaire; and a certain piece of land at Braye. I release all these things, with their men, buildings, and appurtenances, to the aforesaid church, free in perpetuity from all exactions, customs, and jurisdictions, retaining nothing for myself or my successors. Moreover, with the approval of my wife Constance, 538 daughter of King Philip, I give and grant to the church of Saint Stephen and Saint Germaine, and to the aforesaid monks, all revenues due to me from those men and possessions which have been given to them in alms, and the fishing rights of the river Aube; and I ordain that no one shall ever make fulling mills [*molendina batatoria*] or other works for use within the bounds of the aforesaid castle, except through the aforesaid monks. I also grant, in the mills which we hold jointly, that share which I bought from Henry and his heirs, together with the right to replace the miller. Since we wish all these things to remain unshaken and firm in perpetuity, we have caused them to be confirmed by these letters and the impression of our seal. Therefore, whoever knowingly presumes to infringe these provisions shall incur God’s wrath in this world and, unless he repents, shall be subject to eternal damnation in the world to come.

These things were done at Bar-sur-Aube in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1101.

The sign of Erard of Brienne. The sign of Milo, his brother. The sign of Roger of Joigny. The sign of Gausbert, steward, [Col. 1460D] etc.

XCVII. Hugh, Count of Champagne; his mother Alais; his brother Philip, Bishop of Châlons. 1093. (From the records of Saint-Oyend in the Jura.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, HUGH, Count of Champagne, make known to all faithful members of God’s holy Church, present and future, that I, Countess Alais my mother, and Philip my brother, bishop of God’s holy church of Châlons, give as an allod to the church of Saint-Oyend and of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which is being built in the place 539 called Sarmoise, whatever lies between Hilduin’s seat and the river Saulx, etc. Furthermore, we give, confirm, [Col. 1461A] and will that the village called Sarmoise shall remain free and without any disturbance; likewise, that the villagers dwelling there through the aforesaid church shall be free and discharged from all secular customs, shall serve and answer only to the monks serving God there, etc. We further will that, should it happen that the men of the aforesaid village injure my men, my men shall make complaint to the prior of that place and the matter shall be settled by his justice. But if the villagers injure the prior or monks and refuse to submit themselves to right by the prior, the prior shall make complaint to no one other than the Count of Vitry or his officials, because the aforesaid village and all the wood belong to the lordship of Vitry, etc.

[Col. 1461B] No year is appended to this diploma; but the confirmation which immediately follows it, by Philip, Bishop of Châlons and brother of Count Hugh, bears the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1093.

XCVIII. Simon, Count of Bar-sur-Aube, called Count of Champagne. (From the necrology of Saint-Oyend in the Jura.)

On the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September] died Simon, Count of Champagne, a monk of our congregation.

On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January [15 December] died Odo, Count of Troyes.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June] died Hugh, Count of Troyes. 540 On the fifth day before the Ides of January [9 January] died Theobald, Count of Blois, [Col. 1461C] who approved, confirmed, and sealed the gift which his uncle Hugh made to our church.

XCIX. Rainard, lord of the castle of Montbard, uncle of Saint Bernard; Waldric, monk; and Milo, lay brother. (From the first great charter of Fontenay, no. 1.)

To all lovers of holy religion, present as well as future, we have taken care to make known by the testimony of this document that Lord Rainard, lord of the castle of Montbard, for the first foundation of the new abbey of Fontenay—which, with great devotion of heart and with the approval of his wife Aanold, he gave to the Lord God, Blessed Mary, and the brethren who are to serve God in that place in perpetuity [Col. 1461D] and, with God’s help, live there under the regular observance—for the souls of his father and mother, for the remission of his sins, and also out of love for Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, his nephew, and for his brothers Waldric the monk and Milo the lay brother, who with Lord Martin the Hermit were the first builders of the same abbey, gave the territory of Aringes, as the two brothers Rainaud and Walo de Aringes had previously held that land freely. The aforesaid Rainard had bought or exchanged that land from a certain knight of his, Nariod, to whom the same land had devolved by hereditary right through his wife, daughter of the aforesaid Rainaud de Aringes; this gift being approved by Nariod’s wife, named Gertrude, and by the sister of his wife, named [Col. 1462A] Maria. 541 Lord Fergannus, consul of Grignon, also approved this most willingly, as did Lord Humbaud de la Tour with his wife Hodierna, and Lebaud de Grignon with his wife Maria, from whose lordship that land descended.

C. Verric de Châtillon. (From the first great charter of Fontenay, no. 43.)

HULDREUS DE LUCENAY gave to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay one holding at Flacey. Witnesses are Bartholomew de Marmagne and Verric de Châtillon. His son Peter approved this gift, with the same witnesses and with these: Humbert de Fain, Siguin de Tuilly, and Ralph [Col. 1462B] de Fain. The monks received Huldreus into their care in his old age.

Likewise, from the second great charter, no. 27.

HAYMO DE MARMAGNE, entering monastic life under Abbot William of Fontenay, gave in alms to the church of Fontenay the remainder of the land which he, his brother, and his sister possessed toward Saigny, etc. Among the witnesses was Ralph, Knight Templar, through whose hand this was done, etc.

This was done at Châtillon, in the house of Wirric de Pont, which is on the Island.

Witnesses are the aforesaid Ralph, Knight Templar, and Tecelin, nephew of Wirric de Pont.

CI. Girbert de Montbard; his sons Tecelin and Gerard, clerk. (From the first great charter of Fontenay, no. 44.)

[Col. 1462C]

542 GIRBERT DE MONTBARD, with the approval of his son Tecelin, gave to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay a meadow in the place called Deodat’s Meadow.

Witnesses of this matter are Artald, canon of Saulieu; Peter the scribe; and Bruno, son of Lambert the smith of Saulieu.

This gift was subsequently approved by Gerard, clerk and son of Girbert; witnesses are Peter the scribe and Simon, clerk.

CII. Certain extracts from the first great charter of Fontenay, drawn piecemeal from forty-six records contained therein.

[Col. 1462D]

Witnesses of this matter are Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux; Godfrey, monk; and Gerard, brother of the same abbot, etc.; Rainer de la Roche and his brother Nivard.

Under other records: Witnesses to all these gifts made in the presence of Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, are Boso, dean; Evrard, priest of Campinola; Bernard, lord of Montbard; his uncle Andrew; and the brothers Nivard and Rainer.

GODFREY DE SAIGNY gave to Saint Mary of Fontenay all the land that he had within the bounds of Aringes, with the approval of his son Hugh and in the presence of Lord [Col. 1463A] William, 543 abbot of that place. Witnesses of this gift are Godfrey, who was the first abbot of Fontenay; Theobald, priest of Frêne; and Robert, knight of Sainte-Colombe, nephew of the same knight Godfrey.

Under other records: Witnesses of this matter among the knights are Walter, constable, then lord of Montbard, and his brother Nivard.

Under the gift of Hugh the steward: This gift was made at Bussy, in the presence of Guy, monk and brother of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.

Under the gift of Giselbert, knight of Til. This too was approved by Bernard, lord of Montbard, and his sister Milesendis with her husband Rainer.

LEOBAUD DE GRIGNON and HUMBAUD DE ROUGEMONT gave to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay, at the boundary of the two villages of Bonnes and Corcelles, land of their own to be cultivated as a meadow, measured in width according to a certain meadow of Lord Tecelin the Red which adjoins that land, the division being made lengthwise as far as the bed of the river Brenne, etc. Witnesses of this matter were Helirannus Fercannus, consul of Grignon; Godfrey de Saigny; John de Montbard; and Girbert de Châtillon.

BERNARD, knight of ÉPIRY—[Note: [Col. 1463D] You will read in Herbert, book II, *On Miracles*, chapter 37, of William of Épiry, or Spiry, Saint Bernard’s nephew; from this source the author of the *Additions to the Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order* drew. But I do not understand on what ground Walter the constable is here written “lord of Montbard,” unless he was brought into the family by marriage, to which Montbard belonged by hereditary right. Nor do I understand why, in the same first great charter, Rainard is called “lord of the castle of Montbard,” unless this is to distinguish Walter the constable as lord not of that same castle but only of the borough of the same name: namely, the borough which he had held in feudal dependence under Rainard, lord of the castle—whose brother-in-law he was—according to the custom of that age, when the estates of nobles were divided among several co-heirs, yet the principal right of the lordship remained with the head of the family. Since, therefore, according to John the Hermit in the *Life of Saint Bernard*, that Robert to whom the first of this letter is addressed was born of a mother who was the sister of Alais, Saint Bernard’s mother, I am led to conjecture that this Robert was the son of Walter the constable, who by his wife’s dowry was lord of the borough of Montbard. Walter, moreover, was constable not of the kingdom of France but of the Duchy of Burgundy; under the duke’s authority he was, that is, commander of both branches of the military.]—exchanged with the monks of Fontenay, through the hand of Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, and with the approval of his son William, the abbot’s nephew, the meadow called Brolium, etc. [Col. 1463C] Witnesses are William, Bishop of Langres, etc. This too was subsequently approved by Richard, brother of the aforesaid William.

I, STEPHEN, Bishop of Autun, and the chapter of our 544 church, gave to Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, the place commonly called Fontenay, for the construction of an abbey there, etc.

GODFREY DE SAIGNY and his son HUGH, with the approval of Sarah, wife of the same Hugh, gave to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay a field on the slope of another valley on the Saigny side, etc. This gift was approved by Laura, daughter of Godfrey himself, and Elias, Laura’s son.

545 CIII. Conclusion of the first great charter of Fontenay, through the diploma of Stephen, Bishop of Autun, issued in 1136 and authenticated by his seal.

[Col. 1463D]

STEPHEN, by the grace of God Bishop of Autun, to his beloved brother in Christ WILLIAM, Abbot of Fontenay, [Col. 1464A] and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A desire shown to pertain to the purpose of religion and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be brought to completion in deed. Therefore, beloved brother in the Lord, Abbot William, granting your reasonable petitions, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the holy church of Autun and of our office the monastery over which by God’s authorisation you preside; and we secure it by the protection of this present writing and the impression of our seal. We decree that whatever goods or possessions the aforesaid monastery presently holds—namely, both those contained in the charters written on the present parchment and received from our gifts and from those of others, and those which, God granting, it may acquire in future—shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We therefore decree that no one may disturb the same monastery, take away its lands, retain what has been taken, or harass it by rash vexations. If anyone knowingly acts against the text of this our constitution, unless he repents, by God’s and our authority we exclude him from communion with the holy Church, so that both in the present life he shall be alienated from the body and blood of the Lord and in the future he shall be subject to punishment at the divine judgment.

I, Stephen, 546 Bishop of the Church of Autun, have subscribed. I, William, dean, have subscribed. I, Walter, precentor, have subscribed. I, Geoffrey, archdeacon, have subscribed. I, Siguin, archdeacon, have subscribed. I, Gerard, archdeacon, [Col. 1464C] have subscribed. I, Gautier, steward and Abbot of Saint Stephen, have subscribed.

This was done at Autun in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1136, epact 15, concurrent 3, indiction 14.

CIV. Gerard de Châtillon, brother-in-law of Theobald de Salives; Ebles, Count of Saulx-le-Château. (From the second great charter of Fontenay, no. 8.)

THEOBALD DE SALIVES gave in alms to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay everything which he possessed within the bounds of Puits-Franc, etc. Witnesses to this gift are Duke Hugh himself, in whose presence all this was done between Frolles and Uncey; [Col. 1464D] Hugh, son of the same duke; Garnier de Sombernon; Rainer de la Roche; John de Quincey; Gerard de Châtillon, who had been brother-in-law of the aforesaid Theobald; and Raynald, lord of the castle of Grancey. This [Col. 1465A] gift was approved and granted by the wife of the often-mentioned Theobald, named Gundrea but publicly called Sybilla. Witnesses are Lord Constantine, Abbot of Uncey, Gerard, canon, Robert de Saint-Bury, brother of the same lady, etc.; Ebles, Count of Saulx-le-Château; Rainer de Frolles; Bertalph and Herlebald de Grancey; Hugh de Villefleur; Haimo de Salives, etc.

547 CV. Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, lord of the castle of Grignon; his wife, Duchess Matilda. (From the second great charter of Fontenay, no. 9.)

HUGH, Duke of Burgundy, with the approval of his wife Duchess Matilda, gave in alms to the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay everything which he possessed at Puits-Franc. [Col. 1465B] That place, however, descended from the lordship of the castle of Grignon, of which the duke himself was lord.

Witnesses to this gift are Tecelin, archpriest of Aignay, where this was also done; Hugh Cavalgeia; Bartholomew de Sombernon; Peter de Échalot, mayor; and Constantius, provost of Mauvilly.

CVI. Nariod de Montbard; his sons Gualo, Bernard, and Rainer, monk of Fontenay. (From the same second great charter, no. 25.)

Nariodus of Montbarr gave to the church of Fontenay, as alms and with the approval of his sons Gualo and Bernard, all the land he possessed from the grange of Flacey toward Saigny. But he made this alms-deed [Col. 1465C] on account of his son Rainer, whom Abbot William received to become a monk.

548 CVII. Geoffrey of Châtillon, his wife Gertrude, and their sons Hugh and Nivard. (From the same second great charter, no. 40.)

GEOFFREY OF CHÂTILLON gave to the church of Fontenay as alms all his easements in all his lands and woods.

The witnesses to this are Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; Rainer Cavalgeia; and Wirric of Bellen.

This was approved by his wife Gertrude and by their sons Hugh and Nivard.

CVIII. Gerard of Châtillon, lord of Échalot, and his son Milo. (From the same second great charter, no. 46.)

[Col. 1465D]

GERARD OF CHÂTILLON gave to the church of Fontenay as alms whatever he possessed within the boundaries of Puteau-Franc. He granted the boundaries as Hugh of the Valley of Abon, now converted, had divided them, by obedience to Abbot William and with the consent of Theobald of Salives. Moreover, he renounced to the monks of the aforesaid church every tithe from their own land: that is, he would never receive from them, or from another person at Puteau, a tithe from their land. The witnesses are Hugh, duke of Burgundy; Odo, son of the same duke; Warner of Sombernon; Rainer of [Col. 1466A] La Roche; John of Quincey; Rainer, lord of Grancey; etc.

Later, because a dispute arose between the men of Échalot 549 and the monks concerning the boundaries of Échalot and Puteau, and between Gerard and the monks concerning the common pasture of Bergeres, the matter was settled in this manner, in the presence of Lord Odo, the duke’s son, etc. The witnesses are the abbots Bernard of Clairvaux and Constantine of Oigny, Odo the duke’s son, etc.

Thereafter the boundaries of the two territories were either fixed or marked out at the discretion of Constantine, abbot of Oigny. Present at this matter were Lord Robert, son of the duke, afterwards bishop of Autun; Master Robert, then his clerk; Gerard of Châtillon, then [Col. 1466B] lord of Échalot; Lebaud Ordeum, knight; etc. Milo, son of Gerard of Châtillon, granted and approved all this, as his father had done; and he received twenty sous from the benefice of Fontenay.

The witnesses to this grant are Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Langres; Pons, his archdeacon; Walter, canon of Troyes; Milo, dean of Lesigny; Guy, count of Bar; his knight Thomas; Rainer of La Roche; Matthew of Châtillon; Rainer of Pultariis; Lebaud Ordeum; and Gilbert of Tuilly.

CIX. Andrew, lord of Montbarr, his father Bernard, and his grandfather Rainard. (From the Fontenay original.)

[Col. 1466C] In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, GEOFFREY, by God’s grace bishop of Langres, make known to those present and to those to come that Andrew, lord of Montbarr, son of Bernard, son of Rainard, 550 acknowledged in our presence the gifts and grants which he had bestowed as alms upon the abbey of Fontenay. These are: namely, the whole portion of the wood of Segestre lying to the left of the road which leads from the plains of the same wood toward Naelle, as the stone boundary markers placed there indicate; likewise, the division of lands between Fontaines and Segestre, as it had long ago been made in the presence of the countess, the aforesaid Andrew’s aunt, where stone boundary markers were also set; and whatever property the said Andrew possessed [Col. 1466D] within the bounds of Planey, specifically Tuschia.

He also granted that the men of Fontenay might acquire, whether by alms or by purchase, from persons subject to him who held any right there, whatever they could obtain. He further granted them whatever they possessed from Obert of Til, insofar as it pertained to him. He likewise granted them whatever they held from his tenements, and whatever they could acquire by alms or purchase; also all the easements throughout his entire land, both in woodland and on the plain. To name some of these: timber for building, firewood, pannage for swine, and pasture for other animals; except that they may not clear the wood of Jallais for cultivation, though they shall have all other uses there. In the lands they shall have cultivation and pasture for [Col. 1467A] all animals; and in the waters, fishing, except in the forest lying between Pepin’s mill and Saint John’s mill. Finally, whatever his grandfather Rainard and his father Bernard had given and granted to the aforesaid abbey of Fontenay, as was contained in their charters, Andrew likewise granted.

Confirming all these things and securing them with the impression of our own seal, by God’s authority and ours we forbid anyone to presume to inflict any injury upon the men of Fontenay in these matters. If anyone should presume to do so, we strike him with the sword of anathema until he makes fitting satisfaction to them.

CX. Andrew, lord of Montbarr. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

[Col. 1467B]

I, HENRY, by God’s grace bishop of Autun, make known to those present and future that Roger of Semur, with the approval of his wife Ponsia, granted to the church of Fontenay, into the hand of our beloved brother Abbot Arnold, in its entirety the tenement which Richard of Courterabody held from him within the bounds of Fraxine, and which the same Richard had given to the church of Fontenay. Roger retained only the men belonging to that tenement, and received ten pounds from the benefice of the Church.

This was done through the hand of Andrew, lord of Montbarr, whom Roger gave to the Church as surety that he would faithfully observe this gift.

[Col. 1467C] The witnesses to this gift are Andrew, lord of Montbarr; Simon of Curtengi; Theobald, prior of Fontenay; William of Scalleus; William, cellarer; Hugh of Courterabody; and the monks of Fontenay.

552 CXI. Andrew, lord of Montbarr. (From the cartulary of Fontenay.)

I, ANDREW, lord of Montbarr, testify for those wishing to know that Viard of Senevey, his brother John, and Rainer of Chandoisel gave to the church of Fontenay all the arable land which they possessed from Fontenay to Marney, etc., before me and my lord Anseric of Montreal, Anseric the Younger, Hugh of Nigelles, Bernard Nariodus, [Col. 1467D] Andrew of Fontaines, etc.

(Item from the Fontenay original.)

I, GEOFFREY, by God’s grace bishop of Langres, make known to posterity and contemporaries that Milo of Molesme, son of Geoffrey, granted to the monks of Fontenay the easements of the wood called Pratée, within the bounds of Fontaines, for all their uses, etc.

Done publicly at Montbarr, into the hand of Abbot Arnold and through the hand of Andrew, lord of Montbarr, from whose tenement the aforesaid place derives.

CXII. William of Sauz and his wife Ermengard. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

I, HENRY, by God’s grace bishop of Autun, make known to those [Col. 1468A] future and present that Hodierna, wife of Humbert of Rougemont, gave as alms to the church of Fontenay, into the hand of Abbot Arnold, for her own soul and that of her husband, whatever she possessed in the fishery of Curcelle, which was held of her in chief, with the approval of Rainard, lord of Rougemont, of whose fief it was. Osmund, son of the aforesaid Hodierna, wished to contest this. But it is certain that his mother could make a lawful alms-gift, without his consent, from land which she held in chief.

The witnesses are William of Sauz and his wife Ermengard, Saissa, wife of Gilbert of Grésigny, etc.

CXIII. Bernard of Montbarr, lord of Époisses, son of Helvidis. 1210. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

[Col. 1468B]

I, Bernard of Montbarr, lord of Époisses, make known to all present and future that my mother Helvidis, of pious memory, at her death gave as pure alms to the church and brothers of Fontenay ten sextaries of grain—half wheat and half oats—to be taken every year, by the measure of Époisses, from the thirds of Corseinz around the feast of Saint Remigius. She also gave to the brothers of the aforesaid church twenty sous of annual rent, namely from the land of Vassy and from land held of her in chief, to be paid annually on the said feast of Saint Remigius. I approved and granted this alms-gift of my venerable mother to the aforesaid [Col. 1468C] brothers of Fontenay; and, for perpetual remembrance, I have affixed my seal to this present document, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1210.

CXIV. Andrew, lord of Époisses, son of Bernard, brother of Guy, canon of Langres. 1213. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

554 G., bishop of Autun; W., bishop of Langres; and W., bishop of Auxerre, by God’s grace: greetings in the Lord to all who inspect these present letters.

Let all present and future alike know that, whereas a dispute had arisen between the abbot and monks of Fontenay on one side and the nobleman Andrew, lord of Époisses, on the other, concerning [Col. 1468D] men, possessions, and lands situated at Marmagne, which the noblewoman Hyla of Mont-Saint-Jean and her son John had given and granted in perpetual alms to the house of Fontenay, and which the abbot and monks alleged had been seized by Bernard, of good memory, father of the said Andrew; and further concerning three hundred marks of silver, which the aforesaid abbot and monks maintained had been bequeathed to them by the aforesaid Bernard, father of the often-mentioned Andrew: at last, in our presence and that of the noblemen Odo, duke of Burgundy, and Guy of Donzy, together with many others, they came to this form of settlement: of the three hundred marks named above, the abbot and monks shall have one half, and the aforesaid Andrew [Col. 1469A] the other half. With respect to the property at Marmagne concerning which there was a dispute, it was established that Guy, Andrew’s brother and canon of Langres, shall hold that property for as long as he lives; and after Guy’s death it shall return freely and without any contradiction 555 to the church of Fontenay. The aforesaid Guy shall hold this property from the church of Fontenay, in the Church’s name.

Done in the year of grace 1213, in October.

(In the same year and month, Odo, duke of Burgundy, confirmed this very act in the same words by his own charter.)

CXV. Guy, canon, son of Bernard, lord of Époisses. 1220. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

[Col. 1469B]

I, HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Langres, make known to those present and future that Guy, son of Lord Bernard of Époisses, canon of Langres and Auxerre, appearing before us, granted and quitclaimed to the church and brothers of Fontenay whatever he possessed at Marmagne, in men, lands, revenues, and all other things, in exchange for eighteen pounds of Provins currency. The aforesaid brothers of Fontenay are bound to pay the said Guy ten pounds at the fair of Bar and eight pounds at the fair of Troyes around the feast of Saint Remigius. So that all this may remain ratified, at the request of Guy himself and [Col. 1469C] the brothers of Fontenay, we have strengthened this present writing with the protection of our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1220.

556 CXVI. Odo of Issoudun, count of Grignon; his wife Matilda, daughter of Raymond, who was the son of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy, and brother of Henry, bishop of Autun. 1165. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

I, Henry, by God’s grace bishop of Autun, make known to those present and future that the claim which Odo of Issoudun, count of Grignon, brought against the church of Fontenay concerning the alms-gift of my brother [Col. 1469D] Raymond was settled in our presence as follows. The aforesaid Raymond had granted the brothers of Fontenay, for his soul and those of his predecessors, whatever his tenants of the lordship of Grignon might give them as alms from their tenements, provided that the tenant should not lose his tenement. Afterwards Odo of Issoudun, to whom the land of Grignon had come through his wife Matilda, Raymond’s daughter, raised a claim concerning this. Therefore both parties—Odo, that is, [Col. 1470A] and the monks—appeared before me. It was acknowledged and proved by the unassailable testimony of lawful men that my brother Raymond had made this gift before he married the mother of the aforesaid girl, etc. Odo, unwilling to oppose such manifest truth any further, renounced into the hand of Hugh, abbot of Fontenay, every claim which he had raised against the church of Fontenay; and he confirmed as valid the alms-gift so lawfully made, etc. His wife Matilda approved all this. The witnesses are Abraham, abbot of Pratée, etc.

This was done at Saigny on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, and on the next day it was acknowledged and confirmed in the 557 chapter-house of Fontenay, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1470B] 1165.

CXVII. Matilda, countess of Grignon, daughter of Count Raymond. 1196. (From the Fontenay original.)

I, Matilda, countess of Grignon, make known to all, future as well as present, that I have approved and granted all the gifts and alms which my father Count Raymond gave and granted to the church and brothers of Fontenay. I also investigated on reliable grounds the agreement made between my father Raymond, the men of Estalante, and the aforesaid brothers of Fontenay; and I learned as a matter of fact that my father himself set stone boundary markers between [Col. 1470C] the men of Estalante and the aforesaid brothers, so that the said men, their animals, and even their swine should in no way cross the boundaries he had set. Following his example, I will and command that this be firmly observed by all hereafter. I also grant in perpetuity the easements at Mortueau, which my father granted them for watering their livestock. I have further given them fishing in my pond at Estalante: during my lifetime, only for two days and nights before Palm Sunday; and after my death, for two days and nights in perpetuity, for the provision of my anniversary commemoration.

The witnesses to this are Hubert, abbot of Fontenay, [Col. 1470D] and the entire convent of that place; Odo, archpriest of Tuilly; 558 Oliver of Grignon; Matthew of Esté; Pons of Chaace; Milo, his brother; Rainer of Sainte-Colombe; Theobald, provost of Montbarr; and many others.

That all this may remain valid for ever, I have confirmed it with the impression of my seal, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1196.

> **Note:** [Col. 1469D] Many other charters of Matilda, countess of Grignon, dated to the years of Christ 1195 and 1196, survive among the Fontenay records. Duchesne, in *The Dukes of Burgundy*, and the Sainte-Marthe brothers, in the *Royal Genealogy*, book XXXVIII, correctly affirm, on the authority of Robert of Mont, the Chronicle of Auxerre, and other writers of good standing, that this Matilda had four husbands. Accordingly, during the thirty years between 1165 and 1195, she was attached to four husbands: first Odo of Issoudun; then Guy, count of Nevers; afterwards Peter, brother of Philip, count of Flanders; and finally Robert of Dreux. From this one may infer that she, having experienced so many changes of fortune, ultimately withdrew to Grignon, to her first bridal chambers, [Col. 1471C] and, content there with the title of countess of Grignon alone, spent what remained of her life piously.

CXVIII. Matilda, countess of Grignon. Odo, count of Grignon. [Note: [Col. 1471C] Beware, dear reader, of supposing that the Odo, count of Grignon, whom you read of here is the same man whom in 1165 you saw as the first husband of this Matilda. For in this year 1196 Matilda was free after [Col. 1472C] her fourth marriage; and her first husband, Odo of Issoudun, had already died in 1177, if Robert of Mont’s Chronicle is to be trusted. The duke of Burgundy, because he was a kinsman, had secretly carried off Odo’s namesake son and heir. Robert called a relative one related by blood in the second and third degree; this can be seen in the following genealogical diagram.] 1196. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

[Col. 1471A]

Let present and future persons know that I, Matilda, countess of Grignon, have given to the church of Fontenay, for the salvation of my soul, a vineyard which I had received from Erard in pledge for nine pounds of Dijon currency, 559 situated in the parish of Saigny, on the following condition: that the income of the vineyard shall provide for the celebration of Masses; if anything remains, cloth shall be purchased from it to make corporals. Moreover, I have granted that the aforesaid brothers may acquire the said vineyard by whatever means they can. The abbot and monks of the aforesaid church have also promised me that, if the mentioned vineyard is redeemed, the redemption-price received shall be assigned to such a building that, as stipulated above, divine services shall be celebrated in the said church.

Odo, count of Grignon, approved and granted all this, and everything with which the brothers of Fontenay were invested, on the day when these things were done.

The witnesses to this are Odo, archpriest of Tuilly; Oliver of Grignon; Rainer of Sainte-Colombe; Josbert of Mâcon; and Galannus, provost.

That all this may remain valid in perpetuity, I, Matilda, countess of Grignon, have strengthened this present document with my seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1196.

ODO II, duke of Burgundy.

HUGH III, duke of Burgundy.

Hugh II, duke of Burgundy. RAYMOND, count of Grignon.

MATILDA, countess of Grignon, wife of Odo of Issoudun.

ODO the Younger of Issoudun, count of Grignon. Wife: ALIX, lady of Montbarr.

RALPH, heir of his father Odo, having married Margaret, or Sybilla, of Courtenay, dies without offspring; and his lordships return to the dominion of the dukes of Burgundy.

[Col. 1471B] 560 Thus Odo, Matilda’s son—whom in 1196, when you see her call him count of Grignon, was the second of this name among the counts of Grignon, but the third among the lords of Issoudun—was the man to whom, according to Duchesne, privileges granted to the people of Issoudun by him and his wife Alix survive for the year 1190. This Matilda was Raymond’s daughter and Hugh II the duke’s granddaughter. I think Alix was the daughter of Andrew, lord of Montbarr, who, having married Helvidis, lady of Époisses, gave Époisses, her maternal dowry, to their son Bernard, and Montbarr to their daughter Alix. For the author of the genealogical table of Fontenay noted that a girl of the Montbarr family had been betrothed to the son of the count of Grignon. Although he is rather inaccurate in many other respects, I shall not deny him credit in this, since I know from ancient Fontenay records that Bernard, son of Andrew and Helvidis, used only the title lord of Époisses, and not that of lord of Montbarr.

From this, moreover, I seem to discern how Grignon and Montbarr came into the possession of the dukes. That is, through the childless death of Ralph, of whom Alberic writes: 561 Ralph had possessed Montbarr through the inheritance of his mother Alix, and Grignon through that of his grandmother Matilda, niece of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy. This duke, as is clear from no. 105 of the second great charter of Fontenay, no. 11, had also acquired the county of Grignon after Helirand Fergannus (no. 199), who is mentioned [Col. 1472B] in no. 43 of the first great charter. This Count Fergannus seems to have married a daughter of Rainard, lord of Montbarr, so that Andrew, Bernard’s son and Rainard’s grandson, is correctly reported in the documents of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, to have had the countess as his aunt (no. 109).

CXIX. Oliver of Grignon, his wife Floria, and their sons Pons and Hugh. 1191. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

I, GAUTIER, by God’s grace bishop of Autun, make known to those present and future that Oliver of Grignon approved and granted to God and to the brothers of the church of Fontenay all the alms which his father and brothers had made to that church, [Col. 1472C] together with the land called Mont Arlant, in woodland and on the plain, etc. Floria, Oliver’s wife, approved all these things with her two sons Pons and Hugh, etc.

Among the witnesses: Josbert, abbot of Fontenay.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1191.

CXX. Walter, knight of Montbarr; his wife Ermengard, whose brother was Odet, mother Gilla, and Gilla’s children Simon, Maria, and Aaliz. 1215. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

I, Gautier, by God’s grace bishop of Autun, make known to all who inspect this present document [Col. 1473A] 562 that Walter, knight of Montbarr, gave to God and the church of Saint Mary of Fontenay, for the salvation of his soul and those of his predecessors, as a perpetual gift, all the rights he possessed in the forest above that abbey and all the rights he possessed in the territory of the same forest, as far as the great road leading to Saint James. The same Walter also acknowledged that none of his men, nor any other person, ought to have a right of use in the aforementioned forest. This alms-gift was approved and confirmed in good faith by Walter’s wife Ermengard, together with her brother Odet, from whom she held it in chief; by Ermengard’s mother, named Gilla; and by Gilla’s son Simon with his sisters Maria and Aaliz. So that all this [Col. 1473B] may remain valid and firm for ever, at the request of the said Walter, his wife, and Odo, brother of the same wife, we have ordered this present document to be strengthened with our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnation 1215.

CXXI. Extracts from other records of the abbey of Fontenay. (From the second great charter, which consists of forty-seven numbers and ends with the privilege of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, without a date.)

No. 13. Gerard of Échalot, brother-in-law of Gerard the canon, with the approval of his wife Rotrude, gave to the church of Fontenay whatever he possessed at Puteau- 563 Franc and at the Valley of Abon.

[Col. 1473C] No. 23. Ebrard of Villaines gave to the church of Fontenay as alms whatever he possessed from Saigny, in the territory of Flacey and Saigny-le. Among the witnesses: Henry of Montbarr.

In various places in this great charter, Rainer of La Roche occurs at least ten times among the witnesses.

Galo, son of Nariodus of Montbarr.

No. 29. Mauvaslet of Montbarr. His son Hugh. Robert of Montbarr, brother of Odo of Champagne. Again Odo of Champagne occurs among the witnesses, in no. 37; Gerard of Châtillon, Simon of Châtillon, Matthew of Châtillon.

(From originals.)

In the year 1174, Hugh Peccatum of Til gave as alms to [Col. 1473D] the brothers of Fontenay a fourth part in woodland and on the plain, etc.

Andrew, lord of Époisses; his brother Bernard, lordling, lord of Vi, in the year 1232.

Frequent mention is made of the villages of Fontaines in the district of Duesmois and of Fontaines-sèches.

In 1202, Gerard le Broz of Asnières and his wife Margaret give something to the monastery of Fontenay. In October 1273, Alexander of Montagu mentions Ermengard, called Blanche, formerly lady of Sombernon and Esté, then deceased.

(From two cartularies.)

Stephen, bishop of Autun: G., abbot of Molesme, grants him the place in which Brother Martin the hermit lived, so that an abbey may be established there for brothers living under the rule [Col. 1474A] of Saint Benedict.

In the time of Henry, bishop of Autun, and in his charters, Andrew, lord of Montbarr, and Galo of Grignon occur several times as witnesses.

In the charters of Stephen, bishop of Autun, in 1174, Brocard of Montbarr is a witness among others.

Odo of Marmagne, son of Bartholomew of Châtillon and Elizabeth; in a charter of Gautier, bishop of Langres, Bernard of Époisses is witness, in 1196.

To the charters of Gautier, bishop of Autun, concerning the gift of Pons of Chaace and his brother Milo, in 1198, Lord Bernard of Montbarr and Rainer of Saigny, knights, subscribe.

In the charter of Stephen, bishop of Autun, and Gautier, bishop of Langres, [Col. 1474B] of 1173, Bernard Nariodus is mentioned.

In 1202, in a charter of Gautier, bishop of Autun, concerning the gifts of Rainer, knight of Curcelle, Bernard, lord of Époisses, is among the witnesses.

Simon of Montbarr, knight, in 1209, in the records of Haimo, archdeacon of Flavigny.

In 1198, Bernard of Montbarr is, among others, a witness in a charter of Gautier, bishop of Autun, concerning an agreement between the men of Fontenay and Oigny concerning certain woods.

Nicholas of Montbarr, knight, in June 1277.

Hugh of Montbarr, in a charter of Humbert, bishop of Autun, in the time of William, abbot of Fontenay.

[Col. 1474C] In August 1282, Hugh of Saigny, knight, with the consent of his wife Maria, sells a vineyard of his to the abbot and convent of Fontenay.

565 Aaliz, duchess of Burgundy, settles a dispute between the men of Fontenay and Arnulf, knight of Échalot, concerning certain rights of use and pastures.

In the records of Alix, duchess, August 1227, mention is made of Lord Gerard of Sauz; according to whose *porgivation* [reading uncertain], certain boundaries are established between Échalot, Estalante, and Poiseul, at the arbitration of Gervase, chaplain of Estalante.

CXXII. John, knight of Montbarr, son of Beatrice. 1239. (From the Fontenay cartulary.)

[Col. 1474D]

I, HUGH, duke of Burgundy, make known to all who inspect these present letters that John, knight of Montbarr, appearing in my presence, acknowledged that he had given in perpetual alms to the church of Blessed Mary of Fontenay his man Richard of Marmagne, together with all Richard’s heirs and tenements. The said John further gave the said church six dayworks of land situated beside the road before the house of the converted women of Marmagne. The aforesaid John also approved the alms-gift which his mother Lady Beatrice had made to the aforesaid church of Fontenay: two sextaries of wheat and one muid of wine, which the church of Fontenay shall receive every year from the tithe [Col. 1475A] of the said John at Corbeton. The aforementioned John promised in good faith to warrant all this to the said church against every disturber. In testimony of this matter, at the request of the aforesaid John, I have strengthened these present letters 566 with the protection of my seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1239, in July.

CXXIII. Blanche, widow of Hervé, lord of Sombernon, 1242. (From the Fontenay original.)

HUGH, duke of Burgundy, greetings to all who inspect these present letters.

Know that the noblewoman, our beloved and faithful Blanche, lady [Col. 1475B] of Sombernon, appearing in our presence, acknowledged that the late Hervé, her former husband and lord of Sombernon, while in his last illness, gave and granted, in pure and perpetual alms, for the salvation of his own soul and those of his predecessors, to God, the church of Blessed Mary of Fontenay, and the brothers there serving God, one hundred Dijon sous. He ordered that these be assigned for annual receipt from his own demesne land. The aforesaid Blanche, observing the devotion of her deceased husband and wishing to provide for his soul and those of his predecessors, approved the said alms-gift and assigned the said brothers of Fontenay the said one hundred Dijon sous, to be received annually from the proceeds of the fair of Saint [Col. 1475C] Machutus at Sombernon. In testimony of this, at the request of Blanche herself, lady of Sombernon, we caused letters, strengthened with the protection of our seal, to be delivered to the said brothers of Fontenay.

Done in the year of the Lord 1242, in January.

CXXIV. 567 Emaniars, Lady of Sombernon and Esté. 1271. (Extract from the Cartulary of the Abbey of Fontenay.)

We, William, humble abbot of Flavigny; we, Brother Stephen, prior of the Vale of Our Lady near Talant, of the Order of the Vale of Scholars; and the said Simon, master of the house of Saint Anthony [Col. 1475D] at Esté, make known to all who shall see these present letters that Lady Emaniars, called Blanche, Lady of Sombernon and Esté, in her last will and testament—of which we, the aforesaid William, Stephen, and Simon, are executors—has given, released, and granted as perpetual alms to God and to the church of Our Lady of Fontenay, for the salvation of her soul and those of her ancestors, and for the celebration of her anniversary, everything which she had, could have, or ought to have at Nojent and in the territory of that town, etc. And we, the aforesaid executors, have notified and delivered the aforesaid alms-gift to the religious of the aforesaid church of Fontenay, etc. This was done in the year of grace 1271, in September.

Alexander of Montagu, esquire, lord of Sombernon [Col. 1476A] and of Maanlayn, acknowledges the same and promises to warrant it, in the following October.

CXXV. (From the necrology of Fontenay.)

On the fourth day before the Kalends of February died Helvidis, lady of Époisses.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of March died Lord William, lord 568 of Époisses, in the year of the Lord 1326.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of March died Lord Roger of Mortemer, count of La Marche.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April: the anniversary of Pope Honorius.

On the sixth day before the Kalends of April died Lord Robert, duke of Burgundy.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of June died Lord Stephen, bishop of Autun.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of September died Eustachia, lady of Mello.

On the fourth day before the Ides of October died Lord Ebrard, bishop of Norwich.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November died Robert, count of Tonnerre.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of November died Lord Guy, bishop of Autun.

On the seventh day before the Kalends of December: the anniversary of Lord John of Époisses and his brothers.

On the Nones of December: the anniversary of Joanna, countess of Flanders.

On the eighth day before the Ides of December died Lord Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.

[Col. 1476C] On the tenth day before the Kalends of January: the anniversary of Queen Berengaria and her sister, the countess of Champagne.

CXXVI. (From the necrology of Bussières.)

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1130, on this day this monastery of Bussières was founded; its first founders were the most noble lords of Sombernon.

569 On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November: the anniversary of the noble Hervé, lord of Saffres, and all his successors.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of November, special absolution is given to the souls of the illustrious Lord Raymond and his daughter Matilda, countess [Col. 1476D] of Nevers.

CXXVII. The first year of the rule of Rainer, second abbot of Larrivour, was current in the year of Christ 1158, on the sixth day before the Ides of September. (From the cartulary of Larrivour.)

GEOFFREY, bishop of Langres, gives to the monastery of Larrivour and the brothers serving God there the estate of the whole territory of Amorey, in which, he says, they had long possessed from our predecessor, Bishop Vilencus of pious memory, all easements, etc.

Given at Larrivour in the year of the Incarnation 1157, and the first year of the rule of Lord Rainer, second abbot of that same Larrivour, on the sixth day before the Ides of September.

CXXVIII. Hugh, count of Troyes, healed of his wounds. 1103, 1104. (From originals; reported by Camuzat in the *Promptuary*, fols. 121 and 302.)

[Col. 1477A]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, HUGH, count of Troyes by God’s grace, after the affliction of my exceedingly grave wounds 570 and their healing by God, reflecting that in many respects I had offended divine grace, and that I had deserved the aforesaid punishment justly, my sins demanding it—indeed, that I had deserved a far greater punishment—and considering the benefit bestowed upon me by the Lord’s kindness, namely the restoration of my health, resolved to give thanks to the Lord by conferring benefactions upon certain churches, [Col. 1477B] etc. I therefore gave to the church of Blessed Lupus of the monastery of Troyes freedom for the houses of the canons: namely, that henceforth no one should presume to violate them on account of a thief found there, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103.

> **Note:** [Col. 1477D] He introduces a similar privilege, granted to the church of Saint Peter and Saint Saviour at Troyes in the year of Christ 1104, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in indiction XII, in precisely the same words. I believe, moreover, that these wounds were inflicted on Count Hugh when he supported Emperor Henry in the war waged in 1102 between him and Robert, count of Flanders. Concerning this war Sigebert writes under that year: “While Robert, count of the Flemings, was harassing the city of Cambrai, Emperor Henry marched against him; after taking some of his castles, he was compelled by the severity of the approaching winter to return.” Dodechin, the Chronicle of Liège, Meyer, and other more recent writers also mention the same war. Count Hugh appears to have supported the emperor, following the example of his father Theobald. Hermannus Contractus writes under the year 1054: “Emperor Henry celebrated the Easter feast at Mainz; there Theobald, son of Odo, coming to him from Gaul and becoming his knight, promised him his assistance.” Peter Pithou, in his *Commentary on the Counts of Champagne and Brie*, therefore reasonably conjectures that the dignity and title of the Palatine counts of Champagne arose from a grant of the emperors.

571 CXXIX. Hugh, count of Troyes, returned from Jerusalem for the second time. 1122. (From the *Promptuary* of Nicolas Camuzat, p. 286.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful that Lord Hugh, most illustrious Count of Troyes, when he was making his second journey to Jerusalem, at the city of Autun, on the feast day of the holy Apostles Simon and Jude, gave and granted for perpetual possession [Col. 1477C] to the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul of the monastery of Arremar, and to the church of St John the Baptist of the Castle, situated within the walls of the city of Troyes, and to the monks serving there—namely Lord Abbot Walter and his successors—a sextary of wheat, a sextary of wine, bread, wine, and a pork shoulder. All these things the monks of St John of the Castle had customarily given each year at the gate of the city situated toward the Abbey of Arremar. When that same count returned from the holy Lord’s Sepulchre, Lord Abbot Walter approached him and humbly asked him to perform and grant, before his retainers and before lawful witnesses of the city of Troyes, [Col. 1477D] what he had done at Autun. This he did willingly and amicably.

This was done publicly at the city of Troyes, in the cloister of St John the Baptist of the Castle, on the seventh Ides of October—that is, on the feast day of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1122, 572, with concurrent VI and epact XXII; in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II; in indiction I; in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks; and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Hatto, bishop of the city of Troyes.

### CXXX. Odo of Champagne and his wife Sibylla. 1137.

*(From the autograph of the Abbey of Acey.)*

ODO of Champagne and his wife SIBYLLA gave to God and to St Mary of Acey whatever they possessed in the court or estate of Amblie. Charter of Humbert, Archbishop of Besançon, issued in the year of Christ 1137, for the monastery of Acey.

### CXXXI. Garnier of Fontaines, founder of the priory of Bonvaux beneath Talant, of the Order of the Valley of Scholars. 1215.

*(Guillaume PARADIN, book II of the Annals of Burgundy, p. 265.)*

[Col. 1478B]

At this time there arose a new community of religious persons who established an Order called the Valley of Scholars. A gentleman from near Dijon, named Garnier of Fontaines, gave them the site and place of Notre-Dame de Bonval beneath Talant, in order to found there a priory of this new Order; and he endowed it with several rents, by the consent and approval of Duke Odo, who sealed the donations and the foundation of the said place of Bonval with his seal. This was in the year of salvation 1215.

### CXXXII. John, Lord of Fontaines. Enjarranz, or Garnier, of Fontaines. 1220.

*(From the autograph of Bonvaux beneath Talant.)*

[Col. 1478C]

I, Brother THEOBALD, humble preceptor of the Bailiwick of Bures, make known to present and future persons that, if Enjarranz of Fontaines, our man, or his heirs should at any time fail in payment of the three sextaries of oil made from nuts, which John, Lord of Fontaines, son of Lord William of Sauz, gave in alms to God, to Blessed Mary, and to the brethren of the Valley of Scholars, for the salvation of his own soul, that of his mother Lady Belot, and those of his ancestors, to be paid annually on the feast of All Saints [Col. 1478D] for the maintenance of one lamp, the brethren of the Order of the Temple should hold themselves bound by four dayworks of land: two of them situated in the *arbua* [uncertain term] near the castle of Fontaines, and the other two in the territory of Eschiré; by a vineyard situated in the district [Col. 1479A] of Chasoil; and by three sous and six deniers of annual rent; and we should thereafter be bound for payment of the said oil. In testimony of this matter, I have affixed my seal to the present letters.

Done in the year of grace 1220.

### CXXXIII. Abbey of Sept-Fons, of the Cistercian Order, a daughter-house of Fontenay, founded under William, second abbot of Fontenay.

[Note: [Col. 1479D] From this we also learn that the Abbey of Sept-Fons, in the district of Bourbon and of the Cistercian Order—for there are two other abbeys of the same name belonging to the Premonstratensians, in the dioceses of Reims and Langres—was a daughter-house of Fontenay; that is, a colony established from Fontenay by Abbot William. When this occurred cannot be determined from these undated documents. Claude Robert, however, teaches us in the *Gallia Christiana*, writing that he had been informed from a bull of Pope Adrian IV, issued in 1156, that the monastery had been founded in 1132 by Wicard and William of Bourbon.]

*(From the second great charter of Fontenay, no. 38.)*

574 Haymo, knight of Marmagne, gave the church of Fontenay the meadow called the Meadow of Belet, near the monks’ great meadow in the valley of Grignon. In return he received from the monks the land and meadows they held at Marmagne, and a palfrey. [Col. 1479B] This was done between Montbard and Montfort, when Abbot William was leading out the colony for the Abbey of Sept-Fons.

The witnesses are Rainer of La Roche; Gilbert, the aforesaid Haymo’s maternal uncle; Theobald, priest of Fraxino; and Odo, priest of Curcelles.

### CXXXIV. Arms of the Counts of Champagne.

*(Extract from Pierre PITHOU, book I of the Counts of Champagne and Brie, p. 493.)*

These are the seven who may justly be judged to have been the true peer-counts of Champagne. (He had named the Counts of Joigny, Rethel, Brienne, Roucy, Braine, Grandpré, and Bar-sur-Seine.) To this number several have wished [Col. 1479C] to refer the seven gold pieces counter-potent upon a silver bend, which they place on an azure field in the arms of Champagne and Brie. More recent heralds, however, blazon them: azure, a silver bend counter-potent in gold with thirteen pieces. But the *Romance of the Little Saintré*, to which, because of its antiquity, I defer somewhat in such doubtful matters, assigns to a John of Champagne: azure, a silver bend, with two gold cotices or trellis-bands, potent and counter-potent—without numbering them further—and three red labels, which are marks of cadency, etc.

Now, although the potents are still acknowledged by all in these arms, I venture to say that, on the seals of these counts—especially those of King Theobald and [Col. 1479D] Queen Joan, which I have seen in a considerable number—there is far more appearance of fleurons upon this bend than of potents. Yet I have not undertaken here to blazon these arms too scrupulously. I am content to say that, if this is so, they do not seem altogether as ancient as these counts; for it is quite certain that, at the beginning, they did not have so many peers of this rank under their authority. There is likewise very great likelihood, 576 that [Col. 1480A] the overseas enterprises brought us most of these arms and blazons; at the least, they made their use more common, and thereafter more strictly observed, than it had previously been.

### CXXXV. Arms of the Counts of Champagne.

Extract from a letter of Sieur André Duchesne, addressed to Monsieur Nicolas Camusat, canon of the Church of Troyes, on 29 November 1624, and communicated to me by Monsieur Louis de Villeprouvée, Lord of Villette, counsellor to His Majesty and elected official in the election district of Troyes.

As for the potent and counter-potent seal of Champagne, I saw it upon the tomb of Alix, wife of Theobald, Count of Champagne, son of the second Odo, in [Col. 1480B] the church of Saint-Pharon—unless one wishes to say that the tomb was made long after her death. But I have also seen it on seals held at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, before the year 1230. This shows that the potents arose from fancy. For my part, I think that it was a difference adopted by a younger son and thereafter retained by his descendants when they became the senior line.

### NOTICE TO THE READER.

If it is true that Henry the Liberal, who from 1152 was Count of Champagne after his father Theobald the Great, was the first to bear potent and counter-potent charges in his arms, as Monsieur Bonhomme maintains in the article following this one, it must be held certain that such arms [Col. 1480C] were placed upon the tomb of Aalys, wife of Theobald the Elder and mother of Count Hugh, only long after her death, and after the reign of Henry the Liberal, her great-grandson.

### CXXXVI. Memoirs of Monsieur Bonhomme, former canon of the cathedral church of Troyes, concerning the arms of the Counts of Champagne.

Sent to us in September 1659.

577 In the treasury of our Chapter of Troyes I have seen the charter of Count Hugh, entered in the book of Sieur Camusat, with the three seals hanging from it. The first is that of the said Hugh; the third, that of Theobald his successor, to whom he sold the counties of Champagne [Col. 1480D] and Brie; and the middle one, that of Henry the Liberal, son of Theobald. Without doubt they were attached in different years, to confirm the privileges contained in it in favor of the said Chapter of Troyes, according to the time of their respective reigns.

The three seals of these three counts, succeeding one another, have no counterseal. On each seal is impressed a man on horseback, holding a drawn sword in his right hand and, in his left, a shield on his left side, [Col. 1481A] of which only the edge can be seen across his breast, with the inscription of each of the three around the seal:

> Seal of Hugh, Count Palatine of Troyes.  
> Seal of Theobald, Count Palatine of Troyes.  
> Seal of Henry, Count Palatine of Troyes.

All three are thus styled Palatine, as likewise were the subsequent Counts of Champagne down to Joan, wife of Philip the Fair. They had their palace in Troyes, where they held their great sessions twice each year, attended by the seven counts and six peer-vassals. The first term was on the day after Quasimodo Sunday, 578 and the second on the sixth of the following August. Philip the Fair’s contract provided that these great sessions should not be held while those of the Parlement of France [Col. 1481B] were being held.

Each of our counts bore on his shield a blazon according to his fancy: one because of his mother, others because of diverse lands and counties which came to them either by marriage, succession, or deeds of gift.

To tell you that our counts blazoned their shields differently, I know that Herbert, our first Count of Troyes, bore a chequered field of gold and azure in the year 902.

Robert, after 930, having seized Troyes, bore as his blazon a gold panther upon a red shield.

Others afterward bore azure with a silver bend [Col. 1481C] and two gold cotices, one on either side; the silver bend charged with water-waves, and the two cotices likewise.

Others bore upon the silver bend and gold cotices undulating vine-leaves.

Others bore vine-leaves only upon the cotices, and not upon the silver bend.

Henry the Liberal, son of Theobald of the fair lineage, was the first to bear on his shield azure with a silver bend, signifying the River Seine which he caused to pass through Troyes; two cotices potent and counter-potent in thirteen gold pieces, signifying the thirteen count-vassals of the said Count of Champagne: namely, Joigny, dean of the counts; Bar; Auxerre; [Col. 1481D] Tonnerre; Porcien; Brienne; Grandpré; Rethel; Marle; Vertus; Vienne; Bussy; and Brie.

I have in my cabinet the proofs of all that is stated above. 579 Upon the silver tomb which his wife Mary—daughter of Louis the Younger and of Eleanor, daughter of St William, Duchess of Aquitaine, who well knew her husband’s arms—caused to be made, these two verses are engraved in gold:

> Mary reveals the illustrious deeds of the prince,  
> while she veils her husband’s ashes with such a covering.

I have also seen a large red-wax seal, in the treasury of the Chapter of St Stephen, of Count Henry the Liberal, who was its founder. It has a small counterseal bearing the potent and counter-potent charges, and around it [Col. 1482A] the inscription in old French: “Passavant the better.”

His eldest son Henry bore the same, except that he bore Cyprus and Champagne on a divided shield, as King of Cyprus, by reason of his wife Isabella the queen.

Theobald, Henry’s brother, bore azure with the silver bend; and, as cotices on either side, fourteen gold Gothic forms, as may be seen upon the silver tomb which his widow Blanche of Navarre, daughter of Sancho the Wise and sister of Sancho the Strong, caused to be erected for him. It is in the choir of St Stephen’s at Troyes, where these two verses occur:

> In this tomb Blanche, sprung from the kings of Navarre,  
> while she veils the count, reveals with what fire she burns.

His shield is heart-shaped, because in [Col. 1482B] his time the city of Troyes was so formed.

Theobald III by name, surnamed the Posthumous, son of the preceding and King of Navarre through his mother Blanche, bore the arms sent to you in a drawing. And Theobald and Henry, his two sons—of whom the latter was father of Joan, who founded the College of Navarre at Paris and was wife of King Philip the Fair—bore the same.

580 The arms of Theobald the Posthumous are oval, signifying that Troyes was built and enlarged in this shape in 1240, when he had it newly enclosed. Upon all is borne a small red oval shield charged with three gold castles, the ancient arms of Troyes, from which it took its name. At that time there were the King’s Castle, [Col. 1482C] the Count’s Castle, and that of the Viscount, which I saw demolished in 1586.

Theobald, King of Navarre—whose painted arms were attached to this memoir—bore quarterly, within a crowned oval: first, Navarre; second, Champagne with the potent cotices; third, Cyprus; fourth, Brie or Meaux, namely azure, a rampant gold lion. Over all was a small red oval charged with three gold castles, one above another.

### CXXXVII. The lordship of Époisses in the House of Mello.

*(André DUCHESNE, History of the House of Châtillon-sur-Marne, book VII, chapter 1, p. 329.)*

Louis de Noyers also died without children about [Col. 1482D] the year 1409, and had as his heir his sister Marguerite de Noyers, Lady of Pouilly and Pré-Martin, then married to Guy de La Trémoille, son of William de La Trémoille, knight, and of Marie de Mello, Lady of Époisses and Bourbon-Lancy.

*(The same Duchesne, History of the Lords of Couches, p. 166.)*

Jean de Montagu, Lord of Couches, Époisses, and Bellevère. He married Jeanne de Mello, daughter of William de Mello, Lord of Givry, and 581 of his wife Isabella of Bourbon, Lady of La Ferté-Chauderon. This Jeanne had previously been married to Eudes de Til, as a judgment of the year 1424 shows. From the succession of her grandfather Gibaut de Mello [Col. 1483A] she received her lordship of Époisses, which she brought to Jean de Montagu, her second husband.

Extract from the muster held at Sens on Sunday, the seventeenth day of August 1348, communicated to me through the courtesy of Monsieur d’Hérouval, counsellor to the king and auditor in his Chamber of Accounts at Paris.

Monsieur William de Mello, Lord of Époisses, mounted on a bay horse, white at all four legs, is valued at, or accepted for, 200 livres tournois, marked with the mark of the town, etc.

Item, from a receipt of the year 1369:

Let all know that we, Gibaut de Mello, Lord of Époisses, knight, have had and received from Jean le Mercier, Treasurer of the King’s Wars, etc., the sum [Col. 1483B] of sixty-seven livres, ten sous tournois, in francs at twenty sous tournois apiece; for which we acknowledge ourselves fully [Col. 1484A] satisfied and paid. Given at Rouen under our seal, on the seventh day of August, the year 1369.

### CXXXVIII. Extract from two letters written to me from Paris on 11 and 28 November 1659 by Monsieur du Bouchet, knight of the King’s Order, his counsellor, ordinary master of his household, and historiographer.

Certainly the land of Époisses came to Dreux de Mello, son of William de Mello and grandson of Dreux de Mello, 582 Constable of France, through his marriage with Helvis de l’Orme, who had received it from her mother, also named Helvis. I possess a document in which this Dreux is styled Lord of Époisses as early as 1247. It was his grandson of the same name whose wife was Eustache de Lusignan, first cousin [Col. 1484B] of Edward I, King of England. Here is the order of these descents:

DREUX de Mello, Constable of France, died in 1218.

WILLIAM de Mello, Lord of Saint-Bris, died in 1248.

DREUX de Mello, Lord of Châteauchinon, married before 1247 HELVIS, only daughter of HUGH, Lord of l’Orme, and of HELVIS, Lady of Époisses. He followed St Louis overseas and, while in the camp before Damietta, ceded to King St Louis in 1249 what he possessed at Loches and Châtillon by reason of his late uncle DREUX de Mello. He died before 1252.

DREUX de Mello, Lord of Époisses, Châteauchinon, l’Orme, and Saint-Bris, was married before 1259 to the daughter of Anseric, Lord of Montréal, and of Marie de Garlande; for in that year he sought partition of Marie de Garlande’s property from Henry, Count of Grandpré, his wife’s uterine brother. He was still living in 1269.

DREUX de Mello, Lord of Saint-Bris, Époisses, l’Orme, and Châteauchinon, 1276, married EUSTACHE de Lusignan, daughter of Geoffrey de Lusignan, Lord of Sainte-Hermine, Jarnac, and Châteauneuf, and of Joan, Viscountess of Châtellerault. He was still living in 1290. He was father of DREUX de Mello, who married Eleanor of Savoy, widow of William of Chalon, Count of Auxerre and Tonnerre, by whom he had two daughters, etc.

EUSTACHE de Lusignan was first cousin of EDWARD I, King of England, through ISABELLA of Angoulême, 583 who was grandmother to both.

JOHN I, King of England, Isabella’s first husband.  
HENRY III, King of England.  
EDWARD I, King of England.

HUGH X, Lord of Lusignan, Isabella’s second husband.  
GEOFFREY of Lusignan, husband of Joan, Viscountess of Châtellerault.  
EUSTACHE of Lusignan, wife of Dreux de Mello.

[Col. 1483C] This Hugh, Isabella of Angoulême’s second husband, was also Count of La Marche, and was the tenth of that name among the Lords of Lusignan, not the ninth, as Sieur Duchesne stated, since he was unaware of the number of these Hughs.

Here is the proof that Dreux de Mello, husband of Helvis de l’Orme, was already styled Lord of Époisses in 1247. It is drawn from the treasury of the Cathedral of Auxerre.

H., dean, and the entire Chapter of Auxerre, greetings in the Lord.

Let all know that, whereas we had purchased from the nobleman Dreux de Mello, Lord of Époisses, Châteauchinon, and l’Orme, and from his wife Helvis, with the approval and consent of our venerable father Guy, by the grace of God bishop of Auxerre, [Col. 1483D] the borough of Conches near Varzy, and everything which they possessed, held, and owned at Varzy, as is more fully contained in [Col. 1484C] the letters of the aforesaid Dreux and his wife; of the venerable fathers, the bishops of Langres and Nevers; and also in the letters of the aforesaid Father Guy, bishop of Auxerre, from whose fief all the aforesaid things purchased by us are acknowledged to be held, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord 1247, in June.

The lordship of l’Orme is in Nivernais, two and a half leagues from Saint-Léonard, 584 ten leagues from Époisses, and twelve leagues from Saint-Bris; it passed into the House of Chalon-Arlay through the marriage of Marguerite de Mello.

### CXXXIX. Extract from the *History of the Island and Kingdom of Cyprus*, by Étienne de Lusignan, Dominican, chapter 22.

[Col. 1484D]

Hugh, as eldest son, succeeded his father Hugh le Brun II in the County of La Marche, and after the death of his brother Geoffrey, surnamed “the Great Tooth,” in the County of Lusignan. Now the Count of Angoulême had promised him his only daughter, named Isabella; but when they had gone to church to be married, John, King of England, compelled the priest to give her to him as wife. This produced many disturbances and wars, which were finally appeased when the Englishman gave him the government of Saintonge. After the death of the said king, Queen Isabella married this Count Hugh, to whom she had originally been promised; and thus he obtained Angoulême as a third county.

This Isabella, then, although she was the wife of a count, would not on that account abandon her title of queen. Consequently, because of that title, her husband refused to do homage to Alfonso, Count of Poitiers, brother [Col. 1485B] of St Louis, King of France. Great wars even arose between them: Alfonso being aided by his brothers, and this count by Henry, King of England, etc. He died leaving nine children—Hugh le Brun, Guy, Geoffrey, Aimery, William, Agatha, Isabella, Margaret, and Alearde—all begotten by Queen Isabella, 585 who had had four others by King John of England: namely Henry, King of England; Isabella, wife of Frederick II, Emperor; Joan, Queen of Scotland; and the Duke of Lancaster, etc.

Geoffrey received the barony of Jarnac and Châteauneuf. From him descended two children: Geoffrey, who succeeded to his father’s domain and, having married Péronnelle Senille, Countess of Dreux, died without children; and [Col. 1485C] his sister Eustache, who was married to the Baron of Marle—that is, Dreux de Mello—from whom came Count Jean des Lyons, Lord of Arlay, and Amaury, Lord of Craon.

[Note: [Col. 1485D] Duchesne, at the end of book XII of his *History of England*, says that Isabella of Angoulême had seven children by King John, her first husband: [Col. 1486D] namely three sons and four daughters, all of whom he names in order.]

### CXL. Extract from an inventory of one hundred and twelve documents concerning the houses of Saffré and Fontaines, drawn up at Beaune by F. de la Place, royal notary, 19 November 1632.

1. An old letter of the year 1100, speaking of an Allette de Montbard and an Eve de Châtillon, ladies of Saffré and Fontaines. Sealed; entered as no. 37.

2. An old letter of January 1107 concerning certain affairs between Henry and Simon de Saffré, brothers, children of Diane de Montbard and Otho de Châtillon, lords of Saffré and Fontaines. Entered as no. 31.

586 3. An old Latin letter by which Guy de Marrey and Fontaines receives back from a Duke of Burgundy the fiefs of Fontaines, Marrey, and Châtillon, in the year 1129. Sealed; entered as no. 82.

4. Another Latin letter of the year 1147, being a marriage contract between Arvier de Saffré, knight, and Marie de Marrey and Fontaines, [Col. 1486A] by the authority and consent of her father, mother, and the patrons named in the said contract. Sealed; entered as no. 83.

5. An old Latin letter concerning the fiefs of Saffré, in favor of Bernard de Saffré, Lord of Fontaines, dated 1180. Entered as no. 13.

6. Item, a Latin letter written on parchment concerning the fiefs of Saffré and Fontaines, issued by the Duke of Burgundy to William de Saffré and Fontaines in 1187. Entered as no. 11.

7. Item, the alliance of the House of Foix with that of Saffré, of the year 1200. Entered as no. 6.

8. Item, a Latin letter written on parchment [Col. 1486B] concerning certain agreements between Stephen and Bartholomew de Saffré, lords of Fontaines near Dijon, and a man named Jean des Temples, dated 10 May 1200. Entered as no. 7.

9. Another letter showing that Jean de Fontaines gave all his property to William de Fontaines in order to enter religious life. Dated 1200. Entered as no. 53.

10. A letter of the year 1200 in which Constantin de Fontaines and Allette de Montbard make certain agreements together. Entered as no. 58.

587 11. A letter of Bernard de Fontaines containing a settlement with William de Marrey, in part Lord of Fontaines, concerning the property which they had at Châtillon, in the year 1200. Entered as no. [Col. 1486C] 61.

12. A Latin letter by which a Blanche of France grants a portion of her property to Hust de Saffré in 1200. Sealed with two seals. Entered as no. 20.

13. A parchment letter of June 1203 containing a donation made by Allete de Saffré, Lady of Fontaines, to several of her children. Entered as no. 9.

14. A Latin letter of 1206 in which Jean de Fontaines gives his property to his daughter Marie de Fontaines and to his son-in-law Jean de Saffré. Entered as no. 85.

15. An old document in Old French by which Jean [Col. 1486D] de Fontaines obliges Arvier de Saffré to give substantial goods to the poor, in 1227. Entered as no. 86.

16. A Latin marriage contract showing that Arvier de Saffré married Beatrix of Burgundy in December 1230. Sealed; entered as no. 87.

17. A Latin letter written on parchment in which Millotte de Châtillon, Lady of Fontaines and Marrey, makes an agreement with her brother Oudot de Saffré in 1247. Entered as no. 63.

[Col. 1487A] 18. A Latin letter of 1260 showing that Allette de Marrey, Lady of Fontaines, gave all her property to Joseph de Saffré, her nephew, on 6 October of the aforesaid year. Entered as no. 44.

588 19. A parchment letter containing a partition made in 1277 between Arvier and Stephen de Saffré, children of Othelin de Châtillon and Allette de Montbard, lord and lady of Saffré and Fontaines. Sealed; entered as no. 21.

20. A Latin parchment letter showing that Jean de Saffré partitioned his lands of Saffré and Fontaines with Allette de Fontaines, on 13 January [Col. 1487B] 1302. Entered as no. 3.

21. Another Latin letter containing an acquittance for the marriage settlement of Alix de Saffré, wife of Jean de Marrey, Lord of Fontaines, in October 1307. Sealed; entered as no. 73.

22. A parchment letter in Latin of 1315, on the eve of St Lawrence, showing that Jean de Saffré summons his mother Alix Rolin to show by what authority she has taken possession of his land of Saffré. Sealed; entered as no. 80.

23. A letter by which Arvier de Saffré partitions his property with Guillemot de Marrey, Lord of Fontaines, his uncle, in June 1327, on the Monday after the feast of St Barnabas [Col. 1487C] the Apostle. Sealed; entered as no. 46.

24. A parchment letter in Old French in which Jean de Fontaines and Arvier de Saffré, concerning the inheritances of their brothers who had entered religious life, submit themselves to the arbitration of Gaston de Saux, their kinsman, in March 1343. Sealed; entered as no. 76.

25. An old Latin letter in which Pernot de Montbard makes war upon Hust de Saffré, who calls to his aid his cousins 589 of Fontaines and Marrey; and the Duke of Burgundy assists the said Hust de Saffré. In green wax; entered as no. 98.

26. A Latin letter constituting a dispensation for Richard [Col. 1487D] de Fontaines to marry Allette de Saffré, in 1384. Entered as no. 57.

27. A parchment letter of King Charles, by which he promises great benefits to Jean de Saffré, lord of that place and of Fontaines; to an Edme de Saigny, knight, son-in-law of the said Jean de Saffré; and to Philibert de l’Espinace, Lord of La Clette, in 1384. Sealed; entered as no. 18.

28. A parchment letter by which William de Marrey, Lord of Fontaines, made a settlement with Arvier de Saffré concerning the succession to their grandmother’s property, on St Andrew’s Day in 1402. Entered as no. 64.

[Col. 1488A] 29. A parchment letter showing that Jean, Duke of Burgundy, Nantes, Nevers, etc., wishes Hugh de Saigny and Isabella de Saffré to be received as legitimate heirs to all property belonging to Bernard de Fontaines, Lord of Marrey and Châtillon, dated 20 June 1404. Entered as no. 92.

30. The engrossed copy of the decree concerning the lands of Fontaines-d’Ogny, Chenel, and Marrey, at the suit of Monsieur de Beauchamp against Pierre de Saigny. The said properties were purchased by Othelin de Cléron, son-in-law of the said Pierre de Saigny, on the twentieth and twenty-second of July 1405. Entered as no. 52.

590 31. Marriage contract between Arvier de Cléron and Marguerite de Montbéliard, January [Col. 1488B] 1423. Entered as no. 43.

32. Partitions made by Pierre de Saigny, Lord of Saffré, from the succession of Bernard de Marrey, his brother, dated 4 February 1473. Entered as no. 51.

### NOTICE TO THE READER.

If the titles inventoried above could all be found intact, they might have yielded much fine light concerning the kinship of St Bernard. But Monsieur de Cléron, Baron of Saffre, assured me that the originals of these documents had been stolen from him, or else (which comes to the same thing) withheld by some dishonest person to whom he had entrusted them without taking a written receipt.

Nevertheless, from what remains we may conjecture:

1. That the mother of Abbot Robert—of whom Jean l’Hermite says, without naming her, that she was sister to Alethe, mother of St Bernard—was this Diane de Montbar, wife of Outho de Chastillon, mentioned in article 2 of this extract under the year 1107; for the date and the house-name agree.
