This almost makes me abandon the conjecture I had formerly advanced on page 1453: that the father of this Abbot Robert was Wauthier, or Gauthier, Constable of Burgundy, who had married a sister of St Bernard’s mother, endowed with the service-fief of the town of Montbar; and who on that account bore the title [Col. 1488C] Lord of that town. But below we shall offer a more acceptable reason.

2. It seems that Eve de Chastillon, mentioned above under no. 2, was Tecelin’s mother, having at that time other children by Foulques de Sarcelles, whom the monk Alberic in his Chronicle gives her as second husband; and that the instrument of 1107, in which Alette de Montbar is mentioned—who in that case would have been her daughter-in-law—concerned the 591 division of the estate among Eve’s children by her first and second marriages. If this is not so—for I would not venture to affirm it without further proof—it is very plausible that Eve de Chastillon was the wife of Guy de Fontaines, St Bernard’s elder brother, and that Alette de Montbar, her mother-in-law, had entered into some agreement with her concerning the regulation and assignment of her dowry. Whatever the case, I hold that one or the other—that is, either Tecelin’s mother or the wife of Guy, Tecelin’s son—belonged to the house of Grancey. For at the castle of Grancey there is still an old tower called St Bernard’s Tower, because, as immemorial tradition relates, this saint lodged there several times. And the Chronicle of Grancey, although fabulous in other particulars, is not, it seems, to be despised when it affirms that a daughter of the house of Grancey was Lady of Fontaines-lès-Dijon, as wife of that place’s lord.

3. It seems that this Guy de Marrey, who in 1129 received anew from the Duke of Burgundy the fiefs of Fontaines, Marrey, and Chastillon, was the husband of Humberge, [Col. 1488D] or Humbeline, sister of St Bernard; and that he received Marrey anew in his own name, and the other two either in his wife’s name—she having perhaps been heiress to five of her brothers—or in the name of his nieces, two or more daughters of Guy, his brother-in-law, who succeeded to their father, mother, uncles, and aunts after these had entered religion.

2. That the houses of Fontaines, Saffre, Montbar, Marrey, and Chastillon-sur-Seine had, from St Bernard’s century onward, been united by close alliances, and afterward were almost all of one blood; sometimes passing one into another, although the titles, taken from the castles, always remained different. The same may be said of the houses [Col. 1489A] of Sombernon, Saux, Saigny, and Cléron, with respect to the paternal line of St Bernard, namely Fontaines. Yet one must not infer from these alliances what Pierre de Saint-Julien says in his *Mélanges historiques*, p. 478: that Fontaines-lès-Dijon was a cadet portion of Chastillon-sur-Seine. In all antiquity I find no proof of this which would be admissible in the judgment of sensible persons.

592. CXLI. Extracts from the original documents of the houses of Saffre and Fontaines-lès-Dijon. Nearly all communicated to me by Messire Claude de Moisy Cléron, Knight, Baron of Saffre and Villy-le-Moutier, descended from the paternal line of St Bernard.

[Col. 1489D]

1. In the year of the Lord 1204, Gautier, bishop of Autun, grants permission to the nobleman Hervé de Saffre to establish a chapel within his castle at Saffre, in which Mass is to be celebrated daily and Vespers sung by a chaplain endowed by Hervé with specified annual revenues.

2. Guy, knight, son of Hervé, lord of Saffre, settles a dowry upon his wife Aluiz, daughter of Lord William de Tienges, with the consent of Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, in December 1236.

3. Hervier, Lord of Saffre, divides his children’s portions: Guy, the eldest; Hervier—to whom he gives, among other things, all that he possesses at Sombernon held of the fief of Lord Calle de Saux and his heirs; Hugues or Huguenin, Jean, and Étienne, whom he substitutes each for the other; reserving the rights of his wife, still living, and of the heirs she might bear. All confirmed by Ansiaux, Bishop of Autun, in June 1246. No mention is made there of Fontaines.

4. Jean de Saffre, knight, lord of Champ-Renaud; Margaret his wife; and his brother Guy, Lord of Saffre: February 1255.

593.

5. Jean de Saffre, knight, lord of Champ-Renaud, with the consent of his wife Margaret, sells thirty sextaries of grain to his brother and lord, Guy, Lord of Saffre: March 1255.

6. Hervé de Saffre, esquire; William de Saffre, rector of the church of Arnet: October 1273. [Col. 1490A]

7. William, Lord of Fontaines, esquire, in October 1277 buys a piece of arable land from the heirs of the late Humbelin the Elder of Fontaines, situated within the territory of Fontaines.

8. Division of property between Hervé and Étienne, brothers, sons of Guy, knight and Lord of Saffre: November 1277.

9. Agreements and exchanges between Hervier and Étienne, sons of Guy, Lord of Saffre, in October 1279.

10. William de Fontaines, knight: April 1282.

11. Jean, Lord of Fontaines, receives anew in fief [Col. 1490B] from his true noble lord Alexander de Montaigu, knight and Lord of Sombernon, one *corvée* situated in the territory of Fontaines: June 1284.

12. In May 1293 Jean, Lord of Fontaines, and Marie his wife borrow two hundred pounds of pure and lawful Viennese currency, from the personal marriage-money of Agnesota, damsel, wife of Gilet, esquire, their son; and for that sum they mortgage to her certain landed estates, to be retained by her and her heirs until complete repayment.

13. Agnes de Chartretes, damsel, and her husband Gilet de Fontaines, esquire, emancipate their daughter [Col. 1490C] Margaret: Sunday of the Bordes, 1298.

594.

14. Arverius, knight, Lord of Saffre; his wife Beatrix de Buxeria: Thursday, the eve of the Circumcision, 1299. The year 1300 had already begun when reckoned from the Nativity of the Lord; but among the French, the year 1300 was to begin only at the following Easter.

15. Dannot, daughter of Jean, Lord of Fontaines, widow of Hemonin de Montaillot: August 1302.

16. Margaret, widow of Hugh de Buffons, damsel, sells to her brother Lord Gilon de Fontaines certain lands belonging to her, situated in the territory of Fontaines: February 1306.

17. Marriage agreements between Jean, knight, Lord of the Valley of Olligniac, and Helvide de Saffre, widow of Jean, Lord of Muxey. There Helvide mentions her father Hervier, Lord of Saffre; her mother Beatrice; and her brothers, the late Guy, knight, and Jean and Hervier, canons of Langres: Thursday before All Saints’ Day, 1306; and again three days later, namely on the Sunday before the same feast, which that year fell on a Tuesday. [Col. 1490D]

18. Will of Gilles, Lord of Fontaines near Dijon, from November 1312. He chooses burial among the Friars Minor at Dijon, near his father; names as his heir his son Huguenin, and failing heirs of Huguenin, his other son Guyot; gives a landed estate to his daughter Agnes, a nun of Saint-Jean at Autun; settles provision upon two other daughters, nuns, one at Lairé and the other at Leudieu. He names his wife Agnes among the executors.

19. Agnes, Lady of Fontaines, binds herself and becomes surety for Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, for a substantial sum of money: Sunday after the Octave of Saints Peter and Paul, 1313. [Col. 1491A]

595.

20. A division of goods was made between Jean and Hervier de Saffre, brothers and canons of Langres, on the one side; and Hervier, Jean, and Simon, their nephews, sons of Guy, formerly Lord of Saffre and brother of the aforesaid canons, on the other: Wednesday, 4 April 1318. There the canons mention their deceased mother Beatrice, who had been sister of Simon de Buxeria, their maternal uncle, archdeacon of Dijon in the church of Langres, then deceased; likewise their sister Helvide de Saffre, then wife of William, Lord of Chastenay.

21. Jean, Lord of Choiseul, knight, and Jean his son, arrange the marriage of Damsel Jeanne de Choiseul, daughter and sister respectively of the said Jeans, father and son, with Hervier de Saffre, esquire. In settlement of all her claims, both from the side of her late mother Aalys, Lady of Choiseul, and from the side of Jean her father, present there, they give her in marriage the towns and lordships of Vivey and Moilleron, warranted to her for two hundred *livrées* of land, each ten *livrées* being worth one hundred livres tournois. 5 June 1323.

[Col. 1491B]

22. Jean and Hervier, brothers, canons of Langres, sons of Hervier, formerly knight and Lord of Saffre, give their fiefs to Jean and Simon, their nephews, children of Guy, formerly Lord of Saffre, brother of the said canons. Sunday before the feast of Saint Barnabas the Apostle, 1323.

23. Jeanne de Choiseul, daughter of Jean de Choiseul and of his wife Aalys, and wife of Hervier, Lord of Saffre, deals concerning the lands of Vivey and Moilleron, which her father Jean and Gauthier, son of the said Jean, had assigned her as marriage portion, 596 and concerning her right of succession in them. 2 February 1323. In the Roman Church, the year 1324 had already been counted from Christmas Day.

24. Division made between Hervier, Lord of Saffre, esquire, and Jean his brother, canon of Langres, June 1327, on the Monday after Saint Barnabas’s Day. [Col. 1491C]

25. Marriage agreement between Hervier, Lord of Saffre, and Aaliz de Gissey, daughter of William, Lord of Gissey, and Aaliz de la Roche, formerly wife of the said William: October 1330.

26. Simoneta, widow of the late Hugh, Lord of Fontaines, borrows two hundred livres tournois from Guy de Fontaines, canon of Langres: Saturday before the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, 1339.

27. Hugh, knight and Lord of Bera, and Symona de Pontescisse, then his wife and formerly wife of Hugh, Lord of Fontaines, acknowledge to Guy de Fontaines, canon of Langres and brother of the said Hugh, that they owe to the children born of that marriage one half [Col. 1491D] of the movable goods of the said Hugh and Symona, their parents; and, in lieu of that half of the movables—because they might be consumed by use—they will give one hundred and twenty livres tournois, to be divided among them when they separate from their mother’s household. Friday before the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, 1340.

26. Will of Hervier, Lord of Saffre, Knight of Jerusalem, made on the Saturday before the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, 1349. He chooses burial in the church of Blessed Peter at Saffre, beside the tomb of his first wife. He gives something to his sisters Margaret and Halix, nuns at Rougemont; to his sisters Beatrice and Jeannette, nuns at Poligny; and to his daughters Aalix and Jeannette, nuns at Prélonges. He appoints as his heirs [Col. 1492A] his son Jean, his firstborn by his former wife and a Knight of Jerusalem, to one half of all his property; and, for the other half, his children by his second wife, still living at that time. He names as executors of his will Jean de Saffre, canon of Langres, and Simon de Saffre, his brothers.

597.

29. Jean, son of Hervier, formerly Lord of Saffre, by his first wife Joanna de Caseolo, deals concerning his rights with his stepmother Aalix de Gissey, his father’s widow, on the eve of Saint Lawrence, 1349, recalling agreements made by him with his father Hervier on the eve of Saint Clement’s Day, 1346. Again he deals with his stepmother in 1349, on the Saturday after Saint Denis’s Day; and finally in the following year, 1350, on the Monday which was the eve of Saint Lawrence.

30. Jean de Saffre, dean of Langres, makes his will on 4 September 1349. He appoints as heirs: his nephew Jean, canon of Langres, for one third; Jean’s brother Simon de Saffre, esquire, for one third; and Jean, son of Hervier, formerly his nephew, together with Hervier’s other children, for one third. He is buried on the following 9 September, Wednesday. [Col. 1492B]

31. Marriage agreements between Jean de Saffre, knight, and Aalide de Blado [Bled], daughter of Odo, Lord of Blado, widow of Guyot de Gissey, esquire: September 1350.

32. A lawsuit was instituted and pursued in 1350, 1351, and 1352 by Jean de Mussey, Lord of Jours, against the heirs appointed by the will of the late Messire Jean de Saffre, Grand Dean of Langres, buried in 1349 on 8 September, the Nativity of Our Lady. This dean, son of Arvier, Lord of Saffre, and his wife Beatrix, had as brothers Hervier, canon of Langres, and Guy, Lord of Saffre; and as sister Eluis, twice married during the lifetime of her father and mother: first to Jean de Mussey, by whom she had two sons, namely Jean de Mussey, Lord of Jours, and a Hugh who became a monk at Saint-Germain of Auxerre; and in second marriage to Jean, Lord of the Valley of Olligny. Guy, Lord of Saffre, had had three sons: Hervier, father of Jean [Col. 1492C] Lord of Saffre and his sisters; Jean, canon of Langres; and Simon de Saffre. By his will Dean Jean had named his nephews Jean the canon and Simon, brothers, as his heirs, each for one third; and, for the other third, Jean, Lord of Saffre, and his sisters, children of his other nephew Hervier, then deceased. Jean de Mussey, Lord of Jours, claimed one half of the inheritance of his uncle the Dean. The lawsuit was conducted before Robert de Lugny, Chancellor of Burgundy, and before several lords chosen as arbitrators, among whom in 1350 appears Eudes de Fontaines, knight.

33. Agreement of Jean, Lord of Saffre, knight, son of Hervier, Lord of Saffre, and Jeanne de Choiseul, with his stepmother Aalix de Gissey, then remarried in second marriage to Guichard de Valote, knight; she acting as guardian of Guillemote and Huguote de Saffre, her elder daughters by her first husband, the said Hervier. Dated Tuesday before the feast of Our Lady in September 1351. [Col. 1492D]

598.

34. At Dijon, on 1 March 1353, in the house of Eudes de Saulx, Lord of Vantoux, the said Eudes and Haymes de Dambirin, knight, arbitrators chosen by agreement of the parties, pronounce judgment regulating the partitions of the estate of the late Dame Simone de Pontaillé: between, on one side, Jean de Fontaines, Robert, Richard, Isabeau, and Jeanne, brothers and sisters, children of the said Simone by Hugh, Lord of Fontaines, her first husband; and, on the other, Jean Dart, knight in the County of Burgundy, her last husband, and Jeanne, Margaret, and Marie, the daughters she had by the said Jean Dart.

35. Jean de Saffre, canon of Langres, makes his will Tuesday, 13 July 1365. He chooses burial in the church of Langres, in the chapel of Saint Andrew, to the left of the tomb of Hervier de Saffre, his maternal uncle.

36. Jean, Lord of Saffre, knight, was living in 1367, on Wednesday, Saint Matthew the Apostle’s Day, and in 1378.

37. Hugues, or Huguette, de Saffre, sister of Jean, Lord of Saffre, was wife of Huguenin de Varannes in May 1371. [Col. 1493A]

38. Marriage agreement between nobleman Huot de Saigney, esquire, and noble damsel Isabel de Saffre, daughter of Jean, Lord of Saffre, knight, and sister of Philibert de Saffre. Tuesday before Saint Vincent’s Day, 1381. By Roman computation from Christmas, it was already 1382. Huot de Saigney had previously had as wife Isabeau de Blaisey, by whom he had a son named Philibert, already dead at that time, as was his mother.

39. Richard was Lord of the town of Fontaines near Dijon on Monday after the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 1384.

40. Huguette de Saffre, widow of the late nobleman Huguenin de Varennes, esquire, assigns the sum of ten gold francs to her brother Jean de Saffre, knight, Friday after All Saints’ Day, 1385. [Col. 1493B]

41. Hues de Saigney, knight and Lord of Saffre by right of his wife Isabel, consents to the perpetual lease of a vineyard of thirty *ouvrées*, situated in the territory of Gressigny, made to Mathie Crepel, called Duret, and his wife Estiennote, by Messire Jean de Ville-sur-Arce, Lord in part of Gressigny, and his wife Marguerite de Saffre: 24 October 1389. It seems that this Marguerite was Isabel, Lady of Saffre’s, younger sister.

42. Safeguard granted by the bailiff of Dijon, in the Duke of Burgundy’s name, to nobleman Guillaume de Marrey, esquire, Lord of Fontaines-lès-Dijon by right of his wife Dame Marie, for the maintenance and preservation of all their property and rights in the lordship of Fontaines and all its appurtenances: 18 November 1391.

43. In the year of the Lord 1394, on Monday before the feast of Corpus Christi, Étienne Coquel, royal castellan of Colchis, writes concerning a certain matter to the noble and powerful man Lord Jean, Lord of Fontaines, knight and chamberlain of our lord the king. [Col. 1493C]

44. Isabeau is styled Lady of Saffre in part, in November 1396.

45. An instrument dated Friday, 13 February, the eve of Saint Valentine, 1399, proves that Guyot de Saigny, esquire, was brother of Hues de Saigny, formerly knight; that their mother was Marie de Bieuey; and that Hues de Saigny was already dead, leaving as widow Isabel de Saffre, formerly his wife, with their children Antoine and Catherine.

46. Marriage agreement between Huguenin de la Perrière, esquire, and Katherine de Saingney, daughter of the late Hues de Saingney, knight, and of Dame Isabel de Saffre, present at the agreement; in which the property of the said Katherine and of her brother Antoine de Saingney is partitioned. 1 May 1401. [Col. 1493D]

47. Guyot de Saigney, esquire, Lord of La Motte-de-Rouvray-sur-Aube and brother of the late Hues de Saigney, knight, reaches an agreement with Isabeau, Lady of Saffre, his sister-in-law, as guardian of Antoine de Saigney, her underage son; and with Huguenin de la Perrière, esquire, and Katherine de Saigney his wife, concerning a sum which he claimed was owed him: 1403.

48. Isabel de Saffre, widow of Hues de Saingney, receives anew her fiefs from Jean, Duke of Burgundy, Count of Nevers and Baron of Donzy. At Dijon, 20 June 1404.

49. Liébaud de Lugny, knight, and Isabel de Saffre, joint lords of the said place of Saffre, come to an agreement with one another, 1411.

50. Guillaume de Marrey, esquire, Lord of Fontaines-lès-Talant by right of Dame Marie his wife, heiress-daughter of the Lord of Fontaines, esquire, then already deceased, acknowledges that he holds in fief and homage from the Duke of Burgundy the fortified house and fortress of Fontaines, together with all appurtenances and dependencies of that lordship. In the enumeration of them mention is made of a vineyard called [Col. 1494A] Saint Bernard’s Vineyard. At the same time he makes like homage to the said Duke for the fief of Vernoul: 22 May 1413.

51. Guillaume de Marrey and Marie de Fontaines his wife, Lord and Lady of Fontaines-lès-Dijon, arrange the marriage of their daughter Amyote de Marrey with Antoine de Saigney, Lord in part of Bissy-les-Pierres: 25 June 1418.

52. Alexander and Bernard de Marrey, sons of Guillaume de Marrey and Marie de Fontaines, Lords of Fontaines, after the death of their mother Marie, make an assignment of their sister Amyote’s dowry, she having formerly been married to Antoine de Saigny, esquire, Lord in part of Saffre: 28 June 1424. [Col. 1494B]

53. In February 1429 Jean de Champlitte, knight, Lord of Vonges, in the name of his absent wife Odote de Marrey, partitions the inheritance of the late Damsel Marie de Fontaines, formerly daughter of Richard de Fontaines and of Damsel Philippe de Saulx, Lord and Lady of the said Fontaines, with Alexander de Marrey and Bernard de Marrey, esquires, and Perrenote de Marrey, brothers and sister of the said Odote and all legitimate children of nobleman Guillaume de Marrey, esquire, lord of Giry and Gippy in the County of Nevers, and of the said Marie de Fontaines. Alexander acts with the consent and approval of Damsel Marguerite de la Plectière, his wife; and likewise Bernard with the consent and approval of Damsel Alais de Perron, his wife. The four divide among themselves the lordship of Fontaines and all its appurtenances, together with the estate of Oigny near Saint-Julien. Their sister Amyote does not enter into this partition, having received her settlement from her father and mother upon her marriage to Antoine de Saigny in 1418. Mention is made in this agreement of the great tower of Fontaines, commonly called Monsieur Saint Bernard’s Tower, and of the cellar or room of that tower in which my lord Saint Bernard was born. They appoint Girard Boulon their chief officer and mayor of Fontaines. [Col. 1494C]

603.

54. Alexander de Marrey, esquire, lord for one quarter of the fortress, town, estate, lordship, and appurtenances of Fontaines-lès-Dijon, sells all that he possessed there by right of primogeniture or otherwise to the Reverend Father in God, Monsieur Jean Rolin, Bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, for the sum of five hundred and sixty-four francs: 22 March 1434.

55. Amyote de Marrey, daughter of the late Guillaume de Marrey, esquire, and Damsel Marie de Fontaines, Lord and Lady of Fontaines; authorized by her husband Antoine de Saigny, esquire, lord in part of Saffre and Bissy-la-Pierre, partitions the property of her father and mother with Bernard and Alexander de Marrey, her brothers; her sister Perrenote de Marrey, wife of Jean de Chauanges, esquire; and Oudot, Jean, and Huguette, underage brothers and sister, children of her late sister Dame Oudote de Marrey, wife of the late Messire Jean de Champlitte, knight, Lord of Vonges. She accepts as her share of the inheritance the lands, towns, castellanies, and fortified houses of Giry, Gippy, Chastinges, and other lands formerly belonging to her father and mother in the County of Nevers, with high, middle, and low justice; rents, dues, taxes, arable lands, vineyards, meadows, ponds, woods, rivers, ovens, mills, men, women, *mainmorte* serfs, escheats, and all other revenues and appurtenances of those lordships. This agreement was made at Viteau, 16 January in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1438. [Col. 1494D]

604.

56. Pierre de Beffromont, Lord of Charny, deals with Bernard de Marrey concerning certain rights which Bernard claimed in the inheritance of Anne de Saulx, Pierre’s wife, 14 January 1443. In other letters of 5 June 1468, confirming the preceding ones, the said Pierre de Beffromont is styled Count of Charny.

57. Marriage agreement between Antoine de Saigny, esquire and Lord of Saffre, and Katherine de Montbéliard: 20 January 1445.

58. Bernard de Marrey, esquire and Lord of Fontaines, and Damsel Alix Perron his wife, had a lawsuit arising from a dispute with the Lady of Saint-Julien and her officers: 28 July 1446.

59. Pierre and Jean de Saigny, esquires, with the authority and permission of their father, the noble Lord Antoine de Saigny, esquire and Lord of Saffre, divide between themselves the inheritance of their late mother, Damsel Amyote de Marrey, formerly Lady in part of Giry in Nivernais; and jointly, the inheritances they expected from Alexander and Bernard de Marrey, their maternal uncles and full brothers of their mother Amyote. Pierre de Saigny takes as his share of his mother’s inheritance the property in Nivernais. Jean de Saigny is content with the expected inheritances of his uncles Alexander and Bernard, unless their possessions and lordships should diminish through misfortune of war or otherwise; for in that case Pierre de Saigny would compensate his brother Jean with property as near as possible to Grancey Castle, through the arbitration of two of their [Col. 1495A] relatives and friends. Both undertake to marry their full sisters Anne, Jeanne, and Marie de Saigny suitably and honourably. Made 9 March 1448.

605.

60. Another agreement of 26 April 1450 concerning the inheritance of Damsel Amyote de Marrey, by which her son Pierre de Saigny, who had previously received a partition from the property which his late mother had possessed in the County of Nevers, agrees that if Jean, Anne, Jeanne, and Marie de Saigny, his brother and sisters, all children of the said Amyote, prove disadvantaged by this partition, it shall be null; and that all shall return to the same community of property in which they had formerly been, as though no division had been made among them.

61. On 12 March 1458—it was already 1459, reckoning from Christmas Day or from 1 January—the marriage agreements were concluded between Bernard de Bruillart, esquire, and Anne de Saigny; and between Joffroy de Bruillart, esquire, and Jeanne de Saigny: by agreement and approval of nobleman Erard de Bruillart, esquire, Lord of Aisanville and Arcy-sur-Quehure, father of Bernard and Joffroy; and of Antoine de Saigny, esquire and Lord in part of Saffre, father of Anne and Jeanne; as also of Pierre, Jean, and Marie de Saigny, brothers and sister of Anne and Jeanne, all children of Antoine de Saigny. [Col. 1495B]

62. On 1 December 1462 the marriage of Marie de Saigny, sister of Pierre and Jean de Saigny, and Étienne de Ruffey was arranged. From that marriage was born Katherine de Ruffey, married in 1482, on Sunday 9 June, to Pierre de Coublans, son of Guillaume de Coublans, Lord of Boussenois.

63. Alexander de Marrey, esquire and castellan of Vadans, makes an inter vivos gift to the noble and powerful Lord Jean de Poictiers, knight, Lord of Arcis, Vadans, and Souvans, of the whole inheritance of Bernard de Marrey, his brother recently deceased, to discharge a debt of five hundred gold écus owed to him, and in consideration of the great help, friendship, kindness, favours, and inestimable courtesies which he had received from him: the next-to-last day of April, after Easter, 1463.

606.

64. Marriage agreement between Pierre de Saigny, son of Antoine de Saigny, Lord of Saffre, and Roline de Choiseul, daughter of Guillaume de Choiseul, esquire, lord of Clemont. The agreement was made by the said Antoine de Saigny, Pierre’s father; by Catherine de Montbéliard, Antoine’s second wife and Pierre’s stepmother; and by Jean de Saigny, lord of Giry and Pierre’s brother: 18 March 1466. [Col. 1495C]

65. Pierre de Saigny, knight, Lord, in part, of Saffre, Marrey-sur-Tille, and Monsson: 8 March 1484. The same man is still styled Lord in part of Fontaines on Tuesday 12 June 1481, 25 February 1485, and again in February 1486.

66. Bernard de Bruillard, esquire, deals concerning some sum of money from the marriage settlement of his wife Anne de Saigny, sister of Pierre de Saigny, knight and Lord in part of Saffre and Monsson: Friday, 17 October 1483.

67. Marriage agreement between Othenin de Cléron, son of Simon, Lord of Cléron, and Marie de Saigny, eldest daughter of Pierre de Saigny, knight, Lord of Saffre, and Roline de Choiseul: 18 November 1487.

68. Pierre de Saigny and Roline de Choiseul deal with Othenin de Cléron, husband of their eldest daughter Marie de Saigny, 607 concerning the marriages of their daughters Anne and Jeanne, the elder; and concerning provision for Jeanne, the younger, and Marguerite, their other daughters, who were to be placed in religion: 9 August 1488. [Col. 1495D]

69. Pierre de Saigny, knight, and François de Ferrières, esquire, are called joint lords of Saffre on 2 July 1489.

70. Pierre de Saigny is called heir of his father Antoine and of his brother Jean, Saturday, 31 October 1489.

71. François de Ferrières, esquire, is styled Lord in part of Saffre in 1485, 1489, and 1490.

72. The marriage is arranged of Jeanne de Saigny, daughter of Pierre de Saigny and Roline de Choiseul, with nobleman Girard de Chappes, esquire, Lord of Romanney, residing at Flavigny: 1 February 1491.

73. Marriage agreement of Anne de Saigny, daughter of Pierre de Saigny and Roline de Choiseul, with Warin de Saint-Banssonem, lord of Ymonville, son of Ancellin d’Essey, lord of Saint-Banssonem: 23 October 1493. [Col. 1496A]

74. Will of Pierre de Saigny, knight and Lord in part of Saffre, made 4 June 1494. He appoints as his universal heirs the noble Lord Othenin de Cléron, his son-in-law, and Marie de Saigny, his daughter and Othenin’s wife.

75. Marie de Saigny, wife of Othenin de Cléron, sister of Marguerite and Guillette de Saigny, nuns at Trisenon in the diocese of Auxerre: all three daughters of Pierre de Saigny and Roline de Choiseul, 1494.

76. Louis de Brancion, esquire, Lord in part of Saffre: 23 October 1496.

608.

77. Roline de Choiseul, described as widow of Pierre de Saigny: 9 February 1496.

78. Jeannette de Domprey, Lady of Cléron, widow of Simon de Cléron, appoints as universal heirs her sons Othenin and Claude de Cléron; granting life pensions to Messire Simon de Cléron, Abbot of Montbenoît and Goille, and to Jean de Cléron, canon of Besançon and parish priest of Vercel, her two other sons: 22 November 1497. [Col. 1496B]

79. Othenin de Cléron, native of the County of Burgundy, naturalized as a Frenchman by King Louis XII at Melun, September 1500.

80. Othenin de Cléron, styled Lord of Saffre and in part of Fontaines: 7 September 1500, and thereafter 22 May 1523.

81. On 8 February in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1502, the noble and powerful Lady Marie Chambellan, Lady in undivided half of Fontaines-lès-Dijon—which half had formerly belonged to Damsel Marguerite Rolin—wife of the noble and powerful Lord Messire Guy de Rochefort, knight, Chancellor of France, Lord of Pluvot, l’Abergement, Rochefort, and Caseau, took possession of that half of the lordship of Fontaines through her proxy, Louis Servant, castellan of Pluvot. He dismissed all the former officers from their offices, then restored them the same day in the said lady’s name; and the taking of possession was publicly proclaimed [Col. 1496C] in the market halls before the assembled officers and all the people.

82. Louis de Brancion, husband of Jeanne Maillardet, exchanges with Othenin de Cléron, Lord of Saffre, his share in the lordship of Saffre and that of Hiz in Auxois, 609 together with certain other goods and rights, for two hundred francs of annual rent. At Dole, 23 July 1503.

83. Joanna de Saigny, formerly sacristan of Puits-d’Orbe, is elected abbess of the same monastery on 25 June 1504, in the seventh indiction, and is confirmed on 9 July by the vicar-general of Jean d’Amboise, Bishop of Langres. She was the younger sister of the namesake Jeanne who had already been betrothed in 1491 to Girard de Chappes. See above, no. 72.

84. Jeanne de Saigny, sister of Marie de Saigny and widow of the late Girard de Chappes, Lord of Romanney, guardian of her children Jacques, Jeanne, and Katherine de Chappes, comes to terms with Othenin de Cléron, her brother-in-law, surrendering to him what she might claim from the inheritances of Pierre de Saigny and Roline de Choiseul, her father and mother, in exchange for a specified sum of money: 20 December 1508.

85. Dame Catherine de Ruffey, widow of the nobleman Pierre de Coublan, and Claude de Coublan, her son, make a gift of the estate of Saigny near Grignon to Othenin de Cleron and to Marie de Saigny, his wife. 18 March 1511.

[Col. 1499D] 86. Othenin de Cleron makes an agreement with his brother Jehan de Cleron, Lord of Belmont, concerning the inheritances of their late mother Jehannette de Domprey; of Louise de Cleron, formerly their aunt; of Jehan de Cleron, canon of Besançon; and of Claude de Cleron, Lord of Scay, formerly their brothers. 5 June 1511.

87. Jehanne de Saigny is styled Lady of Beurizey and of Romanney in the years 1527 and 1528. It appears that, after the death of her first husband, Girard de Chappes, Lord of Romanney, she remarried a Lord of Beurizey.

88. 610 Marriage contract of Pierre de Montigny, esquire, Lord of Chaumont-le-Bois, and Barbe de Cleron, concluded by Othenin de Cleron, father of the said Barbe, and by Jehan, Claude, and Guy de Cleron, her brothers, [Col. 1500A] after the death of Marie de Saigny, their mother. 6 February 1529.

89. The marriage contract of Chrestienne de Cleron, sister of Claude and Guy de Cleron, all children of Othenin de Cleron and Marie de Saigny, is made with Joachim Du Bois, esquire, Lord of Posainges. 15 September 1533.

90. Marriage contract of Guy de Cleron, son of Othenin de Cleron, then still living, brother of Claude de Cleron, and brother-in-law of Pierre de Montigny, with Philiberte de Moisy, daughter of Jehan de Moisy and Jehanne de Sainte-Croix. 22 December 1533.

91. Barbe de Cleron, widow of the late Pierre de Montigny, esquire and Lord of Chaumont-le-Bois, makes [Col. 1500B] a gift of all her livestock, two beds, and certain other movable goods to Guy de Cleron, her brother. 5 February 1538.

92. Antoine de Cleron, wife of Jehan de Colombier, esquire, Lord of Oigny, releases to her brother Guy de Cleron all that might come to her from the inheritances of Othenin de Cleron and Marie de Saigny, their father and mother, and of their deceased brothers and sisters, for the sum of two thousand livres tournois. 6 March 1541.

93. Philiberte de Moisy, widow and relict of Guy de Cleron, is, on 11 March 1544, called guardian and administrator of the persons and property of Joachim and Bernarde, her children.

94. On the second day of June 1560, the [Col. 1500C] marriage contract is made between Bernarde de Cleron, daughter of Guy de Cleron, knight, Lord of Saffres and Belmont, and Philiberte 611 de Moisy, Lady of Villy-le-Monstier; and François de Pontaillé, son of Louis de Pontaillé: with the consent of Leonard de Pontaillé, knight of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, paternal uncle of the said François; and Antoine d’Oyselet, esquire, Lord of La Villeneuve, and Thomas de Cleremont, knight, Lord of St. George and Rupt, her maternal uncles.

95. On 21 September 1561, the marriage of Joachim de Cleron and Françoise de Pracontal, daughter of Laurent de Pracontal, Lord of Soussé, etc., is negotiated.

96. Arvier de Cleron, Lord of Cleron and in part [Col. 1500D] of Saffres, son of Claude de Cleron, elder brother of Guy de Cleron, divides by arbitration what he possessed at Saffres with his cousin Joachim, son of Guy de Cleron. 23 April 1567.

97. Joachim de Cleron makes his will on 26 October 1567.

98. Joachim and Arvier de Cleron divide the inheritance of their late aunt Chrestienne de Cleron. 11 January 1569.

99. François de Cleron, Lord of Pousanges and in part of Saffres, borrows certain title-deeds concerning the lordship of Gresigny from Joachim de Cleron, Lord of Saffres, his uncle. 1 December 1583.

100. Homage is renewed for the lordship of Fontaines [Col. 1501A] by Humbert de Rochefort. 2 June 1584.

101. Guillaume de Damas, having recently acquired the lordship of Fontaines from the said Humbert de Rochefort, renews homage for it to the Duke of Burgundy on 13 July 1587.

102. The marriage of Antoine de Cleron and Philiberte de Damas is negotiated by their fathers, mothers, and other relatives; François de Cleron, Lord of Pousanges, 612 and in part of Saffres, is present among others. 27 November 1588. Antoine is called son of Joachim de Cleron and Françoise de Pracontal. Philiberte was daughter of Jehan de Damas, Lord of St. Riran, and Magdeleine de Saulx.

103. Marriage contract of Anne de Cleron, daughter of Joachim de Cleron and Françoise de Pracontal, [Col. 1501B] with Jacques de Chenu, esquire, Lord of Souleaux, son of François de Chenu and Marguerite de la Rivière. 24 July 1596.

104. Joachim de Damas, Lord of Le Rousset, on 27 April 1602, renews homage for the lordship of Fontaines, having acquired it by judicial decree against Guillaume de Damas.

105. Joachim de Damas sells the castle of Fontaines to the Reverend Feuillant Fathers in 1613. They subsequently built a church and monastery in its place, with the approval of His Majesty and of all the authorities.

106. Marriage contract between Messire Claude de Moisy Cleron, knight, Baron of Saffres and Villy-le-Monstier, son of Antoine de Cleron and Philiberte [Col. 1501C] de Damas, and Dame Gabrielle Dauion, daughter of Claude Dauion, knight, Baron of Poussay, etc., and Dame Anne de Marcocey. 2 February 1620.

107. Another marriage contract of the said Claude de Moisy Cleron, Baron of Saffres, with Dame Marguerite de Chaugy Rossillon, daughter of Messire Guy de Chaugy, knight, Baron of Rossillon, etc., and Dame Diane de Chastelu. 3 March 1632.

CXLII. Otho de Sauz; Willelma, his wife; and Guido, his firstborn son. 1190. (From the autograph of St. Benignus of Dijon.)

613 I, MANASSES, by the grace of God bishop of Langres, make known to all that, when a dispute had arisen between Lord [Col. 1501D] Otho de Sauz and Peter, abbot of St. Benignus of Dijon, concerning a certain mill which the said Otho was building, contrary to the abbot’s right, in the count’s village, they at last came before us and amicably settled the matter in the following way.

For Otho himself, having been carefully admonished by us, freely granted, without any exception, as an alms to God and to the church of Blessed Benignus, whatever right he had or claimed to have in that mill or in the watercourse. He retained only for his lifetime the fish-holding enclosure which he was constructing above that same mill; but, so that after his death it might pass into the right and ownership of the aforesaid church, he gave it by a testamentary conveyance for the remedy of his soul. And because he had incurred many expenses in building the said mill, it was declared by us and accepted by both parties that the abbot should give Lord Otho twenty-two Dijon pounds; and he did so. The aforesaid alms, of both the mill and the fish enclosure, Lord Otho made into our hand, with the assent of Guido, his firstborn son, Lady Willelma, his wife, and his other heirs.

The witnesses are 614 Lord Peter, abbot of Bèze; Wido de Arc, monk of Dijon; Arnaud, dean of Cuisenay; and Oddo de Grancey, Knight Templar.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1190.

CXLIII. Giles, Lord of Fontaines. 1310. (Extract from the inventory of title-deeds of the Chamber of Accounts at Dijon.)

[Col. 1502B] Giles, Lord of Fontaines, declares that the Duke of Burgundy has granted him permission to crenellate his fortified house at Fontaines, which he acknowledges to be held in liege fief from the said Duke. 1310.

CXLIV. Jehan, Lord of one quarter of Fontaines; Robert, his brother, likewise Lord of one quarter of Fontaines; Simone, their mother, Lady of one half of Fontaines. 1350. (Copied from the original in the Chamber of Accounts at Dijon.)

To all who shall see and hear these present letters: I, Jehan de Fontaines near Dijon, esquire, make known that I have promised fealty and service to the nobleman, my Lord the Count of Roucy, governor of [Col. 1502C] the Duchy of Burgundy on behalf of the King our lord, having the wardship of the said duchy and by reason of that wardship. Namely, for the fourth part of the castle of Fontaines, all the *messerie* of that place, and the fourth part of the jurisdiction of Fontaines. Protesting always to specify further, should there be any other matters not comprised in this present specification. And it is to be known that Messire Jehan Darc, knight, by reason of Madame Symone his wife, holds one half of the said jurisdiction and castle; and Robert de Fontaines, esquire, my brother, one fourth part thereof. In testimony of which matter, I have requested and obtained that the seal used at Dijon in the court of my Lord the Duke of Burgundy for such cases be affixed to these present letters, made and given at Dijon on Saturday, the feast-day of St. Vincent, in the year of grace 1350.

NOTICE TO THE READER.

I see two matters in this title which deserve notice. The first is that Jehan de Fontaines says that he possesses all the *messerie* of the said place, although he held only one fourth part of both the castle and the jurisdiction. He was the eldest of three sons and two daughters. His two younger brothers were Robert and Richard; and his two sisters, Elizabeth and Jehanne. As the eldest, he alone was chief lord of a dominant fief, held only from the Duke of Burgundy. This, in my opinion, is what the word *messerie* means. His co-lords held their portions of the castle and jurisdiction of Fontaines only as [Col. 1503A] dependent fiefs, or rear-fiefs, by reason of which they held immediately from the dominant lord.

The other matter to be noticed is that Simonne de Pontaillé, their mother, married in her third marriage to Jehan Darc, a knight of the Franche-Comté, held, it seems, one half of the lordship of Fontaines as a rear-fief in the name of Richard, Elizabeth, and Jehanne, her other children, who were still under age, as guardian and administrator of their persons and goods. This Richard was subsequently chief lord of the whole lordship of Fontaines; and Marie, his heiress daughter, brought it as dowry to Guillaume de Marey. Thus, together with the blood of the paternal line of St. Bernard, it passed into the houses of Saigny, 616 Saffres, Cleron, and other of the most illustrious families of Burgundy, [Col. 1503B] as will be seen below in the genealogical tables which we have reserved for the end of this volume.

CXLV. Richard, Lord of Fontaines; Jehan, his brother, formerly Lord of the same place; Agnes and Jehanne, daughters of the said Jehan. 1366. (Extract from the original in the Chamber of Accounts at Dijon.)

Richard de Fontaines, lord of that place, having the wardship and governance of Agnes and Jehanne, minors, daughters of his late brother Jehan de Fontaines, acknowledges, in the name and on behalf of the said daughters, that he holds in fief and homage from the most sovereign, powerful, and excellent prince, my Lord the Duke of Burgundy, all the [Col. 1503C] goods and rights which they possessed in the towns of Saulon, Aubigney, and Fénay. Saturday after St. Bartholomew’s Day, in the year 1366.

CXLVI. Extract from a letter of the Baron of Saffres to Monsieur de Chasan, councillor in the Parliament of Dijon, written at Beaune on 24 November 1632, five days after the completion of the Inventory mentioned above on page 585. [Note: [Col. 1503] The numerical notes occurring here and below represent the page numbers of Chifflet’s edition, which you have stated in the text.]

Since you wish to take the trouble to examine the ancient papers of our house, I am sending you the Inventory, drawn up and completed by Monsieur de la Place. If there are deficiencies in the dates, this is because the papers are so old that, for the greater 617 part, they could not read them; and they even failed to include several documents in the Inventory.

NOTICE TO THE READER.

I wished here to report this irreproachable testimony of a lord who was a friend of truth, so that, if some defect is found in the dating of events or in the names of persons in the extracts which I have produced from the Inventory mentioned above, one may endeavor to correct it by some more certain authority. Here is [Col. 1504A] an example. On page 586, number 9, it is said that, in the year 1200, Jehan de Fontaines, wishing to enter religious life, gave all his property to Guillaume de Fontaines. This date is contradicted by several originals cited above, on pages 481, 523, and 525, which teach us that Jehan and Guillaume de Fontaines, brothers, were sons of Calon de Saux, Lord of Fontaines, and that they lived in the years 1267, 1276, and 1282. This makes me believe that, if Jehan de Fontaines relinquished his property to his brother Guillaume in order to become a religious, it was about the year 1280.

CXLVII. Jehannette de Saux, daughter of Marie, Lady of Sauz. 1285. (Extract from the Cartulary of the Collegiate Church of Our Lady of Sauz-le-Duc.)

[Col. 1504B]

In August 1285, JEHANNOTTE de Sauz, wife of Guyot Pleepape, esquire, establishes in the church of Our Lady of Sauz an anniversary observance for her mother MARIE, formerly Lady of Sauz; this is confirmed by GUILLAUME, Lord of Sauz, brother of the said Jehannette. 618

CXLVIII. Epitaph of Marguerite, Lady of Sauz, laid upon a flat tomb before the chapel of St. Anne in the Dominican church at Dijon. 1290.

HERE LIES MADAME MARGUERITE, LADY OF SAUZ, DAUGHTER OF THE COUNT OF VIENNE, WHO DIED IN THE YEAR OF [Col. 1504C] GRACE 1290, IN THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.

In this inscription, the number ninety is divided into eighty and ten, following the manner of ordinary speech, which says “four-score and ten” more commonly than “ninety.” Moreover, I have seen a document of January 1269—that is, already 1270 when reckoned as at present from Christmas Day or the Circumcision—in which Hugues, Count of Vienne and Lord of Pagny, mentions his beloved son and faithful man Guillaume d’Oyselet, husband of MARGUERITE his daughter. Consequently, I consider it more than likely that this same Marguerite, after the death of her first husband Guillaume d’Oyselet, married in her second marriage Guillaume, Lord of [Col. 1504D] Sauz—unless we wish to say that she had a sister of the same name, which is rather rare in families. For this Hugues was the last of the Counts of Vienne; and we do not read that Guillaume, his uncle and predecessor, who held the County of Vienne after the death of his brother Henry in 1233, left any descendants.

[Col. 1505]

619 APPENDIX TO THE DISQUISITION ON THE ILLUSTRIOUS LINEAGE OF ST. BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, in which the so-called charter of Fontenay is examined; the reason why the belt chequered in double rows of silver and scarlet belongs to St. Bernard is shown; and his entire blood relationship and relationship by marriage are discussed more exactly.

PREFACE: On the connection of this Appendix with the Disquisition and its Proofs.

[Col. 1505A]

In undertaking a genealogy hitherto unattempted, I have neither supposed myself ignorant of nothing in it nor been deterred by the Apostle’s warning, given through Timothy, that certain persons should not occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies, which furnish questions rather than God’s edification, which is 620 in faith (1 Tim. 1). Chrysostom may indeed be allowed to interpret this passage of Paul as concerning Hesiod’s *Theogony* and other pagan fables; Ambrose, as concerning the delusions of the Jews in this field; Tertullian, as concerning the dreams of Valentinus the heresiarch. Yet these things do not concern the genealogy of our Bernard—or else the sacred books must be corrected, and the Holy Spirit Himself is at variance [Col. 1505B] with Himself, He who inserted in the books of Genesis, Chronicles, Joshua, Judith, and other canonical Scriptures so many successions of grandfathers and great-grandfathers.

Likewise, a censorious mark must be branded upon Jerome, whose concluding flourish in the *Epitaph of Paula* is this:

> She whom Scipio begot, whom the parents of Paulus brought forth,  
> The offspring of the Gracchi, illustrious progeny of Agamemnon,  
> Lies in this tomb. The ancients called her Paula,  
> Mother of Eustochium, foremost of the Roman senate;  
> She followed Christ’s poverty and the fields of Bethlehem.

I know what precepts the same Jerome gives for the instruction of his Celantia—if it is indeed Jerome, and not Paulinus of Nola, as many have thought. “Never,” he says [Col. 1505C] (*Letter* 19), “prefer yourself to anyone on account of nobility of birth, nor think that persons of more obscure origin and lower station are inferior to you. Our religion knows no partiality for persons; it does not consider men’s social conditions, but regards the souls of individuals, and judges slave and nobleman from their character. The only freedom before [Col. 1506A] God is not to be enslaved to sins; the highest nobility before God is to be distinguished by virtues.”

I read in Hilary of Arles, in his eulogy for his most noble predecessor Honoratus: “The height of nobility is to be counted among God’s children, and the splendor of earthly origin can add nothing to this dignity except through being despised. No one in heaven is more illustrious than he who, rejecting the pedigree of his fathers, has chosen to be known by Christ’s fatherhood alone.” 621 Let us consider the splendor of Bernard’s birth, so that it may appear what he disdained for Christ’s poverty, and so that courage may be given both to those of humble birth, to rest content with the condition at hand as children of God, and to those distinguished by lineage, to trample the pride of their ancestors and aspire to the solid nobility of Christian virtues. Meanwhile, let us not be ashamed of this subject, but rather of our poverty and insufficiency in treating it. For from books already made public we have drawn scarcely any light upon this matter. We therefore had to consult the parchments of many archives; and because we could not penetrate all their recesses together and at one time, we hastily attached to the proofs of our Disquisition, while the press was sweating and the workmen were hurrying, whatever chance offered that served our purpose. Coins of different stamps, whether separated according to their types or promiscuously gathered into a heap, possess the same value and the same price. This Appendix, however, will distinguish all these items, so that it may be understood, as necessary, to what each belongs.

## CHAPTER I. The Fontenay charter is set forth, representing St. Bernard’s paternal and maternal lineage.

[Col. 1506C]

This charter circulates in French; I present it here to you as it came to me, divided for method’s sake into three parts. 622

### FIRST PART OF THE CHARTER OF FONTENAY—GENEALOGY OF ST. BERNARD ON THE PATERNAL SIDE

VERRICUS, Count of Châtillon and Lord of Laignes, had three sons.

ANDRÉ, the eldest, called de Châtillon, became a knight of the Order of Jerusalem after his wife’s death. St. Bernard addressed Epistle 288 to him. He had two sons.

GODEFROY, the second son, became a religious; third prior at Clairvaux; abbot of Fontenay; and finally bishop of Langres.

TECELIN, the third son, was Lord of Fontaines, born and married at Châtillon. By his wife ALETH he had seven children, whose order will be given in the third part of this charter.

GODEFROY, who granted Fontenay a right of use throughout all his lands, had two sons by his wife GERTRUDE.

GERARD de Châtillon, Lord of Eschalo, married to the sister of the Lord of Salives, brother of the Count of Grancey, from whom he inherited, had one son.

[Col. 1507] HUGUE, who had one daughter. NIVARD, who died without heirs. MILO.

N., married to a lord of the house of Tonnerre, to whom she brought the borough of Laignes as dowry.

They had several daughters, one of whom, N., married ROBERT, son of a Duke of Burgundy; their successors have retained the town of Châtillon.

623 ### SECOND PART OF THE CHARTER OF FONTENAY—GENEALOGY OF ST. BERNARD ON THE MATERNAL SIDE

The Lord of MONTBARD had four children.

1. REGNAULD, the eldest.

2. ALETH, wife of Tecelin and mother of St. Bernard.

3. GALDRIC, Lord of Touillon in the territory of Autun, converted by St. Bernard and became a religious at Clairvaux.

4. MILO, a religious at Clairvaux, from where he was sent as prior to Fontenay Abbey.

ANDRÉ, who in 1210 married HELVIDE, heiress of Époisses, had one son.

BERNARD, who had a daughter by his marriage.

BERNARDIN, who had a daughter, N., married to the son of the Count of Grignon.

N., married in 1233 to DROGO de Mello, Lord of Château-Chinon and Saint-Pris. Their son bore the same name.

Their daughter N. married a ROBERT, Duke of Burgundy; and by this means the County of Montbard came into the domain of the dukes in 1286, under the reign of Hugues, Duke of Burgundy.

DROGO de Mello married EUSTACHIA, first cousin of Edward, King of England. She died at Carthage after following her husband with St. Louis, and wished to be brought back to Fontenay, where she lies with an epitaph dated 1270.

[Col. 1507A] ### THIRD PART OF THE CHARTER OF FONTENAY—ORDER OF THE SEVEN CHILDREN OF TECELIN AND ALETH DE MONTBARD

1. GUY, the eldest, was married. At first his wife resisted his conversion; then she consented and became a nun. Several daughters issued from this marriage.

624 2. GERARD followed the profession of arms; St. Bernard predicted that he would be wounded in the side and that then he would desire to become a religious.

3. ST. BERNARD, called de Châtillon.

4. ANDRÉ, who, resisting becoming a religious, had a vision which compelled him to cry, “I see my mother”; he thereupon assented to St. Bernard’s plan.

5. BARTHELEMY, the first to be converted after his uncle Galdric.

[Col. 1507B] 6. NIVARD, who answered his brothers that the division had not been fairly made.

7. HUMBELINE, their only sister; married, then a nun at Jully-les-Nonnains near Molesme.

As its style shows, this charter was copied scarcely more than two hundred years ago. Although it is unknown even to the present inhabitants of Fontenay, I think it was nevertheless called “Fontenay” because it was composed by some monk of Fontenay, partly from the common Life of St. Bernard and partly from the records of Fontenay, though those records were neither carefully examined nor adequately understood. I myself have handled with my own hands every document held at Fontenay; and I have transferred into the Proofs of my Disquisition either copies or at least extracts of all those bearing upon St. Bernard’s lineage. From them the reader will recognize both what pertains to his true genealogy and what the compiler of the charter, in accordance with his own opinion, inserted into it with no slight damage to historical truth.

## CHAPTER II. Werricus de Châtillon was neither a count nor Tecelin’s father; Godefridus, Gertrude’s husband and father of Hugh and Nivard, is likewise unrelated to Tecelin’s lineage; nor are Gerard or Milo de Châtillon; but Eva, the daughter-in-law, perhaps came from the same family.

[Col. 1508A]

Duchesne, at the very beginning of the Proofs to his *History of Châtillon-sur-Marne*, distinguished several Châtillons in France which gave their names to noble families; several others could be added. For we know of at least five distinct Châtillons in the territory of the Sequani. The question concerns the Châtillon family on the Seine, in the Duchy of Burgundy and the territory of Langres: whether it produced St. Bernard and his father, as the first part of the Fontenay charter [Col. 1508B] affirms.

The first author of this opinion, so far as I know, was Robert of Torigni, in his Appendix to Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 1113. “Bernard,” he says, “a distinguished young man, illustrious in learning, character, and lineage, who was afterward to become an example of great virtue, native of the castle of Châtillon in Burgundy, assumed the religious habit at Cîteaux with his full brothers and many other companions, and conducted himself with marvelous religious fervor.” He does not say that Bernard sprang from the family of the lords of Châtillon. Yet recent writers cited above, at page 408, have supposed this, interpreting Robert to mean that Bernard was both illustrious by lineage and born at Châtillon Castle—as though he could not have been born into some other noble family of the castle of Châtillon than that principal family which took its name from Châtillon.

Robert continued his Appendix to the year 1210, at St. Michael’s on the Mount, or in the peril of the sea, where he was abbot. Thus he was remote from Châtillon both in place and in time from Tecelin’s birth—and, as often happens to those far removed, [Col. 1509A] he missed the mark.

But see what led him into error. He had read in Book I of the *Life of St. Bernard*, chapter 1, that Aleth de Montbard, having devoted her son Bernard to God, as soon as she could, placed him in the church of Châtillon—which is known later to have been raised by Bernard’s own efforts from secular life into an order of regular canons—to be educated by masters in letters, and did all she could to ensure his progress in them. Then, in chapter 3, concerning the companions whom Bernard assembled for his purpose: “For they had at Châtillon a single house, their own and common to them all, where they gathered, lived together, and conversed; scarcely anyone who was not of their company dared enter it.”

But if these very words are considered more closely, they plainly establish the opposite of what seemed true to Abbot Robert, Vincent of Beauvais, Paradine, and their other followers. For after Abbot William had stated that Bernard was born in the regions of Burgundy, at Fontaines, the town of his father, he says immediately that, when Bernard passed beyond the care of nurses and attendants, he was sent thence, especially through the efforts of his devout mother, to devote himself to letters in the Church of Châtillon. Fontaines in the district of Dijon lies nearly two days’ journey from Châtillon. There Bernard was cultivated in the disciplines of the liberal arts; and, having at last conceived the plan of a more perfect life, he associated several companions with himself in that purpose. They had their own house, which, according to the tradition of the people of Châtillon, Bernard inhabited throughout the course of his studies for nearly fourteen years, [Col. 1509C] and which about forty years ago was assigned to the Feuillant Fathers by authority of both the royal and civil magistracy. In that house Bernard and his companions secretly held their meetings for some six months before they withdrew to Cîteaux, scarcely admitting anyone else, lest their new—and indeed bold—plan, which would disturb many families, should become public prematurely. Was this, as some imagine, the ancestral house of St. Bernard, the residence of the nobles of Châtillon, which would have been thronged by people arriving from the entire dominion, crowds of servants, and even companies of matrons and girls?

[Col. 1509D] I perceive what our opponents will reply here: that the Fontenay tradition is that Tecelin, Bernard’s father, was born of the Châtillon family, and that this tradition is contained in the Fontenay records. If that is so, I willingly yield to their opinion. Let them show even a single stroke in those records establishing either that Werricus de Châtillon was a count or Tecelin’s father, or that Godefridus and Gerard de Châtillon were born of André, the maternal uncle of St. Bernard. In the Proofs of the Disquisition, you will read of Werricus de Châtillon; Werricus of the Bridge of Châtillon, whether the same as the preceding man or distinct from him; Godefridus, husband of Gertrude; Hugh and Nivard, their sons; Gerard, brother-in-law of Theobald de Salives and father of Milo; Achard, Peter, Reinerius, [Col. 1510A] Girbert, and Matthew—all of Châtillon. Which of these is indicated even in a word as a blood relative of St. Bernard or Tecelin?

The records of Fontenay mention Rainard, Lord of Montbard, and his brothers Gualdric and Milo, maternal uncles of St. Bernard; Guy and Gerard, his brothers; William de Spirey and his brother Richard, his nephews; his kinswoman Milesendis, wife of Rainerius; and several others of his lineage. Yet, among the men of Châtillon, of whom very many are named, not one is in any way indicated as belonging to the line of St. Bernard or Tecelin. It is therefore a fabrication to maintain that these men were Châtillon by origin and family, and that this is proved by the Fontenay records.

I would not deny, however, that some relationship by marriage existed [Col. 1510B] between the Châtillon family and Tecelin’s Fontaines family. For it is established that Tecelin’s descendants possessed some property near Châtillon; and it is conjectured that Eva of Châtillon, with whom in the year of Christ 1100—according to the recension of the Saffres records—Aalysia, St. Bernard’s mother, entered into a certain agreement, was the wife of Guy, St. Bernard’s eldest brother, and brought to her husband as dowry certain houses or lands from the domain of the Châtillon family. But, as I have said, let this remain a conjecture rather than an assertion, until further light shines upon us from elsewhere.

## CHAPTER III. André was not a son of Rainard de Montbard, but a grandson through Bernard, Rainard’s son. There was also another André, Rainard’s brother, omitted from the Fontenay charter or, rather, transferred from St. Bernard’s maternal lineage to his paternal lineage.

[Col. 1510C]

André, Lord of Montbard, is mentioned in certain undated records of Godefridus, bishop of Langres, by which he confirms gifts made to Fontenay monastery by Milo of Molesme. The same André is subscribed in records of Reomaus issued by that same Bishop Godefridus in the year of Christ 1150, at Saint-Pierre-le-Vif in Reomaus, in Peter Roverius, *in Petro Abbate*, chapter 42, and in Illustration 138. An autograph charter of Godefridus, bishop of Langres, has taught us that this André was son of Bernard, who was born to Rainard as father. It bears no date, but from its circumstances appears to have been issued not far from 1160. By it the bishop testifies that André, Lord of Montbard, son of Bernard, son of Rainard, confirmed all gifts and privileges which he had bestowed upon Fontenay Abbey up to that point. “Finally,” he says, “whatever his grandfather Rainard and his father Bernard had given and granted to the aforesaid Abbey of Fontenay, as was contained in their charters, André likewise granted.” The author of the charter therefore wrongly assigned André and Bernard as sons to Rainard.

Moreover, certain records copied into the autograph of the first great charter of Fontenay conclude in these words: “Of all these gifts which were made in the presence of Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, these are the witnesses: Boso the dean, Evrard, priest of Champignolles, [Col. 1511A] Bernard, Lord of Montbard; André, his uncle; Nivard and Rainerius, brothers.” The term *avunculus*, which ancient Latin used only for a mother’s brother, was understood in later centuries also to mean a father’s brother, or paternal uncle. We therefore do not doubt that the André called uncle of Bernard, who was born to Rainard as father, was Rainard’s brother. Nor do we think that the superscription of St. Bernard’s Epistle 288, addressed to André, his uncle, a Knight Templar, ought to be understood of anyone else—an André whom no testimony of antiquity proves to have been Tecelin’s brother.

Accordingly, lest we be compelled to divide the one André, St. Bernard’s uncle, into two men, he must be called the brother of Aleth, Bernard’s mother. For since Bernard de Montbard, Rainard’s son, and St. Bernard, born of Aleth as mother, were cousins; and since it is clear from the autograph records of Fontenay that André was the maternal uncle of that earlier Bernard, Lord of Montbard; André could certainly not have been uncle to both Bernards [Col. 1511B] unless he was brother of both Rainard and Aleth. Therefore André, the Knight Templar, must be restored from St. Bernard’s paternal pedigree to his maternal one.

## CHAPTER IV. Godefridus, bishop of Langres, was not the brother of Thecelin the Tawny, but of the knight Rainerius—either of Acrimont or of La Roche.

William the Abbot, Book I of the *Life of St. Bernard*, chapter 9: “The venerable Godefridus, bishop of Langres, a blood relative of the holy man, his companion in conversion and thereafter in all things his inseparable companion, was accustomed to relate.” Bernard, abbot of Bonnevaux, Book II of the *Life of St. Bernard*, chapter 5: “His venerable brothers were present in his counsels; Godefridus, prior of that same place, was present, his kinsman in flesh and spirit, a wise and steadfast man. By the merit of his religious life and prudence, he afterward became bishop in the Church of Langres; retaining the pattern of holiness, and not diminishing the honor of the rank in which he stood, he perseveres praiseworthily to this day in his going out and coming in.”

They call him a relative in flesh and blood, but state neither the degree nor the line of relationship. The Fontenay charter makes Godefridus the brother of Bernard’s father Thecelin; if this were so, these authors would certainly have called Godefridus either St. Bernard’s paternal uncle or, in the usage of their age, his maternal uncle. A different basis must therefore be sought for their relationship, whether by blood or by marriage.

[Col. 1511D] Rainerius the knight, brother of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, is mentioned in documents of the year 1141, by which the churches of Bar-sur-Aube were adjudged to Ado, abbot of Saint Eugendus, against Adalard, abbot, and the monks of Melun. The records of Morimond Abbey, of which that Odolric was founder, seem to teach us that this Rainerius was lord of Aigremont, son of Ulric or Odolric, and had as brothers Ulric the canon and Gerard Sineterra. If this is so, the passage cited above by us from the Chronicle of Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, will show Saint Bernard’s relationship by marriage to Geoffrey. [Col. 1512A] For Guy of Aigremont—who married Hesceline, lady of Mussy, daughter of Holdoin of Joinville—was the uterine brother of Thecelin Sorus of Fontaines, and of Holdoin and Hayno of Colombey; but he was brother through the father alone of Ulric or Odolric, lord of Aigremont, on whose estate Morimond Abbey stands.

Accordingly, since the Morimond records establish that Rainerius was Odolric’s son, if Geoffrey was Rainerius’s brother, they certainly had as paternal uncle Guy of Aigremont, who was Thecelin Sorus’s maternal cousin. This would have been Geoffrey’s kinship with Saint Bernard: their fathers, though not truly brothers, nevertheless had a common brother, Guy of Aigremont—Ulric’s paternal cousin and Thecelin’s maternal cousin. This is a relationship by affinity: not legal, civil, or canonical affinity indeed, but a popular usage, long received into common speech.

I admit that this can be said with no little plausibility. Nevertheless, the Morimond documents seem to stand in the way. [Col. 1512B] In them Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, confirmed a gift of certain land which Rainerius, lord of Aigremont, had granted to Morimond with the consent and approval of his brothers Ulric the canon and Gerard Sineterra. For how could the bishop, in those records, have failed even once to indicate that these men were his brothers?

I would therefore rather judge that the brother of Bishop Geoffrey was Rainerius de Rosa, who is named at least twelve times in the first and second great charters of Fontenay; he is called Nivard’s brother and the husband of Milesendis, Saint Bernard’s female cousin—the sister, namely, of Bernard, lord of Montbard, and thus daughter of Rainard, Saint Bernard’s maternal uncle. The same man, Rainerius de Rocha or de Rochia, [Col. 1512C] is read as subscribing eight times among the witnesses of the great charter concerning the foundation of Le Val-des-Choues, drawn up in 1135—because of his attachment, I suppose, to the Cistercian order, and especially to Clairvaux, from which Le Val-des-Choues derived, and in which he had both a brother and most of his kinsmen and connections by marriage.

Our conjecture is further confirmed because this Rainerius was also more frequently present at gifts bestowed upon the monks of Fontenay, over whom Geoffrey is known to have presided as their first abbot. If these things are true—as indeed they very closely resemble the truth—it is easy for anyone to recognize Bishop Geoffrey as Saint Bernard’s kinsman in flesh and spirit, because both their common religious purpose and a certain affinity of blood united them. For a man whose brother has married his female cousin, although he falls within no degree of civil or canonical affinity, is nevertheless reckoned and called a relation by marriage in popular usage even today; and this was much more customary in Saint Bernard’s age, before the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, when degrees of affinity and consanguinity, even for purposes of marriage, extended much more widely.

633

## CHAPTER V. The granddaughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard, who was the daughter of the count of Grignon, was not the wife of Robert, duke of Burgundy; nor did she bring the county of Montbard into the dominion of the duke of Burgundy, as the second part of the Fontenay Charter asserts.

The Fontenay Charter contains a manifold error here. History acknowledges only one wife of Robert, duke of Burgundy, the second of that name: [Col. 1513A] Agnes, daughter of Saint Louis, king of the French. Married to him in 1272, she bore him many children and survived him by eighteen years after his death on 9 October 1309. Further, if Agnes was not the duke Robert’s wife, how could Bernard, son of Rainard, lord of Montbard—who was alive around the year of Christ 1130—have had a granddaughter through a daughter who was countess of Grignon, yet still living after an interval of a hundred and forty years?

The Charter’s additional statement that the county of Montbard passed into the dominion of the dukes of Burgundy in 1286, while a certain Hugh ruled as duke of Burgundy, contains nothing true. For in that period the lordship of Montbard did not enjoy the title of a county; and in the year 1286 Robert II was duke of Burgundy. Moreover, Montbard had already come under ducal authority much earlier, as Pierre Roverius shows in *Reomaus*, Illustration 138. There he cites certain records of Moutiers-Saint-Jean from 1235, from which it is clear that Hugh IV, duke of Burgundy, then held jurisdiction over Montbard and exercised it through provosts. This is confirmed by the will of the same Hugh IV, made in 1272, by which he conveyed Montbard by hereditary right to one of his children. Below we shall explain the time and manner in which the lordship [634] of Montbard was transferred to the dukes.

## CHAPTER VI. The Fontenay Charter wrongly states the lineage of Robert the Burgundian’s wife.

[Col. 1513C]

The Charter represents this wife as a native of Tonnerre on her father’s side, and on her mother’s side as Hugh’s granddaughter, Geoffrey’s great-granddaughter, and Andrew of Châtillon’s great-great-granddaughter—Andrew whom it makes Saint Bernard’s paternal uncle. All this is false, as may be understood from what has been said. Here I show only that she is wrongly given as Robert the Burgundian’s wife.

For the wife of Robert in question, son of Robert II, duke of Burgundy, was Joan of Chalon, daughter of William of Chalon, count of Auxerre and Tonnerre, and Eleanor or Elienor, daughter of Amadeus VI, count of Savoy. William had received the county of Auxerre as a maternal inheritance, and the county of Tonnerre, from January 1292, from his maternal aunt Margaret, widow of Charles of Anjou, king of Jerusalem and [Col. 1513D] Sicily, and countess of Tonnerre. A distinguished memorial of her piety survives in the hospital at Tonnerre founded by her, where she was also buried.

Joan’s brother was John of Chalon. Their inheritance was divided so that the county of Auxerre belonged to the brother, while she held Tonnerre. In 1321 she then brought this county as her dowry to Robert, son of Robert [Col. 1514A] II, duke of Burgundy, and grandson of King Saint Louis through his mother Agnes, the king’s daughter. These facts are established not only by several reliable writers of genealogical history but also—and much more certainly—by several original documents which we have read. After the death of William, her husband, Eleanor of Savoy, mother of John and Joan of Chalon, contracted a second marriage around 1307 with Drogo de Mello, lord of Sainte-Hermine.

635

## CHAPTER VII. An examination of what the Fontenay Charter relates concerning the two Drogos de Mello and the wife of the younger, Eustachia; and an explanation of how the lordship of Époisses passed from the Montbard family to those Drogos.

The author of the Charter says that Bernard of Montbard had a daughter who was married in 1233 to Drogo de Mello, bore him another Drogo, husband of Eustachia, cousin of Edward, king of the English; that she followed her husband on Saint Louis’s expedition and died at Carthage; and that she left instructions for her body to be carried to Fontenay, where she lies under an epitaph bearing the year 1270.

It is indeed certain that Eustachia, Drogo’s wife, was cousin to King Edward; in all else there is no credibility. For Bernardinus de Montebarro is fictitious, nor did any girl of this house ever marry into the family of the Drogos de Mello. I shall go further back and explain as follows the connections by marriage between these families, through the passage of the lordship of Époisses among them.

[Col. 1514C] Helvidis, heiress, as I suppose, of the lord of Époisses, was wife to Andrew, lord of Montbard, son of Bernard and grandson of Rainard. Their son was Bernard, lord of Époisses, who in 1210 confirmed gifts which his mother Helvidis, deceased on 29 January, had bestowed upon Fontenay. He did not long survive his mother and is mentioned as already dead in October 1213, leaving three sons: Andrew, who was still lord of Époisses in 1232; Bernard, a young nobleman, lord of Vi; and Guy, canon of Langres and Auxerre.

But when the elder Andrew had died, his widow Helvidis entered into a second marriage with Hugh, lord of l’Orme, and bore him a daughter also named Helvidis [Col. 1514D] de l’Orme. Through her, her husband Drogo de Mello was already lord of Époisses by 1247—after Andrew, as may be conjectured, the childless son of Bernard, his wife’s uterine brother. This Drogo, the first lord of Époisses from his family, was not father but grandfather of the Drogo who was Eustachia’s husband, as you will understand from page 581 and from this brief table.

HELVIDIS, lady of Époisses, had two husbands: ANDREW, lord of Montbard, and HUGH, lord of l’Orme.

From ANDREW, her first husband | From HUGH, her later husband  
---|---  
BERNARD of Montbard, lord of Époisses, 1210, 1213. | ALAYS, wife of Odo II, count of Grignon. | HELVIDIS de l’Orme, wife of DROGO de MELLO; through her they were lords of Époisses by 1247.

[Col. 1515]

ANDREW, lord of Époisses, 1213, 1232. | BERNARD, young nobleman, lord of Vi. | GUY, canon, 1213 and 1220. | DROGO de MELLO, lord of Époisses; his wife was daughter of Anseric, lord of Montréal. He was still alive in 1269. | DROGO de MELLO, lord of Époisses; wife: EUSTACHIA de LUSIGNAN, cousin of Edward I, king of the English, through their common paternal grandmother, Isabella of Angoulême. Drogo was still alive in 1290.

[Col. 1515A] 637

From these facts it may be seen that the distinguished family of the lords of Mello was related by marriage, but not by blood, to Saint Bernard’s maternal line. Let the author of the Charter be trusted concerning Drogo, Eustachia’s husband, going overseas in Saint Louis’s company, and concerning the year and place of Eustachia’s death. For the year 1276, noted above on page 582, concerns not her marriage, but an act performed by Drogo de Mello to recover some inheritance of Eustachia’s paternal uncle, as the very learned Monsieur Du Bouchet informed me in a later letter.

In Fontenay church, between the choir and the high altar on the Gospel side, we saw a black-marble monument said to belong to the spouses Drogo and Eustachia; but of the epitaph formerly borne by bronze plates attached to the marble, no trace remains, since the plates were long ago torn away. There are many other defects in the Fontenay Charter, especially in its ordering of the children of Thecelin and Alays. [Col. 1516A] For it represents Humbeline as born last, whereas John the Hermit asserts that she followed her brother Blessed Bernard in birth order; consequently, being in the middle among six brothers, she had three older and as many younger than herself. The other defects of the Charter will become clear from what we shall say below, drawing upon purer sources, about Saint Bernard’s entire affinity and consanguinity. Let us now set forth several genealogical tables on this subject, in which matters hitherto scattered confusedly and indiscriminately through the *Diatribe* and its *Proofs* may be gathered and arranged in an easy and clear order.

638

## CHAPTER VIII. Table I: Saint Bernard’s paternal family, from Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines.

[Col. 1516B] We gave the passage from Alberic’s Chronicle above, on page 416. From the mother of Thecelin, Saint Bernard’s paternal grandmother, we derive the following line with him:

From an earlier husband, N.:

TECELINUS Sorus, lord of Fontaines. | HOLDOIN.  
---|---  
SAINT BERNARD. | N., offspring of Holdoin. | ALBRIC of Échenay.

The mother of Thecelin, N., had two husbands; her other husband was Fulk of Scey, by whom she had:

HAYNO of Colombey. | GUY of Aigremont, whose wife was HESCELINE of Joinville, lady of Mussy.  
---|---  
ABELINUS. | WERRICUS. | WALTER of Mussy.

[Col. 1515B] Alberic adds that before Fulk of Scey married Thecelin’s mother, he had another wife, by whom he fathered Ulric or Odolric, lord of Aigremont, founder of Morimond. The Morimond records mention three sons of this Odolric: Rainerius, lord of Aigremont; Ulric the canon; and Gerard Sineterra. Perhaps a fourth must be added, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres; but for certain reasons this is less approved by us in Chapter IV of this Appendix.

The conjecture that Saint Bernard’s unnamed paternal grandmother belonged by birth and family to Grancey rests principally on the Chronicle of Grancey. Although that chronicle is fabulous in many respects, its statement that in ancient times one of the daughters of the lord of Grancey became, through her husband, lady of Fontaines does not seem contemptible. For at Grancey Castle there still stands an ancient tower, which from time beyond memory has been called, and is still called, Saint Bernard’s Tower, because he is believed to have stayed there whenever he visited his relatives.

Nevertheless, since Guy, Saint Bernard’s eldest brother, may have married a woman of the Grancey family and she may through him have been lady of [Col. 1516B] Fontaines, I would not affirm anything definitively in this uncertainty. I would say only, disjunctively, that either Thecelin’s mother or Guy’s wife was Eva of Châtillon, and the other a woman of Grancey. Thus, if the former was a woman of Grancey, the latter was from Châtillon; and conversely, if the former was from Châtillon, the other was a woman of Grancey.

Moreover, it seems that Saint Bernard’s consanguinity or affinity with the mother of Asceline, the virgin renowned for holiness, descended from these uterine brothers of Thecelin. As reported in the Chronicle of Clairvaux from Goswin, she was Saint Bernard’s and Bishop Geoffrey’s kinswoman, born in a village near La Ferté-sur-Aube. The same may be said of Josbert, lord of that same La Ferté-sur-Aube, whom the *Life*, Book I, chapter 9, calls Saint Bernard’s kinsman according to the flesh, and in whose place the new abbot is said to have performed his first miracle.

If, as is probable, La Ferté came to Josbert by hereditary right—La Ferté which only a few years earlier had belonged to Saint Simon, formerly count and later monk of Saint-Claude or Saint Eugendus in the Jura—then from this too one may discern how very illustrious Josbert’s family, and hence Saint Bernard’s, was. For Saint Simon is known to have been connected by legitimate blood with both the kings of France and of England, as we have demonstrated more fully in another work not yet published. [Col. 1517A]

The following record from the Clairvaux cartulary should, I think, be understood of Josbert the son rather than of his namesake father: Odo of Champagne and his wife Sibylla approved the whole alms-gift which Josbert of La Ferté had given to the brethren of Clairvaux.
