Since this Josbert’s great benefactions toward Clairvaux survive, one may suppose that an error entered the *History of the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church*, printed at Rome by the Vatican press in 1630. [Col. 1518A] Under Pope Paschal II, page 461, it says that Clairvaux monastery was built at the expense of a distinguished man, Robert. Josbert seems rather to have been written in place of Robert, since the Clairvaux records make no mention of any Robert who deserved well of them in those early beginnings.

641

## CHAPTER IX. Table II: Saint Bernard’s maternal family.

This table, like the following ones, consists almost wholly of the matters set out above; but, where necessary, we shall append a brief explanation of some of its parts.

### FIRST PART OF THE TABLE

1. BERNARD, lord of Montbard — HUMBERGA, his wife.

2. RAINARD, lord of Montbard; wife AANOLDIS. | ALAYS, wife of TECELINUS Saurus. | DIANA, wife of OTHO of Châtillon. | ANDREW, Knight Templar. | GUALDRIC, lord of Tuilly, later a monk; MILO, prior of Fontenay, formerly a lay brother.

3. SAINT BERNARD, with his sister and five brothers. | ROBERT, abbot of the House of God.

### SECOND PART OF THE TABLE

2. RAINARD, lord of Montbard — wife AANOLDIS.

3. BERNARD, lord of Montbard. | N., wife first of FERGANNUS HELIRANNUS, count of Grignon; later of RAYMOND of Burgundy, likewise count of Grignon; or at least his mother-in-law. (See the following Chapter X.) | MILESENDIS, wife of RAINERIUS de Rocha.

4. ANDREW, lord of Montbard; wife HELVIDIS, lady of Époisses, who later married HUGH of l’Orme. | MATHILDIS, Raymond’s daughter by Agnes of Montpensier, his second wife; wife of Odo of Issoudun, count of Grignon.

642

5. BERNARD of Montbard, lord of Époisses. | ALAYS, lady of Montbard, wife of Odo of Issoudun, second count of Grignon of that name, son of Odo I and Mathildis.

ANDREW, lord of Époisses. | BERNARD, young nobleman, lord of Vi. | GUY, canon of Langres and Auxerre.

[Col. 1517B] 1. John the Hermit, as likewise the author of the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif of Sens, informed us that Bernard was the head of the Montbard family, so far as we know. As we noted above in the *Diatribe*, the same author also established for us that Bernard’s wife was Humberga and that one or the other was descended from the counts of Tonnerre. Saint Bernard drew his name from his maternal grandfather; his sister Humbeline, from her grandmother. An old author of the *Life of the Most Holy Peter, Prior of Jully*, has taught us that she was called not only Humbeline, as commonly believed, but also Humberga. These are not wholly different names; rather, the former was fashioned from the latter according to the custom by which the names of infants and children are softened by an affectionate diminutive tenderness.

Thus I do not doubt that Saint Bernard’s sister was first named Humberga at baptism after her maternal grandmother, then called Humbeline throughout infancy and childhood, and later, in marriage and finally in the monastery, resumed her true and original name of Humberga.

2. He should be written Rainard, as shown by the Chronicle of Sens, [Col. 1518B] the first great charter of Fontenay, and the records of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres. In the Fontenay genealogy he is wrongly called Regnald or Regnaud. The same first original great charter of Fontenay has taught us that his wife was Aanoldis. The family of the lords of Montbard descended only from these two, as the second part of this table shows.

2. ALAYS or AELAYS—for John the Hermit calls her by both names; in the necrologies of Saint-Bénigne, Alasya and Alaysa; elsewhere commonly Aalys, Alays, Aelaydis, Aeleth, Aleth. All mean the same and amount to one and the same name. She was truly twice the mother of seven children, because she bore them both to the world and to Christ.

[Col. 1518C] 2. DIANA, wife of Otho of Châtillon, of the Montbard family, in the year of Christ 1107, according to the abstract of the Saffres records. If this source is not mistaken, I think Diana was mother of Robert, abbot of the House of God, on the River Cher in Berry. John the Hermit asserts that he was Saint Bernard’s nephew—that is, born of a mother who was sister to Saint Bernard’s mother. He adds that he received from the mouth of this Abbot Robert the marvelous account he relates concerning the death of Alays, Saint Bernard’s mother; Robert, he says, lived in the monastery under the yoke of regular discipline for more than sixty-seven years.

This agrees with what we read both in the received *Life of Saint Bernard* and in the *Cistercian Exordium*: that this Robert was Saint Bernard’s relative according to the flesh; or, in Peter the Venerable, Book VI, Letter 35, near to him by blood. That the first letter of Saint Bernard, written in the midst of rain yet without rain, bears the heading “To Robert, his nephew,” is either an error of the collector of the letters or belongs to that once common mode of speaking—already noted by others—by which *nepos* (“nephew”) was applied also to a paternal cousin, maternal cousin, or cousin through a paternal aunt, provided he was younger than his paternal cousin, maternal cousin, or cousin through a paternal aunt, or born of a younger father or mother. From this one may infer that Robert’s mother was younger than Alays, Saint Bernard’s parent; and anyone who reads that first letter of Saint Bernard and William the abbot, Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 11, will understand that Robert was an adolescent and almost a boy when Saint Bernard wrote to him.

2. ANDREW, a Knight Templar, to whom Saint Bernard’s Letter 288 is addressed, designating him as his maternal uncle. He is also called maternal uncle of Bernard, lord of Montbard, born of Rainard, Saint Bernard’s maternal uncle. The children assigned to Andrew by the Fontenay Genealogy do not concern him in any way.

[Col. 1519C] 2. GUALDRIC. Concerning him, the *Life of Saint Bernard*, Book I, chapter 3, says: “First of all his uncle Galdric, without delay or hesitation, went over, as they say, feet-first to his nephew’s decision and assented to conversion; he was an honorable man, powerful in the world, celebrated for the glory of secular knighthood, lord of a castle in the territory of the Aedui called Tuillium.”

Here, my reader, you should be informed that there are two castles in the territory of the Aedui with almost the same name: one, Tillium, in the district of Alise, commonly Til; the other, Tullium, called *Tullio* in the Fontenay records, commonly Touillon, of which Gualdric was formerly possessor. At this Tullium is a rural deanery, or archpriesthood, of the diocese of Autun, number 19. Tillium is about five leagues from Montbard; Tullium scarcely two. He conveyed Tullium, but not Tillium, into the dominion of Fontenay Abbey. Several persons in this work are named from the latter, including Hugh Peccatum of Til in the year 1174.

Here one may marvel at the man’s humility: he wished to be surnamed not merely “Sinner,” as very many others did, but “Sin,” which alone man possesses of himself—being indebted to God the creator for his soul, body, and all his other goods. Moreover, the first great charter of Fontenay asserts that this Waldric was then already a monk, together with his brother Milo, a lay brother, and Martin the hermit, the first builder of Fontenay Abbey.

2. If, however, you read in some records that MILO, Saint Bernard’s maternal uncle, then a lay brother, later became prior of Fontenay, [Col. 1520A] beware of thinking that he held this office while still a lay brother. This was never permitted in the Cistercian Order. Rather, hold it certain that Milo, who in humility had wished, upon his first entrance into the Order, to make profession among the lay brothers, was afterwards judged worthy by his superiors to become a monk and presided for some time over the monks at Fontenay, the house whose foundation he had helped initiate. From the year 1113, we infer from the Chronicle of Sens that he withdrew to Cîteaux in Saint Bernard’s company, having renounced the vanity of the world.

## CHAPTER X. Explanation of the second part of this second table, including certain matters worthy of notice concerning the ancient counts of Grignon.

3. Bernard, lord of Montbard, is stated in the records of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, to have been Rainard’s son and Andrew’s father. In the first great charter of Fontenay, Milesendis is also called this Bernard’s sister and Rainerius’s wife; Rainerius, as we more probably think, was Rainerius de Rocha, the same man and brother of Bishop Geoffrey—whence his affinity with Saint Bernard.

4. Andrew’s wife Helvidis, lady of Époisses—what sons she bore him, whom she bore to Hugh of l’Orme, whom she married in a second union, and by what means the lordship of Époisses passed through her daughter and namesake Helvidis de l’Orme to the Drogos de Mello—has already been sufficiently explained above.

It is more laborious to investigate what affinity formerly joined the counts of Grignon [Col. 1520C] to the Montbard family. The cited records of Bishop Geoffrey state: “Also the division of lands between Fontaines and Segrest, as it had long before been made in the presence of the countess, Andrew’s paternal aunt, where stone boundary-markers were also set up.” Andrew’s grandfather, as we have said, was Rainard, and his father Bernard; therefore Andrew’s paternal aunt was Bernard’s sister and Rainard’s daughter. But how was she a countess except through a count for her husband? And whose wife could she have been except that of the count of Grignon, whose territory lay nearest to Montbard Castle and who was the principal lord of many surrounding places?

When Rainard, lord of Montbard, granted the territory of Aringes to Fontenay, that grant had to be confirmed by the authority and consent of the count of Grignon. Thus the first great charter of Fontenay, no. 1, says: “Lord Fergannus, count of Grignon, also approved this with great goodwill.” Under another gift: “Leobaud of Grignon and Humbaud of Rougemont. Witnesses to this act were Helirannus Fercannus, count of Grignon, Geoffrey of Saigny,” etc.

Bernard, lord of Montbard, is himself called several times in this same first charter. Therefore one may suppose that Fergannus, count of Grignon, was Rainard’s son-in-law and Bernard’s brother-in-law; and that, out of regard for or at the request of his beloved wife, he sought to deserve well of her kinsmen, whether monks or founders of Fontenay.

After Fergannus, the county of Grignon is known to have returned to the authority of the prince, namely Hugh II, duke of Burgundy. [Col. 1521A] With the approval of his wife Duchess Mathildis, he gave Fontenay Church everything he possessed at Puteolus Francus. As the records state, this place descended from the dominion of Grignon Castle, of which he himself, the duke, was lord. No more reasonable cause for this transfer of lordship occurs than that Fergannus died either childless or without male offspring. For fiefs of this especially principal kind of vassalage were entrusted by the prince to males alone, although the claims of female heirs were generally observed in this fashion: the estates, together with titles of honor, were conferred upon the husbands they had obtained.

Further, from the records issued by Henry, bishop of Autun, in 1165, we know with certainty that Raymond, son of Duke Hugh II and brother of Bishop Henry, was count of Grignon even before he married Mathildis. Mathildis, born of Agnes of Montpensier, brought her paternal county of Grignon as dowry to Odo of Issoudun. Count Raymond had given the men of Fontenay whatever his *chasati* from the dominion of Grignon might give them from their *chasamentum*, provided that the *chasatus* did not lose his holding. He had therefore granted this already as count of Grignon, but not yet as Agnes’s husband. From this one may infer that Raymond’s father Hugh bestowed the county of Grignon upon him when he betrothed either the widow or the daughter of Count Fergannus to him.

At this period, it is worthy of notice that the first great Charter of Fontenay shows Walter the constable as lord of Montbard—not, I think, of the castle, but only of the borough or town, held as a benefice from the principal lord, Rainard or his son Bernard, who held the castle. [Col. 1521C] We once thought that Walter the constable had acquired this possession through marriage to one of Rainard’s sisters—perhaps she who was mother of Robert, abbot of the House of God, and Saint Bernard’s maternal aunt. But another, much more plausible explanation now presents itself: while Duke Hugh held the county of Grignon, he may have sent his military commander for a time to exercise beneficial lordship over the town of Montbard, in order to assert the dower rights of the widow of the former Count Fergannus, sister of Bernard, lord of Montbard, and to restore them to either her second husband or her son-in-law Raymond.

Forgive me, reader, for groping as though blind amid this scarcity of documents, feeling out conjectures like shadows in this darkness; where certainties are lacking, take at least what is probable in good part.

5. Concerning Alays, I do not know whether I have arrived at a better conclusion. Above we identified a countess of Grignon of this name as wife of the younger Odo of Issoudun; and on no slight conjecture pronounced her daughter of Andrew, lord of Montbard, and sister of Bernard, lord of Époisses. But what a learned friend pointed out from Rigerius in the Chronicle of Lérins—that this Alays was first wife of Archambaud of Bourbon and, after his death, married Odo of Déols, and that he therefore asserts her to have been both daughter of Odo II, duke of Burgundy, [Col. 1522A] and wife of the younger Odo of Issoudun—does not move me from the position which I have advanced.

I admit that Alays of Burgundy had as husband Archambaud of Bourbon, seventh of that name as Duchesne reckons him; I deny that this same woman was married to the younger Odo of Issoudun, for three reasons. First, because of their excessively close blood relationship. It is certain that Odo the duke was brother of Raymond, the maternal grandfather of this Odo of Issoudun. Thus Alays and Odo of Issoudun were related in the second and third degrees of consanguinity. No dispensation capable of removing incest would have been granted in those degrees, especially before the Lateran Council of 1215, when marriages were forbidden up to the seventh degree of affinity or consanguinity.

Second, because of the disproportion of their times and ages. Alays had lost Archambaud, her first husband, in 1169, when Odo of Issoudun, son of Mathildis of Burgundy, was still in the care of nurses or attendants, certainly not yet beyond boyhood. Henry, bishop of Autun, Mathildis’s paternal uncle, teaches us this when in 1165 he calls Mathildis, newly betrothed to the elder Odo of Issoudun, still a girl. How then could Alays, four years after becoming Archambaud’s widow, have taken as husband the still infant son of her younger cousin Mathildis?

Third and finally, because in 1201 Alays was already veiled among the nuns of Fontevraud, as can be seen in Duchesne’s *Proofs concerning the Ancient Family of the Dukes of Burgundy*. Yet in 1212 Alays, widow of Odo of Issoudun, was still living in the world and attended the testament of her son Ralph.

650

If, therefore, any trust is to be placed in that Chronicle of Lérins, I think it should be understood of Odo of Déols, who was cousin or paternal cousin to the father of the younger Odo of Issoudun and therefore closer to Alays in age. For, as Duchesne notes, Odo, husband of Mathildis and father of the younger Odo, was son of Geoffrey, son of Odo, brother of Ralph of Déols. Thus, in the genealogical tree of this house, the branch of the Issoudun family had already been separated from that of the Déols family by a fourth branching at Odo, Alays’s husband. The second husband of Alays, Archambaud’s widow, must therefore be sought in the Déols branch and in its upper division.

This also explains some kinship between these spouses, mentioned in the Chronicle of Lérins: Odo of Déols, whether son or grandson of Ralph, and his kinsman Odo of Issoudun, first count of Grignon of that name, had as wives Alays and Mathildis, who were paternal cousins.

I therefore stand by my conjecture, whose grounds I set out on page 560: Alays, wife of the younger Odo, count of Grignon, appears to have belonged to the Montbard family, daughter of Andrew and sister of Bernard. If a relationship by marriage between her and her husband is to be sought, it would appear in this: Odo was grandson of Raymond by his daughter Mathildis, and Raymond had married either the sister or, perhaps as we said, the daughter of Bernard, Alays’s grandfather.

## CHAPTER XII. Table IV, enumerating the Sombernon lords of Fontaines down to Mary, daughter and heiress of Richard.

[Col. 1523B]

Saint Bernard’s paternal family—that is, the Fontanais family—came down from Guy, his eldest brother, to Claude de Cleron, Baron of Saffres, who survives today, interrupted five times through female heiresses. BARTHOLOMEW of Sombernon, lord of Fontanis through his wife N., daughter of Guy, Saint Bernard’s eldest brother; his sister is mentioned in the Chronicle of Clairvaux as abbess of Poligny, pp. 445, 457, 463, 464, 465, 547, 87, 88.

KALO, whose death occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, pp. 463, 464. TECELIN, pp. 463, 464. GIRARD LI BROS, lord of Asnières. Wife: MARGARET, pp. 465, 437, 563.

[Col. 1525A] At p. 529 and under the year 1237, Hugh de Fontanis, a burgess of Dijon, is noted. Since he is called neither knight nor esquire, and since no mention of him is found in the tables relating to the Fontanais family, we suppose that he was either called de Fontanis from his native place, or perhaps because he was an illegitimate son of one of the lords of Fontanis and was therefore not to be counted among the legitimate descendants.

Moreover, a number of lords and ladies de Fontanis occur in our extracts from the Review of the Saffres and Fontanais tables, pp. 585–590. We considered it a matter of conscience not to insert them into this table, which was compiled from original documents, lest certain matters be confused with doubtful ones. For we have already noted above, p. 617, how erroneous and distorted that Review is, both in the names of persons and in chronological notices. [Col. 1525B]

## CHAPTER XIII. Table V of the de Sauz family, insofar as it concerns the Fontanais family. Who was William de Sauz, whose wife was Belota de Fontanis

The de Sauz family is so illustrious among the Burgundians that it seems worthy of being adequately illuminated in a volume by some expert genealogist. Those seem to me to be telling tales—and playing upon a word—who think that its name was given it from the town commonly called Saulieu, the seat alike of Faustus, a man of consular rank, and of Christianissimus. For that fortress is called *Sidoloucus* in the Roman Itinerary, and *Sedelocus* in the Acts of the holy martyrs Benignus, Andochius, and others of the same school, whom Faustus kindly received in his house in the second century after Christ. [Col. 1526A]

Furthermore, neither do those who today profess descent from this family suppose themselves to have taken their name from the village or castle of Sauz, situated in the land of the Aedui and in the territory of Alise, not far from Semur. The true origin of this house, therefore, lies in the castle now commonly called Sauz-le-Duc, evidently because it was added to the dominion of the dukes of Burgundy; in antiquity it was called Sals, Sauz, and Salion. It might also be pronounced *Salices*, or *Salicem*, after Philip the Fair, king of the French, who in a charter dated 1304 called William, the head of that family, *de Salice*. Or it may be referred to the episode reported by Jonas: when Columbanus and his companions had suffered lack of food at Annegray for nine days, Carantocus, abbot of Salices, divinely warned, sent help through his cellarer Marculf, with carts laden with plentiful provisions; their beasts went before them under divine guidance through the trackless passes and the shadowy recesses of the forests. By the name *Salices*, we think, Jonas here means the village now called Sauz, midway between Vesoul and Luxeuil, from which Annegray is about five hours’ journey distant. [Col. 1526B]

We have scattered a few remarks on the de Sauz family in the foregoing pages, only so far as was needed to show how the Fontanais family became joined to it through the Sombernon line: namely, through William de Sauz, husband of Belota de Fontanis. The following table, I think, will leave his descent sufficiently clear.

656 EVILO, also called Ebalus, Hebalus, and Eubolus, count of Sauz. Wife: Regina, pp. 486, 487, 489, 491, 492, 546. The count died on the fifth day before the Ides of October, p. 520. WILLIAM, pp. 486, 487, 489.

[Col. 1525C] We have deliberately omitted Girard de Sauz, whom the Fontenay documents show in the year 1227, since we are uncertain of his exact place. Likewise, William de Sauz, whose wife Beatrice is mentioned with their sons John and William under the year 1265. Yet one can scarcely doubt that all these are to be reckoned among the descendants either of Count Evilo [Col. 1527A] or of his brother William; but it remains unclear from which of the two, and in what degree.

Another William de Sauz and his wife Hermengard are mentioned in the charters of Henry, bishop of Autun, in the time of Arnold, abbot of Fontenay, p. 553. Nor does this William seem different from the William mentioned in the time of Godfrey, bishop of Langres, and Rainer, abbot of Albéripée, p. 489. For Rainer is known to have been appointed abbot in 1158, as p. 569 teaches; while Godfrey resigned the episcopate in 1161, according to the Chronicle of Clairvaux, p. 82. Therefore Godfrey’s charter seems to have been issued not far from 1159. It mentions William de Sauz, brother of Count Evilo; and the claim concerning a younger William de Sauz is disproved by the priority of these brothers. [Col. 1527B] Hence we regard this younger William, not implausibly, as the son of the earlier namesake. But William, Belota’s husband, must be investigated more closely by the following line of reasoning.

The children of Otho de Sauz, whose grandfather was Count Evilo, or Hebalus, are mentioned in documents concerning the alienation of the county of Langres, drawn up in 1179. I take these children to have been Guy, husband of Elizabeth, who is stated to have been Otho’s firstborn in the charter of Saint-Bénigne, p. 613; Hugh, canon of Langres; and William, to whom Belota de Fontanis was given in marriage and who begot by her the sons John, Kalo, and Otho or Othenin. Perhaps also Elizabeth de Fontanis, whose children Guiard and Adelina are found in the Clairvaux cartulary under 1223; but this is not wholly certain. This connection is strengthened not only by chronological considerations, but expressly by the fact that William, Belota’s husband, had a son Otho, named after his grandfather—as was the most commonly accepted custom in that age, when grandsons were generally named from their grandfathers. [Col. 1528A]

It places at its head Mary de Fontanis, wife of William de Marey, through whom Saint Bernard’s paternal line was carried into most of Burgundy’s illustrious families. Bernard de Marey, her son, boasted that he traced his origin from Saint Bernard’s house and stock.

[Col. 1527C] Just as this de Marey family widely propagated the stock of the lords of Fontanis, so it transferred the lordship of Fontanis itself to outsiders. For Alexander de Marey, the eldest son, sold to John Rolin, bishop of Chalon, in 1434, for 564 francs, his principal right in the whole noble estate, together with his own quarter-share of the lordship. Then Bernard de Marey, Alexander’s brother, reduced to extremity by illness in 1462, gave his quarter-share in the lordship of the castle of Fontanis, with all its appurtenances, to Abbot Humbert and the monastery of Cîteaux. When the duke of Burgundy refused his consent to this gift, lest a noble fief should pass into mortmain, as they say, [Col. 1527D] that quarter-share of Fontaines was sold by the Cistercians for 400 livres tournois—apparently to that same John Rolin, bishop of Chalon. For it is certain that later one half of the lordship of Fontanis came from Margaret Rolin, a kinswoman of the bishop of that name, to Mary Chambellan, wife of Guy de Rochefort, chancellor of France. [Col. 1528C]

Thereafter we find, at least in part, as lords of Fontanis Peter de Saigny, Othenin de Cleron, Humbert de Rochefort, William de Damas, and Joachim de Damas. But since that lordship also passed through other hands and is, as I hear, still disputed today, I did not think it my task to pursue all its possessors—whether alleged or lawful—whether in entirety or in part; especially since these matters now in no way concern Saint Bernard’s lineage.

## CHAPTER XV. Table VII of the de Saigny family, joined to the Fontanais family through Amiota de Marey, daughter of Mary de Fontanis

Under the year 1282, Hugh de Saigny is reported to have granted a certain vineyard of his to the monks of Fontenay for a specified price, with the consent of his wife Mary. Those are mistaken who confuse the names Huo and Hugo, which an earlier age distinguished. Thus, in the original document of Saint Stephen’s, Dijon, which we have published, the children of Hugh Bouins, knight of Vergy, and of his wife Engelvida, are listed as Peter the cleric, Hugh called Bouins, and Huo. Another man of the same family and name—namely Huo de Saigney—in the following century, after losing his wife Isabella de Blaisey and their son Philibert, married another Isabella from the de Saffres family in 1382. Anthony de Saigney, born of this marriage, had as his wife Amyota de Marey, daughter of Mary de Fontanis. Since this family today especially boasts of its blood relationship with Saint Bernard, and admirably reproduces its ancestors’ noble character, it was my intention in this table to disclose its ancient splendor. I begin with its first head known to us and end with Isabella, who interrupted the line transmitted through male heirs down to herself.

In ancient sources the name is used interchangeably as de Saffres or de Saffra. Since among the Burgundians there are some hawks called by this name, and since five such birds appear to be depicted in the heraldic emblem of the Saffres family, there is reason to suspect that this is a case of canting arms, commonly called *armes parlantes*—such as heralds and genealogists know belong to a good many highly illustrious families. [Col. 1531A] I want to warn you of one thing here, dear reader. In the original documents from which we have traced this table of the Saffres lords back almost five hundred years, not a single mention is found either of Fontaines or of the lords of Fontanis. Yet these originals consist of wills, marriage settlements, divisions of property, and other documents of this kind, in which the possessions, estates, rights, dowries, and other concerns of the Saffres family necessarily had to be recorded repeatedly. I mention this so that you may understand, even from this, how little trust the Review of the Saffres Tables deserves, some extracts from which we presented on pp. 585 onward; for it frequently names persons who are asserted to have been lords both of Saffres and of Fontaines. [Col. 1531B]

Still, I would not dare wholly to deny that in earlier centuries some persons held both lordships at once, because of the similarity of the two families’ arms. For the Saffres family displayed birds on its heraldic shield, as did the lords of Fontanis. But because, as we have already noted, this is a canting device among the Saffres, identifying the family by birds bearing its name, it seems native and original to them. Therefore, just as Kalo de Sauz, lord of Fontanis, having set aside the golden lion on an azure shield that is the proper armorial bearing of the lords de Sauz, displayed birds on his tomb as lord of Fontanis, so the lords of Fontanis may likewise appear to have derived from the Saffres family because they placed upon their shields birds adopted from the Saffres. [Col. 1532A] But I wish these things to be reckoned as conjectures, not propositions demonstrated by certain proof. Let us proceed with the rest.

## CHAPTER XVII. Table IX of the de Cleron family, into which the Fontanais family was joined through the Saigny and Saffres lines and survives to this day

About three hours’ journey from Besançon, the capital of the Sequani, between Ornans and Quingey, lies the castle commonly called Cleron, with the adjoining village of the same name, from which an ancient and very noble family took its name. Othenin, born there to Simon de Cleron and Joan de Domprey, took as his wife Mary de Saigny and de Saffres, great-granddaughter of Mary de Fontanis; by her he left descendants through whom Saint Bernard’s paternal lineage has been propagated down to our own age. [Col. 1532B]

Mary de Saigny’s marriage to Othenin fell in the year of Christ 1487. In 1494 he and his wife were named universal heirs of his father-in-law Peter de Saigny. Thereafter, in the secular year 1500, Louis XII, king of France, granted him the privilege of a native subject of the realm. By this grant, though a foreigner, he became the undisturbed possessor not only of Saffres but also, in part, of Fontanis and of the entire lordship of Saigny, near Grignon. He was still alive in December 1533, and he lives even now in his descendants, whose line the following table displays:

## CHAPTER XVIII. An opinion concerning Saint Bernard’s heraldic emblem

On a black shield, a diagonal band chequered in two rows of silver—or gold, as some prefer—and red, such as you see here roughly depicted, is considered by many to be Saint Bernard’s own hereditary armorial bearing.

[Col. 1533B]

[Col. 1533C] Hermann Schedel assigns this to him in the *Chronicle of Chronicles*. Very many painted and sculpted images of this saint, even ancient ones, bear it. Indeed, the same device may be seen in more than one place in the buildings of Clairvaux Abbey, both new and older; thus one may reasonably believe that it was carved upon the walls of his holy house while Bernard was still alive. Edmund de la Croix, made abbot of Cîteaux in 1584, wished that this chequered diagonal band should be placed in the central quarters of his own shield, divided into four parts by the arms of his family and of Cîteaux—evidently in regard to Saint Bernard, at whose sacred remains in Clairvaux he had both taken the religious habit and made his profession. [Col. 1533D]

Even today the custom has prevailed that abbots of the same order who are monks of Clairvaux, or who govern the daughters of Clairvaux—as they say, that is, monasteries propagated from Clairvaux—interweave this same band into their symbolic coats of arms as a token of their veneration for Saint Bernard.

This devotion of the Clairvaux monks toward their most holy patriarch cannot but meet with my approval. A pious opinion—and certainly one by no means imprudent—is enough to sustain it: namely, that these arms in some way at least belong to Bernard and to the house of Clairvaux uniquely beloved by him. But I find it hard to agree with Peter Frizon, author of *Gallia Purpurata*, who assigns the same arms to Peter de Fontanis, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus under Pope Callixtus II, as though he were Saint Bernard’s kinsman. Frizon should first have proved both that this was Saint Bernard’s hereditary armorial bearing and that the cardinal Peter was born at Fontanis in the environs of Dijon, rather than in another family of the same name—of which we know with certainty that there were very many in France. [Col. 1534A]

I would more readily indulge Frizon for assigning the same arms to Martin of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, Stephen of Palestrina, Bernard of Saints Cosmas and Damian, Henry of Albano, and Peter de Bar of Saint Marcellus—cardinals drawn from Clairvaux—although Ciaconius, Cabrera, and Victorello more prudently omitted them in their *Lives of the Popes and Cardinals*.

[Col. 1534B] Yet three considerations prevent me from judging that chequered band to be Saint Bernard’s hereditary emblem. First, in his age I think there were scarcely any arms of that kind, except perhaps those of princes or knights while in arms; and these were not common to an entire family, but personal and individual signs by which men might be distinguished from one another in campaigns. No such arms can plausibly be supposed in Bernard, devoted from childhood to literary studies and intended by parental care for ecclesiastical dignities. Learned persons know, moreover, that the rules now governing hereditary armorial emblems emerged later.

Second, no sensible person can persuade himself that Bernard—a man so conspicuous for contempt of the world, who, trampling underfoot all worldly vanity, had hidden himself in the remote recesses of forests—could have endured having the splendor of his lineage proclaimed by the walls of his wilderness. “But,” you will say, “his descendants arranged it after he had passed to heaven.” Really? Do you not know that Bernard presided over the building not only of the old monastery but also of the new one? In the latter the bones of the deceased earlier ascetics were transferred five years before his death, in 1148, when Saint Malachy, primate of Ireland, was breathing his last at Clairvaux itself? [Col. 1534C]

But let it be granted that his successors did what Bernard had neglected. How then did those successors, Bernard’s equals or near equals, become so mistaken as to attribute to him something which in no way concerned him? He scarcely had, as I have said, either personal or family arms; and if he had any, how were they not transmitted to the succeeding line of the lords of Fontanis? Behold Kalo, lord of Fontanis, who died in 1270: on his stone tomb he bears a shield with a band across the middle and three little birds at the top. John de Fontanis and his son Gilet add two birds at the bottom of the shield, making five in all. Kalo rests at Bonvaux below Talant; John and Gilet in the church of the Franciscans at Dijon, having died one after the other not long after 1300. Here are their surviving arms. [Col. 1534D]

[Col. 1535A] Our opinion, therefore, is that the band chequered in two rows was the armorial bearing of Hugh, count of Troyes, first founder of Clairvaux Abbey. Bernard, as abbot, had it impressed upon the walls of that holy house in perpetual remembrance of benefits received; and pious posterity assigned it to the most holy abbot himself. Since the matter is not of slight importance, let us examine it more closely.

## 671 CHAPTER XIX. Hugh, count of Troyes, first founder of Clairvaux monastery. The place itself was commonly called Clairvaux long before the arrival of the Cistercian colony

It was an exceedingly widespread custom not only among Romans and Greeks, but also among almost all other peoples, to mark the founders of noble buildings for perpetual remembrance by some inscription, or by images portraying them, or at least by symbols and armorial bearings. The same conclusion readily applies to Clairvaux, the most celebrated—one might almost say—of all monasteries in the world. Therefore the chequered band which appears from ancient times impressed upon several parts of its fabric can refer only to its founder. Who this founder was, hitherto unknown to all writers on Cistercian affairs, you shall now learn from us.

Claudius Robert appears in the *Gallia Christiana* to assign Clairvaux’s foundation to Theobald, count of Champagne, confusing its transfer with its foundation, as Angelus Manrique rightly observes in the *Cistercian Annals*, under 1115, chapter 1, no. 4. Yet Robert himself declares Clairvaux founded by an uncertain founder. But he is no longer uncertain to us: informed by the most reverend abbot, we have identified him as Hugh, count of Troyes. We have transcribed the founding charters on p. 513. In them he declares that he gives to God, to the Blessed Mary, and to the brothers of Clairvaux, the very place called Clairvaux, with its appurtenances, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, and lands, “retaining absolutely nothing for myself or my heirs.” [Col. 1536A]

For if, as jurists commonly teach, the founder is the person who provides the ground on which a church is to be built, then Hugh ought much more to be regarded as founder: he not only granted the site for building Clairvaux monastery, but also assigned several productive estates for the perpetual maintenance of the monks of that ascetic community. Thus Saint Bernard rightly says to him in Letter 31:

> “For how can we forget your former love and the benefits which you have so lavishly bestowed upon our house? May God, for whose love you did this, never forget you for ever! As for us, so far as lies in us, we are by no means ungrateful: we keep in mind the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, and, if it were permitted, we would show it in deed.”

There survive splendid memorials of this prince’s religious devotion and generosity toward churches—he who, as Bernard says in the same place, “became from a count a knight, and from rich a poor man”—especially toward the church of Troyes, in Nicolas Camuzat’s *Promptuary*, and toward Molesme and Arrémar, pp. 507, 514, 515, 516, 537 of the prefixed *Proofs*. [Col. 1536B]

Meanwhile, learn from Hugh’s documents for the men of Clairvaux that the name Clairvaux did not arise from their first arrival in that valley, as I see that some modern writers have thought. Rather, it was already commonly called Clairvaux when Hugh granted it to them. This is also made plain by Abbot William, Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 5. For when he says there that Clairvaux had anciently been called “Wormwood Valley,” he sufficiently indicates that, when Bernard led his colony there with his companions, the name Wormwood Valley had long since been abolished and it was commonly called Clairvaux. [Col. 1536C]

Since, then, it is established for us that Hugh, count of Troyes, was the founder of the house of Clairvaux, and no less certain that the façades of gateways, chimney mantels, and other conspicuous parts of buildings were customarily adorned with the arms of their founders, we may infer even from this that the chequered diagonal band affixed to the buildings at Clairvaux was the emblem of Count Hugh—the very device which not a few have considered Saint Bernard’s hereditary arms. Yet I would not therefore condemn the pious custom of those who regard that band as a kind of memorial of so holy a man. It truly did belong to Saint Bernard, because he wished it to be a testimony to his grateful heart toward Count Hugh, and impressed it upon his house of Clairvaux as a kind of token, to be revered by all its members, whether sons of Clairvaux itself or sons of its daughter houses. In that one sign they might recognize both Clairvaux as their common mother and Bernard as their common founder and father. [Col. 1537A]

[Col. 1537B] I see what may here be objected: namely, that the hereditary arms of the ancient counts of Champagne were different—a silver diagonal band on an azure shield, bordered on either side with paired golden strips cross-hatched thirteen times alternately. Further, this chequered band appears nowhere else as the arms of Count Hugh. Yet these objections do not move us, for from the annotations on p. 578 it is clear that Henry, called the Liberal, the first of the counts of Champagne, bore the cross-hatched arms described above with a plain silver band. It is also clear that before Henry the Liberal the counts of Troyes or Champagne had different arms, virtually individual to each one.

I acknowledge that neither this chequered band nor anything else may be seen in Count Hugh’s seals, of which very many survive both at Clairvaux and particularly in the archives of other churches of Troyes. For in them the count is depicted on horseback, holding his shield at such an angle that nothing upon it can be seen. It is enough for me to have identified this as Count Hugh’s personal emblem from the following evidence: he was with complete certainty the first founder of Clairvaux monastery; the chequered band did not belong to Saint Bernard’s family; and, finally, having from ancient times been impressed in so many conspicuous places on the buildings of Clairvaux, it could not—and ought not—to have referred to anyone other than the founder. [Col. 1537C]

## CHAPTER XX. The year and month in which Clairvaux was founded
I have no doubt that the Abbey of Clairvaux was entered upon in the year of Christ, according to the Dionysian reckoning, 1114, in the month of June [Col. 1537D]. For Morimond, the younger daughter, began in July of the same year, on the eleventh day of the month; it was fourth in number among the daughters of Cîteaux, whereas Clairvaux is reckoned third in order of birth. Add to this the author of the Chronicle of Saint Marianus of Auxerre, who writes under the year of Christ 1114:

> In the same year Clairvaux was founded, whose first abbot was Bernard, servant of God, a man distinguished by most renowned holiness; through him the Church of his time flourished anew in the ancient splendor of religion.

Nicholas Camuzat, a reverend man and one highly deserving of the republic of letters, published at Troyes in 1609 the Collections of this Chronicle. He published it from the Pontigny manuscript down through the year 1199 inclusive; the remainder [Col. 1538A], down to 1217, from the Petau manuscript. In his dedication he observes that the author of the work appears to him to have been Robert down to the end of 1210, at which point is written: “Thus far Brother Robert has carried his Chronicle.” From there to the end, and to the year of Christ 1217, he assigns it to Hugh, a Premonstratensian monk of the same abbey of Saint Marianus of Auxerre.

But I myself read with these eyes, at the head of the ancient manuscript itself preserved at Saint Marianus: “Here begins the Prologue of Master Hugh in his Chronicles.” This persuaded me that no author other than Hugh should be sought for this Chronicle: by command of his abbot Milo, he carried it down to the year 1203, where it ends; Robert subsequently added an appendix down to 1210; and thereafter an anonymous writer added what remains to the end, namely 1217 [Col. 1538B]. One might wish that this work, complete and perfected in all its parts, were published. Meanwhile, take in passing what it wrote of Saint Bernard under the year 1153:

> In the same year Bernard, beloved of the Lord, first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux and father also of more than one hundred and sixty other monasteries, having happily completed the days of his life and fulfilled about sixty-three years, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], fell asleep in Christ in the hands of his sons, and from his Clairvaux ascended to the mountain of eternal brightness. He was buried before the altar of the most blessed Virgin Mother; and in the tomb itself a casket containing the relics [Col. 1538C] of the blessed apostle Thaddaeus was placed upon his breast. These relics had been sent to him from Jerusalem that same year, and he had ordered them to be placed upon his body.

The following verses were written concerning him:

> There are bright valleys; but, brighter than these bright valleys, their abbot  
> gave his bright name renown throughout the world.  
> Bright in ancestry, bright in merits, and bright in honor;  
> he shone in eloquence, yet more in religious devotion.  
> Bright too his death, bright his ashes, and bright his tomb;  
> still brighter his spirit rejoices before God.

Yet certain monuments of Clairvaux stand against what we have stated concerning Clairvaux’s foundation in 1114. First, these ancient verses:

> The thousandth year, together with thrice five, is counted,  
> [Col. 1538D] and likewise the hundredth, when the holy man is made abbot.

Then there is the tablet suspended from Saint Bernard’s tomb, upon which one reads:

> In the year of the Lord 1115, in the month of June, [Saint Bernard] was sent with his flesh-brothers and his community to this place, now called Clairvaux; formerly, however, it was called Wormwood Valley.

But unless conjecture deceives me, those verses indicate Bernard’s consecration as abbot at the hands of William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons; this could scarcely have taken place before the year of Christ 1115, since dwellings had first to be established and built at Clairvaux for the new settlers. Therefore, from their first arrival at Clairvaux—which fell in June 1114—the chroniclers of Morimond and Auxerre dated the monastery’s foundation; the men of Clairvaux dated it from the abbot’s inauguration [Col. 1539A].

There remains a difficulty arising from the words of Abbot William, Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 7:

> “When Bernard, newly sent to Clairvaux, was to be ordained for the ministry to which he had been called, and the see of Langres, to which the ordination itself belonged, was vacant, the brethren asked to whom they should take him for ordination. At once the good reputation of the venerable bishop of Châlons, that most celebrated master William of Champeaux, presented itself; and it was decided that Bernard should be sent to him. Thus it was done.”

How, indeed, was the see of Langres vacant in 1115, when Joceran is known to have been bishop of Langres from 1112 [Col. 1539B] to 1125, as we reported from the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne? The answer is ready: at that time the see of Langres was “vacant” in an improper sense—not because there was then no bishop of Langres, but because in that year, 1115, he was absent from his bishopric; perhaps on a journey to the thresholds of the Apostles, or to certain synods, which were frequently convened in those very times by Guy of Vienne, apostolic legate throughout Gaul.

## CHAPTER XXI. At what time the charters of Hugh, Count of Troyes, concerning the foundation of Clairvaux were drawn up; his three journeys to the Lord’s Sepulchre; his titles at different times.

Once the foundation of Clairvaux has been placed in June [Col. 1539C] 1114, it does not immediately follow that the charters by which Count Hugh attested that the house of Clairvaux had been founded upon land granted by him and endowed were issued at that very time. Those charters—following what was most customary in that age—bear no date, although they are originals and sealed with the seals of Count Hugh and Joceran, bishop of Langres. Nor do they appear to have been issued at the very outset of the foundation, because they collect and confirm several donations made to Clairvaux by noblemen, donations which can scarcely be referred to its earliest beginnings.

Thus the foundation of Fontenay Abbey is contained in the charters of Stephen, bishop of Autun, issued in the year of Christ 1136; yet it is certain that it was founded much earlier—indeed, as they say, in 1118—and that a colony from it was sent to Sept-Fons four years before 1136 [Col. 1539D]. We have observed the same practice in the charters of the foundations of Morimond, La Bussière [Alba Ripa], and nearly all the other houses of the Cistercian Order: donations formerly made for their initial foundation are gathered many years afterward into one charter, concluded and confirmed by the privilege and seal of some bishop.

That this was done specifically at Clairvaux is suggested by Count Hugh’s first journey to Jerusalem in 1113. From this he could scarcely have returned to his county in 1114, in June of which year we have assigned the first foundation of Clairvaux [Col. 1540A]. For we know that Count Hugh undertook the journey to Jerusalem three times. The first was in 1113, when, as you may read on page 516, he granted a certain benefaction to the people of Arremar, as he was setting out in pious devotion for the Lord’s Sepulchre. The second was in 1121, or not long before; for in 1122, on the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October], having returned from Jerusalem for the second time—as pages 569, 570, and 571 will show—you will find that he confirmed many gifts to the people of Arremar and their abbot Walter, gifts which he had granted them at Autun shortly before his departure, on the feast of the Apostles Simon and Jude.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, had attempted to prevent the earlier of these two pilgrimages, writing Letter 247 to Count Hugh, in which he reminded him of the obligation of the marital debt; for Ivo did not survive the latter journey [Col. 1540B].

Finally, Hugh’s third and last journey to Jerusalem, during which he also devoted himself to the religious knighthood of the Templars, is inferred from Saint Bernard’s Letter 31; the year is uncertain. It is, however, certain that he was still in Gaul in 1124. For Suger, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, says that Count Palatine Theobald, together with his uncle, the noble Count Hugh of Troyes, took the side of Emperor Henry against Louis, king of the Franks, in the war fought between them before the death of Pope Calixtus; after it the emperor died within a year. Calixtus II died on 13 December 1124, and the emperor on 23 May 1125. That war therefore occupied nearly the summer and autumn of 1124, especially the month of August, according to the Appendix to Sigebert’s Chronicle [Col. 1540C].

After this war, which did not turn out favorably for Count Hugh, no action by him in Gaul is found; nor have I discovered any mention of him even at the council of Troyes, held in 1127 or 1128. Hence I suspect that not long after 1124 he set out for Jerusalem for the third time. When leaving for this final departure, if Peter Pithou is to be believed, he sold his county to Theobald, son of his brother Stephen; disinherited his son Odo; and left pregnant the second wife whom he had married after long before dismissing Constance on grounds of consanguinity. He died overseas on 14 June [Col. 1540D]. His anniversary is certainly entered under that date in the Church of Saint Lupus at Troyes. But in the necrology of Saint-Claude I read his death entered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June]. See page 539.

I now answer the question proposed in a few words: Count Hugh issued the charters concerning the foundation and endowment of Clairvaux after returning from his first pilgrimage to Jerusalem and before undertaking the second, and thus between 1114 and 1121; but the precise year is uncertain.

With respect to the varying titles which Count Hugh assumed at different times, it is noteworthy that he was first called Count of Champagne, even in the foundation of the cell of Sermizelles under the year 1093, though he was only Count of Bar-sur-Aube. Thus his uncle Saint Simon too is called Count of Champagne in the necrology of Saint-Claude, although he had been merely Count of Bar-sur-Aube [Col. 1541A]. Hugh was subsequently called Count of Troyes, when he succeeded his brother Odo to that dignity. Later he styled himself Count of Troyes and Bar together, so that he might be understood to hold a rank above his brother Odo. Finally, he resumed the title Count of Champagne, comprehending under that name both counties—Troyes and Bar—and it is under this title that Saint Bernard’s letter to him is addressed. He also furnished his successors with the precedent that, after the union of the counties of Troyes and Bar, the separate names were abolished and they should be called Counts of Champagne.

Thus, in a twofold sense and at different periods, the designation “Count of Champagne” was used: first for the Count of Bar-sur-Aube; afterward, once that county of Bar had been joined to Troyes, for the Count jointly of Troyes and Bar. Accordingly Hugh first, then Theobald surnamed the Great, and the Counts of Champagne who followed him bore that name [Col. 1541B].

## CHAPTER XXII. What became of Odo of Champagne, disinherited son of Hugh, Count of Troyes; and how he became related by blood to the family of the Counts of Burgundy.

The second wife of Hugh, illustrious Count of Troyes or Champagne and first founder of Clairvaux Abbey, and Odo the son born to him by her, concern him more closely than the chequered belt, which until now we have claimed as his emblem. We therefore append this corollary concerning Odo to our Appendix [Col. 1541C].

Hugh the father deprived Odo of his county, either because he judged him less fitted for so great an honor and office because of his tender age; or because perhaps he had not yet been born—for Hugh is said to have left his wife pregnant when he went overseas; or, finally, because he needed money for domestic matters, and especially for the expenses of his overseas journey, and received the price of his county from Theobald, son of his brother Stephen.

Nevertheless, Odo seems to have received from his father some usufructuary estate, as may be inferred from the cartulary of Clairvaux, where we read that Odo of Champagne and his wife Sibylla approved the entire alms which Josbert of La Ferté had given to the brethren of Clairvaux [Col. 1541D]. For this confirmation of Josbert’s gifts suggests a principal lordship, under whose fief the lord of La Ferté-sur-Aube was held. Royal youths customarily receive such estates carrying paramount lordship from the sovereign prince, so that, in keeping with the modesty of their status, they may at once have someone whom they obey and persons over whom, by prerogative of blood, they exercise authority.

Nor can Odo the elder, Hugh’s brother—and thus the paternal uncle of this younger Odo of whom we speak—be meant here. For from certain monuments we know that the former Odo predeceased his younger brother Hugh while the latter held the dignity of Count of Troyes, and that he had already ceased to live in the year of Christ 1097, long before the foundation of Clairvaux.

[Col. 1542A] The same wife of Odo of Champagne, Sibylla, is mentioned in charters of the Abbey of Accinte, or Acey, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Besançon, under the year 1137.

Nevertheless, Robert of Torigni, Sigebert’s continuator, asserts under the year of Christ 1143 that Odo aspired to his father’s county of Troyes. He writes:

> King Louis captured the castle of Vitry belonging to Count Theobald. When the church there had been set on fire, it was burned, and thirteen hundred souls of both sexes and every age were consumed in the flames. It is said that King Louis, moved by pity, wept over this; and some think that for this reason he undertook the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. He granted the castle to Odo of Champagne, nephew of Count Theobald, who wished on this occasion to recover through King Louis the patrimony which Theobald had taken from him.

Odo was Theobald’s first cousin: the former was the son of Hugh the younger, the latter of Stephen the elder. Thus this author called Odo Theobald’s *nepos* (“nephew”), according to the usage of many in that age, as Pithou observed. The author of the Chronicle of Saint Peter of Châlons, in volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, places the burning of Vitry in 1142 [Col. 1542B].

But Count Theobald’s discord with King Louis did not benefit Odo for long. Peace between them was restored in the following year through Saint Bernard’s mediation; Geoffrey relates in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 3, that Bernard had foretold this outcome five months earlier. Therefore Odo, having abandoned hope of recovering his inheritance and thinking it unsafe to remain longer in Champagne, fled to his maternal uncles, Rainald and William, Counts of Burgundy [Col. 1542C]. For he had been born to Hugh, Count of Troyes, by their sister. If she was called Lombarda or Longobarda, as Pithou notes from certain papers, this was either her personal name or surname, not an indication of her country.

Accordingly, in ancient charters you will read of Odo of Champagne as nephew of Count William, kinsman of Empress Beatrice; and of Count Rainald, Beatrice’s father, as Odo’s maternal uncle. William’s wife was Pontia of Treva, and Rainald’s Agatha of Lorraine; neither was related by blood to Odo of Champagne. Thus there remains no doubt that Odo was born of the mother who was Rainald’s and William’s sister [Col. 1542D].

From the same charters you will also learn that, in the County of Burgundy, Odo possessed as a benefice granted by the counts Camp Pagan near Dole, Quingey, L’Isle, Lobium Portum, and Scanlint or Chanlit, now called Champlitte. I think that the sons born to him by his wife Sibylla were Louis and another Odo, named after his father. In the year of the Lord 1202, when about to go to the Holy Land, this latter Odo gave to the Church of Saint Stephen of Besançon the holding of Aymon Grucel at Pagney. Whether certain noble Burgundian families, which some claim descend from the Counts of Champagne, sprang from these men, I leave for others to investigate.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Corollary concerning the expedition to the East against the Muslims of Andrew of Espisse, kinsman of Saint Bernard.

[Col. 1543A]

The harbor was already in sight; I had already taken in the sails, being on the point of landing, when behold, a letter was conveyed to me from my friend, the most courteous man and one of the few distinguished genealogists, Monsieur Du Bouchet. In it he sent me a notable passage from the Chronicle of Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, by which he thought Saint Bernard’s family might be illustrated. Nor without reason: Andrew of Espisse, mentioned there, was the great-great-grandson of Rainard, lord of Montbard, who was Saint Bernard’s maternal uncle, as you will understand from the table of Saint Bernard’s maternal line which we provided on pages 941 and 942 [Col. 1543B].

Alberic also mentions as Andrew’s father-in-law and companion on the journey John of Arceis. James of Vitry, bishop of Acre, calls him in Book III of the *Eastern History* and in his letter to the Lorrainers “a venerable and very valiant man,” and states that he was captured by barbarians together with his son-in-law Andrew. Yet we have shown from the charters of Fontenay, page 563, that he was still alive in 1232, having returned to his own people. Thus Alberic writes under the year of Christ 1219:

> In this year Henry, archbishop of Milan, and Walter, bishop of Autun, led the expedition of crusaders to the overseas regions; Peter, bishop of Paris, with his brother Walter, the royal chancellor; Milo, bishop-elect of Beauvais, with his brother Andrew; Hervé, Count of Nevers; Hugh the Brown, Count of La Marche in Poitou, with Hervé of Vierzon; Count Milo of Bar-sur-Seine with his son Walter; and with John of Arceis, together with his stepson Andrew of Espisse. On behalf of the deceased Duke of Burgundy came Guy of Thil and Pons of Grancey. Count Renaud of Châteauroux was in England with Savary of Mauléon. There were also many other good knights, all of whom came with many Romans before Damietta [Col. 1544A]. About ten thousand of them engaged the Saracens, suffered loss and endured affliction; many of them and their company being captured, killed, or dying of themselves. Among our men John of Arceis, Walter the chamberlain, and Milo, bishop-elect of Beauvais, were captured.

James of Vitry, who took part in this war, lists many more distinguished men captured or killed in that Book III of the *Eastern History*; and in his letter to the Lorrainers he includes Andrew of Espisse among the captives. Saint Francis, who was present there, had certainly—but in vain—discouraged an engagement with the Saracens at that time, by a divine oracle. Concerning his dealings with the sultan, James of Vitry says a little in that latter letter; Saint Bonaventure, in chapter 9 of his *Life*, says more; and Marino Sanudo in *The Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross*, Book III, part II, chapters 7 and 8 [Col. 1544B].

Saint Francis had gone there burning with desire for martyrdom; he did not obtain that palm, since God’s providence reserved him for other labors. Yet, had he been asked why God had denied him the crown of martyrdom, I think he would have declared himself unworthy of it, in the same spirit as another Francis, at the close of the fourth century thereafter: Francis Xavier, apostle of the Indies and Japan. Already received into heaven, Xavier wonderfully and suddenly restored Marcello Mastrillo from the last extremities of a most difficult illness to strength, and went before him with these words:

> Hail, wood of the Cross. Hail, most precious Cross. I dedicate myself wholly to you forever, and humbly pray that you grant me—though most unworthy—the grace of shedding my blood for you, which Francis Xavier, apostle of the Indies, did not deserve to obtain after enduring so many labors.

If anyone should perhaps reproach such holy men, longing for death and every extremity of suffering, and should instead sing many wishes for long life in the Greek manner—*πολυχρονίας*, “many years”—they would answer him without hesitation, with Ignatius of Antioch as he hastened to the beasts: “Forgive me. I know what is profitable for me” (*Letter to the Romans*) [Col. 1544C].

[Col. 1543]

## SAINT BERNARD’S POSTHUMOUS GLORY ENHANCED.

(Authentic decrees of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, vol. VIII, Rome, 1849, quarto, nos. 4510 and 4516.)

## SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, HONORED WITH THE TITLE OF DOCTOR. ROMAN, OR OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER.

[Col. 1543D] The Lord God filled Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, with the spirit of understanding, as an example and instruction for the faithful. Distinguished by keenness of intellect, gentleness of character, and knowledge of Holy Scripture, he poured forth the utterances [Col. 1544D] of his wisdom like rain. He published so many volumes; he aided the Apostolic See and the Supreme Pontiffs with the greatest zeal and ardor against schismatics; and he assailed and extinguished with voice and pen the errors of the Innovators raging in that age.

Although [Col. 1545A] many centuries had passed, and although only twenty years after his precious death Alexander III, recognizing the holiness of his life and his miracles, had enrolled him among the saints in heaven and his cult had been extended in the Church, the Cistercian Order still desired Saint Bernard to be counted among the Doctors of the Church and honored throughout the world. In that Order the holy Abbot shone as its propagator and outstanding glory.

Moreover, several Cardinal Fathers, recounting his merits toward the Church, together with the same Cistercians petitioned our Most Holy Lord Pope Pius VIII to decree that the feast of Saint Bernard the Abbot be celebrated with an Office and Mass from the Common of Doctors. These petitions were presented in the Ordinary Meeting of the Sacred Congregation of Rites held in the Quirinal Palace on 18 July 1829 by the Most Reverend Cardinal Giulio Maria della Somaglia, then Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Rites. All the other Cardinals appointed to preserve the Sacred Rites likewise showed themselves favorably disposed. Nevertheless, the Most Holy Lord judged that the customary procedure of the Sacred Congregation of Rites ought in every respect to be observed, and therefore wished that whatever objections might be raised should be put forward by the Promoter of the Holy Faith in objections submitted for the purpose.

After the petitioners had attached their responses, at the Ordinary Meeting of 17 July 1830 in the Quirinal Palace, with the Most Reverend Cardinal Don Placido Zurla, Vicar of the City, reporting, the matter was considered at greater length and every objection resolved. The unanimous opinion of the Most Reverend Cardinals was as follows:

> For the favor of confirmation of the title of Doctor, with an Office and Mass from the Common of Doctors and the Epistle in the second place, for the universal Church; to the Most Eminent reporting Cardinal together with the Promoter of the Faith, and to the Secretary with the Most Holy Father.  
> 17 July 1830.

A report of all and each of these matters having been made by me, the undersigned Secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, to our Most Holy Lord Pope Pius VIII, His Holiness approved and confirmed the rescript of the Sacred Congregation in all respects, and ordered Apostolic Letters in the form of a Brief to be issued thereupon. The twenty-third day of the aforesaid month and year.

## POPE PIUS VIII. FOR PERPETUAL REMEMBRANCE OF THE MATTER.

[Col. 1545D] What seemed supremely relevant to the full and abundant enhancement of the honor and praise of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux; what was desired by the illustrious Order of Cistercian monks, which has always deserved most well of this Holy See and in which the aforementioned holy Abbot shone as propagator and outstanding glory; what was to be desired by the whole Catholic Church, to which he gave the greatest assistance by his keenness of intellect, gentleness of character, and knowledge of Holy Scripture—for he published so many volumes, aided the Apostolic See and the Supreme Pontiffs with the greatest zeal and ardor against schismatics, assailed and extinguished with voice and pen the errors of Innovators raging in that age, and repelled by his teaching all haters of the Roman Church [Col. 1546A]—what the prayers of Our venerable brethren, the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, urged, has, by divine disposition, been granted to Our Humility to accomplish.

Although many centuries had indeed elapsed, and only twenty years after his precious death he had been enrolled among the company of Saints by Our predecessor Pope Alexander III of happy memory, who recognized the holiness of his life and his miracles, and his cult had been extended in the Church, still some splendor was to be added to the crown of his virtues and merits: namely, that the title of Doctor, by which Saint Bernard was already called, should be confirmed throughout the universal Church by the supreme decree of this Holy See.

Although Our venerable brethren, the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church charged with preserving the Sacred Rites, had all shown themselves favorably disposed to the requested confirmation of the title of Doctor in the Ordinary Meeting held in the Quirinal Palace on 18 July 1829, Cardinal Giulio Maria della Somaglia of renowned memory, then Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, reporting, We nevertheless suspended such judgment. Observing the practice of this Holy See, We ordered that any objections which might be raised be submitted through the Promoter of the Holy Faith in appended observations.

Once the petitioners had submitted their responses, in the Ordinary Meeting of 17 July of the present year in the Quirinal Palace, with Our beloved son Placido Zurla, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, our Vicar General in spiritual matters in this noble City, reporting, the matter was carefully considered, all objections resolved, and the judgments of the Cardinals of the same Sacred Congregation of Rites found to agree [Col. 1546C]. We judged that the rescript issued on the said day in favor of confirming the title of Doctor, with an Office and Mass from the Common of Doctors and the Epistle in the second place for the universal Church, ought to be confirmed; and We ordered Apostolic Letters on this matter to be issued.

Accordingly, graciously granting the earnest petitions of the entire Order of Cistercian Monks, to which many men eminent in rank and piety had joined their support and requests, by the counsel of that Congregation of Cardinals and by Our Apostolic Authority, by the tenor of these presents, We confirm—and, insofar as necessary, again confer [Col. 1546D]—the title of Doctor by which Saint Bernard the Abbot has hitherto been styled in the said Order and in certain churches. Thus throughout the universal Catholic Church he shall always be held a Doctor; and on his annual feast day, to be celebrated by both regular and secular clergy, the Office and Mass shall be from the Common of Doctors, with the Epistle in the second place, beginning, “The just man,” etc., with an addition to the sixth Lesson and to the Martyrology according to the decree of the same Sacred Congregation of Rites.

Furthermore, We will and decree that this Doctor’s books, commentaries, little works—in short, all his works—shall be cited, put forward, and, whenever circumstances require, employed as are those of other Doctors of the Church, not only privately but publicly in gymnasia, academies, schools, colleges, lectures, disputations, interpretations, preaching, sermons, and every other ecclesiastical study and Christian exercise [Col. 1547A].

Finally, in order that the devotion of Christ’s faithful toward observing this Doctor’s feast day and devoutly imploring his help may be more ardently kindled, in proportion as they find themselves more abundantly refreshed by the gift of heavenly grace, trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and in the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, We mercifully grant and bestow in the Lord a plenary indulgence and remission of all sins upon all Christ’s faithful of either sex who, on the feast day of the same Doctor, being truly penitent and having first made sacramental confession, receive the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist and devoutly visit one of the churches of the Cistercian Order from First Vespers until sunset of that same day; and who there pour out devout prayers to God, as each one’s devotion may suggest, for concord among Christian princes, the extirpation of heresies, and the exaltation of Holy Mother Church [Col. 1547B]. We declare that this Our present concession is to endure perpetually and is in no way included under any revocations or limitations whatsoever of indulgences.

Wherefore, by these presents, We command all Our venerable brethren, Patriarchs [Col. 1548A], Primates, Archbishops, Bishops, and the beloved sons who are prelates of other churches throughout the world, to ensure that what has been decreed above is solemnly published in their provinces, cities, churches, and dioceses, and everywhere and perpetually observed inviolate by all ecclesiastical persons, secular and regular, of whatever Orders, in every place and nation. These things We order and command, notwithstanding Apostolic Constitutions and Ordinances and anything else whatsoever to the contrary.

We further will that the same full credence be given to transcripts or even printed copies of these presents, signed by the hand of a public notary and sealed by a person established in ecclesiastical dignity or by the Procurator General of the said Order, as would be given to these presents themselves if they were exhibited or shown. Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Ring of the Fisherman, 20 August 1830, in the second year of Our Pontificate.

J. Cardinal Albani.

[Col. 1547]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT AND DOCTOR.

[Col. 1547B] Mass from the Common of Doctors, with the Epistle in the second place, beginning: “Justus cor suum” (“The just man [his] heart …”).

The Office likewise from the Common of Doctors, with the antiphon [Col. 1547C] “O Doctor” at both Vespers. The lessons of the First Nocturn are from the occurring Scripture. The lessons of the Second Nocturn are proper, as in the breviaries; and at the end of the sixth Lesson the following is to be added:

> Pope Pius VIII, by counsel of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, declared and confirmed Saint Bernard to be a Doctor of the universal Church; he also ordered that the Mass and Office of Doctors be recited by all, and granted plenary indulgences annually and in perpetuity to those visiting churches of the Cistercian Order on the day of this Saint’s feast.

The lessons of the Third Nocturn: “You are the salt of the earth.” In [Col. 1548B] the Martyrology add: “Whom Pope Pius VIII declared and confirmed Doctor of the universal Church.”

## DECREE.

[Col. 1548C]

The above-written addition to be made to the sixth Lesson in the Office of Saint Bernard, Abbot and Doctor, and to the Roman Martyrology, having been examined by the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Placido Zurla, reporter of the cause, and the Reverend Father Don Virgilio Pescetelli, Promoter of the Holy Faith, our Most Holy Lord Pope Pius VIII approved it and granted that it might be read in the aforesaid Office and Martyrology throughout the universal Church. 23 July 1830.

C. M., Bishop of Palestrina, Cardinal Pedicini, Prefect.

In place of the seal.

J. G. Fatati, Secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Rites.

[Col. 1547]

## BOLOGNA.

*(Saint Bernard is not to be counted among the Doctors in the litanies.)*

[Col. 1547D] The Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Opizzoni, Archbishop of Bologna, requested the Sacred Congregation of Rites to make the following declaration: since, by the Brief of Pope Pius VIII of holy memory, Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, is counted among the holy Doctors, should he be mentioned in the Litany of the Saints among the holy Doctors, or should he be retained among the Priests and Levites [Col. 1548D]?

The Most Eminent and Most Reverend Fathers appointed to preserve the Rites, in the Ordinary Meeting held at the Quirinal on the date below written, judged that the answer should be: “Nothing is to be changed.” 16 April 1831.

[Col. 1549]

# MONUMENTS OF THE SACRED ABBEY OF CLAIRVAUX AND EPITAPHS OF THE SAINTS AND ILLUSTRIOUS MEN BURIED THERE.

*(From the* Fasciculus Sanctorum *of the Cistercian Order, by the Reverend Father Brother Chrysostom Henriquez, Book II, Distinction XLI, p. 407.—Brussels, 1623, folio.)*

## CHAPTER ONE. On the admirable perfection of the Abbey of Clairvaux, which endures there even to the present day.

[Col. 1549A] Before I set down the catalogue of monasteries which our sacred Cistercian Order possesses in the various provinces of the world, it seemed fitting to mention here also the holy relics which the most devout Abbey of Clairvaux cherishes in its bosom. For its blessed soil abounds with holy bodies whose souls already enjoy eternal glory. From its very beginning, when our holy father Bernard laid the first stone there, this happy house has produced, and still produces, immeasurable treasures of holiness and virtue.

From it came forth most holy men who, traversing obscure and deep wildernesses amid forests and mountains, led out innumerable colonies and established monastic discipline in them. In its needs the Church has drawn upon this house, drawing from it the strongest columns for its support, as may be seen in the very many cardinals and bishops raised from it [Col. 1549B]. Many of these resolutely opposed heretics and, by their example and virtue, strengthened Catholics in the faith.

Who could suffice to enumerate the saints whom heaven possesses from this place? Who could tell the wonderful manner and gifts by which the most pure Virgin, Mother of God, has favored this holy congregation? How often, while these holy monks were reaping in the fields, did she wipe the sweat from their faces? How often did she visit and embrace them? How often did she visibly console them in chapter and admit them to her embrace? How often did she nourish with her own hand, with most delightful food, those weakened by abstinence? How often did she enter the dormitory while they slept and impart her blessing [Col. 1549C], that she might defend them against the common enemy of humankind?

I would relate such favors here, were they not more properly reserved for the books that follow. O happy house in which such marvelous things occurred, to which Christ and his most holy Mother so familiarly resorted; in which [Col. 1550A] evangelical poverty, monastic perfection, and apostolic life so flourished!

What fills me with the greatest admiration is that, after so many centuries, religious discipline endures in this holy valley in its original rigor, and that the lustre of the virtues planted here by its first founders has not changed. This must undoubtedly be attributed above all to the Governor of this whole community, who with singular providence watches over this holy congregation; to Mary, His glorious Mother and special protectress of the Cistercians; to its founder, St Bernard; and finally to the prelates who ruled it, whose holiness and foresight the universal Church embraces and venerates. And so that it may more clearly appear that God preserves this holy monastery with singular [Col. 1550B] providence, in this pitiable age, in which charity seems altogether to have grown cold, He chose as its prelate the Very Reverend Father Denis Largentier, a man of outstanding prudence, rare virtue, and great learning. By his zeal and religious devotion rigor is preserved not only in his own monastery, but also in very many other houses of our sacred Order. It cannot be expressed with what solicitude he applies himself to the reformation of the Order, with what zeal he ensures that the statutes of the ancient Fathers are observed and that new laws are in turn enacted for the preservation of our Order. I do not report uncertain matters: although I do not know this Reverend Father in person, I have heard these things, and greater things still, related by the reverend Fathers Bernard Montgaillard, Abbot of Val d’Or; William del Castello, of the monastery of [Col. 1550C] Baudeloo; and Henry vander Heyden, Abbots of Villers. With one voice they all extol the piety, virtue, and zeal of this reverend prelate. To him, therefore, is deservedly due the great religious observance by which this monastery is distinguished. We congratulate him on the diligence with which, by his own example and virtue and those of his subjects, he seeks to extend the name and renown of our [Col. 1551A] Order. We shall speak of the holy and illustrious men who formerly adorned this house by their virtues and now honor it by their bodies; and I shall set down the epitaphs which I found in a manuscript codex of the library of the Dunes.

## CHAPTER II. The epitaphs of the three tombs of saints at Clairvaux follow.

[Col. 1551]

### Epitaph of the most blessed Father Bernard

[Col. 1551A]

Here rests the body of our most blessed Father Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux. He was, in his own day, a man most holy in life and conduct; most illustrious after the Apostles in working miracles; and an outstanding Doctor in understanding and expounding Holy Scripture. Among those at discord, he was a foremost restorer of peace. [Col. 1551B] He was an industrious reprover and corrector of the heresies and errors then springing up in the Church. In many things which he foretold, he was a true prophet. A most devout promoter of monasteries and of the religious life, he was a singular lamp not only of the Gallican Church but also of all Christendom.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, the fifteenth from the establishment of the house of Cîteaux, being about twenty-two years old, he entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions under Abbot Stephen and submitted his neck to Christ’s sweet yoke.
