In the year of the Lord 1105, in the month of June, he was sent with his blood-brothers and his community to this place, now called Clairvaux, but formerly the Valley of Wormwood, where for thirty-eight years he fulfilled the office of Abbot, or good Shepherd. In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1153, after the Order had been extended everywhere, [Col. 1551C] and being father of more than one hundred and sixty monasteries of our Order, when he had happily completed the days of his life and had fulfilled about sixty-three years, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, at almost the third hour of the day, amid the heavy sobs and abundant tears of his sons standing around, he passed to the Lord: to the rejoicing companies of monks whom he himself had sent before him, and to the welcoming ranks of angels whose life on earth he had led. May He who lives and reigns without end make us imitators of his life and sharers in his glory.

### Epitaph of St Malachy, Bishop and Primate of all Ireland

Here rests the body of Blessed Malachy, formerly Archbishop and Primate of all Ireland and Legate of the Apostolic See, a man of apostolic life and glorious in miracles. This is he who instructed in the Catholic faith the peoples of Scotland and Ireland—men, indeed, then barbarous, entering into no marriages, [Col. 1551D] making no confessions or penances, attending no churches, receiving no ecclesiastical sacraments; pagans in fact, Christians in name alone—although they had formerly been converted to the faith through Blessed Patrick. Having driven out barbarism and pagan custom amid the greatest dangers and difficulties, he [Col. 1552A] strengthened them, insofar as he could, in the institutions of the holy Roman Church. Moreover, he spread more widely throughout those lands communities of monks of the Cistercian Order, regular canons, and other religious.

When these things had, with God’s help, been accomplished, he came from farther Scotland to Clairvaux, which he had always desired as the place of his death, the Lord [Col. 1552B] gratifying his pious desire. There, after about three weeks had elapsed, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1148, in the fifty-fourth year of his age, on the night when the anniversary of all the faithful departed is observed, just as he had always desired and foretold—having blessed each person and laid hands upon each one—he bade farewell to the world, was joyfully received by angels, and joined to the most blessed fellowship of the citizens above. This, as the heavenly revelation disclosed, occurred to our most blessed Father Bernard while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass on the following day, during the very Canon of the Mass. May his glorious prayers and merits obtain for us grace before God in the present life and glory in that to come. Amen.

### Epitaph of the most holy Martyrs Eutropius, Zosina, and Bonosa, likewise at the aforesaid Clairvaux

Here are contained the bodies of the most holy martyrs, the sisters Eutropius, Zosina, and Bonosa, which in the time [Col. 1552C] of the happy memory of Pope Honorius III were taken from the altar of the church of St Lawrence in the same city by the venerable Father and Cardinal Conrad, formerly Bishop of Porto, of pious memory. There they had once been honorably and fittingly laid to rest, before that city was reduced to the utter ruin of desolation. Therefore, by God’s gracious providence, they were transferred from that place through the said Reverend Cardinal and sent to Blessed Bernard and the Church of Clairvaux, that they might there be placed more gloriously and venerated with due reverence; and that, by the sacred contemplation of so great a presence, the hearts of the faithful might be stirred to love God more devoutly and serve Him more fervently, through the precious merits and pious intercession of those saints.

To these three holy martyrs a fourth martyr was joined and placed with them, whose name we still do not know. The said Lord Cardinal, Bishop of Porto, sent his sacred body to Clairvaux together with the three named above. [Col. 1552D]

Likewise, Blessed Walta, Cristantia, Petronella, and Domicella, who are among the eleven thousand virgins, were laid with them, together with two heads of certain saints and other relics of very many saints.

## CHAPTER III. On the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church who rest there

[Col. 1551]

[Col. 1551D] After the description of the epitaphs of the saints honorably buried in the church of Clairvaux, we must consider the burial-place of the illustrious men resting there. It should be known that in the same church, as appears from the inscriptions on the tombs, [Col. 1552D] there rest and lie four Cardinals and sixteen Archbishops and Bishops, as well as many other notable men and persons. The inscriptions of them all are noted below.

First, concerning the aforementioned Cardinals.

### Blessed Henry, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

[Col. 1553A]

First, between the tombs of Christ’s most holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, lies Lord Henry, Abbot Henry VII of Clairvaux, of happy memory; afterwards Bishop of Albano, Cardinal, and Legate of the Apostolic See. This Cardinal Henry, Bishop of Albano, a noble and distinguished man, was born at the castle of Marciac near Cluny. Under Lord Robert of Bruges, second Abbot of Clairvaux, he assumed the habit of sacred religion in this house of Clairvaux. Before his fourth year [in religion], while still a beardless boy and yet taking mixed drink, to the astonishment of all he was made Abbot of Hautecombe.

How greatly that monastery prospered under him, spiritually and temporally, with God’s help, is attested even today by the facts themselves and by those who possess its properties. When Lord Gerard VI, Abbot of Clairvaux, had been completed by martyrdom at Igny, Henry was chosen, by the vote of all the Clairvaux community, as Abbot of Clairvaux itself. There he acquired such favor, not only in the Order [Col. 1553B] but also with the Kings of France and England, and with princes and barons, as no man of Clairvaux had possessed before him since Blessed Bernard.

For he gloriously completed two good and magnificent works at Clairvaux, apart from innumerable other benefits. Blessed Bernard, already canonized by Pope Alexander III, who had commanded that the day of his death be celebrated with joy by the universal Church, Henry caused to be raised and re-raised, with venerable bishops and other reverend persons gathered from every side through the venerable Father Lord Nicard, Archbishop of Lyons and formerly Abbot of Pontigny. With the greatest joy and exultation of the whole Gallican Church, he had Bernard religiously and honorably placed in a marble shrine behind the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, as may still be seen today. The illustrious and renowned King Henry of England also caused this church to be most beautifully [Col. 1553C] roofed with lead, out of love and honor for God and for Henry, Abbot of Clairvaux.

While Clairvaux was being increasingly glorified under his hand, he was solemnly elected Bishop of Toulouse by the votes and desire of all. He resisted with all his strength and in no way would accept it. At Cîteaux, at an equal council of abbots and brethren, he was elected Abbot of Cîteaux; this too he refused with all his strength. Pope Alexander III summoned him by name by letter to the Lateran Council, retained him, made him Cardinal, and consecrated him, though unwilling, Bishop of Albano. He sent him as legate to the provinces beyond the mountains and to drive out heretics, giving him authority from the Apostolic See to uproot and tear down, and to build and plant. In vehement spirit he swiftly deposed two archbishops, namely those of Lyons and Narbonne, because they seemed useless and blameworthy. He corrected, insofar as he could, black monks and prelates of many churches. By a miracle he captured a most strongly fortified castle of heretics, [Col. 1553D] defended by a valley; he seized, convicted, converted, and made the chieftains of the heretics acknowledge their error before all.

Afterwards, having visited his Clairvaux and honored it with gifts, he returned to the Roman Curia and was honorably received by Pope Lucius—Alexander having now died—and by the other Cardinals. At length, when Pope Lucius died after four years and Urban succeeded him in the papacy, but himself quickly died within two years, the sounder party of the Cardinals wished to elect Henry Pope. Resisting with all his strength and fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he declared that he would assume no other office than to aid the land of Jerusalem and preach the cross everywhere. Therefore, when Lord Gregory VIII had been consecrated Pope, Henry received from him the fullest legation [Col. 1554A] to the Emperor, kings, princes, and all Christians, for the taking of the cross and for all other ecclesiastical affairs.

Through God’s mercy and the preaching and labor of this holy man, the Emperor at Mainz, with sixty-eight great princes besides others beyond number, was marked with the sign of the cross; and the Kings of France and England alike were signed with the mark of the cross. On coming to Liège, more than sixty-six clerics, out of fear of simony, resigned their benefices into his hand at his preaching; he restored them to them, without simony, in other ways and elsewhere. When, though gravely ill, he hastened into Flanders to restore peace between the Count of Flanders and the Church of Arras, he restored peace between them, not without the astonishment of many.

As his illness grew worse, it would take long to recount how simply he confessed even the smallest sins, and how devoutly he received the Viaticum and the sacrament of extreme unction. Finally, when the hour was at hand [Col. 1554B] for him to pass from this world to God, he was carried before the altar of Blessed Andrew at Arras, as he himself had commanded; and there, amid the words of devout prayer, he happily fell asleep in the Lord, as is piously believed. At last, as he had commanded, his body was brought from Arras to Clairvaux; and here, between Blessed Bernard and Blessed Malachy, on the third day before the Ides of January, after all rites had been performed, he was honorably buried by the Bishop of Langres, about the year of the Lord 1186.

### Epitaph of the same Henry

Beneath this stone lies Henry, once well known to the world,  
An abbot worthy of the Roman cardinalate.  
Despising the fleeting pleasures of the empty world,  
He gave his bodily members to earth and sent back his soul to heaven.

### James, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Bishop of Palestrina

Beside Blessed Malachy, namely in the presbytery [Col. 1554C] on his left, lies Lord James of Piacenza, of happy memory: Archdeacon of Ravenna; afterward monk of Clairvaux; then Abbot of Three Fountains; and finally Cardinal Bishop of Palestrina.

### Blessed Conrad, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Bishop of Porto

In the same presbytery, beside the aforesaid Lord Cardinal James, to the left of the lesser altar, lies Lord Conrad, of happy memory, brother of the former Count Egmi of Freiburg. He was first Abbot of Villers, then of Clairvaux, afterward of Cîteaux, and finally Cardinal Bishop of the Holy Roman Church. The following memorable fact is read concerning him: the sacred fingers with which he was accustomed to offer the host of the Lord’s Body and Blood were often seen to shine with such brilliance that they made the darkness of night as bright for him as noon. He enriched Clairvaux with very many relics, among them the head of St Vincent and relics of Christ’s martyrs [Col. 1554D] Eutropius, Zosina, and Bonosa. He frequently served as legate *a latere*, in which office he magnificently restrained and repressed various heretical perfidies. Finally, when in overseas regions he perceived that the day of his passing from this world was near, he gave the most urgent command that his bones be brought there [to Clairvaux]. His final wish was faithfully fulfilled by the monks of Clairvaux. He died in the year of grace 1227, on the day before the Kalends of October.

### John, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

Between Blessed Bernard and the blessed martyrs lies Lord John de Buxeriis, the thirty-second Abbot of Clairvaux. He afterwards became Abbot of Cîteaux, and finally was made Cardinal Priest of the Holy Roman Church.

## CHAPTER IV. On the bishops buried at Clairvaux

[Col. 1555]

### John, Archbishop of Lyons

[Col. 1555A]

Beneath the step of the high altar, on the left side, directly opposite the Gospel lectern, lies Lord John, Archbishop of Lyons, of happy memory.

### Hugh, Bishop of Langres

Before the altar of Blessed Benedict the Abbot lies the Reverend Father Lord Hugh, Bishop of Langres.

### Manasses, Bishop of Langres

Before the middle of the altar of St Michael the Archangel lies Lord Manasses, venerable Bishop of Langres.

### John, Archbishop of Mechelen

Likewise there, namely on the left side of the same altar, lies Lord John, Archbishop of Mechelen, of happy memory, a humble Abbot of Clairvaux, who for a long time lived in this Clairvaux and conducted himself humbly. [Col. 1555B] Freed happily from the bonds of the flesh, he died in the year of the Lord 1240, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

### Robert, Bishop of Liège

Before the altar of Blessed Andrew the Apostle, on its left side, in an arch, lies Lord Robert, Bishop of Langres and later Bishop of Liège, of happy memory.

### Garnerius, Bishop of Langres

Likewise, before the middle of the altar of the Savior, our Lord and God, lies the Reverend Father Lord Garnerius, ninth Abbot of Clairvaux and later Bishop of Langres.

### Blessed Eskil, Archbishop of Lund

Likewise, there in the arch to the left of that altar lie: first, in the first part of that burial-place, rests a magnificent and eminent man of royal [Col. 1555C] stock, Lord Eskil, of happy memory, formerly Archbishop of Lund and Primate of all Denmark and Sweden. In the time of Blessed Bernard he came to Clairvaux and became a monk there; he showed himself a mirror of the deepest humility and of all uprightness and religious observance, and left his successors an example of monastic perfection. He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1181.

### Radulf, Archbishop of Lyons

Also buried there with him is Lord Radulf, of holy and sweet memory, formerly Abbot of Clairvaux, then Bishop of Agen, and finally Archbishop of Lyons.

### Aleydis, Mother of St Bernard

Likewise there lies the noble lady Aleydis, of pious memory and most devoted to God, mother of the [Col. 1555D] outstanding Doctor and our Father Blessed Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux. She was first buried at Dijon in the monastery of St Benignus. Later, however, the Lord so willing and dealing graciously with us, she was translated to Clairvaux to kindle and enlarge our devotion to humility, and was placed before the altar of the Holy Savior in the year of the Lord 1250, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### Adam, Bishop of Thérouanne

[Note: [Col. 1555D] Bzovius says the following of him: “In this year (namely, 1229), Adam, Bishop of the people of Thérouanne, a man praiseworthy in every part of his life, now worn out by age, resigned his bishopric and [Col. 1556D] professed the monastic life at Clairvaux.”]

[Col. 1556A]

Before the middle of the altar of St Mammes lies our Lord Adam, of happy memory, formerly Bishop of Thérouanne and a monk of Clairvaux.

### Blessed Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres

Before the altar of All Saints lie five venerable bishops. First, buried directly opposite the middle of that altar, is Lord Geoffrey, formerly Bishop of Langres, a man of praiseworthy life and kinsman of Blessed Bernard. He was among Bernard’s first sons, who founded the present monastery with their own blood. He was third Prior of Clairvaux, afterwards first Abbot of Fontenay; having founded and regularly organized that house, he returned to his Clairvaux. There, for many years, especially during the schism that then raged violently in the Roman Church, while Blessed Bernard exposed himself to the dangers of the holy Church in different provinces, [Col. 1556B] Geoffrey performed Bernard’s duties as energetically as he did faithfully. He not only attended to the business and interests of the monastery, but, what is more, whenever need arose he provided vacant monasteries with abbots; and, like another Abbot Bernard, he was regarded as such not only at Clairvaux but throughout the Order.

After the aforesaid disturbances had been quieted, while he held the office of Prior at Clairvaux, he was raised to the see of Langres. Afterwards he went to Jerusalem with King Louis, of pious memory, serving as legate of the Apostolic See. Returning with that King from the said journey, he remained in his bishopric until the death of Blessed Bernard, and for about eight years afterward. He then approached Pope Alexander, of blessed memory, and requested leave to resign; this he obtained, though only with difficulty, by most urgent prayers. Returning with apostolic letters, he bade farewell to the see and again withdrew to Clairvaux. He caused to be built [Col. 1556C] for his own use, on the site from which St Bernard had departed, a chapel, quite humble as may be seen; and, living for about three years and nine months in the house of St Bernard adjoining that chapel, and persevering in holy religious life, he rested happily in the Lord, as is piously believed, about the year of the Lord 1165, on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

### On the Bishop of Sorita, infirmarian of Clairvaux

To the left of the said Lord Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres, toward the cemetery, is buried the venerable Lord Geoffrey of Melun, a Bishop of Sorita, born of the illustrious stock of the French at Sens. Under Lord Robert, second Abbot of Clairvaux, of happy memory, he assumed the habit of sacred religion in this Clairvaux; and, holding various offices under him and several of his successors, he lived praiseworthily among his brethren, with their affection and favor. At last, when the care of the sick [Col. 1556D] brethren had been entrusted to him under Lord Gerard, sixth Abbot of Clairvaux, he was made Bishop of Sorita in Sardinia, in the province of Torres. Ambition did not draw him there, but his profession compelled him, a foster-child of Gaul, to cross over to barbarian customs and a language he did not know. There he lived for seven years; and, bestowing very much upon the monastery of Clairvaux, he scattered [Col. 1557A] the rest among the poor and other places.

Hearing that Blessed Bernard had been canonized by Pope Alexander III, of happy memory, and that the body of the same Blessed Bernard was to be translated under Lord Henry, seventh Abbot of Clairvaux, he came to the General Chapter and hastened thence to Clairvaux. There he devoted himself most diligently to taking part with the Archbishop of Lyons and the fellow bishops. Thereafter, as a fever grew stronger day by day, at the Lord’s summons he passed away—as it is pious to suppose—having devoutly attended him with due honor as far as the celebrated burial, which is visible to this day. He died on the day before the Ides of October, about the year of the Lord 1179.

### On the Bishop of Humanata

After him, toward the cemetery on the northern side, was buried Lord James, Bishop of Humanata, of pious memory.

### Alan, Bishop of Auxerre

[Col. 1557B]

To the right of the said Lord Geoffrey, formerly Bishop of Langres, toward the choir, lies Lord Alan, Bishop of Auxerre. He was raised from boyhood in a certain church of the famous Flemish town called Lille, and under Blessed Bernard assumed the religious habit in this Clairvaux. Afterwards he became first Abbot of the monastery called La Rivour. Presiding over it for twelve years, he labored, with the Lord’s assistance, to enrich that monastery with useful persons and necessary possessions—namely granges, woods, fields, meadows, and pastures. In the final year of Blessed Bernard’s life, he was unanimously elected Bishop by the Church of Auxerre.

He showed great hospitality to all religious persons who frequented his houses. He is known to have bestowed many gifts on his monastery of La Rivour, of which he had been abbot; and upon the abbey of Clairvaux [Col. 1558A] he bestowed all the care he could, often visiting it and contributing such necessary assistance as he was able. At last, after completing thirteen years in the episcopate, he resigned his bishopric with permission of the Apostolic See and returned to his Clairvaux. He stayed at Clairvaux in the house of St Bernard; after the departure of Lord Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres, he resigned his bishopric. Rendering many services to the brethren, and being highly experienced in both the business of the Order and ecclesiastical affairs, he was by no means of little use to Lord Abbot Pontius and his successors down to Lord Peter the Venerable, eighth Abbot of Clairvaux. He died, happily completed in the Lord, on the day before the Ides of October, about the year of the Lord 1181.

### Guy, Bishop of Helenensis

After him, likewise toward the monks’ choir, [Col. 1558B] was buried Lord Guy, of happy memory, monk and Prior of Therloci, later Bishop of Helenensis. He died about the feast of All Saints in the year of the Lord 1327.

### Nicholas, Bishop of Roskilde

Before the middle of the altar of St Martin the Bishop lies Lord Nicholas, Bishop of Roskilde, of happy memory, kinsman of Lord Eskil, Archbishop of the metropolitan see of Lund in the kingdom of Denmark, an exile for the liberty of his church. He died in the year of the Lord 1249, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

### Henry, Bishop of Troyes

Before the middle of the altar of the Most Holy Trinity lies Lord Henry, Bishop of Greater Troyes and monk of Clairvaux, of happy memory.

## CHAPTER V. On other illustrious men whose bodies are interred at Clairvaux

[Col. 1557]

### Stephen de Courcelles

[Col. 1557C]

Before the altar of Blessed Mary Magdalene, to its left, beneath a black marble tomb, lies Lord Stephen de Courcelles, formerly a canon of Toul, who is variously commended in a metrical epitaph as endowed with complete sobriety, piety, devotion, chastity, and humility.

### Margaret, Queen of Navarre

In the presbytery, in a raised tomb, lies Lady Margaret, Queen of Navarre, Countess of Champagne and Countess Palatine of Brie, of illustrious memory. She died in the year of the Lord 1258, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

### Elizabeth, Daughter of King St Louis

In the middle of the choir, in a raised gilded tomb, is buried the heart of the most illustrious Lady Isabella, daughter of St Louis, wife of Lord Theobald, King [Col. 1557D] of Navarre and Count of Champagne. She died in the year 1271.

### Blessed Gerard and Peter, Abbots

In the great cloister, beneath the first arch beside the entrance to the church, rest the venerable men worthy of good remembrance, Lord Gerard, sixth Abbot of Clairvaux, and Lord Peter, eighth Abbot of Clairvaux. The former, after a praiseworthy life, was innocently slain for justice and zeal for the Order. The latter, a most fervent lover of holy poverty and humility, shone with many virtues in his life. May we deserve to have them as patrons with God. Amen.

### Blessed Robert of the Dunes

[Col. 1558C]

Under the second stone arch in the same cloister are the bones of several persons buried in the former chapter-house and translated for the construction of the present dormitory and new chapter-house. Indeed, the diligent reader will find the initial letters of each person’s name there inscribed upon the stones. The place of greatest eminence among the rest is occupied by Lord Robert of Bruges, second Abbot of Clairvaux. With the illustrious Lord Geoffrey of Péronne, Treasurer of the Church of St Quentin, he assumed the habit of sacred religion in this Clairvaux.

When the monastery of the Dunes, which monks of our habit but not of our Order had begun to build, made very little progress and had been entrusted to Blessed Bernard, St Bernard appointed the same Lord Robert Abbot there. Within a few years the entire monastery was built, enriched, and endowed with possessions, and it received beforehand that blessing through whose grace it endures in that place to the present day. [Col. 1558D] A few days before his most happy departure, our most holy Father Bernard, in the presence of his brethren and with great commendation of the man, advised and urged that this venerable man be chosen as his successor. After Bernard’s death, therefore, Lord Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres and former Prior of Clairvaux, named him Abbot. Throughout the whole time of his rule, the Lord granted him such peace both within and without, not only at Clairvaux itself but also among its daughter-houses, that those times seemed most happy.

After three and a half years had passed, when [Col. 1559A] on the holy day of Parasceve he had walked barefoot and had been severely afflicted by the cold, he was seized at the Vigil of the following Saturday with so grave a fever that, only with difficulty, he could be carried from his stall to the infirmary by the brethren’s hands. There, tormented by the same fever for a few days, continually persevering in pure and humble confession, he rested in the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of May, not without the great lamentation of the entire congregation.

### Blessed Serlo, Abbot

Lord Serlo, a man worthy of God, occupies the same place. In the General Chapter of Cîteaux, in the presence of our most blessed Pope Eugenius III, he united Savigny, with its thirty abbeys, to our Order by the hand of St Bernard, and subjected and gave it to the abbey of Clairvaux. After some years he had laid aside the name and office of abbot, in the same year in which St Bernard departed this life and Lord Robert happily succeeded him through the Lord’s ordering, the aforesaid Lord Serlo showed himself Robert’s inseparable companion and attentive servant in all things. In the work of holy preaching, for the edification of the brethren, he labored continually at Robert’s command throughout the whole time that Robert presided; for he imposed this office upon Serlo, whom long practice and gracious kindness had made most ready for this very task. When Lord Robert had died and Lord Fastred had been promoted Abbot of Clairvaux, the same venerable Serlo departed this life on the fourth day before the Ides of September and followed Lord Robert, his father. [Col. 1559B]

### Blessed Humbert, Abbot of Igny

Beside the aforesaid place of greater eminence than the others, on the left side, the first place is occupied by Lord Humbert, a monk of Chaise-Dieu. Already of mature age, he joined Blessed Bernard and served for some time as prior under him. Then, made first Abbot of the abbey of Igny, he conducted himself there praiseworthily for many years and with the greatest reverence, so that no observer, however curious, could scarcely perceive in him an idle word—or even an idle movement. He also organized the monastery of Signy with monks sent from Igny. Later, as the diligent reader will find in the letter written to him by Blessed Bernard, [Col. 1560A] he returned to his Clairvaux and died on the seventh day before the Ides of September. The aforesaid letter, and the sermon which Blessed Bernard delivered in chapter on the very day of Humbert’s death, can instruct the reader quite fully concerning his conduct and the multitude of graces bestowed upon him by God.

### Blessed Odo, Subprior

The venerable Lord Odo holds the second place after him. Under Blessed Bernard he fulfilled the office of subprior, with the great favor of all the brethren, until extreme old age. He was devout and zealous in the divine offices, and industrious in bodily labors. Although grievously injured in body, he nevertheless always went before the others in every task and led them by his example, admonishing and inviting them with effective words. Especially in offering the saving victim, he showed himself so devout that, like Simeon, he too seemed to hold the Child and to caress the little one with wonderful delight. What Blessed Bernard thought of his merits and virtues he showed when, immediately after Odo’s death, as soon as he had finished the first prayer for commending Odo’s soul: prostrating himself on the ground, while all hesitated, he kissed Odo’s feet amid copious tears. [Col. 1560B] He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

### Blessed Gerard of Fars

The venerable Father Lord Gerard, monk of the abbey of Fars, holds the third place after him. He was advanced in years, but so excellent in conduct that he seemed admirable to all rather than imitable. His abbot, endowed with great nobility but excelling still more in religious devotion, a special lover of Blessed Bernard, came to him and, while he was still living, brought him along, wishing to establish in his own or in our region a new abbey from Gerard’s sons. When, for this purpose, he had approached the presence [Col. 1560C] of the excellent Prince Conrad, King of the Romans, he died at God’s summons in the city of Mainz, and sent this venerable Lord Gerard to Blessed Bernard, beloved by all, and to the abbey of Clairvaux. There, after many years, having lived with the greatest religious devotion, he happily completed his course on the seventh day before the Ides of December and rested in the Lord.

## CHAPTER VI. Blessed Tezelin, Father of St Bernard; his brothers and kinsmen; and various disciples of that holy abbot.

[Col. 1559C] Beneath the structure opposite the church, in the cemetery of the abbots, built with stone columns and arches, on the right-hand side of this sarcophagus, are contained the bones of the father of blessed memory and of the full brothers [Col. 1559D] of our most blessed father Bernard, together with the name of Guldric of Tullion, his maternal uncle. Despising the nobility of their lineage and worldly power, in which they greatly excelled, they became monks, founded Clairvaux in their own blood, and left their descendants an example of monastic perfection. There likewise are contained the bones of lay brothers and novices who lived and died happily in the old abbey under the said father, in those golden ages, in that great fervour, in that holy original poverty and austerity, when their pottage was often made from beech leaves and their bread seemed not so much bran-filled as iron-hard.

The bones of these men were brought in procession, with divine praises, from the former abbey, which had been founded in a certain wormwood valley while blessed Bernard was still alive, on All Saints’ Day in the year of the Lord 1148. Hearing the chant of this procession, blessed [Col. 1560C] Malachy, who was in his last illness, was greatly delighted; that night he was laid beside them, lulled into a most sweet sleep. On the anniversary day of all the faithful departed, after the body of blessed Malachy had been [Col. 1560D] solemnly buried, the aforesaid bones were reverently placed in this spot, newly constructed by the present work.

On the left-hand side of the present tomb are contained the bones of lay brothers and novices who died happily in this place while blessed Bernard was still alive. These bones were transferred here from their former tombs because of the construction of the oratory which now stands here. Before the first oratory was built, another had previously been constructed in this place, in which there were only nine altars. In the year of the Lord 1269, both sets of bones were raised from the place in which they had been buried a second time, and, by the hands of the reverend fathers and lords James, by God’s grace Archbishop of Lyons, and Peter, Bishop of Autun, with many abbots and the convent of Clairvaux present at the time of the general chapter, were separately placed in the mausoleum beneath the high altar of the Chapel of Flanders, with solemn honour [Col. 1561A] and especial reverence. Through their devout prayers may we attain grace and glory. Amen.

### John of Aspra, Prior of Clairvaux

In the aforesaid cemetery of the abbots, beside the same building made with stone columns and arches, lies the lord John of Aspra, of pious memory, who died while prior under Abbot Lawrence.

### William, General of the Order

Likewise William of Montacute, Prior of Clairvaux, who afterwards became Abbot of La Ferté and the twenty-first Abbot of Cîteaux.

### Peter, Elect Abbot of Melun

Likewise Peter of Ulmet, prior, elected Abbot of Melun, but he did not wish to go. The monastery of Melun was built in the kingdom of France and was joined to our Reform.

### Otto, Abbot of Luxeuil

[Col. 1561B]

Likewise there lies the nobleman Otto of Saxifont, Abbot of Luxeuil, but afterwards a monk of Clairvaux.

### John Rizevelli

Likewise the lord John, Lord of Rizevelli, afterwards a monk of Clairvaux.

### Abbot Pelagius

Likewise the lord Pelagius, formerly Abbot of Oya. [Note: [Col. 1561] This monastery is situated in the kingdom of France and belongs to the Reform of Castile.]

Likewise the lord Alexander, Abbot of the Valley of Saint Peter.

Likewise the lord Nicholas, Abbot of Caldra.

### William, Archbishop of Rheims

In the great cemetery of the brethren, in its midst, beneath a solemn arch, lies the lord William of Joinville, Bishop of Langres and afterwards Archbishop of Rheims.

[Col. 1561C] Likewise the lord Viard, Dean of the Christian community of Bar-sur-Aube.

Likewise the lord Franco of Cologne, monk and Master of Novices at Clairvaux.

At the entrance to the cemetery, beside the church and facing the gate of the monastery, lies the lord Gerard of Bar, called “the Flower,” brother of the lord Peter, Cardinal and Bishop of Sabina.

Likewise, before the chapel of Aizanville and Saint Eligius: “Here lies Lady Jeanne of Bar, daughter of Sir Gualtier Auserii, wife of Jehan Varnotdon, who died in May of the year 1313.”

In the Chapter House of the monks lies the lord Sagalo, Abbot of Clairmarais, who died in the year 1323.

Likewise the religious John de Montibus, Prior of Clairvaux.

Likewise the religious Peter Godier, otherwise called de Fagis, also Prior of Clairvaux; and the bodies of many others, whose names are known in the presence of God.

[Col. 1561D] In the Chapel of l’Arreyo lies the noble knight Raynald of Grameyo, Lord of l’Arreyo, who caused the chapel to be built.

Likewise, in the same chapel lies Eurad the Elder, Lord of Chascenay, of good memory, a nobleman who died in the year of the Lord 1236, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June].

Likewise, in the same chapel, on the right side beside the door, lie the honourable and devout ladies Lady Simone, receiver of Bar, and her daughter Lady Stephenette Pitoiise.

### In the Cemetery of the Nobles

Beside the wall, at the doors of the church, lies the nobleman Geoffrey, in French Jeffroy, Lord of Joinville, who in his lifetime founded several churches: first, the Abbey of Descurrey of the Cistercian Order; [Col. 1562A] the Abbey of Jeuniuilliers of the Premonstratensian Order; the house of Mascon of the Order of Grandmont; the Priory of Valdomie under Molesme; and the church of Saint Lawrence in the castle of the said Joinville. He died in the year 1132, in the month of August.

Likewise the lord Evrard, priest of Champignolle, who enclosed the abbey with a wall.

Likewise the Count of Grandpré.

Likewise Lord Josbert of La Ferté.

Likewise Hugh, Lord of Plancey.

Likewise Sir Penicars of Durnay, knight, who died in the year of grace 1289, in the month of December.

Likewise Sir Gillis du Pont, esquire, in his lifetime Lord of Revepont and of Maleroy, who died on the twenty-first day of November in the year 1505.

Likewise Adrien Chatoura, son of Jean Chatoura, merchant at Troyes.

Before the great portal of the church lies the lord [Col. 1562B] James, parish priest of Barriville, who died in the year of the Lord 1334, in the month of December.

### Epitaph of the Lord Bonaventure, Bishop of Eu, Who Lies in the Sacristy

Here Bonaventure, whose renown shall never die,  
Dies as one worthy; beneath this tomb he lies buried.  
Lombard by birth, he was truly a citizen of heaven,  
And lived with a pure mind, by the favour of the Godhead.  
For, as a model for our monks, he guided himself.  
Bishop of Eu, he became an exile from his own see  
For the shield of faith, believing it therefore safe  
To come to Clairvaux, hoping there to tread the path  
That climbs to heaven, by following the deeds of the good—  
Sober and chaste, likewise fleeing worldly pride.

Now he follows Christ and has then rejected the world.  
When, under the Lord born from the blessed womb,  
Twice one hundred thousand years, then add ten nine times, and, to complete the number, twice two; he lost his life.

[Col. 1562C]

### Epitaph of the Lord Philip, Count of Flanders and Vermandois

Philip, a prince of remarkable virtue, Count of Flanders, deservedly to be preferred to his predecessors, not only governed Flanders peacefully but also, by his example, urged the neighbouring provinces toward the good of peace. On the third day after his birth he cried out terribly: “Clear the house for me.” When grown, he married Elizabeth, daughter of Ralph, Count of Vermandois. After she died, he sent to Spain for Matilda, daughter of Afonso, King of Portugal; she came to him with royal display and became his wife, in the year of the Lord 1084.

This Philip, the first to bear a lion upon his shield, governed the county of Flanders most vigorously. Abounding in riches and honours, great in wisdom and power, zealous for justice and valiant in arms, he was not undeservedly compared with the Maccabees. [Col. 1562D] When news of his death was heard, his homeland was confounded; grief and fear seized everyone. He died before the city called Acre, during its siege together with the kings of France and England, in the year of the Lord 1191. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Nicholas outside the walls of Acre; but through the care of his wife Matilda he was transferred to Clairvaux and honourably laid within this chapel, which she had prepared for him and herself. Matilda herself was afterwards honourably buried in this same chapel beside her husband.

### Countess Agnes

Behind the tombs of the lord Philip, Count of Flanders, and his wife Matilda, lies in their chapel the most illustrious lady Agnes, Countess of Champagne.

[Col. 1563]

## Poem by Richard, Monk of Grandselve, Diocese of Toulouse, Cistercian Order, in Praise of Clairvaux and of the Religious Discipline There

(*The Complete Works of Bernard*. Paris: Claudius Chevallon, 1536, folio, fol. XXXII, quire d. d. d.)

Richard of Grandselve, in the diocese of Toulouse, was a Cistercian monk, theologian, and poet of no small distinction. Around the year 1160 he wrote a poem in praise of the abbey of Clairvaux. It is printed at the end of the works of Saint Bernard, published at Paris in 1536, folio.

[Col. 1563A]

You who wish to scorn the empty joys  
Of this round world, and contemplate  
And meditate upon Christ’s radiance—  
Then you must seek a place more fitting,  
More ready for good, enriched by goodness,  
Piety, fair estates, and land.

If you hasten there, girded with love of virtue,  
You shall climb in living honour to heavenly dwelling places.  
This is the great place where the heavenly Lamb feeds,  
Whose name and omen shall here alike be disclosed.

You who seek heaven’s rest with faithful mind,  
Make haste: direct your way to Clairvaux.  
It is a straight path to the sky, above all like the sun:  
Burning and shining, leading to the rewards of the kingdom.

It burns away sins and gives the welcome gifts of light;  
It anoints the meek and pricks the faults of the wicked.  
It knows not how to flatter, nor does its discipline grow lax:

[Col. 1563B]

It strikes the slothful, keeping the wicked from sin;  
It teaches the ignorant, sending the instructed toward joys;  
And it washes and cleanses sinners, fouler than beasts of burden,  
That it may restore the gifts they had lost.

Thus purified and wholly cleansed,  
It sends many children and adults to heaven,  
Who, pleasing to the Lord, live blessedly without end.

Flock of Clairvaux, who sing all fitting things,  
You always bear praises on your lips in angelic fashion.  
You continually apply yourself to discipline,  
The medicine of sinners, and so you press on toward joys;  
You keep great watch; you leave no wrong unpunished;  
You chastise the body; you unite yourself with heavenly things.

While, under such care, you desire to live a pure life,  
You become a citizen of heaven, since this is how you wish to live.

[Col. 1563C]

While you dwell in the cloister, if you give your time to Christ,  
Broad kingdoms shall be granted you in the blessed height;  
You shall be joined at every hour to angelic choirs,  
With whom in heaven you shall receive what you now seek.

O happy Valley, which deceives none of its flock  
But leads them all to the rewards of the true light!

[Col. 1564A]

O tranquil Valley, full of excellence of character;  
Devout Valley, holy Valley, wholly fitting;  
Noble, approved, and populous in order,  
Suited to spiritual brethren and beautiful;

Beloved Valley, the true rule of life,  
You direct your companies upward in swift course!  
Cloistered Valley and spiritual dwelling-place!

In you cloistered men also live spiritually,  
Free from evils and sheltered beneath the Lord’s wings;  
From them the monstrous tempter departs empty-handed.

O bright Valley, altar of the divine majesty,  
Very dear to God, a Valley rare indeed—  
There is none in the world, so I believe in my deep heart,  
Like this Valley, so capable of good.

O joyful Valley, Valley filled with goodness!

[Col. 1564B]

Pleasant Valley, good, shining, pure Valley!  
Valley whose mouths resound with the divine voice!  
Royal Valley, you are Christ’s special house,  
Where Jesus is with the Father and his Virgin Mother.

O holy Valley, fragrant with such sweetness!  
Unfeigned Valley, Valley ever blessed!  
Happy is he who, dwelling with you, knows how to live with himself,  
Gathered inwardly, sheltered beneath the cross of the Crucified.

For such a man Christ’s poverty is more delightful  
Than the summit of kingship or the wisdom of laws.  
In this sacred Valley, the decayed, pale, lean flesh  
Fattens the mind that seeks the heavenly kingdoms;

Flesh worn by the heavenly lash enjoys heavenly life,  
And the patient soul gathers the rich fruits of Paradise:  
Thus at last the devout person is saved whole.

[Col. 1564C]

Consecrated Valley, sown for fruitfulness to come,  
You scattered holy seed and brought forth saints;  
And in bringing forth you grow, nor do you yet cease to bring forth,  
Giving birth incorruptibly to those whom the high priest  
Consecrates to sacred altars, working heavenly things on earth.

The wise man runs to this Valley, where I would rather live

[Col. 1565A]

Poor and ragged than rich and luxurious.

This valley is encircled by valleys;  
It fears no assault, for it bears its heart above  
In heaven, beyond the reach of the enemy’s missiles.

Secure Valley, beneath Christ’s unceasing care,  
Saint Bernard consecrated you and blessed you with religious life,  
Following good and slow toward evil.

Farewell, bright Valley, brighter than bright metals;  
Unless you deceive me, you are a straight hill toward heaven.  
If you wish to enter Paradise by the straight path,  
I counsel you: direct your gaze to Clairvaux.

[Col. 1566A]

Behold, Bernard teaches you the memorials of a blessed life,  
Like nard fragrant with remarkable virtue.  
Behold there his true followers, made renowned by fame,  
Who flee the snares and weapons of raging [evil],  
Despising worldly things and bearing Christ in their hearts;  
Among the nations they flourish like flowers through the meadows.

Should I speak, or be silent? As a flower does not surpass its fragrance,  
So goodness yields nothing to honour.  
By examining the gifts of their virtues and the heights of truth,  
And imitating them, you may merit heaven after death.

**Thanks be to God.**

[Col. 1565]

## Description of a Cistercian Journey

Successfully undertaken, with heaven’s favour, by Brother Joseph Meglinger, priest-monk of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Maris Stella, commonly called Wettingen, on the occasion of the general chapter of the same sacred Order, in May 1667. (Lucerne: printed by Gottfried Hautt, 32mo.)

### Brother Joseph Meglinger Praised by the Reverend Father Dom Jean Mabillon

(From *Veterum Analectorum*, vol. IV, Paris, 1685, p. 21.)

Among the religious men of the monastery of Maris Stella, otherwise Wettingen, we saw one, Joseph Meglinger, a learned and modest man, who kindly gave us two little books written and published by himself—he being himself their author and printer. One is the *Cistercian Year*, in which the principal deeds of holy and devout Cistercian monks are related with great elegance. The other is his *Cistercian Journey*, composed on the occasion of the Cistercian general chapter of 1667, to which he himself travelled.

### To the Benevolent Reader

Because I distrust my own ignorance and my own forgetfulness, I exhort and warn you that, if you find anything worthy of censure, you should either endeavour to correct it yourself or, if perhaps meekness and humility deter you from doing so, at least kindly let me know without concealment whatever has troubled you.

—Saint Bernard, in the prologue to the treatise *On the Life and Conduct of Clerics*

### To the Most Reverend Father in Christ, the Most Eminent Prelate and Lord, Lord Edmund, Most Worthy Abbot of the Most Celebrated Monastery of Blessed Mary of Saint Urban, of the Holy Cistercian Order; and Most Deserving Vicar General of the Same Sacred Order throughout Switzerland, Alsace, and Breisgau; My Most Gracious Father and Lord

As I am about to enter the sanctuary of graciousness, in order humbly to burn votive incense upon the altar of gratitude, I am troubled by a single choice of names: by what title I may dedicate to the grace of Your Reverence this small offering, a letter written to a friend concerning my Cistercian journey. If every one of these titles had to be brought forward, this inscription alone would surely fill more pages than the little book itself.

I shall produce one instance out of six hundred. As the rest will become clear from reading the book, it will then shine forth more plainly than midday light by what right I owe this modest labour of mine to Your Reverence alone. It is the opinion of many that fathers of their country are, as it were, deservedly worshipped as certain divinities by such gifts of inscriptions. I willingly and gladly subscribe to that opinion; and I shall honour Your Reverence by the same title neither rashly nor falsely.

For that the Holy Order is our country is plainly shown by those whom their own inclination or the severity of the laws has erased from its roll: we regard them as exiles. Your Reverence is shown to be the father of this our country by your paternal care for us all, exercised through diligent visitation; by the vicarial authority of the supreme Father in the Holy Order; and, finally, by your laborious concern for all the sons of the sacred Order—as will become evident to the benevolent reader in the course of my letter. Indeed, how genuinely I may adorn Your Reverence with this title of fatherhood has recently been shown by the general chapter, by whose authority Your Reverence, chosen among the first four fathers of the sacred Order, represented the person of the Reverend Lord Abbot of Morimond with remarkable sagacity and prudence in that extraordinary situation.

Therefore, in publishing this description of mine, no one had a stronger claim than the common Father of our country. Yet, when I contemplated Your Reverence raised to so lofty a pinnacle of honour, being too conscious of my own lack of skill, I did not dare to address you in person. Instead, I entrusted my eager pen to a friend who has for some years been bound to me in the closest intimacy, and instructed it to recount the whole course of our journey in familiar conversation: partly so that I might more freely pour into his bosom the merriment of jokes gathered on the way, the dulling effect of reverential fear being removed; partly so that, if in composing it I should meet with favourable fortune, I might then seek patronage—certainly nowhere other than from Your Reverence. But if this offspring of my intellect proved unworthy of Your Reverence’s eyes, it might remain unknown and buried in the kindness of my friend.

The letter was completed at the end of the first month after my return. When some of my dearest fellow brothers had leisurely read it, they urged me with pressing arguments to have it printed and dedicate it to Your Reverence. They did not fail to reproach me with ingratitude if I refused. For what else, they said, had Your Reverence done for me than Ananias did for his Tobias, the great one? And that most grateful old man offered him half his wealth in a generous gift; while you, who owe your entire self to him, will not offer at least some token of a grateful heart? They also recalled former benefits bestowed by Your Reverence on Maris Stella: the labours, cares, and anxieties of so many years, by which you bound to yourself both many individuals and all the monks of Maris Stella; and they said that here an opportunity was offered me to declare publicly, in the name of all, the affection of gratitude that was due.

These arguments strongly impelled a will already inclined of itself, so that, although nowhere in this unpolished and unadorned style have I achieved what I wished, and although my unpractised style, refined by such rare exercise in writing, did not please me, I nevertheless conceived such confidence in Your Reverence that I wished not only to offer this little work for reading to its gracious eyes, but also, with the most fitting filial submission, to have it sacredly dedicated under its most celebrated name. Though it is wholly slight, it will nevertheless borrow some worth from so august a countenance; and it will correct its smallness by the greatness of your name, its cheapness by the excellence of your dignity, and its contemptibility by the renown of your patronage.

And so, commending myself together with this little book and our whole Maris Stella to Your Reverence, Father and Lord, I most affectionately pray for your most happy preservation through many years to come, the most desired prosperity of your peaceful government, and finally immortal life among the blessed above. From Maris Stella, on the Kalends of September [1 September] 1667.

Your Most Reverend and Eminent Fatherhood and Lordship’s most obedient servant and son,  
**Brother Joseph Meglinger**

### Approval

We, Brother Gerard, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See Abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Maris Stella, commonly called Wettingen, of the Holy Cistercian Order, by the force of these presents grant to our beloved in Christ Father Joseph Meglinger, subprior and secretary of our monastery, permission to commit to print and make public the description composed by him of the journey which, by our command, he made to the general chapter of the said Holy Order held this year at Cîteaux; since two members of our convent appointed for this purpose have examined and approved it. In witness whereof we have issued these present letters, subscribed in our own hand and sealed with the abbatial seal, at Maris Stella, on the Kalends of August [1 August], 1667.

**Brother Gerard, Abbot**

### To the Very Reverend and Religious Father in Christ, Joseph, upon His Journal

Whence, Joseph, was suddenly given to you  
Such eloquence of tongue,  
With which you write a journal of your journey?

No journey to Rome, no journey to Athens  
Has led you;  
Nor have you gone to Bellerophon’s  
Castalian springs.

But I remember that you visited your mother and your father:  
She gave you milk; your Father gave you sweet honey.

Brother Fidelis Molitor, Prior of Maris Stella, applauded with the affection of a congratulating heart.

### To the Very Reverend Father and Lord Joseph Meglinger, Secretary and Subprior of Wettingen, etc.

Among painters were Parrhasius and Timanthes,  
And Zeuxis’ grape won great applause.  
Deceived birds came to feed upon it,  
But the blow of their beaks upon the panel was vain.

Art had imitated nature with painted colour,  
And the bird declared that what was painted lived.

[Col. 1568A] Whether it was right to say so or not, at least,  
While the bird was deceived by the image, it ennobled  
The work on which it had bestowed its judgment.

Forgive me, venerable Father, my subprior, if I dare  
To disclose my mind concerning this writing.  
I do not speak as a flatterer. Your account  
Of the journey to the Mother of the Order is such:

You portray to the life cities, fields, farms, forests, lakes,  
Meals, meadows, and houses;  
Whoever beholds it thinks he sees all things alive,  
And, deceived, approves his own error.

Thus your [materially uncertain: OCR lacuna] was abundantly fruitful;  
After your return, it brought us many delights.

Well done and be of good heart: behold, Star of the Sea,  
Both your superiors now occupy the printing-press with offspring of intellect.  
One is a musician, this one a historian. Why do you snarl, Zoilus?  
Foolish bird, be gentler toward your own beak.

Brother Gabriel Moser, likewise a priest-monk of Maris Stella and apostolic notary, sang this rejoicingly in token of honour and love owed.

### A Farewell Ode to the Reverend Lord Johann Jacob Mechler, Companion in the Epistolary Theatre of the Journey

Come with me, Jacob, upon paths unknown to me;  
It delights me to leave my homeland  
And travel through lands lying remote  
Beneath the Gallic sun.

And how happy I shall be if I may be granted  
To be your companion at your side, or your attendant!  
Here there is no need for Cretan wax  
Or for Ariadne’s thread.

We do not enter Daedalian deceits  
Or caves impassable by dark paths;  
Rather, more happily you shall enter the bright Valley  
Of the honey-sweet Father.

Though the difficult delays of roads may hinder you,  
Though a thousand dangers and the horror  
Of a squalid inn stand in your way,  
Yet press onward, generous friend, against them.

Whether a soldier at a hanging gate opposes  
Your passage, fearing hidden ambushes, break through;  
Or whether you enter the arch  
And chambers of a hanging inn—

The jaws of Avernus—then, Mechler,  
You need steadfast spirit and a breast  
Of triple bronze, and sticky gold,  
And a helmet scented with smoke,

Changed by the cook, while you send your futile complaints  
Into the empty air, laughed at in French speech  
By the company standing near,  
And moderate rage with laughter.

Then you shall see caves and steep mountains,  
The shadows of forests and narrow valleys,  
The green expanses of full fields  
And broad stretches of lakes.

Indeed, everywhere the sun shall reveal to you  
The savage marks of bloody Mars,  
And you shall lament the ruins of cities,  
Their walls laid waste by flame and sword,

Until wealthy Dole opens to you  
Its famous palaces of the poor,  
And painted bed-curtains, ranged  
In long order throughout the bedchamber.

What need now to sing of the sweet enticements of wine,  
Or its sounding pleasures and gentle whispers in the ears—  
The music of the lily-bearing field?

Or why speak of the grave senate of the council,  
Which the Father of Cîteaux summons  
And gathers here, many fathers of the homeland  
Full of majesty?

But this little book shall lead and bring you back  
For the rest of the way. Do not be reluctant to follow:  
Neither error nor labours hinder you;  
The road is paved with virgin milk.

L. M. P. W. sang this to the author in token of fraternal affection.

### To the Very Reverend and Most Learned Father in Christ, Joseph Meglinger, Describing His Journey

Indeed, examples move more than the precepts  
Of rhetoric which you are accustomed to teach us.  
In practice you demonstrate what true eloquence can accomplish,  
While so fertile a vein of style flows from you:

From a theme so dry, one which a single page  
Could wholly finish, since the journey was only three days’ long,  
You extend it as though the journey had perhaps been long  
For beholding the four quarters of the world.

You broaden narrow material with the freedom  
Of a flying pen, and soar with your genius.

His most obedient brother pupils of rhetoric sang this in token of reverence and affection.

## Familiar Letter Concerning the Journey to the General Chapter of the Holy Cistercian Order

[Col. 1569]

[Col. 1569C] To the very reverend and most learned Lord Johann Jacob Mechler, parish priest in the March of Schwyz, his most upright friend, Brother Joseph Meglinger, greetings.

If you did not know the number of letters which you have received from me over fifteen years, you might perhaps wonder, best of friends, whether the promise by which I had bound myself—to send you an account of the journey which, by heaven’s favour, I undertook to the general chapter held at the chief abbey of Cîteaux and happily completed amid this year’s spring flowers—had slipped from my memory. Yet even if I had promised nothing, since the most sacred law of our friendship has always made common between us, on either side, whatever joyful or adverse events befell us, I could not without fault have excluded you from companionship in so great a happiness of mine.

I shall therefore recount the whole course of the journey in the order established by the successive days—and almost the hours—of the month. Yet I shall not give you a bare journal or diary, [Col. 1569D] for you to run through cursorily like a blind man over an outspread sheet and then condemn to worms. Rather, with no superficial care, I shall lead you about everywhere, as it were by the hand; and I shall depict what I saw freely and almost in living colours. Especially, as occasion permits, I shall not neglect to bring forward the life and miracles of our divinely honey-tongued [Col. 1570C] Father Bernard. With this honey I intend to sweeten the harsh flavour of a style here appearing in public in its first exercise, and to conduct it with the same ease and freedom with which I write all my letters—unless the gravity of the matter adds something of weight, or its cheerfulness some seasoning.

I shall pursue truth with such religious scruple that I shall report nothing except what I have established; and you may be certain that, wherever I append a measure of time or place, it cannot, as the saying is, be found broader or narrower by a fingernail’s breadth.

2. Before I entrust you to the journey, however, you must be taught a few things about the reason for the journey and for the title prefixed to this letter. From it you will at the same time take up a torch for penetrating more deeply into several other matters which, during the course of the narrative, may be less clear to one unacquainted with our affairs. Hear this briefly from the records of our annals.

Saint Robert, a nobleman of Champagne, observed the Rule of Saint Benedict for several years in different monasteries, first as prior and then as abbot. Desiring a stricter life, he withdrew from the monastery of Molesme with twenty companions to the uncultivated wilderness of Cîteaux, so called because of its many pools and cisterns, in the year of restored salvation 1098. In this solitude, by the authority of the Bishop of Lyons, then Apostolic Legate, he laid the first foundations of the sacred institute.

But afterwards, by the command of Supreme Pontiff Urban II, he returned to Molesme, having presided over Cîteaux for little more than a year. Saint Alberic succeeded him in government, endowed by the Queen of Heaven with a white cowl, foreshadowing the brightness of the sacred Order. After Alberic had been taken to heaven, Saint Stephen, an Englishman by nation, succeeded him: he was the man who received Bernard with thirty companions into Cistercian probation in the year of Christ 1113.

Increased by so illustrious an accession, Cîteaux, like a most abundant spring, spread itself far and wide through sacred colonies with such renown that supreme pontiffs, emperors, kings, princes, and all nobility applauded its glory, borne throughout the whole world, with their liberality. Thus our sacred Order took its name from the first monastery of Cîteaux. All the other abbeys sprung from it, like daughters from a mother, had from their origin granted it the prerogative of maternal honour.

In the tenth year from its own foundation it produced the first of these daughters, La Ferté; shortly afterwards Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond. The monasteries subsequently issuing from these four springs honoured their respective mothers, and the abbots of those mothers, with the title of primacy, or of the first fathers in the Order. Bernard had presided over Clairvaux for four years, and Stephen over his Cîteaux for ten, when, wishing to provide piously for posterity through the holiness of laws, Stephen summoned all the abbots to Cîteaux in the year of Christ 1119. With their counsel he drew up the document called the Charter of Charity, in which, among other provisions, he decreed that every year all the abbots of the entire Order should assemble at Cîteaux to deliberate on matters necessary for preserving the Order.

This law was carefully observed in its beginnings; but afterwards it was more rarely put into practice because of the tumults of war and other difficulties. So too in these most recent times, although assemblies had repeatedly been called, the general chapter had been interrupted for more than fourteen years. At last, by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, it was appointed for this present year 1667, and all heads of monasteries were instructed to attend in person or through their commissioners, unless prevented by the most pressing cause.

3. My most reverend Abbot of Maris Stella was possessed by a great desire to behold so celebrated an assembly of so many prelates; but his bodily constitution, prone to illness, directed him to other plans. At the persuasion of the most reverend Lord Vicar General of Saint Urban, it was therefore decided that I should undertake the journey and go to excuse my abbot’s absence.

I can scarcely express what emotions this commission produced in me. A desire to explore foreign regions stirred my heart, and my love for Father Bernard, the Honey-Tongued, kindled it further. I thought that I should behold him almost living upon earth if I were given the opportunity to see those places which brought him forth into this light of mortal life, which nurtured him as a novice, and which revered him as abbot. Yet the magnitude of the undertaking partly drew back my eager mind, as did partly the weakness of my strength, which would doubtless succumb to the hardships of travel. Then I had no experience in affairs of this kind, no practice in such studies, and no knowledge of either the customs or the language of France.

Amid these conflicts of uncertain deliberation, I fixed my attention solely upon the trumpet-call of obedience; under its guidance, I promised myself that, even if I encountered a labyrinth, I should emerge without any other Ariadne. Therefore, having gathered the little baggage necessary for the journey, I left Maris Stella on 25 April. Passing through the town of Mellingen—agreeably situated on the River Reuss, which it spans with a stout bridge and which provides passage for merchandise carried from Italy, Alsace, and the neighbouring region; it had also, some years before, been a useful and very strong obstacle to prevent the heterodox Bernese from joining arms with the Zürichers against the Catholics—I arrived at the village of Sursee at midday, and in the evening reached the monastery of Saint Urban.

4. Since I stayed here for three days, do not begrudge hearing a few things which I observed there concerning this celebrated monastery of our Switzerland. Its situation, indeed, is not especially recommended by pleasantness; for a great wood, commonly called Boowald, lies toward the west, almost taking away the light through the extraordinary height of its trees. The Dutch not infrequently carry these away for use as masts for seagoing ships, first by the Aare and then by the Rhine. There are also many pools, and one might hesitate whether they produce greater benefit from their abundance of fish or greater drawbacks from the unhealthy exhalations of the ground. Yet the inhabitants’ care has largely removed these inconveniences: both by cutting ditches to receive the stagnant water and by clearing the forest over so wide an extent that the air, having gained freedom to circulate, disperses the density of the vapours by suitable movement. Thus the tamed woodland soil is clothed with such fertile grass that scarcely anywhere do Swiss cattle graze with more fortunate abundance. [Col. 1572B] There I saw a very large number of oxen, outstanding for limbs so huge that they resemble elephants. It is certain that the oxen here grow to such a size that a single animal often exceeds a weight of two thousand pounds.

This famous monastery had as founders three brothers—so I have extracted from its ancient records—of full blood: Luitold or Lupold; Wernher (both of whom assumed at Bellevaux the habit of the holy Cistercian Order, dedicating themselves and the monastery to be founded to the Order; the former having there been promoted to the priesthood); and Udalric, a vigorous knight in secular service. They were free barons of Langenstein, the site of their castle, situated about a mile from the monastery, whose ruins may still be seen today. The year of its first foundation on a different estate from that on which it now stands, called Rotha, is unknown because of the monastery’s three lamentable burnings, which consumed most records of its antiquity. Yet the Reverend Father Carolus de Visch, prior of that place, produced from the library of Dunes an extremely ancient chronology of Cistercian monasteries, written four hundred and forty years ago—and therefore judged by him to be wholly true—in which the year 1148 is assigned as the foundation year of the monastery of St Urban. [Col. 1572C]

Many years afterward the foundation was transferred to another neighbouring estate, purchased by the illustrious Lord Arnold, Baron of Kapfenberg—who for that reason too is numbered among the founders—and there construction began in the year of Christ 1191 upon the monastery which still stands. This was precisely the time when the notable city of Lesser Burgundy, now Switzerland, Bern—called by some Arctopolis—received its foundations from Berchtold, Duke of Zähringen, in the last year of Pope Clement III’s pontificate and the first year of Henry VI, Emperor of the Romans. From what mother-house St Urban acknowledges descent you may readily infer from what has been said: namely, Bellevaux, whence its first religious inhabitants came. The same is attested by the most ancient handwritten codices which I myself inspected both at Cîteaux and at the seminary of Dole, besides Chrysostom Henriquez, the very renowned chronologist of our Order, who expressly affirms it in Book II of the *Fasciculus Sanctorum Ordinis*. [Col. 1572D]

The surviving memorial records of St Urban describe a very ample endowment received from its founders. Yet, having also suffered the changes of time and fortune, it did not always prosper in the same course. Certainly its present most reverend superior, Edmund, the thirty-third abbot, now in the twenty-seventh year of his rule, found its condition by no means as flourishing as that which he has now secured for it by his own industry. For, besides enlarging its temporal possessions through the addition of several estates, the castle of Liebenfels, and other advantages, he has adorned the church with a most elegant altar and has rebuilt almost the entire monastery from its foundations, very recently and with equal magnificence. It numbers no fewer than forty religious, who serve the Deity with the highest praise in the observance of regular discipline. [Col. 1573A]

5. Therefore, setting out from this monastery on the afternoon of 28 April, we reached Solothurn, taking lodgings in buildings belonging to the monastery of St Urban. These were at that time inhabited by its procurator, Lord Francis Victor Biis, a most courteous man. Half an hour outside the city, he had met the most reverend lord abbot and his companions and received them in a most polished address. While the household was occupied with preparing supper, the most reverend lord decided to go out into the city to visit certain acquaintances among the senatorial order.

Having already firmly resolved to feed the curiosity of my eyes, I observed the city’s location, commendable both for the fertility of its soil and for the natural defences supplied to it: the navigable Aare surrounds the greater part of the city, while opposite rises the steep and rugged Jura mountain. Several towers crown it, breathing an air of great antiquity, which some date back three thousand years. [Col. 1573B] Yet the houses, refined according to the taste of the present age, show that nothing remains of the crude barbarism of so great an antiquity. The inhabitants themselves likewise are at once gracefully formed by French manners and candidly display, in speech and deed, minds open with Swiss generosity.

The guests, most of them patricians, made this clear by striking experience at supper. They were attended by countless skins full of honorary wine, according to the custom prevalent throughout Germany: magistrates first greet welcome guests with a ceremonial offering of wine. The chief seasoning of the dishes was the moderation of one’s table companions—what we now commonly call discretion—by which everyone retained complete freedom to drink as he pleased. No one was overwhelmed by an importunate host of cups through an inhuman humanity; rather, merely tasting a cup, however illustrious its title, fully discharged every obligation of response. The banquet also broke up early, leaving us, dismissed to our beds, to our rest. [Col. 1573C]

Thus, having early performed the duties of divine worship, we began the second day of our journey under a clear sky, after hastily taking breakfast. A little outside the walls we watched in amazement as many buildings there were being razed to the ground, just as if suburbs were being denied to an enemy threatening siege. When we asked the reason, we were told that senate and people had decided to surround the city with a convenient and not laborious rampart—not that they expected by this shield to repel open war, but because Switzerland is prone to sudden disturbances and they wished to anticipate unforeseen events in good time. Castles were being raised everywhere by the Bernese and others; cities were being enclosed with enormous fortifications, though no enemy was openly identified. They too, finally, intended to ensure that their citizens could neither be despised by the arrogance of others nor fear for their own security.

They then showed us on paper a coloured plan of the work they contemplated, affirming that it would be such that its citizens, without calling in outside assistance, could defend it fearlessly, whether subjects should take arms against the magistracy or foreign force against the city. Having briefly praised their industry and wished them fortune’s favour, within five hours we reached Biel. [Col. 1573D]

6. Biel—called Biela by others—is a small town, but exceedingly pleasant in situation, made so by vineyards, the greenery of meadows, and the neighbouring lake. The sign of the Golden Crown was our lodging; it stood directly before us at the entrance to the principal street, or marketplace. We were received with an exceedingly lavish dinner and feared that an enormous price would be demanded, especially since the quick readiness and attentiveness of the servants seemed to press themselves upon us as if they conformed to the rules of perfect politeness for the sake of the reward they were afterwards to claim. But our fear deceived us so completely that the host accepted only a single gold coin, called a Hungarian, almost less than the fair price, and did so with the most courteous expressions of thanks.

About three hundred paces from the town a boat awaited us. Once aboard, we entrusted the horses to the servants to lead along the lake. This voyage lasted three hours; I wished that the lake stretched all the way to Cîteaux. For the tranquil element, smooth as crystal, reflected the adjacent slopes in a most delightful image. The clouds having been swept away, the sky smiled upon us, while a gentle west wind softened the sun’s rays with a quiet murmur. Such was the sweet play of the temperate breeze that it both caressed us with a perceptible moderation of heat and left the resting serenity of the waters undisturbed by any movement of waves. Another delight for the eyes was added by the unusual sight of vineyards suspended upon the precipices of the neighbouring hills. Hardly anywhere was soil visible in which the vines might fix their roots, though they were then eagerly bringing forth leaves at the beginning of spring; nevertheless, I was told to my astonishment that the genius of the place brings those vineyards to the richest fruits. Amid these delights, and the continuous exertions of the rowers, we disembarked and at once proceeded along a path through vineyards as far as Neuchâtel. [Col. 1574A]

7. If you compare Biel with Neuchâtel, you will scarcely find any difference in size, [Col. 1574B] except that the latter, more closely joined to the lake, enjoys a freer prospect of it. When entering the town I did not notice that there was a castle there; only after the governor of the place had presented the most reverend lord vicar-general with honorary wine did he remind us that the cluster of towers standing about the old buildings was the castle. The French language is used in this city, and it obeys the French Duke of Longueville. By agreement, however, he appoints to the castle Swiss governors from Solothurn, such as the one now residing there, or Bernese governors; for Neuchâtel lies upon the boundary of the territories of both.

Almost all this region is obstinately devoted to Calvin’s sect and tests the patience of religious travellers with sneers and insolent shouting, in accordance with the custom of that doctrine hostile to Catholics. The sign of the Monkey received us beneath a roof sufficiently convenient and agreeable, since the host already displayed the grace of French courtesy by a most dexterous bending of the body, and foods flavoured in a foreign manner pleased us more by their novelty than our domestic fare. [Col. 1574C]

8. Before the night had quite passed, we left Neuchâtel in order to get ahead of the sun’s heat, travelling for two hours by a not unpleasant route among vineyards and fields of easy soil. Easy, I say; for behold, one man with his wife and two shaggy horses was accomplishing the entire labour of agriculture with remarkable economy. One horse pulled the plough, which the woman guided; after every third furrow the farmer scattered seed, and the other horse immediately followed, drawing a harrow.

But the rest of the road had a very different appearance as we proceeded through the most rugged valley, commonly called Kezerthal. A swift torrent divides two steep mountains. Small at its source, it nevertheless sends forth a gloomy murmur through the roar of rocks, increased to horror by the narrowness of the place and the forest. The path runs along the left side of the valley, narrow and midway up the slope, enclosed above by a precipitous rock like a wall and below by a descent no less abrupt. It is often scarcely broad enough to leave room for two horses meeting each other to yield passage in turn. Never, I confess, was it without danger: almost the entire route lay not upon gravel or sand, but over solid, hard rock, worn down by the frequent rubbing of horses’ hooves as if upon a whetstone and polished dangerously smooth for slipping. Enormous stones also hung so lightly above our heads that they seemed capable of falling under the weight of a bird alighting upon them. That they often did fall was shown by recent traces everywhere and by the heaps gathered in the valley below. [Col. 1574D]

9. Yet, having happily completed our journey before noon, we halted for dinner in the village of Couvet; a bundle of boxwood projecting from a window marked the inn. As we passed through the kitchen, I observed there something I had not seen before: the hearth was not raised in a stone structure above the ground, but was made upon the kitchen floor itself. Moreover, no light from the sun was admitted except what entered through the chimney. The chimney’s construction itself carried me into the greatest astonishment. [Col. 1575A] It equalled the entire expanse of the kitchen, resting upon its four walls as a foundation. It was not made of baked bricks and mortar mixed with lime; rather, a floor of fir planks, smoothed by the axe, rose from the walls enclosing the kitchen and lifted itself above the roof in the form of a hollow pyramid, thus conveying the smoke rising from the fire through its most capacious throat into the air. To prevent rain from entering through the same opening that admitted light, they fitted two shutters to the aperture, so that by means of a long cord they could easily be closed or opened as required. The same construction of chimneys was found everywhere along our route.

Six hours remained from Couvet to Pontarlier. Halfway along the journey we entered a gorge where all the valley’s horror and ruggedness seemed, as it were, to have gathered its strength into sinews. A road already sufficiently awkward because of its precipice was obstructed by innumerable fragments of raw stone with many sharp points and by unstable rock. The horses struggled most heavily up the slope through muddy, slippery tracks, their feet caught in the narrow spaces among the rocks, continually threatening themselves and us with either a fall or the breaking of a leg more grievous than a fall. At last we escaped to the summit of the mountain, itself worthy of notice. A sharp and very lofty crag rises there, through whose middle a very narrow road, made not by nature but by steel, may be blocked by a chain of monstrous weight and thickness, joining both rocks through strong hinges of uncertain construction.

Then, passing the castle of Joux, set at a remarkable height upon barren rock bare of grass, we were received by Pontarlier—or, as others prefer, Pontarlin. [Col. 1575B]

10. This was the first city of the County of Burgundy to meet us. The most beautiful weather and the Kalends of May on the following morning invited me to examine it more closely; yet I was almost wet with tears instead of dew, tears drawn forth by half-ruined houses—sad relics of war—standing among newly raised buildings and seemingly still lamenting their own ashes. [Col. 1575C]
