I most pleasantly diluted this sorrow with the generous liquor not now of the Rhaetian vine, but of the Arbois vine. I do not despise the honeyed musts sent by Valtellina, nor its wine clarified into potent strength; yet I prefer Arbois by as much as Paris once preferred Cypris to Lucina. Rhaetian wine is sweet, but it smells of sugar and mulled wine with an effeminate softness. This, however, with manly sweetness breathes neither the Canaries nor bees. The sharp sting that excites the tongue with penetrating titillation gives Rhaetian wine its immediate renown; yet it almost tears the same tongue with an excessively violent bite, so that you can scarcely drain a cup of ordinary size at one draught, and cannot bear it except with your eyes dissolved into copious showers of tears. Arbois wine, on the contrary, while lightly pricking and showing its acidity only from afar, continually inflames lips floating in its agreeable liquor with fresh desire; as one pursues its elusive sting and thinks it hidden at the bottom, one hunts it even by swallowing the last drop.

Nor does it yield in fragrance. Rhaetian wine does not cease to emit the foam of the press and the smell of must, as if still from fermenting lees, until the sweetness—its sole recommendation—has vanished. Arbois, however, brings from the press mature vapours rising gently to the brain, not such as cause the harsh disturbance for which Rhaetian is notorious. Thus it may not inelegantly be called *Ghium*—that is, Chian wine, famous from the island so named in the Aegean Sea. [Col. 1575D] Their effects on health are likewise comparable. Although Arbois does not shine with transparent crystal or garnet-like brilliance, it is not clouded by Rhaetian mists, which Rhaetian wine belches up toward the head to dissolve into a flood of catarrh, while also laying, as it were, mud upon the stomach, more slowly digested than thick cabbage. Arbois, by contrast, generously drunk and followed by moderate sleep, sustains the stomach’s warmth with suitable tempering, removes harmful humours, and settles clouds caught in the brain into cheerful serenity. Forgive my pen for roaming somewhat freely, if only through dry recollection; it might perhaps have wandered farther and more eloquently into praise of this most excellent nectar had it not now been travelling in dry tracks. [Col. 1576A]

11. The Kalends of May had dawned, as I said. In order that divine rites might duly be performed, one part of the servants, with the most reverend lord vicar-general, went to the church which the Augustinian community had been accustomed to occupy from time immemorial; the other remained to guard the baggage. After the first party returned, I proceeded there with the rest. As I drew nearer to the church, I read above the door, written in golden letters, those words of the amazed Moses from the sacred text, Exodus 3:3: “I will go and see this great sight, why it is not burned.” At once I became my own interpreter: I mean that, amid the conflagration of war, this church alone had remained untouched, surviving the city’s ruins. Once I had investigated and learned the truth of the matter, I celebrated the sacred service with a much greater feeling of devotion.

At about its beginning, the importunate devotion of the abundant crowd flowing in had somewhat interrupted it. [Col. 1576B] For men and little children alike answered the opening prayers of the Mass which I led, as many ministers as hearers. When this was finished, we briefly fortified ourselves for the road with breakfast and set out toward Salins. Quite a few villages encountered on that day’s journey had suffered from the war a fate similar to Pontarlier’s. I pitied the great country estates burned and devastated, and at the same time turned my mind’s gaze to the happiness of our Switzerland. “Would that,” I said, “they might learn from this misery not to hate this happiness.” Such are the offspring of wars: not a simple calamity, but one that transmits mournful wretchedness even to posterity. Of once flourishing villages scarcely ten roofs remain, built from heaps of stone to shelter a few people; and even these are fashioned from the ruins themselves, without finish or form, and are no protection against cold, heat, or rain. May the supreme Deity will better things for our country; wretched would it be if, once scorched by this cruel plague, it were to change the hitherto unstained flower of peaceful beauty into a corpse and a pyre. [Col. 1576C]

12. At noon we were delayed in a village entirely like these, called Ala Vye. Some food was readily available, and I made up for the lack of wine. Warned at home that our journey would at times lead through places richer in want than in delicacies, I had made two small vessels out of thin sheet metal coated with tin, in the form of the cases in which small cavalry pistols are kept. I attached them to the saddle as though I had hung such martial tubes there against the ambushes of robbers. Together they held about three *metretæ*—measures, I think, as we call them—more or less. At Pontarlier I had filled them with Arbois wine, destined to be everyone’s spoil at this dinner. These vessels often served us in similar uses.

As the day was already declining toward evening, we entered the city of Salins, situated in the narrow space between two mountains, and spent what daylight remained in viewing the saltworks.

13. It is a most celebrated work, one which the poems of ancient poets [Col. 1576D] might deservedly have sung among the wonders of the world. Our most courteous host led us there. The principal saltworks lay about three hundred paces from the inn. A gate, guarded by several armed men, opened access to the enormous mass of buildings. There those intending to inspect the saltworks receive a token coin, which they must afterwards show to the man who exercises supreme authority over the workers. From the gate one ascends for about fifty paces, and the first door opens on the right. We were not permitted to enter it, because that part of the buildings was occupied only by women and a fixed law forbade the entry of men. As I departed, however, I saw a very long dining hall extending toward the innermost corners of the building. Through its middle ran a continuous line of fire, fed by coals and glowing with white heat; on each side of it, close about it, were arranged circular masses of boiled salt, to be burned by that heat to complete dryness, for they too glowed white.

Not far from there we stopped at another door, and the foreman of the workers, summoned by our host, was present. [Col. 1577A] Having inspected the token and learned from the host why we had come, a workman suddenly flew at my hat—it was new and made of better wool—pulled it beneath his own coat, and, in a comical exchange, set his own worn-out hat, stinking with filth, upon my head. Startled by the strangeness of the thing, I grew angry and, in hesitant, stammering, half-Latin and bad French words, cried out: “So, with open violence, may strangers protected by public good faith be plundered here with impunity while we look on?” As I considered saying more, our host interrupted me with laughter—though those words had already consumed the last farthing of my French resources—and, taking the hat which I had indignantly prepared to throw away, said: “No: he seeks not booty but to oblige you, taking care that, while we penetrate the hidden caverns, water dripping from the rock may not damage this handsome covering.”

The dispute thus settled, we followed our guide with a lantern down a stairway cut in the living rock, like the unbroken spiral of a snail’s shell. [Col. 1577B] Darkness, the horror of the cliffs, and the sound of falling waters filled me with anxious terror. I had scarcely traversed half the staircase when I began to doubt whether it were better to return or proceed. At length, with our hearts pounding amid blind footsteps, we reached the lowest steps. Here a bubbling liquid is received from the rock in a huge pit: either it falls directly into the pit from the neighbouring surrounding wall, or, carried through channels by cut arches, it fills the reservoir. Numerous springs are counted, dispersed here and there within the caverns, which the guide carefully pointed out. He also gave us salt-bitter water to taste in a glass and, not without amazement, showed us an abundant spring of sweet water only a single pace away.

We then returned by the spiral passage and approached the machine by which the briny liquid is conveyed from this deepest cavern to the upper levels. It consists of long straps of worked leather joined together into a continuous but elongated circuit, of such length that it reaches from the top of the building down to the bottom of the pit, and of such breadth that three and three troughs, or wooden vessels holding six or seven *metretæ*, can be continuously suspended in order. These straps rest above upon a windlass. By its revolution, the filled vessels, first immersed in the pit, rise; after passing over the wheel of the windlass, they turn themselves over and suitably discharge their transported liquid into prepared channels. [Col. 1577C] These channels in turn pour the water into an iron pan of vast capacity and circular form, suspended from many iron posts. Beneath it a trench shaped like a cross is filled with fires, burning day and night without any interruption, with such terrible heat that even more than eight paces away one feels its warmth strongly. Until then I had seen no fire which set more vividly before my eyes an image of the flames of hell kindled by divine justice for condemned mortals. “And this,” I thought, “what is it compared with that other most savage, eternal, inextinguishable fire, toward which we blind mortals hurry with a security too cruel for our own destruction, only one step—perhaps many steps—away from death?””

While these thoughts passed briefly through my mind, my companions were already standing at the other salt-pan. It was then resting from the fire. For the pans receive fire in alternating turns, never both at once; in so extensive a structure of iron plates, a corrosive substance, I suppose, not infrequently causes a defect, and in repairing it the heat must be reduced and the water drained off. Finally, after seeing the dining halls where the salt already boiled was stored in heaps, we again made for our lodging. [Col. 1577D]

14. The inn rises to a great height through many storeys. Climbing to its highest room in order to survey the city’s position, I wondered that a city so celebrated and rich from the salt trade was enclosed by so weak a wall, unequal even to light artillery fire. Yet nature had fortified it with her own defences, leaving by a remarkable winding of cliffs only two approaches to the city, where the narrow road between the mountains scarcely allows two travellers to pass together. [Col. 1578A]

The following day revealed this to us not without weariness. As we continued our journey, several troops of donkeys met us and repeatedly blocked those passes with their most troublesome slowness. We sometimes had to wait for a long while in some nook found off the road, until such a troop, containing more than eighty ears, gave us space to proceed. These long-eared animals, condemned to carry wood to the saltworks, each with its own cart, block the whole width of the road; they are either untrained or unable to yield, and would drag into ruin with themselves anyone who resisted. This nuisance occupied nearly three hours. At last, overcoming it and coming out upon the open plain, we gave our spirits free rein beneath the serene mildness of the sky. Yet it refreshed us with its pleasant face no farther than the place appointed for our dinner.

[Col. 1578B] 15. The village is called Chamblai, disfigured by ruins and still displaying from its wreckage the scars of war. While we gave ourselves here to dinner, a damp north wind filled the entire sky with clouds, and for four hours these poured rain upon us. The wind drove it against our sides with such violence that the water worked its way into the innermost folds of our clothes despite the cloaks we vainly held before us. This prolonged inundation and the assault of icy winds had drenched us in no slight discomfort. What increased this into indignation and anger was either the delay or the near injustice of the guards of the city of Dole. For they kept us wholly excluded from the city’s entrance and shelter for half an hour, alleging that no one could be admitted without the consent of the city’s governor.

Meanwhile the entire troop of guards came running up, as if a signal had been given to seize an enemy. As I observed, every eye was fixed upon that one carpet which the servants had spread over a horse appointed to carry baggage. This covering bore, in accordance with the common custom, the family arms of the most reverend lord vicar-general, painted by a Phrygian hand: yellow lilies gleaming from a blue ground. [Col. 1578C] Since French shields too are marked with this flower, those soldiers, judging our intentions from the horse-covering, charged our innocence with the crime of espionage through criminal suspicion. Although the most reverend lord repeatedly declared, without concealing his authority, that we were Swiss and that he was an abbot of the holy Cistercian Order among the Swiss, neither those sacred names nor the harshness of the weather pressing so heavily upon us could extort from them enough respect or compassion even to permit us to take shelter.

At length, better judgement prevailed: it freed the innocent lilies from the penalty of the rain and, having more than satisfied us with the wet Jupiter, admitted us within the walls. Taking an omen from such a contentious entrance, we chose the Golden Sword as our lodging.

16. Adam, the Reverend Father Georgius Millardet, Doctor of Sacred Theology and superintendent of the seminary at St Bernard in Dole, having been informed of our arrival, appeared immediately. Offering us his hand in greeting, this man distinguished among the few by courtesy, learning, and piety offered us his services, and performed them no less promptly than he had promised. For on the following day, the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross, at dawn he brought us to the convent of virgins consecrated to God under our Institute; and from there, after each of us in turn had performed the divine offices, to the seminary house. Having glanced over it as we passed, and tasted a cup of white wine—for this most healthfully takes the place of a breakfast offering—he entrusted us to two companions, under whose guidance we might avoid wandering astray through the city’s crossroads. [Col. 1578D]

17. At their urging we went straight to the great hospital. It rises beside the bank of the River Doubs with a lofty façade, in the splendid style of royal majesty. The entire mass extends into four equal sides of very great length, clad on every outer face with squared stone, without any visible coating of lime even at the joints. Above the first row of lofty windows there hangs a balcony, or stone gallery, fashioned by steel craftsmanship into varied forms, suited to the patients’ use, as they there relieve the discomforts of illness through fresher air and the cheerfulness of looking out. [Col. 1579A]

The interior structure presents two arches supporting one another and then many vaulted rooms on every side. Two of these, surpassing the others in size, held us for some time. They extend along two sides of the building, while the corner where both meet is occupied by a chapel, notable for its screens gleaming with gold and silver. On its altar the most august Body of the Lord is reserved, in a place so suitable that it is visible to the sick lying in the surrounding wards on either side, both for the consolation of sight and, in the final contest and struggle with death—or at other times when necessary—as heavenly food. Twenty beds arranged along the wall were adorned, according to the custom of that country but beyond the lot of such misery, with bright yellow curtains. One ward is occupied by men and the other by women, while the apt disposition prevents their seeing one another.

Everywhere there was such cleanliness that one would say that care for it alone, not care for the poor and sick, was practised here. Each bed had its occupant. Their faces, worn away by the wasting of illness and foul with pallid colour, forcibly compelled the hearts of visitors into fellowship with their pain. The eyes of those lying there, flashing from the hollows of their eyelids, confessed by an eloquent silence the torment hidden within their bodies, and rightly demanded tears from onlookers, as though they themselves had already exhausted all their own. Certainly, under the pretext of curiosity, I stood for some time apart from my companions at the railings enclosing the chapel, lest I should betray the shame of tears welling in my eyes. [Col. 1579B]

For when I had cast my eyes sideways toward the beds in the other ward, I saw there a matron of the highest nobility—as the attendance of servants and the apparel showed—sitting beside the bed of a poor woman and feeding her most precious foods from her lap with such readiness and cheerfulness as if she were pouring sweet wine into her own dearest child. She wiped away, as though it were balm, the discharge flowing from ulcers that tore the sick woman’s cheeks, without the least sign of horror or nausea. She strengthened the afflicted woman by the affectionate tenderness of her manner and the sweetness of her address; finally, she lavished delicacies, money, and ointments upon her. Thus, with a singular feeling of devotion, I judged that I truly beheld here a Magdalene serving Christ the Saviour in this suffering member. [Col. 1579C]

Persons of every rank are received into this hospital without distinction, and the same charity embraces the miseries of all. But what astonished me most was that a small number of virgins, bound by vow to this most excellent service, manage the entire domestic labour. One of them first led us away from the heated room of the sick—lest we should feel horror at the imminent opening of a certain most foul ulcer—to other rooms. These are constructed separately for individual persons, should some more distinguished citizen or someone of patrician family wish to entrust himself to them, as she reported frequently occurred, so that they might recover more quickly when separated from other strangers.

Beside the principal entrance to the building is the apothecary’s shop, where the virgins themselves prepare with their own hands ointments, liquids, and everything, simple or compounded, which physicians’ skill has devised for curing diseases. They preserve these in vessels, cabinets, and glass containers finished with every elegance, equally ready and skilled to dispense, with ingenious dexterity, their antidotes against poisons and their remedies for pains. They are indeed worthy to be preferred, by the whole heaven’s breadth, to all other women’s establishments throughout the world. [Col. 1579D]

18. Having delighted for a whole hour in this spectacle, we then gathered outside the walls another and likewise most ample matter for admiration. Roaming through the city’s fortifications, we wiped away the sadness touching our hearts and the melancholy brought from the hospital with the freedom of jesting. [Col. 1580A] Let my pen, therefore, seized by so mighty a compulsion to marvel, likewise balance itself a little and stride, in triumphant swelling, above the common manner of proceeding.

Truly, when I cast my eyes upon those fortifications, I was immediately lifted by a force greater than, I thought, human into the agreeable boldness of figurative language. I therefore unearthed Ovid’s fabulous war of heaven; and I asked my companions whether the Titans had hurled these fragments of mountains here while they were shattering Ossa and Olympus. For it did not belong to men of inferior and common stature to heap up masses so great. I also did not vainly suspect that Daedalus’ hand had been present in a work which, like a labyrinth, is drawn around through the manifold wanderings of its turns and is terrible even with its brazen Minotaurs. “Why then,” I said, “should I now refrain from laughing at the rashness of that fleeing commander, whom five times five years ago sacrificed several thousand of his men to this monster?”

The walls rising to their greatest height also spread ample terror. They do not shine as though shaved with a razor and coated with plaster; rather, their face, as it were drawn into harsh wrinkles, breathes martial rage and strength through the rawness of unpolished stones. And as though they still raged from the blows of artillery against the walls, they proudly display their scars—which I compared to the spots of skin gnawed by an eruptive disease—though they are slight and not worthy of being called cracks, much less blemishes. Seven bastions project like seven missiles from the circuit of the walls, so looking toward one another for mutual assistance that, from every side, two keep watch for the defence of one. Finally, the depth of the ditch, equal to the top of a tower and showing how great a grave it might become for soldiers, did not permit the eyes, throbbing with alarm, to look upon it for long. [Col. 1580B]

19. Meanwhile the kindness of the lord steward summoned us to dinner, which he had generously provided at the seminary. The first course had been removed when I began to ask my table companion, who had been placed beside me, what mystery that painting contained which I had observed hanging at the church doors in the middle of the city. In suitable colours the artist had depicted a sacred Host, gleaming amid a splendour of rays—the Host used by Catholic priests when, by the power of the divine words, the substance of bread having been expelled, they bring the most holy Body of the Lord under that outward form and expose it to the people for adoration, usually enclosed in crystal and adorned around with golden ornaments.

Pleased by my curiosity, he replied: “There endures there a miracle than which France has scarcely seen a more illustrious.”

“What sort of miracle?” I asked.

“Then,” he said, “as I suppose, you have no knowledge of an event so worthy; I shall therefore briefly relate it to you from the beginning. At the monastery of Faverney, where monks live by the rule of St Benedict, a few leagues from Dole, during the feast of Pentecost that divine mystery whose image the painting displays was exposed during the day to the countless multitude of faithful streaming in from the neighbourhood. And when, in the year of salvation 1608, Pentecost fell upon 25 May, and in the evening burning wax, through the negligence of the sacristan, caught the framework which had been erected in the middle of the altar in the form of a shrine for holding the divine pledge, and the spreading flame reduced all the ornaments of the altar to ashes: that single silver vessel—marvellous to say!—containing God hidden beneath the appearance of bread escaped unharmed. The fire not only did not engulf it, but left it suspended high in the open air above the altar. Such an open and astonishing prodigy could not long be concealed in silence, before the very great concourse of people, having taken in the truth with their own eyes, spread it throughout all the surrounding regions; many drawn by curiosity, more by devotion, to the novelty of so great an event.

“On the already remarkable Tuesday—for it had remained unmoved until then—a certain priest of great probity came from the neighbouring village with all the people entrusted to him, proceeding to this sacred church in the customary order of procession, as we call it. At the altar, first cleared of ashes, he celebrated Mass in the presence of a crowd exceeding all count. As they watched, about the middle of Mass, he raised above his head in the customary manner the Host he had consecrated, for the people to adore. And behold: at the same moment that other Host, which had survived the fire and hung in the air, rose upward through an equal distance; then, after pausing briefly, it followed the priest’s descending hand and, with the gentlest motion, placed itself upon the book lying on the altar. So that so evident a sign of divine mercy should not be drawn either into dispute and mockery by ill-wishers or into oblivion by the ungrateful, Ferdinand de Rye, then bishop of Besançon, committed the entire sequence of events to a public record for posterity, on the sworn testimony of very many witnesses. And in the same year, around the feast of St Thomas, he ordered another of those Hosts—for the vessel had contained two—to be carried to Dole with the greatest solemnity. It remains whole to this day and is displayed there, where you noticed that painting.”

20. After thanking him for his elegant account, I rapidly reviewed the whole story in my mind, that so memorable a monument might be more firmly impressed upon it. Astonished at the deep silence which followed in me, he asked whether I had sufficiently understood what he had said.

“More than sufficiently,” I replied; “and I have fixed it in my memory never to be erased. Would that our sectarians, darkened in mind, would open the eyes of their understanding to the brightness of so manifest a light! They rise up against this most evident truth with an insanity altogether more than frantic. For what mystery of faith did God, incarnate Truth, more zealously commend, establish more clearly, or confirm more brilliantly? In the earliest centuries, although some more difficult doctrines were subjected to controversy by the unlearned, the world nevertheless produced no madness so brazen as to rise to the audacity of detracting from so great a truth. And how many witnesses, in every succeeding age, have been added! Men, surely, who gained for themselves immortality on earth by innocence of life and the glory of learning—and now, without doubt, enjoy it in heaven. By contrast, those who in these latter centuries have been the authors of extinguishing this light, if the gods please, have left no other subject for an account of their lives than filth, wantonness, and unspeakable crimes. Who of sound mind can doubt whether we should assent to these men or to those?

“And moreover, these people bring against us no weapons other than a confession of their ignorance. ‘This thing cannot occur,’ they say; ‘it cannot be comprehended that that immeasurable God, of infinite greatness, should lie hidden beneath so small a particle of bread, be eaten, and be adored.’ Very well. If the hidden things of the divine sacraments must not be believed unless they can be touched, what subject matter will you assign to faith? By manifest and palpable demonstration, tell me the causes and method by which the deity produces, feeds, and preserves throughout the whole world innumerable flies, ants, and creatures of that kind. If you can do this for even one, you will be a great Apollo to me; but, I know, you will not do it even for a louse. And in things so trivial and placed in a condition most abject and beneath your noble station, you will of course bring the light of a mole to bear upon the sun of faith; and, above Paul’s teaching, you will remove the veil of enigma before the happier other life grants the capacity of beholding face to face.”

21. While we philosophized with our whole ardour upon this sublime knowledge, the completion of dinner reminded us that we must resume our journey. Therefore, after giving deserved thanks and warmly praising the charity of the Fathers of the seminary toward us, we set out, accompanied by the lord provost and his companion, proceeding as far as Auxonne: a town not altogether uncultivated, at the edge of the French duchy of Burgundy, strongly fortified and additionally secured by an excellent castle.

But Auxonne will experience in this description the same fortune that I experienced in seeing it. Entering at sunset and departing before sunrise, I could scarcely observe anything memorable except something which made me laugh in the kitchen with prophetic wit. For there a piece of veal was roasting by the fire, turned in swift rotation. Since I could nowhere discover a mechanism furnished with wheels mutually interlocked by the sharpness of their teeth and sharing the motion of a weight through the sequence of wheels—the kind of mechanism, of course, used in our country—suddenly, when a brighter flame sprang up, I saw a wheel made of boards suspended behind the hearth. From its hollow there was indeed a noise, but not the sharp creaking customarily made by wheels. After I had long remained uncertain, the cook at last resolved my doubt. For when the fire had sufficiently penetrated the meat, soon to become a dish for the table, the spit stopped at a single whistle from him; and immediately a dog leapt out of that wooden cavity, solving the riddle of my ignorance and making me laugh at the same time.

When the Most Reverend [father] saw this, he asked what novelty I had observed. I said: “That Roman poet, with his four verses beginning *Thus you, not for yourselves*, would without doubt have added a fifth if he had also lodged at Auxonne. He would certainly have written:

> Thus you, not for yourselves, dogs turn the roast.”

After he learned the occasion of the verse, he approved the wit with a slight laugh and added that it was nothing new to him, dogs claiming this labour as their own through almost all France. We then devoured the food set before us amid the merriment caused by this tale. After a peaceful night, before the sun’s rays struck the highest mountain peaks, we had already covered a league. Having gained an hour’s shade among the thickets, we proceeded very easily, refreshed alike by the coolness of dawn and shadow. And because the plain beneath, then drained by the Saône in thinner streams, afforded us a dry road—whereas otherwise we would have had to continue for half an hour upon a stone-paved way. The inhabitants have raised that road above the ground upon a continual embankment, so that when the river, overflowing its bank, turns the fields into pools, travellers do not lack a safe means of passage.

Then, entering open fields and receiving the sky with the rising sun, we feared that oppressive solar heat would torment us. But a wind from the south suddenly fell upon us with such bitter cold that we immediately untied and put on the cloaks previously fastened to the saddles. For four hours we were battered by that dreadful and intolerable torment; I do not believe that the past winter ever grew cold with so savage a harshness. The stubborn evil admitted no remedy until our lodging at Dijon, called *À la Cloche* (“The Bell”), refreshed us with shelter and fire.

22. Our horses carried us not directly to this inn, however, but first to the residence of the most illustrious lord general. His servants tied the horses outside the courtyard to rings attached to the wall. We ourselves at once obtained access to the lord general, who allowed us merely to perform the duty of greeting after he learned that, already fasting, we had completed a journey of six leagues amid the torment of such cold. Having courteously asked us about the success of our journey, he brought us down from his chamber into the courtyard. Ordering our servants to go before with the horses to the inn, he had the carriage he himself ordinarily used brought out and wished us to be conveyed in it to our lodging.

After giving thanks for such condescension, we reached the inn in rapid course. Not without joy did we praise the honour shown us by the most illustrious lord general—an honour which we knew with certainty had fallen to no one else. I silently considered what I might infer from this gracious outpouring of kindness. And when the Most Reverend lord vicar left me alone, occupied in prayer, while the household was engaged in preparing dinner, I ventured to compare the carriage of Mordecai in Sacred History with our own. Nothing occurred to me which failed to support the aptness of the comparison, except the absence of Haman. Yet I perceive that in this comparison of histories I have almost written you a riddle, unless I briefly explain from what source this royal favour toward Mordecai flowed. Receive, then, the matter briefly from its genuine foundation.

23. From its earliest institution our sacred Order set before itself as its model of life the rigorous austerity of the most ancient Fathers dwelling in Egypt and other deserts, who lived only on herbs and cold water. Thus, for a long time, the eating of meat was abolished among the first monks of the Order, according to the norm of the Benedictine Rule to which we profess obedience; and, beyond this, every kind of food not prescribed by the utmost severity and extreme necessity. Clothing was almost nonexistent, or was coarse stuff made of wool and bristles; patched garments alone were esteemed and used. Intending, indeed, to fight with effective remedies against the dangers of vices, they imposed upon themselves laws of such severity—just as, when we have taught wild beasts to become tame, we also remove the sharpness of their teeth and claws, lest, should they return to their nature, an opportunity readily arise for them to rage. So they completely disarmed the itch of desires, rooted deeply in corrupted nature, by this most simple poverty and their voluntary contempt and neglect of themselves.

But just as such pursuits generally have their greatest force in their first onset and gradually grow languid as time advances, so, when the Order had already spread into various regions and developed differing modes of life, men began to fear that the austerity which had raised up the newborn Order would soon smother it even to extinction, unless, by removing the burden of severity, room were given for breathing. The Apostolic See was therefore asked to permit some relaxation of those very strict laws. Various privileges were obtained, by which the monks were treated more leniently in matters of food.

Yet as indulgence is fatal to genuine virtue, so in various places not only were those extremes of rigour abandoned, but this corruption gradually spread into the remaining laws as well. Thus, with the subsequent misfortune of wars and sects, the Order lost very much of its original splendour. Nevertheless, there were not lacking men distinguished for learning and piety who sought to raise this light, as it were, from its own ashes. Others joined them, drawn by reputation or patronage; but in some cases an unequal prudence of zeal and a premature method of advancing the undertaking delayed its success. For many wished that, after cutting away those privileges by which the favour of the supreme pontiffs had exempted the Order from the rule of abstaining from meat and from other burdens, that crude severity—condemned to the darkness of the cloister—should be restored to the Order without any relaxation.

These efforts were everywhere received with applause. In both the Roman and Parisian courts, moreover, very ample support was furnished to such piety, which bore the not insignificant title of reform; so that it was nearly permitted them alone to be Cistercians, while those who continued to enjoy the use of the privileges were all but excluded from participation in the Order’s name and dignities. Meanwhile no one dared openly resist, since these men, having everywhere preoccupied judgment, had brought matters to such a pass that it was regarded as a great crime even to doubt, much less dispute, the justice of their cause. Yet the controversy remained undecided for many years, all the courts inclining considerably in favour of those who defended abstinence. In the meantime, the minds of many were troubled, uncertain whether they might safely continue using the privileges.

To resolve that doubt, at least for his own province, the Most Reverend lord vicar general of Switzerland, learning that the magnificent Catholic cantons were preparing an embassy to Alexander VII, Roman pontiff, hurried to Lucerne—for business was then detaining him at Bern—and secured the insertion among the instructions given by that magistracy to the ambassadors of the following charge: that the Catholic cantons of Switzerland should ask from the most holy See the favour that those privileges concerning abstinence from eating meat might be confirmed for the monasteries of the Cistercian Order in their province. These prayers did not lack happy success. For the privilege was renewed with the force of supreme authority not only for the Swiss but for the whole Order.

When this had been communicated to the most illustrious Father General, he hastened without delay to the city of Rome. Received with the highest honour by the supreme pontiff, he ascribes to these Swiss letters, as to their source and gateway, whatever goodwill, favour, honour, and grace he experienced there. From this flowed toward us the very ample distinction mentioned above, which, as you will hear, was thereafter to prove fruitful in no ordinary advances. Indeed, scarcely two hours had passed when the most illustrious Father General himself came upon us unexpectedly, together with the Most Reverend lord procurator of the Order, to see whether our lodging afforded us the comfort which he judged due to so welcome a guest. The master of the house was pleased because he had just moved us from a poorer dining room to a somewhat more respectable one. After a most courteous conversation of one hour, they returned to their carriage and residence.

24. On the next day, about the sixth morning hour, the most illustrious Father General made himself readily available to us for the exposition of our business. We did not, however, enjoy his presence longer than until the same carriage carried him away to the royal senate of Burgundy. Hearing that every person was admitted there without distinction, we immediately followed.

Not far from the court—otherwise called, in a half-French expression, the “Parliament House”—I supposed that we had stopped in order to go to a church. For, since there was only one row of windows, I could not discern any stories from the construction of the windows. Then we climbed a narrow stairway into a gallery capable of holding about eight persons, from which, as from a watchtower, we freely viewed the place. First, I praised the remarkable craftsmanship of the painted window glass; yet I did not like the darkness which the colours cast into the otherwise very spacious hall. But the ceiling bore away the prize for beauty, at least in my judgment, hanging over the senators like a heaven. Elegant carvings adorn it with various shields and emblems, so harmoniously distinguished by gold and colours that, besides their majesty, they confer an incomparable splendour upon the place. The gold seemed not so much laid upon the panels by a painter’s art as melted by goldsmith’s hand and fire and applied in sheets of bronze.

The front part of the court is filled with many seats and benches. Those attached to the walls rise in four tiers, the uppermost serving as seats for the senators, or parliamentarians. The president of the senate occupies not a place in the middle of the wall but at a corner, the others following in order along the two walls extending from it. He himself stands out in a red gown and square cap, which we call *biretta*. The others likewise wear black cloaks falling to the feet, with broad sleeves extending to the knees, and black *birettas*. The advocates have the same form of dress. A large throng of them occupies its benches at the back of the hall. We heard two of them argue for an hour, with such exertion of voice, such gesticulation, and finally such rapidity of tongue that nothing troubled me more than that I caught the words alone, without their sense. They frequently interspersed whole passages from Latin works of jurisprudence, from which I understood what was being litigated. After the advocates had argued sufficiently on both sides, all are dismissed; the senators alone decide the suit by a judgment delivered collectively.

Here I recall to your mind, if perhaps you have read in our breviaries or other books the title of our most illustrious Father General, which among other titles describes him as first councillor to the Most Christian King in the supreme senate of Burgundy. This, indeed, is the senate of which I spoke, in which the first place after the president places him among the senators. Nor was it merely his position: his bodily bearing excelled all others. His particularly tall stature and the rest of his bodily proportion harmonized most becomingly with a countenance full of majesty. Above all, the shining grey hair of his lofty head made him at once admirable and venerable, an ornament of senatorial dignity worthier than every adornment of clothing.

25. From this court, a long street led to our lodging. Numerous shops, rich in every kind of merchandise, lined it on both sides; and not a few inn-signs, hanging from the first row of windows, offered a pleasing spectacle to one taking in everything at once. Yet I had expected far better structures of buildings. The greater part consists of timber framing; they fill the spaces between the beams with wickerwork and material woven from hedges, then coat it with lime and clay. You would believe that entire walls of solid stone stood there, unless in places the binding material loosened by age and rain revealed the bare wood.

We also entered the thresholds of several churches, of which there are more than twelve. We found them large indeed, but little finished. The high altar contains almost all the ornament of the whole church; the darkness of the other parts, spiders’ webs, and neglected ornament everywhere place these sacred buildings far beneath the industrious devotion of Germany, whose churches are prepared for the honour of God in a fashion rivaling the heavenly dwellings, no expense diverting minds devoted to true religion from their endeavours to adorn sacred things.

The chief church here is St Benignus’s, displaying the devotion of earlier ages in its immense arches. In its forecourt, a remarkable mass of building suspends, by countless columns, a triple vaulted structure—one vault pressing upon another—for purposes I cannot determine. The mechanism of the clock is also noteworthy: it always prefaces the hour with a melody played by the music of little bells, and then indicates the hour more loudly by a hammer striking the largest bell.

Having wandered through most of the city in this way, we finally visited, a little before noon, the Most Reverend lord abbot of Clairvaux. The house in which we found him is called “Little Clairvaux,” just as that of the most illustrious lord general is called “Little Cîteaux.” The most pious prelate embraced us warmly. Ordering the Most Reverend lord vicar general to sit, he detained him in friendly conversation for an hour. He extended the same condescension to us, who stood bareheaded in the middle, as propriety required. He made up for the slowness of his feet—which the torture of gout grievously afflicted—by the sweetness of his speech, which he poured forth toward us so graciously that I reverently perceived in the successor of the mellifluous Father Bernard a revived grace of affections entering our hearts with a penetrating sense of love.

Meanwhile a glass full of white wine was brought, and he compelled us with welcome force to taste it. For although its exceptionally noble fragrance, which would have invited even an unwilling man, had not overcome our modest reserve, yet, having heard its most holy name—for he said it was St Bernard’s wine—we could not put forward evasions in excuse. Having tasted it sparingly, we returned to our lodging.

26. I spent the morning running through the remaining parts of the city, accompanied by the chamberlain and the keeper of the stables. Along with me, they praised Dijon’s excellent fortifications, though they preferred those of Dole—not in size, but in strength and workmanship. We also passed with interest several handsome residences of great men, popularly called palaces.

Nor did a stimulus for hearty laughter fail us because of the foolish vanity of the women there. When first I observed it, I suspected that I had stumbled either upon Bacchanalian rites or perhaps upon Ethiopian or Arabian barbarian women. For not infrequently women came toward us whose faces, covered with masks of black silk, resembled a spectre blacker than every cooking pot rather than a human being. Astonished at the exceedingly amusing sight and greeting it with laughter, I said: “A pious invention, if women by this art erase the lure of the brow.” But my companions affirmed that another cause lay beneath it: namely, that the beauty and fairness of the face might not be spoiled by sun or dust; they supposed that only beautiful women thus took precautions for themselves.

Later, however, a certain woman revealed another use, and a completely contrary one, when she removed her mask beneath the entrance of her house. She was so ugly, wrinkled, and livid with bile that, if her hair had taken on the form of serpents, I do not know whether this Moorish Gorgon would not have turned us to stone. At least they wish to make us believe that something lies beneath this masked arrogance; or perhaps by this funereal display they perform obsequies for beauty already dead. Many inhabitants of Dijon attend to the array of their other clothes with the same delirium, as I learned from trustworthy report—namely, in order to cover the misery of hunger and domestic poverty.

27. We squandered no fewer than two hours on this walk. Returning from there to our lodging and supper, the Most Reverend lord abbot of Lucelle, Lord Bernardinus, arrived. He had reached Dijon at that very hour and, having paid a greeting to the Most Reverend lord vicar general while passing through, had found convenient lodgings in our neighbourhood. While we escorted him to the threshold of our house, four string-players appeared, eager to season our supper with their art. They would not endure refusal. We ordered them to remain at the door of our dining room and listened for a quarter of an hour, judging unanimously that they deserved to be heard longer. Therefore, to sharpen their fingers, we anointed them with an honourable gift; having received it, they immediately vanished.

They had adorned their art with marvelous concord and sweetness of strings. With a tremulous vibration of their fingers, they most skillfully expressed rapid leaps and lingering phrases. Then a higher voice sang out those sounds with alternating attack and descent; the lower strings returned them in a thicker murmur by elegant imitation. Thus, in rival alternation, they mingled as it were quarrels and embraces; thus they varied harsh and soft sounds with marvelous modulation.

The following day associated those same musicians with us to better effect. For, while quite early we were conducting our business with the Most Reverend lord procurator in Little Cîteaux, the Most Reverend lord abbot of Clairvaux saw us, and a carriage already ready was carrying him thence to his house. Summoning the Most Reverend lord vicar general to himself, he indicated in few words, but words powerful with most effective kindness, that nothing would be more welcome to him from us than if we honoured his table at the approaching dinner with our presence. Nor did he allow us time to prepare an excuse; rather, immediately, by the open service of his servants, he took us into the carriage and carried us with him to his Clairvaux.

28. To pass the time remaining until dinner, the secretary of Clairvaux invited us into the garden, for the Most Reverend [lord vicar general] had gone upstairs to the dining room with the lord abbot. As we readily agreed, he pleasantly poured out an erudite first course of conversation, discoursing elegantly on many matters concerning his most famous valley and nearly all France; finally he asked us about the condition of our country and monasteries. It did not seem right to disappoint the desire for knowledge of so excellent a man. Therefore I said that, if he would not be troubled to listen to me briefly, I would bring forward whatever my sudden and unprepared memory suggested.

Then, being told to begin, I said: “The name Maris Stella, ‘Star of the Sea,’ was born upon the sea, from dangers and propitious light, which saved the illustrious Count Henry of Rapperswil while he was bearing arms against the Saracens. On his return, the angry sea tossed him about for several days in such a manner that, ignorant of where in the world he was, he awaited shipwreck and death at every moment. Dense mists had also taken away the whole sky. Therefore, all human hope abandoned and his mind raised toward heaven, he made a vow to the Virgin Mother, the holy Lady: if she would help him and rescue him from the waves by an outstretched hand, he would consecrate in his dominion a monastery of the Cistercian family under her most august name.

“The Queen of mercy, readily inclined to the prayers of the wretched, did not long delay assistance. That very night she showed from heaven a star of unusual size and brightness, as though a messenger of salvation. Directing his ship’s course toward that Cynosure, he reached harbour safe and sound within a few days. In memory of so great a benefit, he then built a monastery and gave it the name of Blessed Mary of the Star of the Sea. There afterwards the founder himself, after the death of his wife on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, lived a celibate life for nineteen years and received a burial-place in the chapter house, adorned with an epitaph not elegant indeed, but expressive of the pious simplicity of that age. I have copied it into my notebook, if you would like me to read it. It runs thus:

> May the founder, illustrious in blood, be dear to those above.  
> He crossed the seas; with the sword he attacked the pagans.  
> Returning victorious, wearied by the contest of the world,  
> He founded, enriched, and magnificently endowed a cloister  
> With gifts; and, endowing it, with twice a thousand marks; adorning it  
> With six hundred, one hundred, twice fifteen, and eight marks.  
> Receive this man devoted wholly to you, merciful King.  
> May he escape punishment and proceed to heavenly joys;  
> May he rejoice and delight in the embrace of the Bridegroom;  
> Made fit for heaven, may he be blessed in reality without end.  
> In the year one thousand, two hundred, twice thirteen, and one,  
> Count Henry, sprung from noble blood,  
> Founded the cloister, but received eternal rewards,  
> In the year one thousand, two hundred, and forty-six.

“Thus Maris Stella was founded in the year 1227 after heaven had been restored to humankind, and so ample an endowment was bestowed upon it—especially enlarged by the not negligible gifts of the counts of Habsburg, Kyburg, and others; besides those of the nobles of Tillengen, Strettlingen, Mandach, Hettlingen, Schonewert, Warta, Klingen, and Wartenfels. Several persons from these families are buried in the monastery. Consequently, unless the various injuries of time had almost wholly consumed it, Maris Stella might doubt whether there were many monasteries throughout Germany which it would permit to compare themselves with it.

“For, to say nothing of the fires—two of which, in the years of Christ 1448 and 1507, it suffered to the point of utter ruin; nothing of lawsuits, those moths of worldly goods, in which it was almost always entangled with immense loss; and, finally, nothing of whole villages and very extensive rights formerly sold at a most unworthy price, especially while the Swiss were freeing themselves from servitude into liberty—the single devouring Hydra of heresy was sufficient to have overthrown it completely, as was the fate of monasteries in Switzerland and elsewhere. But the most powerful protectress chose to provide better for her clients. She preserved at least the sacred house of her lord sound and intact, although stripped of the greater part of its inhabitants and possessions. After these troubles she gave it abbots most worthy of praise, who through the remarkable industry of many years restored Maris Stella to such honour that it may deservedly congratulate itself and the Order upon its good fortune.

“For, besides lay brothers, it maintains no fewer than forty religious assigned to choir, applying themselves to the studies of theology, philosophy, and humane letters amid exact observance of the divine office. Yet meanwhile it generously expends every week no fewer than twelve measures of grain upon needy people who come to the gate solely for aid. Maris Stella enjoys a pleasant and most healthful site. Toward the east it looks upon Zurich, the foremost city of Switzerland; opposite lies Baden, a town famous for the fortifications of its newly built and very strong castle, for the diet of the cantons, and for its hot springs. On both sides it is enclosed: here by the Jura, most fruitful in vineyards, and there by Mount Claremont, green with thickets and fir trees. These two slopes form a valley through whose middle flows the fish-rich Limmat, carrying many smaller vessels. It curves around Maris Stella toward the north and west in such a way as almost to make it an island, leaving only a small space by which it joins the mainland.

“Maris Stella produced Salemius as its first abbot, with twelve religious. From him the present Most Reverend lord Gerard Burgisser, born in the nearby town of Bremgarten, the thirtieth in number, presides with happy government. All the buildings of the monastery, in the fashion of our age—which hates darkness—admit the free light of the sun into every corner, especially the church, distinguished by the cheerful splendour of translucent glass and the whiteness of plaster. The choir stalls, carved of oak, are renowned for exceptional workmanship. Two organs also animate the music—one of them quite large—which among us receives principal love and care.

“On the left side of the outer church is seen the tomb of Albert I, Emperor of the Romans. When in the year of Christ 1308 he was killed at Windisch, by the river Reuss, by his nephew John at the instigation of certain nobles, he received burial at Maris Stella for one year and three months; then, by command of Henry VII, he was transferred to Speyer, to the other emperors. The church’s surrounding enclosure, no less elaborate, displays in elegant workmanship plaster images of Cistercian monks who flourished either in ecclesiastical rank or holiness. Innocent X, Supreme Pontiff, also enriched Maris Stella’s sacred treasury of relics fifteen years ago, granting relics from Rome of Saints Marianus and Getulius. They now adorn a most beautiful altar and are revered by a great concourse of people because of the miracles by which they are very frequently made famous. Finally, it possesses fairly extensive territorial rights; free from the burdensome favours of advocacies, it honours eight senior cantons with the title of protectors and with an annual acknowledgment.”

29. He received with most eager ears many other matters concerning our Switzerland, sprinkled into these conversations: for example, the slaughter inflicted by Catholics upon the Bernese at Villmergen, and the ancient victories of those same Catholics over various enemies. He did so until he learned that the signal had been given for table. The table was furnished so splendidly that the Most Reverend prelate himself confessed that these feasts owed their cost neither to custom nor necessity, but to our honour.

The table abounded in varied delights of fragrance and flavour, but above all my eyes were drawn to pears of exotic size, as large as both my hands joined together at the finger joints. They still possessed such fresh appearance that in this full-grown spring they seemed to breathe the recent autumn. Surely only the distance of the place restrained me from carrying home one or two of these fruits as curiosities. The arrival of many people, said to be waiting outside to speak with the Most Reverend lord of Clairvaux, ended dinner after a sitting of about two hours.

30. We therefore resolved, after offering words of due gratitude, to go out to the Most Reverend lord abbot of Pontigny, whom the bonds of gout likewise kept in his house. There, admitted without delay, he showed himself very friendly toward us. Among other not obscure signs of kindness, he asked us to visit his Pontigny, affirming that we would never regret the journey. The sacred remains—indeed, the sacred body—of St Edmund, he said, were preserved there, a treasure than which France plainly knows none more wonderful. For those holy limbs had hitherto undergone no change in appearance since death other than if they had been deserted by the soul eight days ago or fewer, though the body had remained whole and incorrupt for more than four hundred and twenty years.

Our pious curiosity was so kindled by this conversation that we nearly promised to go to Pontigny. Yet, having given an uncertain reply, we returned to our lodging, where we found six flasks of Bernardine liquor sent to us by the Most Reverend lord of Clairvaux. Thereafter they sufficed us, until our departure, as a medicinal breakfast and a delicacy.

31. The seventh day of May had dawned, inviting us into the countryside with a most welcome brightness. Therefore, at the very hour when the sun emerged from night’s darkness, we passed beyond the gates, intending to visit Fontaines Castle, from which that most splendid sun of the Order—indeed, of the whole world—Bernard arose. This castle, together with the village beneath it bearing the same name, was already in view, being situated not far from the city walls. Standing upon the summit of a hill, it commands a most delightful prospect over all the broad surrounding country. From the city of Dijon the fields gradually rise for half an hour’s journey, until immediately below the castle the slope ascends more sharply to the heights, inviting [Col. 1589A] crowds of visitors alike to the pleasure of curiosity and of devotion.

This birthplace of extraordinary holiness had always flourished in the celebrated veneration of its inhabitants; but some years earlier the liberality of Louis XIII, King of France, greatly increased its distinction. In 1619 he built there a magnificent monastery for the Cistercians of the stricter observance, of the Congregation of Feuillants; it still entirely awaits the final hand of completion. Arriving there, we found the Reverend Lord Abbot of Camp des Lys, from Austria, who had come by carriage a little before us and had begun the sacred rites as we crossed the church threshold. He was at the altar which now occupies the place where St Bernard came forth from the womb of his devout mother into this light of mortality.

Having learned from a religious Father of the place of this eminent privilege of the altar, I delayed my own devotions until the said prelate had completed the sacred service. Meanwhile two other altars served the Most Reverend Vicar-General and his companion as they celebrated Mass. At last, having found an opportunity for my own devotion, I offered at the aforesaid altar the unbloody sacrifice in honour of the most holy Father: it was he who had made that place precious by his birth.

When all had completed their devotions, we were led through the monastery and Bernard’s paternal home. We congratulated ourselves upon our good fortune in walking through this most noble garden of celebrated virtues, from which so many excellent shoots of holiness had sprung. With curious eyes I traced the footsteps of the innocent child, and said: “Here, surely, in this dining-room his most loving mother spread a bed for her sweet little boy; here she set his table, here his toys. Here, as a little child, he built tiny altars from little images and raised his small hands to the stars. In these corners he turned prayer-beads, counting his prayers. Here he hung upon his mother’s breast for drops of milk; there upon her lips, as she instilled piety into him. Finally, he slipped out through this door when he secretly lavished upon the poor the small coins he had greedily scraped together.”

[Col. 1589C]

32. While I was cursorily reflecting on such things, my companions urged our return, for the day was already declining toward noon. Yet we did not wish to retrace the same road, but, turning to the right, made directly for the Charterhouse. It is distinguished, and, if anything else is, most deserving of inspection. In accordance with the force of the rules they observe, the Carthusians favour dark churches; this one, however, because of its size and windows, has much light. It possesses a very great elegance and abundance of paintings.

The choir is adorned with enormous cast-brass candelabra; and a large eagle of the same workmanship occupies the centre, raised up to support the choir-books. Yet, however rare and elegant these things may be, they are far surpassed by two monuments there: the mausoleums of the Dukes of Burgundy. Whether the matter be art or value, I assign to them the highest estimation among all the things which I have been permitted to examine either elsewhere or on this journey.

Alabaster, carved into manifold artistic forms, comes very near to silver in softness through the fineness of the sculptural work, [Col. 1589D] especially in the figures of the dukes buried there. In them I might almost say that nature has been overcome by art. Indeed, the folds of the garments and the hollows of the drapery falling one into another could not have been arranged more skilfully even by the garment itself. Then the features of the faces, aided by the pallor of the stone conspiring in the service of art, represented so vividly traces of life not yet wholly consumed as it fled the body, that you would have called them not statues but bodies bound in gentle sleep.

The ground upon which these tombs rest supports an immense structure of variegated marble. Upon it stand innumerable figures clothed in the countenances of mourners, as though bearing on their shoulders the upper stone and the effigies of the dukes placed upon it. They have experienced the artist’s hand with such care that each draws its brow and limbs into distinct clouds of grief, different from those of every other. Now the unbroken slab of marble resting upon this lesser troop of weepers—twelve feet long, six wide, and more than a palm thick—shines with the brightness of a mirror, reflecting like glass [Col. 1590A] the figures lying above and the faces of those who look upon it.

The cloister adjoining the church extends for one hundred and fifty paces along its four equal sides. It has attached cells suitable for the followers of that institute, no fewer than seventy; none lacks a well, a garden, a workshop, and two other dining-rooms. After the prior of the place had shown us some of these, we hastened back to Dijon for dinner by a beautiful road, through flower-smiling meadows and the shade of trees.

33. Although excessive heat had inflamed the morning hours, we nevertheless resolved to tour the city again. After walking for some time along the walls, we felt a desire to visit the orphanage, which was said not to be unworthy of our curiosity. Thus admitted without difficulty, we looked for the hospital at Dôle, but found nearly everything inferior.

The building itself is very spacious, divided without any ornament into many workshops and dining-rooms. Some are filled with cradles and the cries of infants; others contain boys and grown youths, who labour partly at various crafts and partly in cleansing wool and then preparing it for spinning and weaving. In another part of the house we encountered several little girls, eight or nine years old, as I suppose, who arranged wool dyed in various colours into elegant pictures with the needle. This house brings up more than two hundred foundlings and orphaned children of this sort. Until they have grown to a proper age, they are trained in the labours of crafts; then, provided with travelling money, they are dismissed and instructed to support themselves by their own industry.

There were countless other things in this great city that might have been recorded here, but which I shall pass over for brevity’s sake. Now I turn to my lodging. As I drew near it, I greeted the Reverend Lord Nicholas, Abbot of the Gate of Heaven, commonly called Tennenbach, who was arriving with a companion. Three years before, he had been summoned from Maristella to become abbot; with great skill, and with no less exertion, [Col. 1590C] he is restoring the monastery, ruined by wars. It is an ancient abbey, situated four hours from Freiburg im Breisgau in a wooded wilderness, founded about the year of Christ 1156. That it was once most celebrated is clearly apparent from the sepulchral stones of many nobles throughout its enclosure. In his honour I thrust myself upon him as companion—indeed, as servant—to the Most Illustrious Lord General, and served as his guide when he returned to our lodging.

34. This fifth day of our stay would at last release us from Dijon; yet we were soon to return on the eighth, and afterwards on the third day of the seventh [the phrasing is uncertain]. Therefore, about the sixth hour of the morning, we celebrated Mass in the church of St Benignus; and, after breakfast, hastened with all the others who were about to attend the General Chapter to the residence of the Most Illustrious Lord General.

At noon the said Most Illustrious Father General set out by carriage toward Cîteaux. The carriages of the chief Fathers of La Ferté, Clairvaux, and Pontigny followed, and ten others altogether, most of them drawn by six or four horses. After this display had gone before, the rest followed indiscriminately, two or three together as the width of the streets allowed, without regard to rank or age. Forty bore the dignity of abbot; then came one hundred and fifty priors and commissioners, attended by one hundred and thirty servants. The French predominated in number; for I learned that two had appeared from Spain, fewer than twenty from the whole of Germany, and nearly all the rest had come from different regions of the kingdom of France.

The horses were of many kinds. Many were small, resembling deer in head and legs and, as I heard, also in speed of running. Yet they were unequal to long journeys: all their strength, as it were compressed into a small body, was exhausted by two days’ labour, and then they became useless until rested. Especially remarkable was the horse upon which the Most Reverend Lord Vicar-General of St Urban rode; the eyes and fingers of all the bystanders were directed at him. And the horse, as if conscious both of its rider and of being observed, heightened its otherwise handsome form by the arching of its neck, the proud manner of its gait, [Col. 1591A] and the spirited springing of its feet—especially while, through the stone-paved city, the hoofs of the clattering horses rang out.

Beyond the fortifications, an exceedingly dense dust, thick like mist, was raised by so great a troop of riders. In the still air and hottest sunshine it did not settle until, after the fourth hour, the mother-monastery of Cîteaux at last opened its gates to us amid the festive pealing of bells. There, after dismissing their horses, all followed the Most Illustrious Lord General as he led the way to the church doors, receiving a blessing with sprinkling of holy water.

A white order of Cistercian monks stood in two lines, one on either side through the middle of the church. Clad in white cowls flowing to the ground, with their eyes fixed upon the earth, they created so lovely a display of modesty that the sight moved every heart with devout emotion. Through this most splendid triumphal entry, the entire multitude of arrivals poured into the inner part of the church and prostrated themselves in prayer for a quarter of an hour.

35. Meanwhile an incredible sweetness from the organ suspended above the great door of the church filled our ears. I frankly confess that scarcely anything has drawn my affections to itself from my earliest years as music has done. I have therefore often attended performances, whether cultivated by voices alone or by instruments; nevertheless, never had I received into my ears so exquisite a compendium of art, the very sap and marrow of music.

Did the trumpet please? This especially, at the opening, shrilled a military call with martial fierceness. Did the flutes delight? The rapidity of the fingers sometimes gathered them by swift repeated strokes into one sound; sometimes, by sudden leaps upward and downward, it combined the large pipes with the small, just as though every corner of the church possessed its own Marsyas sweating in contest with Phoebus.

Then, abandoning pastoral melody, the maker sent a lively breath through hidden machinery into the pipes and pointed horns; [Col. 1591C] bursting forth in the sharpest cries, he suddenly drove them upward through delightful wanderings, and, as they hung aloft and trembled in circling motion, suddenly wheeled them down to the depths. There he commanded them to pause with a sound not long indeed, but weighty; and finally he gathered them together from the middle, the low, and the high registers at once.

Moreover, though outwardly almost nothing could be seen except the long tubes of white metal, the delicate sound of strings was interwoven with the song of the pipes with such ingenuity that I could scarcely doubt that not merely materials from the earth, but also the entrails of little sheep, had been summoned into this harmony. Nor did the wind seem merely to wander at the organist’s discretion: by the distribution of living voices, it seemed almost to range with the freedom of nature itself. For—something I had never even been accustomed to hear described—the pipes formed the human voice, not by a close imitation, but in their own, though tinny, throats. The organist blended this with the flutes so gracefully that now one voice wandered through all the pipes; now the full choir of singers was interwoven in alternating response; now their reciprocal sighs, as it were, struck against one another.

And when this harmony of every tone and voice had sounded forth in one melodious surge, it was heard again as though from afar under the reverberating silence of Echo. Yet this was not a simple play of a sound stealthily returning: the sound continually diminished even to its third repetition, and at last expired, not altogether vanishing, but seeming to deceive us by the illusion of a very long interval.

36. Steeped in these most delightful pleasures, all assembled through the cloister in the inner court. Each followed the Cistercian official charged with domestic affairs, who called us and led us to the allotted rooms. At the great bell’s signal for supper, they then withdrew to their beds. We obtained lodging certainly not among the least convenient: sufficient beds, with a passageway on either side.

At about the middle of the fifth hour on the following day, having hastily performed the opening divine offices, we awaited the beginning of the Chapter. It began shortly afterward at the seventh hour, by which time all, having been summoned, had gathered in the choir. First, Terce—the third of the canonical hours—was solemnly sung, with such gravity that at last I could mentally represent to myself those labours of venerable antiquity in divine worship which, from reading books, I had always considered admirable rather than easily imitable. For they prolonged the deep voice very slowly, inclining it, as it were, toward the ground; and although chant so rendered does not sound melodious, nevertheless, because nearly two hundred voices then joined together, it was adorned with fullest majesty.

With exactly the same slowness we sang the principal office of the Holy Spirit, the Reverend Lord Abbot of Camp des Lys acting as celebrant. That monastery, founded in Austria in 1206, is famous—if any in the Order is. Its abbots are held in the innermost counsels of the Imperial court and in the highest esteem there. Above all, its present superior, who governs with the greatest praise, is so acceptable and familiar to the Roman Emperor [Col. 1592B] that the Emperor commended him in an honourable letter to the General Chapter. Thus the sacred rite was performed in what we call choral chant, while that most elegant organ interposed music sufficient for six hundred musicians.

The ceremonies were performed with exact precision; and amid such a multitude of servants attending the mitred prelate, each fulfilled his own office so carefully and skilfully that you might have thought they moved like the wheels of clocks, regulated to the balanced measure of their weight. When this solemn Mass had ended, we were all admitted to the meeting in the part of the cloister called the chapter-house. It began with the reading of the Charter of Charity (concerning which see above, no. 2), followed by an address from the Most Illustrious Lord General. With the greatest eloquence, fervour of speech, and majesty of voice, he exhorted everyone to unity of mind and to a devout zeal for advancing peace.

After he had finished speaking, he led the three chief Fathers present from the chapter-house into a private room, to select, according to the Order’s custom, the definitores, or lawful judges, by whose authority and prudence laws and statutes were to be framed. The method of selecting them is this: first, the Most Illustrious Lord General associates with himself four definitores from his own filiation; likewise each of the remaining chief Fathers selects four from his own filiation, so that the entire number of electors and elected makes twenty-five definitores. This honour has been preserved unimpaired for the first four Fathers from the very beginning of the sacred Order.

Of the four Fathers, however, the fourth, the Abbot of Morimond, had excused his absence from the General Chapter on pressing grounds. But lest that foremost place, left vacant in a difficult affair of the utmost consequence, should open a path to disputes that might perhaps arise, the Reverend Lord Vicar-General, Abbot of St Urban, was ordered to assume his office and person for the duration of the Chapter. This was a favour as rare as it was honourable, though one neither unequal to, nor undeserved by, his learning and merits.

[Col. 1592D]

37. While these matters were conducted in private, other privileges and decrees concerning the Order were read aloud. After the space of an hour, the Most Illustrious Lord General returned with the others and ordered the names of the definitores to be proclaimed. When these had been read, I was astonished to hear so many monasteries known to me from which definitores were drawn. From the German Congregation alone I noted five, and among the foremost the Reverend Lord Bernardinus, Abbot of Lucelle—an Alsatian monastery once most celebrated and venerable even for its antiquity alone.

It began in the year of Christ 1124 and always flourished with a remarkable abundance of most distinguished men. But as the military tumults of this present age ravage Alsace, Lucelle, caught in the common conflagration, is recovering through the great labour of its present abbot. When, as I have said, the definitores had been named, the assembly was dismissed and released the Fathers appointed to the council for their first session. Thereafter these meetings were held daily for two hours before noon and two after noon. Those who did not participate in the council were free, should they wish to present anything before the assembly, to do so in writing or orally through the notaries.

At the first hour after dinner, a Cistercian professed religious, recently arrived from the Bernardine College in Paris, defended theological theses printed in type on a public sheet. The entire multitude of visitors looked on, while every learned person who wished to test himself in that arena advanced opposing arguments. The Spaniards disputed with especial ingenuity and solidity. Yet he defended himself against all of them with equal vigour and an undaunted countenance, turning back the weapons hurled at him, and won not only victory but remarkable praise from all.

38. On the second day, as also on the third, the solemn Mass preceding the council was celebrated according to the same rites as on the preceding day. The vestments were always changed, but never failed to shine with gold embroidery. The other garments used for private Masses were beyond estimate in value and number. The long inner garment called the alb was splendid around its fringes [Col. 1593B] and sleeve-edges with very fine threads of gold worked through the most delicate linen. The chalices were commended not merely by the richness of gold and silver but by the supreme beauty of their workmanship.

And among so great a number of priests neither a convenient place nor anything else was ever lacking, so that each could engage in devotion as he pleased. For the church, of immense and well-proportioned size, is divided into several ranks of altars, of which I recall there were thirty. The high altar is newly constructed of living stone, most nobly carved with both figures and architectural structures, except that an elegant painting upon stretched canvas makes the middle flat. The wooden decoration of all the other altars is clothed, by an artifice devised not long ago, in an imitation of marble, with a manifold variety of colours most pleasingly gleaming through the lustre of the counterfeit stone.

From the church one enters the cloisters, or ambulatories, by two doors; three of these may be seen, adjoining one another in succession. The one nearest the church is larger than the rest, and does not permit the rule of silence to be violated there; the other two are assigned for conversation and walking. To the left side of the greater cloister is attached the chapter-house, as is customary in all monasteries of the Order. It can contain more than three hundred persons seated and is vaulted with a very broad arch carried by two columns of prodigious thickness.

This same left side is closed near the church door by an altar beneath which rest the sacred relics of the first Fathers of the Order, namely Stephen and Alberic, and others. Not far away lies the tomb of Blessed Alan, a man admirable for learning, humility, and holiness, covered by a stone engraved with various writings. Outside the walls of the chapter-house several benches or bookstands are laden with books, ready for those wishing to devote themselves to devout reading. This side, like each of the other three, is sixty paces long. Near the chapter-house a broad passage leads to the other cloisters; a door only a few steps away gives access to the novitiate. To the second side is attached the refectory, situated between two kitchens.

[Col. 1593D]

39. It is indeed magnificent, raising lofty arches aloft in the form of a church and setting them upon several columns that are numerous but not crowded together.
