It extends sixty-three paces in length and a little more than twenty in breadth. During this Chapter, tables were laid in this refectory, common to both visitors and residents, in seven rows. The first stood at the head of the hall, higher than the rest, for the Most Illustrious Lord General and the chief prelates of the Order. Then two ran along each wall of the building; and opposite them stood two more, four paces away, leaving space for the servants to bring in the food. Finally, the middle part of the refectory, divided by walls fitted with seats, was occupied in two further rows solely by the resident religious.

Eighteen steps, if I am not mistaken, lead up to the lectern for table-reading. At the sound of the great bell all assembled there, whether it was time for dinner or supper; and, led by the cantor, they solemnly recited the customary prayers in voices increasing through the hollow of the vault. A very frugal meal followed, lasting half an hour; and among so many people, the food did not reach all with adequate warmth from the hearth. Yet it was helped by wine, the goodness of which more than compensated for the other lack of accustomed comfort. Finally, when thanks had been given together at the end, each departed wherever the pleasure of walking or companionship led him to refresh his mind. Neither was lacking in so broad a space or amid the company of almost every nation.

40. The greenery of the trees, then unfolding their first masses of leaves, invited us to the pleasantness of their shade. Planted in a fine long row for walking, the arms of their branches joined their tops in the form of an arch. Along the same path of the walk opened a little beech wood, dark with shade; outside it ran a ditch which nourished abundant fish among its still waters and brought coolness to the grove in the heat.

Yet all this is enclosed by a wall extending for a vast distance, forming the monastery’s boundary. Within it also are immense barns for storing hay, adjoining so many stables that during this eight-day period they conveniently accommodated no fewer than two hundred horses. Finally, a long succession of buildings, with their works divided among their respective workshops, stretches from the church all the way to the stables. Though rough and unadorned in their ancient appearance, this whole mass of very diverse and extensive buildings surpasses many towns I have seen in spaciousness and number. This became clearer later from the tower in which the bells hang.

41. Having been admitted by a narrow spiral stair to the highest summit of the church, we then climbed ladders into the tower. Amazed especially at the unusual size of the bells, particularly the great bell, we cast our eyes widely about us. The portion of the tower rising above the church roof is constructed of oak beams, protected from injury by the weather with sheets of lead. The church too had formerly possessed a lead roof; but when heretics plundered Burgundy, it became booty and was put to military use.

From this lofty lookout, therefore, our gaze ranged freely over every far-distant quarter. Various regions could be seen, as though their appearance were fading into bluish obscurity; but the nearer landscape offered a delightful spectacle. Outside the walls, pools showed now a silvery colour, now a green like a tranquil sea. Lightly stirred by the breeze, they played amid the bright reflection of the sky above and the shadows of the adjoining woods. These ponds were almost equal to lakes in size and spread on every side as far as the walls. Hence I not implausibly conjectured that Cîteaux received its name from this, since it is not far removed, so to speak, from a great cistern through this collection of ponds.

42. At last, on the third day, which was the eleventh of May, [Col. 1594D] we obtained an opportunity to go to the chapel of St Bernard—the place in which St Bernard himself, at the age of twenty-three, underwent his novitiate with thirty companions—and there to satisfy our devotional longing. To speak frankly, we indulged it with all our heart. For early in the morning, while the singing of Vigils still held everyone in the choir, we carried there the sacred chalice and the other things necessary for the divine sacrifice; and now priests, then ministers, we celebrated Masses.

Meanwhile there came back to my mind the accounts preserved concerning the admirable rule of life of that most holy novice. Again and again I seemed to myself to be standing either in a heavenly chapel or in an earthly heaven: that is, in the place where an angel clothed in flesh had lived a most chaste life beyond human purity. For what is less human than to live on earth with God alone, without the burden of the senses? And so Bernard spent his novitiate—indeed, his entire course of life.

“For a long time,” says the writer of his Life, “he had been entering and leaving the church of the house”—the church in which we then were—“yet at its far end, where there were three windows, he thought there to be only one; for, having mortified the sense of curiosity, he noticed nothing of the sort.” I therefore set before my mind that mirror of modesty. I contemplated those most pure lights of the eyes cast down to the ground while the mind was fixed upon heaven. I looked upon the most pure youth wrapped in a white garment: now severe against his innocent body with blows; now cast beneath the feet of all, though virtue raised him above all by so great a distance.

The spirit of the place, and the traces of holiness itself still, as it were, breathing in the walls, presented these pictures of memory to me in so vivid an image that, on this first occasion, I had to tear myself away with effort, longing that I might be allowed to breathe day and night that air which such innocence had consecrated. But because beside this chapel stood the hall in which the definitores held their councils, [Col. 1595B] permission to remain there was granted only at dawn.

43. Yet it would be almost endless, and indeed superfluous, to set before the eyes every building of this most extensive monastery with the brush of description. Many still remain, most of them lofty with high vaulting. Among them the infirmary takes first place, not inferior to the refectory and now restored through the recent care of the Most Illustrious Lord General. It is lit by a double row of windows: oblong ones above, smaller square ones below, as many on either side as beds were usually placed for the sick.

Near it is the abbatial residence, finished with every refinement, abundant in immense rooms adorned with tapestries and paintings. Finally, beside the middle cloister stands the library. It is full of books not very numerous but deriving their value from antiquity, nearly all written by hand on parchment. Beside it opens a hall empty of books, but, as its appearance indicates, built to receive them.

It remains for me to show you the chief sight, foremost both in dignity and in value: namely, the vault where the sacred treasure of the church is kept. But because I inspected it more carefully after my return from Clairvaux, I shall defer the account until then.

[Col. 1595C]

44. Now I hasten toward the conclusion of the Chapter, which the sixteenth day of May happily brought. At about the eighth hour everyone was summoned to the chapter-house. They listened to the Most Illustrious Lord General, who again spoke briefly; then the determinations and acts of the General Chapter were read. When these had been recited to the end, the one who performed the office of cantor stepped into the middle of the chapter-house. In a loud voice, using words prescribed by ancient custom, he requested that the Most Illustrious Lord General, by authority of the General Chapter and of the entire Order, should admit to participation in all the Order’s merits first those endowed with ecclesiastical dignity; then the Sacred Imperial Majesty; next the kings—whom he named, each adorned with his proper title and name—and finally the souls, whether of those still living or of those translated to the next age, of benefactors, friends, and persons bound and devoted by other ties.

The General performed this with solemn ceremonies and led the customary prayers from a prescribed book; the entire assembly completed them in alternating response. Finally, a general absolution concluded everything. When all had received it, kneeling, from the Most Illustrious Lord General, they left the chapter-house.

45. Thus the General Chapter, attended throughout these eight days, received a most fortunate crown. The day was already declining toward noon; after a hurried dinner, almost all the visitors departed from Cîteaux at the same hour. We, however, reached Dijon at about the fifth hour of the evening, together with our companion, the Most Reverend Lord Dominic, Abbot of Hauterive. This monastery is among the most ancient, near Fribourg in Switzerland in a vast wilderness, founded about the year 1137—at precisely the time when St Bernard [Col. 1596A] was summoned to Rome and began to suppress the schism of Peter Leo, restoring peace to the Church through seven years of labour. At this time the monastery flourishes in the distinguished renown of regular discipline.

When the aforesaid lord abbot set out for Dôle on the following day, we made for Clairvaux. After travelling five hours we reached Sortillium, a small town lying in a pleasant valley of pastureland. Nowhere did we encounter larger flocks of sheep than in this region. I could not count them, but I readily venture to affirm that one flock often numbered three hundred. Here we obtained a generous meal at a tolerable price, and about sunset took lodging in the dark village of Schelmoesinum.

46. We passed this night more miserably than any other thus far, though not without laughter, which indignation drew from us. For when we asked the hostess whether there was suitable accommodation here, she immediately said: “Indeed there is an inn; but I warn you, gentlemen, it will go better with the horses than with you.” The outcome answered her prediction. There was scarcely a foul-smelling morsel set before us, and four stinking eggs for seven men at supper. The wine too was cloudy, though not turbulent.

In a word, things went coldly both within and outside the house, for a piercing wind entered through the poorly sealed cracks of the windows. To remedy this we made a fire; but damp logs gave out more smoke than flame, greatly inconveniencing our eyes. Moreover, the noise and shouting of twenty soldiers lodging in the same inn prevented rest; and when that occasionally ceased, the thickness of the smoke banished sleep. Yet again and again, in words framed with every show of civility, the hostess offered us for our use whatever in the whole house might please us—bestowing much in ridiculous politeness where nothing was to be found.

I did not dare to compare aloud this innkeeper’s stupidity with the madness of certain people who locate the elegance of French manners in similar mockery. They suppose that only then do they display before a foreigner the artifice of courtly grace with completely Roscius-like agility: when, filling both cheeks with inflated promises, and shaping elaborate verbal formulas into coloured periods, as it were upon a lathe, they promise myriads of attentions, services, and readinesses to serve, and almost give themselves the name of slave—although they would hear nothing more disagreeable than the name “servant,” and harbour nothing less in their minds than even the serious meaning of what they say. I silently rejected the vanity of these men during the sleep-less delay, particularly as the smoke, grievous to the eyes, severely condemned these merchants in smoke.

47. Thus, scarcely waiting for the arrival of dawn, we fled this village and arrived about the sixth hour at the monastery of Hauterive. As we went straight to the church to pray, we were told that the Most Reverend Lord Abbot of Clairvaux had arrived by carriage a short interval before us. The prior of the place immediately [Col. 1596D] led us to him. We found him sitting by the fire and, in accordance with his kindness, gracious toward us. Learning that we had encountered the same wretched lodging which he himself lamented, he refreshed us with a draught of white ambrosia and sent us on to another monastery, still four hours distant, called Longue-Vaux.

The road between these two monasteries was singularly delightful. For the river Alba, rising not far from Hauterive, flows in silent waters through the middle of the valley’s plain; nowhere widening at its sides or increasing with tributary streams, content with its own waters, it carries the wanderings of its channel with remarkable freedom. Now it closely washes the feet of the mountains forming the valley; now, spreading itself among stones and sand as though it sought to catch the sun’s warmth, it creeps on without a murmur.

Although nature granted it no sound, it resounds loudly with the din of workshops, which the labour of the inhabitants has imposed upon it in many places, as though with bridles. Many of these are devoted to forging iron; others, to sawing trees into planks, [Col. 1597A] and enrich their owners with much money. Nor with less usefulness does it moisten the valley into richness of pasture. For although the meadows do not drink water through channels drawn from the river, the moisture insinuating itself among their roots makes them so fertile that all bloom with thick grass.

48. As we advanced through the delights of this valley, midday overtook us at Longo Vado. It is a monastery exceedingly pleasant and healthful both in situation and in the character of the place, founded in the year of Christ 1149 while the most holy Father Bernard was still alive. Its elegant and spacious buildings show that it was once distinguished; but at the present time the church and the monks’ dwellings, neglected as they are, owe their wretched state to that cause over which many monasteries once most flourishing, now beholding their ruin, lament. It is held, namely, by a commendatory abbot: that is, the goods or revenues bestowed upon the monastery by the piety of its founders are divided into three portions, according to the ordinances of kings, with the assent of the Apostolic See. The first portion is taken by whomever the king names—or to whom he commits possession of that monastery (and such persons often still cry in their cradles); the second ought to be assigned to the monks’ maintenance; the third ought to be spent on preserving the buildings. Yet most monasteries are said scarcely to enjoy one twentieth of these three portions. Meanwhile, few either enter them voluntarily or are admitted by these hirelings; and nothing beyond the barest necessities is granted to them.

The prior of such a monastery exercises the abbot’s authority in spiritual government. At this monastery he prepared lunch for us with such ready charity, and dinner for us on our return, as though, amid the greatest abundance of resources, he were lavishly expending these things as superfluities. He seasoned a sumptuous table with such sweetness of character and graciousness of conversation as scarcely anyone had shown during the whole journey. Singular learning and piety likewise shone out from him, while he answered questions with such modesty and introduced other matters with such prudence that, sincerely pitying his condition [Col. 1597C], I judged him worthy to preside under happier circumstances.

49. Nor did he merely satisfy our hunger by the liberality of his food: he also fed our eyes with an object at once most devout and most rare. For, when we had been led from the table into the church, he showed us the inner garment which our honey-tongued Father Bernard used to wear as an under-tunic. Its material is white wool of a light weave, like that of our cowl or outer choir-garment. Its length seems to have reached to the knees. It is not gathered into folds around the neck; rather, a small hood is attached by flat seams, which I suppose was added for use during the night’s rest. For it is no larger than needed to cover the back of the head, and, when folded back, was easily concealed beneath the garment worn over it.

They next showed us the mitre of Saint Malachy, Archbishop of Ireland—of whom more below. Its great value arises from the celebrated sanctity of the man; for the little gold plates adorning its reddish silk are not valued highly in themselves. Finally, as we were about to mount our horses, he invited us into a very large garden. Since six hours’ journey still remained to us, we viewed it only in passing—it was later matched by that of Clairvaux—and, after giving thanks, hurried on our departure. [Col. 1597D]

50. Alba, our constant companion on the road, set us down at about the eighth hour of the evening at the monastery in the most famous valley. Since we shall remain there nearly two whole days, I shall now briefly confess my weariness to you, after resting a little in the refectory.

Having been courteously received through the outer gate, we were greeted by a religious of lower rank—we call those assigned to the monastery’s common services *conversi*, “lay brothers”—and, after our horses had been sent off to the stables, he conducted us directly to the church. There the guestmaster, already informed of our arrival, gave his hand to each of us and, without many words, led us to the high altar, so that, as our holy Rule commands, we might first be joined to God in prayer before being joined to one another in the embrace of peace. From the church he showed us the way to the lodging, signaling with exquisite courtesy how welcome he considered us as guests. [Col. 1598A]

After half an hour had been granted us to recover our breath, I reviewed with weary reflection the whole course of that day’s journey. We had continuously urged our horses forward with spurs, in order to hasten their pace, from the third hour after sunrise until the eighth hour before sunset, taking no more than three hours’ rest. In a dull stupor I wondered at the endurance, both ours and the horses’, which had remained constant through such a troublesome length of road. Not only did my head ache from the burning heat of the blazing sun, but my sides, painfully strained by the jolting of the horses, resentful of excessive labor, grievously afflicted me—especially since throughout all my previous travels I had never experienced this, having always enjoyed vigorous and sound health. I attributed this weakness solely to the preceding night: sleepless, fasting, and uncomfortable.

51. Yet the following supper was an immediate remedy for this sudden illness: the cheerfulness of conversation and the medicinal effect of a most elegant liquor; and also sleep—the forgetfulness of all misery. Though it was not long, it was for the time so effective as if it had been prolonged far into the day. For the windows had not yet brightened with full daylight when, having shaken off sleep, I hurried to the church. There I beheld, not without admiration, the very full choir still engaged in singing Vigils. The chant had begun at the second hour after midnight; and after nearly two hours, when I entered the church, the prayers had progressed a little beyond halfway. Thus deliberately do they render those divine songs, adapting them to a deeper meditation on devout affections; and so reluctantly do they permit themselves to be drawn away from that manner of life which they begin in this mortal existence and are thereafter to continue eternally, in fellowship with those most pure spirits who celebrate the praises of the immortal Deity.

In a quiet corner I joined my own prayers to theirs. After them, casting my eyes more curiously around the whole structure of the church [Col. 1598C], I observed that in size it was not inferior to Cîteaux, though it enjoyed freer sunlight.

52. The outer part of the church is filled with benches, which we call stalls, for the lay brothers; three rows of them are arranged, each rising above the other by a higher step. Unless my memory deceives me, I counted three hundred and sixteen separate seats. For Clairvaux formerly supported as many lay brothers; indeed, fifty men of that class remain even now. They once built a distinct monastery for themselves, with separate dormitory, workshops, chapter-house, and dwellings. The abbot appoints them from the monastery a prior, who presides with the highest authority; apart from him, they choose from their own number one man to whom they give obedience as we do to the conventual prior. He distinguishes his authority by the white color of his clothing; the rest wear dark iron-gray.

Their workshops occupy an immense space and are furnished with every kind of craft and labor. I saw painters, sculptors, and men trained in similar arts; then smiths [Col. 1598D], weavers, and also tanners. Among the last I noticed stones of remarkable size, hollowed out for soaking hides. Their length is more than twenty feet, their breadth more than ten, and their depth exceeds a man’s height to the chest. Elsewhere too through the monastery I greatly marveled at such enormous and unusual stone basins beside the fountains.

53. But I return to the church and its inner choir, which, as I recall, is divided into one hundred and thirty-eight seats. Although in those ancient times more monks assigned to the choir lived together at Clairvaux, they were not all engaged at the same hour in the divine praises. Rather, when one group left the choir, another succeeded it, and then a third; so that the church never rested from the chanting of monks by day or night. Now I heard that about eighty monks are enrolled at Clairvaux.

The whole church rises into a very lofty vault, whose columns, hewn into a smooth form, pleased me more than those at Cîteaux. Behind the high altar, which is not joined to any wall, are three altars: Saint Bernard’s in the middle; Saint Malachy’s on the right; and, beyond it, those of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa are spread over their tombs. So much of these tombs as projects beyond their enclosing wall is covered by another vault, providing space to pass through and to venerate them kneeling in private devotion. Beyond this arch, several other chapels, likewise built with vaulted work and renowned for sacred relics, complete the church. [Col. 1599A]

54. It was the festive day of the triumph which our Savior brought to heaven after conquering death, when he bade farewell to the world, leaving behind the traces of his feet. For this reason everything was performed with the most solemn rites. Half an hour before Sext, they were chanting Prime and the morning office. Before it had ended, I went to Saint Bernard’s altar, intending to offer there the unbloody sacrifice. But another priest was then occupying it, and many abbots and priors besides had already been designated in succession to follow one another in this most sacred work. For not a few had been drawn there either by devotion to Saint Bernard or while returning by way of their own monasteries.

I attended six or seven Masses, meanwhile intent upon the prayers I composed privately. Among them, dearest of friends, remembrance of you was not omitted—if indeed the prayer of a sinner can avail at all, as Saint Bernard used to say—nor of others whom I earnestly commended to the most holy patron. At length a place was granted even to me. The man from whom I received the sacred vestments whispered in my ear that the chalice set out for use at Masses that day was granted in honor of the guests; for it was made noble by the frequent touch of the most holy Father Bernard.

Like a sudden ray from heaven, this utterance entered my mind. Joy and modest shame rushed into conflict, so that I had to collect myself from that struggle and restore myself before I could wholly immerse myself in devotion. “How fortunate,” I thought, [Col. 1599C] “is this lot of mine! If in our Maristella I had been permitted merely to see such a sacred chalice for a brief moment, I should have worshiped Fortune as most lavishly favorable to me. But here, not with my eyes only or by a mere touch, but for almost a whole hour to embrace and kiss so dear a pledge—this already placed me at the summit of happiness and joy.” It is impossible to say how greatly this exultation of the soul stimulated devotion. For I do not remember that, so long as I have borne—unworthily indeed—the most worthy name of priest, I ever handled the divine mysteries with a sweeter savor of devotion.

As I finished Mass, the beginning was made of the greater office, which was celebrated with the most solemn ceremonies. At the customary point in it, a pulpit, set in the middle of the choir by two servants, was reverently ascended, and for nearly an hour a sermon was delivered. An organ blended with the chant with no less elegance than at Cîteaux, though with workmanship somewhat inferior. [Col. 1599D]

55. I spent what time remained after the divine office in the outer part that runs around behind the altars, where the three tombs mentioned above are made of red marble and alabaster or gypsum. White frameworks have been so conveniently built around the tombs that one may kneel down, withdraw oneself into them, and devote oneself to private piety out of the sight of passers-by. Saint Bernard’s tomb, lying in the middle, was crowded with many suppliants; and, as had happened to me at the altar, I did not at once obtain the place I desired. I therefore turned for the moment to the tomb of the holy martyrs. After kneeling for some time in prayer, I bent toward its inner part; and behold, I heard a great sound, as though a sea swelling beneath the agitation of winds were boiling over.

Startled by this roar, I recoiled, and immediately the noise vanished. Wishing to test the matter, I again brought my ear closer, but slowly and gradually; and I perceived the same returning image of the sea. My fear thus turned into devout awe, I quickly finished the prayers I had proposed and went straight to the reverend Lord Vicar-General, since most of the others had already departed. When I asked him what that portentous sound meant, he told me that he too had learned it by experience forty years earlier: those sacred relics had been given to Clairvaux by Conrad, Bishop of Porto, about the year of Christ 1225; and from then through so many years this wonderful marine murmur had continued. [Col. 1600A]

56. At last, after our devotions had been completed and the church left behind, the common refectory received both visitors and residents for dinner. Some sixty sat along the two rows of tables, all alike in deportment and bodily bearing, and so elegantly formed according to the rules of modesty that I was involuntarily reminded of what Pope Innocent II observed in this very place in ancient times. He had convened a council at Rheims in France in the year of Christ 1131 to settle grave disputes. Saint Bernard was present, esteemed by all as possessing no less authority than an oracle; and three years later at Pisa he received the same honor, until at last, by much labor and the glory of countless miracles, he dispersed that cloud from the Church.

Leaving Rheims, Innocent visited Clairvaux with his entire retinue. The gate through which he entered remains blocked to this day in memory of the event, as I myself saw. Concerning his reception, please do not be reluctant to hear the author of Saint Bernard’s Life discoursing. In Book II, chapter 1, he tells the matter thus:

> Returning from Liège, the lord pope wished to visit Clairvaux in person. There he was received most affectionately by Christ’s poor—not adorned in purple and fine linen, nor coming to meet him with gilded Gospels, but in ragged bands carrying a rough cross; not with the thunder of blaring trumpets, not with loud rejoicing, but with subdued chant. The bishops wept; the supreme pontiff himself wept; and all wondered at the gravity of that community: in so solemn a joy all their eyes were fixed upon the ground, nowhere roaming in wandering curiosity, but with lowered eyelids so that they saw no one and were seen by all. The Roman saw nothing in that church that he could desire; no furnishings there enticed his gaze. In the oratory they saw nothing but bare walls. Ambition could long only for their manners, and such plunder could not harm the brothers, since their religion could not be diminished by being carried away. All rejoiced in the Lord, and the festival was celebrated not with foods but with virtues. There whole-wheat bread—meaning bread from which neither flour nor bran has been sifted out—was used instead of fine flour; flat wine instead of Cretan wine; vegetables instead of turbot; and pulses were set out in place of every delicacy. If perhaps a fish was found, it was served to the lord pope, and benefited the community by its appearance, not by its consumption.

They were performing this “comedy,” I say, to the very letter—not as actors masked for a part, but themselves being at once the history and the stage [Col. 1600D]—except that the guests received a more sumptuous table than the supreme head of the earthly world had then received.

57. After dinner, devout curiosity led us through the monastery until late evening. First we ascended from the cloister to the dormitory. An immense vault, divided in two, distributes cells along either side, constructed of oak cut into boards. All are the same size and are not detached from one another; rather, about twenty-five cells are joined in a single row, separated from one another only by a wooden partition. They are no more than eight feet high, and the same number of feet completes both their width and length.

When I entered the dormitory, I thought the cells were chests intended for keeping clothing; on examining them, I discovered them to be cells, truly breathing the poverty and simplicity of our forefathers. For a bed occupies nearly half the cell; feathers are wholly excluded, in accordance with the common usage of France. A coverlet of green or other-colored wool is spread upon a mat with no further ornament. Against the opposite wall is fixed a little table, laden with a few books, an inkstand, and an image of Christ the Savior hanging on the cross. The inner wall, over as much space as the bed occupies, is given to the door; the outer wall is cut by a window no more than two feet wide. The arrangement of the cells is altogether the same in the dormitory of the mother monastery at Cîteaux, as is the site in which they are placed. [Col. 1601A]

58. Where the row of cells ends in the right-hand wall of the dormitory, an iron door opens a vaulted chamber in which the church treasury is kept. About twenty visitors, abbots and others alike, were admitted all together to see it, while the doors were locked. Great chests all around conceal the treasury. When the man charged with this most precious store wished to open the first, after removing three bolts, he warned us that the sacred heads of Saints Bernard and Malachy lay there. Then, once the door was removed, two images fashioned from gold and silver suddenly shone out, rendered so lifelike that at first sight I stood astonished and, fastening my eyes upon them in wonder, waited to see whether they would speak.

The countenance especially of the honey-tongued Father—known everywhere from his image—and here wrought with such fitting skill, moved the deepest marrow of every heart. And indeed I said:

> If Piety wished to assume a face properly her own,  
> Bernard, she would take this likeness of yours.

He painted you with the living brush of his style who, in Book III, chapter 1 of the description of your Life, speaks of you thus:

> In his flesh appeared a certain grace, yet more spiritual than carnal; from his eyes shone a kind of angelic purity and dove-like simplicity. His body was exceedingly thin and without flesh; even his very delicate skin was moderately red in the cheeks. His hair was colored blond and white; his beard reddish, sprinkled with gray near the end of his life. His stature was of honorable medium height, though it appeared nearer to tallness. Serene in countenance, modest in bearing, cautious in speech, restrained in action, constant in sacred meditation, devout in prayer, he trusted in every matter more in prayer than in his own industry or labor. Great-souled in faith, long-suffering in hope, lavish in charity, supreme in humility, outstanding in piety; prudent in counsels, effective in affairs; never less at leisure than when at leisure. Pleasant under reproaches, modest when receiving service, gentle in manners, holy in merits, glorious in miracles, and finally abounding in wisdom, virtue, and grace before God and men. Poverty in dress always pleased him; filth never did.

As these things were recalled to everyone’s mind, every face and breast tingled with desire to embrace this most welcome and so often longed-for pledge, whom in this likeness we venerated as if living. At last the foremost man of the company, having composed himself for feelings of love and reverence—doubt not that his eyes were swimming with joy—threw himself upon the neck of the beloved Father and, covering it with repeated kisses, poured out his whole heart; reluctantly, as I observed, he finally tore himself away. Leaving him, he turned to the image behind, that of Saint Malachy the archbishop, equally admirable in craftsmanship, and again pressed it in a sweet embrace and kiss. [Col. 1601D]

This is that Malachy, Archbishop and Primate of Ireland, renowned for many miracles; and famous even for this single reason: Bernard closed his eyes as he died and honored him with the most beautiful discourse in which his most holy life is recounted. His epitaph is still read at Clairvaux today in these words:

> Here rests the body of blessed Malachy, Archbishop and Primate of all Ireland, legate of the Apostolic See, a man of apostolic life and glorious in miracles. This is he who, with the greatest dangers and difficulties, drove out barbarism and pagan custom, instructed in the Catholic faith, and, so far as he could, conformed to the institutions of the Holy Roman Church the peoples of Scotland and Ireland—men at that time barbarous, contracting no marriages, making no confessions or penances, not entering churches, receiving no ecclesiastical sacraments: pagans in fact, Christians in name alone, although they had formerly been converted to the faith by blessed Patrick. Moreover, he more widely spread through those lands communities of monks of the Cistercian Order, Regular Canons, and other religious. Having accomplished these things with God’s help, he came from farther Scotland to Clairvaux, which he had always desired as the place of his death, the Lord satisfying his devout desire. There, after about three weeks had passed, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the fifty-fourth year of his age, on the night on which the anniversary of all the faithful departed is observed, as he had always desired and foretold, having blessed each person and laid his hands upon each, he bade farewell to the world, was joyfully received by angels, and was joined to the most blessed company of the citizens above. This was revealed from heaven, as it occurred, to our most blessed Father Bernard in the Canon of the Mass itself while he celebrated the solemn Mass on the following day. May his prayers and glorious merits obtain grace for us before God in the present life and glory in the life to come. Amen.

Everyone handles and admires this Saint Malachy’s prophecies concerning the supreme pontiffs, which have hitherto been confirmed by the truth of their fulfillment. The recently elected Clement XI falls under: “Star of the Swans” (*Sidus Olorum*). I leave its exposition to learned men. [Col. 1602B]

59. When this first visitor had thus completed his devotion, all of us succeeded in turn to the same happiness, as one chest was closed and another opened. There were no fewer than eight such chests, filled with sacred relics of incomparable value. The palm before all the rest was won by a reed: the very one which the insolence of mocking soldiers placed in the hands of Christ in his Passion. A golden case, fashioned in the likeness of its original prototype, preserves it. It is a little longer than our ell, with five or six leaves hanging from its stalk and with that black knob which reeds commonly bear, swelling at the top. Measure by your own feeling the savor of devotion with which each of us pressed kisses upon it.

Another chest displayed the head of Saint Mark the Evangelist—I suppose the greater part, or at least the principal part of it—covered by a case likewise adorned with gold and gems. Further, there was the head of Saint Vincent the martyr, once bestowed by Saint Conrad of Porto together with the relics of Saints Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa. In addition, unless I am mistaken, the head of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.

There was also shown an enormous silver panel set with many gems. It opens by means of two wings or doors and displays both a great portion of the Cross of Christ the Lord, which Robert of Nazareth, then Archbishop of Jerusalem, sent to Saint Father Bernard in the year of salvation 1144—and for which he also gives thanks in a special letter, Bernard’s Epistle 175—and three hundred and forty other most noble relics, each placed in its own compartment. Among these the most renowned are: material from the sponge which offered vinegar to Christ the Savior on the cross; material from the crown of thorns; material from the point of the lance that opened his most sacred side; and so on. [Col. 1602D]

Another panel, likewise made from silver plates, contains a far greater abundance of relics. It is said to have belonged to Empress Helena and to have served her as an altar while she traveled. Certainly it is venerable even for its age alone, having remained intact from the time of Helena, who lived about the year of Christ 300, until now. It opens four wings, all filled with innumerable little compartments concealing sacred relics like eyes. I observed many items from the garments of the Virgin Mother, from the instruments of the Lord’s Passion, from the Apostles, and so forth. If a single particle of these things were displayed among us, it would surely be celebrated by a great concourse of people.

I retained most of these things by memory alone; it was impossible to record everything in a notebook, partly because of their abundance, partly because of haste, and finally because of whatever degree of devotion I possessed. I was assigned two sources from which so great a treasury had come to Clairvaux. The first is ascribed to Hugh, formerly Abbot of Saint William’s and afterward, following a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a monk of Clairvaux; he brought many things back with him from Palestine about the year 1221. The second is deservedly attributed to Saint Father Bernard, as may be gathered briefly and clearly from the account of his Life. After his immense labors in quieting the schism that troubled the Roman Church have been recounted, it concludes thus, in Book II, chapter 1:

> When the holy Father returned from Rome, he brought with him precious gifts from the bodies of the holy apostles and martyrs, regarding this as no small fruit of his labor. It is worth recording how he received a tooth of blessed Caesarius among them. When the martyr’s whole head was presented to him, that he might take from it whatever he wished, he asked that one tooth be given him. But for some time the brothers who had come with him labored in vain and could not draw it out at all, although two or three knives which they had applied were broken; the tooth nevertheless remained immovable. Then he said, “We must pray; for we cannot possess it unless the martyr himself grants it.” At last, after prayer, he approached reverently and with incredible ease removed with two fingers what previously could not be moved by iron instruments. [Col. 1603B]

Since almost the whole world was thus generous toward Clairvaux, it is no wonder that so great a treasure flowed there.

I shall now briefly describe what was shown us last. It was that case, in the middle of which crystal surrounds the sacred host, made remarkable by the presence of God incarnate. In common speech it is called a *monstrance*, because it shows that divine mystery to the people. This object, weighty with the purest gold, displays nothing besides the most precious gems. It forms a circle of flowers around the crystal; no one has yet declared whether it is greater in artistry or in cost. A pelican sits upon the summit of its crown, piercing its breast with its beak to feed its young. Pure rubies clothe the bird, arranged with the most fitting proportion in the form of feathers; they depict with consummate art not only the purple sparks apparently flowing from the bird itself, but also the motion of drops leaping from its veins. Yet I have set before you no more than a shadow of this magnificence; from it, however, you may easily estimate the elegance of the actual object. [Col. 1603C]

60. From the dormitory we proceeded through the adjacent cloister of the church, which represents the life of Saint Bernard in sufficiently large and beautiful paintings, into another cloister, and came to the library: truly a grand seat of books, its shelves divided by three vaulted bays. On the right side, cases are loaded with manuscripts only; every codex is tied to the shelves by a small chain, though loosely enough to be conveniently available to anyone wishing to read, while incapable of being removed. The left side contains books in various editions, both new and old print.

Returning from there, we reached the old infirmary, very large indeed, but now serving as a walking place because of various inconveniences that afflicted those living there; another and better building has been assigned for the sick. Attached to it is a place built like a small chapel with a suspended vault. It alone, in all my life, placed me in such a state of happiness that I may justly boast of having seen a miracle.

In the middle of this chapel lies a stone a little longer than the ordinary height of a man, set upon a wall two or three feet high. It is hard as flint and, leaving a rim two fingers broad, hollowed to a depth of one finger. Its purpose is that the cold bodies of persons recently dead may be washed upon it and immediately afterward laid in their bier. This most ancient pious custom still prevails widely in France: bodies are washed almost as soon as the breath has departed. Such stones are shown in all monasteries, including ours, although this practice has ceased among us.

When the little body of Saint Father Bernard received this final office of charity upon that very stone, behold the wonder: it left its shadow so firmly impressed in the hard flint that it continues to this day with indelible permanence. Yet all who have died at Clairvaux ever since have received washing in the same place; no one could easily reckon their number, for Bernard himself, when dying, left seven hundred souls serving God at Clairvaux. This is a miracle, if any in the whole world deserves wonder; and I confess that I could scarcely obtain belief from these very eyes and hands of mine, to which it was granted to inspect and touch it inquisitively and carefully. It is a novelty unknown to all natural science and unheard of in every preceding age: namely, a shadow without a body, such as this one clearly appears in the very light of noon. Head, back, legs, and feet—all these limbs project from themselves a most distinct and visible shadow, exactly as if the sacred naked body itself were waiting there to be washed. [Col. 1604A]

Somewhat bewildered by no slight fear, yet approaching reverently, I began to feel whether the stone produced this shadow by means of a hollow. But the surface was uniform throughout, except that I observed some small pieces near the middle of the stone to have been chipped away with iron. When I asked the cause of this, the answer was that these were traces left by the audacity of heretics. Envious of the most holy Father’s glory, they spread the claim that the monks had applied this shadow to the stone in black pigment. Accordingly, in order to expose the supposed fraud, they dug into the stone with hammers—but without the result for which they were looking. Though the hammer wore away the stone’s outer surface, the shadow always remained whole. Thus may the heretics grind their teeth, able even in this shadow to see their own darkness; with more than beastly savagery they rage against the veneration of the saints, while the wretches are defeated merely in their effort to destroy that shadow.

Before I leave you with this glorious shadow, please hear what Geoffrey, the fourth Abbot of Clairvaux after Saint Bernard, writes concerning the water in which the sacred body was washed, in the sermon delivered on the tenth anniversary of the most holy Father’s death [Col. 1604C]:

> “From the washing of his sacred body, when after his passing we rendered him the funeral rites due according to custom, certain brothers carried [water] to the remotest parts of the world; and, as I learned from their trustworthy report, although the tenth year has now passed, this water not only remains to this day entirely unspoiled, but retains the same efficacy for anyone upon whom it is poured. For although they have already given some of that sacred liquid to many persons seeking remedies—for they affirm that it has brought relief to many—yet, although the vessel has repeatedly been replenished with other water, it remains to this day such as it was on the first day.”

61. From the place of this most splendid shadow we passed through the church into the open light; a few paces beyond its door rises a mausoleum, beneath which is buried the most devout father of Saint Bernard—himself a monk at Clairvaux in extreme old age—together with Bernard’s two full brothers, Bartholomew and Gerard. Thence, after a few more steps, one visits a wooden hut, like a small cottage of the sort customarily erected in fields for cattle. Having entered it and learned that it was rendered famous by Saint Bernard’s residence there during illness, we were seized with devout astonishment that this pile of timber had endured through so many ages: namely, five hundred and fifty years. I shall briefly relate on what occasion it was placed here.

When Saint Bernard, then in his third year in the Order, was appointed abbot of Clairvaux, founded by Theobald, Count of Champagne, and was ordained by the Bishop of Châlons both priest and abbot, his holiness, already shining forth in most brilliant rays, seemed to the bishop worthy of better bodily lodging—so that a body remaining vigorous longer might illuminate the world. The bishop therefore received Bernard into his own house with the greatest reverence and began to urge him to relax somewhat the rigor of his life, restore his strength by gentler food, and then return armed with greater vigor to his former austerity. But, having met with an utter refusal, the bishop went to Cîteaux and there humbly asked the abbot to command Bernard, by his authority, to obey him for a year; and this he obtained out of respect for him.

That he might treat Bernard’s impaired health more securely, he ordered the hut I have mentioned to be built outside the monastery enclosure. Here the most devout Bernard, secluded, was entrusted to the care of a certain utterly worthless quack and itinerant boaster, who afflicted him for a whole year beyond belief. For he offered raw blood as food and oil as wine, and most shamelessly inflicted countless other things upon him, so that Bernard might seem to have been entrusted to him for death rather than recovery. Yet beneath this wolf Bernard, the gentlest of sheep, inhabited the narrow confines of this hut without the least sign of resistance.

It is built square, extending eighteen feet on every side, with no floor or ceiling dividing the upper part from the ground below, the roof alone weighing upon the wretched walls. Though these were brightened by no glass, they shone sufficiently, surely, with the light of holiness from their inhabitant. In place of windows, boards are fitted over cut openings, so that a slight movement may either keep out or admit the air. The bedding, still hanging there, had the same squalid appearance, as did the corner in which he lay.

While I looked upon these things with feelings of compassion, I recalled the blameworthy indulgence of certain magistrates who tolerate that dregs of humanity—the tribe to which Bernard’s persecutor belonged. They fill every marketplace with their cries and feed the credulous populace with the smoke of lies, while with impunity they bring great destruction alike to purse and life. Meanwhile, the great talents of physicians, cultivated by honorable labor for the truth of that most beautiful art, lie neglected—an art which these men corrupt by their audacity.

62. Beside this hut is a chapel in which Saint Bernard not infrequently celebrated Mass. Near its doors a seat is shown upon which he often sat, pouring out the sacred honey of contemplation; and in his final fatal illness he illuminated by his meditations the greater part of the Song of Solomon. But most remarkable of all is the threshold of the chapel. When we read these two words, written in faint letters, “Here he died,” we understood that Bernard had rested his sacred head upon that stone as he sent his most blessed soul to heaven. No one could restrain himself from immediately throwing himself to the ground and reverencing with a devout kiss that hard indeed, but sweet, pillow.

Since I know that you desire to learn in what manner, with what devotion, and finally at what time the holy death of this most holy Father occurred, I cannot set it forth more concisely than by transcribing his epitaph. It reads as follows:

> Here rests the body of our most blessed Father Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux. In his days he was a man most holy in life and morals; most illustrious after the apostles in the working of miracles; an outstanding teacher in the understanding and exposition of Holy Scripture; a pre-eminent restorer of peace among those at discord; an industrious reprover and corrector of heresies and errors then springing up in the Church; a true prophet in many things which he preached; most devout enlarger of monasteries and of religious life; a singular lamp, not only of the Gallican Church but also of all Christendom.
>
> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, the fifteenth from the establishment of the house of Cîteaux, at approximately twenty-two years of age, he entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions and, under Abbot Stephen, submitted his neck to the sweet yoke of Christ. In the year of the Lord 1115, in the month of July, he was sent with his blood brothers and his community to this place, now called Clairvaux, but formerly the Valley of Wormwood; there for thirty-eight years he fulfilled the office of abbot, or good shepherd.
>
> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1153, after the Order had spread everywhere, and being father of more than one hundred and sixty monasteries of our Order, he happily completed the days of his life, having fulfilled about sixty-three years. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], at almost the third hour of the day, amid the grievous sobs and abundant tears of the surrounding sons, he passed to the Lord—to meet the joyful companies of monks whom he himself had sent before him, and the ranks of angels whose life he had led on earth. May he who lives and reigns without end make us imitators and sharers in his glory.

63. While the day sped by amid these sights, the time remaining until supper was claimed by the garden. Extending into four walks of equal length, it left a central space filled with flowerbeds arranged in artistic order, all then blooming with every elegance. Tulips and anemones displayed their cups most splendidly, painted in such dazzling diversity of colors that they overwhelmed the gaze of eyes freely roaming over them.

The walks, three hundred paces in length, raised on each side walls of beech higher than a long spear, clothed in the fresh green leaves of spring. There, however clear the sky, shade never failed the walker, since one of the four sides always stood between him and the sun, although each walk was broad enough to give two carriages ample room to pass. The prospect from the beginning of a walk to its far end was delightful; for distance played deceptively with the eyes, making both walls appear to end in the shape of a narrow point, although they were everywhere laid out in equal parallel lines.

64. Returning from the garden, we inspected the granaries, rich in heaps of grain and fit to preserve wheat for many years. A huge building extended strong vaults conveniently over great distances, so that the grain was secure from the danger of fire while still exposed to the air and thus preserved from decay.

I seemed to see Bernard, the great steward of the household, loading crowds of poor people from those heaps of wheat; and I recalled the famous miracle recorded in the account of his Life in almost these words:

> At one time famine had prevailed in the kingdom of France and its neighboring regions, but the Lord’s blessing filled the granaries of His servants. Until that year, indeed, the produce of their labor had never sufficed for them; and even then, when the harvest had been gathered and everything carefully reckoned, they estimated that it would scarcely last until Easter. When they wished to buy grain, they found no funds, because it was being sold far above the usual price. Thus, in the very season of Lent, an immense multitude of poor people flocked to them. Faithfully distributing what they possessed, and the Lord blessing them for His servant Bernard’s sake, they themselves and the poor who came to them were alike cheerfully sustained by that small provision until the harvest.

Thus every corner breathed upon us the devout remembrance of the most eminent holiness of this blessed Father, wherever we turned our feet or eyes.

65. After the night had passed following a generous supper, we again proceeded, scarcely having greeted the dawn, to Saint Bernard’s tomb. The most reverend lord Vicar-General celebrated Mass at the altar of Saint Malachy, while I celebrated over the tomb of the honey-flowing Doctor. This devotion occupied about two hours. We then went to the chapel of the Counts of Flanders, remarkable for its lofty and spacious vault, but still more remarkable for the treasure of sacred relics resting there in a subterranean chamber.

Because I learned a matter concerning these relics most worthy of hearing, I cannot omit to write it out for you more fully. At the beginning of his sacred colony, which he led forth from Cîteaux, Saint Bernard founded a monastery in the forward part of this valley. It was called the Valley of Wormwood, whether because of the abundance of wormwood growing there or because of the bitterness of the death suffered by those who formerly often fell there among robbers. But as time passed, the number of monks streaming in became so great that the narrowness of the place could not contain them. With the aid of kings and princes, he therefore undertook the construction of a new and larger monastery, which he had almost completed about the year of Christ 1148.

In that very year he solemnly transferred from the cemetery of the old monastery the remains of monks whom he himself had buried, not unaware what worthy honor he was paying them. In subsequent years those sacred relics greatly increased and became renowned for innumerable miracles. They were again raised from the ground in the year of Christ 1296 and honorably deposited in this subterranean vault. There they have lain uncorrupted for so many years—without ornament indeed, but undoubtedly sufficiently adorned by their incorruption.

The number of those sacred bodies exceeds nine hundred, and, as I devoutly believe, has not diminished by even the smallest part through so great a passage of time. I say that I devoutly believe it; nor will I hide from you what moved me to this belief: above all, Saint Bernard’s promise. When he was to send monks to Sweden to found a monastery, he intended among the others to send a certain young man from Utrecht, burning with singular love for the most devout Father. With tears and prayers this man begged not to be separated from him for such barbarous and distant nations, for whose sake, indeed, he had left homeland and world; he said that he had especially entered this sacred institute so that he might be permitted happily to live and die at Clairvaux.

To console him as a most loving father, Bernard promised that he would be buried nowhere but at Clairvaux with the rest of his pupils. The promise did not deceive him. For after he had acted as abbot for forty years in that northern kingdom, he was carried in extreme old age in a litter across so vast expanses of land and sea to Clairvaux. Stricken by a fever for several days, he happily ended his life there and obtained the promised favor of burial.

Since, therefore, the most holy Father Bernard had bestowed and fulfilled the same promise to many others, and since, moreover, as he was passing from this mortal misery to heaven he added among other words of consolation that he would not abandon after death the sons whom he had begotten for Christ, nor permit the dispersion of his flock, but that they would remain at Clairvaux in such fashion that on the decisive day of the Last Judgment all their bones would here be raised again and presented together with him before God the Judge—no one hitherto has called the truth of this oracle into doubt.

Indeed, not many years ago this very thing was confirmed by a new miracle. A Duchess of Lorraine came to see Clairvaux. Allowed, both because of her generosity toward the place and because of her rank, to enter the interior of the church and this Flemish chapel itself, she brought in her noble retinue a certain girl tormented by an enormous toothache, so persistent that all the skill of physicians had been exhausted over many years without effect. When she was told that the objects visible in the subterranean vault were nothing but the sacred relics of Saint Bernard’s disciples, she took up one of the bones reverently, without anyone noticing, and applied it to her cheeks with great confidence. Without delay all her pain immediately vanished.

Inflamed with love for so precious and effective a remedy, she secretly concealed it beneath her bodice, intending to preserve it for the aid of others also. Meanwhile, as the duchess was preparing to depart and had returned to the gates of the monastery, she noticed that the girl was missing. She therefore ordered a search, in case curiosity natural to her sex had led her wandering through the unfamiliar windings of the monastery. Every corner was searched, but nowhere was she seen, until servants sent to the said chapel found her there. By voice and signs they indicated that her mistress was preparing to leave and that she alone was delaying her.

But she, clinging to the open doorway, was indeed attempting to leave, yet in vain. She said that she had long been ready to follow but was wholly unable to get outside the door. Then one of the monks, suspecting what had happened, said: “Perhaps you have stolen something of these relics, and are now being held back by a hidden force. Know that, by Saint Bernard’s promise, none of these bones may be separated until the end of the world unless they themselves consent.”

Convicted, she disclosed her attempted theft, however devoutly motivated; and, having restored the sacred relic to its place, she ran unhindered to her mistress and confessed the entire occurrence, to the amazement of all. One of the religious of Clairvaux related this remarkable miracle to us in the chapel itself, arousing in us a great feeling of reverence and devotion toward this most noble treasure.

66. Leaving this chapel, we went outside the inner gate of the greater monastery and, after two hundred or slightly more paces, reached the old monastery. Bernard and the companions sent with him from Cîteaux built it with their own hands. Church and monks’ dwelling are covered by one roof, and a single floor separates the places for eating and sleeping.

Below, the refectory, paved with no stone, offered bare earth to be trodden by those most holy feet. It is indeed narrow for so great a holiness, illuminated by a few windows not more than a palm in size—windows through which, nevertheless, the splendor of holiness spread over the whole wide world. The kitchen adjoins the refectory and is likewise extremely cramped, yet sufficient for boiling the roots of herbs and leaves of trees upon which these athletes of virtue formerly lived.

From there one ascends by a stair to the dormitory, occupying the same length and breadth as the refectory. There still remain several bedsteads, made of four boards: as long as a tall man’s height and less by half in width, nearly resembling low chests except that they have no lid. A hole cut with an axe gave access, by which one had to climb into them. On examining them, I saw no trace that they had lain higher than ground level; evidently they used straw or dry leaves of trees, thrown into this sort of hollow, instead of feathers. Surely this was a most conspicuous mirror of extreme poverty, at the sight of which our cold age ought deservedly to blush.

67. Above the stair leading from the refectory to the dormitory is a cell inhabited by the honey-flowing Father Bernard. It is certainly small, more like a prison than a chamber, and such as so great an abbot might inhabit. It is only one foot wider than the cells in the dormitory of the new monastery which I described above at number 57, but it is subject to far more inconveniences. It is covered only by a bare roof, through which, though rain does not always penetrate, cold, heat, and a thousand other discomforts intrude. Sunlight enters through the same roof when a few shingles have been removed; a board closes the opening if rain or snow makes this necessary.

Moreover, the stair over which the cell hangs takes away one corner of it from the boards with which it is covered. These boards descend along that side of the cell in a sloping platform, yet were useful to Saint Bernard: he used them as a bed, placing beneath them two other trunks smoothed with an axe in place of a pillow. All these things may still be seen, but on no account touched, because the intrusive devotion of many people, taking tiny but often repeated portions, had almost carried away the whole. Now enclosed by railings, this bed—if indeed it may be called such—is exposed to eyes, not thefts. Within the railings also lies a belt rough with hair and iron, which the most holy Father used to put on to torment his body and which was found upon his bare skin after his death.

Finally, the seat was no better than the other parts of the cell. For besides being raised only a foot from the ground by a wall hollowed out in the manner of a chair, the slope of the overhanging roof did not allow the sitter to raise his head. Consequently, anyone wishing to sit or rise had to bend head and back until, moving one pace away, he had room to stand with head erect.

68. This is the seat from which so many oracles flowed into every region of the world. Upon this throne sat eminent that man of miracles—so calls him John de Bussières, S.J., the most polished writer of this age—especially eminent over the minds which he shaped at will: an Alexander in life; administrator of great affairs; master of pontiffs and kings; almost the single standard of the Christian world, obeyed by earth and heaven alike.

In the obscurity of this corner were born the following twenty illustrious titles, by which a grateful and astonished posterity distinguished Bernard, so that he is rightly and deservedly called:

1. Outstanding, honey-flowing, God-taught Doctor of the Holy Roman Church.
2. Most invincible defender of the Apostolic See.
3. Most zealous champion of ecclesiastical liberty.
4. Most intimate client of the great Mother of God.
5. Great zealot for the house of God.
6. Greatest wonder-worker among the saints.
7. Hammer of heretics.
8. Scourge of schismatics.
9. Herald of the sacred militia.
10. Peacemaker of the world.
11. Father of the fatherland.
12. Teacher of bishops and prelates.
13. Guide into the mysteries for all clerics and religious.
14. One proved and found to be an angel in the innocence of his life.
15. Patriarch by the propagation of the Order.
16. Prophet through foreknowledge of future things.
17. Apostle through the preaching of the Word.
18. Martyr through mortification of the body.
19. Confessor through zeal for the faith.
20. Virgin through purity of mind and body.

69. Beside this cell of the most holy Father is another, rendered famous by Saint Malachy—mentioned above at no. 58—through three months’ residence and his most holy death. It is of proper cellular form, though small. From there we descended to the oratory, such that poverty itself could not have contrived anything more concise. The altar occupies the front; it is visible in precisely the same adornment today, and no other, as that with which Saint Bernard furnished it. That is, on a wooden panel, an image of Christ hanging upon the cross is represented in cheap paint and crude workmanship; beside it are painted the half-figures of the Virgin Mother and Saint John, likewise executed by a brush of scant artistic skill.

Outside the choir, or central part of the church, on the right side is an altar of Saint Lawrence and on the left one of Saint Benedict, marked by likenesses equally simply rendered. Briefly receive from the Life of Saint Bernard the memorable account of these altars (book I, chapter 12):

> Bernard, very ill, when he was afflicted more violently and the pain increased beyond his strength, summoned one of his brethren and ordered him quickly to go and pray. The brother went and prayed at the three altars in that basilica: first, the altar in honor of Mary, Mother of God; and the other two placed around it, in honor of Saint Lawrence the martyr and Blessed Benedict the abbot. And behold, at that very hour the aforesaid Blessed Virgin came to the man of God, attended by those two ministers, Blessed Lawrence and Blessed Benedict the abbot. They came with the serenity and sweetness befitting them, and so visibly that he himself could distinguish the person of each from the very entrance of his cell. Laying their hands upon him and soothing the places of pain with most devout touch, they immediately drove every sickness from him.

70. The day had not yet advanced beyond the eighth hour and invited us to further sights. Therefore, leaving this arena of holiness, we went outside the walls to the place where Saint Bernard is said to have composed a letter in rain without being rained upon. I shall briefly explain, as is my custom, the sequence and cause of this miracle.

Robert, one of Bernard’s relatives, had been offered as a child to the Cluniacs. When he had passed from boyhood and age permitted, he left the monastery of Cluny and, desiring a more perfect life, joined the Cistercians. He was among those sent with Saint Bernard to found Clairvaux. But persuaded by the Cluniacs, and with his tender disposition shrinking from the severity of their rigorous life, he left Clairvaux without taking leave of the holy Father. Bernard for a while concealed the matter and awaited his voluntary return. But judging that neither the young man’s obstinacy nor his error should be endured longer, Bernard withdrew with William, whom he employed to write letters, into a wood near the monastery for privacy and began to dictate a letter as William wrote it on parchment.

Suddenly, in the middle of the work, a heavy rain burst forth, so that the writer wished to gather up the materials and take shelter. But Bernard said: “It is God’s work; write on. The rain will do us no harm.” The writer continued, nearly carried out of himself by wonder, as he saw the flood of the heaviest rain falling a pace or two away, while the two of them sat safely and dry in the open air as though beneath a roof.

The letter was certainly not dry in Robert’s case. Seriously repentant of his rashness, he was moved to copious floods of tears, returned immediately, and some years later was appointed by the holy Father abbot of the monastery of Domus Dei. He departed this life not without a reputation for holiness. The place is half an hour from Clairvaux, in the heart of a forest extending to the very walls. For perpetual remembrance of the miracle, they erected a small chapel in which this marvelous event is depicted.

71. Returning from the grove, we descended into the wine cellars, where casks of unusual size are to be seen. One in particular deserved close inspection above the rest. Since it was empty of wine and its great bottom displayed open doors, it invited my curiosity to enter and inspect the interior construction. But darkness allowed me to do nothing except measure the length with my feet. I found it thirty feet from one end to the other, and eighteen feet high.

It is bound by no hoops or rings of birch, as is customary with our casks. Four enormous beams, joined by cut joints at their ends, enclose the very long oak staves, arranged in six repeated rows. Then, where the circle ends at the four corners of the joints and the beams gape open, the empty space is filled with wedges, so that the entire structure, within the bonds of these timbers as though on a rack, may be loosened or tightened as needed.

You once saw and admired, my friend, the large cask of our cell at Maristella. If you compare it with this one at Clairvaux, how much smaller ours is! For ours measures only seventeen feet in length and twelve in height. In the other cellars, moreover, several vessels no smaller than our Maristella cask swelled with excellent wine.

72. During the very dinner that followed, a report arrived that thirteen thousand soldiers were hastening from France into Burgundy to besiege the town of Dole. Since we had to return home through that region, we hastened our departure. Having immediately given thanks for the great abundance of benefits received, we set out that same day and proceeded as far as the monastery of Longvaux, where we were again received with the greatest kindness.

While we were dining there, the commendatory abbot of that monastery, having returned from hunting and learned of our arrival, sent word through a servant that he wished to speak with us and, if it would not trouble us, that we should come to his house. We could not refuse so courteous an invitation. Following the same servant as guide, we met the abbot at the entrance hall of his residence. Having greeted us politely and eloquently, he led us across the level ground floor of the building to a very spacious hall. Large, highly ornate paintings hung on its lofty walls; most depicted ships tossed on the sea amid storms and their martial engagements: here fire, there shipwreck, swallowing up triremes.

From the hall a stone staircase led to the upper rooms, each splendid in its colors, matching the tapestries that covered both the walls and the tables. The number of paintings placed everywhere was immense, representing the likenesses of kings and princes, especially those of modern France. Some appeared so skillfully executed that they seemed to breathe Apelles, if not life itself.

Moreover, the library was very fully equipped with books, and adjoining it was another dining room containing paintings of rare value. When I took up a light and brought it close to the pictures, the abbot, pleased by my curiosity and plainly rejoicing that he had found observers of his possessions who were not indifferent, pointed out various works with his finger. He declared that some were renowned as the work of Albrecht Dürer, others of Holbein, and indeed of Rubens and Michelangelo of Rome. Having thus inspected the whole house, we went on to the stable and observed, besides a quantity of horses purchased from England, Spain, Pannonia, and Tartary, a bright vaulted ceiling, richly adorned with varied plasterwork and panels, which plainly made the monastery church itself seem an object of envy.

73. Dismissed from this residence, we prepared ourselves for rest. Having breakfasted in the morning, we entered the monastery of Alba Ripa, again distinguished by remarkable charity, and were refreshed by a splendid dinner—so far as the poverty of monks living under a commendatory abbot allowed. We had as guests two religious from that monastery, who used Latin so elegantly that I have scarcely heard anyone speak it with equal ease.

Before the table was laid, one of them offered himself as my companion for seeing the garden. Although I had preferred solitude in order to devote myself to the appointed measure of my prayers, I did not afterward regret having spent that time in most learned conversation. For he brought forth delightful events from history with such faithful memory as if he had wholly devoted himself to this study in order to acquire readiness in narration.

As he scattered many details concerning the life of our honey-flowing Father among his remarks, I began to ask whether Bernard had made this neighborhood memorable by any miracle also. He replied: “It has been handed down that he performed not a few things in this district around Clairvaux. For in this region there is a village in whose lodging-house the most holy Father is said to have contended with a demon in a charming conversation concerning humility of mind. Unless I am mistaken, it is described in nearly this sense in his Life:

> On a certain occasion Saint Bernard, received as a guest with some brethren, was, as was his custom, greasing shoes. The devil appeared to him, transformed into a black monk. ‘O Abbot,’ he said, ‘how great you have now become! Behold, I have come from the ends of the earth to see you, and I find you occupied in greasing shoes. You would not so comport yourself even toward one of your servants.’
>
> ‘But,’ said the holy Father, ‘I have no servants, nor have I ever wished to have them. In the Word of Christ Jesus I have begotten sons for myself, who obey me with all charity and humility. I love and serve them. To show them the way of life, I humble myself in imitation of that great Master who says in the Gospel: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” [Luke III]. God humbled Himself and traversed every path of humility so that we might follow His footsteps. Therefore it does not weary me to follow my Lord and Master; rather, it is fitting and pleasant for me, for love of Him, to occupy myself even in unseemly works and those in which there is no pleasure. Therefore tell your abbot also to do what I do.’
>
> The devil replied: ‘Give me your shoes, and I will grease them.’ Then the servant of Christ, fixing his gaze upon him, recognized by the light of the Holy Spirit the evil spirit, and with indignation and irony said: ‘It is not fitting that one created in supreme beauty and holiness should grease the shoes of me, who am earth and ashes. Away, Satan! And through Jesus Christ I adjure you never to hinder my work or that of my brethren.’ Immediately the devil diminished, contracted himself into a small little beast, and in that form withdrew from their sight.”

74. I followed the flight of the wretched trickster with laughter and asked my companion to continue with this most pleasant material. Without hesitation he said: “A little more than a day’s journey from here lies a small town famous for a delightful deed of the holy Father. It once happened that God’s servant Bernard had business with Count Theobald. As he approached the town in which the count then was, he met a great crowd dragging, by the count’s command, a certain notorious and wicked robber to execution.

On seeing him, the most merciful Father took in his own hand the rope with which the wretch was bound and said to the executioners: ‘Release this murderer to me, for I wish to hang him with my own hands.’ Hearing of the arrival of the man of God, the count hurried immediately to meet him. For he had always loved and honored Bernard with a marvelous devotion. When he saw the rope in Bernard’s hand, by which he was dragging the robber behind him, he was greatly horrified and said: ‘Alas, venerable Father, what did you intend to do? Why have you called back from the gate of hell this gallows-bird, condemned a thousand times over?’

The holy Father answered: ‘I know, most excellent sir, I know that this robber is most wicked and deserving of the extremity of every punishment. Do not think, therefore, that I wish to leave such a sinner unpunished. Rather, I intend to hand him over to executioners and exact from him a fitting vengeance—one that will certainly be so much more fitting as it is more enduring.’

On hearing this, the most Christian prince was silent and no longer dared to oppose the saint’s words. Immediately, therefore, the most kindly Father took off his own tunic, clothed his captive in it, cut off the hair of his head, and joined him to the Lord’s sheepfold, making a lamb out of a wolf and converting a robber. Coming with Bernard to Clairvaux, he thereafter remained obedient until death. Surviving for thirty years, he gave a fine etymological fulfillment of his name, Constantine, by perseverance in good purpose and the most rigorous works of penance; and he passed to the Lord by a holy death.

75. Inflamed by the pleasure of the story and eager to learn more, I then asked whether another place was far away—the place where a blind man, taking dust from Saint Bernard’s footprints, recovered his sight. He hesitated for some time, as if searching his memory, and then said: “It is several days from this monastery; for the account of the Life reports that this miracle occurred in the region of Toulouse, in almost these words:

> At one time the holy man labored in the region of Toulouse against the Henrician heretics. As one of the apostles, he traveled through towns and cities, preaching, healing every illness, and rebuking, refuting, and convicting the most shameful ravings of the heretics. It happened that a certain blind man, having learned the report of the virtues and signs multiplied through the hands of the man of God, was daily encouraged by hope of recovered health and determined to seek out this servant of God, in the hope that by the benefit of heavenly grace abundantly bestowed through him upon wretched mortals, the desired light might also be restored to himself, after the darkness of blindness had been wiped away.
>
> Hastening onward and anxiously inquiring where he might find the saint of God, he heard that Bernard was standing amid a great crowd at a celebrated gathering, spreading the word of life. Stumbling with his feet and running breathlessly, he arrived there, only to be disturbed by sad news: the man of the Lord had already departed and gone elsewhere. Yet what was he to do?
