His desire to recover health compelled him to continue running; but the very thick darkness that had beset his eyes made him slow and less able to move freely.
>
> As he languished in deep distress and sorrow, suddenly inspired by divine grace and conceiving with all his heart hope in the merits of the most blessed man, he said to those around him: ‘I beg you by God’s mercy, lead me to that place where you certainly know that the man of God stood or sat.’ Their kindness immediately granted his request. Coming to the place, he threw his whole body upon the ground, kissed with marvelous devotion the very dust in which the sacred footprints of the man of God had stood, and most earnestly implored the Lord’s mercy through the merits of His servant. When he had done this for a long time and, full of faith, rubbed his eyes with that same dust, suddenly, through the mercy of the Lord—who deigned to make known the holiness of His servant, though absent, even by this grace—he received the light of his eyes.
>
> This miracle not only provided the Catholics with a strengthening of orthodox faith, but also increased for the proud and arrogant heretics the mark of confusion and reproach.

76. He continued his account, gathering the miracles into a brief summary, and added that the most pious Father had indeed worked innumerable miracles throughout every part of France, but that those witnessed beyond its borders, in Germany and Italy, almost surpassed all number. For on his German journey alone, 173 persons deprived of the light of their eyes were enlightened through the merits of the holy man. By his blessing, the use of their limbs was restored to 158 lame persons. By a power bestowed upon him from heaven he raised up 15 persons bent double. Fifty-three mute persons obtained speech through his intercession; 65 deaf persons hearing; and 11 paralytics health. Fifty-five persons whose hands hung shrivelled and, as it were, dead received their desired soundness. The total number of all these wondrous deeds performed in this short time thus amounts to 530. Yet his inseparable companion on these journeys still declares: “Of many of these things here related I saw them done so quickly that I could not recount them as swiftly; and, although nothing is commonly said to be easier than speaking, still to this servant of God, through the grace he had received, the performance of signs seemed easier than the narration of what had been done.”

77. While my companion was thus pouring forth miracles by the hundred, I supposed that he would also mention those reported of the most holy Father in Book III, chapter 6, of the *Life*—deeds which have hitherto held me not only in the highest admiration, but also in the opinion that, among the whole company of saints, no one possessed greater confidence in God than Bernard. Therefore, lest I should appear unversed in so elegant a field of knowledge, I added: “Great are the things, most agreeable companion, that you have related; but do you not think those deeds surpass the rest which he is clearly known to have performed in the above-mentioned region of Toulouse?” The writer of the *Life* speaks thus of them:

“There is a place called Sarlat, where, after he had finished speaking, very many people offered the servant of God loaves to bless—as was done everywhere. Raising his hand and making the sign of the cross, he blessed them in God’s name, saying: ‘By this you shall know that the things urged by us are true and those urged by the heretics false: if your sick people, having tasted these loaves, obtain health.’ But the venerable bishop of Chartres, that great Geoffrey—for he was present and close beside the man of God—fearing, said: ‘If they receive them in good faith, they shall be healed.’ To him the holy Father, not doubting the Lord’s power at all, replied: ‘I would not say this; rather, truly, those who taste them shall be healed, so that they may thereby recognize us as true and truthful messengers of God.’ Then a vast multitude of sick persons, having tasted the same bread, recovered, so that this report was spread throughout the whole province.”

“And what confidence in God was this?” I added. Certainly the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine did not speak vainly concerning our most holy Father, in Book IV, *Controversies*, chapter 4: “Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, was a man wholly apostolic, illustrious no less for the glory of miracles than for the splendour of wisdom. He was distinguished by more miracles than any of the saints.”

78. “Beyond belief,” you will say, my friend, “you have drawn your history from your fortunate memory. Does your letter here speak in precisely the same words as your discourse did there, and no others?” Not entirely in the same words, indeed, but in words not very different. For concerning conversations of this kind, which will occur scattered throughout this journey, I want you to understand this: I give the sense, not the words; indeed, not even anxiously the whole sense. For the most part I omit things which I did not wish others to know, and perhaps sometimes add a few things which no prudent person will doubt could have been said or done.

I return to my companion. Having gone with him to table, I did not even then interrupt the thread of the subject, but during dinner, and afterward all the way to the monastery gate, mingled it with the emotions of farewell. Then, riding on as far as Sortilium, on the following morning, after Mass had been celebrated in the church of the Capuchin Fathers at sunrise, we poured out into the fields, hastening to Dijon. Arriving there about noon, we delayed only as long as was necessary to visit Monsieur Bourée, secretary of Cîteaux, who was then staying at Dijon with friends for the sake of his health, and to take dinner. When these matters had been satisfactorily dispatched, we completed the journey to the monastery of Cîteaux together with the course of the sun. We were at once admitted to greet the Most Illustrious Lord General and were soon conducted to our chamber. But the Most Illustrious Lord, having already dined, meanwhile commended us to his excellent countryman, Father Germanus, a member of the Society of Jesus; he supplied the General’s absence with exquisite courtesy. For, in conversations breathing uncommon learning and much experience, he adorned an otherwise splendid table to our great pleasure, nor would he leave until he understood that we desired nothing but rest.

79. On the following day, after the morning prayers were concluded, wishing to enjoy the freer air and the mildness of dawn—for the weather was clear—I had gone down to the walks of the garden, when the Most Illustrious Father General, newly returned from choir—for he is customarily found there first every day—saw me and summoned me to him. When I had made my way by the stairs and the outer hall to his presence, he ordered me to sit at table. He then began familiarly to ask about the success of the journey to Clairvaux and what had pleased me most along the way.

To each question I replied as modestly as I could: that Cîteaux deserved praise for its greater size and for the brightness of its buildings in comparison with Clairvaux; that the situations of the two places were not very different; but that the pools of Cîteaux seemed preferable to those of Clairvaux, both because their appearance was more cheerful and because fish were more abundant; that the church of Cîteaux too was externally more beautiful than that of Clairvaux, being brighter, somewhat larger, and more richly decorated in more recent workmanship; but that, as regards the choir and the high altar, Clairvaux surpassed Cîteaux. “Yet,” I said, “when I think of the secret impulses of piety that almost force themselves upon one there, of the cloister and the ornaments of the inner church—indeed, even of the single tomb and sacred remains of the most holy Father Bernard—no part of the world will now stand before Clairvaux in my esteem.”

80. He further asked what I thought of the manner of singing and of monastic discipline in France. I replied that in many respects I had changed the opinion I once held concerning the organization of these monasteries: in some matters I had formerly believed too much, in others too little. First of all, the prayers of the divine office, by day and by night, are prolonged with truly great labour to such lengths that they are kept in choir for nearly more than seven hours. It seemed to me that, unless their strength were supplied by a singular favour from above, they must soon succumb.

We Germans, indeed, distinguish the words by a rounded pronunciation exactly according to the prescription of our honey-tongued Doctor [Bernard], and carefully ensure that all voices together meet at one instant at both beginning and end. Yet our national custom prevails in such a way that our manner of singing imposes greater fatigue upon us than the one commonly heard in France. For we raise our voices with a stronger impulse, so that we not infrequently attain the truth of the Davidic song in which he affirms that he cries to the Lord. Since this labour very greatly exhausts one’s strength, no one among us has hitherto approved abstinence from eating meat—even if there were no other reasons—at least for this reason: that such unhealthy aquatic food adds little strength for sustaining that work for which maintenance was liberally bestowed upon us by our founders. Indeed, nothing occurs more frequently in those charters of donation than the statement that such properties are granted to the followers of Saint Bernard “that they may sing praises to the immortal God in this monastery.”

81. Moreover, I added, that law which forbids eating meat chiefly has this purpose: that, once the pleasures are removed from animal appetite—its own weapons, with which it attacks the spirit—the mind may be carried more freely to heavenly things. But in truth, although flesh should be banished from the whole world, ingenious gluttony will never lack a thousand kinds of flavours devised to excite its craving and fatten it through the fires of spices—at greater cost, certainly, but also with greater force toward luxury and lust. Most fish, besides, scarcely deserve even the name of food unless, buried beneath these seasonings, they almost put off their own nature.

For that reason, although the name of abstinence has considerable value in winning popular esteem, we judge that the highest summit of religious perfection does not lie in that alone. We take care first that excessive fullness, burdensome to health and reason, be excluded on every side; but that no one be deprived of necessary nourishment, and that such food be moderate and suited to preserve life and strength for bearing its burdens. But we regard abstaining from the stubbornness of one’s own judgment; freely renouncing conveniences that creep in under the deceptive appearance of consolations; not pursuing them except by command of obedience; and, on the contrary, bearing with peaceful mind troubles, pains, and afflictions arising within oneself or from elsewhere; displaying humility outwardly without an affected guise of sadness, so that one views both others’ honours without envy and one’s own contempt as a delight; restraining the impulses of anger and other vices with the firm rein of reason, as though within prison walls; and finally so ordering oneself wholly by the pole-star of the Deity that governs all things amid every variety of storms, that our will never differs from his—this, at last, we judge the most worthy pursuit of abstinence, and the one on which all our efforts and concerns should be spent.

Yet I do not recall these things so gloriously or boastfully as though we alone were vigorous champions in this arena of piety. Taught now by personal experience, I know that this discipline is held in the highest esteem in these regions; I say it only to establish that the practice of virtues and the eating of meat can undoubtedly coexist.

82. “May God confirm,” the Most Illustrious Lord General replied, “this candid and truly German disposition of yours. It is by no means unknown to me, as likewise is your sincere and constant love for the institutions of the sacred Order and your reverence for its superiors—something which, if ever at another time, I have certainly learned in these troubled latter days, to the great benefit of the whole Order.”

“Most Illustrious Lord,” I said, “no force, no deceit, no passage of time will shake this in us. For we hold as an unquestionable truth that the very name of a body within an Order will perish if unity falls. For how shall we be a body if members united by charity and by conformity to the Institute are not allowed to worship one head?”

As I observed, he received these words with a serene expression, not unaware from what source I had drawn them. Therefore, wishing to hear more on the same subject, he ordered the Reverend Lord Vicar General to be summoned to his chamber on my account. When he arrived immediately and had been detained there for a fairly long time, we prepared together to celebrate Mass. When that had been completed, the custodian of the sacred objects invited us to inspect what they call the treasury.

83. It is no less remarkable in its value—if a few things are excepted—than that which I have above reported seeing at Clairvaux. If you wish to count the number of sacred relics, there is kept here the head of Saint Ananias, he who in Acts of the Apostles, chapter IX, met the Doctor of the Gentiles at Christ the Saviour’s command and brought him light both of eyes and soul. This head, covered with silver, is visible at the back, where the skin, still whole and covered with hair, may be seen.

There are besides the heads of the holy women Faith, Hope, and Charity, and of their mother Sophia, gleaming with gold, silver, and gems astonishingly large. There is also the arm of Saint John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner, enclosed in a golden yet open case. There are plainly large portions of the Saviour’s most sacred cross, and countless other objects fashioned in diverse forms with silver plaques and other ornaments of no contemptible richness. There were also shown the splendid monuments of the dukes of Burgundy and a varied abundance of antiquities, as we commonly call them. Since the number of these things nearly overwhelmed my memory, I retained only these few which I have described.

84. One thing remains worthy of a curious observer; because I observed it attentively, I shall explain it briefly. They presented us with two little books in which the holy Fathers Stephen and Alberic, the first abbots of Cîteaux—as I said near the beginning of the letter—had written with their own hands the rules of the appointed prayers. I venerated these most beautiful pledges of the simplest antiquity and kissed the clearly shining marks of holiness.

The little books do not exceed three fingers’ breadth in width, though they are longer. When closed they appear small, but when opened become three times as large, because their leaves, made of rough parchment, are folded three times downward and on both sides. Nor are the pages filled with writing on both sides, but on the inner side only; so that, although you separate leaf from leaf, no letters appear unless the folds are unfolded. The letters themselves are extremely small, and with a few syllables bring whole periods to completion in the briefest compendium. The books are not bound by any binding or cover, but a cord along one side holds the leaves together lest they come apart. A leather pouch then receives the books, serving the Fathers when they happen to leave the monastery; in it they are even today protected from dust.

85. After this, chests were opened in which sacred vestments and other church furnishings are stored. Their exceedingly rich quantity seems deservedly preferable to the most celebrated treasuries I have seen elsewhere. Gold, worked into woven fabrics through delicate threads, produces several such vestments for seven ministers serving simultaneously at the altar: silk here flashes red, elsewhere purple, then white and blue. Many derive their value from an age extending over no few centuries; others from the person of the donor—for most are royal gifts; all from their material.

Moreover, embroidery distributes its Phrygian artistry amid thickly massed heaps of gold, together with white little gems called *Perilli*, along the borders of the vestments, so as to fill the eyes of beholders with admiration and delight, while leaving them uncertain whether the victory should be ascribed to art or to the worth of the material.

A *faldistorium*, as I believe it is called in Italian, is a seat upon which mitred prelates celebrating Mass sit amid the public ceremonial display. Above it a hanging cloth, like a canopy, spreads its wings in the shape of a royal throne. This throne, suspended around the room where the treasury is kept, long held our curiosity fixed upon it, since its tapestries represented, in most elegant pictures, ancient histories as though upon a stage, in colours most appropriate—though these were almost buried beneath gold and gems. I estimated this work of extremely rare beauty at no less than three thousand gold pieces, though I do not know whether that valuation was below or above its true worth. I remember that I mentioned several other ornaments belonging here above, no. 36.

86. This entire day everywhere supplied material for praise and gratitude alone. For when we had been summoned to the chamber of the Most Illustrious Lord General, a dinner complete in every respect was set before us, distinguished by the value of every seasoning and dish. Then the Most Illustrious Lord got into the carriage with us, accompanied also by his countryman Father Germanus. When the clouds had been cleared away, the open sky gave us some discomfort through excessive heat as we were carried into the open countryside. Yet the pleasantness of the fields, then green with the first growth of crops to come, the shade of the trees, and the gentle whisper of the breeze so shortened the distance that, when the carriage set us down at the castle called Chilly, I seemed to have spent not two hours but only a quarter of one in the carriage.

A very deep ditch encircles it, in the fashion of a true fortification; it makes the place secure, not against the attack of a regular war, but for the purpose of defending itself at least for some time in sudden and unexpected disturbances. From the ditch walls rise to a lofty height, so thick that they could withstand the blow of a lighter artillery piece. The interior arrangement of the buildings contains many great halls and dining rooms. Bright with high windows and splendid with hangings, they are, in my judgment, neither unworthy nor unsuitable even for a royal guest. On the side where the castle faces the rising sun, a wall of squared stone rises from the ditch, affording a broad walk and, below it, a most noble garden that gives material for curiosity and pleasure.

87. Having thus inspected the castle quickly, the Most Illustrious Lord delayed us no more than half an hour before taking us to another estate, called Bourveaux in the local language. Swiftly carried there across level fields, we were led by the steward of the place to the upper parts of the buildings—of marvellous elegance both in architecture and in the workmanship of their cut stone. Looking out from there, we saw a vineyard enclosed without interruption by a circuit of wall, extending, I suppose, in every direction beyond a quarter-hour’s walk.

The wine cellars, to which we were admitted, showed how abundant a vintage it yields each year, and by this abundance we could clearly measure our own poverty. More than two hundred casks, all of equal shape, stood around in three cellars. Pausing at one of them, the cellarer drove a small auger into it, making a little hole; when the auger was withdrawn, no wine followed. But when he pressed the bottom with his knee, a ruddy liquid leapt into a glass like blood spurting from a vein. While my companions wondered that the stream could be stopped without plugging the hole, I too, not ignorant of the matter, approached; putting my thumb into the middle of the cask’s bottom and pressing a little, I stirred the sluggish spring into a gush by the same pressure. When the reason for this had been explained, we tasted sparingly; for it gave off a fiery scent, as of wine almost burnt. Then, remounting the carriage, we returned to Chilly and thence to Cîteaux.

88. As we returned in the swiftly moving carriage, conversation turned to the commendable custom which the French observe at banquets. The dinner of that day, which we had praised for the same reason, provided the occasion for discussing it. For at it the dishes crowned the table on three occasions, while in the meantime liberty was given for a quarter of an hour to take, according to one’s pleasure, whatever pleased each person’s palate. At last, when everything had been removed, a conversation prolonged likewise for a quarter of an hour marked the end of the meal; after that neither cup nor dish appeared.

When these practices were highly praised in the carriage, the Most Illustrious Lord aptly added that he did not approve the custom of the German nation, which often celebrates banquets for two hours or more. For thirst and hunger surely do not last so long amid such continual eating and drinking; what is poured in afterward, therefore, must undoubtedly be a burden rather than nourishment.

“What? Two hours?” another replied. “Indeed, this sedentary battle of cups is prolonged to five hours and more. Surely the law of closer friendship does not permit one to invite a friend to table and dismiss him after one hour has passed. Nor is the courtesy of offering cups confined to the table alone. Stationary skirmishes, like those of boxers in an arena, follow the meal. Indeed, even when leaving, often at the very last thresholds of the house, those about to part thrust upon one another famous cups of health bearing grand titles, until dizziness puts an end to the contest.”

“This is madness,” said another, “not courtesy. What good is this guzzling? And what extraordinary profession of friendship is it to put on the character of pigs in order to please?” This pleasant dispute continued until dinner was over and gave much occasion for laughter. But lest we offend against this same philosophy, we rose from table early and spent the remainder of the day walking.

89. On the following day, having begun with sacred services and discharged them, we applied ourselves to packing our baggage. Thus, when all matters had been arranged, we refreshed ourselves at about the eighth hour with a timely dinner and bade farewell to Cîteaux, especially to the Most Illustrious Father General. In words carefully sought to express our gratitude, we offered him most abundant thanks for his supreme condescension, generosity, and favours toward us; and with due humility commended ourselves and our brethren to him.

Then, passing through the town of Saint-Jean-de-Losne, not large but extremely well fortified by its position and works, we gave our horses fodder and ourselves two hours’ rest in an obscure village, Bariere; and toward evening entered Dole. Changing our former lodging, we chose the sign of the Satyr. Hardly had we been received there when the director of the seminary arrived with two companions and most courteously displayed the greatest kindness both at dinner and on the following morning. Indeed, one of the three most companionably joined us as our guide for two hours toward Besançon. After he had left us, we stopped at the village of Saint-Vit for the delay of dinner and arrived at Besançon sufficiently early. Here the Golden Eagle admitted us beneath its roof. The clock bell had not yet marked the fifth hour of evening, and dinner was not served before the seventh; therefore, having removed the impediment of our boots, we went out through the streets of the city.

90. Buildings extending in an even line enclose streets of enormous length, marked by an innumerable multitude of merchants and craftsmen. Their greatest concentration, however, gathers around a very high bridge, which, because houses are built upon it, resembles a market more than a bridge; every corner is fitted out in the manner of a shop.

A very high mountain adjoins the city, and on its summit stands a church famous throughout the breadth of Europe, which drew our curiosity to itself although we were tired from the journey. Having climbed a steep path for nearly half an hour, we entered the church. Spanned by a very broad vault, it contains many mausoleums of marble and other carved structures of alabaster, wrought with no mean artistry. A chapel joins the right wall; within it, behind the altar, is kept under the guard of the canons and magistrates the sacred shroud in which that celebrated Joseph of the sacred history wrapped the body of our Saviour when it had been taken down from the cross.

It is displayed twice yearly from a position which many believe, not without reason, to have been appointed for this sight by the special providence of God. For outside the church a wall, carried around four corners in the manner of a theatre, extends toward the upper part of the mountain. On the appointed day it is borne there by leading members of both the canons and the magistracy, to the great convenience of spectators flocking from every neighbouring region. Though more than twenty thousand people gather, no one has ever been heard to complain that he did not obtain a view, as he wished, of the precious treasure—whether he stood near or at a more distant place.

91. A few paces from this church stands another chapel, named after its two occupants, the judges of the sacred tribunal. By privilege they possess an authority in disputes involving the conscience of the dying almost equal to that of the highest power on earth. Here, for some time intent upon the city lying below, we were greatly delighted as our eyes wandered without effort through it; for we grasped the entire city at a single view, gathered together like a painter’s work into the compass of a little picture.

The side of the mountain facing the city drops sheer like a wall and serves at once as wall and rampart, being much higher than even the highest tower. On the descent we marvelled at the tireless, almost youthful vigour of our Most Reverend Vicar General in this advanced age, by which he had completed so steep an ascent without a sigh. Observing what we were murmuring about, he smiled with an open countenance and said: “You are amazed that an old soldier has overcome this mountain with such ease. Take courage, and see that after forty years you may have strength as constant for this labour as I remember that, by God’s favour, I possessed forty years ago no less than I do today. The pursuit of piety and temperance, and the security of conscience arising from them, are a sure support for attaining these things.”

Thus, as we went down by another street of the city, our guide, whom we had taken as a companion to show the way, led us among other places to the finely adorned church of the Dominican community. We then had dinner before sleep and determined to set out on the following day at the sixth hour.

92. But through the cunning of my servant we were delayed until noon. He complained that my horse was excessively tired and would that day either perish or at least fail to keep up with the others, unless it were helped by removing part of the burden. This, he said, could conveniently happen if another horse were hired, while mine followed without a rider. But whether he intended to provide for himself and his own fatigue or for the horse was quite evident when, another horse having been brought for me, he threw himself upon mine, intending to ride it all the way to Basel unless another inconvenience prevented him.

For this hired Bucephalus ran comfortably for about fifty paces outside Besançon; then gradually slowly, afterward sluggishly, and finally did not even walk. I applied blows and vigorously spurred him, but I was telling a tale to a deaf man. I think such blows would sooner have moved that Trojan horse than the utterly stupid animal on which I sat. With stubborn immobility it planted its feet, receiving the prick of the spurs, I suppose, as a signal not to run but to stand still. My companions had already gone ahead by one or two stone's throws when, having lingered for some time at a spring, I caught up with them, not without annoyance, and sent the horse back to the city with its guide after paying the price. My own horse, as though taking this as a point of honour, thereafter carried me briskly as far as Mariastein; and my servant’s feet, by a similar reasoning, did not feel weariness.

93. We therefore pushed on vigorously, passing through the town of Baume-les-Dames and arriving at the small town of Clairvaux. After spending the night there comfortably, we equipped ourselves for the road at earliest dawn. Before dinner, which we took at the village of Ottinkurt, we suffered excessive heat; after noon we were harassed by rains, until at last we found lodging in the Alsatian border village of Courtelevante, along with a poor dinner but beds far more wretched. For straw corrupted by rot exhaled its offensive smell even on the following day, our clothes absorbing the stench until the rains washed it away.

Leaving this village at sunrise, we endured very great discomfort until dinner. The road, obstructed by frequent stones, compelled the rider to keep his eyes on the ground, lest the horse be badly led, and to guard against continual fear of a fall through careful handling of the reins. Meanwhile, branches weighed down by rain deprived us of the use of our eyes; being very troublesome, they now caught in our hats, now sent down doubled showers, now suddenly struck our foreheads, wearying both rider and horse. At last, refreshed by dinner in the village of Wolkenspurg, and after four further hours passing the city of Basel, we turned aside to the monastery of Mount Olivet.

94. The sacred feast of Pentecost fell on 29 May. In order that we might observe it with due devotion, we decided to stay and take breath in a monastery familiar to our Order and homeland. Nor was opportunity lacking. The Most Reverend Lord Vicar General, adorned with episcopal insignia—understand the mitre and other such marks—celebrated Mass amid the solemn ceremonies of the ministers; and afterward those virgins consecrated to God received us with a splendid feast.

Although the following day was drenched by continuous rain, it did not prevent me from returning to Basel. When Master Jacob Wolleb learned that I was staying there, he promptly sent a servant and, having invited in honour the magnificent rector of the university, a doctor of law, and other men eminent for learning, graciously included me in an elegantly furnished banquet. After spending almost the whole day with them in familiar conversation, I returned to Mount Olivet a little before nightfall.

[Col. 1620A]

95. At last, on the third day, when the sky had again settled into fair weather, the Most Reverend Lord Vicar General, with his company, intended after Mass early in the morning to make for Saint Urban; I, for my part, intended to go to Mariastein. Ten hours’ travel remained for each of us. We settled our accounts of expenses. When these had been paid, I gave the Most Reverend Lord Vicar General infinite thanks for the patience he had shown toward me; for his singular familiarity and humility, of which I judged myself altogether unworthy; and finally for the highest charity and care which he had bestowed on me throughout the journey.

I promised that, as long as the immortal Deity granted me life, no forgetfulness would ever efface such great benefits; indeed, that I would propagate their memory even beyond the bounds of life, if what I most earnestly desired were permitted me. Meanwhile, I would make up by my prayers for the deficiency of strength wholly unequal to repaying in any measure such generous kindness; and would at least bring it about that he might understand how ready an affection of gratitude and devotion toward him I bore. Then, rendering due thanks also to the other companions of the journey, I went on to the village of Frick. Having dined there, I crossed the rough and level roads, amid no small dangers over the mountain called Bozberg, and saw Mariastein again, from which I had been absent thirty-seven days.

96. Though I reached the threshold of our Mariastein late in the evening, a large crowd of greeters immediately surrounded me from every side. Some asked about the attendance and outcome of the general chapter; others about newly considered matters and statutes; others investigated whether I had completed the journey successfully and what news I brought from those foreign peoples and distant regions. Nor did I lack agreeable material for discourse, which I had gathered so curiously; but gradually I grew weary of telling it, as I was forced so often to reheat the same cabbage.

For, in groups—now three, now four, mixed together—I depicted Dole or Dijon for some, Cîteaux and Clairvaux for others; I lodged these magnificently, those miserably. Then, when each carried his own news to another along with whatever account he had heard, however superficial, everywhere there was kindled a desire to know each matter distinctly. Therefore, to save time, I decided to write to you at greater length the letter owed both by promise and by the right of friendship, so that the things I had brought back impressed only upon memory might not wholly vanish, and that all might receive the reported matters with equal fidelity.

The letter reached its end in a short time. When one or two of the more learned men had read it, they strongly urged me to make it public through the benefit of the press. As nothing much occurred to prevent me from yielding to their wishes, and as they clearly showed me that the description of these most beautiful things, if it reached others, would contribute greatly to the honour of our Mariastein—indeed, of the whole sacred Order—I obtained permission from our Most Reverend Lord Abbot and entrusted it to good fortune. I shall observe from afar whether it gathers applause or derision; I shall attribute the former to the benefits of my Most Reverend Lord Patron, to whose honour it will surely be given, but shall not marvel at the latter amid the licence of this age, which everywhere censures things worthy of praise and exalts things deserving to be put down.

97. This would indeed also be the end of my journey and writing, had not my constant travelling companion, eight days later, led me through Liebenfels Castle to the monastery of Salem. I therefore judged it worthwhile to append a few remarks about it. This royal monastery, to be counted among the most distinguished of the Order, may not only be compared with those principal houses described here by me, but in some respects may even be preferred to them.

If you compare its larger church, lofty with most polished vaulting; then its most elegant cloister, wonderfully adorned with highly artistic paintings; the vault of its richly furnished library and of the chapel beneath it; together with the buildings of its other places—you will certainly place those others far below Salem. Its remaining structures, especially the dormitory, museum, refectory, and the dwellings of the officials, are singularly commended both by their evident spaciousness on every side and by their convenience. Its vaulted wine cellars likewise are filled with great casks. Finally, a modest stream runs through the whole monastery by hidden channels, serving both pleasure and the needs of the workshops.

98. But above all, the great church displays countless altars covered with gold and noble through the painter’s brush; certainly no corner lacks some distinctive ornament. I do not know whether the high altar shines anywhere with greater majesty. Ancient paintings are set within the structures of the side altars; they compel me to confess that I have neither seen nor shall see works of art coming closer in likeness to the truth of nature. So carefully and with such refined diligence do the small images portray their respective faces, garments, and limbs that, without fiction or jest, I affirm that not even Apelles could have added anything.

Outside the vault enclosing the sacred furnishings, a statue of the Virgin Mother is attached to a certain column and is renowned for miracles. During the most recent Swedish war, highly trustworthy witnesses established that it shed real tears. I recently spent three days in this monastery and was treated with such kindliness and generosity that I cannot sufficiently extol, as they deserve, the humanity of the Most Reverend Lord Abbot and the officials.

99. As I was about to depart, already standing almost on the threshold, I asked the Reverend Father Magnus Herbst, superior, bursar, and secretary of the monastery, in what year Salem had been founded and by what nobles endowed. He then led me to the great door of the church and told me to read what was set forth on a large tablet hanging there. I have wished to reproduce it here in the same words; it reads as follows:

“The monastery of Salem was founded and dedicated to God and the Mother of God by Guntram, free baron of Adelsreiten, in the year 1137, under Innocent II, Supreme Pontiff, Emperor Lothair II, and Ulrich II, bishop of Constance. Conrad III, emperor, duke of the Franks and Swedes, confirmed the foundation by granting it imperial protection and exemption. Finally, in the year 1202, Eberhard, bishop of Salzburg, from the noble family of Truchsess, the line of the barons of Adelsreitin having become extinct, assumed Guntram’s place and office and enriched Salem with great benefactions—a true second founder.”

100. And thus, I think, I have abundantly discharged my promise. According to your customary fairness and goodwill toward me, judge my efforts. If you happen to think that you have encountered some harshness or obscurity of style, attribute it to haste and to a work completed in less than a month. Meanwhile, join with me in rendering thanks to the supreme Divinity; to the great Virgin Mother; to her honey-tongued son Bernard; and to her virginal spouse Joseph. For I had earnestly commended, as it were, the course of my journey to their patronage; and thus, by a singular good fortune, I completed it safe and unharmed. Pray also that they may graciously fortify us with their protection for that long journey into eternity, and safely lead us to that homeland for which we were born. Farewell.

[Col. 1621]

## DESCRIPTION OF THE TOMBS AND BURIALS THAT FORMERLY EXISTED IN THE ABBEY OF CÎTEAUX

*(Literary Journey of Two Benedictines, Paris, 1717, quarto, p. 198.—Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, vol. IX, Paris, 1736, p. 193.—MS 357 of the public library of Dijon.)*

[Col. 1621C] Dom Martène and Dom Durand gave, in their *Literary Journey*, a description of the tombs of the Abbey of Cîteaux. The *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions* contain another, drawn up by Moreau de Mautour from his own observations [Note: [Col. 1621D] In his youth M. de Mautour spent the holidays on an old family estate at Brazey-en-Plaine (Côte-d’Or). He often visited the Abbey of Cîteaux, which was only two leagues from Brazey. He returned there three times afterward [Col. 1622D]: his final journey took place in 1721.], and from memoranda supplied to him by Dom Gaudelet, prior of Valette on the Dordogne, a monk of Cîteaux, and Dom Cotheret, Doctor of the Sorbonne and learned librarian of the Abbey [Note: [Col. 1622D] MS 357 of the public library of Dijon contains Dom Cotheret’s remarks and M. de Mautour’s first draft.].

The first tomb seen at the entrance of the Abbey church of Cîteaux, in an enclosed chapel under the porch on the right-hand side, called the Chapel of the Dukes, was made in the thickness of the wall. It rose four feet above the ground [Col. 1621D], beneath a stone arch; and the epitaph engraved upon the frieze of the tomb contained almost nothing but the names of the first three dukes of [Col. 1622C] Burgundy buried there. It read:

> HERE LIE three most illustrious DUKES OF BURGUNDY: ODO, founder of this monastery, who died in the year 1102; HUGH, his son, who died in the year 1142; ODO, son of the said Hugh, who died in the year 1162. MAY THEIR SOULS REST IN PEACE. AMEN.

It appears that this inscription was set up only long after the deaths of these three princes. The site of this tomb, containing a chapel and an altar, was enclosed within the church forecourt by Nicolas Boucherat, the first of that name, abbot of Cîteaux, who had the dividing wall raised in 1584.

Under the same porch of the church, on the [Col. 1622D] left upon entering, stood a tomb about five feet above the ground, bearing this epitaph engraved on its frieze:

> [Col. 1623A] HERE LIES THE MOST SERENE DUKE OF BURGUNDY HUGH III, son of ODO II, who met a glorious death on the eastern expedition against the infidels in the year 1192. He had founded the holy chapel of Dijon in the year 1172. MAY HE LIVE FOREVER IN HEAVEN. AMEN.

Without leaving the church forecourt, one saw another tomb, likewise on the left, rising about five feet above the ground beneath a stone arch set into the thickness of the wall. It was the burial-place of four lords of Vergy, whose coat of arms was painted on the wall beneath the arch, and of a lady of Vergy, believed to have been Elisabeth, lady of Vergy, wife of Hugh of Mont-Saint-Jean. In the same tomb lay two lords of Mont-Saint-Jean, mentioned by the epitaph:

> [Col. 1623B] HERE LIE four illustrious Lords and one Lady of Vergy, and two lords of Mont-Saint-Jean. May they rest in peace. Amen.

After crossing the nave of the church of Cîteaux, one found, on the right-hand side of the choir behind the stalls, a tomb of black and white marble rising about three feet above the ground. It was that of Guy de Rochefort, Chancellor of France, and Marie Chambellan, his second wife. They were represented there in marble, with the following epitaph engraved on the frieze:

> HERE LIES Lord Guy de Rochefort, most upright Chancellor of France, who died on 15 January 1507; and the most illustrious Lady Marie de Chambellan, his wife, to whose fidelity, guardianship, and direction was entrusted [Col. 1623C] the youth of the Most Serene Princess Lady Claude of France, eldest of the daughters of the most pious King Louis XII.

The arms of Guy de Rochefort engraved on his tomb were azure, semy of gold billets, with a silver chief charged with a red lion passant guardant; for a crest, a lion’s head supported by a pair of wings.

Above the tomb of Guy de Rochefort and Marie Chambellan there had formerly been for each a long epitaph in old language, written upon vellum in four columns and set in a wooden frame. Father Martène reproduced both from Palliot (*History of the Parliament of Dijon*), because by the time of his journey they had long since ceased to exist [Col. 1623D].

One had 120 lines, comprising ten stanzas of twelve lines each; the other had 116 lines.

Here are some lines from it:

> Here lies the flower, the title, and excellence,  
> The peerless one, supreme pre-eminence,  
> Honor, worth, perfection among humankind;  
> The true mirror of prowess and valor,  
> The great stream and river of eloquence,  
> The public good, surpassing the Romans;  
> Wise, discerning, setting his hand to all things,  
> Sparing neither mighty, weak, nor strong.  
> To name him: it is Guy de Rochefort,  
> The most accomplished man who flourished in his age.

There was an epitaph of thirty-four French verses, engraved upon a copper plate at the place where Rochefort’s heart lay. It was attached to the pillar [Col. 1624A] of the chapel of Saint Claude in the nave, nearest the middle of the choir.

The fifth tomb stood against the southern gable of the church crossing and contained the bodies of two contemporary bishops, one of Autun and the other of Chalon-sur-Saône. Their names alone were learned from two inscriptions painted in Gothic letters upon the wall above the tomb:

> HERE REST TWO BISHOPS, TRUE SERVANTS OF SOLOMON: HENRY OF AUTUN AND PETER OF CHALON.

The following epitaph was engraved on the frieze of their tomb:

> HERE LIE two most illustrious prelates: HENRY, bishop of Autun, son of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy [Col. 1624B]; and PETER, bishop of Chalon, formerly a monk of this monastery. Both died in the year 1178.

But since it is established (*Gallia Christiana*, IV, 397) that Stephen had succeeded Henry in the bishopric of Autun as early as 1171, it must be acknowledged that the epitaph was later; no use can be made of it.

In the chapel of Saint John the Baptist, on the Gospel side, one saw a magnificent tomb. It was that of Philippe Pot, represented fully armed and wearing a surcoat, lying upon a tomb about six feet high, supported by eight mourners, each bearing upon his arm a shield of one of Philippe’s family alliances. The first shield bore the undifferenced arms of the house [Col. 1624C] of Pot: gold with an azure fess. The second, with the same arms, was quartered with those of the house of Courtjambe, allied to that of Pot. The remaining shields displayed the alliances of Vergy, Blaisy, Montagu-Sombernon-du-Blé, Nagu, Varennes, and Vaudrey.

Philippe Pot died at the age of sixty-six. As he had a particular devotion to the Blessed Virgin, he wished to be buried in the church of Cîteaux, which was dedicated to her. On a pillar supporting the vault of the chapel containing his tomb, one saw a Latin epitaph of forty-four lines. Palliot and Father Martène reproduced it; it began:

> Mourn Philippe Pot, whom pitiless death snatched from the midst of life,  
> [Col. 1624D] whose fame shall endure forever.

Its conclusion was:

> In the year fourteen hundred ninety-four,  
> In the month of September, he gave these limbs to this resting-place.

There was another epitaph in French prose, which Father Martène did not reproduce, though it supplied many details of Philippe Pot’s life. It ran as follows:

> **TANT L. VAUT**  
>
> Here lies Messire Philippe Pot, knight, lord of La Roche-Nolay, of Châteauneuf in Auxois, and for the greater part of Genvray in Charolais; Grand Seneschal of Burgundy; lord of Thorey-sur-Ouche and Saint-Romain. He was brought up in the household of the late Monseigneur the good Duke Philippe of Burgundy—may God [Col. 1625A] absolve him—who made him a knight, was his godfather, and, by election of the knights of the Order of the Golden Fleece, bestowed it upon him and placed it around his neck. He gave him great wealth and honors in many ways and in various offices, according to the age at which he served him; and about two or three years before his death he was first Chamberlain. He gave him the captaincies of the castle and towns of Lille, Douai, and Orchies.
>
> After the death of his said master, Monsieur Duke Charles, his son, retained him in his service as one of his principal Chamberlains, and in general left him all the offices in whose possession he found him. In that service he remained throughout the life of his said lord and master. After that master’s death, the people of the town of Lille, both officers and all others, expelled him from the castle and the town itself by command of the Mademoiselle of Burgundy, then lady of the aforesaid [Col. 1625B] places, and compelled him to withdraw to Tournai. There, at that time, the men of the King and of my said lady came and went. With the consent of the aforesaid lord and lady, the King summoned the said lord of La Roche to that place, wished to have him in his service, gave him great benefits, removed from him the aforesaid Order which he wore, and did him the honor of leaving him his own; and he created him Grand Seneschal of Burgundy.

As for the motto *TANT L. VAUT* (“It is worth so much”), it is claimed that it originated in an adventure of Philippe Pot in Palestine. Having been taken prisoner, Bajazet II gave him only the choice of changing his religion or overcoming a ferocious lion. At the height of the struggle, the knight, full of confidence in the Blessed Virgin’s aid and recalling the ancient miraculous image of [Col. 1625C] Our Lady of Good Hope at Dijon, cried: “TANT L. VAUT!” He thereafter made it the war-cry of his arms.

The Sultan, filled with admiration for the courageous conqueror of the lion, restored his liberty and gave him his own sabre; this led Philippe Pot to quarter his arms with two scimitars, called *badelaires* in heraldic language.

To perpetuate the signs of his gratitude, Philippe Pot had Our Lady of Good Hope painted in a picture in which he was represented kneeling, with his motto *TANT L. VAUT* issuing from his mouth. Beside it one read this rondeau:

> Mother of God, most glorious,  
> Fair, gracious, and *saicoureuse* [sense uncertain]:  
>
> Zaphis [reading uncertain], who ever was upon the earth,  
> Most humbly I come to seek  
> Your precious protection.  
>
> Until now you have preserved for me  
> Honor, life, and health;  
> Under hope of your great mercy  
> I give myself to your will.  
>
> Save me, Lady most blessed,  
> From the prison so grievous  
> Where nothing is seen but cruelty.  
> Keep me from being cast into it,  
> For you are merciful to everyone,  
> Mother of God.  
>
> **TANT L. VAUT**  
>
> And it has been worth so much  
> To him who had recourse  
> [Col. 1626A] To her for whom this word was spoken—  
> Philippe Pot, your suppliant,  
> Whom she has delivered from every evil.  
>
> **TANT L. VAUT**

[Note: [Col. 1625D] *History of the Miraculous Image of Our Lady of Good Hope*, Dijon, 1733, 1777, and 1823. The motto *TANT L. VAUT* was seen in all Philippe Pot’s castles, in every room, over all the fireplaces, and in all the stained-glass windows [Col. 1626D].]

This painting, formerly in the church of Notre-Dame at Dijon, had before the Revolution been given to Madame de Santaucours, a descendant of Philippe Pot. She had it placed at Barbirey.

The seventh tomb, that of Robert of Burgundy, count of Tonnerre, was of black marble, with the figure of this prince in a warrior’s dress, in white marble. It stood in the choir of the church, on the Epistle side, above the seats of the celebrant. This inscription was read above it:

> HERE LIES MONSEIGNEUR ROBERT OF BURGUNDY, [Col. 1626B] Count of Tonnerre, formerly son of Monseigneur Robert, Duke of Burgundy, and of Lady Agnes, formerly daughter of Monseigneur Saint Louis, King of France; he died on the Saturday before Saint Luke’s Day in the year of grace 1334.

This epitaph was plainly modern.

The next tomb, higher than that of the count of Tonnerre and on the same side of the choir, was believed to be that of two prelates who died in the odor of sanctity: Blessed Peter and Cardinal Robert.

Blessed Peter, first abbot of Pontigny, then of Cîteaux, and afterward bishop of Arras, is said to have died in 1203. But since, according to the chronicle of Alberic, the bishop of Arras who died in 1203 was buried [Col. 1626C] at Pontigny, there is reason to believe that two bishops of Arras of the same name had been confused: one, who had been abbot of Cîteaux, died on 18 December 1185, while the other was his successor.

Cardinal Robert had received the purple from Pope Celestine V in 1294. He was the fifteenth abbot of Pontigny, from which he was taken in 1293 to become the twenty-eighth abbot of Cîteaux. He died at Parma in 1305, in the monastery of Saint Martin of the same Order. Its monks sent his body to Cîteaux for burial, as he had directed when dying.

Dom Martène reports the epitaphs of Blessed Peter and Cardinal Robert. Yet at Cîteaux there was no trace of Peter’s, and Robert’s is found only in the *Gallia Christiana* and in the *Annals of Cîteaux*, where one reads:

> [Col. 1626D] ROBERT died at Parma in 1305, in the month of August; transferred from the church of Saint Martin, he was buried in the choir of his own basilica, to the left of the high altar.

Behind the high altar, on the Epistle side beneath the low vaults, stood a shrine containing the heart of Pope Calixtus II, with this inscription:

> BEHOLD, HERE IS THE NOBLE HEART OF LORD POPE CALIXTUS.

The shrine bore two keys crossed saltirewise, and below them two mitres, one crossed by a crozier and the other by a patriarchal cross.

The heart of Pope Calixtus had been brought to Cîteaux in the time of Saint Stephen, its third abbot.

Beneath the shrine containing the heart of Pope Calixtus II was a stone sepulchre in which lay the bodies of two celebrated prelates: Waldemar, archbishop of Bremen, son of King Canute, and Albert, patriarch of Antioch.

Their epitaph follows:

> [Col. 1627A] Besides the noble heart of the most holy Lord Pope Calixtus II, which was placed in the upper part of this tomb, as was shown by the following, indeed most ancient, inscription—barely legible—on the side of the same tomb, on the side by which one formerly ascended to the most august sacrament of the Eucharist, before the year 1667, when the high altar was erected in that splendid and magnificent form in which it is now seen:
>
> “Behold, here is the noble heart of Lord Pope Calixtus.”
>
> Here also lie two venerable prelates of the Church: WALDEMAR, son of Canute, king of Denmark, who, having renounced the bishopric of Schleswig and also the archbishopric of Bremen, to which he had recently been elected, took the monastic habit in this monastery and four years later passed from this life to Christ on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], in the year 1226. He was the first laid to rest and buried in this tomb. And Lord ALBERT, patriarch of Antioch, was the second to be placed in this same sepulchre. In his honor the following decree of the General Chapter of the year 1246 was made:
>
> [Col. 1627C] “For the late Lord Albert, patriarch of Antioch, of blessed memory, who, while at the court of the Lord Pope, out of the greatest devotion which he bore toward the Order, chose his burial in the House of Cîteaux, our mother, a full office is granted throughout the whole Order.”

Opposite this tomb, behind the choir on the Gospel side, stood another in the form of a large shrine, containing the bodies of Saint Palladia and Saint Samnia, two of the eleven thousand virgins, with this inscription above it in Gothic letters:

> HERE LIE the bodies of the holy Palladia and Samnia, who are among the number of the eleven thousand virgins.

Father Martène says that Mass was formerly celebrated upon their tomb.

[Col. 1627D] Beside this shrine, in the thickness of the wall on the Gospel side, was a tomb containing the bodies of four prelates: an archbishop and three bishops—Donat O’Nolargau, eleventh archbishop of Cashel in Ireland; Peter, bishop of Le Puy; Robert de Châtillon, bishop of Langres; and Robert, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône.

The epitaph of these prelates, in Gothic letters, ran:

> HERE THE TWO ROBERTS, BISHOPS OF LANGRES AND CHALON,  
> REST TOGETHER WITH PETER OF LE PUY.  
> WITH THEM IS ASSOCIATED DONATUS, HONORED  
> PRELATE OF CASHEL, AND A COMPANION IN OUR MONASTIC PROFESSION.

Since this tomb was no longer visible because of the new altar built in 1667, this inconvenience was in some [Col. 1628A] measure remedied by hanging on a pillar a panel containing a long Latin epitaph, reproduced by Father Martène.

The twelfth tomb was that of Blessed Guy Paré, fifteenth abbot of Cîteaux. Having died of plague at Ghent on 30 July 1206, his body was brought to Cîteaux.

His epitaph, inscribed on a scroll, read:

> Given to us from the summit of the episcopate,  
> Transferred from Rheims, blessed Guy lies here.

And this other was engraved on the frieze of his tomb:

> THE BODY OF BLESSED GUY DE PARÉ, formerly Cardinal and Legate in Germany, raised from monk and abbot of this monastery to the archbishopric [Col. 1628B] of Rheims; he died at Ghent in the year 1206.

In the sanctuary, on the Gospel side, was the tomb of Blessed Arnaud Amalric. After being abbot of Cîteaux for ten years, he was elected archbishop of Narbonne in 1212. He died in September 1225. His body was brought and buried at Cîteaux, where a mausoleum was erected for him. He was represented in pontifical vestments, with mitre and crozier, with two figures of bishops above and two assisting abbots at his feet. At the base of this mausoleum, though upon a different tomb, was another abbot wearing a mitre, perhaps representing Arnaud in the different dignities he had held. It was alleged that his epitaph had been removed in 1356 by [Col. 1628C] soldiers during the wars of King John.

Manrique and the authors of the *Gallia Christiana* say that Arnaud was buried at Cîteaux, without positively identifying the location of his burial. But they also say that Robert, abbot of Pontigny, afterward twenty-eighth abbot of Cîteaux and then cardinal, was buried where Arnaud was believed to have been buried. They report a Latin verse epitaph, found in the time of Dom Vaussin, abbot of Cîteaux, written on vellum inside the tomb. It was the epitaph reproduced by Father Martène, p. 208, from André du Chesne’s *History of the Cardinals*.

In 1666, when Dom Vaussin, abbot of Cîteaux, [Col. 1628D] had the high altar rebuilt, some tombs had to be removed; but care was taken to preserve their inscriptions and epitaphs. Such were those of Pope Calixtus II, the patriarch of Antioch, the archbishop of Cashel, and the bishops of Le Puy, Langres, and Chalon. They had been transcribed and painted on the outer wall of the sanctuary, and renewed in 1686.

The figure of the prelate visible upon the tomb, wearing a mitre, hands joined, with a small figure at his feet holding a book, could all the more plausibly designate this Arnaud because, according to Ciaconius, Cardinal Robert was not a bishop but only cardinal [Col. 1629A] priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana. Nothing therefore prevents one from believing that this monument was erected in memory of these two great men buried at Cîteaux and brought together, though at different times, in the same mausoleum.

At the base of Blessed Arnaud’s tomb, under one copper tombstone, were buried the bodies of Nicolas Boucherat, the first of that name, abbot of Cîteaux, and Nicolas Boucherat his nephew, likewise abbot of Cîteaux. There was a long Latin epitaph of the first, engraved upon a copper tablet, with his arms attached to the wall. On 2 May 1601, Edme de la Croix, his successor, substituted this tablet for the life-size bronze effigy of Boucherat the elder, which [Col. 1629B] had been removed during the plundering of 1589, along with all the metal in the church, weighing more than thirty-five thousands. From part of that metal the count of Tavannes had two cannon cast, weighing fourteen thousands, which were at the castle of Dijon.

Adjoining the tomb of the two Boucherats was that of Dom Claude Vaussin, abbot of Cîteaux, with a Latin epitaph which stated that he died on 1 February 1670.

In the sanctuary of the church, in the places of the deacons and subdeacons, were buried seven bodies of dukes or duchesses of Burgundy, princes and princesses of their blood: Odo III; Philip, son of Odo IV; Philip, his son; Alix of Vergy, wife [Col. 1629C] of Odo III; Alix of Burgundy, their daughter; and Yolande of Dreux, first wife of Hugh IV.

Among the great persons buried at Cîteaux were reckoned sixty dukes and duchesses, princes and princesses of Burgundy.

Outside the church of Cîteaux, behind the choir, there had formerly been a chapel called Saint George’s, containing several monuments of princes and princesses of the house of Burgundy. But it had been entirely demolished in 1589 by the troops of the count of Tavannes, brother of the viscount of Tavannes, who commanded at Dijon for the duke of Mayenne.

The seventeenth tomb, located in the chapel of All Saints, rose about [Col. 1629D] three feet above the ground. It was that of Philippe de Vienne, lord of Pagny, and Jeanne his wife, daughter of the count of Geneva, both allied to the house of Vergy. They were represented as stone figures lying on their tomb, which bore this epitaph on its frieze:

> HERE LIE Lord Philippe de Vienne, lord of Pagny, and Lady Jeanne, his wife, daughter of the count of Geneva. May they rest in peace. Amen.

In the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene was the tomb of Messire Philippe de Saint-Hilaire, of his wife Marguerite de Vienne, and of their granddaughter Huguette Bouton, who died in 1391.

[Col. 1630A] At the entrance to the chapel of Saint Stephen was the tomb of Jérôme de Saint-Michel, apostolic protonotary, who died at Cîteaux in 1499.

The eighteenth tomb contained the body of Saint Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux, who died in 1134, and those of fourteen other holy abbots transferred to the same place after the consecration of the church, performed in 1193 by Robert, bishop of Chalon. This tomb was at the exit from the church, descending toward the cloister; an altar dedicated to Our Lady had been erected there. On a panel fixed against the wall one read this inscription in Gothic letters:

> The blessed and venerable Fathers, abbots, founders and enlargers of the monastery and Order of Cîteaux, are buried here together: namely, Lord Alberic II, Stephen III, Raynard IV, Gozwin V, Fastred VI, Gilbert VII, Alexander VIII, William IX, Bernard X, William XI, Peter XII, John Robert the Prior, John, Boniface XXIII, a well-ordered and honorable man. May their blessed souls, living in Almighty God, always remember us. Amen.

Near this altar, in the cloister by the wall, to the left of the church entrance, was the tomb of Blessed Alain, a lay brother of the house of Cîteaux, surnamed the Universal Doctor.

Alain’s ancient Latin epitaph was engraved in Gothic letters at the base of his tomb on a stone about two feet square:

> [Col. 1630C] A brief hour buried Alanus in a brief tomb—  
> He who knew the two, the seven, and all that can be known.

[Note: [Col. 1629] “The two” denotes the Old and New Testaments, and “the seven” the seven liberal arts.]

The entire remainder of the monument had been erected in 1482.

Alain was represented on his tomb in the dress of a lay brother, holding a large rosary in his hand, with sheep at his feet, in accordance with the fourth line of the inscription engraved on a banderole surrounding him:

> A brief hour buried Alanus in a brief tomb,  
> Who knew the two, the seven, and all that can be known.  
> Despising the things of the passing age, he became poor;  
> Converted within, he was entrusted with feeding flocks.  
> In the year twelve hundred ninety-four,  
> Devoted to Christ, he put off his mortal body.

On either side of his head was a book. Upon one [Col. 1630D] were written the words: “Several treatises on theology and philosophy”; this book was closed. On the other, opened at the middle, one read: “On the Complaint of Nature; Laughter into Tears; On Parables; From Phoebus to Phoebe; On the *Anticlaudianus*; *autoris mendico* (‘of the beggarly author’ [reading and syntax uncertain]).”

On the faces of the tomb were engraved these words:

> JESUS CHRIST, DELIVER MY SOUL. AMEN.

Above was a stone bas-relief set into the wall. In the center a Resurrection was represented, with the following verse:

> Receive, Christ Jesus, the vows of your servants.

On the left was Alain holding a rosary and a book. Above his head one read:

> BROTHER ALANUS [Col. 1631A] MAGNUS, A GERMAN BY NATION, AN EMINENT DOCTOR.

And on a banderole issuing from his mouth:

> By rising, Christ gives the whole world power to rise.

On the other side, nearer the church of Cîteaux, Saint Bernard was represented with his hands crossed upon his breast and resting lightly on an open book before him. A banderole issuing from his mouth bore this verse:

> By his grievous death Christ overcame the death of the abyss.

Below the bas-relief was this epitaph:

> This great and learned Alanus, admirable in all things,  
> Makes this place of Cîteaux more memorable everywhere.  
> For here he was shepherd, lay brother, and servant;  
> Here still he serves as an example of virtue and honor.  
> Therefore, you religious, lay brothers, and passers-by,  
> Imitate this doctor who lies here below.

[Col. 1631B] This last epitaph was removed in 1712, when the cloister was whitewashed, “because,” says Dom Cotheret, “its style was little suited to do honor to the memory of Alain and to Cîteaux itself” (Dijon MS 357, p. 92).

Near the altar of Saint Stephen, under an arch in the recess of the Chapter-house wall, stood a panel bearing these words:

> GUEST ABBOTS BURIED HERE: [abbots] of Pruliaci, Locedii, Sarneii, Alteresti, Francaevallis, Oliveti, Petrosae, Tyronelli, Boxeriae, Parienagh, Vallae-Sanctae, Walt-Saxen, and many other abbots, whose souls may rest in peace.

Before the chapel of Saint John the Baptist, on the Gospel side, one saw at ground level the tomb of [Col. 1631C] Vincent Marlet, abbot of Bouillon, who died on 10 July 1545.

In the chapel of the dukes of Burgundy, on the right under the porch of the church, were five tombs at ground level. On that situated at the entrance was this epitaph:

> Here lies Lord Guillaume de Marigné.

The other tombs had no inscriptions. Above the altar was a fresco representing Duke Odo, founder of Cîteaux, presenting Saint Robert with the Abbey church. Beside him stood Duchess Mahaut his wife, Hugh II their son, and Odo III their grandson, in ducal costume. At the bottom one read:

> To Odo, to Mathilde his sweetest and most gracious wife, [Col. 1631D] to Hugh and Odo, son and grandson, illustrious dukes of Burgundy, by whose piety and liberality the monastery of Cîteaux was founded and established.

On the other side, the Epistle side, the fresco represented Saint Robert, dressed in black, receiving the Church presented to him by the duke, and three other abbots dressed in white: Saint Alberic, Saint Stephen, and Saint Bernard. At the bottom was this inscription:

> To Lord Robert, first abbot; Lord Alberic, second abbot of Cîteaux; Lord Stephen the Englishman, third abbot of Cîteaux; and Lord Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, who by integrity of character and holiness of life founded, enlarged, adorned, and glorified the Cistercian religious life—the Holy Fathers.

Above the arch containing the tomb of the three dukes just mentioned, one saw in succession [Col. 1632A] five abbots of Cîteaux, painted life-size in fresco and kneeling; each had a Latin inscription giving his name, titles, and date of death.

The first, on the altar side, was Dom Jean-Baptiste Loysier, elected in 1540 and dead in 1559; next came Louis de Baissey, elected in 1560 and dead on returning from the Council of Trent in 1564; then Jérôme de la Souchière, elected in 1564, afterward cardinal, and dead at Rome in 1571; Nicolas Boucherat, elected in 1571; and finally Dom Edme de la Croix, his successor.

On the wall opposite the altar had also been painted images of Nicolas Cossard, procurator of the General Chapter, and Claude Bossu, procurator [Col. 1632B] at the court of Rome, with their inscriptions on the Epistle side. There one also read:

> Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, wrath, and furious anger, to make the land a desolation and to crush its sinners. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, this monastery called Cîteaux began; and on that day the Paschal moon was the fourteenth, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March], indiction VI, epact XV, concurrent IV.

In the choir of the church, above the stalls, the coats of arms and shields of the knights of the Order of Saint Michael, created by Francis I, were formerly seen. On 10 June 1521 he made a large promotion of knights in this church, which he visited expressly with [Col. 1632C] his mother Louise of Savoy and several lords.

On an old panel before the chapel of Saint John one read this inscription:

> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1193, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [17 October], the church of Saint Mary of Cîteaux was dedicated by the Reverend Father Lord Robert, bishop of Chalon; its high altar was consecrated in honor of God, of his Blessed Mother, the ever-virgin Mary, and of all the saints; and it contains these relics, etc.

On the porch of the church were read these verses:

> Hail, holy mother, beneath whom the Cistercian Order  
> Does service, and shines through the whole world like the sun.

And above the image of the Blessed Virgin:

> This church is the head and mother of the Cistercian Order,  
> Which, Virgin Mary, remains devoted to you.  
> By your aid, I pray, keep it standing and protect it; present to Christ  
> [Col. 1632D] The prayers offered within by night and day.

Upon the great gate of the monastery the following verses were written in gold letters:

> Turn your eyes toward us, sweetest Virgin Mary,  
> And defend your house, divine patroness.

The following verses, composed by Gerlon, Abbot of l’Aumône, were formerly to be read in the infirmary:

> The world is passing away: a thing indeed known, yet ever to be feared.  
> Let the world’s passing-away be known to you: the world is passing away.  
>
> The world is passing away—not the world, that is, this fabric of the world,  
> I mean, but the world’s glory: the world is passing away.  
>
> The world is passing away: there are three things—“will be,” “is,” “was”; these three  
> Set the world in motion as they are moved; these three cry, “The world is passing away.”  
>
> The world is passing away; death follows; long life [is] a constrained salvation,  
> A brief life joyful [but] clouded: the world is passing away.  
>
> The world is passing away: may I be strong? I shall not be. May I be beautiful?  
> I shall not be. May I be rich? I shall not be. The world is passing away.  
>
> [Col. 1633A] The world is passing away; [it passes] from nothing into nothing; yet its passing away  
> Does not pass away: the error passes away by whose guidance the world passes away.  
>
> The world is passing away—the world which deceives in every word.  
> In this one thing it does not know how to deceive: the world is passing away.  
>
> The world is passing away; Christ is not passing away. Worship Him who does not pass away;  
> You will say, “I shall not depart without me.” The world is passing away.  
>
> How often shall I repeat, “The world is passing away”? Let the world  
> Cease to pass away, and I shall cease to say, “The world is passing away.”

In the cloister before the refectory there was the half-effaced tomb of an Abbot of St. John . . . . . who died in 1346.

Several abbots were buried before the Chapter House. According to their Latin epitaphs, they were: Lord Baduardus, Abbot of the Place of St. Bernard in Brabant, 1311; Lord John of Breteneria, Abbot of Fons Johannis, 1303; Lord John, Abbot of the monastery of the Place of God in England, in the year one thousand . . . . . . forty.

[Col. 1633B] The following other epitaphs were visible there:

> Robert, whom England bore, is buried here.  
> The abbey of which he was abbot is called Ribresteda.  
> In the year one thousand three hundred and twelve,  
> Lacking one month of its completion, he ended in a peaceful death,  
> On Matthew’s feast; may the merciful Almighty be gracious to him.

> This stone here covers Stephen, born at Dijon.  
> He became a monk, and thereafter Cellarer.  
> Governing Quincey, he was summoned to Pontigny,  
> Which the good father ruled for thirty-two years.  
> In the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred and fifty-eight,  
> On the twenty-fifth day of June, he departed;  
> Through the prayers of Saint Edmund, may he enjoy eternal light. Amen.

Here lies Lord Abbot Elias, formerly Abbot of . . . , who died in the year of the Lord 1280.

On the Calends of October. Pray for him. Here lies Brother John, called Vivien, professed [Col. 1633C] and a lover of this house, a diligent promoter of the proceedings and affairs of Cîteaux and of the Order; likewise an active worker, an opponent of innovations, and also, in temporal matters, one who had held the abbacy in the monasteries of Vallis-Dulcis and Bellae-Vallis and . . . . . . . . . . He died at Dijon, 10 September, in the year of the Lord 1494. May he live in the Lord.

Between the pillars of the doors of the Chapter House and the [Col. 1634A] parlour there was a tomb on which was a crozier, with these two words: “ABBOT OF STANLEE.”

One may perhaps be surprised to see that so great a number of princes and other illustrious persons were buried in the church of Cîteaux, whereas the founder and the three Dukes of Burgundy who died immediately after the foundation were buried only in the church porch. But this must be attributed to the simplicity of the Order’s first fathers, who would not bury laypersons in their church.

The refectory of Cîteaux was more than 120 feet long. Its width and height were proportionate. The former infirmary, which had become the great hall of the dead, [Col. 1634B] was still a quarter larger; it was one of the finest halls one could see. Before the cross set in the middle, these two verses were read:

> Here monks are laid down when they die;  
> From here their souls are taken up and borne aloft.

The most important relic contained in the treasury of Cîteaux was the arm of St. John the Baptist, preserved in a very beautiful silver-gilt reliquary, on which these five Greek verses were engraved:

> A barbarian hand once held the hand of the Forerunner;  
> But afterward the Emperor Constantine drew it forth from there  
> And brought it to the city.  
> He who deposited it in this treasury—  
> This protector of himself—enriched the Empire.

Father Martène translated these verses thus:

> The hand which a barbarian hand  
>
> [Col. 1634C] Formerly possessed—the hand of the Forerunner—afterward, drawing it out from there,  
>
> The Emperor Constantine brought into the city.  
>
> But he who conveyed that same hand into this treasury,  
>
> By which he himself was protected, was enriched in empire.

The Abbey of Cîteaux bore France semé (azure strewn with gold fleurs-de-lis), with at its centre an escutcheon of ancient Burgundy, banded gold and azure in six pieces, with a red border.

[Col. 1633]

## NOTE ON FONTAINES-LEZ-DIJON, THE BIRTHPLACE OF ST. BERNARD

Concerning the priory of the Feuillants, formerly established in his father’s castle, and concerning the room in which he was born, which became the sanctuary of the Feuillants’ church.

(Notice by Abbé Chenevet, in the *Almanac of the Province of Burgundy*, Dijon, 1782, p. 233.—Courtépée, *Description of the Duchy of Burgundy*, vol. II, Dijon, 1777, p. 388.—*Summary of the Life of St. Bernard*, Dijon, 1653.—Archives of ancient Burgundy and of the city of Dijon.—Historical notice by C. X. Girault in the *Historical and Statistical Yearbook of the Côte-d’Or*, Dijon, 1824.—*Description of the Chapel of St. Bernard, restored at Fontaines in August 1841*, octavo pamphlet, by M. Caumont.)

[Col. 1633D] The village of Fontaines [Note: [Col. 1633D] Arrondissement and northern canton of Dijon.], where St. Bernard was born, stands halfway up a hill northwest of the city of Dijon, from which it is three kilometres distant. It has 454 inhabitants. At the summit of the hill, to the west, stood St. Bernard’s castle, of which only a few parts remain; [Col. 1634D] somewhat lower down in front stands the village church, certain portions of which may date from the eleventh or twelfth century. It seems certain that this was formerly the castle chapel, and that it owed its existence to the piety of Tescelin, lord of Fontaines, and Aleth, father and mother of St. Bernard [Note: [Col. 1633D] Tescelin, surnamed Sorus, or the Red, the first known to have assumed the title [Col. 1634D] of lord of Fontaines, was of the house of Tonnerre; Aleth was daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard. Several charters of the years 1104, [Col. 1635C] 1106, and 1113, reported among the evidences of the *History of the Dukes of Burgundy*, show Tescelin holding a distinguished rank at the court of those princes. Tescelin and Aleth had six sons from their marriage, of whom Guy, the eldest, was the only one to establish a family. He [Col. 1635D] left a daughter married to Bartholomew of Sombernon, which caused the lordship of Fontaines to pass into that house; and thence successively through women into those of Saux, Marey, Cléron, and Damas. These various houses possessed the lordship of Fontaines, though divided, according to the usage of the time, into several portions. Some passed to the forebears of the Messrs. Bouhier, others to the city of Dijon, and the seignorial residence to the Feuillant religious.].

[Col. 1635A] It originally depended on the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs near Dijon, given in 801 to the regular canons of St. Stephen of Dijon [Note: [Col. 1635D] A short quarter of a league from Dijon, somewhat beyond the former Capuchin convent, on the left bank of the Suzon stream, there stood a small church called *S. Martini Campaniensis*, from *campis*, *campania*, *prato*, *pratis*, and finally Saint-Martin-des-Champs. As early as 801 it was already a parish church. In the tenth century a small community of canons was established beside this church [Col. 1636C] of St. Martin, and for this reason it was called *Abbatiola S. Martini*, “the little abbey of St. Martin.” A colony of canons from the abbey of St. Stephen of Dijon, they sang the canonical hours, preached, and administered the sacraments at St. Martin and Fontaines. At the end of the [Col. 1636D] seventeenth century it was only a simple chapel. The parish priest of Fontaines, at the head of his parishioners, went there every year in procession to acknowledge the mother-church status of this church and to celebrate Mass there on 11 November (see *History of the Abbey and Collegiate Church of St. Stephen of Dijon*, Dijon, 1696, folio, p. 278).]; it is thought to have been erected as a parish in 1451.

It is first mentioned in a charter of the year 1120.

In that same year Joceran, Bishop of Langres, confirmed to the abbey of St. Stephen the church of St. Martin together with the chapel situated in the upper part of the village of Fontaines: *cum capella quae est in superiori Fontanarum villa*, “with the chapel which is in the upper village of Fontaines.” Popes Calixtus II in 1124, Innocent II in 1129, Adrian IV in 1156, and Innocent IV in 1245 make the same mention in their bulls confirming the possessions held by the abbey of St. Stephen. It should be noted that they confirm to it [Col. 1635B] possession of this chapel together with its cemetery and all its dependencies. It must therefore have been constructed either toward the end of the eleventh century or, at the latest, at the beginning of the twelfth.

The ancient histories, in speaking of the death of Blessed Aleth, which occurred at Fontaines on the Calends of September in the year 1105, on the feast-day of St. Ambrosinian, patron of the chapel of Fontaines, clearly show that he was patron of the place. This is further proved by a charter of the year 1130 and by various documents published by Father Chifflet in his *Genus illustre S. Bernardi assertum*, pp. 415 and 523.
