Blessed Aleth, who died in the odour of sanctity, was buried neither in this chapel nor in its cemetery. [Col. 1635C] Gérannus, Abbot of St. Bénigne, requested her body as a precious relic. Borne on the shoulders of monks to the abbey, it remained there until the fourteenth day before the Calends of April (19 March) 1250. Then, in fulfilment of St. Bernard’s intentions, it was transferred to Clairvaux and placed in the chapel of the Holy Saviour, not far from her son’s tomb. The necrology of St. Bénigne mentioned Aleth in these terms: *Kalendis Septembris obiit Alaisa laica*: “On the Calends of September died Alaisa, a laywoman.”

[Col. 1636A] Some charters teach us that, from the beginning of the fifteenth century, a confraternity under the title of St. Bernard had been established at Fontaines [Note: [Col. 1636D] On 19 October 1415, the brethren of the confraternity established at Fontaines-lez-Dijon in honour of God, the Blessed Virgin, and St. Bernard paid the Duke of Burgundy 200 livres for the amortization of 50 livres of rents intended to provide two Masses a week (see Archives of ancient Burgundy).]; and it is probable that during the same century the room in which this illustrious Abbot was born was converted into a chapel. One might perhaps be entitled to conjecture that the idea came from Bernard de Marey, whose donation to the abbey of Cîteaux will shortly be seen. At least it is certain, from the very terms of this donation, that the transformation of St. Bernard’s birth-room into a chapel had not occurred before 1462; and it will be shown below that it preceded the establishment of the Feuillant religious in the castle of Fontaines in 1614.

[Col. 1636B] Bernard de Marey, who possessed the rights of his mother, Marie de Saulx, Lady of Fontaines, and those of St. Bernard’s family, gave on 20 February 1462 to the abbey of Cîteaux the castle, fortress, and fortified house of Fontaines, where he lived, on condition that it establish there a chapel in honour of St. Bernard, in which the religious serving it should say a Mass every Friday of the year. To this gift he added the fourth part of the house and jurisdiction of Fontaines, the communal oven, and several lands which he possessed there; for the remainder of the lordship was held by his brothers. But Duke Philip the Good refused the letters necessary to validate this gift. The abbey of Cîteaux was therefore compelled to place these properties in qualified hands, since [Col. 1636C] fiefs could be held only by nobles; and it sold them, in fact, for 400 livres to John Rollin, Bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, who had already acquired another quarter of this lordship in 1434 from Alexander de Marey, Bernard’s brother [Note: [Col. 1636D] It was this half which passed to Marguerite Rollin, cousin of that prelate, and subsequently, one after another, to Marie Chambellan, wife of Guy de Rochefort, Chancellor of France; to Joachim Humbert de Rochefort; to William de Damas; and finally to Joachim de Damas, lord of Rousset and Communes.].

Matters remained thus until the beginning of the seventeenth century. During that interval a reformed congregation of the Order of Cîteaux had been established, known as Notre-Dame [Col. 1637A] des Feuillants. Its founder in 1577 was Jean de la Barrière, commendatory Abbot of the abbey of Feuillants, six leagues from Toulouse. Pope Sixtus V approved this reform in 1586, and Clement VIII moderated its severity in 1595. Jean de la Barrière, having come to Paris by order of Henry III with sixty of his reformers, that prince had a house built for them in the suburb of Saint-Honoré, Paris. Henry IV had it completed and granted it all the privileges of houses founded by the Crown.

It was to these religious that Joachim de Damas, founder of the Capuchin convent at Dijon in 1602, decided to sell his castle of Fontaines, in order to convert it into a monastery of their congregation and to have a church erected there in honour [Col. 1637B] of St. Bernard. The sale was made in 1613, and the money for this acquisition was supplied by the gifts of several pious persons. The abbey of Cîteaux opposed this sale and the establishment of the Feuillants at Fontaines, alleging that the lordship of the place had been given to it for the same purpose in 1462. But its opposition was dismissed, and the Feuillants took possession of their new dwelling on Monday in Passion Week of the year 1614.

Louis XIII, who owed his birth to the prayers of St. Bernard, showed himself the protector of the Feuillants. He approved their acquisition; rendered its land inalienable by his letters patent of the month [Col. 1637C] of July 1618 (Appendix, no. 1); declared himself their founder; granted their monastery the privilege and immunities of royal houses; assigned them a pension of one thousand livres; and gave them three thousand livres both for their maintenance and for construction work and the decoration of the chapel of St. Bernard.

Sébastien Zamet, Bishop of Langres, had approved their establishment at Fontaines in 1617. The magistrates of Dijon likewise consented to it; and, further to show their interest in it, they wished to serve as godfathers in 1620 and 1621 at the blessing of their bells (Appendix, no. 2), and contributed by gifts, along with several devout persons, to the decoration of their [Col. 1637D] church [Note: [Col. 1637] Each year the city of Dijon gave the Feuillants an alms of fish on the feast-day of St. Bernard (see Archives of the city of Dijon).].

But the ceremony which, by its splendour and extraordinary magnificence, gave the strongest expression to the sentiments of France and the Province of Burgundy toward St. Bernard was the laying of the first stone of the Feuillants’ monastic church, built in his honour.

On Epiphany Day 1619, it was solemnly placed beneath the first column on the right, in the name of King Louis XIII, by Roger de Bellegarde, Duke and Peer, Grand Equerry of France, Governor of Burgundy and Bresse. Octave de Bellegarde, Bishop of Comminges, blessed it [Col. 1638A] in the absence of the Bishop of Langres, amid an immense gathering of persons of every rank and condition.

Thirty-three smaller stones were placed around the principal stone. All were adorned with inscriptions by which the Supreme Pontiff, temporal princes, kingdoms, universities, and religious orders had wished, as though competing with one another, to raise for St. Bernard an enduring monument of their admiration and piety (Appendix, no. 3).

Devotion to this great saint could not fail thereby to receive new growth. No sooner had Anne of Austria become mother of the Dauphin, who was to be Louis XIV, than she sent one of her [Col. 1638B] chaplains to the Feuillants of Fontaines in 1638 with a letter asking them to offer thanksgiving for nine days to their holy Father, to whom she had vowed herself in order to obtain a son from God (Appendix, no. 4).

Louis XIII had ensured that the feast of St. Bernard was solemnized throughout the diocese of Langres; but since this feast had been observed there only for a few years, Louis XIV wrote to the Bishop of Langres, asking him to restore it. His letters are dated 20 December 1652 (Appendix, no. 5). In them he gives St. Bernard the title of protector of his crown and acknowledges that he owed him the victory of Lens, won on the day of the saint’s [Col. 1638C] feast. Louis XIV wrote on the same subject to the Duke of Épernon, Governor of Burgundy, and to the Parlement of Dijon.

On 25 March 1653 Sébastien Zamet, Bishop of Langres, issued an ordinance directing all his diocesan subjects to celebrate the feast of St. Bernard as a holy day of obligation, abstaining from all servile work (Appendix, no. 6).

On 22 July of the same year, the same bishop established a confraternity of St. Bernard in the church of the Feuillant Fathers at Fontaines and approved its statutes. Louis XIV, his brother, and the Queen Mother had wished to be its first members. By his brief of 2 May 1653, Pope Innocent X had enriched with spiritual favours this new association [Col. 1638D] which, he said, was to be established by the Ordinary (Appendix, no. 7).

After the destruction of the Feuillant monastery by the French Revolution, the confraternity established in its church was transferred to the parish church of Fontaines by Monsignor J. F. Martin de Boisville, Bishop of Dijon. The letters in which he confirms the former statutes are dated 22 January 1823.

The Feuillants’ church, owing especially to the benefactions of Anne of Austria and Louis XII, was oriented north to south. It comprised two domed sections: the choir of the religious, [Col. 1639A] laid out in a semicircle to the north, and the sanctuary to the south. The choir of the religious no longer exists. In 1791 the church was sixty-two feet long and twenty-six wide; the sacristy, twenty-three feet by ten; and the choir of the religious, twenty-three feet by seventeen. It was adorned with sixteen columns: ten of black marble and six of white Flemish marble; their bases and torus mouldings were of white veined marble, and their capitals of alabaster. The high altar, shaped as an ancient tomb, [Col. 1640A] was surmounted by a gilded baldachin supported by four Corinthian columns of Flemish marble, with bases and capitals of gilded wood and pedestals and steps of wood painted to resemble marble. In the middle stood a statue of St. Bernard in gilded wood [Note: [Col. 1639D] This baldachin and its columns are now in Dijon Cathedral. The valuation report does not mention the statue of St. [Col. 1640D] Bernard placed beneath the baldachin; this detail is borrowed from M. Girault’s notice.].

On the exterior walls of the church the following inscriptions were read:

[Col. 1639] On the front, facing east:

[Col. 1639A] “CHAPEL OF BLESSED MARY, LADY OF GRACES.”

[Col. 1640A] “CHAPEL OF ST. BERNARD, FATHER AND DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.”

[Col. 1639] And below:

[Col. 1639A] “HAIL, STAR OF THE SEA, NURTURING MOTHER OF GOD AND EVER-VIRGIN, BLESSED GATE OF HEAVEN.”

[Col. 1640A] “ST. DIVINE BERNARD [the intervening Latin, *AD SOLV DOMESTICV POTENTEM MIRABILIV*, is materially uncertain], powerful in miracles, prays for the King’s welfare on earth and in heaven.”

[Col. 1639B] On the rear, facing west, the inscriptions are mutilated and illegible.

The Feuillants remained at Fontaines until the decrees of 12 February and 11 October 1790 abolishing the monastic orders were put into effect. Their house was then handed over to the secular arm. Its furnishings were sold; and by a report of valuation dated 16 July 1791, Sieur Nogaret, architect appointed by the directory of the district of Dijon, estimated the church, monastery, gardens, orchards, and an enclosure of twenty-one *journaux* of excellent land at the modest sum of 13,000 livres.

The whole was conveyed by report of 17 August 1791, for 21,500 francs, to a company which resold, by deed of 3 July 1793, all the buildings, [Col. 1639C] courts, gardens, and terraces for 9,000 francs, one half payable in the following August and the other in August 1794.

These new purchasers were workmen who bought only in order to profit from the stone and joinery materials. Nearly everything was demolished and sold piecemeal in less than two years; the site, covered in ruins, was resold on 23 March 1795 for 6,000 francs in assignats, worth approximately 2,000 francs, to a third purchaser.

In the Feuillants’ church, the choir of the religious had been demolished, as had the bell tower. The sanctuary was converted into a cellar, and the remainder of [Col. 1639D] the church was occupied by a forge and a stable. The sacristy became a kitchen.

For twenty-five years the church’s two cupolas remained unroofed, bearing four to five feet of demolition rubble and sand. They certainly would no longer exist today without the precaution taken by the old architects of covering them with a barrel vault of dressed white stone.

[Col. 1640B] In August 1821, a fourth purchaser, Monsieur C. X. Girault, at last halted the work of destruction and secured the preservation of the church.

In 1840 the Feuillants’ property again came into priestly hands. Monsieur Abbé Renault, former vicar general and honorary canon of the diocese of Dijon, became its fortunate owner. Thanks to his devout care, the church was restored with much intelligence by M. Caumont, architect and member of the Commission of Antiquities of the Côte-d’Or. As early as 1841, the graceful chapel, emerging from its ruins, could once again be opened to pilgrims drawn by the desire to invoke St. Bernard at the very place of his birth.

It has been seen that the bell tower and choir of the religious [Col. 1640C] were destroyed. What remains of their elegant church consists of three sections, separated from one another by transverse arches decorated with archivolts and pendentives remarkable for the cutting and regular masonry of their polished hard-stone voussoirs, for the precision of the joints, the purity of their profiles, and the richness of their carved and polished ornaments.

The first two sections terminate in domes shaped as royal crowns, adorned with carved fleurons and pearls around their lower circumference.

These domes rest upon complete and very rich Corinthian entablatures. All the mouldings of the architraves and cornices are carved with heart-rays, trefoils, egg-and-dart ornament, dentils, modillions [Col. 1640D] with leaf-shaped soffits, and rosettes carved between the modillions.

The first dome is decorated with the monogram and arms of Louis XIII, and the second with the monogram and arms of his wife, Anne of Austria.

The sixteen marble columns which adorned the church and which were removed during the Revolution, together with their capitals and pedestals, [Col. 1641A] have been modestly replaced with wooden columns of the same dimensions as the old ones. They join the entablatures which form four triumphal arches or porticoes, through which one must pass to reach the sanctuary.

The soffits of the transverse arches, the friezes of the entablatures of the two domes, and the friezes of the four porticoes display a semé of sculpted fleurs-de-lis. These have remained almost intact, while the architraves have been mutilated [Note: [Col. 1641D] This description is taken from M. Caumont’s pamphlet.].

The sanctuary is raised by one step. It is built on a regular octagonal plan. Its present ornamentation, as well as the niche placed [Col. 1641B] above the high altar and the stone statue of St. Bernard which decorates it, dates no earlier than the restoration carried out under the care of Monsieur Abbé Renault.

Yet even if the Feuillants’ church had retained of its former splendour only the bare and decayed walls of this sanctuary, it would nonetheless deserve to be visited with eager reverence, because it rises on the very site of the room in which St. Bernard was born and is contained within the massive thickness of its ancient walls.

The earliest document mentioning the room in which St. Bernard was born is a division of inheritance dated February 1429. It speaks of the great tower of the castle of Fontaines, commonly called “THE TOWER OF MONSIEUR SAINT BERNARD,” [Col. 1641C] and of the cellar or room of the same tower in which my said lord St. Bernard was born [Note: [Col. 1641D] Father Chifflet, *S. Bernardi genus illustre assertum*, Dijon, 1660, pp. 602–603.].

When the Feuillants became owners of the castle of Fontaines, they found this room already converted into a chapel. Louis XIII himself tells us this in the following terms in his letters patent of July 1618: “Now, having been duly informed that at the said place of Fontaines the location where [St. Bernard] was born has since been dedicated and assigned to the use of a chapel, which has been and still is venerated and frequented by a great concourse of people, and that therein many obtain from on high very singular and extraordinary graces and favours through the intercessions of this glorious saint [Note: [Col. 1641D] See Appendix, no. 1.].”

[Col. 1641D] While St. Francis de Sales was preaching the Lenten sermons at Dijon in 1604, “he often went,” says his nephew, “to celebrate in the chapel of St. Bernard at Fontaines, because of the great devotion he had for this honey-tongued doctor, singer of the glorious Virgin [Note: [Col. 1641D] *History of the Life and Deeds of Blessed Francis de Sales*, by Charles Auguste de Sales, Book VI, p. 313.].”

[Col. 1642A] Messire Jean-Pierre Camus, so well known through his association with St. Francis de Sales, relates in his *Eulogy of Piety in Blessed Memory of Monsieur Claude Bernard, called the Poor Priest* the story of a young lady of Dijon who, in 1615, suddenly lost the use of speech.

“Persons of great piety,” he adds, “were of the opinion that this girl and her parents should have recourse to the intercession of St. Bernard and that, for this purpose, she should go every day on foot, for the space of a week, to visit the oratory which had been erected at the very place of his birth, called Fontaines, at the gates of Dijon [Note: [Col. 1641D] *The Spirit of Blessed Francis de Sales*, by M. J. P. Camus, ed. Depéry, vol. I, Paris, 1840, p. LV.].”

Messire F. André Valladier, ordinary preacher to the King, delivering in 1628 the funeral eulogy of [Col. 1642B] Dom Bernard de Montgaillard, Abbot of Orval in Luxembourg, speaks of Fontaines as “a beautiful little round and gentle hill, wholly like the holy Mount Carmel in Judea.” He then continues: “I have had the honour to preach and offer sacrifice there several times in the very room where St. Bernard was born. Since it has always been kept most religiously, it will be kept still more so in future through the devotion of the Feuillant Fathers, who are building there a fine monastery and a magnificent church, greatly frequented because of the outstanding devotion of all this fair city of Dijon—a blessing of which St. Bernard’s birth left it heiress, together with his gentleness, devotions, and divine zeal [Col. 1642C] for the love of God and the perfection of the Catholic religion [Note: [Col. 1642D] *The Holy Mountains and Hills of Orval and Clairvaux*, by Messire F. André Valladier, printed at Luxembourg, 1629, quarto, p. 19.].”

On 31 March 1631, the Marquis d’Effyat, Marshal of France, devoutly visited the birthplace of St. Bernard, in which the Feuillants’ monastery was being built, and offered a silver lamp to be suspended before the saint’s altar. At the same time he founded a perpetual endowment of 500 *livres tournois* for the maintenance of this lamp [Note: [Col. 1642D] See Archives of the Côte-d’Or.].

In May 1667, Dom Joseph Méglinger, a religious of Wettingen in the diocese of Constance, travelling to the Order’s general chapter at Cîteaux, passed through Dijon and had the happiness of celebrating Mass in the Feuillants’ church, upon the very altar [Col. 1642D] that occupied the place where St. Bernard had first opened his eyes to the light—“upon the altar which now occupies the place in which St. Bernard came forth from the womb of his devout mother into this mortal light” (*in altari, quod jam eum occupat locum, in quo de piae parentis utero in hanc mortalitatis lucem progressus est sanctus Bernardus*) [Note: [Col. 1642D] *Descriptio itineris Cisterciensis*, Lucerne, p. 101. In this elegant and witty account of a journey, reprinted above in the *Patrology*, one may read the account of the holy joys felt by the author when he made his devout pilgrimage to Fontaines.].

This altar, raised in so venerable a place, had naturally [Col. 1643A] become the high altar of the Feuillants’ church, and it was intended that the chapel in which it stood should form the sanctuary. This arrangement has been reverently preserved by Monsieur Abbé Renault.

The sanctuary of the Feuillants’ church was then, as it still is today, situated on the ground floor of the great tower of St. Bernard’s castle mentioned in the deed of partition of 1429, cited a little above.

The walls of the sanctuary, which are three, four, and even nine feet thick, could leave no doubt on this point; but a deed of partition from May 1420 proves it conclusively.

This precious document mentions the tower which stood [Col. 1643B] above the castle gate, together with the little house that stood between the said castle tower and the great tower [Note: [Col. 1643C] See Archives of the Côte-d’Or.]. This is all that remains today of St. Bernard’s castle [Note: [Col. 1643C] In 1740, the thick walls of St. Bernard’s castle having been seriously damaged by the inclemencies of the weather, the Feuillants had to plaster the two principal towers in order to prevent their ruin (see Archives of the Côte-d’Or).].

This indication leads us from the entrance gate, where the hinges can still be seen and where the grooves intended to allow the portcullis to drop are visible, directly to the great tower—that is, to the sanctuary of the Feuillants’ church.

A passage from Dumont’s travels shows that in 1689 the sanctuary did not have the octagonal form it has today and already had before the Revolution. “They show,” he says, “the room in [Col. 1644A] which St. Bernard was born. It is a very small, low, square room, made into a chapel. On its door one sees written: ‘Come, my children, and I shall bring you into my father’s house and into the room where my mother bore me’ [Note: [Col. 1643C] *Travels of M. Dumont in France, Italy, Germany, etc.*, vol. I, The Hague, 1699, duodecimo, p. 76 (letter dated Dijon, October 1689).—The inscription placed on the door of the room where [Col. 1644C] St. Bernard was born was drawn approximately from the Song of Songs 3:4.].”

It is probable that in the eighteenth century this small, low, square room eventually came to displease people, and that they wished to bring the sanctuary somewhat into harmony with the rest of the church by cutting it into an octagon within the thickness of the room’s own walls. At what date this regrettable work of embellishment was carried out is unknown, since it altered the form of a place truly consecrated by St. Bernard’s birth.

If one relied upon Abbé De Mangin in [Col. 1644B] his *Ecclesiastical and Civil History of the Diocese of Langres* [Note: [Col. 1644C] Vol. II, Paris, 1765, p. 117.], one might believe that the low, square room still existed in 1765. But it must be noted that this author copied Piganiol de la Force outright [Note: [Col. 1644C] *New Description of France*, 3rd ed., vol. IV, Paris, 1753, duodecimo, p. 30.], who had copied La Martinière [Note: [Col. 1644C] *The Great Geographical and Critical Dictionary*, vol. III, The Hague, 1726, folio, article “Fontaines.”]. La Martinière had copied Corneille [Note: [Col. 1644C] *Universal Geographical and Historical Dictionary*, vol. II, Paris, 1708, folio, article “Fontaines.”], and the latter had merely repeated Dumont’s words.

The following must suffice: the sanctuary is indeed established on the site of the chamber in which Saint Bernard was born; and it was from 1689 onward that it received the form in which we see it today.

[Col. 1643]

## APPENDIX

### No. I. JULY 1618

[Col. 1643D] Louis, by the grace of God King of France and Navarre, to all present and future, greeting. Our dear and well-beloved devout petitioners, the religious of the Congregation of Our Lady of the Feuillants, of the Cistercian order, serving under blessed Saint Bernard, having acquired the castle of Fontaines near our city of Dijon at the beginning of our reign—the place in which, as his paternal home, the blessed saint was born—that acquisition so pleased us that we caused this place to be mortmain in their favor.

Now, having been duly informed that at the said place of Fontaines, the spot where the same saint was born has since been dedicated and assigned to the use [Col. 1644D] of a chapel, which has been and still is venerated and frequented by a great concourse of people, and that there many obtain very singular and extraordinary graces and favors from above through the intercessions of this glorious saint: moved by an ardent desire to do something by which, with the good pleasure of his Divine goodness, we may share in the merits of that saint, and through them be protected throughout the course of our life, assisted and made fortunate in our sincere intentions to establish and maintain good peace and to cause piety and justice to flourish in our kingdom, so that God may thereby be worthily exalted;

[Col. 1645A] Moreover, desiring to advance the honor and adornment of our Province of Burgundy, considering the blessing it formerly brought to France when King Clovis, our predecessor, at the persuasion of Clotilde his wife, daughter of Burgundy, was made the first Christian king; and desiring, for this reason, that the foundation which we intend to make in a place so notable and distinguished within that province may be a perpetual testimony to it of gratitude for so signal a benefit conferred upon this crown;

Also wishing to continue, indeed increasingly to augment, the favors by which we have hitherto assisted the congregation of the aforesaid religious—begun in our said kingdom, approved by the Holy See, and endowed by it with many apostolic graces and privileges; and fruitful, as everyone knows, for the edification of souls; enlarged and fostered by the benefactions of the late King Henry the Great, of most high and praiseworthy memory, our most honored lord and father (may he be in the glory of God)—[Col. 1645B] especially insofar as he became founder of the church and monastery of the Feuillants situated in the suburb of Saint-Honoré in our good city of Paris, which had been erected in honor of the said blessed Saint Bernard; and this under the vow and invocation that it might please the Divine goodness to grant a happy progeny to our said late most honored lord and father and to the Queen, our most honored lady and mother. Since thereafter, and before the year now elapsed, our birth and that of the Queen, our most dear companion and wife, ensued, this also moves us still further to embrace the present occasion, as coming by divine favor, to honor this blessed saint in his birthplace.

For the aforesaid causes and considerations, to the glory of Him who, wonderful in his saints, has adorned the provinces of the earth—which are the firmament of his Church militant—with their several [Col. 1645C] stars, and has wished to decorate and enrich our said kingdom with the splendor of this great and renowned confessor, Father and Doctor of the Church, reformer of peoples, peacemaker of schisms and dissensions, patriarch of religious, worker of marvels, devotee and favorite of the Virgin his Mother: recognizing this place as one of the most venerable in this kingdom, as worthy to be adorned by a church and religious house as it has brought blessing to the whole world, and as the said Congregation has reason to value its enjoyment and possession:

[Col. 1646A] By these presents, signed with our hand, we have wished to make and declare ourselves—and we do make and declare ourselves—Founder of the church and monastery which is to be built at the said place of Fontaines, resolving to extend there our liberality and benefactions as occasions arise. To this end we will that the said house shall henceforth enjoy all the privileges and immunities used and enjoyed, of whatever kind, by other houses of royal foundation in our said kingdom. And, in order to provide for the maintenance at present of some number of religious at that place, to perform divine service there while awaiting the completion of the said building and its establishment in its full regular form and order, we have given and granted, and by these presents do give and grant them, one thousand livres as an annual pension, charged upon the general receipt of our country of Burgundy; and, for the building to be made, namely for the intended decoration of the chapel of Saint Bernard, three thousand livres, payable once during the course of this year, pending [Col. 1646B] the vacancy of a benefice within our nomination capable of maintaining at that place a sufficient number of religious, so that God may be served there as honorably as the prerogative of that place is great. We assign this benefice to them—as we have promised and do promise by these presents—and it shall remain united and incorporated with the said house. When this is done, the said annual rent of one thousand livres shall cease, on condition that the religious inhabiting the said monastery expressly dedicate their public and private prayers and good works to our welfare and salvation, and to the benefit of the whole kingdom.

And in order that the provinces, districts, cities, communities, or places which have been illustrated by the wonderful deeds of the said Saint Bernard—especially our Province of Burgundy and the city of Dijon, to which belongs in particular the happiness of having borne so great a light of the Church—and the prelates, great lords, or other private persons [Col. 1646C] who may have devotion to testify on this occasion their veneration toward the said blessed saint, in order to acquire the help of his intercessions with God, may without difficulty produce the effects of their pious zeal: we do not intend to hinder, but rather exhort all persons to offer their vows and confer their benefactions.

Given at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, in July, in the year of grace one thousand six hundred and eighteen, and the ninth of our reign.

By the King: Poitiers.

### No. II

[Col. 1645]

[Col. 1645D] The city of Dijon gave the Feuillants a bell in 1622; it was the third.

It bore the following inscription beneath the handles:

> The religious city of Dijon knows that the LORD has magnified his mercy toward her when he assigned to her a faithful PATRON and PROTECTOR, whom he established as the great DOCTOR and defender of the whole CHURCH, SAINT BERNARD. In return for this best gift, she renders thanks by pious gifts, earnestly desiring always to have the DIVINE MAJESTY itself appeased through the merits of that same SAINT. +

[Col. 1646D] And lower down, around the bell:

> In the blessing of Saint BERNARD, I was named, with BENIGNO COMPASSORE, Baron of COURTIVRON and chief vice-count-mayor of the people of Dijon, and CLAUDIA DORGE, widow of the most noble late BARON OF THIANGE, as my most welcome sponsors. YEAR 1622.

This bell, broken in 1735, was replaced by another cast at the city’s expense (see Archives of the city of Dijon).

### No. III. INSCRIPTIONS OF THE STONES LAID BENEATH THE FOUNDATIONS OF THE CHURCH AND MONASTERY OF SAINT BERNARD IN THE TOWN AND CASTLE OF FONTAINES, NEAR DIJON

(From the pamphlet entitled: *Sacred to God, Best and Greatest, and to Saint Bernard, for the restoration of the new basilica at Fontaines*, by John of Saint Malachy, Feuillant. Dijon, 1620; 2nd edition, Paris, 1623, octavo.)

[Col. 1647]

[Col. 1647A] The first stone was fitted into the foundations, under the happy auspices and by the special command and pleasure of the Most Christian King Louis XIII, on the feast of the Epiphany in the year 1619, at the celebrated and naturally most delightful site of the sacred building begun within the enclosure of the castle of Fontaines, near Dijon, in honor of Saint Bernard. This feast, made joyful and solemn each year by the gifts of the Kings offered to Christ shining in the humble manger, followed the blessing of the stone, celebrated according to the ecclesiastical rite with devout feeling and solemn ceremony by the Most Reverend Lord Octave de Bellegarde, Bishop of Couserans, Lord of Albrac, and most pious Abbot of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, kinsman of the most illustrious Governor, who happened most opportunely to be in those parts; while musical voices of the collegiate and royal chapel of Dijon raised public rejoicing.

[Col. 1647B] This stone was three and a half feet long and two feet wide. On its upper and more august face it bore the engraved royal arms; then, placed at a distance and in order all around, were these prayers and words composed for the King in capital letters:

> WITH CHRIST JESUS ASSENTING, THROUGH THE MERITS OF SAINT BERNARD, MAY THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING LIVE, REIGN, PIOUS, POWERFUL, HAPPY.

Below were these words:

> By the command and in the name of Louis XIII, Most Christian King of the French and of Navarre, and of his most serene consort ANNE OF AUSTRIA, Roger de Bellegarde, most deserving governor from the King of all Burgundy, commander of the cavalry of France, etc., most devoutly laid this chief foundation-stone, for the construction of a sacred building to God, Best and Greatest, in honor of Saint Bernard—by whose blessed birth and manifest signs the divine mercy has sanctified this hill for itself—on the sixth day of January, in the year of salvation 1619.

[Col. 1647C] Finally, on the lower part of the same stone were the family arms of the most illustrious Lord Viceroy, engraved with the collar of each sacred order of knighthood and the royal sword with which he had long been honored at the royal court. For the excellence of the said lord, these votive words were likewise engraved, arranged at the four corners:

> DEAR TO GOD AND KING, MAY THE VICEROY FLOURISH.

After the stone had thus been religiously and joyfully laid by the aforesaid most illustrious lord, and properly placed in position through the craftsmen’s skill, another stone of equal shape and dimensions was laid over it. No mortar was placed between them, lest the inscription engraved on the inward-facing sequence of both stones, one reversed in relation to the other, should be obliterated; rather, sheets of lead were inserted between them.

[Col. 1647D] On its inner side this latter stone bore the following longer inscription, by which the pious mind of the Most Christian King in promoting and completing this work was more fully and broadly made known to present and future generations; but it was laid away to be seen chiefly by God, by the angels, and by his saints:

[Col. 1648A]

> From this spring—from which, God granting his kindness, at the birth of the honey-flowing Doctor and lyre-player of Mary, Saint Bernard, there flowed a consolation flooding the world with heavenly blessings—there returns, deservedly, the gratitude of the whole world. Louis XIII, the greatest cultivator of justice, Most Christian King of the French and Navarre, determining to erect a solemn and everlasting memorial of his piety toward God and veneration for the saint who adorns his kingdom with so great a splendor, built by royal benefactions a sacred church to God, Best and Greatest, in honor of the said saint, and a religious dwelling for the most humble and devout petitioners, the Feuillant monks. He trusts—as his suppliant desire entreats of God—that through the patronage of Saint Bernard and the prayers instituted and poured forth in this most chosen place of that saint’s birth, he, together with his most serene and beloved consort ANNE OF AUSTRIA, will be endowed both with safety and with the desired offspring; and that thus he will add strength, fragrance, and beauty to the lilies of France, so that at last he may be mingled with the lilies of heaven and, like a lily, may spring up and flourish forever before the Lord.

[Col. 1648B] When, therefore, the aforesaid two stones, as though joined into one, had been placed beneath the first column supporting the right side of the sacred building, many other stones, square in form so that they might more easily be carried and suitably polished with iron, were piled here and there around the circuit. Eager to render in their own way a tribute of honor to the stone marked with the royal insignia and breathing something of majesty, they were set about it in fitting order.

Since, in the series of these stones, each bore, in a medium but clear character, some distinct praise of Saint Bernard, briefly recorded from his deeds, benefits bestowed by him, or benefits undertaken through him, the celebrated and marvelous devotion of the whole Christian world toward the aforesaid saint—known even, for the most part, to persons ignorant of piety—was proclaimed and made public. It was also set before all present how, on that day, the whole world in serene spirit, applauding and rejoicing, was present with the King as he undertook a work whose magnitude was to prepare immense glory for God and fitting honor for that saint, in a place rightly dedicated to his illustrious renown and invocation.

[Col. 1648C] First mention, in the spirit of the bystanders’ festive joy, was made of the inhabitants of heaven: namely, those to whom this undertaking ought especially to matter, not by the prompting of nature but rather by kinship in the Spirit, indeed by zeal for the glory of Christ, whom they behold even in heaven thirsting for the exaltation of his faithful elect, in whose contest they fought watchfully and humbly. These are the father and mother, all the brothers, and the sister of Saint Bernard; all of them possess evident and most abundant testimonies of holiness in their own life and manner of conduct.

[Col. 1648D]

I. Of the pious father TESSELIN, blessed mother ALETH, the five blessed brothers and the sister of Saint [Col. 1649A] Bernard: for the great and final tribute of honor rendered to this place, in which the holy mother happily lived and died, the others received the firstfruits of the Spirit, and to their most beloved son and brother Saint Bernard, conspicuous throughout the world for his merits; sweet rejoicing in God and devout congratulation upon royal piety.

II. Of the HOLY APOSTOLIC SEE: toward Saint Bernard, whom he opportunely upheld by powerful zeal in stormy affairs, through the strength given him by God; supreme devotion.

III. Of the most serene QUEEN MARIA DE’ MEDICI, mother of the Most Christian King LOUIS XIII: toward Saint Bernard, because, from the time of her coming to the royal marriage-bed as wife of Henry the Great of glorious memory, she had, under a vow to obtain offspring through the merits of the said saint, paid him solemn honor at Paris together with the King himself; and thereafter there was granted her a fertility than which none could be thought happier; august and munificent devotion.

[Col. 1649B] IV. Of the most serene PRINCES: the Most Christian King LOUIS XIII, his brother, and his sister, wife of the Prince of Spain; likewise his sister, wife of the Prince of Piedmont; and another younger sister: toward Saint Bernard, by whose merits and prayers they desire to support their high estate and, in God’s good time, obtain offspring; royal and honorable devotion.

V. Of the PRINCES AND MAGNATES OF THE WORLD, especially of the kingdom of France, and of the nobles and courtiers who follow royal piety: toward Saint Bernard, whom all magnify and honor as a vessel chosen by God, who most fruitfully bore his name and the word of salvation before kings, princes, and peoples; serene and sincere devotion.

[Col. 1649C] VI. Of the venerable CITY OF ROME, mother of orthodox faith: toward Saint Bernard, in whom the Lord so gloriously showed forth his saint that, after he had more than once calmed her internal tumults and restored peace to the Church, he was acclaimed Father of the Fatherland; steadfast and renowned devotion.

VII. Of the PROVINCE OF BURGUNDY: toward Saint Bernard, the sun of all its splendor and holiness, whose rays of piety and teaching shine honorably throughout the world; precious and tender devotion.

VIII. Of venerable DIJON, metropolis of the whole province: toward Saint Bernard, whom it continually recognizes, honors, and invokes as its protector; familiar and heartfelt devotion.

[Col. 1649D] IX. Of the PROVINCE OF CHAMPAGNE: toward Saint Bernard, a distinguished treasure of piety given to it by God and commended by special favor; ardent and solemn devotion.

X. Of the PROVINCE OF FRANCE, especially the royal city of Paris: toward Saint Bernard, whom it deserved often to see speaking the mighty works of God and displaying them in deeds, with the Holy Spirit cooperating; graceful and sweet devotion.

XI. Of the PROVINCE OF PICARDY: toward Saint Bernard, mighty in deed and word, whom it embraced and venerated with great piety; effective devotion.

[Col. 1650A] XII. Of the PROVINCE OF NORMANDY: toward Saint Bernard, whom it possessed as a faithful minister of salvation and an outstanding benefactor; exceptional devotion.

XIII. Of the PROVINCE OF POITOU: toward Saint Bernard, whom it admired as a man wholly apostolic, with miracles shining forth on every side; lavish devotion.

XIV. Of the PROVINCE OF AQUITAINE: toward Saint Bernard, to whom, among other benefits, it ascribes the welcome conversion of Duke William, most beneficial and wonderful to the world; attentive and grateful devotion.

XV. Of the PROVINCE OF BRITTANY: toward Saint Bernard, whom it honored as one gloriously triumphing, by the arm of God, over the prince of darkness; exquisite [Col. 1650B] devotion.

XVI. Of the PROVINCE OF TOULOUSE: toward Saint Bernard, whom it glories in having possessed as a restorer of religion, made illustrious by abundant signs from heaven; gracious and diligent devotion.

XVII. Of the PROVINCE OF PROVENCE: toward Saint Bernard, whom it joyfully saw accompanying the Keeper of the Keys of Heaven as he came from Italy into France, and, in so celebrated a court and assembly, relying upon the marvelous authority of the Spirit and the Pope’s favor, conducting the affairs of the kingdom of God; whole and fragrant devotion.

XVIII. Of the PROVINCE OF DAUPHINÉ: toward Saint Bernard, whom it beheld in amazement and joy, radiant with virtues; religious devotion.

[Col. 1650C] XIX. Of the PROVINCE OF SAVOY: toward Saint Bernard, whom he often gladdened by his lovable presence, desired blessing, and the working of great virtues; vigorous and kindled devotion.

XX. Of the PROVINCE OF LORRAINE: toward Saint Bernard, whom she happily found, even to life’s end, solicitous for her welfare and stretching forth his hand valiantly on her behalf, with God cooperating through accompanying signs; pious devotion.

XXI. Of the COUNTY OF BURGUNDY: toward Saint Bernard, whom it proved with great joy to be wondrously adorned with heavenly gifts and illustrious in the grace of healings; dear and genuine devotion.

[Col. 1650D] XXII. Of the KINGDOMS, PROVINCES, AND MANY ILLUSTRIOUS CITIES OF ITALY: toward Saint Bernard, whom they received and honored as an angel of God, performing marvels for their help and consolation and transforming them in their inmost hearts; perpetual and outstanding devotion.

XXIII. Of the KINGDOMS AND PROVINCES OF GERMANY traversed by Saint Bernard, raised up and strengthened in the fervor of faith by innumerable miracles: toward the same Saint Bernard, immense and universal devotion.

XXIV. Of the KINGDOMS OF SPAIN, illustrated by Saint Bernard’s miracles and by the famous deeds and blessed death of his younger full brother, Blessed Nivard, sent there by Saint Bernard to found his order: toward those same saints, celebrated devotion.

[Col. 1651A] XXV. Of the PROVINCES OF THE LOW COUNTRIES: toward Saint Bernard, whom they beheld with the highest joy as another Apostle, everywhere snatching prey from the devil and gathering souls to Christ, in signs and prodigies; holy and notable devotion.

XXVI. Of the KINGDOMS OF ENGLAND AND IRELAND: for the preservation and strengthening of whose ancient piety Saint Bernard rendered marvelous service; to that same Saint Bernard, as though newly born in his own house for the good of the Church, an urgent entreaty to God for aid in their desolation, that he may deal more gently with them or turn it altogether into joy.

XXVII. Of the ENTIRE SACRED ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER: toward Saint Bernard, whom it acknowledges and honors as its most devout father, an eminent promoter before God of its purity and holiness and before men of its dignity; splendid devotion.

[Col. 1651B] XXVIII. Of the DOCTORS AND PROFESSORS OF THEOLOGY of all universities, especially the most celebrated University of Paris, which often entrusted to him precious gains to be offered to Christ: toward him, whom all venerate as taught by God (*theodidaktos*) and as one who greatly draws their studies toward the savor of divine things; graceful and praiseworthy devotion.

XXIX. Of ALL RELIGIOUS ORDERS: toward Saint Bernard, whom they unanimously recognize and honor as a fitting and radiant exemplar of Christ’s life placed in the house of God, and as the faithful and tender guide and father in the spiritual path of beginners, those advancing, and the perfect, administering milk and solid food; attentive and fervent devotion.

[Col. 1651C] XXX. Of ALL ORDERS OF MILITANT KNIGHTS: toward Saint Bernard, whom all religiously hear and accept as a leader in spiritual warfare and as one giving precepts and rules concerning the ordering of temporal knighthood toward God; valiant devotion.

XXXI. Of the ILLUSTRIOUS MONASTERY OF CÎTEAUX and the whole Cistercian Order flowing from it: toward Saint Bernard, chosen prince of all its splendor and holiness; especially of the sons of Clairvaux, toward so lovable and meritoriously exalted a father; most intimate and special devotion.

[Col. 1652A] XXXII. Of the MOST REVEREND FATHER SUPERIOR of the entire Congregation of Blessed Mary of the Feuillants, of the Cistercian Order, of all the monasteries and of every religious of that Congregation: toward Saint Bernard, to be regarded as their father, because by his pious condescension he obtained from God that his paternal home should be built for public consolation and for their use, and because, breathing the good odor of Christ in all his being, he caused royal majesty to undertake this work, drawing after it the Most Christian world; humble gratitude and joyful devotion.

XXXIII. Of ALL WHO, through divine grace inspiring them—and preparing for them heavenly treasures in exchange for earthly ones, and a powerful Friend to receive them into eternal dwellings—have contributed or will contribute their benefactions toward building the sacred church of God, Best and Greatest, wonderful in his saints, in honor of Saint Bernard, in this notable place of his birth; sincere and provident devotion.

[Col. 1652B] These things, moreover, were arranged not merely to adorn the solemn beginning of the sacred building and to extol the mighty deeds of Saint Bernard on that day when, for the unprecedented spectacle of so great rejoicing, a most noble company and the devout people of nearly the whole city of Dijon flocked together; but also so that, if ever in future faith, piety, and true religion should be exiled from their native land—whether through Antichrist reigning on earth for a few years near the consummation of the world, which may Christ avert through the intercession of him whom from the fruitfulness of this hill he gave as a teacher to his homeland and to the Church—and the fury of impiety should blaze in hatred against this fortress and altar of piety, because of its exceptional holiness derived from the saint, even to its [Col. 1652C] destruction: then, when perhaps volumes of the Gospels and writings of the Doctors can no longer be found, nor the voices of preachers heard, these underground testimonies may emerge from the bowels of the earth and the ruins of this building—the stones crying out when men have fallen silent—in praise of Jesus Christ the Savior and in commendation of his glorious confessor Bernard, whose life was Christ.

Just as they will not fear the countenance of tyrants and impious persons, so they will be thrust as darts into their blinded hearts, to their confusion; and to all who remain faithful they will provide grounds for every joy by which they may be strengthened in the true faith.

### No. IV. 29 OCTOBER 1638

[Col. 1651]

[Col. 1651D] BY THE QUEEN.

Most dear and devout petitioners, God having heard the vows of the King, our most honored lord and husband, joined with ours and those of the whole kingdom, by the most happy birth of our most dear and beloved son the Dauphin, whom it pleased His Divine Majesty to give us on Sunday, the fifth of September: not wishing to omit any testimony of the gratitude which we owe his goodness for a grace so earnestly desired, we have resolved to render him our most humble duties and thanksgivings in your church, because of the devotion we have always borne toward the glorious Saint Bernard, founder of your order, and because of our firm belief that his intercessions greatly contributed to obtaining this favor for us.

Desiring to show gratitude for it to this holy soul, at the very place of his birth, and there to offer God our most humble thanks for that blessing which was most desirable to us, we send you for this purpose Master Antoine Colombel, one of our chaplains, because of the esteem in which we hold his virtuous qualities. We have charged him to tell you that it is our intention and desire that, during nine consecutive days, you have the holy sacrifice of the Mass celebrated in your church, so that it may please His Divine Majesty to accept our most humble thanksgivings favorably and to continue his blessings upon the person of the King, upon us, upon our son the Dauphin, and upon this state.

And as we believe, from your piety, that you will worthily do what is fitting to effect our intentions, so you may expect from our affection toward you and your order every good office that you could desire. We pray Divine goodness, most dear and devout petitioners, always to keep you in its holy protection.

Written at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, [Col. 1654A] 29 October 1638. Signed: **ANNE**. And below: **LE GRAS**.

### No. V. 20 DECEMBER 1652

[Col. 1653]

Letter of the King to the Lord Bishop of Langres, asking him to have the feast of Saint Bernard solemnly observed.

[Col. 1653A] My Cousin, although it is our duty and piety to be devoted toward all the saints, and to procure, insofar as lies within us, that they be honored and served in all places which God has subjected to our obedience, we nevertheless believe ourselves obliged to render a more particular cult [Col. 1653B] to those whom divine goodness has made more visibly protectors of this state, and through whose mediation it has pleased him to grant extraordinary favors to our person.

Having therefore learned from the Queen, our most honored lady and mother, that she acknowledged herself indebted for our happy birth to the prayers of the great Saint Bernard, special patron of your diocese; and knowing that the merits of the same saint appeared no less efficacious in giving France the late King, our most honored lord and father, as he expressly testified in his letters patent concerning the foundation he made for the Feuillant religious at the place called Fontaines, where this illustrious saint was born, protector of our crown, who showed himself such at the battle of Lens, which we won over our enemies on the day of his feast: we should consider ourselves lacking in gratitude toward his benefits if we did not promote his honor and glory [Col. 1654A] by every means that God has placed in our power.

Therefore, following the examples which the late King of happy memory has left us, we renew with all our heart the orders which he had given you to have this saint’s feast solemnly observed throughout your diocese. But we desire that this be done more effectively than his orders were, and that what you caused to be observed only during the space of a few years may be religiously maintained throughout our reign and even in all times to come.

For this reason we write this letter to testify that you will do what shall be very pleasing to us by employing your episcopal authority to support our holy intentions, which aim only at the glory of God, the honor due to his saint, and the good of your whole diocese, which has received more particular graces from his assistance than the rest of our state. And, as we expect from your zeal and obedience the effect of the request we make of you, I pray God to keep you, my Cousin, in his holy and worthy protection.

Written at Paris, the twentieth day of December, one thousand six hundred and fifty-two. Signed: **LOUIS**. And below: **DE BRIENNE**.

### No. VI. 31 DECEMBER 1652

[Col. 1653]

Letter of the King to the Duke of Épernon.

[Col. 1653C] My Uncle, having a particular devotion toward good Saint Bernard, special patron of the Province of Burgundy and protector of my crown, and desiring to advance his honor and glory as far as I can, after the example of the late King, my lord and father, I have written to my cousin the bishop-duke of Langres to have the said saint’s feast solemnly observed throughout his diocese and to work earnestly in support of my good intentions. [Col. 1654C] I have wished to inform you of this by this letter and to tell you that you are to see to it throughout the extent of your office. Trusting in your goodwill in this matter, I shall pray God to keep you, my Uncle, in his holy and worthy protection.

Written at Paris, the last day of December, one thousand six hundred and fifty-two. Signed: **LOUIS**. And below: **PHELIPPEAUX**.

### 28 FEBRUARY 1653. Letter of the King to the Lords of the Parlement of Dijon

[Col. 1653]

[Col. 1653D] BY THE KING.

Our beloved and faithful servants, although it is our duty and piety to be devoted toward all the saints and to procure, insofar as possible, that they be honored and served in all places of our kingdom, nevertheless, being obliged to render a more particular cult to those whom God’s goodness has made visibly protectors of this state, and through whose mediation it has pleased him to grant favors, etc. [lacuna] We have written to our cousin the Lord Bishop of Langres to employ his episcopal authority [Col. 1654D] in support of our good intentions, which aim only at the glory of God, the honor due to this saint, and the good of our Province of Burgundy. We have wished to inform you thereof by this letter, and to command and order you to see to it, in all that depends upon you, that our will be punctually fulfilled. Trusting in your zeal and devotion, we shall make this present letter no more express or longer.

Given at Paris, 28 February 1653. Signed: **LOUIS**. And below: **PHELIPPEAUX**.

### 25 MARCH 1653. Ordinance of the Lord Bishop of Langres
SEBASTIAN, Bishop of Langres, Peer of France. The piety of our Kings, which has always been inseparable from the majesty of their crown, has recently moved the King in his goodness to write to us [Col. 1655A] concerning the solemnity of the feast of Saint Bernard, one of the patrons and protectors of this Diocese; and His Majesty has been pleased in his letter to set forth the reasons for his devotion, so that his people, being informed of them, may concur through their obedience with greater zeal and fervour in so praiseworthy a purpose. Among the reasons expressed in His Majesty’s dispatch, the most important, and that which ought to be most deeply felt by France, is the blessing of his birth, which the Queen his mother said she had obtained through the vows and prayers which she made to the great Saint Bernard. Thus, since we can allege nothing more explicit to encourage our diocesan faithful to so just a solemnity, it remains only for us to enjoin upon them—as we do by these presents—that henceforth they celebrate the feast of Saint Bernard, which occurs every year on the twentieth day of August, as a holy day of obligation, on which the faithful shall refrain from all servile works, unless an urgent necessity [Col. 1655B] excuses them, so as to devote themselves more freely to the service of God and to the veneration of this great saint. Moreover, we are particularly bound to this in this Diocese, since we possess the place of his birth and that [Col. 1656A] in which his sacred body rests, and since we have been instructed in the ways of salvation, more than any other region of the Church, by the rare examples of his life and the lofty illumination of his mind. We are further invited to it by the confidence which we ought to have that, just as his intercession obtained for us the incomparable blessing of the King’s birth, so his prayers will obtain for us his preservation for many years, and thereby the joy and happiness of his subjects in living long under the mildness of his rule. This is the thought to which we exhort our diocesan faithful to apply their minds in celebrating the feast of this great servant of God: that the divine goodness may grant us its effect through his intercession, and that to this grace it may deign to add that of the peace so desired by all good people and so necessary to the repose and tranquillity of this Kingdom. Given at Mussy, the twenty-fifth day of March [Col. 1656B] 1653.

SEBAST., Bishop of Langres. By my said Lord: GOURDON.

No. VII. 2 MAY 1653.

[Col. 1655]

Indulgences granted by Pope Innocent X. (See the original in the archives of Côte-d'Or.)

[Col. 1655B] INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful in Jesus Christ: greeting and apostolic blessing. Having learned that in the church of the Feuillants, built at the château of Fontaines in the Diocese of Langres, there is—or is to be—canonically [Col. 1655C] erected a holy and devout confraternity for both sexes under the name and invocation of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, and that it may be the cause of many works of piety and devotion; and desiring that this association, after it has been erected by the Ordinary, may receive more blessings and acquire day by day a new spiritual increase: relying upon the mercy of Almighty God and upon the authority of the Blessed Apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul, we grant by these presents in perpetuity a plenary indulgence and remission of all sins on the first day on which persons place themselves under the protection of this great saint and are admitted into his confraternity, provided that they are truly penitent, have confessed, and have received Communion.

Further, we grant to all brethren of both sexes, present and future, who are contrite, have confessed, and have received the Holy Sacrament, a plenary indulgence at the hour of their death, upon pronouncing with their mouths the sacred name of Jesus, or in their hearts [Col. 1655D] if they lack the means of pronouncing it orally.

Likewise, we grant them a plenary indulgence and remission of all their sins if they visit the chapel or church built in honour of this same saint on the day of his feast, from First Vespers until sunset on the feast day, and therein pray to God for the exaltation of our Holy Mother Church, peace among Christian princes, and the extirpation of heresies.

Moreover, after having received Communion and confessed, the said brethren shall gain seven years and as many quarantines of indulgence by visiting the said church or chapel on Palm Sunday and [Col. 1656B] Quasimodo Sunday, and on the days of Saint Joseph and Saint Anne.

Finally, as often as they attend processions and other divine offices; attend burials, whether of brethren or of other faithful Christians; accompany the [Col. 1656C] Holy Sacrament when it is carried to the sick; or, if prevented from following it, on hearing the bell, recite once the *Pater* and the *Ave Maria* for the said sick; and recite five times the Lord’s Prayer and as many times the Angelic Salutation for deceased brethren; and whenever they call some sinner back into the way of salvation, or teach the ignorant the commandments of God or some other matter which can advance them in the love of God—they shall gain sixty days of indulgence for each of these good works. We will that these present letters be valid and have effect until the end of the world. Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Fisherman’s Ring, on the second day of May 1653, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

G. GUALTERIUS.

WE, JEAN-BAPTISTE BERNARD GONTIER, licentiate in law, provost and canon of the Holy Chapel [Col. 1656D] of Dijon, and Vicar-General of my Lord the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Bishop-Duke of Langres and Peer of France: having received and examined the said Bull and the indulgences contained therein, permit it to be published and posted upon the doors of the churches of this Diocese, together with the confraternity of Saint Bernard comprised in the aforementioned Apostolic Brief. Furthermore, we command our well-beloved parish priests and vicars of parish churches to exhort the people to prepare themselves to merit so great a benefit. Given at Dijon, the fourth day of June 1653.

GONTIER.

By order of the said Lord Vicar-General:

I. BEVREUTTE.

PLENARY INDULGENCES granted by our Holy Father Pope SIXTUS to all the faithful who visit the churches of the Feuillant Fathers on the following days.

[Col. 1657]

[Col. 1657A] SEBASTIAN ZAMET, Bishop-Duke of Langres, Peer of France: Having seen the Bull of our Holy Father Pope Sixtus V, of happy memory, by which he grants and concedes several plenary indulgences to those, male and female, who visit the churches of the Feuillant Fathers, we exhort our diocesan faithful to make themselves worthy of these merits by humble confession of their sins and by receiving the sacred Body of the Son of God; by praying devoutly for the exaltation of our Holy Mother Church, the extirpation of heresies, and peace among Christian princes; and by reciting five times the Lord’s Prayer, *Pater Noster*, and as many times the Angelic Salutation, *Ave Maria*. The days on which they may gain the indulgences are:

The Nativity of Our Lord; the Circumcision; the Epiphany; the Resurrection; [Col. 1657B] the Ascension; [Col. 1658A] Pentecost; Corpus Christi; the Conception of the Blessed Virgin; her Nativity; her Presentation in the Temple; the Annunciation; the Visitation; the Assumption; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of Saints Peter and Paul; the day of Saint Bernard and his entire Octave; and every fourth Sunday of the months appointed to honour the same Saint Bernard.

Done in our château of Mussy, 22 July 1653. Signed: SEBAST., Bishop of Langres. By my said Lord: DOUCET.

The altar of Saint Bernard is privileged on Mondays of every week and on every Wednesday in favour [Col. 1658B] of the brethren.

ERECTION OF THE CONFRATERNITY OF SAINT BERNARD by Monseigneur SÉBASTIEN ZAMET, Bishop of Langres, in the house of the Feuillant Fathers at Fontaines-lez-Dijon:

[Col. 1657]

[Col. 1657B] SEBASTIAN ZAMET, Bishop-Duke of Langres, Peer of France. Although we are obliged to honour all the saints, it seems that we are under an altogether particular obligation to honour those whom France has given to the Church and who have rendered it the greatest services. Now, since no one can doubt that Saint Bernard held first place among the others, whether for the graces which he obtained from heaven for this kingdom or for the number of miracles [Col. 1657C] by which God has wished to make him admirable throughout the world, we have believed that we could find no means more favourable for drawing God’s mercy upon his people than recourse to this great saint, that he might be pleased to obtain from the divine goodness the peace so long desired in this kingdom and deliverance from the evils by which France has been afflicted for so many years. And we ought to hope all the more for this grace from his intercession because there is no saint who has had greater influence with the Blessed Virgin and Jesus Christ, her well-beloved Son, who are the most powerful mediators whom the Eternal Father has given us to obtain his mercy. And because the union of hearts is what renders us more pleasing to God and his saints, [Col. 1658B] we have judged it fitting to erect a confraternity in honour of this illustrious servant of God in the place of his birth. We exhort our diocesan faithful to enrol in this confraternity, so that they may have so powerful an intercessor in heaven. They ought to be prompted to this by the piety and example of our invincible and most Christian monarch, Louis XIV, who has wished to be its first brother, and who has been followed in this devotion by the Queen his [Col. 1658C] mother and by Monsieur his brother. We also exhort those same diocesan faithful who shall be enrolled among the brethren to keep and observe carefully and devoutly the articles and regulations written below, so as to render themselves more worthy of experiencing the effects of the intercession of this great saint, the ornament and light not only of Burgundy and France but also of all Christendom. Given in our château of Mussy, Tuesday the twenty-second day of July, in the year of grace 1653.

Signed: SEBASTIAN, Bishop of Langres. By my said Lord: DOUCET.

REGULATIONS OF THE CONFRATERNITY OF SAINT BERNARD.

[Col. 1657]

[Col. 1657D] 1. Since the end of all associations and confraternities is to honour God in a more particular manner under a saint’s protection, all men and women admitted to that of Saint Bernard must ask him especially for the spirit of piety and fervour with which he served his God upon earth.

[Col. 1658D] 2. Since Saint Bernard during his life had a particular devotion to Christ suffering and to his blessed and glorious Mother, every brother shall endeavour to imitate him in this devotion. To that end, he shall recite daily, insofar as circumstances permit, five *Pater Nosters* in memory of the five wounds, and the *Ave Maris Stella*—“Hail, Star of the Sea”—which he composed in honour of the Most Holy Virgin, and the antiphon [Col. 1659A] *Salve Regina*—“Hail, Queen”—to which he added the words, “O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary”; and he shall add the prayer of Saint Bernard, intending to obtain through his intercession an inward and outward devotion, sincere and true, toward the Son and Mother, who continually intercede for our salvation with the Eternal Father. Then they shall beseech him to obtain for them the grace never to say or do anything by which they might offend him.

3. The place of devotion to Saint Bernard is that of his birth; the days particularly appointed for rendering him honour are the fourth Sundays of the month and every Tuesday of the year.

4. Those who desire to be admitted to the said confraternity shall be admitted by the superior or another religious of the house, who shall enter them in [Col. 1659B] a book designated for this purpose.

5. On the day of reception, one shall approach the sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist, and humbly ask to be received in these terms:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

I, N., take and choose the glorious Saint Bernard as my Patron and Advocate, and I pray God to grant me the grace never to abandon him. For this purpose I beseech you to receive me into this confraternity dedicated to his honour.

The one who receives the brethren shall then say:

“By the authority granted me in this matter, I receive you and enroll you in the society of Saint Bernard, an outstanding worshipper of Our Lord Jesus Christ and of his Mother. In the name of the Father, etc.”

6. Since the most perfect mark of piety is to hear [Col. 1659C] Holy Mass, all brethren are exhorted to do their utmost to attend it every day. In order that they may attend it to glorify God and obtain from his infinite mercy the help necessary to them, upon entering the church they shall beseech Saint Bernard to give them the spirit of fear and reverence with which he entered churches and approached the altars on which rests him whom the Eternal Father has established to be our Judge.

7. On feasts and Sundays they shall occupy themselves with reading [Col. 1660A] some chapter of his life, so that, frequently recalling it in their memory, they may more easily imitate his virtues.

8. Among all the graces which one ought to ask of God most earnestly is that of dying a holy death, since at that moment one is judged either to be admitted into the company of the angels or cast down among the demons. The brethren are advised to pray Saint Bernard to obtain for them the means of confessing before death, as he obtained it for many when he was asked while still in this world.

9. The brethren shall have a very particular charity toward one another; and, when they know someone among them to be in need, they shall relieve him insofar as possible; they shall pray to God for one another and visit one another in sickness.

[Col. 1660B] 10. They shall also take care to gain all indulgences granted them in favour of the confraternity, and all others.

11. To gain the indulgences, they shall say five *Pater Nosters* and five *Ave Marias*, and pray to God for the exaltation of our Holy Mother Church, for peace among Christian princes, and for remission of sins.

12. On every fourth Sunday the litanies shall be said for the brethren at the end of Vespers, and on the feast day of Saint Bernard the procession shall take place at five o’clock in the evening.

SEBASTIAN ZAMET, Bishop-Duke of Langres, Peer [Col. 1660C] of France. Having seen the Articles and Regulations written above for the newly erected Confraternity of Saint Bernard, we have commended and approved them, and by these presents commend and approve them, exhorting all brethren carefully and devoutly to keep and observe them. Done in our château of Mussy, 22 July, in the year of Our Lord 1653.

Signed: SEBASTIAN, Bishop. By my said Lord: DOUCET.

[Col. 1661]

LETTER TO M. THE COUNT OF MONTALEMBERT, OF THE FRENCH ACADEMY, ON THE RELICS OF SAINT BERNARD AND SAINT MALACHY, AND ON THE FIRST SITE OF CLAIRVAUX, by PH. GUIGNARD, CORRESPONDING MEMBER OF THE MINISTRY OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTION, FORMER ARCHIVIST OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AUBE, LIBRARIAN OF THE CITY OF DIJON.

. . . . “Beloved and comely in their life,

in death also they were not divided” (2 Kings 1:23).

[Col. 1661A] MONSIEUR THE COUNT,

You had been kind enough to permit me to address to you, in 1845 and 1846, in the *Auxiliaire catholique* (vol. II, pp. 82 and 216; vol. III, pp. 33 and 427), a series of letters on the relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy and on the first site of Clairvaux. Submitted in 1846 to the competition for the antiquities of France, they were judged by the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres worthy of a highly honourable mention [Note: [Col. 1661B] “M. Guignard, in a series of letters on the relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, has demonstrated that the use of the genuine methods of criticism can lend value to investigations whose object does not arouse universal interest. A highly honourable mention should become the reward of the efforts of the scholar entrusted with the direction of the Archives of Aube.” Extract from the Report made to the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, in the name of the commission on the antiquities of France, by M. Lenormant, at the annual public session of 21 August 1846.]. The indefatigable editor of the complete collection of the Holy Fathers thought that they ought to have a place among the monuments with which he adorns his reprint of the works of Saint Bernard. [Col. 1662A] I therefore have the honour of again placing under your patronage this work, now already a sweet remembrance of the past for me.

I have combined my letters into one, as I had done when presenting them to the Academy of Inscriptions. I have carefully revised them, availing myself of new researches and re-examining the documents which I had first used [Note: [Col. 1661B] Mgr Parisis, then Bishop of Langres, kindly permitted me to consult MSS. IX and XV of the extensive collection assembled by Abbé Matthieu on the history of the whole Diocese, and acquired by the bishopric of Langres. MS. XV contains a complete copy of the two folio [Col. 1661C] volumes of notes extracted from the Archives of Clairvaux by Dom Claude Guyton, around the year 1744 (same MS., p. 526). In 1751, Dom Claude Guyton was keeper of the charters and title-deeds of Clairvaux Abbey (Archives of Aube). In 1845 these two volumes were in the hands of M. Gossin, former counsellor of the Royal Court, residing in Paris. MS. IX contains copies of fragments of a Succinct Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux and of fragments of a History of Clairvaux by Dom André Le Boullenger, the Abbey’s last archivist. According to M. Matthieu, this history was approved on 24 April 1738. That date is plainly wrong: for in 1790 Dom André Le Boullenger was sixty-six years old (*Inventory of Clairvaux*, 24 May 1790; Archives of Aube); consequently, in 1738 he was far from thinking of writing the history of Clairvaux. I believe that 1788 should be read; but every investigation carried out at the Imperial Library to clarify this point produced no result. In 1773 Dom André Le Boullenger was librarian and archivist of Clairvaux; in 1790 he was also sacristan of the abbey. From an inventory [Col. 1662C] of national property of the district of Nogent-sur-Seine, I see that in Year III he resided at Nogent (Archives of Aube). Numerous extracts from MSS. IX and XV will be found in Appendix no. 8.].

I shall first discuss the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, preserved in Troyes Cathedral; I shall then address the history of their bodies, and conclude with a study of the first site of Clairvaux Abbey.

## I. Heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy preserved in Troyes Cathedral

[Col. 1663]

[Col. 1663A] When I had the honour of addressing my first letter to you, Monsieur the Count, on 15 October 1845, the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy rested beneath the high altar of Troyes Cathedral in two wooden caskets unworthy of the name of shrine. They are no longer in the same place today. Since dampness was beginning to rot the caskets, they have been placed in the treasury, pending their replacement by small monuments more in keeping with these distinguished relics.

At that time the head of Saint Bernard, placed on the Epistle side, displayed the front part of the skull and the facial bones; that of Saint Malachy, on the Gospel side, showed the rear part of the skull.

[Col. 1663B] These two heads come from Clairvaux Abbey; but before explaining how they are now at Troyes, it is fitting to gather every testimony concerning their existence before 1790, the period when they remained in the possession of the last of Saint Bernard’s successors, M. Rocourt [Note: [Col. 1663C] Dom Louis-Marie Rocourt, Doctor of Theology of the Faculty of Paris, fifty-first and last Abbot of Clairvaux, initially procurator-general of that abbey, still exercised that office in 1783 (*General Statement of the Revenues of Clairvaux*—Archives of Aube). He succeeded Dom François Le Blois, the fiftieth abbot; but I do not know on what date. In 1790 he was forty-seven years old, as will be seen in Appendix no. 2. During the Revolution, he did not leave the places that bore witness to his former splendour, nor seek from foreign monasteries of his order a refuge worthy of his high station. He preferred to purchase tranquillity and oblivion by every outward sign of profound poverty. Having subsequently retired to Bar-sur-Aube, he spent his long life there in obscurity until 6 April 1824 (*Decennial Tables of the Arrondissement of Bar-sur-Aube*—Archives of Aube). His final illness had unusual features. A callus which he had on his foot became gangrenous, and the foot, consumed by the disease, eventually detached entirely from the leg. Persons who knew M. Rocourt agree that he was one of the handsomest men of his time.].

I find no mention of them before the fourteenth century; and it is probable that they remained joined to the bodies until the devotion of Jean d’Aizanville, the thirtieth abbot [Note: [Col. 1663D] According to *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 809, Jean d’Aizanville was the thirty-first Abbot of Clairvaux; but an unpublished autograph letter of Dom Brice, a Benedictine religious of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, corrects the catalogue given in that work. I publish this important document in Appendix no. 1. Jean d’Aizanville governed from 1330 until about [Col. 1664C] 1348 (*Gallia Christiana*, ibid.).], had them displayed in exceedingly rich silver-gilt busts. A list of the abbots of Clairvaux, written in the fourteenth century, found at the end of manuscript [Col. 1663C] 150 in the library of Troyes, and continuing through Jean d’Aizanville, provides contemporary information [Col. 1664A] concerning the two busts just mentioned. “Jean d’Aizanville,” it says, “a monk and cellarer of Clairvaux, governed for years (left blank, which shows that he was still alive). This man made most excellently gilded silver vessels, in which are deposited the heads of the glorious confessors, Blessed Malachy and Saint Bernard.”

The manuscript Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1664C] Folio XVIII, recto: “Jean d’Aizanville made the heads of the holy confessors Malachy and Bernard.” Here is the title of this Catalogue, composed by Dom Antoine Saulnier, secretary to Dom Denis Largentier: *Elogia singulorum Claravallis Abbatum, a B. P. N. Bernardo, usque ad Rev. admodum P. ac D. Dionysium Largentier, felicis memoriae Abbatem XLIV*—“Eulogies of the individual Abbots of Clairvaux, from our Blessed Father Bernard down to the most reverend Father and Lord Denis Largentier, Abbot XLIV, of happy memory.” In 1845 the original manuscript was in the hands of M. Garnier, lawyer at Bar-sur-Aube. These *Elogia* were continued to 1761 by an unknown author. M. Harmand, librarian of the city of Troyes, made and kindly communicated to me a copy from a copy of the manuscript thus enlarged.], and the *Gallia Christiana* [Note: [Col. 1664D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 809: “Jean d’Aizanville, Abbot of Clairvaux . . . enclosed the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy in most precious little vessels.”] confirm this important notice; but the most curious details are recorded in the Inventory of the Sacristy of Clairvaux, drawn up in 1504 [Note: [Col. 1664D] The Archives of Aube possess two manuscript inventories of the sacristy of Clairvaux: one drawn up in 1504 and the other in 1640. I have found neither among the many manuscripts in the library of Troyes. Only two eighteenth-century copies of the inventory of 1504 survive; they are fairly faulty but correct one another. Manrique cited several passages from it. In Appendix no. 17 I shall give an extract of every article in these two inventories concerning Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy. There also will be found fuller details concerning each of them.]. The following is read under the heading “Heads,” folio VIII, recto.

“Silver-gilt vessel in which rests [Col. 1664B] the head of our most holy Father, Blessed Bernard the Abbot, with an enamelled diadem, having two silver angels at the rear, and at the front two images representing Lord Jean d’Aizanville, Abbot of Clairvaux, maker of this vessel, and his father, in whose time this vessel was made. It should be noted that in the breast of the said vessel there is one large, very precious sapphire, beneath which is another, smaller sapphire, also very precious; it is supported at the front by four silver-gilt lions, and at the rear by two similar ones.”

The description of the bust of Saint Malachy follows, folio 8, recto and verso.
