[Col. 1664C] “A silver-gilt vessel containing sixty-one marks [Col. 1665A] of silver, which the aforesaid Lord Jean d’Aizanville had made, in which rests the head of Blessed Malachy, archbishop, having upon its head a mitre adorned with many precious stones, on the summit of which are six precious sapphires, and on its breast one precious sapphire with many other sapphires and precious stones all around; this head is supported by six silver images.”

Such were the rich reliquaries in which the heads of the two great saints rested.

Dom Joseph Méglinger, a religious of Wettingen in the Diocese of Constance, speaks of them in the following terms on p. 164 of the curious account which he published of his journey to the General Chapter of Cîteaux (*Lucerne*, 1667; reproduced by my care in this very volume of the *Patrology*): [Col. 1665B] “Two images fashioned from gold and silver, so lifelike in their representation that at first sight I stood astonished and, with my eyes fixed on them in admiration, waited to see whether they would speak. Above all, the countenance of the honey-flowing Father, familiar from the portrait commonly seen everywhere and here worked with such artistry, stirred the inmost depths of every heart.”

Dom Martène and Dom Durand tell us in their *Literary Journey* that in the treasury of Clairvaux they saw the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy in two fine silver-gilt busts with very rich enamels, and that they were carried in processions for public necessities [Note: [Col. 1665C] *Voyage littéraire de deux relig. bénéd.*, Paris, 1717, vol. II, p. 98 ff.].

The *Acta Sancti Bernardi* among the Bollandists, [Col. 1665C] which Fr. Pien published separately in 1739, provide some particulars concerning Saint Bernard’s head. They contain the following passage: “The head, stripped of skin and flesh (which we commonly call the skull), enclosed in a silver casket, is kept in the place where the church treasury is stored” [Note: [Col. 1665C] *Acta S. Bernardi, confessoris, primi Claravallensis abbatis, Patris ac Doctoris Ecclesiae, commentario et notationibus illustrata, a Joanne Pinio E. S. J. presbytero theologo*—“Acts of Saint Bernard, confessor, first Abbot of Clairvaux, Father and Doctor of the Church, illustrated with commentary and notes by John Pien, priest-theologian of the Society of Jesus.” Antwerp: Bernard van der Plassche, 1739. One folio volume.—Extract from vol. IV of the *Acta Sanctorum* for the month of August.].

Who could then have suspected that after half a century [Col. 1666A] these monuments of monastic piety would exist only in memory?

The Revolution broke out. As early as 1789, M. Rocourt had sent to the Mint in Paris 993 marks of silver and more than 9 marks of gold from the Treasury of Clairvaux. Three receipts had been issued, one of which was used to discharge the abbey’s patriotic contribution [Note: [Col. 1665D] Second inventory of Clairvaux, drawn up on 19 October 1790 by the delegated administrators of the district of Bar-sur-Aube (Archives of Aube).].

On 19 October 1790, the bust of Saint Bernard was the only silver reliquary remaining in the Treasury [Note: [Col. 1665D] Same source.]. Perhaps a final respect prevented the delivery to the smelter of an image that seemed that of a king amid an empire created by his powerful hand; perhaps also, through a remnant of filial piety, the degenerate inhabitants of the monastery [Note: [Col. 1665D] See Appendix no. 2.] made [Col. 1666B] some efforts to save their founder’s head. Be that as it may, it was only on 3 December 1791 that sacrilegious hands consigned it together with other silver articles destined for the Mint. It is described in these terms in the shipping schedule: “The head of Saint Bernard, his bust, small figures and ornaments in gilded and enamelled silver, and his halo, weighing 79 marks 4 ounces [Note: [Col. 1665D] Schedule of shipment of silverware from the churches, chapels, and suppressed religious communities in the district of Bar-sur-Aube, made to the Director of the Mint in Paris by the administrators of the Directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube, 3 December 1791 (Archives of Aube).—In this schedule Clairvaux appears with sixty-nine pieces weighing 173 marks 4 ounces. In another, dated 18 November 1792, it appears with 27 marks 3 ounces. In a schedule of shipment of old copper, dated 13 September of the same year, it is entered for eighty-seven pieces, excluding fragments. The detailed list shows two eagles, fifty-six candlesticks, and two small statues. Finally, in [Col. 1666C] another statement of materials removed from Clairvaux church, dated 13 Pluviôse, Year III, there are still 5 marks 1 ounce 2 *gros* of silver. I have been unable to find in the Archives of Aube the list of lead and iron fittings torn away at the same period. On 23 February 1792 the administrators of the Directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube sent the Mint nine bells and one signal bell from Clairvaux. [Col. 1666D] Three of them had been exchanged with the church of Couvignon. Approximately, the two largest weighed 7,500 and 5,500 pounds; the smallest weighed 200 (*Schedule of Shipment*, Archives of Aube). Dom Claude Guyton (Matthieu MS., XV, p. 526) cites a document of 1615 showing that the monks of Clairvaux were formerly assembled at the sound of the signal bell, at the usual meeting-place, to conduct their business. This signal bell, he says, was apparently that great iron apparatus which stood in our dormitories above the staircase and served as an alarm for going to the night offices, like those which could still be seen at Clairvaux in 1718, and even in 1744 at Igny and Signy.”].

This shapeless description nevertheless shows clearly that Saint Bernard’s head was contained in a complete bust and not merely in a simple silver-gilt head; all the parts detailed in the inventory of 1504 cited above are easily recognized in it.

[Col. 1666C] Toward the end of 1790, M. Rocourt, seeing the threatening turn affairs were taking, thought of saving the most precious relics in the Treasury [Note: [Col. 1666D] Seals were affixed at Clairvaux from 17 to 24 November 1790. The report of their affixing, drawn up by the delegated administrators of the district of Bar-sur-Aube, exists in the Archives of Aube.]. In the presence of several persons—whose names he was unfortunately unable to cite—he removed from the busts of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy the portions of bone enclosed in them, [Col. 1667A] and applied his seal to them. When times became better, he gave the two heads to M. Caffarelli, Prefect of Aube. The latter presented them to Troyes Cathedral on 24 December 1813; and on 4 September 1816, Mgr de Boulogne, then bishop, exposed them for the veneration of the faithful in the wooden caskets which contain them today [Note: Appendix no. 3.].

Since Monsieur Rocourt had the pious thought of snatching some relics from the destruction that threatened them all, you may perhaps be surprised, Monsieur le Comte, that he limited himself to choosing so small a number and, above all, that he did not seek to obtain the body of Saint Bernard. I shall satisfy your justified curiosity on these two points.

[Col. 1667B] First, Monsieur Rocourt did not limit himself to the two heads whose preservation we owe to him: he also saved several other relics, the details of which are found in Appendix no. 4. As for Saint Bernard’s body, to possess it he would have had to remove it from the ancient tomb in which it then lay in the [Col. 1668A] church. Now this operation could not have been carried out so secretly that news of it would not have spread outside; and the surrounding population, which even in 1793 prevented it from being thrown into the cemetery despite an order of the departmental executive council, would not have permitted it to be carried away from their midst. Besides, in 1790 neither the church nor the abbey had been sold: one could therefore believe, to a certain extent, that Saint Bernard’s tomb would be respected, or at least that, if its destruction became necessary, its bones would be exhumed respectfully and placed again in a neighboring church. The silverware was being sent to Paris; it was urgent to remove from the shrines relics that were no longer to remain there. But [Col. 1668B] it was not evident that the saint’s tomb would be profaned, since only a very slight profit could be gained from removing its materials.

These reflections naturally lead me to speak to you of the bodies of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy.

## II. Bodies of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy formerly preserved in the church of Clairvaux

[Col. 1667]

[Col. 1667B] Monsieur le Comte, in 1148, about three weeks before All Saints’ Day, [Note: [Col. 1667D] “He came to Clairvaux . . . where, after about three weeks had passed . . . he was joyfully received by the angels . . .” (*Epitaph of Blessed Malachy*—Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, dist. XLI).] Saint Malachy arrived at Clairvaux for the second time. He was returning to Rome, hoping that Pope Eugenius III would not refuse the friend of his spiritual father the pallium so [Col. 1667C] ardently desired for the metropolitan sees of Ireland. [Note: [Col. 1667D] “He bore it with considerable distress that Ireland had hitherto lacked the pallium, being zealous for the sacraments, and unwilling that his people should be entirely deprived of any one of them . . . Moreover, he was confident in that man—as indeed in such a man, and one raised from such a profession—and especially because he had been a special son of his own Clairvaux; nor did he fear that he would meet with any difficulty from him.” (*Works of St Bernard*, ed. Mabillon, Paris, 1719, *Life of St Malachy*, XXX.67).] “We received him,” says Saint Bernard, “as a true East coming from on high to visit us. With what splendor of light did that radiant sun illumine our Clairvaux! What a festal day shone upon us at his arrival! It was a day made by the Lord, in which there was rejoicing and gladness! How swiftly and lightly, despite the weakness of my trembling limbs, I flew to meet him! With what joy I threw myself into his arms! What feast-days I then spent with him—and how short they were!” [Note: [Col. 1667D] *Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.70.]

Indeed, God did not permit these two brothers long to enjoy in this world the happiness of dwelling [Col. 1667D] together. On 18 October, the feast of Saint Luke, Saint Malachy, having celebrated Mass, was [Col. 1668B] seized with fever and took to his bed: “We all fell ill with him,” Saint Bernard adds. [Note: [Col. 1668D] “Now four or five days of this our festival had passed, when behold, on the solemn day of Blessed Luke the Evangelist, after he had celebrated Mass in the community with his customary holy devotion, he was seized by a fever, took to bed, and we all with him.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.70).] From that point the holy archbishop foretold his approaching end. Earlier he had wished to rest in the shadow of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1668D] “I have chosen Clairvaux.” (Ibid., XXX.67).] and to give up his soul into [Col. 1668C] the Creator’s hands on All Souls’ Day. His wish—or prophecy—was soon to be fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 1668D] “If it is deemed a simple wish, it was fulfilled; if a prophecy, not one iota failed.” (Ibid., XXX.67).] He wished to be anointed with the holy oil; and his strength still allowed him to descend from the upper floor of the monastery where he was staying [Note: [Col. 1668D] “He lay in the upper chamber of the house.” (Ibid., XXXI.71).], to come and receive the sacrament for the dying amid the monks, and to return to his cell. Saint Bernard could not believe that his friend would soon leave him. [Note: [Col. 1668D] “Who would have believed this man was going to die?” (Ibid., XXXI.71).] “He went up and down easily; his face had color and no gauntness, his forehead no wrinkles; his eyes did not seem sunken, his nostrils were not contracted, his lips showed no tightening, his teeth appeared excellent, his neck was not wasted, his shoulders did not [Col. 1668D] stoop, and his limbs were still strong.” [Note: [Col. 1668D] Ibid.]

[Col. 1669A] Yet on All Saints’ Day, after the day’s festivities, Saint Malachy became very ill. “He was drawing near to the dawn of life, not to the twilight of evening,” says Saint Bernard. [Note: [Col. 1669B] “At nightfall, when the celebration of the day had now somehow been completed by us, Malachy had drawn near—not to twilight, but to dawn.” (Ibid., XXXI.73).] On that very evening, a moving ceremony took place at Clairvaux. The revered bones of Saint Bernard’s first companions were being transferred from the cemetery of the first abbey to that of the new one. [Note: [Col. 1669C] “Thus everything concurred according to his desires, so that by the inspiration of divine mercy he had chosen this place above all; and he also wished to have, after a long interval, this very day for burial, on which the general commemoration of all the faithful is celebrated. And this also deservedly increased our joy: on the same day, by God’s ordering, the bones of our brethren were to be brought here from the former cemetery and reinterred.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *On the Passing of St Malachy*, Sermon I.2; *Epitaph of Blessed Tescelin, father of St Bernard, of his brothers and kinsmen, and of various disciples of the holy Abbot himself*, Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, dist. XLI, VI).] They were regarded as saints because it had been revealed to the blessed abbot that all the monks living with him would be saved. [Note: [Col. 1669C] *Works of St Bernard*, *Extracts from the Great Exordium of Cîteaux*, I; *The Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard Asserted*, Herbert, *On Miracles*, II.XI.] Saint Malachy testified to his joy on hearing the sacred chants accompanying this translation; [Note: [Col. 1669D] *Works of St Bernard*, *On the Passing of St Malachy*, Sermon I.2.] for him they were like a foretaste of the angelic harmonies with which he would [Col. 1669B] soon mingle his voice.

He gladly saw night fall, [Note: [Col. 1669D] “Seeing that the night he had awaited was at hand.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.73).] hoping that it would be followed by a day without sunset. His dying speech consoled those present: “I have loved God,” he told them; “I have loved you. Charity cannot perish.” [Note: [Col. 1669D] Ibid.] And, since his hour had not yet come, he sent the monks away to take a little rest.

Tenderness is anxious. Soon Saint Bernard brought his monks back to the sick man. A great number of abbots from neighboring monasteries had hastened there to attend the final moments of the [Col. 1670A] great archbishop. Psalms, hymns, and devout songs accompanied his departure for his homeland. [Note: [Col. 1669D] “With psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs we accompany our friend returning to his homeland.” (Ibid., XXXI.74).] Then Saint Bernard came forward to receive his friend’s blessing. The latter, already almost motionless, recovered strength to give him one final token of affection and, with trembling hand, to leave him this supreme and moving inheritance. [Note: [Col. 1669D] “He blessed me, and I possess the blessing as an inheritance.” (Ibid., *Letter to Congan, Abbot).]

Nothing on earth now held Saint Malachy; he happily fell asleep in the Lord on the morning of 2 November, while night still reigned; and his eyes, closed by beloved hands, opened again to heavenly brightness. He was fifty-four years old. His calm face bore witness to his peaceful end; death had not altered his features, [Col. 1670B] and he seemed to be asleep. “He was not changed,” says Saint Bernard, “but we were no longer the same men: our tears and groans suddenly ceased; our sorrow turned to joy; our sobs gave place to hymns of thanksgiving.” [Note: [Col. 1669D] *Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.74.]

The abbots took this precious burden upon their shoulders and first carried it to the still unfinished church. [Note: [Col. 1669D] “It is brought into the oratory upon the shoulders of the abbots.” (Ibid.)] Then the holy body was washed and placed in a cell prepared to receive it with honor. [Note: [Col. 1669D] The manuscript *Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux* speaks thus, fol. 6r, at the end of its entry on Gerard, sixth abbot: “His body was deposited before the doors of the church of Clairvaux, in a cell which had once been honorably prepared for receiving the bodies of Saints Malachy and Bernard.” This note is confirmed by *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. [Col. 1670B] 801: “He lies at Clairvaux in the cloister of the Chapter, [Col. 1670C] almost at the very entrance of the church.” And by Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, dist. XXXV, V: “His sacred body, Gerard’s, was deposited before the doors of the Clairvaux oratory, in a cell constructed long ago for receiving the bodies of the holy confessors Bernard and Malachy, in a sarcophagus raised above the pavement.” We see further, in support of the manuscript *Catalogue*, that Peter, surnamed Monoculus, eighth abbot of Clairvaux, was buried beside Gerard: “In Saint Bernard’s first burial-place.” (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 803.) “Where Saint Bernard had first been laid,” says an eyewitness, “we placed him there because of the grace of his merits and because it was the monument of a righteous man.” (MANRIQUE, *Annals of Cîteaux*, vol. III, year 1186, VI.7.)—Positive texts cited in the course of this letter clearly show that Saint Malachy and Saint Bernard were buried in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin immediately after the funeral offices. This cell, of which the [Col. 1670D] manuscript *Catalogue* speaks, can only have been the place of deposition where these venerable bodies were displayed, clothed in their episcopal and priestly vestments; but since they had remained there for some time, it might rightly be called the “monument of the righteous.” —In the *Annales archéologiques*, vol. III, fourth issue, 1845, was published, under the title *A Great Monastery in the Sixteenth Century*, the account of a journey to Clairvaux in 1517 by the Queen of Sicily and the Count of Guise. This document is highly interesting, but it is sometimes at variance with the most authentic monuments. Thus it speaks of a chapel situated at the end of the transept-crossing of the church, on the right-hand side, where one saw the grave in which Saint Bernard was supposedly buried. Yet all Saint Bernard’s biographers say that he was buried on the third day after his death in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin. Now this chapel was at the eastern end of the church, behind the [Col. 1671C] high altar; it was also called the chapel of the Savior. In a sixteenth-century notice of the altars of the church of Clairvaux, to be published after these letters, we find the altar “of our Savior Jesus Christ and his Mother,” placed [Col. 1671D] between those of Saints Peter and Paul and of Saint John the Baptist. And we shall see in Dom Le Boullenger’s description of the choir that the chapel of the Savior, located at the eastern end of the church, stood between that of Saints Peter and Paul and that of Saint John the Baptist. The author of the account, a curious observer rather than a learned one, must have confused the place of Saint Bernard’s burial with the place where his body was displayed in priestly vestments; it was indeed situated on the right, at the end of the church crossing, in the cloister of the Chapter: “in the cloister of the Chapter, almost at the very entrance of the church.”] By a pious theft, Saint Bernard substituted his own tunic for that covering him, [Col. 1671A] [Note: [Col. 1671D] *Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.III.23.] and kept that holy relic as Saint Athanasius had formerly kept Antony’s cloak. Finally, when all the funeral rites had been completed, Saint Malachy was buried in the very chapel of the Blessed Virgin, in whom he had placed his affections. [Note: [Col. 1671D] “When all had duly been performed, Malachy was committed to burial in the very oratory of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in which he had taken great delight.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.75).] He was entrusted to the grave on 2 November in the year of Our Lord 1148. Before his burial, the mere touch of his hand healed a child whose arm hung numb; [Note: [Col. 1671D] Ibid.] and Saint Bernard, offering the saving Host for him on the day of his death, learned by revelation the glory he enjoyed and recited the collect for confessors who were bishops instead of that for the dead. [Note: [Col. 1672C] *Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, IV.IV.21.]

Manrique says that Saint Malachy’s body was placed under a stone arch. [Note: [Col. 1672C] “He himself was laid beneath a stone arch.” (Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1148).] Do these words indicate [Col. 1671B] a particular monument, or do they simply designate one of the round arches which probably enclosed the chapel? I cannot resolve the difficulty, for I know no document capable of clarifying this obscure expression. We possess several epitaphs for Saint Malachy; [Note: [Col. 1672C] See *Menologium Cisterciense*, 5 November; MANRIQUE; Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*.] one, in prose, is drawn from the *Book of Burials of Clairvaux*, a genuine necrology rather than an exact collection of the abbey’s funerary inscriptions. [Note: [Col. 1672D] I searched in vain for this *Book of Burials* among the manuscripts of the Public Library of Troyes; nor does it exist in the Archives of Aube. Manrique cites many passages from it. It is printed in *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, by R. P. F. Chrysostom Henriquez, Cologne, 1631, 2 vols., quarto; vol. II, dist. XLI, and also in this very volume of the *Patrology*.] The others are in verse and attributed to Saint Bernard. When Manrique published the first from the *Book of Burials of Clairvaux*, he judged it to be not very ancient. [Note: [Col. 1672D] “He himself, Saint Malachy, was laid beneath a stone arch, with an inscription added upon the stone containing an epitome of his life. The *Book of Burials* preserves it, though it is more recent, as I judge.” (MANRIQUE, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1148).] It is indeed difficult to believe it was composed before the fourteenth century. It is long and tedious; I shall not quote it. Here are those [Col. 1671C] in verse:

> Do you wish to know who lies here? Lord Malachy.  
> Do you still ask who his heir was?  
> Irish by homeland; holy through the gift of merits;  
> exalted in miracles, he was a bishop in dignity.  
> The legation of the Supreme See added to his burden.  
> He was going to Rome, but from here he takes his seat among the stars.  
> In this valley stands for you a dwelling, a polished stone,  
> in which, Father, your sacred bones have been laid.  
>
> [Col. 1672A] O shepherd worthy, gentle, holy, and kind,  
> I pray that in every hour you may remember those mindful of you.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 1672D] *Menologium Cisterciense*, 5 November; Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1148, XI; *Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XVI.38.]

Were these verses engraved on Saint Malachy’s tomb? This is again a point upon which it is nearly impossible to decide. Details concerning his tomb are exceedingly scarce. Without a drawing preserved by the Bollandists, it would now be very difficult to form an idea of Saint Bernard’s tomb, although for it we are less lacking in documents. But in Saint Malachy’s case we lack both these advantages, and only a few scattered features can give any notion of it. In 1599, a Spanish Cistercian, Dom Bernardo Cardilio Villalpando, was sent to France by the abbot of Fitero in Navarre in order [Col. 1672B] to visit all the houses of the Order and collect noteworthy particulars concerning them. This monk later assembled his notes and composed an *Itinerary*, which, I believe, unfortunately remained unpublished. [Note: [Col. 1672D] Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana nova*; Charles de Wisch, *Bibliotheca scriptorum Ordinis Cisterciensis*.] Manrique was Villalpando’s contemporary and cites him several times; from the descriptions he draws from him, one judges that the author entered into very great detail. Nevertheless, I am persuaded that he did not describe Saint Malachy’s tomb carefully, for Manrique does not invoke his testimony on this matter; and I believe he would not voluntarily have deprived himself of such assistance.

I leave with regret, Monsieur le Comte, this humble stone beneath which the great primate of Ireland sleeps, and which I revere as the cradle of one of those [Col. 1672C] old affections that the community of faith and hope formerly established among peoples better than the community of interest knows how to do in our day.

Saint Bernard, in concluding the history of Saint Malachy’s life, wished for such a happy death for himself, [Note: [Col. 1672D] “I desire these things for myself; I do not begrudge them to him.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI.75).] forgetting in his profound humility that the death of the righteous had long been assured to him. He did not delay long in joining his friend in the eternal tabernacles. “The bonds that held his [Col. 1673A] soul captive being almost broken, the endless day dawned for him. The neighboring bishops, abbots, and brethren surrounded him like a holy multitude. On 20 August 1153, about nine in the morning, Saint Bernard went out like a lamp of the sanctuary and passed from his mortal body into the land of the living. He flew to Jesus Christ his head, to the joyful choirs of saints, to the battalions of angels. Happy day, the object of his life’s entire longing, for which he had ardently sighed and which he had prepared by his prayers! Happy passage from labor to rest, from battle to victory, from death to life, from faith to sight, from pilgrimage to homeland, from earth to heaven!” [Note: [Col. 1673B] “. . . For him the day rose forever . . . the neighboring bishops had gathered with a great multitude of abbots and brethren . . . happily, with Christ as his guide, he passed into the land of the living . . . passing . . . to meet the ranks of angels . . . Happy passage from labor to rest,” etc. (*Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.II.13).]

[Col. 1673B] The saint’s body was washed [Note: [Col. 1673B] “Bernard’s body was brought by the hands of grieving sons, not so much to be washed as to consecrate the waters in its own manner, and was placed upon a stone basin—this is known more by tradition than by written record.” (MANRIQUE, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1153, VII.)—This holy body left its shadow impressed on the stone upon which it had been washed. Villalpando saw it in the sixteenth century. The stone’s surface was all broken by the piety of the faithful who wished to carry away fragments, yet the outlines of the body could easily be distinguished because they were deeply incised.—“Moreover, where it adhered to the stone, it impressed traces which could not be effaced even now, although many scrapings had been taken away from it. To this day, as Villalpando testifies—he is still alive and inspected all these things forty years ago on the mission of Ignatius Fermin Hiberi, abbot of Fitero—the stone is seen at Clairvaux, and on the stone a shadow or likeness of the body: its surface is everywhere worn away and hollowed out, but the lines of the body remain, the impressed figure penetrating deep into the stone.” [Col. 1673D] (MANRIQUE, ibid.)—The account printed in the *Annales archéologiques* discusses this stone in some detail. At the beginning of the eighteenth century Dom Martène examined it; but the preconceptions of a narrow criticism led him to treat very lightly a venerable monument deserving greater attention from him. “It is claimed at Clairvaux,” he says, “that one sees the saint’s shadow on the stone where his body was washed after death, and it was shown to us. Yet I do not know whether it is as miraculous as people imagine; for the shadow cannot be seen from every side. One must stand in a certain position to perceive it, which can occur naturally through the reflection of light.” (*Literary Journey*, vol. II, p. 104.) Dom Joseph Méglinger spoke of it more seriously in 1667 (*Iter Cisterciense*, p. 178): “A prodigy, if any is astonishing in the whole world. I confess that I could scarcely obtain belief in it even from these my own eyes and hands, which were granted to examine and touch it curiously and carefully . . . The head, back, legs, and feet—all these limbs project a most distinct visible shadow of themselves, exactly as though the sacred body itself, naked, were waiting there to be washed. Somewhat shaken by no slight terror, yet approaching with reverence, I began to feel whether the stone, by a hollow in itself, produced this shadow; but there was one continuous flatness throughout, [Col. 1674B] except that I noticed that certain small portions around the middle of the stone had been torn away with iron. When I asked the reason, I was told that these were traces left by the rashness of heretics, who, envious of the most holy Father’s glory, spread the claim that the monks had applied this shadow to the stone with black pigment. Therefore, in order to expose the alleged deception, they dug into the stone with hammers; but without the result they sought. For although the hammer wore away the edges of the stone, the shadow nevertheless always remained whole.”] and clothed in his priestly vestments, [Note: [Col. 1674C] It was not known that Saint Bernard had been buried in Saint Malachy’s tunic; he himself revealed it to his monks. A few days after his death, he appeared to one of the brethren and said to him: “Know, and tell the brethren, that the body of one truly holy, whose garment I too possess, is buried in the oratory.” He meant Bishop Malachy. (*Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.III.23).] was first carried into the chapel of the Blessed Virgin. [Note: [Col. 1674D] “The body, duly prepared and adorned with priestly vestments, is brought into the oratory of the Blessed Mother of God.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.II.14).] It is probable that it was afterward brought back and displayed in the chapel where Saint Malachy had been placed before his burial. [Note: [Col. 1674D] Manuscript *Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux*, fol. 6r—see above, a note on this subject.] The shepherd remained for two further days in the midst of his flock, though dead. [Note: [Col. 1674D] “The dead shepherd remained for two days in the midst of the flock.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.II.14).] The inhabitants of the surrounding country, who had flocked to Clairvaux, filled [Col. 1674A] the valley with their lamentations; everyone hastened to kiss Saint Bernard’s venerable hands and to touch a thousand objects to his body in order to bless them. Yet the monks, fearing that they could not contain the ever-growing crowd, brought forward the hour appointed for their Father’s funeral. [Note: [Col. 1674D] “Anticipating the hour.” (*Works of St Bernard*, ibid.)] Early in the morning of 22 August, [Note: [Col. 1674D] “Eleven days before the Kalends of September.” (*Works of St Bernard*, ibid.)] after the holy sacrifice and devout psalmody, they committed this most pure balm to the vessel that was to contain it and laid this precious diamond in the stone of the tomb. [Note: [Col. 1674D] *Works of St Bernard*, ibid.] He was buried before the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose most devoted priest he had been. [Note: [Col. 1674D] “He was buried . . . before the holy altar of the Blessed Virgin Mother, whose most devoted priest he had been.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, V.II.15).] In accordance with his wish, a small reliquary containing some bones of Saint Thaddaeus was placed upon his breast; his faith and devotion [Col. 1674B] made him desire to be united with that apostle on the day of the general resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1674D] *Works of St Bernard*, ibid.]

Immediately after Saint Bernard’s death, pilgrimages to his tomb began. I shall limit myself, Monsieur le Comte, to naming a few celebrated visitors drawn to Clairvaux by their confidence in the merits of the holy abbot. At the beginning of spring 1154, from distant [Col. 1675A] Scandinavia, Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, first came to the place where his former friend rested; laying aside the mitre to put on the humble monastic habit, he chose to be buried at his side. [Note: [Col. 1675C] “At the beginning of spring in the year 1154, he visited the tomb of the blessed man, formerly his intimate friend, and chose to live and die at his most sacred tomb.” (MANRIQUE, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1154, I).] That same year, a minor prince of Sardinia and Simon, former abbot of Chézy-sur-Marne, followed his example. [Note: [Col. 1675C] “A princelet of Sardinia . . . Simon, abbot of Chézy, followed both men.” (MANRIQUE, ibid.)] Andrew, archdeacon of Verdun, and a cleric named Geoffrey could not tear themselves away from Saint Bernard’s tomb or from his beloved valley. [Note: [Col. 1675C] Manrique, ibid.] In order to sleep in the tomb of his fathers and rest beside his former abbot, so as to rise again with him, Alan left the episcopal see of Auxerre and came to die at Clairvaux. [Note: [Col. 1675C] In 1167 Alan left the episcopal see of Auxerre and withdrew to his former abbey of Larivour, where he made his will in 1182. He then went to Clairvaux, where he died after 1185. (*Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 1675D] vol. XII, col. 295.) In his will he ordered that every monk of Larivour should annually be given a pound of white bread on the feasts of Saint Bernard. He bequeathed to the abbey seven chalices and “all his books, both cloister books and church books . . . . All this was done on this condition and understanding: if he should be buried at Clairvaux in the tomb of his fathers, all that has been said concerning the books shall remain valid and binding; but if not, all shall be void and shall remain neither valid nor binding. Although we took this declaration painfully, since we did not wish for the holy Father’s absence, nevertheless, because it concerned his soul, and because he had long cherished being buried with Saint Bernard so as to rise with him, we granted the burial as he requested, though unwillingly.” (Ibid., *Instrumenta concerning the Church of Auxerre*, col. 136).]

Thus, in Manrique’s view, every order among the faithful seemed to send one of its [Col. 1675B] members to honor the remains of a monk who had been great before God and men; and Christian confidence anticipated the Church’s infallible judgment. [Note: [Col. 1675D] Manrique, ibid.; *Acts of Saint Bernard*, § LIII, 567.]

Finally, in 1174 Bernard was entered in the catalogue of saints by a bull of Pope Alexander III issued at Anagni on 18 January. [Note: [Col. 1675D] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1174, I; *Acts of Saint [Col. 1676C] Bernard*, § LX, 663–64; *Works of St Bernard*, *Canonization of St Bernard*.] A bull of the same pope, dated in the same city and on the same day, carried this happy news to the monks of Clairvaux, then governed by Gerard, sixth abbot. [Note: [Col. 1676C] *Works of St Bernard*, *Canonization of St Bernard*.]

The precise date of the first elevation of Saint Bernard’s body is unknown. A valuable chronicle published by Father Chifflet tells us only [Col. 1675C] that it took place in 1174 and that Guichard, Archbishop of Lyon and former abbot of Pontigny, attended it. [Note: [Col. 1676C] “In the year of the Lord 1174 took place the dedication of the church of Clairvaux, the canonization of Saint Bernard, and his elevation, at which Lord Wichard, Archbishop of Lyon and formerly abbot of Pontigny, was present.” (*The Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard Asserted*, Dijon, 1660, p. 84).] The second, in which the body was placed in another tomb, occurred in 1178. Manrique thought that the elevation of 1174 had been reported falsely; [Note: [Col. 1676C] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1174, II.] but Father Mabillon, followed by Father Pien, demonstrated that the information provided by the chronicle was accurate. [Note: [Col. 1676C] *Works of St Bernard*, *Canonization of St Bernard*; *Acts of St Bernard*, § LXI, 676.] About ten months after Saint Bernard’s canonization, the church of Clairvaux, begun during his lifetime, was consecrated by Gaultier, bishop of Langres. “It is probable,” says Manrique, “that advantage was taken of this solemnity to raise an altar to the new saint.” [Note: [Col. 1676D] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1174, II; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 583 ff.] So long as the church remained unfinished, it appears that a lay brother watched day and night near the chapel of the Blessed Virgin to guard the precious relics contained there. History has even preserved the name of Brother Lawrence, charged with this honorable function. [Note: [Col. 1676D] *The Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard Asserted*, Herbert, *On Miracles*, II.XXX.]

Henry, abbot of Hautecombe, succeeded Gerard [Col. 1676B] in governing Clairvaux. “He was,” says Manrique, “a firm pillar prepared by God for his Church.” [Note: [Col. 1676D] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1177, IV.] Hardly had he received into his hands Saint Bernard’s pastoral staff when he undertook to raise a marble tomb for him. The monument rose quickly. In 1178, Henry, being at the general chapter of Cîteaux, [Note: [Col. 1676D] Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1178, III.] was able to announce to the Order’s delegates that a new celebration was about to be held in honor of their common Father. The impressive assembly, in which archbishops sat together with a multitude of abbots, thrilled with joy; and many of its members followed Henry as he returned to Clairvaux. [Note: [Col. 1676D] “Nor did several of the Fathers who were present at the council leave him.” (MANRIQUE, ibid.)] Among them was Guichard, Archbishop of Lyon, of whom I have already spoken.

[Col. 1676C] The second elevation of the holy body took place with great pomp and with the universal rejoicing of the Church of France. It was placed in its marble shrine behind the high altar. [Note: [Col. 1676D] Manrique, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1178, III.—The manuscript Catalogue of Abbots, fol. 7r, which, like Manrique, followed the Book of Burials, reads: “Having summoned from every side venerable bishops and other reverend persons, he (Henry), through the venerable Father Lord Nicardus [one must read Wichardus], archbishop of Lyons and formerly abbot of Pontigny, caused [the body], amid the greatest joy and exultation of the whole Gallican Church, to be elevated (this word relates to the first elevation performed by the same archbishop of Lyons under Gerard in 1174) and re-elevated, [Col. 1677C] and to be devoutly and honorably placed in a marble shrine behind the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, as may still be seen today.” (HENRIQUEZ, *Fascicul. SS. O. C.*, vol. II, dist. XLI, 111.) The high altar of Clairvaux church was consecrated in honor of the Most Holy Virgin in 1174 by Gaultier, bishop of Langres. (MANRIQUE, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1174, II.)]

“We have [Col. 1677A] celebrated a glorious and solemn feast in our valley,” Henry wrote to the king of England when sending him a finger of Saint Bernard. “How ardently I wished for your august presence amid these joys, more of heaven than of earth! How much greater would have been the solemnity of our rites, and what abundant graces would have been poured out upon you . . . So that bodily absence may not deprive your royal treasury of a share in him whom we have uncovered, I am sending you a precious fragment of relics beyond price . . . Receive a finger of that sacred hand which, by its contempt for worldly riches, deserved to receive from the Lord the fullness of heavenly blessings; of that hand whose touch alone healed the sick, [Col. 1677B] strengthened the weak, reassured men, and drove out demons.” [Note: [Col. 1677D] This letter, published by Mabillon in the Works of Saint Bernard (*S. Bern. Op.*, *S. Bern. canonizatio*), bears the superscription: “To Stephen, king of the English.” There must be an error in this title, since in 1178, the probable date of Abbot Henry’s letter, Stephen was no longer alive. He died in 1154. (Sir Harris Nicolas, *The Chronology of History*, London, 1833.) Consequently, Saint Bernard’s finger can only have been sent to his successor, Henry II.]

At various later periods, Monsieur le Comte, there was a desire to place Saint Bernard’s relics in a silver reliquary; but this plan was never carried out. Jean d’Aizanville, to whom the busts of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy were owed, left at his death an unfinished shrine, for which he had already supplied seventy marks of silver from his own resources. [Note: [Col. 1677D] “In the year in which he died, he had begun a silver casket for Blessed Bernard, and had already provided for it seventy marks of silver from his own funds.” (Manuscript Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux, fol. 18r.)]

In the sixteenth century Tristan de Bizet, bishop of Saintes and formerly a monk of Clairvaux, presented the abbey with a richly wrought gilt-silver shrine for the bones of Saint Bernard. At one end there was [Col. 1677C] a Christ on the cross; at the other, the Blessed Virgin, represented holding the Child Jesus. The twelve Apostles stood around it; jewels were set over the lid. Dom Martène and Dom Durand saw this magnificent reliquary. “There is still preserved in the treasury,” they say, “a large silver shrine which a bishop of Xaintes had caused to be made in order to place Saint Bernard’s relics in it. But the monks, fearing that, if the bones were taken [Col. 1678A] from his tomb, several princes, to whom they could not refuse them, would ask for some, preferred to leave them there.” [Note: [Col. 1677D] Inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux, drawn up in 1640.—It appears from an acknowledgment of Dom Lupin Le Myre, abbot of Clairvaux, dated 17 November 1578, that “Messire Tristan de Bizet was having completed a shrine to contain the relics of Monsieur Saint [Col. 1678C] Bernard.” (Archives of Aube.)—“Tristan de Bizet, of Trojan origin, alumnus of Clairvaux monastery, sixty-sixth bishop of Saintes, died in the year of the Lord 1579. He bequeathed to the Bernardine College in Paris one thousand livres tournois of annual income. His heart lies buried at Clairvaux before the altar of All Saints.” (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 1083.)]

In 1625 the Genoese, on the eve of being overwhelmed by the arms of the Duke of Savoy, had recourse to Saint Bernard and made the solemn vow to take him as patron of the Republic. The holy abbot remembered the promise he had made them never to forget them (*Epist. ad Januen.*, 129); and on the eve of his feast Genoa saw itself delivered by the arrival of the Spanish fleet. Eager to possess some relic of their beloved patron, they dispatched a special envoy to Clairvaux in 1633. He was fortunate enough to obtain a vertebra of Saint Bernard. The Republic received [Col. 1678B] this precious gift with transports of joy (Appendix, no. 5), and wished that a silver lamp [Note: [Col. 1678D] Here is its description, drawn from the Inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux (1640), fols. 26r–v: “Also a large openwork lamp of silversmith’s work; beneath the basin are the arms of the Republic of Genoa, with three crowned escutcheons borne by two griffins, in each of which is a red cross. Above the same basin are three cherubim, to which are attached three chains supporting it; each chain has two knobs. The glass lamp stands upon a large silver knob supported by three other chains, each of which has one knob. This lamp was given to Clairvaux by the Republic of Genoa in the time of the Reverend Father in God Dom Claude Largentier, forty-fifth abbot of Clairvaux.”], suspended before the holy abbot’s tomb, should remain there as a perpetual testimony of its gratitude. [Note: [Col. 1678D] *Acta S. Bernardi*, § LXI, 683–84.—The facts are reported there inaccurately, following Ughelli.]

In 1643 Dom Claude Largentier, in order to satisfy the devotion of Anne of Austria, gave her some particles detached from Saint Bernard’s head, “with all possible reverence and respect” (Appendix, no. 6).

It does not seem superfluous to me to dwell upon all these details. They establish that Saint Bernard’s relics were never moved and that, apart from a certain number of portions removed—which I shall now specify—they remained intact until the Revolution. Father Pien compiled their catalogue [Col. 1678C] in his *Acta*. He first mentions the entry in the Cîteaux calendar printed at Dijon in 1617, marking, on 17 May: “Translation of our holy father Bernard to Avignon.”—This must be understood to refer to a few fragments, since in 1625 the Genoese envoy found the body whole. I have spoken of the finger given to the king of England by Abbot Henry. In Spain, a portion of a rib five fingers long, together with five smaller relics, was preserved at the Escorial. [Col. 1679A] The great monastery of Saint Bernard on the Scheldt, not far from Antwerp, possessed a phalanx from the hand, which was stolen before 1737. Tournai cathedral kept two fine bones; the Augustinian Canons Regular of Cambrai also possessed some. An abbey of Premonstratensians in the diocese of Namur, Floreffe, displayed one. There was one among the Cistercian nuns of Salzines, in the same diocese. [Note: [Col. 1679D] *Acta S. Bernardi*, §§ LXI, LXII.]

In Geoffrey’s Life of Saint Bernard (chap. IV, 27) is found the account of a miracle performed at the monastery of Esrom (diocese of Roskilde in Denmark) by applying portions of Saint Bernard’s beard and hair and one of his teeth. These relics had been deposited at Esrom by his devout friend Eskil, archbishop of [Col. 1679B] Lund.—The Inventory of Clairvaux sacristy, drawn up in 1504, fol. 1v, speaks of a finger of Saint Bernard, and adds these words: “The little vessel for the finger is found empty.” At fol. 5v, a silver vessel intended to contain one of his teeth, which had been taken to Paris, is described. At fol. 10r one reads: “From the rib of Saint Bernard.” His thumb was enclosed in a rich crystal reliquary due to the devotion of Jean d’Aizanville, fol. 11r.—At fol. 13r: “An oblong vessel containing . . . relics . . . namely . . . of Saint Bernard . . . weighing thirteen and a half ounces.”

The inventory of 1640, fol. 9v, speaks of the reliquary in which Saint Bernard’s finger was kept, but only as a memorandum. At fol. 11r one finds: “From the rib of Saint Bernard.” A little further on, on the same folio verso, it is said that Amaury’s tablet contained some of his relics. The thumb reliquary is described at fol. 18r; another is indicated, on the same folio verso, as containing: “From the dust of the head of Blessed Bernard”; a similar entry occurs at fol. 20r. [Note: [Col. 1679D] The account published in the *Annales archéologiques* speaks of Saint Bernard’s arm and his two feet as preserved separately. I know of no document supporting this assertion.]

I have said a word, Monsieur le Comte, about the first pilgrimages to Saint Bernard’s tomb. A few notes gathered concerning these devout journeys in more recent times will conclude this letter, forming a chain of valuable testimonies.

On 28 July 1599, Dom Edme de la Croix, abbot of Cîteaux, wrote to the abbot of Morimond: “I [Col. 1679D] shall do all that I can to be at Clairvaux for Saint Bernard’s feast.” [Note: [Col. 1679D] From the autograph. (Archives of Aube.)]—In 1605 the Venerable Mother Anne of Jesus, foundress of the Carmelites in France, was travelling to Dijon to establish a house of her Order there. “Since Saint Bernard was the guiding star of this journey, as she was going to found a house in his country, the venerable Mother wished to visit Clairvaux. The abbot being absent, she could not see Saint Bernard’s body; [Col. 1680A] [Note: [Col. 1679D] These words show how vigilantly the monks guarded the holy body, since the abbot alone could permit it to be seen.] but she saw the poor dwelling, the very narrow cells, the humble church, the devout choir, where there was an image of Our Lord in the sepulchre which sent fire from its eyes into souls.” [Note: [Col. 1680D] *Life of the Venerable Mother Anne of Jesus*, by Father Manrique, translated by Gaultier; Paris, 1636, 1 vol., octavo.]

A few years later, in 1623, at the beginning of January, Master Husson, provost and canon of the collegiate church of Saint-Sauveur at Metz, was at Clairvaux. He had come there to fulfil “toward God and the blessed Saint Bernard the vow which he had long ago made . . . . . to venerate his holy relics.” [Note: [Col. 1680D] From the autograph. (Archives of Aube.)]

When M. Olier was going on pilgrimage to Annecy in 1647, he wished first to visit Clairvaux Abbey: “He took the road through Burgundy and passed through Châtillon-sur-Seine, famous for the devotion paid there to the august Mother of God. He knew that Saint [Col. 1680B] Bernard had received there several extraordinary graces; and scarcely had he arrived when, that very evening, he went to the church and remained for some time in prayer, prostrate before the miraculous image of Mary. It may be presumed that he received many graces there; at least, he left it profoundly abased in his own eyes, full of contempt for himself. On the following day, when celebrating holy Mass at the altar consecrated under the invocation of the Blessed Virgin, he experienced consolations so vivid that never had they shown more plainly in the features of his face, nor were the pure flames of divine love ever more perceptible in his conversation.

[Col. 1680C] “From Châtillon he took the road to Clairvaux. Being only half a league away, he dismounted, together with those accompanying him, and wished to proceed on foot to the abbey, in silence and in prayer. The character of the place invited him to this and seemed to provide him with an unceasing subject for meditation: it was a very dense and thick wood, such as surrounds most ancient monasteries. He arrived at Clairvaux on the very eve of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, greatly consoled at last to behold the solitude once chosen by Saint Bernard, and admiring how, by the great number of saints he had formed there, he had made an image of heaven out of a desert filled with wild beasts. He remained there two days, so [Col. 1680D] absorbed in continual prayer that it was difficult to draw him away from it; this was his sole occupation on the feast day. On the next day he celebrated holy Mass in Saint Bernard’s old chapel, and then visited all the places within and outside the monastery that recalled some particular incident in the life of the holy founder. Having been led to a small cell [Col. 1681A] of the blessed man, as it was shown there, he remained in it a long time in prayer, and it was not easy to make him leave; this filled the good monks accompanying him with admiration for his person.” (*Life of M. Olier*, Paris, 1841, vol. II, pp. 4–5.)

I cannot, Monsieur le Comte, resist the pleasure of allowing Dom Thierry Ruinart, Mabillon’s devout friend, to recount the visit which this great monk made to Clairvaux in 1701. “When Father Mabillon,” he says, “found himself sufficiently advanced in the composition of his *Annals* to be able to produce two volumes in succession, besides the material already prepared for subsequent volumes, he resolved to begin printing them. But before [Col. 1681B] undertaking this work, he still needed to see certain monastic archives. This gave him a most favorable opportunity to visit Saint Benedict’s tomb at Fleury-sur-Loire and Saint Bernard’s at Clairvaux. He embraced it all the more readily because he had long wished to make this journey, in order to ask God, through the intercession of these two patriarchs of the monastic Order in the West, for the grace worthily to carry out so extensive a design, which he had undertaken only in obedience, for the edification of his brethren, the glory of his Order, and the benefit of the Church. We left toward the end of September 1701 [Col. 1681C] and arrived at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire on the twenty-ninth of that month. After spending three or four days examining certain ancient monuments and what remained there of that famous library, formerly so renowned, we visited the monasteries and archives which presented themselves on our route, and arrived at Clairvaux on the eighth of October.

“On such journeys Dom Mabillon was accustomed, when he began to enter a country or a new diocese, immediately to greet its patron saints with prayers recited for that purpose. But when he approached some place and caught sight of the church of the chief patron or of the saint to whom he was going to offer his vows, he ordinarily dismounted, [Col. 1681D] and knelt down in order to perform more devoutly this exercise of piety which he had prescribed for himself from his earliest years. He did not need all these reminders to awaken his fervor on the day we arrived at Clairvaux; for from the morning when we left Monticramée Abbey, throughout the whole journey he did nothing but sing and recite hymns and canticles, so deeply was he filled with joy [Col. 1682A] at being able once more to visit this solitude which Saint Bernard and so many of his illustrious disciples had sanctified in a special manner. But when, on leaving the wood, we came within sight of that holy house, he was carried away by a devotion so extraordinary that I was wholly astonished. He dismounted and prostrated himself on the ground to make his customary prayer; then, rising without interrupting his prayers, he began to walk on foot for the remainder of the journey. I wished to urge him to remount, as we were accustomed to do on other occasions; but, without even appearing to pay the slightest attention to what I said, he continued to walk bareheaded, [Col. 1682B] although that day the sun was very fierce and the road difficult, and he did not cease praying in this manner until we reached the monastery gate.

“The abbot, who was absent, having learned that Dom Mabillon was to visit Clairvaux, had ordered that everything be opened to him and that nothing be spared to give him a good reception. His wishes were carried out with all the more pleasure because the monks of the abbey were already filled with esteem for so worthy a guest, whose merit and great reputation they knew in advance. One cannot express the joy and cordiality with which he was received in that celebrated house. He spent several days there in continual [Col. 1682C] exercises of piety, which our researches in the libraries, archives, and treasury could not interrupt. And as there are few monasteries where so many traces of sanctity are found as in this one, everything led him to increase his fervor. Each day he celebrated holy Mass on Saint Bernard’s tomb, using the very chalice which that saint had used in his journeys; he visited all the places which that great man had sanctified by some particular act, and carefully noted every circumstance concerning them. Finally, I do not doubt that it was at this time and in this place that he obtained from God strength to continue composing the *Annals* of our Order down to [Col. 1682D] Saint Bernard’s death. He assured me several times that he asked Our Lord every day for this grace, and that, if He granted it, he would die content. God granted his prayers; for, besides the four volumes printed during his lifetime, he left the continuation wholly prepared for publication down to the time of this great saint’s death.” [Note: [Col. 1681D] *Abridgment of the Life of Dom Jean Mabillon*, by Dom Th. Ruinart, Paris, 1709, p. 293 ff.—The all-too-famous Abbey of Port-Royal sent every year a special person to Clairvaux during the octave of Saint Bernard, to bring a paper signed by the nuns, by which they asked God, through Saint Bernard’s intercession, for certain [Col. 1682D] particular graces. This devotion was called a vow because it was accompanied by promises of prayers. M. Varin (*La vérité sur les Arnauld*, Paris, 1847, vol. II, p. 367), from whom I borrow this detail, says that the Arsenal Library in Paris contains the copy of a vow of this kind. In 1687 the canon of Avallon, Lazare-André [Col. 1683C] Bocquillot, had been asked to carry the nuns’ vow to Saint Bernard’s tomb. Might it not be to some devotion of this kind that one should connect the pilgrimage made to Clairvaux in 1628 by the bishop of Belley, Jean-Pierre Camus, with Messire Sébastien Zamet, bishop and duke of Langres? (*The Spirit of Saint Francis de Sales*, Paris, Gaume, 1840, vol. I, p. CXVIII, 14.)]

The neighboring populations did not fail [Col. 1683A] to flock to Clairvaux on Saint Bernard’s feast day, “on which day,” say the Letters of Charles VII, issued at Chinon on 22 March 1459, “many mercers and merchants were selling goods within the enclosure and precinct of Clairvaux.” [Note: [Col. 1683C] Archives of Aube.—These Letters show that the monks of Clairvaux, their judges, mayors, and officers had the right to take and regulate the pints, half-pints, bushels, weights, balances, and other [Col. 1683D] measures of merchants and other sellers of wine, grain, and other goods sold by weight or measure within the enclosure of the said Clairvaux, whether on Saint Bernard’s day or any other day.—On 20 August 1543, one Martin Moysant, styling himself captain of La Ferté-sur-Aube, armed with a dagger and accompanied by ten to twelve companions armed with swords, and with several inhabitants of La Ferté, set up a game of skittles on the high road along Clairvaux’s wall, repeatedly blaspheming God’s name, and declaring that he had indeed set up the said game, and that whoever would say the contrary, he would maintain had lied. (Archives of Aube; original on paper.)]

In 1668, while contagion was raging in the towns of Reims and Châlons, notices were sent by order of the abbot of Clairvaux to all the towns and [Col. 1684A] villages of the district, announcing that no one would enter the abbey on Saint Bernard’s day or on the following Sunday. This prohibition caused great loss to the innkeeper, who accordingly obtained a reduction of four hundred livres in his lease. This sum, very considerable for the period, shows how great the influx of pilgrims was. [Note: [Col. 1683D] Petition of the innkeeper of Clairvaux. (Archives of Aube.)]

### III. Continuation of the History of the Bodies of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, down to 1793

[Note: [Col. 1683D] In Appendix no. 7, under the title *Sacra lipsana S. Bernardi et S. Malachiae* (“The sacred relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy”), I have assembled various notes concerning the cult rendered to these two saints, objects which belonged to them, and places retaining some memory of them.]

[Col. 1683]

[Col. 1683A] Before determining the place occupied by Saint Bernard’s tomb in the choir of Clairvaux church, I think it useful to reproduce the drawing given of it by the Bollandists. The details are probably not perfectly exact; but [Col. 1683B] one has the mausoleum as a whole, and an engraving, however mediocre it may be, becomes precious when it preserves the sole image of a destroyed monument.

A first sketch was communicated to Father Pien by Dom Candide Briger, a Cistercian of Lilienfeld in Lower Austria, together with a letter written from the general chapter of Cîteaux on 8 May 1738. In it he first spoke of Tristan de Bizet’s silver shrine, which contained only Saint Bernard’s cowl. “The tomb,” he added, “placed behind the high altar and surrounded by marble columns, rises about eight feet. The saint’s statue surmounts it. At its foot is an altar upon which [Col. 1683C] the holy sacrifice is offered. A diptych is fastened by iron chains to one of the walls.

“On the first tablet are read these words:

> HERE RESTS SAINT BERNARD, FIRST ABBOT OF THE HOLY MONASTERY OF CLAIRVAUX.

[Col. 1684A] “On the second is engraved the following:

> Testament of the most blessed Father Bernard, abbot.

> “I leave you three things to observe, which, in the course in which I ran, I remember, so far as I was able, having observed: I trusted my own judgment less than that of another; when injured, I did not seek vengeance upon the one who injured me; I wished to give scandal to no one, and whenever it occurred, I allayed it as best I could. Behold, I leave you charity, humility, and patience.” [Note: [Col. 1684C] *Acta S. Bernardi*, *Gloria Posthuma*, I, nos. 6, 7, 8.—This final clause is absent from Alan’s account; it is replaced by this: “Behold how briefly and how clearly, in these words, the servant of God strove to instil humility, patience, and charity into the minds of his disciples.”—At the beginning one also reads *imitanda* (“to be imitated”) instead of *observanda* (“to be observed”). (*S. Bern. Op.*, Alanus, XXX, 82.)—[Col. 1684D] In Mabillon’s time a small picture hung upon Saint Bernard’s tomb bearing this inscription: “In the year of the Lord 1115, in the month of June, he was sent with his blood brothers and his community to this place, now called Clairvaux; previously, however, it was called Wormwood Valley.” (*S. Bern. Op.*, *Notes on Epistle* XXXI.—*Acta S. Bern.*, § V, 60.) Dom Briger does not mention it.]

At the end of his letter Dom Candide Briger promised Father Pien that the abbot of Clairvaux himself would send him a drawing more exact than his own. Indeed, on 29 July 1738 Dom Jean-Antoine Macuson, master of novices of that abbey, sent him a better one in the name of the Reverend Father Abbot; this is the one which the Bollandists had reduced for insertion in their valuable collection (see above, col. 947).

I wished to follow the history of Saint Bernard’s tomb to its end; now, Monsieur le Comte, I return with pleasure to Saint Malachy’s grave. This glorious primate was enrolled among the saints by Clement III on 6 July 1190. [Note: [Col. 1684C] The bull of canonization of Saint Malachy, issued by Clement III, is dated the day before the Nones of July, in the third year of his pontificate (*S. Bern. Op.*, *Life of Saint Malachy*, *Bull of Canonization*), that is, 6 July 1190, following the *Art de vérifier les dates*. This does not agree with the Clairvaux chronicle published by Father Chifflet (*S. Bern. genus illustre assertum*, p. 89), where one reads: “In the year of the Lord 1192, the canonization of Blessed Malachy.” [Col. 1685C] Manrique dates Clement III’s election to 6 January 1188 (MANRIQUE, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1188, I), which does not disturb the date of Saint Malachy’s canonization. I do not know the source of the error in the Clairvaux chronicle. One may see in Father Pagi (*Critica in Ann. Baronii*, Cologne, 1727, vol. IV, p. 685) how Baronius and Manrique were misled by the Great Belgian Chronicle.]

According to the Irish Annalist cited by Manrique, the elevation [Col. 1685A] of his body was solemnly performed at Clairvaux in 1191. [Note: [Col. 1685D] “That same year (1191) . . . was made festive by the solemn translation of the glorious body of Saint Malachy.” (MANRIQUE, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1191, VII.)—“Annals of Ireland, year 1191. At Clairvaux monastery, the translation of Saint Malachy, bishop of Armagh, was honorably celebrated.” (*Britannia*, by William Camden, London, 1607, folio.)]

It appears that the monks had not waited until then to place his remains honorably. Saint Bernard, by saying over him at his funeral the collect for confessors who were bishops, and by declaring in a vision that he was buried in the tunic of one blessed, had in some fashion canonized his friend. I therefore believe that a tomb was raised for him at the same time as for the holy abbot, so as not to grant to one the honor refused to the other. What is certain is that in 1189 Saint Malachy was no longer in the Chapel of the Blessed Virgin, since at that date we see Henry, former abbot of Clairvaux and cardinal legate of the Apostolic See, buried in the choir between Saint Bernard and Saint [Col. 1685B] Malachy. [Note: [Col. 1685D] “Between Blessed Bernard and Blessed Malachy, he was honorably buried by the bishop of Langres.” (MANRIQUE, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1189, I, 8.—HENRIQUEZ, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, dist. XLI, III.—*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 802.)]

Herbert, writing in 1178 and speaking of Saint Malachy’s appearance to a Clairvaux monk, says that this archbishop was honorably buried in the church, *honorifice tumulatus*. [Note: [Col. 1685D] *S. Bern. genus illustre assertum*. Herbert, *On Miracles*, book I, IV.] Would this expression, emphatic in medieval Latin, not designate something more than a simple tomb in the Chapel of the Blessed Virgin? For the stone arch, even supposing it marked a special construction, does not suggest great magnificence and does not justify Herbert’s terms. The bodies of the two saints would thus, from those distant times, have shared a common destiny. Were their shrines of equal beauty? This I cannot affirm for want of documents; it is, however, very probable [Col. 1685C] that there was no very appreciable difference between them. An altar stood upon each tomb, and the Benedictines, in their *Literary Journey*, report that they had the honor of celebrating Mass there. [Note: [Col. 1685D] *Voyage littéraire*, vol. I, p. 98 ff.—According to the account published in the *Annales archéologiques*, [Col. 1686C] Saint Bernard’s tomb and Saint Malachy’s would have been similar.—The following passage, taken from the history of the translation of Saint Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury, written in the first half of the thirteenth century, also seems to suggest the same thing: “Although the bodies . . . of the blessed confessors Malachy [Col. 1686D] and Bernard the abbot, the Great Father of the Cistercian Order, are buried with reverence and honor in marble mausoleums . . . they are nevertheless without any gold or precious stone.” (*Thes. nov. anecdot.*, Paris, 1717, vol. III, col. 1868.)]

Saint Malachy’s canonization confirmed the veneration he enjoyed; but it found him already in possession of a glorious burial place. It carried his cult outside the narrow enclosure of an abbey [Col. 1686A] and brought it as far as his distant homeland, which thrilled with joy in reckoning one more saint among its own. The Cistercian monasteries of Ireland then requested relics of him who had founded them; and through Matthew, archbishop of Cashel, relics were sent to them in 1194 and received with the greatest honors. [Note: [Col. 1686D] Manrique, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1194, II.—*Annals of Ireland*, year 1194.—“The relics of Saint Malachy, bishop, were brought from Clairvaux into Ireland and received with the greatest honor at Mellifont monastery and the other monasteries of the Cistercian Order.” (*Britannia*, by G. Camden.)]

The treasury of Clairvaux preserved separated portions of Saint Malachy’s bones. The sacristy inventory drawn up in 1504, fol. 11r, shows that a bone from his arm was enclosed in a silver arm weighing seven and a half marks, adorned with precious stones and with a ring attached by silver chains. This fine reliquary had been given by Jean d’Aizanville, whose [Col. 1686B] devotion to the remains of the saints we know. The inventory of 1640 mentions Saint Malachy at fols. 6r, 11v, and 81v. The silver arm is described at fol. 18r. At fols. 19v and 20r one reads: “From the dust of the head of Blessed Malachy, primate of Ireland.” The Cîteaux calendar printed at Dijon marks, on 17 May: “Translation of Saint Malachy to Avignon.” But, as we have seen for Saint Bernard, this can concern only fragments, not the whole body.

Toward the end of the thirteenth century we encounter an illustrious testimony of devotion to Saint Malachy. Robert Bruce, who contested the crown of Scotland with John Balliol, endowed a splendid lamp before his tomb. [Note: [Col. 1686D] Appendix, no. 9.] Finally, in 1323 the general chapter of Cîteaux decreed that his feast should be celebrated [Col. 1686C] solemnly throughout the entire Order. [Note: [Col. 1686D] “The Chapter decrees that the solemnity of Blessed Malachy, bishop and confessor, whose body rests in Clairvaux church, shall be celebrated throughout the whole Order with fitting devotion, with two Masses and a responsory at Vespers.” (*Thes. nov. Anecd.*, vol. IV, *Statutes of the General Chapter*, year 1323, col. 1513, no. 1.)]

I would leave a very great gap in these investigations, Monsieur le Comte, if I did not attempt to determine the place occupied in the choir of the church of Clairvaux by the tombs of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy. Two precious documents make it possible to do so exactly. The first is a plan of the church, engraved in the three views of the abbey of Clairvaux drawn in 1708 by Dom [Col. 1687A] Milley, prior of Mores [Note: [Col. 1687C] They may be consulted in the Print Room of the Imperial Library.—See Appendix, no. 10.]; the second is a loose sheet written in Dom Le Boullenger’s hand, on which he indicated the names of the chapels and the position of the burials [Note: [Col. 1687C] This document is in the hands of M. Harmand, librarian of the city of Troyes. See Appendix, no. 11.]. Nine chapels radiated around the choir; yet, on Dom Milley’s plan, the first on the epistle side has no altar marked and appears to be merely a passage communicating with the small cloister. Since Dom Le Boullenger indicated it explicitly, one may conclude that he copied a note earlier than 1708. It would take too long to follow him step by step in enumerating the chapels, and in any case I should merely reproduce what is found in the appendix. I shall recall only that in the fifth [Note: [Col. 1687C] I count nine chapels, as Dom Le Boullenger does.], beginning from the epistle side, [Col. 1687B] rested the Blessed Aleth. Her tomb stood on the left, set into the wall beneath a stone arcade and surmounted by her statue, which Jean de Chalon (fortieth abbot of Clairvaux) had caused to be sculpted in 1508. I now come to the choir, taking care to verify Dom Le Boullenger’s work by means of the Book of Burials published by Henriquez.

Opposite the third chapel, on the epistle side, there stood first the tomb of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus, whose bodies had been given in 1227 by Cardinal Conrad, bishop of Porto, where they had been preserved for centuries. He had added the body of a fourth, unknown martyr [Note: [Col. 1687C] Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. IV, year 1227, §1.]. Beside them rested four of the eleven [Col. 1687C] thousand virgins: the Blessed Walta, Cristantia, Petronella, and Domicella; the heads of two unknown saints; and relics of several others [Note: [Col. 1687D] See *Voyage littéraire*, vol. I, p. 98 ff.—Henriquez, *Fasciculus Sanctorum Ordinis Cisterciensis*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, II.]. Going around the choir, one first encountered the tomb of Cardinal Jean de Buxières, thirty-second abbot of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1687D] “He lies between Saint Bernard and the Blessed Martyrs.” Henriquez, ibid.]. Then came that of Saint Bernard, situated behind the high altar [Note: [Col. 1687D] Henriquez, ibid.—*Acta S. Bernardi*, *Gloria Posthuma*, I, no. 7.—See *Voyage littéraire*, ibid.]. Beside it, still going around the choir and returning toward the gospel side, was buried Cardinal [Col. 1688A] Henry, seventh abbot of Clairvaux, to whom Saint Bernard owed the marble monument enclosing his precious remains [Note: [Col. 1687D] Henriquez, ibid.—Manuscript catalogue of the Abbots, fol. 8r.—*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 802.]. Then came Saint Malachy [Note: [Col. 1687D] “Between the tombs of the holy champions of Christ, Bernard and Malachy, lies Lord Henry of blessed memory.” Henriquez, ibid., III. See *Voyage littéraire*, ibid.]. To his left—that is, one must imagine the observer standing before and looking toward the high altar—lay Cardinal James of Piacenza, formerly a monk of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1687D] “Beside Blessed Malachy in the presbytery, namely on his left, lies Lord James of Piacenza of blessed memory.” Henriquez, ibid.]. Very near, proceeding down toward the gospel side, one came upon the handsome black-marble tomb of Cardinal Conrad, eleventh abbot of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1687D] “In the same presbytery, beside the aforesaid Lord Cardinal James, to the left of the lesser altar, lies Lord Conrad of blessed memory.” Henriquez, ibid.—*Minoris* [Col. 1688D] is evidently a printing error, for, since Conrad’s tomb was situated in the choir, its position can refer only to the high altar. Moreover, the manuscript Catalogue of the Abbots, fol. 11r, expressly says: “His sacred relics were deposited on the left side of the high altar, under a most beautiful mausoleum of black marble.” [Col. 1688D] In the copy of *Gallia Christiana* belonging to the public library of Troyes, and apparently deriving from Clairvaux, vol. IV, cols. 991–992, at the end of the article “Conradus” among the Abbots of Cîteaux, a handwritten marginal note reads: “Near James of Piacenza, beneath a black marble tomb.”], who had enriched the abbey with numerous relics (Appendix, no. 12). Finally, at the foot of the high altar on the left, against the gospel lectern, was buried Jean de Blanchemain, archbishop of Lyons, who left his archbishopric to retire to Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1688D] “Under the step of the high altar, on the left side, directly opposite the gospel pulpit.” HENRIQUEZ, ibid., IV. See *Voyage littéraire*, ibid.].

[Col. 1688B] Dom Joseph Méglinger indicates very precisely the position of the tombs of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus, of Saint Bernard, and of Saint Malachy. “Behind the high altar,” he says, “(which is joined to no wall), are three altars: that of Saint Bernard in the middle; on the right-hand side, that of Saint Malachy; and beyond it lie the tombs of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus. Those same tombs, insofar as they project beyond their wall, are covered by another vault, and provide room to pass through and to venerate them devoutly on one’s knees in private. Outside this arch, several other chapels—the chapels radiating around the choir—likewise built with vaulted work and celebrated for their sacred remains, enclose the church . . . . The time remaining from the divine office [Col. 1688C] I spent in the outer part which runs around behind the altars, where are the three tombs mentioned above, made of red marble, alabaster, or gypsum. White kneeling platforms are so conveniently constructed around the tombs that one, prostrate on one’s knees, can conceal oneself among them and devote oneself to piety apart from the gaze of passers-by [Note: [Col. 1688D] *Iter Cisterciense*, pp. 152 and 156.—Dom Joseph Méglinger relates that, when one bent down beside the tomb of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus, one heard something like the sound of a sea agitated by winds. He assured himself from the Reverend Father Vicar-General that his imagination had not deceived him, and that this extraordinary sound had not ceased to be heard since the bodies of the holy martyrs had rested at Clairvaux (*ibid.*, p. 157).].”

This description confirms the details of the account published in the *Annales archéologiques*: [Col. 1689A] “Behind the high altar there are three handsome and rich alabaster altars, of which the middle one is the altar of My Lord Saint Bernard . . . The said altar is covered by a stone tabernacle with four pillars. The first two stand beside the said altar and serve as columns; the other two, behind that altar, form the covering of the said tabernacle over the altar, and likewise over the vessel in which Saint Bernard’s bones lie, behind the said altar. That vessel is of stone, its cover porphyry-coloured; and on either side of the said vessel or shrine one may kneel to greet the saint, saying the prayer which appears on small tablets on each side.”

The old church of Clairvaux remained in its [Col. 1689B] original state until Dom Robert Gassot du Défens, forty-eighth abbot (1718–1740), altered it from top to bottom under the pretext of beautifying it (Appendix, no. 13). No one lamented the alteration of a monument begun by Saint Bernard; on the contrary, Dom Gassot received very great praise for the zeal with which he adorned the house of the Lord. “He magnificently decorated the house of God,” says the manuscript catalogue of the abbots [Note: [Col. 1689C] Manuscript catalogue, fol. 37r.]. Father Pien adds, in dedicating his *Acta S. Bernardi* to him: “That sacred church which you have restored and adorned will never fail to bear witness to the great affection you have for the house of God” [Note: [Col. 1689C] *Acta S. Bernardi*, dedicatory epistle.]. Yet part of the lower end of the church had been cut away to construct the court [Col. 1689C] of the Abbatial residence [Note: [Col. 1689C] “In his time the hall before the doors of the church was constructed.” Manuscript catalogue, fol. 37r.]. The chapels radiating around the choir had been removed, and the whole structure completely transformed [Note: [Col. 1689C] A plan drawn in 1808 by M. Gilbert, architect of civil buildings at the Ministry of the Interior, while the church rebuilt by Dom Gassot still existed, gives an exact idea of the [Col. 1689D] mutilations it underwent. M. Arnaud, in the *Archaeological and Picturesque Journey through the Department of the Aube*, reproduced, without saying so, the plan of the old church after Dom Milley and that of the rebuilt church after M. Gilbert. It is regrettable that the author of this interesting work devoted only some forty lines to describing Clairvaux Abbey.].

Were the burials in the choir respected? I believe that this may be established, at least for Saint Bernard. For a contract for the choir screen, made in 1739 [Note: [Col. 1689D] Archives of the Aube.], shows that the major [Col. 1690A] construction work had been completed. At that time Saint Bernard’s tomb had not been touched, since the drawing representing it, reproduced by the Bollandists, had been sent to them by Dom Gassot himself in 1738, and the accompanying letter placed it behind the high altar, as formerly. Since the arrangement of the choir had not been seriously altered, nothing made the tombs’ removal necessary. Thus we shall see below that the Revolution found them in their old positions.

As for the burials in the chapels, I do not know what became of them. No doubt they were placed elsewhere. One of them in particular greatly interested me—the burial of the Blessed Aleth—and I should have wished to know its fate; but all the documents I consulted remained silent concerning it.

Further proof that Saint Bernard’s tomb had not been attacked by an incomprehensible vandalism is that it eventually became displeasing. Its architecture was probably thought too old-fashioned, and it was decided to remake it in the modern style [Note: [Col. 1689D] From the middle of the seventeenth century, the monks of Clairvaux were afflicted by the dangerous mania of consulting the variable tastes of fashion in order to alter the instruments of worship, which ought to partake of the immutability of faith.
