In the inventory of 1640, fol. 23v, under chalices, I find four marginal notes, very probably written in 1658, stating that the patens “have been changed to suit the fashion.” Some years earlier, Dom Claude Largentier, forty-fifth abbot, had adorned the walls [Col. 1690C] of his church with a dazzlingly white and exceptionally durable wash: “He caused the church to be whitewashed with a most beautiful, almost indelible crystalline whiteness.” (*Catalogue manuscrit des Abbés*, fol. 34r.)]. It was M. Rocourt, the last abbot of Clairvaux, who conceived this regrettable design [Note: [Col. 1690C] Matthieu manuscript, IX, 266: “Clairvaux is daily embellished by the good taste of M. the abbot, who has just enlarged its enclosure by nine arpents . . . At present (1788) the library, novitiate, bakery, together with their dependent mills and granaries, are being rebuilt from new. M. the abbot [Rocourt] proposes to undertake [for the church] very considerable expenditures: for a superb mausoleum intended to contain Saint Bernard’s body; for erecting the chapels of the apse; paving the choir in marble; making a new sacristy; raising a tower for the bells; and adorning the sanctuary with iron grilles . . .”]. In 1782 he contracted with Guyard, sculptor to the Infant Duke of Parma, by which that skilled artist [Note: [Col. 1690D] *Biographie universelle*, Michaud edition.] undertook to construct a white-marble mausoleum [Note: [Col. 1690D] Extract from the record of the inventory made at Clairvaux Abbey by the municipal officers of that place, 24 May 1790. (Archives of the Aube).] for sixty thousand livres [Note: [Col. 1690D] Second inventory of Clairvaux, 19 October 1790, drawn up by delegated administrators of the district of Bar-sur-Aube. (Archives of the Aube).]. This monument was to have been executed on a [Col. 1690C] very large scale, since a rough-hewn figure of Charity—the only one which reached Clairvaux—was nine feet high. Perhaps a statue of Saint Bernard was intended to surmount it, for the abbey accounts mention bronze bought at Bar-sur-Aube for the model of the saint made by Guyard [Note: [Col. 1690D] Statement of the expenses of Clairvaux Abbey, 1783, p. 34. (Archives of the Aube).]. The artist died long before completing his undertaking, and M. Rocourt had the marbles intended for the mausoleum brought back to France. The greater part was deposited at Lyons, where it remained until the Revolution. When it broke out, an Italian sculptor, Barratta, was to come to Clairvaux to complete Guyard’s work. The rough figure of Charity, the only piece sent to the abbey, remained crated beneath the church portal until 1793 [Note: [Col. 1691B] Second inventory of Clairvaux, 19 October 1790.].

The moment approaches, Monsieur le Comte, when we shall see Saint Bernard’s inheritance pass into foreign hands. But before recounting this lamentable catastrophe, it will be useful to go somewhat back and trace the bones of Saint Bernard’s first companions through their various translations.

In 1148, on 2 November, they were brought from the cemetery [Col. 1691B] of the first abbey in order to be buried in a new cemetery, where a stone monument adorned with columns and arches had been built, not far from the walls of the church choir, to receive them. They were placed on its right-hand side, together with the remains of Saint Bernard’s father, brothers, and an uncle; the left-hand side was reserved for, and successively received, monks, lay brothers, and novices who died during the holy abbot’s lifetime [Note: [Col. 1691B] “Under the structure opposite the church, in the cemetery of the abbots, built with stone columns and arches . . . on the right side are contained”—the present tense of this verb [Col. 1691C] shows that the Book of Burials consists of successive additions, since the same epitaph speaks of the translation of the bodies to the chapel of the counts of Flanders—“the bones . . . of the father and brothers of our Blessed Father Bernard . . . and . . . of monks, etc., who died in the old abbey . . .; on the left side, however, are contained the bones of monks, etc. . . . who died in this place while Blessed Bernard was still living.” (HENRIQUEZ, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, V, Epitaph of Blessed Tescelin.—MANRIQUE, *Annales Cistercienses*, year 1148.—*Menologium Cisterciense*, 2 November.)].

In 1269 these venerable bodies, except those of Saint Bernard’s relatives, [Col. 1692A] who remained in their monument [Note: [Col. 1691C] The testimony of Dom Joseph Méglinger and that of the Benedictines leave no doubt on this point. “Outside [the church] . . . rises a mausoleum beneath which is buried the most devout father of Saint Bernard . . . together with two of Bernard’s brothers, Bartholomew and Gerard.” *Iter Cisterciense*, p. 181.—“Behind the apse of the church is the cemetery of foreign abbots who died at Clairvaux, in which one sees [Col. 1691D] against the church the tombs of Saint Bernard’s brothers.”—*Voyage littéraire*, 1717, p. 99. The account published in the *Annales archéologiques* agrees with these testimonies. Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, VI, Epitaph of Blessed Tescelin.—*Menologium Cisterciense*, 12 August.—Henriquez (*Menologium Cisterciense*, 9 December) observes that, apparently, among Saint Bernard’s brothers buried at Clairvaux there were only Andrew and Gerard. Guy died at Pontigny in 1136 and was buried there, in accordance with Saint Bernard’s prediction. Because he did not wish to permit a sick brother in Normandy to return to Clairvaux so that he might die in “his little nest” (*in nidulo suo*), the holy abbot foretold to him that he himself would not rest in the holy valley. (*Acta S. Bernardi*, §LIX, year 1136.—*Bibliotheca Patrum*, *Exordium magnum Cisterciense*, Distinction II, 10.—MANRIQUE, *Annales Cistercienses*, year 1136, §111.—*S. Bernardi genus illustratum assertum*, Herbert, *De miraculis*, II, XI.) Bartholomew died in 1144 [Col. 1692B] as abbot of La Ferté (*Acta S. Bernardi*, §LIX, year 1144; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 1022, makes Bartholomew die in 1160), where, according to Barnabas de Montalvo cited by Henriquez, his remains rest (*ibid.*). Yet Jongelinus (*Notitia Abbatum Ordinis Cisterciensis*, Cologne [Col. 1692C] Agrippina, 1640, folio) does not mention him in the section on burials of La Ferté Abbey. Nivard, Tescelin’s youngest son, founded the abbey of Spina in Spain in 1147 (*Acta S. Bernardi*, §XLIV, 471; §LIX, year 1147). Henriquez (*ibid.*) reports that in his own time this monastery still boasted of possessing its founder’s body; but Manrique (*Annales Cistercienses*, year 1147, XVIII) admits: “Nivard’s arrival in Spain is more certain than his end.” Only Bartholomew and Gerard are mentioned in Dom Joseph Méglinger’s journey cited in the preceding note.], were raised and transferred with great solemnity to a crypt beneath the high altar of the chapel of the counts of Flanders (Appendix, no. 14).

“It is near the cemetery of the abbots,” say the Benedictines in their *Literary Journey*. “There one sees the tombs of Philip, count of Flanders, and Countess Matilda, his wife [Note: [Col. 1692C] Agnes, second wife of Thibaut IV, count of Champagne, was also buried there. (*Art de vérifier les dates*.—HENRIQUEZ, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, VI.)—*Voyage littéraire*, vol. I, p. 98.]; beneath the altar of this chapel is a fine vaulted crypt in which are arranged the bones of the religious who lived in Saint Bernard’s time. They are venerated as saints, for the blessed abbot had received a revelation that all the religious then living at Clairvaux would be saved. Before [Col. 1692B] this crypt one reads the following verses:

> Here lies in a vault Bernard’s first offspring,  
> Whose lofty mind possesses the heavenly dwellings above.  
> This place is holy: venerating such great tokens,  
> Enter as a suppliant; behold, but do not steal the bones.

And these:

> Bernard’s first offspring, which cultivated this valley,  
> Lies here. If, entering here, you steal bones, you perish.

[Note: [Col. 1692C] “Even today,” says Mabillon, “at Clairvaux one sees the bones of those first holy monks in an underground chapel, arranged wholly for devotion.” [Col. 1692D] (*S. Bernardi Opera*, *Sermon on the Death of Saint Malachy*, sermon I.) Veneration for the bones enclosed in the crypt of the chapel of the counts of Flanders endured until a period quite close to our own. On 24 September 1672, the prior of Clairvaux took from this crypt a whole head, a skull, and two arms, which were given to Mgr de Gondrin, archbishop of Sens, by order of the abbot. (*Registrum secretariatus Reverendissimi in Christo Patris ac Domini Petri, XLVI Claraevallis abbatis, pro anno MDCLXXII*, 1 folio volume—Public Library of Troyes, manuscript no. 14, p. 71.)—See, in the Archives of the Aube, holdings of the Abbey of Notre-Dame-aux-Nonnains, bundle 381, an authentication of relics of the first religious of Clairvaux.—Dom Joseph Méglinger (*Iter Cisterciense*, p. 196 ff.) tells the story of a young lady in the Duchess of Lorraine’s retinue who was suddenly cured, by touching one bone [Col. 1693D] of these holy monks, of a long-standing toothache resistant to every remedy; but she was unable to leave the chapel so long as she retained the relic, which she very much wished to take away with her.].”

As the chapel threatened to collapse, the religious obtained, by decree of the Council of 5 June 1775, permission to transfer it [Col. 1693A] to the church of Clairvaux, together with the bodies it contained.

On 13 November of the same year, the bones of Saint Bernard’s first disciples were removed and placed in a vault made opposite the chapel of All Saints. On the 29th, the remains of the count of Flanders, Matilda, and Agnes were placed in newly built tombs in Saint Michael’s Chapel, with coats of arms and inscriptions [Note: [Col. 1693D] Petition of the religious (copy).—Records of exhumation (Archives of the Aube).—I said above that the bodies of Saint Bernard’s relatives were not transferred to the chapel of the counts of Flanders. Indeed, according to the very record of exhumation (13 November 1775), only “the bones of a quantity of Saint Bernard’s disciples” were raised.—One of the chief reasons why the chapel of the counts of Flanders was not restored where it had been built was that it would have rendered “the prospect defective and obstructed the arrangement of the new buildings” (Petition [Col. 1694D] of the religious, 1775).—The inflexible law of alignment had already been discovered.].

Finally, after six centuries of existence, on 15 January 1792, at ten in the morning, in the district hall of Bar-sur-Aube, the former Abbey of Clairvaux was put up for auction at an opening price of 137,875 livres, 8 sous, and 7 deniers. Since no one came forward to bid, on 10 February following, at the same hour and place, it was awarded, when the candles were extinguished, to Pierre-Claude Cauzon, architect residing at Bar-sur-Aube, for 337,500 livres. All furniture, bells, pictures, and ornaments used for worship, the tombs and reliquaries, and the block of marble deposited beneath the portal were expressly reserved. The purchaser could make no demolition or alteration in the church without giving the district administration two months’ notice [Note: [Col. 1694D] Sale of national property, no. 868, District of Bar-sur-Aube. (Archives of the Aube.)]. He established a glassworks there, and, as the tombs greatly impeded his operations, he [Col. 1693C] addressed the following letter, dated 23 April 1793, to the administrators of the directory of the Aube:

> “Citizens, there exist in the church of the former Abbey of Clairvaux and in the place forming the cemetery [Note: [Col. 1694D] These words designate the choir.], tombs in the form of mausoleums constructed of stone, which, at the sale of the property in February 1791 [Note: [Col. 1694D] This is plainly an error. Besides, errors of this kind are not rare in the documents left to us by the Revolution. Disorder was everywhere.], were reserved by the record of adjudication.
>
> “The purchaser of this property, using the buildings, has just established a glassworks in the church. Furnaces built at very little distance from these tombs have already been in operation for two months, and the purchaser requests that these tombs be removed because they seriously [Col. 1693D] hinder his work by obstructing passage. [Col. 1694A] To this decisive reason is joined another, that of decency. It would therefore be urgent and appropriate to have these tombs opened and examined; and, should they contain bones or relics, to order their transfer by the parish priest within whose bounds the said property lies.
>
> “There still exists in the church forecourt a great timber case containing a colossal figure in white marble, roughly carved by Viard [Note: [Col. 1694D] Guyard.], a French sculptor who died at Rome. This figure too was reserved at the sale. Intended to represent Charity, it now possesses merit only in the intrinsic value of its marble, unless some celebrated artist might [Col. 1694B] wish (sic) to finish the monument. The purchaser of the property likewise requests removal of this block of marble, which interferes with his enjoyment.
>
> “The architect observes that demolition and removal of the tombs will entail no expense for the administration, because the stone and certain parts of black marble of which they are composed will yield a value approximately equal to the costs to be incurred.” [Note: [Col. 1694D] Archives of the Aube.]

Three days after receiving this letter, the directory issued an order directing that all the bones be buried in the parish cemetery. The departmental architect wrote a second time to report on his mission; I do not know the date, but it was at a very close interval. I quote this [Col. 1694C] letter verbatim:

> “To the citizen administrators constituting the directory of the Department of the Aube.
>
> “The architect of the Department of the Aube has the honour to state that, in execution of your order of 26 April last [Note: [Col. 1694D] This order does not exist in the registers of deliberations of the directory of the Department of the Aube; it was probably issued on a loose sheet. A great many such documents, not copied into the registers, are found in the Archives of the Aube.], he went to the former Abbey of Clairvaux in order to open the tombs and mausoleums there. By the opening which he caused to be made of these tombs, he found enclosed within them relics of various persons venerated as saints, such as Saint Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux; Saint Malachy; Saint Eutropius; and others, according to the inscriptions.
>
> “He thought it his duty to respect public opinion by not having the bones of these persons [Col. 1694D] buried in the parish cemetery, as [Col. 1695A] your order directs; he had them deposited in a separate room (sic) of the property, awaiting your further order on this matter.
>
> “From the conference which he held with the citizen parish priest of Ville, in whose parish the property of Clairvaux lies, it appears that the inhabitants would wish to possess in reliquaries the remains of these great men, for whom their veneration is extreme and perhaps dangerous to oppose. To satisfy it, it would be necessary to have three wooden cases in the form of shrines, in which to place the bones contained in the lead cases, and they would transfer them to their church.
>
> “Among the mausoleums and other tombs, the architect [Col. 1695B] found several bones of archbishops, bishops, or abbots, which he had gathered into baskets and which can be buried in the parish cemetery. But a considerable collection of bones, of more than three cubic toises, in a sepulchral chapel [Note: [Col. 1695D] These bones undoubtedly came from the crypt of the chapel of the counts of Flanders.], has also suspended every transfer and burial of bones until you shall have been pleased to decide upon this further matter.
>
> “The architect has also, in accordance with your order, had the marbles and stones resulting from demolition of the tombs and mausoleums placed in one location. It would be necessary to have the administration of the district of Bar-sur-Aube proceed with the sale of these remains, in order to prevent their deterioration [Col. 1695C] and dispersal, and also so that the proceeds may be applied to the costs of demolition and transfer.” [Note: [Col. 1695D] Archives of the Aube.]

I must insert here, Monsieur le Comte, the note drawn up by a former administrator of the directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube, M. Delaine, who was present at the opening of the abbey tombs. You were kind enough to send me a copy of this document, which I knew in 1845 but whose authenticity I had then been unable to establish.

M. Delaine’s Note.

> “In 1793, while serving as an administrator of the directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube, I attended in that capacity, with three of my colleagues now [Col. 1695D] deceased, the opening of the tombs in the church of Clairvaux Abbey, where a window-glass manufactory was about to be established.
>
> [Col. 1696A] That of Saint Bernard contained, beneath a lead coffin, bones forming the skeleton of a man whose head was missing. They were wrapped in a shroud of fine linen, little damaged, which was covered with a piece of fabric woven of silk and wool.
>
> Another—that of Saint Malachy—likewise contained beneath a lead coffin bones forming the complete skeleton of a man who had all his teeth.
>
> In these marble tombs there were, on strips of parchment, several inscriptions in Gothic script, illegible.
>
> I had taken away fragments of Saint Bernard’s shroud and of the cloth which covered it, [Col. 1696B] as well as bones detached from his hands, and one tooth of Saint Malachy.
>
> I kept them until 1814, when they were lost as a result of the war.
>
> There remains to me only a fragment of the piece of fabric, six centimetres long and four centimetres wide, different on its two sides: the ground of one is azure blue, with a design representing a golden-yellow lion; that of the other is golden yellow, with the lion blue.
>
> After the opening of the tombs, the bones were, through the care of the administration, reverently transferred to the cemetery of the parish of Ville-sous-l’Afferté [sic], on which Clairvaux depends [Note: [Col. 1695D] In the secretariat of the Bishopric of Troyes there is a very interesting letter, written on 6 September 1844 by Abbé Jacquinot, former parish priest of Ville-sous-La-Ferté. It shows that this clergyman put the following question to M. Delaine: “You say that the bones were deposited in the cemetery at Ville, whereas we have three hundred witnesses who attest that they were brought to the church, deposited in the choir, then enclosed in the sacristy, and [Col. 1696D] that they were never buried in the cemetery?”—“I know,” he said, “that such was the directory’s order; I was not present at the transfer. We had divided the work among my colleagues; it was one of them who was to attend.”].

[Col. 1696C] We, the undersigned, certify that the foregoing account originates from M. Delaine, our father, former justice of the peace for the canton of Brienne-le-Château, who died at Dienville on 28 February 1850, at the age of eighty-four years and five months; that he wrote it in his own hand; and that, during his lifetime, he recounted to us several times the facts which it contains.

Dienville, this . . . day of March 1850.

Signed: DELAINE the elder, honorary notary; DELAINE, doctor of medicine; DELAINE, advocate before the Court of Appeal of Paris; Alexandre DELAINE, doctor of medicine [Note: [Col. 1696D] The undersigned, former Peer of France and one of the forty members of the French Academy, certifies that the original of the foregoing account is in his possession, together with a fragment of the silk-and-wool fabric there very exactly described. Done at La Roche-en-Breny (Côte-d’Or), 19 November 1854. Signed: Charles, Count DE MONTALEMBERT.].

On 8 May 1793, the administrators of the directory of the Department of the Aube issued a new order, the principal articles of which I reproduce:

[Col. 1696D] “The Directory authorizes the Directory of Bar-sur-Aube to distribute the relics and bones of Saint Bernard, Saint Malachy, Saint Eutropius, and others, found in the former abbey of Clairvaux, [Col. 1697A] among the inhabitants of the parishes of Ville-sous-La-Ferté, Longchamps, and other neighboring places, so that the said relics may be transferred to the churches of those parishes, at the expense of the churchwardens, who shall be bound to provide wooden shrines to contain the bones which the inhabitants of the said places may wish to have in their churches.

“Likewise authorizes the Directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube to have the other bones found in various mausoleums and tombs of the former abbey of Clairvaux buried on the spot, in order to avoid expense.

“Orders that the marble and stones resulting from the demolition of the above-mentioned tombs and mausoleums, together with a block of white marble representing [Col. 1697B] a roughly sketched figure, and the timber frame containing the said block of marble beneath the porch of the former church of Clairvaux, shall immediately be sold on the spot, for the benefit of the [Col. 1698A] Republic, by the Directory and through the diligence of the procurator-syndic of the district of Bar-sur-Aube.

“Done in public session of the Directory, at Troyes, Wednesday, 8 May 1793, Year II of the French Republic, in the afternoon [Note: [Col. 1697D] Archives of Aube].”

Here, Count, ends the information supplied by official acts and authentic documents. It is common knowledge that bones taken from the church of Clairvaux were transferred to that of Ville-sous-La-Ferté; but was their exhumation carried out with the necessary precautions to prevent their being confused? We have no duly drawn-up record to tell us so. It is not for me to collect oral traditions concerning their translation, and those vague [Col. 1698B] recollections which a preoccupied mind often entrusts to an unfaithful memory. When documents are lacking, the historian remains silent, leaving an official inquiry to discover the truth.

## IV. Visit to Ville-sous-La-Ferté.—Researches concerning the first site of Clairvaux Abbey

[Col. 1697]

[Col. 1697B] Ville-sous-La-Ferté lies about three kilometres from Clairvaux. Formerly in the diocese of Langres, this commune was incorporated into that of Troyes at the time of the Concordat. The church of this village, built less than a hundred years [Col. 1697C] ago, is remarkable for an arrangement conformable to Christian requirements; it is oriented eastward and of an elegant simplicity. It has only three altars: that of the choir, and two others placed opposite the side aisles. All three come from Clairvaux. The side altars are adorned with twisted columns and rather finely executed wood-carving. One of them, on the north side, bears a shield with the arms of Saint Bernard [Note: [Col. 1697D] This shield is oval and accompanied by a crozier set upright. It is of . . . , with a chequered bend of . . . , of two rows.—“Saint Bernard, the honour of our Burgundy,” says Paillot, “bore sable, a bend chequered gold and red in two rows” (*La vraie et parfaite science des armoiries*, folio, Dijon, 1660). According to Jongelinus (*Notitia Abbatum O. C.*, Cologne, 1640), the bend was chequered silver and red. Fr. Chifflet (*S. Bernardi genus illustratum assertum*, p. 667 ff.) thinks that these [Col. 1698D] arms belonged to Count Hugh, founder of Clairvaux Abbey. “From this Chifflet infers that Hugh’s emblem was that chequered diagonal band attached to the buildings of Clairvaux, which not a few suppose to be Saint Bernard’s family coat of arms, but wrongly,” says Fr. Mabillon (*Notes on St Bernard*, on Epistle XXXI, 24). From the notes of Dom Guyton, I give in Appendix no. 7 references to several seals bearing Saint Bernard’s arms.].

The choir altar is of marble; above it rises a tabernacle accompanied by very attractive little statues. Paneling with pilasters closes off the choir, leaving between it and the east end of the church space for a small sacristy. Three pictures rest at right angles upon the paneling. The central one represents Our Lord [Col. 1697D] on the cross; it is very mediocre. On either side are full-length, life-size portraits of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy. They are precious canvases, which many museums might envy the modest church that contains them; [Col. 1698B] though executed by the same hand, they are not of equal merit.

Saint Malachy wears his pontifical vestments, with the mitre upon his head; his cope, of very great [Col. 1698C] richness, has ample folds; the head is handsome, but seems fancifully painted. The portrait of Saint Bernard is placed on the Gospel side: I do not think there exists a more magnificent one. The saint stands with his head slightly inclined toward his left shoulder; with his left hand he supports the church of Clairvaux; with his right he holds a Gothic crozier of exquisite workmanship. In the background of the picture a broad window opens, beside which two monks appear to converse; and the harmonious lines and bluish hues of the clear valley recede to the horizon.

The architectural details indicate the seventeenth century; without them one might take Saint Bernard’s portrait for much older. The artist was [Col. 1698D] plainly inspired by old traditions; perhaps he copied some ancient work preserved in the abbey. Every accessory has been reproduced from nature. The church supported by Saint Bernard displays an east end radiating with chapels; [Col. 1699A] a slender spire rises above it [Note: [Col. 1699D] This is wholly in conformity with a charming little etching by Israël Silvestre, representing a view of the church of Clairvaux Abbey in Burgundy.]. The crozier was supplied from the treasury of Clairvaux. The costumes were not chosen without purpose. Saint Bernard wears choir dress; his mantle, slightly raised in front, reveals the lower part of a black scapular. Of the two monks placed by the window, one represents a lay brother in his brown garments; the other is a professed monk, wearing a black scapular over a white tunic.

This is indeed the great abbot as Geoffrey, his scribe, depicts him: “A grace more spiritual than bodily appeared in Saint Bernard. A heavenly brightness shone upon his face; the purity of angels and the simplicity of the dove beamed from his eyes. The beauty of [Col. 1699B] the inner man was so great in him that it showed outwardly and spread over the outer man. His thinness was extreme; his skin was of extraordinary delicacy; his cheeks were slightly coloured . . . and his hair blond, half turning white . . . . His stature rose somewhat above the average” [Note: [Col. 1699D] *Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, I, 1.].

These fine canvases are in very poor condition. One must earnestly wish that a skilful hand should restore them [Note: [Col. 1699D] The parish priest of Ville fully knows the value of the two pictures; and the treasures of his church could not be in better hands than his.], and, above all, that a talented engraver should save them from oblivion. The portrait of Saint Bernard would make a remarkable plate; everything in it is arranged to produce a great effect; all is calm and solemn; the great figure of Saint Bernard dominates majestically; the light is perfectly [Col. 1699C] distributed; a discerning engraver would have only to copy it.

I gladly linger over this description, Count. I seem still to see that image, in which Saint Bernard appeared to me to live again, and from which I could not turn my eyes.

Yet treasures of higher value draw the Christian traveller into the little sacristy of which we have spoken. There, in an old chest which formerly served as a treasury, rest the bones taken from the church of Clairvaux and transferred in 1793 to that of Ville-sous-La-Ferté. Before 1836 or 1837, they were in the baskets used for their transfer; afterwards they were [Col. 1699D] thrown together in disorder into this worm-eaten chest, and the baskets were burned. This wooden chest, mounted on four feet and square in shape, is one metre and three centimetres long, sixty-eight centimetres [Col. 1700A] wide, and thirty-one centimetres deep; it is locked with a key. The bones fill it halfway. Among them one notices especially four skulls; a lower jaw furnished with a few teeth; two femurs of very dark brown, and two others very white. The black femurs are much larger and longer than the latter. There is a large quantity of small bones of the same hue as the white femurs [Note: [Col. 1699D] From the letter of Abbé Jacquinot, an extract of which I cited above in a note, it appears that it was an unbroken tradition at Ville-sous-La-Ferté that Saint Bernard’s bones were black in hue, whereas those of Saint Malachy [Col. 1700D] were very white. The same letter tells us that M. Delaine agreed with tradition in assigning a blackish colour to Saint Bernard’s relics and a clear white hue to those of Saint Malachy. Finally, Abbé Jacquinot reports that Abbé Chrétien, who was present at the transfer made in 1793, had often repeated to the parish priest of La Ferté that it was easy to recognize the relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy: those of Saint Bernard had a grey-yellow hue, somewhat bronzed, while those of Saint Malachy were perfectly white.].

There are also found in this chest: 1. A bag made of two yellowish skins, thick as a little finger, joined by a seam very skilfully and solidly made. This bag, cut open at one end and split lengthwise, is one metre sixty centimetres long and thirty-five centimetres wide.—2. [Col. 1700B] A fragment of violet silk cloth upon which are embroidered golden griffins holding in their claws web-footed birds in white silk [Note: [Col. 1700D] The parish priest of Ville kindly wrote to me on 4 September 1854 that he had found in [Col. 1701C] the old chest another small fragment of silk cloth, with stripes forming squares. He reports three brown femurs and a brown tibia as well.].—3. Finally, a very thin little board (ninety-five millimetres high and twelve centimetres wide), covered with a sheet of parchment projecting over the edges, where it is fastened by small nails. A wooden fitting, nailed to the lower part, suggests that the board was intended to be set upright. The parchment bore four lines of writing; it is wholly eaten away in the centre, but the ends of the lines remain undamaged. There are still almost entire words and fragments of words, which make it easy to restore the [Col. 1700C] meaning. At first sight one recognizes a fine twelfth-century script.

Here is the inscription: [Col. 1700D]

It must plainly be read: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh . . . [Col. 1701A] Between my breasts . . . He shall abide” (*Song of Songs* 1:12).

This half-destroyed inscription would pass unnoticed if one did not compare the text it expresses with a passage in Saint Bernard’s commentary on the *Song of Songs* [Note: [Col. 1701C] Arriving at verse 12 of the first chapter of the *Song of Songs*, Saint Bernard comments on it as follows:

**SERMON XLIII.** *Fasciculus myrrhae dilectus meus mihi, inter ubera mea commorabitur.*

“A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he shall abide.”

[lacuna] “Myrrh, a bitter, hard, and harsh thing, signifies tribulation. Foreseeing that it is about to come upon her for the sake of her Beloved, she speaks this with joy, confident that she will endure all things courageously . . . Therefore she calls the Beloved not a bundle but a little bundle, because she considers light, in comparison with love of him, whatever toil and suffering may threaten . . . Is he not a little bundle, whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light? Not because he is light in himself—for the harshness of the Passion and the bitterness of death are not light—but he is light to one who loves . . .”

2. “I remember that in one of the preceding sermons (*Sermon* 10) I defined the Bride’s two breasts as joy shared with another and compassion . . . But one who passes amid adversities and prosperities knows that dangers are lacking in neither; he wishes to have the Beloved between such breasts, guarded by his continual protection against both, so that prosperity may not exalt me nor adversity cast me down. You too, if you are wise, will imitate the Bride’s prudence, and will not suffer this most dear little bundle of myrrh to be torn, even for an hour, from the governing part of your breast . . .”

3. “And I, brothers, from the beginning of my conversion, in place of the store of merits which I knew to be lacking in me, took care to bind this little bundle for myself and to place it between my breasts, [Col. 1702C] gathered from all the anxieties and bitterness of my Lord.”

5. “And you also, beloved ones, gather for yourselves this most beloved little bundle; implant it in the marrow of your heart; fortify with it the entrance of your breast, so that it too may abide between your breasts. Keep it always, not behind upon your shoulders, but before your eyes . . .” (*Works of St Bernard, On the Canticles*).

These words show that the little inscription can refer only to Saint Bernard. It expressed one of his familiar texts, one of his habitual thoughts. His monks did not wish to separate it from him in the tomb. The parish priest of Ville announces to me in his letter of 4 September 1854 that the board is preserved with the greatest care. It will be remembered that, according to M. Delaine, there were [Col. 1702D] in Saint Bernard’s tomb and in that of Saint Malachy inscriptions in Gothic script upon strips of parchment.].

The humble little board thus becomes a monument to the profoundly mystical spirit of the first inhabitants of Clairvaux; and its presence in the chest reasonably suggests that Saint Bernard’s bones lie there with it.

These, Count, are the treasures which a modest village church has guarded for half a century. Having examined them with the veneration they deserve and the sadness they inspire, I still had [Col. 1701B] to traverse the valley of Clairvaux.

From the cemetery of Ville one sees La Ferté on the right, about three kilometres away. The horizon is bounded by the mountains of Haute-Marne. It was from that direction that Saint Bernard arrived in June 1115, carrying a crucifix given him by Saint Stephen and accompanied by twelve monks representing the apostles [Note: [Col. 1701C] Saint Bernard, arriving at verse 12 of the first chapter of the *Song of Songs*, comments as follows:

**SERMON XLIII.** *Fasciculus myrrhae dilectus meus mihi, inter ubera mea commorabitur.*

“A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he shall abide.”

[lacuna] “Myrrh, a bitter, hard, and harsh thing, signifies tribulation. Foreseeing that it is about to come upon her for the sake of her Beloved, she speaks this with joy, confident that she will endure all things courageously . . . Therefore she calls the Beloved not a bundle but a little bundle, because she considers light, in comparison with love of him, whatever toil and suffering may threaten . . . Is he not a little bundle, whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light? Not because he is light in himself—for the harshness of the Passion and the bitterness of death are not light—but he is light to one who loves . . .”

2. “I remember that in one of the preceding sermons (*Sermon* 10) I defined the Bride’s two breasts as joy shared with another and compassion . . . But one who passes amid adversities and prosperities knows that dangers are lacking in neither; he wishes to have the Beloved between such breasts, guarded by his continual protection against both, so that prosperity may not exalt me nor adversity cast me down. You too, if you are wise, will imitate the Bride’s prudence, and will not suffer this most dear little bundle of myrrh to be torn, even for an hour, from the governing part of your breast . . .”

3. “And I, brothers, from the beginning of my conversion, in place of the store of merits which I knew to be lacking in me, took care to bind this little bundle for myself and to place it between my breasts, [Col. 1702C] gathered from all the anxieties and bitterness of my Lord.”

5. “And you also, beloved ones, gather for yourselves this most beloved little bundle; implant it in the marrow of your heart; fortify with it the entrance of your breast, so that it too may abide between your breasts. Keep it always, not behind upon your shoulders, but before your eyes . . .” (*Works of St Bernard, On the Canticles*).

These words show that the little inscription can refer only to Saint Bernard. It expressed one of his familiar texts, one of his habitual thoughts. His monks did not wish to separate it from him in the tomb. The parish priest of Ville announces to me in his letter of 4 September 1854 that the board is preserved with the greatest care. It will be remembered that, according to M. Delaine, there were [Col. 1702D] in Saint Bernard’s tomb and in that of Saint Malachy inscriptions in Gothic script upon strips of parchment.].

In all likelihood, he had come from visiting Josserand, bishop of Langres. In making for the estates of Hugh, Count of Bar-sur-Aube [Note: [Col. 1702D] *Works of St Bernard*, Notes on Epistle XXXI.—*Acts of St Bernard*, § V, 59–60.—Manrique, *Annals of Cîteaux*, year 1115, 1.], in order to establish there the holy colony of which he was the head, Saint Bernard would naturally have passed through La Ferté. His kinsman Josbert, a noble and wealthy man, lived there [Note: [Col. 1702D] *Works of St Bernard*, Notes on Epistle XXXI.]. This lord could assist Saint Stephen’s poor envoys; and one might suppose that Saint Bernard, appreciating the usefulness of his proximity, or yielding to his friendly solicitations, sought to found the new abbey not far from his residence.

From La Ferté to Clairvaux is about six kilometres; but the succession of little valleys without springs could not attract our saint. The valley of Clairvaux at last presented to his eyes a narrow, wild gorge and a clear brook [Note: [Col. 1702D] “A noble man, also his kinsman according to the flesh . . . A man of high rank and magnificently honoured.” (*Works of St Bernard*, William, IX, 43.)]. At that time the brook, appearing only at the entrance of the valley, disappeared underground and became invisible [Note: [Col. 1702D] This brook received the saint’s name, which it still bears today.]. Saint Bernard judged that he must go upstream to its source, situated about two kilometres farther on. There he again saw the pure water issue abundantly from the mountain [Col. 1702B] and flow eastward, which was then considered an indication of a good spring [Note: [Col. 1702D] “Where the mountain casts it forth, the valley swallows it; and in the place where it rises, there it as it were dies—indeed, is buried.” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Description of Clairvaux*, E.)].

The deep solitude of the woods delighted Saint Bernard; nevertheless, at this spot the valley floor was too constricted for him to think of building a monastery there. On arriving at the spring, Saint Bernard had on his left a low mountain beaten by the north wind; on his right, the much higher mountain faced south. The choice was not doubtful. Climbing the latter, opposite the spring, he stopped halfway up its slope to pitch his tent and establish his colony.

[Note: [Col. 1702D] This note appears at the foot of column 1702, but the callout number (7) has not been printed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 1702D] *Ibidem*—“in the same place.”] [Col. 1703]

[Col. 1705A] I knew, Count, that Clairvaux Abbey had in a sense been founded twice, and that the site adopted by Saint Bernard in 1115 had been abandoned in 1135; but I did not know where the first establishment had been made.

At the western extremity of the monastic enclosure, Dom Milley’s plan indeed shows a building designated *Monasterium vetus* (“old monastery”); one readily recognizes it as the PETIT-SAINT-BERNARD of which the account printed in the *Annales archéologiques* speaks, situated outside the regular precincts and containing a chapel, dormitory, refectory, and Saint Bernard’s room. Yet this is not the foundation of 1115.

[Col. 1705B] For when, about 1135, the monks urged Saint Bernard to change the abbey’s location, [Col. 1706A] they represented to him that it stood in a narrow and inconvenient place, incapable of containing the multitude of religious flowing in from every side. They pointed out farther on the plain and the river that watered it, adding that there they would find space for every dependency of a monastery; that they could have meadows, farms, gardens, and vineyards; finally, they said, if the forest no longer served as their enclosure, they could easily replace it with stone walls [Note: [Col. 1705C] “They therefore pointed out to him the narrow and inconvenient place in which they had settled, incapable of holding so great a multitude . . . They added also that they had considered the suitable plain lower down, and the advantage of the river which flows below; and that there was a spacious place there [Col. 1706C] for all the needs of a monastery—for meadows, farms, thickets, and vineyards—and that, if the enclosure of forest seemed lacking, this could easily be supplied by stone walls, of which there was an immense quantity there.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V, 29.)].

Now the *Monasterium vetus* of Dom Milley’s plan, or the PETIT-SAINT-BERNARD of the account, possessed all the advantages of situation desired by the monks; it stood at the entrance to the valley, not far from the Aube. Consequently the reproaches of Saint Bernard’s disciples cannot [Col. 1706B] apply to it.

[Col. 1705]

[Col. 1705C] To recover traces of the foundation of 1115, one plainly had to penetrate into the valley and find a place where one could have neither meadows, farms, gardens, nor vineyards.

Various pieces of information supplied by an inhabitant of a village near Clairvaux, Arconville, at last brought me happily to the end of my researches. I learned that opposite the spring, [Col. 1706C] halfway up the mountainside, there were traces of ruins and ditches marking out a regular enclosure; I was also told that these ruins were called “a nunnery.” This name revealed ancient Clairvaux to me. Here is the plan of the enclosure marked by the ditches: I observed there heaps of stones which appear to have served for construction, and very old tiles.

[Col. 1707]

[Col. 1709A] It seems evident to me that Saint Bernard built there his first monastery, in which he remained twenty years. All the monks’ complaints apply to this site. This was indeed the narrow and inconvenient place (*insinuant . . . locum angustum et incommodum*), lost amid the forests (*si silvae videatur deesse clausura*—“if the enclosure of forest seems lacking” [Note: [Col. 1709D] These words suggest that the first monastery was not enclosed by walls, and that ditches marked out its precinct. This idea is confirmed when one sees the religious speak of walls for enclosing the new abbey: *facile hoc parietibus lapideis . . . posse suppleri*—“this can easily be supplied by stone walls.”]), where the appurtenances of an abbey could be established only with great difficulty.

Dom Milley’s plan shows that the *monasterium vetus* was a very small building accompanied by a chapel. It stood about two hundred toises from the church. Around it were arranged workshops, workmen’s dwellings, barns, stables, the winepress, and slaughterhouses.

[Col. 1709B] If it were necessary to identify this with ancient Clairvaux, one could scarcely understand why Saint Bernard, anxious to leave it, spoke of a complete abandonment and lamented the uselessness of all the original work. Why, for example, did he raise against his monks the loss of the aqueducts? They needed only to be extended, rather than abandoned, since the water-intakes had already been established [Note: [Col. 1709D] *Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V, 29.].

Yet the monks made an entirely new establishment. Some cut down trees, others dressed the stone and raised the walls; the river was divided into channels, and waterfalls were prepared for mills. Fullers, millers, and tanners installed their machinery, and the Aube, conducted by a thousand subterranean channels, [Col. 1709C] boiled throughout the whole house [Note: [Col. 1709D] *Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V, 31.]. All the workshops of Clairvaux and the workmen’s dwellings are grouped in Dom Milley’s plan around the *monasterium vetus*. It was therefore the first construction of the new abbey; and it is not surprising to find a chapel there, since the great church was not built immediately after the monastery’s transfer.

Saint Bernard, regretfully leaving the profound solitude where he had planted his first steps, but warned by various revelations that he must abandon it [Note: [Col. 1709D] “For the house of cloistered habitation, having been transferred from the narrower places of that valley to a flatter and more spacious site, not without certain divine revelations, was there made great and enlarged.” (*Works of St Bernard*, William, 62.) “. . . though first very many prayers had been poured forth to God concerning this, and certain revelations also had been shown beforehand.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V.)], moved as little away from it as possible while drawing nearer to the plain. Later, as the monastery developed [Note: [Col. 1710D] William of Saint-Thierry, writing about ten years after the transfer of the abbey, observes that the new buildings were already too narrow to contain the multitude of their inhabitants. (*Works of St Bernard*, William, XIII.)], it became concentrated [Col. 1710A] around the church and extended farther toward the valley entrance.

If my opinion concerning the first site of Clairvaux should not seem sufficiently established to you, Count, I would add a few further considerations.

According to the account printed in the *Annales archéologiques*, a room was shown in the PETIT-SAINT-BERNARD or *monasterium vetus* in which Saint Bernard had received Eugene III. But Eugene III did not become pope until 1145; and whatever the date of his visit (Appendix no. 15), more than ten years had passed since the old abbey had been left when he made it. The *monasterium vetus*, therefore, was not ancient Clairvaux.

[Col. 1710B] When Dom Joseph Méglinger visited the *monasterium vetus* in 1667, he venerated there the cell which Saint Malachy had occupied, after his return from Rome, from the first days of October until 2 November 1148, and in which he died. This cell stood near Saint Bernard’s, on the upper floor where the common dormitory was located; the oratory was on the ground floor [Note: [Col. 1710D] *Iter Cisterciense*, 66, 67, 69.]. Thus Saint Bernard, writing the life of his friend, reports that he did not allow the community to come upstairs to him in order to attend, as customary [Note: [Col. 1710D] *Nomast. Cist.; Us. Ord. Cist.*, IV, p. C, V; p. 203.], the ceremonies of extreme unction, and that he wished to descend in order to receive the sacrament of the dying in its midst [Note: [Col. 1710D] “He lay in the upper chamber (*solarium*, that is, an upper room) of the upper house. He is anointed; and, having received the viaticum, commending himself to the brothers’ prayers and the brothers to God, he returns to bed. He descended from the upper chamber on his own feet, and again he nevertheless ascended on his own feet . . .” (*Works of St Bernard*, *Life of St Malachy*, XXXI, 71.)].

But if Saint Malachy died in the *monasterium* [Col. 1710C] *vetus* in 1148, must one not necessarily conclude that the *monasterium vetus* was not ancient Clairvaux, which had already been abandoned for thirteen years at that date?

Besides, one can readily explain how the tradition concerning the abbey’s first site came to be lost even at Clairvaux.

The enclosure situated halfway up the mountainside opposite the Saint Bernard spring, the plan of which I have given above, was not enclosed by walls: ditches traced its circuit, and the forest formed its enclosure (*si silvae videatur deesse clausura*). It contained indeed some stone buildings, but so small and narrow that the oratory, among [Col. 1711A] other things, barely sufficed for the monks alone [Note: [Col. 1711C] “And as the number of those arriving in crowds increased daily, they could not be received within the buildings constructed, and the oratory scarcely sufficed for the monks alone.” (*Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V, 29.)].

After this place was abandoned in 1135, woods encroached upon the ditches and the surface of the enclosure; the buildings, stripped of everything which could serve for the new constructions [Note: [Col. 1711C] Such, it seems to me, is the meaning of these words of Saint Bernard: “If we destroy all these things, men of the world may think ill of us, that we are frivolous and changeable,” etc. (*Works of St Bernard*, Ernald, V, 29.)], soon fell into ruin, and nothing remained that could preserve their memory.

The *monasterium vetus*, where Saint Bernard, as though hesitating and fearing to leave the valley entirely, first fixed the new site of the abbey, and from which it afterward advanced farther toward the plain, gradually took the place of ancient Clairvaux in memory. It too had been in a sense abandoned, since all the great buildings of the abbey were grouped around the church, [Col. 1711B] built about two hundred toises farther on; the *monasterium vetus*, owing to a fate nearly shared with ancient Clairvaux, was bound to be confused with it in tradition.

Yet there remained a vague recollection of the truth, proof of which I find in this curious passage from the *Literary Journey*:

“We were at Clairvaux,” say the Benedictines, “at the time when the monks customarily go, after Easter, to Saint Bernard’s spring, which is half a league from the monastery. On arriving there, they sing a responsory of Saint Bernard, the *Regina caeli*, and each places at the foot of the great cross near the spring [Col. 1711C] small wooden crosses that they make, and drinks the water of the spring from the hand. They customarily go there on the Tuesday after Quasimodo Sunday; for at Clairvaux the monks do not leave the monastery during the octave of Easter, nor during that of Pentecost, any more than during Lent . . . We wished [Col. 1712A] to join the party, and were curious to see this spring, which formerly supplied water to the first monks of Clairvaux. As we passed, a little above the monastery enclosure, we saw a chapel erected on the very spot where Saint Bernard’s letter to his nephew Robert was written [Note: [Col. 1711C] Father Mabillon, annotating this letter, *in [Col. 1711D] medio imbre sine imbre scriptam*—“written amid rain, without rain”—adds: ‘The place where this occurred, near Clairvaux, is made notable by a little oratory, in memory of the event.’ (*S. BERN. Op.*, Epist. 1.) Dom Joseph Méglinger determines the chapel’s position more precisely: ‘We went outside the walls to that place in which Saint Bernard is reported to have composed a letter in rain without rain . . . withdrawing with William, whom he employed in writing letters, to a wood near the monastery for the sake of privacy, he began to dictate to him as he took it down upon parchment . . . [lacuna] This place is half an hour from the monastery of Clairvaux, in the heart of a forest reaching to the very walls. In perpetual remembrance of the miracle they erected a small chapel, in which this wondrous event is seen depicted.’ (*Iter Cist.*, p. 207.) Here I find a further proof of my opinion concerning the first site of Clairvaux. Saint Bernard was writing to his nephew Robert about the year 1119 (*S. BERN. Op.*, Epist. 1); he then lived in the old [Col. 1712C] abbey. The chapel erected at the place where the miracle of the letter *in imbre sine imbre* occurred was very near it. Indeed, if the holy abbot had left the monastery enclosure in order not to be disturbed in his work—‘for the purpose of dictating more privately, they had gone outside the monastery precincts’ (*S. BERN. Op.*, Guillelmus, XI, 50)—he need not have gone far, since the forest immediately afforded him the peace of its deep retreats. Whereas, by placing old Clairvaux at the *monasterium [Col. 1712D] vetus*, one makes Saint Bernard walk half a league before finding the solitude he needed to dictate without interruption.], amid a very heavy rain, without the secretary being inconvenienced or the paper getting wet [Note: [Col. 1712D] *Voyage littéraire*, vol. I, p. 185.].”

Is not the annual pilgrimage to this spring of Saint Bernard, which formerly supplied water to the first monks, a precious testimony of tradition concerning the first foundation of Clairvaux? Why all these commemorative ceremonies, this responsory of Saint Bernard, and this water drunk [Col. 1712B] from the hand, unless it was intended to recall the founder and the poverty of the first disciples, on the very spot where they had initially settled [Note: [Col. 1712D] An inquiry of 11 April 1580 informs us that over the source of Saint Bernard’s spring there stood a fine building of dressed stone, and before it a fine stone cross. Enemies of the abbey had destroyed everything about a year earlier. One witness stated in his deposition that, before the spring was broken up, the water spread at certain places through the valley and cattle were made to drink there. In 1747 the spring was covered by a stone vault surmounted by a high stone cross. Last summer (1854), during the ravages of cholera, a statue of Saint Bernard was placed beneath the stone arcade existing at the source of the spring.]?

Geoffrey, Saint Bernard’s former scribe, in sending the Life of the holy abbot to Archbishop Eskil, wrote to him: “I ask those who may read these lines, if they are displeased by my prolixity (from you I fear nothing of the sort), to excuse me, considering that love suggested lengthy narratives to me.” That too would be my excuse, Monsieur le Comte, if the smallest details did not become very precious when they concern a saint. All the monuments intended to preserve [Col. 1712C] Saint Bernard’s memory have perished. His memory is in some sense forgotten in the places which he made illustrious by so many wonders, and the church of Ville has not an altar at which his image may be honoured. His tomb has been violated; his ashes scattered; the vast monastery, in which he left seven hundred monks when he died, has been turned into a [Col. 1713A] central penitentiary (Appendix, no. 16). It is therefore a pious duty to collect with the greatest care every document capable of restoring at least some image of what no longer exists.

Would I not, moreover, be only too happy to contribute my humble offering to those extensive researches which you have undertaken upon the history of Saint Bernard, and from which you continually promise to let the Christian public benefit [Note: [Col. 1713C] Letter from the Count de Montalembert to the author, 12 September 1854.]?

The ancient abbey of Clairvaux has been overturned from top to bottom; nothing remains save its immense enclosure, witness to its fallen splendour [Note: [Col. 1713C] It follows from a judgment upon a wager, rendered on 14 April 1633 by the lieutenant-general of Chaumont, that the whole enclosure of Clairvaux (8,050 *pieds du roi*, reduced to 402½ cords) exceeded that of Chaumont (7,400 *pieds du roi*, [Col. 1714C] reduced to 370 cords) by 650 feet. *Arch. Hist. de l’Aube*, by M. Vallet de Viriville. Troyes, 1841; octavo, p. 441.], granaries and cellars now used as refectories by female convicts [Note: [Col. 1714C] See *Archéol. dans le départ. de l’Aube*, by Arnaud. Troyes, 1843, p. 229.]. I have passed sorrowfully before its walls, turning away my eyes: the holy and [Col. 1713B] voluntary captivity of the cloister has been succeeded by the enforced captivity of crime. You will share the feelings which filled my soul on rereading this sublime incident from the life of Saint Bernard.

“Saint Bernard went to see Theobald, Count of Champagne, on certain business. As he approached the town where the count then was, he encountered a great troop of men who, by the count’s order, were dragging a notorious thief to execution. At this sight the most merciful abbot, seizing the bonds that tied this wretch, said to his executioners: ‘Give me this robber; I wish to hang him with my own hands.’

“When the count learned of the arrival of the servant of [Col. 1713C] God, he hastened to meet him; for he always loved and honoured him with singular affection and respect. He saw him drawing the thief behind him by the rope; and, struck with astonishment, cried: ‘Ah, venerable Father, what have you done, bringing back from the gates of hell this villain, condemned a thousand times over? Can you save one who has become a veritable demon? You will never succeed in correcting him, and the sole good deed [Col. 1714A] of which he is capable is to die. Let this man go to perdition, since his dangerous life has destroyed that of a great many people. It is better to secure by his death the lives of many persons than to threaten by his life the existence of my subjects.’

‘Most excellent prince,’ replied Saint Bernard, ‘I know that this unhappy man is a great sinner and deserves the cruelest torments; do not therefore suppose that I wish to let him go unpunished. On the contrary, I intend to deliver him to executioners and make him expiate his crimes by a punishment all the more just because it will last longer. You had ordered that he should perish by a brief and momentary punishment; I shall make him waste away by a [Col. 1714B] slow and daily death. You would have left him hanging on the gallows for a few weeks; I shall bind him to the cross and leave him alive amid sufferings.’

“The most Christian prince fell silent and dared no longer contradict the saint. The latter immediately clothed the prisoner in his tunic; and, cutting his hair, joined him to the Lord’s flock, making a sheep from a wolf and a lay brother from a thief. Brought to Clairvaux, this man remained obedient until death, wonderfully answering by his constancy to the name Constant which he had received at baptism. After more than thirty years he departed to God, who, through the merits of our blessed [Col. 1714C] Father, had deigned to preserve him from the twofold death of soul and body [Note: [Col. 1714C] *S. Bern. op. Excerpta ex Exord. magno Cist.*, XV.—*S. Bern. gen. illust. gen. illust. assert.*—Herbert, *De miracul.*, II, 15.—*Menol. Cist.*, 21 June.].”

I remain respectfully, Monsieur le Comte, your most humble and most obedient servant,

PH. GUIGNARD,  
Former archivist of the department of Aube, librarian of the city of Dijon, correspondent of the Ministry of Public Instruction.  
1855—5 March.

[Col. 1713]

# APPENDIX

## No. 1. Correction of the catalogue of the abbots of Clairvaux given in the *Gallia Christiana*

[Col. 1713D] An autograph letter of Dom Ét. Brice corrects the error made in the catalogue of the abbots of Clairvaux supplied by volume IV of the *Gallia Christiana*. A John II, who would have been the twenty-third abbot, was wrongly included in it. Hence, beginning with the twenty-fourth abbot inclusive, one must subtract [Col. 1714D] one from each number expressing the order of succession of the abbots of Clairvaux when using this catalogue.

Dom Ét. Brice’s letter is pasted on the recto of the leaf containing columns 808 and 809, in the copy of the *Gallia Christiana* belonging to the Public Library of Troyes and apparently originating [Col. 1715A] from Clairvaux. I do not know to whom it was addressed: the flyleaf no longer exists. I have copied it exactly.

“It is right, Sir, that those who led you into error should disabuse you by correcting themselves. We entered a John II, abbot of Clairvaux, on the authority of the Book of Fiefs of the Church of Langres. This book is genuine and remains in the King’s Library, no. 9582 b., in the Cartulary of the Church of Langres” (Dom Ét. Brice wrongly copied the former manuscript number, which was 9852 B; the present number is 5188); “and it is because I myself saw and read the charter that I noticed the error there. It consists neither in the abbot’s name nor in the event, but in the date. The one among us who made the extract read, or at least entered, 1281 instead of the 1287 which is there; this agrees perfectly with John III, who thereby is now only the second of that name and was elected in 1286. Thus the twenty-third Abbot John II must be omitted, as others have [Col. 1715B] done; and thereby John III will become the second of that name and the twenty-fifth abbot of Clairvaux, who made the agreement with Guy, bishop of Langres, which I find in the same cartulary called *Man.* in 1280. I do not know whether you would do so ill to read this cartulary for your history of Clairvaux, but one must find someone able to read, which is not so common. I have [Col. 1716A] the honour to remain, with every possible consideration, Sir,

“Your most humble and most obedient servant, Brother ÉT. BRICE. 9 December 1737, from the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris.”

Perhaps Dom Ét. Brice’s letter was addressed to Dom Claude Guyton, who left two volumes of notes extracted from the archives of Clairvaux Abbey, of which I have spoken above? It may be seen that he reports there the text of an instrument of the year 1280 mentioning Theobald, abbot of Clairvaux, with the very evident intention of proving that in 1280 there was no abbot of Clairvaux named John. (See manuscript Mathieu, XV, p. 81.)

In the Archives of Aube I found a paper copy, collated in 1476, of an agreement between Theobald, abbot of Clairvaux, and an English abbot, dated the day of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin in the year 1282. The same repository preserves the original of an agreement [Col. 1716B] between the prior of Cunfin (a dependency of Saint-Claude Abbey) and Theobald, abbot of Clairvaux, dated Tuesday before Easter in the year 1280.—Parchment; seal missing. A fragment of paper has been pasted on the back, upon which one reads: “Remarkable charter proving that it was not a John II who was abbot of Clairvaux in 1280.”

## No. 2. Final act of conventual life at Clairvaux Abbey.—Statement of Clairvaux’s revenues in 1790

[Col. 1715]

[Col. 1715B] In 1790 Clairvaux Abbey consisted of twenty-six professed religious, including Abbot Louis-Marie Rocourt, aged forty-seven; ten lay brothers; and ten affiliated boarders of the house. Three monks were absent. On 24 May of that year, the municipal officers of the commune of Clairvaux notified the abbot, prior, and [Col. 1715C] religious that they were prepared to receive the declaration of those among them wishing to state their intention either to leave the house or remain in it. Their answer, quoted from the official record, was as follows: “The Reverend Abbot told us that, in his capacity as abbot of Clairvaux, he had no desire other than to remain, live, and die in his abbey,” and signed, “Brother L.-M. ROCOURT, Abbot of Clairvaux.” Nineteen religious declared that they intended to take advantage of the liberty granted them by the National Assembly, and signed. Two others announced that they would leave only after obtaining authorization from the Pope. “M. La Ramée (Louis), master of novices, aged fifty-six, professed of Buzet, declared that he wished to remain in the Order and, preferably if possible, in the house of Clairvaux; and signed, Brother LA RAMÉE.” All the lay brothers expressed their intention of making use of the liberty granted by the National [Col. 1715D] Assembly.

Extract from the official record of the inventory made at Clairvaux Abbey by the municipal officers of that place, 24 May 1790, in the presence of the abbot, prior, and religious. (Archives of Aube.)

[Col. 1716B] The same record shows that the annual cash revenues of the abbey amounted to 133,826 livres, 11 sous, 10 deniers:

In wheat, 481 *septiers*, 16 bushels (the *septier* comprising 18 bushels, the bushel weighing 25 pounds);

In oats, 434 *septiers*, 16 bushels;

[Col. 1716C] In rye, 16 *septiers*;

In barley, 47 *septiers*;

In colza seed, 17 *septiers*, 13 bushels;

In peas and beans, 4 *septiers*, 9 bushels;

In 89 thousandweights of straw;

233 capons; 6 ducks; 6 young rabbits; 2 pairs of chickens; 24 cheeses; 7 pigs; 22 ploughing-days; haulage for 42 cords of wood, 225 thousand stakes, and 45 pounds of butter;

In the cutting of 325 arpents of high forest;

In that of 146 arpents, 32 perches of coppice and high forest;

In 55 arpents, 73 perches set apart for heating Clairvaux Abbey, and in 4,393 arpents, 99 perches held in reserve and worked only in urgent necessity, pursuant to an order of the Council.

The sum of 205,734 livres, 18 sous, 4 deniers is owed to the said abbey; the said abbey in [Col. 1716D] turn owes, not including the monks’ clothing allowances, the fees and wages of judicial officers, surveyors, clerks, servants, taxes, minimum benefices, and other items that could not be assessed or determined, the sum of 105,233 livres, six sous.

## No. 3. Certificate of M. Rocourt establishing the authenticity of Saint Bernard’s head

[Col. 1715]

[Col. 1715D] “I, the undersigned, former abbot of Clairvaux, now residing at Bar-sur-Aube, certify to all whom it may concern that the head of Saint Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, which for centuries had been exposed to the veneration of the faithful in the church of that abbey, and of which I gave to Baron Charles Caffarelli, prefect of the department [Col. 1716D] of Aube, officer of the Legion of Honour, to dispose of as he should judge appropriate, the precious remainder that in the year one thousand seven hundred and ninety remained in my possession, and upon which I placed, within the skull, the same red-wax seal whose impression appears below, was removed by me, in the presence of several persons [Col. 1717A] whose testimony I regret that I can no longer add to my own, from the reliquary containing it, when the administrators of the district of Bar-sur-Aube, in the name of and in conformity with the government’s orders, seized all gold and silver objects in the treasury of the said Clairvaux. In witness whereof I have issued this certificate, to serve and be valid wherever necessary. Done at Bar-sur-Aube, the first day of October one thousand eight hundred and thirteen, signed L.-M. ROCOURT, former abbot of Clairvaux.”

Beside it, on the right, is a red-wax seal bearing, on an oval escutcheon, the interlaced letters L. M. R. Below is written:

“Stephen Anthony de Boulogne, etc. Having seen this present instrument under the signature and seal of D. Rocourt, lately abbot of Clairvaux, we permit the holy and distinguished relics of Saint Bernard, abbot, set down herein—first granted to D. Charles Caffarelli, Prefect of the Province of Aube, and by the same [Col. 1718A] Prefect given as a gift to our cathedral church on 24 December 1813, and placed in a silver-plated wooden box closed with glass—to be displayed for the public veneration of the faithful.—Given at Troyes, under our signature and with the affixing of our seal, on the fourth day of September in the year of the Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixteen.

Place of the seal. ‘+ STEPHEN ANTHONY, Bishop of Troyes.’”

These two documents, written on paper, are in the office of the Bishopric of Troyes.

M. Rocourt’s certificate establishing the authenticity of Saint Malachy’s head, and M. de Boulogne’s authorization to expose it, are found in Saint Malachy’s shrine; but since these documents are entirely similar to those just cited and bear the same dates, it is unnecessary to reproduce them.

## No. 4. Investigations concerning the relics removed from Clairvaux in 1790 and 1791

[Col. 1717]

[Col. 1717B] The late M. Girardon, canon of Troyes Cathedral, communicated to me in 1845 some information concerning the relics removed from Clairvaux before the abbey was sold. M. Girardon, a native of Bar-sur-Aube and brother of an administrator of that district, had been well placed to know what was taking place at Clairvaux [Col. 1718B] about 1790; but his great age no longer allowed him to recall precise memories.

It appears that M. Rocourt, together with the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, carried away that of Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr of Spain [Note: [Col. 1717B] In 855 Saint Vincent’s body was translated from Spain to Castres. In 1225 Cardinal Conrad sent his head to Clairvaux (Manrique, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1225, IV, no. 9); accordingly, when the Dominicans of Castres discovered the saint’s remains in their church in 1259, this precious relic was found absent. “But the head of the blessed martyr was not found with the body; for, as faithful antiquity relates . . . the head was kept in a silver shrine and, on principal and feast days, was customarily shown to Christian peoples for veneration . . . but what became of the head, where it went, or where it may be held and remain, is unknown among us and commonly uncertain among all, though various persons affirm different things. For some say that it was conveyed to the Cistercian abbey of Clairvaux by a certain cardinal of the same Order, a legate in these parts.” (*Ex hist. de inventione S. corp. B. Vincentii*, in Bernard Gui, *hist. fundation. convent. O. F. P. Tolosanae provinciae*, *Veter. script. ampliss. collectio*, Paris, 1724, vol. VI, col. 497.) Saint Vincent’s head was kept at Clairvaux in a rich reliquary; Manrique (*ibid.*) gives a description of the vessel containing it: it is the text of the Inventory of 1504. The Inventory of 1640, fol. 8, recto-verso, says: “Likewise, another gilded-silver reliquary in the shape of a cup, in which rests the head of Saint Vincent, martyr. The base is supported by four little gilded-bronze seats upon which sit the four Evangelists; [Col. 1717D] the handle is encircled by eight enamel roundels, and the cup is surrounded by eight images six fingers high, with these inscriptions: Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Mary, Gabriel the angel, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Philip, Saint Mammes, Saint Vincent, and Michael the angel, holding a crown. Above these relief images are eight capitals adorned with stones and as many little towers furnished with relics. In the hollow of the cup is the entire head of Saint Vincent, beside which are some other relics but without their own labels, which in the year 1640 were found [Col. 1718B] completely consumed by the dampness of the place where, five and a half years earlier, the relics had been hidden because of the danger of war. The top of the cover is apple-shaped, ornamented with enamel flowers and stars, from which hangs a little book-shaped reliquary containing relics of Saint Audomar. This head of Saint Vincent was given to Clairvaux by Conrad, bishop of Porto and legate of the Holy See. This reliquary was made in the time of the Reverends Fathers in God Dom Lawrence, fourteenth, and Dom Ralph, fifteenth, abbots of Clairvaux. [Col. 1718C] One arm is missing from an image of Our Lord, and seven settings are empty of their stones.” (Cf. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 804.)], that of Saint Barnabas [Note: [Col. 1718C] Inventory of 1504, fol. 8 verso: “Vessel in which is contained the head of Saint Barnabas the Apostle. The monk Artaud, cellarer of Clairvaux, brought this head. This vessel was made in the time of Dom Evrard and Dom William, abbots, and of Brother Drogo, sacristan of Clairvaux, from thirty marks of silver and one and a half of gold.” Inventory of 1640, fol. 7 verso: “In the cupboard marked E, there is first a fine gilded-silver reliquary, pyramid-shaped, in which rests the head of Saint Barnabas, Apostle. Its base is only of bronze, supported by three heads of gilded-bronze hares, but is covered with silver, with six enamel roses and various precious stones. The handle has six enamel images, above which are represented the mysteries of the Annunciation, with this [Col. 1718D] inscription, ‘Hail Mary, full of grace’; of the Nativity of Our Lord; of the coming of the shepherds to Bethlehem, with this inscription, ‘Glory in the highest’; of the Adoration of the Kings; and of the Presentation of Our Lord in the Temple, with the image of Our Lady holding the child Jesus. Above these mysteries are six capitals with six pillars and as many little towers, in which the relics now have no labels . . . [lacuna] The vessel containing the head of Saint Barnabas, Apostle, is covered by a large capital at the base of which are seen representations of the birth, baptism, transfiguration, crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension of Our Lord. At the summit of the pyramid [Col. 1719C] is a crystal full of relics, which formerly had their labels, but now [Col. 1719D] these are all consumed and effaced because of the dampness of the place where this reliquary was hidden during the wars from 1635 until this present year 1640. The head of Saint Barnabas was brought to Clairvaux by Dom Artaud, and this reliquary was made in the time of the Reverend Father in God Dom Evrard, seventeenth, and Dom William, eighteenth, abbots of Clairvaux. Three stones are missing.”], as well as that of Saint [Col. 1719A] Anne [Note: [Col. 1719D] Inventory of 1640, fol. 18 verso: “Further, a gilded-silver reliquary in the form of a chapel; above is a cross, with a crucifix on one side and the Virgin on the other. It opens in the middle, where there is an oval crystal through which one sees: ‘The occiput of Saint Anne, mother of the Blessed Virgin.’” This was only a portion of the venerable head of Saint Anne kept at Düren, in the diocese of Cologne (*Usuard’s Martyrology with Molanus’s notes*, Antwerp, 1583). The very form of the reliquary leaves no doubt on that point. [Col. 1720C] Inventory of 1504, fol. 10 verso: “Likewise, a well-fashioned gilded-silver vessel without its base, [Col. 1720D] in which is a portion of the head of Saint Anne, mother of the Mother of God, weighing three marks, half an ounce, and one third, whose base also serves to carry the Body of Christ on the day of the most holy sacrament of the altar.” I mention several documents concerning the cult of Saint Anne at Clairvaux, preserved in the Archives of Aube.—15 April 1379.—Permission by John, abbot of Clairvaux, for a lamp before the altar of Saint Anne in Clairvaux church (parchment).—23 March 1383.—Order of the Abbot of Clairvaux for a lamp in honour of Saint Anne and Saint Michael (same).—15 December 1385.—Foundation for the feast of Saint Anne (same).]. M. Hérardin, parish priest of Longchamps, engaged in drawing up the catalogue of Clairvaux Library (letter of the administrators of the Bar-sur-Aube directory to the gentlemen of the departmental directory, 27 August 1791, Archives of Aube), enriched M. Girardon, his friend, with a great number of precious relics. When better days returned, M. Girardon disposed of them in favour of religious communities. But as he kept no register of these various gifts, it is very difficult to trace them. I saw in his hands a small portion of the True Cross, from the abbey treasury, fragments of which he distributed together with his formal attestation. This honourable canon still had one or two vertebrae of Saint Bernard, accompanied by the following certificate:

“I, the undersigned, L. Hérardin, priest serving Longchamps-lès-Clairvaux, diocese of Troyes, certify to all who shall see these present letters [Col. 1719B] that in 1792 (this is an error: 1793 is the date given by the official documents), then residing at Clairvaux, at the opening of the tomb of Saint Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, carried out by the procurator-syndic and members of the district, I myself removed from the tomb two vertebrae of the holy abbot, and divided them for distribution to churches wishing to possess a portion of this precious treasure. I enclosed them in paper tied with a red braid and sealed with two seals like that affixed below these present letters; this packet I delivered to my friend M. Abbé Girardon, canon of Besançon. In witness whereof I have issued this certificate, signed by my hand and sealed with my seal; at Bar-sur-Aube, 8 October 1823. Signed: Hérardin, curate of Longchamps-lès-Clairvaux; seal bearing the interlaced letters L and H.”

At the bottom was written: “I certify that M. L. Hérardin, [Col. 1719C] parish priest of Longchamps, is trustworthy and that credit ought to be given to his signature; at Bar-sur-Aube, 10 October 1823. Signed: L. M. Rocourt, abbot of Clairvaux.” Beside it is an impression in red wax showing a shield bearing, of . . . a chevron charged with three trefoils of . . ., below a fess of . . . charged with three trefoils of . . ., impaled with Clairvaux; surmounted by a count’s coronet and stamped on right and left with a mitre.

I believe that a portion of Saint Bernard’s lower jaw, whose authenticity was attested by the same M. Hérardin, was given by M. Girardon to the archbishopric of Besançon.

In 1845 there was in the office of the Bishopric of Troyes a small packet of grey paper bearing the broken seal of Monsignor de Barral, former bishop of [Col. 1720A] Troyes, with this inscription: “Small rib and neck-bone of Saint Bernard, and pieces of silk and linen in which he was wrapped in his shrine. Bones and relics of Saint Bernard, taken from his shrine at Clairvaux in 1791 or 1792” (an inaccuracy which I have just corrected). These relics had been given by the pious M. d’Arvisenet, former vicar-general of the diocese. A small fragment of blue silk bearing a lion embroidered in yellow silk was attached to the bones.

The church of Ramerupt (district of Arcis-sur-Aube) possesses two notable fragments of the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, given to it by M. Millot, former chief clerk of the court of Troyes. M. Millot received them from Abbé Dolat, parish priest of Sainte-Madeleine in Troyes, who possessed them at third hand. Here is a copy of the authentication accompanying them:

“We, Brother Louis-Marie Rocourt, doctor of theology of the Sacred [Col. 1720B] Faculty of Paris, principal Father of the Cistercian Order, Abbot of Clairvaux in the diocese of Langres, greeting in the Lord all who inspect these present letters and each person concerned. We make known and certify that, on the second day of April in the year one thousand seven hundred and ninety, granting favourably the request of Monsieur Jean Jemelet on behalf of another person, a worshipper of the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman religion, commendable for the integrity of reputation and name, and because of our singular affection for him and Christian fraternity, in the presence of the aforesaid gentleman himself, and also in the presence of Messrs Francis Brelet and Peter Francis Meriot, and further Louis Lavocat, secretary, specially invited and undersigned for this purpose, we removed small particles from the head of Saint Bernard, first Abbot of Clairvaux, and from the head of Saint Malachy, archbishop commonly called of Armagh in Ireland, who while living was bound to Saint Bernard by the most holy bond [Col. 1720C] of true charity and was buried in our church.
