These we gave to the aforesaid Monsieur Jemelet, placed upon crimson-red silk, each separately wrapped above in paper and sealed with our seal and that of our chief monastery. In testimony of this matter, we issued these presents under our handwritten signature and ordered them to be authenticated with the seal of the chief monastery, on the day, month, and year stated above. Place of the seal [Note: [Col. 1720D] The same seal as that described above in reporting the text of the certificate given by M. Hérardin.]. J. JEMELET. P. F. MERIOT. F. BRELET. Brother L. M. ROCOURT, Abbot of Clairvaux. L. LAVOCAT, assistant secretary.”

The authentication is on a folded sheet of bluish laid paper.

The fragments of the heads have been sawn off. Saint Bernard’s relic measures 66 millimetres in length, 18 millimetres at its greatest breadth, and 5 at its narrowest part; [Col. 1721A] its thickness, measured at the two ends, is 7 and 8 millimetres. Its hue is darker than that of Saint Malachy’s relic, whose dimensions, in the order stated above, are: 48 millimetres—15 millimetres—14 millimetres—5 and 6 millimetres. Each fragment still has its piece of red silk and bears the same seal as the authentication, as well as the seal of the Bishop of Troyes, who recognized these relics on 15 July 1850.

Each fragment is enclosed in paper of the same colour as the authentication and marked with the same seal, which need not be broken in order to open the small packets. Their inscriptions are: *De capite S. Bernardi* (“From the head of Saint Bernard”) and *De capite divi Malachiae* (“From the head of Saint Malachy”), in the same hand as the authentication.

I conclude by transcribing a note which M. Du Lac was kind enough to send me on 19 February 1846; it was drawn up by a person who long lived at [Col. 1721B] the Trappist house of Bellefontaine.

“In 1791 Dom Rocourt gave to the Reverend Father Dom Augustin de Lestranges two very considerable portions of the skull of Saint Bernard and of that of Saint Malachy: I have read the authentication. I have also seen the particles given by Dom Augustin to the abbey of Bellefontaine; each was about one square centimetre and 4 to 5 millimetres thick. It is known (the history of La Val-Sainte in Switzerland attests it) that Abbot Dom Augustin gave portions of approximately equal size to a considerable number of his monasteries, and retained at La Val-Sainte a relic large enough to distribute fragments to convents yet to be founded. This history of the Trappe of La Val-Sainte, near Fribourg in [Col. 1722A] Switzerland, is printed at the beginning of the two quarto volumes entitled: *Regulations of the House of God, Our Lady of the Trappe of La Val-Sainte*, Fribourg, 1792 or 1793.

“The relics given to the abbey of Bellefontaine near Cholet (Maine-et-Loire) were stolen from the church where they were displayed on a feast-day in 1826, I believe; but it seems to me that Dom Rocourt’s authentication is still preserved there.

“As for the ivory crozier [of Saint Bernard], Dom Rocourt had taken it away with him. He presented it to Dom Augustin—I no longer know in what year, but well after the earlier Revolution; so far as I can recall, it was in the first years of the Restoration. What is certain is that it is now possessed at Bellefontaine, together with the authentication wholly written and signed in Dom Rocourt’s own hand: I have read it many times. This crozier, moreover, no longer has its shaft or staff; only the curved part remains, beginning at the small [Col. 1722B] knob which was probably attached to the staff. Its end represents a kind of serpent’s head, I believe. The ivory is somewhat yellowish in colour and is nearly everywhere covered with larger or smaller reddish spots. Quite wrongly, it has been overloaded with gemstones, which prevent one from seeing it in all its parts. The pommel or small knob is partly split by a broad, long-standing crack.

“In 1822 or 1824 Dom Rocourt gave a Trappist Father a portion of the mat on which Saint Bernard slept: it consists simply of plaited rushes. Seven or eight pieces, 10 to 12 centimetres long, are preserved at Bellefontaine; but there is no authentication.”

No. 5. Letter of the Genoese envoy upon his return from Clairvaux (MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 55).

[Col. 1721]

[Col. 1721C] My reverend Father and venerable Lord (this was Dom Claude Largentier, abbot of Clairvaux), enriched by so precious a gift, with which I have been favoured through the goodness of Your Reverence and the charity of your Fathers, it could not be otherwise than that my journey should prosper with every favourable success. Thus I arrived in our country on the third of August, and immediately went to the ducal palace. Having been introduced before the Senate and the Most Serene College, after briefly reporting on the office of ambassador imposed upon me, I made it understood, as proof of the care and diligence I had exercised, that I bore with me some treasure of our glorious protector, and of the great kindness I had received from you; I thereupon brought forth this treasure in their presence. This news was received with such inward rejoicing, such outward applause and satisfaction, that I could scarcely explain it. It was at once resolved to have an entire silver image made of him, to place this sacred bone within it at the appropriate spot where his relic ought to be set, and henceforth to carry it in the annual procession held in honour of this great saint on his feast-day. That very hour it was entrusted into the hands of the Most Serene Doge, to be kept until everything should be prepared. But when news of such a thing had spread through the city, the joy received by every person—great and small, nobles and common people—was very great; and all, desirous of hearing how everything had happened, sought every means of discovering how and in what manner it had been obtained. This led them in part to go about asking, [Col. 1722C] seeking to know from what part of the saint’s body it came; one speaking one way, another another, unable to contain themselves for joy. For several days visits to the place where it rested were extremely frequent, and people questioned me more readily about this than about anything else that might have happened to me during my journey, expressing great esteem for such a treasure and a thousand thanks to Your Reverences, your holy monastery, and all the Fathers who dwell there. There was no one who did not wish that merely some one of those whom you most esteem, for the happy outcome of so great an affair, might have been present, that they might report to them how everything had taken place.

At last the saint’s feast-day came, falling most suitably in this season, during which all the citizens are in town—or at least almost all came into the city—and it was the most crowded and celebrated procession held in our time. But because [Col. 1722D] there had not been sufficient time to make the image, the relic was placed in a worked vessel of gilded crystal, in the middle of a very beautiful and very large silver shrine, in which the Blessed Sacrament is ordinarily carried in procession. It seems that several graces and favours have already been received, in part through the intercession of this great saint. The Most Serene senators have since prepared letters of thanks to Your Reverence and your reverend chapter, which I send you enclosed; and they have further ordered that, as soon as possible, a worthy silver lamp be made—if not according to the saint’s merit, at least according to the rank of those who send it. It is already far advanced; and they have [Col. 1723A] further resolved that I should undertake its care, in order to send it safely to you, that it may hang perpetually at the saint’s sacred tomb, as a testimony to the devout affection and gratitude of the Republic both toward the said saint and toward him who has so graciously favoured and enriched it with his relic. The arms of the Republic will be upon it, solely that they may bear witness to the foregoing.

It has not yet been finally determined where the relic is to be kept, because security would have it placed in the public treasury, while piety and devotion would desire it at a suitable altar where everyone could conveniently honour it at any hour. The Republic considers the church built in honour of Saint Bernard somewhat insecure, because the Fathers dwelling there might tomorrow be expelled if that were the Republic’s good pleasure; consequently, they have the use of it only for a time. Perhaps [Col. 1723B] a marble chest will also be made, with a lock made secure by several nails scattered here and there, and it will be placed beneath Saint Bernard’s altar, as more fitting than any other place, since the church has always belonged especially to the Republic. In short, the anxiety to preserve it well has not yet resolved anything definitively.

I believe that Your Reverence and your reverend Fathers, hearing this news, will be greatly satisfied that you granted my humble prayers, and will see in fact that all I said concerning the great and universal devotion toward this saint is wholly true. The only thing that makes the memory of this sad for me is that, having had the favour of being present at the opening of that sacred shroud in which these sacred bones are wrapped, I did not obtain for myself some part of it, however small, to be given to me. Yet I confess that the great reverence I then felt restrained me from asking, so great was the affection [Col. 1723C] and devotion that pressed upon me at that hour. I know well that I have not deserved this sufficiently, but grace might render me worthy of it—for otherwise it would not be grace—and I was likewise restrained from asking for it. As I was conscientious and zealous in entrusting to the hands of the Republic all that was placed in my confidence by him [*sic*], if anything should procure me this favour, it might perhaps be that I was faithful in what was entrusted to me. If there is a means of obtaining it, I leave it to the same charity and goodness that granted it to me the first time; and if I can succeed in obtaining it, it shall remain continually under good guard in our house, in honour and reverence of this great saint. To say more to you would be either presumptuous or excessively distrustful; the saint well knows and understands the intention of my heart: it is only for the greater glory and honour of the Divine Majesty and for the greater relief of my soul. I make to Your Reverence every [Col. 1724A] submission.

The favour could conveniently be granted through the bearer of the lamp when he returns to our region: seal and enclose it in a folded letter, without revealing to anyone the treasure sealed within. May the Lord inspire you and direct all things to His greater glory, and grant to Your Reverence and to all the Fathers every true felicity.

Your Greatness’s most humble and obliged servant,  
Augustin CENTURION.

Genoa, 7 September 1633.

And on the reverse is: “Translation of the letters of the ambassador of Genoa.—A vertebra from the back of the body of Saint Father Lord Bernard, granted to the Most Serene Republic of Genoa through the Most Illustrious and Excellent Lord Augustinus Centurion, etc.”

Dom Claude Guyton adds (*ibid.*, p. 59): “I have seen the original Genoese Italian letter and French-language version [Col. 1724B] of the person called Augustin Centurion, copied above. I have also seen the original letter giving thanks for the relic, from the Doge or Duke of the Republic, dated 17 October 1633. It mentions the silver lamp which he presents to Saint Bernard, to be preserved in our church as a testimony to his enduring and ardent devotion toward so great a protector of their Republic.—Another letter from the person called Giovo, a merchant at Lyons, dated 4 February 1634, through whom this fine lamp bearing the arms of Genoa came to Clairvaux. It was preserved there until 1720 and for so many years, when Dom Gassot, Abbot of Clairvaux, exchanged it in Paris, apparently not knowing the consequences and the dishonour he did to the house in removing such a monument both of Saint Bernard’s holiness and of the Republic’s devotion toward this saint.—And other letters in the Genoese language on the same subject, with French translations attached.—Also the [Col. 1724C] letter of Dom Claude Largentier, in his own name and that of his convent, undated, giving thanks for the said lamp; beneath it is:

> To the Most Illustrious and Most Serene Duke, and likewise to the most distinguished Consuls and Senators of the renowned Republic of Genoa.
>
> Most Illustrious Prince, Most Serene Duke, and all you most distinguished Consuls and most excellent Senators, most honoured and most revered Lords of the renowned Republic of Genoa.
>
> The pledge of your exceptional devotion toward our holy Father Bernard of Clairvaux, conveyed to us [lacuna] etc.—With the reverence and honour that we owe, we earnestly dedicate and pledge ourselves as the most humble petitioners and most devoted servants of Your Most Illustrious and Most Serene Lordship.
>
> Brother Claude, Abbot, and the entire convent of the monastery of Clairvaux.

At the foot of this copy is: 19 April 1634.

No. 6. Authentication of a relic of Saint Bernard given to the Queen.

[Col. 1723]

*Register of the Secretariat of the Most Reverend Father in Christ and my Lord, Lord Claude Largentier, forty-fifth Abbot of Clairvaux.—Begun by me, Brother Antoine Saulnier of Lignot, professed religious and priest of the same Clairvaux, and secretary to the same Most Reverend Lord my Abbot* (1642–1643–1644–1645), 1 small folio volume bound in red leather, pp. 66–67, year 1643. (Archives of Aube.)

[Col. 1723D] We, the undersigned Abbot, Prior, Cellarer, and Sacristan of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Langres, attest and certify to the most Christian, most august, and most pious Queen of France and Navarre, Madame Anne of Austria, Regent, and to all whom it may concern, that the particle of bone presented by us to Her Majesty, for the fulfilment of her piety and devotion toward [Col. 1724D] our most devout father and blessed patron Saint Bernard, first abbot of this house of Clairvaux, was detached and taken from his precious head beneath the left ear, adjoining the jaw, with all the reverence and respect possible to us. In witness whereof we have signed below, continuing our humble prayers to that same Saint, that, as he was in this world and [Col. 1725A] still is in heaven favoured by the Queen of Angels, so he may be on earth protector of Her Majesty, the King, and all their royal posterity; and we make most humble supplication to the said Majesty always to hold the successors, family, and house of this great saint in singular and particular protection. Given at Clairvaux, under the countersignature of our secretary, 26 July 1643. Signed, F. A. SAULNIER.

No. 7. Sacred relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy.

[Col. 1725]

[Col. 1725A] Under this title I gather a number of notes which seemed useful to collect.

## I. CULT OF SAINT BERNARD AND SAINT MALACHY

See in the *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. IV, the statutes of the general chapters of the Order of Cîteaux concerning the feasts of these two saints: 1220, no. 24; 1260, no. 4; 1238, no. 2; 1295, no. 1; 1321, [Col. 1725B] no. 2; 1234, no. 5; 1321, no. 3; 1274, no. 34; 1323, no. 1; 1273, no. 17; 1191, no. 21; 1250, no. 2.

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 391.—Paris, 20 May 1452.—Indulgences granted in perpetuity by Cardinal Guillaume d’Estouteville, legate of the Holy See in France, to all truly repentant and confessed faithful who would help repair the church of Clairvaux, which “in its structures, buildings, vestments, books, and other ecclesiastical ornaments was greatly fallen into decay, ruinous, and defective” [*in suis structuris, edificiis, paramentis, libris et aliis ornamentis ecclesiasticis multum collapsa, ruinosa et defectuosa*] [lacuna], and who would visit it on the feast-days of the Assumption, Saint Bernard, Saint Malachy, Saint Eutropius, Saint Andrew the Apostle, and All Saints.

*Ibid.*, p. 260.—19 June 1512.—The Abbot of Clairvaux grants participation in the spiritual goods of his abbey and its dependent members to all faithful persons of either sex [*utriusque sexus*] who visit the chapel newly erected in honour of Saint [Col. 1725C] Bernard in the collegiate church of Saint Stephen, Troyes, by the venerable and discreet person Dom François Fenot.

(See Archives of Aube—Saint Stephen Fabric, drawer 3, G. 1.)

*Ibid.*, p. 60.—19 January 1669.—Plenary and perpetual indulgence granted by Pope Clement IX (*Dat. Rom. ap. S. M. Maj.*: “Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major”) to all faithful persons of either sex [*utriusque sexus*] who, after confession and communion, visit a church of a monastery of the Order of Cîteaux on the feast-day of Saint Bernard.

*Ibid.*, p. 62.—Copy of the letter of Dom Magloire, monk of Bonnecombe, in the Clairvaux filiation, Procurator General in Rome for the Order of Cîteaux—1669.

“My Lord, your Order has obtained a plenary indulgence in perpetuity for the day of our glorious Saint Bernard. I send you the original Brief, as to his successor, in order that you may be pleased to have it printed and have copies authenticated by certain notaries [lacuna]. It has been seventeen and a half years that I have worked to obtain this favour. Popes Innocent and Alexander VII would not grant it in perpetuity. I brought this affair before the Congregation of Indulgences, in which this great saint found so many servants that it was there concluded, and the Pope signed it with his own hand; and, as I have been told, it is the first and only one of this kind. Edmond de La Croix was unable to obtain it from Gregory XIV and Clement VIII for more than ten years with regard to laypeople.”

*Ibid.*, p. 373.—“Extract from the notebook of collected determinations of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order” [*Extract. e quad. Collect. definition. Cap. Gen. O. Cist.*].

(Before 1669.)—“On the feast of our most holy Father Bernard, let a solemn procession be held through the cloister enclosure, with three stations and two responsories, namely *Blessed Bernard* [*B. Bernardus*] and *For happy indeed* [*Felix namque*], and the antiphon *Blessed be the Lord God the Father* [*Benedictus Dominus Deus Pater*] [lacuna]. In order more meritoriously to obtain the effect of the indulgence (granted for ten years to laypeople by the most holy Clement VIII, but plenary to religious), all persons of either sex in our Order shall fast on the vigil of the aforesaid feast of our most blessed Father Bernard and say the prayers commended to him in the Breviary.”

[Col. 1726B] *History of the City of Paris*, book VI, 243, vol. I (Paris, 1725, folio).

Eudes de Sully, bishop of Paris, established the feast of Saint Bernard in his cathedral in August 1207. For this he assigned a fund from which the payment for Matins was to be taken: six deniers for every canon present, and as much for each of the four priest churchwardens.

Archives of Aube.—11 January 1443.—Gift to the monks of Clairvaux, by the nobleman Regnault de la Mothe, resident at Bar-sur-Aube, of a parcel of vineyard situated at Rouvre (Aube), “burdened with one denier of quit-rent each year to the monks of Clairvaux.” “Provided that the said monks shall be bound to say one Mass of Saint Bernard on one occasion for the intention of the said Regnault.” (Parchment; seal missing.)

Courtépée, *Historical Description of the Duchy of Burgundy*, Dijon, 1777, vol. II, p. 286.—The chapel of Godran College [Col. 1726C] at Dijon, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin and Saint Bernard, was consecrated by Sébastien Zamet, bishop of Langres, on 15 August 1617.

## II. RELICS OF SAINT BERNARD AND SAINT MALACHY

*Literary Journey*, 1717, Part I, p. 99.—Clairvaux.—“We had the honour,” say the Benedictines, “of saying Holy Mass [upon the tombs of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy, with Saint Bernard’s chalice and with Saint Malachy’s]. Both are so small that they are not half a foot high, but their bowl is very broad and shallow.”

*Ibid.*, p. 104.—“In the treasury they show a chalice of an utterly extraordinary kind, which is claimed to have been used by Saint Malachy. It is approximately of the size and shape of the chalices used today; but four little silver bells are attached to the bowl. It is the only one I have seen of this sort; and it is entirely different from Saint Malachy’s chalice shown in the sacristy, with which strangers who have devotion to it are permitted to say Mass. They also showed us several things claimed to have been used by Saint Bernard, including a chasuble. It is certainly ancient; but if it belonged to him, one must say that the monks of Clairvaux were not so hostile to silk and silver ornamentation, since its silk has a gold braid.”

*Ibid.*, p. 148. Prâlon.—“It is said that Saint Bernard came fairly often to Prâlon to console the nuns and support them in virtue by his advice and counsel. A quarter of a league from the monastery one still sees a spring which he is claimed to have obtained miraculously from Heaven; it has retained [Col. 1727A] the name of Saint Bernard’s spring. We were also shown his chalice and all his priestly vestments, and certainly one cannot doubt that they are from that period. The chalice is somewhat larger than Saint Bernard’s chalice at Clairvaux, but it has the same shape, and, to preserve its proportions, its bowl is likewise broader. The paten is the same. The amice is large and has embroidered ornament, like those still used today in cathedral churches on major feast-days. The girdle is like a little cord, in which there are several knots. The maniple and stole are narrow; the chasuble is very large and wholly closed at the bottom, as ancient chasubles are. It is difficult to believe that Saint Bernard, who professed such great simplicity and poverty, had vestments adorned with embroidery; it is more likely that these were the ordinary vestments of the monastery which [Col. 1727B] the saint used, like the others, when he came there, and that they were preserved in memory of him because he had sometimes used them.”

—“The nuns of Prâlon have in their sacristy,” says Father Chifflet, “several relics of Blessed Bernard, among them the alb and chasuble which he wore in performing the sacred rites; and a chalice of gilded silver, broad like a paten and not very deep, very similar to that other which the monks of Clairvaux still religiously preserve as Saint Bernard’s very own chalice.” (*S. Bern. gen. illustr. assert.*, Dijon, 1660, p. 401.)

—Courtépée wrote in 1777, in his *Historical Description of the Duchy of Burgundy*: “The treasury [of Saint Stephen’s, Dijon] contains Saint Bernard’s priestly vestments, which were at Prâlon, an abbey of Benedictine nuns suppressed in 1748.” See *Literary Journey*, 1717, Part II, p. 150.—Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu. “In the sacristy we were shown an ancient [Col. 1727C] alb claimed to have been used by Saint Bernard when he came to Mont-Dieu.”

*Ibid.*, p. 195.—Abbey of Afflighem in Brabant.—“At the side of the church is an image of the Virgin, where tradition says that, while Saint Bernard was praying, the Blessed Virgin spoke to him; and in memory of this event perpetual silence is observed in the cloister. In the treasury they show this saint’s crozier, which has most inappropriately been gilded and enclosed in silver.”

*Ibid.*, Paris, 1724, p. 46.—Cathedral of Laon.—“We saw in the nave the pulpit from which Saint Bernard once preached.”

*Ibid.*, p. 108.—Abbey of Cambron.—“The chasuble of Saint Bernard which is shown there is neither cloth of gold, nor silver, nor silk, but plain cotton. It is used on his feast-day and at all the monks’ first Masses.” (The Benedictines, *ibid.*, pp. 40 and 199, do not acknowledge [Col. 1727D] the authenticity either of Saint Bernard’s cowl at Vauclair or of his chasuble in the treasury of Aix-la-Chapelle.)

See in Dom J. Méglinger’s *Iter Cisterciense*, pp. 145, 49, what he says of an undergarment belonging to Saint Bernard which was preserved at Longuay Abbey.

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 6.—Thursday, 15 November 1753.—A monk of the Premonstratensian Order, professed of Jandeurre Abbey, now held in commendam, prior and parish priest of Coutrisson in the diocese of Toul, two leagues from Bar-le-Duc, told us at Clairvaux that their house in the city of Prague, Hungary, preserves the original letter written by Saint Bernard to Saint Norbert concerning the holy archbishop’s belief that Antichrist was coming and that the end of the world was approaching.

*Ibid.*, p. 213.—14 March 1428 (*more Gallicano computando*, “according to the French method of reckoning”). Dom Thibaud de Bergières, monk of Clairvaux, deposits in the name of the abbot of the said [Col. 1728A] monastery in the hands of the Reverend Father Dom Gilles, abbot of Fécamp (*Fiscampnensis*): “One covered silver goblet, weighing five ounces and one sterling; and a certain silver cup, at the foot of which, in the base, is an image of Saint Bernard with two masks. This cup weighs seven ounces and fourteen sterlings [lacuna]. Done at Rouen.”

*General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, by Dom R. Ceillier, vol. XXIII, Paris, 1763, p. 100—Article on Saint Hildegard.—“XIV [lacuna] Saint Hildegard wrote a letter addressed to the grey monks, a name sometimes given to the Cistercians because when travelling they wore a grey cloak. Saint Bernard’s cloak is still shown at Saint Victor’s Abbey in Paris.”

*Annales archéologiques*, vol. III, p. 286.—“At Châlons-sur-Marne, in the cathedral, a mitre of Saint Malachy is preserved [lacuna]. This mitre bears in its fabric ornaments like those seen here [Col. 1728B] (the author is speaking of a funeral cloth engraved on a tomb, strewn with quatrefoils and medallions in which are depicted alternately lions passant and eagles with outspread wings).”

Dom J. Méglinger says that at Longuay Abbey he was shown “[lacuna] the mitre of Saint Malachy, Archbishop of Ireland, whose greatest value arises from the famous holiness of the man; for the little gold plates adorning its red silk are not highly valued.” (*Iter Cist.*, pp. 145, 49.)

The Charterhouse of Valbonne (diocese of Nîmes) possesses a fairly substantial fragment of the mat on which Saint Bernard died, and a sandal of Saint Malachy. These precious relics were given to it by the present Bishop of Châlons.

I transcribe the information which His Lordship was kind enough to provide concerning their history in the letter with which he honoured me on 26 December 1854. I ask him to accept here the homage of my gratitude.

[Col. 1728C] “It is from Clairvaux that [the relics of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy which I possess] came to me, through the intermediary of Abbé Becquey, vicar general, who had obtained them from the last Abbot [lacuna]. Those of which Abbé Becquey was custodian, and which he obtained upon his request for them, consist of a fairly substantial portion of the mat upon which Saint Bernard died, and a mitre of Saint Malachy, thoroughly authenticated and sealed with the Abbot of Clairvaux’s seal. By the same means I had received two sandals (gilded leather) of Saint Malachy. I thought that I might give one to the Charterhouse of Valbonne; the other was stolen from me by someone I do not know, and I greatly regretted it.

“Sir, that is all I can say about these precious objects, which after me will be placed in the hands of our Chapter and are intended for our church, although Abbé Becquey [Col. 1728D] imposed no condition in giving them to me [lacuna].

“† M. J., Bishop of Châlons.”

I read with keen pleasure the following report in the issue of *L’Univers* of 20 December 1854:

“On Sunday, 5 November, a new church was consecrated at Morrou, Warren County, under the invocation of Saint Malachy, Archbishop of Armagh in the twelfth century.”

“In the parish church of Fontaines-les-Dijon there is preserved, in a reliquary duly verified by episcopal authority, a fragment of Saint Bernard’s girdle—*de zona S. Bernardi*—which appears to come from the monastery of the Feuillants.”

The Dijon Museum possesses Saint Bernard’s cup, which would be much better placed in the cathedral treasury. Here is its description, after the remarkable *Notice of Art Objects Deposited in the Dijon Museum*, prepared by the late M. de Saint-Mémin, [Col. 1729A] Dijon, 1842, p. 141, no. 718.—Cup of Saint Bernard.

“[Lacuna] It would be difficult to determine the earliest date at which (this cup of boxwood root) could have been mounted in the form of a cup upon a foot and within rings of gilded silver, as it is today [lacuna]. If one were to rely upon the date indicated by the form of the angular Gothic characters in the inscription engraved beneath the foot of the cup, whose use was established only in the first half of the fourteenth century, this vessel would have been fitted with gilded silver only about 150 years after Saint Bernard’s canonisation.

“The inscription reads: *CIATHUS SANCTI BERNARDI ABBATIS CLAREVALLIS*—‘Cup of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.’

“In the manuscript history of Cîteaux Abbey by Dom Crestin, one reads that Saint Bernard’s cup, which he had used during [Col. 1729B] his novitiate, was kept there [lacuna]. It appears, nevertheless, that this relic had been transferred to the treasury of Saint Stephen’s Church at Dijon, according to the following documents [lacuna]. In the register of Saint Stephen, fol. 75v, one reads that on 21 February 1659 Sieur Pidard, goldsmith, requested eleven livres for having repaired Saint Bernard’s cup.

“In the same register, fol. 125, one further sees that on 23 November 1663 two gentlemen requested Saint Bernard’s cup to take into the country, furnishing good and sufficient security.”

I believe I should mention here, simply and without deciding its authenticity, that the public library of Troyes displays a carved wooden chair bearing this inscription: “Chair reputed to have belonged to Blessed Aleth, mother of Saint Bernard, bought in 1793 at the sale conducted at Clairvaux by Revolutionary vandalism, and given in 1849 by F. E. Jourdain to the city of Troyes, his native city.”

[Col. 1729C] **Saint Bernard’s Bible.**

Among the manuscripts of the Public Library of Troyes is preserved a Latin folio Bible, 30 centimetres high and approximately 24 centimetres wide, divided into two volumes. The first contains 261 leaves and the second 234. The script is a very regular minuscule of the first half of the twelfth century, in two columns, with painted initials, often gilded and historiated, and headings in red and blue ink.

On the recto of the flyleaf at the beginning of the first volume, a twelfth-century hand wrote in rather large Gothic characters the words: *PARS PRIMA BIBLE BEATI BERNARDI ABBATIS CLAREVALLIS*—“First part of the Bible of Blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.” Beneath it the inscription is repeated in a minuscule script tending somewhat toward cursive, of approximately the same period. These two volumes are [Col. 1729D] no longer in their original bindings.

The last of the inventories of the house of Clairvaux that Pierre de Virey caused to be drawn up when, in 1471, he took possession of Clairvaux as abbot, concludes the entry concerning this Bible with these words: “This is the Bible of my Lord Saint Bernard.”

The leaves containing the Song of Songs are particularly worn.

These interesting details are extracted from a notice inserted in the *Memoirs of the Academic Society of Aube* (Troyes, 1842, p. 246), by M. Harmand, librarian of the city of Troyes. I take this opportunity to express here to M. Harmand my gratitude for the constant kindness with which he was pleased to assist my researches.

**Saint Bernard’s Antiphonary.**

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 258.—11 March 1500.—I, Brother Servais de Sellerie, professed monk of Jardinet Abbey, of the Order of Cîteaux, [Col. 1730A] in the diocese of Liège, acknowledge and confess that I have had and received from the former Abbot of Clairvaux the sum of thirteen gold écus bearing the sun, as part-payment and deduction from the sum of fifty-two like gold écus bearing the sun which I am to receive for writing the last four antiphonaries, in addition to the other eight volumes which I have already made, written, and notated at the said Clairvaux. And likewise, for writing the said four remaining volumes, I have received one hundred and sixty-six quires of good Bruges parchment, and the fine complete antiphonary for the entire year, well written and notated, which at Clairvaux is said to be Saint Bernard’s antiphonary, lent to me as an exemplar. It begins, on the second leaf after the four leaves at the beginning, “On the method, order, and correction of the antiphonary” [*De modo, ordine et correctione antiphonarii*], and with the letter of the fourth responsory, “He shall come unto thee” [*Veniet in te*]; and it ends on the penultimate leaf, “Behold the bridegroom comes” [*Ecce sponsus venit*]. It is entered in the Clairvaux inventory as Y, 17.

Those four volumes of antiphoners, I, the aforesaid Brother Servais, promise faithfully to write, [Col. 1730B] notate, and complete with my own hand in the manner of the aforesaid other eight volumes, for the stated price and sum of 52 gold écus au soleil—that is, 13 gold écus au soleil for each volume—and to deliver them made and completed as soon as I can, up to illumination and binding; and the said former Abbot shall be bound to pay and satisfy this sum. And of the said sum of XIII gold écus au soleil, in deduction from and as so much less of the aforesaid LII similar écus, I hold myself fully satisfied and discharge the said former Abbot and the said church of Clairvaux; likewise concerning the VIII XX VI quires of parchment for making the said four antiphoners; and also, upon delivering to him or to another person of the said monastery of Clairvaux having authority to receive and act in this matter, I shall return and restore the said fine antiphoner of Saint Bernard, belonging to the said church and monastery of Clairvaux. Or, if I should be overtaken by death before the completion of the said four volumes, I promise to have the said Antiphoner returned [Col. 1730C] to Clairvaux. Witness my manual signature here written and affixed on the 11th day of March, in the year 1500, in the presence of Dom Nicole de Paris, bachelor of theology, Prior of the said monastery; Dom Jehan de Vepria, former Prior of the said place; Dom Jacques de Sézanne, secretary; and Dom Estienne de Beaupré, monk of the said Clairvaux. Brother Servais, monk of Le Jardinet.—Afterwards is written: “The Antiphoner of St Bernard is no longer seen at Clairvaux (1744); apparently it was neglected to recover it from Le Jardinet.” (The former Abbot of Clairvaux mentioned in this document is Dom Pierre de Virey, who resigned his office in 1496 and died in 1506.)

## Note on a manuscript in the Public Library of Dijon, commonly called the breviary of St Bernard

Among the manuscripts of the Public Library of Dijon is one whose small size and unusual [Col. 1730D] form make it highly remarkable, and which would nevertheless probably attract very little notice from strangers and visitors, had not the common opinion which makes it the breviary of St Bernard given it a kind of celebrity.

Research that I undertook into everything remaining to us, whether of St Bernard’s body or of objects that belonged to that great saint, led me some time ago to examine this alleged breviary.

I do not think that the manuscript under discussion has been closely inspected by persons at all versed in the knowledge of ancient scripts. At first glance it would have seemed so obvious to them that it was several centuries later than St Bernard that people would long since have refrained from describing it inaccurately.

But had they had the patience to study it in [Col. 1731A] detail, they would soon have realized that it was a liturgical book for the use of the Cistercian Order. Then, on folio 13, after the versicle of the second nocturn at the Matins of Holy Saturday—*Caro mea requiescet in spe*, etc. [“My flesh shall rest in hope”]—they would have read the following, written in red ink in the same hand as what precedes; and they would have possessed every desirable clarification concerning the nature and origin of this curious little volume:

> “Here ends the little book of the temporal breviary, of the nocturnal praise of my Creator Jesus Christ, which I wrote thus for this reason: lest it be stolen from me as another breviary was. Nor, I pray, should He take it ill that I compiled it in such great brevity, because I lacked a more extensive exemplar. And blessed for ever be He who gave me the boldness to begin and granted me the ability to finish, in the year of the Lord 1498.”

This date is written in black ink, as is the title which I shall copy and which begins on the next line:

> “Absolution from punishment and guilt at the point of death, granted by the divine providence of Lord Sixtus IV, Pope, to the brethren of the Cistercian Order in the time of the Most Reverend Father Humbert, Abbot of Cîteaux,” etc.

The formula of absolution occupies fifteen lines. Three lines written in red ink have been erased, in order to write in black the year-date and the *absolutio a pena*, etc.; its writing displays some differences from the characters preceding it.

The note just transcribed establishes:

1. That we have here a booklet (*libellus*) of the Cistercian breviary, containing the temporal cycle (*breviarii de tempore*), namely the night office (*de nocturna laude*);

2. That the monk to whom it belonged had written it in a very small format (*ideo scripsi*), so that, being wholly portable, it might be more difficult to steal; he thus wished it to avoid the fate of another breviary, which its bulk probably obliged him to leave [Col. 1731C] in the choir, where it had been stolen from him;

3. That the same monk asks Our Lord Jesus Christ to pardon his curtailed work, because he lacked a more extensive exemplar. Evidently he refers here to the brevity of his book, which contains only the night office, and then only during the temporal cycle; he cannot mean by the words *in tantam brevitatem compilavi* the many abbreviations which bristle throughout his text, since he could easily have restored abbreviated words from the exemplar before his eyes;

4. Finally, that the copying of this booklet was completed in the year of Our Lord 1498.

Probably wishing later to fill the space left blank on folio thirteen, after the note in red ink, by transcribing the *absolution in articulo mortis*—the absolution at the point of death—granted to Cistercians by Pope Sixtus IV [Note: [Col. 1731D] Died 13 August 1484.] in the time of Humbert, [Col. 1731D] Most Reverend Abbot of Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 1732D] Died 24 or 26 March 1476.], our monk, in order to gain the necessary space, erased the last three lines of the note; he then rewrote the year-date in black ink, adding the *absolutio a pena*, with which the night office ends from Advent through Easter inclusive.

I now turn to the description of the manuscript.

It consists of 36 parchment leaves, approximately 135 millimetres broad and 155 high (pl. B, fig. 1), ending at points I and K in a tab 30 millimetres high (pl. A, figs. 1 and 2). These tabs, placed against each other, are held by a sort of two-branched iron clasp terminating at M (pl. A, fig. 2) in an elongated ring. The [Col. 1732A] two branches spread from M to I and K (pl. A, fig. 1), where they attain a width of 45 millimetres. Three iron nails, riveted on each side, securely hold the branches of the clasp and the tabs together (pl. A, fig. 1).

If the manuscript is imagined suspended by the ring at the end of the clasp, with its leaves folded, fig. 1 (pl. A) represents it seen from the side and fig. 2 (the same plate) shows it from the middle.

But in order to read it, one must first turn it over, so as to hold the clasp between one’s fingers (pl. A, fig. 3), then unfold and refold each leaf in succession. It is impossible to grasp the mechanism of this operation without having pl. B before one’s eyes.

1. Fig. 1. The leaf is entirely unfolded; it is covered with writing over its whole surface; the letters E, F, G, H, I, K indicate the fold lines.

[Col. 1732B]

[Col. 1732C] 2. Fig. 2. The leaf is folded back upon itself at the intersections G and H. Point A is brought onto C, point B onto D, E onto I, and F onto K. One then reads upon half of the verso of the leaf; this verso is still covered with writing over its entire surface.

[Col. 1732D] [Col. 1733]

[Col. 1735A] 3. Fig. 3. Leaving B upon D, F upon K, and E upon I, A–C is brought onto K, and thus a portion of the writing is covered by one third of the verso of the leaf. This third always remains blank, in order to serve as a cover for the folded leaf (pl. A, fig. 1).

4. Fig. 4. If A is left upon C and E upon I, and D–B is brought onto I, one reads upon one third of the verso of the leaf; this third is covered with writing over its whole surface.

The 36 leaves are read in the following order:

1. Pl. B, fig. 4, α.—Fig. 2, β.—Fig. 1, γ.  
   Folios 1 through 13 inclusive, and 23 through 36 inclusive.

2. Pl. B, fig. 1, γ.—Fig. 2, β.—Fig. 4, α.  
   Folios 14 through 22 inclusive.

Folios 7, 10, 11, and 34 are all folded in the same manner.

[Col. 1735B] There ought to be 37 leaves rather than 36, because the first has been torn out; thus the leaf I count as the first is really only the second. That leaf must have begun with the Matins of the first Sunday of Advent. The following leaf, now the first, very dirty externally and with its writing at first almost entirely erased, begins with the twelfth lesson, or the Gospel, of Matins for the second Sunday of Advent.

On the verso are read these words, in a modern and poorly preserved hand: “BREVIARY OF ST BERNARD.”

The first thirteen leaves contain the night office for the temporal cycle, from Advent to Easter.

The fourteenth leaf opens with the indication of the psalms of the first nocturn at Easter Matins, and the thirty-sixth ends with the collect for the twenty-fifth Sunday after Pentecost.

The writing displays [Col. 1735C] some variations and differences in the course of the manuscript, but I do not judge them important enough to take into account.

The rubrics are written in red ink. Through folio thirteen inclusive, the initial capitals, drawn in black ink, are ornamented with a red dot; a few of them, but very few, are made in minium. From folio fourteen to folio twenty-two, the initial capitals, almost without exception, are written in red ink. After folio twenty-two they become much rarer and are replaced by black-ink initial capitals, upon which red dots reappear.

To conclude all that concerns the description of this manuscript, I add that on folio twenty-one is found the night office for the feast of the Blessed Sacrament: “ON THE FEAST OF THE BODY OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.” This indication alone, had it been examined [Col. 1735D] with care, would have sufficed to reject any thought of dating it back to the twelfth century.

At the beginning of this note, I said that if this small monument were to lose the consideration it gains under the usurped title of breviary of St Bernard, it would nonetheless remain a paleographical curiosity.

Indeed, this manuscript faithfully represents those portable breviaries which accompanied regular and secular clergy in their distant travels and of which Mabillon speaks in his [Col. 1736A] treatise on the Gallican liturgy [Note: [Col. 1735D] *De Liturgia Gallicana*, Paris, 1685. “On the Gallican cursus,” pp. 433–434.]. That learned monk had seen two in the treasury of Cîteaux, and transcribed the faithful description given by Father Joseph Meglinger in his *Iter Cisterciense*. It cannot fail to be read with interest because of its close bearing upon what precedes.

> “The little books do not exceed three fingers’ breadth, though they are somewhat longer. When you look at them closed, they appear small; but when opened, they become three times as large, their leaves, made of rough parchment, being folded three times—downward and on both sides. Nor are the pages filled with letters on both sides, but only on the inner side: so that, even if you separate one leaf from another, unless the folds are unfolded, no writing appears. The writing is indeed exceedingly small and, in a very brief compendium of a few syllables, completes whole sentences. They are not bound by any binding or covering; rather, a thread on one side holds the leaves together lest they fall apart. [Col. 1736B] Then a leather pouch receives the little books, serving fathers who may be leaving the monastery; and in it they are even today protected from dust.” [Note: [Col. 1735D] *Iter Cist.*, p. 239.]

Dom Martène and Dom Durand discuss them with less detail in their *Literary Journey* (vol. I, Paris, 1717, p. 222). They were at Cîteaux in 1710. “We also saw,” they say, “in the treasury the ancient breviaries of the monks of Cîteaux, written in a very small script in small removable booklets, which could easily be taken out and given to travellers.”

I should be very tempted to believe that Father Meglinger, during his journey to Cîteaux in 1667, saw there the alleged breviary of St Bernard, which I have described more fully than he, though certainly with less clarity and felicity of expression.

Nevertheless, unless the iron clasp was added later to bind the leaves by [Col. 1736C] holding the parchment tabs firmly together, it is quite evident that Mabillon and Father Meglinger saw two manuscripts different from ours, since the two manuscripts they examined had their leaves fastened by a simple thread. Dom Martène and Dom Durand likewise seem to indicate, by the expression “removable booklets,” that the alleged breviary of St Bernard did not pass before their eyes.

It is true that these little monuments, noticed by four learned men, may from that point have acquired such considerable value in the eyes of the monks of Cîteaux that they replaced the simple thread, which inadequately bound the parchment leaves, with the iron framework that henceforth assured their complete preservation.

These are only pure conjectures; and fundamentally it matters little whether Father Meglinger, Mabillon, or their learned brethren saw the manuscript [Col. 1736D] with which I am concerned. I wish only to establish, in conclusion:

1. That its form was not unusual at Cîteaux, and that our monk of 1498, considering how to make himself a portable breviary secure from thieves, readily found at Cîteaux the model best suited to his purposes;

2. That one of the small portable breviaries preserved in the treasury of Cîteaux, first seen in 1667 by Father Meglinger, in 1682 by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 1735D] Mabillon visited Cîteaux a second time in 1682 with Dom Germain; see Mabillon’s posthumous works, Paris, 1724, vol. II, *D. J. Mabillonii itinerarium Burgundicum anni MDCLXXXII*, p. 12. In [Col. 1736D] 1685 he published the treatise *De Liturgia Gallicana*, in which he speaks of the two manuscripts in the treasury of Cîteaux: “We once saw in the Cistercian treasury two codices of this kind for travellers, which J. Meglinger thus describes in his *Cistercian Journey*,” etc.], and in 1710 by Dom Martène and Dom Durand, was not then regarded as having been the breviary of St [Col. 1737A] Bernard. Father Meglinger, Mabillon, Dom Martène, and Dom Durand would not have failed at least to report that tradition.

Thus, in 1667, 1682, and 1710, Cîteaux did not possess the breviary of St Bernard.

But how does a manuscript in the library of Dijon, certainly derived from that of Cîteaux, today bear this designation? I cannot explain it.

Did it pass from Cîteaux to Dijon with that designation?

I believe I can answer with certainty: no.

If in 1667, 1682, and 1710 people did not believe that Cîteaux possessed the breviary of St Bernard, I do not see how they could have imagined the contrary there later. Accordingly, the catalogue of the abbey’s manuscripts, compiled very probably at the time of its suppression and preserved in the Library of Dijon, makes no mention of this alleged breviary.

[Col. 1737B] What very modern hand wrote these words on the verso of the first leaf: “Breviary of St Bernard”? On what evidence was a fifteenth-century manuscript adorned with such an inscription? Was it done through ignorance or bad faith? These are matters of which I know nothing, and which seem to me of little use to investigate. It is sufficient for me to have demonstrated by conclusive facts that this designation cannot withstand examination for a moment.

I cannot conclude this note without citing a curious passage extracted from a manuscript *General History of the Cistercian Order*, composed at the beginning of the eighteenth century, of which His Eminence the Cardinal Archbishop of Reims was kind enough to communicate fragments to me. There, on p. 49, we read that, when St Robert left Cîteaux to return to Molesme, he left “to his dear children of Cîteaux, as a pledge [Col. 1737C] of his paternal love, all his possessions, consisting of a little diurnal of a most singular construction, and a cup which he used in the refectory, although it was only of wood. Both are still kept most carefully in the treasury of Cîteaux.” Then a note reads:

> “This cup is round and holds about half a setier; it has no handles, but a small round foot supporting it beneath, on which these words are engraved in relief in Gothic letters: F. ROBERTUS. The wood is highly polished, [Col. 1738A] brown in colour, and seemed to me to be chestnut. As for the diurnal, unless one sees it, it is impossible to convey what it is: it is handwritten in a script so small that it almost escapes the eye; its size is no different from ours, and it has a fastening by which to hang it from the belt.”

Here, then, is another diurnal in the treasury of Cîteaux which strikingly resembles the alleged breviary of St Bernard—if it is not in fact that very manuscript—for the last words of the passage just transcribed leave little room for doubt [Note: [Col. 1737D] Since the author had seen the manuscript to which he gives the name “diurnal,” it is impossible to suppose that he meant here the psalter brought to Cîteaux by St Robert and carefully preserved in the abbey treasury. The note placed at the beginning [Col. 1738D] of that psalter, reported by Dom Martène in the *Literary Journey*, vol. I, p. 222, was too clear for the author, who had examined the manuscript, to make the slightest mistake in identifying it.].

Before describing the curious small manuscripts, Dom Joseph Meglinger had believed that they came from St Stephen and St Alberic. These are his own words:

> “One thing remains, worthy of the curious observer; and because I examined it not carelessly, I shall briefly explain it. Two small books were presented to us, in which the holy Fathers Stephen and Alberic, the first [lacuna] abbots of Cîteaux, had written out with their own hand the canons of the prescribed prayers. I venerated these most beautiful pledges of the simplest antiquity and kissed the clearly shining marks of holiness. The little books are three fingers’ breadth, etc.” (*Iter Cist.*, p. 239, 84.)

I shall repeat here what I said above. If Father Mabillon, or Fathers Martène and Durand, had thought that these small liturgical manuscripts had belonged either to St Bernard or to St Robert, St Stephen, or St Alberic, they certainly would not have failed to make this known publicly. Mabillon venerated those ancient Fathers of the Cistercian Order too highly not openly to express the joy he would have felt in touching such precious relics; but on the other hand, he was too learned a diplomatist not to perceive immediately their lack of antiquity. Thus we see that from Father Meglinger he takes only the description, carefully refraining from reproducing what that monk relates concerning the origin of the little manuscripts. Since he was [Col. 1738C] Father Meglinger’s friend, he did not wish directly to refute his assertions; perhaps he also thought that propriety did not permit him publicly to attack traditions accepted at Cîteaux. He therefore remained silent, making his opinion sufficiently known by the words quoted a little above: “We once saw in the Cistercian treasury two codices of this kind for travellers, which J. Meglinger thus describes,” etc.

## III. Places sanctified by the presence of St Bernard. Cells of St Bernard at Clairvaux

[Col. 1737]

[Col. 1737D] Two cells of St Bernard were preserved at Clairvaux. The first was that which William of Champeaux had caused to be built for the saintly abbot in 1117 (*Acta S. Bern.*, § LIX, *Chronol. Bern.*), outside the regular precincts and enclosure of the first monastery (*extra claustra et terminos monasterii*, St Bernard, *Op. Guillelm.*, VII, 32).

“Dom J. Meglinger says: ‘There is to be seen a wooden house, like a sort of hut, such as people commonly set up in fields for cattle [Col. 1738D] ... We were seized with devout astonishment that this pile of timber had endured through so many centuries—namely, five hundred and fifty years ... Fitted together in a square, it extends eighteen feet on each side, with no storey dividing the upper part from the ground; the roof alone weighing upon the wretched walls. The walls had no glass to make them bright, being sufficiently radiant, to be sure, from the light of holiness of their inhabitant; in place of windows, boards were fitted to the cut openings, so that by a light movement the breeze might be kept out or admitted. The same squalor characterized the bedclothes still hanging there, and the corner in which he lay.’” (*Iter Cist.*, p. 181, 61.)

The Benedictines visited the poor cell. “Behind the apse of the church,” they say, “is the cemetery of foreign abbots who died at Clairvaux, in which, against the church, one sees the tombs of St Bernard’s brothers. In this cemetery is seen the Saint’s cell, which William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, had built for him to relieve him in his infirmities. There is no fireplace, for St Bernard was so mortified and detached from the senses that he would not allow a fire to be made for him. But beneath his bed was a great stone pierced in several places, under which a brazier was lit to warm his room without his noticing it. Nothing could be seen more simple than this room and the bed of St Bernard still preserved there; and if a sick abbot [Col. 1739B] was so poorly housed, one may judge what the quarters of healthy and ordinary monks were like. This room adjoins a little chapel, which apparently was built in order to say Mass for him there. It is held that he died there, and an inscription is read which says this quite clearly.” (*Voyage littéraire*, vol. I, p. 99; cf., concerning the chapel, the *Iter Cist.*, ibid.)

The chapel of which the Benedictines speak was built later by Geoffrey, bishop of Langres and kinsman of St Bernard, who came to die at Clairvaux and lived for three years and nine months in the Saint’s little room. It was built upon the very site where St Bernard had ceased to live. “For his own use he had a chapel, quite humble, built on the place from which St Bernard had departed,” says the Book of Burials of Clairvaux (Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, epitaph of Blessed Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, p. 474). This subsequently led people to believe that St [Col. 1739C] Bernard had died in the chapel.

Manrique described St Bernard’s cell (*Ann. Cist.*, year 1153, IX). In 1738 Dom Briger wrote to Father Pien: “Moreover, the house—or rather, cell—almost entirely wooden, and the bed on which he gave up his spirit, survive to this day at Clairvaux” (*Acta S. Bern.*, *Gloria posthuma*, no. 8). The account printed in the *Annales archéologiques* also speaks of St Bernard’s room, located toward the cemetery. In Dom Milley’s plan it is shown as no. 62, behind the choir on the right, about five toises from the east end of the church, under the title *Cubiculum, capella et hortus S. Bernard*—“Room, chapel, and garden of St Bernard.”

The other cell of St Bernard was preserved in the *monasterium vetus*, the monks’ first residence after the abbey’s translation in 1135.

Dom J. Meglinger describes it thus:

> “Above the stairway which leads from the refectory to the dormitory is placed the cell inhabited by the honey-tongued Father Bernard. It is indeed small, more like a prison than a chamber—and such a chamber as so great an abbot might inhabit. For it is only one foot wider than the cells which, in the dormitory of the new monastery, I described above at no. 57 (they are no more than eight feet high and are eight feet alike in width and length); yet it is subject to far more discomforts, since it is covered only by the bare roof, through which, although rain may not always penetrate, cold and heat and a thousand other annoyances make their way in. Through this same roof, by removing some boards, sunlight is admitted, with a board closing the opening if rain or snow makes it necessary. Moreover, the stairway over which the cell hangs takes away one corner of it by means of the boards with which it is covered; these boards descend along that part in a sloping floor, yet provided convenience [Col. 1740A] to Lord Bernard, who used them as a bed, placing beneath them, in place of a pillow, two other logs smoothed with an axe. All these things may still be seen, but may by no means be touched, since the importunate piety of many people, taking small but repeatedly renewed portions, had almost carried off the whole. This bed, if indeed it can be called such, is now enclosed by railings and exposed to eyes but not to theft. Within them also lies a belt rough with bristles and iron, which the most holy Father was accustomed to wear in mortification of the body, and which was found after his death upon his bare skin. Finally, the seat was no better than the other parts of the cell: besides being raised only one foot above the ground, it was provided by a wall hollowed out in the manner of a chair; and the slope of the overhanging roof did not allow the sitter to raise his head. Therefore, whoever wished to sit down or rise had to bend head and back until, moving one step away, he had room to stand with head erect.” (*Iter Cist.*, p. 201, 67.)

It was from this poor cell that St Bernard one night heard angels singing in the chapel of the *monasterium vetus*. Rising carefully, lest he awaken his monks sleeping in the dormitory immediately adjoining his cell, St Bernard went to the chapel, where he learned the *Salve Regina* from angelic lips.

Shortly afterwards, preaching to his monks in chapter on the dedication of their church, he recalled the marvel that had recently occurred there. “He further related certain words concerning events that had lately occurred in the church: ‘Now,’ he said, ‘the holy angels attended your celebration and have by God’s agency taken you under the care of their guardianship.’ He added certain words which made it understood that, before he had set stone upon stone in the building work, that very place had been designated” (St Bernard, *Op. Joh. Eremita*, II, 7).

Even when St Bernard inhabited the little cell which William of Champeaux had caused to be [Col. 1740C] built for him in 1117, the angels had, as it were, marked out for him the site of the church of the *monasterium vetus*.

“One night,” says William, “after he had poured out his soul before the Lord more ardently than usual, he fell into a light sleep and heard the sound of voices from a crowd that seemed to be passing by. Awakening, and as the voices reached him more distinctly, he left his cell and followed their direction. Not far away was a place still thickly overgrown with thorn and briar bushes, but now greatly changed from what it was then.” (*Haud procul aderat locus densis adhuc spinarum vepriumque frutetis abundans, sed nunc longe mutatus ab illo*—William, VII, 34.) “There he saw angels forming two choirs, and their melodious songs filled him with joy. At first he did not understand the mystery of this vision; he understood it later, when, after the translation of the abbey, he saw the church built upon the very place [Col. 1740D] where he had heard the heavenly music.” (“Yet he did not recognize the mystery of that vision until, after some years, when the buildings of the monastery had been transferred, he saw an oratory placed in the same spot where he had heard those voices”: William, VII, 34.)

Nothing less than these heavenly revelations, moreover, was needed to determine the saintly abbot to leave the wild place where he had fixed his first residence (St Bernard, *Op.*, William, 62).

St Bernard, preaching his sixth sermon for the anniversary [Note: [Col. 1739D] It seems evident to me that the six sermons *In dedicatione ecclesiae* were composed for the anniversary of the dedication of the oratory: “the church ... whose anniversary dedication is being celebrated” (*S. Bern. op.*, vol. I, col. 1081 E).] of the dedication of the church of the *monasterium vetus*, delighted in reminding his monks that this was a place “frequented by holy angels” (*quem angeli sancti frequentant*: St Bernard, *Op.*, vol. I, col. 1088).

[Col. 1741A] Father Mabillon observed, with his customary sound critical judgment, that St Bernard’s sermons *in dedicatione ecclesiae* could not relate to the dedication of the great church of Clairvaux, which took place only after his death (13 October 1174; cf. *Menolog. Cist.*, III *Id. Oct.*), but must concern the dedication of the old church, *veteris basilicae* (St Bernard, *Op.*, vol. I, col. 1075, n. b).

Now what was this *vetus basilica*, if not the church—or rather, the oratory—of the *monasterium vetus*? For it is certainly known that St Bernard understood the mystery of the angelic visions only after the translation of the abbey, when he saw the oratory built on the very spot where the angels had formed their heavenly choirs (William, cited passage).

One will be moved in reading the description which Father Meglinger left us:

> “From there we descended to the oratory, which is such that poverty itself could not have fashioned anything more concise. The altar occupies the front; at the present time it is visible in precisely the same furnishing, and in none other than that with which St Bernard equipped it. That is, on a wooden panel, in cheap colours, the image of Christ hanging on the cross is rendered by crude workmanship; and, at either side, the half-figures of the Virgin Mother and St John are painted with the same brushwork of modest skill. Outside the choir, or middle part of the church, is an altar of St Lawrence on the right side, and one of St Benedict on the left, marked by likenesses likewise rendered in simple fashion.” (*Iter Cist.*, p. 205, 69.)

These paintings on wood, so worthy of Clairvaux’s golden age, probably came from the first abbey, whose poor chapel they had adorned. It was probably before them that St Bernard, at the gates of death in 1125 (*Acta S. Bern.*, § LIX; *Chronol. Bernardina*, year 1125), sent one of his monks to pray for him. “They went and prayed at the altars, three of which were in that basilica: the first in honour of the Blessed Mother of God, the two beside it in honour of the blessed martyr Lawrence and the blessed abbot Benedict” (St Bernard, *Op.*, William, XII, 58).

The *monasterium vetus* was visited in 1517 by the Queen of Sicily (*Ann. Archéol.*). In 1605, the Venerable Mother Anne of Jesus “visited the devout ruins of old Clairvaux (*monasterium vetus*), and the cell of Clairvaux with the little bed on which St Bernard was wont to sleep” (*Vie de la V. M. Anne de Jésus*, Paris, 1636). The monks scraped small fragments from it to serve as relics for their guests. I note that St Bernard’s little bed existed at Clairvaux from 1605 to 1673, since Abbot Pierre (Henri) removed a piece from it on 7 January of that year, with every possible reverence (*Reg. Secret. D. Petri*, XLVI, Clairvaux).

Yet, according to MS no. 15 of M. Matthieu, containing Dom Guyton’s notes (p. 343), it was destroyed in 1590 by the garrison which the council of the Union, established at Troyes, had sent to [Col. 1741D] Clairvaux. Probably the destruction was not complete; and several reasons lead me to believe that the account of damage done in the abbey by the soldiers of the League was somewhat exaggerated.

Before leaving the *monasterium vetus*, I wish to explain a sentence of Father Meglinger. After speaking of Pope Innocent II’s visit to Clairvaux in 1131, he adds: “The gate by which he entered remains blocked up to this day in memory of the event, as I myself saw” (*Iter Cist.*, p. 159, 56).

It seems clear to me that Fr. Méglinger here confused Pope Innocent II’s visit to Clairvaux with that made by Pope Eugenius III in 1148. Pope Innocent II had seen the abbey at its first site, of which nothing remained at the time Fr. Méglinger wrote; whereas in his day there might very well still have been, within the enclosure of Clairvaux, some walled-up gateway commemorating the arrival of Pope Eugenius III. What must have made the [Col. 1742A] confusion still easier is that both popes came to Clairvaux after leaving Reims.

The chapel of Saint Bernard (built not far from his cell by Geoffrey) is mentioned in a fourteenth-century deed, of which the following is an extract:

**Concerning the chamber of the abbot of Villers at Clairvaux.**

1336, on the vigil of the Nativity of the glorious Virgin.—For the sum of fifty Florentine florins, John, abbot of Clairvaux, and the whole community grant to “the venerable fellow abbots . . . . . of Villers, Grandpré, and Saint-Bernard’s-place, now present and their successors in perpetuity, one chamber with its appurtenances, situated between the chapel of Blessed Bernard and the chamber of Hungary, which they and their monks, coming to and returning from the General Chapter, shall have, hold, and peacefully possess during the time of the said General Chapter.”

(Archives of the Aube.—Fifteenth-century copy, on paper.)

[Col. 1742B] *Voyage littéraire*, Paris, 1724, p. 75.—Abbey of Saint-Vaast at Arras.—“As we were leaving the monastery, a cross forty or fifty paces beyond it was pointed out to us, and we were told that Saint Bernard, having come to Arras, stopped at this place and would not enter the monastery, because the abbot and monks had refused him a dependent estate which he was requesting in order to build there an abbey of his order. It is said that this is the place where the provostship of Saint Michael now stands, which is rather pleasant.”

In the fragments of the history of the Cistercian Order which His Eminence the Cardinal of Reims was kind enough to communicate to me, I read on page 390 that Saint Bernard, having visited the holy candle of Arras and wishing to show the esteem in which he held that precious relic, caused a cross of extraordinary size to be erected. It remained in the same place for more than three hundred years. Finally, when it threatened to [Col. 1742C] fall into ruin, the monks of Saint-Vaast rebuilt it in 1447, though giving it less height.

In 1439 the abbess of Groeningen gave the abbot of Clairvaux a fragment of the holy candle, by the following instrument:

“We, Sister Margaret, abbess of the monastery of Groeningen near Courtrai, and Margaret Besoentz and Catherine Cornu, sacristan, and the whole convent of the same place, acknowledge that with unanimous consent we have given and granted to our immediate reverend father, the lord abbot of Clairvaux, a certain portion of wax from the candle of Blessed Mary of Arras, from that portion which the most illustrious lady Countess, widow of the most illustrious prince Lord Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Emperor of Constantinople, [the sense is unfinished] which portion of wax had been taken from that very candle of Blessed Mary of Arras, as was afterwards truly discovered and proved by our elders. In testimony whereof . . . . Given . . . . on the last day of February in the year of the Lord 1439, according to the French style.”  
(Archives of the Aube.—Original on parchment.—Only one seal remains.)

Dom J. Méglinger celebrated Mass at Cîteaux *in sacello D. Bernardi*, “in the chapel of Lord Bernard.” “This is the place in which Saint Bernard himself, in the twenty-third year of his life, underwent his novitiate with thirty companions.” (*Iter Cisterciense*, p. 130, 42.)

Fr. Chifflet printed in 1660, in *S. Bernardi genealogia illustrata assertio*, p. 639:

“At the castle of Grancey (Grancey, Côte-d’Or). There still stands an ancient tower which, beyond all memory, has been called and is still today called the Tower of Saint Bernard, because he is believed to have lodged in it when he from time to time visited his relatives.”

The *Notice sur Châtillon-sur-Seine*, by Abbé Tridon (Troyes, 1847), contains very interesting information concerning the ancient oratory of Sainte-Marie-du-Château [Col. 1743A] and the house in the rue du Truchot, famous at Châtillon for the memories of Saint Bernard associated with them.

I read in the proceedings of the general sessions held at Troyes in 1853 by the French Society for the Preservation of Historical Monuments (Paris, 1854, octavo), pp. 169–170, that an old oak at Cunfin (Aube) still bears the name of Saint Bernard’s oak; that there are relics of Saint Bernard at Dampierre (Aube); and that near Bar-sur-Seine there is a chapel dedicated to the holy abbot. It is said to have been erected in remembrance of his passing through. It is further stated that the valley leading to Jully-sur-Sarce (Aube), seat of a nunnery in which Saint Humbeline became a religious, still bears the name Val-Saint-Bernard.

## IV. Seals bearing the arms of Saint Bernard

[Col. 1743]

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 68.—Seal of William, abbot of Clairvaux, appended to a parchment deed dated 11 October 1431.—Circular.—On the field appears a hand holding a crozier; the arm is covered by the sleeve of the cowl. At the top, to the right of the crozier, is the letter S, and to the [Col. 1743B] left, the letter B. At the bottom, upon the crozier, is a small shield representing the arms of Saint Bernard as we have them today.

Ibid., p. 210.—1656, 26 July.—Seals of the abbot and convent of Clairvaux, appended to a parchment act, impressed in wax between two sheets of paper.

That of the abbot is oval. In the middle is a large niche in which stands a prelate, holding in his right hand a crozier without its veil (handkerchief—or tear-cloth) and supporting a church with his left. An S is below the right hand and a B below the left. At his feet is a shield, surmounted in the middle by a crozier, bearing the arms of Saint Bernard.—In the middle of the community’s seal is a [Col. 1744A] large niche occupied by the Blessed Virgin, holding the child Jesus on her left arm. On the right is a bishop, Saint Malachy, titular saint and patron of the church of Clairvaux; on the left, Saint Bernard.

Ibid., p. 449.—1524, 19 May.—Circular seal representing the Blessed Virgin, the child Jesus, Saint Malachy [Col. 1744B] and Saint Bernard. “+ SEAL OF THE CONVENT OF THE MONASTERY OF CLAIRVAUX.”

Ibid., p. 569.—1669, 21 November.—Laurent Gorillon, prior of Clairvaux, vicar-general of the abbot of Clairvaux.

Oval seal, three inches high by two wide, impressed on a host.—In an ornate niche, a regular abbot standing, haloed, clothed in the monastic habit, holding in his right hand a crozier with its veil; a church rests upon his left hand: this is Saint Bernard. Beneath the right elbow, S; beneath the left, B.—Below the feet are the arms of Saint Bernard, surmounted centrally by a crozier. “SEAL OF THE VICARIATE OF THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX.”

## V. Portrait of Saint Bernard

[Col. 1743]

[Col. 1743C] With regard to the portrait of Saint Bernard, I wish to note a sentence of Dom Joseph Méglinger. This religious, recounting the profound impression he had felt at seeing the heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy preserved in the treasury of Clairvaux, expresses himself thus: “The countenance especially of the honey-tongued Father—known from the portrait commonly encountered, and here wrought so elegantly—moved the inmost depths of every heart.”

The words *ex effigie passim obvia notus*—“known from the commonly encountered portrait”—clearly establish that a constant tradition existed concerning Saint Bernard’s portrait. I therefore note that Fr. Méglinger adorned his book entitled *New Portrait of Saint Bernard, the Honey-Tongued Doctor of the Church*, Baden in Switzerland, 1670, octavo, with a portrait admirable in my opinion, and one which bears the closest resemblance to the portrait engraved by Drevet (*Life of Saint Bernard*, by Villefore, Paris, 1704, quarto); to that given by the Bollandists after [Col. 1743D] Puricelli; to the fine painting in the church of Ville; to the eighteenth-century terracotta bust found in the parish church of Fontaines-lez-Dijon; and to ancient enamels which I have seen in various collections.

The profile portraits by Philippe de Champaigne (*Life of Saint Bernard*, Paris, 1648, quarto; small engraving, Paris, at Chereau le jeune) and by Fra Angelico of Fiesole seem to me to depart from the accepted type.

The Benedictines report in their *Voyage littéraire* (Paris, 1717, part II, p. 205) that they found among the Regular Canons of Rouge-Cloître (the Low Countries), [Col. 1744C] “in a manuscript of Saint Bernard, the portrait of this saint, represented in the old habit of the religious of Cîteaux, whose hood was attached to the robe.”

In the first part of the same work the Benedictines again speak of this old habit (p. 6). “In the crossing of the church of La Mercy-Dieu,” they say, “are the tombs of several lords of Prulli, around which religious are represented in the old habit of Cîteaux, with the hood attached to the cowl.”

“At the abbey of La Ferté,” they say on p. 227, “one sees upon the tomb of a lord of Marcilly a religious represented in the old habit of the Cistercian Order, that is, with a cowl whose hood is not separate. We observed the same thing on the tombs of the abbots in the chapter house: all of them, up to 1387, have the hood attached to the cowl. The [Col. 1744D] first who wears the detached hood is from the year 1419.”

Here is, on this subject, an extract from the fragments of the manuscript *History of the Cistercian Order* which His Eminence the Cardinal of Reims was kind enough to communicate to me, p. 408:

“One sees in the church of Longpont Abbey the tomb of Blessed John of Montmirail. It is under an arcade in the sanctuary of the church, on the Gospel side, raised three or four feet above the ground. The saint is seen lying upon his tomb, in a very lifelike raised figure, and clothed in all his regular garments as they were worn at that time. They may serve to decide [Col. 1745A] several questions debated in our day concerning the manner in which the religious of Cîteaux were dressed in Saint Bernard’s time. One sees that they did not wear over the cowl that great hood which falls over the arms and breast and descends behind almost to the heels. Of that whole garment, they had precisely only what served to cover the head: it was sewn to the collar of the cowl and ended in a small point above, almost as the Carthusians still wear it. Their cowl did not have those long [Col. 1746A] and ample sleeves that fall to the ground. They went only to the wrist and were only as wide as was necessary to pass easily over the sleeves of the robe, which were shorter and narrower.”

MS IX of Abbé Matthieu, after reproducing the preceding passage (p. 336), adds: “This costume may still be seen in two representations of Saint Bernard at Clairvaux: one in the church, the other at the entrance gate of the great cloister.”

## VI. Seal of Saint Bernard

[Col. 1745B] On 16 August 1837 M. Deville, director of the Museum of Antiquities at Rouen, announced to the Academy of Inscriptions the discovery of Saint Bernard’s seal. [Note: [Col. 1745C] See M. Deville’s letter to the permanent secretary in Gaume’s edition of the works of Saint Bernard, vol. I, p. 1, col. 928 ff.] This seal, given by a retired officer, M. Pays of Issoudun, [Note: [Col. 1745C] M. Pays wrote to M. Deville when sending him the seal: “This seal was bought from a dealer who had acquired, in 1790, the old copper objects of the collegiate church of Saint-Cyr at Issoudun, [Col. 1745D] affiliated with Clairvaux.” M. Deville adds: “How and why was this seal deposited in the collegiate church of Saint-Cyr at Issoudun? That I do not know”; then he adds in a note: “It should not seem surprising that the monks of Clairvaux allowed the seal of their illustrious abbot to leave their hands, when one sees those same monks putting up for sale the shrine that contained his body in order to pay [Col. 1746C] for some paltry vacancies of their convent.” (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. II, col. 1420.) I make several observations on these passages. The fact that the dealer had acquired the old copper objects of the collegiate church of Issoudun does not necessarily entail that Saint Bernard’s seal formed part of them; the dealer might have obtained it elsewhere. [Col. 1746D] I have proved in the course of my Letter that Saint Bernard’s body had never been placed in the shrine of Messire Tristand de Bizet, bishop of Saintes, mentioned in the extract from the *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum* cited by M. Deville; and that this shrine had never been sold, since the Benedictines still saw it in 1717.], is deposited in the museum at Rouen.

“It is of yellow copper,” says M. Deville, “and oval in shape. It is 40 millimetres long and 30 at its greatest width; its thickness is five millimetres; it weighs 30 decagrams. The reverse is flat and smooth, without the appearance of a handle or attachment.”

It was very properly observed in the *Revue Archéologique*, second year, second issue (1845), p. 99, that Saint Bernard is represented seated upon an abbatial chair whose arms terminate in crudely depicted lions’ heads.

The *Revue* believes that the holy abbot holds a roll in his right hand.

Fr. Mabillon, annotating Saint Bernard’s letter to Eugenius III, written around 1151 (*Epist.* 284), [Col. 1745C] in which he announces that the malice of a forger had compelled him to change his seal, sees a book in the right hand rather than a roll. “Certainly, on Bernard’s own charter concerning the settlement of the dispute between the monasteries of Sainte-Geneviève and Saint-Victor, Bernard’s seal is appended, with his name and likeness, holding a book in his right hand and a crozier in his left.” (*Works of Saint Bernard*, Epistle 284, note d.)

I read in the fragments of the *History of Clairvaux Abbey* by Dom Le Boullenger (MS IX of Abbé Matthieu, p. 434): “Saint Bernard [Col. 1746B] found himself obliged to have another seal engraved. This seal is still shown in the treasury of Clairvaux; it is of copper and oval in shape. Saint Bernard is represented seated upon it, holding his crozier in his left hand and a *pax* [a liturgical kissing-tablet] in his right; and around it is written: ‘+ SEAL OF BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX.’”
