“Saint Bernard’s seal,” says Dom Claude Guyton (MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 8), “which is preserved at Clairvaux, with which the saint sealed an agreement which he made for Saint-Victor-les-Paris, and which remains there, represents Saint Bernard seated.”

In 1594 the abbot of Cîteaux wrote to Dom Denis Largentier, abbot of Tironneau (MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 40):

“I have written to you from Spa, Antwerp, and Brussels . . . . If you find Gaguin’s *History*, you will see in the account of Philip the Fair that, when all the bishops stood against Pope Boniface, the abbot of Cîteaux alone stood for the Pope. We have had our fine privileges, in one of which [Col. 1746C] it is said: ‘You strove with me; you shall sit with me.’ I would not wish to do less than my predecessor in the present affair; but Belleforest of Comminges and Jean de Serres say not a word of it in their histories of France . . . . Being seated is not peculiar to the abbot of Cîteaux: Saint Bernard’s seal represents him seated. Given at Besançon, 14 November 1594.

Your confrere and cousin: Brother EDME, Abbot of Cîteaux.”

M. Deville rightly observed that the Rouen seal is Saint Bernard’s second seal, [Col. 1747A] the one which the unfaithfulness of his secretary Nicholas obliged him to have engraved and which contained his image and name—*continente et imaginem nostram et nomen*, “containing both our image and name” (*Epist.* 284; see also *Epist.* 298). The imperfection of the engraving has always, as may be seen, cast doubt upon the precise nature of the object Saint Bernard holds in his right hand; but I believe that, in accordance with the usages followed in the twelfth century for abbots’ seals, one should adhere with Fr. Mabillon to the interpretation as a book. (Cf. Natalis de Wailly, *Elements of Palaeography*, part IV, ch. VII.)

What was the form of Saint Bernard’s first seal? This is learned from several texts which I shall cite.

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 61.—“Charter from Saint Bernard’s time, on a folio sheet. It is a duplicate original of the agreement concluded between the monks of Vauluisant and the Knights Templar through Saint Bernard’s agency . . . . The second seal [Col. 1747B] is an oval, around which is: ‘+ SEAL OF THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX.’ The field is occupied by a hand holding an inward-turned crozier; its arm is covered by a robe-sleeve and, over the sleeve, by that of the cuculla [cowl] . . . . Along the writing, crosswise, one sees half of each of the following letters: CIROGRAPHUM [chirograph].”

I have thought it useful to transcribe here the agreement of which Dom Guyton speaks, from the cartulary of Vauluisant Abbey (Imperial Library.—Quarto, parchment.—Thirteenth century.—folio 83r).

**Agreement of the monks of Vauluisant and the Knights of the Temple, through the hand of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.**

“In the name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity. Let all present and future persons know that between the monks of Vauluisant and the Knights of the Temple of Colatoire, this settlement was made through the hand of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: that the Knights Templar granted to the monks everything [Col. 1747C] which they had in the territory of Cirilly, from the boundary between the grange of the said knights and the grange of the monks; namely, half the courtyard, half the tithe, and other lands. Thus, henceforth, from the said boundary as far as Sevei, the Knights Templar may acquire no woodland or land, unless it has been given altogether freely as alms, so that he who gives it receives from them nothing of earthly substance.

“Likewise, the monks of Vauluisant granted to the Knights Templar everything which they had from the said boundary [Col. 1748A] as far as the bank of the Venne; thus, in that valley they may acquire no woodland or land, unless it has been given altogether freely by someone, so that he who gives it receives from them nothing of earthly substance.

“Norpaud, abbot of Vauluisant, and Brother Everard, Master of the brethren of the Temple who are in France, approved this.

“And in order that it may remain firm, it was confirmed by the seal of each party, together with the seal of the abbot of Clairvaux.

“Brother Humphrey, Master of the Temple, also approved this.”

The *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XII, col. 231) speaks thus of this settlement: “Norpaud made certain exchanges with the Knights Templar concerning land at Cerilly. To the charter of the exchange is appended Saint Bernard’s seal, in which is represented the hand of a monk bearing an abbatial crozier.”

This, therefore, was Saint Bernard’s first seal, for the agreement which I have transcribed is earlier than the period [Col. 1748B] when the holy abbot found himself compelled to have a seal engraved with a new design.

The names of two persons mentioned in the agreement help to establish its approximate date.

Norpaldus, or Norpaudus, first abbot of Vauluisant, served from 1129 to 1159 (*Gallia Christiana*, ibid.); Everard des Barres, particular master of his Order in France from 1143 onwards, was elected Grand Master of the Temple in 1147. (*Art de vérifier les dates*—one does not find the name Humfredus among those of the Grand Masters of the Temple.)

Now, since he is still called here *Magister fratrum de Templo qui in Francia sunt*, “Master of the brethren of the Temple who are in France,” it is evident that the agreement is earlier than 1147; but it was only later that Saint Bernard changed his seal.

On 7 September 1520, Dom Edme, abbot of Clairvaux, travelling to Rome, arrived with his small party [Col. 1748C] at the monastery of Bonmont in Savoy, “where,” says the account of his journey, “is Saint Bernard’s purse with two letters dictated by him and sealed with his seal, which has the inscription around it: ‘SEAL OF THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX,’ and in the middle is a hand holding a crozier.” (See the curious account of a journey to Rome, begun 23 August 1520 and ended 14 April 1521 by the Reverend Father in God, Dom Edme, forty-first abbot of Clairvaux—published by M. Harmand in the *Mémoires de la Société académique de l’Aube*, second series, vol. II.)

## VII. Documents in which Saint Bernard is mentioned

[Col. 1747]

[Col. 1747D] It would be highly important to collect and publish all documents in which the intervention of Saint Bernard, or his presence as witness, is mentioned; such documents would be valuable for establishing the chronology of his history still more completely.

There are in the Archives of the Aube, among the charter collections of Clairvaux, Larivour, Montiéramey, etc., several original charters in which Saint Bernard is named as a witness. I must even make particular mention of those magnificent parchment documents dating from the earliest years of Clairvaux Abbey, in which the skill of its calligraphers appears in all its brilliance.

The *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* (vol. VI, Paris, 1739) cite several documents in which Saint Bernard’s name appears. Here is the list.

p. 110—In the works of Guibert of Nogent, p. 832, letter of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon (1124).

p. 152—In Chifflet’s *Opuscula*, 4, p. 176, instrument of Hugh, duke of Burgundy (1127).—In the *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, p. 307, charter of Theobald, Count of Champagne, concerning the church of Sparnacum (1127).

p. 370—In Marlot, vol. II, p. 337, letter of Samson, archbishop of Reims (1143).

p. 699—Charter of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon (1146).

p. 723—Diploma of Count Henry (1149).

See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, Instruments, col. 268, charter XXXII (1152).

Here are copies of several documents which *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, merely indicates thus in its article devoted to Montiéramey Abbey:

“To Guy, at the request of Saint Bernard, Bishop Atto gives the church of Clarey; Innocent II confirmed that gift on the Nones of May.”

“Gift of the church of Follis, confirmed by Lucius II, fifteen days before the Kalends of April.”

“At Clairvaux, Guy obtains from Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, the churches of Landreville and Loches.”

[Col. 1749A] Imperial Library.—Cartulary of Montiéramey Abbey; folio, parchment. (There is a copy on paper, folio.)

Folio 48r.—Parish of Clarey.

“Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Guy, abbot of Montiéramey, greetings and apostolic blessing. We commend the things which, from regard for piety and love of religion, are bestowed upon monasteries and other pious places by our brother bishops; and, willingly granting assent to the requests and desires of petitioners, we strengthen them by the protection of our written instrument. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, at the request of our dearest son Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, we confirm for you the gift of the church of Clarey lawfully made to you by the bishop of Troyes, and establish it by the privilege of our written instrument. Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of May.”

Ibid., folio 48r.—Parish of Folz.

“Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1749B] sons G., abbot, and the monks of Montiéramey monastery, greetings and apostolic blessing. We desire that those things which have been done by our brother bishops and the rulers of God’s churches out of regard for religion should be confirmed in their stability, lest they be disturbed by the opposition of wicked men. Therefore, at the request of our venerable brothers Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, we receive your petitions with fatherly kindness and, by the present page of writing, confirm for you and, through you, for Montiéramey monastery the church [Col. 1750A] of Follis, just as it was canonically granted to you by our venerable brother Atto, bishop of Troyes. But if anyone, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against the page of this our confirmation, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Given at the Lateran, fifteen days before the Kalends of April.”

Ibid., folio 85r.—“In the name of the Lord. I, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres, wish it to be known that I have given the churches of Landreville and Loches to Abbot Guy and to the church of Montiéramey monastery, to be freely possessed in perpetuity, with the approval of Dean Clarembald, to whose ministry they belonged, and of the priest Ralph, who held them; upon the following condition: that henceforth the monks shall have the election of the priest; and, while this Ralph holds them, the monks shall have a fourth part of their revenues, excepting baptismal offerings, marriages, burials, and confessions, and the penny from blessed bread [Col. 1750B] and the churchings of women; but after the death or resignation of Ralph himself, they shall have half of the other revenues, apart from the things which we have named, which belong to the priest himself. Witnesses are Lord Alan, bishop of Auxerre; Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; etc. (thus). Done and confirmed by the impression of our seal at Clairvaux, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1152.”

## VIII. Charter of the foundation of Clairvaux

[Col. 1749]

[Col. 1749B] “I find in the fragments of the manuscript history of Clairvaux Abbey by Dom L. Boullenger (MS IX of Abbé Matthieu, p. 351) a copy of the charter of Clairvaux’s foundation, ‘drawn up in the following terms, taken word for word from the original in the abbey archives.’

[Col. 1749C] ‘In the name of the (in the printed editions they add “holy and”) undivided Trinity begins the charter of Count Hugh. Let all present and future persons know that I, Hugh, Count of Troyes, give to God, to Blessed Mary, and to the brethren of Clairvaux the place itself which is called Clairvaux, with its appurtenances, fields, meadows, woods, vineyards, and waters, retaining absolutely nothing for myself (the printed editions read “for me”) or for my heirs. Of this, my knights Acardus of Reims, Peter, and Robert of Orléans are witnesses. And it should be known that Geoffrey Felonia gives his grazing-rights in the territory of Juvancourt, both in wood and in open country, at all times. And if the animals of the said brethren cause any damage, only the principal damage shall be made good, without a fine. I gave all these things in the presence of the above-named witnesses. It should likewise be known that Lord Rainaud of Perecin (the printed editions read *Perceris*, and the *Gallia Christiana* *Preci*—the latter form is now in use) gave to the same brethren pasture and rights of use throughout [Col. 1749D] all his land, especially in the waters, woods, and meadows in the territory of Perecin. Witnesses of this are Acardus of Reims and Robert, my knights. Likewise, it should be known that I, Hugh, Count of Troyes, approve and grant to the same brethren free and undisturbed possession of the land and wood of Aretela. We, Joceranus, bishop of Langres, and Hugh, Count of Troyes, confirm these gifts by his seal and ring’ (the printed editions read ‘my seal and ring’).”

“Two large pendant seals in green wax are attached to this instrument. The first represents Jocevan seated, holding the pastoral staff in his right hand and a book in his left, with the following inscription around it: ‘+ SEAL OF JOSCERANUS, BISHOP OF LANGRES.’

“The second represents Hugh on horseback, wearing chain mail, holding in his right hand a raised naked sword and in the other an oblique shield resting [Col. 1750B] on his left side, upon which nothing is depicted; around it one reads: ‘SEAL OF HUGH . . . . .’”

Since this instrument bears no date, it is difficult to say precisely in what year it was made. The *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 155, among the Instruments, assigned it the date 1115, which it drew from a new extract [Col. 1750C] read upon a framed panel fastened in the cloister of Clairvaux.”

This text may be compared with that which Fr. Mabillon had received from Clairvaux and which had been copied from the original deed—*Ex autographo Clarae-vallensi acceptam referre debemus*, “we must report that it was received from the Clairvaux autograph” (*Works of Saint Bernard*, note on Epistle XXXI, 24); with that published by Fr. Chifflet—*Ex autographo Clarevallensi*, “from the Clairvaux autograph” (*S. Bernard’s Genealogy Illustrated Asserted*, p. 513); and with the *Gallia Christiana* (cited place).

In 1853 I saw exhibited in a case at the public library of Troyes a facsimile copy of the charter of Clairvaux’s foundation with two pendant seals. It is a poor imitation made on parchment in the seventeenth or eighteenth century. In the Clairvaux charter collection at the Archives of the Aube I found several imitations of old documents of the same kind as that just mentioned.

The following document is not out of place after [Col. 1750D] the charter of foundation. MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 448.—“I, Henry, Count of Troyes, wish it to be known to present and future persons that I grant to the brethren of Clairvaux, to possess in perpetuity, whatever my predecessors conferred upon the same brethren: namely, the place itself in which that monastery is situated, with the lands, waters, vineyards, woods, meadows, and fields adjoining the aforesaid monastery, and whatever they have acquired from the fief of my ancestors up to the present day, retaining absolutely nothing for myself or my heirs. I also give to the same brethren pasture and rights of use in waters and meadows as well as woods, in every territory throughout my land, wherever they may freely go. In order that this may remain firm and stable in future, I have caused the present page to be strengthened by the impression of my seal. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1168.”—Pendant seal—round, broken through the middle—the rider and horse are distinguishable, but not the writing.

## IX. Miscellanea

[Col. 1751]

[Col. 1751A] **Itinerary of Saint Bernard from Châlons to Clairvaux in 1146.**

Returning from Germany in 1146, Saint Bernard was at Châlons-sur-Marne on 2 February, where Louis VII had come to meet him; it was a Sunday. (“On the Lord’s Day, the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary was being kept; and Louis, king of the Franks . . . came to Châlons to meet the man of God.”)

Saint Bernard remained there two days (*detentus est per biduum*). He left on Tuesday, 4 February (*egredienti vero feria 3a . . . .*), and came to Donnement, about ten leagues from Châlons.

On 5 February he celebrated Mass at Donnement in honour of Saint Agatha, whose feast was being observed: “on Wednesday . . . . for on that day, in a village of Champagne called Davament, [Note: [Col. 1751D] *Davament* is a copyist’s error. Donnement must be read—in Latin, *Donamentum*. Donnement is a commune not far from Rônay, [Col. 1752D] where Saint Bernard will be seen to arrive. Like Rônay, it belonged to the deanery of Margeries (*decanatus Sanctae Margaretae*).] . . . he celebrated the solemnities of Mass.”

He then came to Rônay, about [Col. 1751B] two leagues from Donnement (“to a town called Rônay”), and then to Brienne, situated at approximately the same distance from Rônay (“on the same road is another castle, called Brena by the natives”).

Finally, he arrived at Bar-sur-Aube, five or six leagues from Brienne; thus he travelled about ten or eleven leagues that day (“on that day we came to Bar”).

On Thursday the 6th he celebrated Mass at Saint Nicholas and returned to his beloved valley: “therefore, on Thursday the holy man celebrated the solemnities of Mass in the church of Saint Nicholas . . . . on that day he was restored to Clairvaux.”

—(*Works of Saint Bernard*, book VI, or *Of Miracles*, ch. XIII.)

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 344:

**Concerning our holy Father Bernard.**

In the year one thousand ninety-one,  
Fontaines Castle gave Bernard birth.

[Col. 1751C] Seven years only having afterward passed,  
The Cistercian Order began in this monastery.

But when the Order had risen to fifteen years,  
The holy man received the religious habit within,  
Under Stephen, drawing thirty companions after him.

Thereafter made the first abbot of Clairvaux,  
The exalted man followed an exalted life and filled  
The world with the light of doctrine and resplendent signs.

He rejected seven bishoprics offered to him,  
Lest fleeting honour impede enduring things.

In vain would I attempt to set in verse  
The rest, which even great books cannot contain.

May he obtain help for us from the Almighty.

Amen.

—The fourth verse shows that this piece was located at Clairvaux; it was probably an inscription.

The edition of the *Grand Exorde* published by Dom Ignace de Ybero (Pamplona, 1621, folio) ends [Col. 1751D] with a mirror for religious, which, I think, readers will be pleased to find here.

**MIRROR OF RELIGIOUS, collected from various sayings of our blessed father Bernard; the monk who looks into it will quickly attain the summit of perfection.**

Let every religious be:

In church, devout.  
In choir, diligent in duty.  
[Col. 1752A] At the altar, discerning.  
In the library, silent.  
In private places, honourable.  
In the cell, studious.  
In the infirmary, a healer.  
Among the brethren, pleasant.

Among secular people, rare.

In nothing, downcast.

In adversity, peaceful.

In prosperity, modest.

In the cloister, enclosed.

In the cemetery, devout.

In the refectory, content.

In prayer, assiduous.

In reading, inquisitive.

In bed, composed.

In counsel, eloquent.

In compassion, dear.

Among the nations, timid.

[Col. 1752B] In obeying, most compliant.

In service, most ready.

In confessing, most humble.

At table, sober.

In the sacristy, trustworthy.

In chapter, modest.

At the gate, brief of speech.

In the garden, hardworking.

In the kitchen, hateful.

In conversation, chaste.

In hospitality, provident.

In appearance, restrained.

And thus in all things he will always be most pleasing to God, and a mirror to men:

Three things become every religious:

To speak little,

To have few intimates,

And to pray much.

[Col. 1752C] Three praiseworthy things in a religious:

The weight of maturity,

Love of the community,

And flight from private property.

Three things to be condemned in a religious:

Lack of devotion,

Dissoluteness,

And wandering.

Twelve abuses of the cloister.

A negligent prelate,

A disobedient disciple,

An idle young man,

An obstinate old man,

A courtly monk,

A litigious religious.

An ostentatious habit,

Exquisite food,

Rumour in the cloister,

Contention in chapter,

[Col. 1752D] Dissoluteness in choir,

Irreverence beside the altar.

A golden admonition.

Enclosed in the cloister, despise worldly applause;

Long for the kingdom, full of wondrous sweetness.

Stand here, and do not cease: after sowing come harvests;

After weeping, applause; after departure hence, Paradise as a dwelling.

Meditation to be practised by day and night.

Your death, Christ’s death, the world’s deceit, Heaven’s glory,

And Hell’s pain—these must be meditated upon by you.

No. 8. Extracts from the manuscripts of M. Abbé Matthieu.

[Col. 1753]

[Col. 1753A] MS. XV (Notes of Dom Claude Guyton), p. 502.—(1143–1157). In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Galeran, Count of Meulan, to all God’s faithful, now and hereafter. We ought to do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith; for thus the Lord instructs us, that we should make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings. Therefore I, Galeran, Count of Meulan and lord of the castle called Gournay, have granted, into the hands of the venerable Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, to the brethren of Clairvaux and to all who belong to the Cistercian Order, free passage for their goods, so that no toll shall be demanded of them either at Gournay or anywhere else among the places belonging to me. And that this grant may remain firm for ever and may not be annulled by any of my successors, I have confirmed this charter by the impression of my seal, adding also the testimony and seal of the Bishop of Paris. I, Theobald, by God’s grace [Col. 1753B] Bishop of Paris, order that this grant be held valid and confirm it by episcopal authority. Its witnesses are Henry of Ferrières, William of Pinu, and Robert of Fromeville, clerics; Bernard the archdeacon; and Ralph and John, canons of the Church of Paris.

—Two pendent seals: the second is oval, representing a seated bishop, with his crozier turned inward: “SEAL OF THEOBALD, BISHOP OF PARIS.” The first is round, impressed on both sides, and represents a lord on horseback: “SEAL OF GALERAN THE COUNT.”

Ibid., p. 504, year 1159.—In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Amen. Frederick, by God’s grace Emperor of the Romans and ever August, to all the faithful, both present and future, for ever. Since it often happens that good deeds once performed are either altered through human inconstancy or [Col. 1753C] erased through forgetfulness, let all know that I, by the will and consent of Beatrice the Empress, my wife, for the remission of our sins and of those of all our predecessors, grant to the house of Clairvaux to possess for ever whatever Guy of Wangionis-Rivo (Vignory) gave and granted to that house from his own fief, together with all other things and his men settled on their holdings in the time of Bernard, Abbot of blessed memory: lands, woods, waters, pastures, and all other appurtenances; and also whatever Bartholomew, son of the same Guy, subsequently granted from the same gift and alms. And lest anyone’s rashness should henceforth dare to violate this, I have thought it proper to confirm it by the impression of my seal. Done at the siege of Chreme, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159. Witnesses: Reynald the chancellor, elected Archbishop of Cologne; Everard, Bishop of Bamberg; Henry, Duke of Saxony; Berthold, Duke of Thuringia; and Adam, Abbot of Ebra.

[Col. 1753D] —The two large round seals are attached to the charter itself. The first represents a seated prince, dressed in a long robe with a mantle over it; a crown on his head, a sceptre in his right hand, and in his left a globe surmounted by a cross: “FREDERICK, BY GOD’S GRACE EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS, AUGUST.” The other, opposite it, represents the seated Empress: “BEATRICE, BY GOD’S GRACE EMPRESS OF THE ROMANS, AUGUSTA.”

Ibid., p. 178 (year 1202).—Bernard, Dean of Bar-sur-Aube, makes a donation to Clairvaux.

The same dean made this gift in the chapter-house of Clairvaux, in the presence of Garnier, formerly Bishop of Langres; [Col. 1754A] he offered it at the altar of Blessed Bernard, while Everard, priest of Longchamp, Brother James, and Brother Matthew, cellarers of Clairvaux, stood by and touched the gift itself.

Hilduin, Bishop of Langres, confirmed this donation along with several others in 1202.

Ibid., p. 454, year 1335.—[Lacuna.] We, Brother John, Abbot of Clairvaux, [lacuna] piously considering the labour which our fellow brethren, especially the monks, endure in the vigils and on the feast-day of our most blessed Father Bernard, in order to render him the fitting and devout praises, whose venerable presence they enjoy, have assigned one hundred livres of small Tours currency to our bursar, to be converted to the common benefit of our church, for the purchase of rents amounting to five livres of small Tours currency. With these rents fish are to be bought, and shall be bought for ever, for a fish allowance to be provided annually on the day of Blessed Bernard for both monks and lay brothers. [Lacuna.] In the year 1335, [Col. 1754B] third indiction, on the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Ibid., p. 523, year 1439, 22 April.—The Abbot of Clairvaux grants a share in all the spiritual goods of the abbey to the very noble and mighty lady, Princess Madame Marguerite de Vaulx, Countess of Saint-Pol, Brienne, etc., on account of her gifts and her very great devotion toward Monsieur Saint Bernard, whose glorious holy body and precious relics, resting in the church of Clairvaux, she had visited in person.

Ibid., p. 212, year 1472, 22 January.—Letters of safeguard granted to the abbey of Clairvaux by Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, in honour of Our Lord Jesus Christ, of the blessed Virgin Mary his mother, and of the glorious holy body of Monsieur Saint Bernard, chaplain of the said glorious Lady and first abbot of that place, who lies and rests in the church and abbey of Our Lady of Clairvaux, the first daughter of our church and abbey of Cîteaux; and in consideration that in the said abbey we and our predecessors, [Col. 1754C] Counts of Flanders, have a fine and devout chapel in which the religious of that abbey are bound perpetually to celebrate, and do celebrate every day, a Requiem Mass for the remedy and salvation of the souls of ourselves, our predecessors, and our successors, the Counts and Countesses of Flanders, who founded and augmented them with various rents and revenues in our lands, for which long ago we gave them our discharge [main levée] . . .

. . . Given at Bruges, the twenty-second day of January, in the year of grace 1472.

Ibid., p. 457, year 1479, 10 December.—The inhabitants of Belaon, diocese of Langres, consent that the religious of Clairvaux may continue to build an iron forge beside their grange at Champigny, for the honour and reverence of God, of Our Lady, and of Saint Bernard, first abbot of the said monastery, where his precious body rests.

[Col. 1754D] Ibid., p. 183, year 1508, 19 January.—Before Jehan Gillot and Étienne Deschiens, sworn notaries at Bar-sur-Aube, Thibaut Henrion of Brousseur [perhaps one should read: *le brasseur*, “the brewer”] and Michau Hurren, cooper, resident at Clairvaux, acknowledge that, of their own free will, because of the particular devotion which they had and declared they had long had toward Monsieur Saint Bernard and toward the church of Clairvaux, in which his precious body rests, and in order to participate in the prayers, orisons, and spiritual and temporal goods which daily take place, prosper, and increase in that monastery, they have given themselves, body and goods, to that monastery, to serve its church and persons according to their ability, both by their trade and otherwise, in all lawful and honest matters.

[Col. 1755A] Ibid., p. 631, year 1587.—An account of the siege of Clairvaux by the Calvinist Reiters relates that, when the Duke of Guise came to the abbey’s aid (1 October), the prince began by going to pray at Saint Bernard’s tomb, “where he remained for a very long time, to the great edification of the religious.”

The account deserves to be copied in full:

“In the year 1587, the German Reiters or Calvinists entered the kingdom of France, fifty thousand men strong, to aid and support the French Calvinists. A large part of them arrived near Clairvaux on the eve of Saint Michael, after dinner, at about three o’clock; and they sent a trumpeter to summon the house, initially demanding lodging for five or six companies. They were told that the late Reverend Abbot Dom Lupin le Myrrhe was in the town of Troyes, and that he first had to be [Col. 1755B] informed of it. The said Reiter enemies numbered about 45,000, in good order, led by the Duke of Bouillon. They extended in length from Chaumont to Latrecey and in breadth from Richebourg to the vicinity of Clairvaux, where they expected to receive their first payment in France, at the said abbey of Clairvaux. But, with the aid of God, the Holy Virgin, the very good patroness of this house, Monseigneur Saint Michael, and likewise our most devout Father Saint Bernard, they were greatly hindered in their wicked enterprise. For the late Monseigneur Henry, Duke of Guise, sent word to our late Reverend Abbot le Myrrhe that there was no remedy but to reach an agreement with the said Reiter enemies of France and promise them what they demanded: namely, 7,000 écus, oxen for salting, and wine in quantity; and that, with God’s help and the favour of the glorious saints mentioned above, we would save the church of Clairvaux; [Col. 1755C] and that even if they burned the rent-rolls, we had woods from which to remake them, since they could not carry off the land and the soil.

“The venerable religious of Clairvaux, hearing this grievous news, withdrew with their Reverend Abbot le Myrrhe to the town of Bar-sur-Aube. All persisted, without interruption night and day, in prayers and devotions in the chapel of Little Clairvaux, where they had all taken refuge—especially on Saint Michael’s day, the day most to be feared, on which the enemy made every effort to enter the abbey.

“Nevertheless, four or five religious, officers of the house of Clairvaux, remained at Clairvaux with great steadfastness to make the necessary arrangements and to administer provisions and munitions to the soldiers in the house defending it. The names of these religious were Dom Bernard Brenay, cellarer; Dom Nicolas Thiefaud of Chaumont, monk of the bakehouse; [Col. 1755D] Dom Jean of Reims, steward; and Captain de Belleguise, a very worthy gentleman, most zealous for this house. All the lay brothers, firmly resolved to fight, were also assembled. The said Lord de Belleguise asked them what their will and resolution might be.

“All together answered that they wished to live or die for the preservation of the said house and to defend their bread.

“Together with the said religious officers, they decided that it was expedient to breach the Ville causeway. This was done by a man named Gautelet [or Gauletet] of Ville, a labourer of the house of Clairvaux. They also decided to break the Tréfou bridge, near Clairvaux, anciently called the Pont au Prieur, about one hundred paces from the abbey on the way to the farm of Outreaube. On Saint Michael’s very night it was broken by a mason, so that on Tuesday morning the whole bridge could be seen to have collapsed against the enemy’s attack; the enemy was at Outreaube, [Col. 1756A] our grange, when the bridge fell with great alarm.

“On Sunday, by permission of our God, a light drizzle began, and continued until Tuesday in such fashion that near Outreaube no horse stood in less than water up to its flanks. This was a special grace of divine goodness, providing for an urgent and perilous necessity. Note that many persons have seen rain lasting a month or three weeks, yet the waters were not then as high as they were on this occasion in two and a half days.

“The greatest outrage which the enemy was able to inflict upon the said abbey was to attack Outreaube. There they knocked down the doors of the cattle-house, very large and spacious as may be seen, in order to set up their cannon and batter down the walls of the abbey. But as they attempted to carry this out, at the first shot the cannon burst, shattered, and [Col. 1756B] broke into pieces. Our valiant soldiers, who were at the Pont du Prieur and, together with the lay brothers, firmly resolved behind a barricade described in the source as “du fou” [uncertain reading], promptly advanced against them within a few hours. They say that they cared nothing for it, for the Reiters—being strangers and ignorant of the ambushes of our good soldiers—had scarcely raised and shown their heads above the said cattle-house at Outreaube before they were greeted with heavy fire from arquebuses and muskets. This caused them to make a gap nearby, in the great field stretching toward the forge; they took large pieces of timber, intending to make a bridge in order to cross the river opposite the sheep-washing place, where five or six had already crossed.

“The soldiers at the Pont du Prieur saw none of this because of the wood along the river. Those others, lying in ambush near Calvin’s Cross, led by the valiant [Col. 1756C] Captain Des Carreaux, descended under cover to cross opposite the washing-place of Pré la Barre and entered the meadow, where the water reached their knees, in order to fire upon the main body of the Reiters and prevent them from crossing the river. When they had approached close under cover, unseen by the Reiters, they fired forty or fifty shots from arquebuses.

“Martin the plumber of Ville, then a servant of this house, was sent with other soldiers to carry arquebuses and stones for firing at the bridge. That bridge was gallantly won by Captain Des Carreaux; their planks and machines were thrown down, many enemies were wounded and cast into the water, and this caused them to return in great shame. A great number fell into the water and were lost and drowned, since the river was swift and high. One of the commanders leading the enemy, enraged by such great [Col. 1756D] fury, swore that he would neither drink nor eat until he had burned the abbey church and roasted all the monks alive. But, thanks be to God, that same night he died miserably, having spoken to no one after he had gone to bed, in the house of the late Laurent Gorillon at Longchamp, then judge of the lands of the Lords of Clairvaux.

“On the very day when they made their greatest efforts, my said lord the Duke of Guise left Vignory, five leagues from Clairvaux, and arrived unexpectedly at Bar-sur-Aube at about six o’clock in the evening, on the last day of September. Immediately my said Lord of Clairvaux, le Myrrhe, was sent to speak with him; he was then at Little Clairvaux in Bar-sur-Aube.

“On Wednesday morning, Saint Remigius’s day, the first day of October, at about seven in the morning, he came to Clairvaux by the Vineyard Gate and, before all else, went to church to say his prayers at Saint Bernard’s tomb. He remained there for a very long time, to the great [Col. 1757A] edification of the religious who stood behind him. My said Lord of Guise then took counsel with the said officers, religious, and my said Lord de Belleguise, went to inspect the strength stationed at the Pont du Prieur, and meanwhile ordered food to be supplied to the soldiers of his company and the Pont du Prieur to be properly rebuilt with pieces of casks and two carts of trapans [uncertain term].

“Nine casks of wine were broached beneath the hall by Dom Jacques Péricard, then wine steward, also on the advice of my said Lord de Belleguise, and a great quantity of bread was carried in sacks.

“It must be noted that when my said Lord Abbot le Myrrhe sent people from Bar-sur-Aube to Clairvaux to carry away the holy bodies and place them in greater safety, the religious and lay brothers sent there—ten or twelve in number—could not in any way lift or move the [Col. 1757B] covering of the tombs in which those holy bodies rested, although it had often been proved that four men sufficed for the same task.

“In thanksgiving, Clairvaux customarily holds every year a general procession on 29 September, the feast-day of the Blessed Archangel Saint Michael, protector of the Church, captain of all the troops of the God of hosts, and invincible defender of the faithful.

“This present writing is attested by Brother C. of Burgundy, religious of Clairvaux, and Brother François Rongeot, Prior, who signed it with their flourishes.”

In the same manuscript of M. Abbé Matthieu, p. 67, I find a document connected with the one just copied:

“I, Balthasar Gobelin, Counsellor to the King and Treasurer General of the extraordinary expenses of his wars, acknowledge that I have had and received in ready money, at the abbey [Col. 1757C] of Clairvaux near Bar-sur-Aube, from the Lord Abbot of the said place of Clairvaux, the sum of 3,000 sun écus: in silver francs of twenty sols each, fifteen quarter-écus likewise of silver at fifteen sols each, together with fifteen sols; borrowed by Monsieur the Duke of Guise, Governor and Lieutenant-General for His Majesty in the lands of Champagne and Brie, and ordered by him to be placed in my hands for use in the duties of my office, including part of the costs and expenses of the army which he led for His Majesty’s service in the said land of Champagne, to oppose the foreign forces entering this kingdom. Of this sum of [lacuna] I declare myself satisfied and fully paid, and have released and do release the said Lord Abbot of Clairvaux and all others. In witness whereof I have signed this with my own hand on the third day of October 1587. Signed: Gobelin.”—On parchment.

Ibid., p. 46, year 1595, 15 June.—Clement [Col. 1757D] VIII, Pope, for perpetual remembrance. Moved by fatherly charity for the salvation of all Christ’s faithful, we willingly dispense, in aid also of the souls detained in Purgatory, the heavenly treasures of indulgences, of which Divine Clemency has appointed us dispensers on earth, insofar as we judge in the Lord that this is beneficially expedient. Therefore we desire to adorn, with a special privilege not yet bestowed upon it, in aid of the souls of the faithful departed, the church of the monastery of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Langres—a monastery exceptionally distinguished among the other monasteries of that Order by the number of monks, lay brothers, donors, and servants, and held in the highest veneration by all because of the abundance of holy bodies and other sacred relics, especially those of Saint Bernard, first abbot of the said monastery, whose body rests in that church. Inclining to the humble petitions submitted to us on this matter by our beloved son Denis Largentier, Abbot of Tyronnel, [Col. 1758A] and trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and the authority of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, we grant that whenever any priest of that monastery alone celebrates a Mass of the Dead at the altar of that same Saint Bernard, in which his relics are enshrined, for the soul of any one of the faithful who has departed this life united to God in charity, that soul shall obtain an indulgence from the treasury of the Church, so that, aided by the merits of Our Lord Jesus Christ, of His Mother the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of all the saints, it may be freed from Purgatory; notwithstanding anything to the contrary. Given at Rome, at Saint Mark’s, under the Fisherman’s Ring, 15 June 1595, the fourth year of our pontificate.

Signed: Vestrius Barbianus.

“The original is in the archives,” adds Dom Claude Guyton; “and a copy is pasted upon a small panel attached to the altar of our Father Saint Bernard.”

[Col. 1758B] Ibid., p. 352, year 1607, 14 January.—Dom Denis Largentier, Abbot of Clairvaux, in appointing a vicar in Ireland, recalls the friendship of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy: “That holy bond of sacred friendship between the most glorious Malachy, formerly metropolitan of Ireland, and our most blessed Father Bernard; the former’s singular love for this Clear Valley, in which, dying, he left his sacred body, a brilliant safeguard of his special and perpetual patronage.”

Ibid., p. 213, year 1611, July.—Louis XIII confirms the privileges granted by his predecessors to the abbey of Clairvaux, “the said abbey being of royal foundation and, on that account and because of the singular devotion which the kings, his predecessors, have always borne toward it, being greatly commended to them as the repository of several holy bodies, notably that of [Col. 1758C] Saint Bernard.”—Given at Paris, in July 1611.

Ibid., p. 213, year 1618, 29 July.—The archives of Clairvaux preserve a long letter which the Reverend Father Dom Denis Largentier, forty-fourth Abbot of Clairvaux, of holy memory, wrote on 29 July 1618 to the Abbot of Cîteaux concerning the affairs of their Order; at its end he tells him: “We shall have the happiness and honour of your presence on Saint Bernard’s Day, in fulfilment of your vow,” etc.

Ibid., p. 217, year 1661, 2 September.—Dom Pierre Henry, surnamed Duchesne, forty-sixth Abbot of Clairvaux, in a letter dated at Clairvaux, 2 September 1661, addressed to Dom Nicolas Perrin, professed religious of Clairvaux, provided by Pope Alexander VII with the cure of Colombey-la-Fosse (district of Bar-sur-Aube, canton of Soulaines), writes: “Since we know that the parish of Colombey-la-Fosse is regular and has been occupied continuously, as it is at present and has been, by religious of our aforesaid house of Clairvaux as well as of another order; and since we know that this place of Colombey-la-Fosse is only two leagues from here, in which our Blessed Father Bernard has shone down to the present day by daily miracles . . .”

—It is known that Saint Bernard blessed a fountain at Colombey-la-Fosse and, by a miracle, imparted to its waters the power to heal various diseases. Water from this fountain, drawn at his command, was changed into wine, to the great admiration of his monks and all those present. (*Life of Saint Bernard*, by John the Hermit, II.12.)

I believe that the miraculous fountain still exists today, and that recourse is had to its healing virtues particularly against fever.

Ibid., p. 400, year 1682, 22 December.—Nicolas de Peiresson, dean of Saint John the Baptist at Chaumont, esquire and lord of Chamarande; his brother Claude de Poiresson, esquire and lord of the said Chamarande; and the latter’s wife, Lady Germaine Geoffroy de Coeffy, establish in perpetuity in the church of Clairvaux, in return for an annual rent of ten livres, three low Masses, in recognition of the particular graces which they have received from God through the merits and intercession of the immaculate Mother of God, Saint Joachim, Saint Anne, Saint Joseph, and Blessed Saint Bernard.

During their lifetimes the Masses shall be celebrated on [Col. 1760A] the day of the Assumption, the feast-day of Saint Bernard, and Saint Joseph’s day; after their death, they shall be celebrated in the chapel of Saint Bernard’s tomb, for the repose of their souls.

MS. IX (*Succinct Catalogue of the Abbots of Clairvaux*), p. 264.—Mention is made of a golden lamp offered at Saint Bernard’s tomb by the Duke of Penthièvre. It is said that this prince was closely associated with M. Rocourt.

No. 9. Lighting before the altar of Saint Malachy and in the church of Clairvaux.

[Col. 1759]

The archives of Aube possess a charter of Robert Bruce by which he gives the abbey of Clairvaux his land of Osticroft, with all its appurtenances, to maintain a light before Saint Malachy’s tomb: “For maintaining a light [Col. 1759B] before Blessed Malachy.” (See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under *Sustinere*.)

This charter is undated, but a passage from the statutes of the general chapter of the Cistercian Order may help to determine, within a few years, the date of its drafting.

In the second collection of definitions of the general chapter, distinction 1, chapter X, “On lighting before the altar on saints’ feast-days,” one reads:

“When the feast of any saint occurs, at an altar consecrated in his honour it is permitted to light not wax tapers, but the light of a lamp or an oil-lamp.” [Note: [Col. 1759D] *Candela*—“an oil lamp,” says Du Cange in his *Glossary*.] (*Nomasticon Cisterciense*, Paris, 1664, folio, p. 277.)

Comparing this passage, which so clearly brings out the spirit of poverty of the early Cistercians, with a request made in 1273 by the Abbot of Clairvaux to the General Chapter [Note: [Col. 1759D] “The petition of the Lord Abbot of Clairvaux, that he may have a light before the tomb of Saint Malachy, is granted.” (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum: Selected Statutes of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order*, year 1273, no. 17, vol. IV, col. 1440.)] that he might be allowed to have a light before Saint Malachy’s tomb, one sees that [Col. 1759C] only a rich endowment in honour of the holy archbishop could be at issue. It seems quite natural to me to think that this was Robert Bruce’s foundation, which gave an entire estate with all its dependencies in order to surround Saint Malachy’s tomb with that splendid display which our fathers so delighted to see around saints’ relics.

I therefore consider myself sufficiently justified, by comparing the permission granted in 1273 to the Abbot of Clairvaux, in not assigning Robert Bruce’s charter an earlier date. The form of the writing, a highly regular diplomatic minuscule, indicates the end of the thirteenth century. Thus this document would have issued from Robert Bruce, rival of John Balliol, whose mother was Isabella, daughter of David, Earl of Huntingdon. (Cf. *The Baronage of England*, by William Dugdale, Norroy King of Arms, London, 1675, folio, vol. I.)

Here is the text of the foundation charter, written on [Col. 1759D] parchment and well preserved:

“Let those present and future know that I, Robert de Brus, Lord of Annandale [Note: [Col. 1759D] Annandale (cf. Camden, *Britannia*).], have given and granted, and by this my present charter confirmed, to God and Blessed Mary and to the house of Clairvaux and the monks serving God there [Col. 1760A] and to serve Him for ever, for the maintenance of a light before Blessed Malachy, for the salvation of my soul and of all my predecessors and successors, as a free and perpetual alms, my whole land of Osticroft, with [Col. 1760B] its rightful and ancient boundaries and appurtenances, and the common easements and liberties belonging to the said land, as Roger son of William Wode and Geoffrey Collan formerly held that land from me: the whole aforesaid land to be held and possessed by the aforesaid monks from me and my heirs freely, peacefully, fully, wholly, and honourably, as any alms is held or possessed more freely and peacefully in all the kingdom of Scotland; in woods and plains, meadows and pastures, moors and marshes [Note: [Col. 1759D] *Mora*: that is, lakes, pools, moor; cf. *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, London, 1652, vol. II, glossary. *Mariscus*: that is, a marshy place, marshland. (Ibid.)], peat-cuttings [Note: [Col. 1759D] *Turbariae*: that is, places suitable for digging turf or peat (cf. Du Cange, *Glossary*).], pannage [Note: [Col. 1760D] *Paunagium*: that is, the feeding of pigs on acorns (cf. *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, ibid.).], and all other easements which may be found or exercised on the said land, free from every secular customary due, exaction, and demand [Note: [Col. 1760D] *Demanda*: that is, an exaction (cf. *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, glossary).]. I also will and grant, for myself and my heirs, that the aforesaid land shall be free from multure [Note: [Col. 1760D] *Multura*: that is, the payment made to the miller from the grain which he grinds (cf. Du Cange, *Glossary*).], and that its tenants shall freely and without hindrance grind in my mills. And I and my heirs shall warrant, hold harmless [Note: [Col. 1760D] *Acquietare*: that is, to render free and secure; an English legal term: “to acquit” (cf. *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, glossary).], and defend for ever against all men [Col. 1760C] and women the aforesaid land with all its appurtenances, as stated above, for the aforesaid monks. And that this my gift and grant may obtain the strength of perpetual validity, I have strengthened this present writing by the protection of my seal. Witnesses: Lords David de Thorthorald, then Steward of Annandale [Note: [Col. 1760D] Annandale, one of the four Scottish stewardships; cf. Camden, *Britannia*.]; Robert de Herice; William of Saint Michael, knights; Master Adam of Kirkcudbright; Lord William of Duncorry; William de Corri; Adam Hendeman; Richard Crispin; William of Aire, clerk; and others.”

—The white-wax seal, pendent from parchment tags, is round and forms a spherical cap on the reverse of the engraved surface. In its field is a fully armed horseman, helmet closed and adorned with a fan-shaped crest, holding a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left; his horse is caparisoned and gallops from right to left.—Legend: “ESTO . . . DEO? . . .,” in Gothic majuscule script. Height of the parchment, [Col. 1760D] nine centimetres; width, twenty-six centimetres.

I have gathered a number of documents relating to the lighting in the church of Clairvaux. In reading them, it will be useful to remember that the use of wax tapers was forbidden by the ancient Cistercian customs [Col. 1761A] upon saints’ altars [Note: [Col. 1761D] This explains the permission granted in 1220 by the General Chapter to the Abbot of Clairvaux: “The petition concerning a wax candle to be hung before Saint Bernard’s relics is granted.” (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. IV, col. 1329.) Without doubt, the Abbot of Clairvaux needed a similar permission in 1255 to accept Matthew of Montmirail’s donation. This lord assured the abbey an annual revenue of eighteen livres tournois, on condition that a wax candle should burn day and night before Saint Bernard’s altar. (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 1061).]; that the early Cistercians used only lamps in their churches; and that only on the principal feasts, when the relics were placed on the high altar, were two tapers placed there, besides the two lamps fixed to the wall on either side. (Cf. *Nomasticon Cisterciense*, *Usages of the Cistercian Order*, chapters LIII, 137; LIX, 153; LXVII, 158; *Institutions of the General Chapter*, chapters LXXXII, 271; IX, 277.)

MS. XV of M. Abbé Matthieu, p. 192.—“I, Hilduin, by God’s grace Bishop of Langres, make known to all, present and future, that Philip, knight of Chaleta, gave to God and the brethren of Clairvaux whatever he possessed in all revenues at Cunfin [lacuna]; the same Philip and, after him, his heir shall offer every year in perpetuity, on Saint Bernard’s feast-day, one wax candle to the church of Clairvaux, worth six Provins deniers [lacuna]. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1202.”

Ibid., p. 71.—“Theobald, Count Palatine of Champagne and [Col. 1761B] Brie, to all, in perpetuity. I have heard, and have been astonished, that when the monks of Clairvaux celebrated their particular and private Masses, no wax light was kindled, but they celebrated with lamps alone being lit; and that danger frequently occurred as a result. Therefore, wishing to remove this danger, I have given to the same brothers of Clairvaux, in perpetual alms, for the purchase of wax for these uses, eighteen pounds of annual revenue in Provins currency, to be received every year at the fairs of Bar from the proceeds of those fairs. The said brothers have, however, given me their assurance in good faith that henceforth they will not celebrate without a wax candle being lit. Moreover, I have given the same brothers, for the use of one lamp, forty shillings of revenue to be received every year at the same fairs of Bar; which lamp shall always and continually burn in the place called the Charnel-house, where rest the bones of the faithful who die at Clairvaux. And so that this [Col. 1761C] may remain known, I have caused the present charter to be confirmed by the protection of my seal. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1222, in the month of March.”—Copied from a collated copy made on 14 August 1664 by notaries.

Ibid., p. 199.—“I, . . . Dean of Christendom of Bar-sur-Aube, make known . . . that, whereas in all movable and immovable things which Constantius, clerk of Villari, held on the day on which this present instrument was made, the brothers of Clairvaux had one half in every respect by the gift of Brother Durand, monk of Clairvaux, as the Clairvaux brethren themselves asserted and Constantius, brother of the said Durand, testified, etc. . . . moreover, the said Constantius shall pay, in acknowledgement of the aforesaid, every year, on the feast of Blessed Bernard, a candle worth twelve denarii to Blessed Bernard himself . . . in the year of grace 1227.”

—The record of this undertaking is also found in the cartulary of Clairvaux (MS no. 703 of the [Col. 1761D] public library of Troyes [Note: [Col. 1761D] There is in the Imperial Library a copy [Col. 1762D] of this same cartulary, likewise from the thirteenth century. It is a quarto volume in splendid Gothic minuscule, with initials alternating vermilion and azure. On the flyleaf one reads: “Bought on 14 Brumaire, year XI (5 November 1802), at the sale of the books of M. Truelle-Chambouzon.—Sold to the Royal Library by Chevalier Armynot, 26 April 1816.” Here are the divisions of the Clairvaux cartulary: *Grangia Abbatis* [the Abbot’s Grange].—*Ultra-Albam* [Beyond the Aube].—*Fravilla*.—*Fontarcya*.—*Bellus-Mons* [Beaumont].—*Champigneyum pro Gomevilla* [Champigney for Gomeville].—*Borda*.—*Moreins*.—*Cornay*.—*Belinfay*.—*Forgie* [the forges].—*Pasture*.]), under the heading: *Ultra-Albam*, CL. Agreement between Constantius, clerk of Villari, and the brothers of Clairvaux.

I extract from the same cartulary the following document, from the year 1215, in which mention is made of a candle rendered upon the altar of St Bernard on his feast day.

*Bellus-Mons*, XVI.

[Col. 1762A] “Peter, Prior of St Peter’s; B., Dean of Bar; Paganus, Official of Langres; and Humbert, Provost of Bar, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord. Let all of you know that a dispute had arisen between the Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux on one side, and Garnier, son of Brother Philip of Chaleta, on the other, because the said Garnier refused to render homage to the Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux for all that the said Garnier had and possessed at Cunfin and throughout its whole territory, just as his father had rendered it to the said Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux, as is contained in the authentic instrument of the Lord Bishop of Langres. At last, the said Garnier, appearing before us and having learned the truth, amicably acknowledged that he held and possessed the said fief from the Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux; and in acknowledgement of the said homage the same G. was bound to render, without delay or postponement, every year, on the feast of [Col. 1762B] St Bernard, upon the altar of that saint, one candle worth six denarii.

“But because he had refused to render the aforesaid homage to the said Abbot and brothers, as he ought to have done, the same G., at the arbitration of B., Dean of Bar, and Erard of the Gate, made amends and rendered them to Walter and Evrard, cellarers of Clairvaux. Concerning the other complaints which they had against one another, the same G., swearing upon the holy things, promised that henceforth he would submit to law before the said Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux whenever the aforesaid Abbot and brethren should assign him a suitable day, as lords customarily do concerning their fiefs; and that whatever the said Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux, either personally or through another suitable person, should adjudge after prior legal procedure, without prejudice to the charters of the brothers of Clairvaux both concerning the matters written above and all complaints which the said Abbot and brothers have against the said G., and likewise concerning the complaints which the same G. claims to have against the aforesaid Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux, he shall observe inviolate within the appointed term, namely [Col. 1762C] by the next Easter.

“And it should be known that the aforesaid Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux shall not draw the said G. outside the castellany of Bar so long as the same G. refuses to submit to law before the said Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux, or at their command, concerning the aforesaid agreements. But if the aforesaid G. should henceforth refuse, which God forbid, to keep in good faith all the matters written above and to maintain them firmly, the said Abbot and brothers shall hold the said fief and all the aforesaid matters in their own hand, without anyone’s objection, until the said G. has made suitable full amends for the aforesaid agreements in the court of the Abbot and brothers of Clairvaux. And so that all the matters written above may remain valid and unshaken, at the request of both parties we have caused the present charter to be made and ordered it to be confirmed by the impression of our seals. Done in the year of grace 1215.”

Ibid., p. 180.—“I, Theobald, Count Palatine of Champagne and Brie, make known to all present [Col. 1762D] and future persons inspecting these present letters that I have given to the church of Clairvaux, in pure and perpetual alms, for the salvation of my soul, twenty pounds of Provins annual revenue for purchasing wax to provide the lighting for Masses in the said church of Clairvaux . . . Done in the year of grace 1231, in the month of May.”

[Col. 1763A] Ibid., p. 17.—(I give this analysis from the original parchment document preserved in the archives of Aube.)

Brother Jehans, Abbot of Clairvaux, authorizes a religious woman of his abbey, moved by great devotion . . . in honour and reverence of the blessed Trinity of Paradise, and also through her great trust . . . in my Lady St Anne . . . and in the blessed martyrs, namely Saints Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus, whose precious bodies rest honourably in the church of Clairvaux, to devote the sum of sixty gold francs of the king’s coinage, which she possessed through her own industry and prudent provision, to the perpetual maintenance by day and night of the lamp [Col. 1764A] placed before the altar of the Holy Trinity in the choir of the lay brothers, and to the establishment of such and similar lights in wax candles as we are accustomed to have before the great altar or around it, and in the said church on the feasts of my lord St Malachy and of our glorious father, lord St Bernard.”

Ibid., p. 5.—Acknowledgement of a gift made to the religious of Clairvaux about sixteen years earlier by Jehan le Pitois, receiver of the royal domains and aids at Bar-sur-Aube, and by his wife Simonette la Rotie, to keep the lamp burning perpetually before Our Lord and the body of Lord St Bernard.

No. 10. Plans of Clairvaux by Dom Nicolas Milley.

[Col. 1763]

[Col. 1763B] The plans of Clairvaux by Dom N. Milley consist of three large sheets, entitled as follows: *Archicoenobii Claraevallensis ichnographia. Tabula 1a* [Ground-plan of the principal monastery of Clairvaux. Plate I].—*Archicoenobii Claraevallensis ad occidentem prospectus. Tabula 2a* [View of the principal monastery of Clairvaux from the west. Plate II].—*Archicoenobii Claraevallensis ad [Col. 1764B] meridiem prospectus. Tabula 3a* [View of the principal monastery of Clairvaux from the south. Plate III].—On each one reads: “F. N. Milley delineavit” [Brother N. Milley drew it]—“C. Lucas D. S. sculpsit 1708” [C. Lucas, D.S., engraved it, 1708]. A large cartouche at the top of the third sheet contains the following inscription:

> TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST REVEREND LORD, LORD PETER BOUCHU, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX; FIRST FATHER OF THE ENTIRE CISTERCIAN ORDER, AND IMMEDIATE SUPERIOR OF THE WHOLE FILIATION OF CLAIRVAUX; AND MOST VIGILANT, ETC.: AS AN EVERLASTING MONUMENT OF HIS DEVOTION, BROTHER NICOLAS MILLEY, A RELIGIOUS MOST DEVOTED TO HIM, PROFESSED OF MOREILLES, PRIOR OF MORIS, OFFERS THIS THREEFOLD DESIGN OF THE PRINCIPAL MONASTERY OF HIS HOUSE. IN THE YEAR OF SALVATION 1708.

[Col. 1763C] The cartouche is ornamented with the arms of the Abbot of Clairvaux, Dom Pierre Bouchu, those of the county of Champagne, and those of St Bernard.

Each plan is accompanied by a Latin legend and a French legend. The contract which I shall transcribe shows that they were printed at Clairvaux itself.

1708, 17 September.—We, the undersigned, have agreed as follows: namely, I, Edme Thevenart, master intaglio printer, promise and bind myself to print, in the residence of my lord the Abbot of Clairvaux, three plates of his abbey: namely, one ground-plan and two perspective views of the said abbey, at the rate of eight livres per hundred prints, one with another; supplying the press and generally everything necessary for the said printing, at which I bind myself to work in person and not through another, without [Col. 1763D] any interruption, beginning on the first day of next October. I, Dom de Montaubon, accept this and promise to pay the said sum of eight livres per hundred of the said prints as the work proceeds; and to provide the paper, a bed, and a room during the course of the said work. Executed in duplicate between us this 17 September 1708. F. de Montaubon—Edme Thevenart.

A receipt written on the back of the foregoing agreement records that Thevenart received 372 livres for 4,600 copies of the plans which he pulled, plus 52 livres 10 sous for printing 1,575 French explanatory inscriptions, at 3 livres 10 sous per hundred (the printer disregarded the extra 75 inscriptions beyond the 1,500), plus 35 sous for grey paper or waste sheets. In all, Thevenart received 426 livres 5 sous, for which he gave a receipt to the Abbot of Clairvaux at Paris on 7 March 1709.

[Col. 1764C] On 8 March 1709 Marie Warangne gave Dom de Montaubon a receipt at Paris for 50 livres 9 sous 6 deniers, the price of trimming 4,038 copies of the Clairvaux plans.—On 14 March 1709 the same woman gave the same man a receipt for 4 livres, the price of trimming 1,575 copies of the French tables of the said plans.

The engraving of these tables had cost 35 livres 2 sous 6 deniers, according to the following receipt:

“I have received from the Reverend Father Montaubon, procurator of the Lord Abbot of Clairvaux, the sum of 35 livres, 2 sous, 6 deniers, for engraving a French table for the plans of his abbey; for which I discharge him. At Paris, this 19 February 1709. Berey.”—Below is written: “Agreed at 1 sou for each engraved word, and 1 sou for three figures.” (These receipts are preserved in the archives of Aube.)

The Clairvaux plans are engraved with great skill. At the bottom of the third sheet is a picturesque representation [Col. 1764D] of the great vat called the *Dolium majus* [Great Cask], famed for its enormous capacity. Dom Joseph Meglinger gives a very exact description of it:

> “. . . We descended into the wine cellars, where casks of unusual size are seen. One especially, above the rest, deserved careful observation. Since it was empty of wine and displayed its broad bottom through open doors, it invited my curiosity to enter and examine its inner construction. But darkness permitted nothing except that I might test its length with my feet; this I found to be thirty feet from one bottom to the other, and its height eighteen. It is bound by no hoops or circles of birch, according to the custom of our casks; four huge beams, joined by cut joints at their ends, enclose in six repeated tiers very long oak boards. Then, where the circle ends at the four corners of the joints, the beams stand apart; the empty spaces are filled with wedges, so that the whole structure, within the bonds of these timbers, may, as if on a rack, be loosened for use or tightened.”

(*Iter Cist.*, p. 209.) According to Dom Le Boullenger (*Fragments of the History of Clairvaux*, MS IX of M. Abbé Matthieu, p. 361), the great vat held 730 muids of wine. Dom Le Boullenger here relates the miracle of the vine [Col. 1765A] planted *in vertice montis qui proximus est Claraevallis* [on the summit of the mountain nearest Clairvaux] by a monk named Christian, and cursed by St Bernard’s brethren (*S. Bern., Op. Joh. Eremita*, II, 10). “One could still see,” he says, “that vine thirty years ago; it was called the great vine,” because of the miracle by which the holy abbot caused its barrenness to cease.

No. 11. Burials in the choir of the church of Clairvaux.—Guillaume Flammeng.—Investigations ordered by an Abbot of Clairvaux to establish the names of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, and Bonosus.

[Col. 1765]

[Col. 1767A] I. Chapel in honour of the Holy Evangelists Mark, Luke, and John.—It was consecrated in the year 1157.

II. Dedicated to St James, Philip, and Barnabas.

III. Dedicated to the Holy Apostles Andrew, Simon, and Jude.—Within the wall of this chapel, on the left side, beneath a stone vault, lies the body of Lord Robert, Bishop of Langres and afterwards Bishop of Liège. (Cf. Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, Dist. XLI, IV.)

IV. It was assigned to the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

V. It is adorned with the name of OUR LORD THE SAVIOUR.—In this chapel rest the remains of four blessed persons.

A. On the left side, beneath a stone arch, buried within the wall, lies Blessed Alix, mother of our holy father Bernard, with her effigy placed above, which John of Chalon, Abbot of Clairvaux, caused to be carved in 1508. (Cf. Henriquez, ibid., IV), where one reads:

> “Likewise, there also lies the noble lady of pious memory and most devout toward God, Aleydis, mother of the eminent Doctor and our holy father Blessed Bernard, first [Col. 1767B] Abbot of Clairvaux. She was first committed to burial at Dijon, in the monastery of St Benignus; but afterwards, the Lord so willing and dealing mercifully with us, in order to stir up and enlarge our devotion to humility, she was translated to Clairvaux and placed before the altar of the Holy Saviour, in the year of the Lord 1250, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April [29 March].”

(Cf. *Acta S. Bern.*, § LIX.—*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 806.—*Menol. Cist.*, 18 October.)

B. Behind the tomb of Blessed Alidis, on the right, one reads on the floor a stone bearing two inscriptions: first, on the forward part of the stone, nearer to those entering the chapel: “Here lies Lord Eschilus, Bishop of Denmark, afterwards monk of Clairvaux.”—Second, on the farther part of the same stone one reads: “Here lies Lord Ralph, fifteenth Abbot of Clairvaux, afterwards Archbishop of Lyon.” (Cf. Henriquez, ibid.)

C. At the very entrance of the same chapel, beneath a marble slab, lies the body [Col. 1767C] of Blessed Garnier, ninth Abbot of Clairvaux and afterwards Bishop of Langres. (Cf. Henriquez, ibid.)

VI. Dedicated under the title of St John the Baptist.

VII. Distinguished by the names of Saints Stephen and Sebastian.

VIII. [lacuna]

IX. Sacred to St Mammes and St Desiderius.—In this chapel lies Lord Adam, monk of Clairvaux and afterwards Bishop of Sora (written in Dom Le Boullenger’s hand).

Following the *Life of Monsignor Saint Bernard, Devout Chaplain of the Virgin* (Paris and Troyes, Gothic quarto), one may read the verse epitaph of Blessed Aleth, composed by Guillaume Flammeng, former canon of Langres, who had withdrawn to Clairvaux. (This epitaph was reproduced by Fr Chifflet, *S. Bern. gen. illustr. assert.*, p. 435.)

I find a very interesting document concerning this person [Col. 1767D] in MS XV of M. Abbé Matthieu, p. 251; here is a copy:

1499, 22 February.—“We, Brother John (Jean de Chalon), Abbot of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Langres, and the whole convent of the same place, to all who inspect these present letters, greeting in Him who is the true salvation of all. We make known that, specially gathered in our Chapter, as is customary, to transact the business of our church, and directing our consideration to the great virtues, gifts, distinguished merits, and most honourable reputation for life of the venerable and learned man Master Guillaume Flammeng, a most devout priest and lately canon of the church of Langres, but now curate and rector of the parish church of Molano (Maulain, Haute-Marne), in the same diocese; and also to the true and perfect affection, devotion, and genuine love which, through many experiences, we most certainly know him to bear toward our Blessed Father [Col. 1768A] Bernard and toward this his church of Clairvaux: hoping for very abundant fruit from his virtuous examples, we have admitted—and by the tenor of these presents do admit—him into our fellowship and society, and into participation in our goods both spiritual and temporal, for as long as he shall live or wish to remain with us. Thus he shall be a full participant in all Masses, sacrifices, vigils, prayers, fasts, abstinences, disciplines, the suffrages of divine worship, and the other spiritual goods which are performed, and which shall hereafter be performed in the said monastery by divine bounty. Moreover, for the duration of his life, he shall have food with us, like one religious priest at the Abbot’s table, whenever and as often as he pleases; or in the convent, if he should ever prefer it.

“On the day of his death, when the Lord shall deign to call him, exequies and divine service shall be celebrated for him as for one of our religious brethren, [Col. 1768B] and he shall be buried in their cemetery. The aforesaid Master Guillaume, meanwhile, demonstrating the real effect of his genuine affection for us and for Clairvaux, lest he appear burdensome to the monastery, has, in acknowledgement of the foregoing, manually delivered to the Cellarer and Bursar of this our monastery two hundred francs of good and sound money of France, actually and in fact expended for the use, needs, and affairs of our church. We acknowledge ourselves satisfied as to their true and actual receipt; we discharge the same Master Guillaume of that sum and promise that we shall be bound to secure his discharge before all persons. And for the observance of all the foregoing, we bind ourselves and our successors, our monastery, and all its spiritual goods, and subject them to ecclesiastical coercion and to temporal justice. Given under the appending of our seals, on the twenty-second day of February in the year of the Lord 1499, according to the French manner.”

—In the margin one reads: “For Lord Guillaume Flammeng, canon of Langres, editor of a Life of our Father Bernard, in seven books, published in 1520 by Jean Lecoq.”—While living at Clairvaux, he composed the epitaph of Blessed Lady Aelis or Aelet, mother of St Bernard, visible near her tomb on a large wooden frame, in fourteen strophes of eight verses each. It was renewed in 1747. (Cf. Brunet, *Manuel du libraire*.—*Biographie universelle*, Michaud ed., Supplement, article by M. Weiss.—M. Carnandet, librarian of Chaumont, announced the publication of the *Life and Passion of Monsignor Saint Didier, Martyr and Bishop of Langres, Performed by Characters at the Request of My Lords the Fellow Members of the Confraternity of the Said Saint at Langres*, composed by the venerable and learned Master Guillaume Flamang, canon of the said Langres; performed in that city by the said brethren in 1482. [Col. 1768D] The quarto manuscript, of 300 leaves, bound in wood, is preserved in the library of Chaumont.

One hundred and sixteen actors appear in the play.)

In 1256, a monk of Clairvaux named Godefroy, charged with visiting in Italy the monasteries of the Filiation, received an order from his abbot, Stephen of Lexington, to obtain every possible piece of information about the names of the holy martyrs whose bodies Cardinal Conrad had given to the church of Clairvaux. This monk’s account has survived: it is found in MS 401 (no. 78, recto) of the public library of Troyes; the handwriting indicates the second half of the thirteenth century.—Similarity of names and a superficial examination led Charles de Visch (*Bibliotheca scriptorum Ordinis Cisterciensis*) to believe that this concerned Geoffrey, St Bernard’s scribe and fourth Abbot of Clairvaux, and that this monk had written the Lives of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosimus, [Col. 1769A] and Bonosus: “He also wrote the Lives of the holy martyrs Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, whose bodies rest at Clairvaux.” But Geoffrey, fourth Abbot of Clairvaux, became St Bernard’s scribe in 1148, according to Casimir Oudin (*De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*); he was at least twenty years old, and consequently in 1256 he would have been 128. That was no longer an age for visiting remote monasteries. Casimir Oudin places his death around 1210.—Besides, Godefroy did not write the lives of the holy martyrs; he merely brought back from Italy the Passion of St Bonosa, as the Bollandists printed it under 15 July, with a prologue absent from their collection but considered too uninteresting to publish.

As for Godefroy’s investigations, they furnish a curious proof of the care taken in the Middle Ages to verify relics. They deserve publication in order to show that monks were not so greatly and [Col. 1769B] naively credulous as some have gratuitously supposed.

### Account of Godefroy

> “In the year of the Lord 1256, when I, Brother Godefroy, a humble monk of Clairvaux, had been sent to Italy to visit the daughter-houses of the said abbey of Clairvaux, I stayed for some time at the Roman Curia, humbly serving the reverend father and lord John, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. At that time, when I came to the aforesaid Curia, the Abbot of Roche in England, a religious and God-fearing man, brought me the command of the venerable father and lord Stephen, Abbot of Clairvaux, to make a careful and faithful inquiry into the names of four blessed martyrs, whose bodies had been honourably brought from the city of Porto, in the time of Pope Honorius III, to the said abbey by the religious, prudent, and devout monk of Clairvaux, *nonnum* Renier of Sena (*nonnum* for *domnum*, see Cange, *Glossary*), chaplain and procurator of Conrad, cardinal of pious memory, then Bishop of Porto; and this by the will and command of the aforesaid Lord Bishop of Porto, so that in the aforesaid abbey of Clairvaux they might be worshipped in Christ with due devotion and reverence, and might be more honourably venerated.

> “For the city of Porto had been reduced to such desolate devastation that scarcely anything but ruins appeared there. The said Lord Cardinal loved Clairvaux with a special prerogative of affection, and indeed had held the office of abbot in that monastery before he was raised to the rank of cardinal. Therefore, wishing to honour the said abbey in the Lord and devoutly inspire it to greater devotion, he caused not only the bodies of the aforesaid martyrs to be transferred there, but also decreed in his last will that the bones of his own body should be brought to the said abbey [Col. 1769D] and buried there.

> “Therefore, wishing reverently to obey my Abbot’s command, I went to the aforesaid city of Porto, accompanied by the Subprior of St Anastasius, an honourable, devout, and prudent man, so that I might diligently and reverently investigate the names of the oft-mentioned martyrs, as the dignity of so important a matter required. When we had come to the cathedral church, hoping there to learn more certainly the names of the said saints, we turned aside to the house of the Archpriest. We found a servant, the keeper of that Archpriest’s house; having obtained nothing certain from him, we returned to Rome on his advice, because he told us that at St Clement’s we would find the aforementioned Archpriest, who could give us fuller certainty concerning what we sought.

> “We therefore sought out and found that Archpriest, a prudent, devout, and circumspect man. Carefully turning over the books which he had at Rome, since at that time he could not find true certainty in accordance with his heart’s desire, he, as a God-fearing man, would not make any complete determination. Yet at our repeated urgent requests, the aforesaid Archpriest went to the city of Porto, carefully searched the books of the cathedral church and others, and, after returning to Rome, declared firmly, [Col. 1770B] steadily, and without any hesitation that the blessed martyrs Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa had formerly been deposited in the altar of the church of St Lawrence in the said city; that Lord Cardinal Conrad had caused them to be removed from that altar by the said monk Renier of Sena and transferred and conveyed to Clairvaux.

> “But I, Brother Godefroy, desiring to obtain still greater certainty, began carefully to inquire whether at Rome there was any church dedicated in honour of the aforesaid martyrs. At last, learning that across the Tiber a certain church had been built in honour of Blessed Bonosa, in which the said virgin was venerated with great devotion, I rejoiced exceedingly. I went to the aforesaid church and questioned its priest, an elderly, mature man of great devotion, concerning the life and Passion of the said holy virgin. I received from him the answer that the body of the said holy martyr had been taken from the altar of the said church of St Lawrence by the above-mentioned monk of Clairvaux, Renier of Sena, in the time of Cardinal Conrad of good memory, then Bishop of Porto, and had been brought by the same monk to Clairvaux with the bodies of the other holy martyrs.

> “Having learned these things, having been informed and testified by many prudent, authoritative, and mature men, I earnestly requested that the life and Passion of the said holy virgin be supplied to me. Having had it copied, I brought it with me to Clairvaux. The feast of the said blessed martyrs is celebrated on the Ides of July [15 July], as is clearly stated in the Martyrology. But because I was unable to remain any longer in the Roman regions, I could not at that time fully investigate the fourth martyr. Some nevertheless believe him to be Blessed Hyacinthus, whose feast is commemorated on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July], or Blessed Vincent, whose feast is observed on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], as appears in the Martyrology. Certain truth concerning these matters may be found if a more diligent inquiry is made at the proper place and time.”

The Passion of St Bonosa, preceded by a prologue and written on fine Italian vellum, follows the account. After the Passion is found a copy of Lessons VII, VIII, and IX, taken from the manuscripts of the Roman Oratory containing that same Passion, which had been sent to Dom Guyton in 1744.

No. 12. Cardinal Conrad.

[Col. 1769]

I. Small bull of Pope Honorius III, dated 6 October 1226, securing to the abbey of Clairvaux the inalienable ownership of the relics given to it by Cardinal Conrad.
