[Col. 1769D]

> “Honorius, Bishop, Servant of the Servants of God, to his beloved sons the Abbot and convent of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian [Col. 1770D] Order, greeting and apostolic blessing. Our venerable brother C., Bishop of Porto, has reported to us that he conferred certain relics upon your church, and has earnestly requested that, forbidding anyone to presume to alienate them therefrom, we should pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon those who presume to act contrary to our prohibition, so that, with those who know of it at least deterred by this fear from such presumption, that church itself may rejoice perpetually in the veneration of the said relics.

> “Therefore, moved by the prayers of the said Bishop and by the charity with which we zealously uphold the honour of that church, by the authority of these presents we strictly forbid anyone to presume to alienate the oft-mentioned relics from it, whether by giving, selling, stealing, or any other method whatsoever. Let no person, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our prohibition or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone knowingly presumes in any way to contravene this prohibition, let him know that he is bound by the chain of excommunication. Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of October [6 October], in the eleventh year of our pontificate.”

(Archives of Aube.—Parchment—the seal is missing—fragments of red and yellow silk seal-strings.)

II. Gift of relics and precious objects made to the abbey of Clairvaux by Cardinal Conrad.

[Col. 1771B]

1227, August.—“Stephen, by divine mercy cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and Peter, Cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil, greeting in the one Saviour to all who inspect these present letters. Let all of you know that, since the nobleman Eginus, Count of Urach and Lord of Freiburg, brother of our venerable father Lord Conrad, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, had pledged to the said Bishop, for two hundred marks sterling, a certain great precious stone called jasper, adorned on every side with precious stones, on one side of which is carved the sign of the cross and on the other side a piece of the Lord’s wood [the True Cross] set in silver; and between the silver and the stone itself are various relics; also two gold ornaments weighing nine marks; a Gospel book with golden covers; a missal with silver covers; a large silver chalice; and a silver casket containing the Lord’s wood, adorned with [Col. 1771C] precious stones and weighing twenty-five marks: the same Bishop, having first obtained from the Lord Pope permission to dispose freely of his property, granted and dedicated during his lifetime, to the monastery of Clairvaux of the Cistercian Order, for the salvation of his soul, every claim and right which he had in these things by reason of the pledge.

“On this condition, however: the monastery is bound to restore all these things to the said count, his brother, if he freely pays back to the aforesaid monastery two hundred marks of good sterling. And so that no doubt may arise concerning these matters in the future, we have caused the present letters to be confirmed by our seals. Done at Anagni in our presence, in the month of August, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory IX.”

(Archives of Aube.—Original on parchment; only a fragment of one of the seals remains.)

III.

[Col. 1772A]

1228.—“To the reverend Abbot of Clairvaux in Christ, and to the whole convent of that monastery: Eginus, Count of Urach and Lord of Freiburg, greeting and an obedience always ready in every matter to the extent of his ability. First, we give thanks to your holiness for the immense and especial reverence which you customarily showed to our lord and brother, the Bishop of Porto of pious memory, while he still lived; and now, to crown all honour done him, through your efforts the bones of the deceased have been brought back from foreign lands and buried among you.

“We therefore, considering the zeal of such great charity and fidelity, bind ourselves to the house of Clairvaux in perpetual services, and shall render them whenever opportunity arises. The ecclesiastical ornaments which are deposited with you, and which we too at one time pledged to our aforesaid brother for two hundred marks sterling, we give, for the remedy of the soul of that same brother and of our own soul and those of our other kinsmen, through the agency of our brother Lord Berthold, formerly Abbot of Lucelle, for your monastery to possess by perpetual and proprietary right, as attested by these letters sealed with our seal.

“But in order that the aforesaid ornaments may be recognized among the rest of your church’s treasure, receive their identifying marks. There is a silver panel studded with gems; a *plenarium* [Gospel-book] covered with gold and distinguished by precious stones; a large chalice adorned with gems and delicately wrought in openwork with the mysteries which Christ bore in the flesh; a missal book covered with silver plates; two golden basins; and a golden roundel filled with precious relic-pledges and encircled with noble pearls. Given in the year of grace 1228.”

(Archives of Aube.—Original on parchment—the seal is missing—red and green silk seal-strings.)

[Col. 1772C] There exists in the Archives of the Aube an original charter on parchment, dated August 1227:

> Conrad, by divine mercy Bishop of Porto and of Saint Rufina . . . [lacuna] . . . in the month of August, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Gregory, Pope the Ninth

—to which is attached the well-preserved seal of Cardinal Conrad. It is affixed by parchment tags. The cardinal, wearing a mitre and clothed in pontifical vestments, is seated on a chair with lions’ heads. He blesses with his right hand and holds his crozier in his left. Legend: “Seal of Conrad, Bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina.”

## Epitaph of Cardinal Conrad

Cardinal Conrad died on crusade, 30 September 1227. By his orders, his body was brought back to France and buried at Clairvaux, not far from Saint Bernard. This epitaph was read at the foot of his tomb:

> HERE LIES LORD CONRAD, WHO WAS FIRST ABBOT OF VILLERS, THEN OF CLAIRVAUX, AFTERWARD OF CÎTEAUX, AND FINALLY CARDINAL BISHOP OF PORTO. WHEN HE WAS STAYING IN THE OVERSEAS PARTS, HE MOST EARNESTLY ORDERED THAT HIS BONES SHOULD BE CARRIED TO CLAIRVAUX, WHERE HE HAD LONG BEFORE CHOSEN HIS BURIAL-PLACE, AND BURIED THERE. HE DIED IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1227, ON THE DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF OCTOBER [30 September].

(*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 992.)

[Col. 1771D] Another epitaph of Cardinal Conrad is found in the chronicle of Villers Abbey in Brabant. It is in verse, and requires some study to understand.

PETIT-Radel, more versed in the knowledge of ancient monuments than in the interpretation of medieval texts, speaks of it thus in the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XVIII, p. 13:

> “We do not transcribe it here, because most of its verses are barbarous and unintelligible, [Col. 1773A] and because, besides, it seems to us to offer no interest, whether historically or literarily.”

I admit that it was easier to pronounce this severe judgment than to grasp its sense properly; but I hope that my efforts to make it less unintelligible will cause it to appear in a more favorable light.

Petit-Radel is mistaken in saying (*loco citato*) that it was written upon the cardinal’s tomb.

A conceit by some monk, it passed from the chronicle of Villers (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 1276) into various collections (*Menologium Cisterciense*, 30 September; Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, “Bishops of Porto”; Manrique).

Here is its text, restored from Henriquez, Ughelli, Manrique, MS. 360 of the Public Library of Dijon—which contains the Chronicle of Villers (late sixteenth or early seventeenth [Col. 1773B] century)—and my own conjectures.

> Live; see that one does not place trusting confidence in time,  
> Where you go as a mortal; how long you flourish in flesh; what blemish you bear.  
> The ear of old men, the stalk of young men, and likewise the herb of childhood,  
> Unequal, yet alike upon their course, are harvest and grass.  
>
> 5. Behold Conrad, shut in the ground, who had securely climbed to so lofty a rank,  
> Now struck down beneath the weight of heaven’s blow.  
> He neither spins nor holds the plough now that he beholds his rewards;  
> Rome, your chief flower blooms above the heavens.  
> The shoot of dukes, O Villers, goes down into your garden;  
>
> 10. Then, O Bernard, it is transplanted into your empty cradle.  
> Soon he deserved to be father of his mother—nay, father of the father  
> Of the Order; at last, O Pope, he deserved to share your authority.  
> Conrad, made radiant by the Pope, was to that sun  
> A full moon; faithful Rome, you were his witness.  
>
> [Col. 1773C] 15. Conrad shaved rough bodies, the beard  
> Of the Order, the neck of the Empire, and Rome’s crown.  
> Daniel in the cloister, Noah in the harbor of his bishopric,  
> Joseph in government, now Benjamin in paradise.  
> In the year one thousand, twice one hundred, and thrice nine,  
>
> 20. Michael’s hand buried him for heaven in its light.

I offer a paraphrastic translation of it: the only kind capable of conveying the multiple meanings concealed beneath these complicated verses.

> “You who live, see—lest one place excessively confident trust in time—where you go as a mortal, how long the flesh flourishes, and what fatal mark you bear. The old man, like a ripe ear of grain; the young man, like a stalk of wheat; and the child, whom I compare to grass, appear very unlike one another; yet I see them, following a common course, come like grass beneath the mower’s scythe. Behold this Conrad, who with a firm step climbed to the summit of honors, enclosed in the grave and cast down beneath the weight of heaven’s blows. This lovely lily spins no longer and directs the plough no longer, since he is gathering his reward. Rome, your fairest flower blooms in the empyrean. The stock of dukes, O Villers, descends into your garden; then it is transplanted, O Bernard, into your empty nursery-bed. Conrad soon deserved to be the father of his mother; more than this, he was judged worthy to be the father of the father of the Order; finally, O Pope, he deserved to share your authority. Conrad, illumined by the Pope’s rays, was for that sun like the moon in its fullness; and you, O Rome, saw him faithfully reflect its splendor, like the bow which God set in heaven. Conrad curbed the heresy with the body of a wild beast; he restored fervor among the monks, like wise old men; he restored to the secular clergy the majesty of command and to Rome the splendor of her crown. A true Daniel in the cloister, Noah in the [Col. 1774A] harbor of his pontificate, Joseph in the exercise of government, he is now Benjamin in heaven. In the year 1227, Michael’s hand buried him for heaven amid the final ceremonies of his feast.”

A short commentary will, I hope at least, justify my attempt at translation.

*Indolis* in the third verse has the sense of “child” or “adolescent.” “*Adolescens, puer*,” says Du Cange in his *Glossary*.

The fifth verse makes a general allusion to the great dignities with which Conrad had been invested, details of which will appear below.

In the sixth verse, *celi* is used as an iamb, whereas *coeli* is actually a spondee. This breach of the rules of quantity may perhaps be explained here by medieval spelling, which wrote *celum* for *coelum*.

*Feriente celi jam pondere fusum* (“now cast down by the striking weight of heaven”) refers to Conrad’s unexpected death, when a fatal fever struck him on crusade. [Col. 1774B]

The author of the epitaph—I dare not call him the poet—having already compared old age in the third verse to a ripe ear, youth to a stalk of wheat, and childhood to grass, compares Conrad in the seventh verse to the lilies of the field, which the Gospel says neither spin nor plough. (St Matthew VI.28; St Luke XII.27.)

In the eighth verse, addressing Rome, he calls Conrad—who was cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and the Pope’s legate—her fairest flower and finest ornament.

*Planta ducum* (“shoot of dukes”) in the ninth verse recalls Conrad’s noble origin.

He was the son of Egon or Eginon of Urach, Count of Fürstenberg and of Freiburg im Breisgau. Through his mother, Agnes or Judith, daughter of Berthold IV, Duke of Zähringen, he was nephew of that Berthold V who was on the point of being proclaimed King of the Romans, and who left him [Col. 1774C] as a hostage in the hands of Archbishop Adolf of Cologne without paying, it is said, his ransom. (Cf. Henninges, *Theatrum genealogicum*, vol. IV, p. 286; Luden, *History of Germany*, French trans., Paris, 1844, vol. V, p. 141. PETIT-Radel, doubtless misled by the *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 586, confuses the duchy of Zähringen with Thuringia.)

In the same verse, the author addresses Villers Abbey in Brabant, of which Conrad became abbot in 1209. (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 586.)

In the tenth verse he addresses Saint Bernard and indicates that Conrad became abbot of Clairvaux, whence the splendor of Saint Bernard’s virtues spread over the world.

Conrad ascended in 1214 to the abbatial seat of Clairvaux, which had become vacant that same year through the death of Guy. (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 804.)

He then became the father of his mother—*matris pater*—in verse 11, Villers Abbey being [Col. 1774D] in the filiation of Clairvaux.

He subsequently became the father of the Father of the Order—in the same verse—when he was appointed Abbot of Cîteaux in 1217. (*Ibid.*, col. 991.)

Verses 12 and 13 refer to Conrad’s elevation to the cardinalate by Honorius III in 1219. (*Histoire littéraire*, p. 8.) He was Cardinal-Bishop of Porto, with the title of Saint Rufina.

Verses 13 and 14 imitate this passage from Psalm LXXXVIII [89].36: “And his throne [shall be] as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven.”

Verses 15 and 16 are certainly the most difficult in the entire piece to understand. *Conradere* does not precisely have the meaning implied by my attempted translation, but it seems that the author used *conrasit* instead of *rasit* merely to make a play upon Conrad’s name.

[Col. 1775A] These two verses appear to me to indicate the labors to which Conrad, after becoming papal legate following his elevation to the cardinalate, devoted himself in France to suppress the Albigensian heresy, and in Germany to reform the morals of the clergy (Labbe, *Councils*, XI, 294); the care which he took to make discipline flourish among the monks; and the distinction which the brilliance of his virtues bestowed upon the Sacred College, whose tiara he refused to accept after the death of Pope Honorius III. But I offer this interpretation only as a simple conjecture.

The final four verses present nothing further that is puzzling.

In verse 17—*Noe portu pontificatus* (“Noah in the harbor of his pontificate”)—the author plays upon the name Porto, of which Conrad was bishop.

[Col. 1775B] Verse 19 indicates the year of Conrad’s death, 1227.

The final verse recalls that Conrad left [Col. 1776A] earth for Heaven on 30 September, the day after the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel. (PETIT-Radel gives the day of his death as 29 September, contrary to all the monuments.)

Several authors have confused Cardinal Conrad of the family of the Dukes of Zähringen with another Cardinal Conrad of Bavaria, likewise a monk of Clairvaux. The latter—the *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 586, falls into this error, which it avoids in vol. IV—was made cardinal in 1142 by Innocent II and died at Bari on his return from crusade. Yet, in the words of Monsignor Louis d’Attichy in his *Flores historiae sacri Collegii* (Paris, 1660, I, 264), “the error is excusable, since both had the same name, country . . . the same rank, and journey.”

Cardinal Conrad Conrad bore, according to Jongelinus [Col. 1776B] (*Purpura D. Bern.*, Cologne, 1644, p. 28), quarterly Urach and Seyn, with an inescutcheon of Fürstenberg.

## No. 13. Note on the purported embellishments of the church and abbey of Clairvaux in the eighteenth century

[Col. 1775]

[Col. 1775B] “Among several expenditures that [Dom Robert Gassot Du Défens] made for the adornment of his abbey,” says the *Brief History of the Abbots of Clairvaux*, “one notes a magnificent portal which he made for his church, an organ, marble altars, fine screens, statues enriched with finished sculpture, and an abbatial court.” (MS. IX of Abbé Matthieu, p. 342.)

From 1729 to 1736 the new stalls of the church were carved.

> [Note: [Col. 1775D] 1729, 25 December.—Contract with a sculptor from Damblin to carve all the stalls of the church for 7,000 livres. He may have one or two assistants, who shall be fed, lodged, supplied with light, and heated like himself. He may go home for a visit every three months, and for this purpose shall be provided with a saddled horse, provided that he remains absent only five or six days. He and his assistants shall eat in the refectory like a religious, except that they shall not take the collation and their supper shall be brought to their room. For the duration of the work, they shall be supplied with a good muid of old wine, to be given to them on feast-days and Sundays by the bottle for a drink. When he has completed his work, he shall be supplied with a cart to convey his tools home. The sculptor maintains that he is answerable only to the Lord Abbot of Clairvaux and his procurator.—Receipt of the amount stipulated above, 8 November 1736. (Archives of the Aube.)]

The old stalls had been removed by his predecessor, [Col. 1775C] Dom Pierre Bouchu. The Benedictines, in their *Literary Journey*, were far from approving the alteration. They speak of it as follows:

> “The church is large, spacious, and beautiful, but plain and without much ornament. The nave was formerly filled with three rows of seats on each side, to accommodate the lay brothers during the office; and from the number of seats one judges that there were formerly nearly three hundred lay brothers at Clairvaux. A few years ago they were all removed, and it was thought enough to retain a small number beneath the organ at the church entrance, where the choir of lay brothers is now situated. The church is certainly more open thereby, but many people think that this removed antiquity made it more venerable. The nave is followed by the choir of the infirm, and this in turn by the choir of the religious, which has nothing but simplicity; but it is a simplicity possessing something grand.”

(*Voyage littéraire*, 1717, [Col. 1775D] part I, p. 99.)

The Benedictines may have read at Clairvaux the following sort of inscription, cited by Dom Le Boullenger (MS. XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 542), from an old manuscript commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict preserved in the abbey library:

> Here are placed the stalls of the church of Clairvaux.
>
> [Col. 1776B] In the upper and lower choir of the priests:  
> one hundred and forty-four stalls.
>
> In the upper and lower choir of the infirm there are:  
> thirty-three stalls.
>
> In the rear choir of the lay brothers there are:  
> three hundred and fifty-one stalls.
>
> And outside the aforesaid choirs there used to be:  
> two hundred and eighty-seven stalls.
>
> Thus, in the total sum, there used to be eight hundred  
> and fifteen seats or stalls in the church of Clairvaux.

I find in the Archives of the Aube various contracts [Col. 1776C] relating to the decoration of Clairvaux church, which I shall merely indicate here.

1736, 12 January.—Contract with a founder from Langres for twelve lecterns and a copper eagle. The final receipt is dated 25 December 1738.  
1737.—Statues of the Blessed Virgin and Saint Robert; contract for two marble chapels and altars.  
1738, 19 August.—Estimate and contract for construction in marble of the high altar of Clairvaux church. It was to be installed on 1 November 1739; the price was 3,050 livres. Receipt, 5 February 1740.  
1739, 22 March.—Contract with a locksmith from Paris for the iron screens of the choir and of four chapels situated opposite the crossing of [Col. 1776D] the church. Receipt, 17 November 1740.

The organ deserves a special notice.

On 20 January 1731, Dom François Fauvre, prior of Notre-Dame-des-Rosiers and procurator of Clairvaux Abbey, concluded a contract with Jacques Cochu, [Col. 1777A] organ-builder residing at Châlons-sur-Marne. By it, the latter undertook, for 1,550 livres, to make a positive organ with an eight-foot façade and sixteen stops:

Eight-foot façade. Eight-foot Bourdon. Four-foot Principal. Four-foot Flute. Cornet. Nazard. Nazard Fourth. Doublette. Tierce. Fourniture. Cymbal. Larigot. Eight-foot Trumpet. Eight-foot Cromorne. Four-foot Clarion. Eight-foot Vox humana. Tremulant and pull-down mechanism.

All materials—wood, tin, lead, copper, and so forth—were to be supplied by the builder. He and his assistant were fed like the religious, except for the collation, which was replaced by supper. No date was fixed for delivery, but it was stipulated that the work should begin no later than [Col. 1777B] 1 April and proceed without interruption.

On 20 July 1732 Dom Fauvre and Jacques Cochu concluded a new contract. This time it concerned the great organ, which Cochu promised to deliver within four years and a few months for 6,000 livres. The conditions were almost the same as those agreed for building the positive organ; only four assistants are mentioned, and Cochu reserved six weeks each year to attend to his private affairs as necessary. The positive organ was not yet completed; it was to be finished before construction of the great organ was undertaken.

Here is the detailed specification:

1. To make six oak-wood bellows, six feet four inches long and three and a half feet wide, with folds and boards properly lined; [Col. 1777C] to make them airtight, with the frames, throats, rockers, and wind-trunks leading to the windchests.

2. Further, to make four divisions of windchest for the great manual, in oak, to receive the stops detailed below; the said windchests to have no borrowing or intercommunication, and to be properly airtight.

3. Further, to make a keyboard of fifty keys, in oak, faced with ebony, with the sharps faced with ivory; the said keyboard extending to upper D (*D-la-ré*), including C-sharp.

4. To make and construct all the action and rollerboards, and to make them operate freely.

5. To make a polished and burnished tin façade, speaking and resonating at sixteen-foot pitch.

6. To make a stopped eight-foot Bourdon, namely twenty-six lower pipes in oak, and all those above them, with all bodies and feet of metal; [Col. 1777D] the said Bourdon speaking at sixteen-foot pitch, in unison with the façade.

7. To make an open eight-foot Flute, namely twenty-six lower pipes in oak, and all those above them, with all bodies and feet of metal; the said Flute speaking at the octave of the façade.

8. To make an eight-foot stop, part of which shall be taken from the façade and the remainder placed inside; all bodies of tin upon metal feet; the said eight-foot stop speaking at the octave of the façade.

9. To make a small stopped four-foot Bourdon, fourteen lower pipes of which shall be oak and all those above them, with all bodies and feet of metal; the said Bourdon speaking at eight-foot pitch.

10. To make a Cornet extending over twenty-seven keys, beginning at C and continuing to upper D; the said Cornet to consist of five pipes on each key, namely Bourdon, Flute, Nazard, Fourth, and [Col. 1778A] Tierce; all these pipes to have bodies and feet of metal.

11. To make a Principal, with all bodies of tin upon metal feet; the said Principal speaking at four-foot pitch.

12. To make a large Tierce, with all bodies and feet of metal; the said Tierce speaking at the third of the Principal.

13. To make a Nazard, with all bodies and feet of metal, speaking at the fifth of the Principal.

14. To make a Nazard Fourth, with all bodies and feet of metal, speaking at the octave of the Principal.

15. To make a small Tierce, with all bodies and feet of metal; the said Tierce speaking at the third of the Doublette.

16. To make a large Fourniture of two pipes on each key, all bodies of tin and feet of metal.

17. To make a small Fourniture of four pipes on each key, all bodies of tin upon [Col. 1778B] metal feet.

18. To make a Cymbal of four pipes on each key, all bodies of tin upon metal feet.

19. To make a Bombarde, with all bodies of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal; the said stop speaking at sixteen-foot pitch.

20. To make a Trumpet, with all bodies of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal; the said Trumpet speaking at eight-foot pitch.

21. To make a Cromorne, with all bodies and bells of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal; the said Cromorne speaking at eight-foot pitch, in unison with the Trumpet.

22. To make a Clarion, with all bodies of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, [Col. 1778C] wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal; the said Clarion speaking at the octave of the Trumpet.

23. To make a Vox humana, with all bodies and bells of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal; the said Vox humana speaking at eight-foot pitch.

24. To make a twenty-seven-key solo Cornet, beginning at C and continuing to upper D, composed of five pipes upon each key, namely Bourdon, Flute, Nazard, Fourth, and Tierce, all bodies and feet of metal; the keyboard shall be of oak faced with ebony, and the sharps faced with ivory.

25. To make a solo Trumpet of twenty-seven pipes upon the same keyboard, with all bodies of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, shallots and feet of metal.

26. (Echo composed of eight stops.) To make and construct an echo windchest of thirty-nine channels’ compass, [Col. 1778D] to receive the stops named below; it shall be of oak, without borrowing or intercommunication, and properly airtight; to construct all rockers and action, with its oak keyboard faced with ebony and its sharps faced with ivory; the said keyboard beginning at bass C and continuing to upper D.

1. To make a Bourdon, with all bodies and feet of metal.

2. To make a Principal, with all bodies of tin upon metal feet.

3. To make a Nazard, with all bodies and feet of metal.

4. To make a Nazard Fourth, with all bodies and feet of metal.

5. To make a Doublette, with all bodies of tin upon metal feet.

6. To make a Fourniture of three pipes on each [Col. 1779A] key, all bodies of tin upon metal feet.

7. To make a Cymbal of two pipes on each key, all bodies of tin upon metal feet.

8. To make a Cromorne, with all bodies and bells of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wire of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal.

26. To make and construct two divisions of pedal windchest of thirty-two channels’ compass, in oak, without borrowing or intercommunication, with their freely working action and rollerboards, and a pedalboard of thirty-two keys, beginning at low F of the compass extension and extending to C.

1. To make an eight-foot Flute pedal with its compass extension, entirely in oak.

2. To make a four-foot Flute pedal, namely its lowest octave in oak and all the upper pipes, with all bodies and feet of metal.

3. To make a Trumpet pedal, with all bodies [Col. 1779B] of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal.

4. To make a Clarion pedal, with all bodies of tin, reeds and tongues of copper, tuning wires of iron wire, wooden blocks, shallots, and feet of metal.

27. To make a tremulant with wind loss; to make a slow-wind tremulant.

For the positive organ as for the great organ, Cochu did not undertake the case, carpentry, carving, or ironwork; I do not know by whom or upon what terms these were executed. A certain Master Jean Gillot of Langres made, for 800 livres, the gallery balustrade consisting of twenty balusters, for which 1,233 pounds of copper were supplied to him. His contract is dated 3 June 1735 and the final receipt, 12 January 1736.

That same year the great organ was completed. Dom Nicolas Similiart, professed religious of Signy and organist, and Bénigne Balbastre, organist [Col. 1779C] of the cathedral and other churches of Dijon, experts appointed by the religious of Clairvaux, spent four days examining Cochu’s work. It was declared sound and acceptable on 29 March 1736; on 7 April following the builder issued his final receipt.

Clairvaux enjoyed its organ for fifty-six years. On 10 February 1792 the abbey passed into the hands of new owners. They were required to preserve the organ and its accessories until they should be removed by the administration, which had reserved them, together with several other objects.

Posters displayed in the district of Bar-sur-Aube and in the principal towns of the neighboring departments soon announced that the organ of Clairvaux was for sale and that it would be auctioned at Bar-sur-Aube on 10 September 1792.

This news moved the churchwardens of Troyes Cathedral. They represented, on 10 August 1792, to the departmental administrators that the organ of [Col. 1779D] Saint Peter’s, placed meanly between two pillars of the choir, did not correspond to the beauty of the building; that sale of the Clairvaux organ would yield only a trifling profit; and that its proper place was in the cathedral, in a gallery to be built above the principal door.

The constitutional bishop, Augustin Sibille, signed the churchwardens’ petition. The departmental directory referred it to the directory of the district of Troyes.

The latter, considering that the Clairvaux organ ought to be counted among works of art, whose preservation accorded with the principles and laws of the National Assembly; and further, that the proposed sale would produce only a modest sum for the nation, granted the churchwardens’ request, on condition that the fabric should bear every expense, [Col. 1780A] and authorized it to sell the old organ of Saint Peter’s to cover part of the cost. (18 August 1792.)

On 29 August 1792 the departmental directory ratified the decision of the directory of the district of Troyes and appointed Sieur Richard, organ-builder of Nancy, to direct the work of removal and reconstruction. It further decided that its decree would take effect only after approval by the Minister of the Interior, to whom an official copy was sent on 14 November following.

The Minister of the Interior delayed his answer. Meanwhile, the purchaser of Clairvaux Abbey demanded the removal of the movable objects reserved at the sale, which he was required to preserve. In his petition to the departmental directory, he said, on 6 January 1793, that he had fulfilled this obligation with the most scrupulous exactitude, [Col. 1780B] and all the more willingly because these objects had hitherto inconvenienced him only slightly; but he intended to establish a glassworks in the church of the monastery, and he warned the administration that the fire, smoke, and movement of numerous workmen might cause great damage to the organ, which was already deteriorating. On the other hand, the directory of the district of Bar-sur-Aube asked to be relieved of responsibility for watching over this precious instrument, which necessarily deteriorated through lack of use and of the care that an organist alone could have devoted to its preservation. (31 January 1793.)

Since the Minister’s answer did not arrive, the departmental directory treated his silence as disapproval of its decree of 29 August 1792. Granting the claims of the purchaser of Clairvaux, it decreed on 11 February 1793 that the organ should be sold at Bar-sur-Aube according to the form [Col. 1780C] prescribed by law.

New notices were posted, fixing the sale for 12 March following. It took place on that day, and the organ was adjudicated for 12,500 livres to Sieur Bernard Lécuyer, building contractor residing at Bar-sur-Aube, with Sieur Joachim Girardon as guarantor.

On 24 March 1793 the Minister of the Interior finally replied that he saw no objection to the organ of Clairvaux being granted to the municipality of Troyes, provided that it bore the costs of installation and removal.

No sooner had Citizens Lécuyer and Girardon learned of the Minister’s letter than they proposed to the departmental administrators that the sale made to them be simply and wholly rescinded, releasing them from payment of the purchase price, since they wished to contribute, as far as lay within their power, to the embellishment of the principal church of the department and to the preservation of a [Col. 1780D] monument of the arts.

After various administrative formalities had been completed, the directory of the department of the Aube accepted the rescission offered by the purchasers on 19 June 1793 and authorized the municipality of Troyes to have the organ in question moved from the church of the former Abbey of Clairvaux to that of Saint Peter at Troyes, on condition that it maintain the said organ, without this, however, prejudicing the nation’s right of ownership in the organ, over which the municipality of Troyes could in no way dispose without the nation’s approval.

Before the destruction of Clairvaux Abbey, René, son of Jacques Cochu, had assisted his father in perfecting his work.

> [Note: [Col. 1779D] A short handwritten inscription pasted [Col. 1780D] inside the case of the great organ states that in [Col. 1781D] 1788, under M. Rocourt, the last abbot of Clairvaux, the organ was restored and enlarged by the addition of Flute, Trumpet, Bombarde, and Pedal stops, by François-Henri Cliquot, organ-builder to the King.]

He was naturally chosen to bring the organ to Troyes. He dismantled it, numbered all its parts, and deposited them [Col. 1781A] in the cathedral beneath Saint Paul’s tower. The grave events which followed from that time caused the organ to be forgotten for many years; and when the existence of this fine instrument was remembered, dust and damp had already seriously damaged it.

On 19 Brumaire, Year XII (11 November 1803), the fabric of Saint Peter’s was legally constituted. The first thoughts of the administrators composing it were for the organ and its restoration. The archbishop-bishop, the prefect, and the mayor promised to support their efforts; but the resources available to them did not correspond to the scale of the undertaking. They therefore resolved to appeal to public generosity, and on 23 April 1804 a subscription was opened for the restoration and installation of the Clairvaux organ in the cathedral church of Saint Peter at Troyes. I do not know what it produced.

[Col. 1781B] On 21 August 1805 the fabric, having obtained permission to cut its reserve woodland, was authorized to apply part of the sum which would accrue to it from its sale to construction of a gallery intended to support the organ. Provisional arrangements were made with René Cochu and, thanks to funds advanced by several churchwardens, work began under the direction of M. Vaudé, architect.

The estimate for the gallery amounted to 34,567 francs 81 centimes.

> [Note: [Col. 1781D] The contract award produced a reduction of 567 francs 81 centimes.]

By May 1807 approximately two-thirds of the work had been completed. René Cochu had submitted his estimate to the fabric on 2 January of the same year; it amounted to 11,050 francs. On 3 December he undertook, on the terms fixed by himself, to repair the organ, place it upon the gallery, and put it into playable condition no later than 20 April of the following year.

In May 1808 the gallery was finished [Col. 1781C] and the organ had been restored there in its former beauty. M. Nicolas Séjean, organist of Saint-Sulpice in Paris, came to examine Cochu’s work. He gave the most favorable report of it. (10 July.) He especially noted the ingenious arrangement of the bellows, which could be set in motion by a child using a single lever. Finally, he judged that the fabric should pay Cochu, beyond the agreed sum, 500 francs

> [Note: [Col. 1781D] The documents consulted in preparing [Col. 1782D] this notice are preserved in the Archives of the Aube and in the archives of the fabric of Saint Peter’s, Troyes.]

for alterations and additions consisting of bass stops, a twenty-three-pipe serpent, and thirty-pipe clarinet and oboe stops.

> [Note: [Col. 1782D] The fabric granted this additional sum to Cochu on 18 September 1808.]

“Dom Pierre Mayeur,” says the *Brief History of the Abbots of Clairvaux* (MS. IX of Abbé Matthieu, p. 342), “had constructed at great expense the superb cloister of the religious, the refectory, bakery, and dormitories; he expended immense sums in decorating the abbey.”

The following document relates to his administration:

[Col. 1781D] MS XV of Abbé Matthieu, p. 617.—Tombs opened in the church of Clairvaux, in the transept on the north side and in the monks’ cemetery before the chapel of All Saints. There were [Col. 1782A] six sepulchral stones or tombs, corresponding to five painted figures lower down on the wall, representing five bishops; and one smaller, heart-shaped carved stone, covering the heart of Dom Tristan de Bizet, monk of Clairvaux, native of Troyes, Abbot of Signy and subsequently bishop of Saintes, who died and was buried in the Bernardins’ college at Paris, and whose heart had been sent to Clairvaux. These six stones rose four to five inches above the pavement. In 1751 the pavement, formerly of brick tiles, was replaced by large stone slabs. The said sepulchral stones were then removed and taken outside. This led to the discovery of the five stones hollowed out and shaped as chests, in which the bodies of the five bishops had been placed, each covered by a flat stone of the same length and width as the said chest. In the five were found some decayed bones, scraps of decayed clothing, decayed wooden croziers, and decayed leather, but without [Col. 1782B] any writing in four of these chests or coffins. In the fifth, which was in the middle, there was found and removed a lead plate about eight inches long and five to six inches wide. Its engraved writing, in eight lines, the last of which are somewhat damaged, reads as follows:

> + On the sixth day before the Ides of November, the lord Godfrey, bishop of Langres, of pious memory, rested in this place in a holy end. Here also he had been anointed and fortified with the divine sacraments through the ministry of the lord Alan, bishop of Auxerre; and, having been washed in the community by the hands of the bishops . . . . . and of Auxerre, he was honourably buried by the abbots.

This shows that Godfrey received extreme unction and the holy viaticum in the church. As for the heart of the bishop of Saintes, enclosed in an entirely embalmed lead heart, it was left in the ground as it was; the coffins likewise were left as they were and covered again with their stones. As for the stones [Col. 1782C] which rose above the paving, they were taken out of the church. In their place, flush with the pavement, black marble plaques were installed, upon which were engraved the names, offices, dignities, and episcopal sees of each bishop.

On 8 September 1771, the bodies of twenty-four Abbots of Clairvaux and the hearts of two abbots of that monastery, placed in the old cloister, were exhumed; after the community Mass, on the eleventh of the same month, they were solemnly deposited in the two side aisles of the church, in accordance with their rank.

It was not possible to exhume the body of St Robert, second Abbot of Clairvaux, because, after his tomb beneath the first arch of the cloister had been opened, his bones were found entirely consumed. (Extract from the official record of exhumation and burial, drawn up and signed by the monks.—Archives of Aube.)

I find in the Archives of Aube a contract [Col. 1782D] made on 2 May 1780 with an Italian to whitewash the whole interior of Clairvaux church and to lay out all the vaults, piers, and columns in panels, for 1,500 livres.

No. 14. Chapel of the Counts of Flanders.

[Col. 1781]

[Col. 1781D] The chapel called that of the Counts of Flanders stood [Col. 1782D] a short distance from the eastern end of the church [Col. 1783A] of Clairvaux, and was oriented as the church was. Monastic tradition attributed its construction to Philip, Count of Flanders, who died at the siege of Acre on 1 June 1191 (*Art de vérifier les dates*), and asserted that he had it built in that very year. It seemed worthwhile to me briefly to discuss both points.

Before petitioning the king for permission to transfer the bones contained in this chapel, Dom Le Boullenger, archivist of the abbey, was charged with investigating its origin. The monk’s work has come down to us, and it is this short memorandum that I shall examine (Archives of Aube).

Dom Le Boullenger begins by admitting that the Clairvaux archives supplied him with no information; he builds his case from printed works. He relies especially on the epitaph of Count Philip reported in Henriquez, on Father Martène in his *Anecdota*, and on [Col. 1783B] the *Journal de Trévoux* (August 1739), to prove that the chapel was built by Count Philip in the very year of his death. He likewise cites, as conclusive, an attestation issued by the monks of Clairvaux on 13 February 1544, in which one read: “the chapel was built by the most illustrious Philip, Count of Flanders.”

Let us briefly examine the value of these authorities.

1. The epitaph taken from the Book of Burials does indeed state that the chapel had been built by the Count of Flanders for himself and his wife: “. . . through the care of his wife Matilda he was transferred to Clairvaux, and honourably laid to rest within this chapel, which he had prepared for her and for himself.” (Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, VI.)

But, to draw a certain conclusion from this text, one would have to establish the antiquity of the Book of Burials as published by Henriquez; and that antiquity is at least highly doubtful. I know [Col. 1783C] that Charles de Visch (*Biblioth. script. O. C.*) attributes the composition of this book to Geoffrey, fourth Abbot of Clairvaux and scribe of St Bernard: “To him is attributed the book on illustrious persons buried at Clairvaux, which is customarily entitled the *Book of Tombs*.” But this is a mere assertion, all the less demonstrated with regard to the text supplied by Henriquez because the latter cited no author’s name.

It is almost superfluous to observe that Geoffrey could have composed only a very small part of the *Book of Burials*, and that it must have grown greatly after his death.

Moreover, Henriquez himself corrected the assertion of the epitaph in the *Menologium of Cîteaux*, where, under 12 August, speaking of the chapel of the Counts of Flanders, he writes: “Matilda, widow of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders, had built it for herself.”

2. Father Martène entered into no discussion concerning the builder of the chapel or the date of [Col. 1783D] its construction; he merely published two charters which we shall mention a little later.

3. Since the *Journal de Trévoux* reported a tradition without examining it, it cannot be adduced as testimony, any more than can the monks’ attestation.

Besides, a serious error on an easily verifiable point, committed by the *Journal de Trévoux*, Dom Le Boullenger, and—on his authority—the monks of Clairvaux in their petition, shows that they may have erred on other points less easy to verify. The error was to give Count Philip and Matilda a daughter Agnes, whom they never had.

“In the same chapel,” says Dom Le Boullenger, “one sees the tomb of Agnes, Countess of Champagne, daughter of Count Philip and Matilda.”

The petition to the king says the same, and the official exhumation record speaks of the bones of Philip, [Col. 1784A] Matilda, and “Agnes their daughter.” A few years earlier the *Journal de Trévoux* had advanced this incredible assertion, and perhaps helped establish so singular a belief.

Yet it could have been known, without great expense of learning, that Count Philip died childless after marrying twice; and Henriquez did not permit one to be mistaken about Princess Agnes, buried beside the Count of Flanders. The following is found in the Book of Burials (*Fasciculus SS. O. C.*, vol. II, Distinction XLI, VI).

**Agnes, Countess**

> “After the tombs of Lord Philip, Count of Flanders, and Matilda his wife, there lies in their chapel the most illustrious lady Agnes, Countess of Champagne.”

It follows from the foregoing that [Col. 1784B] Dom Le Boullenger’s researches had not been guided by very rigorous criticism, and that the monk adhered to the monastic tradition, seemingly confirmed by the epitaph in the Book of Burials.

Some documents, well known to Dom Le Boullenger, should, it seems to me, have clarified the question.

They are:

1. A small bull of Clement III, issued at the Lateran on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the third year of his pontificate (22 January 1190), confirming the concession of burial in their church which the monks of Clairvaux had granted to Count Philip and Matilda:

> “Yielding to the petitions of the noble man, the Count of Flanders, and Matilda, his countess and wife, we grant by apostolic authority to the same church, and confirm by this present written document, their free burial in your church when God shall call them from this present life, according to the concession which, at their request, you have made to them.”

[Col. 1784C] (From the original, Archives of Aube.)

2. A charter of 1191 by which Philip, Count of Flanders, gives Clairvaux the portable chapel which was to accompany him on crusade: “which I carry with me on the journey to Jerusalem.” (See this document in the *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 639.) Pope Innocent III, by a small bull issued at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year of his pontificate (8 December 1204), confirmed this gift:

> “The chapel, which Philip, Count of Flanders, of illustrious memory, bequeathed to you in his last will for the service [or ornament; see Cange, *Glossary*] of the altar, and which . . . . . you possess . . . we confirm.”

(The originals of this bull and of the charter of donation are in the Archives of Aube.)

3. Another charter of the same man, dated 1191, which shows that Philip had given his chapel as a gift—by this must be understood all the equipment, and not the place of worship—to his wife [Col. 1784D] Matilda: “I gave my chapel . . . to my dearest consort, Queen Matilda” (Matilda was the daughter of Alfonso, king of Portugal; she married Philip in 1185.—See *Art de vérifier les dates*); and that Matilda, having enriched it—“since she had enlarged it in many respects”—in turn gave it to Clairvaux church, where Philip and Matilda had chosen their burial: “which she herself afterwards, with my consent and approval, as she had enlarged it, devoutly bestowed upon the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Clairvaux, WHERE SHE AND I, WITH EQUAL DEVOTION, HAVE CHOSEN OUR BURIAL.” (*Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 639.—The original is in the Archives of Aube.)

It seems to me that these authentic documents establish that, before 1191, the Count of Flanders had chosen his burial in Clairvaux church [Col. 1785A] [Note: [Col. 1785D] If the following passage from the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* were objected against the thesis which I maintain: “In the year of the Lord 1191, in the lands beyond the sea, the city of Acre was recovered by the Christians. Among the other princes who died before Acre, the noble Count Philip of Flanders also died. His bones, conveyed to Clairvaux, were decently placed in a stone sarcophagus in his own chapel,” I would reply that the words “in his own chapel” can perfectly well be understood to mean a chapel within Clairvaux church, in which the Count of Flanders had designated the location of his tomb. (*S. Bern. gen. illustr. assert.*, p. 89.)], and not in a separate chapel. It is clear that Princess Matilda wished to be buried in that same church; this shows that she thought of building a distinct chapel only after her husband’s death.

It further seems evident that the two donations of Count Philip and Matilda, wrongly interpreted and understood inaccurately, gave rise to the tradition which attributed construction of the chapel bearing their name to them. I say “attributed to them,” for it is not fully demonstrated that it was built even by Princess Matilda, since Dom Le Boullenger admits that neither Count Philip nor his wife ever endowed it with funds or revenues.

[Col. 1786A] M. Arnaud reports in his *Archaeological Journey* (Troyes, 1843), p. 205, that he found, abandoned in a street at Bar-sur-Aube, a fragment of a tomb in fine black marble, bordered with fillets and one metre wide, with this incomplete inscription:

> HERE LIES THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LADY MATILDA, WIFE OF PHILIP, COUNT OF FLANDERS . . . .

That was all that time had then spared of the later chapel of the Counts of Flanders.

No. 13. Eugenius III.

[Col. 1785]

[Col. 1785B] It is not without interest to trace Pope Eugenius III’s journey in France from the indications supplied by his acts. I record them here from Philipp Jaffé’s *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*; Berlin, 1851, quarto.

**1147**

7, 8 March: at Susa. 9 March: at Ulcia [uncertain place-name]. 26 March: at Cluny. 30, 31 March: at Dijon. 3, 4 April: at Mesnil-Lambert. 10 April: at Troyes. 11 April: in the territory of Troyes. April: at Provins. 15 April: in the territory of Meaux. 20 April: at Paris. 30 April: at Saint-Denis. 24, 25, 28 April: at Paris. 1, 6, 7, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 25, [Col. 1785C] 27, 28, 29, 30 May: at Paris. 1, 3, 5, 7 June: at Paris. 10, 11 June: at Saint-Denis. 12, 13, 14, 17, 19, 22, 24, 26, 29 June: at Meaux. 2 July: at Paris. 14, 15, 16, 17, 23, 28, 29, 30, 31 July: at Auxerre. 3, 8, 13, 15, 22, 23, 24, 25 August: at Auxerre. 6 September: at Auxerre. 14, 17 September: at Cîteaux. 19 September: at Saint-Seine. 25 September: at Auxerre. 6, 10, 11, 12 October: at Auxerre. 13 October: at Saint-Florentin. 24, 25, 26, 27 October: at Châlons. 1, 3 November: at Châlons. 5, 9, 11, 22 November: at Verdun. [Col. 1785D] 29 November: near Trier. 30 November: at Trier. 7, 18, 20, 22, 25 December: at Trier.

**1148**

13, 20, 27, 28, 31 January: at Trier. 6, 13 February: at Trier. 15 February: at Sarranium. 18 February: at Metz. 22, 26 February: at Verdun. [Col. 1786B] 16, 17, 21, 28, 29, 30 March: at Reims. 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14, 18 April: at Reims. 20 April: at Châlons. 23 April: in the territory of Troyes, at Brienne. 24, 26 April: at CLAIRVAUX. 27 April: in the territory of Langres. 29 April: at Langres. 5, 7 May: at Besançon. May: in the Jura mountains. 14, 17, 20, 27 May: at Lausanne. 16 June: at Vercelli.

This simple table somewhat unsettles the itinerary which the *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* (vol. VI, book LXXIX, p. 441) have Pope Eugenius III follow; but the learned authors of that great work did not possess the easy means supplied to me by the *Regesta*, and which can enable others, as it has enabled me, [Col. 1786C] to follow a pope’s travels almost day by day.

It appears from the *Voyage Littéraire* (Paris, 1717, part I, p. 101) that Pope Eugenius III, while he was only a monk at Clairvaux, had been charged with care of the warming-room.

“The warming-room,” say the Benedictines, “adjoins the refectory. The following verses are read upon the door:

> In this warming-room the good monk  
> Must warm himself quietly, or in silence,  
> Showing himself gracious in bearing,  
> And above all preserving peace and silence.  
> For, as it is said, here in patience  
> Eugenius, the holy man, was keeper of the warming-room;  
> But his virtue and great wisdom  
> So exalted him that he became Pope of Rome.”

MS XV of Abbé Matthieu contains a copy of a small bull of Pope Eugenius III which I [Col. 1786D] believe useful to reproduce:

P. 216.—“Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the community of Savigny and the abbots of the monasteries belonging to that house, and to their brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing. The peace of the Church, the concord of brethren, the vigour of religious life, and the state of monasteries are preserved by the bond of unity. For this reason, our beloved sons, the Abbots of Savigny and Beaubec, coming [Col. 1787A] to the Chapter of Cîteaux, humbly petitioned us in person that both they and their whole community might be received, through our dearest son Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, into the unity of the Cistercian Congregation and Order. Accordingly, commending in the Lord their religious devotion, we have rejoiced with them in the duty of paternal charity, knowing that it is written: ‘A brother who is helped by a brother: both shall be consoled.’ Therefore, according to their pleasing-to-God and praiseworthy desire, joining both them and you to that holy fellowship, we decree by apostolic authority that this loving and delightful association be inviolably observed in future times. We command you, then, to render filial obedience according to the ordinances of the same Order all the more readily to our aforesaid son, the Abbot of Savigny, inasmuch as he is known to labour more earnestly for your salvation. But if anyone knowingly attempts to act against this document of our confirmation, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Segnanum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, 1148.” (Cf. Manrique, *Ann. Cist.*, year 1148, chap. VII.)

There exists a *History of the Pontificate of Eugenius III*, by Dom Jean Delannes, librarian of Clairvaux; Nancy, 1737, 1 small octavo volume.—This monk says in his preface that for three years he had been applying himself to a history of Clairvaux Abbey.

No. 16. Clairvaux acquired by the government.

[Col. 1787]

Under a decree of 16 June 1808, the Government became purchaser of the former Abbey of Clairvaux. It was sold to the Government on 27 August 1808 [Col. 1787B] by M. Antoine-Pierre Rousseau, manufacturer and proprietor, member of the electoral college of the department of Aube. Rousseau himself had acquired it from Sieur Cauzon, the first purchaser, on 2 Vendémiaire, Year VIII (24 September 1799).

Clairvaux was sold to the Government for 350,000 francs.

I read the following details in a survey of the buildings drawn up on 8 November 1808 by M. Gilbert, architect of civil buildings attached to the Ministry of the Interior.

**ART. 27.—Church.** “On leaving the cloisters, one enters the church at the level of the transept.

This church has been transformed into a glassworks hall; at its greatest extent, from the portal to the transept, it is laid out and forms a nave and side aisles . . . . . Opposite the nave, in the crossing section, is a rounded apse with columns and a gallery; and to the left, on the north side, a sacristy.”

A report by the same architect states that in [Col. 1788A] 1812 the church was, if not wholly, at least three-quarters demolished.

[Col. 1788B] In the present chapel for prisoners at Clairvaux, I saw in 1846 a fine grisaille painting representing St Malachy in a monk’s habit, with a mitre upon his head and reclining upon his crozier. Angels scatter flowers over him.

Some persons believe they find there an image of St Bernard, forgetting that the great abbot never wore a mitre, and that until his thirty-third successor, Stephen of Soisy, it did not appear upon the heads of the Abbots of Clairvaux.

“Stephen of Soisy,” say the *Elogia* of Dom Antoine Saulnier, “thirty-fourth Abbot of Clairvaux, professor of sacred theology, formerly Abbot of Preuilly, was abbot here for twenty-two years, in the year of the Lord 1380. He was the first mitred abbot.

> This Stephen of Soisy, also called Doctor,  
> First ruled Preuilly and then this house;  
> He presided for twice ten years and two.  
> This lord was the first to be mitred.”

(Cf. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, col. 809.)

No. 17. Extracts from the Clairvaux inventories concerning St Bernard and St Malachy.

[Col. 1787]

### A. INVENTORY OF 1504

[Note: [Col. 1787D] Copies made in the eighteenth century.—(Archives of Aube.)]

[Col. 1787C]

Inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux, made on the fifteenth day of December in the year of the Lord 1504, in the time of the Reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Dom John, fortieth Abbot of Clairvaux, professor of sacred theology (John of Chalon); in the presence of the Reverend Father in Christ, Dom Peter of Virey, senior abbot, and Lords [an apparent error for “Dom”] Nicholas of Paris, prior, and James of Sézanne, sacristan of the same monastery.

**Folio 1, recto and verso. Large panel with doors.**

First is a panel with doors, upon the outer surfaces of which are two raised angels. It was made in the time of Dom William, twelfth Abbot of Clairvaux, and Lords Peter and Drogo, sacristans, from thirty-five marks of silver and two marks of gold. It contains [Col. 1787D] many precious stones, namely sixteen balas rubies, thirty-one sapphires, and other stones of lesser value. In the middle of this [Col. 1788C] panel was placed a portion of the Lord’s Cross, sent to Blessed Bernard by the patriarch of Jerusalem, as Bernard himself writes to the patriarch in a certain letter [Note: [Col. 1787D] *Works of St Bernard*, Letter CLXXV. Note.—The same notable particle of the Lord’s wood is still to be seen in the treasury of Clairvaux.] and which for a long time in his own day was the only one at Clairvaux . . . this panel contains the following relics . . . finger of Blessed Bernard—the little vessel containing the finger is found empty.

**Folio 2, recto. Panel containing the cross sent to Blessed Bernard by Amalric, King of Jerusalem.**

Second is a silver panel containing nine marks of silver and one mark of gold. It was commissioned at Clairvaux by Hugh, formerly Abbot of Saint-Ghislain (St Guislain, Diocese of Cambrai), then a monk of Clairvaux, in the time of Lords Anselm, Peter, and Drogo, sacristans. In the middle of the panel, in the most prominent place, is set the cross which Amalric, King of Jerusalem, miraculously sent to Clairvaux, many years after Blessed Bernard’s death, having been warned by him in a dream, as is more fully contained in the treatise [Col. 1788D] on this matter [Note: [Col. 1788D] Manrique (*Ann. Cist.*, year 1173) recounts the expedition of Amalric I, King of Jerusalem, St Bernard’s apparition to that prince, and the latter’s sending of a fragment of the True Cross to Clairvaux. His account is drawn from ancient manuscripts. It is found again in *Works of St Bernard*, Geoffrey, III, 26. In Manrique, as in Mabillon’s edition, the account [Col. 1789D] ends thus: “A man indeed of good repute and upright conduct, as far removed from suspicion of falsehood as he was free from corruptions of life.”—MS no. 6 of the public library of Troyes, a late-twelfth-century folio, gives the history of the fragment of the True Cross sent to Clairvaux by Amalric: “How the King of Jerusalem, at the appearance and command of St Bernard, sent to Clairvaux the holy cross which he carried in battles.” But after *alienus* [“free”], one reads the following:

> “Let the church of Clairvaux, therefore, rejoice in the Lord, raised to so lofty a rank by such a gift and endowed with the most certain possession of an incomparable treasure; let it glory in possessing the saving wood. Far from here be every ground for doubt and ambiguous suspicion, where certainty, supported by the testimony of so celebrated a miracle and by the authoritative witness of exalted persons, confirms, as a truth established beyond question, a certain portion of the sacred stock. Let others see—those who believe themselves participants in that same blessing—let them see, I say, by what test of truth it is established that what they possess is truly of the wood of the most holy Cross. [Col. 1790D] But we certainly are not permitted to doubt ours, for we are made firm in the matter not now by faith but by the most certain knowledge, through both the miracle of heavenly revelation and the testimony of the king’s piety. Therefore, as we confidently recline beneath the precious shade of this tree, with hearts overflowing we beseech your goodness, most merciful Jesus: reward with a heavenly blessing the giver of this sacred gift, and preserve us, the most devoted servants of your Cross, in the freedom which it itself brought forth. You who live and reign with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.”

This short fragment deserved to be known. It might still serve to establish, against common opinion, that the authenticity of a relic was not without value in the eyes of the credulous monks of the Middle Ages. Those who accused them of foolish credulity did not know that truth is the basis of faith.].

**Folio 5, verso.**—Eleventh is a vessel [Col. 1789A] made in the time of Lords Peter and Drogo, sacristans of Clairvaux, from three and a half marks of silver. In it is placed the Lord’s Cross, which Lord Evrard of Barres, formerly Master of the Temple and afterwards monk of Clairvaux, brought to Clairvaux; he was the uncle of Lord Adam, Bishop of Thérouanne, afterwards monk of Clairvaux. In this vessel was placed a tooth of St Bernard, which was carried to Paris.

**Folio 8, recto.**—The heads follow.

See at the beginning of my letter the paragraphs of this inventory concerning the head of St Bernard and that of St Malachy.

**Folio 9, recto.**—This entry is found: “The things which follow were added to the inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux in the time of Dom Peter of Virey, then abbot, and Dom James of Sézanne, sacristan.”

**Folio 9, verso.**—Two beautiful, large, and tall images of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Bernard, with their [Col. 1789B] feet, diadems, and other ornaments, very finely made, worked, and gilded; together weighing 176 marks, 3 ounces, 7 *tresels* [a unit of weight].

**Folio 10, recto.**—The image of Blessed Bernard by itself weighs 92 marks, 7 ounces, 5 *tresels*, as appears from the statement of the parts of the same image. The body alone weighs 30 marks, 3½ ounces; the head, two arms, and diadem weigh 27 marks, 3½ ounces; the church and crozier without the staff weigh 16 marks, 6 ounces, 5 *tresels*; the foot, with its reliquary but without the crystal, weighs 18 marks, 2 ounces. All these parts joined together make the total weight of 92 marks, 7 ounces, 5 *tresels*. Beneath its foot, in a phylactery, are contained the following relics: namely, of the rib of Blessed Bernard . . . of Blessed Bernard’s cowl and covering, and of the mat upon which he died. The precious and ordinary stones of these images, together with the value [Col. 1789C] and price of their workmanship, are set out more fully elsewhere, namely in the statement delivered and written in his own hand by Dom William Mole.

**Folio 10, verso.**—Two large plain silver plates or discs, for use by the prelate at the high altar, in the middle of which, within a sun-shaped figure, are placed the arms of St Bernard; without gilding, they weigh 15 marks, 5½ ounces.

**Folio 11, recto.**—Other relics in diverse vessels follow.

A crystal vessel with a three-footed silver stand, gilded, in which is placed the thumb of the most blessed Abbot Bernard, covered by a silver little bell, at the top of which is a sapphire. This vessel was commissioned by Dom John of Aizanville; its weight is 4½ marks and half an ounce.

—There is a silver arm of Blessed Malachy, [Col. 1790A] commissioned by the same Dom John of Aizanville from 7½ marks of silver, with precious stones and a ring chained by a silver chain.

**Folio 12, recto.**—A small wooden chest plated with silver, whose lock is of silver, full of relics: namely, of the priestly vestments of Blessed Abbot Bernard and the upper part of his crozier.

**Folio 13, recto.**—Another oblong vessel . . . containing many relics: namely . . . of St Bernard . . . weighing 13½ ounces.

**Folio 15, recto.**—The girdle of St Bernard, of silk, fitted with gilded silver at its ends.

**Folio 16, recto.**—A wooden panel with doors, upon which are painted images of the Blessed Mary and of Blessed Bernard and Benedict—given by Dom Peter of Virey.

**Folio 17, recto.**—An ivory rosary attached to the silver image of Blessed Bernard—given by Lady Catherine Ferrières, wife of the Lord of Dinteville.

### B. INVENTORY OF 1640

[Col. 1790B]

This inventory survives in its original form in the Archives of Aube. It is a paper folio register covered in brown skin; on the front cover one reads the words: “Inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux, made in the year 1640.”—Unfortunately it is mutilated; leaves are missing down to folio 6.—At folio 17, recto, one reads:

> + Inventory of the sacristy of Clairvaux, comprising the small reliquary, the chalices and other silverware, pontifical ornaments, altar frontals, chasubles, copes, linens, tapestries, and other things belonging to the adornment of the Church; made on the fourteenth of May, sixteen hundred and forty, by order of the Reverend Father in God, Dom Claude Largentier, forty-fifth Abbot of the said Clairvaux, in the presence [Col. 1790C] of Dom Didier Gautherin and Dom Benoist Lavandier, and placed in the hands of Dom Antoine le Borgnet, sub-prior and chief sacristan, and Dom Ponce Thibaron, likewise sacristan.

**Folio 6, recto.**—In the fourth cupboard, marked D, there is first a chest covered in sheets of gilded silver, supported on four brass feet. Under the lid there are two rows of relics with their names engraved above them. In the uppermost row are these relics, namely: . . . of St Malachy, bishop . . . This reliquary was made in the time of Dom Guy, tenth Abbot of Clairvaux.

**Folio 7, verso.**—In the cupboard marked E, there is a fine gilded-silver reliquary, shaped like a pyramid, in which rests the head of St Barnabas the Apostle. The handle has six enamel images, above which [Col. 1791A] are represented the mysteries of the Annunciation. Above these mysteries are six capitals with six pillars and as many little turrets, in which the relics presently have no labels. But according to an old memorandum found in this same reliquary, the relics in these uninscribed little turrets are . . . of the covering of St Bernard. This reliquary was made in the time of the Right Reverend Fathers in God Dom Evrard, seventeenth, and Dom William II, eighteenth Abbots of Clairvaux.

**Folio 9, verso.**—In the sixth cupboard, marked F, there is a large table of gilded silver, adorned with diverse precious stones and borders of pearls, commonly called the Table of the Angels. It closes with two doors, above which are two angels in relief; inside, in the middle, one sees an artistically wrought cross containing a portion of the True Cross of Our Lord, sent to St Bernard by the patriarch of Jerusalem. In the whole table there are one hundred and sixteen compartments, square and [Col. 1791B] round, triangular and diamond-shaped, in which are various relics with their names engraved thereon . . . This table was made in the time of Dom William, twelfth Abbot of Clairvaux. In one of the compartments was the finger of St Bernard, but it is no longer there now.

Fo. 10v.—In the seventh cupboard, marked G, there is first a large shrine of gilt silver, made in the form of a chest, prepared to contain the body of our glorious father St Bernard. At one end is a crucifix, and at the other Our Lady holding the infant Jesus. Around it are the twelve Apostles. On the two capitals at the two long sides is a coat of arms bearing two crossed swords with a bar of gold, upon which are two boars’ heads, and in the middle a crozier, the whole surrounded by a cap of green leaves. The lid is strewn with precious stones, and at one end bears the image of Our Lord at the Judgment, and at the other the sending of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1791C] At the very top is a small bell-tower without a bell, upon which is a crucifix. This shrine was given to Clairvaux by Monsieur Tristan, bishop of Saintes, formerly a monk of Clairvaux. [Note: [Col. 1791D] This shrine, given by Messire Tristan de Bizet, is mentioned in a memorandum submitted to Master Adrien Cottin concerning the liberties of the Church of France. (*Thesaurus Novus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, cols. 1419–1420, *Acta varia de schismate Pontificum Avenionensium*.) § IX. Now let us see the evils and inconveniences resulting from the exactions made by the pope. § X. First, from vacant prelacies which he takes: when a bishop or an abbot is promoted, a large sum of money must be paid before the mayor; and this sum cannot be raised without selling the inheritance of the Church . . . as happened at the Abbey of [Col. 1792D] Saint-Germain-des-Prés . . . God knows how many others there are in the kingdom of France, “and at the Abbey of Clairvaux, where there was a noble shrine containing the body of St Bernard, which had to be sold for seven vacancies.” The accusations made by Gallicans against the popes must be accepted only with great caution. Thus, in the two assertions I have transcribed there are two errors. St Bernard’s body was never removed from its tomb before the Revolution; and the shrine which the bishop of Saintes intended for his venerable relics was so far from having been sold for seven vacancies that the Benedictines still saw and admired it in 1717.]  

Fo. 11r.—Same cupboard.

A gilt-silver image, about four feet high, representing our glorious Father St Bernard. At its foot is a crystal mounted in silver, at the four corners of which are twelve pearls joined to four sapphires. Beneath this crystal are: “From the rib of St Bernard”; “from the cowl and coverlet of St Bernard”; “from the cap of St Bernard”; “from the mat upon which St Bernard died.” Around the base are several enamelled windows, upon which is St Bernard bearing the church of Clairvaux; its bell-tower contains a little bell and has a cross at the top. He holds a skilfully worked crozier, adorned with pearls and stones. [Col. 1791D] Behind his head is a diadem embellished with pearls and stones.

Fo. 11v.—Same cupboard.

[Col. 1792A] A table of gilt silver, ornamented with pearls and precious stones, called the Table of Almaricus (the Table of Amaury). In the middle is a fairly large, artistically fashioned cross, containing a portion of the True Cross of Our Lord . . . . . At the four corners of the cross are four compartments covered with crystals, beneath which are various relics. Under the fourth crystal, at the bottom, are relics of St Malachy and St Bernard. The portion of the sacred wood in the middle of the table was sent to Clairvaux by Almaricus, king of Jerusalem . . . . . There is a parchment tablet made in the form of this reliquary, declaring how Almaricus sent this portion of the True Cross at the request of St Bernard, who appeared to him.

Fo. 17r.—In the year 1635, in September, the large and the small reliquary, because of the disturbances and dangers of war, having been removed from the sacristy and hidden in a secure place until March 1640, the dampness of [Col. 1792B] the place in which they were enclosed consumed and reduced to dust the labels of many relics, each of which had its own inscription. They no longer have these, or, if they have any, they are these or similar ones: “The names of these relics are in the book of life.” “They are written in the book of predestination.” “They are unknown to us, but not to God.” “They are unknown by us.” Since the old inventories and certain memoranda which have been found mention relics in particular reliquaries, insofar as it has been possible to identify and judge them probably, and insofar as one could reasonably remember, small slips bearing the names of some relics contained in them have been left on these individual reliquaries, although the relics are now mixed together and it has not been possible to distinguish one from another.

Fo. 18r.—A reliquary of gilt silver, enamelled round about. The base is triangular, upon [Col. 1792C] which three bands support the crystal containing the thumb of our glorious father St Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux. The cover is pyramid-shaped, and above it is a knob of gilt silver. This reliquary was made by order of the Reverend Father in God Dom Jean d’Aizanville, thirtieth abbot of Clairvaux.

Fo. 18r.—A silver arm containing a bone of the arm of St Malachy, archbishop and primate of all Ireland. At the bottom, near the hand, is a border of precious stones and enamelled silver images. On two fingers of the hand are two rings: the smaller is only of brass and has a stone in the middle; the larger is of silver and has three stones. On the back of the hand is the Virgin in enamelled silver.

Fo. 18v.—A reliquary of gilt silver, made in the form of a chapel, with a crucifix at the top. It comes apart at the base and opens in the middle, where there is [Col. 1792D] a round compartment covered with glass on each side, beneath which is: “From the dust of the head of Blessed Bernard”; “from the cowl of St Bernard.”

[Col. 1793A] Fo. 19v.—A reliquary in the form of a goblet, made from a large walnut, held by three silver bands. Upon its gilt-silver foot is written “Guido,” and on the enamelled handle, “I thirst.” Its glass cover has a gilt-silver rim; within it is: “From the dust of the head of Blessed Malachy, primate of Ireland.”

Fo. 19v.—A crystal casket supported by four feet shaped like roses, three of which are of silver and the other only of brass. At both ends are engraved roses, and inside is: “From the dust of the mat upon which Blessed Bernard died.”

Fo. 20r.—A silver reliquary in the form of a tower. On the handle are six enamelled roses, and at the top a small cross, and six windows held by six gilt-silver bands. Inside is: “From the dust of the head of Blessed Malachy, archbishop and primate of all Ireland.”

[Col. 1793B] Fo. 20r.—A small reliquary of gilt silver; the case opens on both sides. On one is Our Lord carrying his cross, and on the other an *Agnus Dei* [Lamb of God]. Inside is: “From the dust of the head of St Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux.” It was made by order of the Reverend Father in God Dom Claude Largentier, forty-fifth abbot of Clairvaux.

Fo. 26r.—Silverware.

Two small silver candlesticks, gilt in several places. Their bases are round, and on the knop is a divided shield, in the middle of which are the arms of St Bernard; on one side are three stars, a stork, and a lion, and on the other side are the same arms.

Fo. 30v.—Pontifical ornaments.

Two croziers.—The first is of gilt silver and comes apart into four pieces. The bottom piece is plain, tipped with an iron point for planting in the ground. The second and third [Col. 1793C] pieces are strewn with fleur-de-lis. The fourth contains the twelve Apostles and the Tree of Jesse, with much foliage around it. In the middle of the upper part of the crozier is the Virgin giving milk to St Bernard. This crozier is placed in a leather case divided in two. The cloth hanging from it has at the top an ornamental goldsmith’s knop, and beneath it a ground of red satin, with gold branches and scattered pearls: on one side Our Lady holding her Son, in gold embroidery; and on the other St Bernard, half-length, holding in one hand the church of Clairvaux and in the other a crozier. The cloth has several bouquets in silk embroidery, and at the bottom a small fringe of white and Isabella-coloured silk.

The second crozier is of white silver . . . . . The cloth has at the top a point of cloth of gold, upon which are St John the Evangelist, St Bernard, and two other monks.

[Col. 1793D] Fo. 58r.—Red copes.

A cope of fine cloth of gold patterned with red velvet; its orphrey [Note: [Col. 1793D] See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Aurifragium*.] in gold and silk embroidery has St Bernard holding the church of Clairvaux, St Robert, St Benedict, St Malachy . . . . . On the hood is “Show thyself a mother.”

Fo. 58r.—Two copes of red damask scattered with bouquets in fine gold and green and Isabella-coloured silk, with golden rosettes . . . . . The orphrey of one has six embroidered panels representing diverse miracles of St Bernard. On the hood is the death of St Bernard.

Fo. 62r.—Panels and curtains serving the high altar.

Two white damask curtains bearing the arms of St Bernard. The bottom is ornamented with a fringe of fine gold and red silk, and all around is a fine gold galloon half a finger broad.

[Col. 1794A] Fo. 63r.—Three panels made in squares of cloth of gold and red damask with flowers of gold and silk; all around is a band of violet velvet, and the fringe is red silk. These panels serve as the backcloth, otherwise as the canopy of yellow and white figured damask placed over the tomb of our glorious father St Bernard on solemn days.

Fo. 63v.—Two curtains of red damask, one of which bears the arms of St Bernard. The fringe at the bottom is green silk.

Fo. 64v.—Violet panels and curtains for the high altar.

Two violet damask curtains, each bearing a shield with the arms of St Bernard.

Fo. 69v.—Coverings for the credence table.—White coverings.

A *mystérion*, or white covering for the credence table, of satin patterned with small flowers; in [Col. 1794B] the middle are the arms of St Bernard. The border is made in squares of yellow, blue, white, and red satin, with a fringe of silk in diverse colours. At the bottom is likewise a fringe of silk in several colours.

Fo. 70r.—Green coverings for the credence table.

A *mystérion* of green Bourges satin, having in the middle two angels holding a chalice upon which is a host, and at the sides the arms of St Bernard.

Fo. 74r.—Coverings of various colours over the piscinas of the high altar.

A piscina-covering of yellow satin; in the middle is Our Lord embracing his cross, and St Bernard at his feet, with this inscription: “Have mercy upon me, O God.”

Fo. 74v.—Coverings for the piscinas of the small altars.—White coverings.

A piscina-covering of white cloth with several inscriptions in red silk, between which are [Col. 1794C] bands made in green silk tapestry. At the bottom are two shields: one of St Bernard, the other bearing a black lion on a gold field. At the bottom is a fringe of red silk.

Fo. 76v.—Red corporals and veils.

A corporal of red velvet, in which Our Lady gives milk to St Bernard, in fine gold embroidery. On its borders is written: “Blessed Bernard, like a solid vessel of gold.”

Fo. 78v.—Corporals and veils of various colours.

Two corporals of blue patterned velvet. One has an embroidered cross scattered with pearls; the other has a paper St Bernard in a roundel of worn old embroidery.

Fo. 79.—White cushions.

Two cushions of white net lace. On one is Our Lady in a sun, and on the other St Bernard kneeling.

[Col. 1794D] Fo. 80v.—Cushions of various colours.

Three cushions in Turkish tapestry, bearing the arms of St Bernard.
