Fo. 81v.—Various ornaments for adorning several places in the Church.

A small shrine of gilt copper, closing with two shutters. Above it are four roundels: one in front, another behind, and the other two at the sides. The one in front is covered by a small crystal, beneath which are relics . . . . . of St Malachy . . . . . At the top is placed a pyramid bearing a cross, upon which is a raised crucifix.

Fo. 82r.—A hanging to ornament the pillars of the pyramid above the choir door, between the seat of the abbot and that of the prior, where the Virgin is holding her Son. This hanging is of violet velvet; at its bottom, on both sides, is the Tree of Jesse, [Col. 1795A] embroidered in gold and silk; and at the top is Our Lord embracing St Bernard. At the summit of the Tree of Jesse is a hood in fine gold embroidery, in which God the Father is represented holding his Son in his arms; above is the Holy Spirit, and beside it two angels.

Fo. 82v.—A frontal for a corporal chest of white satin, on which the Virgin gives milk to St Bernard; above, the Holy Spirit is in a cloud; all in gold and silk embroidery.

Fo. 82v–83r.—The pall, or funeral cloth, of black velvet, with a cross running its full length, made of squares of tapestry, with love-knots and roundels of cut white satin. In the middle is a death’s head of satin, surrounded by silver tears and four flames of gold tinsel. Four shields are also visible: two of St Bernard, surrounded by a chaplet of cut white satin; and the other two [Col. 1795B] bearing the arms both of St Bernard and Clairvaux, and those of the Reverend Father in God Dom Claude Largentier, forty-fifth abbot of Clairvaux, who had this pall made.

Fo. 83v.—Tapestry.

A large piece of tapestry depicting Our Lord praying in the Garden, with St John and St Bernard at its two ends.

Fo. 84r.—A small piece of tapestry in the form of a carpet, at the top of which are the arms of St Bernard; in the middle an angel, and at the bottom the eagle of St John.

Likewise, a small piece of tapestry in the form of a carpet; at the top are the arms of St Bernard within a roundel, and at the bottom St Paul within another roundel.

Likewise, a small tapestry hanging serving as the canopy for the tomb of our glorious Father St Bernard, upon which is Our Lady giving milk to St Bernard; [Col. 1795C] with a coat of arms bearing a broken yellow chevron on an azure field. Above is written: “Like myrrh.”

The Archives of Aube preserve a copy of the contract for the shrine intended by the bishop of Saintes to enclose the body of St Bernard, mentioned in the inventory of 1640, fo. 10v.

This copy is from the end of the sixteenth century or the beginning of the seventeenth; its transcription will be read with interest.

“1577, 27 July.—There appeared in person the Reverend Father in God, Messire Tristan de Bizet, bishop of Saintes and commendatory abbot of the abbey of Saint-Nicolas-au-Bois, diocese of Laon. He declared that from his youth he had been made a monk in the convent and monastery of Our Lady of Clairvaux, of the Order of Cîteaux; had there made his profession; and had so diligently applied himself to study that, through it and by God’s grace, he had been and was provided with great dignities and offices, and accordingly possessed, as he still does, great goods and possessions in the Church. Not wishing to be ungrateful to the said Church and convent, but desiring in some measure to remunerate and recompense it for the spiritual and temporal benefits he had received from it, he had long had, and still had, the wish and intention of having made, in the honour and glory of God our Father, Saviour, and Redeemer Jesus Christ, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of the Most Holy Virgin Mary, and of Monsieur Saint Bernard, a silver shrine, in which to place and repose the sacred bones of the said St Bernard, being in the said church of Our Lady of Clairvaux; on condition that the monks, abbot, and convent of the said Clairvaux associate the said Reverend Lord in the prayers and orisons daily said in the said church and convent, and likewise enter and inscribe [Col. 1796A] in the martyrology and book of benefactions of their said church (the necrology) the contents of these presents, for perpetual remembrance.

“To make this shrine, the said Reverend Lord had summoned before him the honourable men Jacques Beguyn and Jehan Jolly, master goldsmiths living in Paris—Beguyn in the Rue des Lavandières, and Jolly in the Rue de la Vannerie—to whom he declared his wish and intention, and asked whether they would undertake to make the said shrine according to the design he would show them. Beguyn and Jolly consented and agreed.

“Accordingly the said parties, of their own free will and good pleasure and without any constraint, as they declared, acknowledged and confessed that they had made, did make, and now make between themselves, in good faith, the following agreements, promises, and obligations: namely, the said Beguyn and Jolly have promised and do promise, and have in fact bound and do bind themselves, one for the other, and each separately for the whole, without division or discussion, renouncing the benefits of division, order of law, and discussion, to and toward the said Reverend Lord, who accepts this, to make and complete properly and duly, according to the judgment of workmen and persons skilled in such matters, the said silver shrine, three and a half feet or thereabouts in length, three feet in height including the harpies beneath, and twenty inches in width; weighing about one hundred and sixty marks; enriched with images of the twelve Apostles around it, an image of Our Lady holding her child seated at the front end of the said shrine, an image of St Bernard, and a likeness of a kneeling man at prayer in the habit of a monk of the said Order of Cîteaux; to set into it the precious stones that shall be delivered to them; and to make all other embellishments. All is to follow [Col. 1796C] the design for this purpose, initialled by the undersigned notaries, *ne varietur* [so that it may not be altered], of which an identical copy has been delivered to the said Beguyn and Jolly.

“And for this purpose the said Reverend Lord Bishop shall be bound and promises to provide the silver required. Of it, they have now received from the said Reverend Lord one hundred and nine marks, three ounces, and three *gros*, to begin the said shrine.

“To make the said shrine such and as described above, the said Beguyn and Jolly shall be bound to begin within the next eight days and to deliver it made and completed, properly and duly as aforesaid, by the first day of next March, provided they do not lack silver to put into the work. This promise is made on the terms and at the price at which the workmanship of the said shrine shall be appraised and valued by persons skilled in such matters, upon whom the said parties shall respectively agree on one side and the other as soon as the work is completed. The said Reverend Lord promises, pledges, and binds himself to give and pay this price to the said Beguyn and Jolly, or to the bearer: namely, two hundred gold *écus au soleil* within fifteen days from today, and the remainder in proportion and as they need it while making the said shrine. For thus it has been expressly said, agreed, and settled between the said parties, the said Beguyn and Jolly each promising and binding himself in his own right, one for the other and each separately for the whole, without division or discussion, renouncing such rights as above. Done and executed in duplicate in the year one thousand five hundred seventy-seven, Saturday the twenty-seventh day of July.”

I add here an extract from a document also preserved in the Archives of Aube.

1578, 17 November.—Act executed by Dom Lupin Le Myre, abbot of Clairvaux, for the benefit of a certain Master Hardouyn Manchen, residing in Paris. It reads: “. . . . . . . . . In order better . . . . . . . to discharge our [Col. 1797A] conscience of the promise which we . . . have . . . made to Messire Tristan de Bizet, lately bishop of Saintes and at present abbot of Saint-Nicolas-au-Bois . . . . . . first when he promised and gave us the shrine which he is presently having completed to contain the relics of Monsieur St Bernard; and secondly when he gave to us and to our house a complete chapel-set of cloth of gold . . . . . .”

—Copy on paper.—Collated in 1594.

Head of a martyr of the Theban Legion given to the Abbey of Clairvaux.

1260, 2 May.—“To all who shall inspect these present letters, Lady Agnes, Countess of Châtres, greeting and testimony to the truth. We have judged it fitting to make known to you all by the tenor of these presents that, being established in the city of Trier, we gave to the venerable Father Lord John, abbot of Clairvaux (twentieth abbot of Clairvaux), in consideration of the reverence and devotion which we bear toward him and the Order, one head from the Theban Legion, which the abbot of St Martin’s of Trier gave us. In testimony whereof we have given him this present open letter, confirmed by the protection of our seal. Given in the year of the Lord 1260, on the morrow of the Finding of the Holy Cross.”

—(Archives of Aube.)—Original on parchment.—Sealed on a single tag.—The seal is missing.

Altars of the Basilica of Clairvaux.

Loose leaf, sixteenth-century handwriting. (Archives of Aube.)

[Col. 1797] Written at Dijon, eleven days before the Kalends of April, 1855.

[DOCUMENTS]

[Col. 1797]

DOCUMENTS CONCERNING A JOURNEY OF ST BERNARD IN FLANDERS, AND THE CULT OF OUR LADY OF AFFLIGHEM [Note: [Col. 1797D] See *Revue catholique de l’université de Louvain*, 1848, vol. III, pp. 400 and 457. The dissertation preceding the documents we publish [Col. 1798D] is reproduced in the form which it had to take to suit the ordinary readers of periodical works.], collected by the Reverend Father Dom Pitra, of the Order of St Benedict.

[Col. 1797D] One of Belgium’s small towns, Termonde, possesses a church of humble appearance, built by Capuchins: clean, devout, and, like all Belgian churches, rich in works of art and monuments of the saints. The artist will be astonished to encounter there more than one great master—Murillo, Crayer, Jordaens. One of the most remarkable Van Dycks has passed into a neighbouring church, where it shows, at the feet of a crucified [Col. 1798D] Christ, the founder of the convent: one of those poor Franciscans who have always inspired art so happily, even under a Protestant palette. Bereft of its masterpiece, this church has received, as if in exchange, a treasure far more precious: a Madonna glorified by a miracle of St Bernard. Venerated since the eleventh century, it was recently preserved and deposited there by the [Col. 1799A] new Benedictines of Afflighem. Unable to shelter themselves with their Mother amid the ruins of their abbey, or among their fathers’ devastated tombs, they wished to carry the holy statue with them, as though to place their new cradle under the guardianship of her who, eight centuries earlier, protected the nascent abbey.

In days of trouble and anxiety (1848), we were granted, together with brethren, to salute, and with poor pilgrims of Flanders to venerate, Our Lady of Afflighem—or, as she is still called, Our Lady of Peace. Every one of her titles was dear to us; every memory consoling. As we questioned them on the spot, we were astonished by the vicissitudes that had in turn afflicted and glorified this [Col. 1799B] ancient image. Her glory becomes manifest in Flanders’ finest days. Godfrey and his holy mother Ida, then St Bernard, inaugurate this age-old veneration. The peoples follow: in a single day, thirty thousand pilgrims adorn one of her triumphs. An abbey grows in her shadow, until it becomes the mother and head of the Benedictine abbeys of the region. One day Afflighem is dispersed; on that day the statue is broken. Raised again with the restored abbey, it restores to the abbey and shares its splendours. Then, in disastrous days, it falls with it into an oblivion which still endures for both. Not only an illustrious abbey and its whole ancient Order—one of the nation’s great political bodies, creator [Col. 1799C] of Catholicism and consequently of Belgian nationality—but the destinies of all Belgium seemed to us to converge around this humble little statue in a small church of Termonde.

We yield to the desire expressed to us by friends and brethren, by summarizing what they themselves have told and communicated to us. This is not a work of scholarship, but the humble homage of a pilgrim: a devout halt while the shower passes; a hurried pilgrimage through time, perhaps on the day after—or on the eve of—long storms.

I. Starting from the point at which we stand, we shall proceed without embellishment, going back from testimony to testimony, from the very foot of Our Lady of Afflighem to the distant origins of her cult [Col. 1799D] and her abbey.

Almost ten years ago, one of the last surviving members of the Order of St Benedict in Belgium, Dom Vérémond d’Haens [Note: [Col. 1799D] Ignace-Bernard-Marie d’Haens, born in 1771 at Termonde, made profession under the name Vérémond on 23 June 1793 in the Abbey of Afflighem, restored his Order in Belgium in 1838, and died in the [Col. 1800D] monastery of Termonde, among the Benedictines of Afflighem, on 26 August 1846.], gathered at the gates of the hospital sheltering his old age several devoted men who accepted the task of raising from its ruins—if only by saving its name—the Abbey of Afflighem. Before going to his fathers, the old man handed to his disciples, as his most precious legacy, a small statue of Our Lady, which he had seen carried away and faithfully kept until his death by the last grand provost of Afflighem.

[Col. 1800A] This provost was Dom Bede Régaus, certainly one of the men most deserving of being less forgotten, especially in his own country. He loved so passionately his afflicted mother Afflighem, as he liked to call her, that he spent sixty-five years of his life gathering her documents, inventorying her archives, and writing her annals. Fourteen volumes remain of this painful labour. Begun toward the end of a long period of humiliations, it was ended by death in 1807, when the desolation of Afflighem seemed complete forever. Among these doubly historical pages, we found the following, whose heavy handwriting betrays a suffering and weary hand:

“It should be known that tradition teaches us [Col. 1800B] that in the year 1147 [Note: [Col. 1800D] One must read 1146, as we hope to establish.], in the time of Abbot Peter, and not Godescalc, as is said in certain histories, St Bernard visited us and settled there a dispute between the people of Ninove and Dilighem; that this same Abbot Peter, who subscribed the charter of settlement, and with him the entire convent, saw the Saint greet Our Lady, saying: ‘Hail, Mary!’ and heard the statue return this greeting in these words: ‘Hail, Bernard!’—This image stood in the cloister upon its base. There it was cast down by iconoclasts in the winter of 1580 and broken into two parts, apart from the two heads which could not be found. In 1606, after the two parts had been transported to Mechelen, [Col. 1800C] two statues were made from them; our people gathered with the greatest care not only the pieces detached by the chisel, but even the particles of dust . . . This I attest: Bede, provost of Afflighem, 1802 [Note: [Col. 1800D] See below, Documentary Evidence, no. XXIX.].”

This date removes any interested motive from this testimony, which remains important. It is the testimony of the man who, while everything still existed, saw most fully and best the monuments, documents, and chronicles of the abbey; of an old man who could no longer hope, before dying, to see his abbey rise again together with the cult of its patroness. Yet it is an almost isolated protest amid the general discredit which for more than a century has humbled Our Lady of Afflighem. Could she have found favour in days so lightly [Col. 1800D] disdainful of such antiquarian matters, when her church, monastery, congregation, and crown of Belgian abbeys were all passing into nothingness?

Despite Saint Bernard’s great name, Fleury, like Bérault-Bercastel, passed it by; and none of their older or more recent continuators, French or Belgian, appears to have thought of it. Even the more specialized historians, those of the Gallican Church as well as of Saint Bernard, say nothing of it, so far as we know. Godescard does mention it, but merely to dispose of it in a short, almost contemptuous note. [Col. 1801A] [Note: [Col. 1801D] See under 20 August. The note is scarcely fair: for a series of facts there indiscriminately condemned, Mabillon is cited among other authorities; yet neither in the places indicated nor elsewhere that we have searched did Mabillon say anything against the Afflighem tradition. We are glad to add [Col. 1802D] that, thanks to M. Abbé de Ram, who was kind enough to receive our observations, this note did not reappear in the latest Belgian reprint of the *Lives of the Saints* without a severe correction.] More seriously, the Bollandists—Belgian writers and historians of the Church and of the saints—declared against it, at least pending a new inquiry. Let us attempt to carry out the programme they themselves fairly set forth: it is enough, they say, to discover a contemporary testimony, if a continuous tradition cannot be established. Perhaps, by pursuing our course, we shall attain both.

II. At the moment when the uneasy Bollandists withdrew or suspended their approval, a pope ordinarily more exacting and no less competent in such a matter, Benedict XIV, did not hesitate, at Cardinal d’Alsace’s request, to grant a brief of indulgence whose historical recitals it is important to weigh. Although one should not see in documents which merely record the terms of the petition a judgment carrying authority, nevertheless, issuing from a pope and an archbishop of Mechlin, both equally accustomed and obliged to be discreet and reliable, this brief has considerable value:

> “Benedict XIV, Pope, for perpetual remembrance. Attentive in Our paternal charity to the salvation of all, We are pleased on occasion to adorn holy places with the spiritual treasure of indulgences. . . . And therefore We desire, by a special gift, to distinguish in the church of the Abbey of Afflighem, under the invocation of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, an altar of the Blessed Virgin of Afflighem, who, according to tradition, spoke to Saint Bernard. . . . Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, [Col. 1801C] on 11 July 1745.” [Note: [Col. 1802D] See Supporting Documents, no. XXVIII.]

This brief remained unknown; perhaps the many opponents of the Holy See and of Cardinal d’Alsace were feared. Another document, signed by a less suspect name, might have been opposed to them. Boonen, Archbishop of Mechlin, grants numerous indulgences:

> “To increase the homage and veneration shown each day to the miraculous image of the most holy Mother and Virgin Mary, by which she deigned to answer the greeting made to her by her servant and special friend, Saint Bernard, in the Abbey of Afflighem, where it is preserved to this day with great reverence. . . . Signed by our hand and furnished with our seal, at Brussels, 20 May 1647. Jacques, Archbishop of Mechlin.” [Note: [Col. 1802D] Ibid., no. XXVI.]

[Col. 1801D] Boonen was Abbot of Afflighem, through the incorporation of the abbatial mensa into the archbishopric of Mechlin. In 1626 he carried out a celebrated translation of the miraculous statue, hitherto placed in the cloister and thereafter displayed for the veneration of the faithful in a wing of the church. It was likewise under this regime and in this period that the pious and learned Haeften multiplied acts of homage to the glory of Our Lady: litanies every day; a station every Sunday; a solemn procession on the Assumption; an octave with indulgence and [Col. 1802A] procession on the commemorative feast of the Presentation. Then monuments of every kind—paintings from the school of Rubens, woodwork by Jean du Coy, enhanced by elegant inscriptions by Haeften—popularized and authenticated the miracle of Afflighem.

The most exacting doctors of Louvain, Jansenius himself and his disciples, mingled with the people and met, at the feasts of Afflighem, Aubert Le Mire and Sanderus, both of whom gave distinction to this tradition. Molanus assigns it a place in the Belgian Martyrology. Arnold Rayss offered it, as it were, the homage of the University of Douai. The learned Premonstratensian Wichmans made it one of the notable pages of his *Brabantia Mariana*. His brethren of Ninove accepted it along with the chronicle of Baldwin, [Col. 1802B] and the Abbot of Étival, Hugo, did not hesitate to enrich his *Monuments* and *Annals* with it. All orders united in this belief. The Jesuits of Brussels, selected by privilege as custodians of one of the statues made from fragments of the first, relinquished it only reluctantly. Father Berthollet, a contemporary of Father Pien the Bollandist, entered the event without hesitation in his manuscript ecclesiastical history. One understands that the children of Saint Bernard, united with their brethren, celebrated these memories in their annals, in the menologies of the Order, and through a commemorative feast in the Cistercian abbeys of Belgium.

Finally, collected by Phalésius and Odon Cambier, the traditions of Afflighem were transmitted to Mabillon, [Col. 1802C] inserted by d’Achery in the *Spicilegium*, maintained by Dom Martène in the *Annals*, recorded by de Sainte-Marthe in the *Gallia Christiana*, and admitted into dom Bouquet’s great collection of French historians under the safeguard of a national monument and with the authority of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres.

There would be an act of homage of this kind to establish in Belgium; we shall return to it. Let it suffice to add that at this period Our Lady of Afflighem gave her name and patronage to a new congregation which caused the Order of Saint Benedict to flourish again throughout the Netherlands. It is difficult to find, in this age of such serious criticism, [Col. 1802D] a more imposing unanimity of support. And it was needed, as much to forestall the scepticism of another age as to avenge Our Lady of Afflighem for the insults of the sixteenth century.

III. Truly, the Virgin of Afflighem resembles those ancient images which Rome believed associated with the triumphs and funerals of her patrician families. She is bound up with the very history of the Belgian people and shares the vicissitudes of its destiny. In Isabella’s golden age, we have seen her in [Col. 1803A] her most radiant splendour; we might even have claimed a share in the public honours rendered to Our Lady of Peace, whose memory Brussels preserves in golden letters on its Grand Place, inscribed upon one of its principal buildings.

But now come other times: the invasion of the Gueux and the rending of the United Provinces mark an era of violent persecution for Afflighem. Since a policy of secularization prevailed in the councils of Philip II, contrary to the original provisions of the Holy See, the great abbeys were sacrificed to the new bishoprics. After its mensa had been dismembered and its abbatial title abolished, Afflighem, violently detached from the Congregation of Bursfeld, was repeatedly ravaged by iconoclasts and reduced [Col. 1803B] to a heap of ruins. In this desolation, the Madonna was never wholly abandoned; but, since only lay brothers remained about her, in 1670 a sectarian laid hands upon her, overthrew her, and broke her into two principal pieces. From these devoutly preserved remains, a statue was made after the same model and in the same reduced proportions—the statue preserved to the present day.

The chain of tradition was not interrupted. On the one hand, witnesses of the fall saw her raised again; on the other, their testimony leads us to the abbey’s chroniclers, who composed its annals before its documents were dispersed: Amerius, who reaches back to 1531, and an anonymous writer cited by Aubert Le Mire, who from 1519 goes back [Col. 1803C] to the middle of the fifteenth century.

At that period, a chronicle of Brabant, concluded in 1440, and Baldwin of Ninove, writing in 1294, mention the crucial fact: Saint Bernard’s presence at Afflighem. This fact coincides with the saint’s preaching at Tournai, recorded in Herimann’s chronicle by its continuator (1160), and otherwise indicated by Saint Bernard’s companions, his first biographers. These join hands with the chroniclers of Afflighem and Villers, and with the continuators of Sigebert of Gembloux (*HERIMANN, Narratio restauration. abb. S. Mart.*, no. 112; D’ACHERY, *Spicil.*, vol. II, p. 924). And these written testimonies corroborate the immemorial customs which the Congregation [Col. 1803D] of Bursfeld sanctioned by its capitular authority: Our Lady of Afflighem remains inviolate in the cloister, upon her pedestal, at the corner where Saint Bernard encountered her. Every morning, on leaving the dormitory, all the religious bow three times before her, recalling Saint Bernard’s greeting; and great silence, as though still to hear the echo of that miraculous voice, is forever prescribed around the statue that spoke more than seven hundred years ago.

It is probable that every year, on an appointed day, an *elogium* was recited, like that found in the Martyrology of Villers and possibly dating from this period:

> “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November.
>
> “In Belgium, commemoration of the Blessed [Col. 1804A] Virgin, when through the mouth of the statue of Afflighem, in the presence of the convent of monks and of a great multitude of people, she greeted our holy Father Bernard, saying in an intelligible voice: ‘Hail, Bernard!’ This image, as testimony to so great a miracle, is preserved with much honour.”

IV. This striking testimony of the Martyrology of Villers is confirmed by another monument from the same abbey: its chronicle, published by Dom Martène, who clearly distinguished and identified its various parts. The oldest presupposes a contemporary writing about 1221. This contemporary had long lived among his own people, under two or three abbots; he even speaks at the end in a tone of authority that betrays the prelate, and Dom Martène goes so far as to name him: [Col. 1804B] it was supposedly Arnoul, first subprior and then Abbot of Villers. If we allow him more than sixty years of life, we reach 1153, the year of Saint Bernard’s death. Whether abbot or monk, this contemporary of the wonder-worker wrote among surviving eyewitnesses, in an abbey of his Order; and this abbey owed its very birth to the journey we seek to establish. Certainly, if this journey and all these circumstances left memories anywhere, it must have been at Villers; it must have been at a distance of fifty years.

Thus the chronicler of Villers completes the account of the Martyrology of Villers which we have just heard:

> “Since at that time Saint Bernard had come into Brabant on account of his preaching, [Col. 1804C] in order to produce there, as elsewhere, some fruit, he went to the monastery of Afflighem. There he delivered two sermons and left there, as a memorial, the crosier which supported his feeble limbs and which the brethren of Afflighem preserve.”

Now it happens that this inestimable crosier still survives. It has passed from generation to generation for seven centuries, from Saint Bernard to ourselves—even to our unworthy hands, which have been able to touch it. It is mentioned in a series of inventories; in its form, humble yet elegant and distinguished, it bears the stamp of its age and the authentication of its first owner.

> “Whence, then, would this monument come?” Dom Bede asks every sensible person. “To whom would it be ascribed? [Col. 1804D] When and by whom could it have usurped the name of Saint Bernard?”

Here, among his contemporaries, it is already seen and shown in Brabant; it is spoken of at Villers and preserved at Afflighem. Afflighem never relinquished it, except for a few years at the end of the sixteenth century. Transported to Brussels and then to Mechlin with the displaced treasure and convent, entrusted as an abbatial insignia to Archbishop Hovius after the incorporation of the abbatial mensa into his see, Saint Bernard’s crosier was publicly displayed in 1595 in the church of Steenokkerzeel, near Vilvorde. The monks of Afflighem, restored to their abbey, would not rest until this jewel had returned to their church treasury. Phalésius, a witness of the return, [Col. 1805A] recounts its details. A copy of his chronicle, owned by M. Verdussen of Antwerp, had appended to it the record of this restitution. Dom Bede saw it there and recorded the event and all its antecedents before himself placing the treasure in the hands of Dom Véremond d’Haens, restorer of the Benedictines of Afflighem.

We might, it seems to us, stop here: we have found an uninterrupted tradition and two contemporary testimonies, for this mute monument speaks as loudly as the chronicler of Villers. Saint Bernard’s hand is there, and his voice issues from it. Why would he have left at Afflighem the sign of his abbatial rank, yielded the sceptre of his power, abandoned his wonder-working staff? [Col. 1805B] Unless to recall a prodigy; unless to acknowledge a higher power? Saint Bernard’s crosier is inseparable from Our Lady of Afflighem: touch the one, and one hears the other. Yet a more decisive testimony remains.

V. No sooner has light been shed upon one point of history than rays seem to spring up from every side to dispel all remaining shadows. Thus, once the miracle of Afflighem is established by continuous tradition and by a monument still surviving, the history of the nascent abbey is illuminated far and wide by this fact, while also brilliantly confirming it. Its entire heroic age, its twelfth century, rises to bear witness: it is a [Col. 1805C] triumphal acclamation of the Crusades which, to their end, repeats Saint Bernard’s greeting.

There is a predilection of crusaders for Afflighem which is easy to explain if something extraordinary took place there at the time of the holy wars. Thierry of Alsace, who saw Saint Bernard in Flanders and made the journey to Jerusalem four times, rivalled the descendants of Godfrey in generous offerings. Godfrey IV, Duke of Lorraine, was not content, before his departure, to multiply gifts and confirmations of privileges; from the depths of Syria, piously turning his eyes again toward Our Lady of Afflighem, he earnestly urged his sons to love and protect the abbey. Henry, his eldest, hastened to add to his father’s donations; and the latter, on his [Col. 1805D] return, escorted by his two sons, presented himself at the altar of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul and deposited new acts of munificence there. Henry in turn took the cross; and after, as before, his pilgrimage to the holy places, his name occurs on every folio of the abbey’s mutilated cartulary.

Henry II, Duke of Normandy and King of England, and Adelaide, dowager queen, frequently appear there alongside the noble benefactors of Flanders. So great was the resort of knights to Afflighem that Abbot Robert was obliged to build a vast hostelry for them alone, which Saint Louis exempted from every toll. The royal martyr of the Crusades was destined to meet, together with the wonder-working apostle, at the feet of Our Lady of Afflighem.

Thus, as we ascend closer [Col. 1806A] to Saint Bernard, the voices and testimonies appear to increase. Six years after his passage through Afflighem, and during his lifetime, in 1152, an event occurred which serious historians connect with the cult of Our Lady of Afflighem, as well as with the miracle of 1146.

The plague was raging in the city of Brussels and war was devastating the province. It was the period known by a famous and sinister name, “the cradle of Godfrey.” In one of the abbey’s priories, called Our Lady of Lower Wavre, there was a precious shrine. It was transported to Brussels and deposited with honour in the church of Saint Nicholas, so that it might be richly adorned with gold and precious stones. Since miracles occurred on this occasion, the monks of Afflighem wished solemnly to show [Col. 1806B] their gratitude to Our Lady, invoked at Wavre as at Afflighem. It was one convent under one abbot; one family under one mother.

Therefore the whole convent, with the abbot at its head, barefoot and singing hymns, came with its banner unfurled over a distance of four leagues to Brussels. There, having clothed themselves in albs and copes, the monks recovered their treasure, not without difficulty, and bore the shrine of Our Lady of Wavre back in triumph, followed by a crowd of people arrayed in immense files. Witnesses affirm that there were as many as thirty thousand pilgrims, adding that never at any assembly of emperor or pope was there seen a more devout, more honourable, or more numerous procession. Before the eyes [Col. 1806C] of these thousands of spectators, the road was strewn with miracles.

> “But,” says a very ancient chronicle, “the greatest and most memorable benefit was that throughout all this time the wars and seditions were appeased, and among this multitude all enemies reconciled themselves of their own accord, without restitution or satisfaction.”

Hence the popular Belgian devotion to Our Lady of Peace, of the Ark of the Covenant, of Concord. Yet although in fact, owing to its weight and out of respect for the inviolability of the cloister, the miraculous statue of Afflighem did not leave its enclosed sanctuary, Afflighem and Wavre had but one cult and one object of veneration. The image [Col. 1806D] lacking at the priory stood in the cloister of the abbey, and the treasures of Wavre’s shrine formed the jewels of Our Lady of Afflighem. This connection is so real that the most careful historians, Wichmans and Henriquez, did not hesitate to merge these traditions, attribute their honour especially to the Virgin of Afflighem, give her also the title of Our Lady of Peace, and finally carry its renown back to Saint Bernard’s visit.

VI. But even if we had to disregard the inferences and proofs encountered thus far, there would remain a sufficient, decisive, authentic, and contemporary testimony, issuing from the Saint himself—so much the more precious because it responds directly to the sole difficulty which held back the learned Bollandists.

[Col. 1807A] We do not think they would have confined themselves to the negative argument. For although their criticism, beset by a sceptical age, was then more severe—perhaps too timid—they fundamentally admitted the principle which we find formulated in the recent work of their continuators: the tradition of a church is always valid so long as there is no positive contrary testimony. Now we already have more than a mere tradition: accounts and a contemporary monument.

And yet, did Saint Bernard make the journey to Afflighem? Could he have made it in 1146? At that time he was carrying out his great expedition to Germany. The Bollandists collected notes of his itinerary, questioned his travelling companions, [Col. 1807B] and followed the Saint step by step from his valley to the Rhine, then from Germany to Clairvaux, without finding, either in the known accounts or in the plan of the journey, any place at all for his appearance in Flanders.

Perhaps no one admires the *Acta Sanctorum* more sincerely than we do. Precisely because of this esteem, we insist all the more on clarifying this page in Saint Bernard’s life, since one might be tempted—and indeed the decision has already been made—to abandon it in the face of so weighty a censure as that of the Bollandists. [Note: [Col. 1807D] Count de Montalembert, who is preparing a historical monument to Saint Bernard, considered it necessary to write us that he shared our opinion and would gladly see its demonstration developed and published. We may add that the new Bollandists have expressed the same sympathy to us.]

It would seem necessary to reconstruct Saint Bernard’s entire itinerary from Clairvaux to Afflighem; we must limit ourselves to establishing his presence at this [Col. 1807C] latter place. The alleged alibi falls before an official testimony sealed with Saint Bernard’s own seal.

Readers will have noticed, in the first document we cited, a circumstance pointed out by Dom Bede: while Saint Bernard was at Afflighem, he settled a dispute between the communities of Ninove and Dilighem. Does this act of arbitration still survive?

To investigate this, we visited at Ghent the rich repository of the archives of East Flanders, preserved in the government building. M. van der Meersch, archivist, most graciously allowed us to consult what remains there of the documents of Ninove. One may judge our candid and devout joy at seeing again with our own eyes and touching with [Col. 1807D] our own hands a small original chirograph charter, written in full, handsome chancery characters of the twelfth century. [Note: [Col. 1807D] We also owe to M. van der Meersch’s kindness a facsimile of this document, placed at the beginning of this volume. It is regrettable [Col. 1808D] that the wood engraving was unable to reproduce this precious monument more exactly.]

Saint Bernard speaks there in person, dictates there as official arbitrator, and seals the judgment with his seal—with his very rare first seal, perfectly intact here after seven hundred completed years. Our [Col. 1808A] satisfaction was not diminished when we found the document published in several places, especially as its principal point, its date, still appears to us unknown. We hasten, however, to say that the document was edited by M. de Smeth, canon of Saint Bavo’s; that the engraved seal was illustrated by Baron de Saint-Génois; and that as early as 1732 the Ninove charter had been published by Van Gestel in his *History of Mechlin*, and in 1734 by Foppens in his edition of Aubert Le Mire. [Note: [Col. 1808D] Hugo, *Annales Praemonstrat.*, vol. II, p. 227, appendix; Van Gestel, *Historia arch. Mechliniensis*, vol. II, p. 317; Foppens, *Miraei opp. diplomat.*, vol. IV; De Smet, *Chroniques belges inédit.*, vol. IV, p. 751; De Saint-Génois, “Notice sur le dépôt des archives de la Flandre orientale,” in the *Messager des arts et sciences de Gand*.] It remains for us to complete the monument with Dom Bede, by joining to the Ninove charter the duplicate of Dilighem, detached from the same chirographic instrument and drawn up simultaneously.

VII. Since none of the estimable editors had any reason [Col. 1808B] to verify the date strictly, it has been placed confusedly either in 1150 or in 1148. Foppens and Van Gestel move it back as far as 1145. It was probably this false indication which withdrew the document from the watchful eyes of the Bollandists.

It is above all important to establish the date precisely. The history of the dispute itself will establish it.

A short distance from Afflighem stood two Premonstratensian abbeys, Ninove and Jette, or Dilighem.

The latter, founded for Augustinians about 1091, had originally possessed two neighbouring rural churches whose territory, divided by the Dender, lay not far from Afflighem and was included in the domain of the lords of Aalst. [Note: [Col. 1808D] See the topography of these churches in the facsimile.] Count Iwan, [Col. 1808C] when replacing the Augustinians of Dilighem with Premonstratensians, thought it right to detach from it the church of Liedekerke. The diocesan bishop, Nicholas of Cambrai, confirmed this arrangement by a charter, whose original survives in the same repository, dated 1146, tenth indiction, and the tenth year of the episcopate of Nicholas I.

But the Abbot of Dilighem protested and claimed his former rights; Ninove nonetheless took possession. Hence a quarrel which Saint Bernard was called upon to settle. His act of settlement was confirmed by a second charter of Nicholas, likewise surviving and still dated 1146; then by a bull of Eugenius III issued in 1147.

Saint Bernard’s charter can evidently be [Col. 1808D] neither later than these last two acts nor earlier than either Iwan’s donation, the dispute itself, or Bishop Nicholas’s first grant. We are therefore rigorously confined to a short portion of the year 1146.

VIII. Yet every difficulty regarding the date is not removed. The first charter of Nicholas of Cambrai, our point of departure, bears the tenth indiction and the tenth year of his episcopate; it ought to bear the ninth indiction. Moreover, the tenth year of that episcopate, according to the calculation of the *Gallia Christiana* and the *Art de vérifier les dates*, would fall in 1147; the charter expressly bears 1146.

One might pass over the matter of the indiction, for the computation was known not to be perfectly accurate in episcopal chanceries. But the difficulty can be resolved: there was a Roman indiction beginning on 25 March and an imperial indiction beginning six months later, on 24 September. The latter was followed preferentially in territories subject to the Empire. Cambrai was so situated for the greater [Col. 1809B] part of its territory; thus it is necessary to set back by one number the indiction of its charters.

We should like to coordinate the years of Nicholas I’s episcopate with equal certainty. But we face the *Art de vérifier les dates*, corroborated by the *Gallia Christiana*; armed with fourteen charters, they maintain 1137 as the first year of Nicholas of Cambrai. If the tenth year must be assigned to 1147, all our coincidences and the whole structure of our subject are endangered.

But in our favour we have our highly authentic charter; three others preserved in the same archives at Ghent; a fourth recorded in the *Gallia Christiana* itself; and finally fourteen more which the learned archivist of Lille, M. Le Glay, author of the *Cameracum Christianum*, kindly showed us with the scholarly obligingness for which he is known. We thus have nineteen documents to oppose to the fourteen of our predecessors. This anomaly, which might create a formal diplomatic war, must absolutely be reconciled.

It is enough to take into consideration two particulars concerning Nicholas’s elevation to the episcopate.

A letter of Pope Innocent II informs us that Nicholas, still young, was elected before he had been raised to holy orders. A devout and zealous observer of discipline, he had to observe the canonical intervals, and thus could date his episcopate sometimes from his election and sometimes from his consecration. If the latter occurred, as seems likely, [Col. 1809D] around the Easter feasts—that is, at the point then adopted for the renewal of the year—the unavoidable fluctuations of chronology are already understandable.

Moreover, his immediate predecessor had been deposed from his see by a canonical trial. This trial may have been prolonged through several phases; thus the point at which the jurisdiction of one ended and that of the other began remained undecided. If this uncertainty occurred between Christmas and Easter, the dates and diplomas would drift from one year to another.

[Col. 1810A] There seems to be no longer any hesitation concerning the tenth year of this episcopate; and whether we begin from that point or calculate the indiction, the charter of Ninove and Saint Bernard’s journey remain fixed in the year 1146.

We thought we should stop our inquiry there, when two unknown documents came most opportunely to decide the difficulty.

While we were going through the scattered remnants of the archives of several abbeys at the major seminary of Bruges, we found a small charter copied in the middle of a cartulary of the Abbey of Eechout. Ralph, chaplain of Bruges, gives to Saint Bartholomew of Eechout forty sous to be taken from the tithe of Loophout, or of the wood of Lophem. What gives [Col. 1810B] importance to this offering is that Bernard of Clairvaux, Robert of the Dunes, and Leonius of Saint-Bertin are its witnesses and guarantors. The deed was made at Bruges in the year of the Incarnation 1146:

> “The witnesses present were BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux . . . . Done at Bruges, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146.”  
> *Testes affuerunt BERNARDUS, abbas Clarevallensis . . . . actum Brugis ao incarn. Dnicoe Mo Co XLVIo.*

Finally, while conducting these researches at Bruges, we were preoccupied with the thought that Thierry of Alsace, Saint Bernard’s chivalrous friend, could not have offered the holy abbot his noble hospitality without recording its memory in some document of his chancery. Yet it was in vain that we searched all the charters of this prince which passed before our eyes. But a friend in Bruges, [Col. 1810C] the learned Abbé Carton, kindly noted this desideratum. Thanks to him, we came into possession of a charter from the Red Register of Saint Martin of Ypres. According to this document, the Count of Flanders, being on the point of leaving for Jerusalem—and therefore in 1146—*cum glorioso Francorum rege Ludovico Hierosolymam profecturus* (“being about to set out for Jerusalem with Louis, glorious King of the Franks”), confirms the rights and privileges of the chapter in the presence of Bernard of Clairvaux, who signs with Milo, Bishop of Thérouanne:

> *Signum Bernardi Claravallensis abbatis* — “The mark of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.” [Note: [Col. 1809D] See Supporting Documents, no. IX.]

IX. Let us return to the charter of Ninove. It has no designation of either place or time. Could it have been given anywhere other than the Abbey of Afflighem? Once a stay in Flanders has been established, it is enough to permit us to go directly [Col. 1810D] to Afflighem and greet Our Lady there with Saint Bernard.

On examining this precious document further, we observe in it six abbots. Which of them belonged to an abbey situated on Saint Bernard’s route and at the scene of the dispute?

Ninove is three miles from the disputed locality; Dilighem, four. The Dunes, Tronchiennes [Note: [Col. 1809] Or Drongen, of the Premonstratensian Order, near Ghent.], and Châtillon are much farther away. Afflighem is one mile from Liedekerke, somewhat farther from Denderleeuw, and equally distant from Ninove and Dilighem.

Afflighem had even possessed the disputed churches, since after the departure of the Augustinians and before the arrival [Col. 1811A] of the Premonstratensians, Benedictine monks appear to have been temporarily attached to Dilighem.

Afflighem lies on the road from Flanders to Brabant.

Afflighem is the sole Brabantine abbey possessing a specific memory of Saint Bernard’s passage; the only one attesting that it received him; the only one still displaying the holy abbot’s crosier, pledge of that illustrious hospitality; the only one possessing a miraculous Madonna. No tradition brings the Saint either to Dilighem or to Ninove; and there is no trace of any visit either in the contemporary chronicle of Villers, in the continuations of Sigebert, or in Baldwin of Ninove, although he does mention the suit and Saint Bernard’s arbitration.

Finally, Afflighem is governed by Abbot Peter, [Col. 1811B] who heads the four witnesses. He is certainly the most important among them, the one whom Saint Bernard, at the beginning of his mission, would have visited first. Peter discharged important legations before the great men of the age. He sat in the council of the powerful neighbouring bishops; he crossed the seas and appeared on several occasions at the court of the kings of England; he received notable gifts from Queen Adelaide and from her second husband, the Duke of Lincoln. It is less than four years since he was visited by Emperor Conrad with a large retinue of knights.

Afflighem is the abbey of the crusaders, the beloved foundation of the counts of Flanders, Boulogne, and Louvain. Perhaps it already possesses the national standard [Col. 1811C], woven and embroidered by the royal hands of Adelaide, deposited by her in the abbey where she will come to die and lie beside the dukes of Brabant. This Brabantine oriflamme remains in the keeping of Our Lady and Saint Peter of Afflighem; on feast days and at public processions, the abbey has it displayed upon a triumphal car; before going on campaign, the dukes of Brabant receive it from the abbot’s hands, as the kings of France went to take the oriflamme at the gates of Saint-Denis.

Saint Bernard, who summoned all Christian knighthood to war, who could not go to England and was setting out for Germany, could not have dispensed with visiting Afflighem and seeing Abbot Peter; and it is not merely because they are [Col. 1811D] under his abbatial roof that the abbots of Tronchiennes, the Dunes, Châtillon, Jette, and Ninove yield to that of Afflighem the place of honour at the head of the subscriptions to the arbitral charter.

Now, having mastered the time and the place, let us take possession of our charter in its entirety; let us narrow the terms still further and, returning to Saint Bernard, attempt to specify the circumstances of his visit and, if possible, put our finger upon the month and day of his memorable appearance in the abbey of Afflighem.

X. On 31 March 1146 Saint Bernard is at Vézelay and, shortly afterward, at Chartres [Note: [Col. 1811D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 65.].

Having returned to Clairvaux, he writes important letters; negotiates against the proposal to elect him commander-in-chief of the crusade; removes from his path the German monk Raoul, who was about to block his way by a massacre of the Jews; sends ahead his vehement epistles like so many emissaries to the Eastern Franks, the English barons, and the Bohemian and Moravian kings; and arranges everything for his longest absence.

He accepts as his companion his most devoted friend, Baldwin of Châtillon, born in Flanders of the blood of the first crusaders; he chooses two of his monks, Gerard and Geoffrey. The latter, who for fourteen years had been among Abelard’s most celebrated disciples, and for thirteen years since his conversion had been attached to [Col. 1812B] his last master, whom he had never left, will serve as his secretary, carry his seal, and compose the account of the journey. He replaces that Nicholas of Clairvaux who, perhaps humiliated by this choice, from this point onward begins to employ a fraudulent seal and to circulate forged letters from his idle cell. Thus surrounded by Gerard and Geoffrey, guided by Baldwin, the Saint will go first of all to the homeland of Godfrey of Bouillon, there to draw at its source and pour forth in long draughts the enthusiasm for the crusades.

He loved Arras and Alvise, its great bishop; on this same journey he surely venerated the miraculous Candle of Our Lady of Arras. In this year 1146 an unpublished charter shows him in that city, at an assembly of the bishops and abbots of the province [Col. 1812C] of Reims [Note: [Col. 1811D] See Supporting Documents, no. V.]. Could this have been the beginning of his legation?

Could the Saint, while passing through this region, fail to travel upon the *Via Sanctorum*, from Arras to Boulogne, trodden by so many devout persons?—Fail to confer with Clairambault of Arras, one of the luminaries of that age, who, to Abelard’s detriment, did him the honour of commenting on his Boethius?—Or with blessed Goswin of Anchin, Alvise’s successor, a humble sage hidden away among his marshes, adviser to popes, friend of Saint Bernard, again a rival of Abelard, who dared and was able, at eighteen years of age, publicly to confound the doctor in his chair [Note: [Col. 1811D] See the *History of Anchin*, by Dr. Lescalier.]? There can be no doubt that he visited beforehand the place where, in the following year, there would rise like the flowering seeds [Col. 1812D] of his passage Our Lady of Los [Note: [Col. 1812D] D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 924, no. 112. “At the same time,” says the chronicler, who shortly before named the twenty-fourth year of Simon of Noyon, elected in 1122.], Cambron, Villers, and Aune—the first or the principal Cistercian abbeys of these regions. Clairmarais, Vaucelles, and the Dunes had already been founded and lay on his route. Abbot Leonius receives him at Saint-Bertin; and before setting out for the crusade, he accompanies him as far as Bruges and leads him to his friend, in the words of a charter, Thierry of Alsace, who, scarcely returned from the Holy Land, joyfully takes up the cross again and congratulates himself upon it in public acts.

Would Saint Bernard not also have visited Tournai [Col. 1813A], which in that same year, 1146, after forty years of negotiations, finally obtained restoration of its episcopal see, thanks to Pope Eugenius III and, above all, to Saint Bernard? We know that at Tournai there lived one of his dearest correspondents, Otger of Saint-Médard, and one of the most illustrious crusaders, Herimann, abbot of Saint-Martin, “whose footsteps were beautiful, according to an old song, and whose years were eternal, when he passed away on his way to the Holy Sepulchre.” We have seen that Ypres preserves the same tradition and can show in its Red Register authentic proof of his presence with Thierry of Alsace, the most popular of the Flemish crusaders after Godfrey of Bouillon.

Saint Bernard undoubtedly went as far as the [Col. 1813B] shores of the Ocean, to his beloved monastery of the Dunes, to his children, to his brothers, and to holy Abbot Robert, his future successor, who joins Baldwin in forming an escort of honour for him.

An indisputable document shows him at Bruges, surrounded by the devout abbots Leonius and Robert, and noble persons.

This document vindicates the tradition of Furnes, attested by Malbrancq, and that of Nieuwpoort, which still displays a pulpit from which Saint Bernard is said to have preached the crusade. Herimann himself, or his contemporary continuator, reports in agreement with Saint Bernard’s historians that, at his voice, twenty-nine persons of consequence from the Church and diocese of Tournai [Col. 1813C] left the world and followed him to Clairvaux.

[Col. 1813C] And why should we disdain the traditions of Mons and Ghent, where the great voice of the apostle of holy wars retains a stubborn echo in the ears of the people, awaiting the moment when scholarship awakens and brings forth some new testimony buried in the dust of archives?

We wished to avoid these details; they have become necessary in order to make acceptable and plausible the precise identification, as to month and day, of the miracle of Afflighem. If all these matters are assigned their time and place, one will be led from Clairvaux to the gate of Afflighem, and from 31 March, approximately, as it seems to us, to the day fixed by the Martyrology of Villers and the Menologion of [Col. 1813D] Cîteaux: the eighteenth day of October. In 1146, this was Thursday in the third week of October. Everything agrees with this date. From there, urged forward by a first miracle, the Saint moves rapidly and in the following week is at the site of what became Villers, which adopted this date as the anniversary of its foundation. At the end of the month he is at Liège, then at Mainz, and on the first Sunday of Advent at Constance; only there does the narrative of his companions begin.

XI. About the middle of October, therefore, he was travelling on the great road from Flanders to Brabant, “supporting his feeble limbs upon his abbatial staff.” The [Col. 1814A] abbots Goswin of Tronchiennes, Gerard of Ninove, and Walther of Dilighem hasten to meet him. Afflighem is their inevitable rendezvous.

Since the Saint gladly visited monasteries, everywhere making his old Order of Saint Benedict flourish anew [Note: [Col. 1813D] See Supporting Documents, nos. XIV and XV.], multiplying the colonies of the Cistercian reform, or at least arousing a holy emulation, he entered Afflighem and there found the beauty of primitive observance. He needed only to breathe its air in order to see everything; and to say what he admired, one word sufficed:

> “Elsewhere I have seen men; here I see angels. Truly, Afflighem afflicts the man, but raises the soul.”

We could name several of these angels [Col. 1814B], raised above the earth: venerable Albert, who had humbly stepped down from the abbatial seat without losing his noble title, “Marianus, abbot of Our Lady”; the devout prior of Wavre, Walter, to whom the feast of Our Lady of Peace would soon be owed; blessed Francon, first abbot of Vlierbeek; Ingelbert, first prior of Bigard, father and historian of Saint Vivine—another angel of Afflighem, perhaps come hastening at the passage of the man of God. Could we forget Raoul the Silent, who beneath hair-shirt, whips, and iron chains kept for sixteen years the absolute silence of the lamb that is sacrificed, until, when a fire broke out before him, God inspired him to say, “Flame, stop!”—and the flame stopped. [Col. 1814C] It is said that Abbot Peter was “the archangel of these earthly virtues”; but their queen was OUR LADY, whose statue, erected sixty years earlier at the site indicated by the founder, was venerated in the most secluded corner of the cloister, between the dormitory and the church.

XII. Before passing before her, let us enter the chapter-house: never again will a more illustrious chapter be assembled there. Seven abbots are seated, or eight if the old Albert is included. Saint Bernard presides. Blessed Peter and Saint Robert are near him. In the middle of the hall Geoffrey is at the lectern of the scriptorium. Holding a sheet of parchment folded and prepared in the form of a chirograph, he writes in duplicate at the Saint’s dictation:

[Col. 1814D]

> “I, Bernard, called by the grace of God abbot of Clairvaux, to all children of Holy Church: eternal greeting in our Lord Jesus!
>
> “We wish it to be known to all, present and future, that a dispute which had arisen between the abbot of Ninove and that of Jette concerning the church of Liedekerke has been settled before us and religious persons in the following manner: [lacuna].”

He then dictates the agreed conditions: Liedekerke is ceded to Ninove; Dilighem accepts in exchange Leeuwe and a reserved tithe from the church of Erembodegem. The River Dender is to serve as the boundary.

Geoffrey faithfully records the required formulas: [Col. 1815A] he writes, on the right and left, the two identical instruments, except for permissible variations such as the Germanic forms of place-names and certain transpositions of the parties’ names required by usage and formularies. Four monks and four abbots are appointed as witnesses. Peter is placed first, as abbot of the church and place; Geoffrey must honourably subscribe after all the others. Then, on four tongues cut from the margins and hanging from the two charters, he applies white wax twice and twice impresses upon it the seal of the abbot of Clairvaux. This seal is extant, and upon it one recognizes the right hand moving with a crozier set upright, bearing the legend of Clairvaux. Cut vertically through the chirographic inscription, the two documents are [Col. 1815B] matched by their check-signs, verified, and delivered to the parties, to be deposited in the archives of Jette and Ninove for the remotest posterity.

[Note: [Col. 1815C] In examining this charter, we have strictly confined ourselves to what suited our subject; and although we may have appeared overly minute, we are far from having exhausted this interesting study. We might have paused over this chirographic form, as common in the chanceries of northern Gaul as it is rare elsewhere. The topography of this charter; the importance of the disputed places; the patronage of Saint Amand and Saint Nicholas invoked in the case; the resumption of the dispute; the fresh pleadings brought before the tribunal of the Metropolitan and the Supreme Pontiff; and finally a last sentence in 1180, pronounced *ab irato* (“in anger”) by the abbot of Prémontré in order to settle the matter by an act of authority—all deserved at least a less dry mention than this note.

There would have been more to say about Saint Bernard’s companions who appear in this charter: about Baldwin of Châtillon, who still bears there the title of abbot and is found again in Germany; about Geoffrey, a humble monk who would become an important figure through his writings and weighty offices. Finally, without any intemperance of learning, this first seal of Saint Bernard invited an attractive gloss. Contrary to general usage, neither the figure of the abbot nor Saint Bernard’s name appears on it. The hand holding the crozier emerges from a cloud and forcefully expresses divine investiture and the charter’s opening words: “I, Bernard, BY THE GRACE OF GOD.” We cannot refrain from pointing out a very striking resemblance between the crozier depicted upon this seal and the crook preserved by the Benedictines of Afflighem.

On considering Saint Bernard’s second seal, rediscovered at Rouen, and rereading a letter addressed to the Institut de France on this subject, we nearly amused ourselves at the embarrassment [Col. 1816D] of the learned correspondent who, seeing Saint Bernard—as on all abbots’ seals for six or seven hundred years—holding the book of the Rule, asks whether the object might be a mythological hourglass, or, more probably, a church door with capitals, little columns, and a double leaf!—What would it have been if, given over to conjecture, we had examined to what degree this charter might be an autograph of Saint Bernard? We were struck by the resemblance of this handwriting to a small strip of parchment placed among Saint Bernard’s bones, which has been suspected of being an autograph of the great abbot of Clairvaux.

We would at least wish these indicative notes and short studies to give enough value to this charter and this venerable seal that, in the name of ecclesiastical authority, they might be granted a more suitable place—not merely in an archive building, but rather in a church and in the treasury of a cathedral.].

This dispute, which revived later and lasted a long time, must have possessed some importance. The Saint hastened to conclude it, so that he might freely pour out his soul among the devout cenobites. After a first address, he spoke again a second time, and with an accent so penetrating that the memory of it remained and spread far and wide. In the fervour of his zeal, the Saint, ardently expressing his desire to be in all things like his hosts, candidly offered his white habit to these angels. They deliberated: the offer was rejected with equal frankness [Col. 1815C] by the black monks. Yet beneath different colours their hearts remained united; and all together, one last time, went away to pray in the church. The crowd of abbots and white and black monks stretched along the cloisters; all eyes, as they were about to lose sight of him for a long time, followed the illustrious guest. Before all, he stops at the corner of the cloister adjoining the church, [Col. 1816A] bows before the Madonna, and addresses to her the greeting that has always made the Mother of God thrill: “Hail, Mary.” Before all, the statue stirs, bows, and replies: “Hail, Bernard.”

It was too signal a favour for the Saint not to leave a token of his gratitude. Unable to bequeath his white tunic to Afflighem or to bring this holy flock beneath his crozier, he wished his pastoral staff to remain there as a memorial. He detached its crimson crook and laid this wholly golden gift at the feet of Our Lady of Afflighem, in perpetual remembrance of the greeting granted to him on 18 October 1146.

Such was that day in the abbey of Afflighem. We have fulfilled our task, so far as it depended upon [Col. 1816B] us; happy if these pages, written in haste, edify others as they have consoled us ourselves.

After Our Lady, it would remain for us to describe Saint Peter of Afflighem, to place at the feet of its patroness the abbey that grew beneath her wing and spread out like the fringes of her mantle. It is her visible work; it is the virtue issuing from her lips, like Saint Bernard’s greeting.

This completion of our work was nearly finished. Other concerns call us elsewhere, and perhaps our readers’ attention is already far from us. Who, at the present hour of the world, can think of the eve or the morrow? May quieter days and a few serene hours come: we shall recover the ducal abbey, the Belgian congregation [Col. 1816C]—we shall recover the ducal abbey, the Belgian congregation—and its happy motto: “Happy concord.” Until then, trusting in the guardianship of God and of the good Virgin, let us remember Our Lady of Afflighem.

> This statue of the Virgin Mother, Mary,  
> returned Bernard’s greeting in speech.  
> You too, desirous of eternal salvation,  
> greet her often.

## Supporting Documents

[Col. 1817]

### Preliminary Notes

The plan of the preceding work, the narrow limits and unavoidable conditions of a journal article, have not allowed us methodically and chronologically to set out the documents that we had to cite and publish. Without recasting what has been done or retracing our steps, we must nevertheless orient our readers concerning the documents that follow and establish their historical and reciprocal connection.

From the eleventh century onward we find the miraculous statue of Our Lady of Afflighem at the very origin of the abbey (no. II, col. 1823). We set this origin in 1075, against the common opinion which places it ten years later. Our date is established by the death of Saint Anno of Cologne, who blessed Afflighem’s first founders, and by the corrected text of a contemporary chronicle of the abbey itself.

An extract from the work of Francon, second abbot and second founder of Afflighem, reviewed against a well-written twelfth-century manuscript (no. III, ibid.); together with several unpublished pious verses by Amerius on the holy Abbot Albert called Marianus (no. IV, col. 1824), prepares, as it were, the background against which Saint Bernard and Our Lady of Afflighem will meet.

The Saint departs from Clairvaux. As if to set a marker at this point of departure, we publish an unpublished piece, the only one that remains to us apart from Abbot Anselm’s continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux. Lovers of ancient and fine letters will appreciate the exquisite elegance of this little poem. Those who have visited Clairvaux will recognize in this page by the abbot of Gembloux the Clairvaux of old and will find in it precious topographical details veiled beneath an almost continuous allegory. All will forgive us for placing this episode, like a prologue, at the beginning of our *Analecta* (no. I, col. 1821).

We pass abruptly to Arras, where we find Saint Bernard in an assembly presided over by the metropolitan of Reims, attended by the suffragans of Arras, Thérouanne, and Soissons; the abbots of Clairvaux and Mareuil; and the principal members of the chapter and clergy of Arras (no. V, col. 1823). We regret that we cannot dwell upon this document, except perhaps to point to a hitherto unknown council of Arras, to establish at least fully two journeys of Saint Bernard to Arras, in 1132 and 1146, and consequently a double visit to the holy Candle of Arras—which has had the misfortune of being at once too much neglected by the Bollandists and shamefully trodden beneath Voltaire’s filthy feet.

But Saint Bernard must be followed further. We hope later to have some documents leading the Saint to Boulogne, as Father Malbranq suggests; to Ruisseauville, of which Baldwin, his travelling companion, was abbot; to Saint-Bertin, where the abbot and monks seem attached to him, the former through the crusades and the latter through an epistolary correspondence; then all along the *Via Sanctorum*, which passed through Thérouanne, episcopal see of Blessed Milon and homeland of the founder of the Temple and its first knights, so dear to Saint Bernard. We do not doubt that the monks of Clairvaux who, shortly before the charter of Thierry of Alsace (no. VI, col. 1825), visit the site of what became Our Lady of Los, are the holy traveller and his companions. At any rate, the chronicle of Los affirms that the first stone was laid in Saint Bernard’s presence in 1146, while the chronicle of Saint-Bertin adds that several monasteries in Flanders were then visited, restored, or built by Saint Bernard (no. VII, col. 1824).

We lack the lost documents for an unavoidable stop at Tournai, which in the following year obtained, thanks to Saint Bernard, the restoration of its ancient bishopric. The Saint still appears in the stained glass of the fine Romanesque basilica of Our Lady at Tournai. There is even an express mention of this journey, though without dates, in a fabulous work by Hoverlant, who may have produced forty volumes on the history of Tournai which one scarcely dares to cite. More serious is the assertion of Dom Brial who, supported by the testimony of Herimann, of whom we have spoken, places in 1146 a great preaching of the Saint at Tournai [Note: [Col. 1817] See the *Nouveaux mémoires de l’Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres*, vol. IV, p. 508.], and the conversion of thirty notable members of the city clergy, to whom Saint Bernard shortly afterward writes an encouraging letter as an already weary old man. Could Saint Bernard have spoken thus on his first journey of 1132?

We are certain of having Saint Bernard at Bruges in this same year, thanks to the four lines which we exhumed from the abandoned cartulary of the abbey of Eechout (no. VIII, col. 1825).

Finally, the charter of Thierry of Alsace (no. IX) brings us nearer to Afflighem and leads us to Ypres.

What happened at Afflighem is known. We ought to provide a facsimile of the two charters of Ninove and Dilighem, and of Saint Bernard’s seal. We await the reappearance of the Dilighem original in the royal archives at Brussels or in some unexplored collection, as the Ninove original was found at Ghent. It would be curious to put together, after seven hundred and two completed years, these two pieces of parchment, cut apart before the eyes—perhaps by the hand—of Saint Bernard in the chapter-house of Afflighem, *ad perpetuam rei memoriam* (“for the perpetual remembrance of the matter”).

We must no less thank the two learned Belgians, Messrs Van der Mersch and Baron de Saint-Genois, who transmitted to us the facsimile and seal accompanying the double text of the charters of Ninove and Dilighem (nos. X–XI, col. 1825).

A chronicle of Afflighem summarizes the event of 1146 (no. XII), recorded in the Martyrology and chronicle of Villers (nos. XIII–XIV). Amerius of Afflighem puts this account into verse (no. XV).

The documents (nos. XIII and XIV, col. 1827) have a double value for us. The first is testimony from the abbey of Villers, entered in its Martyrology, which fixes the day of Saint Bernard’s visit. Both are also for us a remembrance of our visit to the museum of the new Bollandists, and an occasion to express all our gratitude for their kindly and unanimous eagerness to aid our studies.

In 1153, the numerous monks of Afflighem led a procession in Brussels and continued it to Wavre, followed by thirty thousand pilgrims (no. XVI, ibid.).

In 1160, a pilgrim who came from England and was known for having persecuted the abbey, probably in its overseas possessions, fell ill at the abbey hospice. He was treated there with such brotherly care that, having returned to England, he came back to hide himself under the humblest monastic habit and to die there as a lay brother. We shall find some opportunity to publish in full the rugged, vigorous Leonine verses which he wrote between his two journeys. Here we can only extract a few verses in honour of Our Lady (no. XVII, col. 1828).

[Col. 1819] Amerius acquaints us with the abbey’s old practices for honouring the miraculous statue, practices prior to the reform of Bursfeld (no. XVIII, col. 1828).

In 1460 [Note: [Col. 1819] It may appear extraordinary that we do not possess from this period a greater number of testimonies from the abbey itself. The silence of its chronicles led the Bollandists to pass it over and greatly strengthened the negative argument, then thought so conclusive. First, we oppose to it all these positive documents; then we explain the silence of the abbey’s chroniclers.

In the fourteenth century Afflighem was burned three times, and in the sixteenth it was plundered three or four times by various parties, virtually abandoned and depopulated for twenty-seven years. Its archives were dispersed through seven or eight removals of the monks—to Wavre, Brussels, Mechelen, Louvain, and Vlierbeek. The chronicles that escaped all these disasters and reached the Bollandists are reduced to a continuation of Sigebert of Gembloux and fragments published in d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* under the title *Chronicle of Afflighem*.

As for the continuation, it is only an often interrupted series of notes scattered at long intervals. The entire period of Saint Bernard is absent from it. Messrs Pertz and Bethmann, in publishing this appendix, plainly noted this lacuna. As for the *Spicilegium*: 1. It contains a notice contemporary with the foundation, embracing only the first fourteen years, from 1075 to 1089; we might call these opening chapters, written by a contemporary, the *Exordium Afflighemense* (“Beginning of Afflighem”). 2. In several old manuscripts there existed a conclusion to chapter 10, lacking in the *Spicilegium* and reproduced here; it sharply separates the first portion from the rest of the work:

> “Fulgentius accepted with fear and reverence the burden imposed upon him, and throughout his life laudably governed the aforesaid place, to the praise and glory of the highest Creator, of His glorious Virgin Mother, of the supreme apostles Peter and Paul, and of the entire heavenly court, as the writings and privileges concerning the foundation of the place, its confirmation, and its approval declare more fully.”

It follows from this note that the first chronicler precedes Abbot Fulgentius and the year 1122, while his continuator, the author of this conclusion, was writing after that date. We would be tempted to attribute to the latter chapters 9 and 10, which differ entirely from the preceding chapters. Their author accumulates without order a series of facts plainly extending to 1150. A Brother Arnulf, a lay brother in 1086, is said to have lived sixty-four years in the monastery. Thus it was only after 1150, after Saint Bernard’s visit, that two chapters were added to the chronicle. 3. Still later, other chroniclers supplied various fragments. There are none concerning the period of Saint Bernard’s visit. At least there was nothing continuous until Jean Van der Meeren, known as Amerius, who wrote from 1535 to 1540. Even Odo Cambier was able to send d’Achery only fragments of Amerius. He intended to complete them, but died very young, leaving several unpublished notes.], Abbot Goswin rebuilt the cloister through which Saint Bernard had passed (no. XIX, ibid.).

After the introduction of the Bursfeld reform, and during the Protestant invasion, Afflighem always retained its fervour for the miraculous Our Lady. Jean Solebreck, one of its monks, supplies the proof (no. XX, ibid.).

In 1578 Saint Bernard’s crozier was separated from Our Lady, but was saved and faithfully preserved (no. XXI).

In 1580 the miraculous statue was broken by iconoclasts (no. XXII).

In 1605 the abbey was rebuilt, and the statue remade and restored to the same pedestal on which Saint Bernard had greeted it (no. XXIII, col. 1829).

We add here several dates to the supporting documents:

In 1606 Saint Bernard’s crozier was restored to the treasury of the sacristy at Afflighem.

In 1618 Haeften adorned the cloister of Our Lady with stained-glass windows and had painted there the life of the Blessed Virgin and the miracle of Afflighem.

In 1621 the statue was transferred from the cloister to the left wing of the new church, to the choir of the religious. Haeften maintained the practice of keeping profound silence in the cloister of Our Lady from the stained-glass windows that recalled Saint Bernard’s visit onward (no. XXIV, col. 1829).

In 1624 the solemn Assumption procession began, in which the statue was carried by four Capuchin friars around the abbey.

In 1626 the statue was placed in the middle of the choir beneath a rich canopy and elegantly decorated with Haeften’s inscriptions. He had Crayer paint a magnificent picture of the three Benedictine doctors and panegyrists of Our Lady—Saint Ildefonsus, Saint Anselm, and Saint Bernard—to whom Blessed Rupert was added. At the bottom of the picture one read: “Saint Bernard, greeting her in the same manner, received an answer from the statue.”

In 1627 Jean Verpoorten, prior of Wavre, requested and obtained, to place in his church, the second statue made from the fragments of the oldest one, which had until then been entrusted to the Reverend Jesuit Fathers of Brussels. What became afterward of this second statue is unknown.

In 1627 a new congregation was erected among the Flemish abbeys under the title and patronage of Afflighem (no. XXV, ibid.).

In 1630 Urban VIII granted indulgences for the feast of the Presentation of Our Lady, adopted as the commemoration of the miracle of 1146.

In 1645, a miracle attested by three witnesses and a physician confirmed the faithful’s devotion to small images of Our Lady of Afflighem.

In 1647 the archbishop of Mechelen likewise granted indulgences (no. XXVI, ibid.).

In 1648 one of Afflighem’s most devout monks, Brother Ghislain, died in the odour of sanctity. His innocence and love for Our Lady had earned him the names *Puer Angelicus* (“Angelic Boy”) and *Marianus* (“Devoted to Mary”).

In 1651 another miracle was guaranteed by the declaration of an officer, Baron de Mersele, who, struck by a point-blank gunshot, attributed his survival to an image of Our Lady of Afflighem which he carried upon his person.

In 1655 Rupert Diétrix, forty-second prelate, distinguished himself by his devotion and zeal for the miraculous statue.

In 1657 Odo Cambier continued Afflighem’s tradition through his historical labours and poetic vigour (no. XXVII, col. 1830).

In 1701 Raoul Crucker, still a novice and later grand provost, in his turn deserves mention in this series of testimonies in honour of Our Lady.

In 1745 Benedict XIV issued the brief which we publish (no. XXVIII, col. 1831).

From 1764 to 1770 the church and choir of Our Lady were entirely rebuilt.

In 1774 Paquot investigated Saint Bernard’s stay at Afflighem; his notes are lost.

In 1781 disturbances obliged the provost to alter the hours of the Assumption procession.

[Col. 1821] In 1796 the religious, expelled from their abbey, carried away the miraculous statue.

In 1802 the last provost gave an authentic testimony which we publish as no. XXIX, col. 1831.

In 1841 Dom Veremond d’Haens restored the miraculous statue to the little church at Dendermonde, occupied by the new Belgian Benedictines.

As an epilogue to this work, we give a well-known Cistercian hymn concerning Our Lady and Saint Bernard. We reproduce it if only to give our readers repose after this perhaps wearisome sequence of abridged accounts, scattered notes, and highly disparate documents—no. XXX, col. 1832.
