We do not even dare to say with an abbot of Afflighem: “Perhaps I shall seem excessive; but only to one who is ungrateful both to the Mother and impious toward the Son” (*Videbor forsitan nimius, sed nemini nisi qui fuerit et Matri ingratus et in Filium impius*; below, col. 1824).

[Col. 1821]

# Miscellanea, Mostly Unpublished, Concerning the Cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the Abbey of Afflighem and the Journey of Saint Bernard through the Regions of Flanders in A.D. 1146

## I. Anselm of Gembloux, in Praise of Clairvaux, to the Venerable Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux

[Col. 1821A]

> A sloping valley, which an opposing mountain casts into shade,  
> which a stream flowing with winter waters presses upon,  
> is neither sufficiently fit for grain nor sufficiently suited to the vine:  
> Father Bacchus condemns it; kindly Ceres curses it.  
>
> Far different from this, best of Fathers, is your valley:

The valley is pleasing to both deities in its own fruitfulness.

This too once lay numb beneath a cold shadow;  
and the rank reed floated upon its own shallows.

You were sent by the Lord to a field wrongly left untilled;  
the task of cultivating its waste places was entrusted to your care.

A good servant, you rise to the appointed duties,  
arming your ready hands with ploughshare and sickle.

Your true Sun directs and illumines your steps,  
He who knows not how to submit His brightness to the setting waters;  
and when He breathed at once upon the barren, dark places of the marsh,

[Col. 1821B] the harmful mist and harmful moisture departed.

The valley, once a wilderness, now most splendid Tempe, rightly draws its famous name from the reality.

And lest bracken grow thick, or the most wretched endive  
and thistle luxuriate in fertile ground,

you turn the fruitful clods with the driven ploughshare,  
which you tame beneath the shattering weight of the rake.

Then in equal furrows you bury cereal seed,  
to be multiplied in the return of its own increase.

An image suspended from a stake, together with a drawn bow, terrifies  
and keeps at a distance the destructive birds.

And with the noble shoot *Sorech* of the Lord of Hosts  
a vineyard is planted in a more fruitful place—  
a vineyard through you transplanted from Pharian darkness,  
drawn forth from muddy whirlpools and cleansed.

You plant and arrange the vines in a fixed order,  
setting strong supports beneath their little arms.

Do you not think moisture sufficient for the swelling buds? With the sickle you cut away what is superfluous and luxuriant.

[Col. 1821C] And lest the goat insult the vine, or the sow the planting,  
a squared wall of fencing surrounds it on every side.

[And while the soft] south winds foster it with their gentle breath,  
[the dark citadels of the sky, the cold] of Thrace . . . [lacuna] honey of flavour.

(The folio having been wretchedly scraped, nine verses have fallen out.)

The shoot, changed from the shade of its wild mother,  
learns to grow green beneath the foliage of the Lyaean god [Bacchus].

Now the little bud puts forth its flower and spreads  
a vine-leaf fragrance, through which the woodland extends itself everywhere.

Now autumn commands the laden vine to be raised by its genial cluster  
and its gifts to be gathered.

Now harvest and vintage fill  
the Lord’s granaries with wheaten produce and the vats with nectar.

In these things the delight of bridegroom and bride takes pleasure—  
[Col. 1822A] O Sweet Friend, the work of both is yours.

A most abundant reward awaits you, now a veteran servant:  
for a servant’s merits, the everlasting glory of the Lord.

From Douai manuscript 552, formerly of Anchin.

## II.—1075

This statue, representing the most Blessed Virgin MARY holding her child in her arms, was sculpted from that somewhat soft and whitish stone, or at least from one very like it, sprinkled with a little black sand (which the Germans call *Avenesteen*, the Brabanters *Lavendersteen*). It was of the height of an ordinary man—that is, five feet or more—and wholly antique in workmanship and appearance, with a veil falling from the head onto the shoulders . . . The place in which it was first set up, remained, and was honoured for several hundred years is the cloister, or ambulatory, of the monastery, beside the door leading thence to the dormitory, where its very base may still be seen, projecting from the side of the older church. There another statue of the Blessed Virgin has now been placed, [Col. 1822B] with this inscription:

> Revere this statue of the pious Virgin MARY;  
> and, as you pass by, take care that the *Ave* is not left unspoken.

From the manuscript chronicle of Phalesius.

## III.—About the year 1121. Proclamation of the Blessed Virgin MARY, by Franco, second abbot of Afflighem, newly collated from the manuscripts

And it was fitting that He who came to heal the corrupted mass in Adam should be born not from the seed of corruption but by the power of the Holy Spirit . . . A glass most clean and most solid was sought, through which the Sun of Justice might transmit His fiery rays to drive away the darkness of the nations; a glass from which it might receive an increase of purity and brightness, and suffer no loss of integrity. . . Where on earth could so beautiful a virgin be found, who might captivate with her eyes the King of Heaven [Note: These words and others enclosed in brackets are taken from the Cambrai manuscript, but are wholly absent from the printed editions.], who might draw the Son of God [Col. 1822C] from the bosom of the Father and, by the bonds of charity rather than by force, draw Him captive into her own embraces? Long sought, awaited by the vows of many saints, at last that exceptional woman was found: uniquely worthy, uniquely beautiful, the Virgin MARY. But by whom was she found? Wisdom itself from eternity ordained MARY as its bride; Wisdom itself, in the fullness of time, sanctified MARY’s most chaste womb as its tabernacle; Wisdom itself adorned the temple in MARY, in every glory and beauty beyond the loveliness of all visible and invisible creatures—as much as it willed, and as befitted the One to be born from her. . . Rightly, therefore, every condition, every age, every rank honours MARY with the ANGELIC SALUTATION. Rightly, “Hail, MARY!” [Note: The manuscript reads “adores.” Then, with the printed edition: “Rightly, to MARY.”], every voice, every tongue, and every conscience [Col. 1823A] cries out with the angel: “HAIL, MARY, full of grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women . . .”

For whatever grace the grace of God bestowed upon MARY, though by special prerogative, divine mercy provided it for the salvation of the whole world. MARY is the common good of all, and from MARY’s fullness the solitude of the nations has been filled. Whoever, therefore, thirsts with eager throat for the sweetness of grace, approach with due reverence the fullness of MARY’s womb: such abundance of mercy flows thence, such sweetness of mercy, that neither does its abundance know failure nor its sweetness weariness. Drink, then, drink from this fountain of mercy! Drink, that you may fill your eager throat [Note: The printed editions incorrectly have: “that it may fill.”]; but do not suppose that, by drinking, you extinguish your thirst. Love of eternal things has this distinctive property: it always inflames the desire of lovers and never produces in those who love any weariness of itself.

No mind can estimate, no tongue suffices to recount, how great a grace God has bestowed upon humankind through MARY, the glory of virgins. MARY, star of the sea, light of [Col. 1823B] those who wander, hope of the despairing, comforter of the sorrowful, common joy of all Christ’s faithful: we have not yet done enough for the desire to praise her, nor do we believe it can ever be done enough amid the frailty of this corruptible life. Yet, once her praise’s sweetness has been tasted beforehand, the desire for it is kindled more and more; [but [Note: From the omission of this single passage in the printed editions one may learn how carelessly the works of Franco, abbot of Afflighem, were either published or copied from manuscripts—works issued at Antwerp in 1562 and 1565, Freiburg im Breisgau in 1615 and 1620, Cologne in 1610, and afterwards in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.] the heat of pious desire is cooled, as it were, by a certain divine dew, through daily remembrance of her and frequent repetition of her most sweet name]. For after that singular name of her beloved Son, which is above every name, heaven and earth name no other from which pious minds may conceive so much grace, hope, sweetness, and consolation. For as often as lovers of MARY hear that most sweet name, so often from their devout hearing and from the sweetness of the name heard they draw inwardly some indescribable joy. For the name MARY contains in itself something wonderfully sweet and divine, so that when it sounds in friendly hearts it breathes the fragrance of familiar sweetness. And this is wonderful [Col. 1823C] concerning the name MARY, and very wonderful: it is always heard as though new. MARY, holy Virgin, Mother worthy of God, most gracious comforter, most powerful advocate of those who belong to her. In praise of MARY OURS—OURS, I say, OURS—I may perhaps appear excessive to anyone; but not to anyone unless he has been both ungrateful to the Mother and impious toward the Son . . . (*On the Grace of God*, Book VI throughout).

## IV.—1136. Albert III, abbot, called Marianus

Albert was the third abbot, a true lover  
of the Rule, who shone as its sincere and accomplished fulfiller,  
ever-watchful, equally steadfast, Marianus and a follower of the Fathers.

Amerius, in the manuscript Chronicle, fol. 32, in Beda, *Hafflighem Illustrated*, vol. I, p. 253.

## V.—1146. Saint Bernard attends the council of Arras and subscribes the instrument by which Bishop Alvisus grants the altar of Saints to the abbot of Saint Autbert of Cambrai

[Col. 1823D]

In the name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. [Note: In the original charter only the initial letters are written: *In N. S. E. I. T. P. E. F. E. S. S.*]

I, Alvisus, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, make known to future and present persons alike, in perpetuity. It is clearer than light that every bishop, bearing the office of the apostles, must imitate their example, so that his daily concern is care for all the churches. Knowing and reflecting upon this, I, the least of all the Lord’s priests, desire, insofar as my resources permit, to consent to the pious prayers of Christ’s poor and to relieve their necessities.

[Col. 1824A] Therefore, when we had sat together in the presence of the venerable Samson, archbishop of Reims—Joslan, bishop of Soissons; Milo, bishop of Thérouanne; Alvisus, bishop of Arras; and the abbot of Clairvaux—they jointly presented me, in the course of conversation, with a petition. I judged it fitting to consent to it, for divine grace’s sake and out of reverence for such persons; and therefore I more willingly carried it into effect.

Accordingly, the altar of Saints which Letard, a cleric of Lens, had hitherto possessed and intended to surrender—and did surrender—I have granted and do grant to you, dearest brother in Christ Galterus, venerable abbot of Saint Autbert of Cambrai, at their request and testimony, for the use of your brethren to possess forever, saving in all respects the right of the bishop of Arras and his ministers.

But if anyone after this our decision should attempt with sacrilegious hand to remove it from the church to which, by God’s ordinance, we have assented, let him be anathema with Simon Magus. And that this distinguished gift, so made, may remain valid and unshaken, I have ordered it to be copied, confirmed by the impression of our seal, and marked with the signs of the aforesaid persons and of others.

Sign of Lord Samson, archbishop of Reims.—Sign of Lord Joslan, bishop of Soissons.—Sign of Lord Milo, bishop of Thérouanne.—Sign of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.—Sign of Luke, archdeacon of Arras.—Sign of Peter, provost.—Sign of Nicholas, dean.—Sign of Ansellus, cantor.—Sign of Frumaldus, master.—Sign of Robert and Guy, canons.—Sign of Baldwin, abbot of Maroilles.

I, Alvisus, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, have read over this grant of freedom, subscribed it, and confirmed it with my own hand in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

+ Done at Arras, in the year of the Lord 1146, the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Alvisus, bishop of Arras.

From the original parchment, from which a substantial portion of the seal still hangs by yellowish silk cords.

[Col. 1824C] I, keeper of the archives of Lille, copied, collated, and revised this.

Lille in Flanders, 25 October 1848. Below was written: LEGLAY.

## VI. At Loos near Lille, the monks of Clairvaux mark out a site for founding a monastery, whose foundations, with BERNARD PRESENT AS PROMOTER, as the monastery’s chronicle states, were laid

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Thierry, count of Flanders, make known that the monks of Clairvaux purchased, for the use of the church of Saint Mary at Loos, the land of Bernard of Anakim, which he himself held in fief from Pirron of Bargas; and Peter held that same land from me. And that this may remain unshaken to the aforesaid church forever, we have caused it to be confirmed by the impression of my seal and by this writing, for the remission of my sins [Col. 1824D] and with sufficient testimony. Sign of Roger of Wavrin.—Sign of Peter of Maisnil.—Sign of Hugh of Loos and Clerbald, his brother.—Sign of Lambert, son of Rikir.—Sign of John the Fair.

Done at Lille in the year 1147, on the vigil of Pentecost, while I was setting out for holy Jerusalem for the second time.

From the original parchment, from which the seal, now torn away, once hung, preserved in the same archives at Lille.

## VII. From the chronicle of Saint-Bertin, brought down to the year 1148 by Abbot Simon

(Year 1146). . . And indeed Saint Bernard, after founding and restoring many monasteries through Flanders [Col. 1825A] and Brabant, came into Germany to preach the cross of the Lord. . . Among them were . . . Alvisus, bishop of Arras, our monk, and Leo, our abbot of Saint-Bertin. . .

## VIII.—1146, Bruges. Saint Bernard is present as witness to the grant of Ralph, castellan of Bruges, for the church of Saint Bartholomew at Eechout

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Ralph, castellan of Bruges, for the redemption of my soul have granted forty shillings from my tithe of Lophout to the church of Saint Bartholomew at Eechout in Bruges, with Thierry, count of Flanders, giving consent and confirming it by the impression of his seal.

The witnesses present were BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux; Lemnothus, abbot [Note: This abbot is everywhere else called Leontius or Leontinus. I therefore suspect an error of the notary at this point—unless perhaps *Lemnothus* is a Flemish name, distorted into *Leontius*, in the learned fashion, for the sake of a little Latinity.] of Saint-Bertin; Anselm the Steward; Eustace the Chamberlain; Baldwin of Stupha; and Vodinus, his brother.

Done at Bruges in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the reign of Louis, king of France, while Thierry held Flanders.

[Col. 1826A] From the parchment cartulary and rent-roll of Eechout Abbey, of the Order of Saint Augustine, fol. XXXVI verso, preserved in the major seminary at Bruges.

## IX. Thierry, count of the Flemings, confirms the customs of the chapter of Saint Martin at Ypres before Saint Bernard

[Note: Red Register of Saint Martin, fol. CII, Ypres Library.]

Since the memory of deeds fades through the passing of generations and the succession of events, nothing preserves it more faithfully than the written characters of letters; we have judged it fitting to leave a record for future as well as present persons. Therefore I, Thierry, count of Flanders by divine permission, being about to depart for Jerusalem with the glorious king of the Franks, Louis, granted to Helmar, venerable provost of the church of Ypres, for the remedy of my soul and that of my wife Sibylla, whatever rights or customs his predecessors held from my predecessors, both in the office of alderman and in all other matters, exempt from every exaction. Sign of Lord Milo, bishop.—Sign of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.—Sign of Walter Gonella.—Sign of Gilbert of Bergues.—Sign of Walter, castellan of Saint-Omer.

## X–XI

[Col. 1825]

[Col. 1825A]

+ IN THE NAME . . . OF THE HOLY . . . AND . . . UNDIVIDED . . . TRINITY . . .

I, Bernard, called by the grace of God abbot of Clairvaux, to all sons of the holy Church, everlasting salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ. We wish it to be known to future as well as present persons that the dispute between the abbot of Jet and the abbot of Ninove concerning the church of Liedekerke was settled in the following manner in our presence before religious persons. The abbot of Jet consented to receive as his share the altar and church of Leu with all their appurtenances, namely lands, tithes, rent, buildings, male and female serfs, and any other possessions there may be; and all that the Tenera divides between the parish of Leu and that of Liedekerke, except one tithe in the parish of Erenbaldengem belonging to the church of Leu, which the abbot of Jet shall possess with the other possessions of the same church; while the abbot of Ninove is to retain all the rest belonging to the church of Liedekerke. And that this composition, made at our counsel and urging, may remain valid forever, we ordered this charter to be made and marked it with the impression of our seal, with the following suitable witnesses who were present; the brethren also consenting, and mutually relinquishing by the straw [*exfestucantibus*], of both churches, namely those of Jet and Ninove. Sign of Lord Peter, abbot of the church of Afflighem. Sign of Robert, abbot of the Dunes. Sign of Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon. Sign of Goswin, abbot of Tronciennes. Sign of Everard, monk. Gerard, monk. Gualfrid, monk.

Copied from the Ninove original, now at Ghent, 28 October 1848. The seal still hangs intact.

[Col. 1826A]

+ IN THE NAME . . . OF THE HOLY . . . AND . . . UNDIVIDED . . . TRINITY . . .

Therefore I, Bernard, called by the grace of God abbot of Clairvaux, send everlasting greeting in the Lord Jesus Christ to all sons of the holy Church. We wish it to be known to future as well as present persons that the dispute between the abbot of Jet and the abbot of Ninove concerning the church of Liedekerke was settled in the following manner in our presence before religious persons. The abbot of Jet consented to receive as his share the altar and church of Lewe, with all their appurtenances: namely, lands, tithes, rent, buildings, male and female serfs, and any other possessions there may be; and all that the Tenera divides between the parish of Lewe and that of Liedekerke, except one tithe in the parish of Erenbaldengem belonging to the church of Leuues, which the abbot of Jet shall possess with the remaining property of that same church, while the abbot of Ninove is to retain all the rest belonging to the church of Liedekerke. And that this composition, made by our counsel and urging, may remain valid forever, we ordered this charter to be made and marked it with the impression of our seal, with the following suitable witnesses who were present; the brethren of both churches, namely Jet and Ninove, also consenting and mutually relinquishing by the straw [*exfestucantibus*]. Sign of Lord Peter, abbot of the church of Afflighem. Sign of Robert, abbot of the Dunes. Sign of Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon. Sign of Goswin, abbot of Tronciennes. Sign of Everard, monk. Gerard, monk. Gualfrid, monk.

Copied from the Jet, or Diligem, original, 30 October 1772; there the whole seal had been scraped away, only the complete form of the parchment remaining, around which the wax had been poured. Thus Beda, *Hafflighem Illustrated*, vol. I, p. 389.

## XII

[Col. 1827A]

When, therefore, in the year 1146 Saint Bernard visited the monastery of Afflighem, viewed everything there with wonder, and attended the divine and monastic offices with the servants—or angels—of God, he came upon, in the cloister, beside the dormitory door and near the church gate, a statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom every monk entering the dormitory in the morning was accustomed to greet three times with the angelic salutation . . . When Saint Bernard had greeted the venerable statue of the Virgin Mother of God, saying, “Hail, Mary,” the image itself replied, “Hail, Bernard”; under Godescalc, abbot of this place [Note: Rather, under Abbot Peter: for the charter just quoted makes clear that Phalesius, and many after him, were mistaken.]. Afterwards the holy man delivered two sermons to our monks, in which he desired that the Afflighem monks should live in the habit of the black monks according to the rule of his own institute, while retaining the ancient black scapular of Saint Benedict; but he could not induce Godescalc or the monks to do so. As a pledge of his affection for these religious, he left there his pastoral staff. Departing thence for Gembloux, [Col. 1827B] he bequeathed chasubles to the monks of that place, giving wherever he went a notable testimony concerning both monasteries.—From the manuscript chronicle of Afflighem by Phalesius.

## XIII

In Belgium, the commemoration of the Blessed Virgin MARY, when, through the mouth of the image at Afflighem, in the presence of the community of monks and a large crowd, she greeted the holy Father Bernard in a clear voice, saying, “Hail, Bernard!” This image is kept in great honour as testimony of so great a miracle.

From the Villers martyrology, 18 October.

[From a paper manuscript now preserved in the new Bollandist museum, written in a recent hand and by a recent author indeed, but copied from ancient traditions. See the Cistercian Menology, p. 354 for this day.]

## XIV

[Col. 1827C]

When Saint Bernard once entered Brabant in order to preach, so as to gain some fruit there, as also among other peoples, he visited the monastery of Afflighem and preached there. In memory of this, the Afflighem monks are said to preserve the staff on which he was accustomed to support his weakened limbs. But when he had wished to unite them to the Cistercian Order and had not succeeded, he entered the monastery of Gembloux; and, being received there charitably, left in it his chasuble, which is still there.

From the chronicle of Villers. MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 1269.

## XV.—1146

Bernard says: “MARY, mine, hail!” O blessed Virgin;  
and you willingly answer from the image: “And hail to you, Bernard!”

Under Godescalc, abbot of the place, the event is thus reported:

Then this good spikenard, Bernard, delivered two sermons,  
by which he wished the habits of our monks to become snowy-white.

[Col. 1827D] Neither Godescalc nor any of the monks wished it. He went to Gembloux, leaving part of his staff here as witness; Bernard’s chasuble was left at Gembloux.

Would Afflighem—or would any monk of Gembloux—ever permit  
the black monks’ habit to be compelled [to change]?

You said, Father Bernard, wherever you came:

> “The monk of Afflighem is an angel; the other cenobite is earthly.”

Hence Brabant’s sure and great praise.

Amerius, in the prefatory matter to the Chronicle.

## XVI.—1153. Concerning the Blessed Virgin of Wavre

. . . The abbot of Afflighem and his brethren also came on foot as far as the town itself, Brussels, where, dressed in white and clothed in copes, they arranged a procession of monks with order and dignity [Col. 1828A] in a multitude. And so, singing and praising God and His Mother, with great glory and the applause of all the people—who are said to have gathered that day in the church of Saint Nicholas to almost thirty thousand—they proceeded. The faithful testified that they had never seen a procession so dignified and so well ordered at any assembly ever held, whether of an emperor or by command of the Roman Pontiff. Moreover, the glorious Lady bestowed a benefit which ought not to be passed over in silence but commended above all others: throughout that time many wars already stirred up at the instigation of the Evil One, and disturbances, were quieted and came to rest among her faithful. For when many had assembled from diverse regions, who were reported to be enemies of one another, they were immediately reconciled in peace, without any exaction of money or any satisfaction such as secular persons are accustomed to make in affairs of this sort, being moved solely by the fear of God and love for the most merciful Mother, through the intervention of the faithful.

[Col. 1828B] From the Afflighem continuation of Sigebert, among the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. VI, *Scriptores*, p. 401.

## XVII.—1160. Flowers gathered for the Blessed Virgin Mary from the *Commendatory Poem* of Nicholas Mys, a convert of Afflighem

As the rose is flower of flowers, so that house is house of houses,  
whose fragrance of good character scatters everywhere the thyme of virtues.

Here dwell monks whose holy devotion delights  
the choir of the poles with praise; God is their helper.

Each of them here, soberly fleeing the companionship of Leah,  
desires that MARY may be his own companion . . .

O outstanding people, filled with highest Wisdom,  
whom kindly MARY protects through the seas of the world;  
star of the sea to the world, you are rightly called Afflighem,  
alone without an equal, rejoicing in proportion as you suffer!

## XVIII.—THIRTEENTH AND FOURTEENTH CENTURIES

The monks of Afflighem retained a long-standing custom down to the arrival of the Edmundian reformers: they never entered the church from the dormitory in the morning unless they had greeted that image of the Blessed Virgin MARY three times with the angelic salutation. Whoever was negligent in this underwent a sufficiently sharp rebuke from the Prior in chapter.

Amerius, in the manuscript Chronicle.

## XIX.—FIFTEENTH CENTURY

About 1460 Goswin, the twenty-third abbot, . . . in order to advance the work begun by his two predecessors in constructing the new cloister walks, . . . added a third section himself, which formed the ambulatory of the Blessed Virgin; there he also built stone seats for the foot-washing of the poor.

Beda, manuscript *Hafflighem Illustrated*.

## XX.—Years 1523–1559

John, surnamed Solebrecq, . . . surpassed the rest in piety and observance, but especially in devotion to the Blessed Virgin MARY; throughout his life he was truly [Col. 1828D] Marian. In order to imitate the custom of the ancients, who used to honour and invoke the statue of the same Virgin, displayed in the cloister, with three salutations before entering choir for Matins, he would come before the time of the office and fulfil his desire. This custom had become more difficult in his time because the Egmondians had shortened the way to the church, so that it was no longer necessary to pass through the ambulatory containing the statue.

Beda, ibid., vol. VI, p. 1010.

## XXI.—Year 1578

When the monastery was broken into, Brother Henry De Corte, the custodian, first ran to the church, hid certain more precious objects, and, fleeing, took Saint Bernard’s staff with him and preserved it.

Ibid., p. 1132.

## XXII.—1580

[Col. 1829A]

While our community had been residing at Aalst since the preceding March, when we were expelled from Dendermonde, and while the abbot was everywhere engaged in more important affairs, a new desolation occurred in winter which crushed the spirits of us all. For the venerable statue of the most glorious Virgin Mother of God MARY, which had miraculously returned the greeting of Lord Bernard as he saluted her, was impiously thrown down from its place and broken. This crime was committed by a certain servant left here, infected, as is likely, with the pestilence of heresy. This was related to us by the Reverend Lord Godfrey Pontanus, senior of our congregation and formerly prior at Wavre.

Phalesius, in Beda under this year.

## XXIII.—1605

The newly gathered flock had scarcely tasted the mother’s pastures when the most zealous Prior Cobbartius set his hand to the work and began to labour for the restoration of the whole House. [Col. 1829B] Before all else, zeal for the House of God consumed him, and he was zealous for the honour of the Blessed Virgin MARY. . . The said pieces still lay at the site; Father Judocus Cobbart sent them to Mechelen . . . From them two principal statues of equal form and the same size were sculpted. The religious of the Society of Jesus obtained one through the Reverend Lord Wiringus and displayed it in their college at Brussels. The other, which remained with us, holding the child Jesus on her left arm and displaying a cluster of grapes in her right hand, was placed in the very location where the image had first spoken. It remained there for some years, until—

## XXIV.—1621

The Reverend Lord Benedict Haeften, the first provost after the restoration of the monastery (for his predecessors had been transferred from elsewhere), for weighty reasons moved it into the north wing of the church—which at that time [Col. 1829C] served us as choir—so that access for devout veneration might now be given both to outsiders and especially to the devout female sex, who were excluded from the cloister ambulatory. Consequently, the devotion of the household and especially of the neighbouring people toward the Blessed Virgin is known to have increased considerably. In order therefore to foster and daily advance it still further, the aforesaid provost ordered an artistically wrought and gilded shrine to be constructed. On a tablet hanging before its front he ordered the miracle inscribed in silver letters, enclosed in a short poem composed by himself, as follows:

> This statue of the Virgin Mother MARY  
> returned Bernard’s greeting in a voice.  
> You too, desirous of eternal salvation,  
> greet her often.

At the first location, where the base of that statue itself may still be seen, projecting from the wall of the older church, another image of the Blessed Virgin was set up, with this inscription, dating back one hundred years:

[Col. 1829D]

> Revere this statue of the pious Virgin MARY;  
> and, as you pass by, take care that the *Ave* is not left unspoken.

Phalesius, passim in Beda.

## XXV.—1627

An agreement was entered into among the prelates of three monasteries reformed throughout Belgium, for forming a certain capitular union under the title of the Congregation of the Blessed Virgin MARY Presented in the Temple.

Beda, *Hafflighem Illustrated*, under this year.

## XXVI.—1647. Indulgences granted by James de Boonen, archbishop of Mechelen

We, James, by the grace of God and of the Holy See of Rome, archbishop of Mechelen, greeting to all who shall see these presents.

In order to kindle in the hearts of the faithful devotion toward the most holy Mother and Virgin MARY; [Col. 1830A] and, as far as lies in us, to increase the homage and veneration shown every day to her miraculous image, by which she deigned to reply to the greeting made to her by her servant and special friend Saint Bernard in the abbey of Afflighem, where it is preserved to this day with great reverence: we grant the following indulgences, on the days mentioned below, to all faithful persons who five times devoutly greet the aforesaid image of the most holy Virgin MARY with the Angelic Salutation, so that, through her help, the holy Church our Mother may be exalted and heresies extirpated; that through her mediation Catholic princes may be united; and that through her intercession we may obtain universal peace.

1. On every feast of the most holy Virgin celebrated in the Church, and during its octaves, forty days of indulgence, upon recitation of the aforesaid prayers;

2. On every Saturday of the year, thirty days;

3. On every day of the week, twenty days.

[Col. 1830B]

In witness whereof, these presents have been signed by our hand and furnished with our seal. At Brussels, 20 May 1647. In his own hand: JACOB, archbishop of Mechelen. (Faithful translation of the Flemish original. A. R., monk of Afflighem.)

## XXVII.—1657. Triumphal Song to the Blessed Virgin MARY, while Lord Odo Cambier rejoices

O glory of heaven, radiant Virgin,  
encircled with the flames of the golden sun,  
more beautiful than the stars, as amid lesser fires  
is the moon!

A thousand times hail—and as many times hail!—  
as many gifts as flow for you from generous heaven,  
as many as the deep sea  
rolls grains of sand.

No region lives unaware of your virtues:  
sea of graces, summit of miracles,  
MARY, you are called a miracle  
among peoples.

Whether you choose now the shrine of Loreto,  
which a choir of angels transferred from Palestinian shores  
lest, Saracen, you should profane  
the holy place;

or the sacred ridges of Serrat mountain;  
or whether Lyess of the French pleases you;  
or Apricollis of the Belgians draws you;  
or you dwell at Halle:

a people kneels before your many smoking altars,  
O divine Lady; it pays you vows and honours,  
and the crowd receives and seeks  
certain salvation.

As in returning spring a throng of birds surrounds the dawn  
and, sipping the dew-drenched honeycombs, often greets  
its rosy mother;

[Col. 1830D] as was the applause, when the circle of the stars was born,  
for their Creator when they first shone,  
and all the host of angels  
gave praise to God:

so you are celebrated not only in those places,  
but in every region of the world over which your Son rules;  
nations have established for their Mother  
temples and altars.

Who could recount, Virgin, in Brabant alone  
the sanctuaries consecrated to you?  
Who could sing of the candles, inscriptions, trophies,  
standards, and crowns?

Nor is your Afflighem unknown to the Belgians:  
here for many years the celebrated Virgin established  
an altar dedicated to your worship.

[Col. 1831A]

Here the venerable abbot from Clairvaux, greeting you  
with the angel’s words, received from your own mouth, MARY,  
a welcome answer to his greeting.

Here the crowd prostrates itself before you in vows and on bended knee;  
the monks surround their blessed Mother  
and offer varied praises in song.

Come, mother of beautiful love!  
O Mother of hope! O glory of Zion!  
O present house of God! O ark  
of the hidden covenant!

Render the blessed little one, who hangs upon your arms, favourable to the peoples;  
you bear Him in your hand—  
caress with your hands, O divine Lady,  
Him who thunders.

Here, whenever they say, “Hail, MARY,”  
hear the suppliants; instruct their minds  
toward a better desire, and grant  
the gifts of everlasting salvation.

## XXVIII.—1745. Gracious brief of Pope Benedict XIV

BENEDICT XIV, POPE, FOR PERPETUAL REMEMBRANCE.

In fatherly charity attentive to the salvation of all, we sometimes adorn sacred places with the spiritual gifts of indulgences, so that from them the souls of the faithful departed may obtain the aid of the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ and of His saints, and, aided by these, may through God’s mercy be brought from the pains of purgatory to eternal salvation. Desiring, therefore, to distinguish with this special gift the church of the Abbey of Afflighem, under the invocation of the most holy Apostles Peter and Paul, in the city or diocese of Mechelen or another city or diocese, of the Order of Saint Benedict—in which no other privileged altar, permanent or temporary, is found to have been granted, and if one be found, by these presents we revoke it—and the altar of the Blessed Virgin MARY situated therein, who, as tradition relates, spoke to Saint Bernard: relying upon the authority entrusted to us by the Lord, and upon the mercy of almighty God and the authority of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; and granting the humble petitions made to us in this matter by our son Philip Thomas, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of Alsace, prelate of the metropolitan church of Mechelen by apostolic grant and dispensation, we grant and indulge that whenever any secular priest or priest of any religious order shall celebrate at that altar the most holy sacrifice of the Mass for the soul of any one of the faithful who has departed this life united to God in charity, that soul may obtain from the treasury of the Church an indulgence by way of suffrage, so that, with the merits of that same our Lord Jesus Christ, of the Blessed Virgin MARY, and of all the saints aiding it, it may be freed from the pains of purgatory. All things to the contrary notwithstanding; these presents to remain valid in perpetuity for future times.

[Col. 1831D] Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Ring of the Fisherman, 11 July 1745, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

Below appeared: For Lord Passionei, John Hovius, substitute.—And at the side: “Let it be published.”

Given at Mechelen, 22 September 1745. It was subscribed: Thomas, cardinal archbishop of Mechelen. At the foot: By command of His Eminence, M. Holvoet, Secretary.

From the authentic original at Afflighem.

## XXIX.—1802. The Reverend Lord Beda Regaus, the last provost, renews and confirms the Marian monuments by a final attestation
With regard to the images of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Afflighem [Col. 1832A] (thus), it should be known that we hold by tradition that, when St Bernard was among us in the year 1147, before Lent [Note: [Col. 1831D] It is all the more astonishing that the most learned provost should have been wrong in both elements of the date, because, in his examination and explanation of the records thus far cited from him [Col. 1832D], no one has come closer to the truth; indeed, as we have sufficiently shown above, the true chronological reckoning is established from him.], under our abbot—not Godescalc, as certain histories state, but Abbot Peter—and had settled the dispute between the people of Ninove and those of Dileghem, to whose charter the said Peter subscribed, he, together with our convent, saying “Hail, Mary,” heard the statue reply in greeting: “Hail, Bernard.” This image stood in the cloister upon its base; and in the winter of 1580 it was thrown down from its base by iconoclasts and broken into two parts, apart from two heads which could never be found.

In 1606 the said parts were sent to Mechelen, and two new images were made from them. Our brethren were earnestly charged that not only the notable fragments which might fall away during carving, but even the smallest grains of sand from the said parts, should be preserved.

It therefore happens that, when our religious cast small images, they mix and pour into each one [Col. 1832B] some of the said powder. Certain miracles are attested in connection with these images. Such are those still carried about and distributed to devout believers even today.

I attest this: BEDA, provost of Afflighem, 1802.

Copied from the witness’s own hand.

XXX. Supplement in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of Blessed Bernard, her devout chaplain, who was taken from this world within the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The following hymn was composed:

Now the queen has reclined at table,  
Seated beside her only-begotten Son.

Nard has yielded its fragrance,  
As Bernard draws forth his spirit.

Sweet to the queen’s taste  
Is the sweetness of her fruit;  
Sweet to her smell  
[Col. 1832C] Is the holiness of Bernard’s nard.

While she was reclining at table,  
The fruit brought forth its savour.  
While he was reclining in death,  
The nard offered its fragrance.

That sweet reclining at table  
Is because of the savour of glory;  
This sweet reclining in death  
Is because of the fragrance of grace.

The bride comes from Lebanon,  
To be divinely crowned;  
That Bernard might come  
From the furnace of the Holy Spirit.

Who is this who advances,  
Ruddy as the dawn?  
Who is this leaping over  
[Col. 1832D] The hills, rejoicing with the saints?

This glory is terrible,  
Like an army drawn up in battle.  
This glory is marvellous,  
Like the countenance of Ahasuerus.

Pray to the Lord for us,  
O most sweet little branch of smoke;  
Incline the Father of lights,  
O shepherd, burning like a torch.

(From MS 112 of the Public Library of Liège.) D.

[Col. 1833]

STUDIES ON THE HISTORY OF THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY. RESEARCHES INTO THE PART TAKEN BY THE ORDER OF CÎTEAUX AND THE COUNT OF FLANDERS IN THE CONFLICT BETWEEN BONIFACE VIII AND PHILIP THE FAIR; BY M. KERVYN DE LETTENHOVE. (Presented to the Royal Academy of Brussels on 4 April 1853.—Extract from vol. XXVII of the *Mémoires*.)

“Since love for my native place  
Moved me, I gathered up the scattered leaves.”  
(DANTE)

[Col. 1833A] If the reign of Philip the Fair occupies a distinctive place in the history of medieval France, it is because that reign saw the attempt at once most cunning and most audacious to free itself from every law and every rule, whether founded upon sacred bonds or deriving its origin from the traditional law of the nation. In other times, royalty had nobly gathered around itself all the elements of political life, raising and strengthening itself even as it presided over their regular and peaceful development. By a wholly different course of conduct, at the end of the thirteenth century, it seems able to be great and strong only by isolating itself and surrounding itself with ruins. Thus we shall see it [Col. 1833B] struggle against the papacy in order to acknowledge nothing above itself, even an admonition given in God’s name; then fight the great vassals, so as no longer to find equals at its side, even if it must remain alone to defend France. And if it protects the Third Estate, it is because it does not fear to seek in it the instrument of its passions and hatreds. [Note: [Col. 1833B] Without seeking in the history of England overly familiar examples of the alliance of barons and commons, one may affirm that the alliance formed against the usurpations of Philip the Fair rested upon an entirely national idea, linked to the pious memories of St Louis’s reign, which had protected “vassalage and good customs” (*Dit dou pape et dou roy*). Thus it is found, full of force and life, in the metrical chronicle of Godfrey of Paris, as well [Col. 1834B] as in the Memoirs of Lord Joinville, who, recounting under Philip the Fair the virtues of his grandfather, said: “Great dishonour will come to those of his lineage who refuse to follow him.”]

Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, was the most eminent and illustrious representative of the [Col. 1834A] resistance of the great vassals. That of religious authority was asserted in France by the Order of Cîteaux; but the various phases through which it passed have remained shrouded in deep darkness. Before citing, as the chief object of these studies, the numerous unpublished documents which will serve to establish the details of this twofold struggle, we must pause briefly to recall the relations which had long united the house of the counts of Flanders, and Flanders itself, with the Order of Cîteaux.

In every recollection, these relations stood under the patronage of the great name of St Bernard. It was St Bernard who had come into Flanders to choose Robert of Bruges as the only man [Col. 1834B] worthy to replace him when his fruitful career should have ended. [Note: Henriquez, *Fascic. SS. ord. Cisterc.*, p. 155.] It was St Bernard who had declared that, among all the great vassals, the count of Flanders was the support of the kingdom of France. [Note: *Opera S. Bernardi*, I, p. 205.] The Flemings had answered his call: some by withdrawing into the cloister he had founded, [Note: Gaufredus the monk, *Vita S. Bernardi*, in Bollandists, *Acta SS.*, Aug., IV, p. 309.] others by dying in the crusade he had preached. [Note: *Gesta Ludovici*, in Duchesne, p. 404.] The princes themselves entered, in the footsteps of the abbot of Clairvaux, upon one or the other of these paths. While [Col. 1835A] Thierry of Alsace took the cross, one of his nephews, named Alberon, became a religious in the Order of Cîteaux. [Note: *Chronicle of the monastery of the Dunes*, p. 7.] The count Philip, who died at the siege of Ptolemais, and his wife, the proud Matilda of Portugal, who survived him only to see the misfortunes of Flanders, were buried at Clairvaux Abbey. [Note: Henriquez, *Fascic. SS. ord. Cist.*, p. 417; *Statutes of the Order of Cîteaux*, year 1192; Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, col. 1273.] In more glorious times, Baldwin offered the Order of Cîteaux the imperial banner captured beneath the walls of Constantinople. His daughter, Countess Joan, founded a monastery of the same order in order to obtain from heaven an end to her widowhood, [Note: Manrique, *Annals of the Order of Cîteaux*, under the year 1225; *Statutes of the Order of Cîteaux*, year 1225.] and it was in the humble habit of the virgins of Cîteaux that she breathed her last. [Note: Henriquez, *Menology of the Cistercian Order*, p. 407.] Her alms had been so abundant that, during her lifetime, harvesting began at [Col. 1835B] Clairvaux Abbey with solemn prayers for her. [Note: Declaration of William, abbot of Clairvaux (February 1238, old style, Lille Archives).] Her example was imitated by her sister Margaret and by Guy of Dampierre, who, about to depart for Tunis, thought he could not better call down heaven’s protection upon himself. [Note: Charter of May 1270 (Lille Archives). A sister of Guy of Dampierre was an abbess in the Order of Cîteaux.]

The great Cistercian abbeys repaid Flanders for the benefits they received from the generosity of its princes. The wool of their flocks enriched the Flemish weaver, [Note: Matthew Paris, 1254.] while they also gave a swift impetus to agricultural labour. [Note: The history of the development of agriculture in a remote age, if it is ever written, must be drawn from monastic archives. For Flanders, nothing is more important in this respect than the cartularies of Dunes Abbey.] It was in barren dunes and unhealthy marshes, as the very name of most monasteries indicated, that they had made the soil fertile and created furrows [Col. 1835C] covered with harvests. Learning itself, under the protection of the Order of Cîteaux, went to draw upon the fruitful sources of the University of Paris [Note: “Paris, from the saving fountain of wisdom.” *Book containing various letters*, etc., MS of the Dunes, document no. 636.], in that College of St Bernard founded by Stephen, [Col. 1836A] abbot of Clairvaux, with the support of Margaret of Constantinople, [Note: Letters of the abbot of Clairvaux, 1277 (Lille Archives).—The Order of Cîteaux had other colleges (*studia*) at Toulouse, Montpellier, Cologne, and Oxford.] where Flanders counted celebrated doctors surrounded by disciples as zealous as they were numerous. Above all, the monks of Cîteaux were brothers of the people through their charity and devotion. [Note:  

O good Jesus Christ,  
How good this order is!  
(GILLES LI MUISIS, p. 313.)]

Pilgrims, orphans, and the poor crowded at the gates of their monasteries; [Note: [Col. 1835D] See, in the MS of the Dunes, numerous documents concerning the *porta seu eleemosyna* (“the gate, or almsgiving”), “the poor who continually flock to the gate,” etc. It was a religious [Col. 1836C] of the Order of Cîteaux who served as almoner in the household of the counts of Flanders. At the entrance to Dunes Abbey one read, in letters of gold: “COME ALL TO THE ALMSGIVING, FOR THE HONOUR OF GOD.”] and when the sentence of interdict descended from Arras or Tournai upon the desolate towns and countryside, it was also at the foot of their altars that the people, faithful guardians of political liberty, came to seek the consolations of religious liberty and to prepare themselves for combat through prayer. [Note: [Col. 1836C] Before me lies an opinion by a theologian of Tournai concerning the privilege of Cistercian abbeys in Flanders not to be included in sentences of interdict. After saying: “The brethren ought not to ring so loudly, nor sing so that the people may seem to be summoned to hear the divine office; rather, they should sing in a subdued voice and ring some bell plainly, so that they may appear to do this more for gathering the brethren than for any other purpose,” it adds: “If someone celebrates the divine office in the presence of an excommunicated person, he does not thereby become irregular; much less, therefore, do those become irregular who say the divine offices in the presence of persons under interdict, nor ought they to suffer any penalty.” The papal privilege nevertheless provided: “with those under interdict excluded”; but even this rule was not without exception: “preaching the word of God is excepted and permitted during a general interdict.” MS of the Dunes, no. 222.]

In October 1285, the date of [Col. 1836B] Philip the Fair’s accession, we are still far from the time when the king of France would violently confiscate the county of Flanders and lead to the stake at the Porte Saint-Antoine the Templars, affiliated with the Order of Cîteaux. Yet already we see appearing upon the throne that insatiable avarice which, according to the Florentine poet’s verse, extinguishes in the human heart love of every good thing. [Note:  

“As avarice extinguished in each man  
Our love, through which our deeds are lost.”  
(DANTE, *Purgatorio*, XIX.)]

Among the numerous privileges of the monasteries of the Order of Cîteaux were several securing them immunity from extraordinary charges. At St Stephen’s request, Pope Innocent II had exempted them, St Stephen being the third abbot of Cîteaux, from payment of ecclesiastical tithes; [Note: Lenain, *History of the Order of Cîteaux*, I, p. 254. A manuscript in the Library of the University of Ghent contains a bull of Gregory X confirming and extending the privilege; but its authenticity is doubtful.] and they had [Col. 1836C] likewise obtained the same exemption from the Saladin tithe. “Their prayers suffice us,” said Philip Augustus as he prepared to embark upon the Third Crusade, “since they are of greater use to us through their [Col. 1837A] prayers than others through their gold or arms.” [Note: “Being content with their prayers, through which they were of greater avail than others through gold and arms.” *Cistercium Bis Tertium*, p. 663. The Chronicle of Reims cites a memorable instance of Philip Augustus’s confidence in the prayers of the Order of Cîteaux. Assailed by a storm on his return from Ptolemais, he asked the sailors what time it was. They replied that it was midnight: “Then,” said the king, “we are safe; we need have no fear, for my friends of the Order of Cîteaux have risen to pray for us.”] Nevertheless, this was only an exception. On other occasions the Order of Cîteaux generously contributed to payment of the taxes established by the Apostolic See for the deliverance of the Holy Land. Faithful to the memory of St Bernard, it strove to reawaken Europe’s pious enthusiasm, even as it sent religious to encourage the last crusaders in Syria. [Note: “Monasteries of the Cistercian Order have been built in suitable places”: MARINO SANUDO, III, 7, 3; *Statutes of the Order of Cîteaux*, year 1316: “It is granted to the king of Hungary, when he undertakes the journey to the land of Jerusalem, to have two monks with him.” *Statutes of the Order of Cîteaux*, year 1212; Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, col. 1312.]

Scarcely had Philip the Fair ascended the throne when he received from Pope Honorius IV a four-year tithe for the war in Aragon. [Note: Raynaldi, 1285, 28. In 1290 Pope Nicholas IV urged Philip the Fair to devote this [Col. 1838D] tithe to the defence of the Holy Land. It should be noted that one of the cardinals sent to him for this purpose was Cardinal Benedict Gaetani, later pope under the name Boniface VIII. Raynaldi, 1290, 17.] The same tithe had already been granted to Philip the Bold, and it does not seem to have occasioned complaint. Under Philip the Fair this was no longer so; and [Col. 1837B] a feeling of fear and distrust, seemingly inspired by the future, dominates the letter which the abbot of Clairvaux addressed, about January 1285 (old style), to the principal monasteries of the order. He relates that the abbot of Cîteaux and the abbot of Pontigny had gone to the king and had reached an agreement (*composuerunt*) concerning the amount of the tithe. This agreement was made “to avoid future dangers, loss of souls, and shipwrecks of consciences”; but, though very burdensome, it had been obtained only with great labour and no slight difficulty. In announcing it, the abbot of Clairvaux himself feared “lest so great a sum of this imposition should in some degree alarm you.” The share of one monastery alone—that [Col. 1837C] of the Dunes—in this tithe came to eight hundred livres tournois, [Note: MS of Dunes Abbey, document no. 279. Clairvaux paid only half.] a sum eighty times greater than that demanded from the richest monasteries of Flanders for the Tunis crusade.

The final year of this tithe was collected in 1289. From 1289 to 1291, the confiscation of the property of Lombard merchants and other measures devised for the same purpose occupied Philip the Fair. In 1292 he remembered that a bull of Gregory X had granted a tithe to his father seventeen years earlier, and used this as a pretext for addressing claims to the Order of Cîteaux which were as vehement as they were threatening. [Col. 1838A] The abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux went to Paris and, in the College of St Bernard, caused a protest to be read in the presence of two Flemish doctors, John of Werden and Siger of Gulleghem. It concluded with an appeal to the pope: “Placing themselves, their order, their subjects, and their property under the protection of blessed Peter and Paul and of the holy Roman Church.” [Note: MS of the Dunes, no. 359. The General Chapter of 1290 mentions expenses incurred by abbots “in defending the privileges and liberties of the order.” That of 1292 speaks in terms indicating graver fears: “That the uniform charity of the order may appear to our adversaries terrible as an army drawn up in battle, whenever it becomes necessary among the abbots of any province to hold a convocation or make a contribution in defence of the liberties of the order,” etc.] This appeal against Philip the Fair’s usurpations deserves some attention, because it was lodged in the capital of the kingdom; we shall soon find a more memorable example.

In 1294 war broke out between the king of France and the king of England, and an enemy fleet spread terror from La Rochelle to [Col. 1838B] Bayonne. This time Philip the Fair humbly applied to the Order of Cîteaux (*humiliter fecit supplicari*), to obtain from its generosity a two-year tithe intended to preserve its monasteries and property from the horrors of war. The Order of Cîteaux granted it; and there survives a charter of Philip the Fair in the following terms:

Philip, by the grace of God king of the French, makes known to all that, since the abbots of the monasteries of Cîteaux, La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond, acting for themselves and for the other persons of the monasteries and other places of the Cistercian Order in our kingdom, have thought fit liberally to grant us, for two complete years, a tenth of their ecclesiastical revenues, in aid of the defence and prosperous condition of our kingdom, [Note: [Col. 1838D] “For the protection of the kingdom of France against the English and other enemies.” Letter addressed to the archbishop of Reims, MS of the Dunes, no. 364.] under certain modes and conditions, as is contained in their letters drawn up concerning this matter, the tenor of which is as follows:

To their most excellent prince and lord, Philip, by the grace of God most illustrious king of the French, his devoted brethren Robert of Cîteaux, Rufinus of La Ferté, Simon of Pontigny, John of Clairvaux, and Dominic of Morimond, abbots of monasteries of the Cistercian Order in the dioceses of Chalon, Auxerre, and Langres, and of their monasteries, etc., wish increase of peace and concord, and prosperous and happy success.

It has now come to the public knowledge of the world from ancient times that the blessed kingdom of the French has hitherto stood forth above the other kingdoms of the world as a bulwark of orthodox faith and an invincible safeguard of Catholic purity. In this your kingdom peace has always flourished, the Catholic faith has grown, and the Christian religion, with the Lord as its author, [Col. 1839A] has received happy increase and, once discord—which has stretched its branches as far as the boundaries of the sea—has been banished beyond the limits of your kingdom, will receive happy increase in the future. For the extirpation or banishment of this discord, we believe the aid of all those necessary to whom the tranquillity of your said kingdom most especially restores peace, though to a state little tranquil and secure.

Accordingly, we the aforesaid abbots, desiring the peace and tranquillity of your kingdom, assembled for this purpose at Dijon and, after careful deliberation, have determined that we and all monasteries of monks subject to us, but only those situated in your said kingdom, should assist you in banishing the said discord, as manifest necessity requires. We grant to you on this occasion, for two years and in the name of our Cistercian Order, by special favour, a tenth part of all the rents and revenues of all monasteries of monks of our order situated in your kingdom, because of the said necessity—namely, only such rents and revenues as those [Col. 1839B] monasteries receive and have customarily received and possessed in your kingdom, and as it may happen that they receive and possess—yet under the definite form hitherto observed by the Apostolic See.

This tenth part shall be faithfully collected, without deceit or fraud, by each of us or our successors, in the *generatio* of each one existing in your kingdom [term uncertain], at the terms written below, upon our consciences and those of our subjects. Our pledged word shall be kept without any further retraction whatsoever, expressly and altogether: so that each abbot shall be bound to pay one half at the approaching Resurrection of the Lord and the other half at the following feast of All Saints . . . Nor shall you, lord king, compel anyone concerning this, either yourself or through another . . . . .

And if, by the inspiration of the Lord, to whom it is not difficult to join what is separated, peace should be restored to your blessed kingdom, payment of the aforesaid tenth part shall wholly cease. But if during the said period a truce should be made concerning the said discord, the aforesaid payment shall be entirely suspended for the period during which the truce endures. Provided, however, that by reason of this payment you cannot and ought not to say that you have acquired for the future any right over aids, subsidies, or other payments to be made or granted to you by us or ours; for by these present letters we in no way intend to grant this. [Note: [Col. 1839D] MS of the Dunes, no. 363.]

One readily recognizes the drafting of Philip the Fair’s counsellors in the preamble of this document. It is entirely absent from the text addressed to the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux, and the lines replacing it make us understand better that this concession was voluntary and that the Order of Cîteaux [Col. 1839D] dictated its conditions:

To their venerable and most dearly beloved fellow-abbots in Christ, greeting, and patience in adversity together with sincere charity in the Lord. Since it was recently lamentably represented on behalf of the most excellent prince Philip, by God’s grace king of the French, that the blessed kingdom of France suffers grave vexations and incursions of enemies, through which the tranquillity of all of us and our subjects is assailed, and danger [Col. 1840A] and ruin are threatened to us and our monasteries unless those vexations and incursions are met, while the forces of the said kingdom are scarcely sufficient for this; and since on that account he humbly caused us to be entreated that we should take care to provide him with aid and counsel to root out the said vexations and incursions, so that, once those vexations and dangers were banished, we and our subjects might enjoy the covenant of peace, as we have hitherto enjoyed it: we, indeed, considering that these dangers threaten us and all generally within the said kingdom; considering further that, through the expenditure of the said king’s goods, which he must necessarily lay out because of the aforesaid dangers, our persons and property remain safe; and considering that for these reasons, according to the principle of natural equity and legal enactments, we ought to assist from the goods bestowed on us by God in bearing the burden of so great a weight—therefore, specially assembled at Dijon and with the counsel of good men, we have thought fit to ordain that, etc. [Note: [Col. 1839D] MS of the Dunes, no. 367. Compare the letter of the archbishop of Bourges, 31 July 1294; the statutes of the Council of Aurillac; and the letter of Philip the Fair, 10 February 1294 (old style): Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, cols. 213, 215, and 217.]

When the English had been repulsed, when [Col. 1840B] Guy of Dampierre, led as a prisoner to the Louvre, had left there as hostage his daughter, already betrothed to the son of Edward I, Philip the Fair changed his language. It was not enough that he had promulgated as a sumptuary law an ordinance providing that whoever possessed fewer than six thousand livres’ worth of land should be required to deliver a third of his gold and silver plate to the king, who would determine its value. [Note: [Col. 1839D] *Ordonnances*, I, p. 324; charter of 17 July 1295, in the [Col. 1840D] Lille Archives.] It was not enough that he himself had proclaimed an alteration of the currency, charging his successors with indemnifying those who should suffer thereby. [Note: [Col. 1840D] Letters of May 1295, Paris Archives.] Such was the need for money pressing upon him, as he himself said, [Note: [Col. 1840D] “Since we need large quantities of money.” Letter of 13 April 1296, Rupelmonde Archives.] that he ordered the levy of one hundredth, then one fiftieth, [Col. 1840C] of all movable and immovable property, with no distinction whatever between the property of clergy and that of laity. All France was stirred, and the name *maltôte*, given to this universal tax, has remained as an energetic protest by those who bore it. [Note: [Col. 1840D] William of Nangis, 1296.]

While the bishops hesitated—some because they owed everything to the king’s favour, others because they feared his anger or saw themselves reduced to isolated protests—the Order of Cîteaux was the first to defend ecclesiastical immunities. In every province, the abbots answered the orders of royal officials with an explicit refusal. When certain bishops, at the king’s request, threatened to [Col. 1840D] compel them by virtue of their ecclesiastical authority, they answered with a declaration whose text has been preserved in the diocese of Tournai:

Before you, reverend father and lord, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, I set forth and declare that, although the entire Cistercian Order has been granted by the Apostolic See that neither the order itself nor any member of it is bound to bear the burden of any sudden and extraordinary tithe or other exaction, and although it has been forbidden by those same grants that henceforth any such tithe or exaction—by whatever name it may be called—be imposed upon or exacted from the monasteries, persons, and goods of that order under any form or wording, or that the order itself or any of its members be in any way harassed concerning such matters; and although the same See has decreed that all sentences of suspension, interdict, or excommunication pronounced against the said order, its monasteries, persons, or property on this account, by whatever authority, are null and void and wholly lack force, even if any exactions, collections, or aids whatsoever had been imposed by the Apostolic See or its legates, unless by letters of that See or of its legates making full and express mention of this grant; and although, by privileges of the aforesaid See, the persons of that order or the order itself are not subject to you, even by reason of an offence, except only in matters of faith and without a special mandate of the Apostolic See:

Nevertheless, you have in fact admonished or caused to be admonished the persons [Col. 1841B] of the aforesaid Cistercian Order—that is, abbots, abbesses, and all other persons throughout your diocese—to pay the hundredth, although in law you cannot do so, thereby acting improperly against the aforesaid grants. The said Cistercians neither had been nor could have been summoned by your authority to the imposition of that hundredth, or of any other quota; and, as they had not been summoned, so neither had they consented nor could they consent.

Therefore, since I perceive that my aforesaid Cistercian lords have been improperly and most grievously burdened in all and each of the aforesaid matters; and since I also fear, on probable grounds and plausible conjectures, lest proceedings be taken improperly and in fact against my Cistercian lords, their churches and places, those adhering to them, and all who may wish to adhere to them: on account of all and each of the aforesaid injuries, and lest anything improperly and in fact be done against them, as stated, I challenge and appeal in these writings, as I can and ought, against you, reverend father and lord, by the grace of God bishop of Tournai, and against all and each whom this present matter touches or may touch, to the Apostolic See. In the capacity of procurator and in the name of my aforesaid Cistercian lords, their churches or places, and those adhering or wishing to adhere to them, I request that the appeals which ought to be granted and allowed me be granted and allowed with the requisite urgency. I place my said Cistercian lords, their churches, places, and goods, those adhering or wishing to adhere to them, and all their condition and goods, under the protection of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 1841D] MS of the Dunes, no. 723.]

There can be no doubt that the Order of Cîteaux understood the gravity of the situation in openly opposing the wishes of Philip the Fair; nor that, called upon to choose between the duty speaking to its conscience and the danger threatening its persons and goods, it courageously preferred the danger. In its own history it found memorable examples to which it could only remain faithful.

When, in 1128, King Louis VI unjustly persecuted the archbishop of Sens, the abbot of Cîteaux [Col. 1842A] summoned one of those holy assemblies of the order from which, it was said, a column of light rose up to God. [Note: [Col. 1841D] Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercians*, III, p. 512.] All the abbots affixed their seals to a letter drafted by St Bernard and begged Pope Honorius III to make his voice heard for the liberty of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1841D] Henriquez, *Fasciculus of the Saints of the Cistercian Order*, p. 31.]

In 1296 the same course was followed. A General Chapter was summoned. St Bernard might there have repeated: “Another Herod now begrudges Christ, not exalted in the cradle but in the churches.” The order first replied to the admonition addressed by a prelate friendly to the king, whom we believe to have been Peter Barbet, archbishop of Reims. [Note: [Col. 1841D] This prelate cannot have been either the archbishop of Lyons, who was strongly attached to the pope, or the bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, whose entire revenues Philip the Fair had seized in December 1294. Everything permits us to recognize here the archbishop of Reims, Peter [Col. 1842D] Barbet or Barbette—brother or relative of Étienne Barbette, treasurer of Philip the Fair?—whom Baillet rather naïvely compares to Hincmar because of his zeal for the king’s interests.] In this memorandum, which deserves to be reproduced, the Order of Cîteaux, after declaring itself ready to submit [Col. 1842B] to all taxes established on account of its property or for the defence of the fatherland, vigorously rejects the extraordinary taxes which the Apostolic See had not approved:

Rights, they say, are the greatest gifts bestowed upon humankind by divine clemency from above: namely, priesthood and empire. The former presides over divine matters; empire over human concerns. Elsewhere they are called the two great lights, like the sun and moon [Note: [Col. 1842D] “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.” There are two jurisdictions, spiritual and temporal. Speech of Cardinal of Acquasparta. Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 76.]; and just as gold is more precious than lead, the sun nobler than the moon, and divine things nobler or more worthy than earthly things, so priestly dignity surpasses royal dignity, and the lesser ought not judge the greater when the latter is unwilling and resistant.

Therefore the king has no right to compel unwilling and refusing priests to provide aid, since they are not subject to his empire; for ecclesiastical property is mortified [i.e. dead to worldly claims] and exempt from temporal jurisdiction, and the said aid [Col. 1842C] plainly has the character of a tithe, with which the king ought not to concern himself. The laws cited for this are in the *Authentica*, first collation, near the beginning; *Extra*, *De maioritate et obedientia*; *Extra*, *De decimis*, *Tua*; *Digest*, *On the jurisdiction of all judges*; law *Est receptum*.

Moreover, a son is more bound to his father than a subject to his prince, just as the law says that a son is not bound to support his father if the father has property from which he can support himself—although the cause of one who provides support is highly favored. Therefore a subject is still less bound to his prince, unless the prince’s resources have first been exhausted. For this, cite the law in *Digest*, *On the liberty of farmers*, law *Si quis alimentatorum*.

Moreover, ecclesiastical men ought not be bound to an imposition, because we can do only what we can conveniently do. But, if they were bound to bear so great a burden imposed by the lord king, they would not incur the transgression of an oath, because they are bound to many creditors by the vow of religion, whom they could not satisfy. And the law says: “If a lord falls into perjury because he is unable to give what he swore, and if his vassal can free him with his own money and does not do so, he ought to lose his fief”; and just as the vassal is bound to the lord, so the lord is bound to the vassal. Therefore the king ought, if he can, to release his feudatories at least by his own money from the bond of oath by which they are constrained; otherwise he ought to lose the rights of subjection. The laws cited for this are *Digest*, *On counsel and obligations*, *Si nepos*; 22, question 5; *Extra*, *On competent forum*, *Nisi*.

Moreover, if priests and clerics were bound to the said aid, they would be placed in a worse condition than other persons; and there would follow the intolerable abuse that, under the most Christian king, priests would be treated more harshly than under King Pharaoh, under whom, although all others were subjected to servitude, priests alone and their goods were endowed with liberty, *Extra*, *On immunity* . . . Moreover, if such a new exaction were due and could in any way be made, it could by no means be made without consultation with the supreme pontiff. This is proved by the law which says: “If the country is so impoverished that it needs extraordinary assistance, the governor of the province, having carefully heard the common advantage, shall report to the prince, by whose authority the extraordinary assistance ought to be arranged.” Thus, in ecclesiastical matters, a new exaction is not to be established without consulting the supreme pontiff: chapter *Nova vectigalia institui non posse*, first law, *Extra*, *On the immunity of the Church*; *Code*, *Adversus*, etc.

If churches are bound to such aid by compulsory public service (*angaria*), the poor will be left destitute. Moreover, since certain public burdens are degrading and others honorable, [Col. 1843B] the Church is immune from every degrading burden. Of honorable burdens, some are ordinary and others extraordinary. The Church is bound to ordinary burdens by reason of its property or patrimonies. No one excuses himself from these: chapter “No one may be permitted to excuse himself from the burdens or payments,” second law, Book Ten. Other burdens are called personal, *angaria* or *parangaria*, to which ecclesiastical persons are not bound, except to watches upon the walls: chapter *On Bishops and Clerics*, law *Omnis qui* . . . To extraordinary burdens, whatever these may be, whether pertaining to public utility, piety, or will, the Church is not bound unless they have been imposed by authority of the supreme pontiff; for these are the aforesaid burdens, which are always prohibited unless the prince’s consent is added: chapter *On supplementary imposts*, first law, Book Ten; *Extra*, *On the immunity of churches*, law *Adversus*.

Jurists nevertheless except certain burdens of necessity and piety: for the construction of good works and the redemption of captives; and they say that [Col. 1843C] the Church is bound to these. Yet these things appear to have been altered by chapter 16, question 1. Aid imposed upon churches by royal authority is very far removed from all these. For these reasons and others, which your reverend fatherhood may supply, we abbots, in our own name and that of our churches, ask and beseech that you entreat the king’s officials—whose constant great concern has been to preserve the unity of the Apostolic See and of God’s holy churches—to desist utterly and rest from this great burden newly laid upon our churches; and that you do not compel us thereto, but desist entirely. For without the authority and command of the supreme pontiff, to whom our goods wholly belong, we cannot and ought not obey your admonition and request, nor do we consent. Rather, insofar as we can by law, we object, lest we be reproachfully blamed for negligence, perjury, and disobedience. [Note: [Col. 1843D] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 278.]

[Col. 1843D] The chapter of Cîteaux dared to tell the archbishop of Reims that Philip the Fair showed himself harsher than Pharaoh; it repeated this in the memorable protest which it addressed to Rome.

Pope Alexander IV had formerly borne splendid witness to the religious zeal of the abbots of the Cistercian order and to their devotion to the Apostolic See: “Amid the innumerable storms of the world’s turmoil, which the tempest of burning persecution has stirred up against the Church of God and ourselves, a great remedy has been granted us through God’s providence, since the most fervent charity of you all neither feared dangers nor withheld assistance. We clearly remember, and recall with the giving of every kind of thanks, with what inviolable firmness the anchor of your faith preserved Peter’s little ship, tossed in the storm.” [Note: [Col. 1843D] Henriquez, *Fasciculus SS. ord. Cisterc.*, p. 12.]

The opening lines of the manifesto of the Order of Cîteaux, repeating the end of this bull, recalled the services which it had rendered to Alexander IV and the gratitude which the Holy See had expressed.

“To the most holy father and lord Boniface, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: the abbots, abbesses, convents, canons, priests, and all the clergy of the kingdom [Col. 1844B] of France [Note: [Col. 1843D] It should be noted that bishops are wholly omitted. Their absence and their [Col. 1844D] silence explain why the canons, priests, and all the clergy (*canonici, presbyteri ac totus clerus*) presented their complaints under the protection of the Order of Cîteaux.], the kissing of your blessed feet, and wishes that you may happily steer Saint Peter’s little ship amid the waves of the sea.

“Since, according to the Apostle, we shall all stand before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge, who will bring hidden things to light and illuminate the secrets of darkness, there to receive the reward either of eternal life or of everlasting damnation; and since, in his presence, not only human beings but even angels will tremble—although this ought to occur to the mind of every Christian—many princes, lovers of this world, do not keep that judgment in mind, clinging excessively to worldly things. This is plainly apparent, when they impose so many grievances and burdens not only upon the secular persons whom they govern, but also upon churches and ecclesiastical persons—whom it concerns laymen to defend with all their strength, not to govern, since no power or authority to command them in these matters has been granted to laymen—that the priesthood [Col. 1844C] seems to have been made worse off under them than it was under Pharaoh, who had no knowledge of divine law. For he, after reducing all others to servitude, left priests and their possessions in their former liberty and provided them public maintenance. Modern princes, however, impose virtually all their burdens upon churches and oppress clerics with so many compulsory services that Jeremiah’s lament seems applicable to them: ‘The princess among the provinces has become tributary.’

“Whether drawing tithes or any other things to themselves from the goods of churches, clerics, and the poor, assigned to Christ’s uses; or so nullifying their jurisdiction and authority that they appear to have no power remaining over churches or ecclesiastical persons—things which they ought not by right to do, especially where the resources of laymen themselves are inadequate—they ought humbly and devoutly to receive with thanksgiving what is conferred upon them from the goods of the Church for the common good, provided that the counsel of the Roman pontiff first intervenes, whose concern it is [Col. 1844D] to provide for common benefits. This they by no means do; rather, they cause what has been granted them by power to redound to the injury of the clergy and the impoverishment of the poor.

“And since many counsellors of princes, clerics as well as others, relying on their own prudence and fearing to lose human favor, are afraid to speak freely to them what is right; and since they discern a certain likeness rather than truth itself, suppressing what is more useful, although a likeness should express the truth; and, as though drunk with strong drink and eating a sour grape, they expound with insufficiently cautious discernment the statement that all things are given to the prince’s service and that all subjects and [Col. 1845A] clerics must obey him, and that whoever does not obey the prince shall die—seeking an external, alien meaning, and failing to consider that the distance between kings and pontiffs is known to be as great as that between sun and moon; that princely constitutions do not take precedence over ecclesiastical constitutions; and that ecclesiastical laws cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment.
