“For they now afflict not only secular ecclesiastical persons, but also those dedicated to the Lord God and laboring in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, with tithes and other various exactions. They apply to their own uses the goods of the Crucified One, assigned to the poor and those serving the Lord, so that the goods of the Church cannot provide sustenance for those serving the Lord—although laborers in the Lord’s vineyard ought not be deprived of their penny. They also set aside alms which ought to be distributed to the poor, although those who are not partners in this iniquity ought not to cause harm.

“And because the aforesaid counsellors may be called false prophets, since they take [Col. 1845B] and interpret the words of Scripture otherwise than Holy Scripture says; since, by the conjecture of their own minds, they pronounce all future things as though true without the authority of divine words; and since they do not observe this principle, that in matters doubtful or obscure they should know that what must be done is whatever is found neither contrary to evangelical precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers—when such persons, blinded by favor toward princes, take the lead and begin to guide others, both fall into the pit.” [Note: [Col. 1845C] Perhaps there is here some allusion to Pierre Flotte, who was one-eyed: “half-seeing in body and altogether blinded in mind,” says Boniface VIII in the bull *Verba delirantis filiae*.]

“Whence the Psalm: ‘Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see,’ etc.; ‘and bend their back always,’ etc. And because, most holy father, no one today desires to be martyred for justice, but rather seeks triumph with labor set aside—although it is safer to meet the danger in time than to seek a remedy after the flesh has been wounded—therefore we beseech your Holiness, from whom we wish to know what we are and shall be, with all the affection and desire of a pure [Col. 1845C] heart that we can offer, to extend to this pestilential sickness the assistance of your grace and power. Without these, the clerical estate, which now walks unsteadily throughout the whole world, cannot long endure; for no one dares freely to oppose the powers of this world in defense of the Church, although for shepherds to fear speaking what is right is nothing other than silently to offer their backs and to avoid battle for the house of Israel in the Lord’s conflict. The Lord rebukes them through Isaiah: ‘Dumb dogs, unable to bark.’

“May your reverend Holiness live and flourish, granting us and Christ’s poor some wholesome remedy in the matters aforesaid, together with willing prosperity from the Lord, who drives adversity from the afflicted; so that, beneath the wing of your protection, we may breathe again as we desire, and may feel the shade of gratitude and repose; that, living in peace, we may praise the author of peace, saying with one voice: ‘Glory in the highest,’ etc.—him who through his grace extends his hand to the fallen, cherishes the needy, and consoles the afflicted in their sorrow.” [Note: [Col. 1845C] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 448. I read in the statutes of Cîteaux of 1296, published by Dom Martène and Dom Durand: “Concerning aid to be given to our lord and reverend father Cardinal Robert” (Robert, former [Col. 1845D] abbot of Cîteaux), “and concerning expenses to be incurred in defending the liberties of the Order and transacting certain affairs of the Order, and concerning sending persons to the Roman Curia, the General Chapter entrusts to the lord of Cîteaux and the four first abbots full authority on behalf of the Order”; and further: “because, through the disclosure of the Order’s secrets in recent times, many inconveniences are known to have happened to persons of the Order, and because death and life are in the hands of the tongue, the General Chapter renews the former decree concerning the non-disclosure of the Order’s secrets, adding that it excommunicates, by the very fact, and deposes from office, whatever persons of the Order reveal the secrets of that Order to any persons not subject to the Order, of whatever rank they may be.” (*Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, cols. 1491 and 1492.)]

A former religious of the Order of Cîteaux, Cardinal Simon de Beaulieu, bishop of Palestrina, was then performing in France the functions of papal legate. By virtue of the powers with which he was invested, he required the archbishops of Reims, Sens, and Rouen to summon a council at Paris on 22 June 1296.

[Col. 1846B] The archbishops of Reims, Sens, and Rouen, whatever their zeal for the king’s cause, did not dare disobey an order as solemn as though it had issued from the Pope himself; and in the letters summoning the council they reproduced the words, no less sad than bitter, which Simon de Beaulieu had inserted in his own letters. [Note: [Col. 1845D] Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, col. 221.] Yet the influence of the three primates of northern France was exerted upon the bishops, most of whom were their suffragans. The delegates chosen in the assembly over which they presided to carry the clergy’s complaints to Rome were the bishops of Nevers and Béziers, who upheld the king’s interests with equal zeal. A letter written in the diocese of Bourges, whose archbishop was then the celebrated Giles Colonna, author of the treatise *De regimine principis*, [Note: [Col. 1845D] The letter of Simon de Beaulieu mentioned above is addressed to the archbishop [Col. 1846C] of Bourges, which explains why Philip the Fair became hostile to Giles Colonna, who is said to have written for him his book *De regimine principis*. See Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 64.] informs us that on 28 August the two prelates had not left France. [Note: [Col. 1846C] It is doubtless by the presence of Cardinal Simon de Beaulieu at the Council of Paris, or by the fear felt by the archbishops of Reims, Sens, and Rouen of offending the Pope, that one must explain the protests contained in the letter of 28 August: “With the more watchful eye of poignant compassion, observing the pains and burdens, laments, and outcry of scandals which—alas!—the Gallican Church is known miserably to endure in these days, more grievously distressed by an unheard-of variety of burdens and by the bitterness of manifold persecution,” etc. It is important to note that this letter mentions the special act of appeal addressed to Boniface VIII by the Order of Cîteaux: “the Cistercians, moreover, sending special messengers on their own behalf.” Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, col. 223.]

Before the bishops of Nevers and Béziers had arrived in Rome, Boniface VIII, who had occupied the Apostolic See for one year, [Note: [Col. 1846D] On 25 March 1295 (old style), Boniface VIII had written to the emperor asking him to admit the homage of Guy of Dampierre by proxy, since Guy was kept in his own states: “Because of the grave hazards of wars and dangers of enmities, and also for other reasonable causes.” (Archives of Belgium.)] granted the complaints of the Order of Cîteaux, by placing the archbishop of Reims under interdict [Note: [Col. 1847C] *Gallia Christiana*, IX, col. 120.] and publishing, on 18 August 1296, the famous bull *Clericis laicos*, which we find reproduced in the book of privileges of the Order of Cîteaux. [Note: [Col. 1847C] Henriquez, *Privilegia ordinis Cisterciensis*, p. 84; Dupuy, *Preuves de l’histoire du différend de Boniface VIII et de Philippe le Bel*, p. 14.] It is well known that therein Boniface VIII pronounced excommunication upon clerics who paid tithes without the Pope’s prior assent. The bull *Clericis laicos* was confirmed by the bull *Ineffabilis amoris*, in which Boniface VIII reproached the king of France with having lost a precious possession—namely, the love of his subjects [Note: [Col. 1847D] “He who has lost the hearts of his subjects is reckoned to have lost no little.”]—and announced that he was ready to suffer persecution, exile, and even death for the liberty of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1847D] “Not only persecutions and exiles, but even bodily death, for ecclesiastical liberty.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 19.]

Philip the Fair’s reply began [Col. 1847B] with these words: “Before there were clerics, the king of France had the custody of his kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 1847D] Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 21. Compare what is said in the *Supplication of the People of France to the King*: “Thus the sons of Adam divided the earth and were its lords for more than three thousand years before the time of Melchizedek, who was the first priest,” etc. Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 215.] What followed was worthy of the violence of this opening: “They are permitted—indeed, it is granted to them as an example of pernicious imitation—to give to actors, and, while neglecting the poor, to incur superfluous expenses upon robes, riding equipment, retinues, banquets, and other secular pomp. Who would judge it lawful, under anathema, to prohibit clerics, fattened, enriched, and enlarged through the devotion of princes, from aiding those same princes?” The Order of Cîteaux, to which this vehement attack appears to refer, could have recalled that, when cruel famines devastated France, the poor, far from being abandoned, owed their lives to the generous [Col. 1847C] alms of Cistercian abbeys. [Note: [Col. 1847D] “Relieving the destitution of many thousands with their goods, which they held in common with the poor.” Manrique, *Annals of the Cistercian Order*, under the year 1176. There is no doubt that some abbots of the Order of Cîteaux allowed themselves to be seduced by luxury and pride. A saying of Richard the Lionheart remained famous; perhaps it applied to the abbot mentioned in the [Col. 1848C] statutes of the General Chapter of 1215: “The abbot of Beaulieu in England behaved improperly at table before three earls and forty knights, drinking merrily [Col. 1848D] to Gargocil (?) and keeping a dog with a silver chain to guard his bed; and he brings with him secular servants on horseback, who minister to him on bended knee,” etc. But these abuses were severely repressed, and the General Chapter of 1289 renewed the old prohibitions, “because it does not become the poor and humble servants of God to be adorned with superfluous display.”]

Besides, Philip the Fair did not rely solely upon these diatribes. His intrigues had stirred up Italy’s slumbering dissensions; and within a few days Frederick of Aragon expelled the pope’s legates from Sicily, while the Colonna openly avowed the design of expelling the Pope himself from Rome.

If Boniface VIII had formerly longed, in his ambition, for the day when the tiara passed from the brow of Celestine [Col. 1848A] V to his own, [Note: [Col. 1848D] Raynaldi, *Annales ecclesiastici*, passim.] he made severe expiation for faults preceding his pontificate through all the trials which he had to undergo in order to preserve it. Anxiety and fear had seized that soul, lately so proud: weak and uncertain language, dictated by politics, succeeded protests rendered so eloquent by an intrepid faith. It must be said sadly: Boniface VIII was reduced, in order not to see his authority overthrown in Italy, to lowering and humiliating it in France. [Note: [Col. 1848D] See *History of the Papacy during the Fourteenth Century*, by Abbé Christophe, I, p. 97.] In this reconciliation with Philip the Fair, concluded as a necessity, the mediators he accepted were precisely those bishops whom the act of appeal of the Order of Cîteaux called “clerics, counsellors of princes, fearing to lose human favor,” [Col. 1848B] and whom he in turn stigmatized in the bull *Clericis laicos* by calling them “certain prelates who fear offending temporal majesty more than eternal majesty.”

Twenty-three prelates devoted to Philip the Fair—the first being the archbishop of Reims, who had just resumed possession of his see; the others being the archbishops of Sens, Narbonne, and Rouen, and the bishops of Beauvais, Laon, Châlons-sur-Marne, Langres, Amiens, Tournai, Thérouanne, Senlis, Auxerre, Troyes, Chartres, Nevers, Avranches, Évreux, Lisieux, Coutances, Dol, and Le Mans—had written to the Pope to inform him that most of them were bound by homage, and almost all by oath, to defend the king’s honor. [Note: [Col. 1848D] “Some by homage, nearly all by an oath of fidelity.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 26.] They chose delegates from among themselves to explain to him that they saw the king obliged, by concern for his honor and preservation of his kingdom, to incur great expenses, and that they wished to assist him by granting a subsidy. Boniface VIII hastened to consent by the bull *Coram illo fatemur*, in which he complained bitterly of the defection of the count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 1848D] “With that incitement to dissension now threatening there—the count of Flanders, namely, who was hoped to be a barrier against external disturbances and a great support of aid to the kingdom itself, as one of its principal members—our inmost feelings are embittered thereby,” etc.] and offered, for defense of the French king’s rights, the property of [Col. 1849A] the Church and his own person. [Note: [Col. 1849D] “Indeed, we would expose the resources, power, goods, and our own person of the Roman Church for the preservation of his rights” (28 February 1296, old style). Baillet, *History of the Disputes between Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair*, *Pr.*, p. 326; manuscript of the Dunes, no. 913. Raynaldi adds: “In other letters he commended the outstanding zeal of the prelates in helping the king,” 1297, 45.]

Another bull, *Romana mater*, addressed to Philip the Fair, announced that nothing prevented the clergy from freely granting him a subsidy. [Note: [Col. 1849D] “If . . . the constitution itself does not bind you” (7 February 1296, old style). Baillet, *Pr.*, p. 323.] Since the subsidy was permitted, it is readily understood that it was offered and accepted; and Philip, for his part, no longer forbade the sending to Rome of money collected in France for the maintenance of the Apostolic Chamber, money which Boniface VIII greatly needed. [Note: [Col. 1849D] “To obtain our money for the aforesaid purpose.” Raynaldi, 1297, 48; Baillet, p. 56. The letter [Col. 1850D] addressed on this subject by the Pope to Philip the Fair bears the same date as the bull *Romana mater*. Raynaldi, 1297, 46.]

From this moment the reconciliation of the pope and the king of France was complete.

On 15 May 1297, Boniface VIII permitted the bishops whose names we have already cited to levy, for the king’s benefit, at Pentecost and Saint Remy’s Day, a double tithe upon all [Col. 1849B] ecclesiastical revenues, “by authority of the Church, without invoking the power of the secular arm”; and the following is the preamble of this bull, which we believe unpublished:

“Not long ago it came to our knowledge through your letters, which you jointly sent us, that, through the unspeakable wickedness of the ancient enemy—who, seeking to harm, continually goes about seeking to offend—the condition of the most Christian king of the French was tossed by the waves of manifold disturbance and shaken by the violent tempest of internal crime. Therefore the more sharply did the spur of grief pierce us, and the greater disturbance move the hidden recesses of our breast, inasmuch as we bear that kingdom more especially in the bowels of charity, and are led by a stronger desire that it may abound in prosperous successes and be supported by wished-for outcomes.” [Note: [Col. 1850D] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 911.]

[Col. 1849C] The Pope permitted the use of ecclesiastical censures to compel payment of this tithe, and it was in fact exacted in the diocese of Tournai *under penalty of suspension and excommunication*. [Note: [Col. 1850D] Same source.]

Boniface VIII went still further on 31 July 1297 in the bull *Etsi de statu regni*, declaring that nothing prevented the king of France from demanding ecclesiastical subsidies without the Pope’s prior consent, if the defense of the kingdom was at issue: “that the king may ask prelates and ecclesiastical persons for a subsidy or contribution without consulting the Roman pontiff, notwithstanding the aforesaid constitution or any privilege whatsoever.” [Note: [Col. 1850D] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 40; manuscript of the Dunes, no. 60.] A [Col. 1849D] special bull appointed the archbishop of Rouen, the bishop of Auxerre, and the abbot of Saint-Denis as executors of the tithe, this time permitting the intervention of secular authority against prelates and ecclesiastical persons who would not submit: [Col. 1850A] “that you compel prelates and ecclesiastical persons to furnish such subsidy by our authority, spiritually and temporally, as you judge more usefully expedient, setting aside appeal and, if necessary, invoking for this purpose the assistance of the secular arm.” [Note: [Col. 1850D] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 61.]

Finally, on 9 August 1297, a bull beginning with the words, “The sincere devotion which our dearest son Philip, illustrious king of the French, bears toward the Roman Church has deserved,” granted the king of France one year’s income from all vacant benefices. [Note: [Col. 1850D] Manuscript of the Dunes, nos. 514 and 910. See my notice concerning this manuscript, p. 94, vol. XXV of the *Memoirs of the Academy*.]

Philip the Fair acknowledged these important concessions by Boniface VIII not only by leaving the Colonna faction to its own resources, [Col. 1850B] but also by permitting a tithe reserved for the Pope to be added to the tithes levied for himself, in order to assist the Pope in his war against Frederick of Aragon.

An important document of this period has been preserved in the manuscript of the Dunes: it is an appeal addressed by the dean and chapter of Tournai, so that the generosity of the faithful might support the Pope’s efforts to pacify Italy. A Colonna, Matthew, provost of Saint-Omer, was one of the leaders of this crusade directed against his own family. [Note: [Col. 1850D] Raynaldi, 1297, 41.]

“G., dean and chapter of the church of Tournai, to each and every abbot, abbess, prior, prioress, provost, dean, etc.: everlasting greeting in the Lord.

“The Fisherman’s little boat, always peaceful from its beginning, [Col. 1850C] reddened with Christ’s blood, sailing the sea and tossed by diverse storms of winds, now is tempest-tossed, as it was tempest-tossed in the days of Frederick, formerly emperor of condemned memory; yet it has never failed, as Truth testifies when he says: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail’ . . . We do not believe that any of the faithful is unaware how Frederick, son of the king of Aragon, swollen with envy born of a usurped dominion—whence [the text is corrupt, repeating “of Aragon, envy born of a usurped dominion, whence”] the whole breadth of the world is not enough for two brothers—and with the guile of the condemned Sicilian race, in which the disgrace of ancient blindness has remained, either seeking his own downfall or losing sight in the light, twenty years ago invaded by armed force, with no lack of the taint of treason, the island of Sicily, a special possession of the holy Roman Church; and, seeking more wicked counsels as malice rages, he still holds it occupied, to the prejudice of the Apostolic See and the illustrious king of Sicily.

“Although the said Frederick has at times been urged with fatherly affection by him who unceasingly seeks the salvation of all, to correct his errors through gentle as well as harsh [Col. 1850D] admonitions, he nevertheless, like the deaf asp stopping its ears, does not heed warnings, is not moved by gentleness, and is not frightened by severity—so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in him: ‘When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises.’

“Let the chosen people also hear, the people dedicated to God, how great and innumerable a slaughter of Christians, crowned with martyrdom, has, amid wars renewed by these things, ended their days. For the governance and prevention of these present and future affairs, our most holy father Boniface has so exhausted the treasure and substance of the Roman Church in tribulations and diverse wars—now through mountains and seas, often through trackless and devious shores—that we pass over for the present the costly army which he summoned against the schismatics and exiled Colonnas, sons of perdition, leaders of sedition, venomous parasites of the Roman See, serpents, brood of vipers, most ungrateful men. He now requires speedy and full assistance to bring his undertakings to completion; although from the fullness of his power he may impose tithes upon churches everywhere, in whatever amount and proportion he is able, nevertheless, because things done graciously are more graciously received, we exhort you, etc.” [Note: [Col. 1851C] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 246.]

We know that at the feast of the Assumption in 1298 [Col. 1851B] the Order of Cîteaux paid a further tithe [Note: [Col. 1851C] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 568. The statutes of the General Chapter of 1298 again mention the expenses which were incurred “for defending the liberties of the Order.”] and that a letter written at Compiègne on 25 February 1299 (old style), by John of Sancy, abbot of Clairvaux, announces the levying of two further tithes, combining the account of the king’s threats with the most vigorous complaints concerning the unhappy condition of the Order of Cîteaux:

“To his venerable and in-Christ dearest fellow abbots, J., abbot of Clairvaux: greeting, and, with the consolation of the sevenfold-giving Holy Spirit, the salutary fruit of obedience.”

We have frequently drawn, and still draw, deep sighs with anxious groaning of heart, seeing that in our days our Order is being reduced to servitude through wars, subsidies, contributions, and intolerable tenths, unless divine power comes to its aid. [Col. 1851C] For we do not think that it has escaped your notice in what manner and under what form of words the prelates, abbots, exempt and non-exempt, chapters, and colleges of the said kingdom were summoned and cited by letters of the king of France at Paris, on the octave of the recently past Purification of the Blessed Mary, to render the said king aid for the war in Flanders. But to the reverend father in Christ, our most dear lord of Cîteaux, and to the four first abbots and certain other abbots who were present there on the said day, the peril and pressing necessity of the said kingdom were set forth before the lord king; and we too were urgently requested by the said king, although he could, if he wished, have acted by royal power and privilege in a manner that might perhaps have been intolerable and damaging to us. Therefore, after considering all these matters and holding careful deliberation, following the action of the prelates, though not without distress of heart, we granted to Lord Philip the king two tenths, to be paid during two consecutive years, on behalf of ourselves and of our whole Cistercian Order established in the kingdom of France. By the counsel and consent of the reverend father in Christ, the lord of Cîteaux, and of the first abbots and very many others, and by the paternal authority entrusted in such grave affairs to the aforesaid father and to us, the first abbots, by the general chapter—in matters in which the said chapter cannot be awaited—we command under pain that your goods be exposed to the hands of royal officers compelling payment, and that you contract debts at your own expense under the burden of usury, and under pain of transgression and disobedience, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1851C] MS. des Dunes, no. 926. A letter addressed a few days later to Boniface VIII by the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés offers the same complaints:

“To the most holy father in Christ and his lord, B., by divine providence universal and supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: J., his devoted creature, abbot of the Parisian monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and the entire convent of that place, with their commendation, offer themselves to kiss his blessed feet. The sick and grievously languishing always thirst for health. . . . Therefore, running to the footstool of Your Holiness’s feet, we lay before you our infirmities and pains, under which we are already so heavily burdened and exhausted, almost fainting, that we fear we may no longer be able to rise again: namely, that our monastery is heavily encumbered with debts, because of the expenses which it befitted me, the abbot, to incur at the Roman curia and those which it was necessary to furnish to the lord king of the French for the support of the kingdom; and also because of the devouring abyss of usuries which gnaw at us, as does the evil and painful alteration of the coinage. Our creditors are weary of us and harass us, pursuing us day by day,” etc. [Col. 1852C] (1 March 1299, old style. Archives of Burgundy at Dijon; document communicated by M. Guignard.) What then must have been the condition of the other monasteries, if the royal abbey of Saint-Germain, founded by Childebert, was reduced to speaking thus? Godefroi of Paris says in his chronicle:

> I see no church today  
> [Col. 1852D] That has not been brought to this end,  
> That has not first paid a tenth,  
> A double tenth, and a fiftieth:  
>
> [lacuna]
>
> Those who take it do not thereby perform  
> Their duty toward holy Church.”]

Such was the degree of distress in which this Order, once so powerful and illustrious, found itself—already reduced to hoping for no protection other than that of God.

The count of Flanders likewise saw the hand of Philip the Fair weighing heavily upon him. In vain had he accommodated himself obligingly to royal exactions: the sequestration of the county of Flanders was decreed twice; and Guy himself, invoking the express text of the ordinances of Saint Louis, declared himself released from the oath of homage because the king refused him judgment by his peers, overwhelming him with “injuries, harshness, and oppressions.”

[Note: [Col. 1852D] *Établissements*, I, 49 and II, 27. It is known that, when publishing the ordinances of Saint Louis, Du Cange replaced the word *roy* (“king”) with *chief seigneur* (“chief lord”) in the chapter allowing a vassal, in the event of denial of justice, to summon his lord in order to go to war against the king. It should be added that Saint Louis, on ascending the throne, had sworn that henceforth the king would not pronounce confiscation of the great fiefs without the judgment of the peers.]

[Note: [Col. 1852D] Letter of the count of Flanders to Philip the Fair, 9 January 1296, old style, archives of Paris. I published this important document in my *History of Flanders*, 1st edition, vol. II, p. 559.]

[Col. 1852C] At the moment when the abbots of Floreffe and Gembloux bore Guy of Dampierre’s defiance to Paris, the lord of Blanmont and the lord of Cuyk were travelling to London to hasten the conclusion of a close alliance between the king of England and the count of Flanders.

The following were the terms of the instructions given to them:

[Col. 1853A] These are the words which should be spoken to the king of England, or to his people, on behalf of the count of Flanders.

At the beginning one should speak thus: “Sire, it is desired that you know that my lord of Flanders, my lady of Flanders, all the children of Flanders, and all those who love them—who have known and know the goodwill which they bear toward you—have borne you a very good heart throughout this whole war, and have shown it by deeds, as far as they have been able to do so loyally. Sire, it is true that the king of France has greatly pressed and greatly injured my lord of Flanders; and much more so since the agreements concerning my lord Edward, your son, and Lady Philippa were made than before. This was also because my lord of Flanders would not do, to your detriment, what the king of France required of him and caused to be put before him. The count has always behaved very graciously and very humbly [Col. 1853B] toward the king, continually requesting that he be maintained in reason and right.

“It is indeed true that the duke of Brabant, who is my lord of Flanders’s nephew, and the count of Bar, who is first cousin to my lady of Flanders—and who, sire, are loyal to you—together with many other persons who love you and likewise love my lord of Flanders, have long urged my lord of Flanders to consider his affairs, to seek aid and support, and to join you against the king of France. And because they well knew and know that my lord of Flanders has no power to set himself and his land against the king of France, given the expenditures this would require, they constantly said, and most emphatically maintained, that if he wished to do so, he would have from you whatever he wished. Some reported a sum of money; others made very large promises without naming a sum, sire; and some among those who belong to you said to certain persons belonging to my lord of [Col. 1853C] Flanders that, if the count wished to do it, he would have from you whatever money he wished, and marriages also for his children. Sire, all such statements, and many others, were reported to my lord of Flanders.

“Sire, he, being such a man as you well know him—loyal and honorable—was bound to love you sincerely, while preserving his loyalty in every respect. He never wished to give a definite answer until he had found the king of France wholly in default toward him, after summoning him upon every matter; and he labored to summon the king. For the injuries which the king of France was accustomed to inflict upon him, he resisted more sharply than he had previously done, demanding that right and justice be done him, without negotiating through intermediary or mediation, in hope that if right and justice were done him, he would accept it; but if they were not done him, he might attach himself to that which, sire, had been said to him on your behalf—a thing which he believed he would find very ready when the occasion should arise, according to [Col. 1853D] what had been told him.

“Sire, it has now happened that the count of Flanders has summoned the king of France concerning everything and has found him wholly in default; wherefore clerks of law and divinity have said and say that the king of France has so greatly wronged the count that the count is released from homage, service, fealty, and every due which he owed or could owe him. When the count had ascertained this, he sent to your people to inform them of his answer concerning matters of which he had formerly spoken on your behalf and which some of his own people had likewise reported to him from your people.

“Sire, the count of Flanders made such requests, regarding alliances by which he could better sustain his enterprise against the king, as were not heard in the manner expected from the words heard before. Nevertheless, your people spoke [Col. 1854A] most courteously, saying that they had no greater power, and that you, if one would wait so long, would act more generously than they had power or dared to act. The count of Flanders, sire, had, shortly before your people came to Cambrai, chosen and commissioned the lord of Blanmont and the lord of Cuyk to come to you on his behalf. They had set out, but could not arrive because of the impediment of the weather. And since he also considered that, after he had done and resisted so much against the king of France, once it had been told him that he was released from his obligations, he would wait no longer, he consented to what your people were willing to do for him, reserving always the remainder to the freedom of your judgment, in which he trusts above all things.

“And to complete, sire, all the business and render certain what has been done by your people, and what you will do by your grace—of which men have confidence no less, indeed more, than of what has been done—the count [Col. 1854B] of Flanders has sent you the lord of Blanmont, the lord of Cuyk, and his receiver of Flanders, sufficiently instructed on his behalf. They beg you, for God’s sake, that they may be dispatched swiftly and promptly; for it is urgently necessary that they be quickly dispatched. For, sire, you should know that when the count of Flanders sent here to you, he sent elsewhere to the king of France, through two abbots—the abbot of Floreffe and the abbot of Gembloux—to say and announce on his behalf that the count of Flanders was released from his obligations to him through the king’s own defaults. When this announcement, which has now been made, shall have been delivered, the count of Flanders will expel from all his country, by land and sea, all those who are there on the king’s behalf. Thus war will have begun; and we do not think that you can come to Flanders so soon that the war will not already have begun.”

[Note: [Col. 1853] Archives of the Kingdom of Belgium.]

A treaty was in fact signed a few days later in the chapel of Our Lady of Walsingham. [Col. 1854C] Edward I announced there that he would support Guy with his treasures and armies, and undertook never to negotiate without him: a solemn promise which Edward nevertheless refused to confirm by oath, saying, “for it is our custom not to swear in person.”

[Note: [Col. 1853] Declaration of 2 February 1296, old style, Archives of Rupelmonde.]

Finally, on 25 January 1296, old style, the count of Flanders caused a solemn instrument of appeal to the pope to be read in the church of Saint Donatian at Bruges. All his grievances against the king of France were reproduced therein.

Since the noble man Guy, count of Flanders, after the manner of his progenitors and predecessors, the counts of Flanders, was, by reason of the county of Flanders—which is part of the kingdom of France—one of the peers of the realm, and held the same county from the king of France [Col. 1854D] in fief, the same count, for the said fief, rendered fealty and homage to Philip, the present king of France, as he had formerly rendered them to Louis and Philip of illustrious memory, the predecessors of that king; and the king himself received the same count into his faith upon his fealty and homage. Thereafter, the king, at the discretion of his own will and wholly excluding the judgment of reason, although he ought, by right of fealty and homage, to defend and govern the same count—obedient to him, as he ought to be, as lord and king against all persons—in his rights, and especially in matters pertaining to the fief, attacked him; occupied the rights belonging to the count by reason of that fief and otherwise; plotted against the count’s estate and honor; failed to render him justice and expressly refused to do so; inflicted very many losses upon him; [Col. 1855A] used violence against his person; made a confederacy with the count’s enemies to the latter’s injury; negotiated a confederacy against the count with certain subjects of the count from his land; seemed to seduce them; warned and incited them against the count, their lord, both personally and through his agents.

He also violated and broke the agreements, long maintained between kings and counts, their predecessors, concerning the manner in which the count should be dealt with by law and by his peers in matters which the king owed him, and the count in turn owed the king; agreements transmitted in successive times from kings to kings and counts to counts, renewed by the present king and the same count, and confirmed by oath. The faith having been broken by him, the king pursued the same count in the aforesaid matters, not once only but many times, almost countless times, and in other almost innumerable ways, ceaselessly multiplying grievances against God and justice. Although the count [Col. 1855B] most frequently begged the king to render him justice and refrain from such injuries, he could never obtain a hearing from him. When he requested justice through his peers, which the king ought to have rendered him by law, custom, and the aforesaid agreements, the king regarded himself as offended by this and directed the stings of his indignation against him. The more humbly the count obeyed him—for God, justice, preservation of his honor, the peace which he always desired to maintain with the king, and the acquisition of the king’s favor and grace—the more harshly the king treated him and harassed him with injuries, by these and other things of which it is not only terrible to speak, but dreadful even to think, and detestable for men to hear.

At last, the count, being unable to endure these things any longer, perceiving that through the king’s fault the bond of fealty and homage, agreements and pacts, oaths and faith, subjection and obedience, and every other confederation and obligation [Col. 1855C] which had existed between the king and himself had been utterly dissolved, and that he was entirely released and free from them—because the king recognizes no superior upon earth—has fled for protection and aid to almighty God. But because the count, who henceforth neither ought nor intends to obey that king, since he is not bound to do so by law, reasonably and plausibly fears—and ought to fear, especially since the future may be presumed from the past—that the king himself or another, on account of the foregoing, may unlawfully burden and harass him through the injury of ecclesiastical judges or certain executors, or otherwise, contrary to law and justice; and because the count is ready and offers to stand to law concerning the aforesaid matters and others before the lord pope or any other competent judge, should the king or another wish to proceed against the count in any matter: I, John called Brantin, the aforesaid count’s procurator, in his name and on his behalf, in the presence of [Col. 1855D] the men here present whom I have asked to serve as witnesses, placing the count himself, his estate, those adhering to him and his people, his land and subjects and possessions, under the protection of the Roman curia, appeal or lodge a challenge in writing before the Roman curia against the aforesaid king, against all who believe their interest involved, and against all judges, executors, and other wrongdoers whatsoever. If anyone, in the aforesaid matters or others, burdens, disturbs, disquiets, harasses, molests, or vexes the count, those adhering to him, his people, or his subjects in their persons, lands, possessions, goods, or other things; or does anything unjust or improper, judicially or extra-judicially, to the prejudice of the count, those adhering to him, or his subjects, I urgently request apostolic letters and protest that this appeal or challenge shall be made and renewed [Col. 1856A] at the place and time, and in the manner, required by law. And because the aforesaid lord count, or I, or another procurator, or anyone acting on his behalf, cannot or dare not appeal or lodge a challenge before the king himself or his agents concerning the foregoing, because of fear of that king and his agents—a fear which may fall upon a steadfast man—I protest in the aforesaid capacity that I shall appeal or lodge a challenge, renew the aforesaid appeal or challenge concerning these matters, and notify the king thereof when this impediment has ceased, when we can conveniently do so, and as the law requires.

[Note: [Col. 1855D] Archives of Rupelmonde, no. 858.]

This instrument of appeal, renewed several times in March and May, received the adherence of the abbots of Saint Peter, Saint Bavo, Marchiennes, Ename, Saint Andrew, Oudenburg, Grammont, Dunes, Eeckhout, [Col. 1856B] Saint Nicholas-in-the-Meadows, Saint Nicholas of Furnes, Tronchiennes, and Ninove; of the deans of Bruges, Furnes, Cassel, Seclin, Douai, Courtrai, and Harlebeke; and of the provosts of Ghent, Thourout, Watten, Lo, and Eversam.

[Note: [Col. 1855D] Ibid.; and of Lille; MS. des Dunes, no. 889.]

A letter of 22 June 1297 announced to the pope that the count of Flanders had chosen Michel As Clokettes, John Beck, and John of Tronchiennes to maintain this appeal.

[Note: [Col. 1856D] Ibid., no. 897.]

Guy of Dampierre placed his confidence in the alliance of Emperor Adolf of Nassau and King Edward I of England.

Adolf of Nassau wrote to him on 31 August 1297:

Adolf, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever [Col. 1856C] august, to the distinguished man Guy, count of Flanders, his most dear faithful subject: his favor and every good. We have received with our customary affection the letters of your sincerity recently sent to our highness, and have fully understood their contents. You should know that we are no less troubled by your disturbances than by our own. Therefore, although the rebellion of certain principal princes of the empire and their perverse machinations—by which they do not fear to defile themselves with the crime of lèse-majesté—have hitherto prevented, and still considerably impede, our desired purpose of quickly assisting you against the king of France, nevertheless, under the assurance of loyalty, we declare to you by the tenor of these presents that you may confidently hold that, without dangerous delay, with such armed forces as the urgency of the present necessity permits, we ought to come to see and comfort you, as our beloved kinsman, the noble John of Cuyk, will be able to explain to you more fully. To him we have entirely disclosed the aforesaid situation and [Col. 1856D] our will concerning it. Accordingly, we wish you, taking up a spirit of consolation and courage, confidently to comfort your friends and subjects, knowing most certainly that, if any final negotiations should occur with the aforesaid king of France, we shall in every respect safeguard you as far as possible to us. We have also recently received certain reports about the coming of the illustrious Edward, king of the English, whose aid would truly be thought most advantageous both to us and to you. Whether he comes—which greatly accords with our desires—or does not come—which would be quite contrary to our wishes—we nevertheless wish you to have complete certainty of our assistance. Given at Sélestat, the second day before the Kalends of September, in the sixth year of our reign.

[Note: [Col. 1856D] Archives of Lille.]

[Col. 1857A] Adolf of Nassau succumbed in the struggle against Albert of Austria, and Edward I, who had undertaken not to lay down arms until he had defeated Philip the Fair, forgot this commitment in order to conclude a truce, accepting Boniface VIII as arbiter.

[Note: [Col. 1857D] Rymer, I, III, p. 194.]

The fate of Flanders was to be decided at Rome. Philip, Guy’s son, who had become an Italian prince and was known as the count of Teano after marrying Matilda of Courtenay, went there without delay. He was soon joined by his two brothers, Robert of Béthune and John of Namur, who had left Flanders to defend their father’s interests before the pope.

Before ascending the papal throne, Boniface VIII had acted, in a celebrated lawsuit against the [Col. 1857B] usurers of Arras, as advocate for the commune of Bruges. On the occasion of his accession, it had offered him two rich pieces of scarlet cloth, “in honor of him because he had been advocate in the aforesaid case.”

[Note: [Col. 1857D] Roll in the archives of Bruges.]

It was likewise to Boniface VIII, when he was still Cardinal Benedict Gaetani, that Guy of Dampierre had appealed to remove Guy of Avesnes from the bishopric of Liège, invoking feelings of benevolence and protection which had never failed him: “Having full confidence in the abundance of your kindness, we have recourse to it with all the greater confidence because we have always found it favorable.”

[Note: [Col. 1857D] [Col. 1858D] *Notice sur un manuscrit des Dunes*, p. 30.]

But the situation was no longer the same at the beginning of 1298: it was now necessary to have the pope, who had become Philip the Fair’s ally, accept an instrument of appeal emanating from a vassal in arms against his overlord.

Nothing is more important than the series of [Col. 1857C] diplomatic documents of this period concerning Guy of Dampierre’s negotiations at Rome; readers will perhaps be grateful to us for reproducing them for the first time in their entirety.

On 2 April 1297, old style, Michel As Clokettes and Jacques Beck announced to the count of Flanders that the pope had received them favorably, speaking to them of the affection he had always felt for the house of Flanders. At that time Boniface VIII was besieging the castle of the Colonna and multiplying precautions to secure himself against their attempts.

“Most dear lord, we, Mikieus, your chaplain, and Jacques Beck, your clerk, make known to you that our dear and beloved lord, my lord Philip, your son, [Col. 1857D] count of Teano and of Loreto, and my lady the countess, his wife, were at the court of Rome when I, Mikieus, came to the said court. They had already spoken with our lord the pope, especially concerning your affairs, from whom he received a good answer. Then, sire, after I, Mikieus, had arrived, on the very day of my arrival I was in the presence of our lord the pope and presented your letters to him, in the presence of your aforesaid beloved son and Master Jacquemon, your aforesaid clerk. I explained to him orally, insofar as God enabled me [Note: According to.], your affairs. He heard me most kindly. He answered me very graciously, sire, on your behalf, and [Col. 1858A] recounted the great affection and love which he had long borne toward the house of Flanders and toward you. He said that, please God, he would see to it that your affairs came to a good outcome once the affairs of the kings of France and England came into his hands for settlement. He did not think they ought to leave him without a good peace. He also behaved very favorably toward my lord Philip, your son.

“After that day, most dear lord, we visited all the cardinals and presented your letters to them; we set forth your affairs to them on your behalf and commended you to them. Each one, separately, answered us very favorably concerning you and promised, to the extent of his power, to preserve your estate and honor and the honor of your house of Flanders. Before this, your said dear son had visited them, and told us that he had received a very fitting answer from them. May God grant that the matter may come to a good and honorable end, as we have great hope that it will.

“And, most dear lord, know that my lord Philip, your said son, had left the court when these letters were written, together with the duke of Calabria, son of King Charles, who had come to court at the pope’s summons. He has returned to his own country and will return as soon as he learns news of the arrival of our lords who will come to court for you. It was not yet known in what place the court would be held. It is necessary, sire, that those coming on your behalf come well instructed and well provided for, for very great people will come on behalf of the adverse party. You should know, sire, that the Roman court is very demanding; whoever wishes [Note: Wishes.] to conduct business there must make many gifts, promises, and obligations, especially in an affair as great as you know this to be, in which it is not fitting at present to spare expense. We have provided for you at court the best advocates of the court, but [Col. 1858C] they demand to be well served with their fees; nevertheless, we have retained them.

“It would be good for you to send to court transcripts, written by the hands of public notaries, of all agreements and all privileges by which you wish to be aided. As to the appeals made for you and yours, I, Jacques Beck, your clerk, have sent you several letters delivered by several messengers, namely Gérard Hac, who is of your land of Aalst, and Jean Denis of Lille. In the remainder I have written to you how the pope has retained the matter in part, especially the appeals against the king of France, for settlement; and how he has committed the affair against the archbishop of Reims and the bishop of Senlis to Lord Gérard of Parma, cardinal. It would be good, sire, if it please you, to have citations issued by the judges of the appeals, who are there to perpetuate their jurisdiction, whatever course the affair may take. They have power to reassure you cautiously, and those who adhere to your appeals.

“And, most dear lord, the state and news of the court at present are such that our lord the pope is continuing his war against the Colonna. His host [Note: His host, his army.] is still before a castle called Colonna. He keeps himself more continuously on guard than he formerly did, has himself very closely guarded, and goes out little [Note: Goes out little.]; but at times he has services celebrated in his chapel, and there he has himself very heavily guarded. It is said, sire, that Frederick, who still holds Sicily, has made a very great fleet of galleys; and King Charles, the duke, and the prince his son have made and are making a great fleet against him. [Col. 1859A] Therefore people believe that there will be great war between them in those regions, unless Our Lord brings peace. The bishop of Châlons is still at court; but my lord John of Apremont, bishop, and the primicerius of Verdun have left the court. Our lord the pope has also made many new constitutions, as, most dear lord, I have previously written to you.

“Most dear lord, be advised to ensure that the court is so well supplied that no other failures arise through lack of provision; for this will greatly concern your honor and the advancement of your affairs. It is better to risk consuming [Note: Eats.] a little of one’s own than to lose the great for the small. We have informed our most dear lord, my lord Robert, your son, by letters that if this messenger should reach him first, he should open and read these letters and seal them again with his seal; and that he should then make known to you, sire, his will. If it please you, sire, send us your wishes, and we are ready to carry them out. May Our Lord sustain you in good and long life, in honor and joy, and guard you in soul and body. Given at Rome, the second day of April.”

[Note: [Col. 1859D] April 1297, old style, Archives of Flanders at Lille.]

In a letter written eighteen days later, Michel As Clokettes and Jacques Beck urged the arrival of Robert of Béthune and recommended that he do nothing without learning the exact state of affairs:

“Most dear lord, we Mikieus As Clokettes, your chaplain, and Jacques Beck, your clerk, residing at the court of Rome, make known to you that on the Tuesday at Easter we sent a messenger to our most high and dear lord, my lord the count, your most beloved lord and father, by whom we made known to him the condition and news of the court [Col. 1859C] of Rome. We gave him letters to deliver to you and to inform you of what we were making known to our said most high lord. Know, dear lord, that the pope and your other friends are quite astonished that none of your messengers has yet come to court from near you to inform and advise them of your wishes. We have not yet retained any lodging for you or your people at Rome or elsewhere, nor made any provision, because we cannot know whether the court will be at Rome or elsewhere. Nevertheless, we have done our utmost to discover this; and we are told that, wherever the court may be, the pope will arrange lodgings at his direction for the parties in the business for which you are coming. We can as yet obtain no answer other than this general one.

“Therefore, sire, if it please you, it would be good for you to send ahead of yourself a messenger eight or ten days in advance, to announce your wishes concerning this and other matters. [Col. 1859D] Even if you were as close as Genoa and wished to rest for a short time, we—or one of us—would come to you to tell you about these affairs, insofar as we may learn what should be done; for it is not good to come suddenly to court. We believe that those who are and have been at court for the kings’ messengers have no more definite answer. Make known to us, therefore, if it please you, your wishes and command.

“If you wish to rest at Genoa, as has been said, please take your rest in the houses of those of the company of Restorrimente, and cause inquiry to be made for the said Restor and Truphin, heads of the company, who have very much offered to assist and [Col. 1860A] honor you. May Our Lord sustain you in good and long life, in honor and joy, and guard you in soul and body. Given at Rome, the twentieth day of April.”

[Note: [Col. 1860D] 20 April 1298. Archives of Flanders at Lille.]

As soon as Robert of Béthune and John of Namur had joined Philip of Teano at Rome, they addressed to the pope a memorandum claiming the freedom of their sister, of the lord of Blanmont, and of the other prisoners captured at the battle of Furnes. They ought to have been released under a clause of the truce of 31 January 1297, old style. They principally emphasized the importance to Flanders of the English alliance.

[Note: [Col. 1860D] Rymer, I, III, p. 194.]

Your devoted servants, Robert the firstborn, Philip, and John, sons of the noble count of Flanders, petition Your Holiness to preserve the honor and estate [Col. 1860B] of that count, in whom they place unchanging trust in you; to bring his cause against the king of the French to an end with such speed as may be possible; and to procure for him security to live in peace. If the matter cannot presently be concluded, they petition that his daughter, whom the king holds, be restored to him at once; and that the prisoners and captives whom the king holds—namely, the lord of Blanmont and others—be released, on account of the said count’s war, according to the terms of the agreement made in granting the truce or armistice between that king and the king of England and their confederates and adherents, at least for the duration of the truce.

Furthermore, they petition that, concerning the sentences of excommunication and interdict that have in fact been pronounced against the count, the communities, and the individual persons adhering to him, provision be made with paternal kindness that they be revoked, insofar as proceedings have actually been taken; or at least that everything remain in the state in which it stood at the time of the appeals addressed to you [Col. 1860C]. Likewise, that prelates, notwithstanding the said sentences, be admitted to presentations, and clerics and ecclesiastical persons to benefices, dignities, and orders, and that they be received for all other acts and business and be able to act, both laymen and clerics, in court and outside it; especially since they have declared and do declare the said sentences of excommunication and interdict null. They should be able to do and transact what they could do and transact before the said sentences and the filing of the appeals; and no prejudice should be caused by exclusions on the ground of excommunication or interdict after the aforesaid appeals or sentences.

Furthermore, they petition that provision be made for the churches and ecclesiastical persons of his county who adhere to the count, so that they are not compelled to surrender their goods to the king, to their own injury and destruction, since the king himself and his men, rising against the count and his land, have wrongfully and violently burned and destroyed many churches and sacred places by fire [Col. 1860D].

Furthermore, that careful provision be made that the truce be observed toward the count and his men; and that acts attempted against the truce, past and future, be restored to their proper condition, with restitution for damage, things occupied and carried off, and redress of injuries; and that a suitable executor, or several, be granted to him for this purpose. And because, so long as the king holds that part of the count’s land which he has occupied violently and unjustly, security of truce or armistice cannot be secured for the count and his men, they petition that you arrange for that land to be placed from the king’s hand into your own until the matter has been concluded.

Holy Father, your devoted son, the Count of Flanders, [Col. 1861A] will be burdened and harmed in the following respects if the marriage expected to be contracted between the son of the King of England and the daughter of the Count of Flanders, under agreements made and confirmed by oath between the parents, does not proceed. For it was of great consequence to him and to his family to have the son of the King of England, and future king, as his kinsman and friend; to have royal offspring from the marriage; and to have his daughter as queen, as was to be hoped, if the Lord so disposed.

Furthermore, it was of great consequence to him and to his subjects to have peace and friendship between the lands of England and Flanders, between which there had often been disturbance and war, with damaging loss of persons and property. For the lands are neighbours, and have frequently maintained commercial and trading intercourse, especially in wool from England and cloth from Flanders, and in innumerable other goods customarily found in both places. And because the land of Flanders perceived that this marriage would bring it these and many other advantages [Col. 1861B], it bound itself to pay two hundred thousand livres tournois, which the King of England was to receive on the condition that the marriage went forward. The arrangement was such that the count himself was to contribute nothing from his own resources toward the said marriage. Subsequently, for a reason, it was agreed between the King of England and the aforesaid count that the king gave the said two hundred thousand livres to the count and assigned to him the right which he had in them. The count loses all this if the marriage does not proceed; nor were the men of the country otherwise bound to give it, except on the condition that the marriage went forward. If this condition of marriage fails, Most Holy Father, as you know, the foregoing losses will be followed by others.

These matters, Most Holy Father, the count’s sons, devoted to you, set before you for your information, so that you may recognize the count’s loss and detriment in this affair.

> **Note:** [Col. 1861C] June 1298. Archives of Flanders, at Lille. The following sentence concluded this document: “Not because they wish in any way to oppose your ordinance and will, but because they desire to obey in all things.” It has been erased in the original draft. Another petition, whose precise date I do not know, is composed as follows:
>
> “Holy Father, concerning the provision which Your Holiness intends to make for the Count of Flanders and his men regarding the matters written below, deign to grant your letters [Col. 1861D] and executors, as shall seem expedient to Your Blessedness. First, that his daughter, whom the King of France holds against her will, be restored to him. Furthermore, that those who have been captured and imprisoned—namely Lord Henry of Blanmont and others—be released in accordance with the agreements made when the truce or armistice was granted between the King of France and the King of England and their adherents.
>
> “Furthermore, that the periods for the appeals lodged by the count, and by the communities and individual persons, ecclesiastical and secular, adhering to the count, concerning matters in which the conduct of the King of France and the count may be involved, shall not run; nor shall sentences already pronounced be renewed; but all things shall remain in the state in which they were at the time the appeals were lodged, until Your Holiness judges that some other disposition should be made concerning these matters; and that an injunction be issued that nothing be altered or attempted.
>
> “[Col. 1862C] Furthermore, concerning clerics presented or to be presented for orders, dignities, and benefices by the count and other patrons and prelates who have adhered and do adhere to the count, who have appealed, and who have adhered and do adhere to the appeals lodged—whom the local ordinaries regard as excommunicated, under interdict, and suspended.
>
> “Furthermore, concerning tithes and subsidies not to be paid to the King of France, in accordance with what Your Holiness has elsewhere decreed should be requested and ordained; and concerning [Col. 1862D] revocation of any sentences of excommunication, suspension, and interdict that may have been issued on this occasion; and concerning dispensations, should any persons perhaps have incurred some irregularity on that occasion.
>
> “Furthermore, concerning the observance of truces and armistices, acts attempted against them, past and future, restoration to the proper state, restitution for losses, things carried off and occupied, and redress of injuries. Furthermore, they petition that you deign to provide for ecclesiastical liberty, so that the burgesses of Valenciennes, whom the Count of Hainaut violently caused to be dragged from churches, may be restored to the immunity of the Church.”  
> (Archives of Flanders at Lille.)

[Col. 1861C] A letter of Guy of Dampierre, written at the castle of Petegem on 23 July 1298, gives highly interesting details about what was then taking place in Flanders:

Guy, Count of Flanders and Margrave of Namur, to his dear and beloved sons Robert, Philip, and John, [Col. 1862A] residing at the court of Rome: greetings and a father’s love.

Know, dear sons, that on the octave of Saints Peter and Paul we received at Petegem the letters which you sent us, and carefully understood what they contained: first, concerning your condition; then, how the Apostolic Lord received you honourably and courteously at your first entry, when you paid him reverence, and again when you laid before him our affairs and necessities, for which you had gone there. For this we praise God, praying that, upon this beginning, he may grant you a good course and a better end, so that, once our affairs have been settled according to His holy will, you may return in joy and honour.

Concerning our own condition, we inform you that we were in reasonably good bodily health when these letters were written; but in heart we were greatly troubled, and often are still, pressed by the wrongs, contempt, and damages [Col. 1862B] which the men of the King of France inflict upon us and our men. Every day they harass and oppress them, acting and proceeding contrary to the terms of the forbearance agreed and sworn by the two kings in many respects, and particularly concerning the expressly stipulated clause in the forbearance, “he who holds, let him hold.”

> **Note:** [Col. 1862D] The truce of 31 January 1297 (old style) provides: “That the King of England, his men, subjects, helpers, and allies shall retain what they hold and held on the day when this forbearance was made.” Rymer, I, III, p. 194.

For they arrest, seize, and take at will and without reason, in many places, our men and their goods which had not been taken, seized, or arrested before the said forbearance, nor during the forbearance until now. And they say that, since they hold the chief places of the castellanies, such as Bruges and Courtrai, they wish to have and hold everything within the said castellanies outside the fortresses which were not taken in time of war; and they wish to maintain and establish through their lawyers that the members ought to follow the head. This is plainly contrary to the aforesaid words written in the forbearance, “he who holds, let him hold.” If, by their quibbles and still more by their force, they attained their purpose in this—may it never happen—we [Col. 1862C] would lose nearly all that remains to us

> **Note:** [Col. 1862D] That is, everything which remains to us.

in the castellanies of Bruges and Courtrai, and a great part of the bailiwicks of Ypres and Cassel, which they have put in dispute. In order to settle these disputes, which appear to us highly damaging and dangerous, and concerning which the two marshals—Sir Simon of Melun for the King of France and Sir Geoffrey of Joinville [Col. 1863A] for the King of England—have been unable to agree because of the importunity of the French, who press us on every side despite the forbearance sworn by the two kings and while the negotiation of the affairs is pending before the pope, we have been obliged, as it were under compulsion and to avoid something worse, to set a date with them at Arras, on the octave of Saint Mary Magdalene. There we are to have six knights and four clerics on our side, and the other party the same number of knights and clerics, to instruct the said marshals on the law.

This is very grievous to us: although that which is ours by right is sufficiently stated by the terms of the forbearance, and has not been seized, arrested, or molested by them up to this time … we are compelled by force to submit it to the judgment of their men. And regarding the dispute over Renaix between us and our nephew of Hainaut:

> **Note:** [Col. 1863D] In May 1294, Oste of Trazegnies and Gilles of Wadripont sold Guy of Dampierre what belonged to them in the lordship of Renaix for nine hundred livres tournois, but the validity of this sale was contested by the Count of Hainaut.

after the arguments on both sides had been heard and reported through an inquiry, the marshal of the King of England, the aforesaid Sir Geoffrey, rendered judgment for us; while Sir Simon of Melun, marshal [Col. 1863B] for the other side, rendered a contrary judgment for our nephew of Hainaut. By the authority of the lord of Nesle, who, as we have learned, is the instigator and author

> **Note:** [Col. 1863D] That is: the instigator and author.

of all these wrongs inflicted upon us, our nephew of Hainaut is putting this decision into execution as far as he can, as though the two marshals had rendered judgment for him and in agreement. After these two judgments had thus been given, in order to avoid evil, we requested and offered that the matters be placed in the hands of the two marshals, who should deal with them on the spot and cause all rents and revenues to be taken and collected by their authority, holding them in safe custody until the law should be declared, without prejudice to the party having the right thereto. This offer and request the said Sir Simon and his advisers would not receive; instead, they act upon their judgment in contempt

> **Note:** [Col. 1863D] That is, in disregard.

of the aforesaid Sir Geoffrey and to our prejudice, and issue at Renaix such bans and orders as please them, contrary to reason.

Furthermore, know that the Bishop of Tournai, our adversary to the extent of his power, notwithstanding our appeals—upon which judges have been obtained and a suit is pending at Cambrai—causes whatever sentences he chooses to be published and renewed in the churches of Tournai, Bruges, Courtrai, and elsewhere, as he pleases, to the defamation of us and ours and not without scandal to many. This is very grievous to us.

Furthermore, we inform you, as we have learned, that the King of France causes all the goods of persons of Holy Church who adhere to us and to our appeals to be seized wherever he can find them within his jurisdiction. He has already caused the fruits of this August to be seized; and when those who live under us enter the king’s jurisdiction, he takes and imprisons them for the two fifteenths demanded of all their goods and because they adhere to our appeals. Moreover, the king’s men have taken and seized the benefices of our clerics [Col. 1863D] for the present and following year, so that they cannot enjoy them, although by our privilege granted by the pope they have the favour of being able to enjoy them in our service. Yet nothing can prevail against the king’s force, by which he thus burdens and harries us on every side.

Dear sons, we command, request, and desire that you inform the pope of the aforesaid wrongs and of many others which the [Col. 1864A] king and the Bishop of Tournai inflict upon us and our people in many ways; that you make complaint to him on our behalf; and that you beseech him to provide a remedy through pity and justice, especially against the conduct of the Bishop of Tournai, whom he has in his hand for correction and punishment. We shall shortly send you the entire proceeding concerning him. Speak also concerning the wrongs which the king inflicts on us with the Count of Savoy and Sir Otho of Grandson, and inform them how we are oppressed contrary to right. Ensure that you have them with you, or one of them, when you speak of it to the pope.

Concerning the provost of Braine-le-Lein, we instruct you to act prudently regarding his acquaintance and return, since he is not in the pope’s favour, so that the pope may not, on his account, be moved in any way against you.

Furthermore, dear sons, by this messenger we send you letters to the Company of the Magi, through which you will receive at court four thousand gold florins [Col. 1864B]. We would willingly send you a greater sum of money at once, if we could; but the King of England has failed us in payment of the twenty-five thousand livres tournois which he owes us from time past. Our good people of Ypres and Douai, to whom we are indebted, ought to have been paid from it; and because of this default they are burdened, as are we. We also have our men near the king,

> **Note:** [Col. 1864D] Near the king.

who have long waited there for this payment and are still waiting. It therefore seems good to us that the Count of Savoy and Sir Otho of Grandson should learn from you that we are in distress and loss through failure of this payment, and that, had we received it in time, you would have been provided for more liberally.

Furthermore, dear sons, we are pleased that you have not handed to the pope the letters which you carried, and that you well remember the words which we spoke to you when you left us concerning the matter addressed by those letters. We have not yet changed our intention [Col. 1864C] in what we told you. Indeed, if the pope asks you to remain and to place our affairs in his hands, answer him discreetly and cautiously, and pass on without raising the matter with him. If it were not that the King of France on the other side had submitted himself to the pope, then you could not refuse it; but before doing so, we should wish you to obtain from him, through persuasive arguments and requests, an assurance that he would preserve for us our inheritance which the king has attacked, and that we should not be harassed by him as we have been until now.

Furthermore, dear sons, concerning events in our regions we inform you that the former King Adolph of Germany

> **Note:** [Col. 1864D] Adolph of Nassau, killed on 2 July 1298 at the battle of Göllheim.

was defeated and killed in battle, with his men, by Duke Albert of Austria on the second day of July, between Mainz and Oppenheim. Most say that this duke has great favour among the electors, and he is held likely to become King of Germany; he is approaching Aachen, drawing the people of the country [Col. 1864D] to his agreement, and beginning to make alliances. Therefore we have already sent to him to negotiate and arrange friendship with him, according to what will seem advantageous for us, through the lord of Fauquemont, who has gone there on our behalf in view of present circumstances. We relied partly upon the tenor of a letter from the lord of Cuyck, of which we send you the transcript enclosed,

> **Note:** [Col. 1864D] In this letter John of Cuyck urged the Count of Flanders to send the lord of Fauquemont as ambassador to Albert of Austria in order to seek his friendship.

and upon another letter which our nephew, the Duke of [Col. 1865A] Brabant, sent us. He has sent to the said duke to make alliance and friendship; and both our aforesaid nephew of Brabant and we have sent word on this matter to the King of England.

Nevertheless, we have not yet learned anything certain as to whether he will come into the kingdom of Germany. For although, as is said, he has the electors on his side, except the Duke of Bavaria and the Archbishop of Trier, some people think, not without reason, that if the pope wishes to involve himself in this matter he can make a king as he pleases; for the Archbishops of Cologne and Mainz will fully agree wherever he wishes, according to some. And the Count of Savoy, who is present at court, is, as we understand, very close to the pope; his family, when the pope was in a lower estate, greatly honoured and advanced him. Thus it seems that by this means, which may well have a good outcome, the pope ought and can bring the people of the King of France [Col. 1865B] to reason. We wish you to be advised of this, so that you may proceed more prudently in your affairs. Show these letters to John of Menin and to your secret council; and, for our honour and yours, be diligent and careful in the pursuit of your affairs.

We further wish you to know that, owing to the King of England’s failure of payment, as you may show to his men, we have been obliged at Ypres and Douai to make payments to various persons to whom we were indebted, and you have therefore been supplied with money more sparingly.

Dear sons, we inform you that, just as these letters were being written and the messenger was about to set out, on the Saturday before Saint Mary Magdalene’s Day, we received your letters at Ghent. In them you informed us how the pope had asked and pressed you to place our affairs in his hands; and how, [Col. 1865C] having heard his request and understood his words, sometimes stern and sometimes mild, and having deliberated concerning this with the men of the King of England, and after consultation among yourselves and your council, considering on the one hand the reasons moving you not to do so and on the other the causes which, in light of the present state of the times and affairs, moved and ought to move you, you finally inclined, for the safer course, to his will. You placed all our affairs in his hands, saving our honour and estate and preserving the alliances made between us and the King of England; and the pope caused a public instrument to be made concerning this.

Since it has been necessary to act thus, we accept it in order to avoid something worse, especially because we have also learned that the affairs of the Kings of France and England have been placed in his hands for a complete settlement. For, as our affairs now stand and proceed, we would have no power to live or endure. Therefore, dear sons, we command you to think, labour, and procure, night and day, for the preservation and maintenance of our estate and honour, and your own as well, so that this business may have the good conclusion which God in his grace grants us. We send you the two sealed powers of attorney and the closed letter to the pope, exactly as you requested, without adding or removing anything.

Furthermore, dear sons, concerning the marriage of our daughter to the son of the King of England, consider and work as far as you can to ensure that it is preserved as arranged and agreed between us and the King of England. For if it happened otherwise, you can see and know that we would lose the two hundred thousand livres tournois which we were to give with [Col. 1866A] our daughter and which the said king has remitted and released to us.

> **Note:** [Col. 1865D] This was the dowry which the Count of Flanders had undertaken to give his daughter by the secret treaty of Lierre.

Furthermore, remember to obtain from the pope a remission of the usurious interest which the Crespinois of Arras would exact from us if we remained in our estate. We are so greatly bound for it as you know, and therefore the pope should release us from it. Let the said Crespinois be content, on their side, to come to a fair accounting of what they have received from us and what we owe them. In view of what we have spent in this war, we would have no ability to pay this interest; and, as you know, we are not bound in justice to pay it.

Furthermore, dear sons, arrange that, if we are restored to our inheritance, we may, God willing, be so provided for by the pope that we may withdraw there if the king uses force against us, in order that the ground of discord and strife between us and him may be removed. Furthermore, that the king may not have power to compel us so that every coinage cannot circulate in our land [Col. 1866B]; rather, that they be no worse than the coins minted at the king’s mint, and that we may cause our coinage made in the lands which we hold from the Empire to circulate throughout Flanders without the king’s opposition, since it is as good as, and better than, the king’s coinage.

Furthermore, dear sons, keep in mind that the privileges and franchises which, as if through necessity, during this war we granted to our good towns in order to gain their goodwill—though it has benefited us little—should be annulled, especially all provisions of the said franchises which are or shall be found contrary to law and reason, so that because of them all ground of discord may be removed between us and our heirs and the aforesaid good towns.

> **Note:** [Col. 1865D] Grants of privileges to the communes had been numerous; one sees that they [Col. 1866D] were not very sincere. Yet it is no less true that the towns of Bruges and Ghent had betrayed the count and the country by favouring the French, and one understands why Guy of Dampierre judged them unworthy of the privileges he had granted them.

Above all other matters, dear sons, be diligent and careful, through yourselves and your friends, to inform the pope and those who are well disposed toward him, so that our inheritance may be preserved for us. Furthermore, remember to provide, [Col. 1866C] if you can, that we may mint in Flanders, in the part belonging to the kingdom, coinage of the standard of the king’s money, or better, which may circulate in the kingdom. For to our great loss, unjustly and for a long time, as you know, the king has suppressed our coinage, which we ought to have by our right and which could not circulate in the kingdom because of the king’s power and the poor quality of his money.

We also send you in another writing, enclosed here, wrongs which our men have reported to us as committed against us and our people. Know that Sir Geoffrey of Joinville, William your brother, and our men have requested of the constable and those acting for the king that these wrongs, and many others which we do not send you, committed against us and our party, should be placed in the safe keeping of the two marshals charged with guarding the truce until a declaration should be made as to where they ought by right to remain, however clear our right may be. But [Col. 1866D] we can obtain nothing; it is refused, and they proceed to sue. Indeed, even what we had held before the truce, namely what belongs to our men who have wickedly abandoned us and gone over to the king, we lose through the king’s force: he openly causes it to be taken and collected and has it returned to them.

Furthermore, in negotiating these matters, do not forget to remind the Count of Savoy and Sir Otho of Grandson that they should advise the pope that, if the king had full foothold in Flanders, it is easy to know that what remained would be of little worth to us and our heirs.
