When he had nothing there, and neither hated us nor ought to have hated us, nothing could remain to us; and [Col. 1867A] on this point Sir William of Mortagne spoke to the Count of Savoy when he was in Flanders, as you will remind him.

Given at Petegem, the day after Saint Mary Magdalene’s Day.

> **Note:** [Col. 1867D] Archives of Flanders, at Lille.

This letter no longer found Robert of Béthune at Rome. The mission entrusted to him had been concluded in June by the arbitral sentence of Pope Boniface VIII. It is known that, in restoring peace between the Kings of France and England, it annulled every agreement concerning the marriage of the Prince of Wales to Philippine of Flanders, in order that he might marry a daughter of Philip the Fair. Philippine of Dampierre died of grief in her prison; Isabella of France was to avenge the perjury of the young English prince, who later became King Edward II [Col. 1867B].

Boniface VIII had caused the sons of the Count of Flanders to deliver a declaration recognizing his right to pronounce sovereign judgment upon their claims and grievances. They had not dared refuse it to him, although they consented only reluctantly and in order to avoid greater misfortunes. At that very moment, they were multiplying their representations to the English ambassadors in order that the latter should not abandon them.

Four letters written at Rome provide the fullest details concerning these negotiations.

In the first, the sons of the Count of Flanders relate how, after taking the advice of the [Col. 1867C] English ambassadors, they consented to submit themselves to the pope’s arbitration:

Very dear lord, we inform you that on St Barnabas’s Day [Note: [Col. 1867D] 11 June 1298.] we came before the Pope in the afternoon, at his command; and there were present the representatives of the King of England: namely, the Archbishop of Dublin [Note: [Col. 1867D] William of Hotham, Archbishop of Dublin. He had taken a major part in the conclusion of the truce.], the Bishop of Winchester, the Count of Savoy [Note: [Col. 1867D] The Count of Savoy was son of Thomas of Savoy, who had formerly, as husband of Joan of Constantinople, borne the title of Count of Flanders. He had himself married Mary of Brabant, [Col. 1868D] granddaughter of Guy of Dampierre. He fought at the battle of Mons-en-Pévèle in Philip the Fair’s army and was one of the signatories of the Treaty of Athies.], the Count of Bar, and Sir Otto of Grandson. And we gave the Pope the written statement concerning the grievances which the King of France had inflicted upon you, which he heard from us. We also showed him a public instrument containing the words which the Bishop of Amiens and the Bishop of Le Puy had brought you at Courtrai [Note: [Col. 1868D] I published this document in *Histoire de Flandre*, 1st ed., II, p. 574.]. This instrument states that, after the declaration which you had made to the King that you held yourself released and absolved from all obedience and subjection, they offered, on the King’s behalf, to do you justice through your peers concerning the wrongs which you had done to the King. But it did not say that they offered to render justice concerning the grievances and injuries of which you complained against the King, or concerning anything else. Thus the King’s harshness and failure were again demonstrated.

This instrument was shown to the Pope, to inform him, because the envoys of France, through fraud and falsehood, when they saw that reason could not help them, gave the Pope to understand that the King had always offered you justice through your peers in all your affairs, and that you had always refused it. For this reason the Pope was sometimes somewhat moved against your cause, and spoke of it to certain cardinals. But we showed him, by contrast, through the aforesaid instrument, that you had found so little justice in the King that, although he saw that you complained of him so seriously and in so many matters, he had not offered you justice regarding these things or any others.

We told the Pope clearly that, when the King injured you in your rank, honour, and inheritance—so seriously that the matter belonged to the cognizance and judgment of your peers—you humbly requested that he do you justice, and repeatedly pursued the matter; yet you found neither justice nor moderation. Afterwards you demanded the judgment of your peers; but neither this nor anything else belonging to right or justice could you ever obtain or find from him. Rather, he and his council conceived such great indignation and hostility against you that they always treated you worse than before.

The envoys of the King of France were the Archbishop of Narbonne, the Duke of Burgundy, the Count of Saint-Pol, Sir Peter Flote, Master John of Chevry, Archdeacon of Rouen, and Master John of Montreuil [Note: [Col. 1868D] Jean de Montreuil, one of Philip the Fair’s principal advisers.], cantor of Reims.

Thereafter the Apostolic Lord put a proposal before us and asked us to place your cause in his hands; he would safeguard your honour and rank, and said that otherwise he saw no way in which he could help you. He did this so that he might have an opening and means of helping you against the French. Lord, this proposal seemed to us of very great weight. We told him that the King of England and you were joined by a just alliance, and that his envoys were present, without whom we neither could, wished, nor ought to do anything. We asked that we might take counsel with them and with our own men who were with us. He granted this until the following afternoon.

In the morning, lord, we came to the lodging of the Archbishop of Dublin and set before him and the other councillors of the King of England the affair and what they had heard of it. We requested their counsel, as from those who ought to be wholly at one with us. Thereupon, lord, they consulted separately among themselves and answered us—not as the council of the King of England, but each separately as a friend—that it was dangerous to comply with the Pope’s request and dangerous to refuse it, and that they did not know which course to advise as the better. The Count of Savoy spoke first for himself, and all the others followed him in this manner:

> “The King of France, who is near you, bears great hatred toward you, is a powerful man, and has taken and holds in his own hands a very large part of your land. Those who remain with you are not all very steadfast. Your external friends, such as the Duke of Brabant and the others, are greatly sought after and solicited; and you are not very well provided with men or money. The King of England, because of his affairs in Scotland, Gascony, and England itself—where not all agree well with his will—will never leave England, nor will he ever send you such aid, nor can he provide aid such as may help you. Nor will the people of Ghent or of your country ever willingly receive the English.” [Note: [Col. 1869D] Only a few months had passed since the bloody riots between the people of Ghent and the men-at-arms of Edward I.]

> “And if you do not comply with the Apostolic Lord’s will, you will lose his favour and that of the Roman court, which is a great matter and one that you must carefully preserve; and all this may turn to your great harm.”

They would say no more to us. We considered all this in relation to your cause; yet, on the other hand, great danger might arise from placing so great a matter at another’s discretion.

We then departed from them and took counsel with the knights and clerics who were then with us. In the afternoon we came before the Pope and showed him the great trust which you had in him; how you confidently relied upon your right; and how he stood in God’s place upon earth and was superior to the King of France in spiritual and temporal matters. We asked him to do us justice against the King of France. In order to obtain and secure justice, we offered to place your cause in his hands, as in the hands of a judge and superior. Our brother Philip spoke these words well and fittingly.

The Pope immediately replied that this was to place before him a dispute against the King of France, which he had not at present undertaken; but that it was indeed true that he was superior to the King of France, in spiritual and temporal matters. This reply which we gave did not please him; he said that we had not been well advised to answer thus, and told us again to take better and different counsel, if we thought it good.

He further said that, whatever we might say, this would not prevent his making peace between the two kings; that he would dissolve the alliance, and could indeed do so. And when the King and you swore the alliance, each of you thereby committed perjury, as did the King of France when he swore it; and he said this plainly to their envoys.

Thereupon we again took counsel with the representatives of the King of England; afterwards we consulted your men and ours who were there. By earnest entreaty we obtained a delay until the following day. The Pope granted it until the afternoon of the next day, namely Friday after St Barnabas’s Day.

Afterwards we assembled your council with us three brothers: namely, the provost of Lausanne, Sir Bassian, the lord of Escornay, Sir Gerard of Verbois, the castellan of Douai, Sir John of Menin, Sir Gillon of Renne, Sir Ponchart of Florence, Sir Walter of Wavrin, Sir Robert of Lierenghien, Sir Rason Mulart, the provost of Béthune, Sir Michael As Clokètes, and Master James Bieck. We considered the affair very diligently, in great distress and anguish of heart. We all thought that the less dangerous course was to place the entire affair in the Pope’s hands, with your honour and rank safeguarded, as in the hands of him who stood in God’s place upon earth, in view of the great confidence which you had in him and the good right which you possessed.

The Count of Savoy and Sir Otto of Grandson, with whom we again spoke on the same day before dinner, gave us this same advice. Thus we did so in the afternoon, in the presence of the representatives of the King of England named above, with their assent, and with the alliance between the King of England and you safeguarded; and in the presence of Sir Gerard of Parma, Sir Matthew of Acquasparta [Note: [Col. 1869D] Matthew of Acquasparta, general of the Order of Friars Minor, made cardinal by [Col. 1870D] Nicholas IV.], and Sir Napoleone [Note: [Col. 1870D] Napoleone Orsini.], cardinals [Note: [Col. 1870D] These three cardinals supported the interests of Guy of Dampierre.].

The Pope said very generously and willingly that he would safeguard your right and honour; and wherever right failed you or the matter was doubtful, he would aid you by his favour and in every other way within his power. Further, before he gave it to the King of France, he would give you a county as good as your own, for the King of France had too much land. The Pope has caused a public instrument to be drawn up concerning these matters. Know, lord, that we rely greatly upon our brother Philip and shall rely upon him still more, if God pleases. [Note: [Col. 1870D] Archives of Flanders, Lille.]

The second letter explains the reasons which guided Robert of Béthune and his brothers in the decision which they found themselves compelled to make without being able to consult their father.

Lord, when the Pope proposed that we place your cause in his hands, we were greatly astonished; for we had necessarily either to refuse or to grant his request. We and all our councillors considered the following reasons why refusal might be proper.

First, it was a great danger to place so important a matter at another’s discretion, unless it were in the hands of a man in whom one could trust as much as in oneself. Next, the Pope was a stranger to you, and he knew so much that, if he wished to harm you, he would know well how to find a cause and occasion for excusing and defending himself. Next, through the subsidies and tithes which he had granted to the King of France, and through the favour he showed that King, he had grievously burdened both you and your churches. Next, the Pope, as people say, is a covetous man; and the King, beyond comparison, had greater power than you to serve him from his own resources—or, if not from his own, from the goods of the churches.

On the other side, as to why we ought to grant his request, we considered the reasons set before us by the Count of Savoy and the representatives of the King of England: namely, the power of the King of France; his proximity to you; the great part of your land and people which, as you know, he had drawn over to himself and turned against you; the great expense which you would have to incur in provisioning the towns and places remaining to you and defending yourself; the lack of money and resources to sustain such a war; and the aid of the King of England, the Duke of Brabant, and the Germans, for which you would have to incur greater expense than you could bear, even if they were still willing to help you.

We considered the failure of the King of Germany, concerning whom the Pope himself told us that, if he should again become involved, the Pope would keep him entirely quiet; and that the Pope had, as he told us, three or four such prelates in Germany, each of whom separately would have sufficient power to hinder him, if the Pope wished.

We also considered that the Pope said he would make peace between the two kings without us, and that you would remain alone in the war; that those of your country who remained with you were not very steadfast; and that, if matters proceeded by judgment or arbitration in order to do justice, the Pope might greatly harm you, without your being able to obtain redress. We considered the dishonour which would attach to you: people would say that you were striving to keep all Christendom in turmoil; and we considered the Pope’s anger and indignation. You had good reason to beware of his displeasure and to retain his favour, for many causes—and for one reason among others which you and your council know well. If the Pope moved against you, he would soon take occasion for the war which he was supporting, and all would be involved in it.

We also considered that, if any sentence of excommunication or interdict should come from him against you, or because he who submits his cause to litigation, however clear it may be, is at a disadvantage if any of the sentences pronounced should be upheld, the greater part of your countrymen, whether right or wrong, would take occasion to leave you. And if you angered the Pope, you would not know where to turn for comfort.

The lord of Escornay spoke these words before us and all our council: when he departed from the country, the leading men of the country—those who loved you and the estate of the land most—said to him:

> “You are going to Rome: take care not to return without making peace, whatever it may be; otherwise you will deserve to be dishonoured.”

We also considered the alliance being sought, on behalf of the King, with the Count of Holland against you, as you had informed us, and the whole country. We further considered that, before all worthy persons—namely the cardinals, the envoys of the King of England, ourselves, and our council—the Pope promised us that he would preserve your honour and rank. We understood from these words that you must recover all your land, in such a state that you might hold it freely and peaceably, and that nothing should be imputed to you which might show that you had committed any offence against the King.

After considering all the reasons, one against another, by the advice of all your men, of the representatives of the King of England, of Master Gerard of Parma and Master Matthew of Acquasparta, and by the judgment of us three brothers ourselves, though our hearts were distressed, whatever appearance we made before the Pope in order to retain his favour, we agreed to grant the Pope’s request as the less dangerous of the two courses. For we necessarily had to choose one or the other and could not escape without deciding.

We would gladly have obtained enough delay to send word to you because of the importance of the affair; but in no way could we obtain this, not even a respite of one single hour beyond the time that we have been here. Lord, we have delivered to the Pope our power of attorney on your behalf; but he still wishes to have another, for greater security in the matter. As far as he is concerned, the power already delivered to him is sufficient; nevertheless, he wants another according to the copy which we send you enclosed in this letter. You shall have the date inserted on the day when you seal that power of attorney, and send it to us without delay. Know that this will not prevent the Pope from proceeding in the meantime with the affair, in order to arrange and conclude it, as he has told us. [Note: [Col. 1871D] Archives of Flanders, Lille.]

[Col. 1871D] The third letter, drawn up in the form of a memorandum, reproduces the account of the audience granted by the Pope on 25 June 1298 to the sons of the Count of Flanders, and the words spoken in their name so that Guy of Dampierre might be included in the peace treaty between the Kings of France and England.

In the year of the Incarnation 1298, on Wednesday—that is, the day after the Nativity of St John the Baptist—in the morning, Sir Robert, eldest son of the Count of Flanders, Sir Philip, and Sir John of Namur, sons and envoys of the said Count, came before the Pope in his chamber at St Peter’s. They brought with them the lord of Escornay, the castellan of Douai, Sir Gerard of Verbois, Sir John of Menin, and a man learned in law called Sir Bassian. Also present before the Pope were the envoys of the King of England: namely, the Archbishop of Dublin, the Bishop of Winchester, the Count of Savoy, the Count of Bar, Sir Otto of Grandson, and Sir Hugh of Vere.

There were then set before the Pope on behalf of the Count of Flanders, in the presence of all the aforesaid persons, the following words:

> “Lord, because the Count of Flanders has been unable to obtain right or justice from the King of France, and has been so grievously oppressed by him, the affair has come to the ruin and distress which are evident. Those who are here have, by your will, placed the cause in your hands, while safeguarding the honour and status of the county and the alliance made between the King of England and the Count, from which they do not wish to depart. They have done so as to one in whom they have supreme trust, above all others, and you have undertaken it.

> “Now, lord, they understand that you intend to make peace between the King of France and the King of England without presently including the Count or them in it. This would be too grievous for the Count for many reasons. First, the Count would remain in the war and be deprived of such aid and alliance as that of the King of England, which was made and sworn for good cause and good reason against one who has refused to do right or justice. Next, lord, because a truce has been made between the two Kings, if there is peace between them it must be feared that the King of France will not maintain any truce with the Count; for he has made no truce with him, but only with the King of England, for himself and his allies. If there is peace, the truce therefore has no place. And although the truce still endures and the King of England intervenes to have it observed, the King of France and his men violate it daily and in many cases, as can clearly be shown.

> “Next, lord, if the Count remains outside the peace, those of his country who adhere to him may become discouraged and disheartened. Those also whose hearts are not firmly with the Count may take courage to turn against him, especially those who, before the war openly appeared, had made agreements and arrangements with the King and received letters from him, as has formerly been shown to you. Moreover, lord, it will bring great dishonour and shame upon the Count; his enemies will esteem and fear him less, and the Count may fall into great danger.

> “Since the Count wishes to obey you in everything, the King of France, who will not accept right before you and will not submit himself to you—neither by submission, composition, ordinance, nor agreement—ought not to enjoy such an advantage that the Count should fall into so great peril and distress in his cause. They pray and request that you, in whom the Count and they place their whole trust, provide such remedy and counsel as is fitting. For, lord, they do not refuse peace or wish to hinder it; but they pray that their peace be made together with that of the King of England, and that they not remain without him in the war, for the reasons stated above.

> “For, lord, if you made peace between the two Kings, the King of England would necessarily have to involve himself in the war and assist the Count against the King, with whom he would have made peace, because he is allied to the Count. And to you, lords, who represent the King of England, they request that you speak to our Holy Father so that he may grant our request, that our peace may be made together with yours, and that you may not consent to our being separated from you. For we do not wish to depart from you or from the alliance between the King and my lord; rather, we expressly reserved it in the submission at all times. Even though we granted you leave to submit the matter, we did not thereby grant you leave to make or accept peace without us, leaving us in the war.

> “By the terms of the agreements in the alliance, you cannot and ought not to make peace without us. We further request that you observe toward us the King’s agreement, safeguarding his honour and your own, such men as you are.”

When these words had been spoken, the Archbishop of Dublin said to the Pope: “Lord, we pray you to make our peace together with that of the Count”; and the others followed him. After these words, the Pope became moved according to his will and said that this would not prevent him from making peace between the two kings. [Note: [Col. 1873D] Archives of Flanders, Lille.]

The fourth letter, which likewise recounts the efforts made with Boniface VIII, informs us [Col. 1873B] that they were fruitless. Indeed, by a few words hastily added, it announces that the Pope had pronounced at the palace of St Peter the arbitral sentence which he had refused longer to postpone.

Very dear lord, we, Robert, Philip, and John, your sons, inform you truly and certainly that, on the day after the Nativity of St John the Baptist, we came before the Pope with the representatives of the King of England. Because we had understood that he intended to make peace between the King of France and the King of England without including you in that peace, we showed him the grievances which might result for you and prayed that he would not do so; rather, that he would wait until your peace had been settled and that all the peaces might be made together, for many reasons.

We requested the representatives of the King of England to labour toward this, for the honour of the King and of themselves, and because of your rights. For even if we had consented that they might submit their affairs to the Pope, we had not granted them leave to make peace without you and leave you in war and dispute. Rather, we opposed this, because such was the obligation of the alliance between the King and you, which had been made by the King and you to defend your rights against the King of France, from whom you have been unable to obtain justice.

The King’s envoys there requested the Pope to make their peace and yours all together. After hearing our words, the Pope answered us harshly. He said that, for the County of Flanders, he would not refrain from making peace between the two Kings; that he would make and pronounce peace between them; and that, if there were anything further to say, he would say it at another time. He would have the truce concerning you and the allies observed, but would not pronounce upon your cause at present, because he would have to help you by another means.

He also said that, if we repented of having placed your cause in his hands, he would willingly withdraw from the matter insofar as it concerned you [Note: [Col. 1873D] That is: insofar as it concerns you.]; but he would neither refrain nor delay making peace between the two Kings for anyone.

Take it as certain, lord, that peace between the two Kings will be made within this present week. Therefore consider, lord, your peace and your affairs as you think best; and do not be disturbed [Note: [Col. 1873D] It had first been written: “Do not be alarmed or disturbed.”] by news conveyed to you by anyone other than us, for we shall always inform you of the truth. We especially hope to accomplish good, though there will be some delay. And, for God’s sake, lord, do not fail to send us the two powers of attorney which we requested, as dearly as you value your cause and honour, and the Pope’s aid and favour. We requested these powers of attorney through Ghiselin and Cambier, your own envoys, who brought us your letters and left Rome on the day of the Nativity of St John the Baptist.

Lord, on the evening of the day of the Nativity, we received your letters brought by Michael, our messenger, which speak of the lord of Saint-Venant and others who are said to have come, or to have sent persons, to Rome in order to defame you and injure those who stand with you. Know, lord, that according to what we understand, this is not greatly to be feared, and we shall be very much on our guard. Men from Bruges have indeed come: Gerard Cant and Paul of the Walle [Note: [Col. 1873D] Gerard Cant and Paul Wandewalle were charged with delivering to the Pope a petition from the commune of Bruges. A roll published in my *Histoire de Flandres*, 1st ed., vol. II, p. 601, shows that they dined in Rome with Cardinal Lemoine. Cardinal Lemoine was French, and Boniface VIII treated him rather badly, if one may trust the phrase reported by William of Nogaret: *Picarde, tu habes caput picardicum, sed ego piccabo te*—“Picard, you have a Picard head, but I shall peck you” (Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 339). Nevertheless, he showed devotion to the Pope in his conflict with Philip the Fair.]; the castellan of Bergues has crossed into Apulia, and of the others we know nothing.

Lord, because of the haste required by the kings’ affair, we write nothing else to you now. Cause these matters, lord, to be made known to my lady and wherever you think good.

Lord, after these letters had been written up to this point, we resolved to wait further in order to learn what judgment would be given concerning the two kings. The Pope pronounced that judgment on the following Friday morning [Col. 1874C], in the manner contained in a writing enclosed herein [Note: [Col. 1874D] “In the year of the Lord 1298, on the Friday morning after the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in a full and public consistory at Rome, in the palace of the church of Saint Peter, in the presence of the envoys of the King of France, the envoys of the King of England, the cardinals, and many other archbishops, bishops, and other prelates, and also many others who wished to be present, the Pope pronounced between the King of England and [an omitted party; the text is defective] the following or below-written matters in the manner which follows, etc.” See Rymer’s acts, I, III, p. 200.]. Lord, may Our Lord keep you.

Written at Rome on Saturday, the eve of St Peter and St Paul. [Note: [Col. 1874D] Archives of Rupelmonde.]

Perhaps the sons of Guy of Dampierre accused the Count of Savoy of having supported them with too little zeal. At least they were reproached with having voiced rather sharp complaints; and, because they wished to remain faithful to Edward I’s alliance as long as there was any hope of preserving it, they believed they ought to deny the words attributed to them.

On Monday after the feast of St Peter and St Paul [Note: [Col. 1874D] 30 June 1298.], at the hour of vespers, Sir Robert of Flanders, Sir Philip, and Sir John of Namur, sons of the Count of Flanders, came to the palace [Col. 1874D] of Santa Sabina, to the lodging of the Count of Savoy. They spoke to the said Count, to the Archbishop of Dublin, to Sir Otto of Grandson, and to Sir Hugh [Col. 1875A] of Vere, envoys of the King of England, in the following manner. With them were, of the Flemish party, the lord of Escornay, the castellan of Douai, and John of Menin:

> “Lords, we have been given to understand that you have heard that certain harsh and strange words have been spoken by us and our people against you. We pray you not to believe this, for it is not so; nor have we had, nor shall we have, any desire or intention of the kind. It is true that the Pope has pronounced a judgment between the King of France and the King of England, as you know, in which there is some harshness toward us. We say nothing against the judgment. We have good hope that the matter will come to a good end with God’s help and through the good right which we possess.

> “You know the alliances and agreements between the King and my lord of Flanders. No discord has arisen concerning them, nor has any submission been made, and no judgment has any place in the matter. We firmly believe and confidently trust that the King will observe them for the sake of his loyalty and honour; and my lord will always pray and request him to do so. We ask that you give your aid and good counsel in this matter and that, wherever you can, you will regard us favourably. We would do likewise for you wherever we had the power, as for our good friends.”

They replied that they would gladly do so and would seek, to the best of their power, the Count’s good; that they earnestly desired it; and that the affair had not yet been brought to its end by the judgment. [Note: [Col. 1875D] Archives of Flanders, Lille.]

The Pope’s arbitral sentence contained no reservation in favour of the Count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 1875D] Rymer, I, III, p. 200; MS of the Dunes, no. 923. Baillet, in order to represent the arbitral sentence as adverse to the King of France, asserts that it stipulated that he would restore Guy of Dampierre’s daughter and the towns which he occupied, and would go to the East to fight the infidels. All this is wholly inaccurate.]. In a separate and very short bull, the Pope merely extended the periods for prosecuting the appeal lodged by Guy of Dampierre, so that the settlement of the difficulties might be pursued later. This bull [Col. 1875C] was worded as follows:

> Boniface, bishop, etc. Formerly, between our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious King of the French, on the one hand, and our beloved son, the noble man Guy, Count of Flanders, on the other, concerning certain matters of dispute, lawsuits and contested proceedings having also arisen, several appeals on behalf of the Count himself and those adhering to him were lodged with the Apostolic See on that occasion. We, however, for certain causes which reasonably move us to do so, will that the periods prescribed for such appellants to prosecute their appeals, and the periods fixed by law, shall not run; and that all matters appealed, and matters consequent upon them, shall remain in the state in which they now are until we decide otherwise to make provision concerning them. [Note: [Col. 1875D] MS of the Dunes, no. 277.]

The mission of Robert of Béthune and John of [Col. 1875D] Namur was finished. While Philip of Thiette went into southern Italy, still hoping to serve his father’s cause by making himself useful to that of the Pope against Frederick of Aragon, they sadly resumed the road to Flanders. They had exhausted all the sums [Col. 1876A] entrusted to them, and on 30 July, to meet the expenses of their journey and pay certain debts they had left in Rome, they borrowed at Florence 4,000 gold florins from Guy Bardi. He, like the Louchards of Arras, styled himself a knight, and advanced the money at interest of 4 per cent per month. [Note: [Col. 1875D] Archives of Rupelmonde. For a time the Bardi farmed all the revenues of the kingdom [Col. 1876D] of England. They had a house at Bruges. Villani calls them one of the pillars of Christendom’s commerce.]

A burning fever, the result of anxiety and fatigue, seized Robert of Béthune. He scarcely managed to cross the passes of the Great St Bernard and reach Lausanne, where on 27 August he dictated his will. [Note: [Col. 1876D] I have not found Robert of Béthune’s will again in the archives of Lille. It is summarized in the old inventory. The executors appointed by Robert of Béthune were John of Menin and Gerard of Verbois.]

The following letter was written at Lausanne by Robert of Béthune. He informs his father of his illness and of the delays affecting his return to Flanders:

To the very high, very noble, and very puissant lord, his very dear lord and father, Guy, Count of Flanders and Marquis of Namur, Robert, his eldest son, greeting, filial love, and obedience.

Very dear lord, our delay on the way to you has been longer than we expected, because of the illness of myself and of our brother, who is, blessed be God, now entirely recovered; and I myself was in fairly good condition. But this past Wednesday, while crossing Mont-Saint-Bernard—I had slept at Aosta and came to lodge at Saint-Branchier—a fever seized me, which has since held me severely, a double tertian fever; so that I cannot leave Lausanne, where I am, until God shall have brought me into another condition. On the other hand, dear lord, when we departed from Rome Master James Bieck sought from us two letters of your appeals, which we caused to be kept in order to bring them to you. [Col. 1876C] Please have your council reconsider them, so that you may use them before the month of October begins, unless you have used another letter similar to this one, or unless it is sufficient for your needs; otherwise, thereafter you cannot avail yourself of them, nor of the appeal in respect of these letters, because of the lapse of the year of which the said letters speak in their date. We send them to you in haste, because we shall not be able to come to you as soon as we had intended. Sir, therefore speak promptly with your council. Sir, we understand from those coming from the Roman court, who left after we did, that peace has been made between the King of Sicily and Frederick of Aragon; but we do not know in what precise form.  
[Note: [Col. 1876D] Archives of Rupelmonde, no. 1039.]

On 6 September Robert of Béthune and John of Namur had arrived at Besançon, where they were again compelled to borrow money. A few days [Col. 1876D] later, they addressed from Baume to James Beck and Michael As Clokettes, who had remained in Rome, a letter which we think should be reproduced.  
[Note: [Col. 1876D] Archives of Rupelmonde, no. 990.]

Robert, eldest son of the Count of Flanders, and John, Lord of Namur, sons of the said count, to their good Master James Bieck and Lord Michael As Clokettes, [Col. 1877A] residing at the Roman court for the said count, greeting and good will.

We send you, enclosed with these letters, the transcript of a letter which John of Menin, knight, received at Piacenza from our aforesaid dear lord and father. In it you will see—and it is indeed true—that there are several matters causing great injury to my lord, and that it is urgently necessary for the intention of our holy father the pope to be known, made manifest, and maintained; and that the Bishop of Vicenza, or some other suitable man, should be sent promptly into the country, in order to have the truce or suspension observed, to redress the encroachments which have been and will be made against it, and to restore matters to their proper state. Therefore we command and request you to speak, and have others speak, with the Lord of Parma—[Note: [Col. 1877D] Gerard Bianchi, canon of Parma, a celebrated jurist. He had been created cardinal by Pope Nicholas III.]—to whom we send letters, with our other friends, and with the pope; and to procure a swift remedy, for the matter is in great distress and danger and cannot remain [Col. 1877B] thus for long.

For your information, we recall and set before you the articles contained in the aforesaid letters. First, concerning the presentation of benefices: our holy father the apostolic pope has ordered that matters remain pending and without prejudice until it can be seen how matters shall proceed and what end may be put to the principal dispute between the king and my lord, in which the pope, by his grace, wishes to intervene. Now it appears reasonable that the prelates ought to do nothing in this matter to the prejudice of presentations, of those who are to present, or of those who may wish to present; and that the pope’s will should appear in this regard by his bull, with an executor appointed by him; otherwise the prelates will have reason to say that they do not know the pope’s will in the matter.

Likewise, concerning the heirs of those who have not submitted to the king and have remained with our dear lord and father, and concerning the property which they possessed [Col. 1877C] in obedience to our dear lord before the truce: it is plainly an act by which the French act against the truce or suspension. And when they say that, because they have Bruges and Courtrai or other good towns in Flanders, they should possess the castellany and the surrounding district as members following their head, they are wrong to say this and invent sophistical pretexts, having no basis in reason, in order to proceed against the truce and defraud the agreements of the truce. For it is true, and you know it, that Bruges is a town enfranchised by the ancestors of our dear lord and father and by my lord himself. Within its prescribed bounds it has aldermen and administrators who, outside those bounds, have no jurisdiction, judgment, administration, or power; they represent in no respect the community of the country outside; they are not of its body and cannot bind it, nor perform an act or misdeed for which the latter may be held liable. And if they submitted to the king through their malice or of their own will, [Col. 1877D] this does not concern those outside; consequently the king has acquired no right over those who have not submitted or attached themselves to the king’s party, nor against my lord, to whom the town and country belong, save where they have made an agreement with the king. They did not stand in the place of the count and had no power to do anything in the count’s name that could be prejudicial to him; and he was displeased by what the people of Bruges did as soon as he learned of it, and will be displeased forever.

The people of the castellany and district of Bruges are another body altogether, [Col. 1878A] wholly separate from the people of Bruges. They have aldermen of their own, and an aldermanry, law, and customs distinct from those within the town. The same is true of Courtrai, Lille, the other towns, and the outlying castellanies. These facts are notorious, and you, being of the country, know them. Hence those of the castellanies and the country outside ought not to bear or follow the act of those within the towns, any more than those within ought to bear or follow the act of those outside; for, as has been said, the one and the other are subject to entirely different conditions and laws, and have different judges and administrators.

Likewise, in the matter of Rosnay, they act against the truce, since my lord was in possession of it at the beginning of the truce; and, moreover, while a dispute remains between the two overseers of the truce, it concerns my lord and he wishes the matter to be held in common custody during the dispute. He has made no claim upon the Lord of Nielle, nor does he wish to do so.

Concerning the renewal of the sentences by the Bishop of [Col. 1878B] Tournai, he ought well to refrain while the question is pending. For although the pope has appointed judges in it, the principal question between the king and my lord will necessarily be touched upon and raised in the prosecution of the suit; and this is contrary to the pope’s intention, since he wishes that, for this cause, no period should run against the appeals. If it pleased the pope, it would be good to have his bull and an executor in this matter, especially concerning the bishop’s compelling the appellants and their adherents to renounce their appeals. This is greatly contrary to the reverence and obedience which he owes and has sworn to the Church of Rome. This bishop has committed many outrages and does so every day, relying entirely upon the king’s support and upon the great wealth which he has seized and stolen in the land of Flanders through his bishopric.  
[Note: [Col. 1877D] That is: within his bishopric.]  
It would be very desirable that he could be troubled before the pope, and that the pope should make him suffer, for he has well deserved it.  
[Note: [Col. 1877D] The bishop of Tournai was John of Vassoigne, chancellor of the King of France.]

Likewise, concerning the two fifths which the king seeks to have, and the seizures he makes on their account: the pope’s intention is that the [Col. 1878C] king should not have them, but that they should be paid to the Temple. If the pope would issue letters concerning this, so that our people might not be distrained by the king or his men—who are their enemies and ours—and command our dear lord and father that you and we should assist the executors in levying them by our secular power, he would do well; and we would make the pope’s will plainly known in the matter.

Concerning the release of the Lord of Blanmont and the others held contrary to the agreement of the truce, the pretext concerning the King of Scotland is not true. Nothing was ever said about the King of Scotland; and a matter as considerable and noteworthy as the King of Scotland cannot be understood under general words concerning the release or ransom of prisoners on either side.  
[Note: [Col. 1877D] Philip the Fair refused to restore liberty to Henry of Blanmont on the pretext that Edward I held John Balliol captive, he having become Edward’s prisoner after the battle of Dunbar. It was answered that the general clause of the truce, “all prisoners on this side and that,” could not extend to a prisoner as illustrious as the King of Scotland. John Balliol was handed over at Wissant to the Bishop of Vicenza on 18 July 1299. (RYMER, I, III, p. 210.)]

For God’s sake, good lords, we beg you to be diligent and swift in these affairs, for there is need of it. On the other hand, my lord has informed us that the cross of my lady has certainly been redeemed by you, Lord Michael, or by one of you, for 600 pounds. It would please my lord greatly if you could do it for less. Deduct all that you can, and inform my lord what you have done in the matter. My lord has also informed us that we should learn from you two what you have done with the money which the receiver delivered to you, Lord Michael, since you last departed from Flanders. Therefore write jointly to my lord [Col. 1879A] what has been done with it.

Lords, you know that a little before we left Rome, we took counsel with the Friars Preacher concerning the affairs against the king. There the demand made by Lord Baissans was reviewed, as was the proposal that the Roman council should make another demand. Before entering upon the suit, certain persons said that, on my lord’s behalf, a monition should be made to the king on account of sin, according to the words of the Gospel contained in a decretal. Master James—that is, Master James of the Castle—[Note: [Col. 1879D] It had previously been written: “Master James, the fat and snub-nosed one, whose name we do not remember.”] was to prepare a written document clearly setting out the procedure and terms, and how this monition ought to proceed. Take counsel and agreement whether to proceed with this monition, and how and through whom. Lord Bietremius of Capua was likewise to send us a written document concerning our procedure and our affair.  
[Note: [Col. 1879D] Bartholomew of Capua, logothete of the kingdom of Sicily and papal notary.]  
Obtain and have all these matters in writing, and send them to us [Col. 1879B] as soon as possible; meanwhile keep copies with yourselves in case the messenger does not reach us.

Likewise, you know that concerning the submission which we have made to the pope, saving my lord’s honour and estate, we gave him a procuration; and the pope wishes to have another, principally speaking of my lord’s case. My lord has therefore sent us two procurations. One expressly states, at the end of its tenor, that my lord holds as approved and ratified what has been done by us up to the present, and is dated at the time when it was issued. The other procuration does not contain these words, but is entirely simple in other respects, similar [Note: [Col. 1879D] Similar.] to the one dated at the time of the first procuration delivered to the pope and left with the notary. Take counsel concerning these two procurations and give the pope the one which will better please him, for my lord wishes to do his will, and so do we to the extent of our power. Ensure that, concerning [Col. 1879C] that submission, you have a public instrument expressly stating that, since the pope must preserve my lord’s honour and estate therein, the submission is made in his person and that the pope has received it thus. Also make clear, if you can, whether he undertakes it as pope, in the name of his dignity, so that the submission remains vested in the person of his successor who shall be pope, or in his own individual person, as in Pope Benedict.  
[Note: [Col. 1879D] Here a sentence has been erased: “And also have it made clear that the submission is void if the king does not wish to agree to it, so that my lord is not bound forever [Col. 1880D] while the king remains free at his pleasure.”]

Lords, for God’s sake and out of charity, as we told you when departing, conduct amicably and jointly, by agreement, the matters which you have in hand; and bear yourselves well together, as is fitting for the advancement and security of the affairs which you have in hand and which daily come to and increase among you, and for the honour of persons such as you are. We believe that you have done so and ought to do so in the future; for, lords, the affairs of messengers who are not in agreement are in very perilous hands. If there is anything between you by which one is not well satisfied with the other, inform us or one of us, and we shall provide such a remedy that you shall be satisfied if you are not in the wrong.

We also send you a sealed letter from my lord to the pope, a procuration from my lady, and a sealed letter for our brother. We further send you open and recent grievances, [Col. 1880A] by which it appears that the people of the King of France observe no truce—not because we are yet complaining of this to the pope, but so that the pope may send someone more promptly into the country to enforce the truce and redress the wrongs committed. Master Alexander of Ghent died at Fornovo on Saint Lawrence’s Day. Do not pursue any petition for him; but pursue the others and expedite them to the utmost of your power. Inform my lord or us promptly what you have done concerning the aforesaid affairs and others, and of news from the court.

We further inform you that we have sent a merchant’s letter of the company of the Magi [lacuna] to their associates residing at the Roman court; by that letter [lacuna] Lord Guy Bardi of Florence, knight, is to receive, or cause to be received, at Rome, and by that letter we are to have 4,000 gold florins. Therefore, Lord Michael, we command you to take from it up to 600 pounds for [Col. 1880B] redeeming my lady’s cross, as you have reported to our aforesaid dear lord and father, unless you can do it for less; for if you can do it for less, it would greatly please our aforesaid dear lord and father, as he has instructed us, and as we instruct the said lord. Order him to deliver it to you, and let him retain the remainder for what he lent us at Florence on a previous occasion for our expenses.

We also send you a transcript of a letter which our dear lord and father sends to our lord Gerard of Parma. For under the agreement of the truce the King of France cannot make an alliance with anyone while the truce endures; yet the King of France has newly allied himself with our nephew, the Count of Holland, [Note: [Col. 1880D] John of Avesnes had recovered the guardianship of the young Count of Holland, and it was doubtless through his influence that Guy of Dampierre’s alliance was sacrificed for that of Philip the Fair.] as you may see from the above-mentioned letters. Thus it appears that the king observes neither faith, nor letters, nor truces. Have this said and shown to the said Lord Gerard, and we earnestly request him to be willing to hear these [Col. 1880C] things. Let us have an answer about everything.

Likewise, we ask you to have a citation drawn up and that summons formulated, if it is necessary to summon the King of France. And for God’s sake, as soon as you know, or can learn, the answer which the king will have made to the pope, inform us without delay. May God keep you. Written at Baume [Note: [Col. 1880D] Baume-les-Dames, near Besançon.] on the Tuesday after the Nativity of Our Lady; and deliver the messengers as quickly as you can, for Malis has business at Boulogne-le-Gras, as he has said.  
[Note: [Col. 1880D] Archives of Rupelmonde. Nos. 1008 and 809 must be joined: they are two parts of the same letter.]

We have seen Robert of Béthune go, after the pope’s sentence, to the palace of Saint Sabina in order to declare to the English ambassadors that he still hopes Edward I will fulfil his commitments. Guy of Dampierre, following his example, makes a new effort with the King of England, in whom, [Col. 1880D] as he himself says, he places his final hopes.

To the very high and puissant prince, his very dear and beloved lord, Lord Edward, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland and Duke of Aquitaine, Guy, Count of Flanders and Marquis of Namur, greeting and readiness to do his pleasure according to his power, as is right.

[Col. 1881A] Very dear lord, the very great grief and anguish of heart which I see with my own eyes, and which is also reported to me every day, that the King of France and his people inflict upon me, move me to send so often to you, as to him in whom, after God, I place my supreme confidence and hope: if I am to obtain relief, it will come to me through you. Very dear lord, briefly, the injuries are such that the King of France and his people observe nothing of the suspension which you made, but act against it completely every day. For, lord, by the words contained in the suspension—“he who holds, holds and must continue to hold during the suspension”—those of my land who remained mine, and who have always remained with me, and who until now have reasonably and peaceably remained in possession and enjoyment of what was theirs, have had all the goods which they held on their lands seized by the king this August; and he claims to hold them all himself, saying that they ought to belong [Col. 1881B] to him, especially our goods, in several places.

Dear lord, concerning these injuries and others, Lord Geoffrey of Geneville spoke fully to the constable, and a day was appointed at Arras, where the king was to send knights skilled in arms and acquainted with the law of war, and learned men in law, and we were to send the like. Lord, to that meeting, which was held on the Tuesday in the octave of the Magdalene, we sent knights and clerks. We had good confidence that, if the king’s people wished to consider justice according to the words of the suspension, our right would be preserved. But, lord, this could not be, for although the knights on either side had agreed well, the agreement could not stand. Rather, the constable said that the matter had to remain as he had caused it to be put in writing, and that we should accept it if we wished; and if we did not wish it, we should leave it, for nothing else would be done, whether it was wrong or right. Lord, we send you [Col. 1881C] enclosed in this letter the document as he caused it to be made.

When our people had seen this document, they tried to reach an agreement in some way. Yielding a great part of our right, they prepared another document and, on the advice of Lord Geoffrey, presented it to the constable and the king’s people. Lord, we likewise send this document enclosed in these letters. But this document did not please them; they continued to say that they would do nothing else for us. Certainly, lord, these words are very harsh, and their acts are very grievous to us and our people. We are losing many people who had remained ours, and are in danger of losing more.

Very dear lord, in addition to all these aforesaid injuries, very harsh news has come to us from Rome, which has greatly alarmed us, the people of our land, and all our friends. Lord, it is that the pope has proclaimed peace between you and the King of France, and alliances by marriages, without making our peace with yours. Since this news came to us, the king’s people have tried, and every day try, to break the suspension; they seize our towns, kill our people, take their goods in the fields and houses, seize the aldermen of our towns and put them in prison, and through fear and constraint of imprisonment make them swear fealty to the king.

Certainly, lord, concerning this I need not write many words to you; for certainly I shall never believe, nor have I ever believed, that I should fail to find in you comfort and aid, and that you will always fulfil your duty toward me according to the agreements between you and me. And, very dear lord, by the mercy of Our Lord, may you have compassion on me and [Col. 1882A] upon my estate, and may you comfort me, as one in whom I have placed my estate and honour.

Dear lord, after the things written above, our dear and faithful Waleran, Lord of Montjoie and Fauquemont, returned to us from the Duke of Austria, who has been peaceably elected King of Germany by all the electors unanimously and has appointed the day of his coronation at Aachen for the Sunday after the [lacuna] of August. He has told us for certain that the aforesaid king has a very great desire to make alliances with you by marriages and in all other good ways, and with us also; and that he shows a strong disposition to maintain these affairs, which would bring honour and profit to you and to us. Nor, lord, does he maintain that he wishes to receive advantage or benefit from you or anyone else, as the said Lord of Fauquemont has told us. Know, lord, that he has already sent to us and to our nephew of Hainaut, to settle the [Col. 1882B] discord between us two; and he wishes without fail that there should be peace, and desires above all that we should be at his coronation at Aachen in order to reconcile us together, for in every way he wishes that peace should be made.

Dear lord, I therefore request and pray you to consider and weigh all these things for your honour and ours, for never was there a better opportunity; and do so much that God may thank you for it and we may always be bound to you for it.  
[Note: [Col. 1881] Archives of Flanders, at Lille.]

Edward I’s replies were vague, weak, and unsatisfactory.  
[Note: [Col. 1881] See especially the letter printed in Rymer’s collection of acts, I, IV, p. 1.]  
He felt all the less inclined to help Guy of Dampierre because he saw him drawing nearer to his fall.

The letters which the Count of Flanders received from Rome were scarcely more favourable. Those which [Col. 1882C] we place before our readers cover the five months which elapsed from 19 February 1298 (old style) to 23 July 1299.

Very dear lord, I have waited for the messenger mentioned in the last letters which you sent me, and who was to come promptly after them. I am greatly surprised that he has not arrived. For the cardinals often ask me for news of how your affairs are going in your land, and I cannot answer them well; this grieves me. Certainly, lord, the king has so corrupted the court that scarcely anyone there dares openly to say anything to him except praise; but everyone knows and understands that this is the sovereign’s will. Dear lord, I have laboured, and still labour to the best of my power, that some of your privileges might be renewed; but at present I find no such favour as I should wish. Dear lord, I send you a letter [Col. 1882D] which has been much handled, disputed, and obstructed, and only with great difficulty and [lacuna] obtained. Know that, among the letters which you instructed me to procure against the Bishop of Thérouanne, there was only one by which one might lawfully [lacuna] a letter of justice; it was prepared and opposed at the hearing by the bishop’s procurator. And thereupon [lacuna] the affair required that the pope should command these letters; when he had seen them, he said that he did not wish them to pass and retained them. He said that he wished the [lacuna] of the prosecution not to run against you, and that this should be without prejudice to you. I requested and still request that we have his bull on this point; but I cannot yet obtain it, nor do I know whether I shall be able to do so, because of the small favour which you now find with him. In every event I have entered a protest [Col. 1883A] before the auditor of objections and have his letters concerning it.

Dear lord, if it please you, send more securely to the court, and send letters to the pope and cardinals; and, if there are no secrets in them and it please you, send me their transcripts, so that, if I am questioned about them, I may pursue the matter. May Our Lord keep you and grant you good life. Written at the Lateran, on the Thursday after Septuagesima.  
[Note: [Col. 1883C] Archives of Flanders, at Lille (19 February 1298, [Col. 1883D] old style).]

Not only did Philip the Fair’s influence dominate the Roman court, but the Count of Hainaut also took advantage of Guy of Dampierre’s misfortunes to claim the County of Flanders.

Very dear lord, by several letters I have informed you of the state of the court and of your affairs, which had changed very little when these letters were written, except that, for the present, I have prevented the letter which your nephew, the Lord of Hainaut, sought to procure against [Col. 1883B] you. I have told Lord Guy and the others at court who support him that, if they let such a letter pass, I too shall procure one in your name against him concerning the whole county, and that I have command to do so.  
[Note: [Col. 1883D] This must be understood in the sense that Guy of Dampierre threatened John of Avesnes with claiming the County of Hainaut if the latter disputed the County of Flanders with him. John of Avesnes had, in 1297, borne the arms of the Counts of Flanders, and he hoped that Philip the Fair would revoke in his favour the arbitral sentence of 1246. He therefore multiplied his efforts for several years to establish fully the legitimacy of the hereditary rights based on the marriage of Bouchard of Avesnes and Margaret of Constantinople. Several important memoranda from this period are preserved in the Archives of Lille. One memorandum reads:

“Margaret, led by evil counsel, especially that of her sister Countess Joan, who had conceived a great hatred against her said husband Bouchard because of the war, turned aside to Lord William of Domnapetra and went with him, and entrusted to him her sons John and Baldwin, whom William himself held in prison for about ten years, and inflicted many evils upon them meanwhile, when they had neither guardian nor defender.”

Another memorandum, composed in French, contains the following:

“If anyone should say against the first two children that there was any defect in the marriage of Lord Bouchard and Countess Margaret because the said Lord Bouchard was a subdeacon, or had publicly read the Epistle in churches, or had not solemnly married the aforesaid Countess Margaret, it must be known that before the Council of the Lateran subdeacons had indeed married wives, and their children were legitimate and commonly held as such, and publicly admitted to succession to all honours and all other lawful acts. It must also be known that before the said council not only subdeacons, but acolytes commonly read the Epistles in churches, and still do so.”]

But I would not do this unless you instructed me that you wish me to do it, or unless my lord, your son Lord Philip, advised it. Yet I believe that, through fear that I may do it, they will refrain and forbear from procuring anything against you. I have also, dear lord, spoken with the cardinal who was legate in Germany and whom they claim issued the sentence whose confirmation they seek to procure. He has said that what he did in the matter was done by force and under the compulsion of fear and threats, and that, as soon as he was beyond the power of the King of Germany and his people, he revoked it; he has promised to give me a letter stating that this was so. Master John of Pisa, your procurator, says that you ought to have letters of revocation concerning it. Therefore, [Col. 1883C] dear lord, please inform me of your pleasure and will concerning this and all other matters.

Dear lord, the bearer of these letters is the servant whom my lord, the Lord of Nevers, retained as valet, as I wrote to you formerly; Sir Renier of Pisa was his uncle. Lord, you directed me by your letters to provide him with clothing at two seasons, and I did so at the last All Saints’ Day and at this Easter. You also wished, dear lord, that I should provide for Lord Stephen, the chief usher, and I have done so; but I have done nothing for Lord Giles, because you instructed me in a letter that you would send me a mounted sergeant who would bring clothing and money, but he brought none. Therefore, lord, do as you please.

Dear lord, it would be necessary for you to write to the pope and cardinals [Col. 1884A] in the manner which I formerly wrote to you, and that a new procuration be sent to me, including all your sons; and that the court be supplied with the expenses which it is necessary to make. For it was to depart on the Tuesday after the date of this letter and go to a very wretched and unhealthy place, namely Anagni, the city where the pope was born. Dear lord, may God keep you and all that you love. Written at Rome, on the Wednesday after Easter.  
[Note: [Col. 1884D] Archives of Flanders, at Lille (22 April 1299).]

A letter from John of Menin, reproducing the account of an audience granted by Boniface VIII at Anagni on 13 June 1297, presents the situation in a less threatening aspect; but scarcely have the pope’s words given rise to some hopes than they seem to vanish.

[Col. 1884B] Very high and very noble lords, I, Jean of Menin, your knight, make known to you that on the day when I came to Anagni—namely, the Saturday after Trinity Sunday—I spoke with the pope at great leisure, and laid before him your request upon three matters: first, that you should receive back my lady your daughter; second, that upon surety you should receive back my lord of Blanmont and the other prisoners, according to the terms of the truce; third, that he should cause the truce to be observed towards you, and that what had been done contrary to it should be set right and restored. And I gave him many reasons why this ought to be done for you, and why he ought to attend to it; among others, that, at his request and by his counsel, your children first, on your behalf, and afterwards you yourself when you learned of it, had placed your affairs in his hands, saving your honour, your estate, and your inheritance; and that he had undertaken the matter upon those terms, and had told your children, when they departed from him, that he would cause to be done these three things which I requested of him.

Sire, when he had heard me very fully and [Col. 1884C] at great leisure, he answered me at the outset that everything was true as I had told him. And although I told him that the bishop of Vicenza, when requested on your behalf, had said that no matter concerning your affairs had been laid before him, the pope said that he had been asked to have the truce observed. And I believe, so far as I can understand, that it is true that he had been asked generally, but not particularly concerning you; and therefore he does not wish to involve himself particularly in your case. Nevertheless, I am told that the bishop of Vicenza loves you better than he does the king. The pope himself told me that he is a man beyond suspicion. The pope spoke very courteously of you, and said that he would do for you all that he could, and that he had always been very willing to do so, and was now more so than ever before [Note: [Col. 1884D] *Plus ke onques mais*: more than ever.]. He told me to bring him my petitions in writing and your wishes, and he would willingly give them counsel.

On the morning of St John’s night, sire, I brought him my petition. He read it at once and answered that he would take counsel upon it. I then thought that I should conduct your affair very well and quickly, because I was asking what was right, because it was what he ought to do, because he acknowledged to me as true everything that I said to him, and because of the fair words he spoke to me and the gracious manner he showed me in your name. But since then I have heard no news of your affairs. I do not know what God will put into his heart, but I no longer have as good a hope as I had at the beginning, nor am I easy in heart. You can well know the reason why my hope fails me, as can your children, who know the court. I shall tell it to you, if it please God and you, soon enough; for in no way shall I put it in writing. Yet, sire, wherever I send letters, my words give good encouragement that a favourable settlement for [Col. 1885A] you will be obtained speedily. But, sire, I do not wish to conceal anything from you concerning your affairs or my heart. You shall therefore speak further, sire, with your children and wherever it seems good to you. It may well happen that the matter will turn out better than I hope; may God grant it.

And if it be thus, sire, that I obtain no gracious settlement for you, there is nothing in the world that I ought to ask of him, either for you or for anyone else; rather, with his leave, I shall depart as best I can. [Note: [Col. 1885D] Archives of Flanders at Lille.]

Nothing came to confirm the hope expressed by Jean of Menin. He regarded his mission as ended and prepared to leave the papal court, disturbed by the escape of the Colonna.

Sire, I make known to you news of the court and of this country: last Friday, the Colonna, who have lost everything—towns and castles alike—and who were kept prisoners by order of the pope in [Col. 1885C] a town called Tyble [Note: [Col. 1885D] Tivoli?], departed from there. They were met by a very large armed force near Rome, and at court no one knows certainly what has become of them. [Note: [Col. 1885D] See the *Chronicle* of William of Nangis, 1299.] The pope is troubled by this, and there is fear of great disorder in the country.

On the Saturday before St Peter and St Paul, the king of Aragon, the duke of Calabria, and my lord Philip, your son, together with all the forces the king of Sicily could muster, embarked at Naples and sailed towards Sicily. May God protect them. For this reason, sire, my lord Philip was unable to leave the country and come to court on your behalf. I myself went as far as the bridge of Cypraeu [Note: [Col. 1885D] Ceprano, in the Terra di Lavoro.] to speak with him where he was, near Naples; but illness overcame me, so that I could not proceed. I sent him in writing the affairs for which you had sent me to court, and I withdrew very slowly towards Anagni.

In Lombardy, sire, there is great war, and there was when I passed through: between the marquis [Col. 1885D] of Montferrat, the marquis of Este, and those of Cremona [Note: [Col. 1886D] Crémone.], Pavia, Correggio [Note: [Col. 1886D] Correggio.], and Novara on one side, and the captain and those of Milan [Note: [Col. 1886D] Milan.] on the other. The people of Bologna and Piacenza assist the latter with part of the troops they have sent to those of Milan.

Sire, I am at very great expense at court, both for myself and for my lord Michael, who tells me that he has no money; and I cannot fail him from what I possess. The country here is exceedingly expensive. Please see to it that I have means to obtain money, for there is no week in which we do not spend fifty gold florins or more. Although florins are dear in Flanders because of the currency now in circulation there, they are worth no more at court than they were seven years ago. [Col. 1886A] As of today I have no more than three hundred florins. I have no means either to remain here or to depart from here unless you speedily assist me.

Sire, if I have not obtained a settlement from the pope by the time your messenger returns to me, my waiting here will be worth no more, nor shall I ever be able to bring you any benefit from it. I shall have to leave, unless you send me sealed letters directing me to come to you for your affairs, wherever my own person is required, and to leave your matter in the hands of my lord Michael, your chaplain, who represents you well there, to recall it to mind and pursue it further. Let the letters therefore be properly and carefully drawn up, if it please you to have them made; for neither for me nor for anyone else will the pope do anything except what he wishes.

Know, sire, that it grieves me to remain at court and to spend your resources [Col. 1886B] for so little benefit as I can now accomplish for you there. I can neither remove nor add anything concerning your affairs, and all will be at the pope’s discretion. Sire, my lord Guy of Hainaut, your nephew, is at court seeking some bishopric or dignity. He is not as well supplied with the king of France’s money as people said in Flanders last year; for I understand that he has hands into which to put money, and still spends enough … of his expenses.

It is at the moment when the count of Flanders’s cause appears forever lost that one sees the difficulties emerge which were to divide Boniface VIII from the king of France.

Philip the Fair, who had briefly contemplated raising his brother Charles of Valois to the Empire, was negotiating with Albert of Austria. But Boniface VIII complained of this alliance with a prince whose election he had not approved [Col. 1886C]; and the Flemish ambassadors feared no less the confederation of the king of Germany and the king of France.

Dear sire, the cardinals speak very well for you all, and you have two particular friends: my lord Gerard of Parma and my lord Matthew of Expert [Note: [Col. 1886D] Cardinal Matthew of Acquasparta.]. You also enjoy the court’s favour greatly; but no one has power except the pope alone.

Sire, two hundred florins will be due at the Magdalene feast to my lord Gerard of Parma; and, as I understand, my lord Matthew of Expert was to receive one hundred livres tournois yearly, for three years, one year of which my lord Michael has paid. See that this money is paid, so that what you spend there may be usefully employed. Please attend, sire, to my lord Ponchart’s business. My lord Guy [Note: [Col. 1886D] Gui Bardi. See above, col. 1880.], sire, asks many thousands of florins which he lent [Col. 1886D] for the crusade of Madame, whom God absolve, and another four hundred and fifty florins from the loan he made to my lord your son when he returned from Rome.

Sire, your friends at court, cardinals and others, are very glad, out of love for you, that the treaty of agreement between the king of Germany and the king of France has failed; and I praise God for it. The pope is likewise glad of it, though I do not know why. The pope does not wish him to be called king, but only duke of Austria. I greatly desire, sire, to hear true news that peace will not proceed between the king of France and the king of England, and that the king of England will do towards you what he owes. I believe that peace will not be made, because of a word the pope spoke to me. He told me that long ago [Note: [Col. 1887D] *Très-autan*: for a long time.] he had considered—and still clearly saw—that such great discord as that between the two kings and you could not be pacified unless it were done where all three of you were present in person before him. Therefore, he had considered withdrawing to a suitable place to do this. But during the stay he made at Rome, especially for their affairs and yours, in which he then laboured, illness seized him. He prudently withdrew from the air [Note: [Col. 1887D] *Del er*: from the air, the climate.] in which he had been born, to try whether he might recover in another country. Since then [Note: [Col. 1887D] *Depuis lors.*] illnesses have troubled him greatly and brought him near to death. Even now he is not in a condition to travel out of the country; no one advises it, and without doubt he is greatly weakened and much changed from what he was when we departed from Rome long ago. No one promises that he will live long, [Col. 1887B] or ever regain bodily strength.

When I came before him, he recognized me well and spoke privately with me at length. He said that I need not have brought letters of credence, for he knew well that I came from you. May God grant that he will put his fair demeanour and good words into effect, to your honour and advantage. May Our Lord guard you, sire, in soul and body, and all those who wish you well; and grant you joy from your friends and your enemies.

Dear sire, the king of Aragon, the duke, and my lord Philip your son, with many good men, have already landed in Sicily and, as I understand, have good hope of reconquering the whole country.

These letters were given at Anagni, on the Thursday after the octave of St Peter and St Paul. [Note: [Col. 1887D] Archives of Flanders at Lille (9 July 1299).]

Already in the preceding letter, Jean of Menin and Michael As Clokètes had related that the pope had [Col. 1887C] announced his intention of leaving Rome in order to summon before his tribunal the kings of France and England and the count of Flanders. In his eyes this was the only means of calming Europe’s discords. But he was so burdened by age and infirmities that his strength failed the energy of his resolve, and even the air of Anagni, the city where he had been born, could not restore it. Nevertheless, he gathered the cardinals about him and communicated his project to them, saying that if he should meet death in this work of peace and reconciliation, he thought that he could not die better. He had learned with grief that the affairs of Flanders received no peaceful settlement; and other letters informed him that Philip the Fair, deaf to his remonstrances, [Col. 1887D] was continuing his negotiations with the king of Germany.

Most dear sire, we make known to you that on the Saturday after the Friday [Note: [Col. 1887D] *Le devenres*: Friday.] when II. of Wettre, our messenger whom we sent to you with our letters, and to our lords your children and to several members of your council, departed from us at Anagni, certain news came to the pope from Sicily: the king of Aragon, the prince of Taranto, and Roger of Lauria, who is admiral of the sea, together with those who were with them, joined battle at sea with the forces of Frederick of Aragon, the Sicilians, and the Genoese who were with them. They captured twenty-two galleys; all those aboard were taken or killed. Eighteen galleys escaped, upon which Frederick was present; and among the men of those eighteen galleys a great number were killed. The duke of Calabria, my lord Philip, and the strength of the knighthood and army remained on land there; those on this side have lost little. [Note: [Col. 1887D] On this battle, see William of Nangis, ed. M. Géraud, I, p. 310.]

For this there was held at Anagni, on the Saturday and Sunday after the octave of St Peter and St Paul, a most grand celebration, and the pope has taken as much joy in it as one could have. He has great hope that the enterprise of reconquering the land will prosper. Since then there has been no news worth reporting.

The pope has appointed [Col. 1888B] my lord Gerard of Parma legate in Apulia, and he will depart from court on the Monday after the feast of the Mazzel. This greatly grieves us, for he was the surest help and comfort we had at court. Sire, on the night of the Division of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1887D] 14 July 1299.], we came before the pope and requested a settlement of your affairs. He answered that he had ordered and instructed my lord Matthew the Red to draw up letters concerning them, and told us to go to him. We asked whether it pleased him that my lord Matthew should explain to us the form of our settlement and the state of your affairs. He answered that it pleased him well.

Afterwards we went to my lord Matthew and told him this. He said that the drafts were already made, but that he would tell us nothing of our affair until he had shown them to the pope. He was to do so on the following day, which he had not yet done when these letters were written; and we do not cease [Col. 1888C] to press him. Sire, we firmly believe that my lord Matthew wishes you much good; but, sire, people charge him with being the slowest and most dilatory man [Note: [Col. 1887D] *Om*: man.] alive, and many a business has been lost in his hands through his delay. The pope, on the other hand, is also very slow when he chooses. At present we think that he will give you a favourable settlement in all that he can do; but certainly, sire, we can tell you nothing yet, and we remain continually in fear of a great postponement. Nothing can hasten my lord Matthew in any matter [Note: [Col. 1888D] *De nulle riens*: in no matter. We have read, p. 26, *sur toutes riens*, that is, “in all matters.”], except as he pleases.

And, sire, if it please you, recall me, Jean, by your letters, for I can do no more for you at court. It may well be that I, Michael, shall return with him, if it is thought well to do so. [Note: [Col. 1888D] By a declaration given at Anagni on 27 September 1299, Michael As Clokettes delegated his powers to Gerard of Ferlin, Gilles As Clokettes, etc. Archives of the Council of Flanders at Ghent.]

Sire, after what is contained above had been written, certain news came to the pope, along with letters from the bishop of Vicenza; some cardinals themselves also received letters: the king of France and the king of England have made peace together and have entirely agreed and consented to what the pope ordained and pronounced, in the presence of their messengers [lacuna] at Rome. The marriage of the king of England is proceeding, and that of his son will be carried out according to what the pope has ordained, when the time is suitable. But there was no word, as the letters said, of you, of your lands, or of anything touching you. The king of Scotland and his son have been delivered [Col. 1889A] into the pope’s hands.
