It seems to us, in our small judgment—and so it seems to many people—that the king of France has helped the king of Scotland, of whom there was never any mention either in the war or in the truces, better than the king of England has helped you, who have been included in the war and the truces, and through whom the king of England returned to his own country. Immediately after this news, the pope summoned the cardinals and showed them this affair. When the letters had been read, the pope said:

> “Lords, you see that nothing has been done or negotiated concerning the count of Flanders, which grieves us. But, if God please, by another way we shall help him and bring all the world to peace. If we can, we would willingly go beyond the mountains—not into the land of either king, but into the land of our dear son, the king of Sicily, or into our patrimony, our county of Venice. And if we died on the way, we should think that we died well.”

And, sire, [Col. 1889B] all this still seems to us to be merely words. We do not know whether the arrangement of our affairs, which has been begun as stated above, will be changed because of this news.

Sire, moreover, on the day of the Division of the Apostles, we learned from my lord Matthew of Acquasparta, the cardinal [Note: [Col. 1889D] This is again Cardinal Matthew of Acquasparta, elsewhere called Cardinal of Expert.], that he had received letters saying that the messengers of the king of Germany were at Paris to negotiate an agreement with the king of France. Since then, similar news has come: their men of the great council are, at the time these letters are given, again at Neufchâteau in Lorraine, to negotiate and conclude an agreement together. Concerning this, sire, if we dared say so with leave, we are greatly astonished that we know nothing of your position except through strangers; and it seems that it would be more fitting for the cardinals and your friends to know it from your side, rather than that we should have to learn it from them, if there is anything which you think fit to communicate.

[Col. 1889C] Dear sire, we further make known to you that when I, Jean of Menin, came to court, I, Michael, had neither money nor resources, and I was heavily burdened—and still am—with great debt. Thus we have had to live and continue to incur debts, which I, Jean of Menin, brought to court. We have no means to live more than three weeks after the date of these letters. We seek funding everywhere and can find none; therefore we are in great distress. For God’s sake, sire, give us aid, and quickly, for the need is very great. My lord Gerard of Parma earnestly asks you, sire, to recommend to your favour the affairs of the provost of Bruges. Sire, may Jesus Christ guard you.

Given at Anagni, the day after the Mazzel. [Note: [Col. 1889D] Archives of Flanders at Lille (23 July 1299).]

The count of Flanders replied to Jean of Menin and Michael As Clokettes in the first days [Col. 1889D] of August. He told them that peace had been made between Edward I and Philip the Fair, and that he had no refuge remaining except the pope’s protection.

Guy, count of Flanders and marquis of Namur, to his dear and faithful knight, my lord Jean of Menin, greeting and affection.

We make known to you that the bishop of [Col. 1890A] Vicenza has been in France and in England, and matters have already advanced so far that peace exists between the two kings. Peace has been made in England [Note: [Col. 1889D] A treaty of peace between the kings of France and England had been concluded at Montreuil on 19 June 1299. It states: “The bishop of Vicenza shall go to England and shall make known to the said king of England and to his son the things agreed, which the king and his son are bound to swear.” Rymer, I, [Col. 1890D] III, p. 208.]; the marriages of the king of England and of his son are being arranged, and the king of England and his son have sworn to them. [Note: [Col. 1890D] The oath of the king of England is dated 14 July 1299. Rymer, I, III, p. 210.]

Our son William has been in England to learn the king’s intention. From his reply it seems to us that we shall have little comfort, for he answers that he will always do towards us what he ought. Yet he does not show this to us by deeds, because his actions, it seems to us, contradict his words. He wishes to base himself, and does so altogether, upon the pope’s indulgence and dispensation. As for what he owes us, as you know, namely sixty thousand livres every year [Note: [Col. 1890D] By the treaty of 7 January 1296, old style, Edward I had undertaken to pay the count of Flanders annually 60,000 black livres tournois for as long as the war lasted.], he keeps no agreement with us. Rather, we understand from some of his men that he owes us nothing of the sixty thousand livres, because he says that a truce [Col. 1890B] is not war. Thus in every way he disappoints us, and this entirely through the favours which the pope has granted him and the king of France, such as tenths and other favours, which tend altogether to our destruction.

On the other hand, because the king of Germany sees that the king of France and the king of England enjoy such great favour with the pope, he fears—and we ourselves fear greatly—that he will not ally himself with us because of fear of him. All these troubles arise from the court of Rome, in which we are now so entangled. The pope, who ought to hold God’s place on earth and to be an author of peace as he should be, is not such; rather, he is an author of perpetual war, which will never end. We do not think that either we, our predecessors, or the house of Flanders have deserved this from this court.

Therefore we command you to speak with the cardinals, where you see it fit, [Col. 1890C] and to set forth these our grievances, as you will know better how to do than we can write to you. Likewise make them known to Philip our son, to whom we do not write, because you will speak well to him on our behalf. Upon this, promptly let us know what you advise should be done, and what you can learn of the pope’s intention and of the cardinals’. Know that we are greatly astonished that, since you left us, we have had no news from you. Show these letters to Philip our son, and tell him that we do not write to him because of the danger that letters may be intercepted. Also tell him from us that he should remain near the court in this our need and should not depart.

Know that if the pope fails us [Note: [Col. 1890D] *Nous faut*: fails us.], we are altogether overthrown, for we have no hope in the kings of England and Germany. Therefore diligently ascertain what the pope’s purpose is. If the truce is prolonged, [Col. 1890D] that will be our destruction, unless it is kept towards us better than it has been until now. We would indeed need to know this and be provided for in time. Quickly and without delay let us know what you have learned. Show these letters also to my lord Michael, our chaplain, and take counsel together in all matters. [Note: [Col. 1890D] Archives of Flanders at Lille.]

The bishop of Vicenza, whom the pope had charged with presiding over the conclusion of the peace treaty [Col. 1891A] between Edward I and Philip the Fair, soon went to Flanders. [Note: [Col. 1891C] On 14 July 1299 the bishop of Vicenza had received Edward I’s oath at Canterbury. In August he went near Chartres to receive likewise that of Philip the Fair. His journey to Flanders took place only three months later. On 13 November Robert of Béthune wrote to excuse himself for being unable to come to meet him: *quod partes Gallicanae neque nobis neque nostris ad praesens propter regiam potestatem sunt tutae*—“because the French regions are presently safe neither for us nor for ours, owing to royal power.” He ended his letter with these words: *Scriptum apud Warnestun, oppidum combustum, die Veneris post festum beati Martini hyemalis*—“Written at Warnestun, a burned town, on the Friday after the feast of blessed Martin in winter.” Towards the end of July 1297 Charles of Valois had sacked the town of Warneton, and “it was burned completely,” says a manuscript chronicle, “and no town or house remained from there as far as Lille.”]

Everything suggests that it was at this time, and probably from the bishop’s own hands, that Guy of Dampierre received a bull in which Boniface VIII, attributing his rebellion to pride, urged him to remove every cause of discord before the end of the truces—expiring on 6 January 1299, old style—if he wished to leave his inheritance to his descendants. [Note: [Col. 1891D] Martène, *Collection amplissima*, I, col. 1305. Other papal letters dated 21 July 1299 are found in the archives of the Council of Flanders. [Col. 1892C] In them Boniface VIII likewise urged Robert of Béthune to observe the truce concluded between the kings of France and England.]

The bishop of Vicenza had stopped at Bruges, still under French power, and his first concern had been to order that the truce be observed [Note: [Col. 1892D] Several conferences concerning the protection owed to commerce had already taken place. Guy of Dampierre was represented there by Jean of Bouchavesnes and Philip of Maldeghem. Charter of 20 March 1298, old style. Archives of the Council of Flanders.], and that prisoners from the battle of Furnes be released upon the giving of hostages, in accordance with the agreement made at Paris. [Note: [Col. 1892D] Archives of Rupelmonde.] The count [Col. 1891B] was obliged to restore the king’s coins that had been seized; they were henceforth to circulate in Flanders. His own coinage was to be accepted, though at a reduced value, in payment of what was owed to the king. In December, the bishop of Vicenza attended conferences between deputies of the king and of the count. The following is how Master Bassan, Baissan, or Barssien—who, as a man of law, had accompanied Robert of Béthune to Rome—reported what had occurred to the count of Flanders:

Very dear sire, know that I remained with your men until last Saturday in order to attend the sessions before the bishop of Vicenza. Know well that concerning several articles that touch you deeply, there was great dispute between your men and the king’s men before the said bishop and the constable of France, who was present at this dispute. Many words were spoken by them and by my lord Simon of Melun, which were greatly to your disadvantage, especially concerning your striking coin in your land. They said that you could not do this, because you were neither possessed nor seised of the right to strike coin in your land, which they say belongs to the kingdom of France, in time of war and in time of truce. They therefore said that your coinage ought in no manner to circulate in the kingdom of France, nor in the land held by the king of France in Flanders, especially because they say that your money is false.

I told them that they did no great honour to the king of France by acknowledging in their words that the king’s coinage was not good, since your money was made according to the [Col. 1892A] standard of the said king of France. I said that I and our men were ready to make an assay by fire [Note: [Col. 1892D] By fire.] of each coinage. On other occasions we had appeared with your moneyers and your money at specified sessions, but we could never agree to conduct the assay. Since you refused it, it is clear that our money is as good as, or better than, the money of the said king. By this offer and answer, the said bishop seemed well satisfied.

There were many other disputes between your men and the king’s men, which I could not write as well as I could recount orally. Nevertheless, the final arrangement was that they must accept your coinage at six Parisian deniers in payment of what is owed to them; that your coinage may circulate throughout the kingdom of France without seizure, provided it is sealed with another’s seal than that of the bearer, and provided that the bag in which the said coinage is found is not opened once it has been found sealed. Know well that the bailiff of Damme told me that this point alone vexes you to the amount of ten thousand livres in this year.

Know that uncoined silver (*argent en plait*) could be carried at will, and that what has been seized from you will be returned at a valuation of sixty-five sous per mark. You must restore the king’s coinage which your men have detained and seized in your land. Several other matters have been agreed by the said bishop; I send you the copy enclosed in this letter.

Furthermore, know, sire, that the receivers and I have arranged that my lord Baldwin of Quadypre [Note: [Col. 1892D] Baldwin of Quaetypre, called the Younger. He is probably the person named in Edward I’s letter of 17 March 1299, old style, as Baldwin of Channe.] is to go to the king of England, to speak with him and with the king of Germany’s men concerning what you know has been arranged. He has taken with him in writing the information which he is to state, and he is to depart for England next Monday [Note: [Col. 1892D] *Deluns*: Monday.] to come. We have likewise prepared for him the form of what he is to say to the king of Germany and to the count of Savoy. To God, who guards you. Send me your wishes; I am ready to act.

[Col. 1892C] Given at Ghent, on the Sunday after St Thomas’s Day. Know further that it has been ordered that the commissions which have been made must be completed between now and the Magdalene feast. We therefore advise you to dispatch the scholasticus, so that he may complete the commissions of the inquiries which you have in hand; otherwise, know that he may bring you great peril. [Note: [Col. 1892D] Archives of Rupelmonde, no. 1024 (27 December 1299).]

Guy of Dampierre had withdrawn to the castle of Rupelmonde. [Note: [Col. 1892D] At an assembly of deputies of the country [Col. 1893D] held at Oudenaarde on 3 November 1299, Guy of Dampierre had surrendered the government to his eldest son, Robert of Béthune. By a charter of the following March, he declared that he would be content with the revenues of Rupelmonde.] Betrayed by his allies, Edward I and Albert of Austria; attacked by his nephew, the count of Hainaut; abandoned even by his grandsons, the duke of Brabant and the count of Holland, he had handed his sword to the lord of Moerseke: a sad and supreme acknowledgment of the futility of his resistance and the powerlessness of his efforts.

Nothing is more moving than the letter which Philip [Col. 1893A] of Thiette addressed to the eldest of his brothers on 11 November 1299 from the distant shores of Sicily:

To the very high and noble man, my lord Robert, eldest son of my lord the count of Flanders, lord of Béthune, his most dear lord and brother, Philip, his brother, commends himself to him and stands ready for all his good pleasure.

Dear lord, I received the letters that you sent me, and I am greatly rejoiced when I hear of your good condition, which may Our Lord maintain in prosperity and honour. And as for myself, dear lord, know that I had arranged to leave everything in order to go and pursue my lord our father’s affairs at the court of Rome; but I was advised—both by the king and by my other lords and friends on this side—and the cardinals themselves told his procurators at court, that the pope would be more favourable to the affairs if I were in the service of the Church than if I were at court, and that I should settle them more quickly. [Col. 1893B] Had I thought that they would not prosper the better for it, I should have preferred to be at court to pursue them rather than where I am. For know, dear lord, that I am greatly distressed at heart, both because of the affairs on your side, which have not gone forward, and because of the great danger and great confusion in which we are, unless God helps us. And may Our Lord do His will, in whose hand we all are. Comfort me often, if it please you, with news of your good condition; tell me all your wishes, and I am . . . . . . . ready to do what lies in my power. And I sealed these letters with my ring, because I did not have our proper seal with me.

Immediately thereafter Philip of Thiette added these lines, the expression of a wish which the future was to fulfil only through a thousand perils.

May Our Lord God grant that I may yet see you again in joy! And know, lord, that I greatly [Col. 1893C] rejoice in this, and am in great anguish because I cannot . . . . . . . give counsel in the affairs of my lord our father. And had I wished to remain in order to pursue them, as I strove to do to the utmost of my power . . . . . . . or better to leave; but I shall return there as soon as I can, in order to devote to it all the counsel and help that I can . . . . . . . is right. And know, lord, that we have gained several good towns and castles in Sicily, with some hardship . . . . . . . and we hope that the whole country will come under obedience.

Written at Catania in Sicily, on the feast of St Martin in winter.  
[Note: [Col. 1893D] Archives of Flanders, at Lille.]

On the other side of the Alps, a voice no less sorrowful was raised in reply to him: that of Robert of Béthune, who informed the Flemish ambassadors at Rome that the truces had been broken [Col. 1893D] and that Charles of Valois had already seized Douai, nothing being able to withstand his numerous men-at-arms.

Robert, firstborn son of the Count of Flanders, holding the free [Col. 1894A] administration of the county of Flanders, advocate of Arras, lord of Béthune and Dendermonde, to his beloved and faithful lords John of Menin, knight and his counsellor, and Michael As Clokettes, his most dear chaplain, greetings with the affection of sincere love.

We have carefully read the letters which you wrote to our most dear father and to us. Having considered them, we write to you that you should finally procure for us the love and favour of the supreme pontiff and of the cardinals, and that they should assist us in the great peril in which we stand—especially since the King of France and his men, contrary to the extension of the truces by the most holy pontiff, have entered the land of Flanders for our destruction and that of our land. This ought greatly to move the supreme pontiff and the cardinals, because the said king is wholly disobedient to the commands of the supreme pontiff and of the Roman Church.

Concerning that disobedience of the said king, and many other matters which you are to set forth to the said supreme pontiff, we are sending you, for your information, in a certain [Col. 1894B] schedule enclosed with this letter, several points set out article by article. You are to press these matters with the utmost diligence before the supreme pontiff, especially to learn in what condition the same supreme pontiff intends that we should remain, and what remedy he wishes to apply at present and immediately to our affairs. On the aforesaid matters we are writing letters to the said supreme pontiff; please press most urgently for an answer to them. We likewise send you an enclosed copy of those letters.

Pursue our affairs before the supreme pontiff and the cardinals, as is fitting, diligently from day to day and with every care; for, as you can see, the affair in its present state admits of no delay whatsoever without the complete overthrow of our entire position. With respect to the money and service concerning which you wrote to us, we have made provision and shall make provision with all our power; but you know that we cannot so quickly do what we wished, because we must incur many and diverse expenses [Col. 1894C] in fortifying and defending our land. Nevertheless, we send you the sum of one thousand five hundred florins for your necessities and for payment of the cardinals’ pensions. You should know that, if the king had observed the truces extended by the lord pope and had not risen against us by force of arms, we should have sent you a larger sum, even for rendering service to the lord pope and the cardinals; but we are obliged to commit so much and so great expenditure to our fortifications that at present we are unable to provide more.

Write back to us as quickly as possible concerning the news you receive at court and the pope’s intentions. Furthermore, know that Lord Charles, the king’s brother, occupied our town of Douai on Wednesday in the feast of the Epiphany, notwithstanding the truces, as you will see more fully in the schedule mentioned above. Take care to notify the lord pope of this.  
[Note: [Col. 1893D] Archives of Flanders, at Lille.]

Charles of Valois, master of Douai, advanced toward [Col. 1893D] Ghent, followed by 6,000 men-at-arms. Nevele and other rich villages were given to the flames, and the port of Damme fell into the hands of the French, who found there only an old woman.  
[Note: [Col. 1893D] Guy of Namur was then at Ypres. From that town, on 3 May, he addressed to Robert of Béthune the following letter, in which bitter reproaches mingle with a picture of Flanders’ unhappy condition:

[Col. 1894D] From Guy, your brother.

Most dear lord, this Sunday, the first day of May, we received your letters, by which you instructed us that we should give no credence to the news that we heard concerning Damme until we had certain news from you. On the Tuesday afterwards, lord, we went to the hall in order to obtain . . . . . some definite information concerning matters of which we had spoken to them; and we found them, lord, greatly dismayed, astonished, sorrowful . . . . . We asked them why they were so sad, and they answered that they had ample cause, because Damme had been surrendered; and it was said that it could never have been taken by force. [Col. 1895C] We asked whether they knew with certainty that it had been surrendered, and in what manner; and they answered, No. We told them that we did not act thus. There they showed us that they had spoken with eight of their commonalty’s most capable men, and had required of them, upon faith and oath, an account of their own condition and that of the whole commune—of their willingness and ability to continue living, and of how they could maintain the town. They told us, lord, that of the eight persons whom they had heard, in the form stated above . . . . . . of thirty persons, all agreed that they saw no means . . . . . by which they could save themselves, unless help and encouragement came from you.

Having said this, lord, they requested our counsel in good faith and loyalty, as men who are sworn to us and we to them, that we should advise them loyally according to their condition, that of the country, and yours. Upon this, lord, we took counsel, and it seemed best to us, since we had no certain news of [Col. 1895D] Damme and of the country, and since the matter seemed to us so grave, that we could not properly advise them without sending to you. We told them that we were sending to you, and that it would please us greatly if they likewise sent their own certain messenger, to show you the matter stated above as they had shown it to us. They are sending, lord, one of their young men to show it to you, as has been said above, so they made us understand. They tell us, lord, that they send you no letter, but that their certain messenger will seek orally from you what they have shown us and what we communicate by this letter.

Lord, be pleased to take good and speedy counsel, as you see that the matter requires, and send back to us and to them your will. In loyalty they have taken counsel with us, and they ask your counsel as their rightful lord; above all things they would be sorrowful if they had to part from you. And, lord, the aldermen say that the lack they have of grain, [Col. 1896C] wine, and other provisions is entirely due to you, because in time of truce they showed you, and had sufficiently shown you several times, that for yourself and your men you ought to make adequate provision in the town. This, lord, has not been done, and the people of the town have all followed your example in making no provision. They also ask that you provide yourselves with men-at-arms to help them and the town; and you have not done so, whence they lay all the blame upon you.

On our return, lord, from the hall, the knights and gentlemen who are with us at Ypres came to us in the chamber. One of them showed a letter in the presence of all, which one of his friends had sent him. The letter stated that Damme had been surrendered, together with Lord of Axel, his son, Lord Gerard de Moor, Alard du Bardelar, and many others of the country; and that the men of Aardenburg had a respite to surrender themselves until the following day, [Col. 1896D] the day of May, and that they were to come and surrender before Thursday, failing which they would never be received. They asked our advice; we advised them to send to you. They are sending, and asked us also to send there.

Thus we ask you, lord, to let them know what your other men have done and what you wish them to do, and to do so by your letters. And as to the affairs of Damme and of the country, which people wish to speak of in our regions . . . . . it is a very great wonder that you have made nothing known to us about them, nor to your good people of the town; for everyone comes to speak to us, and we know nothing to say. Upon all these matters, lord, be pleased to make us certain and to send back your pleasure; and, lord, be pleased to believe William le Pisson concerning what he will tell you by word of mouth. May Our Lord guard you. Written on the third day of May.  
(Archives of the Council of Flanders.)]

All [Col. 1895A] the inhabitants, knowing that Philip the Fair had forbidden their being received to mercy, had fled. A son of the Count of Flanders, William of Dampierre, who had married the daughter of Raoul of Nesle, had abandoned them in order to go to Charles of Valois. Shortly thereafter we see him arrive at Ghent in order to urge his father likewise to place himself in Philip the Fair’s hands. A council composed of the old Count of Flanders’ most faithful friends met; among those present were John of Menin, Geoffrey of Ransières, Gerard de Moor, and the lords of Oudenaarde, Mortagne, Nevele, Roubaix, Verbois, and Bondues. William of Dampierre’s opinion prevailed, and Guy set out for France by way of Tournai and Arras, under the guard [Col. 1895B] of the Counts of Boulogne and Sancerre. Guy arrived in Paris on 24 May 1300. Held for several days at the Châtelet during the festivities for the marriage of Blanche, the king’s sister, to the Duke of Austria, he was soon taken to the court at Compiègne: “For the king,” says the chronicle from which we borrow these details, “considered that he did not wish to leave him so close to himself.”  
[Note: [Col. 1896D] Manuscript of the Library of Burgundy, at Brussels.]

It was at the moment when Ghent’s capitulation completed the conquest of Flanders, and at the moment when Guy of Dampierre gave himself up to Charles of Valois, that the alliance of Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair broke irrevocably. A treaty concluded at Vaucouleurs between the King of France and Albert of Austria, the pope rejecting its claims, [Col. 1896A] was enough to bring about the result which Guy of Dampierre had vainly hoped for so long. Boniface VIII, having no longer anything to fear either from the Colonna or from Frederick of Aragon, conceived the twofold design of protecting the Empire against the emperor and punishing the King of France at the same time as the emperor.

The Flemish ambassadors at Rome understood the situation admirably. Taking the initiative in the great struggle that was being prepared, they invoked the rights of oppressed Flanders as the noblest and most legitimate field in which papal sovereignty, uniting temporal with spiritual power, could fight the injustices and usurpations of the King of France. The [Col. 1896B] memorial which they submitted to the pope for this purpose is one of the unpublished documents which casts the greatest light upon the history of the final years of Boniface VIII’s pontificate.

In the name of God, amen.

Since it would be lengthy and would excessively burden gracious ears to recount the manifold and unheard-of injuries and grievances unlawfully inflicted by the illustrious King of France and his people upon the magnificent lord Count of Flanders and upon his county, land, and men, the matter is briefly set forth. Through the mercy of the most blessed father, it is implored on behalf of the count that an appropriate remedy be provided.

For it is now, alas, almost known throughout all the regions of Christendom that the same king, to the count’s injury, once unreasonably detained him against his will, without granting him free power to depart; and that he has hitherto unjustly detained against her will the count’s marriageable daughter whom he held, depriving her of the power to leave and marry. He further inflicted upon the count’s county, lands, and men intolerable injuries and losses, through himself and his men. He invaded the county itself in hostile fashion with an innumerable multitude and an army gathered from every side; he besieged many lands and occupied them by violence. He also despoiled him of the revenue of his inheritance; moreover, [lacuna] riches were with [lacuna] and were burned in the same fire; and [lacuna] slaughters of clerics, religious, and laypeople [lacuna] and most cruel [lacuna] of virgins and nuns, with incomparable devastations and depopulations of the goods and property of the men of that county, were perpetrated almost unto the annihilation of the county itself. These acts were for the most part undertaken after and against a lawful appeal made on the count’s behalf to this holy see. After and against that appeal, the said lord king, in contempt of this see, [Col. 1897B] procured through the bishops of Rheims and Senlis, without reasonable cause, that the count’s land be subjected to ecclesiastical interdict and that he and his adherents be excommunicated in fact. On behalf of the said count, a renewed appeal was made to the same see.

Moreover—and more obstinately still—even after and against the truces and forbearances entered into between the same King of France and the illustrious King of England, for themselves and their confederates, solemnly sworn by both kings, and confirmed and approved in arbitral fashion by the holiness of our lord, while those truces were in force, the same lord King of France, violating them contrary to his royal oath, inflicted many losses and injuries upon the same count, confederate of the King of England, and upon his land and men. Concerning these and many other grievances, and the matters arising from them, the same count petitions the supreme pontiff, before the apostolic see, for judgment and mercy against the said King of France.

[Col. 1897C] That the most holy father pope, and no other, is the competent judge in the foregoing matters, and that the count must necessarily in this matter resort to his examination, is proved by the following.

First, because the same supreme pontiff is judge of all, both in spiritual and temporal matters, even among those who have other secular judges. For he is the vicar of Christ Almighty, as in *Extra, De translatione praelati*, chapter *Quarto*; and such a full vicarship has been entrusted to him that it was explicitly and expressly entrusted to his successors in the person of Peter. By every law he is the successor to the earthly and heavenly empire: “whatever you shall bind,” and the rest; 22, distinction, chapter 1; question 40, distinction, chapter 1; and according to the passage, “Behold, here are two swords,” and according to the passage, “I have set thee over the nations,” etc., as in chapter *Sol.* Although kings exercise temporal jurisdiction and subjects are subject to the king as the pre-eminent authority and to dukes sent by him, this [Col. 1897D] was nevertheless given by Peter and granted by God, the highest prince—God, not a mere human being—whose place the pontiff holds on earth, as in the said chapter *Sol.* Thus, since every power is from the Lord God, it is apparent that the jurisdiction of all persons, temporal as well as spiritual, has been fully given to him as God’s sole vicar.

Just as the lord pope does not lose ordinary jurisdiction if he entrusts an ecclesiastical prelacy somewhere, but may be approached by a simple complaint by all persons, as the laws say, so it is with other powers, because they are from him: for whether the law grants an inheritance or approves one already granted, it is deemed to grant it; *Digest, De verborum significatione*, law *Obvenire*, and *Digest, De iure communi*, 3, 1. This accords with the divine saying: “By me kings reign,” etc., chapter *De s. tibi*, under *De hac summa et plenissima potestate*. That this highest and fullest power resides in the supreme pontiff ought to be doubted by no believer.

The second reason is that the supreme pontiff will without any hesitation be judge over those who acknowledge no judges. Thus the supreme pontiff judges and deposes the emperor, than whom no secular prince is superior, as in *Extra, De re iudicata*, chapter *Ad apostolicam*; *De iudiciis*, chapter *Novit*; and *De maioritate et obedientia*, chapter *Sol.* The King of France also, who acknowledges no superior, as is said in *Extra, Qui filii sint . . . per venerabilem*, is nevertheless judged and deposed by the pontiff for demerits, 15, question [*Alius*]. Therefore it was said of the Roman pontiff: “I have set thee over nations and kingdoms”; and he must be judge over great as well as small. No one may be headless—without a judge established above him—as in the said chapter *Novit*; otherwise law and justice would perish if there were no one to administer them: *Digest, De origine iuris*, law II, §§ *Et originem*.

The third reason is that, before the infliction of such injuries and losses, or at least of most of them, and afterwards, a lawful appeal was made on behalf of the said count to [Col. 1898B] this see. That our lord is also judge in these matters by reason of the appeal is clear in law, because every oppressed person may freely appeal to the Roman see, as in 2, question 6, chapter *Omnis oppressus*, etc.: “all oppressed persons [may appeal] to the Roman Church.” This is true of clerics and laymen, especially where there is no competent judge, as in *Extra, De foro competenti*, chapter *Licet*. In the present case there is no competent judge, because the king acknowledges no superior, as I said above on this point, note preceding, note decision, *Omnis oppressus*.

The fourth reason is that the King of France has notoriously and openly sinned against the count through the foregoing acts; and it is known that it pertains to the supreme pontiff to rebuke anyone for sin, as in chapter *Novit*. The count himself requested, and caused requests to be made, that the king redress the injuries. Nevertheless, because they are manifest and notorious, the supreme pontiff may cause them to be redressed, as in the gloss of Lord Innocent on chapter *Novit*, without admonition by the party, because in notorious matters [Col. 1898C] the order of law need not in every respect be observed, as in *Extra, De iureiurando*.

The fifth reason is the sacrilege committed in the burning of churches and the killing of clerics and religious persons. This is an ecclesiastical crime and must be dealt with before an ecclesiastical judge: 15, question 1, chapter *In canonibus*; *Extra, De foro competenti*, chapter *Consistit*, and there generally in the gloss; 11, question 3, chapter *Canonico*; 17, question 4, *Omnes ecclesiae*; and *Extra, De summa excommunicationis*, chapter *Conquesti*. Moreover, for the count’s detained daughter ecclesiastical judgment must specially be sought, by reason of mercy and liberty, which the laws favour; for anyone may demand the freeing of a captive person: *Digest, De libero homine*, law III, § *Omnibus sit*. Judgment in this is for the ecclesiastical judge, as in chapter *De episcopali audientia*, law *Christianos*; *De episcopis et clericis*, *Si liberi captivi*; and *Extra, De arbitriis*, chapter *Exposita*. Especially if she intends to marry, she must be placed in a safe and secure place, lest through fear she say [Col. 1898D] that she likes what she hates: *Extra, De sponsalibus* and *De procuratoribus*. Also relevant is *Digest, De petitione hereditatis*, law *Haereditatis*.

The sixth reason is that, before the lord king proceeded to so many and such great unlawful acts against the count and began to injure the lord count and his county, the count requested that the king grant him judgment by his peers, which was competent in this matter. The king, repeatedly asked, refused to provide this. Although he had at one time promised to observe justice through judgment by peers, in the end he denied it to him. Therefore ecclesiastical justice succeeded, and the king himself was deprived of the right which he had in the county by reason of the fief, as in *Extra, De foro competenti*, chapter *Licet* and chapter *Exteriore*; and in the *Usus feudorum*, *si de feudo contraria ferentur*, chapter *Domino committente*, and *qualiter dominus prope feudum privetur*, chapter 1, with many similar authorities.

Nor can the lord king claim to be judge in these matters, since he cannot be judge in his own [Col. 1899A] cause, in the Red and Black.  
[Note: [Col. 1899D] “No lord ought to be judge or pronounce law in his own dispute, according to the law written in the code: *ne quis in sua causa iudicet* [let no one judge in his own cause], in the law which begins *unica*, in the Red and the Black.” *Etablissements of Saint Louis*, II, 27.]

This is especially so when his own excesses are or are intended to be at issue, and especially since he would notoriously be a most suspect judge in this cause, being the count’s known persecutor and enemy and entirely unable to bear the name of an impartial judge, as in *Extra, De appellationibus*, chapter *Cum speciali*, and chapter *De asse l. f.*

Judgment is also sought against the king and his men, who, while these truces continued, committed many wrongful acts against the same count and his land. Once peace has been made, the king may perhaps say that the truce did not continue; but that the truce did continue, even after peace was made between the kings, is clear from its term, which term still continues. That our lord can proceed against the king follows [lacuna] both because the aforesaid truces are known to have been sworn by him, because faith must be kept even with an enemy, and because of the sacred character of an oath. For this reason judgment belongs to the Church: *Extra, De treuga et pace*, chapter 1; 22, question 4, chapter *Invocans*; and 23, question 6, [Col. 1899B] chapter *Noli existimare*; *Extra, De electione*, chapter *Venerabilem*; and *De foro competenti*, *Clericis laicos*, of Pope Boniface VIII.

Moreover, the king is bound not only to compensate the losses which he inflicted upon the count after the truces and while they were in force; he has also incurred the penalty established in the compromise, because he did not observe the lord pope’s award.  
[Note: [Col. 1899D] That is: because the king showed the pope disrespect by not observing the truce which he had confirmed.]

The pope is judge both for the reasons stated above and by reason of the contract, or because here at the court—*Digest, De iudiciis*, law *Omnem*; *Extra, De foro competenti*, chapter *f.* and chapter *Romanam*, § *Contrahentes apud sedem istam*—the aforesaid compromises were made and approved. Nor should the lord king say that the truces ended peaceably between the kings, because that might apply as between the kings, but as regards their confederates, especially those expressly named in the truces, such as the Count of Flanders and his county, they still endure until peace has been made with the king; for it was a right which [lacuna] by express provision [lacuna] could not be taken away from him by an act of the King of England: *Digest, De pace*, final law, with many authorities.

Moreover, the form of the sworn truces or forbearances explicitly states that between the kings and their confederates, whether in respect of the war concerning the Church, the duchy of Aquitaine, or likewise the county of Flanders, they were to apply from kingdom to kingdom, land to land, people to people, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 1899D] “As much for the duchy of Aquitaine as for the county of Flanders, from kingdom to kingdom, from land to land, from people to people.” Truce of 9 October 1297. Rymer, I, III, p. 191.]

Accordingly, we who have so sworn may not withdraw, since it belongs to the pope alone to judge an oath and interpret it: *Digest, Ad municipalem*, law *Imperatores*, and chapter *Venerabilem*, 3, final section; and the first gloss on chapter *Innocentes*, there, “the sacred character of the oath,” etc. That our lord can extend the period of the truces or compel their extension is proved because he has this power under the form of the reservation he made to himself, as is apparent from the form: he reserved to himself the power to add and subtract, and once and repeatedly to approve, etc., as in *Digest, De arbitrio*, and the *lex Expens.*, law *Terminato*, 3, final section, chapter *Potest*.

Even if he did not have this by arbitral power, since he sees such great and so grievous discord between the king and the count, from which war might later arise—and especially war between the kings—it is not credible that the lord King of England can or ought to endure the count, to whom he has promised defence upon pledged faith, to be wholly crushed by the lord King of France. Lest our lord seem through dissimulation to favour the latter, he can compel a suitable extension of the truces, as in *Extra*, [Col. 1900A] *De iudicio*, chapter *Novit*, at the end.

Likewise, our lord could compel the King of France to make peace with the count; that he can do so seems beyond doubt from the said chapter *Novit*. The emperor does the same thing, because he proclaims peace to his subjects, as in the *Usus feudorum*, *De pace tenenda*, question, chapter. Indeed, he commands those who govern in the face of enemies to see to it that the peoples of cities do not make war or subject one another, but have peace altogether. (*Authentica*, said *Principium*, chapter *De iniuriis*, and *Digest, De officio praesidis*, law *Congruit*.) *Digest, De usu*, law *Aequissimum*, says this: “The praetor forbids and restrains by his jurisdiction anyone from resorting to arms and quarrels.” This is what that supreme master always taught, in word and deed, who always said: “Peace be with you; I give you my peace; I leave you peace.” These words must be heeded, because they convey a command which must be carried out by the vicar. Such an inheritance left behind must not be rejected or neglected, but maintained and approved.

[Col. 1900B] The writer’s ignorance gathers the foregoing according to the small measure of his understanding. But where supreme authority flourishes, where all perfect knowledge is stored in the breast, where all power and every pastoral office reside, where the highest mercy and clemency are, the interpretation between law and equity may be considered more mercifully and subtly; and, for the Count of Flanders, ever a most devoted son of the Church, wickedly exposed to ruin, may the power of the pious father quickly adopt and apply an appropriate remedy.  
[Note: [Col. 1900D] A copy preserved in the archives of Rupelmonde, no. 1025. At the last line one reads: “This document was given on Tuesday after the day of the Nativity of the Lord.” This very defective copy seems to reproduce a text dictated to an inattentive or ignorant scribe. Although I have corrected its grossest errors, I am far from claiming to have produced a reproduction as accurate as that of the other documents, collated from the original sources with as much care as kindness by M. Le Glay at Lille and M. Van der Meersch at Ghent.]

A letter written by the Flemish ambassadors in the first days of January 1299 (old style) informs us how this solemn declaration was received. In it they invoked papal authority, placed by God above all nations and armed with the two swords found on the Mount of Olives—that is, spiritual and temporal power—not only [Col. 1900C] as the sole refuge of the oppressed against princes who recognized no judge above themselves, but also as the supreme power invested with the right to depose the King of France and the emperor.

Most dear lord, by several letters and several messengers we have written and made known to you the state of your affairs, on account of which we are at Rome on your behalf. We await, and have long awaited, knowledge of your will, without which we can neither know nor proceed either forward or backward in your affairs. Of this you can be quite certain, if you look at and have looked at the letters which we have sent you since St Remy’s day onwards; so much time has passed since you received the letters. Now, concerning several of those matters which existed when these present letters were written, we ought long ago to have learned something further.

On the other hand, lord, we have continually informed you of the great need and distress in which we are for lack of our provisions. Yet of all this, lord, we receive no news. We do not dare say, lord, that no one cares for the affairs or for us on this side; but we greatly fear that [Col. 1901A] you may have some impediment—may God protect you from it—which would be too serious if it prevented you from making known to us your will concerning the matters stated above. Or we fear that, if you have sent messengers to us, they may have been captured or killed, as has happened before. Lord, we shall wait until Easter unless, lord, you send us word here before then.

Concerning this and other matters, we sent our letters to you and to my lord your son through Ghiselin of Lokeren and through Marshal, who departed from us on the Sunday after the thirteenth day of Christmas. On that thirteenth day—  
[Note: [Col. 1901C] 6 January 1299 (old style).]  
—Sir Matthew of Aiguespart preached openly, before the pope, the cardinals, and all present, in the church of St John Lateran, that the pope alone is sovereign lord, temporal and spiritual, over all persons whatsoever, in God’s place, by the gift which God made of it to St Peter and to the apostles after him. Whoever wishes to defend himself against this by exemption or by anything whatsoever, whoever or however great he may be, [Col. 1901B] Holy Church can proceed against him as against an unbeliever, with the temporal and spiritual sword, by the authority and power of God. These words are well suited to the first support for your claims which have been submitted to the pope, copies of which we previously sent you.

On the Thursday which has just passed, we spoke to the pope, reminded him of your affairs, and told him that you were in open war, and that this was through the king. The pope replied that he was well reminded of it, that he was shortly awaiting a messenger, and that he would consider the matter and answer us soon enough. He said that he clearly saw that the king was following evil counsel and that this grieved the pope.

Today, lord—the Saturday after the twentieth day—the pope has made Brother Thetier [Note: [Col. 1901C] Diether of Nassau, Archbishop of Trier from 1300 to 1307.] archbishop of Trier, formerly brother of King Adolf, who was King of Germany. It is said, and we hold it certain, that the agreement and friendship made between the Kings [Col. 1901C] of Germany and France displeases him; and that he has made this man archbishop in order to harm the King of Germany, and that he will procure an impediment or difficulty for him if he can. If anyone were to cause him difficulty, the pope and the Church of Rome would be well pleased; and it seems to them that he and the King of France wish to shake everything.

Dear lord, remember, if it please you, your affairs on this side and us. May Our Lord not forget you, and may He be the guardian of you and of all who wish you well. Lord, we [Col. 1902A] write to no one but you. You shall make your will known wherever it pleases you. These letters were given at Rome, at the Lateran, on the Saturday aforesaid.

Dear sirs, we are sending you this letter by my lord William of Jülich, provost of Maastricht [Note: [Col. 1901C] Guillaume de Juliers, provost of Maastricht.], your nephew, who will bring them to you, or perhaps send them on in advance; for we understand that he is to remain at Bologna as a student. Sir, we have learned, and hold it to be true, that the pope has made a reservation concerning appointments to the archbishoprics of Cologne and Mainz; and those sees will become vacant sooner than is thought, and the pope will place there persons from whom he may obtain support against the king of Germany. Yet he finds no persons suitably prepared; for he will appoint none agreeable either to the king of Germany, or to the king of France, or of England, or to Lombardy. Rather, he will seek powerful persons of the country, who can and ought to oppose the king of Germany. Thus it may well happen that your nephew may attain one of these dignities through the aid of yourself, your friends, and his own, if he is well maintained at school; and, as will be necessary, the archbishops will not be made to die, but the pope will have matters so arranged that the sees become vacant. We believe matters to stand thus, but do not know with certainty how they will turn out. And my lord Guy of Hainaut, your nephew, would have obtained the archbishopric of Trier, as we understand for certain, had it not been for the alliance which his brother has with the king of France.

[Note: [Col. 1901C] 17 January 1299 (old style). Archives of Lille. I place here in a note a much less important letter of Gérard de Ferlin. It is dated 3 March 1299 [Col. 1901D] (old style), and completes the series of documents sent from Rome to the count of Flanders:

“To the venerable and very dear associate J. Makiello, clerk of the most illustrious lord Guy, count of Flanders and marquis of Namur, from Gérard, chaplain of the same lord, on his behalf.

“Dearest sir, you should know that, with my belongings and household, on the Monday before St. Matthias’s Day, I came safely and soundly to the Curia; I desire with affection to know the same concerning you. But on the following Friday your nephew Giles set out at Naples for the king and others to whom he was carrying letters, intending to return as soon as opportunity offered, and to make provision for the lord’s affairs as necessity required. On the following Wednesday I myself set out for the said king, passing through that same Naples; and if the said Giles should need counsel, I shall supply him, as if he were my brother, with whatever is necessary for him. Concerning what my lord instructed John of Villamarci—namely, that he should provide the said Giles with what he needed—I tell you that the same John replied briefly and categorically to me and to the said Giles that he had satisfactorily discharged those matters which concerned the lord, and that nothing remained in his hands by which he could give the said Giles substantial assistance with expenses or costs; and he says that he is prepared to give proof of this. Nevertheless, upon his departure he gave the said Giles six gold florins for expenses, and declared that he would give him thereafter whatever else he might need. The same John is going with me into Apulia, and we shall pass by way of the said Giles; do not therefore doubt that he has been well and sufficiently provided for.

“I know no news to report to you, except what you will be able to judge from the letters which I send to the lord, and that the lord pope is exceedingly severe toward everyone in granting favours. I confidently ask you to think of my brother, and to send me, in confidence, news of your own condition, that of our lord of Marbasio [Gérard de Marbrais?], and your wishes, knowing that with all my heart I would do whatever would conduce to your advantage and honour. Farewell in the Lord. Greet for me all whom you see should be greeted. Given on the Tuesday after St. Matthias’s Day.”  
(Archives of the Council of Flanders.)]

Soon the speech of Cardinal d’Acquasparta received striking confirmation. During the great Jubilee of 1300 the pope appeared bearing the double insignia of spiritual and temporal authority, and cried aloud: “Behold the two swords; here, O Peter, you see your successor; you, saving Christ, [Col. 1902C] behold your vicar.” All Europe had hurried to Rome, and the number of pilgrims crowding the entrances of the holy basilicas eclipsed the most magnificent memories of the city twice queen of the world. It was at once a display of immense religious enthusiasm and a manifestation of the power with which pontifical authority still appeared armed in the eyes of the peoples.

[Col. 1903A] Boniface VIII sent the bishop of Pamiers to order the king of France to restore Guy of Dampierre to freedom; but Philip the Fair replied only by throwing the pope’s legate into prison and summoning the Colonna to his court. At the same time as he received the complaints of the count of Flanders, Boniface VIII remembered the no less vehement and frequent complaints of the Cistercian Order.

[Note: [Col. 1903C] “The clamorous report of many brings to us …” Bull *Ausculta fili*, in Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 50; “On the assertion of many …” Bull *Ante promotionem*, ibid., p. 53. Boniface VIII had already said in the bull *Dudum celsitudini*: “We have received diverse and sorrowful complaints of the Gallican Church.” Raynaldi, 1299, no. 25.]

On 4 December 1301 he suspended all privileges granted to the king for the levying of tithes; the next day two further bulls were published. By the bull *Ausculta fili* he set forth the power entrusted to him as vicar of Jesus Christ and successor of St Peter: “God has appointed us over kings and kingdoms, to uproot, [Col. 1903B] destroy, scatter, and build up in His name and doctrine. Dearest son, let no one persuade you that you have no superior.”

[Note: [Col. 1903C] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 48.]

But one must not believe, as modern historians have too often repeated, that in Boniface VIII’s eyes the papacy was the union—or, more exactly, the confusion—of the two powers simultaneously exercised. Boniface VIII himself said that one could not attribute to him such great folly or blindness as not to recognize the separation of the two powers.

[Note: [Col. 1903D] “We know that there are two powers ordained by God: who, then, ought to believe that there was such folly, such ignorance, in our head?” Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 77.]

The emperor and kings alone exercised temporal power: to them belonged use, action—

[Note: [Col. 1903D] *Actus et usus*: “action and use.” Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 76.]

—and the sphere of facts. Law, however, remained subject to spiritual authority, which was called to distinguish what was just [Col. 1903C] from what was unjust and was invested with unquestionable jurisdiction *ratione peccati*, “by reason of sin”: whether it was fitting to recall an obscure Christian to penitence or necessary to break the crown of the most powerful princes.

[Note: [Col. 1903D] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 76.]

This theory rested on the principle, universally accepted at that time, that society rested upon religion. Religion was at once a restraint upon princes and a protection for the [Col. 1904A] peoples, to whom it offered equality before the supreme tribunal which represented on earth that of God.

Moreover, the bull *Ausculta fili* is of very special interest for the question before us, because it successively addresses the two charges brought against Philip the Fair’s government: on the one hand, the oppression of Guy of Dampierre—that is, of the great vassals; on the other, the oppression of the clergy and religious orders. When Boniface VIII said to Philip the Fair: “You burden peers, counts, and barons … whereas in judgment there ought to be a distinction of persons; yet in your own causes you pronounce law for yourself, and in your own court you assume the roles of both plaintiff and judge,” he repeated what Guy of Dampierre had said in the act of appeal of 29 December 1299. [Col. 1904B] When he addressed other reproaches to the king of France in these terms: “You oppress churches and ecclesiastical persons … you cause tithes to be levied, although no power over clerics has been granted to laymen … ecclesiastical persons are pressed as though under the yoke of servitude … churches have now been made tributary,” he reproduced quite closely the language of the other act of appeal submitted to the Apostolic See by the Cistercian Order.

The second bull, of 5 December 1301, seems to recall the more modest mission which Boniface VIII had performed on behalf of the Flemish communes before his elevation to the papal throne: “Before our promotion to the office of the supreme apostolate, while we were still of lesser station, many credible things were disclosed [Col. 1904C] to us, on the assertion of many, concerning injuries and damages repeatedly inflicted by Philip, king of the French.”

[Note: [Col. 1903D] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 53.]

Jacques de Normanno, archdeacon of Narbonne, to whom these bulls had been entrusted, received orders to leave France; and the bull *Ausculta fili* was publicly burned by the king’s command, on Sunday, 11 February 1301 (old style).

[Note: [Col. 1903D] “The apostolic letters were burned in the presence of the king himself and the magnates, a thing which we read has been done by no heretic, pagan, or tyrant.” Letter of Cardinal Orsini. Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 80. I borrow from the manuscript of the Dunes (no. 574) the following document:

“Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, archbishops and bishops, etc. Since we are sending our beloved son Master Jacques de Normandie, our notary, bearer of the present letters, to the king of France on certain affairs of the Roman Church, we earnestly request and exhort your whole body, commanding you by these apostolic letters, [Col. 1904C] that, when the same notary passes through your regions, you are to receive him graciously and treat him honourably, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and for us; and, whenever you are asked on our behalf by him or at his direction, you are to ensure that he is liberally supplied, while travelling, staying, and returning, with the necessities for the expenses of himself and his household, at the rate of six gold florins each day. [Col. 1904D] If it should happen that the said notary delays for a time in any places or place, we will that the archbishops and bishops not only of those same regions but also of neighbouring and remote regions be bound to contribute to his support, as the said notary may see fit for the distribution and easier bearing of all these charges. Take care, therefore, effectively to fulfil our command, so that you may deservedly be commended for it; otherwise, we shall hold valid and shall cause to be inviolably observed, until fitting satisfaction is made and without appeal, any sentence which he may duly pronounce against rebels in this matter, for which purpose we grant him full power by these present letters, notwithstanding any privileges or indulgences granted to whatsoever persons, places, or orders … Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year of our pontificate.”

Jacques de Normanno received two hundred gold florins from the archbishop of Reims:

“Jacques de Normandie, notary of the lord pope and archdeacon of Narbonne, specially sent by the most holy father Lord Boniface VIII, by divine grace pope, upon certain arduous affairs to the regions of the kingdom of France, to the reverend father in Christ, Lord Robert, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, greeting in the Lord … Since, in order to carry out the aforesaid business, we reached the city of Paris and remained there for some time, we received from you two hundred gold florins for our expenses and those of our household … Given at Paris, on the Sunday after the feast of the Purification [Col. 1905C] of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the year of the Lord 1301.”

This date deserves notice. Eight days later the bull *Ausculta fili* was burned at Paris, and there can be no doubt that Jacques de Normanno received at the same time the order to leave France.]

Among Dupuy’s documentary proofs [Col. 1905A] is found a memorandum written on this occasion by an advocate of Coutances, named Pierre du Bois or du Bos.

[Note: [Col. 1905C] In Latin: *Petrus de Bosco*. Around the same period one finds Gaufridus de Bosco, receiver of the king in the county of Flanders. Guillaume du Bos was Philip the Fair’s bailiff in the Pays de Caux.]

There one reads: “Perhaps it would be expedient for the Roman pontiffs to be poor, as they once were, so that they might be holy.”

[Note: [Col. 1905C] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 46. “If the apostles,” the supplication of the people of France to the king says naïvely, “had done or said as Boniface did, no one would think that they could have converted a single prince.” Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 217.]

More recent research by M. de Wailly—

[Note: [Col. 1905C] *Bibliothèque de l’École des chartes*, II, 3, p. 273.]

—also permits the attribution to Pierre du Bois of a treatise in which he urged Philip the Fair to unite Rome and the patrimony of St Peter to the kingdom of France. Moreover, on its first page appears the maxim so vehemently reproached to Philip the Fair’s ministers in the act of appeal of the Cistercian Order: “Whoever does not obey the prince shall die.” This work of a Coutances advocate, who may have been the confidant and secretary of Enguerrand de Marigny (Enguerrand [Col. 1905B] le Portier took his name from the town of Marigny, four leagues from Coutances), is all the more important because Philip the Fair seems to have drawn several of his ordinances from it.

[Note: [Col. 1905C] Pierre du Bois may perhaps have been the author of Philip the Fair’s [Col. 1905D] celebrated reply to the false bull. See Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 45. Abbé Christophe is mistaken in placing alongside him the university’s procurator, whereas the text he cites mentions only one and the same person: Pierre du Bois, advocate of the king and procurator, not of the university, but of the town (*universitas*) of Coutances.]

There is one observation which must be noted because it gives [Col. 1906A] occasion for an entirely new comparison. Philip the Fair, who in his language and violence so often anticipated Henry VIII, had, like him, the idea that by abolishing ecclesiastical celibacy he would bring the priest wholly into civil society and break the bonds, founded upon self-denial and obedience, that united the priesthood to the supremacy of religious authority. Master Pierre du Bois represented to Philip the Fair that vows of celibacy arose only from the error of certain old men who had forgotten the passions of this world; that they entailed great danger to souls; and that the pope—and, failing the pope, the king—had the right to abolish them, since so many rules prescribed in the old [Col. 1906B] law had been modified in the New Testament. A bull was drafted, and has been preserved in manuscripts in the library of the University of Ghent.

[Note: [Col. 1905D] This false bull runs as follows:

“Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful, greeting and apostolic blessing. Since certain persons, having no knowledge of divine and canonical pronouncements and being ignorant of the power of the Roman pontiff—who is known to hold the place and lordship of Christ throughout the world, both in temporal and spiritual matters—

[Col. 1906B] [Col. 1905] Compare the memorandum in which Guillaume de Nogaret accuses Boniface VIII of having said: ‘Whoever is pope is lord of all spiritual and temporal things.’ Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 331.]

—seeking to know more than they ought, contrary to the Apostle’s teaching, say and believe in heretical fashion that the Roman pontiff, and those who have been promoted to sacred orders, cannot be joined in marriage through a dispensation of the Roman pontiff; considering the Council of Nicaea, the councils of Carthage, and several constitutions of our predecessors; therefore we, having the care of the pastoral office, exercising our power, against which no prince or anyone else either ought or can dare in any way to oppose himself, and wishing to apply a suitable remedy to this heretical disease, considering that our predecessors could in no way have bound us by their constitutions, and that sacred marriage, generally approved by God through its institution in Paradise and confirmed by the actual example of the Apostles, is not forbidden to ecclesiastical persons but ought, as supported by a salutary favour, to be allowed and lawful for all Christians: we therefore, for perpetual remembrance of the matter, by this decree and with the counsel of our brethren, enact that the Roman pontiff and all ecclesiastical persons, secular and regular, of either sex, whatever their rank, order, or religious profession, may, if they wish, be joined in marriage to one virgin man or woman, provided that the aforesaid persons have not completed their thirtieth year in their orders. Yet on the day on which they are to celebrate [Mass], let them abstain from their wives, so that they may more readily obtain what they ask of God. But if sons or daughters are begotten in such marriages, they shall succeed their parents only in patrimonial goods and in ecclesiastical goods not increased in any way. [Col. 1906D] If the parents leave no patrimonial goods, or goods insufficient for the aforesaid children: if they are children of the supreme pontiff or of cardinals, they shall be maintained by the succeeding Roman pontiff; all children of religious persons shall be brought up in the same monastery, with a suitable pension assigned to them, subject, however, to the moderation that they not perish in poverty and that the sacred monastery not be unduly burdened; but if children of parish priests or curates remain, the parishioners shall provide them with victuals and other necessities. Let no one, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone teaches otherwise, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God, and that we shall proceed against him as against a heretic; and we notify our successors that we have ordered these things to be lawful for all. Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third Ides of May, in the third year of our pontificate.”]

From the opening lines, the composition leaves no doubt that it was intended to be attributed to [Col. 1907A] Boniface VIII; Master Pierre du Bois’s opinion confirms this hypothesis. Perhaps the Colonna, then refugees in France, had it given a date corresponding to the proceedings brought against them by the pope. The intervention of the Colonna would be all the more understandable here because, when Boniface VIII raised his nephew Francesco Gaetani to the cardinalate, he compelled him to separate from his wife, sister of Raynaldo Supino, the friend and companion of Sciarra Colonna.

[Note: [Col. 1907D] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 344.]

In any event, neither its source nor its true date can be mistaken if it is placed beside the false bull: “We wish you to know that in spiritual and temporal matters you are subject to us … those who believe otherwise we hold to be heretics.”

[Col. 1907B] We are fully entitled to deny Philip the Fair’s good faith and loyalty, since at the foot of his manifestos against Boniface VIII we find the name of Jean de Pontoise, abbot of Cîteaux, and that of the eldest son of Robert of Béthune: a double falsehood worthy of the legists who had already forged papal bulls.

[Note: [Col. 1907D] Ibid., *Preuves*, pp. 62 and 108.]

After the Estates-General had assembled at Paris on 10 April 1301 (old style), Pierre Flotte addressed to them, in emphatic terms, a long speech very insulting to the pope, and made them sign a memorandum prepared beforehand. Even the clergy adhered to it, though in language more respectful toward pontifical authority.

[Note: [Col. 1907D]

… Pierre Flotte

Preached to them within Paris,

And gave them that good counsel;

Thus they made Paris their Rome.

Their wicked heart made them do it,

[Col. 1908D] When they disowned their father,

And Rome, who is mother of all.  
(Godefroi de Paris, *Chronique métrique*, v. 240.)]

Boniface VIII replied, either directly or through the cardinals, to the [Col. 1907C] complaints of the three estates. It is probably to this period that a great bull belongs in which, while forbidding bishops henceforth to leave their dioceses, he expressed himself as follows:

“Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance. Until now holy mother Church has drawn deep sighs in many parts of the world, because some who preside over her government possess only the name of shepherds. Scattered in different places, roaming about like hirelings, they expose, alas, the Lord’s sheep to wolves; they devote themselves to the service of emperors, kings, princes, barons, and other powerful persons; and under other ingenious pretexts, which for the present we refrain from stating, they are frequently absent. They put temporal and transitory advantage before spiritual advantage, or consider too little [Col. 1907D] that the Shepherd said to His disciples—and through them to their successors: ‘The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep’; and elsewhere it is written that a shepherd is bound to recognize the countenance of his own flock. This cannot be suitably fulfilled while they are almost continually separated from it and so widely forgetful of it. Nor should it be absent from their consideration, to the detriment of their salvation, that [Col. 1908A] they shall answer at the examination of the strict Judge for their administration of temporal and spiritual things which they neglect. We recount these matters only with painful anguish of heart, thoughtfully weighing that the Christian people are very often endangered by defective government, according to the saying: ‘A people without a ruler shall fall,’ and grave scandals have arisen. Therefore, lest by enduring so harmful and condemnable a failure we should, God forbid, incur the divine displeasure—we who, though unworthy, hold on earth the place of Him to whom the Lord committed all His sheep to be fed—we, with the counsel of our brethren, by an irrevocable constitution, desiring beneficially to provide for the souls of all shepherds and flocks, decree that all patriarchs, primates, archbishops, bishops, abbots … shall reside continuously and henceforth serve faithfully in the churches over which they preside, within one month from the day on which this salutary statute comes to their knowledge; otherwise, after the expiration of the aforesaid term, patriarchates, primacies, archbishoprics, [Col. 1908B] bishoprics, and other benefices shall be free and vacant by operation of law. Nor do we wish that anyone may dispense them from residence in those benefices, or from the obligation not to absent themselves therefrom, without special permission of the Apostolic See.”

[Note: [Col. 1908D] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 915.]

In the last days of August, the pope held a great consistory in the presence of the bishop of Auxerre, envoy of the king, and deputies of the clergy. After a speech by Cardinal Matthew of Acquasparta, he himself spoke, saying that although he had greatly loved the king of France, Philip his father, and St Louis his grandfather, he also knew that he had the right to depose him, and that this right might perhaps become for him an imperative duty and a sad necessity. He added: “If the king does not come to his senses, [Col. 1908C] we shall answer in time to come: We know the secrets of the kingdom; nothing is hidden from us; we have felt everything out. We know how the Germans love the French, and those of Languedoc and Burgundy, who can say to them what St Bernard said of the Romans: ‘Loving no one, no one loves you …’ We wish this Pierre Flotte to be punished temporally and spiritually; but we ask God to reserve him for us to punish, as is just. The satellites of this Ahithophel are the count of Artois—what kind of man he is, the whole world knows—and the count of St Paul.”

[Note: [Col. 1908D] By this name Boniface VIII meant the inhabitants of Flanders, whose language resembled Germanic idioms.  
Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 77; Baillet, p. 146.]

No doubt these words later seemed prophetic to most of those who had heard them. A few days after this consistory, perhaps [Col. 1908D] on the night which followed it, a messenger arriving from Flanders announced to the pope that the French army had been defeated beneath the walls of Courtrai by a few townsmen and peasants, hastily gathered and scarcely armed. A lay brother of the Cistercian Order, a deserter—

[Note: [Col. 1908D] The religious rule was explicit: “No person of the Order shall go on behalf of princes against the princes of lands.” *Statutes of the Cistercian Order*, year 1224. “No monk or lay brother shall presume to bear arms.” *Statutes*, year 1282.]

—enrolled in the valiant [Col. 1909A] phalanx which saved the fatherland, had overthrown at his feet the count of Artois, and Pierre Flotte had shared his fate.

[Note: [Col. 1909C] Louis of Velthem, in recounting the battle of Courtrai, takes care to note that Philip the Fair had separated himself from the pope.]

Boniface VIII, without losing an hour, had Michel As Clokettes awakened—

[Note: [Col. 1909C] “Through him I learned that it was so,” says Gilles li Muisis, “because the lord pope had affection for the Flemings.” On this subject the indictment drawn up by Guillaume de Nogaret and Guillaume de Plasian reads: “It will be proved that he procured the Flemings’ rebellion, and that, on receiving news of the said rebellion, he said: ‘The business goes well.’ Likewise, it will be proved that he secretly and continually favoured the Flemings, in words and deeds, by aid, counsels, and favours. Likewise, it will be proved that, over the harm inflicted on the French by the Flemings—not through strength, but through fraudulent deceit and evil guile—the same Boniface publicly showed great joy, rejoicing at the death of French princes and others who perished there, and heaping upon the French insults, affronts, reproaches, and many injuries.” Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 341. Boniface VIII was also accused of having induced Edward to assist, from the proceeds of ecclesiastical tithes levied in England and Ireland, the Flemish communes which triumphed at Courtrai. Baillet, p. 160. Half of these tithes had been ceded to King Edward I by Boniface VIII, 12 March 1301 (old style). Raynaldi, 1302, no. 17. Compare Nicholas Trivet, 1303.]

—and had him brought to the Vatican palace to learn of the triumph of the Flemish communes, which was soon followed, as he had predicted, by the insurrection of Languedoc.

[Note: [Col. 1909D] “Hearing of the Flemings …” Continuation of Guillaume de Nangis, 1302.]

Boniface VIII had convened a council at Rome for the feast of All Saints, 1302. Despite Philip the Fair’s threats, it was attended by the archbishops of Tours, Bordeaux, Bourges, and Auch; the bishops of Angers, Nantes, Vannes, Rennes, Quimper, Léon, Tréguier, Saint-Brieuc, Toulouse, Pamiers, Périgueux, Saintes, [Col. 1909B] Comminges, Rodez, Agde, Lescar, Lectoure, Oloron, Aire, Mende, Nîmes, Carcassonne, Bazas, Le Puy, Autun, Chalon-sur-Saône, Mâcon, Albi, Aix, and Clermont; and the abbots of Cîteaux, Cluny, Prémontré, Marmoutier, Beaulieu, and La Chaise-Dieu.

[Note: [Col. 1909D] Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 86. Dupuy wrongly adds the bishops of Auxerre, Coutances, Noyon, Béziers, and Limoges, who had been sent to Rome as envoys of the king and clergy. It should be observed that none of the bishops who went to the Council of Rome had signed the letters addressed to Boniface [Col. 1910C] VIII concerning the grant of tithes. See above, p. 20.]

On 21 October the king of France ordered his bailiffs to take possession of the property of the prelates and abbots who had gone to Rome, declaring that he feared that their goods might suffer through their absence and that, in his foresight, he judged it far preferable to reserve their custody to himself.

[Note: [Col. 1910C] “Not wishing, because of the absence of those persons, that their temporal goods should be dissipated, and rather desiring that they be prudently preserved, we command,” etc. Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 84.]

[Col. 1909C] This measure seems to have been directed principally against the Cistercian Order.

[Note: [Col. 1910C] In circumstances as grave as those through which the Order had passed in 1296, the General Chapter of Cîteaux renewed the prohibitions published at that time—prohibitions which Philip the Fair’s intrigues had rendered useless: “Abhorring and wishing to punish the pernicious malice of certain perverse persons, who do not fear to disclose the secrets of the Order to seculars, to the detriment of the common good of the Order—for example, when contributions are made within the Order for defending its liberties, revealing this to secular powers, namely barons, [Col. 1910D] princes, and kings, and thereby procuring that such contributions not be paid, or, if they have been paid, that they be seized by those powers—the General Chapter excommunicates the aforesaid traitors of its own Order. Such persons are proclaimed excommunicated, along with other evildoers, on Palm Sunday.” Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, IV, col. 1500.]

Philip the Fair [Col. 1910A] could not have forgotten that the Cistercian religious’ act of appeal had provoked the bull *Clericis laicos*, and he knew that since then their complaints had continued to resound at Rome. It was a former monk of Cîteaux, Simon de Beaulieu, bishop of Palestrina, who had come at the end of 1296 to threaten the king of France with excommunication. Finally, among the cardinals there was one, formerly abbot of Cîteaux, who distinguished himself by his devotion to the pope. If we seek even in Flanders traces of the Cistercian Order’s resistance, we may observe that the abbot of the Dunes, Jacques of Biervliet, made the most vigorous protests against the levying of royal tithes.

[Note: [Col. 1910D] Manuscripts of the Dunes, nos. 914 and 629. An old cartulary of the Abbey of the Dunes summarizes in these terms a bull of special protection granted to that abbey by Boniface VIII: “By apostolic authority he confirms all liberties and immunities granted by the Roman pontiffs, his predecessors, to us and our monastery, as well as the liberties and exemptions from secular exactions granted by kings, princes, and other faithful of Christ.”]

The chronicle of this monastery [Col. 1910B] adds that he had long been attached to Pope Boniface VIII as penitentiary.

[Note: [Col. 1910D] *Chronicle of the Abbey and Monastery of the Dunes*, p. 14.]

The unwavering firmness of the abbot of Cîteaux, Jean de Pontoise, who had succeeded Abbot Ruffin in 1299, no less aroused the anger of the king of France.
