He wished to punish the whole Order for the fidelity which Jean de Pontoise maintained toward the Apostolic See; and one readily understands why he wished to strike it by taking away the vast landed properties that covered the soil of France. Perhaps Philip the Fair had even formed the project of winning over the nobles by restoring to them, in a general confiscation of the Cistercian Order’s goods, all those properties which the abbeys owed to the pious generosity of their ancestors [Col. 1910C].

[Note: [Col. 1910D] See the address of the nobles to the cardinals. Dupuy, *Preuves*, p. 61.]

[Col. 1911A] Nothing reveals more clearly the gravity of the danger than the energy Boniface VIII employed to avert it. On 8 January 1302 (old style) [Note: [Col. 1911C] This letter, dated in the eighth year of Boniface VIII’s pontificate, appears to belong (as Dupuy also thinks) to the year 1302 (old style), and one would have to conclude from this that the ninth year [Col. 1911D] did not begin until after 8 January. The encyclical letters in which Boniface VIII announces his accession to the pontifical see are dated 24 January 1294 (old style). Rainaldi, 1295, no. 7. Yet, if Boniface VIII’s eighth year had begun on 2 January 1301 (old style), then, by changing the date of these letters of protection, they would have to be explained by certain lines of the bull *Ausculta fili*.], he wrote to the abbots of Saint-Étienne of Dijon, Saint-Victor of Marseille, Saint-Paul of Besançon, and other abbots, asking them to take under their protection the possessions of the Cistercian Order, which was exposed to the most culpable and impious persecutions [Note: [Col. 1911D] “To restrain the wicked attempts of adversaries who do not fear to assail ecclesiastical persons and places in respect of their goods and rights, and to harass them with manifold troubles, it is all the more fitting that we apply a suitable remedy, since such disturbances and troubles are known to result, in greater measure, in offence against the divine majesty, loss of ecclesiastical liberty, and contempt for the Apostolic See. Since, therefore (as has reached our hearing), our beloved sons, the abbot of Cîteaux, his fellow abbots [Col. 1912C] and brethren, are being harassed in manifold ways in their persons and goods by certain persons who do not fear to take the name of the Lord in vain, we, etc.” *Privilegia ordinis Cisterciensis*, pp. 86–87; Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 85. A privilege [Col. 1912D] granted to the Cistercian Order at about the same time begins: “Because of the great devotion which you bear toward us and the Apostolic See, we pursue the Order itself and you with heartfelt charity.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 85; *Statuta ordinis Cisterciensis*, 1303. I do not know where Dom Bouiliart, *Histoire de l’abbaye de Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, p. 145, found the assertion that Boniface VIII had belonged to the Cistercian Order.].

How times had changed since Saint Louis had taken pleasure in founding the magnificent abbey of Royaumont (*regalis mons*, “royal mountain”), where he fasted and prayed with Cistercian monks; and since he later wished to die according to their rule, lying upon ashes, just as his mother Blanche of Castile had herself died in the arms [Col. 1911B] of the Cistercian nuns of Maubuisson [Note: [Col. 1912D] Lenain, *Histoire de l’ordre de Cîteaux*, IX, pp. 292, 303. “O how gold has been darkened! Why are the shining examples of Saint Louis, from whom the king derives his origin, obscured?” Letter of Cardinal Matthew Orsini. Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 80.]!

At the same time, the bishop of Tournai, obeying the secret instructions of Philip the Fair, ordered all ecclesiastical authorities in Flanders to cease the functions of their ministry [Note: [Col. 1912D] The sentences of excommunication pronounced by the bishop of Tournai against Guy of Dampierre appear to have been numerous. For that of 1297, see Warnkoenig, I, *Urk.*, p. 67.]. On 7 December 1302 the following protest was solemnly read at Bruges, in the choir of the church of Saint Donatian:

> In the name of the Lord, in the year 1302, on the seventh day of December, I, Michael [lacuna], clerk and procurator of the town of Bruges, in the presence of a public notary: whereas the reverend father, Lord Guy, by the grace of God venerable bishop of Tournai, or his vicars, have recently suspended from the office of dean all the deans of Christendom established in the land of Flanders, and have ordered the seals which they were accustomed to use [Col. 1911C] to be sent to them at Tournai; warning the said deans to obey their commands within a fixed time appointed for this purpose, under penalty of suspension and loss of their benefices; whereas the people of the land of Flanders cannot be beneficially governed without a shepherd or one acting in his stead, nor communicate with one another; and whereas, because of the just fear which can and ought to affect a steadfast person, because of the dangers of the roads, and because of the notorious and manifest war which has long existed and still exists between the French and the Flemings, no one in the whole county of Flanders can have either free access to, or free departure from, the court of Tournai—which lies within the dominion of the illustrious prince, Lord Philip, king of the French—in order to obtain a benefice bestowed upon him if he needs it; or, in connection with matrimonial banns, to obtain and secure them from persons of other deaneries and [Col. 1912A] dioceses, so that one may safely proceed to the solemnization of marriages—which often occurs in the said county, especially in the town of Bruges and its territory, and is customary there; or even to obtain a parish priest or rector for a parish church left vacant by the death of its rector. In all the foregoing matters every dean was accustomed, within his own deanery, to provide and render assistance to the people in the bishop’s place and name; and such things, and similar matters, have customarily been provided and done from ancient times by the deans of Christendom, etc.
>
> [Note: [Col. 1912D] Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 576.]

Shortly thereafter, when Philip of Thiette returned to Bruges, a more important decision was made. It was resolved to beseech Boniface VIII to create bishops in [Col. 1912B] Flanders who, instead of being constant instruments of foreign policy, would preserve among the upright, industrious, and simple populations the religious faith which they had kept intact amid so many excommunications and interdicts, in the midst of the bloodiest wars.

> The clergy and people of Flanders, of the dioceses of Tournai, Thérouanne, and Arras, etc., petition Your Holiness: since very many of them doubt whether they are entangled in sentences of excommunication, suspension, and interdict, imposed by canons or synodal or provincial statutes, or even by ordinary or delegated judges; since moreover many churches of the aforesaid county and dioceses have been violated by the shedding of blood or in yet more violent fashion; and since in certain churches and cemeteries of those same county and dioceses, because their immunity has been violated, or because of the killing, mutilation, wounding, beating, or capture of ecclesiastical or lay persons, divine offices and burials are suspended by provincial or synodal statutes—not without infinite peril to souls, diminution of divine worship, injury to the faithful departed, and great loss to the salvation of the living—and since they cannot obtain suitable remedies in these matters from their own bishops, their vicars, or the aforesaid judges, both because of the most bitter persecution continually raging against them from the illustrious lord king of the French and because the reverend said bishops, showing more favour than is due to that king, [Col. 1913A] grievously oppress them from day to day and inflict manifest injuries upon them: although they are prepared, and always have been prepared, humbly to reverence the said bishops as reverend fathers in Christ and obey their salutary commands, while never for a moment ceasing to defend their country—may you deign, most holy Father, mercifully to aid them in this respect, by entrusting the matter to certain persons who, by Apostolic authority, shall suitably provide, either personally or through others, for the benefits of absolution, reconciliation, dispensation if necessary, and relaxation.

> Likewise, the clergy and people aforesaid petition Your Holiness that, since persons elected to ecclesiastical dignities, to vacant parish churches, or to any other ecclesiastical benefices, and all regular and secular persons of the aforesaid county and dioceses, cannot be presented to the venerable fathers, their own bishops or [Col. 1913B] their vicars, to receive canonical institution and orders; and since their matrimonial and any other spiritual causes cannot be dispatched, for they have no access to the aforesaid bishops, their vicars, or competent judges because of the most bitter war continually threatening them from the illustrious lord king of the French: whence it results that the said churches are deprived of their proper rectors, Christ’s faithful are left without the pastoral care of their own priests, divine worship is diminished, and numerous dangers to souls arise—may you deign, most holy Father, mercifully to provide against these things by commanding one or more persons who, by Apostolic authority, shall suitably supply for each of them, personally or through one or more others, the functions of the said bishops and judges.

> Likewise, Philip, son of the count of Flanders, count of Thérouanne and Lorette, together with the clergy and people of the county of Flanders, petitions Your Holiness that, by [Col. 1913C] your benignity, it may be granted to him that, since the resources of the said Philip and of the lay people are insufficient for the expenses of defending the land of Flanders against the power of the illustrious lord Philip, king of the French, they may lawfully demand and receive from the churches and ecclesiastical persons of the said county an appropriate subsidy for this purpose; and that the said churches and persons may lawfully furnish it, notwithstanding your constitution issued in these matters for safeguarding the immunity of churches and such persons; and that you may mercifully grant remission of any sentences and irregularity which they may have incurred, under pressure of necessity, by acting contrary to that constitution and subsequently taking part in divine offices.

Petition for the creation of one new bishop, or two, in the county of Flanders; the following considerations, however, seem capable of being adduced in support.

[Col. 1913D]

> Although the county of Flanders extends through several dioceses, the episcopal sees to which recourse must be had for the necessary episcopal office, ecclesiastical sacraments, and many other matters are situated in the lands of its enemies.
>
> Likewise, even supposing that, by God’s gift, the war is brought to peace, there will nevertheless remain fear that the inhabitants on either side will persist in their previous mutual insults, from which a dangerous disturbance might arise.
>
> Likewise, the greater part of the county uses the Teutonic language (*ydioma theutonicum*); hence they cannot be suitably instructed by salutary admonitions from their bishops, who are ignorant of their language.
>
> Likewise, the dioceses to which [lacuna] belong are so extensive, and the bishoprics so wealthy, that an appropriate division of them can be made without serious inconvenience.
>
> Likewise, in the county of Flanders there are several dignities, churches, and monasteries so endowed that, without grave prejudice to them, one bishop or two can suitably be supported from some portion of their revenues.

> The clergy and people of the county of Flanders petition Your Holiness: since there are in that county several churches and cemeteries of the dioceses of Tournai, Thérouanne, and Arras which have been violated by the shedding of blood and in a more violent manner; and since in certain churches and cemeteries of that county divine offices and burials are suspended, by provincial or synodal constitutions, because their immunity has been violated or because ecclesiastical persons have been killed, wounded, beaten, or captured; whereby divine worship is diminished, devotion grows cold, the insolence of the least [Col. 1914B] rectors [lacuna] increases, dangers to souls multiply, and the faithful departed lack fitting suffrages and ecclesiastical burial; and since at this time remedies cannot be obtained in these matters from the venerable fathers, their own bishops or their vicars—may you deign, most holy Father, to entrust the matter to another person or others, who by Apostolic authority may supply the functions of the aforesaid bishops in the foregoing matters.

> The clergy and people of the county of Flanders, of the dioceses of Tournai and Thérouanne, petition Your Holiness: since persons elected to ecclesiastical dignities, to vacant parish churches, or to any other ecclesiastical benefices, and all clerics, regular or secular, of the aforesaid county and dioceses, cannot, because of the most bitter war of the illustrious lord king of the French against the Flemings, be presented to the venerable fathers, their own bishops or their vicars, [Col. 1914C] to obtain canonical institution and orders; whence it results that the said churches are deprived of their requisite rectors and ministers, Christ’s faithful are left without the care of their own priests, divine worship is diminished, and many works of salvation [lacuna], while manifold injury arises both to the churches themselves and to their patrons, clerical or lay, and to the persons elected and the aforesaid clerics—may you deign, most holy Father, mercifully to provide that the functions of the said bishops may suitably be supplied in the aforesaid county in these and similar matters.

> Likewise, since ecclesiastical persons elected to ecclesiastical dignities, to vacant parish churches, or to any other ecclesiastical benefices, and all clerics, regular or secular, of the aforesaid county and dioceses, cannot be presented to the venerable fathers, their own bishops or their vicars, to receive canonical institution and orders, and since their [Col. 1914D] matrimonial and all other spiritual causes [lacuna].
>
> [Note: [Col. 1913D] Archives of Flanders at Lille. This document bears the title: “These are the supplications which had to be made at Rome while Lord Philip of Flanders held the administration of the land of Flanders.”]

Yet the events, hastening toward an all too foreseeable conclusion, left Boniface VIII no leisure to give free and independent Flanders those bishoprics which she would receive two hundred and sixty years later from Spanish rule. Philip the Fair, long dissembling—Philip the Fair, whom William of Nogaret depicted as a humble and benign, merciful and gentle person, full of religion, animated by zeal for the faith, wholly devoted to prayer, patience, [Col. 1915A] and modesty—no longer boasted that he did not know how to take vengeance [Note: [Col. 1915C] “A humble and benign person, merciful and gentle, fearing God and men, always fearing to sin in his actions, kindled with the ardour of great religion and faith, daily given to prayer and divine offices, of the utmost patience and modesty, and never moved or cherished war for vengeance against his enemies.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 438.].

On 14 June 1303, in an assembly convened in the church of Notre-Dame [Note: [Col. 1915C] “When a council had assembled at Paris in the church of Blessed Mary.” Chronicle manuscript cited by Raynaldi, 1303, no. 35.], he received—not as king, but as champion of the faith and defender of the Church (Henry VIII also invoked this title in the sixteenth century)—the bill of accusation in which William of Plasian charged the pope with having sought to unite temporal and spiritual power. The representatives of the three estates heard the enumeration of all the charges, most of them so infamous that they cannot be reproduced. Then the grandson of Louis IX, whose beatification that same Pope Boniface VIII had proclaimed [Note: [Col. 1915C]

> It was he who Saint Louis  
> Canonized and exalted;  
> Yet he found his lineage  
> Afterwards a most cruel enemy;  
> When I say it, it grieves me.  
> (*Godefroi de Paris*, *Chronique métrique*, 2210.)

], declared that, although he had wished, as a respectful son, to conceal Noah’s nakedness from the people, his conscience obliged him to comply with the request made by William of Plasian [Note: [Col. 1915C] Should one write Plassian, Plasian, Plessiac, or Plessis; Nogaret or Longaret? All these spellings of the names belong to the period, and nothing better proves how obscure these names were. Plasian and Nogaret assumed the title “knights in the laws.” A manuscript provides me with the text of one such grant of legal knighthood: “Be it known [lacuna] that we grant, by special favour, to our beloved John Marci of Montpellier, doctor of laws, his merits so requiring, that he may, notwithstanding his non-noble status, be invested with the knightly belt whenever he pleases and admitted to all noble acts.” Register of royal grants under Philip the Fair, fol. 123 (Archives of Belgium). The same manuscript contains several documents of interest for the biographies of Enguerrand de Marigny, William of Nogaret, and William of Plasian. See in particular the marriage contract of a daughter of William of Plasian with Raymond Pelet, lord of Alais.], for the convocation of a council to judge the pope. The bishops present assented after some hesitation [Note: [Col. 1916C] “Considering such a matter not merely difficult but most difficult.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 102.]. One voice alone [Note: [Col. 1916C] “The abbot of Cîteaux alone did not assent to them, with indignation and disdain both for the king and the prelates,” *Chronicle of Saint-Denis*, V, p. 150. “The abbot of Cîteaux alone excepted.” Continuator of William of Nangis, 1303; Giovanni Villani, VIII, 62. The verse chronicle of the abbots of Cîteaux calls him: “A thunderbolt thundering against the wicked.” To the abbot of Cîteaux must perhaps be added the abbots of Prémontré and Cluny: *Annales dominicani Colmarienses*, 1303.] had courageously risen to defend the honour of the papacy and protest the sacrilegious usurpation of the Church’s rights and liberties: it was the voice of the abbot of Cîteaux. Philip the Fair, determined to stop before no obstacle, respected neither his pious conviction nor his courageous constancy. While the king had a sentence of death proclaimed against every ecclesiastic who should leave France, because he needed their services [Col. 1916A] in his Flemish war, and while the same penalty was imposed upon royal officers who did not prevent it [Note: [Col. 1916C] Dupuy, *Pr.*, pp. 132–133. Philip the Fair took advantage of this prohibition to have all Italian priests then in France arrested. See the bull *Super Petri solio*, Raynaldi, 1303, no. 36.], the illustrious head of Europe’s most powerful order was dragged to the towers of the Châtelet, guarded by eighty mounted sergeants and eighty foot sergeants [Note: [Col. 1916C] Ordinance of 15 November 1302. Félibien, *Pr.*, p. 615.]. No doubt this was what the king called, as he had when he caused the bishop of Pamiers to be arrested, offering to God the best of all sacrifices by the way of justice [Note: [Col. 1916C] “To offer God, by the way of justice, the best sacrifice.” Dupuy, *Pr.*, p. 630. I find no mention of Jean de Pontoise’s captivity in the statutes of the Cistercian Order for 1303. There I read only: “Since the Order is in great debt and obligated to various creditors.”].

Boniface VIII wished to honour Jean de Pontoise’s devotion by granting him two privileges which passed to his successors. The first was the right to seal with white wax [Note: [Col. 1916D] This was apparently a very important distinction. The emperors used no other wax, and it is reported that when Frederick IV created a duke of Modena, he granted him the privilege of sealing with white wax. De Wailly, *Éléments de paléographie*, II, p. 52.]; the second, the right to place upon his seal the image of the pope seated in Saint Peter’s chair and clad in pontifical vestments. Boniface VIII explained this privilege in the memorable words addressed to Jean de Pontoise: “You sat with me; you shall sit with me” (*Mecum sedisti, mecum sedebis*) [Note: [Col. 1916D] Sartorius, *Cist. bis-tertium*, p. 626. “The Cistercians,” says Saint Antoninus of Florence, “were a great pillar of the Church.”]! Finally, when Sciarra Colonna, after hiding for some time with the Florentine usurer Musciato Francesi, another accomplice in the greed and violence of Philip the Fair [Note: [Col. 1916D] According to Villani, it was Musciato Francesi who advised Philip the Fair to debase the coinage.], entered Anagni crying, “Death to the pope!,” the bull *Super Petri solio* was found there; in it the imprisonment of the abbot of Cîteaux was mentioned among the attacks that called down upon the king of France the thunders of the Church [Note: [Col. 1916D] Raynaldi, 1303, no. 36.].

Boniface VIII survived the outrage at Anagni by only a few days. His contemporaries had accused him of ambition and avarice; in the eyes of posterity he redeemed himself [Col. 1917A] by presenting to martyrdom a brow burdened with eighty-six years [Note: [Col. 1917B] Godefroi of Paris is not favourable to Boniface VIII, but the pontificate of the Avignon popes was enough to make him regretted, and the chronicler-poet adds:

> Dare say that in liberty  
> The Church was held in his time;  
> And I believe, to speak truly,  
> That he suffered all the martyrdom  
> For the Church which he held dear.

]. Hardly had his tomb been opened when the count of Flanders and the abbot of Cîteaux followed him into it. It seems that the last representative of the papacy’s temporal power drew with him the last representatives of the power of the great vassals and religious orders.

Guy of Dampierre ended his days in the tower of Compiègne, and it was in a Cistercian abbey that he was buried.

Jean de Pontoise had already died. Happier than Guy of Dampierre, he had seen the doors of his prison opened; and the continuator of William [Col. 1918A] of Nangis relates that he had resigned the abbatial dignity in order to preserve his Order from the fatal consequences of the king’s resentment [Note: [Col. 1917B] Continuator of William of Nangis, 1304; *Chronicle of Saint-Denis*, V, p. 162. Jean de Pontoise’s abdication did not end Philip the Fair’s persecutions of the Cistercian Order. I shall cite two documents on this subject.

The first concerns the two-year tithe granted by Pope Benedict XI (bull of 14 May 1304, at Perugia, *Ex multiplici negotiorum varietate*, manuscript of the Dunes, no. 338; and Leblanc, *Traité des monnaies*, p. 188), in order that the king of France might improve his currency: “that the coinage, having regard for the common welfare of the faithful, may be restored to the value and weight which it possessed in the time of Saint Louis.”

> To his venerable and most dearly beloved fellow abbots in Christ: greeting, and, after the tribulations and varied oppressions of this passing life, the consolation of eternal blessedness to be awaited. We believe it has not escaped your notice how the two-year tithe was granted to the lord king of the French by the supreme pontiff, and how that same lord king, through his collectors and bailiffs, wished to compel us and ours to an immediate and unprecedented payment, and to levy a separate tithe from every abbey and place of our Order, to the future disgrace and unforeseen and irreparable loss of the Order itself. Therefore the reverend father, the lord abbot of Cîteaux, wishing to ward off present and future dangers and, so far as he could, preserve the honour of the Order unimpaired, approached the royal majesty; and at length, by the favour of welcome grace, not without anguish of heart and affliction of spirit, he reached an agreement with the aforesaid lord king, as had been done on another occasion, as is more fully contained in the royal letters drawn up on the subject, the tenor of which we send you. Wherefore we warn and exhort your whole body in the Lord, and nonetheless firmly command you, by virtue of holy obedience, that each of you pay, without any deduction, the sums imposed upon you in the recently demanded final assessment, calculated in debased coin but payable in good, strong coin of small and old Tours deniers, for two tithes, at the following two terms: to the aforesaid father, the lord abbot of Cîteaux, or to his agent, at Paris, on the octave of Saint Remigius next, for the first tithe; and for the second, on the immediately following octave of Saint John the Baptist. Payment shall be made at the places and terms assigned, under penalty of exposure of your goods to the royal hand and liability for interest should it happen—which God forbid—that a loan must be contracted on that account. Moreover, to avoid expenses and labour, you may make the first payment to the said father or his agent at Dijon, at the time of the general chapter. But if the royal collectors have already extorted or levied anything from you, send or bring letters stating the names of those collectors and the sums paid, and we shall have this deducted in your case and that of the Order, etc.
>
> (Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 609.)

The second concerns the imposition of a fifth in 1305 (*Preuves des libertés de l’Église gallicane*, II, p. 234):

> Pierced to the heart by the stings of acute sorrow, and lamenting that the cause—or rather the plight—of our Cistercian Order and of the whole Gallican Church is being grievously aggravated in many ways, we report that lately at Paris the reverend father in Christ, the lord abbot of Cîteaux, together with the other prelates of the kingdom and ecclesiastical persons, was summoned to deliberate concerning assistance to be rendered to our lord the king. Under pretext of certain privileges newly granted him by the lord pope, and consenting lest we might incur greater burdens through the force of the said privileges, he was compelled, together with the other prelates of the kingdom and other ecclesiastical persons, on his own behalf and ours, and on behalf of the monasteries and places of our Order situated in the said realm, to grant one fifth of all the revenues and proceeds of our Order, payable in two instalments, etc.
>
> (Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 515.)

See also Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, I, col. 1343. We must descend to the final years of Philip the Fair to find traces of reparation prompted either by remorse or by fear of a general uprising. A document preserved in the archives of Lille teaches us that in September 1312 the king exempted the Cistercian Order from all tithes which might be levied in the future; and before me lies a letter of 20 March 1313 (old style), in which he announces that he wishes to assist Clairvaux Abbey—once so celebrated for the splendour and magnificence of its religious ceremonies, but already threatened with utter ruin:

> This monastery, distinguished and noble among other monasteries, is oppressed by so great a burden of so many and such debts that, unless speedy remedy is provided for it, the servants of the monastery must lamentably be dispersed to various places; and consequently the divine office, which has until now been celebrated there so devoutly and solemnly, must be utterly destroyed, and the monastery itself brought to the misery of irreparable desolation.
>
> (Manuscript of the Dunes, no. 868.)

And it was Philip the Fair himself who, before dying, thus set down the sad history of his reign!].

Yet the memory of his holiness and courage remained surrounded by respect, and he was entered in the martyrology of the blessed of Cîteaux, where the history of his life was summarized in a few words: “Through many labours and various perils, by unwearied endeavour, he ascended to the summit of monastic piety” [Note: [Col. 1918D] Henriquez, *Menologium ordinis Cisterciensis*, p. 92; *Gallia christiana*, IV, col. 998.].

This is approximately what the Chronicle of the Dunes also says of Abbot James of Biervliet, who died about the same time as Jean de Pontoise and, like him, was compelled to lay down his authority: “broken by old age and [Col. 1919A] long illness” [Note: [Col. 1919A] *Chronicle of the Monastery of the Dunes*, p. 14.]. This final complaint—equally true of the abbot of Cîteaux and the abbot of the Dunes, of the pope and the count of Flanders—is simply the history of the end of the [Col. 1920A] thirteenth century, that century remarkable among all those of the Middle Ages for its learning and glory, its virtues and genius.

[Col. 1919]

## TWO DIPLOMAS HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED

[Note: [Col. 1919D] Supplied by M. de Jubainville.]

### I. Hatto, bishop of Troyes, at the request of Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and Bernard of Clairvaux, grants to the monastery of Aremar the church of Clerey and the church of Faux. (Between 1132 and 1136.)

[Col. 1919B]

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, HUGH, by the grace of God bishop of Auxerre, and I, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, [write] to all Christ’s faithful.
>
> Everyone who is of the truth gladly hears the truth and bears witness to the truth. Therefore we make known to the whole body of the faithful that Hatto, venerable bishop of Troyes, at our request and through our agency, gave to the monastery of Aremar the church of Clerey and the church of Faux [Note: [Col. 1919] The churches in question are those of Clerey and Faux-Fresnay.], with the approval of Manasses of Villemaur and Falcon, his archdeacons. And in order that this gift may remain firm and unimpaired, [Col. 1919C] the aforesaid bishop and we, by the protection of the apostolic lord Pope Innocent II, of blessed memory, [lacuna]. But lest so manifest a truth, through the age of succeeding times or mute [lacuna] of ours, we have taken care to confirm.

(Original parchment, undated. On the back is written: “Gift made to us concerning the churches of Clerey and Faux.” The seal, which hung by a double parchment tag, is missing.—Archives of the Aube, Moutier-Ancey collection.)

### II. Hatto, bishop of Troyes, at the request of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, “of blessed memory,” grants the church of Lusigny to the canons of Saint Lupus of Troyes. (Year 1143.)

I, Hatto, by the grace of God bishop of Troyes, [Col. 1919D] wish it to be known to all, present as well as future, that the lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of blessed memory, requested of us that we grant the church of Lusigny to the canons of Saint-Loup of Troyes. Since we held that abbot in great veneration because of his holiness, and were altogether unwilling to refuse him anything that he might justly request of us, we granted the aforesaid church in perpetuity to the said canons—namely, to Lord Everard, the abbot, and the other brethren serving God under his rule, and to their successors—saving our episcopal right.

But because a certain knight named Walter the Fisherman had formerly possessed, and had retained down to our own time, a third part of the small tithe, of the offerings on the four principal feasts, and of the churchyard rent, we removed all this from the hand of that same knight by the force of ecclesiastical justice; and we took care to supplement with this, too, the gift which we had made to the aforesaid canons with respect to the other things in that church. This was done on the following terms: the aforesaid abbot and his successors shall be free to choose, whether regular or secular, a chaplain to serve that church. When he has chosen a suitable person, he shall present him to the bishop, and the bishop shall confer upon him, without any opposition, the pastoral care of the aforesaid church. That chaplain, however, shall answer for those matters which pertain to episcopal right, namely for the *circadia* dues and synods.

Moreover, the same church shall pay each year sixteen denarii: namely, eight at the Easter synod and eight at the synod held in September; and in the third year, five solidi. Once these payments have been made by the priest serving in that church, according to custom, at the general synod, that priest shall thereafter remain free and released from every kind of exaction. Our beloved son and archdeacon, Manasses of Villamauro, to whose care that church belonged, cooperated in this matter.

Therefore, since this gift, the sounder the intention with which it was made, ought to be confirmed with correspondingly greater care lest any future challenge should unsettle it, we wished this present instrument to be drawn up concerning it. We have left it fortified not only by the impression of our seal, but also by the attestation of lawful persons, whose names follow.

These, therefore, are the names of the witnesses who were present: Lord Guy, abbot of the monastery of Aremar; Lord Theobald, abbot of the monastery of Derv; Lord Odo, provost of Saint Peter; Manasses, archdeacon of Rumilly; Gibuin, cantor and archdeacon; Stephen of Venizy; Garner of Saint-Remi, priest and canon of Saint Peter; Stephen Lupus, canon of Saint Peter and priest; Eustace; Hilduin of Paulibes; [Col. 1920D] Angelmer of Sézanne; Stephen, son of Girulf; Milo of [lacuna], canon of Saint Peter; Count Guy of Jarre; Lord Helenus, abbot of Arripathorium; Geoffrey of Peronne; Geoffrey of Auxerre; Gancher of La Ferté, monks of Clairvaux.

This was done in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1143, the epact being 13, the concurrent 4, while Louis reigned as king of the Franks and Theobald administered the county of Troyes.

(Original on parchment. On the back is written: “Instrument of Bishop Hatto concerning the church and the lesser tithe of Lusigny,” and, in fifteenth-century characters: “Letter of the donation of the church of Lusigny and of the same tithes.” The seal, which had been suspended by a double parchment tag, is missing.—Archives of Aube, Saint-Loup collection.)

Vices must be attacked by contrary virtues, 385. Vices cannot be uprooted, nor virtues acquired, without great labor, 389. Connection of vices, 387. We are armed against vices by sentences of Scripture, 448. Continual martyrdom is the daily conflict with vices, 1007. The virtues of brothers, rather than their vices, are to be counted and made public, 158. Not everyone is attacked by the same vices, 388. Three calves to be sacrificed to God, 777. Although reproach, when absent, need not be feared, yet when present it wounds the unguarded person, 539. Threefold state of life, 773. One thing is to live according to oneself, another according to God, 375. He lives in vain, or does not live at all, who does not live for God, 203. A monk should not think himself alive if he does not do that for which one lives in a cell, 210. Whether it is permissible to live from another’s labor, 218. Threefold calling, 785. One must not resist calling grace, 193; indeed, one must obey it promptly, 297, 298. Where God calls, counsel is unnecessary, 297. Human wisdom offers faithless counsel concerning a calling, 297. A monk must consider the end of his calling, 637. The bride’s threefold calling in the Song, an indication of vehement affection, 94. Let him now learn to fly from earth to heaven who ultimately wishes to soar into heaven, 1007. Birds denote vain persons, 455. Natural will is a certain appetite of the mind, 226. According to its various appetite it receives various names, 226. It is the origin of diverse thoughts, 228. In itself it is a simple affection, capable of good and evil, 245. How it must be governed, 226. Obedience is its guardian, 226. When will is joined to truth, it is love; when nourished by grace, it is loving affection; when it enjoys possession, it is charity, 226. God has a twofold will, of mercy and providence; likewise, one will permits, another approves, 552. God’s will, as most sacred, is also most secret, 291. A person conformed to the supreme will is united to God by a bond that cannot be broken, 397. Four kinds of human will, 775. Great will toward God is love, 228. One should apply oneself to another’s will rather than one’s own, 797. How much good will and truth avail, 226. How good will must be prepared, and with what care, 225. How rich it is, 1001. Sometimes we seek good will and pursue it more when it flees than follow it when it leads, 29. Will is not good if it does not do what it can, 338. It is not always to be trusted, 211. Necessity, force, and efficacy of good will, 338. A corrupted will receives as many names of vices as it possesses vices, 245. Corruption of the will is not healed at once, 84. A will that turns aside is concupiscence, 226. How many evils a slack will produces, 225. An evil will is free and servile, 132. Self-will attacks, denies, robs, and in a certain way kills God, 708 and following. How many evils spring from the root of self-will, 286. Self-will turns good things into sin, 381. Denial of self-will, 812. Recesses of self-will, 309, 599. Self-will, the cause of salvation and damnation, 369. Pleasure of the flesh does not make people happy, 405. Our two chief enemies: pride of mind and pleasure of the flesh, 1051. Pleasure once passed leaves behind repentance, 389. The pleasures of the world are deceitful and fleeting, 126. Pleasure-lovers denoted by beasts, 455. Some vows are common and others special, 880. Unlawful vows must be rescinded, 880. Blessed Mary was the first to make a vow of virginity, 450, 453. By what eye the bridegroom is wounded, 98. By what lock of hair, 99. Tears give signs of a wounded heart, 98. [Col. 1975] The fox’s den: prudence of the flesh, 298. **Chapter V.**—Concerning an elder to whom the Lord Jesus appeared while he kept vigil on the day of *Parasceve*. Here *Parasceve* means the day on which the memorial of Christ’s Passion is celebrated in the Church. Among the Jews every Friday was called *Parasceve*, that is, “Preparation,” because on that day food and other necessities were prepared for the following Sabbath day, on which it was not permitted either to cook food or to do anything of that kind. Therefore, because Christ was crucified on the *Parasceve* of Passover, the day of his Passion is called *Parasceve*. For churchmen do not call days by the names of idols, as profane people customarily do, who, like pagans, speak of the days of Mars, Jupiter, Venus, and so forth. 1100

**Chapter XIII.**—At Saint Bernard’s command the death of a certain monk of Clairvaux is postponed. 1291

**Chapter XIV.**—Holy angels stand about the bed of a dying monk at Clairvaux. 1291

**Chapter XV.**—Christ the Lord appears in sleep to a lay brother of Clairvaux who tends oxen, urging on oxen with him, pressing the plough-handle, and breaking up the earth with the plough. 1291

**Chapter XVI.**—A certain lay brother of Clairvaux, ignorant of letters and near death, discoursed at length in Latin on the holy Scriptures. 1292

**Chapter XVII.**—A lay brother left Clairvaux three times and was received back three times; at last, truly and long repentant, he tasted eternal blessedness shortly before death. 1292

**Chapter XVIII.**—Concerning Gerard, a lay brother of Moris, a most gentle and devout man: shortly before death, Christ the Lord appears to him with the twelve apostles. 1293

**Chapter XIX.**—A monk of Clairvaux frequently sees evil demons in horrible forms; he sees Saint Augustine, who leads him both to places of punishment and to the abodes of the blessed; he sees the soul of a monk leave the body and hover in the air until it is fortified by a priestly commendation; finally, during Mass, he sees the infant Jesus recoil from a wicked priest. 1294

**Chapter XX.**—Robert, priest at Amiens, a lover and preacher of chastity. There also, a certain chaste woman, accustomed to see the infant Jesus at the time of sacrifice, saw him willingly descend upon the virtuous but recoil from the wicked. 1296

**Chapter XXI.**—Northman, a church bedesman, sees during the divine sacrifice a priest deprived of the kiss of the infant Jesus because of the hatred which stirred him against his fellow godparent. He also sees during the Rogation Days the frivolous songs of women despised by angels and greeted with the laughter of demons. 1297

[Col. 2005]

**Chapter XXII.**—A brother of Clairvaux, accustomed after receiving the Eucharist to taste honeyed sweetness in his mouth, once received Communion after rebuking a friend too harshly and felt an extremely unpleasant bitterness, like that of wormwood. 1298

**Chapter XXIII.**—Another brother of Clairvaux saw Christ the Lord on the holy day of *Parasceve*, as though crucified at that very hour. 1299

**Chapter XXIV.**—Christ appears to a certain elder of Clairvaux while he is in ecstasy and says: “Your sins are forgiven you.” 1299

**Chapter XXV.**—A young monk, wrongly interpreting the devout tears of his abbot as he adored the cross on *Parasceve*, is immediately grievously tempted by a demon to cast off the monastic habit. 1299

**Chapter XXVI.**—The same abbot saw a demon in choir offering red wine in a cup to each monk; one of them, having tasted it, was harassed by a spirit of fornication. 1300

**Chapter XXVII.**—A demon, seen in the likeness of Simon, a monk, leads a Christian lay brother out of the monastery. 1300

**Chapter XXVIII.**—A monk of Clairvaux, thinking of leaving his vocation, saw Saint Malachy in sleep and was struck with the staff of Saint Bernard; he returned to soundness of mind. 1301

**Chapter XXIX.**—A certain lay brother of Clairvaux, trusting in his obedience, dies happily. 1301

**Chapter XXX.**—At the death of a certain religious brother, harmonious angelic music was heard. Boso, one of Saint Bernard’s first-born sons, died with his entire face wonderfully radiant. 1303

**Chapter XXXI.**—Shortly after Saint Bernard’s death, a certain man who contemplated leaving because of the violence of temptations of the flesh is strengthened in his vocation when Bernard appears to him. 1303

**Chapter XXXII.**—Walter, a lay brother, is commanded in a dream by a certain venerable maiden to celebrate the Mass, which he afterward retained in memory. 1304

**Chapter XXXIII.**—While a certain abbot and several others prayed, scents of wondrous sweetness were breathed into their nostrils and tastes into their palates. 1304

**Chapter XXXIV.**—The most blessed Virgin, Mother of God, appearing to a certain brother once and again, assured him of his salvation. 1306

**Chapter XXXV.**—From Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx: a report concerning certain nuns who were accustomed in contemplation to be carried outside themselves. 1306

## Book Two

**Chapter I.**—Concerning the wonderful austerity of life of Dominic, a solitary near the city of León; and concerning evil and good spirits which appeared to him almost continually. 1307

**Chapter II.**—Christ the Lord, appearing to a novice of Clairvaux, blesses him and one of his companions, but passes over a third, evil in name and in fact; after three days he fell away from the Order. 1314

**Chapter III.**—On the day after Easter, a monk of Clairvaux, while in choir, saw high above a shining right hand emerging from the midst, which once and again blessed the chanting brethren in the air by tracing the sign of the saving cross. 1314

**Chapter IV.**—Andrew, formerly archdeacon of Verdun, a man most noble and refined, is converted at Clairvaux together with Geoffrey. When he despaired of persevering, peas of exquisite flavor were seen by him, though seasoned only with water and salt. 1315

**Chapter V.**—A certain monk of Clairvaux is blessed by Christ the Lord appearing to him. 1316

**Chapter VI.**—A remarkable fragrance and taste, together with a heavenly vision, are imparted to a certain brother of Clairvaux. 1316

**Chapter VII.**—A novice at Clairvaux sees Blessed Mary Magdalene standing before the altar, but for the present is denied a vision of the most blessed Mother of God. 1318

**Chapter VIII.**—Prayer with hands joined or outstretched is confirmed by several appearances of Christ. 1318

**Chapter IX.**—Concerning a certain young German who was wonderfully converted at Clairvaux to monastic life and became illustrious for outstanding holiness and divine manifestations. 1318

**Chapter X.**—A monk of Clairvaux, most devoted to the cult of Saint John the Evangelist, learns many things concerning divine matters through him. 1321

**Chapter XI.**—Saint Bernard declares by God’s revelation that the souls of many penetrate heaven immediately upon leaving the body, by a free and unobstructed passage. He also predicts that all who should persevere in the Cistercian Order, while its discipline remained vigorous, would be saved. He foretells concerning his brother Guy that, because he concerned himself excessively with the affairs of the community of Clairvaux, he would die outside Clairvaux. 1322

[Col. 2006]

**Chapter XII.**—To Simon, abbot of Chézy, of the black Order of Benedictines, Saint Bernard denied transfer to Clairvaux as long as he lived; yet he foretold that Simon would die at Clairvaux, which later occurred. 1324

**Chapter XIII.**—Gunnar, tetrarch of Sardinia, becomes a monk at Clairvaux after Saint Bernard’s death, in fulfillment of Bernard’s prediction. 1324

**Chapter XIV.**—Saint Bernard, living at Rome for three years, repeatedly visits his own at Clairvaux. Certain other wonders concerning him. 1324

**Chapter XV.**—When Constantius, condemned to hanging, was being led to the gallows, Saint Bernard rescued him from the executioner; with Count Theobald’s consent, he had him tonsured at Clairvaux and clothed him in the monastic habit. 1324

**Chapter XVI.**—Saint Bernard refutes a slanderous heretic by a prudent answer. 1325

**Chapter XVII.**—At Paris, by words, tears, and groans, he converts several clerics to a holier form of life and takes them with him to Clairvaux. 1326

**Chapter XVIII.**—At Milan, a certain person declared that he had seen Bernard among the apostles. 1327

**Chapter XIX.**—As Saint Bernard prayed, Christ crucified appeared to him, released his arms from the cross, and embraced him. 1328

**Chapter XX.**—For an epileptic monk Saint Bernard obtains that, foreseeing the illness, he can lie down on his bed and avoid the injury of a sudden fall. 1328

**Chapter XXI.**—Saint Bernard appeared several times, not long after his death, to a man first a canon regular and afterward a monk of Clairvaux. 1329

**Chapter XXII.**—The remarkable conversion to monastic life, through Saint Bernard’s aid, of Alexander—formerly canon and teacher at Cologne, later abbot of Grandselve, and finally abbot of Cîteaux. 1331

**Chapter XXIII.**—Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, knows by God’s revelation that Saint Bernard, while still a novice, had on a certain day omitted the seven penitential psalms which he was accustomed to say daily in silence for his mother’s soul. 1332

**Chapter XXIV.**—Concerning Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, who was miraculously supplied with three carts and nine horses; and who, having resigned his office, saw an unclean spirit enter the mouth of Guy, appointed in his place. 1332

**Chapter XXV.**—Fastrad, formerly abbot of Cambron, then of Clairvaux, and afterward of Cîteaux, a man of venerable bearing and great virtues, is divinely commended even at his death. 1334

**Chapter XXVI.**—A certain abbot is warned from heaven not to strive further to shake off the burden of his office. The same man had formerly been delivered from exceedingly severe and frequent headaches by what seemed a miraculous fall of a mass of lead into the middle of his forehead. 1334

**Chapter XXVII.**—Baldwin, knight and lord of Guise, a criminal man, dies at Igny in the monastic habit. Appearing often afterward to Peter, abbot of Igny, he is at last, after long purification, received into heaven through the prayers of the abbot and monks. 1335

**Chapter XXVIII.**—Concerning the plague that devastated the monastery of La Maison-Dieu; and concerning the blessed passage to the higher realms of Abbot Franco and the monk Bernard. 1337

**Chapter XXIX.**—Certain wonders concerning Gerard of Furfa, an old man of admirable piety and exceptional holiness. Saint Bernard appeared to him when he was near death; Gerard also complained after death that he had been buried too hastily while still breathing. 1338

**Chapter XXX.**—Concerning Lawrence, lay brother of Clairvaux, who, rescued from many dangers through Saint Bernard’s aid, brought ten oxen to Clairvaux. 1340

**Chapter XXXI.**—Concerning a monk who died at Burlancourt: it is revealed to a holy man that he was equal in merit to the holy martyrs John and Paul. 1342

**Chapter XXXII.**—A certain devout man who died in the territory of Meaux was found remaining on bare ground, kneeling upon his knees and the joints of his left hand, while holding his right hand to his breast as though striking it. 1343

**Chapter XXXIII.**—A monk of the Cistercian Order, especially devoted to prayer and reading, sees first Saint John the Evangelist, then the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and finally Christ the Lord himself coming to meet him as he was dying. 1344

**Chapter XXXIV.**—As a certain brother struggled with death, a demon appeared in the form of a monkey, mocking him and repeatedly licking a piece of cloth that he had sewn onto his worn scapular without his superior’s permission. 1344

**Chapter XXXV.**—A monk, having taken off his cowl because of the heat of a fever, put on a scapular. When he died in this attire, the gate of Paradise was closed to his soul until, restored to its body, it asked for the cowl and received the penance imposed for having discarded it. 1345

[Col. 2007]

**Chapter XXXVI.**—Concerning Abraham, abbot of Prée in Berry, who while still young was taught to appropriate nothing whatsoever—not even the least thing—without permission. He distinguished Jews by their odor; and because of angelic purity of soul and body, was honored by the Virgin Mary, Mother of God herself, with astonishing proofs of favor. 1345

**Chapter XXXVII.**—A monk of Fontenay, during his final illness, sees certain wonders, foretells his death, and is illumined by divine splendor. 1346

**Chapter XXXVIII.**—Hugh, prior of Fontenay, a man of great religious devotion and learning, dies holily on the feast day of Saint Augustine itself, as he had wished; his blessed soul, met by Saint Augustine among the other heavenly beings, is led into heaven. 1347

**Chapter XXXIX.**—The blessed death of a devout priest, a novice at the monastery of L’Aumône, is commended by several heavenly pronouncements. 1348

**Chapter XL.**—At the monastery of Fontmorigny in the diocese of Bourges, the monk Robert is divinely forewarned of the blessed death he will undergo five days later. 1349

**Chapter XLI.**—Margaret of Saint-Omer, a girl of exceptional beauty, in order to avoid marriage, cut off for herself the tip of her nose together with her upper lip—an astonishing but not imitable act. 1350

**Chapter XLII.**—Concerning a nun who tore out her own eyes, radiantly beautiful in a remarkable way, to safeguard her modesty. The wickedness and unhappy end of William, king of the English. 1351

**Chapter XLIII.**—At Fontevraud, a monastery of the Order of Fontevraud, a nun appeared after death to her companion and testified that she possessed great peace, but did not yet enjoy the sight of God. She said that when her companion joined her on the specified day, both would together be received into glory. 1353

**Chapter XLIV.**—Concerning Mary, a girl of the monastery of Carmes: at first most diligent in assisting the sick with every means; afterward paralyzed, she was distinguished in sickness and at death by prophetic illumination and by other outstanding gifts and privileges of holy souls. 1353

## Book Three
**Chapter I.**—A monk of Grand-Selve, a man of great perfection, appearing after death to Pontius, a monk who later became both abbot and bishop, reveals to him several remarkable matters concerning his condition. 1353

**Chapter II.**—A man restored from the dead said, among other things, that the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, visits the monastery of Grand-Selve three times each day. 1355

**Chapter III.**—A monk of Grand-Selve, sleeping during the night offices, is dragged out of the choir. 1356

**Chapter IV.**—A certain slothful monk, drowsy at the night offices, is terrified by demons. 1356

**Chapter V.**—At Grand-Selve many monks, carried off within a short time by a deadly disease, show that a most excellent reward has been laid up for them in heaven. 1356

**Chapter VI.**—A dying monk at Grand-Selve tastes beforehand the glory prepared for him, surpassing the merits of all men. 1357

**Chapter VII.**—The appearance of two deceased persons at Grand-Selve, for the salvation of those who survived. 1357

**Chapter VIII.**—Brother B., infirmarian of the poor and a most devout man, shortly before death sees Christ the Lord himself and the place prepared for him in heaven. 1358

**Chapter IX.**—Geoffrey, bishop of Séez, while still a monk at Clairvaux, saw a solemn procession of the heavenly orders proceeding toward the infirmary; they are believed to have escorted the departing soul of the venerable old man and priest Tecelinus. 1360

**Chapter X.**—Several remarkable things divinely seen by, or concerning, Geoffrey, bishop of Séez. The incorrupt body of the Lord is found by him. 1360

**Chapter XI.**—Concerning Hungero, and his father and brother Rudolph, who were wondrously converted to the Premonstratensian Order. 1363

**Chapter XII.**—A child drowned in water, laid upon the altar of the blessed apostle Peter, returns to life; he later becomes a cleric and finally a Cistercian monk. 1364

**Chapter XIII.**—A runaway and apostate cleric, brought near death by a fatal illness, requested that his clerical tonsure be restored; yet no skill could shave him. 1365

**Chapter XIV.**—A sick monk of Clairvaux, superstitious in regulating his food and procuring medicines, by the wonderful providence of God’s most merciful Mother both recovers his strength and lays aside excessive concern for himself. 1365

**Chapter XV.**—Concerning Alcherius, a monk of Clairvaux, contemptuous indeed of himself, but most diligent, through love of Christ, in caring for the sick, especially the poor; from Christ’s wounds he deserved to obtain blessing and healing. [Col. 2008] 1366

**Chapter XVI.**—To a certain brother troubled and contrite over his sins, Christ shows how highly he values the tears and mourning of penitents. 1368

**Chapter XVII.**—By another wondrous vision, Christ the Lord instilled in the same brother hope of pardon and of his mercy. 1368

**Chapter XVIII.**—A vision on the same subject, shown to the same brother. 1368

**Chapter XIX.**—At Dommartin, a village in the territory of Toul, the Eucharist, together with its sacred pyx and corporal, escaped flames, while all the objects around it were consumed by fire. 1369

**Chapter XX.**—The sacrament of the Eucharist, stored in a chest, is changed into flesh and disclosed by the sign of a divine light. 1369

**Chapter XXI.**—In the district of Chartres, the greater part of a most sacred host is changed into flesh. 1370

**Chapter XXII.**—On Friday, while a priest is offering sacrifice, the eucharistic host is changed into flesh and the chalice into blood. 1370

**Chapter XXIII.**—While a sacrilegious priest is celebrating Mass, after the consecration had been performed and just before he wished to communicate, the sacred bread vanished in an instant from the paten, and the blood from the chalice. 1371

**Chapter XXIV.**—At Bellesme, a village in the territory of Châlons, the Eucharist secretly sent to a dying woman is made public by an evil spirit. 1371

**Chapter XXV.**—When the Eucharist was brought to a wicked man near death, before he received it he was lifted into the air by demons and dashed to the ground. 1372

**Chapter XXVI.**—A certain lay brother of Bec, near death, is delivered from demonic assaults by the prayers of the whole community; fortified with the sacraments, he departs this life with a good confession. 1372

**Chapter XXVII.**—A lay brother of Longpont, who kept one denarius and one small purse without permission, after receiving the Eucharist at Easter, seemed to have cast a burning coal into his own breast. 1373

**Chapter XXVIII.**—The Eucharist, hidden at the entrance of a pigsty for the health of swine, is divinely revealed and found to have been changed for the greater part into flesh. 1373

**Chapter XXIX.**—A poor peasant, having received the Eucharist on Easter Day and retained it in his mouth, sewed it into his garment in the hope of relieving his poverty. Later, when he was endangered by illness, it was disclosed by him and found wholly transformed into flesh. 1374

**Chapter XXX.**—The Eucharist, placed in a beehive, is found three years later whole and unharmed at the top of the hive. 1374

**Chapter XXXI.**—In Sardinia, much concerning the punishments of the next life is divinely revealed to a certain priest. 1375

**Chapter XXXII.**—A Saracen girl, most desirous of the Christian religion, is slaughtered by a Christian but immoral soldier while defending her chastity, and is enrolled among the martyrs by Pope Alexander III. 1377

**Chapter XXXIII.**—The monks of Bourlencourt are deterred by a fiery apparition from digging up a treasure which one of them had dreamed of. 1378

**Chapter XXXIV.**—Margaret, a pious woman in the bishopric of Rosquélie, long harassed by a barbarous husband and at last cruelly killed, is divinely distinguished by the intactness of her sacred body and by other miracles. 1380

**Chapter XXXV.**—An evil demon tries to avenge the injury done by the breaking and burning of its image. 1381

**Chapter XXXVI.**—When the Christian faith is introduced into Slavonia, demons flee from it with a dreadful noise, like an army defeated, routed, and put to flight in battle. 1381

**Chapter XXXVII.**—A pagan woman, tormented by the sprinkling of holy water, is converted to faith in Christ. 1382

**Chapter XXXVIII.**—King Olaf, who later became a martyr, was reproved after he had, through thoughtlessness, whittled a rod with a knife on the Lord’s Day. He grieved; and, after gathering the shavings and placing them upon his hand as a punishment, he burned them, yet remained unharmed by the flame. 1382

**Chapter XXXIX.**—A bishop accustomed to uttering ridiculous things appears after death with ulcerated and swollen lips; he is freed after seven brothers have observed silence for several days. 1383

# Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux

**Preface.** 1383

**Section I.**—The coat of arms of the Cistercian Order is not derived from the armorial bearings of St Bernard.  

**Section II.**—The nobility of Humbelina, St Bernard’s sister, and likewise that of his sister-in-law—the wife of his brother Guy—demonstrates St Bernard’s noble birth. [Col. 2009] 1385

**Section III.**—Neither St Bernard’s full sister nor his sister-in-law were nuns of the Cistercian Order, but Black Benedictines. 1387

**Section IV.**—On his father’s side St Bernard belonged to the equestrian order, then called the *militia*, and in that rank was of ancient and pure descent. 1388

**Section V.**—Through his mother Aalis of Montbard, St Bernard descended from the counts of Tonnerre and indeed from the ancient dukes of Burgundy. 1391

**Section VI.**—The question concerning the nobility of Aalis, St Bernard’s mother, is resolved from the record of her death on the Kalends of September in the necrologies of Saint-Bénigne, where, without any title of illustrious lineage, she is called merely a laywoman. 1393

**Section VII.**—St Bernard’s illustrious lineage is confirmed from the various connections by marriage of his family. 1395

**Proofs and elucidations of the assertions or propositions in the Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.**

# Appendix to the Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux

**Preface.** 1505

**Chapter I.**—A Fontenay genealogical table is set before the reader, representing the paternal and maternal lineage of St Bernard. 1506

**Chapter II.**—Werricus of Châtillon was neither a count nor Tecelinus’s father. Godfrey, husband of Gertrude and father of Hugh and Nicardus, likewise has no connection with the lineage of that Tecelinus; nor do Gerardus or Milo of Châtillon, though Evanurus perhaps belonged to the same family. [Col. 2013] 1508

**Chapter III.**—Andrew was not the son of Rainard of Montbard, but his grandson through Bernard’s son. There was also another Andrew, Rainard’s brother, omitted from the Fontenay charter, or rather transferred from St Bernard’s maternal lineage into his paternal one. 1510

**Chapter IV.**—Godfrey, bishop of Langres, was not brother of Thecelin the Red, but of the knight Rainerius, whether of Acrimont or of La Roche. 1511

**Chapter V.**—The niece of Bernard, lord of Montbard, and daughter of the count of Grignon, was not the wife of Robert, duke of Burgundy; nor did she bring the county of Montbard into the dominion of the duke of Burgundy, as the second part of the Fontenay charter asserts. 1512

**Chapter VI.**—The Fontenay charter wrongly declared the lineage of Robert of Burgundy’s wife. 1513

**Chapter VII.**—The statements of the Fontenay charter concerning the two Drogos of Mello and the wife Eustachia of the younger of them are examined; and a path is opened for explaining how the lordship of Époisses passed from the family of Montbard to these Drogos. 1514

**Chapter VIII.**—Table I: St Bernard’s paternal lineage, from Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines. 1516

**Chapter IX.**—Table II: St Bernard’s maternal lineage. 1518

**Chapter X.**—Explanation of the other part of this second table, containing noteworthy matters concerning the ancient counts of Grignon. 1520

**Chapter XI.**—Table III, tracing the ancient family of Sombernon to its extinction in the royal family of the dukes of Burgundy. 1523

**Chapter XII.**—Table IV, listing the lords of Fontaines of the Sombernon family down to Mary, daughter and heiress of Richard. 1523

**Chapter XIII.**—Table V, concerning the family of Sauz and its relationship to Fontaines: who was William of Lauz, whose wife was Belota of Fontaines. 1525

**Chapter XIV.**—Table VI, concerning the family of Marcy, attached to St Bernard’s paternal line through Mary of Fontaines. 1528

**Chapter XV.**—Table VII, concerning the family of Saigny, attached to that of Fontaines through Amiota of Marcy, daughter of Mary of Fontaines. 1528

**Chapter XVI.**—Table VIII, concerning the family of Saffres, ending with Isabella, wife of Hugh of Saigny. 1529

**Chapter XVII.**—Table IX, concerning the family of Cléron, into which that of Fontaines was incorporated through the Saigny and Saffres lines and in which it survives to the present day. 1532

**Chapter XVIII.**—An opinion concerning St Bernard’s heraldic device. 1532

**Chapter XIX.**—Hugh, count of Troyes, first founder of Clairvaux Abbey; the site itself was commonly called Clairvaux long before the arrival of the Cistercian colony. 1535

**Chapter XX.**—The year and month in which Clairvaux was founded. 1537

**Chapter XXI.**—When the charters of Hugh, count of Troyes, concerning the foundation of Clairvaux were drawn up; his three journeys to the Lord’s Sepulchre; and his titles as they varied over time. 1539

**Chapter XXII.**—What became of Odo of Champagne, the disinherited son of Hugh, count of Troyes; and how he was connected by blood to the family of the counts of Burgundy. 1541

**Chapter XXIII.**—A corollary on the journey eastward undertaken by Andrew of Époisses, kinsman of St Bernard, against the Muslims. 1543
