[Col. 2015] STUDIES IN THE HISTORY OF THE THIRTEENTH CENTURY.—Investigations into the part taken by the Order of Cîteaux and the Count of Flanders in the conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair.

I.—Charter of Philip the Fair concerning the biennial tithe levied upon the possessions of the Order of Cîteaux (1294).—This tithe was granted to the king in an assembly of the Order of Cîteaux held at Dijon.—He shall remain uninvolved in the collection of the tithe, and it shall cease to be demanded if the war does not continue. 1838  

II.—Declaration of the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux concerning the same tithe.—They believe that they ought to consent to the request made for it by the king, so that he may protect their property against the enemies of France. 1839  

III.—Protests of the Cistercian abbeys of the diocese of Tournai against the collection of the *maltôte* [extraordinary tax] (1296).—They invoke the privilege received from papal authority, whereby they are not obliged to pay either tithes or extraordinary taxes. 1840  

IV.—Memorial in reply to the monition addressed by the Archbishop of Reims.—Spiritual power and temporal power are distinct; the latter has no right to govern the former, which is superior to it.—The king cannot compel the clergy to furnish extraordinary subsidies without the pope’s assent.—Pharaoh himself exempted priests and their property from the common servitude.—The property of the clergy is necessary for the support of the poor.—The legists say that the clergy are bound only by the burdens established *ad instructionem bonorum et redemptionem captivorum*—“for the training of the good and the ransom of captives.” The subsidy demanded by the king is altogether different; and the Order of Cîteaux would consider itself, by submitting to it, guilty of negligence, perjury, and disobedience. 1842  

V.—Instrument of appeal addressed to the pope by the General Chapter of the Order of Cîteaux. There are princes, blinded by temporal interests, who, instead of protecting ecclesiastical persons, wish to crush them with taxes. Far from imitating Pharaoh, who, though an idolater, respected the liberty of priests, they impose upon the clergy almost all their exactions; and they are seen to arrogate to themselves a power which they do not possess, instead of respectfully requesting from papal authority the subsidies necessary for the public good.—The counsellors of princes, clerics and others, not daring to tell them the truth, repeat *quod dantur omnia servitio principis*—“that all things are granted for the prince’s service.”—They forget the distance separating temporal from spiritual power; they rashly usurp what God has reserved for the labourers in His vineyard and for His poor; and they pervert the meaning of Holy Scripture.—Having become blind, they will fall into the abyss and drag the princes down with them.—Yet no one dares expose himself to martyrdom, and no voice is raised in defence of religious authority, shaken in the world.—In this danger, the Order of Cîteaux urgently claims the pope’s protection. 1849  

VI.—Bull of Boniface VIII (15 May 1297).—He permits the collection of a tithe for the benefit of the king of France. 1849  

VII.—Bull of Boniface VIII (15 May 1297).—He appoints as executors of this tithe the Archbishop of Rouen, the Bishop of Auxerre, and the Abbot of Saint-Denis. 1849  

VIII.—Bull of Boniface VIII (9 August 1297).—He grants the king one year’s revenue from all vacant benefices. 1850  

IX.—Letter addressed by the dean of Tournai to the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux, requesting subsidies for the pope.—The Church is threatened with the same calamities as in the time of Emperor Frederick II.—Despite the pope’s warnings and threats, Frederick of Aragon, sprung from a perverse race, persists in usurping Sicily, which belongs to the Holy See.—The pope wishes to put an end to these wars, which have already cost much blood, apart from those which he is waging against the Colonna. 1850  

X.—Letter of Jean de Sancy, Abbot of Clairvaux, concerning two new tithes demanded by the king (25 February 1299, old style).—The Order of Cîteaux is reduced to servitude by intolerable exactions.—The king demanded new tithes, threatening the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux that, unless they granted them, he would have them levied *virtute regia*, “by royal power.”—They yielded, but with grief. 1851  

XI.—Letter of the Abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés to the pope (1 March 1299, old style).—The distressing condition of this monastery.—Causes of its ruin. 1851  

XII.—Instructions given to the ambassadors of Guy of Dampierre in England.—They shall say that the Count [Col. 2016] of Flanders has always greatly loved King Edward I.—It has especially been since the proposed marriage of his son with Philippine of Dampierre was arranged that the king has treated the Count of Flanders with greater severity.—The Duke of Brabant and the Count of Bar had long urged Guy of Dampierre to ally himself with Edward I, promising him that in that event he would have as much money as he wished, while also securing advantageous marriages for his children.—But the count was too loyal to fail in his duties as Philip the Fair’s vassal.—He now finds himself released from every bond of obedience, according to the opinion of theologians and jurists; and while the abbots of Gembloux and Floreffe go to the king of France to notify him of the absence of legal right, the lords of Blanmont and Cuyck seek the support of the king of England. 1853  

XIII.—Instrument of appeal to the pope lodged by the Count of Flanders (25 January 1296, old style).—The Count of Flanders had sworn an oath of homage to Philip the Fair as a peer of the realm, as he had done to Philip the Bold and Saint Louis; but the king held him prisoner, allied himself with his enemies, and behaved towards him contrary to every rule of reason and justice by refusing him judgment by his peers.—The count had no course left but to declare himself free of every bond of subjection and to place himself under God’s protection, since the king of France recognizes on earth no authority superior to his own. 1854  

XIV.—Letter of Emperor Adolf of Nassau to the Count of Flanders (31 August 1297).—Despite the rebellion of the princes of the Empire, he will endeavour to assist Guy of Dampierre against the king of France; he hopes that the king of England will likewise come to Flanders, and even should that prince not do so, he will remain faithful to his commitments. 1856  

XV.—Letter of Michel As Clokettes and Jacques Beck to the Count of Flanders (Rome, 2 April 1297, old style).—They found Philip of Thiette in Rome and went with him to the pope, who received them kindly.—Philip of Thiette has left Rome with Duke-King Charles of Anjou.—It is fitting that the ambassadors sent to Rome should be well supplied with money.—They have selected the best advocates of the papal court.—The pope is besieging the Colonna castle.—Frederick of Aragon and Charles of Anjou are making great preparations to fight one another. 1857  

XVI.—Letter of Michel As Clokettes and Jacques Beck to Robert of Béthune (Rome, 20 April 1298).—They inform him that the pope awaits him impatiently; if he must stop at Genoa, they will go to him to explain the state of affairs. 1859  

XVII.—Memorial presented to the pope by Robert of Béthune, Jean of Namur, and Philip of Thiette. They ask him to restore peace, secure the release of prisoners, maintain the truces, and intervene so that their sister, restored to liberty, may marry the son of the king of England.—Importance of this alliance for Flanders. 1860  

XVIII.—Another petition presented to the pope.—The same requests as in the preceding memorial.—Questions concerning the conferral of benefices and the collection of tithes.—The burghers of Valenciennes, whom the Count of Hainaut had caused to be dragged out of churches, seek the protection of ecclesiastical authority. 1860  

XIX.—Letter of the Count of Flanders to his sons (Petegem, 23 July 1298).—He is in good health, but deeply sad.—The agents of the king of France do not cease to overwhelm him with harassment and demand the castellanies of the towns they occupy.—Dispute concerning the town of Renaix.—Complaints against the Bishop of Tournai.—It is expedient to act in agreement with the Count of Savoy, the king of England’s ambassador at Rome.—It is better not to submit this dispute to papal arbitration.—Albert of Austria has defeated Adolf of Nassau and is making for Aachen.—Guy of Dampierre has sent the lord of Fauquemont to him.—It is presumed that the pope will oppose Albert of Austria’s election.—The Count of Savoy is greatly loved by the pope.—This letter had been completed when the count learned that his sons had submitted to papal arbitration.—He sends them the powers of attorney they requested.—He urges them to insist that his daughter’s marriage to Edward I’s son take place, and also to seek annulment of the privileges granted under necessity to the towns of Flanders. 1861  

XX.—Letter of the sons of the Count of Flanders to their father (Rome, June 1298). They appeared before the pope with the English ambassadors.—They sought [Col. 2017] to establish that the king of France had never consented to submit the Count of Flanders’s complaints to judgment by the peers.—The pope asks to be chosen as arbitrator.—Their hesitation.—They consult the English ambassadors.—They accept papal arbitration, making reservations concerning the alliance with the king of England.—The pope declares that he has no thought of enlarging the already excessively vast possessions of the king of France. 1867  

XXI.—Letter of the sons of the Count of Flanders to their father (Rome, June 1298).—They set out in greater detail the reasons that led them to submit to papal arbitration.—Various reasons.—What they have to fear from the pope.—They also fear being reproached as the sole obstacle to the peace of Europe.—The unfavourable disposition of minds in Flanders.—Intrigues of Philip the Fair in Holland. 1870  

XXII.—Account of the audience granted by the pope to the sons of the Count of Flanders (25 June 1298).—Speech addressed to the pope asking that the Count of Flanders be included in the negotiations between the kings of France and England.—The dangers threatening Guy of Dampierre should it be otherwise.—The Archbishop of Dublin supports these remarks. 1871  

XXIII.—Letter of the sons of the Count of Flanders to their father (Rome, 30 June 1298).—Further details concerning the same audience.—The pope’s unfavourable response.—Arrival in Rome of delegates from the city of Bruges.—The pope’s arbitral award. 1873  

XXIV.—Account of the conference held between the sons of the Count of Flanders and the English ambassadors.—Robert of Béthune and his brothers deny certain statements attributed to them.—They do not wish to do anything against the alliance existing between the king of England and the Count of Flanders. 1874  

XXV.—Papal bull.—He extends the time limits for the appeal lodged by the Count of Flanders. 1875  

XXVI.—Letter of Robert of Béthune to his father.—A fever detains him at Lausanne.—It is reported that peace has been made between Charles of Anjou and Frederick of Aragon. 1876  

XXVII.—Letter of Robert of Béthune and Jean of Namur to Jacques Beck and Michel As Clokettes (Baume, 11 September 1298).—They charge them to inform the Cardinal of Parma of the state of affairs in Flanders and of the need to enforce the truce.—The lord of Blanmont has not been released.—Captivity of John Balliol, king of Scotland.—Redemption of the Countess of Flanders’s cross.—Did Boniface VIII accept the arbitration as pope or as a private individual?—There is discussion of summoning the king of France before the pope. 1876  

XXVIII.—Letter of the Count of Flanders to the king of England.—Confidence which he places in his support.—Non-observance of the truces.—The dangers threatening him.—He begs him to have pity on him.—Favourable dispositions of Albert of Austria, who wishes to settle the difficulties between the Counts of Flanders and Hainaut. 1880  

XXIX.—Letter addressed to the Count of Flanders (Rome, 19 February 1298, old style).—Complaints concerning the complete lack of news from Flanders.—The influence of the king of France at Rome.—Proceedings against the Bishop of Thérouanne. 1882  

XXX.—Letter addressed to the Count of Flanders (Rome, 22 April 1299).—The Count of Hainaut announces his intention to claim the County of Flanders.—His envoys at Rome have been warned that, in that case, Guy of Dampierre would lay claim to Hainaut.—German affairs.—The pope’s departure for Anagni. 1883  

XXXI.—Letter of Jean de Menin to the Count of Flanders (Anagni, 9 July 1299).—He asked the pope to cause Philippine of Dampierre and the lord of Blanmont to be restored to freedom, and to ensure observance of the truces.—The pope’s courteous answer.—Since then, nothing has been done.—A secret reason leads Jean de Menin to hope for nothing.—The Colonna have escaped from Tivoli, and are said to be assembling their adherents near Rome.—Philip of Thiette embarked at Naples for Sicily.—Great wars in Lombardy.—Jean de Menin lacks money.—He considers returning to Flanders.—The Cardinals of Parma and Aquasparta support Guy of Dampierre’s interests.—It is announced that the negotiations between Philip the Fair and Albert of Austria have been broken off, to the pope’s great joy; he refuses Albert the title of king.—Jean de Menin hopes that peace will not be made between the kings of France and England.—The pope’s words on the matter.—The pope’s illness.—He wishes to recover his strength in [Col. 2018] his native country, so that he may go to some suitable place to hear in person the kings of France and England and the Count of Flanders.—Philip of Thiette has landed in Sicily with the king of Aragon and the Duke of Calabria. 1884  

XXXII.—Letter addressed to the Count of Flanders (Anagni, 23 July 1299).—The king of Aragon, the Prince of Taranto, and Roger of Lauria took twenty-two galleys from Frederick of Aragon, the Sicilians, and the Genoese.—Rejoicing at Anagni.—Departure of the Cardinal of Parma for Apulia.—Papal audience.—News has been received of the treaty made between Philip the Fair and Edward I.—Speech delivered by the pope to the cardinals.—He wishes to restore peace everywhere, even if he should succumb in the effort.—Negotiations between Philip the Fair and Albert of Austria. 1885  

XXXIII.—Letter of the Count of Flanders to Jean de Menin.—Journey of the Bishop of Vicenza.—Reconciliation of the kings of France and England.—William of Dampierre’s fruitless attempt with Edward I.—Complaints against the pope.—He is the sole support that the Count of Flanders can hope for, since he expects nothing further from either the king of Germany or the king of England. 1889  

XXXIV.—Letter of Master Bassian to the Count of Flanders (Ghent, 27 December 1299).—Conference in the presence of the Bishop of Vicenza.—Complaints of Simon de Melun against the count.—Disputes concerning coinage.—Departure of Baldwin of Quaetypre for England. 1889  

XXXV.—Letter of Philip of Thiette to Robert of Béthune (Catania, 11 November 1299).—He regrets being far from Rome.—He believes that he can better win the pope’s favour by fighting for his cause.—His sadness.—His wishes.—Successes achieved in Sicily. 1891  

XXXVI.—Letter of Robert of Béthune to Michel As Clokettes and Jean de Menin.—The increasingly deplorable condition of Flemish affairs.—The necessity of having recourse to the pope’s protection.—Charles of Valois has seized Douai. 1893  

XXXVII.—Letter of Guy of Namur to Robert of Béthune (Ypres, 3 May 1300).—The capture of Damme by the French has been learned.—Agitation at Ypres.—The burghers complain that they have been left without defence.—The imminent capitulation of the town of Aardenburg. 1893  

XXXVIII.—Memorial presented to the pope by the ambassadors of the Count of Flanders.—Brief statement of the Count of Flanders’s grievances against the king of France.—Reasons which ought to induce the pope to decide upon those grievances.—The pope is supreme judge in spiritual and temporal matters, as vicar of Jesus Christ.—He is judge among all who acknowledge no superior authority; for this reason he can depose the emperor and also the king of France.—He is judge by virtue of the count’s appeal; it is known that the right of appeal to the Holy See belongs to all the oppressed, and moreover there is no man, however great, who does not have a judge above him.—He is judge because it belongs to him to correct all sinners, and it is certain that the king of France sinned in what he did against the count.—He is judge by reason of the sacrileges committed in the destruction of churches; and he is likewise judge because the imprisonment of the count’s daughter is an ecclesiastical matter.—He is judge because the king, by refusing the count judgment by the peers, wished to judge in his own cause, although he is notoriously the count’s enemy.—He is judge because it belongs to him to ensure respect for the truce which he confirmed.—Finally, it is worthy of the pope to fulfil the mission received from the divine Master, who said: “Peace be with you,” by putting an end to discord and wars. 1896  

XXXIX.—Letter of the Flemish ambassadors to the Count of Flanders (17 January 1299, old style).—Sermon of Cardinal Aquasparta in the Lateran church.—It restates the principal conclusions of the preceding memorial.—The Church’s spiritual and temporal power, which can strike all men, however great, with the spiritual sword and the temporal sword.—Papal audience.—Dieter of Nassau, Archbishop of Trier.—The pope, displeased by the alliance of Philip the Fair and Albert of Austria.—William of Jülich at the school of Bologna.—The sees of Cologne and Mainz will become vacant sooner than is thought.—Guy of Hainaut would have obtained the archbishopric of Trier, had his brother not been allied with the king of France. 1900  

XL.—Letter of Gérard de Ferlin to Jean Makiel (3 March 1299, old style).—He is going to Naples.—Up to that time, nothing has been obtained from the pope. 1901  

XLI.—Papal brief (18 December 1302).—He commends to the bishops and abbots Jacques de Normanno, whom he sends to France. 1903  

XLII.—Letter of Jacques de Normanno to the Archbishop of Reims (4 February 1301, old style).—He has received a sum of two hundred gold florins. 1905  

XLIII.—Spurious papal bull (13 May 1297).—It authorizes the marriage of all ecclesiastical persons of either sex, without excepting the pope.—The pope shall bring up at his own expense the children of his predecessors and those of the cardinals.—The children of religious and parish priests shall receive a suitable pension in monasteries or parishes.—Whoever does not observe the present constitution shall be considered a heretic. 1905  

XLIV.—Papal bull.—Complaints against bishops who sacrifice spiritual duties to temporal interests.—They are forbidden henceforth to leave their dioceses. 1907  

XLV.—Protest of the city of Bruges against the sentence of the Bishop of Tournai (7 December 1302).—Peril to souls; impediments to the celebration of marriages; etc. 1911  

XLVI.—Petition presented to the pope by the clergy of Flanders.—They seek the pope’s protection.—It is urgent to provide for vacant benefices.—A tithe [Col. 2020] is necessary in order that Philip of Thiette may protect the country against aggression by the king of France.—The creation of one or two bishoprics in Flanders would be highly useful, because the bishops to whom Flanders is subject reside in enemy territory.—The Flemish language is not understood by these bishops.—The dioceses are too extensive.—The churches and monasteries of Flanders are sufficiently rich to meet the expenses entailed by the foundation of one or two bishoprics. 1912  

XLVII.—Diploma of doctor of laws. 1915  

XLVIII.—Declaration of the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux (1304).—Distress of the Order of Cîteaux and of the whole Church of France.—They were compelled to yield to the threats of the king’s bailiffs. 1917  

XLIX.—Declaration of the abbots of the Order of Cîteaux (1305).—The same complaints.—The king demanded a new subsidy. 1917  

L.—Letter of the king of France (20 March 1313, old style).—He announces that he wishes to come to the aid of the Abbey of Clairvaux, already so near ruin that divine service there has almost ceased. 1917  

Unpublished charters. 1917  

Index of subjects and words in the second volume. 1921  

Historical index of the life of Saint Bernard. 1975  

Index to the illustrious lineage of Saint Bernard. 1985  

END OF THE ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-FIFTH VOLUME.
